Title: Improving the Quality of Online Public Discourse
Abstract: Online platforms have reshaped political discourse and influence on democratic institutions. While they democratize voice by bypassing traditional gatekeepers, they also serve as channels for toxic content like hate speech, impacting both targeted groups and broader public discourse. These online behaviors have real-world consequences in politics and society. Therefore, it is important to focus on improving online discourse. This includes not just reducing toxic content but also encouraging constructive discussions, a topic that has received less academic attention. In this project, our goal is to examine the quality of online public discourse more comprehensively by focusing on both its toxic and constructive elements. We define toxic content as user-generated content that “express[es] disrespect for someone by using insulting language, profanity, or name-calling; by engaging in personal attacks; and/or by employing racist, sexist, and xenophobic terms” (Kim et al., 2021, p. 924). This includes, at the extreme, outright hate speech that targets individuals as representatives of protected classes. Conversely, we define constructive content as user-generated material that positively shapes public discussion, fosters active democratic participation, and sustains an informed citizenry. This definition aligns, in part, with the notion of deliberation, namely, the process of engaging in rational discourse among actors within the political sphere (Steenbergen et al., 2003). Research on constructive content is less systematic than on toxic content, partly because “constructive” is less clearly defined compared to more easily identifiable categories like toxicity. The project has two main goals: 1) to develop computational methods for the semi-automatic detection of both toxic and constructive content, and 2) to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions against toxicity and for promoting constructive dialogue. Specifically, the project is divided into three work packages: WP1 focuses on developing detection methods and measuring prevalence, WP2 assesses anti-toxicity interventions, and WP3 evaluates measures to boost constructive content. Research will be conducted in multiple languages and settings, including collaborations with Swiss news outlets Blick (German) and 20 Minuten/minutes (German and French), as well as studies on platforms like X/Twitter and Reddit (English). The project potentially faces two main risks:  reliable content detection and data access. The detection of toxic and constructive content in WP1 is critical for the success of later experiments. We plan to use established methods as a fallback, while aiming to improve on them. The second risk concerns data access. We have largely mitigated the risk by securing datasets from major Swiss news outlets like 20 Minuten and Blick, who have also committed to partnership for field experiments in WP2 and WP3 (support letters available upon request). One of our Twitter experiments is already based on collected data. Moreover, the experiments in WP2 and WP3 raise ethical questions. We have designed a multi-faceted approach to mitigate these concerns. The approach, which is described in the research plan, is backed by prior ethics approvals we obtained for similar studies. Collectively, the three work packages will contribute to both academic research and policy discussions on improving online discourse. We will provide reliable causal evidence on the effectiveness of interventions against toxic content and for encouraging constructive dialogue, and we will introduce new computational methods for semi-automatically detecting both types of content. These tools and methodologies can be useful not just for researchers but also for civil society groups and policymakers, and can be adapted for other contexts.
Keywords: Computational social science, Content moderation, Experiments, Interventions, NLP, Natural language processing, Online media, Public discourse, Social media

Title: Elliptic PDEs, free boundary problems, and optimal transport
Abstract:
This project aims to study problems in the fields of partial differential equations and calculus of variations, and has been divided into three parts: 
 * Part A: The one-phase free boundary problem.
We plan to investigate different aspects of the one-phase free boundary problem, both in the local and non-local cases. 
 * Part B: Beyond monotonicity formulas.
We aim to study problems in which the use of monotonicity formulas has been crucial until now, but that are still not understood without this very powerful tool. 
 * Part C: Optimal transport in machine learning
Finally, we plan to continue the study of PDEs and Optimal Transport in the context of problems arising in Machine Learning.
Keywords: Continuous formulation of neural networks, Free boundary problems, Fully nonlinear operators, Integro-differential operators, Lack of monotonicity formulas, Obstacle problem, One-phase problem, Optimal transport

Title: Data-based Optimization of Outcomes: Successful Technology-Supported Therapy (D-BOOST2)
Abstract:
Background and Rationale. Rehabilitation technology has become increasingly applied, especially in neurorehabilitation, over the last 20+ years. Research, and the corresponding funding, seems to be mainly focused on the development and commercialization of such devices. However, once in the market, only very limited guidance exists to support clinicians, specifically occupational (OT) and physical (PT) therapists in the application of the devices and their clinical reasoning.
Clinical reasoning is a particularly challenging task. To choose safe and effective intervention options, therapists must be able to quickly process large quantities of information, such as patient characteristics, knowledge about physiology, motor learning principles, available evidence, and, when applying rehabilitation technology, expert knowledge of the device and its functions. Artificial Intelligence (AI) could support therapists with this task, as it could recognize patterns in prognostic factors, intervention, and outcome data. It could support therapists by recommending those intervention parameters that are most likely to improve outcomes, given the baseline characteristics of the respective patient. Such personalized medicine can boost the effect of rehabilitation technology tremendously.
Supervised machine learning (ML) algorithms have been most successful in recent years. However, large amounts of data to train, test and validate such algorithms are necessary. These data sets require so-called “ground truth”, which means they have to best represent the “truth” without bias. This cannot be done by data scientists alone. To minimize bias during the creation of the data set, close collaboration between data scientists and those knowledgeable about the meaning behind the data is crucial, for example through a user-centered design approach.
This project will provide first steps towards an AI-based clinical decision-making algorithm for technology supported rehabilitation. It is the first multi-device, multi-manufacturer, multi-center project, that includes therapists, industry representatives, academic AI engineers and clinical researchers alike. 
Specific Aims. We aim to build a network of clinics, manufacturers and researchers (work package 1; WP1), define which prognostic factors, therapy parameters and outcome measurements should be provided to the algorithm (WP2), set up a database for development, validation and testing data for the algorithm (WP2), collect the data and prepare it for the AI algorithm (WP3), design the algorithm, train validate and test (WP4), use explainable AI in order to make AI decisions comprehensible and transparent to the therapists (WP4), and conduct a feasibility study (WP5) to assess the effect of the use of the AI-based intervention recommendations on clinical outcomes.
Methods. In a modified user-centered design approach, our multicenter network will define the requirements for the training and test data sets. Once collected, the data sets will then be prepared (e.g., labelled) for modelling with a supervised learning approach. An algorithm able to make intervention recommendations to therapists based on patterns detected in the training data set, will be programmed based on the training data set and thoroughly tested on the test data set. Methods from AI will be complemented by approaches from classical statistical analysis, particularly time series analysis. All stakeholders will be involved throughout the development process.
Results and their Impact in the Field. We expect to create an AI-based system that can make data-based recommendations to therapists about if and which devices to use and which training parameters to choose, based on the given characteristics of an individual patient. We expect that this project will help to standardize, and at the same time personalize intervention with and without rehabilitation technology for individuals with damage to the neurological systems. This will boost the effects that rehabilitation technologies can have on outcomes and maximize the rehabilitation potential for each individual patient.
Keywords: artificial intelligence, clinical application, clinical decision making, decision making support, occupational therapy, physical therapy, rehabilitation technology

Title: Molecular evolution and ecology of Foraminifera and related protists
Abstract:
The evolutionary and ecological studies of microbial eukaryotes, or protists, have been completely transformed by accumulation of genomic and metagenomic data readily obtained from diverse biological and environmental material. The evolutionary history of protists has been profoundly revised by phylogenomics, while environmental genomics brought to light the immense diversity of the microeukaryotic biome and enhanced its ecological importance. Yet, unraveling the evolutionary and ecological information from extremely complex eukaryotic genomes and metagenomes is not always straightforward, and the transformation of this information into practical applications can be sometimes problematic.
Here, we address some of the challenges raised by the deluge of high-throughput sequencing (HTS) data, focusing on molecular evolution and ecology of foraminifera and related protists. The project continues a long-term research that has been conducted by our group on protist phylogeny, taxonomy, and molecular ecology. The project is based on our extensive expertise in the field, the large databases accumulated over the years, and in-house built pipelines for their analyses. It also benefits of a large network of collaborations that facilitates the access to samples, assists in their processing and analyzing the obtained data.
The project comprises two complementary parts. In the first part, we will use single-cell DNA and RNA-seq approaches in order to (1) complement the foraminiferal barcoding database, (2) revise the evolutionary relationships and identify foraminiferal mitochondrial genes, (3) assess the importance of intra-genomic variations, and (4) evaluate the role of bacterial microbiomes in the metabolism of foraminifera and their close relatives. In the second part, we will use environmental genomics in order to (5) assess the patterns of deep-sea benthic diversity, (6) expand the use of fossil eukaryotic DNA as paleoenvironmental proxy, and (7) search for species and genes that could be used as biosensors of environmental impacts. To facilitate the latter tasks, (8) we will develop bioinformatic tools for rapid and accurate analysis of environmental HTS data, focusing on machine learning and ecological network analyses applied to biomonitoring.
The project has significance for both fundamental and applied science. Foraminifera are highly diversified both taxonomically and ecologically, and therefore represent a key model to improve our understanding of the origin and evolution of single-cell eukaryotes. The ubiquity, sensitivity and adaptability of foraminifera prompt their use as a proxy to infer global biodiversity patterns and to reconstruct paleoenvironments and paleoclimates using DNA preserved in the sediment. Finally, we will develop a novel category of DNA-based sensors to assess the environmental impacts of industrial activities.

Title: New Relations Between Voters and Representatives in the Age of Social Media
Abstract:
This project aims to lay the groundwork for a deeper understanding of the relation between voters and elected representatives in the age of social media. Social media platforms like Twitter carry the potential to transform democracies as they allow for direct contact between politicians and voters and thus for more personalized contact between representatives and represented. Academic work on this topic, however, has so far remained highly descriptive and has focussed on the frequency or volume of social media usage by politicians and not so much on the content of their messages. As a result, we lack knowledge about the information politicians portray in social media activity, as well as what the effect of this communication is, e.g. how voters perceive it. The two studies presented in this proposal intend to target this important research gap and to analyse the micro-processes of the content of online communication and how voters perceive it. 
Study 1 (‘What Do Politicians Tweet When? New Quantitative Insight Into the Strategic Use of Personality Traits and Policy Positions’) is an observational study that investigates the tweets of a sample of Swiss and German politicians with the help of machine-learning to find out more about the motivations of politicians to tweet. We focus on Twitter as direct and individualized behaviour is best captured with this platform. Following key ideas in the representation and personalisation literature, we focus specifically on the distinction between personal or policy focussed content and investigate whether the content of the tweets depends on variables such as the incentive to cultivate a personal vote, professionalization of parties and parliament, or career stage in comparative perspective – information that is already available from the SNF project on “Parliamentary careers in comparison”  . Study 2 (‘What do voters want: Policy or Person’) is a two country survey including an experiment that investigates how voters use social media for political purposes and which information they seek in these platforms. A short survey experiment focuses on how feelings of representation and voting intentions of voters are affected by the content of the twitter message that politicians share via social media and whether voters rather appreciate personal appeals about the politicians or information about policy positions and activities communicated via Twitter. Using an innovative survey design, we first extract the demographic personal profile and policy preferences of the participants. We then use this information to present subjects with candidate profiles and Tweets from politicians that are (dis)similar to them on these key dimensions. As such we contribute to the question whether voters appreciate politicians similar or dissimilar to their own personal profile (desire for descriptive representation) and feel better represented by politicians who are like them or who act on their behalf (desire for substantive representation). 
The conduct of these studies in Switzerland and Germany allows for a first insight on variation on relevant influencing variables such as the election system, the importance of parties and the professionalization of the parliamentary system. Importantly, this project forms the base for a larger research agenda that we aim to develop in the next years and where we want to further explore the potential of social media in fostering closer linkages between voters and politicians.
Keywords: online media, personalisation, representation, representatives, voter

Title: Artificial neural networks in reliability prediction for railway applications
Abstract:
Public transport reliability and stability are significant factors influencing service quality and passenger mode choice. Furthermore, unreliable service increases operating costs and reduces revenue. In railway systems reliability is significantly influenced by the technical reliability of infrastructure and rolling stock systems. Reliability can be significantly improved by predicting impending disruption events caused by technical failures of single components or systems. 

A promising method for predicting reliability is through the use of artificial neural networks. Neural networks have already been shown to have considerable potential for predicting reliability and its influencing parameters in general cases where they have been applied to different types of problems either alone or in combination with other methods with good results.

Given the success of neural networks on general problems it is beneficial to assess their potential for predicting reliability in railway systems since reliability is a very important factor in railway operations. Unfortunately, existing neural network reliability prediction methods and algorithms are not directly transferrable to the specific requirements and characteristics of railway applications. Therefore new or refined methods must be developed for application in the railway sector. 

The proposed research project will define and evaluate the potential of applying neural networks in reliability prediction for railway components and subsystems. The research results will not only be highly relevant for direct application in the railway industry, but they will also help extend the state-of-the-art in reliability prediction with machine learning techniques and especially with neural networks. The research is also timely since railway components with a wide variety of monitoring sensors are being rapidly deployed. This means the data needed to develop and test neural networks is just now becoming available.

The proposed research project will evaluate the use of neural networks both theoretically and using a set of case studies. The case studies were selected to consider all relevant types of application of neural networks to railway sector reliability prediction. The case studies are based on real data from railway rolling stock and infrastructure systems. 

The predictions achieved with neural networks can be applied to improve the quality of railway service by anticipating impending failures of railway components or subsystems. Furthermore, they can make possible establishment of more efficient and cost effective maintenance programs and spare part logistics policies, both of which can have substantial economic benefits for railway operators and system suppliers.

Title: STARforM-Lens: Accretion in star formation through the lens of machine learning
Abstract:
The formation of stars and planets is one of the central areas of research in astrophysics, boosted recently to an unprecedented level by the new generation of space- and ground-based observatories, from X-rays to millimeter wavelengths. In this Era of Big and very heterogeneous Data, the combination of data and Machine Learning (ML) is required to break new ground and learn how young stellar objects (YSO) form and evolve before they reach the main sequence. In this context, Gaia has revolutionised our understanding of star formation by greatly contributing to the census of young stellar objects (YSO) in our Galaxy thanks to its superb astrometric capability, providing precise positions, parallaxes, and kinematics. Yet, to this date, most machine learning (ML) contributions to the field have focused either on identifying YSOs or on the supervised classification of YSO based on labeled datasets.  

Photometric variability is an inherent characteristic of YSOs and an important proxy of their mass assembly. The study of photometric variability allows us to simultaneously probe diverse physical mechanisms that occur in the forming star, in its disk and its envelope. Gaia also offers a unique, all-sky capability to study YSO from their time series. Close to 80k were identified in Gaia DR3, and the upcoming DR4 will scale up to a few million YSO candidates, and will release epoch photometry and spectroscopy for all Gaia sources to community, providing a fertile new solid for explorations focused on refining our understanding of YSO evolution and in their protoplanetary disks. 

With STARforM-Lens, we propose to study star formation and its accretion with innovative ML techniques, which were never used so far on such data and on this scientific topic. Gaia data will play a central role as an all-sky survey. The optical data provided by Gaia in DR4 will be complemented with data from numerous all-sky surveys at different wavelengths, providing a more complete coverage of the emission of the central YSO and its surrounding protoplanetary disk. We will employ two distinct ML techniques: firstly, to scrutinise the long-term evolution of YSO accretion by boosting a very large database of panchromatic spectral energy distributions (SEDs) for YSOs with Gaia XP spectra, and employing an ML approach to interpret it, where the SEDs are represented by using a weighted set of simplified models, with the YSO's unknown evolutionary timestamp treated as a latent variable. Secondly, the project will delve into short-term accretion variability in YSO by modeling the heterogeneous data using a shared latent space, leveraging the comprehensive Gaia DR4 data set, which uniquely offers a simultaneous analysis of YSO variability in both photometry and spectroscopy across the entire sky.

STARforM-Lens offers a unique opportunity to paint a novel picture of accretion in star formation, thanks to the immense volume of data sets provided by Gaia DR4 as well as other surveys, and to improved ML tools capable to handle these complex data. STARforM-Lens proposes to go beyond typical ML explorations to provide a comprehensive temporal representation of YSO accretion variability as our window into YSO evolution. We will bridge the gap between evolution at long timescales and short-term variability at human timescales, to better understand the effect of accretion processes in star formation.

Title: Bonding molecular genotyping and phenotyping to outcome measures in AL amyloidosis: A EUropean REgistry and sample sharing networK to promote the diagnosis and management of light chain Amyloidosis
Abstract:
Immunoglobulin light chain (AL) amyloidosis is caused by antibody fragments, light chains (LCs), produced by cells from the immune system called plasma cells (PCs). Amyloid LCs target vital organs and form typical deposits. Therapy is based on anti-PC drugs, aiming at reducing LC production, restoring organ function, improving quality of life, and extending survival. Members of our consortium made substantial contributions to the diagnosis, treatment and management of AL amyloidosis. However, previous studies on the natural history of the disease were limited by low numbers of analyzed patients, limited representativeness of patients’ cohorts, lack of molecular data, and analysis approach.
In the frame of the EUREKA consortium, we will create a single patients’ registry collecting all new cases of AL amyloidosis evaluated at 4 referral Centers across Europe or at their satellite sites, linked to a cross-border biobank and sample sharing network for the study of both disease- causing LCs and PCs with advanced molecular technologies. A fifth site will support the consortium with big data analysis and artificial intelligence applied to health. We aim at 1) defining the impact of advanced molecular technologies to promote early diagnosis and guide therapeutic choices; 2) describing the natural history of the disease in a representative cohort of AL patients in the contemporary era of effective anti-PC therapies; 3) investigating and refining novel advanced technologies to detect with high sensitivity residual disease-causing PCs in patients responding to therapy.
Besides deepening our current understanding of the biology of AL amyloidosis, the data produced within this study will be instrumental in promoting early diagnosis, personalizing individual patient management and in the design of future clinical trials.

Title: Large Scale Weakly Supervised Semantic Segmentation
Abstract:
In the last decade, visual recognition had several significant achievements in certain areas like face detection and robust gesture recognition technology (Microsoft Kinect). Nevertheless, the problem of generic scene understanding remains yet unsolved. We address a stage of scene understanding - semantic segmentation. The task of semantic segmentation is to label each pixel in an image with a label, corresponding to a visual class (e.g. grass, tree, dog, person). It is an important and fundamental problem, addressed by many researchers in the field of computer vision. Having solved this task will make higher level problems like activity recognition and scene description much easier to address.

In many computer vision problems that have been successfully solved, the crucial part was availability of large amounts of annotated training data. Even simple classifiers produce very accurate results if trained on a large training set. Obtaining annotated data for semantic segmentation requires a large amount of manual labor, as each pixel in every image has to be labeled. It takes roughly 5-10 minutes per image for a human annotator to produce the labeling. Ideally, semantic segmentation should recognize thousands of visual classes with high accuracy. Providing a significant amount of data for each class, would require years of human labor.

Recently, we have proposed an approach that require only weak supervision -- user must provide only a list of visual classes present in the image, without having to provide a per pixel annotation. Our main innovation is a Multi Image Model (MIM) -- a data driven graphical model for inferring latent (hidden) pixel labels in the training set and learning appearance models of the visual classes. This greatly reduces the annotation effort and provides results comparable to fully supervised methods.

So far, weakly supervised methods were only tested on small datasets, same that have been used for fully supervised learning. The fundamental hypothesis of this project is that a system trained on a large weakly labeled training set will achieve performance superior than that of a system trained on a small, but fully labeled set. In this project our goal is to scale our current weakly supervised technology to be able to train from large volumes of weakly annotated data. Through this we expect to surpass the performance of current state of the art fully supervised methods that have to use smaller training sets.

Another way of reducing annotation effort we plan to pursue is recycling the annotation already available either in a different format or for different visual classes. Intuitively, it is easier (requires less examples) to learn to recognize a motorbike, when we already know how to recognize a bicycle. This technique is called transfer learning. In our research we have already saw that information from the task of approximate geometry reconstruction could be transferred to weakly supervised semantic segmentation of generic visual classes (grass, tree, car, cat); also a generic object detector, trained on examples from without the considered dataset, can help discriminate between object (e.g. pedestrian) and background classes (e.g. road). In this project we plan to make transfer possible between datasets with arbitrary classes by using a joint hyperprior over structure parameters of our Multi Image Model.
Keywords: computer vision, machine learning, object recognition

Title: Unlocking the Potential of Decentralized Data: Efficient Algorithms for LLM Training and Inference
Abstract:
Summary of the research plan

Background:

LLMs have achieved remarkable success in recent years and are becoming central to many applications. However, adapting these models to siloed and sensitive real-world data like hospital records or financial documents is difficult. Institutions are unwilling to share their data due to privacy and regulatory concerns. FL offers a promising solution by enabling collaborative model development without sharing raw data. Yet, existing FL methods are not well-suited for LLMs: they suffer from inefficient iterative communication, reduced performance under heterogeneous data, and lack mechanisms for long-term adaptation to evolving data or cost-sensitive inference. This proposal addresses these challenges by developing novel methods to fine-tune and use LLMs collaboratively on distributed data silos.

Research Objectives:

We aim to develop scalable, communication-efficient methods for fine-tuning, adapting, and deploying LLMs across decentralized and evolving datasets. Our proposal is structured into three thrusts:
(i) Thrust 1 develops communication-efficient, heterogeneity-robust approaches for federated LLM fine-tuning;
(ii) Thrust 2 designs lightweight adaptation mechanisms for continuously evolving data; and
(iii) Thrust 3 introduces a hybrid inference system enabling institutions to choose, per query, between a local model (efficient but less accurate) and a global model (more accurate but costly), while respecting privacy constraints.

Methods:

In Thrust 1, we avoid repeated communication by having each institution fine-tune its model locally and send it once to a central server for merging. To address data heterogeneity, we propose a novel merging technique that preserves diverse client-specific modules and combines similar ones, resulting in a shared model that is both efficient and performant.
In Thrust 2, we introduce a novel PEFT method based on a lightweight aggregator model trained federatively on top of the merged model from Thrust 1. This aggregator enables ongoing adaptation to newly arriving or shifting client data, without re-training or modifying the underlying base model.
In Thrust 3, we explore a routing policy that, for each query, selects between the local and global model based on a tri-objective function that weighs expected accuracy gain, computational cost, and privacy sensitivity. This allows institutions to make informed, per-query inference decisions that align with real-world constraints.

Contributions and impact:

The project will be advised by Prof. Gauri Joshi, who is a leading researcher in Distributed Machine Learning and a unique expert in Federated Learning. Additionally, we plan to collaborate with the Federated Learning team led by Brendan McMahan at Google, and the efficient inference team at Microsoft led by Victor Ruhle, which includes Ankur Mallick, a CMU alumnus who graduated from Prof. Joshi's lab. Our proposed project will enable collaborative use of LLMs across institutions with sensitive or decentralized data, reducing the barriers to training and deployment in critical domains such as medicine and finance. By addressing communication costs, data shifts, and privacy constraints, our methods provide a foundation for secure, efficient, and adaptive large-scale language model use in the real world.
Keywords: Decentralized Learning, Efficient Federated Inference, Federated Fine-tuning, Federated Learning, LLM Ensembles, Large Language Models, Parameter-Efficient Fine-tuning

Title: Heterogenous Agent Macro-Finance: Models and Methods
Abstract:
In this project, we plan to utilize some of the recent advances in deep learning to develop global solution methods for three important and popular heterogeneous agent macro models: A large-scale stochastic overlapping generations (SOLG) model, a heterogeneous agent New Keynesian (HANK) model, and a search and matching model. We plan to develop reliable solution methods and make the code suites available to the wider profession. 

We propose a series of applications of these models. The first is tied to existing work by Kubler on climate change macro and the green transition; the second application is tied to existing work by Yang on the distributional consequences of monetary policy. The third application is related to Yang's ongoing work on how aggregate risks are transmitted into markets with search frictions and heterogeneous agents. In all our existing work on these problems, the bottleneck comes from a lack of a computational solution method. The main goal of the project is to overcome this.

Finally, we plan to explore synergies between the models, such as introducing monetary policy into the SOLG model or search frictions into the HANK model.

Title: Simulation and Counterfactual Reasoning in Neuroscience
Abstract:
This project will investigate the role of simulations as a form of counterfactual reasoning in the contemporary neurosciences. It will focus in particular on the use of computer simulations in order to produce models of brain architecture and function, not so much in order to simu-late cognitive processes as such ("weak" rather than "strong" Artificial Intelligence according to a distinction proposed by Searle 1980). In classical computational neuroscience, action potentials are modeled by computing numerical solutions to mathematical equations such as the influential Hodgkin-Huxley (HH) equations, which do not admit of analytical solutions. This approach mirrors the traditional use of computer simulations in other areas of science, e.g., physics, climate science or economics. However, in contemporary neuroscience there is also a bewildering variety of other simulation techniques that may or may not resemble the traditional approach. These techniques have rarely been examined from a philosophy of science point of view.
This project will closely investigate the simulation practices of contemporary neuroscience. A first goal will be to provide a survey of different uses of simulation in the contemporary neurosciences. In a second stage, it will treat these simulations as providing scientists with specific counterfactual conditionals the antecedents of which are modeling assumptions and the consequents describe some possible neurological state, structure or process. This counterfactual analysis will be used in a third stage to provide a more integrative view of the different scientific activities of simulation, modeling, experimentation and thought experiments. The relationship between these different scientific techniques has been controversially discussed in the philosophical literature. Viewing them all as involving some kind of counterfactuality will enable us to better understand the commonalities as well as differences with respect to their epistemic role. 
The project will be an integrated part of the DFG Research Unit (DFG-Forschergruppe) "What if? On the epistemological, pragmatic, psychological and cultural significance of coun-terfactual reasoning" (2015-2018, grant application pending), which is a continuation of the existing research unit "What if? On the meaning, epistemology and scientific relevance of counterfactual claims and thought experiments" based at the University of Konstanz (2012-2015). The predecessor to this project, “Counterfactual Reasoning in Biology” (SNSF project Nr. 100018_140885, 2012-2015), is also a part of the DFG Research Unit, a collaboration that turned out to be very fruitful. As the DFG-Research Unit has applied for a three-year prolongation, the current project plans to continue this collaboration.

Title: Improving the precision, stability and robustness of Brain-Computer Interfaces with Bayesian inference
Abstract:
Background and rationale: 

Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) are nowadays considered one of the most promising solutions for restoring motor function after limb paralysis. The principle of BCIs is to record the activity of neurons in the motor cortex using implanted electrodes, and to leverage it to control an assistive external device. During calibration sessions, the recorded neural activity is mapped to an intended motor output, in a process known as decoding. The trained BCI can then be used to restore function for people suffering from tetraplegia. In recent experiments, BCIs have been used by patients to reach and grasp objects with a robotic arm, or to perform handwriting with a computer cursor. However, recording instabilities and lack of robustness are a major impediment to the widespread clinical acceptance of BCIs. Especially, it has been shown that the activity of the motor cortex is highly variable and context-dependent, and is modulated by the nature of the task, the environment, or the mental state of the patient. The mapping between recorded cortical activity and motor output is thus non-stationary, which is a major obstacle to robust decoding.

Objectives:

The overall goal of this research project is to determine the sources of the variability underlying this non-stationarity, and to leverage them to design new BCIs algorithm sufficiently robust to be used by patients in their daily-life activities. Our objectives are twofold:

From a theoretical perspective, the causes for this variability remain elusive so far. I will answer two questions. Firstly, how does instability arise? Using Factor Analysis (FA) to reduce the dimensionality of the recorded population activity, I will quantify how context modulates the latent dynamics of the motor cortex. Secondly, why does instability arise? A normative explanation for the variability of the activity in the motor cortex has not been proposed so far. Here, I hypothesize that the dimensionality of the cortical movement-related activity is context-modulated, which puts constraints on how movement is encoded. I will test this hypothesis using Preferential Subspace Identification (PSID).

From an engineering perspective, no decoding algorithm general enough to handle the non-stationarity of cortical activity exists. Firstly, I will formulate decoding as non-linear filtering problem, which is a robust and efficient framework for estimating motor outputs from noisy observations. Secondly, I will leverage recent developments in machine learning to propose a robust cascade controller for BCI decoding. Finally, I will validate this cascade controller during clinical trials, and compare its performance with previously existing solutions.

Impact for the field:

The goal of this project is to build on recent theoretical developments to improve the stability of the         movement-representation that we are decoding, thus improving the precision, stability, and robustness of BCIs. Moreover, the motor cortex is classically seen as a central area for cerebral motor planning and execution, which dynamics reliably encode movements. The theoretical chapter of this project will help to question this classical view, and to better understand how the cortex maintains a stable movement when its activity is context--wise modulated.

The research project will be conducted in the laboratory of Prof. Jennifer L. Collinger at the Rehab Neural Engineering Labs (RNEL) of the University of Pittsburgh, one of the leading institutions in the field of BCIs, in which funding, participants, and regulatory approvals will be guaranteed. Combined to my theoretical background, this research environment will ensure the feasibility and suitability of the project.

Title: Swarm of Flying Cameras
Abstract:
Autonomous micro helicopters are about to play a major role in tasks like search and rescue, environment monitoring, security surveillance, inspection, etc. If they are further realized in small scale, they can also be used in narrow outdoor and indoor environments and represent only a limited risk for people. However, for such operations, navigating based on GPS information only is not sufficient. Fully autonomous operation in urban environments and indoor spaces requires micro helicopters to rely on alternative localization systems. In fact, even in outdoor environments GPS is not a reliable service and is completely unavailable indoors. One way to overcome this problem is to use motion-capture systems, whose robustness and reliability have recently made micro helicopters able to perform fast maneuvers and even build small architectures (e.g., see the works of Kumar at the University of Pennsylvania and D’Andrea at ETH Zurich). However, these systems are limited to confined spaces and need pre-installation of the cameras, making it impossible to navigate autonomously in unknown, yet-unexplored environments. An alternative solution is to use onboard laser scanners to simultaneously build a map of the environment and navigate through it. However, 2D laser scanners are still heavy; this constrains the vehicle’s minimum weight and size, increasing the risk for people. Therefore, for very small lightweight helicopters, the only viable solution is to use a combination of onboard cameras and inertial sensors. 

Previous work of the applicant has demonstrated successful autonomous basic maneuvers of a micro helicopter using only a single camera and an inertial sensor onboard. Although today’s cameras can have high frame rate, image processing is still limited by the onboard-computer capabilities. As a result, vision-based autonomous maneuvers of micro helicopters are still very slow compared to those attainable with motion capture systems. Additionally, previous works have investigated visual navigation with a single helicopter only. However, there is an interest in using multiple platforms: (i) they can explore, monitor, and map an environment faster and more efficiently than with a single robot; (ii) each robot can share its capabilities or benefit from those of the other team members. However, most works on multi-robot navigation with micro helicopters have relied on motion-capture systems, which allow localizing the robots with millimeter precision and in a common, global coordinate frame. These conditions cannot be achieved with onboard sensors and, notably, with vision, where the robot-localization accuracy is strongly linked to the structure of the perceived environment.

The purpose of this project is to focus on the navigation of multiple micro helicopters in GPS-denied environments (both indoors and outdoors) and on allowing fast, dynamic maneuvers using onboard monocular vision as the main sensor modality. The choice of monocular vision over stereo vision is dictated by the ultra-light weight of the platform that will be used. Due to the use of cameras as the main sensors, to the reduced size of the helicopters, and to the emphasis on multi-robot navigation, we call this system “a swarm of flying cameras.” The main challenges deal with the limited calculation power, the limitations of monocular images, and the highly dynamic motion of the helicopters. The overall goal of the project will be achieved through the interplay of the following subgoals:

1.Fast visual navigation of micro helicopters.
2.Multi-robot vision-based localization and mapping.
3.Vision-based cooperative exploration.

Task 1 aims at enabling fast maneuvers of micro helicopters with limited onboard computing capabilities. To this end, we will investigate methods for fast feature extraction and tracking and local relative-motion estimation to be done on lightweight, embedded computers (e.g., Gumstix or cell-phone GPUs). In task 2, we will investigate methods to estimate both the 3D map of the environment and the poses of each helicopter in a global reference. Most works in multi-robot localization and mapping have been done using laser scanners and for ground mobile robots (i.e., moving in a 2D environments). With flying robots this is more challenging due to the unconstrained motion of the vehicles and due to the lack of range information with monocular vision. Task 3 will study the problem of vision-based cooperative exploration. Again, most works in cooperative exploration have been done for ground mobile robots using laser rangefinders. We will combine the results achieved in the first two tasks and will investigate how to simultaneously compute the next robots’ poses in order to best reconstruct the environment.

The achievement of these goals require expertise in computer vision, robotics, and micro-aerial-vehicle control that the applicant has earned throughout his past research both as a researcher (at EPFL, ETH and the University of Pennsylvania), as a team leader, and as the coordinator of a large European project on micro-aerial vehicles (SFLY). This project will also benefit from the ongoing collaboration that the applicant maintains with the Autonomous Systems Lab at ETH (where the applicant did his PhD and first post-doc) and with the GRASP Lab at the University of Pennsylvania (where the applicant did his second post-doc).
Keywords: Autonomous micro flying robots, Computer vision, Robotics, Simultaneous Localization and Mapping, Vision-based navigation

Title: Towards high-resolution, intelligent, spatiotemporal avalanche forecasting
Abstract:
Predicting snow avalanches in time and space remains a formidable challenge, even though accurate forecasts are essential to saving lives and minimizing costly damage to infrastructure and mobility. Avalanche forecasting still relies heavily on expert interpretation of diverse and heterogeneous data with complex temporal dynamics, resulting in known limitations in objectivity, consistency, and spatiotemporal resolution. Forecasts remain coarse and accuracy suffers - particularly under rapidly evolving or extreme avalanche conditions.

While Machine Learning (ML) models have begun to approach human-level accuracy on average, they still struggle under rare or critical conditions, especially when key processes like weak layer formation, fracture initiation and crack propagation are poorly represented. These limitations become most evident in high-impact situations where reliable forecasts are crucial. However, recent advances in snow-cover modeling, ML methods, and the availability of new data sources such as remote sensing and automated avalanche detection offer opportunities for innovation. The transition to more systematic, model-driven (i.e., both physical and ML models) avalanche forecasting has begun - but major scientific challenges remain in process representation, spatiotemporal modeling, uncertainty estimation, and forecast communication.

The overarching objective of this project is to develop the scientific foundations and practical tools for a next-generation avalanche forecasting system - one that integrates physics-based simulations, advanced ML for forecasting and uncertainty estimation, and expert input to improve accuracy, interpretability, and operational usability. Specifically, we propose to: (a) Develop advanced ML models for avalanche forecasting, using cutting-edge time series forecasting methods and embedding key physical processes (e.g., failure initiation and crack propagation propensity) directly into the model structure; (b) Combine the strengths of human expertise and ML in a hybrid intelligence forecasting framework, leveraging the consistency and scalability of models alongside the adaptive reasoning and contextual insight of expert forecasters; (c) Build a spatiotemporal forecasting system that balances predictability, uncertainty, and computational cost by optimally integrating numerical snow cover simulations - an approach we refer to as intelligent forecasting; and (d) Use agent-based modeling to explore how different representations of forecast resolution and uncertainty affect user behavior, providing insights into forecast communication and interpretation. We are uniquely positioned to address these objectives, with access to a rich variety of data sources - including curated operational datasets and remotely sensed avalanche detections. Using these inputs, we will develop, train, and validate ML models that are more robust to extremes, quantify predictive uncertainty, and enable correction of uncertain forecasts. The envisioned models will build on SNOWPACK, a state-of-the-art numerical snow cover model already used operationally in several countries, facilitating direct transfer of research insights into broader practice.

By assembling an interdisciplinary team of experts, this project will lay the groundwork and propose better decision-support systems tools for avalanche forecasting - enhancing spatiotemporal resolution, integrating uncertainty quantification, and systematically allowing for expert input to control the process. Beyond avalanche forecasting, the developed methods - including physics-informed time series models, hybrid intelligence systems, and agent-based evaluation of forecast communication - will be transferable to other environmental and natural hazard domains. These contributions will advance both the scientific understanding and the operational capabilities in fields where uncertainty, data heterogeneity, and human–machine collaboration remain central challenges.

Title: Stochastic VLSI synapses for robust classification in neuromorphic electronic circuits
Abstract:
Neuromorphic Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI) hardware offers a low-power and compact electronic
substrate for implementing artificial neural networks with distributed plastic synapses. However, this
technology is typically characterized by limited resolution and high intrinsic variability. Therefore,
neuromorphic synapse circuits are inhomogeneous and imprecise and thus the mapping of standard
learning models onto this hardware is practically unfeasible. For this reason, this problem of variability is
considered as an unavoidable “bug” that needs to be minimized. Typical methods used for coping with
device mismatch and limited resolution resort to using very large devices and circuits or to off-loading
the complexity of the synapse model to external digital resources. However, these brute-force solutions
introduce communication bottlenecks and compromise compactness and power efficiency.
In this project I propose to implement a hardware neural network that exploits intrinsic variability
through stochastic learning for implementing efficient and robust VLSI neural processing systems and for
exploring brain-inspired computational principles. The network consists in an ensemble of neurons with
plastic synapses and stochastic learning that receive input from the same sources and that are trained to
respond differently to their input patterns. Preliminary work in this direction has been already carried-out
during my PhD studies, in which I constructed a pattern recognition system and studied its performance
under typical parameter variations observed in neuromorphic devices. This project will proceed further by
identifying the precise role of intrinsic variability in influencing the stochastic dynamics of learning and
thus the network performance in classification. The proposed approach is radically different from typical
machine learning techniques which are based on sequential operations running on conventional fast, precise
and power-hungry electronic hardware. Conversely, it exploits highly distributed and imprecise processing
of unconventional electronic hardware, which is inhomogeneous but also extremely compact and low-power.
Therefore, it offers a novel, brain-inspired strategy for enabling the construction of low-power and efficient
neuromorphic devices as a valid substrate for artificial intelligence and machine learning. Because of its
simplicity, the model used for the proposed study is very general and has potential link with relevant
issues in neuroscience as well, such as probabilistic computation and sensory processing in the brain.
The fellowship will be based in Columbia University (New York City, NY) and thus will take advantage
from the collaboration with world experts in theoretical neuroscience and synaptic plasticity in particular
as well as engineers from industry leaders that are currently exploring neuromorphic technologies and
that are already in contact with that institution. This fellowship fits very well with my competences
in theoretical neuroscience and my interests in neuromorphic engineering and thus represents a great
opportunity for improving my academic profile.
Keywords: ensemble methods, neural networks, neuromorphic engineering, synaptic plasticity, vlsi

Title: Jurassic Globetrotters. Unlocking palaeobiogeographic analyses of Late Jurassic ichnocoenoses of Europe, North Africa and North America through computational ichnology
Abstract:
The Jurassic (201.3-145 Ma), constitutes the central part of the Mesozoic. The Late Jurassic (163.5-145 Ma) is a key period in the study of dinosaur because most of the clades were already well diversified, and because it offers an abundance of fossil remains of dinosaurs from localities all around the world. In some cases, skeletal sites and tracksites are in close stratigraphical proximity (e.g., Lourinhã Formation, Portugal, or the Morrison Formation, USA), allowing inferences about the probable track producer. However, despite the large amount of available track data they have been neglected for palaeoecological and palaeobiogeographical purposes. Tracks are the only evidence left by a living animal (in vivo) in the actual environment where it was walking (in situ), but, despite this fact, their use suffers of several issues: 1) they are the result of complex interaction among the foot morphology, the substrate and the locomotion; 2) the ichnotaxonomy is only partially reliable; 3) lack of objective comparison methods; 4) lack of sufficient digital reference specimens for comparisons (although their number is increasing). 
JuGlo will use the more novel techniques and advances in ichnology (i.e., the science that studies traces) to overcome the issues 3) and 4), and therefore, to improve the quality of ichnotaxonomy. This will allow the pursue of the main objective of the project: using tracks to improve the understanding of dinosaur palaeoecology and the refining the constrains in palaeobiogeographical reconstruction. Six main aims have been identified: 1) innovate ichnology through development of new analytical methods, include Machine Learning (ML) tools; 2) create the largest 3D dataset of Late Jurassic tracks; 3) revision of Late Jurassic ichnotaxonomy; 4) link the palaeoecology and paleoenvironment to the revised ichnotaxonomy to define possible migration routes; 5)  valorise the ichnological collection of JURASSICA Museum.
Counting on thousands of tracks, the unique ichnological collection of JURASSICA Museum will be used to train and test the ML algorithms and will provide high-quality reference material for the development of the project (WP1, WP2, WP3). Fieldwork in the key areas of Europe, North Africa and North America will allow to collect 3D data from known and new tracksites (WP1). These data will be collected via ‘Structure from Motion’ photogrammetry, elaborated with Agisoft Metashape Pro and Pix4D (depending if they are camera or drone images). The 3D dataset will allow developing the ML tools (WP3) and to review the existing ichnotaxonomy of the Late Jurassic (WP4). This will lead to the analyses of the relationships between the ichnofauna and the palaeoenvironment/palaeoecology (WP5) and to the definition of possible migration routes (WP6). 
Scientifically, we expect to improve the discipline of ichnology by extensively introducing new validated methods, and to create a shred collection of digital tracks which, we hope, would also determine a new best practice for digital ichnology and digital palaeontology. Outside the academic world, we expect the project to contribute to improve the interest and knowledge of general public to dinosaur palaeontology. The 3D digital collection can also increase the interest of the public for museum collections and will provide a hinge to diffuse the interest on regional geology and palaeontology and therefore help in the increasing of the tourism in the Swiss Jura (WP7).
Keywords: 3D photogrammetry, Jurassic, dinosaur, ichnology, machine learning, palaeoecology, palaeogeography, sedimentology, virtual palaeontology

Title: Next Generation First-Principles Based Molecular Dynamics with Application to Biomimetic and Materials Design
Abstract:
Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations are arguably the most widely used molecular simulation method today and force-field based classical MD has been highly successful in the simulation of condensed phase systems for both biological and materials science applications. In addition, the advent of quantum mechanical based first-principles MD (FPMD) has enabled the treatment of electronic phenomena such as chemical reactions and photoexcitations. The introduction of multiscale mixed quantum mechanical/molecular mechanical (QM/MM) simulations in combination with a range of powerful enhanced sampling methods has allowed extending both spatial and temporal scales of FPMD. Together with the increase in computer power, it has become possible to perform FPMD with several 100 -1000 of atoms for 10-100 picoseconds. However, the combined challenge of system size, sampling time and high accuracy is still formidable. Ideally, one would like to perform MD simulations with the system size and sampling times typical of force-field based MD but with the accuracy of a high level ab initio method. 
During our previous SNF grant, we have developed multi-rung QML&QMH MD methods that allow to perform simulations with the accuracy of a high level method for essentially the cost of a lower level description. To this end, we have made extensive use of fully time-reversible multiple time step (MTS) integrators. By interfacing the FPMD program CPMD with other quantum chemical programs (GAUSSIAN and TURBOMOLE), we were able to perform e.g. B3LYP or MP2 based FPMD with a 5-10 times reduced computational cost. 
Here we propose, to further extend the versatility and efficiency of these MTS-QML&QMH simulations (via extension into a mixed QM/MM and QML&QMH/MM context; by implementation of stochastic thermostats to minimize resonances; and through the development and implementation of a novel approach for fast exact exchange) and to combine them with approaches from artificial intelligence. Combining force-matched classical force fields with on-the-fly machine learning (ML) for QM force evaluations, it should become feasible to run next-generation FPMD simulations with several orders of magnitude speedup.
These MTS-ML MD approaches in various combinations (MTS-MM&QM(ML), MTS-QML(ML)-QMH, MTS-MM&QM(ML)/MM etc..) will be highly useful for a wide range of applications in biology and material science. In this proposal, we focus especially on applications related to peptide and protein engineering and the development of biomimetic systems for catalysis and light harvesting. The design of such biomimetic systems involves the steps of 1) FPMD or QM/MM simulations of the mechanism of action of the natural target; 2) analysis of the simulation data and identification of the relevant descriptor that influence the function of the natural system and 3) search of chemical and/or sequence space for optimal biomimetic counter parts. For all three steps, we will combine molecular simulations with approaches from artificial intelligence: For step 1), the use of an on-the-fly machine learning approach will enable highly efficient force evaluations that can be used as lower level forces within an MTS scheme. Feature selection and causality inference techniques will be crucial for an identification of the relevant descriptor in the highly dimensional simulation data generated in step 1) and last but not least, in step 3) efficient explorations of chemical and sequence space will be performed with the help of evolutionary optimization algorithms (genetic algorithms and particle swarm optimization) by using and further extending the program toolbox EVOLVE that we have been developing during our previous SNF grants.
Keywords: Biomimetic Design, Computational Biophysics, Computational Chemistry, Photovoltaics, Protein Engineering, QM/MM, artificial intelligence, machine learning, molecular dynamics, multiscale modelling

Title: Learning disentangled graph representations for biomedicine
Abstract:
With recent advances in multimodal data acquisition technologies, vast and diverse volumes of biological omics, imaging, and physiological data are being collected at an exponentially increasing rate. This wealth of data has significantly advanced our understanding of physiological and pathological processes, paving the way for the development of novel healthcare solutions. However, the scale and complexity of such data present major analytical challenges. Biological data often result from intricate modulations across multiple systems, rendering classical signal processing and machine learning methods insufficient for decoding regulatory patterns across various biological targets.

Complex networks (graphs) have emerged as powerful tools to model interactions among biological entities, such as gene regulatory networks and brain functional connectivity networks. These graph-based structures provide effective analytical frameworks for capturing the inherent complexity of biological systems. Given the multimodal nature of biological data, multi-view representations, including multi-view graphs, are often required.

To address the analytical challenges arising from such representations, this project proposes a comprehensive disentangled graph representation learning framework, specifically tailored to the structure of graph-based biomedical data. Disentangled learning holds significant potential across domains such as multimodal machine learning, social network analysis, biology, health informatics, and infrastructure systems. In life sciences and medicine—where large volumes of unpaired and heterogeneous data are common—disentangling shared and unique representations across domains can uncover associations between data modalities and disease characteristics, improve patient stratification, and ultimately enable more effective, personalized therapies.

The objective of this project is to leverage disentangled learning principles to integrate insights from diverse modalities and extract both shared and domain-specific representations across different views—such as across patients or data types. The research is structured around four interrelated thrusts:

T1: Structured Disentangled Multi-View Graph Inference
Develop a framework to infer both common and individual graph structures from multi-    view datasets using observed data.

T2: Multi-View Disentangled Graph Representation Learning
Extend to multiple known domains, represented as layers within a multiplex graph, capturing inter- and intra-layer biological interactions.

T3: Multimodal Disentangled Learning
Incorporate heterogeneous modalities—including clinical, imaging, and genomic data—into the graph learning framework.

T4: Application to Biomedical Data
Apply the developed methods to two key areas: brain connectomics and cancer biology, to learn both disease-level and individual-level representations, ultimately contributing to the advancement of precision medicine.
Keywords: AI for health, disentangled reprepresentation learning, machine learning on graphs, multiview and multimodal learning

Title: Machine Learning for Demand Response (ML4DR)
Abstract: In many countries, renewable energy investment is starting to become economically viable without support. This is leading to the disruption of electric utility’ business and potential grid expansion needs in order to accommodate the increasing amount of renewable electricity. Therefore, it is necessary to find out solutions to minimize these concerns. One of the promising solutions to this problem is the increasing usage of demand response (partial load restrictions). To leverage demand response, it is important to understand customer preferences for adjusting electricity demand to match with power supply. A conventional method to engage consumers is to assess their willingness to allow load control using a survey approach and dispatch their flexibility assuming constant preferences. However, static estimates based on surveys are likely to be imprecise, because consumers have limited experience with demand restrictions and because consumer preferences will vary across time.  Allowing consumers to override device settings, has been shown to increase acceptance of automation, because consumers do not need to anticipate their load shifting cost. Automatic updates of consumer preferences based on override actions could thus reduce the need for static assessments of customer willingness to allow load control and revolutionize the way that the power system is operated. This research thus plans to develop machine learning algorithms for identifying time-varying customer willingness to accept demand response and test how these could be used to automate the price-based device control based on consumer actions in real-time. The efficiency of different learning algorithms will also be assessed using a simulated test case. The practice partner will provide anonymized smart meter data from their customers that can be used to calibrate the machine learning models in a test case. Subject to the agreement of customers, we will investigate to what extent the predictions of consumer willingness to allow load shifting can be improved by the usage of unconventional data sources, such as calendars, location services, social media profiles etc.  This work also provides the design of subsequent field studies to compare the effectiveness between machine learning approaches and survey-based methods (future works).
Keywords: Cost, Demand response, Flexibility, Machine learning, Willingness-to-pay

Title: Phenotypic and Transcriptomic Circulating Tumor Cell Dynamics for Real-Time Assessment of Treatment Response in Neoadjuvant Treatment for Pancreatic Cancer
Abstract:
Background: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the leading causes of cancer-related death. The only curative therapy is surgical resection, however, systemic control via intensive chemotherapy has shown a significant survival benefit. Currently, treatment plans are based on tumor stage and only limited biomarkers are available to plan management according to tumor biology. Furthermore, there is a lack of effective biomarkers that can monitor treatment response in real time. As a result, determination of treatment response is often made too late to alter therapy, leading to progression from potentially curable to incurable disease in neoadjuvant treated PDAC patients. Serum CA19-9 is the only liquid biomarker in routine clinical practice but has significant limitations. Therefore, there is an urgent need to find novel biomarkers that can help to provide precision care to these patients. Recently, assessments of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) have shown promise to fill this gap. Quantitative and qualitative (epithelial versus transitional CTC phenotypes) analyses of CTCs have demonstrated that CTC characteristics change upon therapy and are associated with treatment response and oncological outcomes in different settings. 

Aims: This proposal aims to assess the role of CTCs in individualized treatment of resectable PDAC patients. Phenotypic and quantitative changes as well as transcriptomic characteristics of CTCs will be determined and correlated with patients’ responses to neoadjuvant therapy. Specific aims are: 
1.To assess phenotypic dynamics of CTCs as a biomarker for treatment response. 
2. To assess transcriptomic subtypes of CTCs as a biomarker for treatment response.

Methods: Peripheral blood samples will be collected from 100 PDAC patients prior to initiation and monthly during neoadjuvant systemic treatment until surgical resection. CTCs will be isolated and immunofluorescent staining will be performed for quantitative analyses as well as phenotypic subtyping. Single-cell RNA sequencing will be performed using NOVAseq (Illumina and 10xGenomicsTM). Sequencing data will be analyzed to identify CTC subtypes at the RNA expression level. Histopathological analysis of surgical resection specimens will be performed to determine the grade of treatment response using the College of American Pathologist (CAP) grading system. Traditional statistical tools (e.g. logistic regression) and artificial intelligence based algorithms (e.g. explainable boosting machine) will be used to analyze time-series data in order to determine the earliest point in time when accurate assessment of treatment response can be made and identify transcriptomic CTC characteristics that are associated with treatment response. 

Expected results and potential impact: The findings of this study will help to develop tools that guide personalized therapy in PDAC patients. Assessment of CTC characteristics could potentially demonstrate their role as a new dynamic biomarker providing “real-time” data about treatment response for altering individualized treatment regimens where necessary. Molecular-guided treatment based on single-cell RNA sequencing analyses of CTCs may be implemented into clinical practice to tackle treatment failure.
Keywords: Circulating Tumor Cells, Individualized Treatment, Oncology, Pancreatic Cancer, Precision Medicine, Surgery, Surgical Oncology, Translational Research

Title: The Role of Emotional Interactions in the Polarization of Opinions in Participatory Media
Abstract: The proliferation of online participatory media - such as social networking sites, blogs and online fora - has recently changed Internet users from simple information consumers to participants that actively create, share, evaluate and discuss content.  This recent development provides a number of opportunities and challenges that are the subject of current research. On the one hand, participatory media provide the potential to increase citizens engagement in discussions on political and societal issues. At the same time, there is increasing evidence that - under certain conditions - interactions between users can lead to an increasing polarization of opinions. Group dynamics can lead to the emergence of opposing collective opinions that are often hard to reconcile. This development not only influences online participatory media, it increasingly affects the culture of political discourse. As such, polarization in online media is a relevant phenomenon that can affect the willingness of compromise across social groups. At the same time polarization provides a confrontation of opinions that is a cornerstone of a functional democratic society. A number of individual and collective mechanisms that can result in polarized collective opinions have been identified, e.g. in the fields of opinion dynamics, social psychology, political science and communication studies.  The goal of this interdisciplinary research project is to study the role of emotional interactions in the polarization of opinions. In particular, it will be studied under which conditions positive and negative emotions in online discussions can amplify polarization in online participatory media. We address this question in a quantitative way by means of novel computational methods like the automated emotional classification of texts, machine learning, statistical analysis of large-scale data and agent-based modeling.  Based on our experience in the modeling and analysis of collective emotions, we will for the first time combine findings from the study of opinion dynamics with a quantitative approach to the modeling of emotional interactions. Furthermore, we will test hypothesis from social psychology and political science by means of an analysis of large-scale datasets that will be collected in the project. With this, we make an important and timely contribution to the interdisciplinary study of collective social phenomena in digital democracies.
Keywords: Agent-based modeling, Emotions, Online interaction, Opinion dynamics, Political science, Social media, e-democracy

Title: Participatory Methodology for AI Accountability in the Gig Economy: A Comparative Study of (Digital) Labour Conditions Between the French- and German-Speaking Cantons of Switzerland
Abstract:
The impact of algorithmic management on working time and pay within the gig economy is a subject of international, public and scientific debate. Countries in Europe are developing regulations to enforce algorithmic transparency but the implications of implementing such regulations to assert labour rights are unclear. While researchers are creating tools for algorithmic accountability, there remains a lack of understanding about the practical significance of transparency and the integration of accountability rules into local labour frameworks. There is no study in Switzerland. The few studies that do exist in other countries focus on delivery and ride-hailing, while female-dominated sectors have been ignored.
This one-year project develops a novel participatory methodology at the intersection of sociology of work and data science, to examine the potential of data protection and algorithmic transparency regulations through computational methods for holding platforms accountable, in order to improve livelihoods for digital labour platform workers in various economic sectors in Switzerland. We will collect and analyse data obtained from platforms and workers to compare the use of algorithm in male-dominated (delivery) and female-dominated (cleaning) sectors across cities in four Swiss cantons (Bern, Geneva, Vaud, Zurich).
Our participatory science methodology will establish a collaboration between workers, academics, civic and local organisations to gather and interpret data, and relate it to labour rights. We will take the challenge of accounting for artificial intelligence algorithms, which are complex technical systems that are hard to audit given that their opaque operations are protected by companies. By doing so, we will provide novel evidence for research and policy agendas about how algorithms operate with respect to algorithmic management – more specifically, when and how work tasks, time, and fares' allocation are automated in labour practices. We will equip workers and their unions with data analysis tools for gaining insights into algorithms. The research will show how multiple legal frameworks offer distinct opportunities for algorithmic transparency with the support of legal experts, and will use sociological theory to analyse how algorithms might affect working time, employment status and labour rights for men and women in the gig economy, contributing to a decent work agenda for improving workers’ livelihoods globally.
Keywords: AI accountability, algorithmic management, digital labour, gig economy, transparency

Title: Safety and Performance for Human in the Loop Control
Abstract:
When safety is a crucial requirement, control systems are traditionally designed to act in isolated, clearly specified environments, or to be conservative against the unknown. The overarching goal of this research program is to enable high performance control with safety guarantees for control systems that are in direct interaction with humans. This will be a key step for moving automation into the safety-critical systems of our daily lives, e.g., for allowing the power system to evolve into an active smart grid, balancing flexible personal loads, distributed storage and renewable generation; the transportation system to become a network of interacting semi-autonomous vehicles; robotic systems to provide services and support human tasks, such as delivery, manufacturing, or rehabilitation; and biomedical systems to enhance human capabilities.

The proposed research program will develop new control paradigms that allow the tight integration of human factors in the controller design. The focus will be on interactions that are highly complex, large-scale and distributed, affecting the controller and/or the dynamics of a single system, as well as of a network of systems. While neglecting these interactions can be a severe safety risk, considering the human as an adversary disturbance may cause drastic performance losses or may even become prohibitively conservative. The key feature underlying the developed methods is the capability to leverage predictions of human effects on the control system, enabling highly personalized control on the local scale and efficient operation on a global scale, while ensuring system safety.

The project addresses this challenging problem by exploiting the availability of vast amounts of data, collected by inexpensive sensors at high rates and stored in a distributed manner. The techniques will build on the key technologies of model predictive control, a powerful framework for complex constrained control problems ideally suited to incorporate predictions of human factors into an optimal decision making process, and machine learning, offering the potential to utilize data and to deal with the emerging scale and complexity of human in the loop control systems. The results will be enabled by two novel methodologies: 1) safe learning-based control methods that enable online learning of human interaction from data; 2) distributed plug and play control techniques that cope with human-induced system changes in large-scale networks.

While the developed methods will be relevant for a broad range of applications, the program will study open problems in the area of smart power grids and semi-autonomous vehicles, addressing different aspects of human in the loop systems. It will specifically focus on the human factor in distributed power systems, in order to improve energy efficiency and increase renewable energy generation by advanced demand side management tools, integrating personalized control of energy systems with grid stability control. Active safety systems for semi-autonomous vehicles are developed by a holistic treatment of the complex interactions and interrelation between the driver and the autonomous safety controller.

The outcome of the proposed research program will be a holistic framework for a systematic and automatic translation from data and design specifications to a provably safe and high performance human in the loop controller. The results will enable 1) automatic online identification of human factors from large-scale data; 2) provably safe control systems leveraging complex human models with uncertainties for performance; 3) semi-autonomous predictive safety systems for non-expert human operators; 4) and optimal operation of a network of systems adjusting to human interaction safely on the fly.

The developed methodologies will address fundamental challenges of distributed and learning-based control and will have an important impact beyond the considered problem of human in the loop control. The proposed research revolves around control, learning and optimization, and is not only multi- but also interdisciplinary, addressing control problems beyond the limits of conventional methods.
