Title: Visual Contagions
Abstract:
VISUAL CONTAGIONS focuses on the global circulation of images from the 1890s to the 1990s, prior to the advent of the Internet and the immense paradigm shift in the circulation of images it brought about. The project is hosted by the new Chair of Digital Humanities of the University of Geneva (UNIGE),  led by Prof. Dr. Béatrice Joyeux-Prunel, in collaboration with the international project Artl@s (https://artlas.huma-num.fr/en/), with a team in Computer Vision from the École des Ponts Paris Tech, one in Computer Sciences at the UNIGE, and one in Neurosciences at the Ecole normale supérieure Paris. 

The raison d’être of VISUAL CONTAGIONS is to understand how images have contributed to the globalization of cultures, and their role in the diffusion of symbolic dominations. It poses challenges to the history of art, the visual studies, to global history, the Digital Humanities (DH), and to the cognitive sciences and finds inspiration in the methods of epidemiology. For the period since the 1890s to the arrival of the internet, we start from the unprecedented availability of massive digitized corpora containing images, such as exhibition catalogues, illustrated magazines, posters and works of art. These sources can be crossed with press reviews and archival material, to explain how artistic and media images circulated over the world and how they have helped to disseminate styles and visual patterns, as well as new ideas about politics and about the body.

 Our objectives are 
1) To identify the most recurrent images of the past century, their visual and cognitive features, the characteristics of their authors; 
2) To study their channels of circulation, and to highlight the process of global cultural homogenization through images, to assess its limits, and to question the model of prescriptive centres and imitative peripheries; 
3) To study the impact of images in copies, imitations, visual quotations and the subsequent diffusion of new styles and new ideas about politics and gender; 4) To offer an innovative methodology to analyse iconographic and stylistic diffusions, that can be applied across periods, languages, and disciplines, and later on, for subsequent projects on visual circulation on the Internet, with a specific visual research tool with spatiotemporal result visualization. 

To do so, 
a) Textual descriptions of images (exhibition catalogues, art databases) will be analysed with text mining, semantic analysis and digital mapping, to trace first the circulation of themes; 
b) Images contained in illustrated documents will be extracted and described automatically. They will be labelled according to their content, place and date of reproduction. Then, all images will be compared using pattern recognition algorithms. The methodology has been validated within the Artl@s Project in collaboration with the Ponts-Paris Tech in France (Mathieu Aubry, EnHerit). 
c) The hypotheses drawn from digital analyses will be confronted with the historical analysis of archives and press on 3 particular cases: the global circulation of styles (1890-1990), the transnational diffusion of a visual language of political engagement, and the global convergence/divergence in the representation of women in illustrated periodicals over the same period. 

VISUAL CONTAGIONS will enrich debates on intercultural encounter by including the question of image in globalization. It will help launch subsequent projects for which further funding will be searched: we think of a replicable digital visual search engine to search for and visualize the dissemination of images.

3) to study the impact of images in copies, imitations, visual quotations and the subsequent diffusion of new styles and new ideas about politics and gender; 4) to offer an innovative methodology to analyse iconographic and stylistic diffusions, that can be applied across periods, languages, and disciplines, and later on, for subsequent projects on visual circulation on the internet, with a specific visual research tool with spatiotemporal result visualization. to do so, a) textual descriptions of images (exhibition catalogues, art databases) will be analysed with text mining, semantic analysis and digital mapping, to trace first the circulation of themes; b) images contained in illustrated documents will be extracted and described automatically. they will be labelled according to their content, place and date of reproduction. then, all images will be compared using pattern recognition algorithms. the methodology has been validated within the artl@s project in collaboration with the ponts paris tech in france (mathieu aubry, enherit). c) the hypotheses drawn from digital analyses will be confronted with the historical analysis of archives and press on 3 particular cases: the global circulation of styles (1890 1990), the transnational diffusion of a visual language of political engagement, and the global convergence/divergence in the representation of women in illustrated periodicals over the same period. visual contagions will enrich debates on intercultural encounter by including the question of image in globalization. it will help launch subsequent projects for which further funding will be searched: we think of a replicable digital visual search engine to search for and visualize the dissemination of images.. centres & peripheries, digital humanities, globalization mondialisation, images, visual circulations circulations visuelles

Title: Instantaneous Flexible and Coarse-Grained Docking based on Novel Deep Neural Network Approaches
Abstract: Computational drug design methods have become an important pillar in structure-based drug design (SBDD) for rapid lead discovery and optimization. In addition to molecular dynamics simulations, docking methods are the dominant tool set in computational SBDD for binding-mode prediction and virtual screening. Due to efficiency reasons, docking-based virtual screening typically neglects the flexibility of the protein despite the fact that the protein can adapt its structure to the bound ligand. In spite of significant efforts to incorporate receptor flexibility in docking, current flexible docking approaches are still unable to reliably predict native binding poses or identify active compounds. Due to the enormous flexibility of peptides, particularly challenging is the docking of peptides to flexible, solvent exposed binding sites. Peptide-protein interactions, however, have recently gained increasing attention due to their role in protein-protein interaction interference or in context of accelerated vaccine design, a task of crucial need in the current COVID-19 pandemic.  In light of the tremendous recent advancements in deep learning, the time is ripe for addressing this topic from a different point of view. Thus, in this proposal, we will develop innovative methods combining modern deep neural network (NN) approaches with detailed 3D physicochemical models of protein-ligand complexes with consideration of critical hydration effects. First, based on deep generative flow-based NN, probable protein conformations will be efficiently sampled incorporating the induced-fit effect of potentially bound ligands. In the resulting method, ComplexGenerator, a correspondence between latent space and configurational density of protein structures will be learned on-the-fly, where force-field calculations of the generated protein structure will function as a feedback to the NN. The novelty of our approach is that together with the protein also a ‘ligand model’, i.e. collection of functional groups, will be generated on-the-fly in the binding site. Thus, protein conformations will be generated under the influence of induced-fit to a large variety of potential ligands. Second, a novel flexible docking pipeline will be devised utilizing new concepts for pose generation, refinement, ranking and affinity prediction. Pose generation with flexible protein will be performed with our recently developed graph convolutional NN (GCNN) concept PoseNetDiMa with significantly improved pose generation compared to standard flexible docking methods. PoseNetDiMa relies on a coarse-grained representation of the protein and is trained to predict the distance matrix between ligand heavy atoms and centroids of binding site residues. This distance matrix is translated into poses of the ligand in the binding site. Poses will be refined with a modified version of ComplexGenerator, where the virtual ligand is replaced by the real ligand. Pose ranking will be based on our recently published convolutional NN (CNN) method DeepWATsite with unprecedented accuracy due to the inclusion of hydration information. Finally, a new concept based on GCNN, GAT-MD, will be utilized for free energy calculation of the predicted pose.In a third subproject, we will focus on the topic of peptide-docking. We propose the development of a novel deep NN conditioned by the peptide sequence to identify the likely binding site for a specific peptide on the surface of the target protein. PoseNetDiMa will then be used for docking the peptide into the binding pockets. A coarse-grained representation of the peptide will be used throughout this process. An auto-encoder model will allow the back-mapping of the peptide to a full-atomistic representation for subsequent pose ranking and affinity prediction. All method developments will be intensively validated using retrospective analysis on benchmark sets of existing experimental data. In collaboration with Prof. Ricklin at the University of Basel the methods will also be applied prospectively to flexible protein systems including unknown binding sites and peptide-protein interactions.
Keywords: Computer-aided drug design, Deep neural network, Flexible docking, Peptide-protein docking, Protein hydration

Title: South–North flows of information through translation in the global news agency AFP
Abstract:
News translation practices are often invisible in media organisations (including news agencies) despite the production of news stories in highly multilingual environments. News agencies have become central agents in global news flows because, given their limited resources, most media outlets rely on them for their international news coverage. In spite of this central role, research into news agencies, whether from translation studies or journalism studies, is still partly uncharted territory. Most studies are product oriented, while sociological process-oriented studies are far less represented in translation studies. In addition, literature on news translation is more abundant in G20 countries and most research on news flows in the news agencies focuses on stories that originated in the Global North. This project therefore attempts to counterbalance the distorted distribution of news translation and journalism research by looking more systematically at the translation actors, translation products and translation practices in local bureaux of an international news agency (AFP) that are based in the Global South. The main objective of this project is to investigate to what extent AFP contributes to South–North–South flows of information. 

In terms of research design, the project is structured as a multiple-phased qualitative study over a period of three years informed by Bruno Latour’s sociological actor–network theory approach. In phase A, postdoctoral fellows will conduct field trips to collect data related to the actors (human and non-human) involved in the news production at two AFP’s bureaux in Latin America, two in Africa, at the regional desk for Latin America, at the desk for Africa and at the headquarters of AFP. Phase B is inspired by a sociology of the translation product and will include the collection of news dispatches, graphs, photographs, and videos produced locally, which are possibly translated and edited at AFP’s local bureaux and then sent to regional and/or international customers. In Phase C, a news database will be searched to identify news items that reuse and possibly cite the AFP content analysed beforehand to see to what extent these news dispatches were circulated to multiple media outlets in the Global North and the Global South. In phases B and C, the African and the Latin American sub-corpora will be searched for themes, news values, sources of reported speech and translational relationships.

The relevance of this project lies in its interdisciplinarity, its methodological and theoretical framework (Latour’s actor–network theory), its comparative design and its object – a global news agency in an era of multi-platform journalism. The place of the news agencies in today’s news flows and the role that translation plays in these media outlets are crucial elements for scholars as well as students of translation and journalism. The more pragmatic results of the study, such as multi-skilling in multi-platform environments and the use of machine translation, will be of particular interest to research participants and other journalists. The project envisages collaborative research on this topic that will build bridges between the Global South and the Global North in terms of translation and journalism studies, practitioners and scholars. The project that brings together the applicants, project partners and postdoctoral fellows will also contribute to the flow of information (in this case academic knowledge and expertise) between the Global North and the Global South. Furthermore, the close link between the envisaged impact of this study and the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goal #16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions), which aims at providing access all people to news and information and protecting the freedom of the press, makes it of real significance for the Global South and the Global North.
Keywords: Actor-Network Theory, Convergence, Global South, Journalism Studies, News Agencies, News Flows, News Translation, Translation Studies, news agencies, news translation, sociology of translation, translation studies

Title: ScanOMetrics –  Open-Source Brain Morphometry Assessment for Clinical Routine Using Explainable Deep Learning
Abstract:
Assessment of brain MRI by trained experts is known to be experience and vigilance dependent and may suffer from large inter- and intra-rater variability. However, morphometric analysis has yielded high scientific insight into neurological and psychiatric disorders since its establishment. Unfortunately, these achievements are still largely inaccessible from clinical routine, the main reason being missing software availability in most hospitals around the world. In this project, we aim at closing this gap by providing state-of-the-art, easy-to-use and time-efficient open-source software for morphometry in individual patients. This will foster future developments by other groups as well as access from the realm of patient care. 

We will start from our previous work and experience to step-wise enhance our developments by deep learning based approaches, which recently have proven very successful in the field of medical image analysis (e.g. tissue type or lesion segmentation). Rather than relying on scarcely available human labeled training data, we propose a strategy that mainly utilizes a large amount of weak labels generated with the well-established but computationally expensive reference software FreeSurfer. To make our software’s results “explainable” to the user, we will generate voxel-wise maps of segmentations and output variables, which can be inspected in parallel to the input images. The project will be conducted in a well-functioning and productive team of scientists with experience in brain morphometry and deep learning. To generate training data, we will utilize a large collection of publicly available MRI data and re-use data collected at the Inselspital during other projects. This combination will enable testing on homogeneous as well as on heterogeneous subsamples to assess transferability and reliability. 

The project will be organized in four work-packages (WP). In WP A our existing open-source software for deep learning based morphometry estimation will be extended to include additional variables. WP B will drive scientific exchange between the research groups in Bern and Newcastle (UK) to explore the perspectives offered by a recently found biophysical scaling law of cortical morphology. WP C will make extensive application to “unexpected” input data like the clinically frequent occurrence of MRI with tumors, stroke lesions, resections, MS lesions, dental braces or other artifacts. WP D will deal with the release of the open-source software package. 

This project will train one PhD student (mainly but not only WP A) and up to five master students (WPs B and C). Easy-to-use open-source software will be distributed freely (WP D).
Keywords: brain morphometry, clinical neuroradiology, deep learning, open-source software

Title: Computational design of skills, environment, and collaborative intelligence for assembly robots
Abstract:
This project aims to advance robotic intelligence for the assembly of spatial structures. We envision a future where robots can work collaboratively, have an innate understanding of physical laws, and achieve a level of dexterity and precision that is on par with or beyond human capacity. To this end, this project develops computational algorithms to provide fundamental tools to help us design next-generation assembly robots' dexterous skills, workspace, and collaborative intelligence.

The ability to build functional artifacts from simple parts is a crucial part of human intelligence. Enabling such intelligence in assembly robots has the potential for a large socio-economic impact. First, they hold promises to solve the building industry's productivity stagnation and address the construction sector's imminent labor shortage. Second, they could enable autonomous construction in distant or dangerous places for human workers.

While in recent years, we have seen many impressive prototypes that demonstrate the potential of robotic assembly, the flexibility of these robots is still limited in three key aspects: (1) the robot is only capable of performing simple, preprogrammed skill primitive such as pick and place; (2) the workspace of the robots is usually manually designed, making it hard to adapt to new production needs; (3) the robots display limited collaborative behaviors, which humans enforce through a top-down approach. This project aims to advance the field of assembly robotics by answering the following fundamental scientific questions:
•What enables human’s wide range of manipulation capabilities? How can we enable robots to learn complex manipulation skills from human demonstration in a scalable, effective way?
•What is the relationship between the workspace of an agent and the feasibility of the overall assembly operation?
•How can we enable collaborative assembly behavior to emerge bottom-up, compositionally?

To answer these questions, we structure our research agenda into three parallel streams: (1) Scalable human demonstration for dexterous dual-arm manipulation proposes a new learning-from-demonstration paradigm to facilitate the design of new dexterous robotic manipulation skills; (2) Workspace optimization for robotic assembly explores automated reasoning between workspace layout and assemblability; (3) Physics-aware task and motion planning for collaborative assembly robots investigates automated reasoning that combines logical, physical, and motion constraints.
Keywords: construction robotics, robot assembly, robotic learning from demonstration, robotic workspace optimization, task and motion planning

Title: BREAST CANCER PROGNOSIS AND SURVIVAL: THE ROLE OF ENDOCRINE THERAPY ADHERENCE AND PERSONALIZED FOLLOW-UP CARE
Abstract:
Breast cancer (BC) is the most common cancer in women, with 2.3 million new cases globally in 2022. Advances in screening and treatment have significantly improved survival rates, resulting in a growing population of BC survivors. Survivors of early-stage BC remain at considerable risk of recurrence throughout their lives and face unique considerations regarding follow-up care, late effects of treatment, and quality of life. After initial treatment – such as surgery, chemotherapy and radiotherapy – patients with hormone receptor (HR)-positive BC are prescribed daily endocrine therapy (ET) for at least five years to reduce the risk of recurrence. Many patients struggle with adherence to ET due to its distressing side effects. While incomplete adherence is known to be associated with adverse survival outcomes, intermittent adherence may still provide some benefit over complete non-adherence. However, the survival loss due to partial adherence has not been systematically quantified and may vary widely depending on the longitudinal course of adherence, patient characteristics and needs, and ET regimen. In addition, after completion of initial treatment, survivors of early-stage BC enter a follow-up program that typically includes regular medical visits and mammography for at least five years. Screening for metastatic recurrence is not part of currently recommended follow-up routines in asymptomatic patients. In the absence of recent clinical trial data, the optimal schedule for follow-up care, particularly for the detection of metastatic disease, remains unclear.
In this project, we will analyze real-world data with modern causal inference methods to provide guidelines to improve the care of patients after initial treatment for early-stage BC. The project has two main aims. First, we will investigate the impact of partial adherence to ET on survival outcomes, focusing on populations of extreme age, on drug-drug interactions, and on the real-world adoption of new treatment strategies including gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists, cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 (CDK4/6) inhibitors, and poly ADP ribose polymerase (PARP) inhibitors. Second, we will focus on early detection of loco-regional, contralateral, and distant recurrence by designing optimal follow-up schedules and investigating how ambulatory care data could be integrated for early detection of metastatic recurrence.
I will use data from the French health insurance database (SNDS), which aggregates all the medical and administrative information related to the reimbursement of healthcare expenses in France, both inpatient and outpatient, with comprehensive coverage of the French population. Specifically, the analysis will include over 250,000 patients with BC, representing one of the largest and most detailed BC cohorts in the world. Methods will include advanced causal inference for time-varying interventions, in particular target trial emulation, and deep learning for recurrence prediction.
The project has the potential to provide effective, cost-efficient, and easily implementable evidence-based recommendations for clinical guidelines related to the management of ET non-adherence and the optimal scheduling of follow-up visits, thereby improving both the quality of life and outcome of BC survivors.
Keywords: Adherence, Breast Cancer, Causal Inference, Endocrine Therapy, Epidemiology, Follow-up Care, Health Claims Data, Survival Outcomes

Title: Be Your Avatar: Realtime Tracking and Animation for a Desktop Environment
Abstract:
Tracking and animating humans in motion is a fundamental problem in computer graphics and computer vision. A particularly important question is how to accurately reconstruct the shape and articulation of human hands. Hand motion is a crucial component of non-verbal communication, plays an important role in the animation of humanoid avatars, and is central for numerous human-computer interfaces. While accurate realtime body and face tracking systems have been proposed in recent years, hand tracking solutions of comparable quality are still lacking, in particular ones that can be deployed in the context of consumer applications.
In this project we plan to develop new methods and algorithms for realtime hand tracking and animation with a particular focus on accuracy and ease-of-use. We aim to faithfully reconstruct intricate hand geometry and motion with an acquisition system that can be readily deployed in consumer-level applications. Our goal is to integrate the developed algorithms with existing face tracking technology to obtain a complete system for online human communication in a desktop environment. This system will allow an entirely new form of realtime interactions based on digital avatars, with numerous applications in digital content creation, online interaction and gaming, education and training, or human computer interfaces.
Accurate hand tracking with a non-invasive sensing device in realtime is a highly challenging scientific prob- lem. Human hands are very articulate and therefore require models with sufficiently many degrees of freedom to adequately describe the corresponding motion space. Hand motion is often fast and complex, exhibiting intricate geometric configurations and complicated contact patterns among fingers. In addition, our focus on a single sensor setup to facilitate wide-spread applicability leads to ambiguous and often incomplete input data, caused by significant self-occlusions of the tracked hands.
All these aspects mandate new algorithmic solutions. We will build on our extensive experience in face tracking, geometry optimization, and realtime dynamic modeling to investigate these problems and develop new algorithms for realtime human hand tracking. We will start our investigations by developing an offline system for accurate and robust hand-tracking, using pre-build dynamic hand models tailored to a specific user. We then successively refine our solution towards higher performance and higher usability. This requires new efficient algorithms to meet the realtime goal and sophisticated pre-processing and online learning methods to achieve maximal usability without requiring any additional calibration or user assistance. We plan to integrate and improve state-of-the-art robust optimization methods and machine learning algorithms that allow exploiting the strong spatial and temporal coupling of hand articulation. A novel registration method that combines articulated 3D alignment with high-quality optical flow will be specifically designed for hand geometry and texture.
In the final stage of the project, we will integrate the developed hand tracking solution with our existing face tracking algorithms to obtain a complete system for realtime acquisition and animation of human upper bodies, hands, and faces. This system will enable new forms human interaction in a desktop environment, where users communicate through virtual avatars in realtime. With the increasing proliferation of commodity sensors, we expect our research to facilitate numerous new applications in online communication, with profound potential impact on society.

Title: Vision-based Aerial Swarms
Abstract:
The deployment of an autonomous aerial swarm, here intended as a decentralised system composed of multiple drones (at least 10) capable of autonomously and safely coordinating their trajectories during collective flight, is the next frontier in the science and technology of intelligent flying machines. Despite recent progress in coordination and communication methods, which have led to impressive displays of dancing drones lighting up night skies and theatre halls, these aerial systems are carefully orchestrated by ground computers that accurately monitor and control the motion of the drones. The few autonomous and decentralised aerial swarms described so far, including our own, rely mostly on external positioning technology (Motion Tracking Halls and GPS), intensive communication to share the range and bearing among the drones, and, when tested on real drones, struggle to prevent collisions induced by loss of communication packets and vehicle dynamics. Recent work by our lab and other labs point to the feasibility of adding vision to aerial swarms.
This research proposal aims at developing fully decentralized aerial swarms with robust collision avoidance by means of on-board vision and predictive capabilities. This proposal is a short extension (2 years) of an ongoing project ending in 2019 where we have obtained promising, but preliminary, simulation results indicating the feasibility of the proposed solutions. Our approach builds on biologically inspired swarming methods, such as Reynold’s and Vicsek’s models of collective motion. The proposed work is organized along two parallel and related research lines.
Within the first research line, our theoretical and experimental results indicate that vehicle dynamics and limited sensing, which reduces the information about the relative position of other drones, significantly affect the cohesion and collision risks in dense swarms. In this research proposal, we will enable drones to predict their trajectories and those of their neighbors under the constraints of specific vehicle dynamics and limited sensing. In particular, we plan to approach the problem within the theoretical framework of Model Predictive Control, a powerful computational strategy that can now be implemented in small and lightweight processing boards and is producing impressive results for the control of aggressive drone maneuvers. 
Within the second research line, we will start from our newly proposed method for training convolutional neural networks to produce decentralized and robust swarming control strategies from visual images collected by the drones during collective flight. However, those results were obtained in simulations and the drone were flown in environments with uniform background. In this research proposal, we will develop methods for transfer learning from simulations to indoor environments and to outdoor environments. In a first phase, we will use omnidirectional vision and published models of collective motion for training the neural networks. In a second phase, the visual layout and swarming strategies used for training the convolutional neural networks will incorporate the insights and model predictive control developed in the first research line. We plan to approach the transfer learning problem by using adversarial methods and on-policy imitation learning.
We will validate the methods with a swarm of 10 vision-based quadcopters flying in indoor and outdoor environments. The results of the project will consist in decentralized aerial swarms with predictive control for reduced collision risks and with vision-based coordination among the drones. These methods will be particularly useful for dense swarms where drones fly at short distances to each other and among obstacles. We also expect to develop novel methods for swarming with model predictive control and for machine learning in robotic systems where large data collection is not practical. We expect that these methods will be applicable also beyond the specific swarming models used in this research proposal.
Keywords: Bio-inspired artificial intelligence, Flying robots, Swarm intelligence, Vision-based flight control

Title: Heterogeneous nucleation of metal halide perovskites from solution
Abstract:
In recent years, halide perovskites of general formula ABX3 – where A is a monovalent cation such as caesium (Cs+), methylammonium (MA+) or formamidinium (FA+); B is divalent lead (Pb2+), tin (Sn2+) or germanium (Ge2+); and X is a halide anion (I-, Cl-, or Br-) – have been at the forefront of the materials’ research which are used to make cheaper high-efficiency solar cells, light-emitting diodes, transistors, photocatalyst, and photodetectors. Over the past decade, the solar to power conversion efficiencies (PCEs) of perovskite solar cells (PSCs) has increased from 3.8% to 25.5%, thereby surpassing other thin-film technologies of CdTe, CIGS and including the market leader, polycrystalline silicon. Unfortunately, their commercialization is hampered by their limited stability which directly depends on the morphological evolution during the fabrication process. Control over microstructure evolution is the main problem in the field of halide perovskites. The lack of precise control over the crystallization process creates a risk of forming unwanted defects, photo-inactive structures, pinholes, and grain boundaries. Perovskite electronics are usually manufactured by mixing salts of PbX2 (for example PbI2) and AX (for example FAI) in aprotic solvents on conducting substrates, typically titanium dioxide (TiO2) or tin oxide (SnO2). Therefore, a comprehensive and in-depth understanding of the heterogeneous nucleation of perovskites is imperative for the development of high-performance and stable halide perovskite solar cell modules. Among many perovskites of interest, cubic (a)-phase of formamidinium lead iodide (FAPbI3) have emerged as the champion semiconductor with its nearly ideal band-gap (~1.45eV) for solar cells, superior thermal stability and high-charge carrier mobility. The problem comes from the fact that the thermodynamically stable hexagonal (d)-phase of FAPbI3 is a photoinactive phase, meaning that it does not react to light, thus not a solar power harvester. Whereas a-phase is metastable and the thermodynamic phase transition requires high temperatures of around 150 C. My simulations and immediate experiments have shown that a direct conversion from d to a-FAPbI3 by heating, is not an effective strategy, because hexagonal stacking faults form during conversion and thereby lower efficiency and low stability. Therefore, high-performance PSCs are synthesized via solution processing, where a-FAPbI3 is crystallized in a kinetically controlled approach. Along these lines, a multitude of experimental efforts has been employed to optimize the crystallization processes. However, experimental methodologies are often based on trial and error strategies and fail to provide the underlying mechanism. Moreover, nanoscopic length and time scales that characterize nucleation make this a rather challenging problem for experiments. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can complement experiments by providing atomic-level information on the nucleation processes and therefore can help to design better synthesis protocols. In this project, I take this alternative approach: “I will perform molecular simulations of heterogeneous nucleation of FAPbI3 from solution to understand the fundamental crystallization mechanism and discover control strategies to make highly efficient and stable a-FAPbI3 PSCs”. I will achieve this goal by taking the following steps:
(a) Develop accurate machine learning models of perovskite solutions on TiO2 and SnO2.
(b) Perform long-time brute-force MD simulations and understand solution chemistry FAPbI3 on commonly used solvents.
(c) Carry out nucleation of a and d phases of FAPbI3 on TiO2 and SnO2. Thus, provide quantitative thermodynamic (free energies) and kinetics (rate calculations) details of nucleation process. 
(d) Collaborate with experimentalists to design better fabrication methods for highly efficient and stable PSCs.
Keywords: Ab-initio calculations, Crystal growth, Halide perovskites, Interfaces, Machine learning potentials, Molecular dynamics simulations, Nucleation, Perovskite solar cell, Phase transitions, Renewable technology

Title: Title: Press the power button: The social semiotics of photography in marketing materials – historical, multimodal and ideological perspectives
Abstract:
This project seeks to make a theoretical, analytical, innovative contribution to the field of critical discourse studies, and media anthropology. The project aims to investigate the language of amateur photography through Social Semiotics. In particular, it aims to explore the gender and postcolonial aspects embedded in the imaging tools of daily life. 

This PhD will examine seven amateur cameras, which have fundamentally changed the practice of photography and its social impact, by case study; from the first amateur camera ever invented (1901) to the photo drone (2014). Since the democratization of photography in 1888 (Kodak), the practice of amateur photography has become highly automated through technological developments(1). It has increasingly developed into a more 'progressive practice’: The camera has become an 'image production machine' (Azoulay, 2015: 21). Donna Haraway described this evolution as a ‘technological feast of visualization’, associated with scopic regimes (Haraway, 1991: 188). My hypothesis is that since the invention of the amateur camera (Kodak, 1888), the economic incentives for the technical aspects have been particularly relevant, while ethical and social aspects have mostly been ignored. 

The closer focus of the analysis is the camera instruction manual, which is an empirically and ideologically intriguing document. It has been completely overlooked in social science, discourse studies and media anthropology. I will analyze and contextualize it in relation to conventional marketing materials. The camera instruction manual is a seemingly harmless, behind-the-scenes text, but is an integral marketing tool, in which the social meanings of both photography and photographer are produced and circulated. The instruction manual conveys information explicitly within their legal, technical and economic capacity and implicitly in their social and ethical capacity. It is designed for smooth interaction between the camera and user, with the aim of incorporating these instructions into their habits, thus shaping their image practice. 

I will critically analyze a set of textual and visual data (camera manual, handbook, sales brochure, add, video, interface), within a discourse-(auto)ethnographic framework and from a gender and postcolonial perspective, in order to understand how the gaze of the camera sold by the photography industry is translated and transmitted and how the social meanings are articulated through the practice and form of visuality.

(1) The European Photography Industry Federation estimated 1,138 trillion photographs (Trendreport, 2016). The number of drones sold worldwide is set to increase more than 10-fold to $ 67.9 million between 2015 and 2021 (Trendreport, 2017). The photo industry has announced the ‘smart’ camera, which will be controlled by artificial intelligence.
Keywords: amateur-photography, creative industry, critical discourse studies, gender, race, social semiotics, technology

Title: Targeted Modulation of Complement Activation in Lupus Nephritis Using a Bispecific CATCH-Construct
Abstract:
Background 
The complement system is a highly potent enzymatic cascade supporting our immune system in defense and clearance of microbes and immune-complexes (ICs). Tight regulation is essential to prevent potential self-reactive inflammatory effects. Unimpeded activation causing tissue damage is seen in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), a complex autoimmune disease. Lupus nephritis (LN) is a life-limiting SLE manifestation. Despite available immunosuppressive treatment, 10-20% of SLE patients will show progressive renal disease. LN is characterized by IC deposited at the glomerular basement membrane (GBM). These trigger complement activation via C1q, a pattern recognition molecule starting the classical pathway (CP) of the complement system. The GBM is generally protected from complement attack by binding the main soluble complement regulator factor H (FH). In LN, the GBM has a reduced capacity to bind FH, making it vulnerable to complement attack. 
Aims
The objective of this project is to develop the basis for a novel drug to attenuate site-specific activation of the complement system in LN. The molecule is called CATCH (Complement ATtenuation by Complexing FH to target-bound C1q).  It is a bispecific molecule that will specifically recruit the main endogenous circulating complement inhibitor FH to target-bound C1q in glomeruli. This will attenuate overactivation precisely at the site of inflammation. 
Methods 
CATCH will target a neoepitope on C1q that is only exposed upon C1q binding to a target. This is achieved by generating fragment antigen-binding regions (Fabs) from antibodies from hybridoma cells with unique binding characteristics available at my current lab. Binding properties will be optimized using large language models for intelligent affinity maturation. The binding of FH to the second arm of the bispecific molecule will be achieved by using a well-characterized peptide from the literature with high specificity for FH. Both arms will be expressed separately in established mammalian expression systems and joined using the sortase reaction system. Several tests will be performed to evaluate appropriate affinity, exclude relevant cross-reactivity and demonstrate the capability of complement regulation by the CATCH-construct. 
Results
This project is a pivotal first step in developing a novel bispecific complement regulator drug for LN. In this 12-month project, I will synthesize and characterize a compound with high affinity for both human and murine deposited C1q. This dual affinity not only ensures its effective in vitro functional activity but also positions the compound as an ideal candidate for subsequent in vivo studies in mouse models of LN. 
Impact 
The ultimate goal is to bridge preclinical findings with clinical applications, laying the groundwork for translational research that can directly benefit human health.  Furthermore, CATCH will be a valuable tool for studying complement activation and probing our understanding of the complement system in general expanding our knowledge of a field of research relevant to several diseases.

Title: System-Aware Machine Learning
Abstract:
In machine learning, the design of hardware systems and learning algorithms are often conducted independently. As a consequence, when training machine learning models in practice, the available hardware resources may not be efficiently utilized  by the algorithm. Because the training procedure is an essential component of almost every AI application these inefficiencies impact every single researcher and company applying machine learning in their everyday business. Designing algorithms that  respect and efficiently utilize system resources can contribute to energy efficiency and productivity of the community.
 
The main goal of this proposal is to rethink popular algorithms for training machine learning models to more systematically allow the efficient utilization of memory and computational resources of each component in a heterogeneous system. This is achieved by keeping limitations and bottlenecks of the systems in mind when designing machine learning algorithms. It requires a thorough understanding of the mathematics of the optimization techniques, as well as the bottlenecks of modern heterogeneous systems, in order to find a good balance between theoretical optimality and hardware efficiency. 
Building on my expertise in developing hardware-efficient training routines for generalized linear models, I would like to investigate how these ideas can be transferred to non-convex problems and, in particular, to the training of deep neural networks. This includes a) developing variations of popular learning methods that can take advantage of parallel compute architectures without compromising convergence, b) exploring adaptive data selection strategies in the context of training on limited-memory accelerators, and c) developing communication-efficient frameworks for distributed training on large data sets across multiple compute nodes in a cluster.

This research effort is expected to result in novel, theoretically sound routines for training neural networks that enable effective utilization of available compute, memory and network resources of modern heterogeneous systems.
Keywords: distributed learning, distributed systems, machine learning algorithms, optimization, supervised learning, system-awareness

Title: Directed Evolution by Codon Reassignment (DECodR)
Abstract:
Directed evolution is a powerful tool for engineering proteins for improved function. However, most directed evolution workflows require the creation of large DNA libraries, oversampling of individual variants of unknown identity, and extensive sequencing to determine structure-function relationships. These requirements make development cycles for optimized enzymes long, expensive, and opaque. 
In this research program, we propose a novel method for directed evolution that accelerates the design-build-test-learn cycles. Following development of this method, we propose integrating this approach with automation and machine learning to create an advanced workflow that could be implemented by an autonomous laboratory.
We anticipate that this work will contribute to protein engineering, the study of sequence-function relationships, and computational protein research.

Title: A-Test Autonomic Software Testing
Abstract:
In this project we address the problem of software failures that emerge in production.  We define, develop and validate a holistic approach to automatically generate test cases for exercising software systems with scenarios from production, and revealing bugs that emerge in production, before they cause system failures.   

Software failures in production environments, that is, when the software system runs in the field, are unavoidable, and may have severe consequences. Testing software in testbed environments, before deploying the software in the field, cannot reveal all failures, due to both the combinatorial explosion of execution scenarios and execution conditions that emerge only in production.  Field testing approaches test software systems with data from the field to reveal failures that escape testing in testbed: Ex-vivo testing approaches deal with applications that process data difficult to build artificially; In-vivo approaches exploit pre-designed test cases in the field. Field testing approaches address only few classes of failures that emerge in production, while missing many relevant cases. Machine learning and autonomous system testing addresses the specific issues of testing the behavior of machine learning and autonomous systems.
They deal with built-in learning and adaptive behavior, not with failures that emerge in production.  

In this project, we address the problem of efficiently and effectively revealing general failures that emerge in production: We define an efficient approach to test scenarios that emerge in production by 

1.- generating test templates and general oracles from widely accessible information (code structure, natural language comments, execution traces, reviews, legacy test suites), to capture the relevant information for testing the target system,  

2.- triggering scenarios that emerge in production and have not been fully tested yet, to frame scenarios that may nurse emerging bugs, 

3.- instantiating test templates with the identified conditions, to generate production test cases, 

4.- executing production test cases with sandboxes and digital twins, to reveal emerging bugs, 

5.- generating test suites from the test templates, to minimize the overall effort for software testing.

We exploit

1.- semantic parsing to generate prefixes for test templates from source code and execution traces,

2.- sequence-to-sequence learning to generate general assertions for test oracles from natural language comments and contextual information,

3.- genetic programming to improve test oracles,

4.- deep learning to classify emerging scenarios and trigger new test cases from monitored execution states and traces,  

5.- code generation and software engineering to instantiate and execute test cases from test templates and triggers.  

We validate the approach on retail, autonomous traffic, and learning management systems on both synthetic and real production scenarios, to demonstrate the general applicability and the maturity of the approach to test large software systems in production.

This project impacts both research and production.  It impacts research in software engineering with 

1.- approaches to automatically generate test cases,  
2.- approaches to automatically generate general test oracles, 
3.- methodologies to test software systems for field failures, 
4.- homogeneous environments for seamlessly testing software systems from testbed to production.

It impact on production of software systems with an approach to reduce field failures, recognized as one of the main costs of software systems.
Keywords: automatic generation of test cases, automatic generation of test oracles, deep learning for software testing, field testing, software engineering, software testing, test oracles, testing in production

Title: Managing Artificial-Intelligence-Augmented Decision Making in Organizations: Designing, Adopting and Evaluating
Abstract:
Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based predictions are increasingly being used to augment and automate various managerial decisions within and across organizations. AI technologies possess the ability to (semi)- autonomously acquire new skills and knowledge in performing intelligent and human-like cognitive tasks. In combination with human judgement and decision making, AI’s capacity in mining complex patterns and generating highly accurate predictions from data is expected to improve organizational decision quality, increase decision-making speed, reduce coordination costs and free up managerial attention. As organizations rapidly moved their daily operations online in the face of COVID-19, the generated digital data and the culture of hybrid work has further invigorated the use of new and existing AI technologies. 

Unlike the technologies of the past, contemporary AI is characterized by a fast evolving and complex frontier of emerging capabilities, which includes facial recognition, natural language processing, virtual agents and so on. As a result, on the one hand, AI provides organizations with unprecedented opportunities in enhancing decision making. On the other hand, these opportunities are also accompanied by a host of thorny challenges. Managers are required to oversee all key decisions related to AI in organizations, such as design, development and implementation of AI; allocating resources for its adoption; and governing its use. Furthermore, adoption of AI also introduces a variety of transformations, such as new forms of collecting and processing information, dividing and assigning tasks, and processes for coordinating and decision making. Such transformations can result in individual and collective opposition and thus need to be carefully managed. Decisions, processes and routines within organizations that leverage AI-based predictions also need to be meticulously evaluated and monitored to avoid negative consequences related to unfairness, accountability, trust, privacy and security. As a result, the diffusion of AI into organizations and the transformative changes that it induces require today’s manager to cautiously juggle between the possibilities, changes and challenges of AI. Answers to questions such as how to design effective structures for combining human and AI decisions, how to overcome barriers to adoption of AI in organizations and how to evaluate and monitor the adopted AI for social and economic hazards are critical to inform managers in their renewed roles in the age of AI. In this project, we aim to theoretically and empirically examine these questions and expand our current understanding of management of AI. In doing so, our project aims to contribute to the literatures on management and information systems. 

We will conduct our empirical investigation in both large and small firms, as well as on online platforms (e.g., Uber, Amazon Mechanical Turk, WeWork). Investigating both large and small firms provides contrasting insights on how firm size and culture influence the management of AI. Furthermore, extensive archival records on gig-economy platforms provide transparent and time-stamped data to investigate AI use in automating problems of organizing (such as division of labor and integration of efforts). In order to get the best out of our rich datasets and research contexts, in our projects, we will employ a combination of inductive and deductive and quantitative and qualitative methods, including statistical analysis, qualitative analysis, machine learning, structural equation modeling, and so on. Data collection and preliminary analysis of work packages 1 and 3 has already begun. We aim to begin more extensive data analysis and collection of complementary datasets in April 2023. The research activities of this project will be carried out through the newly formed Laboratory of Artificial Intelligence in Management at the Faculty of Business and Economics (HEC), University of Lausanne.
Keywords: artificial intelligence, management, organization design, organization science

Title: Self-Improving Collaborative Segmentation Platform for Magnetic Resonance Images
Abstract:
Muscular dystrophies and in general neuromuscular diseases are serious illnesses that mostly affect children at a young age, often with fatal outcomes. The development of effective therapies has also been challenging because of the lack of objective biomarkers for the evaluation of the natural course of the disease and the efficacy of the therapy. While MR imaging is a good candidate to provide such biomarkers, an accurate segmentation of the single muscle groups is an important step for the correct image analysis and evaluation.
The segmentation of medical images is a task that has been optimally tackled by deep learning methods in the recent years. However, the accuracy of a deep learning model heavily depends on the type, the quantity and the quality of the data used for the training, and the relative rarity of these diseases often prevents a single site or clinic from having sufficient data for the task, and often from even having the appropriate software tools for an accurate and effective segmentation.
In this project, I propose to develop a collaborative segmentation platform that would be accessible to users around the globe, who can use it as a tool to segment their own images, and by doing so, they would contribute to the improvement of the accuracy of the platform itself. Thanks to the principles of federated and incremental learning, the users would not need to share their data, thus preserving privacy and anonymity. The platform will be developed in a modular way, in order to be extensible to multiple clinical questions and input image modalities and contrasts.
Keywords: Deep Learning, Federated Learning, Muscle MRI, Segmentation

Title: Structure-Based Analysis of TCR and Antibody Repertoires: Advancing Epitope Prediction through Physico-Chemical Insights
Abstract:
Cellular immunotherapy is a rapidly growing field, as shown by the FDA approval of Tumor Infiltrating Limphocyte – Adoptive Cell Therapy for melanoma. To address the variability of polyclonal TIL expansion, T-cell receptor (TCR)-based therapy is gaining traction, as demonstrated by the recent FDA approval of MAGE-A4 therapy. However, finding clinically relevant TCRs for specific tumors remains challenging. Our lab developed TCRpcDist, a structure-based algorithm that calculates TCR physico-chemical distances, demonstrating high efficacy in identifying antigen specificities of orphan tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes in cancer patients. By integrating TCRpcDist with our Tumor Reactive Predictor and koff level predictor, we have identified TCRs for personalized therapy. Noting structural similarities between antibodies and TCRs, we propose adapting TCRpcDist to develop AbpcDist (Antibody Physico-Chemical Distances) using metrics related to key Ab residues for specificity prediction, which is crucial for immunotherapy development for instance to identify Ab for Chimeric Antigen Receptor therapies. The AbpcDist approach will be trained using  databases of known Ab specificities and Ab structures, and in-house experimental data. This method is entirely novel and has not been explored by any other academic group or biotech company.
We hypothesize that TCRpcDist can be significantly improved using recent deep-learning advancements in TCR structural prediction and newly published data. Integrating the updated TCRpcDist with methods like our in-house TCRfp and TCRdist3 in a consensus manner will enhance TCR clustering and deorphanization. We also hypothesize that TCRpcDist can be adapted for antibody clustering and deorphanization. This ambitious program follows six aims. In aim 1, we will retrieve experimental 3D structures and sequence pairs of TCR:pMHC and Ab:antigen complexes from public databases. These will be curated and analyzed to support prediction models. In aim 2, we will enhance the TCRpcDist approach for TCR clustering and deorphanization by incorporating deep learning-based TCR structure predictions, new solvent accessibility thresholds and scoring weights. This will help predict peptide epitopes and associated MHCs, with validation carried out using data from Aim 1 and Aim 4. In aim 3, we will work on improving the predictive ability, interpretability, and robustness of our model to predict the level of avidity of TCRs using structural insights and A. Harari’s data. In aim 4, Prof. Harari will generate experimental data to validate TCR clustering, prospective deorphanization (peptide prediction) and MHC prediction, as well as refinements to the koff model. In aim 5, we will develop and optimize AbpcDist, to cluster Ab based on their physico-chemical similarities and predict binding specificity. We will refine the model using public 3D structures and structural models, and validate against new experimental data obtained in Aim 6. In Aim 6, Dr. Dunn will use proprietary phage display approaches to generate binder panels of scFvs that recognize a model set of up to 10 protein antigens. Epitope predictions emerging from AbpcDist will be validated experimentally for selected scFv/antigen pairs using our expertise in directed mutagenesis and domain swapping/truncation screening techniques.
The project's feasibility is supported by strong preliminary results and the applicant's expertise in bioinformatics, biophysics, protein interactions, and machine learning. A. Harari and S. Dunn at CHUV will supply experimental data for training and validating predictions. Unlike traditional machine learning, our universal and interpretable method does not need retraining for specific antigens, ensuring broad applicability. Algorithms will be open access.
The project outcomes will offer new insights into TCR and Ab responses, aiding the development of novel clinical strategies for treating and monitoring cancer and other diseases.

Title: ASTERIx: Automatic System TEsting of inteRactive software applIcations
Abstract:
In this project, we will investigate the problem of testing interactive software applications.  We  will define and develop a holistic approach to automatically test such applications, and  reveal and remove both unavoidable and emerging bugs, to reduce the impact of software failures.

Interactive applications are software systems that provide services to people who dialog with the applications through different kinds of interfaces.  They are deployed as concurrent desktop and distributed web and mobile applications, which interact with people through graphical user interfaces (GUIs) and wearable devices.  They are popular in many domains, including retail, education, management, finance, entertainment.  Interactive applications are commonly designed as concurrent systems that combine shared memory, message passing and event-driven paradigms.  Failures of interactive applications are unavoidable due to the combination of many factors: the complexity of the testing process, the limitation of the current testing practices, the presence of concurrent failures that manifest non-deterministically, the heterogeneity of interactions with people and environment, and the presence of execution conditions that emerge in the field and are impossible to reproduce and test before deployment. Failures may severely impact the business value of the applications, and may lead to consistent economic loss.

State-of-the-art testing practices do not address all the challenges of preventing failures of interactive applications: 
(i) approaches for testing interactive applications sample the execution space mostly referring to the structure of the interface, largely ignoring the application semantics, and the problem of testing concurrent messages and events exchanged with wearable devices has been only marginally studied so far,
(ii) most approaches for testing concurrent systems target shared memory systems, and only few approaches consider the concurrency issues that derive from message passing and event driven paradigms, which commonly used in interactive systems,
(iii) cost-effective test oracles catch mostly system crashed and regression failures, missing many relevant semantically related problems, 
(iv) testing approaches work before deployment, and hardly deal with problems that emerge at runtime.

In this project we will define and develop an effective and coherent approach for testing interactive  applications, by addressing four main open issues that hinder the automatic testing of such applications: 
- System Testing:Generating system test cases that exercise interactive systems by interacting with the applications through GUIs, mobiles and wearable devices.  We will consider both semantically related aspects of user interactions and concurrency scenarios that emerge from event driven interactions.   We will investigate dynamic model inference techniques for generating system test cases from implicitly available knowledge, and probabilistic analysis and machine learning techniques to learn from system execution, and test the effects of imprecise and noisy data from wearable devices.
- Concurrency testing: Generating test cases and event interleavings for message passing and event driven concurrent systems. We will define current testing techniques that address concurrency failures for message passing and event driven systems, and that generate test cases and event interleavings to exercise the interplay among different concurrency paradigms.
- Test oracles: Generating semantically relevant oracles. We will define techniques to generate test oracles from information provided as natural language and semi-structured comments and annotations, by exploiting natural language processing, and from knowledge that becomes incrementally available when executing the application, by exploiting dynamic model inference and analysis.
- Field Testing: Generating system test cases for field testing.  We will define approaches that dynamically analyse information from field execution to identify emerging execution condition and unpredictable environment interactions, and generate test cases to be executed online for verifying the new execution conditions.

We will study and evaluate the approaches in an integrated and coherent framework for automatic testing of interactive applications.
Keywords: GUI testing, software engineering, software testing, test oracles, testing concurrent software systems, testing in-the-field

Title: pNEUMA: On the new era of urban traffic models with massive empirical data from aerial footage
Abstract:
pNEUMA intends to revolutionize how emerging technologies reshape our understanding of traffic congestion mechanisms, by putting the emphasis on urban networks with disturbances generated by interactions among different types of vehicles. The project targets to better explain the mechanism of congestion formation and propagation in congested multimodal urban environments through massive data from aerial footage and fundamental research prospective. The breakthrough interconnection between local disturbances and their scaling to network effects will enable to develop the new era of urban multimodal traffic models. Our focus will be on disturbances related to lane changes, stops related to pick up and drop off of passengers and cruising for parking. While lane-changes have been extensively studied for freeways, their relation with stop-and-go effects in congested arterials is unexplored, especially when complex multimodal interactions with heterogeneous drivers are considered. Service-related stops of all relevant modes (taxis, buses, delivery vehicles) create static and moving bottlenecks of different magnitude that are associated with long lane-changing phenomena. With respect to cruising for parking, empirical evidence is limited as the physical mechanism of the problem requires data that are spatially far and difficult to obtain.
The realization of the data opportunities requires going beyond the existing simulation-based approaches of modeling congestion with complex models of many parameters that make their validation questionable. We follow an empirical approach to understand these mechanisms. First, we design one-of-a-kind experiment that allows the collection of massive trajectory data with aerial footage from a swarm of drones that was prohibitive before in such large scale. These experiments will monitor accurately almost every single vehicle (moving or parked) that is visible from the skies in the central business district of Athens and their direct interactions with the micro-environment. The size and design of the experiments allows to follow more than half a million vehicles for a 2km2 area for multiple peak periods over a week. Second, based on this massive aerial footage, we will identify hundreds of thousands of local disturbances that occur during the peak hours. 
Third, we will see the interactions of these events with the local environment (other vehicles in the proximity). These interactions among vehicles of different types and the magnitude of the phenomena will allow for determining the spatiotemporal settings that treat the congestion formation and propagation.  Fourth, we will investigate when these local disturbances emerge to critical conditions that create network effects and influence the performance of the network. At the network level, the relationship between traffic congestion and emissions of greenhouse gases, which are associated with global climate change will investigated for the first time in such scale with empirical data. To achieve all these milestones, interdisciplinarity is the backbone of pNEUMA, as it integrates vital inputs from design of experiments, traffic science, network science and machine learning. pNEUMA is a transformative project, as it targets to redefine how we understand and explain complex traffic phenomena responsible for a significant amount of congestion. pNEUMA will develop data that can offer immense opportunities for answering additional research questions that are beyond our interests and expertise. Thus, an open science initiative will create a unique observatory of traffic congestion that researchers around the globe can use to develop and test their own models.
Keywords: cruising for parking, network models, swarm of drones, traffic congestion

Title: Neural Correlates of Dreaming
Abstract:
THE NEURAL CORRELATES OF DREAMING

Background
Dreaming is a particular form of consciousness that occurs during sleep. Studying mental experiences during sleep thus offers a unique opportunity to explain how changes in brain activity relate to changes in consciousness. One unresolved question in this respect is whether dreams are generated in a ‘bottom-up’ manner (starting from activity in low-level sensory brain areas, which is then interpreted and synthesized by higher-order areas, like in perception) or in a ‘top-down’ way (beginning as wishes, abstract thoughts and memories, which are then enriched with perceptual and sensory aspects, as in imagination). 

Aims 
The present project aims at determining how conscious experiences in sleep relate to underlying electroencephalographic activity and if machine-learning techniques can reliably predict periods of dreaming and non-dreaming. It also assesses whether the predominant signal flow in response to transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) during rapid eye movement sleep (REM sleep), when mental experiences are particularly vivid and frequent, follows a ‘top-down’ or a ‘bottom-up’ propagation.

Methods
Experiment 1: high-density electroencephalography (hd-EEG) recordings (256 electrodes) are performed in healthy participants during night sleep in the laboratory. Participants are awakened in pseudorandom intervals and are asked about the presence and content of mental activity. The EEG signal in the two minutes prior to the awakening is analyzed in terms of spontaneous power changes and with machine learning paradigms.

Experiment 2: healthy volunteers participate in a wake session during the day and a sleep session during the night, equipped with TMS-compatible hd-EEG (60 electrodes). TMS is sequentially applied to the left prefrontal Brodmann area 6 and the left occipital Brodmann area 19. After each TMS-session during sleep, subjects are questioned about the presence of conscious experiences. TMS-evoked EEG responses between the prefrontal and occipital areas in REM sleep and wakefulness are compared. 

Importance of the project
This study investigates whether EEG patterns or TMS-evoked activity can predict dreaming. If, as preliminary results suggest, it is possible to determine, in real time, whether a person is dreaming, and also to predict broad categories of dream content, this will open new perspectives in dream research. Changes in dream content form the core feature of many sleep and psychiatric disorders and share features with hallucinations and delirium that represent hallmarks of psychosis. Determining neural correlates of dreaming might thus ultimately open new approaches to the understanding and treatment of these diseases.
Keywords: consciousness, dreams, high density EEG, sleep, transcranial magnetic stimulation

Title: Optimal design and control of compliant surfaces for aquatic locomotion
Abstract:
Natural swimmers often rely on soft, compliant surfaces, allowing them to exploit physical mechanisms such as geometry-induced rigidity, resonance, and damping to achieve stunning speed, efficiency and agility. The cost of this design choice is the complexity of design and actuation required to utilize these additional degrees of freedom. In natural swimmers, this cost has been amortized over millions of years, and evolutionary drive has equipped current swimmers with sophisticated design and control mechanisms.

Most man-made devices instead employ rigid surfaces, and our understanding of the fabrication, design, and control of compliant materials is limited. In recent years, however, the development of soft materials has accelerated, and the corresponding increase in scientific effort holds promise for applications ranging from robotics to renewable energy harvesting. However, a detailed, quantitative understanding of the optimal material properties and actuation strategies for such applications is still lacking. Where nature has had a head-start of many millions of years, we have to play catch-up using modeling and computation.

During my PhD work at ETH Zurich I successfully developed and used accurate, large-scale 3D flow solvers, whereas during my postdoc at Harvard University I have created a software for high-fidelity non-linear elasticity simulations of plates and shells with arbitrary shape, inhomogeneity and anisotropic material response. Throughout both of these phases I have extensively combined such numerical simulation frameworks with reverse-engineering algorithms to find solutions for inverse problems of both design and control.

In this project I propose to combine both numerical techniques into a fluid-structure interaction solver and couple it to evolutionary optimization and machine learning techniques to create a fully integrated inverse-design framework. Using only the solver, we will first systematically investigate the effect of flexural stiffness and actuation of the caudal fin on the performance of rainbow trout, a species within the class of ray-finned fishes. Subsequently we will employ the full framework to inverse-design material properties and control strategies for a polyclad flatworm, a small invertebrate that despite its extremely simple biological design successfully swims by exciting large-deformation waves over its surface. This flatworm is therefore a prime candidate to investigate the design and actuation of compliant surfaces in aquatic locomotion, and through its study I aim to provide qualitative insights and quantitative results that directly impact the performance of engineering devices.
Keywords: actuation, control, deforming, elasticity, fluid dynamics, fluid-structure interaction, learning, optimal, swimming

Title: Out of the Ivory Tower. Providing the Public with Daily Forecast Updates on the State of the Economy in Europe
Abstract: We deliver macroeconomic short-term forecasts on a daily basis to the public. We employ a large amount of data and on a set of different forecasting models in order to generate, each night, nowcast and one-step ahead forecast updates for quarterly GDP growth for several European countries. We then present the continuous flow of now-/forecasts in charts and graphs on an interactive website, accompanied by various meta-information. Our contribution is to provide the public with fast and direct access to information that is often accessible with considerable delay only or not publically accessible at all.

Title: Modelling the Distribution of Atmospheric Water Vapor and Monitoring and Quantifying Atmospheric Rivers using GNSS Radio Occultation
Abstract:
Improving weather forecasts and reducing climate uncertainty are priority research topics. These themes are also a focus in the Decadal Survey done by US leading research institutions. This proposal aims at contributing to these challenges by improving the modeling of water vapor (WV) and the planetary boundary layer (PBL) height using satellite observations. Furthermore, it has the goal of significantly improving the spatio-temporal resolution of atmospheric rivers (ARs) using machine learning (ML) and a combination of complementary datasets. The main technique used is GNSS radio occultation (RO), but we will also exploit datasets of passive sounders and ground-based (GB) GNSS.

RO is very attractive to meteorologists and climatologists because of its long-term stability, high vertical resolution, all-weather capability, global coverage and remarkable absolute accuracy. Furthermore, it is highly complementary to infrared and microwave sounders. With about 20 years of collected measurements, RO can now be used effectively for climate studies. One drawback of RO is, however, that its sampling density is highly non-uniform and too sparse to resolve synoptic variability in the atmosphere. This research aims at using ML to construct RO climatologies (gridded maps of RO products) and detect finer atmospheric structures. The application of ML to map RO data is motivated by the capability of ML to learn from large dataset. Indeed, in previous research, we have demonstrated a proof-of-concept showing the feasibility of ML to map RO data. Our first objective is to build a pipeline to construct continuous (~ 20 years) RO climatologies that will be utilized to study the spatio-temporal behavior of WV. In addition, RO climatologies will be validated with radiometer data.

Furthermore, ML-based RO climatologies will be evaluated with the purpose of detecting and monitoring ARs. ARs are long and narrow bands that transport water outside the tropics and can carry an amount of water comparable to the average water flow at the mouth of the Mississippi river. When they reach landfall, they can lead to (heavy) precipitation. RO, due to its coverage (over land and sea), is a promising method to sense such structures. The large amount of WV in ARs is also reflected in observations of GB GNSS. These data are important when ARs reach continental areas. In this research we aim to exploit GB and RO observations simultaneously to resolve the AR structures.

Moreover, the high-vertical resolution of RO observations has been exploited to model the height of the planetary boundary layer (PBL). The PBL height can be used to characterize much of the diurnal, synoptic, and climatological processes associated with the PBL in a given region (such as cloud characterization,). Similarly to RO climatologies of refractivity (or WV) mapped with ML, we will map PBL heights from RO (and other observations such as microwave sounders). We will create continuous PBL height climatologies, and evaluate them with other PBL height climatologies, such as those from Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) models.

The results of this research will be interpreted with the help of atmospheric scientists working at the host institute. The goal is to use the output to improve the understanding of atmospheric processes related to water vapor or ARs.
