Title: Predictive Modeling of  cART Medication Adherence and Immuno-virologic outcomes among HIV infected Adults in Lausanne, Switzerland
Abstract:
Advancements in human immunodeficiency tritherapy have allowed patients on treatment to achieve a life expectancy similar to those without the disease. To achieve therapeutic goals, it is important to adhere to treatment regimen. 
The monitoring of adherence can be done using several methods such as patient reports, pill count and electronic monitoring. Electronic monitoring allows daily monitoring of medication taking through the use of electronic pill boxes (Medication event monitoring systems, MEMS) that store the time and day of opening. This method is used routinely in care at the pharmacy of the Policlinique Medicale Universitaire since 2004. Currently there is medication adherence data for about 500 patients followed at the adherence programme. 
Few studies have described the erosion of medication adherence over time, but more research is needed to identify the early critical indicators of initial nonadherence signs in HIV. To be able to investigate the effect of medication nonadherence on immune-virologic outcomes, we would like to conduct a predictive modeling analysis of the adherence and clinical data collected retrospectively at our institute in Lausanne. 
The medication adherence data in Lausanne is very unique as it comprises daily medication intake and interview transcripts with patients about the barriers and facilitators to adherence collected routinely in care of a long period of time (12 years). This predictive modeling will be done using state of the art prediction algorithms combining Big Data Science, statistical modeling, behavioral psychology, clinical and adherence sciences. The the University of California Institute for Prediction Technology (UCIPT) has developed a lot of novel methods for big data science analysis and this joint project will combine unique patient data from the adherence clinic in Lausanne with state of the art predictive machine learning methodology at UCIPT.
The analysis of this data can provide unprecedented insights into patient behavior regarding dealing with chronic medication in general, and their struggle to deal with HIV. Consequently, tailored interventions can be developed to prevent nonadherence that can lead to viral failure, and mortality.
Keywords: HIV, Medication Adherence, Medication Event Monitoring System (MEMS), RNA, Viral/blood

Title: Learning context-aware, interpretable representations of the tumor microenvironment to enable AI-driven precision oncology
Abstract:
An overwhelming amount of evidence in the past decade has made clear that tumors are complex ecosystems, where cancer cells coexist and dynamically interact with other cell types of the tumor microenvironment (TME). Several spatial mechanisms within this complex ecosystem contribute to disease progression or treatment response. As a result, several treatments that target TME components have been developed (e.g., immunotherapy, antiangiogenic drugs). To fully understand variability in patient responses and design precise treatments, we need a deeper understanding of the complex interplay between the major TME mechanisms, and how they affect disease and treatment response.

Recently, single-cell and spatial profiling technologies have enabled the measurement of molecular profiles in individual cells, offering an unprecedented opportunity to capture cellular organization within the TME. The wealth of data generated by spatial omics assays is fueling the development of custom artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) models, showing great promise in several tasks in spatial omics data analysis.

However, three challenges limit the breakthrough nature of these developments. Challenge 1: current approaches are based on cell segmentation and mask crucial aspects of a cell’s identity, including its spatial context, molecular features, and morphology. Challenge 2: existing methods ignore the fact that TME mechanisms (e.g., immune infiltration and evasion, signaling molecule exchange, local tissue remodeling) occur across length scales. Challenge 3: existing AI methods to analyze the TME lack interpretability, which limits their ability to uncover new insights on the underlying mechanisms within the TME. 

Advances in AI and in particular self-supervised learning (SSL) and explainability techniques present a tremendous opportunity to overcome these challenges by learning meaningful context-aware representations directly from spatial omics data without the need for segmentation or annotations. Although SSL models have already shown promising results in various histopathology tasks, applying these models to spatial omics has not been pursued so far, and requires the development of custom architectures.

Inspired by the above, the project Learning context-aware, interpretable representations of the tumor microenvironment to enable AI-driven precision oncology proposes the following three interconnected aims that address these challenges.

Aim 1: Generating unified cellular representations from spatial omics. We will leverage vision transformers and self-supervised learning to generate multimodal, unified representations that jointly capture cell morphology, molecular profile, and spatial context.

Aim 2: Generating multi-scale TME representations. We will extend these representations in a multi-scale, hierarchical fashion so that they capture TME mechanisms that occur across length scales.

Aim 3: Discovery of prognostic and predictive spatial biomarkers. We will develop a novel interpretable Graph AI framework that will be trained to predict clinical endpoints, identifying spatial biomarkers of clinical importance. Our goal is to detect clinically relevant patterns of interaction between cancer cells, the surrounding stroma, and infiltrating immune cells, which contribute to aggressive behavior or disease recurrence. 

This proposal is devised as a conceptual leap forward in cancer research that addresses major medical and scientific challenges. In the short term, it will deliver a large collection of breakthrough AI technologies and elucidate novel mechanisms of diagnostic, prognostic and therapeutic significance. The overarching goal of this proposal is to reconcile the stochastic underpinnings of the TME with the existence of robustly reoccurring patterns and thus deconvolve the complexity of the TME into interpretable and clinically actionable findings, paving the way for AI-driven personalized therapy approaches.

Title: Environmental Effects on Molecular Spectroscopy and Reaction   Dynamics: From the Gas-Phase to Droplets and Bulk Water
Abstract:
The overarching goal of this project is to develop, implement and
apply computational strategies to quantitatively characterize,
understand and eventually predict observables and properties of
complex chemical systems in the gas-phase, in and on water droplets
and in bulk water and to interpret them at a molecular level. To this
end, a) techniques based on kernel methods combined with neural
networks (KerNN) and b) kernel-based off-site charge models will be
developed, implemented, validated and used. The spectroscopy,
vibrational and reaction dynamics of tri-, tetra- and polyatomic
systems relevant to processes in the atmosphere and in interstellar
chemistry will be investigated depending on the organization of the
hydration environment: droplet, amorphous solid water, or bulk,
compared with the gas phase. It is of primary interest to
quantitatively characterize whether and - if so - how the particular
water environment leads to changes in the spectroscopy and reaction
dynamics. The systems considered include OClO, HOCO, HONO, the two
smallest Criegee intermediates (CH2OO and CH3CHOO), and
glyoxal. For all molecules, full-dimensional, reactive PESs at high
levels of theory (MRCI+Q or CASPT2 for systems that require multi
reference treatments and MP2 and/or CCSD(T) for single-reference
problems) with triple-zeta basis sets will be used together with
machine-learned representations for the intramolecular PESs. The water
environment will be represented by a CCSD(T)-quality reproducing
kernel for the bonded interactions and a new kernel-based minimally
distributed charge model (MDCM) that correctly describes
intramolecular polarization, i.e. changes of the molecular
electrostatic potential with molecular geometry. Transformative
aspects of the proposed research are the development and application
of generic, scalable, and rationally improvable computational
strategies for quantitative simulations combined based on CCSD(T) (or
CASPT2/MRCI+Q) quality reference data with results from high-quality
experiments to arrive at a comprehensive molecular-level understanding
of the spectroscopy and reaction dynamics of chemical systems in the
gas-phase, in and on water droplets and in bulk water.

Title: Spline methods for the continuous/discrete processing of images
Abstract:
Our aim is to develop a comprehensive framework to address a whole class of problems that are usually formulated in the continuous domain, but call for a digital implementation. Our practical focus is on image processing while the theoretical context is provided by splines. This project started in 1998 and its scope has kept on broadening and becoming more mathematical as more fundamental aspects of splines (in relation to differential equations, wavelets, linear systems, estimation and regularization theory, and stochastic processes) are being uncovered.

The specific spline-related research topics that will be investigated during this term are:

A. Splines and operators: Beyond the theory of RKHS. Splines can be specified as solutions of variational problems with a quadratic regularization that involves a suitable differential operator L and a native space that is a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). We shall generalize the concept by switching to generalized total-variation (gTV) regularization and by enlarging the class of admissible L through the consideration of operators that are not necessarily shift-invariant. The critical point will be to specify the corresponding native space under the constraint of universality (i.e., the ability to represent any continuous function with an arbitrary degree of precision). We are aiming at an extended Banach-space framework that encompasses RKHS but supports the use of more general kernel-type expansions where the kernels are not necessarily positive-definite nor located on the data points.

B. Multi-splines: Cardinal splines are representable using basis functions  that are shifted replicates of a single generator. The extension that we propose in this grant is to consider multiple generators. First, we shall study multi-splines that are direct sums of conventional splines. The challenge there is to construct the shortest basis functions. This will help us to specify a multi-spline calculus for signal processing and develop generalized-sampling techniques. In particular, we shall investigate the use of Hermite-splines for image processing. Second, we shall consider multi-component splines to let us extend the classical techniques to the vectorial setting. The investigated topics will include the construction of vector-valued B-splines, the solution of variational vector-valued problems, and the connection with vector-valued stochastic processes. 

C. Splines and machine learning: The intimate link between splines and RKHS connects them to kernel methods in supervised learning. Our intent is to draw similar connections with deep learning via the introduction of suitable forms of gTV regularization. We shall consider the problem of the optimization of individual activation functions in a deep neural network. We shall investigate the properties of deep-spline architectures where the activation functions are adaptive splines and propose effective training schemes. We shall derive representer theorems, including vector-valued generalizations, for sparsity-promoting  regularization functionals.

D. Splines and inverse problems: We have shown recently that any linear inverse problem with gTV regularization admits a global solution that is a nonuniform spline whose type is matched to the regularization operator. The difficulty is that the underlying spline is adaptive, meaning that the determination of the location of its knots is also part of the optimization problem. Our aim is to develop efficient numerical schemes for finding the continuous-domain solutions of such problems with an arbitrary degree of precision. We shall also consider an extended formulation that involves multiple regularization operators. The methods will be applied to the deconvolution of signals and to the reconstruction of magnetic-resonance images.

E. Splines and stochastic processes: We shall characterize the complete (non-Gaussian) family of self-similar processes as solutions of stochastic differential equations that involve derivatives of complex order. We shall exploit the connection between splines and sparse stochastic processes to develop new ways of generating non-Gaussian processes. Finally, we shall propose an extended functional framework for the MMSE reconstruction of  (not necessarily stationary) Gaussian processes from linear measurements, which we postulate to yield a kind of ``generalized'' splines.

This research should produce: (1) a theoretical impact in the fields of image processing and applied mathematics, due to the novelty and unifying character of the formulation; (2) a practical impact through efficient algorithms and novel computational solutions. The developments in B and D are motivated by concrete problems in bioimaging. The end product will be open-source software that will be made freely available to the biomedical research community.
Keywords: Image processing, Splines, approximation theory, interpolation, inverse problems, machine learning, regularization, sparsity, stochastic processes

Title: Foundations of Market User Interface Design and Applications to the Smart Grid
Abstract:
In the next decade, we will encounter an abundance of new electronic markets in our lives. This has manifold advantages, as market-based systems are often able to allocate resources more efficiently than non-market based systems. Consider, for example, the use of dynamic toll roads, the use of dynamically priced energy, or the many ways in which we can consume content for small amounts of money on the Internet.

In recent years, economists and computer scientists have significantly advanced our understanding of the design of such market-based systems, giving rise to a new field called "market design." This new research area captures many different markets, ranging from matching markets (e.g., school choice problem, hospital-doctor matching, etc.), over combinatorial spectrum auctions, to the design of sponsored search auctions. One common, yet debatable feature of the large majority of the work in this field, is the assumption that the players in these markets are perfectly rational agents. In practice, however, users have cognitive costs, cognitive biases, they have limited time and bounded computational resources for deliberation, in short: "real" humans make mistakes when making decisions in market-based environments.

This research proposal addresses this discrepancy between the common economic models and the actual psychological decision-making processes. We focus, in particular, on the intersection of "market design" and "user interface design," a research area that has been largely ignored so far. We propose new methodologies to design markets user interfaces (UIs) that take users' cognitive costs into account and develop new technological tools that make up for the cognitive limitations. The same way that color-coded planes make the job of an air-traffic controller easier, it is our goal to design market UIs that make economic decision making easier and thereby improve overall social welfare.

The proposal consists of three complementary parts: First, we study the "foundations of market user interface design": how does the way we display information and what choices we offer users affect their decision-making capabilities. The PI has proposed the design of market user interfaces as a new research area in 2011, and we propose the following three new contributions: 1) the development of a behavioral user model to accurately predict user behavior in complex market environments and the identification of the main market UI design levers that we can tweak to optimize market UIs; 2) new methods to automatically design personalized market UIs based on users' cognitive skills; and 3) a collaborative-filtering method to design personalized market UIs based on the information available in a large group of market users.

In the second part of the project we study how to design "smart market UIs for the smart grid." A key element of this part is the design of new learning, planning, and control algorithms to automate the interaction between the smart grid and the user. We propose the following four contributions: 1) the design of semi-automated market UIs involving active/online learning; 2) the design of forward-looking market UIs for the smart grid that take into account predictable changes in the market price as well as endogenous changes in the environment; 3) the design of smart grid UIs for dynamic environments that automatically adapt to changes in exogenous factors; and 4) the design of smart grid UIs for non-stationary user preferences.

In the third part of the project we will develop prototype market UIs for the smart grid. We propose the following two contributions: 1) the development of a prototype market UI for the home heating control problem, i.e., the semi-automated control of a thermostat in a user's house; and 2) the development of a prototype market UI for the electric vehicle charging problem, i.e., a UI that can elicit a user's preferences regarding his trade-off between a fully or partially charged electric car vs. small or large cost savings.

Significance of the Research: The proposed research will lay the essential foundations of research at the intersection of market design and UI design necessary for further study of this area. We will significantly advance both the theory and practice of market UI design. We expect that our theoretical and experimental research will constitute the building blocks of future academic work on this topic. Furthermore, the techniques we develop for the smart grid market (learning, planning, and control algorithms) as well as the specific market UIs for the home heating and the electric vehicle charging problems, will have an immediate impact on research and development for the smart grid, defining the state of the art of market UI design in academic and industry.
Keywords: Active Learning, Artificial Intelligence, Behavioral Economics, Decision Making, Electronic Markets, Hidden Markets, Machine Learning, Market Design, Market User Interfaces, Preference Elicitation, Smart Grid, User Interface Design

Title: Sublinear algorithms for fundamental problems in big data analysis
Abstract:
My research focuses on the design and analysis of efficient algorithms for processing large datasets. The goal of this project is to address two important challenges in this field, as outlined by the following two objectives. 

First: In many modern data analysis tasks, collecting the input dataset is extremely expensive, making it vital to design optimal data sampling strategies. This is common in applications such as MRI acquisition, and spectrum sensing in cognitive radio networks as well as in hyperparameter tuning of machine learning models, where every data sample requires running a computationally expensive training process. These problems typically
reduce to the problem of learning an unknown function using optimal number of samples given some prior belief about its structure. By far the most common way to impose a prior on the structure of a function is through its Fourier transform. Therefore, in many scenarios, there is a crucial need for optimal sampling schemes for learning Fourier structured functions (e.g., Fourier sparsity is a commonly studied structure). There has been extensive research on this problem, however, the practical performance of all these algorithms suffers from either slow super linear runtime or suboptimal sample complexity. Moreover, some fundamental questions in this field are absolutely not well-understood. For instance, the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP) of Fourier matrices is very well understood in the discrete setting, however, no nontrivial bound is known on the sufficient number of samples for recovering all sparse functions using continuous Fourier measurements. My goal is to design practically optimal sample acquisition schemes by exploiting the Fourier structure and furthermore answer the fundamental RIP problem in the continuous regime. 

Second: In many other important data analysis settings, the sheer volume of the available datasets far outstrips our abilities to analyze them. This challenge commonly arises in tasks including parameter tuning of machine learning models (e.g., Google Vizier, a popular Google internal service for performing black-box optimization), training neural networks, and multi-armed bandit optimization. These tasks often require solving numerical linear algebraic problems on typically fully dense kernel matrices, making classical primitives prohibitively expensive. Therefore, there is a crucial need for efficient algorithms that can compress the available datasets while approximately preserving the solution space of linear
algebraic problems that one seeks to solve. Research in this context has led to many very efficient algorithms over the past decade. However, our understanding of data compression solutions for kernel-based learning tasks has remained quite limited. All existing algorithms for kernelized numerical linear algebra tend to be carefully crafted for the specific task and kernel function they aim to solve. As a result, there is no overarching kernel approximation method that works optimally for a wide class of practically important kernel problems. My goal is to develop unified tools and techniques that are applicable to a broad class of kernel approximation problems that are widely used by machine learning practitioners.
Keywords: Big Data, Fourier Analysis, Kernel Methods, Numerical Linear Algebra, Optimal Sampling, Sparse Recovery

Title: Re-assessing patterns in the history of life through artificial intelligence
Abstract:
Inferring diversification dynamics in the fossil record has been a key area of palaeontological and macroevolutionary research for the past 150 years (Phillips, 1860; Simpson, 1984; Newell, 1959; Valentine, 1969; Raup, 1972; Alroy, 2001, 2010a, 2010b; Smith & McGowan, 2011; Benson, 2021). However, the fossil record is notoriously incomplete, and methods such as rarefaction (Raup, 1972; Alroy, 2001, 2010a; Chao & Jost, 2012), richness extrapolators (Chao & Jost, 2012; Chao, 1987; Alroy, 2018, 2020), capture-mark-recapture approaches (Liow et al, 2008; Liow & Nichols, 2010) and Bayesian inference (Starrfelt & Liow, 2016; Flannery-Sutherland et al, 2022) have been used to estimate diversity patterns while accounting for temporal variation in preservation and sampling. Under these standard methods, spatial sampling variation in the fossil record still accounts for a substantial proportion of inferred changes in diversity, producing patterns that reflect the changing geographic range of the record rather than a true biological signal (Vilhena & Smith, 2013; Close et al, 2020a, 2020b). This has sparked the recent development of new approaches to address sampling incompleteness while accounting for variation in the uneven spatial distribution of fossils that can be applied at the regional scale (Alroy, 2020; Flannery-Sutherland, 2022; Antell et al, 2024; Thompson et al, 2020; Hauffe et al, 2022; Dunne et al, 2023; Cooper et al, 2024; Reitan et al, 2023; Franeck & Liow, 2019). However, methods used to estimate how diversification rates change at the global scale (Silvestro et al, 2014a, 2014b; Warnock et al, 2020) do not currently account for this spatial sampling variation, as do those designed to estimate dispersal rates (Hauffe et al, 2022), or latitudinal diversity gradients (LDGs) (Jones et al, 2021), affecting which patterns and processes we infer to drive changing diversity in charismatic groups such as the dinosaurs (Mannion, 2024).

The objective of my research is to develop a new generation of models using simulations and AI to infer more accurate diversification dynamics from the fossil record. I will use these models to answer longstanding questions in palaeontology. In particular, I propose to develop simulation-trained AI models that estimate rates of speciation, extinction and dispersal at the largest spatial scales (global and regional) while assessing potential environmental causes of diversity change and whether there is evidence of trait-mediation. I will further develop a new framework for the estimation of latitudinal diversity gradients from fossil occurrences in light of sampling biases. All software tools produced will be made available to the wider scientific community through open access online repositories, and vignettes will be provided for future users. These methodologies, once developed, will be used to assess the impact of major mass extinction events in the history of marine life (Raup & Sepkoski, 1982; Marshall, 2023), and shed new light on the diversity patterns through space and time of the exceptionally poor fossil record of dinosaurs (Mannion, 2024; Dean et al, 2020).
Keywords: biodiversity, deep learning, macroevolution, palaeobiology, palaeontology, simulations

Title: Mechano-Genomics of Cellular Ageing and Rejuvenation
Abstract:
Cellular ageing is an inevitable and natural process. As cells age, a number of epigenetic factors are altered with consequences including mitochondrial dysfunction, genomic instabilities and metabolic reprogramming. Importantly, recent studies have also highlighted that cellular ageing is accompanied with the loss of mechanical integrity of cells, including altered acto-myosin contractility, nuclear mechanotransduction and gene expression. Collectively, these factors can result in a progressive decline in various cellular organelle functions as well as loss of tissue integrity and onset of various diseases. For example, in connective tissues, fibroblasts alter their matrix deposition properties with ageing, leading to extensive remodelling of the extracellular microenvironment (ECM) that supports tissues and wound healing responses. However, the underlying epigenetic mechanisms of cellular ageing and how ageing fibroblasts can be rejuvenated for tissue regeneration is still unclear. 

My group, in recent years, has made significant contributions towards an in-depth understanding of the coupling between ECM, 3D chromatin organization, and gene expression regulating fibroblast behaviour. In particular, in recent paradigm shifting experiments, we showed for the first time that cell mechanical constraints alone, without the addition of exogenous biochemical factors, can induce partial reprogramming of fibroblasts. Importantly, the re-differentiation of these partially reprogrammed fibroblasts with appropriate matrix conditions resulted in their rejuvenation. Building on these preliminary experiments, I propose to systematically explore the mechano-genomic regulation of ageing fibroblasts and the mechanistic basis of how rejuvenation of ageing fibroblasts can be accomplished for applications in regenerative medicine through the following three aims.

Aim 1: To identify mechano-genomic regulatory modules critical to cellular rejuvenation through partial reprogramming and re-differentiation of ageing fibroblasts using gene expression analysis
Aim 2: To gain mechanistic insights into the processes regulating nuclear mechanotransduction and 3D chromosome reorganization during cellular ageing and rejuvenation
Aim 3: To implant partially reprogrammed ageing fibroblasts into ex vivo tissue models and analyse the mechano-genomic regulatory modules during tissue rejuvenation and wound healing

The proposal is based on the mechano-genomic control of cellular rejuvenation of ageing cells and is completely new to the field. In particular, the outcomes of the proposal will provide an in-depth understanding of the mechano-genomic coupling driving fibroblast ageing, reprogramming and rejuvenation. Importantly, the proposal outlines robust methodology to rejuvenate donor-specific aged fibroblasts, through non-genetic routes, for applications to skin tissue regeneration and wound healing. The proposal is highly ambitious and the success of its goals will provide novel avenues for the field of regenerative and personalized medicine.
Keywords: 3D chromosome organization, Cellular ageing, Cellular rejuvenation, Cellular reprogramming, Gene expression, Light microscopy, Machine learning, Mechanobiology, Tissue repair

Title: Pathological Speech Synthesis (PaSS)
Abstract:
Speech communication involves production of acoustics through movement of articulators (e.g., tongue, jaw) and its perception in terms of different information such as, message, speaker identity, emotional state of person. Speech synthesis systems aim to produce speech that is natural and intelligible like human speech. With the advances in deep learning, today, speech synthesis systems have the capability to match natural human speech in terms of quality. Having said that, speech synthesis research has largely focused on synthesis of typical healthy control speech (adult speech without impairments). There are an increasing number of people across the world with debilitating speech pathologies (e.g., Parkinson's, Laryngeal cancer etc) that leads to breakdown of the synergy between speech production and speech perception phenomena. This in turn leads to issues related to daily life speech communication and quality of life. Thus, there is need for building assistive technologies that can aid in providing better treatment and care, and make the affected people more socially inclusive. 

The goal of the proposed project PaSS is to develop a framework for pathological speech synthesis that is clinically valid/acceptable with the aim (a) to address pathological speech data scarcity issues for pathological speech technology development, (b) to develop tools that could potentially be used for designing care pathway for treatment of patients with speech impairments, and (c) to further our understanding of pathological speech. The proposed research is organized into two research themes (RTs), while  taking into account the challenges related to data scarcity, systematic evaluation of synthesized pathological speech and interpretability/explainability of the developed systems:

RT1 - Pathological speech synthesis with objective speech assessment in the loop. Leveraging from recent advances in few shot speech synthesis, this RT will develop a closed-loop pathological speech synthesis system that is driven by objective speech assessment and validate the developed systems by putting the clinicians in the loop

RT2 - Linking pathological speech synthesis to speech production. This RT will build upon RT1 to explain the developed pathological speech synthesis approaches in terms of physiological aspects of speech production through acoustic-to-articulatory inversion and articulatory speech synthesis models.

PaSS will develop and validate neural speech synthesis and voice conversion approaches for different pathological conditions, namely, dysarthria, Parkinson's disease (PD), and treatment of laryngeal and hypopharyngeal cancer. The research and development will build new synergies in collaboration with GITA Lab, University of Antioquia, Colombia for PD progression and monitoring and the University Cancer Center Inselspital, Bern for the research on treatment of laryngeal and hypopharyngeal cancer. The proposed R&D lies at the intersection of speech synthesis, speech assessment, machine learning (including deep learning), speech signal processing and clinical speech science. PaSS requests funding for one PhD student on full time basis and a postdoctoral researcher on 50% basis for a period of four years.
Keywords: neural speech synthesis, pathological speech processing, pathological speech synthesis, speech assessment, speech synthesis

Title: Unified Speech Processing Framework for Trustworthy Speaker Recognition (UniTS)
Abstract:
The goal of automatic speaker recognition task is to recognize persons through their voice. Automatic speaker verification is a subtest of speaker recognition task where the goal is to verify or authenticate a person. State-of-the-art speaker verification systems typically model short-term spectrum based features such as mel frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs) through a generative model such as, Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) and employ a series of compensation methods to achieve low error rates. This has two main limitations. First, the approach necessitates availability of sufficient training data for each speaker for robust modeling and sufficient test data to apply the series of compensation techniques to verify a speaker. Second,  the speaker verification system is prone to malicious attacks such as through voice conversion (VC) system, text-to-speech (TTS) system. The main reason is that the front-end feature and back-end models of speaker verification system, namely, MFCC and GMMs, are similar to that of VC system and TTS system.

The proposed project aims to address these limitations through development of novel approaches for trustworthy speaker verification. In order to achieve that, through collaboration between researchers from Speech and Audio Processing group and Biometrics group at Idiap, the proposed project focuses along two lines,

1. in on-going DeepSTD project funded by HASLER foundation, in the context of speech recognition, it was shown that speech recognition systems can be built by directly modeling raw speech signals using artificial neural networks. The proposed project aims to build on that approach to develop a generic speaker verification approach that can be used for both speaker verification and speaker diarization.

2. in a collaborative study with researchers from Univesity of Eastern Finland and Nanyang Technical University (Singapore), Idiap have developed a countermeasure approach for state-of-the-art speaker verification system. The proposed project aims to extend this approach along with development of novel anti-spoofing countermeasures using binary features and text-dependent speaker verification.
Keywords: Anti-spoofing, Biometrics, Machine learning, Speaker Recognition, Speaker verification

Title: Research and infrastructure at CECAM: Coarse-grained and multiscale molecular dynamics for active matter
Abstract:
This proposal combines the agreed periodic request for SNSF funding of the Centre Européen de Calcul Atomique et moléculaire} (CECAM)  and a proposal for research activities to be carried out at the CECAM Headquarters (HQ) in EPFL by the Director and Deputy Director of the centre. (Following the changes of the funding programs for infrastructures, the SNSF membership to CECAM is procured via application to the regular scientific calls.)

CECAM is the oldest standing European center for the promotion of basic research and leading edge applications in the area of simulation and modelling. It has fostered or directly contributed to many of the developments that have established simulations as a key component of modern research in areas ranging from materials to biological modelling, from engineering to applied mathematics, from physics to chemistry, and is instrumental in furthering the leading role played by  Switzerland and Europe in this domain. Core activities at CECAM include the organisation of scientific workshops and schools; workshops on algorithmic and software development and exploitation; brain-storming and problem solving events; the development of collaborative research projects for Europe and beyond; and the sponsorship of an international visitors programme. The cornerstone of CECAM's service to the community is its yearly flagship programme of events, selected via independent refereeing and rigorous ranking of proposals submitted  by the broad CECAM community. This bottom-up approach ensures that CECAM is in tune with the most recent topics of interest (recent examples are machine learning and quantum computing) and remains a much appreciated incubator of exciting new developments. The relevance of the center for the community was confirmed in the difficult circumstances of the pandemic via a remarkable response to our on-line activities and an exceptional level of collaboration with our team to mitigate (via postponements or migrations on-line) the effects of this global crises (see also sec. 2.1). This quick response  has strengthened CECAM  as a reference for the field and motivates us even more to constantly improve the level and novelty of the service we offer as a research infrastructure. As described in sec. 2.3, funding of this proposal will contribute to support CECAM's core activities and enable new actions. Among these:  the development of flexible formats for events (in person, on-line, hybrid); the promotion of new initiatives recommended by the recently installed CECAM steering committees in the areas of data driven sciences and High Performing Computing; collaborative projects for exascale ready software development and maintenance; development of new tools for advanced training building on a pilot MOOC course; creation, in collaboration with NCCR MARVEL and other relevant players, of a web repository for reference material  in simulation and modelling. 

In addition, funding is requested for a research programme that takes advantage of the complementary expertise of the applicants. The proposal focuses on the fundamental understanding of active matter, a class of systems that can convert chemical  energy into  motion. This fundamental understanding, with a focus on   the   properties that control the  dynamics of these systems and their collective, emergent behavior is still a challenge. The absence of a reference equilibrium state, and the competition of different physico-chemical processes acting at different scales, require the development of appropriate conceptual  and computational tools. 
As detailed by the actions presented in the two scientific workpackages in sec. 2.3, we will pursue a combined effort to develop  dynamically consistent,  coarse-grained  computational models for enzymatically-driven colloids, extending  state-of-the-art methods for the simulation of active matter. Such  models will be  amenable to a systematic analysis of the emerging  dynamic behavior in response of the different physico-chemical processes  that bring  active colloids  out-of-equilibrium. We will  develop a novel approach, based on solid preliminary work and inspired by Born-Oppenheimer molecular dynamics and a new perturbative extension, to put forward a consistent multiscale algorithm adapted to active matter. This novel approach has the potential to  overcome some of the limitations of current methods in the accuracy of the models without compromising numerical efficiency. 
This will enable systematic progress in the understanding of fundamental properties and emerging behaviour of active nano colloids and nanocolloidal suspensions, with particular focus on nano robots and biocompatible materials.
Keywords: Active Matter, Coarse Grained Molecular Dynamics, Molecular Dynamics, Multiscale Molecular Dynamics, Simulation and Modelling, Statistical Mechanics

Title: Multilepton B decays at LHCb
Abstract:
This funding proposal aims to develop a new research direction within the LHCb experiment 
at the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC) which will be performed during the LHC Long Shutdown 2 
with the data already collected by the LHCb detector in the LHC Run 1 and Run 2

The ideas in the proposal are motivated by the lack of observation of new heavy particles
by the ATLAS and CMS experiments, and are inspired by the recent hints of the
possible lepton nonuniversality seen by the LHCb Collaboration. 

The reported discrepancies with the theoretical prediction in the ratios between various 
semileptonic $b$ hadron decays (e.g. in $B\to K^{(*)}\ell\ell$) are often challenged due
to several inputs non trivial to control. These include possible impact of hadronic uncertainties
in the angular observables, sizeable corrections due to the different trigger strategy between
final states with electrons and muons, and significantly lower efficiency and momentum resolution
in electrons. This proposal constructed to address these points by looking for pure leptonic
$b$ hadron decays which are less impacted by the hadronic uncertainties: $B^\pm\to\ell\nu\gamma^*$
and $B_s\to\ell\ell\gamma^*$ with $\gamma^*\to\ell\ell$ added to the decay chain. 
The role of the virtual $\gamma^*$ in these decays is fundamental: it enhances the decay rates with 
light leptons ($e$ or $\mu$) by orders of magnitude since its presence lifts helicity suppression;
$\gamma^*\to\ell\ell$ visualizes the decay vertex of $B^\pm\to\ell\nu$ in the detector; 
it significantly suppresses backgrounds from other processes; and finally, it removes
the need to use different trigger strategies for different decays (as all the decays can be 
triggered by the same leptons from $\gamma^*$).

Finally, there is an additional point which is addressed in the proposal. 
As this research aims to look for differences between lepton families, its major
ingredient is an improvement in electron reconstruction and identification 
efficiencies thanks to introduction of the machine learning methods. These methods
will allow to more efficiently recognize patterns from the bremsstrahlung emitted 
by electrons when passing through the LHCb detector material, and hence recover lost
energy and reduce low-mass tails in final states with electrons. When finalized,
this work will have an impact on the large part of the scientific output of the LHCb
collaboration. 

By the end of the grant funding period, the developments will be in place to
be implemented into the default algorithms of LHCb during the Run 3 data taking,
and to propagate to other LHCb analyses. The decays $B^\pm\to\ell\nu\gamma^*$
and $B_s\to\ell\ell\gamma^*$ will be 
either observed, or the searches well commissioned to be quickly updated
with the new data to reach the first evidence of these rare processes.
Keywords: LHCb, electron reconstruction, lepton universality, leptons, rare B decays

Title: Compression of Visual information for Humans and Machines (CoViHM)
Abstract: The field of imaging is undergoing two major trends. One one hand, new and richer modalities in imaging are increasing in popularity, which enable new experiences and enhanced understanding through image sensing using mechanisms offering better precision. An example of this trend include a continuous progress in conventional visual representations toward higher quality, higher resolutions, extended high dynamic range and wider color gamut representations. Another example is in the use of new modalities in visual information such as light field and point cloud representations bringing richer functionalities to imaging such as increased immersion and richer interaction with additional degrees of freedom. On the other hand, with progress in imaging techniques based on artificial intelligence and learning based computer vision, the final consumer of visual content is not anymore only human but visual information is increasingly captured to be automatically analysed by machines that perform computer vision tasks without any humans in the loop. If today, the majority of images and video captured are still consumed by humans as opposed to machine, this trend is reversing. In both trends, compression of visual information remains a must in order to produce practically feasible and cost-effective solutions. It is important to note that by far, the large majority of image and video compression algorithms designed, implemented and deployed in the last three decades, have taken into account directly or indirectly the characteristics of the human visual system, in order to compress portions of the visual information with lesser impact on human perception in order to reach more compact representations. This approach does not necessarily result in efficient solutions if the decoded image and video are automatically analysed by machine vision which does not exhibits the same characteristics found in human visual system. There is a need for new and more efficient ways to compress visual information for machines effectively. At the same time, it is important to remind that creation of new categories of visual information coding for machines in addition to those optimal for human perception is not practical in many use cases where the visual information is to be consumed by humans but also analysed by machines. The objective of this research proposal is to tackle this problem, namely, design, implement and validate new visual information coding algorithms that are destined to both humans and machines. The research methodology adopted in this research focuses on three types of visual information, gigapixel and HDR images, light field images and point cloud images. Three doctoral researchers, each focusing on one of the three types of visual information will follow the same general strategy, while adapting each approach to specifics of each modality. In each type, the best latent space representation of the visual information is produced in order to compress the visual information most efficiently. At the same time, each approach relies on learning based techniques where the cost function combines decoded visual information with and without post-processing to enhance its cognitive value, as well as visual analysis for predefined tasks.
Keywords: artificial intelligence, computer vision, gigapixel, high dynamic range, image compression, light field, point cloud

Title: Empowering robots with tactile sensing: towards a general artificial intelligence
Abstract:
Almost everything we do relies on our sense of touch. Autonomous machines, however, only have a basic way of perceiving contact with their surroundings, which limits both their capabilities and their safety. My research focuses on the integration of tactile sensing into robotic systems from a general perspective: Rather than developing task-dependent strategies, it seeks to answer how tactile data can be leveraged in the context of arbitrary applications. The ultimate goal is to address scenarios where machines need to rely on complex interactions with the environment or with humans, especially targeting applications in logistics, manufacturing, and healthcare.

Unprecedented accuracy in sensing distributed contact forces (both shear and pressure) may be achieved by a high-resolution tactile sensor, through a calibration mapping that processes raw tactile data, which are generally challenging to interpret. For the sake of efficiency and generalization, it is highly desirable to extract this mapping in simulation. However, this requires addressing the differences between data observed in simulation and reality, a task that is especially suitable for domain adaptation techniques.

This proposal then addresses the idea of achieving a general artificial intelligence for robots, by pre-training reinforcement learning algorithms (based on trial and error) to facilitate learning new tasks with small amounts of data. This is akin to the capability of the human brain to quickly learn new skills by reusing the bulk of knowledge already available. For tasks that involve physical contact, the integration of tactile sensing with visual feedback has the objective of making robots plan and react to contact, appropriately regulating the resulting contact forces.
Keywords: artificial intelligence, computer vision, deep learning, machine learning, reinforcement learning, robotic grasping, robotic manipulation, robotic skin, robotics, self-supervised learning, sim-to-real, tactile sensing, unsupervised learning

Title: Subject-adapted 3D dynamic bio-impedance models: application to blood pressure monitoring
Abstract:
Arterial blood pressure (BP) acts as a major risk factor for numerous cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, renal and neurological diseases. While in the normotensive population one out of two deaths is of cardiovascular nature, among hypertensive patients it reaches a two out of three ratio. Systemic hypertension is thus strongly correlated with morbidity and mortality and afflicts more than two billion individuals nowadays at a worldwide scale. However, to this day the accurate diagnosis of a systemic hypertensive condition remains limited by the obtrusive and intermittent aspects of its gold standard measurement modality. The clinical demand for a technology providing a non-occlusive, ambulatory-compliant, continuous and unsupervised means of monitoring systemic BP has not been met yet.
With lesser prevalence and mortality than its left heart counterpart, pulmonary hypertension is characterized by its difficult early diagnosis. With symptoms severely lacking of specificity and strongly invasive or limiting measurement modalities, pulmonary hypertension is usually diagnosed at a late stage, when right heart failure has already begun. Providing the medical community with a beat-by-beat non-invasive technique that could detect early signs of pulmonary hypertension is a challenge that remains to be overcome. 
Electrical impedance tomography (EIT) has shown promising results in that matter. Allowing the visualization of cardiorespiratory phenomena such as ventilation and pulmonary perfusion, this technology has lead recent works to show that it could be exploited to assess central BP in a fully non-occlusive, ambulatory-compliant, continuous and unsupervised way. Because of its non-invasive, non-ionizing and low-cost nature, EIT provides an interesting modality for portable BP monitors to be investigated. However, numerous research questions regarding the influence of cardiac motion in EIT signals need to be addressed first. The goals of this research are thus multiple: in a first phase, it aims at identifying and quantifying – through numerical simulation – the various factors affecting EIT impedance changes. To that end, methods and tools allowing the automated generation of subject-adapted 3D dynamic bio-impedance models need to be developed. In a second phase, enhanced EIT images – where cardiac motion has minimal influence – will be reconstructed. Finally, these model-improved EIT images will be validated through the estimation of systemic BP and pulmonary artery pressure in humans and animals.

The precise research objectives of the herein proposed research are thus the following:
1.Investigate and implement methods for the automated segmentation of 4D MR images of the thorax.
2.Use these segmentations for the creation of dynamic 3D bio-impedance models.
3.Exploit said models to study those factors affecting the EIT cardiac signals through numerical simulation.
4.Create a novel EIT image reconstruction strategy where the influence of cardiac motion is minimized.
5.Validate our model-improved EIT images through the estimation of hemodynamic parameters such as systemic BP and pulmonary artery pressure.

This research aims at meeting the clinical demand for non-obtrusive and continuous means of monitoring systemic and pulmonary artery pressure. The research is largely interdisciplinary going from MR image processing, EIT reconstruction and simulation to biomedical signal analysis. The expected outcome is a leap forward in the understanding of cardiac EIT signal genesis, and an opening wedge towards new techniques for the portable and non-obtrusive measurement of BP.

Title: Rapid assessment of bacterial virulence for personalized treatment: using bacterial genome wide and mass spectrum wide association studies of invasive and non-invasive bacteria to identify biomarkers linked with sepsis
Abstract:
Background: The course of infections is heterogenous and determined by host/pathogen interactions and time to treatment. In today’s clinical practice, patient-centric factors assess the outcome and thereby influence empiric antibiotics. For decades, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) profiling was the key for subsequent treatment adaptations. Why is the pathogen’s virulence largely ignored? Bacterial virulence factors are as important as AMR and contribute to clinical phenotypes and pathogen invasiveness. Virulence is variably expressed, similar to AMR, and highly diverse across and within bacterial species. In clinical practise, knowledge about virulence is surprisingly scars and not readily available. Few exceptions show the impact on clinical and epidemiological management, e.g., toxins of Clostridioides difficile or enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli (EHEC). There is clearly a missed opportunity for virulence assessment in current diagnostic practice, which may result in ground breaking changes of clinical management and antibiotic stewardship. 
But how can we unfold this potential?

Objectives: We will develop a diagnostic approach for early bacterial virulence risk assessment using (i) fundamental knowledge on virulence in clinically relevant scenarios (WP1-4), (ii) experimentally validate identified bacterial biomarkers (WP5), monitor markers during infection (WP6), and (iii) translate findings into clinical diagnostic practice (WP7). Our driving hypothesis is that, invasiveness can be determined early.

Methods: First, we screen for potential virulence factors linked to invasiveness of primary sterile sites. We will adapt our machine learning (ML) algorithm for AMR (Weis C et al. Nature Med. 2022) and predict invasiveness from an unprecedented large, MALDI-TOF spectral datasets covering diverse species from an established collaborative laboratory network across 7 countries (WP1). Second, we confirm virulence factors in relevant Gram-negative and -positive bacterial species (ESKAPE): performing bacterial genome wide (bGWAS, WP2) and mass spectrum wide association studies (MSWAS, WP3) from in house and public-available data of invasive and non-invasive ESKAPE isolates. Next, we will adjust the model for patient factors e.g., age, immunosuppression, surgery, etc. (WP4). We will genetically modify wildtype bacteria, using promising candidates from WP1-4, and make isogenic isolates with and without virulence factors (Gibson assembly) for validation of ML algorithms (WP5). Next, we will monitor the expression profiles of biomarkers during clinically relevant infections and we will expand routine MALDI-TOF MS profiling with lipid profiling (negative ion mode and super-DHB matrix) and use Fourier Transform Infrared spectroscopy (WP6). Finally, we will conduct a retrospective quasi study to determine the impact on clinical management (WP7).

Impact: The proposal may result in using bacterial virulence for early personalized evaluation and prediction of outcomes. Thereby, (i) monitoring of patients may be adapted e.g., with additional follow-ups or earlier triaging; and (ii) treatments may be tailored. We generate (iii) a substantial gain in knowledge about virulence in diagnostics with potential for research and the diagnostic industry; (iv) development of bioinformatic tools focusing on virulence, which can be translated to other microorganisms; a list of (v) clinically validated diagnostic biomarkers; (vi) potential “drug-able” targets for anti-virulence treatments and vaccines; (vii) highly characterized biobanks and datasets, which will be made available for the scientific community (FAIR data/sample sharing concepts) as a reference toolbox on virulence, and (viii) a strong translational use case with model character for virulence related research, which could complement other phenotypes, such as AMR.
Keywords: Bioinformatics, Diagnostics, Infection, Invasiveness, MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry, Machine learning, Sequencing, Virulence

Title: Computer-assisted design and biophysical characterization of immunomodulatory and antibacterial peptides and peptidomimetic agents
Abstract: In this study we addressed the need for novel immune-modulators and antibacterial molecular agents using innovative methods and concepts for computer-assisted drug design. The research project was divided into three main sections: i) Development and implementation of adaptive algorithms for the de novo design of bioactive peptides and peptide mimetics, ii) characterization and design of MHC-I binding peptides and druglike compounds, and iii) characterization and design of peptides and peptide mimetics targeting bacterial and cancer cell membranes (antimicrobial peptides, AMPs; anticancer peptides, ACPs). We employed nature-inspired optimization methods like the evolution strategy and the ant colony optimization (ACO) paradigm for the computer-based assembly of novel peptides that exhibit the desired biological activity. The ‘fitness function’ was represented by kernel-based machine-learning systems in the case of in silico design, and actual biochemical in vitro assays in a combination of computer-assisted design with robotic peptide synthesis and testing. A particular research focus was on the understanding of function-determining structural features of AMPs.
Keywords: Anticancer peptides, Antimicrobial peptides, Bioinformatics, Biophysical methods, Chemoinformatics, Computational chemistry, Drug discovery, MHC-I, Membrane, Peptide design, Pharmacology

Title: AutoCare: Leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models for Automated Surveillance of Adverse Events in Cancer Immunotherapy
Abstract:
Background: Cancer is a major global burden of disease, with an estimated 20 million new cases and 10 million deaths in a year. Immunotherapy, particularly immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), significantly improved cancer survival over the past decades, and has benefited millions of patients worldwide. However, the survival gains from ICIs come with the risk of immune-related adverse events (irAEs), which are characterized by inflammatory and autoimmune pathologies. irAEs range from minor inconvenience to life-threatening, and affect up to 80% of patients with fatal cases in 0.3–1.3%. Even when mild, irAEs can negatively impact outcomes and quality of life by requiring early treatment discontinuation, increasing comorbidity burden, and contributing to financial burdens and increased healthcare use. Therefore, it is critical to early detect irAEs to provide timely management and to accurately predict irAEs, especially the severe cases, to mitigate severe harm and reduce mortality. However, as ICIs have fairly recently entered clinical practice and present a very different spectrum of irAEs, many clinicians lack experience in recognizing and managing irAEs. Furthermore, irAEs remain underrecognized and understudied in clinical trials and existing databases, largely due to the time- and resource-intensive nature of manual electronic medical records (EMRs) review. With an increasing number of patients being treated with ICIs, there is an urgent need to develop automated irAE surveillance methods to mitigate the impact of irAE on morbidity, mortality, and quality of life in clinical practice, and advance clinical research.
Large language models (LLMs) offer a promising, cost-effective approach to irAE detection and prediction, leveraging its strong natural language understanding through transformer-based architectures, larger parameter sizes, and extensive pre-training data scales. Moreover, multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) can integrate multimodal data to further enhance irAE surveillance. However, their application to irAE surveillance using EMR data and medical images, particularly in the context of time-series data, remains underexplored.

Aims: The project aims to leverage MLLMs to develop an automated framework for irAE detection and prediction by integrating EMR data with chest computed tomography (CT) images.

Methods: This project will be achieved through three specific aims: (SA1) Develop a multimodal, longitudinal dataset of 13,000 ICI-treated cancer patients by integrating EMR data and CT images, along with a curated irAE sub-dataset. (SA2) Develop an irAE detection framework using MLLMs with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Chain of Thought (CoT) prompting. (SA3) Develop an irAE prediction framework, by integrating radiomics with clinical biomarkers to stratify risk effectively.

Results: I expect to develop MLLM-powered automated frameworks for irAE surveillance with several innovations, including long-context processing, multimodal understanding, a memory bank for time-series data, CoT reasoning, and survival prediction.

Impact: This project will address real-world challenges in irAE research and clinical practice, enabling early detection and prediction to optimize cancer care and improve patient outcomes. Moreover, it will establish automated surveillance frameworks for integrating multimodal data into clinical workflows, with broader applications to other complex medical conditions, ultimately enhancing patient safety, survival, and quality of life, while alleviating financial burdens and healthcare utilization in the long term.
Keywords: Automated Surveillanc, Cancer Immunotherapy, Chain of Thought, Computed tomography, Electronic Medical Records, Immune-related Adverse Events, Multimodal Large Language Models, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Survival Prediction

Title: Searching for new physics at the LHC
Abstract:
Searches for new physics beyond the Standard Model represent one of the pressing pursuits of the particle physics community, with the purpose to resolve major scientific questions related to the origin and nature of matter and the forces that act upon it. The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN offers a unique opportunity for a rich breadth of explorations.

This project proposal focuses on searches for new physics at the ATLAS and FASER experiments of the LHC. New searches are proposed, based on creative developments in detector, trigger processing, and reconstruction at the two experiments. More specifically:

• At the ATLAS experiment, we propose searches that with boost the reach of new physics in multi-jet final states, in Run-2 and Run-3 data. The Run-2 searches aim at advanced explorations of uncovered phase-space. The Run-3 searches will aim at developing new analyses using original trigger selections to be introduced in the context of this proposal, providing unconventional data-sets.

• To prepare the ATLAS experiment for the LHC upgrade (High-Luminosity LHC, HL-LHC), we will initiate a project to evaluate and compare the use of GPUs and FPGAs as accelerators to the TDAQ CPU farm. The aim is to bench-mark their performance using jet reconstruction as an example, and Run-3 data as input to test-beds that will demonstrate their reach.

• At the FASER experiment, we will participate in the high-resolution silicon pre-shower construction, testing, commissioning and operations. We will significantly contribute to the data acquisition aspects of it. We propose to develop photon reconstruction using machine learning and search for axion-like particles in di-photon signatures, using the data collected during operations, in 2024.

The time-span of the project is 38 months, the end-point driven by the current LHC Run-3 schedule, which in turns drives the finalisation of the hardware projects and the collection of data for the completion of a first round of analyses. To pursue the proposed projects, we ask SNF to fund a postdoc and three PhD students for the duration of 38 months. All personnel is currently employed in the group under the ongoing SNF project 200020_19227; this optimises the outcome of the proposed projects with already acquired experience and expertise. One PhD student will complete his thesis within the first 1.5 years and will be replaced for the completion of the project.

The proposed research plan builds on the strengths developed by past and ongoing research in the relevant areas: searches for new physics, especially in analysing multi-jet final states, hadronic reconstruction and triggering as well as the commissioning and operations of a new experiment. This project proposal maximises the outcome of SNF FLARE grants 20FL20_201478 and 20FL21_201474, which cover core-costs for the ATLAS HL-LHC upgrade and the FASER pre-shower construction, respectively.
Keywords: ATLAS, FASER, SUSY, machine learning, searches for new physics, trigger

Title: Optimal Signal-extraction Algorithms for Future Cosmological Surveys
Abstract: The present proposal takes advantage of the expertise available at the Laboratory of Astrophysics (LASTRO) of EPFL in the field of image processing and gravitational lensing, in order to devise new signal processing algorithms for ongoing and future cosmological imaging surveys. These include the ESA Euclid scientific mission, the NASA WFIRST-AFTA mission, and majors ground-based surveys like LSST. This work will be carried out in the context of the second half of the PhD thesis of Thibault Kuntzer and will focus on new galaxy shape measurement methods based on machine learning and artificial neural networks. Similar techniques will be used to tackle a second crucial image processing problem: the measurement of the instrumental Point Spread Function (PSF) and in particular its wavelength and its temporal variations. In this conext we will also investigate PSF algorithms that can cope with blended stars, as almost half of the stars on the sky are in fact double stars, with a significant impact on the PSF modeling. All these methods developed specifically for Euclid will also be applied to wide field sky surveys in the public domain both to do cosmology (cosmic shear) and to do study galaxy formation and evolution with galaxy-galaxy lensing.
Keywords: Cosmic shear, Cosmology, Dark energy, Dark matter, ESA, Image processing, NASA, Weak gravitational lensing

Title: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo Based Algorithms for Sampling
Abstract:
Sampling from a Gibbs distribution is a fundamental algorithmic problem that arises in several disciplines including machine learning, statistics, optimization, theoretical computer science, and molecular dynamics. Formally, one is given access to a function $F: \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and the goal is  to generate samples from the  distribution $\pi(x) \propto e^{-F(x)}$. The aim of this project is to develop fast algorithms with provable guarantees for sampling from such distributions. In many situations, for instance when $d$ is large, such sampling problems become computationally difficult, and Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms are among the most popular methods used to solve them. However, most of the existing guarantees for sampling algorithms can only handle Markov chains that take very small steps and hence can oftentimes be very slow. 

On the other hand, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) algorithms -- which are inspired from Hamiltonian dynamics in physics -- possess the ability to take longer steps. However, obtaining non-asymptotic bounds on the convergence rate of this method has remained elusive; conjectured bounds on its running time would, if true, explain its success in practice. Very recent successes (including a work of the PI) in establishing these conjectured bounds in certain cases have resulted in a renewed interest in the question of why and when HMC algorithms can be provably fast.

The project outlined in this proposal would continue this momentum and contribute to bridging the divide between the theory and practice of  Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC)  algorithms for sampling from high-dimensional distributions. To analyze HMC we will develop new mathematical techniques and introduce new regularity conditions, allowing us to obtain tighter bounds for a large class of situations encountered in practice. We will use the insights gained by our analysis of existing HMC algorithms to design new HMC algorithms along with new methods of tuning their parameters. Lastly, we will implement these algorithms and make them openly available.

Recent works, including that of the PI, synthesize tools and mathematical methods from algorithms and optimization, geometric analysis, probability, and Markov chains, as well as dynamical systems, to analyze HMC algorithms.  These results provide a launching pad for this project and we feel well equipped to analyze such algorithms under these more difficult conditions.
Keywords: Algorithms, Gibbs Distribution, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, Langevin dynamics, Markov Chains, Sampling

Title: ML-edge: Enabling Machine-Learning-Based Health Monitoring in Edge Sensors via Architectural Customization
Abstract:
Wireless Body Sensor Nodes (WBSNs) can acquire bio-signals from patients affected by a variety of chronic conditions, enabling their health assessment while minimally impacting their quality of life. These edge health monitors have to abide to conflicting objectives. They must, on one hand, allow long-term recording sessions while relying on limited power sources, mandating an extremely tight energy envelope. On the other hand, they have to provide precise and detailed health data to patients and caregivers. To this end, embedded bio-signal processing has proved to be a successful enabler: the ensuing smart WBSNs can in fact compute clinical features locally, and only wirelessly transmit compact feature sets instead of raw acquisitions. In this way signal processing can lead to an important reduction of the WBSN bandwidth requirements and their related energy cost.
   Nonetheless, state of the art approaches use digital processing from a somehow low-level perspective, limiting its potential to provide relevant information to patients and caregivers while yielding high efficiency and autonomy. Against this backdrop, the ambition of the proposed ML-edge project is to study the potential of a novel generation of machine learning-based edge sensors to disruptively enhance the capabilities of smart WBSNs.
  We plan to tackle this challenge from multiple perspectives. From an application viewpoint, we will focus our research on developing personalized algorithms to derive highly abstract interpretations of multi-modal bio-signals, in order to be able to detect acute events (e.g., the onset of seizures and migraines), as well as variations in trends in degenerative neurological disorder treatments (e.g., reaction to physical activity exercises in Parkinson's disease patients).
  From a hardware/software co-design perspective, our efforts will instead center on devising domain-specific, heterogeneous digital architectures to support the complex workloads originating from the concurrent processing of multi-modal sources and their ML-based interpretation. In addition, we will develop compiler tools to map the edge-node software to the defined hardware targets, as well as to identify computational hotspots amenable to hardware acceleration.
  ML applications can incrementally improve the fidelity of the employed model as more data is acquired. Therefore, as a third contribution, we plan to propose energy-conscious solutions to harness this opportunity, both by providing a smart selection of the refinement sets and by developing novel training methodologies for the models update.
Our effort will aim at supporting event-based computations at extremely high efficiency levels. We will decline this run-time paradigm in different ways throughout the project: edge-node software will employ complex tasks only when required, while relying on simpler ones when possible. The WBSN architectures will provide a flexible support for different computing demands, aggressively clock- and/or power-gating unused resources. Model refinements will only employ a subset of the acquired data, and use small-bitwidth representations to reduce their workload footprint.
Our planned activities will sit at the crossroads of different fields, giving ample cross-fertilization opportunities among the doctoral students assigned to the project. Its collaborative nature will be fostered by the complementary expertise of the two involved research groups (headed by prof. D. Atienza at EPF-Lausanne and by prof. L. Pozzi at USI-Lugano, respectively), who have an extensive research background in machine learning, embedded systems and bio-signal processing fields.
Keywords: computing architectures, embedded systems, low-power design, machine learning, reconfigurable systems, systems-on-chip, wireless body sensor nodes

Title: Nonexistent intentional objects and singular representations: An Analysis
Abstract: Because they do not appear to fit in the extensional framework that contemporary philosophy has inherited from mathematics-inspired works in logics and formal semantics, nonexistent intentional objects have put philosophers in front of the following dilemma: either reject the framework along with the fruits it can harvest, or deal with nonexistent intentional objects in an intensional framework with all the ontological implications that follow from the adequate semantics (i.e. that nonexistents intentional objects form a kind of object that together share the property of not existing). However, this move may be premature if we can explain singular mental and linguistic representations by invoking mostly intrinsic properties of subjects plus their relations to their mental and extramental environments. Given the pervasive nature of intentional phenomena in thought, speech and communication, and given the importance of singular representations as the starting point of many action-oriented mechanisms, a study of nonexistent intentional objects is instrumental to extend our understanding of how minds work, both individually and in coordination. The insights to be gained from such a study may be precious for the philosophy of mind, ontology, semantics, cognitive linguistics and, possibly, artificial intelligence.
Keywords: intentionality, mental files, nonexistent objects, ontology, philosophy of language, philosophy of mind, presuppositions, semantics, singular thoughts

Title: From Branch to Branch: Unravelling Primate Vision in Arboreal Leaping and Navigation
Abstract:
Primates, including humans and their non-human relatives, possess a highly derived sense of vision for tasks such as object recognition, spatial vision, and detecting and processing of social clues. The early visual cortex underwent a significant transformation at the origin of crown group primates, with the emergence of a near invariant form of vision circuitry in the primary visual cortex (V1). This architectural design has been conserved throughout primate brain evolution and was accompanied by an expansion of neocortex dedicated to vision. In the mouse lemur (Microcebus murinus), a basal primate resembling the primate last common ancestor, V1 covers 20% of the neocortex. However, the visual capabilities and behaviors served by this architecture differ greatly from those in humans, apes, and Old World monkeys. Here we propose a research program to investigate key features of early primate vision. Using the EthoLoop platform, we will study behavior, cognition, and perception in free-ranging mouse lemurs in a controlled naturalistic laboratory setting resembling their arboreal habitat. This platform enables quantitative studies of visually guided navigation, foraging behaviors, and neuronal recording during complex tasks. By adjusting environmental conditions, we can explore visual parameters and infer computational principles. The project combines expertise in quantifying ecological behaviors, theoretical neuroscience and computer vision, and neural recording in freeranging mouse lemurs. The research aims to understand visual processing and cognition during arboreal navigation and foraging. Aim 1: Understanding the strategies of active vision during arboreal leaping: To characterize the different modalities and strategiesinvolved  in visually guided leaping, we will design a novel, parameterizable behavioral leaping task, constrained by physical
features actually observed in natural settings in Madagascar.
Aim 2: Characterizing large scale navigation strategies under varying visual conditions: To gain a better understanding of how the visual conditions affect navigational strategies we will observe freely moving mouse lemurs in the wild, model their behavior and test our predictions under controlled conditions in the laboratory settings. 
Aim3: Revealing the neuronal codes for vision, gaze, posture and space in the mouse lemur brain: To characterize the coding of visual and non-visual features (including motor and posture parameters) we will record the activity of individual neurons under freely moving conditions using electrophysiologyy and portable miniature microscope imaging. Taken together, our studies will open a new perspective on primate vision in action that defined much of the form of vision circuitry still used in the human brain and address several major open questions about potential differences between visual information processing in the primate brain and in that of closely related rodents.
Keywords: Brain, Primate, Vision
