Title: From Test and Treat to Targeted Approaches: Developing a Personalized Risk Model for STI Screening
Abstract:
Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) such as chlamydia, gonorrhea, and syphilis remain a persistent public health challenge. Current "test and treat" strategies, aimed at reducing STI transmission through routine screening, have had limited success in lowering incidence rates. Globally, STI prevention strategies are undergoing significant change, with some countries moving towards reduced testing while others expand testing, even incorporating doxyPEP (doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis). This lack of alignment in clinical guidelines underscores the insufficient evidence base guiding these decisions. Additionally, frequent screening, particularly for asymptomatic individuals, raises concerns in the context of increasing antimicrobial resistance (AMR). There is a critical need to optimize STI prevention strategies by developing more personalized, evidence-based approaches that target individuals based on their specific risk profiles, rather than relying on “one-size-fits-all” testing policies.

This project aims to advance STI prevention by developing and validating a personalized risk assessment tool that will enable tailored STI screening and prevention strategies within the SwissPrEPared cohort, a group of PrEP users with high incidence of STIs. The overarching goal is to shift from traditional blanket "test and treat" models to more refined, targeted approaches that focus on identifying who is most at risk, when, and why. This novel approach will provide insights into STI transmission dynamics by integrating behavioral, biological, and social factors to create personalized prevention strategies. By doing so, it aims to enhance the effectiveness of STI prevention, optimize healthcare resource use, and minimize the risks associated with over-testing and antibiotic overuse.

The research is structured into three work packages (WPs):

WP1: Long-term Trajectories of Sexual Risk Behavior and Health Outcomes: This WP will use longitudinal data from SwissPrEPared to assess STI clustering, changes in susceptibility, and the long-term health impacts of STIs. It will employ cluster analysis, latent class modeling, and other longitudinal methods to identify distinct risk groups, which will inform the development of personalized screening tools.

WP2: Development and Validation of a Personalized STI Risk Tool: Using machine learning, WP2 will develop a tool to estimate individual STI risk based on the factors identified in WP1. This tool will be integrated into the SwissPrEPared clinical workflow, providing explainable, real-time feedback to both clinicians and patients, enabling shared decision-making regarding STI testing frequency. The tool will be developed and piloted using a participatory approach, with continuous consultation from PrEP users and clinicians.

WP3: Public Health Impact of Test and Treat: Mathematical modeling will be used to simulate various testing strategies and behavioral interventions. WP3 will assess the historical impact of the SwissPrEPared program and explore counterfactual scenarios to inform future public health policies and optimize STI testing strategies.

This project represents a paradigm shift in STI prevention, moving away from broad, routine screening toward personalized, risk-based approaches. It marks a significant leap from current clinical guidelines, which typically recommend testing based on broad demographic factors, to a more nuanced approach that tailors testing and prevention efforts to individual risk levels. The integration of advanced analytics, machine learning, and mathematical modeling will position Switzerland as a leader in adapting evidence-based, efficient, and sustainable STI prevention strategies. Once validated, the personalized risk tool can be adapted to other high-risk populations and healthcare contexts, positioning Switzerland at the forefront of global STI prevention efforts.

Abstract:
The search for Charge-Parity (CP) violation, one of the few unknowns left in the Standard Model of particles, is the main goal of long-baseline (LBL) neutrino oscillation experiments. LBL experiments use intense beams of $

A Near Detector (ND) complex, positioned before flavor oscillations occur, measure the neutrino flux and cross section and constrain the corresponding systematic uncertainties in the search for CP violation.
The Japanese LBL neutrino programme is currently defined by the T2K (Tokai-To-Kamioka) experiment. Starting from 2027, the programme will evolve into Hyper-Kamiokande (HK), a 8 times more massive FD compared to Super-Kamiokande used by T2K. T2K and HK will share the same neutrino beamline at J-PARC and the same near detector, ND280. To cope with the large statistics that will be collected at the FD in the next years, also thanks to a higher neutrino beam intensity, a vigorous programme of reduction of systematic uncertainties on the neutrino flux and cross section is carried on by measuring neutrino interactions at ND280, recently upgraded by the T2K collaboration with the construction of a novel 3D segmented scintillator active target and new time projection chambers. The PIs, after conceiving, designing and, finally, upgrading the ND280 complex, with this project aim to exploit the new ND280 data by performing high-precision measurements of the $
u_{\mu}$-nucleus cross-section, boosted by newly developed deep learning (DL) tools, and of the $
u_e$-nucleus cross-section with low gamma conversion background samples. The ND280 measurements at T2K, combined with an active R&D work and detector simulation studies, will lead, thanks to this project, to the conceptual design of ND280++, an additional upgrade of ND280 designed for the Hyper-K high-precision phase after 2030.
The project will give continuity to the French and Swiss leaderships in both experiments and confirm their centrality also in the context of the HK Near Detector. The project milestones are:
(1) perform the first $
u_{\mu}$-nucleus charged current cross section measurement with a comprehensive characterisation of nuclear effects, including the vertex activity, i.e. the signature left in the detector by indiscernible low-momentum particles stopping near the interaction vertex, using the novel DL tools;
(2) perform a high-purity $
u_e$-nucleus charged current cross section measurement, with the rejection of the dominant $\gamma ightarrow e+e-$ background enhanced by SuperFGD, the new 3D granular scintillator active target;

The $
u_{\mu}$ and $

These data analyses will be important also to develop and establish the analysis techniques that will be used at HK ND280 with higher statistics in the final search for CP violation.

Title: Structured-entities Ontology Extension (StrOntEx)
Abstract:
Reference ontologies play an essential role in organising knowledge in the life sciences and other domains. They are built and maintained manually. Since this is an expensive process, many reference ontologies only cover a small fraction of their domain. The goal of this project is to develop techniques that enable the automatic extension of the coverage of a reference ontology by extending it with classes that have not yet been manually added. The extension shall be faithful to the (often implicit) design decisions by the developers of the reference ontology. 

While this is a generic problem, our use case addresses the automatic extension of the Chemical Entities of Biological Interest (ChEBI) ontology with classes of molecules, since the chemical domain is particularly suited to our approach. We achieve our goal by using the leaf classes of the manually curated reference ontology to train a system to predict subclass relationships between mid-level classes and new classes. Thus, our method uses machine learning techniques, but – in contrast to other approaches – does not rely on text corpora as input, but uses the content of the ontology itself. Annotations of classes that provide information that are relevant for the classification of a given entity within the ontology play a key role in this learning task. E.g., in the case of ChEBI these are annotations that represent the structure of chemical entities (e.g., molecules and functional groups). In addition, the axioms of the ontology are represented as logical neural networks, which are used during the training of prediction models. Thus, our approach for ontology extension uses neural-symbolic integration. 

In our previous work we have established the feasibility of the approach by comparing the performance of a number of machine learning approaches at subclass prediction. In spite of the limitations of this initial work, the performance of some of our models compare positively to ClassyFire. The latter is a rule-based system representing the state of the art for this task, and is already being used in the development of ChEBI. Furthermore, our results show that different machine learning approaches are suited for different kinds of chemical entities. Thus, we plan to use an ensemble approach in our project. 

The outcomes of this project will be (a) a benchmark training set for training models for chemical ontology extension, and (b) a system that – when provided with a set of new chemical entities as input – will automatically generate a new ontology that extends ChEBI to cover these entities. The benefit of this work is a novel methodology for extending the coverage of existing reference ontologies. If adopted, it will allow improved interoperability and knowledge integration for the communities that use these reference ontologies. Another benefit will be a novel neural-symbolic architecture, integrating graph neural networks, transformers and logical neural networks. We will also explore methods for explainability of neural networks using neural-symbolic approaches.
Keywords: explainability, machine learning, neural-symbolic integration, ontology extension, semantic data management

Title: Introduction of High Field Optimized Fast 3D MR Spectroscopic Imaging for IDH Typing of Gliomas and Assisted Surgical Neuro Navigation
Abstract:
Introduction – Recently the first commercially available 7T MR-scanner, which is approved for clinical use came on to the market. The main motivation to go to higher field strengths is the fact that better SNR can be achieved in shorter acquisition time, or higher spatial resolution can be obtained in the same measurement time. High field MRI also has drawbacks, e.g. substantially higher specific absorption rate SAR, higher susceptibility related image distortion problems, and longer longitudinal relaxation times. Nevertheless, moving to higher fields is especially beneficial for MR-spectroscopy. This is due to the fact that better signal to noise ration (SNR) is combined with higher spectral resolution. The two most commonly used techniques for spectroscopic imaging (MRSI) are: (i.) relative slow 2D/3D techniques like PRESS and semiLASER based techniques, and (ii.) fast 3D echo planar based (EPI) techniques Although echo planar spectroscopic imaging (EPSI) is a technique that has been introduced by Sir Peter Mansfield in the first half of 80tees, the method is still continuously being improved, and recently very promising applications related to brain tumor diagnostics were published. To be mentioned in this context is the fact that the method can be combined with spectral editing for the detection of 2-hydroxy-glutarate (2HG) in glioma patients. 2HG is only present if the glioma that has mutations in the IDH-gene. It is shown that gliomas having the IDH-mutation have a much better overall survival prognosis. Apart from brain tumor typing, high resolution EPSI imaging also enables investigation the investigation of tumor infiltration using metabolic criteria. In surgery the patients’ preoperative intake of the 5-aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA) before surgery selectively makes malignant glioma tissues fluorescent under blue light irradiation and tumor itself becomes clearly visible during the neurosurgical intervention. The fact that 5-ALA-guided completely-resected glioma patients have a significant longer survival time, underlines the necessity to know the exact tumor boundaries.

Aims – The major aims of the study proposed are manifold: (i.) the development of a novel EPSI-pulse sequence utilizing 3D-radial k-space sampling schemes, that focuses on robustness w.r.t. patient motion, is robust with respect to chemical shift displacement artifacts, includes the possibility of 2HG-spectral editing, uses SAR-reduced RF-pulses, and operate with total acquisition times that are acceptable for clinical routine use; (ii.) comparison of the novel sequence with available conventional EPSI-techniques and semiLASER-based techniques for clinical routine use comparing its performance at 3T and 7T; (iii.) The development of a graphic processor unit (GPU) based fitting algorithm for quantification of 3D-radial EPSI-data based on the existing tdfdfit-algorithm; (iv.) extension of a locally developed machine learning based automatic quality-filtering algorithm to be applied on our novel EPSI-data; (v.) quantitative investigation on the effect spatial non-uniform transmit and receive properties for all relevant metabolites and spatial dependent signal amplitude correction schemes (extension of a locally developed method); (vi.) investigation of the exact effects of selective excitation on J-coupled spin systems, and comparison of these effects between 3T and 7T; (vii.) reproducibility study on 20 healthy volunteers measured twice with the same protocol (10 recorded twice at 7T and 10 recoded twice at 3T); (viii.) pre-operative application of the best suited EPSI-pulse sequence in a total of 40 patients: 20 patients will be recorded at 3T and 20 at 7T using the equivalent protocols; (ix.) co-registration of pre-operative, spatially resolved 3D-EPSI-MRSI data with post-operative 3D-FLAIR and T1c-imaging in IDH-wildtype patients with had complete resection during 5-ALA guided neurosurgical interventions will provide information on whether MRSI-techniques are helpful to predict the tumor affected volume; (x.) documentation of the location of a biopsy, histology to enable a better correlation between MR-spectroscopic patterns and histology.

The sequence will be compared to the performance obtained with another EPSI implementation (Sabati et al., 2015), available via Siemens, as well as the CMRR-implementation of the mega-semi-LASER for 2HG-editing (CMRR Spectroscopy Package, (Marjanska et al., 2012)). The quantification of the EPSI-data of the reference sequence will be performed with the MIDAS package. The EPSI-data of the novel sequence as well as mega-semi-LASER sequence will be quantified using a parallelized GPU-re-implementation of the tdfdfit-algorithm (J Slotboom et al., 1998) made available as separate plugin within jMRUI-spectroscopy package. Co-registration of pre-surgery EPSI-data with post-operative structural MRI-data will be performed with SPM. Statistical analysis and machine learning algorithms will be based on statistical programming language “R”.

Potential significance – (a.) Pre-surgical knowledge of the IDH-status will enable better individual neurosurgical treatment of the patient; (b.) Coregistration of metabolic EPSI-data, with post-operative structural MR-data will give information on the fundamental usefulness of MRSI-techniques to detect glioma infiltration zones; (c.) Improved follow-up of IDH-mutated glioma patients, who typically have a long period of minimal progression, followed rapidly by aggressive growth and transformation to higher grade; (d.) The availability of an imaging biomarker to monitor tumor recurrence would be a major advance for all glioma patients.

Title: Understanding Solar and Stellar Flares with Machine Learning
Abstract:
Flares are highly energetic eruptions on the Sun and stars that have a profound influence on space weather, yet the main questions are still largely unsolved: When and where will a flare occur? How is flare energy dissipated? What are the origins and mechanisms of stellar “superflares”, which are thousands of times more powerful than the strongest ever recorded solar flare? 
The difficulty in obtaining answers to these questions lies in the vast amount of data to be analyzed. Astronomical data sets often exceed terabytes per day, which cannot be analyzed manually and they also challenge the available computational resources when using conventional analysis techniques. Machine learning is a very powerful tool for such studies, commonly used in many computer science applications, such as image analysis, pattern recognition, and classification, however its use in astronomy is still in its infancy. In recent years, machine learning has been tested for astronomical applications, such as classifications of spectra to identify certain types of stars or to find unusual galaxies. This project proposes to use and adapt machine learning tools from computer science to statistically analyze large astronomical databases (e.g. data from SDO; IRIS; ground-based observations such as GRIS and IBIS; Kepler and TESS) with the goal of answering the above open questions and to develop a suite of tools that can be used for many other astronomical data sets in the future. Its uniqueness consists of the interdisciplinary synergy of computer science and astronomical data. In particular, the following specific aims are foreseen:
•Classifying flare spectra from different databases, thus obtaining statistics on the physical conditions (Doppler velocities, turbulence, magnetic field evolution, and heating) during flares. Outlier detection will identify unusual flares and highlight any commonalities among them. The results will be interpreted with radiative transfer modeling and placed within the frame of existing flare models.
•We will attempt to predict flares by using neural networks on a large set of SDO data that cover the entire solar atmosphere from the photosphere to the corona and which span 8 years of observations. This approach will be unique from any previous attempts by including multiple wavelengths in very large data sets, with the hope of revealing the precise conditions necessary for a flare.
•By analyzing the Kepler and TESS database, we will identify and classify stellar flares, for example using k-means clustering, manifold learning, outlier detection, and neural networks. We expect to answer how frequent stellar flares are, how they are related to starspot occurrence, what their global properties are and how similar they are to solar flares (e.g. duration, behavior, wait times). Interpretations will include light curve simulations to explain the observed starspots.
The expected results include a statistical understanding of flares and a suite of analysis tools that can be applied to any large astronomical database. This will not only help us forecast flares and better understand stellar activity in potential habitable systems, but will have extended applications into future astronomical problems that are currently inaccessible due to the large volume of data that need to be analyzed.
Keywords: Astronomical Databases, Big Data Anlysis, Machine Learning, Solar Flares, Solar Magnetic Fields, Space Weather, Stellar Flares

Title: MEWS – Measuring English Writing at Secondary Level. A Binational Comparative Study
Abstract: English essay writing is a key competence in a modern world in which English is the lingua franca of science, business and ihigher education. MEWS will be the first large-scale study on English writing on upper secondary level (10th grade) in Germany and Switzerland and has three main research questions: (1) How proficient are learners in essay writing in English two years before their baccalaureate? (2) What is the effect of individual factors (e.g. motivation, intelligence), family background and extracurricular activities on English essay writing competences? (3) What is the effect of school and classroom factors (e.g. classroom instruction, school types, ‘baccalaureate rate’) on English essay writing competences? Learners’ ability to write English essays will be measured in two populations, the first one from Switzerland (AG, BS, BL, SO, ZH, N = 1500), the second one  from Germany (Schleswig-Holstein, N = 1500) at two time points, gathering a total of four responses from each learner (12.000 essays).  We expect individual factors (level 1), classroom factors (level 2) and system factors (level 3) to be substantial predictors of writing skills on upper secondary level. Based on our literature review, we expect previous writing skills as well as English receptive skills to be the strongest level 1 predictors of subsequent writing skills, followed by cognitive abilities and motivational characteristics, i.e., academic self-concept and interest. Concerning the level 2 effects, we expect learners’ familiarity with the genre of the English argument essay to be the strongest predictor, either because they studied such texts as models and/or actively practiced writing them. The project has a pedagogic focus and will investigate to what degree classroom factors such as peer-feedback, criteria-based assessment or teaching of lexico-semantic structures predict writing skills. Concerning systemic factors (level 3), we expect to find the relationship ‘lower baccalaureate rate = better student performances’ to be mirrored in our data. The final analysis of these groups of variables will be conducted in the framework of multilevel analysis (MLA). Beyond these substantial research questions, the project strives to apply and evaluate modern artificial intelligence (AI)-based techniques of evaluating texts. In addition to rigorously trained human raters, the automated essay scoring engine e-rater® will be used to measure key aspects of learners’ writing skills:  the ability to compose grammatical, well-punctuated sentences, to choose appropriate genre-specific vocabulary, and to structure their compositions coherently by use of connectors and linking words. E-rater will help to overcome high costs associated with human scoring and avoid biased artefacts due to harshness and leniency effects. The project thus lays the groundwork for an exciting new paradigm for teaching und assessing writing competences that will be of great value for teachers, universities and educational governance throughout Europe.
Keywords: English, automated essay evaluation, classroom, competence, writing

Title: Eratosthenes: Deep generative modeling for indoor and outdoor positioning with fingerprinting methods
Abstract:
The proliferation of Location Based Services through smart devices has supported a variety of services. Unlike outdoor positioning, where systems such as the GPS or Galileo are considered a de facto standard, indoor positioning has presented systems utilizing a big variety of technologies and positioning methods. The main categorical division of these methods is set between ranging and fingerprinting methods. Moreover, the recent emergence of the usage of Internet-of-Things (IoT) technologies and their usage in creating Low Power Wide Area Networks (LPWAN) has shaped a new landscape in the field of outdoor localization. The low-power devices used in LPWANs cannot afford the battery consumption of a Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) chip set, such as the GPS. Therefore, an alternative approach is needed in order to localize these low power devices. Similarly, to the indoor positioning, ranging and fingerprinting methods are two main competing approaches for LPWAN positioning as well. Fingerprinting methods generally offer a higher accuracy of localization but suffer from the disadvantage of requiring a tedious and costly data collection phase. Since fingerprinting is a purely data-driven approach, the way data are collected, the volume of the collected data and the way they are utilized in the modeling phase determine the cost and the performance of such methods. In practice, the main barrier that often prevents the selection of fingerprinting is the data collection requirement.
In the Eratosthenes (deep gEneRative modeling for indoor And ouTdoor pOSitioning wiTH fingErprintiNg mEthodS) project we propose a reproducible and systematic study of the potential contributions of generative modeling in fingerprinting localization methods. Our envisaged utilization of generative models is threefold. Initially, (i) we will investigate the concept of fingerprint augmentation through generative modeling. Achieving a reliable generation of fingerprints could have a great impact on how fingerprinting positioning systems are designed, tuned and deployed. Secondly, (ii) we will examine the potential benefits of encoding the fingerprints in the more compact representation of a latent space provided by (variational) autoencoders and operating lightweight ML models on this latent space. Lastly, the most ambitious part of Eratosthenes is (iii) the incorporation of crowdsourced, unlabeled data, in order to strengthen the predictive capabilities of the positioning model, by using Semi-Supervised Learning with deep generative models. Currently, all the volume of unlabeled data that occurs during the operation of positioning systems is only used to feed the model which produces position estimates. Utilizing these huge volumes of data for learning a better latent representation and improving the positioning model would constitute a paradigm shift for the field. 
The indoor positioning research hasn't integrated in a systematic way the recent breakthroughs of the machine learning field. Moreover, during the last few years, there has been an effort to strengthen the consistent evaluation, the comparability and the reproducibility of published works of the field. In this regard, and in terms of the project’s implementation, we will use the most relevant public datasets, that function as benchmarks and will proceed with an open-data, open-code policy. The ambition of the project is to offer a systematic, rigorous, unambiguous, reproducible and consistent overview of the capabilities of generative models to improve fingerprinting techniques, which is a missing piece of the puzzle of the field. The unconventionality of the approach and the potential of a scale-up improvement of the trade-off between improved accuracy and reduced data collection effort is truly appealing. Moreover, the impact of potentially mitigating the barrier of the data collection effort would be the shaping of a new landscape in deployed positioning systems.
Keywords: IoT, deep learning, generative modelling, indoor positioning, localisation, machine learning, outdoor positioning, variational autoencoders

Title: Online Diarization Enhanced by recent Speaker identification and Structuredprediction Approaches (ODESSA)
Abstract:
Speaker diarization is an unsupervised process which aims to identify each speaker within an audio stream and to determine when each speaker is active. It considers that the number of speakers, their identities and their speech turns are all unknown.
Speaker diarization has become an important key technology in many domains such as content-based information retrieval, voice biometrics, forensics or social-behavioral analysis. Examples of applications of speaker diarization include speech and speaker indexing, speaker recognition (in the presence of multiple speakers), speaker role detection, speech-to-text transcription, speech-to-speech translation and audiovisual content structuring.

Although speaker diarization has been studied for almost two decades, current state-of-the-art systems suffer from many limitations. Such systems are extremely domain-dependent. For instance, a speaker diarization system trained on radio/TV broadcast news experiences
drastically degraded performance when tested on a different type of recordings such as radio/TV debates, meetings, lectures, conversational telephone speech or conversational voice-over-IP speech. Overlapping speech, the spontaneous speaking style, background noise, music and other non-speech sources (laugh, applause, etc.) are all nuisance factors which badly affect the quality of speaker diarization.

Furthermore, most existing work addresses the problem of offline speaker diarization: the system has full access to the entire audio recording beforehand and no real time processing is required. Therefore, the multi-pass processing over the same data is feasible and a bunch of
elegant machine learning tools can be used. Nevertheless, these compromises are not admissible in real-time applications mainly when it comes to public security and fight against terrorism and cyber-criminality.

Moreover, after an initial step of segmentation into speech turns, most approaches address speaker diarization as a bag-of-speech-turns clustering problem and do not take into account the inherent temporal structure of interactions between speakers. One goal of the project is
to integrate this information and to exploit structured prediction techniques to improve over standard hierarchical clustering methods.

Speaker diarization is inherently related to speaker recognition. In recent years, the performance of state-of-the-art speaker recognition systems has improved enormously on account of new recognition paradigms such as i-vectors and deep learning, new session compensation techniques such as probabilistic linear discriminant analysis, and new score normalization techniques such as adaptive symmetric score normalization.
However, existing speaker diarization systems do not take full advantages of these new techniques. Therefore, another goal of the project involves their adaptation to speaker
diarization, and thus to fill the research gap in the current literature.

To evaluate the proposed algorithms and to ensure their genericness, different existing databases will be considered such as NIST SRE 2008 summed-channel telephone data, NIST RT 2003-2004 conversational telephone data, REPERE TV broadcast data and AMI
meeting corpus. Furthermore, we will collect a medium-size database that suits our main application involving the fight against cyber-criminality.
Keywords: cyber-criminality, deep learning, i-vectors, speaker diarization, speaker recognition

Title: Differentiating and Broadening the Language of Conflict Transformation – Track Two Dialogue in Asymmetric Intergroup Conflict and Beyond
Abstract:
Background: Intergroup violence such as the October 7th, 2023 terror attack inflicts fundamental harm to individuals and societies. While massive escalations in the Middle East or Ukraine are substantial setbacks for peaceful change, conflict parties eventually must engage in dialogue. Promising approaches, such as unofficial Track Two dialogues need to be strengthened and better understood. However, limited data on differential effects of these interventions exist. Other polarization contexts might also profit from dialogue approaches tested in intergroup conflict. 
Overall Objectives: My 1-year Postdoc.Mobility Return Fellowship assesses the association between process- and outcome factors in Israeli/Palestinian Track Two dialogue based on individual- and group predispositions. I will capitalize on my past investments in setting up assessment formats of a unique conflict dialogue corpus. My objectives are: (i) to assess process- and outcome factors of dialogue based on individual- and group factors; (ii) to investigate broader applications of third-party dialogue approaches within affective polarization settings.
Methods: Computer-assisted text analysis offers reliable measurements of psychological change. During the 2-year Postdoc Mobility fellowship at the Herbert C. Kelman Institute (HKI), I successfully worked and published on data from Kelman’s huge data corpus in collaboration with Stanford’s ‘Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence’ (Johannes C. Eichstaedt). I could show how dialogue impacts linguistic conflict transformation markers. As a next logical step, I will examine the differential dialogue antecedents. During the 1-year Postdoc Return, I would have the unique opportunity to study this rich dataset further, engaging in the first investigations of the differential effects of third-party dialogues using closed- and open natural-language methods such as LIWC or topic modeling in protracted intergroup conflict.
Results & Impact: Linguistic analysis of conflict discourse points practitioners and researchers to effective evidence-based psychological mechanisms facilitating change in intergroup conflict. Expected outcomes include empirical results on distinctive dialogue patterns for conflict transformation. Results and methods applications will also support political decision-making aiming for integrative agreements. A deeper understanding of these effects will contribute to reducing escalation risks in intergroup conflict and affective polarization.
Keywords: Israel-Palestine conflict, Track Two Diplomacy, conflict mediation, intergroup conflict, natural language processing

Title: TOPAZ: Topology of Alzheimer's
Abstract:
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the sixth-leading cause of death for Americans ages 65 years and older. It is an irreversible, progressive brain disorder that slowly destroys memory and, eventually, an individual’s ability to perform even the simplest tasks, such as bathing, feeding, and dressing. Beyond the immediate health consequences, the societal costs are of epidemic proportion, thus making AD a pressing public health and medical problem. With disease-modifying treatment trials still unsuccessful at the present time and only medications to treat symptoms available, an emerging research initiative is to identify approaches to intervene before the damage begins, making it potentially possible to prevent AD.

As AD is known to affect brain connectivity, analysing said connectivity can lead to a better understanding of how the disease progresses. The proposed project is in a unique position: on the one hand, advances in imaging techniques have resulted in a large number of data sets available. The Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), for example, has recruited cohorts that are monitored over a prolonged period of time, using a variety of imaging techniques and reporting numerous clinical scores.  On the other hand, recent advances in data analysis methods resulted in the development of topological data analysis (TDA), a new domain that employs methods from algebraic topology and differential topology to study the connectivity of complex data sets in a variety of different application areas. We propose using these methods to analyse brain connectivity based on neuroimaging data. This will necessitate the development of new TDA methods for handling time-varying data—a challenge that is hitherto only partially addressed by previous research in the context of low-dimensional signal processing or time series analysis. Moreover, making use of recent advances in topology-based machine learning, we also aim to analyse time-varying topological changes in a supervised and unsupervised setting in order to (i) build predictive models (for predicting AD severity and progression), and (ii) to detect patient subgroups (with a similar progression of AD).

This project will generate new knowledge on AD progression, which will help guide future research into the topic. Since this project will be performed under the auspices of clinicians that are experts in AD, it the results of the predictive models and the patient subgroups can also be linked back to clinical scores and lab measurements, for example. This can lead to insights about (clinical) markers that predict AD progression. Finally, we will make our code and analyses publicly available as an open source project to share them with the research community at large and fostering new collaborations.
Keywords: Alzheimer's Disease, Connectivity Analysis, Machine Learning, Persistent Homology, Time-varying Data, Topological Data Analysis

Title: Spectral analysis of fluorescently labeled amyloids
Abstract:
The self-assembly of prion precursors into oligomers and fibers has been linked to several  neurodegenerative and systemic disorders. In particular, the aggregation of Amyloid-ß (Aß), tau and  a-synuclein in brain tissue have been associated with the neuropathological process of Alzheimer’s  (AD) and Parkinson’s disease (PD). Numerous studies have shown that not only these aggregates can propagate from cell-to-cell in a prion-like manner, but their toxicity and linked pathology strongly depends on their conformations, defining different strains of amyloid. The characterization of the biologically relevant strains remains hard to determine experimentally.

To overcome this problem, I propose to implement a computational multicomponent spectral analysis pipeline that will allow to efficiently discriminate amyloid strains. Several fluorescent dyes, such as Congo red and thioflavin, are known to specifically bind to fibrils. Furthermore, their emission spectrum is modulated by the conformation of the fibril. In this project, I will use machine learning to analyze the spectral information of fluorescent microscope image and determine the strains of amyloid. 

The pipeline developed in this project will allow to characterize the composition of brain aggregates in vitro, in vivo and in brain tissue. Such a method could also greatly aid biophysical studies of amyloids by quickly assessing the quality and composition of samples, as well as give molecular insights linked to the different phenotypes. This understanding should lay the groundwork for the development of effective treatments for AD, PD and other neurodegenerative diseases linked to prions.
Keywords: Alzheimer’s disease, Amyloid strains, Machine learning, Neurodegenerative disease, Prions, Structure-sensitive fluorescent probe

Title: Neuronal organization and behavioral functions of multimodal object representations in zebrafish
Abstract:
Background and general aim. Brains learn models of the world that play pivotal roles in cognitive behaviors. An important component of such models are experience-dependent representations of physical or abstract objects that integrate information from sensory systems and memory. However, it remains poorly understood how objects are represented to support computations underlying cognition, how object representations interact with cognitive maps, and how they are used to instruct behavior. We will analyze multimodal object representations in head-fixed, adult zebrafish during active exploration and learning in a virtual reality (VR). We focus on two telencephalic areas, Dp and Dc, that are related to piriform cortex and isocortex, respectively. We will examine multisensory integration, pattern completion, cognitive maps and the geometrical organization of neuronal population dynamics in activity space. Moreover, we will manipulate activity to examine the role of object representations and cognitive maps for behavior and cognition.
Specific aims:
Aim 1: Cellular and molecular organization of Dp. We will analyze gene expression by single cell RNA sequencing and in situ hybridization to classify cell types and delineate functional subregions in Dp/Dc.
Aim 2: Multimodality, geometry and plasticity of object representations in Dp. We will measure activity across large populations of Dp neurons in head-fixed, adult zebrafish during behavior in a VR. We will analyze how representations of olfactory and multimodal objects emerge during exploration and associative learning. Pattern completion within and across sensory modalities, behavioral generalization, and additional processes that may support cognition will be examined through manipulations of objects in the VR. The geometrical organization of representations in activity space and other properties will be analyzed using advanced multivariate methods.
 Aim 3: Object representations and maps in Dc. Similar experiments and analyses as in Aim 2 will be performed to examine multisensory object representations and cognitive maps in Dc. We will specifically explore how object representations in Dp interact with more abstract representations and cognitive maps in Dc.
Aim 4: Causal manipulations of object representations and maps. Using optogenetic approaches, we will manipulate object representations to determine their influence on cognitive maps and behaviors in the VR.
Expected value: We expect fundamental insights into neuronal computations underlying cognitive behaviors that will be of high interest not only in neuroscience but also for translational research and artificial intelligence. The results are likely to go beyond findings obtained in other model systems and to open a spectrum of new opportunities for future studies addressing mechanisms of cognition.
Keywords: Cognition, In vivo imaging, Learning, Multisensory integration, Neuronal circuit, Neuronal computation, Virtual reality, Zebrafish

Title: Validation of Artificial Intelligence Time Resolved Fluorescence method for the real-time monitoring of critical pollutants in industrial and municipal effluents
Abstract:
Due to growing urbanization, industrialization and agriculture, natural water is increasingly threatened by the release of synthetic chemicals into the environment. Both diffuse pollution (e.g., agricultural activities) and point pollution (e.g., domestic and industrial activities) are of high concern because they alter water ecosystem functions and constitute risks for human health (e.g., contaminated food and drinking water), welfare and economy (e.g., access restriction to recreational waters or prohibition of commercial fishing). This project aims at tackling the environmental problem of domestic and industrial point sources of pollution by monitoring critical chemicals in effluents and by providing decision-makers with timely actionable knowledge in order to reduce the release of these compounds in the environment.
While conventional laboratory-based methods usually have good analytical performances, they are poorly adapted to the provision of timely and representative information. They rely on sophisticated sampling strategy (expensive and time-consuming sample transfer to offsite laboratories and sample preparation), thus needing time to provide results. In situ and online analytical techniques are thus urgently needed. 
To overcome these limitations, we will validate a new concept of measure based on time-resolved fluorescence for continuous in-situ monitoring of critical chemicals such as glyphosate, phosphonates, sulphonates, chelating surfactants and PFASs. This project will be based on an earlier patented method on the dosage of limestone and corrosion inhibitors via TRF technique. The technique will be supported by using a standard addition approach and artificial intelligence training (AI-TRF). The quantification procedure will be optimized to monitor a large variety of contaminants commonly present in effluents by both laboratory and mesocosm assays feedbacks. The performances of AI-TRF prototype will be compared to those of conventional laboratory-based techniques (e.g., LC-MSMS, ICP-MS). In a second phase, we will deploy AI-TRF in real effluents to acquire information on the release of contaminants in sewage networks (signaling of exceedance of limit concentrations and production of information on the types of potential sources). In this study, we will focus on (pre)treated wastewaters because they have a less complex matrix than raw wastewaters, but the ultimate goal is to provide a tool that can be deploy at any site of a sewage network to obtain the maximal amount of relevant information.
With this project, we would like to first prove that AI-TRF should be an alternative technology for timeliness quantifications of pollutants comparing to conventional analytical methods currently used by environmental agencies. Secondly, the in-situ TRF installations could drastically increase the spatial coverage of monitoring campaign, thus generating deeper knowledge on critical pollutants, facilitating the development of policies concerning chemical production and consumption as well as on wastewater treatment strategies; thus sustainably preserving the environment. Third, artificial intelligence could support, not only the hard-working tasks normally done continuatively by technical staff, but also the implementation of new generation of state-of-the-art devices.
Keywords: Artificial intelligence training, Chemical pollution of waters, Continuous in-situ monitoring, Domestic and industrial effluents, Mesocosm and in-situ experiments, Time-resolved fluorescence

Title: Hybrid Machine Translation for Morphologically Rich Languages
Abstract:
Hybrid Machine Translation (MT) profits from both data-driven and rule-based methods. In a translation scenario involving a low-resource language, it is reasonable to build a rule-based core system and enhance this prototype in a second step with statistical methods.

In the first two years of the project we have implemented rule-based MT systems for Spanish-German and Spanish-Quechua. In the third year, we will improve those prototypes with statistical methods, e.g. use language models on the target side to rank translation options. Not only will we evaluate both rule-based prototypes compared to the hybrid systems, but we also will compare the two language pairs Spanish-German and Spanish-Quechua. This will be especially interesting due to the fact that we have much more textual material for German than for Cuzco Quechua: We will measure at what rate the hybrid system improves by increasing the amount of training material for the statistical parts, and we will be able to draw conclusions on how the Spanish-Quechua system can profit from more texts (monolingual and bilingual).

We have already trained and evaluated several statistical MT systems Spanish-German that will serve as a baseline for further experiments with our rule-based and hybrid prototypes.

In addition to the MT systems, we have prepared a trilingual parallel corpus of 4000 sentences in German, Spanish and Quechua for treebanking. The Spanish-German part has been annotated and aligned completely, while the Spanish-Quechua treebank will be finished in the third year. The annotation of the Quechua part takes more time, as a suitable annotation scheme had to be developed as part of this project. The treebanks will contribute to the improvement of the MT systems: We will use extracted transfer rules from the parallel trees to expand the grammatical coverage of our MT systems.

The translation systems, as well as the treebanks will be made available through a user-friendly web interface. 

There are several reasons to apply for a one year extension of this project: Firstly, we want to increase the coverage of our machine translation systems by adding and evaluating different statistical parts to the rule-based prototypes. We will use machine-learning techniques to overcome the shortcomings of the prototypes (e.g. how to treat unknown words) and optimize the translation systems.

Secondly, there are several challenging linguistic phenomena in both language pairs that we want to explore further. Those include, among others, the distinction of exclusive and inclusive first person plural forms in Quechua, but also the treatment of German possessive pronouns that are marked for gender of the possessor. As in the source language Spanish possessive pronouns are not distinguished by gender, this information needs to be inferred from the context.

Thirdly, we will bundle a basic language resource kit (BLARK) for Cuzco Quechua, that contains all the tools and linguistic resources we created in this project. As part of this effort we will intensify our cooperation with the Universidad Nacional San Antonio Abad del Cusco (UNSAAC) that has resulted from our visit to Peru in the first year.

Finally, we want to improve the Spanish-Quechua version of Bilingwis, our parallel concordance system. At the moment, the word alignments are extracted from a bilingual dictionary because we did not have enough parallel texts for this language pair to achieve good results with statistical methods. As we have several more parallel texts collected during our trip to Peru, we will add those to the parallel corpus in Bilingwis and improve not only the alignment quality, but also increase the number of translation options for a given query.
Keywords: Corpus Annotation, Hybrid Translation System, Lesser-Resourced Languages, Machine Translation

Title: Party politics and the politicization of health care
Abstract:
This project investigates how political parties have politicized the issue of health care in Western democracies since the 1960s. While health care has often been viewed as a “valence issue”, i.e. a topic with little ideological conflict and broad agreement on its importance, the recent politicization of the COVID-19 pandemic, partisan polarization, and rising support for populist parties have highlighted a more contested partisan politics of health care. This politicization now seems to occur increasingly on a cultural dimension, related to aspects of identity politics (e.g. migrants’ health care entitlements), the environment (e.g. health care sustainability), and public health (e.g. vaccine acceptance), rather than solely on the traditional economic dimension on the role of the state in health care. However, there is a lack of systematic evidence on parties’ emphasis on these distinct ideological dimensions of health care and how this politicization interrelates with voter preferences. Addressing this gap is crucial, as a polarization of health care along both economic and cultural lines could deepen electoral divides and potentially undermine consensus on health care and health care reform in the electorate.
To fill this gap, this project examines three research questions:
(1) To what extent do political parties politicize health care along the economic and cultural dimension?
(2) Do voter preferences predict the type and extent of health care politicization by political parties?
(3) Does the politicization of health care increase electoral divisions among voters?
The project develops a theoretical framework building on the conceptual distinction between economic and cultural ideological aspects of health care. It posits that while all parties may pay more attention to health care due to demographic and fiscal pressures, parties’ choice to politicize either economic or cultural ideological aspects of health care is driven by strategic incentives to attract voters with differing priorities on economic and cultural issues.
The empirical analysis uses a mixed-methods approach, combining a large-N comparative analysis with an in-depth study of four core countries. First, for a sample of 25 Western democracies between 1960 and 2023, novel measures of health care politicization are created by classifying sentences from 2,661 electoral manifestos of 424 political parties, using both human coding and large language models. Because health care provision is often decentralized and regional party positions may differ from national ones, regional party manifestos are also coded for a subset of cases. The data from the party manifestos are then matched with existing individual-level voter surveys to assess the alignment between political parties’ politicization of health care and voter preferences. Second, in the four core countries (Canada, Germany, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom), an original voter-level survey is conducted and linked with the coded party manifestos. This survey allows a detailed examination of the alignment in health care politicization between parties and voters and includes a conjoint survey experiment to provide causal evidence on voter support for different forms of politicization and on the short-term electoral impact of politicizing health care.
This project offers the first systematic analysis of the economic and cultural frames that political parties use when positioning themselves on health care across numerous democracies over more than six decades. It generates new evidence on the alignment between party and voter positions on health care and on the electoral impact of health care politicization through survey experiments. The project illuminates how health care is intertwined with broader electoral transformations and multidimensional political conflicts along economic and cultural lines. Therefore, party politics can no longer be downplayed in the study of health care.

Title: Development of High-Efficiency Push-Button Low-Field Cardiovascular MRI
Abstract:
Cardiovascular disease results in significant morbidity and mortality, making it the leading cause of death in industrialized nations and posing a substantial burden on global healthcare systems. In addressing this challenge, cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) has emerged as a non-invasive and safe technology for evaluating cardiovascular anatomy, function, blood flow, and tissue characteristics to enhance the diagnosis of cardiovascular disease. CMR has earned its reputation as the gold standard for assessing cardiovascular structure, function, and damaged myocardium.

Despite compelling evidence, such as its inclusion in guidelines by major European and American cardiovascular societies, CMR has not seen widespread adoption beyond large urban academic centers in high-income countries. The reasons for this limited uptake include the high cost and time-intensive nature of contemporary CMR, which demands specialized technologist and physician expertise. These factors make CMR challenging to justify in regions with limited MRI resources.

While more cost-effective low-field MRI systems for human use have nearly disappeared from the market due to their lower signal-to-noise ratio, recent progress in hardware, software, and artificial intelligence has generated enthusiasm among academics and industry professionals. These advancements have sparked the hypothesis that such opportunity can be harnessed to create new generations of more efficient, cost-effective, sustainable, and widely accessible low-field MRI systems, even in areas traditionally lacking access to MRI technology.

The recent introduction of high-performing 0.55T systems in the marketplace is a promising development. However, challenges persist in seizing the opportunities presented by these low-field systems to expand their global reach for CMR. These challenges include addressing operator dependence, addressing image quality concerns related to lower signal-to-noise ratios and challenging fat signal suppression, improving exam efficiency, achieving comprehensive 3D organ coverage, and characterizing injured myocardial tissue without contrast agents.

In a deliberate and mechanistic endeavor, a tried and tested team of interdisciplinary investigators is committed to addressing the above challenges. We propose to leverage recent innovations at CHUV with our newly acquired 0.55T system. Our approach involves implementing the "free-running framework" (FRF) that enables highly efficient and user-friendly 3D imaging of the heart's anatomy, function, and blood flow at low field strength. The FRF approach integrates a complete self-navigation concept, eliminating the need for ECG, breath-holds, and navigators. Furthermore, it replaces prospective scan parameter adjustments and scan plane planning with a simple mouse click, enabling a fully flexible and retrospective analysis of 3D image data in both time and space.

By expanding the FRF concept with multiple signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)-enhancing strategies, new innovative fat signal suppression techniques, and proprietary technology for non-contrast characterization of injured myocardial tissue, we intend to thoroughly explore the opportunities offered by these altered physical conditions at low field strength. In a deliberate translational research pursuit, we plan to validate this new technology through reference standard comparisons. This research is aimed at making powerful, time-efficient, and operator-independent concepts available at low field strength to facilitate the global dissemination of CMR for improved patient management.

Title: decodePI: decoding the genetic architecture of protein-protein interactions
Abstract:
Protein-protein interactions represent an essential aspect of most biological functions. A better understanding of how the sequence of two proteins determines quantitatively the affinity and specificity of these interactions will improve our ability to predict the functional impact of genetic variation as well as design new synthetic proteins of therapeutic or bioengineering interests. Recent advances in artificial intelligence and generative biology have opened the door to such developments. However, training deep learning models to predict affinity from sequence will require vast amounts of data that cover the wide and complex genetic landscape of protein-protein interaction affinity.
With decodePPI, we propose to employ deepPCA to systematically mutagenize three human protein interaction domain families: the SH3, bHLH and Death domains. We will quantitatively measure the effects of all possible single amino acid mutants on the whole interaction profile of each family member, generating a dataset of 20 million binding affinity measurements that exceeds publicly available data by several order of magnitude. Our original approach leverages the combinatorial nature of protein interaction domain families to sample a wide and diverse portion of their genetic landscape. Measuring the impact of mutations at this scale, across all members of the same family on the interaction against all other members, is required to detect the full spectrum of mutation impacts in different sequence and structural contexts. We will employ state-of-the-art deep learning approaches to train generative models that predict affinity from sequence for these families. In addition, this project will provide new insights into their biology by revealing the sequence determinants of interaction specificity and their evolution at the level of whole families as well as structural mechanisms of disease mutations found in these families. While the yeast-based deepPCA offers the advantage of a reductionist approach to access mutation effects on affinity, we also aim at developing a similar assay in human cells. This assay would provide complementary to the yeast-based assay by providing information on mutation effects in a protein’s native cellular context, and open the door for high-throughput interactomics directly in human cells.
decodePPI will shed a new light on the genetic architecture of protein function and assess its complexity, a fundamental question with important implications for predictability. The experimental and analytical framework developed here will pave the way towards generalised models of protein-protein interaction affinity and contribute to the generative biology revolution.
Keywords: deep mutational scanning, generative biology, genetic architecture of protein function, protein domain families, protein-protein interactions

Title: Deep learning-based whole-slide image analysis  for immune ecology and cancer prediction in  Barrett’s oesophagus
Abstract:
Barrett’s oesophagus(BO) is the initial step in the progression to adenocarcinoma in the distal oesophagus. The lack of an effective risk stratification system for patients with BO causes frequent avoidable endoscopic interventions, alongside the loss of significant time and resources for patients who will never develop oesophageal adenocarcinoma (OAC). Given its constant selective pressure on pre-cancerous cells, the immune microenvironment is a promising factor in solving this issue. There are two crucial aspects to focus on regarding the tumour microenvironment forward. Firstly, neoplastic cells continuously interact with the immune microenvironment during their evolution. Therefore, the information extracted from the immune landscape can provide measures of the risk of progression. Secondly, immunomodulation treatments have been advantageous recently for many other neoplastic situations and can be applied in BO too.
This proposed project is for a Postdoc.Mobility Fellowship at the Department of Translational Molecular Pathology at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, USA, uses state-of-art AI-based computer vision and ecological spatial statistics. It aims to investigate the immune ecology and tissue architecture in BO in the context of neoplastic progression towards adenocarcinoma. 
The unique Seattle Cohort biorepository of systematically collected endoscopic histopathology biopsies to investigate the evolution of BO ecology and morphology will be employed for this study. The subset, which will be used for this study, consists of 4,284 longitudinal BO biopsies from 24 cancer outcome and 24 non-cancer outcome patients from four locations at three-time points. An AI-based computational pathology tool will be developed for making cancer outcome predictions in BO biopsy images. Firstly, a computer vision pipeline will be developed to classify single cells and characterise the tissue architecture. The deep learning model will be able to map the spatial distribution of heterogeneous cell types in routine BO biopsy slide images. Following the image analysis, BO tissues will be analysed using spatial statistical methods to identify significant patterns. Subsequently, we will test the changes in the immune microenvironment through time in Barrett’s landscape and also aim to define cancer progression-related immune ecology features. Finally, the relationship between genomic changes and immune ecology will be tested.
As the seventh hallmark of cancer, inflammation suppresses anti-tumour response, induces the proliferation of premalignant cells and enhances their survival. Having this knowledge as the foundation, it’s hypothesised that there is a strong link between Barrett’s landscape, immune microenvironment, and carcinogenesis. The discovery of cancer outcome-related landscape patterns requires intensive computation. This study may reveal the interactions between immune and epithelial cells by combining state-of-art computational image analysis tools and spatial ecology statistics.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study that quantifies the spatiotemporal dynamics of tissue inflammation and architecture, followed by spatial analysis based on landscape ecology principles in a sizeable precancer cohort, using fully automated AI-based image analysis tools. This study will create a benchmark for similar pre-cancerous conditions of other organs driven by chronic inflammation.

Title: Semantic SLAM: Adding Semantic Information to Robotic Environment Perception using Visual Object Recognition
Abstract:
The research stay aims to initiate a research collaboration between the host researcher, Prof. Vittorio Ferrari; and the visiting researcher Dr. Javier Civera. The topic of the stay is to fuse object recognition and 3D estimation from the information provided by a standard camera, with the final goal of producing a 3D reconstruction of the scene imaged by the camera which is dense --that is, every part of the scene is reconstructed-- and semantic --that is, every object in the scene has been identified. 
The proposed semantic mapping will be applied to improve the environment perception in mobile robots: while traditional non-semantic robotic mapping is enough for certain basic tasks (e.g., navigation), there is a great interest in semantic mapping in order to robots autonomously perform more elaborated tasks (e.g., grasping an object). Similarly to living beings, a more sophisticated and evolved perception of the environment by a robot always has a consequence a better performance in a wider variety of tasks.
The visiting researcher has a recognized experience in 3D estimation from image sequences with application to robotics. The host researcher has a wide and recognized expertise in object recognition from images. The expertise of both researchers is, in this sense, complementary.
The stay is proposed to produce 3 specific outcomes: First, a detailed road map towards the ultimate goal of dense semantic mapping for robotics with specific mention to the most important research challenges. Second, publications in top conferences and journals with the scientific results achieved during and after the stay. And third, demonstrative code implementing the algorithms and showing experimental results.
The application of the general object recognition research to the specific field of robotics implies a variety of topics scarcely addressed by the traditional research made by the Computer Vision community. Some of this topics are: 1) The need for both semantic and geometric perception, 2) image input in the form of high frame rate image sequences, 3) potential of the algorithms for real-time implementations, 4) strong constraints for sequential, instead of batch, processing, 5) active perception derived from the possibility of robot motion, 6) the possibility to integrate propioceptive robot sensing, and 7) the need for a high robustness. 
This topic list is neither exhaustive nor complete, it will be the first task of the stay to make a complete study of the problem using the complementary expertise of both host and visiting researchers. After that, a demonstrative code integrating the existing state of the art will be developed, in order to have a first system to build future research. Finally, a challenging topic will be selected and research will be focused on a particular problem. The rest of the identified research challenges will be written down in a report and will serve as the basis for mid and long term collaboration.
Keywords: Computer Vision for Robotics, Monocular SLAM, Object Recognition from Images, Semantic SLAM, Structure from Motion

Title: Towards Building Self-Learning and Cooperative World Models
Abstract:
World models are models that allow us to make predictions about the future based on past observations. The ability to predict the future is a fundamental skill for planning, decision-making, and problem-solving, and has a wide range of applications in fields such as robotics, computer vision, and machine learning. In this project, we aim to build world models that can learn autonomously and through collaborative interactions on real multi-modal data, such as images, videos, and audio, and that can be used to develop autonomous robots that can safely navigate unknown environments, among other applications.

An important aspect to make the training of these models scalable is that they are built through self-supervised learning, i.e., from guidance that is directly extracted from data rather than from humans. The project will focus on three key questions: 1) how to develop a representation of the world that allows for predictions of plausible futures, 2) how to adapt to new tasks at test time, and 3) how multiple experts can learn from each other and develop a communication protocol. The first question will investigate the relationship between representations of the future, its uncertainty, and the emergence of abstract concepts. The second question will explore models that can adapt to new data and "reason" with it. The third question will aim to develop a collective intelligence of multiple world models and evaluate the alignment of their communication with natural human language.
Keywords: Representation Learning, Self-Supervised Learning, Unsupervised Learning, Video Processing, collaborative learning, representation learning, self-supervised learning, test-time adaptation, world models

Title: Relational Deep Learning for Reliable Time Series Forecasting at Scale
Abstract: In modern cyber-physical systems, physical and virtual sensors continuously produce large amounts of data. Such pervasive sensor networks acquire partial heterogeneous observations at different rates and scales. The result is a large collection of correlated, heterogeneous, and irregular time series that learning systems should continuously integrate and process for making accurate predictions. Exploiting temporal dependencies as well as relationships across time series, as inductive, architectural, biases, is crucial to building models that can scale. Proper inductive biases, i.e., soft or hard structural assumptions steering the learning system toward the most plausible models, are among the key ingredients for the success of deep learning systems. Graph deep learning methods allow for processing and forecasting any subset of time series while accounting for the relationships among them. This is achieved by relying on message-passing operators and graph-based input representations. The limit of these models is that they only work at a fixed spatiotemporal scale, processing observations at each time step and pair of related sensors. In other words, the processing happens at a single scale, which makes it difficult to account for long-range spatiotemporal dependencies and multi-scale dynamics. The objective of this project is to tackle the problem and overcome these limits toward general relational deep learning for time series forecasting. To achieve this, I will design hierarchical relational forecasting models able to operate on subsets of time series at adaptive spatiotemporal resolutions. The proposed models will be able to jointly process hierarchical aggregates (clusters) at different temporal scales (e.g., hourly, daily, monthly). Said novel approach will enable graph-based predictors to go beyond the modeling of pairwise relationships by directly accounting for higher-order spatiotemporal dependencies. The application potential is endless and revolutionary; however, the resulting forecasting architecture would have to be scalable and reliable. Therefore, a major challenge will be designing neural operators that can scale up effectively and developing uncertainty quantification methods that fit the application constraints. In this regard, I plan to combine deep learning methods with scalable components based on randomization. Moreover, I will design ad-hoc uncertainty quantification methods to provide trustworthy confidence intervals for supporting decision-making. The introduced forecasting methodologies will be applied to tackle high-impact real-world problems in energy analytics and healthcare. The project will be carried out at the University of Oxford in the lab led by geometric deep learning pioneer Prof. Michael Bronstein, with the external collaboration of Prof. Filippo Maria Bianchi (UiT the Arctic University of Norway), renowned graph and time series processing expert.
Keywords: graph machine learning, hierarchical forecasting, relational deep learning, time series analysis, time series forecasting

Title: Large-scale Annotation and Alignment of Parallel Corpora for the Investigation of Linguistic Variation
Abstract:
Translated documents in multiple languages (here: parallel documents) are highly regarded as valuable resources for various tasks in natural language processing and linguistic research. Parallel corpora are useful for tasks as diverse as word sense disambiguation, terminology extraction and contrastive corpus linguistics. The usefulness of these resources for contrastive linguistics, in particular, has increased tremendously with the possibility to automatically align the texts not only on the sentence level but also on the word level.
We propose to align (sentence alignment and word alignment) and annotate (PoS-Tagging and Parsing) a large parallel corpus for the language pairs English-German, English-French, and English-Spanish. For this purpose we will use two large parallel corpora: the Europarl corpus and the UN-Corpus. In addition, we will align the corpus for the language pairs English-Russian and English-Finnish. The latter language pair enables us to include comparisons with a non-Indoeuropean language in the linguistic research.
Linguistic variation at times involves the choice between the use of an element and its omission (articles, relativizers, pronouns etc.). Modelling such zero or null contexts in a corpus-driven approach is particularly challenging because variable zero elements are difficult to retrieve even from annotated monolingual corpora: While it is possible to extract noun phrases without an article from a parsed corpus, such algorithms have poor precision because a vast number of instances will not allow for a definite or indefinite article. Therefore, we propose to use parallel annotated and word-aligned corpora that will enable us to target constructions with variable optional elements in one of the languages. Our goal is to prove the usefulness of such a large aligned and annotated corpus (LAAC) for the investigation of linguistic variation. As a case in point we will investigate variable article use in these languages, and zero articles in English, in particular. We believe that such a LAAC provides a number of advantages for new insights in these areas.
Studying articles in English is of interest and importance because of the growing influence of non-native English speakers whose first languages do not have articles or that use articles in ways clearly different from English. With the help of our LAAC we will retrieve instances of zero articles of the language pairs in the corpus where both languages have definite and indefinite articles (English, French, German and Spanish). The language pairs English-Russian and English-Finnish will serve to model variable article use in English against the background of typological differences.
In addition, we will build a rich database that models factors influencing variable article choice in the language pairs English and German. These factors include lexical variation in the head noun, the internal structure of the noun phrase (pre- and postmodification), syntactic function of the noun phrase but also discourse-pragmatic functions (given vs. new). The aim for the linguistics part of the project is to arrive at a detailed description of variable article use in English and German using a multi-variate analysis. This will prove useful for purposes of language teaching and machine translation. Because of the element of lexico-grammatical variation, large parallel corpora are a prerequisite for this kind of research.
The challenge for computational linguistics lies in the high-quality alignment and annotation of large corpora and the construction of an efficient and powerful corpus query tool that is able to handle these corpora. Efficient query tools for large monolingual corpora exist but the development of such a tool for parallel corpora is highly innovative.

Title: Improved methods for theoretical materials design
Abstract:
Materials design has become one of the most rapidly increasing fields of condensed matter science during the last years. Discovery of novel materials are called for with potential applications in various technologically relevant fields such as energy production and storage, novel electronic devices, data storage, medical application and catalysis. Instead of synthesizing and characterizing novel materials in time-consuming, expensive experiments, theoretical material scientists have started to create databases obtained from all materials known to date and to systematically analyze them with high-throughput computation methods, trying to gain insight on how chemistry and structures are linked to material properties and to extract patterns from the underlying data. New, innovative computational methods are needed to efficiently characterize the continuously growing amount of materials data, and techniques need to be developed to extrapolate materials properties to design novel, undiscovered compounds with improved properties. 

The presented project is aimed at solving two key limitations in materials design. First, most structure prediction methods do not access the knowledge stored in the large structural databases. By combining the Minima Hopping structure prediction scheme and machine-learning techniques a sophisticated method will be developed to explore new chemistries and to discover compounds with improved or new properties in energy applications. The new method will be applied to real-life challenges in materials design to find thermoelectric and hydrogen storage materials, or materials for use in photovoltaic applications. Second, Quantum Monte Carlo methods will be used to refine the energetic ordering of different phases in various compounds to significantly improve the predictive power by going beyond the accuracy of conventional density functional theory calculations used in current approaches. The outcome of this project will be of great value for many material scientists and will considerably accelerate the theoretical discovery of novel materials.
Keywords: Electronic Structure, Materials Design, Simulation, Structure Prediction
