Title: Develop a prototype on-chip PET with improved gamma-ray interaction position estimation and positron range correction using deep learning
Abstract:
Recent biomedical advances have attempted to tackle the biological complexity of living organisms by generating models on chips, called organoids, to mimic some of the structures and functions of real organs and diseases. The increasing potential of organoids in basic research, clinical diagnosis, tissue engineering and drug development brings a burgeoning demand for dedicated measurement equipment. Positron emission tomography (PET) is the most widely applied clinical methodology to investigate in vivo metabolism or molecular pathways. Monitoring metabolism or other physiologic/pathophysiologic processes within organs-on-chip is critical to refine the new organoid technology to resemble closer in vivo physiology and promote its application in new biological models. However, the current imaging devices for measuring PET tracer uptake in either small animals or 2D cell culture, is inadequate to the task of organoid imaging. 
This project proposes a new concept of a dedicated on-chip PET to make molecular imaging of organoids possible. By restricting the focus of the system, the dedicated on-chip PET system will attain the necessary detection efficiency for imaging microstructures. Technically, this project will improve the estimation of line of response (LOR) by developing a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based projected gradient descent method to reconstruct precisely ?-ray interaction positions based on light patterns measured on five surfaces of the continuous crystals. Furthermore, knowledge of the geometric and physical priors of organoid chips will be employed to decode the positron range. We shall develop a penalized on-chip PET reconstruction algorithm to integrate generative adversarial networks (GANs) for correcting the positron range during image reconstruction. We shall employ transfer learning using Geant4/GATE based on realistic Monte-Carlo simulations to accelerate the development of the proposed deep learning methods before proceeding to fine tuning with experimental data. After optimizing the design of on-chip PET based on other Monte-Carlo simulations, we shall construct a prototype system attaining a resolution bettern than 200 µm, i.e. 25% of the positron range. We shall evaluate the prototype system PET for imaging both physical phantoms and prostate cancer organoids.
Keywords: Deep learning, Image reconstruction, Organoid, PET intrumentation

Title: Mechanisms of global timing percetion and their influence on perception and cognition
Abstract:
Perception is unimaginable without its underlying temporal structure. In the auditory domain, percepts evolve from the integration of temporal patterns over the range of several seconds. Timing integration is crucial for efficient segmentation and perception of our auditory environment be it speech, music and even noise that is usually embedded in a stream of sounds (Bregman, 1990). Despite this ubiquitous importance of timing perception, it remains unknown where and how the brain produces this temporal integration. In an interdisciplinary review we summarized existing knowledge on this topic from the point of view of human system neuroscience, animal electrophysiology and animal behavior (Geiser et al. 2014, Frontiers). By means of fMRI we elucidated for the first time mechanisms of temporal Gestalt perception in humans showing that the capacity to perceive temporal Gestalt relies not only on top-down interpretative processing but related specific inhibitory mechanisms in bottom-up sensory processing (Notter et al._a under review). Standard analyses of brain imaging data (fMRI) are unable to distinguish between different activation patterns within identical neural populations. Using a multivariate machine learning approach we were able to show for the first time, that the auditory cortex can distinguish between perceptually different, but acoustically identical temporal patterns. This finding indicates that both sensory and higher cortical areas are involved in the integration of temporal patterns over time (Notter et al. _b submitted).

There is convincing evidence that the basal ganglia play a specific role in temporal integration. With the help of the here requested extension of this project, we aim to elucidate the specific function of this brain area by investigating temporal integration abilities in patients suffering from neural degeneration involving the basal ganglia (Parkinson’s disease).

Title: Nonlocal geometric regularizers for inverse problems in imaging
Abstract:
Imaging makes possible the generation, analysis and visualization of images from physical measurements. The spectrum of these measurements and their associated imaging modalities are constantly expanding, introducing new research problems that require new solutions and reconstruction methods.
In particular, in the reconstruction of an image from noisy measurements of an object, it is necessary to introduce some prior-knowledge about the object in order to obtain accurate and physically meaningful results. This prior-knowledge is usually formulated in terms of the regularity of the solution, and formally analysed in terms of its first order derivatives by classic regularization methods.
Recently, nonlocal regularization techniques have been introduced in imaging to improve classic regularization methods. These techniques define the concept of nonlocal derivatives in order to exploit the repetitive nature of patterns and structures in natural images; they are thus able to better capture the textures and fine details of images, but research is still limited to nonlocal derivatives of first order.
Another way to improve classic regularization methods relies in geometric concepts, like normal vector to a curve or mean curvature of a surface, to obtain more accurate models of the physical world. The resulting geometric models are described in terms of second order derivatives and lead to minimization problems more difficult to solve, but also result in more accurate reconstructions than classic regularization based on first order derivatives.
A simple question then comes to mind: can we derive nonlocal geometric models that improve nonlocal regularizers, in the same way that classic geometric models improved local regularization? Preliminary results suggest that it is possible and this project further investigates this point. 
This project plans to develop geometric models associated to the nonlocal topology of images and apply them to efficiently solve several inverse problems in imaging. To that purpose, second order differential operators can be defined in the nonlocal framework by concatenation of first order nonlocal derivatives, and the geometric concepts of normal vector to a curve or mean curvature of a surface are thus naturally extended to the nonlocal frame. The first goal of this project is to extend traditional geometric models used in imaging to the nonlocal framework and improve existing nonlocal regularization techniques. This will result in minimization problems computationally expensive and difficult to solve. Consequently, the second goal of this project is to design efficient numerical algorithms to compute meaningful solutions, making use of recent advances in convex optimization and spectral graph theory.
Keywords: computer vision, inverse ill-posed problems, regularization, signal processing

Title: Real Estate Bubbles: Emergence, Deflation, Propagation, and Systemic Risk
Abstract:
Much has changed since the last 10 years, when the so-called “great moderation” was regarded as the biggest success of modern economic theory, and research had found that the term “bubble” was not an attractive explanation for the lack of quantitative understanding of real estate prices (Leung 2004). Now we live in the “great experiment” era of central banks in which a plethora of “code red” policies such as QE, zero interest rates, large-scale asset purchases (leading to de facto currency “wars” and their potential debasement) are being put forward, one after another, without any certainty about the social and economic consequences that these policies might bring about. The “great experiment” will likely continue for one, perhaps two or even more decades (in different forms) as in the Japanese scenario, and many new bubbles in part fuelled by these policies are likely to emerge.

 In this context filled with uncertainty, the central role of the real estate market during the 2008 financial crisis and the systemic risks that the market carries has crystalized a number of important research questions, while obliging to revisit others issues from the past. In this proposal, our guiding post will be the questions raised by Hansen (2012) and Brunnermeier and Oehmke (2012) in their respective surveys about systemic risk and bubbles, which resonate directly with our own research agenda. Specifically, this research will address four significant questions: 1) How do real estate bubbles emerge and how do they deflate? 2) How do real estate bubbles propagate internationally and what are their linkages with booms and bubbles in other assets? 3) How agent behaviors, their interaction, and their expectations influence real estate bubbles in the context of financial frictions? 4) How can we characterize and possibly mitigate the systemic risk of real estate bubbles in the economy?

We will approach these questions with the view, which lies at the core of all research conducted by our group, that the origin of crashes is much more subtle than is often thought, as it is constructed progressively by the market as a whole, as an endogenous self-organizing process. In this sense, the true cause of a crash could be termed a systemic instability and any analysis of the market ought to consider the economy as a complex and dynamic system. Methodologically, we intend to follow a Bayesian approach, which will allow us to study multiple theories and to combine standard macroeconomic research with our understanding of economic systems. We will integrate macroeconomic financial frictions into nonlinear dynamic models that allow for different types of interactions among heterogeneous agents (i.e. varying dependence structures), endogenous risks, and analysis of out-of-equilibrium dynamics. Our empirical research will encompass developing and advanced economies to obtain a comprehensive view of the international real estate markets and to avoid the possible misinterpretations that could result from looking at real markets from the sole lenses of the advanced economies. Furthermore, we will maintain an archeological approach to the data; exploring and contrasting several models while applying statistical learning techniques to allow the data to speak by itself. 

The outcome of this research will not only nurture the scientific debate in traditional academic venues. The systemic risk indicators that we will develop will also feed the Financial Crisis Observatory and the Real Estate Observatory. Both initiatives are under development by our group at ETH Zurich, and are publicly available platforms that aim to inform the general public, and serve as scientific tools to analyze complex economic and financial systems.

Title: Testing the Focal Point Theory of International Adjudication: An Empirical Analysis of the ICJ’s Impact on Maritime Delimitation
Abstract:
International Relations and International Law (IR/IL) literatures often see international judicial bodies as serving to further legal certainty and peaceful resolution of disputes through their rulings. Many scholars argue that international courts not only resolve disputes, but also influence the behavior of states that are not parties to those disputes. They do so by clarifying legal principles and providing focal points for cooperation. Scholars have long suggested that focal points could help actors coordinate their expectations and behavior even in the absence of any threat of sanction or any possibility for enforcement. While we agree that the influence of international courts reaches beyond the specific cases they treat, we take issue with the assumption that their intervention necessarily increases legal certainty and reduces future conflict by constructing focal points. Our project adopts an interdisciplinary lens and a mixed-methods approach to examine the degree to which international judicial bodies can and will provide focal points. In this exploratory study, we pay particular attention to the unintended consequences of international judicial decisions. These may include creating opportunities and incentives for states to adopt incoherent rules and principles in the absence of a clear precedent.  
Our contribution will fill two important gaps in the literature. First, the scholarship has overlooked the possible consequences of judicial interventions that do not result in more certainty or focal points. Second, while the ways in which international law and institutions can provide focal points have been widely discussed, we know little about the conditions under which such a focal point will actually emerge. Beyond contributing to these academic debates, our findings carry policy implications for the design of international institutions and challenges facing increasingly legalized international governance structures. Our working theory is that, in many cases, focal points will not be provided either because courts generate rival rules or make complex and case-specific decisions that cloud out any simple and generalizable solution that would stand out as focal. Such decisions give states a great deal of flexibility in the rules they choose to adopt, especially if there are distributional consequences associated with the prevalence of one rule over another. States’ adoption of contending rules makes law more uncertain and increases the chances for further disputes.   
We focus on the International Court of Justice (ICJ) as the most obvious focal point provider, as it is often considered to have the final say in many areas of international law,  which “gives the ICJ a unique ability to create focal precedents.”  The ICJ serves as a most likely case where we can best hope to observe focal points if they are actually created by international courts as the literature suggests. We illustrate and further develop our argument by examining the impact of the ICJ rulings in a pilot study on the law of maritime delimitation. In particular, we focus on the law governing the delimitation of the continental shelf, a body of law marked by the ICJ’s involvement in critical stages of its development. We particularly consider moments in which the ICJ is brought to make pronouncements as to the customary nature of a delimitation rule as potential instances of focal point creation.
To test the common assumption about courts’ role in creating focal points, we create a new, comprehensive database of state positions on continental shelf delimitation. To examine how state practice evolves in parallel to court rulings, we use various cutting-edge methods ranging from change point detection techniques to text mining and analysis through machine learning. Our analysis and findings promise to shed light on how courts’ inability or unwillingness to provide unique focal points influence state strategies and bargaining outcomes—a question so far neglected in the IR/IL literature. After completing this exploratory analysis, we hope to design a larger project where we investigate the courts’ potential to create focal points in other fields of law such as investment law, humanitarian law or international criminal law.

Title: TeleEPI: Integrated care pathway for people with epilepsy based on an unobstrusive AI-powered telemedical system (TeleEPI)
Abstract:
The diagnosis and treatment process of people with epilepsy starts with suspected epileptic seizures. Patients are referred to neurological departments which perform several diagnostic procedures to rule epilepsy in or out, mainly using electroencephalography (EEG). Repetitive short EEG measurements and/or inpatient long-term EEG monitoring of several days are undertaken. Trained personnel perform
the visual evaluation and interpretation of EEG data. This process is time-consuming and requires a high degree of specialization. Anti-seizure medication (ASM) represents the main form of treatment. More than 20 ASMs are used to treat seizures, frequently prescribed in combination
(polytherapy). Finding the proper medication which makes the patient seizure free is often a trial-and-error process which requires several iterations and monitoring of treatment impact and side effects. Several outpatient appointments for routine EEG monitoring are often needed,
especially for more complex patients. An essential input for adjusting and evaluating the treatment effects is selfdocumented epilepsy diaries, where patients report their seizures and other potential epileptic events. However, they are based on pure subjective patient experiences and are
therefore error-prone and sometimes even misleading for medical experts (over- or underreporting of epileptic seizures). The main current gaps and challenges for optimised care in epilepsy are as follows: (1) Complex interaction between stakeholders and information-flows coming from the inpatient but also the outpatient setting.
(2)Error-prone and subjective patient-reported information (seizure over- and underreporting).
(3) Lack of monitoring solutions applicable in the patient’s home.
(4) Not quantifiable influences in standardized inpatient monitoring settings differing from the usual familiar patient environment which often result in a lack of seizure episodes during inpatient monitoring.
(5) High degree of specialization needed to personalize diagnostics and treatments.
(6) Limitations of resources (time and technology) and lack of available experts.
The main focus of this project is to implement and test an innovative digital solution to optimize
care for epilepsy. Our telemedical approach replaces inpatient investigations by continuous, unobtrusive and real-life monitoring at home to optimize treatment decisions for epilepsy based on objective continuously recorded EEG and reporting in a telemedical platform. In this project, we will integrate and improve several existing components of the consortium partners into a comprehensive solution that our clinical partners will implement. The ultimate goal is to find a solution which provides the best possible care, reduces the complexity of care, uses resources more efficiently and achieves optimal outcomes in the sense of high-value care for each patient. The main components of
our system are: (1) Telemedical Platform: We will use AITs telemedical platform which enables simple and intuitive data transfer from medical devices and a broad range of datacapturing
methods. The system allows easy communication between
medical experts and patients. The platform will be expanded to include a digital seizure and nutrition diary (https://kit.ait.ac.at/home-2/). (2) Mobile EEG monitoring: We will evaluate two approaches for mobile EEG monitoring and connect the devices with the telemedical platform. The first
conservative system will use glued standard electrodes and mobile recording hardware (several candidates in the market). The second system will be the wearable seizure monitoring solution EpiCare@Home of project partner Byteflies. (3) AI-based EEG analysis software: We will integrate AITs AI-based EEG analysis software called encevis. encevis is CE-certified and FDA-approved and covers a wide range of EEG analysis as spike detection, seizure detection, electrical source localization and trend analysis tools.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Biosignal Processing, Epilepsy, Home Monitoring, Mobile EEG, Neurology, Telemedicine

Title: ProMiSE: Process Mining Support for End-users
Abstract: The rapid progress of digital transformation requires organizations to find intelligent ways of exploiting the vast amounts of data stored in their information systems to maintain a competitive edge. In this scenario, organizations are increasingly resorting to process mining to discover process models from event data and drive process improvement. Process mining blends principles of data mining and machine learning to extract meaningful process-related information from event data to understand and streamline processes. Over the last decade, process mining has grown into an established discipline, gaining remarkable momentum in both academia and industry. However, despite the unquestioned success of process mining, research has witnessed a lack of guidance for conducting many process mining tasks, such as creating and understanding event logs or explaining the obtained results. Indeed, some process mining tasks, such as data familiarization and process discovery, are inherently exploratory, meaning that neither the analysis goal nor the set of actions that analysts are expected to perform is precisely stated. The analysis process is unstructured and characterized by knowledge-intensive tasks executed repeatedly, as analysts often rely on their technical skills and experience to explore data. This, in turn, challenges the development of guidance for non-expert users, including novice analysts. So far, process mining research has focused mainly on technical aspects to improve algorithms and applications, while user behavior and the needs of process analysts received limited attention. However, gaining a comprehensive understanding of the analysis process, and especially of its exploratory phases, is crucial for supporting novice analysts effectively during the analysis. Thus, the central goal of this project is to gain a comprehensive understanding of how analysts do process mining in practice, i.e., the ``process of process mining'', to develop methodological guidance and operational support to assist novice analysts during the analysis effectively. To gain insights into the process of process mining, we will combine user interaction data with process mining applications (implicit feedback) and subjective insights gathered through retrospective interviews (explicit feedback). Interaction traces will be recorded with the help of a specialized tool, called ProMiSter, during observational studies on exploratory process mining tasks, conducted with process mining experts and novice analysts. For the analysis, we will combine quantitative and qualitative state-of-the-art approaches from data mining, cluster analysis, and grounded theory. The main outcome of the analysis will be a comprehensive understanding of user behavior for exploratory process mining, including frequent patterns of effective and noneffective behavior, analysis profiles, common analysis strategies, and typical challenges. Analysis patterns, profiles, and strategies will, in turn, provide strong empirical evidence for the development of methodological guidance and operational support aimed to assist novice analysts during exploratory process mining, potentially overcoming some of the identified challenges. Building upon observed effective analysis processes, we will derive a set of process mining guidelines providing practical guidance during the analysis. Besides, building upon effective and noneffective patterns of behavior, we will integrate into ProMiSter operational support in the form of recommendations and warnings based on the kind of behavior detected. By building upon the analysis of user behavior, this project will contribute to significantly advance our understanding of how analysts conduct exploratory process mining tasks, potentially providing useful empirical evidence for the improvement of process mining approaches and applications designed to support non-expert users. Besides, the obtained insights and the developed tool and guidelines will be useful to support the training and education of novice analysts and process mining students.
Keywords: Analysis of interaction traces, Process Mining, Process mining guidance, Process of Process Mining, User behavior analysis

Title: Meaning in Life in the Digital Society
Abstract:
This research project investigates the risks and opportunities presented by virtual reality technology (VR) and generative AI (GenAI) for meaning in life. In the last four decades, philosophers have increasingly emphasized that, contrary to a widely held philosophical position, humans are not only motivated either by self-interest or moral demands but additionally, by a pursuit of meaning in life. Digital technologies such as VR and GenAI may contribute to a meaningful life (e.g., by helping us to engage in projects that add meaning to life), but they may also make our lives less meaningful, for example by reducing co-present social experiences. However, the conceptual and normative issues around meaning in life in the digital society have been widely neglected so far.
The proposed research project attempts to address this research gap and provide a conceptual and normative analysis of how VR and GenAI contribute to or disrupt meaning in life. The project focuses on the impact of VR and GenAI on meaning we may achieve through relationships, creating art, and playing games. Can friendships that are being formed and maintained purely in VR be as meaningful as friendships in the physical, co-located world? What if this friend is a GenAI-powered avatar? Does wiring a poem with ChatGPT contribute to a meaningful life? Do games and the gamification of work or self-improvement threaten or contribute to life’s meaning? The three categories of relationships, art, and games are of particular interest because VR and GenAI have and will continue to greatly transform them and because they can make salient different kinds of conceptual questions regarding meaning in life. The project illuminates how VR and GenAI can have both positive and negative influences on how relationships, art, and games contribute to a meaningful life, and will specifically argue for two hypotheses: 1) If used right, those technologies have great potential to help us lead more meaningful lives, although 2) a contact with reality-constraint sets important limits.
The project proceeds in three steps. 1) The first step establishes a conceptual and normative framework regarding meaning in life that builds on, revises, and refines existing hybrid accounts of meaning in life. 2) The second part specifies how relationships, art, and games contribute to the meaningful life (2.1), analyzes how VR and GenAI can undermine meaning in life by transforming relationships, art, and games (2.2), and uncovers ways in which they can enhance or provide new sources for a meaningful life (2.3). 3) In the third part, the results of the previous parts are brought together and sharpened by analyzing meaning in a life predominantly or exclusively lived in VR. This part develops an argument that on the grounds of meaning in life, we have reasons to prefer a life with significant contact with physical reality. This project includes collaborations with the Immersive Arts Space (IASpace) of the Zurich University of the Arts (ZHdK), the aesthetics research cluster of the ZHdK, Prof. Sven Nyholm at the Ludwigs-Maximilans-University (LMU) in Munich, and Prof. Mark Coeckelbergh at the University in Vienna.
This research addresses pressing philosophical questions in normative and applied ethics, specifically in ethics of technology. It furthers our understanding of the value of relationships, artistic creation, and gameplay for meaning in life and helps to identify forms of those practices detrimental to a meaningful life. Furthermore, this project contributes to a much-needed expansion of research in ethics of technology to span beyond concerns for well-being and moral issues to include technological impacts on the meaning of life. By addressing those ethical issues, the project is also of great social relevance. It can advance research which is essential for decision-making concerning the use, regulation, and design of emerging technologies. Considering how quickly VR and GenAI technologies are being developed, it is crucial to address the ethical challenges they raise promptly.
Keywords: Ethics of Technology, Generative AI, Meaning in Life, Virtual Reality

Title: Changes in Wealth and Saving Inequalities over the Last Two Decades: The Role of Social Class and Education
Abstract:
In recent years, wealth inequality has moved to the top of the research agenda in sociology and economics. This topic has become more relevant than ever for two reasons. First, social unrest intensified with movements like Occupy Wall Street that perceived a lack of fairness and opportunity in the distribution of wealth and resources. Second, the availability of wealth data has expanded vastly. Wealth inequality has increased in the United States and some European countries. Yet, we know little about the role of education in exacerbating wealth inequalities and how this interplay with macroeconomic conditions. Not only is this aspect of wealth unexplored, but saving behaviour that largely influences wealth accumulation is also understudied. 

This project seeks to answer the following questions: What is the association between wealth and education, and how has it evolved over time across Western countries? Do economic recessions exacerbate wealth inequalities between different educational groups? What individual-level characteristics predict saving and consumption behaviour? 
  
To cover this gap, this project uses the Luxembourg Wealth Study and the European Union Statistics on Income and Living Conditions. Multivariate regression models will be estimated for each country separately to answer the research questions that do not include macro variables. The second analytical strategy is a three-level multilevel model to analyze the interplay between macro (e.g., GDP output gap) and individual outcome (e.g., wealth). Finally, machine learning techniques will be used to predict consumption and saving behaviour. 

This project is relevant to social policy. If the wealth gap between different educational groups has widened, social policies can intervene to design an optimal wealth tax redistribution. Moreover, if economic downturns drive wealth inequalities, we might better address their repercussions on vulnerable groups whenever they hit again. Finally, analyzing saving behaviour and consumption is crucial at the individual and institutional levels as social policies may intervene to improve saving behaviour.
Keywords: Educational groups, Great Recession, Social class, Sociology, Wealth inequality

Title: Movement and Rest: The Kinetic Body in the Making of Roman Poetry from Catullus to Ovid
Abstract:
This project examines the role of the body and of bodily practices and states (habitus) in the making of Roman poetry, and it does so through the lens of movement and rest. The constantly moving bodies of the goddesses of Fate as they sing (Catullus 64), the sleepless poet tossing and turning in his bed before composing a poem (Catullus 50), the poet as a pantomime or an acrobat (Horace, Epistles 2.1; 2.2), or the poem itself as modeled on a woman in motion (Propertius 2.1) – these iconic figures and motifs of Roman poetry will for the first time be investigated comprehensively and in detail: how are we to understand this emphasis on physical movement in a culture that has long since made the transition to writing? Why is the motif of the kinetic body, which is shaped by performance practices of a distant or imagined past, so prevalent in Roman poetry from Catullus to Ovid? What does it tell us about the nature of that poetry? What does it disclose about Roman views on the “movements of the soul” (generally understood as emotions) and their physical underpinnings? While the tension between performative modes of composition and the written text has been studied extensively in Greek culture, whose tradition of oral poetry has been a major point of interest in the field of Classics for at least a century, in Roman literature physical aspects have been studied primarily in relation to delivery. Accordingly, the focus has been mostly on drama and rhetoric, i.e., genres that are performed in particular settings (the theatrical stage, the court). 
This project proposes a new angle by focusing not on delivery but on the kinetic body as a factor in the production of song and verse, as it is imagined in Roman poetry itself. By putting physical movement at the centre of the enquiry, the project will complement existing research that examines the relationship between the voice and written verse, especially in bucolic, lyric, elegiac, satiric, and epigrammatic poetry. The time span studied extends from the last decades of the Republic to the first ones of the Principate (or from Catullus to Ovid), a period of great tension between Greek and especially Alexandrian influences on Roman literature and a nostalgia for an idealized Roman past; a period, accordingly, of heightened self-reflection in poetry. Close readings and an in-depth scrutiny of the Latin vocabulary of movement and rest with the aid of existing databases will reveal how and to what extent bodily states, postures, and attitudes, as well as motor activities such as walking, gesticulating, or dancing are presented as informing processes of poetic composition in thought, voice, and writing. The study extends to metaphorical references to these bodily states and practices, and it will be complemented by an enquiry into the movements of the soul (animi motus).
The proposed research will offer the first detailed study of how Roman poetry envisions the connection between physical movement and poetic practice. The outcomes will be presented in a series of scholarly articles on poetry from Catullus to Horace (PI) and on Cicero’s concept of animi motus (Postdoc), as well as in three doctoral theses in the areas of bucolic poetry (Vergil), satire (Horace), and elegy (Ovid), respectively. There will be two doctoral workshops and an international conference preparing the ground for an edited volume on the role of kinetic bodies in Roman poetry offering a first synthesis, as well as an interdisciplinary and practice-oriented workshop planned in collaboration with the Literaturinstitut Biel. The project will yield a better understanding of the role of the kinetic body in the binary of voice and writing that dominates much existing scholarship. Moreover, it will add a historical and literary perspective to current research in media studies, sociology, neurobiology, and cultural anthropology that investigates how physical movement contributes to human communication, a question that will become ever more pressing with the rapid advance of artificial intelligence.

Title: Artificial Intelligence and Moral Decision-Making in Contemporary Societies: An Empirical Sociological Investigation
Abstract:
In contemporary societies, concepts of decision, decision-making, and choice are ubiquitous. Many human activities—from politics to love to art—are represented as the outcome of decision-making processes. But this tendency is particularly striking when we consider artificial intelligence (AI). The media speak of a self-driving car that “made a choice” to turn left or right, or we’re told about techniques to build artificial agents capable of “making complex decisions”. Artificial intelligence is a hot topic in public and scientific discourse; modern societies are struggling with this new technology, with its moral, legal, and societal implications. Importantly, these issues are often mediated by decision/choice concepts: AI systems should make “moral decisions,” should be “responsible for their choices,” or should be outright morally good agents.

In a series of recent articles, Abend (2018a, 2018b, 2019) has argued that decisions/choice concepts play a decisive role in social practices and social organization. Social actors put decision/choice concepts to work. They are crucial for moral discourse, too. Decision/choice concepts are one aspect of the “moral background” (Abend 2014), a set of second-order elements that make moral life possible. When morality and decision/choice concepts meet, we speak of moral decisionism.

Previous research in this area is scarce and has significant limitations. For one, there are no studies on the application of decision/choice concepts to AI and its relation to moral judgments. Second, previous research did not properly take the moral and social-structural background of social actors into account. Third, previous research did not systematically compare the effects of different determinants and analyze their interactions. Finally, quantitative, large-scale studies of the general population are missing. In short, a sociological approach to the study of the morality of AI is sorely needed.

In our research project, we employ Abend’s conceptual framework, as laid out in his book, The Moral Background, and his articles on moral decisionism. Our two orienting research questions are as follows: (i) To what extent do social actors describe artificial intelligence with decision/choice concepts? (ii) To what extent do social actors describe artificial intelligence as a moral agent when doing X? We develop an explanatory model identifying situational and individual factors that account for the attribution of decision/choice concepts to AI, as well as moral agency to AI. Methodologically, we administer a factorial survey together with a questionnaire to a representative sample of the general Swiss population. 

Our research project will make several significant contributions to the scientific study of AI and its moral appraisal. We will contribute to various sociological subfields: sociology of decisionism, the sociology of morality, cultural sociology, sociology of science and technology, and sociological theory. Besides, we trust our findings will transcend the ivory tower. They can generate important insights for the design of “moral AI” and “explainable AI,” since being moral and explainable depend crucially on people’s beliefs about AI, for which a representative sample of the population will provide key information. Similarly, well-founded empirical results on decision/choice concepts in AI can inform public sphere discussions and policy-making. The existing experimental data is valuable, but we can benefit from a broader empirical picture: accurate knowledge of public perceptions will be an asset for policy aims, which must be sensitive to the publics and actors it is intended to serve.

Title: Ground Control: closed-loop adaptive control for AM-DED process optimization
Abstract:
Additive Manufacturing (AM) brought terrific innovation in the field of complex shape part manufacturing. Despite the multitude of appreciated benefits, the major drawback that still prevents the industrial stable adoption and integration of such technology in the value chain is the process reliability and robustness. The instrumental turnkey to unfold such challenge is recognized in the process control and optimization. In the DED (Direct Energy Deposition) technology, the current scientific and industrial strategy towards the process control and optimization mostly focus on the 2D and 3D melt pool control. A number of KPIs related to geometry and laser-material interaction are traced and when thresholds are violated a set of empirical rules are triggered to compensate for the laser power. Such practice is mostly based on experience, and it does not take into account the entire dynamics of the deposition process, which goes from the material-laser interaction to material growth models, from the kinematics and dynamics of the machines and feeding systems to the deposition strategy up to the possibility to compensate possible deposition deviations. This results in myopic process control only partially reliable and, most of all, not scalable to any equipment. This project proposal is meant to be considered as a step towards a complete integrated approach to the DED process control problem.
Ground Control (GC) focuses on the process monitoring and control with the objective of transforming Direct Energy Deposition process into an industrially available technology to be disruptively integrated into the value chain. An integrated optimized control platform entitled Ground Control is proposed, bringing innovation on the following aspects: right-the-first-time parts (NO SCRAPS); improved efficiency (energy and material saving); portability, i.e. solution initially developed for a specific machine setup, but, at the same time, scalable to any DED machine architecture and setup.
GC scientific and technical core innovation is the breakthrough on-line control loop architecture efficiently and effectively exploiting on one side the wealth of information gathered from the intensive off-line experimentation, and on the other side the field data from the on-going deposition process. The control solution will be developed as an adaptive hybrid process control and implemented as a control module called GC Adaptive Controller. Its ability to evolve the deposition behaviour relies upon a set of additional modules that will run off-line and on-line, over different time scales: GC Data Set Builder generates a DED process data set for creating a data history of parameters; GC Empirical Modeller is an off-line module that, using the aforementioned data set, processes sensor and control data along with the mechanical, geometrical and quality performance of the manufactured parts (optimal requirements) to generate a data driven process model by machine learning techniques; GC Online Interpreter is an on-line sensor-based elaboration module that interprets the measurements captured during the deposition and identifies the in-control and out-of-control KPIs along with their trends. This will ensure GC Adaptive Controller to persistently close the loop on the laser power, spot, feeding dynamics and kinematic parameters to ensure the matching of the optimal requirements. All the aforementioned modules are designed to synergically cooperate in the unique GC Platform.
The GC Platform relies upon the availability of a CPS-based innovative sensing system that enables process and geometric based parameters as well as an architecture of the CNC allowing the incorporation or triggering of multiple control logics. The benefits of the proposed approach will be assessed on a set of industrial use cases, parts and equipment made available by ARM Laboratory with SUPSI-DTI-ISTePS. 
GC project will produce scientific innovation by developing a novel closed-loop adaptive control solution for DED and its implementation in the GC software platform, optimized for the specific ARM Lab equipment setup but also scalable to be integrated in any DED machine and system. GC will also contribute to establish a solid knowledge ground on DED process by sharing an open database where researchers, students and industrial experts can rely for benchmarking; it will bring industrial innovation by manufacturing a number of round robin parts to be considered as proof of concepts for the enhanced industrial robustness of DED when adopting GC platform. The project is structured over 3 years and 7 work packages.

Title: Unbiased Analysis of Excitatory Synaptic Connectivity in the Aging Cerebral Cortex
Abstract:
Understanding the structural changes underlying the cognitive decline during aging has occupied neuroscientists for many years.  They have relied on light and electron microscopy to understand the extent to which morphological alterations may correlate with functional deficits This decline is believed to reflect changes to the neural circuits and in particular the synaptic connections. However, existing studies have only involved either small sample areas or specific neuronal types. As a result, they have produced apparently conflicting results for different brain regions with regards to the connectivity between neurons while a comprehensive volume analysis of the aging-induced changes through the different layers of a defined region of cortex is still missing.

The goal of this project is therefore to remedy this using a 3D electron microscopy imaging approach along with Computer Vision algorithms free of human bias to compare the structure of synaptic contacts, dendritic spines, and synaptic vesicle pools. This will allow us to analyse the age related synaptic changes in each layer of a single column of the cerebral cortex. This will provide important data about the fundamental elements involved in synaptic connectivity in each layer of a single cortical column. It will also show how these elements change as a result of aging. Finally, it will establish a high throughput workflow for unbiased analysis of cortical connectivity and organelle organisation. This workflow will be applicable across a number of research fields, ranging from characterizing different brain regions to exploring how sensory stimuli and behaviours shape neuronal and synaptic morphology.
Keywords: aging, axon, brain, cerebral cortex, computer vision, dendrite, electron microscopy, synapse

Title: Data-driven Trans-topological Design Exploration of Funicular Structures
Abstract:
This proposal leverages the nascent and growing class of Geometric Deep Learning approaches from Machine Learning (ML) to support the trans-topology structural design exploration of discrete structures based on funicular form-finding (DSFF) during the conceptual design stage. Although DSFF are efficient structural systems, their design is challenging because DSFF are highly constrained systems whereby design feasibility, variables, goals, and requirements, such as preferences for the geometry and force distribution, can be difficult to reconcile, even for experts. The recent popularisation of ML in structural design has led to some promising developments. However, few researchers have developed applications supporting the direct mapping from performance goals to designs or from a given design to the optimal design operation for improving performance according to specific goals. Fundamentally, strategies are lacking for modelling discrete structural systems spanning a trans-topology design space—designs with variable number of elements, such as nodes and members (edges), and irregular nodal connectivity that make it difficult to compare or combine them.
These limitations motivate the applicant’s doctoral research, which develops ML-enabled strategies to support the analyses, limited comparisons, and performance-driven generation of DSFF spanning a trans-topological design space. This proposal expands on those efforts and develops a two-stage project applying a powerful combination of ML approaches: Geometric Deep Learning, Representation Learning and Generative Modelling. It leverages their respective capacities to learn directly from the non-Euclidean datastructures of DSFF to learn a more optimal description, or representation, of design data and to learn complex inverse models conducive for the direct mapping of goals to designs. Specifically, Stage I contributes a computational framework to learn two mappings: one to represent and encode DSFF, irrespective of their sizes, into constant-length data vectors that can accurately capture their topological, geometrical and structural properties, and one to directly reconstruct, or decode, DSFF from their encoded vectors, or latent representations. In doing so, the encoder enables DSFF to be compared,  and the decoder provides a method for generating DSFF derived from the blending or interpolation of vectors corresponding to other DSFF. Crucially, the representation strategy developed in Stage I is adapted within a Deep Reinforcement Learning framework in Stage II to learn to map DSFF to the selection of specific local topology-modifying operations for refining DSFF according to specific structural design goals. The proposed project provides a unified and principled approach for augmenting the author’s current research and addressing its key limitations, in the process developing foundational ML strategies enabling the direct learning and generation of discrete datastructures useful in design. This has broad implications for the field of Architecture, Engineering and Construction, while specifically supporting the direct generation of DSFF and the recommendation of design operations on DSFF according to specific design goals in a trans-topology design space.
Keywords: conceptual design stage, discrete structural systems, funicular form-finding, geometric deep learning, machine learning, structural design exploration

Title: Developing Machine Learning Methods to Accelerate Protein Engineering
Abstract: Inspired by the recent success of Alphafold2 in protein structure prediction, one can envision similar advances in other branches of molecular biology. One branch where current limitations can be overcome using machine learning is protein design. Designing new proteins is challenging because of the high-dimensionality of the space of potential proteins and searching this space with experimental methods is cost and time intensive. Instead, by using predictive and generative machine learning methods, proteins can potentially be designed computationally with less cost and time. This research project consisted of two subprojects. In the first subproject, a new method was developed that enables guidance of generative discrete-state diffusion and flow models with a property-predictive model. This allows the generation of discrete objects such as protein sequences or drug-like small molecules with desired properties. This method is not limited to protein and drug research, but could also be applied in materials research or language modeling. In the second subproject, two methods were developed to analyze selection experiments performed to determine protein fitness. One method provides a mathematical description of selection experiments and can be used to train machine learning models for protein fitness prediction. The other method makes it possible to extract information about the bio-physical properties of proteins from a trained model. Both methods were applied in a collaboration with an experimental research group for the investigation of protein-protein interactions. During this research project, I was working in the group of Prof. Jennifer Listgarten at the University of California, Berkeley.

Title: Accelerated Development of Ferroelectric Nitrides using Ionized Physical Vapor Deposition
Abstract:
The increasing demands of big data and artificial intelligence (AI) necessitate breakthroughs in energy-efficient computing and data storage. Ferroelectric nitrides, such as aluminum scandium nitride (AlScN), have shown great potential for non-volatile memory technologies due to their high remnant polarization (Pr), excellent temperature stability, and compatibility with current semiconductor manufacturing processes. However, high coercive fields (Ec) and limited cycling durability restrict their practical applications. This project addresses these challenges by developing alternative alloying strategies for aluminum nitride (AlN)-based ferroelectrics. Traditional methods to reduce Ec, such as isovalent alloying and strain engineering, often come at the expense of Pr, phase stability, and increased leakage currents. Recent studies suggest that bond ionicity plays a crucial role in determining the coercive field. By incorporating elements with varying electronegativity and ionic radius—such as boron (B), yttrium (Y), and lanthanum (La)—into AlN, we aim to independently manipulate structural properties and chemical bonding environments. This approach will generate insights into how local structural disorder and bond ionicity affect ferroelectric properties, potentially leading to materials with low Ec without compromising Pr.
Building on our previous successes with AlScN, we will leverage the unique advantages of metal-ion synchronized high-power impulse magnetron sputtering (MIS-HiPIMS). This deposition technique can be used to accelerate film-forming metal ions onto the growing film, resulting in enhanced crystalline quality, improved c-axis texture, and a compact microstructure.
The research plan comprises five interconnected work packages. First, we will perform a combinatorial high-throughput screening of AlN-based nitrides with varying compositional complexity. Using HiPIMS for combinatorial depositions minimizes texture gradients, enabling a more reliable materials screening than is possible with conventional deposition techniques. The libraries will be analyzed using automated characterization, including structural analysis and chemical state analysis via X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy to assess cation-anion bond ionicity. Second, device libraries will be fabricated to enable high-throughput testing of ferroelectric properties such as Ec, Pr, and leakage current density. Third, we will develop MIS-HiPIMS deposition processes for the most promising materials. In the fourth work package, these optimized processes will be used to manufacture devices with low film thickness, aiming to achieve low switching potentials alongside high Pr and cycling endurance. Finally, we will leverage the comprehensive datasets generated in the project to establish correlations between material properties and device performance, as well as to develop design principles for new ferroelectric nitrides. Advanced data analysis and machine learning will help identify non-intuitive correlations, while computational modeling will help to understand the mechanisms driving these trends.
By addressing both material and process innovations, this project aims to overcome current limitations in ferroelectric nitrides. The expected outcomes include the identification of novel ferroelectric nitrides with lower Ec and high Pr, as well as the development of advanced and scalable deposition processes to facilitate integration into future in-memory computing technologies. The insights generated in this project will have implications well beyond the development of ferroelectric nitrides for memory applications. For instance, the phase formation in multi-component nitrides during non-equilibrium physical vapor deposition is of interest in many technologies. Additionally, many of the results will directly benefit the development of high-performance piezoelectric thin films, which are essential for 5G and 6G telecommunication.

Title: The Journey of Entrepreneurial Exit: Antecedents, Forms, and Evolution
Abstract:
Entrepreneurial exit is an underexplored yet pivotal phenomenon in the entrepreneurial process. It involves deciding whether and how to leave a venture or instead continue pursuing it. Our longitudinal study aims to significantly advance understanding of how founders formulate decisions regarding both the type of exit—voluntary exit, involuntary exit, or founder persistence—and its form—full, partial, or staggered. We integrate Imprinting Theory and Upper Echelons Theory to examine how founders’ imprinted experiences and team dynamics interact with venture growth to shape founders’ evolving exit preferences. Our study thus responds to calls for process-oriented research to capture the multifaceted, temporal nature of exit.
We utilize a pioneering UK data repository that captures the full history of every shareholder transaction since venture inception. This dataset provides unparalleled granularity by recording every individual share transaction for all shareholders, including minority investors, enabling detailed analysis of the type, form, and timing of entrepreneurial exits. We analyze approximately 5,000 startups and around 10,000 founders, directors, and investors across four key industries: Artificial Intelligence, Biotechnology, Financial Services, and Hardware. By capturing the whole spectrum of possible exits, the utilized dataset enables a comprehensive exploration of different exit types and exit forms. Our aim is to uncover nuanced equity evolution and complex exit trajectories, and thereby to provide new insights into the socially complex decision-making process of founders. Our findings advance entrepreneurship scholarship by framing exit as a dynamic journey shaped by founders’ imprinted experiences, team configurations, and environmental dynamics.
We adopt a mixed-methods approach, combining an empirical analysis of archival data with experimental studies. We employ various empirical methods, including event history analysis, multinomial logistic regression, panel data analysis, and mediation analysis, and precisely operationalize key variables such as founders’ prior entrepreneurial experience, educational and professional diversity, team dynamics, and venture growth stages. Our concurrent experimental approach is designed to supplement and corroborate the findings from the archival data. It thus establishes causality and reveals the underlying motivations and cognitive processes driving exit decisions.
The research team is led by Prof. Dr. Vangelis Souitaris and includes Dr. Djordje Djokovic, a dedicated postdoctoral researcher, and a doctoral student, who will both be funded by the project. Our team has long-standing experience in researching the dynamic domains of entrepreneurship, entrepreneurial exit, and innovation management. Our track record attests to our unwavering commitment to advance knowledge in these fields, just as our extensive research network highlights our standing in the academic community. Moreover, our strong foundation in advanced data infrastructure, modeling, analysis, and data extraction uniquely enables us to harness the full potential of the dataset. Our proven expertise in rigorous empirical research grounded in solid theoretical frameworks will ensure the impact of the proposed project.
Our project makes significant theoretical contributions by explaining how exit decisions result from the interplay of founders’ imprinted experiences, team dynamics, and venture growth stages, integrating insights from Imprinting Theory and Upper Echelons Theory. We will publish our findings in top-tier entrepreneurship and management journals. Practically, the project helps founders navigate exits, aids investors in assessing exit readiness, and supports policymakers in offering tailored assistance. To our knowledge, no current research examines founder exits as comprehensively, positioning our study to provide unique insights into this complex process.

Title: Digital Process Chain for Hollow Core Extrusion
Abstract:
Thermoplastic extrusion 3D printing in large dimensions offers unique opportunities to manufacture geometrically complex and bespoke building elements for sustainable construction. The fabrication process typically consists of stacking material strands in layers. Nevertheless, these strands usually have solid, uniform sections, resulting in dense, heavy, material-intensive parts that require long printing times. To address these challenges, we follow an approach that rethinks the core thermoplastic extrusion: instead of printing with a massive solid cross-section, we investigate printing with hollow profiles. The differentiation of the strand of 3D-printed polymer adds an exciting yet unexplored design opportunity to the printing process, offering structural, environmental, functional, and aesthetic benefits. Our initial experiments have shown that such Hollow Core 3D-Printing benefits from a better strength-to-weight ratio of a custom hollow section compared to a solid one, as well as a significant reduction in material consumption. The non-solid sections of hollow prints allow the process to scale and speed up through increased layer heights and faster cooling rates. Depending on the chosen layer height (resolution of the final print), the material savings can be 50% or higher compared to classical extrusion with a solid cross-section. The main challenge for Hollow Core 3D printing is the increased difficulty of controlling the deposition. There is an increased number of interdependent process parameters. Jointly optimizing the temperature, air pressure, speed, and flow rate makes manual print preparation feasible only for simple designs. Furthermore, even simple prints require careful monitoring. Tiny variations in material batches or ambient conditions lead to local failures. Therefore, it is critical to have control over the deposition to guarantee the structural integrity of the final printed parts. Consequently, we aim to enable large-scale Hollow Core 3D-Printing by establishing a novel digital design-for-fabrication routine consisting of: 
- Customized extruder design to explore the impact and the potential of various extrusion profiles, including a rotating nozzle for an improved extrusion orientation. 
- Establish a closed-loop manufacturing process in which the printer is aware of the desired print result, thereby adjusting the printing parameters in real time. The extrusion parameters are controlled using data-driven control methods to learn optimal print strategies.
- Fabrication-informed design tools, integrating the fabrication and design processes into a single workflow. The designer will be able to freely explore the design space to combine aesthetics and function, while the design tool itself guarantees fabricability. 
- Performative building elements based on Hollow Core 3D-Printing: We explore various applications and develop building elements incorporating details and design languages for Hollow Core 3D-Printing, focusing on lightweight, bespoke concrete formwork. 
The principal applicability will be evaluated for functional goals, such as accuracy, strength-to-weight ratio, fabrication time, reproducibility, and visual appearance, and demonstrated with a family of full-scale building elements. Hollow Core 3D-Printing has the potential to create value by producing more material-efficient, durable, and complex elements within a reduced production time and increased degree of geometric flexibility. If we succeed, Hollow Core 3D-Printing and closed-loop control strategies can impact all areas currently addressed with thermoplastic extrusion 3D printing, but could also open up entirely new fields of application, further increasing the potential of additive manufacturing toward more sustainable construction. The closed-loop control strategies can also be transferred to other materials and extrusion processes with challenging fabrication parameters and material behaviors.

Title: A novel approach to employee well-being: Exploring proactive strategies for psychological needs satisfaction in daily life
Abstract: Employee well-being is a critical aspect of individual fulfillment and organizational success. This is particularly true in today's landscape of work, characterized by increasing digitalization, flexibility, and a strong focus on performance. While these trends, further accelerated by the COVID-19 crisis, offer employees greater autonomy and growth opportunities, they also impose higher demands on self-management and proactive balance between work and nonwork life. Consequently, there is a need to equip employees with effective strategies to successfully navigate their work and nonwork situations so that they feel and perform well in both life domains. My research project investigates needs-based crafting as an innovative approach within occupational health psychology to enhance employee well-being and performance across both life domains. Traditional job design theories viewed employees as passive recipients of their work conditions. This perspective changed with the introduction of job crafting – a bottom-up approach, where employees proactively shape their jobs to align with their skills, needs and preferences. The rich empirical evidence accumulated thus far shows that job crafting is beneficial for employee well-being and motivation. However, existing job crafting models focus predominantly on proactive changes in pre-defined external stimuli and present challenges in their applicability outside the workplace. Addressing this, the needs-based model of crafting, rooted in psychological needs theory, proposes that employees craft their work and nonwork domains to fulfill six core psychological needs referred to as DRAMMA needs: detachment, relaxation, autonomy, mastery, meaning, and affiliation. This approach puts in center employee intrinsic motivation for crafting and thus can capture a wide range of crafting strategies relevant across different contexts in work and nonwork domains. Recently, quantitative scales have been developed to measure needs-based crafting, showing benefits for various aspects of well-being. Yet, a knowledge gap remains regarding the specific crafting strategies employees use in different work and nonwork contexts. My research project aims to fill this gap using ecological momentary assessment and natural language processing to collect real-time qualitative and quantitative data on employee crafting strategies. This innovative approach moves beyond the existing quantitatively focused crafting research to open the black box and provide insights into specific crafting strategies employees use to satisfy their DRAMMA needs across work and nonwork contexts. In addition, it will address the gap in the existing literature on the influences of individual and contextual factors on employee crafting strategies. Finally, the project will generate unique evidence about crafting strategies used by different profiles of employees based on their well-being outcomes. The findings of the project will contribute to the development of recommendations that will serve as an inspiration for employees to develop their own crafting strategies and as a basis for the development of crafting interventions aimed at promoting employee well-being and productivity. Overall, my project offers an innovative perspective on crafting research that will advance the theory and practice in the field of (needs-based) crafting research.

Title: FemiLab: Women’s Brain Health Across The Lifespan
Abstract:
Women have higher prevalence of autoimmune diseases, and are at greater risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease (AD) relative to men. As women's health is historically understudied, little is known about mechanisms underlying epidemiological sex differences in disease, and how factors such as pregnancy and oestrogen exposure influence women's brain health throughout life. 

FemiLab is an international, cross-disciplinary research initiative aiming to push the frontiers of women's health research forward. By applying cutting-edge tools for neuroimaging, genetics, and biostatistics to multiple large-scale datasets, we will investigate how factors linked to pregnancy and menopause relate to brain ageing and AD risk later in life, how these factors interact with genotypes and common genetic variation, and how these associations contribute to epidemiological sex differences in risk and disease. In addition to leveraging data from population-based cohorts such as CoLaus and UK Biobank, FemiLab benefits from collaboration with the ERC-funded project 'BRAINMINT - Brains and Minds in Transition' (PI Prof. Westlye), which focuses on how increased brain plasticity during adolescence and pregnancy involves risk for common mental disorders including postpartum depression. By combining data from several high-quality datasets, we aim to identify groups of women who are vulnerable to accelerated brain ageing or dementia, as well as autoimmune diseases and pregnancy-related mental health problems. 

Research addressing women's biology is not only necessary to obtain a more complete understanding of brain ageing and disease, but also to approach gender equality in health care. With the aim to clarify factors that influence women’s health and disease risk, FemiLab may facilitate the development of targeted, preventive interventions in the general population.
Keywords: brain ageing, genetics, machine learning, menopause, neuroimaging, pregnancy and childbirth, sex hormones, women's health

Title: Gaussian Process Bandit Optimization: Theory and Applications
Keywords: Bayesian optimization, decision support, machine learning
grant_text: gaussian process bandit optimization: theory and applications. many applications in engineering, science and society require us to make decision with uncertain outcomes. a fundamental problem is the exploration exploitation dilemma: the need to trade off gathering information (explore) and making decisions that have proven to be effective in the past (exploit). in many real world tasks, the number of choices is extremely large, and thus we need to make inferences about the outcome of decisions given past experiences. due to its central importance, the exploration exploitation dilemma has been tackled by several communities: the theory community developed principled algorithms with strong guarantees for the multi armed bandit problem (a classical paradigm formalizing the exploration exploitation tradeoff) as well as generalizations; application oriented researchers have developed practical and effective algorithms for response surface methods and bayesian global optimization. however, there is a gap between the wide applicability of the practical methods, and the theoretical rigor of the multi armed bandit approaches. this proposal lays out a basic research program, with the goal of bridging the gap between theory and practice by developing novel approaches towards solving the exploration exploitation dilemma in complex, structured domains that cannot be solved using any of the existing approaches. we build on recent techniques from nonparametric and high dimensional statistics, as well as analytical techniques from online optimization, in order to develop new, principled algorithms for solving decision making problems in real applications. our research will pursue the following inter related threads: (1) new algorithms for dealing with uncertain, high dimensional domains by exploiting recent results from high dimensional statistics; (2) new algorithms that learn to optimize from task context and past experiences; (3) the investigation of fundamental questions on the parallelization of bayesian global optimization; (4) the evaluation of the algorithms on real world applications including information gathering on the web, environmental monitoring and neuroprosthetics. the expected impact of the proposed project includes the development of new theoretical insights and tools, their realization in novel algorithms, their implementation as open source software, and their application in challenging real world exploration exploitation tasks. the success of the project is backed by a significant amount of preliminary research results by the pi and his group. beyond the theoretical and algorithmic insights, the application of the techniques pursued in this proposal can potentially have immediate benefits for society.. bayesian optimization, decision support, machine learning

Title: How sustainable is sustainable finance? Impact evaluation and automated greenwashing detection.
Abstract:
The financial sector has to play a crucial role in combating climate change. Investment flows into sustainable strategies have accelerated since the COVID-19 pandemic, and global assets managed under a sustainability label are on track to exceed $53 trillion by 2025, more than a third of total assets under management. Unfortunately, the boom has been accompanied by rampant "greenwashing," with companies boasting about their environmental credentials. However, to convict of greenwashing, we must answer at least two questions. They take center stage in our research proposal:

-Are the claims made by companies and asset managers credible regarding their environmental impact?
-Does sustainable investing have any visible effect on the real economy needed to transition to a low-carbon economy or achieve other sustainability goals?

In our proposal, we analyze two complementary aspects of impact investing. First, to measure the trustworthiness of environmental and green claims made by the finance industry, we develop an automated greenwashing detection system based on artificial intelligence (AI). Second, to measure the real impact of sustainable investing, we analyze shareholder engagement and sustainability-linked loans as two promising mechanisms for impact. For the shareholder engagement, we plan a real-world experiment with a major index provider. For the new phenomenon of sustainability-linked loans, we discuss and show how it creates the equivalent impact channel for debt investors, which we call creditor engagement, and for which greenwashing is considered as the main concern.
Keywords: Greenwashing detection, Impact investing, Natural Language Processing, Sustainable finance

Title: Non-invasive accurate brain oximetry by innovative near-infrared spectroscopy (BrainOX)
Abstract:
Background and rationale: Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) is widely applied in research and clinical fields to measure the oxygenation (StO2) of the brain. It has, however, been shown that this measurement is contaminated by extracerebral tissue (mostly skin and skull). Although several attempts were made to reduce this influence, the absolute StO2 of the brain was still contaminated by extracerebral tissue in adults. For scientific and clinical reasons it is highly relevant to measure the StO2 of the brain and therefore it is high time to address and solve this problem. The objective of BrainOX is to develop and test instrumentation to accurately measure the StO2 of purely the brain based on near-infrared optical tomography (NIROT).
Methods: The work initiates with simulations in silico by a finite element approach (NIRFAST) to determine the key metrics of time domain NIROT needed to remove the influence of extracerebral tissue. We will specify the BrainOX NIROT setup accordingly, which will be built. It will be tested in a phantom that imitates the adult head with its correct optical properties including brain and extracerebral layers of tissue with real human hemoglobin at varying StO2. This includes developing and establishing a continuous method of reference to accurately determine the StO2 in the phantom, because the current gold standard, the professional blood gas analyzer ABL90, only provides intermittent values, since for each measurement a sample of phantom liquid has to be extracted. Consequently, the BrainOX NIROT setup will be evaluated by comparing its StO2 to the reference StO2 in the phantom part mimicking the brain and by determining how insensitive the BrainOX NIROT is to variations in the extracerebral tissue. Two types of methods of image reconstruction will be developed: 1) methods based on the diffusive physical models of light transport in tissue (more conventional and safe approach) and 2) innovative novel methods based on machine learning (fast but more risky approach). Finally, once the functioning and accuracy of the BrainOX NIROT instrument are tested, a software will be developed that enables real time imaging of the brain StO2. 
Expected results: We expect 4 results: 1) the main result is a BrainOX NIROT instrument that is able to truly measure absolute StO2 of the brain without the influence of extracerebral tissue, 2) a phantom that imitates the adult head and is thus invaluable for testing NIRS instruments in general, 3) a novel method of reference to determine the StO2 accurately and continuously in the phantom and 4) a novel image reconstruction method based on machine learning.
Impact: The main impact will be the functional BrainOX NIROT instrument, which enables clinicians and researcher to truly measure the brain StO2 in adults, which will constitute a major breakthrough. From a technological point of view, this instrument will in the future be developed further to enable high resolution imaging of the adult head. The focus of the BrainOX instrument is to measure the StO2 of the brain in real time. This will enable research in patients with this novel instrument. The phantom and novel method of reference will be invaluable for testing of NIRS instruments in general and is expected to enter the ISO norms on cerebral oximetry. From a clinical point of view, since NIRS has already been shown to be an effective tool in many clinical applications despite its limitations, the feature to truly measure the brain StO2 will strongly enhance its effectiveness in clinical application. We expect that this will lead to a vastly improved outcome and much reduced incidence of brain lesions e.g. during surgery and to a substantial reduction in associated long-term disabilities. From a research point of view, in neuroscience this BrainOX NIROT instrument will be a major new asset, because it truly measures brain StO2, which is what neuroscientists need to assess brain function. This novel, non-invasive, harmless, silent BrainOX NIROT instrument can be applied in natural settings and enables to study e.g. brain development in neonates and children. It will be an invaluable tool for the neuroscience community
Keywords: brain oxygenation, depth resolution, near-infrared spectroscopy, time domain, tissue phantom

Title: Making Image Processing Cheap and Accessible by Self-Designed-Systems Principles
Abstract:
Making Image Processing Cheap and Accessible by Self-Designed-Systems Principles

Image processing is at the core of modern human-life. From hospitals to farmers, many small, medium, and large-scale organizations use image processing to improve the quality of their services. However, image processing is prohibitively expensive, as it requires vast amount of data and computation. Studies have shown that finding a good image processing algorithm can cause up to 3.6x higher carbon emission than a car can during its whole lifetime. In this project, we propose a self-designed image processing system that uses self-designed-systems principles to build an image processing system. Self-design systems define a design space and efficiently build real-world models for each relevant metric, such as time. By means of the real-world models, self-designed systems can quickly navigate in the design space and find the optimal solution. This eliminates the costly design process and hence makes image processing cheap and accessible.
Keywords: Image processing, Machine learning, Self-designed systems
