Title: Biomimetic Compliant Metastructures for Bone Implants
Abstract:
As the global population ages, there is an increasing unmet need for advanced implants to address the prevalence of bone fractures among the elderly. Current bone implants are dominated by stiff materials that lack the chemical composition and architectural cues found in natural bone. As a result, poor osseointegration of implants remains a significant challenge. Often overlooked is the fact that native bone remodels itself with the help of a soft tissue (osteoid), which is highly compliant, biodegradable, and conducive to neo-tissue formation (osteoconductive). Although mechanical metamaterials have emerged as promising candidates, limited progress has been made towards real-world medical applications. A significant knowledge gap exists in understanding the local interactions between cells and metamaterials as a function of design factors such as curvature, pore size, and stiffness - especially when using scaffolds made of bone-mimicking structures and compliant base materials. A key challenge lies in the lack of implant designs and fabrication strategies that adequately mimic native bone tissue and reliably promote mechano-regulated bone formation.

This proposal aims to develop biomimetic, osteoconductive metastructures for bone implants made of compliant base materials, leveraging machine-learning-accelerated inverse design and high-resolution fabrication techniques to overcome current limitations. The central hypothesis is that bone implants with tailored mechanical properties, controlled pore architecture, and enhanced bioactivity can significantly improve cell integration and in-vitro bone tissue formation. To achieve this, the project has four main objectives: 1) to create a computational framework for the inverse design of anisotropic metastructures; 2) to fabricate osteoconductive metastructures made of mineralized hydrogel nanocomposites to closely mimic native bone; 3) to develop mechanosensing techniques for the in-situ characterization of stress distributions in complex metatructures; and 4) to optimize bioactivity for enhanced cell integration and bone ingrowth. These objectives will be addressed by a collaborative theoretical-experimental research program involving five laboratories with interdisciplinary expertise in metamaterials, computational mechanics and machine learning, biomaterials and bone mechanics, polymer chemistry and mechanosensing, and material characterization.

The project’s main impact lies in its potential to revolutionize current bone implant technology, offering new solutions that promote implant integration and long-term biocompatibility, addressing critical gaps in current biomedical engineering approaches for sustainable healthcare solutions. Furthermore, this proposal promises new scientific insight into tissue-implant interactions, osteoconductive biomaterials, and the mechanics of compliant metamaterials. It further delivers new methodologies such as additive manufacturing routes for biomaterials, new techniques for quantitative in-situ stress characterization in complex structures, and a new versatile, generative design pipeline for metastructures with target geometric and mechanical properties, which mimics the natural process of bone formation. It also offers a highly interdisciplinary educational platform.

Title: Modeling Meaning in Text Data for the Social Sciences
Abstract:
New forms of data and advanced statistical techniques provide enormous research opportunities, yet the social sciences fall short of taking full advantage of them. A major obstacle is the lack of analytical approaches that are appropriate to both the questions and the data pertinent to the social sciences. This especially concerns the analysis of meaning in text—understood as shared reference structures that are reflected at the semantic, linguistic, and narrative level. In two subprojects described below, this project will develop methodological solutions to two core challenges in the analysis of text for the social sciences—(A) analyzing how conceptual meaning changes within time-stamped documents and (B) capturing distinct forms of meaning in interviews. Empirical applications of these solutions will explore important questions of history, politics, and culture and provide methodological guidance for the use of computational techniques and new forms of data more generally. Beyond immediate results, this project will lay the foundation and open new opportunities for leveraging modern forms of data and tools for answering questions in the social sciences.

In subproject A, we will develop machine learning methods tailored to the task of tracing the changing meaning and usage of concepts in large corpora of time-stamped documents. Although this is probably the most common format that massive quantities of textual data are and will be released in the near future (e.g. news feeds, media posts, publications, archival data), we still lack tools to analyze the changing meaning of particular concepts and ideas in such data. We will, therefore, develop a novel framework to trace the meaning of concepts through time. We will apply this framework to (i) a corpus of 1,300,000 academic articles to understand and compare changes in how “causality” has been understood in Philosophy, Economics, and Sociology since the 19th Century and to (ii) about 400,000 news reports to provide a data-driven description of the portrayal of “migrants” in the German public media leading up to the Syrian refugee crisis in 2015/16.

In subproject B, we will develop computational solutions to capture and analyze distinct forms of meaning in interview transcripts. Researcher-led interviews have long served as a fundamental source of high-quality data for answering social science questions. Many of these interviews, as well as comparable digital conversations on the new media, are readily available for computational analysis. Despite the enormous potential in this data, we still lack approaches that take advantage of the structures that occur “naturally” in interviews, such as narrative flow and turn-taking, to account for distinct forms of meanings in them. We will build on advances in natural language processing and network analysis to develop techniques that are precisely tailored to capturing different aspects of meanings in both structured and unstructured interviews. We will apply these techniques to (i) unstructured interviews with renowned US chefs to explore different levels of what it “means” to make a career as an elite chef and to (ii) structured interviews from the National Study of Youth and Religion to capture adolescents’ understandings of morality in relation to their socio-economic background. 

We will provide a detailed description of the methodological challenges and step-by-step documentation of respective solutions. Both of the above subprojects will combine new forms of data from various sources and apply hitherto untested algorithms. Providing methodological guidance and best practices for the combination and usage of data from various sources and in various formats has been identified as one of the most pressing needs for the newly emerging field of Computational Social Science. In both subprojects, we will, therefore, detail related challenges, analytic reflections, and solutions. As contributions to textbooks, this will help to improve teaching students in how to use computational tools to collect, combine and utilize both classic and modern, large-scale forms of text corpora for answering social science questions.

This project will advance computational solutions to leverage text as data for the analysis of meaning in the social sciences. In doing so, it will explore important questions of history, politics, and culture and provide methodological guidance for scholars in Computational Social Science.
Keywords: computational social science, network analysis, sociology of culture, sociology of knowledge, text analysis

Title: Machine-learning-driven engineering of quantum moiré nanostructures as (photo)electrocatalysts for the 21st-century hydrogen production
Abstract:
This project will pave the way for a rational comprehension and design of novel/improved catalysts in the context of the water splitting for the hydrogen production at quantum-level details via unprecedented Density Functional Theory-based computer simulations. The engineering of (photo)electrocatalysts (PECs) which use solar power for visible-light-driven water splitting is currently in the focus of worldwide research efforts toward clean and sustainable strategies to meet the increasing demand for renewable energy. However, viable PECs for hydrogen production on a global scale requires the development of devices that are highly efficient (cost/benefit ratio), stable and simple in design. In this context, the project proposes an ambitious and disruptive concept in the (photo)electrocatalysis area to design and to engineer efficient PECs for the hydrogen production via state-of-the-art ab-initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) [1] coupled with advanced machine-learning algorithms, and with the support of the experimental counterpart.
In particular, the project will focus on emerging water oxidation catalysts (WOCs) such as two-dimensional (2D) transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) WSe2 and MoSe2 as Moiré nanostructures [2-4]. A Moiré superlattice is organized as two or more (Van der Waals) layers stacked with a twist or lattice mismatch. The topology mismatching leads to novel quantum devices in which exotic phenomena (such as Moiré potential, flat bands, etc.) arise from Moiré physics, phenomena today not enough investigated due to the novel discovery of Moiré materials.  How Moiré superlattices and Moiré potential can affect the catalytic behaviour? How Moiré superlattices have to be modeled/engineered (layer composition, physical nature (metallic, semiconducting), methods for preparation, twist-angle and stacking order) for enhanced catalytic properties? Which is the best catalytic topology/motif of these homo/hetero junctions? And again, the lack of a quantum electronic structure study/theory make challenging the characterization of Moiré nanostructures as well as a one-to-one comparison/synergy with the few available experimental evidences. In this context, the aim of the project is to fully assess Moiré TMDs as efficient water splitting PECs. WSe2 and MoSe2 are emerging as efficient WOCs [5], however less is known about their (photo)electrocatalytic properties when Moiré nanostructures [6,7]. 
The goal is to develop a theory following two complementary steps: 1) modeling and quantum engineering of 2D Moiré homobilayers WSe2 and MoSe2 and heterobilayers WSe2/MoSe2 in terms of electronic structure, optical and structural properties, conductivity properties, etc. (details below);  2) to fully assess the abovementioned 2D Moiré TMDs as water splitting catalysts revealing the energy (free-energy barriers/changes), the kinetics and the thermodynamics (reaction pathways, minimum energy pathway) behind the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) via DFT-metadynamics technique [8,9] with ad-hoc inclusion of nuclear quantum effects [10-12] (ab-initio Path-Integral molecular dynamics). Machine learning algorithms [13-17] will help and drive the modeling/engineering of Moiré nanostructures enhancing the prediction/investigation (phase-space sampling of the OER) of catalyst performance. 
It is an ambitious but realistic project that aims to push computer simulations and computational material science beyond standard approaches. The novelty/unconventionality is given by the quite virgin research field of Moiré-nanostructures (only few papers available) as well as the computational methods will be employed (DFT molecular dynamics (DFT-MD), metadynamics/machine learning) that aim to overcome the usual DFT-static/single point picture given by most of theoretical studies in the field. Moreover, the proposed project is manifestly per se a multidisciplinary research ranging from computational material science to the practical characterization of devices having a concrete impact into the solar-to-fuel catalysts engineering, in agreement with the ‘future’ hydrogen-economy based society. The project can rely on an experienced applicant in computational catalysis field and on consolidated/renowned national and international experimental partners.

Title: Conversational AI: Dialogue-based Adaptive Argumentative Writing Support
Abstract:
This is a project in the area of Natural language processing (NLP). This is a subfield of Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Computational Linguistics concerned with the interactions between computers and human language. Within the scope of this research project, we aim to explore the potential of adaptive argumentation skill learning with designing, implementing and evaluating dialogue-based adaptive writing support systems to help students to improve their ability to argue in a structured, logical and reflective way.

For this purpose, we plan to research and develop a novel machine learning-based method to automatically assess the quality of students’ argumentative texts. Moreover, we aim to investigate the ability of chatbots, using sophisticated statistical and neural network language models, as a feedback provider to guide students towards building persuasive arguments.

To gain the important training date for the supervised machine learning, we first need to develop a extensive labeling scheme. Therefore, we will develop a novel rich semantic representation for fine-grained argumentation annotations capturing logical, rhetoric and dialectical quality dimensions. Based on this innovative annotation scheme, we will build a large, reusable argumentation corpus. To our knowledge, it is the first of its kind. Therefore, it can become a valuable resource for all researchers in our field.

The argumentation corpus constitutes the data set for our machine learning algorithm, i.e. the algorithm for extracting argumentative discourse structures and assessing the quality of the underlying argumentation. Furthermore, we will explore and build novel dialogue-based argumentation learning frameworks.

Hence, we will develop an argumentative dialogue agent, also called a chatbot, that debates with students with the objective of playfully increasing their arguing skills. This dialogue agent utilises our comprehensive argumentation corpus, as well as large language models and BERT-like architectures. Next, we will extend the dialogue system in the direction of a feedback provider that evaluates the quality of students’ argumentative texts and gives interactive feedback on their lines of argumentation.

The main outcomes of this project will be (i) a novel comprehensive approach to automatically assess the quality of argumentative texts for providing adaptive static feedback; (ii) a proof-of-concept for an argumentative dialogue agent for debating with students on controversial topics with the objective of playfully improving their arguing skills; and (iii) a first prototype of a dialogue-based approach for providing students with adaptive interactive feedback on the quality of their arguments and reasoning chains.

The expected results of our project are interesting for both scientific communities and practitioners. We explore an emerging application field of Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Artificial Intelligence (AI), in particular the potential of educational agents to teach students how to write persuasive texts by engaging in a conversation with the user and providing adaptive feedback about the quality of their argumentation. Moreover, the results of this research project will help companies to develop argumentation learning tools to support the continuous education of their employees, aiming to improve their arguing skills to better match the requirements of today’s job profiles. Nowadays, with the tasks demanding more and more creativity and interdisciplinary cooperation, the ability to argue convincingly is indispensable.
Keywords: Argument Generation, Argument Mining, Argument Quality, Argument Retrieval, Artificial Intelligence, Chatbots, Computational Linguistics, Conversational AI, Large Language Models, Linguistic Resources, Machine Learning, Natural Language Processing, Semantic Representation, Skill Learning, Text Generation

Title: GSP: Signal Processing on Graphs and Fundamental Problems in Machine Learning and Sensor Networks
Abstract:
It comes at no surprise that we are facing today a deluge of information generated by large networks of sensors or data sources. The representation and analysis of such high-dimensional datasets is undoubtedly a very cumbersome task. Fortunately, one can often identify relational structures in large datasets that facilitate the data analysis tasks. 

In many cases, the data structure can be described by a graph representation which underlies signals or functions of interest in the dataset. Contrarily to the classical signal representations on Euclidian spaces, the graph representations lead to richer data descriptions on more topologically complicated domains, such as social networks, sensor networks, or geometrically complex manifolds. When the data are represented on the vertices of a graph, one has to resort to a novel framework and new algorithms for the efficient processing of the information. Spectral graph wavelets offer a flexible method for the analysis of data on graphs, but the in-depth study and understanding of this novel representation, and its application to inference problems or distributed applications still represent important research challenges.

In this project, we want to continue the theoretical development of general techniques for signal processing on graphs and develop the foundations for their application to fundamental problems in machine learning and sensor networks. In particular, we plan to develop the theoretical aspects of the spectral wavelet transform with in-depth understanding of the true role of the graph structure in such a signal transform. Then we will study the application of graph spectral wavelets to graph-based semi-supervised learning problems which represent an important class of data analysis problems in large datasets. In addition, we will extend the graph-based representation and analysis framework to distributed settings represented by sensor networks, which brings important constraints in terms of communication and computation in realistic data analysis problems.

The proposed project certainly defines very important research challenges in the analysis of structured and high-dimensional datasets. At the same time, it certainly offers a high potential for the development of a novel and promising framework for many emerging applications that address the analysis of large-scale medical data, rich social network information or high-dimensional signals in vision sensor networks, for example.

Title: PHENOFLOW: A multifaceted workflow of high-throughput field phenotyping for improved prediction of wheat performance in future climate scenarios based on assessment of dynamic changes of phenology
Abstract:
Plant development is a dynamic process. Morphology, coloration and physiological processes change throughout development and are affected by environmental factors. Annual crops such as wheat need to develop under strongly varying environmental conditions. Assessing the genotype by environment interactions in an automated manner throughout crop development would be highly beneficial to improve approaches in crop modeling and breeding. 
The overall objective of this project is to establish a workflow of robust, automated image processing procedures capturing the performance of winter wheat genotypes. Individual procedures exist for certain traits but are applied mostly on data of few seasons, lacking generic applicability. The specific aims of the project are to i) elaborate robust workflows capturing ‘simple’ and ‘dynamic’ crop traits in high-throughput field phenotyping campaigns mostly based on RGB images taken from close distance ii) determine the response of a high number of wheat genotypes towards several environmental factors at different developmental stages iii) utilize this knowledge to predict the performance of previously analyzed genotypes under current and future climatic scenarios. 
To achieve this, the project will analyze existing and newly acquired images of wheat throughout multiple years at very high spatial resolution (pixel resolution < 1 mm), temporal resolution (at least two imaging campaigns per week) and for many genotypes (dozens to hundreds). This will be done on more than 230’000 images acquired in the ETH field phenotyping platform FIP since 2015 as well as on new data to be acquired in the FIP with a new multi-camera rig rendering an annual data volume of up to 23 TB. Traits such as germination rate and time point, duration of stem elongation or time point of heading will be extracted from these images, leading to an image-based characterization of the developmental progress of all genotypes. Extraction of these traits will be performed with image processing approaches such as color segmentation and with methods of artificial intelligence such as machine learning algorithms and convolutional neural networks. The coordinate system, in which those traits will be quantitatively captured is an adaptation of existing developmental schemes termed DYNAPHEN scale. It allows efficient establishment of environmental response functions useful for crop simulation models. Since annotated images will be made publicly available, this image dataset will form an important training set for data challenges dealing with even more genotypes and environments. The immediate impact of PHENOFLOW is that it will provide a robust workflow for automated trait characterization from single or multiple images, taking environmental co-variables into account, which is required by high throughput field phenotyping approaches. Thereby the project will be of value for the entire field phenotyping community and PHENOFLOW will stimulate future research in crop modeling, breeding, agronomy and physiology. It will facilitate optimized crop management and increase the resilience of wheat to climate change by allowing for more targeted crop breeding.

Title: A New Approach to Preserving Endangered Languages in the Field
Abstract:
Two decades ago, the linguistics community received a wake-up call, when Hale et al. predicted the death or doom of 90% of the world’s languages by the year 2100, and warned that linguistics might “go down in history as the only science that presided obliviously over the disappearance of 90 per cent of the veryfield to which it is dedicated.” Today, language documentation is a high priority in mainstream linguistics. However, the cognate subfield in computer science, language engineering, is yet to participate.

The first half century of research in language engineering and its allied disciplines of natural language processing and computational linguistics — from circa 1960 up to the present — has touched on less than 1% of the world’s languages. For a field which is justly proud of its empirical methods, it is time to apply those methods to the remaining 99% of languages. We will never have the luxury of richly annotated data for these languages, so we must try to do more
with less. For example, we need leaner methods for building machine translation systems; innovative ways to do cross-linguistic bootstrapping via multiple paths; and more effective ways to leverage human effort in labelling data. Such work is the focus of the new international initiative, and already underway in Google’s new ‘Babel’ project which is crowdsourcing aligned text using Amazon’s Mechanical Turk. If language engineering can rise to this, the greatest language challenge of our time, we simultaneously enable multi-lingual technology development at a new scale, and we lay the foundations for a new science of empirical universal linguistics.

Despite the grand scale of these new initiatives, the majority of the world’s languages are oral only, and are left out. This includes thousands of small languages which will probably die out with the current generation. To date, there is no scalable method for acquiring bilingual text for unwritten languages. This project will establish a new method for preserving oral discourse, originating in field recordings made by native speakers, and generating a variety of products including digitally archived collections. It addresses the problem of unwritten languages being omitted from various ongoing efforts to collect language resources for ever larger subsets of the world’s languages. Although no funds are sought for data collection or data preparation, the methods and training provided by the project, together with 100 voice recorders donated by Olympus, will significantly increase the quality and quantity of preserved oral literature from the languages of New Guinea. This will be the first engineering contribution to the problem of language endangerment, and the question of sustainability of linguistic heritage. The model of aligned text to be developed will be significant in that it will be the first to generalise across bilingual texts, interlinear glossed texts, and lexicons.

This approach is innovative in other ways. It harnesses voluntary labour of interested community members who already have access to a wide range of natural contexts where the language is used, and who decide what subjects and genres to record, and who are in an excellent position to train others. They are also able to move around the country to visit other language groups, far more easily than a foreign linguist could. As owners of the data collection activity, they demonstrate a high level of commitment to the task, which plays into the quality and quantity of the resulting materials. The activities easily fit alongside language development activities, adding status and substance to those activities, and potentially drawing a wider cross-section of the community into language development. Only limited supervision by a trained linguist/archivist is required between the initial training and the final archiving.

Title: The Role of the Basal Ganglia in Motor Learning and Adaptation
Abstract:
Many of our daily activities, such as writing, speaking, playing a sport or an instrument, depend on learned motor skills, most of which require executing complex and precise movements in a reproducible and effortless manner. These skills and behaviors also need to be robust to environmental changes, adapting rapidly to new physical contingencies and conditions. The basal ganglia is widely thought to be involved in both learning new behaviors and adapting already learned ones, yet despite numerous studies it has been difficult to establish a direct causal link between basal ganglia function and motor learning/adaptation. One reason for this may be that these questions are, to a large degree, being pursued in humans and non-human primates, models ill suited for large-scale invasive experiments required to dissect the detailed function of the basal ganglia.  

Rodents offer an attractive alternative for studying how complex behaviors are acquired and generated by the brain. I spent the last year developing behavioral paradigms, and experimental tools and techniques for using rodents to address questions related to how motor skills are acquired by the brain and how the motor programs underlying these skills can adapt to environmental changes. A prerequisite for my work is to train large cohorts of rats on complex motor skills. To enable this, I developed a completely automated behavior training set-up that allows for high-throughput training of complex behaviors. I also worked to optimize a novel behavioral paradigm for motor skill learning, and designed and built a motorized manipulandum that will enable me to conduct experiments on motor adaptation similar to ones performed in humans and non-human primates.

With the experimental infrastructure in place, I will spend the next three years studying how the basal ganglia contribute to the process of trial-and-error learning (Aim 1) and motor adaptation (Aim 2). In Aim 1, I will test the hypothesis that the mammalian basal ganglia are involved in generating and regulating the behavioral variability required for trial-and-error learning. I will also test whether the behavioral variability has an ‘instructive’ component, thus directly testing an influential idea of the basal ganglia as a ‘teacher’ of the descending motor control pathway. In Aim 2, I will examine the extent to which the basal ganglia are involved in motor adaptation, by changing the load required to perform an already learned task. In both aims I will manipulate the function of both the input and output of the basal ganglia and observe the effects in motor output and performance.

The initial experiments detailed in this proposal are designed to identify the involvement of different sub-regions of the basal ganglia in the acquisition of a well-defined motor skill through trial-and-error learning, and to further examine whether and how these regions are involved in adapting to changes in environmental contexts. The follow-up phases of this project will build on the outcomes of these initial experiments and use neural recording and transgenic/optogenetic circuit manipulation techniques to test increasingly more detailed hypotheses concerning the role of the basal ganglia in different types of motor learning.

Title: Cyberdelinquency and cybervictimization among young people in Switzerland (16-24 Years Old)
Abstract:
In response to the increasing prevalence of cybercrime and the growing concerns surrounding it, the proposed study aims to analyse this issue in-depth. This research considers a broad spectrum of delinquent and deviant online behavior among young people aged from 16 to 24 years old, both as perpetrators and victims of cybercrime. This kind of research has not yet been conducted in Switzerland. Previous research, both in Switzerland and internationally, has predominantly examined younger population, like student populations, in relation to cyberoffending or has concentrated only on specific aspects of online victimization. There is also a lack of studies that predict cyber delinquency and cyber victimization based on a rich set of concepts derived from criminological, psychological and sociological theories. Furthermore, the widespread use of chatbots and artificial intelligence (AI) systems, which has led to new forms of criminal behavior and online victimization, has been little analyzed. Regarding the official statistics, like police statistics on cybercrime, they provide limited insights into the true extent of cybercrime due to underreporting. Therefore, this study will address a significant gap by offering a comprehensive examination of cybercrime, crucial for developing a holistic understanding of the issue.  

The primary objectives of the research are to explore the scope, nature, and dynamics of cybercrime among youth, identify the most prevalent types of cybercrime in which young people are involved—both as offenders and victims—and assess the consequences of cybercrime (psychological, financial, etc.) on victims. Additionally, the study will examine young people's awareness of online risks, their behaviors in safeguarding personal data, and their ability to recognize illegal online activities. Another key objective is to explore the overlap between cybercrime offending and victimization, shedding light on how these roles are interconnected. By identifying which theories best explain cybercrime behaviors across various offenses, this study will also contribute to filling important gaps in the literature on cybercrime. 

To achieve these goals, a random sample of 8,500 young people aged 16 to 24 from the Swiss resident population will be surveyed, thus covering an age bracket when crime typically is peaking. Using a unified sampling frame, respondents will be selected from the resident register provided by the Federal Statistical Office (FSO). These persons will be invited by postal mail to participate in an anonymous online survey. To improve response rates and for a sufficient net sample for the analyses, one-third of the total contacted sample (30,000 persons) will receive a CHF 10 prepaid incentive and two thirds will not be incentivised. These two conditions –presence and absence of monetary incentives – will be compared in an experimental design to determine the effects of monetary incentivization on response rates and on reported involvement in cyber delinquency.  

This research is expected to have far-reaching implications, including enhancements to academic curricula, particularly in criminology and cybersecurity. The findings will help refine theories of online criminal behavior, pinpoint risk factors, and shape educational programs that reflect the latest developments in cybercrime prevention. Beyond academia, the results will deepen our understanding of digital risks and promote safer online behaviors, leading to practical guidelines for minimizing exposure to cybercrime. The findings will also serve as a valuable resource for public discourse and policymaking. This project has received full support from the Conference of Cantonal Police Commanders of Switzerland (CCPCS) and the Federal Social Insurance Office (FSIO).

Title: Can Artificial Intelligence Improve Economic Policy Decisions? Optimal Assignment Rules for Labour Market Programmes
Abstract: Public employment services allocate limited funds to unemployed persons with the objective of reducing their unemployment duration and improving employment stability in the future, e.g., by assigning unemployed persons to job search assistance or training programmes (which are called active labour market policies,  ALMPs). A large body of literature provides evidence that ALMPs have heterogeneous effects by characteristics of the unemployed and regional economic conditions. Optimal (statistical) assignment rules have the potential to improve the effectiveness of ALMPs. Recently, machine learning algorithms have been proposed to estimate optimal assignment rules. They have the potential to incorporate more covariates and outperform the out-of-sample prediction power of conventional estimation approaches. The proposed research project simulates the implementation of optimal assignment rules for ALMPs using high-quality administrative data that include 5 million unemployed persons. I consider optimal assignment rules for multiple ALMPs and several welfare functions. I test algorithmic restrictions that have the purpose to prevent discrimination. Since the effectiveness of ALMPs could vary between boom and recession periods, I consider dynamic optimal assignment rules that can adapt to economic conditions.
Keywords: Active Labour Market Policies, Causal Inference, Machine Learning, Microeconometrics, Programme Evaluation, Public Policy

Title: Safe entrapment of As and Se in zeolites: Mechanistic understanding obtained from spectroscopic investigations and atomistic simulations
Abstract:
Selenium (Se) and arsenic (As) are anionic hazardous metalloids which may be present in significant quantities in supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs) such as ground granulated blast furnace slag (GGBFS), fly ash (FA) or municipal solid waste incineration (MSWI) bottom ash. SCMs are increasingly used in modern binders as substitute for cement clinker to reduce CO2 emission during cement production. These metalloids pose a potential risk for the environment and human health because their presence in the anionic form implies a high mobility as they are not retained by common cement compounds carrying a negative surface charge. 
The hydration of Portland cement blended with SCMs or the alkali activation of SCM results in the formation of zeolite-type phases among other hydrated cement compounds. Some of these zeolite-type phases belonging to the sodalite and cancrinite families possess the capacity to incorporate anions in their cages and channels thus strongly limiting their mobility. These types of zeolites are also formed during contact of alkaline radioactive waste tank solutions and the sediments beneath the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Hanford Site. The presence of sodalite and cancrinite in cement containing SCMs and in the cementitious materials used in radioactive waste repositories may significantly reduce the mobility of Se anions. 
The detailed mechanism and kinetics of selenium and arsenic incorporation and the thermodynamic stability of As and Se bearing zeolites at relevant chemical condition remains poorly understood. The goal of the present project is to obtain a better insight into the mechanism of the selenium and arsenic immobilization by sodalite- and cancrinite-type zeolites under the high pH conditions and relatively high sulfur or carbonate concentrations relevant for cementitious environments. The project includes:
-Pure sodalities and cancrinites will be synthesized and characterised with scanning electron microscopy (SEM-EDX), powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD), FT-IR, Raman spectroscopy and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR).
-X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) will elucidate the local environment of As and Se species in zeolites.
-The leaching behaviour of Se- and As-incorporated sodalite and cancrinite phases will be investigated in batch experiments.
-Zeolite precipitation experiments in the presence of Se or S anions will be conducted and transformation of the solids will be followed in situ with synchrotron-based pair distribution function (PDF) analysis techniques.
-XAS data will be analysed with advanced theoretical calculations such as FEFF and FDMNES, coupled with molecular calculations.
-Machine learning will be employed to automatize the FEFF and FDMNES calculations based on molecular calculations and the comparison with experimental data.
The gained fundamental knowledge about the formation and stability of Se- and As-sodalite and -cancrinite phases will allow a better evaluation of the potential risks of As and Se present in modern binders and 79Se in cement-solidified radioactive waste, for the environment and for human health. Finally, there is a need for new stable matrices suitable for the immobilization of anionic pollutants such as As and Se. In contrast to other cementitious materials which become unstable under neutral and weak acidic pH conditions, zeolites are stable under most environmental conditions. A detailed mechanistic understanding of the incorporation of As and Se by zeolites of the sodalite and cancrinite families will help to decide whether they are suitable as a stable matrix for the immobilization anionic pollutants.

Title: Establishment of high-precision and miniature genome editors for clinical applications
Abstract:
More than a decade of research on bacterial CRISPR-Cas immune defense systems has paved the way to the development of programmable nucleases, which are powerful tools for genome editing. Further refinement of these technologies in recent years led to a myriad of applications in basic research and biotechnology, and even to the initiation of clinical trials where CRISPR-Cas mediated genome editing is used to treat patients with certain genetic diseases. 
Despite these rapid advances in therapeutic genome editing, CRISPR-Cas nucleases have two major limitations. First, CRISPR-Cas induced DNA double strand breaks (DSBs) have been found to induce complex DNA damage, including large deletions and chromosomal rearrangements, warranting caution for application in patients. Second, DSBs are predominantly repaired by inaccurate non-homologous end joining pathways, as opposed to homology-directed repair from template DNA, making precise correction of pathogenic mutations inefficient. Base- and prime editing are novel genome editing technologies that circumvent these limitations. They consist of Cas proteins fused to either a deaminase or a reverse transcriptase, modifying the target DNA sequence without DSB formation and homology-directed repair. Both systems, however, rely on positioning of the complex in a precisely defined distance to the mutation, which is often not possible with currently available Cas9 proteins due to the requirement of a protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) for Cas9 to be able to bind to DNA (e.g. an NGG motif for SpCas9). In addition, fusing Cas9 proteins to deaminases or reverse transcriptase generates extremely large protein complexes, making in vivo delivery challenging. 
In the proposed project we aim to address these limitations to improve and widen the application of base-and prime editors for therapeutic purposes. For this we will establish novel base- and prime editors by rational protein/RNA engineering and by directed protein evolution. For the latter we will employ various approaches, including phage-assisted continuous evolution (PACE), yeast-based continuous evolution (OrthoRep) and screening of mutagenesis libraries in bacterial survival assays. In aim 1, we anticipate to increase the targeting range of SpCas9 without reducing its specificity. Thus, unlike previous studies that relaxed the PAM requirements of SpCas9 we will develop a library of 64 different SpCas9 variants, each detecting one of the 64 possible trinucleotide PAM sites. In addition, we anticipate to increase the activity of SpCas9 variants for on-target editing while at the same time reducing their activity for off-target editing. In aim 2, we will generate and optimize ultra-small base- and prime editors to improve in vivo delivery. With rational protein engineering and linker screening we will first generate functional fusion proteins between small-sized Cas12f/TnpB nucleases and deaminases/reverse transcriptases. Using directed protein evolution, we will then increase the activity, specificity and targeting range of these novel genome editors. Finally, in aim 3 we attempt to further enhance in vivo base- and prime editing rates by optimizing the locus-specific designs of the RNA components that direct base- and prime editors to their target sites (sgRNAs and pegRNAs, respectively). To achieve this goal, we will first conduct high-throughput base- and prime editing screens in vivo in the mouse liver, and then use these datasets to train machine learning models for predicting optimal sgRNA/pegRNA designs for in vivo genome editing. In addition, we will assess and quantify the influence of chromatin characteristics on the activity of base- and prime editors, and implement this knowledge into our prediction tools. Taken together, the proposed project aims to greatly enhance the CRISPR-Cas genome editing toolbox and thereby facilitate the translation of base- and prime editing into the clinics.
Keywords: CRISPR-Cas, Genetherapy, Genome Editing

Title: Arbeitstitel "Soft Magnetic Robots: Modeling, Design and Control of Magnetically Guided Continuum Manipulators"
Abstract:
Soft continuum robotics combines the precision and dexterity associated with classical robotic arms with the compliance and intrinsic safety of rubber like actuators. These actuators can have a range of applications from lumen inspection and exploration, to microrobot locomotion, to object manipulation in constrained environments. Specifically in medical applications, these devices provide a means to inspect, deliver drug payloads, or implant devices into soft tissue while avoiding the stiffness mismatch between the tissue and the device, which can lead to unnecessary trauma. Common continuum manipulators, such as endoscopes, catheters, and steerable needles, rely on stiff constitutive materials so the forces and torques necessary for their motion can be transmitted along the body via tendons or concentric tubes. Designing devices that are composed of intrinsically soft components is difficult within this mechanical actuation paradigm, because the ability to transfer the mechanical actuation commands along the length of the device requires stiff tendons and large actuator forces to achieve the necessary bending moments and overcome friction. Magnetic actuation of these devices, however, does not carry the same constraints because force and torques can be applied directly to imbedded magnetic materials along the manipulator with a pervasive magnetic field. This allows the device to be composed of very soft materials that do not need to structurally support internal tendon tensions. 

This project theoretically and experimentally investigates robotic tasks performed by magnetic continuum manipulators (MCMs) that are steered by externally generated non-uniform magnetic fields generated by magnetic navigation systems (MNS). MCMs are soft robots that are essentially composed of a slender flexible body comprising a magnet at its distal tip. By generating an external magnetic field, these robots can be steered in a remote manner, thus, opening the way to navigation within the human vessels and cavities. Such robots exhibit a high potential for medical applications (e.g. drug delivery, RF energy delivery, tissue sampling) where their highly deformable soft structure ensures safety and adaptability to interaction with soft organic tissues. The use of these devices is, however, subject to fundamental scientific and technological issues including their fabrication, their control, and their analysis, which was the focus of our prior efforts. 

During the first phase of this project, our MCM technology, as well as our expertise in the field of their fabrication, analysis, and control, have been brought to a higher level of maturity. In the second phase of this project, we will develop application-driven devices to attain the next step toward their clinical-readiness. For this purpose, we will rely on the strong collaboration with medical institutes and hospitals that we have been building for the past three years. New targeted applications range from treatment of brain aneurysms within the Circle of Willis, to exploration of anatomical cavities such as the maxillary sinus or the middle ear are promising as an application for the MCMs. A particular emphasis will be placed on reliable control and localization of the tools for these specific applications, based on the outcome of our prior research. We will also develop our technologies and our fabrication methods of MCMs with the help of industrial and academic partners specialized in the integration of sensors and active parts within millimeter-scale catheters. With regard to fundamental engineering research, we will also extend our ability to understand and characterize the behavior of MCMs and MNS by exploring novel methods for their modeling and their analysis, making use of tools such as deep learning methods and numerical continuation.

Expected outcomes from this application-driven project range from publications in high impact factor trans-disciplinary and robotic journals, to the development of medical robotic systems to a pre-clinical stage.
Keywords: Continuum robotics, Localization, Magnetic Manipulation, Magnetic Navigation Systems, Nonuniform Magnetic Field, Soft Robotics

Title: Cracking the GPCR Code: Decoding Biased Signalling in GPCRs with Machine Learning and Enhanced Sampling for Improved Therapeutics
Abstract: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are one of the most important protein families for pharmaceutical development. The activation of GPCRs by full, partial, and biased agonists governs a wide range of physiological responses through complex mechanisms. Despite recent progress, many details of these activation processes and pathway-selective signalling remain unclear, hindering the rational design of more effective and less toxic drugs. Molecular simulations have effectively contributed to clarify GPCR activation dynamics, but they are hampered by the limited time-scales accessible. To this end, effective enhanced sampling algorithms complemented by machine learning can be very effective. This proposal aims to further develop our advanced sampling, machine learning and cryptic pocket algorithms (Aim 1) to better understand key aspects of GPCR activation, such as the mechanisms underlying biased signalling and the potential of allosteric cryptic pockets for drug development. Our research will focus on two receptor families of major biomedical importance: ß-adrenergic receptors (Aim 2) and opioid receptors (Aim 3). Through established collaborations and partnerships with experimental groups, we will not only validate our computational predictions but also gain new insights into the design of more effective and less toxic drugs.

Title: Inferring the evolution of proteins and of protein-protein interactions using language models trained on sequence data
Abstract:
Proteins play key roles in cells, often through their interactions with other proteins. Understanding the evolution of proteins and of their interactions is a fundamental biological question, with many potential applications in biotechnology, including protein design. Protein sequence data contains key information on protein evolution, and is becoming more and more abundant. The recent progress of deep learning, in particular protein language models trained on multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) of homologous proteins, has been crucial to the recent major advances in protein structure prediction. We propose to use this type of approaches to investigate the evolution of proteins and of protein-protein interactions.

During evolution, random mutations affect sequences, but natural selection acts at the level of biological function. This constrains the evolution of protein sequences. Some amino acids are conserved because of their key functional roles. Moreover, the pairs of amino acids that are in contact in the three-dimensional structure of a protein must preserve their physico-chemical complementary to maintain protein structure and function. In MSAs of homologous proteins, which share the same ancestry and similar structure and function, these coevolving pairs of amino acid sites feature correlations in their amino acid usage. While coevolutionary correlations have been shown to be critical for protein function, they are typically ignored when inferring phylogeny from sequences, i.e. when inferring the evolutionary history of proteins. However, protein language models trained on MSAs capture both coevolution and phylogenetic relationships. We will use them to develop new coevolution-aware methods of phylogeny inference based on evolutionary distances. We will also develop coevolution-aware character-based phylogeny inference methods by using differentiable optimization. We will infer ancestral sequences using these methods. We will compare our inferred trees and ancestral sequences to those from established methods that assume independent sites, and quantify the role of coevolution in phylogeny inference and in protein evolution. We will develop new approaches to disentangle correlations due to phylogeny from correlations due to fitness constraints, using nucleotide-level information, including synonymous mutations. 

Protein language models capture the coevolution between amino acids in protein sequence data in a remarkable way. Coevolution also occurs at the genomic scale, between genes encoding proteins that interact together or are involved in the same pathway. Thus, genome-scale language models hold great promise to inform us about protein-protein interactions and their evolution. Our preliminary investigations focusing on bacterial genomes suggest that this signal can indeed be extracted. We will train genome-scale language models spanning the tree of life, which will be focused on protein-coding genes and informed by protein language models. We will validate our proteome language models by predicting gene essentiality and variant fitness in a genomic context-aware way. Next, we will use these proteome language models to make new predictions of protein-protein interaction networks, and study their evolution. In addition to examining their general features, we will investigate specific protein complexes studied by our experimental collaborators.

This project will provide new phylogeny inference methods that include coevolution between amino acids. This will yield new insight into protein evolution and the genotype-phenotype map, and bridge phylogeny and coevolution. We will produce new proteome language models that capture coevolution between genes. These models will allow us to make genomic context-aware predictions of gene essentiality and fitness, and to infer protein-protein interaction networks and their evolution.

Title: Nerve morphometry with whole extremity coverage in high-resolution MR neurography
Abstract: Magnetic resonance (MR) imaging of peripheral nerves, termed MR neurography (MRN), is increasingly gaining attention for clinical diagnostic evaluation and treatment monitoring of peripheral nerve diseases. It enables morphological investigation of proximal and deeply situated nerve segments not accessible by other diagnostic techniques, including gold-standard electrodiagnostic studies (EDX). MRN at 3 tesla is now clinically used as a complementary tool to EDX and can quantify biophysical nerve tissue properties based on morphology and signal behaviour. To assess morphology and signal behaviour in a clinically feasible and reproducible manner, we have developed a fully automatic nerve segmentation technique for clinical MRN images using convolutional neural networks (artificial intelligence, AI) and proposed a concept of quantitative analysis of nerve morphology and lesion type. However, the approach is currently limited by the MRN sequence characteristics, such as a lower resolution and limited anatomical coverage. With the recent progress in higher resolution MRN, even the qualitative analysis of nerve substructures such as nerve fascicle bundles becomes available nowadays. However, these MRN sequences are 2-D sequences, require long acquisition times (e.g. ~1 hour for an entire lower extremity), and are prone to motion artefacts. The available segmentation techniques do not offer a full anatomical coverage or allow quantification of a substructural morphology. These challenges limit their extended use despite their potential of shedding new insights into nerve pathology. This project aims to develop an entirely new MRN sequence termed "rapid exploratory imaging" (REI) for motion-insensitive, 3-D high-resolution imaging (down to 200-250 micrometres, in plane) that can cover a whole extremity from the nerve roots to the most distal parts within a clinically feasible scan time of around 30 minutes. Along with the sequence, this project aims to develop an automated segmentation technique tailored for assessing the nerve morphology from the spinal roots to the most distal parts including a substructural analysis. The REI sequence development will follow SPACE, a 3-D turbo spin echo sequence. Fat saturation schemes shall be applied to improve image contrast, which will be empirically optimised. Non-Cartesian acquisition schemes combined with parallel imaging, compressed sensing, and AI reconstruction will be employed to achieve our aims of motion resilience, high resolution and fast acquisition times. By adopting our AI, quantitative morphometric analysis of peripheral nerves will be possible through peripheral nerve segmentation. Substructural analysis of nerve fascicles and morphometric quantification of lesions will be performed, resulting in a holistic quantification of the segmented peripheral nerves at multiple scales. In a prospective validation study of clinically and neurophysiologically defined patient cohorts, the developed REI sequence with the morphometric analysis will be clinically tested. The ability to assess proximal nerve segments, the new pathophysiological insights into peripheral nerve diseases through substructural analysis, and the ability to derive quantitative parameters based on biophysical tissue properties are among the key points of this methodology. This could be beneficial in the future for a more optimal treatment monitoring of neuromuscular diseases such as in immune neuropathies (e.g. multifocal motor neuropathies, chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy). Also, the lack of specificity of standard MRN could be tackled by the ability to categorize peripheral nerve lesions more accurately by morphometric data and substructural analysis (e.g. poorly understood "idiopathic" plexopathies could possibly be attributed to a certain pathophysiological process such as inflammatory or microvasculitic).

Title: Combining metric and kernel learning
Abstract:
Kernel and metric learning have become very active research fields in machine learning 
over the last years. Although they have developed as distinct research fields they share 
common elements. One of the most popular approaches to kernel learning is learning a linear 
combination of a set of kernels, usually identified as Multiple Kernel Learning (MKL), 
this essentially corresponds to learning a block diagonal transformation of the concatenation
feature space induced by the concatenation of the feature spaces that correspond to the basis 
kernels. On the metric learning side, probably the most prominent approach is learning 
a Mahalanobis distance in some feature space which in fact corresponds
to learning a linear transformation in that feature space. So both methods learn
linear feature transformations, where in the case of the MKL the learned transformation
has a specific structure. Many of the metric learning methods are kernelized which
raises the issue of which kernel should one use for a given problem, nevertheless
there is no work so far that tries to combine metric learning with MKL. On the other
hand since MKL is learning a special form of linear transformation over the concatenation 
feature space one could use metric learning techniques in order to learn such linear 
transformations or more general forms of them. In fact one can use metric learning techniques 
to learn linear transformations over the feature space induced by any kernel. On the same time, 
and despite the increasing popularity of metric learning methods, there exist so far no 
such method that will scale well with increasing problem sizes, i.e. large feature space 
dimensionality and large number of instances, and on the same time retain a good generalization 
performance.

In the present proposal we want to take a step to address the issues briefly described above. 
More precisely the work described in the present proposal is divided into two workpackages. In 
the first workpackage we link metric learning and kernel learning  methods, by using tools from one 
domain in the other and vice versa. In the second workpackage we will propose metric learning methods 
that can scale well with large datasets. The work of the first workpackage
is divided into two main tasks. In the first task we will combine metric learning with MKL, i.e.
learning metrics over kernels learned by MKL. We will explore different metric parametrizations
which will lead to different learning problems. In the second task we will go on the opposite 
direction and use metric learning ideas for kernel learning. More precisely we will learn linear
transformations of the feature space induced by some kernel, whether this is a kernel that is learned
or it is a standard single kernel. By learning a linear transformation of the feature space we are in
fact learning in the general case a new non-linear, quadratic, kernel. We will experiment with different 
objective functions in order to learn the linear transformations. In the second workpackage we will also
have two main tasks. In the first we will explore the use of stochastic gradient descent methods in order
to improve the scalability of metric learning. In the second task we will go to the extreme case of 
metric learning and we will learn a linear transformation of rank one in order to make metric learning
possible for very large datasets. At first we might think that learning a rank one metric might be too
restrictive limiting its application only to simple learning problems. Nevertheless, by kernelizing it, 
we can  apply it on learning problems of any complexity.
Keywords: kernel learning, large scale metric learning, metric learning

Title: Compact, High-Speed and Specialized Computing Unit for Efficient Generative Artificial Intelligence with Deep Optics
Abstract:
Contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) models’ exponentially growing complexity translates to their proportionately widening skill sets.  Generative AI can create language or image content that can mimic human creativity and understanding. However, to perform such tasks, state-of-the-art generative AI models require immense computational power, leading to increased energy consumption and significant environmental impact. Their energy consumption increases alarmingly, doubling approximately every 100 days, expected to reach 3% of global electricity production by 2026. For instance, classifying an image emits roughly 10 grams of CO2, while generating a single image with AI, due to its iterative process, can emit more than a kilogram of CO2.
Considering the imminent ubiquity of this technology, a paradigm shift in AI computing hardware is imperative to keep developing and deploying these generative models sustainably. As optics is an inherently parallelizable and low-loss modality unlike electronics, where capacitive and Ohmic losses exist, leveraging optical computing for AI can significantly reduce energy dissipation while overcoming scaling limitations. While integrated optical platforms suffer from the same scaling limitations as electronic chips, optical computing systems with three-dimensional connectivity are generally composed of bulky parts placed apart from each other, limiting the volume compute density. The lack of high-performance optical memory units raises the energy cost of optical compute through the requirement of frequent data transfers between digital electronics and optics. This project aims to investigate the potential of optics for realizing compact, high-speed, and application-specific computing hardware for generative AI models with a monolithic architecture based on high-density and thin modulation surfaces with subwavelength structures. The scalable and compact computing platform with three-dimensional connectivity will be specialized for the all-optical realization of generative models with an optical memory for retaining intermediate outputs. We will benchmark this computing principle on different image and language tasks, where the goal will be to achieve comparable sample qualities with modern AI tools while consuming significantly smaller total energy.
Keywords: generative artificial intelligence, image generation, optical computing, sustainability

Title: Co-adaptation of morphology and sensory-motor intelligence in avian-informed drones
Abstract: Drones cannot match the agility, endurance, and adaptability of birds, which can cover long distances, fly in turbulent air conditions, steadily hover against the wind, safely navigate confined spaces, and precisely perch or land in small places. Current drones mostly fall into two categories. Multi-copters offer high agility and autonomous navigation but spend most of their energy and mass on fighting gravity rather than covering distance. In contrast, fixed-wing aircraft offer substantially longer endurance per unit mass but have comparatively lower agility and maneuverability. Unlike drones, birds can achieve both agility and endurance by continuously and extensively morph wings and tail to adapt to different flight conditions and transition between stable and unstable aerodynamic regimes that allow them to switch between high energetic efficiency and high maneuverability. The objective of this project is to develop a methodology for the design and control of agile and energetically efficient morphing drones that leverage the co-adaptation of avian-informed morphology, sensory-motor system, and flight control. The research plan is articulated in three subprojects. The first subproject, conducted in partnership with Prof. Christina Harvey at University of California Davis, will identify a multidimensional morphological space informed by avian anatomy and kinematics that will serve as a frame to design, compare, prototype, and aerodynamically characterize winged drones with diverse morphing wing and tail properties. The subproject will also identify the mechanical, sensory, and actuation design of hardware prototypes with swappable wings and tails that span the morphological space. In addition, the sub-project will automate a robotic aerodynamic characterization platform to rapidly measure forces and moments at different wind speeds, angles of attack, and morphing configurations for the derivation of aerodynamic models. The second subproject, conducted in partnership with Prof. Graham Taylor at Oxford University, will define a set of flight maneuvers and optimization criteria informed by behavioral experiments with birds to identify optimal flight trajectories and control strategies for the extreme configurations of the morphological space by means of optimal control and reinforcement learning methods. This second subproject will integrate the aerodynamic models obtained from the first subproject within an open-source and fast flight simulator that includes visual rendering and interface with widely used machine learning libraries, where all the trajectory optimization and learning experiments will be carried out. In addition, this subproject will augment the lab flight arena with three levels of mechanical assistance for indoor flight tests of short maneuvers and conduct tests of longer flight maneuvers at the LINA drone facilities in Dübendorf, Switzerland. The third subproject will explore the co-evolution of avian-informed architectures within the morphological space and of adaptive control architectures for the maneuvers studied in the second subproject to understand how morphology and control co-adaptation affect each other for faster, more efficient, and/or different solutions. It will combine multi-objective, constraint-based evolutionary algorithms that encode the morphological architecture and the neural control architecture with reinforcement learning methods that learn to fly in a set of maneuvers under a set of optimality criteria identified in the second subproject. It will also develop novel evolutionary methods that encourage and preserve diversity to evolve neural control architectures and local learning rules with fewer learning cycles and sim to real adaptation. Experiments will be conducted in simulation, solutions will be compared to those of the second subproject, with those that are markedly different prototyped and validated in indoor and outdoor flights.
Keywords: Biological inspiration, Drones, Evolutionary Robotics, Robot learning, autonomous flight, co-design, drones, robot learning, robotics

Title: Microscale synthetic transformation by autonomous magnetic-driven reactions
Abstract: The use of autonomously adaptive micromedical devices for long-period in vivo health inspections or advanced minimally invasive medical interventions has attracted increased interest in recent years. Given our successful outcomes from the Swiss National Science Foundation projects Scalable Self-Assembling Robots (#200021-105634 and #200020-118117) at the Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, University of Zurich, and Self-assembling Micro Robots (#PBZHP2-133472) at the NanoRobotics Laboratory, Carnegie Mellon University, this project aims to realize such adaptive functionality by endowing microdevices with synthetically attainable versatile transformation competence represented as advanced microassembly and reconfiguration capabilities. Synthetic transformation is a term used in chemistry, which symbolizes a molecular transformation induced by a triggering molecule. Having reviewed the compulsory demands for autonomously adaptive microdevices, we identified the significant potentiality of realizing artificial synthetic transformation at the micro scale. Toward this end, we derived three fundamental issues to investigate, namely, self addressing, self regulation, and active boundary, which are respectively grounded in engineering challenges (that is, Mechanical internal state, Backward reaction by kinetic energy, and Regulation by boundary). In the proposed work packages, the indicated challenges are addressed by designing physical microcomponents and by performing the aimed transformations (termed reactions) using experiments. We first develop a component that can reflect its neighbor’s conditions and subsequently realize a reaction that brings the system’s states backward. Due to these processes, the system becomes capable of iteratively regaining its initial condition and hence attains stability in the reaction dynamics by organizing a cyclic reaction path. We further upgrade the role of the boundary, such that it can actively regulate the reaction of components. The obtained reactions are subsequently modeled mathematically and analyzed, focusing on the system’s dynamic characteristics. We believe our challenge, adopting biomolecular wisdom into engineering, is a prospective field for the upcoming decade, with the potential outcomes expected to have a broad impact on various research fields, such as robotics, MEMS, biomechanics, and biotechnology.
Keywords: magnetism, medicalrobotics, microrobotics, self-assembly

Title: MED.USE: Medical large language model for reducing resource overuse in the emergency department
Abstract:
Overuse in healthcare, a key component of low-value care (LVC), exposes patients to unnecessary treatments and tests, leading to harm and straining resources. Emergency departments (ED) are key to reducing LVC, by decreasing unnecessary antibiotic use for respiratory infections and limiting unnecessary, costly investigations such as computed tomography (CT) scans. Despite global efforts to reduce LVC, recommendations alone are insufficient to drive change. Effective implementation strategies, and supporting tools are needed. Medical large language models (LLMs) could help integrate evidence into clinical practice, though their real-life impact and safety need further evaluation. 

The goal of this project is to develop a medical LLM-based decision-support system that processes routinely available information and provides recommendations to ED clinicians, aiming to reduce LVC in the ED while being well adapted to the Swiss setting. The focus is on three prevalent clinical scenarios with significant potential for LVC reduction: (1) unnecessary antibiotic prescription for respiratory infections, (2) overuse of CT scans for abdominal pain, and (3) overuse of CT scans for mild head trauma.  

The project is structured into three work packages (WPs) that correspond to three consecutive phases: (1) model development and validation using retrospective clinical vignettes, (2) a silent trial for optimal implementation in clinical workflows, and (3) a randomized controlled trial (RCT) to demonstrate efficacy and safety in real-world settings.

WP1 develops MED.USE, a safe clinical decision-support tool to optimize ED resource allocation and reduce LVC. It involves adapting Meditron70B, a state-of-the-art medical-aligned LLM, to the ED context by using retrieval-augmented generation on guidelines, and expert feedback on clinical vignettes; evaluating and refining the model to achieve a predefined performance threshold using an expert-based multimodal framework and a quantitative approach (e.g., 80% sensitivity and =70% specificity). This improved model will also integrate multilingual voice-to-text technology to transcribe physician-patient consultations and extract key clinical information. Expected outcome: MED.USE, a context-adapted Meditron-70B with proven safety and resource optimization performance on clinical vignettes.

WP2 evaluates the feasibility and acceptability of MED.USE and develops implementation strategies to maximize its uptake and effectiveness. It includes a silent trial where MED.USE runs alongside routine ED care without influencing clinical decisions, to collect prospective data from 20-50 patients per clinical scenario; and implementation science research engaging clinicians, nurses and patients via interviews, observations, and focus groups to identify barriers and facilitators and develop context-specific implementation strategies. Expected outcome: an implementation framework to ensure effective MED.USE adoption and integration into ED workflows.  

Finally, WP3 conducts a multicenter, adaptive RCT to assess the efficacy and safety of MED.USE in reducing LVC in Swiss EDs. Based on the findings from WP1 and 2, the clinical scenario with the most accurate and safe MED.USE model will be selected for evaluation. The primary goal is to determine whether MED.USE reduces LVC compared to usual care. Secondary objectives include evaluating safety (serious adverse events and clinical complications) and assessing economic and environmental impact. This open-label, superiority trial (for efficacy) and non-inferiority trial (for safety) will run in four Swiss EDs (Lausanne, Geneva, Bern, and Basel) over 20 months, enrolling 1,158 patients. Physicians in the intervention group will receive MED.USE recommendations, while the control group follows usual care. Expected outcomes: reduction in LVC prescriptions, maintenance of patient safety, and insights into the economic impact of LLM-assisted decision-making.

Title: The process of habitization, its neural implementation and clinical application
Abstract:
Habits are a fundamental part of the human experience and dominate most parts of our every-day life. They free cognitive resources for other tasks while being “on autopilot”, but they can also become maladaptive or even pathological if they automatically trigger harmful behavior, for example in substance use disorders. Yet, the process of habitization – developing automatic, inflexible routines from often repeated behavior – is still poorly understood. Indeed, most of our knowledge about the transition from deliberate, goal-directed to automatic, habitual behavior comes from animal studies of instrumental learning, but the translation of these findings to the human domain has proven difficult. This is at least in part due to methodological problems in assessing habitual behavior in the lab.

I propose to use computational modeling of instrumental learning processes to elucidate the process of habitization. Therefore, I will combine models of reinforcement learning and drift diffusion models with the classically used outcome devaluation and contingency degradation paradigms to gain insights into the learning mechanisms leading to the expression of habitual behavior. In those tasks, habits are defined as an insensitivity to the devaluation of an outcome, that is, the perseveration of previously learned stimulus-response patterns after the outcome of this behavior has lost its incentive value or the contingency between action and outcome has been decreased. Hence, behavior after the manipulation of outcome value or action-outcome contingency is examined for signs of perseveration while mostly ignoring behavior during the training phase of these tasks. However, most previous studies show large inter-individual variation in the degree of habitual behavior during the test phase. I aim to investigate these inter-individual differences in the development of habits by computational modeling of individual learning processes.

Therefore, we will build computational models of learning and decision making in outcome and contingency degradation tasks and test the validity of this framework in an existing data set (Study 1). For deeper insights into the mechanisms of habitization, we will examine its implementation in one study using functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (Study 2a) and one using electroencephalography (Study 2b) with 60 participants each. Through the combination of the computational models developed in Study 1 with neural data, I can bridge the computational, algorithmic, and implementation levels of analysis proposed by David Marr (1982). Addressing all three levels simultaneously allows for a much more detailed understanding of the process of habitization. Finally, we will test the ecological validity of this framework by assessing participants with a current cocaine use disorder in comparison to a control group of participants. This test will show whether patients suffering from a substance use disorder will show altered learning processes that result in stronger habitual tendencies as suggested by etiological theories of addiction (Everitt & Robbins, 2016).
This research program will reveal how the process of shaping habits from instrumental learning experiences works on a formal level, how it is implemented in the human brain, and how it may become pathological in substance use disorders. These insights into the mechanisms shaping our actions will have a broad impact on many lines of basic and applied research examining behavior shaped by its consequences and repetition. Eventually, this knowledge can be used to design and test interventions to overcome maladaptive habits and develop beneficial ones.
Keywords: computational modeling, experimental psychology, habit, human neuroimaging, reinforcement learning
