Title: The role of serotonin in modulating empathy and prosocial human behavior
Abstract:
Background & Rationale: Affective and cognitive processes play a fundamental role in everyday life and throughout human development. Prosocial feelings (e. g. empathy), social cognition and behaviors are predominantly regulated by the neurotransmitter serotonin. Hence, serotonergic psychotropic compounds such as “ayahuasca” (DMT & harmine) represent ideal tools to investigate different pathways of emotional and cognitive information processing. Additionally, beneficial effects of serotonergic psychoactive substances for psychotherapy of mood disorders have been reported. It is therefore essential to understand the underlying psychological processes contributing to these positive therapeutic outcomes.

Objectives & Methods: The global ayahuasca online survey was created in order to investigate contextual variables, motivations, beneficial effects and potential risks associated with the use of ayahuasca. The analysis of the observational cross-sectional survey dataset will generate important insights about context-dependent and non-specific factors associated with the psychological effects of ayahuasca and everyday life outcomes such as relationship experiences.
The modulation of empathy and prosocial behavior by serotonergic psychoactive compounds contained in ayahuasca (DMT & harmine) will be investigated in an interventional study. Empathy and prosocial behavior will be measured by using a reinforcement learning task (Frank task) with consequences for the participant himself or another participant, and the social value orientation (SVO) task. I expect changes regarding the subjective experience of the self and perception, cognitive flexibility, mindfulness, wellbeing and adaptive value orientation assessed by psychometric measures.

Results & Impact: The project is highly relevant for comprehending the motivations and contexts of the use of the serotonergic brew ayahuasca. Additionally, it will fundamentally contribute to the understanding of empathy and prosocial behavior and their serotonergic pathways. By unveiling the underlying mechanisms leading to potentially beneficial therapeutic outcomes, the findings will also bear potential for the development of novel treatments of stress-related mood disorders, which are known to be characterized by dysfunctional affective and cognitive processing.

Title: Automatic Handwriting Recognition and Writer Identification based on the Kinematic Theory
Abstract:
Handwriting as a means of communication has survived many technological revolutions including the invention of the printing press, typewriter, personal computer, and portable computer. In order to incorporate this convenient and personal way to express ourselves into the digital world, artificial intelligence and pattern recognition are needed, most prominently to transcribe handwriting into computer-readable text and to distinguish different writers in the context of biometric authentication and forensic analysis. Although significant progress has been made in research over the past decades and accurate commercial systems have been developed for constrained scenarios, these challenging problems are still far from being solved.

In this project, we approach handwriting recognition from a novel promising direction, that is from a kinematic point of view. Recent progress in this domain includes the derivation of a mathematical model of the neuromuscular process that generates complex pen movements, alongside with the means to extract the model parameters from sample handwritings. We believe that the integration of this knowledge about the writing process into automatic handwriting recognition systems could be highly beneficial.

Our first goal is the development of kinematic methods for synthetic handwriting generation. The idea is to modify existing handwriting samples by introducing some variance in the pen movement. This allows us to automatically generate a large database of learning samples for training handwriting recognition systems and improving their accuracy. When compared with geometric distortion models, the neuromuscular model is expected to generate more natural handwriting samples that are well suited as learning samples.

Secondly, we apply our kinematic approach to the task of writer identification. This technology allows personalized handwriting recognition and has an important application in forensics to support human experts in their work, for instance by narrowing down lists of candidates that could have written a document in question. We aim to develop novel identification methods based on the behavioral biometrics provided by the neuromuscular handwriting model.

Future applications of the research conducted in this project include biomedical engineering. In particular, the neuromuscular movement characteristics that we develop for writer identification could be instrumental to devise diagnosis and prognosis methods for movement-related medical conditions such as Parkinson's disease. Last but not least the kinematic model of handwritten words and sentences could be interesting for the development of teaching aids that help children learn how to write.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Handwriting Recognition, Kinematic Theory, Neuromuscular Handwriting Representation, Pattern Recognition, Synthetic Handwriting, Writer Identification

Title: Medical, Multilingual and Privacy-Preserving Natural Language Processing in the Clinical Domain
Abstract:
Clinical notes provide a rich source of information about diseases and outcomes of treatments for researchers, and about details of medical care for patients. Analysis of large quantities of clinical notes offers a great potential for medical knowledge discovery. Moreover, learning language patterns in clinical notes can enable us to generate useful medical summaries both for healthcare practitioners and patients. Several factors limit the potential usage of clinical notes, primarily the private and sensitive nature of the information they contain. Coupled with that, the actual amount of annotated text available at any hospital in a specific medical area might be insufficient to enable the identification of relevant clinical signals. Additionally, the different languages in Switzerland necessitate the development of multilingual analysis capabilities. In this project, we propose to develop techniques that will help to overcome these problems and leverage them in the development of natural language processing (NLP) systems for medical records, with two specific areas of applications: (1) extraction of clinically-relevant information from notes in oncology, and (2) summarization of discharge communication. 
The first area of investigation is overcoming sharing restrictions posed by privacy and data protection constraints to enable broader usage of clinical notes for scientific research.  We intend to develop machine learning-based approaches  for the automated identification and neutralization of PHIs (Personal Health Information) as well as for the assessment of the residual risk of re-identification. As we will work on data from multiple centers (Lausanne, Lugano, Zurich), we intend to use decentralized learning approaches, such as transfer learning or federated learning, augmented with privacy-preserving techniques such as differential privacy, to develop a multilingual clinical text de-identification model. We will evaluate the privacy-utility trade-offs of different privacy-enhancing techniques for decentralized learning, and propose potential improvements. The development of a robust multilingual text de-identification algorithm will enable us to safely share data to a central secure high-performance computing infrastructure and develop new multilingual natural language processing (NLP) tools in two carefully selected clinical applications. 
We propose two case studies. The first is in oncology in order to identify adverse drug reactions. In Switzerland, there is a legal obligation for physicians and clinics to report suspected serious or new adverse events of medical treatment to Swissmedic. Despite this legal requirement, Adverse Drug Reactions (ADR) are vastly underreported in clinical practice. The de-identification and pooling of clinical reports will enable us to create the critical mass necessary to train and test advanced NLP techniques based on Large Language Models to automatically identify and flag potential ADRs, which could then be examined by trained pharmacovigilance professionals. While our purpose is to develop techniques that can potentially generalize to several clinical areas, given the experimental nature of our research, we have selected one specific domain where ADRs are frequent (Oncology) and we have enlisted the support of several specialists which will help us validate the usefulness of the system in this particular clinical area. The second case study is about methods for summarizing discharge communications, to adapt the language to the patient's needs. This application addresses a critical issue as existing medical documentation is often difficult for patients due to its complex language and technical terminology. We will use the deidentified discharge letters to finetune Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate paraphrased summaries with improved readability. We will accomplish these investigations using a carefully balanced approach consisting of clinical record annotation in three languages

Title: A-DISCERN: Identifying high-quality online information on medical treatment options
Abstract:
Background: The fast adoption and use of the Internet during the last decade and the proliferation of Web-based applications with the emergence of Web 2.0 made clear that the Internet is becoming a necessity and part of people’s daily life. Nowadays, looking for medical information on the Internet is one of the primary means of health information seeking. However, the promise of the Internet as a decision support system is seriously marred by the fact that the quality of health information on the Internet varies tremendously. Initiatives proposing guidelines, checklists and quality indicators sought to help in solving the problem. Yet, these guidelines and quality criteria are laborious because of the effort and time needed to manually evaluate each criterion when it comes to online health related information. DISCERN (http://www.discern.org.uk) is one of these tools that were developed to evaluate the reliability and the quality of information on treatment choices. 

Aims of the study: The fundamental intention of this research project is to create a system that is able to provide automatically a quality prediction based on the evaluation of an established tool for quality assessment (DISCERN) and to make this assessment easily available to everybody while they are looking at health web pages. Theoretically, this means adding to the informative message of the webpage a meta-message with the intent to reduce or eliminate acceptance of messages originating from low-quality websites.

Methods: The first phase will be dedicated to developing a learning algorithm/predictive model (A-DISCERN) that determines the quality of online text discussing treatment options using features/attributes operationalizing and reflecting the targeted quality criteria comprised in the DISCERN tool. The second phase will include human computation by recruiting users from crowdsourcing platforms to rate the medical texts on the quality criteria investigated in the first phase. Moreover, the second phase will investigate the design of workflow to control and coordinate the work of the crowd with the goal to collect many reliable ratings of medical texts to improve the performance of developed A-DISCERN algorithm. The third phase will focus on implementing the whole system (A-DISCERN system) combining the developed work in the first and the second phase. 

Significance of the project: From the research perspective, the building of the predictive model used to automate the evaluation of the DISCERN criteria will benefit other automation tasks that use NLP in the medical domain (i.e. medical entity and relation identification/extraction). Moreover, the success of coordinating the crowds to work on the rating tasks while maintaining reliable and quality ratings will result in an efficient workflow that could be used in other problems using crowdsourcing. From the application perspective, the final outcome depicted in A-DISCERN system will aid health information seekers to assess the quality of medical texts discussing treatment options, helping people to self-manage and make better decisions concerning their health behavior. In addition, this project introduces new research possibilities that could leverage on the way this project modifies the dyad of usual information seeking into a triad.
Keywords: DISCERN, crowd sourcing, crowd-powered systems, health communication, health informatics, health information quality, human computation, natural language processing, online health information seeking, supervised learning, unified medical language system

Title: The Political Economy of Taxation: Complexity, Authority, Inequality
Abstract:
While the public finance literature has extensively studied the impact of tax systems on economic behaviors (eg. labor supply, avoidance, evasion but also fertility, education), a strand of the political economy literature focuses on the rationale for policymakers’ decision on tax reforms.  This research project aims at bringing these two strands of literature together,  harvesting a wide range of methods and newly available administrative data in the context of France.  The general research question lies at the interaction between the policymaking of tax reforms and the impact they have on the income distribution.  More precisely, I aim to study the notion of complexity of the tax system, which is a product of policymaking on one side, and affects the income distribution and individual behaviors on the other side.

Is complexity good or bad?  or both? All else equal, the simplification advocates can safely criticize tax complexity as imposing wasteful administrative costs on the tax authority and wasteful compliance demands on taxpayers.  But when considering the broader goals of the tax system (raising tax revenue and redistributing revenue among individuals),  there are subtler economic arguments both for simplification and for complexification.  For one,  increasing complexity might expand opportunities for tax avoidance,  which would tend to reduce revenue collections and favor the rich (who have more capacity to exploit avoidance opportunities).  On the other hand, complexification might be a tool to reduce tax avoidance, as more precise rules are needed to close loopholes.  In addition, complexity is associated with more detailed targeting of tax policies.  Targeting is necessary to increase the fairness of the tax system, with more rules taking into account the specific situation of taxpayers  (such as income,  childcare responsibilities,  and disability).   On the other  hand,  there  could  be targeting of tax rules in favor of special interests, such as political campaign donors. 

The proposed project employs empirical methods using new data from France to produce evidence-based insights on the determinants and consequences of tax complexity. I will pursue the following three goals, structuring this research agenda in three projects.  The first objective of this project is to produce a set of measures of tax complexity based on analysis of tax laws using a range of machine learning and natural language processing methods and describe how these measures evolved over time in response to political and economic factors.  The second objective is to shed light on the rationale of policymakers behavior in the law-making process by studying parliamentary members’  behaviour regarding  complexity:  what are the argument used in favor of complexity-increasing reforms?  What are the characteristics (party affiliation, electoral constituency) of the parliamentary members defending these reforms? Third, after going upstream in the making of law, I follow a downstream path and look at the impact of complexity on inequality by identifying individual winners and losers using microsimulation and income tax return data. To achieve my research objectives, I will make use of tools from data science, including natural language processing and machine learning, and applied econometrics.  I will combine these methods with three types of data:  1) administrative tax data; 2) texts of parliamentary speeches and votes of parliamentary members and; 3) annual budget laws enacting tax reforms.

Title: Market Design for Digital Goods:  Subscriptions and de-bundling
Abstract:
Digitalization makes life easier and more convenient for many people and is an important driver of economic growth. Many digital goods do not follow classical production chains. For example, copies of software programs do not have to be assembled from parts in a factory.  Digital goods instead exist as parts of complex technological and economic systems. Traditional models for selling goods often fail to take advantage of these new system, resulting in inefficient markets. While companies constantly develop new business models to sell digital goods, the economic impact of these new markets is often not yet well understood. Curiously, in recent years two seemingly opposed practices have gained traction: bundling different products together through subscription services and de-bundling formerly monolithic products into menu based offerings. 

 
 In this project, I plan to analyze both of these practices through the lens of market design and multi agent systems. This puts the project at the intersection between Computer Science and Economics, requiring a combination of techniques from game theory, artificial intelligence, operations research and microeconomics. As a market designer, my goal is to understand the strategic interactions between all market participants, identify potential inefficiencies and undesired effects and finally propose mechanisms to alleviate identified problems or induce desired outcomes.

 First, I will analyze the incentive structure and revenue implications of bundled subscription services such as software subscription (e.g., Microsoft's Xbox Game Pass or Sony's Playstation Now) or music and video streaming services (e.g., Spotify and Netflix).
 Bundled subscription services allow users to pay a small monthly fee and obtain access to a constantly changing library of titles, often from multiple publishers. This is a two-sided market, where subscription services effectively 'buy' the right to resell the product as part of a subscription. A product is only offered as part of a subscription service when the product's publisher and the subscription service provider come to an agreement. My main focus in this research project will be on how the competitive dynamics vary depending on the existing libraries and contracts of services and publishers. Two specific important open questions I hope to answer are when it becomes optimal for a product publisher to open their own subscription service (e.g., like Disney+) and whether content saturation naturally leads to monopolization once a service reaches critical size in a given segment of the market. 

 The second problem I plan to analyze concerns the opposite approach: splitting formerly monolithic products into a menu of related sub-products. Instead of having to buy the whole product, users can just buy the parts they value highly enough. This type of 'de-bundling' is becoming more and more prevalent for video games and to a lesser degree can also be observed for other types of software. This is somewhat surprising. While product differentiation often increases profits for physical goods, it is generally thought that, thanks to the relative lack of marginal costs, digital goods lend themselves best to be sold as bundles. One of the effects that are not really well understood are the interactions such a business model has with the publishers' incentives when designing a new product. While a monolithic product needs to pose a similar value proposition to a relatively large part of the user base, menu-based products face a quite different optimization problem and features that might be disliked by a majority get designed to extract maximal revenue from a relatively small set of users. I plan to formally analyze these strategic differences in a game-theoretic model and characterize how they affect social welfare and revenue. As the resulting equilibria likely vary greatly depending on whether a product faces direct competition, I plan to do both a monopolistic and a competitive analysis.
Keywords: Bundling, Digital Goods, Market Design, Optimal Product Design, Product Differentiation, Revenue Management, Subscription Service, Two-sided Market

Title: Sparsity in Large-Scale Convex Optimization and Machine Learning Applications
Abstract: With the immense growth of available digital data, algorithmic techniques for the analysis of large datasets have become of crucial importance in many different fields of science and applications. However, the applicability of most such techniques, in particular from the area of machine learning, is still limited by the performance of the currently available optimization algorithms. A more fruitful interaction between the fields of machine learning, approximation algorithms from optimization, and high-dimensional computational geometry could be a key element towards tackling these problems, and to deepen our understanding of the learning methods, which are the two main goals of this project.

Title: Deep Learning Methods for Portable Low-Field MR Imaging in Neurocritical Care of Stroke
Abstract: Portable low-field magnetic resonance imaging (LF-MRI) holds promise to revolutionize neurocritical care because it provides timely, accessible neuroimaging at the point of care with reduced risk to the patient. But a remaining obstacle to its wide adoption is the limited resolution and low signal-to-noise ratio, which hamper the complete characterization of brain tissue. This project aims to establish 3D deep learning methods for LF-MRI image analysis to enable adequate image quality for automated stroke detection. The applicant will work with a highly synergistic team, including world-class experts in MRI physics, machine learning, and stroke treatment. He would bring his expertise in medical image analysis and investigate advanced deep learning methods on unique datasets and develop novel pipelines to overcome the current limitations of LF-MRI. This will establish a sound basis for image analysis and significantly impact the diagnosis and care of stroke patients.
Keywords: MRI, artificial intelligence, deep learning, low-field, machine learning, neuroimaging, stroke, ultra-low-field MRI

Title: Unravelling Europa's tidal evolution through lineament sequencing
Abstract:
Jupiter’s moon Europa is a fascinating icy moon with its global subsurface ocean and a geologically young surface. Europa’s habitability will be explored and characterized by long-awaited space missions Europa Clipper (NASA) and Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer (JUICE; ESA). Linear surface structures, or lineaments, on Europa’s icy surface are expected to evolve out of cracks in the ice shell, stemming from tensile fractures, which might reach Europa’s subsurface ocean. Characterizing the environment that fostered Europa’s rich geologic history, thus, provides insight into the habitability of Europa (e.g. Prockter & Patterson, 2009). However, there are many open questions to address: Is the ice shell thick and convective or thin and brittle?  Are there active plume eruptions on Europa in locations of most recent cracks? How much of the tidal evolution is recorded by mappable linear surface features? Can a sequence of lineaments, ordered by age, unravel the stress evolution and constrain lineament formation mechanisms?
I propose to investigate the tidal evolution of Europa, and its implications for surface-ocean exchange processes that foster habitability. The first work package (WP1) contains the development of the Code for ordering lineaments based on cross-cuttings (Colbox). This makes a temporally resolved analysis of preferred lineament directions possible, since cross-cuttings indicate age relationships. Different double ridge formation hypotheses can be tested. The second work package (WP2) constructs a global picture of Europa, using all existing imagery. I conduct a global lineament azimuth study, with the help of an automated mapping framework. Combined with Colbox, I am equipped to test the agreement between preferred directions of lineaments with a variety of stress models. The stress models are based on different ice shell thickness estimates, thermal profiles in the ice shell, and combinations of spin pole precession and non-synchronous rotation rates. With a Bayesian framework and a stress calculation code proposed by Dr. Alyssa Rhoden (Walker & Rhoden, 2022), this temporal disentanglement can shed light on the formation and evolution of lineaments as a method of tracking Europa’s habitability through time. A better knowledge about Europa’s stress field improves our understanding of tidal heating, which influences the thickness of the ice shell. For example, a thinner ice shell could crack more frequently than a thicker shell. Concretely, my analyses have implications for the planning of observations with the Europa Imaging System (EIS) dual camera system onboard Europa Clipper. Europa Clipper arrives at Jupiter in 2030, making my proposed research opportune. Further, I develop and publish methods that enable a rapid first analysis of new imagery from EIS by automating the sequencing of lineaments and combining it with a deep-learning driven mapping of lineaments. I have acquired the scientific finesse and an international network necessary to pursue my challenging research plan. 
Choosing the Southwest Research Institute (SwRI) in Boulder, Colorado, as a host institution and Dr. Alyssa Rhoden as a collaborating scientist is superb. SwRI provides me with a stimulating, collaborative environment that boosts my career as a planetary scientist. Dr. Alyssa Rhoden is an active and ambitious principal research scientist with long-standing experience with Europa imagery and stress field calculation (Rhoden et al., 2010, 2012, 2015, 2021; Rhoden & Hurford, 2013).

Title: Tuning friction using architected soft surfaces
Abstract:
Friction is present everywhere in our daily life. Many activities, such as walking or riding a bicycle, would be impossible without friction, which allows us to maintain stability. Maximizing useful friction can prevent accidents and increase safety. At the same time, a considerable amount of energy and resources are wasted due to friction. Minimizing unwanted friction improves efficiency and makes processes more sustainable. 

The static friction is the maximal shear load that can be applied at an interface between two solids before the onset of sliding. More than 200 years ago, da Vinci, Amontons, and Coulomb observed that the onset of friction was characterized by the friction coefficient – the ratio of applied shear to normal load at the onset of sliding. The friction coefficient between two materials is often incorrectly considered to be a material pair property. As a consequence, for a given system, it would seem impossible to change or control the friction coefficient on the fly – without having to separate the contacting interfaces and for example apply a coating. 

However, recent studies showed that the friction coefficient is geometry-dependent and can be systematically varied on setups with the same material pair by simply changing the external loading configuration. The reason of this geometry-dependence lies in the mechanism governing the initiation of frictional slip, which has been shown to be a fracture-like phenomenon. Thus, knowing the interface stress distribution, the macroscopic friction coefficient can be predicted using the fracture mechanics framework.

The objective of this proposal is to design soft architected surfaces with morphology that can be actively changed and to exploit these changes to tune the friction coefficient on the fly. In particular, I will focus on elastomeric structures with a network of air channels embedded below the surface and control the internal pressure to quickly and reversibly change the surface morphology. These changes will affect the local shear and normal traction at the frictional interface, which directly control the macroscopic friction coefficient. I will first use a combination of experiments and numerical analyses to characterize the effect of these morphological changes on the frictional properties. Towards this end, I will use the friction-fracture analogy to predict the friction behavior as function of the surface morphology and develop a finite element model (FEM) with a cohesive element representation of the frictional interface with discrete patterning. In parallel, I will fabricate and test the designed soft surfaces to validate and calibrate the model. Finally, I will combine FEM simulations and artificial intelligence (AI) to identify optimal networks of channels resulting in desired properties. These include large changes in both magnitude and directionality of the friction coefficient upon moderate changes in internal pressure as well as unusual dependence of  the friction coefficient on normal load.

I expect the architected surfaces with active and robust control of friction developed as part of this project to allow new enhanced functionalities in a wide range of applications, including transportation, robotics, biological system, and flexible electronics.
Keywords: architectured surfaces, bio-inspired design, fracture, friction, homogenization, nonlinear finite-element analysis, programmable frictional surfaces, soft materials, soft robotics, tunable frictional surfaces

Title: The Forgotten Role of Inductive Bias in Interpretability Research in NLP
Abstract:
For most of its history, the field of natural language processing was primarily focused on the creation of models with a better inductive bias. With the advent of neural architectures, however, that ceased to be the case. This grant proposes to resuscitate the inductive bias in NLP research. Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly becoming ubiquitous in virtually every area of science and industry. Much of the methods used in AI are data-driven, i.e., they rely upon machine learning methods to learn patterns from data directly and make predictions. A fundamental truism in learning systems—both machine and biological—is that a good inductive bias (structured prior knowledge) makes it easier to extrapolate patterns from the observed data and, thus, make more accurate predictions (Mitchell, 1980; Zador, 2019).

However, modern machine learning has shifted focus to statistical learning algorithms whose biases and structure are often opaque or non-verifiable (Vapnik, 2013). This is particularly true of neural network models (LeCun et al., 2015), whose widespread engineering success is tempered by their infamously uninterpretable nature—even to the researchers who design and use them. While ignorance of these biases has profound societal consequences, incorporating biases from well-understood systems can aid the goals and understanding of learning and machine intelligence (Marcus and Davis, 2019; O’Neil, 2016).

The science of language acquisition has taught us that children approach the task of language learning with preconceptions of what their language will look likea. Modern techniques in artificial intelligence, which are widely used to learn and comprehend language are extremely opaque, as their inner workings are unknown. Understanding the structural biases—the implicit assumptions made by a model to process data and make generalizations—of already developed machine learning models, and developing new models which are clearly analyzable—is an open issue. Incorporating these biases will advance technology for languages where data is scarce, and help in other sequential tasks such as time-series data and bioinformatics.
This proposal focuses on identifying and improving the inductive bias of deep learning models whose target domain is natural language—and, more generally, any domains using sequences, such as bioinformatics and time-series analysis. Our proposal is divided into three pillars: §2.3.1 focuses on developing better probing methods to inspect the internals of neural networks, §2.3.2 focuses on the use of artificial (formal) languages to evaluate the inductive bias of existing methods and §2.3.3 discusses the development of neural networks that have an inductive bias tailored to language.
Keywords: Computational Linguistics, Machine Learning, Natural Language Processing

Title: Understanding and Modelling Cryptic Binding Pockets for Biology and Drug Discovery
Abstract:
Over 75% of disease-involved proteins cannot be readily targeted by conventional chemical biology approaches aimed at blocking the substrate binding site. These targets are often deemed ‘undruggable’. However, alternative strategies such as targeting allosteric (remote) or cryptic (hidden) binding pockets offer significant opportunities to target them. In particular, Cryptic binding pockets offer drug discovery opportunities even when no other exploitable pockets are present. Cryptic (hidden) binding pockets are cavities that are absent in unliganded apo structures of a protein and become apparent only when a ligand is bound. Given their promise to expand the druggable genome, cryptic binding pockets are of considerable interest in drug discovery. Unfortunately, not only they are notoriously difficult to identify, but also the molecular mechanism by which they form is still debated, making it unclear what are the best strategy to find them. 

What we do know. Cryptic binding pockets can be exploited to target difficult receptors, seem to be common in the human genome and might have a biological function. Experimental, machine learning and simulations-based approaches, including those that we developed, can be effectively used to locate some cryptic binding sites (especially superficial ones).

What we do not know. It is not clear how most cryptic pockets form; how frequent cryptic binding pockets amenable to drug discovery (druggable ) really are; how many have a biological function; and what is the best computational strategy to predict the presence of both superficial and buried pockets and estimate their ligandability  and druggability. 

What we plan to do. We will address the knowledge gaps and develop a computational platform based on simulations and machine learning to systematically detect cryptic pockets, including buried ones, and explore their ligandability and druggability. In more details we will:

1. Gain a better structural and dynamical understanding of cryptic binding pockets by expanding existing structural data bases. Investigate and classify the conformational dynamics associated with pocket formation. Create a test set representative of different kind of conformational changes to be made generally available together with the expanded database. 

2. Further develop our simulation-based approaches combining complementary enhanced-sampling algorithms and mixed solvents to reveal cryptic sites and quantify the energetics of their formation.

3. Predict new proof-of-concept cryptic sites on targets of pharmaceutical interest, explore their ligandability and druggability by using the new platform and validate them experimentally.
Keywords: allosteric regulation, drug design, free energy calculations, metadynamics, molecular dynamics, protein dynamics

Title: Emotions and International Law
Abstract: This research project proposes to explore the relationship between emotions and international law. While the study of emotions has a rich history in many disciplines including psychology, neuroscience, sociology, and more recently international relations, international law does not deal with emotions in any sustained manner. Law, including international law, is strongly based on rationalist assumptions. The prevailing idea is that law is based on reason and that emotions should be as much as possible excluded from the making, interpretation, and application of law. In this research project I argue that international lawyers and legal scholars must take account of the role of emotions in their study and work to ensure the continued relevance of the field in addressing real world issues. I draw on emerging research on emotions in domestic (mostly US) law, as well as on emotions research within international relations scholarship. Acknowledging and exploring the influence of emotions will enable the field of international law to better adapt to the complex global and societal issues it purports to address, including but not limited to: terrorism, migration, climate change, food safety, populism, and cyber warfare. This research project is divided into three phases: The first phase will delineate the perspective on emotions and the methodological tools that inform the research. The second and main phase will consist of three case studies (fear and anxiety in environmental and food law; empathy, compassion, and dignity in the use of artificial intelligence in warfare; and stigma, shame, and guilt in combating infectious diseases in global health law) through which the relevance of emotions in international law will be studied. The third phase will draw on the case studies to argue for the value and practical implications of engaging with emotions in international law. The central objective of this research project is to open up a new field of study on emotions and international law and thereby to help adapt the field of international law to addressing today’s complex global problems.
Keywords: emotions, environmental law, global health, humanitarian law, international law

Title: Anatomy and dynamics of volcanic systems: insights from a joint seismic tomography and seismicity analysis of Kilauea Volcano
Abstract: Magma transported through the Earth crust is one of the most disruptive but also most informative and relevant processes in Earth sciences. It involves extremely high strain rates and resulting seismic and a-seismic processes, very high and rapidly evolving contrasts in petrology and temperatures, and also considerable volcanic and seismic hazards. Seismic imaging studies as well as earthquake monitoring have proven to be powerful techniques to locate and track magma at mantle depths and in crustal reservoirs that underlie volcanoes, thus aiding in eruption forecasting. However, the connection between crustal magma plumbing systems and related earthquakes, and the underlying regions of mantle melts remains often poorly understood, mostly because the spatial and temporal resolution of seismic monitoring and imaging is not high enough to guide process understanding. The proposed research focuses on clarifying the volume and distribution of melt in volcanic storage regions, as well as the loading such distribution causes on nearby faults. This challenging scientific objective relies on developing a new generation of high-resolution images of seismic velocity structure, maps of b-values distribution, and by solving for loading of faults and stress changes. A joint analysis of the high-resolution velocity structure, the mapping of frequency-magnitude distribution analysis of local earthquakes, and the in-depth modeling of the variation of stress conditions in the Earth's crust will link the observation-driven models to the physical properties and processes that lead to magma generation and large earthquakes. The development of novel imaging methods will focus on leveraging complementary strengths of different seismic datasets through joint inversion (i.e., body wave travel-times, ambient noise cross-correlations, receiver functions, and controlled seismic sources), thus improving the uncertainty quantification, verification and resolution of the final models. Concurrently, by leveraging the improved event detection sensitivity of state-of-the-art Machine Learning based seismic monitoring methods together with the improved knowledge on the velocity structure, we will compile unusually detailed and accurate seismicity catalogues. These catalogues will, in turn, provide detailed insight into the pathway geometries of the conduit system and the loading of faults caused by the geodetic strain of magma movement. This will lead to a better understanding of the underlying causes and physical processes connected to eruptive activity and have also practical implication for volcanic and seismic hazard assessment. The ultimate goal of this proposal is to advance the capability of data-driven geophysical models to constrain melt volumes, geometries, magma properties and fault loading. Thus, we will link imaging to the ability to forecast eruption cycles and seismicity by gaining insights into the mass transport and rate changes through the entire system, including the factors that control stalling versus ascent of magmas. To this end, within the project, we will be studying the magmatic system beneath Kilauea Volcano, Hawai'i. Kilauea volcano is an ideal place to investigate the architecture and dynamics of a magma reservoir as seismicity rates are very high and volcanic processes occur over a relatively short time scale, ensuring the presence of magma in the system today, as attested by the ongoing eruptive activity. It is also an ideal location to study the fundamental process of how deformation gradually loads large faults, and we will analyze how the extension of the East Rift Zone impacts seismicity rates and gradually loads the décollement interface, periodically leading to magnitude 7 earthquakes. We will incorporate existing seismic data collected over the past 40 years from permanent seismic stations operated by the Hawaiian Volcano Observatory as well as from past open access seismic experiments. We will also deploy a dense seismic deployment across the sparsely instrumented Eastern Rift Zone. Title: Universal Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials for Magnetic Systems
Abstract:
Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have become an essential part of the materials science toolbox, combining near–ab initio accuracy with computational efficiency comparable to classical force fields. They allow realistic simulations that include temperature, quantum effects, and disorder, at a fraction of the cost of traditional quantum-mechanical calculations. Recent advances have led to the first universal MLIPs for solids, which can accurately describe a wide range of materials without the need for custom model development.

However, magnetism remains largely absent from current MLIPs, despite its central role in many functional and structural materials such as steels, transition-metal alloys, perovskites, and correlated oxides. This omission limits the predictive power of MLIPs and restricts their use for important classes of technologically relevant materials. Developing reliable models for magnetic systems remains challenging due to the complex nature of magnetic interactions and the high computational cost of generating accurate reference data.

In this Ambizione project, we will lay the groundwork for universal MLIPs that incorporate magnetism. Our aim is to establish a robust data and modelling framework that captures the interplay between atomic structure and magnetic behaviour across diverse material classes.  The project will combine existing and newly generated datasets of magnetic materials to train and validate new technologis for universal magnetic models. We will systematically benchmark their accuracy, transferability, and computational efficiency, ensuring that they are broadly applicable to magnetic metals, alloys, and oxides. Beyond the direct development of MLIPs, the resulting data and models will provide a foundation for future research on strongly correlated materials and machine learning–based electronic structure methods.

Close collaboration with research groups at EPFL and international partners will ensure that the models are tested across a variety of magnetic behaviours and material classes. This project will strengthen the Swiss research community in the field of machine learning for materials science and contribute to the development of sustainable, data-driven approaches to materials discovery and design.

Title: Prevention of postoperative complications by use of artificial intelligence
Abstract:
Background:
Postoperative complications are a huge burden for patients and a socio-economic challenge for health care systems. Despite studies showing that postoperative complications are correlated with intraoperative adverse events (IAE) and surgical skill, no effective intervention to identify IAE and measure surgical performance in real-time during surgery exists. Artificial intelligence (AI) has shown great success in medical image analysis. AI assistance significantly enhances the performance of radiologists in tumor detection. To date, AI assistance in surgery is still missing.

Objective:
This translational research project aims to study the effect of an AI Surgeon Assistant (AISA) detecting IAE, assessing surgical performance, and giving intraoperative feedback on the prevention of postoperative complications.

Specific aims:
1.Development and retrospective validation of AISA in IAE identification and surgical performance assessment
2.Conduction of a prospective pilot study to assess the potential of AISA in the prevention of postoperative complications

Methods:
The multicentric dataset of surgical videos created and annotated during my Postdoc.Mobility fellowship was used to train a deep neural network (DNN) that identifies IAE. To assess surgical performance, we trained a DNN to identify and localize surgical instruments within the dataset. This will allow us to track the movements of instruments over time. Movement trajectories of instruments are a proxy for the skill of the surgeon allowing assessment of the surgical performance. We will correlate the predictions of AISA in IAE identification and surgical performance assessment with postoperative complications as measured by the comprehensive complication index (CCI). Once retrospectively validated, AISA will be programmed to give real-time feedback during surgery. The potential of AISA to prevent postoperative complications will be investigated in a prospective pilot study in a before and after design. For 3 months, AISA will be used to assess IAE and surgical performance without giving feedback. Then AISA will be deployed in the same way for the next 3 months with intraoperative feedback to the operating surgeon. The primary outcome measure will be the CCI at 90 days postoperatively.

Expected results and their impact:
This project assesses if the occurrence of IAE or alterations in surgical performance as detected by AISA are correlated with postoperative complications. The novelty and innovation of AISA is its use as intraoperative assistance through real-time feedback during surgery. In prospective application, AISA will be able to prevent postoperative complications.
Therefore, this translational research project has a potential impact on patients and health-care systems in general by allowing for automated assessment not only of the performance of the surgical team but also by the identification of adverse intraoperative events. Such tools may be relevant for immediate feedback and training of persons performing healthcare-associated interventions.
Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Patient safety, Postoperative complications, Surgical data science

Title: De novo molecular design by deep learning
Abstract: Artificial intelligence methods, and in particular deep learning models, bear potential to support medicinal chemistry and help to improve decision-making in the early phases of drug discovery. This research project aims at critically analyzing the possibilities and limitations of generative deep recurrent networks for de novo hit and lead finding in drug design. The working hypothesis of the proposed study suggests that deep neural network models coupled with multi-objective optimization and active machine learning can be leveraged for the de novo design of bioactive molecules with bespoke properties, such as target panel engagement or selective target modulation. The proposed research project aims to develop a novel concept for rationally addressing the automated generation of focused compound libraries and ligands with desired properties, taking the example of nuclear receptor modulation for proof-of-concept. The main technologies employed are uni- and bidirectional deep recursive neural networks for structure-activity modeling, on-chip microfluidics-based synthesis of focused computer-designed compound libraries, and reporter-gene biological assays. Specifically, the concept of 'active learning' of structure-activity relationships by adaptive deep learning will be implemented. Active learning strategies will be developed for efficient cycling through the design-synthesis-test progressions, pursuing a multi-objective autonomous molecular design strategy. The results of this broad study will not only provide new insights at the forefront of chemoinformatics, but also be of great value for practical medicinal chemistry. Prognoses of the sustainability of the customary pharmaceutical discovery and development practices imply the necessity for adjusted strategies for the future. It has been realized that it will be necessary for the medicinal chemistry community to evaluate the feasibility of fully autonomous molecular design ‘in machina’, and at the same time analyze which aspects of compound generation are best left to a chemically–savvy artificial intelligence or a skilled human mind. The results of this research project will help to identify those approaches and methods that could be implemented robustly by medicinal chemists in the near future, and critically analyze the opportunities and challenges for their more widespread application.
Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Bioinformatics, Computer-assisted drug design, Medicinal chemistry

Title: Urban Positive Clean neigHborhood energy trAnsition: driving innovative solutions for Renovation, diGitalisation and energy Efficiency
Abstract:
The proposal aims to develop a portfolio of innovative solutions to be integrated into the built infrastructure, with the final goal of further enabling positive energy buildings (PEB) and districts (PED) within the future energy landscape. The solutions’ set developed within UPCHANGE will include the integration of renewable energy generation systems in the built environment, digitalization solutions for building energy management and in district energy networks; the proposal will also include a toolkit of solutions for building (and district) performance assessment.
The scientific aim of the project is to enable PEB and PED through innovative technologies, digitalization, sustainability and energy resilience. This will be achieved through diverse solutions encompassing demand-side management analyses, multi functional active facade design and testing, development of a building energy flexibility tool, and digital approaches for data collection and energy profiling and forecasting.
The UPCHANGE solutions relate within both challenge 1 and challenge 2 of the call to: achieving climate-neutral buildings and urban blocks through an increased reliance on local renewables, designing, testing, and developing innovative solutions for active façades, and developing interoperable data management tools and Artificial Intelligence support toolkit for PEBs and PEDs. Additionally, the project also aims to develop demand response strategies for district-scale applications, investigate synergies with energy communities, neutral and PED, and climate neutral cities policies, and demonstrate the feasibility and scalability of the UPCHANGE toolkit through diverse pilot projects in the urban environment.

Title: Towards a Unified understanding of Attention and Social Behaviors in the Wild
Abstract:
Understanding and interpreting people’s states, activities, and behaviors stands as a foundational objective in the field of artificial intelligence. Indeed, the ability to discern non-verbal behaviors, interpret social signals, and infer the mental states of others are crucial components of social intelligence, enabling individuals to predict and understand the behavior of others, anticipate their reactions, gauge their interest, and engage in more meaningful and effective social exchanges.

In particular, gaze and attention form central elements driving many cognitive processes related to intentions, actions, and communications, with many connections with other behavioral cues like head and hand gestures, speaking status, facial expressions, or interactions. While past research efforts attempted to model these cues, the associated tasks were often treated independently which forgoes any possible relationships between them, or in specific settings. 

In light of this, the goal of this research project is to develop holistic and comprehensive models for human attention and social behavior understanding in the wild, where videos feature a wide diversity of scenes, environments, people, objects, and activities.  This implies the integration of social prediction tasks at two different levels: (i) subject-level, where we seek to model head dynamics and facial behavior (e.g. facial expressions, gaze estimation, head/hand gestures), and (ii) scene-level,  by analyzing people’s states and behavior to infer gaze following patterns (where and at what a person looks at), attentiveness, interactions, and social communication, which requires context modeling.

The core idea is to leverage a multi-task co-training framework to model these tasks jointly, thereby accounting for intra-task and inter-task dynamics. The unified model is poised to bring the following benefits: (a) efficiency owing to a single model supporting multiple tasks, (b) improved performance by virtue of multi-task supervision, and (c) strong person/scene representations that can transfer well to person-centric downstream tasks.

Achieving the desired result hinges upon addressing multiple challenges related to the specific tasks themselves, or the overarching unification objective. These can be framed as a set of research questions that will drive our investigations: (a) How can we leverage vision-language models to incorporate a semantic layer into the gaze following task? (b) How should we model head-face-gaze dynamics to infer head gestures and gaze directions? (c)  How can we represent person-centric information given head and body streams? (d) How can we exploit the graph message passing framework or cross-attention models to design fusion mechanisms of subject-level and scene-level information? (e) How to curate data for the tasks of interest, and capitalize on label propagation to learn from a combination of heterogeneous datasets and annotations?

Given the unification end-goal, our approach is to leverage a consistent token-based representation in all our tasks, thereby ensuring compatibility between the different architectural components developed separately. We envision the final architecture to include scene and person transformer encoders followed by a fusion module to allow the exchange of information between each person and the scene or other people. Finally, the updated person tokens will serve as input queries to a transformer decoder before feeding into task-specific prediction heads.

By investigating unified computational models of social behavior and communication in the wild, including how visual attention is influenced by and coordinated with other cues, we expect to impact the research community by advancing the state-of-the-art in human-centric computer vision, providing novel tasks and benchmarks, and contribute to other disciplines that rely on such models to automatically code these behaviors for subsequent large-scale analyses.

Title: Electrophysiological procedures in the interventional MRI environment
Abstract:
Cardiovascular diseases are still responsible for ~17 million deaths annually worldwide, ~25% of which are sudden cardiac death (SCD). Prevention of some of these adverse outcomes is achieved by defibrillator implantation and/or invasive radiofrequency (RF) catheter ablations targeting fibrosis as the arrhythmic substrate. 
While the conventional ablation procedures are performed by highly experienced electrophysiologists, they still result in a substantial relapse rate of ~50%. A key limitation of such procedures is the incomplete visualization of the target scar tissue by currently used voltage mapping and the imperfect control of ablation lesion formation. Interventional CMR (iCMR) can precisely visualize tissue characteristics to delineate the targets for ablation and it can characterize the post-ablation lesion (e.g. by discriminating transmural necrosis vs edema). With the advent of novel active-tracking MRI catheters, precise navigation to the ablation targets appears feasible. Finally, the entire iCMR-guided intervention can be carried out without any x-ray exposure, thus, reducing cancer risk. The current project aims to characterize iCMR-guided ablations of right atrial flutter with focus on 3D cavo-tricuspid isthmus (CTI) motion during ablation and to show the feasibility of premature ventricular contractions (PVC) ablation of right and left ventricular origin. An augmented-virtual-reality (AVR)-simulator developed by our consortium will be refined for 1) more realistic training, and 2) improved personalized procedure planning for safe ablations with high success rate.
Our project intends to establish ablation procedures and its workflows for the invasive management in an interventional CMR system of a set of common arrhythmias and clinical conditions, some of which are potentially life threatening. Within this 3-years project, we intend to treat in a sequential order patients with: 1. typical atrial flutter (RA-Fl); 2. Right ventricular outflow track PVCs and non-sustained ventricular tachycardias; 3. patients with PVCs from the left ventricle in post-myocardial infarction, from the left interventricular septum in patients with mid-line sign, and in patients with the malignant form of mitral valve prolapse. In parallel, the AVR-simulator will be further refined to integrate respiratory and cardiac motion and it will be coupled to the iCMR scanner for improved and more realistic personalized training and procedure planning. To this aim, the project unifies the Electrophysioloy units of the CHUV (University Hospital Lausanne, Prof. E. Pruvot) and the Leipzig Heart Center (Prof. i. Paetsch), the iCMR center of the CHUV (Prof. J. Schwitter), the Federal Institute of Engineering Lausanne (EPFL, Prof. P. Fua), and the research group of Prof. M. Stuber of the CHUV. 
This iCMR-guided approach combined with novel AVR-simulator based training and personalized procedure preparation is expected to result in shorter intervention times, lower complication rates, and better outcome with less relapses. This may also impact positively on costs (while this aspect will not be investigated in this proof-of-concept project). This cost reduction is important, as an increase in the prevalence of post-infarction arrhythmias is expected. If the project is successful, it will demonstrate that ablations of complex arrhythmic substrates as present in PVC patients can be performed safely under full iCMR-guidance. These data can set the basis for randomized controlled trials in this field. We will also better understand ablation lesion characteristics and its impact on arrhythmia recurrence.

Title: Neural Correlates of Dreaming
Abstract:
THE NEURAL CORRELATES OF DREAMING

Background
Dreaming is a particular form of consciousness that occurs during sleep. Studying mental experiences during sleep thus offers a unique opportunity to explain how changes in brain activity relate to changes in consciousness. One unresolved question in this respect is whether dreams are generated in a ‘bottom-up’ manner (starting from activity in low-level sensory brain areas, which is then interpreted and synthesized by higher-order areas, like in perception) or in a ‘top-down’ way (beginning as wishes, abstract thoughts and memories, which are then enriched with perceptual and sensory aspects, as in imagination). 

Aims 
The present project aims at determining how conscious experiences in sleep relate to underlying electroencephalographic activity and if machine-learning techniques can reliably predict periods of dreaming and non-dreaming. It also assesses whether the predominant signal flow in response to transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) during rapid eye movement sleep (REM sleep), when mental experiences are particularly vivid and frequent, follows a ‘top-down’ or a ‘bottom-up’ propagation.

Methods
Experiment 1: high-density electroencephalography (hd-EEG) recordings (256 electrodes) are performed in healthy participants during night sleep in the laboratory. Participants are awakened in pseudorandom intervals and are asked about the presence and content of mental activity. The EEG signal in the two minutes prior to the awakening is analyzed in terms of spontaneous power changes and with machine learning paradigms.

Experiment 2: healthy volunteers participate in a wake session during the day and a sleep session during the night, equipped with TMS-compatible hd-EEG (60 electrodes). TMS is sequentially applied to the left prefrontal Brodmann area 6 and the left occipital Brodmann area 19. After each TMS-session during sleep, subjects are questioned about the presence of conscious experiences. TMS-evoked EEG responses between the prefrontal and occipital areas in REM sleep and wakefulness are compared. 

Importance of the project
This study investigates whether EEG patterns or TMS-evoked activity can predict dreaming. If, as preliminary results suggest, it is possible to determine, in real time, whether a person is dreaming, and also to predict broad categories of dream content, this will open new perspectives in dream research. Changes in dream content form the core feature of many sleep and psychiatric disorders and share features with hallucinations and delirium that represent hallmarks of psychosis. Determining neural correlates of dreaming might thus ultimately open new approaches to the understanding and treatment of these diseases.
Keywords: consciousness, dream, hallucination, high-density EEG, sleep, transcranial magnetic stimulation

Title: Enhancing Computational Pathology for Prostate Cancer using Graph-Based Models for 3D Tissue Analysis, Spatial Transcriptomic and Patient Similarity
Abstract:
The analysis of tissue plays a central role in decoding cellular interactions and linking novel mechanistic insights with changes in tissue morphology. The convergence of novel high-resolution imaging technologies, single cell characterization platforms, and artificial intelligence propel cellular pathology from a technologically stagnant clinical discipline into a center stage position in basic research, disease prevention, early detection clinical management and therapeutic discovery. Empowered by these technologies it will be possible to overcome the limitations of categorical grading systems that do not capture our molecular understanding of disease. Imaging is critical for detecting signals at different scales, setting these into context with the architecture of cells and tissues. Imaging AI plays a fundamental role in the robust and objective analysis of this complex data and linking phenotypic changes to onset and progression of disease.
However, methodological advancements to analyse complex 3D tissue images, link of morphological features with molecular information, and improve our ability to identify related patient subgroups are required to enable the discovery of interpretable histology-based biomarkers that can improve patient care. Addressing these needs is the aim of my two-year SNF mobility grant application supported by Professor Jens Rittscher (Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Oxford Big Data Institute, University of Oxford, UK). Advancing our understanding of prostate cancer which is genetically heterogeneous will provide the context of this methodology development. Working with unique patient cohorts of patients with prostate cancer that are available in Oxford, I will build on my experience in deep learning and imaging to develop graph-based solutions addressing these specific aims:
Aim 1: Interrogate spatial relationships in 3D tissues to advance our ability to quantify changes in the characteristics and appearance of cellular niches within tissues. 
Aim 2: Integrate morphology and molecular information to improve our understanding on how molecular mechanisms govern changes in tissue architecture. 
Aim 3: Identify histology-based patient subgroups to overcome the limitations of categorical grading systems and improve patient management. 
The outputs of this proposal will directly impact our ability for developing biomarkers that better stratify disease, predict response to therapy, and improve patient management.
Keywords: graph deep learning, histology, prostate cancer, spatial transcriptomic

Title: Consequences of Personalized Information Provision Online: Segregation, Polarization, and Radicalization
Abstract: With the ever-increasing importance of machine learning (ML/AI) algorithms and the usage of personal data for the provision of information to voters and consumers, the question of how algorithmic information provision over the web might affect our lives is of substantial relevance. There are concerns that algorithmic personalization in modern web platforms (such as search engines and social media platforms) are a major driving force behind growing political polarization, as citizens are increasingly likely to consume information from like-minded sources, fueling their prejudices and grievances. A particularly concerning trend in this context is the increase in web platforms' capabilities to personalize the provision of information to its users based on the users' personal data as well as the use of more powerful but less transparent ML algorithms (i.e., deep learning). Such systems might contribute to misinformation and political polarization as users unconsciously end up in echo chambers as a result of the personalized filtering. Both for the entities developing AI-driven web information systems, as well as for government regulators and policy makers there is a need for systematic assessments/audits of such AI-driven information systems in order to detect and quantify potentially harmful side-effects for users and (indirectly) for society at large. In this project, we develop the technical infrastructure and scientific framework to conduct field experiments based on ‘bots' (programs that simulate internet users) in order to study whether and how this personalized filtering (such as in search engines, news aggregators, and social media platforms) can lead to informational segregation, polarization, and radicalization.
Keywords: Internet, Mass Media, News Aggregators, Online News, Political Polarization, Radicalization, Search Engines, Segregation, Web Search Personalization, YouTube

Title: Deciphering TCR specificity one epitope at a time
Abstract:
T-cell recognition of epitopes displayed on the surface of infected or cancer cells plays a fundamental role in spontaneous and therapy-induced immune responses. Over the years, experimental and computational tools to identify peptides displayed on Major Histocompatibility Complex molecules (pMHC) have enabled researchers to find many clinically relevant epitopes. In parallel, high-throughput single-cell technologies enable in depth profiling of the TCR repertoire of patients. However, it remains very laborious to determine which TCRs recognize which epitopes.

Recently, we have developed a state-of-the-art deep learning framework (MixTCRpred) to predict TCRs recognizing specific epitopes. These types of models are trained on TCRs interacting with specific epitopes and can provide reliable predictions for epitopes which are part of their training set. Extrapolating these predictions to so-called ‘unseen’ epitopes remains much more challenging. In parallel, we have set up in my group an experimental pipeline to interrogate libraries of CD8+ T cells from donors with pMHC multimers and sequence their TCRs. These data provide reliable models of TCR specificity, as demonstrated in our results with several variants of a Yellow Fever epitope.

Building upon this combined experimental and computational expertise, we aim at deciphering fundamental properties of TCR specificity and develop a robust framework for analyzing and visualizing epitope-specific TCR sequences. To this end we have defined four aims.
-Aim 1: Investigate how the repertoire of epitope-specific TCRs evolves with respect to amino acid changes in epitopes. 
-Aim 2: Investigate how the repertoire of epitope-specific TCRs evolves with respect to changes in MHC alleles.
-Aim 3: Develop an information theory-based analysis and visualization framework for epitope-specific TCRs. 
-Aim 4: Integrate the results of Aim 1&2 in the MixTCRpred prediction framework.

Aims 1&2 include experimental screening of CD8+ T cells recognizing variants of immunodominant epitopes. Aim 3&4 combine algorithmic developments with analysis of data generated in this project as well as public data.

This proposal addresses several outstanding questions in the field. First, our work will provide a very thorough, systematic and controlled investigation of the impact of changes in epitopes and MHCs on the repertoire of epitope-specific TCRs. This is critical to understand how (and how far) models learned on some epitopes can be extrapolated to new epitopes. Second, our proposed framework for analyzing and visualizing TCR specificity will provide a powerful way to rapidly understand and compare the repertoire of TCRs recognizing a large panel of epitopes. Third, our work will pave the way to expanding the range of clinically relevant epitopes for which predictions can be made.

The ability to combine in my group experimental data generation together with developments of algorithms and intuitive visualization tools puts us in a unique position to successfully perform the proposed work. Moreover, the expertise in place at the Department of Oncology at UNIL/CHUV (including access to T cells from donors, a pMHC tetramer core facility, state-of-the-art flow cytometry equipment, and in house TCR sequencing in the group of our project partner, Prof. Harari) represents an exceptional environment to carry out this research project.

The impact of reliable TCR-epitope interaction predictions extends beyond the fundamental questions addressed in this proposal, holding promises for diagnoses or T-cell based therapies. As such, we envision several translational applications of this project, as demonstrated in our recent work on predicting COVID-19 status based on enrichment of TCRs recognizing SARS-CoV-2 epitopes, or designing TCRs recognizing with high specificity the NY-ESO-1 cancer testis antigen (see preliminary results).

Title: The Neuroeconomics of Conflict and Preference Strength in Decision Making
Abstract:
The neoclassical approach to economic decision making endows agents with preference relations, which under appropriate assumptions can be represented through utility functions. This approach is insufficient to account for and organize empirical findings on actual economic decision making for several reasons. Three important ones, substantiated by extensive evidence, are as follows: (i) choice is stochastic, that is, the same agent confronted with the same set of options might choose different alternatives; (ii) decisions often arise from the interaction and even conflict between different behavioral tendencies or decision processes with fundamentally different characteristics (e.g., deliberative vs. intuitive), whose aggregation into a single preference relation can be counterproductive; (iii) preferences are in general not stable and are affected in specific ways by actual choices, that is, choice-induced attitude change feeds back into preferences and affects future choices. Each of these difficulties interacts with established methods of preference elicitation and estimation, posing significant challenges for economic modeling. 

The objective of this project is to develop and test a model architecture for economic decision making, integrating received and new insights from neuroscience, psychology, and behavioral economics and addressing the three challenges described above. If successful, the project can have a significant impact in both theoretical and applied microeconomics by providing a new, mathematically sound but data-driven framework for economic modeling with the potential of sparking a paradigm shift. 

The project relies on three methodological lines. The first is the development of formal-analytical models linking preferences, decision processes, and the possibility of preference change. The aim is to develop a rigorous, analytically tractable, modular architecture. The framework should incorporate formal models of decision processes, possibly different for qualitatively different processes, encompassing e.g. stochastic preference models axiomatized in microeconomics or evidence accumulation models from cognitive psychology. Further, it should include explicit models of central-executive arbitration among processes, reflecting existing evidence on neural correlates of conflict detection and resolution. 

The second line relies on behavioral experiments on decision making where process data, and in particular response times, are collected. Response times are valuable for two main reasons. On the one hand, it is well-known in psychophysics that choice difficulty (e.g., in perceptual discrimination tasks) maps directly into error rates and response times, with more difficult choices resulting in larger error rates and longer response times. Evidence indicates that these phenomena extend to economic decision making, with harder decisions being those with a smaller "strength of preference," roughly linked to a smaller difference in subjective economic value or elicited (cardinal) utility. Hence, response times allow a direct glimpse into differences in such value or utility. On the other hand, response times provide valuable insights into the nature of involved decision processes, because intuitive processes are faster than deliberative ones, and process conflict results in decision delays. These regularities can be used to discriminate among models and build better ones, but evidence from carefully designed experiments is crucial to understand and disentangle their origins.

The third methodological research line concentrates on neural correlates of decision making, specifically those measured with the electroencephalograph (EEG). The corresponding experiments will rely on well-established event-related potentials (ERPs) which index e.g. conflict between behavioral tendencies or decision processes (the N2), the reliance on reinforcement learning (as a main component of intuitive processes; the Feedback-Related Negativity, FRN), or deviations from expectations. Crucially, these neural correlates deliver information that cannot be deduced from pure choice data or response times, and hence are invaluable for model development.

The three lines are strongly interrelated and the project heavily depends on the synergies arising from this multi-method approach. The first line delivers testable predictions (experimental hypotheses) for the other two, and the latter in turn inform model-building by providing empirically sound modeling principles.
