Title: Evolutionary dynamics of chromosomal inversions and local adaptation
Abstract:
Chromosomal inversions are rapidly increasing in interest in the field of evolutionary biology. A search for the
keyword “chromosomal inversions” shows that the number of publications on this topic more than doubled
from 2014 to 2022 (https://app.dimensions.ai/). This renewed interest in chromosomal inversions is in part
driven by the advance of novel technologies that allow us to detect and study inversions in unprecedented
detail. However, despite this plethora of new data, we still know very little about how and why inversions
evolve. We do know, however, that modifications in genome structure, such as chromosomal inversions, can
create genomic landscapes that either facilitate or obstruct adaptation. Understanding this dynamic interplay
between genome structure and natural selection is the central goal of this grant proposal.
Empirical studies have revealed the role of inversions in local adaptation, exemplified by cases like the
Anopheles gambiae mosquito's inversion-linked adaptation to distinct environments. Inversions also fuel
reproductive isolation, a catalyst for speciation, as seen in Drosophila pseudoobscura where specific
chromosomal inversions hinder inter-population mating. Moreover, inversions on sex chromosomes, impact
sex determination and related traits by suppressing recombination in specific regions. These diverse examples
highlight how studying chromosomal inversions can provide crucial insights into the intricate interplay
between genome architecture and the forces of natural selection.
While several hypotheses exist regarding the evolutionary dynamics of chromosomal inversions, empirical
evidence for any of these hypotheses remains inconclusive. Discerning various competing hypotheses will
require deciphering the molecular signatures of local adaptation within chromosomal inversions and the
development of tools for pinpointing selection targets within inversions. On the theoretical side, we lack
realistic models that allow us to understand the conditions driving indirect selection on recombination
suppression via inversions. Such models are also necessary for scrutinizing the temporal sequence of inversion
events concerning locally adapted polymorphisms, providing a window into the chronology of evolutionary
events and their intrinsic connection to adaptation.
To tackle these challenges, I propose to combine mathematical modeling, individual-based simulations,
machine learning techniques, and analysis of empirical data from sticklebacks and fruit flies. This integrative
approach will enable a thorough exploration of the molecular signatures of local adaptation and background
selection within chromosomal inversions (Project 1), the identification of selection targets within these
structural variants using machine learning approaches (Project 2), the determination of conditions driving
indirect selection on recombination suppression through inversions (Project 3), the quantification of
inversions' impacts on both local adaptation and reproductive isolation (Project 3) and the elucidation of the
temporal relationship between inversion events and locally adapted polymorphisms (Project 3).

Title: Learning Properties of Big Data in Parallel and Distributed Computation
Abstract:
As data increases in size, it has become infeasible to perform many modern computational tasks on a single machine. This gives rise to the need for parallel and distributed computation, which is nowadays widespread. On the one hand, the practical realization of these models is in its early stage and so our algorithmic toolbox for these models is in its infancy. On the other hand, one of the cornerstones in modern data analysis is learning and discovering properties of the given data, for which very few parallel and distributed algorithms were developed.

Efficient algorithms: Frameworks for processing data in a parallel and distributed manner, such as MapReduce and Hadoop, are prevalent in modern computation. Although there has been a large body of work on studying properties of data, a small fraction of those results address the increasing need to analyze big data in parallel and distributed settings. My goal is to develop new efficient algorithms for analyzing a broad class of properties of big data in these models. As one of the directions, I want to tackle some of the classical distribution questions (e.g., testing normality or independence of joint distributions).

New communication models: Edge computing is a rapidly emerging paradigm that shifts big data processing from datacenters to the user side (e.g., machine learning computation on smart devices). Since its development is in a very young stage and due to its difference compared to computation in datacenters (e.g., limits on power consumption, storage availability), there is a large number of open fundamental questions related to computation in this framework. My goal is to propose new models of communication between devices in these networks so as to yield efficient computation. To that end, I plan to study dynamic algorithms for updating properties of data that undergo changes.

Title: Intelligent Pressure Offloading Footwear to Prevent Lower Extremity Amputations in People with Diabetes
Abstract:
More than 537 million people globally live with diabetes mellitus, representing 10.5% of the adult population. The World Health Organization estimates that there are ~250,000 non-traumatic, diabetes-related, lower extremity amputations annually in Europe, of which 85% are preventable. These amputations are often a result of an infected foot ulcer coupled with a loss of pain sensation (neuropathy) and abnormally high pressures under the feet (plantar pressures, PPs). Elevated PPs, which are unnoticed by the patient with neuropathy, trigger most foot ulcers and are linked to 94% of amputations.

Current interventions for ulcer prevention and healing focus on offloading these high PPs using a variety of footwear, insoles, or walking retraining. However, these solutions have critical limiting factors that reduce adherence, limit long-term efficacy, and are resource intensive. Furthermore, two underlying constraints of these interventions are an absence of an actively adjusting insole according to real-time needs and the knowledge of the relationships between insole contour changes, biomechanics, and plantar pressures in this population.

The main goal of this use-inspired project is to address these research gaps by using our team’s intelligent offloading footwear to quantify the effects of pressure-offloading and insole contour changes on gait biomechanics. The project’s aims build from current work to produce scientific knowledge on the impact of insole contour changes on biomechanics and PP mapping, and on user perceptions regarding intelligent offloading. The Intelligent Offloading Footwear (IOF) was jointly developed (Prof. Pataky/Prof. Perriard, SNSF-BRIDGE Discovery, 2019-2023); its insole system automatically senses PPs across the foot and offloads high PP areas by altering the insole contour according to the user’s specific pressure needs. This project will scientifically validate footwear performance to offload PPs, producing a tool that is expected to provide more efficient prevention and/or treatment of foot ulcerations and lower extremity amputations when considering its patient compliance, performance efficacy, and reduced customisation need. 

Aim 1 of this project will deliver a passive pressure-contour model to create a database of pressure changes according to insole contour changes. Aim 2 will investigate the influence of active insole contour changes on biomechanics and user perceptions. Aim 3 will generate a machine learning model to quantify the relationship between systematic insole changes and the pressure-offloading efficacy considering data collected in Aims 1 and 2, so as to produce an autonomous algorithm. Aim 4 will integrate the passive pressure-contour model (Aim 1), active PP offloading, biomechanics and user perceptions (Aim 2), and the validated algorithm (Aim 3) into the optimized IOF which will be evaluated in daily life. The completion of these aims will deliver a well-fitting, user-centred, intelligent offloading footwear that efficiently redistributes high PP and is ready for randomized clinical trials in people with diabetes.

This 4-year project uses an interdisciplinary approach by a team of experts (diabetic foot care, machine learning, electronics, gait biomechanics) to 1) generate scientific knowledge regarding passive and active insole contour changes on biomechanics, and adherence perceptions for people with diabetes, and 2) produce validated, intelligent offloading footwear with the ability to prevent ulceration and amputation in people with diabetes.

Title: Graph Analytics in the Language of Linear Algebra: Where Combinatorics Meets Neural Networks
Abstract:
Graph machine learning is an emerging field of artificial intelligence (AI) motivated by the ubiquity of graph-structured data in real-life applications. Graph-powered machine learning techniques exploit the connectivity between graph objects to boost the predictive power of machine learning tasks. In this field, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have proved to be very effective tools. However,  popular GNN architectures are limited in terms of the type and the complexity of the subgraph patterns they can recognise. For instance, cycles, cliques, and frequent motifs can act as highly discriminative features when analysing financial, biological, and social networks, but discovering such patterns using GNNs is extremely challenging. Such complex patterns can be detected by the so called higher-order GNNs. However, the cost of executing higher-order GNNs can be even higher than the cost of detecting these patterns using combinatorial graph algorithms. Yet, traditional combinatorial graph algorithms do not possess any statistical learning capabilities.

This proposal aims to introduce new ways of combining traditional combinatorial graph algorithms and GNNs to build graph machine learning solutions that possess pattern discovery, prediction, and generalisation capabilities beyond those of state-of-the-art GNNs and combinatorial graph algorithms. Our goals include improving the prediction accuracy, the scalability, and the interpretability of graph machine learning solutions both in theory and in practice. We are going to demonstrate the effectiveness of our solutions by analysing financial transaction networks to detect criminal activities, such as money laundering and credit-card fraud. In addition, we are planning to build new AI-powered subgraph pattern search capabilities for knowledge graph exploration.

Furthermore, AI accelerators, such as Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) and Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), have become the hardware architectures of choice for Deep Neural Network (DNN) training and inference. These accelerators offer efficient hardwired execution support for compute-intensive DNN functions, such as dense linear algebra and convolution operations. Mapping graph machine learning algorithms onto similar primitives would enable their efficient execution on AI accelerators that have become ubiquitous in cloud infrastructures, data centres, and edge devices. However, executing GNNs and combinatorial subgraph discovery algorithms on top of the emerging AI accelerators is not straightforward. Whereas GNNs heavily rely on sparse linear algebra operations, AI accelerators are typically optimised for dense linear algebra operations. In addition, combinatorial subgraph mining algorithms are often formulated recursively and expressed using set algebra. Formulating these algorithms in the language of linear algebra is a major challenge. 

A main goal of this proposal is to establish linear algebra as the common language between GNNs and combinatorial subgraph discovery algorithms. We aim to explore an unexplored design space, in which the building blocks of GNNs and combinatorial algorithms can be combined based on linear-algebra-based primitives. Our proposal aims to answer questions such as the following:  
1) What capabilities are needed in GNNs to enable the discovery of discriminative subgraphs? 
2) How can combinatorial subgraph discovery algorithms and GNNs empower each other? 
3) Can subgraph discovery be performed using linear algebra operations on AI accelerators?
4) Can graph machine learning serve as an effective countermeasure against financial crime?
Keywords: Financial Crime, Graph Algorithms, Graph Neural Networks, Linear Algebra, Scalable AI

Title: Learning compositional world models
Abstract:
The world is compositional, or at least, our model of the world is.
It is a hallmark of intelligence enabling "infinite use of finite means", allowing us to rapidly generalize our prior knowledge to new tasks.
We discover this structure solely through observation and interaction with the environment.
What mechanisms support this remarkable ability to modularize procedural knowledge into reusable components?
Advancing our understanding of this question by developing novel deep learning methods is the overarching goal of this project.
We will begin by devising a contrastive learning method that yields representations which explicitly capture the affordances of objects, i.e., not only their physical properties, but also how they can be used when acting in the world.
Building on such representations, we aim to develop world models that are capable of identifying a small set of modular and composable rules that govern the dynamics and interactions of objects in the environment.
Finally, we will leverage the afore developed compositional world models to instantiate methods that support sample-efficient reinforcement learning for rapid acquisition of new skills.
Keywords: artificial intelligence, compositional generalization, compositionality, computational neuroscience, deep learning, modularity, neural networks, reinforcement learning, world models

Title: Sensor Selection for Autonomous Driving applications (SenSel-AD)
Abstract:
The field of autonomous driving has seen significant advancements in recent years and has the potential to increase road safety, reduce traffic congestion, and improve the accessibility and efficiency of transportation systems. However, achieving the efficient design and safe operation of autonomous vehicles (AVs) presents significant challenges. One primary challenge lies in formulating and solving system co-design problems, which involve the formal specification of system functions and constraints, as well as the design of a minimal system that guarantees safety while fulfilling the desired tasks. In addition, comprehensive testing approaches of the whole system and its individual components (i.e. the sensing, perception, planning and control modules) are central to guarantee safety. 
This project addresses these two key aspects with a focus on the perception systems. It builds upon the outcomes of an ongoing collaborative PhD work between ETH and Empa, in which a sensor selection methodology for AVs has been developed. This methodology relies on perception benchmark models derived from real-world sensor data, which characterize the probability that a given perception system (sensor plus object detection algorithm) will detect different object classes under different configurations. On the path planning side, sensing requirements are determined based on collision checks conducted by sampling-based motion planners for various driving scenarios. The optimal perception system is then determined solving a weighted multi-variable optimization problem that minimizes targeted resources, including costs, computational requirements, weight, and energy consumption. This framework does not only provide the optimal perception system for a given scenario or task, but also enables the investigation of the main factors influencing the sensor selection and the AV design, such as the task complexity, or the information requirements from different motion planners.
This follow-up project seeks to further develop and validate the sensor benchmarking and selection procedures. Key objectives include expanding the perception performance models to account for uncertainties and temporal aspects, integrating sensor fusion capabilities, and refining the extraction methodologies for the sensing requirements. Additionally, the project aims to develop a hybrid sensor selection approach, considering sensors' placement on both the vehicles and road infrastructure. Rigorous simulations and real-world testing using the 'move' AD testing infrastructure will be conducted to validate and iteratively refine these methodologies across diverse operating conditions. Ultimately we will apply the novel methodologies to selected use-cases to demonstrate its relevance in real applications.
The research approach leverages open-source databases and advanced data science techniques such as domain adaptation, Bayesian filters, and stochastic optimization, to address critical questions surrounding sensor selection and system validation.  
The outcomes of the project hold the potential to advance the development and validation of innovative sensor technologies, object detection, and planner algorithms. Additionally, through real-world validation experiments, we aim to narrow the gap between simulations and practical autonomous driving applications, thereby improving the reliability and safety of future AVs. Moreover, the hybrid sensor selection approach will facilitate the design of more efficient solutions for complex driving situations, opening up new research directions beyond autonomous driving. In fact, while our primary focus is on AVs, the methodologies developed in the project have broader implications across various domains, including drones, industrial robotics, or smart cities, highlighting the project's significance in advancing the fields of AD and robotics as a whole.

Title: Statistical learning of access-control policies
Abstract: In this research proposal, I address the problem of learning and generalizing patterns from access-control data. Data structures for access-control exhibit a large complexity and are often unintuitive for humans who must administrate them. In many real-world scenarios, this results in high administration costs and security risks. My goal is to automatically identify  statistically significant patterns in such data and to re-configure access-control systems such that the found patterns become apparent. In particular, I will approach the problem of unifying two access-control configurations of different organizations and the problem of generalizing permission request patterns of 200,000 Android applications for mobile devices. I will develop a set of unsupervised machine learning techniques to approach this task. These methods are not limited to access-control configuration but can also be applied in different contexts such as, for instance, to analyze social networks.
Keywords: RBAC, access control, clustering, graph matching, machine learning, mobile devices

Title: MaxEnt-Fin: computational maximum entropy approach to high-dimensional modeling and analysis in finance
Abstract:
Modeling and prediction of fluctuations (volatilities) in financial time series are among the core challenges in Economics and Finance. In the last several years, the accumulation of massive amounts of high-dimensional financial data was accompanied by an impressive development of econometric and machine learning (ML) approaches for the analysis of these data. Besides offering new exciting opportunities, recent applications of the emerging tools to the financial data has revealed some new methodological challenges related to the scalability, sensitivity, and comparability of the algorithms - as well as with respect to the interpretability of the obtained results and the study of the mathematical and statistical properties. For example, time series of stock returns are characterized by relatively few serial observations T (ranging from a few hundred observations with monthly data to a few
thousands with daily data) and by many dimensions n (up to tens or hundreds of thousands, where n corresponds to different companies, but also to characteristics of those companies). Application of popular computational numerical tools from econometrics and machine learning to such “small T, large n” data generally aims at finding increasingly-elaborate models with many parameters that have to be tuned to few high-dimensional observations available. This can lead to a problem known as “overfitting”, i.e. the good quality of fit on the training data is combined with the poor predictive performance of the tuned models. Another limitation is imposed by the computational cost of the common numerical tools, increasing polynomially with the data dimension n.

In this research proposal, we will develop numerical tools based on combining the recently-introduced Scalable Probabilistic Approximation (SPA) methods for adaptive data discretization with the Maximum Entropy principle from physics and information theory. Maximum Entropy principle (MaxEnt) aims at finding as simple as possible (but not simpler than necessary) models fitting the data, being least biased in terms of the underlying assumptions and minimal in terms of the total number of tunable parameters. We will develop a numerical discretization-driven MaxEnt framework for time series analysis and inference of latent cross-sectional interdependencies between different financial time series (like asset returns and credit ratings), allowing for computational uncertainty quantification and risk predictions based on time series from Economics and Finance. 

The research work is structured in three complementary research directions (subprojects) and will be performed by the two PIs, one PostDoc, and two Ph.D. students. (Subproject I) Sparse extension of nonstationary MaxEnt methods from one to multiple dimensions and numerical analysis of the methodology (estimation of computational scalability, sensitivity, and convergence properties). (Subproject II) Development and numerical analysis of discrete MaxEnt methods for scalable and simultaneous entropy maximization, feature selection, and
discretization for high-dimensional “small T, large n” data. (Subproject III) Development and numerical analysis of scalable methods for “small T, large n” transfer learning from econometrics time series - i.e., when transforming the time series to images (e.g., to scalograms) and combining the Deep Learning (DL) network pretrained on “big” image data (e.g., GoogleNet) for feature extraction with MaxEnt and discretization tools from Subprojects I and II. The scientific results will be the content of several research papers to be submitted to top journals in Econometrics, Computational Science, and mathematical foundations of ML methodology. The questions investigated and the methods developed in this project are important both for their topical relevance in the academic community and for the practical implications in the management of financial risks.

Title: Robust Autonomous Navigation in Proximity of Orbiting Objects
Abstract:
Autonomous navigation in proximity of other orbiting objects or more specifically pose (position and attitude) estimation of these objects is a key capability in many space missions, such as On-Orbit Servicing (OOS), On-Orbit Assembly (OOA), Active Debris Removal (ADR), Formation Flying (FF) and more in general Swarms of spacecraft, as well as comet and asteroid Explorations. Generally, pose estimation must be directly performed on board, in real time, in order to enable autonomous relative navigation maneuvering during close proximity operations (as rendezvous, final approach, docking or landing), otherwise infeasible if based on ground-in-the-loop commands, due to communication delays and lack of coverage. Several technologies can be used to for autonomous pose estimation, depending on the operational environment, on the characteristics of the target and on the on-board resources of the chaser. If the target is cooperative (which is usually the case in FF missions and sometimes in OOS missions as well) a radio-frequency (RF) – based relative navigation approach can be adopted in case both chaser and target spacecraft are provided with a RF receiving/transmitting antenna. In Earth orbits, below a certain altitude, it is possible and in general very convenient making use of Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) signals, such as GPS, Galileo, Glonass and Beidou, to perform relative positioning between cooperative spacecraft. If no RF communication link is available between the chaser and the target, pose estimation approaches based on Electro-Optical (EO) sensors can be adopted for pose determination of non-cooperative, known and unknown orbiting target objects.
Following my research activities on GNSS at École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL) and on Vision-based Navigation at California Institute of Technology (Caltech), the main goal of this research project is the design, implementation and testing of novel and advanced approaches and methods, based on monocular camera measurements and also on their fusion with carrier-phase -based GNSS observations (when available), for autonomous navigation in proximity of other orbiting targets. The proposed research project is a scientific follow-up of the Early Postdoc Mobility project on “GNSS/INS/Vision Integration for Versatile On-Board Absolute and Relative Spacecraft Navigation”, as it deeply focuses on autonomous relative navigation between spacecraft and especially on on-board, robust and precise pose determination between cooperative spacecraft and between a spacecraft and uncooperative known and unknown orbiting objects.  In particular,  I propose to develop and validate: 1) two complementary monocular-based methods suitable for pose and shape estimation of  unknown orbiting targets; 2) a  novel image processing method for robust feature extraction and tracking; 3) a Deep Learning based approach for pose initialization of uncooperative targets; and 4) a differential carrier-phase GNSS/Vision integration for precise pose determination of cooperative targets. Preliminary design, implementation and testing showed promising results. It is expected that, following the final design and a rigorous implementation, the proposed techniques for spacecraft pose estimation will outperform the state of the art with higher achievable accuracy and precision and at the same time stronger robustness.
Keywords: Computer vision, GNSS, Machine Learning, Navigation, Robotics, Spacecraft, Spacecraft navigation

Title: Fundaments of human hearing from nonlinear dynamics
Abstract:
The design of intelligent machines that not only communicate semantically with people, but also correctly interpret semantic contents in the emotional context, is pivotal for the development of ICT technologies and unavoidable for a beneficial use in society. This necessity is, in particular, a main bottleneck in the application of artificial intelligence to hearing. To resolve this problem, a number of diverse scientific and technical issues must be mastered. Profound knowledge must be acquired of how sound information is generated, monitored, and interpreted by the nervous system. Uncovering the general physical and the biophysical principles of sound information generation and decoding, fortunately, embodies the ability to implement these insights within lean and real-time capable technical frameworks. Presently, this level of knowledge is not achieved: A physics definition of the most relevant attributes of sound, pitch and timbre, is still essentially missing. The current common approach towards this goal is either by classical linear signal processing or by very detailed implementations of the biophysical templates of often unknown function. Due to the inherent complexity of both approaches, they have not led to efficient implementations of the functionalities required by artificial intelligence. As an example, the mammalian cochlea is fundamentally divergent in construction, functionality and performance from the essentially passive microphone systems used currently, designed only to convert sound pressure linearly into an electric voltage. The biological ear is a strongly nonlinear dynamical apparatus that not only detects sounds, but also provides great signal preprocessing. Nonetheless, its inherent nonlinear dynamics construction principles are relatively simple.
We therefore propose a radically new paradigm. This paradigm is based on a simpler modelling level using the nonlinear dynamics approach, to provide an optimal solution to both the problem of understanding the auditory system at a fundamental level, and to obtain therefrom technological implementations with superior processing capabilities. Auditory processing in biological systems makes heavy use of collective, self-organizing processes, which are central manifestations of nonlinear dynamics. This key element is exploited by nature, but is missing in the complex artificial implementations of auditory systems. Our specific hypothesis is that most of the important features of hearing can be understood and be coded in terms of robust properties of moderately low dimensional dynamical systems. By using this approach for the cochlea, it has become possible to explain a large number of human sound perception phenomena from purely physical grounds. As probably the most important one, the perception of pitch has been explained, including, e.g. the frequency selectivity, nonlinear amplification, combination tone generation, suppression of neighbouring tones, the missing fundamental and the various pitch shift phenomena. Of interest is that all these phenomena are linked, where the link can easily be captured  and exhibited in terms of notions of nonlinear dynamical systems. In our project we will apply this approach to understand unresolved phenomena of human and animal sound perception. We will interpret and study the biological peripheral circuitry (afferent and efferent connections to the cochlea) from a dynamical system point of view. The gained dynamical systems templates provide us with simple technical implementations that we will use to gain further insight into the biology blueprint’s nature, by comparing data from the implemented models with biological data. The paradigm will be cast into an expandable integrated hardware/software platform, that will reproduce the most salient aspects of natural hearing. Being fully accessible on all levels, the framework will be used at different stages of its completion not only as a test-bench for accepted concepts, but also as a predictive tool for unresolved aspects, and to explore the dynamical basis of less understood auditory features, paving the way for their implementation in working applications. We will primarily focus on the pitch as the acoustic feature, to be reproduced by the artificial cochlea and to be extracted by the constructed auditory platform. Pitch is not a fundamental physical quantity, but rather a program of extraction from a wave signal of arbitrary complexity; its evaluation demands both  the ??correct generation of the pitch substrate in the cochlea, as well as the correct extraction of the feature. Pitch, moreover, is the fundamental quality used for efficient mono-channel voice separation and noise suppression.
Keywords: Cochlea Implants, Hearing Robots, Hearing Sensor Periphery, Nonlinear Dynamics Principles of Hearing, Pitch Sensation, Source Separation

Title: Spline methods for the continuous/discrete processing of images
Abstract:
Our aim is to develop a comprehensive framework to address a whole class of problems that are usually formulated in the continuous domain, but call for a digital implementation. Our practical focus is on image processing while the theoretical context is provided by splines. This project started in 1998 and its scope has continued to broaden and to become more mathematical as fundamental aspects of splines (related to differential equations, estimation and regularization theory, stochastic processes, and inverse problems) have been uncovered. 

The specific spline-related research topics that will be investigated during this term are: 

A. Splines and inverse problems 
Splines can be specified as solutions of data-fitting problems subject to a Hilbertian regularization, which involves a defining operator L and a native space (reproducing-kernel Hilbert space). During the last term, we have generalized the concept to linear inverse problems. Specifically, by substituting the $L_2$-norm of the classical regularizer with its proper $L_1$ counterpart, we could prove that the solution is achieved by an L-spline (of a type matched to the operator L) with a minimal number of adaptive knots. We shall extend our formulation by considering additional regularization norms and domains, as well as broader classes of inverse problems. We shall apply our framework to the resolution of nonlinear inverse problems in optical imaging. 

B. Box splines and generalized total variation 
With the advent of compressed sensing, Hilbertian norms and regularizers have been supplanted by their sparsity- promoting counterparts (see also Item A). To accommodate this shift in paradigm, we shall revamp our spline toolbox by replacing the cubic B-splines by continuous piecewise-linear box splines. We shall use these to derive exact discretizations of the total-variation (TV) energy and its second-order extension (HTV) in any number of dimensions. We shall apply the framework to the resolution of concrete inverse problems in the continuum (imaging), using a coarse-to-fine strategy to progressively refine the discretization grid such as to ensure convergence to the continuous-domain solution. 

C. Vector-valued splines 
We shall extend our spline framework to the handling of vector-valued signals. To do so, we shall rely on matrix-valued digital filters and suitable matrices of differential operators, the idea being to exploit inter-channel dependencies. We shall construct vector-valued B-splines/interpolators and characterize the solution of variational vector-valued problems. We shall also make the connection with vector-valued stochastic processes. We shall apply our techniques to the reconstruction and processing of vector fields. 

D. Splines and the k-plane Radon transform
We shall investigate a novel representation of functions on $R^d$  that involves a special kind of spline atoms: the rotated and translated versions of a common (d - k)-dimensional profile, which we call a k-ridge. We intend to prove that these new splines are solutions of variational problems involving a defining operator L and the k-plane Radon transform. The two extreme cases of this extension are connected to the two most popular representations used in machine learning: the radial-basis functions for k = 0, and neural networks with one hidden layer for k = d - 1. 

E. Native spaces for splines 
The specification of a variational spline has two fundamental ingredients: a spline energy (regularization) and a native space. The latter is the largest possible collection of functions over which the defining energy-minimization problem admits a solution. While the theory of native spaces is well-established for Hilbertian energies, the construction of native spaces has remained elusive for other regularization norms, especially for the scenarios where the null space of the regularization operator is nontrivial. We intend to fill this gap by developing a generic construction of native spaces which should cover all the cases that are of practical interest to us. 

We expect that this research will produce: (1) a theoretical impact in the fields of image processing and applied mathematics, in reason of the novelty and unifying character of the formulation; (2) a practical impact through efficient algorithms and novel computational solutions. The developments in A, B, and C are motivated by concrete problems in bioimaging. The end product will be open-source software that will be made freely available to the research community. Topic E is especially important to us because is will provide the theoretical foundation of our lifelong research program.
Keywords: approximation theory, biomedical imaging, image processing, inverse problems, machine learning, regularization, sparsity, splines, stochastic processes

Title: Machine Learning in Byzantium
Abstract:
Whereas a lot of work has been done on improving the performance of machine learning
solutions, very little effort has comparatively been devoted to their robustness to adversarial behavior. This is becoming crucial for (a) machine learning is now often distributed over large scale architectures of which components are not always reliable and (b) applied all the wayfrom image classification, financial trend prediction and gaming to critical settings such as autonomous driving, disease diagnosis and flight control [34].
Essentially, machine learning improves the ability of a computer to solve a problem with
the amount of data available [48]. The computer has a parameter vector (or a model), basedon which it answers questions such as “is there a cat on this picture?”. According to howmany correct answers are provided, a specific cost is associated with the parameter vector.
Learning is the process of updating the parameter vector to minimize the cost.
The increasing amount of data available today [18] as well as the growing complexity of
models (number of parameters) [50] has led to learning schemes that require a lot of computational resources. As a consequence, most industry-grade machine-learning implementations are now distributed [1, 63]. For example, as of 2012, Google reportedly used 16.000 distributed processors to train an image classifier [40]. Many of these implementations adopt a workerserver setting [38]: a single parameter server in charge of the learning procedure, is helped by a set of workers. Some approaches, also motivated by privacy reasons, go even further and consider a peer-to-peer architecture [59]. Each peer, keeping its data locally, collaborates with other peers to improve its own model.
Be they worker-server or peer-to-peer, distributed architectures inevitably raise the issue
of adversarial behavior: in short, a distributed learning solution can only be effective if it
tolerates the inevitable malfunction of some of its workers/peers. Otherwise, not only the
solution will be ineffective, but it could be dangerous as machine learning approaches are now being adopted in critical environments.
Indeed classical fault-tolerance approaches (such as state machine replication) could in
principle be used to circumvent adversarial behavior, but they would clearly lead to inefficient solutions. The goal of this project is to build practical robust distributed learning solutions.
We will proceed in a modular manner by considering different kinds of adversarial behavior,
from asynchronous and curious ones all the way to arbitrary (Byzantine) ones. We will also
consider worker-server as well as peer-to-peer schemes.
For most of the directions considered in this proposal, we recently established pioneering
results [7, 20, 22, 27, 5, 21], some of which [7, 20] are already sparking a promising set of
follow-ups [55, 54, 37, 43, 62, 64, 16, 4, 6, 15, 53].

Title: The evolutionary drivers and phenotypic consequences of chromosome inversions
Abstract: Since their discovery 100 years ago, chromosome inversions have captured the attention of evolutionary biologists, who have long postulated that they might play a special role in adaptation and speciation. This fascination with inversions comes from the fact that there is virtually no crossing-over within the inversion in heterozygous individuals. Thus, these regions of the genome can harbor genetic differences that can differentiate populations or maintain species, even if the rest of the genome experiences gene flow. Indeed, whole genome sequencing studies are revealing that inversion polymorphisms are common between closely related species or populations adapted to divergent habitats or are associated with complex phenotypic polymorphisms within species. Despite a rich body of theory and these recent empirical findings, many fundamental questions about the evolution of inversions remain, including: (1) what are the phenotypic effects of inversions?; (2) are inversions under selection, and what types of selection act on inversions?; (3) what are the targets of selection within inversions?; (4) what are the ecological factors that cause selection on inversions?; and (5) did inversions spread because they captured existing, linked adaptive alleles? We will address these long-standing questions using the threespine stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) system, in which there are three chromosomal inversions that are highly differentiated between stickleback populations adapted to marine versus freshwater habitats across both the Pacific and Atlantic basins. Relative to other systems with inversion polymorphisms, stickleback offer a unique combination of advantages. In addition to well-developed genomic resources, we have the ability to study populations in the wild, do controlled genetic crosses and genetic manipulations in the laboratory, and measure selection on genotypes and phenotypes in semi-natural freshwater ponds. Using this system, we will address several outstanding questions about the evolution of inversions. In project 1, we will identify the phenotypic effects and ecological factors associated with the three inversions by combining association mapping in polymorphic freshwater populations with laboratory crosses on controlled marine genetic backgrounds. We will further use CRISPR/Cas9 technology to “flip” one of the inversions, enabling finer genetic mapping of the causative alleles and putative targets of selection within the inversions. In project 2, we will perform one of the few existing tests of selection on inversions using semi-natural freshwater ponds to determine whether and which type of selection acts on these inversions. In project 3, we will use a novel whole-genome sequencing approach to obtain phased sequences of marine and freshwater inversion haplotypes. This will allow us to determine what forms of selection act on inversions and the targets of selection within the inversions. We will further combine these data with simulations and a novel machine learning approach to test the prevailing hypothesis that inversions contain multiple locally adapted alleles, and further test whether the inversions spread because they captured these locally adapted alleles. Together, these complementary approaches will provide new insights into 100-year-old questions about the evolutionary forces that act on inversions as well as the genetic mechanisms by which inversions affect phenotypic evolution and adaptation.

Title: Ab-Initio Neural Quantum States
Abstract:
The research project aims to advance the description of many-body quantum systems from first principles through the development and application of advanced computational methods based on machine learning and neural network quantum states (NQS). The project is structured into four work packages (WPs), each addressing critical open problems in quantum many-body physics and chemistry.

WP1 tackles continuous-space quantum fluids and solids (helium, high-pressure hydrogen), whose strong correlations defy standard path-integral Monte Carlo and basic quantum chemistry. By deploying NQS with backflow neural architectures, the project aims to uncover superfluid or exotic phases previously inaccessible to conventional methods.

WP2 applies continuous-space NQS with carefully validated pseudopotentials to correlated electron materials such as cuprates/nickelates, fractional quantum Hall liquids, and moiré TMDs. These systems often exhibit intertwined phases (e.g. superconductivity coexisting with charge order, fractional Chern insulators), but theories have been limited by simplified lattice Hamiltonians or approximate approaches. Ab initio-style NQS offer a new perspective on doping-dependent instabilities and topological orders, bridging experimental observations with robust computational insights.

WP3 develops time-dependent NQS to capture real-time electronic and nuclear motion beyond the Born-Oppenheimer approximation. Many transformative phenomena, including ultrafast reactions and photoinduced phase transitions, hinge on strong electron-nuclear coupling where mean-field methods fail. By combining time-dependent variational Monte Carlo with neural wavefunctions, WP3 targets ultrafast regimes in both molecules and solids, potentially elucidating superconductivity in high-pressure hydrides or photoexcited phases in quantum materials.

WP4 establishes a “foundation model” for lattice fermions, eliminating the need to retrain wavefunctions from scratch for each set of parameters. Drawing on Transformer-based ensemble training, the network learns a universal wavefunction that spans different repulsions, dopings, extended interactions, and twisted boundary conditions. This framework drastically simplifies large-scale scans of extended Hubbard-type models, predicting phenomena such as stripe competition or d-wave pairing.

The four work packages are designed to strongly benefit from each other's methodological advances. For example, improved neural architectures developed in one WP can be directly applied to enhance accuracy or computational efficiency in others. Throughout the project, developments will be integrated into the established open-source software NetKet, widely adopted internationally. By openly releasing new computational tools, pretrained models, and detailed documentation, we aim to set a standard of reproducibility and accessibility in computational quantum many-body physics. This commitment aligns with ongoing efforts in Europe to consolidate leadership in the strategically critical area of scientific machine learning, positioning Switzerland at the forefront of developing advanced computational methodologies for quantum science.

Title: Learning Physics-Based Optimal Design of Cardiovascular MRI
Abstract:
Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance (CMR) has become a key imaging modality to diagnose, monitor and stratify patients suffering from a wide range of cardiovascular diseases. Besides the absence of ionizing radiation and the relative operator independence, the success of CMR has been due to the multitude of image contrasts allowing to encode soft tissue properties from the micro- to the macroscale including tissue composition, tissue perfusion, metabolism, mechanical strains and blood flow among many more. At the same time, the plethora of experimental parameters involved in contrast and spatiotemporal encoding, data acquisition, image reconstruction and parameter inference makes end-to-end optimization of CMR a very challenging task. Accordingly, joint optimization of CMR pulse sequences, data sampling, image reconstruction and parameter inference has not been attempted so far. Moreover, as ground truth is missing for any in-vivo imaging situation, rigorous optimal experimental design requires provision of realistic multi-scale in-silico input data which are not yet available. In consequence, the entities of encoding, sampling, reconstruction and inference are typically “optimized” independently using experimental and/or heuristic searches and are hence not guaranteed to be optimal in terms of information yield per unit time. Information-per-unit-time optimality is, however, of critical importance in view of improving the efficiency and accuracy of imaging and for quantifying the ultimate diagnostic sensitivity and specificity.

To address the challenges, a three-stage approach to learning (bio)physics-based optimal experimental CMR design is proposed using 1) Biophysical Simulation and Semantic Image Synthesis to provide large numbers and variations of paired and controllable in-silico ground truth and corresponding artificial CMR imaging data of desired complexity, 2) Parameter Inference and Disease Detection using Deep Networks based on conditional convolutional networks trained on the paired in-silico data and 3) Joint Optimization of Encoding, Sampling and Reconstruction towards optimal information-per-unit-time CMR. To this end, three work packages (WP) are defined as follows:

WP 1 - Biophysical Simulation and Semantic Image Synthesis
* In-vivo shape extraction and mesh generation using mode parameter learning
* Multi-scale biophysical modeling of cardiac function and aortic flow to generate foreground objects
* Background extraction from in-vivo data to train semantic background image synthesis
* Fusion of fore- and background and input into MR physics simulation to generate realistic in-silico images

WP 2 - Parameter Inference and Disease Detection using Deep Networks
* Biophysical model parameter variation and disease modeling to generate paired in-silico datasets
* Training of deep convolutional networks for parameter estimation and disease detection
* Network validation using in-silico MR simulations with different contrast, resolution, artifacts and noise
* Application of networks to process available pre-clinical and clinical in-vivo CMR data

WP 3 - Joint Optimization of Encoding, Sampling and Reconstruction 
* Formulation of encoding, sampling and reconstruction as stochastic meta-optimization problem
* Definition of constraints on encoding, spatiotemporal sampling to guarantee feasibility of CMR experiments
* Implementation of probabilistic relaxation to perform optimization   
* Integration of MR simulation and inference to perform joint optimization for optimal CMR protocol definition

The work outlined is based on documented experience and expertise in biophysical modeling and design of CMR pulse sequences, sampling and image reconstruction schemes, image processing including the development of variational and convolutional networks for image reconstruction, image classification and parameter inference. Close links to colleagues in radiology and cardiology ensure embedding of the proposed research into a clinical context including access to CMR patient data. To this end, the research is expected to enable significant practical advances of experimental and clinical CMR by providing scalable training databases for deep network classification/segmentation applications, quantification of diagnostic accuracy relative to ground truth, CMR system identification and methods optimization delivering gains in imaging speed and information encoding efficiency towards optimal CMR.
Keywords: Biophysical Modelling, Cardiovascular MRI, Machine Learning, Magnetic Resonance Imaging, Optimal Experimental Design, Undersampling

Title: Improving life quality with hypersomnolence using wearable devices and prescriptive intervention models
Abstract:
Central disorders of hypersomnolence (CDH) include narcolepsy, idiopathic hypersomnia (IH), and insufficient sleep syndrome (ISS). The common symptoms of the CDH group are events of sudden and irresistible urge to sleep. Patients with CDH experience sudden sleep attacks during activities such as driving, working, or socializing, which can increase the risk of accidents and injuries. The inability to stay awake or alert can also negatively impact patients' professional and social lives, leading to feelings of isolation and depression. Additionally, chronic sleepiness can increase the risk of obesity, diabetes, and other health problems, further complicating CDH patients' health.

Predicting sleep attacks in CDH patients is crucial for optimizing their care and preventing complications. By identifying when a patient is likely to experience a sleep attack, healthcare providers can recommend strategies to reduce the risk of accidents or injuries, such as avoiding activities that require sustained alertness or taking short naps during the day. Furthermore, identifying triggers for sleep attacks can help patients understand their condition better and adapt their lifestyles to manage their symptoms. 

Cataplexy episodes are temporary losses of voluntary muscle tone triggered by emotion and its are poorly understood. Cataplexy events  are currently impossible to predict. A method for predicting the increased chances of cataplexy would be a valuable addition for medical management regarding patient safety and quality of life.

Evidence from research in mice suggests that changes in ambient temperature can affect the severity and frequency of cataplectic episodes. A drop in skin temperature coincides with increased chance of a cataplexy episode, whereas ambient temperature warming markedly decreases cataplexy expression. This suggests that close monitoring of the relationship between ambient and body temperature of narcoleptic patients may afford prediction of imminent cataplexy. 

In our previous research, core body and wrist skin temperature monitoring has been shown to be a reliable indicator of changes in the sleep-wake cycle and physiological arousal. We also found limited evidence of associations between skin temperature and and cataplexy episodes in patients with narcolepsy. We previously demonstrated the capacity of a non-invasive, wearable device to accurately monitor the core body temperature in healthy subjects, using skin temperature, heart rate, and heat flux measurements.

The main goal of this project is to investigate the possibility of predicting the events of hypersomnolence, including episodes of cataplexy in narcolepsy and excessive sleepiness across patients with CDH, within a prediction horizon that permits taking measures to mitigate their destructive impact. We will use a non-invasive wearable device to measure distal skin temperature, predicted core body temperature, heart rate and variability, and movements. The collected data will be analyzed to identify intervariate and temporal patterns and correlations with events of hypersomnolence. Consequently, we will model the relationships between recorded signals and the events of hypersomnolence in patients using explainable machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques.

The second main objective of the project is to verify the feasibility of proactively mitigating the symptoms of hypersomnolence or cataplexy by means of targeted thermal manipulation. We will conduct a clinical study, whose input will be used to create a novel, prescriptive, data driven model based on the principles of reinforcement learning. Both the predictive and prescriptive models will be clinically validated.

he proposed study will contribute to a better understanding of thermoregulation in patients with CDH, and will have important implications for the management of this chronic sleep disorder, as well as for understanding of sleep mechanisms in healthy population.
Keywords: data science, hypersomnolence, machine learning, predictive analytics, sleep disorders, thermoregulation, wearable devices

Title: Embedding Local Quality Measures in Multimodal Biometric Recognition Systems
Abstract:
The objective of this project is to extend the existing state-of-the-art uni- and multi-modal biometric identity verification and identification methods to incorporate local quality measures. Addressing the issue of data quality is vital for automated multimodal biometric authentication systems that operate on biometric data, usually affected by external conditions and user behavior. Acquiring biometric data of sufficient quality and suitability and using it for reliable decision-making is of critical importance for automatic person recognition systems.
With an increase in identity fraud and the emphasis on security, there is a growing and urgent need to identify humans both locally and remotely on an automatic routine basis. The travel identity documents (e-passports) deployed on very large scale and the increasing use of information sensitive applications, such as e-government, e-commerce, e-banking, and e-health, has triggered a real need for reliable and widely acceptable automated control mechanisms for checking the identity of an individual. Biometrics technologies, using one or more of a person’s distinct behavioral or physiological characteristics, appears as a viable alternative to more traditional approaches such as identity badges, passwords and PIN codes.
Biometric person identity verification (biometric authentication) is a multimodal technology in its own right, with many potential applications. Every biometric modality has some limitations, e.g., a biometric system using single modality may not be able to acquire meaningful biometric data from a subset of users, for example visually handicapped or disabled people. One possible solution to these problems is the endemic use of multiple biometrics. Multimodal biometric systems hold the promise of flexible and robust person authentication avoiding person exclusion or discrimination. The demand for multimodal biometric systems is increasing dramatically, due to security pressures and the need of successful deployment of such systems worldwide. However, our recent studies in international frameworks (e.g. Biosecure Network of Excellence, COST 2101 "Biometrics for Identity Documents and Smart Cards" and COST 1106 "Integrating Biometrics and Forensics for the Digital Age") demonstrate how performance of biometric systems is heavily affected by the quality of biometric samples.
Like any other pattern recognition system, biometric recognition systems use either straightforward global features, which normally describe the whole biometric sample as a feature vector, or local features, which represent local parts (or points) within the sample, being more reliable regarding local variations. In modern local feature extraction techniques, some local feature descriptors are built to encode the relationship between the initially extracted local features within a local area in terms of some measures invariant to global transformations such as rotation, translation and scaling. Local feature descriptors are becoming increasingly popular in biometrics as a means for fast local comparisons.
The state-of-the-art automatic biometric recognition systems are still prone to produce errors. Therefore, one of the most important goals in biometrics research should be reducing such errors. Errors can however come from different sources such as noise and artifacts in biometric samples, non-uniqueness of taken samples, sensing conditions, sensor characteristics, not well chosen feature sets, and unreliable classifiers. These factors cause degradation in biometric sample quality and this would ultimately matter in the ability of the biometric systems for correct recognition. Therefore, the quality of samples can be taken into account in order to improve the recognition rates. That is why many works has been done over the past decade to introduce some quantitative measures of quality for biometric samples. Here, by quality measure, we basically mean the degree of being free from corrupting degradations. Local quality measures represent the quality of local parts within the biometric sample versus the global quality measure which is a measure for quality of the whole sample.
Incorporating local quality measures in biometric recognition systems based on local feature descriptors is a challenging research problem, which has not yet been studied widely. In general, in the present project we will address the problem of how to embed local quality measures in matching using modern local descriptors, in order to obtain better recognition rates, particularly for fingerprint, iris and face modalities. Then, we will investigate the novel approaches for multimodal biometric fusion integrating both local and global quality measures, taking into account the state-of-the-art models already available for incorporating global quality measures. 

Within the two year period of the project the scientific and technological objectives are addressed along the following innovative axes of research and development:
•New local quality measures for fingerprint, iris and face modalities and novel frameworks for embedding them in biometric recognition, especially in presence of modern local feature descriptors.

•New, universal data-driven models and processing techniques for multimodal robust biometric recognition systems integrating both local and global quality measures.

The present proposal results from the main research area of the EPFL-LIDIAP Speech Processing and Biometrics Group (GTPB) and is a logical continuation of research of the ongoing SNSF project “Embedding Quality and Reliability in Multimodal, Multiclassifier Biometric Recognition Systems”, foreseen in the proposal of that project. The present project also will continue fundamental research activities started within the European Science Foundation Action COST 2101 “Biometrics for Identity Documents and Smart Cards” chaired by Dr. Drygajlo, and is in accordance with new European Science Foundation Action COST IC1106 “Integrating Biometrics and Forensics for the Digital Age”, as well as the development activities of two Swiss companies (Covadis and IrisGuard in Geneva), the group participates in.
Keywords: biometrics, fingerprints, iris, multimodality, quality, recognition

Title: Toxicity assessment of New Psychoactive Substances by Artificial Intelligence and in-silico methods
Abstract:
The proposed project lies at the intersection of forensic toxicology, pharmacology and data science. It is a collaboration between Prof. W. Weinmann (Institute of Forensic Medicine Bern, University of Bern) and PD Dr. med. et. phil. F. Hammann (Institute of Clinical Pharmacology, Inselspital Bern) and combines the complementary experiences present in both groups. 
In 2005, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) started referring to drugs that were previously known as designer drugs, synthetic drugs or research chemicals, as New Psychoactive Substances (NPS). These substances, which are not legally controlled when they first occur on the drug market, mimic the effects of classic drugs of abuse by binding to the same biological target. Since their first occurrence, 1228 individual NPS have been reported to the UNODC from 141 countries and territories. Of these, 228 were first reported between Oct 2020 and Aug 2023. According to the UNODC, NPS are 'a matter of great concern and a threat to public health', due to the high number of intoxication reports with roughly ¼ resulting in death. It is well-established that this is a strong underestimation, due to underreporting and missed cases.
In Europe, the European Monitoring Centre for Drugs and Drug Addiction (EMCDDA – with whom we will collaborate on this project) compiles data from member countries to keep track of the continuous proliferation of new NPS. As in many countries the legislation explicitly specifies whether a chemical structure is controlled, NPS escape legal control when they first appear, since their structures are novel. Moreover, even when generic controls are in place (specifying a core structure with potential modifications as controlled substances), designers of NPS still use regulatory loopholes to come up with new compounds. The pace at which new compounds enter the market makes it difficult to keep up, both analytically and in terms of toxicological or pharmacological characterization. However, these data are a prerequisite for risk assessment in order to legally control and remove particularly toxic and harmful compounds from the recreational drug market. Unfortunately, such studies are time-consuming, expensive, and may require approval from the relevant authorities. 
This project aims at filling an important knowledge gap in the toxicological and pharmacological characterization of newly emerging (or even future - sometimes referred to as ‘prophetic’) NPS, following an in silico approach. Specific aims of this project proposal are: (1) to generate Machine Learning (ML) models to predict toxicological and pharmacological characteristics for novel analogs of four NPS classes (Synthetic Cannabinoid Receptor Agonists; SCRAs, opioids, tryptamines, and phenethylamines) by integrating literature and experimental data of existing NPS as a training dataset. Prospective validation with a set of in-house synthesized novel NPS will also be carried out; (2) to determine key structural properties influencing the toxicity of an NPS in order to heuristically evaluate novel compounds prior to generating experimental data. 
The results from this project will be of extraordinary benefit to NPS risk assessment and will thus assist the relevant decision-makers to prioritize those compounds that are of highest concern. In addition, it will allow to define in a cost-effective and timely manner appropriate measures for controlling NPS, with the aim of reducing morbidity and mortality. Importantly, the prediction of toxicological and pharmacological features will not only be beneficial to forensic toxicology (e.g. in the interpretation of post-mortem cases, or drug-assisted criminal assault), it also conforms to the 3R principle, removing (or greatly reducing) the need for animal experimentation.

Title: The risks and benefits of integrating emotions in end of life communication
Abstract:
BACKGROUND AND RATIONALE
There is growing evidence that patient-physician relationships benefit from physicians who develop a degree of emotional closeness to their patients. These benefits are seen in improved outcomes for the patient, the health system, and the physician. However, displaying emotional closeness can be conflicting for physicians, as it requires a degree of personal involvement that has long been taboo in medicine. At the end of life in particular, the medical encounter is laden with emotions; patients are confronted with their mortality and physicians must find the right time and the appropriate words for these discussions. Traditionally, training in these skills was not part of medical education and it has only been in the past two decades that significant progress has been made in upskilling health professionals in end of life communication. Despite these efforts, studies show that families and patients continue to be informed late in the disease progression, and that even after these discussions they remain misinformed. Although emotions and the inner life of the physician have been known to influence communication and the doctor-patient relationship, their effect remains largely unexplored. The reason is largely because decision-making and the physicians’ role in medicine has traditionally been seen to require objectivity. Moreover, despite a shift in training efforts to teach empathy and patient-centred models to younger physicians, the workplace exposes them to the traditional practice of emotional distance, which is often incompatible with their training. How physicians reconcile these two seemingly incompatible worlds across their career remains unknown.

OVERALL OBJECTIVES AND AIMS
In the proposed projects for the Eccellenza Professorial Fellowship, the overarching aim is to explore the role of emotions in medical practice. The main focus is on understanding how are physician emotions present in everyday practice, how are they managed, what is their impact on physician’s wellbeing and on patient care, what do families expect, and whether emotions and communication can be influenced by self-reflection. These questions will be answered in general, but also in the end of life context. The proposed projects are divided into five themes: 1) emotions and the physician, 2) physician emotions and public expectations, 3) physician emotions and experiences of bereaved family members, 4) how emotions are used in current practice, and 5) the place of emotions in medical education.

METHODOLOGY
The main component of the research is a cohort study in which a nested randomised clinical trial will test whether a self-reflection intervention or an anxiety-reducing intervention can affect the wellbeing of physicians, and whether these interventions can impact communication with patients and the physicians’ comfort with communication. Within the cohort, longitudinal changes in burnout, emotional intelligence and comfort about end of life discussions will be tracked during 3 years. To further explore the proposed areas, mixed methods analyses, and qualitative and quantitative single designs will be employed to analyse data from in-depth interviews, cross-sectional surveys, and factorial surveys. The target participant groups will reflect the complexity of roles and actors involved at the end of life: physicians, patients, families, the public, other clinicians, and educators.

EXPECTED RESULTS AND IMPACT
The main significance of this study lies in its timeliness and in its comprehensive approach to a complex subject in medicine. It responds to current and future challenges of caring for an ageing population at a time when medical developments can prolong life almost indefinitely, and where new technologies such as artificial intelligence provide increasingly accurate diagnoses and thus place a greater emphasis on the physician’s ability to communicate with their patients. Ultimately, the proposed projects will provide a deeper understanding of the risks and benefits associated with integrating emotions in the practice of medicine, in order to facilitate end of life discussions with patients and their family members.

Title: Inferring the molecular evolutionary history with multiple-character indels: from theory to practice
Abstract:
Insertions and deletions (indels) are the second most important source of natural genomic variation. Accurate inferences of the evolutionary indel histories may be used to track new variants during epidemics, study effects on protein structure and function, for tumour classification, and prediction of drug targets, and as biomarkers in general.  However, indel variation in genomes remains understudied and the evolutionary signal from indels is not explored due to a lack of tools that can infer indel dynamics. Proper indel handling requires comparative sequence analyses and realistic models of indel evolution to be included in phylogenetic analyses. 
Multiple sequence alignments (MSAs), trees and ancestral sequences are routinely inferred from genomic sequences but  independently, one step after another, and typically without modelling indel evolution. Yet, these objects are interconnected and decisions such as model choice and simplifications made at each step lead to buildup of systematic biases. Ideally, MSAs, trees, and character & indel histories should be inferred jointly.  A recent breakthrough in our team enables such joint inferences using a likelihood-based method based on the Poisson indel process (PIP). PIP is a modification of the classical TKF91 that allows us to compute marginal likelihoods in linear time, but both models allow only single-site indel events. Even though MSAs inferred with PIP display realistic indel patterns and lengths, the inferred MSAs tend to be more fragmented. Building upon this work, we propose to develop a new maximum likelihood method for scalable joint inference of the complete evolutionary history (MSA-tree-ancestors) under a more realistic model that allows multiple residue insertions and deletions (aka. long indels). In order for this to be feasible under long indel models, we will not marginalise over ancestral states during the heuristic search, but rather use likelihoods computed for fixed ancestors, so that the likelihood computation remains linear. To further speed up the inference we will use parallelization, rapid homology pre-detection with fast Fourier transform, parsimony based likelihood prediction, and predicting promising moves in the joint MSA-tree space with novel supervised machine-learning approaches. We will provide open source code and multi-platform binaries. Our method will help those scientists that require MSA, tree and ancestral state inferences for their research, with diverse applications in different domains - from biomedicine and protein engineering to forensics and ecology. In particular, we will deploy the ensemble of our methods for joint inferences with indels (both short and long) on real data: SARS-CoV-2, Swiss HIV Cohort and visual proteins. This will allow, for example, to monitor new indel variants in SARS-COV-2 or to to detect new drug resistant HIV variants and to inform antibody design.
This project will showcase the power of our approaches in applications to real data and allow us to build close collaborations with biomedical researchers. Our method can be embedded in bioinformatic pipelines used in genomic centres, as well as within other sophisticated methods, such as gene-species tree reconciliation or structure prediction by AlphaFold.
Keywords: ancestral sequence, indel model, joint estimation, maximum likelihood inference, molecular evolution, phylogeny, sequence alignment

Title: Novel Machine Learning Approaches for Data from the Intensive Care Unit
Abstract:
Critically ill patients require treatment in specialized settings of intensive care units (ICU) to enable continuous recording of organ function parameters for early recognition of abnormal values, consecutive rapid patient assessment and appropriate interventions. At any given point, a clinician will try to assess if a patient’s condition is improving or deteriorating. The ICU of a hospital is therefore a data-rich environment with many parameters and many longitudinal observations. Machine Learning techniques excel in domains where one needs to describe and control a complex phenomenon and has many observations available. This motivates the use of Machine Learning to support physicians in better and faster understanding the condition of a patient and to support decision making. 

Our research is structured into three broad aims. In Aim 1 we will make data accessible for computational research. This may seem trivial at first sight, but it is a crucial first step that needs to be completed carefully to make use of data from medical facilities that is stored but so far unavailable for research. The size and complexity of the data requires that the information is preprocessed, integrated and stored in formats that computational scientists can take full advantage of. In particular, we will assess different ways to encode, store and access large intensive care datasets. Also, we intend to develop a strategy to transform databases recorded from different sources into a standard format wherever feasible. Subsequent analyses and models in this proposal will rely on standardized data and efficient access mechanisms.

Aim 2 is to develop the necessary methodology and software to predict organ dysfunction defined by specific medical endpoints. We initially intend to focus on three organ systems: circulatory, respiratory, and renal. The goal is to design an early-warning system which can identify patients in need of intervention or additional monitoring with Machine Learning and implement a software prototype for use at ICU of the University Hospital Bern. For this we will use data from ˜55,000 patients from the ICU of University Hospital Bern as well as other publicly available datasets to train, tune and evaluate state-of-the-art Machine Learning methods. We will then develop novel statistical and machine learning approaches to to deal with missing data, multiple time scales, many outliers and other challenges. 

The availability of observational medical data from intensive care units opens the door for retrospective analyses with Machine Learning techniques with the aim to develop decision support systems. Thus, Aim 3 is farther reaching, and intends to advance the state of Machine Learning research in healthcare. This aim considers retrospective uses of large observational datasets, like the one collected  at the University Hospital Bern ICU. Examples are learning abstract representations of patients based on their health data, and predicting treatment policies based on the actions and expertise of many physicians as recorded in this data. This research aims to assist the practice of healthcare with evidence-based support systems powered by Machine Learning, which draw on large quantities and specifics of healthcare data not easily processable by clinicians.
Keywords: Deep Learning, Intensive Care Unit, Machine Learning, Medical Data, Time Series Analysis

Title: Deep Social Force with Big Data
Abstract:
"Understanding humans is the hardest problem for autonomous vehicles"
[Perceptive Automata].
The goal of this project is to model pedestrian behavior in more detail.
So far, pedestrian simulations do not model people avoiding each other
on the right in continental, western Europe which limits any application of
pedestrian simulations to counter flows: people passing by each other in
corridors.
This project brings together the classic field of transportation modeling and
new methods from deep learning, particularly deep neural networks and
differentiable simulations to unlock insights in big data. However,
this project will not do a sweeping black-box replacement of the entire model.
The goal is to generalize the Social Force model [Helbing 1995]
with deep learning while keeping its interpretable nature.
We propose to describe interaction potentials by arbitrary function
approximators in the form of deep neural networks. In this form, Social Forces are
derived from gradients of the neural network using automatic differentiation
with efficient BackProp [LeCun 2012]. The same automatic differentiation
implementation is used to compute the gradients of these potentials.
The more expressive model combined with a more powerful learning technique
will allow to infer the model parameters from larger amounts of data. It will
still be possible to plot these potentials and to interpret their shapes.
Moving from parametric descriptions to neural networks requires more efficient
methods to infer the much higher dimensional parameters. We propose a new
pedestrian model, Deep Social Force, that is tuned in a differentiable
simulation and use Stochastic Gradient Descent [Bottou 2010] to train
the networks on large datasets.
Keywords: Big Data, Deep Learning, Social Force, differentiable simulation, interpretability
