Title: Strategy Selection
Abstract:
The thesis that people possess a repertoire of decision strategies to choose from has been formulated in many areas, including inferential decision making, choice, social interactions, mathematical skill, categorization, and question answering. If one adopts this view, a major problem is then to determine how people select from these strategies to solve given tasks—the strategy selection problem. This problem represents a major theoretical challenge in the cognitive and decision sciences, but it is also a stumbling block for theories in other disciplines, including, for instance, economics, biology, and machine learning, where the problem presents itself in terms of the selection of actions, behaviors, algorithms, operators, routines, and production rules. 
In this project, I contribute to solving the strategy selection puzzle by extending an existing quantitative model of strategy selection. This model predicts how selection emerges through the interplay among the strategies, the workings of basic cognitive capacities, such as memory, and the structure of the environment in which we humans live. Specifically, in Project 1, I extend the memory component of Marewski and Schooler’s (2011) model of strategy selection to quantitatively predicting people’s detailed declarative knowledge of attributes of real-world objects (e.g., detailed knowledge about companies). This extension is necessary to tackle the strategy selection problem for a number of classic models of decision making, including noncompensatory lexicographic and compensatory (e.g., weighted-additive) integration strategies, all of which operate on such knowledge (i.e., by using the knowledge to make decisions). In Project 2, I use the extended memory model to model these knowledge-based strategies’ cognitive niches, that is, the range of situations in which the strategies are applicable. A strategy’s applicability depends, for instance, on whether sufficient knowledge about an object’s attributes can be retrieved. To further model how the interplay of the environment and cognitive capacities leads people to learn to prefer one applicable strategy over another, in Project 3, I integrate the extended model with another existing model of strategy selection, namely Rieskamp and Otto’s (2006) reinforcement learning model. 
Tackling Projects 1-3 will (a) help to address the strategy selection problem for classic decision strategies, providing a refined theory that allows quantitatively predicting which of these strategies people may rely on when making inferences about unknown states of the world. Along the way, I provide a theoretically-grounded method to (b) populate models of memory with realistic, detailed declarative knowledge about real-world objects as well as (c) a theory that allows remedying the experimental decision scientist’s methodological problem of identifying which of various plausible decision strategies a person may use in a decision task. Finally, by integrating the extended memory model and Rieskamp and Otto’s (2006) model, I (d) contribute to building integrative, encompassing models of cognition (cf. Anderson et al., 2004; Newell, 1990).

Title: Motion Models for Monocular People Tracking
Abstract:
Modeling the human body and its movements is one of the most difficult and challenging problems in Computer Vision. Today, there is great interest in
capturing complex motions solely by analyzing video sequences. Potential applications include athletic training, surveillance, entertainment, and electronic publishing.

Most early approaches to monocular people tracking, including some we developed earlier under SNSF funding, involved recursive frame-to-frame tracking and were found to be brittle, due, among other things, to distractions and occlusions from other people or scene objects. Since then the focus has shifted to ``tracking by detection,'' which involves detecting people more or less independently in every frame followed by linking detection across frames, which is much more robust to algorithmic failures in isolated frames.

In earlier work, we showed that, in a multi-camera context, this process could be formulated as an Integer Programming (IP) problem whose solution is a set of trajectories. These trajectories are therefore found as the global optimum of a well defined convex objective function, which makes the process both robust and fast. Since single camera solutions are easier to deploy and therefore more attractive, we have been exploring for the past year how such an approach can be made to work monocularly.

The framework we propose includes two main steps. First, we detect people and their poses in individual frames while taking occlusions into account. Occlusion are handled by an iterative scheme that selects the most likely people detections given what is known about potential occlusions produced by other people, recomputes the likely occluded areas, and iterates. Second, we select among all these detections those that are most consistent across time, according to an appropriate motion model.

During the first phase of this project, we have focused on the first step. We have also run some preliminary experiments involving the second step and will now turn them into a solid well-formalized algorithm during the proposed project continuation. This will involve

 - casting the linking of detected poses at individual time steps into an IP framework,

 - developing algorithms for computing the transition probabilities between poses so as to reliably obtain the desired result when solving the IP problem,

 - developing feedback mechanism from the second step to the first to correct potential mistakes.

In essence, in our earlier work, ambiguities were resolved by using multiple cameras. Here, we intend to show that they can be handled just as well by enforcing continuity on the detected poses. We will endeavor to show that it yields improved performance and results in a truly automated system that can handle generic behaviors in real world environments using videos acquired using a single camera and in potentially adverse conditions.

Title: Closing the loop from functional reorganization of the peri-infarct cortex to recovery of skilled motor functions after stroke
Abstract:
Once a stroke occurs victims suffer from lifelong disabilities including the impairment of speech, vision and motor control. No pharmacological therapy is currently available to stimulate the restoration of function. However, forms of spontaneous recovery exist even without a therapeutic intervention, while the underlying principles of increased plasticity promoting map-shifts and rewiring of neuronal circuitry are not well understood. The brain region adjacent to stroke damage- the penumbra zone – has been shown to be critical for stroke rehabilitation. Thus, understanding the reorganization of the peri-infarct tissue around small cortical strokes and its contribution to functional recovery may inaugurate the development of new treatments and improve rehabilitative strategies. In the project proposed here, we plan to establish a mouse model where the rewiring of neuronal networks and individual neurons in the peri-infarct area can be studied over time within the same mouse during the phase of motor recovery after ischemia. We will use a combination of optogenetics and calcium imaging in the behaving animal, performing skilled motor tasks to study re-mapping and reorganization processes after a photothrombotic stroke in the motor cortex on a macroanatomical and cellular resolution level. Using Deep Learning computer algorithms to explore causal relationships between neuronal rewiring- from cellular resolution to network level - and the behavioral phenotype we hope to reveal the properties of neurons, which reconnect, recode and reorganize compared to those neurons just maintaining their old function. In the last step, we will validate our model and test how forms of sensorimotor training enhance spontaneous rewiring in the per-infarct cortex by understanding the effect of intensive motor rehabilitation on a cellular resolution level. 

In summary, this proposal aims at revealing fundamental principles of neuronal recoding and rewiring as intrinsic repair mechanisms of the brain to react to CNS injuries such as stroke. Understanding causal relationships between neuronal rewiring and recovery of distinct sensorimotor features opens up new possibilities for novel targeted therapeutic approaches or optimized rehabilitative strategies for patients suffering from stroke.
Keywords: neuronal rewiring and recoding, sensorimotor recovery, stroke

Title: LMol: Biomolecular language models for protein design
Abstract:
What is the relationship between the structure, dynamics and function of proteins? Can we computationally predict and tailor new functions into proteins? These are some of the fundamental questions that I plan to address in my academic research program at the Faculty of Biomedical Sciences, Università della Svizzera Italiana (USI), Lugano, Switzerland.
Proteins are remarkable biomolecular nano-machines that perform most essential processes needed for the survival of living organisms. The objective of protein design is to harness this powerful framework in order to engineer new functions into proteins for biomedical and biotechnological applications. Although computational approaches have permitted designing a wide range of new protein structures, they still fail at changing the function of proteins. Currently, no simple physical model permits the modeling of all the necessary disorder, flexibility and dynamics, required for function. The dramatic growth of structural databases for biomolecules would allow a data-driven approach to this problem. Therefore, I propose a Deep Learning project that will shed light and ultimately help narrow the gaps in our theoretical understanding of the functional relationships between sequence, structure and dynamics in proteins. In an innovative approach, I intend to tackle the design process of functional proteins as a language-modeling problem. First, a biomolecular language model will be developed for predicting and designing the interaction networks observed in protein fragments. Then, this approach will be extended for modeling the interactions between proteins and ligands. Finally, these biomolecular language models will be tested for the design of new biosensors from the family of ubiquitous sensory modules (PAS domains). My approach is orthogonal to methods currently used in protein design and will create a new methodology for the design of proteins with distinct catalytic, pharmaceutical and sensing properties. This will have a significant impact on the design of, e.g., antibody therapeutics, new enzymes and molecular probes.
Keywords: Biomolecular language models, Convolutional Neural Networks, Deep Learning, Graph Neural Networks, Graph theory, Protein design, Small molecules biosensor

Title: METATHESIS: Modelling pathological gait with machine learning for treatment selection support
Abstract:
Gait disorders have a large prevalence and induce a dramatic burden on healthcare and are widely spread within the patient population ranging from the elderly and adults (e.g., stroke (CVA), myopathies, multiple sclerosis (MS)) to children with Cerebral Palsy (CP). Gold standard practices for functional diagnosis and treatment selection require analysis by highly specialized personnel with deep technical knowledge and have high costs. The clinical experts assess the gait function by means of instrumented gait analysis, referred as Clinical Gait Analysis (CGA). These assessments are complemented by a clinical evaluation of the neuromusculoskeletal impairments. However, an accurate personalized functional diagnosis, i.e., identifying causes of gait deviations in the neuromusculoskeletal impairments, is difficult to establish and very often several treatment plans may be eligible for reducing motor disabilities. Selecting the most appropriate plan is a complex non-standardized endeavor. Different medical teams can use different decision-making processes, based on the clinical assessment of the patient and, to a large extent, on the physicians' knowledge and expertise, often leading to subjective decisions. Foreseeing the effect that a treatment will have on a patient's locomotion is quite challenging. As a result, outcomes are not always as desired.

CP is the most frequent motor disability of childhood, affecting 17 million worldwide. The estimated healthcare and socioeconomic lifetime costs for CP subjects are between 800,000 and 860,000. The high treatment costs, the irreversibility of some interventions, and the large social impact of the treatment on the life of the patients and their caregivers motivates additional investments in the process of clinical decision making; 25% of CP patients whose treatment followed the CGA-based surgical recommendations, experience a negative outcome and only 37% of the cases have a clinically meaningful improvement over natural progression. Additionally, over the last decades, the proportion of positive outcomes of orthopedic surgeries that improve gait function in children with CP has stagnated. In this project, we will tackle heads on the challenges that the treatment of gait disorders has, starting with applying it to CP.

It is therefore the objective of the project to: significantly improve the current medical practice and the treatment outcomes for gait disorders through patient tailored diagnosis and treatment by significantly reducing the number of cases that lead to a negative treatment outcome. To do so we will support clinicians in: (i) developing a structured and holistic understanding of a patient's condition, and in (ii) selecting the optimal treatment for any patient.

We will address these objectives by developing the digital patient twin to deliver accurate, robust, and explainable gait modeling and treatment selection support. Central to the development of the digital patient twin will be the use of machine learning and in particular generative learning and reinforcement learning algorithms and models. We will train these models on patient data from the clinical partner which include, information on neuromusculoskeletal impairments, diagnosis, gait data (e.g., kinematics, kinetics, EMG, video), medical imaging and notes, information on administered treatments and patient Follow-up.

Digital patient twin: We will develop patient-tailored models to support treatment selection. The overarching approach that we will follow is given a patient's description, namely clinical information as well as musculo-skeletal information, the learned models should reproduce the patient's gait as this is captured by the kinematics curves. By modifying different parameters describing the patient, e.g., muscle lengthening and stiffness, we will be simulating the effect of different treatments and the trained models will output the expected kinematics. 

We will inform and constrain the learning models using domain knowledge. We will consider generative models with latent variables such as Variational Autoencoders. Parts of the latent space can be assigned specific semantics corresponding to factors, e.g., neuromusculoskeletal impairments, that are known to relate to gait deviations. The decoders will incorporate explicit biomechanical models generating gaits that are consistent with physics and human physiology. In the reinforcement learning approaches we will use biomechanical models/simulators to learn patient-specific controllers/policies that accurately reproduce a patient's gait. The learned policies will produce only physics- and physiology-consistent gait. Such models allow us to explore the effect of different treatments by modifying the patient's properties. By explicitly incorporating domain knowledge the learned models will be to a significant extent understandable since they will carry explicit semantics. We will provide further explanations of the models' decisions using saliency that indicate which part of the input data are responsible for the model's decision.

The successful achievement of the targeted results of METATHESIS will have a very significant practical impact: to help improve the mobility of several million significantly disabled people, whose overall quality of life will also be considerably improved. Preserving and improving their mobility is a major challenge that our society is facing and treatment outcomes have not improved since several decades. In METATHESIS we aim to deliver innovative tools to address this necessity, providing clinicians with treatment selection support based on explainable gait modeling.

Title: New approaches to cognition: Developing and testing a multifaceted view on similarity
Abstract:
Current state of research and project motivation. Similarity lies at the heart of many higher-order cognitive processes such as categorization and judgments. To date, however, the mechanisms by which people represent similarity in judgment and decision making are not well understood. Past research has traditionally followed the Euclidean view on similarity, assuming that the similarity of objects is a function of their differences on the features which constitute the objects. However, the Euclidean similarity has several limitations, including that it treats features separately and is insensitive to correlations among features, whereas people can be sensitive to correlated features. Therefore, further research is needed to uncover how people represent similarity. 

Main research question and aim. I argue for a multifaceted view on similarity, which emphasizes that the psychology of similarity comprises multiple useful cognitive similarity mechanisms beyond the Euclidean similarity. My thesis will develop the multifaceted view in four connected theoretical and empirical lines of work, aiming at understanding the processes of psychological similarity representation in higher-order cognition. 

Projects. Project 1 reviews the success and limitations of the Euclidean similarity in cognitive psychology and how machine learning can enrich current psychological theories. In the remaining three projects, I empirically test new hypotheses derived from the multifaceted view on similarity. Project 2 tests how people adapt the way they represent similarity to the current situation. Project 3 tests if an alternative similarity representation can explain a prominent judgmental bias, the conjunction fallacy. Project 4 tests how people represent similarity in real image classification by combining machine learning and cognitive modeling on big data.

Method, expected results, and impact. I use an open-science, open-data, open-code approach. I combine experimental data with inferential Bayesian statistics and computational cognitive modeling, relying on my modeling expertise from my Master’s thesis. My thesis will shed light on human learning, adaptation, and representation of similarity and impact the theories in cognitive and decision sciences and general psychology that are based on psychological similarity. The Ph.D. will result in four publications in international peer-reviewed outlets in the fields of cognitive and decision sciences, general psychology, and machine learning.
Keywords: categorization, cognitive and decision science, cognitive modeling, cognitive psychology, distance, exemplar models, formal models, machine learning, metrics, similarity

Title: Modulating valuation with executive control training: efficacy, neural bases and moderators
Abstract:
1.1 Background 
 
The repeated control of motor responses to stimuli in Go/NoGo (GNG) and Cue-Approach Training (CAT) executive control tasks has been reported to reduce the trained stimuli valuation and to influence behaviors toward them. The real-world efficacy, plastic brain mechanisms and moderators of these interventions remain, however, largely unknown. Our project addresses these questions, with the overarching aim of developing solid, neurophysiologically-informed, and evidence-based interventions to reduce unhealthy food (over)consumption, and in turn the prevalence and severity of related pathologies. 
 
1.2. Working hypotheses 
 
Work-package A: Efficacy of the interventions: We will use stringently controlled intervention trials to test the hypotheses that GNG and CAT trainings i) reduce the valuation of sugary drinks (impacting the motivational more than the hedonic reward component); ii) reduce their real-world consumption; iii) act synergistically and show persisting effects; and iv) the reduction in sugary drinks’ valuation mediates the reduction in consumption. 
 
Work-package B: Neural bases of the interventions: Data-driven multivariate ‘electrical neuroimaging’ analyses of event-related potentials to the trained sugary drink cues and of the underlying brain sources measured before vs. after the interventions will be used to test a series of hypotheses regarding the mechanisms of action by which GNG and CAT trainings reshape the spatiotemporal functional architecture of the cues processing, notably along the attentional, motor and reward pathways.  
 
Work-package C: Moderators of responsiveness to the interventions: We will test the hypotheses that affective learning biases toward sign-tracking in Pavlovian conditioning and/or model-free learning in reinforcement learning moderate the reductions in the cues’ incentive salience induced by the GNG and CAT interventions. We will also test the moderating role of baseline electrical neuroimaging responses to the cues on the responsiveness to the interventions with ERP topographic analyses of covariance. 
 
1.3 Experimental design and methods 
 
We will test these hypotheses with a series of confirmatory, adequately powered, double-blind randomized trials involving 15 days of practice of personalized gamified training with sugary drinks- GNG and/or CAT tasks. Mechanistic control groups, in which our posited mechanism of action, the bias in the stimulus-response contingencies, is neutralized, will allow us to conclude its causal role in the drink-cue devaluation and to control for participants’ expectations of the effects of the interventions.  
 
1.4 Expected value of the proposed project 
 
This translational project is innovative and with broad impact for the following reasons. First, it addresses original hypotheses regarding neurocognitive mechanisms of two main types of response training and on the involvement of affective learning phenotypes and baseline functional activity in these interventions. These investigations will not only reveal the mechanisms underlying response training but also link the response training literature with the broader frameworks of reward-driven learning and behaviors. Second, the project uses stringent designs to address the major health-related challenge of unhealthy eating, with a focus on the efficacy of the interventions on real-world consumption outcomes. Moreover, it uses app-based gamified intervention software immediately distributable to improve eating at the population level or in clinics. Finally, all studies will follow the Registered Report publication route, ensuring the best scientific practice and open science.
Keywords: Brain plasticity, Event-related potentials, Executive control, Response training, Reward system, Source estimation

Title: Together with climate change challenges: firms’ resource acquisition strategies for entering policy-driven nascent industries
Abstract:
Addressing climate change presents both challenges and opportunities for firms, particularly in hard-to-abate industries such as steel and energy, where regulatory pressures and societal expectations drive significant transformations and the emergence of new industries. To enter these nascent industries, firms need to develop and acquire technological capabilities and complementary assets as essential pre-entry resources. These resource acquisition strategies will influence firms’ market entry direction and long-term survival in uncertain and highly regulated contexts. While prior research has explored resource acquisition in market- and technology-driven nascent industries, the dynamics of policy-driven nascent industries—emerging in response to regulatory frameworks and unmet public needs—remain underexplored.

To bridge this gap, this study explores how firms acquire relevant resources during the emergence of policy-driven industries by taking the emerging green steel industry as the research context. Specifically, I will empirically investigate how firms choose resource acquisition strategies (dependent variables: internal development, alliances, acquisitions) to acquire technological capabilities and complementary assets (independent variables). I will also examine contingency factors such as institutional environments and bottleneck resources (e.g., public funding support) that shape these relationships.

To achieve the goals, I will use advanced natural language processing (NLP) techniques to extract measurements from large-scale textual data, including corporate sustainability reports, press releases, and publicly available datasets such as the Green Steel Tracker. The hypotheses will be tested using panel regression models. 

Theoretically, the study will contribute to the resource acquisition and market entry literature by uncovering the unique dynamics of policy-driven nascent industries, where regulatory frameworks and public unmet needs play pivotal roles. Practically, it will provide actionable insights for firms and policymakers on facilitating resource acquisition for market entry and industrial transitions to address climate change challenges. By addressing this gap, the project will contribute to academic research and support real-world efforts to tackle grand challenges like climate change.
Keywords: climate change, market entry, natural language processing, policy-driven nascent industry, resource acquisition

Title: Generative Symbiotic Networks: a novel deep learning approach for biological and artificial vision
Abstract:
In recent years, Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have revolutionized artificial vision systems and shown great promise as a modelling framework for information processing in the brain. However, although DNNs were originally inspired by neuroscience, today’s high-performance neural networks are optimized towards engineering goals, leading to an increasing gap between DNNs and their biological counterparts. This limits them as neuroscientific models (Storrs et al., 2020) and may contribute to their limited robustness in real-world applications (Eykholt et al., 2018). To solve these issues, we propose to bring biological inspiration back into DNN designs by integrating two large-scale aspects of human vision: a dual-stream recurrent architecture mirroring the dorsal and ventral streams, and active information sampling via eye-movements. 

These two aspects, largely overlooked by the machine learning community, are central to human vision. First, the brain’s highly recurrent architecture allows visual processing to extend in time, resulting in increasingly accurate analyses of what is currently seen (Kietzmann, Spoerer, et al., 2019; Spoerer et al., 2020). This recurrent connectivity is divided into two streams, ventral and dorsal, allowing for a division of labor. The ventral stream specializes in object identification, whereas the dorsal stream focuses on spatial aspects of vision, including shifts in attention and eye movements. Second, human vision is based on sequences of inputs actively sampled by eye movements, and information from successive eye fixations is integrated through recurrent processing. Yet, the majority of contemporary DNNs process the whole image at once using feedforward architectures that allow only for a single sweep of information. Incorporating both a recurrent dual-stream architecture and eye-movements therefore promises to be transformative in how we model biological vision, while at the same time helping to create safer real-world AI applications.

To this end, we propose Generative Symbiotic Networks (GSNs), a new kind of DNN that integrates multiple networks into a coherent learning system. This will allow GSNs not only to integrate information over time via recurrent connections but also to sample new evidence in light of the current computational process via simulated eye-movements. To optimize the sampling process for the extraction of relevant information, GSNs furthermore make explicit use of a division of labor, akin to the ventral and dorsal streams. This yields two specialized, yet symbiotic, sub-networks that jointly solve the task of vision. Through these innovations, GSNs mark a turning point in the development of contemporary DNNs, by returning to biology while embracing recent developments in the efficient training of large-scale DNNs. In particular, GSNs combine optimization techniques from deep and reinforcement learning. We will develop methods to train GSNs on large-scale image recognition, allowing both for comparisons with human behavior and neuroimaging, and deployment in real-world AI systems.

To test the ability of GSNs to serve as models of the brain, we will compare them against human eye movements, and assess whether their internal representations mirror effects found in human neuroimaging data. GSNs will furthermore enable us to model how their two streams co-adapt during development and thereby add to the ongoing nature vs nurture debate about the origins of neural selectivity in the visual system. On the artificial vision side, we will test to what extent GSNs lead to more robust AI systems, whether they rely on robust image features and whether they can better withstand adversarial attacks.

Title: A Multidimensional Free-Running Framework for Comprehensive and Quantitative High-Resolution Magnetic Resonance Imaging of the Human Heart and its Vessels
Abstract:
Background and Rationale: 

The SNF generously funded our research project 173129 "A Paradigm Shift in Magnetic Resonance Imaging of the Heart: 5D Imaging - Sample Now and Ask Questions Later" where we developed a new cardiac MRI paradigm in which ECG lead placement, complex scan planning, repeated breath-holding, and time in-efficient acquisitions have been replaced by a free-running image acquisition, where more anatomical and functional information from the heart is collected per unit time than was previously possible, where one single mouse click suffices to initiate a scan, and where a fully flexible and retrospective 3D interrogation of the heart’s anatomy and function is enabled. FRF is so general in its formalism and modular in its design, that it now provides us with the opportunity to leverage its untapped potential in multiple ways: We can now start exploring its boundaries for improved resolution, we can begin to extend its capabilities with new contrast mechanisms for quantitative tissue characterization, and we are in a position to add flow measurements to expand the perimeter of FRF and to research its opportunities. This will critically be supported by the new PilotTone (PT) hardware that surveys physiological motion at a very high frequency conducive of further improved motion suppression as part of FRF.

Overall Objectives: 

To build on the unique capabilities of FRF and extend it with new hardware and software in the pursuit of providing more detailed, better, and new quantitative information about the heart, its anatomy, its function, its tissues, and its vessels. We will rigorously and mechanistically research the boundaries and opportunities of the thus-extended paradigm, and translate it to the clinical setting together with Prof. Jürg Schwitter's team for validation and gold standard comparisons.

Specific Aims & Methods to be Used: 

We will build on infrastructure, tools, and methods available to us and also developed during the original grant period (173129), on new strategic hirings of a mathematician (Dr. Aurélien Bustin), on new collaborations entered in the domain of artificial intelligence (Dr. Jonas Ricardi), and on a tried and tested interdisciplinary collaboration with Prof. Schwitter and his team at CHUV. Both on the acquisition and reconstruction side, new and critical innovation will be added in support of the overall objectives. On the acquisition side, we will extend our free-running pulse sequence with new concepts in support of improved resolution (Aim 1), added contrast mechanisms (Aim 2), and sensitive flow measurements (Aim 3) that add extra dimensions to FRF. Logically, and on the reconstruction side, we will extend the capabilities of our existing reconstruction engine to accommodate this new dimensionality, and we will augment it with new concepts to better constrain motion and improve resolution. By leveraging new hardware and software opportunities available at CHUV, we will rigorously research, translate, and validate this new free-running concept using the following Specific Aims: 

Specific Aim 1: Equip FRF with advanced acquisition and reconstruction methodology to push its resolution boundaries and test the hypothesis that the visibility of anatomical details is significantly improved in vivo. 
Specific Aim 2: Integrate, optimize, test, and validate an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted radiofrequency (RF) pulse sequence design, RF phase cycling methods, and flexible pre-pulse concepts as part of FRF to accommodate new contrast dimensions for tissue characterization.
Specific Aim 3: Expand FRF for flow measurements that are sensitive to the high dynamic range of blood-flow in the chambers and vessels of the heart, equip the reconstruction with extra dimensions to accommodate regularization across the different velocity encodes, optimize the parameter ranges, and validate in vivo. 

Expected Results & Impact for the Field: 

At the crossroads of prior success and new innovation, new hardware, new strategic collaborations, and new hirings, we will leverage existing FRF technology and logically and mechanistically develop it from a framework that provides information about anatomy and function of the heart only into a framework that offers much more quantitative and detailed information per unit time about the heart, its function, its anatomy, its tissues, and its vessels than was previously possible. Through this research, we will gain in-depth knowledge about new data acquisition and reconstruction strategies in cardiac MRI, and about the optimization of their respective components. We will learn for which parameter ranges the methods will work successfully, and we will also learn at which point success meets failure. We will gain insight into the performance of these concepts in gold standard comparisons, and will therefore likely be able to expand the perimeter of knowledge of both data acquisition and reconstruction paradigms in cardiovascular MRI. Provided that this concerns uncharted territory, our findings will contribute to filling a knowledge gap. FRF equipped with a higher resolution, new, needle-free contrast mechanisms, and a higher dynamic range for blood flow measurements, will critically enable future research and discovery and directly support the improved management of cardiovascular disease, the leading cause of death in industrialized nations. Finally, and given that this augmented FRF considerably improves the ease-of-use for the operator as it remains a 1-click solution, dissemination outside of highly specialized academic centers will be facilitated in support of a broader impact for the field.
Keywords: Cardiovascular Imaging, Democratization, Magnetic Resonance Imaging

Title: Rich Context in Neural Machine Translation
Abstract:
Machine translation has been dominated by phrase-based statistical machine translation (SMT) for the last decade, even though SMT comes with some well known limitations regarding the performance of these systems. For instance, phrase-based models need to make strong independence assumptions, and only consider local context during translation, which makes it hard to model phenomena such as long-distance dependencies within sentences.

Recently, a new approach to machine translation systems has received considerable attention: machine translation with neural networks. Even though artificial neural networks have been studied for many years in other disciplines, they are a new and very promising area of research within machine translation. This includes not only end-to-end translation with neural networks, but also phrase-based or syntax-based models with neural components (e.g. neural language models).

In this project, we will work on end-to-end neural machine translation (NMT). We will start with a detailed comparison of NMT with corresponding phrase-based models in order to pinpoint its advantages and shortcomings. Subsequently, we will explore the new opportunities of neural MT with respect to the inclusion of additional information into the translation model: because the translation can be conditioned on arbitrary real-valued input features without having to resort to strong independence assumptions, neural MT can be improved by providing novel types of information as rich context inputs to the translation task, such as document-level information, linguistic annotation, multiple source languages, or side constraints.

It has been rather cumbersome to include document-level information into SMT systems. Neural MT provides a more elegant and straight-forward way to include lexical preferences which have been derived from neighboring sentences. This will help to improve lexical choice which is still one of the major problems in machine translation. Linguistic annotation such as Part-of-Speech tags, morphological features and dependency relations have not resulted in much of an improvement in SMT systems. Still, our intuition tells us that the quality of MT systems should improve with the inclusion of additional layers of linguistic information. We will investigate how to best include linguistic features in NMT. Often we have translations of a given text not only in one language but in multiple languages when we need to create another translation in one more language. Neural MT offers a way to combine the evidence from multiple source languages when translating into a new language.

In this project, we will explore the new possibilities of neural machine translation to advance state-of-the-art MT systems for the three major languages of Switzerland: French, German and Italian.
Keywords: Discourse Processing, Machine Translation, Multilingual Models, Neural Networks, Word Embeddings

Title: The role of bone loss in recurrent anterior shoulder instability - three dimensional image based analysis
Abstract:
Study rationale
Traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation, which primarily affects a young athletic population, often results in traumatic injury to the glenoid rim and-or to the humeral head, increasing the risk of recuring instability. Patients at high risk of recurrence due to significant bone loss and other factors must be identified to guide surgical treatment decision making. For risk assessment, bone loss is currently estimated on CT or MRI using 2D linear measures. Significant variance in measurement techniques and critical thresholds have, however, been reported, and biomechanical studies have shown that measures are inadequate to represent the dynamic effect of defects because they do not consider 3D variations in bone morphology. 
Project Aim
To develop deep learning based algorithms for the 3D analysis of glenoid and humeral head bone loss for more accurate and comprehensive measurement and improved treatment decision making for anterior shoulder instability patients. 
Secondary objectives
1)To study the association between 3D and dynamic bone loss measures and recurrent instability 
2)To study the association between bone loss and shoulder stability to define thresholds for treatment planning
3)To study the effect of bone loss on glenohumeral translations during end-range motion
4)To study the effect of the shoulder muscle activation on joint stability during end-range motion in the presence of varying levels of bone loss
Methods
1)Development of automated methods for the 3D analysis of bone loss from CT or MRI, including a) deep learning based segmentation of the scapula and humerus, b) prediction of the pre-morbid bones c) parametrization of bone loss and defect size and c) dynamic calculation of lesion interaction at end range motion. 
2)Retrospective study of primary anterior instability patients (n=160), to determine association between bone loss (measured in 3D) and recurrence. The instability ratio, calculated via patient specific musculoskeletal modeling will be used determine the association between bone loss and stability of the glenohumeral joint. 
3)In a prospective study of anterior instability patients (n=33), dynamic biplanar radiographic imaging will be used to study the glenohumeral kinematics of the unstable shoulder with high accuracy. Registered to CT derived 3D models, relative pose of the scapular and humeral head during motion will be analyzed to determine the effect of different levels of bone loss on joint stability and the risk of subluxation. The resulting 6D dynamic kinematic information of the glenohumeral joint will additionally be used to drive patient specific musculoskeletal models to investigate the effect of the stabilizing shoulder muscles on joint stability in case of varying bone loss relative to healthy contralateral controls. 
Expected results
1)3D and dynamic measures of bone loss correlate more strongly with recurrence and shoulder instability in primary anterior shoulder instability than previously reported 2D metrics. 
2)Thresholds predicting recurrence based on 3D and dynamic measures of bone loss can be defined for patients having suffered primary anterior shoulder instability.
3)Dynamic stability is reduced in case of bone-loss in the anterior-inferior glenoid due to a decrease in the ratio of translation to glenoid radius which defines the stable motion range.  
4)Muscle force equilibrium at the glenohumeral joint is disrupted in the case of recurring instability and bone-loss due to the changed scapular and humeral morphology and neuromuscular effects, reducing the effect of these compensatory mechanisms in promoting stability.
Impact
This project aims to overcome limitations in current bone loss measurements through the exploitation of deep learning The automation of 3D and dynamic analyses in combination with high accuracy kinematic and musculoskeletal analyses, will allow for the definition of bone loss thresholds to support surgical treatment decision m

Title: Towards a Cheap Personalization of Propaganda with Large Language Models?
Abstract:
Technological advances have changed political communication by making information abundant relative to individuals' attention. For example, with massive amounts of available information, it can be tricky to track domestic and foreign actors' (covert) influence on a country's information sphere. As a very recent technological innovation, large language models (LLMs, like OpenAI's ChatGPT) have been shown to replicate human patterns of language relatively cheaply. Thus, their emergence has also raised discussions about their political impact. One key concern is LLMs' potential to generate floods of low-quality or propaganda content. This concern is particularly salient in light of some early evidence that messages created by LLMs can be as persuasive as human-generated ones.

At the same time, it has been argued that LLMs contain information on human behavior. For example, LLMs have been shown to reproduce typical human biases (e.g., on gender or race). Beyond specific biases, very recent work also documents that LLMs can mimic specific demographic groups based on associations between (implicit) demographic background variables and content they have seen during training. These two observations -- LLMs' potential to create persuasive messages and their potential capability to emulate specific demographic groups -- raise the question of whether they could be used to generate personalized political messages at a low cost or, as an extreme, personalized political propaganda. In other domains (e.g., marketing), personalization is generally seen as effective. Recent public debates have concerned whether such targeting or profiling could also be (mis-)used in political communication: individuals could be rendered favorably disposed to particular interests.

The project aims to provide evidence of whether LLMs can create content for targeted political messaging -- and, if so, how effectively. That is, this research analyzes the persuasive power of targeted content created by LLMs and whether such effects depend on the targets and the type of LLM used. Thereby, a general framework to analyze LLMs' potential for targeted political messaging is developed. It involves reverse-engineering different personas that the LLMs likely have seen in their training and creating content based on them. Then, this content is presented to different individuals in an experimental setting, and its effect on their opinions is measured. The framework is applied to assess whether LLMs can shift opinions on economic policy issues for specific demographic groups.
Keywords: artificial intelligence, causal evidence, large language models, media, persuasion, political messaging, propaganda

Title: Modeling the impact of artificial intelligence auto-segmentation-guided treatment margin reduction on the safety and efficacy of radiotherapy for locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer: an in silico validation study
Abstract:
Background
Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer deaths worldwide. Approximately 25% of lung cancers present as locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer (LA-NSCLC). Conventionally fractionated radiotherapy (RT) combined with chemotherapy followed by consolidation immunotherapy is the standard treatment for inoperable or unresectable LA-NSCLC. When delivering RT, safety treatment margins need to be applied to account for microscopic disease extent and the complex spatial uncertainties. These result in spillover radiation to normal organs at risk (OAR), thus causing excess toxicities and potentially decreasing survival. Adaptive radiotherapy (ART) is a promising strategy to reduce toxicities by continuous monitoring of tumor and surrounding tissues during the course of RT and making timely adjustments to the treatment plan. However, the implementation of ART for LA-NSCLC patients into clinical practice is hampered by the time-consuming and labor-intensive nature of repeat imaging and manually outlining the tumor and OARs, also known as segmentation. However, nowadays patients are routinely being positioned for RT using so-called cone-beam computer tomography (CBCT) scans which are non-diagnostic quality CT scans obtained on the RT treatment machine. These are generally insufficient in image quality to accurately outline the tumor and OARs. Automatic computer-driven segmentation algorithms for diagnostic quality scans do exist and are continuously improving. However, none of them are adequate for segmentation based on CBCTs. Since CBCTs are routinely acquired for patient positioning, autosegmentation based on these images would take advantage of readily available images that are not otherwise used. The team at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK) has developed novel artificial intelligence (AI) methods, such as the deep learning-based “Cross-Modality Educed Learning” (CMEDL) which uses MRI and CT images to inform an algorithm that allows fast and accurate auto-segmentation of target volumes and OARs. This published CMEDL algorithm is currently being extended for auto-segmentation based on CBCTs. We expect that CMEDL will improve auto-segmentation accuracy based on CBCT, allowing fast and reliable auto-segmentation for quick and more precise verification of target coverage in each fraction, facilitating ART with reduced treatment margins for safer and more effective treatments. This will also obviate the need for additional imaging for the purposes of ART and introduce what could be called AI-guided RT (AIGRT).

Hypothesis
The hypothesis of this project is that longitudinal AI auto-segmentation using CMEDL on weekly CBCTs during RT for LA-NSCLC decreases geometric uncertainties in localizing the tumor and OARs and can thus facilitate smaller treatment margins. The resulting decrease in dose to surrounding healthy tissues could reduce the risk of side effects, while target coverage and thus local tumor control are maintained or even improved, compared with conventional treatment margins. Since the internal anatomy during a course of RT is dynamic, real-time dose accumulation maps would allow for confirmation of actually delivered RT dose and allow for dose adjustments during the treatment course as necessary.

Methods
A multi-institutional dataset of CT scans from lung cancer patients from a Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA) dataset (N total = 380, weekly CBCTs for up to 6 weeks, resulting in a total of 1200 CBCT scans) will be used to measure the geometric accuracy and segmentation variability of CBCT-CMEDL auto-segmentation compared to ground truth segmentations by human experts. The Hausdorff distance (HD) values will be used to derive a treatment margin reflecting potential setup accuracy: the AIGRT-margins. A dataset of prospectively acquired CTs from MSK of (N = 200) with biopsy-proven unresected stage II-III LA-NSCLC, treated with definitive intensity-modulated RT (IMRT) will be used to estimate the impact of the smaller AIGRT-margins compared with standard margins on the probability of toxicity and tumor control. On this dataset, treatment plans will be created using deep learning auto-planning software developed at MSK based on 1) the smaller AIGRT-margins and 2) standard margins. Statistics
Geometric accuracy of CBCT-CMEDL tumor and OAR auto-segmentation will be computed using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), surface DSC (SDSC), mean surface distance (MSD), and HD metrics. Dosimetric metrics derived from the dose volume histograms (DVH) will also be computed to evaluate segmentations and determine geometric accuracy. Area under the receiver operating curve (AUC) will be used for comparing NTCP/TCP prediction differences. Statistical comparisons for segmentations and NTCP/TCP model accuracies will be performed using paired and two-sided Wilcoxon tests, with adjustments for multiple comparisons where applicable. Confidence levels > 95% will be considered significant.

AIGRT by means of CBCT-CMEDL auto-segmentation could improve the safety and efficacy of RT for LA-NSCLC patients. To confirm this, the results of this validation study will directly inform the design of a prospective randomized clinical trial, comparing acute toxicity in LA-NSCLC patients treated with definitive chemoradiotherapy with or without AIGRT and reduced treatment margins. The CBCT-CMEDL method will be made available through an open-source software platform and could therefore be integrated into clinical practice without additional costs for the health care system, given that CBCTs are readily available in most Swiss and European radiation oncology departments and regularly applied during RT for image guidance.

Title: An adaptive multi-objective framework for tailoring carbon capture technologies
Abstract:
Identifying the most suitable carbon capture technology for a given application is key to deploying economically attractive and environmentally-friendly capture strategies at a large scale, as needed to achieve a net-zero world.
Most often, research related to carbon capture is carried out either at the laboratory level to obtain materials with outstanding performances or at the industrial level by referring to commercially available technologies that may not be the most suitable depending on the application. My objective is to bridge this gap between lab-scale and industrial-scale research on carbon capture. I propose to achieve this aim by adopting a multi-objective optimization approach to assess the potential of novel high-performing technologies and materials for carbon capture in large-scale future scenarios. Accomplishing this research goal will provide key insights to reduce implementation turnaround time and to facilitate a timely transition to net-zero.
Specifically, I will develop a modelling framework able to assess the technology or the combination of technologies which is optimal for a given capture application. The proposed framework will be highly flexible and adaptable to consider a wide range of emission sources, sinks where the captured CO2 will be stored or utilized, and geographic locations. Depending on the source, the input concentration of CO2 can vary from 0.04% in direct air capture to 25% in the cement industry. Also, different sinks will be considered, e.g., storage and utilization to produce fuels or chemicals, which correspond to different outputs for CO2 purity and pressure. 
Given this wide range of inputs and outputs, a general capture strategy for all applications cannot be the solution. Conversely, tailored strategies must be designed where not only different operating conditions but also different technologies come into play. Such strategies will also include integration of technologies, where the strengths of each technology will be synergistically exploited to reduce separation costs via optimized hybrid processes. 
The selection of the optimal capture process needs to take into consideration not only the costs via techno-economic assessment (TEA) but also the environmental impact of the overall process, via life cycle assessment (LCA). Therefore, the proposed multi-objective optimization framework will include TEA and LCA for different technologies. In particular, for each given application, different technological routes will be optimized with respect to key performance indicators representing cost and environmental impact. Then, the sets of optimized indicators will be compared to identify the best technological solution. I will focus on two technologies, i.e., adsorption and membrane process, as these have evolved as the most promising technologies for gas separation, while I will take monoethanolamine-based absorption (MEA) as benchmark for the calculations. 
Importantly, I will also deploy an open-access online application that will perform optimization through surrogate models derived via machine learning algorithms. This will be a highly impactful tool to drive decisions for materials development and technology selection and it will be highly relevant for a wide scientific community. For example, material scientists will compare the optimized performances of their technology with other processes or materials, and industrial stakeholders will identify the optimal technology for a specific application. 
I have developed broad expertise in modelling separation processes. I have worked extensively on the techno-economic models of membrane- and adsorption-based carbon capture, and on the optimization of integrated processes for the treatment and valorization of polluted liquid and gas streams. Such skills, together with the scientific network that I have started to build in view of the project, will enable me to pursue the main objectives.
Overall, this unique multi-objective integrated approach combining TEA and LCA will obtain novel and important insights on how to make carbon capture strategies more economically competitive and environmentally-friendly, which is key to achieving the net-zero transition.
Keywords: Adsorption process, Carbon capture, Life cycle assessment, Membrane process, Multi-objective optimization, Techno-economic analysis

Title: Towards a Better Understanding of Smooth Minimax Optimization: Stationary Points & Impact of Noise
Abstract:
A core problem encountered in multiple fields--game theory and economics [Von Neumann and Morgenstern, 1944, Myerson, 2013], mathematics, social science, and biology, to name a few--is formalizing learning as interactions between two agents. One player aims to minimize the payoff function, and the other to maximize it. Ideally, min-max training converges to a Nash equilibrium (NE) where no player has the incentive of changing its strategy. 

Over the past several years, such two-player differentiable games gained renewed interest in machine learning as well, in the context of generative modeling and adversarial learning [Goodfellow et al., 2014], multi-agent reinforcement learning [Omidshafiei et al., 2017, Dai et al., 2018, Zhang et al., 2019], robust supervised learning [Madryet al., 2018], hyperparameter tuning casted as a zero-sum game [Maclaurin et al., 2015], among others.  Despite their impressive performance when training succeeds, training such multi-objective agents remains notoriously hard [Chavdarova and Fleuret. 2018, Mescheder et al., 2017]. In particular, poor performance, brittle dependency on hyperparameters, or divergence remain often reported. An understanding of the fundamental differences between single and multi-objective optimization, as well as the stationary points of a minimax game, is currently missing. 

This research project aims to gain deeper insights into the training dynamics of differentiable (smooth) minimax game and ideally develop a practical equilibrium finding algorithm.

We point out two relevant lines of research (i) lack of understanding of the types of equilibria of interest, as well as (ii) large impact of noisy stochastic gradient on the convergence. Currently, it remains unclear whether non-Nash stationary points are of interest for either of the players [Mazumdar et al., 2019], or if these are a subset of the more general global–minimax equilibria (GME) [Fiez et al., 2020, Jin et al., 2020]. Regarding the latter, we showed that under the presence of noise, minimax optimization diverges with high probability [Chavdarova et al.,2019], implying the importance of variance reduced gradient estimates [Chavdarova et al., 2019, 2020].

This project could open a fruitful avenue of further research toward understanding minimax optimization, advancing generative models, and in the long run, learning for general games with more than two players.
Keywords: Generative Adversarial Networks, minimax optimization, smooth games optimization

Title: Bridging Agroecology and Artificial Intelligence: A Participatory Approach to Knowledge Dissemination in Senegal
Abstract:
This project proposes the participatory development of an AI-powered chatbot as a proof of concept to facilitate knowledge dissemination among agroecological practitioners in Casamance, Senegal. Unlike conventional AI in agriculture, which prioritizes industrial farming, this initiative ensures co-design with farmers, extension officers, sociologists, and agroecology experts. The AI model will integrate both global and local agricultural knowledge, bridging scientific research with indigenous practices to provide contextually relevant, multilingual guidance (e.g., Wolof, French).
A key innovation is its community-led development, ensuring local expertise shapes both content and functionality. The project will also critically question AI’s social dimensions, fostering farmer agency, and knowledge sovereignty.
The expected outcome is a functional prototype, demonstrating how AI can be co-created with local communities to support the agroecological transition in a region deeply rooted in land stewardship.
Keywords: Agriculture, Agroecology, Artificial intelligence, Participatory methods, Senegal

Title: From flexible models to process-based networks in hydrology: Using Machine Learning to improve predictions without sacrificing interpretability
Abstract:
Catchment hydrology benefits from a wide array of models with complementary qualities and drawbacks in terms of physical interpretability, ease of setup, data requirements and predictive performance. “Hybrid models” combine different types of models and modelling philosophies and are intended to take the best of each approach, thereby reducing their tradeoff of advantages and limitations. Hybrid models combining process-based (PB) and machine-learning (ML) models in hydrology are a nascent research field, which promises new scientific discoveries and better predictions. 
This proposal combines the recent advances of conceptual models, and in particular the evolution from fixed model structures into flexible frameworks, to the elements that have determined the success of ML models in streamflow prediction. In particular, flexible frameworks have shown to represent a great tool for improving predictions and learn catchment behavior, but arguably lack compelling approaches for model identification. ML models and in particular deep learning methods, on the other hand, consistently beat the prediction performance of traditional fixed model structures, but they are hard to interpret in terms of hydrological processes.
This proposal introduces process-based networks, where the network nodes are represented by the generic elements that characterize such flexible frameworks, which are driven by hydrologically motivated mass conservation equations. These elements can act as processing units each responsible for a particular process or a specific aspect of the rainfall-runoff process. Compared to the activation functions that characterize traditional ML models, such elements are more directly interpretable as catchment compartments with unsaturated and saturated zones, and that connect vertically and laterally in linear and nonlinear ways. The theory and available software infrastructure developed around flexible frameworks and deep learning methods is sufficiently mature to allow the integration of hydrological concepts in modern ML architectures, enabling the access to instruments such as efficient calibration algorithms and parallelization. 
We plan experiments using calibration on many catchments and using static catchment attributes such as topography, geology and soil to benchmark our approach with competing modelling alternatives. The physical interpretability of our proposed approach would enable the investigation of the role of model complexity and processes constraints, to understand which functional representations are characterize each catchment, and “what is learned from where”, that is, to better understand the flow of information from donor to target catchments in model regionalization setups.

Title: Gamification and Active Crowdsourcing in Landscape Perception and Preference Research
Abstract:
Landscapes actualise our existence: they are the perceivable areas of the earth in which our lives unfold. They provide tangible (e.g. food, water, building materials) and intangible (e.g. recreational potential, aesthetic value, inspiration) dimensions to our lives and influence our social, physical, and mental well-being. Understanding how individuals and socio-demographic groups perceive various landscapes has thus become an important consideration in fair decision and inclusive policy making processes regarding our surroundings. 

For effective landscape research, high quality underlying data from a diverse crowd is crucial. However, both traditional expert-based methods as well as modern participatory approaches face several limitations. Traditional methods of generating landscape-relevant information are confined by financial and time limitations, whereas modern crowdsourcing and citizen science approaches often struggle with user engagement, retention, and bias. Gamification - adding entertaining elements to a process - has been found to encourage a diverse audience, increase user motivation and retention, produce high quality data for academic research and has successfully been incorporated into many crowdsourcing efforts. However, even though complementing landscape perception data generation with gamified elements has explicitly been called for, projects remain scarce. 

This interdisciplinary research project will transcend contemporary crowdsourcing efforts by exploiting the unique motivational and spatial characteristics of a novel location-based game to generate rich landscape perception and preference data. The generated data will be analysed using methods from geographic information science, computational linguistics, and machine learning to extract and explore emergent landscape dimensions. The results will showcase the potential of gamification in academic data generation as well as allow for the quantitative interpretation and qualitative characterisation of landscape perceptions within and between individuals as well as socio-demographic and cultural groups. By analysing the developed application and the generated data, this project aims to investigate the hypothesis that location-based games offer a powerful tool for environmental, experiential, and perceptual data generation. This has important implications for both participatory data generation in science more generally, as well as landscape policy and decision making. 

Findings will be published as a set of recommendations based on descriptive statistics derived from the implemented application. Further, extracting salient landscape information from the generated data will allow the compilation of important human-landscape interactions and dimensions, which will be published to complement future inquiries into landscapes. In addition, the assumption of socio-demographic and cultural differences in landscape perceptions will be investigated and significant similarities and differences will be reported, contributing to debates of inclusion and sustainability regarding landscapes. Seeing the participatory nature of the research, the results will be communicated through scientific articles as well as public events to further the academic discourse as well as educate and empower participating individuals.

Title: Remembering the future: A study of work in street trials of driverless buses
Abstract:
Background. Automated Vehicles (AVs) have been hailed as a technology that has the potential to introduce profound changes in transportation and the organization of urban life more widely. As part of this development, driverless shuttle buses have been piloted in numerous street trials across the world. Between 2016 and 2022, according to the Swiss Federal Roads Office, ten pilot trials of AVs for public transportation have taken place in Switzerland. Although the pilot trials bring highly valuable results, the reports and publications do not provide details of the practical knowledge and skilled competence developed by the professional participants: for example, by the operators and technicians who have executed the street trials, solving emergent technical and social troubles on the spot, and guiding passengers or other members of the public in their interactions with the driverless shuttles.
 
Broad objective. In this project, addressing the identified gap, we aim to investigate the details of such knowledge and competence. Turning it from an implicit resource to an explicit topic, we will retrospectively obtain it from the former participants in the street trials of AVs in public transport in Switzerland. By collecting “oral histories” of such trials, the objective is to explore social implications of automated mobility and AI more generally by understanding how former participants account for the organization of pilot trials and their own involvement in it.

Specific aims. Our specific interest is in the ad hoc knowledge and skills involved in pilot trials of AVs. The project seeks to answer research questions such as: How is a street trial of AVs conducted in terms of routine activities by its local administrators and executioners? What kind of “insider knowledge” has been developed for the work of the street, but potentially disregarded (i.e., only remembered and not included in the reports) once the pilot trial is finished? How has the knowledge developed and transformed over the course of the pilot trials, often spanning several years? How was it transmitted and taught to newly recruited employees?

Methods to be used. The project will be based on a methodologically original combination of the procedures of oral history and “coat-hanger” interviewing developed in ethnomethodological studies of work in the sciences. Oral history is an established perspective of collecting witness testimonies that is sensitive to personal and biographical contexts of the narrators. We will interview the former local operators and technicians in the concluded street trials about their practical experiences with AVs as a phenomenon of recent history. The notion of “coat-hangers” will allow us to introduce a list of concrete topics as experienced contingencies, around which the interviews will be structured. Our study will be also grounded in analyses of the large corpus of ethnographic video materials collected in pilot trials of driverless buses in a Swiss town several years ago. We will use short excerpts of these materials (“video coat-hangers”) to serve as reminders for the interviewed practitioners and as resources for the relevant topics to be discussed in detail. 

Expected results and their impacts. The project offers a prospect to contribute significantly to an alternative conceptualization of AI and automated mobility as socially situated phenomena, responding to timely societal challenges. Our research presents a unique opportunity to collect relevant insights into the recent technological developments from their direct participants before they are forgotten. With the advantage of hindsight, we will revisit lessons learned in the concluded projects, comparing and compiling them across different contexts. The outcomes and methodology can be extended to other technologies that are tested through prototypes in pilot trials.

Title: Consolidating the Ontological Analysis Framework for Future Applications: Follow-Up Project to "Reciprocal Enhancement of Terminological and Ontological Resources Through Definition Analysis"
Abstract:
This interdisciplinary work in the fields of terminology, ontology, and natural language processing (NLP) is concerned with natural language definitions in specialized dictionaries and ontologies. It focuses on the modeling of definition contents in view of creating language- and domain-independent tools to help terminologists and ontologists write definitions.

The underlying hypothesis for creating such generic definition-content models is that definitions express characteristics of the types of things to which specialized terms refer. Testing this hypothesis requires using a representation of the types of things that exist in the world, i.e. an ontology. This work uses the categories of the realist upper-level Basic Formal Ontology (BFO). Testing the hypothesis also requires applying these models on corpora of existing definitions to see to what extent the models predict definition contents.

The methodology consists in creating the definition models on the basis of the characteristics of the BFO categories, and using these models as a metalanguage to annotate large-scale multilingual and multi-domain corpora of textual definitions. My previous postdoctoral research aimed at producing the necessary resources for such large-scale corpus analyses: the definition models; definition corpora; computer programs for automatic corpus pre-annotations; an annotation manual for an annotation campaign to create validated training-corpora and to obtain preliminary results.

This follow-up research project aims at: (1) completing and finalizing the resources generated during the previous project to yield preliminary results; (2) testing the different hypotheses to consolidate the proposed ontological analysis framework so that it can be used on large-scale projects and, in the future, applied to the study of other terminological phenomena, such as diachrony and popularization of scientific terms; (3) testing the automation of the annotation task on a large-scale.

The outcomes of this project are expected to have a positive impact on the activity of definition writing and the resulting terminological and ontological resources. Terminological resources will have richer functionalities allowing, for example, for searching the dictionary contents through the definitions. A wider audience will be able to use ontologies as classical terminological resources, and ontologists will benefit from richer and more reliable ontological resources. The results of this research project are also expected to be beneficial to the natural language processing (NLP) and the applied ontology communities: terminological definitions annotated with these types of relational models will allow for better reusability of terminological dictionaries and databases as lexical resources for NLP systems, and for easier domain-ontology development.
Keywords: (semi-)automatic definition writing tools, Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), corpus analysis, definition content modeling, definition templates, definitions, lexico-semantic analysis, natural language processing (NLP), ontologies, terminology

Title: Understanding Tax Enforcement
Abstract:
Governments rely on tax revenue to finance infrastructure, childcare, schooling, healthcare, and social security. Therefore, tax revenues are considerable in most countries. Yet, taxes that are owed are not paid automatically. Between the taxpayer, who needs to pay taxes, and the government receiving the revenues stands the tax collection. Tax authorities are tasked with collecting the taxes and play a key role in tax enforcement.

One of the problems with collecting the taxes that are due is tax evasion. Unfortunately, there is evidence that a considerable amount of taxes is being evaded. In addition to the large costs that tax evasion places on societies, there are tax compliance costs for almost all individuals and companies, including for the vast majority of tax payers paying the taxes in accordance with the law.

Given the importance of tax collection (in particular with respect to tax enforcement and administration, without neglecting compliance costs), it is surprising that thus far very little is known about what people prefer in terms of tax enforcement and tax administration. There is basically no knowledge on which enforcement activities and what enforcement level people prefer for different taxes and what people think regarding activities that can improve enforcement while reducing compliance costs, such as automatic exchange of information to prefill tax declarations (of course, such activities can have other drawbacks, for instance requiring a larger budget for tax authorities). The first objective of this research project is to elicit what type of tax enforcement and tax administration people prefer. The implementation of the research related to this first objective predominantly relies on conducting survey experiments.

The second objective of this research project relates to the use of modern data analytics (including state-of-the-art machine-learning methods) in tax enforcement and tax administration. Thus far, there is only very limited knowledge on the potential of such techniques in tax enforcement (and tax administration more generally). This applies also to the returns to tax auditing – simple estimates suggest that the returns to additional investments in tax auditing are large, but thorough estimates of these returns are missing, in particular when advanced analytical techniques are employed (there is also very little knowledge on the efficiency gains of using data analytics for other activities of tax authorities). The second objective is to understand the potential of modern data analytics in tax enforcement and administration, with a focus on the returns to tax auditing and on understanding which techniques perform best in audit selection. The implementation of the research related to this second objective mainly relies on the analysis of observational data with machine-learning techniques and econometrics.

This project is seen as the beginning of a research agenda situated at the intersection of public finance, behavioral economics, psychology, econometrics, and computer science. The research agenda aims at discovering what type and level of tax enforcement and what kind of tax administration a society desires and how this can most efficiently be attained. The potential societal impact is large, especially because of the large amounts of evaded taxes, but also due to high tax compliance costs. Already a small reduction of tax evasion in one country leads an important increase in tax revenue. Should enforcement and administration practices or investments in tax enforcement change persistently, the long-term effects would naturally be even larger. Reduced tax compliance costs may additionally increase the positive societal impact of this research agenda.
Keywords: audit selection, data science, data science in taxation, machine learning in taxation, preference elicitation, preferences about taxation, survey experiments, tax administration, tax audits, tax enforcement, tax evasion, tax preference elicitation
