Title: SPAD-based random pulse computer for robotics and AI applications
Abstract:
In this project we plan to study, implement, and deploy on-chip integrated circuits necessary to build a fully-programmable computer based on a random pulse computation paradigm, so as to research its suitability for robotics and AI applications.
Today, computing is almost exclusively done via the Digital Computation (DC), based on Turing machine theoretical models. Representing numbers in the positional binary format and using integrated circuits to execute Boolean logic operations, allows for a very fast computation with an arbitrary precision. On the other hand, Quantum Computation (QC) have recently gained momentum. While significantly slower for arithmetic problems, QC can solve a few today intractable problems exponentially faster and with fewer resources.   
A radically different approach to computation is Random Pulse Computing (RPC), initially proposed in the seminal work of John von Neumann in 1956, RPC makes use of counting and combining electrical pulses that appear randomly in time, similar to nerve pulses and inspired by information processing in neurons of living beings. RPC, flashed in the 1960s and was run over by DC in the 1970s, after which it fell into oblivion. Reborn in the mid-2010s, RPC has attracted attention for its economic use of resources, fault tolerant properties, and low power operation; it has thus become a promise to efficiently solve artificial intelligence problems in imaging that are hard for both DC and QC. In addition, RPC promises to be an appropriate approach to deep learning that mimic human brain operations, among others. This is relevant with the rise of AI that currently requires vast resources in the cloud.

Despite the potential of RPC, a general theory of synthesis and analysis of circuits implementing RPC is not available. Even though attempts have been made towards general functional synthesis via expansion into Bernstein polynomials or via a spectral transform approach, these techniques cannot be automated since they require creative guesswork and/or ad-hoc optimizations.
In this project we propose to investigate new, more efficient ways to synthesize complex RPC circuits, motivated by their possible use in AI, in alternative to conventional DC-based in-cloud approaches. Our two original findings, namely the Entropy Budget Criterion (EBC) and the random flip-flop (RFF) circuit, set up an entirely new approach to synthesis and evaluation of RPC circuits, through the merit of the information entropy. This approach readily enabled us to achieve unpreceded improvements in elementary arithmetic RPC circuits, as well as to set some fundamental limits for RPC. However, this was done via an educated guess, while a general theory of synthesizing circuits is still out of reach at this moment. In our research we will use the established fact, that the use of quantum entropy, instead of pseudo-randomness, greatly simplifies RPC circuits and enhances their precision. In addition, we will demonstrate two use cases: 1) the first programmable random pulse computer; 2) an edge-detection image processor. Both will be integrated on monolithic chips by using a standard Si-CMOS process. Namely, we have realized that bio-inspired visual sensing occurs naturally in the technology of single-photon counting cameras, which is a successful research topic at the AQUA Lab at EPFL, where indeed each light sensor (i.e. pixel) encodes information in a random pulse train of quantum origin. Such information can be processed directly by RPC circuits, a major research topic at RBI. Finally, we have recently demonstrated the world's first integrated RFF, on a chip carrying 2800 units. This technology is a crucial asset for reaching the goals of this project.
Keywords: Quantum computing, RPC, Random Pulse computing, Random flip-flop, Random pulse computing, SPAD, Single-photon avalanche diode

Title: Universal and robust stochastic optimization
Abstract:
The vast availability of compute power enabled machine learning models to become larger, more complex and capable of handling large-dimensional datasets. The efficiency of optimization process immensely depends on the properties of the model and the nature of the data available, which poses a significant problem as the complexity of either increases ad infinitum. 

An overarching challenge is to design fast, adaptive algorithms which are provably robust to increasing complexity of the large-scale models and unknown properties of the optimization landscape, while ensuring scalable implementation at a large scale. Having that said, there are two fundamental perspectives to consider: 
(i) provable convergence of standard optimization algorithms requires precise knowledge model and loss function parameters, which are usually prohibitively expensive to even estimate; 
(ii) state-of-the-art methods which show superior performance in practice are predominantly heuristics, lacking theoretical basis.

This proposal presents projects on designing fast, order-optimal algorithms which naturally adapt to the model complexity and loss landscape without prior knowledge of the properties of the model/problem. The goal is to unify the discrepancy between the theory of adaptive algorithms and the practical heuristics employed in practice. The proposed projects has three core thrusts, relying on my research thus far and the preliminary evidence we gathered for projected objectives:

I. The first thrust studies the bias and variance of estimators in stochastic optimization and adaptation to their qualities. 

II. A recent interest in optimization and machine learning is understanding global convergence of higher-order methods, such as Newton's method and beyond, for minimization of smooth losses and finding saddle points of min-max problems, e.g., training GANs. The challenge is understanding their noise-adaptation capabilities and makin them adaptive to smoothness parameters, especially in the presence of uncertainty.

III. A long-lasting challenge in optimization is seamless adaptation to degrees of convexity and obtaining order-optimal rates. Our empirical studies show that one could improve convergence of SGD by locally adjusting the step-size for training residual networks.
Keywords: Adaptive methods, Stochastic optimization, Variational inequalities

Title: RadioClusters on the road to the SKA
Abstract: The project aims to carry out high-impact astrophysics research with the world-leading MeerKAT array, while developing and incorporating novel machine learning techniques to improve the efficiency of the technical aspects of radio data reduction and analysis. The science focus of our synergistic approach is on the environment of galaxy clusters, a key science area for the Square Kilometre Array (SKA). We will use continuum and polarisation data to study faint, diffuse radio sources in cluster environments in order to probe cluster cosmic ray physics and magnetic field properties. These studies require one to find, extract, and characterise low surface brightness, diffuse structure in large volumes of radio data, volumes which will increase dramatically in the SKA era. To prepare for these data extremes, we will investigate machine learning techniques for source finding and characterisation of the target emission and leverage HPC methods such as parallelization to improve the efficiency of existing state of the art software.
Keywords: Anomaly Detection, Astrophysics, Big Data, Cosmic Web, Cosmology, Deep Learning, Galaxy Clusters, Machine Learning, Radio Astronomy

Title: Robust Robotic Scene Understanding  in Complex, Changing Environments using 3D Dynamic Scene Graphs
Abstract: Scene understanding is a crucial capability for intelligent systems, such as autonomous mobile robots, and enables numerous applications ranging from search and rescue and inspection, to industrial as well as service robotics. Recently, 3D Scene Graphs (SG) have emerged as a powerful abstraction and hierarchical scene representation, potentially bridging the gap in world representation between humans and machines. While great progress has been made in online semantic 3D reconstruction and subsequent abstraction, we have identified three major gaps in the current state of the art that hinder the deployment of SGs to complex real scenes and prevent exploiting their full potential for autonomous robots. Most notably, current methods assume a static world, whereas real environments shared with other agents are inevitably subject to dynamics and change. Second, the ability to predict rather than react greatly improves robot performance. However, the capabilities of SGs for prediction have not yet been thoroughly explored. Lastly, as robots are embodied agents, they can move to perceive their surroundings. This enables them to explore unknown scenes and improve their world models, but it is unclear how to use SGs to enable effective robot navigation. The goal of this project is to develop a fully autonomous robotic scene understanding system, overcoming these challenges. Therefore we propose a novel object-centric approach to disentangle spatial and temporal inconsistency in the sensor data and robot map, enabling incremental SG generation in complex, changing scenes. We further propose to leverage the holistic scene information in SGs using Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNN) for more accurate spatio-temporal predictions, and present an Informative Path Planning (IPP) approach for active SG generation. The developed methods, algorithms, and data will be made available to the community through publications in high impact peer-reviewed journals and conferences. This will significantly accelerate the transition of SGs from academic labs onto real robots in challenging everyday situations, enabling higher levels of robot autonomy and improving human-robot communication and interaction. In particular, this provides the models required to answer queries like “robot, where are my glasses - on the counter in the kitchen” with a semantic and metric grounding of the concepts of glasses, counters, and kitchens. This directly enables numerous service robotics tasks such as assistive and support robots, care for the elderly to allow them to stay autonomous at home for longer, interactive augmented reality applications and smart homes, or search and rescue missions.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Autonomy, Perception, Robotics, Scene Graphs, Scene Understanding

Title: Reducing Gender Bias in Detection of Autistic Spectrum Disorders Using a Co-Construction Approach with Computer Vision and Mixed Reality Exercises
Abstract:
Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder marked by deficits in social communication, restricted interests, and repetitive behaviors. Timely diagnosis and intervention are essential for enhancing the long-term prospects of those with ASD. Nonetheless, current diagnostic methods exhibit gender bias, resulting in the underdiagnosis of females with ASD. This project's primary objective is to create a novel, unbiased approach to early ASD detection using a co-construction method involving computer vision and mixed reality exercises. This proposed method addresses ASD diagnosis gender bias by offering an objective, engaging, and accessible detection tool.
The multidisciplinary research team composed of Social Work researchers, neurosciences researchers and computer science researchers will structure the project around 4 main workpackages, with 7 specific objectives:
1.Determine factors for identifying ASD in women without intellectual disabilities, addressing the unique challenges of diagnosing this population and improving understanding of ASD presentation in females.
2.Collaboratively create mixed reality exercises and a computer vision system using input from practitioners and individuals with ASD, ensuring that the developed tools are user-centered, relevant, and effective in addressing the distinct needs and experiences of people with ASD.
3.Develop a set of mixed reality exercises and cognitive game tasks designed to evaluate common ASD indicators and behaviors, with particular attention to incorporating gender-specific cues and scenarios.

Title: Fabrication of Scalable Photonic Neural Networks with Structural Nonlinearity
Abstract:
The energy required to advance artificial intelligence with state-of-the-art electronics is becoming prohibitive. This issue threatens to limit the application of machine learning and other advanced computation. To develop more sustainable approaches, researchers have sought alternatives to conventional electronics. One possibility is to use light, which offers several significant advantages over electrons for computing, including low losses and intrinsic parallelization in both space and frequency. Moreover, light can perform matrix–vector multiplications, the backbone of current deep-learning architectures. However, deep neural networks also require nonlinear activation functions between the individual layers to learn arbitrary relationships between data—a property called universality. In contrast to electrons, photons interact weakly with their surroundings. Thus, optical systems lack strong nonlinearities, limiting the capabilities of all-optical neural networks. Material nonlinearities could be exploited, but these require high light intensities, significantly reducing the energy efficiency of the optical approach.

Very recently, a new approach to nonlinearity (known as structural nonlinearity) was proposed. While in traditional photonic computing an input enters the physical system as an optical beam, followed by measuring the output beam, structural nonlinearity instead encodes the input in the parameters of the physical system. An optical beam is then used to probe the system, leading to a highly nonlinear relationship between the system parameters and the output beam. While photonic neural networks using this approach have recently been demonstrated, important questions remain. Under which conditions are photonic neural networks with structural nonlinearities universal? Which designs should be pursued in experiment? How can they be fabricated at scale to compete with electronic systems?

To address these key questions, this proposal requests funding for an experimental effort to create scalable photonic neural networks with structural nonlinearities. The applicant’s team can fabricate intricate diffractive surfaces (known as optical Fourier surfaces) for use in photonic neural networks. This capability, along with the team’s development of high-speed computational methods to simulate photonic systems, will enable the design and implementation of diffractive photonic neural networks with universal-function-approximation capabilities. A team of 3 doctoral students (one internally funded), bachelor/master’s students, and the applicant will pursue the following objectives: (a) develop and exploit processes to design optical Fourier surfaces for use in diffractive photonic neural networks with structural nonlinearity, (b) advance fabrication strategies to obtain transmissive optical Fourier surfaces in silicon nitride or high-refractive-index polymers for use in photonic neural networks, (c) build and measure diffractive photonic neural networks with structural nonlinearities based on the fabricated optical Fourier surfaces, (d) refine the designs using experimental measurements, and (e) train the system with physics-aware training and benchmark the performance on classification tasks. The expected outcome of this project will be much more expressive, scalable photonic neural networks at visible wavelengths.

Title: Transforming drift studies and monitoring freshwater organisms with the next-generation imaging device for riverine systems.
Abstract:
Many small riverine organisms rely on flow-mediated processes to complete their life cycles. One prime process is drift, a fundamental mechanism of downstream dispersal for aquatic invertebrates and fish larvae. The importance of drift in the life cycle of invertebrates and fish larvae is well documented. Yet, many aspects of drift remain to be quantified. Furthermore, a diverse collection of organisms, including benthic invertebrates and fish, play a crucial role in maintaining clean and healthy rivers and streams, so they are widely used as bioindicators in monitoring schemes to assess the quality of waters. However, the spatiotemporal resolution and laboriousness of current sampling methods used to study drift are considered limiting factors to advancing our knowledge about drift processes and monitoring programmes. The sheer work intrinsic to net sampling results in coarse-grained data about spatial and temporal variation in drift. We must streamline and enhance monitoring of aquatic biota with cost-effective, broadly deployable, and noninvasive methods that provide long-term (weeks-years) and continuous (hourly) data on species presence, abundance, and movement patterns to support research and evidence-based management actions.
With this project, I aim to bring the Riverine Organism Drift Imager (RODI) to fruition. I will capitalise on the prototype development and materialise RODI as an underwater camera system that will revolutionize our capacity to study and monitor drift in freshwater ecosystems. To achieve that, the project is organised into three work packages (WP). WP1. Engineer advances in hardware. Hardware improvements will be engineered for the underwater module and land station. WP2. Develop an image processing pipeline and machine learning (ML) algorithms to screen and classify drifting organisms. Tasks in this WP are distributed in four stages: image acquisition, screening, data storage, and classification of a drift event. Therefore, it will entail the development of efficient algorithms for the screening and classification of drifting organisms, as well as a database. One ML algorithm will be developed to optimize the screening process (identifying and extracting objects of interest in a video frame). A second ML will classify the screened organisms to different taxonomic levels. An image database will be structured to store and annotate images (as needed) from multiple objects (e.g. debris) and drifting organisms (i.e. objects of interest) and serve as input for training and validation of the ML classifiers. WP3. Perform a long-term drift study and calibrate RODI against traditional drift net sampling. We will conduct the first long-term field deployments with RODI to quantify riverine organism drift with high temporal resolution under different flow conditions. We aim to determine how different flow conditions (i.e. steady vs variable flows) impact the drift of invertebrates and fish by obtaining long temporal samples in the Gadmerwasser stream. In parallel, RODI sampling will be calibrated against traditional drift net samples. We will then understand how RODI can contribute as a tool for long-term monitoring and drift studies, capitalising on the knowledge gained with the prototype deployment on the same site.
RODI promises substantial value for both science and practice. This new technology will address fundamental gaps in our knowledge of the drift patterns of fish larvae and invertebrates. On the practical level, it will streamline and broaden freshwater biodiversity monitoring, providing critical data to decision-makers and other stakeholders and thus contributing to the development of more effective management strategies. I envisage RODI as the cornerstone that will support the quantitative and qualitative assessment of the ecological conditions of riverine ecosystems and freshwater diversity, supporting restoration and mitigation goals established by the Swiss Water Protection Law.

Title: The role of cognitive context in persuasion: language comprehension, information evaluation and motivated reasoning
Abstract:
My proposed project deals with the cognitive underpinnings of persuasion from the perspective of linguistics and psychology of reasoning. I look at pragmatic aspects of persuasive and manipulative communication, which I propose to analyze as exploiting language comprehension process and the cognitive mechanisms involved in it (Maillat & Oswald 2009, 2011, Maillat 2013). This situates my research between cognitive pragmatics (Sperber and Wilson 1995, Wilson and Sperber 2012), psychology of reasoning (Kahneman and Tversky 1974, 1983, 2000, Kahneman 2003, Stanovich, West & Toplak 2013, Evans 2003, 2007, Kunda, 1990; Lord, Ross, & Lepper, 1979)  and cognitive sciences in general.
 
I propose to account for persuasion in cases of fallacious (logically or rationally invalid) argument use by applying the model of language comprehension stated in Relevance Theory (Sperber & Wilson 1995) – a cognitive theory of language use – to the analysis of persuasive communication. I extend the Relevance Theoretical model in terms of its claims regarding context selection (a crucial cognitive operation in interpretation process) by using theories from psychology of reasoning to account for the inferential mechanisms driving context selection. I further expand the account of the information that is used for this interpretative process by including in it knowledge representations that are multi-modal and can involve perceived physiological responses to associated affective [emotional] states (as postulated by Barsalou, 1999, 2003, 2008, 2009, Pezzulo et al. 2011, 2013). This allows me to discuss perceptually-grounded emotional components found in mental representations and by extension in the interpretative context.

In my work I combine theoretical investigation with experimental research in the spirit of experimental pragmatics (Noveck & Sperber 2004, 2007, Pouscoulous & Noveck 2009) and experimental psychology of reasoning (Zajonc, 1969, Cacioppo & Petty, 1979, Ozubko & Fugelsang, 2011). My aim is to not only provide a theoretical model for the effects of persuasion but also to empirically test its predictions. In the end I hope to provide insight into the effectiveness of verbal persuasion and by extent to make claims about critical thinking and the critical mind in general.
Keywords: Linguistics, Persuasion, Pragmatics, Psychology of Reasoning

Title: Practical Planning with Ontologies (PPO)
Abstract: This project lies in the intersection of two research areas from the field of symbolic AI, namely AI Planning (AIP) and Knowledge Representation and Reasoning (KR), in particular reasoning with ontology languages. AIP deals with sequential decisions about actions to steer a system towards a desired goal state, while ontologies can describe expressive static constraints on the system's operation. The integration of procedural planning algorithms with reasoning over static knowledge repositories bears a great potential for synergies based on existing data and models, such as business process definitions, knowledge graphs, traditional databases, and operational planning/scheduling models. In this project, we build on the rich foundations of research in both areas to develop practical methods for solving planning problems enriched with background knowledge. On the one hand, we will analyse the relative expressivity of different combined planning and reasoning formalisms and develop compilations into classical formalisms where possible. On the other hand, we will develop these compilations and more dedicated algorithms into practical methods for planning with ontologies.
Keywords: Domain-independent Planning, Knowledge Representation and Reasoning, Ontologies

Title: Prediction of Lake Plankton Abundances
Abstract:
This project leverages a unique, decade-long, high-frequency dataset and cutting-edge interpretable machine learning to transform early-warning systems for harmful algal blooms (HABs) — protecting public health, supporting fisheries, and advancing freshwater ecosystem management.

-- Background -- 
Plankton are foundational to lake ecosystems, driving nutrient cycling and aquatic food webs. The autotrophic algae component of the plankton community, called phytoplankton, is on one side responsible for oxygen production, and on the other it can cause HABs. HABs can disrupt biodiversity, contaminate drinking water, and damage fisheries. Thus, predicting plankton abundances can provide decision makers with early warnings of upcoming HABs, guide mitigation strategies, and offer insights into ecosystem health and climate-driven changes.

-- Existing Limitations --
While progress has been made, predictions of HABs and of plankton abundances in general still face challenges related to data limitations, including frequency, duration and taxonomic resolution. These limitations hinder model training, reduce forecasting accuracy, and often
restrict predictions to coarse indicators like chlorophyll-a. Furthermore, while many current models can capture some predictive relationships, their limited interpretability often restricts deeper ecological understanding.

-- Aims --
We will exploit a novel dataset from Lake Greifensee, Switzerland, which overcomes these limitations by combining high frequency, high taxonomic resolution and range, and long temporal coverage. Using this dataset, we will:

- Develop and compare machine learning models, including interpretable models such as Neural ODEs — a first in lake plankton forecasting — capable of performing predictions based on plankton community dynamics, explicitly integrating ecological theory with cutting-edge machine learning approaches.

- Quantify the added value of high temporal frequency and taxonomic resolution for predictive performance.

- Perform both forecasting (predicting future abundances) and nowcasting (inferring current abundances from other data), enabling early warnings and filling measurement gaps.
 
-- Implications and Impact --
Improved plankton forecasting will support early-warning systems that safeguard public health, mitigate economic losses in fisheries and tourism, and inform sustainable water policy. Our unique dataset and explainable models can serve as national and international benchmarks
for ecological forecasting and guide investment decisions on monitoring infrastructure. Preliminary conversations indicate potential interest from several Swiss cantons in deploying our imaging systems in other lakes. Ultimately, this project aims to significantly advancing freshwater monitoring and HAB prediction, with methodologies that can be adapted to other aquatic ecosystems worldwide.

Title: Developing Bayesian Networks as a tool for Zoonotic Systems Epidemiology
Abstract:
A primary objective of many zoonotic epidemiological studies is to investigate hypothesized relationships between covariates of interest, and one or more outcome variables, through analyses of appropriate data. Typically, the biological, epidemiology and behavioural processes which generated this data are highly complex, resulting in multiple correlations/dependencies between covariates and also between outcome variables. Standard epidemiological and statistical approaches cannot adequately describe such inter-dependent multi-factorial relationships. Bayesian Network (BN) modelling is a generic and well established data mining/machine learning methodology, which has been demonstrated in other fields of study to be ideally suited to such analyses. The accessibility, however, of this methodology to epidemiologists is severely limited due to the sheer breadth and diversity of zoonotic epidemiological data, which is outside the established application areas of BN modelling. 

Two key challenges exist, one technical and one epidemiological. Firstly, no appropriate software exists for fitting the types of BN models necessary for analysing zoonotic epidemiological data, where complexities such as grouped/overdispersed/correlated observations are ubiquitous. This project will develop easy-to-use software to allow ready access to BN modelling to epidemiological practitioners, which is essential in order to make the crucial transition from merely a technically attractive methodology, to an approach which is actually used in practice. Secondly, to demonstrate and promote the use of this methodology in zoonotic epidemiology, relevant and high quality exemplar case studies will be developed showing objectively, situations in which BN models can offer the most added value, relative to existing standard statistical and epidemiological methods. Through the project's collaborators a diverse range of zoonotic data are available for analyses, including cross-sectional and longitudinal studies of antimicrobial resistance in Escherichia coli in farmed pigs in Canada, along with a wide range of different parasite field studies including Echinococcus multilocularis, Taenia, Mesocestoides, Uncinaria and Toxocara collected across eastern Europe and central Asia. 

This project will deliver a range of peer-reviewed publications comprising both methods orientated papers, and pathogen focused studies. The final deliverable of the project will be to provide a valuable addition to the quantitative skills base within veterinary science, by providing PhD level training in applied computational epidemiology of direct relevance to both zoonotic and animal disease research.

Title: Computational Brain Function: Advanced Tools for an Emerging Discipline
Abstract:
The goal of this project extension is to continue the research program that has been initiated by the SNSF professorship grant. In particular, it will allow to consolidate an independent research group dedicated to advanced signal processing in functional brain imaging. This group is jointly affiliated with the Department of Radiology and Medical Informatics at the University of Geneva (UniGE), and the Institute of Bioengineering at the Ecole Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL). The research objectives are to develop innovative tools and analysis schemes for neuroimaging data, and to tackle unprecedented questions about brain function. 

Functional brain imaging is playing an increasingly important role in neuroscience, biology and medicine. Advanced computational tools such as wavelet and machine learning are required to fully exploit the potential of the large and complex datasets at hand, though these tools need to be tailored to the signals under investigation. The scope of the signal-processing techniques that will be developed has been slightly broadened with respect to the main grant based on our experience in the field. While wavelets still play a central role (i.e., one Ph.D. student will finish her thesis on wavelet design for brain graphs to capture network changes in cognitive state and disease), we will also connect with tools from pattern recognition to make our techniques predictive and relevant for diagnosis and prognosis (i.e., this will be the last part of a second Ph.D. thesis). In addition, we will pay attention to make the bridge with groups in cognitive and clinical neurosciences. Finally, recent successful work on scale-free dynamics of EEG microstates will also be further investigated.

Title: Rockaval - Modelling the propagation of rock mass falls using machine learning and a refined energy line approach
Abstract:
Worldwide, residential areas and infrastructure that are built downslope from steep rock faces are potentially threatened by rockfall hazards. There is scientific evidence that further climate warming and permafrost degradation will lead to an increase of rock slope failures (RSF), especially in higher altitudes, further endangering transportation infrastructure and urbanised areas in mountains directly or indirectly. To come up with realistic predictions of the areas that are potentially endangered by rockfall hazards, modelling rockfall propagation, trajectories and/or runout zones is a method that provides important information. However, existing predictive models often lack accuracy and robustness, leading to uncertainties in decision-making processes. This research project proposes the development and testing of an advanced predictive model that integrates geological and topographical data to accurately predict the runout distance of rockfalls, rock mass falls and rock avalanches. 
The research hypotheses from which the RockAval project starts are 1) the dimensionless area below the slope profile of a rockfall trajectory (AUP) is a key variable for the definition of the statistical distribution of energy line angle for a given rockfall event at a given slope. 2) a Machine-Learning based model trained with (AUP) and other covariates of several thousands of rockfall events with varying volumes is capable of accurately predicting the runout of rockfall events ranging from rock particle fall to rock avalanches. To achieve the project goal, our scientific approach can be summarized as 1) the compilation of a well-documented and accessible rockfall past event database, 2) the development and testing of a new statistical models for rockfall runout zone prediction and 3) the application and validation of those models at regional scale. To implement the above described research approach, the RockAval project consists of 5 work packages. The first work packages (WP1) deals with all the management tasks in the project. In WP2, we will carry out the literature review including the assessment of existing Open Data relevant for this project. In WP3 we will compile the rockfall events database. In WP4, we will use machine learning to develop models for simulating rockfall runout zones and test these using 100 well documented rockfall events ranging from rock particle fall to rock avalanches. In WP5 we will apply and validate the best performing model for rock particle fall and blockfall in an area covering approx. 2500 km2 both in France and in Switzerland. We intend to publish 1 review paper, 1 data paper (and the Rockaval database) and 3 research papers during this project. We also intend to propose a session on machine learning for rockfall runout prediction at the European Geosciences Union and organise a Rockaval symposium at the end of the project.

Title: Next-Generation Network Analytics for Time Series Data
Abstract:
Network-based data mining techniques are an important foundation for data science applications in computer science, computational social science, economics and life sciences. They help us to extract knowledge from vast corpora of relational data that capture links or interactions between documents, humans, financial institutions, or genes. However, advances in data sensing and collection increasingly provide us with data that not only tell us who is linked to whom, but also when and in which order these links occur. The analysis of such time series data on networks is still a major challenge. A naive application of network analytic methods discards information on the timing and ordering of links, which however determine the causal topology of dynamic networks. Empirical studies show that this leads to wrong results about the importance of nodes, cluster structures, and dynamical processes. It invalidates applications of current network analytic methods in time series data and limits our understanding of networked systems with dynamic topologies.

Filling this gap, my goal as an SNSF professor is to develop a new generation of network analytic methods for time series data on networks. We will take an interdisciplinary perspective that combines stochastic models of time series data with graph analytic, algebraic and information-theoretic methods. It enables us to reach three objectives, namely to (i) develop network analytic techniques for sequential relational data capturing pathways in networks, (ii) extend these techniques to time-stamped data on dynamic networks with high temporal resolution, and (iii) implement a software package for the analysis of time series data on networks.

A novelty of our approach is the use of multi-order graphical models, i.e. compact static summarisations of time series data that capture the causal topology of dynamic networks. This will help us to advance the theoretical foundation of data science and network analysis. It will lead to scalable, time-aware methods to find important nodes and detect cluster structures in massive streams of relational data. We validate and test them in time series data on software development teams made available by an industry partner. 

The final deliverable of our project is an Open Source software implementation of our methods. A collaboration with the Swiss Data Science Center will help us to disseminate it in the Swiss data science community.  An international network of experts in network science, bioinformatics, computational epidemiology, computational social science, and machine learning will ensure the interdisciplinary impact of our project.

Title: People Analytics at Work. Intensive Case Studies of Pioneering Companies in Germany and Switzerland
Abstract:
People Analytics is part of a more general shift in management relying on data (Davenport 2006). It is focusing on the real-time acquisition, analysis, and prediction of employee performance and engagement, work and collaboration patterns. The fundamental assumption is that human experience and intuition in organizational decision-making should, to a substantial degree, be replaced by data leading to an ’evidence-based’ form of human resource management and a data-driven culture (BI Trend Monitor 2020; Kremser/Brunauer 2019). By collecting and connecting a great variety of data, People Analytics is designed to establish new ways to predict, evaluate, and control individual and organizational behavior (Loi 2020; Sousa et al. 2019; Manuti/de Palma 2018; Leicht-Deobald et al. 2019; Goodell King 2016; Marler/Boudreau 2017), leading to new visibilities and algorithmically imposed hierarchies at the workplace. The high relevance of People Analytics for the future of work stands in stark contrast to a lacking empirical knowledge about the practices and effects of algorithm-based decision-making systems in the area of Human Resources.
The implementation of People Analytics cannot solely be understood from a technical perspective. Quite to the contrary: in the form of a “corporate social graph” (Höller/Wedde 2018), it transfers the socially established logics of social networking to the sphere of work and organization (Staab/Geschke 2019). It relies on the ongoing transformation of work processes and organizational behavior into data, and on continuously connecting this data in manifold ways allowing ever new angles for the analysis of people and work (‘datafication’). How such an algorithm-based logic of social ordering (cf. Yeung 2017) is organizationally implemented, is one main focus of the project. To analyze the production of new visibilities, it draws on insights from the fields of the sociology of quantification (Diaz-Bone/Didier 2016) and ‘valuation studies’ (Lamont 2012) alike. From this perspective, People Analytics are not simply representing organizational reality in an objective manner. Rather, they are characterized by their performativity and reactivity (Espeland/Sauder 2007) informing the employees’ social actions, self-presentations, and identities in various ways. Based on comparative case studies of pioneering companies in Germany and Switzerland, the project analyzes the implementation dynamics of People Analytics. It investigates how a new regime of control based on data, calculation, and – at least in part – on Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning is actually being negotiated. On the case study level, it focuses on work which is both subjectified and algorithmically controlled, hereby revealing the micro-foundations of People Analytics. In a comparative perspective, it analyzes the influence of company-specific data cultures and external software suppliers as well as the impact of national legislation on these processes.
Keywords: Algorithm-based decision making and control, Human Resource Management, Quantification and Valuation, Workforce Analytics

Title: Unravelling the effects of the Miocene global warming event in the tropics
Abstract:
The Miocene climatic optimum (MCO) is a global warming event that occurred between 17-14 million years ago and was followed by a relative short period of cooling known as the Miocene climatic transition (MCT). The MCO is comparable in magnitude to the present and predicted future warming. In the ongoing climate change, it is apparent that temperature is increasing more rapidly at high latitudes than in the tropics. However, it is unclear whether tropical regions were also more resilient to rapid climate change in the past. While paleotemperature estimates are available from high latitudes, the effect of the MCO and the subsequent MCT in the tropics remains unknown, due to gaps in Miocene data and low fossil preservation rates in tropical regions in general. Furthermore, available paleoclimatic models do not provide a robust replacement to empirical data to understand the past climate change in the tropics. In this project, I will evaluate the magnitude of climate and environmental change at tropical latitudes during MCO and subsequent cooling period. 

Morphological traits of fossil mammals can be used to infer the paleoclimate and the traditional approach used linear regressions. I will build upon the most recent developments in machine learning to reconstruct the paleoclimate and paleoenvironment in the tropics using the mammal fossil record. I will use a dataset of 12 functional traits of extant herbivore mammals to train a neural network model for paleoenvironmental analyses. Then, I will use a unique set of trait data of mammals from the La Venta site, the most fossil-rich locality in the Neotropics, to quantify changes precipitation, temperature and primary productivity across a 3-million-year long time frame that includes the transition from the MCO to the MCT. Current evidence suggests that the temperature in the tropics increased less than at higher latitudes during global warming events. I hypothesize that the temperature decrease in La Venta after the MCO was smaller than the ~7°C decrease inferred for temperate regions. This research has the potential to provide accurate estimates of the temperature and other climatic variables in the tropics during the peak of the MCO and the MCT. Furthermore, it will provide a new methodological approach for paleoenvironmental reconstructions using neural networks, which I expect to outperform the regression methods previously used for this task.
Keywords: Global warming, Machine learning, Mammals, Paleoecology, Tropics

Title: Dynamics and Plasticity in System Models
Abstract:
The mammalian brain consists of a huge number of neurons connected to each other in a large recurrent network. Even in the relatively small brain of a mouse and with modern recording techniques only a small fraction of neurons can be observed simultaneously so that the interpretation of observations requires a solid theoretical framework. The project outlined in this grant proposal  contributes to the establishment of such a framework.

  The project is a theory-based modelling project and starts from the well-known facts that cortical neurons communicate with each other by short pulses of electrical activity, commonly called spikes. These spikes are sent across connections to thousands of other neurons. On this background, the project focuses on two separate problems of theoretical neuroscience. The first problem is the  mathematical characterization of the dynamics in a large network of spiking neurons given a fixed set of connections. An important insight from experiments is that the observed  dynamics are low-dimensional. The second problem arises from the observation that connections are not fixed for all time but can change - and this change, called plasticity,  is related to learning.  The project therefore contains two Work Packages (WP) which are broken down into specific subquestions:

 WP1 Neuronal Dynamics on the Systems Level.   
The objective of WP1 is to understand how the low-dimensional dynamics observed in recordings from  large-scale brain networks are linked to neuronal spiking patterns, to properties of  single neurons, and to connections between neurons. In particular, we aim to understand (i) how stochastic spiking of neurons can lead to stable low-dimensional 'rate-coded' dynamics even though the neuronal population is highly heterogeneous; (ii) what  large-scale recordings tell us about the receptive fields and heterogeneity of neurons; and (iii) how models of spiking neurons can be optimized to fit experimentally observed rodent brain activity neuron-by-neuron and trial-by-trial.  

WP2 Synaptic Plasticity for Development of Representations on the Systems Level.  
Visual processing occurs in the mammalian brain across multiple areas in which the representation of retinal images undergoes step-wise changes from local properties (such as edges) to more global properties of objects.  These representations are learned and fine-tuned during development, but we do not know biologically plausible rules of plasticity that enable the emergence of representations in an abstract space of objects. The objective of WP2 is to arrive at biologically plausible rules that can tune connections (without invoking machine learning algorithms that exploit BackProp) to yield a hierarchical representation such that in later areas the representation is more useful than in earlier ones. In particular we aim to understand (i) how an adaptive, and potentially sequential, scheme of learning rules enables fine tuning across different layers and different developmental phases; and (ii) how lateral connections within an area can contribute to powerful representations.

For each of the WPs and all tasks we combine mathematical modeling work with computer simulations.

Title: Next-generation data mining of organismal and ecological trait data across Arthropoda
Abstract:
Insects and other arthropods represent the most numerous and diverse animal group on Earth, with estimates of 5.5 million insect and 6.8 million terrestrial arthropod species (Stork 2018). They have fascinated researchers and amateur entomologists for centuries, leading to a vast accumulation of knowledge about how countless evolutionary adaptations have enabled them to exploit so many ecological niches (Grimaldi and Engel 2005). The most extensive knowledge is often biased towards the more illustrious species and those that serve as models in research, or that impact human health and agriculture. The decades of accrued learning also present substantial variability in terms of what types of organismal and ecological trait data have been collected and with which methodologies. More recently, this knowledge is being extended through the acquisition of increasing amounts of genomic data to explore the genetics underlying these traits. 
Initiatives such as the Darwin Tree of Life (DtoL) and the Earth Biogenome Project (EBP) are already starting to greatly accelerate arthropod genome sequencing (Lewin et al. 2018). This enables large-scale comparative analyses to identify patterns of gene and genome evolution within and between the many Orders of arthropods (Thomas et al. 2020). The ultimate aim is often to then try to understand how these changes relate to observable phenotypic differences between species: how do novelties and shifts arise and how have they contributed to the success of arthropods? Linking genomic evolution to key organismal and ecological traits currently relies largely on the collective expertise of the researchers involved, and many connections remain mostly anecdotal rather than quantitatively analytical. Thanks to ongoing developments in bioinformatics, comparative genomic analyses are generally scalable to increasingly larger datasets. However, even the most informed scientific minds cannot capture and hold the myriad forms of trait data required for large-scale quantitative analyses.
This SPARK project therefore proposes to leverage the power of approaches from next-generation text mining with artificial intelligence and machine learning methods (Moreno et al. 2019), and apply this to kick-start the construction of a comprehensive, centralised, and updateable resource of organismal and ecological trait data across Arthropoda. Methods developed for text analytics and natural language processing of biomedical literature will be leveraged to achieve three major goals: to develop a comprehensive codebase with informatics workflows that collate and assess biological trait data; to build the first large-scale standardised database that collates arthropod organismal and ecological trait data from a wide range of primary (scientific publications) and secondary (reviews, books, databases) sources; and to develop an arthropod trait ontology to power both mining efforts and future research through large-scale quantitative analyses of trait data. Additional outcomes will include assessments of the value of different types of sources for gathering such trait data, and an overview of the possibilities that image analysis could offer to further enhance mining of trait data. There will clearly be many gaps in the knowledge gathered, but the results will help to clearly define organismal and ecological traits that are most difficult to accurately extract from published sources as well as traits that appear to be missing, thereby providing direction to future trait cataloguing efforts.
This SPARK project will therefore bring two usually very distant fields of entomology and informatics together to combine their different expertise and develop modern resources that will greatly benefit researchers working in the fields of arthropod biodiversity and evolution.
Keywords: arthropods, ecology, evolution, resource, text-mining, traits

Title: Chemigenetic Probes for the Near-Infrared Imaging Windows
Abstract:
This proposal tackles the challenges of fluorescent protein-based imaging in the near-infrared (NIR) region by integrating small-molecule engineering and protein design. The central hypothesis is that combining these approaches will yield chemigenetic probes with enhanced photophysical properties beyond 750 nm, providing superior selectivity and contrast for in vivo imaging. Current NIR-emitting proteins lack brightness and coverage past 750 nm, and traditional dyes like rhodamines have relatively short emission wavelengths, limiting deep-tissue imaging. Polymethine dyes, particularly in the NIR-II window (1000–1700 nm), show promise but require a broadly applicable fluorogenic strategy.

To address this gap, we developed polymethine dyes with reversible cyclization, delivering high fluorogenicity in the NIR region. We also created a brighter, more red-shifted NIR-emitting probe than existing proteins. Concurrently, SNAP-tag and HaloTag were engineered for better brightness and binding kinetics, supported by preliminary data suggesting de novo protein design and continuous evolution can boost hybrid probe performance significantly.

The proposal is organized into three main objectives. First, we will develop highly fluorogenic NIR-I probes by refining polymethine dyes for self-labeling proteins like SNAP-tag and HaloTag, involving dye and linker tuning, protein engineering, and high-throughput screening via fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS). Second, we aim to create NIR-II fluorogenic probes by synthesizing extended polymethine dyes and optimizing protein partners to improve binding kinetics and fluorogenicity in the deeper NIR range. Third, we will design minimalistic NIR dyes for enhanced in vivo imaging, focusing on cyclizable merocyanine dyes and engineered CRABP2 variants that facilitate ring-opening for high-contrast labeling.

We will employ generative artificial intelligence and continuous evolution through orthogonal replication, coupled with yeast surface display and FACS, building on early successes in chemigenetic probe engineering. Collaborations with leading in vivo imaging groups will ensure thorough validation and testing against realistic imaging challenges.
Keywords: fluorescent probes, live-cell imaging, near-infrared imaging, protein engineering

Title: Mapping Rho GTPase signaling networks through acute, dynamic stimulation of spatio-temporal signaling fluxes.
Abstract:
Rho GTPases are signaling molecules that regulate cytoskeletal dynamics. Current models state that each GTPase regulates one specific cytoskeletal polymer: Rac1 controls membrane protrusion, Cdc42 controls filopodium formation, and RhoA regulates contractility. Recent developments in technologies to visualize Rho GTPase spatio-temporal activation dynamics have however revealed a much more complex picture. During fibroblast leading edge protrusion, or neuronal growth cone motility, RhoA, Rac1 and Cdc42 are all activated in micrometer-sized, overlapping subcellular domains. Furthermore, their activity fluctuates on time scales of tens of seconds. Such a complex spatio-temporal signaling program most likely serves to precisely position specific cytoskeletal regulating activities to fine tune these morphogenetic events. Understanding this signaling complexity requires a systematic approach to answer two fundamental questions: 1. What are the mechanisms that shape the specific subcellular Rho GTPase activation patterns in time and space ? 2. What is the function of each Rho GTPase with respect to cytoskeletal regulation ?
This proposal builds on novel technologies and conceptual frameworks our lab has recently evolved. Specifically, we have: 1. built 2nd generation, improved RhoA, Rac1 and Cdc42 FRET-based biosensors; 2. performed initial characterization of the function of all Rho GTPase interactors (upstream regulators such as GEFs and GAPs, downstream effectors) during growth cone motility; 3. set up an automated growth cone segmentation computer vision pipeline to characterize their dynamics. One important problem we are currently facing is that “long term application” of any molecular perturbation (by example by means of RNAi-mediated knockdown), alters cell morphology and morphodynamics, affecting mechanical feedbacks that impinge on spatio-temporal control of Rho GTPases. This precludes a clear understanding of the causal events that leads to altered Rho GTPase regulation in response to a molecular perturbation.
Here, by integrating genome editing and chemical biology techniques, we propose to solve this very specific issue, by evolving a technology that acutely applies the perturbation at the same temporal scale than Rho GTPase signaling fluctuates. Using this technology, we will systematically perturb a panel of endogenous Rho GTPase regulators (GEFs and GAPs) on time scales of tens of seconds. We will then record Rho GTPase activation dynamics (using FRET biosensors), as well as downstream cytoskeletal dynamics in response to these perturbations during both neuronal growth cone and fibroblast motility model systems. Our computer vision algorithms will be used to quantify the cellular responses to these perturbations. By answering the two questions mentioned at the beginning of this summary, our integrated approach has the potential to unambiguously deconvolve a spatio-temporal Rho GTPase signaling network at systems biology level. An important component of such a systems biology level understanding, is that it might indicate emergent properties that allow for robust manipulation of cell migration or growth cone motility for biomedical purposes.

Title: Machine learning modular forms
Abstract: The implementation of machine learning algorithms to study phenomena in pure mathematics is a very recent program. In this project we test the accuracy of standard machine learning techniques in the study of classical modular forms, and investigate which specific features of modular forms are the most relevant for different machine learning algorithms.

Title: Basal forebrain regulation of the default mode network
Abstract:
A great deal of the research into brain function has focused on how features of the external world are represented by neural activity. However, much of our cognitive life involves periods of inwardly directed attention, reliant upon intrinsically generated neural activity, often to the exclusion of attention to the external world. Reliance upon internalized models is adaptive, as it allows us to automatically perform repetitive tasks with a high degree of efficiency, freeing up cognitive resources. Externally directed attention also has obvious advantages, allowing us to react to changing environmental exigencies, for example heralding danger or reward availability. Successful behavior thus depends upon the ability to quickly transition between periods of inwardly vs. outwardly directed attention.

In humans, periods of inwardly directed attention, as well as the performance automatized behaviors, has been associated with activation of the default mode network (DMN), originally described as a collection of interconnected cortical brain regions. Recent work, including work from our laboratory, suggests that the basal forebrain, an in particular its’ ventral pallidum (VP) nucleus, serves as a subcortical DMN node. In addition to accumulating correlational evidence, there are now also some causal studies using cell-type specific modulation of VP circuits that support the idea that VP is part of the DMN, and may indeed play a key role in triggering and maintaining a default mode brain state. While an involvement of the VP appears clear, it is unknown which of the efferent VP projections are involved in DMN-related functional modulation. Here, we therefore aim to examine pathways that mediate DMN related activations originating in the VP. We plan to perform optogenetic, celltype- and pathway-specific circuit dissection to assess the contribution of three major potential pathways, involving direct projections to cortex as well as indirect projections via the mediodorsal thalamus and the lateral habenula. The second major aspect of this proposal concerns the question how the newly discovered DMN-related basal forebrain nucleus VP interacts with other basal forebrain nuclei, such as the nucleus basalis, which support attention and allocate brain resources to sensory processing. Indeed, the basal forebrain has long been associated with promoting attention and arousal, and with the newly discovered DMN-related nucleus VP it is unclear how these divergent and, in a sense, opposing regulatory functions are accomplished by the basal forebrain. We hypothesize that the nuclei, similar to the cortical networks, are not active together but rather in alternation, depending on whether the animal is in an inwardly or outwardly focused behavioral state. We also posit that activation of the VP is expected to compromise behavioral performance of an attentional task. We address these questions using suitable behavioral paradigms, analysis of spontaneous endogenous behaviors analyzed using deep learning as well as optogenetics and neural activity during behavior.

We anticipate that our work will be of particular interest to the large community of researchers involved in functional imaging of resting state networks in humans. Our results may eventually provide the basis for novel therapeutic approaches for the multitude of brain disorders that bear relation to the human DMN, by revealing specific subcortical neuronal pathways that could be targeted using deep-brain stimulation or optogenetic manipulations.
Keywords: neuromodulation, neurophysiology

Title: Theorizing identity-based competition: The case of formation and erosion of competitive positions among political parties
Abstract:
Competition is a central process in every society, but its current theorization is unnecessarily restrictive in its focus on product-centric competition. In this project we broaden the theorization of competition to include situations where competition is not primarily on the technical aspects of the products offered, but on the identification of a customer with the identity of an organization – what we term identity-based competition. Identity-based competition is important in many, but not all, markets – and it is central in the competition among political parties.
We draw on the organization theory literatures of identity and social categorization to expand competition theory to include identity-based competition. A core question concerns competitive differentiation, which in product markets is structured around a dominant design or technology. Building on our earlier work, we propose that identity-based competition is structured around an ‘identity template’ – i.e. the taken for granted scale on which organizations can seek to differentiate their identities. The processes of formation and disbanding of identity templates are, however, unclear. We hypothesize, and test empirically, that an identity template forms as expectations of the customers and producers harmonize and become institutionalized around a type of identity differentiation, and that it can be abandoned through a process of de-institutionalization.
The study of identity-based competition requires longitudinal, detailed, data on the identity positioning of competing organizations. Our empirical setting, the democratic systems of the UK and Sweden, is a clear example of identity-competition: parties compete for votes using their organizational identity and voters construct their own identity through their voting. The focus of our study is the abandonment of the Left-Right ideological scale as an identity template, and the formation of a new identity template. The UK and Sweden make an interesting comparison as they differ in the stability of the Left-Right ideological scale as an identity template. This setting lets us observe the competitive process in an unusually detailed manner as the main identity positioning tool of parties, their election manifestos, are available in an open-access content-coded text corpus. Furthermore, the responses of the ‘customers’ – i.e. voters – are tracked in polls and election outcomes are analyzed by the media and political scientists. Modeling the competitive identity positioning of parties, and the corresponding shifts in voter preferences over the period 1950-2019 will allow us to trace the gradual abandonment of the Left-Right identity template, and the formation of a new identity template.
To do this, we must extend the publicly available data in three ways: 1) To capture the competitive formation and erosion of identity positions we will use natural language processing (NLP) methods to mine the manifesto project corpus to identify the evolving identity template in use by parties. 2) To model the role of the voters in the formation of the evolving template we will mine polling and survey data, using relational class analysis methods. 3) To model the internal organizational processes of identity change we will mine archival data on internal party structure, demography and strategies that shape their decisions on competitive identity work.
The outcome of the project is a formulation, and initial empirical validation, of a novel theory of identity-based competition. This is fundamental to how academics, practitioners and policy makers understand markets and democratic systems in modern society. The project is carried out by the PI (USI) and the co-applicant Professor Filippo Carlo Wezel (USI), together with one post-doctoral fellow and one PhD student and an associated researcher Soorjith Karthikeyan of Indian Institute of Management, Udaipur.
Keywords: Competition, Organization Theory, Organizational Identity

Title: AI and Democracy: an Experiment
Abstract: This research project explores the current uses of AI in the citizen-government relation through a broad pluri-disciplinary literature review, 50+ expert interviews, an academic workshop, an online citizen consultation (on AI and democracy), and a survey sent to local and cantonal public administrations in Switzerland (in collaboration with two other academic institutions). This study shows that AI is already used by many governments in Europe to optimise and automate services and decision-making processes, including e-government services, political campaigning, and surveillance. Due to the specific characteristics of AI, these new practices raise numerous ethical and governance concerns, and increase the level of risk and uncertainty in the citizen-government relation. By adopting a design justice perspective, this study also highlight the asymmetry of power among actors in the development, management and use of AI. In this context, there is an urgent need to raise awareness and literacy about AI among citizen.

Title: V-MAV (Cooperative micro aerial vehicles using onboard visual sensors)
Abstract:
The overall aim of the project is to advance the capabilities of visual controlled MAV’s in the are-as of flight behavior and autonomy, cooperative operation, cognitive abilities and in addition to decrease the size of such an MAV. Advances in these areas would enable new fields of applica-tions for MAV’s and path the way to further research topics in mobile robotics. The proposed research proposal is structured into three work packages:

1.Visual-inertial MAV pose estimation and localization using multi-camera systems
2.Embedded vision algorithms for dynamic flight of small scale MAV’s
3.Methods for cooperative visual localization and semantic mapping

Work package 1 will investigate the suitability of multi-camera systems for 6DOF pose estima-tion and localization for MAV’s performing dynamic maneuvers. This will include the develop-ment of visual-inertial pose estimation algorithms exploiting the advantages of multi-camera system geometries.

Work package 2 will investigate embedded computer vision algorithms to facilitate dynamic con-trol and flight as well as a further miniaturization of MAV’s. For this, specific components of the visual control system will be moved to dedicated embedded processors to achieve the necessary high-frame rates for dynamic flight.

Work package 3 will investigate cooperative operation of MAV’s focusing on cooperative visual localization, mapping and cognitive scene understanding and interpretation. In cooperative op-eration MAV’s should be able to share their individual knowledge of the environment and incor-porate knowledge of others with the effect of improving environment mapping and the self locali-zation process. An important part of this research package is cognitive scene understanding. The MAV’s should make use of object detection and classification methods to generate a seman-tic description of the environment to produce a semantically annotated 3D environment map and also to use this meta-information to improve the mapping process (e.g. adapt parameters based on the semantics) or the localization process.

The proposed project will combine the competences of the three involved partners, ETHZ, TUM and TUG. All the three partners have year-long experience in vision controlled MAV through various projects and performed ground breaking work in this area. The common project will ensure the utilization of the combined expertise of the partners.
Keywords: Computer Vision, Micro aerial vehicle, Mobile robotics, SLAM

Title: Design and application of CytoxPred. Machine-learning to predict cancer cell lines targeted by small molecules
Abstract:
A rapidly growing amount of information regarding phenotypic cytotoxicity of small molecules is currently recorded in publicly available databases, such as ChEMBL. This information has reached a level of diversity, quality and extent that allows its exploitation by machine learning approaches to predict the cell lines that could be sensitive to given small molecules. Capitalizing on our experience in predicting protein targets of bioactive small molecules, our overall goal is to develop CytoxPred, a new machine learning model able to accurately predict the cancer cell lines targeted by small molecules. CytoxPred predictions will be generated by reverse screening based on the similarity principle, which hypothesizes that similar molecules are prone to be toxic for the same cell lines. CytoxPred will be built on a highly curated training set of cytotoxicity phenotypic data extracted from publicly available databases. The high quality of data is a key prerequisite for applying properly our own machine learning methodology in order to generate quantitative predictions of cytotoxicity profiles, from small molecule structure.
Importantly and additionally, thanks to our expertise in protein target prediction, we are in a unique position to predict not only the cell lines sensitive to given compounds, but also the mode of action of this predicted cytotoxicity, in terms of possible protein binding. This could open the road to drug discovery and development strategies relying not only on existing experimental information but also on robust biological activity predictions. Here, we will focus on cancer-related compounds and cell lines, to benefit from the expertise of the applicant and research partners in oncology.
We plan to meet these challenging objectives by addressing the following specific aims.
In Aim 1, we will optimize the quality of the data collected from ChEMBL, regarding the target cell line of small molecules, by fine-tuning the selection criteria for data retrieval and by carefully curating the output by our own cancer biology expertise, as well as by crossing-checking with specialized third-party resources including the Cellosaurus, Register of Misidentified Cell Lines, or CanSAR.
In Aim 2, we will build advanced models for CytoxPred by including 2D and 3D similarity between molecules along with other parameters to optimize the description of properties like physicochemistry, kinetics of cell penetration, and propensity to lead to aggregators or to promiscuous compounds.
In Aim 3, we will investigate the feasibility and practicability of the strategy consisting in combining CytoxPred and SwissTargetPrediction, to predict not only cancer cell lines that could be sensitive to given compounds, but also to possibly decipher the mode of action of this cytotoxicity, if it can be explained by protein binding. 
In Aim 4, we will ultimately validate experimentally the predictions made in Aim 2 in selected cancer cell lines, by measuring cell viability and proliferation after in vitro treatment with selected compounds. Moreover, we will validate whether the protein targets predicted in Aim 3 are directly responsible for the observed cytotoxicity. Several experimental validation cycles will be executed to enhance the development pipeline of the in-silico prediction models and to optimize their performance. When possible, for a small number of cases, organoid culture will be setup and final experimental validation will be conducted in transgenic and Patient Derived Xenograft.
The feasibility of the project is endorsed by (i) the long-term experience of the applicant in the fields of cheminformatics, computer-aided drug design, ligand-protein interaction, molecular fingerprints and computational science, and by the considerable in-house computational power as well as (ii) the existing collaboration with Elisa Oricchio’s group whose expertise in cancer genetic and pre-clinical studies using in vitro and in vivo models is expected to have a critical impact on the relevance of the data employed and on the quality of the experimental validation.
The new CytoxPred application will complement the widely used portfolio of computer-aided drug design tools developed by the applicant and provided to the scientific community through freely accessible web sites.

Title: Advanced statistical mechanics and random matrix methods for learning and inference
Abstract:
The spectacular progress of learning algorithms for data processing is transforming the way we do science and solve engineering problems. The applications are advancing at high pace in numerous disciplines, for example, vision and pattern recognition, language processing, genetics, drug design, material science, physical sciences. This progress draws on the intertwined disciplines of high- dimensional statistics, inference, and learning theory. A fundamental mathematical challenge in this nexus is the inference or learning of high-rank objects, generally high-rank matrices. In particular we are in need of a satisfactory theory of statistical and computational phase transitions in the high-dimensional and high-rank asymptotic regime.

This project proposes to use advanced tools from statistical mechanics and field theory (in theoretical physics) to investigate high-dimensional inference paradigms involving learning of high- rank matrices. The paradigms comprise high-rank matrix estimation, factorization, learning weights of neural networks (which all have a host of applications). The aim is to advance our conceptual and technical understanding of these paradigms, notably their phase transitions and statistical-to- computational gaps, by analyzing rigorously solvable models in asymptotic regimes. We propose to use techniques from the so-called large-N matrix models, spherical integrals, and orthogonal polynomials, in statistical mechanics and random matrix theory, as well as new ideas from non- equilibrium statistical mechanics. These techniques have not received much attention in inference and learning, and I strongly believe they will be impactful. The objectives are:

1. Use tools from large-N matrix models and adapt them to rigorously determine information theoretical and statistical limits of learning and inference in high-rank matrix estimation, and specific models of multilayer neural networks. High-dimensional spherical integrals and orthogonal polynomial methods have applications in inference.

2. Study stochastic gradient-flow dynamics (Langevin, SGD) for high-rank matrix estimation and neural networks focusing on the eigenvalue/singular value dynamics of the weight matrices of the layers (similarly to Dyson’s Brownian motion model for eigenvalues of random matrices). Uncover what is the relationship with recent approaches; for example mean-field limits based on Vlasov-McKean equations.

3. Introduce a principled study of non-equilibrium dynamics in inference and learning through the use of well defined multi-bath stochastic gradient flow dynamics. Compare these non-equilibrium estimators with respect to the traditional equilibrium ones.

This research should significantly expand the boundaries of our theoretical toolbox for the analysis of the high-dimensional and high-rank asymptotic regime. The necessary expertise combines methods and insights coming from different disciplines, namely statistical mechanics and other subfields of theoretical physics, information and coding theory, inference. The specific problems tackled are timely and regularly bring together scientists from different horizons, as can be witnessed by recent international meetings, and provide unique training to the PhD students.
Keywords: Dyson brownian motion, high-rank matrix factorization, inference, langevin dynamics, learning, matrix models, multi-bath dynamics, neural networks, random matrix theory, statistical mechanics

Title: Sparse sequence estimation for inverse problems and concomitant sparsity
Abstract:
The research project is in Statistics and in application of Optimization to Statistics. The general research  area is in statistical machine learning which consists in extracting pertinent information from data, mainly with nonparametric methods, to study and analyze phenomena such as astrophysical or financial data. 
Following on Occam's razor's principle that aims at representing objects in the sparsest or most parsimonious manner, researchers have been interested in sparsity.
The goal of the proposed research project is to investigate extensions of the work on sparsity to the situation of inverse problems and concomitant signals recording, using Markov random field, total variation, wavelets, sparsity methodologies, in applied fields such as Astronomy, Medical imaging and Finance. A key idea we are building on is the idea of an estimator defined as the fixed point of a set of nonlinear equations where a differentiable thresholding function is involved. Among other nice properties, differentiability allows derivation of the Jacobian of the estimator needed to estimate the risk unbiasedly based on the result of Stein. Sardy studied some theoretical and empirical properties of this new estimator in the standard regression setting. We intend to extend its use to more complex settings and  to provide improved estimators compared to existing estimators already proposed in the extensive litterature on sparsity, block thresholding and inverse problems. Our goal is to develop and publish methods that are fully automatic and that offer a clear advantage in practice over competitive methods already available.
Keywords: Astrophysics, Block thresholding, Inverse problem, Sparsity, Wavelet
