Title: Evaluating arguments in online discussions: a descriptive study of a normative process
Abstract:
Background and rationale: With the proliferation of social media, online platforms became a central space for the discussion of social and political issues. Although online discussions have been studied from different angles, little attention has been paid to the way in which discussants set normative standards by themselves in these contexts. Studying how people evaluate each other’s arguments in online forums is important to understand the processes that shape public opinion since the perceived quality of arguments influences and reflects individuals’ opinions.

Objectives and aims: This research project draws on argumentation theory to investigate how people evaluate each other's arguments on social media platforms. Its main objective is to develop a procedure to determine which arguments in a discussion are stronger according to people’s evaluation. To achieve this goal, a theoretical model will be constructed to account for the different means that discussants employ to assess the quality of their arguments.

Data and methodology: The data for this project comes from social media posts where users discuss about artificial intelligence controversies. A corpus will be collected by scraping posts from social media platforms. To determine which arguments in a discussion are stronger, three different analyses are performed. The first analysis reconstructs the argumentative structure of discussions to identify how arguments and counterarguments are related to each other. The second analysis consists in annotating the corpus to categorize the evaluative judgments that users make of each other’s arguments. The third step involves including metadata from the social media platforms, such as liking or voting comments, to supplement the previous analyses.

Results and impact: The results of this project should allow us to identify the most important arguments in online discussion according to people’s evaluations. The theoretical model developed for this research should also provide insights on how public opinion is shaped in the context of online discussions. Lastly, the study would provide necessary knowledge in the field of argumentation about the normative standards that arguers employ in their interactions.
Keywords: Argumentation theory, Corpus linguistics, Discourse analysis, Normative standards, Online discussions

Title: RIA: Novel Framework for Generative Architectural Design using AI-Agents
Abstract:
Architects are skilled at discovering and codifying a project’s value system and turning it into a physical artifact. Two main paradigms of design cognition explain this ability: Rational-Problem-Solving (RPS), which is the basis of all computational approaches in generative design, and Reflection-in-Action (RIA), which, despite its closer alignment with design practice, has not been implemented in any computational approach to date. RIA excels in navigating complex or ambiguous problems by dynamically adjusting strategies in response to emerging design problems. Donald Schön refers to the phrase “conversation with situation” to describe the reflexive process of problem-solution co-evolution, that leads to more innovative and tailored solutions beyond what formulaic methods (RPS) can deliver.
The release of ChatGPT has ushered in a new computational era, characterized by multimodal generative AI and Large Language Models (LLMs), that allow us to ‘talk’ to anything. Utilizing the conceptual reasoning and generative capabilities of LLMs, we aim to create an AI-Agent framework based on the Reflection-in-Action (RIA) paradigm, marking a new direction for computational approaches in generative architectural design.
Our main research question is: How suitable are LLM-enabled AI-Agents to develop a generative architectural design framework after the Reflection-in-Action paradigm?
We aim to develop a proof of concept prototype of an AI-Agent equipped with 1) a dataset of architectural strategies (move-impact pairs) and 2) actions grounded in a geometric environment to generate and modify a schematic model of a building. We will extract move-impact pairs via LLM from a large selection of existing architectural projects and their descriptions. The geometric environment will be developed with an open-source geometric kernel. Validation of outputs will be conducted through a custom-built LLM-as-judge routine and architect user studies. The research will be undertaken by a three-member team over 12 months, structured around three main work packages: Dataset, Development and Validation. 
The integration of computational methods in architecture has streamlined and optimized workflows, yet the potential of RIA remains unexplored. This gap is significant because RIA embodies the intuitive, iterative process intrinsic to architectural design, where ideas are continuously evaluated and adjusted based on new information and insights. Integrating RIA into an AI-Agent capable of generating and comprehending the impact of design decisions opens a profound opportunity to build co-creative tools (copilots) that can catalyze innovation in architecture.
Keywords: AI Agents, Architectural Design, Copilots, Design Cognition, Generative Design, Large Language Models (LLMs)

Title: Multilevel predictions of the naturalistic course and treatment response in major depression disorder
Abstract:
The present research project identifies candidate Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) subtypes based on multisource data and examines their predictive power to the naturalistic course of major depression and treatment response. This project focuses on MDD because it constitutes one of the leading causes of disability around the world and is ranked in the top places of the global burden of diseases. Two causes of this large burden are the long-term chronicity and the heterogeneity in the symptoms that characterize MDD. However, most research has considered this disorder as episodic and unitary. Such false assumptions bring detrimental consequences to the prognosis of most depressed patients and consequently, to decisions on the type of care appropriate. To shed new insights on these issues, the present research project aims to identify multilevel markers of MDD subtypes and their capacity to individually predict the course of MDD in terms of remission, as well as their individual predictive power on the response to different treatments, such as exercise treatment, psychotherapy, and pharmacotherapy. The novel methodological framework implemented here is featured by the integration of multilevel data (i.e., clinical, multiomics, and brain imaging). The obtained results will ground a new avenue to the understanding of psychiatric disorders from a multilevel perspective in longitudinal settings.
Two studies will be carried out to achieve our research aim. Study 1 will evaluate the predictive power of multilevel biological systems on the naturalistic course of MDD (i.e., 2-year remission status). We expect to clearly define MDD subtypes based on the integration of multilevel data. Moreover, multilevel modeling will better predict 2-year remission status in MDD than models including a single biomarker. Study 2 will examine the predictive power of multilevel biosystems in response to different therapeutic MDD interventions. Our hypotheses hold distinct predictive scores between MDD subtypes in response to the type of therapy. Also, multilevel data outperforms the predictive power of one-level markers. The aims described will be achieved through the implementation of supervised and unsupervised statistical learning. This methodology is more valuable than traditional statistical approaches because they 1) indicate how well a model works on the individual subject level. 2) They forecast outcomes that are unobserved by inferential methods. 3) They easily handle complex nonlinear interactions between input and output variables. This research project will be carried out at the Department of Psychiatry, University Medical Center (UMC) Amsterdam, under the co-supervision of Prof. Brenda Penninx (Amsterdam UMC), and Prof. Jennifer Labus (University of Los Angeles, California. UCLA). It will utilize collected data from the Mood Disorders Precision Medicine Consortium (MDPMC. https://sites.duke.edu/mdpmc/) an international team of experts aimed to improve the individualization of treatments through disentangling the biology of mood disorders and their variation in response to therapeutic interventions, from a multimodal and multilevel perspective.
Overall, this research project aims to advance precision medicine, which prioritizes predictions over associations, in order to provide personalized benefits to patients. The discovery of multilevel-oriented MDD markers will directly impact current one-size-fits-all diagnostic approaches that assume the existence of syndromes with a fixed set of symptoms identical for all patients. Also, research on prognostic biomarkers of MDD course would have great clinical utility for care planning and targets for intervention. Today, most MDD patients receiving health care take antidepressants. However, the potential side effects on the disease course of such neurochemical modulations are far from clear. Research on multilevel biomarkers with focus on the prediction of MDD recurrence will contribute to better clinical decision-making regarding treatment and remission.

Title: Understanding the climate challenge
Abstract: This research project aims to set up a rigorous conceptual and epistemological framework for understanding the causal and explanatory nature of the possible links between climate change on the one hand and climate extreme events and tipping points on the other hand. The project is structured around two workpackages. The first one will develop an interventionist approach (e.g. involving causal modelling methods) to causal (and explanatory) claims in extreme event attribution studies. This conceptually rigorous framework will facilitate the identification and the elaboration of the relevant sort of causal information that is adequate for the purpose under consideration (adaptation, litigation, communication). The second workpackage will investigate the possibilistic and counterfactual methodology (e.g. in terms of storylines) as a way to manage the deep uncertainties related to tipping points. The global Earth system science perspective on tipping points will be critically assessed combining philosophy of science and social science perspectives, in particular when it comes to human and social dimensions of Earth system tipping points.

Title: Demystifying artificial photosynthesis catalysts with a novel neural network architecture that explains itself
Abstract:
Our goal is to devise a novel water-splitting ruthenium catalyst for artificial photosynthesis (APS), a chemical process crucial for a number of future renewable energy sources. However, the complexity and size of the enzyme and its active site in natural photosynthesis necessitates the use of model systems, such as transition metal complexes, to investigate it. We aim to create a novel neural architecture that allows for accurate and rapid property predictions of such model systems, outpacing traditional methods and enabling high-throughput virtual screening. Moreover, we will design an XAI (explainable artificial intelligence) method that extracts abstractions from the neural network to assist and eventually automate rational design of new systems.
In Phase I, we will assemble a new dataset focusing on ruthenium catalysts for machine learning. Using a machine learning force field trained on density functional theory calculations, we will create a time series dataset for a state-of-the-art catalyst. Concurrently, we will sample single-point data from experimentally verified catalysts and create new data for additional catalysts using a cutting-edge diffusion probabilistic model. This data will be benchmarked with complete active space second-order perturbation theory and density matrix renormalization group. We will gather experimental properties such as turn-over numbers and calculated electronic properties.
In Phase IIa, we propose an original point group adapted neural network architecture, highly effective for the symmetries found in transition metal complexes to predict their properties. By leveraging point group constraints not only for rigid but also non-rigid symmetries (e.g. a rotating group) and treating de- viations from perfect symmetries as perturbations, we anticipate a reduction in the amount of data needed for accurate predictions.
In transition metal chemistry, the presence of different length scales calls for the use of higher-order abstractions, such as ligands or functional groups for designing new model systems and understanding their properties. To make use of this higher-order information, in Phase IIb, we propose a hierarchical approach that agnostically learns molecular abstractions (groups of atoms) through differentiable graph pooling. By comparing these abstractions with functional groups, we can gain insights into when heuristics based on functional groups might fail and when new, task-specific concepts are required. These learned abstractions will then be used as input in a subsequent block of the same network, enhancing the transferability and long-range capability.
Lastly, in Phase III, we will develop a pioneering XAI method that will explain the model in terms of the previously learned abstractions, going beyond current atom-level sensitivity analyses. Based on layer-wise relevance propagation, invented in the Müller group, these explanations will reduce the black-box character of the neural network approach. They make the process accessible to human reasoning and automation, hence suitable for rational design of new model system candidates. Exploring collaboration with the UniSysCat Cluster of Excellence, we aim to devise and synthesize a candidate with machine-assistance.
The power of chemical concepts serves as a driving force behind the development of new APS model systems. By extracting relevant abstractions from a neural network to guide expert chemists, we can establish a new approach for machine-assisted rational catalyst design, closing the loop between data generation, modeling, and explanation.
Keywords: artificial photosynthesis, catalysis, electronic structure theory, explainable artificial intelligence, machine learning, neural networks, ruthenium, transition metal complexes, water-splitting

Title: High-throughput PET imaging by decoding multi-photon signals on long axial field-of-view PET using physics-guided artificial intelligence
Abstract:
The main epistemological objective of the proposed investigations is to test the hypothesis stating that the neoplasia stage of primary prostate cancer may be assessed in-vivo by the combination of  

(i) Prostate Specific Antigen (PSA) biomarker assay,  

(ii) Prostate Specific Membrane Antigen (PSMA) receptor density imaging, and  

(iii) positronium imaging.  

Positronium imaging is a novel method developed at the Jagiellonian University, enabling imaging of properties of positron-electron atoms in humans during the PET diagnosis. The project research hypothesis will be tested by establishing correlations between the PSA value, PSMA receptor density image, positronium lifetime image, and the prostate cancer grade established based on histopathological assessment.  

A combination of these complementary circulating- and image-based biomarkers will be studied for the first time making the proposed investigations pioneering on a global scale.  

In this project, new imaging methods will be developed and in-vitro, preclinical, and clinical investigations will be conducted.  

The methodological purpose of this project is the elaboration of multi-photon total-body PET imaging for high-throughput and enhanced specificity in prostate cancer diagnosis. The specific methodological objectives are: (i) extension of the functionality of the Vision Quadra PET system by the multi-photon data acquisition, (ii) elaboration of the phantom for the calibration of the positronium imaging, (iii) elaboration of the physics-guided artificial intelligence (AI) based reconstruction of multi-photon images, (iv) elaboration of the AI methods for the simultaneous PET and positronium imaging.  

The main research objective of the proposed project is to perform clinical three-photon imaging of patients with prostate cancer using 68-Ga radionuclide labeled PSMA ligand, while the specific aims are: (i) positronium imaging of phantoms, (ii) studies of positronium lifetime in 2D and 3D in-vitro models of prostate cancer cells (spheroids) with different expression of PSMA surface antigen, (iii) performing preclinical positronium imaging of rats model with prostate cancer organoids, and (iv) clinical positronium imaging of patients with primary prostate cancer.  

The proposed research will be carried out at the Jagiellonian and Bern Universities. Bern University possesses the first in Europe long axial field-of-view (LOFOV) PET (Siemens Biograph Vision Quadra) with a length of 106 cm and has acquired unique expertise in diagnosing prostate cancer patients with this modality. In the framework of this project, the Biograph Vision Quadra system will be upgraded for multi-photon detection and will become the first multi-photon LAFOV PET in clinics. The group from the Jagiellonian University has developed and constructed the first multi-photon PET prototype with 50 cm LAFOV and has demonstrated the first multi-photon PET images and first in-vivo positronium images of patients using 68-Ga labeled PSMA. In this project for the first time, this Polish-Swiss collaboration will join their complementary and unique expertise to realize the first positronium imaging of prostate cancer patients on the clinically certified LAFOV PET at the University of Bern. The development of new AI-based multi-photon image reconstruction methods will benefit from the expertise of the Swiss PI in the establishment of artificial intelligence (AI) in a broad spectrum of nuclear medicine imaging and therapy. While the development of positronium as a new biomarker for prostate diagnosis will benefit from the well-established expertise of polish PI in in-vitro and clinical development of circulating- and image-based biomarkers, and in particular from the unique experience as a medical coordinator of the first in-vivo demonstration of positronium imaging in-vivo.   

The expected scientific effect of the joint research of the Krakow and Bern groups will be an established correlation between the (i) standard PET images, (ii) positronium lifetime images, and (iii) the patient’s histopathological data via imaging-guide biopsy or radical prostatectomy. Interpretation of the identified clinical correlations will be supported by studies of the correlations between the degree of prostate cancer malignancy and positronium lifetime determined in the control pre-clinical and in-vitro conditions for rat models and 2D and 3D cell cultures.
Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Biomarkers, Clinical imaging, Diagnostic tools, Positron emission tomography, Positronium, Prostate cancer

Title: 3Dhist: Evolution of colorectal cancer metastases using multimodal 2D and 3D imaging
Abstract:
Colon cancer is one of the most frequent cancers in many parts of the world and despite screening programs is an important cause of cancer death. Cancer spread has several mechanisms and is not fully understood. Particularly the lymphatic system plays an important role in the cancer spread.
The main imaging method to analyse tumours or biopsies of the is histopathology imaging, usually with H&E- (hematoxylin and eosin) and immunohisto-staining. Such cuts are extremely thin (2.5-5 micrometres) and only a small number of cuts across the tumour can be analysed. This means that much information is lost and not the entire tumour can be analysed. In radiology imaging the resolution is often much lower but the entire tumour can be seen in 3D. By extending histopathology imaging towards 3D, we aim to view the entire structure in 3D to better understand the underlying mechanisms. By combining this with micro-CT we also hope to find more information on the structure seen and make links between the complementary information seen in the imaging. The massive amounts of data generated require intelligent tools to detect structures and navigate the data. Data management in the Petabyte range also poses challenges.
This interdisciplinary project is only possible with the involvement of very complementary competencies of the four applicants. The project is thus structured into four sub-projects that have many links, and all require the involvement of the entire group to reach optimal results.
Sub-project 1: Analysis of tumour spread in colorectal cancer by analysing 2D and 3D data. This work package is the clinical partner of the project that will provide tissue samples of patients and use all data and tools developed in the other sub-projects.
Sub-project 2: Set up and validate a new pipeline for highly multiplexed LSM (Light Sheet Microscopy) imaging based on hybridization labelling of antibodies and combinatorial multi-color detection. Applying the pipeline to colorectal primary cancer, lymph node metastases, tumour deposits and liver metastases. The 3D histopathology images will be shared with all partners for analysis and will extend current possibilities for data analysis..
Sub-project 3: Creation of micro-CT images of the same tissue blocks that are used for the 3D histopathology. High resolution CT can then be matched in 3 dimensions with the histopathology images. Specific adaptations based on the tissue to be analysed will help us to obtain a maximum of information.
Sub-project 4: Analysis of 2D and 3D data and combination of several modalities for learning to detect different types of patterns in the massive data volumes that are produced. Patterns such as tumour budding will be analysed. This work package will also work on registration of different histopathology images and also between micro-CT and histopathology images across a variety of scales. Overall, we feel that this project responds to several major scientific challenges and that the understanding of tumour spread but also of imaging modalities, massive data management and intelligent multimodal data analysis. Title: Cross theory rigorous program verification using Constrained Horn clauses
Abstract:
State-of-the-art approaches to automated software verification delegate the computational tasks to solvers for Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) and Constrained Horn Clauses (CHC). The latter enables synthesizing inductive invariants and offers sound but possibly incomplete reasoning about software. Existing approaches to solve CHC either heavily approximate the systems or reduce the analysis to their snippets, thus being unable to verify real-world systems.

The goal of our project is to develop a novel CHC-based verification framework for handling complex programs symbolically and efficiently. We aim at preserving sufficient level of details meaningful for the program developers and users. The project will deliver a set of automated techniques that rely on existing CHC solvers developed by the PI from USI and the partner from Florida State University in the USA. The complementary strengths of these solvers will be combined in a new cross-theory framework that lazily enumerates the theories used in the CHC encoding and applies appropriate techniques provided by the solvers for those theories.

Specifically, the work proposes using the Golem and FreqHorn CHC solvers as starting points for developing a new CHC-solving technology. Golem has the implementations of various efficient algorithms and utilizes Craig interpolation to discover invariants in linear arithmetic. FreqHorn uses the enumerative search boosted by deductive reasoning, and it discovers quantified invariants over arrays. Although our solutions will be well suited for implementation on top of Golem and FreqHorn, they will be generic and potentially realizable on top of other solvers.

We will deliver open-source tools and evaluate them on CHC systems that originate from software from academia and industry. The emphasis will be made on verification of Ethereum smart contracts provided by the industrial partner. The proposal will advance tools for software verification and enable automated reasoning w.r.t. safety properties that otherwise would require many human efforts.
Keywords: CHC, Constrained Horn Clauses, Formal Verification, Model Checking, Program Analysis, SMT, Symbolic Program Analysis

Title: Semantic extraction from Big Visual Data captured by Fixed and Mobile Cameras
Abstract: Recent progress in deploying cameras everywhere, such as in cities and train terminals, or on vehicles and human glasses, makes computer vision algorithms a requirement for extracting semantically meaningful knowledge from such overwhelming volume of data. My focus during the past 18 months was on using fixed cameras to get in-depth insights on human mobility. In fact, in crowded spaces such as train terminals or school campuses, human mobility looks complex, but is often influenced by a few causes only. To validate this claim, I have collected trajectories from more than hundred cameras installed in large public spaces to build a unique dataset of dozen of millions trajectories. This dataset has opened a new wave of research on tracking crowds in large scenes. For the next months, I want to build upon my existing work on forecasting motion behavior given social affinity maps by extending it to mobile egocentric cameras. The recent emergence of Google glasses or GoPro cameras has resulted in the need to extract and summarize the content in the semantic domain to efficiently manage day-long videos. I propose to extract binary low-level features to social affinities high-level features to jointly reason on the relevance of a video segment. Finally, in collaboration with other labs, I will work on detecting and predicting human flows with egocentric vision to guide a self-driven robot navigating in crowded pedestrians-only areas.

Title: Paradox Theory in the Digital Age: Human Actors, Intelligent Machines, and the Emerging Tensions They Create
Abstract:
Paradox research has grown exponentially in recent years (Schad, Lewis, Raisch, & Smith, 2016). By focusing on the sources, nature, management, and dynamics of tensions, paradox theory aims at exploring how organizations experience and deal with the tensions they face (Smith & Lewis, 2011). This proposal explores paradox theory’s current limitations in the context of digital transformation. Digitalization is characterized by the availability of large data sets (“big data”), algorithms that semi-autonomously process this data (“artificial intelligence”), and the increasingly close collaboration of humans with intelligent machines (Daugherty & Wilson, 2018). These developments render several of the paradox theory’s limitations salient: First, paradox theory takes individual cognitive biases as an explanation for organizational actions (Lewis, 2000) and is therefore limited to human actors in organizations. Consequently, paradox theory fails to account for the emergent human-machine interaction. Second, paradox deals with a set of well-established tensions (Cunha & Putnam, 2017). Yet, digitalization creates entirely new tensions, often with wider societal implications, that remain unexplored to date. Third, paradox research focuses on how organizations manage tensions, taking a closed-systems view (Schad & Bansal, 2018). Yet, many tensions in the digital age arise from distributed and open systems that reach beyond such boundaries and therefore cannot be addressed inside the organization.
We address these research opportunities in three projects. Project 1 starts with the paradox literature’s assertion that it is the managers’ responsibility to deal with tensions. Managers perceive tensions, define approaches to address them, and monitor their outcomes. Yet, in the digital age, this human-centric approach fails to explain managers’ close interaction with intelligent machines (Orlikowski & Scott, 2008). Drawing on the philosophy of information (Floridi, 2008), we argue that tensions arising from that interaction demand us to revise paradox theory’s assumptions regarding its ontology, epistemology, and axiology. In a conceptual paper, we develop a new perspective on managing tensions that is relational, emergent, and normative.
Project 2 explores the dynamics of tensions, which are often characterized by escalating cycles. Prior explanations of these escalating cycles are based on individual-level cognitive biases and tend to treat all individuals within an organization the same (Fairhurst et al., 2016). Yet, individuals often display a preference for one side of a tension. External influences such as social media can reinforce their orientations further. The reasons are that algorithms create ‘filter bubbles’ that reinforce the current orientation and draw attention to extreme positions (Schad & Bansal, 2018). Drawing on the attention-based view (Ocasio, 1997), we address how escalation processes unfold through collective action in the context of social media. Using Twitter data, we plan to conduct a longitudinal quantitative study and explore the data through sentiment analysis. We contribute to the paradox literature by complementing the existing atomistic perspective with a social perspective on escalation.
Project 3 challenges core assumptions in the literature on learning paradoxes. These studies emphasize organizations’ difficulties to balance exploration and exploitation (Farjoun, 2010). Organizations display a bias with a tendency to overexploit and underexplore. Yet, the human biases explaining these difficulties may be overcome in the digital age when humans and machines learn collaboratively. Drawing on computer science (Fails & Olsen, 2003), the purpose of this study is to explore how humans and machines can work together synergistically when addressing exploration-exploitation tensions. We plan to conduct a longitudinal, inductive field study in the context of product development projects. We contribute to the paradox literature by developing a perspective of ‘augmented’ learning that describes the interplay between humans and machines.
Keywords: artificial intelligence, digitalization, organization theory, paradox

Title: Algorithms for a Computational Revolution
Abstract:
Today’s world is increasingly reliant on computing services, from mundane tasks such as online shopping, to critical services such as e-government. Two main trends underlie this shift: the algorithms and systems implementing these services must support increasingly many users, and process ever-increasing quantities of data to provide correct service, while the amount of time that users are willing to wait to receive service is constantly diminishing. To address these challenges, system designers are increasingly turning to distribution: splitting computation across several cores, processors, servers, or even data-centers in order to provide fast, robust service to their users. This places immense pressure on algorithms and systems to scale, that is, to continually increase their performance as more computing nodes are added to the system. The scalability limits of current computing architectures are already apparent, and thus several exciting challenges await. How do we design and program complex distributed systems correctly and efficiently? How do we build algorithms to extract every last bit of performance out of the current architectures, and how do we design future architectures to support scalable computation?

Our goal is to take a decisive step towards answering these challenges, by developing a set of algorithmic principles for enabling scalable distributed computation. We aim to provide a detailed understanding of the inherent scalability bottlenecks in the current distributed computing paradigms (either shared-memory and message-passing), and to explore new algorithms, architectures, and tools to overcome these limitations. In particular, we will focus on two approaches. First, we will examine the power of relaxing distributed algorithm semantics, through approximation and randomization, to ensure increased scalability in distributed systems. Second, we will examine new architectures for distributed computation, which can gracefully handle the high contention naturally arising in distributed systems. These approaches are two faces of the same coin. The former aims to achieve scalability by avoiding contention through relaxed semantics, while the latter attacks contention head-on, aiming to design systems which can scale under high concurrency. We plan to apply these approaches to three major upcoming computational challenges: distributed machine learning, highly data-intensive applications, and scalability of cloud computing services.

We expect the impact of our project to be two-fold. Conceptually, our goal is to provide a set of fundamental principles for scalable distributed computation, useful to both theoreticians and practitioners. Practically, we aim to develop these algorithmic insights into a set of working examples for scalable computation, which can be adopted and modified by practitioners to suit their purposes. Thus, a higher-level objective is to bridge the gap between the theory and the practice of distributed computing. We believe that this is an extremely rich research area, with potential for both theoretical breakthroughs and high-impact practical applications, and that creating a center of competence in Switzerland on these topics will be beneficial in the long term.
Keywords: algorithms, computer science, distributed computing, randomization, scalability

apparent, and thus several exciting challenges await. how do we design and program complex distributed systems correctly and efficiently? how do we build algorithms to extract every last bit of performance out of the current architectures, and how do we design future architectures to support scalable computation? our goal is to take a decisive step towards answering these challenges, by aims to achieve scalability by avoiding contention through relaxed semantics, while the latter attacks contention head on, aiming to design systems which can scale under high concurrency. we plan to Title: A data-driven approach to constrain volcanic eruption evolution using geochemistry and geophysics
Abstract: Magma, the product of volcanic eruptions, has a dynamic journey from source to surface. This variability influences eruption magnitude, style, explosivity and duration (eruptive dynamics) as well as the exposure of people and infrastructure to geological hazards. Magma storage depth, its thermal state, and the subsequent path of migration to the volcanic edifice can be partially tracked by direct monitoring: earthquake focal depth, deflation and inflation of the volcanic flank, and erupted volume. By comparison, petrological data, and in particular mineral chemistry, are rarely used as a tool during a volcanic crisis (syn-eruptive petrological monitoring). This is despite informing on magma storage and transport conditions pertinent to short-term forecasting and risk assessment. This includes quantification of magma temperature, pressure and melt composition, key variables governing magma properties and, in turn, eruptive dynamics. To demonstrate the value of syn-eruptive petrological assessment, we propose to sample the products of a well-monitored active volcano (Cumbre Vieja, La Palma, Canary Islands, 19th September 2021 – 13th December 2021) at high temporal resolution (each day to several days). Samples will be processed using a rapid workflow of quantified chemical mapping for major and trace element determination. Magmatic minerals from samples, including from those that bracket shifts in volcanic behaviour (e.g., migration of earthquake focal depth, the start and end of the eruption), will be used as archivists of temporal changes within the volcanic sub-system. Results from chemistry (major and trace element variability), a novel approach to thermobarometry (for recovery of pressure [P] and temperature [T]) and chemometry (to estimate equilibrium melt chemistry [X], density, and viscosity), quantitative textural characterisation (segmentation), and geophysics (seismicity, gas monitoring) will be amalgamated into a multivariate dataset. Statistical and machine learning techniques will relate these parameters to the well-constrained temporal behaviour of the volcano. By combining geochemistry and thermobarometry with geophysics and other monitoring signals, we will unveil the relationships between deep magmatic processes and volcanic eruptive dynamics operating on timescales relevant to continuous hazard assessment during a volcanic eruption.
Keywords: geophysics, machine learning, risk, thermobarometry

Title: The global carbon budget in marine sediments and the effects of the anthropogenic carbon footprint
Abstract:
Marine sediments play a crucial role in the global carbon cycle, serving as the final sink of carbon by sequestering it in the form of organic carbon (OC) for geological timescales. However, there is no consensus on the magnitude of OC buried in marine sediments, and proper estimates of its spatial distribution are still lacking. The factors that affect this final sink of carbon in marine sediments is a delicate interplay between the sources of OC, depositional processes, and environmental conditions. Consequently, to determine the role of marine sediments for the global carbon cycle, a proper understanding of the sources and age of OC is needed. This is particularly essential at a time when the Earth system and the global carbon cycle are heavily perturbed by still increasing fossil fuel emissions, land use changes, and other anthropogenic activities. This causes direct and indirect effects in the marine environment, which will inevitably affect the OC budget in marine sediments. Hence, the overarching aim of this project is to understand and quantify the global organic carbon budget in marine sediments and assess the influence of anthropogenic and climatic perturbations.
Until recently, both the absence of comprehensive datasets and the nascent state of spatial machine learning models hindered progress in this field. However, with the availability of large data and the advancement of spatial machine learning algorithms to understand environmental processes while accounting for sparse or clustered distribution of data, this project aims to develop accurate and robust models that determine the OC budget in marine sediments. Leveraging the output of these spatial machine learning algorithms, I will disentangle the environmental conditions that drive the accumulation and remineralization of OC in marine sediments and identify how their changes associated to expanding anthropogenic perturbations and a changing climate have affected the OC stored in marine sediments. Specifically, we will focus on how direct anthropogenic activities such as river dams and coastal eutrophication have affected the magnitude and source of OC deposited in coastal marine sediments. We will also explore how climate change in Arctic environments, which have already experienced substantial reductions in sea-ice extent, warming temperatures, and enhanced permafrost erosion, have affected the accumulation of the quantity and source of OC deposited in Arctic sediments. Finally, we will predict future trends in the global carbon budget affected by accelerating climate change and expanding anthropogenic perturbations on the global carbon budget.
Providing accurate spatially-constrained estimates of the global carbon budget in marine sediments is crucial in advancing our understanding of the Earth's carbon cycle. Through this project, we will gain insight of the environmental processes that drive the distribution and sequestration of OC in marine sediments, which is essential for its incorporation in global earth system models. The prediction of future trends in the global carbon budget, influenced by anthropogenic and climatic perturbations, will provide invaluable knowledge for informed decision-making and sustainable environmental management that protect sequestered carbon on the seafloor. This project will not only unravel the intricacies of carbon storage in marine sediments but also contribute to the broader mission of mitigating climate change.
Keywords: anthropogenic perturbations, carbon sequestration, climate change, global carbon cycle, global modelling, marine sediments

Title: Collaborative Self-Supervised Learning of Perception Tasks for Robot Swarms
Abstract:
Modern robots rely on deep learning models for solving difficult perception tasks, such as interpreting data from high-dimensional sensors (e.g. cameras) in order to understand their surroundings.  These approaches are typically based on supervised learning, and rely on training datasets that must be labeled, large, and representative of the expected deployment environment of the robot. This is often a significant obstacle when developing new robot systems.
In contrast, humans and animals learn to solve perception tasks from experience, with limited (if any) external supervision.  Their approach is self-supervised, and recent research takes advantage of these concepts in deep learning, with promising applications to robotics.

The objective of this project is to design and demonstrate methods that allow a group (swarm) of cooperative robots to learn useful perception models from scratch without any external supervision. By performing actions (such as moving, blinking lights or bumping into obstacles) and explicitly communicating these actions to their peers, each robot provides precious information that the peers can use to learn and fine-tune their perception models; the swarm supervises itself.  Just like animals hone their fine motor skills by playing with each other, the actions performed by our robots can be seen as a form of group play, that develops and improves the perception skills of all robots in the swarm.

Specific aims: A) develop a system consisting in a small group of 3 identical camera-equipped ground robots, placed at random in an unknown, uninstrumented, delimited environment; without any pre-existing perception ability, robots play by randomly moving, blinking their lights, advertising their actions through a radio link, while collecting sensing data and receiving messages from others; after some hours of play, the group uses the collected data to learn from scratch a visual perception model that, given an image, outputs the relative pose of all visible peers.  B) extend the model described previously to an environment perception task, such as visually detecting long-range obstacles; during play, robots sense and share with peers also their environment interactions (such as bumping into an obstacle); when informed that a peer just hit an obstacle, other robots get weak supervision that is used to learn long-range visual obstacle detection.  C) instantiate the developed techniques to a different scenario: a swarm of nano-drones equipped with pretrained models capable of visually localizing their peers; when deployed in a new environment, in which the models perform suboptimally (e.g. because of unexpected lighting conditions), the peers adapt the models to the new environment by observing each other for a few minutes, without any external supervision. 

Methods. Our robots are provided large amounts of weak self-supervision through their communication with peers and interaction with the environment; this signal can be used for training deep learning models through loss functions designed ad-hoc, e.g. by enforcing state consistency between different timesteps.  In addition, one can learn to extract meaningful high-level representations from perceptual data by training models to solve pretext tasks, i.e. tasks that are not necessarily relevant for the task of interest, but: 1) require similar perception skills and 2) do not require explicit acquisition of ground truth labels, but use otherwise known information for supervision; we hypotesize that, in our context, information shared by peers can be used to define powerful pretext tasks.

Expected results, impact
Achieving robust perception is a key challenge in modern robotics; out project will yield novel methods to tackle this challenge.  We expect that the most practical impact, in the short term, will come from applying the developed methods to finetune existing perception models (e.g. models pretrained by system designers) to automatically adapt to new domains or environments (e.g. deployment environments different than those on which the systems were developed).
Keywords: deep learning, deep neural networks, robot learning, robot swarms, robotics, self-supervised learning

Title: Towards the geographically transferable data-driven human mobility flow generation models (GeoTrans)
Abstract:
Background. Human mobility flow generation is a generative process that assigns inflows and outflows of human mobility to individual geographic units (e.g., regions, cities) based on prior socioeconomic and geographic knowledge. It is fundamental to complement scarce or missing flow data for many mobility-related applications, such as traffic management, urban planning, and emergency response. Moreover, it significantly mitigates the privacy concerns of collecting individual human movement tracking data. Human mobility flow generation mainly follows two approaches: mechanistic vs. machine learning (ML) / deep learning (DL). For data-driven approaches using ML or DL, geographic transferability is crucial, as it means the capability of generating realistic mobility flows across geographic spaces. A model of high geographic transferability can support broader applications with limited or even no re-training and thus reduce the cost of training models. However, to date, the geographic transferability of human mobility flow generation models is under-evaluated, and few solutions have targeted improving the geographic transferability.

Aims. The overall objective of this proposed SNSF Postdoc.Mobility project (GeoTrans), which will be hosted in the Geospatial Data Science Lab at the Department of Geography of the University of Wisconsin-Madison, is to understand the influential factors of geographic transferability of data-driven human mobility flow generation models and hence improve their geographic transferability. I pursue three aims: 1) Model complex geographic characteristics using urban morphology knowledge. 2) Evaluate the geographic transferability of state-of-the-art (SOTA) models. 3) Develop a new human mobility flow generation model with a higher geographic transferability by improving the multi-scale geographic spatial representation capability and using domain adversarial training. The first aim will enrich geographic features in understanding geographic transferability in the second aim, whose outcomes can further guide the development of geographically transferable human mobility flow generation models in the third aim.

Methods. To achieve the first aim, I will collect open mobility origin-destination (OD) flow data worldwide (e.g., in the U.S., Japan, and Singapore). Then, I will prepare socioeconomic and geographic features for the corresponding geographic units. Particularly, I will develop multi-dimensional complex geographic features using urban morphology methods. For the second aim, I will train SOTA models based on the collected OD dataset and the prepared geographic features. I will evaluate their geographic transferability with three metrics: root mean square error, a common part of commuters, and Jensen-Shannon divergence, followed by regression analysis to identify the associations between the three metrics and prepared geographic features. For the last aim, I will develop a hierarchical graph representation learning approach to extract important geographic features at multi-scales. Meanwhile, domain adversarial training will be used to capture useful features shared in both source and target cities to generate realistic human mobility flows. 

Results. GeoTrans will produce the quantitative relationships between the geographic transferability of human mobility flow generation models and socioeconomic and geographic features. It is thus expected to generate a feasible framework to improve geographic transferability and thus gain insights and methods to overcome the geographic knowledge bottleneck impeding geographic transferability in today’s human mobility flow generation models.

Impact. GeoTrans will bridge the knowledge gap between generative AI and geography for human mobility data generation. It will have a significant impact by enabling mobility-informed decision-making (e.g., traffic management, urban planning) across broader geographic areas, particularly in underdeveloped regions, thereby promoting geographic equity in socio-economic development.
Keywords: complex geograhpic characteristic modeling, data-driven, geographic transferability, human mobility flow generation, urban morphology

Title: Single-cell profiling of antibody repertoires and transcriptomes from B cells to determine the relationship with antigen-specificity and aging
Abstract:
The humoral immune response is mediated by B-cells and their vast collection of molecularly diverse antibodies. This antibody repertoire represents both the past and current immunological status of an individual. Recent progress in deep sequencing and bioinformatics has catalyzed a systems level view of antibody repertoires and B-cell responses. However, most studies have relied on deep sequencing in bulk (pooled B-cells), which does not preserve the native variable heavy (VH) and variable light (VL) chain pairing, and thus is unable to recover specificity (antigen-binding) in antibody repertoires. Additionally, to date there has been little research related to how B-cell transcriptional profiles influence antibody repertoires and their cognate specificities. Finally, aging in the immune system, commonly referred to as immune senescence has been shown to dampen adaptive immune responses; while systems level work on T-cells has been performed, there is little information on how aging impacts B-cells and antibody repertoires as well as their direct contribution to age-related homeostasis in certain tissues like the brain. 

The overall goal of this proposal is to answer fundamental and systems level questions related to basic B-cell biology (clonal selection, expansion and evolution) (Project 1) and the role of infiltrating B-cells in the brain (Project 2) within the context of aging in the immune system. This will be accomplished by using single-cell sequencing of antibody repertoires and transcriptomes. Furthermore, our previous expertise in deep sequencing, bioinformatics, genome editing and machine learning will enable us to perform an in-depth and multifaceted set of studies. First, we will perform single-cell sequencing to simultaneously obtain the paired VH and VL chain repertoire and transcriptomes from B-cells of immunized (Project 1) and unimmunized (Project 2) mice (Aim 1). An important aspect of our study will be the use of both young and old mice which will address how B-cells and antibody repertoires are impacted by aging. Next, we will take advantage of the fact that single-cell sequencing will provide us with both the VL and VH chain sequences from B-cells, thus providing the information needed to reconstruct full antibodies with their native binding properties. We will then use our established mammalian cell antibody expression system to screen for antigen-specificity among the highly clonally expanded B-cells (Aim 2). At the conclusion of this aim we will be able to answer several fundamental questions on how clonal expansion and evolution are related to antigen-specificity. Finally, we will use the information on antibody repertoires and antigen specificity and combine it with single-cell transcriptome data to gain a multi-dimensional profile of B-cells (Aim 3). Furthermore, by performing analysis on both young (2.5 months) and old mice (12 and 18 months), we will gain insight into how aging impacts the clonal selection, expansion, evolution and transcriptome profile of B-cells (Project 1) and we will be able to directly gain mechanistic insights into the specificity and potential role of clonally expanded B cells in the brain (Project 2). In addition to single-cell sequencing and antibody screening assays, we will also take advantage of machine learning to determine if antigen-specificity can be predicted from transcriptome clustering. In addition to answering long-standing questions in humoral immunity, this proposal may finally lead to novel approaches for antibody drug discovery and humoral immune profiling after vaccination or infection as well as new biomarkers for B-cell mediated pathologies in the brain.
Keywords: B cells, antibody repertoire, bioinformatic, high-throughput, machine learning

Title: Generative computer vision models to predict anatomical growth in pediatric diffuse midline glioma
Abstract:
Background: Pediatric diffuse midline glioma (DMG) is a rare, yet fatal disease, with currently no curative treatment. Due to the delicate location of these tumors, treatment options and surgical interventions are greatly limited. Radiotherapy (RT) is one of the few life-prolonging treatments, but its therapeutic efficacy varies between individuals. Currently, it is impossible to accurately predict how the tumor will progress for the individual following RT. An upfront understanding of high-risk (i.e. therapy-resistant or progressing) tumor regions would enable patient stratification, individual patient monitoring, and geometric radiation dose adaptations. There is a great unmet clinical need to improve our understanding of DMG RT response and to maximize RT efficacy through personalization. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is the standard of care to diagnose and monitor DMG patients. As such, image generation models provide an innovative strategy towards the prediction of anatomical changes and hence, are a promising tool to address the unmet clinical need  for early and accurate tumor characterization.
Key Objectives: The overarching aim of this project is the investigation of generative space-time computer vision models to provide anatomical tumor growth predictions on MRIs. Specifically, we will address the following hypothesis: i)  Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models (DDIM) guided towards a predefined tumor size based on a mechanistic model fit to longitudinal data can generate images that recapitulate clinically relevant features of tumor growth and response and ii) by training space-time generative models on synthetic longitudinal MRIs we can estimate the tumor growth trajectory in the absence of closely sampled input data.
Methods: In addition to public data, longitudinal (pre-RT, ~3-monthly follow-up until time of death) multi-contrast MRIs and clinical data from ~300 patients obtained from leading international DMG treatment centers will be used to train a slice-based Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models (DDIM) which generates anatomical tumor images. A mechanistic mathematical model fit to longitudinal data will be used to define tumor size as a function of time to serve as the target for denoising guidance of the DDIM. The obtained densely sampled longitudinal tumor growth trajectories will be the basis to train a space-time generative model of anatomical tumor growth allowing for the prediction of tumor response. The model’s performance will be assessed in terms of agreement of true and predicted images in accordance with the Response Assessment in Pediatric Neuro Oncology criteria relative to the baseline image, tumor segmentations, and tumor growth probability maps obtained from repeated sampling. 
Expected Results and Impact: This multidisciplinary project addresses essential questions at the forefront of computer vision and pediatric oncology research from two methodological angles aiming to i) improve patient care through detailed, personalized response predictions and ii) push the boundaries of machine learning for healthcare research through the investigation of new approaches in the realm of generative space-time models. We expect to gain a refined understanding of DMG response to RT through mathematical modeling as DMGs offer a setting to directly assess the tumor’s longitudinal RT response given the absence of surgical intervention. Moreover, we will quantify the performance of a promising generative approach and investigate further combinations of mechanistic and data-driven modeling through synthetic data generation. This project is anticipated as a feasibility study to lay the foundation for generation of synthetic controls in future pediatric (RT) trials, which would greatly improve the potential to quantify the benefit of novel treatment paradigms for these rare tumors. This may further enable RT personalization for a group of pediatric patients, where treatment individualization is inevitable and to date considered the best possible means of prolonging survival and providing symptom relief. By focusing on imaging data that is part of routine clinical evaluation for DMG patients and available, cost-effective RT, this approach could be feasible in many treatment facilities worldwide and provide an important step towards pediatric precision oncology.
Keywords: Computer vision, Diffuse midline glioma, generative AI, pediatric digital health

Title: Serial dependence in perception and decision-making
Abstract:
From moment to moment, visual perception is not a photographic representation of the world but relies heavily on past experience and short-term dependencies: What happened a moment ago has a strong impact on how we perceive the present. Prior experiences can guide current perception but can also induce systematic biases and illusions. In the waterfall illusion, for example, staring at a waterfall for several seconds causes a negative aftereffect in which subsequent static sceneries appear to be moving upwards (Anstis, Verstraten, & Mather, 1998). 
In recent years, it has been shown that prior experience can also bias perception toward previous events positively, i.e., present stimuli appear more similar to past stimuli than they actually are (Fischer & Whitney, 2014). This phenomenon, known as serial dependence, has raised the need for a new understanding of perception: How can these negative and positive effects coexist in the brain? Is there a shared mechanism or distinct stages of perception?
It has been proposed that opposite history biases may originate at different stages of the processing stream (Fritsche, Mostert, & de Lange, 2017), with negative aftereffects arising at early perceptual stages and serial dependence at later, post-perceptual stages. However, the exact nature of the post-perceptual processes involved is unknown: Does serial dependence result from the fact that our decisions or memory traces are systematically biased toward the recent past? How these history biases interact and what is their functional role? Answering these questions can profoundly change our view on human perception in general by revealing a previously unknown hierarchical system in which opposite forces promote the integration or differentiation of information over time. Understanding how such system works may have strong implications in other fields as well, such as in computer vision in which these aspects are rarely addressed, and medicine, where medical diagnosis by visual inspection (e.g., tumor diagnosis) is biased by the history of samples examined.
With the present project, I intend to demonstrate that a hierarchy of serially dependent processes exists in the brain and to characterize their nature, providing the first unifying account of history effects in visual perception. This aim will be realized by a series of experiments in which I will use advanced and innovative methods based on psychophysics, forward modeling of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data, and electroencephalography (EEG) connectivity measures. I will use psychophysical methods to unravel the nature of post-perceptual processes that link perception over time, by addressing the role of decisional templates, mental images and top-down predictions. I will then develop and apply a new approach to reconstruct the emergence of internal – biased – representations from fMRI and EEG data and I will perform the first investigation into history biases from a large-scale network perspective, focusing on time-varying connectivity patterns that relay repulsive or attractive biases along the hierarchy of perceptual processing. Moreover, as a first attempt in translation, I will investigate whether the distorted visual perception in schizophrenia patients is caused by abnormal serial dependency.
The main outcomes of this project can be summarized as follows: 1) Gaining a new and comprehensive insight into the role of prior experience in perception, parsing out repulsive and attractive history biases from both a functional and biological standpoint; 2) Identifying the main sources of history effects in the brain and their interaction during the emergence of perceptual biases; 3) Introducing and validating a new representational-based approach that can relate errors in perceptual reports to activity patterns in fMRI and EEG data; 4) Proposing the first comprehensive theoretical and computational model of history effects. The project will include a collaboration with the University of Iceland, setting the ground for an international research network centered in Switzerland. 
The ultimate goal of this proposal is to provide a new perspective on history biases, validated empirically, which will represent a milestone for future research in the field.

Fischer, J., & Whitney, D. (2014). Serial dependence in visual perception. Nature Neuroscience, 17(5), 738–743.
Fritsche, M., Mostert, P., & de Lange, F. P. (2017). Opposite effects of recent history on perception and decision. Current Biology, 27(4), 590–595.

Title: Multimodal approach for the detection, prediction, and management of Freezing of Gait in Parkinson's Disease
Abstract: Freezing of Gait (FoG), a debilitating motor symptom in Parkinson's disease (PD), manifests as sudden and unpredictable difficulty initiating or maintaining forward movement. These episodes significantly impact daily activities, increase fall risk, and diminish the quality of life for people with Parkinson's disease (pwPD). Current diagnostic methods lack objectivity, making it challenging to predict FoG occurrences in real-time while existing treatments provide only limited relief from FoG symptoms. This research addresses these challenges by investigating the underlying mechanisms of FoG in PD through objective biomarkers derived from the integration of different neurophysiological and biomechanical information. Employing a multimodal approach, this comprehensive analysis aims to: (1) elucidate the complex neural and biomechanical processes contributing to FoG by analyzing together three domains of the neuromusculoskeletal system: brain activity, muscle activation patterns, and movement characteristics, and (2) develop real-time FoG detection and prediction models using machine learning techniques based on characteristic changes in the multimodal data streams. Building upon these insights, a closed-loop wearable stimulation system will be designed and tested to assist in mitigating the freezing. Such device explores three non-invasive intervention modalities attempting pwPD to regain the movements through: haptic feedback for alerting users of impending FoG episodes, functional electrical stimulation (FES) for targeted muscle activation during FoG events, and non-invasive transcranial electric temporal interference stimulation (tTIS) of the basal ganglia to investigate its potential in mitigating FoG severity. The feasibility and effectiveness of this technology in suppressing or preventing FoG events will be assessed in pwPD. Furthermore, by comparing the efficacy of each intervention modality, the study aims to optimize FoG interventional strategies, leading to improved outcomes and potentially opening doors for new therapeutic solutions for the management of FoG in pwPD.
Keywords: Biomarkers, Freezing of Gait, Neuro-Prosthetics, Non-Invasive biosignals, Parkinson Disease, Wearable technology

Title: Trade, Trans-national Infrastructure Investments and Economic Development: Evidence from the New Silk Road.
Abstract: In this project we ask: to what extent large trans-national infrastructure helps structural transformation of developing countries? We study a branch of Chinese Belt and Road initiative (BRI) - large-scale road and railroad construction – implemented in Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan and use a set of innovative datasets and approaches to answer this question. Namely, we use firm-to-firm customs and railroad transactions at finely defined products, spanning at least three countries, granular firm-level information and machine-learning algorithm over satellite imagery to identify new roads and railways in the three countries. This project investigates the three aspects of the BRI investment: a) value added of new roads versus displacement of economic activity b) structural transformation versus “lock-in” in original sectors c) efficient coordination of roads versus strategic/political (mis-)placement.  We answer these questions empirically and structurally. The granularity of the data and a wide range of firm-by-product outcomes offered by the data allows us to causally estimate the effects of roads on structural transformation, and separate displacement of economic activity versus value added effects of roads by keeping the firm-to-firm link fixed. We also are the first to study a trans-national road investment project, as opposed to within-country investment. In a transnational road project, the cross-country coordination becomes key for each affected country in extracting the most benefit from the roads. With the granularity of our data, we are able to better calibrate the spatial, multi-sector equilibrium model to quantify aggregate effect at each location and speak to the optimality and coordination of road placement. Therefore, we also evaluate, whether the road placement benefits all studied countries or, instead, is optimized to help a specific country more.
Keywords: Belt and Road Initiative, Development, Economic Development, Economic Geography, Firms, Infrastructure, International Trade, Structural transformation, Trade, infrastructure investments

Title: Towards Autonomous Molecular Discovery of a ‘Genetic Code’ for Organic Electronics
Abstract:
Chemistry has become extremely proficient in synthesizing molecules and materials with specific structures and characterizing their properties. However, to solve real-world problems like inventing effective and specific drugs for cancer treatment, establishing sustainable processes for carbon capture or developing efficient and cost-effective organic solar cells, it is typically unclear what the exact structures of the functional molecules have to be. Nevertheless, it is usually very clear what kind of properties they need to possess. From a conceptual point of view, to increase the rate of discovery in chemistry, this requires a paradigm shift from designing properties by defining structures to designing structures by defining properties, which is termed inverse design.
Present developments in machine learning and artificial intelligence show great promise to realize genuine inverse design in chemistry. One of the biggest challenges is the practically infinite size of chemical space which makes comprehensive inverse design still an elusive goal. Current solutions to this open problem are the restriction of inverse design campaigns to a tractable chemical subspace, which requires a significant amount of prior knowledge of the problem to be tackled. By restricting chemical space, successful algorithmic implementations of inverse design problems have been demonstrated already based on optimizing sets of computed properties. Large scale applications of these inverse design strategies are yet to be realized for optimization of experimental properties.
In this project, we plan to establish the inverse design workflow for autonomous molecular discovery to establish bottom-up design rules for the prediction of effective donor-acceptor duplexes in the field of organic electronics, with the potential to change how active materials for organic solar cells are invented. The general idea is that donor and acceptor molecules with complementary noncovalent interaction motifs would self-assemble in bulk heterojunctions promoting charge separation and allowing to construct non-fullerene organic solar cells with high power conversion efficiencies at low cost. By establishing a ‘genetic code’ for donors and acceptors, new organic semiconductors could be constructed by linear synthetic coupling of a library of simple building blocks into oligomers.
To achieve this goal, we will use both automatic high-throughput computations and experimentations for the characterization of a large amount of potential donor-acceptor duplexes. The collected data will be compiled in a library, which will be used for training deep neural networks used for inverse design and discovery of even more promising structures enabling autonomous discovery of new promising leads. Finally, large-scale statistical analysis of the collected data will be carried out to establish bottom-up design rules for active materials in organic solar cells and unveil strong non-covalent interaction motifs.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Autonomous Laboratory, Big Data Analysis, High Throughput Computations, Inverse Design, Non-covalent Interactions, Organic Electronics, Organic Solar Cells

Title: Reconstruction of Proto-Western Kho-Bwa
Abstract:
During this postdoctoral research, I will reconstruct Proto-Western Kho-Bwa, the ancestor language of the modern Western Kho-Bwa languages Khispi, Duhumbi, Sartang and Sherdukpen (Tibeto-Burman/Kho-Bwa cluster). These languages are all spoken in the state of Arunachal Pradesh in north-eastern India. 
Until now, not much is known about the genetic affiliation of the Kho-Bwa cluster, and some scholars have expressed doubt about which languages belong to the cluster, and even whether the cluster belongs to the Tibeto-Burman language family at all. Speculation about the affiliation is, however, not supported by any concrete linguistic evidence. 
The reconstruction of Proto-Western Kho-Bwa is an important initial step in a bottom-up approach that will later include the languages Bugun and Puroik too, thus establishing the position of the entire Kho-Bwa cluster. Determining the genetic position of small, endangered linguistic groups and isolate languages in the linguistically diverse eastern Himalayan region is extremely relevant in view of recent genetic studies that reveal the importance of this region in the population history of Asia. The eastern Himalayas have served as an important passageway for people moving between South Asia, Southeast Asia and East Asia, and this is reflected in the linguistic diversity of the area.

I have collected a large amount of data on the Western Kho-Bwa languages, which will enable me to use the comparative method to determine cognate roots, establish regular sound correspondences and reconstruct proto-forms. 
The research will result in three conference presentations, four journal articles and a monograph, presenting the reconstructed onsets, the reconstructed rhymes, the reconstructed roots and affixes, the sound correspondences between the reconstructed forms and the contemporary varieties, and the genetic affiliation of the Western Kho-Bwa languages. 
Furthermore, the research will result in an open-access database of Western Kho-Bwa forms from all varieties, indicating loans and inherited forms, and including lexical roots as well as dependant morphemes.

This postdoctoral research is a logical continuation of the grammatical description of one of the Western Kho-Bwa languages, Duhumbi, completed as a PhD dissertation as part of the SNSF-funded project ‘Strategische Zielsetzungen ins Subkontinent’ (2012-2015). The research will also forge a synergy between the expertise available at the School for African and Oriental Studies in London and the Institut für Sprachwissenschaft in Bern, implementing a systematic and conscientious approach to the reconstruction of Proto-Tibeto-Burman and the linguistic history of Asia, in the same way that the synergy of the knowledge in various institutes and schools in the past made the reconstruction of Proto-Indo-European possible.

Title: Robustness, Causality and External Validity of Statistical Machine Learning, with applications in Digital Health
Abstract:
Background motivation.
External validity or external generalization refers to the situation where results and findings of an empirical study are externally applicable and valid for a new target population which is not included in the study. Assuming that an empirical study finding (often in terms of a statistical p-value) applies to a new slightly different target population will be often massively misleading. Instead, and at the core of this proposal, one needs to develop techniques which allow to transfer results to a new target population in a robust and more reliable way. One of our main applications in this proposal is the field of digital health: a system, model or algorithm for a medical center has to be robustified so that it also works reliably for other centers.    

General goals. We will develop mathematical theory, statistical methodology, efficient algorithms and provide open-source software; furthermore we will work and collaborate on major application problems in digital health, including the reliability and improving external validity of predictions and medical interventions effects.

Specific approaches. It is well-known that modern machine learning algorithms often do not generalize well to new scenarios, We address the topic from at least two different angles. (i) Modeling of heterogeneity and perturbations in large-scale data: we will consider structural equation  and random effect models, thereby using and further developing techniques in causality and empirical Bayes methodology. (ii) Distributionally robust algorithms and corresponding uncertainty assessment: we will consider robustification of machine learning prediction algorithms and also develop the largely unexplored topic of assigning uncertainties (e.g. constructing confidence regions) which are robust in a distributional worst-case or average sense.

Title: Domain-Informed System Dynamics Modelling of Tree Growth and Mortality under Changing Climatic Conditions
Abstract:
Climate change is increasingly impacting global forest ecosystems, reducing tree vitality and increasing mortality rates. These changes in turn compromise forests' ability to sequester carbon and regulate water fluxes, creating a positive feedback loop that reinforces and accelerates climate change. Traditionally, tree mortality was observed at the warm and dry edges of species distributions, but recent findings indicate that dieback is occurring even within core climatic areas of affected species. Reduced tree growth and increasing tree crown defoliation are known indicators for mortality risks. Yet, existing modelling approaches fail to capture the non-linear, time-dependent interactions between climatic stressors and tree functioning.

On the one hand, traditional ecological models make basic assumptions of linearity and stationarity, which fail to capture the complex, non-linear, and time-dependent interactions between trees and their environment. On the other hand, classical machine learning models often capture spurious correlations that severely limit their generalizability and ability to extrapolate outside of their training domain. The latter limitation makes them unsuitable as decision-making tools under rapidly changing climatic conditions.

This project aims to develop a new class of predictive models capable of producing novel insights from existing ecological, physiological, and climatic data. Unlike purely statistical or correlative machine learning models, our approach will combine mechanistic knowledge with deep neural networks in an end-to-end differentiable framework. The model will incorporate observed variables from the ICP Forests Level 1 and 2 networks, remote sensing indices (NDVI), and climatic data to improve predictions of tree mortality and resilience, both in terms of accuracy and explainability. One specific objective of the project is to produce models that reliably extrapolate their predictions to hypothesized climatic or management scenarios.

This project is expected to advance forest modelling by overcoming limitations of current statistical and machine learning approaches, offering improved prediction accuracy and mechanistic understanding. Insights from this project will inform adaptive forest management strategies that optimize carbon sequestration and mitigate the adverse effects of climate change on forest ecosystems. Our findings will support global efforts in climate change mitigation by enhancing forest resilience and preserving biodiversity.

By integrating ecological knowledge with advanced modelling, we aim to significantly improve how tree growth and mortality are predicted, both from a quantitative and qualitative point of view. This effort therefore is a critical step towards more evidence-based conservation and management practices.
Keywords: Climate change, Differentiable models, Forest ecosystems, Forest resilience, Hybrid AI, Machine learning, Predictive ecology, Tree mortality
