Title: Exploring organizational stigma: Positive emotions, contests between evaluative audiences, and consequences of partnering with stigmatized organizations
Abstract:
The aim that I set myself for the Postdoc.Mobility fellowship at the University of Cambridge Judge Business School is to advance research on organizational stigma. 
The first project contributes to the management literature by showing how positive emotions can help stakeholders to make sense of supporting stigmatized organizations. Stigma is a negative social evaluation that results from audiences’ interpretations of an organization and its activities (Hudson, 2008). The literature has shown that emotional reactions are a crucial component of organizational stigma and that stigma elicits negative emotions such as anger and disgust (Ashforth, 2019; Kvåle & Murdoch, in press). However, recent research suggests that positive emotions can help stigmatized organizations garnering acceptance and improving ties with stakeholders (Frandsen & Morsing, in press; Lashley & Pollock, 2020). For this project, I will conduct interviews and collect data on fan forums and social media to study how fans of stigmatized football clubs use positive emotions to make sense of their support and the accusations against the club. The data will be analyzed through an inductive approach (Gioia, Corley, & Hamilton, 2012) and complemented with a quantitative sentiment analysis. A preliminary analysis of fan forums and social media posts that I conducted suggests that fans of stigmatized football clubs express passion, enthusiasm, and pride when reflecting on reasons for their support and use humor and affection in response to attacks against the club.
The second project studies contests between multiple audiences over organizational stigmatization. Stigma rests on evaluations made by heterogeneous audiences, which may reach different conclusions about an organization’s appropriateness (Helms & Patterson, 2014). Thus, the stigmatization of an organization may be contested between stigmatizing audiences and its supporters. I will study contests between supporters of stigmatized football clubs and stigmatizing audiences by collecting longitudinal data on social media. This project will yield important insights into the ‘stickiness’ of stigmatizing evaluations and labels. Social media is the ideal place to collect data for this project because it is a platform where diverse audiences engage. This project also answers recent calls for longitudinal research on stigmatization processes (Zhang, Wang, Toubiana, & Greenwood, 2021) and will advance the field’s understanding of how organizational stigma is constructed, maintained, and removed. I will analyze the data through an inductive approach to build theory from the data (Gioia et al., 2012).
The third project investigates if a high reputation protects organizations from negative consequences that partnerships with stigmatized actors entail. Associations with stigmatized actors can lead to a stigma transfer, which hampers an organization’s performance and ability to attract employees (Hudson & Okhuysen, 2009). I will collect data on football sponsorship deals to analyze if partnering with a sponsor that belongs to a stigmatized category affects the transfer fees clubs pay for players and how a club’s reputation moderates this effect. While clubs with a high reputation will probably not have to pay a transfer fee that is significantly higher than the player’s estimated value, clubs with a low reputation will pay a premium. This means that a club’s reputation could shield it from negative spillovers of the partnership. This project responds to recent calls for research on the relationship between different social evaluations constructs (Pollock, Lashley, Rindova, & Han, 2019) and will provide new insights on how stigma and reputation interact to shape organizational outcomes.
Keywords: Emotions, Identity, Organization and management theory, Organizational reputation, Organizational stigma, Qualitative research methods, Sensemaking, Social evaluations

Title: Trustworthy and Interpretable Atomistic Machine Learning
Abstract:
In the past few years, atomic scale simulations have undergone a profound transformation due to the increasingly common use of machine-learning (ML) techniques as a surrogate model of quantum mechanics, which allows predicting the outcome of an accurate electronic structure calculation at a fraction of the computational cost. This makes it possible to simulate larger systems, longer time scales, and more realistic conditions, extending greatly the scope and the impact of computational approaches to materials and chemical discovery. However, departing from a traditional modeling paradigm that relies on a series of physics-grounded approximations to simplify the description of an atomistic problem requires some caution. Whereas the limits of applicability of simplified physical models are often well appreciated, several aspects of atomistic machine learning are not fully understood yet. 

For example, it is broadly recognized that a combination of symmetry and locality constraints is beneficial to atomistic machine learning, as it incorporates fundamental physical priors into the model. These constraints restrict substantially the design space of structural descriptors, so that most ML frameworks are remarkably similar, built on atom-centered correlations of the neighbor density. It is however unclear what is the impact of the many implementation details, and not even what type of information must be included in a model to ensure they can differentiate between - and hence learn about - structures it have inequivalent geometries and therefore different properties. Another desirable feature of physics-based approaches is their interpretability, as they often generate useful microscopic insights, while data-driven models tend to be more opaque, and provide answers but little understanding. Finally, if would be desirable to achieve a better control of the approximation error of ML models, and their ability to make extrapolative predictions for atomic configurations that differ substantially from those that are part of the training set. 

The broad goal of this proposal is to tackle several of the open fundamental questions concerning established and emerging ML models for molecules and materials, and to provide practical strategies to increase their reliability and interpretability - achieving a level of understanding and error control that can make data-driven techniques as trustworthy and insightful as physics-based ones. We intend to tackle two core questions: (i) what is the expressive power of different ML models, how can it be quantified and optimized to find the best balance between accuracy, and data/energy efficiency? (ii) what is the role of locality in atomistic ML, how can we exploit it to make models more interpretable and insightful, and to obtain more effective uncertainty quantification and active learning? 

These fundamental, and rather abstract, questions have in themselves high intellectual and practical value, but acquire further concrete relevance when seen against the backdrop of the ongoing activities in the PI's group, which include (i) the development of machine-learning models to evaluate interatomic potentials as well as functional properties of materials, (ii) the seamless integration of ML components with explicit electronic-structure calculations, and (iii) their use for solveing technological challenges related to molecular materials, solid-state electrolytes and catalysis. These applied projects provide the context for the more fundamental focus of this proposal, and will ensure the immediate relevance of its formal, abstract findings. A work-package will be dedicated to maximize the synergies between these efforts, and to the implementation of the various proposed methodologies. By releasing these implementations in easy-to-use, open-source software packages, we will facilitate access to tools that allow for the rational design of ML frameworks, for a broader community outside our lab. Finally, this proposal also includes an educational dimension, both through the training of three junior collaborators in a highly-relevant research area, and through the development of a graduate course in atomistic machine learning.
Keywords: atomistic simulations, computational materials design, machine learning, uncertainty quantification

Title: The ecological role of bacterial motility in the ocean
Abstract:
The nutrient landscape for bacteria in the ocean is highly heterogeneous, down to the sub-millimeter scale. As a result, movement behavior is an important ecological strategy to acquire resources for many marine bacteria, involving motility and chemotaxis (the ability to direct motility toward chemicals). As a first example, many marine bacteria home in on the nutrient-rich region—the ‘phycosphere’—that surrounds individual phytoplankton cells, which often leak organic compounds: this is one of the most important forms of microbial interaction in the sea because it leads to a direct consumption of primary productivity. Yet, we still ignore how broad this interaction is and in particular whether it also occurs with the smallest and most abundant marine phytoplankton, the picocyanobacteria, responsible for 25% of the ocean’s primary productivity. As a second example, many bacteria encounter and attach to ‘marine snow’ particles, a rich source of organic matter that forms when dead phytoplankton and other detritus aggregate. Because the sinking of these particles drives a climatically critical carbon flux—the ‘biological pump’—responsible for transforming atmospheric CO2 into biomass and sequestering it in the oceans’ depths, the role of bacteria in remineralizing particles represents a direct link between their microscale behavior and global biogeochemical cycles. Yet, we still do not understand the foraging process and the ‘decision-making’ of individual bacteria as they search for, attach to, consume and eventually detach from particles, because of the lack of an individual-cell perspective in studies of bacteria–particle interactions.
These two ecological scenarios—phycospheres and particles—provide important, ubiquitous examples of the heterogeneity of the resource landscape and how movement behavior can be an important competitive strategy. In turn, the processes shaping the bacterial resource landscape are not homogeneous in the ocean, and in particular are often a strong function of depth, for example because the concentration of phytoplankton cells and particles changes greatly with depth. Yet, we are still in the dark as to how prevalent bacterial movement behavior is over the depth of the water column, significantly limiting our ability to model and predict the ecological and biogeochemical impacts of bacteria.
This project aims to advance our understanding of the forms, prevalence, individuality and ecology of movement behavior of marine bacteria. In three work packages, each addressing specific hypotheses through the development of new or the application of recently developed microscale technology, we aim for the first time to:
WP1. Determine the limits of chemotaxis of marine bacteria to phytoplankton by assessing their ability to exploit the smallest photosynthetic microorganisms (picocyanobacteria) as nutrient resources, through single-cell 3D tracking with digital holographic microscopy and machine learning.
WP2. Understand the real-time decision-making of individual marine bacteria as they use movement behavior to acquire nutrients in a heterogeneous resource landscape, through a novel fluorescent-barcode system (‘microArgos’) to track individual bacteria for hours in microfluidic arenas.
WP3. Quantify the prevalence of motility and chemotaxis toward ecologically relevant compounds over the depth of the ocean water-column, by deploying our recently developed in-situ motility (ISMA) and chemotaxis (ISCA) microfluidic assays allied with ecological characterization and metagenomics.
In addressing these aims, we will illuminate, for the first time, previously inaccessible and yet fundamental features of movement behavior in marine bacteria. Our overarching goal is both to deepen our understanding of the microscale behaviors and biogeochemical roles of these important microorganisms, and to substantially enrich the toolbox for interrogating microscale behaviors in microorganisms in general.
Keywords: Bacteria, Biogeochemical cycling, Chemotaxis, Growth, Microbial ecology, Microbial oceanography, Microfluidics, Motility, Ocean, Tracking

Title: FORESAIT - Forecasting in Social Assistance
Abstract:
This project uses linked register data and advanced machine learning methods to develop a precise, unbiased, and practical model for predicting outcomes in social assistance. Individuals who are on social assistance longer suffer more in terms of mental health and deteriorating skills, creating difficulties finding a job, longer periods of poverty and dependence, and higher costs to the taxpayer. Therefore, a key challenge for social workers in social assistance is to promptly identify at-risk individuals, allowing for early and targeted interventions such as training and job search support. Register databases with granular personal data from large client populations, combined with machine learning technology, presents new opportunities for early risk assessment. Drawing from the literature on predictive risk modeling in unemployment support, the main challenges include ensuring model accuracy to precisely identify those at risk of long-term unemployment, maintaining fairness or avoiding disproportionate errors by socio-demographic group, and ensuring ease of integration into counseling workflows without extra data collection demands.
We develop models predicting social assistance outcomes like long-term receipt, the duration of social assistance receipt, and reasons for social assistance exit using linked data from social assistance, population, social insurance, and health registers. Predictor variables include individual information on current and past socio-demographic, economic, health, and family characteristics as well as macro labor market indicators. We also test models based on survey data including subjective factors such as skills, attitudes, and well-being. We train models using popular supervised machine learning algorithms (e.g., gradient boosting, neural networks), but also test the applicability and performance of the “life2vec” model (https://life2vec.dk/), a recent innovation in machine learning that builds on transformer-based architecture to more effectively use the sequential nature of life events data to predict life outcomes. We train models with varying predictor variables, identifying those that contribute most to model accuracy and that minimize socio-demographic biases. We will prioritize predictor variables that do not impose additional data collection workload for welfare offices, i.e., data that is already routinely collected.
Academically, this project makes novel contributions to the literature on predictive risk modeling in social work. We will provide new evidence on whether statistical models can reach state-of-the art levels of accuracy predicting outcomes of the heterogenous populations receiving means-tested income support, as well as unique evidence on whether the new “life2vec” model is applicable to, and performs well, predicting social assistance outcomes and on whether prediction models based on register data must be supplemented with survey data. With respect to the Swiss social work literature, it is the first study of predictive risk models in Swiss social assistance. More broadly, this project marks a pioneering step towards leveraging extensive investments in case management software and data collection in Swiss social assistance. It is part of an ongoing collaboration between the research team and several local and cantonal social assistance offices to develop and test efficient and ethically responsible prediction systems and data science applications. The project should contribute to a more informed use of social worker resources, leading to shorter periods on social assistance and not only lower public expenses but also improved mental health for clients.
Keywords: Algorithmic profiling, Life2vec, Long-term dependency, Machine Learning, Predictive risk modeling, Register data, Social assistance

Title: Modelling and estimation of unsteady aerodynamic flow at high Reynolds number
Abstract:
In the turbulent atmospheric boundary layer, an increasing number of engineering systems experience aerodynamic unsteady flows, including wind turbines, helicopters, and air vehicles. Interactions with the turbulence in the atmosphere can lead to large load fluctuations, shortened lifetime and reduced effectiveness of aerodynamic controllers. Understanding and modelling these interactions is therefore a key topic in the field of unsteady aerodynamics, but little has been investigated at high Reynolds numbers (> 10^6) where wind turbines and large air vehicles operate. Moreover, at angles of attack near the maximum of lift of an airfoil, the flow becomes three-dimensional (3D). A better understanding of unsteady turbulent flows over airfoils would help to improve the estimation of the dynamic forces and to develop more efficient models to control airfoils in these environments. However, today this is not possible as there is no experimental data at high Reynolds numbers with a controlled turbulent inflow available, in which the dynamic 3D flow structures and their surface pressure responses are measured. 
This SNF-ANR joint proposal focuses on the following three key research challenges:
1. Evaluate the influence of different turbulent scales on the load fluctuations and flow separation over airfoils at high Reynolds number.
2. Develop physics-based low-order models to estimate the turbulent aerodynamic flow with a quantified uncertainty and with a minimum amount of sensors.
3. Implement the most appropriate low-order model into a fast edge computing robust measurement system to estimate the unsteady loads.

Title: Learning with Principles: Theory and Methods
Abstract:
The role of data-driven methods in our modern society is indisputable; the emerging field of data science is now being vastly exploited in various research areas such as drug discovery, decision making, medical image analysis, and artificial intelligence. At the core of data science is machine learning, an interdisciplinary domain that attracts researchers from different areas of applied mathematics and computer science; in particular, statistics, optimization, and signal processing. Despite the astounding recent advances in achieving above-human performances in many machine learning tasks (e.g., image classification), the community is quite far from establishing a comprehensive theory that would explain the success of the state-of-the-art methods (i.e., deep neural networks) as well as characterize their fundamental limitations.

In this proposal, we aim to develop a theoretical framework for “learning with principles” that explains the performance of the current methods and to propose new learning schemes that are interpretable and enjoy solid stability guarantees. We follow the common approach of formulating the learning process as an optimization problem. In particular, we consider the nonparametric setting, where the learned mapping is selected from an infinite-dimensional function space. The choice of the search space will be motivated by the desirable principles we seek for the resulting learning scheme. Broadly speaking, we plan to address the following fundamental questions:

(Q1) When does the optimal solution exist, is unique, and has a parametric representation?
(Q2) How can we leverage the characterization to numerically find the optimal solution?
(Q3) What are the statistical properties of the derived learning scheme?
(Q4) How does the developed theory explain the success of deep neural networks?

To answer Q1, we rely on the advanced tools borrowed from functional analysis — duality theory in particular — developed for the study of optimization problems. By answering to this question, we ensure that the corresponding learning scheme is well-defined and can be recast as a finite- dimensional problem that can be solved numerically.

For Q2, we deploy the existing techniques for numerically solving large-scale learning problems. In this context, online methods are of special interest to us. The desired end-result is a collection of open-source packages that provide robust and interpretable solutions to a broad class of learning problems.

Finally, we rely on recent developments in high-dimensional statistics and deep-learning theory to provide comprehensive answers to Q3 and Q4. The outcome will help the community to understand the behavior of neural networks, especially in high-dimensional settings.
Keywords: Deep learning theory, Functional Analysis, Optimization theory, Statistical learning theory

Title: Evolutionary-scale interpretation of protein functions in the human gut microbiome
Abstract:
Thanks to over a decade of metagenomics efforts, we have a sequence catalogue of over 170 million unique putative proteins from the human gut microbiome. About 40% of these do not have any function assigned (dark proteins), hence limiting our understanding of the well-established relationship between the gut microbiome and human physiology. Current homology-based methods used for functional assignment have reached their limits due to the availability of reference data. But we are now in a new era of computational biology, where deep-learning-based approaches allow us to predict protein structures (e.g. AlphaFold2), functions (e.g. deepFRI), and molecular mechanisms at extremely high levels of detail. This opens the door to further model protein interactions and remote evolutionary relationships (e.g. the Protein Universe Atlas) at unprecedented scales. Following up on these developments, our aim is to construct an integrative view of putative molecular functions and biological roles of proteins from the human gut microbiome by combining deep learning-driven, structure-based function prediction with a large-scale view of the protein universe. 
Our specific goals are to:
1. Construct a catalogue of human gut microbiome protein structures and functions, revising functional annotations and constructing 3D structural models for those without homologs of known experimental or predicted structure.
2. Investigate the sequence and structure diversity of dark proteins in the human gut microbiome in the context of all known proteins.
3. Study the evolutionary origins and histories of such dark proteins, evaluating how they emerged and may relate to those outside the human gut ecosystem.
4. Predict and analyse molecular and biological functions of human gut microbiome proteins by combining 3D structure and conserved genomic context information.

Our large-scale and integrative approach to map and interpret all human gut microbiome proteins, especially those that are difficult to annotate and are thus functionally dark, will lay the groundwork for efficient metagenomic-scale use of this source of biological information. It will provide life scientists a better understanding of gut microbiota metabolic phenotypes, helping to prioritize relevant proteins for experimental characterization and therapeutic exploration.
Keywords: deep learning, genomics, human gut, human health, machine learning, microbiome, protein function, protein structure

Title: AnaGraM: Adaptive numerical methods for time series  analysis of time-dependent dynamical Graphs in the presence of Missing data
Abstract:
Graph-theoretical approaches are becoming more and more popular in many areas of applied science. One of the main reasons for that is a rapid development of graph theory in the last years, relating it to the theory of dynamical systems and, especially relating graphs with stochastic dynamical systems like Markov processes and random walks. These groundbreaking theoretical developments have led to an emergence of a large family of practical applications like (just to mention a few of them): non-linear dimension reduction methods (e.g., based on diffusion and Laplacian eigenmaps); transfer operator approach to dynamical systems; or new engines for internet search such as Google's PageRank algorithm. Graph-related approaches are also getting a lot of attention as tools for analyzing and visualizing the relation between the different components of very large data sets.
The current research proposal is a two-year follow-up of the previous three-year SNSF-project AnaGraph: Adaptive Numerical methods for time series Analysis of time-dependent graphs in context of dynamical systems. AnaGraph was investigating the methodological approaches to data-based inference of non-stationary (i.e., changing in time) graphs in context of dynamical systems. The research program of the AnaGraph-project was outperformed, resulting in 10 scientic papers (7 of them are already published and 3 are in press) in international peerreviewed journals. Computational tools developed in the AnaGraph-project have demonstrated optimal parallelizability on modern hardware architectures of the Swiss Supercomputing Centre in Lugano (CSCS) and are applicable to realistic data analysis problems. Based on a given time series of graph-related observables, developed algorithms allow to identify the temporal changes in the underlying models, as well as to perform a model/data reduction and informationtheoretical comparison of different methods. Main published applications of the methods developed in the predecessor AnaGraph-project were concentrated in two following application areas:
(i) climate/weather/turbulence research; as well as (ii) in computational sociology.
Main methodological aim of this follow-up proposal is an extension of the Finite Element
Methods of time series analysis with Bounded Variation of model parameters (FEM-BV) developed in the previous AnaGraph-project towards the incomplete/missing observational data. Main challenge will be in creating the methods that allow a structure-preserving (in the sense of conservation properties and causality relations of the related dynamical system) inference of the underlying graph structures and missing data imputation. Emerging methods should operate beyond the restrictive stationarity and homogeneity assumption of the standard graph and matrix completion theory approaches. Main practical aim of the current follow-up proposal will be in High-Performance Computing implementation of the developed methods on modern supercomputers and their application to problems in bioinformatics: to gene expression data analysis in genomics, data-driven inference of probabilistic gene networks, their analysis and reduction. The practical problem will be formulated in FEM-BV context as graph problems with missing data and attacked by the methods and tools that were developed in the previous project (i.e., FEM-BV-methods for model inference and reduction) and the new missing data imputation tools that will be developed in the theoretical part of the current project. Previously published work and preliminary results demonstrate that the methods developed in the AnaGraph project have some conceptual and practical/computational advantages in comparison to the standard machine learning tools in this area (e.g., Bayesian mixture models, unsupervised hierarchical Bayesian clustering and K-means methods) in feature extraction for realistic gene expression sets. In a collaboration with external experts from experimental biology, as well as with the local experts in HPC (in the areas of cloud- and GPGPU-computing), graph-related data analysis and classification methods will be compared and evaluated wrt. their HPC-performance and potential in the rapidly developing area of bioinformatics.
Keywords: Gene Ontology, Gene expression analysis, Markov processes, adaptive numerical methods, discrete stochastic processes, graph inference, high performance computing, multiscale processes, nonstationary processes, time series analysis, transfer operator

Title: Search for the neutron EDM at the high intensity ultracold neutron source at PSI with an upgraded high sensitivity spectrometer – Follow-up application II.
Abstract:
Searches for a permanent neutron Electric Dipole Moment (nEDM) with sensitivities better than 10^-26 e·cm are regarded top priority by the particle physics community, since they could reveal new sources of CP violation as predicted by theoretical models beyond the Standard Model (see e.g. [Rai08], [Dub11]). The goal of our international collaboration currently involving 14 European research institutes and universities is to reach until end of 2016 (end of this requested funding period) a cumulative sensitivity better than 10^-26 e·cm with the present apparatus. The new laser-based 199Hg co-magnetometer proposed in this follow-up application will allow for a significant improvement of the nEDM sensitivity and the reduction of several systematic effects.
Here we ask for continuation of funding of a PhD position and a postdoc position for two years. Both will be members of the PSI UCN-Physics group and key figures to the timely realization of the project. 
The postdoc will have the main task to perform nEDM data analysis and coordinate one of the two independent analysis teams of the collaboration, the one centered at PSI where the nEDM experiment is located. The task of the postdoc will be to contribute substantially to the necessary software design and coding and coordinate the development of analysis algorithms for expert systems. He/she will be the central person to design fitting algorithms to combine the data to one nEDM value including all available information. 
The PhD student will continue her work on the development, implementation and characterization of a laser-based 199Hg co-magnetometer aiming at improved sensitivity and the reduction of important systematic effects in the nEDM measurement. In addition to the main task, the PhD student will participate in nEDM data taking and analysis. The academic supervisor for the PhD student will be Prof. Dr. Klaus Kirch, ETH Zürich.
Keywords: high resolution magnetometry, neutron electric dipole moment, ultracold neutrons

Title: Bank Competition for Deposits and Transmission of Monetary Policy
Abstract:
The recent inflation surge prompted central banks across the developed world to tighten their monetary policy by raising their short-term interest rates to levels unseen since the onset of the Great Recession. The broad consensus in the macroeconomics literature suggests that these interest rate increases have an anti-inflationary effect. However, there is less of a consensus on precise mechanics through which an increase in short-term interest rates translates into a reduction in inflation. The lack of precise understanding of monetary policy transmission exposes society to a significant risk of policy error because central banks necessarily rely on estimates of the transition mechanism when deciding how much to raise short-term rates in reaction to incoming inflation developments. A sufficiently large error in the estimate of the transmission mechanism might induce a central bank to move interest rates too high or too little, potentially pushing the economy into a recession associated with high unemployment or vice-versa failing to prevent a costly inflationary episode.

In this project, I aim to contribute to the understanding of monetary policy transmission by developing a structural model of the deposit market and incorporating it into a standard New Keynesian framework used by central banks to guide their policymaking process. The motivation behind this proposal is twofold. First, current New Keynesian models typically either abstract from the existence of banks and deposits or model them using approximations inconsistent with observed data. Second, recent empirical literature (e.g. Greenwald et al., 2023) shows that bank market power in the deposit market plays a crucial role in the dynamics of the passthrough of monetary policy to deposit rates faced by savers as well as business loan and mortgage rates. In light of these empirical findings, the omission of the deposit mechanism in the state-of-the-art monetary models has the potential to cause large errors in policy advice generated by those models.

I plan to use the resulting general equilibrium model to study the role of deposit market frictions in optimal monetary policy design and to explore the implications of changes in the structure of the deposit market (e.g. bank mergers) for the conduct of monetary policy.

Title: Essential Indexicality and Thoughts about Experience
Abstract:
This project explores the relations between two central themes in contemporary philosophy of language and mind, mental indexicality and phenomenal consciousness, in connection with the mind/body problem. The thesis that there is indexicality at the mental level is the thesis that some thoughts, typically expressible with indexicals like ‘I’ or ‘now’, present the world from a particular perspective in the world. Phenomenal consciousness refers to the subjective quality of our conscious experiences: there is, for instance, ‘something it is like’ to see red. Indexical knowledge (of who and where I am in the world) and phenomenal knowledge (of what it is like to see red) share an important feature: they seem irreducible to objective, third-personal knowledge. But how do the two notions of ‘first-person perspective’ relate exactly? This semantic/epistemic question has metaphysical import in current debates on the mind-body problem, since the apparent gap between the phenomenal and the physical knowledge we have of our conscious experiences is exploited in anti-physicalist arguments. One way to resist the anti-physicalist conclusion is to claim that this epistemic gap has its source not in the nature of consciousness (metaphysical gap), but only in the features of our thoughts about our conscious experiences (epistemic gap). According to a thesis we will call indexicalism, the special features of thoughts about our conscious experiences are indexical features: that is, the epistemic gap is explained via mental indexicality. Given indexicalism, phenomenal knowledge will be reduced to indexical knowledge, which is not usually taken to threaten physicalism. However, indexicalism as it has been developed so far, faces important objections that have led many authors to abandon that theoretical pathway. 

The project brings together philosophers with complementary expertise on mental indexicality (on the French side) and on phenomenal consciousness (on the Swiss side) to systematically assess two rival hypotheses about so-called phenomenal concepts (concepts we use to think about the phenomenal character of experience). According to the first hypothesis (the Index-hypothesis), an improved understanding of mental indexicality in general will make it possible to elaborate a version of indexicalism about phenomenal concepts which is not vulnerable to the relevant objections. If successful, it protects physicalism about phenomenal consciousness. According to the second hypothesis, phenomenal concepts are no indexical concepts but genuine property concepts which individuate the properties they serve to attribute by the thinker's understanding of what it is to have the relevant property. This claim (the GPC-hypothesis) leads in a natural manner to an anti-physicalist view of phenomenal consciousness. 

We expect a vivid and fruitful discussion within the project, since the French and the Swiss sides start out with incompatible stances on the two working hypotheses. While important work on both sides in recent years has prepared the ground for elaborating the two working hypotheses, there has been very little direct confrontation of their emerging competing views on the matter. This project is intended to provide the opportunity to do so. Such a confrontation is bound to provide substantial insights into issues that run deep into the origin of the mind-body problem. These insights should contribute crucially to our understanding of ourselves as human beings who are aware of themselves as experiencing subjects with the capacity to reflect on their own conscious states.

Title: Prediction of alternative protein conformations
Abstract:
Proteins are instrumental in biological processes, so solving their three-dimensional structures is crucial for understanding protein functions and related diseases. With the continuous efforts of researchers, around 100k structures of unique proteins have been determined experimentally and computational approaches for structure prediction have been developed. However, these prediction methods face three key limitations: (1) They predict structures based solely on canonical amino acids, yet protein functions require interaction with other molecules. (2) They predict a single structure, despite proteins functioning via multiple conformations. (3) These tools inaccurately predict structures for isoform protein sequences within the context of full-length proteins, indicating a lack of context awareness. This project aims to advance this field by developing structure prediction methods that predict multiple conformations, consider environmental conditions, and have enhanced context awareness. 

My first objective is to predict different protein conformations under various environmental conditions (like pH, and temperature) and in the presence of interacting entities such as ligands, ions, post-translational modifications (PTMs), DNA/RNA, lipids etc. My second objective is to improve the overall accuracy of protein structure prediction for challenging cases by improving the context awareness of protein structure prediction methods. Ultimately, my first objective will result in effective methods for predicting alternative protein structures, which are critical for elucidating biological processes, developing therapeutic agents, and designing functional proteins. My second objective will result in machine-learning models with enhanced context awareness, which is key for predicting accurate structures of protein isoforms and other challenging tasks as well as increasing the success rate of protein design.
Keywords: Alternative protein conformations, Machine learning for structural biology, Protein structure prediction

Title: Efficient Exploration in Structured Reinforcement Learning
Abstract:
Reinforcement learning has emerged as a central paradigm for studying adaptive decision making systems. Algorithms such as the upper confidence bound (UCB) strategy and Thompson sampling are by now well established and theoretically understood to enable sample efficient exploration in many settings. Yet, recent results suggest that these exploration strategies fail to exploit structural constraints that arise from prior information. In fact, most strategies rely on the premise that information is localized such that a near-greedy (reward maximizing) behaviour also leads to efficient information retrieval. This is a fundamental limitation in the design of previous algorithms.

The goal of this research project is to design and analyze efficient algorithms for reinforcement learning where prior information is embedded in the model class, known as structured reinforcement learning. The model structure can for example encode the physical laws of the environment and exploiting such information is key to obtain sample efficient methods. By modifying the standard observation model, we argue that finding exploration policies that generate data to discriminate sub-optimal from optimal policies becomes the central challenge. We expect that resolving this exploration trade-off requires new techniques that will be applicable in a wide range of settings. 

Our first goal is to study the information-theoretic sample complexity in the simplest possible model that requires structured exploration. We will design a learning policy that performs an optimal or near-optimal trade-off between exploration and exploitation. The second goal is to extend the results to the linear setting. This enables the use of features with large state or action spaces, and is recognized as an important step to inform heuristics in modern deep reinforcement learning. Third, we will combine insights from the first and second step to capture the structured learning objective in a parametrized, differentiable policy that can be trained in a modern deep learning system. Throughout our focus is to provide theoretical guarantees for the proposed strategies and evaluate the algorithms on benchmark environments.
Keywords: machine learning, reinforcement learning, sequential decision making

Title: A general bottom-up platform for the rational design of multi-domain biosensors with programmable input-output behaviors
Abstract:
Living cells communicate and respond to their environment through signals mediated by receptors embedded on their surface. Among these, the large class of single-pass receptors are essential for physiological immune and developmental functions, yet they also contribute to the development of severe diseases. They sense a wide variety of extracellular molecules using specific recognition domains, transmitting the binding signals to intracellular regions via long-range conformational changes facilitated by a range of extracellular and transmembrane domains. Their modular architecture has encouraged the empirical construction of chimeric receptors with novel functionalities through native domain swapping and recombination. While this approach has created a few notable molecules that proved useful in cell-based therapies, the rational design of receptors with programmable functions remains challenging, owing to a scarcity of structural information and mechanistic understanding of receptor function, and lack of reliable modeling or design approaches. It has been suggested that inter-domain communication critically controls receptor ligand sensing and signaling, depending both on the intrinsic dynamic switching and oligomerization propensities of individual domains, and the mechanical coupling between them. However, most current modeling and design approaches do not consider these properties and rely solely on optimization of tertiary structures and stability. To address these limitations, we propose to develop and experimentally validate a general computational platform for the design of multi-domain single-pass receptor biosensors with programmable input-output signaling functions that integrates and concurrently optimizes protein stability, oligomerization and dynamic coupling properties through the following aims. 
(1)To design switchable TM domains for optimal signal transmission across membranes.
We will use structural modeling, multi-state design, deep learning and experimental approaches to develop and validate a technique to design TM domains that, following dimerization, are able to switch between precise conformations for optimal signal transmission between the receptor extracellular and intracellular regions. 
(2)To assemble mechanically-coupled multi-domain extracellular regions. We will develop
and validate a technique to assemble and engineer multi-domain extracellular regions that mechanically couple ligand binding and TM regions for optimal signal transduction. 
(3)To expand sensing capabilities and design novel chimeric biosensors. We will leverage
diverse ligand binding domains and designed artificial chemically-controlled switches to expand sensing properties of chimeric biosensors and provide orthogonal ligand-binding stimulus of receptor signaling. 
Through this project, we will not only engineer novel receptors with programmable ligand sensing and signaling functions but also create and release a general modular platform for users to design their own biosensors for diverse applications, impacting the larger basic and synthetic biology community. While our study will accelerate the construction of next-generation biosensors for advanced cell-based therapy and synthetic biology, it will also enhance our understanding of the molecular and mechanistic determinants governing basic and pathophysiological receptor-mediated signal transductions and foster the development of effective therapeutics.
Keywords: cell engineering, computational protein modeling and design, multi-domain protein biosensors

Title: Phase-field modeling of fracture and fatigue: from rigorous theory to fast predictive simulations
Abstract:
The reliable prediction of fracture and fatigue phenomena is of paramount importance in many fields of science and engineering, for applications ranging from biomedical to mechanical to structural engineering; it needs accurate, flexible and experimentally validated models, as well as robust and efficient computational methods. In the past two decades, computational fracture mechanics has been revolutionized by the advent of the variational phase-field approach. This paradigm, which bears relation to Griffith’s theory in classical fracture mechanics, to gradient damage models in continuum mechanics, as well as to phase-field models for phase transformations in computational material science, has opened the pathway to fracture and fatigue simulations of unprecedented flexibility, which is motivating an enormous interest from the academic and industrial worlds alike. While the simplest case of quasi-static brittle fracture under predominant tension is by now well understood and experimentally validated, for more complex problems many open issues remain. Some of these problems, namely: brittle fracture under multiaxial stress states, ductile fracture, and fatigue, are the focus of the present project. For these cases, the few available variational formulations are only able to handle very simple situations and lack sufficient flexibility to be predictive for engineering purposes; the remaining formulations are non-variational and rely heavily on empirical components determined in an ad-hoc manner, thus, they give up several theoretical and practical advantages of variational models which are among the key reasons of their success. Additionally, a comprehensive experimental validation for these cases exploiting modern experimental techniques is still pending.  Finally, the applicability of the phase-field approach to large-scale simulations for industrial applications is hindered by its prohibitive computational cost, determined by the need to resolve a small inherent length scale and to adopt costly staggered solution schemes. 
Against this background, the goals of this project are: to develop a new generation of phase-field models for brittle fracture under multiaxial stress states, ductile fracture and fatigue, able to conjugate the elegant and rigorous variational structure of the original brittle fracture model with the flexibility and versatility required by advanced engineering applications; to thoroughly validate them with state-of-the-art experimental techniques; and to explore novel deep-learning-based approaches to dramatically reduce the computational cost of the related simulations.  To reach these goals, we intend to realize a tight synergy between theoretical modeling, computations with the finite element method, mechanical experiments including X-ray tomography with in-situ testing, and machine learning investigations based on physics-informed deep learning. If successful, the project will deliver rigorous but flexible variational models, suitable for a much larger scope of predictive fracture simulations than currently possible, as well as new experimental results combining global measurements with three-dimensional full-field displacements and fracture patterns under loading up to sub-micron resolution; moreover, the newly developed deep-learning-based tools for the fast solution of parametric phase-field fracture problems will represent a key step towards bridging the gap between academic small-scale high-fidelity simulations and industrial large-scale computations, and will enable future uncertainty quantification and design/optimization problems involving fracture for a large number of applications. Finally, we will initiate a long-term collective effort towards generation and maintenance of computational benchmarks on phase-field modeling of fracture, to facilitate further advancement in the field.
Keywords: deep learning, fatigue, fracture, phase-field modeling, plasticity

Title: Filtering with Spiking Neurons
Abstract:
One of the most fascinating aspect of the brain is its ability to continuously extract relevant features from dynamic environment such as the position of a moving prey from ambiguous visual stimuli or the voice of a known person in a noisy crowd. This problem of extracting hidden and dynamic features from noisy observations can be addressed mathematically by Bayesian filtering theory. It remains however unknown how networks of neurons actually implement such a Bayesian filter.
During the first 3 years of the SNF grant, we made significant progresses at the interface between mathematical filtering theory and its biological implementation. At the single synapse level, we proposed a new spiking neuron model for in-vivo dynamics (Surace and Pfister 2015) that is the key element for the validation of our synaptic filtering theory (Pfister et al. 2009; Pfister et al. 2010). At the neural network level, we proposed the first network dynamic model - the Neural Particle Filter (NPF) - that can perform nonlinear Bayesian filtering whilst implementable biologically (Kutschireiter et al. 2017). This NPF has several relevant properties. On the biological side, since this algorithm does not depend on importance weights, it can be easily implemented by a neural network. On the machine learning side, we could show that due to this weight-less particle filter approach, the NPF avoids the curse of dimensionality (Kutschireiter et al. 2017; Surace et al. 2017). Further, we could directly apply the NPF to an online-learning framework (Surace and Pfister 2016), this way deriving an online learning rule which even becomes local in the limit of small observation noise.
The aim of the present proposal is to extend the original SNF prof grant proposal entitled inference and learning with spiking neurons in two directions. The first project will extend our recent work on the neural network implementation of nonlinear filtering. We proposed the first implementation of nonlinear filtering (the Neural Particle Filter) with a network of neurons, but those neurons were assumed, for simplicity reasons, to be analog neurons (Kutschireiter et al. 2017). Here we will consider a biologically more relevant scenario where neurons are spiking and potentially include refractory periods. We will also study the properties of this new Spiking Neural Particle Filter (SNPF), in particular its scalability in high dimensions.
The second project will apply the SNPF to spiking data that have been recorded in Monkeys performing a decision making task (data from Prof. Valerio Mante Lab, INI, Zurich). The goal will be to bring a new view in conflicting literature about the nature of the statistical model that best captures recorded spiking trains. Some argued that the underlying firing rate slowly ramps up to a threshold - the ramping model (Mazurek 2003; Gold and Shadlen 2007) while others proposed a stepping model where the firing rate suddenly jumps to an elevated firing rate (Latimer et al. 2015). The idea here will be to propose a generalised model which includes both the ramping and the stepping model as specific case and determine to what extent the underlying rate is more consistent with a ramping or a stepping model.

Title: Radiomics as biomarker in multi-modality treatment of locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer
Abstract:
Radiomics is defined as the use of quantitative image analysis algorithms for calculation of a comprehensive set of image phenotypes also called image biomarkers. In contrast to conventional radiological image analysis, this methodology is a) objective and observer-independent and b) allows for a comprehensive description of all available information within medical images. Radiomics is therefore considered as a potential addition to the efforts currently undertaken in the field of precision medicine: to achieve a comprehensive analysis of the cancer phenotype in order to adjust the treatment to the patient-individual cancer characteristics.
The aim of this project is to establish and to use comprehensive radiomics analyses in CT and FDG-PET images for outcome modelling. Prior to all image analyses, the radiomics algorithms will be evaluated regarding their robustness against non-standardized image acquisition and image reconstruction parameters. In addition, a model for quantification of loco-regional tumor spread will be established and its prognostic and predictive value will be compared to the conventional staging system. Machine learning algorithms will be established to correlate the large amount of radiomics biomarkers with clinical outcome parameters. 
The radiomics methodology will be tested based on images acquired within the randomized SAKK 16-00 study of multi-modality treatment for locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Radiomics biomarkers of pre-treatment CT and FDG-PET images, or post induction therapy images and changes of radiomics parameters between these two time points will be analysed. Radiomics parameters will be correlated with available histo-pathological tumor characteristics, primary (event-free survival) and secondary (overall survival, response to induction therapy, failure pattern, pulmonary toxicity) study endpoints.
It is the hypothesis, that radiomics analyses will enable us to build better and more accurate prognostic models than the ones currently based on the TNM system as well as predictive models for identification of patients, who might benefit from neoadjuvant radiochemotherapy instead of neoadjuvant chemotherapy, only.
The radiomics methodology and the machine learning algorithms will be evaluated in cancer patients suffering from NSCLC, a disease with currently very poor prognosis. It is planned to evaluate radiomics and the machine learning algorithms in other cancer sites as well. Additionally, the application of radiomics and the machine learning algorithms are not restricted to Oncology but can maybe successfully used in other medical questions.
Keywords: Clinical outcome prediction, Imaging biomarkers, Radiomics

Title: Causal inference, distribution generalization and heavy-tailed models
Abstract:
The proposal's main objective is to explore new connections between causal inference, on the one hand, and distributional generalization and heavy-tailed models, on the other.

The interface between causal inference and distribution generalization is a relatively new field. Distribution generalization aims to learn a model whose predictions work well in unseen environments. For example, in medical imaging problems, a model trained on x-ray images from hospital A might fail to predict x-ray images from hospital B if the distributions of these images are different. Causality can help in this quest. Causal regression models, which regress the response variable on its direct causes, provide robust predictions for unseen data (Peters et al., 2016; Christiansen et al., 2021). The first goal of this proposal is to study how causality can help achieve distribution generalization across unseen environments in non-parametric models with hidden confounders. In particular, I plan to develop a forest-based algorithm to learn a function that generalizes to unseen domains and works on large-scale data. To do so, I will rely on the control function theory developed by (Newey et al., 1999) and on the theoretical results of random forests (Breiman, 2001; Athey et al., 2019). The proposed method will illuminate possible connections between causal inference and distribution generalization. It will be helpful in applications that need models that generalize to new environments, e.g., the healthcare sector and precision medicine.

Recently, there has been an increasing interest in the intersection between causal inference and heavy-tailed models. One of the main goals of causal inference is to learn cause-effect relationships among variables. While there has been much progress in analyzing causal relationships between random variables, most existing methods are not well suited if the causal mechanisms only manifest themselves in extremes. Gnecco et al. (2021) introduced a novel approach to recovering partial causal information between variables using the signal in the tail of the distributions. The second goal of this proposal is to extend the work of Gnecco et al. (2021) and estimate the causal structure from heavy-tailed data. Title: Statistical Complexity in Financial Economics
Abstract:
Recent developments in artificial intelligence and machine learning have revolutionized many areas of science and technology. The underlying machine learning models share two things in common. First, they are all based on {\it deep artificial neural networks,} a particular class of functions inspired by the multi-neuron structure of the human brain. Second, these artificial neural networks, like the human brain, are incredibly complex and often feature billions of neurons and trillions of links (connections). The remarkable success of these complex models naturally raises the question: 
 What is the mechanism behind their superior performance? How is it possible to train models that often have more parameters than the number of observations on which they were trained? 
 While modern education is largely based on the {\it ``principle of parsimony"}, the modern machine learning revolution has turned the principle of parsimony on its head, leading to the discovery of the {\it virtue of complexity:} In many cases, complex, over-parametrized prediction models perform better out-of-sample, despite generating tremendous overfit in-sample. Furthermore, recent experimental evidence suggests that human beings are already using (and have probably been using for thousands of years) complex models for their decision-making. Indeed, even in everyday life, humans face ultra-high-dimensional sensory inputs (through vision and hearing) and must build predictive models that somehow process these data given only a few observations. Many real-world economic systems are characterized by tremendous statistical complexity. Indeed, the number of factors influencing the observed state of the world is often comparable to or even larger than the number of observations based on which economic agents learn. This project aims to develop novel theoretical and empirical models of economic behavior in the presence of statistical complexity. Using these models to investigate the ability of statistical complexity to explain numerous observed empirical phenomena in economic and financial systems, including behavioral expectation formation, equilibria in financial markets, and the emergence of hysteresis (long-term memory and path-dependencies) in economic data and models. As Susan Athey argues in her 2018 paper "The Impact of Machine Learning on Economics," "I believe that machine learning (ML) will have a dramatic impact on the field of economics within a short timeframe." 

Due to lack of space, I discuss one such direction, which, I believe, can have profound implications for economic modeling. In addition to the surprising statistical properties of predictions in the presence of statistical complexity, the key role of non-linearities in economic dynamics naturally leads to the question: Do economic agents use complex models in building economic forecasts? And, if they do, what are the implications for expectation formation and equilibrium behavior? One of the most important discoveries in recent years is the systematic over-reaction of economic expectations (both in households' expectations and in surveys of professional forecasters).  It turns out that when the shocks driving economic dynamics have varying degrees of persistence, statistical complexity can explain over-reaction and many other observed anomalies in expectations dynamics. Furthermore, it generates novel predictions about boom and bust cycles and excess volatility. These patterns emerge without the need to appeal to any form of bounded rationality. Rather, they are manifestations of the breakdown of the law of large numbers due to insufficient data. Most importantly, statistical complexity generates predictions that are strongly supported by data and are distinct from those of behavioral models. Investigating these effects in the framework of classical economic models (both for the dynamics of asset prices and for macroeconomic dynamics) is an important part of this research project.
Keywords: Asset Pricing, Big Data, Bounded Rationality, Complexity, Economic Expectations, Financial Markets, Learning, Machine Learning

Title: Keeping an eye on drought stress: UAV-based real-time monitoring of physiological tree responses in mature forests during drought events
Abstract: The increased frequency, duration and severity of heat and drought events in the coming years will challenge locally adapted temperate tree species and increase their vulnerability to abiotic and biotic disturbances. Traditional assessments of forest growth, forest structure and crown condition performed every few years by national forest inventories might therefore not sufficiently capture the impact of short-term extreme events on the state of our forests. Current monitoring approaches to study the impact of drought and heat stress on trees either lack real-time data needed to link stress occurrences to specific climatic events and/or causes (e.g., annual tree ring data) or are characterized by too low spatial and temporal resolutions to understand physiological processes at the tree-scale (e.g., airborne and satellite remote sensing data). In this project, we propose a novel methodological framework for near real-time monitoring of tree physiological responses, with the goal of detecting previsual symptoms of drought stress in our forests. To achieve this goal we will use a unique combination of state-of-the-art techniques, including high-resolution repeat thermal and hyperspectral imaging from unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV), leaf-level functional trait measurements including photosynthesis and stomatal conductance, leaf water potential, pigment composition and fluorescence parameters, and continuous environmental parameter time series (e.g., air temperature and humidity, soil water content) at two long-term experimental forest sites featuring controlled irrigation and rain exclusion mechanisms. This unique dataset will reveal the great potential of combining canopy temperature and reflectance by the photoprotective carotenoid pigments to capture drought-stress induced physiological responses at the previsual stage, preceding irreversible structural leaf cell damages. A machine learning model will be used to produce high-resolution spatially-continuous drought stress forest maps, starting from the remote sensing indicators. Although similar methods successfully demonstrated early water stress detection in agricultural systems, like Mediterranean tree orchards, their feasibility for monitoring drought stress in mature temperate forests has, to the best of our knowledge, never been investigated at the high temporal and spatial resolutions provided by UAV imaging. The complexity of forest ecosystems represents a high risk for the applicability of this methodology at an operational level. Crown mixture, shadows and diversity in stand architecture and species composition, are known to challenge the interpretability of remote sensing stress indicators. The high spatial resolution (i.e., centimeter) allowing to capture within-crown variations, coupled with the high turnaround times of UAV-based imaging, currently represents the most accurate methodology to test the feasibility of such a monitoring approach. If proven successful, this novel methodological framework and unique dataset could help to answer (1) which individuals within a population will be more vulnerable to a given drought, (2) which species will be more sensitive compared to others, and (3) do trees respond differently to varying intensities and durations of drought. Answers to such questions could significantly contribute to improve the mechanistic understanding of forest trees’ responses during drought and/or heat events and allow a better representation of the underlying physiological processes in dynamic vegetation models, resulting in more accurate future forest decline projections.
Keywords: UAV, drone, drought stress, forests, plant physiology, remote sensing

Title: The design of trade agreements and global supply chains: A large language model approach and its application
Abstract:
This project is a natural continuation of the applicants’ combined past and ongoing research on preferential trade agreements (PTAs). This project suggests a new approach to computationally retrieve, classify, and analyze legal texts and commitments from PTAs. It is also motivated by the observation that increasing trade in parts and components (the phenomenon also known as global value chains) has grown substantially over the past 30 years and has also been subject to criticism, not least due to concerns about resilience in cases of shocks to the trading system.

To better understand the extent to which the contents of PTAs reflect market developments of increasing firm integration and reliance on production networks over time and with what effect, we propose to significantly expand the DESTA database. The project develops more fine-grained measures of market access obligations enshrined in PTA commitments. It further re-focuses the mapping of PTAs not only along pre-defined chapters but across different parts (treaty texts and annexes) where GVC obligations are visible.  

To do so, the project builds on considerable advances in text-as-data methods, especially in terms of natural language processing via machine learning. We want to use these advances to arrive at a more fine-grained measurement of concepts relevant to an understanding of the design and evolution of PTAs. The development of these algorithms will also support the automatic updating of our database and the provision of key indexes for researchers and policymakers based on the “real-time” integration of new agreements being concluded worldwide.
Keywords: Design, Diffusion, Institutional Design, International Cooperation, Large Language Models, Political Economy, Trade Agreements, language models

Title: SAPIENS: Supporting the API Lifecycle with Neuro-Symbolic AI
Abstract:
As software weaves itself into the very fabric of our world, web application programming interfaces (APIs) turn into the stitches, the glue that holds everything together. Web APIs allow heterogeneous systems to communicate over the Internet, and they provide access to all kinds of data and services. We all use web APIs every day, when we post a tweet, order food online, book a flight, or watch a movie. Supporting the development and maintenance of web APIs can have a tremendous impact both on the productivity of developers and on the quality of the software they produce.

Today, artificial intelligence (AI) is a key ingredient of software development, with tools like ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot changing the way software is created. Anyone can develop software. This might seem compelling at first, but it poses challenges like properly integrating AI into the developer workflow and ensuring the quality of AI-generated software. In the realm of web APIs, AI-driven development falls short. The API lifecycle is complex, as it includes over a dozen phases that involve two parties, API producers and consumers. Activities in these lifecycle phases go far beyond just coding, for example, monitoring (e.g., checking for breaking changes that could affect API consumers), end-to-end testing (e.g., generating flows of HTTP requests to validate the service behavior), or software comprehension (e.g., understanding the API documentation or specification to integrate it into a client application), to name but a few.

To address the challenge of easing a wide variety of complex tasks in the API lifecycle, I conjecture that neuro-symbolic AI (NSAI) is the way forward. NSAI combines the power of neural networks such as pre-trained code models and large language models (LLMs) with the robustness and determinism of symbolic techniques such as invariant detection and constraint programming. As such, it is well suited for the web API domain, where the behavior of neural models trained on thousands of API resources can be constrained by the grammar of API specifications or the runtime information of APIs themselves. Along these lines, I propose the SAPIENS project: Supporting the API Lifecycle with Neuro-Symbolic AI. The goal of the project is twofold: (i) to empower developers in the development, maintenance and consumption of web APIs, and (ii) to improve the reliability of real-world services. To reach this goal, SAPIENS will investigate the following research questions (RQs):

RQ1: How can we tailor AI-supported solutions to the web API domain? The unique nature of web APIs poses challenges to AI-driven development. We will mine and collect extensive API resources and use them to train the first-ever API-centric machine learning (ML) model, which will be intelligently combined with symbolic techniques to support API-related tasks.
RQ2: Can domain-specific NSAI techniques surpass general AI-based solutions for web API development? We will support API design and implementation by combining code-generation heuristics with fine-tuned versions of the API-centric model, and assess the approaches against state-of-the-art techniques—purely neural.
RQ3: How can we leverage NSAI to effectively test web APIs and detect faults? Unlike existing approaches which test APIs via fuzzing (random inputs), we will automate the generation of test oracles, which determine the correctness of the API's outputs. Test oracles enable both testing and monitoring of APIs at large scale. We will integrate LLMs with invariant detection and grammar-directed techniques to generate meaningful oracles.
RQ4: Can NSAI techniques ease the consumption of APIs? To support not only API producers (e.g., developers) but also consumers (e.g., regular users), we will enable the usage of APIs solely based on their specification and natural language queries, via a conversational interface. This will foster a world of Open Data, where anyone can access and use APIs.

The impact of SAPIENS may be translated into: (i) revolutionizing the way in which developers produce and consume web APIs, and (ii) finding critical faults in real-world services. I am highly qualified to lead this project, with a strong background in software testing—having found hundreds of bugs in APIs like YouTube and Amadeus—and web engineering—having created tools and approaches for web API management. To contribute to the project's success, I count on international collaborations (Switzerland, Luxembourg, USA) with top scientists in the field. To transfer results to industry, we will materialize our approaches into plugins for tools such as Visual Studio Code and Postman, the latter being a world-leading API platform with over 30 million users.
Keywords: API lifecycle, neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence, software engineering, web API

Title: Training Overparametrized Models with SGD: the Impact of Noise
Abstract:
The field of artificial intelligence has had many notable successes in recent years, with major applications in areas such as commerce, transportation, healthcare and information technology, and also with fundamental contributions to basic science. These successes have been driven by the advance of deep learning which rests on two complementary pillars: the Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) algorithm and the Neural Networks (NNs). Together they have redefined the way traditional machine learning is being thought, with the advent of a new paradigm: (a) most modern learning architectures are overparametrized, and (b) when trained with SGD, they are able to interpolate the data perfectly and to generalize well.

In spite of these recent successes and advancements, deep learning’s functioning and limitations remain surprisingly mysterious. The need to harness the field with solid theoretical guarantees is growing as deep learning starts being used in sensitive domains such as health care or automated transportation. It has therefore spurred a recent surge of research in that direction.

In this context, almost all these attempts have focused on the gradient descent (GD) algorithm, the deterministic counterpart of SGD to which it is often compared, if not reduced to. This is problematic because gradient descent is too computationally expensive to be used in practice. Moreover, the stochasticity of the SGD algorithm appears as one of the key ingredients of the recent deep learning breakthrough. Indeed, in non-convex optimization, and in particular when training overparametrized NNs, the stochasticity of the algorithm can be useful, e.g., to escape saddle points faster or to select minima with good generalization properties. So far, when mentioned by theoreticians, SGD is at best viewed as an implementation trick to make GD tractable, but it is not studied as a standalone algorithm, with possibly different properties than GD. How and why stochasticity turns out to be an advantage rather than a handicap is still very mysterious. This is precisely what we propose to investigate in this proposal:

What are the role and the impact of the stochasticity of SGD in the training of overparametrized modern learning architectures?

The main ambition of this proposal is to make major progress within deep learning. We aim at providing theoretical guarantees for the algorithms actually used by practitioners, i.e., SGD, in the setting where it is considered in practice, i.e., for overparametrized models. Any progress on these questions will contribute to the general effort of strengthening the theoretical foundations of deep learning and of realigning theoretical and applied research. More broadly, it will have a significant impact in all fields where deep learning plays a role.

Our guiding principle will be to focus on simple models which can be analytically comprehended while showing analogous phenomena to deep neural networks (linear predictors, linear NNs and infinitely wide two-layer NNs). These questions will be addressed leveraging the use of tools such as Lyapunov analysis and stochastic calculus. The project leans on the PI's previous work at the interface of computation, optimization and statistics, namely in stochastic optimization and Monte Carlo sampling methods and their applications in large-scale machine learning.
Keywords: Deep Learning, Implicit Bias, Machine Learning, Optimization, Stochastic Differential Equation, Stochastic Gradient Descent

Title: Neuron Reconstruction from Electron Microscopy Images
Abstract:
Neuroscientists are currently imaging multi-terabyte volumes of neural tissue for the purpose of reconstructing the neuronal circuitry [5,7,8,18], but this unfortunately requires an impractical amount of time to be spent on manually labeling these images. This young field, often termed "connectomics" [26], challenges the computer vision and machine learning community to develop accurate and efficient techniques for automated neuronal reconstruction.
  Despite being an active field of computer vision research, there is currently no application of automated neuron reconstruction methods to real biological questions. From the published methods and from our own experience we believe that this is due to two key problems.
  The first problem is that current algorithms are not practical. The accuracy of state-of-the-art methods is not good enough, meaning that every automatic reconstruction has to be reviewed manually, which is hardly faster than a manual reconstruction in the first place. Furthermore, current methods scale poorly with the size of the data set. At present, they can only process datasets tens of thousands of times smaller than what is needed in neuroscience.
  The second problem is that there is a significant gap between the neuroscience side and the computer science side of neuronal reconstruction. Expert knowledge from neuroscientists is barely included in automatic or interactive reconstruction systems. In the other direction, automatic reconstruction algorithms from computer science are barely used by neuroscientists because they are not made available as usable and publicly available tools.
  Despite coming to the field relatively recently, our method for the automatic reconstruction of neurons from anisotropic EM-image stacks is at present the most accurate one [14]. Furthermore, we have integrated some of our methods into the open source project CATMAID [28] to make our algorithms available to the wider community. Building on our areas of expertise, we propose to address the two key problems of our field through the following four subprojects. We will undoubtedly find more opportunities similar to these subprojects over the course of this project.
  First, the development of a simple visual language will allow us to incorporate expert knowledge as priors in the reconstruction process. Second, by optimizing low-level classifiers with respect to high-level objectives (including expert knowledge), we will unify stages of the reconstruction process that have heretofore been deleteriously separate. Third, the development of a problem decomposition algorithm with global optimality guarantees will allow us to scale up to large image stacks, allowing us to use experts’ large-scale prior knowledge and avoid small-scale approximation artifacts. Fourth, the development of an interactive user interface in CATMAID will get the expert into the reconstruction loop, helping with cases that the automated system finds difficult, which in turn can be used to improve the automated system.
  These improvements over the current state of the art can be seen to directly contribute not only to accuracy and scalability, but also to closing the gap between the neuroscience and computer science approaches to the reconstruction challenge.

Title: MASS: Multilingual Affective Speech Synthesis
Abstract: We propose a project in affective speech synthesis in which we take two orthogonal approaches to synthesis of affect. In the first, data driven approach, we propose to learn affect using deep learning. In the second approach, we propose to use parametric approaches to prosody and formant shifting. We also plan to cover the main Swiss languages; these include German, in which much previous work on affect has been done, and Italian, which is intuitively more emotive, but has previously been overlooked in this and related subjects.
Keywords: Affect, Deep learning, Emotion, Prosody, Speech synthesis
