Title: Chemistry-informed machine learning for reaction prediction
Abstract:
Predicting the reactivity of chemical reactions is important both in practical applications, such as drug or materials synthesis, and in method development, such as finding and optimizing new catalysts. Since the 90's, simulation has become a standard tool to help interpret and sometimes guide experiment. In the last few years, machine learning has emerged as another promising approach that is much faster and also potentially more accurate than simulation. There is a greater need than ever for such tools that can help us accelerate scientific discovery. For the chemical sciences, many of the big challenges involve creating better catalysts for renewable energy storage and conversion and transitioning the chemical industry to renewable feedstocks.

In this project, we will remove some of the obstacles that prevents machine learning from reaching its full potential for reactivity prediction. We will do this by taking the best tried-and-true methods of today, and supercharging them with modern machine learning to create chemistry-informed approaches. All the projects are enabled by advances in automatic differentiation that enable regular chemical theories expressed in numerical code to be merged with neural networks. 

By developing differentiable reactive force fields, we will pave the way for machine learning potentials that can replace density functional theory for reaction simulation. By incorporating inductive bias from force fields and empirical valence bond theory, our chemistry-informed machine learning potentials will need much less training data, and importantly, generalize significantly better outside of their training domain. This will allow them to be trained faster and be used on a broader scale than current methods which are limited by their large need of training data for every reaction. The resulting models will find applications in high-throughput screening and inverse design of reagents and catalysts, and also for high-accuracy dynamic simulations that incorporate solvent effects.

In parallel, we will develop differentiable descriptors, that merge the best of the expert reactivity descriptors developed over the last 50-60 years, with modern deep learning. Descriptors is the go-to method for reaction prediction when very limited data is available, but have recently become less popular due to a perceived dichotomy between descriptors and less biased (deep) representation learning approaches. By developing differentiable versions of the most common reactivity descriptors, we will show that this dichotomy is false, and that descriptors can be seamlessly integrated into deep learning architectures. This will allow the creation of chemistry-informed models with unprecedented accuracy, that work well both in the low- and high data regimes. 

Combining both directions, we will develop differentiable reactive force fields for two important reactions for the pharmaceutical industry, the nucleophilic aromatic substitution reaction and amide coupling. Building machine learning models based on differentiable descriptors of the transition states of the reactions, obtained quickly with the differentiable reactive force fields, we will be able to predict these pharmaceutically important transformations with unprecedented speed and accuracy. These models would find use in, e.g., risk assessment and development of pharmaceutical routes.

Successful completion of this project will have strong impact not only in academia, but also for industry, where reaction prediction is actively pursued by research departments at almost all major pharmaceutical companies. The methods developed in this project have the potential not only to accelerate drug design and synthesis, but also to develop catalysts for larger-scale industrial processes such as polymerization. Another important outcome is the training of the next generation of digital chemistry PhDs, who will play an important role in the digitalization of the Swiss chemical industry.
Keywords: Catalysis, Chemical reactions, Computational chemistry, Machine learning, Synthesis planning, computational chemistry, descriptors, machine learning, reaction prediction

Title: Genome-scale morphological mapping of the mechanisms of cell proliferation
Abstract: This project aims to apply High Content Screening (HCS) techniques to understand the  phospohorylation networks responsible for cell invasion. Specifically, we will use quantitative microscopy to acquire cell morphological data in high throughput. To deal with the very large and highly complex data generated by HCS, we will rely on the supercomputing environment available at the Center for Biological Sequence Analysis / Technical University of Denmark and develop and apply novel non-linear dimensionality reduction and feature selection techniques such as linear embedding, manifolds and ant colonization. The resulting data will subsequently be integrated with data from quantitative mass spectrometry and exome sequencing with new algorithms currently being developed in Prof. Linding's laboratory to generate machine learning based predictive models of cell invasion in cancer.
Keywords: Cell invasiveness, High-throughput microscopy, RNAi screening, Systems biology, bioinformatics, dimensionality reduction, machine learning, supercomputing

Title: Design of a data-driven clinical prediction tool to identify patients with acute respiratory infections at low risk of complications in the emergency department triage
Abstract:
Background and rationale: Acute respiratory infections (ARI) are common and contribute to overcrowding in emergency departments (EDs). Most ARI are benign and self-limited, but they can also cause complications leading to hospitalisation and death. To date, no clinical prediction tool has been evaluated and implemented in ED triage to help nurses identify patients at low risk of complications from ARI and discharge them without seeing a physician, and no tool has included rapid molecular diagnostic tests.
Objectives: Using data from a cohort study of patients seen in the ED triage in Québec, Canada, I aim to test the feasibility and utility of data-driven clinical tools that combine clinical information and rapid molecular diagnostic test results to reliably predict adult patients with ARI at low risk of complications who can be discharged from triage. 
Specifically, I aim to:
i)conduct a systematic review on the use of machine learning to predict risks of complications in ARI (Aim 1)
ii)identify clinical phenotypes of ARI and assess whether the phenotypes predict risk of complications (Aim 2)
iii)build a clinical prediction tool to identify patients with ARI at low risk of complications by using a) the classical approach for prediction modelling (Aim 3) and b) machine learning (ML) methods (Aim 4).

Methods:  I will analyse data from the multicentric prospective study conducted in the ED triage of 4 hospitals in Québec, Canada between February 2022, and March 2023. This includes 1148 adult patients, who presented to the ED with ARI. They collected clinical information (e.g., symptoms, vital signs, comorbidities), obtained nasopharyngeal swabs and analysed them using a rapid molecular diagnostic test. Follow up data on complications (e.g., ED returns, hospitalisation, death) occurring within 7 days were collected by phone and complications within 30 days are now being obtained from the insurance and statistical office. I will conduct the systematic review according to the PRISMA guidelines. To identify the clinical phenotypes of ARI, I will apply latent class analysis, a data-driven statistical clustering approach, to clinical information and results of the rapid molecular diagnostic test. I will build a clinical prediction tool to identify patients with ARI at low risk of complications, first by using state-of-the-art classical logistic regression approaches for prediction modelling, and second by applying commonly used ML steps and use ensemble ML techniques. I will then compare the performance of these two approaches.
Expected results and impact: This project will develop a clinical prediction tool to enable ED triage nurses to identify patients at low risk of complications from ARI and discharge them without evaluation by a physician. This will help reduce ED overcrowding, thus improve the quality of care, reduce waiting time for patients, and reduce financial burden on the healthcare system. Such a tool can afterwards be externally validated in the adult ED triage in Switzerland. A similar study will be set up and adapted for the paediatric population in which ARI is particularly common.

Title: Calibrating Earth Observation-based impacts of drought on mountain forests by monitoring Carbon fixation and transpiration: from individual tree responses to regional scale extrapolation – CALEIDOSCOPE
Abstract:
Drought is a major forest disturbance that is expected to intensify with global warming. Assessing the impact of drought on forests – one of the main contributors to Earth’s primary production and regulators of climate – is fundamental for improving the accuracy of climate change predictions and to propose mitigating options. However, such an assessment is hampered by the lack of an adequate monitoring system that crosses different spatiotemporal scales and that incorporates a mechanistic understanding of the underlying driving processes. Even though Earth Observation (EO) has been the primary tool to assess the frequency and extent of drought occurrence over large geographical areas, it still lacks the necessary ground-based calibration and relative process understanding to also quantify impacts of drought on forest productivity and functioning.
With this project we aim at bridging this gap by linking and calibrating EO forest canopies observations to a unique time-series of tree water use and carbon fixation. By comparing the differences in sensitivity, dynamics, and delays of EO and ground-based observations of the last decade and around two recent major drought events (2015 and 2018), we expect to provide a benchmark for an EO-based quantification of drought impacts on forest productivity and water use. In particular, this study builds upon unique multi-year and daily-resolved tree water use and stem carbon sink observations of differently drought-exposed conifer sites along elevation gradients in the Alps and exploits a new generation of high-resolution multispectral EO sensors to model evapotranspiration. This information together with other spectral indices and EO-derived physiological measures will be used to assess and quantify drought impacts on forest productivity and water use over the heterogeneous Alpine region.
Cutting-edge approaches for timing and synchronizing the dynamics across drought intensity and by differently stressed trees will serve as the back-bone to time and quantify environment explicit tree responses (WP1) for comparison and calibration with various spatially distributed EO datasets at different spatial scales (WP2). The pattern of spatial and temporal matches and mismatches between ground-based and EO drought impacts will be quantified, explained, and accounted for to upscale tree level drought impacts for the studied species at the regional scale by using climate and EO data (WP3).

Title: New Approaches to Constrained Submodular Maximization
Abstract:
Submodular function maximization (SFM) problems have experienced a surge of interest recently. A key driver of this development are numerous recent applications of SFM in fields as varied as machine learning, sensor placements, viral marketing, document summarization, and welfare maximization. That SFM captures such a large set of applications is due to the fact that submodular functions describe a very natural property, namely the property of diminishing returns. For example, in many sensor placement problems, the additional coverage provided by placing one more sensor is the bigger the fewer sensors have been placed so far.

Applications of SFM often require to maximize a non-negative submodular function over some set of (down-closed) constraints. Most SFM problems are hard to be approximated better than a constant factor. Recently, considerable progress has been made in finding constant-factor approximation for constrained SFM, and some of these procedures have been observed to perform very well in practice. However, there are still many open questions around constrained SFM whose resolution seems important to both achieve an even wider adoption of SFM in practice, and also to obtain a better theoretical understanding of constrained SFM. The aim of this research project is to address some of these questions, in particular:

(1) What constraint families admit constant-factor approximations?
(2) What types of constraints admit fast algorithms for constrained SFM?
(3) Is there a unified framework to perform (fast) SFM, which can be applied to a wide set of constraint families?
(4) Under which conditions can we hope to obtain stronger approximation guarantees than the typical hardness bound of 1 - 1/e?
(5) Many of the currently strongest constrained SFM procedures are randomized. Is randomization necessary to obtain near-optimal approximation factors?
Keywords: approximation algorithms, combinatorial optimization, matroids, submodular function maximization

Title: Blocking online alcohol exposure
Abstract:
Background
Alcohol imagery is pervasive online. Exposure to alcohol imagery triggers alcohol use and
harmful consequences. Through recent advancements in the computational abilities of devices and advances in machine learning, it is now possible to develop a plugin which can detect and block alcohol in images. People with an alcohol use disorder are constantly and
sub-consciously seduced to drink through exposure to online alcohol imagery and alcohol ads,
which contributes to relapse and treatment failure. Allowing people with an alcohol use disorder to control their online exposure to alcohol imagery could enhance treatment success.
Objectives
To test a browser plugin prototype that will block alcohol-related images in a sample of 70
participants treated for alcohol use disorder (AUD). The plugin works similarly to the parental control plugins for sex and violence imagery. Specifically, we aim to: 1.) test the feasibility and acceptability of the plugin, 2.) assess the impact of the plugin on perception of alcohol imagery exposure, alcohol craving, and alcohol use.
Methods
The study will be a pilot randomized trial with follow-up at 1 and 3 months with an online
questionnaire. Participants will be randomly assigned (1:1) to receive access to a browser
plugin blocking alcohol imagery (n=35) or to a control group (n=35) (access to the plugin provided 3 months later). Study measures will include: hours of online presence, perception of online exposure to alcohol imagery, alcohol use, and alcohol craving. In the intervention group, acceptability of the plugin will be assessed. Participants will also be asked whether they would be willing to use it in the future. Feasibility will be measured by whether the participants kept the plugin active during the intervention period. As this study will
be a pilot trial, focus will be on descriptive statistics and effect size estimations using confidence intervals, rather than statistical hypothesis testing. We will conduct descriptive analyses on measures of acceptability and feasibility. We will compute confidence intervals to describe range of effects on perception of exposure to online alcohol imagery, craving, and alcohol use.
A subset of 10 participants randomized into the browser plugin condition will be invited to a
one-to-one audio-recorded semi-structured interview about their experiences with the plugin at the end of the follow-up period. Audio content will be transcribed verbatim, coded and analyzed using inductive research methods.
Expected Outcomes and significance
The project will provide crucial information from end users for the adaptation of a worldwide
unique browser plugin to prevent alcohol exposure online. Assessing the acceptability and
feasibility of the plugin will lay the foundation for a future large randomized trial.
Conclusion
This unconventional project will test a prototype of a browser plugin (free, non-commercial)
powered by an advanced machine learning algorithm that will block alcohol exposure online,
allowing people with AUD to control their exposure to alcohol imagery. This has an enormous
potential to facilitate treatment success because people with an AUD will be less seduced by
online alcohol exposure when leaving the clinic and being back in their normal life. This project could position Switzerland as a leader in this approach, which bears minimal burden for the participants and is highly scalable.

Title: Philosophy of Touch in the Digital Age
Abstract:
Digital technologies increasingly mediate social interactions. Far from immaterial, these technologies are located in devices with which human beings are in permanent bodily contact: they track our habits, our movement, our relationships. More importantly, they mediate our contact with one another, as they increasingly determine who we encounter and what enters our perceptual realm. As a result, these digital devices occupy the space between bodies and shape the very nature of their encounter. They transform each individual body into a dataset that is, in essence, quantitative and is always already compared to other data. In doing so, digital media negate the singularity of the individual body. Decisions made based on these data have a profound impact on society by increasing and potentializing tendencies to which society is already prone (e.g., disparities in the treatment between the rich, who are personally catered to, versus the masses, or between white people and people of color). 
To describe and reflect upon the implications of the ways in which digital media transform the relations between individual and collective bodies, my research project engages the concepts of touch and contact. This reflection is based on a double assumption. Pursuing recent philosophical discourses about the community and the political, most notably by Jean-Luc Nancy, Erin Manning and Sara Ahmed, my first assumption posits that the community, characterized as “being-with,” originates in the production of the touching proximity between bodies. While this proximity has traditionally been described—for instance by Nancy—in terms of spatiotemporal simultaneity, digital devices aim at producing proximity-effects despite spatial distance and technological mediations. My second assumption is that far from being a figure of immediacy, touch since Aristotle has been understood in terms of mediality, technicality and prosthetics. However, I argue that digital media actualize a different concept of touch that I call “posthuman,” as touch no longer originates from the human body, but rather consists of coupling bodies to technological devices.
Part I of the project discusses classical philosophical discourses about touch. Here, I uncover a medial understanding of touch and show in what sense this understanding corresponds to a humanist conception. While relying on a medium (from Aristotle’s flesh as metaxu to the stick of the blind from Descartes on), this prosthetic medium is integrated with the body proper and most commonly centered on the human hand. At the end of Part I, I explore a competing understanding of touch as contact from a distance—a type of haunting. Already present in Thomas Aquinas’s theology, the conception of touch as haunting can be traced through the 19th century’s experiments with seances, which flourished significantly around the same time as the appearance of new technical media. Touch as the haunting of the body of a (human) medium from a distance can be conceived of as the prefiguration of the virtuality of contact through digital media. In Part II, I explore—from Marx’s account of workers becoming the organs of the machine to cybernetics and system theory—a posthuman understanding of touch, whereby the body is coupled to and haunted by the medium. While touch traditionally means touching (and constituting) the limit of the touched body, touch as haunting tends to displace and even dissolve the limits of the body. 
In this project, I aim to describe the conceptual shift from human to posthuman touch centered around digital technologies, and how posthuman touch transforms community and the political. To articulate the main issues at stake in this shift: the mediation of digital technologies tends to eliminate the contingency of the encounter with other bodies. It reduces decision-making to computation or, more precisely, it hides the very moment of decision-making that always entails a contingency, as philosophers like Jacques Derrida and Chantal Mouffe have recently shown in order to describe the founding of a political order. Digital technologies—whose predictions are based on past dataset and feedback loops—endanger the possibility of an event as the unpredictable disruption of the existing order. However, I also argue that this posthuman conception of touch can function as a form of engaged, materialist critique of such an order. Thinking the possibility of a critique “in touch” with its object is essential to a nuanced approach to technological transformations. While I approach my corpus in Part I through a discourse analysis to advance a humanist understanding of touch, deconstructing the idea that touch has ever been about immediacy, my approach in Part II is a materialist one: I seek to understand the material and technological conditions of digital media and especially of algorithms to describe the ways in which they affect bodies.
This research proposal forms Part II of the “early Postdoc.Mobility” project I submitted in March 2017, entitled: “Philosophy of Touch in the Digital Age (Part I).” Parts I and II will result in my habilitation writing.
Keywords: Affective Studies, Algorithms, Artificial Intelligence, Community, Digital Humanities, History of touch, Politics

Title: Challenges in International Finance: Exchange Rates Puzzles, Market Segmentation and Machine Learning Approaches
Abstract:
The core of the present project builds upon the developments and outstanding challenges in international finance, with an emphasis on exchange rates. The exchange rates are crucial not only because they represent one of the most important prices in each country, but mainly because trading them constitutes the largest financial market in the world. To illustrate, the daily market turnover is above $5 trillion, and the trading volume exceeds that on all equity markets in the world by a factor of nearly 20. 
Despite its significance, economic theories still struggle to accurately describe the exchange rate determination in international finance. The underlying reason is the fact that exchange rates exhibit several salient features that are in stark contrast with the predictions of existing international asset pricing models.
Guided by this intriguing evidence, I aim to provide answers to the following questions:
1. What are the necessary properties that an international asset pricing model has to satisfy in order to be consistent with the exchange rate empirical regularities?
2. Given these properties, how can we optimally select the factors driving the asset risk premia?
To answer the first question, I allow for the most general market setting, without imposing any underlying structure other than the no-arbitrage condition and derive quantities directly from the prices observed in the domestic and foreign markets. The preliminary findings suggest that international market segmentation is the key economic driver to produce stochastic discount factors (SDFs) which can quantitatively match international asset prices, both under complete and incomplete markets, while being compatible with the exchange rate features. Hence, in the first part of my project, I document new stylized facts that successful international asset pricing models need to incorporate to match the empirical evidence and I provide guidance on how to construct such objects.
To address the second question, my objective is to derive SDFs consistently with the insights acquired, while enlarging the scope of investigation to account for large datasets. Specifically, I want to uncover the factors driving the risk premia on international assets by using machine learning techniques to parse complex interactions of the data that are currently cumbersome to define in a full economic specification. Machine learning employs available data to train a model and then apply the trained model to obtain forecasts from new data. The advantage of this method consists in being able to assimilate different data sources and model their interrelationship, leading to good predictions of the target variable. My ultimate goal is thus to optimally select the set of asset characteristics shaping the stochastic discount factor, under various degrees of market segmentation. Understanding what drives international asset prices is significantly relevant not only for scholars, but also for investors and institutions wanting to hedge the exchange rate risk.
Keywords: exchange rates, international finance, machine learning, market segmentation, return factors, stochastic discount factor

Title: Learning Compositional Representations for Understanding and Generating 3D Environments with Minimal Supervision
Abstract:
This project addresses the problem of 3D scene understanding as well as the task of generating synthetic 3D environments with realistic structure, plausible geometry and appearance, together with full semantic annotations, in ways that are controllable and efficient.  Within the last few years, deep neural networks (DNNs) have fundamentally transformed a large number of research fields. However while DNNs have demonstrated super-human performance on a variety of applications, they still struggle to demonstrate similar capabilities on various perceptual tasks such 3D scene understanding
and 3D content creation. To address this, recently researchers introduced compositional representations capable of encapsulating information about objects in a scene as well as about object relations. Compositional representations inherently encode the structure of a 3D environment as they can reason about the arrangements of objects in a scene and at a finer level about the arrangement of objects into parts. These representations are particularly useful for tasks ranging from physics simulations and shape editing to robot grasp planning.

In particular, our project includes three main objectives: (i) improving existing compositional representations by imposing constraints on the meaningfulness and semantic coherence of the parts instead of only optimizing for the geometry, (ii) developing compositional representations suitable for 3D object generation and (iii) extending existing compositional representations to scenes with multiple objects with the goal of jointly recovering part-based abstractions as well as part-level relations with minimal supervision. A crucial aspect of our proposal is that we want to learn compositional
representations in an unsupervised manner, namely without any part-level annotations, per-part relationships and object relationships. This kind of supervision is typically very hard to acquire, thus we strongly believe that it is important to develop methods that can infer this information directly from data. Due to the multitude of follow up applications that can benefit from our compositional representations, we anticipate that this project will open an exciting avenue for further research on interpretable representations for various tasks beyond scene understanding such as shape manipulation and editing, controllable 3D content creation, robot grasp-planning, AR/VR applications, graphics simulation etc.
Keywords: 3D Reconstruction, Computer Vision, Generative Modelling, Interpretable Representations, Primitive-based Representations, Scene Synthesis, Scene Understanding, Structure-aware Representations, Unsupervised Learning

Title: Group Effects in Oxy-Coal Combustion - GRECO2
Abstract:
Climate change is the central global challenge of our time. While many efforts are underway to decarbonize transportation and energy production, it is acknowledged that with growing energy demand and given the current economic conditions with coal being abundant and cheap, pulverized coal combustion (PCC) will remain a major source of electrical energy. Currently, for example, Japan—the world’s third largest economy per GDP—is upgrading its fleet of coal-fired power plants accounting for more than a third of its power generation as a consequence of the Fukushima nuclear disaster. While the oxy-fuel combustion technology is well-suited to eliminate atmospheric CO2 from PCC especially in retrofitted plants, its implementation is complicated by techno- logical challenges: Besides an inexpensive oxygen separation process, a better understanding of the O2- and CO2-rich combustion is needed in order to optimize oxy-coal burners to maintain flame stability and control pollutant levels. While reduced optical access limits experiments, the high physical complexity of PCC renders direct numerical simulation (DNS) expensive. Less expensive simulation methods, such as large eddy simulation (LES), however, need sub-models valid for oxy-fuel PCC. One fundamental aspect of PCC that has not received much attention is the interaction between coal particle groups and turbulent flow structures. While it is well-known that at suitable particle/turbulence time-scale ratios, particles align with turbulence structures and form clusters, the feedback of such patterns on turbulent combustion is poorly understood. Moreover, as is widely acknowledged in the scientific literature, current LES models are inadequate to represent sub-grid effects of this kind, that are resulting from spatial coherent structures.
Based on our expertise in DNS and modeling of reactive dispersed two-phase flows, we plan to address the listed challenges by conducting in a first step DNS of turbulent PCC. More specifically, we intend to perform parametric studies in canonical setups to obtain a better understanding of the role of, e.g., the turbulence level, the size, concentration, and composition of coal particles, and the effect of radiation. To reduce the computational complexity, we plan to deploy and further develop point particle models. Moreover, these models are of high relevance for LES that lack sub-grid-scale information. In a second major effort, we plan to develop models for the reconstruction of sub-grid turbulence structures by means of emerging machine learning techniques.
The results from this project will increase our understanding of reactive dispersed two-phase turbulence and will benefit applications such as spray and pulverized coal combustion. Furthermore, the planned efforts will provide reference data and insights that will guide modeling efforts. Finally, the models resulting from this project will enable more accurate low-cost simulations that are necessary to eliminate CO2 emissions from PCC being a central contributor to climate change.
Keywords: data-guided modeling, direct numerical simulation (DNS), dispersed two phase turbulence, large eddy simulation (LES), pulverized coal combustion (PCC)

Title: New Image Fusion Methods with Applications to Adult and Fetal Brain Morphometry Studies
Abstract: Image segmentation is a key area of research that has a significant impact on many medical imaging applications. In recent years, merging automated segmentations obtained from multiple atlases (i.e., reference images) has become a standard practice for improving the accuracy and robustness of segmentations. During the doctoral studies of the applicant, he made some contributions in this area by developing fusion methods and evaluating them in the context of segmentation of lymph nodes in the 3D head and neck CT images for radiotherapy treatment planning. There is however still a lot of scope for improvement in fusion methodologies, and there are also many other applications that could potentially profit from such new methods. The first methodological objective of this proposal is to extend our recently proposed Markov Random Field (MRF)-based fusion framework to a more general graph structure, in order to expand its applicability to many other clinical problems. The second objective is to develop new models that could incorporate more prior knowledge into the fusion framework. Finally, we want to adapt and evaluate these methods in the specific context of two important medical imaging applications: (i) parcellation of human cerebral cortex, and (ii) morphometric analysis of the fetal brain. We present our ideas and the context in more detail in the research plan.
Keywords: Atlas-based segmentation, Cerebral cortex, Fetal brain MRI, Markov Random Fields (MRF), Medical image analysis, Non-rigid registration, Parcellation, Ventriculomegaly

Title: Extracting Time-Varying Betas of Latent Factors Via Customized Autoencoder Neural Networks
Abstract: I develop a hybrid methodology that incorporates the econometric identification strategy into neural networks when studying conditional latent factor models. I argue that such an identification strategy is necessary, or the estimates will be subject to an unknown sample-dependent rotation. Moreover, econometric constraints also considerably reduce the computational cost, thus improving the estimation process’s speed. Empirically, I show betas are highly linear in most pre-defined characteristics from the literature. Furthermore, the conditional factors are well spanned by contemporaneous financial indicators, primarily the Fama French 3 factors. Together the results emphasize the value of human knowledge in the era of artificial intelligence. Finally, I conclude that such a hybrid method is feasible for many economic problems as long as certain conditions are met.
Keywords: Artificial Neural Networks, Firm Characteristics, High-dimensionality, Identification Strategy, Large Unbalanced Panel, Non-Parametric Estimation, Time-varying Betas, Unobservable Factors

Title: Biomechanics inspired conservation efforts through an undergrad led Machine Learning application
Abstract: Conservation Physiology describes the field of using morphological data to help inform conservation practices. Nearly all big cats worldwide have been made vulnerable to extinction due to human-wildlife conflicts ranging from the pet trade to bush meat and illegal hunting. One of the most successful ways to conserve these species in areas they have gone extinct is to work towards reintroduction. The challenge of reintroducing apex predators like big cats is the lack of realistic prey capture enrichment in captivity settings. In this proposal, we will test the validity of combining the morphology with biomechanics data to inform more effective reintroduction practices of South African cheetahs. We used videos of captive versus wild cheetahs during agile hunting tasks to determine biomechanical differences between generalized kinematics of the four limbs plus the tail of cheetahs in South African conservation networks. We discuss utilizing a mechanical device to help aid in captive cheetahs feeding habits to encourage more agile behavior for more effective means of reintroduction. We discuss broadly how this field could impact reintroduction efforts world wild by working alongside the communities of individuals involved in the care and reintroduction of all types of fauna. Using our collaboration with the University of Zululand, we will work with undergraduate students to expand the scope of this project around the world for conservationists using a Machine Learning embedded app to understand how biomechanics can impact conservation during animal running.
Keywords: conservation, robotics, technology, wildlife

Title: Artificial Intelligence to Improve the Non-Invasive Identification of the Culprit Vessel in Patient with Suspected CAD
Abstract:
Stress perfusion cardiac magnetic resonance (SP-CMR) has been shown to be highly accurate in the identification of patients with coronary artery disease (CAD) and is recommended by European and UK guidelines for the non-invasive assessment of patients with intermediate pre-test probability of disease. In SP-CMR the identification of the culprit vessels relies on assumptions on the anatomical distribution of the coronaries. These assumptions are based on population-based models of the cardiac chambers endorsed by the American Heart Association (AHA). There is however a significant variability in the anatomical distribution of the coronary arteries and recent data have shown that using the AHA model results in mismatch between myocardial segments and supplying vessels in up to 67% of patients. In practice, this causes a reduction in the diagnostic accuracy of SP-CMR in identifying the culprit lesions, limiting the use of stress perfusion CMR as a non-invasive alternative to FFR in particular in patients with multivessel disease.
In this study we propose to develop a tool based on Artificial Intelligence (AI) to automatically identify the perfusion territory associated with an area of perfusion abnormality, and to integrate this functionality in an automated pipeline for non-invasive perfusion quantification recently developed by the host’s group. This approach will be trained based on the available large dataset of quantitative SP-CMR and validated in a prospective population of patients, where an advanced self-gating 3D coronary angiographic sequence is added to the clinical scan to obtain, in a single CMR session, also additional information on the anatomical distribution of the coronary arteries. The AI based tool developed and validated in this project will facilitate the identification of the culprit vessel and will be used to guide percutaneous coronary interventions. We expect the proposed approach to be particularly useful in guiding complex revascularisation procedures in patients with multivessel CAD.
Keywords: artificial intelligence, cardiac magnetic resonance, cardiology, coronary artery disease, culprit vessel, imaging, non-invasive assessment

Title: Machine Learning Framework for Performance-based Design of Infrastructure Assets
Abstract:
The resources and networks that form our built environment (e.g., buildings, bridges, and lifelines) and societal web are termed infrastructure assets and are critical contributors to the resilience of modern-day communities. While current infrastructure assets are designed to meet life-safety requirements based on prescriptive codes and standards, their response to natural hazards (e.g., earthquakes, storms) exclude considerations of life-cycle costs and innovative design solutions. These considerations are important because, in urban areas of low-to-moderate seismicity (e.g., Switzerland), the seismic vulnerability of infrastructure is likely to have vast socio-economic consequences due to the expected financial losses allocated to infrastructure repairs and downtime. For example, the recent earthquake in New Zealand (EERI 2011) resulted in a socio-economic impact that exceeded 20% of the country’s Gross Domestic Product (Potter et al. 2015). To a large extent, the aforementioned issues relate the lack of performance-based targets in current infrastructure assets to detrimental earthquake aftermath costs. 
While these costs are large, post-earthquake market capital losses have been difficult to quantify before the event.  These financial losses can be mitigated through a performance-based design framework (Cornell and Krawinkler 2000), however, its implementation into engineering practice is still far from being a reality. This transition is challenging because it comprises of computationally intensive tasks, requires the use of parametrized infrastructure models, along with uncertainties associated with the hazard, damage and financial loss estimations that contextualize monetary losses and downtime, and minimizes them over the service life of individual infrastructure assets. We believe that we are now at an opportune moment for making a shift towards performance-based design:
-Over the past years, probabilistic seismic hazard analysis offers a viable tool to characterize the probabilistic nature of earthquake ground motions, as well as the resulting performance of infrastructure assets.
-Digital twins of various fidelities have been developed to realistically simulate infrastructure response from modest damage to collapse. These models can be parametrized and analyzed at a city-scale with sufficient computational resources.
-Structural performance databases have been established to help quantify model uncertainty.
-While non-trivial, economic loss estimations at the system and city-scale level are now made possible through recent advancements in performance-based engineering.
To this end, we propose the development of a data-driven framework to be exploited for decision support in the performance-based design of infrastructure. While the focus of the research is on buildings, it is envisioned that the framework could be generalised to any asset type. In doing so, we will design and implement a python-based platform, which will admit: (i) automated parameterised models of a broad range of code-conforming structural typologies; (ii) uploading/streaming of simulated model responses relating to earthquake-induced damage; and finally, loss estimation in the form of disaggregated expected annual losses. The platform will streamline performance-based design by establishing interoperable tools between publicly-available seismic hazard models and open-source high-end simulation software. Additionally, by leveraging high-performance computing through cloud-based services and machine learning, the proposed streamlined framework would enable rapid predictions (within seconds) of financial loss at a city-scale for a given hazard scenario to embrace community resilience.
All-in-all, we propose an initiative that revolutionises the way we design infrastructure, thereby enabling easy-to-use data science methods and tools that address a highly heterogeneous problem and enhance our experience of the built environment.
Keywords: infrastructure assets, life-cycle cost optimisation, machine learning, natural hazards, performance-based design, regional loss assessment, simulation-based engineering design, uncertainty quantification

Title: DigiLand: A digital approach to changing landscape value through multiscalar geographic text analysis
Abstract:
DigiLand’s overall aim is to demonstrate how multiscalar computational analysis of digitized texts can be used to extract and interpret diverse non-market landscape values (LVs) in global protected areas and multifunctional landscapes in Europe and to explore how these LVs vary across multiple dimensions including language, location, time and stakeholders.

The project is relevant and timely both thematically and methodologically. Contemporary landscape policy focusses on quantifiable, market driven, and instrumental values such as agricultural production or tourism, failing to acknowledge the diversity of world views and multi-layered local contexts when valuing landscapes. The recent report of IPBES on diverse values of nature and recent work on Nature's Contributions to People agree on the need to shift towards more diverse ways of capturing LVs. However, capturing non-market values of landscape, is challenging with traditional methods and data sources. 

We propose addressing this gap by computational analysis of digitized texts, which contain rich, natural language descriptions of landscapes and implicit and explicit statements with respect to LVs. We will apply natural language processing that allows exploration of diverse LVs across locations, time, language, and stakeholders. These methodological advances will enable us to extract locations from text sources, understand emotion and sentiment with respect to tangible and intangible landscape elements, and to compare expressions of LVs in multiple languages. We will perform two case studies: one exploring LVs and protected areas labelled as national parks globally, and a second zooming in on four multifunctional landscapes in Europe to identify changing LVs. Since purely computational methods often miss important nuance, we will use a novel multiscalar approach to combine close reading with distant reading of texts. 

DigiLand will therefore advance the state of the art in two key ways. First, we will develop a suite of tools, specific to the domain of landscape, explicitly exploring LVs, based on current framings of LVs (e.g. Cultural Ecosystem Services and Nature's Contributions to People). These tools will act as a multiplier in landscape research, which currently focuses on social media data and fragmented methods, with little reuse or adaptation to the domain. Second, by exploring the use of textual sources in depth, we will open a new front of research, which takes advantage of scalable, computation text analysis to capture LVs in ways currently not possible. 

DigiLand takes advantage of a unique constellation of expertise. The Geocomputation Group has been at the forefront of developments in methods related to geography and text and in the field of Geographic Information Retrieval. The group has demonstrated how these methods can be applied to understanding the relationship between landscape and language through the analysis of unstructured text. It brings together a core project team and interdisciplinary partners with expertise in LVs, protected areas, landscape multifunctionality, geographic text analysis, and landscape theory. 
The project team is enhanced by a set of project partners with thematic expertise in protected areas, multifunctional landscapes and landscape monitoring from national to global scales. Methodologically, expertise in linguistics, literary analysis of text and computational linguistics brings further key skills.

DigiLand will impact decision-making processes and policy in local, regional, and global discourses for comprehensive landscape management. DigiLand will not just produce scientific outputs, corpora and code, but also hold dissemination workshops for policy makers and local stakeholders and create reproducible pipelines for text analysis of LVs.
Keywords: Social geography and ecology, cultural ecosystem services, digital humanities, geographic text analysis, landscape, landscape value, natural language processing, nature's contribution to people, unstructured text, value

Title: Systems biology approach to identify novel antimicrobials and elucidate their mechanisms of action
Abstract:
Antibiotic resistance is a global threat to the modern world and every year an estimated 700,000 people die due to infections caused by drug-resistant bacteria. Infections with resistant bacteria are responsible for significant mortality and morbidity and the current antibiotic repertoire for existing and emerging hard-to-treat “superbugs” is limited. To tackle this rise in antimicrobial resistance (AMR), research must focus on the discovery of novel antibiotics. Advances in computational methods, such as artificial intelligence (AI), have transformed the biomedical field and are becoming increasingly valuable to make meaningful conclusions from large sets of biological data. A recent and pioneering Antibiotics-AI platform (developed in the host lab) harnessed the potential of machine learning to discover a broad-spectrum antibiotic, that presents unique characteristics and potent bactericidal activity. The model used training data from 2,335 molecules tested on gram-positive Escherichia coli, which was later applied to larger compound libraries: The Drug Repurposing Hub (containing 6,111 molecules) and a subset of the ZINC15 database (>107 million molecules), currently unattainable by any experimental method. Although powerful at identifying novel compounds, successful model-guided discoveries heavily rely on appropriate experimental designs for the generation of larger and reliable training datasets. This proposal, therefore, intends to use experimental and computational systems biology approaches to generate these large training datasets, validate the AI-model’s predictions for antimicrobial effects and investigate their mechanisms of action.
It is well known that underlying biological variations exist between bacterial species in acquiring antibiotic resistance. To understand and specifically target these versatilities, we will use experimental models to target some of the deadliest pathogens: (1) Carbapenem-resistant Escherichia coli, (2) Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, and (3) Multidrug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Around 40,000 compounds will be screened against the strains for antibacterial effects, used as training data for the model, and we will test the top lead predictions for their specificity as narrow-spectrum drugs. These combined efforts will ultimately increase our antibiotic arsenal against bacterial species and elucidate underlying biological mechanisms that will aid our efforts in combating the AMR crisis.
Keywords: antibiotics, artificial intelligence, experimental systems biology, mechanism of action, metabolism

Title: Characterization of tuberculosis drug candidates and their mycobacterial targets
Abstract: Tuberculosis is still the lead cause of death from a single bacterial pathogen. Globally, progress in combatting tuberculosis is jeopardized by spread of multi-drug resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains. Not only is there a need for new TB drugs but also a lack of novel targets. In a recent screen of a comprehensive chemical library we identified several compounds exhibiting promising antimycobacterial activity. We will now investigate these drug candidates and their proposed targets by a combination of biochemical, genetic and structural investigations and in infection experiments. Besides in depth characterization of hit compounds, we will further fuel our drug-screening pipeline with targeted libraries from collaborating partners  localized at University of Zurich and ETH Zurich, respectively. Synthetic derivatives of complex natural compounds with proven antimycobacterial activity, natural products from unique biotopes identified by genome mining and de novo designed compounds suggested by artificial intelligence will be characterized for antimycobacterial activity.
Keywords: chemical library, drug, natural products, non-tuberculous mycobacteria, therapy, tuberculosis

Title: Spatial glycan profiling in skeletal muscle denervation and disease
Abstract: Muscle and nerve communication governs crucial vital processes such as body voluntary movements and breathing. In neuromuscular diseases, effective connection between muscle and nerve is lost, resulting in a pathological response leading to atrophy and a progressive debilitating decline in skeletal muscle function. Strategies to promote muscle reinnervation have remained scarce owing to the limited understanding of the molecular processes that are required to re-establish muscle-nerve communication following denervation. Preliminary data from our lab suggest that expression of glycosylation enzymes is dramatically altered upon denervation. To better understand how aberrant protein glycosylation can affect the spatial temporal dynamics of muscle reinnervation, I propose to develop a novel multiplexed spatial glycan profiling technology that will enable visualization of glycosylation patterns at a single cell resolution in situ and comprehensive mapping of muscle glycosylation spatial temporal dynamics during denervation and reinnervation. I will integrate this approach with single nucleus RNA-sequencing (snRNA-seq) as well as with the CODEX method, a potent multiparametric imaging method, to further elucidate the set of cellular and molecular changes that occur during denervation and to spatially resolve what cell types are pivotal in promoting muscle reinnervation. I expect to identify cell type-specific differences in glycosylation profiles upon interruption of motor neuron-derived signal, capture the cellular source of muscle-derived retrograde signals induced by denervation, and uncover how these processes can be modulated to promote muscle reinnervation. Successful completion of this unique interdisciplinary project will reveal novel insights into the orchestrated process of skeletal muscle reinnervation and identify microenvironmental signals that can be targeted to improve muscle innervation after injury or in disease, potentially leading to the identification of new therapeutic targets for neuromuscular diseases.
Keywords: Denervation, Glycosylation, Machine learning, Neural network prediction, Neuromuscular disease, Single cell multiomics, Skeletal muscle, Spatial proteomics

Title: The Flow: From Deep-Learning to Digital Analysis and their Role in the Humanities Creating, Evaluating, and Critiquing Workflows for Historical Corpora
Abstract:
At the moment, clear-cut workflows and ready-made tools for the implementation of text recognition approaches and methods derived from natural language processing are only available to scholars with in-depth knowledge of information sciences and the ability to code. This problem gets even accentuated when focusing on pre-modern scripts and non-western languages, where scholars need a working understanding of the language and knowledge about the technology used. The proposed project will address this issue by developing digital workflows that build on available technologies, leading to new means of working with historical sources.

In the past decade, machine-learning approaches have been made available that allow for the processing of text in completely new ways. Due to the opacity and complexity of these technologies, however, we see their impact only at the margins of the humanities. With our project, we will further the wider adoption and critical use of machine-learning technologies in the humanities, adopting them to operationalize theoretical perspectives and evaluating the technologies with questions of history and Islamic studies in mind focusing on legal and administrative corpora.

Legal and administrative sources from the 13-15th centuries in England, the 14th-17th centuries in the northern European Hanse area, from the 16-18th centuries in Switzerland and the 19th century in Ethiopia will be analyzed within a praxeological and institutional framework. Research questions in this area profit from the development of digital workflows in particular because of their focus on the analysis of  societal processes, of how law has been practiced and how it affected aspects of everyday life. These processes are usually implicitly present in the relevant documents and this makes them hard to detect. Workflows such as the one suggested in this project address this problem and help to make the invisible visible. We will therefore be able to analyze the respective legal practices of each period and place, refine our understanding of the stabilization as well as the changes in legal practices, and even generate insights in the social life of communities that would otherwise be hard to depict.

The project will lead to…
… the development of Handwritten Text Recognition models for historical languages (historical variants of Arabic, Latin, and Early Modern German)
… machine-learned models for (semi-)automated content extraction from historical languages
… (reusable) implementations of digital workflows, available for small- and large-scale projects
… four Ph.D. theses grounded in their respective fields, applying digital methods for mass-transcribing and analyzing manuscripts
… in-depth insights in four cases studies, tackling questions of institutionalization in different contexts
… the preparation of data stories as a means of science communication (based on teaching activities, the Ph.D. theses, and the developed workflows)
… a conference bringing together leading scholars and scientists to discuss the implementation of digital workflows in the humanities (published as proceedings in digital humanities research by Bielefeld University Press)
Keywords: Deep Learning, Digital Humanities, Historical Sciences, Institutional Theory, Islamic/ Middle Eastern Studies, Law Practices, Machine Learning, Praxeology, Workflow Development

Title: Graph structures, sparsity and high-dimensional inference for extremes
Abstract:
Natural hazards such as heat waves, heavy rainfall or flooding are driven by very few rare events and may have large economic and ecological costs in addition to their potential for severe impacts on human health. The accurate statistical assessment of the small probabilities of occurrence of such extreme scenarios is thus crucial in many different settings. The area of research concerned with the quantification of the risk of these rare events, known as extreme value theory, is a rapidly evolving field with influences from probability theory, statistics and applied science. The analysis of univariate tail distributions, such as the value at risk of a financial asset or the computation of a 100-year flood event in a specific city, is well studied in the literature. Recent advances in theory and practice concentrate on the dependence between rare events in complex multivariate or spatial systems. The motivation for these extensions comes from a variety of different applications, in fields such as hydrology, meteorology, finance and actuarial science. Climate scientists observe an increasing risk of compound events due to a combination of different variables, such as wildfires caused by low precipitation and extreme heat. Similarly, the systemic risk of a financial system depends highly upon the connections among core institutions.

The motivation for these extensions comes from a variety of different applications, in fields such as hydrology, meteorology, finance and actuarial science. Climate scientists observe an increasing risk of compound events due to a combination of different variables, such as wildfires caused by low precipitation and extreme heat. Similarly, the systemic risk of a financial system depends highly upon the connections among core institutions.

Even though research in this area is very active, there is still little understanding of the probabilistic structures of the underlying models. This limits statistical modeling of rare events to fairly moderate dimensions so far, while data sets in risk applications become more complex and higher dimensional. Conditional independence, graphical models and sparsity are key concepts for parsimonious models in high dimensions and for learning structural relationships in the data. For multivariate extremes, these notions have only recently been properly defined and there is still much potential to explore their tight links to high-dimensional statistics, causal inference and machine learning. The main objective of this project is to follow this path and to develop novel mathematical theory and powerful statistical tools for modern applications of extremes. The first part of the planned research agenda tackles the problem of learning extremal graphical structures underlying the data. A version of the highly popular graphical lasso estimator will be developed to perform automatic model selection in extremes through regularization. This opens the door to high-dimensional settings where the number of model parameters is comparable to or even larger than the number of samples. In the second part, directed graphical models and Bayesian networks will be introduced for extreme value distributions. These notions form the basis for causal inference for rare events and have many possible applications, such as the attribution of extreme weather associated with climate change. In real data, the classical assumptions of multivariate extremes are often violated since the dependence becomes weaker for more severe scenarios. Flexible models for this case, called asymptotic independence, are urgently required and will be studied in the third part of this project. Two workshops on graphical models and high-dimensional extremes will be organized within the scope of this Eccellenza grant.

Title: Computational methods for integrality gaps analysis
Abstract:
Mathematical programming relaxations and especially linear programming relaxations have played a central role both in solving combinatorial optimization problems in practice [see e.g. the Concorde's TSP solver by V. C. David L. Applegate, Robert E. Bixby and W. J. Cook] and in the design and analysis of approximation algorithms [see e.g. Vazirani's book]. An important concept is the integrality gap, the maximum ratio between the solution quality of the integer linear program (ILP) and of its linear program (LP) relaxation. For many problems the integrality gap of a natural LP (or SDP) formulation is equal to the approximation ratio of the best algorithm as well as the hardness of approximation ratio and essentially represents the inherent limits of the considered relaxation. The following facts can be observed from the literature review regarding our current understanding of integrality gaps.
•Proving integrality gaps for linear relaxations of NP-hard optimization problems is a difficult task and usually undertaken on a case-by-case basis. Very few and limited attempts have been made to use computer-assisted analysis for this difficult task.
•For several notable and important examples, like traveling salesman problem (TSP), Steiner tree problem (STP), etc., our integrality gap comprehension resisted the persistent attack during the last decades of many researchers.
Inspired by the recent progress in the area of artificial intelligence research using heuristic search methods, within this project we would like to investigate the integrality gap instances and the generation of ``hard'' instances computationally for problems like the traveling salesman problem, the tree augmentation problem, etc. with a ``large'' number of vertices. In this frame we want to combine the most recent theoretical advances and experimental heuristic innovative methodologies to deal with the analysis of integrality gaps. More specifically, we plan to investigate and exploit aspects of polyhedral theory to reduce the search space. Then we combine this information with the use of local search, bio-inspired heuristic techniques and branch and cut techniques for effectively search the pruned space. This approach will allow us to get computer-aided construction of ``bad'' instances, namely problem instances having ``large'' integrality gap values, for the considered LP relaxation.  The aim is to obtain new and better understanding of lower bounds on the corresponding integrality gaps. For example, for the symmetric TSP this will either experimentally confirm or disprove (by computing witness instances) a longstanding conjecture (formulated more than 30 years ago) stating that the integrality gap for the Held-Karp LP is 4/3. Until now an experimental analysis of this kind has been conducted only for very small instances (with at most 12 nodes). Note that the currently known ``bad'' instances that are asymptotically matching the best-known lower bound of 4/3, are ``large'' instances. The general rationale is that computer-aided heuristic search can be a valuable tool for mathematical exploration. It is potentially able to search for much more complicated instances than is feasible manually. Moreover, we plan to use the outcomes of these experiments for driving the theoretical analysis of the considered integrality gaps.
Furthermore, as for the computation of gap instances, obtaining ``hard'', i.e., worst-case, instances for optimization algorithms of NP-hard problems seems to be a very hard task that is usually undertaken on a case-by-case basis. This generalized difficulty has important repercussions even in practice. For example, it often happens that heuristic algorithms are tested experimentally on randomly generated instances or more generally without adequate effort to generate instances that expose weaknesses in the algorithm being tested. Interestingly, our preliminary computational results show that the study of gap-instances can also be useful for the latter purpose.
Indeed, in support of this project application, we developed preliminary research and results that are very promising. More precisely, we consider the computational method proposed in this project for generating metric Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP) instances having a large integrality gap. The obtained computational results show that our method is very effective not only in producing large gap instances but also challenging instances for Concorde, the state-of-the-art TSP solver. As a by-product, we release the {Hard-TSPLIB}, a library of 41 small metric TSP instances which have a large integrality gap and are challenging in terms of run-time for Concorde.  Our approach is general and encompasses many “graph” problems. Extending and improving our preliminary results to many other graph problems will be a feasible short to medium term goal in this project. 
From a broader perspective, this project is a step towards the very challenging and useful ambition to develop a theory/practice for the construction of ``bad'' instances for optimization algorithms. This analysis is not an end in itself but allows us to understand the limits of the considered algorithms with the aim to design better algorithms.
The project will be held at Istituto Dalle Molle di Studi Sull'Intelligenza Artificiale (IDSIA) with a project team supported by the Swiss National Science Foundation composed by 1 postdoc and 2 PhD students for 4 years.
Keywords: Combinatorial problems, Integality gaps, Linear programs, Metaheuristics

Title: Effective Wastewater Management through the Integration of Real-Time Population Mobility Data, Extensive Wastewater Archives, and Advanced Data-Driven Modeling (EMPOWER-DD)
Abstract:
In the future, Switzerland will require significantly improved wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) and increased storage capacity in combined sewer systems. More intense and frequent heavy rainfall will lead to prolonged and more frequent spills of untreated wastewater into the environment. At the same time, rivers will become warmer and experience up to 40% lower flows in summer (up to 74% in some regions), drastically reducing the dilution of WWTP effluents and increasing the toxicity of spills. This challenges the current wastewater management strategy of centralized WWTPs and combined or separate sewer systems.

This proposal aims to enhance the effectiveness of wastewater management by, first, better understanding the pollution of wastewater and stormwater runoff, from big data sets of population characteristics and wastewater flows and quality. Second, we will explore smart data-driven strategies, such as pollution-based real-time control and waste design to stabilize pollution loads during dry weather and achieve (near)-zero emissions during wet weather. Specifically, the project will: i) utilize real-time mobile phone data to better understand wastewater generation, ii) create a big wastewater data set to characterize stormwater pollution better, and iii) employ machine learning and mechanistic models to predict nutrient load dynamics across integrated wastewater systems in real-time. We will also assess how these data insights can improve management strategies, such as pollution-based real-time control and decentralized waste design. These approaches leverage previously unknown spatio-temporal variability in wastewater and stormwater pollution to temporarily retain wastewater in (semi-) decentralized storage tanks, enabling controlled discharge to the WWTP.
Validation will be conducted through extensive monitoring campaigns in an Urban Living Lab, two additional urban catchments of varying scales, and integrated modeling to predict the expected improvements.

Our project brings together a diverse team of experts in urban drainage, applied mathematics, machine learning, stormwater pollution, decentralized wastewater solutions, and resource recovery. This unique combination of interdisciplinary expertise positions us exceptionally well to address this complex challenge.

Our research and methodologies will enhance adaptation to climate change and infrastructure planning, while supporting forthcoming Swiss and European legislation regarding urban wastewater treatment, specifically removing nitrogen, phosphorous, and micropollutants, along with water reuse and public health considerations.

Title: VR-HRC: Virtual Reality-based Multi-Human-Multi-Robot Collaboration in Industrial Environments
Abstract:
Project Overview

Collaborative Robots (Cobots) are being deployed in Industrial environments to support workers in repetitive or heavy-lifting tasks. Cobots typically have Graphic User Interfaces (GUI) and simulation software, making them easier for non-experts to program. However, while this may be an easy way to program one robot, it may not be intuitive for users to program multiple cobots that require collaboration with workers in a factory setting. Let us think of an automotive factory that has an assembly line. Multiple robots may be required for the assembly process, and some of these robots may work alongside humans to help lift a windscreen or provide tools and other parts as needed. The humans who will teach the cobots their tasks will be required to better understand the process in space (three dimensions), while cobots will be required to understand what the humans do around the workspace and adapt accordingly.

In this proposal, we will introduce an innovative virtual reality framework that facilitates collaboration between humans and cobots. This groundbreaking system will empower multiple users to interact with cobots using hand gestures, eye gaze, and speech in a physics-based VR simulation environment, thereby simplifying the process of teaching them industrial tasks. To address the cognitive demands of teaching multiple cobots, we will leverage Artificial Intelligence (AI) methods and will develop intent detection methods from multimodal human data and VR environment data, which will be translated into cobot actions. Generative AI approaches will be exploited, merging robot and human data to train general robot behaviors. Such models will be deployed to the robot for human-like task execution, also allowing for fine-tuning in the case of partially different operating conditions or (similar) new tasks. Human-in-the-loop approaches (e.g., active preference learning) for model refinement will also be exploited to fine-tune such behaviors based on human feedback.

Intellectual Merit

This proposal will advance research in multi-human-multi-robot collaboration in industrial settings by (a) developing intent detection methods that use multimodal human demonstrations to generate multi-cobot actions automatically, (b) developing an innovative physics-based VR environment for multi-cobot factory settings, (c) employing generative AI-based approaches to model, generalize, and simplify the embodied reasoning between humans and multi-cobots, and (d) adopting human-in-the-loop approaches for robot behavior refinement. Our proposed system will be evaluated in pilot studies to ensure its robustness, reliability, and acceptance by humans. To achieve these objectives, the project has the following three thrusts: (1) Multi-Human-Multi-Cobot Sensorimotor Interactions.(2) Embodied Reasoning and Human-In-The-Loop for Multi-Cobot Behavior Refinement and (3) Evaluating the Proposed Methods and Systems with Studies.

Broader Impacts

The proposed work could benefit the manufacturing sector by upskilling factory workers to interact with and teach cobots. Additionally, results will be publicized via regional and national news outlets, local science events, and K-12 outreach. The collaboration between the Dalle Molle Institute for Artificial Intelligence (IDSIA USI-SUPSI) of the Scuola Universitaria Professionale della Svizzera Italiana in Switzerland and Santa Clara University (a predominantly undergraduate and emerging Hispanic-serving institution) in the USA will enable student research to travel between the institutions, fostering knowledge transfer, cultural understanding, and strengthening international research collaborations, thereby amplifying the global impact of this proposal.

Title: Physics and technology for the Future Circular Collider - developing tracking detectors and algorithms for the next generation lepton colliders
Abstract: This research develops state-of-the-art tracking detectors for the FCC-ee, a future electron-positron circular collider at CERN, and by applying cutting-edge modern analysis techniques evaluates its physics reach. The project aims to establish serious options for tracking vertex detectors and to develop detector technologies with excellent precision and granularity focused on adapting CMOS to collisions at the FCC-ee. The FCC-ee collisions will offer a well-understood and very clean environment and will achieve unprecedented precision in the study of the Higgs boson and top quark. The studies in this project will determine the sensitivity of the FCC-ee to relevant Higgs boson and top quark measurements in as much detail as possible taking advantage of recent advances in machine-learning techniques to develop novel experimental methods for the jet-flavor tagging of heavy and light hadrons.

Title: Domain Adaptation for Microscopy Imaging
Abstract:
Imaging modalities such as Electron and Light Microscopy can now deliver high-quality, high-resolution image stacks of neural structures. Manual and semi-automated segmentation or annotation tools are then used to extract structures of interest. However, while the ever growing mass of available imagery should help unlock the secrets of neural function, the required amounts of human intervention remain a major bottleneck. Therefore, there has been great interest in automating the annotation process and most state-of-the-art algorithms rely on Machine Learning.

However, such algorithms still require significant amounts of manual annotation for training purposes. For everyday scenes, this can be done by crowd-sourcing. In microscopy, this is not an option because only experts whose time is scarce and precious can annotate them reliably. This is problematic because the data preparation processes tend to be complicated and not easily repeatable, which means that a classifier trained on one acquisition will not perform very well on a new one, even when using the same modality.

In earlier work, we have investigated approaches that involve acquiring sufficient amounts of labeled training data after one specific image acquisition and then using it in conjunction with a small amount of additional labeled training data that can be acquired quickly after each subsequent one to retrain the classifiers. We  have so  far focused  mostly on  synapse detection and delineation of curvilinear  structures. In  the proposed project continuation, we intend to broaden the scope of this effort  and to develop generally  applicable Domain  Adaptation that  are generally  applicable in  the field of bio-medical image processing.
Keywords: Computer Vision, Microscopy, Transfer Learning

Title: Localized Statistical Shape Models using Kernel Methods
Abstract:
Statistical shape models have become an indispensable tool in medical image analysis. Despite the large amount of research done on shape models, the way of building these models has not changed since their introduction in the 90s. The idea is to model the variability of a shape by taking linear combinations of a set of example shapes. This simple approach is inherently global, as a linear combination is always taken of the full shapes. Therefore a local variation cannot be explained without affecting the full shape. This has been recognized as one of the major flaws of current statistical shape models. In this proposal for a basic research project, we propose to develop a conceptually new approach to statistical shape modeling to overcome this problem. This proposed shape modeling concept will be based on our recently introduced  framework for shape modeling, which is based on kernel methods and Gaussian processes. The use of these concepts from machine learning is fundamentally new in shape modeling. This framework unifies the many different concepts surrounding shape models, most notably nonrigid registration and shape model fitting, into one general and compact mathematical formulation. 

We will extend this kernel-based approach to develop localized and scale dependent statistical shape models. This will allow the model to represent both local and global shape variation around any given point of a shape. We believe that this approach can overcome the problems associated with current shape models. In particular, it has the following advantages:
? A) Decoupling of the local and global variations allows us to obtain a better covariance estimation. The local shape variation is simpler to model and thus needs fewer training examples for obtaining a good estimation. Given some additional example for the global shape, the local models are easy to integrate into a global model.
? B) Images on which the modeled anatomical structure is only partially represented can for the first time be used as training examples for the local model, which greatly increases the number of available data.
? C) Statistical shape models have a fixed point, typically at the center of the mean shape. Deformations far away from this point mostly reflect change in position rather than shape changes. Our proposed approach allows us to perform the alignment separately for each local model, thus separating position from shape information.
? D) Local models built on different scales can be combined in a fitting procedure. This enables us to detect pathologies or fit the model to partial data.

The main research effort will be directed at developing a localized, multi-scale approach to shape modeling. This will be done by extending our approach for shape modeling using kernel methods in two ways: First we extend our registration method towards a multi-scale approach using multi-scale kernels. Second we formulate the new localized multiscale shape models and a new procedure for building these models. To demonstrate their practical use in medical imaging, we will apply our novel models to the problem of registration and model fitting of medical images with pathological or missing data, with the concrete goal of finding being able to fit fractured and traumatized bones.
