Title: Automated Reformulation and Pruning in Factored State Spaces
Abstract:
Automated planning is the problem of finding a sequence of state transitions (plan) that transforms the initial state of a transition system into a desired goal state or proving that no such plan exists. It is a fundamental problem in artificial intelligence, where it is studied by the planning and scheduling and heuristic search communities. We focus on (domain-independent) classical planning, which is concerned with algorithms that are generally applicable, rather than being tailored towards one particular class of transition systems. Classical planning is challenging due to the state explosion problem: transition systems of interest frequently include 10^100 or more states.

The last decades have seen several breakthroughs in the scalability of classical planning algorithms, chiefly through the development of accurate distance estimators for general search methods such as the A* algorithm. However, there is mounting evidence that this line of research is reaching a saturation point, and that further improvements in the scalability of classical planners will have to be reached through other means than better distance estimators.

In the project "Safe Pruning in Optimal State-Space Search" (SPOSSS), we targeted this challenge for the case of optimal planning with a focus on partial-order reduction, a method for eliminating redundancies due to transitions that can be interleaved in many ways. This follow-up proposal widens the scope to also include satisficing planning and to a much more general class of pruning and problem transformation methods than partial-order reduction. The objectives of the project are:

O1: to advance the theory and practice of symmetry elimination for planning. While previous work on symmetries focused on pruning symmetric states within a search algorithm, we will apply a rigorous theory of symmetry elimination to other aspects of state-space search, such as grounding, invariant synthesis, and the automatic computation of abstractions.

O2: to develop general and efficient methods for dominance pruning in transition systems. SPOSSS focused on equivalence pruning, which ignores transition sequences s that can be shown to have exactly the same overall effect as another sequence t. We will investigate more general methods that can also detect and exploit situations where s is strictly less useful than t.

O3: to develop soft pruning methods for satisficing planning. Existing pruning methods designed for optimal planning are hampered by the necessity to be absolutely certain that a pruned transition is not useful. Instead of all-or-nothing pruning decisions, soft pruning methods may decide to deprioritize transitions that are very unlikely to be important for reaching a solution but cannot be ruled out completely.

O4: to develop problem reformulation methods that automatically enrich the description of a transition system to make it more amenable to the distance estimation techniques used in modern planning algorithms, and to abstract away parts of the system that can be solved without search.
Keywords: artificial intelligence, automated planning, problem reformulation, pruning techniques, symmetries

Title: Explore-exploit with Gaussian Processes under Complex Constraints
Keywords: active learning, exploration-exploitation tradeoffs, machine learning, optimization, statistical models
grant_text: explore exploit with gaussian processes under complex constraints. a central challenge in decision making in science and engineering is the explore exploit dilemma: the need to trade exploration (i.e., collecting information) and exploitation (i.e., making decisions identified as effective in the past). oftentimes, the number of alternatives is vast, and consequently we must reason about and predict the outcome of untried decisions based on the collected information. since it plays such a central role, the explore exploit dilemma has been addressed by several communities: theoreticians have developed principled algorithms with performance guarantees for what is known as the multi armed bandit problem (a classical formalization of the exploration exploitation tradeoff) and its generalizations; practitioners have designed efficient algorithms for bayesian optimization and the design of computer experiments that work well on certain real world applications. for a long time, there was a large gap between the empirical success of the practical methods, and the rigor of the multi armed bandit techniques. this proposal is a follow up to an snf project: gaussian process bandit optimization: theory and applications, which started a research program aimed at “bridging the gap”: the goal was to design practical approaches towards solving the exploration exploitation dilemma, that still enjoy strong theoretical guarantees. the methodology revolves around gaussian processes, flexible, nonparametric statistical models, and their use to address challenging exploration exploitation tradeoffs in a principled manner. this line of inquiry has proven to be very successful, with results published at premier conferences and journals, and considerable impact on real world applications in recommender systems, environmental monitoring and experimental design. this follow up project aims to exploit this momentum and the algorithmic insights developed previously, yet explore challenging new problems that no existing approaches can handle. in particular, we seek novel algorithms capable of accommodating complex constraints present in practical problems: safety, dependence and observability. concretely, our research will weave together the following inter related threads: 1. develop novel algorithms for localizing near optimal solutions while satisfying safety constraints; 2. push gaussian process optimization towards more general tasks by accommodating dependency constraints, for example present in multi stage decision and control problems; 3. design algorithms able to operate under observability constraints arising in practical applications; 4. evaluate the algorithms on real world domains ranging from recommender systems to robot learning to neuroprosthetics. in terms of expected impact, we will develop new theoretical techniques and analyses, realize them in novel algorithms, implement them as open source software, and apply them to challenging real world applications. success of the project is supported by substantial theoretical and empirical results by the pi and his group achieved in the prior snf project. beyond furthering our theoretical and algorithmic understanding of the ubiquitous explore exploit dilemma, the application of the techniques pursued in this proposal have the potential of direct benefits for society.. active learning, exploration exploitation tradeoffs, machine learning, optimization, statistical models

Title: Advanced Network Analysis to Study Brain Dynamics in Health and Disorder
Abstract:
Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has revolutionized non-invasive imaging of the human brain and provided fundamental insights into brain function in health and disorder. Brain mapping techniques have gradually been enhanced from detecting isolated, task-evoked brain regions to revealing densely connected networks of brain regions during resting state. While data processing has become increasingly important, an important caveat of most network studies to date is that they rely on a static view of the brain’s functional connections, ignoring moment-to-moment fluctuations. Growing evidence points to the importance of non-stationary network dynamics, however, critical challenges for statistical signal processing need to be overcome first.
Extracting network dynamics from fMRI data is complex and requires a novel framework to map brain dynamics into a lower-dimensional space spanned by neurologically relevant patterns of co-activation (of regions) or co-fluctuation (of functional connections between regions). To that aim, we will build upon recent advances in online dictionary learning and sparse matrix factorizations. This approach will be coupled with new multiscale spatial decompositions to account for brain anatomy, and with recent advanced deconvolution techniques to compensate for hemodynamic effects. The underlying electrophysiological nature of fMRI network patterns will be validated using simultaneous EEG-fMRI recordings in resting state and sleep. Imaging-based markers for clinical measures will be evaluated and validated using pattern recognition and cross-validation. We will show how the dynamic functional connectome provides complementary information that remains hidden to static analysis, and apply them to better understand functional brain organization, and its breakdown in disease and disorder.
Innovation in signal processing, machine learning, modern graph theory, and applied statistics has been a main driving force to advance neuroimaging and fMRI data analysis, in particular. Therefore, we will build on these avances to provide a new framework to disentangle brain network dynamics.
Keywords: brain dynamics, computational neuroimaging, functional connectivity, functional magnetic resonance imaging, graph theory, human brain mapping, network science, sparsity, wavelets

Title: Effect of wind and wave breaking on ocean wave evolution and floating plastic transport using blended machine learning
Abstract:
On the ocean, wind is the main cause of wave growth, and plays a key role in the formation of extreme events such as rogue waves. A natural limit of wave growth is wave breaking. Wave breaking is indispensable when considering the motion of objects on top of the ocean surface, such as oil spills or plastic debris. Because wind and wave breaking are inherently turbulent phenomena, modeling of water waves is much simpler when they are ignored. As a result, despite their crucial role in ocean dynamics, both phenomena are poorly captured in existing models.
Machine learning is a novel method to circumvent the need to explicitly model the turbulent nature of wave breaking and wind forcing. We will investigate wind forcing and wave breaking by utilizing a novel approach of blended machine learning, in which a basic physical model is combined with a learning algorithm, that is trained using measurement data. The project is split into two parts. First, since existing wave-propagation models cannot account for wave breaking, they have a severely limited domain of validity. To model the propagation including and after the breaking event, we will combine the modified nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a long short-term memory (LSTM) recurrent neural network (RNN). Second, we will develop models for particle trajectories on the surface, building upon the improved knowledge of the effect of wind and wave breaking on the wave evolution. These models can then also be formed into a blended model for surface particle kinematics, by training the learning algorithm on existing measurement data.  
With these new models, we expect to make a significant step forward in the description of the evolution of ocean waves and particle trajectories at the surface, with the aim of improving prediction accuracy and reducing damage caused by extreme events and ocean surface pollution.
Keywords: Machine learning, Plastic debris, Rogue wave, nonlinear dynamical system, ocean science, wave breaking, wind forcing

Title: Predictive design in heterogeneous catalysis through machine learning and surface organometallic chemistry
Abstract:
The general aim of the project is to provide new design criteria for heterogeneous catalysts by combining state-of-the-art methods for chemical synthesis, machine learning, and materials characterization to understand, quantify, and predict catalyst structure-function relationships. Catalysts increase the rates of chemical reactions and thereby enable chemical syntheses that are highly energy demanding, with widespread and transformative applications including the removal of pollutants and the production of fuels, commodity chemicals, and pharmaceuticals. A longstanding aim of catalysis is to understand the selectivities and reactivities afforded by specific sites of catalytic materials and to thereby enable predictive design: a priori selection of stable catalysts with high substrate conversion, selectivity, and activity. Such capabilities have been elusive for heterogeneous catalysts in part due to complicated distributions and low absolute quantities of catalytic active sites and the associated challenges in determining structure-function relationships. Correspondingly, design of new catalysts is still largely empirical, inhibiting the targeted development of highly active and stable materials for new applications such as sustainable production of high-value chemicals from biofuel feedstocks.  

Recent advances in synthesis, high-throughput experimentation, materials characterization, and data analytics offer the opportunity to overcome these challenges and enable predictive design in heterogeneous catalysis and will be leveraged for the proposed project. Specifically, well-defined heterogeneous catalysts will be synthesized via surface organometallic chemistry (SOMC) approaches, focusing first on catalysts for olefin metathesis, an efficient and economical reaction, as a case study. SOMC techniques yield catalysts with well-defined catalytic active sites that are amenable to spectroscopic characterization and structure-function correlations. Motivated by emerging applications of olefin metathesis in the upgrading of non-traditional feedstocks (e.g., derived from natural gas or biomass), the influences of substrate and catalyst structure on catalytic reactivity will be elucidated by generating a reaction chemistry database using large libraries of substrates and heterogeneous catalysts. In the past, synthesizing and testing such large quantities of heterogeneous catalysts was typically time-consuming and impractical. Here, robotized high-throughput experimentation methods will greatly enhance the rates of catalyst preparation, reaction testing, and data acquisition. Furthermore, the local structures, interactions, and properties of the catalytic active sites will be established by detailed atomic-level analyses, including multidimensional solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance, X-ray absorption, and in-situ/operando X-ray, infrared, and Raman spectroscopy, as well as electron microscopy and theoretical calculations. The multidimensional catalytic reaction database and structural analyses will provide inputs for neural-network-based machine learning algorithms, which provide means to navigate complex parameter spaces and extract meaningful correlations. Combined insights from reaction studies, spectroscopic characterization, and machine learning analyses will yield fundamental physiochemical understanding of the influences of different structural parameters, providing models to predict catalytic reactivities for challenging substrates and guide future catalyst design and reaction engineering. The machine-learning-enhanced experimental methods provided by the project are expected to be generalizable to other catalytic reactions, enabling de novo development of sustainable catalytic processes, including green routes to fuels, polymers, and specialty chemicals.
Keywords: Chemical engineering, Energy, Heterogeneous catalysis, Inorganic chemistry, Machine learning, Materials, Organometallic chemistry, Reaction engineering

Title: Analysis and Modelling of Space-Time Patterns in Complex Regions
Abstract:
The project deals with fundamental development of a contemporary methodology and exploratory tools for detection, analysis, and interpretation of patterns in spatio-temporal data. An important real case study considered deals with the sequences of forest fire events. A sequence of forest-fires can be modelled by stochastic point processes, where each event is featured by its spatial location and occurrence in time, plus additional information such as burned area, ignition causes, landuse, topographic, climatic and meteorological features, etc. 
The space-time point pattern characterization represents a powerful tool to understand the distribution and behavior of the underling phenomenon and its correlation with socio-economic, environmental and meteorological factors. Many measures describing the space-time distribution of environmental phenomena have been proposed in a wide number of disciplines; however, most of these measures are of global character and do not consider complex spatial constraints, high variability and multivariate nature of events. Moreover, the research on the most sensitive forest fire areas such as the Wildland-Urban Interface (WUI) – the interaction zone between burnable vegetation and anthropogenic infrastructures–, may take advantage of new modeling approaches proposed in this project. 
The main objective of the present project is to carry out a basic research with a strong application part to investigate the complex phenomena and to overcome unsolved methodological problems in characterization of space-time patterns, in particular, forest fires. The most important fundamental tasks of the project are: 
1.Development of a new consistent methodology to detect, quantify and characterize clusters in temporal, spatial and spatio-temporal data based on topological, statistical and functional fractal measures. Adaptation and application of both global (e.g. K-function) and local cluster indicators (e.g. scan statistics) for detection, prospective analysis and ranking of clusters of spatio-temporal forest fire data using irregular shapes and Bayesian extension. 
2.Development of the concept of validity domain which will defeat problems of analysis of clustering in complex inhomogeneous zones. Adaptation of geostatistical tools and methods for the multivariate analysis and anisotropic modelling and simulations of forest fire patterns. Characterization of uncertainties. 
3.Development of new concepts and definition of WUI in the Alpine environment that will combine non-classical techniques in spatial data clustering, remote sensing techniques (e.g. image classification, change detection) and mathematical morphology. 
The practical part of the research deals with an application of the approaches and methods developed for real and simulated space-time environmental data (forest fires, landslides, earthquakes, biodiversity, socio-economic data); the Alpine region being the most important zone of the study. 
This project is multidisciplinary in that it implies expertise in geoinformatics, spatial statistics, forest and environmental sciences. It will provide a response to the increasing demand for environmental monitoring and management tools (assessment of natural and anthropogenic hazards and risks, sustainable development, retrospective success analysis, etc.). The main results will be presented at international conferences and workshops and published in scientific journals. International collaborations necessary for this interdisciplinary project are already established and will be strengthen during the project.
Keywords: Wildland-Urban Interface, forest fires, fractals, geomatics, mathematical morphology, multifractals, patterns of spatio-temporal data, scan statistics, validity domain

Title: Algebraic Reasoning in Adaptive Verifiers
Abstract:
In this project we are advancing the state of the art of
automatic program verification with high degree of
automation and small trusted truth base. This problem is
becoming increasingly relevant because both the demand for
software is increasing. In response, we have a larger work
force with diverse skills engaged in software development,
as well as AI tools that generate plausibly looking code
that is wrong in many cases. To avoid future liability and
technical dept, there is an urgent need for tools that
provide deep validation of software.  

To provide such high guarantees, we have been developing
formal verification techniques and tools for cost-effective
development of verified software using both automated and
human-guided development.  We argue that a key next step to
make both specification and verification more feasible is
better support for algebraic laws in reasoning about
programs.  We propose to develop techniques that enable
proofs of algebraic properties of complex software
components.  Using as a starting point the Stainless
verifier for recursive and higher-order programs [1] and the
Lisa proof checker for set theory [2], we will develop
strategies to prove commonly occurring algebraic properties
of operations, allowing users to benefit from verifiers
without substantial specification effort. Examples of
algebraic properties include equivalence of functions,
mutual inverse properties, associativity, commutativity, as
well as properties of ordering as used in data manipulation
and program termination.  These properties will enable
higher automation for program correctness across a wide
range of scenarios, from serialization and deserialization
(including parsing and pretty printing), parallel
programming (with operations such as map, reduce, scan,
aggregate), more reliable program evolution thanks to
program equivalence verification, and program termination
established by ordering relations.

Whereas our ultimate goal is to produce adaptive verifiers that
learn and improve over time, such direction is beyond the
scope of the project as it was funded; we instead hope to pursue
such avenues in alternative projects.

Title: Reducing Gender Gaps in Credit Markets: Generating Evidence from 7 Countries in Sub-Saharan Africa
Abstract:
Gender gaps in economic outcomes are ubiquitous and particularly pronounced in the global South. Reducing these gaps in sustainable and scalable ways is a policy priority. 

In this project proposal, I seek funding to realize a unique opportunity to make significant scientific progress in one very important domain: Credit markets. Thanks to an established partnership with a prominent micro-credit institution operating in Sub-Saharan Africa, I can study the issues at scale with big data and policy evaluation tools, including machine learning and randomized control trials. The company has a presence in seven African nations (Ghana, Kenya, Liberia, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Tanzania and Uganda) and is rapidly expanding within and across countries. My partnership emanates from a relationship with its Group CEO, Kobbina Awuah, who is finishing his PhD in economics here at University of Zurich, under my supervision, at the end of 2023. Through a Memorandum of Understanding, I will have access to administrative data on millions of loan applications, allowing for very rich and detailed analyses and tools to understand both demand and supply side forces. Importantly, the partnership will involve testing for causal mechanisms using randomized interventions. We will search for “win-win” solutions that are sustainable and scalable: low-cost interventions within the company that both reduces gender gaps and makes the firm more (or at least not less) profitable. 

Over the four-year project, there are three key phases. The first phase (2024-2025), the goal is to: 

i)Build a unique dataset that harmonizes the loans data from all seven countries, containing detailed panel data on millions of loan applicants, decisions by credit officers, and client repayments/default. 
ii)Write a descriptive paper on the gender gaps across men and women on key outcome variables, characterizing what predicts gender gaps, across and within countries.
iii)Develop machine learning algorithms for specific use cases, specified below. The main data here will be “labelled” data (numbers), using standard regression and “supervised” machine learning tools. However, one subproject aims to also include “unlabelled” data in the form of images of the loan applicants, and state-of-the-art deep learning tools for vision, to test for discrimination based on visual input given to loan officers.

Title: Anthropomorphization of AI systems and its Influence on Human-AI and Human-to-Human Interactions
Abstract:
Background: Human communication is often mediated via digital channels, including e-mails, chats, and video calls. In recent years, this trend has led us to communicate through these digital channels and engage with digital entities powered by generative artificial intelligence. Whereas such communication was initially restricted to mundane tasks, such as being forced to engage with one’s telecommunication provider’s notoriously annoying chatbot, interactions with ‘intelligent’ non-human actors (subsequently referred to as AI systems) are now increasing in many aspects of professional and personal life. We interact with AI systems to learn, work, talk, collaborate, write, think, and feel. Crucially, this development toward ubiquitous human-AI interactions may impact human psychology and behavior in many ways. Anticipating those impacts and societal changes is among the greatest challenges in social science.
Aims: The project seeks to explore the impact of AI systems on humans and human sociality. Importantly, how we interact with AI systems will be influenced by the behaviors we have previously internalized when interacting with humans (human-to-human interaction). Yet, as human-AI interaction becomes more frequent, the behaviors, habits, and norms we socially learn in these interactions may shape how we behave in human-to-human interactions. The project seeks to understand whether behavioral changes in human-AI interaction can spill over to subsequent human-to-human interactions, in professional, personal, and romantic interactions. 
Methods:  I will conduct incentivized experiments and longitudinal studies in which participants interact with an AI system. Afterward, they interact with the AI and then answer survey questions about the system. In the second part of the project, we will keep this basic structure with an initial human-AI interaction, after which participants will engage with other humans in behavioral tasks. This will allow us to identify whether treatment effects in the human-AI interaction spill over to the human-to-human interaction.
Impact: The first project aims to expand the current discourse in human-AI interaction, demonstrating the broader social implications of human-AI interactions for human-to-human interaction more broadly. The predicted findings would confirm the hypothesis that AI systems can influence not only humans in a given interaction but also interactions that humans have among themselves—essentially changing the social fabric of our societies. This may be seen as a potential negative future risk, but it could also provide a policy tool to improve human social interactions.
Keywords: artifical intelligence, human behavior, human-machine interaction, organizational behavior, social learning, workplace interaction

Title: Geometric properties of deep visual representations: theory and applications
Abstract: Deep networks are very successful architectures in many visual tasks. Despite the recent advances of these architectures, the geometric properties of deep visual representations are currently not well understood. One of the fundamental geometric properties of any visual representation is its invariance to nuisance variables, such as illumination, viewpoint, and occlusions. The goal of this project is to provide a principled analysis of the invariance of deep visual representations to nuisance variables, and propose alternative architectures with improved geometric properties. This project will allow us to have an increased understanding of the fundamental invariance properties of current deep visual representations, which we will leverage to propose new architectures. These novel architectures will be used to tackle important vision tasks where existing deep visual representations fail due to the scarcity of the data, such as those arising in medical imaging applications. To achieve this project, I will rely on my previous experience on the analysis of the robustness of classifiers, as well as previous works from my host laboratory that laid fundamental theoretical foundations of visual representations.
Keywords: computer vision, deep learning, geometric transformations, invariance, nuisance variables

Title: Multimodal Computational Modeling of Nonverbal Social Behavior in Face to Face Interaction
Abstract:
In the last decade, there is a strong interest on analyzing human actions, especially in smart room applications. However, the intelligence of these systems is limited to performing given tasks, without considering the social situation in the environment or the social behavior of the people in the surrounding. Among the range of applications that provide support systems in rooms equipped with sensing devices, the computational analysis of social interaction is an emerging field of research with the aims of converting these support systems to be socially aware. The research on computational social behavior analysis and this proposed research program in particular, aims to deliver research results that would enable the development of tools to improve quality of life, by collective decision making support systems, meeting support systems and systems for self-assessment, training, and education.
This project proposes to build computational models of social constructs that define the social behavior of individuals and groups in face to face conversations, perceived via audio, visual or mobile sensors. The aim is to automatically analyze the social behavior of individuals during their interaction through their nonverbal signals and build models to estimate several social concepts using machine learning techniques. The novelty of the proposed approach is that it investigates computational approaches that make use of the close relation between related social constructs, such as dominance and leadership, or personality and dominance, during the learning process. The assumption is that these social constructs are related, thus automatic inference for one concept can take advantage of the other. The project follows a joint learning approach that combines the individual characteristics of participants in a group, such as personality and mood, with their social position in the group, such as dominance or roles, resulting from intra-group interaction and relations, as well as the overall group structure. Another novelty of the proposal is related to the usage of social media content to learn social behavior of individuals. Unlike the limited amount of data that is used to build computational models of social behavior, the social media sites provide an excellent and a vast amount of data for natural human behavior. The project aims to transfer the knowledge that can be extracted from the audio-visual behavioral content in social media (i.e. video blogging sites, video discussion sites, video lectures sites, etc.) to small group settings.
My research program is structured in four main phases. The first phase consists of modeling individual characteristics of participants. For this purpose, a database collected from social media will be used together with annotations on personality and mood. Techniques to transfer the knowledge gained through this database to normal small group settings will be investigated in the second phase. The third phase of the project focuses on modeling the group interaction and group structure, and the fourth phase aims at developing a joint learning approach to learn related social tasks.
Keywords: multimodal modeling, nonverbal behavior, social computing, social interaction modeling, social media

Title: HiGrav: High-resolution gravity fields for better flood forecasting
Abstract:
Floods are one of the most destructive natural hazards. They can cause significant damage including loss of human life and destruction of properties and infrastructure. Therefore, real-time monitoring, forecasting, and early warning of floods are essential for disaster mitigation and relief efforts, as outlined in the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030 by the United Nations. Besides rainfall characteristics, the wetness conditions of the river catchment prior to the event are important factors for runoff generation and thus for the magnitude of the flood event. With the advent of the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) twin satellites in 2002 and their successor mission GRACE Follow-On (GRACE-FO) in 2018, it became possible to retrieve terrestrial water storage (TWS) anomalies by measuring temporal variations of the Earth’s gravity field. This opens the possibility of estimating the wetness conditions before and during flood events. However, the use of these data in flood warning systems so far has largely been limited by their insufficient temporal and spatial resolution: standard GRACE/GRACE-FO solutions have a monthly temporal resolution and a spatial resolution of 250-300 km. Thus, the goal of this project is to improve the prediction and monitoring of flood events by using TWS anomalies derived from GRACE/GRACE-FO daily and downscaled to a high spatial resolution of 50 km globally. 

In a first step, we will derive gravity fields with a daily temporal resolution using a Kalman filter approach. This is a significant improvement compared to the standard gravity field solutions. However, it comes at the cost of a worse spatial resolution as the daily coverage of the satellite orbits is not sufficiently dense at the global scale. To achieve a high spatial resolution of the TWS data sets, we will develop new methods based on machine learning to fuse TWS anomalies from GRACE/GRACE-FO with those from hydrological simulations, treating it as a super-resolution problem. To apply these daily highly-resolved TWS anomalies in flood warning and flood monitoring applications, we will develop a methodology to derive them in near real time and predict them into the future with machine learning. 

From the high-resolution TWS anomalies, we will derive a wetness index that will serve as an (early-warning) indicator of flood-prone water storage conditions in river basins. We assess its value relative to other flood-generating factors for different environmental conditions in river basins worldwide of various sizes in the range of few 10,000 km² to several millions of km². A machine learning framework that utilizes this GRACE/GRACE-FO-based wetness index, precipitation forecasts, and other auxiliary data to issue flood warnings will be developed. Furthermore, the gravity-based water storage anomalies will be incorporated into an existing flood forecasting model in selected river basins in Lower Saxony, Germany. The performance of the forecasts based on both the machine-learning approach and the flood modelling system on the regional scale will be evaluated with benchmark hindcast experiments, i.e. by studying in detail its performance for flood events in the past. 
We believe that our new approach to flood forecasting has significant potential to improve the accuracy and reliability of early warnings, setting the stage to reduce flood damages in the future. In addition to flood warning, we also see further applications of our temporally and spatially highly-resolved TWS anomalies such as for quantifying groundwater or soil moisture dynamics.
Keywords: GRACE, downscaling, flood forecasting, gravity field, hydrology, machine learning, physical geodesy, water storage

Title: Principled Numerical Methods for Curved Surfaces
Abstract:
Many popular methods in geometry processing that apply the Laplacian operator lack a mathematical proof of correctness, convergence, or performance. I will add such mathematical understanding to four popular methods: the mixed finite element method for the biharmonic equation, the vector Dirichlet energy, geometry-specific preconditioners for optimization, and developability energies.
Each of these methods is currently used in practice, but the correct conditions that mathematically guarantee a successful application are unknown. This limits their application, as studies and experiments have to be performed to justify each use, and as there are no guarantees for success for any method.
Thoroughly exploring the numerical and computational properties of these methods will vastly increase their utility and birth insights which will inspire novel methods and applications in many fields, including computer graphics, mechanical engineering, architecture, art, robotics, medical imaging, machine learning, and more.
Keywords: Computer Graphics, Discrete Geometry, Geometry, Geometry Processing, Numerical Analysis

Title: Active learning for late-stage drug design
Abstract:
Challenges in solubility, stability, and absorption require formulation development that
can significantly delay the introduction of promising drugs to patients. Active machine
learning allows for rapid model development by implementing a feedback-driven
artificial intelligence that puts the machine in charge of requesting additional data for
iteratively improving predictive accuracy. Coupled to novel organ-on-a-chip assay
systems, active learning workflows have the potential to transform formulation
development and generate in silico models that help streamlining translational drug
design. This proposal aims to establish active learning workflows for rapidly generating
models for various objectives relevant to formulation development using
intestine-on-a-chip systems. In addition to predictive models, such workflows will
generate vast amounts of biological data to deepen our understanding of
organ-on-a-chip systems as well as provide theoretical insights into the learning
patterns of artificial intelligence.
Keywords: Bioinformatics, Computational drug development, Formulation design, Machine learning, Organs-on-a-chip

Title: Orofacial impairment and rehabilitation in stroke patients
Abstract:
Based on the results of Part A (3200B0-108239), a randomized controlled clinical trial is proposed which introduces a rehabilitation programme for impaired orofacial functions following stroke in a new group of patients. The aim is to test the following hypotheses
Structured training of the chewing and facial muscles in stroke patients 
-enhances the oral motor skills,
-improves chewing efficiency and lip force,
-prevents atrophy of the chewing muscles and
-improves the Oral Health Related Quality of Life

Approval from the Ethical Committee is obtained. A focus group of post-stroke patients will be used to present the proposed exercises and refine them according to the comments from the participants as well as a speech-language-pathologist, specialised in oral rehabilitation (LS). Patients over 60 years, who are hospitalized to recover from an ischemic stroke and present with a hemi-syndrome and facial palsy as well as impaired chewing efficiency are enrolled and randomized either to the experimental (n=30) or control (n=30) group. A recent history of neuro-muscular disease and dysphagia are two of several exclusion criteria. After written informed consent is obtained, a dental examination is performed. At baseline, the OHRQoL is evaluated by means of the OHIP-20 questionnaire. Chewing efficiency is quantified using the previously developed two-colour mixing test. The oral motor skills are assessed by means of a Motor-Ability test, where the patient has to assemble two halves of three different test-pieces of increasing difficulty in the mouth. To estimate the lip force, a vestibular oral screen has to be retained behind the lips whist a pulling force is recorded. Bite force is measured on both sides with a force gauge. The thickness of the masseter muscles of the affected and non-affected side are measured using 2D-ultrasound.

The proposed rehabilitation programme begins 14 to 42 days after stroke and comprises a 5-week supervised facial and chewing muscle training by an occupational therapist. Fifteen minutes of gum-chewing therapy is followed by 5 minutes of each of the following myofacial exercises: withstanding pulling forces to an oral screen, pushing a lozenge with the tongue through the oral vestibule and resistive expiration into a spirometer. After one week of supervised learning of the exercises and passing an aptitude test (T0), the patient is asked to perform daily unsupervised self-training in addition to the 2 weekly sessions with the occupational therapist. For the self-training sessions, a video support is developed so that the patient can follow the instructions on a portable DVD player. The Control Group receives an equal number of sessions with the same occupational therapist, yet these are not aiming to improve orofacial function. Evaluations of the orofacial functions are repeated at 2 weeks (T1) and at 5 weeks (T2) with the same protocol except for the masseter muscle bulk (only T2). If the patient is discharged from Hospital before T2 the study continues at domicile or with organised transport, according to the patient’s preferences. As a token all patients receive a complimentary professional oral hygiene session at the end of the intervention period.

The proposed RCT (Part B) suggests an early focussed rehabilitation programme for facial and chewing muscles to improve oral function, prevent chewing muscle atrophy following stroke and increase the patients’ oral health related quality of life.
Keywords: RCT, chewing efficiency, oral health related quality of Life, orofacial function, rehabilitation programme, stroke

Title: Interfacing Neural and Symbolic Knowledge in Natural Language Systems
Abstract:
In this proposal, we outline a research plan to re-design neuro-symbolic interfaces between language models and knowledge graphs by leveraging existing implicit knowledge representations in the language model. Put simply, we seek to measure and localise what the language model already “knows” to figure out what new information to give it, and how best to provide it.

Over the last few years, pretrained language models (LMs) have led to considerable improvements in the fields of AI and NLP, largely due to the considerable knowledge they implicitly capture in their parameters. Despite their empirical breakthroughs, these models fail to transfer to many downstream tasks. They make mistakes that demonstrate they do not learn to use their considerable implicit database of knowledge for new tasks, and their predictions are unexplainable, as language models are statistical “black boxes.” A class of methods to address these shortcomings focuses on grounding language models using knowledge graphs (KG), but these new models do not consider the implicit knowledge already encoded by the language model. As a result, they learn weak, often spurious, alignments between both modalities (language and knowledge graph), yielding solutions that gain little from the KG, and at times, hurt the LM’s performance.

Our objective in this work is to design new neuro-symbolic interfaces between neural language models and symbolic knowledge sources. Specifically, we propose to (1) discover latent knowledge-encoding structures in neural LMs, (2) design methods that effectively connect symbolic knowledge to these latent structures, and (3) develop algorithms for reasoning over these joint structures for robust prediction.

We expect to change how neural models are symbolically grounded by knowledge graphs for robust prediction. Our methods will lead to new approaches for interfacing symbolic structures (e.g., knowledge graphs, semantic networks) with the implicit knowledge in neural language systems. Our research will motivate new methods for faithfully localising various types of knowledge in language models, efficiently selecting symbolic knowledge to complement and ground neural systems, and adaptably reasoning over these joint structures, leading to more interpretable and efficient AI systems.

Title: Machine-Learning for Optimized Ab-initio Quantum Transport Simulations (MALOQ)
Abstract:
Joule heating plays an important role in a variety of nanoscale electronic devices by increasing their lattice temperature in response to an electrical current flowing through them. In conventional integrated circuits (ICs), it might degrade the performance of Si transistors and promote mechanical failures in Cu interconnects. In emerging technologies, it can rather be harnessed to trigger desirable phenomena, such as the reversible crystallization of GST chalcogenides. Being able to control Joule heating in nanostructures is therefore essential. This requires an in-depth understanding of the underlying physics that only advanced modeling approaches can provide.  

To be accurate and of practical relevance, a comprehensive simulation platform operating at the ab-initio and quantum mechanical level is needed. It should capture the interplay between electrical (voltage-induced currents), thermal (excitation of crystal vibrations), and structural (migration of atoms) effects with an atomistic resolution. This can be achieved by self-consistently coupling molecular dynamics (MD), density-functional theory (DFT), and quantum transport (QT) based on the non-equilibrium Green’s function (NEGF) formalism for electrons and phonons. Concretely, an initial atomic geometry is created with MD. Its Hamiltonian and dynamical matrices, electron-phonon coupling, and anharmonic phonon-phonon interactions are then calculated with DFT. This data finally serves as input to a QT solver to obtain the device’s “current vs. voltage” characteristics and local temperature increase, which is passed to a MD package to update the original atomic positions. This MD-DFT-QT cycle must be repeated until a stable structure is obtained. 

The bottleneck of such electro-thermo-structural investigations resides in the preparation of DFT inputs from a given set of atomic coordinates. In the MALOQ project, we will address this issue by leveraging machine learning (ML) techniques, in particular graph neural networks (GNNs) where nodes represent atoms and edges the bonds connecting them. Taking advantage of the most recent progresses in the field, we will develop two ML approaches with ab-initio-level of accuracy, one labeled ML-ESP to predict the entries of large-scale Hamiltonian matrices from small DFT datasets, and one called ML-PDP to perform the same task for dynamical matrices. Our ML framework will also be able to produce the derivatives of both quantities, which correspond to the electron-phonon and anharmonic phonon-phonon coupling elements. With the latter, dedicated scattering self-energies can be computed and used in NEGF. The framework will further involve the development of a custom, multi-GPU code to efficiently train the large, density connected GNNs encountered, while allowing for long-range interatomic and many-body effects to be accounted for.

The ML-enabled building blocks (ML-ESP, ML-PDP, and parallel GNN) will be combined with the LAMMPS MD tool and our advanced in-house QT solver (QuaTrEx) to form the targeted electro-thermo-structural simulation approach. With the proposed enhancements, it will be possible to monitor thermo-induced structural changes in large PCM cells or electromigration processes in copper interconnects with atomically disordered surfaces at an unprecedented level of detail.

The planned work will be conducted by one post-doc (two years) and two PhD students (four years each). All codes developed in MALOQ will be documented and released as open source packages on GitHub. Publications resulting from this research (journals and conference proceedings) will be made open access and thus freely available to the scientific community.

Title: Homeostatic Regulation of Transsynaptic Nano-Architecture
Abstract:
Subtle changes in the molecular organization of chemical synapses may profoundly affect synaptic transmission and animal behavior. Yet, neural systems and animals generally behave robustly for a lifetime, implying a tight homeostatic control of synaptic architecture. Accumulating evidence suggests a ‘sub-synaptic’ molecular organization at the nanometer scale that is coordinated between synaptic compartments. The molecular mechanisms that establish and regulate transsynaptically coordinated nano-architecture remain largely unknown.
The central objective of this proposal is to explore molecular mechanisms controlling transsynaptically-coordinated nano-architecture and its homeostatic modulation. The proposal is based on the discovery of transsynaptically-aligned nano-rings of synaptic proteins that undergo rapid changes during homeostatic plasticity at the Drosophila neuromuscular junction (NMJ). Employing a combination of Drosophila genetics, super-resolution light microscopy and synaptic physiology approaches, we will address the following key objectives:
1. Resolve transsynaptic nano-architecture and its heterogeneity under baseline conditions and during homeostatic plasticity. 
2. Unravel molecular mechanisms underlying the organization of transsynaptic nano-architecture.
3. Scrutinize molecular mechanisms promoting transsynaptic nano-structural homeostatic plasticity.
Super-resolution microscopy-based genetic screens will implicate new molecular mechanisms in the organization and modulation of transsynaptic nano-architecture. The investigation of transsynaptic nano-architecture will be facilitated by genetically-encoded tools for acute protein perturbation and multiplex immunohistochemistry. Synaptic nano-architecture will be examined with Stimulated Emission Depletion (STED) microscopy, as well as Expansion Microscopy (ExM) in combination with STED microscopy or fluorescence fluctuation analysis. Electrophysiological analysis of synaptic transmission will be complemented by optophysiological investigation of neurotransmitter release to link synaptic nano-architecture to synaptic physiology. Newly developed algorithms and machine-learning based approaches will support the analysis of super-resolution imaging and physiology data.
The expected results will not only generate the most comprehensive description of transcellular nano-architecture, but also shed light on the molecular mechanisms shaping transsynaptic nano-organization during homeostatic plasticity. Given the evolutionary conservation of homeostatic plasticity, as well as emerging links between synaptic homeostasis and neurological disorders, our basic research program is anticipated to contribute to a better understanding of the role of synaptic nano-architecture in orchestrating neural function under physiological and pathological conditions.

Title: MAAYA: Multimedia Analysis and Access for Documentation and Decipherment of Maya Epigraphy
Abstract:
While academics in archaeology and epigraphy have made formidable efforts over 100 years to decipher the writings of the Ancient Maya culture, located in a variety of places in Mexico and Central America, and imprinted in multiple media types and artifacts, a significant proportion of the Maya hieroglyphic corpus remains open for scholarly interpretation. This is a long-standing goal that can be accelerated by the rapid progress of computer science, and more specifically of multimedia analysis and information management methods, which today are capable, with varying degrees of success, of organizing, analyzing, and visualizing visual and multimedia collections.

The aim of this bi-disciplinary project is to tightly integrate the work of Maya epigraphists and computer scientists to (1) jointly design, develop, and assess new computational tools that robustly and effectively support the work of Maya hieroglyphics experts; (2) advance the state of Maya epigraphy through the combination of expert knowledge and the advanced use of these tools; and (3) make these new resources and knowledge available to the scholar community through the creation of an online system (which to our knowledge would be one of a kind) that would allow for search, comparison, annotation, and visualization tasks as part of new investigations worldwide.

Our project takes a holistic view to this problem, acknowledging that scholar and technological progress needs to be made at various levels (including data preparation and modeling; additional work in epigraphy; semi-automated visual processing; pattern analysis; and advanced forms of information access and visualization) to achieve qualitative shifts towards deciphering of known (and yet to be discovered) hieroglyphic vestiges of the Maya civilization. At the same time, the computational methodologies that will be investigated in the project are based on principled approaches (probabilistic machine learning, computer vision, and information retrieval), and so the resulting technologies will be applicable to other areas in multimedia retrieval.
Keywords: Archaeology, Computer Vision, Cultural Heritage, Machine Learning, Maya Epigraph, Multimdia

Title: Deep Learning for Graph-structured data
Abstract:
Deep learning algorithms currently achieve outstanding performance in computer vision and speech recognition tasks. This is accomplished by exploiting the regular structure of the data domain in order to draw relevant but strong assumptions about the learning problem. For example, since there are multiple possible ways to position a camera, most regression and classification problems are invariant to translations along the pixel grid. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) use this invariance to reduce the number of parameters and improve generalization.  

Over the last few years, we have seen the first attempts to generalize deep learning methods from grid- to graph-structured data. From bioinformatics (e.g., brain networks), to the organization of human interaction (social networks), human interest (recommendation networks), human knowledge (e.g., Wikipedia), and human mobility (transportation networks), an astounding amount of data exist that posses graph structure. Realizing that for such data standard deep learning falls short, researchers have recently attempted to replicate the success of CNNs by generalizing concepts from the pixel grid to graphs. Building on powerful ideas from spectral graph theory, manifold learning, and graph signal processing, we have witnessed the emergence of new network architectures that exploit the inherent properties of a graph in order to shape and regularize the learning process.

Yet, despite recent progress, current approaches to deep learning for graph-structured data suffer from limitations that hamper their adoption: (i) Their accuracy is dependent on having the right graph as input---yet, in most cases, the graph is either only partially known or it has to be constructed from data in a heuristic manner. (ii) Even though it is understood that depth is necessary to achieve human-level performance, due to graph deformations compounded at each layer it is currently problematic to use graph neural networks with more than a few layers. (iii) By assuming that every training sample relates to the same graph, many current approaches pose requirements that limit their applicability.

By tackling these challenges in a rigorous and reproducible manner, the DLEG project aims to take concrete steps towards making deep learning for graph-structured data an accurate and widely-applicable technology. This should carry substantial scientific impact both on deep learning and computer science, as well as on the many scientific fields that use graphs. Graph structured data are all around us---utilizing them to make relevant predictions brings promise for both scientific as well as industrial innovation.
Keywords: data science, deep learning, graph algorithms, graph-structured data, machine learning, supervised learning

Title: Reasoning about Plans and Heuristics for Planning and Combinatorial Search
Abstract:
Action planning is one of the oldest and one of the central research problems in artificial intelligence. A planning problem arises whenever an intelligent agent (virtual or embodied) needs to decide which activities it must carry out in order to achieve its goals, or as Patrik Haslum put it succinctly: "Planning is the art and practice of thinking before acting."

Classical planning, the most widely studied variant of the planning problem with which this project is concerned, can be formalized as finding shortest paths (optimal planning) or any path (satisficing planning) from a given initial state to some goal state in an implicitly given planning task, essentially a directed graph. Planning is hard because these graphs are often enormous in size in practical applications, comprising 10^100 states or more, precluding the application of traditional "blind" graph search methods.

The most successful planning algorithms of the last decade fall into the general class of heuristic search methods, usually based on A* or a related search algorithm. In this context, the word heuristic, which carries a wide range of meanings in different areas of computer science, is a very specific technical term: a heuristic is a function whose input is a state s of a planning task and which returns an estimate of the distance from s to a nearest goal state. Heuristics are the heart and soul of planning algorithms based on state-space search. Depending on the accuracy of the heuristic estimates, heuristic search algorithms can range from solving planning tasks blindingly fast to being worse than blind search.

Hence, much of the most influential classical planning research in the recent past has been concerned with developing better and better heuristics and furthering our theoretical understanding of existing heuristics. This has led to increasingly more sophisticated approaches. A large amount of human ingenuity has gone into devising today's advanced approaches and developing the underlying theory, especially in the case of optimal planning, where heuristics must satisfy a lower-bound property (be admissible) in order to be safe to use.

The central idea of this project is to shift this burden of sophistication and ingenuity away from the human heuristic designer and onto the machines that perform the heuristic search. Equipped with appropriate reasoning algorithms and representations, computers can derive knowledge about planning tasks more quickly, more reliably and
in more complex settings than we humans are capable of. A planning researcher or practitioner should be able to focus on which information a planning algorithm ought to exploit, without having to worry about how to exploit it in the best way. In other words, we are suggesting a declarative approach to heuristic search planning that enables planning algorithms to reason about plans and heuristics in powerful and general ways.

A key research challenge in this endeavour is identifying an appropriate level of representation at which this declarative information is specified. It should be general enough to capture the concepts that today's state-of-the-art planning algorithms rely on in order to obtain accurate heuristic estimates, yet limited enough to afford efficient reasoning algorithms. In this project, we explore this design space in depth, both theoretically and with an emphasis on efficient practical algorithms.
Keywords: LTL plan constraints, artificial intelligence, automated planning, combinatorial search, heuristic search, operator-counting constraints, potential functions

Title: Modeling the neural correlates of movement
Abstract:
Voluntary movement is a result of a highly coordinated activity between the nervous system and the rest of the body. However, much is still unknown about the quantitative relationship between neural activity, muscle activity, and thence movement. Movement is driven by coordinated activity across a network of reciprocally connected brain areas. Many questions surround the relationship between these different brain regions and their ultimate product: muscle activity and thence movement. Often, these questions have a similar form: how do the properties of one neural population — features of the response, encoded variables, population dynamics, etc. — relate to those of another population. This question has been difficult to resolve even when comparing the neural population activity in primary motor cortex with the muscle response. An enduring hurdle is that the field often lacks appropriate computational frameworks and analytical methods for determining what is shared and what is different between populations. For example, areas that perform very different computations may display superficially similar responses. Conversely, commonalities between communicating regions can be lost amid surface-level differences. It is thus essential that comparisons be guided by concrete hypotheses, constrained both by biological reality and by theory regarding what computational mechanisms are plausible or desirable. 

The goal of this project is to leverage hypothesis- guided analysis methods to characterize and compare populations in data from multiple motor and non-motor areas of the primate and rodent. Modeling such neural activity in the context of movement generation using cutting-edge machine learning models is still a nascent yet growing field. Nonlinear models of neural dynamics, for example, neural networks involving dynamical models such as recurrent neural networks have been gaining popularity due to the rapid advances in computational power that have led to tractable learning of deep and complex network structures. However, the inference of these models is still challenging due to the underconstrained nature of high-dimensional models; thus the question becomes how best to constrain or regularize these in the presence of neural data.

I will develop generalizable dynamical models on data collected on mice and macaque monkeys with the goal of gaining understanding of the computational principles governing movement-related neural activity. Specifically, in Aim 1, I will use a goal-driven architecture to learn a recurrent neural network that reproduces the computational structure seen in motor cortex data recorded during movements made by a macaque monkey at different speeds. In Aim 2, I will explore a data-driven approach to model neural activity from multiple regions while a mouse is making spontaneous and task-driven movements, and explore differences between the dynamics of the neural activity during these modes. In Aim 3, I will combine the two approaches, namely goal-driven and data-driven, to develop a dynamical model learnt using end-to-end training for the generation of task-driven movements. This will help elucidate the role of neural activity from different regions in the context of behavior. While we hope to make significant scientific advances while addressing the aims as discussed below, there will doubtless be computational developments that may even surpass the scientific contributions made while addressing the aims of this proposal.

Title: Artificial Intelligence against Car Dominance– Scenarios for Spatial Sustainability
Abstract:
1.SUMMARY

Background and rationale
The future of urban mobility is increasingly bound to the advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI)– manifested dominantly in the evolving realms of autonomous and connected vehicles. This has started to raise essential questions in field of urban studies. Such questions extend beyond the car user perspective (e.g. safety, comfort), and entail widening the scope of investigations to transformation of public spaces, new logics of mobility, and more broadly, urban experiences. 
Since almost four decades, urban and transport research –under the banner of “modal shift strategies”– has sought a transition from the dominance of car towards the centrality of human, for the ultimate goal of social and environmental sustainability. In this perspective, the speculations on whether or not the wave of autonomous and connected vehicles would be able to introduce a breakthrough in urban mobility depends on its capacity to rectify some of the socio-spatial problematics of the existing car system. Space efficiency is a promise in that direction. Simulations and case-studies have repeatedly shown that autonomous vehicles can liberate significant segments of car-dedicated spaces, for example through reducing the required fleet size by up to 90% (Boesch et a. 2015; Spieser et al. 2014; Zachariah et a. 2014; Martinez and Crist 2015). Nevertheless, it is uncertain  how would/should the liberated spaces take new shapes and for what functions. In particular, what strategies can reappropriate the liberated spaces in a way that they contribute to human-scale sustainable urbanity, rather than feeding even more the self-expansive car system? Answering these questions entails a research agenda that from an urban standpoint can proactively guide the socio-spatial impacts of AI in our future cities. The proposed project will be a pioneering contribution to that research agenda.

Broad objectives
Questions that embody the complexity of human urban experiences in relation to the automobility of today and the ones of future define the broad direction of research that I have begun to explore during the course of my doctoral research. This proposed postdoc will develop a new focus particularly on the topic of urban space and its evolution in the perspective of AI-enabled urban mobility.

Specific aims
Building on the body of research that quantifies the capacity of AI to liberate urban spaces, this project seeks to answer the following question: what potentials do the liberated spaces (surfaces, volumes) hold for redistributing urban land-use, reshaping mobility practices, and rethinking the ecosystem of public space? Concretely, I will develop future scenarios for three urban contexts:  “dense multimodal urban core”, “transit-oriented suburb”, and “car-oriented territories of diffuse urbanity”. 
The generated ideal scenarios will be a major part of the research outcomes. But also, scenario development is the research methodology that I will use to compare various alternation of parameters and to indicate the scenarios that should be prevented.

Methods
Three representative examples of the respective urban contexts will be selected in the greater Boston area (grid size 3x3km). For each case, through analytical cartography of current land-use, car-dedicated spaces will be quantified and mapped along with the patterns of travel demand and modal splits. 
The resulting understanding of the context, together with estimations of Autonomous Vehicle’s space efficiency (extracted from knowledge being created in the domains of Transportation and Computer Science) will be the primary material for “scenario development” (Bishop et. al 2007). Scenarios will address change at multiple scales, from street section, speeds, regulations, right of ways in public space to new mobility corridors, land-use modifications, and complementarity with public transport. A comparative mapping will demonstrate the extent of transformation achieved by the developed scenarios in contrast to the current situation of each case.
Finally, “backcasting methods” (Robinson 1990) will be used to identify the conditions, policies, and events necessary for the realization of the respective scenarios.

Expected results and their impact for the field 
The expected outcomes include (1) three scenarios that (in the format of cartography, descriptive statistics, and narration) depict and detail the socio-spatial benefits that AI may be able to bring to three urban models, and (2) the required policies for those scenarios to be realized. The research also highlights the spatially unsustainable scenarios to be prevented and the corresponding policies to be avoided.
The broad domain of sustainable urbanism aims at informing the process of solution seeking and policy making for the cities. The results of the proposed research will contribute to this domain by addressing the most central urban resource, that is, space, and regarding a timely revolution, that is, autonomous and connected vehicles.
Keywords: Autonomous and connected vehicles, Mobility, Space efficiency, Sustainable urbanism, Urban Space

Title: High-entropy ceramics as dual-functional materials for integrated carbon capture and conversion
Abstract:
In order to close the carbon cycle and minimize greenhouse gas emissions, integrated engineering and scientific solutions will need to take a multipronged approach given the wide range of processes that contribute to climate change, and the fact that carbon emissions are diverse in both their sources and scales. An integrated approach to carbon capture and conversion through materials engineering developments (known as ICCC, CCCC, or ICCU) uses dual-functional materials (DFMs). This process involves chemical looping with fast switching between a CO2 adsorption cycle and CO2 hydrogenation cycle allowing for the conversion of CO2 to methane for more dilute CO2 streams. ICCC technology can specifically help with capturing the range of CO2 emissions at small CO2 point sources while also producing an energy carrier like methane or methanol on a local scale.

The materials design however is quite complex, and materials development is still in its infancy. DFMs for ICCC need to have beneficial material properties for carbon capture materials but also all the beneficial material properties for hydrogenation catalysts. Furthermore, the process conditions between the two cycles need to be complementary (ideally close to isothermal conditions, and ideally at mid-range temperatures). Ultimately this also means that there are accompanying materials engineering challenges for both carbon capture and catalytic conversion processes, but with additional complexities from process considerations. DMFs that allow for a wide range of parameters to be optimized are needed for realizing the potential of ICCC technologies, and there needs to be marked improvement in stability and tailorability of process conditions without loss of CO2 capture capacity or CO2 conversion. 

This project addresses a pressing problem in the low-carbon economy by utilizing a high-entropy materials platform to develop a dual-functional material for integrated CO2 capture and conversion for intermediate temperature regimes (200-400°C). A holistic approach is taken, starting from synthesis and screening studies, through to high-throughput testing and machine learning, and finally to shaping of the final targeted product. Simultaneously, this work will deepen the understanding of the emerging and relatively untested field of high-entropy ceramics for catalytic and gas adsorption applications.
Keywords: CO2 capture, CO2 hydrogenation, dual-function materials, high-entropy ceramics, high-entropy oxides, hydrothermal synthesis, in-situ characterization, integrated carbon capture and conversion

Title: AI-Driven Antitoxin Catalogue (ADAC) - Shifting the paradigm from antivenom discovery to antivenom design
Abstract:
Executive summary: Revolutionising Snakebite Antivenom with a Toxin-Centric Approach
This project introduces a groundbreaking shift in snakebite treatment paradigms, moving from the current reliance on region-specific, animal blood product-based antivenoms towards a universal, toxin-centric approach. Traditional antivenom development focuses on neutralising venoms from specific snake species prevalent in particular regions, resulting in therapies that are not only limited in scope but also pose significant challenges in terms of production, distribution, and cross-regional efficacy. In contrast, our initiative aims to redefine this landscape by targeting broad families and subfamilies of snake venom toxins, pursuing the development of broadly neutralising antitoxins capable of countering a wide array of medically relevant toxins with minimal components.

At the core of our strategy is the computational analysis of snake venom toxins to identify conserved functional epitopes at both the sequence and structural levels. This approach allows us to cluster toxins into target cohorts, laying the groundwork for the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) to expedite the design of innovative small molecule, macrocyclic, and protein-based antitoxins. These antitoxins are envisioned to neutralise entire clusters of toxins, thereby forming a comprehensive catalogue that can be tailored to formulate custom, region-specific antivenoms worldwide. Together this project will not only present substantial promise toward a next-generation treatment for snakebite envenoming, but will also demonstrate how AI can set new standards for precision and inclusivity in global health.
Keywords: Computer-assisted virtual screening, Snakebite envenoming, antitoxin, antivenom, artificial intelligence, de novo therapeutic design, depp learning, drug design, macrocycle, neglected diseases, protein design, snake venom toxin

Title: Behavioral, psychophysiological, and computational signatures of affective influences on information value learning
Abstract:
Humans have a fundamental drive for knowledge. While this drive typically promotes survival, problem-solving, and learning, it also poses key challenges in today’s information-rich world: How do people decide when to seek or avoid information? Why do they sometimes compulsively consume information even when it offers no benefit or leads to adverse consequences? Information-seeking critically depends on how people value information. Individuals are often motivated to seek information for its instrumental utility—guiding decisions and future actions—as well as its epistemic and emotional utility, such as satisfying curiosity, reducing uncertainty, and anticipating positive feelings. These motives highlight the central role of affective processes in shaping information value. However, the mechanisms by which people learn the value of information and how affective processes influence such learning remain unclear. Understanding these mechanisms is essential for better explaining the emergence of both adaptive and maladaptive information-seeking behavior. This project addresses this gap by systematically investigating how affective processes influence the way humans learn the value of information and how this, in turn, impacts information-seeking decisions. 

To this end, the project combines computational modeling based on reinforcement-learning algorithms with behavioral and psychophysiological methods. It is structured into three work packages that aim to characterize (1) how affective processes modulate learning from information prediction errors (i.e., discrepancies between expected and received information) and the integration of information value with reward value; (2) affective responses to information using a multi-level approach encompassing action tendencies, physiological responses, and subjective feelings; and (3) the links between these processes and individual differences in affective traits and compulsive information-seeking behaviors. To promote reproducibility and transparency, the project adopts a discovery-replication approach and adheres to open-science practices, sharing anonymized data, task materials, and analysis code according to the FAIR principles.

By uncovering behavioral, psychophysiological, and computational signatures of affective influences on information value learning, the project aims to advance a mechanistic framework for understanding how affect and emotion dynamically shape information-seeking. Ultimately, it seeks to provide an empirical foundation for developing strategies to mitigate compulsive information consumption—a growing challenge in the digital age.
Keywords: affective processes, affective relevance, emotion, information preferences, information-seeking, reinforcement learning, valence, value
