Title: Medical image retrieval in mANY dimensions  2 (MANY2)
Abstract:
Multi–dimensional visual medical information is increasingly produced in modern hospitals. The imaging techniques evolved to assess the visual appearance of almost every organ with both high spatial and temporal resolution. Functional imaging was also more recently proposed to study the behavior of certain organs. All the specific requirements for imaging each organ bred a wide range of imaging techniques producing multi–dimensional data in the forms of signals, images (2D), image series (3D volumes, videos or 4D volumetric videos) and combinations of modalities (e.g., positron emission tomography (PET) with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)). This comprehensive suite of irreplaceable diagnosis and research tools is perfectly aligned with evidence–based medicine aiming at taking decisions based on proven facts [55]. However, the management of such tremendous amounts of visual information entails several challenges and has lagged behind the imaging physics advances. Visual information with a dimensionality superior to 2 cannot be easily perceived by human observers. Whereas efficient synthetic visualization of 3D objects is made available by computer graphics with 3D rendering, global visualization of 3D textures is a more challenging task. Only virtual navigation in multi–planar rendering (MPR) or semi–transparent visualizations allow observing 2D projections of opaque solid textures. The interpretation of large image data sets based on such visualization tools is time–consuming and entails the risk of omitting important areas. This was recently reported as an important problem in radiological routine by the radiological society of north America (RSNA) [2]. Furthermore, advances in medical informatics enable access to most of the radiological exams to all clinicians through the electronic health record (EHR) and the picture archiving and communication system (PACS). This change of the medical workflow creates a need for computer expert systems able to deliver the right information to the right people at the right time.
Computerized analysis has the potential of allowing comprehensive and systematic interpretation of vast multi–dimensional datasets [16]. It can provide key solutions for both large–scale management of the whole content of the PACS using content–based image retrieval (CBIR) [45] and at the diagnosis level for the interpretation of single image series [25]. In a concern of sparsity and synthesis, 3D computer graphics has been focusing on objects [62]. Shape–based methods allow encapsulating essential properties of objects and thus provide approximations of the real world that are corresponding to human understanding and the human abstraction level. Much less attention has been given to 3D solid texture analysis, although playing a central role in radiology to assess the structural properties of biomedical tissue [64]. Computer–aided diagnosis (CAD) based on 2D texture quantification in radiological images has been an active research field over the past 20 years with the aim of reducing omission errors of pathological tissue by providing systematic second opinions to radiologists. Furthermore, it allows retrieving cases having objectively similar visual properties to orient the diagnosis workup, which proved to significantly increase the diagnosis accuracy, especially when the radiologists have little experience [1]. Only little information retrieval has so far been attempted really taking into account 3D or 4D aspects of the medical data, although for a real integration of visual retrieval into PACS this constitutes by far the largest amount of data to be treated. The state–of–the–art on 3D solid texture analysis and retrieval was reviewed using a systematic methodology in [12]. In our review of the literature we observed that only 91 papers could be found on volumetric texture analysis, where 66 (72.5%) are based on biomedical images. Even fewer papers investigated computerized analysis of 4D datasets. We also observed that the majority of the techniques used for texture analysis do not allow to fully explore texture properties because they require arbitrary choices on scales and orientations, which are difficult when the dimensionality is superior to 2.
The MANY 2 plans pushing the frontiers of current content–based medical image retrieval and analysis approaches from two dimensions to three and more dimensions to exploit the large amount of medical visual data created by modern hospitals in a better way. MANY 2 is the continuation of the MANY project (205321–130046) for years 3 and 4. The results of the first 12 months of MANY consolidated the initial planning for years 3 and 4. In the lake Geneva region, the CIBM (Centre d’Imagerie Biomédicale) combines capacities of several institutions on image creation and image analysis to address some of the production and processing needs. The first year of MANY already showed that combining the expertise of the CIBM with the experience on visual information retrieval and radiology of the research groups involved in this proposal allowed developing innovative image analysis tools. These tools are enabling statistically significant performance improvement when compared to state–of–the–art approaches [13, 30] as well as appropriate clinical integration in [17]. These preliminary results are preparing the filed for years 3 and 4 where the techniques will be extended to four dimensions and multi–modality imaging. In particular, multi–dimensional image analysis using the Riesz transform along with manifold learning using spectral graph theory will enable local multi–scale and multi–orientation texture comparison with infinitesimal angular precision. These methods are expected to allow encompassing subtle structural and spectral signatures of complex pathological tissue alteration in 3D, 4D and multi–modal imaging. Density–based and spectral clustering methods will be used to derive visual words from high–dimensional visual features to identify data structures that are related to medical anomalies. In order to combine visual information from multiple modalities, geometrical fusion rules using voxelwise probabilistic distribution of the tissue classes will be developed. Further statistically relevant validation of the developed tools will be made possible with the creation of high–quality multidimensional datasets containing ground truth and contextual clinical parameters at the University Hospitals of Geneva (HUG). Such datasets already proved to represent high value for the research community in [19]. The developed computer tools and interfaces are planned to be evaluated in the radiological routine at the HUG to cope with the reality of the well–established clinical workflows.

Title: Robustness Aspects of Statistical Machine Learning
Abstract:
Over the last two decades we have witnessed an explosion of data driven by technological advances that have allowed the collection and processing of very large data sets. This data revolution has enlarged the scope of questions that applied researches can seek to ask but has also led them to situations where traditional statistical analysis become unfeasible. Indeed, in fields such as engineering, finance, genomics and neuroscience, much of the applied work relies on extracting useful information from massive data where the number of variables collected can be very large. From a statistics perspective, the increasing availability of large dimensional data has been a driving force behind the impressive recent amount of research devoted to the development of new statistical tools and the growing interest in computational efficiency. Since statistical models are used in practice as approximations to reality, it is therefore natural and important to wonder how statistical procedures behave if the assumptions upon which the models are constructed fail to hold. Hence, robustness towards stochastic deviations from the assumed models is an appealing concept that I will study in this project by focusing on three topics in statistical machine learning.

The first problem that I will consider is differentially private statistical inference. More precisely, I will build on insights from robust statistics to contruct general differentially private parametric inference tools. Title: Design of de novo Influenza A Virus antiviral peptides
Abstract:
Influenza A virus continues to pose a major global health challenge, causing significant disease burden despite the availability of vaccines and antiviral drugs. The emergence of viral resistance highlights the need for new antiviral strategies that act through alternative mechanisms.

This project explores the feasibility of using artificial intelligence–guided protein design to identify novel peptide-based inhibitors that interfere with essential virus–host interactions required for influenza virus replication. The study focuses on conserved components of the viral replication machinery and their interaction with critical host factors, with the aim of disrupting viral polymerase function.

Candidate peptides generated through computational design will be evaluated using established cellular assays to assess biological activity and cellular compatibility. Promising candidates will be further examined for their ability to function within cells during viral infection.

Overall, this work serves as a proof-of-concept for applying deep-learning–based protein design to antiviral discovery. The approach has the potential to inform future therapeutic development against influenza viruses and other priority viral pathogens, while maintaining flexibility for downstream optimisation and translation.
Keywords: Antiviral research, Influenza virus, artificial intelligence, protein design, virus–host interaction

Title: Data-Driven Intelligent Predictive Maintenance of Industrial Assets
Abstract:
Falling costs and increased reliability of sensing devices, data transmission and data storage have fostered condition monitoring to become near ubiquitous for many complex engineered systems. The emergence of In-ternet of Things (IoT), cyber-physical systems and smart factories provides an overwhelming source of data from physical asset monitoring. Even though condition monitoring data have been available for some of the applications for more than a decade (e.g. for critical power generation assets), other areas of industry have only recently started to exploit the potential of condition monitoring systems. 
The amount of data collected per period unit has recently grown by orders of magnitude, potentially resulting in much better information on system condition. System health condition is increasingly captured by different types of monitoring systems, at different time scales, with different types of data, ranging from vibration sig-nals to video streaming. The large volume and variety of condition monitoring data drive traditional model- and knowledge-based approaches too difficult to implement and too demanding in resource usage. 
The proposed research project tackles the challenge of effectively using the diverse, high dimensional, high-velocity condition monitoring data of industrial assets to improve availability and resilience of industrial assets. Intelligent adaptive hybrid predictive maintenance algorithms will be developed in this research project based on a combination of physical performance models and deep machine learning algorithms learning the hidden information, dependencies, and structure in condition monitoring data. The developed framework aims at extracting high-level knowledge representations from high-dimensional condition monitoring signals with a high volume, variety and velocity. The developed hybrid algorithms will close the research gap and enable learning fault signatures from heterogeneous condition monitoring data sources and additionally transferring them be-tween different systems of the same fleet and predict failures based on the learned fault signatures and their predicted evolution in time. The developed approaches will enable a fast and efficient adaptation of predictive maintenance systems to new operating conditions and newly developed systems. A further contribution of the proposed research project is in developing approaches for controlling the remaining useful life (RUL), learning the optimal remedying actions for anomalous system states and integrating the recommendations in a decision support system.
The proposed approaches will not only improve the reliability and availability of critical infrastructure and in-dustrial assets but will also improve their resilience by pre-emptive interventions, improved recovery actions and proactive control of the remaining useful life. The results of the proposed research project will not only benefit the operators, but also the society as a whole by improving the quality of the provided services (including im-proved availability) and reducing the costs of operation and maintenance.
The uniqueness of the proposed research program is in the combination of the cutting edge artificial intelli-gence approaches, physical performance models for addressing the research gaps that are urgently needed by the industry and society.
Keywords: condition monitoring, data-driven predictive maintenance, deep neural networks, fault detection, feature learning, machine learning, prognostics and system health management, signal processing

Title: Bridging the implementation gap: A machine-learning algorithm for the rapid diagnosis of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (RADI-HIT)
Abstract:
Background and rationale
Diagnosing heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) at the bedside is a significant clinical challenge, exposing patients to the risk of delayed diagnosis and unnecessary treatment. Supported by a research grant of the Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF), our team recently developed a user-friendly machine-learning (ML) algorithm that integrates diverse clinical and laboratory data to diagnose HIT more accurately than existing diagnostic tools: https://toradi-hit.org. Nevertheless, authorities and scientific societies require comprehensive external validation before applying ML algorithms to clinical settings. This project hypothesizes that the TORADI-HIT ML algorithm can be implemented effectively in new settings, lead to faster diagnosis, result in a lower number of misclassified patients, and improves medical decision-making. As a result, this also addresses an urgent AI/ML implementation gap in health care. Applying recent analytical techniques to the ML methodology, the study will additionally be used to discover new biomarkers and their interactions for the diagnosis and prognosis of patients with HIT.
Overall objectives, specific aims, and methods
Aiming to fully implement the TORADI-HIT ML algorithm in clinical practice, we will apply it to new settings and populations and assess the usability, the diagnostic accuracy, and the effects of implementation including clinical outcomes. Besides, we will use the study for the discovery of new biomarkers for the diagnosis and prognosis of patients with HIT. 
1.We will use existing data from an external cohort (n=992) to retrospectively validate the TORADI-HIT ML algorithm in a second dataset.
2.We will conduct a multicenter clinical study (n=1’400) to prospectively apply the TORADI-HIT algorithm to new settings and populations and assessing the performance, usability, and effects of implementation on medical decision-making, time to diagnosis, numbers of misclassified patients, and clinical outcomes.
3.In a set of translational research projects using metabolic and immunological phenotyping, we will additionally study the diagnostic and prognostic potential of promising new biomarkers involved in the mechanism of HIT.
4.We will use the clinical and laboratory data obtained to refine the TORADI-HIT ML algorithm and derive prognostic prediction models.
Infrastructure, project linkage, and partners
This project builds on an established infrastructure in terms of (a) an international study group effectively including patients with suspected HIT, (b) a specialized central laboratory with an extensive spectrum of laboratory techniques and biobanking solutions, and (c) an established team developing and implementing functional, machine-learning-based medical solutions. The feasibility of all sub-projects has been demonstrated in pilot studies. A team of key local stakeholders, well-recognized international researchers covering all methodological and infrastructural aspects, and an international study group (12 sites) have committed to collaborate in this project.
Expected results and impact
As one of the very first diagnostic ML algorithms implemented in clinical practice, TORADI-HIT will bridge an urgent implementation gap if successful. It can be used as a role model for the development and implementation of ML algorithms in various clinical settings.

Title: Applying Artificial Intelligence in Strategic Management
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), and in particular machine learning algorithms, is becoming increasingly important for variety of activities in strategic management, ranging from the analysis and prediction of market- and industry trends, via the automation of rapid decision making, to the assessment and selection of target organisations of strategic partnerships. Our prior theory and research has shed considerable light on AI in strategic decision making, assessment of algorithms for particular business problems, and the use of machine learning algorithms research methods within the field of strategic management. The current project aims at developing and appraising machine learning algorithms for the purpose of strategic decision making in organisations. The project has two subproject both aimed at the design and exploration of the behaviour of strategic algorithms.

Title: Learning on Distance Data with Applications in Cancer Research
Abstract:
Traditional machine learning methods usually depend on geometric
information of the data. However, frequently no access is given to the underlying vectorial representation of the data but only pairwise similarities or distances are measured.  Examples of data sets of this kind include all types of kernel matrices, be it string alignment kernels over DNA or protein sequences or diffusion kernels on graphs.
The main goal of the project is to develop new machine learning methods based on relational data that  do not require direct access to an underlying vector space. These new methods will then be applied to such data sets that have no obvious vector space representation. The application areas cover any data sets in form of pairwise distances. Since Mercer kernels can encode similarities between many different kinds of objects (for instance kernels on graphs, images, structures or strings) the methods proposed here will cover a broad scope of application. The main application area will be the analysis of cancer data provided by the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center.
Keywords: biomedical data analysis, clustering, computational biology, feature selection, machine learning, network inference, sparsity

Title: Computational Methods for modeling and analysis of large-scale metabolic networks
Abstract:
Metabolism is one of the most important and most complex cellular processes. Understanding metabolism is central to many problems in health, industrial biotechnology, agriculture and environmental biotechnology. Understanding of how we can manipulate these networks necessitates a systems approach that employs modeling and computational analysis. Engineering principles applied to metabolism permit the repair of metabolic dysfunction in disease, the identification of drug targets in pathogen metabolic networks, and the design of strategies in metabolic engineering for the production of biochemicals.
The advances in functional genomics, bioanalytical technologies and computational methods have led to the widespread use of mathematical modeling and computational analysis for the study of complex biological systems. The most important challenge in these approaches is the uncertainty due to missing information for most of the components in biological networks. The overarching objective of this proposal is the development of a computational workflow that integrates information across different knowledge levels, quantifies and reduces the uncertainty, and produces population of kinetic models of large- to genome-scale metabolic networks that are consistent with the observed physiology and fundamental biophysical laws. These models and the methods from the proposed research plan will enable the analysis and design of metabolic networks for addressing a broad class of problems associated with metabolism.

Title: On-demand Knowledge for Document-level Machine Translation (DOMAT)
Abstract:
Statistical and neural machine translation systems (in short, SMT and NMT) have reached significant quality and speed levels.  Such systems use large amounts of monolingual and bilingual data to train their models and tune their meta-parameters.  As a result, translating a sentence from a language unknown to a user can be done with acceptable quality, and hence a clearly perceived utility.  However, the translation of complete texts is still far from publishable, and requires substantial post-editing by humans.

One reason for this difference is that certain linguistic constraints cannot be reliably translated using only local information, especially when they apply across different sentences.  The homogeneous models used by SMT or NMT systems - very large translation tables or connection weights - are a strength for robust and quick sentence translation, but impose a strong limitation when constraints of different ranges must be taken into account to translate a document.

In recent years, I have pioneered a method to address document-level problems that degrade MT quality, drawing on specific linguistic knowledge as required by each problem.  These methods improved the translation of discourse connectives or verb tenses based on sentence-level or document-level semantic features, or constrained the choice of referring expressions such as pronouns and noun phrases.  For implementation, the methods took advantage of existing approaches, such as factored models, to integrate linguistic knowledge with SMT.  

However, integrating several solutions for dealing with document-level constraints into a unified system is not tractable with current approaches, due to the fact that knowledge sources are heterogeneous and are not tightly coupled with the MT systems.  Moreover, the quality improvements brought by leveraging several distinct knowledge sources may not add up because of interaction between them.  Finally, the need for computing all features for all words or sentences of a document raises strong efficiency issues.

In the DOMAT project, we aim to design a novel approach for providing on-demand linguistic knowledge to statistical or neural MT systems. Both types of systems will be considered to provide comparison terms, as they both have strengths and weaknesses.  The linguistic knowledge will be learned by specific processing modules, which will extract and output features in a format that is usable by SMT and NMT systems.  To make this architecture operational, we will explore strategies to trigger the modules, for instance based on quality estimation or translation confidence.  To populate the architecture, we will build several modules to extract document-level features that are relevant to translation, principally document structure (discourse relations) and coreference (including pronominal anaphora).  The starting points for these modules will be our previous achievements in document-level SMT.

The DOMAT project will mainly support two PhD theses at Idiap/EPFL, one on designing and comparing statistical and neural architectures for integrating  and triggering on-demand knowledge sources in MT, and the other one designing such knowledge sources, which learn specific text-level constraints and output suitable data structures for NMT.

The solutions developed in DOMAT will make tractable the demands for adequate, fluent and efficient translation of large documents, and will result in a principled approach for learning high-level linguistic knowledge to improve translation quality.

Title: Species distributions in neural landscapes
Abstract:
Accurately modelling species distributions is critical for biodiversity conservation, particularly in the face of climate change, as well as for fields such as land-use and land-cover management, agriculture, and ecological restoration. The correlation between the occurrence of a species and the environmental conditions at the sighting location has long been used to model species distributions. While models of this kind have improved through time, they remain incomplete due to their inability to account for biotic interactions and dispersal drivers explicitly, especially under future climate scenarios. Existing efforts to include biotic and dispersal factors have met limitations in data availability, complexity, and accuracy.
In this project, I propose a radically different approach based on a novel algorithm—the “Neural Landscape” (NL)—inspired by the Neural Cellular Automaton (NCA), a model previously used in embryological development. This innovative approach integrates biotic, abiotic, and dispersal processes in a self-regulatory framework, simulating how these drivers interact over time to form the geographical distribution of species. By applying reinforcement learning, the NL will be trained to learn how species coexist, interact and migrate in a shared landscapes, addressing the challenges posed by the fragmented approaches proposed so far.
The project aims to develop a proof of concept using both empirical and synthetic data. The NL will be tested for its ability to accurately simulate species distributions and its robustness when applied to the sparse, opportunistic data commonly used in today’s models. Importantly, the NL’s architecture could overcome the limitations of existing approaches by integrating complex ecological feedbacks while reducing data requirements. Such a model holds significant potential for predicting species distributions under changing climates and may serve as a transformative tool in biogeographical modeling.

Title: Combining machine learning techniques to efficiently determine the need for HCC screening among people with HIV and hepatitis B
Abstract:
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a common cause of morbidity and death in persons living with HIV and hepatitis B virus (HBV) worldwide [1]. Although tenofovir-based antiretroviral therapy, the standard of care for this population, reduces the risk of developing HCC[2, 3], this risk persists even for persons without liver cirrhosis[4]. Because curative HCC treatment is possible upon early detection by liver ultrasound[5], international guidelines recommend 6-monthly screening for persons with HIV and HBV [6]. While currently used hegemonic risk prediction tools successfully capture most HCC cases in this population, their low positive-predictive value constrains their ability to prevent over-screening associated with unnecessary patient concerns, potentially harmful follow-up evaluations and high costs [7]. Reliable and individualized risk assessment tools are required to inform health professionals and patients on the need to screen for HCC and the optimal time-point to start routine screening. In order to overcome shortcomings of currently used prediction tools and measurements, I propose a novel approach combining artificial intelligence techniques to determine the need of HCC screening. I will take advantage of the comprehensive characterisation of the European cohort of patients with HIV and HBV coinfection[4, 8] with a focus on capturing the causal/sequential nature of these longitudinal data. I will apply some of the most recent advances in artificial intelligence, which were conceived and advanced in fields like spoken word and human gesture recognition [9, 10]. This study will be the first to use a combination of machine learning algorithms to explore rich longitudinal data for the development of an HCC risk prediction tool based on clinical and biological events preceding the occurrence of HCC. The overarching goal of this proposal is to develop a machine learning based tool that transforms individual data in personalized probability distributions of time to very early stage HCC. 

AIM 1. To identify HCC-specific patterns in patients characteristics and longitudinal laboratory measurements (“multivariate trajectories”), and to characterise the temporal relationship of these patterns with very early stage HCC.I will do this by identifying patterns among multivariate trajectories of patients diagnosed with HCC. Not all of these patterns will be predictive of HCC development, yet crucial to establish coincidences and discrepancies with patients without HCC. We will then establish, by comparison with the overall population, which of these patterns are specific to people who developed an HCC. Title: Structure Exploiting Optimization Algorithms for Huge-Scale Applications
Abstract:
In the last decade, computational science has entered the age of Big Data, driven by the success of large-scale machine learning applications. These applications demand powerful and efficient algorithms that assist the mining task. Hence, development and theoretical understanding of such algorithms is a fundamental piece in this big puzzle.

The goal of this project is to develop efficient algorithms tailored for the mining and optimization of Big Data models. That is, for the extraction of high-level information and the subsequent identification of optimal decisions. We will only consider algorithms whose efficiency can theoretically be proven---providing such analysis for existing or novel approaches will be our main research task. As a second goal, we aim at deepening our understanding of the learning techniques, e.g. the tools used to exploit the structural information hidden in the data.
Keywords: Algorithms, Convex Optimization, Large Scale Optimization, Machine Learning, Matrix Recovery, Sparsity, Variable Metric

Title: High-precision hadronic contributions to the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon from first principles
Abstract:
The anomalous magnetic moment of the the muon (g-2) is one of the most precisely measured quantities in high-energy physics and therefore provides an ideal test of our theoretical understanding of particle physics at the precision frontier. The results from this most impressive experimental effort over the last two decades offer a unique opportunity to uncover potential new physics beyond the Standard Model (SM). Indeed, the most recent result indicates a discrepancy of about five standard deviations between experiment and the theoretical prediction. On the theoretical side, the interactions among all known elementary particles are described by the SM in terms of fundamental quantum fields. The purely leptonic contributions are determined very precisely by perturbative Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) and the electroweak interactions, while the remaining contributions from the strong sector of the SM are very difficult to determine accurately and currently constitute the dominating source of uncertainty in the theoretical determination. Therefore, corroborating or resolving the discrepancy requires the determination of the hadronic contributions  on the theoretical side to a level of accuracy which matches the experimental precision.

The strong interactions between quarks and gluons are described within the SM by a quantum field theory called Quantum chromodynamics (QCD). Due to the strong coupling, perturbative methods fail and a nonperturbative approach such as lattice QCD is required. In lattice QCD, the quantum field theory is discretized on a finite Euclidean space-time lattice and the partition function is evaluated using Monte Carlo simulation methods. Lattice QCD has seen tremendous progress over the last few years: due to developments on algorithms and computer architectures, simulations are possible directly at the physical point, where the mass values of all the relevant dynamical quarks are set to their physical values, while the lattice volume is kept sufficiently large and the lattice spacing sufficiently small, such that the corresponding systematic errors can be well controlled. Lattice techniques therefore allow nonperturbative calculations of phenomenologically relevant quantities from the underlying fundamental quantum field theory of QCD. Some of these computations have reached sub-percent accuracy which requires the inclusion of isospin-breaking (IB) corrections and electromagnetic (EM) effects from QED. The purpose of this proposal is to perform such nonperturbative lattice computations from first principles in order to determine the leading hadronic contributions to (g-2) to a precision comparable with experiment. Given the latest results from the Fermilab experiment for (g-2) and the conflicting results from CMD3, lattice-QCD computations currently seem to be the only possible way to resolve the discrepancy between theory and experiment.

The main focus of the proposal is therefore the calculation of the hadronic vacuum polarization (HVP) and the hadronic light-by-light (HLbL) contributions to (g-2). To reach the desired accuracy at the permille level it is necessary to include IB and EM corrections in the HVP contribution and perform simulations with dynamical up, down, strange and charm quarks. Within the Extended Twisted Mass Collaboration (ETMC) we have demonstrated the feasibility of these challenging calculations and prepared the ground over the last few years. Our recent results show that the origin of the tension between experiment and SM theory can be interpreted in terms of the fundamental branching ratio of electrons and positrons annihilating into hadrons at low energies. This so called R ratio can be computed within lattice QCD+QED and is another main focus of this proposal. The results can be directly compared to the corresponding experimental measurements, thereby either confirming the SM as the fundamental theory of elementary particles or uncovering new physics beyond it.

Title: Improving Interpretability. Philosophy of Science Perspectives on Machine Learning
Abstract:
These days, machine learning (ML) is all the rage, in science and beyond. ML is used to pre-process job applications, to automatically recognize faces in images or videos, and to classify astronomical objects - to name just a few examples. However, the ubiquitous use of ML also raises questions and concerns. One of the main problems is interpretability: We lack a theoretical understanding of ML models and, in particular of so-called deep neural networks (DNNs). For example, why are DNNs so successful in application? What, exactly, is it that they learn? What is the scope and limit of their success? Since we do not have answers to these questions, we do not understand how DNNs achieve their tasks - they remain black boxes, as it were. This is particularly a problem for science, which is supposed to explain and to help us understand phenomena in the world. Science cannot achieve these goals if its tools are black boxes. The problem has also been acknowledged in the political sphere: The EU's “General Data Protection Regulation” postulates a “right to explanation” for automated decision-making. But what does this right amount to? And how can it be granted to citizens?

In the present project, we will address the problem of interpretability from a philosophical perspective. Our main working hypothesis is that philosophical work on explanation and understanding can help us to make sense of interpretability and to assess approaches that promise a better understanding of ML models. We will thus draw on insights from philosophical research and transfer them to recent discussions about interpretability of ML. One key philosophical finding is that explanation comes in many varieties and defies a straightforward analysis in terms of necessary and sufficient conditions. This suggests that interpretability is not one thing, but rather comes in many different flavors. Our main aim thus is to establish a conceptual framework for thinking about interpretability. The framework will help researchers to avoid confusion, to become clear about the expectations that loom behind the right to explanation and to classify and evaluate existing research programs that propose a better understanding of ML. The conceptual framework will be established by combining a top-down approach with a bottom-up strategy. As far as the top-down direction is concerned, we will draw on distinctions from the philosophy of explanation. As far as the bottom-up direction is concerned, our work will be informed by recent work on ML from computer science. In several case studies, e.g. about Statistical Learning Theory, the so-called Information Bottleneck method and work on causal descriptions, we will try to fit these approaches into our framework. This will not only help us to test our framework and to improve it, but also lead to a better understanding of the approaches and their prospects. The framework will in particular distinguish between explanatory vs. non-explanatory questions about ML, between different levels of generality, and between the subjective vs. objective components of understanding. In a last step, we'll bring this work to bear on the ethics of algorithms. 

Of course, as philosophers, we cannot come up with new explanations of how ML works. But we can get clear about what people are after when they urge for interpretable ML, we can better understand how current approaches to interpretable software hang together, and we can trace the consequences that ML models have for our philosophical view of scientific research in the 21st century. Our aim is to do just this.
Keywords: Deep Neural Networks, Explanation, Interpretability, Machine Learning, Philosophy of Science, Understanding

Title: Beyond the ChatBot: Learning Programming via Novel User eXperience Interface with LLMs
Abstract:
This interdisciplinary project focuses on studying the User Experience (UX) of Large Language Models (LLM) for educational applications, specifically finding novel interactions for tools for first-year bachelor students without programming or computational thinking background. The use of LLMs presents new opportunities for teaching programming, emphasizing the need for ethical and effective utilization to enhance educational outcomes rather than circumvent them. Observations indicate a tendency among students to use such models for completing assignments without grasping the underlying concepts, a practice this project aims to correct by encouraging the use of LLMs as a learning resource to deepen understanding of programming through carefully designed UX.

The project initiates with organizing a workshop that bring together programming instructors and experts in digital learning pedagogy to address potential misuse and opportunities of LLMs in this context. The aim is to harness insights to design an user-friendly interface that facilitates meaningful interactions with LLMs within educational settings. This novel interface, rooted in HCI principles, aims to promote critical engagement with outputs provided by LLMs, integrating them effectively into the learning process while imposing task limitations to deter misuse. The tool's impact will be assessed in comparison to standard chatbot interactions, such as those with ChatGPT, allowing students the freedom to engage the chatbot as they see fit. Evaluation criteria will focus on the level of student engagement and their understanding of programming concepts, aiming to demonstrate the enhanced learning experience provided by the newly developed interaction.

Expected outcomes encompass insights into novice programmers' use and potential misuse of LLMs, the creation of an interaction that foster ethical use, and guidelines for educators on promoting responsible technology engagement. This project aims to marry the capabilities of LLMs with the needs of programming education, ensuring students achieve technical proficiency and a responsible approach to technology use. By focusing on UX in the development of LLM-based tools, the project addresses a critical gap in current programming education, proposing a interaction model for LLM integration that is innovative, user-centric, and educationally sound.

This approach not only seeks to transform programming education by leveraging cutting-edge LLMs but also places a strong emphasis on the ethical dimensions of technology use in educational settings. The project's commitment to an interdisciplinary strategy brings together expertise from computer science, HCI, and educational theory, aiming to forge a comprehensive learning experience that is at once advanced in its technological underpinnings and deeply rooted in pedagogical effectiveness.

By prioritizing the UX, this initiative stands at the forefront of educational innovation, charting a course for the future of programming education that is accessible, engaging, and responsive to diverse learner needs. The emphasis on ethical engagement with LLMs underscores a broader educational imperative to cultivate not just technically proficient, but also ethically aware, future technologists. This project thus represents a pivotal step towards realizing the full potential of LLMs in education, setting a precedent for the development of educational technologies that are as ethically considered as they are technologically sophisticated. Through its comprehensive analysis, development of targeted educational tools, and focus on responsible use, this project contributes valuable insights to the ongoing discourse on the role of LLMs in education, offering a blueprint for future initiatives at the intersection of technology and pedagogy.
Keywords: HCI, LLM, UI, UX, learning, programming

Title: Imaginaries of Artificial Intelligence: The Communicative Construction of AI in China, Germany and the US
Abstract:
BACKGROUND AND RATIONALE: Artificial intelligence (AI) is considered a key technology in contemporary societies, expected to substantially change sectors as diverse as health, warfare, mobility or communication. Consequently, political and economic stakeholders in many countries have allocated considerable resources to AI development, and the technology has been the object of extensive public debates. At the same time, observers and scholars have criticized these public debates for using the concept of AI vaguely and inconsistently, for over-hyping its promise, and for oscillating between naive hopes and dystopian fears. This is indicative of the fundamental interpretative flexibility of broad technologies such as AI: Their development and societal integration is contextual, shaped by political, economic and sociocultural interests, and subject to discursive negotiations in public arenas. These public debates are crucially important. Here, the “sociotechnical imaginaries”, i.e. the societal understandings of the possibilities, potentials and risks embedded in certain technologies, are socially constructed. These imaginaries play a large role in influencing how societies deal with emerging key technologies like AI. 

OBJECTIVES AND AIMS: The projects maps, explains and compares the public imaginaries of AI across countries and over time. It focuses on various stakeholders and different public fora which are indicative of societal views on AI and which play an important role in shaping these views. The analysis is guided by four research questions: 
1. How can sociotechnical imaginaries – for and beyond the case of AI – be understood conceptually and analyzed empirically? 
2. How do key stakeholders from politics, science, corporations and NGOs strategically try to shape prevalent imaginaries of AI, inserting their views into public debate, and which of them are successful in doing so? 
3. What are the dominant imaginaries of AI, their sponsors and implications present in various public arenas?
4. What are the similarities and differences between these public imaginaries of AI in different countries and over time? How do different stakeholders’ strategies to shape these imaginaries compare in different countries and over time? 

DATA AND METHODS: The project makes a conceptual and methodological contribution to the concept of sociotechnical imaginaries, which has gained prominence in scholarship over recent years, but remains underdetermined conceptually and hard to assess empirically. The project will propose a conceptual understanding of public imaginaries that foregrounds the public negotiation of imaginaries and proposes an empirical procedure that allows researchers to assess such imaginaries in large corpora of public communication.
Empirically, the project investigates public imaginaries of AI with a longitudinal and comparative research design. In the temporal dimension, it builds on a longitudinal design that addresses the approx. 10 formative years of AI development, from the 2010s until now. In the spatial dimension, it contrasts characteristics and developments in three countries which are key to the future global development of AI: the US, China and Germany. 
Methodologically, the project combines qualitative, quantitative and computational methods of social science. It uses qualitative expert interviews and document analyses to assess the content, production structures and strategies of different stakeholders trying to influence public imaginaries of AI, and automated and manual content analyses to reconstruct imaginaries of AI in news media, online communication and social media.

EXPECTED RESULTS AND IMPACT: The project provides a comprehensive comparative study on the construction of public imaginaries of AI in the crucial time frame of 2012 to 2021 and in key countries. It contributes to the growing scholarship on the societal uptake of AI and of key technologies more generally. It offers both lacking systematic empirical results as well as conceptual innovation, providing a conceptual understanding of the widely used yet under-defined concept of sociotechnical imaginaries. The project also contains outreach elements to interface with stakeholders of AI development, and provide them with the means to better assess and potentially regulate AI. Thus, we will not only unveil AI trajectories, but also help policy and technology-makers to adjust future trajactories. In sum, the project meets the strong demand for developing expertise both in understanding the unfolding development of AI and in shaping this development for the public benefit.
Keywords: artificial intelligence, news media, science communication, social media, sociotechnical imaginaries

Title: Fast but not furious: rapid Bayesian inference in balanced cortical circuits
Abstract: Sensory perception is fast in human, and nonetheless almost Bayes-optimal. I propose a theoretical approach to this puzzle in which circuit mechanisms for fast dynamics (which I have explored as part of my PhD thesis) will be related to the speed of perception, for wich the computational aspects will be cast in the framework of probabilistic Bayesian inference. The working hypothesis will be that the brain represents posterior uncertainty via sampling, for which the host laboratory has found experimental evidence recently. Title: State Estimation, Mapping, and Planning for Legged Robotics
Abstract:
This proposal seeks support for the fundamental research in perception and planning required to bring legged robots from artificial laboratory environments into real world applications. Legged robots present the possibility of automated systems that are capable of operating in any terrain and, while tremendous progress has been made over the last fifty years, most systems are still constrained to operate in controlled environments. The challenge to move to unknown and unstructured terrain poses fundamental research questions in the fields of hardware design, control development, pose estimation, terrain mapping, and motion planning. These topics are often considered separately but, for legged systems, they are tightly coupled and addressing them jointly is critical for safe and robust operation. State estimates and three-dimensional terrain maps must be accurate and available in real time to ensure the success of both reactive control and deliberative foot placement. Haptic feedback resulting from the comparison of planned trajectories to state estimates must be incorporated back into the map and the planning to ensure robust operation over a wide variety of terrain.

The primary focus of this project is to jointly develop pose estimation, terrain mapping, and motion planning algorithms that form the basis for the operation of legged robotic devices in challenging unknown three-dimensional terrain. In contrast to wheeled or flying vehicles, legged locomotion itself is already a highly complex task and it took nearly fifty years of research until the hardware and control techniques 
have now reached the point to allow legged machines to perform useful tasks. As a result, the high complexity and the lack of adequate hardware platforms forced researchers to artificially decouple the research problem, considering design, control, perception, and planning 
separately. While single elements have been approached by several instances, previous work has so far not been able to tackle the problem in its entirety. This project is a natural extension of our previously funded work developing state of the art legged robotic systems and control tools. Like the few comparable robotic platforms, we have so far concentrated on developing a robust and highly reactive platform that can cope with substantial obstacles and external disturbances while blindly walking or running. Consequently, we have access to a state-of-the-art legged platform and control algorithms, and we can ensure that the research undertaken within this project meshes seamlessly with existing research.

We will draw upon the existing state of the art in perception and planning research from across the spectrum of robotic applications. However, extending the existing research to legged systems raises some unique and fundamental questions. First, state estimation needs to be very fast and precise with respect to the local ground as this is critical to maintain balance an to propel the robot forward. Second, mapping must be conducted with a much higher information density than required for wheeled or flying vehicles, as small-scale geometry is essential to distinguish between good and bad footholds. Third, motion planning must consider the stochastic aspect of the different systems and the environment map in order to attain truly robust locomotion needed to adroitly traverse challenging ground.

The outcomes of this project will be measured with standard tools from each subdiscipline (e.g. comparison with ground truth, planning optimality, runtime, etc.) but, as our focus is to show the benefits of jointly considering these problems for legged locomotion, we will also perform field testing with our quadrupedal robot in outdoor, unstructured terrain. This ensures that our research is rigorously evaluated in a real-world scenario, and that all algorithms operate together to solve the problem is real time.


The successful completion of this project will not only directly contribute to advancing the state of the art in for legged robots, it will also further the expertise at the ETH that can impact the growing Swiss robotics industry. 
The research developed here should be widely applicable for legged and other robots performing search and rescue, autonomous cleaning, and industrial inspection - anywhere a robotic system must operate autonomously in contact with complex three-dimensional terrain.
Keywords: Filter Design, Legged Robotics, Mapping, Optimization, Planning, Rescue Robotics, State Estimation

Title: INsIDER: ImagiNg the Interplay between Axonal DamagE and Repair in Multiple Sclerosis
Abstract:
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic disease of the central nervous system (CNS), which affects ~ 2.3 million people worldwide and is associated with substantial economic burden on MS patients, their families and the entire society. 
Despite significant progress in MS diagnosis and treatment, there remains the need to understand what drives this disease and its clinical progression. Specifically, it is essential to define the interplay between axonal damage - encompassing axonal demyelination, degeneration, loss and disorganization - and axonal repair – namely axonal remyelination and reorganization, which ultimately influence MS evolution and the accrual of disability.
Clinical MS categories are quite heterogeneous. Nevertheless, pathology studies have identified some characteristic traits in early-stage patients with active MS (aMS) and in non-active progressive MS patients (naPMS). Early-stage aMS patients - who are subjects with clinical and/or radiological signs of on-going inflammation - exhibit neuropathological signs of substantial acute axonal damage and significant remyelination. On the other end, naPMS patients - who are subjects with clinical deterioration and no clinical or radiological evidence of disease activity - show less acute axonal damage and remyelination but extensive axonal loss. These characteristic neuropathologic traits of aMS and naPMS patients have not yet been demonstrated in living MS patients. 
The in vivo quantification of axonal damage and repair in MS patients is essential (i) to gain knowledge on MS pathogenesis and its clinical progression as well as (ii) to understand and quantify the effects of current and future neuroprotective and regenerative therapies. 
To this end, INsIDER will combine advanced MRI techniques sensitive to axonal structure and organization to gain new insights into axonal damage and repair in MS.  In fact, MRI metrics derived from models based on diffusion MRI, Magnetization Transfer Imaging, Quantitative Susceptibility Mapping, Myelin Imaging and T1 relaxometry provide complementary and partially redundant information about the axonal structure and axonal organization. Therefore, their combination may increase the sensitivity and specificity to axonal pathology and axonal changes over time.
Through classical and modern machine-learning analysis of multiple advanced MRI data combined with demographic and genetic information, INsIDER will quantify in vivo the differences between aMS and non-active progressive MS (naPMS) patients. Furthermore, INsIDER will validate the most discriminative imaging metrics between aMS and naPMS patients with post-mortem measures of axonal damage and remyelination.  
The specific aims for this proposal are:  
Aim 1. Quantify differences in axonal integrity and organization in aMS vs naPMS patients. 
Aim 2. Quantify changes in axonal integrity and organization in aMS vs naPMS patients over a two-year period. 
Aim 3. Validate the combination of imaging parameters that best differentiate aMS vs naPMS patients using histopathology.
INsIDER will provide new knowledge about the contribution of axonal damage and repair to MS progression and will allow to develop novel surrogate biomarkers to assess disease evolution and future neuroprotective and regenerative treatments.
Keywords: Advanced MRI, Axonal damage, Axonal repair, Disease progression, Multiple Sclerosis

Title: Multiparametric Engineering of Asparaginase by Enzyme Proximity Sequencing
Abstract:
Enzyme engineering is a rapidly evolving field, with applications spanning from industrial biotechnology to human therapies. This field involves mutating a parent (i.e. wild-type) enzyme sequence at the DNA level to generate variants, followed by expression and screening/selecting variants to identify novel sequences exhibiting a phenotype of interest. One major challenge in this field arises when trying to optimize enzymes along multiple fitness axes, such as improving catalytic efficiency, stability, and substrate specificity in a single campaign. Due to the high sequence and structural complexity of enzymes, improvements in one parameter usually come at the cost of another. As such, the solution space to multiparametric enzyme optimization problems is believed to exist on a Pareto frontier of equally good solutions that balance many competing factors. 
While the Pareto frontier is a useful concept, it is not known if these tradeoffs are fundamental to enzyme engineering, or a result of the current limitations in our ability to explore and navigate enzyme sequence space efficiently. If we had access to more comprehensive experimental methods for searching sequence space, along with more advanced computational tools, could it be possible to find enzyme variants that improve across multiple fitness axes simultaneously? This project seeks to advance these science and technology goals in the areas of high-throughput enzyme screening and deep learning to accelerate exploration of vast sequence-function landscapes. Specifically, our project aims to address these questions by applying a multiparametric optimization approach to Asparaginase (ASNase), an enzyme of critical importance for cancer therapy. 

Our novel screening method is called enzyme proximity sequencing (EP-Seq), and relies on localized enzyme-triggered radical labeling of yeast cells to generate an artificial phenotype corresponding to enzyme activity. With EP-Seq, we can screen variant libraries of catalytic enzymes using a one-pot reaction followed by fluorescence activated cell sorting (FACS) and next-generation DNA sequencing. Our goal is to utilize the ultrahigh throughput nature of this screening system to analyze sequence-function landscapes of ASNase on a large scale. 

Ultimately, this research could transform how we think about enzyme optimization and provide new tools that enhance our ability to explore enzyme sequence space efficiently, shifting the paradigm from empirical and random trial-and-error to data-driven streamlined and efficient design of novel enzyme therapies.
Keywords: Asparaginase, Bioengineering, Biotechnology, Cancer therapy, Enzyme catalysis, Enzymes, High-throughput screening, Protein engineering

Title: ULTRA: Ubiquitous Large InTelligent ArRAys
Abstract:
Background and rationale:
The massive amount of available bandwidth at millimeter-wave (mmWave) and terahertz (THz) frequencies is gaining increasing interest for next-generation communication and sensing systems. At those frequencies, multi-antenna transceiver (TRX) arrays are key in overcoming the high path loss and boosting the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Unlike single-antenna TRX, designing large multi-antenna TRX arrays entails multiple significant challenges, and existing arrays mostly rely on look-up-tables (LUTs) and off-line compensation. Such static solutions, however, can neither capture all possible operation modes nor provide real-time adaptivity to the propagation conditions and communication/sensing tasks. 

Overall objectives and specific aims:
The ULTRA (short for Ubiquitous Large inTelligent arRAys) project aims at addressing these large-array design challenges with a holistic approach that jointly considers mmWave electronics, antenna arrays, digital baseband processing, and beamforming algorithms. The main objective is to design large and scalable TRX array architectures at D-band 140GHz with intelligent and adaptive in-field beamforming and calibration. The planned research leverages the complementary expertise of PI Wang (ETHZ) and PI Niknejad (UC Berkeley) on mmWave reconfigurable energy-efficient frontends and large arrays and PI Studer (ETHZ) on digital baseband processing and blind estimation. The project ULTRA will utilize the existing wireless electronics research infrastructure at the IIS institute of ETH Zurich in Switzerland and BWRC center at UC Berkeley in USA. We will pursue the following work packages. 

Methods to be used:
• WP-1: Analytical and Behavior Modeling of Non-idealities in Large Scalable Arrays. 
• WP-2: Designing Reconfigurable D-Band Frontends as Performance Tuning “Knobs”. 
• WP-3: Designing Non-Intrusive D-Band Frontends Performance “Sensors”. 
• WP-4: Blind Array Calibration and Beamforming Algorithms based on novel signal processing and machine learning algorithms.  
• WP-5: ULTRA 140GHz Array System Integration and Demonstration.

Expected results and their impact:
The project ULTRA will result in novel intelligent large-scale multi-antenna array architectures with highly reconfigurable D-band frontends and adaptive array calibration/beamforming, which do not exist today. The research will directly impact applications in beyond-5G and 6G communication, sub-mmWave radar, and next-generation satellite/intersatellite links. For results dissemination, we will provide open access to the research results of the project ULTRA.

Title: Mechanisms of hepatic immuno-sensing and their role in development of non-alcoholic steatohepatitis
Abstract:
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is one of the most prevalent complications of obesity. NAFLD is a spectrum of clinical entities ranging from simple steatosis to cirrhosis. Whereas many patients only suffer from accumulation of fat in hepatocytes, a considerable number of people progresses to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). NASH is characterized by a dramatic increase of inflammatory cells in liver and the development of fibrosis, which may ultimately cause cirrhosis and liver failure. Recent estimates indicate that more than 25% of the global adult population has NAFLD and this disease is rapidly becoming the most common cause for liver transplantation worldwide. Despite its major impact on society, drugs that directly target NAFLD are currently lacking. In particular the signal that initiates inflammation in some patients with NAFLD and causes their progression to NASH presents a promising target. The overall objective of this project is to elucidate the early inflammatory processes in NAFLD that lead to steatohepatitis and fibrosis. We will accomplish this through the collaboration between a strong immuno-metabolic research group in Croatia and a research group in Switzerland that is world-leading on the area of high-dimensional immuno-phenotyping.

NAFLD can be divided in several stages. Initially, an increase of free fatty acids in circulation of obese individuals promotes their uptake in the liver and storage into triglycerides. Accumulation of fat in hepatocytes causes lipid droplet formation (steatosis), hepatocyte ballooning and formation of Mallory bodies. At an unknown point during development of steatosis a hepatic stress response is induced which activates tissue-resident immune cells and recruits leukocytes from the periphery. The ensuing inflammation is associated with hepatocyte cell death and activation of hepatic stellate cells (HSC), which mediate formation of connective tissue. Over time, loss of hepatocytes and accumulation of fibrotic lesions culminates in cirrhosis and liver failure. 
Clearly, a crucial step in the development of NASH is the signaling of metabolic stress from hepatocytes to the immune system and its amplification into an inflammatory response. Very little is known about these events, due to limitations of clinical and preclinical studies. In humans early inflammatory processes in the liver can only be identified with a biopsy. Due to the invasive nature of this procedure and potentially severe complications biopsies are typically only done in late stage NAFLD, when the inflammatory response is already established. Mouse models of NAFLD have so far been a poor pathophysiological representation of human disease. Whereas liver fibrosis is usually established in these models, they do not display signs of metabolic disease and their relevance for the early stages of human disease is therefore questionable. Clearly, there is much to be gained in the understanding of NAFLD by implementing better models of disease in combination with advanced analysis methods. 

At the Medical Faculty in Rijeka (Medri), we have developed a new dietary (SSD) model for NAFLD/NASH. Our preliminary data indicates that the SSD-model induces metabolic disease and initiates a Th17-type inflammatory milieu in the liver resulting in fibrosis. Moreover, our model recapitulates all stages of human NAFLD. Medri has much experience in the field of stress-detection by innate lymphocytes and their role in the initiation of an immune response. In this project, Medri will focus on communication between metabolically stressed hepatocytes and the innate immune system. Our preliminary data points towards a prominent role for IL-17 producing ?d T cells. UZH has been a world-leading research group on Th17-type immune responses and their role in the activation of phagocytes in various auto-inflammatory diseases. More recently, we have done pioneering work on the area of high-dimensional immune phenotyping of myeloid cells. In this project, the UZH will characterize phagocytes in the context of NASH. The collaboration between these two groups thus covers the whole spectrum of early inflammatory processes in NAFLD leading to steatohepatitis and fibrosis.

This project is segregated in three aims. In the first aim, we will identify the hepatic, metabolic stress signals that activate the immune system and identify the innate cells that respond to these cues, with a focus on ?d T cells. Hepatocytes and immune cells will be isolated from steatotic lesions of SSD-mice and analyzed by whole transcriptome RNA-sequencing. Potential candidates for stress-communication will be investigated in in vitro models for leukocyte-hepatocyte interactions. After confirmation of their biological relevance in vitro, we will implement genetic models using mice with cell-specific deficiencies for stress ligands or their receptors. With these models we can disrupt hepatocyte-immune cell interactions in vivo, both in liver cells and in leukocytes. Animals subjected to the SSD model will be analyzed for immunological and clinical parameters, such as liver enzymes in the blood and fibrosis in the liver. Thus, we will demonstrate how the liver communicates metabolic stress and to what immune cells.
In the second aim, we will characterize the response of phagocytes in the context of fatty liver disease. Innate immune cells such as ?d T cells are the first ones to respond to tissue stress, but are generally insufficient to eliminate threats by themselves. Instead, they recruit and activate specialized effector cells such as phagocytes. These cells are efficient at fighting infection, but are also the most destructive in auto-inflammatory diseases such as NASH and are responsible for activation of HSCs. Activated phagocytes represent a spectrum of phenotypic and functional aspects associated with specific events in their local microenvironment. In order to get a comprehensive picture of phagocyte responses, we will apply high-dimensional analysis by CyTOF and FACSymphony. Machine-learning algorithms will be implemented to cluster information-dense datasets into comprehensive biological outcomes. This will generate a picture of the inflammatory processes in the context of NAFLD at an unprecedented resolution and will provide valuable clues into its underlying pathophysiology. 
In the third aim, we will convolute these research lines to elucidate the communication between activated stress sensors of the innate immune system and myeloid effector cells. Our high-throughput datasets will be analyzed to reveal the communication media between innate cells and phagocytes. Using mice with cell specific deficiencies we will confirm which receptor-ligand pairs are involved in mediating liver pathology in the SSD model. Finally, using in vitro and in vivo models, we will identify how the hepatocyte-?d T cell-phagocyte axis results in activation of the HSCs that mediate fibrosis. 

This research collaboration fulfills all goals of the CSRP. It brings together two top level research groups to investigate a pressing issue of both social and scientific importance. The main impact of this project will therefore be identification of new targets for the treatment of NAFLD/NASH. This project builds on the strengths of both groups and generates synergy between them to ascend the level that could be achieved individually. Moreover, it gives the Croatian team access to a level of state-of-the-art research methods that are not available in Croatia. Thus, this project provides a unique opportunity for young Croatian scientists to obtain knowhow on the latest technological advances in the field of immunology. Finally, this project operates in a field about which little is currently known and therefore provides ample opportunity for continued collaboration between the two groups. We therefore believe that this grant is a solid investment in Swiss-Croatian collaboration and friendship.

Title: Analysis and modelling of the mountain permafrost distribution using machine learning
Abstract:
In the European Alps, the significant rise in temperatures and changes in precipitations within the 21st century will lead to deep modifications of the cryosphere components. Because of its strong dependence on climatic conditions, permafrost is certainly one of the most sensitive subsurface materials to climate variations. Both rock walls and sedimentary deposits, such as talus slopes, moraines and rock glaciers, may be affected by this phenomenon and its degradation (manifested by a thickening of the active layer and a warming of the permafrost body) can have various effects on mountain slope stability, such as increasing rock fall activity or rock glacier speed up. It follows that, locally, the torrential dynamics could change over the coming decades because of an increase of the sediment transfer rates.
A deep knowledge of the permafrost distribution at different scales, including the micro scale, has consequently a fundamental importance. Up to now, the different existing spatial models have not been able to simulate the high spatial discontinuity of mountain permafrost and to produce high resolution maps, especially in blocky loose sediments where the ground thermal regime may be strongly affected by air advection processes. An intelligent spatial data analysis and modelling by using data-driven methods (machine learning) can overcome these problems. The key feature of the machine learning (ML) models is that they learn from data and can be used in cases where the modelled phenomenon is hidden, non-evident, not very well described or subject to multidimensionality, namely dependent on multiple factors which can vary if the distribution itself is characterized by a multi-scale component. Therefore, functional dependencies are derived directly from data with a statistical approach and there is any need to appeal to physical models.
The main objectives of this research proposal deal with the data analysis of mountain permafrost patterns at different scales, with the development of a cutting-edge methodology based on ML techniques, spatial statistics and geomatics (GIS, remote sensing). For this study, the most efficient algorithms belonging to the family of kernel based methods for environmental data analysis, modelling and visualisation - Support Vector Machines (SVM), Adaptive Probabilistic Neural Network (AdPNN), Adaptive General Regression Neural Network (AdGRNN), Multiple Kernel Learning (MKL) and Random Forests (RF) - will be used to solve classification problems along with the characterization of corresponding uncertainties. Field investigations carried out in Switzerland provide detailed empirical knowledge on the distribution and characteristics of permafrost in sedimentary terrains. Without any a priori user assumption concerning the relationship between permafrost and its explaining variables and auxiliary information, i.e. topographic and climatic features or geological and geophysical knowledge, ML algorithms will be able to detect spatial patterns in data and to understand their spatial proprieties. The final modelling task will be completed by spatial predictions (classification and mapping) and the validation of the results by comparisons between the produced maps with newly collected permafrost evidences. 
The results of this multidisciplinary study should improve understanding of spatial permafrost data and of the discontinuous distribution of this phenomenon using recent achievements in ML. The most relevant results will be published in scientific journals and presented at forthcoming international conferences and workshops.
Keywords: Environmental modelling, Machine learning, Mountain permafrost mapping, Spatial data mining

Title: Data-driven control approaches for advanced legged locomotion
Abstract:
Complicated multi-body systems, such as legged robots, impose grand challenges in a control perspective. They are high-dimensional, non-smooth and naturally unstable systems that conventional theories in control do not apply. Until today, we can identify two conceptually different methods how the research community tackles this problem, namely template-based and optimization-based controllers. Methods of the former type use simplified descriptions of the complex behavior (i.e. template) as a mean for prediction of the most important dynamics. Very prominent for locomotion are inverted pendulum templates that are used to find the optimal stepping location when moving forward. Using templates has the advantage that the control problem can be solved onboard and in real time. On the other hand, as they only approximate the dynamics, these methods fail if it comes to very dynamic manoeuvers or challenging grounds. The latter method, on the other hand, uses optimization tools together with a physics simulator to find the optimal actuator commands for complete manoeuvers. Unfortunately, even the most advanced algorithms are far away from running in real time. What we need is to have both the real-time capability of the template-based approaches and high performance of the trajectory optimization-based approaches.
Over the past years, we have seen tremendous achievements of data-driven approaches such as deep learning applied to problems like image classification. Despite great results, so far very little (published) research has been done to apply these powerful tools to control of robotic systems. The goal of this project is to fill this missing gap and to develop data-driven control algorithms that ultimately have the potential to enable high-dynamic legged locomotion in challenging environments. We will investigate guided policy search approaches for legged robotic systems with massive parallel trajectory optimizations followed by a deep learning-based policy construction respectively data compression. Thereby we build upon our successfully tested whole-body control and simulation-based parameter optimization tools. For efficient data processing, we exploit the fact that we have enough computation power off-board thanks to GPU computing and large-scale computer clusters. 
Deep learning has been outperforming other approaches due to the abundance of training data and its ability to make a full use of the high dimensional input. Based on this method, our approach foresees to generate enormous amount of high quality training data using accurate simulations to efficiently build high dimensional policies. This will allow us to generate a compact form of trained policies (e.g. neural network) that is light enough to be stored in the onboard computer of the robot and evaluated in the same time required by template-based controllers.
The outcomes of this project and performance of developed controllers will be thoroughly evaluated with real robots that are already available or under development. These robots feature high performance actuation including precise torque control that particularly enables highly dynamic maneuvers.
Keywords: High-dynamic manoeuvers, Learning, Legged Locomotion
