Title: Theoretical conceptualization of terahertz neuromorphic architectures based on antiferromagnetic spintronic devices
Abstract:
AI's rapid development revolutionizes various domains, from cancer treatment to natural language processing. Progress in computing hardware and software, inspired by biological neural networks, drives these advancements. Low-power, highly parallelizable GPUs and labeled data enable training and deployment of artificial neural networks (ANNs). However, ANNs primarily run on traditional von Neumann hardware, causing energy consumption and processing speed challenges. One solution is implementing ANNs on nonlinear physical systems like optics, acoustics, and spintronics devices. Among these, spintronic nano-devices are promising for on-chip neuromorphic computing due to their small size, fast and nonlinear dynamics, CMOS compatibility, nonvolatility, and virtually unlimited endurance. Over the past few years, there have been successful developments of spintronic neuromorphic devices utilizing ferromagnetic materials (FM). Recent advancements highlight the advantages of antiferromagnetic (AFM) systems over ferromagnetic (FM) ones, including absence of stray fields, operation at terahertz frequency, high spin wave velocities, and abundance in nature. Research on AFM-based neuromorphic devices focuses on demonstrating picosecond-duration spiking neurons using AFM topological charges (AFM-TCs) and spin-Hall nano-oscillators (AFM-SHNOs). However, not only these neurons are not put into test to perform a cognitive task in a network, but also the physical realization of spiking neural networks (SNNs) are challenging due to the large number of connections and backpropagation (BP) required. Alternatively, directly training the hardware's physical transformations to perform the desired computations in deep Physical Neural Networks (PNNs) offer the potential to create more scalable, energy-efficient, and faster neural network hardware. The goal of this research proposal is to theoretically conceptualize AFM-based THz PNNs architectures, which are experimentally implementable. To this end I will employ a novel learning algorithm, called the model-free forward-forward (MF-FF) training, which enables direct training of wave-based PNNs locally and circumvents all challenges associated with the hardware-realization of BP. This method is already demonstrated to outperform state-of-the-art hardware-aware training methods in acoustics, microwave and optical implementation. 
I will perform the required micromagnetic and magnetotransport simulations by recently developed multi-physics magnetization dynamics and spin transport simulations package called “Boris Computational Spintronics” (hereafter, “Boris” for short). I will investigate the performance of two different device architectures based on AFM-TCs and AFM-SHNOs to perform the vowel and MNIST handwritten digit classification tasks. The proposed devices can be categorized as the first trainable THz deep reservoir computing implementation. The simplicity of the proposed device layout makes it experimentally implementable and is expected to receive large attention from experimentalists. They offer a pathway to significantly enhance the energy efficiency and speed of deep learning not only during inference but also during the training phase. The research will be carried out at Tserkovnyak Group under supervision of Prof. Yaroslav Tserkovnyak at UCLA who is one of the world leaders in theoretical antiferromagnetic spintronics.
Keywords: Antiferromagnetic Spintronics, Deep Physical Neural Networks, Neuromorphic Computing, Terahertz Magnonics

Title: Random matrix universality in data science and theoretical physics
Abstract:
Random matrix theory has seen tremendous progress in the last decade. The resolution of the Wigner-Dyson-Mehta (WDM) conjecture has triggered a program of universality, and a comprehensive theory of increasingly general random matrix models started to emerge. At the same time random matrices have been used successfully to shed light on various problems in physics, computer science and beyond.

However, there is an increasing disconnect between the comprehensive theory and the applications which have remained largely limited to the simplest matrix models. This project will remedy this disconnect and will build a more "user-friendly" theory of random matrices with concrete applications from physics and computer science in mind. As such the project targets both foundational and applied problem areas.

On the foundational side, we focus on three aspects: First, we will prove the universality of spectral statistics of non-Hermitian random matrices on the mesoscopic and microscopic scale. Second, we will study the universality of Hermitian random matrices with strong correlations. Third, we will prove quantum unique ergodicity for mean field random matrix models on all intermediate scales. 

On the applied side we select four problems for which the existing random matrix theory does not suffice due to either sparsity or correlations. First, we will investigate the sparse Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model and prove the emergence of random matrix statistics in a model routinely used in physics. Second and third, we will study specific Gaussian random matrices with strong correlations related to the complexity of random functions and the Peterson-Thom conjecture from functional analysis. Fourth, we will rigorously investigate the generalisation performance of one-layer neural networks by analysing the correlations imposed by gradient descent. 

The impact of the project will be an application-driven development of foundational random matrix theory, as well novel insights into four concrete and relevant applied problems. The main strength of the proposed project is that the foundational and applied side do not merely run in parallel, but are synergistically intertwined.
Keywords: Data science, Probability, Random matrix theory, Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model, Universality

Title: Intrinsically and extrinsically driven learning of birdsong
Abstract:
This project deals with the vocal template, an auditory memory that vocal learners acquire early in life. Vocal templates are essential in both children and songbirds, they shape the gradually emerging speech and songs during development. However, the template is an intrinsic concept and has remained hard to characterize in experiments because of the large time span between its acquisition and its behavioral expression. Our project will advance our understanding of the formation and use of vocal templates on both computational and neurobiological levels and will elucidate their interplay with extrinsic driving forces of the vocal learning process. 
On a very basic level, it remains unknown how a template is computed from the sounds a juvenile hears, i.e., whether it is extracted as a particular instance of a heard song, or whether it is formed by a composition of multiple songs (which would constitute a mechanism to create truly novel songs). Current evidence points to the template as an instance memory, but explicit tests for existence of compositional templates have never been done. We expose single juvenile birds to two different auditory stimuli presented either in series or conjunctively. By carefully varying the relationship between the two stimuli, we characterize the mathematical operation that governs template formation and reveal the extent to which it is an instance or a composition. 
To gain insights into external influences such as social context (e.g. provided by parents and siblings) on the template-based learning process, we will perform longitudinal observations of juvenile birds while they grow up in midst of a group. We will make use of a unique recording setup that provides us with simultaneous individual-level read outs of vocal and non-vocal behaviors. In these experiments, we will describe the song-learning trajectories and test hypothesized roles of calls and their interactions in mediating a vocal competition in acoustic feature space. 
Our insights will feed into a reinforcement-learning (RL) model that mechanistically describes the vocal learning process. Learning in the model is driven by minimization of a reward prediction error that we assume is signaled by dopaminergic neuros. Dopaminergic neurons play essential roles in acquisition of a template and in modifying song acoustic features such as pitch, but their activity has never been measured during song learning, which is a gap we plan to fill. In a collaborative effort, we will probe for the hypothesized dopaminergic representation of both intrinsic (template) and extrinsic (social interactions) reward prediction errors. The contributions of this project are to advance our understanding of an important neuromodulatory system and its roles during intrinsically (template-based) and extrinsically (social-interaction based) motivated behaviors.
Keywords: Behavior, Communication, Learning, Vocalization

Title: Deep artificial neural network approximations for stochastic partial differential equations: Algorithms and convergence proofs
Abstract:
High-dimensional stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs) arise in many different contexts and are a key ingredient of mathematical models for numerous problems from natural sciences and financial engineering. For instance, high-dimensional SPDEs frequently appear in nonlinear filtering problems in the form of the Zakai equation and the Kushner equation, where the solution of the SPDE describes the conditional probability density of the state space of the considered physical system. High-dimensional SPDEs also play an important role in problems from financial engineering, where the number of dimensions often corresponds to the number of underlying assets of the particular financial derivative in question. Further applications of typically high-dimensional SPDEs include, for example, weather forecasting and modelling of chemical reactions. In these applications the dimensionality of the corresponding SPDE can range from three to many hundreds or thousands or even millions of dimensions.

SPDEs and especially high-dimensional SPDEs can in almost all cases not be solved exactly and large research efforts have been invested in solving SPDEs numerically. However, high-dimensional SPDEs are normally extremely difficult to be solved numerically since existing numerical methods usually suffer under the curse of dimensionality in the sense that the number of operations required for computing the numerical approximation grows exponentially in the number of dimensions. With such methods it is completely hopeless to numerically solve the SPDEs appearing in the above mentioned applications.

A key objective of this research project is to design and analyse a numerical approximation method for solving possibly high-dimensional SPDEs which does overcome the curse of dimensionality. More precisely, the fundamental contribution of this research project will not only be to introduce such a novel method but also to rigorously prove that the new algorithm is indeed able to overcome the curse of dimensionality. Thereby, for the first time we reveal that it is indeed possible to solve high-dimensional SPDEs numerically without the curse of dimensionality. The method appears to be relevant for applications employing high-dimensional SPDEs, such as nonlinear filtering, by allowing overly simplified linearised models to be replaced by more realistic nonlinear models yielding much more accurate predictions.
Keywords: Kushner equation, SPDEs, Zakai equation, artificial neural networks, convergence, curse of dimensionality, deep learning, neural networks, nonlinear filtering, stochastic partial differential equations

Abstract: The goal of this proposal is to prolong our previous grant "Theory and Practice of Reinforcement Learning (RL) & Search". The work funded by this extraordinarily successful project so far led to over 40 publications, some of which won best paper awards. RL is closely related to how animals and humans act  and learn. Without a teacher, solely from occasional real-valued pain and pleasure signals, RL agents must discover how to interact with a dynamic environment to maximize thei future expected reward. The classical approach to RL makes unrealistic strong assumptions such as: the current input of the agent tells it all needs to know about the environment. Our more general methods learn to create memories of important events, solving numerous RL/optimization tasks unsolvable by classical RL methods. Project subgoals include: (1) further improve our state-of-the-art policy gradient techniques and Natural Stochastic Search Strategies, (2) improve adaptive memory-based controllers on RL problems involving high-dimensional state descriptions (HDSD), (3) develop multi-modular  RL methods, (4) combine unsupervised sequence encoders for dimensionality  reduction with RL, (5) use vision-based RL benchmarks to test our methods, (6) devise theoretically optimal ways of maximizing information gain of exploring RL agents exploring their environment.
Keywords: Reinforcement Learning, benchmarks., information gain, multi-modular RL, natural stochastic search strategies, optimal, policy gradients, unsupervised sequence encoders

Title: The Canon of Latent Spaces: How Large AI Models Encode Art and Culture
Keywords: artificial intelligence, cultural studies, digital art history, digital humanities, explainability, multimodality, text-to-image synthesis

images of our written ideas and thoughts in just a few seconds. multimodal ai text to image models have recently become extraordinarily successful in creating realistic and convincing images from from generating illustrations for children’s books to upholding fake news with convincing images of events that never happened the range of potential applications is wide and manifold. but so are the various cultural, societal, ethical and political impacts of these technologies. these models are expected to have a strong impact on creative and media industries. therefore it becomes urgently necessary to understand how and why certain sentences are transformed to specific images and what are the potential implications of the data relations encoded within those models. why does a rainbow Title: Neurofeedback for improvement of coordinated motor function
Abstract:
Operant conditioning, in the form of neurofeedback, consists of measuring one’s own brain activity in an attempt to gain conscious control over a desired set of neurons.  Through repeated activation, neuroplastic changes in brain function follow. Evidence has shown that when successfully learned, neurofeedback can lead to positive changes in behavior. Neurofeedback using functional magnetic resonance imaging, (fMRI), known as real-time fMRI (rtfMRI), has shown potential in inducing local changes in neural activity of cortical and subcortical areas. This method involves measurement of blood oxygenation level dependent (BOLD) signals from a predefined region of interest during a specific task, followed by presentation of this activity to the subject, typically with a delay of a few seconds. While many studies have reported some level of success with this method, it is not clear if coordinated behavior can be improved, what neural mechanisms underlie these behavioral changes, and whether the features of the feedback have a crucial role in learning. Thus our proposal has the three following goals:

1.Behavioral consequences of self-regulation of BOLD signal in motor cortex Previous studies have identified improvements in finger tapping based on self-regulation of motor cortical areas through motor imagery using rtfMRI.  While behavioral outcomes such as finger tapping are a necessary first step in determining the usefulness of neurofeedback, it is not representative of a coordinated task relevant for eventual clinical use.  We would like to investigate whether self-regulation of motor cortex, through motor imagery, results in faster and more accurate force control in a coordinated visuomotor task as measured before and after neurofeedback training.  

2.Visual feedback information In many rtfMRI applications feedback has been presented to the subject by various modalities, including timecourse of the signal and instantaneous value. In this project, we will compare the effect of three conditions: no visual feedback, one with information only regarding current activation, one with both current activation and history.  Thus, we will investigate how the amount of information provided affects performance in a precision grip task, and expect information regarding previous performance to enhance ability to self-regulate motor cortex BOLD signal.

3.Neural mechanisms and connectivity assessment Current studies in rtfMRI have shown local increases of BOLD signal in a desired region of interest. There is some evidence that this increase in ROI BOLD during neurofeedback shows a corresponding increase during a simple motor task. However, it is not clear whether this increase is in a local area or part of a strengthened network. In this aim, we will examine the effect of self-regulation of motor cortex on the functional connectivity of the visuomotor network, which we expect to be strengthened after neurofeedback training.  

Real-time fMRI is currently in its infancy and its potential for eventual use in the clinic is still undetermined. The goal of this set of experiments is to verify on healthy subjects both how rtfMRI can improve a coordinated motor task and why performance improves. Our experiments will provide valuable insights into the nature of neurofeedback and bring it closer to a useful neural intervention for rehabilitation of people with severe motor disabilities such as stroke.  

This research, the only of its kind in Zurich, will pioneer the development of a standardized method for long-term plasticity in the motor system. The group formed for this interdisciplinary project possesses complementary competencies in neuroscience, engineering and rehabilitation. The Rehabilitation Engineering Lab at the ETHZ has carried out pilot experiments with rtfMRI and developed the experimental setup.  The Institute of Neuroinformatics at ETHZ and University of Zurich has decades of experience leading the field of motor control of precision grip.  In addition, clinicians at the Universitätsspital Zürich provide a wealth of knowledge regarding reinforcement learning and fMRI, as well as practical knowledge necessary for a seamless transition to examining stroke subjects in the future.
Keywords: functional brain imaging, motor control, neurofeedback, real time fMRI, stroke

Title: First principle modeling of protein systems with physically-inspired machine learning
Abstract:
Biological macromolecules are the cornerstones of living organisms and understanding their properties is key to accelerate and reduce the cost associated with protein engineering and the development of new drugs.
Computer simulations can provide a detailed picture of molecular-scale interactions and their translation into biological functions, such as a protein's structure, binding affinities to drug-like molecules, and interaction with other proteins.
Despite the steady improvement of computational resources and of electronic structure methods, the size and timescale of relevant biological systems and phenomena prevent direct modelling with first principle methods when using plain molecular dynamics (MD).
Even an effective treatment of the electronic degrees of freedom with classical force fields (FFs) is limited to the folding of medium-sized proteins using dedicated hardware.
As a result coarse-grained (CG) descriptions where groups of atoms are replaced by a single interaction site, or CG bead, have emerged as a bridge between the atomic and the mesoscopic scales.
The goal of such methods is to provide a lower resolution picture of an atomic system that retains its main physical features while averaging out the `unimportant' details. The resulting models effectively extend the timescales and sizes achievable by computer simulation.

Among many proposed approaches, the multi-scale (MS-) CG method aims at reproducing the potential of mean force (PMF) of the all-atom (AA) system with fewer degrees of freedom (DoF). Classical FFs are typically used with molecular dynamic (MD) simulations to generate a large number of samples required to estimate the PMF of the AA system. So far, most of the existing CG models have used simple functional forms for the effective energy function, limiting the expressivity of the models and mostly ignoring multi-body interactions. Although this protocol has been successful in formulating CG models for mixtures of small molecules, the lack of transferability of the CG beads across thermodynamic conditions and system composition has restricted its application to small globular proteins. Possible explanations for this limitation include the simplicity of the CG interaction models, the empirical parameters, and uncontrolled approximations underlying most FF models used to generate the PMF.

The objective of this proposal is to develop a framework to build transferable and systematically improvable CG models to address some of the long standing problems of biochemistry such as predicting the solvation and ligand binding free energies of (macro-)molecules. The applicant proposes to leverage MS-CG and ML techniques to build CG models from first principle references. The large computational burden associated with ab initio methods will be circumvented by building ML interatomic potentials (MLIPs) using density functional theory (DFT) references with an active learning approach and density-functional tight-binding (DFTB) as a baseline. These MLIPs will then be used to perform the extensive sampling of the PMF required by the fitting of a CGSchNet model, a method developed by the host lab. The ML model of interactions at both AA and CG level will be developed to include a variable number of body order correlations using techniques developed by the applicant during his graduate research. The systematic improvability of this framework will be validated on small test peptides and proteins solvated in water. As a second step, it will be used to learn system transferable CG beads from various small proteins. This effort will allow the study of data-driven CG beads transferability across thermodynamic conditions and system composition to increase the range of application for this framework.
Keywords: Coarse-grained simulations, electronic structure methods, free energy calculation, interatomic potentials, machine learning, macromolecules, multi-scale modelling

Title: Towards nonequilibrium ab initio calculations that include nonlocal correlations
Abstract:
Complex quantum materials consist of systems characterized by competing and correlated degrees of freedom whose interplay can give rise to symmetry-broken states. This competition involves spin, orbital, charge and lattice degrees of freedom relevant at comparable energy scales. One way to separate them apart is via fine-tuned laser pulse excitation of correlated systems, which can reveal hidden states of distinct nature. Moreover, dimensionality is an important aspect when it comes to describing the phases of matter. In low-dimensional correlated systems, close to phase instabilities and crossovers, nonlocal correlations become unavoidable to properly capture the underlying phase ordering mechanisms. Up to hundreds of femtoseconds after an impulsive excitation, the order parameter of a transient dynamical phase transition exhibits fluctuations with distinct nonthermal criticality and the electronic band structure can be strongly renormalized. To access nonlocal correlations, single- and two-particle correlation functions need to be calculated consistently, and this is challenging for several reasons. There lacks out-of-equilibrium methods that include both local and nonlocal correlations while treating various degrees of freedom. Dynamical Mean Field theory (DMFT) solely captures local correlations, GW+DMFT only charge fluctuations, the phenomenological time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau (tdGL) only considers low-order microscopic electronic fluctuations and time-dependent Density Functional Theory (tdDFT) doesn’t capture inelastic scattering processes which are relevant for thermalization at long times. In addition, for numerical methods based on the nonequilibrium Green’s function formalism (NEGF), the computational time scales as O(t^2) and memory requirements become quickly overwhelming, prohibiting long-time evolution of systems.
One can work on two main fronts to improve the accuracy and predictive power of one’s theoretical model: the refinement of the effective model Hamiltonian (model-based front) and the elaboration of more efficient computational methods or numerical workarounds to reduce the computational effort (method-based front). The 24 months of this project (mobility phase) would be devoted to alleviating the computational overhead of numerical many-body quantum (NMBQ) methods and using them to address fundamental questions. The usage of the numerical methods – developed and improved during the mobility phase – to perform realistic material calculations would be subsequent to the mobility phase. This mobility phase includes
1. The development of novel methods that combine nonequilibrium DMFT and the Two-Particle Self-Consistent (TPSC) approach which takes care of the nonlocal spin and charge correlations. These methods would be used to compute nonlocal dynamical susceptibilities and self-consistently improve the nonequilibrium DMFT self-energy, a key quantity to access interacting single-particle observables.
2. The elaboration and implementation of numerical schemes that decrease the computational cost of numerical methods based on NEGF. These schemes would make use of memory truncation techniques, compact representation basis to store NEGF, and methods that extrapolate the time-diagonal of NEGF. These schemes would be applied on GW+DMFT, TPSC+DMFT and TPSC variants.
3. Apply TPSC+DMFT and GW+DMFT augmented with the numerical schemes to study the 1) ultrafast renormalization of electronic interactions, 2) processes of dynamical symmetry breaking from a microscopic perspective and 3) the pseudogap physics through photoexcitation.
Realizing the mobility phase would make possible the simulation of nonthermal symmetry-broken states up to experimentally relevant times of the order of picoseconds. This would consequently allow one to study accurately on a theoretical basis the collapse and revival of nonthermal ordered phases triggered and controlled via impulsive excitations. For example, one could study the photoinduced metastable SC state in K3C60 molecular compounds and the photoinduced ferroelectricity in quantum paraelectric SrTiO3 compounds. With these enhanced methods, one could incidentally delve into more fundamental questions such as the role of competing long- and short-range correlations in hidden states and metastable states. One could also examine the role of order parameter fluctuations in nonthermal phase transitions beyond tdGL.

Title: Fundamental Limits of Deep Learning
Abstract:
We are at the center of a revolution in information technology, with an explosion in the volume and richness of data sets, and deep learning represents one of the fundamental paradigms to exploit this very large amount of data. However, despite the ever growing interest in the machine learning community and the wide variety of its practical applications, a coherent framework to understand, devise, and analyze the performance of deep learning architectures has remained elusive. Furthermore, modern deep neural networks typically require large-scale computational resources in order to run the training algorithms, therefore only very few research groups in the world are able to carry out this line of research. These issues call for the development of mathematically rigorous foundations for deep learning, which will provide a principled route for the design of more efficient and accurate learning systems.

The general objective of this proposal consists in the study of the fundamental limits and trade-offs of deep learning. To do so, powerful analytic tools from information theory, high-dimensional statistics and probability theory will be employed. In particular, motivated by the progresses in optimal transport theory and by its recent applications to machine learning, the central idea at the basis of this project consists in regarding a deep neural network as a trajectory that "transports" an initial distribution (represented by the input layer) into a final distribution (represented by the output layer) through several intermediate steps (represented by the hidden layers). To be concrete, consider the case of classification in a supervised setting: one is given a training set with assigned labels and a test set whose labels have to be inferred. The data typically lies in a high dimensional space and has a complex geometric structure, so that simple classification algorithms (e.g, logistic regression) yield unsatisfactory classification errors. The classical solution to this issue consists in adopting more sophisticated classifiers. The originality of this project lies in the fact that we propose to solve the problem by designing a deep neural network that "transports" the given data points into new data points which are easier to classify. In this way, even a naive algorithm like logistic regression will be able to yield excellent classification results. Furthermore, we propose to rigorously analyze such deep architectures, in order to obtain provable performance guarantees.
Keywords: deep learning, high-dimensional statistics, information theory, machine learning, performance analysis, probability theory, transport techniques

Title: Distributed Training of Transformers - Scalable, Private, Robust and Personalized
Abstract:
Our proposal aims to enable the distributed training of recent self-attention neural network models such as transformers, in a way that is efficiently scalable, privacy-preserving, robust to malicious actors, and personalized to each users needs.

Transformer-based machine learning applications have recently lead to revolutionary performance gains on natural language and text applications, which are relevant for a growing set of practical applications affecting billions of end-users, such as personal assistants, writing support or machine translation services. However, significant problems remain to be solved in terms of enabling a decentralized and privacy-preserving collaborative training of such models, to better align data ownership of the participants with the utility resulting from such models.

The present proposal will develop and help productionize distributed and decentralized analogues of current training algorithms for transformer models, which are scalable and efficient, privacy-preserving,  fault tolerant, and support individual personalization of the resulting models.

In addition to foundational research on algorithms, we will also produce open-source software ready to be deployed in practice and in industry applications.
Keywords: Decentralized Systems, Decentralized Training, Distributed Machine Learning, Natural Language Processing, Neural attention models, Privacy

Title: TopoScope: a Topographical Approach to Software Testing
Abstract:
Modern software systems deal with complex inputs, which can be highly structured (e.g., Json documents; service requests), completely unstructured (e.g., images or text processed by a neural network), or a hybrid of the two. The dimensionality of the input space is often huge and correspondingly only a small fraction of all possible inputs can be used to exercise the system during software testing. Hence, the way inputs are sampled from such huge space represents a critical component of any software testing approach. Ideally, representative inputs should be sampled to ensure the intended behaviour in nominal conditions, but at the same time corner case inputs should be also sampled to verify the behaviour exhibited in extreme conditions.

Existing adequacy criteria used for test input selection or generation are mostly based on coverage: a test suite is deemed adequate if upon execution it exercises all code elements targeted by the specific coverage criterion (e.g., branch coverage; data-flow coverage). However, there are multiple ways to cover the same code elements, some involving nominal, others extreme, inputs. With traditional software, the relation between coverage and fault exposure has been shown empirically to be weak. With modern software (e.g., including deep learning components) that processes complex, highly unstructured inputs such a relation is expected to be even weaker. Indeed, recent attempts to extend the notion of coverage adequate test suites to deep learning components were also investigated empirically and found equally ineffective. A novel approach is needed to represent the input space of complex, unstructured inputs and to sample it in order to maximize the effectiveness of the resulting test suite.

In this project we investigate TOPOSCOPE, a novel topographical approach to test software components (e.g., neural networks) that handle highly complex inputs. TOPOSCOPE consists of an input topography construction phase, in which the elements of the input space are organized into an N-dimensional map that preserves the key features of the inputs. The topography of the input space is accompanied by a distance metric, which is used to guide automated test input generation. TOPOSCOPE provides both a diversity oriented and a focused test generator. The former aims at covering the regions of the input topographical map at large, so as to ensure the intended behaviour across the various feature combinations that may occur in nominal conditions. The latter aims at finding examples that belong to a narrow and potentially problematic region of the topographical map.

The project will study black box and white box techniques for the extraction of input features that can be used to create a software input topography. It will design alternative topography construction algorithms, based on different input embeddings, considering human interpretability as an important property of the resulting topographical map. It will evaluate the approach empirically on both traditional and deep learning based software systems. The tool TOPOSCOPE will be released as open source software under a permissive (e.g., MIT) open license.
Keywords: Automated test input generation, Software testing, Test adequacy criteria

Title: From parallel corpora to multilingual exercises — Making use of large text collections and crowdsourcing techniques for innovative autonomous language learning applications
Abstract:
Corpus linguistics has a long-lasting history; even before computers were invented, people analyzed written texts to gain insights into language use. Today, corpora are increasingly used in language learning: Language teachers and lexicographers search for examples that, for instance, illustrate best the use of a particular expression, while being self-contained, using plain language and not comprising element that deflect attention away from the expression in question. Language learners, once being instructed in corpus search techniques, can autonomously explore numerous authentic language examples and prove their assumptions true or false. This technique often referred to as data-driven learning (DDL).

Recent research is concerned with the automatic conversion of corpus examples into exercises in computer-assisted language learning (CALL) applications. State-of-the-art natural language processing (NLP) methods provide a linguistic analysis of the corpus material. Research on technology use in second language acquisition (SLA) showed that the use of corpora in language learning improves learning efficiency.

Most work on corpus use in language learning applications focuses on monolingual corpora. Very few parallel corpora with standard language content (in contrast to translated legal texts etc.) are publicly available. Among those, the recently curated OpenSubtitles2016 corpus stands out in terms of the size and number of available languages. The goal of the proposed project is to exploit this corpus (and possibly other corpora) to extract those translations that benefit language learners most.

To this end, I will apply NLP methods to extract linguistic structures, such as syntactic relations, semantic relations, in particular word embeddings (Karlgren and Sahlgren 2001), and correspondences between words and multiword units of the respective languages by combining word alignment with other annotation layers. I expect that, in line with existing monolingual approaches, features such as lexical complexity and syntactic structures on both languages as well as the kind of correspondence on the lexical and syntactical level, alongside simpler features, such as sentence lengths and the anaphora use, are to be taken into account to determine the suitability of a corpus example for language learning purposes. Surveys on language teachers will be used to adjust the ranking of corpus examples.

The generation of automatically evaluated language learning exercises poses a major problem: How can we reliably judge a given answer to be wrong? A common approach is not to allow free-form answers, but to provide a choice of possible answers, one of which is known to be the correct one, and several other so-called distractors, chosen so as to make them plausible, but guaranteeing their incompatibility with the given context. I will adapt this kind of exercise (among others) to parallel, word-aligned data, which opens up numerous new prospects in terms of answers and distractors (e.g., parallel answers consisting of the correct answer in one language and a distractor in the other). The exercises will be automatically generated by an application prototype that allows its users to give explicit feedback to each exercise. In addition, the application will log all user interactions. The observations crowdsourced in this way will allow us to study user interaction with our application and help towards improving it.

The project comprehends the curation of a parallel corpus for several languages and the extraction of parallel (if possible also multiparallel) corpus examples that are suitable for language learning purposes. Both data sets will be made available so that other applications in corpus linguistics and CALL applications can make use of it. I expect that the crowdsourcing data helps to tailor example selection and exercise generation to the needs of language learners and provide a base for further development of CALL applications.
Keywords: ICALL, NLP, concordancers, crowdsourcing, language learning, parallel corpora, second language acquisition, word alignment

Title: Efficient Discovery of Novel Photoredox Reactions: A Multipurpose Self-Driving Laboratory Approach
Abstract:
Chemical transformations involving reactive radical intermediates offer a variety of selective, nontraditional bond formations. Traditional radical generation methods often involve either toxic radical initiators, high-energy UV irradiation, or high temperatures. Such demanding radical generation methods limit the utilization of radical intermediates in organic synthesis. With the advent of photoredox catalysis, the limitation of generating radical intermediates has reduced significantly. Photocatalysts are capable of generating these intermediates in a controlled manner and under mild conditions. The subsequent challenge is the vast combinatorial space of possibilities of reagents - such as photoredox catalysts, transition metal catalysts, ligands, additives, and light sources (wavelength and power) - as this complexity creates a large and diffuse chemical and operational parameter space. Until now, the exploration typically relies heavily on domain expertise.
Here, we propose an automated experimental discovery platform to search for productive photoredox-catalyzed reactions. A reactivity prediction model (RPM) will virtually screen possible experiments, selecting those to be run based on their predicted reactivity. Following each run, our reactivity classifier algorithm (RCA) analyzes the liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) data, assessing the reactivity of each experiment. Our RCA generates a continuous reactivity score (CRS) that evaluates both the conversion of reactants and the emergence of novel peaks in the chromatogram. To close the loop, the CRSs are used to update the RPM, informing selection of the next round of experiments. This iterative process facilitates the rapid discovery of promising, novel reactions within the initially defined chemical space. By running an intriguing reaction with identical conditions on the platform in parallel, sufficient material for further analysis is synthesized. With purified products, we will fully characterize the main products as well as major by-products of this newly discovered reaction. Moreover, the design of the automated experimental platform allows for efficient closed-loop optimization campaigns for the most productive and interesting new reactions. To this end, Bayesian optimization (BO) algorithms will guide optimization on the self-driving platform, ensuring efficient and streamlined optimization of reaction conditions in an iterative process.
Keywords: active learning, machine learning, photoredox catalysis, reaction discovery, reactivity prediction, self-driving laboratory

Title: Classification of Salivary Gland and Sinonasal Tumors Using Nanopore Sequencing
Abstract:
Background: Salivary gland and sinonasal tumors are characterized by a wide range of types and subtypes, making their histological or cytological diagnosis particularly challenging. The rarity of these tumors further complicates this process. Diagnosis relies mainly on a combination of histomorphology, immunohistochemistry, and molecular methods. In some cases, known genetic alterations can be detected using techniques like FISH, though these tests often have long turnaround times. Recent studies have demonstrated that methylation profiles generated from DNA methylation arrays combined with machine learning techniques can effectively differentiate salivary gland and sinonasal tumor (sub)types. However, a significant drawback of using DNA methylation arrays is the lengthy processing time required for analysis, which generally spans several days or even weeks. This delay can impact timely patient management, particularly in cases where prompt surgical intervention is critical.

Aim: This project aims to evaluate the feasibility of using Oxford Nanopore sequencing as a faster alternative to DNA methylation arrays for diagnosing these tumor types by developing a machine learning-based classifier, utilizing fresh frozen tissue, cytology, or saliva samples.

Methods: Reference data from existing and publicly available DNA methylation arrays will be used as the benchmark, and simulated Nanopore sequences will be generated from these arrays for the development and training of a machine learning-based classifier. The trained classifier will be applied to the Nanopore-sequenced sample probes in order to predict the tumor class. For this latter part, we will extract and sequence DNA from 50 samples of a variety of salivary gland and sinonasal tumors (frozen tissue, n = 30; cytology, n = 10; saliva, n = 10) using Oxford Nanopore technology.

Results: Based on similar studies on tumors of the central nervous system (CNS), we anticipate that Nanopore sequencing will 1) allow for providing a methylome-based diagnosis in at least 80% of the cases, and 2) significantly reduce the time required for tumor (sub)type classification, potentially delivering results within hours rather than days or weeks.

Impact: When applied to native tissue or cytological samples, this classifier could provide a faster alternative to DNA methylation analysis while offering likewise enhanced accuracy compared to conventional histological and cytological methods. This would streamline the diagnostic workflow and improve patient management, particularly for individuals with rare salivary gland or sinonasal tumors, or for cases where rapid surgical intervention is crucial. This diagnostic approach even has the potential for intra-operative application, thereby providing an opportunity to modify the surgical strategy. Last but not least, in addition to its speed, Nanopore platforms offer portability and cost-effectiveness, making advanced molecular diagnostics more accessible to smaller diagnostic centers and resource-limited settings.
Keywords: DNA methylation profiling, Machine learning classification, Molecular diagnostics, Oxford Nanopore sequencing, Precision oncology, Rapid tumor diagnosis, Salivary gland tumors, Sinonasal tumors

Title: Molecular mechanisms of human genome editing
Abstract:
Next-generation genome editing tools are revolutionizing the biological research community and hold promise for the clinical treatment of genetic disorders. CRISPR-Cas nucleases in particular are extraordinarily easy to program. However, what happens after a Cas enzyme targets the genome is not as straightforward. All editing systems to date damage genomic DNA, with the most commonly-used tools introducing a double-stranded DNA break (DSB). The output of genome editing is therefore fundamentally determined by intrinsic DNA repair. While engineering of new Cas enzymes has exploded, far less attention has been paid to controlling DNA repair to track and alter genome editing. We propose to determine aspects by which Cas enzymes interface with cellular machinery to yield genome editing outcomes. The proposed work will provide insight into how human cells keep their genomes safe from harm and may lead to new routes to the treatment of genetic disorders. We specifically propose to develop new tools to explore Cas-induced DNA repair and use them to answer outstanding questions regarding human genome maintenance through three focused aims:

Aim 1: Molecularly monitoring genome editing by visualizing DNA repair. Cas enzymes are not perfectly specific and can impact off-targets. We recently developed a method for unbiased detection of Cas on- and off-targets called DISCOVER-seq that follows the recruitment of DNA repair proteins to a Cas-induced DSB. DISCOVER-seq provides molecular insight into cellular events before edits are cemented in the genome and broadly enables discovery of in situ off-targets in otherwise intractable systems. But DISCOVER-seq is low-throughput, requires large numbers of cells, and has only been tested with Cas9 and Cas12a. We propose to solve these issues by developing Auto-DISCO, which will merge DISCOVER-seq, CUT&RUN ChIP-seq, automated liquid handling, and machine learning. We will use Auto-DISCO to perform real-time tracking of off-targets for thousands of human guide RNAs, determine off-targets and molecular DSB profiles for new Cas enzymes, and develop predictive models of human genome editing.

Aim 2: Tracking HDR search from a CRISPR-Cas induced DNA break. Precise sequence replacement of a Cas-induced DSB via homology directed repair (HDR) is inefficient in human cells. This is a barrier to therapy, since HDR is necessary to reverse the majority of human genetic disorders caused by SNPs. The search for a homologous template sequence is a major component of HDR, but it is not understood how homology search limits HDR. We propose to develop a method for time-resolved tracking of Cas-induced homology search using a proximity-dependent DNA methylase fused to the key Rad51 recombination factor. We will use this approach to determine the distinction between productive and non-productive searches at varying 1D/3D genomic distances and with varying homology. This work will reveal limiting factors to HDR, potentially suggesting new methods to treat genetic disease.

Aim 3: Illuminating the heterogeneity of human DNA repair using single cell transcriptomics. Heterogeneous human tissues express different DNA repair enzymes, react differently to mutations in DNA repair pathways, and generate different types of alleles from identical Cas-induced breaks. Genome editing therapies are therefore challenging in primary tissues that contain many types of cells. We propose to develop a single cell RNA Monitored Editing (scRME) method that marries single cell RNA sequencing with genome editing. scRME will simultaneously track complete single cell transcriptomes and editing outcomes in a single experiment. We will use scRME to determine why genome editing of heterogeneous human CD34+ hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) results in mixed populations of cells with large variation in HDR efficiency and decreasing allele frequency after engraftment. We will ask how transcriptionally-defined HSPC subsets differentially perform HDR and/or take up different indel alleles. This work will lead to improved approaches to predictable hematopoietic genome editing and could suggest ways to increase the efficacy of HDR in heterogenous human tissues.
Keywords: CRISPR, Cas9, DNA repair, genome_editing

Title: Post-truth, Alterity, and Social Media: Perspective Taking and Perspective Blocking in Online Discussions
Abstract:
Our relation to facts, expertise, and knowledge has been the object of profound transformations over the past few years. Expressions such as “alternative facts”, “fake news”, or “post-truth” are now as familiar as they were once thought to be ludicrous. While recent media attention may make them seem more prominent than they actually are, it is difficult to deny that the Internet’s relationship with information and truth has taken, at least momentarily, a turn for the worst. More worrying still, it has been accompanied by a rise in violent and often extremist discourses, that have proliferated in some areas of the Internet and that are often justified by misinformation.
In this context, this project proposes to study how the perspectives of others – as more or less legitimate sources of information and as members of other social groups – are interacted with on social media. In particular, its aim is to explore how perspectives are taken or blocked in discussions about a polarising social event – such as the Orlando 2016 shooting – on the social media platform Reddit. It is also to compare whether and how communities defending extreme political ideologies differ from others groups in this regard, both qualitatively and quantitatively. 
In addition to tackling an important social topic, the proposal also breaks new ground with a mixed-method design, that integrates qualitative insights with recent data science methods. Indeed, there have been, over the past few years, rapid advances in natural language processing and machine learning. However, social scientists, especially social psychologists, have tended to lack the necessary skills to take advantage of them, while experts on machine learning and natural language processing are most often not trained in the micro-details of text analysis, or theories of perspective taking and blocking. Having used in-depth qualitative methods for my PhD thesis, and being currently gaining expertise in data science, I am uniquely positioned to bring these two domains together. 
Combining these methods of textual analysis will, in itself, be an innovative and productive contribution. More specifically, this project proposes to use qualitative analysis and insights to drive the statistical analysis of texts in examining perspectives over large amounts of data, i.e., millions of comments on Internet forums. This is then followed with a quantitative analysis, represented by a quasi-experiment – following the general principles of experimentation to investigate naturally occurring data –, combined with a qualitative exploration of perspective taking and blocking.
This mixed methods project will shed a much-needed light on how we interact with the perspectives of others on social media and on some of the specificities of politically extreme online communities. It will also lead to a state-of-the-art method for combining quantitative and qualitative analyses and explore the vast amount of textual data that the Internet has made available to social scientists.
Keywords: Big data, Machine learning, Misinformation, Natural language processing, Perspective blocking, Perspective taking, Post truth, Social media

Title: Automatic analysis of verbal and non-verbal behavior and provision of feedback in video selection interviews
Abstract:
This project investigates social interaction in personnel selection interviews enhanced by digital technology. We will create a database of applicants participating in video interviews (applicants receive a list of interview questions from a recruiter online and then record themselves answering those questions), which are a newly emerging interview format. We will develop automated procedures for extracting relevant behavioral features from streams of applicants’ verbal and nonverbal behavior in these interviews. This information will be (1) linked to external criteria (e.g., hireability ratings by expert recruiters), (2) used to train machine learning algorithms, and (3) fed back to the applicants. We will assess applicants’ perceptions of this feedback, whether and how they use it to improve their performance in a second video interview a day later, and how they perceive data privacy issues related to the use of their data.
The project addresses three issues mentioned in the call. First, how is digitalization transforming social ties? The selection interview is the gateway to employment and thus the potential beginning of one of the fundamental social ties in modernity: the work relationship. We explore a new format by which selection interviews are conducted in an online, asynchronous manner. Second, how is digitalization transforming the economy? The selection interview is an important personnel selection procedure, which itself is an important component of strategic talent management. The digitalization of talent management is rapidly expanding in practice, but is currently poorly understood in research. Third, how is digitalization transforming our subjective experience? Video interviews are a novel experience for many applicants. Machine learning techniques can be used to extract the applicants’ behaviors recorded on the videos and to some degree infer their personality and social skills. This information can then be fed back to the applicants, potentially changing their subjective experience of the video interview. However, questions like how such feedback is best provided and how the applicant apprehends and uses it are largely unexplored.
The study will yield four main sets of outputs. First, the primary data from the study will lead to publications in scientific journals or conference proceedings in human-computer interaction and organizational psychology or human resources. Second, the data will be used to adapt an existing data collection platform and to improve the quality of algorithms to infer verbal and nonverbal behavior from videos. Third, data about user experiences will inform the development of evidence-based coaching programs for improving applicants’ performance. Fourth, the rich set of data and experience generated will constitute fruitful avenues for further research by the applicant team.
Keywords: Selection interview, Verbal behavior, feedback, machine learning, non-verbal behavior, social computing, social sensing

Title: Exploring common mechanisms for social and non-social autism symptoms: a longitudinal study in the Geneva Autism Cohort
Abstract:
Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD) is a group of highly prevalent disorders that are characterized by persistent deficits in social communication and interpersonal relations as well as by the presence of repetitive behaviors and circumscribed interests. ASD is commonly associated with lifelong disabilities in many individuals. While ASD is usually diagnosed between 18 months and 5 years, increasing evidence suggests that the primary processes responsible for the disorder emerge during the first 6 months of life. However, despite abundant literature, there is still no strong coherent explanation for the co-occurrence of the two major lines of autism symptoms, namely social deficits on the one hand, and restricted and repetitive behaviors (RRBs) on the other hand. 

There is now increasing evidence that deficits in social interaction and altered development of the communicative skills result from a lack of orienting to social stimuli from the first months of life. Following these observations, extent behavioral interventions have been designed to provide the child with increased social learning opportunities, resulting in drastic improvement of the socio-communicative developmental trajectories of many autistic children. There is however way scanter knowledge about the mechanisms explaining the emergence of non-social autistic symptoms, as well as the most adequate intervention strategies to help reduce their eventual burden. Providing a comprehensive account of the mechanisms that drive the emergence of both social and non-social autistic symptoms would be highly important for the future development of more targeted interventions.

In this project, we will focus on two of the symptoms that can be the most invalidating for autistic individuals: difficulties in acquiring language and impaired cognitive flexibility. Following hypotheses by others, we will design a series of experiment to probe the role of primary visual processes and contingency detection in the emergence of social and non-social autistic symptoms. For that purpose, we will combine rigorous experimental EEG and innovative gaze-contingent eye-tracking paradigms in a longitudinal cohort of children with autism, or at risk for autism and their age-matched TD peers. The Geneva Autism Cohort is a uniquely-sized longitudinal effort that follows children from 6 months of age until 12 years. Over this period, we follow the children’s development, from infants at high-risk for ASD, through preschool age and eventual diagnosis confirmation, and then to school-aged children with potential emerging comorbidities. The Geneva Autism Cohort thus provides a promising opportunity to understand the developmental processes associated with autism symptoms at each age.

Our first aim will be to examine the extent to which visual disengagement, sensitivity to contingency and related reinforcement learning processes are altered in this cohort of children and how these processes mature as children grow. Second, we will examine the relationship between these processes and language development, starting with the acquisition of non-verbal communication, then words, and finally sentences, always relating the acquisition of these skills with inter-individual differences in primary attention processes. Third, we aim to bridge the gap between primary attention processes and RRBs by following the maturation of the different processes involved, starting from selective attention to flexibility. Finally, we propose concrete steps for developing novel therapeutic interventions, with the construction of a pilot randomized control trial (RCT) to test the potential of a gaze-contingent eye-tracking technique to remediate social attention in preschoolers with autism. If efficient, this lightweight protocol would represent a low-cost intervention that could be easily accessible for families to provide immediate action for preschoolers diagnosed with autism.

In sum, this project is designed to significantly contribute to our understanding of mechanisms associated with the emergence of all types of autistic symptoms, in a way that will provide concrete knowledge on how to best adapt therapeutic strategies to improve the care of children with autism.

Title: GREECE: Geophysics-assisted Rare Event Estimation in Changing Environments
Abstract: The unprecedented rates by which we impact our environment and climate necessitate revision of the way we estimate occurrence and probabilities of future events that affect ecosystem services, infrastructure and human populations. The challenge is that the weather in a future climate is uncertain, the governing equations guiding our understanding of natural systems are approximations at best, properties and state variables are heterogeneous and poorly constrained, and many impactful events are rare with limited historical data providing guidance. These challenges are exacerbated for non-stationary human-climate systems requiring predictions at ever increasing spatial and temporal resolutions with rapidly growing computational requirements. Predictive uncertainties are particularly high in subsurface systems given a dearth of site-specific data, while transport and storage properties vary over orders of magnitude. These systems also often display legacy effects (memory) that are notoriously difficult to represent in present mechanistic models. The project entitled Geophysics-assisted Rare Event Estimation in Changing Environments (GREECE) will build on current understanding of soil, the vadose zone and groundwater systems, and leverage modern statistical and deep learning methods to answer questions such as: What is the probability that a given (rare) impactful event dependent on local subsurface properties will occur in, for example, the 2050s? What is the uncertainty of this estimate and how can it be reduced? These questions could be related to topics of local soil ecosystems, initiation of landslides, or transfer of pollutants to groundwater. Given the strong uncertainty about subsurface properties and concerning the future climate, a fundamental question then becomes: Where, when and how is subsurface characterization useful for constraining probabilistic predictions about future events that are strongly sensitive to both subsurface properties and a changing climate? The data and the associated modeling to be considered will span near-surface geophysics (e.g., electrical resistivity tomography, electromagnetics, seismic refraction) and subsurface hydrology (e.g., time-series of soil moisture, hydraulic head and tracer data). The project partners include experts in soil physics, hydrogeology, hydroclimatic modeling, surrogate modeling and uncertainty quantification. Frameworks will be developed to estimate probabilities of future events under climate uncertainty given site-specific subsurface data. To make these frameworks computationally and practically feasible for applications involving hydrological and geophysical data, methodological developments will be achieved to (i) gain computational speed-up by multifidelity inversions involving physics-informed neural operators and related approaches, (ii) advance Bayesian optimal experimental design and (iii) develop spatial upscaling procedures. These advances can then be used to gain understanding of the relative contributions to the total uncertainty, in rare event probability estimates, that are due to irreducible uncertainty (climate variability) and reducible uncertainty (subsurface heterogeneity, process descriptions) that can be decreased using data and methodological developments. Demonstrations will be given for various geophysical and hydrological problem types, with specific emphasis given to groundwater recharge in arid environments and leaching of salt in irrigated soils.

Title: New directions in agri-environmental governance: Everyday digitalization in agri-environmental governance
Abstract:
Digital technologies and robotics have opened up intriguing new perspectives for thinking about the future of farming and food. From drone surveillance of crops, to automatic milking systems to weed-killing robots, a good deal of hope is placed in these new technologies, and in their potential for minimizing the environmental impact of agricultural practices and food production (Dutta, Lanvin, and Wunsch-Vincent 2017). For example, programming robots to fight weeds dramatically reduces the amount of herbicides used on specific crops, while simultaneously limiting the soil degradation caused by heavy tractors. Collecting extensive data sets on farms and the food chain, and connecting these to tools and machinery, is thought to harbour great potential for control, monitoring, and optimization. In short, like many other sectors of the economy, agriculture and food have entered the era of Big Data. From an anthropological perspective, this new era is driven by far more than the allure of innovative technologies or intelligent machines. These technological changes are socially and culturally significant, raising the spectre of a fundamental turning point that could impact agriculture and food in some of their essential attributes: the relations between human and non-human (animals, soil, etc.) agents; the place of human knowledge and work in providing for sustainable subsistence; indeed the nature of one of mankind’s oldest links to nature – farming. 
The fast integration of digital technologies in agri-environmental governance (AEG) practices points to new challenges related to processes identified in the first phase. Digitalization quickens and transforms the bureaucratization of governance; it multiplies the potential for building traceability and reinforces practices of control; and it opens new spaces of coordination and knowledge-sharing. Rather than focussing on pioneering experimentations that embody the highlights of this technological turn (such as demonstration farms or prototypical smart machines), often without questioning their viability in real life, this follow-up project will target already common and everyday digitalization in AEG, with the objective of analysing change in the making. Based on a deepening of cases already explored in the first phase (IP-Suisse, Donau Soy, and the alternative agri-food scene in Indonesia), this follow-up project examines the digitalization in AEG through the lens of the same three dimensions – food, knowledge, and autonomy – looking more specifically at: a) how digitalization transforms the configurations of AEG practices; b) how digital technologies reframe the skills required in food production and its governance; and c) under what conditions digital tools promote farmer and consumer autonomy.

Title: Computational Reduction for Training and Inference (CORTI)
Abstract:
This project is a follow-up to the ISUL project, to fund the 4th year of two ongoing PhD theses, and open a new sub-project to investigate a very promising topic that spanned from the research we have conducted, but is too rich to be tackled in the context of the two already running theses.

The ISUL project aimed at developing novel machine-learning algorithms to address two fundamental issues with modern techniques: their need for both very large data corpora and heavy computation. We have developed a series of methods that allow the transfer of structures from an existing network to facilitate the training of a new one, on a different task, for which few data examples are available. Our approaches rely on mimicking the behavior of the existing network not only point-wise, but also in term of local changes. We have in parallel developed techniques that reduce the computational cost of training and inference by relying heavily on sampling to approximate dense weighted averaging.

We structure this new proposal in three sub-projects:

The first sub-project will continue our work on transfer learning first by improving the optimization itself, as we observed that the complexity of the underlying optimization problem is key. Additionally, we will consider using deep generative models to produce synthetic data capturing the joint distribution of the signal components. We can see their use as a Monte-Carlo generalization of our approaches based on first order derivatives to an arbitrary order.

The second sub-project will extend our line of research on sampling for gradient descent and inference. We have recently investigated the use of sampling during inference, and shown that end-to-end gradient-based learning can be generalized to such a context. Our current algorithm relies on sampling an image at a fixed scale to reject poorly informative parts, and does not take into account that different scales may lead to different statistics. This is what we are planning next.

From there, we are envisioning a generalization to sampling the model itself, looking jointly at parts of the model and parts of the signal, and sample along both axes jointly. This can be seen as a data-driven adaptive dropout, that modulates the computation required for a given level of accuracy.

Finally, the third project will initiate a new line of work whose objective is to combine model-selection and training into a unified forward generation of a model, avoiding at the same time the costly back-propagation of the gradient, and a grid-search for the optimization of meta-parameters.

The key motivation behind this new direction is the view of a deep model as a progressive refinement of an internal representation, combined with methods based on information theory that provide criteria to assess if the change occurring at a certain level of an architecture is beneficial to the overall task at hand. Our objective is to leverage these tools and reformulate explicitly the training of a model as the progressive design of a topological deformation of the feature space in low dimension, to avoid back-propagation and gradient descent.
Keywords: Deep learning, Machine learning, Pattern recognition

Title: Free energy estimation for assisting in silico design of materials
Abstract: The main objective of this project is to develop and apply a method to predict the relative thermodynamic stabilities of novel materials at a density-functional-theory (DFT) level of theory, in order to assist in silico material design. This is rendered possible by exploiting advances in machine-learning techniques to circumnavigate the prohibitively large computational expenses otherwise incurred by extensively sampling phase-space using first-principles methods, and employing state-of-the-art free energy estimation techniques in order to accurately and rigorously compute the Gibbs free energy of a given system.  The methodology will be general and transferable, and will be applied to investigate free-energy-related problems of three classes of materials: water, photovoltaic perovskites, and new energy-storage materials.
Keywords: Energy materials, Free energy methods, Machine-learning techiniques, Statistical physics, in silico material design

Title: EFFSIMMSI: Advancing Induced Earthquake Forecasting and Fracturing Dynamics via Innovative Scale-Invariant Seismic Monitoring and Multi-Sensor Integration
Abstract:
Managing induced earthquake risk during underground industrial activities, such as enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) and carbon sequestration, is critical for safety, social and economic reasons. A few well-known examples are the 2006 Basel and 2017 Pohang induced earthquakes related to deep geothermal activities. The abandonment of promising geothermal projects due to large induced earthquakes reminds us how urgent it is to improve our real-time monitoring and forecasting ability. The core ingredients in forecasting seismicity are to increase our understanding of the earthquake preparation and nucleation processes. Those processes have been studied at various scales, from natural fault systems to laboratory fault samples, but all require high-resolution seismicity catalogs and deformation data. In particular, underground research labs, e.g., Bedretto and EGS collab, have been given great hope in helping us better understand fault physics. Processes can be studied in much higher resolution and at various scales in such labs. While labs are an ideal testbed for earthquake mechanisms, it is important to acknowledge that observational science, experimental science, and software design should be coordinated between those different scales to be fully synergistic. However, in current practices, seismic monitoring, a key and fundamental element in data analysis, at different scales are performed using independent tools leading to segregated analysis. A consistent tool that can be directly applied to different scales is in urgent need.

The objective of the proposed research is to move forward from the conventional real-time induced seismicity monitoring that only focuses on large events towards cross-scale high-resolution monitoring that also covers the abundant low-magnitude microseismics. Such advancement in real-time monitoring towards microseismicity is expected to improve our forecasting ability of induced earthquakes and our understanding of fracturing mechanisms. To reach this goal, we will: (1) Develop advanced scale-invariant, multi-sensor seismic monitoring tool by integrating advanced machine learning (ML) based and physical-based methods to better characterize induced earthquakes of different scales in real-time; (2) Investigate whether and how deep-learning catalogs can significantly promote our induced earthquake forecasting ability by systematic benchmarking and by identifying the most relevant features for forecasting, and (3) Study the spatial-temporal evolution and source mechanisms of induced seismicity to uncover physical processes governing the fracturing dynamics. We will apply the developed methods to various scales, including the Utah FORGE EGS site, the ETH laboratory rock physics experiments, the Bedretto Underground Laboratory, and possibly the Haute-Sorne EGS site in Switzerland. Our outcomes, including compiled datasets and developed tools, will be available via open-access data repositories, promoting the use of ML techniques in seismology and revolutionizing our real-time seismic monitoring across different scales and sensor types. Our research will promote reliable induced earthquake forecasting, improve our understanding of earthquake processes at various scales, and hopefully provide new insights into how earthquakes start.

Title: Optimization and implementation of ceftazidime or ceftazidime-avibactam combined with fosfomycin against highly resistant gram-negative bacteria
Abstract: Carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales are a major health problem. One of the few treatment options is ceftazidime/avibactam. However, relapse of infection is observed in up to 15% of the patients, often associated with resistance development. Empiric use of continuous infusion and combination therapies, in particular the addition of fosfomycin to ceftazidime/avibactam seem to be associated with improved outcomes as compared to ceftazidime/avibactam alone. Indeed, also in preclinical models, fosfomycin is often highly synergistic and reduced resistance development is observed in combination with beta-lactams. Yet, the dosing rationale is unclear and massive doses of up to 24 g of fosfomycin are empirically used, frequently leading to sodium overload. The aim of the present project is to define and implement a rational dosing regimen for the combination of ceftazidime or ceftazidime/avibactam with fosfomycin against Enterobacterales. Therefore, we will use state-of-the-art preclinical PK/PD models (hollow-fiber, humanized-PK mouse model) with patient-derived bacterial isolates and pharmacometrics to define optimised dosing regimens. Using whole genome sequencing/artificial intelligence, we will define the link between genetics and the phenotypic bacterial susceptibility as well as synergistic effects, which could be developed into a rapid test to rapidly identity patients that will benefit most from the optimised combination treatment. Lastly, we will implement the optimised, pharmacometrics-guided dosing approach in a proof-of-concept randomized controlled trial.
Keywords: carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales, ceftazidime-avibactam, fosfomycin

Title: Towards data-efficient Bayesian deep learning
Abstract:
Modern machine learning (ML) methods, especially deep learning, have achieved great successes in many applications, for instance, computer vision and natural language processing.
These techniques usually rely on building task-agnostic models and then feeding these models with huge amounts of data (millions to billions of examples), until they learn functions that predict well on these given data.
While this is a successful strategy in domains where large datasets are available, many important problems in the real world do not offer this luxury.
Crucially, this mode of learning also starkly contrasts with human learning, since humans are usually able to learn to perform well on tasks after seeing just a few examples.
We believe that this data-efficiency (or respective lack thereof) is mainly due to three factors: (a) informative inductive biases, (b) reusable neural representations, and (c) knowledge transfer between tasks.

We argue that all these three features can be achieved within the framework of Bayesian deep learning (BDL).
In contrast to the standard deep learning described above, BDL is a nascent research field that marries the ideas of deep learning, particularly expressive neural models with gradient-based training, to the framework of Bayesian inference, with its long and venerable history in probability theory and statistics.
In BDL, the neural network parameters are treated as random variables over which a posterior distribution is inferred using some prior distribution and the data at hand.
During prediction, one then considers all possible hypotheses in this model space, weighted by their respective posterior probabilities, instead of focusing all attention on a single model.

Within this framework, one can naturally accommodate all the aforementioned desiderata of data-efficient learning.
Firstly, inductive biases can be encoded into Bayesian priors for our models, such as weight-space or function-space priors for Bayesian neural networks (BNNs).
Secondly, reusable representations can be learned using deep Bayesian latent variable models, such as variational autoencoders (VAEs).
These models can then in turn be made more performant and data-efficient by specifying priors over their latent variables.
Moreover, these representations can often be trained on unlabeled data and then be reused on downstream tasks where labels are available.
Thirdly, knowledge can be transferred between tasks via Bayesian meta-learning, where related tasks are used to learn a prior that can then be used on the target task.
Keywords: Bayesian modeling, Bayesian priors, data-efficiency, deep learning, machine learning, meta-learning
