Title: Strategies to find the optimal sorbent material and process conditions for direct air capture
Abstract:
Capturing CO2 directly from the air is seen as the last resort. If society fails to control carbon emissions before we exceed a critical CO2 concentration in the atmosphere, direct air capture (DAC) is the only technology available to reduce this concentration. As it has become increasingly likely that we will exceed these limits, humanity must remove large amounts of CO2 from the atmosphere to meet agreed climate targets. This reality has spurred considerable research interest in DAC. As the scale DAC needs to be applied to impact the climate will be gigantic (Gt CO2 removed/year), optimizing this technology in terms of energy consumption and use of resources is essential. There are many different technologies proposed for DAC. One of these possible technologies is to capture CO2 with a solid adsorbent. 

The important advantage of solid adsorbents is that modern reticular chemistry allows us to synthesize a nearly infinite number of possible materials. These materials can then be combined with a separation process with many variables to optimize. This proposal aims to unlock the potential of reticular chemistry for sorbent-based direct air capture processes by developing a systematic methodology to search both the chemical and process design space. This project integrates density functional theory, molecular simulation, machine learning, and process design to identify the most promising material and process combinations to achieve this aim. As a model system, we interrogate the material's space by focusing on porous metal-organic frameworks (MOFs). We can tune the pore shape and the chemistry by combining metal nodes and organic linkers. The design space is initially explored using a five-step temperature vacuum swing adsorption process (TVSA). Our approach is to predict the adsorption properties of the materials using molecular simulations and to feed these properties to a TVSA process model that simulates their performance in the process. The data generated for a diverse set of MOFs will form the training set for a machine learning model that predicts the performance of a particular material and process conditions. 

We plan to develop a methodology to screen the entire chemical design space efficiently, aiming to create an inverse design that allows us to identify the optimal material and process combination. As our methods rely on accurate predictions of the adsorption isotherms, we also plan to improve the force fields systematically. In particular, for those materials that strongly interact with CO2 (chemisorption).
Keywords: carbon capture, direct air capture, machine learning, metal organic frameworks, molecular simulation

Title: eXplainable Artificial Intelligence for histoPATHology (XAI-Path)
Abstract:
Modern medicine is producing massive amounts of data in many different formats (images of many types, signals, structured data, free text, genomics, ...) making the diagnosis and treatment planning increasingly complex for humans who need to take into account all available data and influences, particularly complex data such as images or genomics. With almost all data now being available in electronic format, digital medicine has become a reality. 

Histopathology is one of the last domains where work is still partially carried out with analogue devices, notably microscopes that are used to analyse stained tissue samples on glass slides. Digital Whole Slide Image (WSI) scanners and viewing on computer screens are increasingly replacing these analogue devices and open the domain up for more automatic data analysis also in diagnostic workflows and not only in research where digital data processing has become standard. Part of the problem is the large size of these images, both for visualization and storage (standard images are around 100'000x100'000 pixels at a standard magnification of 40x). Often such images are viewed in multiple magnifications both digitally and under a classical microscope.

Machine learning has changed many fields in the medical domain, first with the analysis of text and structured data, and since 20 years increasingly also for images and signals to help decision making. Within the machine learning techniques used, particularly \emph{deep learning} has led to extremely good results in many focused area over the past ten years, for example to classify chest x-rays or eye fundus images into a number of disease classes. For a few applications human-like performance or even better has been reported, but mainly in retrospective data analysis. Prospective trials with its potentially changing data and possible outliers in the data are more challenging and results have often not been as good as in retrospective analysis, sometimes linked to problems in the model itself or in the underlying data, leading to problems with generalization. Deep learning has also a problem compared to traditional machine learning that uses handcrafted features in that the model is basically a black box and the decisions taken can not be explained easily. Decision trees and handcrafted features are often much easier to understand and also allow finding problems with possibly incorrect decisions.

For combing the outcomes of decision support with all other clinical data of a case the physicians thus require good tools for explaining the decisions, also to identify mistakes that an algorithm can make when the data changes or when the model has learned a spurious correlation based on the training data. Interpretable/explainable AI has thus become a very important research domain that has developed many approaches from heat maps to highlight the regions most important for a decision (as in GRAD-CAM or LIME) to models that use human-understandable concepts such as concept activation vectors or regression concept vectors. Most of these approaches are evaluated rather qualitatively and only few papers exist that run user tests on explainable AI, even though much can be gained and learned from such tests and more quantitative evaluations. All definitions for the terms explainability or interpretability are based on what the actual end user understands, which means that this needs to be adapted for the varying user groups. User tests are normally the best means to to this. Uncertainty quantification is another means for understanding the outcomes of decision support and we plan to also use this aspect.

To properly evaluate a decision support tool with user tests it is important to have a good integration with the used clinical viewing station to use the same environment as clinicians are using in their daily clinical routine. Otherwise, there is a risk that clinicians need to learn a new user interface or modify there behavior. Some histopathology image viewers such as Sectra used in our partner hospital have a plugin mechanism that allows for such an integration.

Lung cancer is the second most frequent cancer in both man and women and by far the most deadliest, being responsible for about 20\% of the cancer deaths. Histopathology is the gold standard for the detailed diagnoses in lung cancer. Several sub-types of small cell lung cancer and non small cell lung cancer exist that need to be analysed. The sub-types give good indications for treatment planning and prognosis.

This project will tackle several of the current challenges of clinical decision support using deep learning and of interpretable deep learning. The use case is in the field of lung cancer research and on histopathology data, a quickly changing and dynamic field in medical data analysis.
Keywords: clinical decision support, explainable AI, histopathology, machine learning, user tests

Title: Navigating the Accelerated Epidemiological Transition in South Africa: The Impact of the Increasing Multimorbidity and Evolving HIV Landscape on Cancer Trends
Abstract:
Background: Sub-Saharan Africa is undergoing a rapid epidemiological transition, facing a double burden of infectious diseases like HIV and emerging non-communicable diseases including cancer and diabetes. This double burden results in complex interactions creating additional health challenges in the region. Both HIV and diabetes increase the risk of developing certain cancer types. To date, the South African HIV Cancer Match (SAM) study, established with support from the Swiss National Science Foundation, has focused on cancer research among people with HIV (PWH). It is based on a linkage of laboratory records from the National Health Laboratory Services (NHLS) and cancer diagnoses from the National Cancer Registry (NCR) and includes data on >9 million PWH for 2004-2021. Expanding the SAM study to include diabetes-related laboratory records will provide a unique opportunity to investigate the impact of the epidemiological transition and coexisting HIV and diabetes epidemics on cancer trends in sub-Saharan Africa.

Aims: As sub-Saharan Africa experiences an accelerated epidemiological transition, we aim to further strengthen the SAM study as a unique resource for cancer research in the region by expanding its scope. Specifically, we aim to 1) construct a new nationwide cohort of people living with diabetes and cancer outcomes in South Africa, 2) compare temporal trends of infection-related and infection-unrelated cancers among people with or without HIV, and 3) examine potential synergistic effects of HIV and diabetes mellitus on cancer risk in South Africa. 
 
Methods: The proposed research is organized in three work packages (WPs): WP1) SAM expansion: We will use state-of-the-art machine-learning based, probabilistic record linkage methods on diabetes-related laboratory records such as HbA1C and blood glucose from the NHLS to identify records belonging to the same person based on names, date of birth, sex, and facility. We will then probabilistically link this diabetes cohort to cancer diagnoses from the NCR. If individuals in the diabetes cohort cannot be linked to the SAM cohort, they will be assumed to be HIV-negative, while PWH in the current SAM cohort not linked to the diabetes cohort will be assumed to be free from diabetes. PWH in the current SAM cohort who can be linked to the new diabetes cohort will be assumed to live with both conditions. All linkages will be performed at the NCR located on the NHLS campus in Johannesburg, South Africa. WP2) Cancer trends in people with and without HIV: Using flexible parametric survival models, we will estimate the incidence rates of infection-related and infection-unrelated cancers among people with and without HIV as a function of calendar year, stratified by sex and age group. We will use Joinpoint models to identify temporal trends in age-standardized cancer rates by sex and HIV status. Among PWH, we will further examine temporal cancer trends by estimating the association of the population-level antiretroviral (ART) coverage on cancer rates using Poisson regression models, stratified by sex. ART coverage estimates for South Africa will be retrieved from the Thembisa model. WP3) Multimorbidity and cancer: We will examine the synergistic effect of both HIV and diabetes by comparing incidence rates of various infection-related and infection-unrelated cancers as a function of age among people living with both HIV and diabetes to those affected by one of these conditions only using flexible parametric survival models.

Impact: The expanded SAM study will provide unique insights into cancer trends in sub-Saharan Africa, as the region faces both a high HIV prevalence and a rapidly increasing burden of non-communicable diseases including diabetes. The findings of the proposed project will be highly relevant for cancer control programs in South Africa and other low- and middle-income settings with a high HIV burden, experiencing an accelerated epidemiological transition.
Keywords: Cancer, Diabetes, Epidemiology, HIV, South Africa, cancer, diabetes mellitus, incidence, record linkage

Title: Organizational learning from product failure: Utilizing artificial intelligence to mitigate the direct and indirect negative spillover effects of product recalls
Abstract:
This multi-disciplinary project aims to deepen understanding of how organizational learning from product failure affects future product development efforts. Learning from negative feedback is a central topic in organization theory, and the notion of adaptive firm response is fundamental to explaining organizational effectiveness, performance, and survival. This is especially true for firms operating in highly competitive, knowledge-intensive industries, where collaboration amongst interdependent, hyper-specialized experts is necessary to timely generate high quality innovation. Collaboration among hyper-specialized experts working on complex tasks often demands greater communication and coordination across the scientific team's knowledge base, leading to higher knowledge integration challenges that can result in reduced product safety and efficacy especially when competitive and economic incentives motivate a race for time-to-market.

Adopting a holistic perspective on organizational learning from product failure, we seek to better understand how a scientific team's knowledge base can predict the propensity of hazards and diminished e?cacy in innovative products, and how a subsequent product recall affects not only firm financial stakeholders, but also triggers negative indirect spillovers that expose the vulnerable firm-dependent stakeholders to significant hazards. In doing so, we will explore how emerging technologies such as Artificial Intelligence, machine learning, and natural language processing can be used for early identification and accurate evaluation of indicators signaling negative product experiences to manage the hazards more effectively and possibly preemptively. The importance of such firm capabilities is twofold: first, learning from product failure can improve internal product development ensuring the development teams possess expertise and complementary knowledge to develop better products. Second, understanding the feedback loop is essential for managerial decision-making as it can help to avoid allocating organizational resources to complaints that do not require attention, while ensuring that critical product failures that jeopardize user safety are attended to. Such firm capabilities enable prompt and cost-effective remediation of critical product failures, as the mismanaging of product failure events can have severe negative repercussions for companies and end users. 

We undertake our empirical inquiry within the context of the pharmaceutical product development cycle, concentrating on pharmacovigilance—activities linked to the identification, evaluation, understanding, and prevention of unintended but harmful events experienced by a patient and attributed to the use of a prescription medication. Using a variety of methodologies including survival analysis based models, panel analyses, machine learning, and natural language processing, we evaluate the capacity of a scientific team's knowledge base to predict the incidence of such adverse events (AEs) in FDA-approved drugs with a focus on interventional clinical studies. Then, we investigate how different types of pharmacovigilance following the marketing of the product might explain the timing of AE reporting and subsequent drug recall. We analyze reporting to the FDA’s Adverse Event Participation system (FAERS), as well as online general-purpose social media platforms, patient-driven communities, and professional-driven networks. Next, we analyze the application of emerging technologies to enhance early signal identification and assessment accuracy, as well as the extent to which firms learn to enhance future product development. Finally, we explore the competitive consequences of drug recalls on the firm, including revisions to the risk structure of its product development portfolio through decreased investment in high-risk products, especially orphan drug-designated therapies that are developed to treat rare medical conditions. In doing so, we highlight the overlooked, but detrimental hazards of product recalls on vulnerable stakeholders, particularly patients with rare or difficult-to-treat diseases who critically depend on product availability and future product innovation. The World Health Organization acknowledges 7,000 rare diseases that affect 300 million individuals worldwide, with more than fifty percent of these cases occurring in children. This grand societal challenge is rooted in institutional, economic, and organizational factors that impede incentives for innovation. We study reasons other than the high financial costs why pharmaceutical companies do not invest in drug development and explore how management theory can contribute to understanding and addressing this social dilemma and stimulate “organization for good”.

Title: NLP in support of Pharmacovigilance: QUality Adverse Drug Reaction AcTIve Control (QUADRATIC)
Abstract:
Pharmacovigilance is the science and activities related to the detection, assessment, understanding, and prevention of adverse effects of drugs, or of any other drug-related problems. It is a critical component of drug safety, and it is essential for the safe and effective use of medicines. Natural language processing (NLP) is a branch of artificial intelligence that deals with the analysis of natural language. NLP can be used to extract information from unstructured text, such as medical reports, and make it available as structured data. 

In the domain of pharmacovigilance, NLP can be used to identify potential safety signals from volumes of data too large for human processing. This can be done by analyzing the text of medical reports and identifying words or phrases that are associated with a particular safety issue. Moreover, NLP can be used to improve the accuracy and completeness of ADR reporting. Traditional methods of ADR reporting rely on manual data entry, which is time-consuming and error-prone. NLP can be used to automate ADR reporting by extracting relevant information from unstructured data sources and populating ADR reports. This can save time and improve the quality of ADR reporting. NLP can also be used to identify potential duplicates and inconsistencies in ADR reporting, ensuring that ADR data is accurate and up-to-date.

In this project, we aim to investigate the potential of state-of-the-art NLP methods applied to the automated processing of clinical records in order to provide reliable signals for the potential presence of adverse drug reactions (ADRs) in the context of pharmacovigilance. Concretely, if the project is successful, the partner hospital will be able to significantly improve the detection of ADRs, and once a similar approach is adopted at other Swiss hospitals, it could have a major downstream impact on public health.

The project will follow an iterative incremental approach, consisting of development of new models and annotation of more data. At each step, the dataset validated up to that point will be used to train the new model to be deployed at the next step. As a secondary effect of this process, a sizable dataset of validated and annotated reports will be incrementally produced.
Keywords: Clinical Text Processing, Natural Language Processing, Pharmacovigilance, Text Mining

Title: Multimodal machine learning for remote sensing information fusion
Abstract:
The research of this project opens new avenues in remote sensing information fusion. Recently, remote sensing has seen important changes, as many new satellite and airborne sensors have been developed and access to optical information has become much easier. Users are now overwhelmed by the sheer amount of information, mainly but not exclusively optical, at their disposal. New strategies for combining and fusing these sources of information are therefore much needed. 

The research will develop the fundamental knowledge and the tools to integrate sources of information of either similar or widely different natures, in view of producing more comprehensive and highly-informative products for endusers working in domains such as post-catastrophe assessment, urban development or climate studies. It will consider different data modalities, such as images from different sensors, but also vector layers, in-situ measurements, zonal statistics or user knowledge. This highly-informative sources are nearly always discontinuous and uncertain, which has so far prevented their efficient use in remote sensing. I will propose solutions inspired by advances in machine learning and computer vision, yet specific to the problematics of remote sensing data, to deal with this unreliability and exploit the complementarities and specific strengths of the different sources into integrated fusing schemes.
Keywords: Crowdsourcing, Data fusion, Hyperspectral imaging, Machine learning, Multimodal, Multisource, Remote sensing, Uncertainty estimation, Very-high resolution

Title: Highspeed Respiratory Motion Prediction in Liver MRI through Simultaneous Ultrasound Acquisition
Abstract:
In MR-guided therapy, the sampling rate is a limiting factor because there is always a trade-off between image quality and acquisition speed. This is a problem in situations where the target structure is subject to respiratory motion. Modelling, predicting and compensation this type of motion has thus become an intense field of research during the past ten years.

The aim of this project is to investigate on algorithms to jointly model respiratory motion data from ultrasound, typically acquired at a high temporal resolution, and MR images acquired at a much slower rate. More specifically, the idea is to apply machine-learning algorithms online (as data comes in) for subject-specific modelling, analysis and prediction of respiratory motion at the acquisition rate of the ultrasound device. Naturally, the algorithms must be computationally efficient in order to be real-time capable.
Keywords: Biomedical Engineering, Image Guided Therapy, Magnetic Resonance Imaging, Medical Image Analysis, Medical Imaging, Respiratory Motion Modelling, Ultrasound Imaging

Title: Predicting the real-world effectiveness and safety of medical interventions
Abstract:
Background: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are key to comparative effectiveness research. Meta-analyses typically use study-level data and aim to identify which is the best treatment on average. However, a treatment that is best on average may perform less well (or may be harmful) for certain patients. Meta-analysis of individual patient data (IPD) from RCTs can address this issue, by utilizing information on patient-level characteristics. However, RCTs usually employ strict experimental settings and inclusion criteria thus hampering the generalizability of RCT findings in less controlled, ‘real-world’ clinical settings. Recently developed methods attempted to incorporate real-world (observational) studies in evidence synthesis, aiming to bridge this gap. However, these attempts only focused on estimating average treatment effects. To this date, there is a gap in methods for making personalized, patient-specific predictions about the real-world effects of medical interventions.

Objectives: The overarching objective of this project is to develop new, reliable methods for jointly synthesising randomized and observational evidence in order to provide personalized predictions for the performance of medical interventions. The project will be implemented with a clear focus on predicting treatment effects in real-life clinical settings. The specific aims of the project are the following: 
(1) To develop methods for selecting patient characteristics to include in meta-analytical prediction models. 
(2) To develop methods for predicting the effects of medical interventions in real-world settings in terms of effectiveness and safety, so as to facilitate a personalized choice of treatments.
(3) To develop methods for monitoring patient outcomes and adapting treatment decisions.
(4) To develop easy-to-use online tools that will utilize all developed methods in order to facilitate and enhance the decision-making process in every-day clinical practice.
(5) To provide proof of concept by evaluating the proposed framework in real clinical examples from depression.

Methods: For the objectives of this project we will explore and further develop (i) machine-learning methods for identifying patient characteristics with strong predictive properties, at the meta-analysis level; (ii) IPD network meta-analysis methods that will combine randomized and real-world evidence regarding a range of alternative, competing interventions, in order to build prediction models for guiding real-world treatment decisions; (iii) methods for building meta-analytical prediction models for disease progression; (iv) tools for making all results available to patients and doctors through easy-to-use web-applications. All methods that will be developed for the purposes of this project will be showcased using real clinical examples. 

Impact: This project aims to help every-day clinical practice move away from the one-size-fits-all approach of treating patients, by using evidence-based methods to tailor treatment strategies to the individual characteristics, needs and preferences of patients. Overall, the project represents a novel approach to integrating different pieces of evidence to answer patient-specific, real-world-oriented questions. The scientific output of this project will be of high interest to research scientists, biostatisticians and methodologists, while the applications to real examples are expected to have a strong clinical impact.
Keywords: biostatistics, evidence-based medicine, meta-analysis, personalized medicine, prediction modelling

Title: DeepLUS4TB: Automated Interpretation of Lung Ultrasound Images for  Tuberculosis Triage using Deep Learning
Abstract:
Background and Rationale: Tuberculosis (TB) is an infectious disease that primarily affects the lungs. Although treatable, 1.6 million people died from TB in 2021. More than 95% of TB deaths occurred in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), partly due to delayed or missed diagnosis when access to healthcare is limited. Timely diagnosis of TB is critical for effective treatment and preventing further spread of the disease. As an affordable, non-invasive, portable tool, lung ultrasound (LUS) is a promising candidate for TB triage in resource-limited settings to identify patients requiring further microbiological testing. However, interpretation of the acquired LUS images depends on the operator and requires expert knowledge.

Objectives and Specific Aims: As outlined in Figure 1, the goal of this research project titled DeepLUS4TB is to explore the applicability of deep learning solutions to support the interpretation of LUS images for TB triage. In Objective 1, novel modular multi-modal deep learning models for TB classification will be developed, aiming to meet the World Health Organization (WHO)’s target product profile for triage tests (=90% sensitivity, =70% specificity). The focus of Objective 2 is to improve the acquisition protocol of LUS images to ensure model robustness, efficiency, and interpretability even in cases when medical expertise is unavailable. In Objective 3, the project will be embedded in a personalized federated learning platform that ensures data sovereignty and ownership. This approach will enable collaborative learning across multiple sites and subpopulations while keeping the data local and under the control of the data owners. 

Methods: Using a LUS dataset collected alongside multi-modal data in an ongoing multi-site observational cohort study in Benin, Mali, and South Africa, existing state-of-the-art deep learning approaches for COVID-19 detection will be adapted and compared for a binary classification task into the classes “TB” and “non-TB”. To include other patient-specific information, a novel modular multi-modal approach will be investigated to boost the performance of the deep learning model. During a research stay at Tintswalo Hospital in rural South Africa, the impact of variations in the operator’s expertise on the performance of deep learning models will be explored. To increase model robustness, an interpretable model will be developed for automatic analysis of LUS videos acquired by non-experts, so-called blind ultrasound sweeps. Finally, an existing federated learning platform will be adapted to the multi-site LUS dataset. The bias between the different subpopulations needs to be addressed with domain adaptation methods to improve the generalizability of the model.

Expected Results and Impact: The delivery of reliable, robust, and interpretable multi-modal deep learning methods that automatically predict a TB triage score based on LUS data is expected. Successful implementation of an automated triage tool could have significant impact for improving TB management in resource-limited settings. It will contribute to early detection and timely treatment of TB cases, preventing the spread and improving antimicrobial stewardship.
Keywords: Deep Learning, Lung Ultrasound, Medical Image Analysis, Tuberculosis

Title: Unified Accelerators for Post-Moore Machine Learning
Abstract:
Investment in machine learning is slated to continue to grow at an exponential rate (roughly 20%/year) thanks to its myriad of emerging applications to improve prediction and decision making in all sectors of society, ranging from science and health to commerce and entertainment. Similarly, improvements in algorithms have led to unprecedented growth in the complexity of deep neural networks (DNNs), resulting in a commensurate increase in demand for computing. Unfortunately, the silicon fabrication processes that have led to an exponential growth in digital platform density and efficiency since the 70s have slowed down (from 41%/year to 15%/year in recent years).

To address this problem, researchers and vendors have resorted to accelerator design for DNNs because programmable accelerators can improve silicon efficiency by two orders of magnitude [27, 15, 23, 26, 43]. Unfortunately, the two popular DNN workloads, training to create models, and inference to use them for prediction, have vastly diverse accelerator requirements and have thus led to a divergence in infrastructure. Training accelerators require floating-point arithmetic, exhibit memory footprints in the range of a few GBs [78] which cannot be easily accommodated on chip, and have been designed for offline use with no latency constraints. In contrast, modern inference accelerators such as Graphcore [19] or Brainwave [15] primarily use fixed-point arithmetic, have on-chip memory sizes ranging from tens up to hundreds of MBs, which is sufficient to accommodate the memory working set of state-of-the-art DNN models and are online services with tight service-level tail latency constraints [48, 15].

In our prior work, we have argued and demonstrated that it is possible to train DNN workloads with a novel arithmetic encoding, called Hybrid Block Floating Point (HBFP), that allows for a majority of the arithmetic operations in (i.e., tensor products) to be performed in fixed-point arithmetic, limiting floating point to a minimal set of operations requiring large magnitude variations (i.e., gradient updates and activations) [12, 35, 69]. Such an encoding creates the opportunity to consolidate the two aforementioned divergent DNN accelerator designs into a unified accelerator that can accurately train DNNs, perform inference without any loss in throughput or impact on tail latency, and enable combined online/interactive training and inference. 

In this project, we propose to investigate a clean-slate algorithm/architecture co-design of unified accelerators for dense DNN workloads (e.g., CNNs, LSTMs, BERT) in both single-node and multi-node systems. In particular, we will investigate the following:

- Numerical Encoding and Training Techniques: Our prior work [14] only investigated minimizing the number of exponent and mantissa bits across entire tensors. Our preliminary results indicate an interplay between block size and the number of mantissa bits requiring a further investigation of the optimal encoding space. We will also investigate error recovery, loss scaling, and mixed-precision to help further minimize encoding.

- Single-node Unified Accelerators: Our prior work [14] only investigated sensitivity to batch size in inference accelerators. Our preliminary results indicate high sensitivity in array utilization and effective throughput to memory hierarchy, interconnect topology, and workloads. 
We will investigate the optimal space for single-node accelerators featuring multiple systolic arrays that are interconnected and backed by a memory hierarchy. These accelerators will include architectural support for mixed-precision for both inference and training. We will also investigate co-designed tiling schemes that enhance accelerator utilization for both uni- and multi-programmed workloads.

- Multi-node Unified Accelerators: We will explore the optimal design space for a multi-node accelerator and the opportunities in inter-node interconnect design to improve the performance. We will also investigate the impact of HBFP on gradient compression, sparsification, and quantization.
Keywords: Accelerators, Learning, Machine

Title: MyVoice: Myoelectric Vocal Interaction and Communication Engine
Abstract:
Silent Speech processing aims at making speech communication available to persons without a voice, and to people who require covert communication in public places. A team of two excellent researchers in Switzerland and Germany, with more than 10 years of experience in the field, proposes to substantially advance their state of the art system, making it a truly European technology which in the future can improve the lifes of hundreds of thousands of speech-impaired persons, and offer an efficient means of private and undisturbing communication to the general public. For this purpose, we ask for funding for two PhD students and two postdocs, for a total project duration of three years.
We (MW and TS) have been working together on using facial electromyographic (EMG) signals, which naturally emerge due to human muscle activity and can unintrusively be captured by surface electrodes, for speech recognition and (re-)synthesis.  Our work includes the first continuous EMG-based speech recognizer, the first EMG-based speech synthesis system which now works in real-time, as well as substantial steps towards training and adaptation with little supervision or even in an unsupervised scenario ("adaptation on the go").  The system was frequently featured in national and international press and TV (Sendung mit der Maus), and won diverse awards (CeBIT Top Ten Attractions 2010, Alcatel Lucent Award for Technical Communication 2012, Biosignals Conference Best Student Paper 2013, Google Faculty Research Award 2019 (TS)).
We build on our existing work in Silent Speech processing with state-of-the-art neural network architectures, where bioelectric traces of articulatory movements of a speaker are captured with small, nonintrusive surface electrodes; this allows capturing speech even when the acoustic signal is not present. In MyVoice we will tackle the key roadblocks which so far have prevented Silent Speech processing from becoming a commercially viable communication tool, and a truly useable speech prosthesis for those persons without a voice; many years of experience have shown us quite clearly where these challenges lie. The fundational/algorithmic part of our research will cover fast and efficient training and adaptation in realistic scenarios, where the recognizer must be immediately usable when a communication scenario arises, despite EMG signal discrepancies between recording sessions; and prosody generation and output naturalness: here one needs to depart from rigid measures of reconstruction accuracy and instead incorporate naturalness constraints into the speech synthesis process, as well as generate a  prosodic contour which is plausible and acoustically pleasant, but also reflects the speaker's intents (for example, marks a question by rising intonation).  This algorithmic part forms the basis for our novel user-in-the-loop training: We have made the experience that users adapt their (silent) speaking style to the machine, which not only improves output quality, but also reduces speaking mode discrepancies, i.e. different articulation styles between normal and silent speech. We aim at making this learning process explicit: while the underlying neural network is trained towards a person's specific EMG patterns, the user likewise receives real-time feedback and can intuitively experiment with the system.

Title: The role of microscale processes on fluid-solid reactions in porous media: unsaturated versus multiphase flow
Abstract:
Porous media are highly heterogeneous and often transient environments, where processes can occur down to the sub-millimeter and seconds scale. In this complex mosaic, the movement of immiscible fluid phases exerts an important control on the mixing and dilution of dissolved chemicals and on processes at solid surfaces. As a first example, many contaminants –such as pesticides or per- and poly-fluoroalkyl substances, PFAS– are found adsorbed in the unsaturated zone. This leads to retarded transport, one of the most important natural forms of groundwater resources protection. Yet, we still ignore the extent to which mixing of these contaminants with the resident water controls their adsorption/desorption, and its dependence on the water content and flow dynamics (unsaturated flow, without displacement of air, and multiphase flow, with displacement of air). As a second example, mineral dissolution in deep aquifers is responsible, among others, for the increase of porosity in CO2 geological sequestration. Minerals such as calcite, dolomite, and clay minerals undergo a reaction with carbonic acid, derived from CO2, leading to a rock dissolution, hence affecting flow patterns. Yet, we still do not fully understand the interplay between fluid flow dynamics, solute transport and mineral dissolution because of the lack of a microscale perspective in studies of fluid–solid interaction. Similarly, subsurface applications that are key in our aims to mitigate climate change and achieve energy transition, such as hydrogen storage, lack a full understanding of microscale processes that allow us to enhance their efficiency.

These two processes –adsorption/desorption (surface reactions without altering the geometry) and mineral dissolution (the geometry evolves)– are examples of the importance of the microscale coupling of physical and mineralogical heterogeneity and flow dynamics on surface phenomena. The rates of these processes are scale-dependent, and in particular, often decrease as the scale increases (i.e., from pore scale to large/field scale), which makes modeling and prediction at large scale difficult and uncertain. While translating mechanistic understanding at the microscale to larger scales is an arduous task, such microscale understanding is key for advancing not only the development of models, but also our conceptual understanding of which processes are important at the scale of applications.

This project aims to advance our understanding of fluid–solid reactions as a function of microscale flow dynamics and to assess the transferability of this control to larger scales. In three work packages (WP), each addressing specific hypotheses through the development and application of microscale technologies and a new modeling approach, we aim for the first time to:

WP1. Quantify the impact of porous media connectivity, liquid phase saturation and flow dynamics on surface reactions, by developing novel functionalized micromodels, which incorporate reactive surfaces, together with fluorescence microscopy and direct numerical simulations.
WP2. Determine the control exerted by liquid phase saturation and flow dynamics on solids dissolution, by quantifying changes at a range of temporal scales, from hours to weeks, of the geometry (by interferometry) in geo-material microfluidic devices, which incorporate physical and mineral heterogeneity.
WP3. Assess the transferability of the microscale observations to larger scales, by performing column experiments together with the coupling of a continuum numerical model and a machine-learning framework.
In addressing these aims, we will shed light on previously inaccessible and yet fundamental features of surface phenomena in porous media. 

Our main goals are both to improve our understanding of the microscale processes governing the fate of contaminants and geochemical reactions in natural systems and industrial applications, and to enhance upscaled modeling of the impacts of these processes.
Keywords: adsorption, aquifers, dissolution, phases saturation, pore scale, porous media, soils, surface reactions, upscaling

Title: Robust Digital Signing with Deep Neural Networks
Abstract:
We propose to develop novel technology that allows to cryptographically sign media content in a robust manner. The problem we address with this comes with the incredibly enhanced capabilities to easily fabricate credible high quality media content and the potential impact this can have on society. We believe it is of great importance to counterbalance these developments with tools that allow to verify integrity and authenticity of media content. Traditional approaches to digitally signing documents seem limited: They are based on simple hashes generated from the content which are sensitive to the tiniest modifications in the data. This, however, is in conflict with standard procedures used to disseminate media content through news portals or social media platforms where content is often compressed for more efficient transmission.
We here propose to build a system that is robust against such modifications in the data but still is sensitive to unwanted manipulations of the content. The system will be composed of various deep neural network models. One model is trained to provide more robust hashes (‘content encoding’) which then can be cryptographically signed. Another component is trained to hide the resulting signatures in the image, not perceivable to the human eye but such that it can be revealed for verification purposes. For content encoding and message hiding we intend to adopt recent developments in deep learning. Our proposal is to combine them with cryptographic digital signing into one single tool chain. To this end we will build an integrated  system that will be  sensitive to forbidden transformations, ie. content modifications, but insensitive to admissible transformations, e.g. compression.
For the proposed work, we will restrict to image data. But the developed technology will lay the foundation for future extensions that will cope with video and audio data.
The proposal is original and unconventional since it combines multiple more or less established technologies from deep learning and cryptography into a system that addresses severe problems that affect society as a whole, specifically in the Western democracies.
Keywords: crypthography, data authenticity, deep fakes, deep learning, image processing, machine learning

Title: Re-engineering informal construction through circular practices and models
Abstract: South Africa has 2.2 million informal dwellers mostly concentrated in urban centers, where approximately 2,700 informal settlements exist. This project proposes an integrated platform to re-engineer informal construction through circular practices and models. In most emerging economies the informal dwellers salvage some waste for informal construction. The informal dwellers usually reuse construction and demolition waste such plastics, cement bags, corrugated iron sheets, steel poles, or timber. Most of these materials are reused by the informal dwellers with little to no attention being given to their potential lifespan, chemical, biological composition, health and safety hazards, environmental impacts and so on. Therefore, the use of material passports to capture information on the repurposed waste is likely to equip informal dwellers with the adequate knowledge on the materials that they are using to construct their dwellings. In the event that there is a need for the dwellers to migrate due to natural catastrophes like floods, the informal dwellers can potentially disassemble their dwellings and reconstruct elsewhere. Making a decision to deconstruct and reconstruct in another location is possible when the informal dwellers are well aware of their building material status in terms of lifespan, quality and composition. Recent advances in deep learning can help process the large datasets  of airborne imagery to audit building components. Derived meaningful insights from the highly unstructured image data will be collected in a construction materials exchange platform to efficiently store and share information. This will help strengthen social capital by providing existing informal construction material businesses an online presence which could allow for increased market demand, new ventures and collaborations.
Keywords: Architecture, Circular construction, Digital empowerment, Engineering and Construction, Material passports, Platforms, Reuse

Title: Abstraction Heuristics for Planning and Combinatorial Search
Abstract:
Automated planning is one of the traditional and central research
areas in artificial intelligence. In this context, planning means that
an agent reasons over its possible courses of action in order to find
out which activities it needs to carry out in order to reach its
goals. For many applications of planning, it is desirable to produce
not just any plan, but one that minimizes some cost metric, a problem
called optimal planning. The most successful optimal planning
algorithms of the last decade fall into the general class of heuristic
search methods, typically using A* or a similar search algorithm.

A heuristic function, or heuristic for short, is a function that
estimates how far away the planning agent is from its goal. More
formally, a heuristic maps states s of the task to be solved to
numerical estimates of the minimal cost of reaching the goal from s.
For a heuristic search algorithm such as A* to be efficient, it must
be supplied with a heuristic that is reasonably quickly computable as
well as accurate (i.e., it should provide estimates that are close to
the actual cost). To provide optimality guarantees, the heuristic must
also be admissible, i.e., never overestimate the true cost.

Abstraction heuristics, such as pattern database heuristics and
merge-and-shrink heuristics, have been a very successful class of
admissible heuristics for optimal planning and related search
problems. An abstraction heuristic maps states from the actual
(concrete) state space of the planning task into a smaller space (the
abstract state space) in a homomorphic manner, i.e., preserving state
transitions and goal states. The cost to reach the goal in the
abstract space then serves as a cost estimate for the concrete space.

Abstraction heuristics have been a subject of intense study in the
planning literature in recent years, leading to several key
breakthroughs both for practical algorithms and in the theoretical
understanding of such heuristics. The latter theoretical studies in
particular have shown that state-of-the-art abstraction heuristics,
despite their significant successes, do not realize the power of the
general approach to its full potential.

The research we propose here aims at reducing this gap between
practical performance and theoretical promises. Specifically, we
pursue three objectives:

O1. To advance the theory of abstraction heuristics in order to
improve our theoretical understanding of their capabilities, their
limitations, and their relationship to other commonly used approaches
for deriving admissible heuristics.

O2. To develop improved abstraction heuristics for optimal planning,
hence raising the state of the art for optimal planning systems.

O3. To transfer the new insights on abstraction heuristics to
applications of optimal search outside of automated planning, in order
to advance the state of the art in these areas.
Keywords: abstraction, artificial intelligence, automated planning, combinatorial search, heuristic search

Title: Real-time detection of High-Frequency Oscillations with a Neuromorphic Device
Abstract:
About 30% of patients with focal epilepsy do not respond to antiepileptic medication, which results in about 200 new patients per year that could benefit from epilepsy surgery in Switzerland. Prior to surgery, intracranial EEG (iEEG) recordings may be crucial to define the epileptogenic zone. The epileptogenic zone is the area of cortex that is indispensable for the generation of epileptic seizures and whose removal is the prerequisite for postsurgical seizure freedom. Intraoperatively, the electrocorticogram (ECoG) can help to identify the epileptogenic zone. However, the delineation of the epileptogenic zone based on currently available standard methods is far from perfect, so surgical resection does not always lead to seizure freedom. New biomarkers for the extra- as well as intraoperative detection of the epileptogenic zone in the interictal state are therefore urgently needed.

High-frequency oscillations (HFOs) in the iEEG and ECoG have been recently established as suitable biomarkers of epileptogenic tissue that may help to identify the epileptogenic zone more specifically than standard methods do. In our previous project, we have devised an automated computer algorithm that is effective in defining and pinpointing a clinically relevant HFO. We validated the algorithm on large iEEG datasets from Montreal and ECoG from Utrecht against postsurgical seizure outcome and also applied it to recordings obtained in Zurich. Using a prospective definition, we have thus obtained a large library of clinically relevant HFO.

In our proposed project, we aim to develop a dedicated embedded electronic device that can quickly and reliably detect HFO. We follow a co-design approach that relies on emerging ultra low-power neural network computing technologies to implement brain-inspired algorithms embodied in Spiking Neural Networks (SNN). Our library of clinically relevant HFO serves as a training dataset for determining the optimal SNN. The SNN is then implemented in neuromorphic hardware, interfaced to a custom low noise amplifier. Being battery-powered, the device is easily integrated in the data stream during clinical recordings, in parallel to the certified medical devices in routine clinical use.

Complementing the technology developments, we record interictally from candidates for epilepsy surgery. The first recordings are with scalp EEG and then - when medically indicated - also directly from the cortical surface during invasive presurgical iEEG and during intraoperative ECoG. This activity will allow us to validate our self-developed device by comparing the sensitivity and specificity of the SNN with the routine data stream and the established HFO detection computer algorithm.

From a neurosurgical perspective, measuring HFO within short time and with sufficient accuracy during surgery is an exciting prospect. While treatment will further be based on clinical standards, rapidly available HFO may be considered in the choice of surgical strategy. In several patients, all necessary information might be obtainable during surgery and the risks of presurgical iEEG might be avoided. This technological advance provides a competitive edge for UniversitätsSpital Zürich and an advantage for the patients.

Looking ahead from the proposed project, we aim to establish HFO as a biomarker for epileptogenic tissue in iEEG and ECoG. Similarly, detecting HFO in scalp EEG by a dense array of neuromorphic devices may monitor the efficacy of an anti-epileptic treatment in individual patients. Independent from HFO, a well-chosen battery of cognitive tasks may indicate the functional integrity of brain structures through iEEG recordings. In a very broad view, we are the first to apply neuromorphic technology in clinical research and create a bridge between the two disciplines.

Title: RATIONAL: Robust Augmented Retrieval for Natural Language Inference over Transformer-based Models
Abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as universal models for addressing language understanding and inference tasks. However, In order to operate factually and rigorously, these models need to be provided with a relevant associated factual context and to reason systematically and controllably over the retrieved evidence. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) became the complementary architectural mechanism which enables LLMs to operate factually, in which a retrieval step delivers the associated facts relevant within a specific task. However, there is a disconnect between the performance of retrieval models, which are grounded on textual embeddings (comparatively lower semantic granularity and performance) and the capacity of LLMs to interpret and operate over these results. As a result, LLMs are currently bound to the comparatively lower performance of RAGs and to their ability to critically reason over these facts. 
RATIONAL aims to develop new methods to support LLMs to perform factual and controlled evidence-based Natural Language Inference (NLI). At the centre of its methodological contributions, RATIONAL will develop: 
(i) new evidence retrieval models which can support crossing the semantic gap between abstract query intents and concrete evidence, by developing novel query augmentation paradigms, sentence embedding methods and contextual retrieval generation methods specialised for crossing the intent-evidence abstraction gap.
(ii) new evidence-based Natural Language Inference (NLI) models which are capable of integrating and reasoning over the retrieved facts in a controllable and critical manner. These new NLI methods will concentrate on the integration of formal epistemological mechanisms and joint quantitative and qualitative reasoning methods to support evidence-based reasoning.

Title: Error-controlled statistical and causal learning via knockoffs
Abstract:
In modern science, researchers often first collect a large amount of data and then try to use it to discover meaningful insights. For example, in genome-wide association studies (GWAS), researchers may have access to millions of single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in thousands of individuals, and the goal could be to identify which SNPs correlate with a phenotype of interest. Such a scientific paradigm, however, may lead to many irreproducible discoveries. This relates to the irreproducibility crisis (Ioannidis, 2005; Begley and Ellis, 2012; Baker, 2016), a major concern for scientific research which has gained a lot of attention in recent years.

The reason for the irreproducibility crisis is complicated, but it is clear that error-controlled statistical methods are desired, as they guarantee to control a certain error rate of the discoveries. For example, a powerful method called the knockoff filter (Barber and Candès, 2015; Candès et al., 2018) was developed recently for variable selection problems, and it controls the finite sample false discovery rate (FDR).

The overall objective of this project is to further develop error-controlled statistical methods based on the knockoff idea, so that more trustworthy and reproducible scientific findings can be discovered. More precisely, we plan to investigate the following two main projects:

A. Data-driven approach to choose hyperparameters of the knockoff method while still providing error control: One of the advantages of the knockoff method is its flexibility. For example, there are many ways to construct knockoffs, and many machine learning algorithms (e.g., lasso, random forests, or neural networks) can be used as an intermediate step of the knockoff method to measure the importance of variables. In other words, there are many hyperparameters. Any pre-set choice of hyperparameters provides the desired error control, but the power of the method can vary largely depending on this choice and the data at hand. This leads to the important problem of choosing hyperparameters for the knockoff method. This problem also relates to other challenges such as de-randomizing model-X knockoffs (Ren et al., 2021) and finding discoveries in multiple resolutions (Katsevich and Sabatti, 2019; Sesia et al., 2020). Addressing this problem is crucial for the practical usage of the knockoff method.

B. Error-controlled causal learning methods based on the knockoff idea: Discovering causal mechanisms is often the highest goal of scientific research. For example, identifying which gene expression levels cause, rather than correlate with, a phenotype of interest would be very valuable. We aim to develop powerful error-controlled causal learning methods for direct cause selection and for causal structure learning problems, based on the knockoff idea. For direct cause selection, we plan to focus on a multi-environment setting where the invariance principle could be used to explore causality (e.g., Peters et al., 2016). For causal structure learning, we plan to build on our recent work on Gaussian graphical models (Li and Maathuis, 2021).
Keywords: Causal discovery, Error-control guarantee, False discovery rate (FDR), Knockoffs, Selective inference

Title: NA
Abstract:
The outstanding crisis of our time, climate change, and also the ongoing war in Ukraine, are forcing us as a society to pursue greater energy efficiency and shift away from fossil fuels towards renewable sources. However, the complexity of the operation and control of power grids is drastically increased by the integration of renewable energy with decentralized feed-in from regenerative energies and dynamic demand responses. Traditionally, power supply by power plants varies on a long time scale in the range of hours. Now, fluctuations take place in the order of minutes. To prevent power systems from becoming increasingly vulnerable to blackouts, the flexibility of power grids urgently needs to be enhanced by improved status control and optimization. For this purpose, a current measurement that is as precise as possible within electrical conductors and power semiconductors is crucial in order to enable efficient control at all levels. The intended cooperation project is thus dedicated to the research topic of ML (Machine Learning) supported quantum sensors based on NV centres with the aim of enabling an integrated regional smart energy system of high flexibility. This corresponds to the first dimension of integration of the call - Smart energy system integration. The success of the future interlocking of regenerative energy sources is guaranteed by the communication between sub-omponents of generation and storage, consumers, machines and people, i.e. relating to the third dimension of integration of the call - Innovation ecosystems and Integration with local & regional development. It primarily depends on the availability of stable, permanent and, above all,decentralized
status recording. The basic prerequisite for this, however, is that the current major shortcomings in the
existing technologies can be overcome in order to make their acceptance possible in the first place.
The primary goal of the proposed project is to put forward a lossless and purely optically connected current measurement in combination with ML techniques for the monitoring of medium voltage power lines and power converters for grid connected batteries and renewables (Fig. 1). Within the planned collaboration, proven research findings from the fields of quantum technologies will be used or further developed in order to connect the sensors and the respective associated quantum elements in a self-calibrating manner without hysteresis and memory effect. At the high level of the system, ML will be used remotely or locally to classify its state from data signals collected at a (small) number of points, allowing for the early identification of disturbances and for proposing efficient countermeasures. At the individual level, ML approaches will be employed to analyse the fluorescence spectra and predict the magnetic field, as well as, the current within the quantum sensors. Also, the charge and health states of the batteries will be derived through prediction from numeral data and image spectra. In a next step, the optimization of battery usage, and ultimately of the power grid, will be carried out by examining the prediction of ML techniques for time series analysis regarding the consumption and photovoltaic production. The time series will, in addition to the data from the quantum sensors, also encompass exogenous variables, such as weather, cloud drift and solar irradiance; the last two will be predicted from sky camera images. In this way, the power distribution of the network, e.g. the scheduling of charging processes and consumption, can be optimized on the base of the ML forecasting. This will affect all involved economic sectors, e.g. municipal infrastructure, industry, agriculture, transport, as connected with the second dimension of integration of the call - Cross-sectoral integration.
Keywords: Distributed current measurement, Graph neural network, Logarithmic imaging, Machine learned calibration, Optically detected magnetic resonance, Optimization of auto-consumption, Prediction of production and demand, Quantum current sensor, Sensing array inversion, Solar irradiation forecasting, Topologocal mapping

Title: Combining MRI markers with sleep EEG features to track brain health and detect pathology
Abstract:
Age has been considered for a long time one of the dominant driving factors of disease progression in multiple sclerosis (MS). Independently of disease duration, older age raises the risk of MS progression and disability accumulation. At the same time, conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) biomarkers, including white matter lesion volume, weakly correlate with disease activity. Recently, advanced MS lesional biomarkers, such as cortical and paramagnetic rim lesions, have emerged as playing an important role in MS progression, but also do not adequately explain disability accumulation. Brain age estimation uses machine learning (ML) to predict the individual age from MRI and it is a potential marker for brain health and integrity. A combination of brain age and advanced lesional biomarkers could provide important insights into disease progression and disability accumulation in MS patients. This may be particularly helpful in expanding our understanding of the causes of cognitive deficits in MS, which are highly prevalent but poorly understood.

In this project, I will retrospectively analyze two unique datasets that include high-resolution MRI scans and cognitive scores of 165 MS patients (with 7 tesla (7T) and 3T scans) and ~1500 MS patients (with 3T scans), respectively, over two to three time-points. I propose three complementary work packages (WP) that, by leveraging structural MRI and novel ML approaches, aim at detecting relevant MS prognostic biomarkers and estimating disease progression. Brain age will be computed per each patient at baseline and at successive time-points. In addition, relevant MS lesional biomarkers will be detected semi-automatically with deep learning. The association between these findings and disability measures will be quantified analyzing cross-sectional data. Finally, I will develop a prediction model that, combining these potential prognostic biomarkers, estimates disease progression on longitudinal data.

This project has strong potential for real-world impact. Identifying MRI biomarkers relevant to brain health would enhance our general knowledge of brain aging. Furthermore, an automated machine learning method able to accurately predict multiple sclerosis progression would enable clinicians to provide a more accurate prognosis and might be useful as a modifiable outcome measure in clinical trials.
Keywords: Brain age, Brain health, Brain pathology, Deep learning, MRI, MRI biomarkers, Machine learning, Multiple sclerosis

Title: Creativity, Imagination and Tradition
Abstract:
Creativity is often defined as the ability of humans to come up with ideas or products that are original and valuable. However, sometimes we call ideas and products creative even though they are not original in any interesting sense, and some cases suggest that creative ideas are not necessarily valuable. Philosophers have proposed various distinctions to account for different levels and kinds of novelty, but the question whether creativity involves value remains disputed. This project aims to introduce a new way to account for conflicting intuitions by distinguishing two genuinely different notions of creativity: process creativity and product creativity. A special focus lies on creativity in the arts, the role of imagination in creative processes and the role of tradition in product creativity.
When it comes to creativity in the arts as well as in everyday life, our main interest is often a conscious and valuable imaginative process, which seemingly can only be ascribed to autonomous agents. This will be investigated as process creativity. However, there is a sense in which non-human animals and artificial intelligence (AI) systems can be creative: when we are concerned with creative ideas or objects, the novelty of the product relative to a tradition is in the center of our interest. This will be investigated as product creativity. 
The following general questions will guide the research. 1. What constitutes the experience of creative processes? The main theses are that novelty is not part of the experience of creating in the arts and that creative imaginative processes in the arts are driven and constrained by aesthetic value within a tradition. 2. What is the role of imagination in creative processes? The project includes a defence of the idea that creativity in the arts necessarily involves rich forms of imagination, such as phenomenal imagination. 3. How shall we define creativity? The main theses are that creativity in the arts is primarily a feature of a process, and that process creativity can influence how we judge the creativity of a product in a derivative sense. 4. How do we ascribe creativity to an idea or product? The project will explore how the idea that we call a new and surprising product ‘creative’ relies on the product being seen within a certain tradition. 5. What are the implications for the notion of imagination more broadly? Focusing on the case of literary fiction, the main thesis is that our engagement with literary fiction is creative, whether we write or read literary fiction. 6. What are the implications for the notion of creativity more broadly? The project aims to spell out the explanatory advantages and consequences of a distinction between process creativity and product creativity as two genuinely different kinds of creativity.
The project is divided into 3 subprojects, to be conducted by 3 researchers. Subproject 1, ‘Creativity and Imagination in Literary Writing’, will address questions 1 to 4 with a special focus on literary writing and will explore general implications for the notions of imagination and creativity, addressing questions 5 and 6. Subproject 2, ‘Culinary Creativity and Tradition’, will put special emphasis on exploring similarities and differences between creativity in the arts and everyday creativity by addressing questions 1 to 4 with respect to elite chef’s cooking and home cooking. Subproject 3, ‘The Creative Person’, will explore the consequences of the distinction between process and product creativity for the creative person, especially in the light of AI creativity. 
The project will contribute to two main areas in philosophy: aesthetics, in particular the philosophy of creativity, and the philosophy of mind, in particular the philosophy of imagination. In the philosophy of creativity, the project will emphasize the importance of looking at different domains separately and distinguishing the defining conditions for creative processes from the defining conditions for creative outputs. In the philosophy of imagination, it will help to further develop the concept of creative imagination and apply the debate concerning constraints on imagination to creativity in the arts by exploring aesthetic values as constraints. Through collaboration with the Webster Center for Creativity and Innovation and the Swiss Literature Institute Biel (amongst others), the project hopes to have an interdisciplinary impact as well as produce an output valuable to a broader audience.
Keywords: Aesthetic Value, Aesthetics, Artificial Intelligence, Creativity, Imagination, Literary Writing, Philosophy of Art, Philosophy of Food, Philosophy of Mind, The creative person, Tradition, Well-being

Title: Data-driven approximation of haemodynamics by combined reduced order modeling and deep neural networks
Abstract:
We are interested in numerical modeling and scientific computing in the fields of vascular flows, in particular for 
the computation of flow indicators for risk factors, for example for the evaluation of the risk of rupture of an anerusims, 
or the risk of heart-stroke. We aim at developing numerical methods to greatly improve the applicability of these methodologies in clinical settings. The project builds on the following main keypoints.

* Reduced Basis and Deep Neural Networks for time-dependent parametrized PDEs: we plan to extend our work presented in [@dalsanto2019pdednn] to the time dependent case. The Reduced Basis (RB) method allows to efficiently solve parametrized PDEs by reducing the dimensionality (i.e. the number of variables involved) of the high-fidelity model. Through its coupling with Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), in [@dalsanto2019pdednn] we show that we are able to incorporate measured data in the simulation: this allows to recover the physical parameters of the problem and - as a result of the proven robustness of DNNs with respect to noisy input - to alleviate the effects of uncertainty. In heamodynamics applications the time dependence plays a central role and the extension will therefore require careful settings and analysis. 

* Reduced Basis and Domain Decomposition methods for modular approximation of arteries: the underlying idea is to approximate the geometry of arteries as a composition of building blocks, such as tubes and bifurcations which are obtained from parametrized deformations of reference geometries. The advantage with respect to employing high-quality meshes of arteries is the development of automatic algorithms to generate such approximated geometries directly from medical images and the fast solution of the equations deriving from the RB method. For this reason, this technique can be considered a valid alternative to the popular geometrical multiscale models (see e.g. [@malossi2013implicit; @blanco2013continuity; @malossi2011algorithms]) for the approximation of the flow in large portions of arteries. As we shall discuss in Section 2.1.2, the modular approach based on the RB method was originally proposed in [@Maday2002195] and further developments have been carried out in [@iapichino2012reduced; @iapichino2014reduced; @iapichino2016reduced]. All these efforts focus on two-dimensional problems and often on the (linear) Stokes equations; in our research, we plan instead to tackle the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations and reduced FSI models [@figueroa2006coupled; @figueroa2009computational].
Keywords: Approximation of parametrized PDEs, Deep neural networks, Finite element method, Machine learning, Modeling of the vascular system, Reduced basis method
