Title: Synergistic effect of arterial stiffness measures and urinary omics studies for the early prediction of pre-eclampsia in high-risk pregnancies.
Abstract:
Background:

Preeclampsia (PrE) affects 5-8% of all pregnancies and is a leading contributor to maternal and fetal morbidity and mortality worldwide. Pathogenic processes leading to PrE initiate months before clinical manifestations. Therefore, there is a window of opportunity for early identification of women who will develop PrE. Currently, there is no accurate tool for PrE prediction. Past efforts to predict PrE have included the use of clinical characteristics, angiogenic factors, and uterine artery Doppler velocimetry (UAD), either separately or in combination. However, the predictive performance of these efforts is variable or modest and needs to be improved. 

The PULSE study is a multinational, multi-center prospective study that aims to determine the predictive value of arterial stiffness and wave reflection measures, alone or in combination with existing predictive tools. This study is ongoing; as of February 2023, 360 pregnant women have been recruited. The PULSE study capitalizes on previous data from our REVEAL study. Briefly, REVEAL, was a prospective study of women with singleton pregnancies at high risk to develop PrE. Arterial stiffness parameters, measured by carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity (cfPWV) and wave reflection measures (augmentation index (AIx) and start time of the reflected wave (T1R)), were assessed every 4 weeks from the first trimester until delivery. Angiogenic factors were measured every trimester, and a UAD was performed in the second trimester, according to clinical practice. We demonstrated that a first trimester 1m/s increase in cfPWV and 1ms decrease in T1R were associated with an odds ratio [OR] 1.64 (95%CI 1.09-2.47) and OR 0.89 (95% CI 0.82-0.96) for PrE, respectively (p<0.05). Blood pressure, angiogenic factors, UAD measures all had, moderate predictive ability for PrE (AUC = 0.71). However, a model incorporating cfPWV, AIx, and T1R had a higher AUC (0.83, 95%CI 0.74-0.92), demonstrating that vascular responses associated with PrE can be detected early in pregnancy.

There seems to be a bidirectional relation between PrE and the kidney4. Kidney disease is one of the hallmarks of PrE with proteinuria as one of the main manifestations. Proteinuria in PrE is caused by a pathognomonic lesion of glomerular endotheliosis associated with the loss of podocytes. When severe, the latter may cause acute kidney injury (AKI). Women suffering from PrE have up to four times the risk of developing chronic kidney disease (CKD) later in their life as compared to women with no history of PrE. On the other hand, patients with CKD are ten times more likely to develop PrE as compared to patients without CKD. In fact, PrE would affect 40% of pregnant women with CKD. 

Vascular dysfunction is an integral mediator of PrE. In fact, endothelial dysregulation seems to be the pathophysiological link to end-organ damage in PrE, such as renal dysfunction 5. Many efforts have been made to find biomarkers, which could detect endothelial damage and help predict PrE. Most of these efforts were concentrated on circulating biomarkers8. Several studies, using urinary proteomics managed to detect urinary biomarkers with potential interest for the prediction of PrE providing some preliminary evidence. However, there is currently no agreement as to which specific urinary biomarker(s) presents the best predictive ability. As the kidney seems to be an important mediator for PrE, focusing on urinary biomarkers of endothelial dysfunction could provide novel tools for the prediction of PrE.

Proteomics and metabolomics are experimental methods increasingly used for the quantification of proteins and metabolites in body fluids. It has been shown that applying proteomics, metabolomics, and machine learning models might allow the prediction of the course of a disease and related treatment responsiveness. 12-14  Thus, studying the differences in urinary proteins and metabolites among patients with and without PrE might allow its early prediction and potential severity stratification. 

Objective: As part of this large prospective cohort study, we aim to identify urinary biomarkers to better predict PrE.

Design: Multinational, multicenter, observational, prospective study.

Patients/Participants: Women with a singleton pregnancy and at least one high risk factor or two moderate risk factors according to the U.S. Preventive Services Task force guidelines, are invited to participate. This 5-year study is being conducted across 8 centers (USA, Canada and the UK) Participants are recruited over three years (100 participants/year/center) to obtain a sample size of 2,400 women. Women recruited from the 5 centers in Canada will constitute the development cohort, and the identified predictive models will then be validated in an external cohort recruited from the US and UK centers.

Interventions: During the participants’ clinical visit between 10-13 weeks’ gestation: 1) arterial stiffness parameters will be assessed via applanation tonometry, and 2) blood and urine samples will be obtained. These assessments will be repeated at 18-21 weeks’ gestation along with a UAD. For the purposes of the proteomics/metabolomics study, we will use data from the McGill cohort (to date n=145 recruited). Urinary samples will undergo targeted omics studies (using mass spectrometry) from samples taken at both visits and at delivery. An experimental subset of samples would be used to define an acceptable lower limit of quantitation (LLOQ) for urinary omics. Identified proteins and metabolites will be fitted into a Support Vector Machine (SVM) - a machine learning algorithm allowing the classification of data into two distinct groups (PrE and non PrE patients). Further analyses will be done within the PrE group to predict late vs. early onset of PrE and its severity. 

Main Outcome Measure(s):  
1.Differences in urinary proteins and metabolites expression profiles between people with PrE and without PrE
2.Predictive value for PrE, including sensitivity, and specificity, negative predictive, positive predictive value and negative predictive value at each measurement time point, including a) late vs. early onset of PrE and b) PrE severity.

Statistical Analysis Plan: 
Only proteins and metabolites whose concentrations will be above their LLOQ defined by the experimental subset of samples will be considered for further data analysis. Proteins and metabolites differences and differential concentrations will be assessed using false discovery rate (FDR). An FDR of <0.01 will be considered significative. Area under the curve (AUC) will be calculated for the machine learning SVM model to assess the predictive ability of the model. 

Implications:
We expect that urinary biomarkers could play a synergistic role in the early prediction of PrE in combination with vascular assessment and could help improve the predictive performance of current tools. Improved PrE prediction would change the paradigm for PrE guidelines as it would identify earlier women who would benefit from closer follow-up and prophylactic measures. It would also allow for concentration of limited health care resources towards those who would benefit most from greater care and reduce burden from women at low risk for PrE. 

Knowledge Translation / Future Directions: Effective PrE prediction and detection of specific biomarkers would also facilitate clinical trials aimed at developing novel preventive and therapeutic strategies. Discovery of targeted urinary biomarkers could help better understand the role of the kidney in the pathogenesis of PrE and could improve our understanding of pregnancy-related kidney disease and hypertension. Following validation, our omics-based prediction model could be translated to a biomarkers-based prediction approach for other diseases.

Title: SYNTH: Evaluating Transformer Models to Generate Synthetic Replications, Nomological Nets, and Peer Reviews
Abstract: The scientific reform movement has identified and implemented methods to improve the robustness, reliability, and replicability of research. However, these methods are labor-intensive and partaking in them is not consistently rewarded. For example, researchers are encouraged to preregister (i.e., declare design, hypotheses, and analysis plan before data collection), and peer reviewers are asked to check that deviations from these protocols are transparently reported. This, however, is quite time-consuming, and reviewers usually do not read preregistrations when they evaluate a full manuscript. This threatens the promise of preregistration. Recent advances in the field of natural language processing have yielded large language models (LLMs), which hold tremendous promise to reduce the costs of tasks that the scientific community has neglected. SYNTH aims to increase research reliability by developing tools to support researchers in three core domains: (1) Synthetic Replications uses a fine-tuned LLM to predict the pattern that survey participants will show when responding to questionnaires (e.g., personality tests). Using this synthetic data will allow reviewers to screen for potential issues of replicability when examining newly developed questionnaires prior to collecting empirical data. As part of the program, a vast selection of existing instruments will be synthetically replicated and empirically re-examined, if the LLM identifies possible concerns about consistency in results. (2) The Synthetic Nomological Net is an LLM-based semantic search engine, which maps thousands of instruments used in the behavioral sciences. As many published instruments may measure the same concept, the engine can be used to identify potential redundancies. Likewise, the Synthetic Nomological Net serves as a tool for researchers, enabling them to proactively verify the existence of an existing measure in the field, thereby preventing unnecessary duplication of effort in creating new ones. (3) The Synthetic Peer is an LLM specially trained to scrutinize and compare preregistration protocols with final research papers, highlighting deviations from the original protocol to aid peer-reviewers in their work. In a collaborative effort with the journal Psychological Science, SYNTH implements a one-year field study to assess the effectiveness of the Synthetic Peer. Alongside the development and evaluation of these novel applications for LLMs in research, SYNTH will also show how putting these applications in the hands of the research community can foster careful risk management and put their use on firm ethical foundations. The program highlights the importance of consent, privacy, fairness, and transparency and uses LLMs exclusively to prioritize, decisions are always made by a human being (concerns often termed ethical artificial intelligence). SYNTH meticulously monitors fairness, potential biases and its impact on the scientific landscape as a whole.

Title: A window into the human mind: Semantic coherence as a marker for adaptive and maladaptive thought
Abstract: Language offers unique insight into our thought processes. In psychotic illness, language is often incoherent and diffuse, revealing a disordered style of thinking characterised by excessively broad semantic association, i.e. a propensity to connect unrelated ideas. This tendency is, to a lesser degree, also observed in healthy individuals with schizotypy, a personality organisation associated with subclinical psychotic symptoms. In this group, broad semantic association can even be linked with creativity (which requires connecting remote ideas) and mental wellbeing. How does the same cognitive feature contribute to mental illness in one case and to mental health in another? This remains yet to be understood, given the lack of studies investigating broad semantic association in relation to both mental illness and health, and to specific neural correlates. The current PhD proposal addresses this gap by means of a combined behavioural and neuroimaging study including both healthy individuals with schizotypy and patients with psychosis. It will use a novel computational approach for analysing natural language to quantify the breadth of semantic association in the thought process directly from the semantic coherence of participants’ speech, overcoming the drawbacks of conventional tasks which fail to capture the essence of disordered thinking. It will examine how semantic coherence contributes to symptoms, psychopathology, creativity, and mental wellbeing, and identify additional factors which may influence these relationships (e.g. intelligence, personality). As a potential neural correlate, it will investigate the asymmetry of the white matter tracts of the semantic system: Broad semantic association has been linked with decreased left-hemisphere dominance for semantic processing in behavioural studies, but more precise neuroanatomical correlates are lacking. With this multimodal approach combining behavioural, computational, and neuroimaging methods, the proposed project will elucidate the grey area in which psychopathology and mental prosperity overlap, furthering our understanding of the near-legendary link between ‘genius’ and ‘madness’, and ultimately, the human mind.
Keywords: 'genius and madness', creativity, mental health, natural language processing (NLP), neuroimaging, neuropsychology, psychosis, schizotypy, semantic coherence

Title: Practical discretisation error estimates for data-driven materials modelling
Abstract:
Modern computational materials discovery frequently involves machine-learned surrogates trained by running density-functional theory (DFT) simulations on a large set of structures. The error in the training data itself is predominantly modelled as small, homoscedastic Gaussian noise, such that the simulated DFT quantities need to be of consistently good quality across the entire data set. As a result simulations need to be run with rather stringent numerical parameters, which in turn drives up computational cost. In contrast recent mathematical advances offer a quantitative approach to model the error. For example, novel perturbation-based error estimates are able to accurately determine the discretisation error, i.e. the error due to the selected plane-wave cutoff Ecut, at a manageable additional cost. With the proposed research programme we strive to achieve two objectives: (1) to develop these discretisation error estimates into a routine tool for materials modelling and (2) to employ such quantitative estimates to overcome the limitations of a homoscedastic error model within Gaussian Processes (GP) regression. In particular we focus on exploring opportunities of such error-informed GP models to reduce data generation costs (by varying Ecut across the dataset) while keeping the impact on the prediction accuracy under control.

To achieve (1) we need to overcome a number of limitations in the existing discretisation error estimates. This includes an extension of the approach to the widely employed norm-conserving pseudodojo pseudopotentials as well as further key DFT quantities: we will target stresses, band structures as well as the estimation of the discretisation error in the structural parameters obtained from a structure relaxation. To gauge our mathematical developments, to determine required parameters and to verify the accuracy of the error estimates we will perform tests on the recently published validation data set, which covers systematically a variety of chemical environments. Finally, we will extend the perturbation-based framework to metallic systems. This requires substantial developments as the setting of the DFT minimisation problem changes --- from the manifold of fixed-rank projectors to its convex hull.

The integration of such discretisation error estimates with GP regression models (objective 2) will be developed in three steps. In each step we test the resilience of the GP's prediction quality to a training with heterogeneous data obtained by re-computing energies and forces of a standard silicon dataset using mixed cutoffs Ecut. First we will develop a heteroscedastic noise model for GP regression, in which the error estimate is used to vary the noise variance. Second we develop a GP surrogate, which not only regresses the DFT energies and forces, but also the respective error estimates. As a result this model not only predicts DFT quantities, but also an estimate for the discretisation error in these predicted quantities --- resulting in a propagation of the quantitative DFT error through the surrogate. Finally we will consider multitask GP approaches, in which for each structure multiple DFT simulations using multiple Ecut values may be employed to feed multiple quantities and errors into a single GP surrogate. This enables the model to pick up on convergence trends, which thus allows predictions (of quantities and their errors) at the highest Ecut level even though the data from all Ecut levels does not need to be available for all structures.

The recent advances in the estimation of DFT errors provide a valuable tool for materials modelling as errors of DFT simulations no longer need to be guessed, but can be computed. With the developments planned in this proposal we perform a first exploration of such error estimates for data-driven materials modelling and provide a solid foundation for any future exploration of this exciting topic.

Title: Understanding Dermatologic Conditions with Human and Artificial Intelligence
Abstract:
The ultimate responsibility for any diagnosis lies with clinicians [24], so that the healthcare system will hardly ever adopt AI-based decision support systems, however performant they may become, if clinicians cannot establish a sufficient trust level. Trust is based on understanding. In a survey, clinicians report their “need to understand the clinically relevant model features that align with current evidence-based medical practice” [135]. In other words, Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) based systems must support their decision-making using the relevant set of diagnostic features. These features are typically available within medical taxonomies, but rarely present as annotations in medical datasets.

In dermatology, more than two thousand skin conditions are distinguished, each associated with a specific set of clinical features (e.g., erythema, body localization, desquamation) requiring domain expertise for identification. Manual data annotation with comprehensive disease-specific feature sets simply does not scale. Furthermore, while some diseases are very prevalent (almost half of the European population is affected by a skin disease [40] such as fungal skin infections, eczema, alopecia or acne), others are exceptionally rare (e.g. ichthyosis variegata with only forty cases reported worldwide), implying that a sufficient number of samples may not even be available. Compounded with the inherent data quality issues of such image collections (e.g., duplicates, low- resolution, poor capturing conditions), there is little hope to achieve XAI-based clinical decision support in traditional supervised settings.

The rationale of our project stems from two considerations. First, diagnostic features in dermatology are highly related to visual cues since clinical practice relies predominantly on visual analysis [83]. Second, Deep Learning (DL) approaches, in particular Self-Supervised Learning (SSL), have demonstrated the ability to learn robust visual representations [94, 126].

This project aims to automatically associate visual aspects of skin lesions with the corresponding dermatology concepts, with minimal dependence on human expert annotations. We will first leverage visual representations learned without supervision to construct a visual concept hierarchy using two different approaches, SSL and Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs), both in Euclidean and hyperbolic space. In a second phase, we will align the learned representations and visual hierarchies with actual clinical dermatology taxonomies and concepts using linear probes and distance-based approaches. The third phase will focus on building XAI-based clinical diagnosis support based on the identifiable diagnostic features. We will start with a baseline inspired from [24], which consists in predicting these features to combine them following dermatologists’ diagnostic pathways. Then, we will explain models built on our visual representations with the identified dermatology concepts. Finally, we will investigate how dermatologists’ decisions are impacted when using our XAI systems both in terms of diagnostic accuracy and fairness.

The proposed approach is well-suited to dermatology because this specialty presents a unique panel of characteristics, particularly a strong reliance on visual features, an extreme diversity of phenotypes, and a large variety of confounding factors (e.g., cloths, tattoos, jewelry), which require extraordinary model robustness. The ability to map visual aspects to medical concepts promises other impacts beyond better explainability for decision support models. The visual representations and taxonomy will enable identification of informative samples and anomalies, such as out-of-distribution samples and label errors, which may be useful for the dermatology community. Likewise, we expect our approach to enable the comparison of expert knowledge with visual concepts learned from data. We will analyze when visual categorization differs from pathological or etiologic categorization and when visual information is sufficient for diagnosis. We plan to perform this analysis on dermatological diagnoses, skin tone, body location, dermatological efflorescences, disease severity and demographic characteristic. We are convinced that through our data-driven approach novel insights on diagnostic pathways in close collaboration with our clinical partners will be gained, similarly to the celebrated case which established the Big Five personality traits in psychology [49].

Title: Predicting vaccine hesitancy among children in Switzerland: A machine learning approach
Abstract:
Immunization is an important tool for reducing child morbidity and mortality rates and improving child survival. However, vaccine hesitancy is a serious obstacle that can lead to the resurgence of previously eliminated diseases. Machine learning (ML) algorithms can be used to capture temporal dependencies and predict vaccination patterns. In Switzerland, there are qualitative studies that confirm vaccination hesitancy as a public health issue, but no studies have applied ML techniques to predict vaccination hesitancy in routine immunization of children.
The proposed study aims to analyze vaccination patterns and behavioral characteristics among children in Switzerland using state-of-the-art ML statistical techniques. In particular, we will 1) explore the main drivers for vaccine hesitancy, 2) assess whether ML models can predict if a child is at risk of not receiving a vaccination, and 3) develop robust forecast models for proactively recognizing population trends concerning vaccination hesitancy.
The study will utilize data from the Swiss National Vaccination Coverage Survey and will include data processing steps such as treatment of missing values, feature transformation, and data cleansing. The ML techniques (random Forests, XGBoost, LightGBM, deep and shallow neural networks, support vector machines, lasso and ridge regression, and naïve Bayes) will be trained and evaluated for accuracy in classifying the number of core vaccines for children and explore features that differentiate vaccine hesitancy patterns
The expected results include the identification of key determinants associated with non-vaccination patterns of children in Switzerland and the development of robust forecast models that can be used for scenario analysis. Having a robust and interpretable model is crucial for healthcare providers and policy makers to identify factors behind low vaccination rates and create more precise interventions and policies to address the issue.
Keywords: Switzerland, forecasting, machine learning, routine immunization, vaccine hesitancy

Title: Certified Correctness and Guaranteed Performance for Domain-Independent Planning (CCGP-Plan)
Abstract:
The research area of domain-independent planning is concerned with the following problem: given formal representations of the world an autonomous agent is situated in, of its capabilities, and of its goals, find a plan (a sequence of actions executable by the agent) that achieves the agent's goals, or prove that no such plan exists. We focus on the classical setting, one of the traditional core areas of artificial intelligence (AI). After decades of intensive research, planning algorithms have recently reached a level of maturity that makes them useful for real-world decision-making scenarios. With this increased maturity of planning algorithms, raw performance is no longer automatically the main concern for AI researchers or AI engineers interested in using planning algorithms in the systems they build. Besides efficiency, increasing demands are placed on the reliability of planning algorithms. We identify two ways in which current planning algorithms are brittle, and we suggest ways to improve their reliability. Specifically, we consider the following two challenges:

1. Certified Correctness: As planning is a model-based approach, there are clear notions of correctness: a sound and complete planning algorithm must return a solution if one exists and report unsolvability when no solution exists. An optimal planning algorithm must additionally guarantee that all solutions it returns are of optimal quality. This means that planning algorithms can be incorrect in three ways. They can return solutions that do not actually solve the given problem, falsely claim that a problem is unsolvable, or falsely claim that a solution is optimal (or bounded suboptimal). While the first kind of error can be detected with plan validators, the other two are much more challenging. In critical applications, possible algorithmic errors, implementation bugs, or even malicious programming (for example due to manipulated programs or ulterior motives of the algorithm implementers) are serious concerns. We investigate planning algorithms that always justify their answers in a way that can be verified independently, automatically, and efficiently.

2. Guaranteed Performance: In many scenarios where a planning algorithm could be used, guaranteeing its correctness is not sufficient. It is also necessary to ensure that in all relevant situations, the algorithm reliably produces a plan within the available computational resources. This is especially true in (common) settings where many similar problems must be solved repeatedly. Current algorithms do not provide performance guarantees, and small differences in the input can make the difference between solutions found within milliseconds, days, or not at all. Due to the PSPACE-completeness of classical planning, there will always be cases where quick solutions are not feasible. However, in many scenarios efficient planning is possible. We propose algorithms that identify such scenarios for individual planning tasks, for planning task structures, and for planning domains.
Keywords: automated planning, certifying planning algorithms, domain-independent planning, formally verified planning algorithms, heuristic state-space search, tractable classes of planning problems

Title: FairMI - Machine Learning Fairness with Application to Medical Images
Abstract:
Algorithmic bias remains one of the key challenges for the wider applicability of Machine Learning (ML) in healthcare.  Statistical modeling of natural phenomena has gained traction due to increased representation capacity and data availability. In medicine, particularly, the use of ML models has increased significantly in recent years, especially to support large scale screening, and diagnosis.  However impactful, the study of demographic bias of newly developed or already deployed ML solutions in this domain remains largely unaddressed. This is particularly true in the medical imaging domain, where it remains challenging to associate demographic attributes with features.

Out of the most recent results, the "impossibility of fairness" establishes some criteria for demographic impartiality cannot be reached simultaneously. Among other factors, the lack of raw data, in particular for intersections of minorities, is one of the greatest issues that remain unaddressed due to their challenging nature.

This proposal addresses three important challenges in the domain of ML fairness for medical imaging: (i) Create novel ways to train ML models for medical imaging tasks, that can be automatically adjusted to become more useful (maximize performance), group or individually fair, (ii) Quantify fairness boundaries of ML models and associated development data, and finally, (iii) Build systems whose joint performance with humans in the decision loop is fair towards various individuals and demographic groups.

To achieve these goals, we will develop a novel evaluation framework and loss functions that take into account model utility together with all aspects of demographic fairness one may wish to address.  A generative framework, trained to isolate tunable demographic features, will provide large-scale data simulation covering minorities and intersections.  We will then study fairness (safety) boundaries through a modified learning curve setup, analyzing and quantifying limits in both ML models and training data. Finally, we will study how humans-in-the-decision-loop affect the fairness of hybrid human-AI systems, and address post-deployment utility/fairness tuning by embedding weight coefficients directly into the trained model.

The development of methods and tools to detect, mitigate, or remove bias will improve the safety of ML models deployed in healthcare.  We expect our work will help define new operational boundaries for the responsible deployment of artificial intelligence tools.

Title: Universal Aspects in the Landscape and Dynamics of Deep Neural Networks
Abstract:
Deep neural networks (DNNs) have shown impressive empirical performance but they are still nevertheless a black-box function modeling data. This is often a significant barrier for practitioners, whose choices most often rely on trial and error, and raises many fundamental questions for theorists regarding why and in which circumstances we can expect these models to perform well.

The learning process of a DNN consists of two major ingredients: a loss function that needs to be minimized, and an optimization algorithm used to find an optimum, in a landscape constituted by the values that the loss assumes for each configuration of the model parameters. Understanding the loss landscape and how the dynamics takes place on it is therefore a fundamental matter which would have a significant impact in machine learning.

Here, we build upon some existing connections between machine learning and statistical physics to unravel the interplay between landscape and dynamics in a series of different contexts: (a) off-equilibrium, (b) equilibrium and steady state, (c) criticality, i.e. emergent collective behavior arising from the competition between energy and entropy. From a practitioner’s point of view, these three aspects will provide precious knowledge on (a) the learning process, (b) the preconditioning of models, and (c) hyperparameter bounds for learning. The approach we propose uses methods and ideas from the statistical mechanics of disordered systems, and will provide a new bridge between machine learning and physics.

We will perform an extensive analysis of the roles of dynamics and loss landscape. More concretely, in each of the contexts described above, we will compare the behavior of Langevin versus Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) dynamics, and the landscape of DNNs with that of a paradigmatic spin glass model. We expect the following broad outcomes:

• A systematic comparison between Langevin and SGD dynamics.

• A systematic comparison between DNN models and some affine complex systems.

• Understanding how the noise in the dynamics affects the effective landscape that is visited, and how this can give rise to emergent collective behaviors of the parameters.

• Using the current understanding of SGD to avoid Hessian calculations in second-order algorithms for the optimization of complex potential energy functionals.

Title: Investigating the interplay between neural circuit structure and dynamics in neurodevelopmental disorders
Abstract:
Investigating the interplay between neural circuit structure and dynamics in neurodevelopmental disorders

Neural circuits are fundamental building blocks of the nervous system and form the basis for information processing and cognitive abilities. Consequently, pathological processes that disrupt the formation of functioning neural circuits can have severe consequences, often resulting in lifelong impairments and reduced lifespan. Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is one of the most prevalent neurodevelopmental disorders worldwide. Despite its heterogeneous genetic basis, a growing body of evidence suggests a convergence to an impaired assembly of the earliest neocortical circuits. Yet, when and how key deviations emerge between the developmental trajectories of healthy and diseased networks remains to be uncovered. Neurodevelopmental defects may manifest as changes in circuit architecture or network-activity patterns. Therefore, parallel measurements of circuit structure and activity across different developmental stages and at single-cell resolution are necessary to elucidate the pathophysiological mechanisms. However, measurements of this nature are unattainable with existing methodologies.

Here, we propose an interdisciplinary project spanning engineering, biology, and computational science to develop novel technological approaches that will (i) enable rapid, parallel topological and functional mapping of neural microcircuits, (ii) facilitate high-throughput screening for network defects in mouse models of autism using measurements across multiple developmental stages, and (iii) uncover novel data-driven insights into the pathophysiology of autism. We will develop a label-free approach to identify monosynaptic connections by harnessing the bidirectional interaction capabilities of our complementary metal oxide semiconductor (CMOS) high-density microelectrode arrays (HD-MEAs) in combination with simultaneous patch clamping in ex-vivo neuronal tissues. Specific tasks will include (i) achieving reliable electrode-tissue interfacing over large areas, (ii) developing efficient electrical stimulation strategies at single-cell resolution covering all cortical layers, and (iii) training classifier models to infer main functional neuronal types based on the rich extracellular electrophysiological features provided by our HD-MEAs.

We will apply this novel approach to highly relevant mouse models of ASD carrying a deletion of the Shank3 or Fmr1 gene. For each model, we will measure spontaneous network spiking dynamics and reconstruct the circuit architecture of the somatosensory cortex. We will conduct circuit characterization at multiple time points during neonatal development. Designated analysis procedures supported by machine learning will be leveraged to (i) identify when and in which pathways developmental trajectories deviate from the wild type, (ii) distinguish between causal and compensatory deviations, and (iii) assess the extent to which the two distinct genetic forms of ASD share defects in circuit assembly. Finally, selected pathways, found to be severely impaired in our high-throughput ex-vivo experiments, will be functionally assessed and characterized in-vivo in collaboration with our project partner, Prof. Camilla Bellone (University of Geneva).

The proposed project has wide-ranging enabling character, as it delivers a novel technological approach and analysis pipeline to rapidly characterize neural circuits. Our circuit mapping method does not require prior genetic modification and is, therefore, applicable to a wide range of neuronal tissues including brain slices and organoids of human origin. A high-throughput circuit characterization has the potential to be transformative for identifying dysregulated pathways in brain disorders, which could subsequently be targeted by interventions. The impact of our approach will be demonstrated by generating novel mechanistic insights into the pathophysiology of autism.

Title: Kernel-based Dimensionality Reduction
Abstract: Many real world problems involve high dimensional and complex data, a challenge for statistical machine learning. Dimensionality reduction (DR) is useful for visualizing data, discovering compact data representations, decreasing computation time, and addressing the curse of dimensionality. While DR has been studied widely in the machine learning community, existing methods are sensitive to noise, sample size, data complexity. Many cannot deal with nonlinear relationships among data components. Although significant advances have been made in recent years, the focus was mostly on supervised learning. Here I propose to design, analyze and implement DR algorithms for unsupervised and reinforcement learning. I will focus on state-of-the-art statistical kernel methods which proved highly successful in a wide range of applications, yielding excellent regressors and classifiers. I will study statistical kernel methods and recent work on kernel-based methods in compressive sensing. I will investigate kernel selection, explore new methods combining Frequentist with Bayesian approaches, and Generative with Discriminative learning, thus marrying different schools of thoughts in statistical learning, to obtain powerful and flexible DR methods. I will also study value approximation for Reinforcement learning in high dimensional spaces. I aim at obtaining automatic kernel selection based on the statistical nature of data, and achieve the best known benchmark results with my kernel-based methods. Autonomous systems that combine unsupervised learning and reinforcement learning will benefit from this. Since humans are extremely good to extract useful information from complex and high-dimensional observations with almost no perceptual loss, I hope the results of my research plan can also shed some light on human decision making.
Keywords: Bayesian approach, Dimensionality reduction, Discriminative learning, Frequentist approach, Generative learning, Kernel-based methods, Reinforcement learning

Title: Synaptic plasticity in system models
Abstract:
Summary of the Research Plan: Synaptic plasticity in system models

Synaptic plasticity is a term that is used in the neurosciences to describe changes in
connections between neurons. Synaptic plasticity can be induced by different stimulation
protocols and manifests itself on diferent time scales: a stimulation protocol that activates
neurons for a few seconds can induce changes that last for hours or days. These long-
lasting changes are thought to be the basis of learning and memory formation in the
brain.

In this grant we will focus on biologically plausible mathematical models of synaptic
plasticity and explore their functionality and potential use in larger biological systems.
The research is organized in four Work Packages (WP).

 WP1. Assembly formation and consolidation in complex neural systems. Recent
models in our lab (partly funded by the previous grant from the Swiss National
Science Foundation) capture synaptic plasticity over multiple time scales from early
potentation to late long-term potentiation. The aim of this work package is to test
these models in challenging systems paradigms corresponding to published experi-
mental behavioral protocols. In particular, we aim for a model that explains the
creation of memories in hippocampus and associated areas and how these memories
are maintained, linked to other memories, and potentially changed upon later recall.

 WP2. Learning by surprise. Synaptic Plasticity is influence by neuromodulators
that could signal surprise, reward, or stimuli that need attention. A simple example of
the interaction of plasticity and neuromodulatos is 'gating', i.e., plasticity is switched
on or off depending on the presence of absence of modulators. Machine learning
research and articial neural networks research shows that this kind of gating could
be important to define the moments when new memories need to be formed. In this
WP we want to explore mathematical theories that are inspired by machine learning
but could be linked to surprise signals in the brain.

 WP3. Deep representations with local learning rules. Modern machine learning relies
heavily on deep networks with multiple layers which are trained by optimized variants
of the BackProp algorithm, a classic gradient descent algorithm. BackProp in multi-
layer networks is biologically questionable because the learning rules are either non-
local or require rather specic feedback pathways to make them local. In this workpackage
we explore whether the BackProp algorithm can be replaced by truly local learning rules,
either Hebbian (cf WP1) or Hebbian under Neuromodulator (cf WP2)
 if the hierarchical multi-area structure of the brain is given. Links to
theories of predictive coding will be explored.

 WP4. Experimental protocols expressed in a formalized language for automatic com-
parison. The results derived from mathematical theories in WP1 - WP3 should make
predictions for experiments. In order to enable a systematic comparison of theory
and experiment we will develop a formal domain-specic coding language in which
experimental conditions (e.g., temperature, duration of exposure, number of repeti-
tions etc) are summarized together with the outcomes of the experiments. The aim
is reduce the comparison of a model with a set of experiments in a specic domain
to starting the domain-specic comparison program.

In all cases we will combine analytical methods with computational simulation work.
Keywords: Integrate-and-fire neurons, Neuron models, Synaptic Learning rules, Synaptic Plasticity

Title: Traffic assignment problem in the era of service-based urban mobility
Abstract:
The past decade has witnessed a rapid growth of shared mobility services such as ride-sourcing, ride-sharing, bike-sharing, etc. These emerging mobility services are reshaping travel behaviors and have already shown profound impacts on traffic dynamics. Given their continuously increasing popularity, we shall anticipate a service-based urban mobility system within three to five decades, where most private vehicles are replaced
by service vehicles belonging to a few mobility service operators. An arising research question is how to model the traffic dynamics in such a service-based urban transportation system. In transportation research, this problem is widely known as the traffic assignment problem (TAP) and has been extensively studied for decades. However, existing traffic assignment models are unable to capture two salient features of urban
traffic dominated by service vehicles: (i) the routing of these vehicles is stochastic and driven by profit, and (ii) the service operator meanwhile imposes different levels of control or intervention on the vehicle routing.
Motivated by the gap in the literature and the practical significance, this project aims to build a general modeling framework, along with analytical and numerical tools, to study the traffic assignment problem in a service-based urban transportation system. The research will be carried out at three levels, each of which corresponds to one major stakeholder in the system:
- User-level: A baseline TAP model for shared mobility services, referred to as sTAP hereafter, will be first formulated for a fleet of homogenous vehicles. The model will then be extended to consider different fleet compositions: (i) a hybrid fleet with heterogeneity in the routing model, and (ii) a competing fleet belonging to different service operators. Two more practical problems will also be tackled at this level. The first aims to better understand the routing strategies of experienced human drivers in real practice. The second regards designing multi-agent learning algorithms that guarantee convergence to
the equilibrium.
- Operator-level: The general control/intervention problem will be formulated on top of the developed sTAP models. Solution approaches will be developed with and without full knowledge of the sTAP models. Results under different objectives and control approaches will also be explored in real-world case studies. Another research focus on the operator level is the coopetition between service operators and the potential of service integration.
- Regulator-level: The trade-off between efficiency and equity will be studied using the metrics of traffic congestion and service quality. The analysis will focus on whether and how self-interested vehicles and profit-driven service operators would intensify traffic congestion and/or sacrifice service quality in certain areas and during certain time periods.
This project brings together the long-standing research on TAP and the emerging research on shared mobility services. It not only creates a new direction in transportation research but also lays a solid foundation for future research on new forms of mobility services. Although originated from a classic transportation research problem, this project introduces methodologies from game theory, machine learning, control, and optimization. It thus creates a potential for interdisciplinary collaborations and contributes to the advancement
of other research communities.
Meanwhile, this project will produce an array of numerical tools for the design and optimization of shared mobility services. Case studies conducted using these tools will generate useful insights into the regulation of emerging mobility services in different urban contexts. The mobility efficiency and equity metrics developed in this project will also support policymakers in the evaluation of long-term urban development programs with mobility services. 
Finally, this project shows a broader impact by contributing to both educational and outreach activities. The former is achieved by developing course materials that connect classic transportation models to the current development of mobility services, and the latter is due to active exposure in top research journals and both national and international conferences.
Keywords: Markov routing game, Mobility-as-a-service, Network design problem, Share mobility services, Traffic assignment problem

Title: Pharmacological determinants of addiction liability
Abstract:
Background & rationale: Addiction appears in a substantial fraction of users with prolonged drug use (e.g., cocaine = artificial reward), while the liability of natural rewards (e.g., palatable food) is low. Natural rewards & drugs have been proven to access the mesolimbic dopamine system. Indeed, dopamine concentrations increase in the Nucleus Accumbens (NAc) when ingesting food & upon drug injection, reinforcing the action & serving as a learning signal. In fact, dopamine transients can easily be transferred to a conditioned stimulus (CS) for both rewards. After only a few trials, the CS starts to elicit a dopamine transient. In this context, the theoretical framework of temporal difference learning (TDL) posits an appealing hypothesis for the difference between artificial & natural rewards. While for the latter, dopamine transients at reward delivery disappear once the reward is fully predicted, drugs (& other artificial rewards) by sheer pharmacological power override this inhibition. As a result, an inappropriate learning signal would cause an overvaluation of the drug-associated CS, further reinforcing the behavior & eventually promoting the transition to compulsion. While very appealing, this theory is not empirically supported nor formally tested in an operant setting that allows for an alternate reward choice. We will monitor accumbal dopamine in a task where the mouse can choose between natural (food) & three artificial rewards (optogenetic dopamine neuron self-stimulation oDASS/cocaine/remifentanil). We posit that the accumbal dopamine transients in response to natural & artificial rewards shape the value of the CS, bias choice, & eventually explain the addiction liability of drugs. We propose the following aims: 
Aim1 a. Characterize the dopamine transients in the NAc evoked by a natural reward, oDASS, cocaine & remifentanil. We will transfect accumbal neurons with the fluorescent dopamine indicator dLight1.2 to monitor dopamine transients in mice that take a natural reward (fat solution), self-stimulate ventral segmental area (VTA) dopamine neurons (oDASS), or self-administer a drug. We will compare cocaine to the faster-acting remifentanil & monitor their effect on the cue-evoked dopamine transient. 
b. Refine TDL theory for an operant setting. We will model the operant task with Q-learning, a model-free learning paradigm that learns the value of actions.
Aim2 a. Predict choice between natural rewards & oDASS, or addictive drugs with accumbal dopamine transients. We will establish a behavioral task where the mouse can select either an artificial (oDASS, cocaine, or remifentanil) or a natural reward (fat solution). We will focus on the trajectories of individual mice from the initial learning phase to the expert stage & how the dopamine transients in the NAc can predict choice. 
b. Build a theoretical framework for the difference between natural & drug rewards. We will construct a model to account for operant, choice behavior not accounted for in the standard TDL model. We will simulate the evolution of the dopamine transient during the learning of drug-associated cues & its impact on choice.
Aim3 a. Monitor the effects of altering the reward value on established choices. We will test how changing the magnitude & kinetics of the artificial reward (e.g., short vs. long oDASS) or devaluation with punishment will affect accumbal dopamine transients & choice. We will also optogenectically modulate dopamine transients to establish links of causality. 
b. Build the theoretical model integrating perturbed reward value. We will simulate the dopamine transients when the artificial reward increases & when the reward is associated with punishment. We will test the model for the predictability of re-evaluating an established choice. 
Methods & expected results: Our project is timely because it harnesses advanced circuit investigation with the recently developed genetically encoded transmitter sensors in combination with oDASS, an optogenetic addiction model where a mouse can self-stimulate chrimson-infected VTA dopamine neurons. Cocaine & the ultrafast opioid remifentanil will be our test drugs. Preliminary data provide proof of feasibility for all aims & proof of face validity for the oDASS but also challenge the prevailing hypothesis explaining addiction liability by the invariance of the dopamine signal at drug delivery. We will implement novel analysis methods (non-supervised clustering algorithms, machine learning) & build a formal model. 
Impact: The current project will yield results that address the fundamental question of why drugs are addictive & why addicts favor drug rewards at the expense of natural rewards. Our results may determine the addiction liability of unknown compounds, inspire novel prevention strategies & help develop rational treatments. The knowledge obtained will pave the way for a general addiction theory that can accommodate substance-independent behavioral versions of the disease.
Keywords: Addiction, Cocaine, Dopamine, Reward prediction error

Title: Targeting Alzheimer's Heterogeneity: combined subtyping of atrophy and small vessel disease patterns to improve precision medicine in memory clinics
Abstract:
Background: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) exhibits significant biological diversity, involving interactions between protein deposits (amyloid-beta, tau, and co-pathologies like alpha-synuclein, TDP-43) and small vessel disease (SVD) from cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) and arteriolosclerosis. These pathological patterns influence clinical phenotypes, cognitive trajectories, and treatment responses. Novel anti-amyloid therapies can slow AD progression but are limited by co-pathologies and the risk of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) with CAA. Additionally, multimodal lifestyle interventions improve cognition and reduce dementia risk, but predictive tools to identify who benefits most are lacking. Identifying AD subtypes in vivo through structural MRI—typical AD, limbic-predominant AD, hippocampal-sparing AD, and minimal atrophy AD—shows promise in predicting disease trajectory and therapy response. However, current methods do not include quantitative measures of SVD. Integrating these measures is crucial to improve patient selection for lifestyle interventions and disease-modifying therapies.
Aims: This project aims to refine AD subtyping using MRI by integrating quantitative measures of regional atrophy and SVD. This will identify subgroups with distinct pathological profiles, particularly regarding SVD etiology, to improve diagnostics, predict cognitive trajectories, and enhance patient selection for lifestyle interventions and disease-modifying therapies (DMTs). Additionally, the project aims to improve detection of CAA for better ARIA risk assessment.
Methods: We will use automated MRI processing to evaluate regional white matter abnormalities, perivascular spaces, and cerebral microbleeds as indicators of SVD, along with grey matter volumes and cortical thickness as atrophy measures. Using publicly available research datasets and memory clinic cohorts from St. Gallen and Karolinska, we will apply supervised random forest classifiers to identify SVD patterns indicative of either CAA or arteriolosclerosis, based on neuropathological assessments and imaging ratings. Unsupervised cluster analyses will refine subtyping, uncovering unique neurodegeneration and SVD profiles. We will also develop continuous scales for SVD typicality—from typical arteriolosclerosis to atypical CAA—and severity, analogous to established scales of atrophy in AD, enabling a simple classification of AD subtypes on four axes. Finally, we will correlate MRI-based subtypes with clinical phenotypes, cognitive decline trajectories, and responses to lifestyle interventions.
Results: We will create an integrated classification system using continuous scales of typicality and severity of SVD manifestations and atrophy. This will identify distinct AD subgroups with unique clinical and cognitive profiles. The study will determine which patients are at risk for rapid cognitive decline and which are prone to cerebral hemorrhage due to CAA, identifying those who will benefit most from lifestyle interventions.
Impact: This project will enhance AD subtyping by integrating patterns of atrophy and SVD on MRI. By identifying distinct pathological profiles, especially in SVD, this refined approach will improve diagnostic precision for detecting CAA, predict cognitive trajectories, and optimize patient selection for lifestyle modifications and DMTs. Ultimately, this will advance precision medicine in AD, significantly improving patient outcomes and treatment efficacy.
Keywords: Alzheimer's Disease, Alzheimer's Subtypes, CAA, Machine Learning, Neuroimaging, Prevention, Quantitative MRI analysis, Small Vessel Disease

Title: A human-centered approach to the application of AI in Emergency Medicine: A scenario-based evaluation of different levels of AI support.
Abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is expected to have a significant impact on healthcare (Mueller et al., 2022; Rajpurkar et al., 2022). The field of emergency medicine (EM) has been at the forefront of discussions on the application of AI in healthcare, with the promise to increase the speed and accuracy of clinical decisions (Grant & McParland, 2019), to better handle patients’ triage (Mueller et al., 2022; Ramlakhan et al., 2022; Farahmand et al., 2017), and to detect/predict high-risk conditions and life-threatening pathologies (Mueller et al., 2022; Ramlakhan et al., 2022; Grant & McParland, 2019). However, the realization of this potential demands a human-centered AI (HCAI) approach to the application of AI in EM (e.g. Ozmen Garibay et al., 2023; Ontika et al., 2022; Auernhammer, 2020), that counteracts the current predominant focus on technical feasibility and fosters a collaborative human-AI performance that exceeds the performance of humans or AI alone and at the same time promotes health and wellbeing.
One of the most basic design questions in this approach concerns the appropriate level of AI autonomy and support during task performance (see Bitterman, Aerts & Mak, 2020). In contrast to previous research of AI systems in EM (see e.g. Tang et al., 2021), we aim to explore, from an HCAI perspective, potentially useful applications of AI in EM and to identify those AI use cases that match to the problems and needs in the participating EM organizations. We plan to do this by conducting a context of use analysis of EM, as a basis for the generation and participatory evaluation of AI use cases in a first study. Building upon these results, our second study aims to investigate what different scenarios for using AI in EM, varying in the level of AI support, might concretely look like for selected tasks and how these scenarios are evaluated by future AI users on psychological process and outcome variables, such as perceived autonomy and trust, and quality of decision making. The second study results in a narrower set of positively evaluated scenarios for the use of AI in EM. Our third study again builds on the results of the second study and investigates how the different selected AI scenarios, varying in degrees of AI support/autonomy, perform regarding these psychological outcomes and decision quality by conducting a randomized experiment. Through these studies, we expect to identify useful use cases for AI in EM from an HCAI perspective, and identify human-AI collaboration scenarios in which human needs are fulfilled. In particular, the question of how much AI autonomy is appropriate in such a setting and how this affects psychological variables will be empirically addressed via these studies. Our research thus provides important insights for the basic research of human-AI interaction and how psychological needs such as human autonomy and user trust influence the use of AI. Furthermore, our research provides practical implications for future research and development of such tools by demonstrating how much AI support/autonomy is desirable when regarding the basic needs and wellbeing of the users.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Emergency Medicine, Human-AI Collaboration, Human-Centered Design, Scenario-based evaluation

Title: Analysis and implementation of low-rank tensor algorithms
Abstract: Numerical methods using low-rank tensor techniques have seen great success in, for example, theoretical physics for the simulation of spin systems, in scientific computing for high-dimensional PDEs, and in signal processing for independent component analysis. The aim of this proposal is to (A) propose numerical integrators for integration of time-reversible tensor ODEs with rank truncation, (B) parallelize low-rank tensor algorithms for optimization and time integration, and (C) apply tensor techniques for regression and decision in machine learning.
Keywords: differential equations, low-rank tensors, machine learning, numerical linear algebra, optimization on manifolds

Title: Multilevel training of DeepONets - multiscale and multiphysics applications
Abstract:
Modeling and predicting the dynamics of complex multiscale and multiphysics problems is a long-lasting challenge in science. Recently, a significant step forward was made by proposing Deep Operator Networks (DeepONets), which can approximate nonlinear operators from data. For a given data, the DeepONets can model complex, possibly unknown, dynamics and facilitate very fast predictions, thus extending the capabilities of current numerical approaches by simplifying computational modeling, discovering unknown models, and providing exceptionally cheap surrogates. For example, fracture propagation in geothermal applications or personalized flow prediction in coronary arteries pose significant computational challenges for traditional numerical methods, which DeepONets can overcome by taking into account available data.

Despite their remarkable predictive ability, the DeepONets suffer from a computationally exhaustive training phase, which limits their applicability and hinders their development. 
During the training phase, the parameters of DeepONet are determined by minimizing a highly non-convex loss functional. At the moment, this minimization process is predominantly carried out using standard deep learning optimization techniques, such as stochastic gradient method, or ADAM. However, arising minimization problems are distinct from those in traditional machine learning, e.g., image/speech recognition.  In particular, they are severely more ill-conditioned, rendering standard first-order optimization approaches ineffective.  Unfortunately, incorporating curvature information using standard deterministic Newton-like methods also falls short due to excessive time and memory requirements needed for solving arising linear systems. 

In this project, we will develop novel training methods by leveraging ideas from multilevel minimization, which will open a new perspective for the efficient training of DeepONets. 
Multilevel methods were originally proposed for solving large-scale linear systems arising from the discretization of elliptic partial differential equations (PDEs), but by now they have been extended to solve large-scale convex and non-convex optimization problems. 
The main idea behind multilevel methods is to employ a hierarchy of auxiliary problems, which are minimized internally to accelerate the solution process of the original problem.
While for PDEs, the construction of multilevel hierarchy is intimately related to the geometrical discretization, it is not yet established how to create the multilevel hierarchy for deep neural networks.  Within this project, we will explore the structure of DeepONet architecture, properties of the loss functional, and the form of the data in the dataset to construct a multilevel hierarchy. This will give rise to novel multilevel minimization techniques, which will serve as a basis for efficient training of a whole new class of problems with large-scale and ill-conditioned datasets. 

Methodologically, we build on the applicant's experience with multilevel methods for non-convex optimization problems and incorporate several algorithmic features, such as trust-region globalization strategy, limited-memory secant methods, or adaptive sampling strategies into the design of proposed methods. This will allow for more efficient and controlled training, with reduced dependence on the hyper-parameters, compared to standard machine-learning approaches. 

Successful realization of this project will enable the use of DeepONets for large-scale multiphysics and multiscale applications and therefore it will directly contribute to the expansion of computational modeling capacities. To ensure the applicability of prospective multilevel training methods to real-life problems, we will design and train DeepONets to predict fracture propagation and to estimate  fractional flow reserve in coronary arteries. As a consequence, the developments made within the scope of this project will also have a direct impact on the computational modeling of fracture propagation and on the diagnosis of obstructive coronary artery disease.
Keywords: DeepONet, Multilevel Methods, Multiscale Minimization, Neural Networks, Scientific Machine Learning, Training

Title: Robusto: Robust brain control of spinal cord neuroprostheses
Abstract:
Problem. We rely on finely-tuned leg movements to move, explore, and even express ourselves through dance. Yet, millions of people lose the ability to walk due to a paralyzing spinal cord injury. This condition has no cure and it often leaves devastating long-term consequences for the physical, psychological, and social well-being of people with spinal cord injury. Restoring functional leg movements is therefore one of their highest priorities.

Opportunity. Previously, my colleagues and I developed a brain-spine interface – a spinal cord neuroprosthesis that used brain signals to control the delivery of epidural electrical stimulation (EES) of the lumbar spinal cord to restore walking in nonhuman primates paralyzed by spinal cord injury. EES recruits large-diameter afferents where they enter the spinal cord through the dorsal root entry zones. The recruitment of these afferents enables the modulation of leg motor neurons located in the spinal segment innervated by the targeted dorsal roots. The understanding of this mechanism of action allowed us to design stimulation protocols targeting individual dorsal root entry zones with a temporal sequence that reproduces natural spatiotemporal activation pattern of motor neurons during walking. Our brain-spine interface decoded locomotor movement attempts from the motor cortex activity to control the delivery of the spinal stimulation, thus ensuring that the activation pattern of spinal motor neurons aligned with the inputs arriving from the motor cortex through cortico-spinal pathways that survived the injury. 

Breakthrough. Under the framework of the ongoing STIMO-BSI clinical trial, my colleagues are clinically testing the brain-spine interface in people with chronic paraplegia due to spinal cord injury. With the brain-spine interface, the first STIMO-BSI participant has regained the ability to stand, walk, climb/descend stairs and navigate complex terrain. Moreover, motor rehabilitation supported by the brain-spine interface mediated a neurological recovery that restored some voluntary leg movement even when the brain-spine interface was turned off. Amazingly, the motor recovery achieved with the brain-spine interface substantially surpassed the recovery reached using the same spinal cord neuroprosthesis controlled by residual movements or buttons, thus indicating that synchronization of spinal EES with motor cortical activity plays a critical role in maximizing the therapeutic outcome.

Challenge. Spinal EES enables movement through presynaptic recruitment of spinal motor neurons by stimulating the proprioceptive afferent fibers arriving from the muscles. However, these fibers also share recurrent projections that send somatosensory signals to the cerebral cortex. Therefore, spinal EES can activate the primary somatosensory cortex that can, in turn, directly activate the motor cortex. However, our brain-spine interface relies on stationary encoding of movement attempts within the motor cortex activity. Therefore, motor cortex responses to spinal EES pose a challenge for robust operation of our brain-spine interface by disrupting the decoding of locomotor movement attempts from the motor cortex activity.

Project goal is to develop and validate machine learning technique that ensure robust use of the brain-spine interface despite the presence of motor cortex responses to spinal EES. To reach this goal, I will first leverage my experience in brain activity analysis to precisely determine the impact of spinal EES on motor cortex activity. I will then use my expertise in brain-computer interface algorithms to design machine learning techniques that enable robust decoding of movement intentions by ignoring the responses to spinal EES. Finally, under the framework of the STIMO-BSI trial, I will demonstrate that these techniques enable a person with paraplegia due to a spinal cord injury to more effectively use brain-spine interface to walk and climb/descend stairs.
Keywords: brain-computer interface, epidural electrical stimulation, machine learning, neural decoding, neuroprosthesis, real-time control, spinal cord injury, statistical learning

Title: Reviving Lost Voices: Economic Expectations from Historical Diaries
Abstract: Almost all economic decisions depend on what individuals expect about the future. This is especially true during volatile economic episodes such as the interwar period between 1918 and 1939. However, unfortunately, surveys about economic expectations are only available past World War II. As a result, researchers approximate expectations, for example, using modern forecasting models to impute expectations from aggregate time series data. Yet, the expectations of ordinary individuals during the interwar period arguably differ from what modern forecasting tools would predict. In addition, such expectations from aggregate data are necessarily silent about expectation heterogeneity, an important feature of modern expectation data. This project pioneers the use of large language models (LLMs) to construct a synthetic household panel of economic expectations for the interwar period by simulating ordinary individuals based on their personal writings. Leveraging diaries from a diary archive, we will process and structure these texts, making them accessible for LLM-based analysis. Once the diaries are transcribed and digitized, they will be used to create a synthetic panel dataset of historical economic expectations. As a first application, this project revisits the role of inflation expectations during the Great Depression and during the German Hyperinflation. These are important historical events that may also inform us about the importance of expectations during severe economic crises today. The historical approach is necessary because such severe crises did not occur more recently. Building on recent research that uses LLMs to simulate economic agents, this project extends the methodology in both scope and ambition. Prior work has demonstrated that LLMs can replicate human behavior in laboratory experiments and human forecasts from the Survey of Professional Forecasters, among others. The full project plan includes a detailed review of the literature. Going beyond existing research, this project is pushing the frontier by applying an LLM approach to historical personal writings, creating structured longitudinal data from actual individuals who lived through important historical episodes.
Keywords: economic expectations, inflation expectations, interwar period, large language models, synthetic survey panel

Title: Spike-based computation and learning in distributed neuromorphic systems
Abstract:
Animal nervous systems are extremely efficient computational devices that allow even brains of simple animals to easily outperform state-of-the-art artificial intelligence for most real-world tasks. Future technologies can benefit enormously, if we learn to exploit the strategies used by the nervous system and implement them in electronic computing systems. The advantage of nature lies in the way that computation is organized, and in its ability to adapt to the natural environment for producing cognitive behavior: rather than using a centralized processor or memory, different physically distributed regions of the brain self organize and learn to process signals from sensors and other brain regions.  Conventional machine learning algorithms, as well as the computing technologies they run on, have not been designed to simulate efficiently these types of massively parallel, inherently variable, continuously adaptive, fault-tolerant, and asynchronously computing local circuits.

In this project we will exploit recently developed mixed analog and digital brain-inspired computing \ac{VLSI} architectures for simulations of spiking neural networks, and address the problem of building efficient low-power scalable computing systems that can interact with the environment, learn about the input signals they have been designed to process, and exhibit adaptive and cognitive abilities analogous to those of biological systems.  This is indeed a daunting task, that requires a true interdisciplinary approach. In particular, a necessary condition for achieving this goal is the existence of computational theories and methods which map directly and efficiently on a computing substrate that emulates the one found in biological neural systems.

We have already substantial experience in developing "neuromorphic" computing devices that directly emulate the bio-physics of real neurons and synapses by exploiting the physics of silicon: we developed several generations of Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI) chips that implement biophysically realistic neurons and synapses endowed with spike-based plasticity mechanisms, that can be used as composable and scalable building blocks for more-and-more powerful artificial cognitive systems.  However, even though we are building more sophisticated generations of these types of devices, and even if other research and industrial groups started to propose similar approaches the use of these bio-inspired computing substrates is still severely limited by our (lack of) understanding of how to "program'' distributed and asynchronous neural systems.  This is in contrast to the classical von Neumann type of architectures that are much more intuitive for human minds to program in a linear, synchronous, and static fashion.  How this can be done for a distributed brain-like architecture remains an open question that motivates this project.

To solve this problem we will study and develop distributed methods of learning, state-dependent computation, and probabilistic inference that can, on one hand, emulate the style of computation used by the brain, and on the other hand (as a consequence) be directly and efficiently mapped onto the distributed spiking neural network systems implemented using our existing and future generations of multi-neuron VLSI devices. Specifically, we will apply dynamical systems and probabilistic inference theories to instantiate biologically motivated learning within and between spike-based computational modules. Building on our recent results that have shown how arbitrary finite state machines, the basic elements of computation, can be implemented with networks of spiking neurons we will arrange such 
networks in distributed and recurrently coupled architectures, and develop learning mechanisms, suitable for VLSI implementation, to train them to perform complex probabilistic inference for recognition and fusion of multi-modal sensory input streams.

By combining our research on probabilistic graphical and spike-based inference computational models with the development of distributed, asynchronous neural computing systems implemented using neuromorphic VLSI multi-chip architectures, we will develop the systematic methodologies required to automatically configure spiking neural network chips to execute user-defined "programs'' and solve high level abstract tasks.
Keywords: Neural computation, Neuromorphic circuits, Parameter tuning, Spike-based processing

Title: Digital Twin of Lung Morphogenesis
Abstract:
This project aims to develop a digital twin of early lung development, integrating molecular signaling, mechanical interactions, and tissue growth dynamics to systematically reconstruct and analyze lung branching morphogenesis. By combining high-resolution imaging data with computational modeling, we will uncover the fundamental mechanisms governing branch initiation, elongation, and stereotypic patterning. Unlike purely data-driven approaches, our mechanistic models provide interpretable insights, allowing us to identify causal relationships, predict emergent behaviors, and refine our understanding of lung development at a systems level.

The first goal is to establish a reaction-diffusion-based digital twin of early lung branching (E10.5–E12.5). This model will integrate FGF10-FGFR2b and SHH-PTCH1 signaling, using experimentally derived tissue geometries to quantitatively reproduce observed gene expression patterns and growth dynamics. 

In parallel as part of a second direction, we will develop a model that captures the remodeling of the lung tree as branches open from E14 onward, progressively adopting a fractal geometry. By quantifying branch angles, lengths, and termination frequencies in imaging data, we will identify the mechanisms driving this transition.

A third objective is to analyze the final stages of lung development (E17.5–E18.5), where deep learning approaches remain constrained by insufficient training data. To overcome this limitation, we will generate synthetic lung images using novel data augmentation strategies to train segmentation algorithms. These models will enable high-throughput analysis of late-stage lung architectures, facilitating the first large-scale characterization of branching from the trachea to the alveoli.

Beyond fundamental developmental biology, this project has far-reaching biomedical and technological applications. The digital twin framework will provide predictive tools for lung tissue engineering, optimizing bioengineered lung scaffolds. Furthermore, it will serve as a synthetic data generator for AI-driven image analysis, improving segmentation and skeletonization of late-stage lung imaging datasets. The methodologies developed will also be broadly applicable to other branching organs, such as the kidney, mammary gland, and pancreas.

Ultimately, this project will advance the role of digital twins in developmental biology, regenerative medicine, and artificial intelligence, demonstrating how integrated mechanistic modeling can transform our ability to simulate, analyze, and manipulate complex biological systems in silico.

Title: Superior Stock Selection based on Deep Learning ? - Evidence from the Cross-Section of Returns
Abstract: The project aims to answer the question if advances in machine learning can be useful in predicting financial returns. Recent proceedings in deep learning show promising results in other research fields. The project contribution to the finance literature would be an in-depth analysis with respect to the cross-section of stock returns. More generally, it would contribute in how far deep learning is suitable for prediction problems, confronting very noisy data. Inspiration as well as crucial for the implementation of the project is the fact, that Google recently open-sourced its machine learning library TensorFlow.
Keywords: Asset Pricing, Cross-Section, Deep Learning, Factor Models
