Title: Brain-Spine/Muscle Interface: Integrating spinal and peripheral stimulation to restore functional hand and arm movements to people with spinal cord injury
Abstract:
Problem. More than 7 million people worldwide live with tetraplegia due to cervical spinal cord injury (SCI). SCI interrupts axons passing along the spinal cord, thereby isolating the spinal motor neurons from the brain inputs. To date, there is no effective treatment. Rehabilitation is long, expensive, exhausting and currently largely ineffective. Therefore, tetraplegia due to SCI leaves devastating long-term consequences for the physical, psychological, and social well-being of people with SCI. Restoring functional hand and arm movements is their top priority.
Emerging therapy. My team and I recently achieved a breakthrough in restoring functional movements after paralyzing SCI using a brain-spine interface (BSI) - a fully-implanted, wireless digital bridge between the brain and the spinal cord. The BSI uses brain activity recordings to infer users’ movement intentions in real time. It then wirelessly controls an implanted neurostimulator that deploys epidural electrical stimulation (EES) over the dorsal spinal roots to recruit proprioceptive afferents coming into the spinal cord. This can reactivate spinal motor neurons and, in turn, contract the muscles. When applied in an intensive training regime, EES can help reorganize spinal circuits to restore voluntary control of muscles after an SCI. This BSI enabled a person with paraplegia due to SCI to stand, walk, climb and descend stairs and navigate complex terrain. More importantly, he has regained voluntary control over his legs, even when the stimulation is turned off.
Limitations. Driven by the success in restoring leg movements, my collaborators and I recently launched the UP2 clinical trial to test whether people with tetraplegia due to cervical SCI can regain hand and arm movements using a BSI system. To date, one participant has completed the main trial protocol. With the BSI, they were able to improve their overall hand and arm motor function by more than 50%. However, the limited specificity of cervical EES, resulting from the high density of dorsal roots in the cervical region, prevented recovery of more complex functional hand movements.
Opportunity. Functional electrical stimulation (FES) can generate muscle contractions by directly recruiting motor neuron axons around the neuro-muscular junctions using electrodes placed over or in the muscles. Recent studies demonstrated that brain-controlled FES can restore some movement after paralyzing SCI. However, FES leads to rapid muscle fatigue. Furthermore, generating even the simpler functional movements through direct FES-enabled muscle recruitment requires the definition of complex algorithms to control the timely activation of dozens of muscles. Still, by enabling precise recruitment of specific muscles, FES complements the current limitations of the BSI system. Integrating FES into the BSI system may enable restoration of complex functional hand movements.
Solution. My team and I will integrate brain-controlled spinal EES and non-invasive FES into the Brain-Spine/Muscle Interface (BSMI) and demonstrate that it can effectively restore dexterous hand and arm movements to people with tetraplegia due to SCI.
Project plan. We will first develop the BSMI by integrating the noninvasive NeuroLife Sleeve FES system into the BSI being tested in the UP2 trial. In parallel, we will expand the automatic BSI calibration procedure to enable calibration of FES and combined EES + FES protocols. We will then assess the efficacy of the BSMI in restoring dexterous hand and arm movements in sessions with UP2 participants. We will use verified clinical tests of hand and arm motor function coupled with our newly-developed motion tracking system to quantify the recovery of functional hand and arm movements. Based on my preliminary results, I expect that the BSMI will immediately allow the UP2 participants to perform a range of functional grasping tasks, which they are unable to perform using only the BSI or the brain-controlled FES.

Title: Accelerated Discovery of Transition Metal-Catalyzed Reactions Through Machine Learning
Abstract:
For the selective formation of carbon-carbon (C-C) and carbon-heteroatom (C-X, where X = O, N, S) bonds, transition metal-catalyzed coupling reactions are one of the most powerful and effective methods. They are essential in the areas of pharmaceutical, agricultural, and material science research and have many applications on an industrial scale. Currently, the discovery of new reactions relies primarily on time-consuming experimental screening studies based on trial and error as the effect of metal ligands, substrates or the choice of solvent on the reaction yield is often difficult to gauge. Many attempts have been made to design a system which predicts the product(s) of chemical reactions given a set of reactants and conditions. While ab initio quantum chemical approaches benefit from their sound physical basis, they are still computationally expensive, and thus, unsuitable for high-throughput settings. In contrast, data-driven methods such as machine learning allow for rapid predictions, however, they are currently limited to organic reactions.

The goal of this research project is to develop a machinery that significantly accelerates the discovery of new transition metal-catalyzed reactions through the application of machine learning and the direct coupling to high-throughput experimentation (HTE). First, we will design a chemical reactivity descriptor that is applicable to transition metal catalysts and suitable for machine learning. Second, we will develop a statistical model based on deep learning to predict the performance of a given reaction. Third, we will train this model on a database consisting of experimental data on chemical reactions. Fourth, to verify predictions on new reactions and to continuously improve the model we will couple it to an HTE setup to form a feedback loop. Title: Tensor Field Networks for Spatially Heterogeneous Real-World Medical Imaging
Abstract:
Deep-learning-based labelling and quantification of medical images stands poised to transform radiological practice, streamlining workflows and allowing precise, repeatable volumetry.  However, most algorithms operating on 3D Magnetic Resonance imaging (MRI) or Computed Tomography (CT) data are trained using standardised datasets acquired in university hospitals, which do not reflect the high variability of imaging data in the real world. For example, in multiple sclerosis FLAIR MR imaging is vital for identifying white-matter lesions: a patient might be scanned at high-resolution (0.5 x 0.5 x 1 mm or better) in a highly specialised research facility, with 3D imaging (1 $mm^3$ isovoxel),  or with lower-resolution 2D imaging (e.g. 1mm by 1mm by 3 mm).  Further, the 2D imaging may not always be acquired in the same direction; the 2D slices may be in the coronal, sagittal or axial directions. There is currently no way to train networks directly on spatially heterogeneous datasets, without resampling the imaging volumes to a common spatial resolution, leading to loss of fidelity when downsampling, and creation of interpolation artifacts with accompanying loss of real-world performance when upsampling.  This limits the potential for translating algorithms from research institutions to clinics.

In this project, we propose a framework for learning from spatially heterogeneous medical images.  In effect, rather than resampling images to make them homogeneous, we resample our neural network during training and when applying it to an image. This allows a single network to perform the same task on both high- and lower-resolution data, and on data with non-uniform voxel sizes.  We will adapt the recently proposed framework of Tensor Field Networks, in which feature extractors are paramaterized not by fixed euclidean grids but by a representation  in terms of spherical harmonics, to segmentation of medical images.  We anticipate that this will lead to smaller training set sizes and better performance on both high resolution 3D imaging and low resolution 2D imaging.  We propose two initial applications of this technology in MRI: brain segmentation for the assessment of neurodegeneration, and lesion segmentation in multiple sclerosis and brain tumor.
Keywords: Deep Learning, Machine Learning, Medical imaging, Neuroimaging

Title: Polaron dynamics from first principles
Abstract: Polarons are quasiparticles characterized by charge localization coupled with self-induced lattice distortions. The presence of polaronic states significantly affects the energetic and transport properties of electrons and holes, attracting interest in physics, chemistry, and material science. Since the pioneering work of Landau and Pekar nearly a century ago, many theories based on effective Hamiltonians treating electron-phonon interactions have been developed. In the limit of strong electron-phonon coupling, the charge localizes over a short length scale comparable to the lattice parameter, forming a small polaron. Conversely, in the limit of weak electron-phonon coupling, the charge localizes over a larger length scale encompassing multiple unit cells, forming a large polaron. Density functional theory represents a powerful tool for the ab-initio study of polarons in real materials. Recent advancements in density functionals indicate that polarons can be accurately modelled by suppressing the electron self-interaction. While this can be achieved at a semilocal level of theory for small polarons, modelling large polarons remains challenging due to the computational cost associated with large supercells. Alternative ab-initio theories based on many-body physics have been developed, aiming to unify the treatment of small and large polarons. Here, I propose to advance the state-of-the-art methods for modelling polarons in real materials, with the goal of studying the dynamics of both small and large polarons at the first-principles level of accuracy. This involves developing density functionals free from self-interaction, in conjunction with many-body theories for polarons. In this context, machine learning techniques based on active learning and equivariant neural networks can be employed to perform large time-scale and size-scale dynamics of polarons. This approach enables the exploration of physical insights into microscopic transport mechanisms involving polarons, without resorting to computationally expensive molecular dynamics simulations. The developed methods will be applied to bulk and surface polarons in materials relevant to energy storage and conversion technology, including transition metal oxides and perovskites.
Keywords: density functional theory, machine learning, many-body theory, polaron dynamics, polarons

Title: NOTUS: Nonlinear Optical Tensor Ultrafast Screening. Application to nano-objects
Abstract:
The research plan outlined in this proposal addresses the evolving landscape of 2D exfoliable materials, especially in the context of van der Waals heterostructures and the integration of 2D materials into complex devices. Advances in deterministic methods for 2D material transfer and placement have created opportunities for fabricating intricate devices, very difficult to achieve through conventional nanofabrication approaches. In the pursuit of efficient identification and characterization of nano-objects on large substrate surfaces, recent progress in image acquisition and machine learning presents a promising avenue. However, direct optical imaging faces limitations due to low contrast of linear dielectric function, prompting exploration into nonlinear optics (NLO), specifically high harmonic generation (HG) techniques. Indeed, HG offers valuable insights into 2D materials by providing detailed information on aspects such as crystal chemistry, structure and symmetry, number of layers, flake orientation, strain, magnetic ordering, and other relevant characteristics.

NOTUS project involves an optical design and software strategy to efficiently determine 2nd and 3rd order NLO tensors. The proposed method optimizes the information extraction from a single-point measurement of NLO high harmonic generated at the focal point of a fast-scanning confocal microscope, significantly reducing the measurement times. The experimental setup involves the generation of complex polarisation patterns in the Fourier plane through the Bessel-Gaussian beam excitation, leveraging a desynchronization of laser pulses along the path, which is usually considered as a drawback. Indeed, this novel approach enables rotationally anisotropic nonlinear harmonic generation (RA-NHG) at normal and finite angle of incidence simultaneously, optimizing the time efficiency of the measurement and giving access to information that is usually not accessible on ultrathin materials.

The proposed research within NOTUS aims to establish a pioneering method to measure NLO tensors of nano-objects. This project is high risk as it combines the development of an innovative optical design and focuses on emerging 2D materials where access to chemical and physical properties rely on limited characterization methods. In addition to its potential for swift localization and detailed characterization of 2D material flakes or heterostructures, this method has the potential to significantly overhaul the measurement of NLO tensors from any material or metamaterial present in the form of nanoparticles, like biomarkers. The broad applicability and detailed information extraction potential make it highly impactful for diverse fields.
Keywords: 2D materials, Heterostructures, microscopy, nonlinear optics, polarization

Title: Open Interaction Systems: an approach Based on Artificial Institutions and Service Oriented Architecture with an application to electronic market places
Abstract:
This research project is in the area of open interaction systems, that is, of software systems in which different programs, regarded as heterogeneous autonomous agents, interact with other agents according to a shared set of rules, in order to achieve their individual goals. A crucial characteristic of this innovative type of systems is that they are open: this means that they are available on the Internet and agents may freely enter and leave them. Major application areas of these systems are e-business (for the creation and management of virtual marketplaces, and for the creation, management, and dissolution of virtual enterprises or supply chains), and socio-technical systems (i.e., systems where human and artificial agents cooperate to achieve certain goals) in the Web 2.0 and 3.0 era.
This research proposal is a continuation of the SNF project 200021-121681 with the title “Open Interaction Systems: An approach based on artificial institutions and reasoning agents with an application to collaborative environments,” funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation from 1st May 2009 to 30th April 2011 and carried out by a Ph.D. student under the supervision of Prof. Marco Colombetti and Dr. Nicoletta Fornara.
In our past works (funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation, by the Hasler Foundation, and by the Swiss State Secretariat for Education and Research) we have defended the view that open interaction systems can be specified as artificial institutions, that is, as systems in which agents play certain roles, are empowered to perform certain actions, and are subject to a set of norms regulating the interactions. In particular we have proposed the OCeAN metamodel, that we now use for the specification of open interaction frameworks, regarded as artificial institutions.
During the on-going SNF project, we have continued our past research on the application-independent design of open interaction systems that allow agents to access a formal representation of the context and of the rules of interaction. Our research work has continued mainly at two levels: the meta-model level, and the architecture level. In particular we have investigated two main problems. 
The first problem concerns an agent’s ability to understand and use at runtime a logical representation of an artificial institution and the interaction system’s ability to monitor the agents’ interaction, in order to apply a form of social control to the actions of those autonomous and self-interested parties. This involves aspects concerning knowledge representation and reasoning. 
The second problem concerns the specification of the complete abstract software architecture (with no reference to a specific application domain) for institution-based open interaction systems that is necessary to enable independent parties to find each other, to interact in an open environment, and to have reliable expectations on the future evolution of the state of the system without necessarily regimenting all agent actions. In particular regarding this problem, after an extensive study of possible alternatives, we came to appreciate the importance for our goals of integrating Agent Oriented Computing (AOC) with Service Oriented Computing (SOC). To achieve this goal we carried out a systematic comparison of the Service Oriented Architecture (SOA) and some of the most widely adopted Agent Oriented Architectures at different levels: objectives, design principles, architectures, and platforms.
We now plan to continue our research by proposing architecture and an infrastructure for institution-based open interaction systems, which combine elements from both AOC and SOC, and by evaluating such a proposal through the realization of a prototype of an open interaction system in the e-business domain, that is, an e-marketplace. Given that these activities are strictly interconnected we plan to carry out them following an incremental development model.
The project will be carried out in two years at the Institute of Communication Technologies, Faculty of Communication Sciences, Università della Svizzera italiana, by a research team composed by Prof. Marco Colombetti, Dr. Nicoletta Fornara and a Ph.D. student.
Keywords: Agent  Oriented Architecture, Artificial Institutions, Electronic Marketplaces, Multiagent System, Normative Multiagent Systems, Open Interaction Systems, Semantic Web Services, Service Oriented Architecture, Service Oriented Computing

Title: Unifying Generative Models and Deep Learning for Counterfactual Reasoning in HIV Therapy Selection
Abstract:
Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV-1) currently affects more than 36 million people worldwide. Treatment for HIV infected individuals requires life-long administration of combinations of antiretrovirals to prevent the formation of drug-resistant strains. The large number of available drugs combined with the high mutagenic rate of the virus make manually searching for a suitable therapy particularly challenging for patients. Developing intelligent clinical decision support tools is crucial to address these concerns.

In this project we propose combining modern deep learning technology with classical generative modelling to infer the effects of a treatment policy on an HIV patient's overall outcomes. Deep learning technology has had a great impact across a multitude of application domains such as in computer vision and natural language processing. Its powerful performance and resulting success may be attributed to the large number of free parameters used in these systems that provide the capacity to exploit large amounts of training data and enable flexible modelling for complex prediction tasks. However, the application of deep learning technologies in healthcare has been limited as a result of their black-box behaviour and potential risks. Consequently, while deep learning has shown promise in applications, much of its success has been limited to relatively simple treatments composed of single drugs -- unlike the HIV therapy selection task. In contrast, generative models have a long history of success in healthcare and produce predictions that may easily be interpreted, but maybe limited in their ability to generalise as a result of fewer parameters. 

This research proposes combining the benefits of deep learning and generative approaches to tackle HIV therapy selection. While the combination of deep learning and generative models is a promising one, the HIV therapy selection task is frequently complicated by the influence of latent confounding when reasoning about the effects of a particular treatment. Latent confounding refers to the existence of an unobserved common cause of both a treatment and the outcomes obtained. It is a problem as it typically biases counterfactual predictions and distorts the underlying effect of interest. In the HIV therapy selection task for instance, socio-economic status may be an indirect confounder of a patient's therapy and hence impact negatively on the observed outcomes. Accounting for the effects of latent confounding is crucial in order to identify reasonable treatment policies for patients with HIV.  Together, these challenges motivate the proposed research project.
Keywords: HIV, causal inference, decision-support, deep learning, generative modelling, interpretability, latent confounding, machine learning

Title: PERPHECT: Deep Generative Networks for Bacteriophage Genetic Edition
Abstract:
Bacterial infections will become highly life-threatening events if nothing is done to curb the current trend of antimicrobial resistance. The paucity of potential new anti-infectives in the pipeline of pharmaceutical industries has called for the development of new treatment strategies and incited a renewed interest in bacteriophage (phage) therapy, i.e., the direct use of natural, microbial viruses for the treatment of bacterial infections, as such a potential alternative.
The close evolutionary relationship between phages and their bacterial hosts entails that their genetic information can be used to predict their interactions. The advent of high-throughput experimental techniques paved the way to genome-wide computational analysis and predictive studies. This has motivated several attempts to use bacterial and phage genome analysis, combined with data about known interactions, to train computational models that can predict interactions between new unknown bacteria and/or phages. 
Phage therapy efficacy may be hindered by the narrow host range and very high specificity of phages which causes (i) that finding the appropriate phages is a difficult task and (ii) obliging to produce and use cocktails of several phages to fight against simple infections. To solve this difficulty, one forward-thinking modernization of phage therapy is to use genetically-engineered (GE) phages. Such engineered viruses can provide substantial advantages over natural phage in terms of host range, immune system recognition, and environmental stability. A limitation for GE-phages is the empirical knowledge that is currently used to guide genetic modifications. Phages are estimated to be the most abundant organisms on Earth with unparalleled genetic diversity, making it impossible for basic research techniques to factor in all possible variables for creating the most active GE phages.
New technologies are further needed to accelerate the design-build-test cycle for engineering phages and to make it possible to translate proof-of-concept academic work into real-world use more efficiently. The application of Artificial intelligence (AI) to this context has potential both to increase the speed at which genomes can be engineered and to enhance the activity of resulting phages. The only applications of AI to phage biology concern mainly predicting species- and/or strain-level interactions, host species prediction, or the identification of novel viral sequences, making the idea proposed in this project highly innovative. 
This project, PERPHECT, focuses on the combined use of Deep Neural Networks, that enable extracting patterns directly from DNA sequences which are relevant to predict phage-bacteria interactions, and Deep Generative Adversarial Networks, that have the potential to create sequences, very similar to naturally occurring ones. The sequences generated with this approach are intended to maximize phage interaction with a target bacterium, while minimizing potentially-perturbing, length-associated effects such as noise, repeats, and non-informative code. Such essential segments are, then, integrated into selected, existing, phage genomes thanks to a genome-editing strategy based on sequence similarity and alignment. Finally, the resulting engineered phage genomes are evaluated in silico by means of several interaction-prediction computational models so as to validate their potential interaction.
Keywords: Deep Learning, Deep-generative networks, Machine Learning, Phage therapy, genetically-engineered phages

Title: Theory and Methods for Storage-Optimal Optimization
Abstract:
Semidefinite convex optimization problems often have low-rank solutions that can be represented with O(p)-storage. However, semidefinite programming methods require us to store the matrix decision variable with size O(p^2), which prevents the application of virtually all convex methods at large scale.

Indeed, storage, not arithmetic computation, is now the obstacle that prevents us from solving large- scale optimization problems. A grand challenge in contemporary optimization is therefore to design storage-optimal algorithms that provably and reliably solve large-scale optimization problems in key scientific and engineering applications. An algorithm is called storage optimal if its working storage is within a constant factor of the memory required to specify a generic problem instance and its solution.

So far, convex methods have completely failed to satisfy storage optimality. As a result, the literature has largely focused on storage optimal non-convex methods to obtain numerical solutions. Unfortunately, these algorithms have been shown to be provably correct only under unverifiable and unrealistic statistical assumptions on the problem template. They can also sacrifice the key benefits of convexity, as they do not use key convex geometric properties in their cost functions.

To this end, we propose a new optimization paradigm for designing optimization algorithms for large-scale optimization problems with structured solutions. We study three inter-related thrusts:

Thrust I: Storage optimal semidefinite programming. Over the last 20 years, semidefinite programming has established itself as a fundamental template for optimization. This thrust develops a new con- vex optimization algebra to obtain numerical solutions to semidefinite programs with a low-rank matrix streaming model. This streaming model provides us an opportunity to integrate sketching as a new tool for developing storage optimal convex optimization methods that go beyond semidefinite programming to more general convex templates. The resulting algorithms are expected to achieve unparalleled results for matrix optimization problems in signal processing, machine learning, and computer science.

Thrust II: Exploiting geometry in non-convex optimization. Storage optimal non-convex methods factor their decision variables in the expected solution structure, followed by alternating gradient descent for each factor. This thrust argues that the factorization idea is best complemented with gradient descent in an appropriate normed space so that we can better escape the curses of non-convex methods. Hence, Thrust II exploits geometric properties of costs functions for storage optimal non-convex optimization.

Thrust III: Applications. This thrust develops solutions to key mathematical problems based on the semidefinite programming template, including convex relaxations to combinatorial optimization and the sum-of-squares hierarchies. We also apply our results to notoriously hard but critical large-scale scientific and engineering problems such as Quadratic Assignment, Fourier Ptychography, Community Detection, and Optimal Power Flow. We also demonstrate algorithmic results on submodular function optimization, which is ubiquitous in machine learning with applications including clustering, sensor placement, subset selection, computer vision, structured sparsity and others.

Impact: If the famous Unique Games Conjecture is true, then semidefinite programming relaxations obtain optimal approximation for a large class of combinatorial optimization problems. By enabling the applicability of convex optimization to large-scale semidefinite programs, we hope to obtain approximate solutions to key combinatorial optimization problems. Essentially, we cannot do better.

Finally, to our knowledge, there are no direct precedents for the idea and realization of optimization methods that sketch the decision variable. As a result, the proposed work partake in a broader vision that randomization can be used to design numerical algorithms and is expected to inspire a new wave of storage-optimal methods to handle ever-increasing dimensions in optimization problems. We also expect new complexity results for the submodular optimization problems due to the new accelerated, generalized proximal gradient descent framework for their continuous relaxations.

Aside from the broader impact in combinatorial optimization problems, scalable convex optimization methods are key in signal processing, machine learning, and other engineering applications. We pursue a number of particularly important scientific applications and unlock new results, including Quadratic Assignment, Optimal Power Flow, Community Detection, and Fourier Ptychography with open source code made available to the broad scientific community via web.

Title: What’s in a Fruit? Connecting Apple Genetics, Sensory Language, and Perception to Improve Breeding
Abstract:
Perennial fruit crops rely on high inputs such as fungicides or irrigation in the face of ever-increasing biotic and abiotic stressors. Modern fruit breeding programs, such as the public ones for apple and pear maintained in Switzerland, strongly emphasize the development of robust varieties that contain multiple, redundant resistances against diseases. For this, high-throughput molecular markers and state-of-the art genomic prediction methods have been co-opted to improve selection of agronomic traits. However, even though some relevant fruit attributes, for example color or aroma components, have a relatively simple genetic basis, fruit quality remains essentially unpredictable. This is not so unexpected. Fruit quality is an extremely complex trait that not only depends on genetics but also management, storage, and ultimately, sensory perceptions and consumer expectations and preferences. Moreover, quality assessments in fruit breeding depends on low-throughput subjective perception ratings. Identifying an apple variety that has market potential thus requires trial-and-error testing and rating of approx. 2000-3000 trees. The complexity of this task, especially with fruit liking largely determined by non-additive genetic effects, makes it unlikely that breeding will soon produce a number of resilient varieties that are also adopted by the global markets. 
In this interdisciplinary project, we will combine statistical learning, computational linguistics, and genetic analysis to link fruit tree genetics to consumer preferences. Through collaboration, we will have access to apple genetic resource and breeding populations, i.e. apples from ~ 350 different varieties and genotyped by a 480K SNP genotyping array. To tackle the stark challenge of predicting fruit quality from genes, will introduces an intermediary layer -  sensory language - essentially breaking the problem into two steps. In a first step, we model the relationship between ~1,600 apple likings and word descriptors (color, appearance, texture, aroma, etc.) for sensory perceptions by different raters. These words-to-rating models will differ in complexity, from Bayesian networks to Random Forest to Neural Networks that can capture complex interactions influencing perception. A key innovation in generative AI—vectorized word representations (embeddings)—will enhance our models: instead of treating words as simple categories (one-hot encoding), we will integrate pre-trained embeddings (GloVe or word2vec) to enrich models with semantic meaning from large text corpora. In the second step, we will model how genetic variation can predict variation in these descriptors (genes-to-words models). The combined genes-to-words and words-to-perception models will offer an initial glimpse into the potential of genomic prediction infused with sensory linguistic analyses for fruit quality selection.
This proof-of-concept study could pave the way for more efficient fruit tree selection approaches, but also inspires new tools to study and understand consumer preferences and sensory perception. More broadly, this may serve as a case study on integrating unstructured data from diverse sources into genetic analyses to enhance crop breeding amid growing agronomic and market challenges.
Keywords: breeding, computer linguistics, horticulture, machine learning, sensory perception

Title: Prospective coding with pyramidal neurons
Abstract:
This Lead Agency proposal is a continuation of the personal SNF-grant of W. Senn on the theory of dendritic computation. In the running project period a key insight has been achieved by suggesting that learning on the level of a neuron implies the prediction of somatic spiking by the dendritic input (Urbanczik & Senn, Neuron 2014). This hypothesis introduces a paradigm shift in viewing dendritic computation and opens the door for a putative computational understanding of the signal processing in pyramidal neurons. So far, general experimental and theoretical research has tried to prove more and more complex nonlinearities in the dendritic processing of synaptic signals. But the mere description of a neuron as a complex input-output element gives only little insight into what dendrites are actually computing. In contrast, regarding neurons, and in particular pyramidal neurons, as intrinsic prediction elements links single neuron processing to a possible broader computational task.

The current proposal extends this single neuron hypothesis by the notion of prospective coding. This notion introduces the idea that the activity of a neuron not only predicts current, but also future synaptic inputs. The proposal takes account of the bipolar dendritic morphology of a pyramidal neuron with a basal and apical dendritic tree. We hypothesize that both the basal and apical tree make independent predictions of the somatic spiking. These predictions are based on within-network projections to the basal tree, and extrinsic or top-down connections to the apical tree. The match between the independent predictions represents a high confidence signal that generates a dendritic calcium spike with a subsequent burst of somatic action potentials. These bursts can then be fed back to the presynaptic neurons that can use them as a teaching signal for their own up-stream synapses. The theory and its experimental verification is divided into 4 subprojects:

SP1: Prospective coding (Lead: Senn lab, 1 PhD). Formalize the concept of prospective coding and show that the independent prediction of future input by the basal and dendritic trees is equivalent to a Bayesian cue combination problem.

SP2: Backpropagation in time (Lead: Senn lab, 1 postdoc). Show that the matching signal for the prediction of future events can be used to train hidden neurons that contribute to these predictions. Apply the theory to the non-Markovian sequence learning problem and to a simplified ball catching problem.

SP3: Novelty coding (Lead: Larkum lab, 1 postdoc – DFG). Test in vivo whether a dendritic calcium spike is representing the match between prediction signals or the match between novelty signals generated by the basal and apical trees. Verify the prediction of the cue combination hypothesis by measuring the neuronal responses to a somato-sensory oddball paradigm with combined auditory and somato-sensory cues.

SP4: Error-correcting plasticity (Lead: Nevian lab, 1 PhD). Verify the hypothesis in vitro whether synaptic plasticity both in excitatory and inhibitory plasticity is error-correcting and hence non-Hebbian. Test whether plasticity involving calcium spikes has a longer induction time window as predicted by prospective coding.

The first two subprojects are yield the formal framework in which the subsequent two experimental subprojects are embedded. The experiments are formulated such that, ideally, they verify or falsify the theory inspired hypotheses. They will be jointly designed and the results will be described in terms of a mathematical model.
Keywords: computational neuroscience, dendritic integration and spikes, learning theory, pyramidal neurons, synaptic plasticity

Title: Algorithmic Bargaining: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Intrastate Bargaining Processes
Abstract:
This research project investigates the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in intrastate bargaining processes. It contributes to the debate in international relations and security studies of how emerging technologies shape the nature of armed conflicts and their resolution. The findings have important policy implications for third parties seeking to use AI to strengthen their role in conflict management and settlement.

The research project is underpinned by the bargaining theory of war, a mainstay of international relations theory that assesses the onset, duration and settlement of armed conflicts. A key proposition of bargaining theory relates to the role of information provision in armed conflicts: because conflict parties have an incentive to misrepresent information about their military capacities and resolve, they do not trust each other’s information. This leads to inefficiencies that can result in war onset or impede conflict settlement. Recent advances in computing power and the availability of big data have led to important breakthroughs in technological applications enabled by AI, opening up new possibilities for conflict parties and third parties to obtain, provide and verify information in the context of armed conflicts. Yet, despite the clear link between AI and information provision in armed conflicts, there is little research into the role of AI in the context of inter- and intrastate bargaining processes. International relations and security studies instead prioritize research on the effects of AI on the nature of military warfare. Peace and conflict studies and grey literature study the effects of AI on conflict initiation and on third-party efforts to settle a conflict, but do not link their findings to wider bargaining processes.

This research project addresses this gap by asking the following research question: when and how will the use of artificial intelligence affect decisions in bargaining processes? It seeks to address in particular how AI-enabled information provision affects the decision of conflict parties to engage in wars or to make concessions to avert a war. 

The research comprises three main research tasks and a multi-methods research design underpinned by a bargaining framework. First, using semi-structured expert interviews, I will map extant and prospective AI applications in the context of ceasefire monitoring missions, providing the first comprehensive descriptive overview of endeavors in this field. Second, I will conduct scenario-based expert assessments into how specific AI applications will likely affect key bargaining obstacles in different ceasefire scenarios. Third, combining process tracing and a set-theoretic possible worlds approach, I will conduct a case study of the OSCE Special Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, a mission that deployed a range of sensory technologies to collect data about conflict dynamics, but subsequently lacked the capacity to comprehensively assess this data. This allows me to trace how existing sensory technology affected conflict violation patterns and progress at the negotiation table, and to assess how the use of AI to process all available data would have likely affected these dynamics. Combined, the findings of the three research tasks allow me to theorize when and how AI applications affect the use of conflict violence and progress towards negotiations in preliminary ceasefires. I will then use bargaining theory to systematically generalize to other instances of intrastate bargaining, building the first empirically founded theory of the role of artificial intelligence in intrastate bargaining processes.
Keywords: Armed conflicts, Artificial intelligence, Bargaining theory, Ceasefires, Information provision, Peace processes

Title: Skeleton Anything Anytask Anytime Anyway
Abstract:
Our research plan is centered on human motion prediction, leveraging the power of skeleton-based models to significantly surpass the current state of the art. The main goal is to develop a suite of methodologies that not only enhance the accuracy and efficiency of motion prediction in autonomous systems but also ensure robustness in their interaction with humans. This ambition is rooted in the belief that a deeper, more nuanced understanding of human movement can lead to safer, more effective autonomous systems across a variety of domains, including self-driving vehicles and social robotics.

Exceeding the State of the Art:
Our proposal aims to improve the limitations of current models by:

1. Developing a singular neural network architecture capable of detecting the skeletons of multiple objects simultaneously, an advancement that could dramatically improve the processing efficiency and scalability of autonomous systems.
2. Creating a versatile, pre-trained model that can adapt to a wide range of motion prediction tasks, significantly reducing the reliance on extensive labeled data and broadening the applicability of our technologies.
3. Addressing the challenge of dataset heterogeneity to enable effective training across diverse motion prediction datasets, which would enhance model versatility and performance in real-world scenarios.
4. Enhancing the robustness of motion prediction models to withstand real-world noise and adversarial attacks, ensuring the reliability autonomous systems in complex environments.

Research Approach and Implementation:
Our approach is divided into four strategic thrusts, each comprising a set of Work Packages (WPs) that target specific challenges:

Thrust 1 ("Skeleton Anything") focuses on the architecture for multi-object skeleton detection.
Thrust 2 ("Skeleton Anytask") is dedicated to developing a universal, adaptable pre-trained model.
Thrust 3 ("Skeleton Anytime") aims to refine motion prediction to accommodate any skeleton configuration.
Thrust 4 ("Skeleton Anyway") seeks to improve model robustness against noise and adversarial threats.

Each thrust is methodically designed to build upon preliminary results, employing a blend of cutting-edge techniques in computer vision and machine learning. The implementation plan allocates 18 months per WP, allowing for deep exploration, validation, and iteration based on ongoing findings and technological advancements. Regular review points will enable the team to adapt to changes in the field, ensuring that our research remains relevant and impactful.

By integrating these elements into a cohesive research strategy, we aim to not only push the boundaries of what is currently possible in motion prediction but also set new standards for the development of autonomous systems capable of seamlessly and safely navigating the complexities of human environments.

Title: Probabilistic Intraday Forecasting of Photovoltaic Power generation for the Swiss Plateau
Abstract:
The installed photovoltaic (PV) power capacity is expected to grow by 300 to 500% in Switzerland until 2035 (Energy Act 2018) and to expand similarly strongly in other European countries (IEA 2019). The intraday forecasts of generated PV power that are in operational use today are mostly based on weather forecast models and tend to produce large forecast errors (Fig. 5), in particular in changeable and cloudy weather conditions. More accurate intraday forecasts of the generated solar power and a better understanding and quantification of the forecast uncertainties are required in order to enable a more cost-efficient solar plant operation and reduce the cost incurred by grid operators and utilities for stand-by and storage capacities as well as suboptimal bidding in the intraday and balancing markets.
Most of today’s state-of-the-art probabilistic forecast models for solar irradiance and PV power are purely based on weather forecast products or historical in-situ point measurements rather than on near-real-time observations of the plant surrounding area (Hong et al. 2016, David et al. 2018), despite the fact that forecasting methods using sensor network and satellite data are believed to have great potential for higher accuracy intraday forecasts with well characterized uncertainties (Yang et al. 2018, Antonanzas et al. 2016). The existing satellite and sensor network based models only provide point forecasts, i.e. a single estimate of the forecast variable, and hence lack an explanation and characterization of the forecast’s uncertainty (Wang et al. 2019, David et al. 2018). 
The goal of this project is to provide a framework for more accurate and reliable intraday forecasts over the Swiss plateau where most current and additional future Swiss PV capacity will be located. Specifically, the project aims to develop more accurate, probabilistic forecasting methods of the global horizontal irradiance (GHI, W/m2) and the resulting generated PV power with quantified forecast uncertainties for forecast lead times of minutes to several hours. This time frame is most relevant for intraday operational risk management and decision support, and weather-model based PV forecasts tend to be outperformed by statistical and machine learning based forecasts including cloud advection models at this time horizon (Antonanzas et al. 2016). We will also investigate correlations between forecast errors across PV plants and scaling effects across the plants’ power generation.
To achieve these goals, we will combine satellite-derived estimates of GHI and data from one of the densest radiation sensor networks worldwide and use probabilistic cloud advection schemes (Pulkkinen et al. 2019) to forecast GHI probability density distributions. We will use statistical and machine learning approaches including deep neural networks to derive probabilistic PV production forecast models and employ them in a case study with four major Swiss multi-MW photovoltaic power plants (Fig. 4).
Our expected results include the provisioning and publication of the forecasting framework and its application and characterization in a case study with the four largest Swiss PV plants, where we will also analyze correlation and scaling effects between the plants. This project will be the first to perform probabilistic surface solar irradiance forecasts and probabilistic PV power forecasts based on satellite imagery, to the best of our knowledge. We expect to provide to the field a more accurate and reliable PV forecasting methodology and a deeper understanding of aggregated PV output modelling for a suite of plants. Extending beyond academic research, this project will facilitate an improved risk management and reduced operational cost through more accurate and reliable forecasts. The forecasting framework and results will be presented and provided to PV plant and grid operators in the course of the project.

al. 2018), despite the fact that forecasting methods using sensor network and satellite data are believed to have great potential for higher accuracy intraday forecasts with well characterized uncertainties (yang et al. 2018, antonanzas et al. 2016). the existing satellite and sensor network based models only provide point forecasts, i.e. a single estimate of the forecast variable, and hence lack an explanation and characterization of the forecast’s uncertainty (wang et al. 2019, david et al. 2018). the goal of this project is to provide a framework for more accurate and reliable Title: Hybrid Approach for Robust Identification and Measurement of Investors Driving Corporate Sustainability and Innovation. Design of Policy Tools for Evaluating the Impact of Specific Investors and Assessing the Quality of Companies’ Investor Bases.
Abstract:
Following several decades of profit-oriented research in finance and economics, we have recently been observing a profound transformation in investor perception and a visible shift towards a sustainable financial system. The list of UN PRI signatories includes already over 2,000 large asset owners and keeps growing every year. Several reports (US SIF 2018) indicate that over 20% of professionally managed assets in the U.S. is already being invested according to the principles of socially responsible investing (SRI). While an increasing number of institutional investors are indicating their commitment to social and environmental sustainability, it remains unclear which investors have the most substantial and lasting effect on the sustainability of companies.
In this project, we intend to measure the extent to which specific investors influence the sustainability of companies they invest in. We focus on the measurable side of sustainability, in particular the environmental impact of the activity of companies, and the level of corporate innovation, measured using patents data. By combining a previously untested dataset with a novel, hybrid methodology, we seek to answer deep-rooted scientific and practical questions such as whether the investor base affects the sustainability and innovation potential of a company. If so, can we identify and highlight investors who are effectively driving the future development of companies across the globe?
By answering these questions, we will provide clear guidance on the design of policy tools to support investors and monitor the investor bases of companies. To maximize the societal and scientific impact of this project, we will use our findings to design two practical tools for policymakers and investors, which will empower them to make more viable and future-oriented decisions concerning sustainability and innovation. The first tool will enable an evaluation of the impact of a specific investor on sustainability, based on their historical behavior. The second tool will provide information whether company’s investor base is likely to promote its sustainable development.
Our approach differs sharply from other projects in this field:
- While the bulk of existing studies either use investor groups, we focus on the impact of individual investors on the evolution of sustainability of the companies they invest in. This will involve building and using untested dataset on investors and company data.
- We extend the scope of the analysis to include crucial investors such as insurers, banks, pension funds, hedge funds as well as sovereign wealth funds.
- We focus simultaneously on sustainability and innovation, which has not been investigated in a comprehensive analysis so far.
- We include European and U.S. companies and investors, in contrast to U.S.-focused studies.
- The proposed hybrid methodology combines linear and non-linear approaches as well as machine learning. It provides a variety of novelties over conventional approaches such as: adaptivity and time variation, addresses the spurious regression problem, and combines linear and non-linear dynamics. We also include a multi-tier data aggregation technique.
- We provide user-friendly assessment tools and seek to maximize usability of results.
Through contacts with national and international organizations as well as public and private sector investors, we will disseminate the research and tools to an academic and non-academic audience.
Keywords: data science, innovation, investor base, sustainability

Title: Neural precision Holographic Volumetric Additive manufacturing
Abstract:
Traditional additive manufacturing (AM) techniques rely on sequential point-by-point or layer-by-layer processes, constructing 3D objects by stacking multiple 2D layers. While widely adopted, this approach inherently limits performance due to its sequential nature, resulting in build rates of approximately 10–100 cm³/hour—three orders of magnitude slower than injection molding. Additionally, the layered structure introduces anisotropy, weakening mechanical properties along the build direction.
To overcome these limitations, a paradigm shift has emerged in the form of Tomographic Volumetric Additive Manufacturing (TVAM), a method we introduced. Unlike conventional layer-by-layer AM, TVAM enables true 3D fabrication by simultaneously solidifying an entire volume of liquid photopolymer through multi-angle dynamic light pattern irradiation. Solidification occurs when each voxel within the resin receives an irradiation dose exceeding a specific threshold.
Most TVAM studies have utilized incoherent light intensity patterning, where only 1–10% of the spatial light modulator (SLM) pixels contribute to the final exposure, leading to significant light loss. By harnessing coherent light patterning—also known as holographic projection—light utilization efficiency can approach nearly 100%. Moreover, this technique enables precise 3D light intensity control within the build volume. By harnessing time-domain multiplexing, sequential phase pattern projections dynamically modulate the 3D energy distribution, enabling voxel-selective polymerization and the fabrication of arbitrary 3D structures. This approach drastically reduces the required number of illumination angles from several hundred to just one or two.
However, two major challenges arise in this process. The first is optical distortions and speckle artifacts, which degrade the accuracy of the projected 3D intensity patterns. Achieving precise holographic control requires a detailed physical model at the nanometric scale to describe wave propagation through the optical system and resin container. The second challenge is the dynamic interaction between light and the photoresin, where local refractive index variations caused by polymerization alter subsequent light propagation. These effects lead to deviations from the intended 3D energy distribution, introducing fabrication errors and structural imperfections.
To overcome these longstanding challenges, this project introduces a breakthrough integration of artificial intelligence (AI), combining a physics-based propagation model with neural network architectures that learn and refine the complex forward model governing both light transport and photopolymerization dynamics. By incorporating real-world experimental data, the neural networks aim to adaptively capture the system’s nonlinearities with high fidelity. A closed-loop camera-based setup continuously acquires physical outputs, enabling iterative refinement of the AI model to optimize phase pattern predictions and actively correct for system distortions. Critically, the ability to fabricate full 3D objects in mere tens of seconds unlocks unprecedented data throughput, allowing rapid generation of large, diverse datasets to accelerate AI training and convergence—a key enabler of this paradigm shift. By embedding AI-driven learning into the holographic VAM process, this research aims to achieve unprecedented accuracy and fabrication speed by orders of magnitude in volumetric printing, pushing the frontiers of high-resolution, high-speed additive manufacturing.

Title: Computational Electrochemistry: Towards the Understanding of Electrolytes at the Molecular Level
Abstract:
In the quest for reducing fossil fuel dependence, finding sustainable solutions to the energy crisis has become a challenge of the utmost urgency. Electrochemistry is a promising solution to these energy challenges as it facilitates the conversion of electrical energy into chemical energy, and vice versa, enabling the storage of excess electricity production in the form of chemical energy.
 
In recent years, electrochemical interface engineering, such as modifying pH, solvent catalyst structure, buffer,, and electrolyte, has gained considerable attentions to improve electrochemical reactions.
The presence and concentration of electrolytes are reported to affect many electrochemical processes, including double-layer capacitance, hydrogen evolution reactions, and carbon oxide reduction reactions. A fundamental understanding of electrolytes at the molecular level is highly desirable, as electrolytes contribute greatly to the efficiency of Faradaics, long-term operation stability, and reaction selectivity. However, the role of electrolyte cation in the electrical double layer and electrochemical reactions is still unclear. For instance, why does the differential capacitance of metal electrodes depend linearly on the electrolyte cation? What is the role of electrolytes in electrochemical reactions and how do they affect their activity and selectivity? What causes the activity to decrease with the size of electrolyte cation on some electrodes while increasing on others?
Some explanations for how alkali metal cations affect activity and selectivity are: binding energy, local electric field, interfacial pH, stabilization of reaction intermediates. However, many questions are still controversial, as the commonly used computational hydrogen electrode model ignores the dynamical nature of electrochemical systems and approximates the applied electrode potential. Indeed, it is non-trivial to simulate realistic electrochemical systems as this requires the electrode potential to remain constant.
The role of electrolytes on free energy landscapes of electrochemical reactions has not yet been examined. Having a precise assessment of the free energy landscape enables direct comparison with experiments, resulting in a molecular understanding of electrolytes.
 
This project will go beyond the commonly adopted computational hydrogen electrode model by considering the dynamical nature of the electrolyte and reaction intermediates within the electrical double layer.
It will attempt to understand how electrolytes, particularly alkali metal cations, affect structural, electronic, dynamic, and reactive properties of electrochemical reactions. More importantly, the simulations will provide a free energy description of the electrochemical reactions with the presence of electrolytes at a constant electrode potential. It will establish the key physical principles for the development of efficient electrolytes for facilitating renewable energy conversion through electrochemistry.

Title: Pyrogenic Cirrus Formation study (PyCiFy): the climatic impact of wildfire-induced ice clouds
Abstract: Extreme events, such as wildfires, and their connection to climate change are gaining significant public attention and are a focus of intense research. To accurately represent wildfire smoke particles in numerical weather prediction and climate models, it is essential to explore the various pathways through which smoke aerosols can influence the climate system. This project investigates the potential impact of wildfire smoke on the formation of high-altitude pure ice clouds known as cirrus. While cirrus clouds typically contribute to climate warming, the microphysical and radiative effects of seeding them with smoke aerosols have not been extensively studied and remain controversial. The PyCiFy project addresses this critical research gap by utilizing satellite remote sensing retrievals to construct extensive datasets for both model evaluation and the development of a machine learning parameterization specifically designed to predict the ice nucleation ability of smoke particles. Integrating the newly-developed ice nucleation parameterization into the ICON-ART model aims to uncover the often-overlooked interactions between smoke, cirrus clouds, and climate. Through sensitivity simulations, we will assess whether the new parameterization improves the modeled cloud cover, precipitation, and radiation patterns, ultimately enhancing our global understanding of this underappreciated climate feedback. This project aims to produce valuable outcomes, including a comprehensive remote sensing dataset, insights into smoke-cirrus interactions, and a novel ice nucleation parameterization for use in global climate models. Given the increasing prevalence of wildfires in our changing climate, understanding the intricate relationships between fires and broader climate dynamics is imperative for more accurate future climate projections.
Keywords: cirrus clouds, climate modeling, ice nucleating particles, machine learning parameterization, model development, pyrocumulonimbus clouds, satellite retrievals, smoke aerosols, wildfires

Title: Context Sensitive Information: Robust Optimization by Information Theoretic Regularization
Abstract:
Data analysis questions in machine learning and statistics are often
formulated as optimization problems where desired patterns in data are
assigned low costs. The search for such low-cost patterns is almost
always affected by random fluctuations that originate from noisy
measurements.  Consequently, we have to distinguish between expected
costs of patterns and their empirical costs. The data analyst is
required to identify the signal in the data and to separate it from
noise. Inferred patterns should generalize over repeated measurements
with identical signal but varying noise.  This requirement of
repeatable experimentation implies that patterns in data should
generalize from one date instance to a second one, meaning that
solutions inferred on the first data set should also yield low costs on
a second data set drawn from the same probability distribution.

A general approach to optimization under uncertainty suggests a
regularization strategy for cost functions by penalizing too complex
solutions. We adopt this philosophy to optimization and advocate an
information theoretic perspective where the uncertainty in the
measurements quantizes the set of patterns and, thereby, induces
granularity in the solution space of learning problems. Effectively,
the distinguishable patterns define a code in a fictional
communication scenario where the stochastic data source in combination
with the selected cost function plays the role of a noisy channel.
Maximizing the so-called approximation capacity determines the
penalized costs of the pattern recognition problem with a data
dependent regularization strength.  The trade-off between
\emph{informativeness} and \emph{robustness} in statistical inference
is mirrored in the balance between high information rate and zero
communication error, thereby giving rise to a new notion of
structure-induced information.

This project pursues the goal to study the general concept of
information theoretic regularization of cost functions in the setting
of continuous and combinatorial optimization problems. The relation
between statistical complexity and computational complexity are a
central question of this study. Robust cost function with optimally
regularized solutions are expected to require low to moderate
computational costs in many real-world settings. Understanding this
algorithmic folklore is of utmost importance for engineering
practice in modeling. 

Two PhD students, one from theoretical computer science / operations research and one from computational science / machine learning, will closely work together to investigate the dependency of statistical complexity and computational complexity. Thereby, the project will substantially contribute to bridge the gap between these two core communities of information technology.
Keywords: Pattern recognition, approximation algorithms, information theory, maximum entropy method, model selection, optimization, robust optimization, statistical learning theory, stochastic programming

Title: Flow Data Inpainting with Neural Networks
Abstract:
Predicting missing flow data is a common problem in various applications and domains, including quantitative flow measurements in test facilities, scientific flow visualization, human-based flow scanning, Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV), or Doppler flow velocity measurements in medical settings. This happens because dense measurements might not be available due to missing sensors, undersampled domains or occluded areas. Various methods have been proposed for data prediction and data fusion, but a main challenge is to handle large areas of missing or occluded data, i.e. where more than 50% of the data has to be predicted. 

In this project, we hypothesize that data recovery in large occluded and empty areas can be learned by neural networks. We therefore propose to develop a deep learning based approach to reliably predict missing flow data. In particular, we will use inpainting approaches that have been successfully used in visual computing, e.g., pixel recovery in images, geometry completion, depth inpainting and view path planning. These inpainting methods cannot be directly applied to 3D flow data, as the underlying physical laws and dynamics of the flow have to be considered. We will therefore synergistically combine deep learning with fluid dynamics, considering the mathematical equations that model fluid phenomena for designing the network architecture, parameters and loss functions. Additionally, special care has to be taken to ensure that temporal coherency of the velocity field data is properly enforced. We aim at a neural approach that has a low memory footprint such that time-varying high-resolution 3D data can be handled.

Our work will be based on a previous proof-of-concept method (unpublished) for flow data inpainting that uses a neural network to predict velocity values of a single frame in a 2D CFD simulation. First results on data sets with large occlusions (50%-95%) show the large potential of deep learning approaches. A significant problem of the current approach is the large memory footprint, restricting the inpainting method to the 2D domain and a single time instance. We propose to develop a novel, low-memory approach for time-varying 3D flow data inpainting with neural networks, aiming at high-resolution flow data sets. The new proposed method will be developed by exploring patch-based approaches, progressive inpainting and multi-scale techniques to reduce memory and to enable reliable predictions especially in turbulent flow regions and near obstacle boundaries. We will further extend the network to learn the dynamics and hence to predict flow data in unsteady flow fields. Lastly, network strategies to combine synthetic and real data will be investigated.
Keywords: Deep Learning, Fluid Dynamics, Inpainting, Neural networks

Title: The Security and Privacy of Real Machine Learning Systems
Abstract:
Many applications of machine learning face clear security and privacy challenges. Yet, our understanding of their vulnerability in practice remains limited. Existing adversarial machine learning research is primarily model-centric: it focuses on showing how the security and privacy of isolated machine learning models can, in principle, be attacked. Yet, machine learning models are rarely deployed in isolation, but rather as one component of a larger learning-based system. As a result, there is a clear gap between our understanding of security and privacy risks of machine learning models “in the lab”, compared to real learning systems deployed in adversarial settings. This makes it challenging for model developers to proactively safeguard their users’ security and privacy against practical threats.

In this proposal, we will build upon, and broaden the scope of our past research on evaluating the robustness and privacy of machine learning models in security-sensitive settings. Our key objectives are to: (1) understand the security of machine learning against realistic attackers, and build up ethical principles for white-hat adversarial machine learning; (2) move beyond the current model-centric view of machine learning security, to instead map the practical attack surface of entire machine learning systems; (3) unify the scattered landscape of attacks and defenses on the privacy of learning systems, and advise practitioners on how to best protect the privacy of their users.

**Research Thrust 1: Robustness Evaluations of Realistic Machine Learning Models.**
The first thrust of this proposal addresses a fundamental question in machine learning security: how robust are real security-sensitive machine learning systems against evasion attacks (adversarial examples)? Our thesis is that no existing attack can reliably succeed against realistic systems. We will thus design new methods tailored to evaluating the robustness of realistic learning systems. Along the way, we further aim to lay down grounding principles for safe and ethical white-hat adversarial machine learning research—building upon well-established white-hat principles in computer security.

**Research Thrust 2: Beyond Model-centric security and privacy.**
Research on adversarial machine learning is primarily model-centric, focusing on vulnerabilities in the training and deployment of stand-alone machine learning models. In our second research thrust, we aim to broaden the scope of this research field by mapping the attack surface of the entire pipeline of modern machine learning systems. This system-wide view will enable us to surface undiscovered vulnerabilities in common components of modern machine learning pipelines, but also new opportunities for pragmatic defenses that go beyond securing a stand-alone model.

**Research Thrust 3: Pragmatic Privacy Engineering and Auditing.**
In the third thrust of this proposal, we aim to embrace a rigorous empirical assessment of the privacy risks of machine learning systems, and help clarify the currently scattered landscape of attacks and defenses in the research literature. Our aim is to provide model developers with the right tools and insights to make informed decisions about the best way to protect and audit the data privacy of their systems. As for machine learning security, we will also strive to go beyond the current model-centric view of machine learning privacy, and study privacy risks that arise within entire machine learning systems.

**Envisioned Impact.**
Machine learning is permeating countless application domains and industries, many of which have strong security and privacy needs. Yet, it remains unclear what risks these systems realistically face in practice, and how to pragmatically mitigate them. This research grant will help us to significantly broaden the scope of adversarial machine learning research, and to study under-explored risks, as well as opportunities for in-depth defenses, in learning systems. Our work will promote open security research in machine learning, and foster the development of an ethically grounded community of white-hat adversarial machine learning researchers. Our goal, ultimately, is to help safeguard the security and privacy of the users of machine learning systems against realistic threats.
Keywords: Adversarial Machine Learning, Computer Security, Machine Learning Security, Privacy

Title: Enhancing Predictive Accuracy of Immunotherapy Response in NSCLC Through Machine Learning-Based Estimation of Clonal TMB
Abstract:
Immunotherapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors (CPI) has provided substantial clinical benefits for patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). These patients can receive anti-PD-L1/PD-1 immunotherapy as a standard treatment in both early and late stages of the disease. However, predicting the response remains challenging with available biomarkers.
Currently, PD-L1 protein expression on tumor cell and tumor mutational burden (TMB) are the primary biomarkers for patient stratification in CPI therapy. Although TMB is acknowledged as a predictive biomarker for CPI efficacy in solid tumors, its universal application has limitations in accurately predicting response. Intratumor heterogeneity (ITH), prevalent in NSCLC, is one reason overall TMB fails to predict response accurately. Recent studies have shown that clonal aberrations, including clonal mutations and predicted neoantigens present in every cancer cell, are better predictors of therapeutic response.
Here, I propose to develop a robust framework for estimating clonal and subclonal TMB from single-region sequencing samples using high-dimensional modeling and machine learning algorithms. I will leverage data from the TRACERx study, which includes a cohort of 421 NSCLC patients with multi-region sampling (1,644 tumor regions) at primary surgery and during follow-up subjected to whole-exome sequencing (WES). The core idea is to utilize comprehensive multi-region WES data to train a model that accurately estimates clonal TMB from single-region samples. This model aims to overcome the limitations of single-region sampling, which often fails to capture the non-uniform distribution of genetic aberrations within tumors.
The results from this study will provide an accurate method to enhance the predictive power of FDA-approved companion diagnostics in clinical settings, offering a robust machine learning algorithm that improves the accuracy and reliability of TMB estimation for better patient stratification and treatment outcomes.
Keywords: Immunotherapy, Intratumor Heterogeneity, Lung cancer, Machine Learning, Tumor mutational Burden

Title: Real-time traffic estimation and control in a connected environment
Abstract:
In the last decades, motorways have become notorious sites of extensive daily traffic congestion, particularly in and around metropolitan areas. Traffic congestion degrades the available infrastructure in the sense of reducing the motorway throughput. Thus, the expensive motorway infrastructure is underutilised ironically exactly at the times it is most urgently needed (peak hours or emergencies). The efficient, safe, and less-polluting transportation of persons and goods on motorways calls for an optimal utilisation of the available infrastructure via suitable application of a variety of traffic control measures such as ramp metering (RM), driver information, route guidance, and variable speed limits (VSL). 

Coordinated RM aims at improving the traffic conditions by appropriately regulating the inflow from the on-ramps to the motorway mainstream. Another control measure for traffic flow on motorways is the display of VSL on appropriate dynamic signs in response to the prevailing traffic conditions. The main idea of VSL is that when a bottleneck is active at a highway location, and congestion propagates upstream, the authorities need to change the speed limit and warn the drivers approaching the end of the queue. This has a direct implication on drivers’ safety (30% less accidents reported in Germany after VSL application), but also, on traffic flow (i.e. can increase the throughput of the bottleneck area). Harmonizing the oscillations of speeds and reducing the stop-and-go traffic during peak hours can result in energy savings, less CO2 emissions and can have a major environmental impact. Moreover, traffic flow is smoother and traffic jams can be delayed and last for shorter periods (i.e. significant delay savings).

The current project focuses on developing integrated control solutions (i.e. coordinated RM and VSL) for managing congestion on motorway networks. A real-time efficient solution of this problem requires the development of new control methodologies that will be based on advanced techniques from the domains of control theory and optimization. The idea is to combine the concept of feedback linearization (due to the nonlinearities of the model) with Lyapunov stability. We aim at designing an optimal controller that utilizes both concepts, and formulate a convex optimization problem (i.e. quadratic) that can be solved online efficiently. The methodology needs to be tested in simulation but also in real life conditions. The derived controllers need to be accompanied with an online estimation scheme that can feed them with appropriate inputs. Depending on the configuration of the sensors (which is site-specific), the spatial and temporal resolution, as well as hardware failures and malfunctions, a traffic control room needs to make sure that has all the necessary machinery in place, so that to provide the state feedback to the regulators, given all the available real-time measurements. This way, the online closed-loop system becomes much more flexible, as it can be applied to sites with sparse measurements and/or frequent hardware/communications failures. The developed estimation engine will make use of machine learning, filtering theory, statistical correlations, and traffic flow theory, and will be able to fill the gaps of missing data in the space and time domains.

In a future connected environment with Vehicle-to-X (V2X) technologies we will have access to traffic data of different nature, that will have inherent differences compared to the conventional loop detector data we are using today. It has to be noted that this scenario is not futuristic but rather quite realistic, as such technologies are already on our roads (e.g. Tesla), and are going to increase incrementally in the next few years. Pilots with autonomous vehicles (AV) are currently run in many places around the world and traffic operators are going to dace mixed traffic (i.e. AV and human driven vehicles) rather soon. The rich data sets that V2X and AV provide need to be integrated with our current data to produce traffic estimates of high accuracy. To this end, the classical models of traffic flow theory that have been used for the last 60 years need to be revisited and modified, in order to accompany the technological advancements of the automobile industry.

VSL infrastructure has been installed recently (and continues to be installed) in highways around Zurich. Traffic operators recognize today that VSL can improve safety, reduce fuel emissions, and also reduce delays during the peak hours that traffic jams occur. The current practice is to use predetermined thresholds for congestion levels and speed limits and create look-up tables for different conditions (e.g. when congestion forms the speed limits go down from 120 km/h to 100 km/h and then 80 km/h). By making this process dynamic and automatic, we can improve its efficiency and enhance the digitalization of traffic infrastructure. The control approach that we propose is novel and is expected to have a scientific impact. A potential real-time field implementation in the traffic network will be one of the first attempts worldwide. Our research group is currently in contact with the traffic operators in the cities of Zurich and Aarau, and also with the Traffic Management Center of ASTRA in Lucerne, that manages all Swiss national roads (i.e. highways and other major roads). We are currently preparing proposals for field implementations in a series of Swiss cities. We aim at implementing the algorithms developed during this project at a Traffic Control Center and regulating the traffic along a stretch of a Swiss highway.
Keywords: Motorway traffic management, Traffic control, Traffic estimation
