Title: Forecasting Mortality: Leveraging Cause-of-Death Data through Neural Network Techniques
Abstract:
Life expectancy is an important input parameter for individuals' lifecycle financial planning and for the financial management of public and private insurance programs, including pensions and life insurance. Demographers and actuaries project life expectancy based on estimates of future mortality rates. In the past few decades, mortality rates have evolved rapidly and there is uncertainty around future trends in mortality and life expectancy. This uncertainty can cause financial risks to individuals and organizations. Insurance regulation in the European Union and Switzerland (Solvency II, Swiss Solvency Test) requires insurers and pension funds to develop statistical models to quantify their exposure to 'mortality risk'. 

This project aims to develop new models to forecast mortality rates using cause-of-death data. We will leverage cause-of-death data through machine learning techniques in order to improve mortality forecasts. Although the need for better methods of forecasting mortality trends, including the impact of cause-of-death trends, has been recognized for some time, such an approach is rarely used. Two of the main reasons behind this lack of cause-of-death data use lie in the difficulty of determining the main cause of death (multiple causes) and modelling the dependence structure of the causes. Modelling this dependence structure is difficult as it is not directly observable. Besides, the fact that  death certificate can list multiple causes of death renders the analysis of cause-specific mortality dependence even more challenging. Therefore, most mortality projections are based on aggregate rates or assume independence between causes. In this project, we aim to improve mortality forecasts at two different levels:

1) Mortality forecasts based on main cause-of-death data: Past studies tend to indicate that in order to forecast aggregate (all-cause) mortality, we usually get better results when aggregate, and not cause-specific, data are used, which contradicts many experts' beliefs. We intend to investigate if more recently widely used statistical techniques may prove the contrary and, thus, be more aligned with experts' beliefs.

2) Mortality forecasts based on multiple-cause-of-death data: Individuals often have multi-morbidity, which leads to multiple causes of death. We aim to analyze and model the relationships binding these multiple causes and assess whether the use of such data may improve the mortality forecasts of cause-specific, as well as aggregated, mortality rates.

Neural network techniques will be mainly used for such analysis. Indeed, recent applications of neural networks to aggregate mortality forecasts proved to be of extreme accuracy. As the benefits deriving from the implementation of neural networks techniques, compared to classical time series approaches, are known to be more important for in-homogeneous time series, the potential improvements in cause-specific mortality forecasts are significant, such time series being highly in-homogeneous. In addition, neural networks are powerful in detecting unidentifiable patterns as well as nonlinear structures and interactions in the studied data. It provides a tool to the research community to implicitly consider the dependence structure existing between the causes of death. We intend to fully exploit the potential of neural network techniques not well-known in the field of mortality modelling in order to improve the forecasting performance of current mortality models using cause-of-death data.

The project will develop new models and provide new empirical results that will (i) extend the current academic research on mortality modelling, and (ii) be useful for practical applications in individuals' lifecycle financial planning and the financial management of public and private insurance programs. The new knowledge on cause-specific mortality forecasting has the potential to impact related research in demography, economy, biology or epidemiology.
Keywords: Aggregate mortality forecasts, Cause-of-death mortality, Cause-specific mortality forecasts, Dependence, Machine learning techniques, Muliple-cause-of-death data, Neural networks

Title: Coral Bleaching in East Africa: Consequences and Adaptations
Abstract:
Coral bleaching is a phenomenon caused by climate change that can negatively impact coral reef ecosystems and thereby affect fish stocks. As a consequence, it poses a threat to the well-being of communities that depend on coastal fisheries. A large portion of coral reefs worldwide is expected to be severely damaged before the end of this century. However, the empirical literature analyzing potential effects on affected communities is very limited. 

The proposed research project addresses this gap through a comprehensive analysis of impacts, adaptation strategies as well as potential consequences of these adaptation strategies to understand the full economic consequences of coral bleaching. It focuses on the four East African countries of Kenya, Madagascar, Mozambique and Tanzania, all of which have sub-populations that depend on artisanal fishing on coral reefs. 

Since coral bleaching can lead to a decrease or collapse of coastal fish stocks, it is probable that it impacts income and nutrition levels of affected households. The impact could be direct for people that themselves depend (fully or partly) on fishing, or indirect through an increase in prices for seafood and other protein sources. We will estimate the impact of coral bleaching on stunting of children (as an indicator for protein malnutrition) and household wealth based on using coral bleaching data from satellite imagery and micro-level data from the Demographic and Health Surveys in the four countries. 

Households may adjust their strategies in response to a shock to their livelihood.  To study the adaptation behaviour of households in response to a coral bleaching event, we rely on panel micro data for one of the sample countries, Tanzania. The National Panel Survey, which was implemented in Tanzania as part of the World Bank's Living Standards Measurement Study, includes the same households across several survey rounds. This allows for controlling for unobserved determinants of household income and examining adaptation behaviour in the form of increased work effort and an expansion of cultivated land. 

Last, we analyze whether coral bleaching has resulted in deforestation. Previous research has indicated that land use change, namely the expansion of cultivated land, can be one potential adaptation strategy. This could imply increased vulnerability as a second order consequence of the adaptation to coral bleaching, potentially leading to a vicious cycle of vulnerability, increasing the impacts of coral bleaching over the medium to long term. In order to answer this question, high resolution land use data sets will be used to analyze the impacts of coral bleaching events on deforestation. 

All questions addressed in this research have a high degree of synergy as they rely on the same rich data sets for both explanatory and control variables and our analyses are similar in their econometric approach. Additionally, the preparatory work for this project in the form of creating of a high-resolution data set on coral bleaching, based on machine learning and satellite imagery, is already being implemented and will be finalized under a separate grant. This means that the research team will have access to a unique data set, increasing both the relevance as well as the benefit-cost relationship of the proposed research. 

This project is more limited in scope than standard applications to the SNSF: We request funding for one Ph.D. student for 15 months.
Keywords: Climate Change, Coral bleaching, East Africa, Remote sensing, Tanzania, climate change, coastal areas, coral bleaching, fisheries, livelihoods, satellite data

Title: First-principles macroscopic properties of phase change materials with physics-based machine-learning
Abstract:
Phase change materials (PCM) are functional materials that can rapidly and reversibly switch between a crystalline and an amorphous phase with a contrasting set of properties, like electrical resistivity or optical reflectance, making them ideal for several technological applications. In particular, the Ge–Sb–Te (GST) alloys have received extensive attention because of their success in digital data storage technologies, from re-writeable DVD and Blu-Ray discs to non-volatile memory platforms. Quantum mechanical (“first-principles”) computer simulations have long been providing a detailed picture of the atomic-scale interactions in PCMs, and have been used to describe the origins of the property contrast between their crystalline and amorphous phases (“one” and “zero” bits). Despite impressive improvements in modern hardware infrastructures and electronic structure methods, the time scale of the switching process or the length scale of these nanodevices make it impossible to directly simulate these devices from first-principles. However successful the community has been in simulating and modeling smaller, well-chosen, and representative atomic structures, the results still invariably suffer from finite-size effects and cannot be fully representative of the real devices.
    Current approaches to circumventing these issues include the use of statistical methods and machine learning (ML) approaches to simulate large and complex atomic configurations. These methods rely on training models from data sets that represent much smaller structures, where it is possible to perform first-principles calculations and use ML to extrapolate to unseen structures. These approaches, as currently applied to study PCMs, mostly focus on building surrogate ML interatomic potential (MLIP) models. They have been successfully used to propose structural models for the amorphous phase of PCMs, to compute the thermal conductivity and even to simulate the active material in nanodevices. However, these ML models typically predict energies and forces on atoms, and therefore lack the knowledge about other properties related to the electronic structure. Thus, they can not be applied directly to predict electrical and optical properties of PCMs, because the latter rely on electronic structure properties like the electronic density of states (DOS) and the polarization.
    The objective of this proposal is to develop a computational framework to predict macroscopic properties of PCMs using size-transferable models for the electronic structure properties, mainly the DOS and the polarization. This project will directly address some of the most central design and modeling needs of PCMs, like their thermal and electrical conductivity, and their optical reflectance. In particular, a novel physics-based approximation will be developed to allow the use of ML DOS models to compute the electrical conductivity, which can be applied directly to PCMs and could, in the long run, be of interest for studying other materials. The computational cost associated with constructing a training set of structural data has already been alleviated by the host lab, which have recently shown how to build an MLIP for the GST family of PCMs. Electronic structure calculations will be carried out for those structural models to achieve highly-converged electronic DOS and polarization data. ML models for those properties will then be trained using artificial neural networks, which are able to accommodate very large training sets compared to kernel methods. As a first step, the applicant proposes to validate the framework against first-principles data performed on a few small GST structures, before exploring the size transferability of the ML models. As a second step, the applicant proposes to study a special case of PCMs characterized by the coexistence of both crystalline and amorphous phases. These structures are the backbone of multi-level storage, where it is possible to store more than a single bit. The proposed research plan provides a foundation to study the macroscopic properties of phase change materials, in models of the same size as nanodevices, from a quantum mechanical point of view.

Title: XAI-PAC: Towards Explainable and Private Affective Computing
Abstract:
Wearable devices, combined with Artificial Intelligence (AI) methods, can bring significant and sustainable improvements to our lives – from improved patient monitoring and decreased healthcare costs to enhanced sports performance and quality of life. Affective computing utilizes the combination of wearables and AI to provide methods for tracking factors related to affective states (e.g., emotions, arousal, valence, and stress). Such methods serve as the first step toward remote mental-health management tools, urgently needed in Switzerland and worldwide, particularly in the wake of COVID-19. However, with AI systems influencing human lives so intimately, end-users must be able to understand those systems. Unfortunately, today’s groundbreaking AI methods are black-boxed (i.e., the decision model and the process are not understandable) and require vast amounts of data – data that are particularly sensitive in the case of affective computing. Hence, it is evident that explainable and privacy-aware affective computing is vital – what can be more private than our emotions, and how can we be sure that the AI “got it right”? This project has three main objectives to pave the way toward eXplAInable and Private Affective Computing (XAI-PAC):

(Objective 1): To develop novel eXplainable AI (XAI) tools for affective-computing methods based on wearable sensor data. The existing XAI solutions are static (i.e., do not allow user interaction) and applicable mainly to image- and text-based models that use only a single data modality. Furthermore, the latest AI systems usually rely on several concurrent machine learning (ML) components, but the existing XAI solutions typically explain only one model within a system. Thus, XAI-PAC will develop multimodal and interactive XAI tools to explain ML models and the interaction between several related ML components.

 (Objective 2): To develop privacy-aware ML methods for wearable sensor data. Federated learning is a relatively new field that promises accurate models while avoiding transmitting potentially sensitive data to a central server. However, federated learning still faces many challenges, such as federated model selection, evaluation, and hyperparameter optimization. Wearable computing magnifies these challenges, adding noise, limited data, and domain shift to the mix. To address these challenges, XAI-PAC will explore privacy-aware personalization and domain-adaptation techniques for wearable sensor data.

(Objective 3): To fuse privacy awareness and explainability into a single approach. In order to achieve private and explainable affective computing, the first two goals are crucial. They are independent as well, and their realization leads to significant advancements in the corresponding fields. The third objective leaps beyond the independent realization of XAI and privacy-aware ML. However, this is not trivial because most XAI tools do not operate under privacy constraints. For instance, differential privacy and federated learning add noise to the ML models to obscure user-sensitive data. Applying XAI tools to federated models could lead to noisy and invalid explanations that do not provide explanatory information.

XAI-PAC will set the basis for an XAI lab at USI, specializing in privacy-aware and explainable AI. The broader impact of XAI-PAC covers health and safety-critical applications – ensuring their understandability and transparency – and foundational research that provides innovative techniques for building accurate, robust, data-efficient, and privacy-aware personalized models.
Keywords: affective computing, artificial intelligence, data privacy, explainable AI, machine learning, wearable computing

Title: New Opportunities at the Energy Frontier
Abstract: The future of particle physics is robust and fragile at once. Robust because the LHC (and HL-LHC) experimental program will produce an enormous flow of high-quality data, which ensures that progress can be made in the next decade. Fragile because the lack of new physics discoveries, if it persists, leaves us uncertain on how to proceed for further investigation. This uncertainties affects the current LHC program, and how to take the best out of it, and even more the design of future experiments. Research in the field should thus be diverse enough to exploit this robustness and to address this fragility at once. The project deals with three subjects, model-independent new physics searches design using Machine Learning techniques, precision LHC physics in the EW and Higgs sector, and future colliders. The first one is an approach to LHC physics where one aims at searching for departures from the Standard Model prediction in a way that is independent of any a priori expectation on how new physics should look like. The second topic aims instead at probing new physics effects of more specific type (though described with the general tool of Effective Field Theories) through the indirect corrections they induce to the SM predictions. As the LHC data-taking proceeds, and the experimental collaborations perform more and more accurate measurements, the latter direction will become more and more relevant. The third topic deals with how we could continue the exploration of the energy frontier on a longer timescale. In particular, I will assess the physics opportunities of a very high energy and luminosity muon collider, whose technical feasibility might be at a turning point thanks to a recent innovative proposal.
Keywords: Beyond the Standard Model, Future Colliders, Large Hadron Collider, Machine Learning

Title: Bridging Regulatory Data Protection Standards and Model Sharing in Healthcare
Abstract:
Sharing of foundation or fine-tuned models trained on confidential, e.g., medical, data is becoming widespread across many sectors, but requires assessment of privacy risks. Data protection guidelines, e.g., from European Medicines Agency (EMA) or International Organization for Standardization (ISO), provide recommendations on the permissible levels of re-identification and inference risk, such as “less than 0.09.” These guidelines, however, are designed to limit risk in the setting of sharing of de-identified tabular data, e.g., electronic clinical records with names and demographic information removed or generalized, but not in the setting of modern machine learning with the release of large language models (LLMs) or other foundation models. In the absence of clear mapping of existing guidelines to this new setting, two undesirable situations happen. On one hand, some institutions refrain from sharing the models trained on private data, which stifles research. On the other hand, other institutions ignore the risks, and release foundation models trained on patient data publicly, which could result in data breaches.

At the same time, a set of formal techniques for privacy-preserving release of statistical data and models known as differential privacy (DP) offers future-proof guarantees against such risks with minimal assumptions. DP provides quantifiable privacy guarantees through the addition of random noise as part of model training. The scale of noise is traditionally controlled by the privacy parameter e. The parameter controls the privacy-utility trade-off: the higher is the noise scale, the better are the privacy guarantees, but the worse is the resulting utility of the models. Moreover, there exist techniques to map the privacy parameter e to bounds on risks that are closely related to those described by the data-protection guidelines. Thus, DP could make for a perfect technical tool to solve the conundrum of mapping existing guidelines to the practice of model release. Unfortunately, it turns out that the existing approaches for translating between operational privacy risk thresholds and the e parameter result in excessive noise requirements, at which the models lose their utility often to the point of becoming practically useless. 

In this project, we aim to develop a framework to precisely map the regulation-prescribed risk levels to noise scale without the standard intermediate step of selecting the e privacy parameter. This framework will enable practitioners to use well-studied, future-proof DP-based technical methods for ensuring strong data privacy protection in releasing large pre-trained or fine-tuned models or their outputs while at the same time meeting privacy risk thresholds recommended by, e.g., EMA and ISO. Our approach will bridge the gap between formal privacy guarantees and practical regulatory guidelines, enabling responsible model sharing in settings with sensitive data such as biomedical or healthcare research.  To illustrate its applicability, we will test and validate our framework on medical machine learning use cases and datasets.
Keywords: data protection, differential privacy, foundation models, large language models

Title: ProMote: Multiscale Process Design through Molecular Modeling of Interfaces
Abstract:
A sustainable supply of our energy and materials demands must be built on novel processes that feature renewable feedstocks, green energy supply, and improved energy efficiency. An efficient design of novel processes needs to account for the interactions of molecules and materials with the process performance that occur at interfaces: e.g., adsorbent materials, heat exchanger surfaces, or membranes.

The ProMote project establishes an integrated material and process design workflow that – for the first time – incorporates rigorous molecular models for interfacial phenomena directly into the evaluation and design of processes. To bridge the gap between the continuum world of process design and the stochastic nature of molecules, the ProMote project proposes the application of classical density functional theory – a molecular-scale continuum description of inhomogeneous systems – in process design and, therefore, to fuse the scales from molecules to processes.

To overcome the computational challenge of applying molecular models at process scales, the project combines efficient mathematical concepts like automatic differentiation with backpropagation – the same concept that powers machine learning and artificial intelligence everywhere – with rigorous physical models that are robust and interpretable due to their physical constraints. In the ProMote project, the integrated design workflow will be demonstrated for three emerging technologies: carbon capture, high-temperature heat pumps, and membrane separations.

The ProMote project tackles the challenge of "How to design materials and processes for complex heterogeneous systems". It lays the foundation for the long-term vision that sees process engineers able to design processes that depend on the intricate interplay of molecules and materials the same way they are designing a distillation column today.
Keywords: adsorption, chemical engineering, classical density functional theory, interfaces, molecular modeling, molecular thermodynamics, nanoporous materials, process design, thermodynamic models

Title: Incorporation of Quantum Effects in Modeling of Biocatalyzed Chemical Transformations
Abstract: Synthetic chemical reactions may involve toxic reagents and solvents, require extreme conditions, and generate substantial amounts of unwanted byproducts. The application of enzymes as reagents offers an opportunity to improve on synthetic chemistry in these respects. Unfortunately, the link between the structure of an enzyme and its function often remains obscure which hampers our mechanistic understanding of the chemical transformations and, hence, ultimately the engineering of enzymes for novel applications. The primary focus of our proposed research is the development of a molecular quantum dynamics simulation method that enables the elucidation of mechanistic details of biocatalyzed chemical transformations based on quantum embedding theories. The realization that chemical transformations occur predominantly in a localized subsystem offers a way to cope with the size of the enzyme systems: We can apply an accurate quantum chemical method for the small subsystem in which the transformation occurs and a fast method for the remainder of the system. The success of these so-called quantum embedding theories is then only contingent on the availability of sufficiently fast and accurate descriptions of the subsystem, the environment, and the coupling between the two. We will develop a quantum embedding theory in which the fastest electronic structure models available today, semiempirical models and density functional tight-binding models, can be applied. The application of rapid electronic structure methods will enable a quantum mechanical description of the whole (or a substantially larger part of the) enzyme. Furthermore, we will develop a machine-learning (ML) approach to obtain electronic energies with a high accuracy based on information extracted from efficient, but less accurate calculations. This ML approach will be integrated with quantum embedding theories to provide a low-cost improvement to the electronic energies for the subsystems. The reliable calculation of kinetic isotope effects (KIEs) based on the electronic energies determined with the ML-augmented quantum embedding theory will require the consideration of quantum nuclear effects like changes in the zero point energies and tunneling effects. For this purpose, we will apply ring polymer molecular dynamics to simulate the reactions in the enzyme. Close collaboration with an experimental research group will provide the opportunity to obtain experimental feedback and to validate our approach by comparing experimental and computed KIEs. The combination of fast ML-augmented quantum embedding techniques and quantum dynamics presented in this proposal will enable the elucidation of mechanistic details of biocatalyzed reactions. These mechanistic insights will be valuable in understanding and in developing biocatalysts.
Keywords: Density-functional tight-binding models, Enzyme kinetics, Machine learning, Quantum embedding theory, Ring polymer molecular dynamics, Semiempirical methods

Title: Implicit social motives and their impact on the direction and intensity of behavior (ISMIB)
Abstract: Social motives like the affiliation and power motives are assumed to be central driving forces of behavior that determine its orientation, direction, and energization. In contrast to the achievement motive, which is the most extensively researched motive, there is only sparse research on the impact of the affiliation and power motives on two important behavioral parameters, namely the direction and intensity (i.e., energization) of behavior. This lack of research is surprising given that social signals are omnipresent in our environment and social contacts are an integrative part of our lives. The present project aims to close this gap in the literature and goes beyond existing work in a number of important ways. First, the project seeks to test a theoretical integration of the motive literature with motivational intensity theory regarding the impact of the implicit affiliation and power motives on the intensity of behavior (i.e., effort-related cardiovascular reactivity). Second, the project elaborates on the expected impact of social motives on the direction of behavior (i.e., behavioral preferences in an implicit reinforcement paradigm). Finally, the project aims at systematically varying different ways of motive activation (e.g., task contexts and nonverbal signals that promise motive satisfaction/dissatisfaction) to enable a broad generalization of the underlying mechanisms and to extend the analysis from the incentive to the disincentive quality of activating stimuli. We aim at investigating these interrelated research questions in a series of 20 experimental and quasi-experimental studies grouped into three work packages addressing one specific question each. The project will be conducted in collaboration between Dr. Kerstin Brinkmann (University of Geneva) as main applicant and Dr. Michael Richter (Liverpool John Moores University, UK) as international co-investigator. The complementary resources and expertise of the two work units allow for synergy effects to take place and for realization of the planned studies in the scheduled time frame. We expect to demonstrate that individual differences in the implicit affiliation and power motives, if activated by relevant incentives or disincentives, exert a direct impact on the direction of behavior but that their impact on the intensity of behavior will be moderated by task difficulty and clarity of task difficulty. By this way, the present project makes a unique contribution to recent research on implicit motives by advancing the understanding of the mechanisms underlying behavioral preferences and effort. We expect that the present research program will provide valuable information for practitioners in various applied contexts.
Keywords: Affiliation Motive, Cardiovascular Reactivity, Effort, Facial Expressions of Emotion, Motivation, Motivational Intensity, Power Motive, Reinforcement Learning, Response Bias

Title: Machine learning accelerated tailoring of nanopores for lithium-ion diffusion
Abstract: The enormous impact of lithium-ion batteries in the global energy scenario has led to unprecedented lithium (Li) demand. The shortage of land-based Li supply entails the need for extracting this element from alternate sources such as seawater or brine. Nanoporous materials such as zeolites have drawn considerable attention in this respect, as these materials could allow for facile Li extraction from seawater and brine. However, a major challenge lies in finding the optimal zeolite structure, out of the million possibilities, that selectively allows the small concentrations of Li+ in seawater to diffuse through, while being indifferent to the higher concentrations of other alkali ions, namely, Na+. In this work, we propose to use quantum simulation techniques like ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) to obtain useful atomic insights into the Li-ion diffusion process in zeolites. We specifically aim to systematically tailor Li exchanged zeolite nanopores, by varying Al distribution, Si/Al ratio, and Li/Al ratio to selectively allow the diffusion of Li^+ over Na+. However, the cost of AIMD simulations limits their use to study a few selected structures, at small length- and time- scales. We, therefore, further propose to develop a machine learning potential with quantum chemical accuracy to help us study the diffusion of Li+ and Na+ ions in millions of zeolites, through an active-learning scheme. Finally, we will develop a machine learning model to predict synthesis conditions of the most promising zeolite structures for Li+ diffusion. Addressing this scientific challenge could help in the design and discovery of potential materials for Li extraction from seawater, as well as other similar energy-related applications.

Title: MRI-based characterization of subgroups in aging and dementia
Abstract:
The state and progression of the cognitive profile of elderly individuals is highly variable and clinically relevant. Sources of variability include effects of healthy aging (including experience and education), acute brain damage, and multiple effects of pathological neuro-degeneration attributed to clinical syndromes. Another part of the variability can be attributed to individual biomarkers. However, a considerable amount of variability in the cognitive profiles and their prognosis remains unexplained. If a disease manifests in a discrete number of sub-types, the implicit characteristics encoded in the grouping may be an additional source of variability. To test this hypothesis, we propose to group individuals based on a detailed biomarker characterization and assess the effect of the grouping variable on the prediction accuracy of the cognitive profile and the prognosis thereof. We propose to implement the grouping with a framework for a data-driven characterization of individuals based on their profile of biomarkers. While biomarkers derived from standard structural MRI are readily available, biomarkers from invasive and expensive procedures are not routinely acquired. The limited set of biomarkers still contains relevant information. To extend the field of application of the characterization to settings with missing data, we propose to use the hidden activation pattern of a deep neural multi-task encoder-decoder network trained with missing data and soft constraints as signature feature representation that is robust to missing data. 

To characterize the individuals, we first extract multiple morphological markers from structural MRI including regional brain volume, regional atrophy, and lesion load. The extracted biomarkers are then used to group individuals using a probabilistic staging model, a model of clustered trajectories, and a model of semi-supervised learning. We then assess the variations in biomarker and cognitive variables across groups and whether the grouping variables contribute to a better prognosis. Our contribution is combining our own recently developed state-of-the-art computerized brain morphometry algorithms and alternative promising markers based on MRI with three existing sophisticated grouping methods and the application/validation to/with a large data set. We evaluate the correlations on a large (N>5000) heterogeneous data set from elderly individuals and on a data set with age range between 22 and 84 years (N=1836). Using longitudinal data (N>200), we will assess the stability of the grouping and the contribution of the grouping to the quality of prognosis. To produce consistent groupings under presence of missing data, we propose the use of a deep encoder-decoder artificial neural network that extracts signature features that are robust to missing data and preserve the cross-subject variance to obtain the same grouping. The level of consistency between the prediction with and without a set of variables is an indirect measure of redundancy. We validate the use case of discovery of biological and cognitive correlates of subgroups in an independent sample after the grouping model was transferred from a large heterogeneous data set to the target sample with missing modalities. 

We expect that the biologically motivated data-driven stratification framework enables the discovery of variants of manifestations of brain pathologies and subsequently increased accuracy in estimating the disease progression. When applied to specific research question, the grouping can lead to the discovery of correlates (for instance a protecting factor) that are present in a certain subgroup. In the long term, refined tools and methods from this project could help to identify non-trivial characteristics that determine the efficacy of an intervention

Title: Predicting outcome after stroke: broaden the perspective
Abstract:
Current treatments of ischemic stroke rely on timely recanalization of the obstructed blood vessel, by either thrombolysis with tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA) and/or mechanically using catheter-based thrombectomy. These therapeutic approaches facilitate vessel recanalization and functional recovery. However, treatment delays and patient-specific factors such as age and comorbidities determine treatment success and the risk of side effects such as intracranial hemorrhage (ICH). The decision for treatment is complex, but needs to be made quickly to avoid delaying recanalization in patients that are likely to benefit.
Although brain imaging is the mainstay of acute stroke diagnostics, current imaging strategies that aim to predict therapeutic success in stroke patients remain insufficient. Potential reasons include selection of imaging predictors from the ischemic side only, and the fact that patient-specific image and clinical data are not jointly considered. Here, we propose a novel prediction approach for treatment success based on vascular adaptations affecting the whole brain, including the contralateral side of stroke. Based on data obtained in animal models of stroke and brain imaging in patients with large vessel occlusion (LVO), contralateral cerebral blood flow (CBF) appears to indicate the brains compensatory response upon ischemic injury. In fact, vascular collaterals facilitate flow from the non-ischemic contralateral hemisphere to the affected side. Contralateral perfusion parameters may therefore indicate the ability of an individual to withstand longer durations of ischemia as well as the response to recanalization treatments. During the first three years of my SNSF professorship, we have investigated vascular function and related imaging findings in a rodent stroke model, and developed models to forecast success of stroke treatments from patient data. Contrary to our initial assumption that the contralateral side of stroke represents a straightforward predictor, we demonstrated that outcome prediction improved only slightly when adding traditional image parameters to clinical variables, regardless of using regions-of interest (ROIs) from the affected, or the contralateral side. However, this finding does not refute our initial hypothesis given that ROI-based analyses have several shortcomings, and are unable to capture all relevant image information. Thus, we developed an interpretable deep learning (DL)-based prediction model that is able to include raw images beside traditional predictors, such as age or sex. In the second funding phase of the project, we will apply these models to large datasets of stroke patients to probe for their potential to achieve a robust and reliable prediction of therapeutic success in individual patients. In our pre-clinical research, we performed in vivo imaging in mouse strains with a different inborn collateral network (C57BL/6 vs. Balb-C). We found that in mice with different amounts of collaterals subjected to stroke and thrombolysis, CBF varied profoundly on the ischemic side. Further, we uncovered significant reperfusion failure in the capillary bed. As hypothesized, laser speckle readouts of cortical CBF showed higher contralateral flow levels in mice with few collaterals and unfavorable response to thrombolysis. In the proposed second project phase, we will analyze single-vessel changes in arteriolar and capillary flow on the contralateral side that may underlie the observed perfusion responses. We will relate function of the contralateral vasculature to the degree of reperfusion on the stroke side as well as to the animal’s functional outcome. Furthermore, we will analyze 3D vascular data in mice, allowing us to examine how stroke alters whole-brain vascular anatomy. Using a translational approach, we aim for a mechanistic characterization of ipsi- and contralateral flow changes in stroke. We will generate and apply imaging predictors to clinical patient data. Thus, I envision i) to deepen the understanding of the basic mechanisms regulating brain perfusion after ischemic stroke, and ii) to improve therapeutic decision-making in acute stroke patients.

Title: RobustSR: Improving the Robustness of Super-Resolution Algorithms to Climate Change and Extreme Events
Abstract:
Recent progress in computer vision has accelerated the development of statistical downscaling, which uses statistical models to improve the spatiotemporal resolution of impactful climate variables, such as extreme temperatures, wind gusts, and precipitation. Machine learning (ML)-based super-resolution algorithms, which learn from data how to best generate high-resolution images from their low-resolution version, are gaining traction because of their improved accuracy and low computational cost once trained. However, they are rarely designed to perform well on extremes, and their robustness is usually only tested in the present climate, where training data are available. These limitations prevent the widespread adoption of modern ML to better constrain uncertainties in the forecasting of local extremes and in the high-resolution projections of climate change.

To address these limitations, we propose leveraging recent developments in deep learning and geostatistics to design hybrid statistical-physical methods helping ML frameworks generalize to climate change and extreme events. We will test these methods for two applications that combine downscaling with prediction over Switzerland: medium-range forecasting and future climate projections. For that purpose, we propose two synergistic PhD projects that address Swiss research priorities. The first project generates spatially-resolved Swiss climate change scenarios that ensure physical consistency and preserve long-term trends, while the second project downscales medium-range forecasts over Switzerland, including small-scale features ignored by the original forecast. In both projects, we will explore the added value of state-of-the-art ML for atmospheric science, which remains challenging to understand. These two lines of research are organized into four Application Work Packages (WP5-8).

These Application WPs rely on four Methodological WPs (WP1-4). First, we design model-agnostic explanation tools to quantify why ML models fail to generalize in out-of-distribution situations (WP1). We then compare feature selection/transformation methods to facilitate generalization to climate change (WP3). In parallel, we compare and develop semi-parametric methods to facilitate generalization to unseen extremes (WP4). These three collaborative projects are complemented by a series of Masters internships exploring the potential of adapting new deep learning architectures to downscale relevant atmospheric fields while maintaining spatial consistency (WP2).

This project will place robustness to extremes and climate change at the forefront of applied ML research, which is critical given our increased reliance on statistical tools for climate adaptation, and timely given the rapid development of ML-based super-resolution algorithms. The Methodological WPs are designed to broadly apply to ML attempts in Earth and environmental sciences, which share similar challenges regarding consistency and generalizability. The Application WPs address pressing operational challenges, aiming to improve publicly-available meteorological and climate products that can be used for decision making and impact assessment. Finally, by pushing the boundaries of physically-informed ML in real-world, challenging applications (high-dimensional, multivariate, stochastic, and involving complex topography), we will contribute to the advancement of ML for Earth system science.

Title: Grammar inference for prediction of disease implications from human protein-coding sequences
Abstract:
This study focuses on two types of proteins that are enriched with disease associated genes, namely proteins with tandem repeats and proteins with highly variable synonymous rates. These types of proteins are common and are often implicated in human disease, pathogenicity and enhanced binding properties. The 
aim is to create a reliable "in silico" system capable of classifying proteins with tandem repeats and highly variable synonymous rates into two classes: those that imply various unwanted properties and those that do not. An immediate use of such a system is as a mining tool for biologists to search big databases for genes that are likely to be associated with disease. The system is to be based on a recent methodology of grammatical inference on biochemical nomenclature, where protein sequences are processed as words in a formal language. At the learning step, grammar inference is used to 
learn automata for classes of proteins with tandems, -- implicating vs non-implicating pathology. An automaton generalizes the idea of the class, and edit distance (defined as the number of "delete", "substitute", and "insert" operations necessary to perform on the word in order that it is accepted by the automaton) is a measure of how "far" a given word is from the class. Thus, symbolic sequences encoding proteins are converted into numeric attributes, and once that is once done, standard machine learning techniques (like logistic regression or support vector machines, etc) are used to do the classification.

Title: Unified Model for Evaluation of Text Generation Systems (UniVal)
Abstract:
The field of automatic text generation has witnessed an explosion in terms of performance within the last few years. The rate at which new models with further reaching capabilities are proposed for a variety of text generation tasks is growing exponentially. Furthermore, with the introduction of ChatGPT, these models have received widespread public attention, accompanied by a growing interest in applying these models in real-world settings. By contrast, the evaluation of such models on academic benchmarks or certifying them for applied settings are far from being solved. 
There is, at present, no reliable, reproducible, high-quality evaluation method for text generation systems. We argue that this stems from the rather ad-hoc nature of all current approaches due to the lack of a theoretical foundation that provides first principles and guidance on how to perform such evaluations.
Evaluation can be divided into human-based and automated evaluation. Evaluation with human raters are cost and time-intensive and suffer often from a low agreement among the human raters. In order to allow for more efficient improvement cycles of models, the evaluation should ideally be performed automatically, significantly reducing cost and providing timely feedback. Thus, significant effort has been invested to propose  automated metrics. These can be categorized into untrained and trained metrics. Untrained metrics such as the widely used BLEU and ROUGE scores are simple to implement, but they suffer from low correlations with human judgments. Trained metrics, on the other hand, have higher correlations with human judgments. However, they are brittle regarding robustness: They need to be retrained for each domain, their scores highly depend on the training data and parameters, and they are susceptible to adversarial attacks. 
In this light, we propose the development of a unified model for evaluation of text generation systems. We base this model on the observation that each aspect of evaluation incorporates various types of uncertainty into the evaluation process, which is rarely accounted for. In fact, the only uncertainty that is usually considered in evaluation procedures is the uncertainty stemming from a (low) number of samples. Other potential sources of uncertainty, such as low correlation between an automated metric and human ratings, are rarely considered in a principled way. We argue that the most viable way forward is to model the whole evaluation process with the various sources of uncertainty. If such sources of uncertainty are explicitly accounted for, we can be much more confident about the robustness and validity of the evaluation outcome.  
In the empirical part of the project, we will evaluate a substantial amount of models and protocols on a large variety of different text generation tasks to showcase the validity of our model. Finally, we investigate how practical evaluation setups can be optimized using our theory, e.g. by exploring how to effectively create a discriminative test set of minimum size, choosing the necessary number of human annotators, and accounting for the error-proneness of automatic metrics. We foresee that the outputs of this project will have a positive impact on both academic research and the development and application of these models in applied settings.

Title: Peirce interprets Peirce. A Computational Exploration of His Original Manuscripts
Abstract: This project focuses on the digital preservation, transcription, and computational analysis of Charles S. Peirce’s original manuscripts. By employing artificial intelligence, natural language processing, semantic web technologies, and advanced data visualization, the team will transform Peirce’s extensive handwritten works into a structured and accessible digital corpus. The project aims not only to improve access to Peirce’s writings, but also to reveal new patterns and insights within his philosophical and semiotic theories, such as his concepts of icon, index, and symbol, through in-depth text and diagram analysis. An important aspect is the creation of knowledge graphs and digital tools that allow scholars to explore the connections and evolution of Peirce’s thought. The consortium brings together specialists in computational linguistics, semiotics, and digital humanities, with a strong commitment to open access and the dissemination of results for both research and teaching purposes.

Title: Precision Medicine Approach for Innovative Outbreak Investigation using Machine Learning Methods
Abstract:
Vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE) are one of many multidrug-resistant organisms (MDRO) that may cause nosocomial outbreaks. Since early 2018, we have experienced an outbreak due to a highly transmissible VRE in our hospital. Our goals are to better understand risk factors for VRE acquisition, elicit hot spots where transmission may have occurred, identify medical devices that may have been a vehicle for transmission, and delineate the optimal approach to tracing contact patients. 

We have assembled highly diverse data of variable quality from electronic medical records generated during the period of the outbreak, covering different aspects of medical care. For comparisons, we labeled any patient with VRE acquisition during the outbreak period as VRE-positive, and patients who had 3 consecutive negative screenings as VRE-negative. Our research to date has identified VRE risk factors and, using a complex network analysis machine learning approach, we were able to establish three main pathways by which the VRE cases are connected: healthcare personnel, medical devices and patient rooms. This network with its multi-dimensionality extends beyond our current contact tracing strategy, which is limited to capturing inpatients based on geographical proximity.

Our goals are firstly to improve the prediction of positive contacts to inform screenings (i.e. MDRO carriers among the screened patients) and to avoid unnecessary screening using suitable temporal and spatial components. Secondly, we aim to provide a generic framework for other hospitals to use as a blueprint for automated outbreak detection, describing which data should be included in the analysis, the preferred methods and benchmarks for measuring success of the proposed approaches. 

Our main deliverables are: 
•An automated system that prepares lists of exposed patients, and identifies those at highest risk for subsequent screening. Importantly, this system will be applicable to all MDRO transmitted by contact (including VRE, but also e.g. methicillin-resistant staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and multi-drug-resistant gram-negative (MDRGN) bacteria).
•An automated system that elicits probable hot spots (e.g. rooms, devices, procedures) based on a network analysis of a hospital system’s human and non-human connections.

In summary, combining traditional statistical methods and new machine learning (ML) approaches we will provide a more complete understanding of such outbreaks, along with a framework for other institutions to adopt.

Title: Learning to Capture and Cultivate Interactions for Intelligent Agents
Abstract:
Intelligent agents that can perceive, reason, and act toward their goals are poised to reshape a wide spectrum of our lives. Notably, current agents parameterized by neural networks and trained on extensive datasets have excelled in specific tasks and environments (e.g., self-driving vehicles, household robots, virtual chatbots). Yet, their performance in broader unconstrained contexts remains limited. They often struggle to handle complex interactions with other entities (e.g., agents, objects) and still lack robustness in the presence of distribution shifts (e.g., changed conditions). In this project, we aim to address these challenges by developing representations that can capture and cultivate interactions beyond the training distribution.

On one hand, we postulate that the key to effective interaction modeling lies in discovering the underlying causal mechanisms (e.g., physical laws, social norms) that govern dynamic interactive processes. Recent studies have shown promise in incorporating causal structures into representation learning in the context of multi-agent or embodied systems. Yet, existing efforts are confined to synthetic settings with strong priors or curated interventions, which are not widely available in real-world scenarios. To bridge this gap, we will explore two new directions: (i) sim-to-real causal transfer, leveraging causal annotations extracted from simulations to capture the invariant mechanisms that are transferable to real-world counterparts; (ii) self-supervised interventions, seeking scalable forms of intervened data pairs from online autonomous explorations or offline robotic datasets without explicit supervision. We will strive to develop a generic paradigm toward causally aware agents, and demonstrate their efficacy in out-of-distribution generalization for self-driving and robotics.

On the other hand, we hypothesize that dynamic interactions, if effectively used, can play a pivotal role in addressing the robustness challenge in broader contexts. Recent studies have revealed the potential of adapting pre-trained models via self/un-supervised learning from unlabeled test examples. However, existing methods remain highly vulnerable, e.g., each can only handle a narrow set of scenarios. To enable more reliable adaptation on the fly, we will explore a new approach that cultivates interactions among multiple elements, drawing inspiration from recent progress in other domains: (i) multi-task model adaptation, investigating the design and interplay of a diverse and complementary set of self-supervised tasks from an adaptation standpoint; (ii) multi-model response adaptation, where foundation models with distinct properties interact as a team of virtual agents to achieve robust and adaptive responses. Our exploration is expected to shed new light on algorithmic designs of dynamic interactions for online adaptation, yielding generic solutions to various problems.

Overall, our project will pursue generalizable and adaptable representations from an interaction-centric perspective, paving the way for the next generation of intelligent agents that can seamlessly integrate into our ever-changing and interaction-intensive society.
Keywords: Causal Representation Learning, Deep Learning, Distribution Shifts, Multi-Agent, Robot Learning, Test-Time Adaptation

Title: Software Analysis for Heterogeneous Computing Architectures
Abstract:
Computational time and energy consumption in computer systems do not come for free. The main objectives of Computer Architecture researchers is to design systems where the time latency and energy requirements are ever decreasing. In recent years many advances have been carried out in modern Software (SW) and Hardware (HW) in order to keep the performance trend high, i.e., decrease both computational time and energy while executing complex and demanding applications. Nevertheless, certain limitations, such as the breakdown of Dennard Scaling and the subsequent, seemingly inevitable, end of Moore’s law economic aspect have posed new challenges that are not trivial to overcome. As a result, Heterogeneous Computing has emerged as a solution in order to realize computer architectures with both general purpose CPUs and specialized HW in order to keep the performance trend increasing.

Selecting the parts of SW applications to be accelerated, i.e., deciding what to accelerate in specialized HW implementations, or HW accelerators, is a significantly challenging task. It requires a deep understanding of the SW characteristics of the application as a whole, as well as a thorough understanding of the identified HW accelerators in order to decide whether any optimizations can be applied onto them, i.e., deciding how to implement them. Furthermore the kind of underlying computer architecture of the platform, where the HW accelerators are going to be implemented, can dramatically affect the performance. Memory latency due to data exchange between HW accelerators and the main memory of the platform can affect the overall latency of the HW accelerators execution. Therefore taking into account the underlying memory hierarchy of the platform can be crucial when it comes to performance.

The suggested project carried out after the completion of my PhD would attempt to tackle the research questions of what parts of an application should be accelerated (selection of HW accelerators), how could they be implemented, while taking into account where these HW accelerators are to be implemented. This can be performed by extending the current work, based on the LLVM compiler infrastructure that has been carried out during my PhD research. I would attempt to A) improve the efficiency of my current tool that performs automatic identification and selection of HW accelerators, B) enlarge the scope of the analysis in order to take more platform characteristics into account and C) integrate this analysis with one that evaluates different types of HW accelerators for the same part of execution.

A fully automated tool-chain would be developed that can both identify and select good HW acceleration candidates, suggest optimizations to be implemented and have them targeted to specific platforms that may vary in HW area resources budget, micro-architecture and memory hierarchy. Such a tool-chain would push the boundaries of the state-of-the-art even further and assist both researchers in the HW accelerator design domain by offering better tools and engineers that would be able to make more informed decisions when deciding on which parts of an application should they focus their efforts on, in order to accelerate a given application. As an outcome this would result into building more efficient heterogeneous computing architectures and boost performance in these systems, both in terms of more speedup and in terms of better energy efficiency. Such an outcome would be substantially beneficial to researchers, as well as other professionals, that could use heterogeneous computing systems, specialized to speed-up their highly time-consuming simulations or Machine Learning applications and, thus, assist them in their work.
Keywords: Accelerators, Analysis, Compilers, Hardware, Heterogeneous, Software

Title: Multi-scale mathematical modelling of pathogen, drug and vaccine interactions: optimising public health and disease elimination strategies
Abstract:
Quantitative sciences and mathematical modelling are increasingly important to understand existing and emerging diseases, and to plan the interventions to tackle them. Models that capture detailed biological, epidemiological and health systems factors, and the complex interactions between, can provide insight into the factors which drive disease dynamics. We have shown that mathematical models can be used to predict the impact of disease interventions; to define the desired characteristics of a new intervention; and to identify optimal deployment strategies. As we move towards elimination of malaria and other diseases, mitigating resistance to current interventions becomes crucial. Since the dynamics of resistance differ between high- and low-prevalence settings, mitigation strategies are likely to change as we get closer to elimination. Defining and quantifying these strategies for different settings and understanding how they differ as pathogens evolve is therefore essential.

In the current global pandemic, we are at a crucial moment to define strategies for vaccine rollout. SARS-CoV-2 has shown a high propensity for mutation, posing the danger that new vaccine-resistant variants may evolve. The proposed project directly examines the dynamics of resistance evolution, and will define strategies for vaccine deployment that mitigate vaccine resistance. Our work will bring theoretical modelling and disease evolution understandings directly to bear on public health policy and vaccine deployment strategy in Switzerland.

Proposing disease models with sufficient detail to evaluate disease interventions presents significant computational challenges for model simulation and sensitivity analysis on one hand, and methodological challenges for model calibration on the other. In phase 1 of the grant we developed machine learning based approaches to solve both these issues. In this prolongation we will adopt our methods to build detailed within-host models of malaria parasite dynamics, and adapt existing individual based models of malaria and COVID-19 to explore evolution of vaccine and intervention resistance.

In Objective 1 we will apply our novel approaches to build within-host models designed to be sufficiently expressive to tackle resistance, and designed with parameterisation to sparse data in mind.

In Objective 2 we will use global sensitivity analysis and the new models to determine key implementation and disease factors driving emergence and spread of malaria genotypes resistant to vaccines, monoclonal antibody therapies, and the spread of mosquitos resistant to insecticide-based interventions.

In Objective. 3 we will adapt our methods from Obj. 2 and our existing individual-based COVID-19 model to determine the key implementation and disease factors driving the emergence of new vaccine-resistant variants of SARS-CoV-2.

We will bring these results together to guide strategies for interventions, for disease control and elimination, especially in the context of resistance. We will promote integration of our model-based research findings into decision making. The proposal builds on the applicant’s previous research and links basic science innovation through to application via new mathematical models, and thus will deliver significant advances for epidemiological modelling and understanding of resistance and disease evolution. While immediately relevant to malaria and SARS-CoV-2, the project will also inform efforts to control other diseases, while sustaining the position of the applicant and Switzerland as global leaders in infectious disease modelling research.
Keywords: COVID-19, Malaria, Mathematical Modelling, Parasite Dynamics, Resistance, SARS-CoV-2, Vaccines, drug resistance

Title: Direct Data-Driven Control
Abstract:
Traditional control systems are designed via a two-step procedure: in the first step, the input and output signals of the plant are used to identify the parameters of a model structure and in the second step, a model-based controller is designed to meet the control specifications. The two-step identification and control procedure works very well for many simple physical systems, where the information about the model structure is available or can be extracted from data. Progress in the field of information science has led to large interconnected systems of systems such that the right model structure for controller design cannot be obtained. This requires the development of new direct data-driven control methods that lump the two-step approach in one optimisation problem. In these methods, the input/output data are used directly for controller design, with no assumption on the model structure or the need for a parametric model. This is a timely topic in the field of control systems and in computer science, where it is referred to as model-free reinforcement learning.

In this project, direct data-driven algorithms have been developed in the time and frequency domain to compute fixed-structure controllers suitable for the distributed control of large systems. In the time domain, a robust formulation characterises disturbances by general sets, with conditions guaranteeing robust stabilisation and performance, together with a safe data-exploration strategy that improves the informativeness of the data without compromising safety. In the frequency domain, new convex synthesis methods for robust multivariable fixed-structure controllers have been obtained from the frequency response of the system and a rigorous description of the uncertainty, guaranteeing the stability and safety of the control system even when the available data are limited or not informative. The controller parameters can be updated if the control performance is deteriorating. Both approaches have also been extended to the distributed control of networked systems and to nonlinear models arising from machine learning.

The algorithms have been validated experimentally on two real systems, in collaboration with EPFL's Laboratory of Bio and Nano Instrumentation and with CSEM: a dual-actuated atomic force microscope and an active micro-vibration rejection platform. These validations increased the microscope's imaging speed by an order of magnitude while preserving image quality, demonstrating the practical impact of these algorithms on high-precision instruments.

Title: Forward modeling and inversion of spectropolarimetric observations in strong chromospheric lines
Abstract:
The project focuses on a key problem in solar physics, namely the measurement of the magnetic field in the chromosphere and transition region. The problem is faced with a spectropolarimetric methodology, exploiting the combined action of the well-known Zeeman effect and of the less familiar Hanle effect in strong resonance lines. The diagnostic potential of the Hanle effect has been clearly highlighted, but its practical application for investigating the magnetic fields of the solar chromosphere and transition region has been hampered by the complexity of its modeling, especially from a computational standpoint. Indeed, this requires considering non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (non-LTE) effects, partial frequency redistribution (PRD) in scattering processes, and to account for the detailed 3D structure of the solar atmosphere.
The project aims to develop and apply a new inversion code, tailored for strong resonance lines, accounting for the Hanle and Zeeman effects, as well as for PRD. To reach this goal, we will (i) carry out forward modeling calculations of unprecedented accuracy, (ii) investigate new non-LTE inversion strategies, and (iii) perform new spectropolarimetric observations. The forward modeling calculations, accounting for scattering polarization and the Hanle effect in the unexplored 3D PRD setting, will be carried out in 3D atmospheric models extracted from state-of-the-art radiative magneto-hydrodynamic simulations of the solar atmosphere. These calculations will provide new insights into the physics of the problem and assess the suitability of simplifying approximations for the inverse problem. Moreover, they will be quantitatively compared to observational data with the aim of setting constraints on the magnetism and structure of the chromosphere. For the inversions, we pursue a two-step strategy, in which the first step is carried out with state-of-the-art non-LTE inversion tools neglecting the Hanle effect. For the second step, which is linear with respect to the radiation field, we will develop fast approximations for the response functions including PRD, Hanle, and Zeeman effects, and exploit machine learning techniques with physics-informed neural networks. The new inversion code will be applied both to already available observational data and to new high-resolution spectropolarimetric observations in strong chromospheric lines, with special focus on quiet and moderately active solar regions. The new observations will be performed with the Zurich Imaging Polarimeter (ZIMPOL) at the German solar telescope GREGOR and by applying for observing time at the new American DKIST. 
The work is organized in three working packages, focused on the following sets of spectral lines: CaI 4227 (WP1), HI Ly-alpha and MgII h & k (WP2), and NaI D1 & D2 (WP3). WP2 takes advantage of the unique observations provided by the CLASP sounding rocket experiments, of which the PI is a team member. The work will be carried out by the PI, two post-doc researchers (1.5 FTE), and one PhD student, with contributions from four scientific partners.
The project will improve our knowledge on the ever elusive magnetic fields of the chromosphere and transition region. Its main contributions will consist of both novel quantitative data on the strength and topology of the magnetic field in these regions, and new plasma diagnostic tools for the community. Moreover, it will foster new collaborations, reinforce the partnership between IRSOL and the Euler Institute of USI, and support the participation of the PI and his group in the international CLASP projects.

Title: Neural fingerprints in bilingualism and dyslexia: neurofeedback training to enhance language learning
Abstract:
Dyslexia is a reading disorder manifested by different subtypes, with phonological deficits being common. A broad range of behavioural deficits beyond reading deficits have been observed in dyslexia, including phonological processing and awareness, processing of rapidly changing information, working memory, statistical learning, procedural learning, visuo-spatial attention and sensori-motor processing. In line with this, brain functional and structural imaging has revealed abnormalities in the function and structure of the auditory cortex, and of regions including the left inferior frontal cortex, occipito-temporal regions, parieto-temporal regions, the cerebellum and subcortical regions. An emerging view in dyslexia research is that arises from an underlying procedural learning deficit, resulting in difficulties with the learning and control of established sensorimotor and cognitive skills, habits and procedures. In contrast, bilingualism entailed the successful learning of the ability to manipulate and control multiple linguistic repertories, at phonological, lexical, syntactic and prosodic levels. Recent work has also shown that the implicit learning of an artificial language, which likely relies more on a procedural memory system, results in more native-like neural responses than the explicit of an artificial grammar, which more likely depends on declarative memory. Neuroimaging research has established the roles of multiple and interacting linguistic and executive brain networks in bilingualism, ranging from low-level auditory regions to higher-level regions involved in phonological awareness and working memory, semantic and syntactic processing, in the processing of linguistic prosody and in domain-general executive and attentional control. Although we have a good understanding of which brain networks underlie these respective levels of language processing, systematic investigations of how language-specific typological differences modulate neural processing in bilinguals are grossly lacking. Similarly, the results of studies on brain structural differences between mono- and bilinguals are very heterogeneous, maybe because language-specific typological differences have not thus been accounted for in such studies.     
The overarching goal of this proposal is to significantly advance our understanding of brain functional and structural underpinnings of dyslexia and of bilingualism, using state-of-the-art brain imaging and data analysis methods. Specifically, ultra-high resolution brain functional imaging will be combined with advanced computational modelling methods (model-based decoding) to identify distributed neural signatures, or ‘fingerprints’, underlying the processing of phonology, prosody and statistical learning dyslexia, and of semantics, syntax, prosody and statistical learning in bilingualism. For the latter, we will study bilinguals who speak pairs of languages that are typologically very different at multiple linguistic levels, or that are more similar to one another typologically, yielding ‘language-specific neural fingerprints’. Careful behavioural assessment of acoustic, phonological and reading skills in dyslexia, and of language proficiency and experience in bilinguals will be performed alongside multi-modal assessment of brain structural features including myelin mapping, auditory cortex characterisation and white matter connectivity to provide detailed neuro-behavioural profiling in dyslexia and in bilingualism. These advances will be used in a complementary subproject to develop a novel intervention (i.e. training) approach, with the primary goal of providing complimentary, causal evidence regarding the functional relevance of the language-specific neural fingerprints in the above bilingualism study, and second, to provide proof-of-concept advances for a new approach aimed at facilitating foreign language learning in healthy monolingual individuals. Specifically, the language-specific neuro-functional fingerprints established in bilinguals will be used as target regions for a real-time functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) neurofeedback training study in monolinguals wishing to learn one of the languages for which neural language-specific fingerprints has been established. Title: The Grammatical Basis of Language Frequencies
Abstract:
Current  computational   linguistic  work  shows   great  interest  in
extending   successful   probabilistic   modelling   to   multilingual
approaches. Many classical applications  and tasks in natural language
processing,  such as  tagging  , parsing  and  recovering of  semantic
representations,   are   being   investigated   in   a   multi-lingual
perspective.

The  computational approaches are  motivated by  the desire  to extend
language technology robustly and  automatically to many languages, but
in  so doing  they  also provide  compelling  computational models  of
problems that are  being studied from a linguistic  point of view. The
properties of these  computational models might shed light  on some of
the  properties   of  the  generative   processes  underlying  natural
language.

In this  research project, we  will investigate the  probabilistic and
statistical  properties  of   a  set  of  well-documented  typological
distributions  of sentential  word order  and word  order in  the noun
phrase.   The  fundamental  research  questions  we will  ask  is  the
following: why  are the frequency distributions of  these phenomena as
they are?

For example,  according to a  careful investigation of the  word order
facts  internal  to  the   noun  phrase  (Cinque 2005),  of  the  24
combinatorially possible  orders of demonstrative,  numeral, adjective
and noun in the world languages, only 14 are certainly attested, while
10  are unattested.  Of  the attested  word orders  only two  are very
frequent, two are frequent, some are  rare and many are very rare. Why
is it so?

We will assume that the underlying grammatical processes that generate
sentences are probabilistic, choosing probabilistic processes that are
known to generate the so-called power-law distributions typical of
linguistic facts.  For example, very few (two, in fact) frequent word
orders comprise the majority of languages in the world, while the
majority of word orders are attested only by a few languages.

   From  the point  of view  of theoretical  and cognitive  studies of
language, the  fundamental question then becomes: why  is it precisely
those  orders that are  the frequent  orders and  the rare  ones rare?
Answering   this   question  can   have   important  consequences   in
investigating the complexity of mental computations.

Understanding the relationship between complex
grammatical  representations across  languages  and their  statistical
distributions will facilitate  the multilingual endeavour described at
the beginning,  will improve performance of the  developed systems and
will  give   us  better  insight   on  why  current   statistical  and
probabilistic techniques are  so practically effective, by elucidating
what fundamental  properties of language they capture  that makes them
such powerful generalizers.
Keywords: Bayesian learning, computational modelling, formal grammar, language technology, language universals, multilingualism, parsing, statistical approaches, syntax
