Title: Low field MR guided response assessment during radiotherapy for glioblastoma patients for adaptive radiotherapy and response prediction
Abstract:
Background: 
Glioblastoma is the most common primary brain tumor in adults, and only has a median survival in the range of one year in population-based studies and between 15-16 months in clinical trial populations. After implementation of combined radio-chemotherapy strategies for glioblastoma, especially incorporating temozolomide after 2005, pseudo-progression mimicking tumor progression has been observed. The clinical question of pseudoprogression vs. progression can significantly impact clinical decision making with direct consequences in clinical practice. The idea of detection of early MRI changes during radio(chemo)therapy of glioblastoma as a potential surrogate imaging biomarker for subsequent discrimination of progression versus pseudoprogression is very appealing, but only few reports have been performed so far. Therefore, there is an urgent need to investigate and characterize imaging biomarkers and establish those for individual decision making in radiation oncology taking longitudinal changes as surrogate of response to local treatment into account. 
Hypothesis: 
Repetitive optimized low-field strength diffusion weighted MRI sequences acquired on a hybrid MR Linear accelerator with 0.35T before and during postoperative radio(chemo)therapy for newly diagnosed glioblastoma are able to detect early treatment-induced tumor/ brain changes and can be used for adaptive radiotherapy planning as well as for response and outcome prediction.
Aims and Experimental design: 
The aim of  this research project is to investigate whether repetitive low-field MRI investigations during radiation therapy allow for improved treatment monitoring and particularly provide a higher accuracy of the clinically relevant distinction between pseudoprogression and true tumor progression. We will implement a low-field strength MRI imaging workflow for glioblastoma patients at a dedicated hybrid MR linear accelerator and evaluate the value of repetitive low-field MR imaging by a novel MR Linac compatible head-coil to monitor tumor volume/ signal changes during the course of fractionated radiation treatment and correlate these to post-treatment outcome.
Pre-treatment 0.35T MR images without intravenous contrast agents can be used for reliable target delineation and calculation of clinically applicable adaptive radiotherapy plans.
Morphological T1/T2-weighted sequences, Diffusion-weighted Imaging (DWI) and Arterial Spin Labeling (ASL) at 0.35T allow for treatment monitoring during radiotherapy.
Advanced DWI techniques such as Intravoxel Incoherent Motion (IVIM) analysis provide biomarkers for tumor response prediction and may be used for machine-learning based tissue segmentation as a basis for adaptive radiotherapy planning.
The analysis of longitudinally acquired low field strength DWI sequences by machine-learning techniques can be used  to discern progression from pseudo-progression.
Expected value of the research project: 
Thus, with the proposed research project we envision an impact in two distinct areas:
Repetitive non-contrast agent based morphological and functional low field MRI imaging with innovative post-processing methods as a diagnostic basis for the implementation of adaptive brain tumor radiotherapy.
Application of these findings in the treatment management of glioblastoma patients to redefine target volume definition for individualized radiotherapy application and improve response assessment and outcome prediction.
This approach will help us to characterize patients who will benefit most from local treatment intensification and spare patients from unnecessary intervention.
Keywords: glioblastoma, low field mri, radiomics, radiotherapy, reponse assessment

Title: In Search of a Geneva Consensus: The Trade-Development Nexus in the GATT/WTO and UNCTAD
Abstract: This research project aims to systematically examine how economic policy doctrines have shaped the trade and development agendas of two key Geneva-based international organisations: the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) and its successor, the World Trade Organization (WTO), as well as the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD). The project introduces the first longitudinal study to track the evolution of the trade-development nexus within these organisations, pinpointing critical junctures where prevailing norms have shifted. The initial work package is conceptual, refining a theoretical framework to explain the evolution of trade doctrines associated with development in intergovernmental economic organisations. The second work package intends to develop two comprehensive corpora of documents examining the evolution of trade and development doctrines within both institutions, including ministerial speeches, policy recommendations, flagship publications, and policy briefs from these IOs. The methods employed range from topic modelling and sentiment analysis to various natural language processing techniques to detect shifts in trade-development doctrines guiding these IOs. After recognising key periods of significant normative change, selected cases will be investigated based on the framework and a set of hypotheses concerning the drivers of change. These case studies will involve in-depth analyses complemented by archival research and interviews with former officials. Ultimately, the findings from this project aim to illuminate the evolution of norms within the trade-development nexus. This research will contribute to ongoing debates in international political economy, development studies, and international organisations. From a policy perspective, the project will offer vital insights into the internal and external factors influencing shifts in trade policy direction at UNCTAD and the GATT/WTO.

Title: Pushing the Boundaries of Sensitivity in Fundamental Physics: Modern Machine Learning for Enhanced CMS and LIGO experiments
Abstract:
Fundamental physics models like the Standard Model of particle physics (SM) or general relativity have been refined over decades in close interplay with experiments. They can describe phenomena such as the Higgs boson and gravitational waves with incredible precision. Despite their success, current models are known to be incomplete because, for example, they lack explanations for astrophysical phenomena like dark matter and a uniform theory of all forces including gravity. Open questions are addressed by a large number of new physics (NP) models. However, no statistically significant signs of NP have been observed indicating that observing NP is only possible through more data, more sophisticated analysis methods or new experiments.

At the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the current Run 3 is expected to double the recorded collision data, and the high-luminosity (HL-LHC) upgrade will again enlarge the datasets by about a factor of ten. Upgrades to the gravitational wave observatories will increase the sensitivity to low-frequency signals, doubling e.g. LIGO's sensitivity. While these upgrades provide excellent conditions for NP searches, they also come with challenges for data recording, selection, and analysis, the major task being identification of tiny signals in overwhelming backgrounds.

In the last years, machine learning (ML) methods have been on the rise, not only but also because dedicated hardware allows the training and inference of large deep neural networks. ML enables fast decision-making and interpretation with performances that transcend other strategies. Thus, it has been proven an ideal tool to handle the ever-increasing amount of data and to identify faint signals, common challenges in high-energy and gravitational wave physics.

Experiments are not capable of storing the complete data triggering the need for in-time filtering of events. Discarded events are ultimately lost for physics analysis. The aim of this project is to develop optimized event selection and identification algorithms utilizing ML methods for the in-time event selection of the CMS and LIGO experiments to enhance sensitivity to NP signals. For the CMS experiment, I propose the first ultrafast isolated electron identification algorithm to be deployed at the initial, hardware-based layer of the trigger system specifically enhancing the sensitivity to low-energetic electrons. For the LIGO experiment, I aim to speed up localization and parameter estimation of gravitational wave events, allowing to extract in-time a large variety of characteristics. Fast parameter estimation would improve multi-messenger astronomy because it allows fast sharing of accurate information about gravitational wave events, beyond the source localization, enabling better and quicker reactions of international space observatories. 

Besides the initial event selection, sensitivity to NP can be enhanced by interpreting results not in terms of one specific NP model, but model independently. This project proposes the first model-agnostic analysis with the CMS experiment targeting events with large-radius jets and being based on modern ML tools. Inputs are proton-proton collision data recorded with the CMS experiment during the current Run 3.

The project contributes to extending the physics reach of the CMS and LIGO experiments by overcoming current limitations in event selection and interpretation with state-of-the-art ML. This will prepare the experiments for challenges imposed by the ever increasing data rate, enhance their sensitivity to NP and ultimately help to broaden our knowledge about fundamental physics.
Keywords: Gravitational wave astronomy, High-energy particle physics, Machine-learning for science

Title: Studying AI Agents' Decisions: Framework & Financial Market Applications
Abstract:
Recent advances in developing foundation models, particularly Large Language Models, are driving automation, with AI agents demonstrating capabilities that may replace human workers in certain roles, with significant economic and social consequences. New frameworks enable AI agents to collaborate autonomously in teams and hierarchies, forming AI-driven firms with AI managers and employees. Established methods allow these agents to interact directly with the economy, accelerating a shift where AI agents, powered by foundation models, increasingly shape economic and business decisions. Although still in its early stages, the evolving Agentic Economy could rapidly take shape in the coming years. Many commentators suggest that 2025 may already mark a turning point in the real-world adoption of AI agents in the economy. To ensure that research insights can meaningfully inform policy decisions regarding the development of an Agentic Economy, it is crucial to explore and establish research avenues at this early stage while its trajectory is still taking shape.

The rise of an Agentic Economy presents profound challenges for business and economics research. At its core lies the fundamental question: what happens when AI agents increasingly make economic decisions? While economics has long studied human decision-making, it is now crucial to understand how AI agents behave in economic contexts—and with what consequences. Although relevant across many sectors, we focus on AI agents’ decision-making in financial markets, where automation is advanced and autonomous agents are already in use. Moreover, financial markets offer a rich foundation for comparison, given established research on human biases, such as non-rational risk aversion shifts during downturns, herding behavior, and speculative bubbles. Studying AI agents in this context can reveal whether they mitigate, amplify, or introduce new inefficiencies and instabilities.

Our research plan builds on two key conjectures: first, that studying AI agents’ behavior and performance is inherently empirical due to the complexity of modern models; and second, that AI agents’ decision-making can be studied in laboratory settings with greater realism than human-focused experiments, which face limitations such as discrepancies between lab and field behavior and broader challenges with human-subject experiments. Building on these foundations, this project makes two key contributions. First, it develops and tests an empirical framework for systematically studying AI agents’ and AI firms’ economic decision-making, including a conceptual experimental design and the necessary technical infrastructure. Second, it applies this framework in a two-track experimental study of AI agents in financial markets: the first track examines individual AI agents making trading decisions, while the second analyzes AI agents within an AI investment firm, where decisions emerge from interactions among AI managers and AI employees. Both tracks will assess key economic behaviors, such as risk aversion shifts, herding, and speculative bubbles, under typical market conditions and during economic crises.

While the fast-evolving AI landscape presents uncertainties, the potential impact on research and policy is substantial. This project aims to equip business and economics researchers, as well as policymakers, with early insights into what could be a fundamental economic shift in the coming years.
Keywords: AI Agents, Economic Decision-Making, Foundation Models, Investment Decisions

Title: ENHANCER: HormEsis RespoNces in PHytoplAnkton NAnotoxicology and ImpliCations for Ecological Risk Assessment
Abstract:
There is growing evidence that engineered nanoparticles (ENPs), when released in the environment, can trigger hormesis response in different organisms, including phytoplankton, and that measurable stimulation effects can occur at concentrations lower than those where the traditional ecotoxicological thresholds appear. Nevertheless, only few studies have systematically assessed the frequency, magnitude and distribution of the hormesis effects of ENPs in phytoplankton species, the underlaying mechanisms and modifying factors. The overall goal of this curiosity-driven and use-inspired collaborative project is to address a major research gap in nanoecotoxicology concerning hormesis, as an underexplored but potentially important response of phytoplankton species, the base of the food chain, to ENPs and its implications for ecological risk assessment (ERA) and sustainable use of nanotechnology. The specific objectives of ENHANCER are: (1) to systematically evaluate the frequency and intensity of hormesis responses in different phytoplankton species, exposed to a large variety of ENPs; (2) to assess the effect of environmental variables, (e.g., natural organic matter, water hardness, pH) on hormesis responses; (3) to improve understanding of key mechanisms driving stimulatory responses in phytoplankton species upon exposure to ENPs, and to generate an unprecedented knowledge on the metabolic “switch” from stimulatory to inhibitory responses; (4) to explore the environmental implications of ENP-induced hormesis with novel artificial intelligence (AI) approaches; and (5) to evaluate potential ERA scenarios under various alternatives. 
To this end we propose to combine high-throughput screening bioassays with different phytoplankton species, assessment of multiple physiological and biochemical endpoints, genomics and metabolomics, AI, and modeling. In order to generate sufficient datapoints for AI, we will employ around 25-30 different ENPs. We will select ENPs that cover a range of characteristics, such as dissolution rate, reactive oxygen species generation, band gap, size, coating type and hydrophobicity. The bioassays will be performed with at least five species representatives of phytoplankton, including algae and cyanobacteria. 
The project is structured around the following work packages: (1) High-throughput screening of hormesis-like responses in representative phytoplankton species; (2) Determining hormesis in different environmental settings; (3) Assessment of ENPs prooxidant potency and antioxidant responses (4) Understanding the molecular basis of switch from stimulatory to inhibitor responses using metabolomics; (5) Artificial Intelligence to predict hormesis and toxicity levels due to exposure to ENPs, (6) Screening Ecological Risk Assessment scenarios. In addition, simplified version of nanoFate model will be developed for educational purposes. 
ENHANCER will advance (nano)ecotoxicology along the following lines: (1) it will produce a rich database of phytoplankton responses to ENPs, with several endpoints and based on a range of exposure conditions; (2) it will provide unique insights in the key mechanisms inducing the stimulation responses and switches from stimulation to inhibition; and (3) it will produce novel AI model(s) for predicting phytoplankton hormesis and ecotoxicology due to ENPs. 
From a broader perspective, the project will provide a very strong underpinning for decision-making by (1) regulators that need to evaluate ENP-enabled products; (2) industrial product designers as they consider the different types of ENPs for their products; and (3) the public at large, by having information to decide on the use of nano-enabled products (e.g., cosmetics, sunscreens, and other personal care products).

Title: The Conversational Consumer: Mapping Voice Interaction Patterns Across Contexts & Time to Enhance AI-Mediated Consumer Touchpoints
Abstract:
Voice technologies from traditional stand-alone devices such as Amazon Alexa, Google Home, or Apple's Siri to voice-mode interactions in ChatGPT and other large language mdoels, have rapidly transitioned into indispensable tools in consumers’ daily life. These conversational AI devices are fundamentally reshaping how people engage with technology, influencing not only consumer behavior but also social interactions, emotional experiences, and their downstream decision-making processes. Despite their growing ubiquity, we still lack a comprehensive understanding of how the linguistic style—particularly the use of more direct commands versus polite requests—affects consumer interactions, experiences, and long-term relationships with these emerging AI technologies.
This research project addresses this gap through a longitudinal approach. Unlike previous research that relied primarily on controlled lab environments and one-shot interaction studies, this project uniquely captures how consumers naturally interact with such voice technologies over extended periods in real-world settings. By examining the evolution of consumers’ employed conversational styles in everyday usage settings, we seek to provide novel insights into how the underlying linguistic patterns used throughout the interaction between a user and voice technology affect consumers' subjective experiences, their well-being, and subsequent decisions across diverse usage contexts.
Leveraging advanced methodologies in speech and audio processing, we systematically explore how subtle variations in conversational style impact consumers’ prosodic fluency (the smoothness and melodic flow of speech), conversational fluency (the perceived naturalness of interaction), and their downstream effects on consumers. Our preliminary research already indicates that polite requests can lead to significantly more fluent and satisfying interactions compared to direct commands, influencing consumers' future relationship orientation with their voice assistants and associated voice technology platforms.
This longitudinal field research pursued in this project spans various real-life contexts, capturing voice interactions not only in private home environments but also in public or mobile settings. This contextual breadth is essential because it recognizes that voice technology usage may vary substantially based on environmental and situational factors such as peoples privacy concerns, their mobility patterns, or the presence of others. The project further explores the capability to naturally adapt and subtly encourage the dynamic change of conversational styles, offering practical insights into how conversational AI can actively support better consumer experiences in AI-mediated marketplaces. Beyond its scientific importance, the findings of this research will also have implications for consumer well-being, demonstrating how voice technology interactions, optimized for natural and intuitive conversational patterns, can mitigate frustration, reduce stress, and improve decision quality.
In summary, by employing a set of unique longitudinal designs to study authentic consumer interactions across diverse real-life contexts, this research advances our understanding of conversational AI beyond traditional lab-based studies and one-shot interactions. The project's objective to reveal novel insights into how contextual factors and sustained use shape consumer experiences will deepen our understanding people’s relationship to and with AI-mediated technologies in the marketplace.
Keywords: Consumer Psychology, Consumer experience, Consumer well-being, Conversational AI, Conversational design, Digital Well-Being, Digital inclusion, Language Formation, Natural language processing, Prosody, Speech analytics, Voice Interfaces

Title: A Transfer Learning Approach to Reduce Participation Bias in Medical Research
Abstract:
Modern research increasingly depends on reliable statistical analyses to understand various phenomena and make informed decisions. In medical research, statistical inference (e.g., interval estimation and hypothesis testing) is crucial for addressing problems ranging from dose finding to precision medicine. However, medical studies often suffer from participation bias, where study participants inadequately represent the broader population of interest. Drawing conclusions about the target population from analyses conducted on data with participation bias can lead to incorrect findings, as seen in the development of many drugs, which primarily rely on male participants, leading to adverse reactions in females. The rise of digitalization in medicine has added further complexity to the analysis of medical data. For example, medical data often include a large number of variables (e.g., genetic information) compared to the available outcomes, and they may have issues such as misclassified results, missing values, and truncated measurements. These complex characteristics of medical data can reduce the effectiveness of current statistical tools, necessitating new methods that can provide accurate statistical inference for complex medical data.

In recent years, transfer learning has attracted increasing attention among statisticians. It allows researchers to use information from different but related studies to solve the target problem. Transfer learning offers a novel strategy for studying medical data with participation bias, enabling researchers to leverage available data to obtain reliable results while ensuring the generalizability of findings.

Motivated by the high potential of transfer learning in analyzing complex medical data, this project will develop a transfer learning framework that can provide accurate statistical inference for complex medical data, particularly electronic health records data, while reducing the impact of participation bias on the results. This project will significantly advance the methodological development and broaden the applicability of transfer learning methods. More importantly, it will have a substantial impact on science by facilitating research findings at a reduced cost through the use of various information sources, and on society by contributing to the reduction of health disparities among populations.
Keywords: biostatistics, electronic health records, gender, health disparities, high-dimensional statistics, precision medicine, public health, statistical inference

Title: Programming self-organization by engineered combinatorial adhesion
Abstract:
Background: During embryonic development, cells organize in time and space to form exquisite patterns of gene expression. Differential adhesion/repulsion clues play a key role in several patterning events, such as the segregation of the different germ layers during early embryogenesis, or motoneuron patterning. However, the extent to which adhesion-driven patterning alone can form predictable three-dimensional structures remains unclear. To a big extent this is due to the complex wiring of natural systems. In animal embryos, chemical, adhesive and mechanical clues act simultaneously and present numerous and intricate relationships. Even if adhesion could be isolated, multicellular eukaryotes present hundreds of adhesion/repulsion mechanisms, which are often expressed at the same time by the same cell type, further complicating its study.
In recent years, few studies have proposed the engineering of synthetic cell adhesion molecules (synCAMs), by replacing the extracellular domain of adhesion molecules by well-known binding partners. SynCAMs permitted the formation of simple patterned aggregates, solely based on synthetic homophilic interactions. While these studies have been pioneering, the programing of adhesion patterning would require to independently tune the different adhesive interaction of each cell population for itself and the other populations within the tissue. Unfortunately, current synCAM systems, based on single-domain interacting pairs cannot be easily scaled up nor tuned for such purpose. 
Overall objective. We aim to engineer a combinatorial adhesion system and to employ it to explore the basic principles of adhesion-driven pattern formation.
Specific Aims: 1st Aim: Generate a repertoire of synthetic adhesion molecules based on Ig repeats. 2nd Aim: Unravel the principles of pattern formation by computational and in vitro approaches. 3rd Aim: Exploring cellular determinants of adhesion-based pattern formation.
Methods: This study will depend on the interdependent application of computational and experimental methods. Computation methods: Mathematical modeling of adhesion systems based on Cellular Potts Modeling (Using Morpheus and Python software). We will also perform deep learning-based pattern classification, in collaboration with the laboratory of Prof. Calin Belta (Department of Engineering and computer science, University of Maryland). Image analysis based on ImageJ and Python. Experimental methods: Cell culture techniques, FACS, Confocal imaging, surface plasmon resonance. Transfection and genetic engineering will be based on previously established methods.
Expected results and impact: The expected impact of these study is twofold. On the one hand, it will provide the necessary tools to start interrogating adhesion-based patterning. Given the widespread role of adhesion in the establishment, refinement and maintenance of patterns, our contribution will surely impact many scientific areas, from developmental biology to tissue regeneration. On the other hand, our synthetic adhesion system will be the first allowing combinatorial interactions. This system could be used for tissue-engineering applications, both alone or in combination with existing techniques, providing the means to generate clinically relevant patterns.
Keywords: Development, Embryogenesis, Engineering, Patterning, Protein, Self-organization, Synthetic

Title: Advanced Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: The goal of this proposal is to improve the theory and practice of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Our extraordinarily successful SNF RL projects so far have led to 60 publications since 2009, four of which won awards. RL is closely related to how animals and humans act and learn. Without a teacher, solely from occasional real-valued pain and pleasure signals, RL agents must discover how to interact with a dynamic environment to maximize thei future expected reward. The classical approach to RL makes unrealistic strong assumptions such as: the current input of the agent tells it all needs to know about the environment. Our more general methods learn to create memories of important events, solving numerous RL/optimization tasks unsolvable by classical RL methods. The originally proposed project subgoals included: (1) Improve scalability of state-of-the-art RL controllers towards high-dimensional observation/action spaces, using Compressed Network Search and unsupervised redundancy reduction through slow feature analysis; (2) Learn through RL to actively focus an internal searchlight of attention, to improve state-of-the-art vision systems; (3) Make further steps towards implementing a full-fledged, self-improving Goedel Machine; (4) Implement and test novel Optimal Ordered Problem Solver-like systems with a programming language based on self-delimiting nets that determine their own effective size and runtime during search for solutions to optimisation problems.
Keywords: Reinforcement Learning, benchmarks, compressed network search, high-dimensional observation/action spaces, natural evolution strategies, self-improvement

Title: Massive Exploration of Optoelectronic Properties with Machine-Learning-Guided Quantum Chemistry
Abstract:
Optoelectronic properties are exploited in various and diverse areas of both everyday life, professional business, and development-driven research. At the same time, because of the complex electronic processes underlying them, they are objects of active fundamental investigations. In recent years, fundamental and development-driven research on optoelectronic properties started to approach due to modern computer architectures and novel algorithms. Parallel and distributed computing allow for a vast number of accurate calculations within affordable time frames, and progress in artificial-intelligence research enables the construction of empirical electronic-structure models by analyzing quantum-mechanical data with machine-learning techniques. This trend accelerates both the development of evermore sophisticated first-principles models and the data-driven discovery of novel materials with promising properties. High-throughput virtual screening (HTVS), i.e., compound discovery by computational analysis of large virtual structure libraries, particularly profits from these developments. Today, HTVS is no longer a mere search tool building on simplistic structure–property relationships, but an increasingly complex endeavor integrating cutting-edge data analysis and electronic-structure models.
However, routine HTVS of advanced materials with promising optoelectronic properties requires achievement of important milestones, which I will approach together with the Aspuru-Guzik research group during my postdoctoral stay at Harvard University. First, we will carry out high-accuracy benchmarks of relevant optoelectronic properties to define a standard for subsequent screening studies. Here, time-dependent density-functional theory, methods based on equation-of-motion coupled cluster, and the density-matrix-renormalization-group approach will be considered. Second, we will develop orbital-based descriptors to select the most efficient electronic-structure method for a targeted accuracy. Entanglement measures of active orbitals derived from the mutual-information concept of quantum information theory are our descriptors of choice. Third, a well-justified screening process is only possible if a rigorous control of all sources of uncertainty can be ensured. For this purpose, we will apply statistical calibration for rigorous uncertainty quantification of property predictions, an approach which I have already developed during my doctoral studies. Fourth, because of the high memory and CPU demands of electronic-structure calculations, we will train machine-learning models based on quantum-chemical data that enable gradient-based property optimizations. This subproject builds on the recently developed autoencoder approach by the Aspuru-Guzik research group.
All of these developments will be combined for the screening of at least 1 million molecules for the discovery of unprecedented organic semiconductor lasers based on organic light-emitting diodes. This work will be conducted in close collaboration with the experimental research group of Chihaya Adachi at Kyushu University.

Title: Towards an Integrated Methodology of Dating Biblical Texts: The Case of the Book of Jeremiah
Abstract:
International scholarship on the Hebrew Bible shares the unanimous consensus that its books, including the Book of Jeremiah, are literary products of the first millennium BCE. Nearly all else is in dispute, for there are no textual wit-nesses to the Hebrew Bible that stem from the biblical period itself, as the discovery of biblical manuscripts from the Dead Sea are all post-biblical. 
For 250 years biblical scholarship has struggled to develop adequate methodologies for the dating of biblical texts, resulting in contentious results for four primary reasons: 1) A dramatic rise in the discovery and study of external evidence (epigraphic and archaeological) in recent decades has challenged traditional (“biblical”) datings. 2) Newer developments in the study of literary growth in the Hebrew Bible have also advocated for taking into account histori-cal linguistics that hitherto have been neglected in the field of compositional analyses of biblical books but suggest quite different results. 3) Different existing methodologies (literary, linguistic, historical, archaeological etc.) have not been sufficiently integrated. They continue to create “conflicting evidences” that have not been addressed in a satis-fying way – neither methodologically nor in terms of specific historical datings. 4) Different academic cultures (e.g. in Europe, Israel, North America) have been entertaining diverse approaches regarding the composition of the Bible. They are, of course, in constant exchange, but biblical studies are still far from finding a consensus approach. This project 1) strives to develop an integrated methodology for dating biblical texts, 2) using the Book of Jeremiah as a case study; 3) it will integrate and refine a significant Digital Humanities (DH) component with regard to linguistic dating, and 4) it will balance the results from “natural” and “artificial” intelligence. The project will include next to the PI (who is working on a 2 vol. commentary on Jeremiah in the Anchor Yale Bible Commentary series) two post-docs. One will work on a monograph assembling, interpreting and evaluating data that are relevant for relative (text x is earlier/later than text/event y) and/or absolute dating (text x is to be dated to year y) of texts in the Book of Jere-miah; the other one will develop a machine learning algorithm that will classify the texts in the Book of Jeremiah in terms of historical linguistics. The PI and the two postdocs will work as a team and interact among each other in bi-weekly meetings in order to balance, adjust and correct their approaches. 
The project includes two conferences and will produce a monograph (by postdoc 1), a (publicly accessible) machine learning tool for linguistic dating (by postdoc 2), a commentary on the Book of Jeremiah (2 vols., by the PI), and several articles (by all three members of the team). All publications will be open access. 
The project’s significance and originality lies in 1) its integrated methodology for dating, 2) its inclusion of a signifi-cant DH component, 3) the mutual integration of results from natural and artificial intelligence, and 4) the dissemina-tion of (continental) European research into the broader academic discourse in the English-speaking world in form of a commentary in a renowned and established series.
In order to ensure the scientific quality of the project, an advisory board will accompany the work of the team and participate in the two conferences. Three Jeremiah specialists (Ronnie Goldstein [HU Jerusalem]; Christl Maier [Marburg]; Hermann-Josef Stipp [Munich], a linguist (Holger Gzella [Munich], an archaeologist/historian (Oded Lipschits [Tel Aviv]), and two DH experts (Willem van Peursen [VU Amsterdam]; Barak Sober [HU Jerusalem]) have agreed to serve in that capacity.

Title: 3D image understanding for urban scenes
Abstract:
The topic of the proposed project is automatic generation of virtual 3D city models, starting from aerial and terrestrial image data. Digital models of our environment form the basis for geographic information systems (GIS) and are required for a wide range of tasks in planning, construction, navigation, etc. Such topographic data has been used for a long time by specialists and authorities, and is nowadays becoming ubiquitous with internet cartography. To this day, 3D city models are generated manually or at most semi-automatically, which is costly and does not scale.

The main data source for large-scale mapping are images and range images acquired with cameras and laser scanners, either from aerial platforms or from mobile mapping systems on the ground. To convert that sensor data to a virtual 3D model one needs to solve two computer vision problems: on the one hand the 3D geometry of the imaged scene must be reconstructed; on the other hand the data must be interpreted, meaning that it must be structured into semantically meaningful entities (buildings, roads, trees, etc.). A crucial point, which has long been known but is still not properly accounted for, is that the two tasks are not independent - objects of different semantic classes have different geometric properties, and vice versa the geometric shape and extent is an important cue about the semantic object class of a surface.

The aim of the proposed project is to develop computer vision techniques able to jointly solve 3D reconstruction and semantic labelling, to automatically generate complete and accurate, interpreted 3D models. Automatic 3D modelling and image understanding have been core topics of computer vision and remote sensing research over the past decades. Both field have now reached some maturity, and a central scientific question is how to integrate the two developments. Specifically, the project aims to develop a probabilistic framework for integrated 3D image understanding in urban scenes, based on aerial nadir, aerial oblique, and ground-level images. Such a model will deliver at the same time better 3D geometry, by allowing one to include category-specific priors for the surfaces’ shape, orientation and layout; and better segmentation of the scene into semantic object classes, aided by the underlying 3D shape and layout.

The technical core contribution of the project shall be a probabilistic graphical model that formalises the a-priori assumptions about 3D urban scenes, together with the necessary inference tools to estimate the geometric 3D shape of a scene and the semantic classes of its individual elements in a single, joint optimisation procedure. A large amount of a-priori domain knowledge exists for structured scenes such as cities, but even simple relations can only be leveraged if both geometry and semantic interpretation are considered - e.g. that building walls are vertical, that roads are smooth surfaces whereas vegetation canopies are not, that roofs are usually higher than the ground, etc.

We are convinced that integrated 3D modelling and scene understanding will significantly enhance the power of automatic mapping and constitutes an important step towards the visionary “3D virtual habitat”.
Keywords: 3d modelling, computer vision, image understanding

Title: Feature Learning for Bayesian Inference
Abstract:
The goal of this project is to use interpretable Machine Learning (ML) to find low-dimensional features in high-dimensional noisy data generated by (i) stochastic models or (ii) real systems. 
In the first case, we are interested in the features imprinted on simulated data by the parameters of the stochastic model. In the latter, the interesting features depend on the particular system. In hydrology, one of the domains considered in this project, they are fingerprints of catchment properties in observed time-series of river-runoff. 
In both cases, the problem is to disentangle the effect of high-dimensional disturbances (noise realizations in the first case or the rain falling on the catchment in the latter) from the effects of relevant characteristics (model parameters in the first case, catchment properties in the latter).
This problem is reminiscent of the problem of finding collective quantities characterizing states of interacting particle systems in Statistical Mechanics. 
Variational Autoencoders (VAE) have been proven to be capable of learning such quantities in the form of order parameters or collective variables, which could then be used to identify phase transitions or to enhance Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations. 

We expect parameter-features of stochastic model-outputs to be of great value for Bayesian inference. They can be used to sample from the Bayesian posterior, in situations where the likelihood function (LHD) is too expensive to evaluate, and one thus has to resort to comparing - ideally sufficient-summary statistics of simulated data with corresponding statistics of observed data as in Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC). 

Instead of comparing summary statistics, we may attempt to sample the product space of model parameters and model states. As this results in an extremely high-dimensional inference problem, sophisticated sampling schemes such as Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) have to be employed. But HMC, which is essentially the same as MD, suffers from slowly-mixing collective features of high-dimensional model-states associated with changing model parameters.
Hence, one of the objectives of this project is to bring the method of biased sampling with collective variables developed for MD to fruition for sampling-based Bayesian inference.
A considerable part of the project is further devoted to the development of ML-methods for summary-statistics learning. Towards this end, we will also employ a robust algorithm for finding the Intrinsic Dimension (ID) of data, which was developed by the PI. 
Not only might this method help to identify the ideal number of summary statistics, but it might also be useful for identifying different phases of the model based on the distribution of the learned features. 
The data ID can guide the design of the architecture of the ML tools leading to higher interpretability.
We will finally apply feature-learning to real data in different domains, either directly to observed data (hydrology), or indirectly to the outputs of the stochastic model that is used to model the data (infectious disease epidemiology). 
We stress that dimensionality reduction, feature learning and interpretable ML are versatile tools that can be leveraged far beyond Bayesian learning and that the application domains of the developed methodology range beyond our two case studies.
Keywords: Approximate Bayesian Computation, Autoencoder, Bayesian inference, Collective Variables, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, Machine Learning, Non-Volume Preserving transformations, Spreading of an epidemic and effect of NPI, Stochastic processes evolving on a network structu, Summary statistics

Title: Revealing adaptations to parasitism using comparative spatial proteomics of anaerobic free-living and parasitic lineages
Abstract:
The evolution of parasitism is a fundamental and fascinating question in biology and evolution. Every extant parasitic lineage has evolved from a free-living ancestor through specific molecular adaptations. These promote host infection and colonization, while avoiding mechanical and/or immune-mediated clearance. Despite the immediate significance of this overarching question in biology to both human and animal well-being and livelihoods, we are very far from understanding how parasitism emerged as a style of life. 

The overarching question informing this proposal is thus stated: how has the transition to parasitism affected proteomes and their subcellular distribution, organelle evolution and metabolic diversification to meet the challenges of shifting from fluctuating environmental habitats to survival within a host, including life-cycle completion and transmission? 

To tackle this ambitious and far-reaching question, we present an interdisciplinary team and approach including spatial proteomic methods, experimental genetics and cell biology, comparative genomics and evolutionary biology, combined with expertise across human and veterinary livestock -infective, and free-living lineages of Phylum Fornicata. Fornicata includes both free-living protist species and human/animal parasites, including Giardia intestinalis (syn. lamblia, duodenalis), a human pathogen of clear zoonotic significance, and closely-related genera Spironucleus and Hexamita, responsible for million Euro losses in the aquaculture industry. 

We propose Fornicata as an excellent case study for comparative high-resolution mapping analysis of the spatial proteome of parasitic and free-living species using hyperLOPIT (localization of organelle proteins by isotope tagging). This is a multiplexed quantitative proteomics mass spectrometry approach to determine the steady-state spatial distribution of hundreds of proteins at high resolution with their resident organelles, sub-organelle niches, and large protein complex level. The technology of spatial proteomics and specifically hyperLOPIT makes it especially suited to comparative approaches of this scale which require team efforts beyond the scope and expertise of a single research group to be successful. 

The project is structured in four workpackages for hyperLOPIT data acquisition, analysis, and functional validation from the following parasitic species: Giardia intestinalis, Spironucleus salmonicida and Hexamita nelsoni; and free-living relatives: Carpediomonas membranifera, Trepomonas and a ´newly-discovered diplomonad lineage” (NDL ‘GhostHex’). 

Combining strong elements of machine learning and computational biology, including comparative genomics, reconstruction of cell biochemistry and compartmentalization, and experimental validation of novel protein clusters, we shall detect gains, losses and adaptations in metabolism, subcellular organization, and strategies for survival in adverse conditions, including parasite transmission. This shall enable us to go beyond a merely descriptive answer to the complex biological question of the evolution of parasitism from free-living lineages by using phylum Fornicata, a complex lineage presenting species with cryptic/undiscovered organelles and novel structures that evade simple interpretation from established models while playing key albeit scarcely understood roles in both parasitic and free-living species.
Keywords: Fornicata, adaptation, bioinformatics, cell biology, comparative, evolution, free-living, genomics, host, hyperLoPIT, infection, microscopy, organellar proteomics, organelle, parasitism, proteomics, protist, transition, transmission, zoonosis

Title: Novel Data-Driven Models for robust and generalisable ultra-low-dose PET image reconstruction and high-quality CT-free PET image synthesis
Abstract:
Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is a non-invasive imaging technique widely used for diagnosing diseases such as cancer, heart conditions, and brain disorders. PET/CT scans provide highly accurate images, but they expose patients to radiation from the injected tracers and the CT scan itself. To reduce radiation risks, it is possible to decrease the dose of tracers and adjust CT settings, but this often lowers image quality, which can hinder medical diagnosis by adding noise and artifacts.

This project aims to develop innovative data-driven approaches, specifically deep learning models, to enhance PET/CT imaging. The goal is to create methods that reduce radiation exposure and scanning time while maintaining high-quality images for accurate medical diagnosis. The project focuses on three key areas: 
1. Improving low-dose PET scans by reducing noise and enhancing image quality.
2. Exploring ways to improve PET scans without needing additional information from CT scans, potentially reducing radiation and costs.
3. Studying how to use deep learning models to create PET and CT scans from low-dose PET data, preserving diagnostic accuracy.

By improving PET scan safety and reducing costs, this research could lead to broader use of PET imaging in clinical practice, benefiting patients by offering more personalized and less invasive diagnostic options. The ultimate goal is to make PET imaging safer, more accessible, and cost-effective for wider adoption in medical diagnosis.
Keywords: CT-free PET, Data-Driven Deep Learning Models, Low-dose PET/CT, Multimodal PET/CT Imaging, Oncologic PET/CT, PET/CT Image Denoising

Title: Developing novel outcomes for clinical trials in Stargardt disease using structure/function relationship and deep learning
Abstract: Stargardt disease is an inherited retinal disease that typically starts to cause visual symptoms during childhood or adolescence. The by far most prevalent form of Stargardt disease (Stargardt disease type 1, STGD1) is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner and caused by mutations in the ABCA4 gene. With the genetic discovery of the disease, novel treatment options are on the horizon, but currently there is no approved treatment for the disease available. One of the challenges for the approval of a drug is to find a sufficient main outcome parameter. In STGD1 disease visual acuity is not a good outcome, because the disease is characterized by a progressive loss visual fields. Functional measures such as microperimetry (MP) show large variability, structural measures such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) are not patient-relevant. We hypotheisze that an optimized estimator of visual field deterioration over time can be developed and that structural data can be used to improve prediction of visual function in STGD1 disease. To test this hypothesis, the data of the ProgStar study, which enrolled 345 patients with STGD1, will be used. Baseline OCT and MP data will be used for the characterization of the structure/function relationship. To refine the structure/function relationship we will apply a deep learning-based model. We will use the structure/function relationship as obtained from the baseline data to predict the future development of visual field decline in STGD1. At the end of this grant we expect to have an improved combined structure/function that can be used in clinical studies involving STGD1 patients. This will facilitate pivotal clinical trials in this field and may accelerate the approval of novel treatments for STGD1 disease.
Keywords: Deep learning, Hereditary macular disease, Microperimetry, Optical coherence tomography, Outcome parameters, Stargardt disease, Structure/function relationship

Title: Avalanche Seismic Monitoring for Automated High-Resolution Forecasting and Characterization
Abstract:
Snow avalanches are the deadliest natural hazards in the Swiss Alps, causing substantial economic losses annually. In the future, climate change is projected to intensify heavy snowfalls and rapid snowmelts, potentially increasing the frequency and severity of extreme avalanches. Precisely determining when, where, how and why avalanches occur is crucial for effective prediction and risk mitigation. However, given the lack of thorough comprehension of the initial mechanical processes and the current experience-based forecasting practices, mostly relying on subjective avalanche observations, providing precise answers to these critical questions remains unattainable today. To overcome this, it becomes essential to leverage technological advancements in novel data-driven approaches and comprehensive databases from reliable data automatic acquisition systems. Automated data can be recorded in real-time independently of weather and visibility conditions by seismic detection systems comprising conventional seismic sensors and cutting-edge technologies like Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS). Despite obvious advantages, DAS systems have rarely been employed for avalanche monitoring, and the methodological transfer and constraints between these systems remain unexplored.

Therefore, our project aspires to pioneer the utilization of unique avalanche databases combining extensive seismic data of over 20 years and new high resolution DAS measurements.  The aim is to advance avalanche forecasting and address knowledge gaps regarding the interplay between external meteorological factors, release mechanisms, snow cover properties and flow dynamics. 
To achieve this, a wide range of innovative methods will be used to exploit our data, including time-series analysis, advanced array processing, and state-of-the-art supervised and unsupervised machine learning methods. Specifically, our goals are: 1) Establish new detection algorithms to automatically detect avalanche activity acquired by conventional and novel seismic DAS technologies while exploring their transferability and operational application. 2) Characterize the avalanche flow type and the internal processes with the unparalleled spatiotemporal resolution of DAS measurements, inferring valuable fundamental parameters for avalanche prediction such as flow velocity and size. 3) Improve our theoretical understanding of avalanche formation by conducting innovative experiments using a multidimensional DAS grid in the avalanche release zone to capture in situ the fracture initiation processes prior to release. 4) Establish a novel forecasting model framework to predict avalanche activity and size with a potential practical use for operational avalanche forecasting in Switzerland.

Collaborating with a team of experts in different fields (snow science, geophysics, data science), we intend to significantly improve avalanche forecasting by combining state-of-the-art measuring methods and novel model approaches. We request four years of financial support to fund the employment of two Ph.D. students hosted at SLF and ETHZ.

The proposed research will result in an unparalleled avalanche monitoring and warning system and will provide a viable tool supporting the authorities in managing avalanche risk. The anticipated outcomes are intended to significantly improve avalanche forecasting, validate novel numerical models utilized in avalanche risk assessment, and contribute to the development of the next-generation early warning systems. Through a better understanding of release mechanisms, the research's impact also extends beyond the avalanche field and is relevant for a wide range of applications, including the detection and warning of other hazardous mass movements like landslides and earthquakes. These implications carry significant benefits for both the scientific community and public safety.

Title: Sonifying Tinnitus from EEG Signals
Abstract:
Background and Significance: Tinnitus is an enigmatic neurological condition experienced by over 10% of adults, marked by the perception of phantom sounds in the absence of external stimuli. For many, it significantly affects quality of life, leading to distress, sleep disturbances, and cognitive impairments. Current diagnosis and research rely heavily on subjective patient reports, leaving an urgent clinical need for objective measures of tinnitus characteristics.

Objectives: This project aims to reconstruct an acoustic representation of tinnitus directly from electroencephalography (EEG) signals. Recent advancements have demonstrated that deep learning-based methods can successfully sonify auditory perception from EEG. Building on this approach, we seek to develop an objective and quantifiable measure of tinnitus.

Novelty: This is the first attempt to apply a zero-shot audio-reconstruction pipeline to tinnitus. Crucially, it does not require any patient-specific data: both model training and inference operate without reliance on individual patient input. Beyond quantification, the approach may leverage introspective deep learning to offer fresh insights into the neurophysiological mechanisms of tinnitus.

Work Plan: The project will be conducted over 12 months by a dedicated postdoctoral researcher, structured into four key phases:
1. Implementation of existing EEG-to-audio software architecture
2. Sonification of published tinnitus EEG dataset
3. Controlled validation with synthetic tinnitus stimuli on healthy participants
4. Final analysis and feasibility assessment

Impact: A successful proof-of-concept promises transformative tinnitus management in three critical ways: (1) providing an objective biomarker for clinical assessment, reducing reliance on subjective reporting; (2) enabling the objective tracking of treatment progress, offering quantifiable insights into therapy effectiveness; and (3) potentially shedding light on the neural origins of tinnitus through deep learning model introspection.

Feasibility and Risks: We minimize technical risks by using a proven deep learning architecture. A parallel approach of both utilizing an established EEG tinnitus dataset and creating a tailored in-lab dataset with synthetic stimuli allows to efficiently probe the method’s robustness in capturing tinnitus-related neural signals. This one-year effort focusses on providing a thorough feasibility assessment and inform future clinical studies involving patients suffering from tinnitus.
Keywords: Auditory Neuroscience, Deep learning, Electroencephalography, Sonification, Tinnitus

Title: Modeling Deformable 3-D Surfaces from Video
Abstract:
Being able to recover the 3D shape of deformable surfaces from ordinary images will make it possible to field reconstruction systems that only require single video cameras, such as those that now equip most mobile devices. It will also allow 3D shape recovery in more specialized contexts, such as when performing endoscopic surgery or using a fast camera to capture the deformations of a rapidly moving object. However, because many different 3D shapes can have virtually the same projection, such monocular shape recovery is inherently ambiguous. Arguably, these ambiguities could be resolved by using a depth-camera. However, even though they are now readily available, such depth-cameras are more difficult and expensive to fit into a cell-phone or an endoscope, and have limited range.

The video-based solutions that have been proposed over the years mainly fall into two classes: Those that involve physics-inspired models and those that rely on a non-rigid structure-from-motion approach. The former solutions often entail designing complex objective functions and require hard-to-obtain knowledge about the precise material properties of the target surfaces. The latter depend on points being reliably tracked in image sequences and are only effective for relatively small deformations.

To overcome these limitations, we have developed approaches that rely on establishing correspondences between an input image in which the 3D shape is to be recovered and a reference image in which the 3D shape is known. We showed that 3D shape recovery under those conditions could be formulated as an under-constrained linear problem. Furthermore, introducing inextensibility constraints and using control points to reduce the dimensionality of the problem turns it into a well-posed problem, which can be solved quickly using convex optimization.

These have proved effective when the surface is well-textured but we have shown in the final stretch of the ongoing project that we can obtain even better results by replacing sparse correspondences by dense ones. Not only are the results more accurate but we can handle surfaces that are only partially textured in the presence of substantial occlusions and illumination changes. However, this improvement comes at a price: Instead of being able to model from individual frames, we have to track from frame-to-frame because the objective function is no longer convex, which makes our algorithm prone to tracking failures.

In the continuation of this project, we will leverage the power of Deep Learning approaches to remove this limitation and preserve the accuracy of dense matching without requiring a priori knowledge of an initial pose. This will involve two main research directions:

- Learn a mapping from image to rough 3D shape. We will train Convolutional Neural Networks to propose multiple 3D shape hypotheses for image patches and recover the global 3D shape by enforcing spatial consistency over neighboring patches.

- Refine the initial estimate in spite of potential occlusions. Since the space of all possible deformations is immense, we do not expect the resulting shapes to be particularly accurate. We will therefore further develop our approach to refining them by better accounting for occlusions and differences on how informative different parts of the surface are.
 
This will result in robust and accurate 3D surface reconstruction algorithms that can truly be deployed in real-world applications.
Keywords: 3D Reconstruction, Computer Vision, Deformable Models, Surface Modeling

Title: Advancing Electrochemical Energy Conversion: Unraveling the Nexus of Activity and Stability in Electrocatalysts
Abstract:
This research project seeks to advance our understanding of catalyst stability during various electrochemical reactions, potentially leading to more efficient and durable catalysts for important chemical processes. The aim is to comprehensively address stability concerns through advanced catalyst synthesis strategies. This will be linked with the development and refinement of experimental methods and electrocatalyst analyses, with particular emphasis on in situ and operando techniques. Last but not least, we will apply machine learning strategies for guiding the synthesis as well as to develop experimental and computational models in a data-driven approach. The imminent goal is to reduce or replace the use of scarce platinum group metals (PGMs in the respective processes. On a broader scale, the obtained experimental results will improve our theoretical understanding of catalyst stability and help to develop theoretical models for catalyst degradation, eventually contributing to establishing a descriptor-based approach to catalyst stability. 
In the proposal, we address three essential energy conversion reactions, the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR), the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), and the selective glucose oxidation reaction (GOR). 
Oxygen Reduction Reaction: This reaction is the limiting process for hydrogen fuel cells and currently Pt-based catalysts are state-of-the-art. The project focuses on Pt-based, compositionally complex solid solution nanoparticles. The goal is to explore the stability of these catalysts during the acidic ORR with a focus on compositional and structural changes of the active phase. The investigations will involve the use of in situ and operando XAS, SAXS, XRD, and total scattering measurements. The work constitutes work package one (WP1). It will be executed by one PhD student (48 months), and a Postdoctoral researcher (24 months) employed by Prof. Rebecca Pittkowski at the University of Copenhagen. Several visits of the Postdoctoral researcher and PhD student between the University of Copenhagen and the University of Bern are planned.
Oxygen Evolution Reaction: The oxygen evolution reaction is the limiting reaction for water electrolysis providing green hydrogen, which is the starting point for sustainable chemicals and fuels. The lack of stable, active, and scalable catalysts for the OER under acidic conditions is one of the most important challenges for electrocatalysis today. In the project, we focus on MnOx-based catalysts. The primary objective is to examine doping approaches as well as introducing structural barriers to metal dissolution during the OER. This part constitutes WP2 and will be executed by one PhD student who will benefit from the work of the Postdoctoral researcher employed in WP1.
Selective Glucose Oxidation Reaction: The third part of the project, WP3, concentrates on the selective GOR using both Au-based compositionally complex solid solution nanoparticles and porous metal foams as catalysts. The main emphasis here is to investigate the mechanisms behind catalyst degradation, specifically related to metal dissolution and side product formation. By gaining insights into these degradation mechanisms, the project aims to enhance the stability and longevity of these catalysts. WP3 will be executed by one PhD student. The closely related topic will allow synergetic effects with the work in WP1 and WP2.

Title: Self-supervised Multimodal Video Representation Learning for Action Recognition
Abstract: Egocentric action recognition is a key task for developing applications in AR/VR (e.g., action guidance and AI assistants) and robotics (e.g., human-robot collaboration and personal assistant robots), as the egocentric views correspond to the views of humans and robots. However, existing research on this task faces two major challenges: 1) the dependency on labeled data, which is expensive to obtain and limits the generalization to other domains, and 2) the focus on a single modality, such as RGB videos, depth videos, or audio sensors, even though the current AR/VR devices provide multimodal data, which is essential to understand egocentric activities in the 3D physical world. The main objective of this project is to devise novel methods for learning effective video representations for egocentric action recognition with multimodal data without labels to overcome the aforementioned challenges. To this end, we will employ sequence alignment as a pretext task of self-supervised learning, which aims to learn embedding space that preserves the temporal information of the data by matching frames from a reference sequence to frames of a target sequence. This embedding space can be leveraged for various downstream tasks such as action recognition, action detection, action forecasting, and frame retrieval. We will pursue this objective through three sub-stages. First, we will jointly learn sequence alignment and 3D hand and object poses, which will enable the embedding space to learn the temporal dynamics across frames and better grounding of 3D hand and object poses. Second, we will explore a novel method to align arbitrary video clips with the assistance of language models, such as vision-language models (VLMs) and Large Language Models (LLMs), which will facilitate action detection in untrimmed videos. Specifically, the proposed method will perform contrastive learning using the semantic embeddings from the vision-language models.  Third, we will exploit multiple modalities, such as RGB, depth, hand poses, head poses, eye gaze, sound, IMU, and 3D point clouds to capture the full complexity of human actions in the 3D physical world. The proposed direction is also highly relevant to the research interests of the host laboratory. The outcomes of this project, including the methods, code, and algorithms, will be disseminated to the research community through publications in prestigious conferences and high-impact journals, such as CVPR, ECCV, ICCV, NeurIPS and TPAMI. This work will substantially enhance the performance and interpretability of action recognition and comprehend the interactions between humans and objects in AR/VR by aligning multimodal sequences. Furthermore, the integration of vision-language models and LLMs with video representation learning will enable the development of assistive AI, which can provide information by understanding and anticipating the context of videos. In conclusion, this project will lay the foundation for many potential applications, such as user guidance and AI assistants in AR/VR and human-robot interaction.

Title: Space-Time Metasurfaces for Optical Analog Computing
Abstract:
With the rapid rise of artificial intelligence in the past decade, neural networks have dramatically increased in size and computational demand, outpacing advancements in CMOS hardware. Simultaneously, photonic devices have seen significant progress in scale, speed, and energy efficiency, prompting researchers to explore micro- and nanoscale optical components for all-optical, analog-based and neuromorphic computing. Many current platforms rely on integrated photonics due to greater advancements in materials development, as well as advanced system-level integration capabilities compared to diffractive and free-space optics. However, the key challenges faced by integrated photonics platforms today are the scalability and the energy efficiency per unit area. Additionally, integrated photonic circuits require preprocessed inputs that convert light from free space to chip-based optical signals, leading to a potential loss of the encoded information.

Free-space optics has the potential to overcome these challenges, offering promising directions for parallelization, energy efficiency per unit area, and additional degrees of freedom for encoding and transmitting information. In this context, metasurfaces, that are two-dimensional arrays of subwavelength scatterers, have emerged as a compact and versatile platform to manipulate the properties of light in unprecedented ways. Active metasurfaces, in particular, enable real-time reconfigurability, allowing dynamic switching between multiple functions. Recently, there has been a growing interest in controlling metasurfaces both spatially and temporally at high frequencies, enabling a synthetic frequency dimension for encoding multi-dimensional information in a single optical element. While existing metasurface platforms have focused on realizing complex spatiotemporal waveform transformations with passive metasurfaces, the potential for reconfigurable photonics in optical and neuromorphic computing remains largely unexplored. This project aims to merge these areas and develop a reconfigurable optical element that can be freely integrated into free-space optical or neuromorphic computing frameworks. 

The proposed project is structured in four parts: (i) development of a scattering matrix formalism to identify the target response from a tunable metasurface for optical analog-based and neuromorphic computers, (ii) appropriate design of an electro-optically tunable metasurface operating at near-infrared wavelengths with target frequency modulations ranging in the GHz regime, (iii) fabrication of the metasurface, and (iv) experimental demonstration of reconfigurable spatiotemporal analog computing operations.  Given the prevalence of integrated photonics in this field, our study will also include comparisons of the compute efficiency and scalability of the proposed metasurface platform with alternative device architectures. This project has the potential to revolutionize the fields of optical computing and information processing by developing energy-efficient hardware capable of engineering increasingly complex spatiotemporal wavefront phenomena.

Title: SIRAFI - System for Improving Regulated Automotive Flows governed by the Intergreen matrix
Abstract:
Can we make dynamic, or even delete in certain cases, depending on the available technologies on a light regulation installation (traffic lights), the intergreen times? Indeed, if a vehicle exits the perimeter of an intersection during the last seconds of the available green phases, actually, the light regulation installation, by the logic of the safety matrix, based on static rules, offers the intergreen time, even if no vehicle is present in the intersection while this v time is no longer necessary. The intergreen time ensures, to some extent, that a vehicle passing at the end of an available green can exit the conflict zone before another vehicle can enter it (next green).
The aim of the project, with the help of observations of existing intersections, prototypical development of machine learning algorithms, and digital twins of transportation, is to analyze and test if these road safety matrices could become dynamic and thus greatly improve road capacity and waiting times for all users while preserving road safety.
This project is proposed for Spark funding because it is an innovative and unconventional idea. Indeed, three main actors are generally involved in the integration and exploitation of light regulation rules; providers of regulated intersection equipment integrating rules determined by transportation engineers, and infrastructure owners (municipalities, cantons).
Transportation engineers determine (rigid) intergreen time matrices based on standard VSS 40 838. If adjustments or derogations are possible regarding the calculation method of intergreen times based on local conditions, these must be justified. However, the matrix remains rigid, and the intergreen times determined between opposing traffic flows are always applied. For safety reasons, engineers as well as infrastructure owners do not deviate from these matrices.
Equipment providers respond to the specifications of the project (client). These specifications generally follow the relevant standards. In terms of innovation, they do not seek to optimize these rigid matrices dynamically. Especially since they are generally required to comply with national and international standards (OCIT – Open Communication Interface for Road Traffic Control Systems), which also establish intergreen matrices as a standard safety element.
Finally, national road research (VSS) mainly aims to update current standards and not to conduct prototypical research if it does not show a certain level of maturity. This prototypical research should be initiated by equipment providers to distinguish themselves from their competitors, but is currently hindered by the aforementioned normative elements.
The various points mentioned above justify a prototypical trial without guarantee of results as proposed by the Spark encouragement instrument.

Title: Adaptive Perception with Event Cameras
Abstract:
Animals and humans continue to inspire robotics and computer vision research, due to their ability to
perceive and act with a low latency, and a high robustness, all while consuming very little power.
Researchers seek to emulate these systems with robotic platforms equipped with standard frame-based cameras running increasingly data-driven computer vision algorithms. However, the speed, safety, and robustness of these systems are limited by the high perceptual latency of frame-based cameras, and computational latencies by these data-driven algorithms, during which the robot is effectively blind. Event cameras are alternative sensors that, instead, capture their environment with independent pixels that measure significant per-pixel intensity changes, and report these as an asynchronous and sparse stream of data, also called events, with low latency and high temporal resolution. Due to this working principle, these sensors adapt to the scene dynamics, and can thus capture high-speed phenomena with low latency, while retaining a low data rate at slow speeds, unlike classical high-speed cameras. However, although the sensor is low-latency, state-of-the-art data-driven algorithms are not: They discard the sparsity and asynchronicity of events in favor of converting them into dense frames, and processing them with standard convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which incurs significant computational latency. Asynchronous and sparse models instead retain this sparsity, by processing the data asynchronously and recursively, but can still not be run in real-time on current hardware. While the adaptiveness of these models is desirable since it explains the efficiency of biological perception, it is also poorly understood, not explicitly controllable, and altogether inefficiently exploited in current asynchronous models. In this proposal, we plan on closing this gap with new event camera-based algorithms that modulate their computation explicitly, and controllably, through the use of latency-aware, dynamic neural networks that adapt their width and depth. Moreover, we plan on guiding this modulation to benefit a downstream robotic platform, by optimizing novel robot-centric metrics. To modulate computation, we will leverage current and past events, as well as events generated while processing. Title: SwarmOps: Human-sensing based MLOps for Collaborative Cyber-physical systems
Abstract:
The rise of AI-enabled Cyber-physical systems (AI-CPSs)1 has revolutionized the healthcare, avionics, automotive, railway, and robotics sectors. In this context, autonomous driving and flights have become a reality through Self-driving Cars (SDCs) and Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), with diverse applications for these systems such as crop monitoring, medical and food delivery, and 3D reconstruction of archaeological and space exploration sites.

Challenge - Using a team of AI-CPSs for real-world tasks is now considered the most credible setup in most applications, with multi-agent collaboration being the future of AI-CPSs. However, current state-of-the-art solutions for AI-CPSs have a limited perception of the environment, which poses significant challenges in real-world applications, such as mapping disaster areas at nuclear power plants or locating people stranded after natural disasters. MLOps, which combines DevOps and Data Engineering practices, is potentially the most effective paradigm for these systems, as it enables reliable and data-centric approaches. Unfortunately, contemporary MLOps solutions are inadequate for teams of AI-CPSs, limiting their reliability, predictability, adaptability, and deployability in
real-world tasks. The major limiting factor for teams of AI-CPSs is the lack of MLOps solutions that can verify their informed, reliable, and safe autonomous decisions.

Goal - The ultimate goal of this project is to enable AI-CPS teams to cooperate in dynamic environments, involving humans and other agents. The project’s innovations will address pressing MLOps shortcomings for AI-CPS teams, focusing on the challenges posed by team interactions of AI-CPSs with the environment and the need of rethinking MLOps abstractions and steps for AI-CPS teams.
