Title: Advancing First-Principles Based Molecular Dynamics To the Next Level
Abstract:
During the last decades, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations based on first-principles (FP) electronic structure methods have evolved into an invaluable tool for the in situ investigation of a wide variety of processes in chemistry, biology and materials science. However, in spite of the exponential increase in computer power and efficient exploitation of massive parallelization, FPMD simulations have remained costly imposing severe restrictions on tractable system sizes and accessible time scales. Through the combination with multiscale methods, in particular mixed quantum mechanical/molecular mechanical (QM/MM) approaches, the size limitations could be widely enlarged while a panoply of dif-ferent enhanced sampling techniques have addressed the time scale issue albeit mostly at the cost of scarifying the real-time dynamics in favor of thermodynamic sampling. In spite of many advances, modern FPMD and FP/MM simulations can only treat few 100-1000 of QM atoms for several 10-100 ps, especially when higher accuracy electronic structure descriptions are used. All the while, the difference in computational cost with respect to ‘classical’ MD based on force fields (FF) has remained large. 
Here, we propose the development of computational methods that can bring FPMD based simulations forward to the next level extending the accessible time windows by several orders of magnitude, in some cases even approaching the ones of FF based MD without giving away neither the accuracy of the FP approach nor the real-time dynamics.  This ‘MD with full FP accuracy for a cost similar to classical MD’ is made possible through combinations of algorithms from conventional computational chemistry with approaches from artificial intelligence (AI). This is a natural continuation of the work achieved during our previous SNF grants, in which we a) introduced the new highly flexible multiscale interface MiMiC based on a multiple program-multiple data strategy that allows for the efficient combinations of differ-ent QM as well MM programs while maintaining fast communication between the processes and b) developed multiple time step (MTS) based multi-rung QML-QMH approaches (in which a lower-level QML method is used to drive and accelerate the actual dynamics with a higher-level QMH method) as well as c) combined MTS machine learning (ML) algorithms to increase computational expedience. In particular, by combining higher-level (HL) and lower-level (LL) quantum chemical (QC) descriptions, we were able to gain at least a factor 5 in speedup. 
Here, we propose to push the efficiency gain of MTS-FPMD based simulations to a maximum through the use of spe-cially tailored, force-matched (FM) FF and mixtures of FF and ML models as LL driver for a variety of QC methods. To this end, we want to a) develop a FM method for highly flexible polarizable FF (flexFF) and mixed flexFF&ML models; b) implement flexFF driven MTS dynamics in MiMiC; c) extend MTS-flexFF(ML)-FP/MM to adiabatic and nonadiabatic excited state dynamics and d) implement fully-adaptive learn-on-the-fly (LOF) extensions. 
From all these developments, we expect an efficiency gain of at least 10-100 times, which will be highly beneficial for a wide variety of applications. In particular, we propose here to tackle two formidable challenges of high societal relevance. We want 1) to help elucidate the multifaceted relation between sex hormones and cancer both by starting to gain fundamental atomistic insights into the hormonal impact on DNA damage formation, response and repair as well as by designing new transition metal (TM) based inhibitors for PARP1, a target for the treatment of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) and 2) contribute to the development of highly-efficient perovskite based solar cells (PSC) with increased stability by investigating the complex role of additives, in particular during the nucleation and growth of the materials as well as in the oxidation protection of Pb-free alternatives.
Keywords: Computational Biophysics, Computational Chemistry, Photovoltaics, QM/MM, artificial intelligence, breast cancer, machine learning, molecular dynamics, multiscale modelling, transition metal anticancer drugs

Title: Crystallization: Optimal control and advanced monitoring (CrystOCAM)
Abstract:
The CrystOCAM project aims at developing a new generation of tools to model, to measure and monitor online, to optimize and control the distribution of sizes and shapes of crystals of a suspension of particles and crystals during the crystallization from solution of organic compounds of interest for pharmaceutical, food and fine chemical applications.

Crystallization is very often the key purification and pre-formulation step of products in the above mentioned industrial sectors. By tuning operating conditions mechanical properties such as tabletability and flowability, as well as features such as purity, chemical stability and bioavailability can be controlled. Such properties are critically influenced by the distribution of sizes and shapes of crystals, which must be characterized through the so called multi-dimensional particle size distribution (nD-PSD), i.e. the distribution of probabilities of the occurrence of certain combinations of two,
three or more characteristic dimensions in the particle population. Describing, measuring and controlling in an optimal manner during process development, scale-up and operation such nD-PSD are at the same time major scientific and technical challenges and great opportunities to make an important change in product quality and process robustness in the
crystallization of organic compounds.

The proposed three-year project will rely on the expertise of three laboratories, in each of which one Ph.D. student will be working: crystallization know-how at the Separation Processes Laboratory (SPL) of Prof. Mazzotti at ETH Zurich; control knowledge at the Automatic Control Laboratory (IfA) of Prof. Morari at ETH Zurich; computer vision and optimization-based control expertise at the new Laboratoire d'Automatique  LA) of Prof. Jones at EPF Lausanne.

The project partners will tackle the challenges above by exploiting important and promising background knowledge, such as a microscopic flow-through cell recently developed at SPL that images individual crystals in suspension and provides sufficient information to reconstruct their three-dimensional structure, or the image analysis and shape reconstruction algorithms developed by Prof. Jones, or the model predictive control and
robust control techniques mastered at IfA and already applied for complex optimal control tasks in chemical processes such as azeotropic distillation or multicolumn continuous chromatography.

The following deliverables are expected:
- Advanced vision algorithms capable of estimating the three-dimensional shape of individual crystals and therefore the nD-PSD of the crystal ensemble online during the crystallization process, so as to enable process monitoring
- Dynamic models of the evolution of the nD-PSD during crystallization and protocols for the characterization of the rates of the key mechanisms involved (nucleation, growth, agglomeration), which will enhance the understanding of the evolution of size and shape during crystallization
- An optimization-in-the-loop controller that will allow for the first time
  optimization and control of the final nD-PSD
- A collection of experimental case studies that will assess and demonstrate the effectiveness of the tools developed within the project
Keywords: control, crystallization, monitoring, particle size distribution

Title: New Approaches to Topological Quantum Computation
Abstract:
Quantum computers outperform classical computers by an exponential increase in calculation speed and therefore have the potential to revolutionize computing. A fundamental diffculty is that the underlying unit of a quantum computer, called the quantum bit, is susceptible to environmental noise which inevitably leads to the loss of quantum information. Topological quantum computers have made it possible to circumvent this problem by storing the information in non-local, topological quantum bits that are inherently robust against local perturbations. The proposed research addresses two important topics in the field of topological quantum computation: (1) New platforms
for topological phases with superconductivity and magnetism and (2) Quantum information processing and Machine Learning. The first project is motivated by the two primary downsides of current experimental realizations of topological quantum bits based on Majorana bound states: The detrimental effects of strong magnetic field on the superconductivity in these systems and their non-universality for quantum computation. The first issue is addressed in a collaborative effort with the theoretical physics group of Professor Liang Fu and the experimental physics group of Professor Jagadeesh Moodera to realize topological superconductor at zero magnetic field hosting Kramers pairs of Majorana
bound states based on an earlier theoretical proposal of the fellowship applicant. The second issue is addressed by studying systems of parafermions which allow for more computational power than Majorana bound states. The second project is an interdisciplinary effort to apply state-of-the-art Machine Learning algorithm for large-scale surface codes of many quantum bits. This approach promises algorithms which are more adaptable to different error models related to different physical realizations of quantum bits. Moreover, it promises a route to optimal or close-to-optimal strategies for error correction in non-abelian surface codes. The broader relevance of the proposed research comprises a multitude of technological applications for quantum computers, such as cryptography or highly effcient search algorithms. In recent years, global players such as IBM, Google, and Microsoft have heavily invested to press the physical realization of a quantum computer forward. For a country like Switzerland, where technological know-how is the most important asset, it is crucial to stay competitive and to remain at the forefront in the race for a quantum computer. As such, the proposed research addresses some of the most pressing problems in the field and provides approaches for new solutions.
Keywords: Condensed Matter Physics, Majorana bound states, Theoretical Physics, Topological Quantum Computation

Title: Metabolite discovery via a biosynthesis-aware chemical language model
Abstract:
Background: The metabolome, the complete set of small molecules within a biological sample, provides an important window into mammalian physiology. Dysregulation of the metabolome can drive disease processes and provide diagnostic or prognostic biomarkers. However, the ability to confidently identify metabolites remains a major bottleneck in contemporary metabolomics, with most data from metabolomic experiments going unused. This limitation leaves fundamental questions about mammalian metabolism unanswered and limits the wider impact of metabolomic technologies.

Aim: The proposed project aims to advance metabolite discovery by integrating in vivo biochemical experimentation (isotope tracing) and chemical artificial intelligence through two key steps:

Aim 1: Create a comprehensive atlas that tracks the incorporation of over a dozen biosynthetic precursors into metabolites across thousands of mouse metabolites.

Aim 2: Develop a biochemical language model trained on Aim 1 generated data. This model will predict metabolite structures from the biosynthetic precursors of each unidentified metabolite, thereby overcoming the current plateau in computational methods for mass spectrometry-based metabolomics.

Methods: Building on preliminary work, I will leverage isotope tracing with over a dozen isotopically labeled precursors infused into mice, coupled with untargeted metabolomics analysis across 23 tissues. This data will be used to define the biosynthetic precursors of every unidentified metabolite and integrate this information into a biochemical language model.

Outcome: I expect the integration of isotope tracing data with AI-driven models to markedly accelerate mammalian metabolite discovery, answer fundamental questions about the size and composition of the 'dark metabolome', and ultimately furnish new molecular biomarkers of disease.
Keywords: computational biology, machine learning, mass spectrometry, metabolism, metabolomics

Title: Man and Machine: When Consumers Collaborate with Autonomous Products
Abstract:
Groundbreaking advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics permit today’s everyday products to evolve into autonomous products, taking over tasks and making decisions on their own. Consumer perceptions of autonomous products mainly reveal two perspectives: On the one hand, people tend to reject autonomous products, for example, because they feel they are losing control or their job and thus feel replaced. On the other hand, people seem to bond with autonomous products—they collaborate with and even create nicknames for them, verbally integrating products into their social lives.

In my research I focus on the collaborative perspective of autonomous products and thus contribute to the pressing issue of how new technologies may coexist in a synergetic way with humans in the future. My primary objective is to improve the understanding of consumers’ perceptions of autonomous products. Based on this goal, two research projects will be carried out in collaboration with Prof. Dr. Stefano Puntoni from Rotterdam School of Management (RSM) at Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) within the SNSF Doc.Mobility fellowship. Specifically, we aim to explain the phenomenon of nicknaming autonomous products: The smarter and more autonomous products become, the more inclined consumers are to call them by a nickname. The CEO of iRobot estimated that 90% of Roomba owners use a nickname for their robotic vacuum cleaner (Vincent, 2018). In addition, companies are actively encouraging their customers to create a nickname for their autonomous products—for example, by inviting them to assign a nickname in the corresponding mobile application.

Despite these observations, we are not aware of any research that either examines the effects of nicknaming autonomous products (our research project I; target journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science) or explains the theory behind nicknaming objects (our research project II; target journal: Journal of Consumer Research). In two preliminary studies, we already demonstrated experimentally that nicknaming autonomous products can serve as a counter against fears commonly associated with autonomy and can thus increase usage intention. In addition, our initial results suggest that some products are more predestined to be given a nickname since product-related drivers exist; moreover, this leads to different types of names (categories). A series of studies conducted at RSM aims to quantitatively validate the preliminary findings and thereby investigate the main drivers that trigger nicknaming, as well as the resulting categories and consequences. The environment of the leading business school RSM with the Erasmus Behavioural Lab (EBL), and especially the close collaboration with Prof. Dr. Stefano Puntoni, a renowned expert in the field of consumer perception of new technologies, create the ideal match for the two research projects. Overall, the proposed research projects add to the literature on human-machine interaction, product innovation, and consumer behavior in the areas of autonomous technologies and naming. In particular, our findings will advance our understanding of the implications of autonomous products on the relationship between humans and products for consumers, firms, and society at large.

Title: Exploiting the full potential of Copernicus Sentinel data for countrywide tree species mapping
Abstract:
Precise and regularly updated information on the state and distribution of tree species, as well as changes over time, is frequently required over large spatial extents by the forestry sector and beyond, in particular for forest management, biodiversity assessments - especially in the context of a changing climate. This proposal is motivated by the increasing need for spatially explicit information on tree species composition by the realms listed above, yet existing research has focused on individual case studies rather than countrywide applications. Such nationwide assessments are particularly challenging but also interesting in alpine countries such as Switzerland, with its complex topography and heterogeneous, diverse and patchy forests. Up to now, no study has successfully addressed these challenging conditions overall, let alone attempted to optimize conditions to obtain better results. Forest inventories, e.g. the Swiss National Forest Inventory (NFI), provide a precise statistical estimation of tree species composition for large areas, e.g. for all of Switzerland, based on stratified samples, but spatially explicit information based on wall-to-wall assessments is missing. 
In this project, we will fill this gap and move from tree species classification on the case study level to analysis at the national level. Our goal is to develop a robust method to classify the nine most common tree species, that comprise 93% of all tree species, with an approx. spatial resolution of 10 m for the whole of Switzerland. This approach is based on innovative remote sensing techniques and freely available input data sets. It fully exploits the potential of multi-temporal remote sensing data using deep learning classification algorithms. It is specifically designed to cope with heterogeneous forests and is thus flexible regarding the choice of classification algorithm and economical regarding training data. The approach enables regular updates and future adaptions. We will benefit from a huge existing and continuously updated data set of training and reference data for tree species provided by national research, monitoring and inventory programs, such as the NFI, the experimental forest management project and the forest reserves network of Switzerland. Thus, cost-effective field work will be minimized and only required as independent reference data. To reach this goal, we will use time series data from the European Space Agency (ESA) Copernicus Sentinel missions (Sentinel-1 / -2), which are at the cutting edge of remote sensing technology and offer excellent opportunities to investigate tree species distribution at an unprecedented high spatial and temporal resolution. These data sets are complementary to the high spatial resolution aerial imagery and Airborne Laser Scanning (ALS) data available for the entire country, which are acquired within a six-year return interval.
We expect the research results to be widely used in scientific as well as practical applications, e.g. in forestry and nature conservation, and we will put a lot efforts on output that matches the needs of potential users. We believe that methodologically, our project will motivate other researchers to build on our approach and apply it to their specific needs.
Keywords: Sentinel-1/-2, biodiversity, classification, climate change, countrywide, deep learning, spatial explicit, time series, tree species

Title: Longitudinal analysis of the Neurocognitive Assessment in the Metabolic and Aging Cohort (NAMACO) study : Step 2
Abstract:
1.SUMMARY 
 
Applicant: Matthias Cavassini Co-applicant: Renaud Du Pasquier Partners: Katharine Darling, Catia Marzolini, Roger Kouyos, Laurent Decosterd, Cristina Granziera, Arseny Sokolov and the NAMACO Study Group*

Longitudinal analysis of the Neurocognitive Assessment in the Metabolic and Aging Cohort (NAMACO) study : Step 2 

1.SUMMARY
Neurocognitive impairment (NCI) in association with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) has been described since the beginning of the HIV epidemic. What has changed over the past three decades is how NCI is manifest. Prior to antiretroviral therapy (ART), uninhibited viral replication in the central nervous system and profound immune suppression led to severe, irreversible NCI in the form of HIV-associated dementia (HAD). Since the development of highly effective ART, HAD incidence is very low. However, as people with HIV (PWH) age on ART, milder, even asymptomatic, manifestations of NCI have been observed. As the population of older PWH grows, NCI represents an important potential health burden and the race is now on to identify the factors which predispose to NCI and influence its course.
Since its inception in 2013, the Neurocognitive Assessment in Metabolic and Aging Cohort (NAMACO) study, with 981 patients recruited from the Swiss HIV Cohort Study, has become one of the largest cohorts in the world set up to examine HIV-associated NCI. The date 2013 is critical as this is described in the literature as the era of modern ART: since 2013, the use of integrase inhibitors has increased and that of ART associated with toxic side effects, including efavirenz, has decreased. Baseline NAMACO study data (at recruitment) have enabled NCI prevalence in Switzerland to be quantified and important clinical questions have been addressed. NAMACO study participants have had a neurocognitive function assessment at two years post-recruitment and a four-year review is almost complete. During this period, much has changed in the NCI field: new terminology; a call for new definitions of NCI stage; and many, surprisingly fundamental, questions remain: how to diagnose NCI, how to treat and how to predict impairment course. In this time, NAMACO has become a high-profile acronym in the field and, with now a high-quality longitudinal database, the study represents a resource for promising collaborations within Switzerland and beyond. The current proposal describes Step 2 of the NAMACO study: the longitudinal analysis of NAMACO study participants, in which we aim to quantify NCI incidence over time and identify predictors of neurocognitive change. Specific aims are:
I. to determine the incidence and predictors of change in NCI among NAMACO study patients at four years post-recruitment
II. to investigate the effect of prescribed drugs with anticholinergic and/or sedative activity on neurocognitive function; 
III. to employ viral genome cluster analysis to examine the role of the virus in NCI aetiology;   
IV. to develop new deep-learning-based classification of NCI by integrating multicontrast MRI and brain-age information.
We believe that this next step will have several important outcomes. It will:
1.improve our understanding of the hitherto-neglected influence of non-ART drugs on NCI course;
2.highlight possible viral as well as host factors influencing NCI development and course;
3.identify novel radiological diagnostic techniques for predicting deterioration in neurocognitive function.
The overall aim of this proposal is to use the NAMACO study dataset to examine the longitudinal epidemiology of NCI and associated factors in a population of aging PWH. Our large and highly-characterised cohort population is a resource which will enable us to address matters of debate in the field of NCI, a field which is evolving in real-time.

Title: Mechanisms of Infection Variability in Virus Entry, Persistence and Egress
Abstract: The number of viruses on this planet is overwhelming and by far exceeds the number of cells and organisms. Yet, not every human being develops severe disease when exposed to viruses, as demonstrated by the ongoing SARS-CoV-2 pandemics. At the level of individuals, reasons for the highly variable susceptibility to viruses comprise genetic and nongenetic factors, such as human leucocyte antigen polymorphism in the major histocompatibility complex gene complex, infection history and preexisting immunity. In cells and organoids, mechanisms of infection variability can be explored at the mechanistic level. Here, we tackle infection variability by focussing on human adenovirus (AdV) species B and C, a DNA virus, which has been the subject of intense investigations in the Greber lab and elsewhere. Our overarching aim is to integrate biochemical, cell biological, genetic, metabolic and immunological approaches to obtain a better understanding of virus infection variability and persistence. AdV infect epithelial cells of the lung, eyes, kidney and intestines, and persist in immune cells. They cause sporadic and unpredictable, mostly local epidemic outbreaks. AdV vectors, classically derived from species C, are broadly used in gene therapy, and increasingly in disease prevention, e.g., vaccination against Ebola and COVID-19. Yet, the molecular mechanisms and variability of infection and persistence of natural AdV in immune cells have remained unresolved. We will scrutinize the process of viral entry before gene expression, followed by viral gene expression in the nucleus, in particular the immediate early promoter E1A, which is active in epithelial cells but not in immune cells. Important questions include, how does the virus sporadically derepress its master regulator, the E1A promoter, and what cellular conditions favor lytic or persistent infections? We take a cellular and molecular approach involving epithelial and immune cells. Part A) focusses on the processes of viral DNA delivery into the nucleus and misdelivery to the cytosol during virus entry. The former leads to infection, and the latter gives rise to innate immune response via cytoplasmic DNA sensors. Part B) explores infection variability of clonal cells in culture using an authentic live cell reporter AdV-C for E1A promoter activity. Part C) explores virus immune cell interactions, such as inducible human pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived macrophages, and human cultured and primary T cells, and asks the question how the virus establishes an immune-paralysed environment in these cells favoring persistence. Part D) investigates the rewiring of immune cells through genetic loops and sphingolipid and glucose metabolites in lytic and persistent infections, and Part E) zooms into the cellular and viral mechanisms of lytic egress from infected cells. Underpinning technology involves virus and host cell genetics, transcriptome, proteome and lipidome profiling of single and population cells, single-cell imaging with label-dependent and label-free microscopy, multiplexed cell marker analyses, computational modelling and machine-learning of infection phenotypes harnessing artificial intelligence. The latter will simplify the interpretation of complex processes, and help identify novel infection phenotypes. Together, this project explores the infection biology and distinct steps giving rise to infection variability of an abundant, clinically and therapeutically important DNA virus. It brings new insight into protective cellular networks with anti-viral functions in human epithelial cells and immune cells, and promises to reveal new connections between metabolism, viral persistence and lytic outbreak.

Title: Minimizing Surprise in Self-driving Vehicles
Abstract:
Transportation is at the dawn of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) revolution with self-driving vehicles that are ever advancing. While tremendous progress has been made in sensor design, data fusion, perception, and planning based on the well-defined driving rules, the current state of technology leads to unacceptable accidents mainly due to unexpected stops. Self-driving vehicles are not safe enough to effectively co-exist with human drivers in the open world and gain their trust.

Our project will enable self-driving vehicles to naturally fit in and follow unwritten but observable social conventions of human driving style. To achieve this ambitious goal, we propose empowering vehicles with the following paradigm: minimize surprise. From the AI perspective, surprise minimization refers to minimizing forecasting errors, uncertainty,  entropy, i.e., anticipating the behaviors of traffic participants.  From a human perspective, the actions taken by the self-driving vehicles should not `surprise’ the traffic participants (e.g., pedestrians, cyclists, other drivers) -- the actions should follow social etiquette.  We will go away from solving classification tasks and learn new representations that minimize surprise in the computational pipeline of a self-driving vehicle: perception, prediction, and planning. Such intelligence is essential to develop safe trustworthy and efficient self-driving vehicles.

On the theoretical side, we will push the limits of representation learning in the context of self-driving vehicles.   We  will  show  the  impact  of  learning representations that  minimize  surprise for multiple tasks jointly. We will demonstrate the impact of self-supervised learning as an auxilary task. We will propose new mathematical methods that model uncertainty and bring interpretability in data-driven methods. We will develop methods that jointly model multiple sequences and generate multimodal distributions. Our work aim to democratize trustworthy self-driving vehicles alongside humans.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Deep learning, Self-driving Vehicle

Title: Beauty of multiple leptons at LHCb
Abstract:
The Standard Model (SM) of particle physics is the most successful theory describing all known elementary particles and their interactions. There are two classes of SM particles of matter: quarks, which participate to the strong interaction and form hadrons; and leptons, which do not. Both participate to the weak interaction. 
The postulate of  lepton universality (LU) in the SM states that couplings of different leptons ($e,\mu,\tau$) to the mediators of the weak interaction are identical. 
In the recent years, this postulate has been challenged by a number of anomalies observed in weak decays of hadrons containing a b quark to final states involving leptons.
In particular, evidence for violation of LU was found in rates of B meson decays to a charm meson, one charged lepton $\ell$ (electron, muon or tau) and neutrino --  $b \to c \ell \nu$ transitions. 
This evidence, if confirmed, does not have an explanation within the SM and would revolutionise the fundamental physics, paving road to a discovery of a new fundamental interaction. 
The limitation in precision of the published studies comes both from theoretical and experimental sides. 
Theoretically, presence of hadrons in the final state involves low-energy strong-interaction dynamics which is difficult to calculate. 
Fully leptonic decays $\Bc \to \ell^+ \nu$, containing only leptons in the final state, are suited to overcome  theoretical limitations, retaining sensitivity to the probed physics interactions. 
However, experimentally, these decays are  challenging, as their visible final state consists of a sole charged lepton. As B_c mesons have spin 0, these two-body decays to leptons also suffer from helicity suppression in decay rate (~ $m^2_\ell/m^2_\Bc$) leading to very low rates for the case of light leptons. It is argued that measurement of $\Bc \to \ell^+ \nu$ is impossible at the current experiments and has to wait decades for a new electron-positron collider to be built. 

My proposal aims to study already now  fully leptonic B_c transitions by exploiting the  $\Bc \to \mu^+\mu^-\ell\nu$ decays. It was shown that decays  $B^+ \to \mu^+\mu^-\ell\nu$, where the extra pair of muons originates from the virtual photon radiation, allow to avoid challenges of a two-body decay. Similar arguments apply in case of the B_c meson. Rates of such processes are linked directly to the rates of the $B^+_{(c)} \to \ell^+ \nu$ decays. While the emission of a dimuon from photon radiation is a rare process, it lifts the helicity suppression of a two-body decay, making the decay rate large enough to be observed experimentally. Importantly, such decays provide a  special experimental signature of three charged leptons originating from a displaced vertex of a $B$-meson, which has rather low background at a hadron collider. First experimental observation of the decays of B^+ and B_c mesons to $ \mu^+ \mu^+ \mu^- \nu$, $e^+ \mu^+ \mu^- \nu$ and $ \tau^+ \mu^+ \mu^- \nu$ final states would allow to test the LU in a completely independent way and provide new constraints on  BSM contributions in the $b \to c \ell \nu$ transitions. 
Datasets recorded by the LHCb experiment at CERN in 2011-2018, and a larger one to be collected in 2023-2024, will be used. Modern data analysis tools based on machine learning techniques and detailed simulations will be used to distinguish processes of interest from  backgrounds. Dedicated calibration data samples will be employed to minimise the systematic uncertainty of the measurement. 

My project is separated in four streams, shared between the applicant and a PhD student. First, the trimuon final state is examined. With the full LHCb dataset, one expects observing the $B^+_{(c)} \to \mu^+\mu^-\mu^+\nu$ decays and measuring their rates with the world-best precision. This requires development of low-momentum muon identification}which will be beneficial for other measurements in the field. Second, the $e^+ \mu^+ \mu^- \nu$ final state is examined, providing a new test of LU. Third, the final state with the tau leptons is studied. 
Finally, work on LHCb detector optimisation for future Upgrades will be performed, to make it possible to study such challenging processes with a greater precision. 
My research will result in at least 3 journal publications based on experimental data and will become a highlight in conference talks.  Phenomenological publications joint with the theorists, reinterpreting experimental results, are also planned.
The principal physics results of this study will include: first observation of fully leptonic decays of the B_c meson and measurement of their rate, which will impose severe constraints on New Physics in $b \to c \ell \nu$ transitions; a principally independent kind of LU tests – the first  test of LU in fully leptonic $B_{(c)}^+$ decays; and extraction the nonperturbative decay parameters useful for theoretical description of any $B_{(c)}^+$ decays. This project will provide an independent test of the puzzle of flavour anomalies and help to clarify what is probably the most exciting deviation from the SM in the last decades.
Keywords: B meson, final-state radiation, flavour physics, lepton universality, rare decays, semileptonic decays

Title: Fate of Polymers in Recycled Asphalt: a Multiscale Approach
Abstract:
Nearly 170 million tons of asphalt mixtures were laid in pavement surface layers in Europe in 2020. Typically, these contain high-quality aggregates and polymer-modified bitumen (PMB). PMB improves the elastic response of bitumen, which in turn increases the resistance to permanent deformation and enhances the cracking performance and durability of asphalt mixtures. As road networks across Europe continue to mature and rehabilitation needs focus on the top layers, the amount of removed aged asphalt mixtures containing PMB and replaced with new mixtures is expected to steadily increase. The crushed material obtained when an asphalt mixture is removed is referred to as reclaimed asphalt pavement (RAP). Due to substantial economic and environmental benefits, there is a push toward using RAP. Unfortunately, RAP containing PMB is systematically downcycled into base layers and secondary applications because of the insufficient understanding of the interaction between aged and virgin PMB and concerns about the long-term performance of recycled asphalt mixtures. As a result, important performance-enhancing properties of RAP-containing PMB are currently underutilized. Therefore, there is an urgent need to gain valuable knowledge about these materials that are becoming more abundant.

One of the concerns with recycling PMB is whether the resulting blend of aged and virgin bitumen will exhibit the response required for performance and durability purposes. Research has shown that some polymers, particularly styrene-butadiene-styrene (SBS) —extensively used in PMB— experience thermo-oxidative breakdown of the molecular structure during service life. Breakdown of the polymer molecular structure can lead to aged PMB with a deficient elastic response and a more brittle behavior. To achieve a satisfactory initial response, a virgin PMB with greater polymer content or other additives may be necessary. More importantly, a satisfactory response is sought throughout the entire service life, so it is of paramount importance to evaluate the impact of aging on blends of aged and virgin PMB. Based on the available literature, no study has yet addressed this topic. Thus, it is critical to perform a fundamental investigation on the effect of aging on the long-term response of blends of aged and virgin PMB. Another concern beyond the interaction at the bitumen level is the presence of chunks of aggregate particles held together by aged bitumen (i.e., clusters) in RAP.
Large clusters hinder the mixing of RAP with virgin bitumen and aggregates, which may result in a non-uniform aggregate distribution within the mixture. Prior research at EMPA showed that clusters yield a deficient adhesion to the surrounding bitumen and aggregates, which introduces a potential source of crack initiation and failure. Also, a non-uniform particle distribution leads to a varying bitumen film thickness and differential properties around the aggregates, which adds another source of localized stress concentration and increases failure potential. Thus, it is evident that further research is needed to identify the acceptable cluster size and the key factors that contribute to the blending of RAP and virgin materials to promote sustainable homogeneous recycled asphalt mixtures.
The current state of research in the area of recycling RAP with PMB shows that a fundamental research is warranted to understand the effect of aging at the molecular level and transfer this knowledge to the macro level. This includes the long-term elastic response of bitumen blends, low and intermediate temperature cracking behavior, and the impact of RAP clusters on particle mixing, bitumen distribution, blending, interface adhesion and, ultimately, the performance of recycled mixtures containing PMB. 

Based on the understanding of the current state of research, the objectives of this project are:
1.To develop a fundamental chemical, morphological, and rheological understanding of the effect of aging and blending of the polymer-bitumen system and the long-term response of blends of aged and virgin PMB (nano- and micro-scale).
2.To investigate the impact of RAP clusters on bitumen distribution, blending, and interfacial adhesion within recycled surface mixtures with PMB (meso- and macro-scale).
3.To determine the relationship between material properties at different scales using machine learning (nano- to macro- scale).

This project will advance the fundamental understanding of ways to recycle asphalt in surface layers for major roads in three main ways: 
•We will determine to what extent the polymer remains active in the reclaimed asphalt and what measures should be implemented to guarantee a similar performance to virgin polymer-modified mixtures. 
•We will determine the most important factors that affect the blending of aged and virgin binders and the effect that blending has on long-term asphalt performance. This can provide the scientific basis needed for designing mixtures with RAP containing PMB.
•We will establish relationships between the multiple scales of the materials using theory-guided machine-learning techniques. 

Three research institutions will work on this project, including Empa in Switzerland, Vienna University of Technology in Austria, and the University of Antwerp in Belgium. The research teams will each address one main topic while closely collaborating, exchanging information, and visiting each other for research stays.
Keywords: asphalt, bitumen, machine-learning, pavement, recycling

Title: Single-Shot Label-Free Imaging using Optical Diffraction Tomography
Abstract: We propose to develop an imaging method that can capture in a single shot sufficient information about the index or absorption distribution of a moving object to reconstruct its 3D shape with temporal resolution in the range of 10-100 microseconds. We combine an optimization inverse scattering algorithm we refer to as Learning Tomography (LT) and neural networks. The proposed research is based on the recent demonstration that LT provides high resolution reconstructions with only four projections for a monolayer of cells instead of hundreds typically used in the direct inversion tomography reconstruction methods. We aim to demonstrate that this remarkable property of LT combined with compressive sampling and neural network processing makes it possible to use the information recorded on a single frame of a high speed camera (CCD or CMOS) to produce high fidelity 3D images. We will demonstrate our technique in an optofluidic platform where the flow of droplets, cells, and other particles will be imaged at very high speed to obtain detailed 3D spatial information.
Keywords: deep learning, holography, microscopy, neural networks, optical diffraction tomography, single-shot imaging, structured illumination

Title: Enabling a high-accuracy and comfortable speech restoration, through neural network-governed conformable wireless sensor networks and deep learning-based biosignals processing
Abstract:
Humans’ ability to communicate stands at the core of our development and livelihood. Yet, making full use of this unique tool continues to remain a challenge for many of us. Recent hardware and software advancements have led to the development of multiple technologies aimed at improving our ability to communicate. However, most solutions’ accuracy is often limited by the low quality of the data input they rely upon, and they are often limited to tackling the verbal elements of human communication, leaving aside non-verbal cues, despite their being known to convey a significant amount of content.

At the same time, attempts to maximize the data input often generate an uncomfortable user experience, due to the need to use multiple sensing devices placed over the user’s skin, and wire them in order to cater for high-energy, real-time transmissions. Moreover, most systems take a single-human approach, choosing to optimize for an intermediary output, rather than the overall quality of the communication process, that by nature involves multiple individuals.

During my postdoctoral fellowship, we aim to investigate the opportunity of developing a biosignal-based communication system capable of performing a real-time, highly accurate translation of mechanoacoustic vibrations and electrical signals into verbal and non-verbal (emotional state, level of fatigue and engagement) communication content, while providing a comfortable, wireless user experience. We aim to achieve this by combining state-of the-art sensing devices into a wireless sensor network, whose communication will be coordinated by a dedicated, AI-enhanced communication protocol. The system will leverage biosignal processing units which rely on deep neural networks to attain state-of-the art processing accuracies of both verbal, and nonverbal biosignals. Moreover, we aim to test our system with multiple individuals engaged in the communication process, thus optimizing for the overall quality of the communication, as well as exploring the potential of enhancing socio-cognitive functions, such as co-creativity and the ability to collaborate.

One of my scientific contributions to the project will go in the direction of creating a dedicated, AI-enhanced communication system that will govern the wireless sensor network in a way that allows it to convey the highest amount of information needed for a high accuracy processing, while intelligently managing the network’s bandwidth and energy resources, to achieve a real-time, very low energy communication. Its ability to manage this complex task will rely on the novel idea of using machine learning techniques to customize the communication protocol’s functional parameters (e.g., node priority in using the channel, maximum attempts of packet retransmissions, length of packet bursts, etc.) to the needs of the application data traffic, thus achieving an optimal energy consumption and latency, without compromising on accuracy. As a second step, the system will integrate dynamic feedback from the unit in charge of content processing, to achieve an even deeper customization of the protocol to the system’s performance needs.

We expect these contributions to significantly advance the prospect of a high-accuracy, seamless biosignal-based communication, as well as other applications aimed at corroborating biosignal data acquired through spatially distributed sensor nodes. We also hope my work on this project to open the way for a new generation of AI-based communication protocols. Such protocols could have a very broad area of applicability, enhancing the potential use of WSNs in numerous applications governed by high traffic volumes and stringent resource constraints, including the one of Wireless Peripheral Nervous Systems.

But beyond the mentioned impact of the project, we hope our research will significantly advance the area of technology-enhanced communication, not only in terms of accuracy, but also through a meaningful exploitation of non-verbal cues and their role in multi-human socio-cognitive processes, such as co-creativity and collaboration.
Keywords: Adaptive communication protocols, Data-driven protocol design, Medium Access Control, Neural networks, Socio-cognitive functions, Wireless Sensor Networks

Title: Striatal serotonin-dopamine interplay underlying addiction-like behavior.
Abstract:
Background & Rationale:
From simple associative learning to pathological compulsion, behavioral adaptations are orchestrated by the striatum's serotonin (5-HT) and dopamine (DA) signaling. DA's role in reward learning and addiction-related synaptic plasticity is well documented. By contrast, the rules governing 5-HT’s modulation of striatal plasticity remain poorly understood. Emerging evidence suggests that serotonin opposes DA-driven compulsive behaviors by altering synaptic plasticity thresholds, yet the underlying cellular mechanisms and behavioral consequences have not been defined.  

Hypothesis:
Serotonin and dopamine jointly determine the induction rules for bidirectional synaptic plasticity in striatal medium spiny neurons (MSNs). By modulating these rules, 5-HT can reverse DA-mediated pathological plasticity and compulsive drug-seeking.  

Objectives & Specific Aims: 
1. Characterize striatal 5-HT and DA dynamics in vivo.
   - Measure spontaneous “oscillations” of extracellular 5-HT and DA in nucleus accumbens (NAc), dorsal striatum (DS), and ventral tegmental area (VTA) using dual-color GRAB sensors and fiber photometry.  
   - Determine temporal relationships, cross-correlations, and stimulus-induced synchronization.  
   - Identify cellular origins via miniscope calcium imaging in DRN and VTA, combined with retrograde tracing and single-cell transcriptomics.  

2. Define receptor-specific effects of 5-HT on striatal synaptic plasticity ex vivo.  
   - Map expression of presynaptic 5-HT1B and postsynaptic 5-HT2A/C receptors in D1R- and D2R-MSNs using spatial transcriptomics.  
   - Quantify how 5-HT receptor activation shifts induction thresholds for long-term potentiation (LTP) and depression (LTD) under high vs. low DA tone using optogenetic stimulation of orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) inputs and whole-cell patch clamp.  
   - Test projection- and cell-type–specific receptor deletions to confirm causality.  

3. Link 5-HT oscillations, synaptic plasticity, and compulsive behavior.  
   - Correlate high-density behavioral features (markerless pose estimation) with 5-HT transients in naïve and compulsive mice undergoing optogenetic DA self-stimulation (oDASS) or cocaine self-administration.  
   - Manipulate 5-HT release temporally (optogenetic stimulation/inhibition) and pharmacologically (selective 5-HT2A/C agonists/antagonists) during identified behavioral epochs to test reversal of drug-evoked synaptic potentiation and compulsion.  
   - Validate findings in cocaine and fentanyl models.  

Methodological Innovation: 
- Dual-color, genetically encoded sensors for simultaneous, real-time measurement of DA and 5-HT dynamics in freely moving mice  
- Cellular-resolution mini scope imaging to reveal population synchrony driving neuromodulator oscillations  
- Projection-specific optogenetics combined with slice electrophysiology to map plasticity induction rules  
- Advanced behavioral clustering (UMAP + hierarchical clustering) to pinpoint action sequences linked to neuromodulator events  

Preliminary Data & Feasibility: 
The Lüscher lab has demonstrated 5-HT1B receptor gating of OFC-DS plasticity, reducing cocaine compulsion (Li et al., Science 2021). Preliminary fiber photometry confirms independent, spontaneous DA and 5-HT oscillations; optogenetic DA stimulation elevates DA without affecting 5-HT. Single-cell transcriptomics identifies key 5-HT receptor expression patterns.  

Impact:  
This project addresses a fundamental gap in neuroscience—defining serotonin’s role in striatal plasticity and compulsion. Results will elucidate mechanisms underlying addiction vulnerability, inform non-addictive therapeutic strategies (e.g., SSRIs, psychedelics), and identify receptor- and

Title: Conceiving, developing and representing a conversational-actor agent - Acting paradigm and theatrical dialog
Abstract:
A conversational agent is a computer application, which strives to imitate the interactions of a dialog with a human being. In the wake of research on artificial intelligence, many agents are currently in use or under development. Yet, performing arts seized this tool very little, even though, historically, theatre is a practice centred on the fact of saying a text. This project aims to conceive, develop and represent a conversational agent on the model of an actor improvising from a text. Using a precise and time-tested acting technique, following some active analysis, we suggest a team of actors and computer scientists work together on the modelling of the behaviour of an actor while he is acting, in order to convert it in an algorithmic translation, relayed to a conversational agent.

Inherited from an exercise by Stanislavski, active analysis involves, for an actor, to redial (redesign) a theatrical text he does not know yet word-for-word: having an incomplete knowledge of the text, he acts by fragments, sometimes with his own words. The method, which may apply on very different texts, supplies furthermore quite a few practical tools, which allow, at least in part, an algorithmic translation. We suggest an iterative process, consisting in a passing of the tools of active analysis to computer scientists, a development of a test conversational agent and a dialog of actors with this agent, in order to conceive, step by step, an actor which would be a conversational agent.

The algorithmic translation is achieved in AIML language: in a XML syntax, it allows the formalization of key words (or group of words) which, once they are detected by the agent in the entry of the user-viewer, produce a fixed answer, possibly in the given context of a discussion, linked to previous exchanges. In the paradigm of functional programming (and no longer procedural programming), the AIML language enables to work, on the one hand, on a symbolic reduction in language (collecting the different ways of saying the same thing) and on the other hand to formalise acting dynamics specific to the actor, such as the management of different situations (contexts) and of tools of active analysis which allow to recompose the text by fragments.
The project proposes furthermore the development of an interaction device (of a dialog), in writing, with the conversational agent, via existing messaging systems (SMS, Messenger, WhatsApp, etc.). This device will be accessible to all. Each of these interactions (conversations) can be considered as a different interpretation of the reference text. All these interpretations (completed simultaneously by the conversational agent, with different user- viewers) can then be represented on stage, in front of a collectively assembled public. Here, we shall ask actors to act as different user-viewers, live (thanks to a headset transmitting the text that needs to be said), in confrontation with the conversational agent, acting as itself with the help of a voice synthesis.

This project, deliberately thought of as being interdisciplinary, wishes to shift the paradigms of the conception of a AI, thanks to the acting tools specific to theatre. The aim is to create a tension on stage between the presence of an actor and an artificial presence.
Keywords: acting, active-analysis, artificial intelligence, conversational agent, dialog

Title: Measuring Posture and Physical In-/Activity to Assess Occupational Sedentary Behaviour
Abstract:
Rational – Sedentary Behaviour (SB) is defined as sitting or reclining with an energy expenditure =1.5 metabolic equivalent (MET). It is among the most frequent human behaviour and in question to cause a plethora of serious chronic lifestyle diseases and premature deaths. Office workers, in particular, are at an increased risk because of their sedentary work. The use of active workplaces is therefore recommended, although we lack evidence whether they have an impact on human health due to inconsistent and non-objective SB measurements. Most evidence for the detrimental health effects of SB is based on self-reports and on device-based methods calibrated to measure posture. Accordingly, we lack evidence whether the activity component of SB (=1.5 MET) is of relevance. Thus, there is a need to develop an objective method to measure posture and activity consistent with the SB definition.
Preliminary Work – We first-ever developed three objective methods to measure posture and activity simultaneously. All methods use a 3-level approach to 1) separate stationary and ambulatory activities, 2) classify posture into sitting and standing, and 3) classify the activity of each posture (inactive =1.5 MET, active >1.5 MET). Accordingly, the methods classify the physical behaviour into five categories: inactive sitting, active sitting, inactive standing, active standing, and walking. The time spent inactive sitting is considered sedentary. All methods have a cross-validated balanced sensitivity and specificity to detect the five behaviours =82.6%, and =82.9% to detect SB.
Objective - The primary aim of the research stay abroad is to analyse the concurrent validity of the two most suitable and accurate self-developed methods in an independent, free-living office worker population.
Research Methods – Based on a sample size calculation, 47 office workers with access to sit-stand desks are recruited. Participants will be equipped with the sensors of the two new methods and the reference criteria for posture (ActivPAL, PAL Technologies, Glasgow, SCO) and activity (indirect calorimetry; K5, COSMED, Rome, ITA). The study records the participants usual desk based office work for two hours, with the allowance of a short break to limit the inconveniences with the facemask of the K5.
For the new methods, the self-developed algorithms are used to create the minute-by-minute behaviour classification. For the reference criteria, each minute is assigned to the most dominant ActivPAL category (sitting, standing, or stepping). Sitting and standing minutes are subsequently classified as inactive (=1.5 MET) or active (>1.5 MET) using the K5 data. Over the entire recordings, methods are compared with Bland-Altman statistics to analyse bias and limit of agreement. A bias <4 minutes is considered highly valid. On a minute-by-minute level, sensitivity and specificity are used. To inspect the validity of the new methods to detect short, medium and long bouts, the sensitivity and specificity analysis is repeated for bouts =5, 6-20, >20 minutes. 
Expected Results – The study will show the free-living concurrent validity of two new methods to measure posture and activity while desk based office work, on a minute-by-minute level as well as for different bout length and over the entire recordings.
Implications – Our 3-level methods are the first that consider both aspects of SB simultaneously: posture and activity. We strongly believe that this approach becomes useful for future studies aiming to analyse the relevance of the activity component of SB, and studies aiming to decrease occupational SB. In the long term, such studies contribute to the development of evidence-based health recommendations for office work.

Title: The Swiss Robotic Disaster Recovery Challenge - Towards versatile robotic locomotion and manipulation
Abstract:
There is agreement in the international research community that it is only a matter of “when” robots will become part of normal human life, and not a matter of “if” robotic technology will ever achieve this stage. Being part of this robotics revolution has reached priority in many countries, e.g., in Switzerland with the National Center of Competence in Research (NCCR) Robotics, in the USA with the National Robotics Initiative, in Europe as a whole due to the Robotics Funding in the European Commission, and in Japan and Korea as a continued effort that started more than 10 years ago. The vision is that robots will assist us in daily life in many scenarios, e.g., in elder care, special needs education, physical therapy, in hospitals, in homes, in space exploration, in hazardous environments, etc. The different tasks and environments for robots will also differentiate the skills they need, as for instance, a home robot will be smaller, less strong, and designed to operate in rather structured human domains, while a robot for outdoor exploration needs to be stronger and deal with complex unstructured, dynamic, and stochastic environments.
In this proposal, we address the latter case and consider disaster relief as the scenario in which such an outdoors robot should be able to operate. Current robotic technology is rather limited in face of unstructured and dynamic environments. However, mobile robots such as humanoids and quadrupeds will change this fact in near future: We envision a new kind of robots that learn to manipulate, to run, and to climb, and that can reach or even surpass human and animal performance in complex natural and human environments.
The tasks which we will investigate fundamentally involve using hands, arms and legs and the whole body in dynamic contact with the environment. Our research aims at robots that will have enough in- telligence, autonomy and learning abilities to fulfill indoor and outdoor tasks with minimum human intervention for several hours.
In order to achieve this goal, our research focuses on achieving robust, dynamic, agile and autonomous robotic control in unstructured environments by means of model based control, force and impedance control, and applied machine learning, with applications to legged locomotion, grasping, field and rescue robotics, prosthetics and bio-inspired robotics.
The technology will be evaluated in a challenge we set ourselves: “The Swiss Robotic Disaster Recovery Challenge”.
This short proposal outlines two PhD research projects that will advance the state of the art in the aforementioned topics: (A) Autonomous control of dynamic locomotion in unstructured terrain, (B) Learning and control of full-body compliant mobile manipulation.
Keywords: Autonomous Robots, control and planning, learning control, locomotion, manipulation, rescue robots, service robots

Title: Artificial intelligence-enabled deep protein fusions
Abstract:
With recent advances in deep learning (DL), some of the most challenging problems in protein science now appear computationally solvable, including protein structure prediction. DL has also been applied to protein scaffolding: Given a desired functional site (FS) structure, the algorithm generates a protein sequence that it predicts will fold to have the desired FS. RFDiffusion, the state-of-the-art algorithm currently, predicted scaffolds for 23 out of 25 benchmark motifs and 5 out of 5 enzyme active sites, as independently assessed by Alphafold2. There is a wide-spread need for such a technology in biology.

Protein fusions, also known as chimeras, are routinely engineered across biology whenever two coding sequences are concatenated. Such tandem fusions are extremely useful and include simple tagging with fluorescent proteins or localization signals as well as intricate sensors such as GCaMP. However, many fusion attempts fail. Many proteins are highly sensitive to tags, sometimes at both N- and C-termini. Even trickier are fusions created to control a protein of interest by domain insertion, also known as domain grafts. Researchers wish to insert light- or chemical-controlled domains into proteins to control signaling or metabolic pathways. However, current approaches can involve a substantial amount of trial-and-error testing. The unreliability of existing approaches is further illustrated by cases where the control logic is inexplicably flipped (light ‘on’ led to more, not less activity). Across biology, a broad variety of protein fusions are needed, as well as better methods for making them.

We propose to apply DL-based scaffolding to create fusions. In brief, we will take two FSs and create scaffolds for the fusion protein. We will validate the DL-generated protein sequences extensively in silico. We will then test DL-generated proteins directly in budding yeast.
Keywords: bioengineering, budding yeast, cell cycle, cell growth, deep learning, diffusion models, directed evolution, quantitative biology, scaffolding, synthetic biology

Title: Enhanced Code Review: Using Context and Learning from Review Experience
Abstract:
Most of today’s industries, from engineering to agriculture to health, are run on software, giving every software defect potentially dramatic and often public consequences. Manual peer code review is widely recognized as most effective at detecting software defects and improving software quality: Several studies showed that properly conducted code reviews support software quality and reliability crucially. Properly doing code reviews, though, requires expensive developer time and zeal: If a reviewer races through a review, only shallow problems and trivial errors are recognized, with the additional risk of generating a false sense of safety.

My goal is to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of code review effort by leveraging context and learning from review experience. The vision and scientific aim at the basis of this proposal are two-fold: (1) To derive a deep understanding of context concerning code review tasks and leverage it to create new models, algorithms, and techniques to enhance automated cognitive support and (2) to modeling code changes as integral components to understanding and automating the code review process as a whole, to learn and transfer review experience.
Achieving our goal and its underlying scientific aim would lead to a significant impact on software engineering research and practice: It will break new ground on reifying and leveraging context for software development, it will advance machine learning models of code by learning to relate code changes to external context, code review statements, and projects as a whole, and it will support practitioners reducing software defects, speeding up the development cycle, and improving overall maintainability and reliability of software systems.
Keywords: code change classification, code inspection, empirical software engineering, mining software repositories, peer code review, software analytics, software metrics

Title: Search for the Neutrinoless Double-Beta Decay with LEGEND
Abstract:
If neutrinos are their own antiparticles - known as Majorana fermions - then an ultra-rare nuclear decay process, the neutrinoless double beta (0?ßß) decay, becomes possible. This process violates lepton number conservation by two units. Detecting 0?ßß-decay would be a groundbreaking discovery and a definite proof of physics beyond the Standard Model. The experimental signature of 0?ßß-decay is a mono-energetic peak at the Q-value of the decay. Various techniques and isotopes are used to search for this phenomenon, with leading constraints on the half-life coming from experiments using the isotopes 76-Ge, 100-Mo, 130-Te, and 136-Xe.  We are involved in the  LEGEND-200 experiment and its successor, the ton-scale LEGEND-1000 project. These  aim to discover the 0?ßß-decay of 76-Ge using high-purity Ge (HPGe) crystals enriched in 76-Ge. The detectors are operated in a liquid argon (LAr) cryostat deep underground at the Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso (LNGS) in Italy.  

The first LEGEND-200 science run took place from March 2023 to February 2024, accumulating an exposure of 76.2\,kg\,y. Data corresponding to an exposure of 61.0\,kg\,y were unblinded, yielding a half-life sensitivity of T1/2> 0.8 x 10^26 y. A combined analysis with the precursor GERDA and Majorana Demonstrator  resulted in a median sensitivity of T1/2 > 2.8 x 10^26 y and a lower limit of T1/2 > 2.0 x 10^26 y (90\% C.L.). These results are included in the first LEGEND-200 publication, which is in collaboration review. 

The background level was  2-3 times higher than expected based on measured material activities and Monte Carlo simulations. This discrepancy prompted  a series of upgrades to identify and mitigate the background sources.  Meanwhile, HPGe detector production is ongoing, aiming to reach the planned 200 kg of detectors for LEGEND-200. A new detector deployment took place in early 2025, with the science run set to begin in April 2025. The next phase, LEGEND-1000, is in advanced preparation stage, with initial construction starting this year and expected to continue until 2030. Due to its modular design, the first set of detectors is scheduled to begin operation by late 2029, while the full-scale data collection is planned to start in 2033.

We are key members of the LEGEND collaboration, with responsibilities spanning detector characterization, calibration, analysis, and R&D. Our key contributions include: Designing, constructing, and operating the systems for source insertion and calibration; analyzing weekly calibration runs and comparing results with Monte Carlo simulations; measuring neutron and gamma fluxes from low-neutron emission calibration sources using our dedicated low-background LiI(Eu) and HPGe detectors, operated underground at LNGS; constructing wavelength-shifting reflectors for the liquid argon veto and conducting R&D for LEGEND-1000; coordinating the production and characterization of new inverted-coaxial detectors for the experiment. We also play a significant role in data analysis, including: Investigating background spectra from the HPGe detectors; the Bayesian analysis for the 0?ßß-decay search; conducting various additional searches for physics beyond the Standard Model; developing machine learning-driven waveform analysis, pulse shape simulations for background modeling, and pulse shape discrimination techniques. At UZH, we operate a small liquid argon detector and a HPGe detector. These are used for R&D purposes and serve as an ideal training ground for bachelor, master, and PhD students.

Title: Interactive, Interpretable and Cost-Effective Machine Learning
Abstract:
Interactive machine learning (IML) is a modern machine learning paradigm of significant theoretical and practical interest, where the learning system and the environment engage in a two-way conversation to collaboratively obtain useful information. It captures a broad range of sequential decision problems arising in pattern recognition and related fields, including adaptive sensing, optimal control, intelligent tutoring, automated diagnostics, and active vision systems, etc. As humans play an intrinsic role in the learning process, it is of crucial importance to develop robust models that not only are predictive and cost-effective, but also yield interpretable insights along with the interaction.

Interactive machine learning has attracted increasing interest in the research community in recent years. However, there is much less work on interpretable IML models: The theory community have developed principled algorithms with performance guarantees for the classical interactive machine learning problems (e.g., active learning), where algorithms only focus on which data instances it wants labeled for training, regardless of the interpretability; in applied domains, as models get more complex in the quest for predictive accuracy, they become more akin to “black boxes” that reveal little intuition regarding why the models make certain predictions. Due to the lack of understanding of existing practical ad hoc systems, it becomes ever more challenging to devise systematic avenues for improvement.

In this project, we will pursue the fundamentals of interactive, interpretable and cost-effective machine learning, with the goal of “bridging the gap” between theory and practice, by reformulating the existing interactive framework to accommodate human interpretability. One way to ensure interpretability of a model is to incorporate explanations. We propose a unified framework that formalizes how IML can expand to include explanations: Different from existing work in the active learning literature which builds purely upon the ?data instance, label? pairs, we explore a novel interactive protocol, involving the tuple ?data instance, label, explanation of the label? per interaction. The benefit of having an additional degree of expressiveness in the feedback is bidirectional, depending on the initiative of the interaction: at training time, the human teacher may provide informative justification to guide the learning process; at run time, the learning system can generate intuitive explanations of its output to enhance model interpretability. However, adding explanations increases the complexity of the learning problem by an order of magnitude. This is a significant technical challenge that no existing theory can capture. In this project, we will investigate both aspects, and build on recent advances from active learning, structured prediction, and machine teaching, in order to develop new, principled and tractable approaches towards practical IML systems.

Concretely, we will explore the interactive learning protocol through the following interconnecting threads:

1. Develop new active learning algorithms to deal with complex, structured hypotheses by learning from explanatory feedback, such as justification of the corrective feedback, or human demonstration;

2. Design novel, dynamically interpretable IML models that interact with human through interpretable predictions at run-time, as opposed to existing offline, “statically interpretable” models which have to trade off model complexity (/accuracy) for human interpretability;

3. Build and evaluate the IML algorithms in real-world applications, including interactive text and image categorization, and active causal inference.
Keywords: Approximation Algorithms, Causality, Interactive Machine Learning, Interpretable Models, Sequential Decision Making, Structured Prediction

Title: Copula Distributions in Machine Learning: Models, Inference and Applications
Abstract:
In the last years, copula models have become popular tools for modeling multivariate data. The underlying idea is to separate the "pure" dependency between random variables from the influence of the marginals. The main focus of research, however, was on parametric (and most often bivariate) copulas in econometrics applications, and only recently "truly" multivariate copula constructions have been considered. Finding principled ways of building these constructions, however, is commonly considered as a hard problem. The machine learning field was largely unaffected by these developments, despite the fact that inferring the dependency structure in high-dimensional data is one of the most fundamental problems in machine learning. On the other hand, machine learners have developed a rich repertoire of methods for structure learning, and exactly these methods have the potential to make copula constructions useful in real-world settings with noisy and partially missing observations. It is, thus, not surprising that there is a constantly increasing number of machine learning publications which aim at using structure learning methods for copula-based inference. 

In general, however, the use of copulas in machine learning has been restricted to density estimation problems based either on Gaussian copulas, or on aggregating standard bivariate pair copulas, while other directions such as clustering, multi-view learning, compression and dynamical models have not been explored in this context.    

In this proposal we will try to close this gap by focusing on clustering, on the connection to information theory (which will also include a connection to dynamical systems), and on finding new ways for using non-parametric pair copulas. From an application point of view, the study of such models is interesting, because inferring hidden structure is presumably one of the most successful applications of machine learning methods in domains generating massive and noise-affected data volumes, such as molecular biology. The precise separation of "dependency" and "marginals" in copula models bears the potential to overcome limitations of current techniques, be it too restrictive distributional assumptions or model selection problems.      

Our proposal is divided into four work-packages which address the following questions:
1) How can copulas be linked to information theory, and what    consequences will this link have on modeling dynamical systems? 
On the application side, these questions are  motivated by studying time-resolved gene expression data and node-ranking problems in gene networks.
2) How can copulas be used for deriving flexible cluster models that can model arbitrary marginals and are robust to noise, missing values  and outliers? The motivation comes from a mixed continuous/discrete dataset containing multi-channel EEG recordings and clinical measurements. 
3) How can we use copulas for simultaneously learning network structures and detecting "key modules" in these networks given external relevance information? Our interest in this question comes from analyzing gene expression data and the aim to detect subnetworks based on clinical variables.
4) How can we use empirical pair copulas  in network learning? The motivation stems from our experience that the problem of selecting "suitable" pair copulas has no obvious solution in practice.   

In the proposed project, we plan to answer these questions,  thereby pushing the state-of-the-art in machine learning problems involving copula distributions.
Keywords: Copula distributions, Graphical models, Information theory, Machine learning

Title: Measuring How Language Models Learn Reuseable Computational Structures
Abstract:
Background — Large language models (LLMs) excel across a range of domains, yet how their internal structure gives rise to both successes and failure modes remains poorly understood. While interpretability work has made progress identifying specific circuits and recurring mechanisms (reused structures), it is still unclear when and why such mechanisms emerge. At the same time, theoretical studies offer insights into expressivity and learning dynamics but often lack tools to isolate internal mechanisms. These complementary lines of work have yet to converge: few frameworks exist that connect mechanistic findings to theory and describe under which data, architectural, or training conditions reusable mechanisms emerge. Broad causal comparisons across tasks and models are rare and existing approaches remain largely correlational.
  
Aims — This project aims to close this gap by establishing a principled framework for measuring mechanistic similarity between internal computations of language models. The first goal is to develop causal, intervention-based similarity measures that allow for precise comparisons of mechanisms within and across models and tasks. These tools will extend existing interpretability methods and enable the identification of reusable computational structures. The second goal is to use these measures to reveal how reusable mechanisms form, under which conditions they arise, and how they vary across architectures and training setups, to generate new insights into the learnability of model internal structure in LLMs.

Methods — We will develop tools for comparing internal mechanisms in language models via causal interventions based on circuit analysis, sparse feature extraction, and targeted interventions. The focus will be on Transformers, including both large scale open-weight pretrained models  and small models trained from scratch. Our experiments will use structured synthetic tasks that support clean, interpretable solutions. We will define causal mechanistic similarity by testing whether there exist some components that produce the same precise change in behavior under targeted interventions. The resulting measures will be applied in systematic studies to track how model size, data diversity, or architecture affect the emergence and reuse of mechanisms for synthetic tasks that have counterparts in large models.

Expected Results — We will develop and release formal definitions, empirical procedures, and implementations for mechanistic similarity, enabling experiments that probe internal computation beyond performance metrics. Applying these tools to simple models trained on joint and diverse tasks will allow us to test fundamental hypotheses about computational reuse and modularity. Thereby, we will improve our understanding of whether and how different data distributions and architectural choices encourage the emergence of general-purpose primitives rather than brittle, task-specific solutions.

Impact — This project addresses a major gap in interpretability research by enabling systematic comparisons of internal model structure. Advancing the understanding of reusable computations will directly support principled model design, improve transparency, and contribute to safer, more reliable AI. More broadly, the tools and findings offer a concrete step toward understanding structured computation in artificial systems, with potential relevance to neuroscience, cognitive science, and dynamical systems.
Keywords: interpretability, machine learning theory, neural networks
