Title: Analysing individual differences and arithmetic problem solving through educational data mining
Abstract:
Understanding mathematical concepts is an essential life skill. To better teach these concepts to children, it is important to have a deeper understanding of their learning process. A valuable approach to understanding how children learn is through educational data mining (Romero & Ventura, 2010, 2013). This approach of data analysis relies on advanced statistical techniques to analyse complex and rich educational datasets and can be particularly helpful in identifying the challenges faced by children while learning. One of the particularly challenging aspects of learning mathematical concepts for children is solving arithmetic word problems. On this specific topic, the Semantic Congruence (SECO) model (Gros et al., 2020) has been developed to account for the difficulties children encounter by describing the different paths and steps that need to be taken to find a solution. Based on this model, an app called Adaptiv’Math has been developed to provide concrete support for children. In addition to helping students learn complex skills, this app can provide researchers with information on the individual differences in strategy use and on children’s learning paths that follow. Identifying these individual differences is crucial, as it can assist teachers in providing targeted support for specific difficulties children face (Dowker, 2005).
The current project aims to leverage educational data mining techniques to test existing theories of learning mechanisms and fill gaps in the understanding of their functioning, specifically in the domain of arithmetic word problem solving. The project has three main goals. The first one is to assess the validity of the Adaptiv’Math app framework by analysing the effect of the app usage on the improvement of students’ performance. The second one is to identify individual differences in the way children learn and in the difficulties they encounter. The last goal is to predict early on the improvement in performance of each child. This is crucial to quickly determine and address the individual needs of students. Together, these goals will allow us to better understand how children learn and the challenges they face to better support their progress.
To achieve these objectives, the existing dataset collected via the above mentioned app will be analysed. This dataset contains data for each child and each performed exercise. The data of approximately 800 children aged between 6 and 9 years old using the app have already been collected in France and these data will be completed with the ones of over 2000 children from several regions around the world before the beginning of the current project. Educational data mining techniques including machine learning algorithms will be used for the analyses. More precisely, multi-level analysis, clustering and prediction analyses will be utilized.
Regarding the results, we first expect the app to have a significant impact on performance improvement. Concerning the second aim, we expect to find individual differences depending on children’s flexibility in changing strategies and performing calculations, leading to different difficulties among children. Finally, we expect to be able to predict early on which children will improve and the type of difficulties they will encounter.
This research project will help us gain a better understanding of how children learn mathematics, which can directly impact educational practices. More precisely, this study will enable us to gain insights into individual differences, providing a clearer understanding of the process involved in tasks such as arithmetic problem solving. Furthermore, early detection of potential challenges faced by children through predictive analyses is central to targeting and addressing difficulties early enough. Finally, assessing the efficacy of the app and the validity of the framework could directly impact teaching as the app is already available for use.
Keywords: Arithmetic word problems, Educational Data Mining, Learning, Mathematical Cognition

Title: Intermolecular Interactions and the Role of Dynamics for Chemical Reactions in Complex Systems
Abstract: The goal of this project is to develop, implement and apply computational strategies to characterize, understand and eventually predict properties of complex chemical and biochemical systems at a molecular level. To this end, techniques including multipolar force fields, (adiabatic) reactive molecular dynamics and neural network-based potential energy surfaces are further developed and used. Multipole force fields will be extended to treat general spectroscopic applications (1- and 2-dimensional infrared spectroscopy), using fluctuating multipoles and describing the energetics of the nuclear degrees of freedom with reproducing kernels. Applications include spectroscopic probes such as -CO, -NO and -N3 for which accurate, fully dimensional potential energy surfaces can be calculated. This will be used to characterize the site-specific dynamics and functional motions of proteins such as insulin, lysozyme, myoglobin and nitrophorin in solution. For insulin, analysis of motions at the dimerization interface will be used to quantify the physiologically relevant monomer/dimer equilibrium which is difficult to do with experimentally established, thermodynamic approaches. To account for vibrational coherences, partial linearized density matrix (PLDM) propagation will be generalized for vibrational dynamics (vPLDM). Nitrosylation of nitrophorin will investigate molecular determinants of NO-signaling in a protein. To study chemical reactions in the gas phase we will use machine learning within the PhysNet neural network architecture to generate fully-dimensional, reactive potential energy surfaces. Here, applications focus on systems relevant to atmospheric chemistry, including isomerization and decomposition reactions of acetaldehyde and pyruvic acid for which fragmentation patterns and final state distributions are important for subsequent reactions. In a next step, PhysNet will be used to investigate double proton transfer in the gas phase and in solution with the aim to characterize the role of solvent in chemical reactions at a molecular level. The present proposal involves two research themes: 1) reactive simulations in the gas- and condensed phase and 2) computational vibrational spectroscopy which both require accurate representations of the intermolecular interactions.

Title: Phenomics and evolution of sexual dimorphism and female colour polymorphism in damselflies
Abstract:
Sexual conflict, arising from antagonistic selection between the sexes and from shared intersexual genetic architecture, can lead to the formation of stable and heritable phenotypic polymorphisms within natural populations. During over 100 years of ecological and evolutionary research, the study of polymorphisms (e. g. colour polymorphisms) has helped to improve our understanding of phenotypic diversification in nature. Many polymorphisms are characterized by a multitude of phenotypic differences in colouration, behavior and morphology as a result of correlational selection, linkage and pleiotropic effects of genes underlying such polymorphisms. Polymorphisms are typically expected to be maintained within local populations by evolutionary processes, such as negative frequency-dependent selection. Yet there are only few studies that have quantified multiple axes of correlated phenotypic variation in addition to colour, which limits our current understanding of the emergence and evolutionary maintenance of genetic colour polymorphisms. 
To address this long standing issue, I here propose a series of research projects that use computer-driven high throughput phenotyping to conduct comprehensive phenotypic analyses (phenomics) of a sexual dimorphism and female-limited colour polymorphisms in damselflies (Odonata; Zygoptera). The overarching goal of these projects is to investigate if and how much female damselfly colour morphs that mimic male colouration to increase their fitness (androchrome females) also vary in other, potentially correlated phenotypic traits, such as morphology, behavior and development. I will investigate such morph differences both within and between populations of a single species and in a broader macroevolutionary context across a large molecular time-calibrated phylogeny of pond damselflies (superfamily Coenagrioniodea).  
This research will be carried out in a collaboration with Prof. Erik Svensson at Lund University, who is an internationally leading expert on phenotypic evolution, sexual selection and female-limited colour polymorphisms. His laboratory has expertise in many analytical techniques appropriate to this project and has 20 years of research experience and expertise on damselfly colour polymorphisms and their evolutionary dynamics in natural populations. First, I will analyze an existing image data set from a long-term population study that has generated evolutionary time series data of Swedish damselfly populations. I will use a combination of classic computer vision and deep learning algorithms to quantify axes of phenotypic variation that have not yet been investigated in this study system. Second, I will conduct a mesocosm experiment using individuals from the same local Swedish damselfly populations to investigate whether androchrome females show alternative developmental trajectories. Finally, I will conduct in-depth phenotyping of an existing image dataset of different damselfly species to investigate the prevalence of androchromatism and male mimicry in other traits across a large damselfly phylogeny. 
The project will close existing knowledge gaps in this important study system and will provide us with a deeper understanding about how sexual dimorphisms in general and female limited polymorphisms specifically might drive phenotypic diversification in nature. The work also follows a longstanding call for a phenomics research programme, and will help to remove image analysis as a longstanding and time-consuming bottleneck in ecological and evolutionary research. Conducting this project in the excellent research environment at Lund University will be an essential step for me to become an independent scientist at the intersection of ecology, evolution, and computer science.

Abstract: Reduced-Order Models (ROMs) serve as cost-effective approximations to full-order models, such as high-fidelity simulations or experiments, and are particularly valuable for multi-objective applications. Despite their advantages, state-of-the-art  ROM strategies often fall short when applied to industry-grade  dynamical systems  due to the presence of significant nonlinearities, multi-physics and multi-scales . As a result, the optimisation of such systems typically relies on trial-and-error approaches or crude models with large uncertainties, which limit design confidence. The typical barrier to incorporating ROMs from model reduction techniques into the design protocol is their lack of interpretability, predictability and generalisability. Indeed, while powerful, typical models from machine-learning provide black-box type models that are not explainable and hence are hard to certify in an industrial environment. Furthermore, existing data-driven ROMs tend to lose their predictive power over longer time horizons. In addition, they  do not generalise well when applied even slightly outside their training domain.  All these lacking features of typical ROMS would nevertheless be critically needed for applications in control and optimisation. In this multidisciplinary project, we seek to improve the state of the art by developing generalisable and predictive ROMs for a wide range of data-driven techniques, from purely data-driven to fully physics-based approaches. Furthermore, by rigorously testing the resulting reduction strategies in industrial-scale applications for control and model identification purposes, we will establish much needed performance comparisons on a range of use cases. This will aid academic and industrial practitioners in their choice of ROM strategies.

Title: Sustaining Knowledge Creation in Online Communities: Enabling, Creating, and Maintaining
Abstract:
Online communities play an increasingly important role in how organizations collaborate and leverage talent across geographic locations. Today in the face of COVID-19 pandemic, as organizations rapidly move their daily operations online, this form of organizing is of ever-increasing relevance even for the most traditional organizations who are forced to adapt rapidly to online collaborations. This project aims to further understanding on how knowledge creation is sustained in online communities that operate in the absence of formal hierarchy and closed organizational boundaries (e.g. Dahlander & Frederiksen, 2012; Faraj et al., 2016; Gulati, Puranam, & Tushman, 2012; von Hippel & von Krogh, 2003; O’Mahony & Ferraro, 2007; Puranam, Alexy, & Reitzig, 2014). We address this emerging question in organization science by examining how online communities organize and coordinate three phases of community activity essential to sustainable knowledge creation (von Hippel & von Krogh, 2003). These phases refer to (a) establishing, nurturing and shaping generative spaces where knowledge flows through new modes of sociality via digital technologies (Faraj et al., 2016), (b) remaining productive in the established generative space in terms of continuous generation of creative ideas (Faraj et al., 2011) and reaching timely consensus on them, and (c) maintaining the generative space with effective resilience against tensions in the form of disputes (He et al., 2020) and membership flows (Butler et al., 2014; Ransbotham & Kane, 2011; von Krogh & von Hippel, 2006).

Advancement and survival of online communities depend on continuous and active contributions by communities’ members. Prior work has argued that such continuity in the activity of online communities requires establishing spaces that ensure unfettered knowledge flows (Daniel & Stewart, 2016; Faraj et al., 2016; Haefliger et al., 2011), continuous generation of creative ideas and consensus over them (Faraj et al., 2011), and ability to maintain the generative space with resilience to disputes (He et al., 2020) and membership flows (Butler et al., 2014; Ransbotham & Kane, 2011). However, openness of organizational boundaries and lack of formal hierarchy pose challenges for organizing and sustaining knowledge creation, reaching a consensus among the community, and resilience to membership flows. Answers to questions such as how online communities maintain the flow of knowledge, how community generates creative ideas and reaches a consensus on them, how disputes are resolved, and how organizational resilience to membership flows emerge are critical for sustainability of online communities. In this project, we aim to answer these questions and expand current understanding of online communities and organization science applied to this phenomenon, by addressing mechanisms for organizing and sustaining knowledge creation within such communities. In doing so, our project aims to contribute specifically to the literatures on organizational knowledge creation, organizational design, and new forms of organizing, as well as the literature about online communities in particular.

We shall conduct our empirical investigation in the context of online communities involved in software development (GitHub), community question answering (Stack Overflow) and music making (BandLab, Soundslates, LoopLabs, and Soundtrap). Extensive archival records on these communities provide transparent and time-stamped data on project and member characteristics, and offer complete digital traces of activities. This provides unique opportunities to examine our research questions related to online communities. Title: Multimodal Clinical Data AI-based Integration for Clinical Research Eligibility Surveillance
Abstract: Clinical research is crucial to allow progress with clinical care, to establish disease characteristics, treatment, and prevention solutions: today’s clinical research is tomorrow’s medicine. Unfortunately, an important proportion of clinical research trials fail to meet patient enrollment goals, resulting in failed trials with wasted investigators’ time and research funding, and exposing patients to risks without offering scientific insight. To improve patient enrollment in clinical trials and address the aforementioned gaps, we propose ground-breaking work building on our previous efforts to capture eligibility criteria from clinical trial protocols, to extract the corresponding clinical information from EHR narratives and ECG tracings, and to match trials with eligible patients automatically. We hypothesize that an automated process based on artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms including natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning can detect patients potentially eligible for a clinical trial to then notify researchers, clinicians caring for the patient, and the patients themselves.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Clinical research, Clinical trial eligibility, Natural Language Processing

Title: Automated Inference of Network Algorithms
Abstract:
After several decades of relative stagnation, the algorithms used for communication over the Internet are now evolving rapidly. A significant driver of this change is the consolidation of control in the hands of a small number of content providers like Google and Netflix. Google, for instance, by virtue of owning the most popular Web browser, as well as several of the most popular Web services, exercises unprecedented control over how networking operates for its services: it can independently make the needed changes for deploying new networking algorithms both at its Web servers and at end users’ devices via its browser, Chrome. Similarly, Netflix users watch movies using Netflix’s code running on both user devices and Netflix servers. This code includes obfuscated algorithms that adapt the video quality to each user’s network conditions – if the network provides high bandwidth, video can be watched at higher quality; if the network conditions deteriorate, video quality can be dynamically lowered. Netflix and other such services can evolve this logic independently, without the knowledge of users and network operators.

The lack of visibility into these network algorithms is inherently problematic: this implies that network operators and researchers no longer understand the logic that governs large fractions of Internet traffic. Researchers cannot reason about the behavior of different Internet services competing for shared network resources. While developing and analyzing new networking algorithms is an extremely active research area, recent work in this direction, e.g., on the type of adaptive video algorithms Netflix uses, does not even compare its results to Netflix or YouTube’s operational systems, because of their opaque nature. We also cannot analyze why such traffic on the Internet interacts fairly or unfairly with other Internet traffic. Likewise, the interaction of network operators’ traffic engineering and shaping mechanisms on such services is only understood to a limited extent via empirical, blackbox measurements.

The goal of this work is to explore methods to automatically infer network algorithms by observing their behavior under controlled manipulation of network conditions. Our objective is not to merely obtain blackboxes that can also emulate this behavior, for example, using machine learning, but rather to recover these algorithms in a human-interpretable form, opening them up to further research and analysis. As a first application, we intend to apply this approach to video services like YouTube to unveil their adaptive video logic and compare it to several recently proposed algorithms for the same problem.

Title: Representation Learning for Clinical Artificial Intelligence
Abstract:
When developing clinical treatment plans for patients, especially for difficult or previously unseen conditions, medical practitioners often rely on experience made with comparable cases either from their own past experience or described in the scientific literature. An important goal in medical informatics is supporting decision making by identifying the literature, the patients that have similar characteristics and the procedures, treatments or laboratory tests that are relevant in the context of a specific patient. In spite of the growing volume of available medical journals and digitized patient records, this often turns out to be a challenging task. Finding reference cases requires methods to summarize, model and search large-scale collections of heterogeneous medical information. This data is typically highly diverse and multi-modal, including physiological measurements, drug prescriptions, procedures, unstructured clinical notes (text) and to an increasing extent, also genetic information. 

This project aims to develop deep machine learning technologies to summarize and interpret this data, empowering medical experts to extract meaning from big medical datasets and biomedical publications. Due to the prevalence of textual resources in electronic health records, we put a special focus on this modality and develop a range of multi-lingual tools for natural language processing. We will demonstrate the effectiveness and flexibility of our methods on the example of three key applications that are relevant in a medical context: 1) Semantically informed document retrieval, 2) Inferring patient dynamics, and 3) Outcome prediction for patient episodes.

In this way, the technology developed in the course of this project will facilitate everyday medical practice as well as clinical research beyond their current, perceived limitations, leading to the development of new treatments, and, ultimately, improved patient well-being.
Keywords: Clinical Decision Support, Deep Learning, Information Retrieval, Medical Data Science, Multi Linguality

Title: Cosmological Weak Lensing and Neutral Hydrogen
Abstract:
Cosmology has undergone very significant progress in the last few decades. Developments in survey instruments have now established the standard LCDM model for cosmology. In spite of the success of this model for fitting observations on large scales, its establishment have opened a number of fundamental questions. These include the nature of Dark Matter and Dark Energy, two mysterious components of the Universe which together make up about 75% of the energy density of the Universe today. Other questions pertain to the initial conditions in the early universe and the nature of gravity on large cosmological scales. Together these problems pose some of the most pressing questions in fundamental physics today. 

To shed light on these questions, several cosmological probes are used and combined to place constraints on the standard cosmological model and its extensions. In particular, weak gravitational lensing has a special role in cosmology as it allows us to map the Dark Matter in the universe and can yield tight constraints on the properties of Dark Energy. It is based on the measurement of the shapes of background galaxies which are distorted due to mass inhomogeneities along the line-of-sight. Another very promising probe is the mapping of the distribution of neutral hydrogen in the universe using the redshifted 21 cm line in the radio band. Using the intensity mapping technique, this probe promises to bridge the gap between the measurements at high redshift from the Cosmic Microwave Background and the low redshift measurement of large scale structures with galaxy surveys in the visible bands.

In this research programme, we propose to develop and these probes to a new level using the extensive forward modelling methods developed in our group. These developments will then be applied to state-of-the art experiments, namely the Dark Energy Survey (DES), the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope (LSST) and the Hydrogen Intensity and Real-time Analysis eXperiment (HIRAX). Our group has an extensive experience in weak lensing measurements, forward modelling, advanced statistical methods, machine learning, and software development. Our group is also currently building the digital correlator for the HIRAX experiment through an associated FLARE SNF funded grant.

This research programme is organised into three synergistic sub-projects which will each be led by a junior researcher. In the first subproject, the junior researcher will extend the forward modelling pipeline we have developed for earlier DES data sets and will apply it to the final DES Year 6 data release. The needed multi-exposure analysis will be important to prepare for and analyse the first data sets of the upcoming LSST experiment. In a second subproject, another junior researcher will develop non-gaussian statistical measures and run the associated simulations for the weak lensing analysis of DES Year 6 and then LSST. A third subproject lead by another junior researcher will consist in adapting our forward modelling tool to the mapping of neutral hydrogen with HIRAX and use it for the analysis of the first data sets from this experiment.

The proposed research programme will have impact not only scientifically, but also for the junior researchers involved, and for the maximisation of the return for several experiments.

Title: Multiscale relationships between forest structures, saproxylic diversity, deadwood decay and carbon cycle in a changing world (MULTIFORDECA)
Abstract:
Globally, forests are pivotal for biodiversity, provide a wide variety of ecosystem services and play a critical role in the cycles of water and carbon. Deadwood plays an important role in all of these aspects, and its role will further increase in importance due to anthropogenic climate change and the goal of achieving net zero emissions in the foreseeable future. It is expected that the amount
of deadwood in forest ecosystems will increase, driven by an increased frequency and intensity of disturbances and by the implementation of biodiversity conservation measures. This will have a profound effect on (1) the composition and diversity of decomposer communities, (2) the residence time of deadwood, and (3) the residence time of carbon in wood and soil organic matter. However, predictions about the strength and direction of these interactions are difficult due to a lack of empirical studies. To fill
this gap, this project focuses on deadwood dynamics in forests, making use of a long-term set of forest inventory and species diversity data across Switzerland covering the most important central European forest types from lowland to high-elevation forests.

We aim at providing a holistic assessment of deadwood dynamics by considering the interplay between abiotic and biotic variables related to climate, management, forest structure and deadwood related, i.e. saproxylic, organisms. As the relevant processes act at different spatial scales, we will analyze the relationships at multiple scales, i.e. from the plot to the landscape.

The project comprises four closely interlinked Work Packages: WP 1 aims at improving our knowledge of the relationship between forest structure and deadwood as well as saproxylic biodiversity from the plot to the landscape scale using state of the art remote sensing technology, Machine Learning methods and a detailed assessment of organisms. In WP 2, deadwood dynamics will be modeled focusing on its temporal variability and decay rates. WP 3 follows the fate of deadwood carbon in soil organic matter and
its contribution to C storage and turnover combining soil fractionation, novel triple isotope techniques and radiocarbon based approaches. WP 4 assesses (i) the role of macro- and microorganisms in wood decay using cutting-edge molecular methods, (ii) synthesizes the functional links and temporal trajectories between decomposers, decomposition and the carbon cycle in relation to climate and management, (iii) synthesizes direct and indirect links between forest structure, saproxylic organisms and ecosystem processes, and (iv) provides an upscaling of the locally derived data sets with a functional and conservation-based focus.

The integration of forest inventory, soil and saproxylic species datasets, top notch remote sensing methods, detailed complementary and innovative field studies, and cutting-edge modelling will provide novel scientific insights on the current and future dynamics of deadwood, the hotspots of functional diversity and species of conservation concern, as well as the deadwood related carbon cycle
and storage of deadwood-carbon in soils.

Title: Mining Goodreads: a text similarity-based approach to measure reader absorption
Abstract:
Over the last decades, with technological advancements, growing digitalization and the development of social media, the act of reading has transformed into a more social interaction (Cordon Garcia, Alonso Arevalo, Gomez Diaz, & Linder, 2013; Merga, 2015), or rather has returned to its once social origins (Nation, 2018). Social media platforms like Goodreads are online environments where millions of people come to share their love for the written word. Members come together to discuss what they read, what they classify as good or bad literature, and they recommend books to one another or even try their hand at writing fan fiction. Thus, in the digital age the act of reading, which has since the latter half of the 18th century been construed as a mostly solitary, immersive act, has started to involve a social component that goes far beyond that of a real-life book club or public poetry reading. First of all, because of the scale on which this takes place and second because of the new opportunities that online platforms offer in terms of social interactions. 
This project focuses on the growing phenomenon of online social reading. It is an exploratory study that exploits a new data source and develops new methodologies. Goodreads holds a wealth of qualitative data about reading experience, text evaluation, and social interactions about reading. It would take an experimental researcher an entire career to gather and analyze even just a fraction of the data that is readily available on this website. So far, this treasure trove of data has not been empirically investigated, and this is partly due to the fact that new methodologies have to be developed to extract the data from the website in a meaningful way. This is exactly the gap that our project aims to fill. In order to investigate meaningful ways in which such a reader review corpus might then be used, we are also developing computational linguistics methods to mine the extracted corpus with a specific reader response in mind, namely absorption – the feeling of being lost in a book (Nell, 1988; Kuijpers, 2014). By analyzing reader reviews on Goodreads using textual entailment and text reuse detection (methods from computational linguistics) and comparing them to statements on the Story World Absorption Scale (SWAS; Kuijpers, Hakemulder, Tan & Doicaru, 2014), we will investigate: (1) the potential of converting Goodreads into an extensive qualitative corpus for the computational analyses of reader responses; (2) the validation of the SWAS through comparison with reviews on Goodreads; and (3) the comparison of readers’ absorption across different genres. It is important to study these online social reading phenomena, as they are becoming exceedingly popular and provide new ways for people of all ages to acquire storytelling and literacy skills (Coiro, Knobel, Lankshear, & Leu, 2014). The potential impact of this project is widespread as it will construct a new corpus of interest to researchers from different fields and develop methodologies that can be fine-tuned to be used on various other online corpora that are made up of natural language.
Keywords: Goodreads, Natural Language Processing, Online Social Reading, Reader reviews, Story World Absorption, Text Mining, Text reuse detection, Textual Entailment

Title: Towards semi-personalized (cluster) medicine with the optimal osteoporotic fracture prediction: artificial intelligence- or current human- based models? The OsteoLaus Project
Abstract:
Osteoporosis is a major public health issue expected to become even more important in the next decades with population aging, which is specifically truer for Switzerland. Clinical consequences of osteoporosis are fragility fractures. Hip fractures are the most serious, associated with a significant increase in death and institutionalization. Although much effort has been made in recent years to improve fracture risk detection and patient management, we are still missing about 30-50% of atraumatic fractures, and are lacking a more precise individual information to better manage patients.
OsteoLaus, a population-based cohort of Swiss postmenopausal women, is by far the only Swiss study with comprehensive data on bone health. Its continuation up to a follow-up period of ten years is of major importance for the validation of the calibration (predicted versus observed) of the current used fracture prediction tool, FRAX, in the Swiss clinics. Moreover, the extension of the follow-up period enables us to study occurrences and associations with a greater power.
Using two large population based cohort followed prospectively (OsteoLaus and Rotterdam cohorts totalizing more than 8,300 individuals), we aim at developing a new fracture model based on artificial intelligence (Machine learning - ML) for fracture prediction. This model will include the best fracture predicting variables (chosen from more than 600 parameters available in both studies) with the hypothesis that it will upgrade fracture prediction to a more specific and complex-but-sophisticated level. The ML approach we are suggesting to use will `teach` us which individual`s risk factors profile corresponds to a certain risk profile. In this way, individuals will be clustered based on their risk profile as defined by their risk factors; and therefore be managed/treated based on their profile. 
Given the economic and social burden of fractures and their incidence, it is a need in the field to provide information on the cost effectiveness (CE) of any suggestive method/tool to be included in the osteoporosis management. Therefore, we will compare the newest AI approach with the most currently used fracture model (FRAX) in terms of clinical costs, personal costs and cost effectiveness performance. In this way, we can provide a full information and decision-making strategy for the actual implementation of our results in clinical practice.

Title: Development of a high-throughput approach for efficient  pharmacotherapy assignment in locally-advanced breast cancer patients.
Abstract:
The proposed research plan is aimed to the development and implementation of a revolutionary methodology that will allow efficient and personalized chemotherapy treatment allocation of breast-cancer patients. Our approach will make use of a unique technical platform developed and validated in the laboratory of Dr. Andrews at the Sunnybrook Research Institute termed as MultiChrome-dye based Multiparametric assessment by Machine learning of cells imaged by High-Content Screening (3M-HCS). This platform allows automated high throughput imaging of hundreds of drug combinations on isolated primary cancer cells using non-toxic dyes, followed by classification of cellular features by the in-house developed software Phindr3D and determination of the cell fate (e.g apoptosis, senescence, necrosis, autophagy).
In this project we will use biopsies  collected from locally-advanced breast cancer patients prior to chemotherapy to create 2D and 3D organoid preparations in GMP-grade defined extracellular matrix and will optimize their conditional reprogramming using cytokine/inhibitor cocktails. Critical milestones at this stage will be 1) increased fraction of reprogrammed disaggregated cells, 2) organoids must recapitulate the main features (determined by a validated antibody panel) of the original tumor without undergoing significant cocktail-induced endoplasmic reticulum stress, 3) rapid growth in reprogramming media, 4) cells should stop dividing but remain viable after removal of ROCK inhibitor from the cocktail. The optimal reprogramming organoid condition will be used to build a chemo-response panel using FDA-approved as well as experimental drugs that will be tested as single agents or used in a combinatorial manner. The chemoresponse measured in the 3M-HCS will be retrospectively contrasted with the actual clinical patient response to determine the predictive value and specificity of the methodology. This working pipeline will provide validation of the whole process (sample handling, reprogramming protocol, imaging etc.), leading to the establishment of standardized operational protocols   that will be used in a future phase-1 clinical trial currently being planned at the host institution. In addition, our 3M-HCS results will be contrasted with an experimental cutting-edge quantitative ultrasound spectroscopy developed and performed by a partner lab from the host institution.
The proposed research aims to solve one of the current bottlenecks of cancer treatment: the discrimination of patients into responders and non-responders to standard chemotherapy regimen. This ab initio classification, based on its speed and expected accuracy, will enhance the quality of life for patients while reducing the economic burden and suffering to non-responsive individuals. Moreover, the high-throughput processing capacity of the 3M-HCS will enable the discovery of alternative and/or unexpected combinations of drugs currently available in the pharmacopeia, thus expanding clinician’s toolbox to manage cases refractory to standard chemotherapy with the consequent impact in their survival.
Keywords: Breast cancer, Cell death, Chemotherapy, Conditional reprogramming, High-Content Screening, Organoids

Title: TinyTrainer: On-chip Training for TinyML devices
Abstract: The TinyTrainer project aims at closing the gap between training and inference of ML systems at the edge, ultimately enabling training on TinyML, MCU-class devices with a power budget of a few mW. In the TinyTrainer project, we tackle the on-tiny-device training challenge with a three-pronged approach. First, we will develop inference accelerators to execute high-quality feature extractors, implemented as DNNs heavily hardware-optimised through aggressive quantisation. Second, we will drastically curtail the computational and storage requirements of backpropagation-based training by leveraging continual learning algorithms and latent reply strategies; we will also develop non-backpropagation-based and few-shot learning strategies for ML systems that can be trained on-chip. Third, we will explore techniques to trigger the on-chip training of small and energy-efficient machine learning systems composed of pre-trained, “upstream” feature extractors and hardware-efficient, “downstream” components. TinyTrainer aims at full-stack development and demonstration: algorithms and architectures will be assessed on silicon prototypes designed during the project and fabricated using advanced CMOS technology nodes.
Keywords: Energy-efficient hardware, Internet-of-things, Machine learning, On-chip training

Title: Predicting outcome after stroke: take a look at the other side
Abstract:
Despite improvements in primary prophylaxis and acute recanalization treatments, stroke remains one of the leading causes of death and disability worldwide. In order to achieve the best outcome possible for the individual patient, therapies have to be administered rapidly. However, the longer the time from symptom onset, the lower the efficacy and the higher the risk of treatment side effects. Although brain imaging is the mainstay of acute stroke diagnostics, current imaging strategies that aim to predict therapeutic success or failure in acute stroke patients remain insufficient. 
Here, we propose a novel prediction approach that is based on immediate and long-term vascular adaptations affecting the contralateral side of stroke. From data obtained through animal models of stroke and imaging in patients with proximal vessel occlusions, contralateral cerebral blood flow (CBF) appears to be particularly suited to predict clinical benefit from recanalization therapies. Contralateral CBF and related perfusion parameters may indicate the ability of the individual to withstand longer durations of ischemia. 
In the experimental part of the project, we will use a thrombin-injection stroke model that does not artificially impact collateral supply. Reperfusion will be achieved through intravenous injection of recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rtPA). To assess CBF and ischemic tissue damage, repeated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) combined with positron emission tomography (PET) will be performed during ischemia, after reperfusion and in the chronic phase of stroke along with behavioral assessments. In the same stroke model, processes influencing CBF on the microvascular level will be directly observed using advanced optical imaging methods. Structural adaptations of the microvascular bed as well as gene and protein expression profiles contralateral to stroke will be analyzed in brain samples. 
In the clinical part of the project, we will analyze stroke patient imaging data in relation to clinical outcome. In addition to a traditional region-of interest (ROI) based analysis we will apply a novel, “unbiased” machine learning algorithm to extract relevant outcome predictors from patient imaging data.
Using a translational approach we aim for a mechanistic characterization of the concept of contralateral flow changes in stroke, and will generate and apply imaging predictors to clinical patient data. With the multidisciplinary study proposed here, I envision i) to deepen the understanding of the basic mechanisms regulating brain perfusion after ischemic stroke, and ii) to improve therapeutic decision-making in acute stroke patients.
Keywords: neuroimaging, outcome prediction, stroke

Title: Sustainable Natural Language Processing for Low-Resource Language Variations
Abstract: Addressing the complexities of language diversity is a big challenge in the field of natural language processing. Despite considerable strides in research, the predominant focus remains on written English and a select few widely spoken languages, driven by data availability and researcher familiarity. However, this limited scope fails to encompass the breadth of linguistic diversity documented globally. Working with languages with scarcer data availability presents multifaceted challenges, further compounded when addressing non-standardized dialects. This project endeavors to navigate the intricacies of non-standardized dialects and low-resource language varieties, spanning the entire NLP pipeline. From data acquisition to methodological development and evaluation, each stage confronts distinct obstacles when engaging with these linguistic nuances. Central inquiries revolve around how to enhance the robustness of natural language models to accommodate diverse language varieties and how to make them useful within low-resource language communities. Through comprehensive exploration and innovative methodologies, this endeavor seeks to advance the inclusivity and efficacy of NLP technologies on a global scale.
Keywords: computational linguistics, dialects, language technology, language varieties and dialects, low-resource, machine learning, natural language processing, neural networks

Title: Physics of multicellular cooperativity: a data-oriented principles approach
Abstract:
This project establishes a data-driven biophysical framework to decode the fundamental principles governing multicellular organisation and function. By bridging statistical physics, applied mathematics, and developmental biology, the project investigates how collections of cells achieve coordinated behaviour through mechanical and biochemical interactions. Recent advances in live microscopy and biophysical manipulation techniques now allow us to investigate these questions with unprecedented precision, allowing for quantitative mapping of cellular dynamics and tissue-scale phenomena.
The research program is built on three interconnected objectives that together build a comprehensive understanding of mechanochemical coordination in tissue morphogenesis. The first objective focuses on the mechanical basis of nuclear positioning during early embryogenesis, using the insect syncytial blastoderm as a model system. By combining hydrodynamic theory with high-resolution imaging data from Drosophila, Tribolium, and Gryllus embryos, the research aims to understand how nuclear density and dynamics couples to cell cycle dynamics. This investigation employs advanced nuclear tracking and velocimetry analysis, alongside geometric analysis of nuclear-driven pseudo-cytoplasmic domains. A key theoretical contribution based on this system would be the development of a hydrodynamic theory for active oscillatory nematics, complemented by model-based inference of nuclear interactions from geometric and motion data of the nuclei .The second objective examines cellular coordination through biochemical wave propagation, with specific application to mammary gland function. This work develops a normal form theory of oscillatory waves coupled to active hydraulics, analysing calcium wave propagation in mammary gland organoids. The research utilizes super-resolution microscopy to investigate the role of cell-cell junctions and employs data-driven discovery methods to identify governing equations. This approach provides insights into how cells communicate across large distances through oscillatory biochemical activity and how these signals couple to mechanical outcomes. The final objective presents an innovative approach to integrate tissue mechanics with spatial transcriptomics in Drosophila notum development. This comprehensive analysis combines quantitative morphometry analysis of approximately one million data points with spatial transcriptomics data covering 7000 genes across 2.7 million combined datapoints. The investigation employs physics-aware machine learning approaches for causality inference and develops generalised hydrodynamic descriptions that can be extended to various geometries and developmental contexts.
The methodological framework combines statistical inference, bifurcation theory and normal form analysis for wave dynamics, hydrodynamic theory for collective cellular behaviour, and physics-aware machine learning for mechanogenomic integration. This interdisciplinary approach enables the extraction of general physical principles directly from biological data, providing insights that span from molecular to tissue scales.
The project's findings will significantly contribute to understanding developmental robustness and pathology, by establishing quantitative frameworks for analysing cellular collective behaviour.
Keywords: biophysics, deep learning, morphogenesis, organogenesis, oscillations, soft matter physics, tissue dynamics

Title: Learning under near-ignorance: models and methods
Abstract:
Can a rational agent learn about a domain from data starting in a condition of ignorance? Addressing this question is important because it is often desirable to start analyzing a problem with very weak initial assumptions, thus trying to implement an objective-minded approach to learning and inference. This question has been most thoroughly investigated so far within the well-established Bayesian learning theory. In this case, ignorance is modeled by a so-called noninformative prior distribution (e.g., a flat one); data are summarized by a likelihood model. Posterior inferences (e.g., predictions, hypothesis testing, etc.) are obtained from the prior and the likelihood by Bayes' rule.

The use of a single - albeit noninformative - prior as a model of ignorance has been criticized by several authors. A more compelling alternative, in our opinion, relies on using a set M of priors that generate lower (\lpr) and upper (\upr) expectations s.t. \lpr(g)=\inf_x g(x) and \upr(g)=\sup_x g(x) for suitable functions of interest g. This expresses very faithfully that one's expectations about g are totally vacuous, which is a clear state of ignorance. These models have been first suggested in [walley, 1991] with the name of "near-ignorance priors". These have been successfully applied to classification problems: by naturally leading to indeterminate (i.e., set-valued) predictions, when the information from data is not enough to draw stronger conclusions, they originate very credible and reliable models. However, in some cases near-ignorance originates also the fundamental problem [piatti et al., 2007] to make learning from data impossible: the set of posteriors may coincide again with the set of priors. This amounts to making data useless, which is clearly a serious issue.

To tackle this problem, we have established some general principles that should govern a well-defined learning process based on near-ignorance, and have specialized them for the case of the one-parameter exponential family. Then we have proved that there is a unique set of priors that complies with these principles, and hence that guarantees both near-ignorance and learning to be attained. We have also shown that the obtained set of priors  reduces to other already known models of prior near-ignorance and thus, indirectly, proven the uniqueness of these models.  Moreover, we have derived new models of near-ignorance that were not available before. We regard these results as a basic stepping stone to properly answer the initial question. This seminal work should now be deepened and extended to fully tackle the question of learning under near-ignorance, and to make it closer to applications. We plan to do this according to the following tasks.
- Extension to the multivariate exponential family: this extension is fundamental as the most  important applications are based on it; this is for instance the case of regression analysis.
- Linear regression: to employ the multivariate model to develop new robust linear regression algorithms. Linear regression is an important area of data analysis, where near-ignorance can provide a leading approach for reliable inference.
- Metrics: to develop new performance metrics to compare a set-valued  estimate/prediction with a single-valued one. In fact, while standard estimators yield determinate (or single-valued) outcomes, those based on near-ignorance lead to set-valued ones. The problem of how to fairly compare through a metric a set-valued estimate  with a single-valued estimate is thus fundamental to judge the quality of the models in practice.
- Extension to the non-parametric case: this extension is important as non-parametric models are spreading in the context of artificial intelligence, because of the increasing computational power. Modeling near-ignorance with a non-parametric model can allow to build very general models for statistical inference.
- Understanding the ultimate relationship between near-ignorance and learning: we plan to go deeper into these questions, exploiting important results derived in the context of Bayesian inference for the consistency  and convergence of posterior distributions.
Keywords: Exponential family, Imprecise probability, Learning, Lower and upper expectations, Near-ignorance

Title: Tracking macrostructural sleep behaviors in infancy using high density electroencephalography (hdEEG) and actigraphy
Abstract:
Background: Infancy is characterized by large transitions in sleep behavior. Poor infant sleep is a burden on families and prolonged infant sleep problems have been linked to later negative consequences for behavior and health, as reported in epidemiological studies. Only few studies have examined infant sleep longitudinally using objective measures. A thorough investigation that includes daytime sleep is lacking entirely. Furthermore, the regional distribution of electroencephalographic sleep (EEG topography) in infants is unknown. 
Specific aims:  1) To quantify the longitudinal development of macrostructural sleep behaviors (duration, variability, consolidation, fragmentation) across infancy in a large population sample. 2) To examine the regional distribution of infant sleep using high-density electroencephalography (hdEEG). 3) To automatize the scoring of infant sleep by means of machine learning.
Material/methods: In 128 infants age 3, 6 and 12 months, actigraphy and sleep diaries are used to quantify sleep objectively. While this data is currently being collected, I will additionally measure hdEEG in a subgroup of 6-month-old infants. This dataset will be used to develop an automated scoring of infant sleep using a machine learning approach.
Expected value of the proposed project: This project will characterize the development of infant sleep rhythms and infant brain activity during sleep. This research will improve our understanding of normative and pathologic sleep behavior development and facilitate sleep stage scoring, which is currently very time intensive. The identification of sleep-related risk behaviors will add important translational value in the context of developmental disorders.

Title: Informed learning-based and data-driven control
Abstract: Being in the era of data, numerous ideas and techniques from machine learning have emerged in learning-based and data-driven control of cyber-physical systems. These approaches fail to perform satisfactorily in the presence of significant levels of uncertainty or when the systems are comparably complex. To improve these approaches and make them further suitable for autonomous and large-scale complex systems, we need to incorporate potentially available side-information about the underlying system. More precisely, the spurious model and decision candidates that are not consistent with the given knowledge are rejected. AS a result, the estimated model and the obtained decision are more interpretable. Furthermore, in various contexts, enforcing particular characteristics and structures facilitates employing more appropriate control strategies. In the current project, the main focus will be on deriving scalable and tractable learning-based and data-driven control techniques that incorporate the available side-information systematically and correctly. Since the given side-information may come from a diverse range and there is no universal treatment for its incorporation, the primary focus will be on more common forms. To this end, we will propose methodologies employing powerful tools and frameworks such as Koopman operator theory, Gaussian processes, and the theory of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces.
Keywords: cyber-physical systems, data-driven control, machine learning, side information

Title: Unconventional Visual Sensors and Processors with Algorithms for Localization and Mapping Operating under Real-World Constraints
Abstract:
Visual sensing and processing has proven to be key in the perception of autonomous systems as it enables the retrieval of a wide variety of cues from the environment. These include the appearance and identity of artefacts, their position and extent in space or their motion. Particularly the spatial awareness of an agent, which could be summarized in the two following questions: ``Where am I?'' and ``Where are things around me?'' is central to many applications. To cite only a few examples, those are driving autonomously in cities, picking parcels in a warehouse, delivering packages from the air, cleaning floors in a house, or guiding tourists in an airport.

The general problem of spatial awareness is captured in what has been coined as Simultaneous-localization and Mapping (SLAM). The problem is for an agent to determine its position and orientation (also known as pose) in a three-dimensional world while creating the map of its a-priori unknown surroundings. While the problem was posed in the early nineties as an interesting theoretical exercise solving yet another instance of some chicken-and-egg problem: How would an agent map anything while it does not know where it is? Or, reciprocally, how would it report its position without any idea of what the map should be? In the last ten years, the practical interest in the SLAM problem emerged in robotics applications in need of spatial awareness.

Although, SLAM algorithms have been under development for the last thirty years, the design of reliable systems operating under real-world constraints is still considered to be an open problem. Such constraints are, for instance, the need of robustness against a wide range of variations in illumination or viewpoints combined with low latency requirements under a limited power-budget embedded in a small form-factor. We shall be more precise about the quantification of those, later in this proposal.

SLAM sensing and processing pipelines complying with such tight specifications typically produce a large amount of data and require enormous computing resources. Hence, their implementation commonly uses multi-core architectures with several Central Processing Units (CPUs) and General Purpose Graphics Processing Units (GPGPUs). The size and power-consumption of these devices limit their use in mobile applications such as small battery-powered apparatus, for instance, virtual reality gears, room-cleaning robots, or miniaturized unmanned air vehicles...

Concurrently, the developments of material technologies, lithographic processes, and assisted VLSI design enables the conception and fabrication of new visual sensors and processors. Unfortunately, such visual sensors and processors are not widely in use because of 1) their limited availability 2) the difficulty in their use and the limited available support (ecosystem in terms of software and interfaces are not always available) and most importantly 3) the lack of understanding of some of their working principles. This is explained by the fact these are almost exclusively academic research projects produced in a few prototypes by hardware groups often targeting different objectives than algorithmic vision research groups. This is one of the gaps we aim to close.

Through my research, I have been focusing on the use of such ``unconventional'' devices to develop algorithms solving vision problems under tight real-world constraints. A red-thread I have been pursuing is the idea of deporting more intelligence close to the sensor and developing distributed, parallel algorithms processing next to where light is transduced. Examples of algorithms and systems I have developed include a real-time algorithm performing joint High-Dynamic Range imaging and Tone Mapping implemented on a near-focal plane processor (NFPP) running under $1.2\si{\watt}$ of power and enabling the capture of $120$dB of dynamic range compressed on 8-bit images \cite{martel2016parallel,martel2016real,martel2016patent}, a monocular, passive depth estimation system based on focus measurements performed using a tunable liquid lens providing up to $150$ depth frames per second with up to $128$ depth levels under $1.6\si{\watt}$ \cite{martel2017high,martel2017real,martel2017live}, an active stereo system using Dynamic Vision Sensors (DVS) to recover depth based on stereo-matching of events actively generated by a magneto galvanometer driven laser \cite{martel2018stereo,martel2018live} and others \cite{martel2015toward,martel2016neuromorphic,martel2016demonstration,moeys2017color}.

In this line of research, this proposal suggests using opportunities these new sensors and processors have to offer for designing a new generation of spatially aware artificial vision systems. Those systems could sense light differently --than in conventional cameras-- and process as much as possible close to the sensor without the need of expensive data-transfers often dominating their latency and power-budget. In particular, I will consider sensors producing temporal events (DVS), processors containing processing elements alongside photosensitive elements in each pixels (NFPP) and multi-spectral and polarized imagers. The goal is to develop novel algorithms exploiting the peculiarities of these devices. These include both algorithms for localization and mapping: 1) a robust tracking/pose-estimation system on a NFPP working under a wide-range of illuminations, 2.1) an algorithm to assess the quality of viewpoints based on normal reconstructions in a polarized imaging system for mapping, 2.2) the investigation of Near-Infrared for pose-estimation in low-light conditions and human scenes, with 1) and  2) built around 3) the design of an event-driven SLAM pipeline to perform updates using these estimates.  To design efficient spatially aware systems, this project can solely be carried out with an interest in all the disciplines in artificial vision ranging from the hardware up to the algorithmic level.
Keywords: Artificial vision, Dynamic Vision Sensors, Near-focal plane processing, Simultaneous Localization and Mapping, Spatial awareness, Vision sensors

Title: Neural Oscillations as Predictors of Psychosis
Abstract:
Aims:
This study will attempt to predict the transition to psychosis on a landmark sample whose size is unmatched by any other study in the world. The study design of the North American Prodrome Longitudinal Study 2 (NAPLS-2) allows to investigate brain activity in clinical high risk (CHR) individuals longitudinally (repeatedly over time) and observe whether the anomalies identified at baseline worsen over time thereby leading to psychosis. Owing to the rich and varied set of experimental paradigms assessed in NAPLS 2, the proposed project will allow identifying neurophysiological paradigms that are most sensitive to conversion to psychosis. These paradigms could subsequently be selectively implemented in early detection clinics in Switzerland.

Methodology:
We will assess 242 Healthy Controls (HC), 199 CHR individuals who did not convert to psychosis (CHR-NP) and 72 CHR individuals who converted to psychosis (CHR-P) on three different EEG paradigms collected as part of NAPLS-2. NAPLS-2 is a consortium of eight universities (including prestigious universities such as Harvard, Yale and UCLA) with the largest CHR sample in the field and allows for advanced analyses and statistical power that cannot be performed in single-site studies. In particular, we will assess neural oscillations during the (1) visual and (2) auditory oddball paradigms, along with the (3) mismatch negativity response. Analyses will include: assessing neural oscillations using time-frequency analyses, phase locking value, and lagged phase synchronization across frontal and temporal regions. We will also make use of advanced machine learning algorithms (artificial intelligence) to identify multivariate patterns of brain activity predictive of transition to psychosis.

Hypotheses:
•Compared to both CHR-NP and HC, CHR-P individuals will demonstrate altered theta activity during both the P3a and P3b response during context-updating processes elicited by oddball target and novel stimuli.
•During the P3a and P3b response, CHR-P individuals will have reduced frontal-temporal phase synchronization of theta neural oscillations compared to both CHR-NP and HC due to lower grey matter volume in both of these brain regions.
•The auditory oddball paradigm will yield markers more predictive of conversion to psychosis than the visual oddball paradigm.
•Compared to both CHR-NP and HC, CHR-P individuals will demonstrate lower early theta activity during the MMN response that will be associated with lower MMN amplitude.
•Following the deviant tone, CHR-P individuals will have reduced frontal-temporal phase synchronization of theta neural oscillations compared to both CHR-P and HC due to lower grey matter volume in both of these brain regions.
•In CHR-P and CHR-NP individuals, aberrant frontal-temporal phase-synchronization and lower theta oscillations following deviant stimuli in the MMN paradigm will be associated with psychotic symptoms and neuropsychological deficits.
•Variation in brain structural (acquired via MRI) and functional data (acquired via EEG) among CHR individuals will be predictive of the individualized transition to psychosis.

Expected value of the project:
Currently in Switzerland, about 32,000 people are affected by schizophrenia and the average cost per patient has been estimated to be about EUR 39,000 in the year 2012 alone. Therefore, the early detection of psychosis potentially leading to enhanced treatment approaches will not only benefit the national economy in the long run but also help the patients and their families to get ready for a possible transition to psychosis. An early detection could allow for an early intervention, that is, the patients could undergo mild treatments such as a psychological intervention or administration of low-dosage antipsychotic medication. This study is unique as it is the first to investigate, repeatedly over time, a rich and varied set of experimental paradigms on the largest sample of CHR individuals worldwide. The main findings could help clarify whether brain abnormalities identified at baseline worsen overtime and allow for the individualized prediction of transition to psychosis.
Keywords: EEG, Machine Learning, Mismatch negativity, Neural Oscillations, Oddball Paradigm, Psychosis, Schizophrenia

projects in the area of english learning: asset (assessing student’s english texts) and mews (measuring english writing at secondary level) . while asset was concerned with teachers’ diagnostic competences when judging english student texts, mews generated a large corpus of authentic learner texts with holistic ratings by trained humans and assessment software. trace combines these projects to achieve following objectives: 1) generating detailed ratings of text qualities for a large corpus of authentic student texts, achieving highest possible objectivity by combining human ratings and english learner texts accurately by comparing their assessment to human and machine made benchmark scores (study 3); 3) building a comprehensive, free online training tool and evaluating its effectiveness with a large sample of pre service english teachers (study 4, 5 & 6). empirical studies have shown scoring consistency to be relatively low when raters do not use analytic assessment practices (i.e., apply detailed criteria to student texts) (dempsey et al., 2009). therefore, in study 1, human raters will assess a large portion of texts from the mews corpus using analytic criteria Title: Transforming tissue engineering through a deep dive into dynamic organ physiology
Abstract:
Engineered living tissues, which aim to functionally replace human tissues damaged due to disease, injury or congenital defects, have gained significant prominence in modern medicine. These engineered tissues have also demonstrated promising results as models for disease modeling and drug testing. Current tissue engineering approaches use cells (animal or patient-derived) seeded or encapsulated within biomaterial scaffolds. During maturation (tissue growth), the scaffolds and the culture media provide the right topographical or chemotactic cues for the cells to proliferate, differentiate and deposit the tissue-specific extracellular matrix (ECM). A major challenge with current tissue engineering approaches is creating functional tissues for dynamic organs (e.g., lungs, heart, etc.), which undergo repetitive physiological motion with volumetric dilation-contraction. Dynamic tissues pose specific design challenges which are overlooked by conventional approaches: 1) Auxetic tissue characteristics, where the tissues expand across multiple directions simultaneously, and 2) Anisotropic cellular and ECM arrangement, which impart a directional variation in the tissue properties. Bridging these two design challenges requires a complete re-thinking of how we design and fabricate engineered tissues. In addition, it is equally important to use the right cells and biomaterials which mimic the composition of the native tissues, as well the tissue maturation conditions mimicking the growth and function in vivo. 
To be able to solve this multi-faceted challenge, we will develop new synergistic deep learning (DL)-based design and computational tools to analyze the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans, and identify patient-specific conformant designs for the cardiac meshes which demonstrate Poisson’s ratios similar to the native tissue (Objective 1). Then, volumetric bioprinting (VBP) with or without tomographic projections will be used to rapidly fabricate the tissue constructs based on photo-clickable decellularized extracellular matrix (dECM) resin encapsulating human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived cardiac cells (Objective 2). The cardiac tissues will then be maturated in custom dynamic culture bioreactors which provide electrical, mechanical and biochemical stimulation to achieve biomimetic tissues (Objective 3), which will be evaluated for their pre-clinical effectiveness in improving cardiac function post myocardial infarction in rat models (Objective 4).
Given the established expertise in high-throughput volumetric printing and development of new photoclick biomaterials, the Zenobi-Wong group will be the ideal host lab for the Ambizione. To be able to achieve the challenging tasks in the Ambizione project, I have gathered a consortium of experts (see letters of collaborations in the Annexes) – 1) Prof. Fanny Yang (Department of Computer Science, ETHZ) – for helping develop the DL models, and 2) Prof. Maximillian Y. Emmert (Institute for Regenerative Medicine, University of Zurich), for providing the cells and performing the animal surgeries. By combining the otherwise distinct fields of deep learning, and tissue engineering and biofabrication, the project will provide a framework for optimizing the tissue design and fabrication for dynamic organs. A human cell-based biomimetic cardiac model could also reduce animals used in research or elucidate disease mechanisms. The new innovations in tissue design and materials, fabrication and maturation will transform conventional tissue engineering approaches and open-up new collaboration opportunities. The Ambizione project will be a steppingstone in my career as an independent researcher, with my lab investigating the frontiers of interdisciplinary science and creating impact by meaningfully engaging society.

Title: Development of a Universal Neural Network-based Potential Energy Surface
Abstract:
Machine learning (ML) methods have gained increasing popularity in the field of computational chemistry in recent years. Provided they are trained on appropriate reference data, they allow to circumvent the need for a solution of the Schrödinger equation and allow substantial speed-ups. It has been shown previously that it is possible to generate accurate ML models that generalize to large structures by training them only on smaller molecules and that their predictions follow known trends of the periodic table and are chemically meaningful. These findings suggest that it should be possible to systematically generate a large set of reference data with the purpose of teaching an ML model the general rules of chemistry. A ``universal'' model would be a computationally efficient alternative to ab initio methods. In particular, deep neural networks (NNs) are a promising method for this purpose because of their scalability to large datasets. However, current NN-based approaches only consider nuclear degrees of freedom and lack a way to include information about the electrons, i.e. the total charge of a system and its spin multiplicity.

The aim of the proposed research project is (a) the generation of a systematically constructed set of ab initio reference data covering general rules of chemistry and (b) the development of a deep NN architecture that takes the same input as ab initio calculations, i.e. information about both electrons and nuclei. By training the NN on the generated dataset, the aim is to construct a universal NN-based potential energy surface (PES) applicable to a wide range of chemical problems. Due to its favourable scaling and computational efficiency, the NN-based PES could be applied to study large systems that are out of reach of current ab initio methods. The impact of an efficient and accurate alternative to ab initio calculations would probably be similar to the introduction of density functional theory (DFT) and potentially lead to new insights. Possible applications include reactive molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, the study of protein folding dynamics and the search for new drug-like molecules, catalysts, or other compounds with desirable properties.

Title: Decision making in a complex world: Towards a process-level theory of risk taking
Abstract:
This project aims to contribute to a better understanding of how people navigate the modern world full of risk and uncertainty. Specifically, with increasing choice autonomy and a growing number of lifestyle options in the Global North, it is more and more in individuals' own hands to what extent they expose themselves to (life)-critical risks (e.g., risky behaviors that threaten physical and mental well-being). Moreover, although cultural, societal, and technological innovations have rendered several aspects of life safer than ever, such innovations almost by definition bring along novel risks and uncertainties (e.g., applications of artificial intelligence in medicine and other crucial domains of life).

Importantly, people do not approach these diverse risks and uncertainties in an absolutely static manner. For this reason this project not only examines how and why people differ (i.e., from person to person) in their risk perceptions and actual risk taking – but also studies how individual persons vary regarding their risk perceptions and risk taking across time and different situations.

Addressing this and related questions requires developing a comprehensive process model of risk taking. To this end, this project will establish a unifying theoretical framework and integrate process-level explanations that have been proposed by disparate theories of the behavioral sciences. Moreover, in developing and testing such a model, this project will make use of novel assessment technologies to also investigate risk taking in real-life contexts (e.g., by means of app-based measurements aimed at collecting continuous and situation-specific data) – rather than exclusively examining the psychological processes related to risk taking in the lab.

Ultimately, process-level explanations of individual differences in risk taking may be essential when it comes to designing novel choice architectures, preventions, and interventions. In addition, a more precise understanding of individual-level risk taking may also contribute to a better understanding of human behavior in the context of systemic risks (e.g., human-induced climate change, financial crises, political radicalization). In the latter, individual decision making scales up and causes ripple effects, and as such may not necessarily have immediate effects on individuals' own lives, but potentially dramatic consequences for society at large.
Keywords: decision making, ecological assessment, modeling, risk taking

Title: Nonstationary graphical model discovery
Abstract: The goal of the proposed project is to characterize the fundamental (i.e., algorithm-independent) limits of the problem of estimating the statistical dependencies between the components of a non-stationary vector random process from finite-time observations. The insights gained through this characterization shall then be used to develop inference algorithms with provable performance guarantees. Knowledge of the statistical dependencies between the components of a non-stationary vector random process, commonly represented in a dependency graph, drastically facilitates storage and processing in the high-dimensional case (i.e., when the vector process consists of a large number of scalar element processes), as is the case in numerous modern applications in fields as diverse as information technology, machine learning, biology, medical imaging, chemistry, geosciences and many more. On the other hand, there are numerous applications in, e.g., neuroscience, genomic research, social network analysis, financial and economic time series analysis, and medical time series analysis, where statistical dependencies between vector process components hold information on underlying phenomena that one would want to identify. In most of these applications, the available time series data is multivariate and non-stationary and can hence be modeled as a non-stationary vector random process. Estimating the statistical dependencies between the components of a non-stationary vector random process is challenging as non-stationarity makes the statistical dependencies to change over time, so that the dependency graph underlying the observed process varies in time. Prior work in this broad area is mainly concerned with the estimation of dependencies between the components of multivariate (static) distributions or multivariate stationary vector random processes. In both cases the underlying dependency graph does not change over time. The literature on non-stationary graphical model discovery is very scarce and a corresponding general theory is missing. Considering the fact that in many practical applications (in particular the ones listed above) the processes under consideration are non-stationary, there is an urgent need for the development of a general theory and corresponding inference algorithms.One central element of the proposed project is to build on the theory of so-called underspread random processes, i.e., random processes with small high-lag time frequency correlations, a property often encountered in practice. Underspread processes have an approximate Fourier algebra underlying, which allows for a theory akin to that for stationary processes. We will argue and demonstrate by way of a concrete example that underspread processes constitute a good model for many phenomena in the real world.
Keywords: conditional independence graphs, nonstationary random processes, sparsity
