Title: Text Clustering with Styles
Abstract:
This research proposal focuses on the design, implementation and evaluation of text clustering algorithms based on styles.  Under this general formulation, one can find different applications.  Given a set of documents (or text excerpts), the targeted system may regroup works written by the same author (authorship attribution), according to the same genre (news, romance, play, poetry, etc.), text types ((verbatim of) spoken vs. written speech), political views (left-right, government-opposition), author’s profile (age, sex, socio-cultural psychological, education, background, etc.), or written during the same time period.  Such a system may provide answers in different domains, as, for example, in literary domains (e.g., what are the stylistic differences between Molière and P. Corneille) or in linguistics (e.g., what are the different styles used by teenagers on online forums).  In information retrieval (IR), instead of presenting the retrieved items only according to their similarity with the query, we can regroup them into clusters according to a given criterion (e.g., from surveys to specialized articles).  The internet offers other pertinent applications such as profiling different user types to detect the presence of cyber criminals (e.g., sexual predators, identity thieves).  
The targeted style-based clustering system is mainly based on an unsupervised model where the needed features to discriminate between the different groups (and sub-groups) are not learned from a set of training instances.  Within this general context, we are targeting the following four main objectives.  
First, we want to design, implement and evaluate different inter-textual metrics able to effectively discriminate between the various styles present in a given corpus.  Such an inter-textual distance (or similarity) must be non-negative, symmetric and respect the triangle inequality.  Moreover it must be stable and robust (small variations or small errors in the input must result in small distance variations).  The measure should have a clear interpretation for the end user (no black-box system).  
Second, we want to select and evaluate various text representation strategies, focusing mainly on lexical-based information such as word types, lemmas or based on more sophisticated tools such as part-of-speech (POS) categories, along with the sequence of these items.  The selected representations must also be able to give a pertinent key to interpret the inter-textual distance between two texts or clusters.  
As a third objective, strongly correlated to the second, we want to work with various languages other than English.  The question is to determine how we can generalize conclusions obtained from English to other languages, in particular with languages having a more complex morphology (e.g., Finnish, Hungarian) or certain Asian languages (Japanese, Chinese) showing radically different linguistic characteristics. 
Forth, we want to analyze, and have a better understanding of, the underlying variability and uncertainty related to the automatic assignment proposed by the system.  Such an indication must be easy to understand for the end user.
Keywords: authorship attribution, digital humanities, digital librairess, inter-textual distance, natural language processing, text clustering, text representation

Title: Decoding Biases in Antibody-Mediated Immunity to Advance Vaccine Development
Abstract:
B-cell-mediated immunity is a critical component of the adaptive immune system responsible for pathogen clearance and protection from re-infection. B-cell receptors (or antibodies, in the secreted form) are proteins from the immunoglobulin superfamily that mature to recognize antigenic features that are distinct from host’s endogenous biomolecules. These features are called epitopes and they typically consist of peptidic elements in proteins exposed on the surface of the pathogen, but can also include glycans and lipids. Epitopes can be thought of as molecular surfaces that antibodies interact with. Depending on the inherent properties of these surfaces they will have higher or lower probability of being targeted by antibodies. This is a phenomenon known as immunodominance. The present study aims to identify the molecular determinants that regulate the formation of immunodominance hierarchies in antigens. In other words, we seek to understand what makes epitopes "attractive" for B-cells. 
Towards this goal, we will study the recurring molecular signatures in antibody-mediated immunity across a larger group of healthy human subjects seropositive to common viral antigens (e.g., SARS-CoV-2 Spike, influenza HA, Human Papillomavirus), due to prior vaccination and/or infection. We will apply a hybrid approach based on electron-microscopy-based polyclonal epitope mapping (EMPEM) and next-generation sequencing of epitope-specific B-cells to identify the immunodominant conformational epitopes in each antigen and link them to specific B-cell clones targeting them. The focus will be on epitope and paratope features that occur frequently in a given population. We hypothesize that through structure-based analysis of these high-probability immune outcomes we can uncover the molecular rules driving B-cell-mediated immunity leading to novel tools and concepts for antigen engineering. 
 The study will consist of three Specific Aims:
-SA1: Identification of antigenic structural determinants of epitope immunogenicity 
-SA2: Identification of B-cell receptor features associated with immunodominant epitopes
-SA3: Design and evaluation of antigens with tailored immunodominance hierarchies 
In addition to answering the fundamental immunology questions, the results from this study will provide a roadmap for future structure-guided vaccine design efforts, enabling to engineer vaccine candidates with tailored on- and off-target reactivity. Furthermore, through development of computational workflows for modeling of B-cell responses we aim to reduce the volume of animal immunization experiments during pre-clinical evaluations of vaccine candidates; thus, simultaneously augmenting and accelerating the process.
Keywords: antibody, cryoEM, electron microscopy, epitope, immunity, immunodominance, machine learning, next-generation sequencing, vaccine, virus

Title: Relating semantic to symbolic structures in Swiss scientific research. Mapping topic spaces with a focus on the twinning of the digital and ecological transitions (2010–2025)
Abstract:
Science is increasingly regarded as a critical resource for understanding problems and identifying solutions to current crises, such as global warming, biodiversity loss, pandemics, and their dramatic consequences on populations. However, science is not homogeneous, but a complex ecosystem structured both semantically and symbolically. In this project, I emphasize that mapping scientific research is key to informing science policy and researchers about the diverse and often competing definitions to problems and methods for addressing them. Semantic similarity across research topics may vary, hence reflecting a diversity of the meanings associated with these topics. Additionally, different values may be linked to these meanings, hence endowing certain definitions of problems with higher credibility than others. Symbolic structures, which derive from the uneven distribution of scientific credibility, materialize in the form of funding and citations.
In this one-year project, I aim to develop an approach to relate semantic to symbolic structures, hence identifying what is said, by whom, with what meaning and associated value, or credibility. I emphasize that such endeavour is key to understand why certain problems and solutions are (not) privileged over others. Asking (Q1) What is the semantic and symbolic structure of Swiss scientific research? I aim to classify and map the topical landscape of research in Switzerland on a global scale, hence emphasizing on general principles of structuration. To do so, I will draw on all SNSF granted research projects as recoded in the SNSF grant data portal since 2010, as well as all applicants’ publications as cataloged in the Web of Science database. Asking (Q2) What is the semantic and symbolic structure of research focusing on the digital and ecological or ‘twin’ transition? I aim to delve deeper into the complex issue of sustainability, considering its polysemy and varied applications, to capture how Swiss scholars handle, define, and dispute the crucial task of integrating research on digital technologies with sustainable development goals. Such a ‘zoom’ will help refine the findings from Q1 by focusing on the meanings accorded to sustainability and associated terms, and where it situates in the global topical landscape.
This endeavour requires both methodological consolidation and innovation. By consolidation, I mean to benefit from the state-of-the-art approaches to mapping semantic and symbolic structures. Semantic structures are best approached using topic modeling techniques, which have proven their efficiency for grasping the different meanings attributed to various problems, either by classifying (Latent Dirichlet Allocation) or mapping semantic similarities (BERTopic). Symbolic structures are seminally approached using social network and geometric data analysis. By innovation, I mean facilitating the cross-fertilization of these methods to relate semantic to symbolic structures. Enhancing our understanding of the interplay between semantic and symbolic structures, along with emphasizing on topics pertaining to the so-called twin transition, will hopefully facilitate the identification of nodes of convergence across scholarly approaches to problem-solving. I believe this knowledge is key for the scientific community to gain deeper self-awareness and foster greater cohesion across scholars aiming to enhance our understanding of sustainability and transitions issues. Furthermore, a better knowledge of how funding allocation shapes the range of scientific approaches to addressing today’s major societal challenges will benefit funding agencies, political authorities, and society as a whole.
Keywords: BERTopic, Bibliometrics, Deep learning, Latent Dirichlet Allocation, Sustainability, Switzerland, Topic modeling, Twin transition

Title: Quantitative EEG during REM sleep: an early biomarker of cholinergic neurodegeneration
Abstract:
Background and rationale: The degenerative process of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is believed to start decades before the clinical onset. A prodromal phase of AD, termed mild cognitive impairment (MCI), offers the opportunity to detect AD before the dementia phase, although not all individuals with MCI will progress to AD. Promising markers of AD derived from positron emission tomography (PET), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and quantitative EEG (qEEG) have been identified in patients during wakefulness. However, qEEG slowing during rapid eye movement (REM) sleep has been shown to be a more powerful tool than waking EEG to discriminate patients with AD from healthy controls. The rationale for studying qEEG during REM sleep is that cholinergic basal forebrain neurons, which degenerate early in AD, play a major role in cerebral cortex activation during REM sleep, at a time when several other neuronal systems that contribute to cortical activation during wakefulness are less active, leaving the cholinergic influence unmasked. 
Project idea and objectives: We propose that REM sleep is a more sensitive state than wakefulness to detect early AD-related cholinergic degeneration. The main objectives of this project are: 1) to assess the predictive value of baseline REM sleep qEEG to identify MCI subjects who will progress to AD, 2) to build a machine learning model to predict AD conversion from large-scale clinical and paraclinical input data, and 3) to validate REM sleep qEEG as a surrogate biomarker of cholinergic neurotransmission integrity in humans.
Methods: At baseline, 140 MCI subjects and 45 healthy controls from the community (age range: 65-85 years) were assessed with neuropsychological battery, blood tests (for APOE genotyping), full-night polysomnography (PSG), waking EEG, and brain MRI. At 3-year follow-up, a second neuropsychological assessment will be performed to classify the participants in one of the following groups: normal cognition, MCI, or AD. Baseline EEG slowing during wakefulness and REM sleep was measured with the [(delta + theta)/(alpha + beta)] ratio and between-group differences will be assessed at 3-year follow-up using repeated-measure ANOVA. Baseline clinical and paraclinical (APOE genotype, PSG, qEEG, MRI) data will be used to build a machine learning model to correctly predict which MCI participants will convert to AD. A subsample of participants will be tested with a cholinergic PET scan using 18F-fluoroethoxybenzovesamicol (18F-FEOBV), a radiotracer that binds selectively to the vesicular acetylcholine transporter.
Expected results: We predict that REM sleep qEEG at baseline will better discriminate MCI subjects who will progress to AD than wakefulness qEEG. We expect that REM sleep qEEG slowing will be retained in the machine learning model as one of the features that allow the most accurate prediction of AD conversion. Concerning the PET study, we predict that REM sleep qEEG slowing will be associated with a decreased 18F-FEOBV uptake in specific brain regions (i.e., cingulate, precuneus, and temporoparietal cortex, as well as superior, middle, and medial frontal cortex).
Impact: REM sleep qEEG has the potential to become a reliable non-invasive and low-cost biomarker to help identify individuals at risk of progressing to AD. The identification of these vulnerable subjects is crucial to develop and test the efficacy of treatments that could prevent or slow the progression of AD.

Title: Long-range acoustic sensing based on a far-field causal entanglement
Abstract:
Far-field acoustic imaging and detection devices were long thought to be inescapably limited by a fundamental constraint: the diffraction limit. To be well resolved, two individual features must be separated by more than half the shortest acoustic wavelength. Recently, advances in metamaterials or deep learning have made it possible to circumvent this limit, but these techniques require a high level of design or post-processing computational cost and, moreover, often operate only in a narrow frequency range.

In this proposal, I propose to overcome this diffraction limit in a completely different and unconventional way. I will to use intensity singularities and their resulting field dislocations for non-intrusive sub-wavelength detection at a long distance.
In 2D acoustics, the singularities of the intensity field are pairs of topologically related isolated points around which an acoustic vortex and a saddle form respectively. The point-like nature of these singularities makes them extremely promising for accurate acoustic detection.

The singularities become lines in 3D. Instead of adopting the conventional foliation representation of the field (succession of 2D parallel planes), I study here these dislocation lines directly using a 3D streamline representation. Preliminary simulations have shown that the generation of a pressure singularity at a 3D space position effectively creates two dislocation ellipses, one hosting the vortex, the other hosting the saddle. An interesting (unpublished) feature of these ellipses is that their size can reach tens of wavelengths, while the distance between the vortex and saddle lines is less than a tenth of a wavelength.  A small scatterer placed on the vortex line will consistently change the whole ellipse, allowing the presence of a scatterer, which can be 1/10 wavelength in size, to be automatically detected at several wavelengths away by sensing the other side of the ellipse. Indeed, two singular points on the ellipses are topologically entangled, meaning that they must always exist together: a disturbance at one point is causally repercuted on the other.

Over this one year effort, I will conceive, build and conduct the first acoustic experiment capable of observing these unique line singularities, study their physics and apply them to sensing. Non-intrusive acoustic sensing methods have to be deployed to detect the change in the ellipse without disturbing the field itself. Among others, optical fiber scanning or synthetic schlieren  tomography  will be developed. These methods have only been used in acoustics to image very simple fields, like standing waves or focused beams. I propose to extend their applicability to image acoustic wave in more complex situations and quantitatively measure the acoustic intensity from the 3D images obtained.

This research is paving the way to novel super-resolution detection techniques and sub-diffraction limit imaging devices in acoustics, and will have a considerable impact for the experimental investigation of complex acoustic fields.
Keywords: Detection, Dislocation, Imaging, Singularities, Super-resolution

Title: Evaluating ‘Interactive Problem Solving’– Cognitive-Affective Process Assessment and Impact of Unofficial Mediation in the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict
Abstract:
In many regions of the world, intergroup conflict and hostility remain pertinent problems. They often involve mass violence and fundamental harm to the well-being of the entangled citizens and whole societies. Intergroup contact, particularly unofficial ‘Track Two’ mediation, is a valuable approach aimed at changing intergroup disputes and achieving sustainable conflict transformation, thereby supporting official ‘Track One’ diplomacy. Scholars such as John Burton and Herbert Kelman have developed fundamental conceptualisations in this field, utilizing seminal theories of social psychology. However, despite excellent scholar-practitioner work on conflict transformation, hardly any research to date has systematically addressed the impact of specific microfoundations such as cognitions or emotions, describing the exact psychological processes between participants and facilitators that influence process outcome. 
Without these foundations, we remain ill-informed about concrete functional mechanisms and, most importantly, about the basis for transfer effects that are essential for the enduring impact of unofficial mediation. My project, ‘Evaluating Interactive Problem Solving’ is addressing this gap in our understanding of individual conflict transformation by analysing selected mediation protocols from Kelman’s renowned data corpus spanning several decades within the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. I am applying for the SNF Postdoc Mobility Fellowship to expand my research skills towards a more applied setting and fill this crucial gap on the psychological aspects of individual conflict transformation and mediation processes.
Keywords: 'Track Two' diplomacy, Israel-Palestine conflict, conflict mediation, intergroup conflict, natural language processing

Title: Towards a Comprehensive SCI Prognostic Model: Leveraging Multi-Modal Clinical Assessments
Abstract:
Background: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is a complex condition with diverse clinical presentations and recovery trajectories. Accurate long-term prediction of recovery is essential  for treatment planning, patient management, and the design of clinical trials. However, this remains challenging due to the significant variability in injury characteristics, individual treatment responses, natural recovery capacity, and the limitations of current clinical assessments.
 
Problems and gaps: Standardized frameworks such as the International Standards for Neurological Classification of Spinal Cord Injury (ISNCSCI) and the American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) Impairment Scale (AIS) are essential for assessing the severity and neurological level of SCI. However, they only offer a partial view of the recovery process. Additional assessments, including blood tests and neurophysiological measures (e.g., motor evoked potentials, nerve conduction studies), could enhance predictive accuracy. However, their integration into predictive models is hindered by inconsistent data collection, variable timing, and measurement scale differences. The fragmented nature of SCI datasets further complicates assessing the full impact of these measures on recovery outcomes.

Key objectives: The goal of this project is to enhance long-term recovery prediction in SCI by incorporating neurophysiological assessments and blood markers alongside standard neurological evaluations and patient demographics. Using advanced machine learning (ML) techniques, the project aims to improve predictive accuracy and clinical utility, leading to more personalized and effective treatment strategies.

Methods: This project explores multi-modal integration using state-of-the-art ML approaches, such as multi-task learning and multi-branch deep networks with the goal to improve recovery prediction. A key innovation of the project is the employment of  adaptive weighted-masking strategy, which ensures missing clinical assessments do not exclude patients from analysis. This method maximizes dataset utilization and enables the development of a more generalizable and clinically applicable recovery model. The integration of heterogeneous data sources will be a core aspect of this work, allowing for more precise and clinically relevant prediction.

Expected results: The project expects to generate a robust, generalizable long-term recovery prediction model that integrates multiple data modalities, even in the presence of incomplete clinical assessments. By prioritizing key clinical assessments and features, the model aims to provide more accurate and interpretable recovery prediction, ultimately leading to better patient stratification, prognosis, and treatment strategies.

Impact: This project will enhance the predictability of SCI recovery, benefiting clinical decision-making and improving patient outcomes. By developing a decision-support tool for clinicians, the study aims to facilitate more personalized treatment plans and optimize future clinical trial design. Additionally, this work has the potential to stimulate broader adoption of advanced ML techniques in SCI research, bridging gaps between computational models and clinical practice.

Title: Analysis and Design of Self-Supervised Learning Methods
Abstract:
Since the breakthrough performance of AlexNet on the Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC) in 2012, neural networks (NN) are being used in virtually any area of computer vision. This breakthrough was made possible by the development of better learning methodologies for neural networks and access to better hardware (GPUs, in particular). However, another important factor was the availability of very large annotated datasets. These datasets were built through crowdsourcing internet services, such as those offered by Datatang and Amazon. These services allow researchers to collect annotations of images by distributing the task to workers worldwide. Unfortunately, they also come with a number of limitations. The main one is their high cost, despite crowdsourcing being a very efficient and effective work distribution system. This has become even worse as Amazon’s Mechanical Turk just increased in 2015 its fees from 10% to 40%. Moreover, depending on the complexity of the task, the manual preparation of annotation is not only expensive, but also time-consuming and might require expertise that is not always available in sufficiently high numbers (e.g., annotation of medical imagery). In contrast, a large quantity of unlabeled images and videos is readily available.
These limitations motivate us to look at the unsupervised learning approach. Our main challenge is to define meaningful learning tasks without using manually assigned labels. Towards this purpose, in this project we propose to investigate a recent unsupervised learning paradigm called self-supervised learning. In self-supervised learning, instead of training a system to solve a given task, one trains it to solve a (related) pretext task, where labeling comes for free from the data. For example, given frames of a video one can use half of them to predict the other half.
The labels are then taken directly from data "for free".
We therefore look at re-casting unsupervised learning as a supervised learning method where the labels are extracted directly from data. We formalize the set of all possible freely-available labels as those that we can directly extract from the data itself. We decompose the data (grayscale intensities or RGB values at all pixels and their corresponding 2D coordinates) into two disjoint sets: one that forms the new labels and the other that forms the new data. The choice of how the original data is decomposed will depend on the nature of the data (e.g., the imaging modality) and of the task. Our objective is to achieve a performance comparable to that of supervised methods on tasks such as classification and localization.
Keywords: neural network unfolding, neural networks, self-supervised learning, transfer learning, unsupervised learning

2. improving the accuracy of estimated wave field parameters with arrays. this will be achieved by considering the broadband nature of seismic waves and by exploiting the time invariability of seismic parameters over long recordings; 3. the estimation of additional quantities of interest with array recordings, such as surface wave attenuation (q factor), directional properties of surface waves, and the composition of the wave field; 4. extending the domain of applications to larger arrays including temporary large arrays and data from the swiss seismic networks; 5. application of the new methods to derive structural information for seismic stations in regional networks; Title: New methods to infer population dynamics from the fossil record
Abstract:
The study of extinct species, which represent the majority of all organisms that have ever lived, is essential to understand the evolutionary dynamics governing species origination and extinction and shaping biodiversity. As the field of paleobiology is entering the era of big data, with millions of records already available and many more to be digitized, there is an increasing need for novel theoretical frameworks and computational tools to make the best use of these data.

In this project I will develop a suite of mathematical models to infer the evolution of population size throughout the lifespan of species based on their fossil record and determine how population dynamics scale up to macroevolutionary processes of speciation and extinction. I will also implement a method to improve the dating of paleontological samples thus making downstream analyses of fossil occurrences more robust. These methods will set the basis for a new generation of computational paleobiology and expand the scope of evolutionary analyses.

A second part of the project is devoted to applying the new methods to empirical data to tackle crucial evolutionary questions. I will use rodents of North America as a model system to determine the links between population dynamics, extinction risk, and species longevity. I will also analyze a plant fossil dataset of unprecedented size to model how Neotropical forest, which today harbors the most biodiverse habitats on Earth, originated and evolved since Cretaceous, i.e. during the past 140 million years.

This project will bring substantial scientific progress on two fronts: The new methods will change how the fossil record is used in evolutionary biology research bridging micro- and macro-evolution to determine the links between population dynamics and the speciation and extinction processes. The empirical studies will reveal how environmental changes alter animal and plant communities in terms of species composition and their abundances.
Keywords: Bayesian methods, artificial intelligence, extinction, fossils, macroevolution

Title: Differentiable simulations for mechanistic insight and catalyst design
Abstract:
The goal of this project is to develop an algorithm for atomistic reaction mechanism elucidation of complex heterogeneous systems based on the combination of quantum chemistry, machine learning potentials (MLPs), and differentiable simulations (DiffSim) that can then be turned into a catalyst design and optimization approach. After validating our methodology on the methanol to olefins (MTO) reaction, we are applying it to gain new insights into the oxidation of methane to methanol and improve on the existing catalysts for that reaction.

Understanding chemical reactions on an atomistic level is crucial for the development of efficient and sustainable chemical processes. Theoretical models can provide such crucial insights, but they are trustworthy only if they include all energetically accessible structures and reaction paths, which necessarily requires the automated exploration of the relevant reaction space in order to be feasible.

Overall, this project aims to enable such models based on a workflow that can simulate complex reactive systems with sufficient speed and accuracy, and then design a catalyst to enhance the rate of a desired reaction from end-to-end, requiring only the desired chemical transformation as an input.
Specifically, the method development in this proposal includes an out-of-the-box combination of two powerful technologies in unprecedented ways, the application of recently established MLPs in long atomistic simulations in combination with the unique concept of DiffSim that has just been developed by the Gómez-Bombarelli group.
Additionally, we are proposing the novel ansatz DiffCat in which we apply the DiffSim framework in order to determine the ideal catalyst structure from an atomistic simulation. We will validate the developed algorithms through the reproduction of the MTO reaction mechanism and apply the algorithm to unravel the active sites and mechanisms involved in the oxidation of methane to methanol over copper loaded zeolites with experimental collaborators.

Our methodology is enabled by high-throughput first-principles-based calculations that constantly improve an MLP that then allows for sufficiently long and accurate simulations. The simulations are guided towards the chemical transformation and catalyst of interest by a bias potential learned through DiffSim. Fallback strategies include approaches based on Bayesian optimization and a genetic algorithm in order to optimize both the pores and the site distribution of zeolite catalysts.

Anticipated outcomes include new algorithms for the elucidation of complex reaction mechanisms validated by the application to the highly relevant MTO reaction. We hope to gain new insights into the active site and reaction mechanism of the oxidation of methane to methanol and leverage our developed algorithms to improve on the existing catalysts. The studied reactions are focused on methanol, a central building block for sustainable chemical processes with long-term significance, while the studied models are advantageous for our theoretical models. The required structural models are too large to afford extensive sampling with density functional theory (DFT), but are still tractable to calculate reference energies of single structures with DFT which offers a good compromise between cost and accuracy for these systems.

The project’s outcomes are anticipated to advance the field of zeolite catalysis and theoretical chemistry by providing a comprehensive algorithmic approach for mechanism elucidation and catalyst design. Moreover, the project aims to enhance the understanding of a crucial reaction for the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions. Ultimately, the development of efficient catalysts is expected to have broad implications for industrial processes, paving the way for sustainable and optimized chemical transformations.
Keywords: Catalyst Design, Differentiable Simulations, Machine Learning, Mechanism Elucidation, Molecular Dynamics, Theoretical Chemistry, Zeolite Catalyst

Title: Large-scale learning and Vision for GeoVisipedia
Abstract:
The GeoVisipedia project aims at coupling humans and computers for the benefit of the envi-ronment and quality of human life. 

We will create an open web-service that brings together human knowledge crowdsourced via the internet and sophisticated machine learning (ML) and computer vision (CV) methods to analyse remote sensing images acquired by satellites, airplanes, or unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV). We will build upon the already existing knowledge, tools, and webservice of the Visipedia project http://www.vision.caltech.edu/visipedia/index.html) that is lead by my host Prof. Pietro Perona (California Institute of Technology, CalTech, Pasadena) and Prof. Serge Belongie (Cornell Tech, New York). 

The main idea of the Visipedia project is to apply sophisticated state-of-the-art machine learning (ML) and Computer Vision (CV) methods to object recognition problems specified by an expert in that particular field (e.g., an ornithologist for bird species recognition) who has no deep insight into ML and CV. After an expert has specified a particular task, she/he provides guidelines and example images with corresponding annotations to a wide "crowd" of amateurs via the internet. These non-experts then help detecting further instances of the particular object through, for example, annotating further training examples that can be employed to learn an automated classifier. Additionally, non-experts can upload bird photos themselves where different bird species are recognized using the trained classifier. 

With the GeoVisipedia project proposed here, the Computer Vision laboratory at CalTech and the Institute of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing (lead by Prof. Konrad Schindler) at ETH Zürich (ETHZ) will combine their complementary expertise in human-in-the-loop, large-scale learning and remote sensing data analysis, respectively, to add a geospatial component to Visipedia. 

Our idea is to transfer and extend the concept of Visipedia, which is already successfully running for bird species recognition, to object recognition in georeferenced overhead imagery acquired by satellites, aircraft, or unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV). For example, an environmental agency can upload a high-resolution aerial data set of a natural reserve and specify example annotations of deer. Amateur users can then help to manually annotate further deer to finally learn a classifier which detects all deer in the natural reserve to count the population. Title: Recursion in action across primates
Abstract: What is the fundamental nature of the difference that separates human cognition from that of other animals? A difference of nature (Descartes, 1637/2006, pp.47–48) or of degree (Darwin, 1871/1896, pp.34–35)? In this work, I propose to tackle the question by focusing on the comparative analysis of recursive mental capacities involved in nested cup manipulation across humans and chimpanzees. Recursion has been argued to constitute the definite cognitive ability that distinguishes us from other primates, and to underlie—among other things—the singularity of our language faculty (Berwick & Chomsky, 2016). The nested cup task, on the other hand, has proven particularly suited to the investigation of primates recursive abilities in a comparative and developmental perspective, given both the structural and developmental parallels that exist between the syntax of language and that of action (Greenfield, 1991). Yet, if early experiments on the nested cup task did tend to support the specificity of human recursive capabilities (Conway & Christiansen, 2001) latest results are not so clear-cut: adult chimpanzees, for instance, do seem capable of producing all types of recursive operations available to humans (Hayashi & Takeshita, 2022). More work is therefore needed to understand whether human and non- human primates recursive abilities actually differ in any specific way and if so how. In this research project for a twenty four months postdoctoral mobility at Chubu Gakuin University under the supervision of Pr. Misato Hayashi—a renown primatologist and leading expert of the nested cup task—I propose to focus on the statistical analysis of sequences of nested cup manipulations across primates, rather than individual units as what has been done so far. My general hypothesis is indeed that a qualitative difference does exist between human and non-human primates recursive abilities, but that this difference is one of degree rather than kind. More precisely, I build upon work which argues that non-human primates recursive abilities may in fact be limited by their reduced working memory capacity (Read, 2008) and postulate that the qualitative difference between humans and chimpanzees recursive abilities lies in the depth of the nested structures both species are able to process. I propose to test my hypothesis by carrying out a statistical analysis of nested cup manipulations across humans and chimpanzees in order to compare the patterns—rather than single types—of recursive combinations that both species are able to produce at various stages of their development. My methodology requires no further experiment on either chimpanzees or humans, as I make use of already available video recordings of past nested cup experiments accumulated by Pr. Hayashi over the past twenty years. If my results prove conclusive, they will contribute to a better understanding of our cognitive similarities and differences with other primates, notably by providing a specific characterization of the recursive patterns that may be shared or specific to each species. If they confirm the existence of a gradual continuum between primates recursive abilities, they will also contribute to the debate on the origin of human language by supporting a more gradualist scenario, contra the saltationist hypothesis favored notably by proponents of the biolinguistics enterprise (Berwick & Chomsky, 2016).
Keywords: action grammar, cognitive development, comparative cognition, evolutionary linguistics, hierarchical complexity, language evolution, machine learning, nested cup, object manipulation, primatology, recursion, syntax

Title: Active learning for late-stage drug design
Abstract: Challenges in solubility, stability, and absorption require formulation development that can significantly delay the introduction of promising drugs to patients. Active machine learning allows for rapid model development by implementing a feedback-driven artificial intelligence that puts the machine in charge of requesting additional data for iteratively improving predictive accuracy. Coupled to novel organ-on-a-chip assay systems, active learning workflows have the potential to transform formulation development and generate in silico models that help streamlining translational drug design. This proposal aims to establish active learning workflows for rapidly generating models for various objectives relevant to formulation development using intestine-on-a-chip systems. In addition to predictive models, such workflows will generate vast amounts of biological data to deepen our understanding of organ-on-a-chip systems as well as provide theoretical insights into the learning patterns of artificial intelligence.
Keywords: Bioinformatics, Computational drug discovery, Formulation design, Machine learning, Organs-on-a-chip

Title: Computational and neurophysiological mechanisms of multisensory-motor integration
Abstract:
Sensory feedback from various sources is continuously integrated to form a coherent representation of the body. This flexible internal model plays a fundamental role in motor control by providing real-time information about the body's position and movement. In this process, sensory feedback is dynamically reweighted based on bottom-up factors, such as inter-sensory coherence and the relative precision of each sensory modality. Additionally, multisensory integration can be influenced by top-down control mechanisms, amplifying the neural representation of task-relevant information and/or inhibiting irrelevant or distracting stimuli based on current goals. Perhaps surprisingly, this is a complicated computation: although we have computers that can play chess and produce language, simple manual reaching and posture remain major challenges for artificial intelligence. 
In neurological diseases where one sensory modality is compromised or unreliable, the brain can rely more heavily on other available sensory information, thereby adapting physiologically to the sensory deficit. However, brain damage can impair top-down control mechanisms, leading to maladaptive distortions of body perception and motor behaviour, also independently of unisensory deficits. Neurotransmitters such as dopamine may play a critical role in the regulation of multiple stages of the multisensory integration process. Indeed, conditions characterized by dopaminergic dysfunction, such as Parkinson’s disease, are characterized by altered sensory weighting and reduced top-down cognitive control on multisensory-motor integration processes. 
The goal of the current project is: a) to define the computational bases of the interplay between bottom-up and top-down factors contributing to multisensory-motor processes b) to explore the role of dopamine in their modulation by studying Parkinson’s patients as a model and c) to unravel their neurophysiological bases by modelling electroencephalography (EEG) recordings.
Keywords: Closed-loop motor control, Cognitive control, Computational modelling, Multisensory integration, Parkinson disease

Title: The molecular landscape of Alzheimer's disease: building predictive models of cognitive decline and cognitive resilience in high-risk individuals
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the leading cause of dementia in the elderly. The hallmark of AD is a slow progression of neurodegeneration through stages of cognitive decline, ultimately leading to death. The cause of AD itself is biologically complex and multifactorial and begins decades before the observation of clinical symptoms. The accumulation of amyloid-  (A ) aggregates in neuritic plaques (degenerating neurons around an A  core) within the brain and hyper-phosphorylated tau proteins as neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs) are thought to contribute to the onset of neuronal degeneration. Genetic predisposition to AD has revealed a link with the immune system. Thus, the role of the immune system has become a major topic of investigation in the etiology and potential treatment of AD. Changes in composition and activation of resident and infiltrating immune cells as well as astrocytes are suggested to play a central role in the ongoing neuronal injury, beneficial or detrimental responses to injury and potential physiologic compensation. Interestingly, some genetically predisposed individuals never display AD neuropathology and furthermore, some individuals who have AD neuropathology never present with AD dementia. Thus, there appears to be a molecular program of resistance to disease despite high risk on the one hand, and on the other hand a program of compensation that leads to cognitive resilience despite AD neuropathology. A major barrier to understanding the immune and neuronal phenotypes and mechanisms behind these effects is that multiplexed subcellular imaging of human brain is extraordinarily difficult. Conventionally, neuropathologic assessment is based on images captured using pigment precipitation or fluorescent reporter-tagged antibodies. However, the multiplexing ability of these approaches to study subcellular features is confounded by spectral overlap and high auto-fluorescent background of adult human brain. Recently, a new method called multiplexed ion beam imaging (MIBI) has been developed which uses elemental isotope-tagged antibodies and mass spectrometry readouts. In this way, MIBI bypasses auto-fluorescent signals and spectral overlap between reporters and massively increases the multiplexing capacity in a single image. The central goal of this study is to use MIBI to analyze archival and newly existing brain samples to generate a deeper understanding of the molecular mechanisms which lead to phenotypes associated with cognitive resilience, despite high genetic risk for AD. We will analyze a range of human brain samples originating from healthy aged individuals (resistant), those with AD neuropathology but no dementia (resilient) and those with AD neuropathology and AD dementia (positive). Using MIBI we will capture unprecedented detail of neuroimmune interactions within a spatial context, AD risk gene products as well as genomic, proteomic and metabolomic features of neuronal, glial, and vascular elements. With this high dimensional data, we will use computational approaches and deep learning to build predictive models of cognitive decline and cognitive resilience, thereby shedding light on the molecular drivers and mechanistic pathways that underlie AD dementia as well as successful brain aging and exceptional cognitive resilience.
Keywords: Alzheimer's disease, Cognitive decline, Cognitive resilience, Deep learning, Dementia, High dimensional data, Multiplexed Ion Beam Imaging (MIBI), Neural networks

Title: What role do statistical learning mechanisms play in developmental dyslexia? A behavioral, computational and EEG approach.
Abstract: The aim of this research project is to investigate the hypothesis that developmental dyslexia might not just be a language- specific deficit but also result from a general impairment in learning statistical structures, of which natural languages are an example. To this aim, I will combine behavioral, neurophysiological (EEG) and computational methods in collaboration with the multidisciplinary research team led by Pr. Daphne Bavelier, who is a renowned expert in learning and brain plasticity and the supervisor of my doctoral thesis. This multidisciplinary approach will further our understanding of the neural mechanisms that are impaired in dyslexia, and provide important information for the development of efficient interventions.
Keywords: Development, Dyslexia, Learning, Statistical, electrophysiology

Title: External Knowledge for Low-resource Machine Translation: from Tokenization to Decoding (EXOMAT)
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have considerably changed the landscape of natural language processing thanks to very large neural networks trained on commensurate large datasets.  Their impact, however, has been weaker in the field of machine translation, despite emerging multilingual competencies of LLMs for 5-10 languages that are frequent in the training data.  Improving translation quality when training data is scarce remains an open problem.  The EXOMAT project explored novel strategies for low-resource machine translation, by considering the use of several types of external knowledge. The EXOMAT project designed: (1) a novel method for improving multilingual subword vocabularies; (2) a novel strategy for decoding based on recombination of fragments with a quality estimation criterion; and (3) a reasoning-based approach to translate inter-sentential dependencies with LLMs.  In addition, (4) EXOMAT contributed to a study of the use of reinforcement learning for data selection when training multilingual neural MT systems that include both high and low-resource languages. These tasks were carried out as the last part of a PhD thesis completed at EPFL, with additional support from a senior engineer with PhD. Two published papers and one paper under review summarize the achievements of EXOMAT.

Title: Effect of preterm birth on cortical dynamics of learning
Abstract:
Preterm birth is a leading cause for neurodevelopmental delays and has been associated with a large range of disorders including sensory processing, executive functions and emotional regulation. While a number of these impairments persist throughout adulthood, several studies reveal that behavioral compensation allows the individuals preterm (PT) to reach performance levels comparable to those born full-term (FT), and that the differences are only observable at the neural level. This suggests that the neural development of PT children follows distinct pathways from their FT counterparts, resulting in a delayed acquisition of skills and competences. The acquisition of any skill or behavior can be seen as an act of learning, whether it be implicit or explicit, relying on mechanisms of plasticity to transform the appropriate behavior from a cognitively demanding task into an automated response. To date, most imaging studies involving functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) on learning have focused on pre/post comparisons or quantifications of the involvement of individual brain areas, thus disregarding the dynamic, non-linear and inherently inter-areal nature of learning processes in the brain. In addition, while learning abilities have been assessed in PT children through standardized testing batteries, the neural correlates sustaining the acquisition of new behaviors has only been weakly studied in PT children. This proposal addresses this question through two main objectives: (1) Adapt analytic methods currently defined for the treatment of resting-state (RS) brain imaging data to task-based paradigms to capture the individual transients of learning in young healthy adults; and (2) leverage these methods to describe developmental differences in learning processes between FT and PT children. 
fMRI relying on blood oxygenation level dependent (BOLD) signal has proven to be a reliable non-invasive tool to study neural activity both at rest and during task execution highlighting among others, patterns of atypical brain development. However, most studies addressing the neural basis of learning have focused on the involvement of individual brain areas or have considered the inter-areal functional connectivity (FC), yet only in its static form, i.e. averaged across blocks of data acquisition. These approaches may be too simplistic to capture the intrinsically interregional and dynamically non-linear nature of learning processes. This project proposes to adapt two methods developed on RS data to task-based paradigms: the variability of the BOLD signal and the innovation-driven co-activation patterns framework (iCAPs). The variability of the BOLD signal has been associated with neural flexibility and knowledge representation, and could, therefore, be a marker for local plasticity. The iCAPs framework extracts large-scale, dynamic networks with temporal and spatial overlaps, thus describing network interactions in finer detail. Leveraging these methods will unveil unobserved aspects of learning and will generate a deeper understanding of the developmental processes specific to PT children. 
This project aims at studying for the first time the fine-grained dynamics of learning in a population affected by premature birth. The outcomes have the potential to impact several domains of in-vivo and translational research, with methodological developments in the field of dynamic brain imaging and characterization of the neural processes underlying learning in a broad sense in PT children.
Keywords: Functional connectivity, Motor learning, Preterm birth, Statistical learning, fMRI

Title: Multilayer taxonomy of nodal marginal zone lymphoma
Abstract:
The extranodal, splenic, and nodal MZL are the three main malignant disorders derived from marginal zone B-cells. They are recognized as separate entities by current classifications of lymphoid tissue tumors. While the clinicopathologic presentation, genetic characteristics, diagnostic definitions, and therapy of extranodal and splenic MZL are clearly characterized, the specific clinical, pathologic, and genetic aspects of NMZL remain largely undefined. The lack of typical markers makes NMZL diagnosis difficult, time-consuming, and not readily reproducible. The term NMZL currently includes a heterogeneous collection of cytologically distinct tumors, whose pathogenesis and biological features are incompletely understood. Moreover, NMZL are incurable tumors with no available specific clinical management. Their heterogeneity represents a barrier not only to the diagnosis but also to the successful deployment of novel, biologically targeted therapies. Molecular profiling studies have recently proposed new molecular classification systems for some lymphoma entities that are heterogeneous like NMZL. Hence, molecular subtyping is the next step in the precision medicine of lymphomas. Molecular subtypes can be delineated and validated through multilayer molecular profiling of the tumor coupled with machine-learning bioinformatics. They are ultimately defined by the most enriched combinations of genetic alterations and transcriptional subtypes.
The International Extranodal Lymphoma Study Group is a non-profit academic organization aimed at advancing biological studies to improve the treatment outcome of extranodal lymphomas. Investigators from more than 300 sites in Europe, Australia, North America, Latin America, and Asia have joined IELSG studies.
Here, we propose the IELSG52 study. It has a retrospective, observational, multicenter design and aims to recruit at least 500 pathologically confirmed NMZL biopsies and their clinical annotations. The IELSG52 study seeks to resolve the biological heterogeneity of NMZL into more homogeneous and manageable subgroups of tumors that rely on shared oncogenic programs.
The IELSG52 study is expected to produce insightful results that would:
- provide valuable aid in establishing the diagnosis and prognosis of NMZL
- enable the selection of optimal therapy for individual patients
- provide a biology-based framework for the design, conduct, and interpretation of clinical studies on novel targeted agents.

Title: Automation of pharmacometrics modeling by deducing mechanism-based models from neural ordinary differential equations
Abstract:
Mathematical-statistical modeling in pharmacology, also called pharmacometrics (PMX) modeling, is an interdisciplinary field that applies ordinary differential equations to support decision-making in drug development, and clinical practice. However, PMX modeling is in some sense an iterative trial-and-error process since several models are developed and tested to characterize the given data. Therefore, the current PMX modeling approach is time-consuming, labor-intensive, and consequently computationally costly, meaning it can be a bottleneck when it comes to drug development and clinical application.

Automation of modeling processes is a hot topic. However, current automation approaches just test standard PMX models and among those the “best” model is selected. But it is obvious that the best model is often not a standard model but a tailored modeled considering distinctive features of the patient population. As example, in neonates and especially in pre-term neonates, strong maturation processes occur that must be taken into account.

In this grant application, the main goal is to propose a PMX modeling automation workflow that (i) deduces automatically a tailored mechanism-based PMX model, and (ii) is less-time consuming and consequently less resource-intensive than current approaches. This is achieved by applying neural ordinary differential equations, i.e., differential equations with neural networks in the right-hand side, in a first step, allowing to learn the mechanism from the given data. However, since neural networks are in some sense a “black-box” and often have poor extrapolation capabilities, in the next step, the trained neural networks are applied to deduce a mechanism-based PMX model that no longer consists of neural networks. This is achieved by approximating the behavior of the neural networks with a combination of small PMX components in an automated workflow. Since we have the trained neural networks, our automated workflow entirely operates on a “derivative level”, i.e., solely utilizing the right-hand side of the differential equations. This tremendously reduces computational costs because no solving of the differential equation is necessary. 

The novelty of the proposed automation workflow based on neural ordinary differential equations is that, for a given patient population with distinctive features, it deduces automatically a tailored interpretable mechanism-based PMX model, and simultaneously strongly reduces computational costs. In summary, the proposed automation workflow might have two major advantages. First, it accelerates drug development. Second, it accelerates application of PMX models in clinical application, especially for populations where complex mechanisms, such as maturation processes in neonates, must be modeled.

Title: Microstructural Impacts of AI on Strategy Processes, Organizational Design, and Continuous Adaptation
Abstract: This research project comprises four interconnected studies examining how advanced artificial intelligence (AI)—specifically machine learning and generative AI—affects strategy processes, organizational design, and adaptation. Drawing upon the microstructural approach to organizing and recent findings on human-AI collaboration, we examine the implications of integrating AI technologies into organizational strategy-making and implementation processes. In different studies, we investigate how AI systems influence the formulation and adaptation of strategies, shape centralized and decentralized organizational structures, and impact managerial control and coordination. Furthermore, we analyze the broader organizational consequences, including effects on employee behavior and organizational culture. The project aims to advance the theoretical and practical understanding of how AI may contribute to the emergence of new organizational practices.

Title: Unified Navigation Framework for Embodied Reasoning
Abstract: This project aims to train a general-embodied navigation agent that bridges the gap between RL-based navigation and LLM-based semantic understanding and reasoning through our proposed Unified Navigation Framework (UNF). This framework results in a resilient, semantic, and commonsense-informed navigation policy, which can execute a wide range of navigation tasks. To train such a policy, we propose to generate a wide range of verifiable language-conditioned navigation tasks in simulation, and then train a set of navigation agents that require increased semantic understanding throughout the project. We specifically investigate the interplay of a low-level locomotion policy and a high-level LLM, where bi-directional information parsing and joint optimization are key research questions. In the final version of this project, we aim to discover emerging reasoning capabilities. The project is co-developed with the San Francisco Fire Department K9 unit to establish evaluation metrics and evaluate its capability in real-world search and rescue operations.
Keywords: Embodied Reasoning, Legged Robotics, Navigation, Reinforcement Learning

Title: The space in between: where local meets global in human vision
Abstract:
In the last seven decades, vision research has been heavily influenced by a framework where the visual scene is analyzed by a hierarchy of “filters” (Kruger et al. 2013; Hilgetag & Goulas 2020). Processing is largely feedforward and the filtering components operate independently of each other. For example, a visual scene is first analyzed by edge detectors in primary visual cortex V1, whose outputs project to higher and higher visual areas, eventually leading to object recognition in IT (DiCarlo et al 2012). At each area, local neural circuits compute basic aspects of visual processing, such as contrast, and operate independently of other circuits. This framework can account for many psychophysical phenomena, such as surround suppression and others (Morgan 2011). In addition, this architecture is extremely successful in computer vision where it forms the backbone of deep neural networks (Richards et al 2019), which can outperform humans in tasks such as object recognition (Weyand et al 2016).  
Because it is assumed that local circuits operate independently from each other, the majority of vision research uses simple stimulus displays with a single target or with a target and few extra elements (Morgan 2011). For example, observers may be asked to indicate the orientation of an isolated Gabor patch, and stimulus contrast is varied to understand how the Gabor is processed. Powerful techniques such as noise image classification can be used to characterize the underlying perceptual mechanisms in great detail (Ahumada 2002, Murray 2011, Neri, 2018). However, this approach fails when more complex stimuli are presented, as both Peter Neri and Michael Herzog have shown in the last decades coming from very different research directions (Neri 2011, 2014, 2017; reviews: Herzog et al., 2015; Herzog & Manassi, 2015).

Title: Welcome to the team Dr. Watson: New Roles and Responsibilities in AI-Supported Healthcare Teams
Abstract: Exponential growth in data generation and compute power combined with advances in machine learning have led to artificially intelligent applications (AI) that have the potential to outperform humans in various cognitive tasks. Researchers speak of a paradigm shift from “mind to machine” that will fundamentally change the way humans work. We do not know, however, how this change will affect professional roles, teamwork, and the distribution of control and responsibility between humans and AI within these new socio-technical-systems. In this study, we explore these questions in the example of healthcare teams (i.e., physicians and nurses), because there the potential opportunities but also the risks of AI are especially high. To this end, we also assess the viewpoints of various stakeholders (e.g., healthcare professionals, AI developers, patients, management, policy makers) to provide an all-around perspective. In sum, the proposed research will make significant contributions to science by exploring how effective work processes – and the technology to support these processes – can be best designed in unison while we still have leeway. The broader impact beyond science consists in providing managers, regulators, politicians, and the general public with the relevant knowledge to make informed decisions on the use of AI in current and future work systems.
Keywords: Artificial intelligence based decision-making, Digitalization, Human-system-integration, Professional roles in healthcare, Teamwork in healthcare

Title: Neural theories of compositional learning
Abstract:
Research summary
The overarching goal of the proposal is to develop neural models of compositionality—specifically, how to learn tasks by decomposing them into subtasks according to a task grammar. Aims 1 and 2 address increasingly complex task settings and their corresponding experimental predictions, while Aim 3 focuses on the most generalized case.
Aim 1: We will develop a neural model that decomposes motor tasks into sequences of simpler motor primitives, utilizing a combination of inverse and forward models. The inverse model will be trained to generate the parameters of motor primitives in response to specific goals, while the forward model will predict the outcomes of these motor primitives. This fully differentiable model will enable learning the appropriate combination of primitives without requiring explicit feedback. We argue that this form of compositional learning can considerably accelerate the acquisition of complex motor tasks, particularly through offline learning during sleep. The experimental predictions of this model will be tested in an escape task in rodents, developed by Tiago Branco, from UCL.
Aim 2: This aim explores how to learn tasks that can be interpreted as linear combinations of other tasks. We will assume the model has already acquired a set of related tasks and will investigate how it can learn new tasks through simple reinforcement learning and discrete hypothesis testing. This form of learning, for which there is experimental evidence even in animals, has largely been neglected. To test the experimental predictions of this approach, we will collaborate with Valentina Borghesani at the University of Geneva, using brain imaging in human subjects.
Aim 3: In the third aim, we will expose a recurrent neural network (RNN) to a set of tasks generated by a task grammar applied to a set of behavioral primitives. This time, no prior learning will be assumed. The goal is for the network to discover both the behavioral primitives and the associated grammar without explicit feedback. We predict that learning of new tasks from the same grammar will be greatly accelerated in models that explicitly learn and represent the grammar and the subtasks involved in task generation. The work will rely on a dual architecture with an action RNN in charge of generating the behavior and a context RNN responsible for learning the task grammar. 
By focusing on non-linguistic compositional representations in animals, this work might shed new light on the neural basis of what led to the emergence of natural language in humans.
Keywords: compositional, compositionality, general intelligence, grammar, hypothesis testing, modularity, neural learning, predictive coding, recurrent neural networks

Title: Towards understanding fish swimming patterns in critical flow
Abstract:
River fragmentation and channelization reduce the aquatic biodiversity and impede fish migration. Adaptation of river restoration measures to accommodate hydraulic requirements of the fish during their migration can help mitigate environmental impacts. Greater understanding of the mechanism that underpin how fluid-structure interactions affect fish swimming and behaviour is required to enhance restoration measures adapted to the hydraulic requirements of fish. Modern flow visualisation and measurement techniques allow fine resolution observation of fish kinematics and simultaneous flow measurements. Such techniques can provide insights into the fine-scale mechanisms of fish swimming under standardized conditions and reveal the influence of complex hydrodynamics, e.g. vortices, on fish propulsion. How fish behave at larger-scales, and adapt their swimming routes to navigate critical flow fields (zones of complex flow, where water velocities partially exceed fish swimming speeds), remain poorly understood. Such understanding allows for adaptation of renaturation measures in rivers to the swimming requirements of selected target species. 

Recent technological advance now enables the use of Infrared light Particle Image Velocimetry (IR PIV), which is not visible by fish. IR PIV will help map complex flow fields while at the same time enable fish swimming behaviour to be captured using IR cameras. We assume that ca. 100 rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss Walbaum, 1792) will modify their swimming behaviour at three different flow fields (treatments) to enhance their locomotory performance. Multiple descriptors of the recorded fish swimming trajectories (e.g. location, swimming speed, swim path length, sinuosity) will be computed and used to train a Random Forest model for prediction of the flow treatments and to identify swimming patterns as similar response of multiple fish to specific flow conditions (Objective 1). Further, we will use Generalised Linear Models (GLMs) to identify which flow factors (e.g., water velocity, flow direction, eddy size and number) predict trajectory descriptors to explore the relationship between flow and swimming patterns (Objective 2). Finally, we will predict swimming routes of the fish for the given flow regimes of the treatments using the flow data to train an Artificial Neural Network (Objective 3) on the swimming trajectories recorded. Artificial Neural Networks capable of predicting the swimming trajectories of fish in flow fields would be a breakthrough achievement because they can use complex swimming patterns and generalize on previously unseen data for prediction of expected swimming routes. Therefore, our findings will form the basis of Artificial Intelligence-based tools for assessing flow in newly designed hydraulic structures (such as fish passes). Such tools will describe the hydraulic effect of such structures on the swimming behaviour of target species without testing on live fish, and thereby reduce the need to use animals in experiments by replacing them through computer simulation.

This experiment applies modern, state of the art approaches to investigate swimming behaviour in response to complex flow and opens the innovative research field of swimming pattern analysis. We will build basic evidence needed to better understand the underlying mechanisms of performance enhancing swimming patterns exhibited when fish are challenged under complex flow regimes and the importance of swimming routes for successful negotiation of the flow fields. These findings will open up new avenues of research in the field of animal movement using modern technologies, such as Artificial Intelligence (AI). Our findings will contribute to the conservation of biodiversity by advancing evidence-based river restoration that accounts for the impact of flowing water on the swimming behaviour of fish.

Title: New Algorithmic Building Blocks and Benchmarks for RandomizedOptimization Heuristics (AlgoBench)
Abstract:
Context:
Optimization plays a pivotal role in a myriad of domains ranging from logistics and engineering to artificial intelligence. While exact solving techniques are effective for certain problems, complex scenarios often necessitate alternative approaches. Randomized Optimization Heuristics (ROHs), including evolutionary algorithms, estimation-of-distribution algorithms or simulated annealing, have emerged as versatile tools for solving these complex optimization challenges. Runtime analysis of ROHs on theoretical benchmarks has proven a fruitful way to deepen our understanding of ROHs, and has lead to several algorithmic ideas from the PI and others that have entered optimization portfolios like Nevergrad, which is an open portfolio of ROHs developed by Facebook Research in collaboration with the research community. 

Objectives:
This project aims at advancing and improving the pipeline from theoretical insights to practical applications through two work packages (WPs), each to be addressed by one PhD student. Firstly, the last years have revealed several failure modes of ROHs. This opens the possibility of improving our optimization portfolios by designing new algorithmic building blocks to mitigate these failure modes. Due to our solid understanding of these failure modes, this may introduce new algorithmic ideas that are not in the standard toolset of ROHs. WP1 is dedicated to the development, analysis, and implementation and integration of these building blocks into the IOHprofiler framework, which is an open framework which allows researchers and practitioners to easily access these building blocks. 

Secondly, for turning theoretical insights into practical success it is important that the theoretical benchmarks on which ROHs are analyzed capture well the landscapes of real problem, albeit in a simplified way. The community has developed an informal suite of theoretical benchmarks that represent certain types of landscapes. For example, OneMax is representative for an easy hill-climbing task, LeadingOnes for a harder hill-climbing task, Jump for a landscape with a misleading gradient, and so on. While the suite of theoretical benchmarks is adequate for many types of landscapes, the PI and other groups have identified one particular weakness in the last years: local optima are represented by only a handful of frequently studied theoretical benchmarks, and these benchmarks do not represent the full spectrum of local optima that may occur in practice. Based on some recent developments, WP2 thus aims at developing new theoretical benchmarks for local optima in a more systematic way, and to develop an understanding for how various ROHs can cope with them.

Impact and Relevance:
The proposed research stands to significantly impact both the theoretical understanding and practical application of ROHs. The new algorithmic building blocks will improve our optimization portfolios, thus improving our ability of optimization. The new benchmarks will deepen our understanding of ROHs in the context of local optima, and will improve our ability to bring theoretical insights into practice. Moreover, the algorithmic building blocks and the new benchmarks are likely of a nature that introduces a stronger history-dependence into the optimization process than current techniques can deal with. Thus, part of the proposal is also to develop new methods to cope with dependent random processes and improve our capabilities for the analysis of ROHs.

Title: Hybrid Creativity: How Artificial Intelligence Can Defy or Reinforce Human Creative Performance
Abstract:
One popular and highly successful strategy for spurring innovation in private and public organizations is to integrate consumers and external stakeholders into the innovation process (Afuah and Tucci 2012; Chesbrough 2003; Poetz and Schreier 2012). Eighty-five percent of the 100 most valued brands already use digital platforms such as OpenIdea, Crowdspring, HYVE Crowd or proprietary platforms such as LEGO ideas (eYeka 2015; LEGO 2021). 
Although these digital platforms are widely used, human behavior still hinders them from performing to their full innovation potential. In this project we focus on three vexing behavioral barriers to human creativity endemic to digital platforms. First, people tend to suffer from cognitive fixation, that is, we have difficulty letting go of previously seen common concepts and ideas (Hofstetter et al. 2020a; Smith et al. 1993). Second, we tend to follow a path of least resistance when generating ideas and do not step out of it if not externally required (Moreau and Dahl 2005). Third, when selecting ideas, we tend to suffer from novelty aversion, rejecting highly original ideas because they are associated with greater evaluation uncertainty and are thus more frequently rejected (Girotra et al. 2010). These three barriers significantly reduce the quality of ideas that come out of digital innovation platforms.
AI may offer a way out of these three traps. For instance, using transformer or generative adversarial neural networks, AI approaches can better explore solution spaces without cognitive limitations, offering inspirational input to humans that can enable them to overcome cognitive fixation. Until now, however, these opportunities have been under-researched.
The goal of this project is to complement behavioral science research on human creativity with recent developments in AI to find ways to overcome the three aforementioned barriers to human creativity. We investigate a “hybrid creativity” approach, in which humans and machines interact in novel ways that can improve joint creative performance, and ask, “How can we best use AI to improve human creativity?” Guided by this main research question, we will conduct three related sub-projects, all aiming at publication in top-tier scientific journals in the fields of marketing and management.
Conceptually, we draw on behavioral theories related to the three barriers such as SIAM model (Nijstad and Stroebe 2006), the Geneplore model of creativity (Finke et al. 1992), self-efficacy theory (Bandura 1997), and distraction-conflict theory (Baron 1986). Drawing on these theories, we argue that AI approaches can both help overcoming these barriers and harm individual creative performance on digital innovation platforms. Understanding how AI could help us will allow us to design meaningful interventions that aim to improve human creative performance on platforms. The deliverables of this research project are 1) an understanding of psychological mechanisms of hybrid creativity and actionable interventions that should be considered when AI is intended to increase individual creative performance and 2) exemplary AI tools are publicly available, implementable, and testable on innovation platforms. We strive to publish the results of our research in leading journals of the fields of marketing or information systems research, such as the Journal of Marketing Research, Marketing Science, Information Systems Research, or Management Science.
Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Consumer behavior, Consumer creativity, Digital innovation, Technology perception
