Title: Functional Causal Models for Multivariate Extremes
Abstract:
In the last years statistical modeling of extreme events has gained a lot of interest. These events may occur in many different sectors, often with dramatic consequences. Some examples are flooding, heat waves, extreme wind speeds and rainfalls, epidemics, drought or famine periods and the financial crises started in the 2008, when many operators went bankrupt at the same time. In all these cases it is fundamental for governments and regulators to understand deeply the underlying processes, taking into account how the different factors interact with each other. Moreover, it is important to detect causes that may facilitate extreme events, as well as to develop methods to predict such extremes in the future with the aim to put in place the best measures to minimize their impact. The mathematical and statistical challenges emerge from the highly nonlinear (causal) dependencies that occur between extremes, and from the fact that an extreme event can be caused by the interaction and summation of many variables. These subtleties, if missed, can lead to wrong conclusions and eventually to an underestimation of the real risk involved. Extreme value theory is a widely used tool to model extreme events and many advances have been made in the recent years to cope with the multivariate case. Its practical use in complex situations still remains challenging.

The objective of this project is to link functional causal models with extreme value theory as a powerful tool to overcome these limitations. Functional causal models are an alternative to Bayesian networks that permit to model complex dependencies taking advantage of powerful techniques already used in the machine learning community. They can further be used to discover causal relations between the variables under analysis and answer to counterfactual queries. The project is divided into two parts, each of which applies the proposed methodology to a different field. In the first one, I will study functional causal models for space-time modeling of extremes to monitor extreme occurrences in space and time in order to correct the system only when it is necessary. Furthermore, the causal nature of the estimated model will suggest which actions are the most recommendable to minimize the risk of severe consequences. In the second part, I will use functional causal models in the context of climate change attribution and attribution of extreme events to infer to what extent human and natural forcing impact climate extremes. Following some previous line of work, I will use only observational data and historical records, instead of relying on computational intensive and idealised simulations from computer-based models. When causal inference is performed using observational data only is fundamental to determine under which assumptions the causal structure of the phenomena of interest can be fully identified and this will be a crucial objective of the project.

The successfully application of functional causal models in the context of multivariate modeling of extreme events will help to spread the use of machine learning techniques in the extreme value community and in many fields of practical applications.
Keywords: causal infernece, climate change attribution, extreme value theory, machine learning, statistical methods

Title: TRUST-ME: TRUstworthy enhancement of job SaTisfaction and productivity using Micro-sensing in work Environments
Abstract:
For almost a century, employee productivity and job satisfaction have been a topic of interest. They are sometimes in conflict, with employers pursuing productivity at the expense of employee satisfaction. Other times they are aligned, as satisfied employees tend to be more productive, and employees that feel productive are usually satisfied. Over the years, awareness of the importance of good work conditions for physical and mental health has grown, and legislation to protect workers has followed. However, new concerns such as precarious employment (i.e., the “gig-economy”) have also led to increased stress and worsened mental health among the workforce. Technology has seemingly tipped the scales the wrong way in recent years. Today, so-called “technological supervision” – the automated management of employee schedules, from warehouse staff to hotel housekeepers to software developers, in a quest to maximize efficiency – is increasingly creating physical and mental exhaustion among those managed in this way. The COVID-19 pandemic, with the increase in remote work, has only exacerbated these problems. There is thus a need for approaches that increase productivity, job satisfaction, and employee well-being without sacrificing one for the other.
Recent developments in sensing technology (e.g., video- and audio-based and wearable sensors) and advanced artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms are promising personalized digital tools for monitoring well-being and boosting productivity. At the same time, awareness of privacy issues and the possibility of unpredictable and undesirable outcomes of AI have grown, prompting interest in the development of privacy-preserving technology and trustworthy AI. By combining expertise in sensing technology, privacy, user experience design, and explainable AI, this project will develop a new approach for monitoring job satisfaction, wellbeing, and productivity. The project will (1) offer insights into the complex relations at work in AI-driven privacy-aware workplace monitoring and (2) create powerful yet explainable AI that provides actionable productivity insights.
The TRUST-ME project will utilize the expertise from two separate institutions. Swiss partner USI has expertise in security, privacy, and trustworthy AI. Slovenian partner JSI has expertise in machine learning for sensing and modeling psycho-physiological constructs, including employee wellbeing. The proposed project will thus explore the problem domain via two critical strands of investigation: (1) multimodal monitoring and modeling of job satisfaction and productivity (led by JSI) and (2) multimodal, secure, private, and explainable AI for productivity assessment (lead by USI). 
The first strand will employ physically unobtrusive workplace sensors for knowledge workers, such as computers (which can sense typing patterns, mouse movement, and application usage), cameras, and eye trackers. These will be used to obtain psychological constructs of interest, e.g., satisfaction, wellbeing, engagement, self-perceived productivity, and affect. We will model these constructs' interrelation using multi-modal sensor inputs and multiple sources of ground truth based on novel deep-learning methods involving deep supervision and bi-directional learning. This approach will represent the problem domain more accurately, alleviating the impact of noise in ground truth otherwise obtained via (subjective) questionnaires.
The second strand will implement tools and techniques for maximizing user security and privacy in this context, including quality and integrity of data, access to data, and adequate privacy and confidentiality controls. We will use federated learning to build models on user-trusted local devices instead of sending potentially sensitive user data to a central location (where employers could misuse it). Additionally, we will develop multimodal explainable AI methods to provide transparency and end-user understandable reasons for the findings of the TRUST-ME models. We will exploit this to create a dashboard that will provide users with insights into their well-being and productivity while clarifying how the system came to these conclusions. Both employees and employers will receive information at the right granularity without intruding on employees’ privacy. TRUST-ME will lay the foundation for future sensing interventions to improve job satisfaction and productivity while respecting ethical values such as privacy and autonomy. 
Both strands of the investigation will come together in a validation study with academic knowledge workers, software developers, and administrative staff. This study will provide inputs into the design of the TRUST-ME approach, data for training and evaluating the machine-learning models, and feedback on the dashboard presenting their outputs.
Keywords: explainable AI (XAI), federated learning, human-centered computing, job satisfaction, machine learning, productivity, sensors, trustworthy AI

Title: The role of diffuse radiation for a long-term arable crop rotation at Oensingen, Switzerland (Acronym: DiRad Oensingen)
Abstract:
Relevance — Diffuse radiation plays an important role for ecosystem productivity. However, its effect on the cropland C budget is largely unknown. Global crop yield modeled by Mercado et al. (2009) indicate a 25% increase in the net carbon sink due to increased diffuse radiation during the years 1960–1999. However, direct field measurements are scarce. Thus, these model results clearly stress the need for validation with in-depth experimental field measurements as proposed here.
Overall Aim — The overall aim is to improve our understanding of how diffuse radiation affects the CO2 budget as well as the water use efficiency of crops. We will test and develop an integrated method with long-term as well as intensive field campaign measurements at one representative arable site in Switzerland (Oensingen CH-Oen2).
Working Hypotheses — We aim at answering the two major questions: (1) How large are the differences in growth response to diffuse radiation among crop types?; and (2) Why is the observed response to diffuse radiation so variable between crop types? To answer these questions, we will test three working hypotheses:
1.The effect of diffuse radiation on growth and thus net ecosystem productivity depends on crop type. This will be tested at the Oensingen flux site (arable site) using the typical crops in its crop rotation (winter wheat; winter barley; rapeseed; potatoes; peas/beans).
2.On days with clear sky but high loads of aerosols, net ecosystem productivity shows the largest enhancement due to the increased fraction of diffuse radiation.
3.On an ecosystem scale, the relevance of diffuse light conditions is most pronounced during peak growth when concurrent improvements of water use efficiency (WUE) are expected under diffuse light conditions.
Methodical Approach — The proposed PostDoc candidate has developed a novel data mining approach to disentangle the climatic effect from the ecosystem properties and to understand the biophysical mechanisms that drive photosynthesis in relation to available diffuse and direct radiation. This approach uses an artificial neural network in combination with existing long-term data that are complemented with intensive field surveys during two cropping seasons a the Oensingen arable flux site, Switzerland.
Expected Value of the Proposed Project — Improved functional understanding of crop responses to diffuse radiation that can be used by mechanistic simulation models to adequately represent the C cycle of European croplands; quantitative assessment of the effect of diffuse radiation on gross primary productivity, evapotranspiration, and their ratio WUE.
Keywords: Crop growth, Diffuse radiation, Net ecosystem productivity, Water use efficiency

Title: Interpretable artificial intelligence for computational biology: extracting new insights from single-cell proteomic data.
Abstract:
Since its reintroduction in seminal works by Bengio and others, deep learning has become one of the most active fields in machine learning, with astounding performance in a broad area of applications such as computer vision, speech recognition and natural language processing. However, with the improving performance of artificial intelligence (AI), the community has come to realize that for a model to be trusted, it must be not only accurate, but also explainable. Simply put, if users do not trust a model or a prediction, they will not use it, especially in a sensitive domain such as health care. 

This proposal focuses on demonstrating how Interpretable Artificial Intelligence can lead to the generation of new biological insights in computational biology, a flourishing field where the recent application of deep neural networks (DNNs) to long-standing problems such as the prediction of functional DNA sequences, the inference of protein-protein interactions or the detection of cancer cells in histopathology images has brought a break-through in performance and prediction power. However, despite initial achievements, many of these models are built as black-boxes and have failed to provide new biological insights. This project rests on the recent demonstration that interpretable approaches can shed light on the underlying biological principles driving model decisions. 

Our application area will be the analysis of single-cell mass cytometry (CyTOF) data from tumor samples. CyTOF technology is achieving tremendous high throughput in the number of profiled cells, with some of the most recent datasets consisting of millions of single cells. In this project, we will develop state-of-the-art deep learning networks to model CyTOF data, and use recent methodologies developed at IBM Research – Zürich on automatic architecture-search in order to optimize the architectures and hyperparameters and identify the best performing model for each learning task with a minimal computational effort. We will develop novel interpretable approaches exploiting different conceptual approaches. For instance, we will investigate how to produce disentangled representations that clearly and disjointly map latent and data generative factors. We will also explore architecture-constraint models, which can enhance the interpretability of certain components of the network. Finally, we will investigate parallels with Lagrangian mechanics in physics and develop approaches to identify invariances that can highlight underlying mechanisms. 

We will validate the generated explanations first through a literature search, to rule out unlikely explanations, and then through experimental perturbation experiments, which  will be performed by Prof. Bernd Bodenmiller’s lab, a pioneer of the development and application of mass cytometry to tumor profiling and a long-established collaborator of the group of computational biology at IBM Research – Zürich. In summary, this research programme will provide an in-depth understanding of how new biological insight can be extracted cumbersome deep learning models, and how interpretability approaches can deepen our understanding of the mechanisms driving key biological processes.
Keywords: cancer, computational biology, deep learning, interpretable artificial intelligence, knowledge extraction, single-cell proteomics

Title: Multidimensional polarization and its consequences for democracy in Europe
Abstract:
A key feature of politics today is its multidimensionality. Historically, a single dimension between left and right has been used to capture (the mainly economic) ideological differences in society. However, from the 1970s onwards, a second dimension of political conflict has emerged in most European countries. With the advent of new political parties and issues, an opposition has materialized over cultural issues, such as immigration. As a result, party polarization—or the degree to which political parties disagree ideologically—is now multidimensional, and the continued use of a single left-right dimension obscures a more complex, fragmented political landscape.

But what are the consequences of multidimensional polarization for the functioning of democracy? I argue that multidimensional polarization could diffuse ideological conflict across different, cross-cutting dimensions. At the same time, this increased complexity may undermine established party-voter relations, as new ideological disagreements are brought to the fore. Thus, multidimensional polarization is potentially a double-edged sword, lowering partisan hostility but at the cost of decreased political engagement. 

Although the multidimensionality of voter and party preferences is now widely accepted, existing studies of polarization continue to rely on a one-dimensional left-right conception and operationalization of party disagreement. This is a surprising disconnect, given Europe’s well-documented history of societal division, party system fragmentation, and electoral volatility. As a result, despite its undeniable normative implications, we do not know the consequences of multidimensional polarization for democracy.

My proposal develops an ambitious research agenda that focuses on three core aims, which are tackled in three related work packages (WPs): [1] to map multidimensional polarization among political parties across Europe (1970–present), and to analyze its consequences for [2] political engagement (e.g., voter turnout) and [3] partisan hostility (or affective polarization). It will do so through a mixed approach that combines innovative statistical methods (e.g., machine learning; WP1), observational analyzes across more than 20 European countries (WP2+WP3), and panel data studies (WP2) and experimental research designs (WP3) in country case studies. The project’s output will consist of high-impact publications, a comprehensive dataset for public use, initiatives for international collaboration and network-building, and public outreach about societally relevant questions.

This Ambizione project makes clear theoretical, empirical, and normative contributions. It provides a novel theoretical argument about the consequences of party polarization in a multidimensional political landscape, offers cutting-edge studies that will provide much needed data and measurement instruments for future research, and enhances our understanding of the desirable and undesirable ramifications of multidimensional polarization for democracy in Europe.
Keywords: Europe, democracy, dimensionality, polarization, political parties, turnout

Title: In vivo and in vitro structural analysis of flagellar/ciliary motors and regulators
Abstract:
Eukaryotic flagella and motile cilia are bending organelle powered by ATP-driven microtubule-based sliding of dynein. However the molecular mechanism of flagellar/ciliary bending is still unclear. More than 400 component proteins are known, but many of them have not been characterized. Dynein, the key motor protein, has a variety of isoforms and each isoform has a fixed locus on the 96nm periodic unit in flagella/cilia, as we proved in the past study. However we do not know the meaning of these isoforms in the context of motility yet. Biochemical studies revealed a number of regulatory pathways in flagella/cilia: phosphorylation, calcium. However, the molecular mechanism of regulation must be still investigated. Here in this application, we propose structural studies of flagella/cilia and component molecules (dyneins and regulators) both in vivo and in vitro. 
To elucidate flagellar/ciliary bending mechanism, we need structural biology at various scales: from single dynein molecule to the molecular networks inside the entire flagella/cilia. Our group has been working on 3D structural analysis of dyneins and regulatory proteins in vivo in flagella/cilia, using cryo-electron tomography and 3D image analysis (3D image averaging and classification). We succeeded to map dynein isoforms in flagella, which demonstrated the fixed position for each isoform, conformation of dyneins and its change induced by nucleotides as well as the structure of the radial spoke, a complex of signal transducers to dynein. These findings present highly integrated nature of this organelle and usefulness of cryo-EM technique to elucidate the bending mechanism. In this application, our proposal will go beyond and cover widely from atomic resolution crystallography of individual regulatory proteins, which form large complex (radial spokes and the central pair apparatus) in flagella, single particle analysis from cryo-EM to visualize entire radial spoke complexes, dyneins interacting with microtubule at pseudo-atomic resolution, and in vivo 3D visualization of dyneins in the various stages of motility and regulation, using cryo-electron tomography and further development of image classification technique. The project involves biochemical analysis for purification and antibody production to label proteins in flagella/cilia and identify them in microscopic/tomographic images.
Our research will enable characterization of single dynein molecule, crosstalk of two heads of dynein dimer, integration of dynein isoforms into complexes (dynein arms), functional mechanisms of such regulators as radial spokes and central pair apparatus, and entire networking of these molecules in the axoneme, mainly from the structural aspect.
Keywords: axoneme, cilia, cryo-EM, crystallography, electron tomography, flagella, motor protein

Title: Robust structure learning of Bayesian networks
Abstract:
Bayesian networks mix graphs and probabilities in order to perform reasoning under uncertainty. Their main advocate, Judea Pearl, has been awarded in 2011 the prestigious "ACM Turing Award" because, among other things, "this work not only revolutionized the field of artificial intelligence but also became an important tool for many other branches of engineering and the natural sciences". The graph of a Bayesian network describes the dependence relations between the variables in a domain, while its (probabilistic) parameters encode their strengths. A Bayesian net can be learned from data, be queried to assess the probability of events given observations, and help on decision making.

For Bayesian networks to be successful, a crucial, and a very challenging, task that must often be addressed is how to learn the dependency graph (the "structure") from data. This is typically achieved by searching the space of graphs while trying to optimize a score that measures how well a graph fits the data (or other domain knowledge).

Structure learning has been, and still is, the subject of intense, cutting-edge, research. At present time, there are very sophisticated algorithms for this task. However, these methods fall short to consider the reliability of their results. Two undesired outcomes are then possible: (i) that there is a structure with a slightly better fit than the others, but which is heavily prone to structural changes under small variations in the data (or personal beliefs); (ii) that there are many structures with similar score that lead to different outcomes in applications, so that the choice among them is highly arbitrary. Problem (i) is severe in applications, such as genomics, where the focus is often on understanding the underlying mechanism that should be modeled by the network. Problem (ii) negatively affects the application of Bayesian networks to prediction as in the data-mining task of "pattern classification", because structures with similar score can, in some cases, lead to quite different prediction accuracy.

In this project we aim at developing reliable (or "robust") structure learning methods. Our standpoint is that to achieve reliability, we should have methods able to infer from data, and work with, multiple candidate structures. In this we are inspired by the field of "imprecise" (or "credal") probability, where it is widely acknowledged that robustness is entangled with sets of models (and in particular sets of probability distributions). We will proceed according to the following plan:

- We will start by studying current methods for structure learning and the reliability of their results, through *sensitivity analysis of optimal structures*. The idea is to understand which characteristics can be borrowed from them.

- We will *develop algorithms that deliver sets of candidate structures*. To this end, we will first deliver new, state-of-the-art, algorithms for the traditional case of (standard) structure learning. Then we will work upon them for our set-based methods using k-best ideas (i.e., finding the k most-probable structures) when the focus is on precise probability, as well as imprecise-probability criteria, such as maximality (which will yield the more structures the less information in the data).

- We will *develop robust score functions and models based on imprecise probability*. We will employ decision criteria such as "maximum entropy" and "maximin" in order to produce a single, robust, structure out of the multiple ones when this has to be the case. We will also keep on working with multiple structures and, whenever needed, probabilistically average over them (by "credal model averaging" in the case of maximality, and Bayesian model averaging in the k-best case).

- We will *extend the above methods to the case of incomplete data*. Few approaches handle missing data to date. 

- We will develop these methods with (some) *accuracy guarantees, and we will formally study their complexity*.

- We will *specialize robust structure learning to problems of multi-label classification* (where an object can belong to multiple categories). Current methods are still limited in this.

- We will *apply robust structure learning to genomic and clinical real data sets*. Working with these data sets is especially relevant, because dealing with incomplete and multi-label data is often unavoidable. Also, by using more reliable procedures, we intend to improve on current methods, yielding results that have pratical impact.
Keywords: Averaging, Bayesian networks, Credal and multi-label classification, Imprecise probability, Multiple models, Robustness, Structure learning

Title: Generalized Positional Encoding for Machine Learning
Abstract:
In the last few years, the progress in Machine Learning (ML) has been overwhelming, with application milestones in nearly all fields of Science and Engineering. This astonishing success is very largely due to a shift in paradigm from extracting handcrafted features to automated representation learning, i.e letting ML handle the whole pipeline from learning a good representation of data to feeding it into a classifier/predictor/regressor. 

But representation learning has its drawbacks. First, in order to learn the structure of each data sample, algorithms need to be exposed to massive amount of data where they can pick up correlations and build patterns. This requires the capacity to collect and curate data at ever larger scale, which raises several problems. On one hand, only few actors have the capacity to crawl internet scale datasets. For some applications, data in such quantity is simply not available, a problem some look to solve by using large pre-trained "Foundation Models" in the hope they will become generic enough and can be fine-tuned to expressive representations for any task. On the other hand, even in the unlikely event such  datasets would become openly available, the energy and, ultimately, environmental cost of the necessary computing infrastructure weakens our pretense to a sustainable future. 

In the event the data is structured, in the sense that it is expressed over a structured domain (images, videos, graphs, sequences of symbols ...), we can leverage the known structure into effective inductive biases that dramatically increases the efficiency of learning models. Even large scale pre-trained transformers leverage structure - when available - via positional encoding of tokens. However, structure cannot always help. First, there are large amounts of data that do not exhibit any pre-defined structure. Second, the underlying structured domain might be partially or fully unknown or very noisy. In these cases, there is simply no a priori well-defined inductive biases. Third and finally, data is most often a mix of structure and attributes and the latter do not necessarily correlate well with the underlying domain leading to poor performances even with good inductive biases.

In this project we will explore new ways to do representation learning by exploiting the intrinsic structure of datasets, aiming at designing new ML algorithms and systems that are less data hungry and can deal with highly misaligned structure and features (heterophily). Taking inspiration from graph neural networks, intrinsic neural representations and transformer architectures, we will construct and study a new theory of data-driven operators that can be used to understand the structure of data and exploit it efficiently thanks to novel generalized positional encoding. We will then aim at designing an efficient numerical implementation of this technique into novel ML systems and benchmark their efficiency on key tasks.
Keywords: artificial intelligence, machine learning, neural networks, spectral methods

Title: Hippocampal rhythms underlying local and non-local reinforcement learning
Abstract:
Background: Adaptive behavior requires learning which actions are more likely to result in beneficial outcomes. Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a powerful framework for understanding how we learn the relationship between actions and outcomes either directly or from inferred (i.e., not directly experienced) associations based on an acquired model of the environment. In humans, such local and non-local forms of learning (often also referred to as model-free and model-based, respectively), are linked to midbrain dopaminergic activity including the functions of target projection regions such as ventral and dorsal striatum, sectors of pre-frontal cortex and hippocampus (Daw et al., 2005; Dolan & Dayan, 2013, Wunderlich et al., 2012). 
A persistent question in cognitive neuroscience is how the brain links immediate rewards to past or inferred events, the ‘so-called’ credit assignment problem. A candidate mechanism is hippocampal neuronal replay, a phenomenon whereby neural activity elicited by previously experienced events is sequentially reactivated during states such as sleep and rest (Liu et al., 2019, Schuck & Niv, 2021, Singer et al., 2009, Ambrose et al., 2016, Igata et al., 2021). Recent human evidence from the host lab showed local and non-local learning are supported by different expressions of replay, with different spatio-temporal characteristics (Liu et al., 2021). Yet, the temporal organization of replay within ongoing brain oscillatory activity, and particularly in the human hippocampus, remains unknown. More specifically, the role of high-frequency “ripple” (100-200Hz) and theta (4-8Hz) oscillations - two major hippocampal-related rhythms linked to memory consolidation processes - in RL has not been examined. Additionally, whereas previous studies provide evidence linking deep brain oscillatory activity to RL, the causal role of specific hippocampal rhythms has not been established.

Aims: In this proposal, I will develop a multimodal approach combining associative neuro-imaging (WP1) and causal manipulation of hippocampal activity (WP2) to study the functional role of specific patterns of oscillatory activity in relation to local and non-local RL. 

Methods: In WP1, I will investigate the temporal relationship between hippocampal replay and brain oscillatory activity during local and non-local learning. Here I will avail of existing magneto-encephalography (MEG) data and computational characterization of associated behavior (Liu et al., 2021; n = 29), as well as existing methods pioneered by the host lab (Liu, et al., 2021; Higgins et al., 2021). In WP2, I will investigate the causal role of specific hippocampal rhythms in local and non-local RL in healthy humans (n = 30), exploiting transcranial temporal interference stimulation (tTIS), a non-invasive brain stimulation technology, allowing focal stimulation of deep brain regions (Vassiliadis et al., 2024, Wessel et al., 2023), including the hippocampus (Violante et al., 2023). 

Results: Based on previous literature, I expect to find associative (WP1) and causal (WP2) evidence for an involvement of high-frequency “ripple” and theta oscillations in local and non-local learning, respectively.

Impact: This dual, associative and causal approach can provide fundamental insights into the potential coordinating role of specific deep brain rhythms in RL, opening a horizon for their modulation in patient populations with impaired RL, for example compulsive disorders.
Keywords: electro-encephalography, hippocampus, magneto-encephalography, memory, oscillations, reinforcement learning, replay, reward, transcranial temporal interference stimulation

Title: Learning Shape Perception
Abstract:
The field of artificial intelligence is currently experiencing its second big rise. The current success is mainly based on recent advances in machine learning and pattern recognition algorithms as well as the growth of datasets. In the machine learning community this lead to a redefinition of hard problems in the field. Current face processing systems, for example, are inefficient in two particular ways - they need a lot of data and they cannot generalize well to new tasks. Human intelligence, learning, and perception are still far from being in reach for current systems. Humans learn to solve a lot of tasks during their life and they can easily adapt to new tasks with no or very little additional training data. We can, for example, answer novel questions we did not explicitly train on, like what is the number of birthmarks on the left cheek or tell what is unique about the lips of a person. This shows a huge gap between human learning and machine learning. Computational models for human perception and learning are a step in this direction. In this research project, we will build such a model on the developmental trajectory of human face perception and contribute to close this gap.
Our contribution is, to build a novel learning strategy that mimics human learning. Since human learning itself is not understood, building such a model includes theory and a computational model of human learning. To focus on the theoretical and computational part of this challenge we will focus on shape perception of faces in particular since face perception is very well studied across all age groups. In the literature, there are experiments with infants and toddlers as well as with young and older adults [10]. Research results suggest that face perception is still improving in the early 30s. Not only faces, but also the visual system to process image input is well-studied and we can build on the results of those studies.
We will base our research on recent results on face perception supporting inverse graphics in biological face processing. We will build upon this system which is a combination of deep learning and generative models based on statistical shape models and computer graphics with one major change - an additional parametrization of the generative model to change the complexity of the model. We define the complexity of the model by the details it contains (model resolution), by its flexibility (statistical) and by the rendering process (image formation). This enables to mimic increasing visual acuity, depth perception, color vision, sensitivity to contrast and illumination in the visual system from infants to adults as well as adding complexity to the model early on, as well as in later stages.
We expect the following benefits of this additional parametrization from a machine learning perspective: the initial simpler model bootstraps the later learning steps in a curriculum learning sense and enables self-teaching, which results in improved performance on the machine learning side. Additionally, from the perspective of biological face processing, we will evaluate if this model, with increasing complexity during the learning process, fits neural processing data in non-human primates better than previous models.
To summarize, in this research project we will:
- synthesize the results of cognitive and neuroscience research with face models of different complexity.
- extend a current generative face model with additional parameters to vary complexity in both rendering and modeling.
- train such a model with curriculum learning by continuously increasing its complexity.
- combine self-supervision with a continuous curriculum learning approach.
- evaluate the overall model by its fit to behavioral and neural human data.
The desired outputs of this research project are more efficient machine learning strategies for inverse rendering, based on insights from the learning process in humans for face perception. We will evaluate the final model not only by its inverse rendering performance but also on how well it fits behavioral and neural data.

Title: Negentropic Explorations of Radio: Alloys of Matter and Information
Abstract: This project proposes a humanities exploration of machine learning techniques, using methods characteristic for art and design research. Starting from an ambition to address the persistent and foundational dualism in modern thinking (e.g. nature – culture, subject - object, mind - body), the project engages with technology and computation in an experimental way. The experience of working with machine learning algorithms opens up a space of thinking which is characterized by synthesis in place of analysis: creating alloys rather than cutting apart. I propose to work with these processes as procedures for encoding and decoding information from noise (data), and demonstrate them as negentropic, synthesis-oriented ways to acquire knowledge. I will work with radio signals, both naturally occurring and man-made, and identify patterns, events, activities in the data on different types of transmissions. I will work with the data set from the Radio Signal Identification Guide Wiki. With this data, I will produce two case studies: the first one focusing on spectrogram images of all signals; the second one focusing on abstracting from existing categories in the dataset and reorganizing it according to subjective preferences of researchers. Browser-based tools or digital observatories for organizing and navigating this data in meaningful ways will be developed in scope of the project and used in both studies. These observatories will be presented at two workshops with invited experts. The design of digital observatories, workshops and their results will be documented in a peer-reviewed article. These outputs will address the articulation of similarities and difference beyond simple ontological distinctions onto matter or information, subjects or objects. I see this work as an experimental setup for further work on methods for engaging with abundant information. In the future, I hope to apply these methods on more complex datasets while continuing to explore digital corporeality.

Title: Probabilistic Mechanical Intelligence
Abstract:
The energy consumption of information and communication technologies already exceeds that of the airline industry, and this is poised to grow considerably with the advent of artificial intelligence. For example, generative models - that is, models that generate images, music or answers to questions by sampling from a probability distribution that is conditioned on inputs  such as text prompts  - has been an area of particular growth and energy requirements in AI. One of the pressing questions is how to address this problem while we continue to benefit from further developments in AI systems.

Mechanical computing has been proposed as an ultra energy efficient platform for computing. Mechanical systems at the nano- and microscale are particularly promising due to their high quality factors (low damping). These so called Nano and Micro Electro Mechanical Systems (N/MEMS) are indeed capable of performing computations. At the nanoscale a distinctive phenomenon becomes inevitable: thermodynamic fluctuations that typically are treated as errors. While both computational capabilities as well as thermomechanical noise have been intensely investigated in N/MEMS, the two have not been leveraged together to implement low-power generative AI. Rather than treating noise as harmful to information processing, I will exploit it as a natural source of stochasticity, turning NEMS into (traditionally computationally expensive) random number generators -- at zero energy cost. On this basis I propose to theoretically design a network of NEMS that can be conditioned by mechanical forces at input degrees of freedom (DOFs). The network passively processes the random fluctuations together with the input such that output DOFs sample from a target conditional distribution. In this way, the NEMS network combines random number generation with neuromorphic computation and eventually embeds a generative AI. I call this AI a Probabilistic Mechanical Intelligence. 

I plan to test the approach by learning a conditional distribution of images given labels on the MNIST dataset. The input labels will be encoded as forces on the input DOFs. The network parameters will be optimized so that the amplitudes of the output DOF represent i.i.d. samples from the conditional distribution of pixels values given a label.

 To simulate the stochastic (Langevin) dynamics I use an already established code. For the inverse design I use adjoint methods and combine them with training tools from probabilistic machine learning (ML). I will in the first step design a small network, such that its output DOFs passively sample from various Gaussian and non-Gaussian distributions. Then I will design networks that sample from conditioned distributions upon forcing of input DOFs. I will finally test the approach on an actual machine learning task. I chose MNIST, because it is a well understood benchmark and requires a limited number of training parameters. The impact of the proposed research is to establish NEMS as a new platform for probabilistic AI.

The work will use my expertise in inverse design of mechanical systems, acquired during my PhD at ETH Zurich, along with the experience in mechanical artificial intelligence that I gained during my stay at Harvard at the group of Katia Bertoldi. Joining Prof. Adams' lab -- a world leading research group in AI with focus on probabilistic methods -- I plan to learn how to analyze and train probabilistic mechanical networks. Furthermore, Prof. Adams collaborates with the Mirco/Nanofabrication Center, which will guide my theoretical research towards systems that can be realised.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Green Computing, Inverse Design, Mechanical Computing, Stochastic Processes

Title: Mapping risks for child labor and deforestation in global commodity supply chains:  A proof-of-concept study with novel digital monitoring tools in the cocoa sector in the Ivory Coast
Abstract:
Emerging laws in Europe and Switzerland require companies to conduct due diligence on human rights risks and deforestation, which poses new management challenges for companies with complex global supply chains (see Swiss Federal Council 2021, European Commission 2022, European Union 2024). 

With this project, I want to test a novel way of addressing human rights risks in global supply chains, by combining earth observation technologies with field audits. This approach acknowledges the limits of current supply chain traceability of raw materials to the source of origin and introduces an innovative risk monitoring approach that can create a heat map of high-risk geographical areas. Based on this data, companies can develop improved strategies to address human rights issues in their value chain and emphasize the remediation of root causes. 

Concretely, I propose to use earth observation data to identify locations that combine recent deforestation and informal agriculture activities for cocoa production (based on the spectral signatures of the plant cover). The Earth observation data will then be integrated with socioeconomic datasets (such as proximity to social infrastructure) that are predictive of child labor risk.  Field visits will be used to ground-truth the analysis to determine the statistical probability of child labor at each location. The methodology will include a machine learning (AI) component to reduce uncertainty through an iterative learning process.

To test the effectiveness of this methodology, I propose a proof-of-concept study in the context of child labor in cocoa farming in the Ivory Coast. The elimination of child labor in global supply chains has been a key priority for companies and policymakers for several decades. 70% of child labor happens in the agriculture industry (UNGC 2021). The cocoa sector is notorious for high risks of child labor, including in the Ivory Coast where 40-45% of the world’s cocoa is grown, securing the livelihoods of approximately two million farmers and their families (Swiss Platform for Sustainable Cocoa n.d., Johnson 2022). Recent reports estimate that nearly one million children work in cocoa in the Ivory Coast, which is every third child in the Ivorian cocoa growing regions (NORC 2020). 

Between 17-25% of cocoa in the Ivory Coast is non-traceable and procured through the indirect supply chain that is often associated with cocoa production in deforested areas of protected forests (Renier et al. 2023). These forest areas have been subject to legal and illegal logging activities over decades. While farming activities in deforested areas are prohibited, the soil in these areas remains fertile which attracts farmers to these isolated areas to grow food or start growing commercial crops such as cocoa (Barima et al. 2020, Pearce 2019). Based on export volumes, it is likely that cocoa from these areas ends up in the supply chains of global brands, too. This situation merits an analysis of alternative approaches to monitor and remediate human rights risks in the cocoa supply chain, and to fulfill the new legislative requirements. 

In short, I will assess to what extent earth observation technology can help companies to set up an effective, risk-based due diligence approach to human rights and deforestation, including in remote areas of their supply chain, based on a pilot study in the Ivory Coast.
Keywords: business and human rights, child labor, cocoa supply chains, ground-truthing, human rights due diligence, mixed methods research, monitoring technology

Title: The future of radiomics: understanding, Validating and Increasing the Specificity of Imaging Biomarkers for personaLizEd medicine (VISIBLE)
Abstract:
The promises of personalized medicine in oncology have been hindered by its dependence on slow, costly and invasive molecular analyses. In addition, the analyzed tissue samples are most often acquired from either a highly localized tumor region or from the grinding of whole tumor mass, which does not allow to accurately capture molecular heterogeneity [69]. Recent studies in the emerging field of radiomics1 showed strong evidence that Quantitative Imaging Biomarkers (QIB) have the potential to surrogate and even surpass biopsy-based molecular assays in well-defined applicative contexts [2,129]. Whereas such imaging biomarkers neither have the spatial resolution of histopathology nor the molecular specificity of assays, they have the potential to capture the global intralesional heterogeneity of tumor phenotypes in a non-invasive way [114,144].
Two main groups of QIBs were proposed in the literature of radiomics: intensity and texture. Thanks to their interpretability and ease of implementation, intensity-based measures were widely used in many applica- tions to predict Overall patient Survival (OS), Disease-Free Survival (DFS) and response to treatment [12,17]. Texture-based imaging biomarkers measure complex dependencies between voxel values at multiple image scales and directions [37]. They can provide precise measurements of local tissue architectures associated with cell proliferation, angiogenesis and necrosis [5, 21, 43]. However, there are many obstacles preventing their serene integration into clinical routine [135]. First, unlike intensity-based biomarkers, texture attributes are mostly informative when forming large groups. Two major consequences of the latter are (i) the challenge of apprehend- ing the relation between multivariate analyses of texture attributes and targeted disease outcomes [115], and (ii) the need for large-scale studies to validate multivariate analyses while respecting ten-to-one ratios between the number of samples and attributes [16]. Second, commonly used approaches for texture analysis suffer from important limitations in terms of robustness, invariances and specificity [36]. Third, although the promise of radiomics relies on quantifying tissue heterogeneity, most studies are aggregating voxelwise imaging measures over entire tumoral volumes allowing neither to characterize distinct tumor habitats nor to reveal the complex relationships between imaging biomarkers and underlying physiological processes.
In this proposal, solutions are detailed to overcome the aforementioned limitations. These solutions are justified by recent theoretic analyses detailed in our recent book on Biomedical Texture Analysis (BTA) [33]. Previous work already showed the importance of the identified limitations, where novel trainable and highly- specific texture operators achieved state-of-the-art performance in a variety of applications [24,34,45,49,53, 57,64]. However, further research efforts are required to (i) develop texture operators fulfilling all optimiality criteria defined in [33] and (ii) investigate the importance of the criteria in the particular case of radiomics oncology studies. Second, the project will innovate in the validation of the developed methods by moving from tumor- to habitat- level validation (i.e., seeking for cancer hallmarks [68,81]) based on high-quality, innovative and large datasets gathered at the Lausanne University Hospital (CHUV), international collaborations and public sources. These will include collections of subjects with sub-tumoral local ground truth based on localized stereotactic core biopsies for histopathological and molecular analyses [86, 87] as well as molecular tracers of hallmarks (e.g., cell proliferation, hypoxia, angiogenesis) [88,112]. While being expensive and difficult to use in clinical routine, the aforementioned biomarkers can be used transiently to consolidate the link between QIBs and tumor habitats. The proposal will primarily focus on Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC) [138] and Head and Neck Cancers (HNC) [119] as they are two important cancer types with most data and knowledge available [2,105,106]. They are also best imaged using Computed Tomography (CT) and Positron Emission Tomography (PET) images, where voxel values have a direct and absolute physical interpretation.
Keywords: convolutional neural networks, deep learning, interpretability, medical image analysis, molecular imaging, nuclear medicine, oncology, open-access, personalized medicine, radiology, radiomics, texture analysis, web platforms

Title: Online Data Center Modeling
Abstract:
This project will create a common data model and representation for the state of an operational data center, driven by real-world use-cases and deployments, which can serve as a solid foundation for cross-layer management of entire distributed hardware and software stacks.  

Modern data centers are the crucial infrastructure for storing, processing, and distributing information for applications that touch all walks of life, including health care, finance, communications, and other industries. However, data centers are also complex, dynamic, highly networked systems and, as such, their capacity, performance, behavior, and failure modes are difficult to predict, understand, and plan for.

A recent survey of federal agencies in the United States reports that 94 percent of federal data centers experience downtime as a result of data center complexity.  Reports of data center outages have become commonplace. Notably, outages involving Amazon's EC2 Cloud Computing facilities in turn took down many important websites, of which Reddit, Github, Foursquare and Airbnb were only the most high-profile.  A recent outage at Visa left customers unable to use their credit cards.

Less visibly, our commercial collaborators in this project confirm a truism in the industry: ensuring that the applications in a data center meet their performance and availability targets in the face of changes in offered load, reconfigurations, upgrades, and equipment and software failures is an extremely difficult problem that costs companies dearly in expense, energy, and employee time. 

A major reason for this complexity is that the many conceptual layers involved in an enterprise data center (physical network connectivity, physical and virtual machines, link layers, VLANs, routing, service-oriented architectures, application deployment, etc.) are managed today by tools and techniques which focus on only one or a few layers. Worse, these layers are typically operated by different divisions in the organization, creating a strong barrier to the development of commercial management solutions.  


These layers are also becoming more complex in themselves.  An key example of this general challenge is the rise of Software-Defined Networking (SDN) techniques, which promise considerably more efficient and flexible networking at the link and IP layers through a centralized "controller'' which dynamically creates forwarding table entries in switches.  However, this power comes at the cost of increased complexity. SDN control software is itself a complicated distributed system,
that must maintain distributed state gathered from a variety of heterogeneous devices using asynchronous communication. Anecdotally, network administrators have been hesitant to deploy SDNs, because the increased automation makes it harder for them to track down problems and generally understand anomalous behavior in the system. As a result of this reluctance, many networks only partially deploy SDNs, until they gain familiarity and confidence, leading to difficulties in which SDN and legacy network software co-exist in the same network.


More importantly, today's SDN controllers to date (primarily based on the OpenFlow standard) operate at the level of IP flows rather than taking a global view of the data center state which can be reasoned about online.  Moreover, they expose no internal representation that would allow the network layers they manage to be coupled to other layers of the stack (such as the several application levels, or the physical infrastructure).

This project will take a radically different approach.  Rather than focussing on mechanisms to control and manage subsets of a data center, we will create a data model and \emph{representation} of the state of a data center which can be populated and driven by logs, traces, and configuration information; queried by operators to determine global properties of the system (such as traffic matrices), and drive online workload-driven simulations to explore the effects of configuration changes. Such a data model and schema for a modern data center does not
at present exist.

Beyond these immediate applications, we argue that without such a foundational substrate, any attempt to manage an entire data center will result in a management system which is ad-hoc, brittle in the presence of changes, and highly specific to a single context - in short, it will resemble the "home-grown'' systems in use today. 

We are in a highly advantageous position to carry out this work. Our collaborators in industry have data centers and networks which are highly instrumented, and have agreed to share this instrumentation data with us.  

The work is also timely from a technological perspective: modern server technology can process the large volumes of trace data generated by a center (about 2TB/day in the case of Amadeus for example) in a compact space, and parallel data processing systems are appearing in the research community which can integrate graph processing, data streams, stored relational data, and continuous, incremental online queries within a single framework - exactly the workload that data center modelling presents. 

The primary goal of the proposed project is not to focus on the systems issues involved in building such as system. Instead, we plan to leverage existing research systems such as Naiad and ongoing work at ETH into parallel data processing and information management, as much as possible in the short term. As the project matures, we expect that the process of developing the data center model will provide insights into system design, that will lay a foundation for future systems work.

Neither will the project address the "actuation'' part of data center management - it will concentrate solely on building and maintaining a representation rather than taking any action based on this.   There are several reasons for this.  Firstly, we feel strongly that without a clear logical foundation in representation, control policies will be too ad-hoc, and it is essential to get this representation correct first.  Secondly, it is easier to deploy a prototype system operationally in a real data center (something we plan to do in this project) if it both delivers value to operators (by providing information views not otherwise available to them) and poses no threat to the infrastructure, instead merely ingesting trace data and providing a query interface over system state.  

Instead, the work in the proposal will perform the vital task of creating, refining, deploying, and validating the abstract representation of the state of a data center.  In doing so, we will build upon but extend recent work in applying ideas from both knowledge representation and programming language semantics to understanding the operation of networks, including existing work by the PIs themselves.

If successful, we expect the results of this project to have a broad impact far beyond providing useful tools for data center operators.  Our goal is to provide a shared substrate for diverse data center management functionality, analogous to the way that the relational model of databases provided a common substrate for tabular data.  Such an extensible model can act as a disruptive incentive to the management software industry, serve as a basis for interoperability, comparative benchmarking, and verifiable SDN controllers. In the longer term, we hope to greatly further our understanding of design principles for the control planes of networks and distributed systems.
Keywords: Data center, Data modeling, Networking

Title: Autoimmune T cell responses in acute and chronic myocarditis
Abstract:
Myocarditis is a prototypical inflammatory heart disease that leads to the loss of cardiomyocytes and frequently precipitates fibrotic remodeling of the myocardium culminating in heart failure. Autoimmune inflammatory myocardial disease is mainly caused by the activation of CD4+ T cells that recognize major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II-binding peptides derived from the contractile protein myosin heavy chain 6 (MYH6). Cardiopathogenic murine and human CD4+ T cells are activated through various mechanisms including the recognition of microbial mimic peptides derived from commensal Bacteroides species. The risk to develop T cell-driven myocarditis is thus determined by the genetic background with the ability of MHC II molecules to present heart-specific peptides, the presence of cross-reactive peptide mimics in the microbiome, and the T cell receptor (TCR) repertoire that is shaped by the peptide-MHC (pMHC) complex. The complexity of pMHC-TCR interaction, particularly in human T cell-driven diseases, requires novel computational approaches with iterative circuits of data analysis and interpretation followed by experimental validation to resolve the key immunological processes underlying myocardial inflammation.
The planned research is based on the hypotheses that (i) phenotypical and functional changes of heart-specific T cells accompany and critically determine the disease course during myocardial inflammatory disease in humans, and that (ii) cardiopathogenic T cell activity can be tuned by altering specific pMHC-TCR interactions.
To provide critical insight into the immunopathological mechanisms underlying acute and chronic inflammatory myocardial disease in humans, we are currently enrolling patients with acute myocarditis patients and patients with inflammatory cardiomyopathy in the ImmpathCarditis study. We anticipate that the assessment and documentation of patient data and the combined microbiome, serum antibody and proteomic analyses of patient samples in Aim 1 will provide a critical resource for clinical phenotyping of acute and chronic myocarditis. The work in Aim 2 with high-resolution T cell analyses will identify TCRs specific to MYH6- and/or the bacterial peptide mimic and will establish the basis for an advanced model of pMHC-TCR interaction in CD4+ T cell-driven myocardial inflammation. We envision a two-step integrative data analysis approach for the work in Aim 3 with initial phenotypic clustering of clinical data and a separate analysis of high-dimensional immunological and molecular data. We anticipate that these analyses will reveal a set of serological and immunological markers that guide the distinction of clinical phenogroups in myocarditis patients. The work in Aim 4 will use deep learning-based prediction methods and advanced modeling approaches including AlphaFold2 to characterize and to modulate pMHC-TCR interactions that determine the activity of murine and human cardiopathogenic CD4+ T cells. 
In sum, the project will provide a comprehensive analysis of the molecular and immunological pathways that control the activation and differentiation of heart-specific T cells in acute and chronic human myocarditis. We anticipate that the integrative analysis of clinical, immunological and proteomic data has the potential to identify serological and immunological markers that can be used to differentiate clinical phenotypes in myocardial inflammatory diseases and thus improve patient diagnosis and management. In addition, the advanced understanding of the T cell-driven immunopathological circuits operating in the inflamed human myocardium and the focus on specific pMHC-TCR interactions will be instrumental in the future development of peptide-based modulation of T cell activity.

Title: Optimized photonics structures for a new generation of Kerr microcomb devices.
Abstract: Optical frequency combs (OFCs) measure optical frequencies with an unprecedented precision, allowing myriad applications in optical metrology, high-precision spectroscopy, optical atomic clocks, attosecond science, astronomy, and quantum information processing. More recently, Kerr microresonator cavities have emerged as a promising candidate for the extreme miniaturization of OFCs down to the millimeter scale in micro- and nano-fabricated resonator systems. This approach has seen tremendous progress over the last 10 years, going from theoretical prediction to a fully self-referenced ‘Kerr microcomb’ system based on integrated components. One of the most intriguing discoveries in this field has been the observation of a unique type of mode-locking via the formation of temporal dissipative Kerr solitons (DKS). These breakthroughs promise new chip-based combs technologies for miniaturized optical clocks, compact dual-comb spectrometer and LIDAR, and new sources for optical telecommunications, where they can replace 100’s of lasers. All these applications of OFCs place different requirements on the comb properties. For instance, in telecom application, a high power per comb line is required, over a moderate spectral span. On the other hand, metrological applications seek typically to bridge one octave, with high power in the wings of the comb to allow self-referencing. So far, engineering the comb properties relied on small variations of simple resonator geometries. The main goal of this proposal is to leverage the recent development in inverse design methods (via constrained optimization, machine learning methods, ...) to develop algorithmic tools that will allow tailoring arbitrary photonic structures, in which Kerr combs with a set of specified properties will be generated. Although inverse-design methods have been successfully demonstrated to optimize linear functionalities, the main challenge here will be to adapt these tools for the nonlinear problem of DKS generation. This approach is especially promising to manipulate the dispersion of the resonator to an unprecedented level, and to study the impact of this parameter on the DKS dynamics. This has the potential to unveil novel nonlinear dynamics and provide new avenues in the field of microcombs, such as the long-standing goal of generating a comb in the visible spectral region.
Keywords: Inverse design, Nonlinear optics, Optical frequency-comb, Optimization, Physics

Title: Regulating the Algorithmic State with Regulatory Sandboxes
Abstract:
AI technologies (AI) are infusing all dimensions of our social and working environments. They are the last layer of information technologies deployment, which were already considered an enabler for government efficiency. They support the transition from ‘e-government’ to ‘digital government’ and, finally, ‘smart government’. 
This rapid evolution could lead to a paradigm shift in public administration – the ‘new public analytics (NPA)’  – and is a source of major concerns, especially for legal scholars who are called to scrutinise this evolution to ‘ensure public accountability for NPA techniques’. Indeed, public authorities and private organisations that perform public tasks – in an analogue or digital manner – are bound by the law (the rule of law principle). AI technologies' development, deployment, and use in and for the public sector must fulfil the legal framework and its requirements. 
From a regulatory perspective, AI technologies pose the ‘Collingridge dilemma’, meaning that either regulators do not have enough knowledge about the technology being developed to formulate a precise regulative response (e.g. artificial intelligence), or they are too late and no longer able to turn back the impacts of technology (e.g. social media). Two paths have been proposed as possible answers to overcome this dilemma. The first is anticipation, or prospective evaluation – in which regulatory tools such as data protection impact assessment have been developed. The second focuses on regulating the innovation process. In this last case, instead of projecting uncertain eventual outcomes, the goal is to fix the ethical and legal boundaries of the “social experiment”. In deploying AI systems, global actors view regulatory sandboxes as a panacea for tackling this issue and help the AI deployment for mitigating social, environmental, and individual risks. Many entities like the European Union or Switzerland have enshrined experimental instruments in their legal systems. However, using Pasquale’s metaphor about AI, implementing regulatory sandboxes remains a ‘black box’. 
In this context, the proposed project aims to address the following questions: How do regulatory sandboxes foster AI in the public sector? and for what purpose and what impacts on public sector-designed AI and on public administration? 
While the regulatory sandbox tool has been mainly studied from different legal perspectives, an in-depth empirical study of its implementation in the context of digital transformation, especially public administration, is still missing. Adopting an empirical and comparative case-study approach, the project will map the implementation of regulatory sandboxes for AI in comparative public administration, exploring the normative and organisational elements that surround their deployment, as well as their the practical implementation, stakeholders’ attitudes and potential impact on the technology. It will offer guidance to policymakers and lawmakers in drafting experimental clauses and implementing regulatory sandboxes. 
Finally, from theoretical and normative perspectives, the project aims to contribute to discussions about the legal compliance of regulatory sandboxes to administrative law principles, the regulation and governance approaches of AI, the sociocultural dimension of AI technologies and the side effects of regulatory sandboxes in unlocking AI in the public sector.
Keywords: AI, Artificial Intelligence, Experimental Legislation, Public Administration, Public administration, Regulation and Governance Studies, Regulatory Governance Studies, Regulatory Sandbox, Regulatory Sandboxes, Rule of Law

Title: Multi-modal speech sensing based on 2D and 3D optical and acoustic signals for identity recognition and authentication
Abstract:
Human speech perception is a process that takes into account both acoustic and visual speech information but yet most automatic recognition systems are typically based on one of the two modes. In this project we will combine the strong between-speaker differences of acoustic dynamics and facial movement dynamics and to build more reliable person identification systems. Facial movements are usually extracted from 2D frontal facial images. Visual 3D facial features obtained with 3D cameras improve the accuracy of facial feature extraction, especially for non-frontal facial images.
One goal of this project is to develop a sensing platform to collect both the 2D and 3D optical speech characteristics and the acoustic signals. Dynamic information including 3D facial movements and speech rhythm will be used to improve speaker recognition and authentication. Compared to previous identity recognition methods that usually use either the 2D face or the voice of an individual, the here proposed scheme will be more robust since it is based on simultaneous visual (2D and 3D) and acoustic dynamic speech sensing. Another goal is to investigate the relationship between the acoustic dynamics of speech and 3D facial dynamics and thus pave the way to predicting voices from faces and faces from voices. The obtained deeper understanding of the acoustic and face dynamics of speech will have an impact on various speech technologies, including: automatic speech recognition, lip modelling for speaking face synthesis, real time human computer interface applications and speech-based password authentication.
Keywords: 3D sensing, Authentication, Identity-recognition, Speech-sensing

Title: PRISM-FILD: Precision Medicine through Redefinition of Diagnosis and Management using Integrated Systems and Multilevel Data in fibrosing interstitial lung diseases (fILD)
Abstract:
Interstitial lung diseases (ILDs), a heterogeneous group of pulmonary disorders, present a significant clinical challenge due to their complex pathogenesis and unpredictable progression. Fibrotic ILDs (fILDs) can evolve through primarily fibrotic pathways (e.g., idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis - IPF), inflammation-driven mechanisms (e.g., systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease-associated ILDs - SARD-ILD), or may remain stable (e.g., post-ARDS). Present diagnostic and prognostic tools rely on multidisciplinary discussion (MDD) combining clinical, functional, imaging, histopathological, and laboratory data. However, these approaches often fall short in precision, leaving many cases poorly characterized or classified as “unclassifiable ILD.” This lack of resolution hinders timely diagnosis, prediction of disease progression and optimally targeted therapy.

While antifibrotic drugs reduce lung function decline in progressive fILDs, they do not reverse disease or improve symptoms. In contrast, immunomodulators may be effective when inflammation dominates, but they may cause harm when applied to predominantly fILDs, such as IPF. Thus, accurate differentiation between inflammation-driven and fibrosis-driven phenotypes is crucial. Current evaluations still neglect key factors such as longitudinal disease behavior, environmental exposures, genetic susceptibility, or the biological heterogeneity present even within the same diagnostic label.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) presents a transformative opportunity to overcome current limitations in the diagnosis and management of ILDs. While recent advances have shown that AI can match or exceed human experts in specific radiological pattern recognition tasks, existing clinical tools remain limited in scope. They typically focus on single data modalities-most often imaging-and are restricted to specific ILD subtypes (e.g. IPF). To date, no clinically validated AI system offers a comprehensive, multimodal approach that integrates diverse data types-including clinical parameters, radiology, histopathology, omics, and longitudinal patient information-to support robust stratification, accurate diagnosis, and reliable prognosis across the spectrum of ILDs. This represents a critical unmet need and a unique opportunity to develop next-generation AI-powered tools that reflect the complexity of real-world clinical decision-making.

Despite growing interest in AI-powered approaches for ILD, implementation into clinical decision-making remains limited. Preliminary applications of AI to imaging and clinical data show promise, but systematic, large-scale integration of multimodal data-including high-dimensional omics-has not yet been achieved. Our group and others have shown that distinct protein signatures, identified through proteomics, correlate with ILD subtypes and may serve as valuable markers for stratification and treatment guidance. However, these insights have yet to be operationalized in AI models capable of supporting clinical decisions.

Given the variability of ILD progression and drug responses, a paradigm shift is needed: from static, phenotype-based classifications to dynamic, biology-informed endotyping. AI, when fed with comprehensive multimodal data-including longitudinal clinical records, high-resolution CT scans, liquid biomarkers, and histopathology-has the potential to deliver individualized risk assessment, disease trajectory prediction, and therapy selection support. 

This project aims to close a critical gap in the management of fILDs by developing and validating an AI-driven, multimodal system capable of redefining fILDs based on distinct inflammation and fibrosis endotypes. By integrating advanced imaging, detailed clinical data, and high-dimensional proteomics from international longitudinal cohorts, we will apply cutting-edge AI methodologies to enable earlier, more accurate diagnoses and personalized prognostication.

Title: Proof-of-concept for developing NLP-based PROM assessment: improving distress management in patients with cancer
Abstract:
Background: The importance of integrating patient’s perspectives in assessing the success of cancer treatment is well established. To this effect, Patient Reported Outcome Measures, or PROMs, have been developed.  Their systematic assessment has been shown to substantially improve symptom control and patient-reported quality of life. Psychological distress in cancer patients is one such measure and poses a substantial burden, with prevalence rates of 35-60%. Effective interventions targeting distress require effective screening. However, current screening rates, reported at <50%, are insufficient. Recent technological advances in the field of artificial intelligence (AI), opens possibilities for novel screening approaches. 

Aim: The aims of the study are primarily to demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of large-language-model (LLM)-based Patient Reported Outcome Measure (PROM) screening in cancer patients, using distress assessment in breast cancer patients as a case-in-point. Secondarily, we aim to a) evaluate whether integrating LLM-based analysis of semi-structured interviews can improve the consistency of detecting emotional distress and b), to evaluate the trend of self-reported health-related quality of life (EORTC QLQ-C30 questionnaire) from baseline to 3 months.

Design: We plan the study as a prospective, monocenter observational proof-of-concept trial, aiming to recruit a minimum of 30 patients of a maximum of 50 patients with breast cancer at our center over a one-year period, spanning 2026. We wish to demonstrate that a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Large Language Model (LLM), compact enough to be run within a hospital, is capable of flagging patients requiring referral for psycho-oncological support. Open-question semi-structured interviews performed during cancer nurse consultations, derived from items from the validated Hornheider Screening Instrument (HSI), will serve as source data.  Performance of the NLP model will be determined by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) predicting necessity for referral in comparison to the defined gold standard, the NCCN Distress Thermometer, at baseline. We set the benchmark for success at an AUC of 0.80. 

Significance & impact: Although the importance of integrating PROMs into routine cancer care is well recognized, implementation is so far lagging behind. Potential barriers to routine PROM assessment are on the one side patient hesitancy or lack of literacy to fill out lengthy, burdensome questionnaires and on the other side lack of resources by the health care provider to collect, analyze and act on PROMs. We aim to address these barriers by trialing a proof of concept to automatically derive a PROM, namely distress, from patient interviews. This holds the potential to reduce patient barriers by integrating PROM collection in the setting of a trustworthy, appreciative conversation with a member of the care team. On the other hand, this approach also holds the potential for automating PROM assessment and hence reducing required resources from the care team.  We are confident that our approach can, if demonstrated to be feasible, facilitate the integration of PROM assessment and hence substantially improve patient care.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Breast Cancer, Distress, LLM, NLP, Patient Reported Outcome Measures
