Title: Trusses beyond trusses: the mechanics of woven and straw-based architected materials
Abstract:
We propose a new class of lightweight architected (meta-)materials with controllable mechanical performance, exceptional energy absorption and stiffness, and tunable nonlinear active and passive reconfigurability. This is achieved by expanding the design concepts of truss-based metamaterials to woven, knotted, and straw-based cellular networks. Towards their optimal design, the objectives of this project are (i) a detailed physical understanding of the mechanics of woven and knotted lattices and of structures including straw-like elements, (ii) an efficient, validated computational framework for the prediction of the mechanical behavior of such structural architectures, (iii) the theoretical-computational tools required to parameterize the design space and to efficiently optimize the design of structures containing woven and/or straw-type connections, and (iv) prototypical demonstrations of the functionality achievable by such architected materials.

For woven and knotted lattices, we introduce a beam-based representation for individual slender fibers, which accounts for frictional contact and large deformation and is calibrated by experiments on 3D-printed base materials, followed by the integration into braided configurations and complex networks. For straws made of series of elastic frusta, we examine the stable states and the transition pathways between stable configurations - with and without internal pressure being applied as a means of actuation. All models are implemented within a massively-parallel and variational open-source computational library, resulting in a comprehensive and powerful numerical framework for predicting the complex quasistatic mechanical response of structures. Validation is achieved by comparison with the deformation of representative 3D-printed structures, using high-speed feature tracking for detailed in-situ observation of the mechanical response to different loading scenarios. Experiments are of increasing complexity, starting with elementary units of individual woven and knotted units as well as straws, and building up to two- and three-dimensional networks.

Based on the parametrization and exploration of the combined topological-geometrical design space - both at the microscale (of individual fibers and frusta) and at the macroscale (of the topology or graph of a truss network), we apply optimization techniques and machine learning for the inverse design of architectures to identify structure-property relations and to predict designs having target functionality. To highlight the achievable performance of this new class of architected (meta-)materials, we focus on active and passive reconfiguration as well as on impact energy absorption as benchmarks of practical relevance for applications ranging from soft robotics, aerospace and deployable structures to functional textiles and adaptive wearables, vibration isolation and impact protection - for all if which this research promises new design concepts and presently unavailable computational models.

Title: 5liber Learning-UAV: Artificial Intelligence-based Ultra-tiny UAVs
Abstract:
Despite incredible progress in the last few years, current generation small-size unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are not yet comparable to what biological evolution could achieve in one of the most successful and widespread classes of animals: insects. In particular, while it is possible to fabricate small and even insect-scale drones (i.e., called pico-size) capable of flight [1,2,3], it is not yet possible to provide such a drone with the level of intelligence for an autonomous flight that insects find natural, despite their relatively uncomplicated brains. In this project, we want to tackle specifically this problem, providing an insect-sized drone with the onboard intelligence enabling bio-inspired autonomous navigation capabilities. Similarly to elementary biological organisms, we aim at a standalone onboard intelligence, meaning the capability of making decisions depending only on onboard computational and sensing resources -- i.e., no ad-hoc infrastructure, no remote computers/servers. However, State-of-the-Art (SoA) insect-size and nano-size drones (i.e., ~10 cm diameter and few tens of grams in weight) still lack a meaningful level of autonomy, contrary to their larger counterparts [4,5,6,7], since their tiny power envelopes and limited payload do not allow to host onboard adequate computing power for sophisticated workloads.
In this project, we aim at key innovations pushing the SoA in terms of standalone intelligent flying robots further, in the direction showcased by biology in insects. First, we want to provide flying robots with the capability to explore an environment avoiding obstacles using exclusively local information and onboard computation (standalone navigation). Second, we aim at raising the level of intelligence of the drone by making it capable of learning and fine-tuning its behavior on the field, adapting to new and different environments. Third, we want to pursue this target on an insect-scale drone, that we will design to fit within a few cm2 and sub-10-grams mass, and capable of high-level onboard sense-and-act capabilities. Our target form factor is smaller than SoA commercial nano-size UAVs, aiming at a size between nano- and pico-size UAVs, or what we call “Fünfliber-drone” (i.e., 5liber-drone) because of its dimensions fitting within a 5 Swiss Franc coin -- comparable to a dragonfly.
To achieve these ambitious objectives, we will take advantage of recent advances in both microcontrollers and highly efficient SoC’s, as well as of novel artificial intelligence and robot control based on deep, continuous and reinforcement learning.

Title: Effects of airborne pollen on cardiorespiratory health and allergic symptoms
Abstract:
Introduction
As the duration and intensity of the pollen season increase due to climate change, allergies to airborne pollen are also increasingly common in Europe. Yet, it is not well recognized that high pollen concentrations may increase respiratory and cardiovascular events, leading to mortality and excess hospitalizations. Moreover, combined exposure to pollen, air pollution and weather conditions could have synergistic effects, that alter the allergenicity of pollen - a research area which has been hardly explored.
Aim
I aim to investigate how short-term exposure to pollen is related to mortality, hospitalization and allergic symptoms, both on its own and synergistically with air pollution and weather. Moreover, in light of increasing allergy prevalence, I aim to study how the relationship between pollen and health has developed over the study period, and which subpopulations might be most at risk. 
Methods
I will develop spatiotemporal exposure models of pollen for the years 2003-2022 based on a network of 14 pollen measurements stations in Switzerland. These maps will allow me to attribute individual exposure to pollen, air pollution and weather by location and by day, and will be used as the exposure metric for the health analyses. 
For the health endpoints, I will use large, real-world datasets without selection bias: individual cause-specific mortality is available from the Swiss National Cohort (2003-2018) and hospital admissions from the hospital admission database of the Federal Office of Statistics. Taking advantage of the efficient case-crossover study design, I will investigate the population effects of pollen on daily respiratory and cardiovascular mortality and hospitalization, accounting for air pollution and weather as time-varying confounders. I will investigate: trends in how pollen affected each outcome over the last 16-year study period; identify potential interactions with air pollution or weather; and explore the effect modifiers age, sex and urban/rural residence.
To explore individual sensitivity, I will study repeated accounts of self-reported symptoms from the “e-symptoms” app, launched in 2012 by aha! Swiss Allergy Centre and CK-care. Using random forests machine learning techniques, I will analyze the user base’s symptom severity reports in relation to actual prevalent pollen, air pollution and weather triggers, and the diagnosed allergies they indicate. The trained model will allow me to predict personalized symptom severity for future days based on pollen forecasts and provide personalized prevention recommendations and thus enhance quality of life for the allergic population. Ultimately, as a single user contributes more symptom reports, I will be able to gradually improve their personalized symptom prediction based on their personal sensitivity, which is derived from their previous reports. Data collection is already ongoing, and will continue throughout the study until 2022.
Significance
This highly innovative project utilizes available nationwide health datasets and a systematic smartphone-based data collection method, to better understand the role of pollen in self-reported symptoms, respiratory and cardiovascular diseases at both personalized and population levels. This study will add substantially to the small body of scientific evidence that airborne pollen is adversely related to severe health effects such as mortality and hospitalizations. The project will prevent and reduce health effects due to pollen, which constitute a large burden on health and economy. This is particularly relevant in light of the increasing prevalence of allergies and the earlier start to and lengthening of the pollen season.

Title: Exploring the power of regularization for reliable machine learning
Abstract:
As machine learning models enter applications in the real world at a rapid pace, it is important that they are not only accurate but also reliable. In particular, they should be reliable under natural distribution shifts and produce reliable predictions that are robust against adversarial corruptions and attacks on the input.

The recent storyline for large machine learning models states that fitting the training set perfectly leads to optimal generalization performance whenever the model is sufficiently overparameterized. In that regime, regularizing the model reaps no benefits. While this is at odds with the common intuition of overfitting, theoretical works were able to prove this observation for heavily parameterized linearized and random feature models. However, the data speaks differently when the focus turns to reliability. In fact, recent papers show empirically that stopping before algorithm convergence increases adversarial robustness for neural networks. In this project we will both build on the power of regularization to detect and train with minority samples and develop theory that helps to understand when and why regularization can increase adversarial robustness.

Our theoretical setting will first align with previous work that focuses on the impact of overparameterization on generalization, in the context of linear or random feature models. Even though these results would be interesting in their own right, a major motivation driving the recent line of theoretical work for overparameterized models is to understand deep neural networks (DNN), models that have become hugely popular in practice. Ideally, we would like to claim that the insights from the fixed feature models actually carry over to DNNs. However for this purpose, it is crucial for us to conduct extensive experiments for both the linearized and NN models, and observe their dependence on varying architectural structure, the degree of overparameterization, or the data distribution. This approach should help to prove theorems that are closer to explaining the robustness of DNNs under distribution shifts and adversarial perturbations and help to gain intuition for which settings it is still crucial to employ early stopping and regularization.

In summary, this project will investigate two different types of robustness where the power of regularization is crucial for reliability:
A. Provide new theoretical insights that are able to characterize when regularization can increase the robustness of large models while not benefitting standard prediction performance
B. Develop an active learning algorithm in the distribution shift setting that improves current domain adaptation methods in settings where the test distribution contains vastly different data points and new labels are necessary

The impact of this project is potentially profound: Data distributions in the wild change constantly and hence we urgently need models that address these changes in a satisfactory way. Improving active learning for distribution shift is one important step to learning models that can adapt to shifts in a cost-effective way. On the other hand our theoretical insights on the power of regularization for reliability could complement the modern storyline that has so far revolved around the virtues of overparameterized models without the need for regularization.
Keywords: adversarial robustness, distribution shift, domain adaptation, early stopping, high-dimensional statistics, machine learning, out-of-distribution detection, overparameterization, regularization, reliability

Title: Firm Disclosure via Social Media –  The Use of Twitter for Disseminating Non-GAAP Information and Management Guidance
Abstract:
Firms increasingly use social media, particularly Twitter, to disseminate information (Jung et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2015). While social media has become a common disclosure channel for firms (Best and Caylor, 2019), research on Twitter to date is largely generic with little insights into firms’ motives to use social media and the actual content of the disseminated information. In this project, we aim to analyze S&P 1500 firms’ disclosures via Twitter from 2013-2020 for informational and strategic purposes. We focus on two specific types of firm disclosures in two separate manuscripts, namely reporting of management-adjusted earnings (non-GAAP) and firms’ forecasts (management guidance), respectively. Twitter, as a corporate communication channel, has very specific characteristics that provides fruitful ground for investigation. Namely, the brief publishing format of Twitter allows managers to emphasize disclosures and timely updates about the firm can be immediately released to a large, diverse set of investors. Results from our project are expected to contribute to the current regulatory debate on non-GAAP measures and the use of social media for information dissemination of management guidance. 
The proliferation of non-GAAP reporting has been steadily increasing (Black et al., 2018), which led to specific non-GAAP regulations for traditional communication channels. In the U.S., Reg G of the 2002 Sarbanes-Oxley Act requires a reconciliation from non-GAAP to GAAP earnings in firms’ disclosures. To date, social media is less regulated than other information channels (e.g., Bartov et al. 2018) and firms can provide shortened and/or less transparent information by using Twitter. Hence, non-GAAP disclosures via social media may be inherently different from earnings releases. In the first paper, we aim to provide detailed insights into the determinants of non-GAAP tweets. Further, by comparing tweeted non-GAAP information with non-GAAP information disseminated through traditional channels, we analyze the nature of the non-GAAP disclosures (e.g., earnings vs. other information, exclusion types etc.). We further investigate the extent to which non-GAAP tweets appear to be associated with strategic disclosure behavior.
In the second paper on management guidance via Twitter, we first analyze firms’ Twitter information using natural language processing (NLP) and optical character recognition (OCR) to categorize the content of the tweets and to identify guidance-related tweets. We then analyze the timing of the guidance-related tweets to identify whether and which firms follow a guidance policy via Twitter (i.e., with regular, persistent guidance), and how this relates to their “former” established guidance policy documented using more traditional channels (e.g., IBES Guidance from press releases and conference calls). We further compare the accuracy of the guidance information in the tweets with the other/prior forecast information in the guidance sources. By that we analyze the accuracy of the highlighted guidance in the tweets and whether firms provide such information via Twitter strategically or whether it acts as another practical mechanism of information dissemination. Finally, we analyze whether there is a differential market response, as well as liquidity effect, to guidance dissemination via Twitter compared to (or in addition to) traditional guidance disclosures.
Our project addresses recent calls to analyze the increasing volume of unstructured data (Lewis and Young, 2019). Not only have the narrative parts of annual reports, analyst reports, and conference calls increased, but also social media posts further add to the (unstructured) information available to firm stakeholders. Finally, understanding how guidance through social media channels can help managers’ efforts to provide an early outlook to firms’ financial performance will likely be informative and consequential to investors, analysts, policymakers, and researchers in the accounting and finance areas.
Keywords: Firm Disclosure, Management Guidance, Non-GAAP Earnings, Social Media

Title: Into the Mind of the Machine: Implications of Fixed and Adaptive Algorithms on Consumer Perceptions and Behavior
Abstract: Algorithms are the backbone of the new cutting-edge technologies of the digital age including autonomous products, artificial intelligence (AI) or the internet of things. Many different kinds of algorithms exist that are lively discussed in the computer science literature. For consumers, however, the inside of a machine typically constitutes a black box. Integrating research streams from consumer behavior and computer science, we open the box and inform consumers about two major categories of algorithms: fixed (following parameters pre-determined by a programmer) and adaptive (following parameters that can be altered in the course of operation). Since former consumer-centered research on perceptions of algorithms and AI typically treats algorithms as a generic concept, this work is the first to examine the effect of informing consumers about the specific type and working style of algorithms implemented in products and technologies. The main objective of this project is to investigate how information about the characteristics of the underlying algorithm alters consumer reactions directed to a technology (e.g., a smart product). Extending former research on consumers’ perceptions of algorithms and building on our own former research that adaptive (vs. fixed) algorithms are perceived as more creative and human-like, I propose that information about the implemented algorithm will significantly influence consumers’ behavior directed towards technologies and evaluations of their produced outcome. In a mixture of behavioral lab and online experimental studies during the anticipated research stay at the Columbia University, I aim to collect complementary behavioral evidence for our initial work and extend our research focus.
Keywords: AI, Algorithm, Artificial Intelligence, Automation, Creativity, Smart Products

Title: Making Program Analysis Fast
Abstract:
Computers have become an integral part of our lives and have revolutionized the way we
interact and communicate with the world. From simulating complex physical and biological
systems to enabling powerful smart phones, computing plays a fundamental role in modern
society. However, programming those computers is still a difficult, time-consuming, and
error-prone activity. Thus, ensuring that programs work correctly and efficiently remains
a fundamental problem in computer science. In particular, as programs grow larger and
more complex, the need for automated reasoning tools and techniques that can ensure that
programs behave as they are supposed to, has increased dramatically. Because of the need
for such automated techniques, the last decade has seen tremendous progress in software
analysis tools. Techniques once considered purely theoretical have been improved [13, 24]
and are now applied in complex real world settings including device drivers [2] or largescale
safety critical systems such as flight control software [6].

A fundamental challenge in developing automated reasoning engines
is striking a careful balance between cost (both space and time) and the expressive power
of the analysis engine (precision). Achieving this balance is critical: an analyzer that is too
imprecise can fail to verify correct programs, while an analyzer which is very precise can be
too costly (e.g., run out of memory or require weeks to finish) to be useful for real world
programs.

The main goal of this proposal is to develop new algorithms, data structures,
and techniques that significantly speed up program analysis. This way, we bridge the gap
between analysis cost and expressiveness and programs that previously could not be analyzed
in a reasonable time frame become amenable to analysis and verification. Our high
level approach is to import performance optimization techniques that were developed in the
distinct domain of high performance computing to program analysis. Specifically this includes
the development of architecture-cognizant optimizations, autotuning, and program
generators for program analysis.

Our proposal is inter-disciplinary: to make progress we
need to combines ideas from two distinct areas of computer science: high performance
algorithms and optimizations (represented by Prof. Dr. Markus P¨uschel) and program
analysis and verification (represented by Prof. Dr. Martin Vechev). Our preliminary results
(described later) have been highly encouraging: in a recent paper on the subject [44] (about
to appear), we show in many cases almost an order of magnitude speed-up compared to
(already optimized) analysis engines. We believe that our proposal can have significant
impact on both the algorithmic side but also in terms of practical tools to be released and
adopted by the research community and by industry.

Title: Olfactory-based strategies for swimmers and robotic devices
Abstract:
Olfaction, the detection of chemical substances through smell, plays a significant role in migration, social interaction and feeding of many animals. In marine environments, some prime examples are the migration of eels and salmon over hundreds of kilometers, or the predation of sharks using their sense of smell. Robotic applications based on chemical sensing can be used to find gas leak sources, rescue trapped people, detect drugs and explosives, or coordinate collective behavior.

Investigating odor-based source detection in natural and robotic contexts requires a multi-faceted approach. It incorporates sensing, neural processing, an actuation system, and body mechanics. The surrounding fluid environment affects the plume evolution and interacts with body deformations, resulting in locomotion. Most existing studies for olfactory-based sensing rely either on integrated models that drastically simplify the fluid environment, or on costly, inflexible robotic experiments that complicate the use of machine learning techniques.

With this proposal I wish to use my knowledge of fluid dynamics, biolocomotion and machine learning to reverse-engineer chemical source localization strategies in a simulated fluid environment. Using reinforcement learning, I will optimize the swimmer’s strategic behavior and compare with existing bio-inspired and statistical algorithms for odor source detection. Progressively increasing the complexity of the swimmer, from a point-wise agent to a complete neuromechanical representation, enables me to distinguish all facets of the arising cognitive behavior. Collaborations with the RoboBees team enable implementations of such strategies in practice, ultimately leading to improved robotic strategies and new insights in natural swimmers’ behavior. 

In a wider context, this neuromechanical model coupled with reinforcement learning and accurate fluid dynamics can be used for studying other cognitive tasks, such as predation, escape responses and collective coordination. I believe that the work outlined in this proposal will provide exciting new insights in how cognitive behavior arises, for olfactory-based locomotion and, eventually, for a wider range of unsteady locomotory patterns.
Keywords: biolocomotion, chemical sensing, cognitive behavior, machine learning, neuromechanics, robotics, source localization

Title: Second-Order Layers in Deep Networks for Visual Recognition
Abstract:
Automatically recognizing objects and people in images could have impact in a wide variety of domains, such as security and autonomous navigation. Unsurprisingly, visual recognition has therefore been one of the fundamental goals of Computer Vision since the beginning. Over the years, great progress has been made, which can be roughly equally attributed to the advances in Machine Learning and the development of new image features. With the advent of Big Data and the renewed popularity of Deep Learning, this progress has recently accelerated significantly.

In particular, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), that jointly learn features and classifiers, have played a crucial role in this acceleration. CNNs are multi-layer architectures in which the output of the previous layer is convolved with a series of filters learned from data. In essence, this convolution process computes a weighted sum of the values output by the previous layer, either locally for convolutional layers, or globally for fully-connected ones. By performing such a linear operation, each filter can be thought of as computing first-order statistics from the previous layer output.

Psychophysics experiments have shown, however, that, to discriminate different textures, humans strongly rely on second-order statistics, such as covariance, which depend quadratically on the input measurements. This was exploited in Computer Vision by the Region Covariance Descriptors (RCDs), which represent an image region by a covariance matrix computed from local image features. In previous work, including our own, these RCDs were shown to outperform standard, first-order, features in many visual recognition tasks. However, these second-order descriptors have always been extracted from handcrafted features, and are thus currently unable to deliver the performance achieved by deep networks.

Our goal is therefore to introduce second-order statistics in Deep Learning architectures. In particular, we intend to focus on CNNs, which provide, in their inner layers, local representations from which covariance matrices can be computed. To this end, we will investigate two different scenarios:

- One covariance descriptor as final image representation. The nature of the lower layers of the CNN will remain unchanged in that they will still compute first-order statistics, but the final layer will encode one covariance matrix, which will be fed to a classifier.

- Local covariance descriptors in the inner network layers. Second-order statistics will be computed in the lower layers of the network. These second-order layers will then act as input either to first-order layers, or to other second-order ones.

To interface our second-order layers with either the classifier, or first-order layers, we will account for the fact that covariance matrices, which are symmetric positive definite (SPD), form a Riemmannian manifold, and can thus not be studied under Euclidean geometry. This has proven crucial in previous work on RCDs from handcrafted features, including our own. We will therefore leverage our expertise with the SPD manifold to develop a generic and effective framework to incorporating second-order statistics in deep networks. In this framework, the parameters of all layers and the final classifier will be learned jointly, which will combine the benefits of deep architectures and of second-order statistics, thus yielding even more powerful models.

We are confident that our framework will further improve the performance of visual recognition to the point of making it practical for real-world applications. Furthermore, we expect that our approach will have repercussions beyond the Computer Vision community, and motivate others to go beyond standard, first-order Deep Learning architectures.
Keywords: Computer vision, Convolutional neural networks, Deep learning, Region covariance descriptors, Riemannian geometry, Visual recognition

Title: Fast algorithms for accurate crystal defect simulations: Towards computer-aided materials design
Abstract:
Humanity is currently facing its biggest environmental challenge requiring breakthrough energy technologies. To ensure energy efficiency, the development of novel materials, specifically metallic alloys, becomes indispensable. For example, alloying tungsten, the primary candidate for plasma-facing materials in nuclear fusion power plants, with rhenium increases the fracture toughness at elevated temperatures by a multiple, compared to pure tungsten, and, therefore, the lifetime of reactors (Ren et al., 2018, IJRMHM 75). Its behavior under irradiation yet remains to be investigated, however, many of the underlying mechanisms cannot be directly observed in real experiments. This requires a computer-aided materials design approach in which these mechanisms are quantified by simulation in order to predict experimentally-observed phenomena. The state-of-the-art computing hardware and algorithms can simulate hundreds of atoms by direct atomistic simulations with density functional theory (DFT) which allows for an accurate prediction of ideal crystalline properties, such as phase stability or elastic moduli. However, in realistic materials many critical properties, such as yield strength or fracture toughness, are determined by the microstructure and, hence, require a multiscale approach. Presently, multiscale simulations are prohibitively expensive with DFT and, in lieu thereof, carried out with empirical interatomic potentials (EIPs). However, existing EIPs can, at their best, only suggest a qualitative mechanism but remain inadequate for a quantitative understanding of multicomponent systems and chemical interactions.

The recently-emerging class of machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) holds great promise to push these frontiers to a new level. However, for larger systems, possibly involving tens of thousands of atoms, their development is still in its infancy. In particular, there exists no straightforward approach to generate training data for atomic neighborhoods which are not just representative of the bulk material, i.e., in the vicinity of defects, such as dislocations, cracks or grain boundaries. However, a hypothetical, perfectly-trained MLIP---although orders of magnitude more efficient than DFT---will still be too expensive for large-scale problems. Therefore, the proposed project follows a novel approach combining machine learning, multiscale modeling and state-of-the-art numerical methods.

The first part of the project is devoted to the development of a novel training procedure with controllable accuracy for MLIPs to be used in atomic-scale simulations of dislocations and their interactions with point defects. The proposed algorithm follows a top-down approach by extracting the training set directly from the large-scale simulation. This will be achieved using active learning to identify only parts of the atomistic domain where the MLIP becomes inaccurate, and out of which the algorithm subsequently constructs the training configurations. This idea stands in contrast to the classical bottom-up approach, where the potential is trained with respect to a huge, predetermined database, often decoupled from the actual quantities of interest.

In practice, simulating dislocation motion is performed using infinite arrays of infinitely long, parallel dislocations. However, this method requires very large cell sizes to mitigate spurious effects from the image dislocations. This will be addressed in the second part which is devoted to the development of an atomistic/continuum coupling method, circumventing this problem by restricting atomic resolution to a region around the dislocation core, coupled to a very efficient exterior discrete boundary element method such that the overall computational cost scales with the size of the fully atomistic region.

The proposed algorithms will be applied to study dislocation motion in pure bcc W and W-H systems. In hydrogen-based nuclear fusion reactors the transport of H atoms through dislocation propagation is expected to play a crucial role for the embrittlement of W-based materials, but, to date, no EIP exists to quantify the contributing mechanisms. Therefore, the results will shed new light on previous studies and pave the way towards a complete understanding of design-relevant processes for future devices. Moreover, the proposed methodology is by no means restrictive and will be used in future research to study related problems, such as hydrogen embrittlement in iron-based materials or defect-solute interactions in bcc metals to quantitatively characterize high-strength steels.
Keywords: Active learning, Atomistic simulation, Atomistic/continuum coupling, Discrete boundary element method, Dislocations, Learning on-the-fly, Machine learning potentials, Multiscale modeling

Title: 3D in Wildlife Conservation and Management: Integrating Demography, Dispersal, and Decision Making
Abstract:
Successful wildlife conservation and management depend on decisions about how and when to best allocate limited resources to respond to threats affecting endangered species or to mitigate human-wildlife conflicts. However, making these decisions is challenging, particularly when critical information about the system in question is missing. In wildlife ecology, uncertainty often arises from population models that overlook or inadequately represent critical life-history processes. A key life history process frequently neglected in these models is dispersal – the transfer of individuals between sites or social groups – despite its important role in sustaining population persistence. This omission is particularly critical in social species, most of which are endangered, as reproduction in these species is often limited to a few breeding individuals within each group, and individual dispersal decisions can significantly affect the reproductive success of existing groups and the formation of new groups. A lack of understanding of a species' dispersal behaviour, its interaction with the environment, and the influence of group social structures on dispersal patterns can therefore result in inaccurate population models, hindering reliable population forecasts and optimal decision making. 

To address these challenges, I aim to (1) develop individual-based models (IBMs) that more accurately incorporate dispersal processes, and (2) integrate these IBMs with advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models to identify the most effective conservation actions under anticipated environmental and anthropogenic change scenarios. 

To achieve these aims, I will use empirical data from two social species as case studies: the mountain gorilla (Gorilla beringei beringei), a species of conservation concern in Africa, and the dingo (Canis dingo), a species involved in human-wildlife conflict in Australia. 

I will first create a spatially realistic, socially structured IBM that accurately reflects the local demography and movement patterns of dispersers and resident groups in each species; this will be achieved by incorporating detailed knowledge about dispersal, combined with methods I co-developed during my PhD, which aim at reducing uncertainties in survival estimates and in predictions of where dispersers will settle. To test the performance of this ‘dispersal-enhanced IBM’, I will compare how well it reproduces empirically observed population-level estimates of both species, such as population abundance or group sizes, against a dispersal-naïve IBM. 

Second, this dispersal-enhanced IBM will be combined with deep reinforcement learning to derive the optimal conservation strategy under focal scenarios, such as habitat loss, disease outbreaks, or climate change; this will be achieved by simulating population dynamics considering different management actions and training a neural network to learn the optimal decision sequence.

I will be hosted by Monash University in Australia to collaborate with the leading scientists in the field of AI modelling for conservation decisions. I have established collaborations with the Dian Fossey Gorilla Fund and the Myall Lakes Dingo Project, both of whom will provide access to extensive data on the two case study species.

Ultimately, this project will not only enhance my skills in demographic modelling for applied purposes but also provide a significant advancement in wildlife conservation and management, showcasing the promising integration of IBMs with deep reinforcement learning approaches in AI-driven decision making.
Keywords: decision science, dispersal ecology, individual-based modeling, population ecology, population viability analysis, stochastic dynamic programming, structured decision making, wildlife conservation and management

Title: Collaborative machine learning
Abstract:
Background: Machine learning has traditionally involved *centralized* learning -- training large models on vast datasets which are collected from users. However, there have been growing privacy concerns and regulations regarding the collection and permanent storage of such datasets.

Collaborative learning represents an alternate paradigm wherein users form a loose federation and collaborate with each other to train a machine learning model, without transferring any raw data thereby enabling privacy-preserving learning.
However, the performance of collaborative learning currently significantly lags its centralized counterpart, mainly hindered by the heterogeneity in the tasks and datasets across the users.

Goals and methods: The goal of this proposal is to develop theoretically sound and practically performant algorithms for collaborative learning. While centralized learning is restricted to training a single model for all users, in collaborative learning each user is free to personalize their model to their particular task and dataset. This can be leveraged to overcome heterogeneity and match or even exceed the performance of the centralized approach. Building on my expertise in developing efficient algorithms for distributed and federated optimization, I would like to investigate how to adapt these techniques for personalized collaborative learning. Concretely, I hope to a) use techniques from knowledge distillation to develop model-independent communication protocols for transferring knowledge between users, b) use ideas from domain adaptation and multi-task learning in order to leverage shared information while personalizing models to each user's task, and c) develop robust and private frameworks which can ensure that malicious agents cannot derail the training or extract sensitive information.

Outcomes: I expect the research outlined in this proposal will result in new algorithms and techniques for communication efficient, personalized, and robust collaborative machine learning. Further, our impactful theory advances will go beyond collaborative learning as well, towards a more fundamental understanding of domain-adaptation and multi-task learning. Finally, I expect to produce reusable open source software to ensure fast dissemination and broad real-world applications of the research.
Keywords: Collaborative learning, Distributed Optimization, Distributed learning, Federated learning, Privacy-preserving machine learning

Title: NA
Abstract:
Reinforcement learning (RL) is the study of agents that interact with an environment by observing states and acting according to a policy that ideally maximizes expected cumulative reward. Traditional model-based RL systems learn a simple predictive model of the consequences of their actions, and use this model to adjust the parameters of a controller. Human beings employ essentially the same strategy, but are clearly much more sophisticated than that. RL methods typically use the predictive model to simulate the future step-by-step (millisecond by millisecond), an awkward strategy that ignores the enormous potential efficiency of abstract reasoning. This strategy seems unlikely to scale to complex real-world problems. Instead, humans learn to ignore insignificant details and think about the past and the future in terms of abstract concepts such as objects and relations between objects, which are compact representations of complex spatio-temporal patterns. 

The main goal of the current proposal is to develop neural systems that are similarly capable of abstract reasoning. We are interested in systems that learn to extract simple concepts and their relations from an observation stream, and that learn to think in a greatly compressed, almost symbolic, "concept space" to quickly identify high-level strategies for future behavior. Based on our previous work, we think that we are now in a great position to make progress in this field, which seems central to the future of RL.
Keywords: Deep Learning, Learning to reason abstractly, Learning to think, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Neural Networks (NNs), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Reinforcement Learning (RL), Supervised Learning (SL), Unsupervised Learning (UL)

Title: AIIDKIT: Artificial Intelligence for Improved Infectious Diseases Outcomes in Kidney Transplant Recipients
Abstract: Kidney transplant recipients face a sustained risk of infections beyond the immediate post-transplant period, complicating traditional risk assessment and often requiring extended prophylaxis with associated adverse effects and costs. To address this, the AIIDKIT project aims to develop a highly personalized artificial intelligence (AI) model using advanced deep learning to predict not just the likelihood, but also the specific type and causative organism of infection in this population. This initiative will leverage a rich retrospective dataset from the Swiss Transplant Cohort Study (STCS) and the Brazilian Botucatu Medical School Hospital (HCFMB), encompassing detailed longitudinal data (including comprehensive patient profiles with pre-, intra-, and post-transplant information, donor and organ characteristics, clinical events, and laboratory results) from over 3,300 kidney transplant recipients with up to 10 years of follow-up. Our novel scientific approach lies in modeling the entire transplant trajectory as a sequence of clinical events and observations, utilizing cutting-edge deep learning architectures such as attention mechanisms and, uniquely, graph neural networks to capture both temporal dependencies and complex interrelationships within the multimodal data. Specifically, we will investigate graph-based attention networks to model dynamic relationships between patient characteristics, treatments, and infection occurrences. This approach differentiates itself from existing initiatives by moving beyond traditional risk factors and leveraging the power of deep learning to learn intricate, personalized patterns directly from the longitudinal data, enabling a more granular and clinically actionable prediction of infection risks. This project has the potential to significantly refine our understanding of post-transplant infection dynamics and contribute to more targeted and effective clinical interventions, ultimately improving patient outcomes and optimizing resource utilization.

Title: Data mining for precipitation nowcasting
Abstract:
This project establishes a bridge between data mining, machine learning and meteorological research by proposing innovative approaches for efficient processing of the growing amounts of meteorological data which are being captured and stored nowadays. More specifically, data-driven methodologies and algorithms will be developed for spatial prediction of meteorological variables and particularly for short-term forecasting (nowcasting) of precipitation in the regions of complex mountainous topographies. This project will investigate in detail complex dynamic processes in the boundary layer such as orographic precipitation and convective storm initiation and evolution for which vast datasets become available due to advances in remote sensing technologies.

Weather radar offers high spatial and temporal resolutions relative to other sensing technologies and is becoming an essential tool for precipitation studies, retrieval of wind fields, quantitative precipitation estimates and forecasting. However, the assimilation of high resolution radar data in numerical weather prediction models requires the sophisticated description of microphysical processes to be effective and is thus computationally demanding. Thus, precipitation nowcasting is commonly approached using extrapolation-based models, expert-based systems and conceptual models. Data mining along with machine learning methods, in particular Support Vector Machines (SVM), provide the necessary theoretical and algorithmic support for building efficient data-driven nowcasting models. The philosophy underlying the project is to learn, in a statistical sense, the non-linear relationships which link spatial patterns of precipitation and of convective initiation to the atmospheric and topographic conditioning factors.

Two main case studies will be considered in detail. The first one is related to the nowcasting of orographic precipitation in the Alps by exploiting methods of sequence retrieval and of dimensionality reduction. The approach is based on the embedding of radar images in a phase space characterizing the evolution of main image patterns and meteorological forcing. The phase space is constructed by applying principal component analysis on a large radar data archive where the instances are the images (every 5 minutes) and the dimensions are the image pixels and by stacking atmospheric forcing variables. The evidence of similar radar sequences in the archive is used to guess the future evolution of the system. The forecast can be computed by combining the evolution of the trajectories which follow the retrieved sequences. Weather radar images, wind and instability conditions will be used for the task.

The second forecasting exercise considers the initiation and evolution of thunderstorms using SVM extensions for target detection, classification and regression. The environmental conditions which lead to thunderstorm initiation can be modelled by training SVM models on a representative set of initiation and non-initiation points. Their evolution and variation of internal energy is also a function of the environmental conditions which need to be extracted from suitable spatial locations, typically the ones in front of them. Radar, satellite images and features, outputs from numerical models, digital elevation models and sensor networks will be used for the task.

Several scientific questions will be explored during the project such as the precipitation predictability in space and time, optimal embedding of the data, relevance of predictor variables and sources of uncertainty. Being at the interface between meteorological and machine learning research, the project is innovative and particularly important in our increasingly data-driven world. Basic fundamental research about the predictability of precipitation and its modelling in complex topography using novel data mining methods is the basis for setting up effective hydro-meteorological early warning systems.
Keywords: Convective initiation, Data mining, Orographic precipitation, Precipitation nowcasting, Sequence retrieval, Support vector machines, Weather radar

Title: Smart microscopy for spatial optogenetics: dissecting Rho GTPase signaling in cell migration and neuronal morphogenesis
Abstract: Rho GTPase signaling networks play a pivotal role in controlling cytoskeletal dynamics, which underpin essential cellular processes such as cell migration and neuronal morphogenesis. These networks generate dynamic, subcellular signaling patterns that fluctuate on timescales from seconds to minutes and length scales of microns, orchestrating local cytoskeletal rearrangements. While the importance of these signaling networks is well-recognized, understanding how specific cytoskeletal rearrangements depend on the spatio-temporal dynamics of the different Rho GTPases and their interplay, has remained a central challenge. After the seminal discovery that Rho GTPases control the cytoskeleton in 1992, the next two decades have focused on mapping the functions of the Rho GTPase network components (GTPases, GEFs, GAPs, effectors). Later, biosensor imaging has revealed that Rho GTPase signaling fluctuates on time scales of tens of seconds and length scales of single microns, that the Rho GTPase network can form signaling patterns, that Rho GTPases crosstalk with each other, and that cytoskeletal dynamics feed back on Rho GTPase signaling. The contemporary challenge is now to precisely map the Rho GTPase network circuitry that produces such complex signaling patterns. For that purpose, we need technologies to perturb Rho GTPase signaling dynamics at the exact time/length scales they are fluctuating. Optogenetics has emerged as a powerful tool to study spatio-temporal Rho-GTPase signaling, because it enables controlled perturbations of signaling dynamics at these precise time and length scales. The ability to deliver spatial light inputs using digital mirror devices or galvo mirrors allows one to spatially control optogenetic actuators. This for now has taken advantage of human input to specify which subcellular region of interest is activated, limiting experimental throughput. New advances in microscope automation and computer vision enable automation of such experiments, allowing to systematically dissect how spatio-temporal Rho GTPase signaling contributes to cellular morphodynamics. In such experiments, real-time image analysis is combined with adaptive targeted illumination in order to apply specific illumination inputs and/or control specific outcomes. The Pertz and Kapitein labs have independently pioneered such smart microscopy methods to optogenetically control cell behavior in real-time with yet unmatched precision, at the same time allowing to scale up experimental throughput. We propose to join forces and pursue the following three aims. In Aim 1, we will build an open-source software for real-time optogenetic control, integrating genetic actuator/biosensor circuits to dynamically perturb Rho GTPase signaling and simultaneously measure cell morphodynamics, cytoskeletal, and Rho GTPase signaling dynamics. It includes human supervised and machine learning-based unsupervised methods to explore spatio-temporal Rho GTPase signaling dynamics at scale. In Aim 2, we will perform smart microscopy experiments to probe subcellular Rho GTPase networks governing cytoskeletal dynamics in migrating cells and neurons, aiming to reveal how signaling orchestrates cytoskeletal rearrangements and uncover conserved or unique Rho GTPase signaling network structures. In Aim 3, we perform smart microscopy experiments to explore how subcellular Rho signaling dynamics feeds back on the dynamics of the whole cell. This will provide new insights into cell polarization during cell migration and axonal specification in neurons. Our project will both advance the understanding of spatio-temporal Rho GTPase signaling in regulating cell morphogenesis and deliver a robust, open-source smart microscopy platform for automated spatial optogenetics that can be applied to any cell biological problem.
Keywords: Rho GTPase, Rho GTPase signaling, biosensor imaging, cell migration, computer vision, cytoskeleton, neuronal morphogenesis, optogenetics, smart microscopy

Title: Towards Creative systems with LINGuistic modelling (C-LING)
Abstract:
Language  is  predominantly  viewed  as  a  means  for  information  exchange  in  the  field  of  AI  and natural language processing.  However, this overlooks the important role language plays as a vehicle for creative thought.  This  aspect  of  cognition  is  unique  to  mankind,  crucial  for  innovation,  and  currently  under-explored in  AI.  As  an  example,  inventions  such  as  the  mobile  phone,  or  the  glass  canoe,  have  come  to  life  in  people’s minds by means of combining known concepts in unseen ways. The  field  of  NLP  has  mature  methods  to  capture  the  meaning  of  words  and  the  way  they  relate  to  each other.  At  the  same  time,  a  number  of  researchers  have  started  questioning  the  learning  capacity  of  these large language models and concerns regarding short-cut learning, bias and inability to generalise are growing. Creative tasks, such as the ones specified in this project, require a high level of generalisation that allows the system  to  cut  across  patterns  found:  across  domains,  time  periods,  as  well  as  different  languages.  They  are therefore  a  perfect  testbed  for  measuring  the  generalisation  power  and  actual  level  of  intelligence  of  current systems. 

This  project  aims  to  investigate  what  aspects  computational  models  need  to  perform  creative cognitive  tasks,  from  generating  relatively  simple  novel  concepts  to  more  complex  and  structured  ideas, across  multiple  domains  and  languages.   More  in  particular,  it  aims  to  answer  what  types  of  structured  and unstructured knowledge are needed and what models best integrate these types of knowledge. 

Current  neural  language  models  are  trained  on  large  amounts  of  text  data  and  used  successfully in  many  NLP  applications  as  models  of  language  use.   However,  as  shown  in  previous  work,  such  statistical models  might  capture  word  associations  well,  but  they  are  not  sufficient  for  tasks  that  involve  reasoning  or generalisation across domains, which is the case for the creative cognitive task we study.  Previous work from cognitive  science  used  symbolic  methods  to  model  conceptual  blending.   However,  these  methods  are  often not scalable.  We plan to use hybrid neural-symbolic methods for modelling creative thinking, which will allow us  to  add  structure  in  our  models  and  integrate  insights  from  cognitive  science.  Furthermore,  we  will  exploit differences  in  embeddings  and  knowledge  across  domains  and  languages/cultures  to  inform  the  models  for novel concept creation. 


We expect to build a variety of computational models for the range of creative tasks  we  defined  from  novel  concept  generation  to  the  generation  of  more  structured  complex  ideas,  across domains  and  languages.  This  will  lead  to  insights  w.r.t.  the  limitations  and  capabilities  of  neural  and  neuro-symbolic  approaches  on  such  creative  tasks.   In  addition,  we  will  learn  in  how  far  we  can  leverage  cognitive theory  for  building  creative  systems.   Our  research  into  creative  processes  will  impact  the  field  by  pushing towards  AI  tools  that  are  more flexible  and  resourceful than  current  technologies,  which  will  lead to  the  level of innovation and diversity needed for human progress, while better exploring the wealth of data available.
Keywords: AI, creativity, deep learning, lexical change, lexical innovation, natural language processing, neologisms, neuro-symbolic methods

Title: Solving Stochastic PDEs: new algebraic and analytic approaches
Abstract:
According to Martin Hairer's regularity structure theory, the scheme of solving a semilinear Stochastic PDE (SPDE) consists of an algebraic step and an analytic step. The general goal of this project is to use new methods to study both algebraic and analytic steps so that one can solve a larger class of SPDEs beyond currect knowledge both theoretically and numerically. 
More precisely, we will mainly focus on the following two problems:
(a) Non--classical models in regularity structures: This part concerns with both algebraic and analytic steps. In terms of the language of regularity structure theory, the driven noise of a given SPDE will be lifted to a model which involves with lots of algebraic structures (the algebraic step). Once the model lifting of noise is fixed, then the solution map of the underlying SPDE depends continuously on the lifted models (the analytic step). The classical regularity structure theory requires that the noise possesses a Hölderian continuity, and cannot encodes the case that it only has a certain Besov type regularity or discontinuities. Here, we want to develop new tools to solve SPDEs with non--Hölderian noises. Since this is quite an ambitious goal, we propose to restrict ourselves to the rough paths regime, i.e. the 1-dimensional regularity structures, and consider some intermediate steps. A first intermediate setp is to establish the Lipschitz--continuity of the Ito--Lyons map with respect to certain Besov topologies and prove the existence of mild solutions to Burgers--like SPDEs with 1-dimensional periodic boundary condition driven by Levy processes (whose pathwise regularity may have a Besov type). A second intermediate goal we want to achieve is to study more concrete examples of SPDEs with non-Hölderian noises which may illuminate us to find a unified approach to deal with the general case and develop the Besov and cadlag rough path theory. 
(b) Reservoir computing of regularity structures: This part concerns mainly with the analytic step. According to the above description, one can realize that solving SPDEs via regularity structure theory shares the same essential inner structure with the so--called reservoir computing, a special approach from machine learning. The more interesting phenomenon is, in the setup of rough path regime (i.e., the 1-dimensional regularity structure theory), one can extend models by constructing signatures such that the solution map is even almost linear with respect to the extended models, so that the learning of the readout map in the corresponding reservoir computation can be reduced to a linear regression. The natural question is whether the same extension exists for general regularity structures, such that the above reservoir computing approach is valid for solving SPDEs with higher dimensional boundary conditions. More precisely, we will investigate whether most of currently known regularity structures, in particular those induced by Hopf algebras possess the same extension property as rough paths (which are group--like elements of a specified Hopf algebra).
Keywords: Machine Learning, Regularity Structure, Rough Paths, Stochastic Partial Differential Equations

Title: Reciprocal Enhancement of Terminological and Ontological Resources Through Definition Analysis
Abstract:
Definitions are central to terminological and ontological resources. Definition writing is therefore an activity essential to the development of useful and reliable resources. Definitions are included in such resources in order to ensure that they fulfill the function of conveying information about the meaning and usage of terms in the domain. They are intended to enhance communication or to help ontlogists in data annotation. To enhance their quality, these resources should include natural language definitions with the appropriate and relevant content. Producing definitions is however time consuming, costly and requires proper expertise in this activity, among other things, with regards to the type of contents that is relevant to defining terms. 

The general objective of my research is therefore to create generic, language- and domain-independent tools to assists terminologists and ontologists in natural language definition authoring. This objective requires creating language- and domain-independent definition models that can be implemented in such (semi-)automatic tools. It also requires testing these models on corpora of existing definitions to see to what extent they can be used to predict definition contents. Completing and testing a full operational framework for definition authoring for terminological and ontological resources, indeed, requires large-scale multilingual corpus analyses in order to obtain statistically significant results. The results would then be used to implement the ontological models predicting the contents of definitions in a definition-authoring tool that can be used in terminological resources and ontologies. These analyses, however, require the (semi-)automatic annotation of large amounts of definitions. Such annotation tasks rely on external resources, such as manually annotated training corpora or terminological lexicons.

This research project aims, more specifically, at realizing the necessary groundwork for such large-scale corpus analyses through the analysis of natural language and logical definitions. The outcomes of this project will be a set of resources that can be used for the automation of definition analysis and generation: ontologically annotated French and English training corpora, term lexicons, lists of expressions marking relations, a manual for the annotation of the internal structure of definitions and annotation methods using existing ontologies. This project will also yield preliminary results on the tested hypotheses through analyses of the manually annotated data.

To attain these goals, I maintain that it is possible to reciprocally enhance terminological and ontological resources through definition analyses. These analyses are based on the ontological analysis framework that I have proposed in my PhD thesis [1] and that I am currently improving in the Department of Philosophy at the University at Buffalo under the supervision of Professor Barry Smith, Director of the US National Center for Ontological Research and Professor of Philosophy, Neurology and Computer Science at the University at Buffalo (NY, USA).

Several factors are known to determine or influence the contents of definitions. Among all the known factors that may constrain definition contents, the one that should, prima facie, be the most 'neutral' with respect to domains and languages is what I have called the 'ontological factor' [1].

My research is based on the assumption that the type of entity in the world referred to by a term being defined has an influence on the contents of the definition. The novelty of my approach is that the categories (entity types) and their corresponding relations that constitute the definition models are based on the categories of an existing realist upper-level ontology, the Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), and their specifications [2,3]. This choice is motivated by the fact that this ontology is aimed at representing the types of things that exist in the world, their properties, and their relations to other types of entities. The methodology for corpus analyses that I developed implies segmenting each definition according to the general genus+differentiae pattern and tagging each segment with the corresponding entity type for the genus and relation for each differentia using the proposed relational models based on BFO.

In this project, I propose to improve my analysis framework by taking advantage of other ontologies extending BFO, such as the Information Artifact Ontology (IAO) or the Gene Ontology (GO) also developed in Buffalo. The idea is to use existing ontologies, inter alia their logical definitions, to facilitate the analysis of the contents of natural language definitions. Conversely, I also propose to use the results of small-scale corpus analyses of definitions to enhance the quality of natural language definitions in ontologies. Annotating definitions with ontologies and adding textual definitions to ontologies both imply getting a better understanding of the relations between logical and textual definitions.

I will therefore use the improved ontological analysis framework and methodology to annotate the natural language definitions constituting the corpora to be analyzed and compared to logical definitions. This will produce the data necessary to test the applicability of the models to predicting definition contents and to realize large-scale corpus analyses. To summarize, these methods involve the reciprocal use of ontologies to annotating definitions and of the results of natural language definition analyses to enhancing ontologies.

The outcomes of this interdisciplinary research project would not only have a positive impact on the particular activity of definition writing and the resulting terminological and ontological resources. Terminological resources would have richer functionnalities allowing, for example, for onomasiological queries. A wider audience could use ontologies as classical terminological resources, and ontologists would benefit from richer and more reliable ontological resources. The results of this research project would also be of particular interest for the natural language processing (NLP) and the applied ontology communities: terminological definitions annotated with this type of relational models would allow for better reusability of terminological dictionaries or databases as lexical resources for NLP systems and for easier domain-ontology development, a field which has growing ties with terminology.

Title: Ecosystem Mapping in Challenging Environments with 3D Deep Learning
Abstract:
Background
Unprecedented human pressure on ecosystems through global climate change and local interference could have catastrophic cascading impacts on billions of people, necessitating widespread monitoring of ecosystems. To monitor ecosystems that can not be surveilled at sufficient resolution by satellite or aerial imagery, it is necessary to devise in situ surveying methods that are scalable in terms of data acquisition and the labor cost of data analysis. Creating 3D digital twins reconstructed from cheap consumer cameras is a promising candidate for scalable surveys, enabling change detection down to the resolution of fine-grained structures, for example branches of individual trees or coral colonies. However, current 3D reconstruction face severe limitations in challenging real-world ecological scenarios. While the use of deep neural networks has led to staggering advances in 3D computer vision in the last years, these improvements have focused heavily on urban, driving, or indoor scenarios, while progress on domains outside of the training data is not objectively measurable. For existing 3D vision algorithms, reliable 3D reconstruction in natural settings, such as dense forests or underwater environments like coral reefs and kelp forests, remains notoriously hard due to imagery with repetitive textures, strongly varying lighting conditions, or moving objects.
Aims The proposed project will drive development of AI-based 3D computer vision algorithms that generalize to real-world environments in ecological applications. The aim is to create substantial and tangible progress on the fundamental tasks of image matching and monocular depth estimation, which are the fundamental building blocks of any 3D vision pipelines from 3D mapping to robot navigation.

Methods 
First, a diverse and challenging benchmark 3D vision dataset spanning various natural en- vironments that are challenging for current 3D vision algorithms will be created in a series of short field campaigns, including forests, coral reefs, and kelp forests. This dataset will allow objective evaluation of existing 3D vision algorithms and allow training 3D deep neural networks to adapt to these challenging natural scenarios. In particular, we will devise efficient fine-tuning techniques for adapting state-of-the- art 3D foundation models to ecological domains, streamlining the adaptation of novel 3D computer vision techniques in ecological monitoring applications.

Results 
The expected result is that an objective 3D vision benchmark will expose a significant per- formance gap of state-of-the-art 3D vision algorithms between the urban/indoor training domains and challenging natural scenarios. As a remedy, the expectation is that a relatively small amount of high- quality domain-specific data can be used to effectively bridge this performance gap by means of transfer learning, significantly improving the state of the art in 3D vision in challenging ecosystem monitoring settings.

Impact 
More accurate and reliable 3D vision algorithms in natural environments will catalyze the use of 3D vision pipelines in ecological monitoring. This will unlock potential in environmental robotics, and democratize environmental surveys by reducing the equipment and labor cost, potentially leading to innovative citizen science solutions in biodiversity monitoring. This line of research paves a clear path for future research on the promising intersection of artificial intelligence with environmental science for tangible impact in ecology and conservation.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Climate Change, Computer Vision, Ecology, Machine Learning

Title: Behavioral Biomarker for Temporal Lobe Epilepsy
Abstract:
The mechanistic bases of temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) are not well understood. A major impediment to progress towards evidence-based, rigorous preclinical, translational research into the TLE is that the experimental approach often requires labor-intensive 24/7 video-EEG monitoring of seizures and rests on the inherently subjective scoring of behavioral seizure phenotypes by human observers along the Racine scale.
The aim of the proposed research is to explore the transformative potential of state of the art machine learning (ML)-assisted 3D video analysis to phenotype mice with acquired epilepsy in an automated and high-throughput manner (Aim 1) and to correlate TLE-specific neuronal circuit activity with subtle behavioral dynamics that are not captured by current technology (Aim 2). The central idea rests on the discovery that complex animal behaviors are structured in stereotyped modules (“syllables”) at sub-second timescales that are arranged according to specific rules (“grammar”) that can be detected without observer bias by a combined 3D imaging (Kinect™) and ML method. The ML-assisted 3D video analysis technology will be adopted for epilepsy research to test if there are TLE-specific behavioral syllables and associated transition probabilities that might not be discernable by a human observer. In addition, it will be determine if behavioral syllables in chronic TLE are invariant between animal models of TLE. In order to comply with current standards of research into TLE, the presence or absence of TLE will be determined using conventional 24/7 video-EEG (vEEG) recordings and analysis. Synchronous acquisition of vEEG and 3D video will be used to assess if aberrant neuronal network activity is associated with the expression of specific behavioral syllables. Intervene upon local seizures or interictal spikes using closed-loop optogenetics will help to verify if these TLE-specific behavioral syllables are related to the certain hippocampal ensemble activity.

Title: Network Analysis to Predict Eligibility for Epilepsy Surgery
Abstract:
One percent of the world’s population suffers from epilepsy, one third of whom have a drug-resistant form. Epilepsy surgery, which consists in resecting the part of the brain involved in generating seizures (i.e., the epileptogenic zone, EZ), is the most effective treatment option to achieve seizure freedom in these patients. About thirty percent of patients undergoing epilepsy surgery are, however, not seizure free. This high rate of surgical failure has motivated the search of electrophysiological biomarkers to better localise the EZ or predict success of surgery.

Epilepsy is considered a disorder of neural networks, involving multiple cortical and subcortical regions. The epileptic network can be estimated and characterised using several tools, among them high-density EEG, MEG and in some patients, intracerebral EEG. A growing body of evidence has shown that an increase connectivity of this network was linked with the severity of the disease and bad surgical outcome. Network analysis therefore appears to be an ideal biomarker to aid surgical decision-making. These results however come from studies with a small number of patients and must be validated on a larger cohort. Furthermore, it is not known to what extent the non-invasively estimated network corresponds to the true network, which hinders its interpretability and thus its clinical application. 

The first objective of this proposal is to better characterise the non-invasively estimated network by taking advantage of simultaneous intracranial EEG and high-density EEG or MEG recordings available at the HUG and at the APHM in Marseille, respectively. Networks derived with non-invasive recording can be directly compared to those obtained with ground-truth intracranial recording thanks to the simultaneous recording settings. The second objective is to find the network features which best describe the severity of epilepsy and use these to train a machine learning algorithm on a large cohort of patients admitted for presurgical evaluation to identify those who are suitable for surgery. Finally, the trained machine learning algorithm will be prospectively applied to patients at the HUG and a patient-specific report will be compared to the decision made by the clinicians. This final step is of utmost importance as such algorithms usually fail at the stage of clinical application.

This project is expected to highlight a specific set of connectivity metrics and features able to describe brain networks non-invasively. This set of metrics will be beneficial not only to the epilepsy research but to the entire neuroscience community. It is also expected to probe the relevance of network analysis in studying epilepsy. The second deliverable of the project is the clinically relevant machine learning algorithm to predict the eligibility for epilepsy surgery based on non-invasive recordings.

Title: CONNECT-CARE: Inclusive Healthcare Access and Personalized Health Management for Children and Adolescents (CONNECT-CARE)
Abstract:
The proposal addresses the urgent global epidemic of obesity, impacting billions of individuals worldwide. Obesity significantly elevates the risk of chronic conditions such as type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, imposing substantial burdens at both individual and community levels, as well as incurring enormous economic costs for healthcare systems. Current guidelines mainly focus on acute treatment rather than long-term therapy, with important differences based on gender and socioeconomic background. Moreover, traditional community-based health strategies face significant challenges in effectively reaching and supporting vulnerable populations like young individuals, low-income families, and migrants. These challenges significantly contribute to health inequalities and hinder the effectiveness of current programs. This highlights the urgent need for novel multidisciplinary approaches with patient engagement at its core to implement effective prevention strategies.

The project aims to develop and implement an innovative and interactive platform to empower children and adolescents in managing their health and adopting healthier lifestyles. With ground-breaking digital tools at its core, this new platform will go beyond traditional prevention strategies by reshaping the way young individuals access and

engage with healthcare systems. Through implementing a streamlined and bidirectional user-healthcare interaction as well as introducing an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted personalized obesity management approach, the project will transform how young individuals receive and perceive health messages. To achieve these aims, the project will use data from primary healthcare systems, encompassing clinical, socioeconomic, behavioural, and cultural aspects, to allow for the development of a pan-European Youth Empowerment Hub (YEH), which will harbour all digital tools and resources including the personalized obesity management platform (NutriFit Advisor) and an online educational platform. The YEH will be seamlessly integrated into the healthcare system for a bidirectional interaction between users and health professionals, improving healthcare providers' capacity to deliver services efficiently. The feasibility and effectiveness of the YEH and its digital solutions, will undergo evaluation in two randomized-controlled pilot studies in Spain and Denmark.

The implementation of a bidirectional communication platform with AI at its core will serve as a transformative tool, reshaping the relationship between users and healthcare providers. By facilitating seamless interaction, it will enhance healthcare access for users while simultaneously improving service delivery for healthcare providers. Furthermore, the project will establish the AI-assisted NutriFit Advisor as a trusted and reliable tool for young individuals, addressing a critical need for more tailored and effective health interventions. Finally, the emphasis on prevention, supported by better use of tools and data to improve the quality of obesity care, will contribute to more cost-effective and personalised care. In summary, this project will shift the paradigm of healthcare delivery towards more patient-centred and digitally-enabled models transforming health and care in daily life, and ultimately leading to better health outcomes.
Keywords: AI, Computational persuasion, Explainable AI, Nutrition support, Obesity
