Title: A novel approach to first-principles inverse materials design leveraging algorithmic property derivatives
Abstract:
The development and understanding of materials is a common theme when tackling major challenges of the 21st century, such as health care, green chemistry, energy production and storage. Indeed, many of our current solutions are fundamentally limited by the physical and chemical properties of the materials we have at hand. To overcome these fundamental limits, the computational discovery of novel materials has become a vital tool, as exemplified by the numerous success stories leading to the development of novel semiconductors and materials for electrocatalysis, hydrogen storage, Li-ion batteries. A common discovery strategy is inverse materials design, where the search through a large design space of candidates is directly guided by the targeted materials properties. A variety of methods has been proposed for this purpose. Commonly these employ first-principle property simulations based on density-functional theory (DFT) — either to directly drive the design space search or to train a statistical surrogate, which is eventually employed in the discovery process. In contrast, the use of DFT property derivatives, i.e. derivatives of the predicted property value with respect to the structural parameters, is hardly explored. However, viewing inverse design as a global optimisation of the property with respect to the materials structure, it seems natural to guide the search based on property derivatives as well. This is backed up by recent promising work in the Bayesian optimisation literature, where the inclusion of such derivatives improved the efficiency of global optimisation procedures. Motivated by this perspective, the goal of this work is to explore the use of property derivatives for inverse design.

A key obstacle for this research is that such DFT property derivatives are not readily available in standard DFT codes. Moreover, considering the large number of possible properties one might want to target, it would be a considerable effort to manually implement all associated property derivatives. An alternative to this manual approach is algorithmic differentiation (AD), which establishes a generic framework to compute arbitrary derivatives. Of note, once established in a DFT code, this technique has the potential to save years of human development time and thus enable rapid prototyping of novel derivative-enabled methods — well beyond the application in inverse materials design we target here. The use of AD in DFT simulations is still in its infancy. Codes supporting AD have only recently begun to appear, but have already stimulated flagship research such as the design of novel machine-learned DFT functionals. So far AD-enabled applications have been restricted to Gaussian basis sets. However, with the density-functional toolkit (DFTK), a first plane-wave-based code has been recently equipped with AD support opening the way to use AD-based property derivatives.

To guide our method developments, we will focus on the strain-based engineering of band structures, a setting in which inverse design has lately been applied with remarkable success. Employing strain to alter the physical or chemical properties of semiconductors is an established tool, which has generated billions of dollars of product value. However, the experimental realisation of ultralarge tensile strains in diamond nanoneedles has recently lead to unexpected paths for reversible metallisation and superconductivity in diamond. Many exciting opportunities for systems under strain remain to be uncovered making this a timely application to focus on in this research.

In the past, AD has shown to be an enabling technology which stimulates high-impact breakthrough research. A prime example is statistical learning, where AD in the form of backpropagation has made gradient descent methods possible — forming the basis of modern machine learning. With this project, we want to provide a first example for the use of AD in DFT-based inverse design, specifically enabling the use of recent progress from the global optimisation literature. Considering the ubiquitous role derivatives play in DFT property calculations (phonons, elasticity, Raman spectra, NMR shielding constants, Hubbard corrections, ...) this work strives to provide an flagship example where AD-based approaches facititate cross-disciplinary fertilisation and unlock fundamentally new ways of developing simulations.

Title: Investigating the Role of Microbiota in the association between Mood disorders and Obesity in Young Adults of the Community
Abstract:
Background: Major depressive disorder (MDD) and obesity are major public health challenges, with increasing rates in youth accompanying unhealthy lifestyle. While the association between MDD with obesity has been established, it may vary according to subtypes of MDD and the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. The gut microbiota, the community of microorganisms residing in the gastrointestinal tract, has emerged as a significant player in human health, modulating metabolic responses and interacting with the central nervous system in the gut-brain axis. This intricate interplay between microbiota, obesity, and MDD and its subtypes should be better characterized, especially in young populations that carry a potential for early intervention and prevention to reduce the risk of later cardiovascular disease (CVD).
Aim: We will perform the first follow-up of our population-based cohort of young adults to prospectively explore the links between MDD and obesity and their interplay with gut microbiota. By collecting prospectively psychiatric and somatic data along stool samples, we will (i) assess the association of MDD and its subtypes with increase in adiposity markers and cardiometabolic conditions (ii) address the association of microbial community composition and function with MDD, and its subtypes, as well as obesity, and (iii) evaluate the possible mediating role of the microbiota in the association between obesity and MDD. 
Methods: In the first follow-up of the CoLaus|PsyCoLaus Offspring cohort, we expect to include 1200 participants aged 18 to 41 about 6 years after baseline. As performed at baseline, we propose a somatic assessment to gather comprehensive data on cardiovascular risk factors (CVRF) and medication use through interviews, along with biochemical and anthropometric measurements as well as actigraphy. The psychiatric evaluation will consist of a semi-structured diagnostic interview designed to elicit criteria for DSM-IV/DSM-5 disorders and specific subtypes of MDD. These assessments will collect information on: a) recent adverse life events and stress, b) lifestyle (physical activity, diet, smoking), c) physiological factors (cortisol, sleep, circadian rhythm, HPA-axis, inflammation), and d) psychological factors (personality, temperament, coping style, self-esteem). In addition, we will assess gender through a questionnaire and collect stool samples. The fecal microbiota will be sequenced by deep shotgun metagenomics to allow for the species-level identification of microorganisms and the reconstruction of functional abilities in the community. Inferential statistics as well as machine-learning approaches will be applied to identify clinical and microbial features associated with MDD, its subtypes, as well as obesity, while considering potential confounders in the rich clinical data. 
Expected outcome: By exploiting the longitudinal clinical data, this study will clarify the direction of association between MDD and its subtypes with adiposity and cardiometabolic conditions, investigating the role of sex and gender as potential mediators. The cross-sectional analysis will identify microbial biomarkers, taxonomical and functional, associated with different subtypes of MDD and obesity, while accounting for factors impacting the microbiota. This will allow us to generate novel hypotheses on potential pathophysiological mechanisms driving the interplay between the microbiota, obesity and MDD. Finally, this study will build a biobank of stools for molecular analyses and preserved microorganisms for subsequent culture studies or animal models. 
Impact: Given the faster weight gain in young adults compared to other age groups, increased insight into the microbiological, psychological, physiological and behavioral links underlying MDD, CVRF, and ultimately CVD will enhance the development of innovative intervention and prevention strategies that could provide both mental and physical benefits from an early age.

Title: KIND: Investigating the Link between Type 1 Diabetes Management and Nerve Vitality in Children and Adolescents
Abstract:
Background: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) affects 8.75 million individuals worldwide, including an increasing number of pediatric patients. Switzerland has 26,600 affected individuals, with numbers increasing. Among the long-term complications of T1D, diabetic neuropathy (DN), which includes diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN) and cardiac autonomic neuropathy (CAN), is the most common one, impacting quality of life and increasing healthcare costs. Prevention is paramount as no specific medical treatment options are available. Yet current diagnostic methods are either burdensome, costly, and infrequently performed, such as nerve conduction studies (NCSs), or are not sensitive enough for the clinically inconspicuous stage of DN typically found in children and adolescents, limiting their effectiveness in pediatric populations.
Objective: This study aims to enhance our understanding of DN in pediatric T1D patients through holistic longitudinal monitoring, combining state-of-the-art clinical assessments with innovative digital biomarkers. The research objectives are: (1) determine how clinical factors affect peripheral nervous system (PNS) development over time in children and adolescents with T1D, including the differential impact on motor, sensory, and autonomic compartments of the nervous system; (2) develop a novel digital biomarker from real-world lifestyle tracking using wearables (e.g. physical activity) and continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) metrics that can predict DN onset and progression. We seek to better understand the pathophysiology of DN in a pediatric population and establish low-burden, individualized screening tools that can improve early detection and long-term prevention and progression of DPN and CAN in pediatric T1D patients, making monitoring more accessible and cost-effective.
Methods: We will conduct a 24-month prospective observational study with children and adolescents (age =5 years) with T1D at the Children’s Hospital of Eastern Switzerland (OKS). Our comprehensive assessment integrates multiple data sources: (1) the gold standards for clinical measurement of structural – nerve cross-sectional area (CSA) via high-resolution ultrasonography – and functional – nerve conduction velocity (NCV) via NCS – changes of the PNS; (2) CGM and metabolic parameters (e.g. C-Peptide); (3) wearables capturing relevant lifestyle factors; and (4) demographic data. Assessments will occur at baseline, 12 months, and 24 months, with wearable monitoring for one month preceding the main annual examination. Our interdisciplinary approach combines the neurophysiological and diabetological expertise of the OKS team with the digital biomarker and data science capabilities of the University of St. Gallen (HSG) team. For analyzing the relationship between biological factors and nerve function (RQ1), we will employ multiple regression models. For designing predictive digital biomarkers (RQ2), we will develop personalized machine learning models. This research builds on previous collaborations between OKS and HSG, in which the data collection infrastructure was developed and first pilot studies were conducted successfully.
Expected outcomes: This research will yield: (1) comprehensive characterization of DN onset and progression in pediatric T1D, including structural and functional changes in (un)myelinated nerve fibers; (2) novel digital biomarkers for early detection of DN using low-burden, continuous monitoring outside clinical settings; (3) identification of modifiable risk factors with the strongest influence on various components of nerve function; and (4) foundation for targeted, individualized preventive strategies. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, and presentations at international conferences. Ultimately, this research aims to establish new standards for patient-centered DN monitoring and prevention in pediatric diabetes care, reducing the long-term health and economic burden.

Title: Towards a Clinically Valid Digital 6-Minute Walk Test in Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension
Abstract:
The ATS guided 6-minute walk test (6MWT) is a non-invasive and easy to administer sub-maximal functional assessment for exercise capacity 1. It is performed under clinical supervision and evaluates the total distance (6MWD) patients walk back and forth at their own pace along a 30m walkway 1. Initially developed for cardiopulmonary disease the 6MWT is currently one of the (if not the) most widely used functional assessments in Cardiovascular and Cardiopulmonary Diseases (CVD and CPD, respectively) 2 In pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), a progressive disease of the pulmonary vasculature, the 6MWT is one of the gold-standards to assess prognosis and acts as efficacy proxy for therapeutics. A major limitation of the 6MWT is its dependence on clinic visits. This limits the administration frequency to few assessments per year, which is sub-optimal for close monitoring and provides only a snapshot of true functional performance. In times of pandemic, this limitation became even more apparent, leading to late diagnosis, decompensation, and adjustment of treatment in PAH patients. Given the rapid adoption and recent successes of digital devices, such as wearables, in medicine and healthcare 6–8, it is highly probable that a digital 6MWT, that can be performed at home or in the community (further referred to as e6MWT), could add considerable value 9. For instance, continuous assessments of e6MWTs may allow for closer disease progression monitoring in PAH, a high-priority target enabling early therapy initiation and response evaluation – factors associated with better quality of life and disease progression. Economically, it would help cut down on healthcare expenditures by reducing frequency of expensive clinic visits. 

Previous research using smartphone based e6MWT has shown good acceptability in PAH patients, but sub-optimal analytical validity (thus how accurate an algorithm performs in the target population), while clinical validity was not evaluated at all. Related research in CVD has come to a similar conclusion and particularly found that smartphone estimated e6MWT distance (e6MWD) was largely inaccurate when based on regular manufacturer provided algorithms. This is consistent with preliminary results from an ongoing clinical trial (DyNaMITE: NCT03893500), evaluating wearable based e6MWT in PAH. One potential remedy brought forward was the use of other measures, such as the total step-number during an e6MWT, which was found much more robust compared to e6MWD but no clinical evaluation has been performed. Existing evidence thus suggests that towards a clinically useful e6MWT for functional outcome assessments, it is necessary to introduce more robust alternative outcomes (what will further be referred to as e6MW{X}) and/or improve upon manufacturer provided e6MWD estimates.  Moreover, it is of utmost importance to provide evidence for clinical validity. Overall, the goal of this project will consequentially be to develop a clinically valid e6MWT by introducing more accurate e6MWD and/or e6MW{X} measures and both clinically and analytically validate those measures in PAH. Towards this, the project will build upon the DyNaMITE trial, to date, the largest clinical trial assessing use of app and wearable based e6MWT in PAH and the first one to allow for assessment of clinical validity

The specific aims of this project are: (1) Develop and analytically validate robust, personalized e6MWD estimation approaches using Apple Watch e6MWT sensor data. To do this, PAH patient and e6WMT specific characteristics will be exploited. Data from the DyNaMITE trial will be used for refinement and evaluation of analytical validity; (2) Develop and evaluate algorithms to calculate additional e6MW{X} measures based on Apple Watch e6MWT sensor data, including gait-parameters (GP), heart rate (HR) based parameters and temporal parameters (relative changes at n-minutes). To refine algorithms and evaluate analytical validity of gait-parameters a study with 20 PAH patients will be conducted where additional ground-truth data from validated devices will be collected; (3) Evaluate clinical validity of e6MWD and e6MW{X} in PAH and explore potential beyond PAH. This will be based on clinical data from the DyNaMITE trial and applicability beyond PAH will be evaluated on the large-scale My Heart Counts dataset.  

Discussion of Results and Potential Impact of the Findings: The results of this project will determine whether, and which, e6MWT derived digital measures could be used as replacement or addition to regular, in-clinic, 6MWD. If at least one measure shows signs of analytical and clinical validity, this could significantly change clinical care practices in PAH and beyond. It may also eventually accelerate research into much needed new therapies by providing, potentially more accurate and objective, digital endpoints to clinical trials.  Since the used e6MWT setup is supported by the non-profit social media and device development group PHaware, findings would be quickly translated into practice, benefitting a large global network of practitioners and PAH patients. Lastly, findings from this project, could proof applicable to the > 10 other conditions where the 6MWT is commonly used as a functional outcome assessment.

Title: MOTVS: Human-oriented ubiquitous mobility
Abstract: MOTVS has a unique ambition to develop a new mobility paradigm capable of efficiently managing large-scale networked systems through flexibility, cooperation, and collectivity. The project intends to revolutionize how emerging technologies reshape mobility by putting emphasis on improving the quality of life for people and avoiding uncontrolled competition that jeopardizes efficiency. The breakthrough interconnection between systems and humans will enable innovative services to citizens that have not been realized before, improving mobility and making its operation safer, greener, and more efficient. Identifying new means on how to govern such a complex social system in resilient and sustainable ways composes MOTVS’ vital objective. To achieve this, interdisciplinarity is the backbone of MOTVS, as it integrates vital inputs from optimization, control, machine learning, traffic science, and game theory to reform the travel of people in cities.
Keywords: cooperation, game theory, mobility, multimodal transportation, optimization, ride-sharing, sustainability, traffic management, transportation

Title: CardioTwin - Precision Cardiology based on Digital Twins
Abstract:
Wider research context / theoretical framework: The treatment of cardiovascular diseases relies increasingly on device-based therapies that need to be further improved to enhance efficacy by tailoring these to the pathophysiology of a given patient. The grand challenge in achieving such personalized precision therapies is to identify optimal device and deployment options. Physics law based virtual-heart technology that replicates a patient’s anatomy and electrophysiology (EP), referred to as digital twin model, shows high promise as a transformative tool addressing this challenge. However, fitting of parameters to patient data and generating reliable predictions remains challenging.

Hypotheses / research questions / objectives: The overall objective is to develop uncertainty-aware virtual-heart technology for the automated generation of mechanistic high fidelity ventricular digital twins (VDTs) of human ventricular EP from routine non-invasive clinical data. VDTs will incorporate personalized representations of the ventricular conduction system enabling these to replicate electrocardiograms (ECGs) during intrinsic activation, and to predict ECGs and electrograms (EGMs) in response to pacing therapies.

Approach / methods: Developments include an automated workflow for the generation of VDTs, a real-time in silico forward EP model for ECG and EGM computations, a multi-fidelity uncertainty quantification (UQ) framework to quantify the impact of observational uncertainty, and identification techniques for inferring probabilistic EP model parameters. These will be applied to calibrate virtual cohorts of healthy subjects, patients undergoing ablation of infarct-mediated ventricular tachycardia (VT) or cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT). Calibrated models will be validated, and their predictive power evaluated. UQ will provide estimates of confidence in predictions.

Level of originality / innovation: The main innovation of the project is the development of a systematic and automated approach for generating EP VDTs from clinical data. Importantly, the project proposes a paradigmatic shift from pointwise parameters estimates towards probabilistic modeling approaches. Demonstrating the ability to personalize EP function and to predict therapeutic responses with statistical bounds will boost credibility and expand the scope of modeling toward a precision cardiology tool. VDTs will also play a pivotal role in transforming medical device development in industry, as devices can be developed faster at cheaper costs.

Primary researchers involved: The projects build on the expertise of Dr. Plank in modeling cardiac EP and in building workflows for generating VDTs from clinical data, and Prof. Krause and Dr. Pezzuto in parameter identification techniques for cardiac EP problems, multi-fidelity methods and UQ. The development of the core parameter inference technologies is based on the expertise of Dr. Pock in probabilistic modeling, optimization, and machine learning.
Keywords: adjoint optimization, cardiac electrophysiology, computational cardiology, nonlinear inverse problems, parameter identification, uncertainty quantification

Title: Unupervised Learning of Interactions from Real Data
Abstract:
Our ultimate goal is to build an agent that learns to operate in the real world (i.e., to plan actions, such as navigation around obstacles or to grab objects) without direct supervision. In our own definition, an agent is a machine that can observe data through several sensors (e.g., cameras and microphones) and that can perform actions such as changing its position or interacting with objects. An agent can learn either by direct interaction or through passive observation of the interactions between other agents. In this proposal we focus on the latter learning strategy. We investigate methods for an agent to build a representation of the observed data, i.e., an internal model of the environment, the agents in it and their interactions. In contrast to related work we do not learn from simulated data, where the agent is aware of its own actions, but directly from real data. The agent learns this representation by making and validating predictions of the observations with it. In particular, the learned representation aims to predict the consequences of actions and to determine what actions are needed to produce changes to other agents.To tackle this goal, a first aspect is to choose the data to learn from. Unfortunately, collecting examples with labels, which are needed to train with supervised learning methods, does not seem a viable solution. Manual annotation of objects and actions is quite costly, error-prone, time-consuming, may be ill-defined, and may introduce undesired bias into the training. A second aspect is whether the proposed “passive” learning is even possible and thus if one should instead focus on learning through direct interaction, i.e., with a physical agent (a robot) or a simulated one (e.g., in a videogame). Using a robot to learn through direct interaction with the real world is challenging, because the interaction process requires either a very long time (physics and technology limit the speed of operation of a robot) or working with several robots in parallel, which is costly. Working with simulations faces instead limitations due to the gap between the simulated and the real environments. Moreover, current research in self-supervised learning, representation learning and disentangling of factors of variations shows that passive learning is possible and its full potential is still largely untapped.Our proposed approach is to make an agent learn about objects and other agents through passive observation of their interactions. Our approach is to use existing datasets of real images and video sequences and to learn representations of the environment (e.g., global attributes such as illumination and the point of view of the agent), of the objects (attributes such as their location, pose, category, 3D surface, appearance – texture, materials –) and of the actions (e.g., actions can be associated to changes of the object attributes). 
We expect that solving the above objectives will have a strong impact in both science and industry. Building object representations that will enable the detection, prediction and learning from object interactions without human annotation has the potential to solve machine learning problems at a large scale without data privacy concerns (e.g., in the medical and military fields, in the banking and insurance industry).

Title: Topological phases and phase transitions in frustrated magnets
Abstract:
I propose to study exotic phenomena, such as topological order and quantum spin liquids (QSL), in frustrated magnetic models and materials. The project focuses on, but is not limited to, the following topics:

1. Effective field theories for quantum spin liquids
    a) Tensor-network representation of QSL wave functions
    b) Chiral topological orders in Heisenberg models
    c) Topological band theory of fractionalised quasiparticles, novel paradigms of topological order and transport
2. Applications to experimentally relevant systems
    a) Quantum spin ice on the pyrochlore and kagome lattices
    b) Kitaev honeycomb model and alpha-RuCl3
    c) Machine-learning approaches to spin-liquid physics

These projects reinforce each other but can be carried out with minimal interdependence. Projects in Stream 2, in particular, relate closely to neutron-scattering and muon-spin-rotation experiments carried out at PSI, while theoretical projects in Stream 1 will benefit from collaboration with established groups at UZH, ETH, PSI, and institutions beyond Switzerland.

I request funding for a PhD student, who will (at least initially) focus on developing computational approaches using insight from field theories of QSL physics. This background will allow them to broaden their expertise in both computational and analytical directions as they mature.

Successful completion of the proposed research would greatly enhance our understanding of topological order in QSLs, yield testable predictions for a range of materials of topical experimental interest, and potentially open novel directions for topologically ordered matter that are not anticipated by the current state of research.
Keywords: condensed matter theory, frustrated magnetism, higher-order topology, neutron scattering, quantum spin liquids, topological order, topological quantum computing

Title: From Uncivil Disagreement to Political Unrest? A cross-platform & cross-national analysis of the offline consequences of online incivility
Abstract: Over the last decade scholars in communication and the social sciences have increasingly deemed social media as the space where uncivil political discourse primarily unfolds. However, we know little as to how different social media platforms’ affordances impact the scope and effects of online uncivil conversations, that is, negative, impolite and offensive verbal exchanges that derogate non-like-minded views and threaten individuals’ freedom and human rights. To fill this void, a first aim this project will address is analyzing online behavioral data across four broadly used social platforms (Facebook, Whatsapp, Twitter & YouTube) in Brazil, Israel, Spain, Switzerland, and U.S. These platforms are governed by different moderation policies and content personalization features and, by extension, different potential to unleash uncivil exchanges. To date, the vast majority of studies within the research domain of political incivility or hate speech are solely focused on Twitter. By comparing tried-and-tested machine learning models against our own supervised text classifier, this project will bring novel empirical evidence to understand levels and dimensions of online political incivility in multi-platform media environments. A second and central puzzle this study will contribute to solve are spillovers from the online domain to offline political activism and participation across different countries.  A broad array of studies shows that social media can invigorate political participation offline by helping protests and social movements to organize and mobilize their members. However, to date very little is known as to how the kind of unrestrained and at times inflammatory content that individuals engage with in social media affect their political activity outside the online domain.  Studying these online-offline dynamics is important in light of recent political events in the U.S. or Brazil, which illustrate how rapidly elite incivility can fuel violent extremism and democratic backsliding. To address this gap, we will track the conversations and declared offline activity of selected political groups and individuals during protest events and election times. A third and last contribution of this project will be to provide a set of recommendations for policymakers and social platforms to combat incivility. To this end, we will use an online experiment that employ different platform affordances and strategies to counter incivility, from content moderation to the use of sanctioning messages. We will build a dynamic online forum that help us to (a) refine our understanding of online-offline causal relationships among individuals with different political predispositions and to (b) identify potentialities of different platform affordances and optimal conditions for civil political exchanges to happen. All materials used in the project, including code to fit our incivility text classifier to new data in several languages will be made available to the scholarly community.
Keywords: cross-national, cross-platform, incivility, participation, political communication, social media, spill-over effects

Title: General neural solvers for combinatorial optimization and algorithmic reasoning
Abstract:
Combinatorial problem-solving and algorithmic reasoning have been longstanding blindspots of deep learning
architectures despite their significance for real world applications and theoretical computer science. This is
evident even in the most recent breakthroughs on language models like ChatGPT, which are still unreliable
when it comes to performing even elementary algorithmic operations like sorting small lists of numbers.
A fundamental challenge that underlies the lack of success in achieving those capabilities for neural
networks is the difficulty of fusing discrete computation and neural network architectures trained with gradient
descent. Even though advancements have been made in integrating specific kinds of discrete computation
through problem-specific continuous relaxations and reinforcement learning, there is no general framework
that can tackle a wide range of combinatorial and algorithmic problems. This research plan aims to rectify
this by proposing a comprehensive approach to neural combinatorial optimization that can deal with the
diverse challenges posed by those problems.
My approach relies on novel continuous relaxations of arbitrary discrete functions, with the goal of
improving the algorithmic and combinatorial capabilities of neural network pipelines in a computationally
efficient fashion. At the same time, by leveraging the ability of neural networks to exploit patterns in realworld
data distributions, the project is aiming to advance the state of the art in combinatorial optimization.
Furthermore, I will utilize polynomial time reductions between combinatorial problems to rigorously study
the inductive biases of neural networks and formulate new notions of invariance for data-efficient learning.
Finally, motivated by recent advances in multi-task learning for algorithmic problems, I will be taking
advantage of the relationships between NP-complete problems to formulate efficient multi-task learning
procedures for combinatorial optimization.
The benefits of such a framework are twofold. First, advances in combinatorial optimization have applications
in chip design, transportation networks, software verification, and community detection. Additionally,
improving the combinatorial capabilities of neural networks can have a significant impact on models used for
important applications like protein design and language generation. Second, it will advance our theoretical
understanding of the capabilities of models to solve hard combinatorial problems and will lead to a formally
grounded understanding of multi-task learning procedures.
I believe that Stefanie Jegelka’s group at MIT is uniquely positioned to facilitate this kind of research
since the group has led the charge in algorithmic aspects of machine learning, e.g., by setting the foundations
of algorithmic alignment and studying the capabilities of modern neural network architectures often
employed in those tasks. The PI also is a leading expert in topics related to combinatorial and discrete
optimization, which will be essential for this project.
Keywords: algorithmic reasoning, combinatorial optimization, machine learning, neural networks, representation learning

Title: Automated Synthesis and Repair of Infrastructure Code
Abstract:
Software systems have become the backbone of our society that control critical functions and support the workflows and processes of our daily lives. To enable the constant and pervasive use of software systems on a scale that is required by today's civilization, engineers need to build, manage, and evolve underlying software infrastructures in a reliable fashion. 
Thus, building systems with quality that are predictable and repeatable to enable proper scaling, often to hundreds or thousands of machines, is a major challenge, where manual installation and configuration is infeasible. 
Recently, infrastructure code has emerged to address some of these challenges and introduce structured infrastructure automation, and thus more reliability and reproducibility, that can make use of the same environment and tools ecosystem as program code (e.g., versioning, program analysis, testing). 
However, infrastructure code is quite a novel concept and has only in very recent years gained wide-spread traction in production software systems. While the underlying infrastructure systems have been well studied in systems research, the way that these systems manifest as formalizations of their infrastructure and are evolved in a programming language is in need for better understanding and ripe for investigation. 
Further, the nature of software infrastructure requires new systems to be constructed in a trial and error fashion that is not suited to a typical software development workflow. This results in legacy infrastructure systems that are bound to implicit knowledge of engineers to be reproducible.

This proposed research aims to make these implicit actions to achieve infrastructure explicit and improve the reliability of software systems by leveraging techniques from programming language and software engineering research to support engineers to build reliable and reproducible infrastructure code. I want to investigate two approaches to improve the workflow and state of the infrastructure code ecosystem: program synthesis and automated program repair for infrastructure code.
The goal is to leverage the growing volume of infrastructure code on open source platforms such as GitHub. More precisely, I want to exploit human knowledge in these codebases and leverage their expertise and past efforts to enable new learning, inference, and code transfer techniques.
For infrastructure code synthesis, I want to develop methods that employ program synthesis from examples that combine running queries on existing infrastructure systems and optionally learn from software histories to synthesize new infrastructure code. This approach can help engineers automatically generating programs that are correct by construction that does not impede their typical workflow of building and evolving such systems. It can also be used to migrate the behavior of legacy systems to modern systems, thus supporting software evolution.
In infrastructure code repair, I want to generate correct patches to fix defects in infrastructure source code by learning from similar fixes in existing source code bases. I have already conducted initial work by performing data mining and initial analysis on the population of infrastructure code files on public software repositories, providing the basis for the investigation of the proposed research. 

I have the opportunity to work with the world-renowned group of Prof. Martin Rinard specifically, and within the broader programming language and software engineering research community at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) more generally, where I have already spent a 10-week research visit in 2016 (which resulted in a publication in a top-tier venue). Because of the nature of computationally intensive research conducted within MIT, it provides the necessary infrastructure and testbeds to enable the experimental side of this proposed research.

The resulting work will enable engineers to create resilient infrastructures by generating correct infrastructure code by construction (synthesis), or automatically patch them based on learning from past fixes (automated repair).
Keywords: automated program repair, configuration management, machine learning, program synthesis, programming languages, software engineering

Title: Home Style in Global Governance
Abstract:
National governments are accused of being evasive and opportunistic in their presentation of international organizations (IOs), thereby exacerbating their crisis of legitimacy. Indeed, IOs have been described by leading scholars as ‘inviting’ or ‘ideal scapegoats’ (Moravcsik 1994, Tallberg 2002). Yet empirical evidence on how governments present IOs to domestic audiences is limited to a small number of studies. The overall aim of this project is to provide the first comparative, quantitative study of how governments from across the world present IOs in their domestic public spheres. Inspired by Fenno’s 1978 classic, I call this their ‘home style’. 

How do national governments present IOs to domestic audiences? Why do they present them in this way? And what are the consequences of these presentational strategies for the legitimacy of global governance? These are the questions I aim to tackle through my project, which methodologically combines cutting edge text-as-data methods (to build and analyze original datasets on communication of IOs by national governments) and survey experiments (to causally identify the effects of these presentational strategies the legitimacy of IOs). My project is divided into three work packages (WP). In the first one, I build on my existing work to conduct an exhaustive study of home style in the EU, covering all 28 EU member states between 2010 - 2020. This will involve scraping government websites for speeches by national leaders and identifying mentions of the EU in these speeches, which are then classified with supervised and large language models (LLMs). The outcome is a book project on home style in the EU. In WP2, I extend the focus to IOs and governments beyond Europe, in particular using the growing text as data infrastructure of machine readable parliamentary speeches to identify mentions of 75 different IOs in parliamentary speeches of five legislatures outside of the EU (Switzerland, USA, Canada, India, New Zealand). In the final work package (WP3), I use an original online survey experiment in the USA and India (n = 6,000) to causally identify the effects of national governments’ presentation of IOs on perceptions of IO legitimacy.

This research will make a number of important contributions. Theoretically, it will provide an original argument on why governments present IOs the way they do, one that challenges the stereotypical view of governments as evasive, opportunistic blame shifters. With that being said, the patterns uncovered will show that the ways governments present IOs at home still presents deep problems for the legitimacy of IOs. Empirically, the project will also produce original datasets on the presentation of the EU by national leaders (WP1) and on the domestic presentation of IOs in parliamentary debates (WP2) that will prove a valuable resource for the research community in International Relations (IR) and Political Science.
Keywords: Blame, Communication, Global Governance, International Organizations, Legitimacy, National Governments, Text as Data

Title: Zika virus: causality, open science and risks of emerging infectious diseases
Abstract:
Background
Zika virus infection was established as a cause of congenital abnormalities, including microcephaly, and of Guillain-Barré syndrome during a Public Health Emergency of International Concern that the World Health Organization (WHO) announced in February 2016. The Public Health Emergency ended in November 2016 but substantial gaps remain in the causality framework of Zika complications, knowledge about population level susceptibility to Zika virus infection and the risks of the newly recognised route of sexual transmission of Zika virus. 
Objectives
1. To produce a web platform that will allow the production and updating of living systematic reviews of evidence about Zika virus infection; 2. To estimate key parameters that will allow refined inferences about the sexual transmissibility of Zika virus in endemic and non-endemic settings; 3. To investigate the seroprevalence of antibodies to Zika virus in different geographic settings and to use seroprevalence data to allow estimation of the duration of immunity after Zika virus infection. 
Methods
1. We will produce an open access web application to produce living systematic reviews that allow continual updating of evidence about causal associations between Zika virus and its complications, and emerging research questions. The application will automate searching and deduplication, use text mining and machine learning to assist screening and allow automated updates of review output for rapid publication. 2. We have developed a sexual transmission framework to identify key parameters needed to understand the potential for ongoing spread of Zika virus through sexual transmission. We will analyse data to determine the duration of persistence of Zika virus in semen, vaginal fluid, urine, breast milk and other bodily fluids. We will then use a transmission model to estimate the per sex act probability of Zika virus transmission. 3. We will use data from ongoing longitudinal studies and repeated cross-sectional studies in Nicaragua that will determine antibody levels to Zika virus using new diagnostic tests (taking into account exposure to dengue and chikungunya). We will apply “back-calculation” methods to determine the duration of immunity of Zika virus infection. We will also pilot a method for the collection and assessment of seroprevalence data collected in a range of settings that have experienced new Zika transmission since 2013 and where Zika is presumed to be endemic to improve understanding of population level susceptibility to Zika virus infection.
Timeline: The project will last four years
Importance and impact
This project has considerable importance for research on Zika virus infection and transmission. Whilst vaccine development is advancing rapidly, there are still important gaps in our knowledge about vulnerability to Zika virus in large proportion of the world’s population that lives in areas where Aedes mosquito vectors are distributed. The project objectives are aligned with the research agenda of the WHO and with international initiatives to increase capacity for preparedness for infectious disease pandemics. The outputs are therefore relevant to current research priorities. By working within a culture of open science and with the living systematic review network, our research outputs, including publications and software will be publicly available as quickly as possible.

Title: Advancing Neurofeedback in Tinnitus (ANT) Closing the loop with stimulus design and neural feature training
Abstract:
Background 
Tinnitus is the perception of noise or ringing in the ears when no corresponding external sound is present. It affects about 15 to 20% of the western population and in 20% of these cases leads to severe impairment of quality of life. No effective treatment options have been discovered yet, leaving this population without an urgently needed cure. Neurofeedback (NFB) is currently evaluated as a treatment option to coun- teract the maladapted neural substrates of chronic tinnitus and other chronic diseases. NFB is a non-invasive technique used to alter neural activity by displaying an auditory or visual feedback of its own activity. NFB setups are composed of closed-loop systems integrating elements such as neural signal processing, feedback presentation, and training paradigms.

Motivation 
Despite the increasing attention these methods attract in the fields of neuroscience and clinical practice, a demonstrable knowledge gap in NFB research exists. No systematic research has been performed yet on the impact of NFB-stimuli and -settings on trained neural activity, specific versus unspecific effects, cognitive load, participant motivation and cognition, specificity of neural targets, or the long-term effects of NFB training. In most current research approaches, simple feedback parameter visualisations or sonifications are implemented, which mostly follow poorly specified frameworks of operant conditioning. Moreover, the critical link between behavioural effects and training of neural correlates remains to be demonstrated.

Objectives 
Our overall goal is to provide a treatment option for individuals suffering from tinnitus by the use of NFB training. To do so, it is necessary to improve neurofeedback (NFB) through (i) a systematic development of advanced feedback stimuli and (ii) development of a NFB protocol with tinnitus-specific neural targets, and (iii) evaluate the potential of NFB tinnitus treatment at home.

Methodology 
All project partners will collaborate in a tightly synchronised project implementation. The step- wise evolution of the work will aim towards and pivot around therapy of tinnitus as an exemplary clinical use case. First, the design and validation of a set of visual and auditory NFB stimuli will be addressed, based on a systematic assessment of stimulus-specific neural reactions as well as cognitive, affective and motivational consequences of stimulus exposure. Second, based on these stimuli, the validation, localisation, parameterisation, feature extraction, and NFB protocol design will be carried out in parallel. In addition, feasibility studies evaluate needs and requirements for tinnitus home-treatment.

Expected Outcomes 
Main outcomes of the research project will be best practice methods, data-sets, visual and auditory stimulus designs, and software tools, which will be made openly available for the scientific community, treatment practitioners and the broad public. In addition, all outcomes will be disseminated through high-impact publications in neuroscience and behavioural science, as well as the fields of cognitive ergonomics, sound-, visual- and interaction-design.

Project Consortium 
Uniting three research groups from the domains of clinical neuroscience (University of Zurich, UZH, University Hospital Zurich, USZ), cognitive psychology and user experience evaluation (Bern University of Applied Sciences and the University of Fribourg, BFH-UFR), and visual and interaction design (EPFL+ECAL Lab, Lausanne), the proposed research consortium will be the first of its kind to address these issues from a multidisciplinary perspective and expertise.

Title: From Metabolic Pathways to Ecosystem Resilience: How Metabolic Versatility Shapes Microbial Habitat Ranges and Responses to Environmental Change
Abstract:
Background
It is largely unknown what factors influence the global distributions of microorganisms and their responses to environmental change. While habitat generalists are known to tolerate disturbances better than habitat specialists, the physiological basis of this resilience is unclear. Recent studies suggest that generalists exhibit greater metabolic versatility, with multiple alternative pathways for energy and carbon metabolism, indicating that metabolic versatility may be a key factor for both habitat range and perturbation tolerance. However, it remains to be systematically tested whether metabolic versatility is a predictor of the global distribution and stress resilience of microorganisms.

Aims
This project will resolve how metabolic versatility vs specialism influences the global distributions of microorganisms and their response to environmental change. To do so, I will (i) develop a quantitative tool to predict the metabolic versatility of a microorganism, (ii) map how versatility predicts the abundance and occupancy of microbes across global soils and oceans, (iii) characterise the life history traits of metabolically versatile vs constrained microbes, and (iv) test how versatility predicts resilience of microbes to simulated environmental change.

Methods
The proposed project is a systems-level study using both field and laboratory data. A tool to quantitatively predict metabolic versatility in energy and carbon metabolism in microorganisms will be developed, leveraging an in-house database of metabolic processes and key genes. This tool will be applied to >100,000 bacterial and archaeal genomes to assess the taxonomic distribution and variability of metabolic versatility. Applying the tool to genomes from global marine and soil metagenomic studies will make it possible to resolve the link between process-specific metabolic versatility and habitat specialization. Life history trait frameworks will be applied to discriminate metabolically versatile vs constrained organisms as e.g. opportunists, competitors, or stress-tolerators. Finally, I will test the predictive power of metabolic versatility for community shifts under environmental perturbations by training and evaluating a machine learning model on soil microcosm experiments simulating four common climate extremes.

Results
This work is expected to systematically and quantitatively determine to what extent microorganisms across the tree of life are versatile with respect to energy and carbon metabolism. It will also reveal the relationship between metabolic versatility and habitat specialisation, resolve the life history strategies of metabolically versatile microorganisms, and test metabolic versatility as predictor of perturbation tolerance under environmental change.

Impact
The proposed work allows me to systematically test whether a microorganism's metabolic versatility profile is a predictor of its habitat range and its tolerance to environmental change. In the process, this work will deepen ecological theory by gaining new insights into the functional factors governing microbial community co-existence and resilience. This has implications for ecosystem monitoring and ecosystem projections under Earth’s changing climate, and for the assembly of stable communities for biotechnological applications.

Title: Motivations and tools to encourage contributions on Wikipedia
Abstract:
In this project, we aim to elicit the principles that motivate people to contribute to peer-production platforms. We plan to put these findings into practice by implementing novel tools offering personalized recommendations that encourage contribution to Wikipedia, minimizing the disruption of the user's experience.


*The role of Wikipedia.* 
Since its creation in 2001, Wikipedia grained a prominent role in democratizing knowledge. Thanks to a community of volunteers that invest their time in writing, it became the largest encyclopedia ever existed. Today, with billions of views every month, Wikipedia is one of the most visited websites globally, and it represents an extraordinary resource for readers and researchers. Besides its role as a free knowledge platform, it also has an important function in fueling the progress of computer science research, serving as the central dataset for the development of language models, graph models, and knowledge representation. 

*Problem and research opportunities.* 
Given the crucial role of Wikipedia in many fields, maintaining high-quality content is a critical mission with wide-spectrum repercussions. Currently, despite its popularity, much content is still missing. Wikipedia is based on the open-collaboration model, and editors are a crucial resource to expand and maintain its content. Keeping the global editor community active and engaged is vital for the long-term future of Wikipedia and all the associated projects.

*Research objectives and milestones.*
We focus our effort on understanding and designing systems to motivate people to contribute to Wikipedia. Our research proposal is organized into three milestones:

== A: Understanding motivations ==
Elucidating motivations that lead users to edit the content is crucial for designing systems to encourage contributions. We aim to understand what we refer to as "in-the-moment motivations", representing the reasons that triggered the urge to edit a specific part of the page. We plan to rely on both quantitative methods based on surveys and qualitative leveraging Wikipedia server logs.

== B: Tool to fix image Alt-Text == 
Every image in web documents should be associated with the property alternative text to summarise the visual content in a textual form. This information improves the accessibility for millions of people with sight impairments or limited Internet access and supports automatic systems such as search engines in indexing and retrieval. Despite this crucial function, on Wikipedia, millions of images have an empty alternative text. We plan to implement an in-page recommender system to close this gap.

== C: Personalized recommender system ==
Based on the experience gained from the previous steps, we will implement an in-page recommender system to address multiple issues on the page, going beyond the alternative text of images. The system will be based on incentives that emerged in the motivation study (A) to deliver a personalized recommendation that maximize the probability of a contribution, minimizing the annoyance. The recommender system will incorporate a real-time adaptive behavior based on user history and implicit feedback employing a reinforcement learning (RL) approach (i.e., contextual bandit).

*Contributions.*
This research project introduces three unique scientific contributions with broad implications beyond Wikipedia. First, the study (A) on in-the-moment motivations will reveal the kind of incentives that engage users to work toward a desired goal on peer-production platforms. Second, the tools to add the alternative text to Wikipedia images (B) will provide insights on how to use these incentives to engage editors. 
Finally, the personalized recommender system (C) provides a novel contribution by developing the principle of unobtrusive design. The tool, borrowing from nudge theory, will focus on the challenging objective of maximizing participation and minimizing annoyance using RL methods. Additionally, beyond the scientific community, our contribution will positively impact the quality of Wikipedia with repercussions for millions of web users.

Title: Towards Theoretical Foundations for Foundation Models
Abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) and, more broadly, foundation models have achieved remarkable breakthroughs across a wide range of fields, including natural language processing and computer vision. At this critical juncture in their development, it is essential to establish a principled understanding of these models to ensure effective quality assessment, social responsibility, and the ability to guide and regulate their use. While various theoretical frameworks are emerging in the literature, our proposal puts forth three interconnected strategies to unravel the properties, functionalities, and core principles behind foundation models. Rooted in information-theoretic and statistical thinking, these approaches are distinct in the specific tools they employ. The three key research directions we aim to explore are as follows:

Thrust 1 - How Foundation Models Learn Structured Data.
The complexity of foundation models resists straightforward analysis, unlike the elegant techniques used in linear systems, such as Fourier analysis. Instead, we propose a novel approach by focusing on how foundation models behave when exposed to mathematically structured data, using Markov models as an entry point. Markov models have a long, well-established history, and we draw from this deep well of knowledge. However, our approach diverges significantly from classical Markov theory, which traditionally focuses on questions of convergence and mixing times. In contrast, foundation models introduce a new challenge: they operate with many relatively short, independent Markov batches. Our goal is to develop a comprehensive theory of these Markov batches and leverage this understanding to disentangle the complexities of foundation models. Early results are promising. For instance, we’ve demonstrated that a transformer architecture, with only three layers, can effectively represent Markov processes of arbitrary order.

Thrust 2 - Fundamental Limits of Prompt Compression.
In this research thrust, we aim to explore foundation models through the framework of information theory. A prime starting point is the task of so-called prompt compression. Prompts are the inputs to the large language model. They have to be cleverly engineered to elicit the desired response. We propose to understand and design this process from the perspective of information theory, and more specifically, rate-distortion theory. The key challenge lies in finding the optimal trade-off between prompt compactness and response quality. In recent work, we show for small databases that there is a large gap between the performance of current prompt compression methods and the optimal strategy, and we propose a query-aware, variable-rate adaptation of a prior work to close the gap. By fully leveraging the connection with information theory, we aim to develop a deeper understanding of prompt engineering for foundation models.

Thrust 3 - Prediction, Learning, and Games with Self-Consuming Models.
A defining feature of foundation model training is data heterogeneity, driven by the vast and varied data scraped from the internet. This marks a significant departure from traditional supervised neural networks, which typically rely on more homogeneous datasets, such as labeled images. What makes this shift even more intriguing and challenging is the emerging trend where a substantial portion of training data for new foundation models is generated by earlier generations of these models. Recent studies have already documented instances of ``model collapse,'' where learning procedures break down due to self-consumption, raising critical questions about the statistical limitations in such scenarios. To address these challenges, we will develop suitable information measures and explore a variety of statistical modeling techniques, including innovative adaptations of the classic Polya urn model.

Title: Enhancing new physics searches in ATLAS with advanced trigger strategies
Abstract:
This project aims to push the frontiers of new physics in hadronic final states at the ATLAS experiment by combining recent advances in triggering with novel analysis techniques. It builds on developments that now make possible searches previously limited by trigger constraints and contributes to advancing ATLAS’s trigger capabilities for the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC), enabling a richer hadronic physics program. Using data from Run-3 and anticipating HL-LHC challenges, we will address key questions through three research efforts, organized into dedicated work packages (WPs).

WP1 focuses on exploring physics beyond the Standard Model using Trigger-Level Analysis (TLA) to target multi-jet final states. TLA enhances sensitivity to low-mass and rare processes by utilizing trigger-level data, enabling lower jet thresholds and increasing statistical reach. We will optimize the TLA workflow, including rethinking jet calibration, and analyze the new TLA+Partial Event Building (PEB) data stream, used for the first time at ATLAS. This will open opportunities for studies of electroweak SUSY and exotic Higgs models, and inform future HL-LHC strategies.

WP2 targets long-lived particles (LLPs) producing delayed jets, a key signature often missed by standard triggers. New trigger selections implemented in 2024 have created datasets tailored for such events. We will analyze these using advanced timing and reconstruction techniques, improving sensitivity to BSM scenarios with slow-moving particles.

WP3 addresses the hadronic reconstruction challenges posed by HL-LHC conditions, particularly high pile-up. Our efforts will focus specifically on employing machine learning for real-time jet reconstruction and flavor tagging. These developments are crucial for maintaining sensitivity to key signatures such as HH ? bb¯bb¯ and enabling inclusive hadronic triggering under extreme HL-LHC conditions.

The work will result in physics publications, new algorithms, and software for HL-LHC triggering, contributing directly to ATLAS’s long-term physics goals and enabling physics discoveries.

The research plan builds on the strengths of past and ongoing work in multi-jet final state searches, hadronic reconstruction, and triggering at ATLAS. It maximizes the impact of previous investments, which have supported the ATLAS construction and its HL-LHC upgrade.

Title: Adaptive control with approximate Bayesian computation and differential privacy
Abstract: In this project, we shall examine the interaction between information theoretic notions of privacy, insufficient statistics and optimal control. More precisely, we shall develop efficient algorithims for near-optimal control of complex systems where there is a need for privacy for some aspect of the used data.

Title: Derivation of pediatric sepsis phenotypes using machine learning applied to clinical, functional and genomic data from the swiss pediatric sepsis study
Abstract:
Sepsis is severe infection, leading to life-threatening shutdown of organs. Sepsis represents a leading cause of death and disability in children: Over three million children die each year due to sepsis and one out of three childhood sepsis survivors will suffer from ongoing health problems. In fact, the risk of acquiring sepsis is never as high as during early childhood. A recent resolution by the WHO endorsed by Switzerland highlighted that sepsis is a global threat, demanding urgent actions to improve understanding and therapy of sepsis. 
While it is well known that bacteria and other pathogens such as viruses cause infections, the  mechanisms underlying the severe response of the body to infection which ultimatively results in sepsis are not well understood. There is a need for studies in children with sepsis which investigate the genetic and immunologic features of the disease.

The landmark Swiss Pediatric Sepsis Study is a national observational multicenter cohort study including all 10 major children`s hospitals which recruited 1204 children with bacterial sepsis in Switzerland. 
The purpose of the new project is to investigate the clinical, genomic, and functional information from this unique study. We suspect that different children develop different patterns of their body`s response to infection. Using new methods, such as Artificial Intelligence, we aim to find groups of children which are particularly unwell due to sepsis, and which are more likely to one day benefit from specific interventions. For this purpose, we will investigate the genes involved, as well as markers of the body`s response to infection.
As a first objective, we will explore the role of genetic variation to understand why some children are very vulnerable to sepsis. 
As a second objective, we will then compare how the immune system of different children responds to sepsis. It is possible that we may find that some children with sepsis suffer from underlying alterations in their immune system, which makes them more susceptible to sepsis.
Finally, using new computational methods, so called machine learning, we will try to integrate the wealth of genetic, clinical, and functional data to gain a completely new perspective on why some children become severely unwell due to sepsis.

This world-wide largest contemporary study on bacterial sepsis in children has the potential to identify key mechanisms determining sepsis risk and sepsis outcomes in children. Our hope is that it can thereby improve our understanding of the progression from infection to sepsis. Ultimately, we hope to gain a better understanding of the individual susceptibility to sepsis. Thereby, we hope to help to enable better treatment of children with sepsis in the future, for example through personalized medicine.

Title: 3D Reconstruction and Simulation of Deformable Bodies with Geometric Deep Learning
Abstract:
3D data acquisition, shape augmentation and physically-based motion computation of deformable materials are long-standing problems in computer graphics. A particular challenge is the simulation of soft tissue and faces due to their highly nonlinear viscoelastic properties and complex interplay with musculoskeletal systems consisting of bones, muscles, tendons, ligaments, and other connective tissues. Therefore, the simulation of soft tissue and faces in particular, involve a large degree of manual processes and are difficult to control by users. Prediction and manipulation often require a re-simulation of the entire dynamics with computationally expensive physics solvers and manually optimized parameters.

In this proposed project, we revisit this long standing problem and tackle it by using data-driven methods and deep learning. Convolutional neural networks have been proven to work very well in various tasks involving regression from one domain to another, in fully supervised or self-supervised settings. Most previous works are largely restricted to problems that are represented in Euclidean domains such as images. Our project will explore the emerging field of geometric deep learning that generalizes the convolution operator to non-Euclidean data, such as 3D meshes, point clouds or implicit functions. We focus particularly on the representation and dynamics of soft bodies, such as soft tissue and faces. We use priors from geometry and physics in the learning process and enable a disentangled representation of the geometry and an efficient computation of the dynamics in the latent space.

We apply our geometric deep learning methods to (WP1) 3D reconstruction of the geometry from single image inputs, (WP2) prediction of augmented shapes with trained models using geometric priors, and (WP3) computation of the dynamics in the geometric latent-space for reduced simulation of soft bodies.

Our work will forward the knowledge in 3D modeling and simulation with deep learning methods. In particular, we will contribute to the exploration of geometric deep learning architectures, which are highly relevant for graphics applications and are currently under-explored. The developed methods have a large potential to speed-up and improve the quality of current approaches: 3D data acquisition will be simplified, the forward predictor can be used for physically-based shape augmentation, and the latent space dynamics allows an efficient computation of the physics. Our methods can be applied to soft bodies in general, but we expect a particularly large impact on the research on modeling and simulation of soft tissue and faces. Our work will improve applications such as medical simulations, digital prototyping, visual effects and computational robotics.

Title: Improving patient safety in surgery by use of artificial intelligence
Abstract:
Background
Postoperative complications are a major challenge in surgery. They result in significant patient morbidity, sometimes even death and pose a huge socio-economic burden for health care systems.
Artificial intelligence (AI) powered assistants have revolutionized transportation and are now standard equipment in airplanes and motor vehicles, making locomotion significantly safer. Worldwide, three times as many people die within 30 days after surgery than in road traffic accidents. Yet, no AI assistants to increase patient safety in surgery exists up to date.

Objective
This translational research project aims to apply AI to prevent intraoperative adverse events (IAE) and to assess surgical performance with the ultimate goal to improve patient outcomes.

Specific aims
1.Creation of a dataset of surgical videos and patient outcomes
2.Development of an AI Surgeon Assistant (AISA) that identifies IAE and assesses surgical performance in surgical videos
3.Prospective validation of the effectiveness of AISA in the prevention of postoperative complications

Methods
First, a dataset containing already recorded videos of more than 600 laparoscopic weight-loss surgeries performed in two academic teaching hospitals and corresponding clinical and outcome data will be created. As one of multiple board certified surgeons, I will annotate and rate the surgical videos regarding IAE and surgical skills using validated scores.
Second, I will train a convolutional neural network (CNN) to identify the most critical phases of the interventions. Third, I will develop an event recorder detecting IAE during these critical phases. An existing CNN developed for event detection in videos, will be trained on the annotated dataset. Fourth, a CNN will be trained to monitor the surgeons’ intraoperative performance through surgical skill analysis. The observations of the event recorder and the continuous skill assessment will then be correlated with each other and with patient outcomes. The primary outcome is severe postoperative complication. This framework of AI algorithms is called AISA. The effectiveness of AISA to prevent postoperative complications will be investigated in a randomized controlled trial.

Expected results and their impact
I expect the occurrence of postoperative complications to increase with the number of IAE and to decrease with good surgical performance. I therefore hypothesize, that the continuous intraoperative feedback of AISA will reduce postoperative complications.
The AI Surgeon Assistant developed by this translational research project will improve the outcomes of patients undergoing surgery and will significantly reduce health care costs.

Title: Design and analysis of numerical methods with high ergodic accuracy for Langevin-type dynamics
Abstract:
In a wide range of applications in biology, chemistry, physics and computer science, one faces the challenge to sample from the invariant distribution of an ergodic stochastic differential equation (SDE). In particular, the recent progress in data science led to the emergence of new sophisticated dynamics, in order to improve the sampling quality and handle the stochastic gradient approximation. As the variety of dynamics evolves, there is a need for efficient numerical methods for their discretisation. The primary goal of this research project is to design novel numerical methods for a widely used family of dynamics: Langevin-type dynamics, which are modifications of the well-known Langevin system. To guarantee the efficient use of these methods in practice, our approach focuses on two important mathematical properties: ergodic accuracy and stability. In particular, one key objective is the characterisation and generalisation of a superconvergence property observed for one method in standard Langevin dynamics.

The first impact of the project concerns the abundant applications in data science, as the designed methods will be used in the training of machine learning algorithms. These methods will improve the current ones in terms of accuracy thus bringing a substantial gain of computational time and precision. Furthermore, our derivation being based on a mathematical analysis, the project is highly relevant for the numerical analysis field, where the approximation of ergodic SDEs is an especially active topic of research. In particular, the proposed analysis of the superconvergent phenomenon in a generalised setting is a significant advance.
Keywords: Bayesian sampling, Langevin dynamics, ergodicity, invariant measure, numerical analysis, stochastic differential equations

Title: PONs - People-Opinion Networks: A study of polarization in word embeddings and social networks in Switzerland and Southern Africa.
Abstract:
This multidisciplinary research collaboration will bring insight and methodological development on how opinions get polarized in the media and social media in Switzerland and Southern Africa. We propose a novel method, using Natural Language Processing and grounded in social psychological theory, for studying how social networks develop around opinions and become polarized. 
Our overall objective is to study polarization in a framework that jointly considers opinion-based and social structure definitions of polarization. The way to do this is to link two networks, one derived from each approach. While the social-structure network is straightforward to construct, the opinion-based network is not clear at all, and we develop an opinion-based network extracted from word embeddings.
Our first aim and deliverable is to develop a network representation of social opinion that can be used to study polarization. We propose a novel method for extracting opinion-based networks from word embeddings trained on media and social media data.
Our second aim and deliverable is to link social networks and opinion networks in multilayer representations that we call People-Opinion Networks (PONs). The social networks will be developed from interactions between agents on social media. The opinion networks that we extract from word embeddings will also include agent names, and we will use established methods to link the two structures, creating multilayer networks.
Our third aim is to use our multilayer PONs model in a comparative investigation of polarization in Switzerland and South Africa. We will perform cross-sectional and longitudinal analysis of polarization in both media and social media. These investigations will be informed by the view (from social psychology) that polarization arises from intergroup comparisons, and that the emergence of polarization depends on the spread of opinions between groups. These investigations will exploit the full potential of our multilayer PONs representation for investigating how polarization arises from potentialities in both social and opinion structures
Our investigation will focus on debate around migration in Switzerland and South Africa. We will study opinion and interaction around two polarizing events in each country between 2010 and 2020. For each of the four instances of polarization we will sample data from three time periods, three months immediately before, during, and immediately after the polarizing event. In each of these twelve samples periods we will collect two layers of data: (1) media data from a broad spectrum of newspapers and news sources; and (2) social media data from Key Opinion Makers (journalists, politicians, etc.), their followers, and a sample of other users extracted by keywords. 
?The research collaboration thus proposes to make an original contribution to science, developing a novel method to study social polarization and social change dynamics more generally. In the process, we will also be training the next generation of South African social science researchers with links to leading labs groups in Europe and skills in cutting edge data science methods.
Keywords: natural language processing, opinion polarization, opinion-based groups, social media, social networks

Title: Designing for Freedom: Leveraging AI technology for digital self-determination
Abstract:
This research project sets out to identify the most promising design and governance strategies to leverage artificial intelligence (AI) technology for digital self-determination. Much of AI research and contemporary discourse are concerned with accurately identifying the potential risks and harms associated with the technology. While that is important, the (positive) ideals and values that might guide a desirable digital future or inform regulatory efforts often remain underspecified. This is a missed opportunity, particularly with respect to the concept of personal freedom, which enjoys broad appeal and contemporary popularity, particularly in the digital context. Both characteristics make it uniquely fit to serve as an emancipatory ideal for our digital 21st century and help us devise concrete strategies for digital empowerment.

The project builds on research undertaken in my dissertation where I demonstrated the relevance of understanding personal freedom as self-determination in the digital realm. Inherent to this conceptualization of freedom is the FREE framework, a set of principles that create the background conditions for freedom as self-determination online: friction in design, responsibility in action, equality of standing, and embeddedness in scope. In the postdoc mobility project I apply the FREE framework to the empirical reality of the 21st century digital realm and identify innovative strategies to leverage AI technology for digital self-determination. I do this through an innovative and novel combination of theoretical and empirical research, including interviews, policy-analysis, and fieldwork. I will produce a body of work that provides high value to scholars and policymakers interested in questions such as: When is friction in design conducive to digital self-determination, and what lessons can we learn from food and drug regulations to promote responsible AI development?
Keywords: AI ethics, normative philosophy of computing, political philosophy, political theory, public policy
