Title: Exploring new realms of biodiversity: Mapping functional realms to understand and conserve the global structure of species interactions
Abstract: The effective functioning of earth’s ecosystems sustains biodiversity and human well-being, but many ecosystems are under threat from habitat loss and climate change. Unfortunately, we have a limited ability to conserve ecosystem function because we lack a global understanding of species interactions across trophic levels, which are key drivers of ecosystem dynamics. The objective of the proposed research is to take steps towards mapping the global structure of trophic interactions and ecosystem function by introducing and applying the concept of the functional realm. We will focus primarily on the trophic interaction of seed dispersal, and aim to 1) quantify and map functional realms for seed-dispersing vertebrates; 2) understand how ecological, evolutionary and geologic drivers influence realm formation; and 3) assess the conservation status of, and threats to, each functional realm. We expect that functional realms will not correspond directly to any known classification such as plant biomes or zoogeographic realms, but may show influences of both in the configuration their borders and their spatial relation to one another. By mapping functional realms for the trophic interaction of seed dispersal, our results have the potential to better integrate species interactions into global ecology, aid conservation and restoration efforts, and address long-standing debates about the convergence and divergence of ecosystem function.

Title: Edge-Companions: Hardware/Software Co-Optimization Toward Energy-MinimalHealth Monitoring at the Edge
Abstract:
The proposed Edge-Companions project aims at a breakthrough in the hardware/software co-design of Multiparametric Health Companions (MHCs). These devices are devoted to the monitoring of patients affected by chronic conditions, acquiring and interpreting bio-signals such as electroencephalogram (EEG), electrocardiogram (ECG), photoplethysmography (PPG), respiration, and motion sensors, among others. Motivated by the tight design constraints that characterize MHCs, in this project, my aim is, together with my EPFL team, to maximize energy
efficiency and minimize resource requirements while maintaining high levels of precision in detecting episodes of clinical relevance.

The innovative co-design solutions that we plan to introduce in this domain will be validated against three real-world scenarios: detection of epileptic seizures, assessment of cardiovascular diseases, and assessment of lower limb joint health through gait analysis. The addressed scenarios are of particular relevance in light of today’s demographics and lifestyle changes, which are causing a fundamental shift in the
demands facing healthcare provision, from ailments caused by pathogen agents to ones caused by chronic diseases. This situation requires novel solutions to cope with long-term multi-parametric monitoring of patients to avoid hospitalizations, improve the quality of life of subjects, and reduce costs for healthcare. Multi-parametric health companions promise an effective solution to this context. However, MHCs must present a very high energy efficiency while confidently detecting real-time episodes of clinical relevance (such as epileptic seizures or cough monitoring) from data acquired in real-life conditions. 

Such conflicting requirements require careful optimizations across the entire hardware/software stack. This stack should be dynamically tailored to each of the two computation phases composing MHC applications: first, features extraction, in which relevant attributes in the time and/or frequency domain are computed from acquisitions after accounting for noisy patterns; second, features interpretation, in which bio-signal attributes are evaluated to perform health assessments or detect acute episodes. Both phases will be optimized at hardware and software levels.

Regarding features extraction, at the software level, we plan to develop algorithms for the incremental classification of biosignals, conditionally navigating at run-time from smaller to larger feature sets depending on contextual (patient-specific) information and on the (data-dependent) confidence of classification. In this way, computational efforts will only be invested when required, that is, in highly challenging cases. Then, at the hardware level, each feature will be efficiently computed by employing domain-specific hardware accelerators. 
Regarding features interpretation, at the software level, we plan to innovate edge Machine Learning (ML) algorithms by studying the benefit of personalized federated methodologies, which combine generalized and patient-tailored models with on-device training when processing features derived from the sensed data. Then, at the hardware level, architectural explorations will be performed, exploiting the ensuing model-level parallelism and the regular computing patterns exhibited by ML by introducing novel approaches for computation-in-place (in- and near-memory), which will avoid energy-costly data transfers.

As a result, research efforts on feature extraction and interpretation will be cross-fertilizing, opening opportunities at the software level for novel methodologies for automated ML-based feature discovery, and enriching feature sets derived from expert knowledge. Moreover, at the hardware level, they will pave the way for the design of heterogeneous, accelerator-rich nano-meter hardware architectures, tailored to the requirements of the MHC domain. All developed hardware and software components will be released as open source.

Title: Automated Decision-Making and the Foundations of Political Authority
Abstract: The project’s aim is to contribute to a re-assessment of the foundations of political authority (PA) in the context of automated decision making (ADM). Our general research question is: How is the executive exercise of political authority transformed by ADM and what does this mean for its con-ceptualization and justification? The general working hypotheses is: If properly understood and designed within its socio-technical context, ADM-supported PA can be justified. We expect our results to support this hypothesis at least regarding a certain domain of executive PA. An inter-disciplinary team of philosophers and computer scientists addresses the research question by applying the methods of analytical philosophy to conceptual and ontological analysis and devel-oping it further by using insights from organizational decision-making theory (ODM). This approach is complemented by empirical research adopting ethnomethodologically-informed, experimental and design methods from Information Systems (IS) research, computer-supported cooperative work (CSCW), and science and technology studies (STS). At the heart of our inquiry are two ex-perimental use cases of executive government authority that use drones to support (a) law en-forcement and (b) authoritative emergency response. For the scientific community this project is expected to present a novel and more complete conceptualization as well as justification of ADM-supported political authority. It is expected to present: a unified conceptualization as well as justification of political authority as practical and coercive authority; a more concrete theory of the accountability and legitimacy conditions of politi-cal authority taking into account the agential capabilities of ADM; a socio-technical analysis of the design of ADM-driven executive government; a socio-technical analysis of how the design can be brought more in line with justificatory standards and normative goals of political authority. From a broader societal and use-inspired perspective this project expects to give guidance to the citizenry at large and more specifically to the executive regarding the normative framework and design of ADM-driven government.
Keywords: accountability, automated decision making, big data, justice, legitimacy, machine learning, organizational decision making, political authority, public policy

Title: Can talking to machines improve financial decision making?
Abstract: Policymakers and scientists are increasingly using narratives for communication rather than simply sharing information. In addition, social welfare organizations are now using stories to promote policy objectives.  People differ in many ways that are relevant when it comes to behavioral change in general and financial decision-making specifically. Any intervention - nudges, edutainment, information campaigns, or legislative changes - can have heterogeneous effects among the targeted population. How do we know what information should be incorporated into a particular treatment, and how should the information be framed and delivered? Moreover, how can we address heterogeneous attitudes and needs when developing communication campaigns for increasingly polarized societies? In this proposal, we tackle both challenges, namely the heterogeneous attitudes and the question of what makes a good story for development outcomes. We propose a proof-of-concept study exploiting edutainment campaigns using short films on financial literacy in Ghana. The contribution of the proposed project is to use recent methodological advances in order to create a strategy, or platform, for designing experiments that have information treatment arms that consist of narratives in the form of videos. There have been significant advances in computational social science that provide the tools for optimizing the design of digital content and in the development of information interventions to improve financial literacy.  The proposed project builds on these two affluent research areas to develop a technology for designing the treatment arms employed in experiments that use video narratives as the primary intervention.
Keywords: adaptive experiments, behavioral change, behavioral economics, financial literacy, machine learning, narrative communications, natural language processing

Title: From Thought to Voice: Decoding hierarchical neural mechanisms of speech for next-generation neural prostheses
Abstract:
Background: Speech is a cornerstone of human communication, transforming abstract thoughts into fluent vocal expressions through a hierarchical organization of neural mechanisms. In this hierarchy, high-level linguistic representations are progressively converted into precise motor commands for articulation. However, the exact neural processes and the roles of distinct cortical regions in this transformation remain poorly understood. This gap not only limits our fundamental understanding of speech production but also hampers the development of effective neuroprosthetic devices to restore communication in individuals with speech impairments, conditions that affect approximately 2.2 million people in the UK and 5 million in the US. Traditional direct neural decoding methods often struggle due to limited data. In contrast, neural network models, which have proven highly effective in understanding sensory processes, are trained on extensive datasets and generate rich, task-driven representations. These models offer a promising alternative by overcoming data limitations and enhancing both neural encoding and decoding, thereby opening new avenues for decoding the complex neural signals underlying speech.

Aims: This project has two main objectives. AIM 1: To uncover the hierarchical neural mechanisms of speech production. We will characterize how speech representations evolve from high-level linguistic representations to articulatory processes across distinct cortical regions. AIM 2: To develop a computational framework for neuroprosthetic speech decoding by aligning neural activity with task-driven models.

Methods: We will integrate computational neural network models with intracortical neural recordings from human subjects. Large language models (LLMs), trained on extensive datasets, will capture structured linguistic information, while text-to-speech (TTS) models will simulate phoneme articulation. By aligning the representations derived from these models with neural activity recorded from language and premotor cortices, we will evaluate the biological correspondence of model representations. The decoding framework will first be validated using offline data and subsequently refined for real-time applications.

Expected Results: We expect to reveal a clear hierarchical organization of speech-related brain regions, demonstrating how high-level linguistic reasoning is progressively transformed into articulatory execution. Furthermore, by leveraging task-driven models as an intermediary, we anticipate a significant improvement in neural decoding accuracy, paving the way for a real-time speech neuroprosthesis.

Impact: By integrating neuroscience, artificial intelligence, and neuroengineering, this project will advance our understanding of speech production mechanisms and contribute to the development of next-generation brain-computer interfaces for speech restoration. These advances have the potential to significantly improve communication for individuals with speech impairments, ultimately benefiting millions worldwide.
Keywords: Brain-computer interface, Hierarchical processing, Neural alignment, Neural decoding, Representation learning, Speech neuroprosthesis, Speech production, Task-driven modeling

Title: Detecting New Physics at 40 Megahertz: Scouting for anomalous events with unsupervised AI in the CMS hardware trigger
Abstract:
After having analyzed almost 200 inverse femtobarns of data produced by the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), no signs of New Physics (NP) has been observed. We know physics beyond the Standard Model has to exist in order to explain certain physical phenomena, and the reason for it passing undetected can be due to a) its signatures not being observable in current particle colliders, b) us not being sensitive to it using our currents methods of detection or c) the cross section of the signal is too small and more data is needed. Addressing b) and c) will be crucial for the future success of the largest experiments at the LHC, CMS and ATLAS, and is what will be the focus of this project. 

The ultimate limiting factor for many searches for New Physics is the hardware event selection system of the detectors, the so-called Level-1 (L1) trigger. Tens of terabytes of data per second are produced from proton-proton collisions occurring every 25 ns, an extreme data rate that can not be read out and stored. The rate is therefore reduced by a real-time event filtering system which decides which collision events should be kept for further analysis and which should be discarded, reducing the event rate from 40 MHz to 100 kHz. High selection accuracy in the trigger is crucial in order to keep only the most interesting events while keeping the output bandwidth low. These selection requirements are based on reasonable assumptions as to what a possible New Physics signal might look like in the detector, but also implies that New Physics signals could be systematically rejected by a typical set of online selection algorithms.

Recently, it has been proposed to deploy a novel '40 MHz data scouting' system, a stand-alone system connected to the L1 trigger through high-throughput optical links and fed to a system consisting of FPGAs and GPUs. The system will acquire the L1 trigger data at the full bunch crossing rate of 40 MHz, with no selections applied, and analyze certain interesting topologies at the full rate. Up until now, the object resolution at L1 has been too poor to be used in physics analysis, but this will change in the next phase of the LHC program. Between 2024 and 2027, the LHC will undergo a substantial upgrade into 'High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC)', in order to be able to deliver a factor of ten more data. This includes a substantial upgrade of the trigger system, for the first time including tracking and high-granularity calorimeter information, resulting in offline-like resolution at L1. This will make 40 MHz scouting extremely relevant.

Detecting signals with small cross sections in the scouting data will be problematic. The large increase of data produced during HL-LHC not only increases signal rates, but results in significantly higher background rates. A high-luminosity database of anomalous events with a large suppression of background events is needed, to enhance New Physics signals with small cross-sections. 

The aim of this project is to dramatically increase the physics reach of the CMS experiment by detecting anomalous events in real-time in a model agnostic way using AI, creating a high-luminosity anomalous dataset for novel physics searches. It consists of two main goals:

- Detecting anomalous events at 40 MHz in a signal-agnostic way on scouting system FPGAs and in the Level 1 trigger, creating high-luminosity anomalous databases for novel physics searches, and serve as a guide to the experiment of where triggering efforts should be focused.
- Designing a real-time signal-agnostic analysis for HL-LHC running downstream of the buffered scouting data.

The project will deliver novel and unbiased datasets for New Physics searches, allowing for signal-agnostic analyses to be performed, as well as providing a novel dataset to be analyzed for existing searches where high background suppression is crucial. In addition, the developed algorithm allows to give feedback to the experiment in real-time regarding interesting regions of phase-space to trigger, making sure potential New Physics signals are not discarded by the current trigger algorithms. Through technical achievements like establishing nanosecond inference on dedicated FPGAs in a distributed system, it will pave the way for other ML applications being developed for HL-LHC.
Keywords: Anomaly detection, Autoencoder, CMS Experiment (CMS), Data scouting, FPGA, Large Hadron Collider (LHC), Machine Learning, New Physics, Real-time analysis, Trigger

Title: Persisting post-stroke cognitive impairment 3 and 12 months post-stroke: multi-modal biomarkers and prediction model for risk assessment
Abstract:
Achievements in stroke therapy led to a dramatic reduction in stroke severity. However, despite this therapeutic success, our preliminary data of n~433 stroke patients demonstrated that ~77% of them suffer from relevant cognitive deficits in the acute stroke phase. Such a high prevalence of post-stroke cognitive impairment (PSCI) was observed despite mild stroke severity (NIHSS 24h <5 in 80% of patients) and even in a young subgroup (<55 age old). In our sample, about 50% of patients recovered from PSCI, but PSCI persisted in others (persisting PSCI). Tools to predict persisting PSCI are missing until now, but would be required to provide intensified therapy where needed. Understanding individual cognitive trajectories across the first weeks post-stroke is a necessary step to establish an effective cognitive therapy after stroke. The purpose of the project is to establish prediction algorithms that identify patients at risk of persisting PSCI across acute/subacute and chronic stroke phases. Specific aims of the study are: To identify risk factors and to establish a prediction model for persisting PSCI at 3 and 12 months post-stroke (=acute/subacute and chronic stroke phase correspondingly).

Methods. We assess post-stroke cognition in patients with the first ever stroke by performing longitudinal neuropsychological testing with assessment of all cognitive domains <10 days, 3 and 12 months post-stroke. Using the presence of PSCI at 3 and 12 months as a binary variable to predict, we will train a high-dimensional machine learning algorithm with demographic, stroke, clinical and neuropsychological parameters as a baseline model, and further include i) brain imaging parameters, ii) proxies of cognitive reserve, iii) serum biomarkers as inputs. We expect to establish a prediction tool for persisting PSCI at 3 and 12 months post-stroke. 

Significance. The present project should provide new insights into PSCI-burden, establish easily applicable screening tests for stroke units to uncover PSCI, improve therapeutic decisions and hence patient care, and provide new approaches for therapy and prevention of PSCI. Overall, the project should improve personalized treatment prospects. Given the rising number of young stroke patients, a reduction of PSCI would improve their social and occupational integration. Given the ageing of the population, reduction of PSCI in older adults might help to reduce the prevalence of dementia. In case of positive results, we seek to conduct a therapeutic trial on patients at risk of PSCI.

Title: Predicting Individual Unobserved Heterogeneity to Target Policies: Applications and Robustness
Abstract:
Detecting and describing heterogeneity in the effect of a covariate on an outcome is key to applied microeconomic analysis and causal inference. However, while we now have a well-established set of tools to describe heterogeneity when it can be observed (see recent related books on the subject Huber, 2023; Chernozhukov et al., 2024; Gaillac and L’Hour, 2025), there are many contexts where this heterogeneity is not observed and needs to be modeled. Quantifying these effects is pivotal for policy; for instance, targeting treatments to subgroups where they are most effective. Random coefficients models, where the coefficients are individual-level specific but drawn from the same distribution, offer flexible modeling. They have a long tradition in econometrics (see in the cross-section context Beran and Hall, 1992; Gautier and Kitamura, 2013; Masten, 2017; Hoderlein et al., 2017; Gaillac and Gautier, 2022). However, currently these methods often rely on unrealistic assumptions, limiting policy applications.

This project aims to advance knowledge on how to exploit this unobserved heterogeneity to make policies more efficient by developing the tools to predict it at the individual level to improve the targeting of appropriate populations. It focuses on developing computational tools, high-impact applications, and theoretical robustness.

Building on Gaillac (2024), the project integrates advancements from three areas. Firstly, Empirical Bayes (EB) methods have shown impressive results in both capturing unobserved heterogeneity and using it to inform policy. Secondly, Gaillac (2024) shows that recent tools from the Optimal transport (OT) literature allow to gain robustness to the support of the regressors, which was one of the usual critical assumptions in the literature. Lastly, Gaillac (2024) describes how to combine this with Machine ML tools developed in the heterogeneous treatment effects literature to describe the unobserved heterogeneity.

The project objectives are twofold. First, we develop practical tools to improve policy design and applications.  Starting with developing user-friendly Python and R packages integrating OT methods with ML to handle unobserved heterogeneity. This will also be illustrated by two main innovative applications aimed at improving the targeting of public policies. 

Second, we will make theoretical advances to improve the robustness of EB predictions. We first extend the method developed to allow for more flexible models. We then consider a partial identification approach to improve the robustness of the prediction. Finally, we will extend the method to a certain class of heterogeneity, which will improve the stability of the method in higher dimensions.

The goals of the project are both to gain a better theoretical understanding of the models used for forecasting as well as to consider their impact once they are used for decision making by policy makers, such as public employment services. The results will make these theoretical advances in exploiting heterogeneity, both observed and unobserved, more applicable to public policy design.
Keywords: Causal effects, Empirical Bayes, High-dimension, Machine learning, Optimal transport, Unobserved Heterogeneity, Unobserved heterogeneity, Value added

Title: Robust segmentation-based methods for remote sensing VHR image analysis
Abstract:
This project establishes a bridge between optical remote sensing, computer vision, machine and visual learning by proposing innovative approaches for efficient and accurate segmentation- and object-based very high resolution (VHR) remote sensing image analysis. The proposed processing tools aim at improve current models for VHR data analysis and at proposing new and innovative techniques for their interpretation, in particular for Earth observation and environmental sciences tasks. This project intends to introduce in the remote sensing community analysis methods based on robust segmentation, with particular attention to the issue of classification of VHR remote sensing images exploiting semi- and weakly- supervised methods. 

Nowadays, many commercial satellites provide optical images with meter and sub-meter spatial resolutions. To properly process this kind of data, standard pixel-based approaches are no longer effective, and state-of-the-art object-based methods are often inefficient, since unable to generalize well on other datasets automatically. Additionally, the collection of ground truth data is a very expensive task, since VHR images cover large geographical areas with ground projected sampling distance of few decimeters. Thus, the amount of detail present in these image is often misleading, with respect to the semantic and information class to which pixels belong. One possible solution is to consider objects as entities, and processing the images on this object-based assumption. Adapted model to process them are then needed, and will be developed with the most advanced machine learning tools, offering frameworks able to deal with this problem instantiation.

For these reasons, advanced computer vision and visual learning tools will be coupled to fundamental and applied machine learning to solve, with the bias of knowledge coming from the remote sensing optical image processing domain, the issue of image analysis and information extraction from VHR data with limited user intervention. Computer vision and visual learning fields offer a variety of tools to solve the aforementioned problems, but in turn they are not robust to remote sensing data, since objects composing the image are not distributed as standard images (foreground / background, spatial complexity, etc). For this reason, knowledge from both fields will be coupled and merged to solve the issues jointly thanks to advanced statistical machine learning theory.

From the machine learning point of view, besides the large variety of classification and pattern recognition methods, theoretical concepts will be elaborated to tackle specific issues that are now limiting the processing and classification of VHR data. To minimize the user intervention when providing labeled examples, particular attention will be paid to the possibility of reusing already learned models of image interpretation, to propose robust solutions that are able to generalize well not only on a single dataset (image) but also on other similar datasets. This way, the generalization with very limited user intervention will improve the processing efficiency. In more details, objects composing the VHR image extracted with state-of-the-art computer vision and visual learning paradigms will be analyzed using kernel-based methods for classification, clustering and feature extraction / manifold learning. 

This project will provide a series of very innovative approaches and concepts to deal with remote sensing VHR optical images, and will be among the first contributions trying to tackle the VHR image processing issues explicitly with advanced computer vision methods. The developed techniques will be tested on both natural and remote sensing VHR images, to validate the proposed approaches in real world scenarios. Being a project at the interface of different disciplines, several fundamental questions will naturally arise and their consideration will strengthen the robustness of the proposed methods, particularly by exploiting the multidisciplinary nature of the research project.
Keywords: computer vision, image processing, kernel methods, machine learning, object-based image analysis, remote sensing

models for vhr data analysis and at proposing new and innovative techniques for their interpretation, in particular for earth observation and environmental sciences tasks. this project intends to introduce in the remote sensing community analysis methods based on robust segmentation, with particular attention to the issue of classification of vhr remote sensing images exploiting semi and weakly supervised methods. nowadays, many commercial satellites provide optical images with meter and sub meter spatial resolutions. to properly process this kind of data, standard pixel based approaches are no longer effective, and state of the art object based methods are often inefficient, since unable to generalize well on other datasets automatically. additionally, the collection of ground truth data is a very expensive task, since vhr images cover large geographical areas with ground projected sampling distance of few decimeters. thus, the amount of detail present in these image is often misleading, with respect to the semantic and information class to which pixels belong. one possible solution is to consider objects as entities, and processing the images on this object based assumption. adapted model to process them are then needed, and will be developed with the most advanced machine learning tools, offering frameworks able to deal with this problem instantiation. for these reasons, advanced computer vision and visual learning tools will be coupled to fundamental and applied machine learning to solve, with the bias of knowledge coming from the remote sensing optical image processing domain, the issue of image analysis and information extraction from vhr data with limited user intervention. computer vision and visual learning fields offer a variety of tools to solve the aforementioned problems, but in turn they are not robust to remote sensing data, since objects composing the image are not distributed as standard images (foreground / background, spatial complexity, etc). for this reason, knowledge from both fields will be coupled and merged to solve the issues jointly thanks to advanced statistical machine learning theory. from the machine techniques will be tested on both natural and remote sensing vhr images, to validate the proposed approaches in real world scenarios. being a project at the interface of different disciplines, several fundamental questions will naturally arise and their consideration will strengthen the robustness of the proposed methods, particularly by exploiting the multidisciplinary nature of the research Title: Physics based Computational Photography
Abstract:
When we perceive a scene, we not only use our capability to see, but efficiently use other senses (hear, smell, and touch) to interpret the physical environment. Current camera technologies do not allow to capture such information and are additionally limited to low-dimensional signal acquisition. As a consequence, many photography and computer vision applications do not yet perform to the quality we would like: they do not yet give us consistently the image we "see'', nor do they accurately retrieve the image we want.

We believe that using more physical sensor data can help us better imitate human-like performance in machine vision systems. Most cameras are not stand-alone anymore, but built into mobile electronic devices which contain a number of other sensors, such as GPS, audio, motion, and compass. As such, we can record as many physical properties of the scene needed in order to get additional knowledge about the conditions under which the image was taken. One goal of this research project is thus to develop solutions that allow mobile devices to simultaneously capture multi-sensor data. We will not limit ourselves to current smart phones, but will develop the ideal multimodal "camera'' with potentially custom sensors and sensor alignments.

We will use this additional data to improve various applications in computational photography, specifically image enhancement, image annotation, and image visualization. Up to now, research on multimodal image processing has focused on sensor data that is physically correlated (i.e., accelerometer data and image). We plan to go a step further and perform a thorough investigation about the relationship between different sensor data. The extracted or learned correspondences and differences between the different physical measurements are then applied to concrete imaging applications.

The following major research goals will be investigated by two PhD students:

-We will use a versatile hardware platform and develop an open-source software that allows us to simultaneously capture data from multiple sensors, with the possibility of recording several instances of the same sensor type. The software can then be used to collect, use, and share multisensor data.

-We will analyze the relationship between various sensor measurements and their potential use for computational photography and computer vision tasks. This involves both investigating analytic relations between sensor data, as well as machine learning for sensor data where such a mathematical relationship does not exist.

-We will develop algorithms that improve image quality by using multisensor data. For the evaluation of the image quality, we will use both state-of-the-art objective (computational) quality metrics as well as subjective (human observers) quality assessments.

-We will use the multisensor data to create new ways of annotating and visualizing potentially large image collections. The use of these additional sensor measurements will allow us to create more relevant and accurate annotations, as well as provide us with new ways to organize and represent image collections.

-We will analyze the hardware and algorithms that we develop with respect to collaborative sensor networks.
Keywords: Collaborative Multimodal Sensing, Computational Photography, Image Enhancement, Image Visualization, Multimodal Sensing

Title: Abiotic Organic Complexity (AOC) - Key to the evolution and detection of carbon-based life
Abstract:
The long-standing mystery about the origin of life on Earth and its potential uniqueness is closely related to the origin of organic chemical complexity in the earliest history of our Solar System. We must understand the physical and chemical processes at play during the different stages of Solar System formation and follow the evolution of organic matter from its origin in the interstellar medium (ISM) toward prebiotic molecules and eventually to the building blocks of carbon-based life. The stepping stones towards the emergence of carbon-based life are the so-called Complex Organic Molecules (COMs), i.e., carbon-based molecules composed of at least six atoms (including carbon and hydrogen) that are of potential relevance to prebiotic chemistry. Comets preserve a chemical record reflecting the Abiotic Organic Complexity (AOC) of the early Solar System. They might have delivered substantial amounts of organic material to young planetary surfaces through impacts, which, in turn, might have helped kick-start life on Earth.

An unprecedented milestone in cometary science was the European Space Agency’s (ESA’s) Rosetta mission that studied comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko (hereafter 67P) in situ for two years. Its electron-ionization (EI) mass spectrometer (MS), the Double-Focusing Mass Spectrometer (DFMS), collected invaluable data on the chemical composition of the tenuous cometary atmosphere, the coma. Thanks to exceptional mass resolution of the DFMS, these data provide first-ever access to a comet’s abiotically emerged COMs. The proposed research project will reveal how AOC is key to the evolution and detection of carbon-based life in three work packages:

(1) Inventorying AOC: It was previously demonstrated how individual COMs can be identified from single Rosetta/DFMS mass scans. In this project, we will establish the first comprehensive (abiotic) census of cometary COMs based on such mass scans and derive from it both the molecular complexity distribution and a list of potential biosignatures with cometary sources.

(2) Characterizing AOC: We will use the high-resolution Rosetta/DFMS data as a unique testbed to develop data-driven methods to characterize 67P’s AOC, from multivariate statistical methods and chemical networks to machine-learning approaches. These methods will allow for the extraction of unbiased information on organic complexity.

(3) Forming AOC: Based on results from WP1 & WP2, we will explore the formation history of the cometary AOC in two ways: first, by comparing 67P’s COM census to that of the ISM and second, by investigating the census for indications of dominant bottom-up or top-down formation pathways.

By uniting in situ mass spectrometry and organic (astro)chemistry with applied mathematics and data science, this project takes full advantage of the archived Rosetta/DFMS data and is truly interdisciplinary. We expect impactful and high-gain output at a moderate risk. The project will outline the cometary perspective on our own origin and potential uniqueness, which is strongly entangled with the origin of COMs in the early history of the Solar System and hence with many research fields of space science concerned with organic matter, from planetary sciences to astrochemistry and astrobiology.

Furthermore, this project will support the search for signs of extraterrestrial life by establishing abiotic benchmarks and reference values, such as the organic complexity distribution and a review of potential biosignatures with cometary sources, and provide cutting-edge tools and methods to extract information on organics from complex EI-MS data. This makes the project extremely timely and a key asset for ongoing and future space missions dedicated to the search for signs of life in Solar System bodies like Jupiter’s – and later probably Saturn’s – icy moons. Our work will strengthen and complement the Swiss involvement with mass spectrometers on ESA’s Jupiter ICy moon Explorer (JUICE) and Comet Interceptor missions, and crucially contribute to the emerging national research community focused on the origin and prevalence of life.
Keywords: Comets, Complex Organic Molecules (COMs), Data science, Interstellar medium, Mass spectrometry, Prebiotic chemistry, Search for life, Space missions

Title: Neural networks on graphs and their filter design
Abstract:
The promise of neural networks that we can model any complicated problems attracts researchers in almost every field. However, in reality, it is often not as simple as we think. Studies point out that it is crucial to integrate human intuition into neural networks. For example, studies in human activity analysis suggest that it is best to separate temporal and spatial information, and this can be an important prior in human activity learning. Similarly, in an image classification task, neighboring pixels are more important than far-away pixels, and convolutional neural networks, which are particularly designed to utilize this prior, have become a major breakthrough in this field.
One of the interesting approaches to applying prior knowledge to neural networks is to utilize a graph structure in discrete mathematics, known as a graph neural network (GNN). Using vertices and edges in a graph structure, one can allocate data to different vertices and define their relationships on the connecting edges. A transportation network can be a good example: speed sensors and road connections on a map can be easily translated to nodes and edges on a graph. 
The main challenge in GNN is that operations for data defined on a graph must be handled differently, compared to conventional ones. It is an important question to ask what kinds of prior information can benefit from a graph structure and how we can efficiently structure them on graphs. 

The overall objective of this project is to develop methods to include various priors in graphs. 
In particular, this project plans to develop graph convolutional networks (GCNs) with structural priors. In studying transportation networks and solving traffic forecasting problems, for instance, it is observed that short-term and long-term predictions require different information. 
This idea inspires the need of creation of graph filters that can be utilized differently depending on the duration of the time window (e.g., 30 min, 1 hour, 6 hours, etc.).
In this project, therefore, we plan first to implement a new graph filter in the application of transportation networks. Then we can further extend its application to other areas such as human activity analysis which is one of the research topics in the host laboratory. 
This work is expected to enhance the performance of GCNs with dedicated structuring and also increase their interpretability. And furthermore, this can extend the applicability of GCNs to a wide range of applications.
Keywords: Graph filter, Graph neural network, Graph signal processing

Title: Learning and Inference via Information Measures
Abstract:
There is a longstanding and deep connection between information measures and learning algorithms. This involves superficial aspects as well as rigorous mathematical connections. Probably the most visible connection concerns the use of information measures as imposed figures of merit in learning algorithms. Cross-entropy, for example, is often used as a loss function when optimizing classification models like logistic regression and artificial neural networks. More fundamentally, rigorous connections between information theory and learning algorithms have been established, for example, for principal components analysis (PCA) or multi-armed bandits. To goal of the work proposed here is to further develop such rigorous connections by leveraging recent progress on information measures. Specifically, our interest is, (i), in information measures as an analysis tool for learning and inference algorithms, and (ii), in information measures as an inspiration and guidance in the design of learning and inference algorithms. It is this deep connection and mutual inspiration that is at the basis of the three concrete research vignettes that we propose to investigate:

Vignette I - The Generalization Error of Learning Algorithms.
Overfitting and the generalization behavior of learning algorithms are important questions. Information measures can shed some light on them, as evidenced in a substantial line of recent work in the community. In recent and on-going work, we have established a set of fundamental bounds. We propose to substantially strengthen this by incorporating more relevant classes of learning algorithms and encompassing more realistic models, as well as leveraging emerging progress on information measures.

Vignette II - ``Common Information Components Analysis.''
Information measures have inspired many algorithms over time. Leveraging one of our very recent results, we are proposing a new algorithm to accomplish universal unsupervised feature extraction. This algorithm is inspired by an information measure referred to as Wyner's common information, a principled way of identifying the common aspects of multiple random variables. The resulting algorithm extracts features that best express the commonalities between two (or multiple) data sets.

Vignette III - The Price of Distributed Learning and Inference.
Information measures are powerful tools to quantify communication constraints. If learning and inference have to happen in a distributed setting, split into a number of terminals, this can often be abstracted into a limitation on how much communication is allowed between these terminals. For one and the same inference task, executed on a single machine versus executed on a distributed set of machines, what is the fundamental penalty in quality of inference?

While these three vignettes are all different in their specifics, their common thread is the leveraging of recent progress on information measures.
Keywords: Feature Extraction, Generalization Error, Information Theory, Machine Learning, Signal Processing, Statistical Inference

Title: Efficient and reliable anharmonic free energies of molecular crystals using diffusion Monte Carlo and machine learning
Abstract:
Molecular crystals are ubiquitous in the pharmaceutical industry and show great promise in technologies based on organic photovoltaics, porous materials for gas absorption etc. However, often these materials are known to exist in several polymorphic forms that are very close in energies but exhibit different physical properties. This is a great risk especially for the pharmaceutical industry; a meta-stable polymorph of a drug may undergo a phase transition to a more stable form -- with completely different properties -- during the course of manufacturing or storage. The pharmaceutical industry has therefore spent a lot of resources on high throughput crystallization experiments to screen polymorphs of drugs. However, these screenings can neither tell if a given polymorph is the most stable form at the conditions of crystallization nor about the existence of other competing polymorphs. Within this perspective, theoretical crystal structure prediction (CSP) has great potential in guiding the experimental crystallization of the polymorphs of a compound. 

While CSP studies have shown reasonable success in a series of blind tests -- by predicting the experimentally observed polymorphs -- they are not able to consistently discern the most stable polymorphs of a compound. This is because many drugs exhibit competing polymorphs with free energy differences less than 1kJ/mol, which is much lower than the error of current CSP methods This error comes from the approximation made while describing inter-particle interaction made using force-fields or dispersion corrected density functional theory, as well as from the proxies of the anharmonic free energy -- such as lattice energies or harmonic free energies -- used for calculating the stability. Anharmonic free energies accurate to within 1 kJ/mol can be calculated in principle by combining path integral (PI) free energy calculations to include exact anharmonic and quantum fluctuations of nuclei, with diffusion Monte Carlo (DMC) to  accurately describe the full range of interactions in molecular crystals. Unfortunately, these calculations can require up to a million force evaluations and are therefore extremely labour intensive. Therefore to make CSP methods genuinely predictive, it is important to develop fast and efficient ways of combining different state-of-the-art techniques.

The objective of this proposal is to develop an accurate and efficient workflow to combine PI free energy calculations with DMC energetics. In the first step, the large cost of performing explicit ab initio PI calculations, will be alleviated by using machine learning (ML) techniques to interpolate energies and force calculated on a set of reference structures using DMC. A novel scheme would be used to automate the selection of the reference structures and to validate the ML model. In the second step, a novel thermodynamic integration scheme -- requiring just one simulation -- would be used to calculate the corrections on the free energy obtained with the ML model. Overall, the applicant proposes to calculate the quantum free energy of a polymorph to within 1 kJ/mol using up to a thousand force evaluations at DMC level.

The scheme will be validated on the polymorphs of ice by comparing against experimental sublimation energies. It will then be used to perform a CSP study in collaboration with the group of Prof. Sarah Price, on understanding on isotope dependent polymorphism in pyridine. Our technique will advance the state-of-the-art of CSP by conclusively determining the most stable and potentially new polymorphs of pyridine, as well as by providing references for determination of approximate methods such as density functional theory.
Keywords: Crystal Structure Prediction, Diffusion Monte Carlo, Machine Learning, Path Integral Molecular Dynamics

Title: Exploiting sparsity: communication over wireless networks and analysis of mass spectrometry data
Abstract:
Data generated in many modern applications has an extremely high number of dimensions. In order to store, process, and transmit the hight-dimensional data efficiently, one needs to exploit the structural properties of the data. Many natural data sets have a structural property called sparsity: When the data set is represented in a suitable basis, it can be described by a small number (relative to its dimension) of  parameters. Sparsity has been successfully exploited in a variety of applications, including recording and compression of photo, audio, and video signals, MRI, radar, computer vision (for image recovery, super-resolution, denoising, etc.), and more. In this project we propose to study how sparsity can be used in: (i) communication over ad-hoc wireless networks and (ii) analysis of the data obtained by mass spectrometry (MS) measurements in the field of proteomics (large-scale study of proteins). 

Part I of this project is in the field of wireless communication. In radio channels, the channel state information (CSI) is a sparse signal, i.e., CSI can be described by a small number of parameters, relative to the dimension of the signal space. Knowledge of the CSI at the receiver is crucial for efficient communication. Our own research supports the fact that sparsity of the CSI allows one to obtain the CSI in a single-input single output (SISO) wireless channel (i.e., a wireless channel between a single transmitter and a single receiver each of which employs a single antenna) at a negligible cost in terms of power and bandwidth. The situation changes in ad-hoc wireless  networks (i.e., wireless networks without any fixed infrastructure). Here, each individual channel is  sparse, however the total number of channels is large. It is thus unclear whether the required CSI can be obtained in ad-hoc wireless networks at a low cost. State of the art protocols proposed for communication over ad-hoc wireless networks assume that the full CSI is available globally. To design a practical system, this assumption needs to be removed. In this project we propose to explore how the required CSI  can be obtained optimally in ad-hoc wireless networks. Furthermore we propose to study how the initial lack of CSI impacts the capacity of such networks. Information-theoretic results obtained in this area can shed light on how to design ad-hoc wireless networks in the future.

Part II of this project is in the field of data analysis for MS. In proteomics, researchers use MS measurements to determine which of the possible 10^4 types of peptides (and, hence, which proteins) are present in complex sample mixtures. Modern methods for MS generate data sets of enormous dimension, i.e., sets with up to 10^9 data points. Because the number of types of peptides that need to be detected is significantly smaller than the number of available data points, the data set produced by MS is an example of a sparse signal. Currently, biologists use ad-hoc methods available in off-the-shelf statistical software to process the MS data. These methods, which are very useful in the analysis of classical MS data, fail to deliver adequate results when used to analyze the data obtained through cutting-edge high-performance MS methods. In this project, based on the ideas from the rapidly developing area of compressive sensing (CS), we intend to develop signal recovery algorithms that systematically exploit sparsity in MS data.
Such algorithms can significantly improve the accuracy of peptide detection and speed-up the MS data acquisition leading to advances in the technology used in proteomics.

Title: Using machine learning to make brain-based predictions
Abstract: With the help of machine learning algorithms it is possible to extract patterns and make predictions based on very complex data sets. In the field of neuroimaging these algorithms are increasingly used to predict cognitive ability or disease state. During the planned visit at the Child Mind Institute I aim to enhance my machine learning skills and apply the gained knowledge to a data set I am currently working on. With this data set I investigate the possibilities to predict age from neuroimaging data on a single subject level. In the future, these techniques might be used to make brain-based predictions of complex behavior or disease.

Title: Predicting Ruminal pH Using Non-invasive Exhaled Breath Biomarkers in Dairy Cows: Toward a Future Diagnostic Tool for Subacute Ruminal Acidosis (RumiPHeX)
Abstract:
Background and rationale: Ruminants play a vital role in converting human-inedible feedstuffs into high-quality protein through their unique rumen microbial ecosystem. This microbial fermentation produces volatile fatty acids (VFAs; mainly acetate, propionate, and butyrate) which contribute over 70% of the energy required for milk synthesis in dairy cows. However, excessive VFA and lactic acid production can lead to a drop in ruminal pH, resulting in ruminal acidosis. Subacute ruminal acidosis (SARA) is characterized by ruminal pH dropping below 5.6 for more than 180 minutes per day. Although cows with SARA often have no clinical signs, they may suffer from reduced feed intake, impaired digestion, milk fat depression, gastrointestinal damage, liver abscesses, and lameness. Effective real-time, continuous monitoring of ruminal pH is crucial for optimizing dairy production, ensuring rumen health, and promoting sustainability in ruminant livestock systems. Recent advancements in bovine exhalomics (exhaled breath analysis) offer a promising, non-invasive alternative for monitoring metabolic challenges through breath-based biomarkers.

Overall objective: This project aims to develop a non-invasive exhalomics-based model for ruminal pH prediction, and to better understand the associations and dynamics between key exhaled breath metabolites and ruminal pH.

Methods: This project will first use 20 multiparous lactating dairy cows in a 2 × 2 crossover design with two treatments: (1). high-starch SARA-induction diet, and (2). low-starch control diet. Exhaled breath samples will be collected and analyzed together with ruminal pH “ground truth” data. The predictive modeling framework will integrate: (a). Random Forest & Gradient Boosting Machine for feature selection and dimensionality reduction; (b). Generalized Additive Models for predictive modeling; (c). SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) values to determine key breath biomarkers influencing ruminal pH predictions; and (d). Cross-validation for model robustness and accuracy assessment. 

Expected results and broader impact: This project is expected to establish a non-invasive, exhalomics-based model for accurately predicting ruminal pH in dairy cows. The resulting model will enable a real-time, non-invasive ruminal pH monitoring, and eventually, enable a farm-ready diagnostic tool for ruminal acidosis for precision livestock management. By integrating machine learning and breath biomarkers, this project also pioneers an innovative approach to monitor physiological function of ruminant animals, paving the way for future advancements in precision livestock farming and sustainable livestock production.
Keywords: Animal welfare, Dairy cow, Exhaled breath, Prediction model, Ruminal acidosis, Ruminal pH

Title: Adversarial Examples in Machine Learning
Abstract: The goal of this project is to investigate Adversarial Examples in Machine Learning, slightly perturbed inputs that cause automated predictive models to fail. On the one hand, I plan on exploring the vulnerability of machine learning models in security-sensitive settings (e.g., network intrusion detection) by setting up state-of-the-art defenses and trying to find systematic gaps in them.On the other hand, I want to gain a deeper formal understanding of the reasons why adversarial examples exist, and why they generalize across different model architectures.This will be a more mathematically driven exploration, into the theory of neural networks and their training dynamics.A better understanding of the limitations of machine learning approaches would have general applications to data analytics and could also pave the way to more robust learning approaches that would be beneficial beyond security-critical domains.
Keywords: Adversarial Examples, Deep Learning, Machine Learning, Robustness, Security

Title: Putting "Backpropagation and the brain" to the test
Abstract:
Deep Learning is the state-of-the-art in training artificial neural networks (ANNs), with immense advances in practical applications made in the past decade.
On the other hand, research in computational neuroscience has revealed a zoo of different brain areas, connection schemes, cell types, and neuron and system states, producing however only limited understanding of the exact mechanisms by which learning leads to complex function.
This raises the question whether the highly efficient learning system that is the brain implements a form of Deep Learning.

My aim is a better understanding of how biological systems can learn efficiently, starting from the high degree of functionality of trainable ANNs, and bringing this approach closer to the biological brain. In particular, the state-of-the-art in training artificial networks is the error backpropagation algorithm.
My proposal describes a realistic implementation of this method in a hierarchical model of cortex, treating data from animal experiments as an important ingredient in the development of the model. Implementing Deep Learning across the cortical hierarchy using neuronal populations, my model makes concrete predictions about connectivity, information pathways, activity in deep and superficial layers, and plasticity.
I aim to test this model and its predictions using recordings from cortical neuron populations.

Applying my experience as a model builder, my approach is to first create a concrete cortical microcircuit model, using fully dynamical populations of neurons with dendritic integration zones and time-continuous learning. In order to describe the cortical hierarchy closely, the theory is constructed in accordance with current experimental evidence, e.g. of prediction mismatch coding and information pathways in visual cortex.
I will then study this model using extensive computer simulations, including robustness tests for parameter variations, large noise found in biological systems, and ablations.
Based on my model, I will make predictions for animal experiments and test them using the existing setup for recording cortical neurons in sensory and motor cortices of mice at the Neural Computation Unit (NCU) of Prof. Doya, as well as re-analyzing already recorded data of the lab.

This work will contribute to a deeper understanding and functionalization of learning schemes in cortex, and more generally, of learning with physical neurons.
Working with data from experiments, the main result for my model will be the validation/falsification of its predictions for biology, and the ability to corroborate the hypotheses underlying my theory with experimental evidence.
In the end, I expect to be able to provide an analysis differentiating between my model (implementing a Deep Learning approach) and classical predictive coding models of learning in cortex.

I will study a functional theory of learning in the brain, with the aim of bridging the gap in understanding which has grown between computational neuroscience and machine learning. Here, even a falsification of my approach would lead to important insight.
In the long term, this line of research can contribute to a better understanding of human learning and associated disorders.
Keywords: Biophysical models, Cortical hierarchy, Deep Learning, Learning algorithms, Network models, Neuromorphic hardware

Title: Integrating High Resolution Monitoring and Trait-based Modelling to Understand and Predict Phytoplankton Dynamics (AQUASCOPE)
Abstract:
Phytoplankton community dynamics are controlled by bottom-up (water physics and chemistry) and top-down (natural enemies) drivers. However, the relative importance and direction of these drivers on taxonomic compositions and relative abundances are not well established in natural communities: they vary in time and space and also depend on trait-mediated physiological and ecological interactions. The goal of this project is to quantify the relative effects of interacting drivers on lake phytoplankton, within taxonomic and size-based categories. We aim at (re)designing trait-based theoretical and data-driven models in order to make accurate predictions of plankton food-web changes — and therefore ecosystem processes and services — across environmental gradients in space and time. The project AQUASCOPE features three connected work packages (WPs): 1) the application of new methods for in situ monitoring, 2) data analysis, and 3) trait-based modelling. 
WP1 (CH-Research assistant) will gather in situ readouts of simultaneous physical, chemical, and biological observations at high frequency and spatial resolutions, including morphological traits of individual organisms (size, shape, and pigments). We will count and phenotypically characterise interacting plankton species by combining automated scanning flow-cytometry (organismal size range 1 um – 1 mm) with underwater imaging (dual-magnification: 10 um – 150 um and 100 um – 1.5 mm). Plankton monitoring will be supported by in situ sensor measurements for water physics and chemistry, an automatic sample collector for laboratory analysis of nutrients chemistry, and meteorological conditions. Data will be gathered over spring and summer in three lakes of different trophic state and across relevant temporal and spatial ecological gradients. 
WP2 (CH-PhD student) will benchmark underwater imaging with scanning flow-cytometry and microscopy data to estimate densities and traits within and between taxonomic groups of phytoplankton and zooplankton. WP2 will review and apply data mining tools to explore patterns in the large and rich dataset, focusing particularly on trait and taxa co-occurrence changes over seasonal, depth, and lake gradients. Using a machine learning approach to cope with the complexity of the data, WP2 will test hypotheses about how bottom-up and top-down interact and influence size-abundance relationships in phytoplankton and zooplankton. WP2 will finally apply machine learning to: 1) estimate growth responses of species and functional groups to environmental drivers and 2) quantitatively study how responses and trade-offs govern taxa-relative abundances in phytoplankton natural communities.
WP3 (DE-PhD student) will use physio-ecological processes (e.g. nutrient acquisition, growth rates, and food-web interactions) and their size-scaling properties to develop theoretical models of how physical forcing, competition for resources, and grazing from specialist or generalists shape: 1) size distributions of prey and predators, 2) size-abundance and other trait-abundance relationships of phytoplankton communities, and 3) abundances of different plankton taxa and functional groups. Informed by observations (WP1) and data-driven hypotheses of species responses to environmental gradients (WP2), theoretical models (WP3) will be used to make predictions of how plankton community structure changes under different scenarios, including changes in seasonal patterns, different future climate change scenarios, nutrient pollution, and different food-web structures.
AQUASCOPE will evaluate underwater imaging as a new tool for research and routine lake plankton monitoring. The collected data will allow us to refine concepts and theories in community ecology, particularly of how chemistry, physics and species interactions can shape the dynamics of phytoplankton communities over time and space from a trait-based perspective. Quantitative understanding of drivers and mechanisms that control community structure will allow us to make forecasts of changes in plankton biodiversity across environmental gradients, including algal blooms. The international and cross-disciplinary nature of this collaborative project will be an ideal ground for promoting skill acquisition and independent thinking in the PhD students, thus fostering their future scientific career.

Title: EARLY DETECTION OF ALZHEIMER’S DISEASE USING A ‘SURROGATE HUMAN DISEASE MODEL’
Abstract: Alzheimer’s disease is a neurodegenerative disease that affects an estimated 35 million people worldwide and is the leading cause of dementia in elderly people. It is progressive brain disorder that causes a slow decline in memory, affects an individual’s ability to everyday activities, and eventually leads to complete dependency. With the proportion of elderly people in the population increasing, the burden of Alzheimer’s disease is expected to become significantly greater over the next few decades. Beyond its immediate health consequences, the societal and economic costs are of epidemic proportion and thus, make Alzheimer’s disease a public health priority worldwide. With disease-modifying treatment trials unsuccessful at the present time and only medications to treat symptoms available, an emerging research initiative is to identify approaches to intervene before the damage begins with the ultimate goal to make Alzheimer’s disease preventable. Important steps in disease prevention include the identification of risk factors and discovery of prognostic biomarkers. That is why we are proposing a project that leverages existing multi-dimensional data sources and harnesses the power of machine learning to identify risk factors and biomarkers that are most associated with Alzheimer’s disease and its progression. To overcome major limitations of Alzheimer’s disease research (no clear disease onset, lack of appropriate animal models, lack of sensitive and specific biomarkers), our work introduces an entirely new and unconventional concept in the field of neurodegenerative diseases – the idea that the biomarker search and risk factor identification can be expanded to a ‘surrogate human disease model’. Traumatic brain injury is a very suitable surrogate human disease model as it is a central nervous disease with an acute onset that initiates long-term neurodegeneration processes triggering pathological features that closely resemble those of Alzheimer's disease. Advanced machine learning techniques, such as transfer learning, will aid the knowledge translation from traumatic brain injury to Alzheimer’s disease. In transfer learning, the goal is to build an algorithm based on one dataset and then utilize the gained knowledge to subsequently employ the same algorithm on different, yet related datasets. We envision that our unprecedented and unconventional approach could become a common strategy to overcome barriers to the classic bench-to-bedside biomarker discovery. Understanding how different diseases along the neurological spectrum relate to each other will provide potentially new insights into the etiology, classification, and design of novel therapeutic interventions. Knowledge gained from this project may lay the ground work for public health initiatives aiming at preventing Alzheimer’s disease and have major implications for other neurological diseases hallmarked by cognitive impairments, including Parkinson’s disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
Keywords: Alzheimer’s disease, Early detection, Human disease model, Prevention, Risk factors, Traumatic Brain Injury

Title: DeepDrought: Is access to Deep soil water a critical tree trait for Drought stress release?
Abstract:
Recent evidence highlights a significant link between European forest die-offs and the combined impact of drought and unusual warmth, particularly notable in increasing instances of insufficient winter and spring precipitation and the resulting inadequate deep soil water storage. There is a critical lack of detailed understanding of how deep soil water availability and root water uptake contribute to plant drought mitigation and overall forest health, especially under current climate change trends and increased atmospheric demand.
DeepDrought's primary goal is to enhance our understanding of how trees depend on deep soil water during drought stress. Our specific aims are to advance understanding of how climate change affects root distribution and root zone moistening and, with it, the ability of trees to take up, store and use deep water resources. Moreover, we aim to develop more accurate predictions of species-specific responses within the Soil-Plant-Atmosphere Continuum.
The project is divided into two work packages (WP) to achieve our aims. WP1 empirically analyses root distribution in the context of plant water stress indicators. WP2 seeks to improve our ability to predict future drought vulnerability. First (Task 1a), the project will use a unique Swiss-wide root distribution data set covering up to 3000 sites from which we will first derive root species-specific distributions via stratification of the dataset and, with machine learning models, predict root depth and distribution across Switzerland. Additionally, the project will compare root distributions from two comprehensive soil inventories (172 sites) conducted in 1993 and 2024, examining changes in root distribution over time. Next, we will relate the root water uptake (RWU) dynamic to plant water stress. RWU is available from previous projects for two supersites and across 16 sites as part of the Swiss Long-term Forest Monitoring Program. We will explore how RWU dynamics affect plant water stress proxies such as tree water deficit (TWD, Task 1b) and water use efficiency (WUE, Task 1c). TWD is automatically derived from high-resolution dendrometer measurements (10 min) at these sites. Still, our research will focus specifically on TWD at pre-dawn as an indicator of plant water dynamics. Further, we will establish 25-year carbon and oxygen isotope measurements of tree rings on contrasting tree species, enabling estimation of WUE and underlying leaf gas-exchange responses as a long-term but low-resolution indicator of tree physiology.
Simultaneously, the project will improve predictions on species-specific drought stress (WP2) by incorporating plant water storage (i.e. capacitance) into an existing Soil-Vegetation-Atmosphere Transport (SVAT) model, enhancing its ability to simulate plant-water interactions accurately, which will be rigorously tested against physiological measurements at super sites (Task 2a). This improvement effectively narrows the gap between hydrological models and the complexities found in real-world forest ecosystems. The SVAT model will then be utilised across various Swiss locations to uncover trends in how plants depend on deep soil water under diverse environmental conditions (Task 2b). Lastly, the project will employ the model to forecast future water availability and drought stress for the Swiss forest, exploring the potential impacts of climatic changes until 2100 (Task 2c).
DeepDrought will advance our understanding of soil-plant-water relationships by linking RWU with crucial plant physiological parameters, offering deeper insight into how trees respond to changing climate conditions. Its innovative approach to include plant water status into an SVAT model will amend these rather hydrological models with a physiological perspective. DeepDrought could, therefore, serve as a blueprint, making significant contributions to tracking and predicting climate impacts on forest health, enabling more informed forest management decisions.

Title: 7DayHouse: Fabrication-aware Design
Abstract:
The architecture, engineering and construction (AEC) sector must respond to an ongoing global housing crisis. By 2025, a third of the world’s urban dwellers—1.6 billion people—could struggle to secure adequate housing. In recent years, Europe has faced an exceptionally high demand for urban housing. This demand is fueled primarily by urbanisation, increased immigration, and demographic trends towards one-person-households. 
To meet this demand, the European housing industry needs to develop high-end, customized solutions. However, it is questionable if the current system for the design and construction of housing is responsive enough to rapidly deliver customized housing without compromising architectural quality.  The current housing process requires a long, bespoke process and the end customer has few options for customization. Instead, public or private developers forecast the customer demand and build a “stock” of available homes from which the end customer must select. A small percentage of detached or duplex homes might use architectural services for individual customization. This process is expensive and can take years to complete. 
New technologies might help. However, proposed software solutions such as generative design solutions are not fabrication aware. Meanwhile, emerging fabrication-aware design systems for industrialized construction do not yet provide the design flexibility required by architects. To solve this, we imagine a radical systems transformation of the process to design and construct a home. In this new system, the end customer should be able to receive a fully-customized design solution generated within one day. Furthermore, this design solution must link with industrialized production capabilities so that the home can be fabricated, assembled, and completed at a final location within one week. We call this solution the 7DayHouse (7DH).
This research will focus specifically on Day 1 of the 7DH. The novel contribution will be the creation of a fabrication-aware generative design tool that can create and iterate the design of a fully-customized home within one day. Within the new Centre for Computationally Augmented Design established at ETH Zurich, we will combine state-of-the-art research in artificial intelligence and generative design with emerging research on mass customization for industrialized construction. We will model for design requirements (WP1) and production constraints (WP2) to create an adaptive “kit-of-parts” library that represents supply chain capabilities. These parts will form the basis for an augmented, fabrication-aware design tool (WP3) that will use an interactive genetic algorithm to generate optimal design solutions that can be visualized and iterated in real time for an intuitive and immersive customer experience in a virtual environment (WP4).  
We will operationalize the tool through the design of a customized, prefabricated timber “top-up” unit. Top-up units are lightweight rooftop extensions built on top of existing buildings. They can increase sustainable urban densification. Generating fabrication-aware design for the top-up unit will enable a first fundamental investigation while anchoring the research in a practical demonstration. Once validated, we believe the methodological steps can be adapted to create fabrication-aware generative design tools for many other typologies of future homes. Such a tool can have a broader impact to address challenges that will face the global housing sector over the next decades.
Keywords: Digital Fabrication, Generative Design, Industrialized Construction, Kit-of-Parts

Title: VTS: Verbal tenses and subjectivity: an empirical cognitive approach
Abstract:
This research project aims at investigating the pragmatics of verbal tenses and their relation to subjectivity in two languages: French and Romanian. In the cognitive pragmatics approach of language, the meaning of temporal markers such as verbal tenses, grammatical aspect and temporal adverbials is determined during the interpretation process under the combined pressure of the linguistic context, the general world knowledge mutually manifest to the participants at the communicative act and pragmatic cognitive principles, all guiding the inference toward the most relevant interpretation, which corresponds to the meaning intended by the speaker (Relevance Theory, RT, Sperber & Wilson 1986; Wilson & Sperber 2004). The question that arises given this framework of language comprehension is the place occupied by subjectivity in the interpretation process of a discourse in general, and of verbal tenses in particular. Does it belong to the linguistic context (in other words, is it encoded at the lexical and/or grammatical levels of a language), is it a purely pragmatic phenomenon or is it a phenomenon situated at the semantics-pragmatics interface (in other words, the result of an inferential process triggered by linguistic elements). 
The current state of the research is largely unbalanced between these two Romance languages both regarding the verbal tense system and subjectivity. The research will build on the rich state of the art regarding the pragmatics of verbal tenses in French (Moeschler et al. 1998, 2012; Moeschler 1998, 2000a, 2000b, 2015; Saussure 2003, 2011; among others) and regarding subjectivity with application to French but not only (Benveniste 1966; Banfield 1982; Fleischman 1990, 1995; Vuillaume 1990; Tahara 2000, 2004; Reboul 1992, 2000; Schlenker 2004; Moeschler 2014) and it will be carried on two levels. At the first level, we aim at proposing a fine-grained and comprehensive model of the relations between verbal tenses and subjectivity in French. At the second level, we aim at developing a cognitive pragmatic model of verbal tenses in Romanian, with a focus on verbal tenses that are more likely to have subjective usages. 
 Hence, the main output of VTS will be an empirically (corpus-based and experimental) and fine-grained theoretical cognitive pragmatic model of temporal markers and subjectivity in two Romance languages. The research will be carried out by a unified team with complementary competences: the applicant, specialist in the pragmatics of temporal markers and connectives among others and native speaker of French, a post-doc, native speaker of Romanian, mastering French and English, and specialist in theoretical and experimental pragmatics and corpus linguistics, and a candoc, native speaker of Romanian with a solid knowledge of pragmatics. The research team will be located at the Department of Linguistics from University of Geneva, which has the material and human resources necessary to successfully carry out the research presented in this project. 
This project will provide an answer to questions regarding the status of subjectivity, its role for the processing of temporal markers and the nature of the semantics-pragmatics interface.  Besides the fundamental contribution of this project to a less investigated language in a cognitive pragmatic framework, it also aims at proposing a model that is applicable to several fields such as translation studies, Natural Language Processing (NLP), statistical machine translation (SMT) and language teaching (Romanian L1-French L2 and Romanian L2).
