Title: Accurate and Fast Reconstruction of Magnetic Resonance Fingerprinting for Water-Fat Separation in Neuromuscular Diseases
Abstract:
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) gained popularity in recent years for diagnosing and monitoring neuromuscular diseases (NMDs). MRI can image both the peripheral nerves and skeletal muscles involved in NMDs. While MRI for neurogenic NMDs is mostly performed qualitatively, myopathic NMDs are increasingly assessed using quantitative MRI. For instance, CSA and volume quantify muscle trophicity, intramuscular fat fraction and global T1 relaxation time quantify degenerative processes, and muscle water T2 and water T1 relaxation time quantify edema. However, quantifying several MR parameters at interest is slow and hinders the wide adoption of quantitative measures for NMDs into the clinics. A quantitative MRI method capable of fast and simultaneous MR parameter mapping is the recently proposed MR fingerprinting (MRF). While the MRF acquisition is fast, the reconstruction of quantitative MR maps from MRF data is slow due to a computationally expensive dictionary matching. Nowadays, there exist a few attempts to replace this dictionary matching by deep learning, which showed that fast and accurate MR parameter reconstruction from MRF might be possible. Regarding NMDs, combining MRF with dedicated accelerated deep learning-based reconstruction would be of significant impact for their monitoring.
The main objective of this project is to develop an accurate and fast MR map reconstruction method from MRF. We will perform the MR map reconstruction based on MRF-WF, a MRF sequence tailored to NMDs with fat fraction and water T1 relaxation time maps. The main hypothesis is that accurate and fast MR map reconstruction from MRF-WF is possible through dedicated deep learning-based methods. Based on the nature of MRF data, we will first investigate the reconstruction from image space and second from k-space MRF-WF data. While image space-based MRF reconstruction has been performed, the k-space-based reconstruction requires novel methodological developments, mainly to cope with the huge memory requirements. In a third part of the project, we will investigate the reconstruction of high-resolution MR maps from low-resolution input data by means of super-resolution, which leverages the rich temporal information of the MRF signal evolution to reconstruct accurate high-resolution MR maps. We will compare our reconstructions to dictionary-based and state-of-the-art dictionary-free reconstruction approaches in all experiments.
By the end of the project, three different reconstruction methods for MRF should be available: image space, k-space, and super-resolution reconstruction. Successful reconstruction from image space and k-space would result in a time gain of 10 hours and 20 hours per MRF-WF examination, respectively. Therefore, the application of MRF-WF in clinical routine for quantitative MR-based NMD assessment would be possible. Additionally, super-resolution reconstruction could yield high-resolution maps from low-resolution MRF scans. Generally, all methodological developments might be applicable to other MRF sequences, and would, therefore, be of relevance to the whole MR image reconstruction community as well as other diseases.
Keywords: convolutional neural network, deep learning, image reconstruction, machine learning, magnetic resonance fingerprinting, neuromuscular diseases, quantitative magnetic resonance imaging

Title: What Explains Household Insurance Demand?
Abstract:
Insurance markets worldwide are not only large, but their proper functioning can greatly impact household welfare. Canonical theories of all major types of insurance predict that wealthier households demand less insurance since they can self-insure to avoid frictions in the insurance markets. However, recent empirical support for these theories challenges the conventional wisdom but faces severe data limitations. To obtain a comprehensive perspective and identify the causal drivers of household insurance demand, we employ novel data combined with a novel methodology. We have compiled a unique panel dataset with household- and contract-level information on the demographic and financial situations of a representative sample of over 100,000 household-year observations in China. 

Beyond wealth, the data enables us to study how a broader range of economic, psychological, and social factors shape household insurance choices. For this, we use a novel dynamic modeling approach that separates cross-sectional differences from changes across a household's life cycle, including shifts in age, family composition, and financial situation. This framework leverages recent advances in machine learning and allows us to recover the underlying preference structures driving household insurance demand without the need to impose restrictive parametric assumptions.

Title: Training with Linear Minimization Oracles at Any Scale
Abstract:
In the current landscape of deep learning, optimization methods like SGD and Adam remain foundational—but they operate under a significant limitation: they treat neural networks as black boxes, ignoring the rich structure of architectures designed with specific tasks in mind. This research project seeks to change that paradigm by introducing a unified, geometry-aware approach to optimization—one that deeply integrates architectural properties into the optimization process itself.

At the heart of the project is a new class of optimization algorithms built on norm-constrained conditional gradient methods, such as stochastic Frank-Wolfe variants. These methods treat learning as a constrained optimization problem, where constraints are carefully chosen based on the geometry of the network (e.g., spectral or operator norms). This shift not only leads to more stable and efficient training but also lays the foundation for automatic generalization and hyperparameter transfer across different models and scales.

One of the most innovative aspects of the plan is the SCION framework (Stochastic Conditional Gradient with Operator Norms), which leverages architectural insights—such as weight matrix norms and initialization strategies—to ensure that optimization dynamics align with the network’s design. Through this lens, widely-used optimizers like Adam can be reinterpreted and generalized into non-Euclidean settings, enabling better performance and adaptivity, especially in modern architectures like Transformers and state-space models.

The research is structured around three synergistic work packages:

WP1 develops the theoretical backbone: new optimization algorithms that combine the strengths of steepest descent and conditional gradient methods. These methods incorporate layer-specific constraints and adaptive stepsizes, making them not only stable but also inherently scalable.

WP2 brings these tools to bear on modern network architectures, analyzing and extending them through representation theory and norm-based optimization. Key directions include improving linear attention mechanisms for long-sequence modeling, designing modular spatial masking for vision transformers, and leveraging norm-constrained contrastive learning for multimodal settings.

WP3 focuses on real-world applications, pushing the boundaries of what test-time training, graph modeling, and hybrid architectures can achieve. It explores how models can adapt dynamically at inference, how reasoning can be embedded in network activations, and how Transformer-SSM hybrids can be optimized efficiently using novel training strategies.

Underpinning all of this is a commitment to scalability and sustainability. As data continues to grow exponentially, the project addresses the urgent need for more computationally efficient training methods. By aligning optimization with architecture and training dynamics, the proposed methods have the potential to cut training costs dramatically—reducing not only runtime but also environmental impact.

This research represents a bold step forward: it moves beyond treating neural networks as opaque optimization targets, instead recognizing them as structured, interpretable systems. Through this deeper integration of optimization and architecture, the project promises to deliver not only faster and more robust models but also a more principled foundation for the future of machine learning.

Title: DEEP: Deep Learning Resource-Efficient GPU Orchestrator
Abstract:
The exponential growth of deep learning (DL) models and their adoption is facilitated on the one hand by modern hardware (GPUs), and on the other hand by the availability of larger datasets. However, even if the training and deployment of deep learning applications is widely used in large-scale data centers, these exhibit low hardware utilization, barely reaching 50%, as shown by studies performed on Microsoft and Alibaba clusters. This waste of hardware resources is exacerbated by the expensive price of GPUs, while contributing to an unsustainable carbon footprint of AI systems. In fact, less than 15% of large-language model training can lead to a carbon footprint equivalent to the average yearly energy consumption of a US household.

Several factors contribute to deep learning applications not fully utilizing existing hardware resources. Potential problems in this context may include: (i) not having a large enough dataset to warrant a large model, e.g., transfer learning, (ii) deployment on resource-constrained devices at the edge may require smaller models, (iii) the ideal batch size for training the model may not be large enough to utilize all the GPU resources, or (iv) there may be data preparation and movement bottlenecks at various points in the deep learning pipeline.

Achieving effective utilization of hardware resources requires novel resource managers and schedulers that are aware of the resource needs of end-to-end deep learning tasks and the characteristics of modern hardware. The goal of this project is to reduce hardware resource needs for deep learning tasks through novel resource management and scheduling methods, thereby improving the sustainability of deep learning applications. To achieve this goal, the project will develop techniques for co-location aware resource management across deep learning tasks over shared clusters of servers composed of CPUs and GPUs. To achieve collaborative resource management, the project will utilize modern fine-grained co-location methods on GPU hardware departing from extreme approaches such as exclusively assigning GPUs or coarser-grained GPU sharing mechanisms. Furthermore, rather than focusing on specific stages of deep learning applications, this project will adopt an end-to-end and holistic view from data management and loading to deep learning training and inference.
The outcomes of the project will benefit data scientists at institutions of different sizes through optimizing performance and sustainability of their workloads while preserving their productivity.

Title: Intrinsic timescales in the extended auditory network
Abstract:
The ability to quickly react to changes in the environment is a fundamental skill for survival. Brain disorders, including disorders of consciousness, have impairments in detecting novel events, which reflect disease severity. To develop novel interventions and diagnostic tests, we need to improve our understanding of the neurobiological mechanisms that mediate detection of events in the world around us, already at a fundamental research level. 
Our brains have the astonishing capacity to process isolated stimuli, integrate those over longer intervals, and form predictions about future states of the world which can facilitate perception. To study the neural mechanisms supporting these computations, the current experimental framework is to investigate the latency and characteristics of evoked brain responses to sensory stimuli, using non-invasive techniques like electroencephalography (EEG). However, evoked responses to external stimuli co-exist with spontaneous fluctuations in neural dynamics. These fluctuations occur in the absence of external stimulation, and unfold over multiple intrinsic timescales which quantify the characteristic time over which neural signals unfold, in patterns of oscillatory and non-oscillatory activity. Across multiple metrics, species, and modalities, intrinsic timescales are organized in a hierarchical manner along brain circuits, and differ across brain states, including sleep and wakefulness, or in brain disorders. Yet, evidence about the functional role of intrinsic timescales in representing and integrating stimuli of the environment to form predictions remains sparse. 
The goal of the proposed project is to study the neural mechanisms mediating the organization of intrinsic timescales in wakefulness and sleep and their relevance in processing environmental information, using state-of-the-art recordings of intracranial and scalp field potentials and single neuron activity in humans, in combination with machine learning to model and analyze these signals. 
This project will provide mechanistic insights into how intrinsic dynamics support auditory processing and predictions. Understanding the functional relevance of intrinsic timescales is needed to develop circuit-specific interventions and diagnostic tests for patients with neurological disorders who have altered intrinsic dynamics and impairments in sensory processing.
Keywords: auditory deviance, auditory processing, electroencephalography, intracranial electroencephalography, intrinsic timescales, multivariate pattern analysis

Title: Managing the Algorithm: Prompt Engineering for AI-based Systems as an Emerging Business Skill
Abstract:
Today, artificial intelligence (AI) is pervasive as it influences a lot of different areas in our private and working lives, for instance through AI-based conversational agents, which are applied in various usage scenarios. Enabled through the advancements of natural language processing (NLP) achieved by large language models (LLMs), AI mimics our human natural intelligence. In this context, it can lead an intelligent conversation with a human counterpart as recent examples such as ChatGPT show very impactful. Interacting with these intelligent AI-based agents through conversational dialogs is nowadays an omnipresent foundation of everyday life. LLMs offer a unique opportunity for individuals to develop and enhance their modern competencies, such as communication, reasoning, creativity, and problem-solving, by interacting with these AI systems through natural language dialogs. On top of that, creating new value with AI is a transformative competency for the future (OECD 2018). 
Nonetheless, generative AI and LLMs also face difficulties, such as the need for technical skills, the risk of producing wrong or meaningless outputs (oftentimes called hallucination), and the lack of reasoning needed for approaching complex problems. Thus, the improvement of communicating with AI-based systems is a critical endeavor. By using prompts, which are textual instructions and examples of the desired interactions, users can enhance the quality and relevance of the AI outputs. However, engineering prompts comes with several challenges. First, prompting in itself is a challenging task that involves active research on the direct and indirect effects of prompts on generative AI models, and lacks established workflows for prompt engineering, which requires extensive experimentation and evaluation by NLP experts to avoid undesirable AI outputs. Second, understanding the process of how AI-based systems produce outcomes based on user inputs is critical for generative AI outputs but not well understood. Third, although managing algorithms through effective prompts is an important skill, there is a critical lack of what defines prompt engineering as a business skill. Prompt engineering not only relates to understanding the technical aspects of AI-based systems but also involves the ability to apply this skill effectively and creatively in a variety of situations such as analytical thinking, strategic planning, decision-making, and negotiation in collaboration with an algorithm. The goal of this project departs from prior techno-centric research and introduces a skill-based approach to prompt engineering as the critical key for enabling individuals to manage algorithms. Thus, the main research question (RQ) is based on the question “How can prompt engineering for business skills in generative AI-based tool environments be conceptualized, designed, and evaluated?” Guided by this RQ, the project is built upon three work packages, all aiming at publications in top-tier journals and conferences.
Conceptually, we draw upon a skill development perspective to overcome the aforementioned challenges and answer the main RQ. We argue that effective prompt engineering strategies allow for improved skills in the business domain. Understanding how to conceptualize prompt engineering from a skill perspective and how to design effective learning processes is a time-critical endeavor for research to provide scientific evidence in this novel research area. The project has three overall deliverables: First, we provide a conceptualization of prompt engineering skills in the business domain. Second, we design a learning process based on worked examples to embed prompt engineering strategies into higher education business teaching. Third, the project provides empirical insights into the effects of prompt strategies and contributes to research related to worked examples when considering the interaction with emerging generative AI technologies.
Keywords: business skills, digital learning, generative artificial intelligence, management education

Title: IMAGES, INNOVATION, AND CULTURAL CHANGE
Abstract:
The image we project, the style we chose, the clothes we wear, the haircut we have, the glasses we pick, all of these decisions represent key ways in which we express our personal preferences. Do I chose to express my individuality, and look completely different from anyone around me? Do I wear the same suit and tie as everyone else? Every one of us, every day, makes choices of personal style. But the clothes we wear and the styles we pick are not only driven by personal preferences. They also reflect society-wide trends and jointly determine the visual culture of an age: Is it permissible to deviate from what others wear? Can a man have long hair, a woman short hair? Do the styles we pick and the extent to which we deviate from others predict how we interact – which parties we support, or whether we join protest movements?
The proposed project combines methods and approaches from cultural economics, big data analysis, and machine learning. In particular, I plan to exploit a unique source containing millions of images to analyze cultural change over time and space. Since the 1930s, almost every American high school student has had their yearbook picture taken before they graduate. These portraits show how graduating seniors present themselves to the world – how they want to be seen and remembered. Images are available in much greater volume and at much greater levels of geographical granularity than other sources that can be used for cultural history and the economics of cultural change. 
The project will draw on methods from computer science and the economics of innovation to analyze this corpus of high school portraits for the period 1930-2010. It will first develop and apply methods to analyze image similarity. Crucially, these have to remain computationally tractable in such a large set of images. In addition, I intend to apply and extend methods that allow us to assess how innovative styles in images are, using machine learning methods to classify style attributes and emotional expressions.
These methods will then be applied to two main topics: a) the rise and fall of American individualism b) the hippie revolution: from long hair to social protest. For both topics, I will be able to draw on a much wider range of regionally and locally disaggregated data than previous work, allowing us to pinpoint the geographical origin of new cultures and subcultures.
Keywords: Images, artificial intelligence, cultural change, innovation, political protest movements

Title: Gravitational Probes of Dark Matter
Abstract:
Despite enormous efforts within the fields of particle- and astrophysics, the nature of dark matter (DM) is still completely unknown. Neither direct-detection experiments nor recent collider-searches have revealed any hint of DM, putting the long-lasting search back to square one. This project aims to investigate the nonlinear regime of structure formation, searching for hints of the underlying DM sector.

Many DM scenarios affect the way structures form at small and intermediate cosmological scales, well known examples are warm, mixed, or self-interacting dark matter. Other popular candidates are sterile neutrino DM, ultra-light axion DM, or more generic DM species interacting with dark radiation or with standard model particles. Depending on the specific scenario, major progress beyond the current state-of-the-art can be achieved by either increasing the accuracy of previously probed intermediate scales or by pushing the frontier of structure formation towards smaller, currently untested scales. With this proposal, I aim to make significant contributions to both.

In the near future, dedicated weak-lensing surveys will provide a wealth of new data ideally suited to constrain DM models at intermediate scales. However, without a better theoretical understanding of the strong gas-ejection processes around galaxies, it will be impossible to truly benefit from these surveys. I plan to develop a new technique based on a parametrisation of gas profiles around galaxy clusters which aims to modify gravity-only numerical simulations mimicking baryonic effects. A preliminary version of this model with only two free parameters is able to reproduce the large variety of different power spectra predicted by current hydrodynamical simulations. With this proposal, I plan to further develop this promising model and to constrain its parameters using individual (or stacked) observations of galaxy- and cluster-outskirts from X-ray, Sunyaev-Zel’dovich, and galaxy-galaxy lensing measurements. This will allow me to perform highly improved predictions of the weak-lensing shear and peak statistics in the nonlinear regime and to develop unprecedented constraints on mixed, interacting, and decaying DM scenarios.

Upcoming observations of neutral gas in dwarf galaxies offer particularly promising tests of the dark matter sector, since they probe both the abundance of galaxies and the inner DM distribution. Recent observations have revealed some tensions with the standard DM model, but both theoretical and observational uncertainties remain large. I plan to run simulations with varying astrophysical feedback and DM parameters and I will develop new methods (based on machine-learning) to determine the circular velocity of dwarf galaxies. This double-track approach will allow me to dramatically reduce current uncertainties and to truly establish dwarf galaxy observables as competitive probes of the DM sector.

Strong gravitational lensing has the potential to provide information about structure formation of the dark regime below the scales of dwarf-galaxies, making it an ideal probe for dark matter. However, very accurate information about (sub-) halo numbers and profiles for alternative DM scenarios are required, a crucial step that is missing in current strong-lensing analysis pipelines. I plan to develop analytical models of sub-halo properties for a large variety of DM candidates. These models will be calibrated against zoom-in N-body simulations with and without embedded stellar potential. The final goal is to develop the first pipeline for strong lensing predictions that is applicable to generic DM models.
Keywords: Cosmology, Dark Matter Physics, Gravitational Probes, Numerical Simulations

Title: Structural Improvements of Attention Models (SIAM)
Abstract:
Large artificial neural networks are now the technology of choice to deal with complex high-dimension signals such as images, videos, sound, or natural language.

Since 2017, after having demonstrated remarkably good performance in natural language processing, attention-based models have gained in popularity across application domains. However, despite their success, this class of models still has several limitations that hinder an even wider adoption.

Attention models are in particular computationally heavy, and require massive amounts of memory to run, making them impractical for many use cases. State-of-the-art methods now rely on architectures with up to several hundreds of billions of parameters that require hardware worth several hundreds of thousands of dollars for inference, and millions of dollars for training. These requirements severely hinder the research in the field by restricting it to a few large-scale corporations. Moreover, besides hurting the pace of research,  the potential of those methods in many economic sectors will make those requirements societal and political issues.

Surprisingly, the structure of these models has not evolved much since their inception in 2017, and virtually all the state-of-the-art architectures have extremely high number of parameters and a quadratic complexity with respect to the sequence length. We aim in this project at proposing structural changes to (1) speed up inference, (2) reduce memory footprint in spite of high parameter count, and (3) allow massively distributed training on computing nodes with both limited resources and low bandwidth communication channels. We will apply the resulting models to standard benchmarks in natural language processing and computer vision, and to world models for image-based reinforcement learning.

These objectives are naturally structured in three sub-projects targeting those three aspects, and will be conducted by as many PhD students.

We will address the question of speed in inference through two main approaches. The first will be to modulate the allocation of computation in a non-uniform manner across the sequence's tokens, by reducing their number thanks to a smaller number of ``pooling tokens'' generated dynamically. The second will be to set dynamically the dimension of the keys and queries per token with a new architecture that operates with multiple parallel pathways of different complexities.

To reduce the memory footprint, we will first couple standard sparsification of the parameters with a L1 penalty, and multiple levels of parameter quantization, resulting in a hybrid architecture that allocates bits in a non-uniform manner across parameters, keeping high precision for subparts of the evaluation that require it, in the spirit of cascade quantization. We will then combine them with non-linear low-rank techniques developed for computer vision.

Finally, a very important effort will be put on the development of a transformer architecture that allows distributed  optimization. Our key idea is to move the effort from the design of a distributed and generic optimization scheme to an architecture that can accommodate a vanilla optimizer distributed over multiple nodes with low bandwidth connection. The bulk of the information extracted during training will be moved from the weight matrices of the attention layers to static key-value sets that can be optimized separately. This will require in particular an analysis of the way transformers encode information, to allow the characterization of the type of data that are required for distributed training, and in particular how much completely disjoint datasets allow to obtain a unified model if it is an assembly of parts trained in isolation.
Keywords: Deep learning, Machine learning, Pattern recognition

Title: Visual Question Answering and Visual Turing Tests for Medical Imaging
Abstract:
Recent Deep Learning (DL) developments have been particularly exciting in the medical field, as large Neural Network methods have surged and brought impressive new capabilities. At the same time, the black-box nature of these has raised many concerns, by scientists and doctors, as to what these methods are doing, what their biases are, and when and where they ultimately fail. For this reason, understanding the inner workings of DL methods has becomes a vital research focus for medical image computing, as well as other research fields in Artificial Intelligence.

In this context, Visual Question and Answering (VQA) methods that query the content of an image by means of an explicit text question, offer an exciting new pathway to discern the inner workings of DL. In effect, they allow direct model probing with respect to the inputs in much the same way as a Turing Test. This hence offers an ability to verify and identify whether DL methods are reasoning about images appropriately – a critical objective in medical image computing. To this date however, VQA methods in medical image computing are ill-suited as (1) current research on VQAs has largely been driven by the computer vision community, whereby the question of how to leverage clinical and domain-specific knowledge remains unexplored and (2) the methodology by which VQAs are evaluated relies on simple count statistics or natural language processing metrics that do not relate to the clinical tasks VQAs in medicine would be tasked to answer. 

As such, the current project has two goals. The first is to develop new VQA methods that can reason about the content of medical images in similar ways to domain experts by taking into account domain-specific knowledge from medical applications. The second is to design methods that can validate and verify that VQA methods are evaluated with respect to their clinical objectives in an unbiased way.

To do so, our project proposes, on the one hand, to develop new computational VQA methods that are tailored for medical applications. These will include Question and Answering modules that can be added to existing DL methods, methods to integrate domain-specific knowledge into VQAs as well as VQAs for sequential reasoning. To validate VQAs, we will explore the recent Visual Turing Test (VTT) framework and re-focus its use for concept validation in medical domains. Here we will design methods for concept-centric questioning policies, VTTs for sequential reasoning and designing VTTs that can cope with broader VQA answering spectrums. By the projects end, we will have designed novel methods that can provide in depth understanding of DL functioning in VQA methods and ensured representative evaluations of these for concept-oriented objectives. 

Ultimately, the project will yield insightful new developments in a research area that is under pressure to give more information to clinicians, its ultimate users. Hence, it has major impact potential for the research community (technical and clinical) and industries looking to commercialize medical image computing methods. To bridge our results to these communities we will disseminate our results through publications, websites and conferences, but also through community led algorithmic challenges.
Keywords: Machine Learning, Medical Image Analysis, Model Validation

Title: REPORT-IT - Advancing Liver Parenchyma and HCC Reporting and Classification through Multiparametric MRI and Visual Language Models
Abstract:
Multiparametric liver MRI (mpMRI) is crucial for assessing chronic liver disease (1-4) and hepatocellular carcinoma (5), generating anatomical and functional information. Diagnosing chronic liver disease (CLD) and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) based on mpMRI is complex (6), requiring a deep understanding of liver physiology (7), lesion differentiation (8), and clinical context due to the wealth of generated data (9) and the influence of prior interventions (10). Liver segmentation in mpMRI is essential for the quantification and localization of quantitative imaging biomarkers within lesions and adjacent liver segments, with respect to adjacent liver segmental borders, portal veins and hepatic veins. Machine learning in mpMRI streamlines segmentation and feature extraction tasks, improving efficiency and accuracy (11). Multimodal large language models (MLLM) (12), or more specifically, vision-language models (VLMs) (13-15), have transformative potential in liver mpMRI analysis and automated report generation (16), therefore facilitating healthcare communication. This project fills an important research gap, utilizing mpMRI for localization and characterization of HCC and the adjacent liver parenchyma. It explores the potential of VLMs in generating structured reports based on mpMRI, which has not been investigated before.
We hypothesize that VLMs can characterize HCC lesions by giving a correct “Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System (LIRADS) score, as compared to the LIRADS score given by the interdisciplinary tumor board conference. The primary aim of this project is to compare the true positive rate (LIRADS 4 or more) and false negative rate (LIRADS 1 and 2) in tumor board confirmed HCC lesions (defined as LIRADS 4 or more in tumor boards), as well as the false positive rate (LIRADS 3 or more), between VLM1 with unstructured mpMRI input, and a VLM2 enriched with additional structured quantitative and annotated multiparametric mpMRI data. Other parameters such as size, location, or radiomics features will be analyzed as secondary aims of the project. 
REPORT-IT includes 6 work packages (WP). WP1 is dedicated to prospective patient inclusion and mpMRI acquisition, and analyzing mpMRI of patients with tumor board confirmed HCC in Lucerne, Zug and Bern. WP2 will refine the existing algorithm for segmentation and labelling of liver segments, liver lesions, liver veins, portal veins, and the spleen on T1 weighted sequences, acquired before and after contrast medium administration. Based on this 3D-cartography, structured parameters from coregistered mpMRI quantitative sequences will be assigned to focal liver lesions, liver segments, vessels, and spleen in WP3. In addition, mpMRI parameters will be combined, e.g. to assess the wash-in and wash-out portion of the area under a perfusion curve in an HCC-lesion, compared to the proton-density fat fraction (PDFF) and the liver MR elastography (MRE) stiffness in the surrounding liver segment. WP4 will fine-tune a VLM training pipeline based on unstructured mpMRI inputs from WP1 and formal original LIRADS scores from interdisciplinary tumor board reports (VLM1), as well as a second model with additional structured multiparametric inputs from WP 2–3 (VLM2). WP5 will validate and compare the performance to grade CLD and HCC of between VLM 1 and VLM2. In addition, external validation will be performed in a fully characterized US dataset of mpMRI with HCC (17). WP6 is used to disseminate the findings of the previous work packages and to present the results in national and international conferences and in peer-reviewed scientific journals.
REPORT-IT will develop and compare two novel VLM-models to streamline and standardize liver mpMRI interpretation and generate accurate non-invasive structured reports in patients with CLD and HCC.

Title: HatCh: Habitat change mapping with historical aerial imagery and deep learning
Abstract:
Habitat mapping is critical for biodiversity planning and ecosystem management. Historical habitat changes impact biodiversity and landscape function significantly. The post-World War II era saw accelerated changes in European landscapes and habitats through a decline in traditional agriculture and increasing urbanisation and infrastructure development. While broad extent satellite data is available dating back to the 1970s, historical aerial imagery has been captured in many areas since the 1930s providing valuable insights into landscape change. The Casey Jones aerial mapping project (1945-1946) captured high-resolution black and white images over most of central and northern Europe and northern Africa and has recently become publicly available for Switzerland. This dataset offers a unique opportunity to assess the status of European habitats prior to rapid changes. However, historical imagery presents challenges for habitat mapping due to low spectral resolution and variable quality. Advances in machine learning, including deep learning, offer significant opportunities for habitat mapping from black and white imagery, though they require extensive training data. 

Structured into five work packages, this research project will address crucial knowledge gaps in the history of Swiss habitats and the implications for biodiversity and ecological infrastructure. The following research questions will be addressed: 
-What are the criteria for habitat typologies to allow for assessment and monitoring using (historical) earth observation data? (WP1)
-What role can deep learning and machine learning techniques play to facilitate delineation of habitat types from black and white imagery? (WP 2 and 3). 
-How has habitat composition and configuration in Switzerland developed since the mid 20th century? (WP 4) 
-What is the relationship between habitat change and current day biodiversity and ecological connectivity in Switzerland? (WP5)

The applicant and project partners form a strong team with complementary expertise in: machine learning including deep learning for ecological applications; spatially explicit statistical modelling; landscape history and the driving forces of landscape change; habitat connectivity analyses; and the ecological relationship between habitat and species. With extensive recent experience in habitat mapping (with both historical aerial imagery and modern satellite imagery) this team will support a Ph.D. candidate to define a flexible and hierarchical habitat typology and develop innovative methods based on deep learning to map Swiss habitats at five time steps (1946, 1980s 1990s, 2010 and 2023).  Landscape characterisation will be used to quantify the spatial complexity of each map. Trajectories of change over time will be quantified considering how the amount, spatial configuration and connectivity of habitat types have changed between time steps and within strata defined by biogeographical regions, elevation and cantons. Finally, the implications of these changes for biodiversity will be examined in a random forest modelling approach using biodiversity metrics derived from the Swiss biodiversity monitoring program and the Swiss breeding birds atlas. 

This work will identify areas with significant habitat changes, guiding potential restoration efforts and improvements in ecological networks. The habitat typology developed will be an adaptable approach that can be applied in other countries. We will offer methodological advances in the use of black and white imagery in mapping habitats, that can be applied in the majority of western, central, and southern Europe as well as North Africa and Iceland thanks to the availability of ‘Casey Jones’ imagery. The historical habitat maps, the assessments of spatial complexity, and the spatially explicit quantification of habitat change will be valuable inputs for studies in which the history of habitats is important.

Title: Data Economy: Organization, Innovation and Regulation
Abstract:
This project studied how data, artificial intelligence, and regulation shape organization, innovation, and market outcomes in the digital economy. Across firm-level, project-level, and market-level settings, the results show that data-intensive and open forms of innovation matter for firm performance but depend critically on organizational choices. Startups that engage with open-source communities become more likely to obtain funding; digitization improves the allocation of investments in uncertain creative markets; algorithmic recommendation outperforms human curation on average, but not uniformly; and digital automation increases profitability while reshaping labor demand, operational processes, and the mix of tasks and workers. Related work also broadened the project’s scope to questions of reuse, standardization, and imitation in digital and creative markets.

The project further documented how data advantages and regulation interact in digital markets. It measured extensive off-platform tracking, showed that returns to data depend on scale, scope, and the ability to combine browsing data with demographic information, and analyzed how shifts in browser technology and governance affect contributions, product quality, and competition. On regulation, the project found that the GDPR reduced websites’ interactions with web technology providers while increasing concentration among leading firms, and that roam-like-at-home regulation generated substantial consumer welfare gains in mobile internet use. Additional research highlighted the tension between AI innovation and the supply of training data: legal and economic rules governing copyright, data access, and reuse affect both innovation incentives and the willingness of creators to continue supplying content. Overall, the project produced a coherent body of empirical evidence on how firms create value from data, how regulation redistributes that value, and how digital markets evolve under AI, privacy, and access constraints.

Title: Utilizing Deep Learning in Map Generalization (DeepGenln)
Abstract:
Map generalization (short: generalization) is a cartographic process responsible for deriving from a source database a target map or database at a reduced scale, reducing the contents and complexity of the map, while preserving the structural characteristics of the source data. It is of fundamental importance in digital cartography and GIS, serving tasks such as the creation and maintenance of geospatial databases at multiple scales, cartographic visualization at variable scales, and controlled data reduction. Map generalization is an ill-structured problem that cannot be solved by mere geometric or image processing operations, and hence the automation of this process is challenging. Since the mid-1990s, the prevailing paradigm for automating map generalization was based on knowledge acquisition from expert cartographers, allowing to define constraints that in turn can be used to drive optimization models and generalization algorithms. The main difficulty with this approach is its dependence on explicit knowledge about how to carry out map generalization, even when part of the knowledge acquisition process is supported by conventional machine learning (ML).
In recent years, deep learning (DL) has been successfully introduced in related areas, such as computer vision and image processing, and several new DL architectures have been developed that may be beneficially exploited for the purposes of digital map generalization, even holding the promise of eventually leading to end-to-end solutions. We therefore believe that the time is ripe to explore whether a paradigm shift is possible in how the automation of map generalization is approached, by more directly exploiting the implicit cartographic knowledge contained in published map series to perform map generalization, without the need of first making it explicit.
We thus propose to explore the utilization of DL in map generalization. We will focus on the use of three particular DL architectures — convolutional neural networks (CNNs), generative adversarial networks (GANs), and graph convolutional neural networks (GCNNs) — that hold potential for map generalization, and for which early work has been published for specific tasks of generalization, with encouraging results. We will address three particular limitations of existing solutions. First, while existing results have been trained on map data that represent only a limited range of generalization patterns, we will collaborate with two national mapping agencies (swisstopo in Switzerland, and IGN in France) to build a large training set database that can be used for training and benchmarking of DL solutions, and for which advice from expert cartographers in sample selection as well as data augmentation procedures is used to ensure that a comprehensive, balanced set of sample cases is represented. Second, while so far only isolated solutions directly imported from existing DL solutions for image processing have been reported that mainly rely on a single type of DL architecture, we will integrate different architectures and propose domain-specific objective functions for the DL architectures in an attempt to create end-to-end solutions. And third, while none of the published papers has studied the transferability of results, owing to the fact that our database will contain training samples from two national mapping agencies, we will be able to investigate to what extent neural networks trained on a particular training set (e.g., on French IGN maps) can be transferred to maps of another producer (e.g., swisstopo maps), and vice-versa.
The proposed project is expected to lead to insights regarding the following points: strategies for selection and augmentation of training samples and their influence on the results that can be achieved; performance of particular DL architectures for specific tasks of map generalization; performance gains that can be achieved by domain-specific objective functions; performance of integrated, end-to-end DL solutions; and transferability of trained NNs to similar maps of other producers, and other scale ranges. As a tangible result a large training set database of map samples from two countries will be published for use in training and benchmarking DL solutions by international research.
Keywords: deep learning, digital cartography, map generalization, open science, training data

Title: A Unifying Geometric Framework and Fast Algorithms for Image Processing
Abstract:
Images and Imaging is ubiquitous and many research questions have not been answered to full satisfaction, yet. We propose to research and develop a unifying framework, new mathematical models and efficient algorithms for inverse problems in image processing, with a broad variety of applications in computer vision and biomedical imaging. 

We believe that the Beltrami framework has great potential as generalized regularizing functional, in particular if equipped with a weighting function that allows multiplicative coupling of the data term with the 
regularization term of the specific inverse problem. Indeed, the resulting energy functional has very interesting fundamental properties, such as geometric regularization interpolating between Gaussian and TV
smoothing, re-parametrization invariance, applicability to any Riemannian manifold and intrinsic data-dependent modulation of the local regularization strength.

Research in related fields, s.a. compressed sensing and optimization theory, has led to very efficient optimization algorithms, which may be applied to the weighted Beltrami framework as well. We postulate that the weighted Beltrami framework represents an important step towards a unifying variational framework for geometric image processing, with a high degree of generality and a multitude of beneficial properties. Therefore we propose to research, if and how other inverse problems in computer vision, image processing and other related domains can be generalized by the weighted Beltrami framework, and to develop robust and
fast numerical schemes to optimize them.

Title: Games, Networks, and Society
Abstract:
This is a proposal for a continuation of a current project  on evolutionary games on networks, an area
in which we have worked during the last years with good results. We propose to complete and 
extend the research further to
areas that have not been investigated enough or at all up to now. In particular, we propose to study
iterated games on static and dynamically changing complex networks and to investigate more
sophisticated forms of agent behavior in populations based on machine learning ideas. Moreover,
following a recent strand of research of the first part of the project, we propose to continue  experimental
work on simple games in the laboratory, extending it to dynamical cases. This aspect of the project is
important because it would allow us to compare real players behavior and various learning models
with the goal of improving the latter on one hand, and of suggesting interesting experimental settings
by using numerical simulations of the models on the other hand.
Keywords: evolution, experimental games, games, learning, networks

Title: Querying the Digital Archive of Science: Distant Reading, Semantic Modeling and Representation of Knowledge
Abstract: The archive of science is the place where scientific practices are sedimented in the form of drafts, protocols of rejected hypotheses and failed experiments, obsolete instruments, outdated documentation, internal correspondence, and other leftovers. Today, just as science goes more and more digital, so does its archive, giving rise to new research practices and opening new frontiers of knowledge for the historian (from big data to the longue durée). These collections clearly differ from the traditional lieux de mémoire filled with thoroughly selected and carefully stored tangible objects. What do these new digital repositories do to archival items? What regimes of knowledge and memory do they presuppose? How can they be made meaningful for queries of the historians and of the wider public?  To answer these questions, my thesis will outline new hermeneutics for the digital archive of science, looking both at its infrastructures (Linked Data technologies) and its methods (distant reading). Mixing theoretical reflection with case studies based on the archives of CERN and EPFL, my study will assemble the elements of a humanist (instead of engineering-oriented) ontology for the scientific archive, transferring concepts and perspectives from the history of science into a computational language. By questioning the epistemological foundations of the digital archive of science, as well as the ways of processing and interpreting such an archive, my research will provide a critical contribution to the good practices of both the computational history of science and the archival policies of scientific institutions.
Keywords: archives of science, digital methods, distant reading, history of science, knowledge representation, semantic modeling

Title: Neuroscience-Inspired Machine Learning for Interpretable and Data Efficient Medical Imaging
Abstract:
Machine learning (ML) algorithms regularly break records when it comes to achieving high prediction performances on different tasks. In healthcare, these methods can study patterns that correlate to medical conditions by studying available healthcare records and other patient data to provide clinicians automated diagnosis and management tools. Several successful ML algorithms were recently proposed to solve different problems in the medical field. These algorithms often achieve exceptional results at the cost of interpretability, since most of these models are working like a “black-box”, where it is hard to understand and explain the predictions or the decision-making of these successful ML models. However, the clinicians want to make the model’s output accountable. Furthermore, these methods often require a high amount of annotated data to solve different tasks efficiently, which is sub-optimal for data-limited domains such as healthcare.

Goal: The goal of this research project is to tackle interpretability and data efficiency in ML for medical imaging.

Approach: Humans are proficient in terms of providing explanations of our decision-making and learning with few examples. Our approach is to use this proficiency and mimic the radiologists in terms of
• a decision-making method for interpretability based on solving a body of tasks, i. e. detecting different organs in the given image, identifying the image plane, recognizing the texture, degradation, brightness of the organ, identifying the sizes and relative positions, indicating abnormalities, etc. The combination of each of these tasks provides the final diagnose and also insights into the decision-making,

Title: The Effects of Income Inequality on Psychological Functioning
Abstract:
A careful examination of the literature on the relationship between income inequality and psychological functioning reveals inconsistent findings: Some empirical studies show that living in an unequal area is negatively associated with happiness, life satisfaction, and mental health (grouped under the term “psychological functioning”), but just as many studies show that this effect is null or even positive. The general goal of this project is to clarify the nature of the effects of income inequality on psychological functioning. The project is structured in two parts that use different approaches to achieve this general goal. Part I. seeks to answer the question: “WHY does inequality negatively AND positively predict psychological functioning?,” whereas Part II. seeks to answer the question “WHEN does inequality negatively OR positively predict psychological functioning?”

The goal of part I. is to investigate an opposing processes model accounting for the opposite effects of income inequality on psychological functioning. I argue that income inequality generates both negative (e.g., anxiety vis-à-vis downward mobility) and positive (e.g, hope vis-à-vis upward mobility) social emotions, which should impair and improve psychological functioning, respectively. A preliminary study with 1,970 participants—funded by the NCCR LIVES in preparation for this project and conducted in July 2018—provided preliminary support for this idea. In part I., I will first run a pre-registered exact replication of the preliminary study (Study I.1a) and a conceptual replication using large national representative data sets (Study I.1b). Since correlational data does not enable one to draw causal inference, I will then run a first pre-registered experiment inducing income inequality and a second pre-registered experiment inducing social emotions (Studies I.2a-b).

The goal of part II. is to investigate the individual and contextual moderators of the effects of income inequality on psychological functioning. Specifically, I intend to identify the at-risk versus resilient individuals (lacking/holding particular resources) and the at-risk versus resilient areas (distressed/thriving communities) for which income inequality is appraised as a threat rather than a challenge and—by extension—impairs rather than improves psychological functioning. In Part II., I will first run a pre-registered meta-analysis on the link between income inequality and psychological functioning (Study II.1a). Second, I will use a machine learning-based approach with survey data sets to identify the most important individual moderators of the effects of income inequality (Studies II.1b-c) as well as a confirmatory approach with a longitudinal data set to confirm these moderation effects (Study II.1d). Third, I will run exploratory studies again using longitudinal data to identify the contextual moderators (Studies II.2a-b) and confirmatory studies using behavioral big data (Studies II.2c-d).

The project is expected to have a large impact on the field of the psychology of inequality, because it integrates the conflicting findings that have been reported over the last 20 years in the literature, while using multiple sources of data (survey-based, preregistered experiments, big data) and advanced analytical tools (e.g., multilevel modeling, meta-analysis, machine learning). Given the political dimension of the subject, the project is also expected to attract media coverage and have a societal impact. At the same time, the risk of obtaining inconclusive results are low, because most hypotheses are derived from preliminary or exploratory studies. Moreover, project feasibility is high, because the project relies on primary data collected using crowdsourcing platforms or secondary data sets that are publicly available and because most subparts involve a collaboration with a research specialist of the subtopic. Finally, the project perfectly fits the agenda of the host institution (the NCCR LIVES / LIVES Center) at the epistemological (interdisciplinary framework), thematic (vulnerability/resilience in the face of inequality), and methodological (longitudinal, multilevel studies) level. The project includes a research stay at the UNC-Chapel Hill, USA, to further strengthen my research network.
Keywords: Distressed communities, Emotions, Happiness, Income inequality, Life satisfaction, Mental health, Multilevel modeling, Psychological functioning, Ressources, Social comparison

Title: Ribosome synthesis in mammalian cells
Abstract: Ribosomes are large molecular machines that drive biosynthesis of proteins in all kingdoms of life. The biogenesis of ribosomes is an extremely complex pathway that involves many accessory non-ribosomal proteins and small RNAs. These factors collectively promote rRNA maturation and ribosomal protein deposition. Ribosome biogenesis (RB) is a highly energy demanding process that is stimulated in response to nutrients and growth factors, and diminished by cellular stress. Deregulation of ribosome synthesis is of medical importance, as it leads to various syndromes and is linked to tumorigenesis. Most knowledge on eukaryotic RB comes from studies in yeast, while comparatively little is known in mammalian cells. Here, we propose a comprehensive, interdisciplinary approach at the interfaces of biochemistry, cell biology, systems biology and bioinformatics to fill these gaps. To identify the repertoire of factors involved in human ribosome biogenesis, we will perform genome-wide RNAi-screens on 40S and 60S biogenesis. Our RNAi screening assay is imaging-based and relies on a panel of cell lines carrying fluorescent reporter proteins. Evaluation of the high content screening data will involve assisted machine learning techniques for image analysis as well as bioinformatics tools for prediction of off-target effects and identification of protein networks. In parallel, we will characterize assembly intermediates of human ribosomal subunits on the proteomic and RNA level. We will exploit the screening and proteomics data to study the molecular function of selected trans-acting factors in ribosome assembly, export and maturation. Further, we will investigate how signaling pathways and transcription factors cooperate in the control the synthesis of ribosomal proteins and rRNA. Our goal is to expand the understanding of the mechanisms that govern the formation of a fundamental macromolecular complex in human cells.
Keywords: 40S subunit, 60S subunit, RNAi screening, image analysis, nuclear export, rRNA processing, ribosomal protein, ribosome biogenesis

Title: Establishing Novel MR Criteria for the Assessment of Malignant Glioma Progression
Abstract:
Introduction – Due to recent changes in glioma treatment, e.g. combined radiotherapy with temozolomide (RT/CT), and anti-angiogenic therapy (AAT), the traditional Macdonald criteria for tumor response evaluation are increasingly recognized to be not adequate any more, since effects of pseudo-progression and pseudo-response are not covered by these criteria. In order to overcome these problems, the Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology (RANO) Working Group is an international effort to develop new standardized response criteria for malignant glioma, but according to their recent 2010 paper with updated response criteria, should to be regarded as ”a work-in-progress”, rather than definitive criteria. Since the formulation of the Macdonald criteria in the beginning of the nineties, many novel MR-techniques have become available, now widely used in clinical routine, that allow for the non-invasive retrieval of morphological, functional and metabolic properties of brain tumors. In the same 2010 paper of the RANO group, it was pointed out that there is an urgent need to investigate whether these contemporary state-of-the-art MR-techniques (i.e. diffusion weighted imaging, dynamic susceptibility contrast enhanced perfusion, imaging, MR-spectroscopy (MRS)) are able to fill the gap in the proper evaluation of tumor progression. The underlying neuroradiological study should be seen as a structured systematic multimodal attempt to implement these state-of-the-art MR-techniques as indicated in the 2010 RANO paper.
Aims – The goal of our proposal is to identify those MRI/MRS-parameters that are complementary indicators of tumor progression status, thus investigating the added value of functional and metabolic MR-information to the currently proposed RANO criteria. To do so, this study foresees the acquisition of T1-, T2-weighted, perfusion, diffusion-weighted MR-images, as well as localized MR-spectra of de novo glioma patients before, during and after treatment by neurosurgery, radio-chemotherapy and/or anti-angiogenic therapy. We intend to investigate the tumor progression in time by determination of 82 MRI/MRS-related parameters that characterize the morphological, functional and metabolic fingerprint of the tumor during a two years follow-up period. The collected MR-data will be analysed by a special software tool that has already partially been developed in house for this purpose, a so called MRI-MRS brain tumor progression analyzer, allowing for both MRI and MRS data analysis within one application. Large parts of the application, i.e. DSCE-perfusion (including Dynamic Histogram Analysis (DHA) and image texture analysis), quantitative MRS, and image segmentation have been established yet in our institution. Algorithms supporting the MR-parameter extraction will be developed in order to automate its retrieval as much as possible, simultaneously minimizing operator dependent biases. The tumor progression analysis tool will also enable the overlay of RT-dose maps onto the MR-images, allowing for studying the exact spatial dependency of dose effects of RT on the 82 MR-parameters.
Methodology – Patients with de novo gliomas will undergo routine structural MRI according to the RANO guidelines. Additionally perfusion- and diffusion-MRI, as well as MR spectroscopy will be performed on a 1.5T MR-scanner. Patients with high grade glioma (grade III or grade-IV, proven by biopsy) will be prospectively enrolled in the study. Structural and functional MRI-parameters will be determined before therapy and during a follow up of twenty four months: (a.) T1-enhancing tumor volume; (b.) peritumoral volume (derived from T2w images); (c.) perfusion parameters: cerebral blood volume CBV, tracer transfer coefficient Ktrans, dynamic histogram analysis (DHA) center- and width-parameters (d.) apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC); (e.) spectroscopic parameters: choline, creatine, N-acetyl aspartate, myo-inositol, lactate, glycine and glutamate/glutamine concentrations as well as mobile lipids and macromolecular baseline. The T1, T2, perfusion and diffusion images will be analyzed by means of texture analysis determining 11 parameters per MR- modality. A total of 82 MR-derived parameters will be put into “disease progression state vectors” p and will be examined and correlated to the clinical parameters. For 90 patients the values of these progression state vectors p will be determined at first diagnosis, together with changes in these vectors during and after therapy. In a first descriptive step, parameters originating from the different individual MR-modalities will be compared separately using longitudinal data analysis, identifying the time dependency of those parameters that significantly change during the course of the disease. It is assumed that the course of the disease can retrospectively being classified correctly into one of the extended RANO therapy response states after radio-chemotherapy (RT/CT): progressive disease (PD), complete/partial response (CR/PR), stable disease (SD), pseudo-progression (PsP), and after further progression and renewed ATT and/or CT the pseudo-response (PsR) state. All data at first diagnosis will be used to further verify the observations from our previous work on tumor classification by DHA analysis. In a second step, besides standard survival analysis (Kaplan-Meier survival curves and hazard models) advanced statistical classification methods, using support vector machines, investigating the possibilities to distinguish PD from PsP, and CR/PR from PsR from the 82-dimensional disease progression state vectors p will be performed. 
Potential significance – The availability of MR-derived markers that discriminate between PD and PsP or CR/PR from PsR is assumed to have a big impact on therapeutic treatment of malignant glioma: ineffective treatment could be modified at an early stage, and the error of stopping apparently non effective treatment could be prevented. The tumor analysis and classification software to analyze the MRI/MRS tumor data, developed during this study, will be made publicly available.
Keywords: Diffusion, MR-Imaging, MR-spectroscopy, Perfusion, RANO criteria, classification, glioma, image processing, pseudo progression, pseudo response, texture analysis

Title: Cognitive Software-Defined Networking
Abstract:
The future of computer networks will evolve around developing networked systems that have a deeper awareness of their operations and environments and are capable of learning relationships among network entities and network protocols. In this paradigm, network entities will track the dynamics of their behavior and the attributes associated with the traffic exchanged in the network, and report this information to an intelligent controller. Ultimately, the intelligent controller will use this information to learn, plan, and orchestrate the network such that end-to-end and network-wide performance goals can be met. This move, while perceived visionary now, it is inevitable given the scale and complexity of network architectures today. This will pave the way for building network architectures that are agile to meet new needs and challenges. This is particularly important as new software systems are rapidly emerging for new applications; from large-scale software systems that deal with massive data (e.g., cloud computing, big data), to the adoption of the Internet of Things, and the tactile Internet that caters for low latency applications. 

In this project, we explore how machine learning techniques can help solve networking problems. There exists already a diverse set of network management services that can be boosted with machine learning algorithms and the rise of network programmability will accelerate this move. In this project, we leverage SDN to design intelligent management services for emerging networks. This project targets network resource management problems. Examples of such services include task placement, network flow scheduling, traffic engineering, relay selection, bit-rate selection for streaming and so on. These problems are often regarded as difficult online decision-making tasks where the outcomes largely depend on understanding the complex workloads and the environment. We will explore how to translate key resource management services in the network domain into a learning problem. The fundamental goal of this project is to design intelligent network management services that can learn and optimize the long-term performance impact of their decisions. Ultimately, we want to explore if machine learning can provide a viable alternative to the status quo network management techniques.
Keywords: Cognitive Networking, Network Architectures, Networked Systems, Software-Defined Networking (SDN)

Title: Designing and Training Hybrid Hierarchical Quantum Neural Networks with Quantum Advantage
Abstract:
Recent years have witnessed a rapid increase in the amount of produced data, due to a wide availability of embedded devices, and a rapid adoption of IoT devices in our daily lives. At the same time, Moore's law has started to show its limits~\citep{kumar2015fundamental} and many forecasters expect it to end in the next decade. This is especially bad timing considering that many critical problems will require processing even larger amounts of data in the near future.
There is therefore an urgent need to increase the amount of computational power. Among the possible solutions to solve this problem, quantum computing is a strong contestant given the rapid progress that has been made in the past few years. IBM just cleared the 100-qubit mark with its new \emph{Eagle} processor and significant progress is expected already in the coming year~\citep{ibm_eagle}.

At the same time, the field of machine learning (ML) has made tremendous progress in the last decade. Deep Learning has become a key technology solving complex problems, such as beating humans at complex games~\citep{silver2016mastering}, driving cars autonomously~\citep{bojarski2016end}, or folding proteins~\citep{senior2020improved}. However, a key limitation of deep networks is the \highlight{extremely expensive computation time required to train such networks using large amounts of data}. A fundamental question that has been at the core of the entire field of quantum ML is whether a quantum-enhanced neural network can prove to be beneficial over purely classical neural networks. This question is of high significance as a \highlight{positive answer would give rise to a new generation of powerful ML models}. To address this grand challenge, we present the following three overarching goals: \textbf{i) Quantifying quantum advantages:} a key incentive for quantum information science is the possibility of achieving a so-called quantum advantage, by which a quantum computer solves a practically relevant problem faster or more accurately than any available classical computer. Our contribution towards this goal will be to \highlight{develop theoretically sound metrics to quantify such an advantage}. For instance, we propose to quantify the degree of complexity required to approximate certain classes of functions using a quantum network vs a classical network. A concrete application for such results would be the possibility to design quantum networks that outperform classical networks.
\textbf{ii) Hierarchical learning:} A key idea in the design of classical networks is the concept of building hierarchical functions, where a potentially complex target function is decomposed into a nested sequence of simpler functions. The recent work by~\cite{allen2020backward} highlights the benefits of this type of representation, which is also shown in~\cite{ghorbani2020neural} to be superior to kernel methods. Due to the current restrictions of quantum devices, such architectures have not been fully exploited for quantum networks. In this proposal, we lay the foundations for developing such hierarchical methods. We propose to create \highlight{hybrid quantum-classical networks} to exploit the benefits of quantum circuits while addressing some of their shortcomings. We expect this will \highlight{open up new research directions to create more powerful quantum networks}.
\textbf{iii) Developing more efficient training procedures:} classical networks are powerful models due to their hierarchical and non-linear structure. A significant barrier to developing hierarchical quantum networks is the \highlight{inefficiency of current training procedures}. We address this problem by developing new hybrid analytical/derivative-free methods that exploit quantum noise and the structure of ML problems. Such training methods have applications to other fields of ML, e.g. in reinforcement learning or black-box adversarial attacks where analytic gradients are not always available.

Finally, the proposal provides research training opportunities for a diverse group of students. We emphasize it is interdisciplinary in nature as it involves a collaboration between experts in quantum science and in ML. Both types of expertise are essential to the success of the proposal.
Keywords: Deep Learning, Machine learning, Quantum Deep Learning, Quantum Machine Learning, Stochastic Optimization

Title: Swiss Primary Hypersomnolence and Narcolepsy Cohort Study
Abstract:
Background: Central disorders of hypersomnolence (CDH) affect about 1-2% of the population. Narcolepsy with cataplexy (today named narcolepsy type 1, NT1) is the only disorder with well-defined biomarkers. Etiologically, NT1 is thought to arise from an autoimmune process leading to a loss of hypocretin (Hcrt) neurons in the lateral hypothalamus. In the absence of validated biomarkers, CDH other than NT1 (the so-called “narcolepsy borderland”, NBL) remain difficult to diagnose. Controversies also exist in terms of etiology, time-course and treatment of NBL.
Aims/hypotheses: The main aim of SPHYNCS is to assess known markers and new analytes in a comprehensive systematic phenotypization of NBL that will improve our understanding and lead to the assignation of new immunological and non-immunological biomarkers of NBL. The main hypotheses are the following: 1) a subgroup of NBL patients represents an early/incomplete form of narcolepsy, in which biomarkers of both an autoimmune response and NT1 are detectable. Accordingly, few of these patients will eventually evolve into NT1; 2) a systematic phenotypization of NBL patients using established as well as new biomarkers (obtained from neurophysiological and “multi-omics” approaches) will improve our understanding of the characteristics and determinants of CDH. 
Patients and methods: For this prospective large “phenotypization” study, 9 certified Swiss sleep centers which belong to the Swiss Narcolepsy Network (SNaNe) will include over 3.5 years an estimated total number of 500 newly diagnosed patients (age: 14-70 years) with NT1 and NBL. About 40 patients with excessive daytime sleepiness/hypersomnolence due to severe sleep apnea (SA) and about 40 gender- and age-matched healthy subjects will constitute the concurrent controls populations. Assessments in these 3 populations will include sleep-wake and other questionnaires, full polysomnography, two-week actigraphy, monitoring with another wearable device in the familiar home setting, vigilance/attention tests, blood and (in selected patients) cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) measurements. After 6 months, the evolution will be assessed clinically and by questionnaires; blood collection and measurements and (when clinically indicated) sleep-wake tests will be repeated. Innovative methods to monitor sleep-wake cycle, assess immune responses in blood and CSF (e.g, T-cell library and high-dimensional single cell analysis), genetic markers (e.g. exome and targeted sequencing of candidate genes) and “multi-omics” (e.g. transcriptomics, proteomics/peptidomics, metabolomics, microbiomics) will be used. SPHYNCS data will be merged with those of the European Narcolepsy Network database, and used to build a predictive model with machine learning approach to develop diagnostic models for NBL and to identify factors that predict progression to NT1.
Expected value: This project will increase our understanding of CDH and clarify the relationship between NT1 and NBL. The identification of new biomarkers will lead to the identification of novel solutions for an early and precise diagnosis, monitoring and treatment of CDH.

Title: Embracing Phylogenetic Incongruence Among Genetic Loci
Abstract:
Phylogenetic trees depict evolutionary relationships among biological entities, such as genes, individuals, and species. They are fundamental to evolutionary biology, and their relevance extends to all of biology, including epidemiology, comparative genomics, oncology, developmental biology, host-pathogen interactions.

One major complication arises whenever the characters making up an entity do not all share a common evolutionary history—a phenomenon referred to as phylogenetic incongruence. For example, phylogenetic incongruence arises when, among the loci used to infer species phylogenies, there is presence of incomplete lineage sorting, hybridization, introgression, lateral gene transfer, duplication and losses, etc.

In this SNSF professorship extension project, we will continue to develop process-agnostic, general-purpose phylogenetic inference methods, and we will use these advances to tackle long-standing biological questions complicated by multiple sources of phylogenetic incongruence. Specifically, we will (1) improve the scalability, usability, and interpretability of our emerging software tool treesignal, which models incongruence using a machine learning framework; (2) contribute toward resolution of the Avian Tree of Life by employing methods that side-step genome assembly and annotation and cope with multiple sources of incongruence (in particular incomplete lineage sorting and genome annotation artifacts); (3) investigate the functional consequences of allopolyploidization (hybridization followed by whole genome duplication) in crop genomics, with a special focus on upland cotton.

If successful, the project could resolve highly contended phylogenies, and shed light on genes related through hybridisation, many of which have been neglected to date due to methodological limitations. Ultimately, we believe that process-agnostic analysis of incongruence among loci has  the potential to become a routine step in phylogenetic analyses.

Title: Machine learning and sampling-based metaheuristics for stochastic vehicle routing problems
Abstract:
In recent years there has been an increasing interest for Stochastic Optimization Problems, where some form of uncertainty is taken into account directly into the model. This produces more realistic models, since in the reality many events or quantities are normally affected by uncertainty (e.g. travel times for a vehicle routing problem) due to unpredictable factors such as traffic or weather conditions. Stochasticity makes however the problems more difficult to solve from a computational point of view than their non-stochastic counterparts. This fact is intrinsically moving the Optimization context closer to data-driven sciences like Machine Learning.

One of the challenging aspects of stochastic uncertainty from an optimization perspective is that already the computation of the objective function of a problem, given a solution, often becomes very complex. In this project we will use Monte Carlo sampling and metaheuristic algorithms to make stochastic optimization problems – stochastic vehicle routings in particular – tractable. We will then move further towards a data-driven optimization paradigm by bringing Machine Learning into the game. We will first use techniques from such a domain to improve the performance of the Monte Carlo sampling-based metaheuristics, and later fully combining Monte Carlo sampling and Machine Learning to solve Stochastic Vehicle Routing Problems. Parallel computation, based on GPGPUs, will play an important role in making possible such a data- driven optimization approach.
Keywords: Machine learning, Metaheuristic algorithms, Monte Carlo sampling, Stochastic optimization
