Title: MIONA: Machine Learning for Ionospheric GNSS and VLBI Data Assimilation
Abstract:
The ionosphere is the ionized part of the Earth’s atmosphere. Models and forecasts of the ionospheric electron content are critical for navigation, positioning, and timing as well as for satellite operations, aviation, and telecommunication. In science, such models are important to enhance our understanding of the dynamics of the solar-terrestrial space, including the solar wind and the geomagnetic field. Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) is a prominent space geodetic technique capable of deriving such ionospheric models. Although significant advances have been achieved over the past years in the determination of ionospheric models and forecasts, they still suffer from insufficient accuracy and spatio-temporal resolution for certain high-precision applications (for example single-frequency radio observations). 

In the project “MIONA: Machine Learning for Ionospheric GNSS and VLBI Data Assimilation”, the goal is to develop and realize new approaches for the refined determination of ionospheric models and forecasts. Currently, observations of the space geodetic technique very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) are not considered in global ionospheric models. While VLBI lacks the dense coverage of GNSS, the new technological developments in the VLBI Global Observing System (VGOS) based on broadband delays allow the precise determination of dispersive effects. It is thus worth investigating the impact of VGOS data when assimilated into ionospheric models based on GNSS. We expect novel findings in this regard since VGOS observations have not yet been thoroughly investigated for ionospheric parameter determination. 

In addition to multi-constellation GNSS and next-generation VLBI data, we will incorporate data from various other sources that are related to the ionosphere and space weather, including solar and geomagnetic indices and models. By developing new machine learning architectures, we will perform optimal data fusion that will improve the quality and spatio-temporal resolution of our ionospheric models. These models will be updated in near real-time and predicted into the future based on a combination of Kalman filtering and machine learning. Our improved ionospheric models and forecasts will be provided operationally to the scientific community and society.

In addition to the ionospheric products, the project MIONA will contribute to a better understanding of the determination of ionospheric parameters from GNSS and VGOS, in particular regarding their systematic and random differences. We will learn which external data sources are sensitive to the ionospheric electron content and most suitable for data fusion. Furthermore, we expect new insights into the application of machine learning techniques for geodetic time series combination and prediction. Finally, the improved models will enhance our understanding of the ionosphere and its interaction with space weather, enabling future research in this field.
Keywords: GNSS, VLBI, ionosphere, machine learning, space geodesy

Title: A symbiotic bidirectional neuro-muscular interface to restore sensory-motor function in artificial legs (SYMBIO-LEG)
Abstract:
Current technologies are not able to provide effective clinical solutions to trans-femoral lower limb amputees. Commercial prostheses can provide a limited voluntary control and no sensory feedback to the users, which makes impossible to the user’s nervous system (NS) to achieve an effective and natural sensory-motor integration. This causes serious problems as: falls due to unexpected perturbations, asymmetric walking and balance inducing bone pathologies, higher power consumption (with occasional hearth failures), feeling the prosthesis as a foreign body (with consequent abandonment) and phantom limb pain (PLP) occurrence. 
The effective replacement of the highly efficient neural communication system (NS to muscles, and natural sensors to the NS) poses outstanding challenges, in terms of speed, number of communication channels, and power efficiency. Current “neural interfaces” between the residual NS and the artificial leg suffer limitations both regarding their selectivity and especially the way of use. The proposer recently showed that intraneural interfaces can be used to restore an effective and natural bidirectional communication link between the NS and an artificial hand for trans-radial amputees (Raspopovic et al., 2014, Oddo et al., 2016). In this proposal we aim at extending this successful approach for the control of leg prostheses in trans-femoral amputees. In particular, the SYMBIO-LEG proposal aims at (i) developing an innovative fully symbiotic closed-loop nerve-machine control of lower limb prosthesis and (ii) testing it with trans-femoral amputees. 
The focus of this proposal will be the development of the optimal bidirectional communication between the NS and the leg prosthesis thanks to the deep understanding of the “Electro-Neuron” interactions, which will be unveiled by novel dedicated models. In this way we will replace the highly redundant nervous system communication by a limited (but optimized) set of artificial channels. Moreover, advanced models will enable to explore the high-dimensional space of electrical stimulating parameters (amplitude, frequencies, etc.), and recording possibilities (configurations, filtering policies etc.), which are both intractable by means of “brutal-force” approach. Particular effort, also, will be dedicated to the development of the “brain of the system”: a portable intelligent and adaptable controller, which will contain the most advanced encoding and decoding biomimetic algorithms, based on deep-learning, neural networks and model-based behavior.  
The SYMBIO-LEG will be clinically tested with 1-2 trans-femoral amputees at the CHUV to assess quantitatively its physiological (metabolic cost, phantom pain, embodiment, confidence), neuroplasticity (learning) and biomechanical (kinematics and kinetics during walking and balance) effects on amputees. The hypothesis of our proposal is that our advanced symbiotic communication system will able to cyber-human system (user, neural interface, prosthesis) to evolve and adapt in order to deal with unexpected and unplanned real-life situations. In this way the cyber-human system will be able to evolve, increasing its effectiveness in real-world conditions and becoming more adaptive (to changing tasks and situations), more robust (against surprises), more effective (learn from the past to anticipate or predict the future), more natural (becoming a new part of the body of the user).
Overall, SYMBIO-LEG project will: i) allow achieving an unseen level of therapeutic and quality of life benefits for highly disabled leg amputees, who are currently affected by important functional and psychological problems, ii) propose a unique set of communication and computational tools for the effortless and efficient communication between robotic devices and human nervous system, iii) augment our overall knowledge about the symbiotic use of neural interfaces and human NS, in particular regarding the issues about the neuroplasticity, tuning, learning, adaptation, both on the algorithmic and NS side.
Keywords: Neuroprosthetics; artificial limbs; PNS

Title: Data-Driven Animation Synthesis for Stylized Characters
Abstract:
Digital avatars are increasingly used in different domains such as learning and healthcare. Digital avatars can positively impact the behaviors, attitudes, motivation, attention, and engagements of learners and can be used at various locations like classrooms, museums, and historical monuments to deliver learning content. In psychiatry and mental health counseling, digital avatars have been demonstrated to significantly reduce psychological distress. Similarly, interacting with digital avatars has been shown to support open communication and to increase the levels of trust as well as facilitating positive behavioral and cognitive changes. While those applications involve realistic and stylized characters, we focus on stylized (toon-shaded) characters to avoid Uncanny Valley effects (i.e., drop in empathy associated with avatars if they become too realistic) and to simplify modeling.

Many of these applications involve dyadic (one-to-one) communication between the user and the avatar, where the communication should be natural and responsive. Since human communication is inherently multi-modal and under the assumption that human-to-avatar communication follows the rules of human-to-human communication, the avatar requires adequate body language and facial expressions for realistic interactions. The goal of this project is to automatically infer the facial and body animation of an intelligent digital avatar in dyadic human-to-avatar conversations from human-to-human conversations using machine learning models. Compared to traditional motion capturing, learning the animations from data allows for automated, richer, and less repetitive movements.

For training such machine learning models effectively, different input modalities need to be considered. First, speech significantly affects (facial) motion (e.g., phonemes lead to different mouth shapes). Second, past research has shown that a person’s inner state can be communicated through non-verbal cues: the face is a primary channel through which emotions are expressed and intention can activate certain facial action units in the upper face. Thus, a dataset that is used for training such a machine learning model on the described task needs to reflect those input modalities. Since no adequate dataset is publicly available, we plan to collect a dataset in the lab consisting of voice and video recordings of human-to-human conversations. The data collection will be designed to trigger diverse (facial) movements and internal states (emotion and intention) of the participants.

The purpose of the collected data is manifold. First, it allows us to explore correlations between the input modalities (speech signal, emotion labels, and intention labels) and output modalities (facial expressions, eye gaze, head rotations, body joint location, and rotation angles). These correlations can be learned using machine learning models for automatic avatar animation. The correlations between speech and facial expressions as well as emotions and facial expressions have already been explored widely. However, less attention has been drawn to the impact of intention on facial expressions and body language, which is an essential concept for intelligent digital avatars that follow the belief-desire-intention (BDI) model.

Second, correlations between movements (i.e., face and body) and speaker characteristics (e.g., gender, age, ethnicity, personality) can be investigated. Our goal is to incorporate such attributes in the machine learning models to improve the animation generation qualitatively. A key disadvantage of pre-recorded animations is the problem of retargeting, i.e., new motion capture needs to be performed for each character. With a data-driven approach, inferring different motion styles is possible if the training data is diverse. By employing a statistical model that can disentangle content from style (e.g., vector quantized variational autoencoder), we can allow for artistic control in the style such that the inferred motion corresponds to the target character. Thus, no new motion capture data needs to be collected for a new character.

Title: Cosmology with 3D-Maps of the Universe
Abstract:
We have long known that our Universe is expanding. But surprisingly, at the turn of last century, astronomers demonstrated that the expansion is accelerating! To explain this acceleration, the unknown “Dark Energy” ingredient was added to the Universe content. The nature of Dark Energy has become a key question in Cosmology and Fundamental Physics, and many dedicated observational projects are underway or planned in the near future to solve this puzzle. Massive galaxy and quasar redshift surveys will trace the large-scale structures of the Universe. At the same time, wide field imaging surveys will map the weak lensing distortion to reconstruct the total matter distribution.
Following the very successful Baryonic Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS), I have designed and started in Sept. 2014 a 6-year project on the Sloan telescope: the extended-BOSS (eBOSS) survey. eBOSS enables high-precision distance measurements at epochs spanning the emergence of Dark Energy in the Universe (within 0.6<z<2). Finally the accurate measurement of the power spectrum on small scales may shade new light on the nature of the Dark Matter.
In this project, we propose to strengthen our team and expertise to leverage our strong investment in new projects as well as on our leadership (in eBOSS and 4MOST) in order to lead the advancement on several key questions of cosmology (Dark Matter, Dark Energy, neutrino masses, non-gaussianities, galaxy formation). To achieve this project, we will develop new algorithms and innovative machine learning approaches to cope with the factor of ~10 increase in the flow of spectroscopic data starting in mid-2019.

Title: Developing the Next Generation of Ice Sheet Models for Assessing Future Evolution and Tipping Points in Antarctica
Abstract:
The future evolution of the Antarctic Ice Sheet and its impact on sea level rise is a critical concern. Despite advancements, current models exhibit large uncertainties, rarely project beyond 2100, and face risks of tipping points leading to rapid, irreversible mass loss. These challenges arise from difficulties in calibration, initialization, and the computational demands of high-resolution, millennial-scale simulations needed to explore parameter space.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning and parallel computing offer transformative potential for ice sheet modeling by accelerating computations and enabling efficient data assimilation. Physics-informed deep learning integrates ice flow physics with data, overcoming traditional computational bottlenecks. While proven effective for mountain glaciers, these techniques remain unexplored for marine ice sheets and shelves, representing an opportunity to improve uncertainty quantification and model fidelity.

This project aims to advance the Instructed Glacier Model (IGM, https://github.com/jouvetg/igm) to simulate marine ice sheets and shelves, incorporating calving, ocean melt, and grounding-line processes. Leveraging GPUs, we will significantly accelerate performance over traditional methods. Using this efficiency, we will optimize Antarctic Ice Sheet initialization for alignment with observational data and perform high-resolution ensemble simulations to reduce uncertainties in future projections.

Title: Scalable Root Cause Analysis for the Internet of Things
Abstract:
Ubiquitous computing is the growing trend toward a world in which physical objects of all kinds could sense, communicate, analyze, and act or react to people and other machines autonomously. The idea of network of smart devices communicating and transmitting data over Internet originally proposed in 1982, and is referred to as Internet of Things (IoT). Since then, confluence of technological advances as well as modern data analysis and learning techniques has significantly evolved the vision of IoT and made a paradigm shift toward autonomous control and human-out-of-the-loop-computing.

Radio-frequency identification (RFID) and machine-readable identifiers provide a way to automatically identify and track the objects and people in daily life. The ultimate goal is to smarten the physical objects such that they can sense the physical world, autonomously transform to different states, and seamlessly communicate with human beings as well as other devices. The interconnection of these smart devices is expected to help automation in nearly all fields, from environmental monitoring, to infrastructure management, to manufacturing, and smart cities.

Consider an intelligent rail transportation system equipped with different types of sensors connected to the Internet. Various sensors located on tracks of a rail transportation system provide us with huge amount of data from how each wheel crosses the track, the speed, vibration, angle and rpm, and amount of pressure on that wheel. We also have access to other sources of information, such as weather information including temperature, humidity, etc. The goal is to exploit streams of information from different sources to enable the system to predict a failure that hasn’t happened before, and to further find the root cause of the failure in an autonomous manner.

To this end, we need techniques able to sift through huge amount of confusing and conflicting data from various sources in search of nuggets of insight that may inform better decisions. For situations where we need to combine evidence from different sources, data may be incomplete or inconsistent, and the underlying environment may be time varying, probabilistic models are the most appropriate tools for deriving informed decisions. However, model-based techniques in general require a deep understanding of system behavior to construct the models. Even in cases where automatic model construction is feasible, the model cannot tell what the deeper root cause is. In addition, the methods for computing with the probabilistic models do not scale well when the dataset is massive. As data volumes in modern applications increase faster than the ability of individual computers to process them, we need to look at ways to adapt our computations using parallelism or streaming methods.

We will design computational tools to analyze massive stream of information from thousands of sensors sending data in real-time, and to intelligently act to it. To validate our methods, we will have access to real data from Volkswagen, Boeing, and Bosch that give us access to their proprietary sensor network dataset and open venues for new and relevant areas of research. The predictive analythics alerts personnel to identify potentially hazardous events, enabling them to make the right decisions at the right time with minimal service disruption. In addition, the framework allows for tracking the root cause of different types of failure and can be used to maximize the safety and security of the system.

Objectives The fundamental goal of this project is to exploit large-scale data collected by large sensor networks to build methods for predictive as well as prescriptive analytics. We believe that the new computational methods will have application in several domains, including medical and healthcare systems, building and home automation, environmental sensing and urban planning.

The main objectives of this proposal are as follows:
• Model the rapidly generating stream of data from sensors as time series to allow recording historical trends.
• Use data summarization techniques to extract the representative time series elements from the data generated by thousands of sensors to enable large scale data analysis.
• Designmachinelearningtechniquestoanalyzethesummarizedtimeseriesdatainreal-time, make inference about the state of the system, and perform intelligent actions.
• Use the developed models and algorithms to predict the potential failures that hasn’t happened in the past, and identify the root cause of failures in an autonomous manner.
Keywords: Data Summarization, Internet of Things, Machine Learning Methods, Root Cause Analysis, Sensor Networks

Title: Unlocking the Potential of Data Processing on FPGAs in Cloud Computing
Abstract:
Cloud computing is a ubiquitous technology that significantly impacts the lives of millions, from sectors such as education, healthcare and entertainment, to the way people communicate, work, collaborate or access information. It offers on-demand services, including data storage, computational power, and high-bandwidth networks, with elastic resource allocation, all while abstracting the management and maintenance of the underlying infrastructure from the user. These advantages have led to a growing number of businesses migrating their operations to the cloud, making it the foundation for many data-intensive systems, such as big data analytics, data management, and artificial intelligence.
    
The high computational requirements of data-intensive applications and the stagnation of CPU scaling-up capabilities, i.e., the end of Moore’s law, have led to a cloud environment characterized by (1) resource disaggregation and (2) domain-specific accelerators (GPUs, TPUs, FPGAs, etc.). Resource disaggregation means that computational and storage resources are spatially separated and connected through the network, resulting in significant data movement within the cloud. Domain-specific accelerators refer to digital chips tailored to perform specific operations (e.g., parallel processing units, memory hierarchies or matrix-multiplication) to achieve cost savings, better computational performance, and energy efficiency.

FPGAs are one such domain-specific accelerator, attracting significant interest from both industry and academia due to their low latency, parallel specialized pipelines, and high power efficiency. Current research investigates how FPGAs can be used to accelerate individual compute-intensive tasks and outperform CPU-based implementations, but often overlooks their optimal positioning and utilization within the cloud infrastructure. This oversight limits their potential effectiveness in terms of application performance, integration cost, and energy use.

The goal of my project is to analyze the optimal positioning and utilization of FPGAs in the cloud. By doing so, I aim to reduce data movement and fully unlock the potential of FPGAs for processing data on-the-fly as it traverses the network, considering their internal architecture and the needs of data-intensive applications.

Firstly, I will investigate the data processing needs of the applications running in the cloud (e.g., databases, stream processors, large language models, machine learning). These needs will be categorized into (1) applications’ main operations and (2) pre-/post-processing operations. I will then analyze how the latter can be mapped to on-the-fly data transformations and data analytics operations on the FPGA.

Secondly, I will explore how the entire chain of smart devices (i.e., devices that integrate programmable logic such as FPGAs) present in the cloud’s infrastructure, from smart storage to smart NICs and smart memories, can be leveraged to reduce and streamline data movement by offloading the pre-/post-processing operations.
    
Finally, I will use the two previous results to develop a computational model for cloud
applications, with the FPGA as a data reduction and pre-/post-processing device. This model
could be used to predict the future computational needs of cloud applications and map them to the corresponding hardware.
    
Mapping applications’ computational requirements to hardware is of paramount importance for the entire future system design spectrum, from chip architecture, i.e. chiplets, to distributed systems. While this project focuses on finding the role of FPGAs within cloud architecture, its results and methodologies can be applied to other domain-specific accelerators such as GPUs or TPUs. If successful, this project could significantly enhance cloud computing efficiency, by shifting tasks currently performed by CPUs to secondary outcomes of data movement. Leveraging data movement with computational tasks will, in turn, influence the design of distributed systems and inspire new algorithmic problem-solving methods.
Keywords: Cloud Infrastructure, Computational Models, Data Movement, Data Processing, FPGA, SmartNIC, SmartSSD

Title: CArDiac pErfusion aNalysis on myoCardium manifolds using gEometric deep learning and quantitative [82Rb] PET imaging (CADENCE)
Abstract:
Cardiovascular atherosclerotic disease remained the leading cause of death worldwide in 2020. Its major manifestations are regrouped into Major Adverse Cardiac Events (MACE). Each year, cardiovascular diseases cause 3.9 million deaths in Europe and over 1.8 million deaths in the European Union, with an estimated to cost of €210 billion. While cardiovascular risk scores can be approximated with unhealthy patient behavior, clinical manifestations, family history and genetics, they often do not suffice to identify a large majority of MACE and their consequences. Myocardial Perfusion Imaging (MPI) is a powerful non-invasive functional tool for risk stratification, as well as for identifying the consequences of MACE. It is recommended by clinical practice guidelines. Modern multimodal imaging technologies based on [82Rb] Positron Emission Tomography (PET) yield quantitative MPI to assess ischemia of the myocardium and its consequences with unprecedented performance via the quantification of the Myocardial Blood Flow (MBF). Its visual assessment is performed via territorial perfusion analysis on Polar Maps (PM) with controlled positioning of feeding arteries and heart anatomy. However, the complexity of multimodality cardiovascular imaging of this dynamic organ has been shown to be subjective to high inter- and intra- observer variability with semiquantitative visual assessment alone. In addition, subtle local spatial patterns that are invisible to the naked eye could identify early alterations of the perfusion related to an increased risk of MACE, microvascular disease or to assess myocardium viability after infarction.

In this context, modern Artificial Intelligence (AI) has the potential to be of high added value due to its ability to fully exploit and aggregate the wealth of modern MPI to address clinically relevant endpoints with little or nonexistent observer discrepancies. While many studies already demonstrated the feasibility and promises of AI for MPI analysis, none of them were based on [82Rb] PET. In addition, all existing AI methods analyzed flattened PMs without considering their inherent polar geometry, which is far from optimal since strong space-varying distortions occur near the center (apical region). Only one study used Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) as a first approach to incorporate the irregular structure of PMs, which achieved a large performance gain (˜ 10%) when compared to conventional CNNs, suggesting that it is crucial to adequately manage PM geometry.

In this proposal, we plan to further develop the latest advances in Geometric Deep Learning (GDL) to adequately analyze the MPI signal over various geometric representations including the PM, 3D as well as on myocardium surface manifolds, the native space of the MPI signal. The investigation of this vast and unexplored research space is expected to significantly push the boundaries of how MPI can be used for clinical purposes. We will address three important clinical aims: (i) MACE risk prediction, (ii) the diagnosis of Coronary Microvascular Disease (CMD), and (iii) the assessment of myocardium viability after a myocardial damage related persistence of ischemia. The proposed models are expected to outperform current AI methods for the analysis of [82Rb] PET/CT, which could be easily implemented in clinical practice.

Title: Monitoring water related mass-balance changes in the Swiss Alps with passive seismic interferometry
Abstract:
At the interface of seismology, hydrogeology, and energy sciences, this proposal aims to advance the knowledge of how Earth's shallow fluid systems change over time and space. Being able to closely observe and monitor these processes is pivotal in enhancing our understanding and management of critical resources such as water and energy, as well as geohazards. Switzerland is already heavily affected by climate change, with long hot and dry periods in summer, inexorably melting glaciers and snow-poor winters. In particular in the Swiss Alpine region, these mass-balance changes have significant impacts on slope stability, induced seismicity and groundwater recharge. 
Such mass-balance changes modify stresses in the subsurface, affecting speed and attenuation of seismic waves crossing the regions. Switzerland has one of the densest seismic monitoring networks in the world, allowing us to work toward  a near real-time monitoring of the stress state of the subsurface.
We will develop a real-time monitoring framework for Switzerland using cutting-edge seismic interferometry methods to probe the 4-dimensional (space-time) changes in subsurface fluids. 

The proposed research will tackle the following aspects:

1.Methodological advances: Quantify the impact of various parameters on seismic veloci-ty.
2.Process understanding: Assess long-term velocity changes at selected locations with the in-troduction of unsupervised machine learning and study the interaction of mass balance changes (crustal stress changes) and geohazards such as rain induced seismicity and landslides.
3.Application: Scaling up to assess the spatial distribution of long-term velocity changes across Switzerland. Make maps available on the SED website that update the crustal stress daily.

With the outcome of this project, we expect to make a large step forward in the understanding and real-time monitoring of stress changes in the shallow crust and their implications for geohazards.

Title: Early-stage structural design exploration through human-machine PEER collaboration
Abstract:
Design builds on the designers’ own experience and therefore it often lacks creativity and diversity. Structural design, namely architectural forms that satisfy equilibrium principles, is often limited to the replication of catalogued forms and conventional solutions. Design space exploration (DSE) describes the incremental generation of multiple design variants (design options). DSE is believed to stimulate creativity and diversity and it is recently supported by digital (computational) means. Despite the vast development of computational tools in architecture and engineering practice, computers (machines) are still far from being used as collaborative partners that contribute, with their own intelligence, to the design process and the DSE. During my PhD I worked on the automated generation of early-stage structural forms (represented as bar networks in static equilibrium) aiming at DSE of structural forms. Finally, I implemented a fully operational computational framework named Policy-based Exploration of Equilibrium Representations (PEER). The research, techincally supported by PEER algorithms/methods, will focus on the development of a new intelligent design workflow that establishes advanced human-machine peer collaboration for thorough and well-controlled DSE of structural forms.

Understanding the impact of design decisions is key for thorough DSE and well-controlled automated generations of equilibrium representations (i.e., bar networks in static equilibrium). Human intelligence has limited capacity of predictability and synthetizing long sequences of decisions as chess playing proves. The research will advance the DSE of structural forms, through machine intelligence. During automated generations of structural forms as part of DSE, the machine, promoted as an intellectual designer, will foresee and prevent undesired design situations, imposed by early human-made decisions. Precisely, it will suggest sequences of design decisions that result in thorough exploration (i.e., generation of the highest possible number of design variants) and well-controlled solutions (i.e., avoidance of intersecting bars and high node valency). Despite the machine intervention in the design process, the (human) designer will still be able to steer the design variants with regards to subjective criteria and preferences (i.e., aesthetics). Concretely, I will investigate the coupling of reinforcement learning (RL)—a particular area of artificial intelligence (AI)—with the PEER framework. After, I will determine if RL counterbalances the limitations of human intelligence and whether RL grants additional control to the output design solutions.

The results of this research will enable a synergy between the human and the machine. The new intelligent design workflow will dodge premature design fixation and will provoke creativity and diversity. In particular, this research will unveil uncatalogued structural forms and will synthetize systems that provide a balanced answer to complex architectural/structural contexts. Inside academia, direct applications to the teaching of structures in schools of civil engineering and architecture are foreseen. Outside of academia, interested architectural and engineering offices will benefit from the automated and intelligent generation of diverse early-stage structural design variants.

Title: DEEPER: Developing AI Methods for Integrating In-Situ TEM to Probe Atomic-Scale Dynamics of Battery Materials
Abstract: The goal of this project is to develop a method allowing to overcome the spatial resolution limitations imposed by the liquid medium in in-situ electrochemical liquid-phase transmission electron microscopy (ec-LP-TEM), through a combination of machine learning (ML) and phase-field modeling (PFM), in the goal to track the atomic-scale dynamics of LIBs materials during operation. LIBs are essential for advancing clean energy and sustainable development. However, challenges such as capacity degradation, limited lifespan, and safety concerns hinder their ability to meet future energy demands to achieve carbon neutrality. These issues are closely linked to the complex aging and degradation of electrodes, including cracks, defects, and structural distortions. During repeated charge-discharge cycles, Li-ion migration within and between cathode grains generates stress and strain, leading to structural and morphological transformations. These changes are key drivers of degradation, impacting capacity retention, cycling stability, and overall safety. Understanding Li diffusion pathways and their interplay with the simultaneous atomic-scale transformations is crucial for optimizing current cathode materials and developing next-generation materials that enhance battery performance to meet the evolving demands of future technologies. This requires real-time observation of atomic-scale processes within single particles. In the last decade, in-situ LP-TEM has demonstrated an unprecedented ability to investigate materials under their application conditions. However, the thick liquid medium required by the biasing system limits the real-time acquisition of atomic-scale information. By developing a method that combines this technique with PFM and ML algorithms, this challenge can be overcome, enabling the extraction of atomic-scale data during battery operation. DEEPER will represent a significant step forward in in-situ TEM for battery materials, providing deeper insights into the complex mechanisms behind LIB aging and degradation. Ultimately, DEEPER will pave the way for using in-situ TEM to understand previously inaccessible local processes in batteries.

Title: EEG based microsleep episode detection in the maintenance of wakefulness test and the driving simulator using a machine learning approach
Abstract:
Road traffic injuries are the leading cause of death for those aged 15-29 years. Excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) is estimated to be the underlying cause in up to 15-20% of motor vehicle accidents (MVA), and is most often caused by socially induced sleep deprivation or poor sleep hygiene in otherwise healthy individuals, followed by medical disorders, or the intake of drugs. Methods for reliably objectifying sleepiness are urgently sought, primarily for sleepiness detection while driving but also for predicting the risk of sleepiness induced accidents during laboratory assessments of patients. The EEG is widely recognized as the gold standard for determining sleep-wake stages and their sudden, as well as gradual, changes. In the clinical and scientific context, standard EEG scoring criteria are generally applied, in which sleep is scored based on 30-s epochs. These sleep criteria consider neither the occurrence of microsleep episodes (MSE) nor the local aspects of sleep demonstrated in both animals and humans. Falling asleep is a gradual, not a sudden, process and shows fluctuations between waking and sleep. Particularly when assessing objective sleepiness in the context of driving ability, MSE of short duration originating in any brain area become an important criterion.
We aim to characterize and identify MSE by defining visual scoring rules for MSE as short as 1 s, extracting relevant features based on quantitative EEG analyses, and by developing machine learning algorithms to detect MSE. First, we will only consider occipital EEG leads but will extend our analyses to central EEG leads in a second step. Our algorithms will be trained and verified on MWT data of patients and subsequently applied to MWT data of sleep deprived healthy individuals, and simulated driving conditions. In the driving simulator, we will investigate the association of MSE with impaired driving performance and spontaneously perceived sleepiness (SPS). In the context of fitness to drive assessments, one generally assumes that the perception of sleepiness precedes the occurrence of MSE. Our approach should allow to validate or disprove such an assumption. Previous studies mainly assessed relationships based on mean values or pooled data. Our aim is to take inter-individual variations into account and relate single events (i.e. MSE) with quantitative EEG measures. Therefore, we intend to track the sleep-wake transition zone (e.g. occurrence of MSE, vigilance fluctuations) with high temporal resolution on a second-by-second basis. 
In summary, we intend to develop and formulate the first standardized MSE scoring rules worldwide and to establish reliable automatic detection algorithms. This will have a major impact in sleep medicine and research and open new areas of research and diagnostic procedures. Since sleepiness is among the most frequent causes of car accidents, and an important risk factor for train and truck drivers and in many surveillance tasks such as air traffic or nuclear power plant control, reliable diagnostic tools to judge fitness to drive or fitness on the job become essential for reducing car and work accidents, catastrophic incidents, and the immense costs related to excessive daytime sleepiness.
Keywords: driving performance, excessive daytime sleepiness, fitness to drive, machine learning, microsleep episodes, quantitative EEG analysis, sleep onset, spontaneously perceived sleepiness, wakefulness to sleep transition

Title: Correlated oxides for Neuromorphic Computing
Abstract:
Our society produces several Exabytes of data every day. How to handle such amount of information has become a critical issue, especially with the end of downscaling and Moore’s law. Nature might offer a solution to this: animal brains are very good at processing large amounts of data and extracting patterns from them. Neuromorphic computing is a new computation paradigm which mimics biology by creating artificial neural networks composed of two basic elements: neurons and synapses. 
One way to tackle the problem is simulating this neural networks in a computer. This approach, used in machine learning, has become extremely popular in recent years. It is, however, a very inefficient and slow way to mimic nature. In order to rival the brain, neuromorphic computing must be implemented at a hardware level: it is imperative to find materials that behave as neurons and synapses.
Resistive switching, an effect in which the resistance of the material changes when a voltage is applied, has great potential. There are two types of resistive switching: volatile and non-volatile, ideal for implementing neuronal and synaptic functionalities, respectively. Despite of this, no viable, resistive switching-based neuromorphic hardware has not been found yet.
In this project, I argue that correlated oxides, concretely those that feature an insulator-to-metal transition (such as VO2), offer a unique opportunity. Based on my postdoctoral research results, I show that both volatile (neuron) and non-volatile (synapse) resistive switching can be observed in the same material. I propose using ion irradiation to locally modify the properties of the oxide, which will allow to pattern a complete neural network on a single substrate. I also show how heat transfer can be used to create submicron, self-amplifying artificial neurons. Combining these two elements it might be possible to implement the first fully scalable neuromorphic hardware.  
This research will be hosted by Jean-Marc Triscone’s group at University of Geneva. I will use thin film growth, nanolithography and focused ion beam techniques to fabricate oxide nanodevices that I will subsequently measure using a high speed electric transport setup.
If the project is successful, it may have  important implications on the development of Neuromorphic Computing, paving the way towards oxide based neuromorphic hardware.
Keywords: Correlated Oxides, Neuromorphic Computing, Oxide electronics

Title: Novel approaches to quantum cryptography on networks and the quantum--machine learning interface
Abstract:
This proposal addresses several issues of rapidly growing technologies, such as quantum information and machine learning. As real-world networks of small quantum devices become a reality, there is a demand for cryptographic protocols which are native to networks. At the same time, larger quantum devices, quantum computers, are limited by data corruption due to environmental noise, a challenge that we hope can be made easier with clever theoretical proposals. Finally, the exploding field of machine learning is resorting to larger and larger models, making training and evaluation difficult.

The goals of this proposal are to 1) create novel, semi-device independent quantum cryptography protocols that are native to networks, 2) explore the potential of quantum hyperdimensional computing, a yet unexplored potential solution to noise in quantum computers and 3) understand the implications of a quantum-inspired speedup of machine learning, which promises fast execution even without dedicated hardware. The three topics are at the interface of quantum and classical information theory, and aim to leverage the strengths of each field to solve the challenges of the other.

The impact each of these projects could be profound: novel protocols designed for the reality of a quantum internet, a new paradigm for designing quantum algorithms in a more noise robust manner, and a potential speedup of neural networks, with foundational implications on complexity theory due to asymptotic speedups. Even if these ambitions are not met, out understanding of these critical areas will advance significantly, and the results will be of interest to both the quantum and machine learning communities.
Keywords: Bell nonlocality, machine learning, quantum algorithms, quantum cryptography, quantum information theory, quantum networks

Title: Deep generative molecular backmapping across chemical and conformational space
Abstract:
Chemical compound space is the set of all possible molecules or materials. It has been estimated that with a maximum of 17 heavy atoms of C, N, O, S, and halogens, there are 166.4 billion molecules. Therefore, the exploration of chemical space is a challenging task. In this regard, coarse-grained (CG) models can be a powerful alternative to reduce the magnitude of the problem.
CG models aim at reducing atomistic degrees of freedom (DOF) by aggregating atoms in interaction centres called beads. In the case of transferable CG models, the reduction of DOF induces an effective reduction of chemical space by generating a degeneracy of the molecular representation. Although this can be considered a downside of CG representation, it becomes a great aid for the exploration of chemical space. Currently, transferable CG force fields (FF) can be used in many applications with outstanding results. Nevertheless, the process of back mapping, which is transforming a CG conformation to all-atom (AA) resolution, is still very cumbersome. Recently, the use of machine learning (ML) techniques has been proposed as a way to build bridges between CG and AA representations. Unfortunately, most of the application of ML for CG force fields are system specific, which make them ineffective for the exploration of chemical space. 

In this project, we propose a generative ML method to back map across compositions and conformations obtained with the popular MARTINI CG FF to AA resolution. The proposed model will use state-of-the-art techniques such as equivariant graph neural networks and diffusion models for the back mapping task. The specific aim of this model is to create a method that can be used in high-throughput screening. This will accelerate the design of chemical compounds based on desired molecular interactions or macroscopic properties.

The generation of a suitable training dataset for the new architecture will also be done to ensure a thoughtful exploration of chemical and conformational space. In this regard, skills obtained from my PhD studies in the exploration and construction of chemical databases will be applied. It is expected that the generated database can be used as a starting point for the training of a model that can back-map structures at low computational cost and, at the same time, that is transferable and easily extensible. Additionally, the obtained model can be used in combination with existing ML techniques for the study of more complex biomolecular problems. Furthermore, we will study the effect of reducing chemical space with CG by comparing the AA landscape for free energies of transfer between solvents with the corresponding one at CG resolution.

Finally, the proposed applications will be in the direction of biological and drug discovery problems. The first proposed application is the calculation of partition coefficients and free energies of transfer between solvents across chemical space. This allows for a rational design of compounds with specific solvation properties. It is expected to identify molecules with ideal solubility properties to pass lipophilic membranes.  The second application will be toward high-throughput screening of small molecules that can stabilize the G-quadruplex DNA complex, a relevant therapeutic target because of its relationship with the inhibition of the telomerase enzyme. This enzyme has been identified as key for the apoptosis of cancer cells. It is expected that sets of molecules with strong binding potential can be identified from the interactions between the complex and different ligands.
Keywords: Backmapping, Chemical Space, Coarse-Grain, G-Quadruplexes, Generative Machine Learning, Partition Coefficient

Title: WiLoC: Wireless Localization with Channel State Information: Algorithms, Analysis, Defenses, and Deployment
Abstract: Positioning services for wireless devices play an increasingly important role in our daily lives and many applications already rely on precise location information. While on-device positioning systems, such as the global positioning system (GPS), enable ubiquitous localization of mobile devices in outdoor environments, they require line-of-sight (LoS) connectivity to multiple satellites, which renders them ineffective for indoor applications and dense urban scenarios with tall buildings. To enable accurate positioning for such scenarios, powerful off-device positioning systems have been proposed in the past, i.e., systems that perform positioning at the infrastructure base stations (BSs) or access points (APs). However, such methods heavily rely on geometric models, require LoS propagation conditions, and require accurate calibration and synchronization among the transmitter and receiver(s). Recently, off-device positioning systems that process channel state information (CSI) with artificial neural networks (NNs) have emerged. Such systems enable accurate positioning under challenging propagation conditions, but are supervised, i.e., require the acquisition of large datasets consisting of CSI and ground-truth location (obtained from an external reference positioning system), are susceptible to hardware impairments, cannot adapt to dynamic changes in the environment, and pose severe privacy and security risks, as the network providers can localize users without their consent. This project, called WiLoC (short for Wireless Localization with CSI), lays out an interdisciplinary research agenda spanning algorithms, analysis, and hardware aspects in order to (i) resolve these drawbacks and (ii) develop a prototype system to demonstrate the efficacy of the planned research.
Keywords: Adversarial examples, Channel state information, Machine learning, Neural networks, Wireless communication, Wireless positioning

Title: Autonomous vision controlled micro aerial vehicle
Abstract:
Autonomously flying robots are the logical heir of ground based mobile robots. The ability to fly eliminates many restrictions of ground based robots in terms of navigation and obstacle avoid-ance.
In this proposal, we consider a micro aerial vehicle (MAV), in particular a quadrotor helicopter, as the base platform for a flying robot. In contrast to a ground robot, the control of such a MAV is more complicated. In particular, there is no safe state for it in the absence of any control inputs. A ground robot can easily be put to a safe stop by switching off the control inputs. A MAV however always needs control inputs to keep flying, in the absence of any control inputs it would crash. One of the challenges therefore is to create highly reliable basic control for a MAV, such that it can be handled in similar manners as a state of the art ground robot.
Partially this has been achieved in the previous project (SNF:200021-125017) for controlled environments. There the focus has been on developing basic flight operations, e.g. vision con-trolled take-off, hovering and landing. Also local visual SLAM restricted to a small operation area could be achieved, as well as basic obstacle detection with visual sensors.
The focus of this project is to extend the MAV’s capabilities for operation in larger, uncontrolled and dynamic environments. In order to achieve this, we propose to investigate along the follow-ing areas:

1.Reliable vision based flight control using combined stereo vision and inertial readings
2.Dense 3D environment mapping and scalable SLAM for MAVs
3.Path planning and avoidance of dynamic and moving obstacles based on trajectory pre-diction

For task 1, we will further the coupling of IMU and stereo vision. We will investigate how the IMU can be used to filter outliers in the vision estimates or in the feature matching. We will also analyze the integration of inertial measurements into the vision processing queue, on one hand to speed up the computation, and on the other hand to make the algorithms more robust in certain critical situations.
For task 2 we will investigate 3D mapping by multi-view depth map fusion to enable path planning and obstacle avoidance for MAVs. The map representation needs to allow obstacle avoidance in 3D, e.g. flying above and below obstacles, which is a significant difference to ground robots. We will also investigate special properties of MAVs to create a well targeted SLAM algorithm which is lightweight and scalable. The attitude control of a MAV together with accurate attitude measurements restricts the motion to a quasi-planar motion. This can be exploited in a visual SLAM algorithm.
In task 3 we will investigate path planning and advanced obstacle avoidance methods especially targeted for MAV, using the increased movement capabilities compared to ground robots. Here we also would like to investigate strategies to avoid dynamic and moving objects. From camera input, we want to detect, track, and predict moving objects, and use this information to compute an optimal avoidance strategy.
Robotics and this project especially require interdisciplinary research. The project needs exper-tise in MAV robotics research as well as computer vision research. These necessary compe-tences can be provided by collaboration of our two research groups, the Computer Vision and Geometry Lab (CVG) and the Autonomous Systems Lab (ASL).

Title: Integrated multi-omic and clinicopathological analysis of BRCA-mutated high-grade serous ovarian cancer in patients with poor survival: identification of predictive biomarkers for personalized treatment
Abstract:
In the era of personalized medicine where we transition from organ-based diagnosis towards individual molecularly distinct diseases, the tailoring of treatment in cancer is increasingly important. This is particularly true for ovarian cancer where there is little treatment stratification within the different histological or molecular subtypes, and novel treatment options are urgently needed. It is evident that the various histotypes of ovarian cancer share an anatomical location, however, they show strikingly different epidemiology, altered biology, and consequently different disease outcomes. Advanced stage tube-ovarian high-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC), the most common histological subtype is characterized by an initial response to treatment, relapse, and the progressive development of chemotherapy resistance. Pathogenic germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 gene mutations (gBRCApvar) are found in up to 17% of HGSC patients and are associated with better initial chemotherapy responses, reflected in increased 5-year survival. Despite improved medium-term survival, there are BRCA-deficient patients that show an uncharacteristically poor response to treatment and short survival.
Traditionally, much of the focus in HGSC research has centred on patients with the most common range of typical outcomes. Our research is taking an unconventional approach of studying clinical outliers since these may provide a stronger insight to the determinants of patient outcome. Specifically this proposal involves BRCA-deficient HGSC in patients who demonstrated unusually rapid progression and/or short survival. It is currently unclear whether differences in treatment response and survival of gBRCApvar-carriers is associated with the type or position of BRCA mutation, or other clinical or genomic changes in the tumours.

Hypotheses:
1.Combined proteomic, high-resolution genomic, and immune (i.e., ‘mutli-omics’) analysis of tumour samples from BRCA-deficient HGSC patients with exceptionally poor survival will provide insights into factors influencing patient survival.
2.Insights into determinants of survival gained from these patients may provide therapeutic strategies to improve outcomes in all HGSC patients.

Aim 1: Validate and further investigate promising predictive biomarkers experimentally and in independent ovarian cancer cohorts.
Aim 2: Build and evaluate the use of a multi-omic machine learning model to predict survival and HGSC therapy response.

To our knowledge, this is the largest comprehensive multi-omics study of BRCA-deficient patients of any cancer type, and will provide the first detailed multi-omics landscape of BRCA-deficient HGSC patients. The data generated in this proposal may reveal clinically useful prognostic biomarkers and significantly enhance the international knowledgebase of the poor prognosis group of BRCA-deficient HGSC. Moreover, predictive targets and response patterns and pathways identified will be useful for stratifying patients in clinical trials investigating ovarian cancer.
Keywords: BRCA-deficient, High resolution genomic, Immune analysis, Multi-omics, Poor survival, Tubo-ovarian high-grade serous carcinoma

Title: Functional Connectivity and Computational Role of Apical Dendritic Tufts of Layer 5 Pyramidal Neurons in Mouse Neocortex
Abstract:
The neocortex of the mammalian brain enables extraordinary cognitive abilities and learning capabilities in higher mammals and humans. Despite decades of research and substantial progress in revealing neocortical structure and function, still today a deeper understanding of the anatomical and physiological basis of the computational power of the neocortex is missing. Part of the challenge is the highly complex functional organization with many neuronal subtypes and across multiple levels: from local connectivity within the 6-layered microcircuit to embedding of specific cell types in the large-scale cortico-cortical and brain-wide circuitry. The neocortical projection neurons, the pyramidal neurons, have a prominent apical dendrite that reaches towards the brain surface and forms a tuft of dendrites in the most superficial layer 1. In these tufts, pyramidal neurons receive a multitude of synaptic inputs from a wide range of regions, which are integrated in a complex manner and shaped by the nonlinear properties of the dendrites. The coupling of the apical dendritic tuft to the soma and the interactions of apical dendritic and somatic compartments are considered crucial for the generation of action potential bursts, which can strongly influence larger-scale dynamics and brain states. Previously established concepts have assigned various functions to the apical dendritic compartment, including gain modulation, coincidence detection, transmission of prediction errors, multiplexed information transfer, and non-linear integration of higher-order information. Furthermore, adaptations of dendritic activity and dendro-somatic coupling are considered key potential mechanisms for learning-related changes in brain dynamics, but experimental data are scarce. Overall, the computational principles governing dendritic dynamics during learning and the underlying functional connectivity within local and long-range neural circuits remain poorly understood. 
Recently, we longitudinally tracked the activity of apical tuft dendrites of layer 5 pyramidal neurons while mice learned a tactile discrimination task. We discovered two types of functional changes, which we recognized do match two distinct components of the prediction error in classical temporal difference reinforcement learning. Casting our results into a model suggested that gain modulation via apical dendritic tuft activity governs the recruitment of appropriate, i.e., task-relevant, subsets of pyramidal neurons. Guided by our model, we aim here to investigate more deeply which long-range inputs are integrated in layer 5 apical tufts and how they influence somatic output during learning. We will work towards three major aims: (Aim 1) Identification of anatomical and functional tuft connectivity with long-range axonal inputs from various probable source regions; (Aim 2) Measurement and analysis of learning-related activity changes in the most prominent of these input paths and their correlation with functional changes in the dendritic tufts. In addition, we aim to assess dendro-somatic coupling and changes in gain modulation across learning by simultaneous dual-depth imaging in layers 1 and 5; and (Aim 3) Optogenetic manipulation of specific long-range inputs, guided by our model predictions and tailored to either hinder or promote learning. We will also iteratively refine our computational model, with the goal of establishing further direct links between specific mathematical terms and the dynamic features of tangible neural compartments or pathways. We expect fundamental insights into the role of layer 5 apical dendrites in cortical information processing, bearing high potential relevance for understanding of large-scale brain dynamics, brain state modulation, as well as cognitive functions and dysfunctions. Our results may also inspire novel learning algorithms or neuromorphic chip designs for implementing learning in artificial systems.
Keywords: calcium imaging, dendrite, learning, neocortex, neuronal network, prediction error, pyramidal neuron, reinforcement learning, sensory discrimination, two-photon imaging

Title: Incentives for Acquisition of Data and Knowledge
Abstract:
Data Science is an emerging paradigm to help people make better decisions based on data. Often, this data must be acquired from other, self-interested sources, such as in crowdsourcing, surveys, or medical studies. Because the data is used for important decisions, it is very important that the data be accurate, relevant and novel. The subprime financial crisis of 2008 and the Enron scandal of 2002 are vivid examples of the consequences that can result from decisions based on inaccurate data.

Much attention has been given to filtering data after it has been received. However, a crucial dimension that has received less attention is to motivate data sources to make an effort to provide only accurate and relevant data in the first place. The most  straightforward incentive is to pay for the data. However, anyone could submit random or redundant data just to get compensated. In many cases, it is not possible for the receiver to verify the accuracy of data, nor to know what data could help it learn a better model. Thus, it has no way of knowing what data deserves to be paid. This problem stands in the way of many useful applications of data science in fields ranging from digital medicine to information security.

The issue has been studied in the context of crowdsourcing predictions. Surprisingly, through interaction of multiple data providers it is possible to devise schemes that reward only accurate and truthful data. They are prediction markets and peer prediction and increasingly used in private and also public settings. However, so far both  approaches only apply to single predictions with small answer spaces. 

The goal of this project is to develop similar reward mechanisms for a broader class of data, in particular data that can be used for machine learning from examples. It will provide, for the first time, an incentive scheme for data providers so that only high-quality and relevant data is paid. This will enable many broad opportunities for crowdsourcing in data science.

Beyond incentives for quality, we will also address the issue of malicious data providers who manipulate the learning result to an outcome that favors them. Here, rather than just being given low incentives, such data providers must see their data excluded from the learning process. This can be achieved through reputation systems, a technique closely related to the incentives we are developing.

The project defines formal models that fit a range of actual scenarios, and then develops generalizations of both the prediction market and the peer prediction models. We prove their incentive properties through game-theoretic analysis and uncover the assumptions required. We simulate practical scenarios to estimate the average cost and efficiency of our incentive mechanisms.
Keywords: Computational Game Theory, Data Science, Multi-Agent Systems

Title: Bridging the gap between machine learning and geostatistical simulations
Abstract:
This project aims at using machine learning (ML) to improve state of the art methods to produce realistic spatial interpolations. The proposed solution overcomes the limitations that are currently present in the existing methods. The current interpolation methods are vital tools in various fields, from geology and hydrogeology to earth surface sciences (e.g., remote sensing, climate modeling, weather, ecology). All these fields of study require the interpolation methods in order to understand how a variable evolves in space. Each interpolation method suits a specific field of study best; this project focuses on interpolations that produce spatially coherent structures applied to remote sensing (in particular on the enhancement of poor – and usually cheap – satellite images). To handle the variability in the spatial structures and also to take uncertainty into consideration, many different interpolations are required (each called a simulation). Each interpolation represents a different scenario, respecting underlying spatial structure. Nowadays methods can enhance poor satellite images, however, they only use a small fraction of all the information available, and therefore we are still relatively far from the optimal outcome.
This problem of generating structurally coherent interpolations was historically addressed by two distinct approaches: 1- Gaussian random fields which uses a mathematical framework and 2- multiple point statistics (MPS) which uses images of analogues to obtain the information needed for the interpolation. While the first approach is mathematically robust, the major issue lies in its inability to simulate complex structures. In contrast, structural complexity is embedded in the training images used by MPS algorithms to do simulations. However, these solutions come with some limitations of their own, for instance they need to be placed over a grid and they cannot well reproduce the rare events (usually extremes). But probably the most critical limitation is that extrapolating to new (unencountered) scenarios is impossible. Finally, both approaches require extra algorithmic parameters or mathematical models to be tuned. These parameters are sometimes hard to determine and need extensive trial-and-error.
Current solutions are either limited to simple models, or by the impossibility of generalizing structures to new situations. In all cases, current approaches struggle with huge datasets. This project aims to develop a 3rd approach that challenges these established facts, by proposing a state-of-the-art Machine Learning approach that will allow extrapolation, reproduction of complex structures, self-parametrization using the significant dataset available in remote sensing field. The proposed approach in this project capitalizes on sequential simulations that are well known as operational strategies. Furthermore, ML will allow quick adaptation to new situations and datasets by learning from the previous case studies.
Keywords: Geostatistics, Interpolation, Machine learning, Multiple-point statistics, Statistical simulation

Title: WHEAT.AI: Learning Agronomic Intelligence at Landscape Scale with Earth Observation and Machine Learning to Improve Winter Wheat Cultivation
Abstract:
Our research proposal, "WHEAT.AI: Learning Agronomic Intelligence at Landscape Scale with Earth Observation and Machine Learning to Improve Winter Wheat Cultivation," aims to revolutionize the way we gain ecophysiological and agronomic knowledge by leveraging modern machine learning techniques and earth observation. This initiative uses the example of winter wheat cultivation in Switzerland as its focal point.

The main goals of this project are:
- To develop and evaluate a sophisticated machine learning model named “WHEAT.AI,” designed to predict the Leaf Area Index (LAI) time series for winter wheat using data on weather, soil, and cultivation types (conventional and organic farming).
- To investigate the impact of soil characteristics, weather conditions, and cultivation types on crop growth and yield, thereby enhancing our understanding of the risk and resilience factors in winter wheat cultivation.
- To compare and validate the WHEAT.AI model against mechanistic models and field experiment results, ensuring its reliability and applicability to real-world agricultural practices.

The project surpasses the current state of the art by:
- Utilizing transformer-based deep neural networks (WHEAT.AI) for precise growth modeling and yield prediction, moving beyond traditional time-series and function-fitting models.
- Leveraging a unique, comprehensive, multi-year, country-wide dataset (MYWG), which includes LAI observations, environmental variables, and detailed information on cultivation types over more than eight years across the entire agricultural landscape of Switzerland.
- Using the WHEAT.AI model to investigate the impact of soil characteristics, weather conditions, and crop management practices on plant growth and yield.
- Bridging the gap between earth observation and crop physiology by integrating ecophysiological knowledge into earth observation approaches.

The project is structured into three main work packages (WPs):
- WP1 focuses on building and evaluating the WHEAT.AI model based on the MYWG dataset, fine-tuning strategies for specific situations, and comparing the model against an established mechanistic model.
- WP2 and WP3 delve into analyzing the risk and resilience factors for growth and yield, utilizing both the MYWG dataset and predictions from WHEAT.AI. This includes examining the effects of weather, soil, and cultivation practices.

In conclusion, we believe that the synthesis of this truly interdisciplinary research will be groundbreaking. Just as modern machine learning has revolutionized applications such as protein folding and weather forecasting, we envision how systems like WHEAT.AI may revolutionize how we investigate ecophysiological processes of plant growth at the landscape scale and identify risks for crop production. This will be evaluated by addressing exciting research questions. Moreover, the proposed research will be pivotal for earth observation applications, demonstrating a new way for gap-filling and denoising time series data of plant traits beyond typical satellite data-driven approaches.

Title: Collaborative and Data-Centric Large Language Models
Abstract:
This research proposal tackles critical challenges in the development and deployment of large language models (LLMs), such as immense computational demands, data privacy concerns, and a lack of transparency in training and decision-making processes, which hinder their safe use in sensitive domains like medicine. We propose an algorithmic, data-centric, and collaborative-learning-based approach that emphasizes architectural innovations and advanced training methodologies to enhance LLM capabilities while ensuring transparency and understanding of their inner workings. 
Our research focuses on three key areas. First, we aim to improve data efficiency of training LLMs, by developing automatic data selection methods as well as an improved curriculum of vast amounts of training data. Second, we aim to customize and improve collaborative learning methods, specifically federated and decentralized learning, for pretraining and fine-tuning LLMs, with the goal of enabling new applications on currently untapped private data, as well as personalized on-device AI models, without compromising each user's data sovereignty.  Third, we explore improved modularization of LLMs, allowing the re-use and exchange of parts of already pretrained models. We also enable better quality responses within the same computational budget, by adaptivity of test compute to the level of difficulty of the current generation step.
Integrating these three research directions aims to produce LLMs that are more efficient, transparent, and adaptable, suitable for deployment in critical sectors such as healthcare. By advancing collaborative training frameworks, we seek to democratize AI development, fostering an inclusive and ethically responsible AI ecosystem.  In addition to foundational research on algorithms, we will also produce open-source software ready to be deployed in practice, enabling many applications in a global and multilingual context.
Keywords: AI, Collaborative Learning, Data Selection, Efficient Training, Large Language Models, Optimization, Training Data

Title: Neural network control with dissipativity and performance guarantees (NeCon)
Abstract:
Motivated by the widespread use of control systems in engineering and the extensive availability of system models and control techniques for guaranteeing local stability and dissipativity, the NeCon project aims to develop and demonstrate novel control design methods based on Neural Networks (NN) for preserving these crucial features while improving the system performance. 
The proposed research plan comprises foundational advances as well as applications to real systems. At the methodological level, existing methods will be extended by developing wide classes of centralized and distributed dissipativity-preserving NN controllers for nonlinear interconnected systems. To this purpose, we will leverage the compositional properties of dissipative systems and their built-in stability features. Control design will be cast into optimization problems for general cost functions accounting for a rich set of performance specifications. Moreover, optimization-friendly parametrizations of control policies will be provided for efficiently searching in the set of NN controllers by using standard backpropagation and gradient descent methods. Our results will enable the exploitation of deep NN for maximizing controller flexibility and guaranteeing desired closed-loop behaviors even if the optimization stops prematurely.
Besides model-based control design, we will study Imitation Learning (IL) algorithms exploiting data generated by sophisticated expert controllers and the modeling power of NN architectures to synthesize dissipativity-preserving policies that are easy to implement and that can smartly adapt to changes in the system dynamics or interconnection topology. IL will also be used as a paradigm for migrating controllers from centralized to distributed architectures or between different distributed configurations.
As a proof of concept, the new approaches will be validated on district heating systems by conducting real experiments on the NEST building available at Empa, with the goal of replacing costly optimization-based controllers with regulators that are more scalable and easier to implement.
The proposed research will contribute to the long-term vision of smoothly combining control theory with NN for operating a broad range of systems in a reliable and efficient way. NeCon is also expected to have a substantial impact on industry, by providing tools for making nonlinear control design accessible to non-experts and by promoting more efficient use of resources through the maximization of flexible performance criteria.
Keywords: Distributed control, District heating systems, Imitation learning, Neural network control, Stability and safety

Title: Learning and Exploration under Perceptual and Value Uncertainty
Abstract: Organisms often face the challenge of navigating a world riddled with many sources of uncertainty, be it ambiguous sensory inputs or unreliable behavioral outcomes. Most existing research only considered either of these two sources of uncertainty in the contexts of perceptual decision making for the former, and reinforcement learning and value-based decision making for the latter. We aim at developing a unifying experimental and theoretical account of human adaptive behavior subject to both perceptual and value uncertainty. To do so, we will design and conduct psychophysical experiments that combine perceptual inference and value-based learning tasks. Namely, subjects are encouraged to maximize reward through reinforcement learning in an environment where both stimuli and rewards are unreliable. We will then use computational modeling and statistical model comparison to probe how those two forms of uncertainty jointly affect behavior. One potential outcome is that humans solve the perceptual inference and value-based learning tasks independently. Alternatively, perceptual and value uncertainty interaction cannot be explained by accounts that considered the two processes independently. Our data-guided computational approach will allow us to identify the strategies used by subjects to solve the combined task and to generate new empirically testable hypotheses about complex behaviors.
Keywords: computational modeling, decision making, directed exploration, human behavior, pscychophysics, reinforcement learning, statistical data analysis, uncertainty

Title: Computer aided Methods for Diagnosis and Early Risk Assessment for Parkinson`s Disease Dementia
Abstract:
Neurodegenerative disorders begin insidiously in midlife and are relentlessly progressive.  Currently, there exists no established curative or protective treatment, and they constitute a major and increasing health problem and, in consequence, an economic burden in aging populations globally. Parkinson’s disease (PD), following Alzheimer’s disease (AD), is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder worldwide, estimated to occur in approximately 1% of population above 60 and at least in 3% in individuals above 80 years of age. In Switzerland, about 15’000 persons are diagnosed with PD. In addition to motor signs, which due to recent medical progress can be treated satisfactorily in most cases, non-motor symptoms and signs severely affect the well-being of patients.  They include mood disorders, psychosis, cognitive decline, disorders of circadian rhythms, as well as vegetative and cardiovascular dysregulation. Neurodegeneration in PD progresses for years before clinical diagnosis is possible, at which time e.g. 80% of dopaminergic neurons in the Substantia nigra are lost already. Therefore, any clinical targeting disease modification, prognosis and personalized treatment including guiding the indication for deep brain stimulation (DBS) requires reliable and valid biomarkers.
The main goal of this research project is the identification of a pertinent set of genetic and neurophysiological markers for diagnosis and early risk assessment of PD-dementia. Our approach has a distinct interdisciplinary basis, in that it fosters close collaborations between physicians, neuroscientists, psychiatrists, psychologists, computer scientists and statisticians.   
Based on current research findings we postulate that a combination of (1) quantitative electroencephalographic measures (QEEG, e.g. frequency power and connectivity patterns and network analysis), (2) genetic biomarkers (e.g. MAPT, COMT, GBA, APOE) and (3) neuropsychological assessment improves early recognition and monitoring of cognitive decline in PD. To test this hypothesis, this project proposes an interdisciplinary long-term study of patients diagnosed with PD without signs of dementia, among them a subgroup of patients undergoing DBS. 
The workup of the proposed study includes collection of clinical, neuropsychological, neurophysiological and genotyping data at the baseline, as well as at 3, 4 and 5 years follow-ups. Sophisticated statistical models that can deal with noisy measurements, missing values and heterogeneous data types will be used to extract the best combination of biomarkers and neuropsychological variables for diagnosis and prediction of prognosis of PD-dementia.  Besides this clinical perspective, this project further aims at deciphering the unknown disease mechanisms in PD both on a genetic and neurophysiological level, with particular emphasis of the interplay of genetic markers and temporal changes in the functional connectivity of the brain over time.
