Title: ACTWELL: Activities, Contexts, and Traits in Well-Being in Everyday Life Longitudinally
Abstract:
Most people (69%) rate well-being (WB) as the most important life outcome (Diener & Oishi, 2000). While objective quality of life indicators has overall increased in many countries around the world in the last 10 years (OECD, 2020), subjective well-being (i.e., life satisfaction, affect), has continuously degraded over the last ten years with a recent aggravation in the COVID-19 pandemic (Clifton, 2022). Rising levels of loneliness, depression, and anxiety are deteriorating many peoples’ WB (Holt-Lunstad et al., 2015; World Health Organization, 2022; Xu et al., 2018) and were estimated to cost the global economy US$ 2.5 trillion in 2010 (e.g., absenteeism, turnover, treatment; World Health Organization, 2022) with a projection of around US$ 6 trillion for the year 2030. Swiss citizens report high overall WB (OECD, 2020), but research indicates that the WB of vulnerable groups (e.g., young people, elders) is asymmetrically impacted in times of crises (e.g., during the COVID-19 pandemic; Kuhn et al., 2021). Currently, WB is mostly investigated in long-term panel studies quantifying WB over years and decades (e.g., Helliwell & Aknin, 2018). These studies are paramount for the overall assessment of WB trends, but they cannot provide the fine-grained information needed to understand WB in the complexity of daily life. In contrast to strategies to address long-term WB developments (e.g., economic decline), interventions on sudden environmental and geopolitical crises call for a better understanding of the behavioral, contextual, and dispositional factors that impact WB in-vivo. Understanding of WB in daily life could inform the development of monitoring and warning methods to anticipate and intervene in circumstances that indicate or precede low WB. The development of such intervention- and support mechanisms requires an intricate understanding of how WB is manifested naturalistically in daily life and which behavioral and contextual markers are indicative of current and changing levels of WB.
Here, we leverage seven secondary big datasets (CH, DE, USA) on naturalistic behavioral and contextual sensing data from smartphones to describe, predict, and to explain self-reported overall- (life satisfaction) and momentary WB (positive/negative affect). In six work packages (WP1-6), we will perform a systematic literature review (WP1) that will inform the computational extraction of subjective (experience sampling, questionnaire data) and objective behavioral (mobile sensing data) and contextual (e.g., locations, weather) markers of WB (WP2). Using machine learning, we will analyze how WB is reflected in patterns of behavior and contexts across individuals (WP3) and within individuals across time (WP4). Additionally (WP3+4), we will investigate which behaviors, contexts, and traits are most predictive of WB levels within- and across datasets and individuals. Finally, the longitudinal nature of our data will allow us to identify behavioral patterns that precede different WB levels at later points in time (WP5), providing first insights on potential causal mechanisms of behaviors and contexts on WB.
Our project will generate a comprehensive picture of how WB is manifested in the behaviors and contexts of peoples’ daily lives and how this information can be used to predict levels of WB and its changes. The identification of markers of WB across people and the degree to which these are person-specific will not only inform WB theory, but also provide actionable evidence for further research and the development of scalable and in-vivo deployable detection-, support-, and intervention strategies.
Keywords: Daily behavior, Machine learning, Mobile sensing, Personality, Well-being

Title: SwiftLink: Machine Learning Strategies for Adaptive Multimedia Navigation
Abstract:
The acquisition of large collections of multimedia data is now generalized in all social processes. The cost of acquisition, storage and dissemination has been drastically reduced due to the advances made in related hardware and communication domains. It is still not clear however whether optimal strategies exist to take the most advantage of these multimedia collections. Information search systems come as a solution to mine and retrieve information from these collections. In the case of exploration, information networks are generally manually organized via moderated user communities (eg Wikipedia or YouTube). Fully automated solutions generally come from the domain of Adaptive Hypermedia, creating information networks from the information content.

Via the SwiftLink project, we wish to explore a new direction for the automated creation, adaptation and maintenance of information networks. This project, mainly supporting the PhD work of M. Marc Vonwyl, extends an initial 2-year phase (SNF grant number 200021-119906).  After a thorough and comprehensive state-of-the art of adaptive navigation systems and related issues, we have already identified and implemented strategies for item representations and the creation and exploration of an initial interlinking network. In parallel, we have looked at the issue of semantic propagation between digital items over such a network.

We now propose to continue with defining short- and long-term adaptation strategies of the item network in place.  First, in an online interactive process, based on estimates of the user mental state, we wish to augment the user's browsing efficiency and increase her/his satisfaction. We propose to look at adaptive constrained techniques that will allow for structuring and summarizing the collection of items based on constraints implicitly or explicitly set by the user during previous navigation actions. We will also investigate in the direction of the newly developed techniques around transductive learning where only part of the data is labeled and the rest is unlabeled but known.
This forms an original line of research in the field, offering new challenges such as the design of interactive adaptation techniques using this learning framework.
Then, from a long-term (offline) perspective, collaborative user interaction is collected and used as an extra source of semantic information to perform lasting adaptation and incrementally enhance the initial bootstrapping content-based navigation system.

Large-scale issues related to the handling of the item collection at a global scale will be taken into account, in close relationship with our current efforts for the development of a distributed multimedia indexing and retrieval engine.

The evaluation of the proposed methods and systems will be done both from a technical machine learning and data mining perspective and also from a user-centric perspective, assessing the utility and usability of the proposed systems. The project will inherit from several achievements of the \viper\ group in the domain of multimedia representation, multimodal fusion, interactive learning, information propagation and collection navigation. There is also a strong potential for collaboration  and a clear link with the current research made in several projects where the group is active.
Keywords: Multimedia information management, adaptive hypermedia system, and retrieval, information browsing and navigation, information management, information retrieval

Title: Innate Immunology in Kidney Transplantation: Elucidating Natural Killer Cell-Driven Alloreactivity in the Context of Rejection Pathophysiology and Treatment
Abstract:
Background 
Chronic kidney disease is a significant global health issue, for which allograft transplantation is the best treatment. Despite medical advancements, 20-30% of patients lose their transplants within a decade due to rejection. Traditionally, rejection was categorized as T cell- or antibody-mediated, but recent research has challenged this dichotomized view and the role of the innate immune system, particularly natural killer (NK) cells. Studies indicate NK cells might contribute to rejection, triggered by various factors including distinct gene polymorphisms. Nevertheless, treatment remains challenging, but a novel CD38 antibody (felzartamab) shows promise and is currently being tested in kidney transplant recipients with antibody-mediated rejection (ABMR). This project aims to understand the complexities of rejection, exploring genetic factors and potential therapies with a special focus on NK cells.
Aims
The project builds upon a previous postdoc.mobility project (P500PM_214237) and comprises two aims:
1.Pathophysiology: Investigating the importance of NK cell genetics in unselected transplant cohorts, focusing on the activating NK cell receptor NKG2C. 
2.Therapy: Investigating the impact of felzartamab versus placebo in patients with ABMR, with a specific focus on NK cells, utilizing the Molecular Microscope Diagnostic System (MMDx).
Methods 
For the first aim we will establish a cohort of 3000 consecutive kidney transplant recipients from Basel, Vienna and Prague. In this population we investigate the potential of a deletion in the KLRC2 gene encoding for the NKG2C receptor to develop microvascular inflammation and clarify whether other potential triggers of NK cells, such as delayed graft function, have an impact on the behaviour of NK cells. 
For the second aim we will use the data from a phase II randomized, controlled, double-blind phase 2 pilot trial to investigate the CD38 antibody felzartamab in late ABMR (NCT05021484). The objective of this analysis is to use the MMDx project to investigate the treatment effect of felzartamab on ABMR with special focus on NK cells. Applying machine learning algorithms, we will analyse the change of gene expression analysis and pathogenesis-based transcripts under the treatment with felzartamab or placebo and its relation with NK cell burden. 
Results 
This project aims to reexamine the role of the NK cells system in kidney transplant rejection. Divided into two aims, this project involves a meticulous and precise examination of NK cells in kidney transplantation. 
Impact 
The results of these investigations will aid in enhancing our fundamental understanding of the complex immunological processes during transplant rejection and improve the risk stratification before kidney transplantation.
Keywords: Kidney Transplantation, MVI, Natural killer cells

Title: PHASER-QUAD: Parsimonious Hierarchical Automatic Speech Recognition and Query Detection
Abstract:
This project proposal is intended to merge and extend the support for two ongoing and strongly complementary projects on “Parsimonious Hierarchical Automatic Speech Recognition” (PHASER, 200021-153507) and “Adaptive Multilingual Speech Processing” (A-MUSE, 200020-144281), to cover the last two years of the respectively funded PhD students Pranay Dighe (PHASER) and Dhananjay Ram (A-MUSE), in addition to Dr. Afsaneh Asaei (PHASER) as one of the leading postdocs in the field to assist PhD students supervision.
After a brief overview of the last 2 years of achievements in the two projects, we describe in details the
research activities foreseen to further anchor the novel parsimonious and hierarchical paradigm for the
closely related tasks of speech recognition and query detection (hence the project acronym PHASERQUAD). The goal of this project is to exploit and integrate in a principled way recent developments in posterior-based Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Query-by-Example Spoken Term Detection (QbE-STD) systems, hybrid HMM/ANN systems, exploiting Hidden Markov Model (HMM) and Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), Deep Neural Networks (a particular form of ANN with deep/hierarchical and nonlinear architecture), compressive sensing, subspace modeling and hierarchical sparse coding for ASR and QbE-STD.
The resulting framework that we have been building upon quite successfully relies on strong relationships between standard HMM techniques (with HMM states as latent variables) and standard compressive sensing formalism, where the atoms of the compressive dictionary are directly related to posterior distributions of HMM-states. The proposed research thus takes a new perspective to speech acoustic modeling as a sparse recovery problem which takes low-dimensional observations (at the rate of acoustic features) and provide a high-dimensional sparse inference (at the rate of words) while preserving the linguistic information, preserving temporal and lexical constraints.
To that end, we have proposed novel paradigm for speech recognition and spoken query detection based on sparse subspace modeling of posterior exemplars. To further develop the hierarchical, sparse-based, ASR and QbE-STD systems, and demonstrate their potential on the hardest benchmark tasks, several challenging problems will be addressed over the next two years (resulting in two distinct high-quality PhDs): (1) sparse posterior modeling tailored for speech recognition and detection objectives, (2) exploiting the low-dimensional structure of posterior space for unsupervised adaptation in unseen acoustic condition, and (3) hierarchical structured architectures that can go beyond the topological constraints of HMM for high level linguistic inference.
Exploiting and further developing our various, state-of-the-art, speech processing tools (often available as Idiap open source1 or integrated in other systems like Kaldi2), the resulting systems will be evaluated on the three different, very challenging, databases: GlobalPhone (multilingual), AMI (noisy and conversational accented speech), and MediaEval for QbE-STD.
Keywords: Automatic Speech Recognition, Deep architectures, Hierarchical posterior-based acoustic modeling, Hierarchical sparse coding, Parsimonious structures; Multilingual, Query-by-Example Spoken Term Detection, Searching large multilingual audio archives

Title: A physically-constrained downscaling approach based on dynamical downscaling and machine learning
Abstract:
Climate change has significant impacts on our planet and human societies. Global climate models (GCMs) provide valuable insights into large-scale atmospheric circulation but are limited by their coarse spatial resolutions, making it challenging to accurately simulate small-scale features and dynamics. Regional climate models (RCMs) offer an opportunity to enhance our understanding of local and regional climate dynamics by downscaling GCM results with higher resolution and better representation of physical processes. They can reduce biases and assess uncertainties associated with GCM projections at the local level, potentially constraining climate sensitivity. However, RCMs require significant computational resources and long run time. An alternative, statistical downscaling, which uses empirical connections between large-scale and local-scale climate to obtain regional projection, is cheaper and faster but struggles with representing spatial variability and may not perform well for future climate due to its reliance on historical observation data. Machine learning (ML) techniques show promise in the field of statistical downscaling as they are good at regression tasks. However, most of the existing models use surface data or summed quantities of a single column as predictors. Developing a ML statistical downscaling model by using all vertical levels up to tropopause as inputs, which will allow the ML to exploit all relevant physical information and train it with both the historical and future data from the dynamical downscaling results by RCMs, is therefore promising.

The main objective of this work is to develop a physically-constrained ML downscaling approach for precipitation to address its regional uncertainty in a changing climate. The specific tasks include constructing a ML framework that is physically constrained through incorporating the full vertical structure of the atmosphere as predictors and includes local and non-local information to improve spatial variability following Prof. O'Gorman's previous works on parameterization using ML. The framework will be made physically explainable through layer-wise relevance propagation. The ML model will be trained using  the bias-corrected dynamical downscaling data in both current and warm climates (results from the applicant's PhD project). Additionally, more dynamically downscaled datasets based on convection-permitting model simulations in Europe and North America will be used to investigate the model's spatial and temporal portability. The developed downscaling approach will be applied to specific regions to explore its potential in constraining regional precipitation uncertainty under climate change and provide valuable information for impact studies and policymaking concerning climate change adaptation.
Keywords: dynamical downscaling, machine learning, regional climate projection, statistical downscaling

Title: Generative Graph Models at Scale: Discrete Diffusion, Transferability and Requirements
Abstract: Generative models are becoming the mainstream nowadays in numerous domains where artificial intelligence is deployed. Yet, generative models have not yet developed much for graph data, while such representation are quite pervasive in various domains of science, like chemistry or biology, and in countless applications of societal importance, such as mobility or social networks. The purpose of this project is exactly to bridge this gap, and develop generative and informed graph models at scale. That is, generative graph models capable of generating graphs with a large number of nodes, which may further feature properties that are proper to specific applications. Scalability is a challenge of generative graph models that sets the problem apart from other generative problems. This is true for three reasons: (i) Graphs are discrete entities and generating discrete entities in large dimensional spaces is often intractable; (ii) Generating a graph requires selecting some connections among a quadratic number of choices - this is more difficult than generating elements of a sequence as is the case of language models or collections of spatial values as is the case of image generative models; and (iii) Data for training graphs is more scarce - this makes the use of large models difficult. These three challenges motivate our three proposed research thrusts. In Thrust I we will build scalable models based on improved discrete diffusion processes that progressively add or remove edges. This reduces the combinatorial complexity of exhaustively exploring the graph space. In Thrust II we will learn by transference. The idea here is to train generative models for small graphs that we later transfer to larger graphs. This reduces the computational complexity of training diffusion models in large graphs. In Thrust III we incorporate requirements in generative models. This reduces the sample complexity of the search space. Within these three thrusts we will utilize molecular graph generation as a case study, in which we leverage our techniques to solve problems of interest in molecular discovery and protein design. The project will develop new theory and methods that will provide important foundations for the development of graph generative models, which could eventually be deployed to enable new scientific discoveries in chemistry or biology, or new applications of high societal impact in health or mobility.
Keywords: Generative models, Graph representation, Machine learning, diffusion models, generative models, graph generation, molecule generation

Title: Feedback control of camera networks for tracking and surveillance
Abstract:
The proposed project aims to develop control algorithms
to enable the automation of surveillance tasks for networks 
of cameras. The control problems of interest in this context
involve both continuous decision making (selecting the 
pan-tilt-zoom inputs for the cameras) and discrete decision 
making (e.g. the combinatorial allocation of tasks to cameras).
Moreover, they also involve substantial stochastic uncertainty
(regarding the movement of the targets, measurement noise and
errors, etc). The problems of interest can therefore
be formulated in the framework of stochastic hybrid systems. 
Building on the proposing team's earlier experience with stochastic
hybrid systems, research is proposed here along three themes: 
Methodological development, computational development for 
on-line implementation, and experimental validation. 

In terms of methodology, we propose to develop a two tier 
control architecture. At the lower level, controllers to optimise 
the execution of individual tasks by individual cameras will be 
developed, based on the theory of stochastic reachability
and dynamic programming. The higher level will involve a 
supervisory controller allocating tasks to different cameras. 
The design here will be based on probabilistic temporal logic 
and the decisions will make use of the solution of the lower 
level problems (loosely speaking, the probability of successful 
execution of individual tasks).

In terms of computational methods, we propose to exploit the
surveillance problem structure to develop fast approximations 
to the solution of the lower level dynamic programs as well
as state estimation algorithms necessary to implement the
resulting controllers based on the camera data. The computational
methods will in turn be used to experimentally validate our 
methods on a test-bed available to the proposing team. The 
test-bed comprises two surveillance pan-tilt-zoom cameras,
several robots serving as targets, and the necessary hardware
and software to support the operation of these.

We stress that the proposed work is complementary rather than
competitive to computer vision, artificial intelligence, and
image processing approaches to surveillance problems. Here we 
concentrate on the purely control theoretic problem of moving 
the cameras in an optimal way to maximise the probability of 
accomplishing given objectives. Our methods assume that image 
processing algorithms are already available to extract the 
position of targets from the images collected by the cameras; 
indeed such algorithms are available for the test-bed on which 
our methods will be validated. On the other hand our methods 
provide a foundation on which more advanced computer vision 
methodologies (e.g. to extract contextual information and 
construct high level objectives) can be based.
Keywords: Automatic Control, Networked control systems, Pan-tilt-zoom cameras, Surveillance

Title: Automated Detection of Archaeological Sites in the Andes (ADArcheoSA)
Abstract:
Altos de Arica refers to the highlands of the Andean transect of 18S, between the coast of Arica and the altiplano of Parinacota, laying at 3000 - 6000 m asl. It identifies a highland region of the Atacama Desert bordering Peru and Bolivia, now incorporated into Chilean territory. Since prehispanic times, this arid transect has been characterized by strong socioeconomic and cultural interactions of distinct ecological zones, especially because of the complementarity of their resources and economic potentials. Colonial archives describe the region as a multiethnic space, with complex settlement systems generally located on high points. The territory is known for its well-preserved remains of large stone architectural complexes dating back to the Inca period, used by rural village communities through times as small farms (estancias) with large housing complexes, corrals and terraces. These settlements were mainly associated with pastoral and agricultural activities. 
Although the archaeological sites show relatively good preservation status due to the arid climate, the scientific research mainly remains locally confined as a consequence of the geopolitical fragmentation. In particular, due to the difficult terrains, traditional archaeological surveys and post-processing work are labor-intensive and extensive surveys are rather an exception. Moreover, with the rapid economic growth leading the urban development, mining, and industrial agriculture to expand into previously unexploited high lands, the Andean archaeological and cultural heritage is further threatened.
ADArchaeoSA aims at providing a powerful mechanism to speed up and automate the archaeological site detection process and to produce a more complete archaeological map of Altos de Arica. To this end, the research will combine multi-temporal and multi-sensorial satellite imagery with the most cutting-edge Machine Learning techniques. It will develop a groundbreaking quantitative approach to extract information (object of interest) from a series of selected satellite images over extensive areas not yet surveyed and reveal still unknown archaeological sites. The results of this innovative approach will be embedded into wider discourses on landscape change, resilience and dynamics, creating an opportunity for the development of an anthropological critical perspective about the complex current policies of heritagization, multiculturalism, and environment in a pluri-national frontier zone.
Keywords: Andes, Cultural Heritage, Landscape Archaeology, Machine Learning, Remote Sensing

Title: Supercool: Design methods and tools for superconducting electronics
Abstract: The growing interest in superconducting electronics (SCE) is related to the search for a scalable computing technology that can match and extend the current performances of CMOS at lower energy cost. The SCE technology will be very relevant to the design of fast computing systems in the twenties, to address challenging complex computational problems as, for example, related to artificial intelligence, security, weather prediction and environmental modeling as well as bio-med-discovery and drug design. Whereas prototype circuits of medium scale have been successfully designed and tested, the realization of complex and powerful computing systems is hindered by the lack of design tools. Indeed, the features of various incarnations of SCE, such as rapid single flux quantum (RSFQ) and adiabatic quantum flux parametron (AQFP) circuits - that support deeply pipelined and/or wave pipelined circuits - render design more complex. There are no commercial design tools for logic and physical design of SCE and research tools can cope only with limited-scale design. It is the purpose of this research to provide a framework for the logic design of SCE circuits with various technological flavors. Thus this research proposal addresses: i) logic models that capture common features as well as competitive advantages of different SCE realizations; ii) algorithms that manipulate models in the search for optimal implementation in terms of performance (i.e., latency) and area; iii) synthesis and optimization software tools that enable designers to map functional specifications of SCE systems in register-transfer languages (RTL) to optimized netlists of logic gates; iv) algorithms and tools for verifying implementation correctness. In particular, this research will exploit the essential features of SCE circuits expressed as majority functions, as well as a related Boolean algebra and its extension to synchronous circuits. Research will address both theory and practice, and will produce both methods with verifiable properties and open-source design tools. Extensive experimentation and exchanges with an industrial partner will provide us with a means for achieving impactful research results.

Title: Machine Learned State-to-State Reaction Networks
Abstract:
The broader goal of this project is to develop, implement and apply
computational strategies to quantitatively characterize the evolution
of chemical reaction networks and to interpret them at a molecular
level. Such reaction networks play important roles in processes
ranging from combustion to the genesis of molecules under interstellar
conditions and arise in atmospheric chemistry and rarefied
gases. Depending on the application, the relevant state space for the
internal rovibrational states of reactants and products can differ
considerably but invariably affects reaction outcomes. In high-energy
processes (combustion, atmospheric entry), all internal states can be
populated due to the high energies available whereas for reactions on
cold grains, as in interstellar chemistry, primarily translational and
low rotational degrees of freedom are expected to be active but the
time scale for molecules to collide are long.

This research project develops a machine-learning-based, generic,
state-resolved, and generalizable approach for small-molecule reaction
networks in the gas phase and on surfaces. It is based on
machine-learned models that relate state-resolved initial states
(collisional energy and ro-vibrational states) with final state
distributions of the products. These models are trained on a
comparatively small number of explicit quasi-classical trajectory
(QCT) simulations using high-level machine-learned interaction
potentials. The state space of an atom+diatom reaction contains ~10^8 state-to-state cross sections which would require ~10^{13}
QCT simulations for converged results for one collision
energy. Machine-learned models have been shown to be efficient and
useful for such tasks and will be employed in the present project
together with Monte Carlo sampling of several small-molecule reaction
networks for [N,O]-containing species. The work will provide
molecularly resolved information about the chemical evolution of a
collection of species and their distributions. Furthermore, the
trained models can be used in more coarse-grained simulations, such as
direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC). In a second subproject the
diffusion and reaction of small molecules on amorphous solid water is
characterized from QCT simulations and from solving the Smoluchowski
equation. Such an approach paves the way for a state-resolved
understanding of reactivity at low temperatures. Both methods
developed in the present work are generic and it is anticipated that
they can be generalized to atmospheric reaction network models and
combustion. Importantly, the approaches account for thermal
nonequilibrium which is prevalent for processes on surfaces and
grains, and for rarefied gas flow.
Keywords: Chemical Reactions, Diffusion, Machine Learning, Molecular Dynamics

Title: A Machine Learning-Based Approach to Predict Post-Treatment Drinking Behavior in Patients with Alcohol Use Disorder
Abstract: Efficient clinical practice requires tools that can accurately predict post-treatment symptom trajectories, thereby helping patients and clinicians make informed decisions regarding the type, intensity, and treatment duration. Despite a large body of research (Adamson et al., 2009) on associations between specific predictors and post-treatment outcomes in alcohol use disorder (AUD), these inference statistic-based models lack the ability to provide adequate predictions for individual patients. The recent integration of machine learning (ML) algorithms in the clinical research domain has demonstrated the efficiency and reliability of ML-based models for various applications, such as research in AUD populations (Mak et al., 2019). However, it remains to be investigated how ML algorithms can be used to improve individual, post-treatment outcome prediction for patients with AUD. The proposed project aims to address this clinically relevant gap through two phases: (i) Develop and train ML algorithms to generate valid and reliable post-treatment outcome prediction models for AUD patients’ drinking behavior. Secondary analysis of longitudinal data from 745 patients with AUD will be used to develop these computational models. Title: Fair AI in Heterogeneous Societies
Abstract:
Important decisions affecting people's lives are increasingly made by
artificially intelligent (AI) systems. Examples are judicial
decisions, allocation of students to universities, charging stations
to electric vehicles, and workers to different tasks. Currently, these
systems follow fixed decision algorithms. We would like to improve
them to learn to adapt their decision policies to the motivations,
behaviour and knowledge of people. When such an AI is used at scale,
it must also take into account broader societal considerations, such
as fairness and privacy.

I will develop and evaluate for automatically aligning AI behaviour
with societal values. I will move away from existing work in fairness
in machine learning (focusing on meritocracy and group fairness) and
closer to concepts in social choice theory. The central novelty is
explicitly handling population heterogeneity, and extending fairness
notions from decisions about individuals to heterogeneous groups.
Another novel aspect of FAIHS is that inference will be done
indirectly, rather than via surveys, as traditionally done in
behavioural analysis. A final groundbreaking aspect is that the AI
will be interacting with a segment of society, instead of being a
passive observer. This requires inferring human preferences and
behaviour, and taking them into account when acting.

One is matching problems: assigning students to universities, teams to
jobs, or doctors to hospitals.  In job matching, workers repeatedly
interact with an AI that assigns groups of individuals to jobs. After
a job is completed, the AI obtains feedback which it can use to
improve future matches. Feedback can be explicit: ratings given
separately by each worker and employer, or indirect: by measuring the
overall quality of the job after it is completed. While FAIHS will
not only consider matching problems, they are emblematic of the issues
involved when an AI interacts with a population, and will be used as
an example throughout this proposal.

The will be grounded on reinforcement learning (RL), social choice
(SC) theory, Bayesian inference (BI), mechanism design (MD),
differential privacy (DP) and algorithmic fairness (AF). All of these
areas have strong links with decision theory. RL in particular deals
with the problem of single agents learning how to act in an unknown
world through interaction and reinforcement. SC focuses on the problem
of how to act, given heterogeneous (but known) preferences of multiple
agents. At its core, this project will generalise the RL problem to a
SC setting, adapting appropriate fairness concepts from there. We will
also consider a more general concept of heterogeneity, where
individuals vary in characteristics, information and preferences.

The is to balance the needs of heterogeneous institutional decision
makers (DMs), individuals and society at large, under
uncertainty. FAIHS will develop AI policies that adapt to the unknown
preferences of the individuals through interaction.  It will develop
appropriate fairness concepts that take into account both uncertainty
and population heterogeneity. It will develop inference methods for
estimating preferences, as well as algorithms for optimising policies
given utility and fairness constraints under uncertainty.


My plan is to develop, analyse, implement and test algorithms for
inferring intentions and social preferences, adapting to human
behaviour, and achieving fair outcomes under uncertainty. While this
may not be trivial, my work on fairness, egalitarian games and
multi-view and human-AI collaboration renders me well-equipped to meet
these challenges. We will deal with fairness notions for decisions
over populations by defining appropriate notions of expected
contributions of individuals and use them to derive fair algorithms.

The theoretical model and algorithm development will be
complemented by extensive experiments. These include case
studies of university admissions, job matching, as well as more
abstract collaborative tasks, designed to test the quality of our
methodologies. These will be done through interactive
simulations, due to the nature of the problems considered. In
the later part of the project, we will conduct online experiments with
humans and an interactive AI system, in order to both infer
human preferences and the effects of the AI on their behaviour.  These
will focus on job matching, where humans are assigned to various jobs
by the AI, as well as collaborative tasks, where humans and the AI
must work together towards a goal. These will enable us to indirectly
measure fairness ideals in human behaviour.

The project will be organised in two axes. The first is
problem structure: First, decisions affecting each individual
independently (e.g. hiring specific applicants) and later, decisions
affecting everybody (e.g. setting a hiring requirement). This includes
settings with multiple stakeholders, whose interaction with the
population the AI mediates. The second axis is the amount of
information known about utilities, knowledge and behavioural types of
individuals.  Both axes require developing fairness ideals, models
and algorithms for inferring and aligning the preferences of
individuals and DMs. We expect that our research will bring closer
together the fields of social choice and fair machine learning,
through novel problem settings, new algorithms and the publication of
theoretical and experimental results.
Keywords: Bayesian inference, algorithmic fairness, differential privacy, mechanism design, reinforcement learning, social choice theory

Title: Improving the variational density functional theory for excited electronic states with machine learning
Abstract: Photochemical processes can be spatially and temporally controlled, a highly desirable feature for modern technology, especially nanotechnology. Given the complexity of their nonadiabatic evolution following photoexcitation, simulations offer the most effective way to model and predict photochemical reactions. While sufficiently good methods exist for propagating nuclear populations among multiple electronic states and simulating the photochemical mechanisms, obtaining accurate excited electronic states efficiently remains the main bottleneck. Because accurate wave function (WF) methods become impractical for computing excited electronic states of realistic systems due to their poor scaling with system size, approximated methods such as the variational density functional theory (DFT) are employed instead. While the latter method can easily simulate a photochemical mechanism in large and condensed phase systems, its accuracy is still not as reliable as the WF methods. That is because the current variational DFT methods only utilize exchange-correlation functionals (XCFs) originally developed and optimized for ground electronic states. Furthermore, the total electron density is not complete information required to describe an excited electronic state. Thus, this project aims to apply recent developments in constructing XCFs with machine learning (ML) techniques for the design of XCFs specifically tailored to describing the excited electronic state in variational DFT. In a stepwise approach, an excited state XCF that connects the electronic density with the energy of the excited electronic state will be constructed by ML. Firstly, on a single system and for each excited electronic state separately. Then the XCF will be trained to describe multiple excited electronic states over a wider range of conformational space, including the regions of conical intersections between different electronic states. The ML-XCF will be expanded to simultaneously include the diagonal and off-diagonal electronic densities necessary for a more accurate description of the multi-configurational character of excited electronic states into the variational DFT method. Finally, the ML-XCF will be trained on a larger set of different molecular systems to make the ML-XCF transferable to systems beyond the training set. In all cases, WF results will be used as reference data for ML. This project will establish an ML framework for designing XCFs specifically tailored to constructing excited electronic states with WF-based method accuracy by the variational DFT method. In the quest for advancing simulations of photochemical reactions, variational DFT with such XCFs becomes a reliable method for computing excited electronic states.
Keywords: Density functional theory, Electronic structure, Exchange-correlation functional, Excited electronic states, Machine learning

Title: The multilingual voice of Swiss federal institutions: Bringing translators’ profiles and needs to the fore
Abstract:
Institutional multilingualism is vital to the functioning of the Swiss Confederation. Translators are essential to ensure that federal institutions can work and communicate with citizens in all the national languages of Switzerland. As of now, we know little about the translators who carry out this important and socially relevant work. Moreover, with new developments in technology and artificial intelligence being reported almost daily, we know little about how these translators perceive and manage a fast-changing technological and informational landscape and whether their technological needs are being met. This project intends to fill this gap through a survey and interviews of federal translators and key stakeholders, combined with a content analysis of a sample of past and present vacancy notices. Applying these robust social science methods, it aims to uncover the multilingual voice of Swiss federal institutions.
As far as other institutional contexts are concerned, most notably the Directorate-General for Translation (DGT) of the European Commission, more literature is available on the translators’ profiles, the competences requested by the market and the new challenges the sector is facing. Also, previous studies have started to shed light on human factors involved in translation technology. The scarce consideration of Switzerland may depend on the fact that the technological development of the linguistic services of the Swiss Confederation lags behind compared to other institutional settings, such as the EU. To the best of my knowledge, profiles and needs of federal translators have not been investigated yet. It is particularly important to fill this gap, since Switzerland has been held up for a long time as an exemplar of institutional multilingualism and knowing more on the actors involved can open up fruitful discussions and exchanges with other institutional settings.
Against this background, the overall objective of this project is to broaden our knowledge of the production of multilingual texts within the language services of the Swiss Confederation, focusing on the actors involved. The specific aims are to paint a comprehensive picture of federal translators’ profiles and needs and to work out potential solutions to existing pain points. Several stakeholders can benefit from this project. Participants themselves, i.e. the language services of the Swiss Confederation, will have the opportunity to improve on current practices and organisational structures. Also, this study will provide the research community with empirical data on an institutional context that has been scarcely investigated until now, thus adding a new term of comparison for further studies in the field of sociology of (institutional) translation. Finally, the findings can be used in the field of academic training to check the adequacy of current curricula.
Keywords: Institutional multilingualism, Swiss Confederation, machine translation, sociology of translation, translator's competences, translator's needs

Title: AIgoritmic Assistance in Market Design
Abstract:
The field of market design has seen notable advancements in both academic and practical domains. Current empirical research in this area extends beyond merely testing matching mechanisms and delves into the broader decision-making environment participants face; this project aligns with that trajectory. Positioned at the intersection of expansive AI literature and market design, this project considers various applications of market design and empirically tests whether the use of AI can improve outcomes. 

In this project, AI is applied to market design problems in three distinct ways. First, AI can provide personalized advice through predictions derived from observables, simplifying behavior in complex environments (two subprojects). Second, AI enables designers to uncover previously inaccessible information using machine learning techniques and share it with participants (one subproject). Third, AI can be employed to improve efficiency by overcoming behavioral mistakes (two subprojects). Outlined below are four subprojects exploring these ideas.

Subproject 1: Experimental Test of Online Dispute Resolution Systems (ODR)
ODR systems, employed by giants like eBay and Amazon, address customer disputes and aim to establish a settlement before escalation to court. This project experimentally assesses ODR's performance against unstructured free-form bargaining in one-dimensional and multi-dimensional disputes. The research will explore three main ODR mechanisms: direct one-shot, sequential with bid revisions, and ODR with AI-assisted recommendations.

Subproject 2: Reporting Preferences in Multi-attribute Assignments
The matching process often requires participants to express preferences over various attributes, which can be complex. This research aims to design and assess different methods for preference reporting while keeping the matching mechanism fixed. Six preference reporting methods, ranging from the most complex like ranking all alternatives to more streamlined approaches including ones with algorithmic assistance. 

Subproject 3: Causal Effect of Transparency in College Selection Criteria on Social Gap in University Applications
The social gap in academic aspirations is well-documented. We hypothesize that opaque college admission criteria may deter low SES students due to anticipated discrimination and self-stigmatization fears. First, using machine learning on data from previous years we identify the most meritocratic programs among the prestigious ones. Next, we test whether highlighting these programs boost applications from low-SES students.

Subproject 4: Design of Rating Systems Robust to Heterogeneous Tastes
This project tests the effectiveness of online rating systems when product preferences differ significantly among users. The project first tests the efficiency of traditional rating designs. Alternative rating designs are then developed, including algorithm-based recommendations, to counteract potential efficiency losses stemming from diverse tastes.

Together, these studies assess how improved information design and algorithmic tools impact efficiency, fairness, and decision quality in complex economic settings.
Keywords: algorithms, experiments, market design, matching

Title: Orchestra in Class, a novel booster for executive functions and brain development in young primary school children
Abstract:
Rationale. How to optimally stimulate the developing brain is still unclear. Executive functions (EF) exhibited substantially stronger far transfer effects in children who learned to play a musical instrument than in children who acquired other arts. 
What is crucially lacking is a large-scale, long-term genuine randomized controlled trial (RCT) in cognitive neuroscience, comparing musical instrumental training (MIP) to another art form and a passive control group. The collected data will allow, using machine learning, to build a data-driven model of children's interconnected brain and EF development over the first 2 years of their academic curriculum (6-8 years), with and without musical or visual arts enrichment. 
Aims/objectives. Our study aims to show that Orchestra in Class (OC), compared to Visual Arts (VA) training, may benefit EF and their cerebral substrates in young children from public primary schools. If our hypotheses prove accurate, more widespread adoption of musical practice instruction would allow integrating (neuro)scientific findings into the public education system.
Background. Real-life interventions, like musical practice or dancing, may generate far transfer of learning and brain plasticity more easily than focused cognitive training because they are complex and variable. However, underlying brain and behavioral mechanisms and their relationships following long-term MIP in a group setting remain largely unknown. 
The effectiveness of active music making can be explained by 1) the direct involvement of core EF, particularly working memory (WM), 2) the fact that the auditory system processes input faster than any other sensory system, and 3) the rewarding nature of active music making, which may serve as a neurochemical scaffold for reinforced learning.
Methods. Through a genuine RCT, we will compare the impact on brain and behavior of 2 years of OC interventions versus VA (active control group) and standard education (passive control group, PCG). Both art interventions will take place twice a week for 45 minutes in school class size groups. The VA groups serve to control for the contextual influences of stimulating regular group interventions and homework, and the PCG for general child development and test-retest effects. We will recruit 132 6-7 years old children at local primary schools: 44 randomly assigned to the OC, 44 to the VA intervention, and 44 to the PCG. Recruiting in public primary schools promotes socioeconomic diversity. 
Data collection. Data collection will consist of yearly (baseline, after 1 year, after 2 years) 1) comprehensive EF psychometric testing, thus far transfer, and of near transfer (musicality, drawing), 2) academic achievements and 3) multimodal structural and functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging ((f)MRI), including fMRI with WM tasks in the auditory and visual domain.
Hypotheses/outcomes. We anticipate that learning to play a complex instrument in a group setting (OC) will provoke multiple far transfer effects to EF underpinned by brain plasticity. VA may induce some specific advantages in the visuospatial domain. But we expect the developmental driving force of OC to be superior because 1) music instrumental practice is more multisensory, 2) group music performance involves dynamic interactions, and 3) this “real-time” activity implies continuous WM updating. WM is a core component of EF and academic achievements. Associated functional and structural brain plasticity following OC may manifest in temporal, (medial & lateral), prefrontal and superior parietal areas, cerebellum, basal ganglia, and the corpus callosum. 
Scientific relevance. This project can potentially promote novel educational tools within the school curriculum, particularly OC, reinforcing brain development in core cognitive domains in the early stages of academic training. No systematic knowledge exists on the links between brain function and structure, EF outcomes, and academic progress in a 2-year RCT following 2 distinct art interventions in young children compared to a passive control group. We aim to compare OC, VA, and PCG to determine which neural substrates better predict WM, EF, and academic improvement.
Interdisciplinarity. The consortium comprises experts from human & social sciences, neuroscience, biomedical engineering, cognitive & developmental neuroscience, developmental psychology, educational sciences, and computer science. Experts in MIP and VA education will participate as scientific partners.

Title: ArchiMed: Mining medical archives and pathological collections in the digital age. Artificial intelligence at the frontiers of biology and the humanities
Abstract:
At the intersection of cultural and biological heritage, the project develops an interdisciplinary methodology to read and re-interpret two exceptional and massive collections of human biological materials and paper registries in Strasbourg and Geneva amassed over the 20th century. Our radical approach combines artificial intelligence (AI) for the analysis of paper technologies (autopsy and histopathological reports, patient files, expertise reports) with archeogenomic analysis of paraffin-embedded specimens. This double analytical strategy will be further affiliated with social histories of patients and diseases and literary studies of recordkeeping. This will lead to a proof of concept integrating the archeogenomic, histopathological and historical search for biomarkers in biological tissue collections.
This project confronts the difficulties of analysing voluminous medical collections. The Strasbourg pathological collection includes over 1.5 million specimens in paraffin blocks and even more histopathological slides; the Geneva neuro-pathological collection includes over 130,000 paraffin blocks, humid specimens and histopathological slides. Five teams (historical, literary, clinical, pathological, bioinformatics and archeogenomics) will co-develop a systematic AI model for data identification, extraction and transformation into a databank. Then three interpretative axes will focus on rare stages of syphilis, cancer and neurodegenerative diseases. This will involve the search for biomarkers, but will also comprise cross-disciplinary studies combining archeogenomic analyses with exposomic and humanities approaches (social history, nosographic construction, etc) with the goal of opening up and improving clinical diagnosis. Finally, an ethical and meta-level reflection will contextualise practices of collecting human remains for medical research from the late 19th century to the present.
Keywords: archeogenomics, artificial intelligence, biobanks, cultural heritage, cultural studies, digital humanities, digital pathology, histopathology, medical collections, retrospective exposomics, syphilis

Title: Machine Learning for Complex Discrete Probabilistic Models with Limited Data
Abstract:
Modeling discrete data is a core task in modern machine learning with applications ranging from sensor placement, experimental design, and recommender systems, to image analysis, and gene interaction discovery in cancer research. While past approaches have oftentimes been based on optimization techniques, there has been growing interest in harnessing the power of discrete probabilistic models, because they allow for more robust reasoning under uncertainty, and provide a principled way to learn from noisy data. On the negative side, both learning discrete probabilistic models from data, and performing inference in them, that is, computing various probabilistic quantities of interest, are known to be computationally hard problems in general. Therefore, there has been an ongoing research effort towards finding models and algorithms that render these problems feasible in practice.

In this research project, we want to focus on discrete probabilistic modeling and inference, while taking into account two important desiderata, both of which are crucial in many practical applications. First, we want to venture beyond classic pairwise models and consider more complex higher-order interactions that are often present in real-world systems. Second, we want to focus on the small data setting, which often arises in applications where data is naturally scarce or expensive to get hold of. The combination of these factors creates an intriguing tradeoff between the desire to consider richer model classes on one hand, and the need to impose structured prior assumptions for statistical and computational efficiency on the other.

In light of this tradeoff, we want to investigate both theoretical and algorithmic aspects thereof, while being informed by and evaluating our proposed methods on real-world applications. On the theoretical level, we plan to characterize relevant model classes, and create a framework for learning models that have guarantees with respect to inference efficiency. On the algorithmic level, we plan to leverage results from combinatorial optimization and continuous sampling to improve on existing discrete inference methods. Finally, on the application level, we plan to evaluate our methods on real-world domains, such as genomic analysis, material synthesis, and computer systems architecture. An important aspect of this project is that we plan to consider these three levels in tandem rather than individually.
Keywords: complex systems, discrete models, machine learning, probabilistic inference, sampling, submodularity

Title: Collective Movement and Decision Making in a Multi-level Society: A bird`s eye view of Wild Gelada Monkeys
Abstract:
A multi-level society offsets the costs and benefits of group-living by continually changing the group size and composition. The hierarchically nested social structure seen in the multi-level societies has evolved across animal taxa, including humans, who spent the longest time in the known history living in modular hunter-gatherer societies. Thus, a deeper understanding of the functional complexities of multi-level societies is necessary to get insights into origins, evolution, and future of human sociality. However, the fundamental questions regarding collective movement, consensus decision making and fission-fusion dynamics in multi-level societies remain unexplored. This gap in our knowledge is perhaps due to methodological limitations imposed by numerical, spatial and temporal extents of multi-level societies.

Nevertheless, the latest technologies like Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are enabling the tracking of large animal groups in a natural environment in a cost-effective way. In this study, we will investigate collective movement and decision-making in a multi-level society of wild Gelada monkeys (Theropithecus gelada) in Ethiopia. Combination of UAV based aerial imaging and state-of-the-art computer-vision algorithms will allow us to simultaneously collect high-resolution (30Hz) location data on multiple gelada individuals. This enormous amount of data will be used to infer movement patterns, leadership, and fission-fusion dynamics within and between different levels of social organisation in geladas.

The results of this study will provide fundamental insights into the functioning of a multi-level society of a non-human primate, which could help us to understand the evolutionary roots of collective behaviours in modern humans. Furthermore, this will be one of the few studies to empirically test conceptual and mathematical models of collective behaviours in complex biological systems in natural settings, while establishing the novel methods for future field-based studies. Finally, understanding the movement patterns of geladas will contribute to future conservation efforts of this endemic species, which is threatened by the imminent habitat loss.
Keywords: Collective Behaviour, Consensus Decision-making, Fission-fusion dynamics, Multi-level Society, Non-human primates, Theropithecus gelada

Title: 3D Capture of Free-form Specular Shapes using Mobile Devices
Abstract:
During the last decades, a substantial number of techniques have been developed in order to capture 3D models from a set of input images or videos [Debevec et al. 1996; Levoy et al. 2000; Pollefeys et al. 2004; Newcombe et al. 2011]. Among those, reconstructing three-dimensional models of cities has been of broad interest, either using street-view image data acquired by camera-mounted cars or internet photo-collections [Frueh and Zakhor 2004; Snavely et al. 2006; Pollefeys et al. 2008; Xiao et al. 2009; Nan et al. 2010]. While those techniques are evolving and improving very quickly as research in computer vision and graphics increases, they are often limited to non-reflective surfaces. In particular those techniques struggle with windows as these do not reflect sufficient laser-light back to the range sensor or due to their reflective nature violating the Lambertian assumption underlying most image-based techniques. Similarly, specular surfaces offer challenges to those techniques which will in the end reconstruct erroneous data when reflections occur. Due to the fact the appearance of such surfaces are due to distorted reflections of the world around, correspondences between different images are not linked to the surface points themselves, and hence are difficult to estimate. This makes conventional 3D reconstruction techniques very hard to handle in urban environments or industrial settings where many objects are reflective such as windows or cars among others.

In this project, we propose to tackle the challenging problem of reconstructing reflective surfaces using practical methods with the only use of a mobile device (a Smartphone, a Tablet or a hand-held video camera). We build upon our previous SNF project where we explore the geometry of reflective surfaces and proposed an approach for urban reconstruction of window surfaces using the reflection of lines in the scenery. Instead of using lines, we propose to use the reflection of a known reference object. This allows obtaining a dense correspondence mapping at each image which will be used to accurately reconstruct the specular surface. This reference object will be the screen of a mobile device or simply the natural environment previously captured with other methods. This will provide a practical approach to capture real-world free-form reflective surfaces with the only use of a mobile device. To achieve this goal we propose to estimate the geometric extrinsic calibration of all the elements of a smartphone or Tablet (such as the screen, the front and the rear cameras) by exploiting the fact that they are rigidly connected. Using a single planar mirror, it is possible to establish correspondences between each of the non-overlapping cameras and the screen of the device. The geometric calibration of a mobile device can be exploited in order to offer a simple approach to reconstructing specular surfaces from multiple views, by exploiting the fact that an image displayed on the screen can serve as a reference pattern for computing correspondences.

The overall goal of designing and implementing a reflective surface capturing system will be achieved by focusing on the following subgoals:
•The calibration of mobile devices, and in particular on how to estimate the relative poses of the cameras (front and rear cameras) of a smartphone with respect to its screen.
•The analysis and understanding of free-form reflective surfaces and how they can be re-constructed from the reflection of a known reference object (like a pattern on the screen). 
•The integration of multiple views on to improve the accuracy of the 3D reconstruction.

Practically, the developed methodology would allow to faithfully reconstruct reflective surfaces and objects for planning, visualization, and simulation, where nowadays models look artificial (e.g. houses with perfect mirrors as windows), require a huge amount of manual interaction (somebody adding the windows manually to the scan/model) or simply cannot be obtained in real-world situations. Second, the developed techniques have the potential for a much broader impact, e.g. they could enable automated quality control processes in manufacturing and civil engineering, to scan for defects or to detect stress or pressure visible through subtle deformations of the material's normals, and finally might even be deployed to autonomous cars or other robotic vehicles to be able to interact in or scan more complex environments. Third, the methodology developed for calibrating mobile devices will open doors to new possibilities in mobile vision applications with strong impact to end customers.
Keywords: 3D modeling, Camera Pose Estimation, Computer Vision, Shape from Reflection, Shape from Specularities, Structure-from-Motion

Title: Hippocampal circuits for the discrimination of social threat from social safety
Abstract:
The discrimination between previously encountered threat- and safety-associated conspecifics is critical for the ability of an animal to obtain access to resources while avoiding harm. Failure to achieve this discrimination can lead to the display of fear responses towards safe social stimuli, social avoidance and withdrawal, hallmark features of social anxiety disorder (SAD). SAD is the most common anxiety disorder with an estimated lifetime prevalence of around 5-12.1%. However, the neural mechanisms underlying SAD remain little known, preventing targeted therapeutic interventions. 

Since the influential studies of patient H.M. by Brenda Milner and colleagues, the importance of the hippocampus for social memory in humans, i.e. our ability to encode and recall past experiences with other people, is well-established. Social memory is thought to comprise social novelty recognition memory - distinguishing novel from familiar individuals - and social episodic memory - experience-dependent learning of social information, including conspecific identity and the valence (e.g., threat) associated with the social experience.
The Siegelbaum lab and others have shown in mice that the hippocampal CA2 region, a rather unexplored structure in the dorsal hippocampus, is required for social novelty recognition memory. In contrast, CA2 is not needed for contextual or spatial memory, commonly thought to depend on the hippocampus. In my SNSF postdoctoral studies in the Siegelbaum lab I significantly expanded on this finding by showing that the hippocampal CA2 region is also needed for social fear discrimination memory (SFDM) as one type of social episodic memory. By implementing a new variation of a social fear conditioning (SFC) paradigm, I found that silencing CA2 abolishes an animal’s preference for safety-associated conspecifics after SFC, leading to indiscriminate avoidance of both safety- and threat-associated individuals, reminiscent of phenotypes linked to SAD. I found that CA2 is in contrast not required for the discrimination of threat- from safety-associated objects ( Kassraian et al., 2024, Nature Neuroscience). 
This cements CA2's cardinal role for social behaviors, in line with the enriched presence of receptors for the ‘social’ neuropeptides arginine vasopressin 1b and oxytocin in CA2.  However, despite the critical importance of social behaviors for many species and their vulnerability to neuropsychiatric disease in humans, the broader hippocampal circuit mechanisms which support this function are not known.  In addition to receiving direct input from entorhinal cortex (EC), the main cortical input to hippocampus, CA2 receives input from the dentate gyrus (DG), through 1. disynaptic EC->DG->CA2 and 2. trisynaptic EC->DG->CA3->CA2 pathways. DG mature granule cells (mGCs) are critical for the dissociation of similar sensory cues and environments, a function called 'pattern separation'. Moreover, DG serves in mammals as one of only two sites of adult neurogenesis, and DG adult-born granule cells (abGCs) support pattern separation and mitigate stress susceptibility. This gives rise to my overarching hypothesis, supported by my strong preliminary data, that DG, as an important hippocampal input region to CA2, supports CA2's role for SFDM when social stimuli are 'similar' (same strain) but not when they are 'dissimilar' (different strain). I will test this hypothesis by pursuing the following three aims:

Aim 1: I will delineate the role of CA2 PNs, CA3 PNs and DG mGCs for SFDM with similar or dissimilar social stimuli with chemo- and optogenetic silencing methods during SFC encoding or recall. This approach will also allow me to test the hypothesis that the DG->CA2 and not the DG->CA3->CA2 circuit subserves SFDM for similar social stimuli. 

Aim 2: With multi-region in vivo one-photon calcium (Ca2+) imaging and through the use of Machine Learning decoders, I will test the hypothesis that both DG mGCs and CA2 PNs encode representations of social identity to support SFDM, but that an identity-independent representation of social valence is computed locally in CA2.  

Aim 3: I will test the hypothesis that DG abGCs contribute to SFDM of similar and highly similar social stimuli by chemogenetically manipulating abGC activity. Additionally, by combining Ca²? imaging from CA2 PNs with simultaneous silencing of mGCs or abGCs in independent cohorts, I will test my hypothesis that disrupting DG mGC or abGC activity impedes CA2's ability to form distinct social representations of similar social stimuli. 

Impact: Social memory is a cognitive ability underlying a broad range of social behaviors and often disrupted in neuropsychiatric disorders. Yet while the CA2 region is recognized as a key hippocampal hub for social memory, little is known about how broader hippocampal circuits support episodic social memory, such as social fear discrimination. This study will address this critical knowledge gap by dissecting the DG-CA2 circuit with an integrated behavioral, circuit-level and computational approach. Findings will significantly advance our understanding of how hippocampal circuits process social information and the specific roles of different regions therein. This will provide key insights into the neural basis of social behaviors and the role of the hippocampus therein in health and in disease. As social avoidance is a widely observed across a range of neuropsychiatric disorders such as social anxiety disorder, autism spectrum disorder and schizophrenia, understanding how hippocampal dysfunction contributes to a loss of social fear discrimination memory is of cross-diagnostic relevance.
Keywords: Hippocampus, Memory, Social behaviors, Social fear, Social memory, Systems Neuroscience

Title: Towards Burnout Risk Detection using Word Embeddings
Abstract: In Switzerland, more than one million people feel often stressed at their work place. The number of people feeling stressed has increased massively over the last ten years and is estimated to cost multiple billions of francs each year. Sometimes, this stress can lead to a burnout syndrome. Last year, the WHO has included burnout in the 11th Revision of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11) as a syndrome.Burnout identification is complex, because it overlaps with other syndromes. To identify burnout in clinical intervention, inventories are used. Inventories are psychological tests, where the person concerned fills out a questionnaire. The currently used metric, in both practice and most studies, measures burnout with self-test inventories, and is criticized in the literature. The state-of-the-art does not use free-text questions in the inventories or interviews, even though there have been promising approaches in the literature. One reason is the concern that evaluation of such free-text questions generates a large overhead. On the other side, it has been shown that inventories with scaling questions have major limitations such as users faking their results, extreme response bias, defensiveness and social desirability bias. Natural language processing provides new capabilities to reason about text contents in an automated way. This has already been proven for different psychological applications including implicit association tests and suicide risk assessment. In particular, language modeling by using so-called word embeddings has notably improved the efficiency of natural language processing tasks in the recent past.In this project we propose to investigate on a new approach of burnout detection based on open questions, analyzed using the power of traditional and contextualized word embeddings. The approach developed in this project will enable new methods to measure burnout, both in clinical intervention and in preventive measures.
Keywords: burnout detection, natural language processing, psychology, social computing, word embeddings

Title: Resolving molecular mechanisms underlying reduced fish cell population growth upon chemical exposure
Abstract:
Fish are a fascinating and tremendously important group of organisms. They populate a huge variety of habitats in different climate regions, from lakes and rivers, to the deep sea and reefs, to wetlands and bays, while providing manifold ecosystem services. At the same time, fish are sensitive to a variety of stressors, including chemical pollution. Many fish have the capacity to bioaccumulate chemicals, which in turn can impact fish health. It is for these reasons that fish play a key role in the environmental risk assessment of chemicals, with impact on survival and growth being measured in laboratory experiments as proxy for fish population health. Yet, such laboratory animal experiments are ethically problematic, very resource intensive in terms of man power, time, testing volumes, etc. and a significant bottleneck in chemical risk assessment, a fact that is increasingly recognized regulatory agencies world-wide.
  
It is in light of these matters, that we, together with other research groups, have developed strategies that inform about the chemical’s impact on fish survival, bioaccumulation and growth by a combination of fish cell-based and computational models. Because the fish cell-based models are, in fact, permanent fish cell lines, these strategies can significantly reduce, if not eliminate, the need for animal experimentation. A combination of conventional animal experiments, cell-based experiments and computational modelling has provided convincing evidence that a decrease in cell proliferation and/or increase in cell death is behind the retardation of growth seen after chemical exposure of fish: the number of cells, measured in vitro upon exposure to chemicals of varying structures for less than a week, leads to an excellent agreement with fish growth measured after month-long chemical exposure. At the same time, chemical exposure that does not lead to reduced growth in fish also does not cause a reduction in cell number in vitro. These results raise a very important overarching question: how can chemicals with very different structures and presumably different mechanisms of biological action lead to the same overall outcome - reduced cell population, ergo reduced fish growth? Being able to answer this question would mark an important milestone from a fundamental as well as an applied science point of view. It would, for the first time, allow delineating different paths of reduced fish cell population growth, hence furthering knowledge in fish physiology and toxicology. It would moreover facilitate the transition from in vivo to in vitro testing based on transparent chemical structure-biological mechanism relationships along with detailed knowledge on the breadth and limits of the applicability of the in vitro assay. 

Indeed, so far, the ecotoxicology community has not been able to provide a molecular, mechanistic answer to this question. With the research proposed here, we now wish to shed light on the molecular response networks activated inside the fish cells upon chemical exposure and leading to reduced cell population growth. We plan to achieve this using a systems toxicology approach, via a combination of cell-based chemical exposure experiments, cell-based morphological and functional profiling, genome-wide gene expression measurements, analysis via bioinformatics and network-based approaches and confirmation of the in vitro results in an in vivo system. Cell-based morphological and functional profiling will be performed via multiplexed fluorescent assays, thereby capturing the cellular phenotype, but also by measuring of the cellular composition and energy state. Together these measurements will form the cellular phenotypic profiles that will be used to differentiate between the effects of the different chemicals. Gene expression analysis will be based on high-throughput sequencing, i.e., RNAseq-based transcriptomics (yielding transcript abundance) and Riboseq-based translatomics (yielding translational efficiency, meaning the number (and position) of translating ribosomes on each transcript). The acquired functional profiling and omics datasets will be analysed using statistical, machine-learning and network-based methods to find transcriptional, translational and/or phenotypic biomarkers with predictive value for retardation of fish cell population growth. Finally, the identified biomarkers will be tested in vivo in zebrafish to confirm that the mechanisms behind reduced cell population growth in vitro are also act in live animals. 

The described systems biological approach will allow us to meet the following objectives: 
•To identify molecular pathways leading to reduced fish cell population growth upon exposure to different chemicals
•To identify at which level (transcriptional, translational, phenotype) these pathways converge to cause reduced fish cell population growth
•To establish whether the same molecular pathways are also active in growth retardation in living fish.
Keywords: Alternatives to animal tests, Cell population growth, Chemical risk assessment, Computational network analysis, Fish cell lines, Molecular mechanisms, Reduced fish growth, Translational responses

Title: Robust Causal Estimation from Complex Data
Abstract: Causal inference from real-world data is often hindered by selection bias, unmeasured confounding, heterogeneous data sources, and model misspecification. At the same time, the increasing availability of large and diverse datasets offers new opportunities to mitigate these challenges through data fusion—that is, the integration of information from multiple observational or experimental sources. This project develops a general framework for causal data fusion that accommodates heterogeneous populations, complex data structures, and both cross-sectional and longitudinal settings. We aim to establish nonparametric identification conditions, design doubly and multiply robust estimators that achieve semiparametric efficiency, and characterize the efficiency gains possible through the joint use of multiple datasets. Furthermore, when causal parameters are not identifiable from existing data, we propose algorithms for designing targeted experiments that enable identification and efficient estimation. Across these components, the project advances methodological foundations at the intersection of causal inference, semiparametric statistics, and modern machine learning, with applications in medicine, economics, public health, and the social sciences.
Keywords: Causal Inference, Complex Data, Data Fusion, Doubly Robust Estimators, Efficient Estimation, Semiparametric Statistics
