Title: Prediction with Big Data
Abstract:
Understanding financial asset returns lies at the core of empirical asset pricing. The bulk of the academic literature often exclusively focuses on a single predictor and a single asset. However, practical concerns are more sophisticated and challenging. First, given that hundreds of predictors have been discovered by the literature, researchers and practitioners become increasingly concerned about whether they can simultaneously benefit from all information available. Second, the comovement between returns across many assets such as stock and bonds undergoes a significant change over the last decades. Therefore it is also interesting to understand the economic origin of the covariation based on a large set of economic variables. In reality, these two issues are also concerns of asset managers who want to employ big-data techniques in asset allocation, and policy makers who want to design optimal fiscal and monetary policy based on rich economic data sources.
Understanding the covariation of risk premiums across assets from a big- data perspective has not been sufficiently explored. One important reason is that big-data techniques in finance are often not developed for multiple- response equations. This project fills this gap by employing the “spike-and-slab” (SAS) approach, which allows for such an extension in a Bayesian setup. Unlike other target-oriented big-data approaches, the SAS approach further allows for statistical inference and hypothesis testing. It does not require one to fix the model, but learns about the specification from all possible models. Thus, it minimizes model risks. It has been used in economics only recently and only for toy examples. This project attempts to establish the framework for predicting returns across assets and understand the linkage between their covariation and the macroeconomy.
Keywords: Bayesian statistical learning, Big data, Prediction

Title: Assessing the environmental context of past urbanization dynamics using sedimentary archives (CIVES)
Abstract:
Project CIVES: Exploring the environmental and ecological context of past urbanization dynamics using sedimentary archives 

Several modern European cities have Iron or Roman Age legacies and went through different cycles of economic and environmental changes, including crises and collapses related to societal reorganizations or environmental deterioration. However, only little is known about the environmental and ecological context of early urbanization dynamics in Europe. One of the reasons for this knowledge gap is that chronologically precise and temporally highly resolved palaeoecological time series from sediment archives are very rare or completely lacking in most areas of Europe, so that the comparison with the archaeological and historical evidence remains difficult. A main objective of the project CIVES is to close this gap for selected study areas in Switzerland, Italy and Greece. Specifically, the project will reconstruct the ecological and environmental context of early urbanization dynamics in Europe to better understand how the establishment, growth, stability and vulnerability of urban centers was related to land-use, environmental (e.g. climate) and/or ecological (e.g. biodiversity) factors. In addition, the project will assess the environmental and ecological consequences of early urbanization dynamics (e.g. forest disruption, pollution). 
The main objectives can be summarized as follows: 1) We will use temporally highly resolved and precise sedimentary time series as decadal-scale evidence of environmental, ecological and land use change during the past 3000 years, when towns and cities established in Europe. New multiproxy time series will be generated by investigating (annually laminated) lake sediments with physical (e.g. radiocarbon dating), geochemical (e.g. X-ray fluorescence), palynological and sedaDNA approaches. 2) We will compare palynological and sedaDNA samples from lake surface sediments with inventories of remote sensing and surveys. 3) We will establish transfer functions for down-core application to improve the inferential basis for land use and vegetation reconstructions, using statistical and machine learning approaches. Such inductive land-use transfer functions for palynology and sedaDNA are lacking today. Their implementation will allow a first comparison with established deductive models for quantitative palynological reconstructions. 4) We will compare our qualitative and quantitative reconstructions of land use and vegetation (including biodiversity) with independent palaeoclimatic time series to explore the long-term links between land use, vegetation and climate change. 5) Taking advantage of the outstanding chronological precision and temporal resolution, we will connect the reconstructed land use and environmental time-series with archaeological and historical evidence on town foundation, growth, crises and collapses to assess the potential ecological and environmental drivers and consequences of early urbanization processes. The comparison of the new palaeoecological evidence with the available palaeoclimatic and archaeological data will be based on the independent chronologies of the considered proxies and use numeric tools such as ordination techniques including external driving variables, cross-correlation analyses to explore leads and lags as well as generalized additive models (GAM) and change point analyses to investigate non-linear linkages 6) Finally, we will assess the relevance of the CIVES project outcomes for future urbanization dynamics under global change conditions. 

The project will provide new insights into the roles of environmental (e.g. climate, fire) and ecological factors (e.g. vegetation, biodiversity) for ancient European urbanization dynamics with an emphasis on past land use activities that connect the societal and natural systems. Furthermore, we expect advances in the understanding of past urbanization impacts on the environment and ecosystems.

Title: Deep Structured Representation Learning for Visual Recognition
Abstract:
Automatically recognizing and segmenting objects in images and videos is central to a wide variety of application domains, such as security and autonomous driving. Visual recognition has therefore been one of the fundamental goals of Computer Vision since its inception. In the past few years, with the increasing amount of images and videos available online, Deep Learning, and particularly Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), have delivered spectacular progress in this field. In contrast with earlier approaches that first extracted handcrafted features from the images and then trained a classifier on these features, CNNs learn the features and the classifier together.

However, while there has been great advances in terms of network architectures, classifier types and optimization strategies, the representations extracted by CNNs have remained largely unchanged. Each layer applies filters followed by a nonlinear transformation to the output of the previous one and, sometimes, a pooling operation. This is a much less diverse repertoire of image operations than those that were used previously, which include Bags of Visual Words and spatial pyramids, Region Covariance Descriptors, and, for image sets and videos, Subspace-based descriptors. In the past, all these structured representations have proven highly effective at modeling a wide variety of problems. Furthermore, as shown in recent work, the limited diversity of CNN operations makes them unsuitable for a range problems.

In other words, structured representations have essentially been discarded from current Deep Learning architectures, even though they have proven their worth in earlier approaches. The goal of this project is therefore to develop new deep architectures that leverage the representation power of structured descriptors within an end-to-end learning formalism. To this end, we will pursue the following research directions:

- Learning histogram-based representations. We will develop architectures that jointly learn a codebook and a representation of the input image such that the latter relates to the elements of the former. In particular, we will study the use of generative models to learn interpretable codebooks.

- Learning subspace-based representations. We will develop architectures that model image sets as linear subspaces, encoded via an orthonormal matrix computed from the global representations of the individual images. We will study different ways to extract these subspaces, as well as different layer types to transform a subspace into a different one or into a vector.

- Learning the structure of a network. A severe drawback of deep networks is that there is no principled way to automatically determine the best architecture for the problem at hand. Developing new layer types, as we propose, will only add to this problem. To overcome this, we will develop algorithms that learn the network structure, including the number and type of layers and the number of units per layer.

In an ongoing project, we have begun developing deep architectures that extract covariance-based representations. Here, we aim to expand this to other structured representations, which will require us to introduce entirely different architectures. The purpose of this proposal therefore is to continue and expand our previous research direction and encompass it in a single project on the more general topic of learning deep structured representations for visual recognition.

In short, our project will enrich the repertoire of representations that Deep Learning can exploit, while at the same time providing automated design tools to incorporate them into a working architecture. We are therefore confident that it will lead to significant advances in visual recognition and motivate other researchers, in this and other fields, to go beyond standard Deep Learning architectures.
Keywords: Computer vision, Convolutional neural networks, Deep learning, Structured image representations, Visual recognition

Title: Shifted snowmelt timing and recurrent summer drought in alpine grassland: deciphering the role of soil biota and symbiotic partners for the distinct plant species responses
Abstract:
Drought intensifies with climate warming. Drought affects all organisms (plants, soil microorganisms) as well as soil processes by inhibition the provision of substrates, blocking diffusion and transport for microbes. In alpine ecosystems, the long winter may partly release from summer drought provided a thick snowpack covers the ground.
We will here exploit an already established climate change experiment in an alpine grassland in the Swiss Alps to resolve fundamental questions on the effects of drought and the contribution of the long winter period. The experiment is unique, because it combines variable snowmelt timing (by snow manipulations) with summer drought (rain-out shelters for 5 and 10 weeks). Plant community responses aboveground seem to diverge from the belowground signals. We assume this is equally true for the rhizosphere, inhabited by a special microbiome and influencing the plants’ reactions and the nutrient relations closest to the roots. But roots are commonly colonized by symbiotic partners, arbuscular mycorrhiza (AM) and Dark Septate Endophytes (DSE), adding to the complexity of these interrelationships, but rarely accounted for.

In the previous experimental years, we observed a decrease in aboveground biomass under drought, but clearly with species-specific sensitivities, ranging from negative to positive response (for the dominant sedge species). The 5-wk drought led to a stimulation in root production and root production under 10-wk drought equaled that of the controls. Despite clearly higher root production, ecosystem respiration was strongly reduced, indicating a negative impact on soil microbes under drought. Overall, drought responses (above- and belowground biomass) showed no interaction with the snow manipulations, highlighting the asset of the fully factorial design. 

We aim at deciphering the role of soil microbes and fungal endophytes as they presumably mediate these distinct plant responses to drought. We will use DNA metagenomics for bacteria, archaea and fungi in the different soil compartments (rhizosphere vs. bulk) and will additionally focus on genes/enzymes of the nitrogen and carbon cycle. Collecting rhizosphere from fine roots of different plant species allows to assess the AM and DSE colonization in these roots. A similar machine learning approach (as already applied for the root scans) will be developed and will assist to quantify the fungal structures in the microscopic images at high throughput rates. 
Alpine soils beneath a thick winter snowpack are tightly “thermostated” at 0 °C. Soil processes are continuing and presumably levelling out drought effects during the growing season. We will expose static CO2 soda-lime samplers (to be constructed) and cation-anion resin membranes over winter to assess winter CO2 and nutrient fluxes and compare them to the fluxes during the summer. Soil samplers (for soil microbes) will be prepared in autumn, which will then be pulled through the snow pack without exposing the soil to freeze-thaw cycles. Because these winter methods are challenging, they will be tested in the single species (SPS) experiment with guaranteed access and residence in winter (Alpine Research Station Furka ALPFOR). Within this  SPS experiment, the most abundant plant species of the snow manipulations / drought experiment are available as monocultures, again exposed to summer drought (plus controls). Explaining co-variables (C, N, pH, microbial C / N in rhizosphere vs. bulk soil) as well as physiological plant responses (e.g., osmotic potential) will be included and associated with the analysis of the microbial life under drought and the enduring snowpack in winter.
The insights gained here will advance our understanding on the interrelationships at the interface between plant roots / symbiotic endophytes and the rhizospheric microbiome and help to elucidate the mechanisms of summer drought vs. winter processes in alpine grasslands. The project is planned for three years.

Title: The Exoclimes Simulation Platform: General Tools for Understanding Exoplanet Atmospheres
Abstract:
The discovery of planets outside of the Solar System, known as exoplanets, is one of the most dynamic and rapidly growing fields of astronomy and astrophysics.  Exoplanet science is inexorably becoming an interdisciplinary endeavour involving the generalisation of techniques from atmospheric science, planetary science, geology and geophysics, Bayesian statistics, machine learning, etc.  A central and emerging theme of exoplanet science is the characterisation of the atmospheres of exoplanets.  The detection of water in exoplanetary atmospheres using the Hubble Space Telescope is now routine.  From the ground, state-of-the-art spectrographs are measuring high-resolution spectra that enable the robust identification of atoms and molecules.  There is clear motivation to develop, in parallel, cutting-edge theoretical methods to simulate, interpret and understand the physics and chemistry of these exoplanetary atmospheres.

At the Center for Space and Habitability (CSH) within the University of Bern, I lead the Exoplanets & Exoclimes Group (EEG).  We are broadly interested in the theory, simulation and phenomenology (interpretation of data) of exoplanetary atmospheres.  Our key project is the Exoclimes Simulation Platform (ESP), which aims to provide the exoplanet community with a set of publicly available computer codes for simulating and interpreting exoplanetary atmospheres (www.github.com/exoclime).  Two grants from the Swiss National Science Foundation (SNF) were awarded in 2014 and 2016 for developing the ESP.  These grants have exclusively funded Ph.D students.  To date, the ESP offers a general circulation model (GCM; THOR), a radiative transfer solver (HELIOS), an opacity calculator (HELIOS-K), a chemical kinetics code (VULCAN), a chemical equilibrium solver (FastChem), a Mie scattering code (LX_MIE), a retrieval code (HELIOS-R2) and a machine-learning retrieval code (HELA)—written by both Ph.D students and postdocs.  With the core set of open-source codes now established, we enter the next phase of transitioning from technology development to cutting-edge applications and problem-solving.

In the current SNF proposal, we request for 10 Ph.D years to support 4 students.  Chloe Fisher will develop a novel method combining cross correlation analysis with supervised machine learning to interpret high-resolution, ground-based transmission spectra of exoplanets, thus completing the final year of her Ph.D.  A new Ph.D student will be hired to interpret spectra of brown dwarfs following a multi-pronged approach: using a state-of-the-art retrieval code to infer atmospheric properties, which will guide the construction of next-generation model grids using state-of-the-art radiative transfer and chemistry codes.  These model grids will serve as training sets for our random-forest machine-learning retrievals.  Continued funding for Sinan Li will enable her to devote three years towards computing three-dimensional virtual laboratories of ultra-hot Jupiters and using the output of these GCMs to train random forests for interpreting multi-faceted space-based data.  These virtual laboratories will also be used to understand how high-resolution spectra measured by next-generation spectrographs (e.g., ESPRESSO) are constraining atmospheric dynamics in ultra-hot Jupiters.  A second, new Ph.D student will be hired to complement the work of Li by working towards a fully coupled (dynamics-radiation-chemistry) GCM that will allow the construction of virtual laboratories of super Earths and mini-Neptunes, which are anticipated to exhibit considerable physical and chemical diversity.  

Besides advancing the state of the art of exoplanetary and brown-dwarf atmospheres, the proposed work leaves behind a legacy of fully reproducible science using open-source computer codes developed as community resources.
Keywords: atmospheric fluid dynamics, exoplanets and exoplanet atmospheres, graphics processing units (GPUs), numerical algorithms, radiative transfer

Title: Mapping fire risk and natural habitats vulnerability in the mountainous biodiversity hotspot of northwest Yunnan, China.
Abstract:
Vegetation fires are a common disturbance in several ecosystems and are often considered by the general public as unwelcome destructive phenomena. Several regions of the world are confronted with an intensification of catastrophic wildfires which are difficult to control and have huge impacts on natural habitats, atmospheric composition, human infrastructure, and public health, bearing massive economic costs. Fire ecologists attribute these negative consequences not only to climate change, but also to ineffective fire management policies based on poor understanding of the role of fire in ecosystems, in particular how fire regimes work. Flammable ecosystems experience recurrent fires and are characterized by a dominant fire-adapted and fire-dependent vegetation. On the other hand, those regions where wildland fires occur rarely are in general covered by fire-intolerant species and old-growth forests, or lack burnable biomass (deserts, glaciers). Since the domestication of fire, humans have had a significant impact on these fire systems by either introducing fire or increase its frequency in regions that did not experience such activity, or by aggressively suppressing them to protect environmental and property assets, as it has been the case in modern times.
As a follow-up of the work performed during my doctoral thesis, I would like to investigate the impacts of recent fire occurrences in the mountains of northwest Yunnan, China (NWY). Owing to extreme environmental gradients, mountainous regions host a high variety of life zones and niches with extremely rich biodiversity. For the same reason, they are also very sensitive to changes in climate patterns and land use practices. Northwest Yunnan is among the hotspots of fire activity in Yunnan province and southern China but the spatiotemporal characteristics, controlling variables, and short- to long-term impacts of these fires on the environment, as well as future predictions of risks have never been assessed. By using a recently developed conceptual framework of long-term fire risk and vulnerability inspired from IPCC’s climate change Outcome Vulnerability model and a georeferenced burned areas dataset of the past 30 years, I plan to:
1.Analyze the different factors controlling fire occurrences in NWY (fire susceptibility), with a strong focus on the interactions between environmental factors (climate/weather, landcover, topography) and human factors (population density, proximity to natural areas). 
2.Assess the ecological consequences of fires through time (Sensitivity of land systems to fire) in terms of habitat fragmentation, resilience and recovery capabilities of different vegetation types, and the impacts on several key faunal species.
3.Combine the previous results to define and rate risk areas of high vulnerability where major management resources should be deployed for the best effectiveness (improve resilience and adaptive capacity).
4.Using future scenarios of climatic and socioeconomic change, predict and map the potential evolution of fire risk in NWY and identify sensitive areas that need particular care.
The methodology will rely on a strong spatial modeling base by the means of Remote Sensing and GIS processing technologies for data creation, manipulation, and output in the form of maps. Objective 1 will adopt machine learning models to find patterns out of 30 years of fire occurrences and the considered explanatory variables, and produce a map of probabilistic risk of fire. For objective 2 instead, I plan to combine Remote Sensing and field work in various locations that burned at different dates to assess vegetation recovery, and install camera traps to study occurring wildlife. Policy-oriented data, such as conservation priority areas and protected areas boundaries. will be incorporated to produce a map of habitat sensitivity to fire. A fire/vulnerability index for the region applied on a combined map will be the main output of objective 3, which together with the different outputs of objective 4, will consist in a final product that will be a valuable knowledge base for local land/fire managers. In fact, fire management operations consume huge economic and human resources, not to mention the difficulties encountered in remote mountainous areas, and the high danger to firefighter’s lives. These results will provide a better understanding of the local ecosystems resilience to fire and improve the effectiveness of management operations.
Keywords: conservation, ecosystem vulnerability, fire management, mapping, mountains, risk assessment, wildland fires

Title: Measuring, Understanding, and Predicting Mutual Fund Performance Worldwide
Abstract:
Mutual funds have emerged as primary investment vehicles for households worldwide: Over the past decade, the number of regulated open-ended funds has increased from 86'301 in 2010 to 122'528 in 2019 with total assets under management of USD 54.9 trillion (Investment Company Factbook, 2020). Although only 8% of all mutual funds are domiciled in the United States (and, hence, 92% of all funds are located in other countries), academic literature on the topic has almost exclusively focused on investigating US funds. As a consequence, the evaluation, understanding, and prediction of mutual fund performance worldwide is not well understood.

In this research project we empirically study the performance and trading behavior of actively-managed mutual funds on a global scale using various econometric techniques. Specifically, we ask the following research questions: 1. Do mutual funds outperform when it matters most to investors? 2. How do mutual funds trade cross-sectional stock market anomalies? 3. Are machine learning techniques helpful to predict future mutual fund performance?

In Phase 1 of the project, we evaluate state-dependent performance of actively-managed mutual funds. While it is generally established that, unconditionally, active funds underperform their benchmark, we examine whether active funds deliver value for investors during periods of economic downturn. In a pre-test, we find that risk-adjusted performance of mutual funds is indeed positive with annualized 0.35% during recessions periods. We expect to confirm this result also on our full data sample and to answer research question 1 with "yes". Hence, our research can solve the puzzle why investors still prefer to invest in active mutual funds (instead of passive ones) worldwide.

Phase 2 seeks to understand mutual fund performance by studying funds' trading behavior. To do so, we exploit detailed equity portfolio holding data and examine how funds engage in the trading of 241 cross-sectional stock market anomalies (such as, e.g., value, momentum, or reversal). We expect that successful mutual fund managers trade anomalies wisely, in a way that they are buying (selling) stocks that are undervalued (overvalued). Our results will answer research question 2 and shed light on the actual trading strategies of mutual fund managers on a global scale.

In Phase 3, we predict mutual fund performance using 30 individual fund- and manager characteristics (such as, e.g., turnover, active share, or manager experience). For this purpose, we apply machine learning techniques, such as boosted regression trees and neural networks, which are particularly suited in such a high-dimenstional setting. In a pre-test, we already show that -- when combining eight common mutual fund characteristics to a joint predictor variable -- a standard deviation increase in the predictor leads to higher future fund performance of 2.5% p.a. Hence, machine learning is expected to be of great value in the prediction of mutual fund performance.

To answer our research questions we will apply the most comprehensive global mutual fund database up-to-date. It is composed by merging data from (i) reported returns and characteristics, (ii) detailed equity portfolio holdings, and (iii) manager characteristics for individual mutual funds in more than 39 countries over the period from 1980 to 2020.
Keywords: International Performance, Machine Learning, Mutual Funds, Prediction of Fund Performance, Stock Market Anomalies, Trading Behavior

Title: Mapping Lope: A Cartographic Exploration of the Comedia Nueva
Abstract:
In recent decades, the “spatial turn” has significantly reshaped the study of space within the Humanities and Social Sciences. In academic literary studies, a substantial body of research explores space in literature and literature in space, with some focusing on “distant” (data-driven) reading. In the specific case of Lope de Vega, the most prolific playwright of the Spanish Golden Age, scholarship has predominantly focused on the geographical settings of the dramatic action and their connection to genre and subgenre classification, as well as to their historical context.

Despite these significant advancements, the absence of appropriate tools has thus far hindered a comprehensive analysis of Lope de Vega’s literary geography. This project aims to address this gap through a detailed analysis of the full set of toponyms referenced in Lope’s dramatic corpus. The study has two primary objectives: first, to reassess the relationship between architextual classification and literary geography; second, to explore the connections between this set of toponyms and the political, social, and cultural circumstances of his time.

My research will adopt an interdisciplinary approach, integrating methodologies from Philology, Literary Geography, and Digital Humanities. The project aims to develop and implement a machine-learning-based workflow to automate the extraction of place names from Lope’s dramatic corpus and visualize these data through interactive maps and statistical analyses. To extract toponyms, I will fine-tune a Named Entity Recognizer code (Flair, spaCy) that has already been successfully tested in two case studies. This methodology will enable me to conduct quantitative analyses (distant reading) by generating statistics and dynamic maps (Leaflet map, Peripleo), providing an unprecedented perspective on Lope de Vega’s use of toponyms and facilitating the identification of spatial clusters in his work. These quantitative studies will be complemented by qualitative analyses (close reading), which will uncover new dimensions of the role of toponyms by examining their function, placement, and connections.

By joining the PROLOPE research group at the Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona, I will gain access to modernized critical editions of the plays in my corpus. Moreover, this collaboration will allow me to benefit from the expertise of leading scholars specializing in Lope de Vega’s work, participate in various projects in the field, and take advantage of a strong infrastructure in Digital Humanities.

This project represents a unique opportunity to advance understanding of the role of space in Lope de Vega’s work and in 17th-century European theater. Furthermore, the methodology employed has significant potential for application across a wide range of authors, genres, and disciplines. Although similar interdisciplinary approaches have been applied in smaller-scale studies, they have not yet been implemented on a dataset of this scope, encompassing 360 plays, or with this depth of analysis. The project’s outcomes will be published on the PROLOPE project website, allowing users to explore interactive maps through filters such as place name, genre, subgenre, play title, or date. Additionally, all codes and workflows developed during the project will be released as open-source resources, ensuring unrestricted access for other researchers.
Keywords: Cartography, Digital Humanities, Literary Geography, Lope de Vega, Philology, Spanish theatre

Title: Open many-body quantum systems and machine learning
Abstract:
Many physical phenomena take place in an equilibrated and closed system, the latter meaning that the system under consideration is assumed ideal and does not interact with any other system in the universe. Equilibration refers to the system having had time to settle, and transient behavior has passed. 

Recent advances in condensed matter physics have started to uncover the possibilities of open systems, in which an external source constantly adds energy to the system and in which the system itself may lose energy to its environment. In particular, such driven & dissipative systems often involve a periodic driving leading to physical phenomena with no equilibrated counterparts.

The aim of this research proposal is to study such driven & dissipative systems, and identify the possible new phases of matter that may arise from them. To achieve these goals we make use of both advanced analytical techniques as well as advanced numerical methods, including the option of applying machine learning techniques to fundamental physics.
Keywords: Machine Learning, Many-body localization, Non-equilibrium, Open systems, Topology

Title: Preventing antibiotic resistant infections by personalized microbiome manipulation
Abstract:
The clinical introduction of antibiotics has alleviated tremendously the public health burden caused by bacterial pathogens, but their use does not come without a long-term cost: While antibiotics reduce the pathogen load in the individual patient, they also generate a selective pressure for the emergence of resistance at both the individual patient and the population level. In order to avoid that the infection-related burden for public health returns to a level similar of pre-antibiotic times, it is crucial to understand how we can use antibiotics in a multi-objejctive framework, to both treat the individual infection but also avoid the emergence of resistance at the population level. The Kishony lab has shown that the host gut microbiome is a reservoir for pathogens which potentially seed infections at other body sites (e.g. urinary tract or open wounds, unpublished results) and that new resistances after antibiotic treatment are mostly driven by the replacement of a pathogen strain in the gut microbiome community(Stracy et al., 2022)?. The relationship between resistances to different antibiotics is complex and can be synergistic (“cross-resistance”), neutral or even antagonistic (“collateral sensitivity”)(Imamovic & Sommer, 2013; Lázár et al., 2014; Podnecky et al., 2018)?. Therefore, a given antibiotic treatment, while selecting for higher resistance to it, can promote or reduce resistances to other antibiotic treatments, and thereby influences the probability of future resistant infections. 
During my research stay in the Kishony lab, I would like to complement my knowledge in genomics and metagenomics with the lab’s expertise in machine learning, computational biology and electronic health records to develop new antibiotic treatment strategies to not only treat ongoing infections, but also preventing future resistant infections by leveraging strain replacement and collateral sensitivity through microbiome manipulation. To this end, we will i) measure the relationship between different resistances in pathogen enriched microbiomes from patient fecal swabs, ii) describe the connection between these different resistomes states in  Enterobacteriaceae communities and isolates from same patient samples from different time points for which we have metadata on the antibiotic treatment and build a reinforcement learning model that would describe the antibiotic treatment path for which not only a present infection can be treated but also possible future infections remain easily treatable and iii) evaluate the performance of this model compared to current clinical practices in both retrospective and prospective cohort studies. A successful completion of this project will pave the way for a possible paradigm shift from a short-sighted view of treatment to a look-ahead strategy that devises optimal current treatment by considering future treatment step and  future outcomes, but also yield significant insight into the dynamics of microbial communities upon disruption through antibiotics uptake. In a more general view, it will also provide new tools to control microbial community properties through targeted interventions.
Keywords: Antibiotics, Electronic health records, Machine Learning, Metagenomics, Microbial evolution

Title: Domain-specific Statistical Machine Translation
Abstract:
Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) systems can be built quickly when sufficient training material is available. But for many language pairs and application areas there exist only small amounts of high quality human-translated texts. The general question in this project is how we can best adapt an SMT system to a particular application domain when only a limited amount of in-domain human-translated texts are available as training data.

In the first months of the project we have prepared a domain-specific parallel corpus of Alpine texts in German and French as the result of a digitization project on the yearbooks of the Swiss Alpine Club. Since 1957 the SAC has published its yearbooks in parallel French and German versions. We have turned this material into a unique corpus of more than 4 million words in both languages.

We have run an extensive series of SMT experiments on this corpus. They have confirmed our expectation that even a limited domain-specific corpus results in much better in-domain translation quality than an order-of-magnitude larger out-of-domain corpus or even a general MT system like Google Translate.

In this proposal for extension of the project we first survey the recent developments in SMT in general and in domain adaption for SMT in particular. We then describe our accomplishments in the first year of the project and re-state our tasks for the second year. We have followed the project schedule closely and our publications testify the recognition of our work.

We apply for a project extension of two years. In this period we will continue our work in a number of directions. We realized that the exploitation of comparable domain-specific corpora for the enlargement of  training corpora is important for improving the SMT quality. Recent work on extracting parallel sentences from Wikipedia pages confirms this point. This will be our first line of activities.

Second, we will contrast and compare our work with competing approaches. This means that we need to run controlled experiments on the methods proposed by other researchers, for instance on domain adaption through caching the recent history, through corpus identifiers in factored SMT, and through creating synthetic corpora by automatically translating in-domain monolingual corpora.

Third, we observe a tendency to include linguistic information in SMT systems and to combine rule-based and statistical MT in hybrid systems. We will include linguistic information ranging from named entities over specific word reordering to dependency parsing. Our German dependency parser is partly rule-based and will thus be able to account for properties of the source language. We propose to combine these hybrid systems with domain adaptation methods. 

Finally, we plan to enrich our parallel French-German treebank, which we have built in the first year of this project with a shallow semantic layer of geographical tags. The parallel treebank and the annotated parallel corpus will be showcases of our work through a combined web-based Alignment Search System and machine translation system for Alpine texts.
Keywords: Domain Adaptation, Machine Translation, Natural Language Processing, Parallel Corpora

Title: In silico prediction of phage-bacteria infection networks as a tool to implement personalized phage therapy
Abstract:
The emergence and rapid dissemination of antibiotic resistance worldwide threatens medical progress. As a consequence, medicine might face a return to the pre-antibiotic era in a very soon future. The paucity of potential new anti-infectives in the pipeline of pharmaceutical industries urges the need for alternatives to fight this public health problem. Phage therapy might represent such an alternative. This re-emerging therapy uses viruses that specifically infect and kill bacteria during their life cycle to reduce/eliminate bacterial load and cure infections. These viruses, called bacteriophages or phages, have been co-evolving with bacteria for billions years, controlling bacterial populations and epidemics, and contributing to their genetic exchanges. With the advantage of having low impact on the commensal flora, as they are highly strain specific, some phages might, nevertheless, harbor virulence factors and drive horizontal gene transfer mediating dissemination of pathogenic traits including antibiotic resistance, calling for their careful selection before their therapeutic use (see below “Phage lifestyle inside the bacteria”). 

The success of phage therapy mainly relies on the exact matching between both the target pathogenic bacteria and the therapeutic phage. Therefore, having access to a fully characterized phage library is necessary, although not sufficient, to start with phage therapy. An essential and obligate second step to conceive personalized phage therapy treatments is the capacity to predict the interactions between the target pathogen and its potential phage. The long term goal of the proposed research is, therefore, to develop quantitative and predictive in silico models of phage-bacteria infection networks. These models will describe the interactions between phage and bacteria and will serve to fasten the selection of effective phages to propose phage therapy in a personalized fashion.

To efficiently predict successful phage-bacteria interactions suitable for phage therapy, we will develop a novel in silico methodology that will, ultimately, enable the selection of phage candidates from an existing phage library to target a given pathogenic bacteria. To achieve this, we will combine genomic information with state-of-the-art bioinformatic and machine learning techniques, taking advantage of the growing amount of interaction data already available as well as of our own data to keep uncovering new phage families. We will ensure that our methodology brings explanatory power along, thereby shedding light on the relevant genomic features underscoring the interactions. To challenge our approach, we will eventually prospectively validate our methodology using paradigmatic pathogens (Pendleton et al. 2013). For this, we will construct the phage-bacterium infection networks around those pathogens, to identify single phages and/or phage cocktails with extended bactericidal activities, as assessed in different models of infections, including a Galleria melonnella model of infection and a rat endocarditis model. We expect our methodology to drive a paradigm shift in phage therapy, by offering a time-sparing and easy-to-use way to accurately select phages for each individual patient. The methodology will be made available online and several future developments of this project are already envisioned.
Keywords: A. baumannii, E. coli, K. pneumoniae, P. aeruginosa, bacteriophages, in silico prediction, interaction

Title: A mechanistic theory of functional responses: zooming into movement behaviour to understand and predict predator-prey interactions
Abstract:
The dynamics of ecological communities arise from a large number of individual interactions, such as the consumption of prey by a predator. A critical factor determining the dynamics of interacting populations is how the strength of interactions among populations (number of interactions per unit time) varies as a function of population density. The shape of this relationship, known as the functional response (FR), has profound implications for the coexistence, collapse, or cyclical behaviour of two or more interacting populations. Although FR theory was originally derived from process-based models of how individuals move and interact, in practice, FRs are estimated experimentally by measuring the number of prey consumed after some time period across a range of prey densities. Despite the empirical measurement of thousands of FRs, our understanding of how the shape of the FR emerges from individual movement and behaviour remains limited. This limitation has led to two main challenges. First, even in simple scenarios when the predator feeds on a single-prey type, different predator-prey pairs can exhibit qualitatively different FR shapes, resulting in fundamentally different dynamics at the population and community levels. Nevertheless, a mechanistic understanding of the factors determining whether a given predator-prey pair will exhibit one FR type versus another is still lacking. Second, the empirical approaches that have been used to measure FRs in simple single-prey contexts do not scale well to the more complex, but also more common case of predators that feed on multiple prey. In this context, the number of experimental replicates required to measure multi-prey FRs increases exponentially with the number of prey, and consequently, multi-prey FRs have been measured in only a few cases.
We propose to solve these two fundamental problems by reconnecting FR theory with its mechanistic basis in movement behaviour. Since the original formulations of FR theory, movement ecology has made enormous strides thanks in part to technological advances in GPS tracking and computer vision tools. This work across a diverse range of species has revealed general principles of movement behaviour: first, individuals often transition among distinct movement modes characterised by different movement parameters; and second, individuals are capable of biasing movement towards or away from nearby individuals in ways that qualitatively change interaction dynamics. However, these principles have rarely been incorporated into FR theory, leaving their implications for the dynamics of interacting populations unexplored.
To bridge this gap, we aim to integrate two major but largely separate subdisciplines of ecology—movement ecology and functional response theory—by developing a theory of functional responses that incorporates general principles of movement behaviour. To accomplish this, we combine mathematical models and experiments within a highly tractable system—protist food webs. This system facilitates high-resolution, high-throughput measurements of both individual behaviour and functional responses. We will first explore how different single-prey FR types emerge by measuring the movement behaviours of predators and prey under varying conditions and developing models that account for transitions among distinct movement modes and the degree of random and directed search. We will then extend this approach to model predator and prey behaviour in multi-prey contexts to explore the mechanistic basis of density-dependent transitions in predator diet (prey switching). Finally, we will test the ability of these models to predict the shape of functional responses across multiple predator-prey pairs in both single-prey and multi-prey contexts. In doing so, we aim to overcome prevailing challenges in single and multi-prey FRs and to develop new theory that links general principles of movement behaviour to the dynamics of interacting populations.
Keywords: food web, foodweb, functional response, movement ecology, predator-prey dynamics, trophic interaction

Title: Learning generative models for molecules
Abstract:
Machine learning models are particularly good in solving forward prediction problems in which given some input structure there is a unique well-defined target value that we want to predict. The inverse problem, i.e. given a desired target value to be able to sample structures that exhibit it, is more challenging  because it has an underspecified, one-to-many, structure. Generating molecules with desired properties is a particular challenging application of that setting partly due to the fact that the set of molecules which have a given property is structurally very diverse and highly multimodal. 
 
In addition we also need to deal with discrete nature of the underlying structures. Directly optimizing over discrete structures with respect to target properties is problematic: gradients are unavailable and we can not directly estimate the change in a structure that would correspond to the desired property change. Generative models  hold considerable promise for such problems as well as for the more general setting of inverse modelling. 

In this project we have two overarching objectives: to develop generative models and algorithms that are able to do single-step molecule generation given some desired property as well as style transfer; in the latter we want given some input molecule to be able to sample molecules that are similar to that and exhibit a desired property. 

Most approaches to these problems involve a two-step process, which is not only computationally expensive, since at inference time we need to solve an optimization problem, but often requires retraining for new target values. Moreover, because they hinge on a second optimization step, their use is limited to models that are defined over continuous latent spaces where optimization is amenable. Being able to do single-step generation while it has an interest per se, it will also open up the space of generative models to discrete latent spaces, since we will not be constrained anymore by the additional optimization step.

The objectives that we set above lead to a particular choice of generative models that we will be using, namely the ones that make use of latent variables, such as Variational Autoncoders and flow-based generative models; the latter are so far quite under explored for the molecule generation problem. Conditional generation and style transfer have shown surprising 
success in domains such as computer vision and natural language processing. However such an approach, if not carefully designed, can lead to pathological cases, in particular when the conditioning  factor has a weak information content with respect to the generated structures, where either the latent variable or the conditioning variable are ignored by the model.
Note, that such pathologies are by far not specific to the molecule generation setting. Thus one of the specific aims of the project will be the appropriate crafting of the objective functions that will ensure that all model components and inputs to the model are used as intended and no reductions to trivial cases arise. In addition, our preliminary work has shown that autoregressive have a performance advantage for conditional generation over latent variable models such as variational encoders, nevertheless they cannot be used for style transfer. Thus one of our specific aims will be to get the best of the two worlds while delivering models that are able to address both tasks and achieve very good performance. A final specific aim is to explore discrete latent variable models for the molecule generation problem. While this is a challenging task, we believe that discrete latent spaces are more appropriate for the inherently discrete setting of molecule modelling. Perhaps not surprisingly, given the challenge of the task, there is quite limited work with such models and we want to address this gap. 

The models and algorithms that we will develop in this project will be of interest for other than the molecule generation settings. Inverse modelling appears in many different settings, robotics, modelling of physical processes, and many more, while discrete data structures are  very common in many domains. Thus the results of the project will be of direct use there.
Keywords: flow-based models, generative models, inverse problem, molecules, variational autoencoders

Title: Reliable Open-Source Large-Scale Machine Learning
Abstract:
Machine learning methods have seen a tremendous surge of interest in recent years in many scientific and industrial applications. However, major roadblocks still appear when facing datasets which exceed the storage capacity of a single computer, as distributed machine learning algorithms are often unstable, vary hugely in performance on different systems, and are not accessible to many users.
In this project, we aim to improve this by pursuing two research directions. First, we will develop new resource-adaptive algorithmic building blocks for distributed machine learning, which are more robust and flexible with respect to changes in the underlying hardware and software systems, and improve their usability for the end-users, both in a cloud computing environment or on specialized compute systems. Secondly, we want to improve knowledge and accessibility of distributed machine learning for researchers and practitioners, by providing verified and scalable reference implementations under an open source license. This will be done as part of the first public benchmarking suite for distributed large-scale machine learning, comparing both algorithms as well as underlying hardware and software frameworks in a transparent and reproducible way.
Keywords: Algorithms Benchmarking, Distributed Machine Learning, Large Scale Data Analysis, System-Adaptive Algorithms, Systems Benchmarking

Title: Precision Medicine in Molecular Radiotherapy using Deep Learning
Abstract:
Over the last decade, the emergence of effective RadioPharmaceutical Therapy (RPT) with the advantages of localized tumor efficacy and tumor cell specificity, has promoted a rapid expansion in molecular radiotherapy research. Parallel advances in theragnostic, integrating therapy and diagnosis, have enabled a paradigm shift from the current one-size-fits-all strategy to personalized medicine. The introduction of theragnostic in molecular radiotherapy enables clinicians for therapy selection/ adaptation, personalized treatment planning, and early assessment of treatment response. In pursuing precision medicine in RPT based on the patient-specific biology, molecular pathology, tumor burden, and dosimetry, this research proposal will focus on two main pillars: i) To bring the full capacity of theranostic dosimetry-based planning to RPT setting by developing a practical dosimetry workflow and user-friendly tool, and ii) To develop a prognostic and decision-support model for 177Lu-labeled RPTs based on quantitative biomarkers from pretherapy imaging and pathology to ensure optimal efficacy and economy. There is growing evidence that personalized dosimetry-guided RPTs may be beneficial for therapy outcome. To this end, the first essential step is establishing a standardized workflow of personalized dosimetry that an international effort is underway to accelerate its clinical translation. In the second step, we aim to develop a predictive model for response to 177Lu-DOTATATE and –PSMA therapies using quantitative imaging biomarkers, in order to improve evidence-based selection of candidates for these treatments and further optimize clinical trials and individual care. To accomplish these goals, the following steps are required:
1.Personalized dosimetry workflow: i) Evaluation of the previously-developed dose calculation engine against FDA-approved software; ii) Imaging protocol optimization for theragnostic dosimetry using machine/ deep learning algorithms.
2.Decision-support tool: i) Extracting Radiomics features and handcrafted quantitative biomarkers from pre-therapy imaging; ii) Building a learning-based model to estimate the therapeutic absorbed dose from pretherapy images (68Ga PET images); and iii) Training a prognostic model based on Radiomics signatures, dosimetric indices and clinicopathological information to predict treatment outcome efficacy; 
One of the main barriers to dosimetry-guided personalized molecular radiotherapy is the lack of dosimetry tools that are validated yet practical for the clinical setting. To improve the current workflow, we aim to develop and validate a platform for patient-specific treatment planning that is clinically practical. Accordingly, the retrospective dose profiles calculated using the developed toolkit, allow evaluation of the treatment response to the one-fits-all strategy (it was reported that tumors mostly receive suboptimal doses [6]) that is essential for the establishment of a standardized personalized clinical workflow and/or randomized control trials. According to the ongoing prospective clinical trial underway at the University of Michigan (UM) on full-time-point 177Lu-DOTATATE, we aim to investigate the predictive value of Radiomics/ Dosiomics signatures derived from pretherapy 68Ga PET images along with clinicopathological information for treatment-response, striving at assisting clinicians for pre-therapy patient selection and decision-making. The proposed methodology is adaptable to 177Lu-PSMA therapy where its prospective trial is anticipated in early 2022 at UM. Currently, there is minimal evidence on patient eligibility for 177Lu-DOTATATE and -PSMA RPT and no standardized criteria have been established, yet. Thus, the proposed research project for outcome prediction of these types of treatments with encouraging responses and well tolerable side effects can aid clinicians in further optimization of trial designs and individual patient management. Furthermore, this prognostic model is a useful tool in randomized clinical trials for candidate selection and stratification of patients to responders and non-responders groups.

ii) building a learning based model to estimate the therapeutic absorbed dose from pretherapy images (68ga pet images); and iii) training a prognostic model based on radiomics signatures, dosimetric indices and clinicopathological information to predict treatment outcome efficacy; one of the main barriers to dosimetry guided personalized molecular radiotherapy is the lack of dosimetry tools that are validated yet practical for the clinical setting. to improve the current workflow, we aim to develop and validate a platform for patient specific treatment planning that is clinically practical. accordingly, the retrospective dose profiles calculated using the developed toolkit, allow evaluation of the treatment response to the one fits all strategy (it was reported that tumors mostly receive suboptimal doses [6]) that is essential for the establishment of a standardized personalized clinical workflow and/or randomized control trials. according to the ongoing prospective clinical trial underway at the university of michigan (um) on full time point 177lu dotatate, we aim to investigate the predictive value of radiomics/ dosiomics signatures derived from pretherapy 68ga pet images along with clinicopathological information for treatment response, striving at assisting clinicians for pre therapy patient selection and decision making. the proposed methodology is adaptable to 177lu psma therapy where its prospective trial is anticipated in early 2022 at um. currently, there is minimal evidence on patient eligibility for 177lu dotatate and psma rpt and no standardized criteria have been established, yet. thus, the proposed research project for outcome prediction of these types of treatments with encouraging responses and well tolerable side effects can aid clinicians in further optimization of trial designs and individual patient management. furthermore, this prognostic model is a useful tool in randomized clinical trials for candidate selection and stratification of patients to responders and non responders groups. . precision medicine, radiomics, radiopharmaceutical therapy, machine learning, theragnostic dosimetry

Title: HIV-1 Transmission in Switzerland: viral transmission traits, superinfection and drug resistance
Abstract: This translational research project is a continuation of SNF 130865. We aim to unravel traits of HIV transmission in three conceptually different situations of high clinical relevance: transmission leading to de novo infection (Aim 1), spread of HIV between infected individuals (conferred to as superinfection (SI); Aim 2) and transmission of drug resistant virus (Aim 3). The proposed studies are based on two renowned longitudinal studies with extensive biobanks: The Swiss HIV Cohort  and the Zurich Primary HIV-1 infection study (ZPHI). AIM 1. Here we will determine whether specific genotypic and phenotypic viral traits of transmitted/founder viruses (T/F) exist. Characterization of T/F viruses, the earliest virus population that emerges in a newly infected individual, is of high interest as understanding their transmis-sion pathways may open avenues for prophylaxis and treatment. Current data on T/F virus features led to intriguing in-sights, but no definitive picture of genetic and phenotypic traits of  T/F viruses has emerged. A limitation of previous studies was that features of  T/F viruses had to be compared to unrelated viruses from chronically infected patients as transmitting individuals were in most cases not identified.  Here using phylogenetically linked T/F viruses and their transmitters we will be able to study phylogenetically linked transmitter-recipient pairs. Thus far we identified 79 acutely HIV infected (recipients) and 107 chronically infected individuals with genetically related HIV strains which are their likely transmitters. Plasma samples close to estimated time of infection will be chosen for virus genomic analysis from transmitters and recipients to retrieve full length HIV-genomes employing Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) followed by haplotype reconstruction. T/F virus will be compared to variants present in the transmitter regarding, length, specific mutations, deletions/insertions, glycosylation sites, charge and frequency to define whether stochastic or non-stochastic transmission occurs. If genotypic traits are identified, gene transfer and mutagenesis experiments will be performed followed by phenotypic analysis to discern  if  indeed signifying characteristics of T/F viruses exist. To this end we will compare transmitter and T/F viruses for features implicated in shaping transmission including replication capacity, sensitivity to neutralizing antibodies and entry inhibitors, entry kinetics and interferon sensitivity.  AIM 2: Here we will  systematically explore frequency and risk factors for  HIV-1 superinfection in the SHCS and ZPHI. A first phylogenetic screen based on pol sequences has revealed 150-312 potential SI cases. By retrieving longitudinal plasma samples before patients went on antiretroviral therapy  we will seek to confirm SI by full length NGS and define approximate time points of  SI events. In a detailed virus genomic analysis we aim to reconstruct haplotypes, study recombination events.  A specific emphasis of our studies is on  determining risk factors for acquiring SI using detailed patient, disease and host genomic data available. Viral fitness of  initial circulating and superinfecting strains will be computed using machine learning techniques. To test whether SI is prevented by neutralizing antibody responses,  those will be compared among superinfected and non-superinfected individuals. Finally, viral setpoint of cases and controls will be compared to determine the impact of SI on disease progression. AIM 3: Here we will investigate transmission  of HIV-1 drug resistance mutations (TDR) within the SHCS, specifically focussing on the non-B compared to the subtype B epidemic, newer drugs, and reversion rates of  TDR.  We will study TDR prevalence over time for B and non- B subtypes in all drug naives and, specifically, in recently infected individuals. We will particularly focus on newer drugs. In patients with TDR we will determine reversion rates for specific TDR and fitness cost by taking into account the pol genotypic backbone indepen-dently of  TDR. Furthermore, by performing phylogenetic analysis we will study whether there are differences in transmission dynamics between B- and non-B subtype TDR. This analysis will reveal whether TDR in the non-B subtypes is increasing as would be expected due to the recent, wide spread roll out of antiretroviral drugs in developing countries.

Title: HistoRiCH: Historical river change – Planning for the future by exploring the mapped past
Abstract:
Summary
Switzerland’s historical maps build a unique knowledge base for studying landscape change over the last 150 years. So far, such maps are mostly used for local to regional projects, e.g. by manually digitizing map elements. The overarching vision of this research project is making this rich source of spatio-temporal information accessible – nation-wide and to its full temporal depth – for a quantitative analysis of changing freshwater ecosystems in a management context. The project has three primary objectives:
1.From maps to features. Development of robust digital map processing methods for extracting hydrological features from scanned historical maps. The aimed-for vector data of rivers and lakes spans extended areas and time periods allowing for a seamless reconstruction of the development of the shape and topology of freshwater ecosystems.
2.From features to metrics. Derivation of ecological metrics from those extracted hydrological features to characterize ecosystem structure and function. Specifically, novel metrics must be developed that exploit the newly gained temporal depth and acknowledge the poor data qualities and high uncertainties to be expected when processing historical map sources.
3.From metrics to application. Unlocking historical knowledge for present-day management of freshwater ecosystems (e.g. river restoration, biodiversity conservation), under consideration of the hydrological and morphological factors driving the observed change. This requires establishing a better understanding of how historical landscape change impacts on present-day ecology.
The three objectives will be addressed through tight-knit collaborations in the interdisciplinary project consortium. The ETHZ cartography group addresses the data-centered challenges around the development, validation and application of digital map processing methods. This involves the development of machine learning algorithms tailored to the extraction of hydrological features from historical maps. The ZHAW geoinformatics and ecohydrology groups embed the extracted features into the ecological context by developing quantitative metrics characterizing the static structures and dynamic functions of the studied freshwater ecosystems. Multi-scale and sensitivity studies combined with error propagation approaches will tackle the expected variable data qualities. The Eawag river restoration group investigates the application of the generated knowledge base for research and practical management. This requires a multi-scale analysis of the factors driving landscape change (e.g. urbanization, hydrology) in order to interpret the observed changes, assess their impact on present-day river ecology and derive practical recommendations for an informed use of historical maps.
This project will contribute to the fields of digital cartography, geographic information science, image processing and freshwater ecology. The digital map processing algorithms are transferrable to the evolution of further landscape aspects such as urban areas, forests, or transportation infrastructures, both in Switzerland and in other areas with similar historical maps. Uncertainty-aware spatio-temporal data processing techniques gain importance for exploiting multi-scale, low-structured big (spatial) data. The contributions to freshwater ecology lie in the extended set of multi-scale and dynamic metrics and guidance for their application for freshwater management. Our joint contributions will form the methodological basis for our vision of a standardized nationwide data base for tracking and reconstructing the development of the Swiss river network from the past to the future. Incorporating this information into existing national spatial data infrastructures (e.g. geodata4edu.ch, map.geo.admin.ch) will provide an excellent tool for ecologists, river engineers, and regional planers.
Keywords: Cartography, Ecological Metrics, Feature Extraction, Freshwater Management, Geoinformatics, Historical Legacies, Historical Maps, Mapping, Ontologies and Semantics, Restoration

Title: See ColOr_II (Seeing Colours with an Orchestra II)
Abstract:
In the research domain of vision substitution, exploration is the act of perceiving and understanding the various components of the surroundings, as well as the spatial distribution of the main constituents. Since June 2010 we have been investigating user perception by means of a prototype based on three distinct modules related to central vision, peripheral vision and obstacle detection. Each module provides the user with a sound representation of parts of video frames captured by a 3D camera. We have been validating two of these modules (the local and the global module, corresponding to central and peripheral vision, respectively) with a number of experiments. Videos on the local module are available on http://www.youtube.com/guidobologna. This proposal will extend the research that will come to an end with the current See ColOr_II project (See ColOr_II -  Project 200021_127334, June 2010 - May 2012, with a PhD student). 

The local module provides the user with the auditory representation of a row containing 25 points of a captured image. The key idea is to represent a pixel of an image as a sound source located at a particular azimuth angle. Moreover, each emitted sound is assigned to a musical instrument, and to a sound duration depending on the colour and the depth of the pixel, respectively. The global module allows the user to explore a captured video frame. For instance, it is possible to compare two distant points (in terms of colour and depth) by pointing two fingers on a touchpad representing the current environment picture. The specific use of the local module, thus focusing only on a small portion of the captured scene leads to the tunnel vision phenomenon. A current research question is to determine whether the addition of a global vision mechanism provided by the global module allows the user to become aware of the surroundings in real time, with colours and 3D.

To recognise an object in the current See ColOr prototype the user relies on colours, but in some situations colour is inadequate. For instance if a door has the same colour as the wall, it will be impossible to distinguish it. Furthermore, it could take too much time in some cases to identify a specific object. Thus, we propose to investigate how well machine learning models (such as neural networks, SVMs, decision trees, etc.) can learn to recognize classes of objects relevant to visually impaired individuals. In addition, we aim at making it possible to inspect panels such as bus stops. As a consequence, we propose to look into text from frames captured by a 3D camera. The difficulty compared to the state of the art in the domain is the resolution, and the angle of view that has consequences in character distortion. The research will be performed in text detection, segmentation and rectification, but not in the reading part itself (existing open source programs will be used). 

Recently, in computer vision a substantial progress has been achieved by extracting locally invariant features from images. Among several types, invariant features can be learnt by supervised learning models to detect objects from different view angles and at different scales. Image databases such as LabelMe (http://labelme.csail.mit.edu/), includes a great number of annotated object classes that will be used as a starting point to our research.  Among other possible models of supervised learning, artificial neural networks will be very relevant to put into operation the recognition module. Specifically, neural networks have been successful in many recognition tasks; moreover, they can reach a decision very quickly, as they are parallel distributed models. Finally, other models such as SVMs or ensembles of decision stumps will be compared to neural networks on the predictive accuracy performance. 

Once an object is detected, we propose to represent it by a characteristic sound (“earcon”) that will be triggered from either the local module or the global module. Another novelty will be a guiding tool that will allow the user to grasp an object. The idea here is to sonify the x-y-z coordinates of an object by left-right spatialisation, pitch and sound duration, respectively. The same tool will be used in some situations to make it possible for the user to be in a better location to inspect a text panel. Here our research investigation will be at the experimental level, as we will focus on an experiment that will determine whether the guiding tool is accurate and efficient to reach and to grasp objects.

Our system for visual substitution puts forward four novel aspects. First, by its architecture presenting local/global modules, and recognition modules See ColOr_II will imitate the visual system by providing the user with essential cues of vision (local, global and cognitive) by means of the auditory channel. Second, the simultaneous sonification of colour and depth is a characteristic that does not appear in any other electronic travel aid. Third, we propose to carry out new experiments such as exploring the 3D environment with its colours, finding specific objects and inspecting panels with relevant text information. Finally, the research proposed here will put forward cheap components and non-invasive devices, such as notebooks, Kinect 3D cameras, headphones (possibly bonephones [Wal05]). They could be adopted by the visually impaired community, once a 3D camera will be miniaturised on sunglasses.
Keywords: 3D camera, computer vision, image processing, machine learning, multi-modal interaction, sensory substitution, sound spatialisation

Title: Forecasting midlatitude storm impacts beyond current predictability limits
Abstract:
Extreme storms are a major natural hazard in the extratropics. These storms can cause substantial economic damages, induce flooding, and can interrupt transportation networks, electricity supply and even lead to casualties. The risk of extreme weather systems, and extreme extratropical storms in particular, is expected to increase with climate change, especially in Europe. However, while midlatitude weather is dominated by cyclones, it is particularly challenging to predict weather in the midlatitudes beyond ten days. Skillful predictions of extratropical storms, on timescales of several weeks to months, rely on the connection between storm tracks and large-scale atmospheric variability modes that can often be predicted beyond the synoptic time scale, thus providing a potential for extending the predictability limits of storms to timescales longer than a few weeks. An in-depth understanding of the dynamical processes controlling the predictability of extratropical storms over the North Atlantic and Europe in winter is essential for skillful sub-seasonal to seasonal (two weeks to two months) prediction of these high-impact weather systems in current and future climate and for assessing their potentially devastating impacts. Such predictions can provide early warnings for society and reliable information for decision makers in sectors such as public health, energy, ecosystems and water security.
Here, I propose research aimed to identify the role of dynamical precursors governing extreme winter storms in the Northern Hemisphere midlatitudes, and particularly the Euro-Atlantic region, to improve the prediction of storms on sub-seasonal to seasonal time scales (i.e., timescales of several weeks to months) by combining state-of-the-art climate model simulations, statistical and machine learning postprocessing methods and risk assessment models. As such, this study represents a pioneering approach, with the aim of connecting persistent atmospheric modes and predictability of extreme weather events. 
The improvement of midlatitude storm forecast skill on timescales longer than a few weeks will be done in three work packages (WP): (1) We will identify the dynamical drivers governing the frequency and intensity of extreme winter storms using a series of state-of-the-art numerical experiments under current and future climate conditions. (2) We will use state-of-the-art statistical and Machine Learning tools to develop an improved forecast of extratropical storms in the North Atlantic and over Europe using operational weather forecasts; (3) We will build an impact model to assess the predictability of storm impacts in Europe through linking physical risk with economic loss estimations.
The proposed research is expected to improve the understanding and prediction of midlatitude storms on sub-seasonal to seasonal time scales and to provide more accurate forecasts of the impacts of these storms. In addition, the outcome of this research can be used for prediction of extreme storm hazards in future climate, which is essential for climate change adaptation over Switzerland. As such, the significance of this research extends well beyond demonstrating atmospheric predictability, and has the potential to provide early warning for society and stakeholders and reduce the risk due to extreme weather in the future.
Keywords: atmospheric dynamics, atmospheric predictability, climate change, climate impacts, natural hazards, storm tracks

Title: Learning to classify abnormal events with statistical relational learning and distributed data sources
Abstract:
Machine learning techniques have been applied with great success to a wide
variety of problems such as behavior recognition and forecasting, classification of devices and events, and finding regularities in large datasets. It is widely recognized that machine learning works well when sufficient data is available to unambiguously identify the desired result.

In this project, we focus in particular on learning to recognize abnormal
behavior such as malware and configuration errors in network traffic data.
We obtain the data through NexThink, a spinoff company of our group, but also other sources. We also plan to consider other data such as RFID traces or financial transactions. Such data is by nature relational and distributed, and we would like to study how a combination of relational and distributed learning can be used to learn to detect abnormal events.

Besides the fact that relational models are a more natural fit for network
traffic, they also offer a richer vocabulary for specifying the learning
objectives. In feature-based methods, rare events tend to get classified
as outliers. In relational learning, the learning objective can specify more

We also consider how such sharing can be combined with methods for protecting privacy, and how this will affect the learning process.

doctoral students currently working on these issues.
