Title: Coding Strategies for Caching Systems
Abstract:
Coded Caching for content delivery networks is emerging as a promising strategy to address issues of spectral gridlock and congestion. Content delivery networks are special in that requests are typically concentrated during peak hours—a movie delivery network will experience many more requests during the typical evening hours than during the rest of the day. Hence, if delivery takes place only after the requests are received, this will inevitably lead to strong network congestion during peak hours, and thus, result in slow delivery and poor quality of overall service. It may appear that this problem is fundamental and cannot be alleviated. However, one emerging asset that can be leveraged is the wide availability of cheap memory devices at the end users or at intermediate servers in the network. In that case, one can strategically place partial contents in anticipation of the actual requests, and this will reduce the requirement for communication bandwidth at delivery time, thus resulting in faster content delivery. The research proposed here aims at developing coding techniques and corresponding fundamental performance bounds for such coded caching systems.
Part I—Models and Fundamental Information-theoretic Limits.
The first and major thrust of the proposed research concerns the development of modeling frameworks for caching systems, and within these models, the derivation of fundmental performance limits. The most powerful tools that lead to fundamental bounds on data compression and communication come from Information Theory, and the proposed work plans to leverage these tools in the first place.
Part II—Code Constructions for Caching.
The second key thrust of the proposed research concerns the development of code constructions for caching systems. Our preliminary work has revealed a strong connection between the problem of coded caching and the classical problem of reliable communication over noisy channels that has been intensely studied over the past seventy years. Exploiting this connection, we propose to study several substantially different classes of code constructions, including convolutional codes, low-density parity check codes, polar codes, and most importantly, universal code constructions of the type of the well-known Lempel-Ziv codes. This part of the work will have a smaller analytical and mathematical component, and more importantly, will contain in-depth numerical simulation and algorithm development, all the way to a full end-to-end system prototype that can be applied to any given data base.
Part III—Extensions: Secrecy, Real-time Constraints, andWireless Models.
There are myriad extensions that will be studied, based on practically motivated additional constraints on the caching problem. For example, it may be undesirable for the cache contents itself to reveal too much about the data base. A more challenging extension concerns the adaptation of the techniques to the case of wireless connectivity. In that case, generally, the caching strategy should be designed jointly with the wireless coding
strategy, and again, the challenge would be to understand fundamental performance bounds. Finally, there is an intuitive connection to communication-constrained Machine Learning and emerging Big Data systems that will be explored in more detail.
Keywords: Data Compression, Error-control Coding, Information Theory, Signal Processing

Title: Stochastic modelling of mosquito behaviour in response to environmental conditions
Abstract:
Background
Understanding mosquito foraging behaviour is of fundamental biological interest and practical importance for preventing infectious diseases such as malaria and dengue. Mosquitoes sense CO2, skin odours, heat and moisture with high sensitivity, but how mosquitoes use this information to navigate towards a human in turbulent air flow is yet unclear. Tracking experiments in wind tunnels are an advanced model to study mosquito host seeking flight but have important limitations and the results from current regression-type analyses are hard to generalise to field settings. In addition, such analyses typically rely on summary statistics of whole trajectories and thus don’t account for autocorrelation and behavioural changes within trajectories. Therefore, new analytic frameworks and predictive model for individual mosquito flight trajectories are needed to advance understanding of mosquito host seeking behaviour. 
Aims
I aim to improve the understanding of mosquito foraging flight in response to the environmental conditions with respect to airflow, CO2, skin odour and heat. In particular, I will (A) Provide a framework to analyse mosquito flight on the level of individual trajectories and simulated data on airflow, CO2 and odour along each trajectory; (B) Model mechanistically how mosquitoes use sensorial information on air velocity, CO2 odour and heat to navigate during foraging flight; (C) Asses to what extent the experimentally observed mosquito foraging flight trajectories are driven by cue-following and identify flight patterns which relate to other behavioural modes.
Methods
I use computational estimators of intrinsic dimension (ID) to analyse behavioural modes within single trajectories. I use Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) stochastic processes and modifications thereof, which depend on environmental covariates as predictive models of mosquito movement at the trajectory level, and fit them to data by computational Bayesian methods. Depending on the success in addressing the objectives with the OU approach and depending on timing, I may also use stochastic simulators fitted to data by approximate Bayesian computation and a machine learning simulator trained with reinforcement learning. The lab experiments that generated the tracking data and the computational fluid dynamics simulations that generated the data on environmental conditions were performed by collaborators.
Results
I expect to deliver an analytic framework based on intrinsic dimension to cluster behavioural modes within single trajectories. Thus, I will be able to quantify for each trajectory the alignment of behavioural switches with changes in the local environment. I will likely find that mosquitoes enter and exit cue-following behaviour and I will be able to indicate under what environmental conditions and in what areas of the wind tunnel this is likely to happen. I have already partly succeeded in fitting of a stochastic movement model to tracking data to quantify the attractiveness of the cue source while taking into account the full time-series data. It is difficult at present to forecast how well the proposed predictive movement models fit to the real data. However, I will likely be able to test whether the hypothesis that a fixed sequence of behavioural modes depending on certain cue combinations guides host seeking flight is supported by the experimental data. 
Impact
A predictive model of mosquito flight trajectories depending on high-resolution environmental conditions is a flexible tool to optimise design of mosquito control interventions such as odour-baited traps. Thus, my work has potential for an important public health impact. In addition, my approach in modelling animal movement in response to high-resolution environmental conditions may be extended to other species.

Title: Three Dimensional Simulations and Optimization of Fish Schools
Abstract:
We wish to perform hydrodynamically accurate simulations of ?ows past self-propelled 3D, ?sh-like  swimmers to examine the interplay between of hydrodynamics, learning and optimization in the formation and dynamics of ?sh schools. We will investigate the capability and mechanisms by 
which such swimmers to exploit vortical structures in a cooperative manner. 
In this work we aim to study ?sh school dynamics by physically accurate simulations of interacting two and three dimensional swimmers. We believe that the combination of the accurate ?ow simulations and learning/optimization algorithms for ?sh schools is a novel approach that 
would help distinguish between hydrodynamic interactions and learned or optimized patterns of behaviour. 
In this context, the focus of this work entails two interlinked components: 
• the simulation of ?sh schooling focusing on resolving accurately the ?ow-structure interactions 
and hydrodynamic interactions of multiple swimming bodies. 
• the investigation of ?sh schooling behavior as determined by various learning scenarios and  resulting in energetic e?ciency, defense against predation, etc. 

These goals require the development of state of the art numerical methods for multiple, complex, de- 
forming bodies immersed in a ?uid. In the context of optimization we will develop novel algorithms 
that combine reinforcement learning and stochastic optimization to help quantifying member and 
group traits such as sel?sh or altruistic behaviors as well as leadership in the context of the ?sh 
school. We expect that the results of these simulations will provide state of the art understanding for the governing mechanisms of collective behaviour of swimmers and will have relevance for realistic engineering and robotic devices.
Keywords: fish schools, flow simulations, flow-structure interactions, reinforcement learning, robotics

Title: Learning student-centered collaboration in the social network teacher education. A mixed-methods study on collaborative activities related to the learning processes of pupils
Abstract:
Collaboration among teachers is significant for the immediate handling of professional tasks, such as team teaching (York-Barr et al., 2007) or in implementing legal requirements such as inclusive schooling (Mavropalias et al., 2023; Sannen et al., 2021), and it has a positive impact on students’ learning outcomes (e.g., Ronfeldt et al., 2015). Collaboration is usually considered a professional standard for educators (Decuyper et al., 2010; Vangrieken et al., 2015) and is demanded as content in teacher education (e.g., Thousand et al., 2006). However, novice teachers often feel inadequately prepared for collaborative activities (Keller-Schneider, 2020). There is a lack of empirical knowledge regarding what current student teachers are learning about collaborative activities, particularly those focused on students’ learning processes (student-centered collaboration) in their education (Bauer & Fabel-Lamla, 2020).
In this project, we are interested in the learning opportunities for student teachers from a sociocultural perspective (Resnick et al., 1991), situated within social interactions. Collectively, these can be described as a social network (McCormick et al., 2011) shaped by the student teachers and other educators through social activities (Engeström, 1999; Kreis & Brunner, 2022). First, this investigation aims to understand what student teachers learn in social interactions and with whom, in terms of student-centered collaboration, referencing which tools are used, and how significant they perceive this for their professional development. Second, we seek to examine the extent to which the perspectives of student teachers in primary education (PE) and secondary education level 1 (S1) diverge. Third, data will be collected using a mixed-methods approach, wherein student teachers are tasked with describing their social network maps either to a peer or to a chatbot. The study will investigate how conversations between student teachers differ from those with a chatbot in terms of content clarity.
Approximately 200 student teachers from PE and S1 will be surveyed about learning opportunities related to student-centered collaboration at the end of their studies. A data collection tool will be developed, whereby student teachers use a web application to enter aspects of the above research question on an egocentric network map. Subsequently, an initial group of student teachers will discuss their egocentric network map with fellow student teachers. In previous applications (Galle et al., 2022), these data have provided a rich dataset, but a trained person capable of asking probing questions has been lacking. A second group will conduct this conversation with a chatbot based on a large language model (a type of AI algorithm). The goal is to develop the chatbot to assume the role of a researcher and ask stimulating follow-up questions.
The data will be analyzed using structuring qualitative content analysis (Kuckartz, 2014) using MAXQDA software. Collaborative learning opportunities will be described, codes quantified, and differences between PE and S1 student teachers quantitatively calculated. It is hypothesized that S1 student teachers, due to a longer study duration compared to PE student teachers, will reference more people and provide a more in-depth description of collaboration. In addition, a method will be explored to aggregate egocentric network maps into an overall network map, aiming to identify extant social structures in learning opportunities and compare those in PE and S1. To assess the data quality of the two aforementioned groups (fellow student teachers vs. chatbot), responses regarding content clarity will be rated using evaluative qualitative content analysis (Kuckartz, 2014), with differences calculated quantitatively.
Student-centered collaboration plays a crucial role in enhancing students' learning. The aim is to understand which social learning opportunities are available to student teachers and how significant they are for their professional development. The comparison between PE and S1 could provide indications of the structural conditions of such learning opportunities. The data collection tool with the chatbot has the potential to collect quantitative data from many student teachers as well as qualitative descriptions of individual cases. Notably, the chatbot could serve as a reflective tool within teacher education programs.
Keywords: KI, activity theory, chatbot, collaboration, collaborative activity, cooperation, data collection with Chatbot, large language model, learning, professionalization, social network, social network approach, social network map, teacher education, team work

Title: Astroparticle Physics in Space: DAMPE and HERD Missions
Abstract:
The Space Astroparticle Physics Group at the Department of Nuclear and Particle Physics (DPNC) of the University of Geneva is a leading multi-disciplinary research group in the areas of cosmic ray physics, gammy-ray and X-ray astronomy, Dark Matter search and space instrumentation.      
Astroparticle physics research in space has been making rapid progress in recent years. Advanced particle detection techniques typically used in accelerator experiments have been successfully applied to detectors deployed with satellites or onboard space stations. Unprecedented measurement precisions have been achieved, and the frontier of direct cosmic ray detection has been pushed to the 100 TeV, and soon to the PeV, region. Space astroparticle physics has become an essential ingredient of the so-called multi-messenger astrophysics, which, by bringing together astroparticle physics, astrophysics and astronomy, provides a powerful multi-discipline tool to explore and understand the physics of extreme phenomena in the Universe. 
The Geneva group has been playing a prominent role in this progress. The group has made key contributions, in both hardware development and data analysis, to several major space missions. Currently the group participates in AMS-02, DAMPE, HERD, POLAR/PLOAR-2, PAN/Mini.PAN and eXTP. The research plan of this request focuses on the direct cosmic detection in the TeV-PeV range with the DAMPE and HERD missions: 
A) DAMPE: Direct measurement of cosmic ray electron flux to above 10 TeV, and that of nuclei (in particular helium, carbon and oxygen) up to 100 TeV/nucleon, using increasingly larger datasets, of up to 8 years of observation, of the DAMPE mission. Machine Learning techniques will be deployed for particle identification, energy correction and direction reconstruction in order to extend the energy reach and to improve measurement precisions. Monitoring and calibration of the DAMPE Silicon-Tungsten Tracker, which the group proposed, and has led its construction and in-orbit commissioning. Production of large Monte Carlo datasets, which are critical for exploring the particle energy range that can never be reached on ground.  
B) HERD: Prototype tests, beam test data analysis, detector calibration and simulation of the HERD Fiber Tracker (FIT), which is proposed and being developed by the Geneva group, financed by the Swiss Space Office, and is currently in the baseline layout of the HERD detector, Science preparation, including layout optimization, software development and the extrapolation of data analysis techniques developed for DAMPE will be carried out, in view of the first data from HERD, which is expected to be launched around 2025. 
The combination of the DAMPE and HERD activities provides a coherent leading-edge research project in the next few years for the group. Both experiments are based on the so-called calorimetric method, i.e. using large calorimeters to precisely measure the energies of high energy particles, and the Geneva group has led or is leading the developments of the tracker for both detectors, thus allowing the project to benefit from significant technical and scientific synergies. Timewise, the DAMPE mission is currently in excellent operation condition and will continue to collect data for at least 4-5 more years, at which point increasing statistics is no more critical, when HERD will start to be operational, overlapping with DAMPE measurements with a 10 times increase in statistics, and more importantly extending the measurements towards PeV, the so-called “knee” region in the cosmic ray spectra. 
The Geneva group collaborates closely with the Department of Astronomy of the University of Geneva and EPFL on these research projects.

Title: High resolution soil moisture: physically based hydrological modeling and downscaling
Abstract: Soil moisture, intended as the water content in the unsaturated soil top layer, is an essential dynamic hydrological property. In fact, being the boundary between land and atmosphere, it plays an important role in the water and energy balance processes. It impacts the energy partitioning between latent and sensible heat at the surface, but also affects the generation of surface runoff (e.g., Merz and Plate, 1997), and several biogeochemical cycles. Furthermore, soil moisture is also essential for diverse applications which require high-resolution estimates of soil wetness over large areas, in the field of natural hazards (landslides, floods, droughts) but also for management decisions (e.g. crop monitoring for irrigation and management decisions). Soil moisture information can be retrieved in several ways: from in-situ or remote sensing measurements or through hydrological modeling. Each of these has advantages, but also limitations. Here, the focus is on estimates based on physically based hydrological modelling, which, compared to measurement based estimates, allows additionally to carry out scenario and sensitivity experiments. This is very important in the context of climate change and analysis of extremes. The limiting factor for model application at the large scale is the computational cost, which only allows simulations at large scales with coarse resolutions (e.g. 1-2 kilometers). The main objective of this research project is to explore how we can obtain higher resolution soil moisture estimates over large domains by combining physically based hydrological modeling with downscaling techniques, similarly to what is being done with remote sensing data. This research will be carried out on two case studies, one small catchment in Switzerland (Napf) and a large river basin in the United States of America (Upper Colorado River Basin). These are selected because of their differences in climate, soil properties, and size. Simulations of the hydrological and land model ParFlow-CLM will be used for the downscaling (coarse resolution model) and as high resolution moisture reference (higher resolution model). Different techniques of geospatial, regressive, and machine learning downscaling will be tested. Their performances will be evaluated in a validation step using statistical measures both based on cell-to-cell and pattern comparison. Of key importance will also be the transferability of the different techniques, i.e. how easily they can be applied to different domains and how robust their performances are. Finally, an example of the usefulness of a high resolution soil moisture estimate will be provided in the context of landslide prediction and understanding of vegetation patterns.

Title: DeepScan: A Deep Learning Model for Automatically Grading Students' Drawings and Feedback Provision
Abstract: To assess students' understanding of mathematical concepts, teachers often employ open-ended problems that can take the form of written responses like short answers and essays. With the rapid advancement of natural language processing, these written responses can now be effectively analyzed and graded automatically.  However, mathematical open-ended work also involves the use of figures, diagrams, and graphs which require students to use digital canvases or upload pictures of their handwritten work on most Learning Management Systems (LMSs). Unfortunately, there are currently few or no available solutions to automatically grade and provide feedback on these types of open-ended responses. This project aims to address this problem in detail by utilizing computer vision, deep learning, and meta learning to develop a robust solution.
Keywords: automatic grading of mathematical graphs, automatic grading of open-ended responses, computer vision, deep learning, e-learning, meta-learning

Title: Approximate references. Indexical procedures and the representation of discourse objects.
Abstract:
The present project is part of my PhD thesis, which aims to describe approximate referential (indexical) procedures in contemporary French discourse. In linguistics, reference is the process by which the speakers talk about the world, i.e., the process by which the language is able to evoke and to point at the world’s objects. Referential (or indexical) procedures are thus means used by speakers to refer to these extralinguistic referents. Among the referential expressions, some introduce a new referent (e.g., the indefinite noun phrase in "Il était une fois une princesse […]"), while others recover a referent already available for the speech participants (e.g., "[…] La /cette princesse / Elle avait de nombreux prétendants"). The latter are called anaphoric expressions. There are two main conceptions of anaphora: one that considers anaphora as a textual and semantic dependency of an expression to what is called its antecedent, i.e., another expression in the preceding text; another that treats anaphora as a cognitive process through which an object already present in the shared knowledge of the interlocutors is retrieved. Under these two conceptions lies the idea that the role of anaphoric procedures is the “resolution” of the anaphoric expression and therefore, a univocal identification of the intended referent.
The purpose of my project is to show that speakers often produce approximate anaphoric references, which do not target a well-determinate object, but, on the contrary, leave its identity underspecified. The expressions specialized for such references are, among others, the pronoun "ça", the anonymous collective "ils" (e.g., as in "Ils ont encore augmenté les impôts"), poor semantic-content expressions like "cette/la chose", "ce/le truc", etc. These linguistic designators are very productive in discourse, particularly in spoken language. However, the subject hasn’t drawn much attention in literature on reference and anaphora. My project has the following goals: i) to identify the expressions that present an inclination towards approximate references; ii) to analyse them in their context of occurrence; iii) to measure the consequences of their account for a general theory of referential procedures in linguistics.
This project is carried out following an empirical and qualitative approach: I work on attested examples in contemporary French, extracted from various written and spoken corpora, in order to capture the phenomenon in a wide range of discourse genres. Numerous authors have studied the question of anaphora with recourse to examples constructed for the purpose of their own analysis, therefore often under their own judgement of acceptability, which partly explains the lack of interest to approximate references in linguistics. The exclusive recourse to attested data for this study of indexical procedures, in particular through spontaneous conversation evidence, has seldom been undertaken. For that purpose, the theoretical framework adopted is a context-constructive approach of discourse: the discourse is the result of a mental collaborative construction by the interlocutors and evolves as the communication unfolds. The anaphoric expressions point directly into the discourse model at the referents, which are thus conceived as cognitive representations, or discourse objects. This conception is compatible with the idea that the speaker can perform approximate references and that the addressee can adapt to underspecified representations, which behaviours the present project aims to examine.
The motivation of this work is the need to develop an appropriate model of reference in linguistics. This study will provide a better understanding of effective indexical procedures in linguistic usage by taking into account approximate references as common practices. The intended audience are linguists working on semantics, pragmatics, syntax, interaction, cognitive linguistics, as well as psycholinguists or orthophonists, all of them being inevitably confronted with anaphora among their respective data. Researchers in language didactics will also find interest in this study. Indeed, in grammar or linguistics manuals, the presentation of anaphora is systematically based on a textual conception. A more reliable and suitable model will give clues as to which linguistic competencies (e.g., interactional, cognitive, argumentative, etc.) the speakers need to handle in order to use anaphoric expressions. Finally, this research will also benefit to researchers in NLP (Natural language processing), regarding the difficulties set by underspecified expressions for automated anaphora resolution.
Keywords: approximate reference, discourse anaphora, discourse model, discourse object, indexical procedures

Title: Real-Time Automatic Sleep Scoring and Sleep Patterns Monitoring during LIFU stimuli tuning
Abstract:
Background/Rationale.  To date,  real-time automatic sleep scoring algorithms are limited to few specific applications. Recently, many scoring algorithms have been developed, but almost all of them are designed for offline applications. The few automatic systems running in real-time are nearly always used to facilitate the delivery of acoustic stimuli at targeted phases (e.g., SleepLoop - University Medicine Zurich). My aim is to test and to optimize my automatic sleep scoring algorithm in real-time and in the context of ultrasound stimulation.
My contribution will be part of a larger framework assessing the use of Low Intensity Focused Ultrasound (LIFU) to deep brain structures, and thalamus in particular, in the context of loss and recovery of consciousness in healthy volunteers as well as in the pathological brain (e.g., Disorders of Consciousness [1]). One branch of this program addresses the use of LIFU in different phases of sleep in healthy volunteers and requires knowing the sleep phase of the subject, thus real-time sleep scoring. The ultimate clinical goal of this project is to evaluate the ability of this technique to allow modulating transitions from deep-sleep stages to the awake state, and to be able to modulate the transitions from a sleep stage to the other with the external stimuli. As stated in [1], LIFU trains are delivered with a specific setup of the hardware. This setup may have to be customized on each subject, thus rendering the pre-setting not effective for the ultimate clinical purpose. Hence, in this study there is also the need to develop offline an automatic system able to forecast the optimal stimulation setup.

Objectives/Aims. Aim1. Validate our sleep scoring architecture in real-time, in the context of ultrasound stimulation. Aim2. Develop an automatic tool monitoring sleep patterns and features online. Aim3. Develop a machine learning based regressor able to forecast the optimal LIFU setup (e.g. LIFU pulse repetition frequency or duty cycle) for an efficient sleep modulation procedure. Clinical Assessments. Assessment1. Assess the efficacy of LIFU, a novel, safe and non-invasive technology, as a means of recovering the awake state from the deepest sleep state SWS. Assessment2. Assess the preliminary efficacy of LIFU as a means of modulation of sleep stages, i.e. transitions from deep to shallow sleep stages.

Methods. Deep learning optimization techniques will be used to enhance my sleep scoring algorithm in the new context of ultrasound stimulation. In order to develop the tool forecasting the optimal LIFU personalized setup, machine learning algorithms will be employed, together with features selection methodologies. Several evaluation metrics (e.g. per-class F1-score and the Cohen’s kappa) will be employed to assess the goodness of our algorithms. In this study, I also have the opportunity to learn how to set-up and administer LIFU stimulation, thus gaining additional knowledge from the expertise within the MontiLab.

Expected Results/Impact. Despite the change of domain (dataset and recording hardware) and despite the likely impact of LIFU stimuli on EEG waves, I expect the sleep scoring system to reach high performance (>85% in overall accuracy). I also expect that it will be possible to validate the hypothesis, through different offline analysis and ML algorithm development, that each subject needs a customized stimulation procedure. From a clinical point of view, the primary expected outcome is the efficacy of LIFU in modulating states of awareness and arousal and, in particular, its recovery from states of unconsciousness. Indeed, this specific research project is part of a three-pronged approach assessing the ability of enhancing recovery from states of unconsciousness including anesthesia [2], patients with disorders of consciousness [1], and sleep [3].
Keywords: Deep Learning, Low Intensity Focused Ultrasound, Machine Learning, Real-time Automated Systems, Sleep Patterns, Sleep Scoring

Title: From beauty to strangeness: a flavour approach to probing new interactions
Abstract:
The Standard Model (SM) has been standing for over 50 years as our best theory of particle physics, describing sub-nuclear phenomena with great precision. Experiments have validated it to a remarkable degree.
However, the SM fails to accommodate essential phenomena observed in Nature. It does not, for example, provide an identity to a striking 84% of the matter contained in the Universe.
Our understanding of the remaining part -the fundamental fermions, i.e. quarks (q) and leptons (l), that compose the matter we are made of- is not devoid of problems, either. For instance, we have yet no explanation for the large abundance of matter compared to antimatter.
Moreover, the fundamental fermions of the SM come in three copies. The origin of this property, called flavour, is completely unknown. The parameters that describe the fermion masses and flavour mixings inexplicably span 12 orders of magnitude, and show a hierarchical pattern that the SM leaves unexplained.
This lack of understanding concerns both the quark and the lepton sector.
To answer these fundamental questions of Nature, a theory that complements the SM with New Physics (NP) should be found, based on findings informed by experimental data.
In the quark sector, ideal laboratories to look for NP are flavour-changing transitions, where effects due to NP could be enhanced.
Recent measurements of such transitions have opened cracks in the SM: intriguing anomalies have emerged in the decays of beauty (b) hadrons, suggesting the possible presence of new particles.
An additional puzzle is present in the lepton sector. The three neutral leptons, neutrinos, are the most elusive particles of the SM. Their flavour structure is also hierarchical, though we cannot tell why their masses are so small, nor why they have a mass at all. Neutrinos naturally undergo flavour-changing oscillations, with large mixing angles.
New theories aimed at explaining the flavour structure of the SM as well as the b-anomalies also predict modifications of the neutrino sector.

This project addresses the flavour problem by undertaking two complementary Aims.
Aim 1 scrutinizes rare quantum-loop quark-flavour changing processes. These are sensitive to effects from new virtual particles, thus probing NP at a mass scale much larger than the range currently available for direct searches. The LHCb experiment, a forward arm spectrometer at the LHC devoted to study the decays of hadrons containing heavy quarks, has detected several anomalies in b->sll transitions. These anomalies could turn into imminent discovery of NP if independently confirmed. This can be achieved by looking at different processes governed by the same quark-level transition. I propose two new methods to do so:
1. the first ever inclusive amplitude study of b->sll transitions at a hadronic b-factory, to take full advantage of the LHCb luminosity;
2. the analysis of angular observables in rare 5-body decays, observables never probed up to now.

Aim 2 fills large gaps in our knowledge of the neutral lepton sector. Neutrinos interact only weakly: therefore, we have scarce information on their scattering cross-sections. On the other hand, neutrino interactions are a golden resource for applications that range from astronomy to the study of the inner compositions of protons and neutrons. I propose here a novel approach to the reconstruction of electromagnetic and hadronic showers, by using machine learning and tracking detectors. This idea has immediate application in upcoming neutrino physics experiments aimed at measuring neutrino cross-sections at LHC energies for the first time, and it will also enable the use of the same detectors to look for dark matter in an as of yet unexplored mass domain.
Keywords: B physics, LFU, amplitude analysis, flavour, flavour anomalies, neutrino, new physics, real-time neutrino physics

Title: Magnetic field effects on hydrodynamic instabilities in dense plasma mixing
Abstract:
The proposed research investigates how magnetic fields influence the growth of hydrodynamic instabilities and heat transport in dense plasmas, processes that play a critical role in inertial confinement fusion. While magnetic fields have been shown to improve fusion performance by enhancing energy confinement and reducing instability growth, the physical mechanisms responsible for these effects are not yet well understood. This project aims to establish a fundamental, experimentally grounded understanding of how magnetic fields modify instability development and material mixing in dense plasma flows.
Addressing this challenge requires experiments with high spatial and temporal resolution capable of producing benchmark-quality data for validating radiation–magnetohydrodynamic simulations. Such data are essential for improving predictive modeling capabilities in high-energy-density plasma environments.
The experimental program will use a pulsed-power platform capable of generating intense soft X-ray radiation and multi-Tesla magnetic fields to produce dense, well-diagnosed plasma flows. A comprehensive set of diagnostics, including optical and X-ray techniques, will provide quantitative measurements of plasma density, temperature, velocity, ionization state, and magnetic field structure. The research is structured in three stages: first, characterization of uniform planar ablation flows; second, investigation of interacting plasma flows to study mixing layers and instability growth; and third, examination of how externally applied magnetic fields alter instability evolution and plasma morphology. The resulting datasets will serve as benchmarks for validating radiation–magnetohydrodynamic models through direct comparison with synthetic diagnostics.
To maximize insight and efficiency, data analysis and simulation workflows will be supported by machine-learning tools for rapid diagnostic interpretation and optimization of model parameters. This integrated experimental and computational approach will enable faster feedback between observations and simulations and support adaptive experiment design.
The outcomes of this research will advance understanding of magnetized plasma dynamics, improve the reliability of numerical models, and inform the design of future inertial confinement fusion concepts. Beyond fusion energy, the results will be relevant to a broad range of high-energy-density and astrophysical plasma phenomena where magnetic fields, radiation, and hydrodynamic instabilities play a central role.

Title: Chemical Space Inspired Building Blocks and Peptides for Medicinal Chemistry
Abstract: The chemical space of all possible molecules of interest for medicinal chemistry is extremely large and difficult to grasp. Our goal is to develop computationally driven workflows connecting the theoretical concept of chemical space to actual computations with large databases of molecules, design, synthesis and activity testing in the laboratory. Such workflows can have a transformative effect on drug discovery by uncovering new dimensions and compound classes. We combine computational and experimental approaches in the areas of small molecules and peptides.  The first part on small molecules aims to identify and synthesize new building blocks for medicinal chemistry from the chemical space databases GDB originally developed in our group, which enumerate all possible molecules up to a given size, with focus on GDB20 and on polycyclic diamine drug cores as synthetic targets The second part on peptides addresses further developments of our chemical space guided approach to peptide design, with specific projects on machine-learning guided design of antimicrobial peptides, on stereorandomization for antimicrobials and for protein aggregation inhibition, and on mRNA transfection reagents towards vaccine development.
Keywords: antimicrobial peptides, chemical space, cheminformatics, computer-aided synthesis planning, dendrimers, machine learning, peptides, protein aggregation, small molecule drugs, transfection reagents

Title: Logic for synthetic biology
Abstract:
Synthetic biology demonstrated success in engineering simple genetic circuits that are encoded in DNA and perform their function in the cellular environment. However, there remains a need for rigorous quantitative characterization of such small devices and their mutual compatibility. 
In this project, we argue that biologists can greatly benefit from a logical framework which will set grounds for automated reasoning within the modeling process. The starting point of such a framework is a logic for expressing experimental observations. Title: The new frontier of twistronics: twisted bilayer oxides beyond vdW
Abstract:
Two-dimensional (2D) materials are at the forefront of research, due to their unique properties and potential for downscaling next-generation electronic devices. The emergence of twisted van der Waals (vdW) 2D materials and their inherently fascinating features has led to the rise of the field of twistronics: rotating one monolayer relative to another can alter the electronic properties of the single layer, revealing exceptional behaviours in the combined structure. These twisted bilayers create a superstructure known as moiré pattern, where exotic physics phenomena, such as superconductivity, topological effects, strong electronic correlations, emerge. In this context, considerable attention has been given to the well-known graphene and TMDs. However, 2D materials beyond vdW remains largely unexplored, opening a world of fascinating possibilities. Recent findings on 2D perosvskite oxides underline a promising direction to extend the range of interesting materials beyond vdW exfoliable systems, thereby opening new frontiers in twistronics. The aim of this project is to explore the realm of twisted bilayer perosvkite oxides (TBPO). The project will greatly benefit from the extensive expertise of the host group, the group of Prof. E. Kaxiras at Harvard University, a world leader in the study of twistronics. The group had contributed to the first discovery of superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) in 2018, and their knowledge on both the physics and the computational methods will be fundamental on the project’s success. The project will moreover leverage the state-of-the-art machine learning (ML) techniques, which are emerging as powerful tools for studying large systems containing thousands of atoms, as the moiré superstructures. In particular, recent implementations will provide access to properties beyond the electronic band structures, like the electronic transport and the superconducting critical temperature. 
The project aims to achieve the following results: 
- the discovery of fascinating phenomena in a new class of materials for twistronics - twisted bilayers perovskite oxides - beyond vdW monolayers combinations;
- the theoretical prediction of phonon-limited electronic transport and superconductivity in these structures, and understanding how these properties can be tuned by varying the twist angle.
- the application and benchmarking of emerging ML algorithms to study complex moiré superlattices, representing a key advance for the field of twistronics.
The project will be organized as follows:
- the first part will focus on the geometrical relaxation effects of TBPO, in particular the 2D phase of BaTiO3, which has been recently studied experimentally. I will investigate spontaneous corrugations arising from the twisting of two monolayers with respect to each other. To this end, I will train a ML force field using established equivariant neural networks, as implemented in NequIP;
- in the second stage, I will devise a continuum model Hamiltonian for three TBPO (ATiO3, A = Ba, Ca, Sr), building on preliminary results of the host group, and leveraging their large knowledge in these computational methods. Here, I will explore the angle-dependent electronic band structures to identify exotic phenomena.
- lastly, I will investigate electron-phonon related properties. To this end, I will employ recent deep-learning methods using DeepH to first train an Hamiltonian model able to reproduce the moiré electronic bands. This model, combined with the previously trained force field, will serve as the key building block to infer the electron-phonon coupling (EPC). From those, the targeted properties will be computed.
To summarise, this study will serve as a cornerstone in twistronics by exploring a novel class of promising materials, and by establishing new methodologies to study complex moiré systems.
Keywords: 2D, density-functional theory, electron-phonon, electronic band structure, electronic transport, machine learning, moire, twistronics

Title: Interacting random walks
Abstract:
Interacting random walks refer to a variety of models for complex large-scale disordered phenomena, motivated by questions in statistical physics, biology, economics and statistics. The interaction feature of these models produces long-memory effects which cannot be analyzed by the tools of classic probability theory.

Our project aims at developing generic tools, at understanding better its deep links with other topics, as well as to tackle new questions and applications. More specifically, we intend to work on the following topics:

- Gaussian free field (GFF), Branching random walks (BRWs) and Random interlacements
- Random walks in random environment (RWREs)
- Self-interacting random walks (SIRWs)
- Particle systems, forest fires and percolation

These are fundamental models of probability, which gather essential phenomonological structure and difficulties in stochastic processes and statistical physics.

The GFF is at the nexus of most of these models. For instance it is intimately related to random interlacements through the isomorphism theorem. The level set of the GFF and random interlacements bear a key difficulty, in that their percolative structure is mean-field and not local. Important progress has been done on this, and several questions on the critical values remain open.

The BRW, which describes a randomly moving cloud of branching particles, was  introduced in the context of physics and population genetics ; it is also deeply related to the 2d GFF, and consequently to quantum gravity. Indeed, it has proved to be a fundamental tool in the understanding of the maxima of the GFF. One other very interesting direction concerns the BRW with selection, on which we have a strong expertise : several conjectures of physicists remain open.

RWRE is a fundamental model in statistical physics, describing the movement of a particle in a highly disordered medium. It has been introduced as a model of DNA chain replication and crystal growth (see Chernov and Temkin) or turbulent behavior in fluids through a Lorentz gas description (Sinai 1982). Fundamental questions have resisted repeated and persistent attempts to answer them, in particular invariance principles, ballisticity conditions in the non-reversible setting, and in the case of a dynamic environment. The project gathers some of the world experts in that area.

SIRWs are random processes evolving in an environment constantly modified by their own behavior, being for instance self-repelling or self-attracting. They describe a variety of phenomonological behavior and provide a good theoretical tool for learning behavior, with a link to game theory and statistical learning. This is a relatively new subject, which has recently shown deep relation with quantum field theory, Anderson localisation and the KPZ universality class. One important goal is to understand the structure of this apparently very diverse family of models.

Random walks may interact not only with their environment but also with each other, as a system of particles. This can for instance provide models for random growth, forest fires and self-organised criticality. We shall explore the connections with the (deterministic) coagulation-fragmentation equations, which often provide most useful hints for explaining properties in the random setting.

Finally, note that all these models share deep connections and a large class of technical tools. For instance techniques from RWRE, such as renewal structures and environment seen from the particle have found fruitful applications into the study of SIRWs or the propagation front of infectious models. Also, BRW is a central tool to investigate RWRE on trees.

The project will favor collaboration between french and swiss teams, already close scientifically, and will stimulate common research projects and co-supervision of doctoral theses and post-doctoral researchers. An annual conference will also be organized, alternatively by each team of the project.
Keywords: Gaussian Free Field, branching processes, dynamic environment, forest fires, interacting particle systems, percolation, quantum field theory, random interlacements, random walks, random walks in random environment, reinforced random walks, self-interacting processes, stochastic differential equations

Title: Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance-Based Digital Twinning for Biophysics-Enhanced Electrophysiological Sensing
Abstract:
Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance (CMR) delivers detailed insights into the heart's tissue composition, motion, strain, perfusion, and blood flow dynamics. However, the capability to simultaneously derive diagnostic information on the electrical activity of the heart is limited due to the intrinsic interaction between electrical sources and the (electro)magnetic fields used in CMR systems. These interactions distort the Electrocardiography (ECG) signal and, as a result, ECG features are generally non-diagnostic. The magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) effect, in particular, prevents the detection of pathological ECG features, compromising, for instance, monitoring of stress CMR and CMR-guided electrophysiological (EP) interventions. For these and other CMR applications, cardiac digital twins can aid to not only integrate, augment and contextualize various measurement data by embedding biophysical models, but may also enable correction of the MHD effect under different physiological conditions of the patient. To this end, rapid data-driven hemodynamic digital twin updates are required, which is currently an open issue.

The present project proposal aims to realize concurrent CMR and diagnostic ECG via rapid data-driven spatiotemporal digital twinning of function and hemodynamics. To achieve the objective, a three-stage approach is envisaged based on 1) Concurrent Function and Flow Imaging, which will provide simultaneous time-resolved data on cardiovascular function and hemodynamics, 2) Rapid Shape Learning, Data Augmentation and Biophysical Modeling to derive dynamic cardiac and aortic anatomical models, blood velocity vector fields and functional models and 3) Biophysics-Enhanced Electrophysiological Sensing to update spatiotemporal cardiac and aortic digital twins and output diagnostic ECG signals for guiding diagnosis and interventions. The value of our approach will be demonstrated for CMR stress testing and CMR-guided EP interventions. The program is structured in four work packages (WP):

WP1 - Concurrent Function and Flow Imaging
* Synthesis of cardiac and aortic flow data using personalized biophysics simulations
* Design and implementation of PC-BSSFP sequences and reconstruction
* Optimization of volumetric (PC-BSSFP) and navigator (PC-NAV) data acquisition
* Data collection and protocol refinement in volunteers 

WP2 - Rapid Shape Learning, Data Augmentation and Biophysical Modeling
* Extraction of cardiac and vascular anatomy from PC-BSSFP data
* Navier-Stokes-based flow augmentation to interpolate/extrapolate/augment flow data
* Physics-informed neural networks to simulate cardiac function
* High-fidelity models and physics-informed neural networks to simulate MHD effect
* Low-rank modeling and ablation experiments to inform and refine data acquisition strategies

WP3 - Biophysics-Enhanced Electrophysiological Sensing
* Recording of volumetric PC-BSSFP and PC-NAV data along with 4-lead ECG traces
* Integration of real-time digital twin updates using PC-NAV and ECG data
* Extension from 4- to 12-lead CMR-compatible ECG unit

WP4 - Application to Cardiac Stress Testing and Electrophysiological Interventions
* Integration of PC-NAV into CMR stress perfusion protocol
* Pilot CMR perfusion study on cardiac patients under rest and stress condition
* Incorporation of PC-NAV into active catheter tracking protocol; addition of holographic display
* Data collection in patients prior to and during CMR-guided EP interventions

The work envisaged is based on documented experience and expertise in CMR pulse sequence design and image reconstruction, image processing, biophysical modeling, image data synthesis and inference using classical and physics-informed machine learning as well as clinical translation of novel methodology. The research will permit significant advances of CMR-guided diagnostics and interventions by enabling concurrent CMR imaging and diagnostic surface ECGs under both rest and stress conditions.

Title: Improving hepatocellular carcinoma screening in Switzerland: new strategies.
Abstract:
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the second leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide and the fifth in Switzerland. The stage of disease at time of diagnosis determines prognosis and treatment effectiveness. To enable early detection of potentially curable HCC, clinical practice guidelines recommend semi-annual surveillance with liver ultrasound (US) with or without serum alfa-feto protein (AFP). However, US and AFP are known for limited HCC diagnostic accuracy.
In this context, in order to achieve a higher diagnostic performance of HCC screening, different alternative strategies need to be tested. First, the use of CEUS could be a valuable tool in case of lesion found on US in order to reduce false positive rates allowing diagnostic of benign lesions during the exam. Thus, this will increase US specificity and decrease the rate of US-related unnecessary complementary investigations. However, it was never tested in the context of HCC screening. Alternatively, a novel concept of abbreviated MRI (AMRI) screening strategy has been conceived. AMRI consists in the selection of sequences designed to answer the targeted question of HCC detection, thus reducing time and cost while maintaining high diagnostic accuracy. Multiple AMRI protocols have been proposed, with retrospective investigation allowing to the conclusion that Dynamic (Dyn)-AMRI is the most accurate protocol for HCC screening, with higher diagnostic performance than non-contrast (NC)-AMRI and gadoxetate-enhanced hepatobiliary phase (HBP)-AMRI. However, these results require prospective validation in screening conditions, particularly regarding the head-to-head comparison of US to each HCC screening alternative that is missing. Moreover, Dyn-AMRI was never tested prospectively with the proper intravenous (IV) contrast (extracellular contrast agent instead of gadoxetate acid), with expected higher diagnostic performance. Moreover, NC-AMRI presents the advantage of not requiring IV contrast injection that - despite its lower sensitivity compared to Dyn-AMRI - needs to be consider in the context of screening. In complement to AMRI, recent progress in deep learning (DL) for medical imaging evidenced that it is now robust enough for routine clinical use including for cancer detection. DL could be used as an additional tool for radiologists, for detection sensitivity improvement and/or for reduction of interpretation time, both crucial in a screening context. Lately, as any screening test needs to be cost-effective in the cost-health system where it is intent to be used, a cost-effectiveness analysis integrating each potential strategy within the particular Swiss HCC screening population and health system is required. Even if preliminary results evidenced the cost-effectiveness of AMRI in North America, it was never tested in Europe and cost effectiveness of CEUS and DL for HCC screening are currently unknown.
The ultimate objective of the present project is to develop and validate a novel screening strategy for HCC screening suited to at-risk patients in Switzerland. This precise, safe, available and cost-effective method will help detecting asymptomatic HCC at an early, curable stage, which ultimately should reduce death burden from HCC. In order to achieve this objective, the project will comprise three work packages (WP):
- WP 1: Compare the diagnostic performance of US, CEUS and AMRI for HCC detection in an at-risk population. 
- WP 2: Exploratory aim: Develop and test a DL model for HCC detection based on AMRI.
- WP 3: Perform a cost-effectiveness analysis comparing US to different alternative screening strategies for HCC in Switzerland.
A prospective observational study comparing US, CEUS and AMRI head-to-head for HCC screening in patients at risk followed in Lausanne University Hospital is planned. Imaging follow-up will continue as long as the patient does not develop HCC. Data from WP 1 will be used to train the DL model and to perform the cost-effectiveness analysis comparing each alternative strategies for HCC screening. Target enrollment for this study is 330 patients, as this is expected to yield 30 patients with HCC.
Keywords: Abbreviated MRI, Cancer screening, Contrast-enhanced ultrasound, Cost-effectiveness analysis, Hepatocellular carcinoma, Machine learning

Title: Understanding individual differences in predisposition to aggressive phenotypes and their modulation by stress
Abstract:
Aggression and violence represent a great burden to individuals and societies, highly contributing a broad range of problems worldwide. Most of the share of the violence in society stems from the general population (i.e., not patients) and attempts to reduce aberrant aggression from happening has proved to be a difficult task. A major deterrent allowing the progress of research in humans is the lack of appropriate instruments to elicit and measure aggression in the lab, frequently relying on either subjective ratings or 2D-based computer tasks, that suffer from response bias, low standardization, low experimental control and poor immersive capabilities. Recent developments on virtual reality (VR) provide improved ecological validity, reproducibility, and robust experimental control. However, to date, the few VR studies to investigate aggressive behaviors in humans have mainly focused on ‘fictious’ violent video games or fictious scenarios. Therefore, it would be important to develop novel VR scenarios in which aggressive acts can be provoked in meaningful and credible situations. On the other hand, the field has traditionally focused on a discrete number of specific behavioral and/or physiological parameters when attempting to characterize aggression phenotypes. This focused approach is rather limited in the conclusions it can deliver. Our lab has developed a pilot study contributing VR scenarios with ecological validity leading to a high degree of engagement on the side of the participants, and capable of capturing the range of aggressive tendencies including both proactive and reactive components.  
In this project, we capitalize on recent developments in VR technology coupled with detailed analyses of behavioral and physiological responses to develop standardized semi-naturalistic immersive VR environments capable of eliciting in participants both reactive and proactive aggressive behaviors. We will recruit 550 participants from the general population and refine and validate our recently developed VR aggression tests and, then, apply various computational methods (e.g., Bayesian modeling, machine learning) to the multi-dimensional data acquired with the overarching goal of understanding which behavioral and physiological markers define specific aggression typologies, eventually providing relevant biomarkers of aggression. Further, we will study how exposure to stress affects individuals’ behavioral and physiological responses when confronted to tests for aggression using the newly developed VR scenarios. The specific AIMS of this project are:
1. To develop and refine standardized semi-naturalistic immersive VR environments capable of eliciting reactive and proactive aggressive behaviors.
2. To perform a deep behavioral and physiological phenotyping of individuals in order to enrich the characterization of meaningful features to better understand the aggression profiles
3. To identify clusters of individuals showing distinct aggression profiles through unsupervised clustering from key indicators of aggression from a VR paradigm.
4. To identify psychophysiological predictors of different aggression profiles.
5. To investigate the impact of stress exposure on individuals’ aggressive responses and physiological concomitants. 
We expect that our project will deliver groundbreaking knowledge of the behavioral and physiological architecture of human aggressive behavior, and how it changes under stress, that will greatly advance knowledge on human aggression and open key avenues to advance research in order to develop effective treatments.
Keywords: aggression, anxiety, autonomic nervous system, cortisol, empathy, fear, virtual reality

Title: Queerness as gap: an artistic research project on how digital interfaces restrict queerness and how it can be recovered.
Abstract:
In an increasingly digital world, where online spaces shape our daily interactions and self-expression, the intersection between technology and identity has become a focal point of inquiry. Early internet scholars envisioned cyberspace as a realm of liberation from physical constraints, particularly for marginalized communities of Queer individuals. Yet, despite efforts by cyberfeminists in the 1990s to carve out more inclusive digital spaces, the internet has often reflected and perpetuated offline inequalities, reinforcing gender and racial biases. Recent studies have highlighted the ambivalent nature of online platforms, offering both opportunities for self-expression and new forms of surveillance and control. This research project Queerness as gap seeks to explore the impact of digital interfaces and artificial intelligence on Queer identities within online environments. Drawing on insights from Science and Technology Studies (STS), media studies, and digital art, the project aims to dissect how AI technologies constrain and shape Queer expression. Through a series of case studies, including experiments with facial recognition software, neural machine translation, and conversational AI, the project will investigate how these technologies mediate Queer identity online. Additionally, media digital arts practices form part of the practice-based research to develop affective experiences, counter and critical AI apps that challenge normative assumptions and foster critical reflection with the public and within the Queer community.   
Queerness as gap will contribute new insights into the socio-technical dynamics of digital culture and AI, and their implications for Queer communities. These findings will contribute to the interdisciplinary field of STS, advancing theoretical and empirical understandings of how technoscience impacts queer communities and shapes values. The project's outcomes will be disseminated through academic journals, conferences, and public exhibitions, promoting critical engagement with digital media and fostering greater inclusivity within online spaces.
Keywords: Digital art, Digital identities, Gender, Queer AI, Queer studies, Science and Technology Studies (STS)

Title: Innovative Computational Methods for Ultra-Fast Simulations of Coupled Physical and Chemical Processes Using Machine Learning and GPU Parallel Computing
Abstract:
Simulating coupled physical and chemical processes is not only scientifically challenging, but computationally intense, due to the usual high computing costs of chemical reaction calculations. Examples of environmental and engineering problems that involve these coupled processes are: reactive fluid flow in porous media, remediation of polluted groundwater, ore forming processes, fuel combustion in engines, geologic carbon storage, geothermal energy systems, enhanced oil recovery. Both chemical and physical processes are strongly coupled. In a porous medium, for example, chemical reactions alter fluid and rock composition, which change their physical and chemical properties (e.g., rock porosity and permeability, fluid density and viscosity), ultimately affecting how fluids flow and how heat and chemical species are transported.

Chemical reactions in fluid flow simulations can account for over 99% of all computational costs. Ideally, a more balanced cost would be preferred when simulating physics and chemistry together. However, by analyzing the nature of the computations involved in each case, it appears to be impossible that this can ever be achieved in complex cases. When simulating physical processes, this usually means solving sparse systems of linear equations, resulting from the discretization of partial differential equations that govern conservation laws. The computing cost for modeling chemical processes, on the other hand, include the (i) computation of thermodynamic properties of dozens to hundreds of species using intricate equations of state that model the non-ideal behavior of fluid and solid phases (e.g., aqueous, gaseous, solid solutions); (ii) solution of a system of non-linear equations to calculate chemical equilibrium states or to integrate the differential equations governing the chemical kinetics evolution of the system. These two-step operations occur at every mesh cell, at every time step in reactive transport simulations.

This short analysis shows that the cost of modeling chemical processes is, in general, substantially higher than that for modeling physical processes. Thus the question arises: 

    How can chemical processes be calculated as fast as, or perhaps faster than, physical processes? 

Achieving this goal is this project's main objective:

    Enable complex simulations of fluid flow and heat transfer, coupled with chemical reactions, to be performed substantially faster, by a few orders of magnitude, by essentially decreasing the computing costs of chemical reaction calculations. 

From the previous analysis, this seems impossible to accomplish in most cases, especially when complex chemical systems with dozens to hundreds of phases and chemical species are considered. It is indeed a difficult task if conventional numerical methods are used. However, this project goes unconventional: it employs a special machine learning algorithm that can learn on-demand how to rapidly and accurately predict future similar chemical reaction calculations. The smart predictions mainly consists of a single small matrix-vector multiplication, and are thus faster than the full, conventional chemical reaction calculations by orders of magnitude. A proof of concept of this algorithm is presented in Leal et al. (2017).

This proposed research project is not purely theoretical, which would limit its usefulness for the applied scientific community, more concerned in developing new technologies and understanding complex phenomena, rather than numerical methods! The most meaningful benefit of this research for the scientific community will be an open-source numerical simulator implementing all the here-proposed innovative computational methods that will permit them to increase chemical model complexity and yet be able to make faster simulations. This simulator will be benchmarked against experimental data and other simulators, as well as used for modeling complex deep geothermal systems that use CO2 as the geothermal energy extraction fluid. This will be done in collaboration with experts in the field from various institutions as described later.
Keywords: GPU parallel computing, chemical equilibrium, chemical kinetics, chemical reactions, machine learning, reactive transport

Title: Text-based Nudges for Well-being: Causal Effects of Linguistic Properties
Abstract:
Ensuring healthy lives and promoting well-being for all is a global priority and a United Nations sustainable development goal. To that end, behavioral nudges aiming to promote online and offline well-being emerged as a promising approach to be used by stakeholders in conjunction with traditional policies. For example, online counter-messaging interventions can reduce harassment, while dish labelling interventions can successfully promote healthy and sustainable dietary choices. However, although designing behavioral interventions is an active research area, recurrent limitations emerge. It remains difficult to isolate the causal effect of the intervention on behavioral outcomes, and it is challenging to link the outcomes with specific features of the textual nudge.

We propose a project that leverages natural language processing and causal inference to understand how to use linguistic cues for behavioral interventions. First, we will develop methodological approaches for identifying causal effects of linguistic properties of nudges and, second, we will derive empirical insights about their effectiveness. The general approach in this project will be to combine ideas from observational and quasi-experimental identification with modern language model representations to minimize the impact of confounding factors. The project focuses on two well-being applications related to online and offline interventions.

The first empirical study in the proposal will leverage behavioral nudges to improve online spaces. Through a collaboration with Nextdoor, we will conduct a study with the goal of improving toxicity detection and examining the effectiveness of behavioral interventions urging users to reconsider posting harmful content. We will design an observational framework to identify the causal effect of linguistic properties of a nudge on the success of the intervention. The findings will be validated via A/B tests with Nextdoor users. Nextdoor is willing to incorporate tested nudges into the product features. We believe that the project will help Nextdoor fight harassment and racism on its platform. The methods and the findings will have wide implications for designing online communities where all participants feel connected, respected, and safe.

The second empirical study attempts to discover how to use linguistic cues to promote healthy and sustainable dietary behaviors. We will aim to discover how to make the language of sustainable and healthy food appealing by analyzing online recipe descriptions. Findings will be validated by varying the wording of dish names and descriptions through collaboration with Stanford dining halls. This study will have clear implications for fostering healthy habits and improving public health.

The project will be advised by Prof. Dan Jurafsky, who is the leading researcher in computational linguistics and a unique expert in the studies of the language of food. Additionally, we assembled an interdisciplinary team with two psychology experts. The first outcome will be a framework that allows the isolation of causal factors of linguistic properties across domains. The second outcome will be empirical findings about strategies for promoting well-being. The findings will be validated through field experiments and will have broad implications for content moderation, civility, and health research. Beyond research communities, the contributions will have immediate takeaways for practitioners and policy-makers.
Keywords: A/B tests, NLP, anti-social behavior, causal inference, computational social science, data science, health, nudges, well-being

Title: Sparse and hierarchical Structures for Speech Modeling (SHISSM)
Abstract:
Computer science is currently witnessing the emergence of major research activities, arising (more or less independently) from multiple disciplines (statistics, linear algebra, human brain research), and being applied in different ways in multiple application areas, including big data mining, statistical pattern recognition, computer vision, and speech processing (synthesis and recognition). These emerging research areas, which will be investigated in the context of SHISSM , include (1) more and more focus on posterior-based features and systems; (2) revival of (brain-inspired) Artificial Neural Networks in the form of deep/hierarchical architectures (referred to as Deep Neural Networks - DNNs); (3) full exploitation of modern compute resources (big data, large GPU-based processing); (4) sparse coding seeking sparse representation of the processed signals; and (5) compressive sensing and sparse recovery, aiming at modeling the speech signal in large-dimensional sparse spaces (reminiscent to what is believed to happen in the human brain), resulting in simpler processing (e.g., recognition) algorithms.
Building upon several predecessor projects, which resulted in strong theoretical and experimental outcomes, SHISSM is thus very ambitious and aims at developing a better theoretical understanding allowing for a principled combination of ‘deep’ (hierarchical) and ‘sparse’ architectures, driven by advanced statistical modelling (posterior-based approaches, as estimated at the DNN outputs), compressive sensing, sparse recovery, and the formal links recently identified by the PI of this project between Hidden Markov Models (HMM) and compressive sensing, also exploiting posterior distribution estimated by DNNs. 
SHISSM is thus an interdisciplinary project tying together these important emerging areas in the context of speech modeling, and Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) in particular, although its impact is expected to go go far beyond speech. Ideally, the targeted framework should result in a unified model, more performant on complex pattern recognition tasks, while also providing interesting biological motivations. In the particular context of speech modeling, and has already demonstrated through some of the PI’s work (discussed later), the resulting approach should be more effcient and more performant that standard HMMs (or hybrid HMM/DNN systems currently considered as state-of-the-art), while also being more biologically-sound, and relevant to other related areas such as speech synthesis, speech coding and human speech intelligibility modeling. 
This project proposal is intended to consolidate and extend the efforts currently being developed in the context of the the Swiss NSF project PHASER QUAD (2 years, 200020 169398), supporting two excellent PhD students (Pranay Dighe and Dhananjay Ram1, whom should nearly have defended their PhD thesis by the start of the present project).
Exploiting recent developments around the above research areas, and further developing our various, state-of-the-art, machine learning and speech processing tools, often available as Idiap open source libraries2, as well as through the GitHub site3, or integrated in other open source toolkits like Kaldi4), the resulting systems will be evaluated on the several international benchmark databases (including, depending on the type of research, TIMIT (phones), Phonebook (words), Switchboard (sentences), AMI (noisy and conversational accented speech), GlobalPhone (multilingual), and ITU subjectively scored data (for human auditory modeling).
Keywords: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), deep architectures, deep neural networks (DNN), hierarchical posterior-based ASR, hierarchical sparse coding, human auditory modeling, sparse recovery modeling, speech intelligibility modeling

Title: Expanding acetabular fracture classification using 3D CT analysis and deep learning techniques
Abstract:
Background and rationale:
The existing acetabular fracture classification system of Letournel based on radiographs lacks reliability in non-expert surgeons and inclusivity due to changes in trauma mechanisms, demographics, and diagnostic innovations. Recent and current modifications in the diagnostic work-up of acetabular fractures are still needed to overcome the issues noted above. Thus, due to the shift from high-energy trauma in young people to low-energy trauma in a geriatric population and the increase of technological capabilities such as CT scans and 3D modelling, a new classification system is desperately needed. In conclusion, the Letournel system and plain radiographs remain the mainstay of initial fracture classification, followed by additional CT scans assessed using a decision tree algorithm. For a 3D classification system of acetabular fractures to gain clinical acceptance, it must be reliable and efficient. Leveraging CT segmentation and deep learning technologies, an automated algorithm capable of 3D modelling and classification can be developed. Such a computerized solution could provide clinicians with consistent, reliable, and efficient fracture classification support. Finally, such a system should provide a reliable framework to support the study and treatment of new fracture patterns emerging from the shift to low-energy trauma.

Overall aim:
To evaluate whether an automatic classification algorithm based on modern technologies, such as deep learning, can improve the reliability and inclusiveness of acetabular fracture classification, thereby enhancing surgical planning and patient outcomes.

Specific objectives:
(1) To assess the automatic algorithm's performance in acetabular fracture classification by comparing its reliability against that of senior consultant acetabular surgeons.
(2) To identify and incorporate novel acetabular fracture types into the existing classification system, using data analytics and correlation with morphology and hip diagnostic factors.

Methods:
In contrast to using a deep learning model for direct classification, we will explore a two-tiered classification algorithm to address the limitations of fracture type distribution inhomogeneity and the variation in fracture type sizes. In the first tier, we will investigate a deep learning-based classification model to classify the high-frequency (approx. =10%) fracture types (BC, PW, Tr+PW, AC) and group the rest into an “other” category. Then, for cases that fall under the “other” category, we will investigate a second-tiered, more specialised geometry-based classification approach to differentiate among less frequent fracture types (approx. <10%) or an “uncertain” type. Hence, we will leverage the power of deep learning for the most common cases while still accurately classifying rarer ones using alternative methods.

Impact:
This research project aims to revolutionize the diagnosis and treatment planning of acetabular fractures by integrating AI, particularly deep learning. Our two-tier system initially combines deep learning with traditional machine learning for reliable results but aims to transition to a purely deep learning-based algorithm as more CT data becomes available. The focus isn't limited to acetabular fractures; the framework can be adapted for other joint injuries and conditions like osteoporosis. From a research perspective, the project will enable follow-up studies on various factors, such as coxometry and postoperative assessments, and plans to expand into a multicenter study for greater generalisability. Open-source sharing of code will encourage collaborative advancements, and the project will ultimately position the Department of Orthopaedic Surgery at Inselspital as a global leader in acetabular fracture management. Future work includes uncertainty analysis to validate the reliability of AI-driven decisions.
