Title: Machine learning structure and site dependent DFT+U parameters
Abstract:
Density functional theory (DFT) has become the primary method for electronic structure calculations in condensed matter physics, chemistry, and material science. DFT calculations applied to transition metal oxides however suffer from the self-interaction error that leads to an over-delocalization of electrons in transition-metal d-derived orbitals. At the DFT level of theory, this shortcoming can be corrected by using the DFT+U method or hybrid functionals. The former has the advantage of being computationally affordable with a cost only slightly higher than that of a plain DFT calculation, whereas the latter is significantly more expensive especially for extended systems. The main drawback of the DFT+U method consists in the choice of U, which for many years was treated as a parameter to be empirically fitted to experimental data. An alternative approach consists in the self-consistent determination of U from linear-response theory and does not rely on any experimental input. While in a bulk calculation all symmetry equivalent transition metal sites share the same U, the situation becomes more complex when the symmetry is broken, for example by surfaces or point defects. For these situations, it was recently proposed to compute U in a self-consistent and site-dependent approach such that transition-metal sites with a different coordination environment or oxidation state will acquire different U values. While this method results in improved structural and energetic properties for transition metal perovskites, it is computationally significantly more expensive than a plain DFT calculation, yet still cheaper than a hybrid functional calculation. To circumvent the computational burden associated with the self-consistent site-dependent formalism, we propose here to apply machine-learning (ML) techniques based on feed-forward artificial neural networks (ANN) to train a model that predicts a site-dependent U based on structural information only, as illustrated in Figure 1.
 
This will reduce the end-user computational cost of a site-dependent DFT+U calculation to the one of a plain DFT+U calculation. In the present feasibility study, we will apply the approach to TiO2 and hence learn a model for Ti 3d U values that will be validated for the low-symmetry Magnéli phases. The learned model will constitute the beginning of an open-access database of ML models for all transition metal elements in the periodic table, thus enabling highly accurate site-dependent DFT+U calculations at an affordable computational cost as required for example for realistic defect calculations in large supercells.

Title: Understanding Coupled Ionic and Electronic Dynamics in Battery Electrode Materials using Quantum Machine Learning
Abstract: The central scientific goal of this proposal is to enable reliable and accurate simulation of energy materials. Developing novel energy materials can have a huge social, economic, and environmental impact. However, the difficulty in such atomistic modeling is to bridge the vastly different time-scales and length-scales that are involved in the dynamics of these systems. A new computational approach is required since the existing quantum calculations are too complex and costly to be performed for the required duration and the system sizes. To enable such modeling, we need a fast and cheap, yet accurate method to sample atomic conformations as well as a method that can describe the energetics and interactions between particles accurately. The method we propose is motivated by the significant progress that quantum machine learning methods have made in materials modeling. Here, we propose to use advanced sampling techniques based on a newly developed method, so-called Boltzmann generators. This method enables us to generate statistically independent conformations of a complex system in one-shot. Such development will overcome the current limitations of the atomistic modeling of energy materials in realistic conditions. This is essential on a fundamental level for the understanding and design of new materials, whose development is required to overcome many of the intrinsic weaknesses of currently used energy materials. Addressing this scientific challenge can propel the large-scale deployment of novel materials for clean energy technologies.
Keywords: Quantum machine learning, energy, machine learning, materials

Title: Development and Validation of A Multi-modal Image-based Model Generation Method for Non-invasive Dynamic Assessment of Femoroacetabular Impingement (FAI)
Abstract:
Background.
Femoroacetabular impingements (FAI) is defined as a painful dynamic abutment between the hip socket and the femoral head. It is a major cause of primary hip osteoarthritis and one of the key risk factors that may lead to early cartilage and labral damage in young adults. The therapy of FAI involves the surgical resection of the impinging areas of the acetabulum and the proximal femur. Based on a strong research experience on FAI, we know that its diagnosis is difficult and that the current gold standard is problematic as it requires the direct intraoperative visualization of the impingement conflict. A less invasive approach relies on a radiological analysis of standard 2D radiographs and MR images – a task however not automated and whose quality depends on the physician’s expertise. Virtual 3D impingement simulations provide a more objective and accurate way to study FAI but most approaches rely on CT scans, which expose patients to high doses of radiation. MR images were used as a non-invasive alternative to build 3D models for FAI analysis but the resulting approaches were often not fully automatic or required conditions sometimes incompatible with clinical setups (e.g., MR images with large field-of-view (FOV))

Contents and Objectives of the Research Project.
This project will develop an efficient method to generate 3D anatomical models using Computed Tomography (CT)-free imaging protocols that are used in clinical routine in order to support computer-assisted diagnosis and surgical planning of FAI. We will devise a fully automatic approach based on multi-modal images combining 2D X-ray radiograph with 3D Magnetic Resonance (MR) Images acquired with small FOV. In order to achieve this goal, we are aiming to develop A) a fully automatic, machine learning based approach for segmenting 3D MRI data acquired with small FOV; B) a disease-specific, articulated statistical shape model (DS-aSSM) based 2D-3D reconstruction technique to generate 3D patient-specific models from 2D X-rays; and C) a robust multi-modal data fusion method to fuse models generated from A) and B).

Scientific and Social Impact of the Research Project
Although there are many risk factors contributing to hip osteoarthritis (HOA), it is now generally accepted that more subtle bony abnormalities associated with FAI and/or developmental dysplasia (DD) contribute substantially to HOA.  Various studies have suggested that computer-assisted 3D modeling techniques can help clinicians to better understand the dynamic and static factors of FAI – via patient-specific pre-operative planning and intra-operative assessment. Capitalizing on standard FAI diagnosis imaging protocol, i.e., conventional X-rays and MRI, to reduce radiation and to avoid unnecessary disruption to the standard clinical workflow, the proposed CT-free 3D anatomical model generation approach will facilitate a future wide-spread access of computational simulation and virtual surgical planning techniques for patients with FAI and address a key social challenge of our society.

Title: Stroke treatment goes personalized: Gaining added diagnostic yield by computer-assisted treatment selection (the STRAY-CATS project)
Abstract:
Stroke is the second most frequent cause of death and a major cause of disability in industrial countries: in patients who survive, stroke is frequently associated with high socioeconomic costs due to persistent disability. In clinical practice, advanced neuroimaging techniques are increasingly employed for a quick, reliable diagnosis and stratification for therapy.  Tissue-at-risk estimation is frequently performed by MRI, with the infarct core being identified as an area of restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (DWI-MRI). The surrounding severly hypoperfused and  potentially salvageable tissue tissue (i.e. the “penumbra”) is characterized by its delay in arterial transit time using perfusion-weighted MRI. The clinical image interpretation is routinely performed as a visual analysis done by neuroradiologists and/or neurological stroke experts.

There is class I evidence that intravenous thrombolysis is a safe and effective therapy within an estimated time frame of 4.5 h after stroke onset. Very recently, four prospective studies demonstrated the superiority of mechanical thrombectomy in proximal vessel occlusions within a time frame of 6 h after stroke onset. Mechanical thrombectomy has thus become the treatment option of choice to achieve an early and sustained revascularization of proximally occluded vessels in specialized stroke centres2. The recent advent of mechanical thrombectomy has now raised an urgent question that needs to be answered: “can we predict advantageous tissue survival if mechanical thrombectomy is successfully applied compared to the natural course of disease in the presence of sufficient vs. insufficient collaterals?”  The availability of a safe, reproducible and reliable information about the expected tissue salvage would allow not only to select patients that would benefit from mechanical thrombectomy, it would further allow to select patients for revascularization in a time window that exceeds 6 h if sufficient collateral flow enables sustained tissue survival.  

It is essential that indicators for further success of endovascular therapy can be calculated as soon after admission as possible, in order to save as much of the brain tissue as possible: "*time is brain*". Computer-assisted and automated tissue segregation of the infarct core and salvageable penumbra using compound information from multimodal MRI offers a novel and robust standardized solution to this problem: while simple thresholding based on perfusion and diffusion imaging provide only a crude estimate of the tissue at risk, machine-learning approaches based on multimodal MR data overcome the limited accuracy of linear analyses. The proposed machine-learning approach incorporates thus two separate goals, i) to quantify penumbral collateral flow in the acute emergency setting and ii) to identify fingerprints that disentangle salvageable vs. non-salvageable tissue based on machine learning in a “big data” approach based on multiparametric imaging.   We will provide means for i) by transforming the interpretation of image features into an interpretation of the underlying stationary flow field. This will allow us to combine information of all available MR imaging data, to quantify the collateral blood flow in the individual patient before and during intervention, and to compare 4D flow patterns at a population level. We will ii) build on our existing predictive models of stroke outcome, incorporating FLAIR and SWI maps and making use of the "big data" that have been acquired during the last years in more than 1000 patients that underwent intraarterial thrombolysis or thrombectomy. Our overall goal is to investigate if, given sufficient training data, predictive maps of the infarction can improve on the current "penumbra" concept as a tool for identifying patients who will have a favourable response to reperfusion therapy.
Keywords: Machine learning, Magnetic resonance imaging, Mechanical Thrombectomy, Stroke

Title: Convex Q-learning: Optimal policy learning under distribution shifts
Abstract: This research project aims to develop a novel computational framework for learning optimal policies under distribution shifts in a statistically principled manner. By integrating convex Q-learning with distributionally robust optimization (DRO), the project seeks to overcome limitations in existing reinforcement learning approaches, which struggle with long-horizon problems and handling uncertainty including distribution shifts. The research is structured into four key components: developing a tractable formulation of convex Q-learning that incorporates distribution shifts, designing recursive algorithms that enable online learning, benchmarking the proposed methods against state-of-the-art techniques in statistics, economics, and computer science, and releasing an open-source software library to facilitate further research and application. The project will yield both theoretical and algorithmic advancements. On the theoretical side, it aims to establish new statistical efficiency results, providing deeper insights into the generalization properties of robust policy learning. On the algorithmic side, it will focus on developing recursive formulations that leverage stochastic approximation, enabling real-time learning in dynamic environments. The integration of convex Q-learning with DRO presents a novel approach that mitigates computational intractability and ensures policies remain robust under distributional shifts. This research has broad interdisciplinary significance, with applications in economics, energy systems, and control problems. Additionally, it will contribute to the reinforcement learning and statistics communities by offering new perspectives on learning robust policies under uncertainty. The development of a publicly available software library will support education and further research, ensuring long-term impact. Dissemination through academic journals and major conferences will further extend the project's influence across machine learning, operations research, and economics.
Keywords: Distributionally Robust Optimization, Markov Decision Processes, Optimal Policy Learning, Reinforcement Learning, Stochastic Approximation

Title: EdiSE: Energy-Driven Integration in Software Engineering
Abstract:
As digital transformation accelerates, software development has expanded across domains– driving up the energy needed to power the computers and cloud infrastructure that run this software. Digital technology now contributes 4% of global greenhouse gases (GHG) emissions, with energy consumption rising 9% annually. Despite growing awareness of energy consumption, optimization efforts have mainly focused on hardware rather than software. The software engineering (SE) community has identified various energy patterns–best practices to reduce energy consumption, such as efficient data structures and algorithms, programming languages, or libraries–and energy anti-patterns, their inefficient counterparts. However, many programming operations (e.g. loops) in popular languages like Python or C++ remain unexplored in terms of their energy impact, particularly in energy-intensive domains, e.g. data-intensive and AI systems. Identifying energy-efficient practices is a manual and time-consuming task. Even when known, their adoption in development workflow remains low due to lack of awareness, expertise, tool support, and tight deadlines.
SE tools and processes – profilers, linters, AI-based assistants, or code review practices – rarely consider energy efficiency, limiting their impact. As AI-based coding assistants grow
with their own carbon footprint, it is crucial to prevent reinforcing inefficient coding practices and instead refactoring them into energy-efficient alternatives. Addressing these gaps requires a holistic framework for identifying and integrating energy-efficient practices into
software development workflows. Our vision is to redefine how software is designed and assessed in the era of sustainability. By treating energy efficiency as a core software quality attribute – on par with performance and maintainability – we can align the interests of various stakeholders (business, governments, developers, and private citizens, etc.) with the societal goal of ensuring sustainable consumption, Goal-12 defined by United Nations. We do so by devising theories, models, and tools to optimize code energy efficiency while balancing other performance aspects and reshaping developers’ mindsets towards a greener digital future.
Keywords: Empirical Software Engineering, Energy Efficiency, Green Software Engineering, Human Computer Interaction, Machine learning, energy-efficient programming, green IT, green software engineering, software engineering

Title: Computation of positive semidefinite factorizations and their application in physics and machine learning
Abstract:
This research plan describes projects which form the continuation of the work I did during my early postdoc.mobility fellowship at MIT. These projects are interdisciplinary as they draw motivation from both physics and machine learning. 

* Motivation from physics. Given quantum states and measurement operators it is straightforward to compute the probability for measuring specific measurement outcomes. However, oftentimes we need to solve the inverse problem, namely, from measured data we need to infer what the underlying density matrices and measurement operators are. This difficult problem appears in the analysis of quantum experiments (e.g., superconducting qubits) and in the computation of the 1-way quantum communication complexity of Boolean functions. All but one of the proposed projects are concerned with the computational solution of this inverse problem. 

* Motivation from machine learning. Classical models are ubiquitous in our descriptions of general phenomena. This becomes particularly evident when recalling that probabilistic models are classical and vice versa. Large parts of science are concerned with fitting the simplest possible probabilistic model to measured data. On a computer, this task is often infeasible because the simplest model is still too complex to reconstruct. Assume the considered system is indeed best described  in terms of a probabilistic model. Then, whatever model we fit to the measured data, this model represents a compression of a more complex probabilistic model. It is easy to see that we encounter a continuum of choices when searching for a model that represents the compression of a higher-dimensional probabilistic model. We want to select the model that preserves most of the appealing features of probabilistic models. Previously, I showed that under some conditions (sparsity of the probabilistic model and uniqueness of the compressed model), positive semidefinite (psd) factorizations (i.e., quantum models) form a class of models which preserves some operational features of probabilistic models (operational interpretation of the 1-norm). One of the proposed projects aims at a deeper understanding of the relation between compressed probabilistic models and quantum  models. All other projects aim at the computation of psd factorizations of measured data.
Keywords: Analysis of systematic errors, Positive semidefinite factorizations, Quantum Tomography

Title: Dissecting corticostriatal circuit involvement in action learning through reinforcement
Abstract:
According to current models of action learning through trial and error, if a random exploratory action leads to reward, certain dimensions of the action are assigned with credit for the reward – the dimensions are reinforced. Through reselection of those dimensions it is established which aspects of the action are contingent with the reward – the action is refined through practice. The striatum is crucial for this process of action learning. It receives glutamatergic input from sensory, motor, and associative brain regions, and incorporates reward information through phasic dopamine input. The glutamatergic input from cortex is hypothesised to provide the necessary efference copy of the performed/ongoing action, allowing assignment of credit to the relevant dimension of the action through synaptic plasticity at corticostriatal synapses. I will investigate how this mechanism unfolds in the corticostriatal network of the mouse. 
I have developed a novel head-fixed joystick task for mice, which enables selective reinforcing of specific dimensions of skilled forelimb actions. Using this task I will investigate if and how these dimensions of the action are represented in neural activity patterns of the corticostriatal circuitry during learning, how they emerge, and if separate subcircuits are needed to learn specific dimensions. 
Two distinct neuronal classes project from cortex to striatum, intratelencephalic (IT) and pyramidal tract (PT) neurons. I show that for mouse forelimb circuit, these cells are distributed across widespread cortical areas with specific distinctions in their locations. I will use a battery of neurogenetic tools to optically record and manipulate the activity of these neuronal populations while mice are learning and performing new forelimb actions. This will allow me to assign specific action dimensions to distinct cortical areas, cell-types, or activity patterns, and inform which cortical regions are involved in reselection and refinement of the action.

Investigating action learning in a versatile but controlled task, I will be able to ask the fundamental question: which sensorimotor corticostriatal information is needed for which aspects of motor learning through reinforcement. These experiments will extend knowledge of motor control theory and pave the way for future studies on corticostriatal circuit function and dysfunction in disease.

Title: A technician‘s mathematics? The new social realities and new mathematics of German-speaking technical practitioners around 1600.
Abstract: My project is dedicated to the study of how mathematics was shaped by technology and technicians in early modern Europe. Epitomized by the proliferation of fields of application of artificial intelligence, computational technologies profoundly shape our world and will continue to do so in even more significant ways. Taking a historical perspective on mathematization in and of society is essential for an understanding of developments like these. In this respect, scholars have often turned to the epoch of the Scientific Revolution, crediting it with the origin of (modern) science. In the last three decades, however, the classical narratives have been challenged from various angles. One consequence is that studies of the changes in natural knowledge systems have increasingly shifted their focus of analysis from the intellectual to the more practical sphere. As part of this turn, my research is centered around the analysis of German treatises in mathematics written by technician-mathematicians around 1600. The emergence of a specific mathematical and computational culture out of technological craftwork will be delineated, if possible, by the identification of instances in their works that reveal conceptual shifts, which may have been related to their technical practice. The close reading of texts and examination of technical objects will be complemented by an examination of the socio-economic, technological, institutional, and political factors that enabled (or held back) the transmission of knowledge between technology and mathematics, respectively. My research would thus offer a new analytical approach to the field of science and technology studies that accounts for the historical-cognitive materiality of mathematics and assesses the German-speaking practical mathematical culture of technicians at that time (including in particular Jost Bürgi). Beyond providing the basis for a different perspective on the transformations in the study of nature in early modern Europe, my project would offer a view on mathematics as a computational practice that is more suitable for the increasing reliance on technical tools (computers) and can challenge the “immaterial” and elitist public image of mathematics. Finally, understanding the sociopolitical dimension of formal knowledge is a pressing task in the light of the Anthropocene.

Title: Winter Climate Prediction with Machine Learning
Abstract:
In-depth knowledge and understanding of past climate change and variability is crucial to create an adequate framework in which the current and future climatic change, climate extremes and their impacts (economic, social and ecological), can be assessed. Currently, reliable high-resolution climate information of the past 150 years is provided by climate reanalysis products. Essentially being climate models in tandem with weather observations, such data allow for analysis of past climate variability on high spatial and temporal resolution.

New scientific endeavors (so called paleo-reanalyses) expand that timeline to the last 400-500 years by incorporating environmental proxy data and historical written evidence. Despite best efforts of assimilating a wide array of climate data, most such data are biased towards the boreal growing season, covering roughly the months April to September. Reliable large-scale information for the winter season is currently sparse to non-existent. 
Current winter climate over large parts of the Northern Hemisphere is changing rapidly and non-linearly (Winter 2019/2020 in Europe was the warmest on record). Attributing winter climate extremes to natural or forced (via greenhouse gas increase) variability is highly discussed in the scientific community, with no clear consensus emerging. Identifying a better framework for these climate winter extremes is therefore of both academic and societal importance, enabling better guidance on measures concerning future climates.

A possible way to fill in missing winter climate information is the use of seasonal prediction products. Currently, potent seasonal prediction products are computationally extremely expensive. A new emerging field of seasonal prediction with low-cost machine learning algorithms shows promising results, is however untested for paleo climate applications.

The aim of the WINTER project is therefore to combine cutting edge machine learning tools and long-term climate reanalysis products in order to improve the winter climate understanding for the past 500 years at hemispheric scale. More specifically, the project will use neural networks and random forest models to establish a gridded climate product for the boreal winter season that is more skillful than the baseline climate model winter performance, allowing for a better understanding of climate variability and extremes. Furthermore, the machine learning algorithm will be tested against state-of-the-art seasonal prediction products. As such, the project will also contribute to the improvement of prediction products in the seasonal-to-subseasonal (S2S) framework of the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).

If successful, this project will create the most reliable high-resolution winter climate data for the past 500 years worldwide. The initial focus will be on the Northern Hemisphere, due to higher data availability, but can easily be adopted for the Southern Hemisphere. The combination of cutting-edge machine learning tools, novel paleo-reanalyses and modern seasonal prediction products is unprecedented and will contribute considerably to the understanding of seasonal climate prediction, climate reconstruction methods and large-scale climate variability.
Keywords: Seasonal Prediction, climate, extreme events, machine learning, prediction, reanalysis, variability

Title: Coherent Rendering
Abstract:
Photorealistic images created using computer simulations have become an integral part of our society. Humans are fundamentally visual creatures, hence almost any creative process requires our ability to predict and modify the visual appearance of objects or materials that do not yet exist. Computer-generated images also serve an essential role as part of the scientific method, where they are used to test computational models of reality against photographs or other types of visual data.

Physically-based algorithms for generating these synthetic photographs known as renderings perform an intricate simulation of the interaction of light and matter. The main problem with these methods is their cost: an hour-long animation sequence can easily consume millennia of computation time, restricting high-fidelity rendering to narrow sets of use cases. Rendering algorithms are slow because they are incoherent: seen from a high level, they perform an unstructured random exploration of a high-dimensional probability distribution with pathological behavior. We propose three directions that will revolutionize the design of rendering algorithms:

1. Coherent Markov Chain Monte Carlo, a new approach to stochastic sampling that evolves large groups of coherent samples within a general domain. ?

2. Regularized light transport equations that model physical reality in a way that is suitable for systematic exploration. They are intrinsically smooth and support different levels of approximation, which has a number of exciting applications in the context of machine learning and inverse rendering.

3. Compiler technology to map high-level descriptions of coherent sampling algorithms to concrete implementations that run efficiently on modern processor architectures. ?
The proposed research lies at the frontier of statistics, physics, programming languages, compiler technology and processor architecture and has significant potential for impact beyond computer graphics.
Keywords: coherent monte carlo sampling, inverse rendering, photorealistic rendering

Title: Basics of visual processing: from elements to figures
Abstract: Vision is the most important sense and understanding vision is crucial in fields as disparate as neuroscience, psychology, medicine, engineering, computer science, and philosophy. Yet after decades of success, vision is a mystery. Although the processing of low level features in single elements, such as orientation and colour, has been characterized in great detail, vision research has not succeeded in linking low level vision to high level object recognition, because mid-level, contextual vision has turned out to be an impenetrable barrier. One reason is that low level vision depends as much on mid-level vision as the other way around because the way an element is perceived changes dramatically when it is put in context or when the context changes. As we have shown previously, perception of a single element potentially depends on the configuration of most other elements in the visual field. Very little systematic work has focused on mid-level vision. Here, we will make the first steps, both experimentally and theoretically, towards a framework in which vision is always contextual. We will first collect large volumes of data how humans group single elements into figures and how figural processing determines low level processing. Furthermore, we propose that vision is usually not only contextual in space, but in space and time. In the next step, we will investigate systematically how humans extract figures from spatio-temporal displays. Based on these data and existing models, we will try to create a unified framework in which figure extraction depends on time consuming, recurrent processing linking activity of neurons across the entire visual field. As a first attempt in translation, we will use our experimental and modelling results to characterize visual, contextual deficiencies in schizophrenia. The current project continues previous work, generously funded by the Swiss National Science foundation (SNF), bringing different research avenues under one roof.
Keywords: Pattern recognition, Schizophrenia, Vision

Title: Untangling the relationship between voice and face: A cross-modal approach to talker identity
Abstract:
Humans have evolved a remarkable faculty of recognizing individuals through voice and face. Just by hearing a short utterance like “hello”, or taking a glimpse of a face, a tremendous amount of information would have been communicated to us: Is this person I know? Is s/he in a good mood? If s/he is a stranger, how old is this person? Is s/he the type of person I like? There also seems to be a mysterious link between voice and face — We seem to possess a mental calculus to envisage what a person might look like when we hear a voice, or speculate what a person might sound like when we see a face. We would feel surprised if the real face or voice turns out to be too different from our imagined ones. A most recent success in deep learning technology achieves high-accuracy predictions of faces from voices based on massive web-harvested data (Oh et al. 2019). Both human and machine performances point to a strong interconnection between voice and face. Nevertheless, we still have very insufficient knowledge regarding some of the fundamental questions on the nexus between the two domains. A better understanding of these issues will be of significant value in forensics, medicine, AI and the entertainment industry. The overall objectives (OBJECTIVES I to III below) of my proposed project hence revolve around addressing these questions. 

OBJECTIVE I: What are the links between voice and face morphology? The hardware of our speech organs plays an indisputable role in shaping our voices. Our unique anatomical dimensions of speech organs inevitably leave traces in the acoustic signal of the voice, i.e., “voice as anatomy made audible” (Nolan 1999). The craniofacial architecture provides the housing for, and partially functions as speech organs. It is reasonable to assume that hidden links between voice and face exist, and people may resort to these links to make predictions between both domains.  

OBJECTIVE II: What are the links between temporally dynamic features in voice and facial movements? Human communication is a dynamic process. Our articulatory facial movements develop over time, so do the acoustic variables in voice. It has been demonstrated that people can attribute the correct voice to a silent talking face, but not to a static face image (e.g., Kamachi et al. 2003, Lander et al. 1999, 2007). Also, my previous work showed that temporally dynamic characteristics in the acoustic signal hold important speaker-specific information (e.g., He and Dellwo 2017, He et al. 2019). The two strands of research warrant investigating the dynamic relationships between both domains in more depth, which will yield illuminating messages on the manifestation of talker characteristics.
 
OBJECTIVE III: Do people have similar judgments of a person’s voice from the face? Despite the fact that people can formulate a mental representation of a voice when seeing a face, it is still unknown whether different people have similar or divergent judgments; and how different the imagined voices are from the real voice. Investigating whether the judgments can be explained by the findings from OBJECTIVES I and II is enlightening to our understanding of the complex nexus between voice and face. 

To address OBJECTIVES I and II, the electromagnetic articulograph and electroglottograph with a larynx endoscope will be used. Craniofacial landmarks, articulatory movements, vocal folds activities will be recorded simultaneously with the acoustic voice data. The relationships between the facial and voice characteristics can then be modeled. Re OBJECTIVE III, a neutral voice will be synthesized. The participants will then adjust various acoustic features of this synthesized voice after seeing a face until they arrive at a voice that they believe belongs to the owner of the face. Comparisons can be made between predictions, as well as between the predicted and real voices. The outcome of the project will be of a unique value to our understanding of the role of acoustic and visual information in identity coding. Such information is relevant cross disciplines from phonetics/speech sciences over psychology to biology. It will also be immensely useful in applications involving forensics and public security (e.g., cross-modal person identifications, ear-/eye-witnessing biases, and composite sketching), clinical speech science (e.g., a reference multimodal database of a healthy population), artificial intelligence (e.g., avatar-voice matching in human-machine dialog systems), and the entertainment industry (e.g., finding optimal voices in film dubbing and for animated characters).
Keywords: acoustic analysis of speech, articulatory measurements, forensic speech science, morphometric analysis of face, talker idiosyncrasy, voice-face relationship, voice-from-face prediction by humans

Title: Financial Market Microstructure, Big Data, and AI
Abstract:
Well-functioning financial markets provide liquidity to efficiently allocate resources and are fundamental to economic growth. A crucial aspect of designing, regulating, and monitoring financial markets is the ability to learn from the past and make informed decisions for the future. However, the limited availability of historical data restricts the ability to study the past. In contrast, the recent explosion of data and the rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI) introduce new risks for the foreseeable future.

To date, little is known about how to (i) estimate liquidity in the past when high-frequency data are not available and (ii) simulate the impact of AI on financial markets in the future. At the core of both issues is the lack of a practical understanding of how the price of an asset is determined in financial markets, which prevents connecting high-frequency to low-frequency data and hinders realistic simulations. In the last two years, I have been working on a model of price formation that predicts and explains novel testable relationships among key variables in financial markets. Here I conjecture that such a model may be used to connect the microstructure of financial markets to macroscopic effects. The goal of this proposal is thus to finalize the model and use it to improve estimation and simulation in critical applications. To do so, this proposal is articulated around three parts. Each part involves empirical analyses using the NYSE Trade and Quote (TAQ) database.

(Part I): The main objective is to explain relationships among variables. I propose to do so by finalizing and validating a price formation model based on the last chapter of my PhD thesis that I have further developed during my postdoctoral research.
    
(Part II): The main objective is to estimate liquidity from low-frequency data. Specifically, I propose to (i) use the relationships in Part I to construct estimators of liquidity from low-frequency data, (ii) estimate liquidity in the historical sample when high-frequency data are unavailable, and (iii) study liquidity in the cross-section and the time series since 1926.
    
(Part III): The main objective is to simulate the impact of AI on financial markets. Specifically, I propose to (i) simulate financial markets as trading games where AI agents learn to trade by maximizing their utility in an environment based on the model in Part I, (ii) perform theoretical analyses of the equilibrium and simulation studies of the dynamics, and (iii) identify emerging trends by comparing the theoretical and numerical results to the empirical data.

The project foresees collaborations with world-leading experts in market microstructure and artificial intelligence. The expected outputs are academic publications, open data containing liquidity estimates, and open-source software implementing the estimators and simulators developed in this project. Overall, this project contributes to a deeper understanding of how financial markets functioned in the past, function in the present, and will function in the future.
Keywords: artificial intelligence, data science, finance, financial markets, market microstructure

Title: ML-based radiative transfer parametrization for high-resolution weather and climate simulations over complex topography
Abstract:
In this project, I plan to develop an ML radiative transfer parametrization for high-resolution ICON simulations which includes the 3D effect of the topography.
The goal is to improve the forecasting performance of near-surface temperature and of triggering of convections and to massively reduce computation cost.
The ML parametrization will be trained with the COSMO-2 reanalysis dataset created by MeteoSwiss which contains 5 years of hourly data stored at 2 km scale over Switzerland.
Keywords: Machine learning, Numerical stability, Weather and climate models

Title: Behavioral and neural mechanisms of primate cognition
Abstract: Neural computations emerge from the collective activity of large populations of interconnected neurons. To decipher the principles underlying these computations, we combine behavioral experiments in humans and non-human primates with large-scale neural recordings, causal perturbations of the neural dynamics, modern methods from statistics and machine learning, and computational modeling. We focus on the visuo-motor system, which provides the dominant mode of interaction with the environment in primates, and reveals the interplay of a variety of perceptual, cognitive, and motor processes. The visuo-motor system provides a degree of experimental control that is unmatched by other modalities, and will allow us to move beyond artificial, impoverished behavioral paradigms towards studying brain function in naturalistic settings. We aim to obtain a comprehensive characterization of the neural population dynamics in these settings, to reveal the corresponding neural computations with mechanistic models, and to test quantitative predictions of these models with precise causal perturbation of the dynamics. The resulting understanding of the neural computations underlying cognitive functions will provide us with a powerful platform to elucidate the neural underpinnings of cognitive impairments in psychiatric disorders.
Keywords: artificial neural networks, attention, awake behaving primates, cognition, decision making, dynamical systems, electrophysiology, executive function, population responses, prefrontal cortex

Title: AIDO: AI-enhanced design optimization
Abstract:
Engineering the systems needed to tackle the pressing challenges of today’s world, such as electric vehicles or high-performance energy conversion systems, requires holistic techniques and methods that cross the barriers of disciplines. Indeed, as the boundaries of technologies are pushed to look for more energy-efficient, resource-limited or personalized systems, all components need to be refined and their interactions cannot be neglected anymore. As an example, designing a high-efficiency heat pump requires choosing the geometry and properties of a radial compressor, high-speed bearings, an electric motor, a supporting rotor and a thermally-adequate housing. In this setting, effectively exploring the design space—i.e., the domain of all possible solutions—by hand to find designs that match the specifications is tedious and difficult, and often leads to inefficient, costly and over-engineered solutions. Artificial intelligence (AI) methods, developed in computer science, are increasingly used to tackle these issues, specifically multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) and machine learning (ML). There are, however, limitations that, up to now, block their use for complex and highly-constrained design problems.
This project aims at investigating the use of hybrid approaches, where ML is used to learn on-the-go a problem’s structure and assist an MOEA, focusing specifically on the challenges posed by tight constraints, an often overlooked area. In the first step, two different ways to combine ML with MOEAs will be developed. Specifically, the search operator of MOEAs will be (i) augmented by a learning repair operator aiming at improving solutions to meet the constraints or (ii) replaced by a generative operator learning a latent representation of the design space with valid constraints. This step builds on bridging the latest advances of both ML and MOEAs. In the second step, the two approaches as well as established methods are rigorously compared. To showcase the practical efficacy and relevance, two applications will be considered: the design of automotive actuators, and the design of morphology-personalized bikes. The final step will assess if design principles can be extracted from the learned models, and provide engineers with insights into the considered design task and into the search process. Title: nextSTEPS: Next-Generation Stem Cell Therapy as an Emerging Paradigm for Stroke
Abstract: Stroke is a leading cause of disability and death affecting one in four people during their lifetime. Stroke survivors have only limited therapeutic options and are often left with considerable disabilities. First-generation cell therapies have shown promising preclinical results in animal stroke models but have not been confirmed beyond doubt in a clinical setting. Major uncertainties remain regarding (1) the graft’s immunocompatibility to the recipient; (2) initial graft survival after transplantation; and (3) graft delivery and retention at the injury site. Here, my team and I, aim to develop and preclinically validate advanced, allogeneic cell therapies for stroke that will help to overcome these current limitations. We will use our recently generated GMP-compliant neural progenitor cells (NPCs) as a scalable and well-defined cell source. To ensure high translational potential, improved immunocompatibility of NPC grafts was previously established by the targeted disruption of human leukocyte antigens (HLAs) to circumvent the host’s immune response. The safety in the immune evasive cell grafts will be ensured by the incorporation of a genetic safety checkpoint that will allow selective elimination of the transplants in case of cancerous transformations. The current poor graft survival rates will be considerably improved through incorporation of cells into functionalized and compressible dual release cryogel microcarriers before transplantation. Cryogels will be functionalized with fast-releasing pro-survival factors and slow-releasing pro-angiogenic factors to mitigate the recipient’s hostile stroke microenvironment. So far, transplanted cells can only reach the site of injury in sufficient quantity after direct injections into the brain as the blood brain barrier (BBB) remains barely permeable to cell grafts even after stroke. We plan to generate “smart cells” that express a brain-shuttle system to allow improved graft migration across the brain barrier and retention at the injury site following endovascular injection. The graft will be genetically equipped with surface proteins that facilitate migration across the BBB and a single chain antibody fragment to bind injury-specific antigens present only in the stroked tissue. All cell grafts will be transplanted and preclinically validated in our previously established immunosuppressed and humanized mouse models of stroke. To assess graft survival and migration, luciferase expressing cells will be longitudinally tracked using non-invasive in vivo bioluminescence imaging. All mice will undergo regular detailed kinematic testing to assess recovery based on our recently developed deep learning-based software. The direct contribution of the transplants to functional recovery will be determined through loss-of-function studies using a chemogenetic system to selective silence the cell grafts during behavioral analysis. Recovery-associated tissue responses will be evaluated with regards to scarring, inflammation, neural and synaptic loss, vascular repair, and maturation in the peri-infarct tissue. For in-depth graft characterization, brain slices from the injury regions will be identified and transplanted cells will be evaluated for electrophysiological activity, morphology and cell fate using spatial and single cell transcriptomics. Revealing the molecular and cellular graft phenotypes will provide insights into the graft composition and may uncover which neurons are required for regeneration-associated tissue responses and functional recovery. This highly multidisciplinary approach will combine aspects of neuroscience, molecular biology, and tissue engineering and enable us to overcome major limitations of current cell therapies. The gained knowledge will directly contribute to the development of safe and effective cell therapies for brain injuries in the foreseeable future.
Keywords: behavioral neuroscience, biomaterials, cell therapy, deep learning with DeepLabCut, immune compatibility, neuroscience, regenerative therapy, spatial single cell transcriptomics, stroke, therapeutic angiogenesis, translational research

Title: Multiscale transmission dynamics of rabies in Africa: The urban-rural interface
Abstract: Background and rationale: Dog mediated rabies, although entirely preventable, kills every year over 25’000 people in Africa. In the foregoing SNF project 310030_160067 we demonstrated that two consecutive dog mass vaccination campaigns were sufficient to interrupt rabies transmission for more than two years in N’Djaména the capital of Chad. We confirmed the mathematical assessment by a phylodynamic analysis of rabies virus (RABV) sequences. The re-introduction of rabies from the outside of the city was captured by a meta-population model which indicated that importation of latently infective dogs is the most likely cause, rather than the heterogeneity of transmission or underreporting. Research in Bangui, Central Africa suggests that chains of transmission in the city are too short to sustain the transmission and that regular import of latently infective dogs is needed to sustain transmission. The research questions arising are thus: 1) Can rabies transmission in an African city be interrupted or reduced by avoiding the (human-mediated) import of latently infective dogs? 2) Can rabies reservoirs be identified that sustain transmission (Re>1) and what are their characteristics? 3) What is the effect of dog movement restriction on the transmission of dog rabies in a free roaming context?Overall objectives and specific aims: 1) We aim to understand the role of (human-mediated) dog importation on the transmission dynamics of rabies by creating a ring of permanently staffed vaccination posts around N’Djaména. 2) We attempt to identify rabies transmission reservoirs in urban areas with high dog densities. 3) We assess the effect of dog movement restriction on occurrence of rabies outbreaks in a rural context. Approach and methods: 1) The Institut de Recherches en Elevage pour le Developpement (IRED) in N’Djaména estimates weekly passive dog rabies incidence since twenty years which serves as baseline for the effect of the  vaccination. A ring of 13 permanently staffed vaccination posts will be maintained during 12 months at all road entries to the N’Djaména district. In collaboration with the security sector, all cars entering N’Djaména will be checked for transported dogs. After informed consent of the owner, dogs will be vaccinated against rabies and distemper, unless the owner presents a valid vaccination certificate. A lateral photograph will be taken from each dog for their identification by machine learning algorithms. Weekly changes of dog rabies incidence will be assessed by IRED before, during and 24 month after the ring vaccination intervention. 2) To identify rabies reservoirs that sustain transmission, the origin of each dog entering N’Djaména will be recorded. In the most important places of origin (>80% of imports), active surveillance of rabies will be initiated to collect as many rabies strains as possible for a phylodynamic analysis. This will include the city of Sarh, one of the cities known for dog exports, who has a high dog-to-human ratio. 3) Participatory transdisciplinary stakeholder processes will be used to identify locally adapted dog leashing practices in Sarh, Southern Chad. An incentive-based dog leashing scheme (with daily walks), embedded in the ongoing Program for Guinea Worm Eradication (PGWE), will be implemented in 20% of the dog population for its effect on reducing the transmission of rabies. Rabies transmission will be followed as above before, during and 24 months after the leashing intervention.  Expected results: We expect 1) a strong reduction or even interruption of transmission of rabies in N’Djaména by the vaccination of imported dogs, 2) to identify and characterise source areas of dog export that sustain rabies transmission as reservoirs, 3) the unequivocal identification of dogs by smart phone based machine learning algorithms, and finally 4) a reduction of rabies incidence by dog leashing.Impact: While it is known that dog mass vaccination is the most cost-effective way to eliminate rabies, African national governments are currently still reluctant to invest in dog mass vaccination campaigns. Any alternative  intervention as tested here plays thus an important role to progressively reduce human rabies exposure to reach the zero-human rabies goal by 2030.
Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Machine learning, Mass vaccination, Metapopulation model, Rabies elimination, Transmission dynamics

Title: Why Do So Many Patients Undergo Unnecessary Surgery? Financial Incentives and Overuse in Hospital Care
Abstract:
Recent OECD estimates suggest that up to 20% of health spending in developed countries is wasteful or even harmful to patients (OECD, 2017a). Linked to this, a large body of research documents that adherence to clinical guidelines is often low leading to a lot of patients receiving care that makes no differences to their health (Pronovost, 2013). Medical overuse is undesirable because it contributes to preventable harm, suboptimal patient outcomes and considerable waste of resources.

The main objective of this research project is to study overuse in hospital care in Switzerland. Despite the relevance of the topic, relatively little is known about the magnitude of the problem and the underlying factors that influence overuse in daily practice.

In the first work package, we plan to compile an extensive catalogue of guideline-based indicators of overuse in hospital care that can be measured in routine data (i.e., claims & administrative hospital data). Our focus will be on high-volume, elective, surgical procedures, diagnostic tests, imaging services, and medications of questionable value for patients. We intend to systematically extract guidelines from major medical associations and platforms such as “ChoosingWisely” and “smarter medicine” and synthesize systematic literature reviews on the topic. Clinical experts and medical coders then help us refining the catalogue. To enable the transfer from guidelines to routine data, we gather the relevant diagnosis, treatments, and patient characteristics necessary to assess guideline conformity and provide the corresponding medical (e.g., ICD-10-GM) and tariff codes (e.g., DRG codes). Once the guidelines are mapped onto the data, we quantify the extent of overuse in Switzerland.

In the second work package, we build on the previous work package and study the interplay between financial incentives and overuse. We lay a special focus on the question as to how financial incentives in private insurance affect medical decisions. Going beyond average effects, we plan to identify patient subgroups in the data that are most (least) affected by financial incentives. For example, private insurance might especially lead to overuse among low-risk patients, whereas severely ill patients are hardly affected by them. We make use of “meta-learners”, a recently introduced class of machine learning techniques designed to study such effect heterogeneity and flexibly “learn” what factors systematically influence overuse in hospital care.
Keywords: Adherence to Clinical Guidelines, Financial Incentives, Machine Learning, Overuse in Hospital Care, Routine Data

Title: FightAMR Novel global One Health surveillance approach to fight AMR using Artificial Intelligence and big data mining
Abstract:
This project aims to develop new AI-powered surveillance solutions to identify increased risk of AMR
emergence and direction of spread through the food-borne route based on the 'One Health' concept, and capable to detect the appearance of known and novel AMR traits. The solutions will be suitable for
deployment in low-to-high income countries. While there have been many studies on AMR in livestock, environment, and human, they often focus on a specific sector and/or rely on a specific analysis (antimicrobial usage or whole genome sequencing) but not necessarily on integrated data analysis. Our goal is to strengthen big data approaches to integrate surveillance across human, animal, environment with the food chain to assist interventions to prevent AMR caused by resistant enteric bacterial pathogens.
We plan to devise a real-time monitoring method capable of pinpointing geographical locations and routes which -at any point in time- may be at higher risk of developing AMR. This will be achieved by a triangulated approach: i) Understand the conditions leading to higher risk of AMR, by developing a cloud-solution embedding auto-adaptive learning to integrate and mine public data from different sources (metagenomics, phenotypes, satellite, etc) at different scales (region/setting/country, etc) and subjects (humans, animals etc); ii) Perform an AI-guided experimental sampling collection campaign of unprecedented scale and coverage; iii) Identify monitorable biomarkers indicating increased risk of AMR and direction of spread, embedded in deployable surveillance solutions.
Keywords: AMR surveillance, Artificial intelligence, Big data mining, Machine learning, One Health

Title: VaultML: Preventing privacy leaks in machine learning
Abstract:
Machine learning has tremendous potential to increase performance, revenue, and quality of life. However, its reliance on data and inference power raise a wide number of privacy concerns. The research community has focused so far on two directions to address these concerns: allowing to train machine learning models on private data, and allowing users to query models with private data, without revealing the raw data itself.

Advances in these directions focus on privacy issues associated with inputs for the models. However, recent research shows that the outputs of a deployed model (i.e., its predictions) can be as sensitive as its inputs. Notably, they can be used to infer information about the model's training data, recover parts of the data, or even "steal" the model itself. Previous work neither addresses concerns associated to the privacy impact related to the predictions and classifications themselves, regardless of the privacy of inputs. 

The overall objective of VaultML is to understand and prevent privacy issues at the output of machine learning processes. Concretely, we have two goals: 1) to develop measurement tools for quantifying the privacy of machine learning models; and 2) to develop defenses that, applied on models or on user's input to the models under deployment mitigate the privacy impact stemming from the pervasive use of machine learning.

For the first objective, we will develop methods to quantitatively measure the susceptibility of models building upon classic techniques for estimating information leakage. As for the second objective, we will use the understanding gained using the tools to quantify information leaks to inform the design of defenses. Concretely, we will use these insights to repurpose techniques well known in the machine learning domain, e.g., generalization techniques or adversarial examples, to enhance the privacy protection of users data at the time of training and upon deployment.

The results of VaultML are of interest both to privacy researchers, machine learning practitioners, and ultimately society as a whole. On the one hand, the capability to deploy models that do not leak information not only benefits end users whose data is protected, but also helps concealing businesses secrets and simplifies regulation compliance. On the other hand, empowering end-users to better control the inferences that can be made from their digital fingerprints, not only improves their individual privacy, but also has the potential to protect society from the risks induced by the availability of massive data.
Keywords: Machine Learning, Privacy, Quantification, Systematization

Title: Modeling People and their Clothes in Crowded Scenes
Abstract:
Current algorithms for modeling clothed people mainly fall into one of two categories, those that model the external surface of the clothed body without modeling the body itself and those that model the body while ignoring the clothes. The former have been shown to work remarkably well on very clean images in which the person can be precisely outlined but rarely account for poor lighting or occlusions that are frequent in the real world. The latter are more robust but do not fully exploit the information the shape of the clothes provides about that of the body. Furthermore, in neither case are many provisions made for the fact that there may be many people in the scene and that they may occlude each other.  As a result, whereas modeling people wearing tight-fitting clothes is fast becoming a mature field, handling subjects wearing looser garments remains an open problem when it is to be done in everyday settings where people may hide each other, precise outlines are hard to estimate, and shadows often complicate matters. 

In this project, we will handle this more difficult task of modeling people and their potentially loose fitting clothing from video. This will include modeling individuals as well as multiple people interacting with each other.  In the process, we will also develop new approaches to representing complex surfaces whose topology can change and to modeling their interactions. 

We believe that this will have an impact beyond the specific topic of people and their clothes, for example in the field of Computer Aided Design where such models are crucial. Finally, by deploying our algorithms in the real-world setting of drones filming people, we will prove that the potential of our technique goes beyond lab environments, which eventually will lead to technology transfer from Academia to Industry.
Keywords: Computer Vision, People Tracking, Pose Estimation, Surface Modeling

Title: Digital Originals in 3D
Abstract:
This project employs a combination of complementary imaging technologies with the objective of attaining a new level of visual quality in 3D models. This objective is accomplished by combining accurate and precise photogrammetry 3D mesh data with extended texture data obtained through Reflectance Transformation Imaging (RTI). Hence, we will enhance, integrate, and streamline the digital capturing, processing, and dissemination of objects and their digital representation in 3D. We will create a generalized and seamless workflow representing the content creation and provision pipeline to reach this goal. For 3D data acquisition, we will incorporate and streamline two cutting-edge technologies: RTI and Photogrammetry. We rely on automated acquisition for high reproducibility and explainability of data. The resulting datasets are automatically post-processed with the help of machine learning, compressed, and converted into a streamable 3D file format. The streamable 3D file format allows for public exploration and investigation with highest rendering quality.

A significant challenge for both Photogrammetry and RTI methods is the necessity for high reproducibility. We address this need through the utilization of an automated capturing rig. This approach enables the capture of high-quality datasets, which can then be processed optimally to obtain 3D shapes and textures. The rig is equipped with the necessary lighting and camera-platform to place sensor devices at any 3D location and angles within the rig's reach. With this setup, sensors can be optimally positioned for high-quality acquisition. The combination of the automatic rig, which contains a camera and a light dome, significantly extends the sizes and shapes of objects that can be scanned.

We also acquire an enhanced set of metadata. The combination of technical metadata on the capturing process as well as material properties plays an instrumental role in the accurate interpretation of the models. The metadata explicitly delineates the quality of the measurements and provides a comprehensive understanding about what and how data has been generated. 

Indeed, high-quality 3D objects are significant in data volume. This project addresses the challenges of storage, loading times, and real-time interaction with high-quality 3D objects by developing innovative file formats and streaming technologies similar to modern game engines including adaptive mesh and data streaming. The aim is to facilitate web-based dissemination and visualization of 3D objects and metadata. Therefore, we respect communities like the International Image Interoperability Framework (IIIF) for standards and collaborate with DaSCH for flexibility, access, and data management. Thus, this project, in collaboration with DaSCH, the IIIF consortium, and Virtual Culture, will enhance archival storage, dissemination, and interoperability standards for better performance and data quality in web environments. Our last objective is to improve capturing technical metadata for reproducibility and significantly advance file and metadata formats, ensuring sustainability through close cooperation with the IIIF technical committee.

For visualization and exploration, we will examine state-of-the-art rendering technologies such as physically based rendering, non-photorealistic rendering and, last but not least, the very latest gaussian splatting method. Thus, our method allows the real-time representation of 3D objects with a new level of visual quality, enabling new applications in conservation, restoration, preservation, exhibitions, online collections, research, and education. It will allow instant identification of techniques, materials used and differences in execution, condition, and damage. In addition, our approach offers new interaction paradigms and advanced possibilities for virtual exploration and documentation of 3D artifacts.
Keywords: 3D Imaging, 3D reconstruction, Computer Graphics, Data processing & streaming, Digital Twin, Imaging, Photogrammetry, RTI, Textures

Title: REMEDY (Reducing Mistriage in Emergency Departments: A Path to Improved Triage Accuracy through Real-time Evaluation and Artificial Intelligence)
Abstract:
Background: The demand for emergency care varies and can change rapidly. Triage is the first step in the emergency department (ED) process, aiming to identify patients needing time-critical interventions, relieve suffering, ensure safe discharges, and efficiently use available resources. Despite the recognized importance of accurate triage, about 20% to 30% of patients experience incorrect triage level assignment, known as mis-triage. Factors leading to poor triage performance remain unclear. Current studies on triage evaluation may not accurately reflect real-world practices, and there is no standard to determine patient acuity. The use of surrogate outcome measures such as hospital admission, Intensive Care Unit admission, and mortality rates as markers of (predictive) validity is controversial. Many triage evaluation studies rely on retrospective data, written scenarios, or electronic health records, which may be biased. Furthermore, few studies have assessed the clinical impact of mis-triage, leaving its causes and consequences unclear. 
Overall objectives and specific aims: The RemEDy project aim to improve triage processes in EDs by defining optimal processes and quantifying confounding factors that impede effective triage. The RemEDy project will achieve this trough the following aims: 1) To develop an evidence- and consensus-based triage evaluation instrument for real-time assessment 2) To identify and analyze clinician’s and patient’s characteristics and ED metrics related to mis-triage and its consequences 3) To develop and validate an AI algorithm to support triage decision-making 4) To develop a targeted training program for triage clinicians and assess its effectiveness. 
Methods: Identification of mis-triage and improvement of triage processes in the ED will be addressed with a multi-phased mixed methods project methodology. 
1) Scoping Review and Delphi Study: In work package (WP) 1 a scoping review, following Joanna Briggs Institute guidelines, to identify existing knowledge on triage evaluation will be conducted. A triage evaluation instrument will be developed, guided by the results of the scoping review and the consensus opinions of expert clinicians and patient representatives determined by a modified Delphi study. 2) Multicentric Observational Study: In WP2, trained triage experts will use the developed triage evaluation instrument to identify mis-triage in ‘real-time’ during routine clinical practice in the ED, which has never been done before. This will be a multicentric, prospective observational study, conducted across seven EDs in Switzerland over 6 months. 3) Artificial Intelligence Algorithm Development and Validation: In WP3, AI triage algorithm to recommend triage scores and predict mis-triage, using both pre-existing and real-time data from the observational study will be developed. The algorithm will be validated and updated with new clinical data to enhance predictive performance and clinical decision support, providing recommendations and warnings about potential over- or under-triage. 4)Training Development and Pragmatic Trial: In WP4, a training program for triage clinicians will be created using the Behavioral Change Wheel methodology, followed by a pragmatic trial to assess its effectiveness.
Expected Clinical Relevance: RemEDy aims to improve the quality and safety of care in EDs through enhanced accuracy in triage. A comprehensive understanding of mis-triage and other possible triage system defects will allow for the identification of potential areas for improvement, leading to the development of measures to avoid them.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Delphi Study, Emergency Department, Emergency Severity Index, Multi-center study, Pragmatic Trial, Triage, Triage training, artificial intelligence, emergency medicine, emergency nursing, implementation science, mis-triage, nursing science, triage

Title: NEWS - Newborn Early Warning Signs
Abstract:
Sepsis and meningitis are major causes of morbidity and mortality in the
neonatal population. Despite vigilant clinical assessment of infants in the neonatal
intensive care unit (NICU), diagnosis of sepsis and necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) often
does not occur until an infant has significant hemodynamic compromise. Analysis of heart rae variability becomes more and more relevant in predicting outcomes over short and long time. Thus decription of apnea, bradycardia and desaturation (ABD-events) are of major importance to predict future potentially life-threatening events. Combining biomarker screening with predictive monitoring of physiologic markers for assessing risk of sepsis or NEC and for detection of early-stage illness could prevent progression to severe illness and shock.
The neonatal intensive care unit's database for surveillance and storage of
cardiorespiratory parameters (Clinisoft®), allows us to prospectively characterize
development of ABD-events over time.
To examine the contribution of infection, acute and chronic inflammation, in
development of cardiorespiratory dysfunction there are ongoing prospective studies of
term and premature infants at the NICU and paediatric intensive care units at the Karolinska University Hospital Solna. There cardiorespiratory recordings (Clinisoft®) of ABD- events are correlated with routine inflammatory biomarkers & medical records. We then further examine how physiomarkers (ABD-events) & biomarkers may act as Newborn Early Warning Signs (NEWS) for infection, inflammation and need for increased therapeutic interventions. 
In this project, our objective is to develop machine learning based methods for using low frequency labeled data (Clinisoft) in conjunction with the high frequency unlabeled data. Using pattern recognition we develop better physiomarkers (cardiorespiratory indexes) as NEWS that will help to predict short-term outcome and enable rapid therapeutic interventions.
Keywords: Autonomic Control, Heart Rate Variability, Machine Learning, Preterm Infants, Risk Prediction, Time-series Analysis

Title: The Rationales and Risks of Systematization: A Pragmatic Account of When to Systematize Thought
Abstract:
The ideal of systematicity has shaped philosophy since its inception, animating efforts to explicitly justify thought and action in terms that are consistent, coherent, complete, and parsimoniously principled. But in recent decades, this formerly unquestioned ideal has become sharply contested.
There are still rationalist and scientistic advocates of systematization who hold on to the idea that the demand for systematization is ineluctable because inherent in rationality itself—we could not make any sense of things without systematization, they insist. Moreover, being more systematic than ordinary thought is what grounds philosophy’s claim to being scientific (in the broad sense of wissenschaftlich) and its claim to attention. The task of the wise is to systematize, Aquinas said, and it is by systematizing that philosophers earn their claim to being listened to.
But there are now also pluralist and particularist critics of systematization on all sides: philosophers of science have argued that scientific understanding does not resemble a unified pyramid deriving everything from a single set of principles, but a patchwork of inconsistent models of particular domains; and in ethics and political philosophy, the idea that to be rational just is to think as systematically as possible, at the limit by disciplining one’s thought into a neatly axiomatized theory, has been accused of betraying an overly rationalistic conception of rationality—we can think rationally and critically by reflecting honestly about the particular case, and we should, because we have a better hold on reality’s complexities if we preserve the kaleidoscopic richness of unsystematized thought.
Because reflections on systematicity are dispersed across disconnected subfields and lack a shared vocabulary and focus, however, it is unclear how the views of advocates and critics of systematizations relate to each other. To make headway, I propose to resituate and evaluate the defences and critiques of systematization within a pragmatic perspective that focuses on the rationales and risks of systematization: on the practical pressures that drive systematization and the problematic practical consequences of systematizing. This allows me to integrate seemingly incommensurable views of systematicity by pursuing four questions: (1) To what extent is systematization a practical necessity, and just how much systematization is minimally required? (2) What rationales for greater degrees of systematization might there be that even critics can recognize? (3) What are the risks of systematization? (4) Where systematization is inappropriate, what task is left for philosophy, and what might it base its claim to attention on?
My overall aim is to develop a pragmatic account of systematization that answers these questions and helps us determine when and how far we should systematize. Specifically, I aim to: (A) formulate rationales for systematization and the forms of systematicity they call for; (B) identify the different risks of systematization that give us reason not to systematize further or more widely than we need to; (C) indicate, on the basis of these risks and rationales, the appropriate degree of systematization in different contexts, and evaluate the threat posed to the ideal of systematicity by the rise of AI; (D) bring out in what respects even critics of systematization still endorse and exemplify certain forms of systematization, thereby finding a basis for their claim to Wissenschaftlichkeit and attention in what I call “practical congruence.”
Methodologically, the project is innovative in connecting previously unconnected discussions of systematicity and integrating them within a pragmatic perspective. The output of the project will be my third monograph, along with five articles testing its key ideas in selective peer-reviewed journals, and the organisation of a major international conference. These results will be directly relevant to how philosophers understand one of their discipline’s guiding ideals, which has been thought to be foundational to their self-conception and authority. But the results will also bear on the value of systematization in other disciplines. Moreover, the question of the value of systematicity is made urgent by society’s increasing reliance on AI: deep learning neural networks, in particular, are black boxes yielding outputs that precisely lack integration into humanly intelligible systems of reasoning. By trying to better understand the place and rationale of an ideal that is so directly in tension with society’s increasing reliance on opaque AI, the project bears on one of the central challenges of the 21st century.
Keywords: particularism, philosophical methodology, rationalism, rationality, reflective equilibrium, systematicity of thought
