Title: The Neuroendocrine Control of Human Reproduction
Abstract:
Congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (CHH) is a rare genetic disorder characterized by absent puberty and infertility caused by GnRH deficiency. The clinical overlap with constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP), a common and transient form of GnRH deficiency, makes it virtually impossible to differentiate these two entities in patients prior to age 16, leading to delay in treatment and psychological burden for patients and family. Clinical heterogeneity occurs not only for the reproductive phenotype, but also for the CHH-associated non-reproductive phenotypes (i.e. cleft lip/palate, sensorineural hearing loss, etc.). Genetic heterogeneity also prevails in CHH, with over 40 loci known to underlie the disease either alone or in combination. Further, variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance illustrate the complexity of the phenotype-genotype correlation. 

This project will focus on clinical, genetic and basic aspect of GnRH neuron biology, employing a multidisciplinary and translational approach to address the current challenges in the field: (1) A more timely and accurate diagnosis of CHH can provide significant relief of psychosocial burden for both patients and families. We therefore propose to improve the early diagnosis of CHH by validating machine learning to distinguish CDGP from CHH. (2) The clinical heterogeneity in CHH with variable frequency of associated phenotypes make it difficult to conduct an efficient clinical evaluation for each patient. We aim to promote personalized medicine by demonstrating the role of genetics in guiding clinical assessment. The present work will challenge our traditional view of the classification of syndromes based on constellation of phenotypes. (3) The dogma that a congenital disorder such as CHH is permanent has been challenged by the discovery of HH reversal in adulthood, suggesting the implication of GnRH neuron plasticity. We will investigate the contribution of environmental factors in CHH reversal to improve clinical management of CHH. (4) Despite the advent of next generation sequencing, the majority of patients remain without molecular diagnosis. Recently, the increasing affordability of whole genome sequencing (WGS) allows to screen large CHH cohorts for variants in regulatory non-coding regions, previously not accessible by whole exome sequencing.  Yet, interpretation of identified rare variants remains challenging. We propose to combine WGS with transcriptomics to increase the yield of molecular diagnosis and translate these findings in clinical genetics. The discovery of novel genes in CHH will also shed light into the ontogeny of GnRH neurons and their regulation. (5) Finally, we will use the CHH patients-derived iPSC and genome editing technologies to functionally validate the genetic makeup of each patient, along the evaluation of potential individualized treatments.
Keywords: GnRH deficiency, Human Genetics, Hypogonadism, Neuron biology, Pubertal disorders

Title: Exploring the effects of audience-organization linguistic alignment on access to social benefits
Abstract:
A wealth of studies shows that organizational members tend to adopt similar behaviors, language, beliefs, values and norms -i.e. to culturally align to one another and become more similar on one or several cultural dimensions- and that this tendency is an important driver of organizational performance as it facilitates communication and coordination within organizations (for reviews see Chatman & O’Reilly, 2016; Giorgi, Lockwood, & Glynn, 2015). Like organizational members within organizations, organizations within markets tend to become similar to their peers by adopting the same features and behaviors, which also generally have a positive impact on organizational performance, as audience members tend to expect and reward conformity in markets (for reviews see Durand & Thornton, 2018; Hannan et al., 2019). Organizational members’ alignment to one another within organizations (within-organization alignment) or organizations’ alignment to one another within markets (between-organization alignment) have thus both been extensively studied and associated with organizational performance in past research.
Comparatively, audience-organization alignment, i.e., external audience members’ tendency to become similar to the organizational members they interact with in terms of behaviors, language, beliefs, values or norms, has been less studied. Some studies show that potential hires benefit from displaying some levels of similarity in socio-demographic background to the organizational members in charge of hiring them (Rivera, 2012; Rivera & Tilcsik, 2016). However, potential hires are a relatively specific kind of audience, which are being evaluated by existing organizational members for their potential in becoming a good organizational member. Little research has examined how cultural alignment between, e.g., clients, suppliers or investors and organizational members may impact organizational performance. In fact, most research on social evaluation in markets presents audience members as external observers, clearly separated from organizations (as in, e.g., Boulongne & Durand, 2021; Pontikes, 2012), and does not expect them to culturally align with organizational members. Yet, greater audience-organization cultural alignment should lead to more efficient and rewarding interactions between organizational members and external audience members. This could in turn lead to positive organizational and audience-level outcomes –such as more positive organizational evaluations or increased likelihood that audience members’ requests are met.  
With this project, we set out to address this research gap. We focus specifically on audience-organization linguistic alignment, i.e. audience members propensity to rely on the same semantic content and syntactic rules than organizational members to structure their verbal exchanges. Within- and between-organization linguistic alignment is a known and important driver of organizational evaluation and performance which recent research has studied extensively (e.g., Barlow, Verhaal, & Angus, 2019; Corritore, Goldberg, & Srivastava, 2020; Lix, Goldberg, Srivastava, & Valentine, 2022; Srivastava, Goldberg, Manian, & Potts, 2017). An examination of the effect of audience-organization linguistic alignment on organizational performance thus seems a natural point of departure to lay out the groundwork for a systematic study of audience-organization cultural alignment and its effect on organizational performance. 
To study audience-organization linguistic alignment and its impact on organizational performance, this project uses a unique dataset of nearly 400,000 emails exchanged between the Caisse d’Allocations Familiales (henceforth CAF), or Public Benefit Office, a French agency in charge of distributing social benefits to people in need, and its beneficiaries. This data was collected through a research partnership with the CAF of Seine-Saint-Denis, a French department in the north of Paris (henceforth CAF93, after the number associated with the French department of Seine-Saint-Denis). A key and novel contribution of this project is that we can measure the level of linguistic alignment between a focal beneficiary and CAF officers during a particular email exchange using natural language processing. Furthermore, leveraging longer-run outcome data on beneficiaries, we are also able to assess the consequences of audience-organization linguistic alignment for beneficiary’s ability to access welfare benefits. Finally, through our on-going research partnership with CAF93, we would be able to have a direct impact on the policies applied by CAF93 to reduce the non-take-up of social benefits, one of the main objective of CAF93, and a problem common across many OECD countries and programs (Hernanz, Malherbet, & Pellizzari, 2004; Marc et al., 2022) which constitutes a major roadblock to succeed in limiting social inequalities.

Title: Deep learning-assisted improvement of image quality and quantitative accuracy in hybrid PET/CT imaging
Abstract:
Advanced multimodal and multiparametric imaging technologies using positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT) are playing a critical role to achieve the full potential of quantitative imaging biomarkers as diagnostic techniques transition from the systems to the molecular level. PET/CT image quality is challenged by various image degrading factors and the frequent occurrence of artifacts (misregistration, halo, metals, truncation) hampering reliable visual interpretation and accurate reporting. Likewise, quantitative imaging biomarkers using PET/CT is still challenged by the lack of reliable and robust attenuation, partial volume and motion correction methodology enabling to produce artefact-free, quantitative PET images, robust and reliable quantitative metrics for routine use and advanced tools for multiparametric imaging suitable for research applications. Advanced image-derived PET metrics including radiomics combined with sophisticated deep learning (DL) algorithms have emerged and are producing a paradigm shift in medical imaging research. However, the performance of DL algorithms is challenged by robustness and generalizability issues, which can be addressed through validation in multi-institutional and multicentric clinical studies and the use of federated learning strategies to circumvent the need for sharing clinical datasets. Yet, despite the significant progress, the adoption of these advanced techniques in the clinic faces several challenges from both methodological and practical standpoints. As such, further research and development efforts are still required to address the many open research questions. Advanced algorithms enabling to improve image quality, simplify and optimize image acquisition and reconstruction protocols and enable quantitative imaging biomarkers using DL must be developed and validated in clinical setting.
We request funding to develop and validate in clinical setting novel advanced algorithms enabling to exploit the full potential of qualitative and quantitative multiparametric imaging biomarkers using DL algorithms in clinical oncology. We propose a robust methodology enabling to push forward the development and widespread adoption of DL-assisted qualitative and fully quantitative multiparametric PET/CT imaging to routine clinical practice for the assessment and characterization of disease spread and recurrence. 
We foresee to develop innovative algorithmic approaches for improved qualitative and quantitative multimodal and multiparametric whole-body (WB) PET/CT imaging towards improved clinical diagnosis, monitoring of treatment response, radiation therapy planning, prognostic modelling and outcome prediction using DL.

Title: Visual Search +  New Approaches in Content-Based Image Retrieval
Abstract:
Visual Search +
New Approaches in Content-Based Image Retrieval

With an exponential growth in both the generation and sharing of digital photographs, the topic of Content-Based Image Retrieval (CBIR) has become increasingly important across all disciplines. This is particularly true as the model of manually tagging content and context within every media file becomes unsustainable. While automation in keyword tagging can be found in products such as facial recognition software, by maintaining textual descriptions of visual media, both the stored labels and attempts to match them are grossly limited by the semantic gap. Nevertheless, with the inevitable advancement of image processing to transcode qualitative attributes into quantifiable data, design will play an ever-increasing role in providing the bridge for users to access this information through visual means. Visual Search + explores the ways in which this bridge can be built, through the formation of an interdisciplinary team consisting of junior researchers from the departments of computer vision and interface design. 
This research strives to make progress beyond the well-explored low-level CBIR attributes (color, contour, texture) and broaden the contextual interpretation of images by computers through reducing the sampled imagery to one type, portraits. A focus is placed on images involving the face, due to its crucial role in everyday communication. Furthermore, while the innate human ability to recognize and process features within the face exists across all mediums, there remains a great limitation to articulate and describe them in detail. Using the 3D Morphable Face Model, a technology capable of analyzing 2D photographs in regard to face attributes such as eye gaze, head tilt, age, sex, mouth activity, facial expression, beard, among others, this collaboration pushes the technology to meet time restrictions imposed by the real world environments of content management and retrieval. It is with this challenge that the 3D-MFM will also be utilized to generate an unlimited set of sample training imagery, used to teach Fast Image Detectors how to describe and quantify visual attributes with concise speed and accuracy. 
For each facial attribute extracted, a visual module will be designed for the query of numerically stored data. Exploring the possibilities and usability of both 2D and 3D widgets, visual qualities within the image will be retrieved through the abstracted visual representation of those very same qualities. Realized through a web application environment (Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP), this will allow for the seamless connection of an online graphical user interface, with a database used to store all extracted information, after having been populated through offline image processing.
Through a collaborative venture of the Graphics and Vision Research Group at the University of Basel and the Visual Communication Institute of FHNW HGK Basel, Visual Search + yields the real world application and user consideration of cutting-edge computer vision techniques, while providing the field of design an opportunity to realize investigations of interface design through the underpinning 
of developing technology.
Keywords: Content-Based Image Retieval, Design Research, Interface Design

Title: Triage against the Machine: Can Artificial Intelligence reason deliberatively?
Abstract: This project investigates the ability of artificial intelligence (AI), specifically large language models (LLMs), to emulate human deliberative reasoning—a cognitive process fundamental to democratic and sustainable decision-making. Unlike AI’s typical reliance on pattern recognition and statistical learning, human deliberative reasoning is inherently social and context-dependent, evolving to assess arguments within group settings by incorporating reciprocity of reasons (the collective identification of relevant reasons) and reflectivity of reasons (the integration of these reasons into decision-making). Using the Deliberative Reason Index (DRI), this study evaluates the extent to which LLMs can replicate intersubjective reasoning by simulating real-world deliberative processes across various scenarios, including non-dialogical, role-playing, and dialogical chain-of-thought simulations. The expected outcomes suggest that LLMs may struggle to match human deliberative reasoning due to their lack of social and contextual adaptability, potentially impacting the efficacy and sustainability of AI in democratic decision-making processes. This investigation aims to delineate AI’s potential and limitations in democratic governance, providing insights to guide future AI development and its responsible integration into decision-making contexts.
Keywords: AI, cognitve bias, decision-making, deliberation, democracy, reasoning

Title: Neural Networks for Learning Graph Embedding and Graph Matching
Abstract:
The proposed project is concerned with graph-based pattern recognition. Research in this area can be roughly divided into three time periods, viz. the eras of graph matching, graph kernels, and graph neural networks. The overall objective of the present project is to develop and research robust methods which combine the best ideas and methods that emerged from these three eras(1). This way, we aim to introduce novel graph-based methods that significantly exceed the current state of the art, both in terms of speed and accuracy. Due to their power and flexibility, graphs indeed play a pivotal role in many disciplines in science and industry and the research of efficient and accurate graph-based methods has become a crucial challenge. Therefore, both the relevance and potential impacts of the proposed project can be considered very high. We envisage three relatively independent lines of research that will be investigated by two PhD students and one postdoctoral researcher.
- Line of Research 1: We will employ existing graph embedding frameworks, more specifically the resulting vector space embedding, as ground truth for designing, developing, and training of novel graph neural networks. The aim is to learn graph embeddings that minimize the difference of the learned and the ground truth embed- ding. Major benefit of this procedure is that the embedding of unseen graphs can be accomplishment incomparably faster than with the original techniques.
-Line of Research 2: We will learn graph matchings using graph neural networks. To this end, we plan to omit the global pooling layer and directly infer node map- pings based on the learned node embeddings. Initial ideas include exploring clustering and/or assignment algorithms that can be applied to the learned node embeddings. The advantage of this method is that it derives explicit mappings of the substructures of the underlying graphs (which is both valuable and often necessary in applications).
- Line of Research 3: We plan to explore new (interdisciplinary) applications for graph-based pattern recognition. In particular, we seek to address data challenges where graphs are not currently used, even though they would be the natural approach for formal pattern representation. We believe that this will enable us to define break- through and pioneering algorithms in various scientific fields.
Along the three lines of research, several open research questions need to be answered to push forward the frontier of current knowledge. These questions range from technical issues (e.g., Which architectures are best suited for the target tasks?), over conceptual issues (e.g., Which novel applications are suitable for graph-based methods?), to empirical issues (e.g., To what extent do the proposed methods improve and accelerate the current state of the art in graph-based pattern recognition?).

(1) We are aware that there have already been some efforts in this direction. However, the present research proposal is original and defines new frontiers and addresses relevant open research questions.
Keywords: Graph Kernel, Graph Matching, Graph Neural Network, Graph-Based Pattern Recognition, Structural Pattern Recognition

Title: Pixel2Paleo: Exploring lake sediments with high-resolution imaging techniques to discover biogeochemical fingerprints of paleoenvironments
Abstract:
Studying past climate and environmental changes is vital for understanding the present and making meaningful scenarios for future Earth system dynamics. Lake sediments are natural archives and preserve valuable information about past conditions. However, traditional methods of analysing sedimentary archives often lack the temporal resolution and comprehensiveness required to fully unlock their potential. Additionally, due to the analytical limitations, the traditional inductive approach is used, where one selected proxy reconstructs one past variable. This project represents a pioneering effort in utilising advanced imaging methods to unravel the intricate relationship between lake sediments and past climate and environmental conditions.

Our objectives in this project are to explore sediments with the deductive approach for patterns in a combination of proxies, which would code the interplay of environmental variables. We aim to explore high-resolution imaging techniques resulting in a pixel resolution of 50–200 µm containing up to 3,000 variables per pixel to examine the biogeochemical fingerprints embedded within lake seasonally laminated sediments.

To gain a full understanding of the impacts of environmental variables (temperature, trophic states, and catchment) on the deposited lake sediment, we will analyse modern sediments (~200 years old) linkable with observational data. Furthermore, the understanding of sediment biogeochemistry will be followed by laboratory incubation experiments of the previously analysed sediments to assess post-depositional alterations and the stability of preserved signals. The knowledge gained in the first two parts of this project will then be applied to older sediments (up to 16,000 yr BP) to test the reliability of reconstructing past environmental and climate conditions using sedimentary fingerprints. This research aims to answer the following questions (RQ):
1. How does the composition of organic matter at low, medium, and high lake trophic levels differ?
2. How do temperature, light and oxygen impact sediment composition?
3. How unique are the sediment biogeochemical fingerprints of cold and warm climates of the Earth’s history?

To answer these RQs and achieve our objectives, the team comprising the PI, a PhD student, and a research assistant will explore a suite of cutting-edge, high-resolution imaging techniques: µXRF elemental mapping for high-resolution elemental distribution maps, Mass Spectrometry Imaging (MSI) for simultaneous detection and spatial mapping of compounds, and Hyperspectral Imaging (HSI) for in situ sediment characterisation based on spectral signatures. Employing data science approaches, e.g., supervised and unsupervised pixel clustering and neural networks, on our complex data will enable a thorough understanding of sediment composition and reveal patterns linked to past climate and environmental events.

The outcome of this project will be a better understanding of the complex sediment composition and the link between the sediment composition and the environmental factors at its deposition. Results will be publicly accessible as a fingerprint and image database correlating biogeochemical sediment composition with specific climate and environmental conditions. This resource, open to contributions from other researchers, will facilitate more accurate interpretations of lake sediment records linked to past climate and environmental changes. With this knowledge, we can better anticipate the future behaviour of lake ecosystem services. The fingerprint database has the potential to significantly advance the field of paleoclimatology and bring more targeted conservation strategies for lake ecosystems in the face of future environmental challenges.

Title: Uncertainty Quantification for Optimal Transport
Abstract: The aim of this project is to develop statistical methods for carrying out inference and uncertainty quantification in the Wasserstein space W of probability measures on Rd.  The Wasserstein space is the natural setup for many real-world phenomena, ranging from computer vision to life sciences.  Existing statistical theory in Wasserstein space is unsatisfactory or restricted to the one-dimensional case.  In this project we aim to establish limit laws for random elements in the Wasserstein space, establishing the foundations for carrying out the elementary statistical tasks of testing hypotheses and constructing confidence sets in Wasserstein space.
Keywords: Distributional Limits, Non-Euclidean Statistics, Optimal Transport, Statistical Inference, Uncertainty Quantification, Wasserstein Distance

Title: RODI: ROle based speaker DIarization
Abstract:
Speaker Diarization (SD) is the task of inferring  who spoke when in an audio stream and is an essential step  for facilitating the search and the indexing of audio archives, increasing the richness of automatic transcriptions and extracting high level informations on human conversations.  It involves two simultaneous unsupervised tasks: (1) the estimation of the number of speakers (2) associating speech segment to each  speaker.  Typical diarization applications  consists of Broadcast audio and meeting recordings. Most of the recent efforts in the domain have addressed the problem using  machine learning and signal processing techniques. On the other hand, current approaches completely neglect the fact that the data represents instances of human conversations which present predictable patterns induced by the role that each participant have in the discussion.
Conversations are one the most common form of human  interaction and "while appearing unconstrained and spontaneous, are governed by principles and laws which give rise to ordered and predictable behavioral patterns" [Orestrom83]. 
In recent years, many studies have shown that the turn-taking  extracted from speaker diarization  can be statistically modeled  and used to classify the role that each speaker has in the conversation. Those roles can be formal (as in Broadcast recordings) or informal (as in meeting recordings). Reversely we propose to integrate in the diarization system, the statistics on the speaker interactions induced by their roles. 

 The goal of this proposal is to enhance  speaker diarization of meetings and broadcast data  through the combination of traditional audio processing techniques with the  information on the conversation structure coming from the roles that participants have. The project is organized in two research tracks:
1- Statistical representation and estimation of the  speakers interactions conditioned to their role.   
2-Integration of this information into the speaker diarization system.

We propose  three case scenarios  of increasing difficulty to address the problem. 

Case scenario A assumes that the number of speakers and their role are known. The research will focus on the statistical modeling of the turn-taking and on the integration of this information in the diarization.

Case scenario B assumes that the number of speakers is known, but their role is unknown. The research will focus on the estimation and the integration of the role information obtained by an automatic classifier.

Case scenario C assumes that both the number of speakers and their roles are unknown. The research will focus on how  the information on turn-taking and roles  affects the estimation of the number of speakers and the associated speaker time.

The development and the evaluation will be carried on meeting recordings and broadcast audio data collected in the framework of the Rich Transcription evaluations. Progresses will be estimated in terms of Diarization Error Rate which is the official metric proposed by NIST for benchmarking this task. The project will build on a recently finished thesis on speaker diarization which produced significant advances in the field of information fusion in this task. The research proposed in RODI will try to bridge the gap in between two different fields (automatic speaker segmentation and analysis of human conversations) that are closely related thus we ask to fund a dedicated PhD student to support the project. The student will join IDIAP and be enrolled in the EPFL EDEE doctoral school.
Keywords: Automatic role recognition, Human conversation analysis, Speaker clustering/diarization

Title: OPtimal Estimation in RAndom Generative mOdelS:  Theory, Thresholds, Tractability
Abstract:
Probabilistic models are ubiquitous in science and engineering. Statistics, Machine Learning, Information theory, signal processing, statistical physics –among others– are fundamentally based on them. Given this ubiquity, it might come as a surprise that we lack a satisfactory mathematical theory, even for very simple questions, on the optimal learning possibilities of efficient algorithms when dealing with data generated from these models. 

In OperaGOST, I wish to address this challenge, and to provide an answer to the following three fundamental questions for a large classes of probabilistic models: 
What is the best possible results one could hope for, regardless of any algorithms? 
For which distributions of data can the learning task be treated efficiently?  
What are the optimal algorithms, in terms of accuracy and computational complexity, for this task? 
Any progress on these questions would imply a dramatic advance in our understanding of random probabilistic structures, their interaction with efficient computation, and on the theory of learning from data, with far-reaching impact across multiple theoretical, applied and practical domains. 

In this project I wish to address these questions with an interdisciplinary approach that will leverage on the use of tools from mathematical physics and statistical mechanics, but also from information theory, optimisation and random matrices. It builds on the PI experience and track-record in methods of disordered systems and their successful applications to challenging computer-science problems. Indeed, the modelling strategy and the analysis proposed in the OperaGOST project originates from studies of phase transitions in models of condensed matter physics, Yet most of its objectives and anticipated applications belong to the fields of machine learning, computer science, and statistical data processing. 

It is the unique synergy between the theoretical statistical-physics inspired approach and the scientific application in computer science that makes the project original, its objectives achievable, and enables the promise of a leap forward in our understanding of the ability to learn from data.
Keywords: Algorithms, Information theory, Replica methods, Statistical Physics, Statistical-to-computational gaps, Statistics, Theory of learning

Title: eeGPT: Analysing Electroencephalograms with Generative Pre-trained Transformers
Abstract:
The Electroencephalogram (EEG) stands as a pivotal and time-tested diagnostic tool in epilepsy patient care. However, the intricate analysis of EEGs demands substantial time and expertise from highly specialized professionals. The introduction of wearable or implantable EEG devices, capable of ultra-long-term recordings spanning months or even years, has intensified this challenge. Artificial Intelligence (AI) holds the potential to offer innovative solutions. Consequently, our aim here is to harness cutting-edge AI techniques to address this critical healthcare necessity.

Specifically, our main goal is to advance EEG analysis by recent AI methods from Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPT), hence we design EEG + GPT = eeGPT. eeGPT aims to 1) exploit huge amounts of unlabelled EEG data, which have been and will be continuously collected from long-term monitoring devices; 2) ease adaptiveness for supporting different tasks for epilepsy diagnostics and therapy with few labelled data; 3) work with highly compressed representations of EEG to facilitate efficient wireless communications with long-term monitoring devices for battery saving.

State-of-the-art deep learning models are limited in their capabilities, particularly in the following two ways: patient-specific or task-specific limitations. To address the first limitation, eeGPT will provide a novel holistic view over multi-channel time-series by attending to time and channel information simultaneously. To address the second limitation and make use of unlabelled data, eeGPT will be pre-trained in a self-supervised manner on a non-specific task, namely predicting the next state of the EEG signal. eeGPT then can be fine-tuned by medical experts to support many different tasks that are demanded for personalized epilepsy treatment. This is not where its advantages end: eeGPT will devise new tokenization to operate with compressed representations of EEG while maintaining high fidelity.

In Work Package 1, we will build an instance of eeGPT based on our preliminary intracranial EEG foundation model. We will then thoroughly evaluate its capabilities and limitations, especially with a reduced number of electrodes and temporal compression, and further evolve it to be able to make a transition to challenging extracranially recorded EEG. In parallel, in Work Package 2, we will work on EEG data collected at the Sleep-Wake-Epilepsy-Center of the Inselspital. We will curate, organize, and label three EEG datasets: labelled routine scalp EEG, labelled vigilance/sleep polysomnographies (PSGs), and unlabelled ambulatory and in-hospital long-term EEGs. These three datasets will provide about 10000 hours of recordings, a scale that is critical to the generalization performance of generative AI methods. In Work Package 3, we will pre-train and fine-tune eeGPT with our EEG datasets aiming for supporting various tasks (e.g., detection of epileptiform signals and seizures, duration and depth of sleep, occurrence of diffuse slowing and other non-epileptiform changes, etc.) for epilepsy therapy, and eventual robust operation with compressed representations of EEG.   

eeGPT will thus combine clinical insights and sizeable EEG datasets with emerging generative AI methods to lay the foundation for improving ambulatory care of epilepsy patients.

A broader view of eeGPT reveals that it addresses two known and treatable risk factors for Alzheimer's disease, the most prevalent form of dementia: epilepsy and sleep disorders. Given the rising proportion of older individuals in industrialized nations, dementia is anticipated to inflict significant distress on patients and their families. Moreover, it poses a formidable challenge to healthcare systems and society as a whole. Consequently, any new instrument, like eeGPT, that enhances the treatment of dementia's risk factors and thereby mitigates cognitive deterioration, will be of immense significance.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Brain-inspired Computing, EEG, Epilepsy, Generative AI, Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT), Long-term Patient Monitoring, Machine Learning, Neurology, Sleep

Title: The combination of new data sources with statistical learning to tackle the robustness problem in traumatic stress studies. From interpretation to prediction and back?
Abstract:
In light of the recent replicability crisis in psychological science, also clinical research needs to rethink its scientific practices. Considering digital and technical developments, new opportunities have emerged during the last years with the potential to crucially change perspectives in the field of traumatic stress studies. Hereby, digital advances have an impact on both how data is collected and how it is analyzed. With respect to the first, new options for recruitment and data collection were invented in the last years: Crowdsource-based data collection via social networks or commercial tools is an easy-to-use, time-and cost-efficient option. Likewise, as a response to the Open Science movement, researchers also gain more and more access to large-scale data sets, since storage of data within repositories becomes a more common practice. Also, due to technical advancements modern computer devices allow more complex and computationally-intensive statistical models. This has led to the broad availability of machine-learning algorithms that have the potential to also reliably prediction human behavior, and thus provide an answer to the replicability crisis also with respect to traumatic stress studies. However, currently both large-scale datasets in combination with data-driven algorithms have not been incorporated in traumatic stress studies on a frequent basis and little is known about its potential in this area. One reason might be that applying these methods requires to find answers to a number of unsolved and critical issues. 
The aim of the project is to investigate how both new data sources and methods of analyses can lead to an altered scientific perspective for clinical psychology and traumatic stress studies in light of the replicability crisis. More specifically, the project has the following objectives: 1) To identify already-existing large-scale datasets for its applicability for traumatic stress studies. 2) To test the usefulness of data-driven models in order to extract relevant predictors (mental) health outcomes after exposure to traumatic stress over the course of time. 3) To compare the robustness of findings by transferring findings from one data-set to another independent data-set. 4) To discuss opportunities of data-driven models in solving the replicability crisis and its options in lights of its-often limited interpretability. 
In a first step, different open-access data repositories will be searched for suitable data sets that have investigated trauma-related variables. In a second step, predictive models by means of machine-learning algorithms will be built in order to establish robust and stable prediction of health outcomes over the curse of time that. Their predictive performance will be tested on a random chosen new data set of the available ones that has not been used for model building. Additionally, findings will be compared to already published results that have applied traditional statistical models. We expect robust models that can predict health outcomes over the course of time. However, specific variables used in the different datasets might vary, thus also compromising the generalizability of results. 
Altogether, this project serves as the basis for a better understanding of how digital advances can change scientific thinking in clinical psychology and will add valuable insights into the debate about how to combine traditional statistical models with predictive models that offer high predictive accuracy but low interpretability.
Keywords: PTSD, clinical psychology, machine learning, panel data, traumatic stress studies

Title: Tail-robust Analysis of High-dimensional Nonstationary Time Series
Abstract:
Overview: Time series analysis has played a central role in statistics, economics, finance, and social sciences. Advances in data collection technologies now allow researchers to gather time series data from numerous locations or nodes. As a result, high-dimensional time series data have become widespread in applications like sensor networks, health monitoring, natural language processing, and infectious disease analysis. Most existing techniques for analyzing dependent data assume stationarity in the data-generating process; however, this assumption can be unrealistic over extended periods. A more practical approach is piecewise stationarity, which assumes stationarity only within time segments separated by change-points. While mean change detection has been extensively studied, less attention has been given to autocovariance change-point problems. The cross-sectional and temporal dependencies captured by autocovariance matrices are crucial for understanding modern time series data. Moreover, high dimensionality, heavy-tailed distributions, and temporal dependence introduce new challenges in time series analysis, including autocovariance matrix estimation, change-point detection, and statistical inference. This proposal focuses on developing a tail-robust analysis framework for high-dimensional nonstationary time series under weak conditions. The research plan is organized around four coherent  research aims. In Aim 1,, we will develop two types of tail-robust autocovariance matrix estimators for high-dimensional time series, accommodating general non-linear temporal dependence with weak moment conditions. Their non-asymptotic properties will be meticulously studied. Building on this foundation, Aim 2, focuses on developing a statistical framework for detecting change-points in autocovariance structures. We will design of a novel statistic to assess autocovariance structure changes for nonstationary time series. Leveraging the unique properties of this statistic, we will introduce a recursive segmentation algorithm to learn the number and locations of multiple autocovariance change-points.  In Aim 3, we will address three closely related inference problems in high-dimensional nonstationary time series analysis: (a) Gaussian approximation for tail-robust autocovariance estimators; (b) bootstrapping for non-stationary time series; and (c) testing the presence of autocovariance change-points. In Aim 4, we plan to demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through interdisciplinary applications. Our goal is to tackle complex, real-world time series analysis problems across various domains.

Intellectual merit: This proposal aims to develop a new tail-robust framework for analyzing high-dimensional, nonstationary time series. To achieve this, the PIs will investigate a series of well-defined research problems, including the development of novel methodologies, robust algorithms, and rigorous theories. We will also create open-source, user-friendly software packages for implementation in real-world applications. Completing this project will fill existing knowledge gaps in the literature, provide key insights into modern time series applications, and serve the data-driven society with innovative time series analysis tools.

Broader impacts: This proposal aims to inspire new ideas to push statistical theory and methodology development forward.  The proposed research projects will (i) produce innovative theories and methodologies for analyzing modern time series data; (ii) stimulate new quantitative investigations across various scientific fields; (iii) provide the data-driven society with effective and efficient software packages; and (iv) offer undergraduate and graduate students a unique educational experience by involving them in cutting-edge, interdisciplinary research.
Keywords: Change point analysis, High-dimensional data modelling, Nonstationary process, Robust estimation, Time series analysis

Title: Unraveling Determinants of Reverse Shoulder Arthroplasty Outcomes: A Causal Bayesian Network Approach Integrating Clinical, Imaging, Biomechanical, and Genetic Data
Abstract:
Background: Reverse shoulder arthroplasty (RSA) has become the preferred option for primary shoulder arthroplasty. Initially used for rotator cuff tears in older adults, it is now widely used to treat osteoarthritis, failed shoulder replacements, and fractures at all ages. Despite its expanding use, RSA reports a significant complication rate, with up to 8.9% of patients experiencing complications within two years of surgery. Beyond infections, the leading causes of implant failure are mechanical, including glenohumeral instability, scapular fractures, component loosening, and restricted mobility, especially limitations in internal rotation. A deeper understanding of these complications is essential to improve RSA procedures, for example through more personalized surgical planning as well as enhanced functional and structural evaluations of the patients.
Objectives: The main objective of the proposed research is to improve the understanding of the determinants of RSA successes and failures, by collecting and analyzing preoperative and postoperative data for a large cohort of patients. Established and novel methods from complementary fields, including orthopedic surgery, imaging, biomechanics, and genetics, will extend an existing registry, to unravel the complex mechanism of RSA outcomes.
Previous work: In recent years, the applicants have initiated a shoulder registry, which already includes nearly 1000 patients, and developed patient-specific tools to quantify the biomechanics and structure of the upper limb. Further research is needed to extend patients’ evaluation and link preoperative information with clinical outcomes.
Methods: Clinical, imaging, kinematic, and genetic data will be collected for the patients who will undergo RSA at the university hospital in the next four years, for those who already had this procedure, and for control subjects. Advanced patient-specific musculoskeletal modeling integrating kinematic recordings will be used to evaluate joint stability and mobility. Additional analyses will be performed using finite element models, specifically to assess complications like bone fractures and implant loosening. Machine learning will be used to extract patient-specific structural features and complications from radiological images. The extensive observational mechanical, but also clinical, structural, functional, and genetic, data will be analyzed with causal Bayesian networks, which are powerful methods to test causal inferences and control for confounding variables.
Significance: The project is expected to advance both shoulder care and bioengineering. By building and analyzing a large multidimensional dataset, it will unravel important determinants of RSA outcomes. This is expected to enhance patient outcomes and minimize revision surgeries, for example, by stimulating more personalized treatment strategies, particularly with improved usage of individual data and patient-specific risk assessments. Original methods and expertise will be developed during the project, which could serve beyond RSA and upper limb pathologies.

Title: Hidden Quantifiers
Abstract:
Hidden quantifiers lie at the heart of some of the most well-studied theorems and methods of mathematical logic. A theory of first-order classical logic admits quantifier elimination, one of the main tools of model theory, if all occurrences of  quantifiers in a formula can be "hidden" (modulo the theory) using quantifier-free formulas. Similarly, Skolemization, a key ingredient of automated reasoning methods, "hides" occurrences of quantifiers in formulas by introducing new function symbols. Less obviously, quantifiers may be hidden at the propositional level using modal operators, yielding various disguised fragments of first-order logic.

The goal of this project is to study hidden quantifiers in the setting of universal algebra, focussing on classes of ordered algebras related to nonclassical --- in particular, substructural, modal, and many-valued --- logics. Hidden quantification for these classes takes various forms. Firstly, although the first-order theory of the class might not admit quantifier elimination, it may still be possible to define quantifiers with weaker properties. Most notably, Pitts'  uniform interpolation theorem for intuitionistic logic reveals propositional "bisimulation" quantifiers and the existence of a model completion for the theory of Heyting algebras. Part A of the project aims to develop a general theory of uniform interpolation and quantification, building bridges to model-theoretic properties such as amalgamation, coherence, and existence of model completions, and fixpoint properties studied in computer science. This theory is expected to yield not only new uniform interpolation results for  logics and classes of algebras, but also theorems and tools for characterizing and calculating uniform interpolants when they exist.

Parts B and C will consider hidden quantification at the propositional level, focussing on  ordered algebras with modal operators. Part B aims to establish a correspondence between fragments of quantified logics and "order-based" modal logics used to model concepts such as necessity, belief, and spatio-temporal relations in the presence of uncertainty or vagueness. This correspondence will be used to address open axiomatization, decidability,  and complexity problems for both these modal logics and the associated fragments. Part C aims to establish similar results for ordered groups with operators by extending relationships between orders on groups and validity in ordered groups to this setting. Such algebras not only provide semantics for "continuous" modal logics, but also serve as a basis, via categorical equivalences, for studying other residuated structures such as divisible and cancellative residuated lattices.
Keywords: Interpolation, Logic, Ordered Groups, Proof Theory, Universal Algebra

Title: Improving the accuracy of electrochemical simulations with physically grounded machine-learning approaches
Abstract: Electrochemical systems play a crucial role in numerous technologies for energy storage, electro-catalysis and nanoelectronics. When considering devices like batteries and capacitors, in particular, one is typically interested in studying the solvation and reaction processes that take place at the interface between the metal electrodes and the electrolyte solution. For this reason, the computer simulation of an electrochemical system must satisfy four main requirements: i) an explicit description of the electrolyte that is suitable to perfectly screen the electrode charge fluctuations, avoiding finite size effects, ii) a quantum-mechanical description of the electronic structure relaxation processes between electrodes and redox species in solution, iii) a simulation box larger than the typical Debye length of the electrolyte along the direction orthogonal to the metallic plates, and that extend for several nanometers along the directions parallel to the electrode surfaces, iv) simulation trajectories long enough to  converge the slow thermal relaxation process of the ions in solution. Many computational methods have been proposed over the past decades to simulate electrochemical systems. On one hand, density functional theory (DFT) based approaches are suitable to deal with the quantum nature of the system. However, DFT methods present a computational burden that is too high to be compatible with an explicit description of the system, and they usually circumvent the charge compensation problem by replacing the electrolyte solution with a continuum medium. On the other hand, classical molecular dynamics (MD) methods have been developed to enable the simulation of realistic electrochemical cells that include all the atomistic details of the system. In this case, the major drawback is the lack of a rigorous quantum-mechanical description, needed to predict electrochemical reactions. By and large, no existing method can  simultaneously meet the four requirements previously mentioned without relying on severe approximations. The objective of this proposal is to make use of physically grounded machine learning (ML) approaches to overcome the limitations associated with the first-principles simulation of electrochemical systems. The essential requirement of constructing a ML model that can predict  electronic-structure properties, such as the electron density, while incorporating long-range physical interactions, is made possible by the methods developed by the applicant during his PhD thesis. In the first part, the proposed ML framework will be trained on a set of finite electric field DFT calculations, that are suitable to simulate a relatively small electrochemical cell in the presence of an applied voltage drop. This learning effort will be used to assess the prediction accuracy  of the interaction energy between the (electrically polarized) metal and the electrolyte solution over an arbitrarily wide range of distances. In the second part, the possibility of learning the charge density distribution and the field-dependent Fukui functions of the metal, defined as the electron density response with respect to a smooth charge variation, will be used to characterize the redox centers over the electrode surface in response to the solvent distribution, as well as to obtain an estimate of the interfacial electric capacitance. Finally, these achievements will be exploited to carry out a data-driven MD simulation of a sufficiently large electrochemical cell, including a thermally relaxed description of the ionic solution beyond the Debye screening length. Applications of this framework will involve a system made of a lithium metal slab in contact with a room temperature ionic liquid. In perspective, the proposed research plan lays the groundwork for solving the long-standing problem of adopting an explicit representation of the electrolyte within the first-principles modeling of electrochemical reactions.
Keywords: density functional theory, electrochemistry, long-range interactions, machine learning

Title: A virtual reality and machine learning approach to predict physiological vulnerability to stress from high-density locomotor data
Abstract:
Psychosocial stress is deleterious to health and can affect the development of diseases, including psychopathologies and cardiovascular disorders, making the identification of at-risk individuals an extremely valuable resource. Here, we aim at developing a novel diagnostic tool, that can be measured ubiquitously, to identify physiological stress susceptibility based on behavioral data. An important innovation of our approach is to put forward locomotor features during exploration of novel (virtual) environments as a means to predict physiological vulnerability. Preliminary results from our approach indicate that indeed it is possible to predict the individual stress response using machine learning with these locomotor features collected outside stress. Given our promising existing results, we expect to achieve a refined model with the added subjects and a generalization stress task. To this end we will use an intermediate disease effector as dependent variable; specifically, heart rate variability (HRV; an index of vagal brake on sympathetic nervous system activity), proved itself to be a critical intermediate mechanism of disease. We will collect high-density locomotor data of exploration in non-threatening immersive virtual environments (IVEs), inspired in exploratory tasks for behavioral phenotyping in the rodent literature: an empty room and an elevated alley. We will then apply state-of-the-art machine learning techniques to these high-density locomotor features in order to learn how predict the HRV based stress response in a third IVE where threat is ubiquitous. Finally, we want to study the capacity of our model to generalize to a different stressful situation for which the model was not trained, and expand this sample to females while broadening as well the age range.
We will recruit 120 healthy participants (60 males and 60 females) with ages 18-48 years-old. A virtual reality (VR) head mounted display will be used to immerse participants in the different IVEs: two exploration and one threatening IVEs of 90 seconds each where we have already been able to predict HRV from behavior; one stressful challenge in VR lasting 10 minutes that has already been tested and validated in the lab for stress elicitation. 
Behavior in the exploration IVEs will be assed via position tracking and motion capture using already developed behavioral features. Feature selection will be performed on the training set and the resulting features will be used for statistical model learning with state-of-the art regression-like models such as extreme gradient boosting. We will use explanatory machine learning to understand the impact of each feature in the model’s decision for each individual subject. The stress response will be quantified using cardiorespiratory data (respiration and electrocardiogram), which will be recorded wirelessly. Given the vast number of available HRV formulas, we will use the most widely used time- and frequency-domain formula for parasympathetic activity. The stressful challenge in VR will be further quantified using salivary cortisol and alpha amylase.
The discovery of non-invasive biomarkers for disease is a key goal in contemporary biomedicine. So far, daily locomotor data passively acquired through either room sensing technologies or wearables (i.e., digital phenotyping) has been used to predict disease progression in elderly populations or in individuals at risk for self-reported anxiety, depression or stress. However, our study will go beyond as, to date, no study has demonstrated the prognostic value of behavioral data as a predictor of stress vulnerability using objective (i.e., not self-reported) stress measurements. In addition, given the heterogeneity of life challenges and conditions in human subjects, establishing a diagnostic value of real-life behavioral data from passive digital phenotyping approaches to predict stress vulnerability is still extremely challenging. Our approach provides a key and highly necessary a priori step, as it will gain relevant information (that later could be used to interpret data from real life and digital technologies) by probing subjects under experimentally controlled situations in VR environments. We expect our project to contribute with a major step in the field of physiological stress susceptibility.
Keywords: Behavior, Bio-markers, Heart rate variability, Machine learning, Prevention, Stress, Virtual reality

Title: Modeling of Beam-Induced Motion in Cryo-Electron Tomography
Abstract: We intend to improve the resolution of cryo-electron tomography reconstruction through the development of novel algorithms. Recently, single particle analysis has experienced a revolution in terms of resolution, for the first time producing reconstructions of biological macromolecules at a near-atomic scale, without the need to crystallize them. Single particle analysis, however, still requires a purified solution of the molecule in question, while tomography allows researchers to observe the molecules in a near-natural state. Reconstruction from tomography, though, is still limited to less than half the resolution of single particle analysis. We assume that this is largely due to the motion induced in the cell volume by the electron beam, which leads to slight misalignments between the individual images of the sequence and thus to blurry reconstructions. We expect that by actively modeling that motion, we will be able to significantly improve the resolution of tomography reconstruction, bringing it closer to the resolution of single-particle methods. We will adapt current state-of-the-art variational approaches from the field of computer vision to serve as a basis for our algorithms.
Keywords: computer vision, cryo-electron microscopy, cryo-electron tomography, electron cryo-tomography

Title: Coding Theory and Sparse Recovery
Abstract:
Sparse recovery is an interdisciplinary area at the intersection of high-dimensional geometry, signal processing, combinatorics, and theoretical computer science which in the recent years has caught tremendous attention from researchers, largely due to several exciting breakthroughs as well as fundamental applications in a wide range of areas.

The most important sub-classes of sparse signal recovery include compressive sensing, combinatorial group testing, and low-rank matrix completion. The basic goal in compressive sensing is to identify a hidden sparse vector, typically over the real or complex domain, using measurements that each reveal the inner product of the hidden vector with a carefully chosen "measurement vector". Group testing is a similar problem, but over the Boolean domain {0,1}. In this variation, each measurement picks a set of the coordinate positions and reveals whether the sparse support of the unknown vector contains any of the chosen positions. Finally, low-rank matrix completion is a matrix-form variation of sparse recovery, with the goal of learning a hidden low-rank matrix by revealing as few entries of the matrix as possible. The structural properties of the hidden object in all these variations, namely sparsity of the vectors or the low rank property of the matrices, allow for measurement designs that make it possible to reconstruct the unknown vector or matrix using a substantially lower number of measurements than its dimension.

Among the vast number of applications of sparse recovery that signify its importance, one can mention compressive imaging, biomedical imaging, machine learning, sensor networks and network coding, data streaming, digital communication, metric embedding, molecular biology and DNA library screening, data compression, pattern matching, software testing, inference in surveys and recommendation systems, and many others.

In this project, we will investigate direct and indirect connections between sparse recovery problems and tools from coding theory. This will include explicit construction of optimal, or near-optimal, measurement schemes using error-correcting codes and codes from randomness extractors and related objects. Moreover, we will work on connections between sparse recovery and list-decodable codes, generalized sparse recovery problems allowing arbitrary or larger classes of measurements, and their connections with harmonic analysis of Boolean functions. Finally, we will touch upon adaptive measurement designs as well as constructions of Johnson-Lindenstrauss projections that are geometric objects related to compressive sensing and subject of substantial attention in high-dimensional geometry.

Some of the above-mentioned directions form a continuation of my Ph.D. thesis work and parts of my current post-doctoral research funded by a Swiss NSF prospective researchers grant. Further than that, the proposed project features a number of completely different directions, such as applications of tools from harmonic analysis, additive combinatorics, and high-dimensional geometry in attacking problems related to sparse recovery.
Keywords: Combinatorial group testing, Compressed Sensing, Dimensionality reduction, Error-correcting codes, Low-rank matrix completion, Randomness extractors, Sparse recovery

Title: Scaling Laws for Neural Network Models of the Primate Visual Ventral Stream
Abstract:
Artificial neural networks have revolutionized our ability to model the brain. Compared to early small-scale models, the latest state-of-the-art neural network models have vastly improved our explanatory power of cortical neural activity. Our community typically builds new models of the brain in a trial-and-error fashion: following some intuitive idea, we codify it into a computational model, train it on task-related data, and hope that this model's brain alignment is better than what we had before. But this lacks a guiding principle for improving models and costly in terms of compute to train larger models. At the same time in machine learning, the latest model improvements mostly stem from one key factor: scale. Larger models are trained on larger datasets with larger compute budgets. These models are guided by scaling laws that have been established with small- to mid-sized models. 

We here propose to "scale the neuroscience way" and scale up model building with the goal of improving brain alignment -- specifically for the primate visual ventral stream -- rather than solely performance on computer vision benchmarks. By testing the brain alignment of architectures of different sizes, image distributions of different quantities, and objective functions, we can establish scaling laws that allow us to extrapolate which combination of model components is likely to be the most brain-like. In other words, we will be able to use these scaling laws to efficiently experiment with models at a small scale and then only scale up those architectures, objectives, and image distributions that are the most promising. This approach might lead to a vastly more efficient discovery of neural models of the brain's visual system, which we believe will ultimately help us understand the brain and mind, and be key components of clinical applications.
Keywords: artificial neural networks, deep learning, primate vision, visual neuroscience, visual object classification, visual ventral stream

Title: Enabling Drug Discovery with Small and Dirty Data
Abstract:
Identifying ligands that bind to a biological target is both an important step and a limiting factor in modern drug design. Tremendous efforts have been made to classify the drug features that affect their target binding properties. However, due to insufficient available data and uncertainties from experimental measurements, salient drug features are difficult to find. Tackling this problem in an automated, scalable fashion requires efficient filtering techniques and ways to systematically represent chemical compounds at sufficient resolution.

Some methods have successfully extracted useful information from the available data, such as the work of Lee et al. [1]. These approaches typically use molecular graphs [2,3] or descriptors based upon structure alignment [4-6] to represent molecules, proteins, and other compounds. Such coarse representations often have difficulties describing many important features in chemical compounds, such as non-covalent interactions, or distinguishing between conformers in a systematic and efficient manner. This raises the question of whether a more efficient representation could improve the information extraction process.

My Ph.D. research has focused on the development and deployment of machine learning models for predicting fundamental quantum mechanical properties [7-10], such as energies, forces, and dipole moments. While this work fundamentally differs from the aforementioned approaches for assessing ligand binding affinities, certain aspects are poised to tackle the shortcomings of existing methods. 

One area of my research with promising applicability in ligand discovery is the field of molecular representations. A complete and efficient representation of compounds, capable of uniquely distinguishing any changes in geometry is necessary to accurately model quantum mechanical properties. Hence, numerous representations of compounds have spawned from quantum chemistry related machine learning.

I propose that these representations developed to predict energies and forces can be used in combination with molecular dynamics sampling to obtain an ensemble of representations. This ensemble can be  aggregated via Boltzmann sampling to generate ligand representations. This ensemble forms a more realistic representation than molecular graphs, since the compounds are treated as continuous objects living on a potential energy surface, instead of as a rigid body. This project would explore whether such generalized representation of ligands and targets can help in identifying and understanding the drug features relevant to target binding.

It is conceivable that this way of representing ligands can improve the accuracy of current models and therefore help to identify new drug candidates.  Furthermore, the insights gained from this project could also help guide neighbouring areas of research to shift from discovery to design.  

Compared to my previous research where I developed representations but focused on clean and noise-less data of relatively low complexity in this Cambridge postdoc I will instead pivot towards complex biological problems featuring noisy experimental data. As such, this postdoc together with Alpha Lee will be an invaluable experience for me. I will learn important aspects of modern drug design, which is a field that I intend to pursue further throughout my career.

Title: Collaborative Vision-based Perception, Towards Intellingent Robotic Teams
Abstract:
Following the boost in popularity of Robotics research over the past decade we witnessed truly impressive advancement in the technology available. Right at the forefront are small Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) equipped with onboard cameras, recently demonstrating that vision-based autonomous flights without reliance on GPS are possible, sparking great interest in a plethora of areas. With society and industry pushing for robot-assistive systems to automate cumbersome tasks, such as inspection and maintenance, a vast amount of research effort is dedicated to relevant technologies. Current solutions, however, still lack in portability and generality struggling to perform outside the controlled laboratory environment, with onboard robotic perception constituting the biggest impediment. 

The emergence of bio-inspired dynamic visual sensing, and with their fusion with existing visible-light and inertial measurements open up new horizons in robotic perception, capturing the interest in the Computer Vision and Robotics communities. While with the potential to revolutionise the field, the heterogeneity of these sensing cues poses great research questions in understanding how to process and combine them. Moreover, inspired by nature's swarming behaviour enabling teams to address problems that individuals cannot (e.g. ants building a bridge to transport members of their colony from one side to the other), the transition from single intelligent robotic agents to a robotic team promises to revolutionise the way that we perceive robotic automation today.

In this spirit, continuing on the fundamental and high-impact work conducted as part of my ongoing SNSF Professorship grant, the focus of this research plan lies with addressing remaining key questions in developing advanced robotic perception capabilities of a swarm of UAVs with a plethora of potential applications ranging from search-and-rescue and industrial inspection, to digitisation of archaeological sites and crop monitoring. With previous and ongoing work predominantly focusing on resource-limited and highly agile rotorcraft UAVs, my aim is to explore and further develop robotic perception under some of the most challenging circumstances, promising to push the boundaries of robotic perception in general. As the advances to robotic intelligence envisioned in this work are largely platform-agnostic and are key in addressing the perceptual uncertainties present in real robotic missions, this work has great potential in transforming the way we consider the employment of Robotics today.

Title: A novel machine-learning approach for robust neutrino detection
Abstract:
In this project, I will develop a novel machine learning (ML) approach for robust neutrino detection by mitigating data–simulation differences in liquid argon time projection chambers (LArTPCs), which is an emerging detector technology for accelerator-based neutrino experiments. This will resolve an open problem, and allow a promising ML-based reconstruction chain to be confidently applied to neutrino data analysis. Ultimately this will be a vital step to deliver physics goals of the flagship Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE). 

Understanding neutrinos may hold the key to answering one of the most puzzling questions in physics: why is the Universe matter dominated? Neutrino oscillation is a newly discovered tool for probing unknown physics, in which electron-, muon- and tau-neutrinos change their identity as they travel. Neutrinos are difficult to measure as they interact very rarely, so kilotonne scale of detectors and intense neutrino sources are required for precision measurements. DUNE is a future accelerator neutrino oscillation experiment designed to resolve a number of outstanding questions. The main DUNE detection technology is LArTPCs, which produce high-resolution images of charged particles generated by neutrino interactions. ML algorithms are powerful techniques well suited to the complex task of identifying and reconstructing neutrino events from such images. 

A recent development, led by the group at SLAC, to address these challenges is a full data reconstruction chain that consists of innovative machine learning algorithms. While its performance is impressive on simulated LArTPC images, a demonstration for a physics analysis with real data is vital. Critically, as this chain is optimized only using simulation, it may be vulnerable to discrepancies between simulation and real data. For this chain to work reliably on real LArTPC image dataset, an equally innovative solution is needed for an accurate modeling of detector physics effects with precision. 

Through this proposal, I will develop a ML approach compatible with the reconstruction chain which is currently being developed, to identify and mitigate data–simulation differences, and strengthen the ML recon- struction chain against them. I will use real data from a prototype LArTPC to benchmark the performance of this new ML approach through an analysis of neutrino-induced neutral pions (p0’s). The p0 decay to two photons, which produce electromagnetic showers in the detector, is a standard candle to characterize the detec- tor response, and is important because the main DUNE oscillation signal will be identified by electromagnetic showers from electrons. 

There are four key stages to this project: 
• Stage 1: develop criteria for selecting neutrino induced p0 interactions using detailed simulation.?
• Stage 2: develop a differentiable simulator to improve the fidelity of the detector simulation; build adversarial training of a discriminative model to be robust against the potential remaining data–simulation differences. 
• Stage 3: contribute to the commissioning and operation of the ArgonCube 2×2 prototype detector, which will produce LArTPC neutrino beam data of a similar quality to that expected in the DUNE experiment.
• Stage 4: evaluate the novel ML approach using neutrino-induced p0 data from the ArgonCube 2×2 detector, and measure the p0 production rate to provide useful information for the DUNE physics program. 

This project will mark an important step for robust neutrino detection using ML framework for LArTPCs. The impact of this project is not limited to DUNE, and will benefit all LArTPC-based experiments. Carrying out this project at SLAC will allow me to work with world experts in the field, and will put me in a good position to develop into a future leadership position in this area.
Keywords: Particle Physics, liquid argon (LAr), machine learning, neutral pion, neutrino, reconstruction, time projection chamber (TPC)

Title: Artificial intelligence and machine learning to improve the diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction
Abstract:
Background and rationale
Cardiovascular disease including acute myocardial infarction (AMI) remains the leading cause of death worldwide with 17.6 million people dying per annum. Each year, more than 12 million patients present with suspected AMI to the emergency department (ED) in Europe and North America, resulting in substantial resource use and contributing to ED crowding. Prompt recognition of patients with AMI is crucial to guide investigation and timely treatment and can improve survival. The major innovation in the early diagnosis of AMI in the last years was the clinical introduction of high-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn) assays, which has improved the early diagnosis of AMI. Therefore, international guidelines recommend the use of hs-cTn testing to enable earlier diagnosis of AMI with a fixed diagnostic threshold derived from a healthy reference population. Applying these recommendations in a stepped wedge cluster randomised controlled trial across 10 secondary and tertiary care hospitals in Scotland demonstrated that testing reduced length of stay but did not improve patient care or outcomes. 

Objectives and specific aims
It is well known that cardiac troponin concentrations are influenced by age, sex, time of symptom onset and comorbidities, such as kidney disease, and new approaches that individualise the use of this biomarker are needed to guide clinical decisions. To improve the early diagnosis of AMI, it is our aim to develop a machine learning algorithm that incorporates these variables and can accurately predict the likelihood of AMI and report probabilities for individual patients to guide better clinical decisions. 
We hypothesize that:

1.A machine learning algorithm combining cardiac troponin with key clinical variables can improve the diagnostic performance of hs-cTn for AMI in patients with comorbidities. 
2.Use of this algorithm in clinical practice to estimate the probability of AMI will improve clinical decisions in patients with suspected AMI and reduce diagnostic uncertainty. 

Methods
We plan to train and test a machine learning algorithm called CoDE-MI (Collaboration for the Diagnosis and Evaluation of Myocardial Infarction) that will combine hs-cTn with age, sex, comorbidities, and other variables into a clinical decision support tool to improve the diagnostic performance of cardiac troponin. We will develop this using data from our previous randomised controlled trial population (High-Sensitivity Troponin in the Evaluation of Patients With Acute Coronary Syndrome [High-STEACS]; NCT:01852523) which enrolled 48,282 consecutive patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome. We will then externally validate its performance with our collaborators in patients from Switzerland, Australia, and New Zealand. Finally, we will integrate CoDE-MI into clinical practice in a proof-of-concept clinical trial. 

Results and impact
We believe that our algorithm will improve the diagnostic performance of hs-cTn and will be generalisable across different healthcare settings. Further development to enable the algorithm to be embedded into practice across different healthcare systems could lead to a more individualised assessment for our patients, reduce diagnostic uncertainty, ED crowding, and patient’s anxiety by improving the selection of patients for early discharge and hospital admission for further investigation and treatment.
