Title: Comprehensive analysis of determinants of polyethylene wear and the related tissue response to improve outcomes in total hip arthroplasty
Abstract:
Approximately 10% of individuals in Western countries require total hip arthroplasty (THA) in their lifetime. The leading long-term cause of THA revision remains wear and wear particle induced inflammation. Although highly cross-linked polyethylene (HXLPE), today’s best choice for acetabular sockets, has mitigated mid-term wear issues, long-term concerns persist with variable clinical performance among products. Particularly, we have detected deviations from specifications that greatly influence the implant’s wear performance. Confidentiality of material properties and processing data limits analysis, and there is a lack of comparative studies correlating implant properties with clinical and histopathological outcomes. Wear particles from HXLPE are smaller and biologically more potent than those from conventional polyethylene and are often undetectable in routine histology, underscoring the need for innovative diagnostic methods. This project will characterize the in vitro and in vivo wear behaviour of polyethylene (PE) sockets from retrieved THA components, particularly HXLPE, to identify product-specific differences and their relation to failure modes and tissue response. Through collaboration with centres in Switzerland, Germany, Austria and the USA, we will analyse ~5’000 retrievals to ensure robust statistical power. Our central hypothesis is that structural and property differences among PE brands directly affect the in vivo wear performance, associated tissue response and ultimately medium- to long-term implant failure. We will test our hypothesis with the following work packages (WP):
-WP1: Collect retrieved PE sockets from revision THA with corresponding periprosthetic tissue samples and clinical information. Retrievals and clinical data will be obtained from an international multicentre network of reference centres in revision THA.
-WP2: Characterize the chemical structure and cross-linking degree of PE from all major THA brands and their impact on mechanical properties and wear resistance. Samples from the bulk of the material will be characterized using Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, mechanical testing, and tribological testing.
-WP3: Precisely analyze the relationship between absorbed dose and the trans-vinylene index in HXLPE through controlled irradiation campaigns conducted in high dose-rate gamma and beta irradiation facilities. The absorbed dose in polyethylene will be accurately determined using well-established alanine dosimetry.
-WP4: Determine in vivo wear rates for HXLPE bearings in THA and assess how wear volume and patterns relate to material design and clinical factors. Wear will be assessed from retrievals with an optical coordinate measuring machine. The impact of various factors on in vivo wear will be assessed via multiple regression and novel artificial intelligence-based methods.
-WP5: Characterize histopathological patterns associated with HXLPE wear in THA in relation to material design and clinical confounding factors. Histopathological analysis will be augmented by a novel FTIR imaging (FTIR-I) approach to identify and locate intra-cellular wear debris.
This project will characterize material properties and wear behaviour of revised THA components, offering a unique opportunity to determine with sufficient statistical power the determinants of PE wear in THA, particularly for HXLPE, integrating product specificities as well as the corresponding tissue response. Benchmarks for material properties and processing will be established, improving implant development and failure analysis. A unique histopathological approach augmented by FTIR-I, currently available only at our collaborating institution in the USA, will be implemented in Switzerland, establishing an innovative reference centre in Europe. More cost-effective methods will be developed for broader application. Beyond improving patient-related outcomes, the findings may be expected to reduce medium- to long-term revision rates by ~50%, significantly alleviating the burden on healthcare systems.

Title: Customer Interactions with Generative Artificial Intelligence
Abstract:
Advances in large language models and the associated establishment of the user-friendly application ChatGPT have led to a focus of public attention on generative chatbots in a very short time. Compared to previous chatbots, generative chatbots do not rely on predefined response alternatives and can therefore provide completely new and unanticipated responses. Furthermore, they are usually able to consider entire conversation progressions and react to their own mistakes. These characteristics lead to generative chatbots being perceived and treated as very human by their users and they might even offer social value (see social response theory). Therefore, the technology has great potential to revolutionize the interaction between chatbots and customers and will increasingly replace human service agents.

International top-tier marketing research has often limited chatbot studies to simple interaction illustrations or, at most, experiments with rule-based chatbots. This research often investigated superficial features of chatbot anthropomorphism (e.g., the name of a chatbot) and did not benchmark chatbots with human service employees. Moreover, in the field of text analysis, previous marketing research generally did not make use of the advanced methodology of modern large language models. This has led to a clear consensus among researchers that further exploration is needed in these specific domains.

To address these research gaps, we plan to conduct two experimental studies. We assume that the occasion of a customer interaction plays a decisive role in optimizing the customer interaction with chatbots. Therefore, we will use both negatively and positively connoted scenarios (e.g., a service recovery and a recommendation scenario) in our incentive-compatible experiments.

The first study will focus on how customers perceive generative chatbots compared to human service agents and traditional chatbots. We hypothesize that generative chatbots excel over human service agents during positive interactions, while the opposite may occur in negative scenarios. Furthermore, we intend to explore ways to optimize the interface between generative chatbots and human service employees. We expect that a redirection to a human service agent will be perceived more negatively with a generative chatbot than with a traditional chatbot.
For our second study, our sole focus will be on generative chatbots. We plan to employ cutting-edge text analysis techniques derived from large language models to evaluate different strategies for adapting to customer interactions. According to communication accommodation theory, such adaptations usually have a positive effect on interaction partners. In our study, we therefore want to examine the effectiveness of adaptation strategies frequently used in marketing research (i.e., personality matching, language style matching, empathy, social vs. formal orientation). We assume that personality matching is most successful in positive interaction occasions, while empathy should be most successful in negative interaction occasions.

The implications of this research project go far beyond the focus on marketing. Generative chatbots promise to transform many aspects of our society, from serving as educational tutors to fulfilling diverse roles in healthcare, including support for mental health care. Optimizing the interaction behavior of generative chatbots is also highly important in these application fields, among others.

Altogether, this research contributes to research and society by providing an understanding of interaction satisfaction with generative chatbots, investigating the role of anthropomorphism in chatbot interactions, exploring personalized adaption strategies in chatbot communication, and providing and evaluating real-world applications and implications for generative artificial intelligence.
Keywords: anthropomorphism, chatbots, communication adaptation, customer interaction, customer relationship management, generative AI, large language models

Title: AI-based Risk Assessment for Clinical Trials on Medicinal Products: A Large-Scale and Integrative Approach
Abstract:
Background and rationale: Clinical trials (CTs) are essential for developing new drug treatments, but they are costly and subject to high failure rates. Artificial intelligence (AI) methods offer the potential to improve the efficiency and success of such CTs by enabling more accurate risk assessment and improving drug safety and efficacy prediction. However, current AI-based CT risk assessment approaches face limitations like selection bias, limited data diversity, and siloed risk categories.
Overall objectives and specific aims: This project aims to overcome these limitations by creating a comprehensive and integrated AI-based approach for CT risk assessment. Specifically, we will i) build an integrated risk assessment benchmark for drug safety, efficacy, and operational risks using CT protocols and results, ii) design deep learning models, particularly graph neural networks (GNN) and transformer-based language models (LMs), to jointly learn multiple risk categories, and iii) investigate the generalization of AI models for CTs in large retrospective and prospective studies.

The dataset will include demographics, intervention details, CT phase, sponsor, adverse events, outcomes, trial status, and protocol modifications across selected therapeutic areas. Data will be cleaned, preprocessed, and labeled for quality improvement. Phase 2 focuses on developing deep learning models (GNNs and LMs) to simultaneously learn safety, efficacy, and operational risks in a multi-task framework. These models will be trained on the integrated benchmark, using features like drug structure, CT design, and participant characteristics. Performance will be evaluated with appropriate metrics for imbalanced data (e.g., F1-score, MCC). Phase 3 will prospectively evaluate a diverse subset of ongoing trials across different interventions, conditions, and phases. The best model from retrospective data will be applied to infer risks of prospective studies, and results will be compared to actual outcomes. We will also explore a use-case comparing AI predictions with physiologically-based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) simulations for drug-drug interactions. These experiments will retrospectively and prospectively assess model performance, early risk identification, and generalizability across diverse CTs.
Expected results: We anticipate delivering a comprehensive benchmark dataset and improved machine learning models for CT risk assessment, alongside insights into their real-world performance. Specifically, we expect to i) provide a unique open benchmark dataset for CT risk assessment, fostering further research; ii) develop robust and scalable open-source machine learning models for accurate prediction of drug safety, efficacy, and operational risks; iii) offer actionable insights for researchers and clinicians to optimize trial design, mitigate safety and efficacy risks, and reduce failure risks; and iv) advance digital trials research by establishing a strong foundation with open data and models. In particular, we expect to answer whether AI methods can generalize CT risk predictions across modalities (molecular structure, free text, hierarchical/categorical data), conditions, and interventions.
Impact: This project has the potential for significant scientific and practical impact on clinical research and drug development. Scientifically, it will contribute to digital trial design and management by demonstrating machine learning's feasibility in enhancing CT risk assessment. In practice, results may lead to tangible benefits in drug development, including improved CT efficiency and success, enhanced patient safety through early risk identification, accelerated drug development and faster access to new treatments, and reduced associated costs.

Title: Cognitive sequelea of adolescent recreational substance use
Abstract:
Substance use is highly prevalent among Swiss adolescents and young adults, with potential long-term consequences for cognitive well-being. Substances such as alcohol, tobacco, and cannabis have been proposed to be particularly neurotoxic during the highly neuroplastic and sensitive period of adolescent brain maturation. Indeed, several cross-sectional and a few longitudinal studies suggest that an early age of onset and frequent use of these substances during adolescence is associated with impaired cognitive performance and less educational success in later life. These previous studies came with notable limitations, however. First, cross-sectional studies typically used small and highly selective samples, assessed substance use by self-report only, and could, by design, not address the directionality of effects. Second, the few longitudinal studies tended to be underpowered, relied on self-reported substance use only, started their substance use assessments past the age of typical initiation, or were limited to one or few adolescent substance use assessments. Most of these studies also had a low prevalence of adolescent substance use, limiting statistical power to detect associations with later-life cognition. Third, sex-differences were neglected in nearly all studies, although animal studies suggest differences in developmental vulnerability between sexes. Finally, previous studies did not adequately address polysubstance use and concurrent use or chronic consumption of specific substance combinations, which are, however, normative patterns of use in adolescents today.
We propose to address these limitations by leveraging a unique, large-scale cohort study with 9 main assessments from ages 7 to 24 to investigate the developmental neurotoxicity of early substance use on young adult cognitive functions. The Zurich Project on the Social Development from Childhood to Adulthood (z-proso, N=1,675, 52% males), funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF, No. 198052), has investigated the social, educational, and psychological development of participants at ages 7, 8, 9, 11, 13, 15, 17, 20, and 24. Importantly, up to 6 self-reports of substance use (prevalence and frequency) per person are available between ages 11 and 24 in z-proso. At age 20 (in 2018) and 24 (in 2022), the study also collected hair samples. Funded by the SNSF (No. 189008), the age 20 hair samples were already assayed for ~100 illegal substances and medications and their main metabolites by state-of-the-art toxicological analysis. Part of the here proposed work is to additionally assay the already collected age 24 hair samples.
The fine-grained z-proso substance use questionnaire revealed a high burden from substance use. For example, self-reported 12-month prevalence at age 20 was: cannabis use=56%, cocaine=11%, Ecstasy=12%, codeine=13%, and use of at least 2 illegal substances=25%. The age 20 hair tests suggested that 3-month self-reports underestimated the prevalence of most substances by 30–60%, demonstrating the urgent need of objective measurement of substance use. Importantly, at age 24 (data collection was finished in August 2022), three well-established tests of the Core Battery of the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB) were also administered, assessing four core domains of young adults’ cognition: attention, working memory, visuo-spatial declarative memory, and executive functions.
Thus, the richly characterized unique z-proso data set will allow us to predict young adults’ cognitive performance across core domains, using both the self-reported and objectively quantified measures of adolescent and young adult substance use. It will also allow us to investigate potential sex difference in the developmental neurotoxicity of the substances. Importantly, at all of its 9 main assessments, z-proso extensively characterized sociodemographics, child characteristics (e.g., symptoms of anxiety, depression, pro- and antisocial behaviors, ADHD, and later also psychosis), earlier indicators of cognitive functions (e.g., school success), and other potential confounders/covariates. The longitudinal data also allow for an examination of the directionality of effects and to apply propensity score modeling techniques that are suitable for causal analysis of observational studies. Our research aims include to test:
1) cross-sectional associations between substance use and cognition at age 24,
2) longitudinal associations between objectively quantified substance use in hair (age 20 and 24) and cognition at age 24,
3) associations of different substance use trajectories between ages 11 and 20 and cognition at age 24, 
4) cross-sectional and longitudinal associations of cognition and real-life functioning at age 24, and
5) the prediction of cognition from adolescent and young adult substance use with the use of artificial intelligence.
New findings revealed that legalization of cannabis in the US has driven young adults’ rates of cannabis use to an all-time high (1). In this era, it is crucial to understand the potential cognitive costs of early substance use. The present study has outstanding potential to overcome limitations of previous work, and to generate important new knowledge on the impact of early life substance use on cognition. Its insights can inform ongoing debates of legalizing cannabis and other substances, including in Switzerland, which has high rates of substance use among young people, and where a legalized cannabis market is expected within the next few years. Of note, we aim not only to investigate the effects of alcohol, tobacco, and cannabis use but also of substances such as Ecstasy, cocaine, prescription opioids, and polysubstance use, which have been scarcely investigated in longitudinal study designs and which were used at high prevalence rates at age 20 in the z-proso cohort.
The proposed project leverages a rich, long-term-longitudinal existing data collection in a cost-effective way to examine important questions about the role of substance use in young adult cognition at a unique scale. Results of the proposed project have the potential to provide substantial and significant new insights into the study of the developmental neurotoxicity of adolescent substance use on cognition. Thus, we expect that our findings will inform addiction research, prevention, and policymaking in important new ways. Our proposal requests funding for one PhD student, one postdoc, consultant costs for an international expert on causal modeling, and assaying the age 24 hair data to analyze the above research questions with the exceptional z-proso data set.

Title: Probabilistic inference schemes in forensic handwriting examination: a diagrammatic approach to support evaluation and reporting
Abstract:
General context: The comparative examination of handwriting is a reputedly challenging area of forensic practice because of its strong reliance on expert judgement by individual examiners. Unlike the chemistry- and physics-based branches of forensic science, comparative handwriting examination does not currently invoke any standardised quantitative measurements, except for research purposes and with a restriction to selected handwriting features. Usually, forensic handwriting examiners express and summarise their observations in terms of qualitative verbal descriptors (e.g., ‘similarities’ and ‘differences’). This gives rise to a fundamental two-fold problem. On the one hand, scientists face the problem of how to assess the probative value of observations made during comparative examinations, and on the other hand, they face the problem of how to communicate and convey their evaluation in a case-tailored, transparent, logical, robust and intelligible way. These tasks are further complicated by the fact that they need to be conducted under circumstances of uncertainty that inevitably accompany all practical proceedings. The extent to which conclusions of forensic scientists can be trusted in this area of practice thus became a major focus of attention and is considered by several critics from the legal disciplines as being vague at the least. This skepticism, which in some jurisdictions fueled intense debates over legal admissibility, is further supported by the fact that the practice of some scientists could be demonstrably shown to be unreliable. In combination, this reveals the interdependency between scientific and legal issues.

Practical needs, relevance and main research issue: As in various other areas of forensic science where the evaluation of scientific results under uncertainty plays an important role, many committed forensic handwriting specialists have begun to converge in their opinion that probability theory should be employed as a measure of uncertainty, that is a reference approach when evaluating results of handwriting examinations. This has led to the proposal of a few formative probabilistic approaches, but these take either a rather general form (involving only a few variables), or they are confined to the study of the discriminative potential of selected handwriting features (without considering other aspects of a case as a whole). In-depth and systematic studies of how to define probabilistic frameworks at levels that usefully approach the intricacy of real cases have not yet been reported. Due to this lack of fundamental research, scientists face difficulties in practical applications, despite their increasing interest in probabilistic reasoning schemes. This project proposal thus recognises this as the bottom-line research issue, summarised in terms of the following question: How can forensic scientists substantiate a probabilistic conclusion about results of handwriting examinations?

Methodology, method and expected research outcomes: This project is based on the understanding that the substantiation of expert conclusions, using probability, is a problem in inference analysis, based on coherent argument construction. It relates to the wider context of expert knowledge elicitation, representation and analysis, which is a main theme pursued in the so-called information sciences and statistics. Over the past few decades, these disciplines have seen the development of so-called diagrammatical (or graphical) probability frameworks, in particular Bayesian networks, that have operational capacities to deal with real-world problem domains. The use of Bayesian networks as a method for knowledge representation and analysis has already been studied - and found to support probabilistic analyses at an unprecedented level - in several theoretical and practical forensic science applications, but to only a limited extent in the context of handwriting examinations. As the primary objective, this research proposal thus seeks to rely on Bayesian networks within a general methodology for structured expert knowledge elicitation and analysis in order to build diagrammatic inference structures that have the potential to become part of the scope of resources that forensic experts need to substantiate probabilistic evaluations and conclusions in cases involving the results of comparative handwriting examinations. At a time when justifiable and reasoned approaches to inference in forensic science represent common aims of both scientists and other participants in legal proceedings, fundamental research on probabilistic inference structures using a diagrammatic probability framework can be considered as timely, useful and novel.
Keywords: Comparative handwriting examination, Evaluation, Forensic science, Graphical probability analysis

Title: Ultra-Compact Non-linear Metamaterial Wave Processors for Analog Deep Learning
Abstract: Information processing based on tailored wave-matter interactions emerges as an appealing alternative to conventional digital processors in terms of speed and energy consumption, in particular for low-latency low-power Internet-of-Things sensors with artificial intelligence (AI). We will introduce locally resonant metamaterials with non-linear and programmable inclusions as an ideal platform to implement ultra-compact AI wave processors, the compactness being of particular relevance for common long-wavelength signals like microwaves and sound. We will develop a generic semi-analytical model of such wave processors based on coupled dipoles. We will fabricate acoustic prototypes mainly targeted at processing temporally encoded information (e.g. in speech) and radiofrequency prototypes mainly targeted at processing spatially encoded information (e.g. for gesture recognition).
Keywords: Metamaterials, acoustics, analog signal processing, artificial intelligence, radio frequencies

Title: Models, Algorithms, Software and Repositories for Synthetic Biology and Biotechnology
Abstract:
Recent advances in omics techniques have led to an ever-growing amount of available data about cellular behavior. As the complexity and volume of biological data are increasing, it becomes essential to efficiently store, organize and retrieve, integrate, and analyze the data in order to be able to extract critical information about biology. The overall objective of this proposal is to develop repositories and computational tools and methods capable of furthering our holistic understanding of complex metabolic processes by leveraging from massive amounts of available omics data. 
The proposed research is organized into three parts: (i) Repositories and tools for predictive metabolism: ontology-based databases of human and drug metabolism will be developed together with a framework for predicting the metabolic fate of drug molecules that will allow us to propose new drug candidates and enhance drug repurposing studies; (ii) Analysis and design of steady-state models of metabolism: we plan to develop versatile and computationally efficient methods for consistent  integration of protein and mRNA expression data together with thermodynamics into constraint-based models; this will improve the scope and accuracy of predictions of genotype-phenotype relationships, and it will represent a salient step toward one of the overarching aims of systems biology – the construction of reliable whole-cell models; and (iii) Analysis and design of dynamic models of metabolism: we propose to develop novel methods based on concepts of generative adversarial networks for construction of large- and genome-scale kinetic models that exploit idiosyncrasies of deep learning architectures to generate parameters of models with desired properties with unprecedented efficiency and scope; we also plan to develop a novel method that considers the effects of intracellular crowding on enzymatic reactions that will provide us with information how kinetic mechanisms should be modified to model accurately enzyme reaction networks under crowded, non-ideal, conditions.
Apart from augmenting our capabilities for analysis and design in biotechnology and synthetic biology studies, these methods will also facilitate research and discovery in many other areas of scientific and industrial importance where metabolism plays a fundamental role such as medicine (e.g., personalized medicine, cancer, infectious diseases, metabolic disorders), pharmacology (e.g., drug design, drug mechanism elucidation), specialty and commodity biochemistry (e.g., biocatalysts for biofuels, polymers), microbiology (e.g., microbial communities, biodegradation and bioremediation), nutrition, toxicology, and agriculture.
Keywords: Models of metabolism and macromolecular expression, databases, dynamic models of metabolism, machine learning, mathematical modeling, metabolic engineering, metabolic pathways, process systems engineering, repositories for predictive metabolism, sustainability, synthetic biology, systems biology, uncertainty analysis

Title: Nonparametric Variational Representation Learning for Natural Language Understanding
Abstract:
In recent years, attention-based models like Transformers have radically improved the performance of natural language understanding (NLU), demonstrating the appropriateness of attention-based representation for language. In (Henderson, 2020) we show that these representation share many characteristics with those found in traditional computational linguistics (e.g. graph structure), except that they do not automatically learn multiple levels of representation nor their entities (morphemes, phrases, discourse entities, etc). Motivated by this challenge of entity induction, our recent work has discovered a very non-traditional perspective, which characterises attention-based models like Transformers as doing nonparametric Bayesian inference. Given an input text, our Nonparametric Variational Information Bottleneck (NVIB) Transformer infers distributions over nonparametric mixture distributions (Henderson and Fehr, 2023). We have even shown that pretrained Transformers can be converted into equivalent NVIB Transformers, and regularised post-training (Fehr and Henderson, 2023).


This reinterpretation of Transformers, combined with their unprecedented empirical success, leads us to
postulate the hypothesis that natural language understanding is nonparametric variational Bayesian inference
over mixture distributions. This claim of the adequacy of NVIB leads to two fundamental challenges which are
not currently being addressed, each with an associated technological aim:

1. How can NVIB support inducing graph-structured representations at multiple levels of representation?
   Making deep learning representations interpretable.

2. How can NVIB enable controlling the information in representations?
   Making deep learning representations controllable.

For the first challenge, we will extend our previous structure processing methods (Mohammadshahi and Henderson, 2020, 2021, 2023; Miculicich and Henderson, 2022), developed for set-of-vector representations, to mixture-of-component distributions. And we will focus on unsupervised learning methods, rather than our previous supervised learning methods. To extend these models to multiple levels, we will take the approach of embedding all levels in one big mixture of non-homogeneous components, which are computed with iterative refinement. This extends our previous work on iterative graph refinement (Mohammadshahi and Henderson, 2021; Miculicich and Henderson, 2022), adding the induction of the nodes of the graph and the induction of multiple levels of representation. Learning representations which are interpretable as linguistic structures will be a testbed for the general aim of deep learning of interpretable representations.

For the second challenge, we will leverage the information theory behind NVIB to model both inferring implicit information and removing private information. We will investigate the use of KL divergence as a measure of entailment in semantic inference. Title: View Sets for 3-D Object Detection and Recognition
Abstract:
Object recognition is one of the most fundamental issue Computer Vision has to address if it is ever to truly emulate Human Vision and to find a wide field of application. In the past few years, remarkable progress has been made in that direction thanks in no small measure to novel approaches to recognizing image patches [Lowe04,Miko04b,Winder07,Hua07].  In a first phase of the project we now seek to continue, we have shown that formulating this recognition task as a classification problem led to reliable real-time implementations that perform well even when perspective or lighting change drastically [Lepetit06a,Ozuysal06a,Pilet06a,Ozuysal07]. In a second phase, we demonstrated that training our classifiers could also be massively sped-up by formulating new patch descriptors, thus allowing both training and recognition to be performed online [Calonder08].

However, in our early approach as well as many others, patch recognition relies on ad hoc image features, which are computed on the basis of image gradients, with SIFT [Lowe04] being the best known example.  Our own features that we refer to as Ferns [Ozuysal10] are an exception to this rule but can also been understood as measuring the contrast between neighboring pixels.  The study of mammalian brains offer ample evidence that such features play an important role in human and animal vision and some cell arrangements in the visual cortex appear to behave as Gabor filters.  However, other cell arrangements in the same cortical areas appear to implement very different features [Olshausen05], which raises the possibility that one must go beyond simple gradient-based features to truly emulate the brain and improve the performance of our recognition algorithms.

We therefore recently developed and evaluated a method to learn image features instead of designing them by hand.  Examples of learned features are shown in Figure 1.  While some of them correspond to contour detectors, others are indeed more complex. By pooling the features extracted from an image, which is an operation similar to the one performed by the local histograms in SIFT and by the complex cells in the visual cortex, we obtain a representation of the image that is compact and more discriminative than the original image itself: This representation is well adapted to object recognition and outperforms the state-of-the-art on CIFAR-10, a recent and very challenging benchmark.

However, our method is still limited to a short pipeline, while there is evidence that by extracting features from the image representation itself, one can obtain a better representation, in terms of both compactness and discriminative power [Hinton06a].  We therefore now want to use our current method as a brick and stack several instances of it to obtain a better discriminative image representations, and thus improve the performances.  We believe this approach to be promising because a layered architecture closely matches what is known about the visual cortex and can represent very complex transformations.

This will result in a principled way to produce robust image features, with many potential applications. First, the new features will be more complex than those that have been used so far, which seems to be a requirement for efficient object recognition [Mutch06,Fidler10,Zeller10].  Manually designing such complex features is very difficult, and our approach offers a promising way of overcoming this difficulty. Second, it will become easy to develop features for images acquired using sensors other than ordinary cameras, such as infrared cameras and lidars, for which existing features are clearly suboptimal.

Finally, we will apply our image representation to online learning. We evaluated our current representation on object category recognition only.  It requires a large set of training images, and a slow training stage to build a classifier applied to the image representations.  This is not applicable for some important scenarios, for example, a robotic system that has to continuously learn new objects online. We want to use the image representation of objects to learn as templates, and detect these objects by matching their templates against the representation of the incoming images.  It would then become virtually instantaneous to learn new incoming objects by simply adding new templates to the database.

In short, we intend to develop a robust representation of images appropriate for recognition purposes that should be useful for many Computer Vision algorithms. Furthermore, because it will be partially inspired by our current knowledge of the first layers of the visual cortex, this line of research could help us unravel some of the mysteries of the human visual system.
Keywords: Computer Vision, Object Recognition

Title: NAST: Neural Architectures for Speech Technology
Abstract:
Recent years have seen the replacement of many component technologies in speech processing with the deep-learning of deep neural networks (DNNs).  Such systems typically perform much better than the older component technologies.  The same time period has (not independently) seen such technologies move from academia to industry.  Areas such as speech recognition and synthesis that were once regarded as research fields are now ubiquitous applications, typically in the context of the "GAFA" (Google, Apple, Facebook, Amazon) companies.  These companies have led advances based on large data and computational resources, and more recently on end-to-end approaches.

Responding to this trend, much academic research in speech technology has moved into what might be called peripheral technologies.  In the case of the applicant here in Switzerland, that has meant focusing on geographical issues, in particular multilinguality and the closely related issues of paralinguistics and adaptation.  Of course, many of the solutions to these issues lie in deep-learning; however, the data resources can be rather small, putting us in a position to compete with the GAFA companies.

In research threads on multilingual recognition and emotional synthesis, we are finding that, in order to do deep-learning with such limited resources, it is helpful to cast techniques from signal processing, from bio-inspired computing and from Bayesian statistics into neural components.  Integrated into neural networks, the components provide "explainability" that is not present in abstract sigmoid units; it is then clear how they might be adapted to variations in speaker and language.

In NAST, the objective is to consolidate the two (application directed) research themes above into a single theme around neural architectures.
Specifically, the EU H2020 project SUMMA, although geared towards multilingual speech recognition, is yielding results in Bayesian methods and recurrence.
The SNSF project MASS, focusing on emotional synthesis, has cast muscle models as neural components.  We intend to blur the distinction between recognition and synthesis since the proposed techniques are applicable to both; this also reflects theories of physiological processes.  We aim to create what might be called a toolkit of neural techniques.  This toolkit already contains rudimentary muscle models, initial Bayesian recurrence and vocal tract warping.
A key feature of all the neural techniques is that they will be trainable in an end-to-end manner.  This will allow them to be fully optimised in the context of the application at hand, be it recognition or synthesis of speech or emotion.

In a first thread, we propose to develop the muscle models developed for intonation synthesis by driving them using spiking neurons.  Whilst quite ambitious, the thread builds on initial work by a masters student, and is written with multiple chances to back off to more conventional techniques.
Indeed, the most likely and influential outcome will be a hybrid of spiking and conventional neurons in a coherent framework.  In a second, more incremental thread, we propose to consolidate the work of two doctoral students.  In finishing their doctoral studies, they will provide neural components for the
toolbox that will feed into their own work, that of the first thread above, and into a new task on factoring waveform synthesis.  Each thread is written to allow interactions both within the thread and between the two, with many components being reused across tasks.

In a technology sense, we may hope that the work will allow adaptation to speakers, to emotions and to languages with better quality and on smaller amounts of data.  For particularly under-resourced or localised dialects, we hope to enable these capabilities where they would not otherwise exist.  The resulting networks will have fewer parameters, allowing them to be smaller and faster.  More generally, the tools will enable the concept of "explainability" in DNNs; rather than seeking meaning in networks of
otherwise abstract activations, we provide activations that are fundamentally based on explainable processes.

The concept of the toolbox, whilst being distributed across several open-source packages, will enable transfer of the technology to the academic community, to industrial collaborators here in Switzerland, and hopefully to the GAFA companies.  The students will be complemented by several post-doctoral
researchers in the Idiap speech group working on Innosuisse, EU and industrial projects; they will aid both the research and potential impact.  In a more philosophical sense, we hope to build a bridge between the engineering of the GAFA and the speech "sciences" to which academic speech technology has often looked for inspiration.
Keywords: Neural networks, Physiology, Speech processing

Title: NeuMath: Neural Discourse Inference over Mathematical Texts
Abstract:
Recent advances in NLP enabled by Deep Learning based architectures bring the opportunity to support the interpretation of textual content at scale. The application of natural language inference methods can facilitate scientific discovery, reducing the gap between current research and the available large-scale scientific knowledge. Contemporary NLP models, however, are still limited in their ability to interpret abstract and mathematical knowledge. 
The articulation of mathematical arguments is a fundamental part of scientific reasoning and communication. Across many scientific disciplines, expressing relations and inter-dependencies between quantities (usually in an equational form) is at the centre of the scientific argumentation. 
NeuMath aims to address this gap by building neuro-symbolic representation models which can support mathematical natural language inference (MNLI). The project will develop models which can jointly represent and reason over two symbolic modalities (natural language and mathematical expressions) and will build the foundations to deliver embedding models which can interpret and support the generation of mathematical arguments (by leveraging available large-scale scientific corpora). 
The project will pioneer neural representation paradigms with novel semantic control/explicit representation mechanisms over embedding spaces (the injection of structural biases) aiming to enable explainable, multi-hop and abstractive MNLI inference. NeuMath will focus on the design of representations which facilitate the transference of inter-sentence and inter-document relations into inference relations and will develop novel neuro-symbolic architectures which can efficiently represent multi-type/multi-hop inference. 

The project provides a head-on approach a paradigmatic area in the AI and NLP spaces: the development of models which can approximate the flexibility of neural models with the rigour and abstraction capability of symbolic models. MNLI provides an ideal problem space to push the envelope of explainable and precise NLP models. These features dialogue with requirements for the application of AI in economic areas of high national relevance, such as pharmaceutical and finance. More specifically, the ability to interpret mathematical discourse at scale can be a fundamental infrastructure to catalyse scientific discovery.
Keywords: Discourse representation, Mathematical Natural Language Inference, Natural Language Inference, Natural Language Processing

Title: Data-Driven Distributionally Robust Optimization: High Dimensional Statistical Analysis and Decision-Dependent Uncertainty Formulations
Abstract:
While our society gets shaped by the ongoing data revolution and by the engineering breakthroughs in the energy sector, there is a growing need for data-driven optimization models outputting reliable decisions, that are insensitive to input misspecification. However, despite having access to large amounts of data for training, the performance of standard models (such as empirical risk minimization) has been observed to be heavily affected by the inherent statistical uncertainty present in the data. One important real-world example happens in renewable energy markets, where the overall long-term financial return is severely affected by a very limited number of spikes in the energy prices, which are generally not captured by data and forecasts.

Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) has recently emerged as a powerful and principled tool to robustify data-driven optimization models, with many numerical experiments suggesting that DRO has the potential to address this issue. DRO formulations are nowadays routinely employed in diverse areas, such as machine learning, control, estimation and filtering, as well as further downstream application fields such as robotics, power systems, renewable energy markets, and finance, to name a few. 

Despite such promises, our current theoretical understanding of DRO is limited to scenarios where: (i) the dimension of the problem is very small compared to the number of samples, and (ii) the uncertainty is exogenous, that is, it does not depend on the decision. However, assumption (i) is often invalidated in modern applications, from machine learning, where the state of the art models employ billions of parameters, to power systems, which are extremely large-scale systems. Moreover, real-world applications are often subject to decision-dependent endogenous uncertainty, invalidating assumption (ii). One such important example is the price-maker setup in renewable energy markets.

This project aims at addressing these limitations by studying DRO problems in regimes where: (i) the dimension of the problem and the number of samples are large and of comparable size (commonly known as the high-dimensional regime), and (ii) the uncertainty is decision-dependent. Specifically, by leveraging tools from high-dimensional statistics, optimal transport, and stochastic approximation, this project aims at understanding what are the:

    (1) statistical properties of DRO problems in the high-dimensional regime;

    (2) computational and statistical properties of DRO problems with decision-dependent uncertainty.

Such advancements would have big impact on both the methodology and applicability of DRO. First, they would enable us to study the performance guarantees of DRO problems in such regimes, and to understand what is the proper hyperparameter tuning (which is crucial for the advantage offered by such methods). Secondly, they would open the door to countless real-world applications in large-scale problems governed by high levels of uncertainty, such as machine learning and power systems. My ultimate aim is to employ these advancements in automatic control, to develop distributionally robust controllers for systems with state-dependent uncertainty, and in renewable energy markets, for robust trading under the price-maker setup.
Keywords: Data-Driven Optimization, Energy Systems, High-Dimensional Statistics, Robust Optimization, Stochastic Control, Transportation Systems

Title: Data-POETRY: Data-informed POlicy Exploration for TRansportation and energY
Abstract:
As our energy system is transformed in the fight against climate change, it is a challenge to balance the technical complexities and big-picture objectives with their impacts on people and communities. Policy is used to support and guide the transition. Recent policies have started to move beyond cost and CO2 emissions to include other objectives, like increased flexibility or support for low-income households. However, researchers lack the right quantitative modeling tools to inform policymakers about these new designs and their impacts on the larger system. Existing models are too computationally expensive to go beyond scenarios to produce better policy mixes that address these multiple objectives.

This project aims to fill that gap by developing a new modeling suite to assess and optimize energy transition policy mixes. We use machine learning meta models to facilitate the optimization and overcome computational limits of existing methods. Though real policymaking and politics cannot be optimized, applying optimization methods to energy system policies can yield many valuable insights: identifying new policy directions, evaluating complex policy mixes, and helping objectively balance trade-offs between multiple objectives like total costs or emissions and household-level price increases or local air pollution. 

“Data-POETRY: Data-informed POlicy Exploration for TRansportation and energY” will focus on transportation electrification, a sector with high emissions and direct impacts on daily life. In the project, we will: 1) connect existing models in a new pipeline to simulate impacts of electric vehicle (EV) charging policies in the European electricity system; 2) use machine learning meta models to replace complex components; and 3) leverage the meta models' reduced computational complexity to directly optimize the EV policies.

We plan to investigate three policy case studies: vehicle purchase subsidies that shape EV adoption, charging infrastructure investments that shape EV driver charging behaviors, and pricing signals that shape the EV charging process. These cases address important policy challenges and cover a wide range of model types, including logistic regression, agent-based modeling, and optimization. In each, we will consider multiple optimization objectives  including cost, emissions, distributional impacts, and health impacts of local air quality. 

The project will make several contributions. The use of machine learning meta models to facilitate policy optimization introduces a novel approach to the field of energy policy modeling. The case studies will contribute critical insight on the use of meta models for integration in a larger optimization and on their success at representing different types of models used for energy and transportation systems. Further, the results will contribute important insights to support better policies for the EV transition and reveal the trade-offs between cost, emissions, equity, and health objectives in their design.

Title: Development of a Neural Network Potential with Accurate Electrostatic Interactions
Abstract: In recent years, a new generation of interatomic potentials based on machine learning techniques has been introduced. These potentials, which provide a direct functional relation between the atomic positions and the potential-energy, combine the accuracy of electronic structure methods with the efficiency of simple empirical potentials. Because of the absence of system-specific terms they allow to perform extended simulations of a large variety of systems. Most of these potentials rely on atomic properties like energies and charges depending only on the local chemical environments of the atoms.  Such local charges are, however, unable to capture long-range charge transfer. This prevents the accurate description of systems in which distant structural features have global effects on the charge distribution in the system. Examples for such systems are semiconductors including defects, polar surfaces of oxides and metal-organic molecules with different possible metal oxidation states. In order to overcome these intrinsic limitations of current machine learning potentials, we propose to combine high-dimensional neural networks with the charge equilibration neural network technique. The resulting new method will be generally applicable to all types of systems, which we will demonstrate by analyzing the potential-energy surfaces of different model systems covering all types of bonding using the minima hopping method.
Keywords: Machine learning, charge equilibration, force fields, neural networks

Title: Moralizing exclusion: Exclusionary attitudes and morality in party politics
Abstract: Some parties advocate exclusionary stances, exhibiting prejudice towards disadvantaged outgroups and opposing policies that advance their wellbeing. Indeed, xenophobia, racism or sexism have been connected to the platform and support base of some parties, primarily on the far right. Other parties oppose these exclusionary policies, advocating measures to accommodate minorities. A central aspect of contemporary politics concerns how these two kinds of parties interact. Given that exclusionary attitudes are often seen as morally troubling, moral rhetoric should be central to these interactions. Still, despite growing scholarship on the role of moral arguments in political campaigns and on the consequences of the far right's rise for mainstream parties, little is known about how morality plays out in mainstream parties’ strategies to compete against the far right. This dissertation empirically explores four aspects of these dynamics of moralized competition, with a focus on Western democracies with strong far-right exclusionary parties, like Spain, Germany or Austria. Specifically, I test: i) how mainstream parties use rhetorical moralization when competing against exclusionary parties, ii) whether said attempts are electorally successful, iii) how exclusionary parties might make their exclusionary policies appear more acceptable, iv) and whether mainstream and exclusionary parties strategically appeal to minorities by using moral language and descriptive representation in their campaign advertisements. To do so, I leverage a combination of original survey experiments and observational designs for causal inference using textual and visual data, as well as natural language processing and computer vision methods. Thus, this project promises to significantly advance our theoretical and empirical understanding of the role of exclusionary attitudes in party strategies, electoral competition, and moralized political speech.
Keywords: Electoral campaigns, Exclusionary attitudes, Far-right parties, Morality and politics, Political communication

Title: Neuromorphic Attention Models for Event Data   (NAMED)
Abstract:
The field of embedded computer vision has become increasingly important in recent years as the demand for low-latency and energy-efficient vision systems has grown. One of the key challenges in this area is developing intelligent vision systems that can efficiently process large amounts of visual data while still maintaining high accuracy and reliability. To address this challenge, NAMED project leverages the promising combination of event-based sensors, cognitive attention, sensors fusion, and hybrid models. Event-based sensors mimic the biological retina: they asynchronously measure per-pixel brightness changes and output a stream of events that encode the time, location, and sign of the brightness changes (positive or negative). In addition to eliminating redundancy, they benefit from several advantages over conventional frame cameras, from which they fundamentally differ.  The most important advantages are the temporal resolution (µs), the high dynamic range (140dB), the low-power consumption (mW), and high energy efficiency of the processing due to the reduced redundant information to process. Cognitive attention refers to the selective processing of sensory information by the brain based on its relevance and importance to the current task or goal. It involves the ability to focus one's attention on specific aspects of the environment while filtering out irrelevant or distracting information. Sensor fusion and hybrid models refer to the way to process data with both traditional frame-based camera and event-based cameras investigating on the sensor and model fusion to improve both energy efficiency and accuracy performance by using the benefits of both sensor and machine learning models. 

Inspired by the human visual system, the project focuses on designing efficient and low latency embedded computer vision systems to enable applications that require both such as new generation of robotic and wearable devices. To achieve this goal, the project will exploit a unique combination of interdisciplinary expertise in cognitive science, neuromorphic computer vision, electronics and embedded systems and robotics, we aim to develop novel energy-efficient neuromorphic attentional models and hybrid models for event-based sensors and embedded vision, which offer significant advantages over traditional computing approaches, as described above. The objective is to enable lightweight embedded solutions evaluating the model in a novel hardware research platform to optimize and evaluate the solution for real-world robotics scenarios, augmented reality and virtual reality that require low latency, embedded processing, and robustness in the perception. The project will also contribute to the development of the broader field of neuromorphic computing and event-based sensing, by providing new insights into the design and implementation of attention mechanisms in these domains and the potential to fuse together deep networks and spiking neural networks and event-based sensors with neuromorphic sensors.
Keywords: Attention Model, Embedded Vision, Energy efficient embedded systems, Event Based Camera, Event Data, Machine learning at the edge, Neuromorphic Processing

Title: Rage against the Machine: Advancing Knowledge on Consumer Price Fairness Perceptions in AI-Infused Marketplace Transactions
Abstract:
With technological advancements made in recent years, firms increasingly rely on artificial intelligence (AI) in pricing. While AI in pricing may be a game changer, it may also have pitfalls. To date, it is unclear how consumers will react to being confronted with new forms of marketplace transactions. To enable firms to engage in these transactions effectively, it is thus imperative to investigate the consequences of AI in pricing. Specifically, this proposed research examines the role of consumer price fairness perceptions in response to marketplace transactions involving AI. 
Despite important contributions made previously, extant research so far does not account for the developments made in the field of AI which will increasingly take part in exchange relationships that to date are considered to take part between price setter (firm, seller) and (human) buyer. This will include AI agents as price setters, price communicators (e.g., chatbots), prices set by humans assisted by AI, price perceptions of goods generated by AI, price perceptions formed in the presence of AI, and in the future even AI acting as consumers in reference transactions (e.g., humanoid robots). Given that price fairness perceptions are highly subjective, and that AI is in many cases met with consumer skepticism, perceived threat, and even speciesism, it is proposed that participation of AI in any way needs to be accounted for in such settings. 
In response, the goal of this research is to comprehensively answer the question how consumer judge the price fairness in AI-infused pricing settings.  In answering this question, our project contributes to the literature streams of behavioral pricing that covers price fairness, and consumer reactions to AI. The results help managers to anticipate consumer reactions to prices in situation in which AI is involved in the exchange relationships relevant for price fairness judgments. Ultimately, firms who are better able to make such predictions will outperform others in pricing, and gain a competitive advantage leading to higher profits and firm success.
Keywords: artificial intelligence, consumers, fairness, pricing

Title: FLAME (Fair, Lightweight, Affordable, Multimodal, and Explainable) Machine Learning Methods for Predicting Alzheimer’s Disease Using Personalized and Adaptive Multimodal Biomarkers
Abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) affects 50 million people worldwide and is projected to overwhelm 152 million by 2050. Identifying targeted AD biomarkers facilitates early and accurate disease prediction, allowing for timely treatment and disease management. Despite growing efforts to join machine learning and biology insights, AD biomarker discovery and disease prediction are facing five major challenges. (i) Most of the AD-related biomarkers are developed from data from Caucasian populations collected in Europe and North America. This omits ethnicity-specific patterns from non-Caucasian samples and individual traits due to socio-economic factors from other regions, as well as their interactions with age and gender. (ii) Most of the state-of-the-art predictive models require trained experts, high-performance computers and GPUs. Yet, AD is a global health threat; such exorbitant requirements prohibit communities with limited resources and decentralised healthcare systems from benefiting from scientific and technological advances. (iii) AD is associated with neural, genetic, proteomic and clinical factors. AD biomarker discovery and prediction, therefore, need to integrate these data, but by doing so one must confront intra-modality changes, inter-modality dynamics, and asynchronous and incomplete multimodal inputs at different time points. (iv) While multimodal data analysis improves our understanding of AD evolution and elevates prediction accuracy, collecting all these data for each subject – simultaneously – just for disease assessment is unfeasible, costly, and sometimes invasive (e.g., obtaining CSF data via lumbar puncture). (v) Present machine learning-based approaches in general and those for AD prediction in particular often lack transparency. This impedes clinicians from understanding models and trusting predictions. Here, we propose the FLAME framework, consisting of five aspects: Fair, Lightweight, Affordable, Multimodal, and Explainable, each aimed at addressing one of the challenges. Particularly, (1. Fair) FLAME studies up to 14 datasets consisting of subjects from Asia, Australia, Europe, Latin America and the US (including African American cohorts) covering populations of Asian, Caucasian, Latin American and African descents and a wealth of modalities, including neuroimaging (MRI and PET), CSF/Blood, SNPs/WGS, RNA-seq, and cognitive tests, different age and gender groups, various disease stages, and multivariate disease outcomes measuring distinct faculties affected by AD (e.g., executive function, memory, language, and visuospatial function). (2. Lightweight) FLAME is a lightweight machine-learning framework. It requires minimal computational resources and maintains robust predictive accuracy and clinical relevance. (3. Multimodal) FLAME aligns and analyses heterogeneous modalities, even when incomplete, and maps their individual and joint effects to disease outcomes via machine learning. (4. Affordable) FLAME builds an affordable clinical AI system that minimises the number of required tests or imaging sessions, adapts to available (sometimes limited) data, and recommends, strategically, the most informative next available data modality needed to collect and analyse. (5. Explainable) FLAME provides clear, interpretable insights into a hierarchy of feature importance (which features drive predictions) and the biological and clinical interpretation of these features. Applying FLAME to up to 14 diverse datasets, we aim to (a) improve our understanding of potential multimodal biological underpinnings of AD and its disease evolution, (b) support explainable clinical decision-making, timely treatment and appropriate AD management, (c) advance personalised AD prediction cross-sectionally and longitudinally, considering biomarker variability, population patterns and individual differences, and (d) accommodate more users, including those with limited computational, human, and data resources, to unite machine-learning and biology to combat AD.
Keywords: AI in healthcare, Alzheimer’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Biomarker discovery, Clinical decision support, Disease prediction, Low-resource settings, Machine learning, Multimodal biomarkers, Multimodal data, Personalised medicine, Predictive modelling

Title: Integrated, fast on-chip combs and detectors for coherent THz photonics
Abstract:
In recent years there has been a growing interest in integrated Mid-IR and THz photonics for telecommunication and sensing. Particularly, the emergence of advanced techniques making use of coherent multimode sources offer new possibilities to bridge microwaves and higher frequencies. In the visible and telecom range, integrated silicon photonics  already makes extensive use of on-chip optical elements as splitters, modulators,  high-confinement waveguides and high Q resonators embedded in a planar platform to achieve highly performing devices like micro-resonator frequency combs. In that case the missing element is the source, due to the indirect bandgap of silicon.

In the THz frequency range, a prominent candidate for source integration is the THz quantum cascade laser. Recent advances in the high temperature operation of these devices,   combined with  their frequency agility  and the possibility to operate as frequency combs as well as very fast detectors make them extremely appealing as key building blocks for THz photonics.  

Such achievements allow to envision a planarized photonic platform comprising sources and detectors as well as passive components for signal routing and manipulation. 
We plan to leverage on the most recent advances of our laboratory and other groups to develop key elements for coherent THz photonics based on THz quantum cascade gain medium. Most of the advancements in the device performance and the integration capabilities are offered by a newly developed planarization approach to the fabrication of THz quantum cascade lasers and THz detectors based on regenerative amplification. We want to combine such planarization technique with novel integrated photonic design techniques based on inverse design and deep learning that allow an advanced control over the many relevant parameters of the optical components such as reflectivity, dispersion, optical confinement and wavelength multiplexing.
Specifically, we plan to organize our work along the following research directions: 

1. Wide bandwidth, dispersion-compensated planarized THz QCL combs targeting both FM and AM operation. We will explore dispersion compensated ridge lasers, concentric rings endowed with broadband photonic elements to promote temporal soliton formation and their extraction. Advanced RF control will enable switching from FM to AM combs over bandwidths larger than 1.5 THz. Pulses at 1 ps length are expected to be attained with RF control and dispersion compensation.

2. Inverse-designed photonic components (splitters, achromatic couplers, wavelength division multiplexers, low loss waveguides) To adequately exploit the advancements in the comb and detector sections, we will target the development of frequency agile photonic structures to route and process both RF and THz signals, as they will be integrated on the same ground plane. 

3. High temperature, ultrafast regenerative quantum detector based on planarized resonators. Leveraging on our recenz advances, we will employ opimized, high performance two-well gain active regions embedded in a variety of resonant cavities to achieve fast (>20 GHz) THz detection on Peltier thermoelectric coolers (Tdet > 190 K).
Keywords: Frequency combs, Integrated optics, Quantum cascade, Terahertz

Title: Addressing the Code Quality Decay Problem by Forecasting Code Design Flaws and Applying Refactoring Operations
Abstract:
During maintenance and evolution activities, the source code can drift away from its original design, possibly increasing complexity and leading to design flaws. In the literature, these design flaws are often referred to as the terms anti-patterns or code smells. Code smells are symptoms that indicate the possible need for refactoring the source code. They are not bugs and do not interrupt the program functioning, but could increase the maintenance cost and promote bugs' introduction in the future. 
To remove the design flaws, refactoring techniques have been proposed in industry and academia. Refactoring has been defined as a technique restructuring an existing code, altering its internal structure without changing its external behavior. Basically, the only goal of refactoring is to improve specific quality aspects of source code. 
In this research proposal, I aim to develop techniques addressing code quality decay problem by forecasting design flaws, recommending and applying refactoring operations. I target three main goals in the context of this research:
Goal 1: Forecast code design flaws. My first goal is to forecast code design flaws that will experience a quality decay in the near future using machine learning classifiers. I  aim to develop techniques to predict when a code component is deviating from good design principles before design flaws are introduced.
Goal 2: Investigate code quality proxies. In this goal, I aim to build the empirical knowledge needed to advance the state-of-the-art in refactoring recommender systems. I want to validate the existing assumption that quality metrics and code smells are reliable proxies to evaluate code quality as perceived by developers. In particular, I want to investigate if quality metrics and code smells perceived by developers are aligned to the ones identified by automated detection tools used in refactoring recommenders. 
Goal 3: Recommend and automatically apply refactoring operations to prevent the forecasted code quality decay.
Finally, I want to investigate the possibility to design a new generation of "data-driven" refactoring tools able to recommend meaningful refactorings learned from refactoring activities performed by developers in open source repositories, rather than recommending refactorings aimed at maximizing some quality metrics or removing code smells. Towards this goal, I will study the types of refactoring transformations performed by developers in pull requests that can be learned by a Neural Machine Translation model.
Keywords: Code quality decay, code design flaws, software maintenance, software refactoring

Title: Exploring the frontiers of Nuclear Physics with multi-task deep learning
Abstract:
Modern physics aims at the understanding of the fundamental forces in nature, their symmetries, and the resulting complex interactions between the building blocks of matter. While, high-energy physicists utilize the powerful tool of perturbation theory, when the relevant energy scales are smaller and the examined systems involve the strong nuclear force, ab initio methods become progressively intractable. To this end, effective theories have been constructed that can approximate the exact dynamics to an adequate level of precision providing valuable insights, which are obtained at a lower computational cost.

Nuclear physics is the study of nucleons, i.e. protons and neutrons, and the strong nuclear force which holds them together, at the low-energy regime of atomic nuclei. Quantum chromodynamics (QCD) is the underlying theory of the quarks and the gluons, which are the constituents of the nucleons and the mediators of the strong force, respectively. However, QCD can only provide perturbative results at energy scales achievable at particle accelerators like the LHC. Non-perturbative ones can also be obtained using a space-time lattice and numerical simulations on supercomputers, but at present only for systems that involve very few nucleons. Consequently, theoretical predictions have to rely on simplified descriptions such as mean-field theories, where an average interaction is introduced in order to reduce the many-body problem into an effective one-body problem.

One of the most prevalent modern approaches of devising predictive models in science is the use of artificial intelligence (AI) and in particular machine learning tools (ML) such as deep neural networks (NNs). NNs are universal function approximators, which by training on large datasets, can uncover intricate patterns and correlations that might be challenging for traditional analytic methods. However, the unprecedented computational strength of  NNs comes with the trade-off of reduced interpretability, which poses challenges for their direct application in theoretical disciplines. 

The objective of my project is to develop a deep learning model that predicts with world-leading precision the properties of atomic nuclei. By employing multi-task learning (MTL), the model aspires to become the first example of a general-purpose AI for theoretical nuclear physics applications, in the sense that it can predict the values of a large set of diverse nuclear observables. Most importantly, the proposed NN architecture is based on a latent embedding representation space shared between the different tasks, that allows for meaningful interpretations corresponding to well-known physical principles. This result into improved reliability of its generalization capabilities. Motivated by this feature, I intend to use the model in order to explore the uncharted territories of the nuclear landscape and thus address important unresolved problems in nuclear and particle (astro-)physics.
Keywords: Flavour Physics, Interpretable Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Multi-task learning, Neural Networks, Nuclear Astrophysics, Nuclear Physics, Representation learning

Title: Combining Molecular Dynamics and Machine Learning for Free Energy Calculation with Quantum-Mechanical Accuracy
Abstract: The goal of the present project is to develop a methodology for performing rigorous free-energy calculations with quantum-mechanical (QM) accuracy by coupling replica-exchange enveloping distribution sampling (RE-EDS), which we introduced in 2016, with our recent machine learning (ML) approach for QM/MM molecular dynamics (MD) simulations for condensed-phase systems. Free-energy changes represent the driving force behind all isothermal-isobaric molecular processes. Thus, the accurate prediction of free-energy differences has been a long-standing target in computational chemistry, with a high relevance in the context of pharmaceutical, material, biological and environmental sciences. While a QM/MM set-up with electrostatic embedding enables the description of the solute or ligand with QM accuracy, the associated computational cost is still too high to permit direct free-energy calculations at this level of theory. Thus, most free energy calculations are performed using classical force fields, although such force fields provide a lower accuracy. To achieve our goal of direct QM/MM free-energy calculations and go beyond the current state-of-the-art techniques, we aim at exploiting the inherent sampling efficiency of the RE-EDS method combined with the speed-up offered by ML models to evaluate the energies and forces of the QM solute or ligand. Our (QM)ML/MM method involves a high-dimensional neural network potential (HDNNP) trained to predict the difference between a semi-empirical method and DFT. The delta-learning scheme simplifies the learning task and thus reduces the required training set size drastically. Through electrostatic embedding in the MM environment, long-range interactions are incorporated appropriately such that condensed-phase systems can be simulated. RE-EDS is best suited for the combination with (QM)ML/MM owing to the following features: (i) it is straightforward to construct an EDS reference state with QM Hamiltonians, (ii) only the end-states need to be sampled with EDS (no pathway-dependence, no intermediate states), (iii) it is a multi-state method providing superior sampling efficiency, and (iv) a minimal effort is required to estimate the system-dependent parameters thanks to replica exchange. The envisioned (QM)ML/MM + RE-EDS methodology will enable us to (a) study enzymatic reactions within a fully flexible environment, and (b) estimate the binding free energies of a protein to a series of ligands with QM accuracy. The approach will be made available to the community as an automated pipeline implemented in open-source software packages.
Keywords: Free energy calculation, Machine learning, Molecular dynamics, QM/MM

Title: Deep Learning Theory and Practice
Abstract:
A recent approach to better understand the behavior of neural networks (NNs) is to study them in the
large width limit (i.e., letting the number of neurons per layer go to infinity), since the theory becomes
simpler and more intuitive in this limit. The first approaches to studying these limits by Neal [1996],
Jacot et al. [2018], Lee et al. [2018] became very popular but failed to explain some of the most intriguing
properties of practically used NNs (namely, multi-task learning, feature learning, and transfer learning) as
we mathematically analyzed in Heiss et al. [2021]. New approaches study such limits of deep NNs with different (less artificial) hyperparameters [Yang and Hu, 2021, Parhi and Nowak, 2022, Heiss et al., 2021, Jacot et al., 2022] so that these important properties (such as multi-task learning) can be well explained mathematically. For my postdoc, we want to both extend this theory and exploit some of the far-reaching practical implications of this theory. Prof. Bin Yu’s research group at UC Berkeley is the perfect place to do this, as they are particularly strong in connecting deep learning theory to practice. In particular, we want to better understand the phenomena that occur in practice in transfer learning (Project 2). We also want to use insights from Heiss et al. [2021] to make NNs more energy efficient (Project 3) and more interpretable (Project 4a).
For Project 4b, we will apply a network architecture (NJ-ODE) developed in Zurich (to which I
contributed in Andersson et al. [2023]) to analyze the temporal dynamics of the gut microbiome of infants.
In project 5, we want to work on uncertainty quantification, building on Bin Yu's PCS framework for veridical data science.
