Title: Understanding and Designing User Trust in Smart Personal Assistants
Abstract:
Based on recent technological advancements in the field of Artificial Intelligence (AI), it is predicted that Smart Personal Assistants (SPAs) such as Amazon`s Alexa, Google`s Google Assistant and Apple`s Siri will run on 870 million devices by 2022. This significantly increases the exposure of many to this technology in both B2B and B2C settings. These Information Systems (IS) provide assistance by engaging with users via natural language and have been promised to fundamentally change the ways how we perform tasks, consume services and products, and interact with our environment. However, SPAs face problems in terms of user acceptance, and one major source of these user reservations is a lack of trust. SPAs represent a novel class of IS that are characterized by high degrees of interaction and intelligence. These capabilities may fundamentally affect how people develop trust in these systems as for instance they are perceived by users as increasingly human and at the same time less predictable. Thus, we need to generate insights on how to build user trust in SPAs to avoid disuse – unrealized potential due to rejection of SPAs. In specific, there is a lack of a concise conceptual approach for studying user trust in SPAs as well as of empirical insights on how user trust in SPAs forms and evolves over time. Moreover, we are missing general design guidelines on how to develop more trustworthy SPAs. Therefore, in the scope of this project we plan to answer the following three research questions: 

RQ1: How should trust in Smart Personal Assistants be conceptualized? 
RQ2: How does trust in Smart Personal Assistants form and evolve over time? 
RQ3: How can insights from literature on trust be leveraged to design more trustworthy Smart Personal Assistants?

To answer our research questions, this project proposal consists of two interwoven components: the first component focuses on conceptualizing trust in SPAs based on theoretical reasoning as well as the analysis of semi-structured interviews and on empirically investigating what drives user trust over time based on field experiments. This component resembles the behavioral part of the project aiming to increase our understanding of user trust in SPAs and to explain how it forms, and thus, how it can be influenced. The second component focuses on systematically deriving insights from the literature on trust in order to design SPAs in such a way that users are more likely to form trust and respectively continue trusting the system. Thereby, we combine different research methods such as semi-structured interviews with SPA designers and users as well as field experiments. This component resembles the design-oriented part of the project, aiming to use behavioral insights as a basis to design or redesign existing SPAs using a thorough design science research approach. 

Taken together, this project contributes to the body of knowledge by developing a conceptual approach for studying trust in SPAs and generating insights on the evolution of trust including changes in antecedents and consequences of trust over time. Moreover, we contribute to theory by creating a nascent design theory for building more trustworthy SPAs. Overall, these insights will help us to better understand how trust in SPAs can be systematically built.
Keywords: antecedents and consequences of trust, evolution of trust, smart personal assistants, trust in smart personal assistants, trust networks, trustworthy design

Title: Problem Solving with Domain-Independent Dynamic Programming: Theory and Practice
Abstract: Domain-independent dynamic programming (DIDP) is a recently proposed framework for modeling combinatorial optimization problems using dynamic programming and solving them with a general purpose solver. Initial results show strong performance using a heuristic state-based search solver, thus demonstrating the success of problem solving approaches developed in Artificial Intelligence (AI) on problems traditionally studied in Operations Research (OR). This proposal seeks to develop the theory and practice of DIDP-based problem solving by theoretically characterizing DIDP from computational and knowledge representation perspectives; by understanding its relationship to the problem solving paradigms embodied in constraint programming, satisfiability, and AI planning; and by developing novel domain-independent heuristics for DIDP through the adaptation and extension of techniques from AI planning and decision diagram-based optimization.
Keywords: automated planning, constraint programming, decision diagrams, dynamic programming, heuristic search

Title: HisDoc III : Large-Scale Historical Document Classification
Abstract:
In HisDoc III we target historical document classification for large amounts of uncategorized facsimiles with the intent to provide new capabilities for researchers in the Digital Humanities. In particular, we will address the task of categorizing document images with respect to content, language, script, and layout. To do so, we will leverage the expertise gained from our previous projects HisDoc and HisDoc 2.0. In HisDoc we have shown that historical Document Image Analysis (DIA) can be effectively applied to extract layout structures and textual transcriptions and in the current HisDoc 2.0 project we successfully retrieved additional paleographic information. The novel contributions of HisDoc III will be complemented by these methods to cope with large document collections.
Existing methods are largely based on supervised learning and thus require an extensive amount of labeled training data. Therefore they are not directly applicable to classify collections of heterogeneous manuscripts with a large variety of layout structure, textual content, degradation traces, and other artifacts. While this problem is already relevant for homogeneously digitized books, it becomes even more crucial for isolated pages and the tremendous amount of yet non-cataloged and unexplored fragments distributed over many libraries around the world.
The objective of HisDoc III is twofold: (i) fundamental research on combined text- and image-based classification methods and (ii) making developed technology useful for libraries, archives, and researchers in the Humanities. Firstly, for the classification of documents we will study novel deep learning methods for large amounts of unlabeled text and image data. These methods will be complemented by structural approaches based on document graphs. For the combination of these diverse approaches we will investigate Multiple Classifier Systems on the one hand and integrated neural network architectures on the other. Secondly, we will combine three ideas for making methods useful for libraries: (i) novel means for reducing the needed amount of ground truth by unsupervised machine learning and alternatively bootstrapping combined with active learning; (ii) intuitive computer-assisted presentation and annotation tools; and (iii) making our systems publicly available as Web services.
To demonstrate the suitability of the HisDoc III research results, we will design novel computer-assisted workflows in collaboration with an advisory board compiled of scholars, librarians and archivists. A particular focus is speeding up the generation of catalog and database entries and devising ways to present methods and results in an understandable way.
In HisDoc III, we formulate novel research ideas, solve fundamental problems in DIA, and make innovative tools and services available for the research community. We expect this project to become a catalyst for the development of innovative solutions for the Digital Humanities.
Keywords: big data, cultural heritage preservation, deep learning, digital humanities, document classification, document image analysis, historical documents, scructural learning

Title: At the two upgrade frontiers: machine learning and the ITk Pixel detector
Abstract:
The PI proposes to explore the two principal ATLAS upgrade frontiers: the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) upgrade and state-of-the-art machine learning (ML). The ITk upgrade of the ATLAS Pixel detector is key to the HL-LHC project. Contributions to the in-house construction steps and associated quality control are proposed, in line with FLARE grant 20FL20 201478. Complementary to this crucial hardware upgrade, the PI will leverage modern ML to maximize the physics output in high energy particle physics by incorporating the domain knowledge directly in the model building for performant, interpretable and reusable ML modules. Concrete applications in the area of the PI’s core particle physics expertise, i.e. top quark physics, flavor-tagging and searches for physics beyond the Standard Model, will be used to demonstrate and analyze the added benefits of the proposed methods, and they will at the same time lead to explicit knowledge gain in particle physics.

ML has come a long way from classification and regression tasks in science, and in particle physics in particular, and it has made formidable quantum leaps on several fronts in the recent years which open ever more doors for breakthroughs in science. One of the overarching themes of this proposed research is to represent particle physics data as graph models, supporting arbitrary relational structure between the naturally unordered particles (nodes) of arbitrary size, and communicating their interaction through the presence or absence of pairwise connections (edges). These models combine two key advantages over other ML models: they allow to imprint the physics in the form of the very flexible structure of graphs and they provide additional flexibility in the representation of properties of nodes, edges, and the graph as a whole.

Three specific use cases are proposed to showcase the large range of promising applications of graph models:
1) optimum association of reconstructed objects to the top-quark decay products in tt¯ events, benefiting the many analyses involving top quarks by reducing combinatorial background; 2) improved flavor-tagging based on the full decay chain topology of b- and c -jets; 3) learning a physics-inspired representation of Standard Model (SM) processes to design powerful signal-agnostic tests for the presence of new phenomena in form of anomalies in the data. In all cases the physics is conveniently encoded in the graph models by use of Monte Carlo (MC) simulation. Thanks to the high-fidelity of the simulation, reduced performance due to mismodeling is expected to play only a minor role but will be studied. Simple but effective attention mechanisms are used to help the models focus on the information which is relevant to the task at hand. Additional flavor-tagging innovations are proposed building on the graph model, and a proposed tt¯+charm measurement combines the top and the flavor-tagging work.

The search for physics beyond the Standard Model (BSM) remains one of the priority goals of the LHC. The lack of experimental signs and the uncertainty regarding the theory guidance heralds a new era hinting at reconsidering the current search strategy, which is focused on classic and theoretically-founded signatures. This formerly well- motivated catalogue of highly specialized searches collapses in this new context to a set of rather arbitrary hypothesis tests. In the absence of any theory prior the traditional search strategy is far from ideal, and one would prefer a much broader search for deviations from the SM. The PI proposes to extend ATLAS’s physics portfolio to anomaly detection maximizing the search generalizability for a given small and acceptable loss in sensitivity. The emphasis is on automation and a reduced complexity of the data analysis.

The proposed graph-based approach achieves these goals by primarily capitalizing on the MC modeling to test for deviations from the background hypothesis. With the BSM anomaly search strategy being still in its infancy, multiple diverse approaches are required to cast an as broad and fine net as possible over the LHC data. In this spirit the PI proposes a second complementary search for anomalies in form of a resonance which is one of the fundamental search strategies for new phenomena. The key innovations are two-fold: the analysis complexity is alleviated through data-derived background estimates and a data-derived anomaly metric which makes the compute- and human-intense simulation and analysis of MC events superfluous.
Keywords: Anomaly detection, Flavor-tagging, HL-LHC Pixel upgrade, Machine learning, Searches for BSM physics, Top-quark physics

Title: Neuromodulation-induced plasticity of hippocampal networks – diagnostic and prognostic value for mood, cognitive and motor outcome in depression
Abstract:
The successful prevention and treatment of major depressive disorder (MDD), the leading cause of disease burden worldwide, depends on understanding mechanisms governing the heterogenous expression of associated mood, cognitive and motor function deficits. Despite advances in identification of the structural and functional organisation of depression circuits in humans, we lack knowledge about their association with individual clinical phenotypes, their temporal evolution, or their sensitivity to therapeutic interventions designed to produce long-lasting therapy-induced plastic changes. The aim of our project is to bridge this gap by studying from a lifetime and sex differences perspective the mechanisms by which electro-convulsive therapy (ECT) induces brain plasticity to modulate mood, cognition and motor function. We have published our experimental results to date to justify the feasibility of our approach.
Our plan is to integrate existing large-scale behavioural phenotypic information and prospective trajectory-based temporal models of individual clinical ECT related outcomes, neurobiologically enriched with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) features, to generate predictive statistical models. The main scientific objectives are: 
i.Address to what extent MDD-associated mood, cognitive and motor function profiles can be identified in the community-dwelling population and how they evolve in both sexes over a lifetime. 
ii.Establish how anatomical MRI data associated with MDD profiles can be interpreted in terms of neurobiological properties of local and distributed brain features of interest. 
iii.Validate causal models that integrate ECT- and pharmacological treatment-induced affective symptom improvement, cognitive and motor performance, catecholamine plasma levels, functional and anatomical imaging data.
The project’s novelty is twofold – the sophisticated in vivo studies of tissue property and neural activity changes associated with ECT therapy will not only help understanding the missing link between current descriptive assessments of human brain plasticity and underlying neurobiological mechanisms in depression but will also open new fields for related research in healthy and diseased brains. The results will also potentially promote acceptance of modern ECT by the general public and should rationalise its targeted deployment by psychiatrists.

Title: Self-Supervised Learning for Earth Observation: Leveraging a wealth of multi-modal data
Abstract:
Deep Learning approaches have proven highly successful across a wide range of downstream tasks from vastly different domains. However, adapting this technology to domain-specific tasks is hampered by three challenges: (1) supervised learning typically requires large amounts of labeled data, which can be prohibitively expensive to acquire, (2) the use of model architectures that are constrained by their inductive biases and (3) the focus on single data modalities imposes limitations on the learning process.

Recently, new Deep Learning paradigms have emerged that provide promising avenues to overcome these limitations. Self-supervised learning approaches address (1) by pre-training architectures on unlabeled datasets, enabling a more efficient use of labeled data. Attention-based Transformer architectures, able to learn long-ranging relationships in data, have shown their ability to overcome (2). Finally, (3) is resolved by utilizing freely available multi-modal data to supplement existing datasets in a data fusion approach, from which (1) and (2) are likely to benefit, as well. While these new approaches have already shown excellent performances separately, there are reasons to assume that their combination leads to superior performance.

Probably one of the most impactful application areas to implement and evaluate these approaches is the field of Earth Observation (EO), which naturally provides vast amounts of multi-modal data in the form of satellite observations, geographic, topographic, as well as concurrent environmental data. In this project, we lever- age the growing body of publicly available multi-modal EO data in combination with self-supervised learning and recent Transformer approaches. The fundamental research goal of this project is to explore ways how self-supervised learning can take full advantage of multi-modal data to learn rich, task-agnostic representations and how to leverage the versatility of tailored Transformers in such a setup. For this purpose, we will implement different backbone architectures (including Transformers) and train those utilizing different self-supervised learning setups in combination with data fusion, multi-task learning and knowledge transfer elements. We will evaluate the utility of the different learning approaches and architectural designs on common EO-related downstream tasks to identify the most promising setup. Our experiments will mainly utilize the large-scale BigEarthNet dataset, which we will extend with freely available supplemental data as part of this project to explore their utility. We will validate our findings by applying our approaches to real-world challenges and competitions. This project will yield three key contributions: (1) a publicly released set of pre-trained models for EO applications that can be readily used by the EO community, boosting its scientific output; (2) a systematic approach to train models on small-sized labeled datasets, opening new possibilities for EO-related research; (3) unique insight into how multi-modal data can be leveraged with data fusion methods to learn task-agnostic representations in a self-supervised way and how these representations can be exploited by Transformer (and other) architectures, thereby informing other Deep Learning domains featuring multi-modal data.
Keywords: Data Fusion, Deep Neural Networks, Earth Observation, Multi-modal Data, Remote Sensing, Self-supervised Learning, Transformer

Title: Information-theoretic analysis of deep identification systems
Abstract:
This project is a further extension of the concepts and methods obtained in the scope of SNF project number 200021--165672,  ``Information-theoretic forensic physical object identification" and research performed in the Stochastic Information Processing Group during the last two years. In the previous studies, we addressed a number of theoretical and practical problems of physical object identification using novel techniques of data encoding and searching in high dimensional spaces. The main challenge of the preceding SNF project was to introduce theoretical foundations of physical object identification based on high dimensional forensic features in large-scale databases and experimentally validate it on the newly acquired PharmaPack dataset.

In the continuation, we will extend the work on physical object identification, specifically for anticounterfeiting. Ever cheaper and sophisticated manufacturing technology has widened the range of counterfeited products considerably. Next to packaging and fake medication, industrial and aerospace parts are being cloned. Traditional countermeasures tend to invasively alter an object, based on the assumption that the alteration is either hard or economically unfeasible to reproduce. Our earlier work incorporated anti-counterfeiting as a natural consequence of the fact that the measured forensic features were hard, if not impossible, to clone.

Further more, we envision that any verification of any objects' authenticity should be executed by an ordinary consumer, using a mobile phone. Enabling the end user in such a way would be a significant step against counterfeiting, which is highly scalable and cost efficient next to enabling other applications such as product track-and-trace thus covering a complete delivery and distribution chain.

However, recent developments in machine learning, notably the rise of adversarial architectures, have empowered counterfeiters. It enables informed attacks against verification systems that successfully leverage all available information, such as the original data (distribution) next to knowledge on the targeted identification architecture. This type of informed adversarial attack may generate a sample that simultaneously fools both a human expert and an automatic verification system. An early study in our group performed in 2012 and published at WIFS2012, predicted these attacks and modeled the performance consequences of informed attacks on both identification and authentication systems. 

In summary, this creates a necessity to properly handle these newly emerging security requirements and to reconsider the theoretical foundations derived in the assumption that the attackers and counterfeiters are uninformed. 

The theoretical detectability limits of counterfeits hinges on a number of important aspects and assumptions. These include modeling the attackers' knowledge of the original, the manufacturing processes and the inherent limitations of using mobile devices for verification. All these factors remain largely unexplored and ill defined. 

In conclusion, it is timely and important to identify, introduce and apply new principles into the design, analysis and optimization of identification architectures. The goal of the present proposal is to extend and further develop a new information-theoretic framework for physical object identification using deep representations and apply it to practical systems. This goal will be achieved based on a novel interpretation of links between machine learning, variational inference, information-theoretic coding, models of the production process, attacks, physics of uncloneble features and particularities of identification taking the specifics of mobile imaging into account. Finally, the field also currently lacks public datasets which are needed to gain reproducible results and benchmarking. 

As detailed in the proposal, the envisioned theoretical framework of physical object identification relies on recent concepts and our own findings in information theory, sparse approximation, deep variational inference, adversarial machine learning and physical production.

In the scope of this proposal, the following subjects will be investigated:
(A) Information-theoretic analysis of deep identification systems: architectures, performance and complexity;
(B) Universal image processing for deep identification systems;
(C) Database construction and enrollment;
(D) Information-theoretic analysis of attacks and countermeasures in identification systems.
Keywords: adversarial attacks, anticounterfeiting, clonability, database, deep identification, information-theoretical analysis, mobile imaging, security, unsupervised learning

Title: Strengthening the Role of Generative Machine Learning in Psycholinguistics
Abstract: Recent advancements in generative machine learning have revolutionized computers' ability to process human language, automating aspects of language learning and usage that were previously considered exclusive to humans. Though not every aspect of language has been mastered by these models, a growing number of models demonstrate near-human proficiency in text generation and nuanced syntactic tasks, as well as speech recognition. Despite these advancements, cognitive science and psycholinguistics have yet to fully harness the capabilities of high-performance language models in their text and spoken forms. Considerable advances in psycholinguistics have been made to date using insight from surprisal theory and biases in cross-linguistic distributions of language properties. Nevertheless, further research is necessary to bridge the gap between the recent and technologically advanced machine learning engineering and linguistic inquiry. This interdisciplinary proposal aims to address these challenges by integrating modern generative machine learning with scientific inquiry into the nature of human language, through 1) the analysis of longer discourse contexts and refinement of surprisal theory, 2) the incorporation of spoken language stimuli and spoken language models (end-to-end automatic speech recognition) for the the enhancement of surprisal theory, and 3) the leveraging of modern compute clusters for training smaller language models for insight on machine vs. human language learning biases. Through three pillars—“Beyond the Sentence,” “Beyond the Text,” and “Beyond a Single Model”—the proposal seeks to advance psycholinguistics and cognitive science by applying recent language and spoken language modeling advancements to address fundamental questions in psycholinguistic theory.

Title: Neurobiological mechanisms underlying social motivation hypothesis in ASD
Abstract:
Haploinsufficiency of the SHANK3 gene causes a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by impaired social interaction and repetitive behaviors classified within autism spectrum disorders (ASDs). We still lack a detailed understanding of the pathophysiology of these core symptoms: What is the origin of social deficits in ASD?  The "theory of the social motivation of autism" posits that social interactions are not rewarding for a child with ASD and thus provides a framework for the investigation of emerging social deficits and their pathophysiology. There is, however, a dearth of knowledge about the neural bases that lead to reduced social motivation. Two distinct scenarios are conceivable. Social deficits may be due either to the reduced reward value of social interactions or to the inability to learn the association of actions and rewards (reinforcement learning). We propose here to dissect the behavioral, circuit, and cellular mechanisms underlying the social motivation hypothesis using the Shank3 knockout mouse model carrying the deletion of exon4-22 (Shank3 ?4-22 mouse model). 

The reward circuit has been implicated in motivated behavior. This circuit comprises the projections of dopamine (DA) neurons from the Ventral Tegmental Area (VTA) to the Nucleus Accumbens (NAc). DA released in the NAc modulates synaptic plasticity of glutamate afferents, which is the substrate for learned motivated behavior. Here, we predict that accumbal DA transients arise during social interaction, modulate the induction of social-evoked synaptic plasticity (SESP) and thus reinforce instrumental behavior. The altered behavior in Shank3 deficiency mouse model may thus be explained by impaired SESP. To test this hypothesis, we will use in-vivo and ex-vivo electrophysiological approaches, fiber photometry methods, optogenetic tools and behavioral tasks in Shank3 knock out mouse model to implement 3 specific aims: 

Aim 1. We will use instrumental reward tasks to unravel the reinforcing properties of social interaction (approach to social stimuli), social reinforcement learning (association between action and social interaction), and social effort (strength of motivation to interact) (Behavioral mechanisms). 
Aim 2. We will characterize the neuronal circuits underlying social motivation deficits. Using in      vivo electrophysiology, we will first examine the properties of VTA DA neurons. We will then use optogenetic tools to develop closed-loop approaches to rescue social behaviors in the mouse model and to test the causality between activity and behavior. (Circuit mechanisms). 
Aim 3. We will examine the synaptic mechanisms underlying the social motivation deficits. We will use ex vivo slice physiology to investigate the induction and the expression of SESP in the NAc. We will investigate shared synaptic mechanisms between different reinforcers (social, food, and optogenetic stimulation of DA neurons) and examine the mechanisms underlying reinforcement-based therapeutic intervention. (Synaptic mechanisms). 

The results of our study will provide the behavioral and circuit mechanisms underlying the social motivation hypothesis and will contribute to understand the neuronal bases of behavioral interventions.
Keywords: Autism Spectrum Disorder, Reward circuit, Social Interaction

Title: Cochlea-Like Audio Sensing with Embedded Event-Driven Processing for Ambient Intelligence
Abstract: This proposed research project aims at building a complete event-driven system in CMOS including a cochlea-like acoustic sensing front end and a signal processing stage with hybrid analog/digital computation. The expected adaptive and ultra-low power consumption of the system resulted from the combination of 'event-driven' and 'hybrid analog/digital computing' may open doors for its applications in wireless acoustic sensor networks for ambient intelligence, which has great potentials of enriching human being's daily life in an unobtrusive and affective way, and especially may help disabled and elderly people gain more convenience of performing routine tasks in ambient assisted living. Other applications, like hearing aids and cochlea implants can also profit from the developed technology.
Keywords: Ambient Intelligence, Analog/Digital Computing, Audio Sensing, Cochlea, Embedded Event-Driven Processing, Machine Learning, Wireless Acoustic Sensor Networks

Title: The role of governance in public sector digitalization (RoGoDi)
Abstract:
This research aims to investigate how public organizations can steer digitalization initiatives towards better outcomes, such as improved performance and increased public value. This is important as, for more than a decade, digitalization has defined changes in public administration (Filgueiras & Almeida, 2021) and, as such, represents the key post-New Public Management reform (Torfing et al., 2020). Significant public resources have been dedicated to a variety of digitalization initiatives ranging from scanning documents to using artificial intelligence to automate service delivery (Neumann et al., 2022; Gartner, 2021; Mergel et al., 2019). Despite this, these initiatives frequently result in failure (Goh & Arenas, 2020; Neumann et al., 2019). 

The baseline for this research is the omnipresent argument that attributes of digitalization initiatives (such as the scope of an initiative or a type of utilized technology) define the outcomes: e.g., large-scale initiatives utilizing cut-edge technology almost always founder (Wiewiora & Desouza, 2022; Yaraghi, 2015; Gingnell et al., 2014; Holgeid & Thompson, 2013). The proposed solution for reaching better outcomes has been to prioritize small-scale initiatives utilizing mature technology (OECD, 2001). However, this is not always possible. Our research aims to investigate whether the forms of governance in public sector digitalization matter, being the key element in the process from designing a digitalization initiative to ensuring it delivers the expected outcomes, and whether some governance configurations are better in this respect than others. Thus, this research project develops an exploration into how public governance contributes to governmental outcomes in  the era of public sector digitalization (Schou & Hjelholt, 2018) based on the following overarching research questions:

1.Which governance configurations do public organizations adopt to govern digitalization initiatives? 
2.Does governance matter to the outcomes of digitalization initiatives? If so, how does it make a difference or why does it not?

Given that governance of public sector digitalization is strongly contextualized (OECD, 2021), we focus on one country to limit the number of contextual factors at play. As a result of its politico-administrative structure, strong reform efforts for digitalization at all state levels combined with lively discussions on the role of governance in this endeavor (e.g. eID or e-voting initiatives), as well as a high permeability of knowledge and experience between the private and public sector in a position-based public sector employment regime, Switzerland presents a variety of governance configurations, digitalization initiatives and the outcomes thereof.

The research project puts forward a mixed-methods research design, starting with a quantitative part in the form of an original survey of stakeholders involved in the governance of public sector digitalization in Switzerland, followed by a qualitative part in the form of a multiple-case study utilizing stakeholder interviews. The quantitative part of the research will establish whether governance makes a difference, while the qualitative part will investigate how governance makes a difference, or why it does not.

This research represents both a science-driven and a use-inspired approach, as its findings will inform both the theory and the practice of digitalization in the public sector. The empirical evidence about whether governance matters to the outcomes of digitalization might enlighten future decisions on how digitalization should be governed. The findings will contribute to avoiding undesirable outcomes in future digitalization of the public sector and facilitate the design of better governance structures across organizations and state levels by proposing standards and guidance on the governance of digitalization in the public sector.
Keywords: adaptive governance, agile governance, governance, mixed methods, modes of governance, public sector digitalization, public value, tentative modes of governance

Title: Large Language Model Society: Opportunities and Risks for Information Seeking
Abstract:
The release of ChatGPT in late 2022 marked a watershed moment in artificial intelligence, comparable to how the Mosaic web browser democratized Internet access in the 1990s. While organizations have long utilized AI systems, the widespread adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) by the general public represents an unprecedented shift in how society interacts with AI technology. Each week, over 800 million people use ChatGPT alone, increasingly seeking information through its conversational interface rather than relying on traditional search engines.
However, these systems are imperfect and pose significant societal risks. Despite their massive adoption, we lack a comprehensive understanding of how the general public uses LLMs in daily life, what outputs they prefer for different tasks, and the associated opportunities and risks as we progress toward a society where everyday LLM use becomes the norm.

This project aims to promote the positive societal impact of everyday LLM usage for information seeking. It will examine user online browsing patterns to understand how people engage with LLMs in daily life, assess existing LLM-mediated information access systems across search engines and conversational chatbots, and analyze human preferences for these systems. Additionally, it will evaluate the fairness implications of personalized LLM outputs in everyday tasks to ensure equitable access to information.

The project leverages natural language processing (NLP) and computational social science (CSS) methods to comprehensively examine the societal impact of everyday LLM usage. We will analyze large-scale online tracking and survey data from thousands of users and conduct systematic audits of LLM-powered information access systems using real-world queries and prompts.

Expected Results: The project will deliver three major outcomes:
A comprehensive framework for understanding LLM-mediated online information seeking behaviors. Empirical insights into LLM output quality for information seeking tasks and its alignment with human preferences. Systematic analysis of fairness implications and practical bias-mitigation solutions in personalized LLM outputs.

This project will provide crucial insights for ensuring that the growing integration of LLMs into daily life promotes rather than hinders equitable information access.
This research will have broad implications across multiple stakeholders. For researchers, it will advance the understanding of real-world LLM usage patterns and establish robust evaluation methodologies. Practitioners will benefit from guidelines for developing more effective and equitable LLM-powered information systems. Policymakers will gain insights to inform regulations around AI-mediated information access, while society as a whole will see contributions toward the responsible deployment of LLM technology that ensures equitable benefits for all user groups.

Title: Operational digital twins of complex industrial systems based on physics-informed deep learning with integrated structural inductive bias, physics and domain expertise
Abstract: Digital transformation has enabled a tight monitoring of the system conditions of complex industrial systems. The digital informational about the physical system and its operation can create a digital entity on its own representing the digital twin linked to the physical system across its entire life cycle. Digital twin technology has been creating large expectations particularly in the field of intelligent operation and maintenance. Some of the most complex requirements on the digital twins arise in the context of real-time update frequency, automatic connectivity, factory environment as integration breadth, multi-physical behavior as digital model richness and look-ahead prescriptive simulation capabilities. High-fidelity physical performance models and deep learning algorithms have been occasionally applied for these types of applications. Physics-based models are, however, expensive in their development and are not available for all systems in a sufficient resolution. Furthermore, they often come with a large computational burden for real-time updates. Also, they are often only available at the prototype level and may not be adjustable to the instance level of a specific system under its specific operating conditions. Additionally, they may not capture all of the underlying sub-processes which may result in significant gaps between digital twin models and the operational state of their physical counterpart. Data-driven approaches, such as deep learning (DL) algorithms, developed as digital twins have been typically limited to the specific operating conditions and the unique configurations. The high diversity of system configurations and operating conditions has been preventing the generalization and the scalability of DL approaches. DL algorithms are known to have a limited extrapolation ability. However, extrapolation is required in the presence of new operating conditions and also for predicting the evolution of the system conditions over long time periods. Al-so, the integration of domain expertise and prior knowledge on the underlying physical relationships has been limited within the data-driven digital twin methodology. Additionally, the interpretability of the developed data-driven methods has been limited, which has prevented the acceptance of the developed models by domain experts. Moreover, the data-driven models are often lacking the generalization ability, are not scalable and cannot be applied beyond the operational regimes the algorithms were trained on (lacking the extrapolation ability). The proposed research project tackles the challenge of developing methodology for hybrid digital twins of complex industrial and infrastructure systems combining the learning capabilities of machine learning algorithms with the interpretability and extrapolation abilities of physics-based approaches. The ultimate goal is to improve the availability and the resilience of complex industrial assets. The proposed project has two main methodological contributions: Firstly, hybrid digital twin methodology developed in the proposed research project will integrate the relational inductive bias representing structural information of the measurement locations and their inter-relationships for developing physics-informed graph neural networks that will improve the generalization ability and the scalability of the developed algorithms. Secondly, the proposed research project will develop methodology to learn disentangled physically-interpretable factors of variation and to integrate the governing (partial) physical relationships. Furthermore, the learning will integrate domain expertise either defined by experts as rules or learned by reinforcement learning algorithms. Moreover, the proposed research will develop a holistic framework for operational digital twins that fuses purely data-driven, purely physics-based and hybrid algorithms combining different types of inductive bias representing physical relationships. The proposed hybrid digital twin will not only improve the reliability and availability of critical infrastructure and industrial assets but will also improve their resilience by preemptive interventions. The results of the proposed research project will not only benefit the operators, but also the society as a whole by improving the quality of the provided services (including improved availability) and reducing the costs of operation and maintenance.
Keywords: Graph neural networks, Hybrid digital twin, Intelligent maintenance systems, Physics-informed neural networks

Title: Neural Correlates of Dreaming
Abstract:
THE NEURAL CORRELATES OF DREAMING

Background
Dreaming is a particular form of consciousness that occurs during sleep. Studying mental experiences during sleep thus offers a unique opportunity to explain how changes in brain activity relate to changes in consciousness.
 
Aims 
The present project aims to determine how conscious experiences in sleep relate to underlying electroencephalographic activity and if machine-learning techniques can reliably predict periods of dreaming and non-dreaming.

Methods
Fourty-four high-density electroencephalography (hd-EEG) overnight recordings (256 electrodes) were performed in seven healthy participants in the laboratory. Participants were awakened at pseudorandom intervals and asked about the presence and content of mental activity. 741 questionings were performed. The EEG signal in the two minutes prior to the awakening was analyzed in terms of spontaneous power changes and with machine learning paradigms.

Preliminary results
In Non-REM (NREM) sleep, high frequency power in the 15-20 Hz range, and a low density of sleep spindles and slow waves reliably predicted sleep consciousness. In REM sleep, sleep consciousness was associated with high gamma power (25-40 Hz) over the fronto-central regions, and low theta power in the occipitial and central midline regions. 

Importance of the project
Our preliminary results suggest that dreaming is associated with specific EEG features. This constitutes a major step in dream research, as it will eventually enable researchers to determine, in real-time, whether someone is dreaming. More generally, changes in dream content form the core feature of many sleep and psychiatric disorders and share features with hallucinations and delirium. Determining neural correlates of dreaming might thus ultimately open new approaches to the understanding and treatment of these diseases.
Keywords: consciousness, dreams, high density EEG, sleep

Title: Graph Signal Processing and Learning in Smarter Cities Applications
Abstract:
Urban analytics and modeling inevitably involves an extremely large volume of data, coming from possibly every visible or invisible corner of the modern city environment, that are produced by millions of its inhabitants. But volume is not the only problem in modern data analysis. Data are increasingly complex, with many structures behind the observations made by individual sensors: mobility data may follow physical constraints of the environment, and behaviors of a group of people may be influenced by the friendships among them. To understand such structures is one of the key challenges in our attempt to capture the intrinsic relations between different entities and the true cause of the observational signals, even more so in the context of urban data analytics and modeling.

Graphs are powerful mathematical tools to model structured and networked data. Traditionally a representation that reveals the pairwise relations (edges) between entities (vertices), graph-based data representations can be complex and flexible enough to incorporate the structures and dynamics of the data, yet remaining reasonably simple and efficient for processing. First, data of interest can be associated with either the vertices or the edges of the graph. In the former case, it could be observations from the entities, for example readings from various types of physical sensors; in the latter case, it could be information defined based on the strengths of the relations between the entities, for example a measure of ``social affinity" between two different persons based on the number of common friends they have. Second, a graph can evolve as relations between entities evolve. Examples include physical distances between mobile sensors that are constantly moving, or friendships in a social network that might evolve along time. Third, since the complexity of the data may be attributed to the increasingly common fact that there exist multiple types of relations between the same set of entities, such as different kinds of interactions between the same group of people, a multi-layer graph can be used to model such relations where the layers share the same vertex set but have different edges.

In this project, we propose to develop novel techniques in the intersection of signal processing and machine learning on graphs, and apply them in the context of urban analytics and modeling. Specifically, we are interested in studying three related questions: (i) how to understand the relations between various physical and ``social" sensors to make sense out of large volume of city data, (ii) how to efficiently capture the dynamics in human behaviors and environmental changes, and (iii) how to take into account multiple factors at the same time to explain the complex interactions between human activities and city environments. The new development in this project would not only contribute to the emerging research field of signal processing on graphs, but more importantly, also shed lights in the understanding and designs of future Smarter Cities in the modern era of global urbanization.
Keywords: Complex and structured data, Human and urban dynamics, Signal processing on graphs, Smarter Cities applications

Title: Navigating Trust in Generative AI: An Information Theory and Optimal Transport Perspective
Abstract:
In the era of big data, with recent advances in data-driven machine learning frameworks coupled with growing concern about trust and responsibility in artificial intelligence (AI), it is desirable to deepen the foundations of trustworthy and responsible machine learning (ML). Recent advances in this socially-critical research area suggest that mathematical tools from information theory and optimal transport theory will play a pivotal role in the next decade of machine learning applications. The development of responsible AI foundations has a direct practical impact on societies by creating new opportunities, e.g., in healthcare, education, and biometric technologies, thereby improving people's quality of life around the world. However, to the best of my knowledge, there is currently no general framework that unifies and generalizes the existing models and establishes connections with interdisciplinary fields, such as digital health and biometrics. Ensuring reliable and accurate ML models builds trust in technologies, benefiting society and individuals. Prioritizing trustworthy ML research is crucial for AI's responsible development and use for the greater good.

My research aims to comprehensively study and integrate the four pillars of trustworthy machine learning: (i) accuracy/utility, (ii) privacy/confidentiality, (iii) fairness, and (iv) complexity. To realize this objective, I intend to leverage my expertise in areas such as information theory, functional analysis, probability and measure theory, and optimal transport theory. Specifically, my goal is to develop trustworthy machine learning applications by employing tools from optimal transport theory and information theory. This comprehensive approach is designed to ensure that our machine learning models are not only accurate, but also respect privacy and confidentiality, uphold fairness, and effectively manage complexity.

My previous research, including my PhD work on the Complexity-Leakage-Utility Bottleneck (CLUB) model and my ongoing work on the reSponsible fAir FacE Recognition (SAFER) project, forms the groundwork for this proposal. The CLUB model serves as a unified theoretical framework that broadens many existing privacy/fair models, providing fresh insights into generative and discriminative models used in machine learning.
Keywords: Fairness, Generative AI, Information Theory, Privacy, Responsible Artificial Intelligence, Trustworthy Machine Learning

Title: SWISS SECOND - the impact of disease activity on secondary brain alterations in epilepsy patients five years after the first seizure
Abstract:
According to the WHO, epilepsy ranks as the neurological disorder with the second-largest burden of disease in terms of disability-adjusted life years. Epilepsy also imposes substantial economic burdens, including increased health care needs, premature death, and lost productivity. Increasing clinical evidence suggests that immediate medical treatment is associated with a better prognosis within the first five years following the index event. 

While several studies have demonstrated that prior seizures are an independent risk factor for seizure relapse in patients with new onset epilepsy, limited research has explored the impact of recurrent seizures on brain health at the structural and molecular levels during the early stages of the disorder. We aim to identify imaging surrogates for seizure freedom five years after they have experienced their first epileptic seizure. This will form the basis of a holistic multi-domain neuroimaging approach to unmask predisposing factors of disease progression after a first seizure. We make use of newly developed in-house methods: i) deep-learning based structural analysis of brain damage, ii) echo planar spectroscopic imaging to determine the interplay between GABA and Glutamate, iii) MR-based measures of neuronal-currents in epilepsy and iv) simultaneous EEG-fMRI, and apply them to the well phenotyped cohort of patients we have recruited as the lead institution of SNF SINERGIA project CRSII5_180365 (SWISS FIRST). Working with the developers of these methods and direct access to a unique image acquisition framework at the Translational Imaging Center Bern (3T and 7T) is expected to provide new insights into the structural, molecular and physiological correlates of early and progressive brain damage and its consequences for brain health impairment in epilepsy patients. 

Our DL-based brain morphometry method has been independently validated and recommended as being most accurate at resolving atrophies in the submillimeter range. It will ensure reliable longitudinal monitoring of disease to distinguish progressive vs. stable trajectories. The non-invasive depiction of abnormal brain activity associated with neuronal current induced oscillating magnetic fields is the first of its kind in clinical MRI scanners and will be complemented by an in-house developed and timely setup of simultaneous EEG/fMRI recordings at 7 T MRI. We will further incorporate a unique methodology for determination of slowly progressive subtypes of epilepsy, by investigating imbalance in excitatory vs. inhibitory neurotransmission through the in-house developed and patented SLOW-EPSI MRSI. 

We expect advances in knowledge by looking into previously unexplored predisposing factors for disease progression related to the intrinsic pathophysiology in patients with early epilepsies. Identification of risk factors and informed control of seizures may facilitate the prevention of progressive structural, cognitive, and behavior damage in future studies. More detailed knowledge about predisposing factors of disease progression in subtypes of non-lesional epilepsies may open a future avenue for targeted therapeutic management of patients, preserving brain health for those living with epilepsy.

Title: The “Sentometrics” toolbox: enriching decision-making with sentiment information from news articles and corporate disclosures
Abstract:
This research project contributes to the analysis of sentiment in texts by asking whether “a deeper understanding of textual sentiment maximizes its information value”. A wealth of various forms of texts written on connected economic and financial topics have become cheaply available at large scale, presenting an increasingly important driver of the economy. Texts express either a positive, a negative or a neutral tone, textual sentiment, providing incremental information to quantitative data. Natural language processing and machine learning techniques have made significant progress in associating sentiment to texts. What lacks, however, is a decomposition of sentiment, knowledge about the underlying multivariate process of how sentiment is generated, and a framework for accurate statistical analysis. Understanding sentiment at a deeper level is key to grasping the full information potential of the big data sets texts are, with a focus on news articles and corporate disclosures. 

We put forward three research questions, that each target a distinct feature of textual sentiment. First, we ask if the dimensionality of sentiment and its evolution provides supplementary information as opposed to single sentiment estimates. Second, we question if a more precise estimation of textual sentiment improves its informativeness. Third, we research the added value of linking the cyclicality of textual sentiment to other cyclical variables. Our overarching hypothesis states that accounting for the dimensionality, precision, and cyclicality of textual sentiment enhances its information value.

Our methodology is to develop a three-layered framework called “Sentometrics” that addresses the research questions, intertwined with a desire to obtain a deeper understanding of textual sentiment. The first layer consists of a dynamic factor model that reveals the common components of textual sentiment. The second layer is a time-varying stochastic model underlying the generation of positive and negative words in texts. Such a parametric approach is entirely new to the textual sentiment literature. The third layer integrates textual sentiment into a regime-switching model. To validate our main hypothesis, we will deploy this enhanced textual sentiment modeling in three specific economic and financial applications, focusing on the supplementary information value that is obtained. The validation exercises will cover respectively the prediction of macroeconomic indicators, trading performance, and covariance matrices. We analyze extensive firm-specific textual data, that is, media coverage, annual reports, and quarterly earnings press releases, across the largest European countries. 

A successful development of the “Sentometrics” toolbox fills in the gap of missing econometric tools to decipher textual sentiment, making it possible to extract and exploit more detailed information on the sources, dynamics, and uncertainty of sentiment in texts. Our applications may improve risk protection of companies, banks, and financial institutions, potentially increasing the stability of the financial markets and the economy. As the modelling is set up application-free, it can be deployed in multiple subsequent research settings, including marketing, politics, and web intelligence, effectively providing a means for many fields to use textual sentiment as an optimally informative variable.

Title: Clinical Prediction Models for Surgical Outcomes: Addressing Methodological Challenges in Implementation, Data, and Analysis
Abstract:
Clinical prediction models can support surgical decision-making by identifying patient profiles that are at an increased risk of poor outcomes. While artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled decision aids demonstrated potential in enhancing shared decision-making and improving patient satisfaction, there remains a significant gap in implementation. Furthermore, few studies describe stakeholders’ preferences regarding the use of clinical prediction models. The adoption of decision support tools needs to be accelerated by (i) improving their transparency and reporting standards, (ii) addressing their implementation barriers, and (iii) aligning their development and implementation with stakeholder expectations to maximize their clinical impact. Simultaneously, the growing deployment and development of modern machine learning and AI models have sparked debates about their performance in comparison to regression models, particularly when citing issues relevant for surgical databases, including varying sample size, atypical outcome distributions (for example ceiling effects in patient-reported outcome measures), and number and strength of predictive ability of prognostic factors. 

The Clinical Prediction Models for Surgical Outcomes (CPMSO) project aims to address the challenges of implementation, data, and analysis by establishing standardized guidelines, ultimately improving the reliability and adoption of AI-driven decision support tools encompassing prediction models for surgical outcomes. Research Objective (RO) 1: To develop and validate a consensus-driven set of recommendations that support the implementation of prediction models for surgical outcomes in patients with musculoskeletal disorders. RO2: To assess the impact of data characteristics ((i) sample size, (ii) outcome distribution and (iii) number and predictive ability of prognostic factors) on the performance of machine-learning, regression, and Bayesian models for ordinal/continuous outcomes.

METHODS. In working package (WP) 1 related to RO1, we will (1) systematically map existing evidence on the implementation of prediction models in joint surgery through a scoping review, identifying methodological challenges and factors influencing their clinical adoption. We will also (2) explore the perceptions, needs, and implementation barriers of key stakeholders—including patients, healthcare professionals, and researchers— regarding prediction models for surgical outcomes, using focus group discussions. Based on these findings, we will then (3) develop and assess the relevance of a set of consensus recommendations addressing key issues for the implementation of prediction models for surgical outcomes. In WP2 related to RO2, the apparent and bootstrap-validated overall, discrimination and calibration performance of models predicting ordinal/continuous outcomes will be compared, including machine-learning, regression, and Bayesian models. First, data simulations will be generated, for which key data characteristics will be controlled ((i) sample size, (ii) outcome distribution and (iii) number and strength of predictive ability of prognostic factors). The validity of our findings will then be assessed using four nationwide surgical databases focusing on the prediction of pain (Numeric Rating Scale [0-10]) one year after surgery. Databases will be standardized to the Observational Health Data Sciences and Informatics (OHDSI) format, facilitating the further steps of analyses, which will include handling of missing data, predictor selection, model development, and internal validation.

EXPECTED RESULTS AND IMPACT. RO1, linked to WP1, will produce key recommendations for implementing prediction models for surgical outcomes, a crucial step toward enhanced decision-making and achieving better health and socioeconomic outcomes for patients and the society. RO2, linked to WP2, will provide methodological guidance on selecting optimal models for ordinal/continuous outcomes based on key data characteristics. The findings will be published in peer-reviewed journals and presented at international scientific conferences. The CPMSO project aims also to develop a professional network of experts, and support the integration of currently developed predictive analytics tools supporting surgical decision-making in Europe.

Title: AI4Flex.Data: AI-Driven Cross-Engine Optimization of Concurrent Workloads
Abstract:
Data has gone from being scarce to being super-abundant. Never before has it been so easy to collect large data quantities, due to the large-scale infrastructures available in the cloud. However, the increasing workload diversity in modern use-cases (i.e., lately seeking to harness unstructured data to fuel AI innovations) has led to the proliferation of specialized data management systems, each targeted to very narrow types of workloads. As a result, developers have had to reinvent the wheel again and again, thus slowing down our ability to quickly adapt systems to new trends. This has led to siloed systems, high maintenance costs and wasted engineering cycles. Even worse, the byproducts of this fragmentation – incompatible APIs, disparate functionality, inconsistent semantics – impact the end users, who commonly need to interact with multiple distinct systems to complete their tasks and to have expert knowledge to use them in the appropriate manner. However, at their core these specialized data systems are built on the same set of logical components, data structures and algorithms. 
We are motivated by our own experiences. In 2021, one of Italy’s largest banks started a migration from an on-prem Teradata data warehouse to a cloud-hosted BigQuery warehouse. 30 thousand workloads were ported, over the course of 3 years. Unsurprisingly, after one year of using BigQuery, the bank is evaluating another evolution in their data storage strategy because of cost and vendor lock-in concerns, but one not involving rewriting workloads. At the same time, workloads are becoming increasingly complex, to the point where single engines cannot efficiently support the types of analytics users wish to perform (e.g., matrix multiplication). In an experiment comparing PostGRES and Spark, we observed nearly three orders of magnitude difference in performance time (for a 1000x1000 dense matrix multiplication, PostGRES took ~166 minutes vs. 6 seconds in Spark). Such results suggest that workloads combining multiple operations (in this case extracting the discrete entries in a dataset and using them for matrix multiplication) can massively benefit from distributing these operations between various engines. 
This project is centered around the ideas of seamless portability and cost/performance efficiency of workloads that are transactional, analytical or a combination of the two. We propose AI4Flex.data, a system that optimizes workloads according to user goals by distributing their operators between different engines via learned models that replace traditional core components in these engines. AI4Flex.Data will be developed as a virtualization layer that decouples user-facing APIs used to express workloads from the underlying execution engines and runtimes. Under the covers, AI4Flex.Data will first map workloads written in SQL, code (e.g., Spark/Dataframes), no-code (e.g., IBM DataStage) to an intermediate representation (IR) (e.g., directed acyclic graph (DAG)). This not only eliminates the problem of incompatible APIs, but also ensures workload portability, significantly cutting migration times. Second, AI4Flex.Data will decide which engine(s) best fit a specific workload while choosing the appropriate provisioning and right-sizing for each engine and aiming to match a user’s specified cost/performance goals. Learned models have been able to outperform traditional optimizers, but their application has been limited to single-engine setups. Core technology developed in this project will deliver zero-shot learned models that are generalizable for unseen workloads and engines, in a distributed scenario where specific operations run on the engines that are most optimized to support them. To train such zero-shot models, we will develop a novel pipeline to generate synthetic workloads directly as IRs. Finally, we will answer a fundamental question for the research community: How effective are learned cost models on actual distributed optimization tasks?

Title: Reassessing the anatomy and evolutionary history of Permian sauropsids
Abstract:
Amniota is the clade of tetrapods that contains Sauropsida (i.e. reptiles and their closest relatives) and Synapsida (i.e. mammals and their closest relatives). Sauropsids arose more than 300 Ma ago in the Carboniferous and intensively diversified during the Permian, a period during which an abundant array of groups cohabited. The Permian diversity consists of a mix of lineages that either diversified without leaving descendants or that include the earliest representatives of groups that are still present today, making this period an important time for the understanding of sauropsid origins and diversification. Although hundreds of species of Permian sauropsids are recognized, much of their skeletal anatomy remains unknown and their phylogenetic relationships are still debated (e.g., Ford & Benson, 2020; Simões et al., 2022). Descriptions were generally restricted to the externally visible aspects of the fossils, limiting the amount of information that can be gathered. The increasingly intensive use of micro-computed tomography (µCT) in vertebrate paleontology over the last 30 years has allowed providing bone-by-bone reconstructions and descriptions of the external and internal anatomy of fossils with far greater accuracy and detail than previously possible with traditional methods. µCT scans also recently provided new insights into the evolutionary history of several early sauropsid lineages (e.g., Simões et al., 2018; Griffiths et al., 2021; Hunt et al., 2023), but its application to early-branching Permian taxa remains extremely rare and must be expanded to better understand the anatomy, evolutionary history, and diversification of the group.
My aim is to use µCT and state-of-the-art image segmentation techniques to digitally study a key selection of Permian sauropsid skulls. I, particularly, propose to segment and describe the skulls of Eunotosaurus africanus (Parareptilia), Owenetta rubidgei (Procolophonia, Parareptilia) and Captorhinus aguti (Captorhinidae), which belong to groups for which the phylogenetic relationships are debated and need to be clarified. These works will allow to identify new anatomical features that provide information about the acquisition of lineage-specific traits, and that will be transcribed into new phylogenetic characters. Then, I will assess the impact of my anatomical investigations by updating the latest phylogenetic matrices that were computed to analyze relationships among amniotes (e.g., Ford & Benson, 2020; Simões et al., 2022). I will perform a series of analyses using different methods (i.e., parsimony vs. Bayesian inference), of which the results will shed new light on sauropsid relationships and their morphological diversification during the Permian.
Keywords: Anatomy, Diversity, Evolution, Micro-computed tomography, Morphology, Permian, Phylogeny, Sauropsids

Title: Towards semantic interpretation of 3D Point Clouds and images in Urban Environments
Abstract: The proposed project aims to develop methods for the automatic detection and recognition of objects in urban environments, by analyzing the data delivered by mobile mapping systems, namely 3D point clouds from terrestrial laser scanning together with co-registered photographic images. While the geometric part of urban mapping is well understood, semantic interpretation and labeling of the data is still a largely open problem, but is required to create detailed maps with semantically tagged objects (e.g. trees, road signs, street lights, etc.). The expertise of both the host institution and the visitor is an ideal combination for such a project: the host institution is an established research center in photogrammetry with a strong computer vision flavor, the visitor is a computer vision researcher interested in photogrammetric applications. The project is intended as a first step in a longer-term research collaboration.
Keywords: laser scanning, mobile mapping, object detection, photogrammetry

Title: Local Learning in Neurally Inspired Computing Systems
Abstract:
This project aims at combining key properties of biological nervous systems with state-of-the-art machine learning methods to create computing systems that operate in a way fundamentally different from traditional ones, and excel at tasks that are notoriously difficult for today's computers.
The results will lead to strongly improved ways of learning and inference in neural networks, and deep networks in particular.
Even though deep neural networks have become synonymous with great breakthroughs in artificial intelligence over the recent years, they are by no means comparable to real brains in terms of efficiency, learning, or inference performance. 
While being loosely inspired by biological neural systems, artificial neural networks starkly differ from their biological counterparts in almost every respect.
This project focuses on principles of localized computation, which can be observed in biological brains, and which could lead to enormous improvements in scaling behavior and efficiency if incorporated into current machine learning models.
Being highly interdisciplinary by definition, the project will not only lead to theoretical models, but also detailed methods for applying the investigated principles to physical neural network realizations.
The research will result in a closed-loop prototype system demonstrating the advantages of these developments.
Keywords: analog electronics, deep learning, distributed processing, machine learning, neural networks, synaptic plasticity, vlsi

Title: Compute-aware Deep Neural Networks on the Edge
Abstract:
Edge artificial intelligence (AI) is quickly gaining both visibility and importance with the increasing billions of smart devices deployed in homes, office spaces, and on person. Ensuring that on-device algorithms perform reliable inference with low-latency and high compute efficiency on these resource-constrained hardware platforms is critical. State-of-art deep neural networks frequently have a large number of weight parameters to achieve high task accuracy under a wide range of operating scenarios. The large memory footprint of these networks does not match the limited memory and compute resources of edge devices. 

CA-DNNEdge aims to develop compute-aware networks that can dynamically limit the number of updates within the network while still allowing the network to perform the task with high accuracy.  The project will focus on convolutional and recurrent stateful architectures that exploit brain-like sparse-computing and learning principles to maximise energy efficiency. It will investigate the tradeoff between the energy efficiency, latency and task accuracy of a network operating in real-time dynamic environments. CA-DNNEdge will develop new bio-inspired architectures that enable continual learning. The algorithms will be co-developed together with hardware-aware training methods to enable optimal performance from the hardware deployed in these resource constrained scenarios.
Keywords: compute-aware networks, continual learning, event-driven computing, event-driven deep networks, hardware-aware networks, neural architectural search, neuromorphic processing

Title: Understanding Human Visual Processing through Deep Learning in Virtual Reality
Abstract:
The human visual cortex is the most advanced visual processing system that we know of. If we understand how it works, we can design more efficient and intuitive computer interfaces. This proposal aims to develop new state-of-the-art deep-learning models of human-computer interaction in virtual reality (VR). 

The use of VR is two-fold, (1) it allows unprecedented control and access to the user's visual space and the actions they perform, and (2) the 3D visual input and freedom in a virtual environment allow users to use their full visual processing capabilities; this is not possible with a traditional 2D display. Deep-learning models are biologically plausible, and can model visual processing with a detail unprecedented in human-computer interaction models.

First, we will first explore what deep-learning architectures are best suited to model user interaction. Then, the models will be analysed using several techniques to infer new insights in human visual processing. Finally, the models will be applied to help the user for task-assistance and optimization.
The results of this research will be submitted to main conferences in the field, and a final journal publication will present the complete work.
Keywords: deep learning, human visual processing models, human-computer interaction

Title: Very Large Sets of Heuristics for Scene Interpretation (VELASH)
Abstract:
This project is a one-year renewal of the three-year VELASH project, which started in September 2009. The objective of VELASH is to design novel algorithms to facilitate the development and the use of very large families of image feature extractors for object detection in natural scenes.

In coordination with the European MASH project, we have created over the last two years a collaborative platform to allow multiple contributors to develop and test such image feature extractors collaboratively.

In VELASH, we have adapted Boosting to deal with multiple families of feature extractors, and have developed new generic procedures extremely efficient in that context. This new techniques have been validated on object classification and detection on canonical databases (INRIA pedestrians, CIFAR, Caltech 101, etc.)

The objective of this renewal is to move from monolithic models, and to extend state-of-the-art part-based object detection methods. Our objective is twofold. First, while current methods mainly exploit variants of histograms of gradients -- which result in edge-based templates stable to local deformation -- we want to leverage the multiple modalities provided by the many families of feature extractors we have already implemented. Second, we will investigate the modeling of the joint behavior of features computed on individual parts, instead of relying on strong assumptions of conditional independence.
Keywords: Large feature space, Object detection, Part-based models, Pattern recognition

Title: When atrial fibrillation leads to heart failure – Data-driven cluster analysis to guide treatment and improve outcomes
Abstract:
Background and rationale: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most prevalent cardiac arrhythmia and is often associated with the development of heart failure (HF). When both conditions are concomitantly present, they lead to an increased morbidity and mortality. Despite important recent advancements in diagnostic technologies, the characterization and treatment of AF patients at risk of developing HF remains a challenge. Advancing knowledge for AF patients at risk of developing HF or providing care for AF patients with HF to minimize further adverse outcomes requires large comprehensive longitudinal datasets, adequate statistical approach and the possibility for external validations.
Aims: Uncover patterns and associations (clusters), thereby identifying patients with AF at risk for HF development, adverse cardiovascular events and likely to benefit from invasive treatment strategies.
Methods: Leveraging prospectively-collected research data from a large AF-ablation registry in place since 2011, data collected within the AF and Digital Health Clinic and large-scale data from patients’ Electronic Health Record (EHR), a comprehensive dataset will be created encompassing unselected AF patients presenting to the University of Michigan (UofM) over the past decade. Machine learning methods, specifically clustering algorithms, will be applied to identify patient clusters at risk of developing HF and/or further adverse outcomes and highlight subgroups likely to benefit more from invasive over conservative treatment strategies. 
Expected results and impact: Clustering of AF patients depending on their risk of HF development and likelihood to respond to specific treatments using high-dimensional data will allow for the development of elaborated tools for integration into the patients EHR. Once established, the methodology will allow for enrichment of the models with further, prospectively collected data and data from other institutions. These complex but comprehensive models integrated in the EHR will provide physicians with an instantaneous evaluation of all available data to guide diagnostic and therapeutic measures in an efficient, safe and cost-effective way.
Keywords: atrial fibrillation, cluster, electronic health record, heart failure, outcome research, phenotyping, prognosis, unsupervised machine learning
