Title: Towards a General Theory of Mechanism Design for Economies of Automated Agents
Abstract:
Over the last decade, artificial intelligence (AI) has led to numerous exciting advances for our society ranging from language translation to cancer detection and to the entertainment industry. In the near future, the presence of AI in our society is expected to increase, with AI agents (AIs) driving our cars, adjusting the temperature in our houses, or assisting our military operations. While supporting our activities, AIs will struggle for shared resources. For example, a self-driving car will benefit from taking a shortcut only when not many other cars are choosing the same road. Unmanned aerial vehicles assisting teams of marines will contend for a limited number of available missiles. It will then be important to design central entities, called economic mechanisms, that coordinate resources between different AIs operating in their own interest.

Designing effective economic mechanisms is the focus of a celebrated branch of the microeconomic theory called mechanism design. Mechanism design has found several applications in our society, including the design of spectrum auctions and matching markets. At the same time, it has not yet found applications in complex domains like road allocation or military operations. The main reason behind this failure is that, in these domains, agents are not fully rational, with not properly formed preferences that may change over time. However, things may change for the better when it comes to AIs, as they respect rationality assumptions much better than humans. This opens up the question of whether the field of application of mechanism design can be extended to more complex economies of AIs to induce more efficient allocations of our societal resources.

The goal of my research project is to move a first step towards developing a theoretical framework for mechanism design in (complex) AI economies. To achieve this goal, I plan to 1. build a simulator of AI economies, 2. define an approach to derive a proper mechanism for each simulated economy, and 3. develop models to predict the performance of a given mechanism in a given economy.

I plan to build my simulator of AI economies on top of Atari 2600 game environments. These environments are particularly appealing as they 1. introduce a variety of tasks qualitatively similar to the ones AIs are expected to undertake in real-world (e.g., driving games, action games), and 2. provide game scores that can be used to assess the performance of the mechanism. I will modify the Atari 2600 game environments by introducing commonly shared resources (e.g., shortcuts in driving games, or bullets in action games) allocated by a central mechanism.

Given the novelty of the project and the wide use of Atari 2600 game environments to assess advances in machine learning, I expect that even simple preliminary results can be of general interest to the AI community.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Mechanism design

Title: From Semantics to Argumentation Mining: a Context-Independent Lexicon of Indicators of Argumentative Discourse Relations
Abstract:
In everyday communicative arenas we exercise our logos to argue for issues of personal as well as public interest. Those discussions are nowadays spread on the Web, where user-generated comments (forums, tweets) augment the more traditional media, bringing the negotiation of opinions to a global dimension. Argumentation Mining is the recently expanding field in Computational Linguistics aimed to automatically extract arguments from a wide variety of text genres and contexts. The mining of arguments constitutes a true challenge since it entails not only detecting which discourse units are claims and which are premises supporting or attacking them (argumentation structure) but also the inferential relations (e.g. causal, analogical) that bind them (argument schemes). Knowledge about linguistic items that indicate the presence and the type of such argumentative relations is crucial: they constitute features to train reliable machine learning algorithms and they are useful clues for the expert analyst to build guidelines for manual annotations. However, a comprehensive context-independent lexicon of indicators of argumentative discourse relations is lacking. This is due to the scarcity of corpora annotated at the levels of both argument structure and argument schemes: the indicative role played by linguistic items has to be uncovered by looking at their recurrent correlations with argumentative features. Moreover, it is necessary to carry out a deep semantic and pragmatic analysis in order to account for their polysemy and assess their predictive potential outside a specific context. 
On these grounds, the main goal of this project is to investigate how do we speak about the way we reason. More specifically, I aim to contribute to Argumentation Mining by i) proposing feasible guidelines for the annotation of argument structure and schemes, ii) providing a comprehensive empirically validated and theoretically justified English lexicon of indicators of argumentative relations and iii) offering an argumentatively annotated mixed-genre corpus about highly debated energy issues and an analysis of their argumentative patterns. To achieve these goals, I will combine computational methodologies and linguistic analyses. First, guidelines for the annotation of argumentative components, structures and schemes will be proposed and tested in annotations of a sample of 20 discussion threads (ca. 1600 comments) taken from Changemyview, an inherently argumentative subReddit where users discuss issues of common interests and award a “Delta point” to the users that have persuaded them. Taking as a benchmark the AIFdatabase, which collects the main corpora annotated as arguments, the created corpus of discussion threads (ca. 4800 argumentative relations) would be the first non-monologic corpus annotated at the level of both argument structure and argument schemes. Second, patterns of lexical items recurrently associated with argument structures and schemes will be automatically retrieved. Their hypothesized indicative role will be investigated through a corpus-based analysis of their semantic and pragmatic properties (e.g., semantic type of proposition in scope) as well as ad hoc compatibility tests. The qualitatively-validated list will be enriched through bootstrapping techniques in a non annotated corpus. The validity of the lexicon across domains and genres and its relevance for argument mining will be tested carrying out supervised machine learning experiments. Finally, argumentative patterns typical of the energy contexts will be identified and discussed through qualitative analyses. 
The results of the project will have an impact on i) Computational Linguistics by advancing Argumentation Mining, ii) Linguistic Semantics and Pragmatics by uncovering the implicit inferential meaning of indicators of discourse relations and iii) Discourse Studies by providing a validated taxonomy of informal reasoning to be exploited for educational purposes, as well as an analysis of oil drilling and fracking polylogues able to increase public awareness about controversies related to energy extraction. The devised methodologies have the potential to transfer across different domains and applications that tackle globalized communication.
Keywords: Argumentation Mining, Argumentation Theory, Corpus Linguistics, Discourse Studies, Pragmatics, Semantics

Title: Frontiers in NMR crystallography
Abstract:
The spatial arrangement of atoms is directly linked to chemical function. Determination of atomic-level three-dimensional structures, through the introduction of a range of physical methods, and most notably from single crystals by diffraction methods, has transformed molecular and materials science over the past 60 years, leading to today’s structure-based understanding of Chemistry. Despite this revolution, if the system under investigation is not periodic, or is located on a surface or at an interface, as in many functional materials, atomic-level three-dimensional structure determination is elusive. Archetypal examples are devices for solar energy conversion, amorphous drug formulations, nanoparticles, or cements, for which there is today no routine method to characterize their structures with atomic-level precision. Given the rapid current increase in the relevance of such systems, there is today an acute need for methods to determine structures in such cases, and this is now one of the key fundamental challenges in chemistry.

For example, the atomic-level structures at the surfaces and interfaces in hybrid perovskite materials are thought to define the mechanisms that lead to both stabilisation and efficiency of the photo-active phases. Despite a range of probes (XRD, TEM, XPS, EXAFS, etc.) typically being deployed, complete structure determination in such non-crystalline multi-component systems is usually not possible with conventional techniques. 

The overall goal of this project is to address this problem by developing methods to determine the atomic-level structures of complex non-crystalline materials. We propose to do this with novel Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy approaches, enhanced by Dynamic Nuclear Polarization (DNP), in combination with advanced computational methods.

Specifically, we seek to extend the scope of DNP enhanced NMR crystallography methods: (i) by developing multi-dimensional super-resolution 1H NMR experiments for assignment and structure determination in solids, through ultra-fast magic angle spinning and new approaches to error mapping; (ii) by providing new strategies for dynamic nuclear polarization enhanced NMR through innovative approaches to generating hyperpolarization; (iii) by introducing new strategies for structure determination from chemical shifts through machine learning and large scale data mining approaches; and (iv) by applying the methods to systems of high interest, specifically the structure and dynamics in lead-halide perovskites, and amorphous drug formulations.

This will result in robust and broadly applicable methods for atomic-level structure determination in materials where structure and dynamics are currently the most inaccessible. This objective is not possible today, and the impact will be transformative, as it will provide the possibility for rational design of better properties in all of the above areas, where today atomic-level structures can only be inferred or determined partially by other methods.
Keywords: Dynamic Nuclear Polarisation, Molecular Structure, NMR Spectroscopy

Title: Machine learning in design of 2D materials: forward and inverse design of graphene kirigami
Abstract:
Since its discovery in 2004, graphene has attracted tremendous attention due to its unique properties making it a promising material for various applications. Graphene's poor toughness and stretchability, however, has raised great concerns regarding its applications in large-scale devices where crack-like flaws are irresistible. As such, different methods have been proposed to tailor the microstructure of graphene to achieve enhanced mechanical properties. One of the promising methods to toughen and increase the stretchability of 2D materials and in particular graphene is by introducing patterned cuts, the so-called kirigami design. 

Making kirigami-inspired cuts is an emerging technique, which has received considerable attention due to its efficacy in improving the graphene properties, especially stretchability. Introducing controlled distribution  of cuts is an effective method for tailoring mechanical properties of graphene. However, the design space created by cutting patterns is massive and cannot be explored by conventional methods. On one hand, a predictive model describing the mechanical behavior as a function of cutting pattern is lacking and on the other hand molecular dynamic (MD) simulations, despite their promise in studying the mechanical behavior of materials at atomic level, are quite costly. As such, finding the optimum cutting that could lead to the graphene with targeted or optimized properties are not accessible by conventional methods and thus the creation and implementation of new design approaches such as state-of-the art Machine Learning (ML) or Deep Learning (DL) algorithms are required. 

The proposed project thus follows a multi-scale novel design approach based on ML-based algorithms empowered by MD simulations to predict the mechanical properties of kirigami graphene in terms of the kirigami pattern. This will shape the first main goal of this proposal which is the forward design of graphene. Moreover, this research proposal aims to shed light on inverse design of kirigami graphene where the goal is to find the kirigami patterns that yield optimized or targeted mechanical properties, such as stretchability or toughness. We expect that the new design methodologies proposed in this research plan will make the solution to this inherently complex problem tractable.

The main DL algorithms implemented in this proposal are Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and  Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). CNN is a supervised learning method which generally requires a large labeled training dataset. Therefore, a special focus will be devoted to developing ML algorithms which require less labeld data. Strictly speacking, a hybrid ML architecture combining CNN and GAN based on an adaptive learning and optimization strategy is proposed. The hybrid model will be trained only using the \enquote{useful} portion of desgin space and thus greatly reduces the need to perform expensive physics-based simulations. In addition, a conditional GAN combined with a CNN solver is proposed for the forward and inverse design of graphene kirigami (GK) where the ML network learns to propose cutting patterns based on the \enquote{user-defined} material inputs. 

In this research proposal we aim to build upon machine-learning approaches for design of graphene with targeted or optimized mechanical properties by tuning its microstructure directed by kirigami patterns. The machine learning methodologies will enable us to (a) explore the vast design space created by the microstructures and (b) identify the optimized designs with targeted or optimized properties. The developed multi-scale computational framework will pave the way towards a complete understanding of mechanical behavior of graphene in the presence of kirigami patterns and provide a promise towards the design of graphene with desired and/or unprecedented mechanical properties for a wide range of applications.
Keywords: 2D materials, Deep learning, Generative Adversarial Network, Genetic Algorithm, Graphene, Molecular Dynamics

Title: PEDAID3 - Positive Energy District supported by AI and Data-Driven-Decisions
Abstract:
Positive Energy Districts (PEDs) support the vision for future urban energy systems by enhancing energy efficiency and enabling renewable energy generation from individual buildings to entire city districts. By adopting the PED approach, urban areas contribute to regional and national energy systems by smoothing peak production, managing demand, and supporting energy exchange and storage. Still, realising PEDs presents challenges, particularly in providing effective situational awareness and decision support to various stakeholders. This requires the integration of multiple distributed data sources, such as renewable energy installations, and the management of dynamic, multidirectional data streams, including interactions like Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G). PEDAID3, standing for Positive Energy District supported by Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Data-Driven Decisions, addresses these challenges through three key developments: 

> A Stakeholder-Centric Framework for Holistic PED Modelling. 
> Co-Created PED Solutions grounded in this Framework. 
> A Multi-Stakeholder Decision Support Platform integrating the Co-Created PED Solutions. 

The Stakeholder-Centric Framework identifies stakeholders, challenges, and enablers for PED planning, monitoring, operation, optimisation, and defines performance metrics aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals, encompassing energy, environmental, economic, and social impacts. It also incorporates strategies for secure data management that comply with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), ensuring data accessibility and interoperability. 

PEDAID3 adopts a strategic, people-centred approach to PED planning, monitoring, operation, optimisation, prioritising Co-Creation with stakeholders to ensure the Solutions meet community needs, privacy standards, and support collaborative urban management. By engaging public administrations, urban authorities, utilities, and community members, the project fosters public acceptance and acommunity-buildingolvement in PEDs. PEDAID3 also contributes to broader community-building efforts, fostering collaboration and knowledge exchange among cities, stakeholders, and research and innovation actors. 

Developed based on the Stakeholder-Centric Framework for Holistic PED, the PED Solutions include a Data Management System, Urban Energy and Spatial Planning tools, and Data-Driven AI Algorithms, enabling detailed simulations of energy demand, production, flexibility, and sustainability impacts across urban areas. These Solutions also facilitate the assessment of how adjustments to charging infrastructure locations and renewable energy installations impact the overall performance of PEDs. This cross-sectoral approach empowers stakeholders to make informed decisions. 

The PEDAID3 Multi-Stakeholder Decision Support Platform consolidates these PED Solutions into a unified, adaptable Platform with customisable dashboards, tailored to the specific needs of each stakeholder and supporting the planning, monitoring, operatio,n, and optimisation of PEDs. This enables each stakeholder to view metrics relevant to their specific interests, all supported by a seamless and robust data management approach. The Platform seamlessly integrates diverse, distributed, and dynamic data inputs, managing multidirectional data streams that encompass energy, environmental, economic, and social data. 

The PED Solutions and the Platform will be validated at laboratory level, corresponding to Technology Readiness Level 4 (TRL 4), using data from Municipal Parking Company of Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Lugaggia Innovation Community (LIC) by Azienda Elettrica di Massagno, Riga Technical University Campus, Municipality of Cheremule, and Municipality of Rzeszów. The validation will showcase the Platform's capability to support PED planning, monitoring, operation, and optimisation, emphasising its adaptability, scalability and replicability across Europe, in alignment with the PED Transition Pathway.
Keywords: Data Management System, Decarbonization, Holistic Co-Creation Framework, Multi-Stakeholder Platform, Urban Energy Management

Title: Fast and Quiet Raster Data Acquisition Systems
Abstract:
Sparse sampling/Compressive Sensing enable fundamentally faster measurements for a variety of raster data acquisition (RDA) systems such as Scanning Electron Microscopes, Scanning Probe Microscopes, Confocal Microscopes, Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopes, Focused Ion Beam Systems, and related techniques. The up to 200-fold speedup works by using the underlying structure of natural images whose data can be sparsely described in a suitable representation space. Images, for instance, have a mostly sparse representation in the discrete cosine transform, a quality that is heavily used for image compression. This approach would be an alternative to multibeam scanning microscopes which increase imaging speed based on  multiplying the number of beams, making the instrumentation much more complex and expensive.

The crucial flaw of raster data acquisition systems is their linear mapping of pixels; pixel after pixel, a single point of interest is rastered along a grid pattern. This rectangular rastering inside the field of view leads to slow throughput and from an information science perspective to a massive overhead from measuring redundant data. With compressive sensing, the measurement can be reformulated to use a much smaller subset of measurement locations from which the entire field of view can be faithfully reconstructed. 
In addition to the slow throughput, rastering a point of interest along the field of view can also damage the sample and introduce noise. Beam damage in electron or bleaching in light based microscopes can be reduced using compressive sensing by massively reducing the electron and photon doses. For noise in raster acquisition systems, the measurement of random locations converts spurious noise into white, which could otherwise erroneously mimic spatial data. 

The proof of concept to utilize sparse sampling for these raster acquisition techniques has shown great promise. As is usual with big advances: “there is no such thing as a free lunch”. Using compressive sensing has notably created new issues that we will address in this project.

Firstly, the measurement of random locations or along paths that deviate from the usual rectangular patterns leads to new imaging artifacts that are due to inaccuracies in the sensor location or due to the type of path used. Based on the instrumentation, the positioning problems can be due to nonlinear piezoelectric effects, such as hysteresis or creep, or due to mechanical backlash. These effects need to be studied and compensated and we propose active as well as passive means to improve the fidelity of the measurement location in the field of view. 

Instead of transforming coherent noise into white noise by the measuring on random locations, we propose the exact removal of spurious noise from the data using accurate time-tagging of every measurement. From the time-trace of the incoming date, we can remove time-dependent coherent noise via Fourier analysis before using the data to reconstruct the image information. 

In addition to these technical issues, we propose the use of specialized sparsifing bases in the sparse reconstruction. This data-structure guided choice requires knowledge of the underlying physical principles, such as scattering or atomic/molecular structures. We emphasize in this part the use of analytical bases as the sparsifying bases depending on the type of data structure. These efforts will lead to a more accurate reconstruction and will further reduce the required measurement time; further reducing beam damage. 

In the light of machine learning advances, we also propose to use convolutional neuronal networks, specifically to compare their performance with the analytical dimensionality reduction schemes described above. The crucial aspect is here to work with actual experimental training sets because simulated noise has been shown to perform worse in the CNN recovery.

Title: Reference production and the evolution of person agreement: Corpus-based typological and computational approaches
Abstract:
Quantitative methods have been gaining ground in comparative linguistics, most notably in dealing with global linguistic diversity and the evolution of language families as well as variation in language use, language change and linguistic diversification. 
Here we deploy quantitative corpus-linguistic methods to investigate the choice between referential null forms and overt person forms, and its interaction with the evolution of person agreement across diverse languages. This investigation targets a vexed puzzle in comparative linguistics, namely how the cross-linguistically ubiquitous possibility of null reference (“pro-drop”) can be reconciled with the likewise ubiquitous tendency towards the evolution of person agreement, which presupposes an increased use of overt person forms? Likewise unresolved to date is the discrepancy between the postulated cross-linguistic uniformity of mechanisms of referential choice and variable cross-linguistic preferences therein. Our project will be the first of its kind to tackle these quandaries through extensive cross-linguistic corpus analyses that implement cutting-edge quantitative methodologies from corpus linguistics, natural language processing as well as phylogenetic comparative methods. In doing so we will be able to determine the relative importance of discourse-functional and structural factors on referential choice and the evolution of person agreement, as well as the role of phylogenetic, areal and socio-cultural features of diverse languages in explaining cross-linguistic diversity. This project will thus fill a glaring gap in usage-based approaches to the typology of reference production and grammatical relations, and grammatical systems more generally, which have only rarely been addressed in first-hand empirical studies of actual language use. It will also contribute to explaining the development of grammatical complexity, and more generally to the areas of language processing and cognitive sciences, as well as human communication and interaction, and their socio-cultural underpinnings. 
The project will draw on corpora of unprecedented detail of annotation and cross-linguistic breadth that have been designed precisely for research of the type pursued here, enabling the extraction of relevant information with a minimum of theoretical preconceptions, thus enabling evaluation of all relevant functional and structural factors. We focus on two language subfamilies and linguistic areas: for Oceanic languages, we will deploy phylogenetic comparative methods to assess the influence of areal and socio-cultural vis-à-vis phylogenetic factors in referential choice and the evolution of person agreement throughout the family. For Iranian languages, we will draw on historical corpora to reconstruct referential choice and the evolution of person agreement, supplementing earlier philological work. 
Envisaged outcomes are a series of academic articles in which we report unprecedented insights into the conditions of null reference and person forms within and across languages, and in relation to models of emerging person agreement. The annotated corpus will be made available to the scientific community and will constitute a central resource for future cross-linguistic research on reference production and grammatical relations, and other areas of human language grammar and communication.
Keywords: corpus-based typology, evolution of grammatical structures, grammatical relations, person agreement, phylogenetic comparative methods, quantitative corpus linguistics, reference production

Title: The molecular basis of egg cell specification and zygote activation
Abstract:
Plants are the heart of agricultural production as they provide us with food, feed, fibers, and fuel. In order to breed crops for a sustainable agriculture in light of climate change, we have to gain a better understanding of the processes underlying plant reproduction. Apomixis, a form of asexual reproduction through seeds, occurs naturally in around 500 plant species. Their seeds are genetically identical to their mother plant. The harnessing of apomixis in crops has the potential to revolutionize agriculture. For instance, apomixis would allow the fixation of any heterozygous genotype, including that of highly productive and vigorous F1-hybrids. These are favored in agriculture but have to be laboriously produced every year anew and are available for a limited number of crops only. Through apomixis, hybrid genotypes could be maintained over several generations, making hybrids more broadly available. While synthetic apomixis has successfully been established in monocots, it has not yet been achieved in dicots, mainly because the molecular mechanisms underlying the initial steps of seed formation, fertilization and the initiation of embryo development, are poorly understood.

Plant eggs are highly specialized cells that acquire a quiescent state to await the arrival of the sperm cell, despite containing most molecules to initiate embryogenesis. Upon fertilization, the zygote loses quiescence and is activated to enable embryonic development. The molecular basis of this fundamental process in the plant life cycle remains unknown, due to egg cells being an extremely rare cell type that is deeply embedded in maternal tissues, hampering experimental amenability. This project will provide insights into the molecular regulation of very early reproductive events. Building on our recent results and the development of novel approaches, we will address the following questions:

(1)How are egg cell specification and the establishment of quiescence regulated? 
(2)What molecular changes occur upon fertilization that activate the egg cel for embryo formation?
(3)Can the egg cell be induced to form viable embryos in the absence of fertilization? 

To address this, we will use a combination of genetic, molecular, and bioinformatic approaches that we developed and/or adapted to allow the analysis and manipulation of egg cells and zygotes in the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana. We will use egg cell-expressed nanobodies to deplete candidate transcription factors that regulate the specification and function of the egg cell. Furthermore, based on transcriptomic data generated from reproductive cell types collected by laser-assisted microdissection, we will mutate candidate cell genes by using CRISPR/Cas9 to study their role in the transition from quiescence to activation. Transcriptional profiling will help us to assess early transcriptional changes in the egg cell induced by sperm arrival. We will also identify candidate genes involved in parthenogenesis, i.e., the formation of viable embryos in the absence of fertilization, which will be tested in transgenic plants. For this purpose, we will apply advanced bioinformatic tools for transcriptome analyses based on artificial intelligence algorithms, such as deep neural networks. 

Although this project addresses key developmental questions that stand at the beginning of seed formation, our findings will establish a scientific basis to engineer parthenogenesis in dicots, which include some of the most important crops like pulses (lentils, beans, peas) and oil crops (rapeseed, sunflower, safflower). The insights gained into the mechanism of egg cell specification and activation will be published in international, peer-reviewed journals that guarantee open access. All data and materials generated in this project will be deposited in public repositories to make them available for further scientific investigations.

Title: Integrating hierarchical data structures in machine learning methods: Challenges, solutions, and opportunities for psychological research
Abstract:
Answering complex research questions with statistical models can be challenging in everyday research practice. Many datasets in psychology are hierarchically clustered, for instance, when students from multiple classes are assessed, or when multiple measurements per person are collected. This means that predictors can be present at different levels (e.g., describing students at the individual-level and classes at the cluster-level), and that autocorrelations in longitudinal data need to be controlled for. Furthermore, it would be desirable to use more flexible methods, such as decision trees or random forests from machine learning, to describe complex, non-linear psychological dynamics. However, current decision tree and random forest algorithms do not adequately account for the hierarchical structure of predictors. As a consequence, researchers risk drawing the false conclusion that predictors are relevant even when they have no true effect.
In this research project, we will develop an integrated framework that will allow researchers to use machine learning methods reliably for hierarchically clustered data in order to explore non-linear effects between predictor and outcome variables and complex temporal dynamics.
In Work Package 1, we will demonstrate that current decision tree and random forest algorithms can lead to false conclusions when applied to hierarchically clustered data. When cluster-level predictors are included, researchers face a risk of false-positive research findings. Using simulation studies, we will demonstrate in which conditions false-positive effects can occur. Building on a new extension of the score-based statistic, which is the basis for modern, unbiased decision trees and random forests, we will propose a solution that allows researchers to reliably use cluster-level predictors in decision trees and random forests. We will extensively test the proposed solution through further simulation studies and illustrate application scenarios.
In Work Package 2, we will adopt our extension for cluster-level predictors developed in Work Package 1 to a generalization of decision trees: model-based recursive partitioning. First, we will integrate our extension for cluster-level predictors and provide a toolbox for its application in psychological research, including recommendations for sample size planning and assumption testing. We will also outline, discuss, and highlight how our extension of the model-based recursive partitioning method can be used to explore non-linear, temporal dynamics in longitudinal studies in an automated and data-driven way in empirical psychological research.
In Work Package 3, we will further assess and extend the machine learning methods with regard to analyzing a special type of hierarchically clustered data: longitudinal data. In longitudinal data, multiple measurement occasions are clustered within each person. In contrast to "classical" hierarchically clustered data, longitudinal data possess an autocorrelation structure (carry-over effects from one timepoint to the next) that must be taken into account. We will examine the consequences of ignoring the autocorrelation structure in decision tree and random forest algorithms and propose and evaluate potential solutions to account for autocorrelations.
The research project builds upon previous research by myself, researchers at the University of Zurich, and three national and international project partners in the fields of machine learning, multilevel modeling, and applications in psychology. The proposed extension of machine learning methods to hierarchically clustered data is crucial for psychological research, as it opens up the possibility to explore complex psychological processes, such as temporal dynamics, without the risk of encountering false-positive research findings. All developed method extensions will be implemented in the free open-source software R, ensuring accessibility to empirical researchers worldwide.
Keywords: data exploration, decision tree, hierarchical data, hierarchically clustered data, longitudinal data, longitudinal modeling, machine learning, model-based recursive partitioning, multilevel modeling, random forest, simulation study

Title: Mathematical Models for Analog Data Sciences: the Continuous Way
Abstract: This proposal focuses on the development of mathematical methods that are inspired by the remarkable progresses in data sciences but fundamentally adapted to the analysis of continuous- domain signals. Towards this objective, we propose to investigate two research directions. In the first and main one, we consider continuous-domain generalizations of the traditional sparsity- and structure-promoting optimization procedures. In this setting, an unknown analog signal is to be reconstructed from some measures y that only give a partial access to the relevant information. This includes beautiful mathematical challenges: the theory has to be adapted to the infinite-dimensional functional-analytic setting, and adapted practical implementations must be proposed. The expected outcomes are a theoretically sound and innovative statistical analysis of the performance of the proposed reconstruction scheme and algorithmic applications of these schemes in various settings on real data (astronomy, climatic data, echo-acoustic), for various geometries (Euclidian, periodic, or spherical), in collaborations with signal processing scientists and statisticians. The second research direction focuses on machine learning tasks for the analysis of analog signals. We propose to contribute to the construction and application of deep learning architectures that are tailored to continuous-domain 3D image analysis. A specific attention will be given to geometrical invariances, in particular the rotation invariance, that can be captured efficiently with continuous modeling. Expected outcomes include a theoretical characterization of relevant architectures and the exploration of innovative invariant methods for specific applications such as bio image analysis.
Keywords: Continuous-domain optimization, Equivariant neural networks, Sparse statistical learning, Sparsity-promoting regularization

Title: EMPHASES: Assessing EMergent PHenomenA in complex Social-Ecological Systems with time series of settlement and habitat networks
Abstract: Nature and biodiversity are not only essential for the existence of human societies, but are also threatened by the expansion of cities and transport infrastructure. As much as human societies depend on networks of settlements that are well connected by roads and rail (i.e. settlement networks), animal species also depend on networks of well-connected habitats (i.e. habitat networks). Interactions within these networks (e.g. land-use transport interactions and metapopulation dynamics) as well as between the networks (e.g. those found in urban and road ecology) give rise to complex system dynamics. Therefore, coupled settlement and habitat networks are considered a complex social-ecological system (SES). To understand how settlement and transport infrastructure growth affects biodiversity, we need to unravel the combined effects of the network-internal and -external interactions on their long-term evolution: an analysis that has never been performed with empirical data. Complex systems theory provides useful concepts for such a challenging analysis. In complex systems, emergent phenomena arise from the interactions between the subcomponents of the system and are subject to laws that cannot be derived from those governing the subcomponents. Networks have frequently been used to study emergent phenomena. In this project, we will study the dynamics of settlement and habitat networks for more than a century and assess how these dynamics give rise to emergent social and ecological phenomena. Our study area is the densely populated Swiss Plateau. In work package 1, we will classify and vectorise a time series of historic topographic maps since 1870. We will classify a range of natural and manmade feature classes with state-of-the-art deep learning image classification techniques. With GIS modelling methods, the quality of these classifications will be enhanced and corrections that are necessary for the vectorisation will be made. In work package 2, we will construct time series of settlement and habitat networks from the classified historic maps and further historic databases and documentation. As attributes of the networks, we will include the main interacting variables within and between the networks. The evolution of the networks will be described with a range of network metrics. In work package 3, we will detect emergent social and ecological phenomena that are relevant for the sustainable development of urban regions (e.g. those relating to species richness and socioeconomic indicators), describe them with mathematical functions (where possible) and assess their temporal stability. Furthermore, we aim to explain the phenomena with the dynamics in the interactions within and between the settlement and habitat networks. We will also assess possible feedbacks of these emergent phenomena to the networks. This project will not only increase our understanding of the long-term dynamics of settlement and habitat networks, but also provide information to design sustainable planning solutions for countries where the period of rapid population and urban growth is yet to start. Furthermore, we will make the map products available to the scientific community.

Title: Bayesian symbolic learning to aid in the design of sustainable chemical clusters (LEARN-D)
Abstract:
Background: Meeting the climate targets and the Sustainable Development Goals calls for a profound transformation of industry, including the chemical sector, which will have to shift to renewable carbon to curb its emissions. This transition will require deploying integrated facilities combining fossil and renewable technologies with carbon capture processes. The design of such integrated systems poses significant challenges that remain open. Notably, conventional process design tools –initially developed for fossil processes– focus on single isolated facilities (rather than integrated clusters) and apply fairly simple models and environmental metrics. Therefore, novel computational tools are still required to design the integrated chemical facilities of the future and provide valuable insights into how to best transition to more sustainable chemicals and fuels. 

Project goals and methods: This project will provide computational tools for designing integrated chemical clusters for low-carbon chemicals and fuels production by combining machine learning algorithms, process simulation and the latest impact assessment methods. We will formulate hybrid mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLPs) models integrating first principles and analytical equations derived via Bayesian symbolic learning, where the planetary boundaries (PBs) concept will be employed to identify designs operating within the Earth’s ecological limits. We will test and refine our approach in the optimization of highly relevant low-carbon chemicals and fuels, providing general design guidelines and valuable recommendations for practitioners and policy-makers. 

Relevance: This project will develop computational tools to design the chemical facilities of the future, leading to significant reductions in carbon emissions, water and energy consumption. It will also provide clear quantitative evidence on how to best transition to sustainable chemicals and fuels, including which technologies to prioritize, how to optimally deploy them (and where) and how to minimize their potential collateral damage. From a modeling viewpoint, this research could lead to a new class of computational tools for designing complex sustainable engineering systems. Our algorithms will automatically build simplified analytical models from data using MINLP methods and a corpus of well-established equations. Furthermore, our model-building tools combining machine learning and mathematical programming could facilitate the discovery of governing equations in science and engineering. Similarly, the application of the PBs concept will find applications in the absolute environmental assessment of other engineering systems.
Keywords: Bayesian symbolic learning, life cycle assessment, low-carbon chemicals and fuels, planetary boundaries, process optimization, sustainability

Title: Measurement reliability of individual differences in sentence processing (MeRID): A cross-linguistic perspective
Abstract:
Theories of human sentence processing generally assume that the cognitive mechanisms involved in language processing are qualitatively identical not only across speakers of a language but even cross-linguistically. However, within the history of cognitive science, this assumption of an idealized human cognition has not remained uncontested and several researchers have pointed out that individual differences should play a more prominent role in theories explaining human cognition (e.g., Estes 1956; Levinson, 2012). Indeed, over the past decade, evidence has accumulated indicating that individual differences in a comprehender’s cognitive capacities play an important role in sentence processing (e.g., Vuong & Martin, 2014; Nicenboim et al., 2015; Farmer et al., 2017). Although these studies demonstrate the impact of individual differences on sentence processing, it is still not well understood how different components of domain-general cognitive capacities interact and how this affects language processing (Kidd et al., 2018), and whether individual differences in psycholinguistic effects reflect quantitative or qualitative differences in the way individuals process language. In other words, it is not yet understood whether we have to assume qualitatively different mechanisms (or strategies) as a function of a comprehenders cognitive capacities or whether individual differences in psycholinguistic effects can be explained in terms of quantitative differences in certain processes, e.g., the same retrieval mechanism for all humans, but differences in retrieval latencies as a function of working memory capacity. 
From a methodological point of view, the first step for a principled investigation of individual differences in sentence processing is to establish the test-retest measurement reliability of the impact of individual differences in cognitive capacity on theoretically relevant psycholinguistic effects (Parsons et al., 2019).  We can’t take this measurement reliability as a given because of the so-called reliability paradox (Hedge, 2017). It states that test-retest measurement reliability at the individual level is necessarily lower for manipulations with high between-subjects reliability (i.e., replicability at the group level). However, it is likely that precisely effects with high replicability at the group level constitute the set of well-established psycholinguistic phenomena which build the foundation of sentence processing theories. 
In this project we will investigate the test-retest measurement reliability of individual differences in cognitive capacities on phenomena of sentence processing that are well-established at the group level and of high theoretical relevance, namely effects of predictability and dependency locality. To this end, we will collect a large-scale behavioral reading data set with comprehensive psychometric assessments of all participants, including the measurement of working memory capacity, cognitive control, IQ and reading fluency. In order to achieve ecological validity, we will not only compare reading data obtained in a naturalistic reading paradigm (reading corpus) with data recorded in a classical planned experiment with manually constructed minimal pairs, but also take a cross-linguistic perspective by comparing one relatively well-studied Germanic language (German) with another Germanic, but to date understudied language (Danish) and two understudied Slavic languages (Croatian and Czech). Generalizability of our findings will be further increased by a cross-methodological approach in which we directly compare self-paced reading and eye-tracking data in a within-subject subject manner. Subsequently, we will investigate to what extent different classes of established psycholinguistic theories can account for the observed data and whether the empirical data points towards a quantitative or a qualitative role of individual differences in sentence processing. To this end, we will analyze the scanpaths of the readers in a data-driven manner using traditional and deep learning-based sequence clustering techniques to possibly detect clusters of reading strategies which we will then correlate with the different psychometric measures. Finally, we will extend established computational models of sentence processing to compare how well the models perform when accounting for individual differences in sentence processing in terms of quantitative differences in certain scalable parameters in comparison to models that assume different cognitive mechanisms for different (groups of) participants. Our results will shed light on the question whether a theory assuming the same cognitive mechanisms subserving language comprehension in all humans is empirically plausible, or whether we should rather develop psycholinguistic theories that account for qualitatively different processing strategies.
Keywords: Croatian, Czech, Danish, German, computational cognitive modeling, eye-tracking, individual differences, psycholinguistics, sentence processing, slavic languages

Title: N2O-SSA: Combining measurements, modelling and machine learning to improve N2O accounting for sustainable agricultural development in sub-Saharan Africa
Abstract:
N2O is a strong greenhouse gas emitted during microbial N cycling in soils, particularly N-fertilised agricultural soils. Fertiliser use in sub-Saharan Africa is currently relatively low, and increased fertilisation to drive higher agricultural productivity is predicted in coming decades. There is great potential for climate smart agricultural techniques in this region to ensure food security while minimising environmental impacts and greenhouse gas emissions. However, financial investment in sustainable agriculture in sub-Saharan Africa is very low, in part due to the scarcity of data, in particular regarding N2O fluxes and emission factors. This study aims to develop and implement a novel measurement technique to monitor N2O fluxes and isotopic composition, and thus infer N2O production and consumption pathways for the first time in sub-Saharan Africa. We will investigate various computational approaches to simulate N2O fluxes across sub-Saharan Africa and understand drivers and causes of uncertainty, with a particular focus on causal inference. We will develop an optimised modelling framework to allow robust predictions of future N2O emissions in a changing climate, to contribute to closing the data gap and fostering sustainable agricultural development in this region.

This project will be divided into four work packages, led by a PhD student and a postdoctoral researcher employed by this project. The primary goal of WP1 will be the development and rigorous testing of a coupled chamber-preconcentration-isotopic measurement system in the laboratory and field in Switzerland, including automated data analysis software to facilitate rapid quality checking and troubleshooting. The aim of WP2 will be to deploy the system at an experimental field site in Kenya to monitor N2O flux and isotopic composition through a dry-wet seasonal transition for two crop types and two fertilisation levels, in close collaboration with project partners at the University of Eldoret. The site is representative of agricultural practices in the region, and offers the strong infrastructure and knowledge basis needed for successful measurements. WP3 will focus on the application of machine learning to improve current N2O flux models, in particular to characterise uncertainty and improve computational efficiency to allow robust predictions in a range of conditions. The main aim of WP4 will to explore the application of causal invariance algorithms to understand drivers of variability in N2O production pathways, and thus develop a customized flux generative model for robust predictions of N2O.

This interdisciplinary project is a unique combination of biogeoscience and machine learning methodologies with clear relevance for both research fields and beyond. The scientific relevance for biogeosciences centres around the new knowledge of N2O causal drivers in the understudied tropics, which represent a region of high uncertainty in current predictions. The project is also highly relevant for machine learning research, focussing on the interface between observational data and machine learning methods, and the application of novel techniques for spatiotemporal data. The wider impact of this project will result from model development, which will provide new, robust data for N2O fluxes and emission factors in sub-Saharan Africa, and efficient modelling tools that can be used to investigate the impacts of climate change as well as management and mitigation policies on emissions. Furthermore, the project will strongly contribute to education and capacity building, strengthening ties between research communities in Europe and sub-Saharan Africa.
Keywords: Biogeochemic modelling, Isotope spectroscopy, Machine learning, Nitrous oxide, Sustainable agriculture

Title: Estimating and reducing prospective errors: a mathematical foundation of cortical computation
Abstract:
The proposal tries to lay a theoretical ground for neuroscience, following the example of theoretical physics. In physics, the basic laws of motions and interactions can be derived from the unifying principle of least action. The theory starts with a “single formula”, from which, for instance, Newton’s law of motion can be derived. Given initial positions of particles in a force field and some target positions, the principle characterizes the path of the particles from the initial to the target positions. Inspired by this example, we propose here to develop the Neuronal Least Action (NLA) principle for neurobiology, from which not only the neuronal and synaptic dynamics can be derived, but which also entails that the voltage trajectory (activity pattern) across a neural network produces a desired behavioural outcome. 

The key notion of the theory is the one of a prospective error. Errors appear in behaviour and ultimately can be expressed as errors in the motor output. But those motor errors are caused by errors in the brain, and each single neuron aims to minimize its contribution to the error, effectively by minimizing its own ‘dendritic prediction error’. Because the environment changes in time, the cortical activity must be corrected prospectively, and this is done through apical dendrites that learn their individual prospective errors. The prospective dendritic errors correct the somatic activity right in time, so that – upon a sensory input stream – the motor output is pushed in real time towards a targeted behaviour.    

The NLA principle states that the voltages of the involved neurons move along a (high-dimensional) path that minimizes the total dendritic prediction errors across all neurons. Because the NLA principle connects behavioural errors in the periphery with dendritic errors in the brain, it gives recipes of how the involved elements can achieve this task. For instance, it suggests how

(i) behavioural errors can backpropagate into the brain,
(ii) local excitatory and inhibitory neurons can support the error representations, 
(iii) dendrites can extract prospective errors,
(iv) synaptic plasticity across the circuitry can learn to estimate errors and improve neuronal activity.

The project aims to work out the details of these recipes, so that they eventually become useful to create (a) experimental predictions and (b) biologically inspired machine learning algorithms. Yet, to achieve this goal, a strict mathematical theory is necessary at the first place, and this will be the focus of the project. The collaborators with their clinical (T. Proix), experimental (F. Helmchen) and neuromorphic background (M. Petrovici) will help shaping the development of the theory towards the envisaged applications.

So far, only the general idea of the NLA principle has been presented (Senn et al., eLife 2024), with previous links to backpropagation in the brain (Sacramento et al., NeurIPS 2018), microcircuit learning (Haider et al., NeurIPS 2021), and dendritic prediction errors (Urbanczik & Senn, Neuron 2014), to cite some key steps. Here, we will extend and develop the NLA principle in 3 directions: 

1.temporal NLA that includes memory processing on different time scales (dendritic filtering and threshold adaptation), 
2.attention-based NLA that takes up transformer-like self-attention calculated in cortical layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons, and gain modulating cortical layer 5 pyramidal neurons,
3.spike-based NLA, with an exact gradient learning rule for spiking networks.

The project is expected to impact its neighbouring fields of experimental neuroscience, machine learning, and neuromorphic engineering. It will suggest how cortical microcircuits and dendrites could implement the ideas formulated above, (i)-(iv); how transformers, as currently most powerful AI algorithm, can be implemented in real-time within a neuronal circuitry; and how spike-based neuromorphic chips may be designed to perform these operations.

Title: Uncovering peptide-mediated chemokine receptor signal transduction mechanisms through deep-learning
Abstract:
G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) constitute the largest family of signaling receptors. They receive stimuli from the outside in the form of light, odorants, neurotransmitters or hormones and translate these signals into important specific intracellular functions. A wide range of diseases are associated with various forms of GPCR dysfunctions. While major structural insights have been gained into the activation of receptors sensing small molecule ligands, our understanding of peptide-mediated GPCR signal transductions remains largely phenomenological. Understanding how protein structural perturbations upon ligand binding are transmitted over long-distances within allosteric proteins to elicit specific functional responses is critical for drug discovery and therapeutic protein design but remains very challenging. In this proposal, we will develop and apply integrated deep learning, molecular dynamic (MD) simulations, protein modeling, engineering and experimental approaches to delineate, validate and reprogram how GPCR structure and dynamics change upon peptide ligand binding and sequence variations, and how these perturbations are allosterically propagated into selective cellular responses. We will focus on chemokine peptide-activated receptors as they orchestrate critical immune responses and represent attractive pharmacological targets. The research will be carried out through the following aims.
(1) To develop and validate computational deep learning approaches for inferring ligand-specific GPCR signaling responses. We will further develop a Deep Learning (DL) method trained on MD simulations for inferring and interpreting allosteric interactions and pathways that mediate ligand-specific signal transductions at an unprecedented level of resolution and accuracy. We will validate the approach against large functional, structural and dynamics datasets available on model GPCR systems. GPCR variants with new activities will be designed based on the allosteric predictions and validated through structural dynamics measured by NMR spectroscopy.
(2) To decipher the peptide activation mechanisms in CC chemokine receptors. We will apply the DL approach to investigate the sequence, structure, dynamic and signaling relationships in the CC chemokine receptor-ligand system. We will exploit large-scale mutational datasets on the receptors and peptides to map binding and activation determinants. We will also test the predictions through cycles of design and experimental validation of new CC receptor variants.
(3) To uncover the peptide activation mechanisms in CXC chemokine receptors. We will apply our computational approaches to delineate the mechanistic underpinnings of peptide ligand activation in the CXC chemokine receptor family using deep scanning mutational libraries and various receptor-peptide complexes. These findings will be validated through new designed CXC receptor variants. Lastly, we will carry out a global comparative analysis of allosteric signaling determinants in chemokine receptors, to reveal novel principles of peptide-mediated activation and evolutionary relationships in this family.
This study will uncover family-wide allosteric underpinnings of peptide-mediated chemokine receptor activation and provide a unique deep learning tool for inferring ligand-mediated protein signaling. The project will impact the design of personalized and selective drugs and the development of GPCR-based biosensors for basic and therapeutic applications.
Keywords: G-protein-coupled receptor, cell signaling, computational protein modeling and design

Title: Synchronised brain – coordinated mind: The role of prefrontal slow oscillations in interregional neural communication and cognitive coordination
Abstract:
Even seemingly simple cognitive tasks frequently require efficient coordination of a range of different task sub-components, such as perception, attention, transient storage of information, voluntary suppression of distracting information, selection of adequate actions, etc. It is well-known that a distributed network in the neocortex of the human brain, the so-called multiple demand network is involved in this cognitive coordination process. However, it is not clear, yet, how this network coordinates cognition. Based on previous studies we suggest that slow rhythmical brain activity in the medial parts of the prefrontal cortex (frontal midline theta activity) play an essential role in dynamic coupling and de-coupling of distributed cortical networks, depending on the specific demands of a task. We here propose a research programme comprising three work packages that should identify fronto-medial slow oscillations as a unified mechanism of cognitive coordination. In the first work package we will test young, healthy human participants on working memory tasks that require the flexible storage of either spatial or figural information. Dependent on the exact requirements we hypothesise that frontal midline theta activity will couple task-relevant and de-couple task-irrelevant posterior brain areas. Experiments using passive recording of electrical brain activity will be followed-up by experiments in which transcranial magnetic brain stimulation is used to mimic the previously recorded brain activation patterns. We will try to interfere with either spatial or figural working memory performance by stimulating posterior brain areas specifically in time intervals that are associated with either a medial prefrontal cortex coupled or de-coupled state. In a second work package we will extend these findings to visual attention tasks. We will use a similar approach as in work package one to investigate whether frontal midline theta activity is instrumental in orchestrating (re)orientation of spatial attention. This would suggest that the hypothesised brain coordination mechanism is not specific to working memory processes but more general. To further test this idea of a unified control mechanism, in a third work package the proposed approach is applied to behavioural inhibition, i.e. execution versus inhibition of actions. Largely independent of working memory and visual processing constraints, a vital role of frontal midline theta in coordinating sensorimotor networks during behavioural inhibition would clearly speak for a unified mechanism of cognitive coordination identified by this proposed research project.
Relevance and future applications of these findings would certainly be important for neuropsychiatric and neurological research as there is a large variety of clinical conditions with difficulties in cognitive control, such as schizophrenia, autistic spectrum disorder, obsessive compulsive disorder, Tourette syndrome, etc. A better understanding of how cognitive control is established in the human brain should also lead to potential therapeutic applications in conditions with compromised cognitive control. Moreover, these findings might be important to implement in artificial intelligence so that parallel processing can be coordinated more efficiently.

Title: Longitudinal Brain Tumor Segmentation with Uncertainty Estimation using Fully-connected Conditional Random Field and Perturb-and-Maximum-Posterior-Marginal Estimation
Abstract:
Background:
Automated brain tumor segmentation from multimodal MR images has the potential to leverage diagnosis, treatment, patient follow-up, radiomics studies, etc. However, despite progress in brain tumor image segmentation current algorithms still lack spatial consistency and do not provide a measure of certainty of their results, which is critical for adequate exploitation of results in subsequent steps.
Methods:
In the proposed project we aim at developing an automated multimodal MR brain tumor segmentation. Based on preliminary results, we will extend our previously proposed supervised-based segmentation approach with a fully-connected Conditional Random Field (CRF) regularization module, featuring improved segmentation accuracy and spatial consistency of tumor compartments. To produce measures of uncertainty of the segmentation results, we will further develop a perturb-and-maximum-posterior-marginal estimation technique. Both improvements feature low computational costs, in agreement with the requirements of the clinical workflow. The approach is to be evaluated on both local glioma datasets and publicly available databases used for benchmarking of brain tumor segmentation algorithms. The evaluation will lead us to test the following hypotheses: 
Hypotheses:
H0) Employing a Fully Connected Conditional Random Field (CRF) approach for brain lesion segmentation yields improved segmentation results, in terms of accuracy and spatial consistency, as compared to a standard pair-wise CRF.
H1) Segmentation uncertainty can be obtained through a perturbation & MPM approach under a fully-connected CRF setup.
 
Expected added value of the proposed study:
The project will provide improved accuracy and spatial consistency for automated quantification and delineation of brain tumor compartments. The ability of the proposed approach to yield uncertainty measures of the segmentation opens up opportunities to create time-effective human-machine interfaces necessary to monitor and correct results of the automated approach. This can have a substantial impact in clinical scenarios such as radio-therapy and neuro-surgery, where a precise delineation of the tumor is needed in order to precisely target the tumor while preserving as much healthy tissues as possible. In turn, uncertainty estimates of the segmentation can be used as data-quality measures for high-throughput radiomics studies relying on these segmentation results to extract imaging biomarkers of diagnosis, assessment of prognosis, and prediction of therapy response.
Keywords: Brain cancer, Glioma, Longitudinal brain image analysis, MRI, Medical image analysis

Title: Optical measurements and weak decays searches with liquid xenon detectors
Abstract:
Currently the main open questions in astroparticle physics are related to the nature of dark matter and neutrinos. To shed light into these, xenon based experiments have been extensively used. The best limits on direct detection of weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) dark matter candidate and neutrinoless double beta (0vßß) decay are coming from experiments using xenon.
The project addresses two important aspects. The first goal is to improve the understanding of the microphysics in liquid xenon (LXe). Many experiments rely on measuring the light produced by the particle interactions scattering off xenon atoms. With detectors requiring larger and larger volumes, up to more than 2 m in one dimension, understanding the light propagation and attenuation in LXe is a bottleneck in providing accurate results, both on the physics of xenon and the detector itself and on the physics results coming from these experiments. Measurements on the light attenuation in LXe are outdated and report different results. Furthermore these measurements were carried out in small setups.
Recent results on this topic are coming from experiments using liquid argon as target medium. For this purpose I propose to carry out a new measurement of the light attenuation in LXe with a large setup. The University of Zurich is a unique place for this scope, not only in Switzerland but in the World, as it is the only place where a cryostat with an inner vessel of 312 cm in height and 24.8 cm in diameter, and related infrastructures, as cryogenics and xenon storage, working with LXe, have been already commissioned. The cryostat is now equipped with a purity monitor and soon will be upgraded with a time projection chamber (TPC). The TPC will be equipped with an array of photomultipliers and silicon-photomultipliers at the top and bottom, respectively. The goal of this project is to equip the TPC with a system to shine vacuum ultraviolet light with a wavelength of ~175 nm, corresponding to the scintillation in LXe, and to measure optical properties as the light attenuation in LXe and extract related quantities of interests, such as the Rayleigh scattering, group velocity, Sellmeier coefficients.
The second goal of this proposal is to expand the physic reach of the LXe TPC detectors, in particular with the XENONnT experiment, a multi-tonnes scale dual-phase TPC, currently taking data with the main goal of WIMP dark matter search. Its precursor, XENON1T, has already demonstrated the capability for such type of detectors to look well beyond the WIMP energy range and to be able to give substantial contributions to the neutrino field with the first measurement of the two-neutrino double electron capture of 124Xe and a stringent limit on 0vßß of 136Xe. However the latter is still not competitive with dedicated experiments due to the high background rate at the energy of the decay, around 2.5 MeV. Here I propose to extend this work to new physics channels, such as the zero-neutrino double electron capture (0vECEC) of 124Xe, the first of this kind in xenon dual phase TPCs. Due to the complex signature of the resonant 0vECEC, comprising X-rays, Auger electrons and gamma cascades, machine learning algorithms will be necessary to tag signals coming from this decay. Furthermore, background rejection in the region of interest of these processes can also be improved by exploiting these tools, such as the available python packages of sklearn and keras.
Keywords: dark matter, double weak decays, neutrino, optical properties, time projection chambers, xenon

Title: Fast Separation of Auditory Sounds
Abstract:
Interpreting acoustic scenes is an important engineering task, reaching high levels of sophistication in speech recognition applications such as recognizing what has been said, who said it or which language they spoke in. Current systems that solve these tasks typically require speech to be acquired by a close-mounted microphone from well-controlled acoustic environments and fail in realistically-changing environments with added noise, natural room reverberations, and competing talkers. By contrast, none of these realistic situations present significant difficulty to human speech communication. The representations chosen by biological systems appear to be tuned to the statistics of natural sounds, both reflecting the overall distribution of these sounds and adapting to their local statistics on a range of timescales.  By contrast, the first stages of present engineering systems tend to be off-the-shelf signal processing algorithms, with no sensitivity to global or local sound statistics.

Our goal is to build a new front-end processor for sounds that extracts in real-time features based on these biological principles in a way that is resistant to the presence of distractors and noise; to integrate this front-end with state-of-the-art speech-processing algorithms; to allow for adaptation of this front-end based on changes in input statistics; and to build a robust, real-time, compact hardware implementation of this sound processing system. We take advantage of recent developments in computational source streaming models, bio-inspired feature extraction methods which depend on the input statistics, advances in neuromorphic sensor technology, and embedded systems for real-time performance. These developments provide a unique opportunity to combine knowledge in these different areas to construct a novel acoustic processing system. We will validate this system on a task relating to aspects of human speech in different environments including other talkers and reverberance.

This project intends to achieve two important objectives: first, it will advance the state of the art of machine speech recognition by using algorithms that determine acoustic features based on the statistics of the environments and the temporal coherence observed in the auditory cortex; and second, it will build a real-time source streaming system composed of a continuous-time sensor front end coupled to standard digital architectures such as microprocessors or FPGA boards, for easy reconfiguration of the system architecture. The operation of the system in real-time allows for exploration of biologically inspired acoustic algorithms that can also be used in embedded applications like hand-held devices and for use in setups for scientific behavioral experiments.
Keywords: biomimetic acoustic system, efficient coding, natural statistics, source streaming, statistical acoustic features

Title: Large scale approximate Bayesian inference of neural dynamics and connectivity from calcium imaging
Abstract:
Calcium imaging is enabling scientists to simultaneously measure the activity of thousands of neighbouring neurons, but at the expense of being an indirect method. The indirectness of the measurement, the slow decay of calcium transients compared to the time course of the underlying neural activity, the limited signal quality, as well as the expected increase in scale of the data provide the formidable challenge for machine learning to infer underlying quantities of interest using scalable methods.
My first aim is to devise fast inference methodology for point process driven diffusion, with practical application to calcium imaging data and the inference of spikes. Secondly, I develop methods to capture nonlinearities in the diffusion process describing the membrane potential, such as refractoriness. Thirdly, I extend the inference methodology to populations of neurons and the synapses connecting them. 
My main hypotheses of this project is that calcium data can be used to infer microcircuits, and that approximate inference based on message passing will deliver a scalable tool for it.
I envisage as major output of the project to provide widely applicable analysis tools to infer the dynamics of neurons, specifically somatic potential and spikes, based solely on calcium imaging, as well as the structure of neural connectivity.
Inference of synaptic strengths and neural dynamics is of utter importance, because interconnected networks of synapses represent memories, and changes in synaptic efficacy, which depend on neural dynamics, are implicated in learning.
Keywords: Bayesian inference, Calcium imaging, Connectomics, Machine learning, Message passing, Point process, Spiking neuron, Stochastic dynamical systems

Title: Test Code Quality: A New Dimension of Test Code Effectiveness
Abstract:
Our society runs on software: Ranging from financial transactions to health treatments, and more, we rely on software systems. Unfortunately, in such a context the emergence of serious faults that sometimes lead to dramatical societal consequences is the rule rather than the exception, as we witness too often in the news. Therefore, the creation of mechanisms to ensure the correct functioning of software and avoid the introduction of faults is of the greatest urgency.
Software testing is a crucial activity that developers perform to produce high-quality and reliable software. However, determining the effectiveness of software tests is an open research and practical challenge. To assess test effectiveness, many organizations rely on metrics like branch or mutation coverage; unfortunately, the academic community pointed out that those metrics are not optimal as they (i) cannot provide a comprehensive view of test effectiveness and (ii) are computationally too expensive to be computed within modern development contexts such as Continuous Integration. 

With the project presented in this proposal, I aim at facing these fundamental challenges, thus bringing testing research to the next level. First, I propose to reformulate the concept of test code effectiveness considering multiple aspects at different levels of granularity and build a comprehensive theory of the factors impacting test code effectiveness, with the goal of automating the identification of test instabilities. Among such factors, I conjecture that test code quality is a fundamental dimension of test code effectiveness, which has been poorly considered in the past: For instance, the research my co-authors and I conducted has provided initial compelling evidence that the design quality of the test cases relates to serious problems, such as test flakiness and limited ability to find faults in production code. Second, I aim at facing major challenges related to developers' awareness and testing adoption. I propose the definition of a new generation of test code checkers that may precisely pinpoint the location of test instabilities, quantify their impact on test code effectiveness adopting machine learning techniques, and enable a continuous runtime feedback on the improvement of the production code due to tests. Finally, the key idea of my research proposal is to ease the adoption of testing practices by (1) defining the concept of machine learning-guided automatic test case generation and repair, where the information related to the most-impacting test instabilities coming from machine learning analyses done by the devised test code checkers are used as input of search-based algorithms that optimize the generation/repair of individual tests based on the identified properties, thus making the generation dynamic in nature and dependent on the need of a test; and (2) exploiting crowdsourcing mechanisms with the aim of integrating human reasoning into test generation, thus complementing the capabilities of automatic test generators.
The expected long-term benefits of this research are a deeper scientific understanding of testing, improved test effectiveness, and better quality software. My strong track record in software testing, test code quality, software analytics, and empirical software engineering, together with the envisioned collaborations within the Department of Informatics and the University of Zurich, form a unique basis that enables me to perform and lead this project. My unique international collaborations with top scientists in the field enable high-quality scientific results and a rapid industry uptake of the results.
Keywords: Empirical Software Engineering, Machine Learning, Software Quality, Software Testing
