Title: The medieval masonry bridge: Towards a construction history of arch bridges built before 1550
Abstract:
This project aims at a multi-perspective in-depth study of European masonry arch bridges built before ca. 1550 A.D., with particular focus on documenting the incremental evolution of the present bridge fabric and interpreting traces of construction site procedures. Although the wide-span masonry bridge is certainly comparable to the cathedral as a feat of medieval building activity, very little is known about the construction technology employed for medieval bridges, because the earliest pictorial records of masonry bridge construction date back only to the 16th century (thus yielding the terminus ante quem of 1550 for the present project). On the other hand, traces of scaffolding and centering, as well as repairs and rebuilding, abound in many bridges, but their interpretation requires precise data: In the absence of reliable and high-precision surveys, hypotheses about the construction procedures and repair history typically remain rather arbitrary. 
Construction of medieval masonry arch bridges resumed in the 11th century, separated from the flourishing ancient Roman bridge building by a gap of several centuries. Nevertheless, many medieval bridges show clear proof of inspiration by ancient precedents, or even make use of actual Roman remains. Therefore, some insight into Roman bridge building is evidently required to understand the resurgence of masonry arch bridge construction in the Middle Ages. Furthermore, bridges were always particularly liable to receive damage, and needed repair. Bridges that have been transformed more than once promise to provide particularly rich traces of construction procedures. Such bridges include Roman bridges repaired in the Middle Ages, as well as bridges built from scratch in the Middle Ages and maintained until the present era. 
The current project will provide an overview of medieval bridges and high-precision documentation for some representative clusters of bridges. The sample of the case studies is based on criteria of span, actual presence of traces of temporary works, richness of building, maintenance and rebuilding history, and coherence of context. Evidently, historic cutting-edge states of technology can best be observed in particularly challenging bridges, so that small bridges (less than 6 m or 20 ft span) are excluded from the project unless they are of clear importance as models for nearby larger bridges. Important traces of construction procedures are typically located at great heights, in the middle of the stream, on the upper side of corbelling stones, or difficult to access due to other reasons; this is why detailed documentation of such features is typically absent even today. In order to overcome these problems, the project will make use of state-of-the-art surveying techniques. Specifically, it will rely heavily on structure-from-motion (SFM) based on terrestrial and ‘drone’ photography (mostly not actual drone photos, but pictures made by cable-mounted camera and other ad-hoc devices), and on complementary laser scanning. Creation of single-stone-precision geometrical surveys will furthermore make use of automated feature extraction from digital images. All three techniques have already been developed and used extensively in other projects of the applicant’s group at ETH Zurich. They will be exploited to create high-resolution 3d models of the bridges.
The outcomes of the project will include reliable and detailed documentation (colour-coded building phase plans) of a relevant set of medieval bridges, improved understanding of historic construction and constructional procedures, detailed insight into the complex building history of selected bridges, and new information on possible and probable knowledge transfer from antiquity to the Middle Ages.
Keywords: Construction history, archaeology of elevation, bridges, middle ages

Title: Information-theoretic forensic physical object identification
Abstract:
This project is a further extension of methods obtained in the Stochastic Information Processing group during the last 3 years.  In our previous research, we addressed a number of theoretical and practical problems of image identification using short robust fingerprinting codes and established important information-theoretic limits on the trade-off between  identification rate, complexity and memory. The main challenge of the preceding studies was to introduce theoretical foundations of reliable content identification and to develop a practical framework for the identification of physical objects based on their unique unclonable features. The developed algorithms have been tested experimentally on a specially created database, FAMOS, that contained multiple acquisitions of unique microstructure images originating from 5'000 packages that were acquired with special cameras in the controlled environment. These results have been published in several journal papers and presented at many reputable international conferences with acceptance rates below 30%. Additionally, we have submitted 2 patents, one of which has already been granted and received the distinction of the Latsis PhD award 2013 of the University of Geneva. This success and our new findings make it possible to extend the achieved results to other challenging applications related to physical object protection which recently emerged in the multimedia security and forensic community and the anti-counterfeiting industry.

However, many previous results, identification algorithms and theoretical limits assumed that the quality of the acquired images is relatively high, which was a valid assumption for a controlled verification environment. In practice, many applications require physical object identification in the public domain, preferably using  mobile phones. This in turn creates additional constraints on the quality of the images, algorithmic complexity, memory, communication traffic and security. Additionally, the recent trends in identification technologies necessitate performing the identification in high-dimensional space, where methods developed for short codes and vector quantization face considerable difficulties. Finally, the anti-counterfeiting industry urgently seeks technologies capable of identifying objects not only based on their individual microstructures, but also according to their fine-grained visual design capable to distinguish even minor differences in appearance and  reliably authenticate the original object from its cloned counterparts. This creates a necessity to properly handle these new emerging security requirements and to reconsider the theoretical results derived for the assumptions for short codes and a high signal-to-noise ratio used in the previous fingerprinting techniques.

It should be noted that the majority of existing identification techniques at most address the recognition of physical objects while fine-grained recognition is still considered major challenge. Furthermore, the distinguishability of fake objects and clones is largely non-addressed. Moreover, there is no public database of original products, their look-alike copies produced by re-design or copies produced by just scanning and printing as in the case of packages. Finally, the identification techniques dealing with such applications are largely unexplored and lack a thorough theoretical analysis. Thus, it is very important to identify, introduce and apply some common principles into the design, analysis and optimization of these identification techniques. In this context, the goal of the present proposal is to extend and further develop a new information-theoretic framework for physical object identification in the high-dimensional space of forensic features and apply it to practical systems. This goal will be achieved based on a novel interpretation of links between the  encoding techniques, machine learning and forensic identification  which will be theoretically introduced and explored in this project.

As detailed in the proposal, the proposed theoretical framework of physical object identification relies on recent concepts and findings in information theory, high-dimensional embedding and sparse approximation, coding theory and machine learning.

In the scope of this proposal, the following subjects will be investigated:
(A) Information-theoretic analysis of physical object identification performance, complexity and memory storage;
(B) Creation and enrollment of  databases of original and fake objects; 
(C) Practical implementation, optimization and validation.
Keywords: anti-counterfeiting, cloneability, content fingerprinting, database of faked objects, information-theoretical analysis, machine learning, physical object protection, random projections

Title: Large Scale Variational Approximations to Bayesian Learning for Sparse Generalized Linear Models
Abstract:
Machine learning (ML) seeks to automatize the processing of
large complex datasets by adaptive computing, realizing the full potential
of which requires decision-making from uncertain knowledge. Today, most
ML work settles for the lesser goal of penalized estimation, which
is supported by robust and scalable algorithms. As estimation eliminates
uncertainty rather than quantifying and managing it properly, many laborious
tasks are left to be done by hand. For all but mildly ill-posed problems, the
user has to specify additional constraints in order to obtain useful
solutions, and truly automated decision-making (e.g., tuning data acquisition
during an experiment) is out of the reach of such technology.

It is well known that most of these limitations can be overcome by Bayesian
reasoning about uncertain knowledge, which unfortunately remains
infeasible at scales demanded by many real-world applications. However, with
substantial recent progress in variational approximations, computational
limits of Bayesian inference are being pushed. Both penalized estimation and
variational inference lead to optimization problems, yet while the
former operates on single points u, the latter manipulates
probability distributions Q(u) over points. These quantify
uncertainty in what u should be, valuable information which is neglected
in estimation. The main goal of this proposal is to substantially advance the
state of the art in approximate Bayesian inference for continuous variable
(sparse) generalized linear models. In marked contrast to both penalized
(sparse) estimation and discrete variable variational inference, nearly all
relaxations known to date are poorly characterized as optimization or saddle
point problems (e.g., convexity, convergence, numerical robustness). Commonly
used solvers are algorithmically naive and do not link up with recent progress
in numerical optimization. They cannot be used to address most large scale
applications, for which penalized estimation remains the sole viable
alternative to date.

Based on our prior work, we propose a novel perspective on continuous variable
variational Bayesian inference, with the realistic prospect of decreasing
runtime by several orders of magnitude, narrowing the gap to penalized
estimation substantially. In order to make real progress, the fine structure
of a variational problem needs to be understood. By using novel decoupling
transformations, elementary subproblems can be reordered according to their
relative computational complexity, which can lead to dramatic speedups without
altering the problem or compromising convergence. While we demonstrated the
feasibility and effectiveness of this program for a local lower bound
relaxation, the present project addresses expectation propagation (EP),
a more flexible and accurate, yet also substantially more challenging
approximation. EP is not an optimization, but a saddle point problem. Commonly
used algorithms lack convergence proofs, and numerical instabilities can be
severe. A novel provably convergent and highly efficient EP solver will be
developed in this project.

With a clean understanding of subproblems, not available in previous work, we
can begin to systematically focus on the hardest ones. For continuous variable
variational inference, computing Gaussian (co)variances is the bottleneck
at large scales, a primitive all but neglected previously. In collaboration
with numerical mathematics experts, recent algorithms will be adapted and tuned
to our framework. By combining numerical methods with graphical model message
passing, we anticipate to substantially advance the state of the art for
model-based Gaussian variances, which is required in order to sensibly
address large scale applications of interest here. The prominent role of
Gaussian variances implies a novel computational perspective on variational
inference. In situations where no algorithm is known to approximate variances
uniformly accurately, only such variational methods are scalable which are
robust to such errors to some degree. Unfortunately, all EP algorithms to date
diverge in such a situation. One of the most ambitious of our goals is to
robustify EP (or a modification thereof) in order to end up with the first
scalable solver for this powerful approximation.

Apart from immediate speedup benefits, a computationally systematic approach to
continuous variable variational Bayesian inference allows fundamental questions
to be approached. Independent of algorithms, can we group model
setups in terms of inherent hardness of approximate inference, and what are
the determining factors? Comparing two approximations, is one inherently
harder to solve than the other, and if so why? While such questions have been
successfully addressed for discrete variable and purely Gaussian inference, they
are essentially open for widely used setups of interest here. This project
will address some of them.

Beyond increased accuracy, novel expectation propagation algorithms developed
in this project will allow us to tackle problems not previously addressed at
scales of interest here. We aim to research how Gaussian (co)variances, by
means of expectation consistency conditions, can help to improve approximations
to discrete variable and hybrid model Bayesian inference. A major motivation
to develop scalable Bayesian technology is the application to parameter
learning and adaptive acquisition optimization for magnetic resonance imaging,
whose feasibility in principle we have established in prior work. We will
also address Bayesian inference for large spiking neuron models, advanced
hierarchical scale-mixture models for natural images, and classification with
many classes.

Anticipated outcomes of this project will have high impact on probabilistic
machine learning, laying the foundations for a novel computational understanding
of variational inference methods and raising the bar for scalable Bayesian
computations. We
propagate a modern approach, beyond simplistic coordinate descent, to solving
variational relaxations, anchoring them in the hierarchy of standard numerical
optimization problems. The decoupling transformations, double loop structure
for the sake of scalability, and the focus on reductions to (sparse)
reconstruction and, in particular, Gaussian variances are new generic
principles for continuous variable inference, by no means restricted to
applications addressed here. Advantages of an approximate Bayesian treatment
are easy to motivate for each of the latter, and their challenging nature
constrains methodology along immediately fruitful directions.
Keywords: Approximate Bayesian Inference, Bayesian Statistics, Medical Image Processing

Title: Principles for collaborative, immersive molecular visualization and modeling through low-cost virtual reality on the web
Abstract:
Research in chemistry and structural biology seeks to understand structure-function relationships in various kinds of molecules by combining experimental atomic structures with various types of coarser experimental information as well as models, chemoinformatic or bioinformatic predictions, large databases, and of course literature. While integration of such wealth of information requires computation-intensive procedures to properly sample molecular conformations and positions, the action of human experts is always key, as it is their experience, knowledge about the underlying chemistry, physics and biology, and hours of visual inspection of the data and 3D structures, what drives research forward and distils the ultimate interpretations. Human experts can identify problems in data, make connections between disparate pieces, recall observations relevant to the study problem, etc., all currently impossible for computers. In turn, computers can identify patterns, compare information, build models and do literature and database queries at a throughput inaccessible to humans. Thus, as in other realms of science and technology, fluent human-computer interfaces that streamline human thinking, experience and intent with the calculation power of computers could enormously assist those areas of science and technology dealing with molecules, by helping human experts to explore, filter and make sense of data, setup complex calculations, analyze the outputs from such calculations, and very importantly, by facilitating thinking and exploration of hypotheses in 3D augmented with all relevant data at hand. Today’s interfaces for molecular visualization and modeling are however very far from this “dream tool”, let alone enabling interactive collaboration between multiple users.
    Here we propose to explore the components required for interactive handling of 3D structures and data in an immersive virtual reality (VR) environment where collaborating researchers can manipulate virtual molecules in a natural way while the computer on-the-fly computes relevant mechanics and experimental observables, and overlays data. We propose to employ a low-cost device called Oculus Quest 2 (400 CHF) which provides exquisite hand pose estimation, produces highly immersive VR experiences, and includes a web browser with full WebXR capabilities -a technology and standard that all vendors of VR sets are including as it breaks the cross-platform barrier and facilitates multi-user VR.
    We will exploit the joint experience of applicants and partners in atomistic small molecule modeling, coarse-grained modeling of biological systems, experimental biophysics, web programming, and webVR to develop this project in 3 aims: Aim 1 is to build on our preliminary work and on proof-of-concept tests on an Oculus Quest 2 device to tune how users interact with virtual atoms or groups of atoms through the hand pose estimation inputs of the device, using visualizations tailored specifically to either small molecules or large molecules like proteins and nucleic acids. We will then adapt (i) the rigid body physics-based force field from our moleculARweb website (for chemistry education using commodity augmented reality) to provide basic molecular mechanics for small and large molecules, (ii) the ANI neural network developed by project partner Roitberg’s group to get accurate energies and forces in real time for small molecules, and (iii) the Martini force field to treat proteins at a coarse-grained level together with project partner Dr. Souza team. In Aim 2 we will develop ways to achieve collaborative work; first simply streaming particle coordinates from a controller device to a secondary web app that other users can view on any regular device or in another Oculus device; then, to allow two users using Oculus devices to act on the same molecular system at the same time. In Aim 3 we will invite members from research groups working on molecular structures to test molecular modeling experiences using our VR prototype and regular mouse-keyboard-screen, both individually and in pairs, to test their abilities to achieve certain tasks on each setup and thus objectively assess the effects of the VR tool.

Title: Electro-Opt: Machine Learning-Assisted Electrolyte Optimization for the Nitrogen Reduction Reaction
Abstract:
The production of ammonia is one of the most important chemical processes that is essential to support the global population. Currently, it is produced via the Haber-Bosch process, which produces 1-2% of global CO2 emissions. On the other hand, the electrochemical N2 reduction reaction (NRR) poses an attractive alternative: it could be powered by renewable energy and particularly amenable to delocalized small scale production. However, virtually all electrochemical interfaces would preferentially activate protons over N2, favoring H2 evolution over NH3 synthesis. This poses a major challenge for the development of NRR catalysts. To date, only Li and Ca electrodes in organic solvents reliably produce ammonia. Nonetheless, they are plagued by low rates and efficiency. For Electro-Opt, we intend to use a data driven experimental approach augmented by machine learning to unravel the factors controlling N2 reduction and design and realize more efficient interfaces.

The guiding principle for Electro-Opt is that the selectivity of the Li-mediated systems originates from the solid electrolyte interface (SEI) that is formed under reductive potential: this SEI inhibits the proton transport to the electrode thereby tuning the selectivity. The structure of the SEI and its properties are demonstrated to depend on the electrolyte composition. Consequently, the choice of the organic solvent, metal salt, proton donor, and additives have a direct influence on the NRR.

The aim of Electro-Opt is to optimize the electrolyte composition by increasing the understanding of the relationship between the electrolyte and the NRR using data-driven modelling. This we will achieve by using the automated set-ups available at Imperial College. These automated set ups will assist us in collecting large amounts of data. Also, they will produce more reliable data by eliminating the human error. Using current vs potential measurements, impedance spectroscopy and the ion chromatogrophy we will obtain data on the stability, activity, and selectivity of the Li-mediated system. The acquired data will be used to train machine learning models. Investigating these machine learning models will highlight the important properties of the electrolyte, their contribution and interesting electrolyte compositions. In addition, we will employ optimization algorithms to find more active electrolyte compositions. Combined, these findings will aid in designing experiments to further unravel the physics behind the NRR of the Li-mediated system, which will be used to scale up this process.
Keywords: Ammonia, Automation, Electrocatalysis, High Throughput, Lithium, Machine Learning, Nitrogen Reduction Reaction

Title: Big Data for Precise Interventions: Data-driven Development in India and Kenya
Abstract:
Current trends in the field of international development emphasize the potential of “big data” for planning, implementing, and evaluating development interventions. The widespread proliferation of digital devices, coupled with processes of datafication, has resulted in new data sources (e.g., data exhaust or online content), various types of data (e.g., location data), and novel ways of analyzing datasets (e.g., through artificial intelligence (AI)). According to the United Nations (UN), one of many data-enthusiastic organizations, “(n)ew sources of data (…), new technologies, and new analytical approaches, if applied responsibly, can enable more agile, efficient and evidence-based decision-making and can better measure progress on the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in a way that is both inclusive and fair” (UN n.d.). Data-driven methods and technologies are supposed to measure and compare development outcomes at the global level on the one hand, and to achieve higher impact through “precise” and “people-centered” interventions at the local level on the other hand. Unlike previous top-down and one-size-fits-all approaches, data-driven development is seen to align global development concerns and local needs. However, the lack or underfunding of data infrastructures in many low- and middle-income countries, particularly in the “Global South,” poses critical questions about the availability and use of “granular” data for “precise” development interventions. Furthermore, increased efforts to bridge those data gaps by private actors, such as global tech companies, data analytic firms, or development consultancies, raise important concerns with regard to emerging modes of governance, public-private relations, and international collaborations. 

This project will critically examine the shift towards data-driven development in India and Kenya. It investigates how data is used not only to monitor or evaluate but also to perform development through three ethnographic case studies: health, education, and justice – three sustainable development goals which have all been framed in similar terms: the importance of achieving universal access through context-specific approaches. Building on debates in anthropology and Science and Technology Studies (STS), this project will explore data infrastructures, data practices, and new modes of governance that are emerging through the quest for data-driven development and that enable and enact certain visions and versions of development. How are data for development interventions sourced, produced, and made “actionable”? How are the tensions between universality and granularity that data-driven development initiatives are imbued with negotiated? What are the social, economic, and political ramifications of data-driven development?  For example, what kind of interventions and target groups emerge through data-driven development? And what modes of governance does data-driven development foster? As countries at the forefront of digital and data-driven development in the Global South, India and Kenya are particularly suitable sites through which to critically reflect on the use of data for development.

Employing a multi-sited approach and applying ethnographic methods such as participant observation, qualitative interviews, and (digital) document analysis, the research team academically contributes to the anthropology of development, the anthropology of data, and the anthropology of governance. The project will also be relevant for development and data practitioners, as the nuanced ethnographic insights and micro-level contextualizations of data-driven development approaches will go beyond abstract debates about the opportunities and limitations of digital and data technologies dominating current development discourse.

Title: K-GraphLink: Knowledge-Graphs Linking physical world and code for task planning
Abstract: The project envisions the development of a graph representation that abstracts the physical world mapping it to a graph with relevant and functional attributes. This representation allows to create precise task planning based on this graph model, with the connections between the real objects, represented as graph nodes, allowing exact predictions to be made based on graph reasoning, which is not possible with conventional Large Language Models (LLMs). Indeed, knowledge graphs are among the most effective methods for mapping and querying complex relationships, and this method is also employed in this context, with the representation of functional properties in node and edge attributes representing a novel innovation. The method is utilized as an illustration in two pertinent domains. The former pertains to robotics, where graphs already play a significant role in task planning; the latter focuses on engineering design, an area that has recently gained significant relevance due to LLMs (large language models) and generative AI. Nonetheless, the field still faces challenges in terms of description and representation of systems and consistency of modeling and planning.
Keywords: AI Agents, Affordance reasoning, Electronic Design Automation, Graph Neural Netwoks, Knowledge Graphs, LLMs Agents, Large Language Models, Multi-Agent Systems, Multi-Modal Embedding, Planning in Robotics

Title: Charting the individuality of neural progenitor state transition sequences by hyperspectral time-lapse imaging
Abstract:
Neural progenitor cells generate the cellular diversity of the brain by activating different gene expression programs associated with fate choice, specification, and differentiation. Extensive work characterized the critical steps of gene activation underlying the diversification of neural lineages, yet we do not know to which extent activation sequences are stereotypical, whether they unfold identically in different individual cells, or if significant dynamical heterogeneity exists among cells. Are all neurons of a particular time generated through exactly the same sequence of regulatory events? Does the exact order matter to the outcome?
While, in principle, omic technologies, such as single-cell RNA sequencing, could support this kind of inquiry, a key technical limitation of these techniques is that they are destructive: a cell can be measured only once. Thus, single-cell RNA-seq analyses only reconstruct trajectories as averaged trends from cell population ensembles. Here, I propose to overcome this limitation in the study of neural development, extending and applying live transcriptomic recording technologies. I will obtain accurate recordings of entire timecourses of gene expression dynamics from several individual neural progenitors. This will be achieved thanks to live Raman microscopy, a high information content hyperspectral imaging modality that can be paired with machine learning and spatial transcriptomics to obtain high-accuracy prediction gene expression profiles. I propose recording Raman time-lapse movies of human iPSCs being differentiated towards differently patterned neural progenitor cell pools. Raman-modality movies will be augmented into transcriptomic movies using a deep learning model trained with a training dataset of coupled Raman images and spatial transcriptomics profiles. The results will be unique timecourses tracking gene activation sequences in real-time as neural progenitors undergo specification in vitro toward forebrain-, midbrain-, and hindbrain-like identities. These time course data will constitute a unique resource to address questions untractable before. We will learn about individual cells' gene expression dynamics and the heterogeneity of specification velocities, and we will determine if dynamically defined subtypes of cells exist as we hypothesize. The application of this new live omics approach will open new research directions and new ways to study settings where brain development or homeostasis is impaired or perturbed.
Keywords: brain development, live imaging, neural stem cells, raman microscopy, single-cells, transcriptomics

Title: Machine Learning for Electronic Properties
Abstract:
Despite the constant increase of computational power, atomic-scale modelling of matter is still limited by the need for a trade-off between the accuracy of electronic-structure methods that evaluate atomistic properties from first principles, and the associated computational cost. Reducing the expense of property evaluation without compromising on the accuracy is important, because many of the physical effects that should be accounted for to achieve predictive materials modelling - such as nuclear quantum effects, anharmonic fluctuations or activated transitions between (meta)stable states - require large-scale simulations and very long sampling time. 

The application of machine-learning techniques to materials modelling has been growing traction as a possible solution to this conundrum. Only a few reference electronic structure calculations need to be performed to generate training data, that are used to build a surrogate model based on a general representation of structures and statistical regression. Since the early attempts, this line of research has led to the development of interatomic potentials for pure materials and multi-component systems, as well as to the prediction of energy and properties of small organic molecules. Crucial ingredients for efficient ML models are the choice of a training set that covers uniformly the range of configurations that one wants to study, and the use of a representation that is consistent with all of the fundamental symmetries of the problem. Following these prescriptions it has been possible to develop machine-learning schemes that can effectively predict the stability of molecules, elemental solids and molecular crystals, and even assess the activity of potential drug candidates. 

The purpose of this proposal is to develop machine-learning techniques to predict the main ingredients of an electronic-structure calculation, such as the electron charge density, or the density of states. Besides the intrinsic value of evaluating these quantities inexpensively, the core ingredients in an electronic structure calculation provide a stepping stone to more transferable machine-learning models of energy and other ground-state electronic properties. The main concepts that we will use to achieve these goals are (i) the decomposition of the target property in local contributions, inspired by the nearsightedness principle for electronic matter, that guarantees a transferable ML model; (ii) the use of symmetry-adapted descriptors that can generate models of tensorial properties without assumptions of a rigid molecular geometry; (iii) the use of Gaussian process regression, a simple yet powerful ML framework. 

We will apply the resulting ML schemes to the study of hydrogen-bonded systems (both aqueous systems and molecular materials). Prediction of the charge density will allow us to for instance to compare directly with experimental electron charge densities from high-resolution X-ray diffraction or to learn from high-end electronic structure methods, and to visualize in real time indicators of inter and intra-molecular bonding. Learning the density of states gives a more robust approach to predicting spectroscopic properties and band gaps, and provides a simple strategy to treat long-range charge transfer effects and to predict the band energy - that can be combined with the exchange-correlation function computed on the ML charge density to reconstruct the full DFT energy of a system. 

Particular attention will be devoted to the open science aspects of this endeavor, by making data for the ML models publicly available, and by developing an open-source library for ML regression that is fully interfaced with modelling tools such as LAMMPS and i-PI. By training two doctoral students and one post-doc in a field at the intersection between materials science, artificial intelligence and data science, this proposal will also educate young researchers in subjects that are of strategic importance for the Swiss manufacturing and services sectors.
Keywords: atomic-scale modelling, computational materials design, electronic structure, machine learning

Title: Controling The Spread of Epidemics: A Computing Perspective
Abstract:
Can we control the spread of fake news or infectious diseases? This problem is not new, but is still important. This proposal aims to design a principled framework to answer this question based on the theory of gossip protocols. These represent an efficient mean to disseminate information in a peer-to-peer network and have been long used to model the spread of infectious diseases [20] or rumors in social networks [11, 19]. More recently, gossip protocols have led to significant advances in the fields of peer-to-peer machine learning [33] and decentralized optimization [10, 12].
Consider individuals (agents) connected in a social network. Normally, we would like communications between individuals to be efficient and information to spread quickly. In fact, nobody wants their status on Facebook to be updated 3 days after publishing it. Accordingly, any agent that tries to slow the information spread will be considered as an adversary to the system [17]. Similarly, trying to monitor the communications is usually seen as a violation of individuals privacy [18]. But when information travels fast and without any control, it makes the system vulnerable to the quick spread of fake news through the network.
In this project, we aim to turn adversaries into algorithms and control the diffusion of information in gossip protocols. The originality of our approach is to take inspira- tion from methods traditionally considered as adversaries by previous works; essentially turning previous vulnerabilities to our advantage. In particular, we aim at devising ways to stop fake news and even locate their sources. We will also study the impact of our approach in the domain of peer-to-peer machine learning and optimization. Besides, the findings of this project could benefit governments designing policies to slow the spread of epidemics. For most of the research directions we present in this proposal, we have established pioneering results over the years [5, 6, 16, 17] that provide a solid basis for our investigation.
Keywords: Adversaries, Distributed Computing, Gossip algorithms, Privacy

Title: Improved learning algorithms for recurrent neural networks
Abstract:
The remarkable success of artificial neural networks in solving complex tasks has established them as promising models for understanding learning in biological neural networks — our brains. However, their core learning algorithm, backpropagation, requires mechanisms that cannot be directly implemented in biological circuits. While researchers have proposed various biologically plausible alternatives to backpropagation, these efforts have primarily targeted
feedforward networks. These networks miss a fundamental feature of biological neural circuits: their rich recurrent connectivity. When considering recurrent networks, a fundamental challenge emerges: the standard deep learning algorithms that work well for feedforward networks struggle to effectively train recurrent architectures. In this proposal, we identify this challenge as the critical bottleneck in using deep learning as a normative theory for biological learning, and we propose to address it.

Recurrent networks have long been identified as difficult to learn, particularly for capturing long-term dependencies, which partly motivated the shift toward Transformers in deep learning. This challenge stems from their iterative nature, where the same function is repeatedly applied, causing parameter changes to have compounding effects across time. The recent revival of recurrent architectures through deep state space models has demonstrated that these challenges can be overcome, albeit through architectural modifications that diverge significantly from brain-like structures. This breakthrough has opened a promising path for training recurrent networks, making it particularly timely to revisit and improve the optimization properties of more biologically realistic architectures. We propose two complementary research directions building upon recent advances in optimization theory of these architectures. First, we aim to develop optimization algorithms specifically designed for recurrent architectures, focusing on their unique exploding behaviors and the complex parameter interactions they generate. Second, we will investigate how modularity — a principle central to deep state space models as well as biological neural circuits — can be leveraged to improve learning.

This project will have implications across several research fields. These advances will provide insights into biological learning mechanisms: while we know that biological circuits solve complex optimization problems as they learn new tasks, we don’t yet understand how. By uncovering effective learning algorithms for artificial recurrent networks, we will generate testable hypotheses about potential biological solutions. For the broader computational neuroscience community, our work will provide essential tools to improve the training
of recurrent neural networks with brain-like architectures, enabling more realistic modeling of neural circuits. Beyond neuroscience, this work will also advance deep learning through novel optimization techniques for recurrent architectures, continuing to revive interest in these theoretically powerful yet largely untapped models.
Keywords: backpropagation, biologically plausible learning, computational neuroscience, deep learning, optimization, recurrent neural network

Title: EASEML: Toward a More Accessible and Usable Machine Learning Platform for Non-expert Users
Abstract:
There is little doubt that machine learning and data science is going to be the revolutionary force of science and society in the coming years. However, the usability of
current machine learning infrastructure and platform is obscure at best. From our
experience working with users in astrophysics and biology, and in the private sector
with companies such as Zurich Insurance, Mercedes-Benz, and a Swiss telemedicine center, it is clear that the emerging bottleneck for machine learning to play an even more revolutionary role is not the availability of techniques, instead, it’s the accessibility and usability of learning systems and platforms. In the present proposal, we plan to build upon, and significantly go beyond, our recent research on declarative machine learning, scalable distributed learning systems, modern hardware support for machine learning, and learning theory. Our key objectives were: (1) to enable a platform that is significantly easier to program, and faster or cheaper to train and to massively deploy on a diverse range of infrastructures, (2) to develop the foundations for automatic management of the machine learning workload and system relax- ation for machine learning systems, and (3) to scale up and continue our support for leading scientists and Swiss private sector.
Keywords: data science, machine learning systems

Title: Fast forward genetic simulations to study the genomic signals of selection with deep learning
Abstract: Cost effective whole-genome sequencing (WGS) techniques have revolutionized the fields of population and quantitative genetics. Nowadays, we can use high throughput sequence data with millions of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNP) to infer past demographic events like changes in population sizes, migratory routes, genetic admixture between sister species (e.g., between modern and ancient Humans), or find the signals of genes under positive or negative selection. All these inferences inform us about the natural history of our and other species. Moreover, interrogating co-variation of SNP and phenotypic data we can gain a better understanding of the genetics of polygenic traits like human diseases and aid in their diagnosis and treatment (e.g., type 2 diabetes, Alzheimer, schizophrenia, obesity). All these inferences use sophisticated statistical techniques based, for most of them, on relatively simple underlying theoretical models (e.g., ignoring selection). In many cases, inference methods are set in a Bayesian framework which necessitates to solve a likelihood function. However, faced with the sheer increase of WGS data, such likelihood-based approaches become impractical and have been replaced with simulation-based approaches in likelihood-free frameworks. Among them, deep learning methods who train a set of connected artificial neural networks (ANN) to learn about the data are currently developed and have been shown to outperform most other approaches. As much as WGS has revolutionized whole areas of biological sciences, deep learning is currently revolutionizing data sciences. However, those approaches are extremely greedy, they necessitate swathes of training data to be able to learn meaningful representation of the data and make predictions.This project proposes to develop fast forward-time individual-based simulation (IBS) tools to generate genome-scale SNP data to allow researchers to develop and use simulation-based inference methods. To date, this has been done using backward-time, coalescent-based simulation tools to generate genome-scale neutral genetic variation with only limited capacity to incorporate the effects of selection. The field now needs to advance its capacity to efficiently model genome-wide patterns of molecular variation under genome-wide selection (positive and negative). The project aims to achieve this by developing new computational solutions based on parallel optimization. The main target is to accelerate the recombination process by developing new algorithms who take advantage of cutting-edge computer acceleration on graphical computing units (GPU). Multiple levels of parallel computing are proposed, on GPU and CPU with large expected gains in computing time (>10x). Further optimization of memory usage based on bit-wise data structure to model SNP data will allow for large reduction of the memory footprint of the simulations (8-32x).The second core part of the project is to develop and train a deep learning ANN to infer signals of polygenic selection at a quantitative trait. The ANN will use a recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture to learn high-level dependencies in the WGS data provided by our fast forward IBS. It is theoretically expected that polygenic selection causes small, correlated changes in allele frequencies at the many loci of small effect that influence the quantitative trait under selection. Detecting selection at many loci with small effects is one of the most challenging inference problem and requires modeling and understanding complex patterns of genome-scale linkage disequilibrium (LD). No current method is able to use WGS data in a likelihood-free framework based on simulated WGS data to address this challenge. The project will fill this gap and help understand under which conditions signals of polygenic selection can be detected. Potential applications are manifold, especially when applied to Human genomic and phenotypic data.

Title: G3E: Geometric Generative Gaze Estimation model
Abstract:
As a display of attention and interest, gaze is a fundamental cue in understanding people activities, behaviors, and state of mind, and plays an important role in many research fields like psychology, Human Robotics Interaction (HRI) or Human Computer Interfaces (HCI). For these reasons, many computer vision based gaze estimation have been proposed. Some achieve high accuracy but require expensive or specialized hardware. A solution based on consumer hardware is needed and to minimize intrusion and accommodate user's movement, remote cameras with wide enough field of view are preferred but lead to the challenge of low resolution imaging. From a methodological viewpoint, two main approaches exist. Geometric ones based on explicit eye geometry models can be very accurate but rely on high resolution images to fit and track the local features (glints, pupil center...) used to estimate the geometric parameters. On the other side, appearance based methods, which learn a direct mapping between the eye image and gaze parameters avoid feature tracking, but often need test data close to the training set in terms of user, gaze space, and illumination conditions.

Leveraging on our previous work, we propose the current G3E project to investigate a novel head-pose independent gaze estimation method that takes advantage of the appearance and geometric methods. It relies on an appearance based probabilistic generative process that model the generation of head-pose independent eye images recovered thanks to the use of consumer RGB-D cameras. By using an explicit geometric gaze model, we will handle head pose and gaze direction in a unified framework, allowing 3D space reasoning and extrapolating to gaze directions not seen in the training data. On the other hand, by modeling the generation of semantic regions (eyelids, cornea, sclera), we will decouple the gazing process and user geometry from the ambient conditions (color appearance), while avoiding the critical local feature (cornea/iris) fitting and tracking problems of standard geometric methods.

The project will study different modeling options to address the problem (details of geometric model, eyes coupling, image stabilization), and in particular several inference schemes to achieve the difficult learning from low resolution images. In a second thread, we will investigate the bayesian properties of the model to address the unsupervised learning and adaptation to user (eye geometry), session, and interpretation, by leveraging on relevant priors (eye color palettes, multimodal communication patterns like eye-contact or gaze-aversion and human attitudes in dynamic human-human interaction settings).

The project will thus address a fundamental component towards human-human or human-computer communication perception, and will make an important contribution in the fields of social signal processing, which aims at the development of computational models for machine understanding of communicative and social behavior, or in HRI and HCI like for multimodal information desk design.
Keywords: HCI, HRI, focus of attention, gaze tracking, graphical model, human interactions, unsupervised adaptation

Title: Understanding the underlying structure of remote sensing images: improving adaptation in classification models with artificial intelligence techniques
Abstract:
In this project, I propose to develop theoretical solutions to practical limitations in remote sensing data analysis.
I propose to study the underlying structure of high resolution remote sensing data, to characterize its nonlinearities and to study the variations of this structure when acquisition conditions change. This way, it will be possible to develop adaptable classification models that can process images of different zones, taken at different times and by different sensors, thus filling a major gap in current remote sensing research and meeting the endusers expectations. The project aims at creating models that can be applied to several images, thus allowing to surpass an important limitaiton to the use of remote sensing images in real world applications. 
To ensure this last point, the project also aims at developing validated applicative tools for applications needing landuse maps or environmental parameters retrieved from remote sensing data. To this end, real case studies in landscape genetics, disaster management and atmospheric modeling will be considered.
Summarizing, the project will participate in scientific advances in the fields of machine learning and fill theoretical gaps in current remote sensing image processing research that prevent the field to meet users' expectations.
Keywords: Disaster managment, Landscape genetics, Machine learning, Multitemporal image analysis, Remote sensing, Statistical models

Title: African Futures: Digital labor and Blockchain Technology
Abstract:
Considered by some as “the most important conversation of our time” (Tegmark 2017), the emergence of artificial intelligence and digitally-mediated work represents a fundamental challenge for most developing economies. Coupled with jobless economic growth, rising human productivity, and the exponential increase of the available labor pool, few jobs can be said to be safe from automated labor. In developing economies in particular, the future may not even hold enough jobs for everyone. Paradoxically, the exposure of the global South to automation as well as the lessons it may offer to address changing conceptions of digital work and production in an internet-enabled economy have been largely overlooked in the literature. This research project will strengthen the empirical knowledge on changing trends in employment in the global South by way of a two-pronged approach to the increasingly interconnected global division of labor: i) app-based work mediated by online service platforms, and ii) the use of blockchain technology in mining sites for ethical sourcing, traceability and proof of origin. 

With dwindling formal employment opportunities, a large number of Africans are turning to temporary employment or tech-enabled freelance work in digital economies. With the prospect of a jobless future, self-employment, or independent contract work, the African experience of on-demand labor should inform debates on automation, computerization and non-standard forms of work. Second, the research will examine the introduction of blockchain technology in African mining contexts. Despite the potential to perform an integral role in the functioning of global supply chains, ethnographic research is needed to assess risks and challenges of empowering or further excluding the participation of artisanal miners. Taken together, this research investigates how these forms of individual and collective labor will inform future studies of human labor performed alongside automation and the transformative impact of technology over our digital lives. How can we valorize digital work and human labor in light of dehumanizing experiences and the desire for human autonomy and flexibility?
Keywords: Africa, Digital economy, Digital labor, Work

Title: Scripts and orthography in corpus-based language typology
Abstract:
The project addresses automatic extraction of morphological features from corpora for the purpose of language typology. The proposed stay is the first step in our planned long-term collaboration aimed at a better understanding of the degree to which specific morphological marking strategies (e.g. tonal patterns, inflection, derivation, reduplication, etc.) enable languages to encode information. 
     In order to use corpus data for the purpose of language comparison, we need to take into account the fact that writing conventions in corpora differ from language to language. We thus need to assess the impact of a) scripts and b) orthography on the observations regarding the distribution of morphological and lexical types in corpora of a wide range of languages. 
    During the proposed visit, we will perform initial experiments on a relatively large set of parallel corpora. Using general tools (such as taggers, morphological analysers) and our own custom scripts, we will extract from the corpora the data that will be used to measure the information encoding potential of a language in different settings. Measures of information encoding potential include type-token ratios, the
entropy of word type distributions, the shape of word type distributions etc. The overall aim is to establish how much the information encoding potential changes when a particular factor is neutralised. During the proposed stay, we will investigate whether the observed changes depend on the scripts and orthography, which is a necessary piece of information for all future studies in this direction.
Keywords: information measures, language typology, morphology, multilingual corpora, natural language processing, quantitative analysis

Title: High-Throughput Biofabrication and Machine Learning to Identify Drug-Induced Cardiac Side Effects
Abstract:
Problem 
The drug development process takes over 12 years and $2 billion before a compound reaches patients.1 33% of drug candidates fail during late experimental evaluation (lead optimization and preclinical safety studies), due to cardiac side-effects. These failures occur due to the limited biological relevance of current experimental in vitro and in vivo assays, and the limited predictability of computational drug screens to predict mechanistically complex side effects.

Current Approach 
Pharmaceutical drugs are developed in a stepwise process; first, virtual drug libraries (>100’000 candidates, target-to-hit, hit-to-lead) are screened using computational descriptors and high-throughput experiments. Next, drug candidates are optimized using simple experimental in vitro systems (e.g., 2D cell monolayers, >1000 compounds, hit-to-lead, lead optimization), and in preclinical in vivo (animal model) evaluation (10-100 compounds). Critically, most drugs which induce cardiac side effects (e.g., ventricular arrhythmia), are discovered only during in vivo preclinical safety evaluation, or following market launch. This delay occurs due to the mechanistically complex nature of these side-effects, which are poorly captured in current in vitro assays. Furthermore, interspecies differences in cardiac biology complicate detection of side-effects during in vivo animal studies. Here, the use of more physiological, three dimensional human tissue models could enable better detection of side-effects prior to costly, late stage drug experimentation (hit-to-lead, and preclinical studies), or drug withdrawal.

Our Approach 
We will combine a scalable human cardiac tissue biofabrication platform with a machine learning pipeline, to predict and validate drug-induced cardiac side effects. Drug compound libraries will be screened in high-throughput for changes in engineered heart tissues (EHTs). The generated data will be used alongside drug chemical structures, to develop a machine learning model to predict drug-induced cardiac side effects.
Keywords: Biofabrication, Cardiac Tissue Engineering, Disease Models, Drug Development and Discovery, High-Throughput Drug Screening, Machine Learning

Title: Multi-agent learning from demonstrations and human-feedback
Abstract:
Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is a fundamental driver of the next generation of AI, offering the potential to revolutionize complex domains from autonomous vehicle fleets to large-scale logistics. Despite this promise, current successes are overly reliant on (i) hand-engineered reward signals that are notoriously difficult to design, (ii) controlled settings that lack real-world adaptability, and (iii) scalar objectives that often fail to capture complex societal or ethical nuances. This leaves critical questions regarding the alignment and autonomy of these systems in dynamic environments.

This project addresses these challenges by establishing a reward-free framework for multi-agent systems that leverages human demonstrations and comparative feedback. We focus on three complementary objectives: (i) Establishing theoretical foundations for multi-agent imitation and inverse reinforcement learning to infer optimal policies from expert demonstrations; (ii) Extending Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) to multi-agent settings to align agent behaviors with evolving human values and learning processes; (iii) Developing a reproducible benchmark of realistic environments to validate the scalability and stability of reward-free learning.

Our goal is to ground MARL with theoretical rigor and human-centric strategies, moving beyond predefined reward functions toward autonomous systems that align naturally with real-world objectives.
Keywords: Imitation Learning, Machine Learning, Multi-agent learning, Reinforcement Learning

Title: Metabolic and neurobiological mechanisms of motivation and its modulation by stress
Abstract:
There are important individual differences in motivated performance, and motivation is key to individuals’ achievement and well-being. In addition, motivation can be drastically reduced by chronic stress, and constitutes one of the hallmarks of stress-related disorders such as depression. Although motivation is multifaceted, we focus here on approach, or reward-based motivation, given its importance for mental health and accomplishment, and because its behavioral and cognitive constituents, as well as neurobiological underpinnings, are not well understood. However, given that motivation is a global construct, advancing mechanistic understanding requires new approaches capable of dissecting performance into specific motivational components and achieving meaningful clustering of individuals. Therefore, it will be paramount to progress in our understanding of the mechanisms that lead to individual differences in specific components of reward-based motivation and its modulation by stress.
Our previous work has shown a causal role for mitochondrial function in the NAc and revealed important links between specific accumbal metabolites and behavior, including aspects of motivated performance in humans. This proposal aims at gathering pioneer understanding of the metabolic and neurobiological underpinnings in the NAc of individual differences in specific elements of reward- and effort-based motivated performance. It also aims at understanding how chronic stress affects precise motivational components and their underlying mechanisms.  
The specific AIMS of this project are:
1. To investigate how specific components of reward- and effort-based motivated performance relate to specific accumbal metabolites.
2. To relate individual variation in accumbal metabolic profile predictive of differences in specific components of motivated performance to its molecular and cellular underpinnings in a cell type specific manner.
3. To deepen our understanding of the behavioral architecture of motivation; what are the phenotypic commonalities that cluster individuals? 
4. To determine how clustering of phenotypic differences in motivation map to accumbal metabolism and neurobiological mechanisms.
5. To establish how chronic stress affects the behavioral architecture of motivation, and corresponding accumbal metabolic and neurobiological mechanisms.
6. To establish causality from identified cell type-specific molecular mechanisms to the regulation of mitochondrial, neurobiological, metabolic and behavioral processes.

To achieve these aims, we will apply deep behavioral phenotyping, computational modeling, machine learning approaches and neurobiological analyses to decipher the architecture of effort-based motivation and its regulation by accumbal metabolism. We expect to gather novel information highly important to develop targeted treatment interventions.

Title: Discovery of mechanistic principles in cell signaling through hypothesis learning and automated experimentation
Abstract:
Mechanistic models of biochemical pathways have been successfully formulated for many cellular systems, which has tremendously furthered our understanding of biological processes and network architectures evolved in living systems. Amenable to analysis with tools developed for dynamical systems, evaluation of such models revealed that familiar engineering principles such as bistability, ultrasensitivity, or noise attenuation have evolved in biochemical networks to achieve specific goals. However, for most cell signaling and regulatory systems, detailed mechanistic models are still lacking because of biological complexity, i.e., nonlinearity and stochasticity of biochemical reactions, and insufficient measurements of molecular players involved in reactions. And where such models exist, e.g., in the form of differential equations, we typically have only rough estimates for the parameters that usually come from population-averaged measurements. To make a leap forward and to aid the discovery of new mechanistic insights in cell biology, we propose to build an automated hypothesis learner/validator – an integrated approach comprising wet-, hard- and software. It combines optogenetic actuators, molecular biosensors, real-time closed-loop microscopy, and mathematical optimization with a reasoning system. The aim of the platform is to autonomously learn and validate hypotheses about a biological system monitored and perturbed in real time. This will generate information for adaptive selection of quantitative symbolic relationships that best describe the data.

This project is an ambitious attempt to integrate novel theoretical approaches (active learning of models from data), cutting-edge technology (automated real-time closed-loop microscopy) and the latest cell biology techniques (optogenetic actuators and live-cell biosensors), and to apply them to discovery of mechanistic insights into biological systems. Given the large amount of existing optogenetic actuators and biosensors, this methodology can also be translated to other systems. Processes developed during this project will enrich our experimental toolkit to interrogate cell signaling and offer an enormous potential to generate and learn hypotheses from biological data in an automated way.
Keywords: bioinformatics, cell biology, image analysis, machine learning, mathematical modelling, microscopy

Title: Ideological Ad Targeting in Consumer Markets and the Political Market Place
Abstract:
Digitization has revolutionized advertising, paving the way for new business models and marketing strategies that harness highly detailed user data and statistical learning to target (potential) customers and voters online. While more sophisticated targeted advertising has benefited companies and could potentially lead to better-informed consumers and voters, it has also raised concerns regarding its negative side effects on consumer privacy and unintended economic, social, and psychological consequences.

The highly targeted political advertising by Cambridge Analytica and ideologically driven advertising practices on Facebook have further fueled public concern about targeting based on users' political preferences. Despite the economic and social significance of this issue, little is known about how firms and political parties or campaigns ideologically target consumers and voters on the internet.

In this project, we adopt a novel methodological approach to study online advertising: examining online advertising using artificial targets. We propose implementing this approach in two parts: Part 1 investigates whether and how firms target individual consumers based on their ideological preferences, while Part 2 explores how political parties and candidates target voters during election campaigns.
Keywords: Ad Targeting, Brand Ideology, Online Advertising, Political Advertising

Title: Determinants of trade policy without aggregation bias
Abstract:
The “protection for sale” model by Grossman and Helpman (1994) is the workhorse setup used in international trade to understand the political economy determinants of trade policy. The model suggests that policy-makers weight social welfare and political contributions by industry lobbies when deciding the structure of trade protection. A key parameter in the model is the weight that the government places on social welfare relative to political contributions. If a large weight is put on social welfare, then industry lobbying will have no impact on the equilibrium structure of protection, whereas a small weight is likely to result in a lot of influence by industry lobby and high levels of trade protection for those industries.

A problem highlighted by the empirical literature that tested the predictions of the protection for sale was that most estimates of the weight put by governments on social welfare relative lobbies’ contributions were too high and at odds with what would be suggested by estimates of welfare costs. 

A potential explanation for this very large estimated weight on social welfare when explaining the determinants of trade policy is aggregation bias. All studies use as the level of observation the “industry” with only around 100 industries in most studies. This is because production data, which is necessary to structurally estimate the protection for sale model, is only available at that level of disaggregation. However, trade policy does not get determined at the industry level, but at a much more disaggregated level: the tariff line. For every industry, there are on average around 50 tariff lines (if we use the widely used six-digit Harmonised System classification). More importantly, most tariff schedules show a lot of heterogeneity within industries and across tariff lines. 

The objective of this research project is to estimate the protection-for-sale determinant of tariffs at the most disaggregated level (HS six-digit level) to avoid aggregation bias. This will be done for a large number of countries, as in Gawande, Krishna and Olarreaga (2016). The variable that is currently missing to be able to estimate such an equation at this level of disaggregation is production data. All other necessary data (tariffs, imports, exports and trade elasticities) is available at the six-digit of the HS. Therefore, the first stage in the project will consist in estimating production data at the six-digit level of the HS for a large number of countries.

Title: Computational biomicroscopy: advanced image processing methods to quantify live biological systems
Abstract:
Microscopes have traditionally relied on exquisite optical components. With the advent of image digitization, computation now plays an essential role, both in the imaging formation process as well as the quantitative analysis of the acquired images.  

The goal of this project is to develop imaging approaches that leverage two classes of computational tools: machine learning approaches and signal processing using sparse approximations. Their application in the general field of computational imaging is highly promising.

Specifically, the first aim of the research in this project is to overcome resolution limitations in low-photon, three-dimensional fluorescence microscopy by use of machine learning techniques in deconvolution and optimal imaging parameter determination. The second aim is to address computational artifacts in digital holographic microscopy, a technique that allows collecting images over wide fields of view and focal ranges using fairly inexpensive hardware devices yet that requires carefully designed computational tools for post processing. There, we propose to work in a generalized sampling framework that can be adapted precisely to experimental acquisition devices while retaining the advantages of classical signal processing implementations (fast Fourier transforms). This framework is also particularly well-adapted for performing non-linear approximations in sparse signal representations. 

The proposed methods will be implemented and become part of an imaging platform recently set up at Idiap, which allows acquiring and disseminating microscopy data and tools in a reproducible research framework.  The developed techniques should also allow future development of microscopes with inexpensive components and simplified hardware designs.
Keywords: computational photography, developmental biology, holography, image processing, machine learning, microscopy, signal processing

Title: Optimising outcomes in psychotherapy for anxiety disorders (OPTIMAX)
Abstract: Anxiety disorders, such as phobia, panic disorder or generalized anxiety disorder, are the most common class of mental disorders present in the general population. They are hugely disruptive, place psychological distress and role impairments on individuals and their families and create a serious economic burden for society. Psychological psychotherapies, such as cognitive behavior therapy (CBT), based on principles of basic cognitive and behavioral science and implemented via standardised treatment manuals, are amongst the most effective treatments for such disorders. These treatments are nevertheless only moderately successful in initiating and sustaining individual change in anxiety. The present program of research aims to improve outcomes in CBT for anxiety. To achieve this objective, a multi-method research program is proposed combining a large-scale clinical study with experimental laboratory paradigms. First, we will in a randomised controlled clinical trial examine genetic, endocrine, demographic and clinical predictors of response to CBT for anxiety. Using cutting-edge machine learning analysis methods will enable classification of subtypes of individual treatment responses based on these multiple predictors. Second, drawing from basic neuroscience science findings, we will in the laboratory examine the potential of (i) brain stimulation and (ii) memory reactivation during sleep to enhance learning during CBT. The projected findings will lead to important theoretical and clinical innovations in forecasting treatment outcome and break the ground for improving current psychotherapy for anxiety disorders that forms an ever-growing burden for society.
Keywords: anxiety, autobiographical memory, cognitive behavior therapy, mechanisms, psychotherapy, sleep

Title: Quo vadis, Clio? Assessing Use and Abuse of AI Workflows in Historical Research
Abstract:
This project proposes to explore a new avenue for the methodological advancement of historical research by implementing and critically assessing the massive integration of AI tools into scholarly workflows, aiming at the work environment of ‘classical’ historians who have no particular background in Digital History. Since the release of ChatGPT the latest, we all have become aware of the massive disruptive potential of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) in general and Large Language Models (LLMs) in particular. We all have made our own experiences with both the amazing capabilities and with equally amazing shortcomings of these new technologies. What we need now is a systematic Technology Assessment (Technikfolgenabschätzung) and the development of new best practices in dealing with these new technologies. While AI tools can facilitate various aspects of research, they also pose risks, such as producing biased results or encouraging approaches that violate the principles of good academic practice. The project aims to promote critical reflection on these technologies and provide practical insights for their responsible use in the field of history. 
The project is built around an experimental historical case study, which will be dissected into discrete research steps and workflows. For each step, the project team evaluates where AI tools can be implemented, assesses the advantages and challenges they bring, and considers their compliance with scholarly standards. Special attention is given to identifying potentially abusive uses of AI, such as shortcuts that compromise academic integrity or generate misleading interpretations. Moreover, the project seeks to establish principles and guidelines for employing AI in ways that align with the highest standards of good scholarly practice. 
Quo vadis, Clio is a highly unconventional and interdisciplinary research project that combines the revision of ‘classical’ methods of historical research with the introduction of AI workflows and, above all, a Technology Assessment approach. The transformative potential of this project lies in its ability to advance informed methodological innovation within the historical discipline. It aims to broaden the scope of critical engagement with AI technologies beyond specialists in the field of Digital History, addressing the implications for historical research as a whole.
Keywords: AI for historians without DH background, Artificial Intelligence in historical research, History didactics, Large Language Modells, Methodology in historical research, Technology Assessment

Title: Subseasonal prediction of compound extremes driven by the stratosphere (STRATcompound)
Abstract: Extreme weather and climate events such as hot or cold spells or precipitation extremes can have severe impacts, for example for human health, ecosystems, agriculture, and infrastructure. When such weather extremes occur as compound events, meaning that multiple drivers or hazards jointly trigger an impact, then the damages can be amplified. It is therefore crucial to anticipate such hazards and their impacts as long as possible in advance. While many compound extremes will increase in frequency or severity in a changing climate, it is not yet understood if they can be anticipated on the timescales that allow for emergency preparation, that is, several weeks to months in advance, so-called subseasonal to seasonal (S2S) timescales. There is indeed potential for S2S prediction if at least one of the compounding factors is remotely driven. An important driver of compound extremes is the stratosphere, which can trigger surface weather extremes. These extremes can lead to a variety of hazards that occur concurrently or consecutively in a cascading manner, but they have not yet been considered in a compound event framework. The focus of the here proposed research lies in identifying compound extremes related to precursors in the extratropical stratosphere. The envisaged hazards include storm series that can lead to excessive precipitation (WP1), temperature extremes such as marine and land cold air outbreaks and hot spells (WP2), compound extremes modulated by the tropics and driven by the stratosphere (WP3), as well as cryospheric extremes such as snow droughts and permafrost thawing (WP4). Both dynamical and artificial intelligence-based subseasonal prediction models will be used to identify the forecast skill of compound extremes and to identify the role of the stratosphere. Sensitivity studies will be performed to attribute the extremes and to understand the links between the drivers and the compound extremes, to identify the origins of predictability and to understand compound extremes driven by the stratosphere in a changing climate.
Keywords: compound / multi-hazard events, compound extremes, extreme events, stratosphere, stratosphere - troposphere coupling, subseasonal prediction

Title: Human Behavior on Networks: Connecting Models and Experiments
Abstract:
Advances in the field of complex networks have created a solid ground for the understanding and modeling of diverse complex systems. 
A line of research that has proven particularly interesting is evolutionary game theory on networks, in which agents, located on the nodes of a network, interact with their neighbors through a game while their own actions are described by a strategy subject to an evolutionary process. 
The issue of whether population structure can foster cooperation in social dilemmas has been addressed by many, but theoretical studies have yielded contradictory results so far. 
Recently, the largest-scale experiment (up to date) with humans playing a spatial prisoner's dilemma game on different networks revealed that the network structure does not influence cooperative behavior, and that humans do not consider neighbors' payoffs when making their decisions.
In this project we propose to develop theories and models that incorporate the input of these experiments, in order to shed light on the manner in which people interact with each other.
Our main target is to understand if the absence of network reciprocity is a general feature of evolutionary dynamics that are not based on payoff comparison, and what are the effects of introducing non-economic factors in the strategy update process. We also plan to develop an evolutionary model to reproduce the different human behaviors observed in experiments.
Keywords: adaptive systems, agent-based modeling, complex networks, evolutionary game theory, mean-field theory, moody conditional cooperation, reinforcement learning, stochastic processes, voter model
