Title: UNSUPERVISED LEARNING OF 3D MODELS FOR OBJECT DETECTION AND CATEGORIZATION
Abstract:
Object detection and categorization are fundamental problems in computer vision and the first steps towards building intelligent systems capable of interacting with our environment. Unfortunately, these are problems of baffling complexity due to the high dimensionality of visual data and its highly nonlinear dependency to nuisance factors such as viewpoint, scale, illumination, intra-class object variability, clutter, occlusions and noise.

Inspired by recent approaches, we propose to investigate a novel detection and categorization approach focused on the 3D shape of objects. The novelty in our approach lies in how we learn the 3D model from data and how we use it for detection and categorization. During training we propose to build a 3D model of an object directly from images of a category. At runtime, we use 3D models at two levels: locally, to select valid 2D landmarks in images and, globally, to certify that the collection of selected 2D landmarks is the projection of a known 3D geometry. To deal with intra-class variability, a key ingredient in our approach is the design of feature descriptors invariant to texture variations. These descriptors are used to establish landmark correspondences both during training and testing. Textural information is only used at runtime for the category selection.
Keywords: 3D reconstruction, categorization, convex optimization, object detection

Title: LONG-SB Study: Revealing the neural basis of long-term cognitive development of children with open spina bifida
Abstract:
Background: Spina bifida is the most common birth defect with direct central nervous system involvement. Incomplete neural tube closure sets the stage for spinal damage and results in cerebral, visceral, and peripheral neural impairments. In the open form, approximately half of affected children will not be able to walk independently. Developmental delay is common, characterized by lower IQ, difficulties with language, executive functions and attention. Developmental impairments persist and necessitate life-long support. The early identification of individuals at risk for developmental impairments is of high clinical value and has great translational potential. 

Knowledge gaps: Children with open spina bifida show a specific spectrum of cognitive deficits. However, we still don't fully understand the reasons behind this and why there is variability in how these difficulties manifest among different individuals. While prenatal corrective surgery improves motor outcomes, the spectrum of neurocognitive impairments was reported to be the same as after postnatal correction. We hypothesize that while the secondary damage due to the exposed spinal cord is ameliorated by the prenatal surgery, there is a vulnerability window before surgery, particularly due to the large-scale and rapid establishment of the brain’s neural circuitry during the mid-gestational stage. To fill the gaps in our understanding, the LONG-SB study will have the following goals:

Goal 1. To characterise the anatomical basis of neural circuitry dysmaturation in open spina using a distinctive, single centric, longitudinal prenatal and neonatal MRI dataset and an image analysis approach optimized for this cohort.

Goal 2. To characterise the spectrum of neurocognitive impairments in open spina bifida, focusing on learning, memory, attention and executive functions at school age, and establish links between the developmental dysmaturation of neuromorphology, neural circuitry and cognition.

Methods: Our study will first focus on the improvement of methods to quantify cerebral development in fetal and neonatal MRI. Next, we will enroll data of over 195 infants who underwent prenatal surgery for open spina bifida, collected in a unique single-center cohort study running for over 12 years (WP1). Longitudinal MRI are available pre-, post-operatively, prenatally, and neonatally in all cases. At two years of age, cognitive development was assessed with the Bayley-III scales. Over 70 children reaching 8-10 years of age will be prospectively called back for an in-depth assessment of neurocognitive development, focusing on attention, memory, learning, executive functions, fine- and visuomotor functions, extended by parental questionnaires. In WP2, MRI analysis of cerebral dysmaturation will include a volumetric measurement of brain tissues through image segmentation and structural connectivity analysis, and we will characterize what clinical variables are linked to impaired cerebral development. In WP3, we will characterise the specific neurocognitive developmental profile in spina bifida and will use MRI analysis to reveal links between early cerebral dysmaturation and such impairments.

Significance: Fetal surgery for open spina bifida in Zurich is a successful, internationally acknowledged therapy that already improved the lives of over 200 children and their families. Based on this clinical experience, the LONG-SB study will contribute to the field with new computational imaging and analysis techniques. Our study will provide further evidence for altered vulnerability in spina bifida, in other words, whether there is a specific link between dysmaturation of certain neural structures during this period and the very specific spectrum of cognitive outcomes. This new knowledge will be important to create individualized support to help the affected children develop to their full potential, and to reduce the socio-economic burden associated with this disorder.
Keywords: child development, executive functions, fetal MRI, fetal surgery, magnetic resonance imaging, neurodevelopment, pediatrics, spina bifida, working memory

Title: Reconceiving and Improving Multi-Perspectivality and Rationality in Argumentative AI (M-Rational)
Abstract:
With the introduction of the transformer architecture Vaswani et al. (2017) and its recent evolution into Large Language Models (LLMs), a number of approaches developed in Natural Language Processing (NLP) reached a level of performance that makes them ready (or almost ready) for deployment in real-world settings. Many of these applications are evolving from a text classification perspective (e.g. sentiment analysis, information extraction) to complex reasoning tasks including in complex domains of discourse. Some of these domains of discourse, such as political, ethical and legal reasoning, requires an interpretation model which not only models processes of inference, both formal and material, but also requires the acknowledgment and integration of multiple assumed perspectives and value systems.

The dominant paradigm for the construction of these systems involves the notion of a human-grounded feedback, the use of annotations, instructions or post-hoc validation for the training or evaluation of these models. This paradigm, when applied to complex and multi-perspective domains, bring the inherent risk of introducing severe subjective biases into these models. As generative language models march towards widespread application, developing new methodologies for integrating multi-perspective reasoning capabilities into these models becomes a matter of strategic societal importance.

This project focuses on the development of new conceptual resources and methods to support the development of Natural Language Inference (NLI) models which deliver multi-perspective reasoning. To achieve this ambition, it is conceptualized across four main pillars: (i) a novel conception of multi-perspective reasoning based on inferentialism (MPR), (ii) a novel conceptual understanding of perspectival rationality inspired by the philosophy of science, (iii) the development of novel mechanisms for controlling LLMs in order to deliver MPR and (iv) new evaluation methodologies for MPR models.

In NLP, there has been a long-standing orthodoxy of unifying disagreeing perspectives – be it in the creation of a training dataset or in the evaluation of the output of LLMs – into one single ground truth, usually by majority vote. More recently, however, researchers have started to explore ways of appreciating and exploiting the plurality of perspectives (what we call perspectivality) that can become visible in the context of challenging tasks such as the computational assessment of argument quality.

However, the basic issue with this positive conception of perspectivality is that, to this day, it suffers from both a theoretical and a practical deficiency. On the theoretical side, it is not clear (i) how exactly to understand the notion of a perspective, including basic aspects such as the question of what such perspectives are perspectives of, how to give an exact account of such perspectives, and what makes such perspectives rational positions in the space of reasons (rather than simple aberrations or noise). M-Rational will develop conceptual answer to these basic questions. Our project aims to chart new terrain, neither forcing everything into the Procrustean bed of a single unified ground truth, nor collapsing into a debilitating “anything goes” relativism. On the practical side, M-Rational will contribute to evolving the state of the art in NLI and argumentation reasoning by shaping the sub-theme of multi-perspective argumentation reasoning, i.e. models which can interpret and critically augment arguments, mapping representative stances, eliciting underlying premises (assumed facts, definitions) and maximize logical validity. Combining with the philosophical part, the project will also modify the very notion of what it means to make progress at argument reasoning in multi-perspectival settings by reconceiving the goal of the task as such.

Title: Noise-Adaptive Optimization Methods and their Robustness Properties
Abstract:
Randomness is regularly present throughout most machine learning (ML) pipelines, including the initialization of the parameters of a model, in the groundtruth labels, or in the optimizer.
While these various sources of randomness have been studied in the literature, they are often considered under simplifying assumptions that do not capture the observed empirical evidence in modern deep learning models.

In this proposal, we focus on non-convex optimization where a common practice is to assume that the noise is bounded and derive convergence rates to achieve first-order (and sometimes second-order) stationarity. While important, these guarantees have at least three important limitations: i) they do not specifically describe the behavior of the algorithm in some regions of specific interest (e.g. valleys or local minima), ii) they do not fully exploit the properties of the noise to improve convergence, and iii) they do not give a precise characterization of the type of minima that are more likely to be chosen by an optimizer depending, for instance, on its width, height, etc.
Crucially, the latter properties are connected to the robustness and generalization of the chosen solution. Understanding such properties is therefore of practical relevance as ML models are now being frequently deployed in real-world applications such as self-driving cars.

In this proposal, we define four overarching goals in order to enhance our understanding of the role of stochastic noise in non-convex optimization, as well as to develop new noise-adaptive optimization methods. Each goal corresponds to one work package (WP). i) First, we aim to introduce new tools to characterize the behavior of stochastic methods for optimizing non-convex functions. We will base our analysis on continuous-time representations that have become a popular tool in ML. Our main focus will be to derive analytical expressions for mean exit times from various regions of interest, including saddle points, valleys and local minima.

We will address the general noise regime (i.e. not assuming the noise goes to zero as in many existing work). This is of practical relevance in ML, where one can not necessarily assume that the level of noise is small. Instead, large levels of noise have been shown to be beneficial~\citep{zhou2019toward, wei2019noise, xie2021positive}.
The tools we will develop are general enough to apply to a broad range of applications in ML as well as other fields of science. We will also conduct an extensive experimental evaluation on modern neural network architectures to validate and orient our theoretical analysis.

ii) Second, we will study the effect of changing the properties of the noise, producing novel types of stochastic algorithms that are noise-adaptive. This will include developing new analytical tools for fractional Brownian motion, as well as for self-excited processes where the noise can be driven by a chosen function. Both areas are to the best of our knowledge unexplored in ML.

We expect that this direction will lead to new algorithms with faster rates of convergence and more control over the targeted minima.

iii) Third, we will use the results developed in i) and ii) to analyze the robustness and generalization properties of stochastic optimization methods.

iv) Fourth, we will use the results derived in the first three WPs to analyze the properties of gradient-adaptive methods that are commonly used in ML but also differ from non gradient-adaptive methods in terms of generalization~\citep{wilson2017marginal}. We will also propose a new variant of stochastic optimization methods that are both gradient- and noise-adaptive.

Finally, the proposal provides research training opportunities for a diverse group of students. We emphasize it is interdisciplinary in nature as it will involve a collaboration between mathematicians and computer scientists. The tools developed in WP1 and WP2 are of general interest in the mathematical community and will be applied to applications of practical interest in the field of ML. We also aim to organize a conference/workshop mid-proposal to gather mathematicians and computer scientists interested in applications of continuous-time stochastic processes to ML.
Keywords: Generalization for machine learning, Machine learning, Non-convex Optimization, Stochastic Optimization, Stochastic differential equations

Title: From model-based to data-driven design: Signal processing and control of noisy nonlinear systems
Abstract:
Mathematical models of dynamical processes provide the critical link between real-life applications and techniques for prediction, monitoring, and control. Models are obtained from observed data via system identification methods. These methods, however, do not take into account the subsequent use of the model for design. The issue is currently addressed by trial-and-error human interaction. A rigorous high-gain approach, investigated in this project, is to merge the data modeling and model-based design subproblems into one joint problem, called data-driven design. Its benefits are theoretical optimality and automation of the overall design Process, which reduce the cost and increase the design reliability.

This project studies data-driven signal processing and control from noisy data of nonlinear systems. Three approaches are investigated: 
1. methods with provable properties for exact data from classes of nonlinear systems,
2. effective convex relaxations for noisy data from general nonlinear systems, and
3. adaptive data-driven control.
The first approach is based on embedding of the nonlinear system's behavior into the behavior of a linear time-invariant system. The second approach is based on machine learning techniques such as sparsity promoting regularizers. The third approach is based on the data-enabled predictive control method developed at ETH-Zürich. The effectiveness of the methods will be validated on metrology, robotic quadcopter, and power electronics testbeds
Keywords: data-driven control, data-driven signal processing, model predictive control, system identification

Title: Prediction rule ensembles: Interpretable models for psychological research
Abstract: In this project, we will further develop prediction rule ensemble (PRE) methodology, a novel data-science method that uniquely balances accuracy and interpretability. Prediction rule ensembles consist of a small number of very simple decision trees (or rules), which make it easy to apply empirical research findings to decision making in clinical practice. As such, PRE methodology holds great promise for improving evidence-based practice in psychology. Therefore, the goals of this project are: 1) Extending PRE methodology such that multilevel dataset structures, which are particularly common in psychological research, can be handled. 2) Disseminating the extended PRE methodology, through the development of publicly available, well-documented software, tutorial papers and a workshop.
Keywords: decision tree methods, machine learning, multilevel analysis, psychological research methods, statistics

Title: Tackling distribution shifts in machine learning methods for medical image analysis
Abstract:
Methods based on machine learning have shown remarkable promise towards automating analyses of medical images. Such methods typically consist of a training phase (where parameters of a model are estimated using empirical data), followed by a testing phase where the trained model is used to analyze previously unseen test data. A key requirement for good performance is that training and test images be sampled from the same probability distribution. Deviation from this requirement (known as distribution shift) is ubiquitous in medical imaging and often leads to substantial performance degradation, thus forming one of the main hurdles to clinical translation of such methods.

In this project, we will develop methods to improve robustness of machine learning methods towards distribution shifts in medical images. We will consider multiple types of distribution shifts, including those caused by changes in acquisition settings, imaging artifacts, demographic variability, as well as anatomical abnormalities. Further, we will tackle such shifts in different types of machine learning models - namely, discriminative as well as generative models.

To summarize, we propose to tackle hitherto neglected, but important distribution shifts across a wide spectrum of machine learning methods and applicable to many medical image analyses. We believe that progress in this research direction will greatly enhance the trustworthiness and reliability of machine learning methods, thereby facilitating their translation into clinical practice, and ultimately improving the efficiency and reach of healthcare systems.
Keywords: deep learning, healthcare, machine learning, medical image analysis, medical imaging, out-of-distribution generalization, reliable AI, robustness, trustworthy AI

Title: Greening the deal: Do acquisitions boost or block environmental transformation?
Abstract:
Transforming today’s society into one that is more sustainable relies crucially on green transformation undertaken by the private sector. Recently, many industries have seen a surge in “green deals” (BCG, 2022). These mergers and acquisitions (M&As) have the potential to promote environmental transformation by encouraging green innovation through research synergies and technology adoption, but business consolidation can also reduce competition and lead to "killer acquisitions" that stifle future innovation (Cunningham et al., 2021). M&A deals may also be used as a tool for "greenwashing", to improve “green image”, rather than genuine environmental transformation:  Not only is the acquired research not developed further, but it also leaves stakeholders with the impression that the acquiring company has taken substantial steps towards becoming more sustainable. Given the scope for opposing effects, it is unclear whether and when M&A activity is beneficial for green transformation. This project aims to fill this gap by providing comprehensive, data-driven analysis of the impact of M&A activity on substantive green innovation at the firm-level and contrast these findings with the effects of M&A on “green image” and financial performance.

Interest in the impact of mergers on innovation has grown significantly in recent years among policymakers, investors, and academic researchers alike (Gilbert, 2020). The topic remains controversial and most of the progress in research has been made in the theoretical modeling of effects. There are only a handful of studies that apply real-world data to assess the effects of mergers on innovation, and of those that have, the majority focus on mergers in the pharmaceutical industry. The novelty of the proposed project is to focus on the impact of M&A deals on green innovation, as well as to consider implications for greenwashing and firm performance using a large, cross-industry dataset. Moreover, this project will develop and apply novel methods to measure sustainability and green innovation using natural language processing (NLP) algorithms to process the rich textual information contained in patents and company statements. 

To evaluate the cause-and-effect relationship between mergers and green innovation, the data will be analyzed using differences-in-differences analysis combined with propensity score matching. The outcomes for firms involved in green deals will be compared before and after the merger, benchmarking outcomes against similar firms that are either involved in non-green M&A or not involved in M&A at all. To assess the extent to which greenwashing motives may be at play, the analysis will track measures that capture the “green image”, as communicated by firms themselves, pre- and post-merger. The impact of green deals on financial performance measures will also be analyzed. The key challenges and risks for this project will be to merge firm-level variables across diverse data sources for a large sample of firms, to develop sufficiently rich and accurate measures of green innovation, and to convincingly estimate the causal effects of mergers.  

The findings of this research will be of great interest to policymakers, business leaders, investors, and other stakeholders who are concerned about the environmental impact of corporate actions. By shedding light on the role of M&A activity in promoting or hindering green transformation, our study will contribute to the development of more effective policies and strategies that accelerate the transition to a sustainable economy - and thus to a sustainable society. Ultimately, this research will help to bridge the gap between theory and practice by providing practical recommendations for firms, investors and policymakers seeking to achieve their sustainability goals.
Keywords: economics, environmental eonomics, finance, green innovation, greenwashing, management science, mergers and acquisitions, text analysis NLP algorithms

Title: Safe Pruning in Optimal State-Space Search
Abstract:
State space search, i.e., search in large, usually implicitly defined transition systems, is one of the foundational techniques in several research areas in computer science and its applications, including automated planning, directed model checking, and many classes of optimization problems. We focus on explicit-state search, where search algorithms consider one state of the transition system at a time, often (but not necessarily) guided by approximate distance information using algorithms such as A*. Moreover, we focus on the optimal setting, where solution algorithms must guarantee that no cheaper solution than the one reported by the algorithm exists. Recent research has shown that in many practical contexts including search domains studied in optimal planning there are fundamental limits to the scalability of classical search algorithms, even under very optimistic assumptions. In this project, we focus on the development of search techniques and state space pruning techniques to extend classical search algorithms to overcome these limitations, by not having to explore search states that are provably redundant.

The above-mentioned scalability issues are due to the fact that as planning tasks grow in size, a combinatorial explosion happens not just for the number of states, but in many cases also for the number of states that are part of optimal solutions, which all need to be considered as possible alternatives by a standard search algorithm in order to prove optimality of the solution. However, in many cases these potential solutions are not interestingly different; for example, they might vary only in the order in which certain independent subgoals are achieved, and a deeper analysis would reveal that all possible orderings are in a formal sense equivalent.

There are two lines of research, originating from the model checking community, that attempt to address this problem by pruning redundant parts of the state space: partial order reduction and symmetry elimination. While a significant body of work on both approaches exists both in planning and in model checking, we believe that this line of research is not yet sufficiently developed and warrants further investigation. In particular, most of the work on partial order reduction in planning has been developed in isolation without sufficient comparison to other approaches. Moreover, several of the key papers that apply partial order reduction to planning and related problems are theoretically flawed, claiming to be complete and/or optimality-preserving when in fact they are not. It is perhaps telling that none of the recent winners or runners-up of the International Planning Competitions (IPC) made use of partial order reduction or symmetry elimination techniques.

In this project, we investigate sound and complete state space pruning techniques for planning based on partial order reduction and symmetry elimination. The overall goals are to better understand the existing state space pruning approaches in the literature and how they are related to each other, to develop new techniques for state space pruning based on the better understanding obtained, and to apply partial order reduction and symmetry elimination to new algorithmic problems where they have not been considered before such as grounding of operators and the computation of invariants.
Keywords: artificial intelligence, automated planning, partial order reduction, symmetries

Title: Outdoors seen from inside out: Impact of views and daylight composition on our visual experience
Abstract:
This project aims to deepen our understanding of the perceptual effects of daylight and views out, with a focus on view content, view access and compositional qualities of daylight accounting for factors like sky type and façade design for instance. While a visual connection to the outside through views has long been acknowledged as beneficial to one’s perception of an indoor environment, we still lack the means to evaluate its criticality, and have no way of anticipating how its combination with the increasingly innovative façade systems that emerge today from the construction industry may ultimately affect our comfort, cognitive performance and attention, and our overall well-being. 

Existing metrics describing daylight performance are typically limited to illumination potential and to the avoidance of visual discomfort, while façade performance tends to be based on material properties and heat exchange considerations. Building upon recent progress on advanced glazing and shading technologies but also on the effects of glare, contrast, visual cues in views and on the psycho-physiological effects of daylight and façade patterns, we aim to shed new light on the importance of view content and daylight conditions and on the influence of their combination in the perception of an indoor space – and thus in its adequacy towards our psychological and physiological well-being. 

The methodological approach will be based on a series of experiments in monitored environmental conditions which will rely on a combination of controlled and semi-controlled user studies. They will be conducted either on screen, in Virtual Reality with High Dynamic Range photographs, or in real spaces. Subjective self-assessments will be supplemented by an ad hoc selection of biomarkers. This approach will thus require us to reach out to fields of science remote from building engineering: environmental psychology from which most findings on benefits of views come from, psychophysics from which evaluation methods for cognition and attention will be drawn, and vision research and computer science, in particular regarding semantic image segmentation. 

This project will advance knowledge about the benefits of daylight and views out, of which we are intuitively aware and yet that have been under-explored in terms of their actual impact on human well-being, in particular as far as perceived comfort, cognition and attention are concerned. Although the immediate contribution of the project is mostly fundamental (deepening our understanding of these effects), it can have a significant impact on future standards for building envelopes as well as on practice, as we are living an era of exponential expansion of façade technology development and innovative design, in which evidence-based guidance can become a game-changer.
Keywords: daylight, facade pattern, gaze, glare, perception, view, virtual reality

Title: Identification of neuroanatomical changes that predate transition to psychosis and could predict the individual risk of developing schizophrenia: an MRI longitudinal study in adolescents and young adults
Abstract: Schizophrenia is a mental illness of unknown etiology that usually begins during adolescence or young adulthood and that is characterized by abnormal thought and distorted emotional responses. There is no cure and patients have to cope with many of the chronic and debilitating symptoms for the rest of their lives. Recent pathophysiological models suggest that the development of schizophrenia could be described in three stages: the prodromal phase, the first psychotic episode and the long-term chronic phase.  During the prodromal phase, there is a gradual deterioration of global functioning and appearance of attenuated psychotic symptoms. Thus correct identification of at-risk patients during this prodromal phase is a promising approach to study the etiological process and to allow an early management of patients before the development of chronic schizophrenia. Patients within the prodromal phase and showing the highest and most imminent risk of psychosis are classified as “Ultra High Risk” (UHR). They are adolescents or young adults seeking help and meeting a combination of clinical symptoms and functional decline. Among UHR patients, 30-40% convert to frank psychosis within a year if left untreated but there is now emerging evidence that early social and medical interventions could avoid transition to full-blown schizophrenia. Even if the etiological process that underlies schizophrenia is still unknown, various neuroanatomical abnormalities have been associated with each of the different states of the illness. Neuroimaging studies during the prodromal phase and transition to frank psychosis are still nascent and their results obtained on a small sample of patients are largely inconsistent. Moreover, neuroanatomical abnormalities seen during these early phases could represent a combination of pre-existing (traits) and ongoing changes (states). Hence, the aim of my project is to: 1) characterize the baseline (traits) and longitudinal (states) neuroanatomical changes associated with transition to psychosis in UHR patients to allow a better understanding of the pathophysiological process underlying schizophrenia; 2) determine the predictive utility of these changes to enhance the distinction between UHR patients that subsequently convert to psychosis (UHR-T) and those that do not (UHR-NT). Methodologically, my project is based on the structural analysis of 3T MRI brain scans obtained in the context of the largest cohort ever collected of drug-free and medication-free UHR adolescents and young adults. To identify the UHR group, young people have been assessed by an instrument specially developed: the Comprehensive Assessment of At Risk Mental State (CAARMS). This implies that they are aged between 15 and 29, are seeking help and meet criteria for one or more of the following groups: 1) Attenuated Psychotic Symptoms group; 2) Brief Limited Intermittent Psychotic Symptoms group; 3) Trait and state risk factor group. After recruitment subjects have been scanned at baseline and then every 18 months for three years or until conversion to psychosis since 2008. Thus processing of MRI brain scans followed by the cross-sectional and longitudinal comparison of morphometric data between UHR-T and UHR-NT as well as the implementation of a Support Vector Machine (SVM) that can identify which features best discriminate between two groups of individuals should allow to characterize the neuroanatomical changes associated with transition to psychosis and to determine the predictive utility of these changes at an individual level. Since February 2012, I have processed all baseline MRI brain scans to extract cortical thickness measures through a semi-automated surface-based analysis tool. I have also run a preliminary group comparison between all UHR (regardless of further transition) and controls and found no difference in cortical thickness at baseline. Even the implementation of SVM failed to classify individuals at above-chance levels. The lack of baseline differences between UHR and control individuals suggests that no brain changes are attributable to the impact of confounding factors like drugs-use in our sample.
Keywords: Adolescent, At Risk Mental State, Brain, IRM, Longitudinal, Machine Learning, Psychiatry, Psychosis, Schizophrenia, Support Vector Machine, Ultra High Risk, Voxel-based Morphometry

Title: Peptide Biodiversity: Advancing Human Health Through Nature's Pharmacological Treasures (Biodiversity2Drugs)
Abstract:
The Biodiversity2Drugs project operates within a comprehensive experimental framework that places strong emphasis on the sustainable and responsible exploration of terrestrial and aquatic peptide resources for human health benefit. This framework is built upon the recognition that nature boasts rich biodiversity, encompassing a vast array of organisms, from bacteria to mammals, which have evolved a wide range of bioactive peptides. The primary research questions that drive this project revolve around identifying, characterizing, and harnessing these largely unexplored peptides. To tackle these questions, a diverse group of scientists are teamed-up from 15 academic research institutions in 13 countries. This team is complemented by 10 self-financed partners from Australia, India, Germany, the UK and the USA. 

The core hypothesis underpinning Biodiversity2Drugs is that these nature-derived peptides, especially those interacting with cellular receptors, have substantial potential to serve as novel therapeutic lead compounds. The project adopts a pioneering approach, introducing a unique combination of computational analysis and high-throughput methodology that respects biodiversity by minimizing the ecological impact of peptide sampling while maximizing inherent therapeutic value for mankind. To achieve these objectives the project has been organized in 6 (+1) work packages (WPs):

WP (0): Coordination, Dissemination, Reporting, Communication, Outreach/Policy
WP (1): Peptide Mining and Biodiversity
WP (2): Peptide Evolution and Ecology
WP (3): Computer-Assisted Ligand Mapping and Optimization
WP (4): Green Peptide Chemistry Pipeline
WP (5): Pharmacological Screening and Validation
WP (6): Translation for Societal Impact

The project's primary objectives include addressing urgent clinical challenges across multiple domains, encompassing inflammation, infectious diseases, autoimmunity, pain, metabolic disorders, neurodegenerative diseases, and cancer. This endeavor employs state-of-the-art methodologies such as artificial intelligence (AI)-driven modelling, alongside a focus on eco-friendly peptide production to ensure alignment with sustainable practices. Comprehensive in vitro and in vivo characterization forms a pivotal component, facilitating a deep comprehension of peptide interactions with cellular receptors and their physiological impact. The overarching goal is to identify lead peptides with specific pharmacological profiles, holding promise for clinical development as drugs or diagnostics, or potential research probes. Collaboration among academic and industrial partners, coupled with a commitment to sustainability, underscores the project's objective: harnessing biodiversity for the responsible and scientific development of tools and drugs. In essence, the Biodiversity2Drugs initiative seeks to leverage nature's rich biodiversity to advance medical science and therapeutics.

The project stands out for its innovative exploration of peptide biodiversity, an underexplored domain in Nature-Based Solutions, offering potential applications for new therapeutics. It enriches our knowledge by intertwining ecological and evolutionary aspects of these peptides to shed light on their structure-function relationships. The paradigm-shifting approach to drug discovery distinguishes itself through data-driven comparative peptidome mining, combined with advanced computational tools, high-throughput activity screening and green chemistry of bioactive peptides across diverse organisms, incorporating sustainability practices in sampling and production. Leveraging artificial intelligence for peptide optimization and fostering interdisciplinary collaboration on a global scale, the project drives innovation in peptide-based drug discovery. Its holistic examination of peptides within their natural contexts not only opens avenues for pharmaceutical breakthroughs but also underscores the significance of creating biological knowledge and preserving biodiversity. Positioned as a pioneering force, Biodiversity2Drugs is set to uncover groundbreaking discoveries and transformative drug leads, revolutionizing pharmaceutical research and healthcare.
Keywords: biodiversity, drug discovery, nature-derived peptide, peptide library, peptide synthesis

Title: AI-Driven Methods for Patient-Specific 3D Head Models Using Multimodal and Incomplete Data for Facial Skull Injury Reconstruction
Abstract:
3D head models, generated from CT and MRI, are becoming essential in modern clinical procedures due to their detailed anatomical accuracy. Extracting these models from imaging data is relatively straightforward, allowing for the creation of precise 3D representations of the post-trauma state in facial-skull injury patients. However, for surgical planning of skull injury reconstruction, bones need to be realigned and implants placed to restore the facial shape and appearance prior to the injury. The only reference doctors have for this pre-injury state is a set of photographs of the patient, which are inadequate for surgical planning as they lack 3D information and integration with anatomical data.
This underscores the urgent need for advanced methods capable of generating highly detailed 3D models of pre-trauma head morphology, accurately capturing both soft tissue and bone. These models serve as references and enable 3D implant design and simulation of treatment outcomes.

In this project, we address the fundamental challenge of creating a 3D patient head model representing the *pre-trauma* state, which cannot be captured using conventional imaging. This involves unique scientific hurdles, particularly the integration of partial and multimodal data, which we will tackle using AI-driven methods. The key idea of this proposal is to 3D reconstruct the patient's face by leveraging pre-trauma 'in-the-wild' photographs and post-trauma partial 3D scans of the unaffected, healthy areas of the face. We estimate the bones from the 3D facial surface, using partial healthy bone data as a constraint in our AI-driven skull estimation method, and integrate as prior a high-fidelity model of the orbital bones to ensure precision in both reconstruction and function. This 3D head model can be integrated with physics simulations to compute soft tissue deformation resulting from bone realignment and implant placement. This enables us to solve an inverse problem by determining treatment parameters through an optimization process. 

In this collaborative project between ETH Zurich and the University Hospital Zurich, we leverage our expertise in Computer Graphics and medicine to significantly improve the treatment of facial and skull injuries. Through a continuous interplay of core research, technology transfer, and clinical evaluation, we advance knowledge in utilizing multimodal and partial data within AI, geometric modeling, and simulation. Our work enables the computation of 3D head models for facial-skull trauma patients, representing their condition prior to injury for the first time. This 3D reference has the potential to revolutionize treatment planning by supporting surgical strategies and facilitating person-specific digital implant design. This research will not only reinforce Switzerland's tradition of clinical excellence in Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery but also position us at the forefront of scientific innovation, leveraging AI and Computer Graphics to significantly improve patient care.

Title: Acceleration of complex motor learning by skill level-dependent feedback design and automatic selection
Abstract:
Provision of augmented (extrinsic) feedback is a common strategy to accelerate motor learning of real life tasks in sports or in rehabilitation. Trainers/therapists observe the learner, evaluate the performance, and use their expertise to provide adequate feedback. More and more, observation of the learner’s performance is enhanced by technology. Technical systems measure relevant kinematic and kinetic variables, which a human trainer can hardly sense in a precise, objective, and consistent manner. Technical systems also enhance the (human) possibilities to mediate the measured performance to the learner, e.g. by visual displays, headphones/speakers, or robots. However, these multilayer, technical possibilities to provide augmented feedback have rarely been evaluated.
The mediated information of feedback displays should be adequate to the current skill level of the learner. For instance, in the early learning phase of a complex task, which involves several muscles and is high-dimensional, augmented feedback should mediate the movement structure so that the task itself is understood. In a later phase, feedback designs should help to fine-tune the movement. In simple task learning, fine tuning might be required from the beginning on as movement task itself is known a priori. Therewith, principles derived from simple task learning can hardly be generalized to other learning phases than fine-tuning. Only when complex tasks are investigated, the impact of different feedback designs along the multiphase range of learning can be determined. Such knowledge is crucial, as a learning process can only advance if an inappropriate feedback design is replaced by a more effective one at the related skill level. Experienced trainers/therapists know when to change their feedback, i.e. they recognize when the learner cannot profit from a feedback (anymore). In technical training systems, a concept on how to select adequate feedback along a learning process of a specific, real life task has not yet been evaluated.
In this project, a concept to enhance training of a complex, real life task by technical systems is developed and evaluated at the example of rowing. Thereby, firstly, feedback designs are proposed based on existing literature and own experiments. The feedback designs are evaluated along a complete learning process to determine when being appropriate. Thereby, criteria have to be derived that monitor the process of learning. Secondly, to automate switching to the most effective feedback, a reinforcement strategy for individualized learning is developed. Data of previous subjects will allow an estimation which feedback is most effective at the current skill level. In addition, data of the current subject is considered to adjust the reinforcement strategy to the individual as the effectiveness of a feedback design is assumed to depend on the subjects. Fourthly, the concept is compared to unsupervised concepts, e.g. with fixed or random provision of the same feedback designs. Therewith, this project contributes to the understanding of complex motor learning and optimization of augmented feedback designs and concepts in real life tasks. The gained results have a direct impact in sports and rehabilitation, where the application of technical systems such as training simulators and rehabilitation robotics become more and more popular.
Keywords: Automatic Switching of Feedback, Complex Human Motor Learning, Multimodal Feedback, Multiphase Learning Process, Personalized Feedback, Reinforcement learning

Title: Learning faces from DNA
Abstract: The problem of recovering the geometric structure of the human face from DNA is an importantinstance of genotype-to-phenotype mapping, one of the Holy Grails of modern genetics.Successfully solving it leads to a breakthrough in many applications, ranging from personalizedmedicine to biometrics and forensics. However, the problem is complex involving the jointmodelling of known and unknown associated genetic interactions with related facial features. Toalleviate many of the difficulties involved, we invert the problem, by learning a mapping from thefacial geometry to the genetic features. As the facial structure is the overt, integrated, andmeasureable endpoint of all relevant genetic features and their interactions, the task is no longer toextrapolate partially given genetic features and their interactions, but to learn relevant facialfeatures to classify onto any set of associated genetic features. With advanced deep learning thatintrinsically deals with non-Euclidean geometric data, we can learn face-to-DNA mappings. Thespace of learning parameters can be restricted by integrating biological knowledge into thenetwork’s architectural design. This forward face-to-DNA mapping is of value on its own leading toface-to-DNA biometrics, e.g. confirm whether the face of a suspect matches with DNA found on acrime scene. Also, an actual face will be reconstructed from DNA by “reversing” the neural networkin order to synthesize faces with prescribed genetic features.
Keywords: 3D shape analysis, biometrics, face-from-DNA, facial reconstruction, genetics, geometric deep learning, imaging

Title: How individual-level choices drive collective consumer behavior in social networks
Abstract:
Many managerial decisions aim to influence collective consumer behavior, e.g., to stimulate the adoption of a new service or to promote sustainable consumption.
Collective consumer behavior results from the aggregation of many interconnected individual-level choices, whose dynamics determines the success or failure of new products and their creators. There exists a rich literature on both the drivers of individual-level choices and the collective dynamics of adoption processes, but only few studies integrating both perspectives. Specifically, the consumer behavior literature mainly focuses on the individual level by identifying the main drivers of consumer choices via experiments and surveys, but the obtained individual-level results are usually not integrated into dynamic models of innovation growth. On the other hand, the innovation growth literature mainly focuses on the collective level, by modeling the aggregate market dynamics of an innovation. The models are usually not calibrated on empirical individual-level behavior, which can results in misleading aggregate predictions of new product success. Studies integrating empirical individual-level choices and collective behavior are rare, yet much needed to improve marketing interventions aimed at influencing collective behavior.

This project is the first systematic effort to connect empirical individual-level choices with the collective success of new products and their creators in social systems. It will focus on three interrelated stages along a product’s lifecycle: the product’s creation (Work Package 1, WP1), its early adoption (WP2), and its collective adoption by a social network of individuals (WP3). The project has three main goals: (1) understand how individual-level creative strategies predict and drive the long-term collective success of product creators (WP1); (2) understand the role played by different groups of early adopters in the collective success of a new product (WP2); (3) understand how to integrate individual-level behavioral heterogeneity and social network structure to predict the collective success of a diffusion process as well as improve seeding policies (WP3). For each of the three goals, we will not only advance theoretical understanding, but also derive managerial implications for seeding policies. These ambitious goals will be achieved via a rare combination of traditional methods in consumer behavior (such as discrete-choice models and experiments) with social network and machine learning methods.

The impact of this project will be ensured by original research publications in leading management journals (such as Management Science and Journal of Marketing Research) and interdisciplinary journals (such as PNAS and Nature Communications) as well as four additional outputs: (1) a “golden standard” dataset on individual-level choices in presence of social signals and private information, which researchers can use to calibrate simulations of collective consumer behavior; (2) a review article that summarizes the state-of-the-art on seeding policies, including the project’s findings; (3) a manager-oriented article aimed at Harvard Business Review; (4) a software package and online platform that researchers and managers can use to test different seeding strategies for different products under different network configurations. Beyond marketing science and practice, this project aims to become a reference point for scholars interested in predicting and managing collective social behavior, which is a timely challenge that involves disciplines as diverse as sociology, economics, and complexity science.

To achieve this project's objectives, the research team has to meet high standards: A rare combination of skills from various fields is needed, namely marketing, social sciences, statistics and computer science. Based on the applicant's earlier research and his affiliation with the “URPP Social Networks” at the University of Zurich, he is in the unique position to put together such a team. Given this remarkable opportunity to address a key question in marketing science, the applicant would greatly appreciate the support by the SNSF to fund this project.
Keywords: Innovation growth, Marketing, Online communities, Social Influence, Social Networks

(2) a review article that summarizes the state of the art on seeding policies, including the project’s findings; (3) a manager oriented article aimed at harvard business review; (4) a software package and online platform that researchers and managers can use to test different seeding strategies for different products under different network configurations. beyond marketing science and practice, this project aims to become a reference point for scholars interested in predicting and managing collective social behavior, which is a timely challenge that involves disciplines as diverse as sociology, economics, and complexity science. to achieve this project's objectives, the research team has to meet high standards: a rare combination of skills from various fields is needed, namely marketing, social sciences, statistics and computer science. based on the applicant's earlier research and his affiliation with the “urpp social networks” at the university of zurich, he is in the unique position to put together such a team. given this remarkable opportunity to address a key question in marketing science, the applicant would greatly appreciate the support by the snsf to fund this project.. innovation growth, marketing, online communities, social influence, social networks

Title: Deep Learning in Multi-type Named Entity Recognition for Biomedical Event Extraction
Abstract:
In this project, I want to exploit a new technology – Deep Learning – in order to improve the important task of event extraction in the area of biomedical text mining.

In the Life Sciences, knowledge is scattered across an abundance of scientific publications. Currently, the most comprehensive index of biomedical literature, PubMed, lists more than 27 million records, which are being updated with well over 20000 new entries per week. Finding relevant information has become a tough task, as most findings are only available in texts written in natural language, which is not easily accessed through automatic methods. Furthermore, in the era of “Big Data”, methods are available that allow for analysing and meaningfully interpreting massive amounts of information; however, these methods require the data to be represented in a structured, machine-readable format.

Accurate and efficient tools are needed to address these challenges. Text mining provides means for extracting structured knowledge from natural-language text, which are generally classified into distinct tasks: named entity recognition (detecting mentions of genes, chemicals, diseases etc.), entity linking (assigning identifiers to these entities), and relation and event extraction (finding relationships between entities). Tools that solve these tasks – separately or in a sequential pipeline – are useful in many applications. For example, information retrieval benefits from the correct recognition of biomedical entities: When searching for documents concerning the protein CPA1 (carboxypeptidase A1), an adequate tool is expected to find not only mentions of the abbreviation and the full name, but also the occasionally used short form CPA. Furthermore, “CPA” might also refer to a disease (cardiopulmonary arrest) and possibly to other, unrelated concepts, thus challenging the tool to exclude irrelevant matches. As another example, event extraction is used to enrich comprehensive biological models, such as regulation or pathway networks. Such models can be used to predict the potential effect of a certain chemical on a range of biological targets, which is a powerful instrument for detecting drugs that might cure a certain disease. These models are constructed by connecting a large number of relational facts (such as protein–protein interactions), which are in part extracted automatically from text collections.

In recent years, Deep Learning has set new standards in many areas of artificial intelligence. In many fields of natural language processing, the application of deep neural networks has improved performance of standard tasks. For biomedical texts, however, it seems that Deep Learning has not yet been studied quite as well as for other domains. Little is known, in particular, about its effects on the tasks of biomedical named entity recognition and entity linking, which are initial steps of a typical text-mining pipeline. The goal of the proposed project is to study the potential benefits of applying deep neural networks to biomedical named entity recognition. The proposed method will be evaluated at different stages in a text-mining pipeline that includes entity linking and event extraction.
Keywords: deep learning, event extraction, named entity recognition, natural language processing, text mining

Title: The algorithmic (public) sphere: new media, knowledge production and access to information online
Abstract: Internet developments and algorithmic advances have been intrinsically linked in recent years, one powering the other. The extensive deployment of algorithms in managing and curating knowledge online evolved towards their integration in decision-making processes at many levels, from standard-setting to sanctioning measures. This project analyses the effects of algorithmic control and corporate ownership on the (re)constitution of public deliberation space(s). Building on an original analytical framework for governance mechanisms, it critically examines emerging rules and norms for algorithm-driven access to information on a hard-soft law continuum. The dimensions examined here apply to past and current regulatory initiatives, divided into three categories: legal enshrinement (rules that are binding), institutional consolidation (specialised bodies and lines of work) and modelling (soft rules for shaping behaviour, ranging from good practices and guidelines to influential statements or resolutions). Investigating how the individual and the collective access to information is reshaped through key algorithmic decisions, this project makes an initial inroad into the multifaceted governance of new media and knowledge production. Mixed methods are employed here for capturing the complexity of the field, including an initial mapping exercise for existing regulatory and self-regulatory initiatives, as well as content analysis and expert interview. Beyond its academic value, this study is timely for policy-makers and media law experts, but also for developers working on machine learning and artificial intelligence.The findings of the 18-month research project will be disseminated in both academic and policy communities via specialised articles, policy briefs and contribution to public discussions.
Keywords: access to information, algorithmic governance, decision-making, new media, public deliberation

Title: Statistical Frontiers in Dynamic Network Modeling
Abstract:
This project explores statistical advancements in Relational Event Modelling (REM) to analyse dynamic networks where interactions occur in continuous time. REMs can be used to study anything from social interactions, financial transactions, patient transfers and alien species invasions, capturing fine-grained temporal dependencies.

This project will focus on making REMs more interpretable, faster and more robust. In particular, it will focus on three challenges: (i) The role of time – understanding how network effects evolve across different time scales and how past events influence future interactions, in connection with novel goodness-of-fit strategies; (ii) Computational bottlenecks – improving efficiency in estimating network covariates to enable scalable analysis of large datasets; (iii) Causal inference in dynamic networks – such as disentangling homophily (preference for similar others) from social influence (behavioral adaptation due to interactions).

Building on prior work in theory and applications, this research will integrate modern statistical learning techniques to enhance REM's capabilities. The goal is to develop more robust causal inference methodologies, improve computational efficiency, and refine the modelling of temporal dependencies in dynamic networks. These advancements will contribute to the broader field of statistical network science, making REM a more powerful tool for understanding complex event-driven systems.

Title: Integrating Symptom-Based Network Analysis and Multimodal Normative Modeling for Transdiagnostic Pediatric Mental Health Research
Abstract:
In recent years, Switzerland and other Western countries have seen a concerning increase in the prevalence of mental health disorders, reaching unprecedented levels. Mental health disorders usually require long-term specialized medical and behavioral support, which causes a significant economic and social burden. Importantly, many mental health disorders begin to emerge during childhood and adolescence, which are critical stages in human development marked by essential neural reorganization. To advance our understanding of the pathophysiology of mental health disorders and identify clinically relevant biomarkers, it is therefore crucial to strengthen our research efforts into the developing brain. However, a significant challenge facing current pediatric mental health research is the reliance on traditional diagnostic labels and group-average case-control studies. Emerging research from genetics, system neuroscience, and behavioral science has challenged the validity of traditional diagnostic labels that have been developed largely blind to the underlying neurobiological pathology. To address these limitations, initiatives such as the Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) have been established, which aim to refine the classification of mental disorders by mapping neurobiological and behavioral dimensions that cut across diagnostic categories. Despite these efforts, a transdiagnostic approach that moves away from case-control comparisons has been adopted in only a limited number of pediatric mental health studies to date. This may be attributed, at least in part, to the insufficient availability of large-scale transdiagnostic pediatric datasets and adequate analysis methods that can effectively capture commonalities across diagnostic categories, model patient heterogeneity, and facilitate individual-level statistical inferences.
To address this gap, in this project we aim to develop a novel analysis framework that integrates two powerful methods: symptom-based network analysis and multimodal normative modeling. The benefit of symptom-based network analysis is that it considers mental health disorders as co-occurring clusters of symptoms within complex networks, allowing us to provide explanations for commonalities across and heterogeneity within diagnostic categories. Normative modeling shifts the focus away from group-level comparisons that rely on traditional diagnostic labels towards characterizing how each individual pediatric patient differs from the neurotypical pattern and how these deviations relate to behavior and clinical outcome. Currently, normative modeling is restricted to a single data modality. Here, we develop novel normative models that combine structural MRI and functional EEG data to improve our understanding of the complex interrelationships between structural pathology and dysfunctional neural mechanisms. To accomplish this, we will use an existing large-scale (N>4000) transdiagnostic database from the Healthy Brain Network (HBN) initiative. As part of the initiative, children and adolescents (age: 5-21 years) with diverse mental health problems underwent clinical interviews, cognitive and behavioral testing, as well as EEG and neuroanatomical MRI. Importantly, our new analysis framework allows us to subsequently leverage unsupervised machine learning to identify behavioral and neurobiologically homogeneous subgroups of pediatric patients across diagnostic categories. Identifying transdiagnostic subgroups has significant clinical implications, as it enables clinicians to stratify patients into appropriate clinical trials or interventions, leading to a more efficient use of healthcare resources and potentially improved patient outcomes while reducing costs. Finally, building on our analysis framework, we predict future clinical outcomes by implementing predictive modeling, which can enable early detection of diagnostic markers and tailor therapeutic intervention strategies to the individual. Overall, our project aims to provide a more comprehensive understanding of inter-individual variability in pediatric mental health disorders, irrespective of diagnostic boundaries. By doing so, it has significant clinical implications, as it can help clinicians to better identify and treat pediatric mental health disorders, ultimately improving outcomes for children and their families.
Keywords: EEG, clinical outcome prediction, multimodal, neuroanatomy, normative modeling, pediatric mental health disorders, symptom-based network analysis

Title: Probabilistic learning in deep cortical networks
Abstract:
To survive and thrive in continuously changing environments animals must constantly translate the information provided by the external world into appropriate behavior. In practice, however, this proves difficult because sensory information is almost always incomplete, sparse and noisy. Furthermore, their ability to hold and transform information is limited. Thus, the internal representations of information acquired by an organism – and, ultimately, the decisions that it can make – are fundamentally uncertain.
Uncertainty can be dealt with in a principled manner within the mathematical framework of Bayesian probability theory, which offers a method of formalizing and combining prior beliefs with available data in a rational and, in some sense, optimal way. The solid theoretical grounding of the probabilistic approach and its practical appeal have led to countless applications in almost every field of engineering and science. The ubiquity of Bayesian inference is however not limited to engineering and scientific endeavor: mounting evidence from behavioral and neuroscience studies supports that humans and primates, but also simpler organisms naturally process information according to the rules of probability theory.
In line with such empirical findings, the idea that the brain performs probabilistic inference is highly influential in theoretical neuroscience, that has inspired models for a wide range of tasks, from sensory perception all the way down to behavior and decision-making. However, the majority of neuroscience theories do not approach learning as a problem of probabilistic inference. This is striking, as learning plays a crucial and natural role in probabilistic modelling and learning can itself be understood as a problem of probabilistic inference, with the goal of seeking plausible models that explain observed data. Such models are then used as the basis to make predictions. Importantly, unlike in non-probabilistic approaches, predictions are explicitly (and quantitatively) informed by model uncertainty. Model uncertainty arises naturally because data is limited and noisy: a set of observations is therefore expected to be consistent with many different models. Neglecting this will often result in overconfident predictions, poor generalization, as well as the inability to communicate prediction uncertainty to downstream neural circuits.
The aim of my research is to address this major problem and develop models of probabilistic learning in cortical neural circuits that represent parameter uncertainty and leverage such knowledge when making predictions. I will model cortical learning as an inference process in which synaptic weights correspond to model parameters. Because exact Bayesian inference is intractable in neural networks, my first objective will be to develop a biologically-plausible approximate inference method, resorting to a type of approximation known as stochastic variational inference. This leads me to consider the hypothesis that synapses evolve stochastically by sampling from distributions of approximating models that are consistent with data, and that their temporal variability encodes uncertainty. As a second objective, I will then develop a unified model which takes into account both synaptic weight and neural activity uncertainty, which plays a pivotal role in probabilistic theories of perception and decision-making. Finally, for my third objective, I will increase the level of biological realism of my models. This will allow me to better capture existing experimental data and propose novel experiments.
I will focus on a class of models that I termed deep cortical networks (DCNs), that lie at the intersection of neuroscience and machine learning while keeping a balance between biological detail and computational capability. This will allow me to connect with ongoing research in artificial deep neural networks (DNNs; where Bayesian learning is an active and important current research direction) while advancing our understanding of if, and how, cortical circuits adjust and acquire information probabilistically. If my research is successful, it will result in novel, experimentally-falsifiable neural circuit learning models, as well as artificial neural networks with improved performance.
Keywords: Bayesian parameter inference, deep cortical network models, deep neural networks, model uncertainty, neuroinformatics, probabilistic learning, theoretical neuroscience

Title: Health Behavior Informatics and Multimodal Machine Learning for Automatic Healthcare Decision Support
Abstract:
Understanding of verbal and non-verbal behaviors is a crucial component of the mental health diagnosis, clinical decision and therapy. Combining verbal and non-verbal behaviors with physiological information, therapists and psychiatrists make a wide range of clinical decisions, including medication management, psychotherapeutic interventions, and assessments on clinical course and severity. Thus, analysis of human communication dynamics of clinical interview and therapy is critically important to create technologies that are able to understand and actively participate in these types of interactions. That is why, automatic analysis of human communication has recently drawn much attention in computer vision, affective computing and social signal processing community for healthcare decision support, because: i) The recent progress in speech, facial expression and gesture recognition
allows us to start with automatic analysis of verbal and non-verbal behaviors are critically important
components of the mental health diagnosis. ii) Multimodal analysis allows us to discover the specific behavioral and physiological markers of mental disorders. iii) Automatic recognition of human multimodal behaviors and patterns in physiological changes has shown the advantage and promise of using computer science techniques to support traditional clinical practice.
The project aims to provide efficient models and methods to detect behavioral and physiological markers associated with mental disorders for support healthcare decision. This approach is naturally linked to the question of how to prevent mental disorders, rather than treating them at the latest stage when individuals suffer, as well as social and economic cost have already occurred. Furthermore, the models and methods that will be designed and developed to discover the specific behavioral and physiological markers can be applied to support a wide range of mental disorder diagnosis. The development of automatic behavioral and physiological marker analysis is expected to have an economic value and impact on society, since it could be used for healthcare support all
over the world.
We are interested in discovering dependencies among: low level verbal and non-verbal cues (gaze, body orientation, turn taking patterns, presence of negative words, tone and prosody of voice, face expression), high level behavioral codes (e.g. acceptance, positivity, blame, negativity, approach-avoidance, emergent leadership, extroversion, engagement, rapport, involvement), physiological changes (e.g. patterns in blood pressure, heart rate, sweating, expiratory flow rates) and emotion states (e.g. being exited, bored, sad, angry). In particular, we aim to provide the automatic multimodal evaluation of clinical interviews and the planning of therapy process using technologies and computational modelling of multimodal signals.
The aim of the project is to carry out the automatic analysis of various verbal and non-verbal behavioral cues as well as patterns in physiological changes during clinical interviews and therapy sessions for mental disorders, such as schizophrenia, depression, suicidal ideation and sleep disorder.
Keywords: Computational Modelling, Health Behavior Informatics, Healthcare Decision Support, Multimodal Machine Learning, Multimodal Signal Processing and Fusion, Pattern Recognition

grant_text: a high throughput microphysiological platform to analyze the role of the aging human vasculature in melanoma metastases. the effective treatment of metastatic melanoma is an unmet clinical need since less than 50% of patients survive at 5 years after diagnosis of advanced disease. this dismal prognosis is mainly due to the formation of brain metastases for which no effective therapies are available. of all cancer types, melanoma has the highest rate of cerebral tropism, with over 40% of advanced patients developing brain metastases. clinical observations have shown that patients above 70 years old have metastatic melanomas with the most aggressive prognostic features, which result in the highest mortality rate. surprisingly, the impact of physiological aging on the pattern of melanoma metastases is largely unexplored when studying the biological mechanisms driving cancer cell dissemination. pre clinical and clinical studies have shown that blood vessels and lymphatics experience structural and functional changes during physiological aging, including compromised cell cell junctions and increased vascular permeability, particularly in the blood brain barrier (bbb). this compromised vascular function coupled with the loss of vascular identity genes increases the transmigration of circulating melanoma cells in the brain (i.e. extravasation). however, a detailed mechanistic explanation of the higher rate of melanoma cell transmigration through the vasculature of old patients is still lacking, partially due to the absence of reliable models that: 1) recapitulate features of vascular aging; 2) allow high throughput (ht) parametric studies to identify drivers of melanoma cell extravasation. to fill this gap, we propose to: 1) design a high throughput system hosting 3d perfusable human bbb minitissues; 2) compare bbb models derived from human donors of different ages and validate them at the molecular and functional level by comparison with human brain tissue biopsies and published datasets; 3) analyze the biological mechanisms driving the age dependent extravasation of melanoma cells and provide a list of candidate targets involved in melanoma extravasation for functional perturbation; 4) perform a crispr based screening of the most promising targets and validate them a key aspect of the proposal is the multidisciplinary integration of microvascular network (mvn) biofabrication, multi omic characterization of human brain vasculature, and design of a data analysis methodology that exploits artificial intelligence to combine experimental data with existing databases to identify and rank pathways underlying melanoma extravasation. during the project we then expect to: 1) design and microfabricate a ht platform hosting human 3d minitissues that allows to perform large scale experimental campaigns; this platform is fully integrated with ht biofabrication strategies and ht analytical techniques, and can find applications in any other field requiring screening of compounds or drugs (e.g. combination of chemotherapies on patient derived cells); 2) provide a detailed molecular and functional analysis of the differences characterizing the human bbb during aging, which can have consequences in other disease models including neurodegeneration; 3) identify drivers of melanoma extravasation through the bbb by combining the molecular and functional profile of vasculature and cancer cells through ht live confocal imaging, automated quantification of local vascular permeability and cutting edge spatial transcriptomics; the design of a novel data analysis pipeline is expected to discover potential mechanisms of extravasation also shared by immune cells during inflammatory processes or other phenomena involving immune cell mobilization; 4) validate the identified targets through a functional crispr screening and human tissue microarrays, which provide a higher clinical relevance and are often neglected in basic biology studies.. aging, biofabrication, blood vessels, human microvascular networks, melanoma metastases, microphysiological systems, blood brain barrier

Title: Fourth-Generation Neural Network Potentials for Molecular Chemistry
Abstract:
Machine learning potentials (MLP) have become an important tool for performing atomistic simulations with the accuracy of electronic structure methods but at a small fraction
of the computational cost. To date, most applications have been reported in materials science, while organic molecules have been primarily studied for benchmark purposes in vacuum. Although most chemical reactions occur in the liquid phase, applications of MLPs to solvation and molecular chemistry in solution are still very rare. Apart from the complexity of the involved configuration space, a major challenge for studying these systems is the need for a highly accurate description of intra- as well as intermolecular interactions, from strong covalent bonds via hydrogen bonding to electrostatic and dispersion interactions. A particularly crucial aspect is the charge distribution in the involved species, which cannot be captured correctly by most current MLPs based on local
properties like environment-dependent atomic energies and charges. Recently, we have developed a fourth-generation high-dimensional neural network potential (4G-HDNNP), 
which combines the accurate description of local bonding and reactivity with long-range
interactions based on the global charge distribution in the system. This global description is not only essential for molecules containing delocalized electrons, e.g. in aromatic groups or conjugated $\pi$-systems, but also if the molecular charge is changing, like in (de)protonation, which is a key step in many types of reactions in organic chemistry. All these systems can in principle be studied by 4G-HDNNPs, which explicitly take into account the global charge distribution resulting from reactions, different functional groups and varying total charges, making this method a promising approach for molecular chemistry. The goal of this project is to explore the applicability of 4G-HDNNPs to molecular chemistry in solution by focusing on two major aspects, the quality of the density functional theory (DFT) reference data and the generalization of the 4G-HDNNP method. High-quality reference data will be obtained by benchmarking the accuracy of exchange correlation functionals beyond the Generalized Gradient Approximation (GGA) level to Quantum Monte Carlo and Coupled Cluster calculations, and by including dispersion and self-interaction corrections (SIC). The 4G-HDNNP will be extended by employing new descriptor types for structural discrimination that are applicable
even to difficult situations like conical intersections and by the introduction of charge constraints, which, along with SIC and constrained DFT calculations, will allow to overcome the integer charge problem in both, DFT and the 4G-HDNNP, in a consistent approach. This new set of computational tools will be implemented in the open-source software RuNNer and applied to representative solute-solvent model systems covering important scenarios in synthetic organic chemistry.
Keywords: machine learning, solvation effects
