Title: Improved methods for theoretical materials design
Abstract: The proposed research is aimed at developing and applying machine learning methods to study energy materials. In particular, I will use novel artificial neural network potentials to explore the surface structures and thermodynamics of TiO2 nano particles, which are touted as promising materials for environmental friendly hydrogen production. In contrast to similar research projects, I will investigate the materials properties not only for highly idealized conditions, but in environments which reflect realistic conditions encountered in water splitting applications. Ultimately, the goal is to establish design rules for new, improved photocatalytic materials. By going beyond the conventionally used approximate conditions, the expected results from this project will be of value for a better understanding of surface structures and their chemical activity for a wide range of materials.
Keywords: Interface, Machine Learning, Photocatalysis, Structure Prediction, Surface, Water Splitting

Title: Uncovering age-dependent changes in the budding yeast kinase signaling network
Abstract:
To maintain homeostasis, cells use a complex homeostatic signaling network (HSN) to sense and respond to external conditions and internal cues. Loss of the homeostatic capacity has been identified as one of the key deficits of aged organisms ranging from yeast to humans, increasing frailty and disease predisposition. An extensive kinase signaling network forms the backbone of the HSN and changes in protein kinase activities in aging have been shown to drive specific losses in cellular homeostasis. There are now multiple lines of evidence to suggest that specifically modulating the kinase signaling network associated with nutrient sensing can increase both lifespan and healthspan, improving maintenance of the global homeostatic signaling network.
It remains unclear how changes in kinase activities results in an age-dependent deregulation of the HSN and deterioration of proteome functionality. A detailed understanding of the causes of declining cellular functions during aging can be gained via systems-level studies of changes in kinase-signaling and proteome integrity.
 The overarching goal of my proposal is to understand how and why the HSN fails with age and give rise to different aging phenotypes. I will address this in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, which has served as an excellent model organism for aging research and to perform holistic systems biological studies. The proposed experiments, (1) will enhance our understanding of phosphorylation-dependent control of the HSN in yeast; (2) uncover signaling nodes in the HSN that are prone to age dependent failure; (3) and determine molecular aging trajectories that affect cellular homeostasis on the systems-level. 
To define the kinase signaling network at high resolution I previously developed rapid-robotic-phosphoproteomics (R2-P2), a method that enables large-scale quantitative phosphoproteomic studies8. This method enabled me to create the most comprehensive atlas of phosphorylation-dependent signaling in budding yeast up to date. I will now use this this resource to infer kinase activities, predict functional phosphorylation sites and compute logic models of signaling network modules to gain a better understand-ing of HSN control.
Concurrently, I have established an experimental system to enrich replicative aged yeast cells and applied a series of proteomic assays to measure protein abundance, phosphorylation, thermal proteome stability and protein turnover to identify alterations in signaling and proteome deterioration as a function of age. Analysis of protein level measurements revealed prominent changes in proteome integrity such as decreased abundance, high-turnover, and destabilization of proteins in biosynthetic pathways and destabilization of large protein complexes. Conversely proteins in energy metabolic pathways showed increased abundance and stabilization. I now plan to identify causal connections of age dependent proteome changes with phosphoproteomic responses in aging. Finally, age-dependent changes in the phosphoproteo-me will be integrated with the high-resolution kinase signaling network to identify parts of the HSN that are degrading during aging. 
The proposed project is a continuation of my research that I have performed during the last 3.5 years as a postdoc in the group of Prof. Judit Villén at the Department of Genome Sciences at the University of Washington. For my return phase I propose to finish this project in the computational biology group of Prof. Pedro Beltrao at the Institute of Molecular Systems Biology at ETH Zurich. Scientifically and professionally I will profit enormously from joining the Beltrao group. It will allow me to establish a novel expertise and gives me the possibility to apply their predictive machine learning models and post-translational regulatory network tools on the extensive proteomic framework I have built within the context of yeast signaling and aging.
Keywords: Aging, Bioinformatics, Computational Biology, Machine Learning, Mass spectrometry, Phosphorylation, Proteomics, Signaling, Systems Biology

Title: Legal Data Analysis (LDA) – A New Research Frontier for Legal Scholarship (in Switzerland)?
Abstract:
In the knowledge and network society, insights from data have become an essential resource. In large part, legal scholarship is yet to discover the potential of the computational analysis of legal data. “Legal data” refers to textual data contained in legal documents (judgments, contracts, statutes etc.). The project focuses on the contribution of legal data analysis (LDA) to legal scholarship. LDA refers to the application of computational techniques that use natural language processing (NLP), machine learning (ML), and other data science methods in order to automatically extract meanings or semantics from legal text corpora. LDA methods can be used for legal text-based predictions, classification, complexity measurement etc. 

The project aims to make a pivotal contribution in the endeavor to further align legal scholarship with digitalization. It seeks to impact legal methodology by constructively integrating LDA into doctrinal legal research (DLR)-designs. The central research question addressed by the new project is if and how LDA advances the process of legal knowledge production (with special emphasis on Swiss law). The specific aims of the project are:

• to identify the practical challenges faced by large-scale empirical legal research (ELR) projects (WP 1),
• to outline how LDA transforms ELR and advances the process of production of new legal knowledge (WP 2),
• to assess the implications of data-driven legal knowledge production from a theoretical and legal methodological perspective (WP 3),
• to identify areas of Swiss law that could benefit from LDA with a view to designing further interdisciplinary projects (WP 4).    

The project will build on a multi-method approach, combining qualitative methods (literature review, explorative interviews) with quantitative methods (data science). The expected results will include, first, an improved understanding of how the goals of legal scholarship can be advanced by using LDA. Second, the project will generate domain-specific expertise and knowledge on the applicability of selected data science methods to various legal contexts. Third, a dataset (relating to legal interpretation) will be released open access on which LDA methods are tested.
Keywords: empirical legal studies, legal data analysis, legal method, machine learning, natural language processing

Title: Reconciling geological and modelled reconstructions of Alpine glacier evolution from the Last Glacial Maximum into the Holocene
Abstract:
Quaternary glaciations have left numerous geological footprints in the landscape of the European Alps, especially during and after the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM). Despite extensive field evidence and dating constraints, the chronology of the glacier evolution is far from being well understood. Yet, understanding the relationship between climate change and glacial response since the LGM is important for setting current global warming and related glacier response into a long-term and dynamic context. Numerical models accounting for the glacier thermo-dynamics and mass balance have proven to be promising tools for simulating ice extent evolution under a variable climate. However, existing flow modelling reconstructions of the LGM Alpine Ice Field generally produce far too thick ice compared to observed trimlines, and the comparison of modelled extents to geological records such as moraines remains so far limited to maximum extents and largely ignores the transient record of deglaciation. These discrepancies between field- and model-based reconstructions is largely due to spatially too coarse models (>1 km) that do not resolve the complex relief of the Alps. 

Clearly, none of the existing and well-established traditional ice flow models can achieve the resolution required (200 m) in large scale and over timescales of several tens of millennia, either because they are computationally too expensive or because they are lacking essential physical processes. In contrast, the new Instructed Glacier Model (IGM) -- recently developed by the applicants -- utilizes deep-learning to manufacture a cheap ice flow emulator trained from physical glacier models. This permits in turn to speed-up the overall model by several orders of magnitudes with minor loss in accuracy, and thereby to achieve very high-resolution. Building on this IGM approach we aim in this project to simulate the maximum state and deglaciation of the last glaciation in the European Alps in agreement with the geological record. This will be done by (i) further developing IGM to include ice thermo-mechanical effects and a module for sediment transport and moraine production, and by (ii) performing with this model a large number of transient simulations of palaeo glacier evolution in the Alps since the LGM and through the Holocene. These applications will aim to (i) resolve the issue of LGM ice thickness (ice sheet versus ice field) and (ii) produce dynamic simulations of deglaciation and Holocene glacier fluctuations (including minimum extent) by newly integrating geological records (such as trimlines, dated moraine sequences, erratic boulders, etc.). Ultimately this project will produce a well constrained high-resolution transient reconstruction of ice extent over the Alps and enhance our ability to interpret the palaeo record and our understanding of the spatio-temporal response of glaciers to climate variations from the LGM through the Holocene.
Keywords: Climate, Deep Learning, European Alps, Geomorphology, Glacier, Ice flow modelling

Title: Exploring Conditioned Pain Modulation in horses: a quantitative AI supported approach
Abstract:
Personalized pain therapeutics is attracting great interest due to the tremendous inter-patient variability in the response to analgesic therapy. Quantitative pain phenotyping aims to identify and quantify traits that can predict individual differences in outcomes from pain-relief treatments. One of the most promising pain phenotypic domains is Conditioned Pain Modulation (CPM), which offers a quantitative measure of the body’s ability to filter nociceptive information and to modulate pain processing. 
The phenomenon that led to the discovery of the CPM was named “Diffuse Noxious Inhibitory Control” (DNIC), and actually originated from experiments with anaesthetized rodents. CPM, on the other hand, refers to psychophysical testing of pain modulation in conscious, wakeful subjects. To fill the gap between DNIC and CPM research, the Descending Control of Nociception (DCN) paradigm was developed leading to experiments in awake, behaving rodents. The main limitation of this paradigm is it focuses on solely nocifensive behavioural responses, while differences in personality, mood, and emotional states are not accounted for. 
This project aims to lay the foundations for a novel CPM paradigm in conscious animals. The use of the term `CPM’ in animals is intentional, stressing the importance of investigating not only nociceptive responses to quantifiable test stimuli and conditioning, but also cognitive appraisal of noxious inputs.
Our animal model in this project is the horse. Assessment and management of pain in horses is one of the biggest challenges of veterinary medicine at present. With the increasing societal awareness for animal welfare and growing criticism toward negative consequences that equestrian sports and “use” of horses might have on their well being, there is pressing need to make tangible progress in the neglected field of research of horse pain. But another reason for choosing the horse is that a large amount of experience is presently available to allow characterizing the equine personality traits, mood, and emotions in the context of health as well as in painful conditions. 
The aims of this project are, therefore: 
1.Developing clinical tools for a personalized approach to diagnosis and therapy of pain syndromes in horses; 
2.Promoting translational research providing evidence for cross-species comparison of CPM/DCN mechanisms. 
3.Developing novel AI tools for non-invasive quantification of pain responses in horses based on facial expressions, body language and other associated elements. 
To this end, we will collect data in experiments with healthy horses, as well as from clinical cases. 
We will use AI approaches developed in our previous work on recognition of pain and emotions from facial expressions in various species to develop non-invasive pain quantification instruments that will be correlated with other assessments, including clinical assessment, personality assessment and validated pain assessment instruments such as grimace scales. 

This multi-disciplinary project will provide an unrivalled frame of research, contributing not only to the field of equine pain medicine and animal affective computing, but also to the fundamental understanding of endogenous descending controls, using an original, highly advocated back-translation approach. Investigating CPM in conscious horses, free to display their behaviour and emotions during and around testing, would provide a unique opportunity to evaluate individual influences on CPM outcomes for non-human animals.

Title: A Market-based Approach for Querying the Web of Data
Abstract:
The Semantic Web is to computers what the traditional Web is to humans. The goal is to expose data in a way such that machines can easily find the information they are looking for. If implemented properly, a semantic search would lead to the desired results much faster than using a traditional search engine. To enable this vision, the data needs to be exposed in a machine-readable format, and RDF has to be adopted as the de-facto representation of Semantic Web documents. RDF documents co-exist with HTML documents and also link to other RDF documents, leading to the so-called Web of Data (WoD).

In contrast to the traditional Web, the majority of WoD datasets only exist due to subsidies from research projects or governments. This leads to a number of problems. First, when a research project ends, it is often the case that an endpoint simply disappears (because servers are costly). Second, RDF data is often out of date or has otherwise low data quality (because maintaining data is costly). Third, and most importantly, the majority of data that exists somewhere in some form is simply not available as RDF documents (because creating the RDF dataset and making it available is costly). The reason for these problems is simple: on the WoD, datasets are usually queried by algorithms rather than viewed by people, which removes the traditional incentives for publishing and maintaining data. In particular, advertising, the main source of income for search engines, does not work in this environment where machines process the data and automatically filter out unwanted information. This raises the question: How can the WoD free itself from purely relying on government subsidies and overcome the problems listed above?

We propose the use of a global market for querying the WoD, where queriers must pay for receiving results, and data providers get paid for answering queries. This creates a financial incentive for data providers to publish and maintain data. Additionally, this also enables the economically efficient allocation of resources in the WoD. Our approach takes into account the value from querying service-providers (or end-users), as well as the data providers costs. In contrast to prior work, we use market mechanisms that handle the “combinatorial aspects” of the problem in a principled way. Instead of using a “large-market” argument or “market equilibrium prices,” our market mechanisms are grounded in mechanism design theory which allows for a formal analysis of the market’s efficiency and incentive properties.

Our explorations break new ground in large-scale data organization. While prior work has investigated the technical means for the Semantic Web and Linked Data for the past 12 years, these explorations have never included the economic viability; it was always assumed that money would come in some way. The scientific impact of our work, therefore, lies in spearheading new investigations into the economic viability of the Semantic Web vision. Furthermore, this project pioneers investigations in pricing truly large, diverse, and complex information services a topic of utmost importance with the advent of big data and data science.
Keywords: Combinatorial Auction, Distributed Query Optimization, Economic Methods for Computational Problems, Federated Databases, Game Theory, Market Mechanisms, Mechanism Design, Semantic Web, Web of Data

Title: MIQmodel: Context-aware Mobile Internet Quality Model
Abstract:
On a growing scale, we use mobile applications and services ‘on the move’ (e.g., in a car or a train) to fulfil critical goals that rely on prompt and to-the-point mobile interactions ranging from last minute information about the important meeting we are about to join, to a health procedure that can save our fellow train passenger’s life. The challenge arises from the fact that the service-ability of these applications and our experience rely on the connection quality provided by the underlying mobile networking infrastructure, supporting the data exchange between the mobile device we use (e.g., a smartphone) and some remote application server(s) (situated somewhere “in the cloud”). This underlying mobile networking infrastructure we denote as the Mobile Internet (MI), and its connection quality as MIQ. As research studies show, the MIQ is a best-effort level quality. Nevertheless, the users develop high MIQ expectations; the more they value the utility of the mobile application at hand, and the more critical the use of this application is to their personal goal, the more critical they become of accepting a given experienced MIQ. It is especially so, if the experienced MIQ is surprisingly different from their expected MIQ. The MIQ contributes to the overall user experience (QoE); the QoE also embraces the service design (user interface) and service information quality, which are not treated in here. 
   The MIQ is defined by its speed, accuracy, dependability of the mobile connection establishment and then the subsequent MIQ stability. We denote these as Quality of Service (QoS) criteria for MI, which further depend on the user’s complex context (location, time, mobility speed and heading, access network, etc.).
   We present research project on developing timely and accurate contextual MIQ model that predict MIQ for mobile users in different context. We research the predictive accuracy, speed and computational complexity of the MIQ model, as well as we focus on precision and recall of this model to predict MIQ ‘surprises’, via modelling and predicting unexpected (by the user) MIQ conditions (e.g., bad access network). The model is based on a proactive assessment of QoS and MIQ context, and predictive modelling of MIQ for any future point in time. The MIQmodel is user-centric and enables to proactively control interactive applications, in order to meet the user’s expected MIQ levels and enable them to meet their goals. It contrasts with the current operator-based approaches – focusing on providing access to their wireless networks, yet not assuring the user’s experience for mobile applications. We evaluate our research with real network quality measurements data collected ‘in situ’ with a set of real mobile users ‘on the move’.
   The proposed project lies at the frontier of Human-Computer Interaction (HCI), pervasive and ubiquitous computing, network performance management, machine learning and predictive analytics. The project is timely - there is a significant need for research and commercial interest for mobile networking solutions, as smartphones became personal communication and computing devices affordable for the masses. Additionally, there is a growing number of applications providing time-constrained services to their mobile users, relying the success of their delivery, hence their users’ experience, on the ‘best-effort’ quality of the underlying wireless networks.
   To conduct the proposed research we have the necessary equipment including latest smartphones as well as infrastructure for collecting smartphone-based data from mobile users called mQoL Living Lab (mQoL-LLab). So far our research focused on the ‘basic’ system (QoSIS.com) for collecting network performance data from mobile users and using simple machine learning on that data. The next step taken in the project is to do in depth research and model the user’s experience and expectations in context, and its relation with mobile networking. Mr Fanourakis - the PhD student proposed for this project has already started some initial research towards it. 
   There are various potential exploitation areas of the MIQmodel research, including novel application development leveraging MIQmodel in their application quality management, and mobile networking solutions by network operators, leveraging the model towards enhancing their users’ experience ‘on the move’. The MIQmodel will be initially exploited via our on-going research projects and collaborations in the area of mobile networking, especially applied in healthcare, where the lack of quality assurance for mobile services can even result in endangering the patient’s life. It is our moral obligation to ensure quality in this emerging area, propelled by the exponential needs of the ageing, and chronically ill population.
Keywords: human factors, machine learning, mobile Internet, mobile networking, mobility, quality of experience, quality of service

Title: Multicompartment in vitro models of the nervous system
Abstract:
Neuroscience is the largest scientific discipline, because understanding the nervous system is one of the grand challenges of this century. Many top-down techniques exist to study brain activity including EEG, MEG, fMRI and other imaging tools but these have limited resolution both in space and time. Optogenetics enables us to visualize neural functions at high resolution in animals, and we also have a plethora of tools to study the molecular details of fundamental physiological processes, including optogenetics, gene-expression analysis, patch-clamp and other single-cell methodologies. In addition, we use machine learning to analyze our data and computational models help us understand the observed complex behavior.
Nevertheless, there is little doubt that we are only at the very beginning of our journey towards comprehending the nervous system. In addition, our aging society suffers from Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, chronic pain and many other related diseases and clinical trials often fail in humans due to difficulties in translating the results of animal experiments in this area.
This project tries to address this problem by developing complex in vitro models using human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) derived neurons and glia to capture essential features of the in vivo physiology. Recent advances in microphysiological systems will be used to build a nerve-on-a-chip that resemble the C-fibers of sensory neurons. A multicompartment microstructure will provide the geometric constrains to guide axonal growth and connect cells together according to the desired design. A high-density microelectrode array (MEA) will enable stimulating the in vitro nerve and the monitoring of action potential propagation in each individual axons. Myelination will be attempted by adding Swann cells into the hydrogel-filled nerve compartment. The effect of drug-exposure will be evaluated based on the electrophysiology recording, e.g. activity-dependent slowing, to establish the differences between healthy and damaged nerves. We will also build a memory-on-a-chip system to investigate synaptic plasticity and its diseases. The well-defined small neural networks will provide reproducible data that will be used to optimize biophysical computational neural networks. The models then in turn will suggest more complex networks which will be validated with experiments in an iterative manner. Finally, the most promising nerve-on-a-chip and memory-on-a-chip systems will be also realized using patient-derived cells in order to discover digital biomarkers based on the observed activity patterns. 
During previous projects, the Laboratory of Biosensors and Bioelectronics developed a unique toolbox that enables the proposed experiments: We can build small neural networks with single cell precision using an automated pick-and-place process, we can maintain stable culture conditions over weeks without human intervention using a custom made incubator with embedded liquid handling capabilities, we have established the means of interacting with the networks using MEA, and we have already developed the first version of the computational models and data-analysis tools. As such, we are in a privileged situation to perform this project.
Besides developing a platform that enables advanced in vitro studies with human neurons, the project will also answer fundamental neuroscience questions related to memory and learning, develop reliable computational models with predictive power, and provide alternative means to animal experiments. The comparison of data obtained from systems that are built using healthy and patient-derived cells will enable us to discover digital biomarkers of diseases and treatments, which provide a novel approach to drug discovery.
Keywords: brain-on-a-chip, computational neuroscience, iPSC-derived neurons, in vitro disease models, in vitro drug testing, in vitro neuroscience, microphysiological systems, nerve-on-a-chip, plasticity

Title: Combining artificial intelligence and environmental DNA to improve the prediction of marine fish range shifts under global change
Abstract: Species range shifts are one of the most frequent response to ocean warming. These shifts, which are expected to increase with future changes, have economic, social and human health implications. However, no clear rule can explain differences observed among species in range shifts, with climate no being the only factor involved. What happens for non-exploited and rare species? SHIFTeDNA proposes to fill this gap by analyzing an existing eDNA metabarcoding fish dataset collected from the poles to tropical seas. Based on this unique global database, we aim to i) revisit current fish distributions ii) predict accurate range shifts fish response to climate warming. We will use the last refinement in machine learning to analyze the millions of sequences available. We will build a reference database for 15000 marine fish to assign eDNA sequence to a species. The results will contribute to a better understanding of marine fish biogeography and a sustainable conservation of those resources.
Keywords: DNA metabarcoding, biodiversity, bioinformatics, climate change, environmental DNA, machine learning, monitoring

Title: Integrating Neuropsychological Models of Learning and Decision Making
Abstract:
Many decisions can benefit from learning. For instance, physicians improve their diagnoses on the basis of previous experience. Learning can help in avoiding mistakes and is therefore central for advancing personal and societal development. In the last two decades, cognitive neuroscience has greatly promoted our understanding of the neural mechanism underlying human learning and decision making (e.g., Glimcher et al., 2009). However, the two questions of how decisions emerge and how decisions are improved by learning have until now been mostly addressed independently from each other. The proposed research project aims at connecting neuropsychological models of learning and decision making to improve our understanding of both phenomena and to integrate them in a comprehensive theory of decision making.
Among psychological and economic theories of decision making, sequential sampling models (SSMs) offer a precise description of the cognitive process underlying decisions and are strongly supported by empirical evidence (Busemeyer and Townsend, 1993; Fehr and Rangel, 2011; Ratcliff and Rouder, 1998). The principle of SSMs is that evidence about available choice options is accumulated over time until an internal threshold (of required evidence) is met and a decision is made. A particular strength of SSMs is their ability to conjointly predict how and how quickly people decide. Neural representations of evidence accumulation have been found in cortical areas including the medial prefrontal cortex (Gluth, Rieskamp, & Büchel, 2012; Hare et al., 2011) and the intraparietal sulcus (Basten et al., 2010; Gold and Shadlen, 2007).
The learning-based improvement of decisions, on the other hand, is captured by reinforcement learning (RL) models (Sutton and Barto, 1998). At its core, RL uses the difference between expected and actual outcomes (i.e., the prediction error) to adapt future predictions and choices. On the neural level, the prediction error has been linked to phasic firing of midbrain dopamine neurons (Schultz et al., 1997; Tobler et al., 2005). 
As outlined above, existing literature targets only one of the two phenomena of learning and decision making at the same time. SSMs are tested under stationary conditions for obtaining stable estimates of model parameters, such as the height of the decision threshold. To derive choice probabilities, RL models use an exponential choice rule which is oblivious to the underlying decision mechanisms and unable to predict response times. The goal of this proposal is therefore to extend the scope of both approaches by using RL to model the change in SSM parameters in dynamic decision environments and by applying SSMs to RL scenarios for predicting both how and when decisions are made. Neuroimaging techniques, including electroencephalography (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), are used to support the cognitive modeling results as well as to understand how adaptive decision processes are implemented in the human brain.
Keywords: EEG, cognitive modeling, evidence accumulation, fMRI, preferential choice, reinforcement learning, reward

Title: VidFuncta: Neural Ultrasound Video Compression and Vision-Language Model
Abstract:
Background and Rationale: Ultrasound is a widely accessible and cost-effective imaging modality, yet its interpretation is challenging due to operator variability and poor standardization. During the Postdoc.Mobility fellowship at Yale, Julia Wolleb has focused on developing deep learning tools to support lung ultrasound (LUS) interpretation, particularly for tuberculosis triage. These efforts led to the creation of VidFuncta, a framework leveraging implicit neural representations (INRs) to compress and analyze entire ultrasound videos efficiently. The rationale is to build generalizable, low-cost  clinical decision support tools that can operate in real-world and resource-limited settings.

Objectives and Specific Aims: Building on the foundation of VidFuncta, the proposed return project aims to extend and refine the framework in two key directions. The first objective is to improve the quality and clinical utility of INR-based compression for ultrasound videos. Specifically, the goal is to preserve high-frequency image features that are essential for accurate medical interpretation, while maintaining high compression rates to support scalable data storage and sharing. The second objective is to transform VidFuncta into a multimodal framework by integrating clinical text data from expert ultrasound reports. This will enable the development of a vision-language model (VLM) tailored to ultrasound, allowing for interactive clinical applications such as automated report generation and an ultrasound-specific chat model. 

Methods: To achieve these goals, the project is structured into clearly defined tasks spanning a 12-month period. For Objective 1, the focus will be on enhancing the performance of VidFuncta’s compressed representations. This includes experimenting with alternative activation functions beyond the standard sinusoidal setup used in SIREN networks. Wavelet-inspired and variable-periodic activation functions will be tested to better preserve high-frequency content. Once the optimal configuration is identified, various compression strategies will be assessed by adjusting the size and dimensionality of the 1D representation vectors. 
For Objective 2, the project will leverage a large annotated dataset of 35,000 cardiac ultrasound videos and their corresponding clinical reports, collected from Istanbul Medipol University. These video–text pairs will be aligned and used to train a contrastive vision-language model. The compressed video representations from VidFuncta will be matched with text embeddings obtained from a pretrained language model. Training will optimize a contrastive loss function to align similar video-text pairs in a shared embedding space. The effectiveness of the vision-language model will be evaluated through retrieval tasks and report generation performance.

Expected Results and Impact: The expected outcome of this project is a next-generation framework for automated ultrasound interpretation based on VidFuncta, combining efficient data compression with clinically meaningful representations and multimodal learning. The improved compression module will allow for scalable and affordable ultrasound data storage while preserving diagnostic fidelity. The vision-language extension will enable interactive applications, such as automated reporting and interactive decision support, tailored specifically to ultrasound. These innovations are expected to make ultrasound AI tools more accessible and reliable, with potential impact in both high-income healthcare systems and resource-limited environments.
Keywords: Deep Learning, Implicit Neural Representations, Medical Image Analysis, Ultrasound Videos, Vision Language Models

Title: Harmony or Dissonance: A Quantitative Analysis of Asset Managers' Proxy Voting Behavior
Abstract:
Institutional investors are increasingly expected to incorporate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) considerations into their stewardship activities and proxy voting decisions (Majoch et al., 2017; Hoepner et al., 2018). Despite being widely acknowledged as a significant mechanism in theory, proxy voting’s practical impact has proven challenging for both academics and investors to quantify (McNulty & Nordberg, 2016; Barko et al., 2022; Broccardo et al., 2022). This difficulty arises not only from the unwieldy and dispersed nature of proxy voting data, which often lacks standardization and easy accessibility, but also from the complexity of tracing direct outcomes from specific voting actions to tangible corporate changes (Dimson & Karakas, 2015). Meanwhile, the 2024 proxy voting season is anticipated to feature an unprecedented number of ESG-related shareholder proposals, highlighting the escalating importance of investor impact through proxy voting, and underscoring the growing social relevance of this research topic (The Economist, 2024).
Recent studies have delved into the voting behavior of ESG funds, revealing a complex landscape where these funds, despite their sustainability mandates, may vote contrary to ESG principles in pivotal votes (Griffin, 2020; Li et al., 2023). This discrepancy raises critical questions about the integrity of asset managers' stated voting strategies versus their real actions. However, a significant challenge persists: accurately determining asset managers' stated preferences. A detailed examination of their proxy voting guidelines, which explicitly state their voting intentions on various issues including sustainability, is essential for this purpose. Yet, despite their significance, these documents have largely been overlooked in existing research, leaving a gap in our understanding of their influence on voting behaviors.  
This project aims to bridge this gap by conducting a comprehensive examination that pairs a detailed quantitative text analysis of the world's largest asset managers' proxy voting guidelines with a quantitative analysis of their voting records. This approach will not only assess the content and intentions outlined in the AMs' guidelines, but directly juxtaposes these intentions against concrete actions taken in sustainability-related votes. By comparing stated preferences with the preferences revealed by real-world behaviors, this research seeks to measure the extent of AMs' commitments to sustainability in theory (guidelines) and in practice (voting records), thereby providing a novel insight into the discrepancies between professed sustainability intentions and concrete voting patterns across multiple managers.
The proposed project utilizes a unique dataset of asset managers' voting records, with a specific focus on sustainability-related votes, as identified in partnership with two leading sustainability organizations. Currently the data covers the twelve largest Swiss asset managers and the global “big three” (Vanguard, State Street Global Advisors, and BlackRock) with plans to expand the coverage to dozens more asset managers in Q2 of 2024. The approach not only innovates in the use of experts’ identification of sustainability-relevant votes, but also in its analytical framework. Employing political science methodologies including ideal point estimation for the quantitative analysis of the voting records (Imai & Olmsted, 2016; Bolton et al., 2020) and natural language processing (NLP) techniques like topic analysis and sentiment analysis for the analysis of the proxy voting guidelines (Grimmer et al., 2022), the study brings a novel perspective to corporate governance and ESG.
The findings could serve as a critical resource for asset owners from pension funds to retail investors, policymakers, and corporate governance scholars, providing a more transparent and accountable framework for assessing asset managers' commitment to ESG principles. Furthermore, by rigorously highlighting and quantifying the discrepancies between proclaimed and actual voting behaviors, this research has the potential to catalyze a shift in industry standards specifically in the areas of AM transparency and accountability in sustainability practices. By making the insights accessible to the wider public domain, the results should stimulate change towards greater alignment between stated preferences and behavior. This, in turn, should lead to a more aligned investment landscape, fostering a broader movement towards more authentic commitments to corporate sustainability.
Keywords: Asset managers' voting behavior, Corporate governance, ESG, Sustainable finance

Title: Precision-Medicine for Neurological Disorders: Harnessing the Power of Big Data and Machine Learning for Biomarker Discovery and Drug Repositioning Strategies
Abstract:
BACKGROUND AND RATIONALE: Traumatic neurological disorders, such as spinal cord injury (SCI) and traumatic brain injury (TBI), have a devastating impact on the patients, caregivers, and society, reducing quality of life and massively burdening the health care system. Countless clinical trials have failed to identify effective disorder-modifying treatments for patients suffering from SCI or TBI thus far. This is a growing problem because of the increased incidence of SCI and TBI in many countries, likely due to greater numbers of falls in elderly individual (i.e., ageing population) and concussion in sport- and military-related activities. However, prior to chasing new treatments, we need to reconsider the design of traditional clinical trials in traumatic neurological disorders. Furthermore, innovative drug discovery strategies, such as drug repositioning, have to be considered to expedite the development of effective treatments for patients with SCI and TBI.
OVERALL OBJECTIVES AND METHODS: The first objective of the proposed research is, thus, to create and implement an innovative strategy to guide clinical trial designs as an alternative to the traditional “one-size-fits-all” approach. Specifically, this part of the project aims at analyzing high-dimensional datasets with machine-learning methods for biomarker identification in patients with SCI and TBI. Incorporating biomarkers into earlier phases of clinical trial development serves multiple purposes, ranging from informing patient stratification/ selection, safety and efficacy assessment, trial enrichment, to supporting the dose selection. The second objective is to identify commonly administered medications that modify neurological and functional recovery after acute SCI and TBI. The primary “innovative” method we are applying is observational drug effectiveness and safety studies. Observational studies will be performed using concomitant medication data from historical (i.e., Sygen and NASCIS) and contemporary data sources (i.e., TRACK-SCI, TRACK-TBI, CENTER-TBI). Drugs with beneficial effects should be considered as a potential therapy to enhance neurological or functional recovery. This would be possible through a drug repositioning strategy.
EXPECTED RESULTS: The application of clustering methods (e.g., k-means clustering, topological data analysis) will identify common features amongst patients with SCI or TBI, respectively, and subsequently divide the initial heterogeneous population into disjoint and more homogeneous supergroups (i.e., clusters). We hypothesize that these subgroups exhibit different trajectories in terms of how the recover. For the second objective, we expect to find drugs that (alone or in combinations) will significantly impact (i.e., beneficial or detrimental) neurological recovery following SCI or TBI, while others won’t have any effect.
IMPACT: The fundamental importance of the proposed project stems from the fact that even in the era of “modern” medicine traumatic neurological disorders (i.e., SCI and TBI) remain incurable, leaving millions of patients with permanent disabilities. Burdening the patient, caregivers, and the society as a whole, traumatic neurological disorders are one of the greatest threats to public health according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Thus, expediting the development of effective treatments constitutes a priority area of research for patients, but also the society as a whole. Biomarkers have the potential to enhance public health by novel means of understanding and diagnosing disorders, and providing strategies to determine responses to new treatments. Lastly, we are proposing an innovative and feasible approach that utilizes existing clinical trial data to identify drugs potentially modulating neurological recovery. Information gained from this study will be critical to best standards of care guidelines for the acute pharmacological management of SCI and TBI.
Keywords: Machine Learning, Neurological disorders, Polypharmacy, Precision medicine, Spinal Cord Injury

Title: Event-based representation and learning of stochastic systems on graphs
Abstract:
Deep learning has achieved remarkable success in inverse problems, simulating physics, and learning dynamical systems. It relies on highly parameterized networks trained on massive datasets which yields strong predictive performance, but often complicates interpretation of results. In domains such as Earth science or engineering, it is important to complement these large-scale approaches by structured, well-understood signal processing methods grounded in solid theoretical foundations.

Here we propose to develop such foundations for a class of stochastic dynamical systems on graphs. We are motivated by the observation that pressing signal processing challenges in Earth science, engineering, neuroscience, and social science share this underlying structure. In particular, we focus on scenarios where data arise from event-driven observations alongside classical synchronous sampling. Event-based observations naturally appear in seismology (earthquakes), finance (market crashes and abrupt signals), and neuroscience (action potentials), and are increasingly used by design in engineering systems (neuromorphic sensing). These events result from a hidden stochastic process driven by complex
domain-specific mechanism, and often unobserved variables. A key example is the stress in seismology, which couples multiple degrees of freedom so effectively that one can represent it via a  combinatorial graph. We seek to make inferences about signals (sampling theorems), the underlying system (system identification), or the graph itself (relational inference). To this end, we organize our work into three packages:
- WP1 - Parametric jump–diffusion models and uniform sampling: We begin by developing new parametric models for stochastic dynamics on graphs, focusing on jump–diffusion processes. This includes deriving physically informed drift terms (e.g., pseudodifferential or Fourier integral operators) and studying their properties. We then establish fundamental principles of sampling and system identification for these models, assuming regularly sampled observations. Key goals
include (i) characterizing identifiability under sparse or noisy data, and (ii) understanding how graph constraints improve the well-posedness of the underlying inverse problems. 
- WP2 - Event-based sampling and reconstruction: In parallel we will address asynchronous, event-driven observations that arise naturally in many physical, biological, and financial systems. We will unify currently disjoint ideas from point processes, neuromorphic sampling, and jump–diffusion modeling to form a coherent theory of event-based inference on graphs. This will include generalizing classical sampling theorems to event-based linked stress-release models and designing new algorithms for reconstructing both the system state and the underlying graph from irregularly spaced observations.
- WP3 - Deep foundation models for seismic data: We complement the work on foundations by exploring deep-learning approaches—especially state-space and transformer-like models—to handle multi-scale or long-context data that combine event streams and continuous signals. We will favor designs that embed physics-based constraints and graph priors learned from WP1–WP2. Here we will benefit from our recent expertise in building state-of-of-the art foundation models for
seismic data, and access to unique datasets and expertise through collaborations. 

Throughout the proposal we focus on the class of jump-diffusion processes, which naturally capture both smooth variability and sudden, event-like changes. They also serve as suitable signal models for event-based or neuromorphic observations, where events can be viewed as points on the jump manifold. Our goal is to build theory and algorithms to estimate different aspects of these continuous dynamical systems from partial, noisy observations.

Title: Improving Hardware Design with Deep Learning
Abstract:
The constant growth in performance and area/energy efficiency requirements of everyday applications has, in the last decades, influenced researchers to design more and more performant and efficient specialized hardware. Hardware accelerators have emerged as a viable solution to satisfy such requirements and address the end of Moore’s law and the breakdown of Dennard scaling.
However, hardware design is a complex process. It requires the description of millions of transistors that have to work in parallel in order to perform complicated tasks. Traditionally, Integrated Circuit (IC) design has relied on Hardware Description Languages (HDLs) to describe the logical components and their interaction at a Register Transfer Level (RTL). Nonetheless, the HDL design flow requires the concurrent definition of both functionality and implementation from a low-level view, and it does not scale for large applications. Therefore, such approaches cannot easily target complex applications or support the generation of circuit variants with different area and latency targets, as often required in case of different performance and cost constraints.
High-Level Synthesis (HLS) helped designers in this process. HLS tools allow the design of ICs starting from high-level specifications allowing designers to guide the synthesis process by using directives able to steer the resulting implementation according to the desired performance and requirement goals. While HLS allows to easily define vast design spaces for a given hardware specification, determining the performance (latency) and resource requirements (area, power) of each implementation still requires time-consuming syntheses. Moreover, the number of possible implementations of a design explodes exponentially with the number of applied directives, while, in general, only a few of them are Pareto-optimal – i.e., they show the best cost/performance tradeoff – from a performance and resources perspective.
Various HLS-driven Design Space Exploration (DSE) strategies have been proposed to identify (or approximate) the set of Pareto-implementations while minimizing the number of synthesis runs. These approaches aim at imitating or learning a model of the HLS tools to pre-estimate the effect of the HLS directives and steer the HLS exploration process. While mandating very few synthesis runs, such strategies struggle when coping with multiple, interdependent optimizations. Hence, they are often limited to capturing the effect of only a few directives. Nonetheless, existing methodologies are rarely considered together, as an ensemble of knowledge, during the exploration process and the choice of the proper DSE strategy is often mandated by the domain of the design to be implemented in hardware and by the designer experience. Moreover, previous attempts to automate this task using statistical inference have failed due to the limited expressiveness of vector-based representations of the input data. 
I aim to exploit the recent advancements in Geometric Deep Learning (GDL) to process and evaluate, in the form of graphs, candidate HLS optimizations for a given computational kernel and create a DSE framework able to leverage prior knowledge coming from existing DSE methodologies and from the outcome of past DSEs. This can be performed by extending a recent work that I have published, which showcased promising results while applying Transfer Learning (TL), and by learning, from input graphs representing an abstraction of the design specifications, a model able to generalize the effect of the HLS directives without needing a pre-characterization of the HLS tool.  Such a framework would push the boundaries of the state-of-the-art by offering the possibility, for the first time, to apply Deep Learning (DL) techniques in the context of HLS-driven DSEs.
Keywords: Deep Learning, Design Space Exploration, Hardware accelerators, Hardware design, Hardware/Software codesign, High-Level Synthesis

Title: Optimized Visualization Methods for Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics Data
Abstract:
We propose an extension of the project "Optimized Visualization Methods for Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics Data" (SPHvis+) in order to address further needs in the visualization of smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) results.  Besides the methods realized in the first funding period for isosurfaces, Lagrangian coherent structures, and direct volume rendering, further visualization methods have turned out to be highly desirable. One of them is a method for extracting free surfaces as triangle meshes, which is still not solved in a fully satisfying way, despite recent publications. Another goal is a visualization of the interface surfaces in multi-phase flow. Finally, for the huge data sizes of simulation results computed by our cooperation partners, we need to extend parallelization from the GPU level to the level of a multi-CPU/multi-GPU cluster.

The main objective of this proposal remains to visualize SPH data directly, i.e., without prior resampling or triangulation. Our approach is to respect the kernel functions that were used for the simulation and to reuse them also for visualization. The obvious advantage is that at each point in the domain any interpolated value is exact with respect to the SPH representation. However, it means that visualization algorithms relying on the cell structure of grids cannot be used but must be adapted or replaced by new algorithms. Compared to other data representations, SPH data allows us to compute gradients and second derivatives efficiently and in high quality. This fact is exploited for several types of visualization problems where a predictor-corrector strategy can be used. This holds formline-type feature extraction, but also for isosurface extraction and for computing Lagrangian coherent structures (LCSs). Both prediction and correction steps make heavy use of derivatives, therefore this strategy is appropriate.

After having designed and implemented methods for computing vortex core lines, isosurufaces,  streak surfaces, and Lagrangian coherent structures directly from SPH data, we intend to add two additional types of surfaces to our visualization tool box. Free surfaces are, somewhat surprisingly, not yet available in sufficient accuracy from existing implementations. Either the correct volume of the set of particles is not respected or the smoothing operation is not done consistently with the SPH representation. We plan to build on the free surface extraction method of Marrone et al., but replace the second stage in order to reduce discretization artifacts. Besides free surfaces, another surface of interest is the interface between two fluid phases such as water and oil. The extraction of interface surfaces is in some sense a symmetric version of the problem of free surface extraction. We will exploit this symmetry to obtain higher-quality results in shorter computing time.

Another goal of the proposed project is to extend parallelization of our algorithms from a single GPU to clusters of CPUs and GPUs. While interactivity or near-interactivity has been a goal of the first funding period, the goal is now to handle extremely large datasets which were computed on large clusters. We will achieve this by a modification of our acceleration structures in such a way that subtrees of the data hierarchy can be assigned to nodes of a cluster, such that each subtree is handled as in our current implementation. The proposed project extension will add to the state of the art in SPH visualization and reinforce the message that SPH data deserve special methods, different from point-sampled data. It will also create synergies with partners such as Anritz Hydro and the Swiss Center for Scientific Computing, and by this, with the NextMuSE FET-Open project. And finally, it will benefit our teaching activities by generating interesting topics for Master's theses, and by providing real-world cases  for courses and practical exercises.
Keywords: Free Surface Reconstruction, GPU Computing, Parallelization, Scientific Visualization, Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics

Title: Automatic Summarization of Electronic Health Records
Abstract: Primary care physicians spend considerable shares of their working hours performing clerical duties such as writing and reading patient records. To reduce this burden, automatic document summarization can allow them to quickly catch up with the medical history of a patient while reducing the risk of missing critical pieces of information. As health records grow in length over the course of the patient’s lifetime, locating relevant case-related information can become difficult and time consuming. To address this issue, I propose designing models based on deep neural networks that can produce contextualized summaries based on requirements specified by doctors in an interactive manner. Title: Stochastic Model-Data Fusion on Networks: Disease Spread and Cascade Failure
Abstract:
Many processes and phenomena encountered in scientific research and industrial applications can be represented by networks. Their specific topology accounts for the interactions among the components and the emerging collective behaviour of the whole system. Despite their omnipresence, common modeling approaches either lack fine-grained interactions necessary to probe the fundamental mechanisms or rely on too many degrees-of-freedom which render them intractable in practice. Besides, the parameters controlling nodal interactions and the network connectivity remain largely uncertain.  Therefore, reducing the complexity of the network description to the essential and quantifying its uncertainty against the available real-world data are of prime importance in diverse applications. We aim at developing a stochastic model-data framework to elucidate processes on high-dimensional network and focus on two important examples of emerging crisis: disease spread in the population and cascade failure of power grids.

To prevent the healthcare system from being overwhelmed and protect the vulnerable population, it is necessary to support interventions that can guide us through the highly likely recurring epidemic waves. The possible epidemic scenarios should cover varying levels of disease severity, disease spread, and immunity response. The heterogeneity of the immunity response and social mixing, typically stratified by age-groups, demand a fine-grained stochastic network descriptions. Such models are necessary to outline surveillance, vaccination programs, and epidemiological measures. 

Local exogenous disturbances in power grids might cause  system-wide disruptions. The increased uncertainty of the power generation due to integration of renewable energy sources and to the ever increasing electricity demand call for robust yet efficient predictions of the energy flow. Efficient and accurate network models can detect early-warning signals and prevent reaching the tipping point of cascade failure. Moreover, they  can help us to design more resilient grid structures that can better withstand contingencies across supply, demand and transmission.   

The central idea of our methodology is to cast the description of random and multi-dimensional network processes into a stochastic model-data framework. After devising a generic description of stochastic processes, a machine learning (ML) approach is pursued to learn efficient reduced representations. The resulting dynamics is further mapped into interpretable stochastic evolution, which is used to quantify the uncertainties and to optimize the observability of the system in the Bayesian framework. 

This methodology will be employed to improve predictive modeling, to anticipate the spread of epidemics and provide optimal monitoring and early warning of large-scale power failures. Besides allowing more efficient simulations, such models provide tools to optimize the network structure and plan mitigation strategies. The proposal brings together ideas from data-driven and stochastic modeling to address large-scale human vulnerabilities to epidemics and power outage. Most importantly, the improved understanding and the resulting toolbox will offer a platform to support preparedness, control and intervention in case of critical events affecting the complex networks emerging in the health and industrial sectors.

Title: MentalWords - Analyzing Textual Data to Better Understand Mental Health Diseases and Providing an Additional Data Source for Clinical Professionals
Abstract:
Different studies show that stress at the workplace or regarding care work has become a prevalent societal problem. Persistent situations of stress can lead to mental health problems, such as, e.g., depression, anxiety, or burnout. Detecting mental illness is difficult, as they are the consequence of many different factors and manifest in a variety of both physical and mental symptoms. Furthermore, the symptoms of different mental health problems can overlap, making it unclear which underlying condition should be treated. In clinical intervention and field research, mental health problems are typically detected by using so-called inventories, with scaled-response questions. However, it has been shown that such inventories can have limitations, such as social desirability bias, defensiveness/denial or extreme response bias. 
Whereas the use of free-text questions is promising, the evaluation of such questions generates a large manual effort and is thus not often used in practice. New technologies from the field of machine learning and natural language processing (NLP) provide ways of automatically processing text. However, there are three main challenges: (a) most research in the field is relying on social media, there is a scarcity of clinical data being available for NLP in mental health research, (b) the clinical distinction between burnout, depression and other related problems is challenging, as symptoms might be overlapping, (c) it can be difficult for the concerned groups of patients to express themselves in a written form. 
In this project, technical and medical researchers will closely collaborate with a clinical partner to collect transcribed data from different groups of mental health patients and from the working population without clinical evidence of a mental health condition. We aim to develop a data collection protocol that integrates as smoothly as possible into the clinical workflow to limit the overhead of the clinical partner to a minimum in the long term. We analyze the transcribed data to explore the differences and overlaps between the groups and develop an ensemble classifier to identify indication for burnout, depression and anxiety in German text data. Finally, we aim to release an open access dataset to make the anonymized data available for further research.

Title: GraphQueryML: Using Machine Learning to Optimize Queries in Graph Databases
Abstract:
Query optimization, i.e., the translation of a declarative query statement into an efficient query execution plan, is one of the central problems of database systems research. Even after four decades of research many sub-problems of query optimization are still unsolved. Acknowledging the fact that an increasing number of data sets is graph-structured and, in particular, represented in the Resource Description Framework (RDF) or in the Property Graph (PG) data model, this proposal explores the important open research problem of using machine learning for optimizing queries in graph databases. (1) We will design and
develop a general query optimization framework that uses machine learning with focus on deep reinforcement learning. (2) We apply our framework to the optimization of SPARQL queries in RDF databases. (3) We will study the optimization of Cypher queries in property graph databases. Our approach has the great potential to enable novel discoveries both in the scientific community as well as in industry. In particular, the data-intensive bioinformatics community with the wide adoption of RDF databases will be benefit from accelerated queries across multiple RDF databases and thus enable shorter scientific discovery cycles.
Keywords: Graph databases, Machine learning, Query optimization, Relational databases

Title: Computational principles of affect in social learning and decision making
Abstract:
How do we learn about and from others based on their affect (i.e., feelings)? Science has much to say about learning in objective contexts. From algorithms playing chess to organisms seeking food, the computations involved in adaptive learning and decision making are increasingly well understood. When it comes to affect, however, the corresponding computations are more elusive. Intuitively, this might seem unsurprising: Unlike objective states, affect is inherently intractable and should not be expected to adhere to clear computational principles. However, recent research challenges this intuition by documenting how affect can align with computational principles. This is promising, as a more precise understanding of the subjective holds promise for elucidating contexts that cannot be understood based on objective features alone. Past research has begun to act on this promise, showing that people’s own affect can explain their choice behavior beyond what can be explained by objective features. However, this does not speak to social functions of affect in terms of computations involved in observing other people's affect.
The objective of this project is to address this gap and identify systematic computations that tie others’ affective responses to observers’ inferences. To this end, it addresses two questions from a computational perspective: How do we learn about (1) and from (2) others based on their feelings? By revealing systematic computations that link affective responses to social inferences and behavior, this project aims to inform fundamental research along with a broader perspective on how expressions of affect (be it human, artificial, public, or private) may relate to social cohesion.
Keywords: Affect, Intergroup bias, Reinforcement learning, Social decision making, Social learning

Title: Measuring and Modelling Catastrophic Landslides and Debris Flows
Abstract:
Every year, landslides kill thousands of people and cause billions of dollars in infrastructure damage worldwide (Petley, 2012).  Landslides are a common and costly natural hazard in Switzerland, as demonstrated by the recent landslide that impacted the town of Bondo, in Canton Graubünden, killing eight people.  Increased development pressures in high risk areas, as well as melting permafrost and increased frequency of severe rainstorms, is expected to change landslide risk worldwide.  Developing a detailed understanding of the fundamental mechanisms that govern landslide motion is crucial for managing this changing risk in the future.
Some of the most catastrophic landslides are flow-like landslides, such as debris flows, where the failed material behaves as a fluid.  The mechanisms that govern flow-like landslides are poorly understood at present, which limits the ability of researchers and practitioners to manage landslide risk.  The three most important mechanisms that govern flow-like landslide motion are: 1) longitudinal sorting, which leads to destructive surges 2) liquefaction, which dramatically increases the area impacted by the landslide and 3) material entrainment, which can increase the volume of the flow by orders of magnitude.  New methods to measure and model these mechanisms are urgently needed to manage landslide risk in the future.  
Through developing and applying new field data collection techniques, performing innovative analogue experiments and implementing a cutting edge numerical model, we will generate important new insights into these three important mechanisms.  Specifically, the objectives are: 1) measure longitudinal sorting and entrainment in moving debris flows, 2) quantify how liquefied strength governs flow-like landslide motion and 3) develop a new numerical modelling framework that leverages recent advances in computing architecture to simulate the interaction of the three studied mechanisms.
The Mountain Hydrology and Mass Movements group at WSL, which is the host institution for this research project, operates the Illgraben Debris Flow Observation Station (IO), and has two state-of-the-art analogue modelling facilities.  This existing infrastructure will be leveraged to perform novel field and analogue modelling investigations.  High frequency LiDAR sensors, which provide high-resolution measurements of the surface of objects, will be installed in the IO measure longitudinal sorting and entrainment in moving debris flows.  This data has not been previously collected, and will provide unique insights into these mechanisms.  This dataset will be made available to the scientific community to encourage further innovation.  Analogue experiments, which systematically vary the factors controlling liquefied strength, will be performed to quantify how liquefaction influences landslide runout.  The results from both the field and laboratory investigations will be incorporated into a new numerical modelling framework.  This numerical model will simulate the interaction of longitudinal sorting, liquefaction and entrainment, which is beyond the current capabilities of similar models.
The novel field and laboratory data will provide an unprecedented level of detail about the mechanisms of longitudinal sorting, liquefaction and entrainment.  Incorporation of this data into numerical models will illuminate the physical causes that govern the motion of flow-like landslides and reveal a new fundamental understanding of this landslide type.  This new understanding of landslide mechanisms is crucial for managing landslide risk in an uncertain future.

Title: VISION-EAR: VIsualize Sound transmissION with dynamic phase-contrast micro-tomography of the human middle EAR
Abstract:
An important source of disability, particularly in children, is the impairment of sound transmission through the middle ear leading to conductive hearing loss. An improved understanding of the biophysical properties of middle ear structure and function are of considerable international scientific interest because of the ability to directly apply such knowledge to surgical methods of hearing reconstruction. However, detailed investigations of middle ear hearing mechanics have been challenging due to the anatomically small dimensions (the three middle ear bones are the smallest bones in the body) and the middle ear’s location within the confines of the temporal bone. 
Over the past 4 years our group has designed and executed an innovative approach to investigate the human middle ear biomechanics by using synchrotron-based X-ray phase contrast imaging (SR X-PCI). This sophisticated imaging method provides ultra-high-resolution (micrometer) imaging quality paired with excellent soft tissue contrast to permit histologic level details of the human ear. Furthermore, we are internationally the first research group to succeed in performing dynamic imaging of the movements of the human ossicular chain using this technique. This newly developed dynamic imaging method unlocks a new pathway by which the mechanics of hearing can be rigorously investigated. With this proposal, divided in four workpackages, we aim to push the resolution of the dynamic SR X-PCI to break new grounds in the understanding of middle ear biomechanics in normal, diseased and reconstructed states. This research will provide critically important information for otosurgeons, who can use lessons learned to improve outcomes for patients undergoing hearing restoration surgery. 
In a first step, we will leverage our previously acquired datasets of static SR X-PCI data to build a new ultra-high resolution finite element (FE) model of the human middle ear. We will validate against temporal bone specific data from dynamic SR X-PCI and laser Doppler vibrometry. With a massive increase in resolution and a direct experimental description of material properties we expect to exceed the accuracy of present FE models. This approach allows us to simulate the dynamic behavior of the middle ear in different conditions (normal, diseased, post-surgical) to inform experiments and surgeons. The second step will combine artificial intelligence modeling and digital volume correlation to automatize the analysis of the large datasets generated by dynamic SR X-PCI. With direct correlation of segmented data, such as the tympanic membrane, it will be possible to depict complex within structure movements. Presently this is not feasible, due to limitations in data-analysis pipelines. Thanks to technical refinements at the Swiss Light Source beamline currently underway, we will push the resolution of dynamic SR X-PCI to a new level. After upgrades to the beamline are complete, we will perform dynamic SR X-PCI on 20 temporal bones under acoustical stimulation at higher frequencies than were previously possible. The higher resolution will permit better descriptions of 3D micromovements at mid to high frequencies. Finally, we explore translational experiments via imaging of the reconstructed ear. With direct experience in otosurgery, our group has developed an onsite minimally invasive endoscopic approach for ossicular chain reconstruction while keeping the tympanic membrane intact. This approach will allow us to experimentally define the interactions between reconstructive materials and the mechanical efficiency of the human middle ear. In these experiments, we will directly compare autologous grafts to titanium-based implants and use the data to further test and refine our FE model. This novel approach will define previously unidentified factors influencing the hearing results from reconstructive middle ear surgery.

Title: Using Machine Learning to Reveal the Neurocomputational Architecture of Theory of Mind
Abstract:
Virtually all aspects of social behavior depend on our ability to infer and respond to the beliefs, intentions, and emotions of others - an ability known as "Mentalizing" or "Theory of Mind" (ToM). This capacity underpins personal, cooperative, and competitive interactions alike, and its impairment is seen as a hallmark of various neurodivergent phenotypes, including Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD). The cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying ToM are therefore a research focus of various disciplines such as neuroscience, psychology, psychiatry, and economics. Yet, our current understanding remains constrained by experimental paradigms and models grounded in narrow theoretical frameworks, which capture mainly static and simplified aspects of ToM.

This project aims to transform our understanding of the neurocomputational basis of ToM, by integrating cutting-edge machine learning, a novel experimental paradigm, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). Although prior research has associated ToM with activity in brain regions such as the temporoparietal junction (TPJ) and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC), the precise computations these areas perform - and how they interact dynamically to support mentalizing - remain largely unknown. Existing theory-driven models offer mainly correlational insights into these computations and have limited explanatory power for capturing inter-individual differences or deficits in ToM.

The central innovation of the present project lies in the application of Disentangled Recurrent Neural Networks (DisRNNs), a novel machine learning approach designed to extract interpretable, modular latent variables from behavioral data. Applied to interactive tasks that evoke adaptive mentalizing, DisRNNs enable data-driven discovery of the dynamic computational components underlying ToM that are free from assumptions imposed by predefined cognitive theories. When integrated with neuroimaging and brain stimulation, this approach provides a powerful framework to identify the neurocomputational processes that causally support mentalizing behavior.

We will train DisRNNs on behavioral data from ecologically valid tasks designed to elicit adaptive mentalizing during cooperation and competition - two fundamental contexts in which ToM is essential. These models will identify latent cognitive variables that best explain behavior across contexts. We will then map these variables onto neural activation patterns using fMRI and assess their causal relevance, by comparing behavioral effects of simulated synthetic lesions in the models to behavioral disruptions observed in TMS experiments, as well as to behavioral deficits in individuals with high-functioning ASD. Finally, we will use combined TMS-fMRI to investigate causal dynamics within the brain network representing the DisRNN-identified cognitive processes, revealing how specific brain regions interact to support mentalizing.

By leveraging a novel but validated paradigm, a state-of-the-art machine learning framework, and sophisticated neuroimaging and brain stimulation techniques, this integrative project promises a significant leap in our understanding of ToM. It will uncover the computational architecture of social cognition, reveal its neural implementation, and offer mechanistic insights into social impairments. Ultimately, these insights may inform targeted interventions and diagnostic tools for neurodivergent populations, including those with ASD and BPD.
