Title: Computational design of soluble and functional membrane protein analogues
Abstract:
Proteins are essential to virtually all biological processes, and their functions are dictated by their three-dimensional structures, which are determined by the sequence of amino acids. Traditional methods of protein engineering have relied heavily on modifying existing proteins, a process constrained by the limitations of natural sequences and structures. In contrast, de novo protein design starts with the desired structure or function and works backward to create a sequence that will fold into the target protein. This bottom-up approach allows for the creation of proteins with entirely new functionalities that may not be achievable through natural evolution or traditional engineering techniques. Recent advances in computational design, such as the development of machine learning-powered algorithms capable of accurately predicting protein structure from sequence, have opened new avenues for the design of novel folds. These tools enable the rational design of proteins with specific functions, allowing for the exploration of fold space that would be difficult to access through natural evolution alone. In recent work from our group, we have analyzed the structural diversity of the protein fold universe in relation to the cellular environment, and observed that the fold space is not homogeneously distributed and that some folds only exist in the membrane proteome. Sparked by this observation we attempted to computational design soluble analogues of membrane proteins and we successfully showed that the membrane folds were designable and experimental structures closely mimicked those of the native membrane proteins. Membrane proteins are cornerstones of biological activity, both due to their sophisticated mechanisms to transduce signals across the membrane often including conformational transitions as well as for the importance that they bear as drug targets (54% of FDA-approved drugs target membrane proteins). Therefore, we aim to explore the opportunities within these systems to tackle fundamental challenges in protein design such as those of the design of ligand binding capability and conformational heterogeneity in de novo proteins. Furthermore we will also explore the potential of the soluble membrane protein mimetics in the development of candidate biologics (e.g. antibodies and monobodies) for the modulation of their function and ultimately in drug discovery. Within this proposal we aim: to improve the computational framework to handle bigger folds, ligand binding properties and multi-state design (Aim 1); expand the space of folds for membrane soluble analogues where proteins with other structures and functions will be attempted (Aim 2); design of structural dynamics features and ligand binding capabilities for functional purposes (Aim 3); exploration of biotechnological applications applications for the soluble membrane analogues in the realm of the discovery of conformation-specific biologics for drug development (Aim 4). 
In summary, we propose a research plan that spans an interdisciplinary approach from experimental to computational research that tackles fundamental research questions as well as unsolved problems with translational  potential in the domains of computational protein design for function and drug discovery for challenging targets .

Title: Dissecting catecholaminergic regulation of flexible decision making
Abstract: Cognitive flexibility is a fundamental aspect of adaptive decision-making, enabling organisms to adjust their behaviour in response to changing environmental contingencies. A critical component of this process is the ability to balance exploitation of known rewarding strategies with exploration of new possibilities, a function that is regulated by key brain regions such as the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and the medial orbitofrontal cortex (mOFC). The ACC has been implicated in monitoring outcomes, evaluating cost-benefit trade-offs, and implementing behavioural adjustments in response to uncertainty, while the mOFC is essential for representing state-dependent value and updating these representations when contingencies change. Catecholamines, particularly dopamine (DA) and norepinephrine (NE), play a crucial role in this regulation. DA has long been associated with reinforcement learning via reward prediction error (RPE) signalling, whereas NE, traditionally linked to arousal and attention, is increasingly recognized for its role in encoding unexpected uncertainty and facilitating adaptive shifts in cognitive and behavioural strategies. Despite these insights, there is limited direct empirical evidence linking real-time DA and NE activity to exploratory decision-making. To address this gap, this project aims to characterize NE and DA dynamics in the ACC and mOFC during voluntary versus instructed exploration in a multi-armed bandit task and to link these catecholaminergic signals to uncertainties in neural state representations, assessing how they track and/or regulate state transitions and flexible decision making. This will be achieved using a combination of fiber photometry to record real-time DA and NE release in ACC and mOFC in mice using genetically encoded fluorescent indicators, alongside computational modelling using probabilistic state representation frameworks to analyze relationships between neuromodulator activity and entropy in neural state models. It is expected that NE activity in the ACC will increase during voluntary exploratory switches, supporting its role in exploratory actions, whereas NE in the mOFC will correlate with entropy updates, indicating a function in updating internal models of the environment. Additionally, DA signals are anticipated to reflect reward prediction errors and/or policy-shaping rather than directly modulating uncertainty. By refining models of neuromodulatory control over cognitive flexibility, this study will provide critical insights into the mechanisms underlying decision-making and has potential implications for understanding psychiatric conditions such as ADHD and schizophrenia, where deficits in flexible behaviour are common.
Keywords: Cognitive flexibility, Decision-making, Dopamine (DA), Exploration-exploitation trade-off, Neuromodulation, Norepinephrine (NE)

Title: Towards Top-Down Feedback in Deep Learning: Integrating Probabilistic Hierarchical Models into Deep Neural Networks
Abstract: The performance of Computer Vision systems has significantly increased in the last decade due to advances in deep learning. However, Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are still far from achieving human-level performance at most visual recognition tasks. One major reason for this performance gap is that DNNs are inherently restricted to make decisions via feed-forward processing. We know from research on biological vision and computer vision that top-down feedback is of central importance for the robust recognition of objects in real-world environments. In this project, I propose to introduce a top-down feedback mechanism into Deep Learning systems by integrating probabilistic hierarchical models into Deep Neural Networks. This novel technology will be particularly useful at visual recognition tasks where the object appearance varies drastically due to changes in the objects pose, lighting, partial occlusion, background clutter or the camera's viewpoint.
Keywords: Computer Vision, Deep Learning, Object Analysis

Title: AI-powered Reflective Writing: Developing an Open-Source Tutor to Enhance Students’ and Educators' Metacognitive Skills
Abstract:
Metacognition and reflective writing is a critical skill for students, fostering deep learning, self-awareness, and hence, crucial to achieving the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals. However, many learners struggle with structuring their reflections effectively and receiving timely, personalized feedback. While Artificial Intelligence (AI)-powered writing support tools have shown promise in improving academic writing, their role in fostering reflective writing remains largely unexplored. As universities seek innovative ways to support students’ metacognitive development, understanding the potential and limitations of AI-powered reflection tools is both timely and necessary.

This 12-month project is designed to investigate whether and how conversational tutoring can support students in their reflective writing skills. Specifically, the focus lies on the examination of two AI-interaction modes—(1) structured guidance for writing reflective texts and (2) offering adaptive feedback—and whether these modes differentially affect the quality of the final reflection texts.

Further, we will investigate the effect of our reflective guidance on students' perception of their reflection skills and their progress. Offering guidance and feedback should help students gain confidence in their skills and allow them to experience self-efficacy in regard to their ability to write reflective texts. However, while AI-powered writing aids have shown promise in some educational domains, their application to sustained reflective practice is nascent and unproven. The project’s success is uncertain—negative findings are equally valuable as they provide novel insights into how AI can (or cannot) support deeper reflection skills.

The project’s innovative character lies in its combination of adaptive AI-powered feedback with a structured reflection framework, providing a human-centered approach to reflective writing support. By analyzing both qualitative and quantitative indicators of student engagement and skill development, this project can advance the understanding of how AI can support reflective learning processes. Findings will be disseminated to educators, along with practical recommendations for integrating the tutor as an open source tool in educational institutions in Switzerland. This research contributes to a growing conversation on responsible AI in education, offering actionable insights into the design, implementation, and impact of AI-powered reflection tools.
Keywords: AI-based Feedback, Metacognition, Open Source Learning Tool, Reflective Writing

Title: Quantum synchronization and quantum phase transitions in arrays of nano- and optomechanical systems
Abstract:
We will explore novel aspects of quantum synchronization in networks of self-sustained oscillators. This includes even-odd effects in the number of levels of the synchronization nodes and the dependence on network topology (number of neighbors and interaction range). Another interesting direction that we will study is frustration effects and possible links to frustrated quantum spin systems. Furthermore, we will investigate symmetry-breaking pattern formation in synchronization networks (quantum chimera states). 

Using unsupervised machine-learning schemes, we will investigate phase diagrams of models that exhibit synchronization or other types of long-range order. We will also  explore neural network architectures that involve physical insights and recent innovations in machine learning to compute steady states of driven dissipative quantum systems. Finally, we will continue our work on quantum control and 
will investigate the control of open quantum systems.
Keywords: chimera states, condensed-matter theory, machine learning, optomechanics, quantum coherence, quantum synchronization

Title: Deep NEWS (Deep Machine Learning based Newborn Early Warning Signs)
Abstract:
Deep NEWS - Deep Machine Learning based Newborn Early Warning Signs –

Background and rationale 
Newborn babies in neonatal intensive care units may rapidly develop cardiorespiratory dysfunction, for example, upon developing sepsis or necrotizing enterocolitis. Clinical symptoms are unspecific and aided by analysis of biomarkers with limited sensitivity and specificity. This type of analysis is time-consuming and requires a biological sample, such as blood or cerebrospinal fluid or requires additional tools such as x-ray or ultrasound examinations. Recent discoveries have established that infections affect vital signs, such as heart rate and breathing of babies at a very early stage of disease. Detecting and analysing changes in heart rate and breathing may lead to a diagnosis up to 24 hours earlier than that obtained by current clinical practice. 
Objectives 
We hypothesize that factors such as perinatal transition, disease-induced inflammation, and other morbidities alter cardiorespiratory control in newborn infants. This dampens the ability to respond to environmental stressors, which may cause adverse clinical events that could ultimately result in death. Therefore, early detection of changes in the respiratory or heart rate pattern, such as apnea, bradycardia and desaturation using deep machine learning algorithms, may serve as patient-specific physiomarker for loss of cardiorespiratory control (acronym Deep NEWS, derived from Deep machine learning based Newborn Early Warning Signs). Such an approach may enable rapid therapeutic interventions prior to occurrence of life-threatening events. This study aims to continue to investigate how changes in vital sign fluctuation are related to acute clinical deterioration in newborn infants. 
Aims 
The specific research questions addressed in this project are: 
1) How is the cardiorespiratory pattern altered during early development and how can changes due to normal development be separated from changes related to disease? 
2) How are patient characteristics (e.g. gestational age, birth weight, sex) and treatment strategies (e.g. different levels of respiratory support; medications) related to the cardiorespiratory pattern in babies? 
3) Can changes in cardiorespiratory pattern be used as clinically feasible physiomarker to predict adverse events such as systemic infections, bleeding (e.g. from the lungs or cerebral) or necrotizing enterocolitis in neonates?
Methods 
Participants in this study are newborn infants hospitalized in a neonatal intensive care unit of the Karolinska Hospital in Stockholm, Sweden. We will utilize their vital signs, e.g. heart and respiratory rate and oxygen saturation, already recorded and stored at the Karolinska Hospital. All study participants are under physiological development and come with known descriptors, such as gestational age, birth weight, and sex. Therefore, we perform a longitudinal study to separate development-related and disease-related changes in the cardiorespiratory parameters. Clinical information about the patients will be extracted from different systems (e.g. laboratory results, patient chart information, nurse reports). Given the multiplicity, entanglement and high-recording rate of vital parameters, data analysis will be built upon novel machine learning algorithms (deep learning). 
Expected results and their impact 
We expect to learn more about physiological and pathological fluctuations of different vital signs, their influence on each other and their usefulness in predicting future clinical deterioration. The ultimate goal of the project will be to develop a tool for risk assessment and disease prediction that quickly can be implemented into clinical practice. This will aid clinicians in evaluating the benefits of intervention strategies for some of their most critically ill patients. This physiomarker-based patient state assessment, performed in realtime should allow physicians to decide quicker about the need of potentially lifesaving interventions.
Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Autonomic control, Big Data, Cardiorespiratory stability, Machine learning, Monitoring, Neonatology, Prediction

Title: “The AI of Theseus”: A Mathematical Formalization of the Identity of Artificial Intelligence Systems
Abstract:
Modern artificial intelligence (AI) systems, such as conversational agents, medical decision-support systems, and online platforms, use machine learning (ML) models to perform a number of tasks and assist humans in everyday decision-making. 
A distinctive feature of these ML models is their evolution over time to adapt to changes in the environment they operate. Despite the dynamic behaviour of the ML models powering AI systems and while researchers are actively investigating the epistemology and ethics of human-AI interactions, a discourse on the nature and persistence, i.e., the existence at different times, of modern AI systems is missing. Without a clear understanding of what AI systems really are and how they may possibly change over time over time due to the dynamics of their ML models, our ability to learn from and interact with these technologies is hindered. This gap is also a notable source of societal risk, as evidenced by recent concerns raised by healthcare regulators. Just as in the case of the evolution of personal identity, defining the identity over time of these AI systems is key to ascribe responsibility in human-AI interactions and manage the risks stemming from the use of this technology.  
To address this issue, our project has two goals: (1) to investigate the ontology of modern AI by introducing a mathematical formalization that defines the ontological kind and identity criteria of AI systems, and (2) translate this formalization into a societal risk taxonomy, outlining mitigation strategies for the different societal actors engaged in the regulation of modern AI. To achieve (1), we will use mathematical category theory, which has recently started to attract the interest of researchers in computer science and formal philosophy. Using mathematical categories, we will explicitly formalize the structure and transformations of modern AI systems, defining their ontological kind and identity criteria, by relating them to the persistence conditions of the ML models these systems use to execute their intended functions. As a result, we will also determine when a ML-based AI stops existing, although this may contradict common sense, as in a modern version of the ship of Theseus puzzle of identity. 
To achieve (2) we will steer an ELSI (ethical, legal, social implications) dialogue with academics and experts from AlgorithmWatch. Through the dialogue, we will translate the mathematical formulation of the ontology and identity over time of modern AI into a taxonomy of societal risks and define their mitigation strategies. Then, we will assess the societal impact of the (lack of) persistence of AI systems that are embedded in the services we access in everyday life. 
The novelty of the project is twofold. First, its mathematical category-based methodology promotes an original approach to the formal philosophy of modern AI artefacts. Our results will provide a much-needed ontological standing to modern AI systems and support the rigour of the philosophy of modern AI domain. Further, they will promote new philosophical inquires relating the epistemology and ethics of AI to the persistence of these systems. Finally, the ELSI dialogue will contribute to the development of ethical guidelines and policies that ensure AI systems are trustworthy and robust over time, enhancing transparency and accountability in AI applications.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Category Theory, Ethics, Identity, Machine Learning, Ontology, Time

Title: Towards Quantifying the Synthesizability of Materials
Abstract:
The discovery of new materials is an essential ingredient for technological progress. It is generally agreed upon that simulation methods can make important contributions to this field and extensive research activities are under way worldwide. In this context unbiased structure prediction methods have revealed a large number of possible structures for numerous materials. However only a relatively small fraction of these structures can be found in nature or can be synthesized in the laboratory. This observation poses fundamental and technological challenges. One would like to understand whether the unobserved structures can for some hitherto unknown fundamental reason not exist or whether simply the correct synthesis recipe has not yet been found. If they can not exist, synthesis should not be tried for these materials. If they may exist, simulation could give guidance to synthesis efforts. Since a time resolved atomistic simulation of the actual nucleation and growth processes occurring during synthesis is not feasible in connection with a high-accuracy description of the potential energy surface, we will use concepts from thermodynamics to predict the final structure without following the relevant processes in time. In this context, it will be necessary to develop much more efficient methods to calculate free energies. To understand the behavior of the free energy at formation conditions 
requires developing improved methods to calculate this quantity at high temperatures, where the harmonic approximation breaks down. To obtain the correct energetic ordering at room temperature, it is frequently necessary to include nuclear quantum effects into the free energy calculations. Applying some of the latest mathematical tools, we will develop novel algorithms that are considerably more powerful than the existing ones. Finally we will also search for new quantities that can be obtained from 
the potential energy surface at affordable numerical cost and that contain relevant information about the synthesizability of a material. All these new methods should then finally allow to directly assess the synthesizability of a material. The new methods will be used for several materials that have potential applications in energy production and storage. Preferentially materials will be used that have already been studied in the group and for which fast machine learning force fields will be available when the project starts.
Keywords: free energy methods, materials discovery, structure prediction

Title: Sensing User Attention During Everyday Interactions Toward Anticipatory Human-Computer Interaction
Abstract: Human attention is at the core of many tasks in human-computer interaction (HCI). This project investigates new computational methods to sense, understand, and model user attention and its allocation during everyday activities. A novelty of our work is that we do not only focus on overt shifts of attention, which can be measured through eye movements, but also, for the first time, shifts of covert attention using microsaccades that indicate mental focus. This is a challenging task but, if successful, has the potential for significant impact in HCI given the community's long-standing interest towards building user interfaces that can adapt to the users' attention and anticipate the users' intention. This project has three objectives. First, we explore a generative approach based on recent advancements in machine learning to sense overt, also known as visual, attention robustly. Second, we investigate new methods to predict shifts of covert attention. Towards this goal, in stark contrast to previous studies that explored highly controlled and laboratory settings, we study more challenging everyday interactive scenarios. The project's final objective is to validate our findings on the task interleaving problem, i.e. the challenge of predicting how and when users switch from one task to another. By working on methods to sense user attention, our work lays the foundation towards a new generation of anticipatory user interfaces.
Keywords: Anticipatory User Interfaces, Attentive User Interfaces, Covert Attention, Eye Tracking, Machine Learning, User Attention, Visual Attention

Title: Bioinspired Asymmetric Catalysis
Abstract:
Nature contains a myriad of catalytic systems with intricate and specific reactivity. Within this proposal we draw inspiration from nature with respect to the design of catalytically active small molecules, the discrimination between and activation of substrates, and the structure of reactive intermediates. In doing so, we focus on developing practical methods for use in organic synthesis and illuminate relationships between features of small-molecule catalysts, in particular peptidic catalysts, and those of enzymes. In the past, we have established tripeptides as highly reactive and stereoselective catalysts for C–C bond-forming reactions and developed methods for performing stereoselective reactions with bioinspired fluoroacetate enolate equivalents with enzyme-inspired organocatalysts. In this proposal, we will build on this knowledge substantially. We will focus specifically on the following goals:

Aim 1. Our previous studies showed that peptidic catalysts have features of both enzymes and small molecules. Now we will probe the chemoselectivity of peptidic catalysts by challenging the performance of already developed catalysts in compound mixtures. The reactions will be done in aqueous media with increasingly complex mixtures that mimic cellular environments.

Aim 2. We have gained deep insight into the conformational properties of the tripeptidic catalyst H-DPro-Pro-Glu-NH2. We will now use and expand this knowledge to rationally modify the conformation of ProProXaa-type catalysts such that their diastereoselectivity can be switched at will. Control over the conformation will also be utilized to achieve a) kinetic resolution, b) products containing quaternary stereogenic centers, and c) reactions with substrates that could interfere by coordinating to or reacting with the catalyst or reactive intermediates. The results will provide unprecedented insight into the reactivity, stereoselectivity, and chemoselectivity of chiral secondary amines.  

Aim 3. The exquisite substrate selectivity of enzymes arises from differential coordination. Our studies suggest that different coordinating moieties can also be used for selective substrate activation with peptidic catalysts. We will see whether this concept can be applied to difficult catalytic C–C bond forming reactions with acrylonitriles and alkynes. 

Aim 4. We have in the past successfully used combinatorial library screenings in combination with the optimization of the lead structure to develop peptidic catalysts. We will now explore the value of machine learning, a methodology that does not rely on mechanistic insight, as an alternative tool to expand the scope of peptidic catalysts. 

Aim 5. We developed the first enantioselective aldol reaction with fluoroacetate surrogates. Related surrogates allowed us to access fluorinated Mannich-type and conjugate addition products. This methodology opens intriguing prospects for the synthesis of fluorinated derivatives, including pharmacologically relevant polyketide substructures. We will build on these results and expand the methodology to a) consecutive aldol reactions with fluoroacetate and b) fluorinated oxindole derivatives. 

These aims are rooted deeply in organic synthesis and will enlarge the toolbox of stereoselective transformations. In addition, the aims are far-reaching, allowing us to reveal whether peptides could play a now-unknown role in nature—as catalysts.
Keywords: C–C bond formations, asymmetric catalysis, chemical biology, peptides

Title: Digital technologies and the future of innovation
Abstract: This proposal contributes to our understanding of how digitalization is transforming the economy. The overarching objective is to advance knowledge on how digital technologies disrupt inventive activities. Specifically, the proposal puts forward two exploratory studies. The first study deals with the automation of inventions and the consequences it has for the organization of inventive activities. The second study deals with the protection of inventions in the blockchain era and proposes a radical re-think of the intellectual property (IP) system. The project, which spans a total duration of 18 months, also discusses concrete managerial, legal and policy implications arising from the research. The proposal is particularly relevant to the “Digital Lives” call by the SNSF. The first study fits into the broader theme of the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on the organization of jobs. The second study fits into the broader theme of how blockchain will alter the economy. We focus on one sector of the economy, namely inventive activities, which is often seen as the last bastion of human superiority over machines. A key feature of the proposal is a focus on thought-provoking questions. The first study addresses the question of whether AI can be used to automatically produce inventions. The second study will exploit blockchain technology to rethink the IP system from scratch. The funding provided by the SNSF through this call seems to us the perfect opportunity for exploring such questions.Another distinguishing feature of the project is a dive at the source of the technology by exploiting insights collected either from close interactions with startups or by careful study of startups’ business models. This research design ensures that the studies will be conducted with a sound understanding of the technology and will be grounded in reality.The proposal only scratches the surface of the issues and, therefore, offers rich opportunities for follow-on research. The first study is the starting point for a deep examination of how AI will augment or displace creative work. The second study provides a fairly concrete context in which to re-imagine and study the direct legal consequences of blockchain technologies.
Keywords: blockchain, computer-generated inventions, data science, intellectual property, management of innovation

Title: Numerical relativity at exascale
Abstract: The scientific community is building the next generation of gravitational-wave detectors, both on the ground and in space, that will measure gravitational waves from merging black holes and neutron stars up to 100x more accurately than before. To make sense of the data we need numerical simulations that match this accuracy, and we cannot wait 100x longer to run simulations that already take weeks to months. We need to elevate numerical relativity to exascale supercomputing, leveraging the vast computational power available in current and future supercomputers to simulate merging black holes and neutron stars at 100x higher accuracy. I propose to achieve this goal with a combination of high-order numerical methods, supercomputing techniques, and machine learning. Specifically, I will develop massively parallel simulations of merging black holes with discontinuous Galerkin methods, a class of spectral finite-element methods that are particularly suitable for parallelization. I will GPU-accelerate these methods and run the simulations at scale on the most powerful supercomputers in Europe to reach the accuracy needed for the next generation of gravitational-wave detectors, specifically for the upcoming European LISA space mission. The catalog of simulations produced by my research project will inform the LISA waveform modeling community and will be used to interpret gravitational-wave observations from LISA.
Keywords: Black holes, Computational astrophysics, Gravitational waves, Numerical relativity

Title: Integrated analysis of high spatial and spectral resolution images
Abstract:
The topic of this proposal is automatic extraction of high-resolution spectroscopic information from remotely sensed images captured by airplanes or satellites. The starting point of the research is that imaging sensors in the visible and infrared spectrum have either high spatial or high spectral resolution, but not both. High spatial resolution sensors (digital cameras) typically record a panchromatic band covering the complete visible spectrum, and a few so-called multi-spectral bands with rather broad spectral coverage (blue green, red, near infrared etc.). On the contrary, high spectral resolution sensors, also called imaging spectrometers, have many (up to hundreds) contiguous bands with very narrow spectral bandwidth, which allow them to capture continuous reflectance spectra across the visible and infrared wavelengths. Due to physical limitations, it is currently not possible to build a single sensor with both high spatial and high spectral resolution. Thus, to obtain detailed spectral information and geometric detail it will in the foreseeable future be necessary to use two separate sensors and combine their observations. The two datasets can either be acquired simultaneously, if the recording platform is equipped with both instruments, or recorded independently (but with small temporal delay) and co-registered in post-processing.
The research theme of the present proposal is the integrated analysis of such datasets, in order to synergistically exploit their respective advantages. Such integrated processing shall enable one to derive information which has on one hand the fine geometric resolution of modern cameras, and on the other hand  the detailed and identifiable radiometric signatures of modern spectrometers. The main goal of this project is to combine hyperspectral unmixing and data fusion. In this way, one can take full advantage of the sensors’ complementary strengths, namely distinctive spectral reflectance distributions revealed by spectroscopy and rich texture visible at high geometric resolution. Taken together, spectral surface properties can be localized more accurately and assessed at a higher spatial resolution, leading to more accurate and more detailed extraction of semantic, biophysical and biochemical parameters.
While the idea to combine the two data sources is not new, previous work has either concentrated on disentangling the radiometric signatures that make up a pixel’s spectrum (spectral unmixing), or on increasing the resolution of hyperspectral images by fusion with a high-resolution images (image fusion). I.e., the two problems are dealt with separately. On the contrary, here we will combine the two tasks in one joint formulation, in order to exploit the correlations between the two data sources. We argue that such an integrated formulation will improve both parts: unmixing is supported by the high-resolution image, which makes explicit the spatial distribution of the spectral information within one hyperspectral sample, and has a larger portion of spectrally pure pixels (“endmembers”); fusion on the other hand also benefits from unmixing, which provides a basis of physically plausible spectral endmembers, as well as their local abundances. The integrated approach will be evaluated on several datasets with ground truth, both for the aerial case (APEX and ADS sensors) and for the satellite case (Hyperion/ALI), and including end-to-end testing for two important application areas, land cover and vegetation properties.
The integration of high spatial resolution imaging with imaging spectroscopy has not yet been investigated in depth, and the two research communities have (too) little interaction. One aim of this project is to bridge this gap. To that end, we build on one hand on the expertise of the ETHZ Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing Group in optical remote sensing, and computer vision, including a recently started research line in hyperspectral image analysis; and on the other hand on the extensive experience in imaging spectroscopy of our partners at the University of Zurich Remote Sensing Labs (RSL). The project addresses a fundamental scientific question of remote sensing. At the same time has considerable practical innovation potential: more detailed earth systems monitoring will play an important role for addressing challenges of high societal relevance, such as of food security, sustainable planning etc.
Keywords: computer vision, high spatial resolution imaging, hyperspectral imaging, image analysis, information fusion, remote sensing, satellite and aerial sensors

Title: In vivo dopaminergic modulation of plasticity at  cortico-striatal circuits during learning.
Abstract:
Reinforcement learning allows animals to adapt to new environments and is critical for survival. Unfortunately, reinforcement learning can also occur in maladaptive ways, which are thought to contribute to drug addiction and other brain diseases. These disorders are extremely difficult to treat, in part because of our limited knowledge of the molecular and circuit mechanisms that underlie reinforcement learning. While a wealth of literature implicates changes in cortico-striatal synaptic strength in reinforcement learning, nearly all such studies have evaluated synaptic changes ex vivo. Such preparations are useful for isolating the contributions of specific molecular mechanisms, but they are highly artificial and only capture a single “snapshot” of the learning process at the time the animal was sacrificed. There is a need for novel methods to turn these static “snapshots” into dynamic “movies” that assay changes in synaptic strength longitudinally as animals gain new experiences and form new associations. 
To address this need, during my Early Postdoc.Mobility fellowship I developed and optimized a novel in vivo preparation for examining cortico-striatal synaptic strength in awake behaving mice. This preparation allows me to understand dopamine-mediated dynamic changes of cortico-striatal synaptic strength during hyperdopaminergic states and investigate molecular effectors responsible for those changes. During the Postdoc.Mobility fellowship, I propose to use this preparation to test fundamental questions about the modulatory role of dopamine at orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) inputs to dorso-medial striatum (DMS) neurons during reinforcement learning. Specifically, I will test the hypotheses that (Aim 1) dopamine modifies coordinated neuronal activity at OFC-DMS networks; (Aim 2) dopamine modulates cortico-striatal plasticity in vivo during reinforcement learning and (Aim 3) OFC-DMS plasticity is a necessary component of dopamine-mediated reinforcement learning tasks. 
Funding this research proposal will facilitate an unprecedented longitudinal examination of the modulatory effects of dopamine onto excitatory synaptic plasticity during reinforcement learning in awake animals. Furthermore, it will bring new insights on the role of excitatory cortical inputs to the dorsal striatum, thus contributing to the refinement of models of basal ganglia function. Considering the number of psychiatric diseases linked to striatal impairments, these results have a large potential impact on therapeutic-oriented research. Finally, the development of this new methodology will offer to the scientific community a tool to investigate neuronal plasticity in vivo in circuits beyond the basal ganglia.
Keywords: dopamine, dorso-medial striatum, orbitofrontal cortex, plasticity, reinforcement learning

Title: Toward machine learning of electronic properties of metal-organic frameworks: material representation in feature space
Abstract:
Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) have emerged as a versatile class of materials for a range of applications. By changing their building blocks, the metal centers and organic ligands, one can tune their properties. This structural tunability, however, leads to the challenge of finding the optimal material among thousands of materials for a given application. Computational methods have played a significant role in design and discovery of MOFs by large-scale screening of MOF databases for gas separation and storage.
Large-scale screening of MOFs for their applications in which their electronic properties are essential (e.g. (photo)catalysis, sensing, etc.)
is prohibited due to the exceedingly large computational cost.
In this project, we propose to use machine learning (ML) to make such screening possible.
We propose to extend the ML tools developed for inorganic transition metal complexes
to MOFs by adapting the material representation to the periodic structural nature of MOFs and including MOF specific features to the material description.
ML in chemistry and material science is emerging as a tool to accelerate the computational search of the material space by prescreening the materials
and providing insight into their behaviour by revealing structure-property relations hidden in high-dimensional data.
This approach can provide valuable insights on the importance of structural features on different electronic properties of MOFs,
e.g. importance of local vs. global and chemical vs. topological features.
Eventually, a predictive ML model will be used for discovery of MOFs with desired electronic properties.
Keywords: artificial intelligence, clean energy, high-throughput screening, machine learning, metal-organic frameworks

Title: Dipyridamole and EEG biomarkers in restless legs syndrome: A placebo-controlled crossover study across sleep-wake states
Abstract:
Background. Restless legs syndrome (RLS) is a neurological disorder characterized by an urgent need to move the legs, especially during rest and at night, often disrupting sleep and causing periodic leg movements (PLMs). Clinically, RLS combines two core phenomena: deficits in sensorimotor integration and a state of persistent hyperarousal. These distinct features are linked to dopaminergic and glutamatergic dysfunctions, respectively. Recent evidence suggests that the adenosinergic system may bridge these abnormalities. Brain iron deficiency (BID) – a central mechanism in RLS – leads to cortical and striatal downregulation of adenosine A1 receptors, resulting in heightened cortico-striatal glutamate transmission and increased cortical excitability. Adenosine, a key sleep-promoting neuromodulator, normally reduces wake-promoting neurotransmission and supports sleep homeostasis. A deficit in adenosinergic signaling therefore contributes both to hyperarousal and unleashes neural mechanisms involved in the spinal inhibition of PLMs. Hyperarousal may help explain EEG alterations observed in RLS patients, such as increased beta and gamma activity, decreased slow-wave activity (SWA) during sleep, and possibly a sleep pressure accumulation. Dipyridamole (DPD), an adenosine reuptake inhibitor, has recently demonstrated clinical efficacy in RLS by improving symptoms and sleep quality. However, the neurophysiological mechanisms underlying these improvements remain poorly understood.
Aims. This study aims to clarify how DPD, a specific adenosinergic agent, affects the neurophysiology of RLS by analyzing EEG biomarkers of sleep-wake regulation. Specifically, it investigates whether DPD reduces cortical hyperarousal, enhances sleep homeostasis, and improves sleep macro/microstructure. It further explores whether changes in EEG markers correlate with clinical improvements, helping to identify predictive biomarkers of treatment response.
Methods. The study will recruit 30 RLS patients and 30 healthy controls. RLS participants will complete two 2-week treatment phases (DPD vs. placebo), separated by a 1-week washout, in a randomized, double-blind crossover design. DPD will be up-titrated to a maximum of 300mg/day. After each phase, clinical assessments (IRLS, CGI, MOS/ESS) and neurophysiological tests (PSG, MWT, m-SIT) will be performed. EEG data will be analyzed using time–frequency and complexity-based methods. Key features will assess cortical hyperarousal (beta/gamma power), sleep homeostasis (SWA, theta power), and sleep stability (sleep parameters, CAP, sample entropy measures, ORP). Title: Heterogeneous Face Recognition
Abstract:
Face recognition has existed as a field of research for more than 30 years and has been particularly active since the early 1990s. Researchers of many different fields (from psychology, pattern recognition, neuroscience, computer graphics and computer vision) have attempted to create and understand face recognition systems.
One of the most challenging tasks in automated face recognition is the matching between face images acquired in heterogeneous environments. Use-cases can cover matching of faces in unconstrained scenarios (e.g. at a distance), with long time lapse between the probe and the gallery and faces sensed in different modalities, such as thermal infrared or near infrared images (NIR) against visible spectra images (VIS). Successful solutions to heterogeneous face recognition can extend the reach of these systems to covert scenarios, such as recognition at a distance or at nighttime, or even in situations where no face even exists (forensic sketch recognition).
The key difficult in matching faces from heterogeneous conditions is that images of the same subject may differ in appearance due to changes in image modality (e.g. between VIS images and NIR images, between VIS images and sketches images) introducing high intra-class variations. With these variations, a direct comparison between samples generally results in poor matching accuracy. Heterogeneous face recognition algorithms must develop facial representations invariant to these changes. In this proposal, we present three strategies to cope with these challenges.
We will start by investigating manifold learning techniques. The key idea of manifold learning is to learn a joint mapping that project images, of different modalities, into a subspace where these projections can be compared directly with a simple distance function.
As a second step, we will investigate generative approaches for face recognition. Generative approaches compute the likelihood of an observation (face image) or a set of observations given the a statistical model of the subject. In this environment, cross-sensor or hetereogeneous matching can be regarded as a session variability information the model needs to cope with, compensating for them during the enrollment and probing.
Finally, a combination of both techniques will be investigated. This combination can be carried out in two different ways. At first, we will investigate score level fusion between the joint map learned with manifold learning approaches and the generative approach. We will then investigate the possibility to provide face images projected with the manifold learning techniques as input the generative face recognition systems.
Keywords: biometrics, generative modelling, heterogeneous face recognition, manifold learning, session variability

Title: Shared intratumor transcriptional heterogeneity and predictive models for patients’ clinical outcome
Abstract:
Background
Until recently, the term of cancer heterogeneity was mostly mentioned in respect to genetic aberrations. Lately however, several studies reported the presence of transcriptionally different populations of cancer cells within the same tumor; the observed transcriptional states were shared across tumor samples. This phenomenon, which we refer to as shared intratumor transcriptional heterogeneity (SITTH) is the focus of our proposal. Previous work, which reported SITTH based on a limited number of single cell RNA-seq experiments, could not scale up to infer the prognostic value of SITTH for most cancer types. For the same reason of the absence of large-scale studies, possible molecular drives of SITTH (mutations, copy number aberrations, etc.) could not be reliably determined. Of note, several pan-cancer works offered a different definition of intratumor transcriptional heterogeneity based on the overall transcript variability without requiring for transcriptional states to be shared across samples. This definition of intratumor transcriptional heterogeneity is valid and provided valuable insights, however it describes a different biological phenomenon than the one we focus on in this proposal.

Project objectives
Here, we propose to develop an automated computational method to detect shared transcriptional states from bulk tumor RNA-seq data and assess SITTH. This will allow us to use thousands of already profiled tumors from dozens of cancer types together with available clinical and molecular information. Specifically, we aim to (1) build and experimentally validate a computational method to assess SITTH based on bulk RNA-seq data, (2) assess the prognostic power of the designed SITTH index for patients’ stratification, and (3) detect cancer type-specific or pan-cancer molecular and clinical factors associated with SITTH in a pan-cancer study. These factors will include activities of signaling pathways and cancer hallmark processes, genomic variants, epigenetic events, immune cell infiltration, and also metastatic vs primary tumor location site, tumor size, stage, and cancer molecular subtype. 

Methodology
Computation methodology will include the extension of the convex analysis of mixtures to a hybrid neural network architecture by borrowing the recent idea of a variational autoencoder for probabilistic non-negative matrix factorization. The project will also employ regularized linear and non-linear survival models to assess the predictive power of the SITTH index, along with other clinical and molecular factors, in a variety of cancers. We will use state-of-the-art bioinformatics tools for the analysis of single cell RNA-seq data and for the assessment of tumor microenvironment composition from bulk RNA-seq data. We will experimentally validate discovered associations between SITTH and clinical or molecular features in selected cancer types using immunohistochemistry and single cell RNA-seq.

Expected results
In sum, this project aims to create the first fully automated computational method to characterize shared intratumor transcriptional heterogeneity from bulk RNA-seq data. The application of this method on data available from large scale cancer studies such as cancer atlas TCGA will allow us to infer the predictive power of SITTH for cancer patient survival and treatment outcome. Moreover, we will detect clinical and molecular features associated with SITTH, which has a potential to provide novel treatment strategies.

Impact and significance
Our pan-cancer study has a potential to demonstrate that a gain of transcriptional heterogeneity by malignant cells contributes to treatment resistance across cancer types and discover possible, potentially targetable, drivers of cell plasticity. Moreover, we will discover molecular biomarkers associated with transcriptional heterogeneity and propose gene expression signatures characterizing high SITTH. In the future, these biomarkers may be used in clinics for patient stratification and choice of therapy.
Keywords: Algorithms, Bioinformatics, Cancer, Heterogeneity, Machine learning, Predictive survival models, Signal deconvolution

Title: Writing with Ghosts: Creativity and Authenticity in AI-Assisted Screenwriting
Abstract:
Recent advances in machine learning have sparked passionate debates about the implications of artificial «intelligence» (AI) for artistic practice. As audiovisual artifacts generated by neural networks now often equal or exceed the quality of human creators, many artists perceive AI as a threat to their livelihoods. Serious ethical concerns about the origins of the data used to train AI models underscore the potential perpetuation of societal inequalities, exploitation of creative labor, and inadvertent promotion of cultural appropriation. These issues became evident during the writers' strike in the U.S. film industry in 2023, as screenwriters expressed fears that large language models (LLMs) could exacerbate already strained labor conditions by fueling wage squeeze, estrangement from embodied co-creation, rush for results, and inauthentic creativity. 
Despite these concerns, screenwriters also proactively use LLMs as productivity tools and collaborative sparring partners. This contradiction between apprehension and adoption remains largely unexplored in current scholarly research. While recent literature highlights the polarized discourses about AI adoption in creative practices, few studies systematically investigate how practitioners navigate and rationalize the ambivalences of LLMs in their real-world workflows. As a result, insights and tacit knowledge from professional creative practice remain underrepresented, resulting in a gap between theoretical discourse and practical application.
To bridge this gap, the proposed research adopts a novel, sequential mixed-methods approach within a practice-led, participatory research design to explore screenwriters' lived experiences with AI tools. We critically interrogate how artistic self-understanding, sector-specific labor practices, and notions of creative authenticity are evolving amidst rapid technological change. Specifically, we ask: (1) how the use of LLMs is reshaping screenwriters’ notions of artistic originality; (2) what metaphors or mental models—such as collaborator, sparring partner, assistant, or friend—screenwriters adopt when conceptualizing AI interactions; and (3) how screenwriters navigate tensions between efficiency gains from AI tools and ethical concerns related to technological displacement.
The study will focus on practitioners in German-speaking countries (Germany, Austria, Switzerland), allowing for comparisons across differently structured but culturally comparable labor markets. Specifically, we will: (1) conduct a quantitative online survey distributed through screenwriters’ professional associations to broadly map attitudes, practices, and narratives toward AI integration; (2) select four to six participants from the survey respondents for a guided auto-ethnographic study to document detailed experiential reflections and creative interactions with AI tools; and (3) validate, triangulate, and refine findings through a concluding participatory focus group discussion. This methodological arrangement ensures robust and multifaceted insights into the fraught relationship between human creativity, professional writing, and AI technology.
The study will be presented as an academic research paper targeting the ACM CHI (Computer-Human Interaction) conference. Results will also be disseminated through screenwriting associations and other creative partnerships.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Augmented Creativity, Computer-Human Interaction, Large Language Models, Screenwriting

Title: Modelling of uncertainties in the process chain from the starting material to the crimp connection for reverse material and process optimisation
Abstract: This research project aims to develop methods for optimizing entire manufacturing process chains while accounting for material and process uncertainties, at the example of  electrical copper-zinc connectors. These are increasingly needed due to the increasing electrification of vehicles and the general digitalization of the industry, and their performance depends on the complex interplay between the manufacturing process steps. The connector performance to be optimized is defined by three key criteria: geometric characteristics, mechanical strength, and electrical resistance. The goal is to develop a simulation methodology that predicts the performance of crimp connections based on process and material parameters, while considering uncertainties. A full scale process chain model and a universal surrogate model will be created to harmonize the simulation of different process steps and speed up simulations. Also, for the first time, invertible of these models will be analyzed. The project involves two phases: first, developing a process-spanning simulation and data collection via soft sensors; second, optimizing performance through a reverse process model. The methodology will be tested on various materials and crimp geometries to expand its industrial applicability.
Keywords: electrical connector, machine learning, manufacturing, numerical simulation

Title: Guided Large-Scale Exploration of Meteorological Data
Abstract:
Improving our understanding of atmospheric processes is key to several main challenges of the 21st century. Among others, we need to understand and predict climate change better in order to estimate the future habitation state of Earth for varying scenarios. Along with the gradual increase of extreme weather situations, more and more people are affected by hurricanes, floodings and droughts. Thus, meteorologists around the world improve individual aspects of the forecasting models. From year to year, the simulated data becomes larger and more complex due to technological advances of computing resources, simulation methods and measurement devices. Due to this rapid growing of available data, new data analysis methods are desperately required to gain insights into the complex meteorological processes. Scientific visualization is a powerful approach to this problem, as it enables humans to use their perceptive and cognitive capabilities to process and analyze patterns. Inspired from these needs and the feedback of the meteorologists from MeteoSchweiz in Zürich and the German Climate Computing Center (DKRZ) in Hamburg, we set out to build a new interactive exploration pipeline for guided large-scale meteorological climate data analysis.

Continuous Space-Time Exploration. The exploration of highly resolved meteorological 3D attributes such as the 3D flow, the air temperature, the precipitation or the cloud water content is challenging. All attributes together give rise to a significant amount of occlusion, which makes it difficult to see the internal structures. A successful visualization fulfills two criteria: relevant information is always represented and occlusions are removed to provide a clear view. There are still many problems to solve before existing methods are applicable to large meteorological data: adjacent data is often correlated and can be reduced, meaningful geometry has to be selected automatically, and time-dependent data has to be handled frame-coherently. Our first goal is an interactive framework that allows the detailed exploration of geo-spatial meteorological data, which allows meteorologists to explore the correlations between the weather attributes in space and time.

User Guidance. The exploratory navigation through a data set is important, though for large data sets an unguided search is a tedious serial process. The spatial domain is large and the time series easily covers decades of data. For this reason, we will concentrate on user guidance. We envision an exploration tool, in which users are offered choices during their exploration, based on previously visited structures or initially indicated preferences. Instead of randomly navigating through a domain, the system will provide story arcs that the user can follow, for instance a series of hurricanes with similar extend and duration. The creation of these story arcs requires both manual annotations for training, as well as feature extraction for assistance in the annotation of events.

Automated Annotation. Finally, we further automate the annotation process through machine learning. First, features in the scalar and vector fields are learned with auto-encoders or generative adversary networks. These unsupervised learning methods project the data into a low-dimensional feature space, also known as latent space. Second, using supervised learning we correlate the latent space with annotations and visualization parameters that were placed by an expert. Over time, the system learns to annotate, which leads to a semi-interactive workflow, in which domain experts can take corrective action. This learning process opens up another dimension that is highly relevant in visualization: the visualization of uncertainty. The low-dimensional feature space, the data-driven annotations, and the underlying meteorological data are uncertain. Uncertainty visualization of 3D data is a recognized challenge in the visualization literature.
Keywords: Climate Science, Feature Extraction, Flow Visualization, Machine Learning, Meteorology, Scientific Visualization

Title: Machine Learning for Communications
Abstract:
The field of machine learning has seen tremendous advances in the past few years, largely due to the abundant processing power and the availability of vast amounts of data that enable effective training of deep networks for complex models. The main motivation for using machine learning usually comes from that fact that in some areas, such as image recognition and natural language processing, constructing hand-crafted models that are elegant, tractable, and practically useful is nearly impossible. The field of communications, however, is built on precise, but often simple mathematical models that are well understood and have been shown to work exceptionally well for many practical applications. Unfortunately, the ever-increasing demands have forced communications systems designers to push the boundaries to such an extent that in many applications conventional mathematical models and signal processing techniques are no longer sufficient to accurately describe the encountered complex scenarios. Specifically, there is an increasing number of cases where rigorous mathematical models are either not known or impractical from an analytical, or even computational perspective. 

At this point, machine learning methods may come to the rescue as they do not require rigid pre-defined models and can extract relevant and meaningful structure from large amounts of data to provide useful results. In fact, contrary to many other machine learning applications, in communications it is relatively simple to collect such labeled data, either from simulations or from testbeds or the massive amount of every-day communication, making the training of machine learning algorithms for numerous applications comparatively straightforward. The two aforementioned observations render machine learning an ideal tool that carries the potential to augment and revolutionize signal processing for communications and even exploit communications for further applications. Some well-known
research groups have recently started to venture into this area, but the idea is still very much in its infancy and there is a number of pressing issues that need to be addressed, such as:

1. Applications: Machine learning algorithms can, in principle, learn to perform any task from the data they are given. However, since in the field of communications we already know how to solve many problems optimally, it is crucial to carefully identify the applications where machine learning is actually beneficial and not a re-invention of a (needlessly complicated) wheel.

2. Architectures: Different applications require vastly different machine learning approaches and architectures. Thus, it is important to identify the best architecture for each scenario and to develop novel architectures and approaches whenever necessary.

3. Adaptability: In most communications applications, and in particular in wireless communications, the environment can change rapidly over time. Machine learning algorithms need to be able to adapt, either through appropriate offline training or through low-complexity and fast-converging online training.

The main goal of this project is to exploit expert knowledge from the communications field to put machine learning to service where conventional signal processing struggles to achieve the expected quality of results. To this end, we propose to examining a number of concrete practical applications. The first application is to employ neural networks in order to perform digital self-interference cancellation in full-duplex radios with better performance and lower complexity than existing approaches. The second application has to do with using machine learning techniques in order to perform blind detection of channel codes, as well as joint detection and decoding of coded non-linear modulation schemes. As a final application, we propose to employ machine learning techniques that exploit the residual self-interference signal in full-duplex radios to build context-aware radios that can make inferences about the environment in which they are operating.

recognition and natural language processing, constructing hand crafted models that are elegant, tractable, and practically useful is nearly impossible. the field of communications, however, is built on precise, but often simple mathematical models that are well understood and have been shown to work exceptionally well for many practical applications. unfortunately, the ever increasing demands have forced communications systems designers to push the boundaries to such an extent that in many applications conventional mathematical models and signal processing techniques are no longer sufficient to accurately describe the encountered complex scenarios. specifically, there is an increasing number of cases where rigorous mathematical models are either not known or impractical from an analytical, or even computational perspective. at this point, machine learning methods may come to the rescue as they do not require rigid pre defined models and can extract relevant and meaningful structure from large amounts of data to provide useful results. in fact, contrary to many other machine learning applications, in communications it is relatively simple to collect such labeled data, either from simulations or from testbeds or the massive amount of every day communication, making the training of machine learning algorithms for numerous applications comparatively straightforward. the two aforementioned observations render machine learning an ideal tool that carries the potential to augment and revolutionize signal processing for communications and even exploit communications for further applications. some well known research groups have recently started to venture into this area, but the idea is still very much in its infancy and there is a number of pressing issues that need to be addressed, such as: 1. applications: machine learning algorithms can, in principle, learn to perform any task from the data they are given. however, since in the field of communications we already know how to solve many problems optimally, it is crucial to carefully identify the applications where machine learning is actually beneficial and not a re invention of a (needlessly complicated) wheel. 2. architectures: different applications require vastly different machine learning approaches and architectures. thus, it is important to identify the best architecture for each scenario and to develop novel architectures and approaches whenever necessary. 3. adaptability: in most communications applications, and in particular in wireless communications, the environment can change rapidly over time. machine learning algorithms need to be able to adapt, either through appropriate offline training or through low complexity and fast converging online training. the main goal of this project is to exploit expert knowledge from the communications field to put machine learning to service where conventional signal processing struggles to achieve the expected quality of results. to this end, we propose to examining a number of concrete practical applications. the first application is to employ neural networks in order to perform digital self interference cancellation in full duplex radios with better performance and lower complexity than existing approaches. the second application has to do with using machine learning techniques in order to perform blind detection of channel codes, as well as joint detection and decoding of coded non linear modulation schemes. as a final application, we propose to employ machine learning techniques that exploit the residual self interference signal in full duplex radios to build context aware radios that can make inferences about the environment in which they are operating. . coding and modulation, communications, full Title: Metric methods for linear and non-linear transformations
Abstract:
The overall objective is to use and develop ground-breaking metric methods for the study of products of randomly selected transformations. The rationale for this is that such compositional products appear all over natural and social sciences when modelling the time development of a system, especially in a random environment. They are also a cornerstone issue in dynamical systems, for random walks on groups, and appear in evolution differential equations. Moreover, in machine learning it has been empirically observed that natural data tends to have a compositional structure (the momentous rise of deep learning). Some leading researchers in the listed areas have expressed the need for new tools. Our metric space methods provide a new general approach that has already demonstrated its power and is destined to complement linearity as a foundational concept. The specific aims include the following:
•to establish multiplicative ergodic theorems for bounded, linear operators. This is in particular motivated by the study of certain stochastic partial differential equations,
•to study a new framework for the theoretical understanding of deep learning, with results regarding random initialization, drop-out and the stochastic gradient descent method. In particular, we plan to investigate a newly discovered depth threshold phenomenon of neural networks. This is ongoing work with B. Avelin (Uppsala),
•to deepen the metric methods for holomorphic maps in several complex variables, notably Wolff-Denjoy theorems and an extension of Carathéodory prime-end theory to higher dimensions. This is in collaborations with F. Bracci (Rome), L. Arosio (Rome), and M. Fiacchi (Pisa),
•to advance an entirely new line of attack on the 70-year-old invariant subspace problem in operator theory,
•to prove a multiplicative ergodic theorem for surface homeomorphisms that extends a spectral theorem of Thurston. Joint project with C. Horbez (Paris).
Although the span of these goals is strikingly broad, with our approach several key issues are interconnected. Thanks to this and the strength and expertise of my collaborators, progress is expected on each subproject. Significant partial advances are nearly guaranteed thanks to the novelty of the methods and the current status of our research. Via cross-fertilization, progress on one part will lead to new insights for another. In particular I expect to learn and take advantage of techniques from several complex variables, optimization and stochastic game theory, and import parts of them to a purely metric setting. Several of our new methods can be viewed as metric analogs of functional analysis. In view of the wide range of the applications it could be argued that there is a new theory emerging. Such a metric theory would provide a tool-kit, far beyond the contraction mapping principle, especially adapted for scientific studies of nonlinear phenomena across disciplines.
Keywords: Deep learning, Ergodic theory, Holomorphic maps, Metric geometry, Operator theory, Random walks

Title: Beyond Traditional Elites: Influencers’ Agenda Setting Powers in the Digital Age
Abstract:
The advent of digital democracy and social media has shifted the balance of power in political agenda-setting, giving rise to a new online elite of Social Media Influencers (SMIs) capable of shaping public discussions and agendas. For instance, German influencer Diana zur Löwen has used her platform to promote mental health awareness, influence public attitudes, and even impact the German coalition agreement. Italian fashion influencer Chiara Ferragni advocates for social causes such as raising funds for a new hospital wing during the COVID-19 pandemic, while Swiss influencer Anja Zeidler mobilized her 300,000 followers against the MERCOSUR free-trade agreement in 2019, prioritizing environmental concerns in the political agenda. However, it remains unclear whether SMIs can consistently leverage their significant follower numbers to set public debate topics beyond their usual areas of expertise. Thus, this research project aims to explore the role SMIs in the political agenda-setting process and their influence on traditional political elites within digital democracies.

Specifically, I seek to examine the extent and quality of political content produced by SMIs, assess the effectiveness of their communication strategies, and determine the degree to which they shape traditional political elites' agendas. The objectives include analyzing the scope and nature of SMIs' political engagement on two major social-media platforms – Instagram and YouTube –, an evaluation of their communication strategies' effectiveness in resonating with online audiences as well as an investigation of SMIs’ influence on traditional political elites’ agendas and discourse. To achieve these objectives, the comprehensive data collection will focus on English and German speaking SMIs from Europe and North America between 2019 and 2023. I will employ a combination of supervised classification techniques, sentiment analysis, and advanced correlational methods to explore the relationships between SMIs, political content, audience engagement, and traditional political agendas. Additionally, online experiments will be conducted to assess SMIs’ ability to alter the issue priorities of their online audiences.

This project holds significant academic, methodological, and practical implications for the fields of political science, political communication, and digital democracy. It contributes to a more profound understanding of political agenda setting in the digital age and offers valuable insights into the nature and effectiveness of political content shared by SMIs. Methodologically, the project will develop and employ innovative computational methods to analyze online political content, expanding the methodological toolkit in political science and providing broader applicability across various areas of the discipline.

On a practical level, the findings will inform political actors, advocacy groups, and communication professionals on the most effective strategies for engaging with online audiences and shaping political discourse. By identifying factors contributing to the success or failure of political content on social media, this research can guide the development of targeted communication strategies for political engagement and advocacy.
Keywords: agenda setting, digitalization, elites, public policy, social media

Title: Advanced Cooperative NeuroEvolution for Autonomous Control
Abstract:
The overarching goal of this proposed work is to further improve and
apply our state-of-the-art methods for evolving recurrent neural
networks.  Our coevolution-based algorithms have already shown great
potential in a variety of applications and have outperformed previous
methods in thorough experimental studies.  Here we will push the
coevolution concept to the limit by developing ways to scale the methods
to high-dimensional inputs, such as vision.

There are many real-world problems for which programming a solution
directly is not feasible.  Typically, these problems involve
controlling some system by repeatedly measuring its state and
selecting the best action from a set of possible choices.  Because the
environment can be very complex (i.e. non-linear, high-dimensional,
noisy, unstable, etc.)  it can be difficult, if not impossible, to
know in advance the consequences of a sequence of such actions.


The field of Reinforcement Learning (RL), has
contributed many methods that,
in principle, can solve these types of problems.  However, in
practice, they have not scaled well to large state spaces or partially
observable environments (POMDPs).  This is a serious problem because
the real world is continuous (i.e.~an infinite number of states) and
artificial agents, like natural organisms, are necessarily constrained
in their ability to fully perceive their environment.


More recently, methods for evolving artificial neural networks or
neuroevolution (NE) have shown promising results on continuous,
partially observable tasks. We have made important contributions to
this area with methods that use cooperative coevolution to
automatically design recurrent neural networks (i.e.\ networks with
memory). Instead of evolving complete networks directly, networks are
built from subpopulations of components that are coevolved to work
together to solve a given task. Our Enforced SubPopulations (ESP) and
CoSyNE methods are particularly effective examples of this approach
that has been a applied to many diverse reinforcement learning
problems including finless rocket control, and supervised time-series
prediction.

While these results are encouraging, NE to date has only been applied
successfully to control tasks with a limited number of inputs
(typically less than 100). However, to solve sophisticated tasks in
real-world domains such autonomous robotics, much richer sources of
sensory information such as vision are required.  High-dimensional
inputs imply much larger networks and a correspondingly large search space,
which can cause evolution to converge before finding a solution.  

To scale neuroevolution to these conditions, we propose the following 
multi-faceted approach:

(1) Develop new, more powerful neuroevolution algorithms based on
  our own previous methods (work plan items 1 and 2)
  using insights from an empirical analysis of cooperative coevolution
  (item 3).

(2) Reduce the dimensionality of the input space by evolving
  non-redundant codes using the principle of predictability
  minimization,
  that can be used to preprocess inputs to evolved the evolved
  controllers (item 4).

(3) Explore new methods based on our recent groundbreaking 
  work to delay convergence in the space of
  large networks by sustaining diversity in the behavior of candidate
  controllers instead of in their genotypes (item 5).
Keywords: behavioral diversity, coevolution, neuroeovolution, recurrent neural networks
