Title: Development of a prognostic model of aneurysm sac expansion/shrinkage after endovascular repair (EVAR) by omics approach and machine learning
Abstract:
Background and rationale. The invasive treatment of abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) leads to severe stress-related responses and activates various inflammatory cascades. Currently, AAA is treated either using open surgical repair (OR) or endovascular aortic aneurysm repair (EVAR). Thereby, it is being used in up to 80% of elective and 60% of ruptured AAA cases. However, EVAR bears an increased risk of secondary intervention and long-term mortality compared with OR. Different outcomes have been observed after EVAR treatment: aneurysm sac shrinkage, stability or expansion of the treated aorta. Patients with aneurysm sac shrinkage have a significantly lower risk of long-term mortality, late complications and secondary interventions. In contrast, aortic sac enlargement and even sac stability, observed in more than 50% of cases, is associated with an increased risk of AAA rupture and mortality. Interestingly, virtually nothing is known about the pathophysiological mechanisms leading to sac shrinkage, especially in EVAR-treated patients without endoleaks. Endoleaks after EVAR can lead to an increase in aortic diameter and thus do not reflect the pathophysiological processes leading to either aortic sac shrinkage or stability/expansion in successfully implanted endo grafts. No study to date has performed proteome and transcriptome analyses of patient's blood to define circulating biomarkers associated with changes in the AAA wall after EVAR treatment using machine learning (ML) in order to develop a reliable predictive model of aortic sac shrinkage or expansion. 
Overall objectives and specific aims. The study aims to analyse plasma and blood cells from patients after EVAR treatment in a follow-up manner using data from proteomics and transcriptomics as well as clinical findings and 3D reconstruction of the diseased aorta. By applying ML, we intend to develop a reliable prediction algorithm including relevant disease-related circulating biomarkers associated with aneurysm sac stability/expansion or shrinkage.
Methods. The study is designed as a retrospective-prospective exploratory study. All patients between 30 and 80 years will be included, who underwent or will undergo standard EVAR of a degenerative infrarenal aortic aneurysm at the Department of Vascular Surgery and which do not show an endoleak postoperatively. Exclusion criteria will be patients with hereditary diseases, trauma, or individuals suffering from inflammatory disorders or interfering with the project outcome. Matched healthy volunteers will be used as a control group for comparison. Blood samples will be collected at different time points: 1 day prior to EVAR, 6 weeks, 12 and 24 months after the treatment. Blood will be separated into plasma and blood cells, followed by protein and RNA extraction, as well as extended proteomics and transcriptomics analyses. The data will be further validated by western blotting, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), and quantitative RT-PCR. The resulting big data sets will be analysed by ML, applying various known algorithms to develop a reliable predictive model of AAA sac shrinkage or expansion. The advantage of such an approach is that it allows us to adapt the predictive model appropriately for individual patients aiming for personalised medicine.
Conclusions and expected results. AAA sac shrinkage has been considered a surrogate parameter of successful EVAR treatment. In contrast, aortic sac stability/expansion is associated with complications and increased mortality. Nonetheless, nothing is known about the mechanisms leading to the corresponding changes within the aortic wall. Because of the lack of tissue samples from these patients, an extended blood analysis using a state-of-the-art approach (omics, ML) will allow us to develop a reliable predictive model of aneurysm sac behaviour, reflecting the corresponding changes within the aneurysm wall after EVAR.
Keywords: AAA expansion, AAA shrinkage, Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA), Aortic sac shrinkage/expansion, Circulating biomarkers, Endovascular repair (EVAR), Proteomics, Transcriptomics, endovascular aoritc aneurysm repair (EVAR)

Title: Supervised Deep / Recurrent Nets
Abstract: Supervised artificial recurrent neural networks with adaptive feedback connections are more powerful in sequential data processing than classical statistical methods such as Hidden Markov Models or Condtional Markov Fields. Our deep feed-forward networks also set records in many real-world pattern recognition benchmarks. The goal of this project is to analyze and further improve state-of-the-art algorithms for training recurrent and deep neural networks, also exploring how much they can benefit from massively parallel GPU architectures. The networks will be applied to high-dimensional problems (e.g., object detection) and challenging real-world benchmarks, such as prediction/compression, handwriting recognition, image recognition.
Keywords: LSTM RNN, Recurrent neural networks, deep neural networks, pattern recognition benchmarks, sequence learning, time series prediction

Title: Biological nanopore sequencing of long digitally-encoded polymers
Abstract:
Our society produces data at the impressive rate of few exabytes per day; trend that is continuously escalating creating for the future significant storage and archiving issues. At the current pace, supports based on silicon or magnetic tapes will become soon unsustainable, thus that new alternative concepts and technologies need to be explored to store information at higher density.  Synthetic information-containing polymers have recently emerged as a potential solution as they can offer unparalleled chemical flexibility to optimize storage density and long-term stability. However, analytical methods for decoding the molecular information stored in these synthetic polymers still hold significant drawbacks, which to date prevent the widespread use of this emerging technology. 
In this proposal we respond to this technological need by developing a framework based on biological nanopores, which are used to decipher digital information stored in synthetic sequence-defined polymers. This project is a synergistic collaboration between French researchers (CNRS, Strasbourg) specialized in digital polymer synthesis and Swiss scientists (École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne, EPFL) expert in biological pores and nanopore sensing. The applicants have already reported a proof-of-feasibility, in which engineered pores of the aerolysin pore-forming toxin family were used to sequence digital oligo(phosphodiester)s. The present project aims at advancing the state of the art in order to develop further this bio-inspired platform for retrieval of large data volumes in real-world applications. To do so, both the molecular structure of the polymers and the reading strategy will be optimized to match the analytical needs. First, the chemical properties and information content of the monomer bits will be investigated using molecular modeling and simulation, in order to understand which parameters (e.g., size, rigidity, bulkiness) affect the polymer-pore interactions. These rationally designed monomer bits will be prepared by automated phosphoramidite chemistry, polymerized and characterized in order to obtain linear chains with sizes ranging from 10-mers to 100-mers, containing terminal oligonucleotides to better guide pore translocation. Existing aerolysin pore mutants, along with newly engineered variants and alternative pores from the aerolysin superfamily, will be tailored to match polymer features in order to accurately decrypting the information therein encoded. The concurrent development of a deep learning framework will facilitate and automatize the decoding of digital polymers, contributing at the same time to guide the discovery of the optimal alphabet of digitally-encoded moieties tailored for aerolysin-based pores. As the field of information-containing macromolecules is still in its infancy, this bio-inspired platform specifically developed to define and decode them will surely open exciting novel opportunities to deliver practical solutions for the field of molecular data storage as well as for other areas such as materials traceability and anti-counterfeiting technologies.
Keywords: biological pores, chemical synthesis, data storage, deep learning, informational polymers, modeling and simulation, nanopore sensing

Title: Ethical dimensions of digital technology-assisted physiotherapy: fundamentals for ethics education of physiotherapists
Abstract:
Background and rationale:
This project aims to identify the needs of physical therapists regarding the use of digital health technologies and to define ethical case vignettes for the use of digital health technologies in physical therapy practice. Nowadays, more and more digital technologies are used in physical therapy and rehabilitation, such as robotic rehabilitation (Martin et al., 2014; Stahl & Coeckelbergh, 2016), health apps and wearables (Hussain et al., 2015), virtual reality for stroke rehabilitation (Rowe et al., 2022), or tele physiotherapy (Rausch et al., 2021). This development requires a new responsibility for physical therapists to critically examine ethical aspects of digital technologies. As digital health technologies also incorporate artificial intelligence, physiotherapists must be able to check that the principles of the ethics of new technologies and artificial intelligence have been respected, such as explicability and bias removal, or respect for user autonomy (Diagnostic Médical et Intelligence Artificielle, 2022; Radclyffe et al., 2023). Therefore, therapists need skills and competencies that go beyond the mere application of technologies. This raises new ethical issues in physical therapy practice (Rowe et al., 2022; Stahl & Coeckelbergh, 2016). Physical therapists must justify the use or non-use of a particular technology. They need to know the intended use and limitations of different technologies and be able to use them or not according to ethical principles. For this purpose, physical therapy orients itself to clinical ethics based on the four basic principles developed by medical ethicists Tom I. Beauchamp and James F. Childress. The four principles of ethical practice are described as follows: Respect for Autonomy, Non-Maleficence, Beneficence, and Justice (Beauchamp & Childress, 2019). In relation to health services are also Public Health Ethic Principles more and more relevant beside Biomedical Perspective (Mertz, 2018).

Overall objective and specific aims:
To further develop the competences of physiotherapists in the use of digital health technologies, the training of the skills required must keep pace with the development in the field. The knowledge and ethical case vignettes acquired in this project will allow to improve this training in educational programs. In specific, this project aims to 1) scope ethical dimensions that need to be considered by physiotherapists when using digital technologies in their practice and to identify ethical conflicts that arise within these ethical dimensions, 2) identify physiotherapists’ views on ethical dimensions of digital technology use and to identify their needs related to knowledge and competences, 3) develop case vignettes ethically relevant for physiotherapy practice, and 4) translate case vignettes into an effective toolkit for education to reflect on ethical questions.

Methodological approach: 
We plan to conduct 1) a scoping review on ethical conflicts arising in digital technology-assisted physiotherapy practice; 2) focus groups with physiotherapists and patients to explore their views on the ethical dimensions of digital technology-assisted physiotherapy and focused ethnography in various medical settings; 3) the development of case vignettes based on the results from studies 1 and 2 and their validation in an expert workshop and an online Delphi survey; and 4) the translation of the developed case vignettes into various educational material.

Expected results: 
This project will provide insight into the ethical dimensions of digital technology-assisted physiotherapy from both physiotherapists and patients view. These ethical dimensions will be adopted in case vignettes to be connectable on game-based learning-tools (e.g., moral games). At the end of the project, a toolkit to use in ethics education will be available.

Impact: 
A toolkit for the training of ethical decisions in digital technology-assisted physiotherapy will form a significant basis for future ethics education. But research will also benefit from the development of ethical case vignettes: they will be available for the assessment of physiotherapists' competences in ethical decision making.
Keywords: Digital Health Literacy, Digital Health Technologies, Ethics, Gamification, Health Services Research, Public Health Ethics

Title: Health inequalities and the prolongation of working life
Abstract:
Current demographic and economic developments in Western societies fuel a trend of extending working life. The public and academic debates about postponing retirement age give little attention to heterogeneity in aging. This project aims at examining the effects of the transition from employment to retirement on health outcomes for different social groups. In particular, we explore how the extension of working life and later life health conditions influence each other. One the one hand, we examine how retirement transition patterns, such as gradual or direct retirement transitions, affect individuals’ health outcomes. On the other hand, we investigate how adverse health conditions affect labor market integration during late careers and transitions to retirement. 

To this end, we adopt an interdisciplinary life course perspective that comprises both individual and institutional level factors. We draw from secondary data from Switzerland, as well as Sweden and the United States. We apply methods that allow for causal inference (such as difference-in-difference analysis), longitudinal methods (such as fixed-effects or sequence analysis) as well as methods appropriate to analyze particularly large or small datasets (such as machine learning or Bayesian statistics).

Our project contributes to unveiling the mechanisms that underpin health inequalities in the prolongation of working life. We aim at identifying which mid-life associated factors may best explain health differentials in the transition to retirement. These factors may offer effective targets for early intervention, improving health outcomes in old age. As ever more working lives end in late retirement, it is becoming increasingly important for researchers and policy makers to understand how this affects health in late life.
Keywords: Disability and illness, Health inequality, Life course sociology, Retirement transition, Working life extension

Title: Relational Identity and AI Agents: Conceptual and Ethical Issues
Abstract:
The boom of artificial intelligence technology in the last decade has triggered a marked increase in research on the ethics of AI. The increased application of AI, from the prediction of recidivism to predictive policing, hiring processes, recommendation systems, and artificial companions, has raised a host of ethical issues. One concern that has been voiced repeatedly is that AI will challenge human identity. But AI will not just change what it means to be human, it will also change what it means to be me. The issue how AI will challenge individual identities has however been neglected in the ethical debate so far. This project aims to make a crucial contribution to closing this research gap by investigating how interacting with artificial agents influences personal identity.
You construe your individual, characterizing identity in interaction with others which let you be part of groups, tell and show you whether they think you are kind or funny, advise you on life plans or which book you should read, and make life-changing decisions about you. AI has already begun to enter into such interactions with people – e.g., software recommends music, products, and online content based on user preferences – and will likely do so in ever more domains of our lives. Interacting with AI agents that are often opaque, biased, cannot engage in true moral reasoning, and with whom we likely have highly asymmetric relationships changes those relational dimensions of our identity. In this research project, I analyze the impact of AI agents on relational identity on a conceptual and ethical level.
First, I investigate to what extent AI agents can take the role of human agents in relational identity constitution and analyze how AI agents differ from human agents in this role. To this end, I review the literature on relational narrative identity and characterize AI agents along key concepts of opacity, objectivity/bias, and capacity for moral reasoning. Second, I investigate the ethical issues arising from three kinds of interactions with AI agents that are particularly relevant for their potential influence on relational identity: close relationships, AI as decision-making help, and AI as decision-makers. It is ethically relevant for our identity interests how AI we may form close relationships with (e.g., care robots, sex robots, or other companionships robots or chatbots) react to us and what kind of behavior they enforce or discourage. AI that helps us in making personal decisions, for instance through recommendation systems, could enforce stereotypical identities, eliminate deliberation processes that allow us to identify with and take responsibility for choices, and make recommendations without adequate moral reasoning. AI that makes decisions about us (e.g., by predicting the likelihood of future recidivism for sentencing) categorizes and characterizes us without providing explanations or opportunities to negotiate. Those three sketches of ethical concerns regarding AI agents and relational identity serve as hypotheses that are investigated and developed in this project.
Considering how quickly AI systems are being developed, it is crucial to timely address the ethical challenges they raise. This project can advance research which is essential for the current efforts in the regulation and ethical development of AI.
Keywords: AI Agents, Artificial Intelligence, Ethics of AI, Narrative Identity, Relational Identity

Title: Efficient statistical and computational tools for large space-time datasets with an emphasis on distributed memory parallel computing
Abstract:
Statistical models are indispensable to analyze and interpret space-time data, such as remotely sensed data, climate model outputs, and environmental measurements. However, increasing data sizes make it impossible to use standard geostatistical methods, as their computational workload exceeds the available resources. Although more algorithmic machine learning methods can handle large data volumes, they often lack interpretability and do not carry uncertainty estimates. Therefore, the search for efficient statistical models that can be run on large computers is an active and important field of research. During my SNSF Early Postdoc.Mobility project (May 2018 to November 2019) I develop and assess new approximate Gaussian process models (AGPMs) that make the analysis of large space-time datasets more efficient. Given the success of those AGPMs, it is appropriate to plan for additional support to refine and adapt the statistical results to different types of environmental datasets. In this way, the project will evolve from an interesting theoretical exercise to valuable and interdisciplinary contributions to science. 

The aims of the project are to:
- Investigate statistical properties of two new distributed memory parallel inference methods for AGPMs.
- Use the NCAR supercomputer facility to apply AGPMs to massive datasets including LiDAR based canopy height measurements, climate model outputs, and censored arsenic water contamination data.
- Strengthen collaborations with statisticians and other scientists to promote the use of the new AGPMs.

Although not obvious from an international perspective, an appointment at CSM with another visiting scientist status at NCAR is a unique situation for my research, not matched in other locations:
- Prof. D. Nychka (CSM), Prof. S. Bandyopadhyay (CSM), and Dr. D. Hammerling (NCAR) are renowned experts for space-time models and computing.
- NCAR has the necessary supercomputers and the know-how to run the models on large datasets.
- Nearby institutions including the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the Colorado State University, and the University of Colorado build a strong statistical community.

As mentioned in the invitation letter of Prof. D. Nychka, he will fund the last three month of the 18 months project with similar conditions as the SNSF. Therefore, I apply for 15 months SNSF funding and plan the project for 18 months.

Title: FRIDAY: Frugal, Privacy-Aware and Practical Decentralized Learning
Abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms currently dominate the computing landscape, primarily exploiting end-user data. The exponentially increasing volume of data used for training machine learning (ML) models, coupled with the growing size of these models, renders training on a single machine impractical. Consequently, major global stakeholders train and host these models in massive data centers, raising concerns about energy consumption, privacy, and overreliance on external providers. These concerns call for novel distributed infrastructures that address these challenges.
Federated learning (FL) systems offer a promising first step towards addressing these concerns. FL allows users to train a model on their private data and share only model updates with a central server, which then merges these updates and sends the resulting aggregated model back to users. Decentralized learning (DL) offers an alternative to FL, going a step further by eliminating the need for a (trusted) server that represents both a communication bottleneck and a privacy threat. Instead, participants in DL directly share their model updates with other participants using peer-to-peer topologies and gossip algorithms. Since DL requires minimal additional infrastructure and is relatively simple to deploy, it is an attractive alternative to FL to execute ML tasks in many industrial scenarios, such as healthcare and IoT settings. DL architectures, however, face challenges originating from (1) data heterogeneity (also known as non-IIDness) as different users possess
datasets with varying characteristics, (2) system heterogeneity as participants have varying capabilities in terms of memory, storage, computing power, and network, and (3) privacy concerns as in DL the bar to mount privacy attacks targeted at individuals is lower than in FL. While there have been recent theoretical advances in DL, the practicality of such systems in resource-constrained and heterogeneous settings remains to be demonstrated.

FRIDAY deviates from existing approaches by considering realistic DL settings where not all users have equal computational resources. FRIDAY will devise learning services that enable collaborative, frugal and privacy-aware learning. The originality of FRIDAY lies in its system-oriented approach, which aims to bridge the gap between decentralized algorithms and practical learning systems. To harness the power of peer-to-peer infrastructures and make DL practical, it is crucial to account for the wide range of data and system heterogeneity commonly found in real-world scenarios. Concretely, we will conceptualize, implement, and extensively experiment with innovative and practical decentralized architectures that are frugal and privacy-aware. 
We have identified three primary research questions to delve into the practical aspects of decentralized learning, building on our past research and recent advancements in decentralized architectures:
(RQ1) How to build practical \ac{DL} systems that facilitate model training in realistic and large-scale scenarios?
(RQ2) How to build frugal DL systems that reduce key system properties, such as computational and network overhead, while maintaining high model accuracy? 
(RQ3) How to enhance the privacy of DL systems by selecting from the wide range of alternatives found in FL, including differential privacy,  hardware enclaves, and secure aggregation, while customizing the solution to ensure
compatibility with intended target applications?

The success of our project hinges on our ability to implement and experiment with such systems at a large scale, with real-world traces and on a wide range of datasets. The project will output open-source software that fosters research and promotes the adoption of the developed systems. Ultimately, we anticipate FRIDAY to significantly impact both academia and industry, paving the way for practical, efficient, and privacy-aware distributed learning systems that satisfy diverse settings an

Title: Fast, Scalable Graph Pattern Mining on Evolving Graphs
Abstract:
Graph pattern mining is an important area of Big Data that aims to discover complex structural patterns in graphs. This enables wide-ranging applications, such as finding chemical interactions or 3D protein structures, analyzing communities in social networks, mining frequent motifs in networks, analyzing semantic data, or detecting suspicious credit card transactions.

Graphs evolve over time to reflect changes in their structure, e.g. users join and connect to each other in social networks. Current general-purpose graph mining systems can only execute algorithms on static graphs. The few systems that support dynamic graphs are not general-purpose as they require fixed pattern queries that are less expressive. Since graph mining algorithms require enumerating all subgraphs of interest contained within a graph dataset, they are expensive to execute and it is, therefore, desirable to design systems that only process the changes to the graph.

We propose to design the first distributed, general-purpose graph mining system for evolving graphs. Our system offers a streaming model where changes in pattern instances resulting from updates are output with low delay, enabling a new class of efficient, continuous pattern mining applications. Unlike existing systems that rely on data parallelism, this new graph mining system takes a task-parallel approach, combining an update-driven graph exploration technique with a novel canonicalization method that allows exploring changed pattern instances in a highly-parallel, co-ordination-free manner.

I have implemented a prototype of this new graph mining system. Preliminary results on a single machine compared with state-of-the-art systems show significant performance improvements. Our system is faster than Delta-BigJoin, a popular fixed subgraph query system by 1.3X to 30X depending on the algorithm, while supporting a more general computation model. We also achieve 7-8X runtime improvements over static recomputation from scratch. Furthermore, I expect the final system and optimizations to achieve at least 1-2 orders of magnitude more in performance improvements.

I would like to pursue this research during a mobility postdoc at MIT with Prof. Tim Kraska. I plan to scale out the system using Apache Spark and implement a sharded graph store to support large graphs. Moreover, our task-parallel system is amenable to several performance optimizations. For instance, we can support a pattern pruning API that will allow programmers to leverage domain-specific knowledge to aggressively prune the exploration and speed up computation. I will also investigate caching of partial subgraphs matching the pattern of interest to reduce recomputation as the graph is updated over time.

During this postdoc, I also plan to explore further extensions of this work by using GPUs to execute graph exploration and by employing NVMe SSDs to speed up the graph store and increase the caching capacity of the system. Finally, I will explore recent machine learning techniques in connection with graph mining, both by applying techniques such as learned indexes to speed up subgraph enumeration and by leveraging my new graph mining system in a machine learning pipeline that enables real-time anomaly detection in logs.

This project will provide a fast, scalable, open-source graph pattern mining system for evolving graphs that can significantly advance the state-of-the-art. This software will facilitate the development of new, interactive applications in the disciplines that rely on graph mining. For example, computational biologists could leverage incremental graph mining to detect common structures in protein-protein interaction networks with low delay, or data scientists analyzing social networks could interactively analyze communities. We expect the research to also provide more generally applicable results with respect to graph store design, adaptive graph partitioning, and task parallelism in graphs.

Title: Predictive modelling of clinically significant depressive symptoms after coronary artery bypass graft surgery
Abstract:
Background and rationale: In patients undergoing coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery as a treatment for coronary heart disease (CHD), the prevalence of clinically significant depressive symptoms (CSDS) is about 30%. This is 4-fold higher than the 12-month prevalence in the general population. In patients with CABG, CSDS are associated with poor quality of life and an increased risk of morbidity and mortality. Although meta-analyses show a slight decrease in CSDS from pre-CABG (19-37%) to post-CABG (15-33%), the majority of patients will not experience remission of CSDS. Moreover, psychological and pharmacological interventions have little effects on pre-CABG CSDS, whereas psychological depression treatment post-CABG requires several sessions to be effective. Several predictors of post-CABG CSDS have been identified, but there is no prognostic prediction model. Moreover, predictors related to increased inflammation and impaired interoception, both emerging key concepts to explain depression, have not been scrutinized in CABG. 
Overall objective: The overarching aim of this project is predictive modeling of post-surgery CSDS in patients with CABG using pre- and perioperatively collected data.
Methods: We will develop a prognostic prediction model for CSDS, assessed with the widely used Patient Health Questionnaire-9, 6 weeks post-CABG, using demographic, health behavior, psychometric, medical, inflammation and (cardiac) interoception data. Data analysis will be performed using machine learning algorithms. We will recruit a total of 350 patients from cardiac surgery departments in two different hospitals, anticipating a loss to follow-up of ca.15%. From the final cohort of 300 patients, 200 will be recruited in Hospital I for the training set to build the best suited statistical model of CSDS and another 100 in Hospital II for the test set to validate the final model. To avoid model overfitting, a nested cross-validation approach will be used. One analysis approach will perform a binary prediction using a PHQ-9 cut-off score =10, proposed for depression screening in patients with CAD, and one will perform regression using a continuous PHQ-9 score. In addition to the comprehensive prediction model, a “light solution” model will also be calculated and evaluated with candidate predictors that are available in all cardiac surgery centers to increase generalizability. The data will additionally be used to develop exploratory prediction models of anxiety symptoms, CABG-surgery induced posttraumatic stress, and poor quality of life to generate hypotheses for future studies. 
Expected results: We expect that the developed prediction model can detect patients undergoing CABG who will develop CSDS post-surgery. We further expect our project to yield important information on a predictive value of inflammation and interoception for post-CABG depression. 
Impact for the field and beyond: For clinical practice, the prognostic prediction model will allow for an identification of patients at risk of developing CSDS post-CABG yet before undergoing surgery. To prevent the development of post-CABG CSDS, clinicians could initiate precision medicine decisions before/early after surgery based on patient-specific modifiable predictor variables. Patients at risk could be better monitored for CSDS and other indices of psychological well-being in the postoperative period such that established treatments can be offered depending on the psychosocial status of the individual patient. Moreover, the identification of risk factors for post-CABG CSDS could greatly advance the knowledge about mechanisms linking depression to CHD risk and inform influential hypotheses of the pathogenesis of depression, such as the inflammation hypothesis and aberrant interoception.
Keywords: Behavioral cardiology, Cardiovascular disease, Computational Psychosomatics, Coronary artery bypass surgery, Depression, Inflammation, Interoception, Machine learning, Prediction, Psychocardiology, Psychological wellbeing

Title: Identification of blood protein biomarkers in infant victims of Abusive Head Trauma (AHT)
Abstract: AHT including shaken baby syndrome (SBS), is one of the most severe forms of traumatic brain injury (TBI) in infants under the age of two. It has a higher morbidity and mortality than accidental trauma in infants. AHT affects almost 40 infants per 100,000 live births per year and one-third of cases are misdiagnosed.  Indeed, in cases of silent AHT, clinical symptoms may overlap non-specifically with those of atraumatic infants with acute malaise (such as non-febrile convulsions, or Brief Resolved Unexplained Event (BRUE)). Pediatricians will not systematically screen infants for intracranial haemorrhage (ICH) with radiological examinations to avoid unnecessary exposure to ionising radiation in the developing brain. Conversely, in cases of accidental TBI, all cases with a severity of 13 or less on the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) are referred for radiological investigation. Currently, there is no screening test that would assist the standard clinical practice in identifying, within the infant’s population suffering of malaise, children with ICH at risk of mild to moderate AHT (GCS: 9-12/13-15). Our pilot study  highlighted the serum increase of proteins physiologically enriched in the brainstem, eye and spinal cord in the infants with severe AHT (GCS: 3-4) compared to atraumatic controls. Several proteins elevated in AHT serum have N-glycosylated site-specific post-translational modifications (PTMs) typical of proteins secreted from tissues into the bloodstream. This multidisciplinary project aims to improve the diagnosis of mild to moderate AHT in infants, that we named silent AHT, through the proteomic identification of a panel of functionally related serum markers that reflect the pathophysiology of AHT at the molecular level. Based on our proteome analysis of the world's largest blood cohort of AHT in children (UPMC Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh, USA) and experience with mass spectrometry (MS) analysis of PTM, we aim to test the hypothesis that serum protein expression profiles, together with N-glycosylation levels of proteins potentially secreted from tissues, provide the baseline knowledge for computational machine learning (ML) to obtain serum signatures that discriminate pediatric silent AHT. Our project has four specific aims: i) Aim 1 is to apply bioinformatics tools, also based on ML,  to discover panel of proteins that discriminate the silent form of AHT in recently acquired serum protein dataset in the pediatric cohort from Pittsburgh biobank measured using advanced MS. The cohort includes the large number of silent and severe AHT cases, as well as atraumatic control and accidental TBI cases in children.  ii) Aim 2 is to record complementary N-glyco-proteomes of the same infants using a previously developed MS platform for the measurement of enriched N-linked glycosylated serum proteins via hydrazide chemistry. This step will provide in-depth proteomic analysis of infant sera, enriching for low abundance and tissue secreted proteins. iii) Aim3 is to objectively evaluate the predictive performance of the biomarker protein panel for silent AHT identified in Aim 1/2 by using an independent serum collection from a prospective multicenter cohort (Hospices Civils de Lyon, Saint-Etienne University Hospital and University Hospital Geneva). iv) Aim4 will be dedicated to the creation of a novel, publicly available web data portal of proteomic datasets generated across different types of pediatric TBI within this project dedicated to AHT. The financial aspect has been secured for proteomics analysis of Aim1 and the sample collection within Aim3. The requested grant would allow further steps within Aims 1, 2, 3 & 4 to develop a novel serum biomarker panel that will form the basis of a point-of-care tool to select high-risk children with suspected AHT.

Title: Mechanisms for social learning
Abstract: Our decisions are shaped by the people surrounding us; we tend to eat at restaurants where others eat, to like people that are popular, and ask for advice when we face particularly difficult decisions. This propensity for social learning is shared among both humans and non-human animals. For humans, social learning is the basic mechanism underlying both our diverse and complex culture, and a range of maladaptive behaviors, such as herding in financial markets. Evolutionary biology has demonstrated that social learning increases adaptive fitness, but knowledge about the computational and neurobiological mechanisms underlying social learning is limited. The aim of the project is to provide such knowledge, by studying human social learning in terms of the underlying neural computations and brain systems. In particular, we ask how adaptive social learning strategies, such as copying the behavior displayed by a majority of others and copying the behavior of others when individual learning has costly consequences emerge from basic computational and neuropsychological reinforcement learning mechanisms. Moreover, we are interested in how these mechanisms can cause both adaptive behavior such as cooperation and maladaptive behaviors. We plan to achieve this by using quantitative behavioral observation, combined with formal computational modeling and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). The proposed research will elucidate the computational and neuropsychological mechanisms underlying learning in social environments, which in turn will provide insights into the basic building blocks of human culture.
Keywords: Conformity, Reinforcement learning, Social behavior, Social learning, fMRI

Title: High-frequency ambient seismic body waves: Unlocking a high-resolution probing signal
Abstract:
Recent developments in seismic processing have enabled the ambient seismic wave field as a source to study and monitor Earth structure. Ambient noise is attractive because it is ubiqui-tous, continuously available, and comes at no cost. However, a staggering proportion of stud-ies only use ambient surface waves which offer very limited resolution at depth. An enormous seismic remote-sensing and monitoring opportunity lies in high-frequency ambient body waves (>1 Hz), potentially providing a much clearer view of the subsurface, from the crustal scale to the exploration scale. Yet this part of the ambient seismic background is still largely a terra incognita, with little understood characteristics and sources.

The paucity of empirical evidence of high-frequency ambient body waves, in my interpretation, is less an immutable fact than a challenge in signal recovery. In the proposed two-year post-doc at the Marine Physical Laboratory (MPL) at Scripps Institute of Oceanography (SIO), I will explore and understand this largely unknown part of Earth’s background vibrations. This will be achieved by a cross-disciplinary combination of signal recovery techniques from ocean acoustics, radar, sampling theory, and seismology (seismic interferometry).

Researchers at MPL have been at the forefront of studying ambient body waves since 2005. The project will combine my industry-academia experience in ambient seismic noise with the MPL team’s world-class expertise in advanced signal processing and cross-disciplinary Earth system analysis.  The time is favorable for this project: large and spatially dense seismic net-works that lend themselves well to array-based processing are available today both in academia (e.g. Transportable Array in US, Hi-Net in Japan) and industry (e.g. LB3D in Long Beach, US CA). Development of processing improvements will occur in tandem with modeling body wave generation mechanisms and high-resolution studies on a crustal and exploration scale.

With this project I will establish myself as an expert in the analysis of weak signals in datasets from distributed and continuously recording data sources. The project will also enable me to extend my personal network in leading US research institutes (UC San Diego, CalTech, Stanford, UC Berkeley). This will lay the ground for a research career in Earth system monitoring innovations.
Keywords: Adaptive filtering, Array processing, Big Data, Earth system monitoring, Machine Learning, Seismic interferometry, Seismic noise

Title: Circuit organisation and function of vulnerable dopaminergic neurons in Parkinson's disease
Abstract:
Parkinson’s disease (PD) is the second most common degenerative neurological disorder affecting millions of individuals worldwide - approximately 6.1 million people in 2016 (Vos et al. 2017). The pathological hallmark of this disease is the degeneration of midbrain dopaminergic (DA) neurons causally linked with motor deficits, which are the basis for PD diagnosis. Although PD patients also exhibit non-motor symptoms such as deficits in cognition and motivation, which apparently are present before diagnosis and almost inevitably emerge with disease progression (Chaudhuri, Healy, and Schapira 2006). It is generally thought that DA subtypes show differential vulnerability during the progression of PD (Kamath et al. 2022), and it is therefore important to uncover the role of the DA subtypes that are responsible for the early phase of PD symptoms. In order to understand the progression of the disease and to develop new treatment approaches, it is crucial to understand the functional role of primary vulnerable DA neurons.

Recent studies have suggested that the vulnerability of DA subtypes is linked with expression of the markers Aldh1a1 or Agtr1 (Kamath et al. 2022; Liu et al. 2014). Moreover, unpublished data from the Meletis laboratory shows that expression of the marker Anxa1 marks a DA neuron subtype that shows high vulnerability and degenerates in a mouse model of PD. In this project, we aim to take advantage of this newly identified subpopulation of DA neurons (Anxa1+) which we hypothesise is responsible for the manifestation of the cognitive and motivational disturbances in the early phases of PD. For this purpose, we have designed and generated a mouse line which will allow us to specifically study the role of the Anxa1+ DA neuron subtype in PD progression (i.e. Anxa1-Flp mouse line). This project proposal is articulated in 3 aims: 

Aim 1: The physiology of Anxa1+ DA neurons. We aim to identify the circuit organisation (monosynaptic inputs and projections) of Anxa1+ DA neurons based on anterograde and retrograde tracing experiments including monosynaptic rabies tracing using genetic strategies in Anxa1-Flp mice. Moreover, we aim to define the role of Anxa1+ DA neurons during cognitive and motivated behaviours, focusing on reinforcement learning and behavioural flexibility.

Aim 2: The pathophysiology of Anxa1+ DA neurons. We aim to study in two models of PD - a mild 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) lesion as well as injection of alpha-synuclein preformed fibrils (PFFs) - the role of Anxa1+ DA neurons in the progressive dysfunction.

Aim 3: Define the molecular events in Anxa1+ DA neurons in the early events of PD. We aim to investigate the molecular events underlying progression in PD models (6-OHDA and PFFs) focusing on Anxa1+ DA neurons including non-cell autonomous degeneration.

These findings could open a revolutionary way to investigate PD and will uncover potential new circuit-based therapeutic approaches.
Keywords: Dopamine, Neurodegeneration, Parkinson, Substantia nigra, Vulnerable neurons

Title: Optimizing the Provision of Rehabilitation Services Through Explainable Recommender Systems (SmartRehab)
Abstract:
Clinical databases collect vast amounts of data daily, including treatments, test results, and patient reports, but they are currently underused. This happens because much of the collected data is not well systematized to be analyzed, and its value in medical decisions is regularly underestimated. To date, the distribution of health services is managed in multiple systems, which complicates information delivery to healthcare professionals and patients. The complexity of information and lack of data exploration may lead to suboptimal treatments, resulting in over or undertreatment, which implies additional healthcare costs and far-reaching effects on patient health and well-being.

This project aims to contribute to this area of research by implementing recommender systems that support healthcare professionals' decision-making processes. The project will use data from a rehabilitation clinic in Switzerland that cares for persons with spinal cord injury (SCI). Our system will analyze data from the first rehabilitation, which happens after acute care and lasts six to eight months. SCI is damage to the spine that leads to irreversible physical impairment, also known as paraplegia and tetraplegia. First rehabilitation is designed to support persons with SCI to get used to their new condition, and to give them the tools to make them as independent as possible. The healthcare professionals involved during this phase include physicians, nurses, physiotherapists, logopedists, and psychologists, among other therapists.   

In contrast to other clinical pathways, we focus on rehabilitation because healthcare professionals, together with the patient, define what services are required given the characteristics and needs of the patient. Thus, decisions about the provision of services can be revised and updated depending on the development of the patient. Until now, SCI has presented healthcare professionals with the challenge of analyzing complex individual cases and developing the appropriate treatment procedures crucial for patients in the early months of recovery. Recommender systems can support health professionals by giving them information about what worked best for similar patients in the past. 

Conventional health recommender systems (HRSs) rely on artificial intelligence (AI) to support healthcare decision-making and often lack explanatory power, raising ethical concerns and undermining the trust essential for understanding and acceptance of algorithmic decision-making. Therefore, this project will leverage recent developments in explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) for HRS. A hierarchical recommendation and explanation mechanism for optimal SCI rehabilitation services is proposed using a novel XAI design and evaluation framework at the system, interface, and algorithm levels. These algorithms include explanation-aware recommendation techniques that can generate a wide range of feature-, text-, and path-based explanations and inferences. The outcome of this project will be a web-based platform called "SmartRehab," which will provide healthcare professionals with explainable recommendations for SCI rehabilitation services through a user-friendly interface to support their decision-making. The platform will also track the impact of the recommendations on patient assessment. Additionally, the project will measure the explainable algorithms' performance and the user-friendly interface's usability and acceptability through offline and online evaluations. The evaluation will consider the system goals from the perspective of healthcare professionals and AI experts. 

This project is led by the Lucerne University of Applied Sciences and Arts (HSLU). HSLU is responsible for designing and implementing explainable methods in recommendations that will be integrated into the beta version of SmartRehab. In addition, this project collaborates with the University of Lucerne (UniLU), health professionals at the Swiss Paraplegic Center (SPC), and the Swiss Paraplegic Research (SPF) to comprehensively analyze the use case and thoroughly test and provide feedback on the system developed. The objective is to provide feedback on the system and ensure it is functional and user-friendly. The project's ultimate goal is to deploy a prototype of SmartRehab that can optimize medical decision-making in SCI rehabilitation. It will translate into optimizing patient functioning and reducing the cost of services. The project also considers rigorous ethical considerations. As a result, it provides a solid foundation for expanding current solutions by establishing a standard for using HRS for rehabilitation services.

Title: Improving Priors towards Automated Prescreening of Brain Magnetic Resonance Images
Abstract:
The need for high throughput radiological assessment of Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) data is increasing. On one hand, health-care relies more and more on patient images and on the other hand, the number of individuals at risk who should be screened regularly for early detection increases with the ageing population. Both of these developments lead to increasing use of MRI - due to its resolution, contrast and non-ionizing nature – and put pressure on radiologists to increase assessment throughput and pay higher attention to subtle early disease effects. The main limitation of the current radiological practice in meeting the demand is the need for extensive human interaction in analyzing images. Arguably, the most viable solution is to develop algorithms that can automatically prescreen images to accelerate assessment.

Two important components of automatic image prescreening are: (i) detecting abnormal lesions, one of the main uses of MRI, and (ii) extracting anatomical measurements that can indicate degenerative conditions. Both have been central goals for computing research and automatic algorithms have been developed. Despite the advances, current methods are not used in clinical practice. The two key issues are: algorithms do not perform as well as humans in detecting lesions, and algorithmic image quality requirements for extracting accurate measurements differ from the ones used in clinical practice and necessitate longer acquisitions.

In this proposal we aim to develop algorithms to address both of these issues and focus on structural brain imaging, an area MRI is widely used in, as the application area. Our observation is that both issues arise due to a common technological limitation: current image priors that are at the core of algorithmic approaches do not accurately represent anatomical variability in large image patches, i.e. areas covering a number of neighboring voxels. Recent developments in unsupervised learning and release of unprecedentedly large datasets, such as Human Connectome Project and UK Biobank, are motivating for the development of new algorithms that can encode priors with higher representation power. Based on this we propose two specific aims:

1. General-purpose lesion detection in brain MRI: First aim is to develop algorithms for detecting abnormal lesions of any type in a voxel-wise fashion. To this end, first we will develop methods to estimate prior distributions over multi-modal image patches through unsupervised learning with Random Forests (RF) and neural networks (NN). Then, we will develop outlier detection algorithms that can use the estimated priors.

2. Segmentation with fast acquisitions: We will develop segmentation algorithms robust to artifacts due to subsampling in k-space with the goal of reducing acquisition times necessary for extracting measurements. For this, we will first develop methods to estimate joint priors over intensities and segmentations in image patches using unsupervised learning with NN. We will then develop joint reconstruction-segmentation and post- reconstruction segmentation algorithms that use the estimated priors to overcome the artifacts. We focus on segmentation of subcortical and cortical structures whose morphology is sensitive to neurodegeneration.

Successful completion of the proposed project would advance the state of image priors and their use for medical image computing. It would facilitate algorithmic approaches to accelerate radiological assessment of MR images and allow research studies to expand cohorts with similar resources using shorter acquisitions. Here our focus is on structural brain imaging, however, we aim to develop generic methods that can be applied to other modalities and organs.
Keywords: MRI, faster acquisition, image priors, lesion detection, medical image analysis, segmentation, unsupervised learning

Title: Self-assembly of neuromorphic particle networks
Abstract:
Artificial intelligence systems consume the amount of energy of a power plant, while the human brain operates on the energy equivalent of a lightbulb. This inefficiency arises because conventional computers separate memory and processing, requiring constant data transfer. In contrast, the brain’s interconnected network of neurons stores and processes information simultaneously.

To address this inefficiency, we can design brain-inspired computer architectures that imitate these neural networks. Instead of manufacturing such systems in costly silicon-chip factories, we can harness self-assembly, where microscopic building blocks spontaneously form networks. These self-assembled networks can reconfigure themselves by breaking and reforming connections, much like how the brain rewires itself during learning. 

My proposed research aims to create neural networks by self-assembling colloidal particles. The goal is to design and optimize particle networks from the ground up, first utilizing guided assembly to understand and control information processing “synaptic gaps”. These foundational experiments will then drive a computational study investigating networks with diverse self-assembly-derived structures and reconfigurability. This project will establish a novel research direction toward the experimental realization of structured and rewireable brain-inspired computers. 

By bridging the gap between artificial intelligence and neuroscience, we can develop transformative, energy-efficient, and cost-effective computing technologies for artificial intelligence.

Title: Retinex: From Shadow removal to aneurysm assessment
Abstract:
"Not all light is created equal." Indeed, the light we perceive is a superposition of many different phenomena. In a very simplistic approach, for example, one can model the amount of light reflected from an object and measured by the eye (or a camera) as proportional both to the brightness of the illumination shed onto the object, and the rate of reflectance of the object's surface. Now, when we are interested in an object's reflectance as a descriptor of its material properties, e.g. in order to tell a "white" sheet of paper from the "brown" table it is laying on, we need to normalize for variations in the scene's illumination. This is a job which the human visual system is rather good at. Conversely, if we are interested in getting a good estimate of the incoming illumination, we need to get rid of the local modulation by the surface reflectances. Either way, it is a problem of decomposing an observed intensity image into an underlying field of illumination and reflectance. Retinex is the corresponding concept in image processing and computer vision for this task --- however, a multitude of different flavors of retinex have been developed in the past 40 years, each of which is rather specific to the application it is intended for.

Here, we propose to perform research on retinex in two main directions: First, we want to bring order into this plethora of retinex implementations, and unify them within a single, simple but general framework --- they all deal with the same reflectance-illumination decomposition problem, after all. Indeed, we have obtained some very promising preliminary results in this respect, and would like to exploit the many opportunities and potential generalizations of our proposed model. Second, we propose to apply retinex within a very useful clinical application, namely the assessment of aneurysms based on contrast-agent flow observed in digital substraction angiography (DSA) images. Here, retinex will help extract the contrast-agent concentration from single DSA frames, and its tracking over subsequent frames allows simple inference of blood flow patterns, which from much more complicated computational fluid dynamics studies are known to be relevant predictors of aneurysm rupture risk, and later also help evaluating the eventual treatment outcome.

Title: Deciphering the regulatory impact of transcription factor dose on cell (re)programming
Abstract:
Cellular reprogramming —the process of converting one cell type into another— is controlled by transcription factors (TFs) that bind to specific DNA sequences to regulate gene expression. However, despite significant research, lab-based cell reprogramming remains inefficient and variable, suggesting gaps in our understanding of the underlying regulatory mechanisms. While several factors may contribute to this reprogramming heterogeneity, we focus here on one specific factor: TF dose and its effect on molecular and cellular outcomes. Despite its importance, TF dose has been largely understudied, since research has mainly considered the presence or absence of TFs without detailed exploration of their dose-response effects. Emerging evidence now suggests that TF dose plays a critical role in shaping cell fate by modulating gene expression patterns and chromatin dynamics, often in a non-linear manner, leading to either desired or aberrant outcomes in reprogramming.

To address this, we propose to investigate how TF dose influences transcriptional and chromatin landscapes and ultimately cell fate at the single-cell level, integrating expertise from the Deplancke and Zenk labs in single cell multi-omics and cell culture models with advanced machine learning (ML) expertise from the Brbic lab. Using an innovative single-cell (sc) technique, scTF-omics – adapted from the recently developed, dose-sensitive single-cell TF overexpression assay (scTF-seq)-, we will generate multi-modal datasets (TF dose, gene expression, and chromatin accessibility) in two distinct cellular contexts: 2D mouse mesenchymal stem cells (Aim 1) and 3D human brain organoids (Aim 2). These datasets will capture temporal changes in cell states, allowing us to build and apply ML models to address two key questions (Aim 3): i) what transcriptional mechanisms drive diverse TF dose-dependent gene expression responses (like constitutive, linear, monotonic or non-monotonic responses)? and ii) can we infer gene regulatory networks (GRNs) underlying specific cell lineages or states, and predict how TF dose impacts these GRNs? Using an active learning strategy, we then plan to iteratively refine the ML models by experimentally validating their predictions and incorporating the resulting data back into the model.

By elucidating the role of TF dose in reprogramming, we aim to provide new insights into TF dose-dependent gene regulation and establish foundational principles for engineering cell states, with ultimately broad implications for regenerative medicine and therapeutic applications. Taken together, our project tackles key challenges in single-cell biology and cellular (re)programming by integrating cutting-edge technologies and AI-driven approaches to unravel the complexities of transcriptional regulation underlying cell fate determination.

Title: Massively Parallel Optical Reservoir Computing with Frequency Multiplexing
Abstract: In response to the computation bottleneck of conventional Turing-von Neumann machines, the quest for more efficient tools has never been stopped. Among others, optical computing has appeared as an interesting solution. The high speed and inherent parallelism of optical computing has shown promising potential for a variety of computing paradigms, from Ising machine, neural networks, to deep learning. In particular, a special type of neural networks termed reservoir computing, can greatly benefit from the random yet fixed coupling in the light transmission through scattering media. Leveraging millions of the pixels of spatial light modulator and camera, such optical system performs large-scale parallel computation at the speed of light. Recent studies, in particular in the host group, have successfully use the optical reservoir computer to predict the motion of chaotic system, without pre-knowledge about its model. The objective of this project is to further push the capability of parallelism by frequency multiplexing. Indeed, most of the optical reservoir computers are simply implemented on single laser sources, while the frequency degree of freedom is generally overlooked. Relying on my past experience with optical frequency combs and the expertise of optical computing from the host group, the concept of broadband reservoir computing can be merged seamlessly. With massively parallel frequency multiplexing, this project expects outperformance of optical reservoir computing compared to conventional computer towards large number of nodes, and would ultimately push the reservoir size to an unprecedented level. In addition, the feasibility of adapting integrated microcombs will also be explored, which could potentially reduce the form factor, cost, and complexity of such optical reservoir computing systems.
Keywords: optical computing, optical frequency comb, reservoir computing, scattering media

Title: ‘Windows’ into Mars’ potentially habitable subsurface in the context of NASA’s Perseverance extended mission
Abstract: The search for ancient biosignatures on Mars has largely focused on sedimentary environments, such as the Jezero Crater delta, where the Perseverance rover landed and will collect samples for future return to Earth. However, this approach assumes that life on Mars had enough time to develop photosynthesis, which may not be the case given the early loss of surface water and habitability on Mars. Alternatively, anaerobic microbial life may have evolved in the subsurface of Mars and left clues in ancient rocks that are not affected by crustal recycling. In this project, I propose to explore the potential of subsurface life on Mars by studying the polygonal ridges in Nili Planum, a region of Noachian basement rocks adjacent to Jezero Crater. These ridges are hypothesized to be formed by hydrothermal processes and may contain hydrous minerals that indicate astrobiological activity and biosignature preservation. I will use orbital and laboratory data to determine the composition of the polygonal ridges and compare them to other examples of exhumed hydrous deposits on Mars. Furthermore, I will map the global distributions of polygonal ridges using machine-learning techniques in collaboration with world-leading experts in the field. This project will advance the science in the exploration of subsurface life on Mars and provide high-priority sampling sites for Perseverance’s extended science mission.
Keywords: Astrobiology, Biosignatures, Hydrothermalism, Mars, Spectroscopy

Title: Finding neural correlates of discrete behavioural events
Abstract: Source separation is a well-known problem in signal processing. The most famous example is the cocktail-party problem where the aim is extracting a voice of interest from a mixture of voices and noise. The problem of separating sources affects many fields including brain imaging. When using EEG, isolating the signal of interest is a task that has been studied for a long time but has not yet reached satisfactory results. Interestingly, many of the tools that are used for speech separation can also be applied to separate sources of activity in EEG. The study of behaviour is one of the applications of EEG particularly affected by the problem of source separation. To limit this problem, behavioural studies are carried out in controlled environments, nevertheless, the results from these studies are biased towards behaviour observed in the lab and cannot be extended to behaviour observed in natural conditions. Also, during lab behavioural studies only short timescales can be investigated and important long timescales, such as weeks, are missed. While there are portable solutions to capture EEG, it is more difficult to capture discrete natural behaviour. One promising solution comes from the tracking of smartphone interactions. This type of monitoring can last for months and can capture behaviour for a wide range of timescales. This project aims to find neural correlates of discrete behaviour by applying techniques of signal processing and machine learning that I studied and developed during my Ph.D., to the problem of unmixing EEG sources. To adapt these techniques to EEG I will leverage the unprecedented dataset collected by the lab of Arko Ghosh containing around 500 hours of simultaneous recordings of EEG and smartphone use. The dataset contains pure forms of passive touch and pure touch movements that will be used as ground truth signals for a new generation of multichannel beamforming filtering techniques to create mappings between discrete behaviour and corresponding brain activity. This project will also adapt the successful model that I recently proposed for speech separation to the problem source separation in EEG, namely I will train a neural network model on the large amount of data available to me and use discrete behaviour as a time-varying cue to isolate corresponding neural processes from EEG. Finally, I propose to create an encoding model to reconstruct the isolated neural activity using only the discrete behavioural data. This project can lead to high-impact scientific output such as broadening our theoretical understanding of natural behaviour, extending the study of natural behaviour outside of the ideal conditions of the lab, and reducing the number and complexity of assumptions generally made in EEG processing (e.g. high number of electrodes). This research will have an immediate impact on the way EEG is used for analyzing behaviour and a long-term impact on the development of real-time tools for behavioural analysis that can be applied to the monitoring of neurological and mental health in real-world environments.
Keywords: Digital signal processing, Discrete behaviour, EEG, Machine Learning, Source separation

Title: Early Fake News Detection on Social Media
Abstract: Recent years have seen a large increase in the amount of fake news posted on social media. Although fake news is a problem that exists for a very long time, the increasing popularity of social media has facilitated fake news dissemination and has exacerbated the problem and its consequences. In this project we plan to focus on early fake news detection (i.e. detect if a news article contains false information as early as possible after its publication) by combining information extracted from different modalities including content and images. First, we will develop models that capture the life cycle of fake news to understand which stories attract more attention and why. Then, we plan to develop effectiveness metrics that are appropriate for the early stage prediction problem. Finally, we plan to develop models for early fake news detection that will combine multimodal information extracted from content and images. The outcomes of the proposed research will contribute to the theoretical and methodological development of sophisticated fake news detection systems.
Keywords: deep learning, effectiveness metrics, fake news detection, multimodal detection, social networks

Title: The interplay between environment and collective behaviour in a natural setting
Abstract:
Understanding of complex systems relies upon our ability to bring into light how emergent properties arise from interactions among the individual components. In collective behaviour, complex coordination and decision- making abilities can emerge from localized rules of interaction. The prevailing paradigm in the study of collectives has been to consider every individual “self-propelled particles”, inspired by collective processes in physical systems, and to model their interactions in empty environments. Similarly, most experimental studies are conducted in artificial enclosures with minimal structural complexity. While this approach has been highly influential in bringing into light the general concepts of collective motion and decision-making, it fails to take into account many features present in natural systems. Individuals are not particles, but are rather probabilistic decision-making entities that must make sense of complex streams of potentially informative sensory input from their social and physical environment, and translate these into a sequence of behavioural decisions. In nature, collective behaviour often takes place in structured environments, which impose a set of constraints that can affect the way individuals sense their environment and interact with each other. These constraints may play a significant role in how selection acts on behavioural traits, thereby shaping social interactions, and can thus have a strong impact on how individuals integrate information from their peers. In order to further our understanding of collective behaviour, it is thus important to move towards a more realistic framework that integrates this biological complexity.
Obtaining detailed, quantitative data on animal groups in the wild is the ideal solution to study the complexity of natural systems, because it captures the selective environment in which behaviour evolved. While recent technological advances now allow for the automated tracking of multiple individuals, implementing such technologies in the wild represents a significant challenge. In nature, environmental conditions are highly variable, and many of the techniques than can have been developed for laboratory studies cannot be readily implemented in the field, especially underwater where there is considerable dynamical refraction and scattering of light. Benefiting from the recent advances in computer vision and machine learning, I have recently developed a pipeline to obtain 3D trajectories from multiple individuals, with a high spatiotemporal resolution, from field observations on groups of coral reef fish. In the current application, I propose to build upon my recent progresses to study how these groups of fish interact with their physical environment, and how this shapes their social interactions.
I first propose to investigate how groups of damselfish Dascyllus marginatus avoid collisions during collective escape manoeuvres. This species of coral-dwelling planktivores forms small groups of individuals that live in close association with a coral, in which they can retreat when threats appear. Uncoordinated actions during collective escape can have dramatic consequences, and it remains unclear whether animals use specific mechanisms to avoid such problems during these extremely fast events. Second, I aim to investigate whether water flow around the coral head creates turbulence that affects the spatial positioning of the fishes, thereby shaping their social interactions. Finally, I want to investigate how the structural aspects of the coral head might drive group spatial dynamics and composition. Altogether, this project will allow to investigate in depth how animals interact with the physical structures that play a central role in their ecology, and how their behaviour as a collective can be influenced by the environment in which it occurs. This approach will allow to bring ecological relevance and to further the integration of the environment in the study of animal collective behaviour.

Title: A Learning Approach to Image Restoration and Motion Estimation without Ground Truth Data
Abstract:
This project aims to develop novel learning-based methods for image restoration and motion estimation that do not require collecting ground truth data. Learning-based methods have demonstrated the capability of achieving a very high performance not only on semantic tasks, but also on low-level computer vision tasks, such as image restoration and motion estimation tasks. These tasks typically require a large data set of input-output pairs, where, for example, in motion estimation the input is a pair of subsequent video frames and the output is the latent optical flow. While this data enables a very effective training of neural network models, collecting such pairs is very often costly (e.g., it requires specialized hardware) or does not scale well (e.g., parallel capture requires multiple replicas of the same specialized hardware). One way to address this limitation is to generate synthetic data either with a rendering engine and then adapt the domain gap with real data or by directly learning to generate realistic data. 
We aim to use this framework to address image restoration tasks such as denoising, deblurring, super-resolution, demosaicing, reflection separation, and motion estimation tasks such as optical flow estimation and tracking. Because of the broad applicability of this framework to problems where the image-formation model is (at least partly) known, we expect this project to make a substantial impact in both academia and the industry.
Keywords: deep learning, generative models, image restoration, motion estimation

Title: “Learning from others” – Harnessing patient narratives to generate personalized disease course scenarios in persons with Multiple Sclerosis
Abstract:
Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a neurodegenerative disease that affects younger adults and generally has an unpredictable disease course and outcomes. Many people with MS share their stories and experiences to help others learn from them. These narratives are a valuable resource for chronic disease research or even long-term disease course scenarios, but they are hard to process and analyze systematically. Recent advances in large language models (LLM) can help to combine and present such narrative information in a succinct and person-tailored way, which would benefit MS research and improve MS management and patient-doctor communication concerning current health status and future scenarios.

Building on a prototype software, existing MS research databases, and publicly available patient narratives, this project aims to harness a novel LLM architecture (Retrieval-Augmented Generation, RAG) that operates in a tightly controlled, secure environment and utilizes locally stored data to generate personalized data summaries and disease course scenarios for people with MS from multi-modal data (structured clinical data and surveys, unstructured narratives). Measures are set in place to ensure data privacy, data security, and data ownership.

Our project will fine-tune an existing RAG prototype and examine its capability and usefulness for summarizing structured and unstructured MS data and for generating personalized disease scenarios. The main data source is provided by the Swiss MS Registry (SMSR) and consists of 1039 anonymized free-text timelines of major life events since MS diagnosis, which will be enriched by data from two linked Swiss MS databases and free-text patient narratives from public websites. All data will be converted into short text statements that include the unique person identifier, the time, and an event description, which will serve as input and data source for our MS-RAG. For this project, we will actively involve the community of MS researchers, neurologists, and people with MS, who will guide model fine-tuning and contribute to evaluating the accuracy and usefulness of the MS-RAG-generated summaries and scenarios.

Work package 1 aims to produce and evaluate personalized summaries of disease histories. Our MS-RAG will be given anonymized, narrative timelines of 30 participants from the “major life events” study as input and prompted to generate summaries for medical professionals or persons with MS. The summaries will be evaluated by 10-15 stakeholders for their readability, clarity, and usefulness (as Likert scales). Next, personalized summaries will be created for all 1039 “major life event” survey responders and analyzed with natural language processing methods (BERTtopic) to describe and assess the plausibility of broader disease course patterns in the study sample.

Work package 2 aims at creating and evaluating personalized MS disease course scenarios. The MS-RAG will receive anonymized data and life stories of 30 persons as input and generate three scenarios over 5 years for each person, informed by the pool of available free-text narratives. The scenarios will be qualitatively compared with actual outcomes and expert opinions to measure their accuracy and usefulness in an online survey. In a stakeholder workshop, we will also explore how these scenarios can improve patient-doctor communication and shared decision-making in healthcare, as well as examine associated risks of such scenarios.

Combined, our MS-RAG architecture and the project findings promise to make complex, multimodal research data more accessible for MS management. They will further contribute to reducing information overload for medical decision-making, thus enhancing opportunities for persons with MS and healthcare providers “to learn from others”. Moreover, our systematic stakeholder involvement in development and analysis will yield important insights into how novel LLM-based technologies can be productively employed in MS management, as well as into perceived risks.
