Title: Interpretability-Guided Deep Learning for Medical Image Analysis: Applications to Medical Image Classification, Retrieval and Segmentation.
Abstract:
Background 
Artificial Intelligence (AI) in medical imaging applications is making a large impact in healthcare due to its ability to extract high-dimensional information of rich predictive value for many tasks, such as image classification, segmentation, localization, registration, prognosis, etc. However, as the research in this area progresses, we discover important issues about AI in medical image computing, such as sensitivity to confounding biases, shortcut learning, vulnerability to attacks, over- and under confidence, etc. The challenge in investigating and understanding these phenomena is exacerbated by the “black box” nature of AI systems. In this regard, the area of interpretability of AI systems emerged as a necessity to further leverage our understanding of AI systems, and to develop effective mechanisms to audit and monitor them. In healthcare applications, trustability, and ultimately patient safety, is of utmost importance to ensure that AI systems are successfully translated into clinical practice. Based on our previous and recent findings, in this project we aim at investigating how interpretability saliency maps, a common strategy to yield pixel-wise attribution maps, can be used beyond provision of interpretability information, to leverage AI systems in three different areas of importance: (i) inductive bias for model training, (ii) informative sample selection in active learning, and (iii) as distance metric for sample retrieval. 
Aims and Methods
In the proposed project we aim at developing a novel graph-based information unit based on the information contained on saliency maps for all class label explanations available per sample. This novel information unit, referred to as Multiclass Saliency Graph (MSG), is composed of nodes corresponding to individual saliency maps per class label, and edge weights characterizing their similarity. We will investigate different ways to characterize inter-, and intra-sample saliency information contained in MSGs for inductive bias, sample informativeness, and as a novel sample distance metric for sample retrieval. To show benefits of the proposed novel MSG information unit, we will apply our findings to three different medical imaging tasks: (i) multi-class medical image classification, (ii) medical image retrieval, and (iii) multi-sequence medical image segmentation, using own and publicly available medical imaging datasets, featuring multi-site-multi-class lung scans, and multisequence MRI datasets of brain tumor patients receiving radiation therapy. For each of these tasks, the approach will be evaluated using standard machine learning and clinically oriented metrics, as well as interpretability-oriented metrics including expert-based saliency maps. The evaluation will lead us to test the following main hypothesis: 
Hypothesis: 
H0: Multiclass Saliency Graphs yield rich sample information and can enable (i) improved model training and performance, (ii) improved learning rates in an active learning setup, (iii) improved inter-sample distance metrics, and (iv) improved interpretability of trained models.
Expected impact of the proposed study
By investigating a novel mechanism that jointly yields improved model training, performance, and model interpretability, we expect to make contributions to fighting the black-box nature of deep learning systems while fostering improved generalization, fast learning rates, and model performance. By evaluating the proposed approach in different clinical imaging tasks, we expect to highlight its pluripotency to combat many of the issues hindering clinical translation of deep learning systems. Beyond AI-based imaging tasks, and under the framework of personalized medicine, the proposed approach can be extended to non-imaging information datasets, towards improved model performance and interpretability in multi-omics clinical scenarios.

Title: Towards biologically-interpretable generative models of population coding
Abstract:
The amount of functional and biological data we can collect in the brain is exploding. We are now able to record the simultaneous activity of up to a million neurons via light beads microscopy (LBM) calcium imaging. In addition, the fine transcriptomic subtypes of the recorded neurons can be revealed via post-hoc transcriptomics. While this type of multimodal, large-scale, cellular-resolution data may offer us an unprecedented opportunity to unveil the biological underpinnings of the neural population code, the analysis of such data represents a major challenge and calls for the development of dedicated, biologically-interpretable machine learning methods.

We propose to test a new data analysis approach that uses machine learning to learn concise and biologically-interpretable representations of neuronal population activity on a first-of-its-kind dataset, namely LBM calcium imaging of visual cortex combined with post-hoc transcriptomic identification of the recorded neurons.

Our method is explicitly designed to take advantage of large numbers of neurons in large-scale recordings for it is inspired by the theory of neural fields. The proposed method is, in a sense, the "dual" of current nonlinear latent variable models. In short, our model assumes that there exists a low-dimensional latent embedding "space of neurons" and that a neuron's coding properties are determined by its location on this space. Then, at any given time, our model represents the individual firing rates of all neurons as a neural field, i.e., a smooth function over the latent space. To enable efficient learning from large-scale recordings, this nonlinear model will be expressed as a deep generative model, more specifically, a variational autoencoder. Transcriptomic data will enable us to put biological labels on the recorded neurons and thereby endow the latent embedding space with biological interpretability. Moreover, in analogy with the benefit of behavioral labels for latent variable models, these biological labels could improve the consistency of the embedding of neurons on the latent space and allow us to combine data from different animals.

This method will provide us with a comprehensive picture of the nonlinear contribution of each neuron subtype to the representation of sensory and non-sensory information in visual cortex and it will shed light on the structural basis of high-dimensional population coding. In addition, as our generative model uses the language of neural field theory, it should help us design data-driven mathematical models of emergent population dynamics in cortical networks of neurons.

Title: SENSIF Innovative multiplex paper-based electrochemical biosensor and artificial intelligence for smart  periprosthetic joint infection and AMR diagnostic
Abstract: SENSIF will develop a new device for supporting correct diagnosis and efficient treatment of Periprosthetic Joint Infection (PJI) close to the patients based on i) the use of synovial fluid as biological sample, ii) combination of multiple biomarkers with artificial intelligence (AI), and iii) exploitation of paper-based technologies for their several outstanding features including high sensitivity and easy mass-production. PJI has been selected as a case study considering i) the significant burden on the healthcare expenditure and the quality of life of the patients due to the presence of bacteria resistant to the few antibiotics with proven anti-biofilm activity, ii) the challenge in the diagnosis of this type of infection in timely fashion, even following 2018 Philadelphia International Consensus Meeting criteria, and iii) the need to support the prudent and rational use of antimicrobials and reduce overprescription. SENSIF will establish a pillar in the management of infection by combining the diverse and complementary skills and infrastructures of SENSIF consortium constituted by i) the physicians with relevant expertise in PJI, ii) data scientists with experience from developing AI-based methods for diagnostics, iii)  biomolecular scientists with expertise in diagnostics orthopedic disease, and iv) two companies, one (SME, start-up company) with skills in the development of miniaturized point-of-care devices prototype and the other one (large company) with its activity focused on the development, manufacturing, and selling of orthopaedic medical devices.
Keywords: Diagnostic, Infection, Joint Prosthesis, Orthopeadic, Point-of-care

Title: Investigation into finite temperature atomic-scale crystal plasticity through generative deep learning
Abstract:
This research proposal aims to develop a computational framework, by combining statistical mechanics with the generative deep learning, that will enable an efficient sampling of finite-temperature atomic configurations, effective computation of the free energy, and examination of the thermally activated processes underlying crystal plasticity. The developed computational framework will then be applied to determine the influence of external load and temperature on the rates and mechanisms of the thermally activated cross-slip processes in fcc Ni and hcp Mg crystals.

The plastic deformation of crystalline materials is primarily governed by the evolution of linear defects, called dislocations. The evolution of a dislocation network entails various thermally activated processes involving atomic-scale interactions with different crystalline defects and the underlying crystal structure. Cross-slip is a thermally activated dislocation mechanism that is important for dislocation multiplication, dynamic recovery, and dislocation patterning. Understanding the specific mechanisms and computing the rate-of-occurrence associated with the thermally activated atomic-scale processes as a function of temperature and external load is crucial for modeling and controlling the plastic deformation of crystals.

Finite-temperature behavior of a system, e.g., a crystalline defect, depends upon its free energy, a key thermodynamic quantity whose calculation from the atomic description of the material requires enumerating the equilibrium atomic configurations (microstate) accessible by the system at the prescribed temperature. The rate of a thermally activated process is, furthermore, a sensitive function of the associated free energy barrier. Conventional atomistic simulations, i.e., molecular dynamics (MD) and Monte Carlo (MC), are plagued by the time-scale problem and are particularly ineffective in examining the thermally activated processes and computing the free energy barrier of a transition. Furthermore, various complexities and heavy computational costs involved in the existing free energy computation techniques compel the introduction of numerous approximations and use of relatively easily calculable zero-temperature properties that fail to account for key finite temperature behaviors.

The real valued non volume preserving (RealNVP) neural network offers an efficient way to generate the equilibrium finite-temperature microstates and determine the associated free energy. For instance, a RealNVP based sampling framework, Boltzmann generator, has been demonstrated to generate equilibrium microstates from the NVT ensemble and applied to simple and molecular systems. The Boltzmann generator leverages the invertible structure and tractable training associated with the RealNVP to learn a transformation from the Gaussian distribution to the desired Boltzmann distribution of the NVT ensemble. The microstates are then generated in "one-shot" from the trained network. The loss function used in the training of the Boltzmann generator, furthermore, provides an efficient means to determine the free energy of the system. Thus, the RealNVP based sampling framework holds promise in facilitating a systematic investigation of the temperature-dependent behavior of crystalline defects.

The major hurdle in the application of the Boltzmann generator to crystalline defects arises from the associated computational complexity of O(N^2), N being the number of atoms. The O(N^2) scaling prevents the handling of a large number of atoms which is required in the modeling of crystalline defects. To solve this critical issue, we propose a new deep learning architecture for the Boltzmann generator that reduces the computational complexity of the algorithm to linear O(N) in the number of atoms. To examine the thermally activated processes, we propose to incorporate the Boltzmann generator into the finite temperature string method to facilitate an accelerated sampling of the equilibrium microstates and efficient computation of the free energy barrier. The developed framework will then be benchmarked by applying it to study the behavior of point defects. We will, next, apply the developed framework to examine the effects of stress and temperatures on the cross-slip rate of straight and jogged screw dislocations in fcc Ni, and influence of temperature on the cross-slip rate of the pyramidal <c+a> screw dislocations in hcp Mg.

We believe that the proposed research will introduce an efficient computational framework to shed light on various atomic-scale finite-temperature phenomena controlling crystal plasticity. The efficient generation of equilibrium microstates and computation of the free energy will encourage the application of the Boltzmann generator to a wide range of problems in materials science. This research will further help reveal the finite-temperature cross-slip mechanisms of screw dislocations in fcc and hcp crystals.

crystal structure. cross slip is a thermally activated dislocation mechanism that is important for dislocation multiplication, dynamic recovery, and dislocation patterning. understanding the specific mechanisms and computing the rate of occurrence associated with the thermally activated atomic scale processes as a function of temperature and external load is crucial for modeling and controlling the plastic deformation of crystals. finite temperature behavior of a system, e.g., a crystalline defect, depends upon its free energy, a key thermodynamic quantity whose calculation from the atomic description of the material requires enumerating the equilibrium atomic configurations (microstate) accessible by the system at the prescribed temperature. the rate of a thermally activated process is, furthermore, a sensitive function of the associated free energy barrier. conventional atomistic simulations, i.e., molecular dynamics (md) and monte carlo (mc), are plagued by the time scale problem and are particularly ineffective in examining the thermally activated processes and computing the free energy barrier of a transition. furthermore, various complexities and heavy computational costs involved in the existing free energy computation techniques compel the introduction of numerous approximations and use of relatively easily calculable zero temperature properties that fail to account for key finite temperature behaviors. the real valued non volume preserving (realnvp) neural network offers an efficient way to generate the equilibrium finite temperature microstates and determine the associated free energy. for instance, a realnvp based sampling framework, boltzmann generator, has been demonstrated to generate equilibrium microstates from the nvt ensemble and applied to simple and molecular systems. the boltzmann generator leverages the invertible structure and tractable training associated with the realnvp to learn a transformation from the gaussian distribution to the desired boltzmann distribution of the nvt ensemble. the microstates are then generated in "one shot" from the trained network. the loss function used in the training of the boltzmann generator, o(n^2), n being the number of atoms. the o(n^2) scaling prevents the handling of a large number of atoms which is required in the modeling of crystalline defects. to solve this critical issue, we Title: Striding Towards Multidimensional Place and Social Space; Advancing Statistical Modeling Approaches for Social and Spatial Spillover in Latent Variable Models
Abstract:
Spatial dependence occurs when cases in a statistical analysis have a systematic relationship on a variable in space. For example, cultural traits tend to be more similar in nearer regions. Social dependence occurs when cases who are more socially engaged share a systematic relationship on a variable. For example, close friends have a stronger impact on opinion formation, compared to acquaintances. These forms of dependence are distinct from dependence in time. Simply put, time moves in one direction and thus earlier measurements can impact later measurements, but not vice versa. Spatial or social dependence are multidirectional and thus accounting for these effects require a more complex procedure to that of temporal dependence. 
When analyzing spatially or socially dependent data, the statistical approach must account for the dependence in order to make valid inference. The class of model which can measure these effects originated in the field of economics (LeSage & Pace, 2009). In both situations, social and spatial, the statistical approach is identical; however, the operationalization of the dependence and how it is measured differs. The behavioral sciences, in particular psychology, have largely ignored these approaches in training and research. For example, the cross-country analysis approach frequently erroneously treats countries as independent units (e.g., Horn, 2009; Pokropek, Borgonovi, & McCormick, 2017; Kövi et al., 2019). The lack of utilization of spatial/ social network approaches in psychology in part can be explained by the frameworks lack of orientation towards traditional approaches like latent variable modeling.
To fill this methodological gap, I recently developed a novel statistical approach which incorporated a psychological sciences hallmark analysis, Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) with spatial/ social auto-regressive effects (Roman & Brandt, 2021). This approach has great utility in many fields and is broadly applicable to any setting which has multidimensional constructs and spatial or social dependence. While this model was a good first step, more work is needed to develop this framework to have the flexibility needed for broad application. 
This project aims to make spatial/social network SEM more accessible to researchers by further developing the framework established in Roman and Brandt (2021) and by making the tools accessible to researchers. Multi-group and longitudinal adaptations are proposed to maximize the empirical applications of the models. The models will be developed, evaluated with simulation studies, and typified with empirical examples utilizing existing data. The project culminates in the development of open source (R package) implementations of the models in an effort to increase the accessibility of the approach to applied researchers and to improve the scientific impact of the project. 
The project is feasible, novel, and impactful. In Roman and Brandt (2021), I establish the utility of the spatial/ social network auto-regressive SEM combined approach. The adaptations I propose follow existing developments from other approaches and are thus likely to succeed. Each of the proposed models are inherently novel as no existing approach can simultaneously accommodate spatial/social dependence in conjunction with latent predictions and multi-group specifications or longitudinal measurements. The approaches are impactful in that they allow researchers to theorize and test new empirically relevant confirmatory hypothesis that could not be tested with existing methods. While the proposal targets psychological research, the models can be applied to a wide range of research designs, phenomena, and disciplines.
Keywords: Bayesian, Machine Learning, Multi-Level Structural Equation Modeling (MLSEM), Multi-group SEM, Social network auto-regression, Spatial auto-regression, Structural Equation Modeling (SEM)

Title: Automatic and patient-specific 3D MRI models of hip cartilage and labrum – a morphological and biochemical analysis for improved surgical decision making
Abstract:
Background and rationale
Joint preserving surgery aims to optimize biomechanics in hip deformities to stop or delay progression of degeneration. Good long-term results depend on correct indication and surgical correction of all relevant pathologies. This can be challenging, especially if early arthritic changes, mixed or borderline deformities are present. Today’s imaging modalities have their limitations: Radiographs are only a 2D representation of the 3D hip anatomy and early degenerative changes of labrum or cartilage are not detectable. CT allows segmentation of osseous anatomy, however, is associated with radiation exposure and does not give information about soft tissue. Standard morphologic MRI is limited to detection of advanced cartilage damage while biochemically sensitive MRI such as gadolinium enhanced MRI (dGEMRIC) of cartilage can be used as a more sensitive cartilage biomarker. In clinical routine a more detailed morphologic 3D analysis of cartilage and labrum and assessment of dGEMRIC indices is not routinely feasible due to the laborious task of manual segmentation. Current deep learning technologies including convolutional neural networks can potentially allow automatic segmentation of the entire hip joint. 

Overall aim
To develop a deep learning approach to automatically segment 3D MRI models of hip cartilage and labrum for a more detailed morphological and biochemical analysis and improved surgical decision making in young patients with hip deformities.

Specific aims
(1) To develop and validate a deep-learning approach for fully-automated MRI-based 3D hip models of bone, cartilage, labrum 
(2) To perform intraoperative and histological validation of cartilage damage using 3D model-based dGEMRIC analysis
(3) To define normal and abnormal 3D labrum and cartilage morphology in patients compared to asymptomatic volunteers

Methods
(1) Retrospective study including 100 hips who underwent direct MR arthrography at 3 Tesla including a newly developed 3D dGEMRIC sequence (3D MP2RAGE). An expert reader will perform manual ground truth segmentation of bone, cartilage and labrum which serves as training data for the neural network. A 3-fold cross validation will be performed to evaluate segmentation accuracy. A software for visualization and calculation of dGEMRIC indices and 3D morphologic cartilage (thickness, size of the surface area, volume) and labrum (width, cross sectional area, volume) parameters using the 3D models will be developed.
(2) Prospective study of a minimum of 50 hips / 25 hips with preoperative direct MR arthrography including dGEMRIC at 3 Tesla undergoing surgical hip dislocation or total hip replacement. The neural network will be used to generate 3D models of hip cartilage for topographic dGEMRIC analysis which will be compared to intra-operative- (Beck classification) and histologic cartilage damage (Mankin score, intensity of safranin-O staining) using receiver operating characteristics analysis.
(3) Prospective study of a minimum of 400 patients with preoperative direct MR arthrography including dGEMRIC at 3 Tesla and 40 hips from asymptomatic volunteers will be included. The neural network will be used to generate 3D models and calculate 3D cartilage (thickness, size of the surface area, volume) and labrum (width, cross sectional area, volume) parameters which will be compared among different hip deformities and asymptomatic volunteers.

Expected results
(1) A neuronal network can generate accurate (minimum dice coefficient of 0.8) and fully-automated MRI-based 3D hip models (bone, cartilage and labrum) for calculation of dGEMRIC indices, 3D morphologic cartilage- and labrum morphology.
(2) A dGEMRIC threshold can be defined which allows an accurate detection of intraoperative and histologic cartilage damage.
(3) Reference values of 3D cartilage and labrum morphology for normal hips and different hip deformities can be defined.

Impact
This application aims to exploit the great potential of deep learning technologies to establish a segmentation pipeline for the entire hip joint which paves way for routine use of a new dGEMRIC technique as a robust, clinically and histologically validated biomarker. The proposed methodology will enable calculation of 3D morphologic parameters of cartilage and labrum to a level detail which to date has not been feasible on a routine basis. Overall, these achievements have great potential for improved surgical decision making in young patients with hip deformities and early joint degeneration.
Keywords: MRI of the hip, biochemical cartilage composition, deep learning, delayed gadolinium-enhanced MRI of cartilage, hip osteoarthritis, image segmentation, joint preserving hip surgery, musculoskeletal imaging

Title: The curious brain: Dissecting the neurocomputational mechanisms of curiosity and reward, and their impact on incidental learning.
Abstract:
Curiosity is a fundamental component of human activities and societies. Although it may appear to motivate actions without direct needs or benefits, there is growing evidence that it has adaptive value. Curiosity is defined as the desire to acquire knowledge, and it aims at reducing ignorance and uncertainty, eventually favouring the optimization of behaviour. Researchers have distinguished two types of curiosity: instrumental curiosity refers to the exploration of the environment with the aim to learn its rules, while non-instrumental curiosity refers to spontaneously seeking epistemic knowledge in absence of clear utility. However, research on curiosity is scarce, and little is known about its neural and computational mechanisms. Some scholars suggested that knowledge might be treated as an intrinsic reward - an idea consistent with observations that curiosity-driven actions engage dopaminergic brain circuits overlapping with the reward network, and that humans (as other animals) learn how to maximize the probability of future reward. Decades of research on reward processes, known as reinforcement learning (RL), have demonstrated the crucial role of a frontal-striatal brain network, notably including the ventromedial prefrontal (vmPFC) and orbitofrontal cortex (OFC). The striatum encodes prediction errors (PEs), which drive the learning. However, no research directly compared RL and curiosity. 
Here, we propose a novel cognitive task including reward, instrumental curiosity and non-instrumental curiosity, allowing us to study similarities and differences between these conditions. Behavioural performance will be measured with computational modelling, while brain activity will be recorded with high-resolution 7-Tesla fMRI acquisition. The effect of reward and curiosity on incidental memory will also be assessed to unravel their influence on learning and functional brain dynamics at retrieval. We will build an innovative computational model to probe hierarchical predictions, PEs and uncertainty about reward probabilities during decision making with curiosity-driven options. Crucially, we will extend this model by including a branch that encode computations about the perceived advantage of exploring the environment instead of exploiting it (i.e., non-instrumental curiosity). Our modelling approach will allow formally testing the hypothesis that uncertainty drives the need for knowledge, and probing for the first time whether the striatum is also involved in learning to explore, beyond learning to exploit. Through functional and effective brain connectivity analyses, we will test the hypothesis of a dual involvement of the striatum in encoding both how and whether to exploit reward, with its corticopetal projections to different prefrontal regions responsible for updating (i.e., learning) these two complementary variables.  
Our project has several innovative and unconventional aspects as it will bring formal computational principles and neural foundations to seemingly freely chosen behaviours associated with curiosity. This work should encourage a novel approach to the scientific study of curiosity and foster its integration in cognitive sciences and clinical research. Our model could be usefully applied to study reward processing deficits in neuropsychiatric disorders such as depression or apathy, promote interventions enhancing curiosity-driven learning in attention deficit hyperactive disorder (ADHD), or even improve artificial intelligence tools and robotic engines.
Keywords: Brain, Computational modelling, Curiosity, Reinforcement learning, Reward, Striatum, fMRI

Title: Deploying machine learning for multi-physical fields simulation of metal additive manufacturing
Abstract: Marking its evolution as a central feature of the Fourth industrial revolution, additive manufacturing broadly refers to the layer-by-layer 'printing' of spatially precise on-demand 3D structural objects with enhanced design freedom relative to conventional manufacturing technologies. Effective contribution of metal additive manufacturing (MAM) to the vision of Industry 4.0 necessitates addressing key challenges related to mechanical reliability of the printed parts and their costs. Due to the lack of a better alternative, trial-and-error strategies are often adopted to optimise MAM process conditions. A deeper understanding of the various physical phenomena associated with MAM process might be achieved through numerical simulations, that would in turn enable a more systematic optimisation of process conditions required to achieve the goal of 'first-time-right' high-quality production.A thorough quantitative understanding of the MAM process requires insights from different types of computer simulations, namely: thermal, mechanical, metallurgical, and fluid-dynamics. The extremely high computational cost of such multi-physical fields simulations has been addressed in previous research by either decreasing the simulation domain size and/or by adopting gross simplifications. Instead, this project proposes to exploit the power of multiscale modelling and machine learning algorithms to realise reliable component-scale simulations for MAM. The underlying idea originates from the incremental build nature of MAM and the fact that the involved phenomena during deposition of the material increments are very similar at each location. The variation in the characteristics of the deposited increments does not originate from a significant change in the involved physics but only from a (modest) change in the imposed boundary conditions. Component-scale simulations of MAM process can therefore be considered as solving a large number of nominally similar small-scale models, each under different boundary conditions than the rest. The computational cost of such repetitive simulations can thus be significantly reduced by employing a specific class of machine learning toolboxes called 'metamodels', i.e. parsimonious statistics based learners. We have already demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed idea for thermal analysis of selective laser melting (SLM) process.The proposed research aims to develop a flexible simulation platform which, for a given set of SLM process conditions, trains and validates a metamodel on the basis of few small-scale high-fidelity simulations that incorporate thermal, mechanical, and microstructural computations. For a given geometry and process parameter set, the platform will use the metamodel for predicting a range of relevant parameters/characteristics within the SLM build ? such as temperature history profiles, hot spots, residual stress distributions, part distortion, and microstructural parameters like grain size and texture. The prediction results will be subsequently exploited by a crystal plasticity finite element (CPFE) framework for assessing the mechanical response of SLM components. Importantly, the existing high-end experimental facilities at Empa, ETHZ and PSI will be employed for dedicated experiments to i) understand the involved physical phenomena, ii) accordingly derive relevant numerical models, and iii) ultimately evaluate the reliability and effectiveness of the proposed simulation strategy.The project will benefit from ongoing collaborations with researchers from Empa (Dr Leinenbach), ETH Zürich (Dr Marelli, Prof De Lorenzis & Prof Mazza), Bremen Univesity, Germany (Dr Mohebi), and Northwestern University, USA (Prof Wagner). The proposed research requires the involvement of three PhD students, where the laboratory of the PI at Empa has committed to funding 50% of the PhD positions.
Keywords: High-fidelity simulations, Metal additive manufacturing, Microstructure, Thermomechanical modelling, cientific machine learning

Title: Pesticide exposure mixtures and neurobehavioral health outcomes in farmer and non-farmer families
Abstract:
Background: Research has shown that exposure to pesticides used in agriculture can cause adverse health outcomes. Yet, there is a paucity of data on independent and joint health effects resulting from co-exposures to multiple pesticides. At the same time, enhanced agricultural production, increased pest resistance and epidemic outbreaks of vector-borne diseases in the face of climate change have led to increased and diversified use of pesticides.
Overarching goal and specific objectives: The goal of my 1-year Postdoc.Mobility Return Fellowship is to assess the association between exposure to mixtures of pesticides and neurobehavioural outcomes in highly exposed farmers in Uganda and farm children in South Africa. Thereby, I will scientifically capitalize on my past investments in designing and setting up of these unique cohorts. My specific objectives are: (i) to assess the exposure to multiple pesticides and the cross-sectional association of single and combined active ingredients with neurobehavioural outcomes in smallholder farmers in Uganda; and (ii) to investigate the exposure to multiple pesticides and the predictive association of single and combined active ingredients with the change in neurobehavioural test performance in South African children over two years.
Methods:  During the 2-year Postdoc.Mobility fellowship at Utrecht University in The Netherlands, I successfully worked and published on data from two cohort studies, which I co-initiated with 300 farmers in Uganda and 1,000 children of farmers in South Africa. Using self-reported questionnaire-based exposure data, I showed that increased exposure to glyphosate leads to poorer visual memory in Ugandan farmers and that different activities related to pesticide exposure (e.g., working on fields or picking fruits from the field) lead to neurodevelopment impairments in children living in areas with intensive agricultural production in South Africa. As a next logical step, to deepen the pesticide exposure assessment, I successfully acquired funds to analyse urinary bioactive metabolites of multiple pesticide active ingredients. As a result, in 2020, a total of 2,300 urine samples from both cohorts will be analysed for 30 metabolites of major pesticides. During the 1-year of the Postdoc.Mobility Return Fellowship, I will have the unique opportunity to continue my research on this rich dataset to investigate the association between mixtures of multiple pesticides using the metabolite data and neurobehavioural outcomes in farmers and children from two different settings in Africa. Accounting for the highly correlated pesticide exposures, I will use high-dimensional statistical methods such as Bayesian model averaging (BMA) procedures to disentangle the effect of individual pesticides within a mixed and highly correlated exposure situation (single effect) or the Bayesian kernel machine regression (BKMR) to quantify the summed (synergistic) mixture effects.
Expected outcomes and significance: These will be the first studies investigating the health effects of pesticide mixtures based on urinary metabolite data in farmers and children in Africa. The results of the studies will pave the way for further studies on mixtures of multiple pesticides and neurobehavioural outcomes in Africa and beyond. A deeper understanding of the effects of co-exposure to pesticide active ingredient mixtures will help to improve future study designs and prevention strategies to reduce the health risk of pesticides.
Keywords: Agriculture, Exposure assessment, Exposure mixtures, Farmer families, Low- and middle-income countries, Pesticide

increased pest resistance and epidemic outbreaks of vector borne diseases in the face of climate change have led to increased and diversified use of pesticides. overarching goal and specific objectives: the goal of my 1 year postdoc.mobility return fellowship is to assess the association between exposure to mixtures of pesticides and neurobehavioural outcomes in highly exposed farmers in uganda and farm children in south africa. thereby, i will scientifically capitalize on my past investments in designing and setting up of these unique cohorts. my specific objectives are: (i) to assess the exposure to multiple pesticides and the cross sectional association of single and combined active ingredients with neurobehavioural outcomes in smallholder farmers in uganda; and (ii) to investigate the exposure to multiple pesticides and the predictive association of single and combined active ingredients with the change in neurobehavioural test performance in south african children over two years. methods: during the 2 year postdoc.mobility fellowship at utrecht university in the netherlands, i successfully worked and published on data from two cohort studies, which i co initiated with 300 farmers in uganda and 1,000 children of farmers in south africa. using self reported questionnaire based exposure data, i showed that increased exposure to glyphosate leads to poorer visual memory in ugandan farmers and that different activities related to pesticide exposure (e.g., working on fields or picking fruits from the field) lead to neurodevelopment impairments in children living in areas with intensive agricultural production in south africa. as a next logical step, to deepen the pesticide exposure assessment, i successfully acquired funds to analyse urinary bioactive metabolites of multiple pesticide active ingredients. as a result, in 2020, a total of 2,300 urine samples from both cohorts will be analysed for 30 metabolites of major pesticides. during the 1 year of the postdoc.mobility return fellowship, i will have the unique opportunity to continue my research on this rich dataset to investigate the association between mixtures of multiple pesticides using the metabolite data and neurobehavioural outcomes in farmers and children from two different settings in africa. accounting for the highly correlated pesticide exposures, i will use high dimensional statistical methods such as bayesian model averaging (bma) procedures to disentangle the effect of individual pesticides within a mixed and highly correlated exposure situation (single effect) or the bayesian kernel machine regression (bkmr) to quantify the summed (synergistic) mixture effects. expected outcomes and significance: these will be the first studies investigating the health effects of pesticide mixtures based on urinary metabolite data in farmers and children in africa. the results of the studies will pave the way for further studies on mixtures of multiple pesticides and neurobehavioural outcomes in africa and beyond. a deeper understanding of the effects of co exposure to pesticide active ingredient mixtures will help to improve future study designs Title: Data-driven Methods for Artist-directed Physically-based Simulations
Abstract:
Currently, business models in film and animation are changing dramatically. There is a high pressure on industry for producing content at much lower costs. At the same time, the expectations of the audience for better visual effects are increasing. To date, these demands are contradictory requiring new methods that satisfy both needs.

Such visual effects include physically-based simulations of materials ranging from liquids, smoke, fire, elastic objects to cloth. These simulations gained massive importance in the past years and are nowadays ubiquitous in computer graphics applications. However, they are not well integrated into the workflow of artists, contributing to the problem stated above. The creation of physically-based simulations for high-end animations in feature films or effects in computer games is a permanent iterative process: The constant interplay requires tools to change the scene setup iteratively, and efficient computations are needed to avoid long waiting times. Efficiency is even more critical for animations in TV productions - constituting the biggest market for animations - where simulated effects must be ready in instant time and at a low budget. Artistic control must be provided as well, as simulations serve as a tool to tell a story and often a behavior that does not adhere entirely to physical laws is even desired. To cope with this, our simulations must provide high stability.

This project aims at supporting the artists’ workflow for creating physically-based simulations from sketches to final results. The foundation will be based on data-driven concepts: Establishing an abstract model that matches the input from a user to 3D example simulations. We envision an artist sketching the dynamics in 2D and instantaneously seeing the simulation results in 3D without bothering too much about physical parameters and long waiting times for the computation. We also envision a set of tools to interactively control the global shape and motion of the material either physically-plausible or non-physically (such as cartoon deformations), or to synthesize high- frequency details (such as turbulence patterns) from examples in a temporally coherent way while ensuring stability of the methods. This must all be possible without possessing any knowledge about the underlying physical laws and methods. To reach these goals, we propose to combine for the first time a) Physically-based simulations, b) Artist control, and c) Machine learning.

The Computer Graphics Lab (CGL) at ETH Zurich provides a particularly strong environment for performing this type of research. The applicants have a long track history of innovative research on physically-based simulations. The lab’s work has been recognized by multiple publications at the prestigious conferences in graphics ACM SIGGRAPH and Eurographics, and was awarded with the Technical Achievement Award (SciTech Oscar) in 2012 for the Wavelet Turbulence method. Due to the strong ties of the CGL with Disney Research Zurich, Disney (including Pixar), and the Art School of Zurich, we have access to professional lab and production artists. Professional artwork can be used in this project, and our collaborators are included during the concept development and especially the evaluation process.
Keywords: Artist control, Computer graphics, Data-driven, Machine learning, Physically-based simulation

Title: Molecular level understanding of crystal nucleation and polymorphism by in-situ optical spectroscopy combined with deep learning-assisted simulations
Abstract:
Self-organization of individual atoms/molecules into ordered structures results in new solid state physical properties. Often, atoms and molecules can pack in more than one structure. This so-called polymorphism is an important topic of research in a wide range of fields, because each polymorph can have different physical properties (e.g., solubility, color, electrical conductivity etc.). For example in the field of pharmaceutical science, some drugs are inefficient unless they are in the right polymorph. Typically, a trial-and-error approach is a common strategy to develop a recipe to obtain desired polymorphs. This is because the microscopic description of how crystal nucleation occurs and how different polymorphs emerge is yet to be established. The biggest challenge to experimentally study crystal nucleation has been the stochastic and heterogenous nature of the nucleation occurring at nanometer scale. This nature has been particularly detrimental for the application of optical spectroscopy in this field.
This proposal aims to establish the molecular level understanding of crystal nucleation and polymorph control by using novel in-situ optical spectroscopy methods recently developed by the group of the applicant along with the theoretical simulation method developed by the partner (Simine group at McGill university). We target two types of crystallization processes:  i) the crystal nucleation rate is “low” that the number of crystallization events is countable (e.g., crystallization of amino acids and pharmaceutical compounds from solution), and ii) the crystal nucleation rate is “high” that a countless number of nano-scale crystals form and grow (e.g., Calcium carbonate precipitation). For the first, single crystal nucleation spectroscopy (SCNS) will be used. SCNS can record Raman spectral evolution of crystal nucleation in solution one nucleation event at a time. For the second, time-resolved dynamic light scattering (DLS)/Raman microspectroscopy will be used. This method allows one to track the temporal evolution of size distribution at tens of ms time resolution while Raman spectral evolution can be simultaneously recorded to access the structural information (i.e., polymorphism).  For both studies, theoretical simulation by Simine group will be accompanied. The biggest advantage of this collaboration is that we can use spectroscopic data as a key connection between the experiments and theories. This allows us the direct comparison of the results at different stage of crystallization, not by the statistical values such as nucleation rate J that has been a popular parameter to compare between experiments and computer simulations. 
The successful outcome has a multitude of impacts due to the ubiquitous nature of crystallization. First of all, crystallization is of importance in many fields of academic and industrial researches, and therefore the obtained microscopic understanding of crystal nucleation will be of high interest for a broad audience. Secondly, understanding polymorphism will lead to its rational control, which could have a huge economic impact for food, pharmaceutical, chemical and materials industries.
Keywords: Crystallization, Raman/THz Raman spectroscopy, Single crystal nucleation spectroscopy, deep-learning assisted simulation, in-situ optical spectroscopy, time-resolved dynamic light scattering

Title: Terahertz operation of nanometer scale resistive switches
Abstract:
The computational challenges imposed by the rising paradigms of Big Data, Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) urge the development of new hardware platforms which are able to overcome the inherent limitations of traditional, CMOS-based von Neumann architectures. The latter are exemplified by the power hungry and bandwidth-limiting permanent data transfer between separate processing, memory and storage units (`von Neumann bottleneck'), the speed mismatch between CPU and RAM (`memory wall') and the serial nature of data processing.

Crossbar networks of two-terminal resistance change devices (`memristors') offer a viable alternative. Beside the advantage of simpler device structure and nonvolatility, multibit operations up to a few GHz frequencies have been demonstrated, which cost 3-4 orders of magnitude less energy compared to CMOS-based solutions. On the architecture level asynchronous operation, co-localized information processing and storage are naturally supported providing a flexible and up-scalable platform for the hardware implementation of artificial neural networks (ANNs) and neuromorphic computing. The first experimental realizations of all-memristor ANNs utilizing memristor-based artificial neurons and synapses are extremely promising. On the other hand, the potential of ultimate down-scalability to the single atomic scale has remained greatly under-explored in terms of high-speed device operation. Consequently, state-of-the-art resistive switching devices operated at 1-10 GHz rates could not yet set foot in the frequency domain of the latest telecommunication technologies extending up to 72 GHz.

Seeking the ultimately dense and fast neuromorphic hardware platform, the project envisions resistive switching devices with atomic scale switching volumes and up to THz operation rates. These will be realized by the unconventional and highly challenging approach of integrating ultimately fast, bottom-up atomic structures into top-down semiconductor architectures at the wafer scale. If successful, the project will facilitate the integration of future telecommunication technologies into neuromorphic circuits, providing the enabling technology for a plethora of low-power, autonomous AI applications.

For this purpose we will fabricate vertical device stacks of Ta/Ta2O5/Pt confined in nanopores of non-switching, insulating matrices. The nanopores will be created in suspended membranes by state-of-the-art focused ion beam techniques down to 2 nm in diameter. The ideal membrane material (SiNx, hBN) has a higher breakdown electric field than the switching oxide. Reduced membrane thicknesses are expected to yield to electroforming-free resistive switching operation. Furthermore, the utilized membrane and switching oxide materials must be transparent to THz radiation at ~10 nm thicknesses. In pursuit of high-speed resistive switching, first the establishment and basic characterization of hysteretic current-voltage traces will be carried out at low frequencies. Next, resistive switching induced by THz radiation will be investigated. The latter will be focused and amplified by a special electrode design acting as a receiver antenna at THz frequencies. The achievable field strength will be simulated by finite element calculations in COMSOL Multiphysics. Resistive switching will be identified via the changes in the transmission spectrum according to the different absorption in the high and low resistance states of the switch or, alternatively, by detecting a DC current contribution generated by the THz field.
Keywords: Terahertz, electrical transport, focused ion beam microscopy, resistive switching

Title: Reconciling inter-hemispheric proxy-model temperature inconsistencies during the past-millennium by using tree-ring anatomy – RECONSPHERE
Abstract:
Background: The markedly different reconstructions of Northern and Southern Hemisphere (NH, SH) temperature histories over the past millennium are puzzling, given the agreement of model simulations between the hemispheres. Resolving whether the hemispheres have different sensitivities to anthropogenic, volcanic and other climate forcing is critical to understand and evaluate the efficacy of climate model projections. Thus, it is urgent to clarify whether NH-SH model vs. proxy inconsistencies are related to shortcomings in the proxy records. Tree-ring anatomy, which is based on quantitative wood anatomy (QWA), is a timely and cutting-edge proxy to elucidate this inconsistency. This is largely thanks to recent advances in accuracy and the ability to capture key aspects of historical climate, combined with recent time-saving AI-assisted advances in data production.

Objectives: We seek to determine if the causes for the known inconsistencies between extra-tropical NH / SH temperature reconstructions can be explained by using advanced tree-ring anatomy techniques to produce new high-fidelity proxy-data.

Specific aims: Using the new proxy data we aim to: i) reassess the NH-SH expressions of putative climate periods such as the Medieval Climate Anomaly and Little Ice Age, ii) evaluate whether the modest or absent cooling in SH following volcanic eruptions is related to the inability of previously used proxies to detect these extreme events, rather than an inherent lack of SH climate response to volcanism, and iii) investigate if both intra- and inter-hemispheric patterns of modern warming can be found more coherent using wood anatomical techniques, especially given the sometimes observed absence of recent warming in NH, known as “divergence”.

Approach: We will establish a coarse but representative extra-tropical SH-NH network comprising 16 key millennial-length tree-ring anatomy chronologies, applying novel AI-based image analysis. The resulting temperature reconstructions will be developed using various wood anatomical traits using well-established reconstruction techniques. We will subsequently compare the new NH-SH reconstructions with previous state-of-the-art proxies and climate models and test for convergence in volcanic signals and long-term trends.

Expected results: We hypothesize that our new reconstructions of past millennium temperature will reconcile previously observed model-proxy inconsistencies, provide new and more detailed evidence concerning the temporal and interhemispheric consistency of volcanic cooling, as well as provide a fresh perspective on the long-term development of NH-SH temperature histories, including the stigmatized “divergence” problem.

Impact: This study will place current warming in an unprecedentedly precise historical context and provide a new long-term perspective on the SH-NH climate system dynamics. This perspective will be invaluable for assessing model predictions of temperature change and will feed directly into forthcoming editions of the IPCC assessments of climate change.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Little Ice Age (LIA), Medieval Climate Anomaly (MCA), SH-NH temperature history, current warm period, divergence, quantitative wood anatomy, tree ring proxies, volcanic cooling

Title: A theory-driven approach to understanding the neural circuits of proprioception
Abstract:
Biological motor control is versatile and efficient. Muscles are flexible and undergo continuous changes requiring distributed adaptive control mechanisms. How proprioception contributes to perception, adaptive control and motor learning is not fully understood. From behavioral experiments, proprioception has been hypothesized to be related to different functions such as action recognition, redundancy reduction, postural control or body localization. At present, it is not clear how these functions are implemented by the proprioceptive pathway. 

We will develop a framework for studying the proprioceptive pathway using goal-driven modeling. We will create computational pipelines to synthesize large-scale datasets of proprioceptive stimuli for model development, leverage machine vision and biomechanics to model the system, and develop a platform to generate and test predictive models of the proprioceptive system. Taken together, our proposal aims to elucidate fundamental principles of sensorimotor control. Moreover, we aim to seamlessly integrate modern machine learning, large-scale data science, biomechanics and neuroscience. We believe that developing detailed, biologically-inspired models of the proprioceptive system might ultimately lead to effective therapeutic approaches and for sensory-enhanced neuroprosthetics.
Keywords: computational neuroscience, deep learning, muscle spindle, perception, proprioception, somatosensation, somatosensory cortex, task-driven modeling

Title: Supermassive black holes and their large scale environment: triggering, evolution and feedback
Abstract: The last twenty years have brought forward evidence of coevolution between galaxies and their central super massive black holes. During the active phase of accretion of matter onto the supermassive black hole induced energetic gas outflows affect the star formation and shape the bulge of the galaxy creating the observed black hole mass - stellar velocity dispersion relationship. This relationship is observed both for galaxies with dormant black holes (normal galaxies) and for galaxies that show signs of active accretion (active galactic nuclei, AGN). The common gas reservoir that is responsible for the star formation and the feeding of the black hole can undergo cycles of expulsion and re-accretion into the galaxy. Such phenomena are thought to take place in galaxy groups and clusters and tentative evidence are witnessed with perhaps the most striking example the Perseus cluster. This project will focus on the study of AGN triggering, feedback onto the host galaxy and AGN-galaxy coevolution as a function of their large scale environment. The AGN populations recovered using selection criteria across the electromagnetic spectrum, namely in the X-rays, infrared, radio, and optical wavelengths will be used to test AGN unification scenaria. The expected outcome of this project is i) the determination of the AGN X-ray luminosity function inside clusters and in the field ii) test unification schemes of AGN as a function of environment density iii) study infalling AGN inside clusters, why don't we observe more AGN? iv) investigate the feedback of AGN onto the cluster v) finally we will provide a probabilistic machine-learning mechanism to identify AGN using their broad band colors. This work is state-of-the-art within the current capabilities of X-ray satellites and a precursor of future X-ray and infrared space missions
Keywords: active galactic nuclei, active galactic nuclei triggering, coevolution, feedback mechanisms, galaxies, galaxy clusters, luminosity function, machine learning, supermassive black holes

Title: Together with the climate change challenge: stakeholder value proposition and organizational performance
Abstract:
Firms face increasing pressure from their stakeholders to respond to the climate change challenge. As a result, they need to balance stakeholders’ demands for their social responsibility and the need to maximize corporate profitability. Responding to this challenge – and doing it well – will be a significant competitive differentiator in the years ahead as it is creating extensive and novel business opportunities. Even though companies have pledges and ambitions for this grand challenge, how to better achieve the landing of a win-win strategy – i.e., balancing commercial goals while tackling the climate change challenge, is still elusive. Prior research highlights the important role of stakeholder engagement for long-term competitiveness, but we still lack sufficient knowledge about how firms can better engage their stakeholders to tackle the climate change challenge. Meanwhile, from the perspective of stakeholder theory development, how to measure firms’ stakeholder orientation level and its relationship with organizational non-financial performance are still largely underexplored.
Thus, this project aims at addressing the over-arching research question: How does stakeholder orientation influence firms’ actions to tackle the climate change challenge? Two important aspects regarding the emerging phenomenon will be explored: 1) how firms can form stakeholder value propositions via business model innovation to tackle the climate change challenge; 2) how firms’ aspirations/ambitions for climate change mitigation are shaped by the level of their stakeholder orientation. 
In the first study, taking the lens of business model innovation as the base, I will conduct an in-depth single case study of a platform-based entrepreneurial firm, to investigate how it designs multiple business models to create stakeholder value propositions, and how it balances the commercial goal and the goal of facilitating carbon emission reduction. In the second study, I will take the lens of stakeholder theory, investigating the relationship between stakeholder orientation level and firm target-setting difficulty of carbon emission reduction. Selected advanced natural language processing (NLP) will be adopted to construct the patterns of stakeholder orientation from firms’ sustainability reports. 
The first study will contribute to business model literature by exploring multiple business model configurations and the creation process of stakeholder value propositions. The second study will provide a novel methodological perspective to deliver a new construct and empirical measures of stakeholder orientation, contributing to the development of stakeholder theory as well as strategies for grand challenges. Jointly, these two studies can also provide important managerial insights to firms about how to stay with climate risk to develop potential business opportunities via business model innovation and to what extent stakeholder orientation will shape organizational performance.

Title: The impact of disappearing firn on mountain glaciers (deFIRN)
Abstract:
Summary
Glaciers are increasingly losing mass due to sustained climate warming. In many mountain ranges, even the highest parts of glaciers are now affected by warming. These glacier accumulation areas, which have historically gained mass on an annual basis, are dwindling because of decreasing snowfall and increasing melt. This implies that glacier firn, the porous layer of old snow that slowly converts to glacier ice, is increasingly exposed to melt. As a result, the firn hydrology changes, often leading to retention of excess meltwater, and firn areas thin or shrink, in many places giving way to bare glacier ice. Here, we label these ongoing changes the firn transitions. These firn transitions feed back on glacier mass balance, but the strength and relevance of these feedbacks remain to be quantified. A major hurdle is the ability of parameterizations to represent firn and albedo processes in glacier mass balance models. These parameterizations often date from when glaciers and climate were closer to equilibrium, or, in many cases, are completely absent from the models.

This research proposal focuses on the changing firn and newly exposed bare ice areas and quantifies their impact glacier mass balance. Thereby we focus on mountain glaciers of the mid-latitudes because their meltwater is relevant to infrastructure and agriculture. Initially, we will measure the processes pertaining to firn transitions. We will focus on glaciers in the Alps and Central Asia, which we already monitor or where historic data exist. Based on the measurements, we will develop process-based parameterizations for firn and albedo, which we will implement into a glacier-scale energy and mass balance model to assess the interplay of firn transitions with glacier mass balance. Subsequently, we will integrate the parameterizations into a computationally efficient regional-scale glacier surface mass balance model. Along each step of model development, from the point-scale to glacier-wide and regional applications, we will quantify improvements in model accuracy and advance only process parameterizations that achieve significant gains. We will use a machine-learning based clustering approach to ensure computational efficiency in our regional-scale model. Finally, we will deploy the latter to estimate the impact of firn transitions on glacier surface mass balance sensitivity for entire mountain ranges and to advance the accuracy of geodetic glacier mass balance measurements.

The project will address the representation of fast-changing glacier surfaces and firn, which is important to better understand glacier response to a quickly changing climate. We will create a foundational set of measurements spanning temperate and continental climatic conditions. The project will strongly improve process understanding, from micro- to regional scales, and provide process-based tools that will enable the research community to assess current and future changes of mountain glaciers as well as their impact on water availability.

Title: PAuSE: Pathological Speech Enhancement
Abstract:
Digital communication plays a vital role in our daily lives, occurring in many different forms including mobile communication, meeting through teleconferencing platforms such as Zoom, and using voice-activated agents such as Apple’s Siri or Amazon’s Alexa. Since we live in a noisy world, the recorded microphone signals in these digital communication applications are often contaminated by background noise. Background noise causes signal degradation, thereby impairing speech quality and intelligibility and decreasing the performance of many signal processing techniques required in several applications for a high fidelity communication experience. To deal with background noise, speech enhancement approaches aiming to recover the clean speech signal are indispensable. As such, a wide range of speech enhancement approaches have been proposed in past decades, with e.g., the traditional statistical model-based approaches and the more recent deep learning-based approaches having shown strong enhancement performance. 
Statistical model-based approaches generally rely on a Bayesian framework and assume that the clean speech spectral coefficients follow a Gaussian or super-Gaussian statistical distribution. Deep learning-based approaches generally rely on a large amount of training data to learn a mapping from noisy signals to clean signals. Although these approaches have shown advantageous enhancement performance, they have been devised for scenarios where the target speakers are neurotypical speakers, i.e., speakers that do not exhibit any speech impairments. However, many pathological conditions such as hearing loss, head and neck cancers, or neurological disorders, disrupt the speech production mechanism, resulting in speech impairments across different dimensions. As a result, the statistical distribution of pathological speech differs from that of neurotypical speech and preliminary investigations show that state-of-the-art enhancement approaches can yield a considerably lower performance for pathological signals than for neurotypical signals. Although conditions resulting in pathological speech are widely prevalent, speech enhancement approaches specifically targeting pathological speech, e.g., through using appropriate statistical distributions or training data, have never been established.
The PAuSE project aims at developing model-based and deep learning-based speech enhancement approaches that yield an advantageous performance for pathological speech. For model-based approaches, we will derive Minimum Mean Square Error and Maximum A Posteriori estimators exploiting appropriate statistical distributions for pathological speech signals. For deep learning-based approaches, we will target two different research directions to deal with the lack of extensive pathological speech training data. First, we will develop approaches which rely only on neurotypical training signals but exploit knowledge of pathology-specific acoustic features that impact enhancement performance. Such approaches will be based on feature-aware networks, where the feature information is directly embedded in the network or different networks are specialized to enhance signals with different feature profiles. Second, we will develop approaches that also exploit the typically scarcely available pathological training data. Such approaches will be based on pathology-aware networks, augmentation strategies specifically targeting pathological speech, and transfer learning and adaptation strategies. The conducted research will provide a better understanding of the deterioration of enhancement performance for pathological signals. Combining this knowledge with novel estimators and training frameworks will produce enhancement approaches with a strong performance for the growing group of pathological speakers.
Keywords: deep learning, enhancement, model-based, noise, pathology, single-microphone

Title: A Computational Modeling Approach to Understanding Sequential Decision Making
Abstract:
Sequential decision making – a decision where available options are encountered successively - is a hallmark of our everyday life. When we search for a job or an apartment, we may decide to accept or reject it without knowing potential future options. How do human choices differ from computational models and optimal decision making approaches for such problems? What can we learn from such differences and how can we enhance human sequential decision making? Despite extensive studies of sequential decision problems in economics and political science, with ample assistance from computational modeling, the associated psychological processes of the decision maker remain largely unexplored. 

The goal of this dissertation is to help understand and predict how people respond in situations that require sequential decisions by developing computational models and linking them with psychological processes. I will employ prominent modeling approaches such as sequential sampling and reinforcement learning and enhance them by state of the art Bayesian inference techniques to integrate experimental data. I will implement these algorithms to sequential decision making tasks and conduct a comparative study of their predictions and respective response times with those of human decisions. I will use these models to understand how people are affected by variations in the temporal separation of the options and the possibility of selecting options that they may have previously rejected.  

This work will contribute to the theory of psychology as well as to applied decision making. Understanding the psychological processes that underlie sequential decisions will help quantify the conditions under which people may succeed or fail in such tasks. In turn, this will provide knowledge necessary for structuring decision problems in order to assist humans in making critical decisions that reflect their fundamental individual preferences.

Title: Growth Kinetics Interaction of Staphylococcus aureus and Dolosigranulum pigrum
Abstract:
Background: Several recent studies on the bacterial microbiota of the upper respiratory tract have shown that colonization with Dolosigranulum pigrum, a benign commensal, is an informative predictor for the absence of Staphylococcus aureus, a major cause of mortality and morbidity in all age groups in developed and developing parts of the world. Given these recent findings we hypothesize that D. pigrum has superior fitness in colonising the surfaces of the nasal passages, and is likely be able to inhibit growth of other bacteria, including S. aureus, that inhabit the same niche.
Indeed, preliminary data generated in the lab of Dr. Katherine P. Lemon by Dr. Silvio Brugger show a direct inhibition of methicillin-resistant S. aureus JE2 by all tested D. pigrum isolates in an in vitro co-culture assay. The mechanism by which D. pigrum might inhibit S. aureus growth is currently subject to investigation, and increasing knowledge about growth dynamics and fitness of both D. pigrum and S. aureus are needed to further support this investigation.

Aim: To quantify parameters of growth of Staphylococcus aureus including both methicillin sensitive (MSSA) and resistant variants (MRSA) and D. pigrum alone and when grown together on agar plates, and determine the change in fitness of MSSA and MRSA in the presence of D. pigrum.

Methods: In order to quantify fitness, a high-throughput method already established for the growth analysis yeast and termed “quantitative fitness analysis” (QFA) will be adapted for our study. 
In QFA the microbes are grown in a rectangular array of independent neighbouring cultures on agar plates, and growth is recorded over time through time-lapse high resolution photographs of the plates. The images are then processed with an open source purpose-built image recognition software, and the image data can be used with the QFA R package for the open-source statistical software R. Growth curves are conveniently constructed by QFA R, which also includes mathematical modelling tools to derive logistic population model parameters and calculate fitness summary statistics. 

Implications: The knowledge of growth parameters, and possible changes to them when species interact, would give valuable insights into how D. pigrum and S. aureus compete with each other and may provide some evidence on the mechanism of action of the yet unknown metabolite(s) from D. pigrum that suppresses S. aureus growth. In the future, knowledge of the growth dynamics and interaction could also prove to be useful in a potential development of probiotics that oust S. aureus from their reservoir in the human nose to reduce the risk of S. aureus colonisation and dissemination, e.g. in healthcare institutions.
Keywords: Bacterial growth interaction, Dolosigranulum pigrum, Quantitative fitness analysis, Staphylococcus aureus

Title: Understanding protein design and evolution using geometric deep learning
Abstract:
Proteins are the fundamental building blocks of life. They have evolved to specifically interact with other proteins, nucleic acids, metabolites, and membranes in order to form complexes whose structural architecture and mechanism are at the basis of any biological function. We further leverage these natural nanomachines to our advantage in medicinal and biotechnological applications, where it is key to finely control their structure, stability and function. While experimental and computational methods have achieved in the past key advances for our ability to investigate and engineer the structure, dynamics and function of protein complexes, several facets still remain difficultly accessible. In this context, the rise in recent years of machine learning and its application to biology with methods like AlphaFold has revolutionized protein science, opening unexpected possibilities to discover new biological insights and engineering solutions.

During our previous SNSF grant, leveraging these advances in deep learning, we have developed the Protein Structure Transformer - PeSTo, a novel geometric transformer that provides a simple, yet elegant and accurate way to predict protein binding interfaces. Because the model is based only on atomic coordinates and element labels, it can learn and predict protein interfaces with other proteins, nucleic acids, ligands, cofactors, and virtually any kind of molecules. We have recently shown that this model can be repurposed (rebranded CARBonAra) to design protein sequences that fold and are functional while taking into account a given molecular context.

Here we propose to expand PeSTo’s and CARBonAra’s architecture to push further the frontier in protein science, trying to understand the principles at the basis of protein design and evolution. We will capitalize on CARBonAra’s unique capabilities to grasp structural constraints to amino acid variability, to extend its ecosystem with new features that can better sample and score protein designs, as benchmarked with extensive computational and experimental tests (Aim 1). We will then apply these methods to study trade-offs between protein structure, stability, dynamics and functions, central to our ultimate goal of creating new structure-informed models of protein evolution, which we will test on ß-lactamase enzymes (Aim 2). Specifically, we will use CARBonAra to pinpoint relevant ensembles of residues accessible to large-scale saturated mutagenesis in order to better illuminate unexplored high-order epistatic interactions.

We expect that with the new methods and protocols developed here we will not only be capable of designing more functional proteins but will also contribute to better understanding fundamental protein biophysics, with the overarching goal of informing models of protein evolution that can simulate evolutionary trajectories with high structural and functional detail. In summary, building on the original PeSTo geometric transformer we will provide powerful new ways to sample the protein sequence space with implications for protein engineering and evolution.

Title: NA
Abstract:
Sleep apnea (SA) is a highly prevalent breathing disorder affecting about 23% of the general population globally and contributes to the development of cerebro- and cardiovascular comorbidities. SA is typically diagnosed by single-night in-hospital polysomnography (PSG). This measurement is expensive and technically complex and further affects the patients' sleep behavior, as it takes place in an out-of-home setting. This aspect could introduce bias and lead to diagnostic inaccuracy. Furthermore, inter-night variability in SA severity detection may ultimately lead to over- or undertreatment if only one night is considered for diagnosis. Therefore, novel solutions that are easy to use, cost-effective, and applicable for long-term use in unattended home settings are of high interest in sleep medicine.
This project aims to develop and validate an optical solution for monitoring SA, with the characteristic of being unobtrusive and applicable for use over multiple consecutive nights without disturbing the patients’ sleep. Based on photoplethysmography (PPG) signals obtained from a wearable sensor – placed either at the wrist or the upper arm – a variety of vital signs can be measured continuously. These include parameters such as blood oxygen saturation (SpO2), heart rate (HR) and HR variability (HRV), and respiration. All these parameters are affected by SA and, thus, are recommended by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) for unattended monitoring. In addition to this traditional set of parameters, we make use of CSEM’s long-standing expertise in PPG-processing and exploit the information of advanced pulse wave analysis (PWA) features and continuous blood pressure (BP), both of which are known to be influenced by SA events, leading to surges in BP and sympathetic activation. We hypothesize that using such advanced PWA features and continuous BP monitoring can significantly improve the performance of PPG-based SA detection. Since no public dataset is available that contains high-quality PPG signals (i.e., with sufficient frequency information as required for the reliable extraction of advanced PWA features), we will first perform a clinical data acquisition study at the sleep center of the Cantonal Hospital St.Gallen (KSSG) and record a large dataset with synchronous high-quality PPG and PSG as gold-standard reference for SA detection and classification. Using these data, we will develop and validate multi-parametric machine learning (ML) algorithms to predict SA severity using the abovementioned PPG-derived parameters via two approaches: a) the first is based on feature engineering and multimodalities, with a model combining advanced PPG-derived features according to the quality of the PPG signals recorded; b) the second approach is based on feature learning and focuses on the development of an interpretable NN architecture to predict SA severity directly from raw PPG signals.
Unobtrusive monitoring of SA is essential to maximize the patient’s acceptance and adherence, thus allowing monitoring over multiple nights - either as a follow-up to clinical diagnosis (i.e., to confirm or refine PSG-based diagnosis) or as a treatment follow-up to improve compliance and control for SA treatment efficacy. Even though not expected to replace PSG, our solution would help to decrease the socioeconomic burden by reducing the steadily rising healthcare costs and improving the quality of life of SA patients.
Keywords: blood pressure, photoplethysmography, pulse wave analysis, sleep apnea, wearables
