Title: Low back pain: Unveiling the contribution of motor control adaption using biomechanical modeling and neuroimaging
Abstract:
Background: Low back pain (LBP) is a major health issue. Treatment of chronic LBP is still a major challenge due to a lack of pathophysiological understanding. Thus, understanding LBP pathophysiology is a research priority. Adaptions of motor control likely play a significant role in chronic or recurrent LBP because motor control is crucial for spine posture, stability and movement. Different motor adaption strategies exist across individuals with LBP and two phenotypes representing the opposite ends of a spectrum have been suggested; i.e. "tight" control and "loose" control over trunk movement. The former would be associated with reduced trunk motor variability, the later with increased trunk motor variability. This conceptual framework is very useful to explain maintenance and aggravating of LBP because motor control adaptations are expected to have long-term consequences, such as increased spinal tissue loading, associated with degeneration of intervertebral discs and other tissues. Several knowledge gaps need to be addressed to test the validity of this framework: 1) Do loose/tight control phenotypes indeed exist and/or do other motor control adaption strategies exist? 2) Is reduced/altered paraspinal proprioceptive input associated with LBP related to neuroplastic cortical changes, thereby affecting the organizational structure in sensorimotor cortices and top-down trunk motor control? 3) Do psychological factors influence the organizational structure in sensorimotor cortices and motor control strategies?
To address these knowledge gaps, the objectives of the current project are: I) To establish motor control phenotypes in LBP. Proprioceptive weighting and biomechanical assessment of dynamic movement tasks, including subject-specific spine kinematic variability and its relationship to pain duration, negative pain-related cognitions, segmental loadings and paraspinal muscle forces, will be performed. II) To test whether cortical proprioceptive maps differ between healthy subjects and patients with LBP. Brain activation in response to thoracolumbar vibrotactile stimulation will be interrogated using functional magnetic resonance imaging data and univariate and multivariate analysis based on machine learning. III) To test whether proprioceptive maps demonstrate a relationship to spine kinematic patterns, pain duration and negative pain-related cognitions in LBP patients. Team: The team is well suited to carry out the proposed research; the PI has a track record in neurophysiological and brain imaging investigations of pain in healthy and chronic pain populations. Exceptional knowledge regarding MR physics and engineering is provided by Dr. Stämpfli and Prof. Dr. Schütz. Profound expertise in the assessment of proprioceptive functioning, spine kinematics and biomechanical modeling is provided by Prof. Dr. de Bruin and project partners Dr. Schmid and Dr. Senteler. Impact: The interdisciplinary approach combining spine kinematics, biomechanical modeling and neuroimaging has the potential to disentangle the biopsychological interactions underlying individual motor control adaptions in recurrent and chronic LBP. We anticipated that this will be of major therapeutic importance.
Keywords: biomechanical modeling, functional magnetic resonance imaging, motor control, muscle spindle, non-specific chronic low back pain, proprioception, somatosensory reorganization, spine kinematics, vibrotactile

Title: Learning Robust Control for Autonomous Robots
Abstract: We aim at formulating an architecture for simultaneously learning robust closed loop controllers and optimal plans with an emphasis on the application to the high dimensional nonlinear, hybrid and stochastic continous state-action spaces found in robots with arms and legs. We propose to use a combination of robust nonlinear control and reinforcement learning. As key contributions, in this project we will develop two main tools to solve this challenging control problem: (1) a robust iterative nonlinear optimal control method and (2) online certification methods that can be used to assess new candidate controllers before they are being rolled out on the real system. We will integrate these methods into a comprehensive learning robust control framework for a high performance torque controlled quadruped robot with arms. Herewith we address an important gap for the application of learning control to real demanding robotic control problems. While we gear our application and tests towards robots with arms and legs this research has large benefits for many other control problems in robotics (e.g. agile autonomous flight of quadcopter) and beyond.
Keywords: Autonomous Robots, control and planning, learning control, locomotion, manipulation, rescue robots, service robots

Title: Successful Design Choices for Human-Artificial Intelligence Collaborations in Accounting
Abstract:
The rapid development and adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in corporate settings raise many questions regarding how organizations can structure and optimize human-AI outputs. First, this involves fostering AI adoption by motivating people to acquire the necessary skills and knowledge and understanding employees trusting behavior towards AI recommendations. Second, it involves optimizing task performance through the implementation of carefully designed human-AI collaboration strategies and appropriate performance measurement tools. This collaborative project aims to build an “Accounting AI lab” between the accounting departments of the universities of Lausanne and St. Gallen to investigate questions related to the implementation of AI tools in organizations and the role of management control. The project will produce a series of papers, targeting top tier accounting and multidisciplinary journals. They will employ mixed methods, including a series of laboratory and field experiments, empirical archival data, as well as surveys.

Part 1 focuses on AI adoption in the finance function to benefit from human-AI collaboration. Prior studies suggest that adoption depends on employees having the appropriate skills and knowledge to use AI tools. To gain insights into the fast-evolving use of AI in organizations, we will we design and conduct a survey with finance executives from various European countries, along with an empirical analysis on the evolution of skills and knowledge requirements in accounting and finance job posts. The objective is to get insights from practice regarding the various uses of generative AI in accounting and finance, the purposes, challenges, and risks of its implementation as well as to understand how AI contributes to the workforce transformation.

Part 2 addresses the issue of trust in AI, which is essential if employees are to get the most out of these tools, and the role of performance measurements to build or rebuild trust in AI. Recent findings are mixed concerning trust in AI, with evidence consistent with AI aversion – with subjects trusting more human advice than AI advice – and others supporting AI appreciation (Burton et al. 2020, Logg et al. 2019). We argue that AI aversion or appreciation bias is task and subject dependent. We will design three experiments to capture AI appreciation and use both subject characteristics such as gender, knowledge, personality traits, and task characteristics such as difficulty, creativity, and data processing need as moderators. In addition, the AI aversion literature relates mostly to ‘one-shot’ lab experiments that studies dispositional trust but do not capture the evolving nature of learned trust. We design a randomized and controlled field experiment to explore whether the AI aversion or appreciation bias holds over time and after providing subjects with performance feedback.

Part 3 addresses human-AI collaboration strategies and the role of performance feedback. While recent papers promote augmentation – human collaborating with AI – over automation – with AI substituting humans (Raisch and Krakowski 2021), we know little about how these various human-AI collaboration strategies relate to task performance (Raisch and Fomina 2024). In addition, management control literature solely analyzes the effects of performance feedback on tasks performed exclusively by humans (e.g., Eyring et al. 2021, Eyring and Narayanan 2018, Hannan et al. 2013). Thus, the question is whether the feedback  to humans affects the interaction with the AI tool and whether any potential change in behavior depends on the design of the human-AI collaboration strategy. In this third part, we will design an experiment to shed light on two research questions: (1) Does the human-AI collaboration strategy affect performance? (2) Does performance feedback affect the way AI tools are used?
Keywords: AI appreciation, Collaborations in Accounting, Human-AI collaboration, Human-Artificial Intelligence, Management control, Performance measurement

Title: A “Neurometric” Approach to Cognitive Aging
Abstract: Cognitive functioning is a key determinant for the quality of life at older ages. Although older age generally comes with some decline in cognitive functioning, there are considerable individual differences in the rate and onset of changes in cognition and to what extent different domains of cognition are affected. Understanding the principles of these individual differences has become increasingly important in light of the projected increase in the population of older adults. Complementary to psychological studies that have assessed the multifaceted nature of cognitive aging, neuroscientific studies have shed light on the neuronal correlates. Whereas a majority of the neuroscientific studies have focused on rather isolated aspects of cognition, recently more integrative and comprehensive approaches have been initiated in the form of large-scale research initiatives that have examined mainly magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) measures in relation to age-related changes in various cognitive domains. Although these initiatives have contributed to new insights in the localization of the cerebral functions that change with cognitive aging, a comprehensive view into the actual cognitive processes, taking place at higher speed, is so far lacking. To fill this gap, we developed a test battery, which includes seven electroencephalography- (EEG) and eye-tracking based paradigms that assess key domains of cognitive aging. These paradigms offer temporally proximal EEG-, eye-tracking-, and behavioral-measures that are associated with the underlying processing steps of cognitive task performance. By assembling output measures of different tasks and modalities, we have the goal to obtain a comprehensive neurocognitive profile that characterizes individual differences in cognitive abilities at the level of processing steps. In a first study we will assess the test-retest reliability of the test batteries’ output measures in a sample of 90 healthy elderly individuals. In a next step, we will use the sufficiently reliable output measures for a factor analysis in an independent sample of 140 healthy elderly individuals to derive neurocognitive profiles that are based on latent features. Using these profiles, we will examine how the latent features are related to to an extensive set of standardized psychological tests and to existing neuroanatomical measures. These important steps may provide insights about the functional meaning of the latent features. Next, we will test whether the neurocognitive profiles may help to characterize subgroups of healthy elderly participants that are at risk for developing age-related cognitive impairments. This sample will then be extended with 100 mildly cognitively impaired (MCI) elderly individuals and we will examine the sensitivity and specificity of the output measures to differentiate between healthy elderly subjects and MCI patients. Finally, a last subproject is dedicated to making the data and procedures fully available to the research community. Therefore, we believe that this research project not only would empower numerous future studies, but on its own would importantly complement other aging research initiatives. More importantly, we see potential that the test battery or parts of this approach can be translated to clinical application, for instance in the diagnosis of early markers for cognitive impairment, as EEG and eye tracking are relatively low in cost and readily applicable to a wide population. Lastly, this project will be marked by strong collaborations and hence promises to facilitate scientific careers and future research projects.

Title: Improving symptom management in endometriosis: Development and Evaluation of an AI-Driven Interactive (Chatbot) Patient Decision Aid
Abstract:
Background: Endometriosis is a chronic, oestrogen-dependent, and inflammatory gynaecological disease affecting approximately 10% of reproductive-age women. Characterised by endometrial-like tissue outside the uterus, it leads to a wide spectrum of symptoms and associated conditions, including pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, and dyspareunia, often coupled with fatigue, infertility, depression, and anxiety. The complex nature of endometriosis results in a significant impact on patients’ quality of life. While advancements in symptom management have expanded treatment options, the challenge now lies in delivering precise, individualised recommendations that address the multifaceted nature of the disease. 
Project Overview and objectives: This project aims to develop and evaluate the usability, accessibility, acceptability and feasibility of an AI-driven interactive patient decision aid (patient facing chatbot and care team interface) made available through an existing shared decision-making platform (Fora Health).  Using a woman’s demographic profile, current clinical guidelines and evidence-based information, including but not limited to the Vaud University Hospital's (CHUV) endometriosis website, a comprehensive AI-driven endometriosis patient decision aid (PtDA) will present symptom management options such as hormonal therapy, surgery, manual therapies, pain management consultations, and psychotherapy. It will provide personalised, multilingual information to empower women aged 18-49 to make informed decisions, incorporating both medical and non-medical approaches, with a focus on fertility concerns and addressing the unique needs of socially disadvantaged women.
Methods: The research team will use a mixed-methods, participatory, and user-centred approach in collaboration with multidisciplinary stakeholders to ensure successful dissemination and implementation. The project comprises four studies:
(1) Scoping and Design: Using the Photovoice method, 15-20 women will identify their information and decision support needs regarding symptom management.
(2) PtDA Prototype Development and Alpha Testing: Focus groups and think-aloud methods with 15-20 women will refine the PtDA for usability, functionality, and patient preference alignment.
(3) Beta Testing (Field Test): The PtDA’s usability, accessibility, and acceptability will be tested in real-life conditions by 15-20 women using web analytics and an online questionnaire based on Morville's user experience framework.
(4) Randomised Controlled Feasibility Trial: Feasibility of a full-scale randomised controlled trial (RCT) will be assessed, with knowledge data as the primary outcome (60 participants).
Impact of the project: This AI-driven interactive PtDA aims to promote shared decision-making in endometriosis management by enhancing patient knowledge, enabling more informed decisions, optimising the use of appropriate treatments, and ultimately improving pain and symptom management, resource utilisation and quality of life. The insights gained from our work are potentially transformative for digital decision aids across a wide variety of topics, providing patients with personalised, comprehensible information outside of consultations with providers. By the end of the project, we will have created a tool that empowers women with endometriosis to make more informed treatment decisions, improving their quality of life. The study will also contribute to advancing the science of decision aid development by refining methodologies for usability, accessibility, and acceptability in digital health tools. Finally, the findings will lay the groundwork for a future definitive trial to test the tool's impact on patient-centred outcomes in a full-scale RCT.

Title: Cardiac Trigger Localization and Arrhythmia Identification System Using 3-D Esophageal Electrocardiography
Abstract: In electrophysiology, there is a gap in diagnostic methods when the non-invasive methods, such as standard 12-lead Electrocardiograms (ECGs), are not sufficient but an invasive catheter mapping examination is inappropriate or not applicable. Recent results from a clinical trial have shown that it is feasible to estimate the electrical cardiac activity on the heart surface from 3-D esophageal electrocardiogram signals. Therefore, we will derive the mathematical methods and generalize the idea towards a new diagnostic modality in cardiology and towards a working prototype of an esophageal heart analyzing tool.
Keywords: Arrhythmia Diagnostics, Biological signal processing, Esophageal Electrocardiography, Model-based signal processing, Unsupervised learning

Title: Ontological Models for Feature Selection in Definition Writing for Terminological and Ontological Resources
Abstract:
Definition writing is an essential activity in the development of terminological and ontological resources. This activity is still mostly realized manually. It would nevertheless greatly benefit from the assistance of (semi-)automatic definition writing tools. Such tools would not only accelerate the writing process but also enhance and guarantee the consistency and, therefore, the overall quality of the produced definitions and ontologies integrating these definitions.

The main objective of my research is to find theoretically founded operational answers to feature selection in terminological definitions. In particular, my research aims at discovering and defining formalizable principles and rules that can be implemented in a (semi-)automatic tool intended to assist terminologists and ontologists in writing definitions. For such a tool to be reusable in different terminographic and ontological contexts, by terminologists or ontologists working in different languages and on different domains, it should use generic models that are domain- and language-independent.

Typically, definition writing consists in extracting all available information about a term/concept/referent from a corpus constituted of texts written by experts in the domain under scrutiny. The information thus extracted is combined to form a concise and informative sentence. However, not all the information thus extracted is relevant to defining. One of the most challenging tasks of definition writing is therefore the selection of defining information. The main questions raised by this activity which have to be answered in order to develop adequate tools to assist in definition writing are: On what grounds is this selection done? and What kind of information is relevant to define?

To answer these questions, I made the hypothesis that domain-specific conceptualizations, which are “described” by terminological definitions, refer to different kinds of entities in the world and that their properties and relations have an influence on the information that is relevant to define these concepts. The relevance of the defining features is also governed by other factors, such as the organization of the conceptual systems which underlie terminologies, and other kinds of more pragmatic factors. Nevertheless, the one factor that is the most “neutral” regarding conceptualizations is the level of reality. Therefore, in order to be able to design generic tools to assist terminologists and ontologists in producing relevant definitions, independently of the domain or the language in which they are working, I propose to create defining models based on the properties and relations characterizing each type of entity. 

The entity types and their corresponding relations which constitute the proposed relational models are based on the categories of an existing realist upper-level ontology, the Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), and their specifications [1]. This ontology, founded by Professor Barry Smith and his colleagues, is aimed at representing the type of things that exist in the outside world, their properties and their relations to other types of entities. Entity types are organized according to philosophical distinctions and they are consistent with the scientific knowledge of the world. 

Methodologically, the objective of my research is to adapt these categories to creating relational models and use these models to describe the internal structure of existing definitions. Large-scale multi-domain and multilingual corpus analyses should thus enable to test the hypothesis and, if verified, to implement these models in a (semi-)automatic definition writing tool. A pilot experiment based on a corpus analysis of a sample of 240 terminological definitions extracted from 15 domains yielded very encouraging results, with almost 75% of the relations expressed in the analyzed definitions pertaining to the models associated with each entity type. This empirical study showed, moreover, which relations (characteristics related to each entity type) in these generic models are most relevant in terminological definitions. However, the adaptation of BFO entities to these generic models and to the description of the internal structure of the definitions has brought up different questions which should be considered carefully with a specialist of these matters.

This interdisciplinary research project is, thus, aimed at consolidating the groundwork done in my thesis, validating the obtained preliminary results and extending the scope of the empirical work based on corpus analysis of existing terminological definitions. This project has in addition a more theoretical scope: to deepen specific questions related to the interface between the proposed ontological approach and the more conceptual or lexico-semantic approaches traditionally adopted in terminology. A better understanding of their interrelations would not only help with implementing rules for semi-automatically annotating large amounts of definitions, but it would also contribute towards an integrated theory of definitions in terminology.

Title: YouStream 3D: Immersive Context-Aware Personal Communications
Abstract:
We are witnessing an integration of computer-communication technologies on an unprecedented scale. People, devices, and computers interact in ways unforeseen before. Future predictions speak of even more fundamental changes lying ahead spurred by the ever increasing amount of digital content pervading our lives. At the heart of these technological advances lies our drive to interconnect and share information, anywhere and anytime. In particular, social networking applications are increasingly becoming a landmark of our online existence. For instance, according to recent statistics, we spend on average 15 minutes on YouTube every day and more content is uploaded there in 60 days than all three major US networks created in 60 years. The unparalleled scale and massive content production of online social networks raise a new set of challenges for the reliable delivery and understanding of content in such environments. Even the most powerful content delivery networks today such as Akamai and Limelight are not capable of serving such large audiences, simultaneously. The anticipated personalization of the streaming process in the future, according to different viewing times, client devices, and viewing angles, e.g., as in online games, will only augment the complexity of the problem further. Equally important, the fusion of online communities and media sharing sites has brought to the forefront unfamiliar phenomena such as audience-content interaction and interdependencies. Finally, the proliferation of smart mobile devices has promoted yet another layer of complex context-driven time-varying interrelations between people, locations, and data.

The project will investigate intelligent multimedia systems that will address the new engineering and scientific challenges that are introduced by the fusion of community sites, content production tools, the proliferation of multi-camera arrays, and the advent of virtual worlds. Our systems will account for the plethora of contextual information generated in such scenarios to efficiently and reliably deliver immersive multimedia communication to all corners of the worlds. Important applications spanning telecollaboration and telecommuting, environmental monitoring and disaster relief, as well as telemedicine and health care, will all benefit from the advances in networked multimedia that the project will enable. In conjunction, we will study novel techniques for efficient quality-of-experience aware signal processing and communication of decentralized information sources in loose coalitions of networked devices, as frequently encountered in social networking settings and wireless mesh networks, in general. Our distributed protocols will take advantage of the inherent robustness and bandwidth scalability of such environments and will exploit concepts from reinforcement learning, Pareto optimality, and network coding to comprehensively advance the state-of-the-art. They will incorporate energy-aware aspects for further power efficiency and energy conservation.

The present proposal represents a continuation of the ongoing Ambizione project PZ00P2-126416. During the course of our investigations, we have made a number of exciting discoveries that were not anticipated at the time when the original project was formulated. They pointed us to new fruitful directions of research that could lead to further important insights into the context-driven and media-rich information systems of the future. However, due to the limited time span of the present project, we will not be able to explore all of them. Therefore, we feel it is important to continue the present project along the research investigations described in this proposal. To summarize the contributions of the ongoing Ambizione project PZ00P2-126416, we published to date two book chapters, six journal papers, and 20 conference articles. Many of these studies are reviewed in Section 2.2. of the proposal that describes our investigations relevant for the present proposal. The author has been invited to give talks about this research at numerous academic institutions recognized internationally for their excellence. There is an additional number of articles that are either in review or will be submitted this year, based on our ongoing investigations. It should be mentioned that the present project has stimulated very fruitful collaboration relationships with a number of research institutions throughout the world, of which the author is particularly proud. I believe that with the additional funding support anticipated by the present proposal further important research contributions of the same nature will follow.
Keywords: cloud computing media, content delivery, context-driven information processing, decentralized networking, multi-graphs, multiple view video systems, online social networks, peer-to-peer systems

Title: Towards an early-warning tool against enteric virus contamination of coastal watersheds - PreVir
Abstract:
Enteric viruses arising from human sewage spill-over into water catchments represent a threat to human health through water-using food production or water-based recreational activities. Despite continuous efforts in wastewater treatment and microbiological monitoring of water bodies, viral contamination of food during production still occurs in Europe, with adverse health effects on consumers and economic consequences on food producers. Filtering large amounts of their growing waters, shellfish are both a food, and a sentinel of the microbial quality of their environment. Shellfish contamination by norovirus, an enteric virus, is indeed the most frequent setting in viral foodborne outbreaks in Europe and an important problem in the world as well. Importantly, while this contamination is known to be affected by rainfall, the exact impact of weather events, and especially extreme hydroclimatic events, is not known. Additionally, shellfish farmers and stakeholders using water for recreation require information to enable adaptation to the events. Here, we aim at contributing to the safe and sustainable use of water, especially for shellfish production, by (i) acquiring new knowledge of the viral contamination in catchments, and (ii) co-developing an early-warning tool helping end-users to mitigate the impact of this contamination upon extreme hydroclimatic events. 

Indeed, although water quality and quantity are known to affect the transport or persistence of infectious enteric viruses, the impact of extreme hydroclimatic events on the viral contamination of watersheds is not well understood. Thus, we identified key scientific and technological questions that were only partially addressed by previous studies. How do floods and droughts alter the dynamics, diversity, and infectivity of enteric viruses in water catchments up to shellfish beds? Can the contamination of shellfish be predicted from water quality, meteorological or other parameters, under normal conditions and during extreme events? Finally, how does this translate to an infectious risk? By answering these questions, we will generate new knowledge that we will use to develop process-based and machine-learning models of viral contamination and viral infectious risk in shellfish and coastal waters. Through contacts already established with stakeholders and the organization of dedicated workshops in multiple countries, we will co-construct an early-warning tool answering the needs of European end-users.  

The project addresses the second topic of the call “Tools for water management – in the context of hydroclimatic extreme events”, by developing an early-warning, decision-support tool, based on new data and risk models, that will help the shellfish industry and coastal communities to enforce mitigation measures against contamination by enteric viruses. It adopts a catchment-to-sea perspective, necessary for this anthropogenic contamination diffusing from land to sea through watersheds. It will focus on the impact of floods, storms and droughts to ensure adequate adaptation of the mitigation strategies to climate change and increasing frequencies of these extreme events. Moreover, through building new models and using advanced computing technologies like neural networks, it will also contribute to smartening the water system. Our trans-European consortium gathers complementary expertise in environmental virology, virus epidemiology, water quality and modeling, that will be enriched through our contacts with stakeholders, to contribute to the management of the water resource contamination by enteric viruses.
Keywords: Enterovirus, Machine learning, Norovirus, extreme weather events, mitigation measures, shellfish, water quality modeling

Title: PHASER: Parsimonious Hierarchical Automatic Speech Recognition
Abstract:
PHASER takes a new perspective to the Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) problem, expressed as a hierarchical sparse recovery problem. More specifically, the project will exploit and integrate in a principled way recent developments in posterior-based ASR systems, hybrid HMM/ANN systems, exploiting Hidden Markov Model (HMM) and Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), Deep Neural Networks, compressive sensing, sparse modeling and hierarchical sparse coding for ASR. The sought approach should be able to model temporal properties, exploit model parsimony and hierarchical decoding structures, while also integrating the phonetic and lexical constraints currently being modeled through the pre-defined HMM topology.

Besides further research and development in these areas, one of the key pivots of the present proposal also lies in the recent identification of strong relationships between statistical HMM techniques (with HMM states as latent variables) and compressive sensing formalism, where the atoms of the compressive dictionary can be automatically estimated from posterior distributions of HMM-states.

Exploiting and further developing our various, state-of-the-art, ASR tools (often available as Idiap open-source or integrated in other open-source systems like Kaldi), the resulting systems will be evaluated in different context, including isolated word and continuous speech recognition, as well as multilingual recognition.
Keywords: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Deep Architectures, Hierarchical Posterior-based ASR, Hierarchical Sparse Coding

Title: From quantum theory to machine learning and back -- Quantum-inspired machine learning & machine learning-assisted quantum research
Abstract: Both quantum information and machine learning, by design, are suited to deal with high-dimensional data, and both, in their own distinct ways, have their weaknesses in precisely this. For example, state-of-the-art deep neural networks resort to the use of billions, if not trillions of parameters, requiring massive amounts of specialized hardware to run. In quantum theory, even for table-top experiments, we have difficulties handling the high-dimensional latent Hilbert space which could explain the results and the physics of our quantum experiments. In the current research project I propose to utilise the strengths of each to support the weaknesses of the other, with the goal of providing tools for quantum information theorist and machine learning researchers, and not just solving open questions, but also raising new ones.
Keywords: Bell nonlocality, machine learning, many-body physics, neural network, quantum correlations, quantum theory, quantum-inspired, tensor network

Title: Post-selection causal inference for cluster level parameters – theoretical and machine learning perspective
Abstract: The causal nature of numerous phenomena has been recognised in many fields and thus leading to the development of various methods for its study and analysis. The general public is concerned with the environmental impact of greenhouse gases or the influence of fake news. Likewise, scholars are frequently interested in the average effect of a certain medical treatment or an exposure to a chemical substance. The outcomes are very often stochastic variables which manifest an intrinsic clustering. In particular, studies on causal impact has a long tradition in biostatistics where measurements reveal temporal dependence because they have been collected for individuals over time. Similarly, observations from different geographical locations display spatial resemblance. In the past few decades, statisticians have attempted to develop valid strategies to select the confounding factors in order to estimate correctly the causal parameters. The issue is particularly severe in up-to-date, big data settings where the number of covariates may exceed the observations. Nevertheless, it has been a common practice to disregard the influence of a data driven model selection procedure while constructing confidence intervals and tests for treatment parameters. This negligence results in erroneous conclusions with far-reaching consequences for practitioners. Despite the shortcomings, no one to the best of our knowledge has studied the theoretical and empirical properties of causal estimators for clustered data. Thus, our goal is to construct and investigate valid post-selection confidence intervals and tests for cluster level parameters. More specifically we will examine two-step strategies of Belloni et al. (2014) as well as Dukes and Vansteelandt (2019) and Dukes et al. (2020) and extend them to account for the cluster level parameters. In addition, we are going to investigate statistical properties of novel estimators, in particular post-selection uniform convergence. Afterwards, we attempt to analyse the post-selected estimators obtained by implementing nonparametric and machine learning techniques. Specifically, we are going to make use of the ensemble algorithm superlearner to estimate the ingredients of the collaborative targeted maximum likelihood estimator (C-TMLE) of van der Laan and Rose (2011). Then we plan to assess the sensitivity of the post-selection confidence intervals for cluster level estimators. Finally, we will compare the numerical performance of the theoretical and machine learning strategies and apply our methods to case studies. We intend to show that ignoring the selection process in the inference for cluster level parameter is harmful, leads to wrong theoretical results and substantially affects real data analysis. Our comprehensive study will fill an existing gap in the theory and practical research on clustered causal processes.
Keywords: causal inference, clustered data, high-dimensional, machine learning, post-selection, targeted inference, uniform convergence

Title: Coestimating selection and demography
Abstract:
Detecting signatures of past selective events provides insights into the evolutionary history of a species by evidencing adaptive events. The identification of molecular targets of selection in humans, for instance, pinpoints biologically relevant differences between us and other apes. In addition, inferences regarding selection provide important functional information by elucidating the interaction between genotype and phenotype. Since positions in the genome that are under selection are functionally important by definition, detecting signatures of selection has also been used extensively to identify functional regions or protein residues. Finally, inferring the molecular locations at which selection is acting may help us to predict responses to selective pressures in organisms such as viruses, which would revolutionize the management of pandemics and the development of drugs. 

Unfortunately, the demographic history of a population or species is a major confounding factor when inferring past selective events. Indeed, neutrality tests are very sensitive to violations of the underlying demographic assumption of constant population size – and it is often impossible to distinguish between adaptive or demographic processes in putatively identified regions. After a population bottleneck, for instance, false positive rates of up to 90\% are not uncommon. Current approaches to deal with this problem rely on the assumption that selection is acting on a few loci only, while demography affects all loci equally.  A two step procedure has been proposed in which a set of selectively neutral loci are used to calibrate a demographic model against which putatively selected loci are compared. However, recent evidence suggests that selection may be common in the genome of many organisms and a priori knowledge on the neutrality of markers is often difficult to obtain. As a result, this approach suffers from high false negative rates – not to mention relying on very strong assumptions regarding the pervasiveness of adaptive mutations.

There is currently no flexible approach to estimate demography and selection jointly. However, recent advances in computational approaches offer new hopes to tackle such an inference. A particularly promising approach is Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC), a technique to sidestep analytical likelihood calculations with simulations. To this end, ABC has been used to infer a wide range of evolutionary scenarios such as population bottlenecks, population splits and migration, but also to distinguish between a classic selective sweep and recurrent selective events.

Here I propose to develop an ABC framework to estimate demography and selection jointly, and to apply it to a variety of organisms with very different evolutionary histories. Major new developments are needed to reach this goal. Firstly, the application of ABC to large scale data sets is tenuous without novel techniques to reduce the computational effort required. I will address this through various innovations including new ABC-MCMC algorithms with increased performance, an efficient recycling of simulations, and extending recent approaches to hybridize ABC with traditional full-likelihood methods. Such a hybridization will enable us to profit from the rich literature on full-likelihood solutions to simpler problems and to take linkage properly into account. Secondly, the joint inference of demography and selection calls for new models and new sets of informative summary statistics. I will approach this challenge by integrating models established to infer either selection or demography alone and through current techniques to explore a large space of summary statistics, such as PLS or machine learning algorithms. 

The proposed innovations will allow me to work towards answering some of the most controversial questions in evolutionary biology, namely the importance of adaptation in shaping genomic variation. I will approach these questions by inferring genome-wide selection coefficients from unique data sets of four organisms representing various selective and demographic histories: Deer mice (Peromyscus maniculatus), HCM viruses, Drosophila melanogaster and humans. These estimates will not only have broad implications for the management of pandemics or the development of new drugs, but will also greatly improve our understanding of the mode and tempo of the process of adaptation.

Title: Augmenting versus hindering ? The role of emotions for collective human-AI decision-making
Abstract:
Through recent technological advancements in artificial intelligence (AI), organizational decision-making is fundamentally changing (Kellogg, Valentine, & Christin, 2020; Lebovitz, Lifshitz-Assaf, & Levina, 2022). AI is being used to support complex decisions such as the selection of job candidates or diagnosing diseases (Lebovitz et al., 2022; Shrestha, Ben-Menahem, & von Krogh, 2019; Smith & Telang, 2018; von Krogh, 2018). However, decision makers often perceive algorithmic advice to be inferior to those of humans, and are averse to their input (Dietvorst, Simmons, & Massey, 2015). Understanding the drivers behind this resistance will be critical for the successful and sustainable deployment of AI in a growingly digitized world.
Research to date has focused on cognitive challenges to people’s successful adoption of AI technologies. However, algorithms have been shown to not only evoke cognitive reactions but also strong negative feelings, such as internal stress (Kellogg, Valentine, & Christin, 2020). To prevent these negative emotions from hindering effective human-AI decision-making, research is needed to understand and address them. Furthermore, existing studies of AI decision-making mainly focus on individuals, even though decisions within organizations usually involve a diverse set of stakeholders whose experiences with these tools may vary, requiring a team-level analysis (Glikson & Woolley, 2020). 
Building upon the research conducted as part of my Postdoc.Mobility grant, the proposed one-year research plan aims to address the role of emotions when teams develop and collectively make decisions accompanied by AI tools. Specifically, this research sets out to pinpoint why, how, and for whom emotions hinder human-AI decision-making in teams and to subsequently design interventions to overcome these challenges and sustain the well-being of diverse team members. More precisely, I plan to work on the following projects: a) an ethnographic study of emotional dynamics of emergency teams using an AI-based alert to predict sepsis in children; b) an ethnographic study of designers developing and healthcare staff using AI technologies to monitor patients’ health status at distance; c) a theory paper on emotions and human-AI decision-making; and d) an interdisciplinary project on leveraging large language models (generative AI) for patient-provider messages
This research will advance theory on the emotional underpinnings of human-AI decision-making in teams and identify strategies that will enable teams to make effective decisions supported by AI tools. The findings will be submitted to top-tier outlets. Based on insights from real-world applications, I will develop recommendations and host workshops to support decision-makers to augment team decision-making through AI technologies. In the healthcare sector, small improvements in team decision-making can result in large benefits for society by increasing patient safety, quality of treatment and reducing costs.

Title: Inducing Semantic Representations from Multiple Data Sources
Abstract:
Deep natural language understanding is a core long-term objective of the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP).  Statistical approaches to NLP have been making progress towards this goal, but further progress is being hampered by fundamental limitations of the traditional statistical NLP methodology.  The traditional methodology uses supervised learning methods applied to large amounts of data annotated by linguistic experts.  The existence of such corpora for semantic role labelling (SRL) has enabled recent progress in extracting these shallow semantic representations from text, but these corpora are only available for a few languages, they only cover a limited vocabulary of words, and often they only annotate a subset of the semantic relations.  In addition, further progress towards deeper more informative semantic representations is limited by the notorious difficulty of devising sound and complete representations for deep semantic content, and of annotating data with such representations.  For NLP tools to reach levels of semantic analysis even approaching what humans take for granted, we need to develop and exploit new machine learning methods which can automatically induce new semantic representations from unannotated data.

In this project we will develop models of semantic analysis that are trained on both annotated SRL corpora and on data that is only weakly correlated with linguistic meaning.  A very powerful source of data that is weakly correlated with natural language semantics is corpora of sentences and their translations (called parallel corpora).  A sentence and its translation provide different evidence about their shared meaning, so we will use large parallel corpora to induce representations of this shared meaning.  In our previous work, we have shown that this shared meaning is often manifested in shared patterns of semantic roles.  In this project we will exploit this experience to develop models for cross-lingual semantic role induction.  To do so, we will develop models that jointly model multiple languages and their semantic roles.  A single model will be trained both monolingually on SRL corpora and multilingually on parallel corpora.  It will then be tested monolingually on any of the languages in the parallel corpus, even if there was no SRL corpus for that language used in training.

The approach we will take to this ambitious objective builds directly on recent advances in NLP and machine learning.  In machine learning, Bayesian latent variable models provide a formal framework for learning and reasoning about representations that are not labelled in the data.  In recent years, there has been steady progress in inference (computing probabilities) and learning (estimating parameters from data) for a variety of Bayesian latent variable model designs.  Building on monolingual Bayesian models of semantic role labelling, we will exploit results on topic modelling to induce classes that allow us to label verbs that are not annotated in the training data.  Then we will exploit results from Bayesian multilingual models of part-of-speech tagging and syntactic parsing to extend to multilingual models.  Our previous research on latent variable models make us well placed to combine these techniques and solve the additional problems necessary to devise efficient and effective methods for this complex task.  We expect to be the first to develop a Bayesian latent variable model of multilingual semantic role labelling.

By combining insights from research on Bayesian latent variable models, semantic role labelling, and parallel corpora, we will develop a model that combines the advantages of linguistic knowledge about semantics, supervised training on the explicit annotations in SRL corpora, and unsupervised training on the weakly correlated evidence in parallel corpora.  Developing such a model is a key step in progress towards deep analyses of natural language meaning.  The complexity of the task and the amount of relevant data also make this project an important test case in developing effective methods for combining partially supervised and weakly supervised machine learning techniques.
Keywords: latent variable models, machine learning, natural language processing, parallel corpora, semantic role labelling

Title: Conversational Interfaces as Preference Expression Modalities
Abstract:
Recent advances in natural language processing and the adoption of conversational interfaces gradually transform how consumers interact with firms (BI Intelligence, 2016; Dale, 2016; Hirschberg & Manning, 2015). The use of conversational interfaces as a new interaction paradigm between human consumers and conversational agents has been declared as the “next operating system in commerce” (Suri, Elia, & van Hillegersberg, 2017; The Economist, 2016) and is expected to transform how humans search, shop, and express their preferences. Recent industry reports further indicate that conversational interfaces will be integrated by at least twenty-five percent of all offered customer service and support operations by 2020 (Gartner, 2018). Not surprisingly, the conversational interface market is soaring at a thirty-one percent annual growth rate and predicted to exceed $1.34 billion by 2024  (Global Market Insights Inc., 2018), illustrating the significant impact of conversational interfaces on the future of commerce. However, fundamental research on the underlying mechanism of how conversational interfaces alter consumer search processes and choice remain scarce and academic research is predominantly concerned with design and technology-related issues rather than the consequences for consumers. Specifically, the majority of prior work on anthropomorphic agents and conversational interfaces examined either factors related to optimizing the design features of conversational interfaces (Landis, 2014; Lokman & Zain, 2010), factors related to user perceptions and acceptance (Boden, Fischer, Herbig, & Spierling, 2006; Comendador, Francisco, Medenilla, Nacion, & Serac, 2015), or how conversational interfaces can learn in an unsupervised fashion through interactions with the a user (Serban et al., 2017). Research remains scarce in terms of the downstream consequences of how these interfaces may fundamentally alter consumers’ search, preference expression, and ultimately choice experience, how they affect their purchase decisions, and the psychological mechanism that explains these effects. 
The current research program aims at providing a theoretical framework for the underlying psychological processes of how these conversational interfaces affect consumer decision making. Specifically, we examine the question of how these interfaces fundamentally alter consumption experiences and consumer preferences, and explore potential downstream consequences of conversational interfaces. Specifically, the current research is specifically designed to identify the underlying psychological process of how conversational interfaces can create more intimate consumer-firm relationships, how greater intimacy can by altered by structural and contextual features of the interfaces (such as built-in turn-taking of more humanoid properties of the interface), and how greater intimacy between consumers and firms can ultimately alter consumers’ susceptibility to influence attempts. 
To unravel the process by which conversational interfaces (and particularly different interface properties, such as conversational style or humanoid appearance) affect consumer’s preferences and actual choices, such as their susceptibility to influence attempts to trade them up to more premium product choices, we will conduct a series of experimental studies in both field and laboratory settings. The grant applicant has already built the needed infrastructure to complete the envisioned experiments as well as a series of initial, foundational studies. These promising initial findings will be extended and more rigorously tested in the proposed research plan of this grant proposal (see sections 2.2 and 2.3 for details).
The findings of this research will have substantial theoretical implications for future work at the intersection of marketing, the psychology of consumers in technology-enhanced environments, human-computer interaction and will provide insight into the psychology of consumers in a ‘digitized’ society (see related section under 2.5 for details).
Keywords: Consumer Decision Making, Conversational Interfaces, Field Experiments, Laboratory Experiments, Natural Language Processing

Title: New vertex reconstruction to search for rare Higgs bosondecays at the CMS experiment
Abstract:
In particle physics, we study nature at its most fundamental level by observing particle collisions. The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN offers the unique opportunity to study particle collisions at highest energies and challenge our current understanding of fundamental particles and forces. 

The Higgs boson is a central part of the Standard Model of particle physics as it provides the mechanism behind electroweak symmetry breaking. It is the only fundamental scalar that has been observed so far and might well be the portal toward a wider sector of new particles and fields. Characterizing the properties of the Higgs boson by measuring its couplings to other Standard Model particles is one of the main goals of the physics program at the LHC to explore the possibility of physics beyond the Standard Model. 

I propose a research program to search for new physics effects in rare decays of the Higgs boson. Specifically I am interested in the decays of the Higgs boson to gauge bosons and pseudoscalar or vector mesons. These decays are much suppressed in the Standard Model such that a potential observation would hint to new physics phenomena. To date the branching ratios of these decays are only weakly constrained experimentally or completely unexplored.  

The research program will be carried out with the CMS experiment at the LHC and use the data that has been or will be collected during the LHC Run 2 (2015-2018) and Run 3 (2022-2025). The proposed search channels have complex signatures in the detector and are challenging to reconstruct experimentally. In particular, the measurements rely on an excellent performance of the tracking detectors to precisely reconstruct displaced vertices from the decay of long-lived particles. An integral part of this project is the development of new methods for vertex reconstruction based on state-of-the-art machine-learning techniques. This development will be crucial to exploit the full physics potential of the LHC, especially in view of the high-luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) upgrade, where particles from an average of 200 simultaneous collisions will need to be reconstructed.
Keywords: Higgs, Higgs physics, High-energy physics, LHC, Particle physics, Vertex reconstruction, particle physics, pixel detector

Title: Leveraging generative AI to identify and probe naturalistic complex behaviors in Virtual Reality
Abstract: To elucidate the dynamic link between brain and behavior, we need to be able to quantify and manipulate complex behavioral repertoires in naturalistic, laboratory contexts. We propose to address this challenge by combining generative AI technologies to detect behavioral patterns with virtual reality (VR) technologies to simulate naturalistic social interactions and environments. We will develop machine learning methods to quantify animal behavior in natural social contexts. We will study two models of social animals: fish and monkeys. Both exhibit interpersonal interactions and collective behaviors, but exploit the sensory inputs differently (e.g. vision, hearing) with different levels of cognitive flexibility. The first goal will be to develop tools for automatically generating ethograms from videos collected in both the wild and laboratory environments. We will then build agent-centric behavioral models of social interactions. The second goal will be to leverage these models in the VR systems we are developing. This will enable us to simulate social interaction contexts to manipulate individual and collective behaviors in both animal models.

Title: Ensemble Inference of Gene Regulatory Networks
Abstract:
The maintenance of normal cellular functions and the regulation of appropriate cellular responses to environmental and genetic perturbations depend critically on a network of interactions among cellular molecules. The reconstruction of such networks from high-throughput cell biology (omics technology) has become a major focus in systems biology, including the inference of gene regulatory networks (GRNs). The knowledge of GRNs and particularly how such networks differ in healthy and disease cells, can provide insights for understanding the pathogenesis of important diseases such as cancer and finding possible treatments. Despite intense efforts in the last two decades, the inference of GRN from gene expression (transcriptomics) data is still unsolved. This inference problem has often been said to be underdetermined, suggesting that there exist multiple indistinguishable solutions. 

In this project, we propose to develop and use ensemble inference framework and algorithms to address the reconstruction of GRN from gene expression data. The ensemble strategy represents a significant deviation from existing network inference methods, but a necessary one for tackling the underdetermined issue of the GRN inference. In this approach, we aim to identify an ensemble of (indistinguishable) GRN structures that are consistent with available expression datasets. As the number of such structures can be intractable, we will determine only the upper and lower bounds of the ensemble. Using the property of transitivity, we can construct the members of the ensemble from these bounds if desired. Here, we plan to expand our previous ensemble inference algorithm in order to enable: (1) the inference of the nature of gene regulatory interactions (activation/inhibition), and (2) the integration of multiple types of datasets, including perturbation, time-series and observational data. 

Here, we view the GRN inference as finding the causal relationship among genes. We will adopt different strategies for extracting causal information depending on the type of data. In particular, we will use steady-state expression data from gene perturbation experiments to produce gene accessibility lists, recognizing the fundamental limitation in such data for differentiating direct and indirect regulations. Meanwhile, we will transform time-series expression data into a causal ordering among genes. Finally, we will build a Markov equivalence class of Bayesian networks from observational dataset. Here, we will employ and extend existing algorithms in the analysis of each of the aforementioned data types. The main challenge and thus the novel contribution will be in the integration of the disparate causal information to produce tight bounds of the ensemble.
Keywords: ensemble modeling, gene regulatory networks, machine learning, network inference

Title: Motion Models for Monocular People Tracking
Abstract:
Tracking people and recovering their 3D motion is one of the most difficult and challenging problems in Computer Vision. Today, there is great interest in capturing complex motions solely by analyzing video sequences, both because cameras are becoming ever cheaper and more prevalent and because there are so many potential applications. These include athletic training, surveillance, entertainment, and electronic publishing.

During the first year of the ongoing project we have focused on using a single Kinect depth camera. We have shown that we could successfully extend our earlier multi-camera approach to computing probabilities that people are present in the scene at any given time using input from a single depth-camera and in such a way that occlusions are correctly handled. During the remainder of the ongoing project, we will work on linking these detections across time and inferring temporally consistent 3D poses. In the project continuation we are now requesting, we will return to using an ordinary video camera while applying the lessons learned to achieve the same result, but without requiring the additional depth information. This will allow us to operate in settings where depth-cameras do not work well, such as outdoors or at depth ranges beyond their capabilities.

The approach we propose to investigate relies on the idea that, instead of using multiple cameras to resolve ambiguities as we did in earlier work, we can use images taken by a single camera over time to achieve the same result by enforcing temporal continuity.

Title: Finding early biomarkers of premature adrenarche to prevent long term consequences – AdmiR3
Abstract:
Background: The physiology of adrenarche and impact of premature adrenarche (PA) on later disease remain unknown. But the risk for earlier pubertal maturation, the polycystic ovary syndrome, infertility, and metabolic disorders including insulin resistance and dyslipidemia is increased in some individuals that had PA. So far only few studies have investigated PA individuals longitudinally and none of them compared the characteristics of PA patients versus control individuals at the specific time points of the developmental events of adrenarche, puberty onset and completion, rather than at fixed ages. Likewise, no study so far has used an unbiased multi-omics approach to unravel the physiology of adrenarche and PA on human biomaterials. 

Study aim: To characterize the natural course and consequences of PA in children from the onset of adrenarche to the start of puberty (4 years outline of this study), and to form a cohort that can be followed throughout puberty into adulthood. It will compare clinical, metabolic and transcriptomics data of PA individuals to matched controls at time points given by defined pubertal developmental events in order to find early biomarkers of later disease as well as targets for preventive measures. In addition, identified candidate markers will be investigated for their (patho-)mechanistic impact on adrenal steroidogenesis using molecular and cellular in vitro methods. 
WP1 - Comprehensive phenotyping. A cohort of 30 PA children and 90 controls will be recruited and studied prospectively at 4 time points from the onset of adrenarche to the onset of puberty assessing clinical data and collecting biomaterials.
WP2 - Metabolic profiling. Collected serum samples will be comprehensively profiled including steroid profiling (LC-MSMS) and protein profiling (Olink). 
WP3 - Transcriptome profiling and bioinformatic network analysis. Biosamples will also be profiled for differential expression of small RNAs by RNA sequencing. All data will be analyzed by a multi-omics approach using machine learning. 
WP4 - Validation of data in a Finnish cohort. A collaboration with a Finnish group will be started that studies an independent cohort in parallel to compare data and exchange knowledge.
WP5 - Validation of identified biomarkers and networks through mechanistic in vitro studies. Data confirmation for disease causing effects will be performed with established experimental in vitro models.

Expected Results and Impact: Our proposed studies will provide insight into the developmental event of adrenarche and its regulation, which when occurring prematurely and/or deregulated might result in adverse health outcome. The study aims at finding markers and targets for diagnostic, therapeutic and preventive care of PA. It shows that early life events matter, and that studies in children are important to reveal opportunities for early interventions or even prevention of adult disease.

Title: Interactive Cognitive Systems, Indoor Scene Recognition for Intelligent Systems
Abstract: Humans usually refer to rooms and arti cial environments in terms of their visual appearance (the corridor), the activities they usually perform in them (the tness room) and the objects they contain (the bedroom). The nouns used to represent these environments epitomize their semantics and allow them to use abstract representations while easily communicating their spatial concepts. In order to simplify the interaction between humans and arti cial agents, and to enable a high-level reasoning using abstract spatial concepts, the human representation of space should also be understood and reproduced by arti cial agents. For example, a robot s de nition of \oce", should point to the same set of places that a human would recognize as such. The main goal of this project is to develop a system able to visually learn such semantic concepts and to take advantage of them also in working scenarios which di er from the original ones. Taking inspiration from biological models of human perception, we identify two main components for the representation of indoor scenes: (1) a description of the global appearance of the image in term of image features, and (2) a description of the local landmarks present in some regions of the image. From a computational point of view the two representations could be regarded as a global appearance description of the scene, for example by means of statistics of visual features, and as a statistical representation of the co-occurrence of local concepts and scene categories. The design and integration of computational models of these two perceptual components, suitable for indoor place categorization, constitutes the core of our research. This project is a two-years renewal of the project ISC Interactive Cognitive Systems, track `Indoor Scene Recognition for Intelligent Systems, that started in 2011. The fund covers for the salary of Mr. Marco Fornoni, a PhD student at EPFL. During the rst two years of the project, we casted the problem into that of learning from multiple cues. Our contributions have been a principled online Multi Kernel Learning algorithm able to combine optimally multiple features while providing theoretical guarantees on the expected performance, and a global feature representation encoding at the same time task-driven and data driven spatial information. The combination of these two contributions has led us to obtain the state of the art in the eld, as measured on reference benchmark databases. The objective of this proposal is to move forward on this path, and to address three main open issues: (a) with respect to the feature representation, we will develop methods for encoding local landmark information, Rather than building object-based representations, we will take advantage of the Image-to-Class paradigm proposed in the NBNN classi er [34], casting it e ectively into the Multi Kernel Learning framework; (2) with respect to cue integration, we will move from a global to a local Multi Kernel Learning formulation, so to be able to assign di erent weights to di erent samples, over the multiple cues. Lastly, we will develop domain adaptation methods able to cope with di erent features and classi ers in the source and target tasks, so to enable intelligent systems to learn semantic spatial concepts from images collected on the Web, and use them in their own situated settings.
Keywords: Computer Vision, Cue Integration, Kernel Methods, Machine Learning, Place recognition, Robot Vision

Title: Intelligent Platform for Drug Response in Precision Oncology (Resubmission)
Abstract: This project aims at developing a new portable device based on electrochemical sensors, pharmacokinetic models, and state-of-the art machine learning algorithms. This new device will be the very first ever-conceived single-device capable of fusing real-time data dealing with molecular concentrations in the patient’ blood and patient’ metadata to provide robust clinical recommendations for dosage adjustments in precision oncology. In pharmacological treatments, the scope of precision medicine is about tailoring a precise delivery of therapeutic compounds neatly adapted to the patients’ characteristics. This mainly means adapting the dose to the exact disease-profile of each individual patient as well as to his metabolic behaviour right during treatment administration. This last is the most difficult to establish since it relies on genetic predisposition, epigenetic influences, and acquired characteristics (phenotype, senescence, comorbidity, comedication), all patient features that have complex interactions among them as well as with the patients’ environment and life-style. Following the time-evolution of drugs concentration in patients’ blood is also more difficult in case of therapeutic cocktails which, on one hand, are much more efficient and effective in cancer therapy than each single therapeutic agent while, on the other hand, are more difficult to monitor-in-time because different drugs strongly-interact in both patients metabolism and drug sensors. Therefore, the main objective is here to establish a new tool for precision oncology by developing a micro-fabricated system that integrates: electrochemical sensors for measuring several anticancer drugs commonly used in chemotherapy; all the electronic circuits required for sensors reading as well as for data elaboration and communication; local intelligence based on machine learning algorithms as implemented on hardware; dedicated fluidics to separate serum from patients’ blood and to drive the serum to the sensors; a user interface to interact with the system by using any mobile device (tablets, smart-phones, smart-watches, etc.). The electrochemical sensors will be micro-fabricated on a dedicated platform realized in silicon or in ceramic. The electronic circuitry will be realized with off-the-shelf components; the algorithms for local intelligence will be, implemented on hardware with off-the-shelf computing systems (e.g., FPGA or Edge-TPU) once optimized and robust enough for the application. Data fusion and data mining will be used in optimizing the algorithms by considering data from sensors and other source of information relying to the patient’ characteristics (age, weight, classification as metaboliser, etc.), and to the drugs delivery (name, administered dose, time of administration, etc.). The drug monitoring will be tested with lab samples in the presence of other spiked interfering metabolites, and further validated with patient’s samples by comparing with independent lab measurements. The originality dealing with the sensors part of the platform is also assured by the project need to design and realize an electrochemical biosensor for busulfan, sensor that has never been reported in literature so far. Moreover, the final platform will be capable to provide the simultaneous detection of busulfan, methotrexate, 5-fluorouracil, cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, and etoposide with a single multi-panel device. This also has never been reported in literature so far.
Keywords: Analog Design, Anticancer Drgus, Biosensors, Chemotherapy compounds, Data fusion, Deep Learning, Electrochemical Sensors, Embedded systems, Fluidics, Machine Learning, Multi-panel systems, Nanosensors

Title: HORD GNN: Higher-Order Relations and Dynamics in Graph Neural Networks
Abstract:
Complex biological, man-made systems and social relationships can be formalized as graphs (networks), with graphs being rich representations accounting for both structural and functional dependencies (edges, links) that exist among entities (nodes) and compose the networked system. Within this vast application framework, machine learning tools can be applied, boosted by the availability of large –and heterogeneous– data streams and unprecedented computational capabilities. By making explicit functional dependencies existing among entities as well as assigning mixed numerical and categorical information to nodes and edges, we take full advantage of prior knowledge about the problem as relational inductive biases. As proven by the literature, this setup becomes beneficial to the inference engine addressing the application needs, in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. It follows that machine learning architectures have evolved and have been suitably extended to deal with sequences of graphs, though most of the current research has focused on independent graphs drawn from the same probability distribution (i.i.d.) with a fixed set of nodes and a known topology defined by binary relations. Not rarely, these amenable hypotheses are inadequate in complex biological setups and man-made systems where functional dependencies among the different entities are latent and change over time. Extension to general high-order time-evolving interactions in terms of spatiotemporal dynamics (e.g., those associated with epidemic diffusions) or to instances where dependencies are latent and must be discovered from data (like those modeling particle collision jets) urge for major research attention. As such, addressing these two aspects represents the major goals of this proposed HORD GNN project. More in detail, the project objective is twofold and will result in three research lines. The first objective aims at overcoming the assumption that relations and interactions are fully observable, i.e., that the graph is known a priori. This pushes the research to consider (research line 1) advanced hypergraph-based representations and methods proposed to account for high-order latent relations. Suitable data representations and graph learning algorithms based on hypergraphs will be investigated. Then, the focus will be on the definition of a statistically sound processing framework, ultimately leading to grounded, effective, and efficient methods. Within this research line, we will also address embedding techniques with algorithmic relational inductive biases to map hypergraphs into vector embeddings that allow reconstructing the underlying graph representation whenever needed in the processing pipeline. A reference, high societal impact, application on power consumption forecasting in smart power grids will be considered, with a graph learning methodology to exploit latent dependencies among consumption patterns in the grid.  The second objective focuses on accounting for the temporal aspect with graph state-space models where the state of a dynamical system is represented in the form of a (hyper)graph. Within this frame, research line 2 aims at advancing the state of the art to produce predictive models where states and -optionally- inputs are (hyper)graphs either given by the application or learned from spatiotemporal relations observed in the data. This research requests extension and redefinition of mathematical operators -standard for vector data-, but no counterpart exists for graphs dealing with multiplex and hypergraph structures, ultimately leading to Graph Kolmogorov-Wiener filters, Graph Kalman Filters, and suitable extensions to nonlinear graph predictive models. A reference application involves the study of macroscopic brain dynamics through EEG signals. Research line 3 covers aspects of both objectives from a different perspective and aims at providing a novel Reinforcement Learning framework for learning composable policies to solve control problems in Markov Decision Processes where states, and eventually policies, are represented as (hyper)graphs capturing the structure of the system at different abstraction levels. We will study the expressive power and transferability of graph representations in this context, both in terms of value function approximation and policy learning. Then, we will exploit the compositionality of graph representations to design a novel algorithmic framework for hierarchical reinforcement learning where systems will be represented as multilayered graphs of interacting sub-modules. The proper hierarchy (graph) of controllers can be fixed by the designer or, again, learned to maximize reward accumulation. Finally, we will address the setting where the structure of the system under analysis can change over time. The reference application involves control of physical systems such as musculoskeletal models in the Learning to run competitions and the ones in the DeepMind control suite. 
I strongly believe that the proposed research plan will produce groundbreaking results, hence advancing this field to an unprecedented level by providing theoretical results and grounding methodological achievements; open-source Python libraries will be provided to permit entrepreneurs, practitioners, and researchers to take full advantage of public research outcomes.
Keywords: Graph Neural Networks, Graph representation learning, Graph-Kalman Filters, Hypergraphs, Predictive Graphs Neural Networks, Reinforcement Learning on Graphs
