Title: RoboMix2: Mixed Event-frame-based On-device Learning on Mixed Spiking-artificial Neural Networks for Robotics
Abstract:
Biology has always inspired scientific evolution, from the aerodynamic shape of airborne vehicles taken from predatory birds [1, 2] to optimization algorithms guided by nature [3], such as particle filters and ant colonies. Along the same line, recent advancements in robotics have leveraged i) novel event-based cameras inspired by biological visual pathways [4], ii) energy-efficient spiking neural networks (SNNs), mimicking biological neurons [5], and iii) tiny machine learning (TinyML) algorithms capable of continuously evolving and adapting [6], like mammals [7]. Event cameras offer low motion blur and high dynamic range, with lower bandwidth and power usage compared to synchronous frame-based cameras [4], which are complementary, by providing dense and easier-to-track features [8]. Similarly, SNNs complement artificial neural networks (ANNs), as they are robust to noise, low-latency, and operate with discrete events that occur at specific points in time [9, 10]: the perfect fit to exploit asynchronous events (spikes) from an event camera. Finally, continual on-device learning of TinyML models can mitigate the general problem of domain shift, i.e., well-trained models underperforming in
real-world domains due to semantic gaps. 
Combining these three conceptual cornerstones, and deploying them on hardware and software running on-boards of a robot promises to unlock unprecedented accuracy and reactiveness, at extreme energy efficiency. It will then become feasible to design miniature aerial robots with the extreme agility of hummingbirds, creating novel capabilities and enabling applications with significant economic impact. Unfortunately, at present, the power requirements for these cutting-edge advancements is still in the order of several Watts or more, preventing widespread adoption of these techniques, combined as a whole, aboard miniaturized robots. Consequently, the current State-of-the-Art (SoA) either exploits a subset of these technologies [11, 12, 13] or relies on bulky and power-hungry devices [14, 15]. In the RoboMix2 project, we want to deliver the first generation of ultra-low power (ULP) neuromorphic devices for miniaturized robots, capable of on-device learning of mixed event-frame-based SNN-ANN. To unleash the full potential of these bio-inspired advancements, we will address this challenging scenario from both the standpoint of hardware design and algorithmic methodologies. The RoboMix2 project will leverage mixed event-frame sensing and mixed SNN-ANN computing, like brains in mammals, combining different sensory perceptions and pathways [16], leveraging the strengths of all and limiting the weaknesses of each. Therefore, we will explore µs-level resolution interfaces for multiple event-frame streams, energy-efficient and ULP hardware design for SNNs and ANNs inference, and hardware accelerators for fast on-device learning of TinyML. Contextually, the project will pioneer a new class of hybrid TinyML models combining a frame-based feature-rich ANN with a faster event-based SNN, capable of on-device continual learning, fine-tuning themselves during the mission, with self-supervised strategies.
By addressing the key task of visual odometry in two complementary use cases (UCs), a kg-scale unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) and a sub-50 g miniaturized unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) (i.e., nano-UAV), the project will demonstrate i) its general applicability, and ii) its effectiveness under the most severe constraints (i.e., power envelope, payload, and form factor) of a nano-UAV. The hardware-software co-design at the heart of our use-inspired project will pave the way towards a new class of embedded ULP neuromorphic digital devices (i.e., Neuro Devices) of wide interest and applicability. The targeted Neuro Device can boost the performance of any robotic platform, improve safety in autonomous driving cars, and even be deployed at the edge, like in smart buildings, for accurate scene analysis and monitoring.

Title: Recommendation System for Academic Mobility
Abstract:
Exploring research environments is a common practice in academia. Although conferences and workshops help keep scholars up to date on their field, career mobility remains a vital activity to establish long-term and long-distance collaborations. Although well-known institutions are often excellent places for boosting careers, it is difficult to fully grasp the quantity and diversity of available institutions.

This project is intended to help scholars understand the research environment around them and utilize its opportunities by providing them with a recommendation system for academic mobility.

This system is conceived as a web-based application that invites scholars to type their name or copy and paste their ORCID identifier. The answer to such a query is a dashboard displaying potential institutions that matches the interests of every single user. The application relies on a large dataset created during the Early Postdoc.Mobility. Its core structure is composed of scholars, institutions, and publications collected respectively from three datasets, namely ORCID, ISNI, and Crossref.

While the current Early Postdoc.Mobility is aimed to visualize and analyze collaborations from all over the world, the proposal for a Postdoc.Mobility is to predict academic mobility by using the recent techniques of artificial intelligence. This method will be applied to the academic careers available on the ORCID dataset, the text analysis on publication abstracts calculated with techniques of Natural Language Processing (NPL), and the collaborations that exist among institutions all over the world.

The central idea is to design a recommendation system that provides an informative dashboard customized to the user. His/her personal data provided by ORCID will be compared with statistical methods to the global database to offer him/her a personal overview of the academic environment. With consideration of the critics and capabilities of artificial intelligence, the project aims not to pursue an infallible recommendation system but rather useful information to critically think about their academic career. The aim of the system is to provide contextualized and customized information, showing the travel choices made by other peers, the opportunities around the world, and the patterns of academic mobility.
Keywords: Academic Mobility, Computational Social Science, Data Visualization, Digital Humanities, Self-recognition

Title: Philosophical Research in the Age of AI
Abstract: Since its inception as a scientific discipline in the 1950s, the field of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has raised deep philosophical questions about the possibility of machine thinking and the nature of the human mind. With the dramatic increase in data and computing power since the turn of the millennium, it has become possible to physically realise what were previously only theoretical ideas. The ensuing developments have given rise to both hopes and concerns in modern societies. While in some areas the scale of potential harm caused by AI-driven technologies has alarmed many observers, the same technologies have generated euphoric expectations, when applied to other purposes such as cancer diagnosis or the fight against climate change. For philosophy, in addition to the theoretical problems about human intelligence, ethical, political and societal issues of great importance and urgency have arisen. Although many philosophers have been captivated by these problems and issues, they have given comparatively little attention to the impact that the systematic use of AI technologies might have on their own discipline. The main goal of this project is, therefore, to explore the potential of using state-of-the-art AI technology in, and for the purposes of, philosophical research. As the chosen approach is practice-orientated, the plan is to examine various use cases in which different tools are tested and refined. While the focus will be on identifying possible benefits of using AI tools in philosophy, the project is critical by design in that it will also assess the potential harms that might arise. However, in order for the critical assessment to go beyond the obvious and identify issues that lie beneath common applications, advanced user skills are required. A deeper and more accurate understanding of the opportunities and risks of AI will only emerge through active experimentation and methodological integration into research practices. This will, in turn, allow for new and perhaps more fruitful perspectives on theoretical problems in the philosophy of mind, as well as practical problems in the ethics and politics of AI.
Keywords: AI for Humanities, Epistemology, Epistemology of Algorithms, Ethics of AI, Philosophical Methodology, Philosophical Research, Philosophy of AI, Philosophy of Computer Science, Philosophy of Mind, Politics of AI

Title: TEDI for Precison Oncology
Abstract:
Cancer management will increasingly rely on stratified and personalized therapies based on the characterization of molecular signatures that are predictive of individual responses to treatments. However, while promising this field is still rudimentary owing to a paucity of validated biomarkers. We believe that we can contribute to filling this gap by exploiting the information yielded by transposable elements (TEs), a prominent yet largely untapped product of genomic analyses. TEs, some 4.5 million of which can be readily identified in the human genome, contribute more than 50% of our DNA hence are the repository of a major part of our genetic heritage. But so far this information has been left essentially unexploited because the high repetitiveness of TE-derived sequences very significantly complicates their analysis. The use of improved DNA and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) methodology combined with in-house optimized analytical pipelines has allowed us to reveal that the transposcriptome, or TE-derived transcriptome, provides a high-density barcode for cell identity, differentiation stage and activation status. We recently applied this know-how to oncology, and taking colorectal cancer as a paradigm obtained the proof-of-principle that TE-based biomarkers (TEBBs) can serve to stage tumors, evaluate their clinical prognosis, predict their response to particular drugs, and point to novel therapeutic avenues. 
Based on these premises, the present proposal will test the potential of TE-derived information (TEDI) to i) provide a molecular sub-categorization of tumors to complement their clinical staging; ii) identify the source of a tumor of unknown origin; iii) generate biomarkers predictive of the response of tumors to specific treatments; iv) suggest new pharmacological targets for treating tumors; and v) uncover neo-antigens for cancer immunotherapy.
Using a wide range of methodologies, including genomics, proteomics, immuno-peptidomics, molecular biology, bioinformatics, machine learning and artificial intelligence, this project will be articulated around the following specific aims:
1.Further develop TEDI-targeting methodology.
2.Define TEDI signatures and identify diagnostic and prognostic TEBBs for many cancers.
3.Apply this methodology to reveal the source of metastases of unknown origin.
4.Seek disease-specific TEBBs in liquid biopsies.
5.Delineate TEBBs predictive of the drug sensitivity of cancer cells.
6.Unveil TE-driven targets that could serve for developing anti-cancer drugs.
7.Identify TE-derived tumor-specific antigens that can be targeted by immunotherapy.
Keywords: biomarkers, cancer, genomics, transposable elements

Title: Is More Always Better? The Future of Climate Change Science
Abstract:
Climate science and climate modelling are central to understanding and addressing the climate challenge. On a global level, they have been highly successful: attribution claims about the anthropogenic cause of global warming or claims about global long-term trends for climate variables such as temperature are extremely robust. However, essential regional projections for certain climate variables remain highly uncertain because of fundamental inadequacies and biases in the models. At the same time, in the face of the increasingly devastating impacts of climate change, there is a pressing need for climate change information at the regional and local scales, particularly in view of adaptation. Accordingly, a strong push exists to develop ever more complex, higher resolution climate models, exploiting ever-increasing computational power and ever more sophisticated data-driven machine learning tools. However, this ‘More is Better’ (MIB) strategy raises fundamental epistemic questions: How far can high-resolution modelling and data-driven techniques be pushed? How can their uncertainties be properly handled? And which types of information and models are most relevant for addressing the climate challenge? By addressing these issues, this project aims to provide a systematic picture of the epistemic foundations of climate science and climate modelling, including their value-laden and normative dimensions. 

To this aim, the project is structured into two main parts, involving a senior scientific collaborator (Part A and Part B) and a PhD student (Part B). Part A will articulate the MIB strategy's fundamental epistemic strengths and weaknesses in three main steps (A1-A3), taking state-of-the-art climate modelling initiatives implementing the MIB strategy as study cases. In the first step, the various purposes of the MIB strategy (such as understanding or decision-making relevance) will be disentangled, and their corresponding epistemic requirements and challenges will be identified (A1). The project will then address the extent to which these goals can be achieved, given the nature of the complex non-linear systems involved (A2) and the opacity of the deployed machine learning tools (A3).

Part B will show how every implementation of the MIB strategy is entangled with specific value-laden and normative dimensions. In the first step (B1), we will articulate these dimensions in detail and show how the planetary ambitions of the MIB strategy in climate modelling raise new challenges for the management of values in science. In a second step (B2), Part B will examine to what extent the novel approach to climate change information in terms of physical climate storylines can improve the integration of value-laden and normative dimensions while counteracting some of the epistemic issues of the MIB strategy.

In light of the climate challenge, there is an urgent need to reshape the relationship between climate science and society, that is, to reshape The Future of Climate Change Science.
Keywords: climate change, climate modeling, computer simulation, instabilities, machine learning, modeling, policy relevance, uncertainties, understanding, value management, values and science, values in science

Title: Development of an AI-enabled robotic solution to predict the most effective front-line technique and assist the operator in performing mechanical thrombectomy for the endovascular treatment of acute ischemic stroke
Abstract:
Stroke is the leading cause of disability worldwide and the third leading cause of death. According to the World Health Organization, around 15 million people worldwide suffer a stroke each year. In the majority of cases, stroke is caused by a blood clot blocking a cerebral blood vessel, reducing the blood supply to an area of the brain. This area gradually dies off, resulting in the loss of associated neurological functions, leaving the patient unable to speak, understand, or move a part of their body. The longer the occlusion, the more the patient's neurological functions and survival are affected. However, there is a time window during which restoring blood flow downstream of the occlusion site could save a certain number of neurons and restore their function. Rapid reopening of the vessel could significantly reduce the risk of brain death and restore the neurological function. The advent of mechanical thrombectomy (MTB) represented a breakthrough in the treatment of acute ischemic stroke (AIS). MTB involves the mechanical removal of the clot occluding the cerebral artery and is considered effective in a relatively high number of patients (80-90%), but with very variable delays. The reopening time is related to the number of MTB attempts made by the operator to retrieve the clot. Nowadays, a number of MTB techniques are available and depend on several factors that are unfortunately unavailable at the time of patient admission, such as clot consistency and extension.
In our previous work, we investigated if information about the clot could be inferred using a robotic device equipped with a force sensor.  We measured the forces exerted on the micro guidewire during the penetration of the clot (i.e., the first phase of MTB) and we found that clot consistency and location could be obtained with this technique. Our goal is to extend this approach and develop robotic strategies that not only allow the identification of the clot characteristics, but also provide guidance for the operator on the most effective choice of MTB technique to retrieve the clot from the occluded vessel.
We envision the following two-fold approach. 1) Development of robot-assisted approaches for navigation based on merging imaging and force sensor information, including teleoperation solutions of haptic guidance and shared control between the robot and human. 2) Prediction of MTB technique using artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms. To achieve this aim, we will use in vitro acquisitions to train and assess the predictive value of an AI solution that would provide the operator with the best technique, based on the information acquired by the robotic device during clot penetration. 
Finally, we plan to conduct a preliminary animal study to evaluate the efficacy and the safety of our robotic solution. Implemented in a clinical setting, this approach could improve the endovascular treatment of stroke given that it will provide the operator with the adequate MTB solution and assistance in removing the clot, based on information unavailable until now.
Keywords: AI, Human Robot Interaction, Interventional Neuroradiology, Ischemic stroke, Mechanical Thrombectomy, Robotic assisted endovascular treatment, Robotics, clot extraction, endovascular

Title: Encoding Multiple Physical Intelligences into Self-Assembled Micromachines
Abstract: Artificial intelligence enables robotic machines to autonomously adapt to their surroundings and perform complex tasks. Unlike large robots, micro- and nanorobots cannot host bulky computational units to generate computational intelligence. The intelligence of small-scale robots, including sensing, control and adaptation, can only stem from their physical bodies and is known as physical intelligence. Developing and evolving physical intelligence in micro- and nanomachines will significantly advance the intelligentization of these devices. Despite growing efforts in this field, encoding diverse physical intelligence into one small-scale machine is still essentially unexplored. The main challenge is the lack of suitable strategies for combining incompatible functional agents and embedding different response mechanisms in one device. The overall objective of the project is to address this challenging question in microrobotics. I will develop a directed self-assembly strategy to construct micromachines with various physical intelligences that can effectively perceive and adapt to a changeable microenvironment. The expected output of the proposed project will address fundamental questions in robotics as well as advance the development of intelligent microrobots for diverse applications: (1) Encoding multiple physical intelligences into one micromachine will enable us to partially answer one fundamental question in robotics: “how to increase the intelligence of small-scale robots?. (2) In turn, by addressing this question, we can develop “conceptual intelligent micromachines” that integrate diverse modular systems to perceive and process information as well as to generate feedback. (3) Moreover, the project is interdisciplinary thus will generate impact on diverse research fields spanning from materials science, biomedical engineering to synthetic biology.
Keywords: microrobotics, nanocapsules, physical intelligence, self-assembly, supraparticles

Title: Unleashing the full potential of high-performance Cherenkov telescopes with fully-digital solid-state sensors camera
Abstract:
This project aims at establishing the small-size single mirror telescopes (SST-1M) as relevant actors among imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes and anchor them in the multi-messenger instruments network.
To do so, we propose to consolidate the SST-1Ms design and operation in view of joining a scientifically relevant observatory. 
With a strong Swiss lead in its development, these telescopes were initially designed for the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory. Despite being ultimately not selected for the array, the two prototype telescopes have since demonstrated exceptional performance. Operated at the Ondrejov Astronomical Observatory under less than ideal conditions, they have still managed to achieve impressive results.
The Crab can be detected with 5 sigma significance in less than 3 hours for monoscopic observations and 2hours for stereoscopic. It observed its first extra-galactic blazars, 1ES1959+650 and more recently, it measured a hardening of the MRK421 spectrum for energies above 2 TeV and consequently produced an Astronomers' Telegram.

These results have encouraged the pursuit of relocating them to a more suitable observation site.
The Swiss, Czech and Polish SST-1M collaboration is in advanced discussion with the Hanle Observatory in India which host the Major Atmospheric Cerenkov Experiment Telescope (MACE), a 21~m Cherenkov telescope.
In parallel, the SST-1M collaboration is studying the added value when part of the future The Southern Wide-field Gamma-ray Observatory (SWGO). Eventually, both locations offer the advantages of high altitude and the opportunity for the SST-1M system to contribute within a larger observatory framework.

The interdisciplinary project is structured around three main goals, each addressed in its own work package:
1) Mechanics upgrade and telescope protection for long term operations: The project seeks to refine the mechanical design and environmental control systems of the telescopes to adapt to high-altitude conditions, including heating, cooling, and protection when not in use. This effort will be coordinated by M.E.R. M. Heller at UniGe with support of the  mechanics group department.
2) Optimisation of stereo trigger: To improve noise rejection and reduce the energy threshold, offering larger overlap in energy with larger telescopes, we plan to enhance the telescope's trigger logic with advanced algorithms, including clustering and artificial intelligence. Prof. Andres Upegui from HEPIA will lead the work package and collaborate with M. Heller from UniGe.
3) SST-1M joins the multi-messenger era: In order to be part of the multi-messenger astrophysics effort, a bi-directional alert system will be developed: the SST-1M will connect to standard multi-messenger alert systems and a real-time analysis will be implemented.  In parallel, the optimisation of the location of SST-1M and potential future telescopes with respect to the existing MACE telescopes will be done via differential programming. Eventually, the performance of such an array for the study of extended sources will be performed. These tasks will be supervised by M. Heller and Prof. T. Montaruli at UniGe.

This initiative requests funding for two postdocs and two engineers to ensure the SST-1M telescopes can perform optimally at a prime observation site, thereby contributing significant scientific data. This effort builds on Switzerland's significant investment in constructing these telescopes and aims to fully realise their scientific potential.

Title: Music across borders: Harnessing AI to translate music for singability and accessibility
Abstract:
As early as 2010, translation studies experienced a “technological turn” (Cronin 2010: 1), fostered by the new large-scale availability of technology, the web, and Statistical Machine Translation (SMT). In 2016, Neural Machine Translation (NMT), first launched by Google Translate, significantly enhanced the quality of machine translation (MT) outputs (Klimova, Pikhart, Delorme Benites, Lehr and Sanchez-Stockhammer 2023: 664), giving way to a “new era” in translation studies (Hongtao 2023: 466). In 2022 further advances in artificial intelligence (AI), natural language processing (NLP) and large language models (LLM) led to the release of ChatGpT (2022), the user-friendly AI chatbot by OpenAI; the wider accessibility of Generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGpT fostered a new revolution in the translation field (Hongtao 2023). Given these remarkable technological advances, studies investigating the potential of technology in creative areas of translation that were previously considered the exclusive domain of human translators, such as literary translation, are starting to flourish (e.g. Hadley et. al 2022; Youdale 2022; Rothwell, Way and Youdale 2023); the possible economic benefits of MT in these areas of translation are also being recognised (Hadley 2023). In this context, GenAI and ChatGpT are attracting particular interest (Rothwell, Way and Youdale 2023: 9), given the possibility of tailoring their translation outcomes via prompt engineering (e.g. He. 2024; Gu 2023; Gao, Wang and Hou 2023, etc). 
Until recently translation technology has not been considered particularly relevant for the highly creative processes of music translation. Within the new-born subfield of translation studies named “music and translation studies” (Greenall, Franzon, Kvam, Parianou 2021: 21–22; Redzioch-Korkuz 2024: 66), and specifically, within its sub-domain of “song translation studies”, however, “[r]easons are given to ponder [..] the functionality of AI translations” (Franzon, Redzioch-Korkuz, Gaska 2024: 6). Although not much studied yet due to the novelty of both the field and the technology, AI appears to have good potential to facilitate singable translation of lyrics (Kodura 2024). Additionally, given its already proven capacity to facilitate accessibility for disabled users (e.g. Choi, Lee, Kim, K. Lee, Yoo, S. Lee, and Hong. 2024; Cheng, Huffman, Zhu, Su, Kushalnagar, Wang 2024), AI can be relied upon to facilitate music translation for accessibility purposes. Seeking to contribute to both these contexts, my study explores the potential of Gen AI to assist translators in the multi-disciplinary practice of interlingual and intersemiotic translation of lyrics for performance and hearing-impaired audiences. 
The lack of multidisciplinary expertise on the part of translation or music professionals is a major difficulty in music translation practice and research (Susam-Saraeva 2008: 189; Redzioch-Korkuz 2024: 66); it renders music translation rarely practised and costly (Desblache 2019), but also causes significant shortcomings in research on accessible translations of music, which often come as an afterthought in many contexts (Harrison 2014). Specifically relying on prompt engineering and interdisciplinary research and methodologies to customise ChatGpT’s output, my project will first investigate how AI can help translators who are non-music experts understand the constraints of singability and produce singable translations of lyrics; after adjusting musical criteria for singable translation (Low 2017; Apter and Herman 2016) to work as intersemiotic translation criteria that can maximise music perception by hearing impaired audiences (e.g. Choi, Jeon, Lee, Noh, and Hong 2024; Holmes 2017), I will explore how AI can assist translators in understanding the requirements for music accessibility and in creating accessible translations of music. The object of my research is vocal-pop music for choir; in my experiments and evaluations, I rely on “participant-oriented” research methodologies (Saldhana 2014) and the collaboration of music experts, translation professionals and relevant audiences (e.g. musicians, translators, hearing-impaired audiences and the general public). Pre-agreed collaborations with award-winning Italian Choir Coro Anthem, and Zürich Choir Ars Cantata are in place for this project.
Keywords: Creativity, GenAI and prompt engineering, Intersemiotic translation, Music accessibility, Song Translation

Title: Development and Application of Rapid Conventional and Unconventional Quantitative Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Abstract:
The magnetic resonance (MR) signal can be sensitized to a large variety of tissue parameters, as reflected by a vast range of dedicated clinical MR pulse sequences designed to generate contrast even for very subtle tissue alterations with high specificity and sensitivity. Such MR images can be acquired reasonably fast, but their contrast is a non-trivial weighting of various intrinsic and extrinsic parameters and thus not a direct measure for a specific tissue property. As a result, pathological alterations are not identified from a measurable, objective change in tissue properties but rely on a subjective reading of contrast differences on a physically meaningless scale that is affected not only by various random factors but also by instrumentation. Quantification of the MR signal in terms of the underlying biochemical and biophysical tissue parameters is thus generally thought to be the key to MR methodology to push conventional MRI beyond its current limits. It is thus not surprising that the promise of MRI in the tradition of scientific instrumentation has attracted considerable interest in the MR scientific community ever since. Especially, the continuous improvement and progress in scanner hardware and reliability has not only facilitated quantification, but also stimulated the development of a wide variety of methods for the extraction different biophysical and biochemical parameters. Noteworthy, although quantitative MRI dates back to the early 1970s, research and development is not only ongoing but performed world-wide with increased interest and effort.

Unfortunately, MR-based tissue quantification is typically a very time-consuming process and can be biased by numerous factors. It is thus not surprising that over the years and even for the most fundamental MR tissue parameters, such as tissue relaxation, a whole ‘buffet’ of MR methods have been proposed to tackle the ‘reliable quantification in reasonable time’ problem for successful translation and application in the clinics. Only recently, the extraction of MR tissue quantities has become an even more important paramount goal since artificial intelligence and machine learning has entered the field of MRI relying on the availability of large amounts of standardized and comparable, such as quantitative, MRI data. 

We have more than a decade of experience in the development and translation of new quantitative MRI methods to the clinical setting. Recent developments, such as spiral readouts and configuration-based imaging methods have shown good prospects and high potential towards a ‘reliable quantification in reasonable time’ for a wide range of tissue parameters. In this research proposal, we further elaborate and extend our recent methodological achievements in a consequent and innovative manner to develop reliable tissue biomarkers for the detection of widespread pathophysiologic processes, as well as subtle and diffuse tissue alterations with high specificity and sensitivity.

Title: Candidate-Based Segmentation Methods for Biomedical Image Processing
Abstract:
In this research plan, we propose to address three open problems of current 
state-of-the-art methods for biomedical image segmentation. (1) We propose to 
increase the expressiveness of multicut- and candidate-based methods for image 
segmentation by generalizing both approaches into a versatile framework, which 
we call the candidate multicut (CMC). (2) We propose to incorporate biological 
priors in a principled way into segmentation methods with global objectives, in 
particular, into the CMC. For that, we aim to design an interpretation layer, 
which is more suitable to express priors than a model operating on supervoxels 
alone. (3) We propose a sparse interactive learning framework based on 
structured support vector machines, such that partial ground truth annotations 
can be used for learning. Together with a confidence measure for inference 
decisions, this framework has the potential to be used for interactive training 
of model parameters, which is particularly useful for large datasets.

We present our proposal in the context of two challenging biomedical image 
processing problems: the reconstruction of the 3D shape of neurons from electron 
microscopy images and the 2D segmentation of cells in light microscopy images.
Keywords: Biomedical Image Processing, Connectomics, Electron Microscopy Image Segmentation, Light Microscopy Image Segmentation, Neural Image Segmentation, Neural Reconstruction

Title: Hypermedia Communities of People and Autonomous Agents
Abstract: The HyperAgents project aims to enable the deployment of world-wide hybrid communities of people and autonomous agents on the Web. For this purpose, HyperAgents defines a new class of multi-agent systems (MAS) that use hypermedia as a general mechanism for uniform interaction such that they are: (i) aligned with the Web architecture to inherit the properties of the Web as a world-wide, open, and long-lived system, and (ii) transparent and accountable to support acceptance by people. We refer to this new envisioned class of Web-based MAS as Hypermedia MAS. The HyperAgents project proposes: (1) to define an architectural style for Hypermedia MAS that induces the above-mentioned properties, (2) to define declarative languages and mechanisms for specifying, enacting, and regulating interactions among people and autonomous agents in Hypermedia MAS, (3) to develop an open-source software infrastructure for Hypermedia MAS that enables the deployment of hybrid communities on the Web, and (4) to demonstrate the deployment of prototypical hybrid communities in two application areas: (i) Industry 4.0 and (ii) tackling online disinformation. To undertake this investigation, the project consortium brings together internationally recognized researchers actively contributing to research on autonomous agents and MAS, the Web architecture, Semantic Web, and to the standardization of the Web. Being able to harness the collective power of Web-scale hybrid communities and to focus it on specific problems would have extensive implications in a broad range of domains: for manufacturers, it could enable distributed intelligent manufacturing at global scale; for citizens, it could enable access to transparent and trustworthy online information. We expect that the work conducted in this project will break new ground in AI and Web research and that its applications will cut across society.

Title: Reverse engineering of swarming dynamics
Abstract:
Swarming behavior is ubiquitous in nature. The collective response of groups of bacteria, insects, fish, etc allows their communities to achieve tasks far beyond the capability of the single individual. Such self-organized behaviors exhibited by social animals are found to rely on simple local interaction rules rather than on a centralized or global knowledge. This "swarm intelligence" has been subject of research in many fields, from mathematics and physics to robotics, due to its appealing properties of robustness, distributedness, scalability and flexibility.

Experimental studies tried to infer interaction rules, mainly via video tracking techniques, while theoretical studies focused on handcrafting these rules to reproduce patterns observed in nature. Such bottom-up approach cannot establish whether a given observed collective behavior is optimal nor it can provide a direct link to its function.

In this context, we wish to develop automatic design algorithms for the reverse engineering of collective behavior to identify local rules that optimally allow to achieve a specified objective (energetic efficiency, foraging, defense against predation, etc). In a novel attempt to understand how the flow environment affects the emergence of collective behavior, we will apply the developed algorithms to fluid dynamic simulations accounting for flow mediated interactions between flying or swimming agents. The ultimate goal is to transfer the behavioral and fluid mechanics knowledge gained to obtain a swarm of flapping micro aerial vehicles (RobotBees).

The combined use of theoretical, computational and robotic investigations is a unique feature of this proposal. By applying automatic design algorithms to the computational study of swimming and flying swarms, we hope to get new insight into how and why schools or flocks arrange in certain configurations. Furthermore, the reverse engineering of behaviors of multiple flying robotic devices, if successful, will pave the way to a number of exciting applications. 

The understanding of swarming dynamics and mechanisms is certainly a challenging problem, but it carries the promise of being beneficial in a wide range of engineering applications, from collaborating underwater devices and swarms of unmanned air vehicles to energy harnessing applications.

Title: Reliable Machine Learning for Networked Control (RL4NetC)
Abstract:
Safe and efficient operation of large-scale Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs) such as automated transportation systems and the continent-wide electricity grid rely on the delicate orchestration of massive sensing, actuation, and communication carried out by many interacting agents.  A significant complication is that agents in CPSs are often myopic. That is, they can only interact with their immediate surroundings. This limitation is typically due to geographical distance, privacy requirements, or cyberattacks that partly disable the communication network. Under such constraints, it is very difficult — oftentimes impossible — to ensure fail-safe and optimal operation of large-scale CPSs.

The field of Machine Learning (ML) yields powerful tools helping agents learn how to make sense of and interact with complex environments optimally. The success of ML and universal function approximators such as Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) is famed in fields such as computer vision, recommendation systems, and speech recognition. The opportunities that ML offers for interacting with large-scale dynamical systems while reliably complying with strict safety requirements are much less understood.

In the RL4NetC project, we take on crucial challenges hampering the deployment of ML-based algorithms and architectures in large-scale CPSs. We specifically aim to address the following research questions. (i) How can we formally certify the safety and numerical reliability of ML-based control architectures, such as distributed control policies parametrized through DNNs? (ii) Well-established and widely used control paradigms for safety-critical CPSs, such as Model Predictive Control (MPC), may lead to poor performance in large-scale applications due to the propagation of uncertainties. How do we exploit ML to improve the global performance in the face of uncertainty? (iii) Large-scale applications are affected by the curse of dimensionality. How do we scale up our solutions to CPSs made up of hundreds of coupled subsystems?

The RL4NetC project tackles the challenges (i)-(iii) in a principled and mathematically rigorous manner. We plan to establish innovative connections between keystone paradigms in control theory for large-scale systems — such as Port-Hamiltonian (PH) system theory and MPC — and fundamental tools of ML — such as DNNs, neural Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs), and regret minimization in Reinforcement Learning (RL). By explaining how large networks of physical systems behave when they are interfaced to ML algorithms, we can achieve the level of performance, dependability, and scalability that is absolutely necessary for real-world CPSs. In the near future, our societies will rely on increasingly complex and interacting infrastructures — making them safer and more sustainable is a worthy endeavor towards scientific progress and technological innovation.
Keywords: data-driven control, distributed control, machine learning for control, model predictive control

Title: Integrating urban form and sociotechnical potentials of decentralised energy supply for sustainable urban development
Abstract:
Both Switzerland and the United Kingdom (UK) have ambitious goals for increasing their use of renewable energy and reducing CO2 emissions. In particular, the Swiss Energy Strategy 2050 aims at phasing out of nuclear energy by 2035 and a possible 50-80% reduction in CO2 emission by 2050. Similarly, the UK aims at obtaining 15% of its energy consumption from renewable resources by 2020, as well cut its CO2 emissions in 2050, from the present value, by 80%. These aims can only be reached through a great increase in the production of renewable energy. One way to do so is building large solar farms in rural areas. Another, and complementary, way is to increase the on-site solar-energy production in urban/rural areas, an idea that forms a major part in the concept of decentralized energy supply. 

The term ‘decentralised energy supply’ means that the energy is produced close to, or at, the site where the energy is used. This is in contrast with centralised energy supply where the energy is normally produced by large power plants and transported through a network or grid to the consumers. The benefits of a decentralised energy system include reduced (i) dependency on fossil fuels, (ii) CO2 emissions, and (iii) energy costs and risks of peaks in energy prices, as well as (iv) greater energy security, partly through better balance between demand and supply. An additional benefit is that decentralised energy is generally from renewable resources, in particular solar energy through photovoltaics (PVs) for electricity production. 

Decentralising of the urban energy supply, particularly through the use of PVs, requires a comprehensive assessment of their sociotechnical and techno-economic co-evolution. The project therefore aims not only (a) to improve and refine our knowledge of the resource and technical PV potential for Switzerland and the UK, with application to other areas (e.g., Africa), but also (b) to analyse how solar energy technologies and associated social acceptance and affordability evolve together, and (c) how their co-evolution may affect sustainable urban development and energy policies. More specifically, the project aims at exploring (i) the effects of physical urban forms, particularly urban density and the shapes of rooftops, at national scale on the efficiency of energy production through PVs, and to connect urban forms to (ii) different sociotechnical aspects of decentralised electricity production and (iii) and to the associated socio-economic parameters (costs, acceptance, affordability, etc.), as well as (iv) to the energy policies of the local energy production. The results will be analysed within the framework of the projected climate scenarios for 2035 and 2050.

In this project a comprehensive assessment and comparison of the physical and sociotechnical aspects of decentralisation PV-produced electricity supply for a sustainable urban development for both Switzerland and the UK at national scale will be explored. When refined, some of the results should be transferable to other areas, with different geographic and cultural frameworks, such as Africa which has a very high irradiation and the potential of producing highly decentralised PV electricity, at a comparatively low cost, in virtually every part of the continent. Currently, the share of people without access to electricity in Sub-Saharan Africa, however, is on the increase (from 587.1 million in 2008 to estimated 968.3 million in 2030). One aim of the project is thus to transfer the results from the detailed study of the decentralised PV potential in Switzerland and the UK to developing areas such as in Africa, which are highly favourable in terms of solar-energy potential. 

The main technical methods for analysing the PV electricity potential in this project are as follows: (1) Entropy analysis of regional urban density, (2) GIS spatial analysis for urban energy planning (shapes of buildings and rooftops), (3) statistical methods for analysing socio-economic potential, (technology and electricity costs, including subsides), as well as regulations, policy implementations, and CO2 emissions, (4) machine-learning techniques together with GIS for modelling the potentials of PV electricity production, and (5) clustering methods to identify the sustainable development patterns as regards decentralised electricity production from urban to suburb and to rural areas.
Keywords: Decentralised electricity production, Solar energy, Urban development, Urban form, Urban sustainability

Title: Improving Alzheimer’s disease detection with GRACE (Graph-theory Reinforced for Ameliorating Clustering and Estimation)
Abstract: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder affecting 50 million people worldwide and is expected to affect 152 million by 2050. In Switzerland, 150,000 people (315,400 by 2050) are affected by AD or another form of dementia. AD patients’ typical life expectancy following diagnosis is three to nine years. Central to disease management and timely treatment of AD is the early and accurate identification of AD. Changes in brain networks precede AD symptoms and are, therefore, important biomarkers for early AD detection. Critical to detecting brain network topology and patterns related to AD is graph theory. A chief way to model brain networks via graph theory is to use a weighted graph whose nodes represent brain regions and weights on edges delineate connectivity strengths between nodes. Nevertheless, existing algorithmic graph theory devices for brain network-based AD detection are insufficient or ineffective. For example, clustering algorithms aimed at discovering brain modularities or network communities confront difficulties due to their sensitivity to parameters, suboptimal clustering (irreversible merging) and difficulty in interpretation. In parallel, graph measures used for AD studies are facing obstacles. For example, thresholding, a common practice for defining brain graphs, omits weaker but potentially biologically relevant edges. Graph measures defined on such unweighted graphs fail to capture crucial connectivity strengths. Graph measures defined on weighted graphs are derived from structural graph theory and may not fully reflect neurobiological processes and do not account for small-world properties of brain networks. Here, to address these issues and improve AD biomarker identification and disease prediction, I propose a programme consisting of four work packages (WPs), uniting algorithmic graph theory, machine learning, neuroscience, and neuroimaging. The first WP develops a new optimal deterministic clustering algorithm which will outperform current methods in terms of optimality, removing the need for manual parameter tuning, and better interpretability. In the second WP, we develop new neurobiology-informed graph measures that better depict underlying neurological processes as AD progresses and account for the small-world properties of the brain network. In the third WP, employing these new algorithms and measures, we discover disease-specific edges, hubs, and subgraphs using neuroimaging data. To evaluate the neuroscientific relevance of the findings, we use these network features to predict AD status, AD-related cognitive scores, and longitudinal progression using machine learning. To evaluate the reproducibility and generalisability of the methods, we first perform cross-validation using data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). We then further test and validate the findings in two independent imaging datasets from the Vrije Universiteit Brussel. The last WP builds an analytical toolbox for brain network identification, clustering, and network-based outcome prediction. Taken together, the WPs may be extended to the study of other neurodegenerative diseases, providing a generalisable approach to understanding brain network (dys)function in health and disease. To summarise, our past work in brain connectivity studies, brain disease prediction, biomarker and machine learning method development, and our preliminary findings on AD prediction using imaging biomarkers and brain networks have laid an encouraging foundation for executing the WPs of this proposal. Supported by this grant, we are committed to making further methodological and neuroscientific contributions to the early, timely and accurate detection of AD.
Keywords: Algorithmic graph theory, Alzheimer's disease, Brain network, Disease prediction, Graph theory, Machine learning, Network biomarkers

Title: An AGE clock for RESIlience in SweaT- AGE RESIST
Abstract: Aging is defined as the “progressive loss of physiological integrity, leading to impaired function and increased vulnerability to death”. The vulnerability is increased by the loss of resilience and stress resistance. Different biomarkers/tests, such as the pan-mammalian epigenetic clock, the inflammatory aging clock (iAge), and the timed walking test, have been developed and are applied within the R&D environment of aging. However, these biomarkers/tests cover single biomarker types only, are laborious, and mainly depend on specialized laboratories. A diagnostic tool integrating several types of biomarkers for aging in parallel, continuous, and real life is still lacking for convenient application in everyday life. In this cutting-edge project, an interdisciplinary consortium of renowned researchers from world-leading academic institutions have teamed up to develop the first wearable sweat-sensing platform to determine the biological age of resilience non-invasively, continuously, and lab-independently. Building on the successful research work from Aging, Wearable Sweat Sensing, Physiology, and Translational Medicine, a test is developed to determine if a person is physiologically resilient regarding the biological age. The AGE RESIST project is planned as follows: (i) Explore novel sweat-based molecular biomarkers to build up an age clock of resilience using machine learning algorithms, (ii) prospectively validate the biomarkers, (iii) implement the biomarkers into a cutting-edge wearable sweat analyzing platform, and (iv) a proof-of-concept study is conducted to demonstrate the feasibility to apply the sensing platform directly on humans. This project is highly innovative and promising as it (I) translates the knowledge gained from basic aging research over many years into a clinically applicable test, (II) determines the biological age of resilience from sweat, which is a completely novel approach, (III) fosters non-invasive, continuous, and lab-independent health monitoring by advancing the field of clinical wearable sweat analysis, (IV) once successfully validated, provides great potential for clinical medicine to guide surgical/therapeutic indication and rehabilitation especially in older and frail patients, and (V) brings world-leading and international researchers from different academic fields into close discussion and collaboration with the public, patients, physicians, and regulatory to develop a clinically meaningful solution.

Title: Image data validation for AI systems
Abstract:
Deep learning has lead to huge advances in longstanding problems of computer
vision, natural language processing, signal processing and robotics. In the near
future, deep learning will allow the automation of many critical tasks like
medical pathology detection, medical diagnosis, or autonomous driving. However,
deep networks are known to provide confident but wrong predictions when they
process images that do not belong to the training distribution. Given that
acquisition devices, data transmission systems, human operators, and software
can all fail in unexpected ways and lead to corrupted images, a deep network
might produce inaccurate results, if not, dangerously misleading ones, in these
critical tasks.

This project will focus its research efforts in developing a data validation
method that can identify whether an input image can be safely processed by a
deep network or not.

The project is inspired on our preliminary work on deep data
validation, where we designed a simple architecture that
reaches state-of-the-art performance. However, data validation is a challenging
problem, and the capacities of our method are still very limited for practical
purposes. As such, the current project has two goals. The first is to build a
strong data validation system that reaches a performance suitable for real-world
applications. The second is to incorporate temporal consistency into the
validation to deal with sequences of images.

To do so, our project proposes (i) to explore deep learning architectures that
exploit the multiscale nature of images in order to detect a large range of
potential issues; (ii) to explore the performance of methods for one-class
classification and integrate them into our system; and (iii) to devise an
architecture inspired on recurrent neural networks that can analyze sequences,
thus enabling us to incorporate time consistency to the validation process.

By the end of the project, we will have developed a comprehensive methodology on
data validation that will have a potential impact not only in the research
community, but also in a large number of industries that will be able to build
more robust AI systems. We will disseminate our results through publications,
conferences, tutorials and websites.
Keywords: anomaly detection, data validation, deep learning, image processing, machine learning, out-of-distribution detection, outlier detection

Title: In-Situ Atomic-Scale Monitoring of Interface Deterioration in All-Solid-State Batteries
Abstract:
All-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) are considered a promising solution to the safety issues and energy density limitations of conventional Li-ion batteries containing combustible liquid electrolytes. However, the Achilles' heel of ASSBs is their long charging times, attributed to the high internal resistance for Li-ion transfer across the solid electrolyte/electrode interfaces. The proposed research project aims at deepening the understanding of Li-ion transport in rechargeable ASSBs during realistic battery operation. The project has two main goals. First, it aims at unequivocally identifying the processes responsible for impedance enhancement and performance degradation in working solid-state battery devices with increasing charge/discharge cycles. This project therefore focuses on identifying the sources of resistance and monitoring the mechanical and/or chemical processes at these locations. This information will allow us to elucidate the electrochemical degradation mechanisms of ASSBs and provide important guidance to design more efficient and robust batteries. Second, in addition to improving battery performance, this project aims to contribute to the development of the in-situ electrochemical electron microscopy capabilities for energy storage devices at Empa. For this, a state-of-the-art probe aberration corrected scanning transmission electron microscope (STEM) and various in-situ holders with in-situ electrochemical, electrical biasing and heating capabilities are available at the Electron Microscopy Center of Empa. Besides, as part of the project, additional air-free transfer holders will be purchased to prevent exposure of the microbatteries to air and moisture.
The research objectives will be achieved by using a variety of cutting-edge operando imaging and spectroscopy STEM techniques. The work will be carried out by a 4-year doctoral student and a 2-year postdoctoral researcher (which will be co-financed by SNSF and Empa) working in close collaboration.
The project goals will be achieved by addressing four work packages (WPs):
WP 1: Functional microbatteries will be optimized and tested on MEMS-chip sample supports for in-situ electrochemistry studies in the S/TEM.
WP 2: The electric potential distribution across working devices will be visualized with high temporal and spatial resolutions to characterize the solid electrolyte/electrode interfaces. This will be made possible by differential phase contrast (DPC-)STEM and 4D-STEM, which will be optimized for low beam currents to ensure the integrity of the beam-sensitive lithium-ion battery materials. 
WP 3: Time-resolved operando electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) data will be acquired to (i) visualize the Li-ion dynamics and (ii) elucidate the electrochemical/chemical degradation mechanisms of ASSBs. For this, the spectral data sets will be analyzed by applying advanced machine learning algorithms. 
WP 4: In this last WP, the methodologies developed in the previous WPs will be combined in an all-inclusive TEM platform to get an improved understanding of how, where and when degradation mechanisms and battery failure occur.
Finally, this project shall contribute both to the scientific advancement in the field of energy storage and to the development of the in-situ electrochemical electron microscopy capabilities at Empa. Since other research groups in Switzerland will be able to use and benefit from them, this proposal will enable Swiss researchers to stay at the forefront of the current worldwide trend towards high-resolution observations of dynamic electrochemical reactions in electron microscopy.
Keywords: All-solid-state-batteries, Dynamic events, Electron energy-loss spectroscopy, In-situ electrochemical testing, Interfaces, Li-ion transfer, Scanning transmission electron microscopy

Title: The Evolutionary Interplay of Cooperation and Communication in Canids
Abstract: Why and how have humans evolved a communication system so fundamentally different from anything in the animal world, including great apes? While the gap between human and ape intelligence has turned out to be smaller than originally thought, the gap between their communication systems has remained considerable. It has therefore become increasingly clear that human language requires more than just high intelligence. One hypothesis is that language has originated from a unique juxtaposition of intelligence and hyper-cooperation. Although all higher primates cooperate, humans are undisputedly and fundamentally more cooperative in virtually every aspect of life. Human hyper-cooperation is especially evident when raising offspring, a cooperative breeding system that is fairly common in birds and some mammals, but mostly absent in non-human primates. To investigate the interplay between cognition, cooperation and communication, we therefore propose a research programme on a highly intelligent and highly cooperative mammal -  wolves - which are cooperative breeders like humans. We will carry out our studies within an ecologically valid framework, that is, to study communication when cooperation is most necessary, i.e., when finding food, avoiding danger and raising offspring. In doing so, we will use new technology and leverage progress in machine learning to monitor the behaviour and communication of naturally interacting wolves and combine these data with targeted cooperation experiments. Conceptually, we will treat cooperation as a process that requires initiation, maintenance and termination. We will also consider that, in real-life situations, the relative payoff between participants is almost always uneven, in extreme cases even negative for one partner, which generates extra communication challenges. We further want to understand the role of individual differences and relationship qualities. We will collect the same data from domestic dogs because their cognitive capacities are comparable to wolves, but they are not considered cooperative breeders, something they have lost during 30,000 years of artificial selection due to domestication. Our longterm goal is to utilise these new empirical data to develop a better-informed evolutionary theory about the role of cooperation during the transition from animal communication to human language.

Title: Towards a PREcise DIagnosis in Ciliopathies - PREDICT
Abstract: Ciliopathies are rare Mendelian disorders caused by dysfunction of primary cilia, sensory organelles protruding from the cell surface playing a crucial role in signal transduction during development and cell function. Clinically, ciliopathies can involve most organ systems, displaying substantial phenotypic variability and overlap between ciliopathy disorders. This makes predicting the precise outcome for a given patient particularly difficult, especially for progressive features. This project aims at providing a precise diagnosis to patients, to enable tailored surveillance and treatment, focusing on progressive retinal and renal phenotypes in patients with selected ciliopathies and recurrent causal mutations. PREDICT will rely on large previously collected cohorts of patients with ciliopathies to generate a comprehensive dataset for selected patients, combining detailed phenotypic information with whole genome sequencing and transcriptomic analyses to provide a holistic view for selected individuals. Using this patient-derived information in combination with the extensive publicly available data in databases and the literature, PREDICT will use artificial intelligence to generate predictive models for specific endorgan involvement. These models will be tested in vitro using simple cellular assays based on fibroblasts and/or human urinary epithelial cells which will provide a quantitative measure of ciliary dysfunction. Predictions will further be tested in more complex cellular models based on induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived retinal and renal organoids, as well as in vivo using zebrafish models. Taking advantage of the wealth of biological information available on ciliopathies, in particular concerning protein interaction networks, these validations through functional assays will circumvent the limitation of poor statistical power inherent to rare disorders. Cellular assays will further serve as diagnostic tools for improved classification of ciliopathies, using high-content imaging and transcriptional signatures. Models and algorithms developed in PREDICT may serve as paradigms for other rare Mendelian disorders to improve our ability to provide an accurate prognosis, which is a requirement for precision medicine.
Keywords: Ciliopathies, Zebrafish, artificial intelligence, genomics and transcriptomics, iPSCs, multimodal molecular diagnostics

Title: Deep learning and computational fluid dynamics to improve prediction of coronary events: leveraging data from FAME 2
Abstract:
Background and rationale: Despite significant advances in its treatment and prevention, coronary artery disease (CAD) remains the biggest cause of mortality worldwide. The identification of lesions during invasive coronary angiography (ICA) that will be responsible for a future myocardial infarction (MI) remains challenging. Even with the use of our best anatomical and haemodynamic risk stratifiers, up to 8% of treated patients with CAD still present with coronary events in the ensuing two years. This highlights the need for improved risk stratification of coronary lesions. Two tools that could potentially improve the identification of high-risk CAD are deep learning (DL) and computational fluid mechanics (CFD).

Aims: The study will use data from the Fractional Flow Reserve Versus Angiography in Multivessel Evaluation (FAME) 2 trial, a randomised controlled trial that evaluated if fractional flow reserve (FFR)-guided percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) would be superior to optimal medical therapy (OMT) in patients with stable CAD. We will evaluate if the risk stratification of coronary lesions can be improved using: Objective 1: a DL-based algorithm to interpret ICA images of coronary lesions; Objective 2: 3D models of the coronary arteries and CFD-derived haemodynamic parameters.

Methods: For the proposed work, 567 patients (799 stenoses) who did not undergo revascularisation will be included (OMT group + registry group). The primary endpoints at 2-year follow-up will be (i) MI, (ii) urgent revascularisation (UR), (iii) cardiovascular death, and (iv) a composite of all three. For each patient, ICA at the time of randomisation will be labelled with a customised tablet and stylus using our specialised software, including the identification and segmentation of all major coronary arteries and first-order branches from at least two angiographic projections. All coronary lesions for which FFR was measured as part of FAME 2 will be annotated. Cropped images of lesions (patches, 224x224 pixels) centred around each annotated stenosis will be extracted automatically by the software. Objective 1: DL will be used to classify coronary lesions (patches) as either future culprit (FCL) or non-culprit (NCL) for each study endpoint, using our previously developed DL model (ResNet18). Performance of the network will be measured using four evaluation metrics: (i) classification accuracy; (ii) sensitivity; (iii) specificity; and (iv) F1 score. The predictive capacity of DL will be compared with: (i) diameter stenosis, (ii) area stenosis, (iii) invasively-measured FFR. Objective 2: 3D models of each patient's coronary arteries, generated using our own developed approach, will be used for haemodynamic simulations to derive the following CFD parameters: (i) FFR, (ii) wall shear stress, (iii) helical flow, (iv) topological shear variation index (TSVI). The correlation between these parameters and each endpoint will be assessed. The predictive capacity of CFD parameters will be compared with (i) diameter stenosis, (ii) area stenosis, (iii) invasively-measured FFR, (iv) DL.

Impact: This study will aim to demonstrate that DL and CFD can improve on currently available risk stratification tools, and ultimately lead to a reduction in coronary events in patients with CAD.
Keywords: Computational fluid dynamics, Coronary angiography, Coronary artery disease, Deep learning, Myocardial infarction

Title: The monocyte-to-phagocyte transition during tissue inflammation and immunopathology
Abstract:
Chronic inflammatory diseases are widely held to be mediated through aberrant lymphocyte activation and their invasion into affected tissues. In T cell-driven autoimmune diseases, such as Multiple Sclerosis (MS), Crohn’s disease (CD) and Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) for instance, helper T (Th) cells are widely considered to initiate and orchestrate the inflammatory cascade, which leads to tissue destruction. We propose that the immunopathology observed in these conditions is not directly executed through T cells, but that their instruction of myeloid cells -and in particular monocytes- through cytokines regulates the phagocyte behavior upon tissue invasion. During inflammation, Ly6Chimonocytes are rapidly mobilized from the bone marrow (BM) and recruited into affected tissues. Upon invasion, they develop into tissue macrophages and represent the primary mediators of immunopathology. The mechanisms underpinning the monocyte to tissue phagocyte transition (MTPT) and the cytokine networks involved are being increasingly better understood. What remains however largely unresolved are the mechanisms which govern pathogenic monocyte-derived macrophage (MoMAC) behavior and the effector mechanisms leading to tissue destruction. Using experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) and scurfy as preclinical models of tissue immunopathology initiated by T cells, we will pursue the following aims:
1) Molecular characterization of the MTPT to identify candidate transcriptional regulators and effector mechanisms of MoMACs.
2) Conditional targeting of transcriptional regulators of MTPT and MoMAC pathogenicity licensing.
3) Conditional targeting of MoMAC effector functions in preclinical models of type 1 cytokine-initiated tissue inflammation.
Overall, we propose to systematically map the network of monocyte-derived phagocyte-driven immunopathology across various inflammatory disorders.
Keywords: Immunopathology, T cells, cytokine networks, machine learning, macrophages, mononuclear phagocytes, neuroinflammation, single cell analysis, tissue invasion, transgenic mice

Title: Lymphoid neogenesis in cancer
Abstract:
The tumour microenvironment (TME) contains various stromal and immune cell populations that influence disease progression and response to therapy. In chronically inflamed tissues, infiltrating lymphocytes can form ectopic lymphoid organs termed tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) via the process of lymphoid neogenesis. TLS structurally resemble follicles of lymph nodes and can exert similar functions such as priming of antigen-specific T cells and mounting ectopic germinal centre (GC) reactions. In the TME, TLS development correlates with increased infiltration of adoptive immune cells and improved patient survival in a growing list of solid tumours. Thus, TLS are proposed to be in situ sites of anti-tumour immune response activation.
We recently observed that the development and prognostic value of TLS differ significantly between various tumour types. Further, we saw that TLS are increased after immune checkpoint inhibition (ICI) in patients that responded to the treatment, while they had no predictive relevance at baseline in any of the analysed tumour types. These findings reveal a complexity of tumour-associated TLS biology that is currently poorly understood. This project is designed to increase our basic understanding of the interactions between tumours and the immune system focusing on tumour-associated lymphoid neogenesis. Specifically, we aim to answer the following questions: Which tumour-intrinsic factors influence lymphoid neogenesis? Do TLS differ in tumours with opposing prognostic associations? What is the difference between tumour-associated TLS and lymph nodes (LNs)? Are TLS needed for the efficacy of immunotherapies?
We will employ two unbiased approaches to analyse tumour-associated TLS: Spatial transcriptomics and computational histology. Spatial transcriptomics is a novel RNA sequencing technology allowing unbiased gene expression profiling in a spatial context. We will use this technology for in-depth characterisation of TLS in human tumours and for the development of novel experimental models where TLS relevance in anti-tumour immunity can be assessed. Computational histology refers to a unique deep learning algorithm that we have recently developed for high-throughput quantification of TLS and GC in histological images. With this approach we will measure TLS density in all diagnostic scans available from of The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and correlate it with the deposited molecular and clinical data. This will allow us to identify novel factors that influence lymphoid neogenesis in the TME of various cancers. We will use mouse models to validate our findings and to test the importance of lymphoid neogenesis in the context of immunotherapies. Additionally, independent patient cohorts will be used for validation analysis by quantitative pathology that involves multiplex immunofluorescence and multispectral imaging.
The results of this research program will contribute to our general knowledge regarding the role and development of TLS in cancer as well as to the identification of novel biomarkers for predicting patient survival and response to immunotherapy. Last but not least, it will contribute to the identification of new immunotherapeutic strategies for cancer.

Title: Overturning probability of uplifting structures under far-field earthquake excitation
Abstract:
During the last few decades, there has been an increasing interest on the rocking oscillator (or “inverted pendulum”, as Housner (1963) named it) mainly for 2 reasons:
a)Using rocking as an earthquake hazard mitigation design strategy has been proposed. The uplift of a structure works as a mechanical fuse, limiting the forces transmitted to the ground. Some few rocking structures have already been built worldwide.
b)The rocking oscillator describes the behavior of essential equipment (like computer servers or laboratory equipment) not anchored to the ground. 
“Rocking spectra” that describe the response of rigid blocks to acceleration pulses have been developed. They are convenient, because the pulse is described by only 2 parameters (peak acceleration and dominant period). This makes it possible to present the results in the form of 2d spectra. However, for most cases the pulse alone is not enough to describe the overturning potential of a true ground motion.
On the other hand, research based on recorded or synthetic ground motions has failed to define a “good” intensity measure of the ground motions, capable of describing their overturning potential. The use of PGA is considered to be simplistic and does not give enough information about the ground motion. Other intensity measures have been proposed, but not enough evidence is given on their applicability limits.
The goal of this research proposal is to use synthetic ground motions and well established mathematical tools to understand the dynamics of the earthquake response of rocking oscillators. It will be attempted to explore intensity measures for rocking structures and define their applicability limits. The principal idea is to use stochastic ground motions, calculate the overturning probability for given ground motion statistical properties and stochastic filter parameters and then check which properties (or combination of properties) are important to the overturning probability. This project proposal is organized following these four main objectives: 1) Stochastic study of the planar rocking motion; 2) Stochastic study of the 3d rocking motion; 3) Sensitivity analysis – Feature Selection Strategies; 4) Formal Dimensionality reduction – Feature Extraction Strategies.
It is worth noting that dimensionality reduction is useful in many disciplines. Therefore, powerful mathematical tools have been developed that, to the applicant’s knowledge, have never been used before in Earthquake Engineering.
Rocking seismic response modification technology is targeted towards special structures, such as bridges, tall slender stand-alone structures and high performance buildings. In bridges the rocking concept is widely applicable to precast modular bridges because it needs no monolith connections between the precast columns with the precast bridge deck. Therefore, the use of this concept may reduce the overall cost and facilitate faster construction, which is crucial especially when traffic is affected during construction. The stochastic analysis of rocking objects can be used in the framework of Performance Based Earthquake Engineering to quantify the failure probability of rocking structures. This can be a contribution towards putting aside vague terms that are widely used in engineering practice (like “redundancy”) and being able to compare structural systems in the only scientific way: By comparing the probability that they reach a specific performance level. This will give a tool to design engineers to decide whether a rocking solution could be optimal.
Moreover, there is a growing interest from the industry in quantifying the failure probability of essential or expensive equipment. The results of the proposed project can be used in assessing the probability of overturning of equipment stored in the ground floor and can be easily extended to systems resting on upper floors of buildings.
Keywords: dimensionality reduction, dynamic response, earthquake excitation, foundation uplift, high-performance computing, rocking systems, uncertainty quantification

Title: Artificial Intelligence in Medicine - The AIM at Glucose Project Intensive Care Units
Abstract:
Background: Even after a plethora of studies in severely ill patients, it is still unclear what the optimal blood glucose range is. Contradicting trials have not only sparked a large debate in the intensive care community, but have also harmed patients by hypoglycemic events. Perhaps a therapy confined to two glucose ranges (i.e. diabetics and non-diabetics) might be too simple. Herein, artificial intelligence algorithms can help to find the optimal glucose range for a given patient. 
General Aim: Our goal is to engineer an artificial intelligence [AI] algorithm that is able to aim at an optimal blood glucose range in an ICU instead of simply titrating insulin to a one-size fits all range.
Methods: We will retrospectively analyze MIMIC-III, an open-access database of 61,532 admissions from 2001–2012 in six ICUs at a Boston teaching hospital. We include all patients with a stay over 1 day and blood glucose readings. We are going to stratify eligible patients by diabetic status and admission diagnosis. The main endpoint is to predict a personally optimal glucose range for a single patient. For this, we are going to train a reinforcement learning algorithm. It assumes a Markov decision process to model the decision-making process. The function itself uses temporal difference learning to maximize the long-term reward. As our main reward/outcome, we are going to use the minimal, daily sequential organ failure assessment [SOFA] score. Results are going to be externally validated in the Swiss Inselspital ICU database from Bern.
Discussion: This proposal offers the opportunity to engineer a publicly available AI algorithm that can predict an optimal glucose range for a given patient. This algorithm can later be externally validated in an RCT. We offer a novel analytic approach that has never been implemented. With your support for AIM at Glucose, I will not only be able to offer a new AI algorithm. Besides learning valuable “Big Data” skills, I could later build up a clinical machine learning team at the very research competitive Kantonsspital Aarau and form a hub for teaching.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Glucose Metabolism, Intensive Care Units, Machine Learning, Reinforcement learning
