Title: Heterogeneous Catalysis: from Single-Sites to Supported Nanoparticles  from Molecular Principles
Abstract:
Chemical processes based on heterogeneous catalysts will be one of the key pillars of sustainable chemistry. A longstanding problem of this field has been to establish more rational approaches for catalyst discovery and development based on structure-activity relationships, similarly to what has been implemented for their homogenous counterparts. Towards this goal, one needs to understand the structure (and the dynamics) of the active sites and the underlying reaction mechanisms, which is particularly challenging for heterogeneous catalysts, where only a small fraction of the material participates in the reaction. In that context, our laboratory along with others have implemented strategies to tackle this issue, focusing on Surface Organometallic Chemistry (SOMC), which is based on preparing materials with tailored, ultimately well-defined, surface sites and characterizing them at the molecular level by employing state-of-the-art spectroscopic and computational approaches including solid-state NMR, Operando X-Ray Absorption Spectroscopy, ab initio molecular dynamic and machine learning to name but a few. This approach has already been successfully applied to generate highly active “single-site” catalysts based on well-defined supported organometallic compounds, to understand the surface sites of highly dispersed supported metal oxides or supported mono- and bi-metallic nanoparticles, that used in industrial settings for numerous applications, e.g. metathesis and polymerization of olefins, propane dehydrogenation or COx hydrogenation. Despite several advances, challenges remain to bridge the gap between heterogenous and molecular catalysis. For instance, one would like: 1) to understand how active sites are generated from high-valent metal sites found in supported metal oxides, 2) to identify descriptors that are readily measured and calculated, as a first step towards obtaining robust and predictive structure–activity relationships, 3) to obtain information of the ligand environment of metal sites, directly by probing its electronic structure, 4) to explore the synergy of bi-metallic systems to design efficient catalysts for hydrogenation and selective oxidation processes and explore surface chemistry of elements that have never been studied in SOMC, despite their notable chemistry and implication in selective catalysis.
In the context, we propose to broaden our exploration of the fundamentals of heterogeneous catalysis and surface chemistry regarding supported single-site catalysts and nanoparticles, with a specific focus on the aforementioned challenging topics, that will be developed in three independent and complementary work-packages. WP-1 will concentrate on studying activation processes in supported single-site catalysts, focusing on a case study with olefin metathesis. WP-2 will be devoted to developing solid-state NMR methodology to directly evaluate the electronic structures of metal sites, focusing on challenging low gamma nuclei. Finally, we plan to expand our molecular-level understanding of supported bimetallic nanoparticles and develop selective de-oxygenation and de-hydrogenation processes, exploring on the one hand group 9 metals towards bi-functional catalysis, focusing on selective hydro-oxygenation reactions (HDO), and on the other hand the surface chemistry and the promotional effects of heavy pnictogen (Sb,Bi) in the context of developing efficient catalytic processes (e.g. selective oxidation reactions with molecular oxygen), that are today untouched area of SOMC.
Keywords: NMR, alkane conversion, alkene conversion, heterogeneous catalysis, nanoparticles, single sites

Title: Networking for Immersive Communications (NICO)
Abstract:
Communication systems tried to improve the quality of communication to become close to real in-person communication. The vision of immersive communication is to enable interactions with remote people and environments such that users get the impression to be really inside a remote or virtual environment. Immersive communications may add additional services and functions and even improve real in-person communication. Augmented reality, virtual reality, and haptics are key technologies to enable immersive communications, with extreme requirements in terms of bandwidth, reliability, and latency. The targets are few milliseconds, combined with high-bandwidth (e.g., for 360 ° video), and/or high reliability (e.g., 99.9999 %, for interactive sensor/actor based applications such as haptics). NICO addresses these extreme challenges and requirements by a set of various approaches on protocol, network architecture, and implementation architecture level. In NICO we intend to come closer to these targets by addressing the following interrelated research challenges, which have to be considered in an integrated way.

- viewport prediction algorithms in 360 °, video based on sensor-based localization, tracking and rotation/movement predictions using advanced machine learning (ML) concepts in order to improve users' Quality-of-Experience (QoE),

- disruptive methods to identify QoE parameters in immersive communications combining system measurements and psychological behaviors,

- implementation of an advanced integrated hardware and software platform including operating system scheduling for user-level virtualization and the support of hardware accelerators for immersive communication processing in order to support low latencies and high throughput, 

- novel mechanisms to minimize latencies by (extended) caching mechanisms exploiting in-network processing for immersive communications,- novel network protocols based on information-centric networking and network coding to support low-latency communication, 

- original algorithms and mechanisms for service migration to minimize latency between mobile users and service entities, including the novel concept of Floating Services.
Keywords: Future Internet, Immersive Communications, Mixed Reality, Quality of Experience

Title: Towards Integrated processing of Physiological and Speech signals (TIPS)
Abstract:
Speech processing research has largely focused on modeling the activity of voice source and the activities in the oral cavity. However, speech production is intrinsically related to other physiological activities, such as respiration, heart activity, which can undergo changes due to a variety of reasons like mood or emotion, social or environmental setting (e.g., loud versus quite environment), or neuro-degenerative diseases (e.g., Parkinson's disease) or stroke. These changes in turn can affect speech communication. In the speech community, there is very little research that has undergone to understand the relationship between speech and physiological activities, such as respiration, heart rate.

Idiap and CSEM are currently involved in developing a platform, where speech and physiological signals are collected in a synchronous manner through a wearable cooperative sensor and processed to develop novel speech- and physiology-based applications. Building on the outcomes of this collaboration, the proposed project TIPS aims to investigate the relationship between speech signals and physiological signals under different speaking conditions (read, spontaneous, group conversation, public speaking and speech under cognitive stress), and develop methods,
1. to predict physiological parameters from the speech signal
2. to improve mental stress detection by combining speech and physiological information
3. to robustly segment utterances in terms of words and phrases by jointly modeling speech and physiological signals.
The outcomes of the proposed project is of interest not only to the speech community but also to other fields, such as social computing and health care to name a prominent few.

The proposed research will be carried out in collaboration with CSEM, who will assist with their expertise in sensor development and physiological signal acquisition. We will also collaborate with an executive coach and expert on spoken word, who will help us in developing methods to detect mental stress in public speaking. Finally, we will also collaborate with the German Aerospace Center (DLR), Braunschweig to acquire speech and physiological data under cognitive stress conditions, specifically air traffic controllers data, and develop novel speech and physiology-based cognitive stress measurement methods.

TIPS will fund two young researchers, one PhD and one Postdoc, and will train them at the interaction of speech processing, physiological signal processing, sensor fusion and machine learning.
Keywords: mental stress detection, physiological signal processing, sensor fusion, speech processing, wearable sensor

Title: Credal networks made easy
Abstract:
Graph-based approaches to uncertainty and statistics usually fall under the headline of graphical models. These are very important, and widespread, models in Artificial Intelligence. In this proposal we focus on Bayesian networks, decision nets, and in particular on credal networks (Section 2.1.1).

Bayesian networks mix graph and probabilities in order to compute inferences under uncertainty. Decision nets can be regarded as Bayesian nets extended to deal with decisions. These are precise-probability graphical models, in the sense that the probabilities used to build the model, as well as the probabilities computed by the model, cannot be subject to imprecision. Credal networks are instead an imprecise probability model: i.e., a credal net can be regarded as a set of Bayesian networks, or, in turn, a set of joint mass functions.

Credal networks are very expressive models compared to Bayesian networks. Our research, for example, has shown that credal nets nicely unify a number of models and problems [11,8]. Moreover, credal nets have applications in pattern classification: the supervised data-mining task of learning a model from data that is later used to assign new objects to one of a number of pre-established categories. In this case, credal nets have given rise to the new paradigm called credal classification, which is important to do reliable predictions. 

However, there are important open problems that limit the application of credal nets: (i) there is no truly efficient algorithm for credal nets that can give guarantees on the quality of the (approximate) solutions provided. On our view, this is the most urgent problem to address in the field of credal nets. (ii) Such an algorithm could lead to address and solve many important problems, such as decision-theoretic problems, and also to the development of new models for classification (these two aspects are related as doing classification can be regarded as a special decision problem). (iii) When we focus in particular on classification, we find another key issue: we are limited in our understanding of the quality of the predictions made by credal classifiers, because we have not yet a clear and principled metric to empirically measure their performance. This is a fundamental problem credal classification is experiencing, and one that is very urgent, too, to give it credibility.

By this proposal we want to overcome these problems, according to the following plan.

(1) We will develop a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) for credal networks (with bounded treewidth, and bounded maximum number of states per variable; see Section 2.3.1). We believe this algorithm, which has long been searched for, will be a turning point for research on credal networks: it will scale down the computational complexity of credal networks to a level (bigger, but still) similar to that of Bayesian networks. We will give both a theoretical proof and numerical experiments to show that the theoretical claims are effective in practice.

(2) We will use the new algorithm to solve complex decision-theoretic problems and investigate applications to game theory (Section 2.3.2).

(3) We will derive a principled new metric for credal classifiers. We will provide the first metric for credal classifiers that is derived from general principles and some reasonable assumptions (see Section 2.3.3). The metric will output a single number to measure the prediction of a classifier, and will apply to credal classifiers as well as to traditional classifiers. Experimental tests will be carried out to validate the metric.
Keywords: algorithms, classification, credal classification, credal networks, decision networks, decision theory, graphical models, imprecise probability, updating algorithm

Title: A molecular dynamics study of water crystallization using deep neural network potentials of ab-initio quality
Abstract:
Water is essential for life and technology. Its ubiquitous character is illustrated by the number of fields in which it sparks interest, such as biology, materials science, and environmental chemistry. Water also provides the most famous example of a freezing transition, the transformation of liquid water into ice. If this transformation occurs through homogeneous nucleation, then a nanoscopic ice cluster is formed inside liquid water. If the ice cluster is smaller than a critical size, it will dissolve, and if it is larger than the critical size, it will grow. The small time and length scales involved in nucleation represent a hurdle for experiments and atomistic simulation has been a useful tool to provide insight into the process.

In spite of the maturity of computer simulation techniques, the modeling of water remains challenging. In many cases the need to describe water accurately requires the use of ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations. In this context usually density functional theory (DFT) approximations are used and the recently introduced DFT functional SCAN has proved to give a much better description of water than its predecessors. However, AIMD simulations are prohibitively expensive for large systems and long timescales, being limited to a few hundred atoms and a few hundred of picoseconds at most. Using classical molecular dynamics (MD) that use semiempirical force fields it is possible to study relatively large systems (10^5 molecules) albeit with reduced accuracy compared to AIMD simulations. A possible way to bridge the time and length scales between AIMD and classical MD is by using neural network inter-atomic potentials. These potentials are trained using the energies and forces from ab initio calculations providing ab initio accuracy with linear scaling and a computational cost slightly higher than a traditional semiempirical force field.

The overall objective of this project is to study homogeneous ice nucleation using molecular simulations with unprecedented accuracy in the description of water. The specific aims are obtaining insight into the nucleation mechanism, and calculating nucleation rates and nuclei sizes as a function of temperature. These will be compared to experimental results and simulation predictions using less accurate force fields. To achieve these objectives we will first perform AIMD to train a deep neural network potential. Afterwards we will calculate the nucleation rates and nuclei sizes using classical MD. Crucial to the success of these calculations is the use of enhanced sampling methods. We plan to use metadynamics, forward flux sampling, or the seeding method in order to access the required timescale.

We expect to settle long standing debates regarding ice nucleation and assess the accuracy of the SCAN functional in describing this phenomenon. Our study would pioneer the use of ab-initio quality force fields in the study of ice nucleation.

Title: Learning to reconstruct tissue structures with generative AI
Abstract: Advances in spatially resolved single-cell technologies have paved the path for generating comprehensive spatial maps of cells at high resolutions. The capability to capture spatial organization within tissues provides an opportunity to gain insights into cellular self-organization, cell-cell interactions, and their impact on the phenotypes and functions of cellular communities. Despite significant progress, the understanding of the mechanisms driving functional and spatial organization within tissues remains incomplete. This is to a large extent due to technological limitations: existing technologies for capturing spatial context of cells are either limited in the number of genes that can be measured, or lack the single-cell resolution. On the other hand, vast amounts of single-cell RNA sequencing data (scRNA-seq) has been generated; however, scRNA-seq data does not preserve the spatial context of cells. In addition, existing analyses are mainly focused on a single dataset at a time, and lack insights about shared spatial patterns across datasets. In this project, we will develop AI methods that will learn underlying mechanisms governing spatial organization of cells from large collections of existing spatial datasets and enable the generation of tissue structures from cells’ molecular profiles. These methods will help to overcome the limitations of existing spatial and scRNA-seq technologies and generate new insights about the underlying mechanisms that affect tissue organization and cell-cell interactions. We propose a highly interdisciplinary project that will develop new machine learning tools with an impact on spatial biology. While progress in these aims builds towards the overall goal of reconstructing tissue structures from molecular features and developing “AlphaFold for cells”, in parallel we will develop new computational methods that will be valuable for the single-cell and spatial omics community, as well as machine learning community.

Title: Attention Sensing in the Workplace: Towards the New Future of Work
Abstract:
In recent years, computing technology has fundamentally changed how we work. In particular, information workers have seen a significant shift towards fragmentation of work in which employees work on several tasks throughout the day, switching between them frequently, even every couple of minutes. While task switching can be beneficial as it may also include breaks, such as reading the news or browsing social media, too many distractions may have harmful effects or even lead to tasks not being completed at all. Consequently, understanding how people work, their behaviours, how they manage everyday tasks, and what makes them productive have emerged as core research questions in human-computer interaction (HCI). One of the most important metrics to quantify the workplace is productivity, which is closely related to worker performance and thus relevant for employees and organisations alike.

In this project, we propose a novel research direction that (1) aims to understand, quantify, and improve productivity through models of user attention. In stark contrast to prior research that has mainly analysed productivity through classical performance metrics (e.g. task completion time or number of completed tasks), passive sensing, or application usage logs, we are first to sense and analyse users’ visual attention, i.e. observing eye movements, in the context of productivity. Our project will lay the foundations for better understanding workers’ attentive behaviour and how they are linked to productive or distracting behaviours in the context of work. Based on our analyses and insights, we will (2) develop the first computational models to predict user productivity based on attentive patterns (e.g. the number of attention shifts from one application to another) as well as interactive behaviour, such as mouse or keyboard dynamics. Lastly, (3) we will devise computational methods (e.g. based on deep reinforcement learning) that can optimise user tasks according to different levels of attention with the goal to maximise productivity at the workplace. Based on these methods, we will propose a novel task scheduler that will be able to adapt a user’s schedule optimally by matching their attention patterns, which is linked to their level of concentration and focus, to tasks of appropriate dificulty and complexity. For example, if a user is in an attentional state that is more likely to lead to disruptions, our task scheduler will propose cognitively simpler or more mechanical tasks. These advances will be instrumental for a better understanding of user behaviour at the workplace and for actively supporting them in their quest for higher productivity and well-being.
Keywords: Attentive User Interfaces, Machine Learning, Productivity, User Attention, Visual Attention

Title: Decarbonizing industry by smart electrification (DecInEL)
Abstract: In view of the policy objective of net zero carbon emissions, the deepest possible level of decarbonisation must be achieved for all sectors including industry. Industry is the most challenging sector to decarbonise due to the higher complexity, heterogeneity and temperature levels compared to the service sector and households. Considering the various challenges and trade-offs with energy carriers such as biomass (sustainable supply, air pollution etc.) and green gasses (need for very large amounts of renewable electricity) industry decarbonisation by electrification of heat supply up to 200°C (using heat pumps) is an energetically convincing concept, especially when combined with heat integration, heat storage and renewable energy use (renewable electricity and other renewables). We refer to this concept as smart electrification. Considering that approximately two thirds of all process heat in Switzerland is required at below 200°C (own estimate), smart electrification is an essential decarbonisation strategy which is being neglected also in other countries. As essential constraint and keeping in mind the evolution of industrial production in the past decades, we assume electrification of heat supply as retrofit measure in existing plants (brownfield), thereby considering the typical constraints encountered in such a context. Against this background, the overall research question of the DECINEL project is how deep decarbonisation of manufacturing industry (without high-temperature processes) can be achieved by electrification of existing plants at lowest possible cost and in a safe and resilient manner. To answer this question, the DECINEL project is organised around four tasks of different size, thereby collaborating with industrial partners, which will contribute data: Task 1 (smallest task) frames the project and deals with spatial top-down analysis of 10 to 20 industrial hotspots in terms of energy demand, CO2 emissions and other characteristics (subtask T1.1 and T1.2); it also includes the scale-up of bottom-up results (from T4) to the national level (T1.3, see below). Task 2 and 3 provide the project’s methodological backbone. In Task 2 (largest task), we develop a novel optimisation framework for process design allowing to identify the opportunities and limits of deep decarbonisation of existing industrial plants by means of direct and indirect heat integration (T2.1), heat pumps (T2.2) and utilisation of renewable energy sources (T2.3). One of the novelties consists in using the Simulated Annealing algorithm which ensures that the identified solutions do not differ too much from the original design (“neighbourhood moves”), thereby leading to a design that is suitable for retrofit (as opposed to a greenfield design). The retrofit model will be applicable both for continuous and non-continuous processes as well as multiple operational cases (MOC) and will ultimately allow to analyse the trade-offs between CO2 abatement and costs. In Task 3, we develop novel methods for operational strategies and real time process optimisation of the processes designed in Task 2. To this end, we will prepare a data and model library under realistic operational conditions (T3.1), an artificial intelligence (AI)-based multi-criteria optimisation method for operational strategies (T3.2) and its further development for real-time operational optimisation of processes (T3.3). In Task 4 we test the newly developed methods in case studies for a chosen sector (e.g., food) by developing generic energy profiles (T4.1) and applying the newly developed process design tools (T4.2) and operational strategy tools (T4.3). Subtasks T4.2 and T4.3 will provide detailed understanding of the viability of the methods (e.g., on computational time). Through scale-up to the national level, they will also offer insights into the realistically achievable potential of country-wide decarbonisation of industry by smart electrification (T1.3).
Keywords: Pinch analysis, decarbonisation, energy efficiency, industry, operational strategies, optimisation, process design, retrofit, spatial analysis

Title: Households' Risk through Deep Data Analysis: Mobility, Credit, Consumption, Mortality, and Voting
Abstract:
The current project aims at investigating three main topics of research utilizing the wealth of information available through the novel big (or deep) data on consumers’ credit behaviour provided by Experian. In a nutshell, the Experian data cover all credit transactions through credit reports at the monthly frequency from 2004 to this day, so that individuals, and households are followed overtime. The cross-sectional coverage is virtually the entire adult US population. The intent is that of establishing a unique research agenda, and research group able to tackle several issues concerning consumers’ behaviour for the years to come. The acquisition of the complete data, ultimately every credit transaction of the entire US population is recorded in such data, will allow to establish a unique research group and research agenda which would make us the leaders in Europe in these areas of research. To my knowledge very few researchers around the world have access to such wealth of information, I had access to similar data in the past as a Senior Economist at the NYFed and the Federal Reserve System, one of the very few institutions worldwide that has access to similar data, so that I am fully aware of the research potential they can unlock. Acquiring these data will give us the ability to lead the way in Europe and will make the research group a focal point for the Worldwide research community. The possibility of research given by the data are seemingly endless, while in this proposal we focus on three closely related topics, those are just a tiny subset of what is possible with the brainpower and resources we can put together overtime. To assure the success of such an ambitious project the current proposal includes the request for funding for computing equipment as well as personnel that might look a bit out of the standard requests. Let me reiterate that the data provided by Experian cover virtually the entire population of the US, potentially at the monthly frequency with thousands of transaction attributes, this means that the complete database is quite large, in the order of tens of terabytes. Handling such a vast wealth of data requires appropriate computing power as well as personnel. To be clear, while the Experian data focus on recording credit transactions, delinquencies, and so on, they also record major life events such as mobility, family formation, death. As the data have a very detailed geographic identifier (precise address) and individual social security number, it is obvious that we can merge them with other data sources and potentially with other administrative data if we receive the due authorizations to do so.
In the current proposal, we will develop three closely related areas of research:
1.Credit and Default behaviour in the wake of the Great Recession;
2.The effects of “Gentrification” and “De-Gentrification” on consumers;
3.Big (Deep) Data and their contribution to the analysis of credit behaviour.
In the first line of research we will investigate the relationship between borrowing behaviour, house price dynamics, and delinquencies in the wake of the great recession. The current narrative, mostly based on work by Mian and Sufi (2009, 2015), points towards the negative effects of too lax borrowing criteria which have generated a large amount of bad loans opened by sub-prime or lower credit score borrowers. Those loans have then determined the large financial crisis and the great recession due to the changes in the housing price dynamics. However, a closer look at the actual borrowing behaviour through individual data will show that the old narrative is, at least, incomplete. That older narrative misses the fundamental life-cycle dynamics of borrowing behaviour. Our initial results, based on data that were accessible to this researcher as an employee of the Federal Reserve, show that in fact it is younger and better borrowers we should look into to explain the large growth in credit between 2003 and 2007 and not the subprime borrowers. These facts are crucial in understanding the nature of the financial crisis and subsequent great recession and therefore essential for the formulation of policy responses. 
Clearly the house price dynamics, housing supply, credit, and labour market conditions should be jointly investigated to fully understand the drivers of consumers’ behaviour and delinquencies. In this view, in the second research line, we then analyse the effects of large increase or fall in house prices within a local area (commuting zone or zip code) and their crucial consequences on consumers. On the one hand the effect of Gentrification (or a steady and large increase in house prices) should have a positive wealth effect on home-owners, therefore potentially improving their consumption profiles and lowering their delinquencies rates. At the same time renters might suffer from the increase in house prices as rents will respond to that. To our knowledge very little is known about the consequences of gentrification and de-gentrification in terms of geographic mobility, consumption, and delinquency as resulting from steady and large increase or fall in housing prices. We therefore aim at filling the gap in the literature by combining data on credit behaviour with data on prices and labour market in the US. Credit data will give us a unique opportunity to consider delinquency directly, and as the amount of consumption out of credit cards is now around 50% of total expenditure (much higher in large metropolitan areas) in the US, we can use credit card balances to infer a measure of total consumption through a dynamic budget constraint formulation. Moreover, the dynamics of geographic mobility across owners and renters are crucial forces for equalization of differentials across markets and deserve a central attention in policy making.
A natural extension of the two areas of research above is our third line of research in this proposal. We aim at the development of predictive models of delinquency, consumption, and mobility outcomes exploiting the wealth of data acquired for this project. The aim is to build forecasting models of behaviour based on promising new approaches developed within the big (deep) data revolution. The current frontier in econometrics combines methods from statistics and machine learning and has shown great promises. Of particular interest are Deep Learning models which involve neural networks and have been shown to be extremely powerful tool for prediction and outlier detection (LeCun et. al. 2015, Schmidhuber, 2015) Furthermore, they can be used for unsupervised learning, which can provide novel insights into how high-dimensional models are to be constructed, the number of consumer types in a population or developing new approaches to delinquency (and the other aforementioned outcomes) in credit data.
Keywords: Big and Deep Data, Consumer behaviour, Credit, Delinquency, Gentrification and De-Grentrification

Title: Machine Learning Simulation of Many-Body Quantum Matter
Abstract:
The field of artificial intelligence has seen a prodigious rise in the past years, driven by both technological and methodological breakthroughs driven by Machine Learning (ML). In recent times, ML methods and ideas are being increasingly adopted to solve fundamental problems in Physics [1]. The PI and coworkers have played a founding role in the adoption of ML techniques to quantum many-body Physics [2–4], obtaining new state-of-the-art results in the numerical simulation of interacting quantum systems [2,5], and in traditionally challenging tasks in quantum computing [3,6] with the introduction of Neural-Network Quantum States (NQS). 

Goal of this Project is to research, deploy and promote the systematic application of modern ML methods to a variety of fundamental problems involving strong correlations, for which several ambitious and high-impact results can be expected in the near term. The Project is structured in 4 Work Parts (WPs) each corresponding to the planned work of a PhD student for 4 years.  

WP1’s chief goal is to devise and apply NQS methods to study open challenging fermionic lattice problems in Condensed Matter theory. For example, to address the existence of stripes and superconductivity in spinless 2D fermions; the possibility of obtaining a compact variational representation of infinite-dimensional lattice fermions with ANNs. ML methods will also be used to attack, potentially with unprecedented accuracy, the long-standing issue of the stability of superconductivity in the 2d Hubbard model.   

WP2’s goal is to study open problems involving frustrated spins in two and three dimensions.   We will adopt methods of increasing complexity, ranging from neural-network correlators for 3 dimensional problems, to novel SU(2)-enforced neural-network states for two-dimensional problems. Models that will be tackled are the J1-J2 model, the Shastry-Sutherland model (also in connection with EPFL’s experiments) and Pyrochlore Heisenberg models.  

WP3 will use existing and novel continuous-space NQS to study problems emerging with ultra-cold quantum gases out of equilibrium. For example, we will study the quench dynamics of a one-dimensional gas featuring long-range dipolar interactions; the role of dimensionality in the thermalization process in continuous space; the existence of an effective maximum velocity for information spreading.    

WP4 will aim at providing methodological advancements to remove, as much as possible, the variational bias due the specific functional form adopted in a neural-network quantum state. This will be achieved combining NQS with ground-state path-integral projection methods. A fully-differentiable neural fixed-node approach will be introduced and adopted to further improve the accuracy for fermionic and frustrated spin problems.       

A common theme of all WPs will be the release of the methodological advancements as fully open-source tools for a wider community, under the umbrella of the NetKet project.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Fermions, Neural-networks, Quantum, Quantum Dynamics, Ultra-cold atoms

Title: Pathways to Intensive Cross-Sectoral Climate Policy
Abstract:
The evidence on climate change is unequivocal. The window of opportunity to limit global warming to an average surface temperature increase below 2°C is closing rapidly. More ambitious policies than those currently implemented are necessary. Meanwhile, most research has assumed a problem-oriented perspective, primarily advancing the conceptualization of various barriers to policy adoption. The objective of this cumulative dissertation is therefore to advance the theorization and empirical analysis of solution-oriented political enablers of ambitious climate policy in four papers.

This dissertation develops a theoretical framework for politically enabling ambitious climate policies in the first paper. Its core is a typology of six political enablers. These include, for instance, the science-policy interface linking the factual knowledge generation by scientists with the political domain. To contribute to the supply side of one of the most widely recognized organizations at the science-policy interface in the climate domain, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the second paper compiles a systematic map and database of over 50,000 research articles as an underpinning of the upcoming IPCC special report on cities. Based on the results from a machine learning pipeline rooted in artificial intelligence, I discuss three approaches that will be critical to improving the supply side of the science-policy interface: i) systematic evidence synthesis for policy advice based on robust findings, ii) cross-city learning where similar problems and solutions exist, and iii) the use of computational methods, such as remote sensing. These will be crucial to closing the identified knowledge gaps for small and fast-growing cities -- those cities that have the largest future mitigation and adaptation potential.

The third and fourth papers contribute to policy design, communication, and framing as political enablers of more ambitious climate policies. The third paper evaluates the relative predictive power of established explanations in the literature on support and mobilization based on a pre-election survey before the Swiss CO2 Act in 2021 to advance theory building. The results show that beliefs and policy instrument preferences have the highest predictive power implying that communication and framing during political campaigns should aim at fostering positive beliefs about the effectiveness of the policy design. Building on these insights, the fourth paper shows that perceptions related to the effectiveness of prior benefit-inducing policies, such as renewable energy subsidies, can foster public support for more ambitious carbon taxation at the ballot -- a recently developed theoretical approach to politically enabling public support for ambitious climate policies called policy sequencing.

The results of this dissertation have key implications for academic research as well as for policymaking. Academically, this dissertation contributes to conceptualizing political enablers and, specifically, the supply side of the science-policy interface and policy design through the extension of policy sequencing theory to cognitive aspects related to the perception of benefits. Empirically, I provide robust evidence using mixed methods, combining computational methods, such as machine learning rooted in artificial intelligence, experiments, and qualitative conceptual approaches. For policymaking, the results provide important implications: For instance, when designing policies with a sequencing approach, communication to raise awareness of policy-induced benefits from the sequencing strategies, will be key to securing public support. Thus, activating political enablers combined and sequentially can become more than the sum of its parts.

Title: Full 3D Scene Understanding from a Single Image
Abstract: The aim of this project is to compute a full digital 3D reconstruction and semantic labeling of a scene where only a single image, potentially containing depth information, is given. While 3D reconstruction from images is a well studied problem in computer vision, most of the existing works use datasets containing many images which jointly observe the whole scene and only reconstruct the geometry not taking into account semantic labels. Only recently, approaches have emerged that jointly reason about geometry and semantic labels. When only a single image is given most of the existing approaches restrict the problem to finding a 2.5D depth map of the scene and semantically label pixels. The main limitation of such a representation is that it does not allow the description of all the information of the scene. For example such a representation does not allow the representation of the backsides of object which cannot directly be observed from a single viewpoint or surfaces which are hidden, such as a wall or the ground behind furniture. This however often is important information,  for example for a robot arm grabbing an objects the geometry of the back side does matter. In the proposed project the goal is to reason about the geometry and semantic labels of the 3D scene as a whole including the not directly observed and obstructed geometry. The means to do this is to exploit symmetries, shape priors and reasoning about repeating objects in the scene. A tight coupling between semantic classes, objects and geometry will allow to use interdependencies between semantic classes and geometry, for example ground is expected to be flat and horizontal. The key question to be addressed in this project is how much information can be extracted out of a single image.
Keywords: 3D Reconstruction, Scene Understanding, Semantic Labeling, Single View Reconstruction

Title: Specificity, selectivity and pharmacokinetics of compstatin: a comprehensive multidisciplinary analysis
Abstract:
The complement system plays a major role in innate immunity as it confers immune surveillance and first-line defense against non- or altered-self entities such as microbes or apoptotic cells. Yet, misguided complement activation may trigger or contribute to severe clinical conditions or complications, including autoimmune, hemolytic, inflammatory and age-related disorders and transplant rejection (PMID) [1]. Owing to its cascade organization, involving ~50 plasma proteins, receptors and enzymes, complement provides multiple points for novel pharmacological intervention [2]. However, few complement-targeted drugs have reached the clinic, and the available options primarily target peripheral steps in cascade initiation or effector generation. For many acute-phase or multifactorial complement disorders, blocking the activation of the central complement component C3 is considered important [3]. Derivatives of compstatin, a peptidic inhibitor of C3 activation [4], are the most advanced compounds in this class, with two candidate drugs being evaluated in clinical trials. However, its narrow species-specificity for primate C3 currently restricts a broader exploration of potential benefits of C3 inhibition in various established animal models of complement disorders. Furthermore, despite considerable progress in structure optimization, some pharmacokinetic and physicochemical properties of the compstatin class remain to be improved to fully unleash its unique therapeutic potential.
The main objective of this project is to understand target binding and complement inhibition by compstatin in the human system at the atomic level and identify key determinants of its narrow species specificity. We will utilize this knowledge for designing compstatin analogs that recognize non-primate C3 and, for example, inhibit mouse, rat or pig complement. Simultaneously, we will assess compstatin’s target selectivity for C3 over the orthologous C4 and C5 proteins and explore options for achieving C4-, C5- or pan-specific inhibitors for research or clinical applications. Finally, we will analyze and optimize the pharmacokinetic properties of compstatin with special emphasis on solubility and bioavailability.
The proposed rationalization and optimization efforts will be driven by well-established in silico simulation techniques such as molecular dynamics simulations, free energy methods, homology modeling, and post-MD analyses, supported by novel approaches based on deep learning (Prof. Markus Lill, Computational Pharmacy). Thanks to project collaborations with strong experimental groups, in silico findings will be experimentally verified by employing peptide synthesis and characterization, chemical modification and labeling, and target binding and functional assays in vitro (Prof. Daniel Ricklin, Molecular Pharmacy) as well as pre-clinical assessments of cellular permeability in vitro and in vivo (Prof. Henriette Meyer zu Schwabedissen, Biopharmacy; all at University of Basel).
Our studies are expected to extend preclinical evaluation options of compstatin-based drugs in animal models and enhance their pharmacokinetic profile, thereby facilitating clinical development of this important inhibitor class. Selectivity studies with C4/C5 may provide insight into complement activation and potentially reveal novel inhibitors. Finally, atomic level insight into the structure-activity/property relationships of cyclic peptides may be used for the design of this compound type in general.

Title: Improving the Argumentation Skills of Students Through Artificial Intelligence
Abstract:
Argumentation is an omnipresent foundation of our daily communication and thinking. The ability to form convincing arguments is not only the fundament for persuading an audience of novel ideas but also plays a major role in strategic decision-making and analyzing different standpoints especially in the context of digitalization and its influence on jobs. This has been recognized by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), which named these so-called metacognition skills a major part of their Learning Framework 2030 (OECD 2018). However, educators face difficulties in providing individual learning support for argumentation skills to students due to traditional large-scale lecture sizes and the growing field of distance learning scenarios such as Massive Open Online Course (MOOCs). Therefore, students often suffer from the lack of support, such as formative feedback in their individual learners’ journey. With the help of new adaptive argumentation learning systems, students would be able to learn autonomously and independently of the instructor, time, and place.

Keeping organizational and economic limitations in mind, the effective use of technology-based applications seems to be a viable approach to improve the quality of argumentation learning in large-scale and distance learning scenarios individually. More specifically, a promising way to support students to learn structured argumentation and enable teachers to convey it to classes of large sizes and independent from location might be the usage of adaptive technology-based applications in a pedagogical scenario for a student’s learning journey. Therefore, recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) such as argumentation mining (AM) seem to be a promising approach, since Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Machine Learning (ML) offer scalable analyses of text in various other domains, such as court statements, newspaper articles, or user-generated content. Therefore, I aim to explore the potential of adaptive argumentation skill learning based on Artificial Intelligence (AI) by designing, implementing, and evaluating a new technology-enhanced pedagogical concept to actively support students in developing the ability to argue in a structured, logical and reflective way. Based on this goal two paper projects will be conducted. Both projects will be carried out with Ken Koedinger from the Human-Computer Interaction Institute of Carnegie Mellon University (CMU) in Pittsburg, USA. In paper project 1, we aim at investigating to what extend does an adaptive argumentation writing support system (AAWSS) based on AI foster student’s logical argumentation in social and political discourse, e.g., when writing student essays. We aim to publish our results at the leading HCI outlet the ACM Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI) 2022. In paper project 2, we will build on our generated design knowledge from our previous research and paper project 1 to conceptualize a process model in the form of a web platform to empower researchers and educators to develop an AAWSS to foster students’ metacognition argumentation skills in different domains. We aim to develop a manuscript for the journal Management Information Systems Quarterly (MISQ) (VHB JourQual 3: A+ & FT 50 journal). 

Hence, I firstly bridge the boundaries of argumentation learning and argumentation mining to help students to learn logical argumentation in social and political discourse by examining a pedagogical scenario for adaptive argumentation learning. I contribute not only new rich argumentation annotation schemes, argumentation corpora, and novel ML models, but most of all, insights into the overall embedding, design and effects of an adaptive argumentation learning tool based on NLP and ML. Thus, my research will contribute to theory and practice, by providing a) empirical insights on the effects of AAWSS on logical argumentation of student in political discourse and b) design knowledge through a step-by-step process model for researcher and educational designers to build their own AAWSS in the field of IS and HCI.
Keywords: Adaptive Argumentation Learning, Adaptive Writing Support Systems, Argumentation Mining Algorithms for Education, Design Knowledge, Intelligent Tutoring Systems, Meta-Cognition Skill Learning

Title: Object Detection with Active Sample Harvesting (DASH )
Abstract:
Practical deployment of Machine Learning techniques relies on the existence of large training data sets, which exhibit all the difficulties to be met in practice, and are labeled by human experts.

While critical, the production of training data remains a subject poorly studied. Efficient labeling has been tackled with active learning, to concentrate the human effort on the examples which truly influence the learning. The production of unlabeled data, however, has not been studied in itself.

The objective of this project is to address these two tasks, and to develop novel, efficient, and mathematically sound procedures to produce very large quantities of labeled data to train part-based object detectors.

The first part of this proposal focuses on the extension of active learning to the particular situation of object detection with part-based models. We will define multiple levels of information,spanning from the mere presence of an object in an image, to the locations of its individual parts. From there, instead of simply identifying subsets of samples whose labels are likely to be informative, the procedure we envision will select pairs of samples and levels of labeling, so that the ratio information / labeling cost will be maximum.

The second part will address the production of unlabeled data. We introduce the idea of "data harvesters", web-crawling daemons built upon goal-planning algorithms. These harvesters will model the relation between information attached to the web source of images (web site, extual context of images, date and time, gps coordinates, camera type, etc.)  and their usefulness for training. From this model, harvesters will implement goal-planning strategies, to properly balance exploitation and exploration, trying both to localize good sources of data for training, and to download data from the ones already identified.
Keywords: Active learning, Machine learning, Topical Web-crawler, Unsupervised learning

Title: Respiratory Motion Correction in MR-Guided Cryoablation
Abstract:
The proposed project will leverage recent progress in hybrid ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (US-MRI) technology, to develop synergistic software and hardware technology that is aimed at improving surgical and interventional guidance in the presence of respiratory organ motion. Our approach to this problem is to exploit the relative strengths of MRI and US imaging in novel ways. To accomplish this goal, we will further develop our simultaneous US-MRI acquisition technique as well as machine learning algorithms that handle high bandwidth US data toward estimating motion and deformation in MRI images.

MR-guided cryoablations are minimally-invasive procedures aimed at killing tumor tissues through freeze-thaw cycles, while MR images are acquired to help monitor the size, shape and location of the evolving iceball. We have developed ties with a clinical collaborator who performs kidney cryoablations and will apply our developed technology to the problem of breathing motion during these procedures. In a pre-scan calibration ("learning") phase, simultaneous US-MRI will be acquired over a short period of no more than 5 minutes. The type of ultrasound data we acquire is unconventional. We use a single-element US transducer to acquire a raw RF fingerprint of the abdominal configuration, here referred to as USrd signal. This is in contrast to 2D US imaging where arrays of transducers are used in conjunction with subsequent post-processing for image-reconstruction. One such fingerprint is recorded in conjunction with each acquired MR signal, with the MR scanner software controlling the timing and triggering of the whole US-MRI hybrid setup. After obtaining these training data, non-rigid image registration will be performed on the MR images in order to extract motion information (displacement maps). Machine learning techniques will then be employed to correlate US and motion information to obtain a model for 3D displacements as a function of the USrd signal. The USrd patch is to be kept in place throughout the minimally-invasive procedure and the model will be used to deform each acquired free-breathing MR image to a reference position, presumably full expiration. The result will be motion-corrected intra-operative MR images, which will allow the radiologist to more accurately position the ablation needles and monitor the growth of the iceball around the tumor. This monitoring and guidance essential to ensure that the entire tumor (plus a safety-margin around it) is 'eclipsed' by the iceball to ensure proper treatment are reduce the risk of recurrence while preserving as much as possible the surrounding healthy tissues. As opposed to current procedures where breathing motion complicates the image interpretation, our advances will hopefully lead to faster procedures with better outcome. 

The technology will be validated at the Brigham and Women's Hospital (BWH), in the 'AMIGO'  advanced multi-modality suite, one of the world's most advanced imaging- and tracking-focused surgery suites. Kidney cryoablations are already performed in AMIGO, and we will test the potential added value of our technology as part of these procedures.

Title: MicroLearn: Micropower Deep Learning
Abstract:
Sensors and wearable technologies are gaining popularity, with people increasingly surrounded by “smart” objects, from phones to clothing, from glasses to watches, from home automation to healthcare. Smart, connected products are made possible by vast improvements in processing power and device miniaturization and by the availability of ubiquitous wireless connectivity: The clear trend is toward a trillion connected devices, the “Internet of Everything” (IoE) vision. The IoE creates formidable research challenges. In particular, a trillion sensor-rich connected devices are going to produce a mind-boggling quantity of data and potentially useful information. However, the data by themselves do not provide value unless we can turn them into actionable, contextualized information. Big-data mining techniques allow us to gain new insights by batch-processing and off-line analysis. However, this is not sufficient: in-situ real-time feature extraction, analysis, classification, and local decision-making are essential for a truly scalable and robust IoE infrastructure. 
Machine learning technologies are used with great success in many application areas, solving real-world problems in entertainment systems, robotics, health care, and surveillance. More and more researchers are tackling classification and decision-making problems with the help of brain-inspired algorithms, featuring many stages of feature extractors and classifiers with lots of parameters that are optimized using the unprecedented wealth of training data that is currently available. These deep learning techniques are achieving record-breaking classification accuracy results  on very challenging problems and datasets, and routinely surpass more mature ad hoc approaches as well as humans. Deep learning techniques are extremely flexible and can be applied to various data sources, performing at best when information is spatially or temporally well-localized, but still has to be seen in a more global context. However, deep learning approaches are still not suitable for mobile devices (and even less for wearable, ultra-miniaturized IoE devices) because, in their current embodiments, they require massive amounts of computational power.
The MicroLearn project aims to push beyond the current power walls for deep learning  This requires working on algorithms, architecture, circuits as well as design methods for deep learning under extreme constraints: tiny energy buffers (batteries), miniature energy harvesters, low-power and low-cost logic and memory devices. Specifically, the project aims to study and develop the basis for a new generation of deep learning engines operating within a power envelope of a few mW. 

The project’s technical objectives are:
•Reducing the digital computational load, by curtailing the raw digital bandwidth produced by sensors through mixed-signal techniques which mix feature extraction with traditional analog-to-digital conversion.  
•Increasing the energy efficiency of digital computational cores with massively parallel near-threshold accelerators, which retain flexibility and high performance on the application domain, while at the same time significantly reducing power with respect to general-purpose parallel instruction-set processors. 
•Optimizing deep-learning algorithms to target ultra-low power hardware with limited computational and storage capabilities. Focus will be on robust training of classifiers with reduced numerical precision and weight compression techniques. Semi-supervised and unsupervised techniques for ultra-low power devices will also be explored in this context.
•Demonstrating algorithmic, circuit, and architecture innovations by developing real-life demonstrators of full-system prototypes based on advanced fabrication technologies.  
The research questions, appropriate abstractions and architectural concepts corresponding to the technical objectives are investigated in three work-packages, dealing respectively with mixed signal front-end (WP1), near-threshold processing (WP2) and power-aware learning algorithms (WP3). One last work-package (WP4) is dedicated to system integration prototyping and assessment.
Keywords: Deep Learning, Low Power Embedded System, Mixed Analog-Digital Signal Processing, Near-Threshold CMOS Design, Parallel and Heterogeneous Computing

Title: Leveraging next generation 7 Tesla MRI to enhance diagnosis and therapeutic monitoring of diabetic polyneuropathy
Abstract:
This project aims to advance the understanding, diagnosis, and treatment of diabetic polyneuropathy (DPN) by utilizing next-generation 7 Tesla (7T) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) technology combined with advanced image analysis techniques. DPN is one of the most common complications of diabetes, affecting up to 50% of diabetic patients and leading to significant impairments in quality of life. Despite its prevalence, the precise mechanisms underlying nerve damage in DPN remain unclear, particularly the relationship between metabolic factors, nerve microstructure, and functional impairment. The core of this project focuses on leveraging both the enhanced spatial resolution and functional imaging capabilities of 7T MRI to visualize and quantify structural and metabolic changes in peripheral nerves in the lower leg. This recently introduced technology allows for unprecedented visualization of nerve lesions and microvascular structures that are undetectable using standard 3T MRI. The study will also employ computational methods to detect and quantify nerve damage, improving the accuracy and reproducibility of peripheral nerve imaging. A critical component of the project is the exploration of therapeutic interventions, specifically the use of GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R) agonists, a newer class of diabetes drugs known for their neuroprotective effects. The study will investigate how GLP-1R agonist therapy affects nerve structure and function in DPN patients, aiming to identify biomarkers that can predict patient response and optimize treatment strategies.
The research will follow four main objectives (work packages):
1. Develop and optimize a dedicated MRI protocol for high-resolution imaging of peripheral nerves and establish standardized methods for quantifying nerve structure and function.
2. Identify structural and functional changes in the nerves of DPN patients using 7T MRI, distinguishing between different types of diabetes (type 1 and type 2) and control groups.
3. Correlate MRI findings with clinical assessments, such as quantitative sensory testing (QST), serological markers, and nerve conduction studies (NCS), to refine patient stratification, improve diagnostic accuracy, and determine imaging biomarkers of DPN severity.
4. Evaluate the therapeutic impact of GLP-1R agonists on the structural and functional regeneration of nerves by assessing structural and functional nerve changes before and after one month of GLP-1R agonist treatment in individuals with type 2 diabetes, as well as imaging parameters, that allow stratifying therapy success. 
The project will be carried out over two years and includes the recruitment of healthy control subjects, alongside diabetic patients, both with and without DPN, assessed through NCS, at the Geneva University Hospital. Imaging and clinical data will be collected and analyzed to provide a comprehensive view of nerve health and progression in DPN.
This project aims to combine cutting-edge imaging techniques with sophisticated data analysis to yield essential insights into the pathogenesis of DPN. It seeks to identify novel diagnostic biomarkers and explore innovative therapeutic approaches. The outcomes will be shared through peer-reviewed journals, contributing to advancements in clinical practices for the management of DPN and related neuropathies. Moreover, the project will offer an educational platform, fostering the development of researchers and students in the fields of advanced imaging and computational analysis.

Title: New paths in neutrino-nucleus modeling for neutrino-oscillation experiments
Abstract:
The experimental confirmation of neutrino oscillations sparked off an enormous experimental and theoretical interest in the oscillation properties of these particles. Worldwide, several collaborations are working on the extension of our knowledge about neutrino masses, mixing angles and the CP violating phase. The analyses of neutrino-oscillation experiments, however, suffer from the tension between the need for fast and efficient Monte-Carlo simulations and for a detailed microscopic description of the nuclear processes governing the neutrino-nucleus interactions.

The goal of this project is to combine the expertise of the Ghent group in microscopic modeling with the experience of the Geneva partner in experimental analyses using generators. We aim at developing a well-defined algorithm for the description of advanced aspects of neutrino interactions, suitable for implementation in the analysis of current and future experiments. We wish to join forces to develop methods for efficient multivariate MC generation based on neural networks, of direct use in neutrino-oscillation analyses.  The main breakthrough to achieve this purpose will come from recent developments we have made in Artificial Intelligence techniques suitable for particle physics applications. It has been shown in recent work led by the University of Geneva that modern Neural Net technology are able to reduce the time needed to sample complex probability density functions as the one required for the Monte Carlo event generation considerably. 

The combination of cutting-edge neutrino-nucleus interaction models (Ghent) with advanced numerical models (Geneva) will propel the understanding of these interactions forward and will strongly impact the sensitivity of the search of particle-antiparticle asymmetries and other beyond-standard-model phenomena in neutrino oscillations. In this way we will be able to make strong contributions to the future successes in this field.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Neutrino cross-sections, Neutrino oscillations and CP violation

Title: Storytelling and first impressions in face-to-face and algorithm-powered digital interviews
Abstract:
The structured selection interview is a valid predictor of job performance, often featuring so-called past-behavior questions, which invite applicants to tell a story about a past work situation. Applicants’ storytelling responses are often suboptimal. Moreover, it is unclear what they reflect: Mastery of a specific competency, or a more general trait (e.g., charisma). Recently, asynchronous digital interviews have emerged, where applicant behaviour (typically nonverbal) is videorecorded and automatically analysed via machine learning algorithms. Applicants perform worse in these interviews than face-to-face. The cause of this difference is poorly understood; moreover, the criterion validity of digital interviews for predicting job performance is unknown. Analysis of verbal behavior is less advanced, being limited by automatic speech recognition (ASR) and standards for defining content for natural language processing (NLP) analyses. Storytelling in response to past-behavior questions provides a yardstick for “good” content, and could be identified by building state-of-the-art ASR and NLP approaches allowing integration of verbal and nonverbal behavior.
This project is an interdisciplinary collaboration between psychologists and computer scientists with three goals: (1) Understanding how storytelling performance reflects the mastery of a specific competency versus more generic abilities (charisma), (2) understanding processes behind performance differences in technology-mediated versus face-to-face interviews, and (3) improving the verbal pipeline for AI-powered digital interviews by improving ASR and NLP. We start by analyzing existing data on how applicants respond to past-behavior questions in digital versus face-to-face interviews (Studies 1 and 2). In the main study (Study 3), participants complete a work sample to measure task performance, and later are asked to tell what they did in a simulated interview, in either a face-to-face or a digital condition. Participants’ behavior in the interview and work sample will be transcribed and coded to compute criterion validity. Responses in face-to-face and digital conditions will be compared. The data will be used to build an ASR and to extract storytelling using end-to-end machine learning. The planned research will make key contributions to personnel selection research and computer science, in terms of scientific publications, software development and training and education.
Keywords: Selection interview, machine learning, non-verbal behavior, social computing, storytelling, validity, verbal behavior

Title: What is a healthy dairy herd?
Abstract:
Health is a complex and multifaceted concept, influenced by a diversity of factors. Nonetheless, in the field of animal health, particularly in livestock medicine, the prevailing paradigm has been disease-centric and health is often depicted as the absence of disease. This neglects the myriad of factors that contribute to health and narrows down the spectrum of interventions aimed at promoting health.
In the Public Health realm, the determinants of health model has been widely embraced to provide a comprehensive overview of the dynamics of population health. Despite the calls for a more holistic understanding and more systemic interventions in the food production sector, such model is still lacking for livestock health. 
This projects aims to address this critical gap and pioneer the development of a determinants of health model for livestock populations. Drawing upon insights from various data sources and combining advanced analytics and transdisciplinary concepts, we will start by co-creating with relevant stakeholders a determinants of health model for dairy herds. In this process, we will review scientific and grey literature using natural language processing techniques; this will be complemented with the exploration of large language models to identify factors that are associated with dairy health. To ensure the development of a nuanced and comprehensive determinants of health model, dairy health experts and farmers will be interviewed in the subsequent step of the project. We will conduct interviews to investigate the relationships between the different identified indicators and group them into relevant determinants, taking the human determinants of health model as a foundational basis.
Subsequently, we will explore the generalizability of the model to other livestock species and production sectors. This process will involve online focus groups with experts from veal, swine, and poultry sectors. Discussions will evaluate the adaptability of the dairy-tailored model, highlighting sector-specific considerations and management practices. 
Finally, in-person focus group workshops with key stakeholders will be used to explore the potential applications of the model in animal health surveillance. Participants will be asked to identify, from the previous elaborated network of indicators and the determinants of health model, factors that can be monitored and that constitute feasible intervention points in the livestock production systems. This would pave the way for a more structural surveillance concept, moving away from disease-focused monitoring and closer to a health promotion ethos.
The timing of this project is very pertinent and a determinants of health model for livestock holds promise to be influential in various dimensions. For example, it can be highly relevant to inform the development of future agendas for the sustainability and transition of food production systems. In addition, using a common framework to better understand human and animal health will foster a shared understanding of health, which is critical for the successful operationalization of integrated approaches to health, such as One Health. 
In summary, this innovative project will develop a pioneering determinants of health model for livestock population, combining the use of artificial intelligence techniques with transdisciplinary-inspired methodologies. Such model would represent a paradigm shift in the field of animal health, from its current disease-centric view to a more holistic and resilience-promotion concept.
Keywords: Determinants of health, Livestock, Prevention, Stakeholders, Sustainability

Title: Polypheny-DDI: A Flexible Polystore-based Distributed Data Infrastructure
Abstract:
In recent years, data-driven research has established itself as the fourth pillar in the spectrum of scientific methods alongside theory, empiric research, and computer-based simulation. In various scientific disciplines, increasingly large amounts of –both structured and unstructured– data are being generated or existing data collections that have originally been isolated from each other are being linked in order to gain new insights. The process of generating knowledge from raw data is called Data Science or Data Analytics.

The entire data analytics pipeline is quite complex, and most work focuses on the actual data analysis (using machine learning or statistical methods) while largely neglecting the other elements of the pipeline. This is particularly the case for all aspects related to data management, storage, processing, and retrieval – even though these challenges actually play an essential role. A Distributed Data Infrastructure (DDI) supports a large variety of data management features as demanded by the data analytics pipeline. However, data science projects are typically very heterogeneous in terms of data models, access characteristics, and performance expectations in a way that exceeds current DDI systems. Moreover, in order to integrate, continuously update, and query data from various heterogeneous applications and to address the needs of data science applications, DDIs must overcome inherent structural heterogeneity and fragmentation of the data to be analyzed.

Recently, polystore databases have gained attention because they help overcome these limitations by allowing data to be stored in one system, yet in different formats and data models and by offering one joint query language. In past work, we have developed Polypheny-DB, a distributed polystore that integrates several different data models and heterogeneous data stores. Polypheny-DB goes beyond most existing polystores and even supports data accesses with mixed workloads (e.g., OLTP and OLAP). However, polystores are limited to rather simple object models, static data and exact queries. When individual data items follow a complex inherent structure and consist of several heterogeneous parts between which dedicated constraints exist, when the access goes beyond exact Boolean queries, when data is not static but continuously produced, and/or when objects need to be preserved in multiple versions, then polystores quickly reach their limits.

At the same time, these are typical requirements for data management within a data analytics pipeline. Examples are scientific instruments that continuously produce new data as data streams; social network analysis that requires support for complex object models including structured and unstructured content; data produced by imaging devices that requires sophisticated similarity search support, or frequently changing objects that are subject to time-dependent analyses.

The objective of the Polypheny-DDI project is to seamlessly combine the functionality of a polystore database with that of a distributed data infrastructure to meet the requirements of data science applications. It will focus on i.) supporting complex composite object models and enforcing constraints between the constituent parts; ii.) supporting similarity search in multimedia content, and iii.) supporting continuous data streams and temporal/multiversion data.

The project will design, implement, and evaluate models and system components for an advanced polystore-based distributed data infrastructure. From a systems perspective, we will extend the polystore system Polypheny-DB towards Polypheny-DDI, leveraging and combining expertise of the research group on polystores, multimedia data management and retrieval, and data stream management. The Polypheny-DDI system will be released under an open source license.
Keywords: Data Streams, Distributed Data Management, Multimedia Data Management, Polystore Database

Title: Stabilization of fully inorganic lead halide perovskite nanomaterials
Abstract:
Lead halide perovskite nanomaterials offer an attractive and sustainable route for developing efficient photovoltaic, photocatalytic and light emitting devices, given their low cost and low CO2 emission manufacturing and excellent tunable optoelectronic properties. However, the poor stability of perovskites has halted technology implementation. We aim to understand and address perovskite degradation to enable cheap and environmentally friendly optoelectronic production. Achieving this is urgently needed for accelerating the energy transition and building the sustainable future our society requires.
The primary and overarching question we hope to address with this proposal is: what causes material degradation in perovskite nanomaterials and how can we avoid it? We hypothesize that perovskite degradation involves charge transfer reactions leading to material reduction/oxidation. This is intrinsically an electrochemical problem, and its degradation thermodynamics is given by the relative energetic positions of the conduction and valence bands and decomposition redox potentials. We aim to leverage thermodynamic stability by shifting the band edge and decomposition redox potentials through material nanoengineering.
To guide our experimental pursuit of stabilization strategies we will use machine learning assisted density functional theory modelling. Once promising perovskite nanocrystal candidates are selected, they will be synthesized, and we will use in-situ electrochemical absorption and emission spectroscopy to measure their band edges and decomposition potential positions. This research will contribute to our understanding of perovskite degradation to enable cheap and environmentally friendly optoelectronic production.

Title: The Linguistic Capacities of Neural Networks: A Perspective from the Philosophy of Animal Psychology
Abstract:
The project proposed here attempts to apply concepts and distinctions that have been developed in the philosophy of psychology as well as the philosophy of mind to neural machine translation systems. There seem to be no principled reasons why this application should not be possible, as the relevant abilities should be ascribed based on the same criteria, irrespective of whether the being in question is a human infant, a non-human animal or a computer algorithm. Still, some of the criteria might have to be extended or reconceived, as the kind of being of computer algorithms does differ strongly from that of living beings.

If successful, the project would provide a highly innovative perspective on the linguistic and hence cognitive sophistication of neural machine translations systems. The results of this project could then provide the ground for a novel angle on what it still takes for AI research to reach strong AI. Furthermore, it could invite a reassessment of what it means in general to have linguistic abilities.

Of central importance for the project is the fact that neural machine translation systems defy Searle's famous Chinese Room Thought Experiment. Rather than merely correlating strings in the target language with strings in the source language, neural machine translation systems infer their own representations of semantic relations from the training data with which they are provided. It is the guiding research hypothesis of this project that this marks a watershed with regard to the linguistic and hence cognitive capacities that these systems should be credited with, and that the conceptual tools from the philosophy of mind and psychology are particularly suited to evince this: The project conjectures that, while it is misguided to ascribe human-level linguistic competence to these algorithms, it is true that these algorithms, other than traditional SMT-systems, are on equal footing with young children when it comes to linguistic abilities.
Keywords: AI, Deep Learning, Machine Translation, Neural Networks, Philosophy of Language, Philosophy of Mind, Philosophy of Psychology, Wittgenstein
