Title: Data-driven Trans-topological Design Exploration of Funicular Structures
Abstract:
This proposal provides a follow-up application to an SNSF Doc.Mobility project that is currently under development by the same title. The project is motivated to leverage the nascent and growing class of Geometric Deep Learning approaches from Machine Learning (ML) to support the trans-topology structural design exploration of discretised structural networks based on funicular form-finding (DSFF) during the conceptual design stage (CDS). Although DSFF are efficient structural systems, their design is challenging because DSFF are highly constrained systems whereby design feasibility, variables, and goals, such as preferences for the geometry and force distribution, can be difficult to reconcile, even for experts. The recent popularisation of ML in structural design has led to some promising developments, with researchers applying ML support design exploration according to specific goals. However, the majority of approaches lack support for the modelling of trans-topology design space—designs with variable number of elements, such as nodes and members (edges), and irregular nodal connectivity that lack the familiar properties as common systems of coordinates, global parameterisation that conventional vector-based approaches in ML depend. Consequently, the opportunity to compare or learn from DSFFs has largely remained unmet, much less to make predictions over them or to generate them directly from performance goals. 
These limitations motivate the applicant’s doctoral research, and the applicant’s initial SNSF Doc.Mobility proposal to combine Geometric Deep Learning—methods for learning form non-Euclidean datastructures like DSFF—with various advanced ML approaches to support (I) the direct generation of DFSS designs from performance goals, or from the blending of existing designs, and (II) the iterative refinement of input DFSSs according to select performance goals. Technically, the two parts respectively combined GDL approaches with (Graph) Representation Learning and Generative Modelling, and Deep Reinforcement Learning. Promising results were developed from the fellowship, which provided technical proof-of-concept demonstrations for all initially proposed tasks, along with foundational contributions that support better learning on mesh-based discrete datastructures. However, there remains outstanding limitations that reduce the usability of the research. This follow-up application is motivated to provide improvement and completion to select under-developed and under-performing tasks in both parts by focusing on their common challenges.  In particular, the key focus is to improve the implementation’s robust handling of infeasible or unfamiliar inputs, which this follow-up will address with relevant specialised adaptations in both parts.  The proposed follow-up will contribute technical ML knowledge and techniques supporting the application of the novel combination of ML methods to structural design, especially strategies supporting the use of ML to solve inverse design problems mapping performance to design, where the handling of infeasible targets is an acute concern.   It will also provide a meaningful completion to the initial fellowship, resulting in applications conducive to versatile design scenarios. Finally, the combined research efforts will have broad implications for the field of Architecture, Engineering and Construction, supporting the direct generation of DSFF and the recommendation of design operations on DSFF according to specific design goals in a trans-topology design space.
Keywords: Equilibrium Shell Structures, Geometric Deep Learning, Inverse Model, Machine Learning, Reinforcement Learning, Structural Design Exploration, Structural Form-finding, Structural Optimisation

Title: Rational Design and Development of uPAR-targetingRadioligands for Theragnostic Application
Abstract:
Background: Radioligand therapy (RLT) involves the intravenous administration of radioligands that specifically target tumor lesions to damage cancer cells through the emission of particle radiation. This concept has been successfully applied for metastasized neuroendocrine tumors and prostate cancer. The development of new RLTs is needed to enable the treatment of other cancer types at advanced stages when other treatment modalities are no longer applicable. Our goal is to design, synthesize and evaluate novel radioligands for RLT of cancers that express the urokinase-type plasminogen activator receptor (uPAR), a promising target expressed across multiple tumor types. This goal is to be achieved through rational design using molecular modeling and artificial intelligence (AI) enabling the development of radioligands that effectively treat tumors without damaging healthy tissue.
Status of Own Research: Prof. C. Müller brings extensive experience in radiopharmaceutical development and preclinical research. She has been at the forefront of developing novel tumor-targeting radioligands modified with an albumin binder to enhance their pharmacokinetic profiles. One of her notable accomplishments was the clinical translation of a novel radioligand for targeting the prostate-specific membrane antigen into an on-going Phase I study, where it is being evaluated for the treatment of metastasized prostate cancer. More recently, she has developed uPAR-targeting radioligands, derived from the known AE105 peptide structure, which have been modified with an albumin-binding entity to enhance blood circulation and, consequently, tumor uptake. Dr. X. Deupi brings extensive expertise in analyzing the relationship between protein sequence, structure, dynamics and function. His research integrates molecular modeling, data science and AI methods to interpret complex datasets. Within the field of radiopharmaceutical development, his group utilizes computational approaches to guide ligand optimization prior to their experimental validation in vitro and in vivo. Over recent years, Dr. Deupi has supported the rational design of radioligands targeting various clinically relevant proteins, including G protein-coupled receptors, the angiotensin converting enzyme-2 and the uPAR. His contributions demonstrated how computational techniques can validate biological insights and direct structural modifications to optimize radioligand binding modes, enhancing their suitability for RLT.
Goal of the Project: Our goal in this project is to develop novel radioligands for targeting uPAR-positive tumors and enable their use for RLT of metastasized cancer. Therefore, it is essential to design radioligands with functional groups that optimize tissue distribution, ensuring specific accumulation in tumor lesions while minimizing uptake in normal tissue. Such characteristics will be crucial to enable efficient and safe RLT, ultimately facilitating clinical translation. To achieve this goal, we will use molecular modeling and AI tools to rationally design new uPAR-targeting ligands. These AI tools will incorporate both existing and newly acquired preclinical data, along with information from the literature. The proposed radioligands will be synthesized and preclinically evaluated, both in vitro and in tumor-bearing mice, to obtain feedback for further optimization. 
Expected Value of the Proposal: The success of RLT in treating neuroendocrine and prostate cancers shows its potential to control the disease and improve patients’ quality of life. Developing new RLT concepts applicable to a broader range of cancer types would allow more patients to benefit from this type of therapy. uPAR is a particularly promising target for advancing RLT, as its expression increases with disease progression and remains mostly absent in healthy tissue. If this project is successful, the top candidate among these radioligands is likely be translated into first-in-human clinical studies.
Keywords: AI, Molecular Modeling, Radionuclide Therapy, Radiopharmaceutical, Rational Drug Design, Tumor Therapy, cancer therapy, radioligand, radioligand therapy, urokinase receptor

Title: Interpretable Machine Learning for Chemistry-Guided Reaction Optimization
Abstract:
The optimization of chemical reactions is one of the core elements of synthetic chemistry. Despite this, it mainly relies on ineffective lengthy trial-and-error campaigns. This research proposal aims to develop new machine learning- and data science-based approaches that can accelerate the optimization of chemical reactions without the need for large experimental data sets. The implementation of optimization algorithms has the potential to fast-track research and give scientists more time to focus on creative tasks that lead to innovation and progress. 
Specifically, a new Bayesian optimization (BO) algorithm will be developed that incorporates chemical domain knowledge, extracted from the model itself, by applying techniques from interpretable machine learning. This will make BO more efficient and allow it to be conducted in large, high-dimensional, and weakly defined search spaces that are typically encountered in the optimization of chemical reactions. Furthermore, a strategy for virtual ligand optimization based on molecular heat maps is introduced. The developed algorithms will be applied in the optimization of a stereoconvergent metallaphotoredox-catalyzed synthesis of valuable chiral beta-amino acids. As showcased in this real-world example, these new optimization strategies will allow researchers to accelerate the often highly time-consuming optimization of chemical reactions.
Keywords: Asymmetric Catalysis, Bayesian Optimization, Data Chemistry, Ligand Design, Reaction Optimization

Title: Harmonic decomposition of the 3D morphology of surfaces for simulating the growth of soft shells and plates
Abstract:
Growth processes of living tissues, such as skin, brain tissue and petals, are caused by environmental stimuli such as temperature, light, humidity or electrical currents. These stimuli act unevenly on the tissue sheets and cause different growth in size and volume. The differential growth of the thin elastic sheet leads to curvatures and thus changes in the shape of the sheet. Recent developments in materials science have made it possible to fabricate structures that exhibit similar shape change capabilities. However, understanding of such shape changes is limited because most studies do not consider hierarchical aspects of growth or systematic geometric decompositions of such shapes.

In this project, I will study the growth of thin elastic plates and shells using new harmonic analysis methods to decompose open and closed 3D surfaces. First, I plan to add more topologies, such as cylindrical or annular surfaces, to the current mathematical analysis methods. Then, I will use these methods to find simpler approaches for the 4D printing of such structures. Finally, I will provide general mathematical solution methods for growth problems that use computers to answer how a specific geometric shape can be transformed into another shape. 

In addition to the direct benefit of 4D printing of structures, a better understanding of growth processes has numerous other applications: from a better understanding of biological growth in flowers and tissues, to applications in artificial muscles, robotics, and metal forming. In addition, harmonic decomposition analysis methods are used for many applications, such as the classification of microstructures, geological particles such as rocks and gravel, and medical imaging using machine learning. So my new methods will directly benefit these research areas.
Keywords: geometric programming, growth, morphogenesis, surface parameterisation

Title: Enhanced Infrastructure Management Using Data Sensing and Computer-Aided Stochastic Interpretation
Abstract: Monitoring the structural characteristic responses  bridges and buildings can help understanding their behavior, detecting anomalies, and quantifying the need for rehabilitation. During the last decades, measuring instruments have evolved to a point where cheap and reliable sensing technologies are now commercially available. The bottleneck is related to data interpretation because the amount of data involved is so large that it is financially and practically unfeasible to process it manually. This project addresses three aspects of this challenge: (1) Develop a self-learning anomaly detection methodology that does not require human intervention, (2) Propose a framework for quantifying what are the admissible modeling uncertainties for satisfying performance targets, (3) Investigate the robustness of Bayesian updating in the context of large-scale civil structures. Solving these challenges requires developing synergies between data sensing, stochastic data-interpretation and infrastructure management. In addition to these theoretical research axes a fourth objective is to apply and validate the methodologies in (1-3) using data obtained on large-scale structures and networks.
Keywords: Bayesian networks, Data analytics, Infrastructure management, Machine learning, Probabilistic methods, Sensing

Title: Delineating Trees in Noisy 2D Images and 3D Image-Stacks
Abstract:
Tree-like structures appear at many different scales and in many different contexts. They can be micrometer scale dendrites in light microscopy image-stacks, centimeter-scale blood vessels in retinal scans, or meter-scale road networks in aerial images. Extracting them automatically and robustly is therefore of fundamental relevance to many scientific disciplines. However, even though the topic has received sustained attention ever since the inception of the field of Computer Vision, both robustness and automation remain elusive. Fully automated techniques exist but require very clean data; substantial amounts of manual intervention is required for any other kind.

In this project, we will therefore develop a fully automated approach to addressing these shortcomings. We will first develop an approach to finding optimal trees that accounts both for global image and geometric properties. We will then implement a practical algorithm to build near-optimal ones in an acceptably short time, even though the underlying problem is closely related to one known to be NP-Hard.
Keywords: Computer Vision, Delineation, Dendritic Trees

Title: Automatic Dataflow Modeling for HPC Applications
Abstract:
Whether it is climate change, artificial intelligence or quantum physics, scientific progress today requires ever increasing computational power. New, powerful supercomputers are being continuously designed to fulfill the practically boundless demand for high performance computing. Modern supercomputers are complex, heterogeneous systems containing a staggering number of processing units working in parallel, ranging from commodity processors like those in personal computers to powerful accelerators specifically engineered towards scientific use. Using such systems is challenging, as the computational work must be divided among many processing units. On these systems, the task usually requiring the most time and energy is transferring data to, from, and between the distributed memory of these processing units, as well as accessing the local memory of each individual processing unit. 

Therefore, ensuring that the data moves as little as possible is paramount to achieving good performance and 
low energy consumption, and even the decision of which processing unit configuration to select is difficult without a detailed understanding of both application and hardware. Recent work shows how programs expressing dataflow explicitly can be optimized to reduce the runtime up to eight times compared to solving the same problem without a data-centric approach. By creating an intermediate representation called a Stateful Dataflow Multigraph (SDFG) and applying transformations to this SDFG locality is significantly improved. Having dataflow be explicit in the code requires a complete rewrite for most applications.The difficulty and productivity loss in rewriting entire scientific programs, result in optimizations needing a data-centric representation remaining out of reach for most scientific endeavors.

In this project, we wish to generate data-centric representations of arbitrary parallel programs - similar to SDFGs - to allow many locality-improving optimizations to be applied even to applications without explicit dataflow information. We will expand polyhedral loop analysis and taint analysis techniques to create dependency hypotheses and determine which code regions benefit most from optimizing locality.  We will measure instrumented versions of these applications in various configurations to test these dependency hypotheses and focus on critical performance hotspots. After iterating this process to refine our hypotheses, we should ideally create a complete SDFG based on dependence models for the application and allow the optimization process to start. Even an incomplete collection of SDFGs for parts of an application should allow significant optimizations to locality.

This kind of analysis has never been attempted, and would not be possible without leveraging cutting edge research in dataflow programming and performance modeling. It requires expanding state-of-the-art performance measurement and instrumentation techniques. The main challenge is creating a code analysis method to incorporate static and dynamic information to create SDFGs for parts of the code and then iteratively linking these together if possible. Developers could take advantage of optimizations previously restricted to dataflow programming and make informed decisions about which hardware configuration is best for their application without needing either a performance expert or a complete rewrite of their application.
Keywords: Data flow, Performance analysis, Performance modeling

Title: Efficient high-dimensional estimation and differential privacy
Abstract:
High-dimensional estimation problems form the mathematical foundation for a variety of fundamental machine-learning tasks, including regression on predictive data, clustering of geometric data, and community detection in large-scale graph data.
Past years have witnessed dramatic advances in our algorithmic understanding of these problems, particularly in the robust estimation setting,
where an unbounded adversary can alter a certain fraction of the dataset arbitrarily.
Much of the progress in this setting has been enabled by the sum-of-squares method and the proof-to-algorithm paradigm.
Recent works suggest that extending this paradigm could achieve similar progress for efficient estimation in privacy-preserving settings,
where algorithms operate on sensitive data and must ensure that their outputs do not compromise private information.

This project aims to develop a unified framework for designing efficient differentially-private algorithms applicable to a broad range of high-dimensional estimation tasks involving predictive data, geometric data, and graph data.
Recent extensions of the proof-to-algorithm paradigm to the privacy-preserving setting will serve as a starting point.
The project seeks to create new tools for identifying and reasoning about inherent trade-offs between computational efficiency and privacy.
Finally, the project seeks to leverage insights from designing polynomial-time private estimation algorithms to develop practically efficient private estimation techniques.

Title: Microenvironmental orchestration of phenotype plasticity in colorectal cancer
Abstract:
Background and rationale:
Recent work on colorectal cancer (CRC) has demonstrated that cancer cells are inherently “plastic” meaning that they can switch their phenotype without underlying genetic alterations. It is to be assumed that phenotype switches occur in response to tumour microenvironment (TME) stimuli and altered host conditions, and consequently that phenotypic plasticity is the primary mode of cancer cell adaptation during tumour evolution.

Objectives and aims:
My primary objective is to determine the mechanisms of molecular cross-talk within the CRC TME that lead to cancer phenotype switching. I aim to establish a computational model to interpret spatial transcriptomics (ST) data, and then to use the model to determine how tumour cell genetics combine with microenvironmental cell type composition and distribution, and related TME gene expression programmes, to produce tumour cell gene expression and histopathological phenotype. Further, I aim to establish if and how treatment reprograms tumour cell phenotypes.

Methods:
I will primarily use computational methods to interrogate ST and matched digital pathology (DP) data from well-characterised CRC cohorts, including metastases, where there is existing genomic data. Matched ST and DP data simultaneously measure cell type, spatial location and gene expression phenotype of 100,000s of cells across tissue sections and genetic alterations can be inferred from ST data. I will construct and validate a machine learning model that integrates microenvironmental and cancer genetic data to predict cancer cell gene expression phenotypes. Post hoc analysis of the model will determine the role of the TME in controlling cancer cell plasticity.

Expected results and impact:
My project should establish how the TME controls cancer cell gene expression, potentially indicating promising directions for new TME-directed therapies to control CRC. In addition, it will reveal fundamental new biology about the cellular cross-talk that regulates colorectal cancer cell phenotypes.

Title: Set-theoretic Foundations of Computation with Applications to Satisfiability Modulo Theories
Abstract:
The starting point of our research is the state of the art in two areas of theoretical and applied computer science. 

The first of these areas is classical computational complexity theory, which is concerned with the classification of algorithmic problems (encoded as countable sets) in classes of problems determined by certain abstract computing machine models. To fully classify a decision problem one must prove two facts. First, one must show that the problem is solvable by the abstract computer defining the class. Second, one must show that solving any other problem in the class reduces to solving the decision problem. It has been observed that the latter is typically much harder since one needs to encode any abstract computer of the class in some decision problem while in the former one only needs to provide an instance of an abstract computer. 

In this project, we want to demonstrate that the encoding of such abstract computers may be simplified using linguistic formalisms developed in the theory of verification of sets, multisets and arrays. A key insight from verification is that checking the truth value of sentences in  these formalisms reduces to checking the truth value of sentences of the theory of arithmetic without multiplication (the so-called theory of linear integer arithmetic). By enhancing these formalisms with non-linear relations, we hope to demonstrate how to encode a wide range of machines belonging to complexity classes ranging from NP to NEXPTIME. 

The second of the areas of interest is constraint solving as it is practised in the area of satisfiability modulo theories (SMT). While developing extensions of linear arithmetic we hope to answer some long-standing problems about the computational complexity of deciding theories of interest for SMT. At the moment, there exist a number of fragments of non-linear arithmetic whose decision problem lies between NP and NEXPTIME, but for which a precise complexity classification is not known. We expect that this classification will have an impact in the practice of constraint solving since NEXPTIME is one of the first classes known to contain problems that are not solvable in polynomial time. 

If time permits we will experimentally validate our results as well as develop heuristic principles to decide on the feasibility of automating SMT problems.
Keywords: Automated Reasoning, Logic in Computer Science, Satisfiability Modulo Theories, Theory of Computation

Title: Beyond novelty: Everyday AI use in medical education and practice
Abstract:
The projected research aims to explore the integration of ‘artificial intelligence’ (AI) into everyday professional activities in healthcare, particularly medical imaging in cancer care. It will examine AI’s impact on clinical practices and healthcare education, addressing challenges related to explainability and ethics, and seeking to provide an in-depth understanding of how AI transforms professional practices in healthcare. Grounded in the sociological approach of ethnomethodology and conversation analysis (EM/CA), the project will investigate how AI is integrated into routine medical activities and teaching. The research aims to move beyond novelty and exoticism in social studies of AI, offering empirical contributions to discussions on everyday AI use. Our state-of-the-art review highlights the interplay between novelty and routine in technology studies, emphasizing the need to study AI as a social phenomenon. It identifies knowledge gaps in understanding the routinization of AI in medical practices and the practical activities involving various forms of AI, and underscores the importance of bottom-up ethnographies of ordinary medical activities, focusing on the integration of AI systems. Responding to these needs, the project is driven by two interrelated research questions: (1) How is medical experts’ work with AI in education and decision-making organized in situ and in real time? (2) How do participants orient to, and make mutually relevant, the instructional character of these settings? In addition to the applicant involved as a PI, the project involves three team members: two postdoctoral researchers and one research assistant. Our long-term collaborations with image-based personalized medicine experts at HES-SO and Lausanne University Hospital (CHUV) have laid a strong foundation for this research, serving as a springboard for exploring issues of broader sociological and societal relevance.
 
In terms of methodology, our research will employ EM/CA to study the detailed organization of social activities involving AI in healthcare. It will use ethnographic fieldwork, video-based observation, and in-depth interviews to understand the integration of AI in medical practices. The research is divided into six work packages, each with defined goals and deliverables, scheduled to start in March 2026 and conclude in February 2030. We will begin with a comprehensive literature review of relevant research in the sociology of technology and image-based personalized medicine utilizing AI. In parallel, we will engage in ethnographic fieldwork to observe and understand the activities and tools used in medical settings, focusing on AI integration. The subsequent studies will be grounded in collecting and analysing video recordings of educational and decision-making activities involving AI-based tools. Through detailed analysis of video data, we will identify recurrent phenomena and practices specific to teaching and working with AI in personalized cancer care. The findings will be disseminated through presentations at conferences and publications in relevant journals, contributing to broader scientific discussions. Our research will provide insights into the situated details of integration of AI in healthcare, with results relevant to educational curricula, public debates on AI, and policy design. By advancing the understanding of how AI technologies are embedded in routine professional work, the project will contribute to the sociology of AI and medical education. Ultimately, the research will help establish a sociological conception of AI technologies that support human expertise and care, moving beyond their novelty to become integral parts of everyday medical practices.

Title: Open-Set 3D Scene Understanding for Functional 3D Scene Representations
Abstract:
In the last decade, significant progress has been made in 3D scene understanding to detect, perceive and segment objects and people in real-world 3D scenes. These functionalities are relevant for deploying and training autonomous agents, as well as synthesizing virtual humans in interactive worlds for AR/VR applications or gaming. Existing methods typically recognize furniture elements (e.g., chairs, tables, and beds) and building elements (e.g., walls, floors, and doors), which serve as a proxy representation for modeling scene interactions (e.g., sitting on a chair, opening a door, looking at a screen). In fact, more fine-grained interactions and functionalities (pressing a button, turning a knob) are not possible since existing work generally operates on rather coarse 3D scene representations (point clouds, meshes) which typically fail to represent such fine details.
The goal of this research project is to develop new 3D scene representations that directly incorporate fine-grained functionalities and interactive elements without loss of relevant functional details. These functional 3D scene representations go beyond currently used object- and scene-level representations which can only serve as a coarse approximation of possible scene interactions.
This objective will be achieved via multiple intermediate goals:
First, we utilize the zero-shot capabilities of  visual-language models for detecting scene functionalities from images.  Then, inspired by recent advancement in neural rendering, we develop an approach for representing functional scene elements as a set of geometric primitives with associated interaction labels. Lastly, we explore the use of human-scene interactions via visual-linguistic modalities to further enhance the proposed functional 3D scene representation.
Keywords: 3D scene understanding, 3D vision, computer vision, instance segmentation, scene representation, semantic segmentation

Title: Polarimetry to bridge the gap between in-situ and remote sensing observations of atmospheric aerosols (BISAR)
Abstract:
Aerosols, tiny particles in the size range from a few nanometers to tens of micrometers, are ubiquitous in the atmosphere. Their chemical, physical and optical properties are highly variable in space and time as they have a rather short atmospheric lifetime and originate from many different natural and anthropogenic sources. Two major environmental impacts of atmospheric aerosols are their adverse effects on human health and their contributions to climate change, the latter being driven by radiative forcing from aerosol-radiation and aerosol-cloud interactions. Understanding and constraining aerosol impacts often requires columnar or global scale observations, where ground-based and space-borne remote sensing approaches come into play. Polarimetry, i.e. measurements of angular and polarization dependence of light scattering by particles, is the central tool to enable aerosol property retrievals from remote sensing data. However, the inverse problem can be ill-posed, thus typically requiring simplifying assumptions. Furthermore, independent validation against e.g. detailed and accurate in-situ measurements is difficult.
The major objective of this project is to bridge the gap between in-situ and remote sensing measurements by advancing approaches to retrieve aerosol physical and chemical properties from polarimetric measurements widely applied in aerosol remote sensing. New polar nephelometers were developed and characterized to provide in-situ measurements of light scattering as a function of angle, wavelength and polarization. Existing traditional retrievals were adapted for this measurement space as well as new machine learning based approaches. Extensive laboratory experiments provided polarized phase functions of various pure and mixed aerosol types along with independent physical, chemical and auxiliary optical characterization. These comprehensive optical data sets served to test forward calculations of different complexity levels and assessing polarimetric retrieval algorithms under well-constrained conditions. Field deployment at sites equipped with in-situ and remote sensing capabilities provided polarized phase functions and physico-chemical properties of different atmospheric aerosol types with to goal to compare with remote sensing observations and to validate polarimetric property retrievals and aerosol typing.
Retrieving light absorption from polarimetric is a major challenge. Results depend on aerosol representation chosen for the optical kernel and considerable systematic bias can occur. This study demonstrated using laboratory experiments that considering particle morphology of black carbon aggregates can make unbiased absorption retrieval possible. Applying these findings to a field data set demonstrated that treating black carbon containing particles as a separate non-spherical component in the aerosol retrieval can provide considerably improved absorption retrieval compared to commonly applied retrievals that assume spherical shape.
The research on the aerosol light scattering phase function and the development and assessment of deep learning based retrieval algorithms is, on the one hand, fundamental, on the other hand, it directly serves research needs driven by sustained expansion of atmospheric in-situ and remote sensing observation networks and corresponding efforts to integrate data chains all the way to real-time assimilation of measurement data and derived products in e.g. atmospheric composition forecasts.
Keywords: aerosol radiation interaction, aerosol retrieval, atmospheric aerosol, polarimetry, remote sensing

Title: Importance sampling for large-scale unsupervised learning (ISUL)
Abstract:
This project aims at investigating two key issues for the training of large neural networks over large scale training sets. All the developed techniques will be benchmarked on standard image classification and object-detection data-sets, on pedestrian detection and re-identification, and on controlled data-sets produced over the course of the project.

We structure this proposal in two sub-projects. The first will investigate a general strategy based on importance sampling to deal with very large training sets. While the current common approach to learning is the stochastic gradient descent, very few efforts have been invested in the choice of the ``re-sampling'' strategy. Virtually every state-of-the-art method uses a uniform visit of the samples over the learning, without prioritizing according to computation done previously.

Our objective is to develop a general framework to apply importance-sampling to gradient-descent and other optimization schemes so that they concentrate the computational effort over problematic and informative samples.

The second sub-project will investigate a central, and currently poorly addressed, practical issue when using large neural networks, which is the meta-optimization of the network structure itself. We are interested in studying approaches to avoid the requirement for the standard and computational intensive combination of meta-parameter grid-search and hand-tuning.
Keywords: Computer vision, Deep learning, Machine learning, Pattern recognition

Title: Protein quality control and degradation from the endoplasmic reticulum
Abstract:
Summary of the research plan
Background-The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is the major biosynthetic organelle of nucleated cells. It produces lipids, oligosaccharides and about 40% of the eukaryotic cell’s proteome. The ER contains molecular chaperones and folding enzymes that welcome nascent polypeptide chains and assist their conformational maturation. The structure and assembly of newly synthesized proteins is checked by quality control factors that prolong ER retention and folding attempts of proteins exposing misfolded domains, hydrophobic patches, charged residues in intra-membrane domains, unpaired cysteines or peptidyl-prolyl bonds in the wrong configuration. Terminally misfolded polypeptides are degraded to prevent ER clogging with aberrant gene products. Most of the polypeptides entering the ER are covalently modified at asparagine side chains with a conserved (from yeast to humans) oligosaccharide composed of 2 N-acetylglucosamine, 9 mannose and 3 glucose residues. In the last two decades, it has been established that sequential removal of terminal glucose and mannose residues from protein-bound oligosaccharides determines the engagement of molecular chaperones and folding enzymes such as oxidoreductases and peptidyl-prolyl cis/trans isomerases that catalyze rate-limiting steps of protein folding programs. Oligosaccharide processing also determines interruption of futile folding attempts and selection of terminally misfolded proteins for clearance from the ER, which requires translocation into the cytosol for degradation by the ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS) via ER-associated degradation (ERAD), or segregation in ER subdomains that do eventually vesiculate and are removed from cells via ER-to-lysosome-associated degradation (ERLAD).

Objectives-We aim at dissecting the pathways activated by mammalian cells to remove polypeptides that fail attainment of the native structure in the ER. Emphasis will be given on establishing the mechanisms that regulate segregation of misfolded polypeptides within specialized ER subdomains that are eventually subject to lysosomal clearance. 

Methods-The mechanisms of selection of misfolded proteins for clearance will be investigated with a series of model proteins derived from disease-causing mutant variants of alpha1-antitrypsin and will be validated by testing the fate of other folding-defective polypeptides such as disease-causing beta-secretase and pro-collagen variants. Model proteins are designed to explore the role of protein-bound oligosaccharides, polymerization and aggregation propensities, membrane anchoring and localization in sub-compartments of the early secretory pathway including the ER itself, ER exit sites, intermediate compartment. Experiments will be performed in cultured mammalian cells, including patient-derived cell lines. Genome editing (CRISPR/Cas technology) will be used to generate cells lacking genes-of-interest or expressing tagged versions of endogenous proteins-of-interest. The vast expertise and technological knowledge available in the lab, crucial tools such as conformation and polymer-specific antibodies specific for the model proteins under investigation, new-generation protein trafficking reporters developed in our lab for steady state and time-resolved visualization of intracellular transport routes in confocal light scanning microscopy and in transmission electron microscopy, will be implemented with deep learning approaches, also developed in our lab, for unbiased and automated segmentation and classification of fluorescence and electron microscopy images, which are instrumental for quantitative assessment of experimental results.  

Expected results and impact-We will investigate the features of defective gene products that determine engagement of ERAD or ERLAD for destruction. We will mechanistically characterize the ERLAD pathways engaged by clients with different topology, localization, chemico-physical features. Client-specific pathways likely rely on different ER-phagy receptors and likely use different transport routes for delivery to the endolysosomal compartments (i.e., micro- ER-phagy, macro-ER-phagy, LC3-dependent vesicular delivery). We will establish when, and to what extent, ERAD and ERLAD pathways collaborate to control efficient clearance from cells of aberrant gene products. We will establish new technology for time-course monitoring of the events under investigation in light and electron microscopy and for their quantitative assessment. Understanding the mechanisms and identifying the regulators of protein clearance will offer diagnostic and prognostic disease indicators; their modulation is expected to offer therapeutic opportunities in protein misfolding diseases.

Title: Multiscale dynamics of dog rabies elimination
Abstract:
Multiscale dynamics of dog rabies elimination 

The aim of this project is to elucidate the contributions of population vaccination coverage and the vaccine immunity of individual dogs on the interruption of dog rabies transmission; determine the role of population density of dogs in the transmission of rabies; and identify the optimal frequency and coverage of vaccination campaigns. The proposed project will help define the most cost-effective dog mass vaccination strategies for rabies elimination in Africa and Asia. Rabies is a zoonotic disease that is responsible for substantial human mortality in Asia and Africa, but recent studies have suggested that elimination is possible.  

We hypothesize that the population level aspects of vaccination coverage contribute more to the dynamics of dog rabies elimination than the kinetics of protective antibodies within individual dogs; and that the transmission of dog rabies is density dependent below a threshold of 100 dogs per km2.

Approach: In 2012 and 2013 we vaccinated 18,200 and 20,000 dogs in N’Djaména, Chad, reaching a population coverage of more than 70%. Dog rabies incidence dropped from one rabid dog per week prior to the mass vaccination to less than one rabid dog in eight months afterwards. The last rabid dog was recorded in January 2014.  Because of the multiple scales (between dogs and within dogs) in rabies transmission and immune dynamics, this unique data set will be used for comparative mathematical modeling approaches with individual based (contact networks and machine learning) and population-based models. First, we use dog to dog and dog to human contact network data, collected by observational studies, to extrapolate individual dog contact networks to a citywide contact network as a basis for rabies transmission models. Next we will develop metapopulation models that extend an existing compartmental model into 4 or 5 interconnected sub-models, based on the spatial heterogeneity of dog populations in N’Djaména, with assumptions of both frequency-dependent and density-dependent contact rates. Finally we will develop an individual dog based machine learning model and simulate the kinetics of protective antibodies in new populations. The three sets of models will be calibrated to existing data from the previous vaccination campaigns and compared by goodness of fit measures that evaluate parsimony and determine best fitting models (and model assumptions). The models will be used to predict the effectiveness of vaccination campaigns at various frequencies and coverage levels in preventing rabies epidemics due to imported cases. These predictions can then be validated against numbers of any new dog and human rabies cases through the project duration. 

Expected results and societal impact: This project will generate new knowledge on dog rabies transmission dynamics and potential for elimination; provide advice on optimal vaccination strategies; and identify the most realistic and parsimonious models for the follow-up of forthcoming dog mass vaccination campaigns in Africa and Asia in the framework of the Global Alliance for Rabies Control (GARC).
Keywords: Contact network model, Machine learning, Mass vaccination, Metapopulation model, Rabies elimination, Transmission dynamics

Title: “In vivo histology” correlates of atrophy in the aging brain
Abstract:
Motivation and research question: There is a large body of empirical evidence from clinical and large-scale general population studies demonstrating the associations between increasing age and neurodegeneration on brain anatomy. The anatomical signatures and atrophy patterns derived from computational anatomy were found to be heterogeneous across the population and even within clinical syndromes. However, the atrophy patterns derived from T1-weighted magnetic resonance images (MRI) do not allow for straightforward neurobiological interpretation of the underlying (patho)physiology that is essential for more reliable detection of preclinical stages of neurodegeneration. Novel computational tissue properties based on multi-parametric MRI provide biologically interpretable maps of myelin, iron content, and free tissue water. Based on the hypothesis that there are in vivo measurable microstructural correlates to heterogeneous brain atrophy in elderly individuals, I will determine the spatial patterns of the statistical associations of microstructural brain tissue properties (myelin, iron content, and free tissue water) with distinct pre-clinical anatomical signatures representing the heterogeneity in brain anatomy. My goal is to contribute to the understanding of differential effects of brain pathologies and typical ageing by deriving a biological interpretation of the statistical association maps.

Materials and Methods: I will analyze a rich set of already acquired longitudinal data from a large-scale  community dwelling cohort of cognitively unimpaired mid- and old age participants from Lausanne, Switzerland. The rich set of demographics, cognitive tests, cardio-vascular risk factors and psychiatric evaluation complements a unique brain anatomical MRI protocol. I will standardize regional volume estimates based on age, sex, and intracranial volume to an external reference data set and reduce bias due to acquisition hardware and protocols. After obtaining normative ranges, I will use machine-learning derived models previously trained on a data set of more than 30’000 participants to stratify homogenous subgroups with distinct atrophy patterns. I will close the loop by assessing the spatial correspondence of macro- and mesoscopic estimates of atrophy and underlying tissue properties using the established voxel-based quantification (VBQ) of relaxometry-based multi-parameter mapping. Finally, I will validate the resulting fingerprints of neurodegeneration in clinically ascertained cohorts of patients with positive biomarkers for Alzheimer’s disease that have undergone the same MRI protocols.

Impact: My project is a unique combination between data-driven characterization of ageing-associated brain atrophy and in-depth investigation of the underlying tissue properties using large-scale longitudinal data in the community dwelling population. I provide an adapted analytical framework for data integration honing on my extensive experience and expertise in statistical modeling and data analysis. The work will result in biologically interpretable maps of spatial statistical associations between computational brain anatomy signatures and tissue properties. The interpretation of these maps will bridge the cumulated evidence stemming from computational anatomy and morphometry studies on brain volume with novel neuroimaging parameters indicative for underlying tissue property changes. The proposed analytical framework that benefits from machine learning derived patterns from big data in the general population is readily applicable to other fields of imaging neuroscience research in brain health and disease.
Keywords: Aging, Machine learning, Magnetic resonance imaging, Neurodegeneration

Title: Functional Data Analysis for Complex Systems
Abstract:
Networks (namely, graphs with context dependent structure) play a central role in a host of disciplines, both as as the primary data structure associated with the phenomenon under consideration (for instance, the flow of (mis)-information in social networks, latent representations of developmental trajectories in cells in individuals) or as an integral component in representing high dimensional data in sophisticated multi-step machine learning pipelines. While tremendous advancements have been made in the formulation and application of network driven techniques on data,  theoretical understanding of such models and accuracy of ensuing statistical pipelines remain in their infancy. Leveraging the synergies between the complementary expertise of the two PIs, the goal of this proposal is to understand the foundations of two major sub-domains in this field: 

(I) Optimal transport for multilayer networks and trajectory inference for complex systems:  Network representations of multilayer valued data e.g. same patient over multiple time points, or multi-population patient data across different tasks have become a major thrust for methodology development in areas like network neuroscience. Our main goal is the development statistically principled techniques for network summarization, clustering, and extraction of principle directions of variation building on Gaussian process optimal transport techniques from functional data analysis, and specifically the representation of Procrustes metrics on covariance operators via the the Wasserstein distance between corresponding Gaussian processes.  The second aspect of this theme, motivated by single cell RNA-seq (developmental trajectories of cells) and network neuroscience (brain networks evolving at different rates in the development of diseased states),  is to understand optimal transport based methods for registration (time synchronisation) and supervised learning tasks, including network clustering after quotienting-out the underlying developmental trajectory as well understand the instability of currently proposed OT-based techniques. 

(II) Continuum scaling limits in Graphical models:   Driven by areas such as gene-expression data from cancer genomics, the main goal of this theme is the study of high-dimensional data with underlying dependency structure modulated by a latent network connecting the features. Methods and corresponding advancements in mathematical techniques include (a) Thresholding pipelines from covariance and correlation matrices and local weak convergence of associated objects to limit infinite structures and implications for thresholding schemes; (b) Hierarchical Representation learning for complex systems and their connection to convergence to continuum scaling limits via connections between linkage clustering and thresholding; (c) Structured alternatives, penalized estimation and limiting distributions of random adjacency matrices including Localization phenomena for eigen-vectors and their use in  hub-detection. Our goal is to understand asymptotics for both classical Gaussian random fields, as well as recent machine learning driven models (e.g. Maarten Gaussian processes). 

The research proposed is motivated directly by the PIs' current collaborations with Social Network scientists, Neuroscientists and Single cell-RNA-seq (UNC) and Biophysics, Molecular Dynamics, and Computational Neuroscience (EPFL), and a major motivation for the proposed research is to provide guidance for domain experts regarding the accuracy and correctness of proposed techniques. Success in the proposed research will require frequent and in-house collaboration with domain experts in these disciplines, whilst also leading to research projects across a spectrum of computational and technical ability and providing vertical integration of research groups from undergraduate to postdoctoral research foci.
Keywords: Procrustes analysis, continuum limit, covariance kernel, covariance matrices, functional data, functional data analysis, geometrical statistics, graphical model, networks, optimal transport, random graphs, random networks, statistical optimal transport, synchronisation

Title: Joint behavior and neural data modeling for naturalistic behavior
Abstract: In the words of behavioral-geneticist Jerry Hirsch, "Nothing in neuroscience makes sense except in the light of behavior." The quest to decipher the intricate workings of the brain hinges on our ability to comprehensively quantify behavior and causally understand the relationship of neural circuits to actions. Yet, several challenges remain. Extracting robust 3D postural data in complex environments remains difficult. Due to new nonlinear machine learning tools, joint modeling of neural and behavioral data to do hypothesis- and discovery-driven science is becoming possible, yet explaining how the inferred latent spaces are linked to features of the neural code is an open problem. Here, we aim to advance the state-of-the-art in animal behavioral analysis and propose new explainable joint modeling of neural and behavioral data methods. These are critical for us to be able to ask fundamental questions about the neural population dynamics during naturalistic behavior. Collectively, we propose a synergistic set of three aims that build state-of-the-art computer vision for behavior, explainable artificial intelligence methods for multi-modal behavior & neural data modeling, and leverage these advances to answer questions about the neural representations of behavior in naturalistic settings.
Keywords: 3D pose estimation, Interpretable AI, action recognition, animal pose estimation, computer vision, deep learning, joint modeling, naturalistic behavior, neural coding, neuroscience

Title: Developing data-driven spatial analysis methods for inferring spatiotemporal evolution from dialect data
Abstract:
The goal of this project is to develop a methodological framework  in a step-wise fashion for inferring spatiotemporal change from the current distribution of the phenomena dialect (in this case dialects spoken in Switzerland and Japan). The framework should be flexible enough to be applicable to other data sources and hypotheses from the broader humanities, such as demography data or the evolution of cultural habits. 
The first work package (WP1)  proposes to quantify the impact of different geographical factors (e.g. physical and sociocultural isolation factors) on linguistic relations, using current linguistic data. Language change is implicitly incorporated as the driving force that lead to the current linguistic situation. WP1 will lead to new linguistic insights that constitute the building blocks for WP2 and WP3, where spatiotemporal language change will be the explicit focus.
WP2 is a spatiotemporal analysis of language change over relatively short time spans. It aims to contribute to showing evolution paths of languages by comparing different age groups to infer which regions do presently and will in near future undergo the most profound change. Geographic factors as identified in WP1 are hypothesised to have a major impact on short time change of dialects.
WP3 will use current dialect data to infer language change over longer time spans, i.e. hundreds of years, posing a fundamental methodological challenge. GIScience approaches applicable to this problem are concerned with reengineering probable routes from incomplete or sparse movement data, but usually focus on small spatial extents and short time spans. Biology and recently also linguistic typology applies phylogenetic approaches for inferring language trees from current language data, but often ignore spatial evolution paths. The goals of WP3 will be to combine the two methodological frameworks , and model dialect change as a phylogenetic sequence of dialects that follows probable evolution paths in space. In addition to new insights in dialect change, WP3 will make a strong methodological contribution to both GIScience and the humanities.
Keywords: apparent-time constructs, dialectology, diffusion modeling, geographic information science, language contact, language evolution, machine learning, route inference, route planning, sociolinguistics, spatial analysis, spatiotemporal analysis, syntax

Title: Novel Methods for Spatio-Temporal Image Interpolation
Abstract:
Digital images and video are omnipresent in our world, and have become our central means for analysis, documentation, education, and entertainment in virtually all areas of our modern society. Thus, there is an enormous interest in techniques to efficiently process, modify, and enhance captured image and video data. While methods for image and video filtering like denoising or stylizations seem rather well-understood, the task of (spatio-temporal) image interpolation offers a lot of fundamental research challenges, but also exciting applications. Basically, image interpolation requires computing novel “in-between” images from a set of given images or a video. For spatial image interpolation one considers a few cameras and aims at generating novel views from intermediate virtual camera viewpoints in order to explore the scene from an arbitrary viewpoint. Applications include virtual camera flights in sports broadcasting, modification of the depth impression of stereoscopic 3D movies during post-production, or interactive scene exploration and free viewpoint applications from photographs. Similarly, temporal image interpolation considers a single video stream and generates intermediate frames between the captured ones. This is required in frame rate conversion in order to playback footage on devices with different frame rates, e.g. 100Hz (common TV sets) vs. 24Hz (common for cinema projectors), or for the creation of super slow-motion effects at frame rates that exceed the capability of today’s standard cameras. Combining spatial and temporal interpolation leads to spatio-temporal image interpolation where the user can place virtual cameras at novel viewpoints and and modify the flow of time.
However, the problem of image interpolation is inherently ill-posed, as it requires the analysis and synthesis of non-rigid 3D motion of scene elements, as well as handling changes in the viewpoint of the camera and the reconstruction of missing, e.g., occluded information solely from a set of 2D images. Despite those questions being investigated in computer vision and graphics research for many years, fundamental questions remain unsolved. In particular it has turned out that existing solutions are not suitable for the ever increasing resolutions and frame rates of today’s images and video, both in terms of quality and efficiency. Hence a fundamental rethinking of image interpolation strategies is required.
The goal of this project is to do basic research that addresses the remaining challenges and results in novel approaches and algorithms for spatial, temporal as well as spatio-temporal image interpolation1. First we will analyze the currently most promising existing solutions, e.g., optical flow-based interpolation, and investigate whether those classical formulations can be modified and extended to process high resolution and high frame rate data. In those classical approaches, the motion analysis and the actual interpolation are often two decoupled, consecutive processes. Hence, in a second phase we will consider a tighter integration of the analysis and synthesis phase, which can for instance be achieved by adding the interpolated images as additional unknowns to a energy-based optical flow framework, resulting in a joint estimation of motion and interpolated images. Thirdly, we want to explore fundamentally new techniques that depart significantly from classical formulations, e.g., by relaxing the interpolation constraints and to synthesize novel images that only approximate the given input images in a visually plausible way. For instance, a synthesis algorithm might decide to remove or introduce novel image content for achieving an overall better visual quality. To achieve these goals, this project also includes the development of a unified software framework that allows for an efficient implementation of the various motion analysis and interpolation strategies, as well as designing and building a novel benchmark that addresses shortcomings of existing benchmarks in the research community and provides a more appropriate, practically oriented evaluation platform. Finally, an important criterion for utility of the developed techniques is an efficient parallel implementation on GPUs or other multi-core platforms.
The Computer Graphics Lab (CGL) at ETH Zurich provides a particularly strong environment for performing this type of research. Prof. Markus Gross has a long track history of innovative research on novel view synthesis form images; see Section 2.2. Dr. Henning Zimmer who is a postdoctoral researcher at CGL is a leading expert in optical flow analysis and author of some of the currently best performing methods in this field. In addition, the group has strong connections to industrial research partners in the field of image and video processing in Switzerland such as Liberovision (www.liberovision.com) and Disney Research Zurich (www.disneyresearch.com) which will provide valuable input on practical requirements in terms of quality and efficiency as well as help building our new interpolation benchmark. Close collaboration is planned with the video technology group led by Dr. Alexander Hornung at Disney Research Zurich, which provides additional expertise in motion estimation and image warping for novel view synthesis.
Keywords: benchmarking, computer graphics, computer vision, high resolution, interpolation, parallel implementation

Title: Quantum Decision Theory and its Practical Applications
Abstract:
Decision theory underlies essentially all the social sciences, including economics, finance,political sciences, psychology, and so on. It is also employed in studying the evolution of various social systems, where the evolution equations that describe population dynamics are constructed so as to provide the maximum  of utility, or fitness, for the species of the considered social system. The standard utility theory is based on the maximization of expected utility, under a given set of lotteries or prospects (von Neuman and Morgenstern, 1953; Savage, 1954). This theory assumes that, when making a decision, humans are fully informed and absolutely rational. These assumptions have been questioned from the very early days of the creation of decision theory, starting with the famous St. Petersburg paradox (Bernoulli, 1738). A variety of other paradoxes have been observed, proving that humans generally do not follow classical decision theory. An account of many such paradoxes can be found in Camerer et al. (2003) and Machina (2008). Recently, our group has advanced a novel approach to decision theory, invoking mathematical techniques used in quantum theory, because of which this approach has been called Quantum Decision Theory (QDT) (Yukalov and Sornette, 2008). The mathematical basis of this approach has been developed in several publications (Yukalov and Sornette, 2009 a,b,c; 2010 a,b; 2011). The development of our QDT has reached a level of maturation such that it is time to have at least one Ph.D. student join us and to work with on-going experimental tests. The goal of this project is therefore to continue developing the Quantum Decision Theory (QDT) and to use it for practical applications. At present, it seems that QDT is prone to become the sole parsimonious predictive decision theory that allows for the quantitative resolution of all existing paradoxes of classical decision theory and makes it possible to explain many timedependent effects in decision making. We also plan to develop this theory for the practical purpose of portfolio management. Concretely, the following problems will be considered.
1. The relation between Quantum Decision Theory (QDT) and classical decision theory, based on the maximization of expected utility. The goal is to consider a growing list of classical problems tackled by classical decision theory and attack them with QDT to account for paradoxes and develop falsifiable predictions.
2. Quantitative resolution of the best known paradoxes of classical utility making, including the Bernoulli St. Petersburg paradox (Bernoulli, 1738), Allais paradox (Allais, 1953), independence paradox (Allais, 1953), Ellsberg paradox (Ellsberg, 1961), Kahneman-Tversky paradox (Kahneman and Tversky, 1979), Rabin paradox (Rabin, 2000), Ariely paradox (Ariely, 2008), disjunction effect (Tversky and Shafir, 1992), conjunction fallacy (Tversky and Kahneman, 1983; Shafir et al., 1990), isolation effects (McCaffery and Baron, 2006), combined paradoxes (Yukalov and Sornette, 2009b,1 2010b, 2011), planning paradox (Kydland and Prescott, 1977), and dynamic inconsistency Strotz, 1955; Frederick et al., 2002).
3. Explanation of the attenuation effect (Charness et al., 2008) caused by provided information and decision makers interactions. 
4. Application of Quantum Decision Theory to portfolio management.
5. Use of Quantum Decision Theory for quantum information processing, quantum computing, and creation of quantum artificial intelligence.
6. Collaboration with the group of Prof. H. Heinimann at ETH Zurich for explaining and interpreting, in the frame of QDT, the results of their experimental studies of decision making. 
The development of a decision theory, such as the proposed QDT, that is free of the numerous paradoxes plaguing the classical decision making would be a major breakthrough. The development of the general theory to the level at which quantitative predictions become possible would provide essentially more relevant and robust decision making, cascading into the social sciences. Given our recent output, there is little uncertainty that our endeavor will be highly successful. Overall, we can say that the present research proposal has a remarkable low-risk high-return potential impact.

Title: Towards safe water reuse in agriculture: integrated design and monitoring of treatment trains for pathogen and micropollutant removal
Abstract:
Water scarcity and climate variability increasingly impact agricultural production, threatening global food security, nutrition, and livelihoods. The use of treated wastewater in agriculture, e.g., for irrigation, could mitigate these effects, but its potential remains largely untapped. The absence of treatment targets for emerging contaminants, such as organic micropollutants (OMPs), and the difficulty of verifying compliance during operation contribute significantly to safety concerns around water reuse. These concerns are linked to two research gaps: (1) the absence of frameworks for systematic assembly and comparison of treatment trains (cost and environmental impact) that remove both traditional as well as emerging contaminants, and (2) the need for approaches to monitor the performance of agricultural water reuse systems during operation.

For my postdoctoral research, I propose to focus on two objectives both centered on the integrated design and monitoring of agricultural water reuse systems, each independently addressable: 
(A) Literature and modeling study: Develop a framework to systematically assemble and evaluate technology trains designed to remove both pathogens and OMPs using approaches from quantitative sustainable design.
(B) Experimental study: Develop a soft sensor (software-based model) for real-time prediction of pathogen and OMP removal in an agricultural water reuse system (membrane bioreactor with UV disinfection) using machine learning.

While this proposal focuses specifically on OMPs as one type of contaminants of emerging concern, the approaches that will be developed during the project will also be applicable to other types of contaminants.

My prior research was focused on risk-based monitoring of the microbial water quality in decentralized non-potable water reuse systems. With my expertise in water quality analysis, risk assessment and machine learning, I am confident in approaching this ambitious project with a results-oriented approach. The German Environment Agency and the Technical University of Berlin, my host institutions, are excellently equipped to support the project, and will grant me access to full-scale and laboratory-scale agricultural water reuse systems with online sensors, necessary laboratory facilities for microbial and chemical analyses, as well as a network of experts working on relevant topics (including water quality analysis, water reuse technologies, machine learning, and life-cycle assessment). 

In view of rising temperatures and climate variability, I strongly believe that water reuse will be a critical component of sustainable water management for agriculture, promoting long-term water security and contributing to global food security. The proposed research project will enable me to address current bottlenecks in agricultural water reuse, and provide me with the necessary tools and comprehensive expertise to identify promising future research avenues for pursuing a career focused on water reuse within Switzerland.
Keywords: contaminants of emerging concern, monitoring, soft sensor, wastewater treatment, water reuse

Title: Deep Causal Models for Legal and Political Texts
Abstract: This research proposal outlines an approach for taking the plain text of documents, along with an outcome of interest, and automating the discovery of latent treatments in the text that are causally related to the outcome. While previous work has estimated causal relations from text in controlled lab experiments, or analyzed correlations between text features and outcomes in observational data, a notable gap in the literature is how to recover causal effects of language in the field. This method will be useful to social scientists because a range of theoretically important questions concern phenomena that are embedded in text. In this project we will apply the method to judicial opinions and news stories.
Keywords: causal inference, computational linguistics, deep learning, judicial precedent, partisan news, political economy, text data

Title: Machine-Learning-Assisted Modeling and Design of Two-Dimensional Material Interfaces for Heterogeneous Catalysis
Abstract:
Background and rationale of project: 

Two-dimensional (2D) materials have emerged as promising heterogeneous catalysts due to their high specific surface area and unique electronic properties. Despite numerous experimental demonstrations, only a minor fraction of 2D materials have been explored, leading to poor understanding of the structure-property relationship (SPR) and hindering new material design. The colossal size of the configuration space (> 10^6 data points) makes it impractical to solve the SPR by conventional density functional theory (DFT) methods within reasonable computation time. Moreover, DFT approaches often fail to model the multiconfigurational electronic structures and long-range interactions which are crucial for their catalytic behaviors. 

To overcome the limitations of conventional approaches, this proposal aims to implement machine-learning assisted SPR (ML-SPR) models for 2D material catalysts, which has been successfully demonstrated for predicting catalytic activity of metallic surfaces. Particular effort will be focused on: i) effective generation of large-scale training datasets, ii) inclusion of long-range interactions in ML models, iii) understanding intrinsic catalytic mechanism thermochemistry on 2D material interfaces. A robust ML-SPR framework based on graph convolutional neural network (GCNN)is proposed to correctly capture both chemi-and physisorption on 2D heterogeneous interfaces, to perform material screening for various electrochemical reactions, including water splitting, CO2 reduction, molecular catalysis, etc. The ML-SPR framework provides insight into design rules on these materials and identifies ideal materials for experimental validation.

Objectives: 

• Develop a unified GCNN framework to encode interfacial chem- and physisorption
• Build machine learning potential for long-range interactions based on physically informed graph convolutional neural network (PIGCNN) 
• Use developed ML-SPR methods to screen two-dimensional materials for electrocatalysis applications  
• Applying ML-SPR for various electrocatalysis systems (water splitting, CO2 conversion, oxyanion reduction, molecular catalysis, etc.) on 2D material interfaces 
• Systematic comparison of prediction accuracy and uncertainty between different ML-SPR approaches

Methods to be used: 

The major method involved in the research is graph-based convolutional neuralnetwork (GCNN) on high performance computing (HPC) platforms. Particular effort will be paid to designand optimize the model for 2D material interfaces, as well as performance comparison with other materialscreening algorithms.

Expected results and impact:

The research project is expected to develop transferable machine learning models suitable for capturing both short- and long-range interactions, and further apply to study theheterogeneous catalysis on 2D materials interfaces. The developed ML-SPR model will help bridge thegap between theoretical and experimental studies of 2D-material-based catalysis. In addition, the proposed machine learning models unify chemi- and physisorption scenarios, which also has broad application on many other interfacial phenomena including optoelectronics and energy conversion.
Keywords: Heterogeneous catalysis, Machine learning, Material discovery, Neural network, Renewable energy, Two-dimensional materials

Title: AutoLegis: Automated detection of styleguide violations in legislative drafts
Abstract:
The proposed project aims to develop methods for the automated detection of violations of linguistic guidelines in legislative drafts, and to implement and evaluate them in a prototypical tool. Its most important innovative contribution is the enhancement of the method of error modelling, which was developed for automated style checking in technical writing, to meet the requirements of legislative editing -- a domain  largely out of reach for state-of-the-art style checkers.

Error modelling means that texts are searched for specific features that indicate a potential styleguide violation. For two reasons, this task is more challenging in legislative drafts than it is in technical manuals. Firstly, legislative language is considerably more complex than technical language. Secondly, while linguistic guidelines for technical writing contain relatively simple typographical and grammatical rules (e.g. that measurement nouns should be abbreviated or that future tense should be avoided), a substantial number of legislative drafting rules are concerned with domain-specific discourse-related issues (e.g. that one sentence should not contain more than one norm or that legal definitions must not contain normative elements). Formulating detection strategies for violations of these latter type of guidelines is not trivial.

We propose to tackle the problem by enhancing the method of error modelling with concepts from legal information retrieval. We plan to develop detection strategies that exploit and combine domain-specific information from multiple levels of analysis: layout information, document structure, conventionalised key phrases, morphological features and syntactic patterns.

To provide proof of concept, we plan to implement a tool that automatically annotates legislative drafts with such mixed-level information and then searches them for combinations of features that indicate a potential violation of legislative drafting guidelines. Detected passages will be highlighted in the draft, and an appropriate help text will be made available to the user.

The project focuses on German-language legislative drafting in Switzerland.
Keywords: Authoring Tools, Automated Style Checking, Legal Linguistics, Legislative Drafting, Natural Language Processing

Title: Document Synchronization Across Languages
Abstract:
The development of multilingual neural language and translation models has enabled new techniques for natural language processing, including machine translation, prompt completion and automatic summarization. However, most current techniques focus on generating documents from scratch. It is an open question whether the maintenance of existing text collections can be automated with similar techniques. In this project, we focus on the comparison, updating and synchronization of content across different documents and language versions and explore the potential of deep learning techniques for this family of tasks. By developing annotated datasets, evaluation methods, algorithms and machine learning models, we will lay the groundwork for diverse applications in information retrieval, content management, automatic text generation and quality assurance. 

Two research objectives will guide our work: 

1. Recognizing fine-grained semantic differences between documents: We aim to develop machine learning approaches for recognizing various types of word-level or sentence-level differences between related text documents. Such methods could potentially be used to identify errors in translations, to classify edits in a document, and to analyze the variation in a set of documents. To this end, we plan to assemble a collection of document pairs, such as website translations or documents with edit histories. We will construct a taxonomy of fine-grained differences and use it to annotate the documents with a gold standard, which we will then use for training and evaluating machine learning systems. We will also study methods for computationally representing and visualizing the predicted differences. 

2. Automatic editing of text based on reference documents: We will study the task of synchronization, where a document is edited based on a reference document, or even a set of reference documents. Our main goal is to generate editing suggestions that are useful for human editors. We will explore several approaches for generating such suggestions, including the use of large language models, machine translation systems, or custom models. We will also study how to evaluate the quality of the suggestions and aim to demonstrate the techniques on real-word use cases, for example by creating suggestions for extending Wikipedia articles based on articles in another language, or based on a newspaper archive. We hope that our research will enable the efficient maintenance of large, multilingual text collections, such as technical documentation or textual knowledge bases. 

In this use-inspired research project, we strive to promote the adoption of our techniques in research and industry. We will use open-source language and translation models and publicly release any custom models and implementations. We will also publicly release the data we collect, and we expect that participating in or organizing shared tasks will be an effective way to promote our contributions
Keywords: computational linguistics, cross-lingual nlp, large language models, machine translation, natural language processing, semantic textual similarity, text editing
