Title: Intelligent Mobility Services
Abstract: Today’s society is extremely dependent on mobility. Many different transport modes are available to support mobility, e.g., walking, cycling, public transport, individual car traffic, (shared) taxi services, car sharing etc. Mobility is more and more based on basic ICT (Information and Communication Technology) services to make mobility more energy-efficient, faster, and secure. Examples for basic ICT services are localisation and navigation (both indoor and outdoor), mobility prediction of vehicles and traffic congestion prediction. Such basic ICT services are increasingly based on Machine Learning (ML) techniques. This project focuses on supporting such basic ICT services and how to make use of Machine Learning for these. Traffic congestion is one of the biggest problems for major cities in the world. How to efficiently utilize the existing road networks to optimize vehicle traffic is the key to build intelligent transportation system (ITSs). Therefore, ITSs should explore multiple data resources to provide suggestions to travelers in moving, such as providing route recommendations with users’ preferences, e.g., shortest path, minimum travel time, safest route, etc. To provide such recommendations, accurate predictions about users’ or vehicles’ future locations and trajectories are important. Various types of ML algorithms have been developed to solve practical problems. However, most of the currently ML-based problem solvers require manual operations, which means that the optimal model selection and (hyper)parameter tuning operations are all done manually. Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) automates the whole Machine Learning procedure and enables the system to adapt to different scenarios. Therefore, an ITS should utilize AutoML techniques, such that it can provide optimal recommendations for different traffic conditions and user requirements in an automated way. Such ITSs can be used for both individual car and (shared) taxi traffic as well as car sharing. (Shared) Taxi and car sharing services have another requirement, i.e. customers need to find their way to the taxi stand or to the shared car. Often such customers are ordering their taxi from an indoor position and then need to find their way to the taxi system. In such case, a personnel navigation system is needed, in particular, when customers are at places they are not familiar with. So, many typical taxi orders are made from indoor users, e.g., in shopping centres, train stations, or airports. How to get users’ accurate indoor locations and recommend closest pick-up points are essential to provide good user experiences. However, GPS positioning is not available in such indoor environments. Therefore, the combination of Pedestrian Dead Reckoning and radio signals is a good solution for indoor positioning. We propose an efficient probabilistic model together with an enhanced particle filter to provide accurate and stable indoor positioning for commodity smartphones in smart building environments. Both parts of the project, namely indoor positioning and mobility prediction could be part of an integrated mobility application, where a user first navigates through a train station and airport and then takes a shared taxi or car and finally makes use of mobility prediction for the car travel. Both parts, mobility/congestion prediction and indoor localisation will be integrated into a common demonstrator

Title: A Higher Level for Neuron Reconstruction
Abstract:
To better understand the brain, the substrate of our cognition, we require detailed knowledge of its structure, in particular its ``wiring diagram''. Unfortunately, an exact diagram of even the tiniest part of a brain is still not available today!

Thanks to great advances in volume electron microscopy, human experts can now reliably trace individual neurons. Unfortunately, the effort for a manual tracing of {\it all} processes in the gigavoxel images that are now becoming standard is prohibitive: it is measured in multiple decades. And yet, a fully manual tracing still is the current state of the art.

The reason for this sorry state of affairs is that automated methods still break down in the multiple parts of a typical volume image where neural processes become very thin, the staining is imperfect or the signal-to-noise ratio is poor. And yet, the high agreement obtained between independent human tracings testifies to the fact that these obstacles are, in principle, surmountable.

We propose to work on next-generation algorithms that surpass the state of the art in a number of ways: Firstly, we will develop higher-order factors that can capture properties such as shape. These factors will be used both post hoc, to evaluate predictions based on local evidence alone, to obtain uncertainty measures that can be used for interactive training or semi-manual tracing. The same factors will also be used during inference. The resulting optimization is very hard and calls for an informed generation of competing hypotheses which we will also develop and refine. An important part of this proposal is a structured learning framework, where we wish to learn from cheap annotations: skeletons rather than pixel-level annotations. To that end, we will also need a meaningful error metric, which we are confident we can find based on a concept of edit distance.

In summary, we will leverage some of the latest techniques in computer vision and machine learning, and push the boundary in a few important places. We thus hope to enable neuroscientists to ask new questions, and answer them, based on the massive amounts of data they currently generate.
Keywords: Biomedical Image Processing, Connectomics, Electron Microscopy Image Segmentation, Neural Image Segmentation, Neural Reconstruction

Title: MetaDiv: Ecological and Evolutionary drivers  of phytochemical diversity
Abstract:
Through the lens of chemistry, every organism, biotic interaction, and ecosystem, reveals a unique skeleton of molecular structures. As sessile organisms, plants produce throughout their lifetime an astonishing diversity of compounds to cope with the abiotic and biotic constraints of their environment. Phytochemical compounds have been shown to enhance tolerance against abiotic stresses such as UV radiation or extreme temperatures and increase resistance against herbivores and pathogens. This phytochemical diversity, commonly named “the plant metabolome”, is directly linked to an individual’s genome, physiology and environmental context, thus offering a novel perspective to mechanistically explore ecosystem functioning. Furthermore, many molecules produced by plants display pharmacological properties, making them an invaluable source of medicines (e.g. anticancer, antibacterial, analgesic, anti-inflammatory, antitumor, or antiviral). Accordingly, most of the global population directly uses natural products as their primary source of medicine, and 70% of drugs used for treating human health are derived from natural product discovery programs. Sadly, time is running out. Earth is experiencing a major biodiversity crisis, with estimates placing 20% of known species at high risk of extinction. Importantly, these estimates do not consider the large number of rare and as yet undescribed species for which the metabolome remains unknown. There is thus a critical need to explore the hidden diversity of natural compounds produced by vegetation at the global scale. In doing so, we may finally be able to mitigate the repercussions of this irreversible loss of fundamental information for ecological research and human society.
The time is ripe to integrate recent advances in analytical chemistry and ‘big data’ analytics for exploring the molecular diversity of thousands of species simultaneously, to enhance our understanding of ecosystem functions, the processes underlying biodiversity, and novel drug discovery programs. Given this unprecedented land use change and massive destruction of regions possessing untold value to medicine and scientific research, characterizing and comparing phytochemical diversity at global scale is poised to become one of the hottest topics in functional, community and ecosystem ecology in the next decade. Through the project MetaDiv, I will be able to position myself, and my research group, at the forefront of this field. Based on an unprecedented phytochemical dataset including thousands of plant species form arctic, temperate, equatorial, and Mediterranean ecosystems grown across multiple botanical gardens of Switzerland, coupled to the latest generation of High-Resolution Mass Spectrometers, as well as the latest methods in molecular networking and machine-learning, I aim to obtain a first image of the phytochemical landscape worldwide. With the project MetaDiv I intend to: 1) accurately characterize phytochemical diversity across thousands of plant species, 2) identify the evolutionary and ecological drivers of phytochemical diversity variation, 3) provide new predictive tools for characterizing phytochemical diversity, and 4) merge the extrapolated facets of phytochemical diversity with current biodiversity metrics.  By combing our metabolomic data with existing repository on plant community, environment and phylogeny, we will not only advance the field of fundamental ecosystem functioning research, but also contribute to society through drug discovery programs and biodiversity conservation.
Keywords: Botanical garden, biodiversity, functional ecology, metabolomic, open science, plant metabolome

Title: Probing variation in viral proteomes through interaction profiling and structural modelling
Abstract:
Viruses are enormously diverse and, despite their highly limited repertoire of protein-coding genes, they have evolved a wide range of pathogenic mechanisms of increasing clinical relevance worldwide. Their evolution is extremely rapid and under different constraints than that of cellular life. Due to this, evolutionary relationships between and to viral proteins can not typically be detected by raw sequence-based comparisons. However, remote relationships across viral proteins infecting hosts from all three domains of life have been discerned through protein structure comparisons. Viral proteins contain unique characteristics distinguishing them from their hosts: a less densely packed structure, weaker inter-residue interactions, high occurrence of short disordered regions, a greater abundance of polar residues, and lower destabilising effects of mutations. These characteristics allow them to form unique interactions, such as adopting multiple oligomeric states and conformations with different functions, rapidly evolving against interaction-inhibiting drugs, hijacking host functionality, and inhibiting interactions with host immune proteins. 
All viral proteins are potential targets for therapeutics, which usually rely on two routes - antibody drugs, vaccine and immunotherapy strategies that take advantage of the vertebrate adaptive immune response, and antiviral drugs that inhibit the functionality of viral proteins crucial for replication. However, the small viral protein repertoire, our limited knowledge of viral proteomes and the capacity of viruses to evolve sophisticated immune and drug evasion strategies, greatly hinders therapeutic design, with many common pathogenic viruses still resisting treatment. Both viral evasion tactics and therapeutic design predominantly hinge on the dynamics of viral protein interactions. 
The field of protein bioinformatics has seen a rapid expansion in the past years, with deep learning methods combining evolutionary information hidden across billions of protein sequences to advance protein structure prediction, remote homology detection, the prediction of interactions with other proteins, peptides, and ligands, and inferring the effects of mutations. These advances in methods have been accompanied by the development of large databases and new resources linking millions of proteins across the tree of life based on evolution, structure, and interaction predictions that were far beyond the reach of previous methods. Thus, we are at a unique point in time where we can leverage the advances in protein bioinformatics and the growth of sequencing data to structurally characterise entire viral proteomes and their interactions. 
In this project, I will develop computational methods to guide therapeutic discovery against viruses while minimising the chance of evasion by (1) uncovering remote relationships in viral proteomes to better characterise their interaction profiles, (2) modelling their complexes and interfaces with host immune proteins and potential therapeutics, and (3) pinpointing critical residues on surfaces and interfaces linked to observed variants. By advancing remote search and protein complex prediction, I will characterise the viral protein universe to answer long-standing questions on viral evolution and pathogenicity. Further, I will combine predicted immunogenic and druggable regions with the implications of mutations on structural stability and binding in interactive viral proteome maps. These methods and predictions will be concretely applied and experimentally validated in three clinical applications, on identifying (1) key viral-immune interactions in transplant settings, (2) variants related to antiviral drug resistance, and (3) epitope mimicry events linked to autoimmune responses. Thus, with this research, I aim to aid in the identification of potential targets for antiviral therapeutics, immunotherapy, and vaccines, support informed tracking of viral infections and potential variants of concern, and increase our understanding of the underlying mechanisms of viral evolution, variation, and escape.

Title: MLin: Machine Learning Input Data Processing as a Service
Abstract:
Data is the lifeblood of machine learning (ML). Yet, our system infrastructure for managing and preprocessing training data in ML jobs lags significantly behind the vast advancements in hardware accelerators, software frameworks, and algorithms that optimize model training computations. The input data pipeline is the part of an ML job responsible for extracting data from storage, transforming data on-the-fly (e.g., randomly augmenting, filtering, shuffling, and batching elements), and loading data to a training node (e.g., GPU). As hardware accelerator performance continues to improve, feeding data at a sufficient rate to saturate accelerator compute capabilities is increasingly challenging. The high cost of accelerators compared to their CPU hosts makes it particularly important to ensure that accelerators operate at high utilization. Hence, the input pipeline is critical to the end-to-end throughput, resource cost, and accuracy of model training. Unfortunately, optimizing input data pipelines is challenging for users as it involves handling larger-than-memory datasets, reasoning about data transformations that affect training dynamics, and parallelizing processing to avoid input data stalls. Furthermore, although input data pipelines are frequently re-executed in ML training workflows (e.g., during hyperparameter tuning), existing systems miss the opportunity to reuse input data computations across jobs.

The key research question we explore is: how can we raise the level of abstraction for input data processing in ML jobs while automatically optimizing data pipelines to improve performance and resource efficiency? Our objective is to enable input data processing as a service for ML jobs. We propose MLin, a multi-tenant system architecture that allows users to define their input data pipeline through familiar APIs (e.g., tf.ata operators in TensorFlow) while the service takes care of efficiently executing input pipelines by transparently applying optimizations and elastically scaling resources for data processing. To our knowledge, MLin is the first system to propose a centralized view of input data processing across ML jobs, which we explore how to leverage across three phases in our proposal: 1) elastically scaling resources for input data processing to improve performance, 2) reusing input data processing computation across jobs to improve resource efficiency, and 3) recommending input datasets and data augmentations to improve model accuracy.
Keywords: cloud computing, computer systems, data processing, machine learning

Title: Unsupervised data-driven discovery of material laws
Abstract:
In the past decade, machine learning techniques have experienced a tremendous boost and nowadays permeate our everyday life. This renewed blossoming, which can be partially attributed to the remarkable performance of deep learning architectures, has led to several advances in data-rich and model-limited fields such as social sciences, finance, advertising and marketing [BN20]. At the same time, machine learning is quickly establishing itself as a game changer in many fields of science and technology. It is becoming clear that its tools are key enablers which can empower scientists and engineers to accelerate the development of novel materials, processes and technologies. 
More recent and much less developed is the role played by machine learning for advancing scientific discovery in domains traditionally dominated by mechanistic models, such as solid mechanics, which is the domain of interest in this proposal. Due to parallel advances in experimental techniques, this field is rapidly becoming data rich. The simultaneous availability of first-principles models and large sets of high-quality data offers a unique premise for data-driven approaches enabled by machine learning tools and bears an enormous potential to transform the field. The exploration of this potential started very recently and, despite a rapidly growing interest, is still in its infancy. 
In this project, we focus in particular on material modeling, a crucial component of solid mechanics. The objective of this project is to uncover the potential and explore the unprecedented possibilities offered by machine learning for material modeling in solid mechanics, while leveraging state-of-the art knowledge in this domain. As opposed to the current paradigm of assuming a priori known material laws and identifying their unknown parameters through data, our goal here is to i) discover the material laws themselves using unsupervised, interpretable, data-driven and mixed data-physics-driven approaches; ii) encode complex material behavior in deep neural networks by exploiting the synergy of unsupervised deep learning with domain knowledge. To reach this goal, we intend to start by developing and evaluating novel ideas and concepts for simple and reversible material behavior such as in hyperelasticity, and then tackle increasingly challenging cases of more complex and/or irreversible nature including heterogeneous and anisotropic hyperelasticity, plasticity, viscoelasticity, damage and combinations thereof. Our new approaches will be enabled by last-generation machine learning technologies, most notably sparse regression, sparse Bayesian learning and deep neural networks. Also, we will depart from artificially generated data and subsequently leverage the availability of high-quality experimental data through state-of-the-art experimental techniques including three-dimensional digital image correlation and micro-tomography with in-situ testing equipped with digital volume correlation. Additional data will become available through collaborations with well-known research groups, which will provide experimental results on human brain tissues and metamaterials. Finally, we will initiate a potentially long-term collective effort towards the generation of a data repository on the mechanical behavior of materials to be used as basis for data-driven modeling and simulation in computational solid mechanics.
The ultimate vision of the project is the possibility of discovering or encoding, starting from virtually no assumption, any arbitrarily complex, potentially irreversible material model with an a priori unknown number and meaning of the internal variables, along with the corresponding parameters, based on only measurable data. If achieved, although probably only to a partial extent in the proposed project, the new approaches would not only lead to substantial savings in the time and cost of material identification procedures, which are ubiquitous in research as well as in industrial practices, but also represent powerful new tools for surrogate modeling and scientific discovery in material modeling and more in general in computational solid mechanics.
Keywords: advanced materials, bayesian learning, constitutive laws, digital image correlation, neural networks, sparse regression

Title: Dynamic Vulnerability Analysis of Containerized Applications
Abstract:
Cloud based infrastructure alleviates the challenge of managing and maintaining application services across large distributed computing environments. However, the need for faster deployment, better performance and continuous delivery of application services has led to the introduction of containers.Container is a virtualization approach that sits on top of a physical machine and shares its host Operating System (OS) kernel and services. The benefit of using containers over traditional virtualization approaches will lead to its growing adoption in the industry by 40% annually. Moreover, it is also expected that 47% of information technology service providers are planning to deploy containers in their environment.

However, the use of containers come with a cost of security concerns. Firstly static bug detection techniques suffer from high number of false positives, which challenges the credibility of the tool’s effectiveness in bug detection. Secondly existing container analysis tools (such as Clair, Anchore, Dagda) provide a limited analysis coverage for security bug (also known as vulnerability) detection.Therefore, in this project, we will address the aforementioned concerns. To overcome the problem of false positives, we will use a software bug detection technique that will leverage different software metrics (e.g., code complexity) to build a prediction model. The model will predict the presence of bugs in the code. To overcome the limitation of analysis coverage, we will analyze a running container (i.e., Docker) image by using runtime verification; which is a dynamic analysis technique that helps in detecting bugs while the program is running. Hence, we propose a novel security bug detection technique called DiVA (Dynamic Vulnerability Analysis) which combines bug prediction and runtime verification technique. DiVA will verify only those execution points of the program where the prediction model will show the presence of bugs. Thereby, improving the bug detection analysis.

The project is in the scope of Distributed Computing Applications (DCA) research group at department of Information Technology, Uppsala University, Sweden, which specializes in leveraging cloud solutions and machine learning to solve complex problems. This project is also in line with Omar Javed’s research interest which includes dynamic program analysis, mining software repositories, virtualization and runtime verification.
Keywords: Application containers, Monitoring and verification, Prediction, Security vulnerabilities

Title: Empowering Computational Science using Data-Centric Programming
Abstract:
As high-performance programming is approaching the exascale era, scientific program complexity is increasing beyond the skill-set of the average domain scientist. With the ubiquity of accelerators, such as GPUs and FPGAs, in supercomputers and data centers, a scientific computing application needs to coordinate between multiple programming languages, communication interfaces, and undergo meticulous adaptations with respect to the target hardware and topology. This creates a situation where scientific programs need to be optimized, sometimes by other software engineers, to the point where domain scientists can no longer modify them on their own. The characteristics of current hardware architectures indicate that the bottleneck disallowing applications from running faster has recently shifted from computation to data movement, which can be confirmed by surveying current application optimization methods for CPUs, GPUs, and FPGAs.

The overarching goal of the proposed research is to change the landscape of computational science, promoting a separation of concerns between the scientific code and the optimizable, hardware-mapped representation. We will do this by designing a data-centric programming model for parallel and distributed applications. Using data-centric parallel programming and a graph-based Intermediate Representation (IR), our preliminary results show that applications written in a high-level language can match the speeds of expert-tuned assembly code, which approaches hardware peak performance.

We will design the model to map efficiently to multi-core CPUs, GPUs, FPGAs, and interconnected clusters thereof, using existing high-level languages for the domain scientists. Performance engineers will then interface directly with the IR, applying transformations interactively without modifying the original code. Towards this goal, we will formulate an infrastructure for data-centric graph rewriting, and provide a set of reusable transformations. Title: The effect of media on voting behavior: Evidence from Switzerland
Abstract: Media plays a crucial role in modern democracy, as it is the first source of information for most voters. In principle, more information about policy decisions and outcomes should strengthen the accountability process, improving political selection and therefore allowing better policies. This project will contribute to the existing literature by studying under-researched topics such as the quality of journalism and the interaction of media and culture. The empirical context is newspapers in Swiss localities.

Title: EcoDynCast: forecasting alien invasive species range dynamics with graph neural networks
Abstract: Invasive alien species (IAS) pose an increasing threat to biodiversity, ecosystems, and economies. Driven by climate change, global trade, and land-use changes, their range and numbers are expected to grow, requiring robust predictive models to guide management strategies. However, current predictive models often fail to account for key transient ecological processes, including dispersal and demographic shifts, and typically overlook long-range dispersal due to human activity. These gaps hinder accurate forecasting and the development of appropriate mitigation efforts. Opportunistic datasets provide high-resolution spatio-temporal data on species occurrences that could inform dynamical models. Yet these datasets are characterized by shallow temporal signals, which can only be leveraged with strong ecological priors. This project aims at developing \texttt{EcoDynCast}, an ecologically informed, data-driven dynamical model designed to forecast the invasion dynamics of IAS using opportunistic data. The key innovations of our approach are (i) the combination of deep learning with a process-based reaction diffusion framework, to mitigate shallow signals in datasets, and (ii) the introduction of a data assimilation scheme permitting to mitigate biases in opportunistic datasets. The reaction-diffusion model consists of a multi-layer perceptron and a graph neural network, to model demographic and spatial dynamics respectively. By distinguishing these two components, we can directly embed ecological principles within the model’s architecture, and constrain the components with prior knowledge on realistic growth and dispersal rates as well as invasion corridors. Opportunistic datasets bear strong spatial, temporal and taxonomic biases, which must be accounted for when used for training. The proposed data-assimilation scheme leverages expert survey data to correct these biases and permits aligning model prediction with the opportunistic datasets. The project will be organized into two main work packages. WP1 focuses on the development of the dynamical core of the model under an idealized scenario with unbiased synthetic data. This initial phase will allow us to refine the dynamical core architecture and validate its performance in predicting ecological dynamics in a simplified setting. WP2 focuses on assimilating biased opportunistic datasets with a real-world application to model the invasion dynamics of \textit{Ambrosia artemisiifolia}, a widespread invasive plant in Europe. WP1 and WP2 will permit the elaboration of a new dynamical species distribution model benchmark to support future developments. By combining cutting-edge machine learning with ecological first principles, \texttt{EcoDynCast} represents a novel and unconventional approach to IAS forecasting. It directly aligns with the objectives of the Spark program by pushing the frontiers of ecological modeling and scientific machine learning. Beyond IAS management, our project could have broad impacts in biodiversity conservation, as it is also appropriate for modeling species range shifts under climate change. Overall, \texttt{EcoDynCast} aims to establish a new paradigm for dynamically predicting species distributions, ultimately supporting more effective environmental policy and conservation planning.

Title: An integrative multi-omics approach to investigate cerebral and systemic biological pathway alterations with clinical relevance in early Alzheimer’s disease
Abstract:
Besides amyloid pathology and tau-related neurodegeneration, multiple other molecular alterations and pathway dysregulations have been observed in Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Their inter-individual variations, complex interrelations, and relevance for clinical manifestation and disease progression remain poorly understood, however. Heterogeneity at both pathophysiological and clinical level complicates diagnosis, prognosis, treatment, and drug design and testing. Recently developed high throughput “omics” are unbiased data driven methods which allow addressing a wide spectrum of disease related changes at different endophenotype levels. 
Here, our main objectives are 1) to investigate in depth the systemic and CNS molecular AD endophenotypes by using integrative multi-omics analysis; 2) to relate the identified molecular and pathway alterations to core AD pathology, clinical manifestation, and disease progression and, 3) to derive novel multimodal blood-based biomarker signatures for individual diagnosis, differential diagnosis and prediction of disease progression. To this end, we will use a dataset from an existing thoroughly characterized, longitudinally followed up cohort, and acquire new data in subjects with normal cognition and with AD and non-AD cognitive impairment. Single-omics from paired CSF and peripheral blood samples including Proteomics, Metabolomics, Neuroinflammation, Methionine metabolism, Fatty acids, Lipidomics and Ionomics will be considered. Statistical approaches including machine learning and graph-based analysis will be applied to explore associations of molecular alterations with a) amyloid aggregation, tau pathology, neuronal injury, regional brain atrophy, and b) cognitive decline within single omics modalities. In parallel we will apply a data-driven integrative multi-omics factor analysis approach to address interrelations of multiple pathophysiological alterations across different omics levels. This will generate a latent factor representation of the dataset complexity to extract common axes of variance, and identify analytes associated with  markers of core AD pathology or independently contributing to variance. Pathway enrichment will identify pathway alterations related to core AD pathology and/or, independently contributing to clinical severity, and disease progression over time. Blood sampling and targeted analysis at follow-up visits will be performed to relate dynamics of systemic alterations to clinical progression. To validate and extend the findings while addressing multiple possible confounders, we will acquire a new independent cohort from 3 Swiss university centers including subjects with AD, non-AD cognitive impairment, and controls; and perform targeted omics related to the identified mixed pathophysiological alterations. For additional validation, we will use clinical and omics data available from a large multi-cohort biomarker discovery project (EMIF consortium). Finally, blood-based biomarker combinations that best diagnose cerebral AD pathology and predict rapid cognitive decline will be determined in the first cohort and their performance will be verified in the independent multicenter cohort. 
Taking multiple clinical and endophenotype levels into account, this project will allow for the deep exploration of pathway alterations and improve our understanding of the mechanisms involved in cerebral AD pathology, associated systemic alterations, clinical manifestation, and progression of the disease. It has a high potential for biomarker discovery and translation to clinical application. We expect the results to lead to personalized medicine approaches for both diagnosis and intervention.
Keywords: Alzheimer Disease, Biomarkers, Brain volumetry, Disease Mechanism, Multiomics, Systems Biology Approach

Title: Environmental Treaty Design: Typology and Effectiveness
Abstract:
This research project aims to identify the treaty design variables that are the best predictors of political, economic and/or environmental progress of international environmental legal systems.
The first part of the investigation uses tools developed in the field of natural language processing to extract information on a large number of treaty design features from the texts of multilateral environmental agreements (MEAs), combined with network analysis, topic modelling and other text analytics in order to gain a comprehensive overview of the hundreds of multilateral environmental agreements that have been adopted over the last few decades.
The second part of the enquiry involves web-based collection of political data on treaty participation as well as relevant economic and environmental data on the objects of regulation of the agreements so as to see whether there are any statistical relationships between design variables and observed developments.
Much has been written about how to design successful agreements, yet most empirical studies are small-scale and/or limited by a disciplinary focus. My research innovates in that it develops/uses (i) a common typology of rules across all areas of international environmental law, (ii) computational tools that have never been applied to the study of MEA texts to the best of my knowledge, (iii) a combination of legal, political, economic and environmental data that are usually studied in isolation, and (iv) the latest visualisation, regression and machine learning techniques to reveal patterns and hopefully identify which types of legal rules and combinations thereof are best suited to address large-scale anthropogenic imbalances in ecosystems around the world.
Keywords: Complex systems, Empirical legal studies, Global environmental governance, Global public goods, Information extraction, Institutional design, International law, Linked open data, Multilateral environmental agreements, Natural language processing, Network analysis, Policy evaluation, Regime design, Text analytics, Text mining

Title: Neuromorphic X-ray tomography for advanced biology and materials science applications (NeuroTom-X)
Abstract:
Synchrotron-based X-ray micro-computed tomography is the reference technique for a number of studies investigating fundamental properties and functions of materials and organisms. Third-generation (and upcoming 4th-generation) synchrotrons like the Swiss Light Source (SLS) allow performing these in situ, operando and in vivo with unmatched spatial and temporal resolutions. However, the increased use of imaging technologies has created a big data bottleneck in terms of data storage, management, processing and visualization. High-speed dynamical imaging experiments currently either produce exorbitant amounts of data, shifting the challenges to the data processing side, or remain limited in temporal resolution, thus hindering further progress in experimental designs. Therefore, overcoming these by revising data acquisition and signal processing methods and pipelines is of paramount importance to enable a range of new studies, capable of answering fundamental and applied questions in biology and general matter research.

The underlying project is to leverage the recent advances in neuromorphic imaging sensors and computing, time-based sampling theory and machine learning to develop an X-ray based neuromorphic vision system that will enhance current spatial and temporal imaging resolution capabilities by at least an order of magnitude in a plethora of time-resolved experiments. We further hypothesize that with our approach we will significantly reduce data production rates, thus facilitating real-time data processing approaches, and enabling smart data acquisition type of experiments. As embodiments of the newly developed platform, together with our project partners, we will address and answer scientific questions from independent scientific fields, thanks to the here proposed methods.

The project involves a number of interdisciplinary techniques, including modeling, assembly, calibration and characterization of equipment combined with devising novel algorithms and pipelines for end-to-end processing of the event-based data streams. We will (a) first develop a dual imaging instrument for high-speed X-ray tomography that integrates neuromorphic and standard image camera sensors; (b) study minimal data representations for reconstructing signals of interest by applying time-based sampling theory; (c) develop data-driven (deep) learning-based image enhancement methods with efficient event-data processing architectures for real-time reconstruction and inference; and (d) apply our methods to study novel nano-architected metallic lattices as well as pulmonary microscopic dynamics.

To the best of our knowledge, the dual neuromorphic X-ray tomographic imaging system will be the first of its kind. We will not only be able to answer urging scientific questions, being currently inaccessible by other methods, but the developed techniques for event data stream processing will also be applicable to generic image processing and computer vision tasks. The project will tighten the collaboration between experimental and computing groups at times when imaging challenges are shifting to the data processing side and thus guarantee PSI’s / SLS’s world-leading position in time-resolved X-ray micro-tomography. Finally, the generic question on how event-based sensing can be utilized in dynamic X-ray image enhancement tasks will be of uttermost importance, e.g. for clinical applications such as interventional radiology or in high-throughput industrial imaging.
Keywords: Computed tomography, Phase-contrast imaging, Signal processing, X-ray microscopy, additive manufactoring, high-speed imaging, respiratory physiology

Title: Detecting Troll Activity in Online Social Networks
Abstract:
Online Social Networks (OSNs) are computer-based technologies that enable users to create content and entertain social relationships. OSNs have rapidly grown from an aggregation channel to a global phenomenon that has elicited a paradigm shift of our society, by transforming the way people access the news, share opinions, make business and politics. In such a scenario, accuracy, truthfulness, and authenticity of the shared content are necessary ingredients to maintain a healthy online discussion. However, in recent times, OSNs have been dealing with a considerable growth of malicious and fake accounts, which purposely undermine the integrity of online conversations by sharing false and inflammatory information in OSN platforms to influence the public opinion and sow conflict on social or political issues. Recent studies found evidence that these malicious actors play a disproportionate role in manipulation and misinformation campaigns globally, highlighting the pitfalls of OSNs and their potential harms to several constituents of our society, ranging from politics to public health. Bots (i.e., software-controlled accounts) and trolls (i.e, human operators often tied with political movements) represent the most recognized categories of malicious entities acting in such efforts. Although the attempt of OSN providers to purge their platforms, the nefarious activity of bots and trolls has not entirely stopped. While the detection of bots has established solutions, the automated identification of troll accounts represents an open challenge for the research community. Existing approaches analyze the activity of accounts tied to Russia’s troll farm and involved in the Twitter online discussion during the 2016 US Presidential election. To enable the detection of such trolls, these efforts use language cues and Twitter accounts’ metadata. Such solutions, other than being limited to a unique OSN, exploits linguistic markers strictly related to the trolls under analysis.
In this project, we aim to launch an innovative computational tool for automatically detecting troll accounts in OSNs that is agnostic both on the online platform under scrutiny and on the origin and purpose of the malicious users. The targeted solution strives to be generalizable to different OSNs and scenarios (e.g., in the political, health, or social context). The novelty of our solution is also in the proposed methodology, which does not merely target to identify troll accounts in online platforms, but also aim to understand and characterize their malicious activity. The rationale is to infer a set of online incentives that may steer trolls’ behavior and utilize such cues for distinguishing them from non-troll accounts. To perform such analysis, we intend to rely on Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL), which is a machine learning framework that has the main goal of finding the motivation (in the form of rewards) behind an observed behavior. In our scenario, we plan to employ IRL to infer the rewards that could have led troll and non-troll users to perform their online activity. We then consider to exploit the estimated rewards as features of a supervised learning algorithm aimed at classifying such accounts. The differences in the predictive features between the two classes of accounts might enable a principled understanding of the distinctive behaviors reflecting the incentives trolls and non-trolls respond to. While these objectives represent ambitious and critical challenges in the race towards healthy online ecosystems, our pioneering approach, given its generalizable nature, can potentially impact and curb the activity of malicious actors along different dimensions, not only related to the manipulation of public opinion in the political context, but also, and more generally, in the fight against every form of online harassment and abuse in OSNs (e.g., cyberbullying).
Keywords: Disinformation, Fake-news, Opinion manipulation, Troll

Title: TACT-HANDS: Improving control of prosthetic hands using tactilesensors and realistic machine learning
Abstract:
Intuitive and robust control of poly-articulated prosthetic hands by amputees is an as-yet unsolved problem, largely due to: (1) inadequate sensorization in the hand and in the human-machine interface; and (2) inadequate machine learning methods to detect the intent of the user. These problems cannot be easily solved since prosthetic hands pose severe limitations on weight, price, size, cosmetics and power consumption. They cannot be equipped with standard robotic sensors and, at the same time, a practical, reliable intent detection method is simply not yet available. 

In TACT-HAND, we will employ and evaluate a new generation of tactile sensors coupled with realistic machine learning methods to overcome both problems. Firstly, we will build a lightweight, wearable human-machine interface based upon high-resolution tactile sensors to augment/substitute traditional surface electromyography. Secondly, we will design and apply fast, incremental and intuitive machine learning methods to fully exploit the tactile interface and provide stable intent detection. Thirdly, similar sensor technology will be employed to build a tactile dataglove to sensorize a commercially available hand prosthesis. The aim is to advance the state of the art in prosthetic hand control with better grasping and manipulation together, including higher stability and reliability.
Keywords: Learning and adaptation with tactile sensors, Prosthetic hand control

Title: Toward High-Throughput Quantitative Analysis of Nanoparticle Pollution in Environmental Samples
Abstract:
The aim of this research project is to develop and demonstrate a high-throughput measurement system and analysis strategy for the concurrent measurement and quantification of all types of inorganic nanoparticles (NPs). This research expands on an emerging nanoparticle detection method termed single-particle inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (sp-ICPMS), which is one of the few analytical methods that is capable of detecting, sizing, and counting ENPs at environmentally relevant concentrations. We will expand on conventional sp-ICPMS by leveraging the detection power of new ICP time-of-flight mass spectrometry (ICP-TOFMS) instrumentation in order to simultaneously quantify diverse inorganic NPs from a single sample. ICP-TOFMS is uniquely suited for sp-ICPMS because it provides high-sensitivity full-spectrum mass analysis at high time resolution so that individual NPs can be distinguished based on their multi-elemental and/or -isotopic composition; no other commercially available ICPMS instrument can provide these measurement features. Unique properties of ICP-TOFMS will be used to overcome natural nanoparticle interferences based on single-particle element “fingerprints” and also improve speed of analysis and sample utilization through rapid, multiplexed determination of inorganic NPs. 
The development of this new sp-ICP-TOFMS measurement system is motivated by growing concern about the impact of engineered NP (ENP) pollution and the need for robust analytical methods for the detection of nanoparticles in complex environmental matrices. ENPs in the environment are difficult to detect because they are small (hundreds to millions of atoms), dilute in terms of total mass concentration, and are present in complex matrices that may even contain naturally occurring NPs that mask the signals of ENPs. The research outlined here overcomes these challenges and offers a viable solution for comprehensive inorganic NP measurements. To meet the ultimate goal of comprehensive inorganic NP analysis, significant analytical methodology and instrumentation development are required and will be attained through meeting five specific research aims: 1) development of a sample-introduction system with online calibration for measurement of diverse inorganic NP types; 2) improvement of particle-number concentration measurements via online measurement of NP uptake; 3) improvement of measurement sensitivity based on redesigned sample-introduction system and hardware modifications to the ICP-TOFMS; 4) development and evaluation of a method to distinguish diverse natural NPs from ENPs based on element “fingerprints”; and 5) demonstration and validation of the approach for the analysis of NPs from wastewater treatment plants in Switzerland.

Title: Artificial intelligence-enabled tumor boards for curative loco-regional therapies of colorectal liver metastasis
Abstract:
Background and rationale: Curative-intent loco-regional therapies for colorectal liver metastasis (CLM), such as surgical resection or thermal ablation, offer good long-term prognosis. Surgical resection is the gold standard, with local effectiveness of 89%-98%, and percutaneous thermal ablation is a viable alternative, with 50%-95% local effectiveness for selected patients, especially with the introduction of advanced technologies. While ablation can be repeated within months and multiple times, repeated resection is possible but more challenging and consequently limited in application, especially following major hepatectomy approaches. To date, interdisciplinary tumor boards decide on a treatment approach based on the feasibility of a treatment according to tumor size and location and overall patient health. Thus, if resection is not feasible, ablation is considered. On-going randomized controlled trials are evaluating ablation vs. resection for CLM. However, these trials are powered for non-inferiority and do not address the critical issue of patient selection based on molecular, radiologic, and physiologic biomarkers. Such biomarkers, such as TP53/RAS co-mutation or SMAD4 mutation, have been reported as strong predictors for new intra-hepatic metastasis, a major driver in poor overall survival, and are typically available at the time of the tumor board meeting3. Furthermore, such trials sustain competition be-tween disciplines instead of encouraging interdisciplinary treatment strategies, as practiced in leading centers like The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center4. Personalized treatment must optimize a tradeoff between local tumor control and the possibility of repeat treatment of new intra-hepatic metastasis, which emerges in most patients with CLM. Therefore, it is crucial to develop risk models to predict the chance of local control following specific treatments and the probability of requiring repeat treatment for new lesions within a short period.

Objectives: The aim of this project is to build a treatment recommender system for curative-intent local therapies for colorectal liver metastasis based on molecular, radiologic, and physiologic biomarkers. 

Method: I will first perform a retrospective analysis of data (imaging, clinical, laboratorial, genomics, and pathologic) from the institutional registries of patients who underwent surgical resection of CLM to build a predictive model for intra-hepatic progression local and elsewhere within the liver new metastasis. I will identify a combination of molecular, radiologic, and physiologic biomarkers available at the time of the tumor board meeting with predictive capacity for local and distant tumor progression. This predictive model will be combined with a previously developed predictive model for percutaneous thermal ablation (during my Early.Postdoc Fellowship) to create a treatment recommender system. The individual models will produce independent predictions of local and distant intra-hepatic progression following each treatment. The system will then recommend the treatment with the optimal tradeoff between local tumor control and the potential for re-peat treatment. These models will then be evaluated in a prospective observational study to test the predictive accuracy and compare overall and disease-free survival between patients treated as recommended and those treated as anti-recommended.

Expected results and impact for the field: This research will identify biomarkers for tumor-specific and personalized allocation of curative-intent loco-regional therapies for patients with colorectal liver metastasis. Furthermore, the results from this project will be used to initiate a clinical trial where eligible patients are allocated according to the treatment recommender system. This work will advance the understanding of patient selection criteria for curative-intent loco regional therapies for CLM and thereby improve long-term outcomes.
Keywords: artificial intelligence, interventional oncology, personalized medicine, precision medicine, surgical oncology

Title: The origins of syntax
Abstract:
Background and rationale
According to most theories, syntax is what separates human language from other communication systems. But how did it evolve? A number of hypotheses have been put forward, with no consensus. A first one states that syntax can evolve once the size of the lexicon surpasses a threshold and combinatorial signalling becomes more beneficial. Second, research on artificial grammar has forwarded the idea that syntactic processing is a computational achievement, suggesting that the emergence of syntax is linked to brain size evolution. A third view is that syntax is a reflection of event perception, whereby events are decomposable into grammatical functions (actor, action, patient), a cognitive predisposition externalised in human language. The rationale of this project is to address these hypotheses with a broad comparative research programme on non-human primate communication and cognition, including great apes, in the wild and captivity.

Objectives
The goal is to generate empirical evidence to better understand how and why primate communication and cognition transitioned into human syntax, to develop a comprehensive evolutionary theory of syntax.

Specific aims
The proposal is for four systematic studies on the natural syntax of key non-human primate species, both in the wild and in captivity, in terms of structure, flexibility and cognitive underpinnings. We will collect new data sets and analyse existing ones, taking advantage of recent developments artificial intelligence and machine learning.

Methods
We will carry out observational studies and field experiments in primate species in their natural habitats across Africa to assess the range of syntactic patterns and their flexibility. We will carry out targeted behavioural experiments with great apes at Basel Zoo, using touch screens and eye-tracking technology. We will use machine learning to screen existing and new databases.

Expected results
Data will provide a more complete picture of the phenomenology of primate syntax. Within species, we expect variation caused by socio-ecological factors, especially predation pressure and social complexity. For great apes, we expect event perception in terms of agents, actions and patients, and pragmatic use of syntax during social interactions. We expect these datasets to enable substantial theoretical progress towards a unified evolutionary theory of syntax.

Impact
Language is uniquely human but its evolution is not. Empirically driven comparative research on syntax is of key importance in making progress. We expect results to be of interest for several scientific disciplines concerned with the evolutionary history of humans, including anthropology, psychology, cognitive science, biology and linguistics.

Title: Strongly-Coupled Immersed Boundary Methods for Fluid-Structure Interaction
Abstract:
The interplay between fluid flow and deformable structures is of fundamental
relevance in many areas ranging from engineering applications such as energy
harvesting using smart materials and the optimization of aerodynamic devises to
bio-fluidmechanics in order to enhance our basic understanding of the propulsion
mechanisms of animals as well as the blood flow through the aortic valve and the
cardiovascular system. However, the accurate prediction of the complex
interaction between fluid and deforming structures at reasonable computational
costs remains a challenge for state-of-the-art numerical solvers.

To that end, the immersed boundary method (IBM) has proven as an efficient tool
by alleviating the need of expensive meshing and re-meshing approaches such as
arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian (ALE) formulations. In addition, the IBM allows
the use of Cartesian meshes for the fluid for which extraordinary robust and
efficient numerical solvers exist. Despite these advantages, the IBM was long
perceived to lose its benefits for high Reynolds number flows. Recent advances,
however, are starting to break these limits with the development of
higher-order accurate schemes and adaptive grid refinement techniques.

Notable is the recent development of the immersed boundary lattice Green's
function (IBLGF) method, which has shown to accurately capture both laminar and
turbulent external flows for stationary and (prescribed) moving geometries at
minimal computational cost. Efficiency was achieved by employing lattice Green’s
functions (LGF) on formally unbounded staggered Cartesian grids, which allow a
minimal and adaptive computational domain as prescribed by regions of
significant vorticity, while implicitly enforcing free-space boundary
conditions. In combination with specialized time integration techniques and
adaptive block-refinement (AMR) the IBLGF reduces to simple discrete Poisson
problems, which can be solved efficiently using parallel fast multipole methods.

In the first part of the proposed project we shall take advantage of these
benefits and extend the IBLGF to a strongly-coupled immersed boundary method for
elastic bodies undergoing large displacements. In this regard, we will address
pertinent issues related to efficiently enforcing the nonlinearly coupled
fluid-structure interface conditions, which, in contrast to weakly-coupled
methods, allow for small solid-to-fluid mass ratios and large body motions.
While the fluid part will be solved by the IBLGF, we will discretize the solid
using a finite element procedure.

In the second part of the project we will employ the newly developed FSI-scheme
to address both fundamental and engineering relevant problems. As a first
application, we shall use this technique in the realm of biolocomotion, where
we will focus on the propulsion mechanisms of flapping flight and self-propelled
swimming.  In particular, using optimization techniques such as multi-objective
evolutionary optimization algorithms or deep reinforcement learning techniques,
we will determine optimal kinematics for maximum performance of single and
multiple individuals. This will shed light on the illusive underlying mechanisms
of animal locomotion and the role of hydrodynamics in fish schools and swarms.
The optimization procedure requires multiple fully coupled fluid-structure
simulations. Therefore, the efficiency gained in the first part of the project
will become essential. This insight will have significant implications for
designing novel bio-inspired propulsion mechanisms for robotic devices. 

In a second step, we aim to investigate energy harvesting applications, where the
fluid kinetic energy is targeted as the energy source and maximum output power
is achieved by exploiting fluid-structure instabilities such as aeroelastic
flutter to couple structural motion to flow forcing. To that end,
cantilever-type piezoelectric transducers have shown promising results but
require thorough investigation for maximum power output. Here, we will take a
similar approach as above and use numerical simulations to understand the
fundamental mechanisms and, based on these results, design optimal harvesting
devices. This will significantly impact engineering applications and enable
fully autonomous, maintenance-free devices, which cannot easily be powered by
external sources.
Keywords: Biolocomotion, Energy Harvesting, Fluid-Structure Interaction, Immersed Boundary Methods

Title: MAchine Learning to Boost the Early diagnosis of acute Cardiovascular conditions (MALBEC)
Abstract:
Background, rationale and objectives: Acute cardiovascular diseases (ACVD) including myocardial infarction (MI), acute heart failure (AHF), pulmonary embolism (PE) and acute aortic syndromes (AAS) are the most common cause of death in Switzerland, Europe, and the United States. Early and accurate diagnosis of ACVD is a prerequisite for the initiation of evidence-based therapy. In the last two decades, the early diagnosis of ACVD has been transformed by the clinical introduction of three cardiovascular biomarkers, which quantify disease processes inherent to the different ACVD: high-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn) for MI, B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP, or NT-proBNP) for AHF, and D-dimer for PE and AAS. Together with the physician’s clinical assessment and the 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG), these biomarkers are central to the diagnosis of MI, AHF, PE, and AAS. Unfortunately, current clinical management of patients with suspected ACVD, including the real-life use of these biomarkers, is still suboptimal and prone to errors. Limitations include that 1) diagnostic information is gathered piece by piece and each piece interpreted in isolation; 2) current diagnostic algorithms address exclusively one single ACVD (e.g., MI) and ignore the need to evaluate multiple conditions simultaneously; 3) current disease-specific diagnostic algorithms apply single biomarkers with binary cutoffs and binary decisions, ignoring the profound effect of confounders such as age, sex, body mass index and renal dysfunction; 4) lack of integration of the quantitative information provided by the 12-lead ECG; 5) limited flexibility with specific timepoints for serial blood draws, which is challenging in busy emergency departments (ED); 6) failure to differentiate between type 1 and type 2 MI, although both require completely different therapy; 7) lack of integration and visualization as a decision support tool within the electronic patient record. All these lead to avoidable morbidity/mortality and treatment costs. The overall objectives of this project are to improve the early diagnosis and management of ACVD by overcoming these limitations. Therefore, this project has two main aims: first, to develop and implement a clinical decision support tool that integrates and visualizes results of established diagnostic variables (e.g., ST-segment elevation in the 12-lead ECG) in a dashboard and, second, to derive and validate human-simulatability machine learning (ML) models that integrate information from the three main diagnostic pillars to rapidly inform the diagnostic probability for six ACVD in patients with acute chest pain and/or acute dyspnoea. 

Methods: Within our interdisciplinary consortium and using a unique dataset of more than 150,000 extensively characterized patients enrolled in randomized controlled trials and observational studies we will initiate six work packages (WP). WP0 runs in parallel with WP1-4 and will use a Java-based multi-platform mirth connect server with a plugin mechanism to develop and implement a clinical decision support in a dashboard as part of the electronic patient record in the ED. In WP1-4 we will derive, internally and externally validate novel ML models with three different classifiers (XGBoost, autoML and an interpretable neural network) for a six-level nominal outcome (STEMI, NSTEMI type 1/type 2, AHF, PE, and AAS). Using transfer learning, state-of-the-art pre-trained models based on 2.2 million and 400,000 ECGs will be exploited to optimally extract ECG features from the 57,000 patients with available digital ECGs. In WP5, the MALBEC models will be implemented in the clinical decision support tool.

Expected results and clinical impact: We anticipate that the MALBEC models will outperform current diagnostic algorithms in safety, effectiveness, and flexibility, and therefore also clinical acceptance and adherence. This will translate in medical and economic value for patients, physicians, and institutions.

Title: Synaptic plasticity in system models
Abstract:
In the neurosciences, synaptic plasticity refers to changes in connections between neurons. Synaptic plasticity can be induced by short stimuli and leads to changes that last for hours or days. These long-lasting changes are thought to be the basis of learning and memory formation in the brain. We focus on biologically plausible mathematical models of synaptic plasticity and explore their functionality and potential use in larger biological systems, exploiting similarities, but also differences, to Machine Learning. 

The research is organized in four Work Packages (WP).

WP1. Learning by 'surprise' signals. Synaptic plasticity is influenced by neuromodulators that are released at moments of surprise or reward. A simple example of the interaction of plasticity and neuromodulators is 'gating', i.e., plasticity is switched on in the presence of a modulator. Machine learning research shows that gating by 'surprise' could be important to form new memories or modify existing ones whenever the expectations arising from the current world knowledge are disappointed.

In this workpackage we want to explore mathematical theories that are inspired by machine learning but linked to surprise signals in the brain and described as Hebbian plasticity gated by neuromodulators, so-called three-factor rules. Furthermore, we would like to extract and use surprise signals in spiking neural networks.

WP2 Learning by 'novelty' signals. Curiosity is a natural drive to explore an environment so as to gain information and discover 'novel' states or objects. In machine learning, curiosity (search for information gain) has been modeled in the form of ad hoc signals that play a role akin to reward in the theory of reinforcement learning. In this workpackage we want to formalize notions of novelty and curiosity and implement these in a biologically plausible neural network of spiking neurons
with a generalized three-factor learning rule.

WP3. Learning by 'sameness' and 'contrastive' signals. Modern machine learning relies heavily on deep neural networks with multiple layers which are trained by the BackProp algorithm. BackProp in multi-layer networks is biologically questionable because the learning rules are either non-local or require rather specic feedback pathways to make them local. In this work package we explore whether deep neural networks can be trained with alternative learning rules that are generalizations of three-factor rules that include not only Hebbian contributions from pre- and post-synaptic neurons and gating via neuromodulators, but also a signal that conveys whether the current stimulus is, or is not, of the same kind as the previous one. A positive sameness signal could be generated by the brain during observation of, say, a rotating object, by linking information across time whereas a negative ('contrastive') signal could be generated after a saccade to a distant location.

WP4 Quantitative comparisons between plastic network models and recorded data. We plan to extract parameters of neurons and synaptic plasticity rules from spiking data from networks of up to 1000 recorded neurons. The methods will be developed exploiting modern algorithms and rst tested on articial data (system idencation), before they will be applied to two sets of experimental data. Extracting neuronal and network parameters from experimental data is a challenge in itself, but our long-term goal is to extract parameters of neurons embedded in a network not only at a given
moment in time, but to follow parameter changes of neurons and their connections over time during behavioral learning progress. 

In all cases we will combine analytical methods with computer simulations.
Keywords: Integrate-and-fire neurons, Neuron models, Surprise and Novelty, Synaptic learning rules, Synaptic plasticity, Three-factor rules of plasticity

Title: Sparse solutions of underdetermined systems: retroactive applications, algorithms, inference, and new perspectives
Abstract:
The discovery of the possibility of sparse solutions of underdetermined systems is the pivotal achievement of statistics, and in a broader context of data science, at the turn of the 21th century. Earlier, it were rather solutions of overdetermined systems, that is, the presumption that data should dominate in quantity the complexity of concepts they lead to, that accompanied the evolution of the ideas and techniques of statistical data analysis from the 17th century until reaching their maturity by the end of 1940’s — subsequently followed by the vigorous growth in all areas of statistical methodology and its engineering applications (statistical machine learning in particular).

We propose to participate in a similar process that is underway now: to use the state-of-the-art knowledge of approaches capable of obtaining sparse, and more generally any solutions in the underdetermined systems, to investigate certain retroactive applications, in a few selected areas where this capability can lead to novel methodological advances. We aim at developing comprehensive technologies qualified of delivering the results in data-analytic practice: they are, among other things, to be accompanied by efficient algorithms, and embedded into the wider statistical framework capable of gauging their behavior in stochastic terms (inference), and also tried on few stimulating examples from the practice of data science. We also propose research on a more fundamental level (new perspectives) further enhancing technologies capable of achieving sparsity and related objectives, not missing any opportunity of furthering the conceptual understanding (“theory”) of relevant aspects — via probabilistic, but also other means.
Keywords: Artificial neural network, Change point detection, Machine learning, Model selection, Regularization, Sparsity

Title: Repair of lysosomes and homeostasis in cystinosis: unlocking molecular mechanisms and therapeutic targets
Abstract:
Background and rationale. Epithelial cells that line the proximal tubule (PT) of the kidney rely on an intertwined ecosystem of vesicular trafficking pathways to efficiently ensure the reabsorption of essential nutrients and maintain homeostasis. The lysosomes stand at the crossroads of this network owing to their ability to process incoming molecules, sense and signal nutrient availability, and sort receptors and nutrient transporters, dictating the differentiation of the tubular cells, hence their physiological homeostasis. Recent evidence shows that remodeling programs mediate the reformation of new lysosomes following the degradation of extracellular and intracellular cargos. Signaling pathways and transcriptional programs also enable tubular cells to constantly monitor the levels of intracellular metabolites and fine-tune the metabolic activities of lysosomes to sustain homeostasis.
Defects in lysosome-residing enzymes or proteins can lead to PT dysfunction and proximal tubulopathy. Recessive mutations in CTNS, the gene encoding cystinosin (CTNS), cause cystinosis, a lysosomal storage disease characterized by early and severe dysfunction of PT cells, progressing towards chronic kidney disease and life-threatening complications. How, mechanistically, the increased levels of cystine within lysosomes, reflecting its defective export through CTNS, disrupt the lysosome and affect cell-fate decisions in the kidney tubule epithelium remains incompletely understood, hindering the development of new disease-modifying therapies.
Taking cystinosis as a paradigm of defective lysosomes causing PT dysfunction and proximal tubulopathy, and using a combination of preclinical models, cell-and lysosome-based function assays, and disease-relevant screening technologies, we aim to:
1. Decipher how lysosomes direct cell fate specification in the kidney tubule epithelium. By combining animal and cell-based models with gain- and loss-of function interventions and pharmacological approaches, we propose to conduct in-depth mechanistic investigations of how the lysosomal mobilization of cystine through CTNS directs cell-fate specification and differentiation in the kidney tubule epithelium. These studies will help identify how cystine sufficiency instructs kidney tubular cell fate decisions and whether alterations in this process drive proximal tubulopathy and kidney disease development in cystinosis.
2. Dissect mechanisms of lysosomal reformation and their roles in normal and diseased PT cells. By using physiologically relevant PT cellular systems, along with high-throughput protein profiling of intact lysosomes, and super-resolution imaging techniques, we plan to investigate whether and how the nutrient transport activity of CTNS regulates the reformation of new lysosomes during cargo degradation ? an evolutionarily conserved, homeostatic pathway that preserves the requisite number of functional lysosomes within the cell. These studies will help uncover the effector mechanisms exploited by kidney tubular cells to fine-tune the functions of lysosomes in response to physiological perturbations of homeostasis and their implications in pathogenic challenges, such as the progressive storage of accumulating undegraded materials in cystinosis.
3. Identify targets and cystinosis therapeutics. By synergizing prior knowledge-based approaches and artificial intelligence (AI)-powered, target identification engine with a cross-species screening and validation workflow, we aim to develop an integrated drug discovery platform to enable the identification targeted candidate therapies for individuals living with cystinosis and accelerate their therapeutic translation to the clinic.
Expected outcomes and impact. From these studies, we expect to unravel fundamental principles governing the identity, functions, and plasticity of lysosomes in the context of growth, metabolism, tissue homeostasis and disease, and to accelerate the effective translation of new therapeutic agents from preclinical systems to clinical benefit for individuals living with cystinosis and other lysosome-related disorders.
Keywords: Autophagy, Differentiation, Epithelial cells, Growth, Homeostasis, Kidney proximal tubule, Lysosomal storage disease, Lysosome, Metabolism, Signal transduction, Therapeutic intervention

Title: How China Climbs the Tree of Trade Success
Abstract:
China is on its way to become the leading economy in world trade. On the one hand, it should not surprise us that a country with a population of some 1.4 billion is big in every regard. However, what is startling is the speed of change at which China went from an essentially invisible economy to one of the leading countries. A lot of that has been enabled by its first gradual and since the 1990s its aggressive opening up to foreign trade.
In the past 20 years, in particular since its membership in the World Trade Organization in 2001, two important developments happened: on the one hand, China has gained large weight in many countries’ imports; and on the other hand, China has largely transformed from a global producer of “simple” (labor-intensive) goods such as textiles and apparel to one that competes with economies at the technological frontier in terms of electronics, solar panels, etc. Clearly, these two aspects are intertwined, but in politics and academic research alike there is currently a focus on how China’s emergence has transformed life and wellbeing in developed countries. E.g., the very inception of the so-called U.S.-China trade war by the former U.S. president Donald Trump, the increasing number of WTO anti-dumping cases against China, and the numerous studies on the local labor market effects of China (Dauth and Südekum 2012; Autor, Dorn, and Hanson 2015; Egger, Kaynak, and Rydzek 2020) are all examples of this type of attention. What goes much more under the radar in this debate is that China’s transformation has helped reduce poverty for about one-fifth of the world’s population, that it progresses rapidly to a country of reduced resource waste, and that it swiftly climbed the ladder of technological and qualitative progress. For instance, a picture of some major road in one of China’s big cities would have mostly shown people on foot, on bicycles, and on motor vehicles. Now, instead, one would see not only many western luxury cars but also Chinese cars which look like western ones. The sample of cars on a Chinese road nowadays is not much different from the one which one would see in leading developed countries. And the fraction of electric-engine taxi cabs is larger and grows faster than in most western economies. 
This project is devoted to looking inside of China’s success by using merged firm and trade-transaction data for the period from late 1990s to 2013. This data-set contains information on accounting variables of firms and great detail about their trade (exports and imports), ranging from the product details, the trading partners (countries), the value and quantity traded. Moreover, what is known as well is the spatial and sectoral information about the firms in China. These ingredients permit assessing where (in terms of regions, sectors, products, and trading partners) success (in terms of productivity and quality improvement) was largest, to which extent it happened through churning (weak firms exiting and strong firms entering) or upgrading of existing firms, etc. These insights can improve our understanding of the economic roles of trade, as we can learn drivers and consequences in an environment of rapid change.
Keywords: Bayesian modelling, Chinese economy, document parsing, factor analysis, firm Behavior, international trade, latent factor models, machine learning, micro-level trade analysis, network analysis
