Title: Description, prediction and origin of human decision-making
Abstract:
Decision theory underlies all social sciences, including economics, finance and political sciences and is also crucial in engineering sciences as a bridge between “mechanical” solutions and their human and social acceptance and implementations. The classical view assumes that people often use cognitive heuristics (or biases) to save effort, but they would be more accurate if they made “rational” choices based on logic and statistics. However, the conditions required to apply classical models of rationality — such as knowledge of all the feasible options, their state-contingent outcomes and related probabilities — rarely hold in most decisions we face. In these situations, several studies have shown how simple strategies often outperform more complex ones.
In this proposal, we address an outstanding problem in decision theory: the development of a systematic theory of choice, able to answer both the descriptive question (“In which scenarios do people employ which heuristics?”) and the normative question (“When should individuals use a heuristic instead of a sophisticated approach to make better decisions?”).
To reach our objective, we consider the following research questions:

1. Formalization of heuristics: what is the neuro-psychological process underlying human bounded rationality?
2. Ecological rationality of heuristics: what was the adaptive problem faced by our ancestors where a given cognitive bias was evolutionary optimal?

We plan to address the first question via computational models of decision-making, empirically validating and extending our recently developed Random Field Decision Theory. This is (to our knowledge) the first model for individual decision-making relying on the statistical mechanics of disordered systems.
We propose to address the second question using tools from evolutionary game theory and agent-based modeling, as well as insights from evolutionary psychology and recent advances in axiomatic theory of choice.
We expect to generate a range of new models delivering falsifiable empirical predictions (e.g. relationship between response time and type of preferences). These will in turn drive the design of laboratory experiments for suitable hypothesis testing. Broadly, the first project serves also as fuel for the second, providing new observations which need to be rationalized in the realm of evolutionary psychology.
Our aim to shed light on the computational and evolutionary origin of human decision-making would have a remarkable impact on: i) the efficacy of policy implementation; ii) the development of reliable and biasfree artificial intelligence agents; iii) the adaptive intelligence of organizations, shaping in turn technological innovations.
Keywords: computational models of decision-making, dual-process theories, ecological rationality, evolutionary psychology

Title: MAD4WW: Hybrid Mechanistic and Data-Driven Modelling for Wastewater Processes
Abstract:
Today's water resource recovery facilities (WRRFs), also known as wastewater treatment plants, are facing a complex multi-criteria situation because they do not only protect human beings and the environment from adverse impacts of wastewater, but are also required to contribute to solving global challenges such as climate change. Computer models are powerful tools to support the operation and optimization of WRRFs to navigate through this intricate task. Yet, current models are either not designed to predict all nowadays-relevant compounds and emissions or their application to real systems represents a difficult challenge due to the complexity of full-scale plants. By combining the strengths of data-driven approaches with knowledge-based, mechanistic models, hybrid modelling is a promising approach to overcome these challenges. However, hybrid modelling is an emerging field and to leverage its full potential for widely used, understandable and solid support tools, there is a huge research need especially with regard to interpretability, reliability and generalization of this modelling technique.

The objective of this proposal is to systematically investigate the potential of hybrid approaches in the context of modelling nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions from biological wastewater treatment. Being a strong greenhouse gas (265 kgCO2-eq) and an ozone-depleting substance, N2O mitigation is a top priority. In our modelling process, we will address above research gaps and explore potentially groundbreaking new approaches including the use of genomics data within three specific aims:

AIM 1: Investigating how machine learning tools can support process understanding (interpretability) and thus improve mechanistic model building in a full-scale context (generalization).
AIM 2: Systematically exploring hybrid modelling architectures with a special focus on relating to operational parameters (interpretability) and on developing novel approaches.
AIM 3: Developing an uncertainty framework (reliability) and investigating generalization of hybrid models.

A concrete output of this project will be an encompassing novel model package to predict N2O emissions from biological wastewater treatment. Beyond that, this project shall clear the way for a new age of efficiently using data from full-scale WRRFs and substantially contribute towards next generation wastewater models that shall help WRRF operation to meet stringent effluent quality and concurrently address today's global challenges.

The interdisciplinary environment at Eawag as well as years of experience in wastewater treatment, greenhouse gas emissions and modelling render our team just predestined to conduct the proposed research.
Keywords: Biological Wastewater Treatment, Data-Driven Modelling, Hybrid Modelling, Mechanistic Modelling, Nitrous Oxide Emissions, Stochastic Modelling, Wastewater Process Engineering

Title: “KernelCD phase2”: Change Detection in Remote Sensing Images Using Kernel Based Machine Learning Algorithms
Abstract:
One of the most challenging problems in remote sensing and Earth observation is the detection of changes occurred between two acquisitions of the same geographical area at different times. Such detections are crucial for environmental and urban monitoring, post-catastrophe assessment and natural hazard mapping. Many techniques that aim at addressing the problem starting from different assumptions exist, and among which difference image analysis and post classification comparisons are the most utilized.
In the current “KernelCD” project (SNSF Grant No. 200021-126505), the problem of detecting changes in optical images was successfully addressed by applying methods coming from the machine learning community. In particular, supervised and unsupervised kernel-based techniques were developed specifically for change detection. For the supervised methods, the approaches proposed were designed with accent on accuracy, while light computational load was preferred for the unsupervised ones. Finally, robustness was the main criterion for the success of feature extraction techniques, last topic proposed in the current “KernelCD” project. Despite the success of this first part of the project, the potential of such developments for the applicative domain remains underexploited. One of the main limiting factors remains the recourse to single-source sensors. In order to fully accomplish the aim of “KernelCD”, new methods specific for multi-source data need to be developed. To this end, we ask for a second part of “KernelCD” (“KernelCD” phase 2) in this proposal.
In this second part of the project, a one year prolongation, we aim at developing approaches specific to multi-source, multi-modal and multi-temporal remote sensing image processing, with focus to accurate and robust change detection. On the one hand, the methods designed will be able to deal with noisy environments and will be robust with respect to heterogeneous input sources. But on the other hand, they will maintain strict accuracy standards and information extraction capabilities. As for the current “KernelCD” project, these problems will be tackled by considering the most recent developments in the machine learning and pattern recognition communities. Kernel-methods have been poorly documented in the remote sensing community for multi-temporal data-fusion applications: we aim at filling this gap by building on the knowledge acquired from the current “KernelCD” project, and by proposing high-level research by introducing novel techniques for change detection under these conditions. Particular attention will be paid to kernel-based nonlinear feature extraction / manifold learning and dimensionality reduction methods, which will be applied to data-fusion tasks (thus adopting a feature-level fusion approach). On these bases, once the data structure is described, a comprehensive change detector (generating change maps) will be developed. Considering of heterogeneous sources available is a compulsory step, as the changes react differently depending on the type of sensor. For the new detector, the lacks of information of a specific sensor will no more constitute a limitation. This continuation allows a natural ending of the “KernelCD” project: the development of novel advanced techniques dedicated to multi-temporal multi-source data processing. 
The “KernelCD” phase 2 starts from the achievements of its precursor, which have been appreciated at international level by publications, invited talks and fruitful collaborations. It is therefore a natural evolution of the project that will increase its positive impact on to both theoretical and applicative scientific communities.

assessment and natural hazard mapping. many techniques that aim at addressing the problem starting from different assumptions exist, and among which difference image analysis and post classification comparisons are the most utilized. in the current “kernelcd” project (snsf grant no. 200021 126505), the problem of detecting changes in optical images was successfully addressed by applying methods coming from the machine learning community. in particular, supervised and unsupervised kernel based techniques were developed specifically for change detection. for the supervised methods, the approaches proposed were designed with accent on accuracy, while light computational load was preferred for the unsupervised ones. finally, robustness was the main criterion for the success of feature extraction techniques, last topic proposed in the current “kernelcd” project. despite the success of this first part of the project, the potential of such developments for the applicative domain remains underexploited. one of the main limiting factors remains the recourse to single source sensors. in order to fully accomplish the aim of “kernelcd”, new methods specific for multi source data need to be developed. to this end, we ask for a second part of “kernelcd” (“kernelcd” phase 2) in this proposal. in this second part of the project, a one year prolongation, we aim at developing approaches specific to multi source, multi modal and multi temporal remote sensing image processing, with focus to accurate and robust change detection. on the one hand, the methods designed will be able to deal with noisy environments and will be robust with respect to heterogeneous input sources. but on the other hand, they will maintain strict accuracy standards and information extraction capabilities. as for the current “kernelcd” project, these problems will be tackled by considering the most recent developments in the machine learning and pattern recognition communities. kernel methods have been poorly documented in the remote sensing community for multi temporal data fusion applications: we aim at filling this gap by building on the knowledge acquired from the current “kernelcd” project, and by proposing high level research by introducing novel techniques for change detection under these conditions. particular attention will be paid to kernel based nonlinear feature extraction / manifold learning and dimensionality reduction methods, which will be applied to data fusion tasks (thus adopting a feature level fusion approach). on these bases, once the data structure is described, a comprehensive change detector (generating change maps) will be developed. considering of heterogeneous sources available is a compulsory step, as the changes react differently depending on the type of sensor. for the new detector, the lacks of information of a specific sensor will no more constitute a limitation. this continuation allows a natural ending of the “kernelcd” project: the development of novel advanced techniques dedicated to multi temporal multi source data processing. the “kernelcd” phase 2 starts from the achievements of its precursor, which have been appreciated at international level by publications, invited talks and fruitful collaborations. it is therefore a natural evolution of the project that will increase its positive impact on to both theoretical and applicative scientific communities. . change detection, environmental monitoring, ground cover classification, hyperspectral, kernel methods, lidar, multi source, remote sensing, Title: Direct and indirect impacts of mining in the Amazon
Abstract:
The Amazon rainforest plays a crucial role in supporting human well-being by contributing to climate stability, conserving biodiversity, as well as sustaining local food production and livelihoods. However, this ecosystem is vanishing at an accelerated rate. Mining activities in land system analysis have been identified as a land use with small spatial extent, but large spillover impacts. In particular, artisanal gold mining has direct impacts on forests, but also leads to broader water contamination, biodiversity loss and land conflicts. Within this research, I aim to provide a step change in our understanding of mining activities in the Amazon, their direct and indirect impacts on the forest ecosystem, as well as the interaction with other deforestation drivers. Moreover, I am interested in studying the effectiveness of the linked environmental governance. To this end, I aim to create an extensive and deep learning-based high-resolution map documenting mining activities over time. Utilizing this novel data foundation, I will study the vast indirect land use impact of industrial and small and artisanal mining, as well as the spatial interconnection between the agricultural and mining sectors, especially with regards to its expansion. Using a desk-based conceptual analysis on mechanisms of different stakeholder commitments, I will assess the stringency and implementation factors of governance in the Brazilian gold mining sector. I will examine the impact of different conservation policies and assess the stringency of recently formulated due diligence commitments with resepect to environmental and social outcomes.
This research fills various pressing research gaps such as the type and extent of mining activities in the Amazon and their indirect drivers of deforestation. More broadly, the outcomes of this research will support Amazon conservation efforts while addressing present land conflicts and related humanitarian crises in the region. The research will have direct impact through the interaction of both local stakeholders and global players involved in the mining sector. The ultimate goal is to devise solutions that promote a thriving Amazon characterized by standing forests and free-flowing rivers, as well as decent livelihoods for local communities.
Keywords: Amazon, Artificial Intelligence, Land systems, Mining, Remote Sensing, Voluntary Sustainability Standards

Title: Investigating the connectomic fingerprint of cerebral small vessel disease
Abstract:
Background and rationale
Cerebral small vessel disease (SVD), highly prevalent in the aging population, has a strong impact on individuals’ behavioural, cognitive and motor function. The long-term SVD effects on individuals’ quality of life and cognitive performance explain the significant emotional and socio-economic burden on patients and caregivers. Despite major advances in the field, our understanding about the relationship between spatial and temporal characteristics of SVD-related brain anatomy characteristics and the resulting clinical phenotype is still limited. 

Overall objectives and specific aims
Given our recent findings brought empirical evidence for the existence of four well-defined SVD subtypes, the main goal of this project is to provide a detailed understanding about the spatial dependency between SVD-associated brain pathology and related clinical signs and symptoms. To this aim, we combine methodological developments for automated delineation of SVD-induced lesions from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data with implementation of the “connectome” concept characterising whole-brain structural networks. Specifically, we aim to 1) test the accuracy of already implemented, (semi)automated lesion detection methods versus manual lesion detection; 2) investigate the spatial relationship between lesion-based connectome maps from healthy individuals and individuals’ cognitive performance, apathy scores and recent cerebrovascular events; 3) investigate the structure-function relationship between individuals’ structural connectomes with cognitive performance, apathy scores and recent cerebrovascular events; and 4) develop and validate a prediction model for cognitive outcome using machine learning techniques.

Methods to be used
We use state-of-the-art longitudinal clinical data, MRI and statistical frameworks to characterise clinical phenotypes of different SVD subtypes according to our established CADMUS classification. We combine two prospective clinical SVD registries from Switzerland and the United Kingdom, Bern PRO-SVD and Oxford SVD (n = 235), including standard cognitive and behavioural assessments, additionally to a multi-contrast MRI ptotocol. After testing the accuracy of already implemented methods for automated lesion detection against manual labelling, we will map the patients’ lesions on normative connectomes derived from >1000 healthy participants from the CoLaus|PsyCoLaus cohort. We then analyse the spatial relationship between the resulting connectome maps with individuals’ cognitive performance, apathy scores and cerebrovascular events across SVD subtypes. Using machine learning techniques, we will test the predictive accuracy for cognitive outcome after validation with longitudinal data.

Expected results
Combining clinical cohorts with large-scale epidemiological data, we will describe structure-function relationships through brain networks defining SVD-associated cognitive and mood dysfunction and cerebrovascular events. Finally, we will develop and validate a connectome-based prediction model for cognitive decline in SVD.

Impact for the field
Mastering the challenge of predicting SVD’s clinical outcome will provide new avenues for adequate prevention and therapy of a highly prevalent and devastating disorder. A better understanding of affected brain networks could pave the way for personalised treatments targeting specific brain networks using non-invasive brain modulation techniques.
Keywords: Apathy, Cognition, Connectomics, Diffusion-tensor imaging, Magnetic resonance imaging, Small vessel disease

Title: Learning unbiased habitat suitability at scale with AI (deepHSM)
Abstract:
Global loss of floral and faunal species is accelerating at disconcerting rates. A continuation of this trend will likely result in degradation of ecosystems and ecosystem services, potentially in loss of suitable living conditions. Counter-measures like protection of endangered species, habitat restoration and reduction of pollution are urgently needed, but require a thorough understanding of the habitat suitability and current distribution of species on a global scale.
Habitat suitability maps (HSMs) are often obtained through species distribution models (SDMs), which attempt to explain the living and reproduction conditions of a species based on environmental variables typically related to climate and topography. SDMs are generally based on a series of hand-selected environmental variables, lightweight statistical models, and a number of species presence records obtained through field sampling, museum collections or hand-drawn distribution maps. SDMs are used widely, but the low number of presence records, as well as the lack of expressivity of the statistical models used, often limit their accuracy. Moreover, computational limitations, as well as geographical biases, limit the potential for SDMs to be extended in an accurate way and to large scales. In parallel, machine learning has shown tremendous success in interpreting large-scale data in various disciplines. This is mostly attributed to high-capacity algorithms like deep learning, as well as availability of big data from crowdsourcing efforts used to train the algorithms. Deploying machine learning has the potential to provide the urgently required upscaling of SDMs, but efforts have so far been scarce. Crucially, the benefits and implications of using ML for habitat suitability mapping are poorly understood.
The aim of deepHSM is to assess biodiversity trends at scale using machine learning. We will develop the next generation of SDMs able to map complex interactions with the environment for many species at once, while integrating and building on expert knowledge from both data science and ecology.
We will first create deep learning-based SDMs able to ingest large volumes of data. To this end, openly available repositories will be used, consisting of remote sensing satellite products and climatic data on the one hand, and species occurrence records from crowdsourcing portals on the other hand. These deep SDMs will then serve as a foundation for a series of studies addressing the shortcomings mentioned above. First, we will develop novel concepts to augment deep SDMs with expert knowledge about specific survival and reproduction requirements for species, and to explicitly model biotic interactions between species. Second, we will investigate means of eliminating data and modelling biases of the accessibility of locations, as well as individual uploader preferences of occurrence records uploaded to the mentioned portals. This in turn permits estimating the credibility and confidence of SDM maps per location.
Together, these studies pave the way for models that allow quantifying floral and faunal distribution with high accuracy, high reliability, and at scale. Crucially, deepHSM envisions SDMs that reason on big data, while simultaneously listening to the knowledge gathered by biologists and ecologists over decades. The result is a digital characterisation of biodiversity through data science that builds on expert- and community-provided knowledge across the globe. deepHSM not only has the potential to derive new insights into biodiversity, species losses and conservation, but further opens up avenues to create a global community, from data-contributing enthusiasts over conservationists to ecologists, that works hand-in-hand towards a better understanding of species distribution and their protection.
Keywords: Earth observation, deep learning, habitat suitability, machine learning, remote sensing, species distribution models

Title: Implantable Autonomous Wireless Bio-Electronics for High-Resolution Monitoring and Detection of Epilepsy in-vivo
Keywords: Bio-electronic interfaces, Cortical microelectronic implants, Wireless cortical implants

clinical environment within the context of epilepsy treatment consisting in detecting and subsequently resecting incriminated areas. the determination of the epileptogenic areas as well as the development of future implantable systems aiming at early detection or prediction of the seizure both are in need of autonomous implantable recording systems that enable patients to be monitored in their home environment. to this extent, portable and autonomous solutions to cortical implantable recording systems must be provided. no such full system exists to date, though several research groups achieved resulting in a fair understanding of block level engineering issues and their potential solution. a true system level approach is needed to enable the systematic study and further development Title: Intelligence through the Eyes of Imagination
Abstract:
While artificial intelligence is intensively researched in philosophy (2000+ entries on Philpapers), human intelligence is under-explored – it doesn’t even have a dedicated entry in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. This situation is puzzling since it is reasonable to assume that we need a clear concept of human intelligence to determine whether it applies to machines. 

This project aims at a conceptual analysis of human intelligence relying on the tools developed in the imagination literature and the tight connections between imagination and intelligence. The analysis of human intelligence can benefit considerably from the literature on imagination, since: (i) the structure of key debates about their nature are similar, and (ii) many kinds of imagining play a central role in intelligence. 

(i)   In detail, what “imagination” and “intelligence” refer to (i.e., their extensions) and how they are defined (i.e., their intensions) are hotly debated issues. What is the extension of imagination? How many sui generis mental states does the lay term “imagining” refer to? The consensus is that no “single something” (Kind, 2013, p.144) corresponds to all senses of imagining. Instead, there are several sui generis imaginative states such as supposing, being creative, synthesizing, etc. Likewise, in the intelligence literature, psychologists have wondered since Spearman (1904) whether a single something influences specific cognitive performances. General intelligence (or “g”) is taken by some to play that role. Similarly, just as there could be several kinds of imaginings, there could be several distinct kinds of intelligence, such as creative, emotional, or visuospatial intelligences. As to the intensional dimension, we face up to 12 definitions of imagination (Stevenson, 2003) and 53 definitions of human intelligence (Legg & Hutter, 2007). There is no consensus on the desiderata these definitions should satisfy. “Chaos itself can go no farther!” (Spearman, 1927, p.14)

(ii)   As Spearman also observed (1927, p.13), approaches to intelligence often incorporate imagination. According to a first approach (Sternberg, 1999), creativity is a sui generis kind of intelligence. Since creativity is much discussed in philosophy as a kind of imagining, we may consider creative imagination as a component of intelligence. Another approach (Gardner, 2006) is favorable to Emotional Intelligence, which is strongly correlated with the ability to put oneself in someone else’s shoes. This can be identified with the imaginative ability to get immersed in fiction or characters. If so, imaginative immersion is particularly relevant for EI. Finally, in the psychometry of general intelligence (Wechsler, 1997), visuospatial processing tasks, such as manipulating and rotating shapes, are so strongly associated with mental images that it is natural to posit a necessary connection between them. Hence, three of the most discussed senses of imagination – creativity, immersion, and mental images – seem to play crucial roles in approaches to intelligence. 

My project of analyzing the concept of intelligence through the lens of imagination has two facets: (A) clarifying the desiderata for a robust sense of intelligence by using tools developed in the imagination literature and (B) determining the specific relationship(s) between imagination and intelligence. 

To achieve my goals, I shall (A) examine empirical debates on intelligence and redeploy the methodology from my Ph.D. dissertation to establish criteria for a robust sense of intelligence. This, I hypothesize, will shed light on (i) emotional and (ii) so-called “crystallized” intelligence. Additionally, (B) I shall explore the relations between intelligence and imagination by investigating empirical data on (iii) creativity and (iv) mental imagery. This will help disambiguate the kind of imagination at work and the exact relation between these imaginings and intelligence. Determining the nature of intelligence and its interaction with other psychological traits are taken as essential issues for future empirical research (Protzko & Colom, 2021).
Keywords: Aphantasia, Creativity, Emotional Intelligence, Gf & Gc, Imagination, Intelligence, Nature of intelligence

Title: Deep learning-based Ultrafast Ultrasound Image Reconstruction: simulations, transfer learning and sparse arrays
Abstract:
Background: Ultrasound (US) imaging is one of the safest, cheapest and, widely accessible imaging modalities used in medical diagnosis. Particularly, a technique called ultrafast US has recently attracted attention since it achieves frame rates of multiple kilohertz, enabling the analysis, for instance, of flow motion and micrometer tissue displacements induced by shear waves that propagate through tissue. Ultrafast US imaging is already at the origin of several pioneering imaging modes such as functional neuroimaging and shear-wave elastography.
Because ultrafast acquisitions are performed using unfocused wavefronts, resulting images are of relatively low quality (compared to focused wave imaging), characterized by broad main lobes (low lateral resolution) and high diffraction artifacts (low contrast) caused by side lobes (SLs), grating lobes (GLs), and edge waves (EWs). Such artifacts can be detrimental to both diagnosis and displacement estimation techniques, the latter being the core objectives of most ultrafast US imaging modes.
Three-dimensional (3D) real-time US imaging will become a key enabler for diagnosis and treatment of several diseases. Nevertheless, it requires several thousands of transducer elements, increasing the hardware complexity and computational cost. Sparse array imaging has proved to be a solution to reduce the cost and complexity of 3D US scanners. In this context, it exists a clear need for affordable, potentially portable, ultrafast US image reconstruction methods capable of producing high-quality 3D images from single ultrafast acquisitions.

Objectives: This project is a continuation of the research pursued at the Signal Processing Laboratory (LTS5) of EPFL focused on the development of advanced ultrafast ultrasound imaging reconstruction techniques. Preliminary results have demonstrated the potential of deep learning for reconstructing higher-quality ultrafast images in two-dimensional (2D) imaging. Thus, this project has a twofold objective. First, it aims to further improve ultrafast ultrasound imaging reconstruction techniques capable of acquiring higher-quality images using state- of-art deep learning methods. Second, it aims to adapt and apply the developed reconstruction techniques to three-dimensional (3D) imaging through the use of sparse arrays.

Expected results: At the end of this project, we expect to have improved the current image reconstruction techniques for 2D and to have developed affordable image reconstruction techniques for higher-quality 3D ultrafast US imaging.

Impact: The reconstruction techniques will allow to improve the accuracy and robustness of ultrafast imaging modes and also to reduce the cost and complexity of 3D US scanners. With better image reconstruction techniques, we will get higher-quality images on affordable, possible portable devices, that can potentially enhance the diagnosis and treatment of several diseases, which is our ultimate goal.
Keywords: Deep learning, Image reconstruction, Sparse arrays, Transfer learning, Ultrafast Ultrasound

Title: Hanging manipulator for gardening applications
Abstract: Switzerland is the land of Alps, with mild weather and considerable precipitation. There is great potential for food production, but sustainable farming seems hard to achieve. Many farms are too small to be economically viable. This factor together with the hilly type of terrain in some parts makes the application of large-scale agricultural machinery economically and technically difficult, and the dimensions are yet too large to install infrastructures like those in greenhouses. Robotic manipulators mounted on wheeled bases are yet promising solutions in these scales, though not practical in steep gardens. This project aims at proposing a different robotic solution for midsize and hilly gardens in Switzerland. We consider reaching plants from the top by using a cable-driven robot. An upside manipulator mounted on this robot carries gardening and farming tools. Being solar-powered, this platform solves the locomotion problem and assists the gardeners with artificial intelligence.
Keywords: Autonomous Gardening, Control, Hanging Robot, Manipulator, Mechanics, Smart Farming, Solar Power

Title: Advanced Learning for Tracking and Detection in Medical Workflow Analysis.
Abstract:
Research in computer vision has made a remarkable impact in many real world situations and had provided robust solutions.  For example, face detection algorithms have been integrated in most mass-consumer digital cameras. This has been made possible by the combination of robust feature extraction with statistical learning algorithms.

In this project we want to similarly advance object detection and tracking by considering a challenging and complex scenario. Surgical work-flow recovery is crucial for designing context-sensitive service systems in future operating rooms. Abstract knowledge about actions which are being performed is particularly valuable in the operating room (OR). This knowledge can be used for many applications such as optimizing the work-flow, recovering average work-flows for guiding and evaluating training surgeons, automatic report generation and ultimately for monitoring in a context aware operating room.  Our objective is to analyze the events happening in the medical operating room, equipped with multiple cameras, in order to prepare the necessary input for fully automatic work-flow analysis.

Title: Learning optimal features for land-cover classification
Abstract:
The aim of the proposed project is to learn optimal image features to improve automatic image interpretation. The novelty of the work will be to employ statistical feature learning methods rather than handcraft image features for each sensor type and each definition of classes. In particular, we target land-cover classification in difficult areas such as for example urban zones. Land-cover maps are required in many environmental and planning tasks. Current large-scale projects relevant for Switzerland include the periodic update of the European CORINE land-cover datasets; the more recent Urban Atlas, which specifically targets land-cover in the notoriously difficult urban zones; contributions to the land-use layer of the Global Climate Observation System (GCOS, local coordination by MeteoSwiss); and the national land-use inventory (“Arealstatistik”, maintained by the federal bureau of statistics BfS).

The main scientific objective is the development of a generic feature learning framework, which can be adapted to different mapping tasks and image sensors. The project includes the practical implementation of a software prototype for processing input images and delivering image features (usually in the form of multi-channel feature images), which can then be used in any commercial or in-house classification workflow. The question which features are optimal to semantically classify image content is a fundamental, and - except for a handful of classes in open terrain - still open question of remote sensing. It becomes more relevant as ever larger amounts of raw data are collected by a growing arsenal of different sensors.

In the field of statistical learning, there has recently been important progress on data-driven feature learning, which we plan to leverage for the project. These recent advances have been successfully employed for different classifications tasks, including image classification in computer vision, which proves their potential for remote sensing. Although the primary focus is on the features (since only information captured that is captured in this step is available for the subsequent classification), the project will also investigate which classification methods to use with the learned features, since not all classifiers are suitable for all sets of features (e.g. some popular parametric methods are problematic in high-dimensional feature spaces). From both our own experience and the consensus in the literature, we expect that modern discriminative methods like support vector machines and random forests will be most appropriate.

In the project we will develop a dedicated software prototype, but also use open source software, and occasionally commercial products. In particular, a lot of high-quality code for machine learning is available in open source research libraries and general-purpose statistics packages, which we will exploit. On the other hand, end-to-end tests of classification performance will use both research software and commercial remote sensing tools: commercial packages provide well-tested implementations of standard methods, which are also widely used in practice; but important modern methods are not included in current packages, and vendors typically do not document their implementations in sufficient detail. Therefore end-to-end testing will use both conventional remote sensing tools and state-of-the-art classification software.

We believe that the exciting developments in automatic feature learning, which have already been successfully applied to several other problems, hold great promise for remote sensing.
Keywords: image processing, remote sensing

Title: SentiVol: Sentiment Analysis and Bayesian Model Averaging for Volatility Prediction
Abstract:
We propose to investigate the impact of sentiment and activity volumes of social media, financial news, and search engines on stock volatility. We use state-of-the-art sentiment analysis tools to process a large amount of heterogeneous data gathered from various sources which include Twitter, StockTwits, Reddiit, Google Finance, Nexis, Google Trends and Wikipedia. Our research questions are then (i) whether sentiment analysis and internet activity variables provide predictive power when used jointly with a large set of other economic predictors, (ii) what is the nature of this potential impact, and (iii) how can this information be used to generate improved volatility predictions. Our proposed approach is based on Bayesian regression models with spike-and-slab priors. This allows for dealing with high-dimensional data and for doing Bayesian model averaging which results in improved predictions compared to using one single model. We will investigate various model extensions to account for phenomena such as regime switches, non-linearities, and interactions among predictors. In addition, we plan to apply a Bayesian regression model that jointly uses low-frequency and high-frequency return data to generate more precise volatility estimates and, consequently, predictions. In summary, the goal of the project is to contribute to the development of the next generation of volatility prediction models that combine sentiment signals with advanced statistical methods.

Apart from publishing our results in peer-reviewed international academic journals and presenting them on conferences, we plan to set up a web page called “Open Observatory for Sentiment in Volatility” that does real-time volatility prediction based on our results. This will serve as an early warning device for high market volatility. Furthermore, we plan to initiate a follow-up project in cooperation with industry participants in order to apply the results gained from this research.
Keywords: Bayesian modeling, Large amount of heterogeneous data, Sentiment and behavioral analysis, Volatility estimation and prediction

Title: Understanding and promoting goal-directed behaviours in older individuals
Abstract:
Goal directed behaviours (GDB), a complex coordination of various cognitive, emotional and affective processes in order to intentionally attain desired goals, are particularly relevant in everyday life of older individuals. In this population, extreme reductions in GDB decrease one’s quality of life and well-being, and subsequently diminish one’s autonomy. Recently, clinical geriatricians proposed that apathy can be conceptualised as an extreme reduction in GDB. However, to date, no theoretical model connects the processes at play in GDB and in apathy reduction. Moreover, we still lack insight into how normative cognitive deficits and motivational and affective processes in ageing are translated into concrete everyday difficulties and how they impact both goal pursuit and apathy. A comprehensive, integrative perspective to understand the complexity of everyday manifestations of GDB and apathy in older individuals is thus needed. Such a perspective would also allow for designing effective intervention programmes aimed at achieving GDB, thereby reducing apathy and increasing quality of life.
The specific aims of this project are: (1) Conduct semi-structured interviews of older adults’ testimonies of (a) their everyday difficulties in GDB, (b) apathy manifestations, and (c) spontaneous compensation strategies to face such difficulties; (2) Assess indicators of cognitive, motivational and affective processes that influence GDB difficulties and manifestations of apathy; (3) Adopt a mixed-methods design, combining both quantitative and qualitative approaches , to analyse together interviews and tasks/questionnaires data to reach an integrative model of GDB difficulties and apathy; (4) Design individualised interventions to promote GDB in daily-life, learn and adapt useful strategies for specific GDB, and transfer learning to untrained GDB. We will address these questions in two studies. In Study 1, we will conduct interviews and administer objective tasks and questionnaires in order to address aims (1), (2), and (3). Study 1 will additionally provide a model to design individualised interventions (aim 4) using implementation intentions and meta-cognitive training. The effectiveness of these interventions will be assessed in Study 2 with both an intervention and a control sample.
This work is expected to contribute both at a theoretical level, by providing insights into older adults’ everyday difficulties in GDB, and on clinical practice, by designing effective interventions that can be used in daily life to promote GDB. Given the ageing of Western populations and their growing loss of autonomy, this work is important from both a societal (providing knowledge to ameliorate effective interventions and to increase older adult’s autonomy) and individual (increasing well-being and quality of life) perspectives. Understanding GDB difficulties and designing appropriate interventions to promote functional autonomy is therefore of critical importance at both the individual and societal level.
Keywords: Everyday situation, apathy, goal-directed behaviours, individualised clinical interventions, mixed-methods

Title: MaRVis: Magnetic Resonance Vision
Abstract:
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is an essential tool in clinical practice for diagnosis, treatment planning and assessing therapy efficacy. Despite numerous advances in acquisition technologies, even in the most advanced centres MRI is used in a standard, non-personalised mode. An acquisition protocol is hand-picked among a set of predefined ones prior to imaging, minimally modified and executed without further adaptations. Contrary to this mode, today's advances in machine learning and medical image computing allow us to conceive autonomous imaging systems that actively participates in the imaging by understanding the content, adapting the acquisition on the fly and searching for the best evidence to help clinical tasks. Here, we propose to develop technologies towards realising this vision. 

An autonomous imaging system integrated within an MRI has the potential to revolutionise medical imaging. MRI is able to create multiple maps in 2D and 3D displaying different tissue characteristics and function at high spatial resolution and with excellent contrast between different tissue types, all without using ionising radiation. An intelligent system that can drive the acquisition autonomously can more effectively leverage this versatility to acquire better images for each patient while accelerating the overall scan, leading to better patient-care and higher throughput, even paving the way towards using MRI as a quantitative screening tool in clinical practice.

While an autonomous MRI system must be composed of hardware and software components that closely interact with each other, at its core algorithms are needed to automatically interpret data as it is being acquired and extract information to guide the rest of the system. In this project, we propose to develop the algorithms that make up this core and create a Magnetic Resonance Vision (MaRVis) system. Leveraging advances in machine learning and the release of large scale imaging datasets, we organise our work along three aims: 

Aim 1. Advanced image reconstruction from partial measurements: The first aim is to develop image reconstruction algorithms for MRI that go beyond the state-of-the-art. We target algorithms that can reconstruct images with extreme undersampling ratios at a quality that allows extracting semantic information via anatomical modelling and abnormality detection, and quantify inherent uncertainties. 

Aim 2. Semantic understanding and content-aware strategies for MRI:} The second aim focuses on developing algorithms that can extract semantic information during an acquisition from partially available measurements, and on designing and demonstrating strategies to leverage the extracted semantic information together with prior clinical knowledge to guide further acquisition. 

Aim 3. Robust multi-contrast integrated representations: Lastly, we will develop deep learning algorithms that are robust to contrast changes and domain shifts inherent to MRI, and construct representations of the data that integrate multiple-contrasts and semantic information for better interpretation and quantification.

Successful completion of the MaRVis project will provide an algorithmic framework that opens up new avenues for how MRI can be used in clinical practice and research. By making content information available on the fly, the developed framework will enable content-aware adaptation and personalising acquisitions and motivate further developments towards acquiring optimised observations in terms of resolution, Signal-to-Noise ratio (SNR) and set of contrasts. Results in this project will take crucial steps towards realising an ultimate autonomous MRI system and can become the key motivation for future research on related hardware and cyber-physical systems, as well as other imaging systems, such as Computed Tomography.

Title: Algorithmic Bargaining: How Artificial Intelligence Affects War Onset and Termination
Abstract:
Background and rationale: In our age of rapidly expanding data, progress in processing power, and ever more sophisticated algorithms, artificial intelligence (AI) has begun to permeate every aspect of armed conflicts. There is little doubt that the use of AI will change the nature of warfare. But how does AI affect international security more broadly and conflict parties’ propensity to enter or terminate wars more specifically? Existing scholarship focuses predominantly on the military use of AI to tackle this question, ignoring a quieter transformation that is taking place: that of AI opening new possibilities for conflict actors to gather and analyze vast amounts of conflict data to make better predictions about the expected trajectory of a conflict. This lack of research on the role of AI-enabled information provision in armed conflicts is an important gap, as bargaining scholars have long identified imperfect information as a key rationalist explanation for war.

Research question and aim: This research project addresses this gap by asking the following research question: how does the ability of conflict actors to gather and analyze conflict data with the help of AI affect their decisions to initiate war or settle an armed conflict? The aim is to develop a mid-range theory of when and how non-military AI applications affect strategic decisions about war and negotiated peace.

Research methods and data collection: The research employs a multi-methods research design. The main research activity consists of synthesizing and generalizing the findings of my previous Postdoc.Mobility research (grant 202993), aiming to develop a theory on the effects of AI on war onset and termination. To accomplish this, I will use analytic narratives that integrate a rationalist framework situated in the bargaining theory of war with empirical illustrations drawn from a set-theoretic counterfactual case study of the war between Russia and Ukraine. 

Contributions and impact: This research project will contribute to our understanding of how technological changes currently underway will likely affect international security in the coming decade. By showing when and how AI can potentially decrease the risk of war onset or facilitate settlement, it adds important nuances to existing scholarship, which tends to highlight the risks of AI in the context of armed conflicts. The findings are policy relevant, as they can inform government priorities and investments in the development and governance of AI technology.
Keywords: armed conflicts, artificial intelligence, bargaining, emerging technology, information provision, war onset, war termination

Title: MiNI: Multimodal Neuromuscular Interface
Abstract:
The “Multimodal Neuromuscular Interface” (MiNI) project seeks to enable natural, controller-free interaction with extended reality (XR) and related technologies through direct unobtrusive sensing of peripheral muscle activity, with a particular focus on the hand and fingers. MiNI is designed to capture the user’s neuromuscular signals at their biological origin and integrate them into a real-time closed loop system that decodes motor intent and delivers feedback seamlessly via wearable XR technology.

At its core, MiNI takes the form of a low-profile, skin-like interface that integrates surface electromyography (sEMG) and pulse-echo ultrasound technology. This combination is expected to capture both the electrical activation patterns and the mechanical dynamics of muscles, thereby enabling robust decoding of user intent and estimation of biomechanical states (e.g., joint angles and generated forces), even in conditions where single-modality solutions would fail. Signals will be acquired using tiny, energy-efficient electronics that consume less than 10 mW of power while running multimodal embedded machine learning models. These models are expected to recognize hand gestures and estimate generated forces in real time at the edge with less than 20 ms latency. In practice, MiNI will make it possible to drive XR applications with everyday gestures, facilitating smoother remote collaboration, more intuitive prosthetic control, and novel forms of robotic interaction.

Title: Skills and Attitudes through Machine-Based Adaptive attention guidance (SAMBA)
Abstract:
Driven by societal and digital changes, educational institutions are bound to adopt innovative teaching approaches and technologies contributing to the promotion of 21st century skills (i.e. Self-Directed Learning skills) to meet the new challenges within the context of the fourth industrial revolution (4IR). One such teaching approach is adaptive learning, in which the pace of learning, learning objectives, content, or instructional concepts (e.g. inquiry-based learning (IBL) or distance learning) are tailored to students’ individual needs. This is particularly required in Self-Directed Learning (SDL) environments. In learning environments that aim at SDL development, learning is driven by the students' own activity rather than by predetermined inputs from lecturers. In blended and purely online learning environments, high amounts of data can be recorded for each student to enable the application of learning analytics and use collected data to constantly monitor the students’ progress, adapt the instructions or the instructional content, and provide personalised guidance which might develop SDL skills. Attention guidance is one such activity that needs to be optimised in this context as students may inhibit their self-direction by not applying attention correctly. An important function of attention guidance is to highlight the learning content (text, diagrams, graphs, etc.) while students are interacting within the SDL adaptive learning application – this can assist students to appropriately guide their own attention and in doing so support their self-direction. However, this process is inefficient and time-consuming when employed manually by lecturers. To address this drawback, a more feasible approach would be to create an automated system that is able to provide optimised attention guidance based on students' data that resulted from interactions with the blended learning system that would ultimately contribute to SDL skills development. 

The aim of the proposed project is to supply cutting-edge research through machine-based adaptive learning SDL environments (further on called the “SDL adaptive learning application”) with the focus on improving the students’ attention in order to stimulate their SDL development. The first goal is to investigate to what extent the attention can be measured based on different types of data collected from students (mouse tracking and keyboard activity, log data, pre- and post- knowledge tests and pre- and post- SDL perception tests). The second goal is to integrate machine learning into our SDL adaptive learning application in order to adapt attention guidance to students' personal needs and thus improve it. The final goal is to evaluate the impact of the proposed SDL adaptive learning application on SDL skills and attitudes. Title: Planning and Heuristic Search -- A Joint Perspective
Abstract:
A central problem in Artificial Intelligence is to automatically find
a sequence of operators that transforms a given start state into a
state that satisfies a goal condition. Within Artificial Intelligence,
there are two subfields -- "planning" and "heuristic search" -- that
have studied this problem from different perspectives with little
cross-fertilization. However, in the last decade it has been
recognized that important results can be achieved by integrating
research results from the two subfields.

This project will bring a prominent researcher in heuristic search
(Holte) together with a leading researcher in planning (Helmert). The
overall aim of the project is to stimulate a close and ongoing
collaboration between these two subfields by exchanging technical
knowledge, sharing software, and joining together the perspectives of
planning and heuristic search. In particular, the project intends to
investigate related techniques that have been studied independently by
Holte and Helmert, to better understand the differences and
similarities of these techniques, and to provide the basis for a
systematic integration.
Keywords: abstraction, heuristic search, planning, sharing software

Title: PREdicting biomarkers in DYsTonia: defining the paradigm of monogenic dystonia to implement the diagnosis and prognosis of undiagnosed forms
Abstract:
The three main objectives of this project are, 1) to increase the diagnostic yield in dystonias, by detecting previously unrecognized etiological gene variants or by identifying less penetrant disease-predisposing alleles; 2) to study prioritized gene variants in 3-D human-derived cellular models to validate the underlying mechanisms; and 3) to identify prognostic markers, based on the detailed molecular study of the 3-D disease models, which will be used to predict also the course of undiagnosed patients. 

The outlined objectives will be developed through a strategy based on five work packages (WPs), and executed conjointly by the consortium.
WP1: Harmonization of existing clinical data and collection of biological samples necessary for the genetic, cellular and biomarker analyses.
WP2: DNA sequencing aimed at discovering the genetic causes of dystonia in enrolled patients, assessing by OMICS approaches the effect of selected variants on striatal organoids, and generating data for identification of prognostic biomarkers.
WP3: Generation and systematic characterization of iPSCs-derived human striatal organoids, to establish a novel human model of dystonia for the validation of genetic variants’ pathogenicity and to identify new biomarkers predictive for disease progression.
WP4: Bioinformatic and statistical analyses, which will be essential to elaborate and integrate clinical, molecular and cellular data to identify prognostic biomarkers.
WP5: Impact, dissemination and management. Combining studies in patient cohorts with innovative human disease model systems, we expect to provide a comprehensive analysis of gene-level alterations, disease mechanisms, and predictive biomarker signatures in distinct dystonia subgroups.
The results of the project will have immediate repercussions on patient management in terms of defining and predicting the course of the disease, genetic counselling for family members, and choosing the most tailored treatments for each distinct dystonia syndrome.
Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Biomarkers, Electrophysiology, Mass spectrometry-based methodologies, Monogenic Dystonia, OMICS, Polygenic risk, iPSC-derived brain organoids

Title: Modelling of Students’ Ability Development by Hybrid Graph Neural Networks
Abstract: This research project addresses challenges posed by the large amounts of data generated by modern educational technologies, including massive open online courses, intelligent tutoring systems, and computer-based formative feedback systems. These technologies promise adaptive personalization of the learning process by collecting rich data -- data which also offer valuable insights into knowledge structure and development. Such data is typically characterized by: a large number of tasks, a significantly larger pool of learners, and a longitudinal component; extreme sparsity because each learner interacts with only a small fraction of available tasks; and high amounts of noise due to situational and motivational variance among assessment scenarios and learners. Such characteristics present computational and methodological challenges that we propose to address by combining advanced machine learning techniques with parametric modelling from item response theory and dynamic modelling methodology. By bridging the gap between data-driven machine learning approaches and psychometric educational measurement methods, this research leverages modern computational techniques for extracting information from data, and combines it with existing statistical approaches for understanding such extracted information. The planned approach can be characterized by five innovative characteristics: (1) Advanced Machine Learning: We will adopt and optimize state-of-the-art machine learning methodologies, specifically Bipartite Graph Neural Networks, for analyzing big sparse longitudinal data. Synthetic data will be used to investigate the computational and psychometric properties of such models. The goal is to find the most suitable approach for handling this complex data. (2) Explainability Enhancement: To enhance the explainability of machine learning outputs, we will develop model outputs and explainability approaches inspired by key parametric models for student performance and item characteristics, as well as for learning gains and fluctuations in student characteristics over time. This integration involves the development and testing of various interpretability layers, to ensure that the machine learning results are understandable to researchers and practitioners. (3) Model Application: A series of behavioral experiments, involving teaching experts and students, will test the applicability and comprehensibility of the developed models and explanations. (4) Application to Real-World Data: To demonstrate the tractability and value of the approach, we will apply it to data already collected from online learning software, with tens of millions of unique observations from hundreds of thousands of students. (5) Software Development: We will develop open source software for understanding the knowledge space representations from GNNs in interpretable, parametric inspired approaches, and similar for the continuous-time dynamics from developed recurrent neural net approaches. (6) Impact Assessment: We will assess the potential impact of the methodology on educational outcomes using a range of approaches. These approaches include studies to validate the multidimensional item components, assess the quality of explanations generated by the models, compare adaptive testing algorithms based on Graph Neural Networks and Item Response Theory, and measure the impact of recommendations based on this methodology on students' learning outcomes.

Title: DBox: An Interactive Problem Decomposition Framework for Computational Thinking and Beyond
Abstract:
Every great programmer, from novice to expert, shares one foundational skill: problem decomposition—the practice of breaking down problems into solvable parts, central to computational thinking. However, most programming environments offer little explicit support for structured decomposition, often leaving learners to rely on trial-and-error or instructor guidance. While techniques like worked examples and subgoal labeling help learners recognize structure, they do not scaffold the dynamic, top-down construction of decomposition strategies.

As AI tools become more powerful, users increasingly need to articulate complex goals in ways machines can act on. This challenge is especially evident in programming, where tools that automate tasks from natural language prompts often suffer from a gulf of envisioning, as user intent fails to translate into effective output from large language models (LLMs). Without strong decomposition skills, both learners and professionals risk over-relying on AI, engaging in inefficient trial-and-error, or struggling to debug vague or ineffective prompts. Despite this growing need, there is a lack of explicit design to support structured decomposition across both educational tools and professional workflows.

To address this gap, we propose DBox, a structured decomposition framework that integrates visual scaffolding, interactive refinement, real-time adaptive feedback, and computational validation. Our approach enables users to construct structured problem breakdowns explicitly through an interactive visual interface. Unlike traditional bottom-up, trial-and-error methods, DBox encourages top-down planning, allowing users to externalize, refine, and revise their decomposition strategies before diving into implementation. The interface uses a box metaphor that helps users organize and iterate on their thinking as their understanding of the problem evolves.

Under the hood, we propose to integrate LLMs and computational validation to provide early feedback on decomposition strategies, helping learners assess solution structure before implementation.  Rather than waiting until execution time to identify flaws, users define key test cases and expected variable values that are compared with system-generated predictions. This process helps validate logical consistency and surface structural issues before any code is written, shifting the focus from debugging implementations to strengthening design soundness.

We will evaluate DBox across three distinct user groups to understand its impact across different learning and professional contexts.
In introductory computer science courses (CS1), DBox-Code is used to examine how the system improves decomposition strategies and conceptual understanding. For early-stage learners, DBox-Block integrates with a Scratch-like block-based environment to explore how visual scaffolding supports foundational skills. In professional settings, DBox-IDE is embedded in standard development environments, supporting modularization, structured reasoning, and clearer intent expression in AI-assisted workflows.

This work contributes to human-computer interaction, software engineering, and programming education by addressing a core challenge: helping learners and professionals develop and apply effective decomposition strategies. By scaffolding this skill explicitly and providing intelligent feedback during the design phase, DBox empowers users to think more clearly, collaborate more effectively with AI tools, and remain active participants in the problem-solving process.

Title: Neural and behavioral markers for the motivational negative symptoms of schizophrenia - a longitudinal approach
Abstract:
Background: The motivational negative symptoms of schizophrenia include avolition, asociality and anhedonia. These symptoms strongly contribute to impairments in social and occupational functioning as well as quality of life. At the same time there is a lack of evidence-based biological and psychosocial treatment approaches. Recent research employing behavioral experiments and functional neuroimaging has linked negative symptoms mainly to dysfunctions of the reward system. Despite these advances, treatment development is still hindered by a lack of biomarkers that can reliably link clinical symptoms to pathophysiological mechanisms. 

Aims: This project will define a set of neural and behavioral markers that can serve as biomarkers for treatment development for motivational negative symptoms. For this purpose we will establish (1) that these markers are robustly associated with negative symptoms, (2) that this association is longitudinally stable and (3) that this association is stable across centers. Furthermore, we will assess the longitudinal predictive power of each neurobehavioral marker for motivational negative symptoms. Finally, we will explore whether a combination of markers can improve cross-sectional and longitudinal prediction and be useful for defining mechanistically informed patient subgroups.

Methods: We will conduct a longitudinal study in two centers. In each center, we will recruit 66 patients with schizophrenia (132 overall) and 30 control participants. These participants will have a full assessment of psychopathology, behavioral measures and functional magnetic resonance imaging at intake and at 3 months. In addition, a follow-up psychopathological assessment will be performed in patients 9 months after intake. Behavioral markers will be derived from tasks assessing reinforcement learning, effort-based decision making, goal-directed behavioral control and option generation. Functional magnetic resonance imaging markers will be obtained with tasks assessing reward anticipation, reinforcement learning and working memory. Analytic approaches will include state-of-the-art computational modeling of behavioral and imaging data using a reinforcement learning framework and dynamic causal modelling as well as unsupervised classification approaches.

Expected value: Establishing a set of neural and behavioral markers can serve treatment development in several ways. These markers will improve our understanding of motivational negative symptoms by bridging clinical phenomena and pathophysiological mechanisms. This should lead to the identification of potential targets for biological and psychosocial interventions. The established neural and behavioral markers can also be used as endpoints in clinical trials. This approach will allow to better define the mechanisms of action of biological and psychosocial treatments. Overall, we believe that this project is of high importance, because it will allow transforming the promising results of recent behavioral and neuroimaging research into a set of markers that will considerably improve the foundation for treatment research on the negative symptoms of schizophrenia.

Title: Mining Regions: Pollution, politics, and structural change
Abstract:
Global demand for minerals is expected to significantly increase during the next decades (Herrington, 2021). The World Bank estimates that the production of metals, such as graphite, lithium, and cobalt could increase up to 500% over the 2010 to 2050 period to meet the demand for clean energy technologies (Hund et al., 2020). This demand is increasingly met by mineral extraction in developing countries. However, resource extraction has not unequivocally benefited developing countries, and for some, it has been an outright curse (e.g., Sachs and Warner, 1995). Mining can be a source of structural change and development, but it also causes pollution and conflict over the distribution of rents generated from mineral extraction (see Van der Ploeg, 2011; Cust and Poelhekke, 2015, for excellent overviews). 

My project sheds new light on mineral extraction's local and regional costs and benefits by combining state-of-the-art econometric techniques with recent advances in data science. I leverage advances in machine/statistical learning to generate the first global dataset on mining activity (part I). Economists have extensively studied the local effects of natural resources but are constrained by the lack of annual data on production by mining site (Cust and Poelhekke, 2015). Part I provides this information and allow researchers to include the intensive margin of mining in their empirical analysis. Part II focuses on mining-related pollution. I combine remotely sensed pollution proxies with survey data to investigate multidimensional pollution patterns in response to mining (i.e., pollution of water, vegetation, soil, and air), highlighting the behavioral response of the local population. Ex ante, it is not clear if the behavioral response to mining amplifies or mitigates pollution (Aldeco et al. 2019). Still, the relationship between mining and the behavioral response is of first-order importance to assess the local environmental costs of mineral extraction in relation to the generated economic output. 

My project also closes important gaps in the literature on the resource course (Sachs and Warner, 1995, 2001) by studying the role of ethnic diversity/segregation and relative resource endowments for political conflict, as well as political representation in space. More precisely, part III develops a theoretical model that relates the spatial interaction of mineral wealth (Morelli and Rohner, 2015) and ethnic diversity/segregation (Alesina and Zhuravskaya, 2011; Esteban et al. 2012) to the probability of local and national conflict. The model is then calibrated to geo-referenced mine and census data across Africa and used to predict the relative risk across space caused by future mining activity. Part IV focuses on the political representation of mining regions. A potential explanation for a local resource curse, apart from conflict, is that mining regions do not benefit sufficiently from the generated mineral revenues (Acemoglu et al.. 2004; Bhattacharyya et al., 2017; Asatryan et al., 2021). Part IV provides the first systematic empirical evidence on how the spatial distribution of mineral wealth affects the political importance of cities and regions within a country by exploiting plausibly exogenous variation in the mineral wealth of the discovered deposits (as in Caselli and Michaels (2013) and Berman et al. 2017)). In summary, the project generates frameworks and data that can help to properly assess the costs and benefits of mineral extraction for mining regions.

Title: Macro-Finance  with Heterogeneous Households
Abstract:
Macroeconomic research studies the relationship between aggregate economic quantities such as GDP, unemployment rate, and inflation. To do that, macroeconomists build models to replicate the economy, use economic data to quantify them, and then use the calibrated models for predictions. Traditionally, these models focus exclusively on aggregate quantities and only model a single representative household. Such models, by design, disregard differences across households and do not take into account how income and wealth are distributed. 

Increasingly available household-level data, together with advances in computational methods, led to a paradigm shift: we now know that the response of aggregate quantities to macroeconomic shocks critically depends on the underlying heterogeneity at the household-level (e.g., Kaplan et al., 2018; Bhandari et al., 2021). The household-level heterogeneity, in turn, is amplified by the differential impact of macroeconomic shocks. While substantial progress has been made (e.g., Azinovic et al., 2019; Auclert et al., 2021), incorporating heterogeneity into equilibrium models remains a computational challenge, limiting the realism of macroeconomic models.

My broader research agenda aims at making progress on these two closely connected topics: the incorporation of household heterogeneity into models of the macroeconomy and the advancement of computational methods necessary to solve them.

Title: Blue Networks. How the Locus Coeruleus controls and reorganizes brain activity
Abstract:
The Locus Coeruleus (LC) is a tiny brain stem nucleus that provides norepinephrine (NE) to most parts of the forebrain and contributes to myriad brain functions, including arousal, sensory processing, nociception, sleep/wake cycles, cognition and stress responses. What remains poorly understood is how such a small structure affects so many distinct processes. Until now, much experimental work has been devoted to determining how LC neurons change their firing properties under various behavioural conditions. These studies have led to the realization that the mode of LC activity matters. For example, a phasic mode with a background firing rate of ~3Hz and strong burst responses to salient stimuli (2-4 spikes at 15Hz) is associated with improved executive function and task engagement. A high tonic mode with background activity of ~6Hz is associated with hypervigilance but greater distractibility during attention tasks and weakened short-burst responses. A recent hypothesis states that different firing modes of LC promote specific behavioural responses by selectively engaging distinct brain networks. Indeed, human neuroimaging studies have shown that periods of increased arousal, compatible with the phasic mode of LC, are associated with the recruitment of the prefrontal and posterior parietal cortices and with improvements in executive function. In contrast, exposing subjects to prolonged, stressful stimuli, thus mimicking the high tonic LC mode, causes the mobilization of the insula, the amygdala and sensory-motor cortices, compatible with hypervigilance. Crucially, controlled empirical validation of these observations is difficult because it is impossible to accurately control the levels of LC activity in humans. 
In my previous work, I found that chemogenetic excitation of LC in mice – which mimics strong and sustained LC activation – leads to the recruitment of networks similar to those that have been reported after stressful stimuli in humans. However, the role of the LC/NE system is not limited to stress, and distinct modes of LC activation can have specific effects on behaviour. In this Eccellenza proposal, I will focus on understanding how different activation modes of the LC cause changes in brain network dynamics. The proposal is organized into three interconnected projects. First, I will apply a series of precise and controlled optogenetic manipulations of the LC in mice during anesthetised and awake task-free functional MRI (fMRI) recordings (Project 1). This will provide the first causal evidence that LC firing modes are able to mobilize different brain networks. Using these data, I will study how properties of fMRI signals align with different NE receptor distributions in mice, and test whether there is agreement with changes observed in humans before and after stress induction using an existing dataset (Project 2). This will allow me to establish a translational back-to-back comparison of LC/NE effects on fMRI dynamics in both species. In the third part of the project, I will test how different modes of LC activity change the brain’s ability to encode the saliency of a stimulus. To do so, I will combine LC optogenetics-fMRI with an auditory odd-ball task in awake mice (Project 3). Finally, I will integrate these experimental data into new computational models that are calibrated to mouse data and able to simulate the microcircuit mechanisms through which the LC/NE system regulates network dynamics, thus mechanistically explaining our interventions. In conclusion, this project will lead to a systematic and analytical description of how the LC/NE system regulates local and global network organization, which is key to understanding how LC promotes distinct behavioural responses.

Title: Causal structures for quantum systems
Abstract:
Quantum theory is exciting and paradoxical. On one hand, it is among the most precisely tested physical theories, at the core of modern technology. On the other hand, quantum theory defies our understanding of space-time: the mechanics of its causes and effects is not fully understood one century after its inception.

In particular, composite quantum systems exhibit strong correlations that cannot be explained in the paradigm of 19th century physics. Even if the underlying mechanism is still unclear, tools are currently available to link the correlations of quantum or classical systems to their causal structure, i.e. the architecture of their subsystems. Currently, these tools only apply to the simplest cases. In the last three years, however, methods inspired by the field of machine learning have shown encouraging progress towards a general description of quantum systems and their correlations.

My aim is to employ these developments to create practical and efficient tools to characterize the causal structure of quantum systems. To achieve these goals, I will employ my expertise on quantum correlations developed during my PhD thesis, and combine it with novel methods coming from the field of machine learning, such as probabilistic graphical models. In contrast to most physical theories where internal models are required, these tools work externally from the correlations present in experimental data. Because they make no assumptions about the inner workings of the devices, they apply to a wide range of experimental systems. I will look particularly for implementations in quantum photonics devices, broadening research collaborations beyond my current network in Europe.
Keywords: Bell inequalities, Causal structures, Device-independent information processing, Quantum information, Quantum networks, Quantum nonlocality
