Title: Machine Learning Methods for Clinical Data Analysis and Precision Medicine
Abstract:
In the last years, enormous progress has been made to gather as many information as possible about an individual patient, on the molecular level of gene activity and mutations as well as on the clinical level as for example patient treatment history. A single patient visit at a hospital may result in tens of thousands of measurements and structured information, including clinical factors, diagnostic imaging, lab tests, genomic and proteomic tests, and hospitals may see thousands of patients each year. Also, DNA sequencing is nowadays a standard, fast and relatively cheap procedure. All these developments in medical information technology have resulted in an overwhelming amount of data, often measured over a long period of time. The ultimate aim is to use all this vast information for a medical treatment tailored to the needs of an individual patient. To turn the vision of precision medicine into reality, many methodological problems remain to be solved:

(i) there is an urgent need for the integration of the heterogeneous (or multi-modal) patient data currently available, for improved disease diagnosis, prognosis and therapy outcome prediction. Instead of learning on one data set exclusively, as for example just on images or just on genetics, the aim is to improve learning and enhance personalized treatment by using as much information as possible for every patient. 

(ii) On the other hand, longitudinal analysis, where observations are made across multiple time points, is a proven epidemiologic study design that has so far been underutilized in clinical studies, due to budgetary concerns and due to missing ability to analyze this data. A patient usually visits a hospital multiple times, or is hospitalized over a certain time period. This results in time-stamped data for every patient. Depending on the disease, this might result in very long time-series data, with irregular time intervals, and many missing values. These are difficult challenges which require new machine learning methods for the efficient analysis of large amounts of longitudinal multi-modal clinical data, with the goal of gaining insights and making predictions about disease phenotypes, disease progression and response to treatment. 

The aim of my proposed research is to provide a complete framework for the analysis of high-dimensional time-series data with multiple diverse data types and ensure accessibility both for researchers and physicians. The proposed developments range from methods focusing on the integration of multiple, possibly very different data types, to advanced machine learning methods that allow time-varying analyses of complex biomedical multi-modal time series data.
Keywords: Biomedicine, Clinical Data Analysis, Heterogenous Data Integration, High-dimensional Data Analysis, Longitudinal Data Analysis, Machine Learning, Personalized Medicine, Precision Medicine, Supervised Learning

Title: AI-Supported Human-Computer Interaction with Large Volumes of Historical Documents
Abstract:
The present project is in the area of computational analysis of documents using machine learning and natural language processing (in particular, large language models (LLMs)). It is based on a collaboration between the applicants’ research groups and the research center Diplomatic Documents of Switzerland (Dodis), which is the center of excellence for the study of history of Swiss foreign policy.
The overarching goal of the project is to research novel algorithms to automate and support the process of studying, understanding, selecting, and editing documents at Dodis. In particular, we strive for a unique solution that allows both experts and interested laypersons to have a written conversation with an artificial system which has in turn access to Dodis’ large document corpus. We aim for a framework that is composed of two building blocks. First, a conversational artificial intelligence (CAI) that accurately answers user questions and follow-up questions and challenges incorrect assumptions, and second a high-quality summarization component that provides accurate and useful summaries of documents avoiding hallucinations.
Both fields of research (i.e., summarization and CAI) gained momentum in the last years and elaborated models are available. However, to further push the boundaries of current understanding and implement a solution that is actually usable for Dodis, substantial efforts in research are required. First, although Dodis will contribute an extensive corpus of real-world documents including ground truth transcripts, we face the major challenge that state-of-the-art OCR is prone to errors for historical typewritten documents and is largely unable to extract (implicit) meta-information from the documents that could be valuable for subsequent research (e.g., the document type or recipient). Second, existing (locally executable) models for summarization produce questionable summaries that are hardly usable for Dodis’ research purposes. Moreover, while public LLMs such as GPT provide grammatically and linguistically sound summaries, the results often do not reflect the historically important aspect of the document (moreover, the summaries are still not precise enough, i.e. they contain hallucinations). Third, we observe that open platforms like Dodis are based on the idea of keyword search which are not able to answer specific questions in natural language. On the other hand generic CAI platforms provide very vague or even false answers to specific questions on Dodis documents (as they do not have good access to the necessary documents). It is a major research challenge of this project to enable natural language interactions with a novel CAI system based on the large amount of documents available. The aim is to provide highly accurate and verified answers to specific user questions without hallucinations.
We start our research by selecting and preparing large-scale ground truth training sets for building the envisaged systems. We will first research and empirically evaluate existing models for all tasks and systematically document all limitations (e.g., fabricated facts or similar). Major contribution of the present project is then to develop and research novel approaches that use large knowledge graphs to guide and improve both the summarization and CAI processes. In the experimental phase we use both automatic evaluation metrics and human-based evaluations. Last but not least, the writing of scientific papers and doctoral theses is also part of the present project.
The significance and impact of the proposed project is manifold (ranging from unique and novel data sets for document analysis to more robust document workflows using LLMs). One of the most important impacts is, however, that the present project might result in radically different services, which can be interpreted as first – yet significant – step towards a more natural human-computer interaction with large archives of historical documents.

Title: Combining large-scale electrophysiology, retrograde tracing, and spatial transcriptomics to probe tumor-neuron networks
Abstract:
The project aims to investigate the complex interactions between glioblastoma (GB) tumor cells and neuronal networks, with the goal of developing new therapeutic approaches. Glioblastomas are the most prevalent and aggressive primary brain tumors in adults, with poor prognosis despite comprehensive treatment.

Recent research has shown that GB cells can form functional connections with neurons, which promotes tumor growth and invasiveness. This tumor-neuron communication likely contributes to therapy resistance.

The research team plans to combine advanced technologies:

    - Retrograde tracing using rabies viruses to map neuronal connections with tumor cells
    - High-density microelectrode arrays (HD-MEAs) for capturing neuronal activity patterns
    - Spatially resolved transcriptomics for single-cell gene expression analysis
    - Defined human cell culture models using induced neurons

The main objectives of the project are:

    - To track and characterize the formation and dynamics of tumor-neuron connections in defined human cell culture models
    - To identify molecular signatures of tumor-induced pathophysiological alterations by integrating electrophysiological and transcriptomic data
    - To screen FDA-approved drugs to assess their effects on tumor-neuron networks and use machine learning to predict new compounds
    - To validate the most promising targets in patient-derived xenograft models and combine them with standard-of-care therapies

The project combines the expertise of two research groups: the team at Heidelberg University Hospital with extensive experience in neuro-oncology and tumor-neuron interactions, and the team at ETH Zurich with specialized knowledge in neuronal network electrophysiology and human cellular models.

The expected outcomes include:

    - A better understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying tumor-neuron communication
    - Identification of new therapeutic targets
    - Development of multi-modal methods for functional and genomic characterization of tumor microenvironments
    - Validated targets with the potential to be translated into clinical trials

This interdisciplinary project could lead to new treatment strategies for glioblastomas by targeting the previously poorly understood tumor-neuron networks, potentially improving patient outcomes.

Title: Evolving on the edge: assessing the genomic impact of ancient human expansions
Abstract:
The colonization of the world by modern humans has consisted in a series of range expansions that have left deep traces in the genetic makeup of the modern populations. Indeed, range expansions consist in a series of founder effects leading to a progressive loss of genetic diversity along the expansion axis, which is still observed today between Africa and the Americas. However, these expansions have led to the spread of neutral or mildly selected variants that happen to be by chance on the front of the expansion, and to their increase in frequency in newly colonized territories, a phenomenon called genetic surfing. Genetic surfing has a genetic signature that looks like the effect of positive selection and selective sweeps, but it is not considered in the interpretation of most selective scans done in human populations. Moreover, while the genetic surfing of single neutral or selected variants are well understood, their impact on surrounding genomic diversity (i.e. the extent of linkage disequilibrium around the surfing variant, the proportion of the genome affected by surfing events, or the genomic distances between surfing DNA segments) have not been investigated. In addition, human expansions are mainly studied by looking at modern individuals a long time after the expansions have stopped, when the original expansion signals have been blurred by later migrations and population movements. In order to better understand the genomic impact of range expansions on past and current human populations, we propose in this project to model the evolution of large genomic regions in one- and more realistic two-dimensional expansions and to examine the genomic diversity of ancient individuals that lived on or close to large past spatial expansions. 

The proposed realistic modeling of spatial expansions will not only allow us to uncover their exact signatures on neutral and functional genomic diversity over a given geographic landscape, but it will also allow us to define sets of statistics that will be used in a machine learning approach to distinguish their effects from those of selective sweeps at single loci and, importantly, over the whole genome, which is essential to understand the recent evolution of modern human populations. The sequencing of ancient individuals that lived on or close to the edge of the Danubian Neolithic expansion, from Western Anatolia to Germany, will allow us to study the full temporal dynamics of this expansion, detail the mode of dispersal of Neolithic farmers and their level of interactions with previous and later people. By sequencing about 50 ancient genomes at ?10X coverage from individuals scattered along the whole Danubian corridor, we will assess the exact genomic impact of the expansion process and check theoretical predictions of an increasing mutation load developing over long-lasting range expansions. In addition, we will also examine the genomic diversity and predicted health status of other ancient individuals being closer to more ancient (Paleolithic) human expansions in various parts of the world (Northern Eurasia and the Americas), and thus contrast the effects of hunter-gatherer and farmer expansions. In order to make correct demographic inferences from ancient genomes, we will also develop new methods to estimate the past demography of ancient populations where individuals are sampled at different times and different geographic locations, which is a great challenge and unaddressed problem in current conventional population genomic analyses. Our project, which will include modeling, genomic simulations, model testing, methodological developments, and analyses of ancient full genomes, represents a fully integrative approach to the study of range expansions, which are an important component of recent human evolution that has certainly conditioned the genetic diversity and potentially the health status of modern populations. It will also have a lasting impact on archaeogenomic studies, as it will provide new statistical tools for the integration of ancient genomes into proper model-based analyses, which are key to infer the evolutionary processes underlying observed genomic diversity patterns of ancient populations.

Title: Enhanced sampling in the latent space of Boltzmann generators
Abstract:
This proposal aims at developing a new method for molecular simulations of rare events by combining enhanced sampling techniques with Boltzmann generators - deep neural networks designed for efficient sampling of equilibrium states.
Molecular simulations are playing an ever-increasing role in modern science, with applications in fields as varied as physics, chemistry, biology, and material science. They provide key microscopic insight and speedup discovery of new materials or new drugs, via large virtual pre-screening of possible candidates. Molecular dynamics and Markov chain Monte Carlo are widely used to sample the equilibrium Boltzmann distribution. However, despite the impressive improvements of both algorithms and hardware, molecular simulations are still severely limited by the sampling problem. This problem arises from the mixed multiscale nature of many phenomena of interest (chemical reactions, protein folding, crystal growth, and nucleation etc.), that present long-lived metastable states, with rare transitions between them happening on much longer timescales, which are out of reach for molecular simulations. Numerous enhanced sampling techniques have been developed to mitigate this issue, but they are typically not easy to generalize and require a non-trivial handcrafted effort for each different system.
Recently, a new sampling scheme has been proposed, Boltzmann generators, that brings a novel perspective on this long-lasting problem [Noé et al., Science 365.6457 (2019)]. Instead of directly sampling in the physical space, Noé et al. showed that it is possible to train a deep neural network to perform a change of coordinates and map all the metastable basins of the hard-to-sample Boltzmann distribution into a single Gaussian basin. One can then easily perform one-shot uncorrelated sampling in this latent space, and map back the result to obtain the exact Boltzmann distribution, thanks to a simple reweighting. This new method is completely general and, if scalable to the large systems, has the potential of solving the sampling problem. 
The overall objective of our research project is to significantly improve the efficiency of Boltzmann generators, and thus extend their applicability to more systems. The specific goals are in two distinct directions: 1) Combine Boltzmann generators with techniques from the field of enhanced sampling, such as metadynamics and expanded ensembles. We want to devise a method for performing enhanced sampling in the latent space of Boltzmann generators, in order to improve the sampling efficiency despite the possible limitations of the learned mapping. Importantly, our approach is complementary to efforts of the machine learning community for improving the learning capability of the type of neural networks used in Boltzmann generators. 2) Apply Boltzmann generators to study phase transitions in condensed matter systems for the first time. To achieve this, we will have to overcome some technical difficulties, making use of previous experience in devising collective variables for phase transitions. 
Our research will help extend the capabilities of Boltzmann generators, making them competitive with other advanced enhanced sampling techniques. This will be a crucial milestone in proving them as a valid alternative to traditional sampling methods. Machine learning is already outperforming previous state-of-the-art techniques in various fields of computational sciences, and the possibility that it might greatly improve the sampling efficiency of molecular simulations is a fascinating challenge to pursue. The expected impact is significant, allowing simulations of many important phenomena which are hard to study using available methods, such as crystal growth, and protein folding.
Keywords: deep neural networks, free energy calculation, machine learning, molecular simulations, normalizing flows, rare events, statistical mechanics

Title: Can we use artificial intelligence to uncover strategies in human cognition?
Abstract: The ultimate goal of this research program is to advance our understanding of one of the main cognitive determinants of human behavior: working memory (WM). WM is the limited-capacity system that keeps a small amount of information accessible for ongoing thought and action, and is considered the cornerstone of human cognition. There is broad consensus on the notion that WM plays a central role in goal-directed cognitive behavior such as learning, reasoning, and language comprehension. However, there is currently little agreement on how WM works. In particular, there is a long-standing fundamental debate centered on how several pieces of information can be maintained simultaneously in WM. Several strategies of WM maintenance have been proposed, but evidence for the spontaneous use of these strategies is inconsistent across different studies. These studies have mainly relied on one of the following behavioral approaches: (1) Ask participants which strategy they have used to maintain the to-be-remembered information, (2) Examine performance regarding the to-be-remembered information, and (3) Examine how a secondary task is disrupted by simultaneously trying to maintain the to-be-remembered information. However, across these approaches, no coherent picture has emerged. With the current research project, we aim to move the field forward by developing and testing a new approach to uncover which strategies are used to maintain information in WM. We propose an innovative method that combines artificial intelligence techniques with experimental, behavioral paradigms. Our aim is to develop a tool that can detect whether individuals are using a particular strategy while trying to maintain information, without requiring participants to be able to report this strategy, and without relying solely on reduced data (i.e., averages or variance) from either secondary task disruption or memory performance. We plan to start with detecting (1) one of the most agreed-upon maintenance strategies, called verbal rehearsal (i.e., repeating information verbally in our head), and (2) a fairly standard WM paradigm requiring maintaining information while processing a secondary task. The innovation of our project lies in our use of recent advances in artificial intelligence to build a detector that considers information from memory performance and secondary task disruption in parallel, and takes into account the entire pattern of data without any loss of information. This endeavour is inherently risky, since it defies the traditional research approach where data are averaged and statistically compared between carefully constructed experimental conditions. However, if successful, this new method could be applied to other, more contested maintenance strategies, across a wide range of task settings and populations. Moreover, we believe the same method could be applied to examine strategy use in other domains of cognition (e.g., reading and mental arithmetic). We have the combined technical skills and domain knowledge to ensure that this project will be conducted according to the highest standards. Therefore, any outcome, positive or negative, can be considered a gain in knowledge for the field, and will be publicly documented (including open data).
Keywords: artificial intelligence, cognition, deep learning, strategies, working memory

Title: Promoting Honesty in Business: The Role of Contemplation Questions
Abstract:
Honesty is a cornerstone of society and business life. It fosters trust, cooperation, and fair markets. Yet recurring scandals – from financial crises to cases of fraud and misreporting – show that dishonesty remains widespread, and that laws and compliance programs alone cannot guarantee ethical choices. This interdisciplinary and cross-institutional project therefore explored another path: strengthening honesty and people’s capacity for moral self-governance with the help of contemplation questions (CQs). These are simple, structured questions that aim to help individuals pause and reflect when confronted with ethically ambiguous and difficult situations. Examples include “Would the public approve of my decision if they read about it in the newspaper?” or “Would I like the person I see in the mirror after making this choice?” Many companies already use such questions (often referred to as checking questions) as decision aids to support employees when faced with workplace challenges, but their effectiveness had never been tested systematically.

Our research proceeded in three steps. First, based on interviews (with compliance and ethics experts) and surveys with German employees, we derived a) a taxonomy of typical ethical workplace conflicts where honesty is at stake, including tensions between honesty and loyalty, customer exploitation, authority obedience, profit goals and self-protection, and b) a categorization of CQs into five groups linked to different reference groups and associated norms (Self, Peers, Company Policy, Law & Reputation, Universal Principles).

Second, we conducted a series of (large-scale) experiments with samples of the German working population to test the effectiveness of CQs. Contrary to our expectations, CQs did not automatically promote honesty. Their effect depended on individual differences: for people with a strong moral identity, CQs encouraged honesty; but for those with weak moral identity, CQs backfired, and even fostered dishonesty. This suggests that some individuals may use CQs to rationalize questionable behavior. These findings, robust across studies, reveal a striking risk: tools designed to support honesty can, in some cases, produce unintended boomerang effects.

Third, in light of these insights and rapid advances in artificial intelligence, we developed an AI-based coaching tool to enable interactive, repeated CQ practice. An advanced AI-coach, tested in an intervention study with professionals, increased users’ confidence in their moral judgments more than it improved decision quality, revealing a potential confidence-competence gap. 

Overall, the project demonstrates that while CQs can strengthen honesty under specific conditions, they also entail unintended risks, underscoring the double-edged nature of ethical decision aids. Given that many governance frameworks and compliance guidelines recommend the use of CQs, our findings highlight the need for systematic evaluation before broad implementation. More generally, the results underscore the importance of assessing not only intended but also unintended effects of ethical decision aids.
Keywords: Behavioral Economics, Behavioral Ethics, Business Ethics, Compliance and integrity, Contemplation questions, Digital gamebased learning, Digitalisation, Honesty, Self-regulation

Title: Towards Improved Optimization of Variational Inequalities
Abstract:
Gradient-based algorithms are a popular class of optimization methods that are widely used to solve various problems in machine learning and other fields. However, these algorithms can be unstable when applied to zero-sum games, multi-player games, and other variational inequality (VI) problems, which involve finding a solution that satisfies certain constraints and maximizes the value of a particular objective function. This instability can manifest in various ways, such as rapid divergence from equilibria or convergence to limit cycles, where the algorithm revisits a set of non-solution points with probability 1.

To address these issues, we are conducting a research project to understand the properties that an algorithm must possess to avoid or escape limit cycles and to understand the role of noise from stochastic gradients in these problems. Our primary tools for this study will be more precise ordinary differential equations (ODEs), which can track the original discrete-time methods more closely and provide theoretical convergence guarantees for some classes of problems. The continuous-time perspective could also suggest new insights into accelerating these methods, as the terms in the continuous-time dynamics often have physical interpretations.

Overall, our goal is to improve the stability and convergence of gradient-based algorithms for solving zero-sum games and other VI problems, which will have significant implications for machine learning and other fields that rely on these methods, such as game theory and economics.
Keywords: Continious-time analysis, Game-theory, Limit cycles, Machine Learning, Min-max problems, Optimization, Variational Inequality

Title: Understanding and detecting early psychosis: A network approach
Abstract:
Improving early detection of psychosis remains a substantial challenge in research and in clinical practice. Such early detection of the first signs of psychosis is paramount, however, in order to avoid onset of psychosis or prevent increases in severity. There are currently two early detection approaches to define clinical high risk among emerging psychosis, defining a basic symptoms (BS) criterion, or an ultra-high risk (UHR) criterion. There is considerable room to improve psychosis prediction and the current project aims to fill this gap. Previous approaches mostly aimed to detect psychosis using regression, multivariate modelling or machine learning approaches and have shown some inconsistencies between studies, hence indicating the necessity of refinement and improving precision models in this field. Network Analysis (NA) has been rarely exploited for at-risk mental state for psychosis. Further criteria such as protective factors are essential to improve the prediction, which only few studies have focused. 

Specifically, I will apply NA, an innovative explanatory data analytical approach, to data on psychopathological symptoms in a sample of 150 ultra-high risk persons for psychosis. The main question of this project is what factors associate and predict psychosis among at-risk individuals. A network will thus be constructed (i) cross-sectionally to identify interrelations between the psychopathological symptoms and neurocognitive measures (ii) prospective longitudinally to identify dynamic associations between psychopathological symptoms, neurocognitive measures and protective factors. The proposed research project will try to push forward efforts to understand the psychopathological pathways, the influence of protective factors on psychosis and predictors for psychosis. Finally, the findings of the study can also improve the implementation of specific treatment for this population by providing treatment targets in order to avoid conversion to full-blown psychosis.
Keywords: early detection, network analysis, psychosis, resilience, risk and protective factors

Title: Machine Translation and Animation Assessment for Swiss German Sign Language
Abstract:
I propose a two-part project dealing with Swiss German Sign Language. The first part involves sign language machine translation, the second sign language animation assessment, i.e., the evaluation of virtual signers, or "avatars". The project is embedded into my PhD project "Trainslate", where, together with two Deaf researchers, I am building a system that automatically translates German train announcements of the Swiss Federal Railways into Swiss German Sign Language. The final output of our system is an avatar that signs the train announcements in real time on a mobile phone. 
The research questions I propose to investigate during my stay abroad are:
R1.1 (sign language machine translation): How can non-manual features be included in the final output of a sign language machine translation system? 
R2.1 (sign language animation assessment): What is the best design of a user evaluation study that will assess the comprehensibility of a DSGS avatar signing train announcements?
R2.2 (sign language animation assessment): What is the best design of an online survey that will assess both the acceptance and comprehensibility of a DSGS avatar signing train announcements?
Keywords: avatars, machine translation, sign languages

Title: Potential for ancient habitability and deep crustal materials preserved in the rim of Jezero crater, Mars
Abstract: This 12-month research project extends from recent discoveries about distinctive geological ridges on Mars, which have been shown to have a magmatic rather than hydrothermal origin through analysis of high-resolution imagery, spectral data, and machine learning-based mapping. The project aims to investigate the Jezero crater rim to understand potential habitable environments, biosignature preservation, and how excavated materials inform Mars' deep crustal composition and chronology. The specific objectives include mapping hydrated mineral exposures along the western rim and analyzing complex stratigraphy to reconstruct geological history, utilizing multiple datasets including CRISM spectral parameters, CaSSIS color composites, and HiRISE imagery with stereo-derived DEMs, complemented by iSALE-2D shock physics simulations. This research will directly support the Mars Sample Return campaign by identifying key geological units that could preserve evidence of ancient Martian life and provide essential context for understanding Mars' early crustal evolution, with particular relevance to NASA's Perseverance rover mission and the broader search for signs of ancient life on Mars.
Keywords: Astrobiology, Geology, Mars, Spectroscopy

Title: RIMES - Robust Integrated Modeling for Energy and Engineering Systems
Abstract:
Modern engineering research has to deal with complex and integrated systems, characterized by large amounts of available data. Energy systems and engineering design problems are fundamentally – and increasingly – uncertain, and models must inevitably rely on simplifying assumptions, inaccurate forecasts as well as limited or incomplete information. Recent research has shown that the consideration of uncertainty can dramatically improve the reliability of engineering design as well as the resilience and robustness of decisions and plans drafted based on the outcomes of energy system models. Yet, for a range of reasons – spanning from methodological (e.g. difficulties in characterizing uncertainties, complex and nonlinear formulations) to practical (e.g. computational tractability) limitations – uncertainty is to date very seldom accounted for in engineering research. This project aims to address these limitations, working towards the vision of a systematic consideration of uncertainty in energy systems and engineering models.

The contribution of this project lies at the intersection of the operations research (OR) and engineering domains, and its fundamental innovation is the development of novel modeling, optimization and data science methods to enable the consideration of uncertainty in energy systems and engineering applications. Concretely, the project develops along three main research streams that naturally complement each other: (i) the formalization of a methodological framework to consider uncertainty in engineering models; (ii) the development of novel whole-energy system optimization models for the planning of regional energy systems; (iii) the application of the developed uncertainty framework to energy systems planning in the context of the energy transition in Switzerland and Europe.

The latest developments in the data science and OR domains (such as machine learning, deep learning, data-driven optimization, distributionally robust optimization, among others) provide methods that assist in making rational decisions and predictions in an increasingly interconnected and fast-paced world. This project contributes to a wider adoption of such methods throughout the engineering domain and to champion a wide range of cross-disciplinary collaborations, which are essential in modern engineering research.

Besides its scientific contribution, the project can be highly impactful on society and industry, contributing to a wider adoption of advanced modeling and optimization methods in the engineering domain and beyond to address major societal challenges. In particular, this project is timely in respect to the Swiss energy transition and to the commitment of various countries to reach net-zero emissions by 2050. In this context, action needs to be undertaken in the near term if we are to keep within a 1.5-degree temperature rise to avoid the worst effects of climate change. By providing rigorous modeling that includes uncertainty, this project will be central in ensuring that policy-makers have the best information to make these pivotal decisions.

The project is hosted by the Department of Mechanical and Process Engineering (D-MAVT) at ETH Zürich and is performed in close collaboration with a network of academic institutions (Imperial College London, EPFL and UC Louvain, among others), research centers (CIRAIG – Polytechnique Montreal) and industry.

Title: Neural circuits mechanisms of forelimb motor adaptation
Abstract:
To perform successful actions, motor commands must be adapted by taking into account the current goal of the animal as well as a change in the environment. The central nervous system has the remarkable ability to adapt to these changes with ease in healthy individuals. For example, we can rapidly adapt to typing on a unfamiliar keyboard, or riding a new bicycle. This process called motor adaptation – namely, the ability to learn from environmental perturbations to restore performance – has also been demonstrated in various laboratory tasks such as a physical perturbation to the limb or a task that decouples visual feedback to limb or eye movements.

Since the pioneering work of Shadmehr & Mussa-Ivaldi in the 1990's, the use of force field perturbations during forelimb movement has become a powerful way to study the behaviorally-observable mechanisms underlying motor adaptation. Despite the successes of these studies, our understanding of neural mechanisms underlying motor adaptation remains elusive. We recently translated these paradigms to a mouse model in order to study neural circuit mechanisms. We found that for forelimb adaptation, the somatosensory cortex (S1) was essential for learning to adapt (Mathis et al, Neuron 2017), but inactivation did not disrupt motor control. The finding suggests a unique role of cortex for adaptive learning. Yet, how S1 encodes perturbations and systematically adapts to these perturbations remains unclear.

(2) What are the cell-type specific representations of kinematics across sensorimotor cortex? (3) How do these neural representations change during motor adaptation at both the individual neuron and population level?

Taken together, our proposal collectively aims to elucidate fundamental principles of behavioral and neural representations of efficient adaptive motor control. Moreover, we draw on the power of mice as a model system of forelimb control, develop new behavioral paradigms, leverage advances in machine learning, and deploy large-scale neural recordings during skilled behaviors. We believe that understanding detailed neural circuit mechanisms underlying motor adaptation will lead to novel and effective therapeutic approaches for neuroprosthetics and rehabilitation strategies.

Title: Structure based engineering of photo-catalysis using Free Electron Lasers
Abstract:
1. Summary:
We will demonstrate with this proposal that time resolved measurements at FELs such as SwissFEL can provide mechanistic insight into enzymatic reaction of proteins and enable the development of structure based design of protein variants with altered properties. We also aim to substantial  improve the analysis of time resolved crystallography data. The three main objectives are:
We will extend on the measurements my group has already obtained with bovine rhodopsin within the scope of my current SNF grant “Analysing protein dynamics in receptor signalling relevant to pharmacology”. Ultra-short time points in bovine rhodopsin below 1 ps will yield information on the electronic processes underlying the reaction mechanism of retinal isomerization in rhodopsin. A main focus will be placed on data analysis: In collaboration with Abbas Ourmazd, we will explore novel methods for the analysis of time resolved data based on geometric machine learning; this will allow the analysis of protein dynamics with temporal resolution well beyond what can be achieved by current binning methods. 
We have recently solved the structure of a bi-stable visual pigment, Jumping Spider Rhodopsin1 (JSR1). Comparison of JSR1 with the monostable bovine rhodopsin will allow us to mechanistically understand the underlying structural features differentiating mono-stability from bistability. The comparison of the dark-state structure of JSR1 with that of bovine rhodopsin and other class A GPCRs revealed an interesting N-terminal fold, which seems to be conserved among bi-stable rhodopsins. In addition, the specifics of the water network in JSR1 indicate that there is a common activation mechanism between mono- and bi-stable rhodopsins. In this project, we will perform time resolved measurements of JSR1 using serial crystallography at the SwissFEL and SLS covering at least a time span ranging from pico- to milli-seconds. This will allow us to elucidate the activation mechanism of JSR1 and compare it with that of mono-stable bovine rhodopsin and to identify structural features that provide a mechanistic explanation for the two different enzymatic reaction mechanisms in the two rhodopsin families. As JSR1 is structurally more closely related to non-visual classA GPCRs compared to bovine rhodopsin, we also expect novel insights into the general mechanism of classA GPCR activation. 
The possibility of recombinantly expressing JSR1 combined with a remarkable high thermostability makes this protein a very interesting candidate for the development of molecular switches, which can be used for example in optogenetic applications. We will use the static and dynamic structural information generated at SLS and SwissFEL in combination with molecular modelling to predict mutations altering the reaction mechanism of JSR1. Of particular interest are mutations altering the spectral properties of  the protein towards a distinct wavelength separation for cis to trans and trans to cis isomerisation. Mutants allowing a full spectral separation of both reactions would be a suitable basis for the development of on-off molecular switches for systems engineering and in optogenetics. Our studies with JSR1 revealed that the protein is able to activate Gq protein as well Gi protein in a cellular context. Together with structural information of JSR1, as well as the structural analysis available in the literater including data we have obtained with rhodopsin G protein complexes we will propose and characterise modifications of JSR1 leading to higher specificity of JSR1 for individual G-proteins.

Title: Text Mining Banks' Pillar 3 Reports: Dictionary, Topic Analysis, and Prediction
Abstract:
In response to criticism of the policy failure subsequent to the recent 2007–09 global financial crisis, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (hereafter BCBS) promoted several regulatory amendments of the Pillar-3 framework with as objective to improve the communication of sufficient, comparable, and comprehensive information on banks’ capital adequacy and material risks (BCBS 2009, 2015). Despite BCBS’s continuous efforts, academics criticized that banks reporting is “increasingly lengthy and poorly integrated,” and “non-comparable across exposures, firms, and time” (Ryan, 2012, p.299). Applicants such as the American Bankers Association (ABA) expressed two similar concerns in a comment letter to the BCBS that constant policy changes in Pillar 3 reports “would also cause undue burden for reporting institutions, which have devoted substantial resources to developing regulatory reporting processes for Basel III” (2014, p.2).
In response to the debate on banks’ reporting, in this project, we will use machine-learning tools to develop a specific text analysis framework for banks. To our knowledge, there exists no research focusing on the text of banks’ reporting. Using a sample of European listed banks from 2004 to 2017, our objective is to reveal how banks formulate their reports along aspects such as complexity, boilerplate, and similarity over time and across banks. Based on this framework, we will measure the sentiments expressed by banks along various aspects such as risk/uncertainty, litigation, accounting & finance, in addition to positive/negative sentiments that have been extensively studied. Our concentration on European banks is motivated by the fact that compared to the voluminous studies for the U. S. setting, research on Europe appears to be lagging, which is in contrast to the enforcement of Basel rules in Europe.
We will also examine the predictive content of words used in Pillar 3 reports: what is the incremental value of text in addition to financial numbers to predict banks’ future performance, both from an accounting prospective by focusing on future net interest income and from a market prospective by focusing on items such as future stock market volatility and liquidity.
To achieve our first objective, we extend and adapt the existing dictionaries of textual analysis to a bank-specific context. Earlier text analysis used the Harvard Psycho-sociological Dictionary, which contains a large quantity of words mostly related to sociological work or to literature, but less relevant to corporate reports. Loughran and McDonald (hereafter LM 2011) demonstrated the necessity to apply field specific dictionaries and they built a relevant dictionary for specific use in finance. However, LM 2011 focused on negative words. Other tone categories such as positive and uncertainty-related words were almost the same as in the original Harvard dictionaries. Words such as “disclose” and “liability” are counted as negative tone in the LM (2011) dictionary but in general, in accounting and finance they are not considered as having a negative meaning. 
Second, the existing textual analysis has concentrated on corporate annual reports, 10-K filings, and alternative information sources such as press releases and conference calls. The most common source of textual analysis is corporate 10-K forms (i.e. Lawrence 2013, Lehevy, Li and Merkley 2011, LM 2011, 2014). 10-K forms are the mandatory annual report filings required by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), adapted from the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. Banks publish however not only annual reports but also other reports or filings demanded by the policymakers of banking industry and capital markets. These types of reporting sources are easily accessible but have not yet been addressed by textual analysis.
Third, unlike firms in the industry, banks and financial institutions are confronted with at least two reporting regimes enforced by different regulatory bodies. On one hand, European listed banks are required to disclose the nature and extent of risks arising from financial instruments according to International Financial Reporting Standard No. 7 (IFRS 7); on the other hand, risk disclosure requirements of Pillar 3 issued by BCBS is mandatory for all banks under the supervision of the national banking regulator. Although in many aspects, IFRS 7 and Pillar 3 disclosure are roughly identical, many banks disclose risk-related information in these two reports in an either complementary or overlapped way, which renders text analysis for bank reporting much more complex than for industry firms.
We already performed preliminary research along the lines described above. After scraping from the annual reports, Pillar 3 documents, and all texts published by the BCBS on internet, we created an initial list composed by 8’884 words. Inspection of this list of words revealed the emergence of two new categories that contain terms relevant to (1) accounting & finance and (2) uncertainty & risk. This identification led us to extend the five-category dictionaries of LM (2011), which are positive, negative, litigious, strong modal, and weak modal wording, to seven categories. In addition, we survey the Pillar 3 disclosure requirement and identify 41 abbreviations of specific terms that are commonly used by banks, such as ABS Asset-backed securities (ABS), Advanced measurement approaches (AMA), Risk-weighted assets (RWA) etc. We include these bank specific words into the new category of accounting & finance, which reflects banks’ business models and typical risk exposures. This new classification enables us to overcome the drawback of “applying no business word lists to accounting and finance topics......the misclassification of word lists may add noise to the tonal measure and lead to spurious results”, as criticized by LM (2011, p.62).
Our first hypothesis is composed of two sub-hypotheses: banks text wordings are determined by Basel regulatory revolution; by banks business nature and risk exposure. To test these two sub- hypotheses, we will perform five types of textual analysis, that is: (1) word count, (2) boiler plate (3) cosine similarity measures, (4) FOG, a measure of text complexity, and (5) NER, a measure of text preciseness. Among which, we are the first to apply the NER measure of “specificity” for banks’ risk disclosures in Pillar-3 reports, which advances prior studies for 10-K filing (Campbell et al., 2014; Hope et al., 2016). Third, by analysing the word list from 2004 to 2017, our work overcomes one common drawback of prior research that employed a static list across periods without reflecting the change in reporting regulation. The coverage of both pre- and post-crisis samples may also enable us to examine how the sentiments and informativeness of pillair 3 disclosure changed as a response to the global financial crisis.
Beyond the above contribution on textual analysis, we contribute to the literatures on banking and finance. Our second hypothesis examines whether the change in wording is predictive of banks’ profitability, stock market volatility and liquidity. We expect that textual analysis have incremental value over plain numbers. The test of this hypothesis also serves as an additional validation test of our dictionary (i.e., Jegadeesh and Wu, 2013).
Overall, our study fills up an interdisciplinary research gap between accounting and finance by identifying a list of terminologies derived from both areas, and by examining the economic consequences of textual differences from both angles. Unlike most accounting studies that focus on examining textual readability whereas finance studies are more interested into analyzing textual tone, finance sentiment, and valuation. Our study may offer timely policy implication regarding the efficiency of Basel rules in improving banks transparency and the stability of overall financial system.
Keywords: Basel rules, Pillar-3 reporting, Risk disclosure, Textual analysis, Uncertainty

Title: Stochastic Control for Real-Time Navigation Aid in Emergency Building Evacuation.
Abstract:
Human navigation in an emergency evacuation is a crucial problem. It arises in a large variety of environments from urban buildings to remote landscapes and with many different forms of life-threatening hazards such as fire, toxic contamination or epidemics. In an emergency building evacuation, commonly, very simple predetermined strategies are applied. They do not account for the complex evolving environment consisting of the hazard and humans. These strategies are either static, such as  exit signs, and thus they do not take the state of the hazard into account, or they depend on current measurements of the states only. The inability of these strategies to use the real-time locations of specific hazards, to predict hazards evolutions and to update their navigational plans accordingly can make the predefined strategies unsafe. 

In an era of smart networking, mobile computing and sensing, more sophisticated techniques should assist humans in life-threatening situations. There is a substantial benefit in making decisions in real time through fusion of information available from several types of building and wearable sensors. The adaptation of navigation strategies to an occurring situation increases the chances of successful navigation and consequently the survival rate in safety critical situations. 

The long-term goal of this project is to design a real-time decision support system to assist humans in safety critical evacuation missions. Within this project, we aim to lay the foundations for this goal, through advancing control theory and algorithms necessitated by this problem. Hence, the main focus of this project is on the following aspects: 

1) Capturing the requirements of a search and rescue mission as an objective function of a control problem. The approaches needed here lie in the intersection of formal methods and control; 
2) Developing probabilistic models of the environment and updating them online based on sensor data so as to incorporate them in real-time control algorithms. This problem requires incorporation of probabilistic learning with control;
3) Synthesizing feedback control policies for complex objective functions captured by a formal language, while taking into account the uncertainties in the probabilistic models. 

In this project, the general control theoretic questions raised above will be addressed with respect to the needs of  the emergency evacuation application. The theory and algorithms will be validated on simulation scenarios. Finally, it is hoped that the developed theory and algorithms would have far-reaching applications in other domains of robotics and artificial intelligence.
Keywords: Data-driven Control, Dynamical System, Formal verification, Multi-agent Control, Optimal Control, Optimization, Real-time Feedback, Stochastic Control

Title: UNISON: Universal Structure-Aware Output Learning for Natural Language Understanding and Generation
Abstract: Over the last few years, language models parameterized by deep neural networks have positively impacted many real-world natural language tasks. Language modeling provides a unified framework for tackling virtually any language problem based on pretraining on unlabeled or labeled data and then finetuning on labeled data.  However, state-of-the-art language models require a massive amount of data to learn to predict output sequences and are computationally efficient when the output sequences are very long.  This project aims to address these limitations of language models by proposing new sample efficient output parameterizations that can be optionally grounded to explicit human knowledge and computationally efficient model designs that allow them to scale to arbitrarily long output sequences and increase decoding efficiency.   These improvements have a positive impact on real-world tasks such as machine translation, text alignment, style transfer, next word prediction and help make the current paradigm cost-effective and accessible to a broader audience.
Keywords: adaptive language modeling, data efficiency, efficient language models, knowledge grounding, large-context attention, output representation learning

Title: Learning complex networks for economic data: theory, methods, and algorithms
Abstract:
Network data analysis is an essential tool for understanding complex systems, from global trade to social interactions. Despite its growing role in data science, the field faces challenges due to high dimensionality, intricate dependencies, and methodological limitations in capturing these complexities.

This project integrates techniques from statistics, econometrics, and machine learning to develop novel methodologies with strong theoretical foundations and computational efficiency. A collaboration between the University of Geneva and the Free University of Bozen-Bolzano ensures a multidisciplinary approach, leveraging complementary expertise to create scalable, interpretable models that push the boundaries of current methods.

A key focus is multiview networks, where multiple types of interactions coexist among entities. Existing methods struggle with view- and node-specific dependencies, often leading to overly complex, less interpretable models. To address this, we propose a framework that blends latent variable models from statistics with factor models from econometrics. Our inference approach, based on the Laplace approximation of the likelihood score, integrates observable covariates and unobserved factors to enhance accuracy and maintain tractability. This ensures rigorous statistical guarantees, particularly in developing asymptotic properties as network size and complexity grow. Applications include trade networks, social media, and other domains requiring deep insights into heterogeneous network structures.

Another major focus is dynamic networks, where evolving temporal and structural dependencies over the networks must be captured efficiently. Existing methods often face computational bottlenecks and struggle with high-dimensional data. To overcome this, we extend the existing network autoregressive models by incorporating nonlinear dependencies and enabling data-driven discovery of network topology. Unlike standard methods that rely on predefined graphs, our framework adapts dynamically to real-world networks and it accommodates Gaussian, binary, count, and mixed data types. To conduct inference, we introduce a novel composite likelihood approach and provide its statistical guarantees (asymptotic theory), integrating machine learning-based optimization for large-scale computation. Applications span credit and trade frictions, tourism flows, and social networks where evolving structures must be understood and predicted.

Our research is structured around three core aims: (1) developing a unified theoretical framework for latent variable models in networks, (2) deriving inference procedures for learning graph topology in high-dimensional, time-varying networks, and (3) implementing and validating methodologies through efficient algorithms for real-world network data.

By advancing modeling and inference techniques for network data, this research benefits economics, social sciences, engineering and other research fields. The integration of statistical, econometric, and machine learning methods, combined with the collaborative expertise of two leading institutions, ensures significant contributions to the field. Our work enhances the ability to analyze, interpret, and predict complex network behaviors, paving the way for more robust decision-making in interconnected systems.
Keywords: Asymptotic theory, Laplace approximation, Latent variables, Network data, Partial Likelihood, Random fields, Statistical inference, dynamics, factor models, graph topology learning, network data

Title: Big Data Lives. Anthropological Perspectives on Tech-Imaginaries and Human Transformations
Abstract:
How individuals and societies aim to live in the future is channelled through and inextricably linked to the use of technology. Today, artificial intelligence (AI) and Big Data technologies are key elements in popular narratives about the future of mankind. What these developing technologies promise is enticing, as well as frightening. Public debates about AI and its effects on civilization tend to be heated. Famous figureheads conjure up distant, contrasting futures where we are either at the mercy of selfish machines, or have managed, with their help, to banish illness and war, and end all the world’s problems. Rather than argue for either side in this debate, our research project endeavours to understand the effects of human engagements with AI and Big Data technologies that acquire and manage personal data on behalf of states, intelligence agencies and commercial corporations.

This research project brings together three geographically diverse, ethnographic case studies. Each study explores the on-going implementations of technological infrastructures to provide insight into technology-driven, societal transformation as it happens: the implementation of China’s Social Credit System (SCS) on a national scale in 2020 (sub-project A by Lucien Schönenberg); a landscape ethnography that examines the “Virtual Border” – comprised of surveillance cameras, sensors, radar systems, and Integrated Fixed Towers (IFTs) – between the USA and Mexico (sub-project B by Darcy Alexandra); and sensor enabled, wearable technology in the context of a booming, digitalised healthcare system in Austria (sub-project C by Sophie Wagner). All three projects deal with initiatives that promote “better/safer futures”. Aiming to instil moral behaviour, inventing security threats that demand counteraction, or claiming to develop research while pushing a growing market and a country’s status as ‘ideal for business’ all produce troubling impacts on the freedom and privacy of individuals and radically alter notions of transparency, responsibility and trust. They bear witness to the ways in which Big Data based technologies add unprecedented degrees of complexity to the management of individual lives.

We acknowledge that the existence of Big Data based technologies has the potential to radically alter individual perception and subjectivity, and that it might be productive to rethink the human/technology dichotomy. Therefore, this research project investigates the relational existence of technologies and social phenomena. Our aim is to add a specific, human-centred approach to the discourse about AI and Big Data, and contribute to the dynamic understanding of human ontologies.
Keywords: Algorithms, Artificial Intelligence, Big Data Technologies, Human Transformation, Privacy, Self-tracking, Social Credit System, Surveillance, Tech-Imaginaries, Virtual Wall, Wearables

Title: Deep multi-target tracking
Abstract: Current solutions for tracking multiple objects in videos achieve reasonable performance under specific conditions but typically break down when applied in unconstrained scenes. In this project we will specifically address the limitations of current tracking approaches and develop more general models, making them accessible to a wider range of tasks. We will do so (a) by exploiting the rapidly growing amount of annotated data, part of which we have already collected in our recently published benchmark; and (b) by integrating both low-level cues from state-of-the-art deep learning and and high-level cues from geometric scene understanding in a joint framework.
Keywords: 3D scene understanding, convolutional neural networks, multi-target tacking, visual tracking

Title: Ab initio design of CO2 activation catalysts enabled by machine learning
Abstract:
The increasing environmental constraints to reduce CO2 emissions triggered the search for renewable energy sources and alternative feedstocks. The conversion of CO2 into fuels and chemicals represents a promising alternative, but also a challenging one due to the low reactivity of this non-polar molecule. One of the ways to activate CO2 is by using heterogeneous (solid) catalysts. Most of catalysts are however based on precious metals or suffer from deactivation, bringing the need for the development of novel inexpensive and stable materials.  A common approach to find new catalyst is to synthesize and test libraries of materials experimentally. Nevertheless, due to the overwhelming number of possible materials and compositions, only a selection of candidates can be tested within reasonable time and cost, and those are usually only slightly different from already known catalysts. 
A different strategy to tackle this problem is the computational screening of materials. By simulating large sets of materials in silico, the chances to find new catalysts are significantly increased compared to the experimental approach. Nevertheless, the accuracy needed to correctly predict reactivity is high and therefore requires the use of ab initio electronic-structure methods that present a prohibitive computational cost for the evaluation of millions of material candidates. Machine learning (ML) techniques have recently emerged to alleviate this caveat by providing efficient and flexible self-adaptive interpolation schemes that allow reducing the number of electronic-structure evaluations needed to simulate specific proprieties for large sets of materials.
The primary goal of this research is to accelerate the discovery of catalysts for CO2 conversion by combining density functional theory (DFT) calculations and ML methods. In particular, state-of-the-art ML algorithms will be applied to obtain quick yet accurate predictions of CO2 adsorption energies and geometries on metal oxide surfaces. These materials present Lewis acid/base sites on which the CO2 molecule is adsorbed and activated before the C-O bond cleavage. Both CO2 binding energy and adsorbed structure indicate the extent of activation. A database of DFT calculations will be created and used as a training set for the application of two approaches: (A) the direct ML model prediction of stability and structure of the adsorbed CO2 from easily calculated material proprieties (e.g., properties of the isolated atoms, bulk materials or clean surface) and (B) the use of ML interatomic potentials to describe the CO2-surface interactions. 
The models derived from ML will be applied for the identification of promising CO2 activation catalysts out of thousands of different oxides at a fraction of the computational cost required by the direct application of DFT. Furthermore, the developed methodology will be applicable to predict the adsorption of other molecules or reaction intermediates on surfaces of different materials, paving the way for ML prediction of reaction barriers and the study of complex surface reaction networks.
Keywords: Density functional theory, First principles modeling, Heterogeneous catalysis, Machine learning

Title: Predictive chance modelling: Exploration of a new approach to professional decision-making in child protection
Abstract: Much of empirical research in the field of child protection is concerned with the risk of maltreatment and how to predict that risk. Knowledge about what service responses work to alleviate the risk of maltreatment lags behind. One major reason for this is methodological: research designs that allow us to estimate the efficacy of interventions in child protection have been hard to come by. As empirical knowledge is lacking, social workers in child protection have expressed their urgent need for more evidence on the efficacy of different kinds of interventions for specified groups of clients. The objective of the proposed study is to explore the potential of novel techniques in predictive modelling for estimating the chances of service responses in child protection to succeed, an approach we call “predictive chance modelling” (PCM). The predictive models will draw from an existing administrative dataset (N = approx. 15’000 cases) provided by the Office for Youth and Vocational Guidance in the canton of Zurich, which is one of the largest service providers for child maltreatment in Switzerland. Predictive models to be developed, tested, and systematically compared will include more traditional regression techniques, non-linear classification models (such as neural networks), classification trees (such as random forests) and Bayesian adaptations of both regression and non-linear modelling (such as Bayesian logistic regression and Bayesian neural networks). The modelling is embedded in an explorative user-oriented design that will bring together stakeholders from the field, including frontline social workers involved in service planning, management of the Office for Youth and Vocational Guidance, and representatives from the local Child Protection Authorities. The goal is to make the results of our predictive models interpretable, by way of visualization, to professionals, and to explore whether PCM is seen as potentially helpful by practitioners in the field. Discussions shall also revolve around the preconditions that would have to be met if PCM approaches should be further developed towards implementation in professional decision-making. The proposed study will provide empirical findings and methodological insights about the efficacy of service responses in child protection. It might also pave the way for more detailed inquiries into the professional, technical, legal, and ethical requirements for PCM to play a useful and legitimate part in the future development of child protective services.
Keywords: child protection, child welfare, intervention, machine learning, predictive modelling, service response

Title: Enhancing Student Performance Through Formative Feedback in Large Scale University Lectures
Abstract:
Today's world is changing faster than ever before. Students graduating from university find a world, which is highly volatile. Decisions need to be made under high uncertainty. The problems to be solved are often complex and interdependent. Large amounts of data lead to ambiguity during decision-making. Consequently, a shift in the compositions of skills and knowledge is needed. In the past, students could mostly rely on the knowledge they once learned for a longer period. Today, however, students need to constantly acquire new knowledge and the required skills shift more and more towards critical thinking, collaboration and communication. In my research, I am focusing on the students' ability to provide high quality feedback, which belongs to the group of communication skills. I chose this skill, because it is especially important, for team members of agile teams, which in short iterations need to constantly adjust their shared understanding of the project aim and the current status.
To train the students skill in providing feedback two essential factors are needed a) a realistic teaching-learning scenario in which students are challenged to train such a skill and b) the provision of formative feedback, which, according to Hattie (2015), is one of the most important factors for student performance. A major challenge is that most universities can hardly provide such conditions due to the increasing lecture sizes and their financial resource constraints. The numbers provided by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and Bundesamt für Statistik (Federal Office for Statistics) mirror this development. According to the OECD (2016), between 2005 and 2014 the number of students at universities rose by 15 percentage points in the US, 29 in Germany and according to the Bundesamt für Statistik (2017), 28 in Switzerland. Consequently, the major challenge I aim to address is how can a challenging teaching-learning scenario that includes formative feedback to help students develop their ability to provide high quality feedback be created. My key boundary condition is that lecture sizes keep growing while available resources are limited. Thus, increasing the teaching resources by scaling the number of teaching assistants and applying a tutor feedback model such as the one proposed by Marjanovic (2016) does not seem viable.
Hence, I aim to leverage the potentials of modern IT and propose a solution using peer feedback, in which students a) find a nearly realistic teaching-learning scenario in which they can train their ability to provide feedback and b) receive automated formative feedback during the course of writing their feedback to a peer's work. To achieve my goal - especially the part related to providing automated but meaningful formative feedback - we will use 5,252 student peer feedbacks, which we gathered over the last three years in one of our large-scale lectures to train a supervised machine-learning algorithm. 
The expected findings of my research are empirical data, describing the characteristics of high quality feedback from the students’ perspective. Furthermore, our hypothesis is that through providing formative feedback on the students’ ability to provide feedback, we can improve this skill. Thus, my research will contribute to theory and practice, by providing a) descriptive knowledge of the feedback characteristics, and b) empirical insights showing the value of providing automated formative feedback on the students’ ability to provide feedback. I contribute to practice, since I provide insights for distance learning vendors on how to implement the peer feedback process effectively.
Keywords: Higher education, Large-scale lectures, MOOCs, Machine Learning, Online education, Peer feedback

Title: Improving Diagnostics for Patients in the Emergency Department using Machine-learning Algorithms and Biomarkers
Abstract:
Diagnosis is particularly challenging in the emergency department (ED), where resources are strained by overcrowding, time is limited, and patients often present early in their disease course prior to manifesting many of the tell-tale signs of specific diseases. Yet, the efficient diagnostic decision-making is the foundation for a rapid and accurate treatment. Successful treatment is associated with an improved patient outcome. 

A significant example for the improvement of patient’s outcome due to early and adequate goal directed therapy is the treatment in sepsis. Sepsis is caused by an infection that leads to a dysregulated host reaction. It is a life-threatening condition with up to 6 million patients dying worldwide. Despite recognition of its importance, early recognition of patients with sepsis remains a major challenge and is key for early and adequate goal directed therapy.

I will work on an interdisciplinary project with the objective to combine data from biomarker and other molecular diagnostic tests with clinical data that is routinely available in the electronic health records (EHR). The aim will be to generate reliable sepsis-related outcome predictions. We will combine traditional biomarker-based diagnostic approaches with data science and health information technology methods (data scraping, machine-learning and bidirectional real-time communication with the EHR) to identify patients at high risk of sepsis, septic shock, intensive care unit (ICU) admission and death. The long-term goal with this prediction model is to generate a clinical decision support at the individual patient level (personalized medicine). We will base our project on the innovative machine-learning based tool that reliably stratifies patients by risk of adverse outcome (admission, ICU admission, death) at time of ED arrival. It was developed by the Johns Hopkins University and is used for ED triage across all ED of the John Hopkins Health System. This tool is able to process data and provide EHR-embedded decision support in seconds, and outperforms gold standard triage tools in risk-stratification. 

The first aim is to derive and validate a predictive model for sepsis and sepsis-related adverse clinical outcomes using data from the EHR. To achieve this, we will conduct a retrospective cohort study, in which we will apply machine-learning methods to routinely available data collected from EHR to generated predictive models with high capacity for identifying ED patients at increased risk for sepsis, septic shock, ICU admission and in-hospital death. Second, using this predictive model, we will conduct a prospective cohort study to evaluate the additive value of biomarkers (monocyte distribution with and rapid antigen testing) in accuracy of diagnosis and adverse outcome prediction (aim 2). We will collect data of all patients who present to the ED over a 9-month period, and incorporate these values in our model. The last aim is to test the predictive model for the prediction of treatment outcomes: responsiveness to fluid and antibiotics administration in patients with sepsis.
Keywords: Diagnostic, Emergency Medicine, Machine-learning, Molecular diagnostic, Risk stratification, Sepsis

Title: Transfer Learning for Object Detection
Abstract: Many classes of objects can now be successfully detected with statistical machine learning techniques. Faces, cars and pedestrians, have all been detected with low error rates by learning their appearance in a highly generic manner from extensive training sets. These recent advances have enabled the use of reliable object detection components in real systems, such as automatic face focusing functions on digital cameras. One key drawback of these methods, and the issue addressed here, is the prohibitive requirement that training sets contain thousands of manually annotated examples. We present three methods, based on transfer learning, which make headway toward reducing labeling requirements and in turn, toward a tractable solution to the scene understanding problem. In particular, instead of building detectors from the ground up, we propose to transfer knowledge acquired from previously learnt category detectors to new target class and in so doing, enable the learning of a new target category using a limited number of training samples.
Keywords: Computer Vision, Image Processing, Machine Learning, Object Detection, Transfer Learning

Title: Development of a novel, integrative proteogenomics approach to discover the entire protein-coding potential of prokaryotic genomes
Abstract:
Large advances in Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) technologies have led to an enormous increase of genome sequences. However, our ability to accurately and comprehensively predict all protein-coding open reading frames (ORFs), has lagged behind: large discrepancies exist for the total number of ORFs predicted and the precise protein start sites. Moreover, the recent identification of unannotated short proteins that carry out key biological functions has further emphasized these shortcomings. Today, we thus do not know the entire protein-coding potential of any organism, not even the best-studied prokaryotes.     
Yet, the knowledge of all protein-coding genes is one crucial aspect to fully capitalize on the genome information and decode its function. It is relevant for all levels, from small, focused experiments, to large functional screens, systems biology studies that depend on complete quantitative data series, up to accurate prediction of gene regulatory, interaction and metabolic networks. In view of the re-emergence of infectious diseases and the lack of novel antibiotics to combat the increasing multi-drug resistance, a comprehensive protein inventory is also expected to contain novel classes of targets for antimicrobial defense strategies.

To address this knowledge gap, we propose to further develop and validate a novel, integrative proteogenomics approach capable of discovering the entire protein-coding potential of prokaryotic genomes. In a first phase, we will exploit the very deep proteomics and transcriptomics data acquired during the previous grant for the a-proteobacterium Bartonella henselae, a model for host-pathogen interaction. We will extend them with the actual genome sequence, enriched 5’ end mRNA transcripts and NH2-terminal protein datasets, allowing us to identify alternative protein start sites and to establish how many ORFs have been missed in two infection biology relevant conditions. In parallel, we will further develop the basic prototype of our proteogenomics approach which differs from existing solutions in several ways: it i) can integrate reference genome annotations with results of gene prediction algorithms, and in silico predictions, precisely capturing their overlap and differences in an informative gene identifier, ii) creates an extensive yet minimally redundant protein database which, combined with stringent control of the false discovery rate, allows to achieve better statistical power for novel genome hits and prevent spurious identifications, and iii) shortens the time-consuming, tedious analysis of potential novel genome hits. Testing our approach in pilot studies has, in each case, identified unannotated ORFs, including short proteins, differentially regulated proteins, membrane-associated lipo-proteins and metabolic enzymes. A major focus will be to program a computational expert system that largely extends the functionality and level of automation of the prototype, and allows to critically assess prioritized candidates in the visual context of functional annotations and experimental data.  

In a second phase, we aim to provide further proof for the general validity of our proteogenomics solution by applying it on selected model organisms of biological, medical and agricultural relevance. These will include Staphylococcus aureus, a medically highly relevant Gram-positive prokaryote. We will assess the extent of missed protein-coding ORFs on a more comprehensive scale by analyzing existing proteomics data from many different conditions. Based on the promising results, we are convinced that the potential impact of our integrative proteogenomics solution is high, and that it can enable us to more fully exploit the functional information encoded in genomes.
