Title: Turning noise into data: a discovery strategy for new weakly-interacting physics
Abstract:
With the discovery of the Higgs boson in 2012 by the ATLAS and CMS Collaborations, the Standard Model (SM) of particle physics is now complete, and it forms a robust definition of the strong, weak, and electromagnetic interactions with matter. Nonetheless, it is clear that the SM is an incomplete description of the universe: there are multiple observed phenomena such as the existence of Dark Matter (DM) which are not explained by the SM. The experimental High Energy Physics (HEP) collaborations at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) are hard at work looking for clues that would provide explanations for these phenomena, and possibly point towards an ultimate theory of particle physics.

The LHC delivers so many proton-proton collisions to ATLAS and CMS that it is not possible to record them all. The collaborations must quickly sort through the incoming information and save only what they deem to be important; the ATLAS strategy prioritizes higher-energy or otherwise rare collisions.
This choice works well for many applications, and it was fundamental to the discovery of the Higgs boson. However, it also discards the vast majority of the data of interest in searches for low-energy weakly-interacting new physics, thus limiting the sensitivity to new low-mass particles which could explain the nature of DM or other low-energy phenomena.

This project proposes a solution: it is possible to recover an enormous yet currently unused low-energy dataset by turning the additional “noise” collisions recorded in every event into useful data. This novel approach, hereafter referred to as the Data Interpretation Strategy for COmplete Vertex Event Reconstruction in High Energy Physics (DISCOVERHEP), provides a means of searching for new weakly-interacting physics at a level that dramatically exceeds traditional approaches. I propose to build a team which will develop and make use of this new dataset in the search for new weakly-interacting physics. I will focus on hadronic physics (interactions with quarks and gluons), as this has traditionally been challenging to study at low energy and thus remains a mostly-unexplored area with a large discovery-potential.

The proposed project is divided into four Work Packages (WPs). WP1 focuses on the development of the tools needed to reconstruct every event in the ATLAS dataset with respect to every vertex in the event, thus providing the enormous low-energy proton-proton collision dataset needed to conduct searches for new physics. WP2 represents the first analysis of this unique dataset using a traditional dijet resonance search, which is expected to provide dramatically improved sensitivity to new low-energy weakly-interacting physics models (including dark matter mediators) compared to competing approaches. WP3 exploits jet substructure techniques in this new dataset to identify low-energy jets inconsistent with Standard Model quarks and gluons, thus probing currently uncovered areas of parameter space in the search for more complex new physics models such as strongly-coupled dark sectors. WP4 exploits modern machine learning techniques and this novel dataset to generically search for anomalous low-energy hadronic interactions, thus probing a wide variety of different models of new physics, and which may point the way towards unexpected new forms of physics that would be missed using traditional directed search strategies.

There are many well-motivated models of new low-energy weakly-interacting hadronic physics, and it is thus important to cover a wide range of possible options. The proposed research program does exactly this through both direct searches for specific well-motivated models of new physics and a generic search to minimize the impact of preconceptions on the forms that new physics may take. The proposal will furthermore probe low-energy weakly-interacting hadronic physics to unprecedented precision, thus expanding the ATLAS physics program and potentially leading the way towards new discoveries.
Keywords: ATLAS, Anomaly detection, Hadronic physics, High energy physics, Jet reconstruction, Machine learning, Particle physics, Physics beyond the standard model, Pileup, Weakly-interacting physics

Title: Highly Adaptive Computational Models of Biomedical Tissue in Radiological Images: Digital Tissue Atlases and Correlation with Genomics (MAGE)
Abstract:
Modern multi–dimensional imaging in radiology yields much more information than the naked eye can appreciate. As a result, errors and variations in interpretations are currently the weakest aspect of clinical imaging. Computerized quantitative image analysis can make better use of the image content by yielding exhaustive, comprehensive and reproducible analysis of imaging features, which spawned the new fields of “radiomics” and “imaging genomics”. It has the potential to surrogate and surpass invasive biopsy–based molecular assays with the ability to capture intralesional heterogeneity in a non–invasive way. Personalized phenotyping of the manifestation of the disease can be used to diagnose, assess treatment response, and predict prognosis with higher precision. Neither radiomics nor imaging genomics are mature fields of study, though. First, current computational models of biomedical tissue in multi–dimensional radiological protocols lack the appropriate framework for leveraging local image directions, which showed to be most relevant to characterize the geometry of 3–D biomedical texture. Second, most approaches proposed in the literature are assuming that the tissue properties are homogeneous over the tumors or organs, which is inadequate in most cases.
In this proposal, we will address these two challenges. First, highly adaptive computational models of biomedical tissue will be learned from the data to optimally characterize their discriminative multi–dimensional geometric properties in one–versus–all (OVA) configurations. A desirable property of the models is that they can be “steered” analytically to enable rotation–covariant image analysis. To the best of our knowledge, it constitutes a unique framework that gather both supervised model learning and rotation–covariance. Whereas most of radiomics approaches proposed application–driven methods, preliminary results showed that the framework can model a broad range of 2–D and 3–D biomedical tissue types in radiological images. The models can be trained to segment, classify and retrieve desired tissue categories. Second, the tissue properties will be localized in the anatomy or within the lesions to construct prototype architectures of the radiological phenotypes.
The methods will be used to study two groups of diseases: glioblastoma multiformes (GBM) and interstitial lung diseases (ILD). GBM tumors measure often several centimeters in size and are occupying a large amount of voxels in magnetic resonance (MR) images. ILDs are most often diffuse and are characterized by large lung regions with homogeneous tissue types. Therefore, multi–scale texture–based tissue characterization of both disease groups is expected to be best suited for modeling their radiological phenotypes. Two large cohorts of patients will be used to investigate the groups of diseases and validate the developed methods: The Cancer Image Archive (TCIA) and the Lung Tissue Research Consortium (LTRC), which are both initialtives of the National Institutes of Health (NIH). Radiology images with homogenized protocols and molecular data are available for each patients in both collections. The digital models of the radiological phenotypes will be correlated with the genomic profiles to unveil complex relationships between structural, functional and molecular properties of biomedical tissue. The advances in methods and knowledge will translate into immediate benefits to the patient by designing personalized biomarkers to predict diagnosis, survival and treatment outcome while avoiding invasive and expensive biopsy sampling as well as gene sequencing. The methods, the consortium and the cohorts of patients that this proposal is gathering is unique in many ways and is expected to allow for a significant breakthrough in the emerging fields of radiomics and imaging genomics.
Keywords: gliobastoma multiformes, image processing, imaging genomics, interstitial lung diseases, machine learning, radiogenomics, radiomics, steerable filters, texture analysis, wavelet transform

Title: Understanding the role of inhibitory circuits in controlling plasticity and in implementing network-level objectives
Abstract:
One of the great outstanding questions is how the brain processes information—even solving mundane everyday tasks like grocery shopping poses complex computational challenges. The brain solves these challenges with ease using neural networks. Most neurons in these networks are “hidden neurons,” which are neither directly connected to sensory input nor the output of the circuit. How these neurons connect to contribute to computation at the circuit level remains elusive. Importantly, not all of their connections can be hard-coded. Thus our brains have to set them up somehow. To that end, neural circuits must “know” their objectives and rely on some form of “optimization algorithm” to implement them. However, neither objectives nor the algorithms by which the brain achieves this feat are unknown. This proposal’s overarching goal is to study the fundamental objectives and circuit mechanisms involved in setting up functional connectivity.

Because hidden neurons do not “know” their contribution to the computation carried out by the whole circuit, one essential requirement to establish their tuning is higher-order feedback. Feedback has to be relayed through dedicated elements of the biological wet-ware and directly influence learning at hidden neurons. Although there are many possible ways of achieving this, the pervasive inhibitory circuitry seems most promising for several reasons. First, inhibition fulfills all temporal requirements of a rapid control mechanism needed to prevent run-away plasticity at excitatory synapses. Second, widespread experimental evidence has implicated inhibitory interneurons in the gating of plasticity. Third, inhibition has an essential role in theories of predictive coding and putative links to credit assignment. Last, the circuit position of certain interneuron types seems ideal to receive long-range feedback and, thus, to regulate synaptic plasticity by impacting calcium dynamics. Yet, how the diverse inhibitory interneurons work together to establish functional circuits and which high-level objectives these circuits optimize remains mostly elusive.

To elucidate the role of inhibitory circuits in circuit-level learning, we will study how interneurons can receive and process higher-order feedback to steer synaptic plasticity at hidden neurons and optimize circuit-level objectives (WP 1). Similarly, we will investigate prediction and its relation to inhibitory neurons as one putative circuit-level objective for unsupervised learning in neural networks (WP 2). To tackle these questions, we will develop theories and computational models at different levels of abstraction and compare their activity to data from our experimental collaborators. On the one hand, we will continue to use deep neural network models to study the computational merits of prediction as a general objective for unsupervised learning in neural networks. On the other hand, we will build biologically constrained spiking neural networks (SNNs) and train them with supervised and unsupervised objectives using our expertise in surrogate gradient techniques. Moreover, we will use SNN simulations, data-driven plasticity models, and tools from dynamical systems to study how inhibition can transmit higher-order feedback to hidden neurons and control synaptic plasticity. Finally, we will use data from our experimental colleagues to verify and iteratively refine our models. To that end, we will develop open-source simulation and analysis software for the quantitative comparison of model activity with high-dimensional in-vivo recordings (WP 3). In short, we propose understanding neural computation by studying the “biological algorithms” that tune neural connectivity instead of inferring their function directly.

In summary, the research in this proposal takes a new approach to conceptually understand neural computation at the network level. Our work will shed light on the mechanistic role of diverse inhibitory circuitry, which previous theoretical models have mostly ignored. Conceptualizing the role of inhibitory neurons in controlling plasticity will be an essential step toward understanding both brain function and dysfunction.
Keywords: computational neuroscience, dynamical systems, excitatory-inhibitory balance, interneurons, learning, machine learning, neural networks, self-supervised learning, spiking neurons, synaptic plasticity, unsupervised learning

Title: Exploitation and Upgrades of the CMS experiment at the LHC:  the next phase
Abstract:
This funding proposal (excellence grant) seeks support by the SNSF to continue the successfully ongoing SNSF-funded research program of the PI, carried out in the context of the CMS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, Geneva. The current grant (finishing in September 2020) is a streamlined physics analysis program with clear emphasis on precision studies of the Higgs boson (differential measurements of Higgs production using its di-photon decay channel and limits on the Higgs self-interaction via the search for di-Higgs production) and on searches for physics beyond the Standard Model (SM) (supersymmetric particles and Heavy Neutral Leptons (HNLs)). This is complemented by novel approaches to event reconstruction based on modern machine learning tools and by contributions to the Phase-2 upgrades of the ECAL barrel electronics and Precision Timing Layer (barrel part).
In view of the upcoming LHC run schedule and the corresponding modest increase of statistics to be expected during the period of this new proposal, the strategy will be adapted, since it is not very meaningful to continue analyses that consequently would not result in significantly new physics insights (such as the di-Higgs search, the search for supersymmetry with the MT2 observable or the search for HNLs using W boson decays). Therefore, the main goals of this new proposal are: (a) Continue the Higgs program (focus on the di-photon decay channel of the Higgs boson) in areas where further improvements in the systematic uncertainties and novel interpretations of the data can lead (i) to new results and/or (ii) to preparing the path towards future high-statistics analyses at the end of Run-3 and during the High-Luminosity phase of the LHC. These efforts will continue along the lines of employing novel machine learning methods and other event reconstruction improvements, as well as novel theoretical interpretations of the available data. (b) In terms of searches for new physics, the idea is to scrutinize previously untouched datasets (in particular the so-called CMS B-parking data set for a novel search for HNLs) and to measure not yet explored observables such as R(J/?), in order to address the important topic of possible signs of violations of lepton flavour universality. (c) Again, these activities will be complemented by contributions to the operations and Phase-2 upgrades of CMS, with emphasis on the ECAL barrel electronics and barrel Precision Timing Layer. 
As previously, the planned research efforts are in excellent synergy, complementarity and close coordination with the other CMS efforts at ETH (groups of R. Wallny and C. Grab), whose focus is on the optimal Physics exploitation of the CMS Pixel detector and on its upgrades. Finally, this excellence grant will allow the PI and his group to maintain and strengthen its standing in the competitive environment of the CMS experiment, and complement other investments related to detector operations and upgrade efforts.
Keywords: CMS Experiment, Electromagnetic Calorimeter, Higgs Boson, LHC, New Physics Searches, Upgrades

Title: Decoding the HGF/c-MET Axis in Neutrophil-T Cell Crosstalk for Optimized ICI Therapy
Abstract:
Background. Despite major progress in harnessing adaptive immunity for cancer therapy, ICIs remain effective only in certain patient populations and tumor types. Recent findings from our group show that specific irAEs—especially ICI-related colitis—are strongly associated with improved clinical outcomes, where a high HGF/CXCL9 cytokine signature correlates with superior survival. Patients in this “double-high” cluster exhibit enhanced neutrophil activation and memory T cell responses. Notably, ICI-treated neutrophils secrete elevated HGF, while c-MET expression is upregulated in both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. These c-MET+ T cells display higher levels of key chemokine receptors (CCR1, CCR2, CCR4, CXCR3), as well as CD27 and CD62L, suggesting distinct migratory and functional phenotypes that may be critical for tumor infiltration.
Hypothesis. ICI therapy drives a coordinated remodeling of neutrophils and T cells, leading to robust HGF secretion and enhanced T cell tumor infiltration through CXCL9/CXCR3 interactions. HGF-mediated c-MET activation on T cells boosts anti-tumor immunity but may also exacerbate irAE severity through excessive inflammation. Neutrophil–T cell crosstalk thus emerges as a pivotal regulatory mechanism, and by targeting the HGF/c-MET/CXCL9 axis, we aim to optimize T cell infiltration and activation while maintaining a favorable therapeutic window.
Overall Objective. This project translates these mechanistic insights into clinically actionable strategies to improve ICI therapy. By pinpointing how neutrophils, HGF, and T cells interact, we will: (A) Identify predictive biomarkers linking systemic cytokine levels and tumor-intrinsic factors with patient response and irAE severity, (B) Develop AI-driven approaches integrating multi-omics data, spatial immune parameters, and clinical outcomes for personalized risk stratification and (C) Investigate novel therapeutic combinations (e.g., c-MET agonists, HGF/CXCL9 mimetics) that harness neutrophil–T cell synergy to enhance ICI.
Specific Aims.
1.Aim?1: Determine the immunomodulatory role of HGF and CXCL9 in ICI therapy and how HGF/c-MET axis modulates T-cell and non-immune cell (endothelial, epithelial, fibroblast) interactions.
2.Aim?2: Elucidate how neutrophils and c-MET/HGF axis modulate the CXCL9/CXCR3 axis and T-cell migratory capacity.
3.Aim?3: Validate c-MET/HGF effects on tumor immunity in animal models.
4.Aim?4: Integrate digital pathology, spatial transcriptomics, scRNA-seq to explore HGF/c-MET/CXCL9 in tumor immunity.
5.Aim?5: Assess the prognostic and functional significance of c-MET+CXCR3+ T cells in ICI responses.
Expected Outcomes.
1.Neutrophil–T cell Crosstalk: Elucidate how HGF-secreting neutrophils regulate T cell infiltration, chemokine gradients, and tumor immunity.
2.Biomarker Discovery: Identify predictive markers for ICI response and irAE severity based on HGF, CXCL9, and c-MET+ T cell dynamics.
3.Mechanistic Model: Establish a multi-compartmental framework linking systemic (blood), inflammatory (colitis), and tumor (TME) interactions.
4.Targeted Interventions: Develop new therapeutic avenues (e.g., c-MET and HGF agonists, HGF/CXCL9 modulation, novel bispecific antibodies).
5.AI-Powered Clinical Tools: Build machine-learning models integrating multi-omics and spatial data to guide personalized immunotherapy.

Title: Deep Learning Models for Continual Extraction of Knowledge from Text
Abstract: Machine reading extracts valuable knowledge from text (e.g., in the form of entities and their relationships) and stores these in a knowledge base or knowledge graph for further usage. This is a task of continual reading and learning based on the texts and the knowledge already acquired. In this project we port this task to a deep learning framework, where fundamental research is needed to represent both the unstructured text and the structured knowledge in an integrated way. This is challenging also because the extraction is performed with limited supervision of annotated training data. While continually learning and updating the extracted knowledge, the model has to avoid acquiring incorrect knowledge. We evaluate the continual learning models with two use cases: extraction of biomedical knowledge from a publication feed of biomedical documents, and extraction of facts from a newsfeed.
Keywords: Continual learning, Deep learning, Distant supervision, Information extraction, Natural language processing

Title: RING: Robust Intelligence with Nonconvex Games
Abstract:
We address one of the most formidable challenges of the new AI era: building robust intelligence while facing the perils of uncertainty.  Uncertainty is omnipresent in every corner of the machine learning pipeline, from data generation, model selection, system dynamics, and algorithm design, all the way to prediction and decision making. Besides data uncertainty, typical sources of uncertainty include but are not limited to: model uncertainty, dynamics uncertainty, adversarial uncertainty, task uncertainty, and causal uncertainty. 

Extensive groundwork has been laid to deal with data uncertainty through the lens of stochastic optimization that drives tremendous progress of machine learning especially deep learning. However, when tackling other types of uncertainty, existing research has settled for rather disconnected solutions, to name a few: (a) Bayesian methods (to address model uncertainty), (b) reinforcement learning  (to address dynamics uncertainty), and (c) adversarial machine learning (to address adversarial uncertainty), and (d) meta-learning (to address task uncertainty). Moreover, they often fall short of either  scalability to accommodate the ever-growing data and model complexity in modern applications, or  theoretical guarantees to justify their efficiency; and worse still, they are not adaptive to coping with a mixture of uncertainties. 

Bridging these gaps would require a significant departure from the state of the art. This project  seeks to substantially advance the theory, algorithms, and practice of robust intelligence by grounding it in a novel, principled, and unified framework --  contextual Stackelberg game --  that reins in a broad spectrum of learning paradigms under uncertainty. To achieve the expected breakthroughs, this project integrates three complementary thrusts.

Thrust I: Foundations of contextual Stackelberg games. This thrust establishes fundamental theory and algorithms for solving generic contextual Stackelberg games, with a primary focus on the challenging nonconvex setting. We will develop provably efficient algorithms by rethinking the bias-cost-variance trade-off and taming the nonconvexity.  As a side product, this will also close a number of theoretical gaps on nonconvex zero-sum games. 

Thrust II: Bridging contextual Stackelberg games and robust intelligence. This thrust demonstrates the prospects of contextual Stackelberg games for addressing various learning tasks under uncertainty, with a primary focus on meta-learning and reinforcement learning. Based on the game perspectives, we will develop brand new theories and provably efficient algorithms for meta-learning and reinforcement learning, with improved sample efficiency, generalization, and trustworthiness.

Thrust III: Bridging the theory and the practice through interdisciplinary applications. The third thrust is devoted to evaluations and advancement of these efficient algorithms in several societally critical applications, including  energy-efficient motion control for smart transportation and  autonomous control for digital agriculture. 

Expected Impact. The proposed game framework will enable a systematic study of various machine learning paradigms under uncertainty, and offer a fresh route to design universal algorithms with scalability, provable guarantees, and adaptivity,  which are lacking in the current state-of-the-art. The close synthesis of optimization, games, and uncertainty-aware learning would promote automatic synergies among several seemingly disparate subfields of machine learning, which in turn will help cross-fertilize the theory governing them as well as broaden their applicability. Such synergies are quintessential for advancing the deployment of ML/AI in societal critical domains when a mixture of uncertainties is prevalent.
Keywords: machine learning, optimization

Title: Bringing Light in the Darkness of the Patient Journey: Digital Biomarker for Monitoring and Predicting Disease Severity in the Daily Lives of Rheumatoid Arthritis Patients
Abstract:
Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease that affects about 0.5-1% of the population worldwide and leads to inflammation of joints, resulting in severe pain, swelling, and stiffness. The current strategy for treating RA is the "treat-to-target" approach. Patients typically receive methotrexate as first-line therapy, but about 50% of patients are switched to a biologic after three months due to an inadequate response to therapy. Approximately 30-40% of patients do not respond well and are switched to another biologic. The process continues until the right medication is found. However, this trial-and-error approach places a significant burden on patients and the healthcare system. There is a clear need to find a more efficient approach to managing RA.

This study aims to investigate the feasibility of developing a digital biomarker to monitor disease activity and predict treatment response in RA patients using passive sensor data collected from smartphones and smartwatches. Specifically, we aim to develop a digital biomarker to detect disease worsening in daily life and predict treatment response (remission) in RA patients early enough using passive sensor data from smartphones and smartwatches, and machine learning. We plan to run a 3-month pilot study with RA patients to collect passive sensor data and patient-reported outcomes from smartphones and smartwatches of RA patients. The data will include physical activity, sleep patterns, heart rate variability, pictures of joints, and joint temperature. After the 3-month period, we will collect laboratory measures to assess the treatment response (remission vs non-remission). We will use machine learning algorithms to analyze the data and develop a digital biomarker that can detect days with disease worsening (flares) and predict treatment response.

The digital biomarker developed in this study could provide a non-invasive, unobtrusive, and efficient method for monitoring disease activity and predicting treatment response in RA patients. This could lead to earlier interventions and improved disease management, reducing the burden on patients and the healthcare system. The use of passive sensing from smartwatches could also increase patient compliance and reduce attrition rates compared to active sensing methods. The development of a digital biomarker for RA patients could significantly improve disease management and reduce the burden on patients and the healthcare system. This study could pave the way for the development of similar digital biomarkers for other inflammatory chronic diseases.
Keywords: digital biomarker, digital health, disease monitoring, machine learning, remote monitoring, rheumatoid arthritis, smartphones, wearables

Title: Melise - Machine Learning Assisted Software Development
Abstract:
The usage of Machine Learning (ML) models to support software engineering tasks has witnessed considerable interest from both academics and practitioners in the last year. Building an ML model takes several steps ranging from the elicitation of the requirements, feature engineering, and model training, to evaluation and deployment. This typical pipeline often contains feedback loops: for instance, unsatisfactory training results may loop back to the feature engineering phase. However, once deployed, ML models often become a static entity, in the sense that they are rarely updated or re-trained. We believe this is a huge missed opportunity: a vast amount of data is continuously generated during the development process, e.g., issue tracker posts, user reviews, or repository events, and a static ML model cannot gain any advantage from it. In other words, while a specific software project keeps evolving, the ML model supposed to support its development practices remains unchanged. As a consequence, this can lead to a loss of accuracy of the model itself, slowly but inevitably becoming obsolete.

The goal of our project is to investigate whether the data stream created in software development can be successfully exploited to re-train ML models and, consequently, to improve them. However, such a data stream is not the only piece of information that we aim to use to accomplish this task. While this constitutes passive information, we plan to gather an additional active stream provided by the developers. Indeed, we want to implement a user-based feedback loop mechanism with the goal of continuously improving ML models. Our goal is to use it in a reinforcement learning fashion: every time a warning produced by the model is assessed by a developer, we can re-train the model and, for instance, reward it in case correct warnings were generated.

In this project, we will focus on bug prediction and effort estimation as ML models. We claim that software evolution and ML model evolution need to go hand in hand, and feedback loops are key for that. We plan to create a comprehensive benchmark dataset that can be used for selecting generalizable and effective defect prediction approaches. We will devise a feedback loop exploiting both active (user-based) and passive data streams, with the goal of continuously improving ML models. As a result, we will devise the necessary foundations for ML-assisted software development that takes into account learning from the context and avoiding the typical concept drift of ML.
Keywords: AI for SE, machine learning, mining software repositories, software engineering, software evolution

Title: Data-Driven Workflow for Generality-Oriented Ligand Design in Nickel Catalysis
Abstract:
Homogeneous transition-metal catalysts are essential for the synthesis of pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and fine chemical ingredients. Palladium dominates among other metals and advances in Pd-catalyzed cross-coupling have been enabled by appropriately designed ancillary ligands that, when coordinated to the metal center, enhance its selectivity and activity. However, the high cost and scarcity of precious metals has propelled the search for more sustainable alternatives based on earth-abundant elements. While tremendous progress has been achieved in nickel chemistry, minimal effort has been dedicated to identifying new ligands suited to its unique properties. “Re-purposing” ligands that have proven successful in related Pd-catalyzed reactions, although being the most common strategy, is inefficient, as the design principles do not always translate well between the two metals. Subtle properties, such as a ligand’s ability to perform reliably across a broad substrate scope, may be affected non-intuitively. Therefore, there is a need for methods capable of building comprehensive yet reliable reactivity pictures and establishing structure–activity relationships that quantify and predict how ligand generality changes in Pd vs. Ni-catalysis, accelerating reaction optimization and new ligand design for challenging cases.
This fellowship aims at developing a data-driven workflow to (1) assess and quantify the generality of Pd- and Ni-based catalysts in terms of both their substrate scope and applicability in distinct cross-coupling reactions, and (2) identify more active ligands for low-performance areas of chemical space. It will use chemical space maps with reaction-agnostic descriptors to rationalize trends in catalytic behavior over a range of transformations and statistical models to relate structural features to function, enabling the inverse design of superior ligands. High-throughput experimental data will be integrated with reactivity profiles generated in silico, and predictions from the maps will be validated experimentally, providing a feedback loop that enables model refinement. These achievements will provide a transferable platform for exploring new privileged ligand classes tailored to the mechanistic demands of nickel, and streamline the development of more sustainable and efficient cross-coupling methodologies.

Title: Deep-Learning & Remote Sensing for archaeological research in the Island of Euboea, Central Greece
Abstract:
As long as archaeologists have studied the past, the investigation of the location and distribution of archaeological remains in their surroundings has been a central endeavour in the discipline. However, the study of ancient settlement development and land use are complex phenomena and several potential hazards may contribute to affect the location and preservation of archaeological heritage. These hazards can be of different nature: geological, climatic or human-induced, as many modern activities crucial for subsistence living. Particularly, in the most recent years, climate-change related sudden events have been uncovering and destroying archaeological sites, especially in the Mediterranean basin. The island of Euboea, the second largest island in Greece, has recently suffered from catastrophic large wildfires, extreme rainfall events and flood phenomena resulting in the destruction of more than 120k acres of pine forest, razed homes and hundreds of displaced people. Such extreme weather phenomena, compounded with coastal erosion and human activities (agriculture, industry etc.), besides being a significant global challenge, represent an existential threat also for the high number of coastal cultural heritage sites. Is there any way to identify and document these sites before these predictable catastrophes make them disappear? 
Deep learning and Remote Sensing methods emerged as an invaluable metric and have found multiple uses in every field of application, and archaeology is no exception. They are essential analytic methods to support archaeological research as a type of non-destructive methodology, to collect the necessary information across different spatial dimensions - from local to the supra-regional contexts - and to produce predictive and susceptibility maps of still unknown and endangered archaeological sites. Moving from the results obtained within the ADArchaeoSA project, this research will aim at identifying higher risk areas on the Island of Euboea where known, and still unknown, archaeological sites may be located, and to define high-priority zones in which to target archaeological prospections and investigations. The automated procedure based on object detection algorithms and applied to high resolution multi-spectral satellite and LiDAR images, will enable to recognize and identify different types of sites, extracting information from the images in a systematic way, either above or below ground level. The procedure will allow: i) to produce an extended geo-referenced archaeological database for the Euboea region; ii) to identify sites at risk by cross-referencing the prediction results with modern environmental hazard maps; ii) to ultimately gain a more comprehensive knowledge of past land use in the Eastern Mediterranean. The results will be relevant to archaeology and beyond by providing valuable insights into ancient cultural landscapes and, in a contemporary perspective, to help modern society, heritage managers and environmental planners respond to the challenges associated with climate and environmental changes by providing critical tools and input to decision-making for archaeological and heritage conservation.
Keywords: Central Greece, Climate Change, Deep Learning, Landscape Archaeology, Remote Sensing, Risk Assessment

Title: Science Communication in the Age of Artificial Intelligence. Assessing the Swiss Science Communication Landscape
Abstract:
BACKGROUND AND RATIONALE
Generative AI (GenAI), epitomized by the rise of large language models (LLMs) such as GPT, will fundamentally change societal communication in many realms. This includes public science communication—communication from and about science-related issues to non-expert audiences, including its production, content, use and effects—which has risen in importance. The project maps how GenAI impacts and changes the science communication landscape in Switzerland—both currently and in the next years.

OBJECTIVES AND AIMS
The project focuses on current and future changes and their assessment by relevant players and stakeholders of science communication. In five work packages (WPs), it analyses individual scientists as well as communicators from scientific organizations and institutions of higher education (WP1), intermediaries such as science journalists and influencers (WP2), and citizens as important audiences of public science communication (WP3). For these groups, the project assesses their knowledge of and attitudes towards science communication and GenAI, their use of and interactions with GenAI, and the impact GenAI has on them. In addition, the project assesses broader socio-technical contexts of science communication and GenAI, including relevant public and sectoral debates and expert assessment and foresight on ethical, legal, regulatory, societal, and technological aspects of AI and their development (WP4). The concluding WP5 integrates the results across WPs and enables feedback from and exchanges with the science communication community in Switzerland.

DATA AND METHODS 
The project combines state-of-the-art social-scientific quantitative and qualitative methods with computational approaches to triangulate current and future changes in science communication related to GenAI. Given the rapid development in the field of AI, longitudinal designs are applied that go beyond cross-sectional snapshots to trace developments over time and understand them and their implications in a broader context. The project builds on extensive experiences of the project team in researching science communication and AI in Switzerland and beyond, an interdisciplinary advisory board of scholars and practitioners, an established network within science communication research, but also among professional science communicators and science journalists. 

RESULTS AND IMPACT 
In light of the profound changes GenAI will likely bring to science communication, the project would be of great value for the Swiss science landscape—at a time when GenAI is still in its formative phase, when guidelines and regulations are being developed and when the science communication community can still influence its development and use. The project would be of high academic relevance, filling a research gap by presenting findings on GenAI’s impact on science communication in Switzerland, adopting a holistic, integrative, and original approach by including scientists, professional science communicators, science intermediaries as well as audiences and by reconstructing changes over time. Findings would be presented in leading scholarly journals and national and international conferences. In addition, the project would have considerable societal and practical implications, providing different players in science communication with a basis for assessing and reflecting potentials and challenges of GenAI. For outreach, results will be published in sectoral and public-interest publications, presented at practitioner congresses, and be discussed in workshops with experts.

Title: Genomic innovations underlying arthropod success and diversity
Abstract:
The comparative approach has been a cornerstone of biological research for centuries. By observing the similarities and differences in species morphologies, life histories, and ecologies, we have refined our understanding of species relationships and learned about their biology and evolution. The ability to obtain genetic blueprints in the form of whole genome sequences from many different species means that the resolution of our observations is now increasingly enhanced and extended: to thousands of genes and billions of nucleotides. Comparisons that identify genetic and genomic similarities and differences have disentangled complex species relationships and advanced understanding of biological function and evolutionary processes at molecular, organismal, and ecosystem levels. The diversity of organisms on Earth today represents many varied evolutionary solutions to life’s challenges. Their common ancestry means that the comparative approach offers the opportunity to reconstruct the history of events that have resulted in currently observable genomic and biological diversity. The questions that this research project therefore seeks to address centre on: (i) what kinds of genomic changes or innovations lead to or facilitate which kinds of life history adaptations and species diversifications? And (ii) what are the rules or constraints governing how genomic evolution proceeds in a manner that maintains viability while allowing or even promoting the generation of biological diversity?

Studies exemplifying the state-of-the-art in the field of characterising the genomic basis of animal diversity show that complex gene repertoire evolutionary gain and loss dynamics likely provide the substrate from which diversity can emerge. Early radiations were accompanied by gene family innovations, conservation, and losses that likely underlie key functional shifts in multicellularity, development, homeostasis, and immunity. In younger lineages too, genetic and genomic changes can be associated with adaptations and diversifications such as enhanced immunity and trade-offs amongst vision, smell, and echolocation abilities of bats. As the most successful group of terrestrial animals, arthropods demonstrate a vast array of evolutionary adaptations to exploit ecological niches across many different ecosystems. This diversity makes their biology fascinating to study, as models for understanding fundamental biological processes, as well as because of the impacts they have on humans and their critical roles in maintaining a healthy planet. This, together with accumulating arthropod genomics resources, make them ideal for investigating how conservation or divergence and gains or losses of functional genomic elements give rise to the splendour of animal biology.

This project therefore aims to (i) apply computational comparative approaches to infer evolutionary histories of genomic elements and quantify genomic innovations across arthropods; (ii) apply machine learning and text mining methods to enhance gene- and organismal-level functional characterisations; (iii) use these quantifications and characterisations to learn the rules governing how genomic evolution proceeds and how it generates functional-biological diversity; and (iv) apply the same challenges (infections) to multiple species of Drosophila flies to test the functional implications of genomic innovations in terms of gene expression on a system-level biological response, i.e. immunity.

By addressing these aims, this project will establish a new set of quantifiable evolutionary features with which the field can characterise element evolutionary histories and genomic innovations in order to explore how these changes relate to observable phenotypic differences. The research will lead to advancements in the field on the one hand covering comparative genomics methodologies, and on the other providing insights into how evolution works and how biodiversity is generated and maintained. Results will demonstrate the importance and highlight the benefits of applying genomic technologies at increasingly complex scales to understand the diversity of life on Earth.
Keywords: arthropods, biodiversity, ecology, evolution, function, genomics

Title: Learning the activation mechanism in G protein coupled receptors from free energy calculations
Abstract:
Project summary
Background - G protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) are relevant drug targets, with approximately 26% of marketed drugs targeting this receptor family. These receptors exhibit intrinsic conformational dynamics that govern their activation, interaction with intracellular effector proteins, and subsequent signal transduction cascades. The activation mechanism of GPCRs unfolds over long timescales and involves intricate conformational changes, including the roto-translation motion of transmembrane helix 6 (TM6) and alterations in the contact maps of specific amino acids, referred to as microswitches. Obtaining a comprehensive understanding of GPCR activation mechanisms is highly sought after, as it would facilitate the design of biased signaling ligands. These ligands selectively activate specific microswitches and promote the coupling of the receptor with a particular effector protein, thereby preserving the desired pharmacological effect while minimizing adverse effects. While structural studies utilizing techniques like X-ray, Cryo-EM, and NMR have shed light on some aspects of GPCR dynamics, a comprehensive understanding of their activation mechanisms remains elusive. Atomistic simulations offer promise in elucidating GPCR conformational ensembles, although the large scale and extended timescales of GPCR conformational changes pose challenges for traditional simulation protocols like standard molecular dynamics.
The project - In the present project, we focus on adenosine receptors (ARs) and beta-adrenergic receptors (BARs), with the aim of developing a computational strategy to investigate receptor activation mechanisms at the atomic level. The study seeks to achieve three main objectives: 1) characterizing receptor functional states during activation, 2) understanding the effects of ligands on receptor states, and 3) examining receptor interactions with effector proteins.
Research strategy - The research is structured into six thematic Work Packages (WPs), each dedicated to a specific receptor subtype. Each WP encompasses tasks such as data collection, generation of conformational states, simulation of activation pathways, and binding simulations with effector proteins. The research approach entails studying receptors in both the apo and holo forms complexed with ligands exhibiting various activity profiles ranging from agonist to partial agonist and inverse agonist. Advanced free-energy calculations based on path collective variables metadynamics, along with machine learning algorithms like AlphaFold 2, are employed to enhance the sampling and prediction capabilities of receptors' conformational changes, leveraging existing structural data while overcoming dimensionality issues and limiting timescale.
Impact - The research outcomes will significantly advance our understanding of receptor functionality. Firstly, we will reveal whether the investigated receptors assume key functional states, including intermediate and pre-active states, during their transition from the inactive to the active state. Secondly, our inquiry will elucidate the influence of the diverse ligands on the receptor's conformational equilibrium and subsequent interaction with effector proteins. By comparing structures obtained for diverse receptors within the same receptor subgroup (i.e., ARs or BARs), and when bound to different ligands, we could provide a structural foundation for understanding selective receptor activation and ligand-biased signaling pathways. This information is essential for designing ligands with tailored pharmacological activity and has the potential to revolutionize drug design for neurological, cardiovascular, and inflammatory disorders in the case of ARs and BARs, with significant societal and economic impact.
Keywords: G protein coupled receptors, G protein-coupled receptors, adenosine receptors, beta-adrenergic receptors, computational modelling, drug design, free energy calculations, funnel metadynamics, ligand-biased signalling, molecular dynamics, structural biology

Title: THE CREATIVE APE: Investigating the evolutionary origins of creativity in chimpanzees and bonobos
Abstract: Creativity is central to our species’ extraordinarily rich behavioural variation, and to our ability to adapt, innovate, and thrive in a rapidly changing world. In many ways, humans are the ‘Creative Ape’. While clearly exceptional; whether human creativity uniquely defines us remains unknown. The Creative Ape Project investigates the evolution of creativity by examining its expression in our closest living relatives: chimpanzees and bonobos. By quantifying, for the first time, the creative capacities of wild non-human apes, we will establish whether and how humans are uniquely creative, along with the underlying drivers that shape creative expression across species. The project explores four interconnected topics: i) Making mavericks, ii) Funny guys and arty-types, iii) Lone ape geniuses, and iv) Creative ape economies. We employ a comprehensive approach that leverages long-term datasets, new field data, detailed manual video-coding, bespoke automated deep-learning models, and advanced modelling, to extract rich information on the ways in which apes solve problems in their daily lives. With a collective 200+ years of observations across sites and individuals, our project uses video and observational data across communities of wild chimpanzees and bonobos who live in the rainforests, mountains, and savannas of Africa. In sum, we will operationalize the study of creativity in non-human species, and shed light on the drivers and consequences of our own creativity.
Keywords: behavioural diversity, communication, creativity, great apes, tool use

Title: Deciphering Truth in a Maze of Misinformation: A Signed Network Approach
Abstract:
Recent debates, such as those on climate change, have pointed out that content shared on social media often lacks professional involvement, leading to the widespread dissemination of false information. Furthermore, online users tend to inhabit echo chambers that reinforce existing biases and disregard opposing viewpoints, making fact-checking and debunking less effective. This calls for the design of innovative tools to assist non-expert users in identifying unreliable sources. To this end, it is crucial to understand how individuals form their opinions and beliefs in an environment full of conflicting sources of information.

In the interdisciplinary research on misinformation and opinion formation, network science has emerged as a valuable framework. Traditional approaches focus on information and opinion propagation within a social network. However, they overlook the crucial aspect of how individuals independently form their opinions by browsing an external network of contrasting information sources and decide which sources to trust. 
The interconnection of sources is only partially addressed in a recent paper (M. Medo et al., Communications Physics, 2021), where the authors study the performance of a simple rule to detect unreliable nodes within a signed network of information sources (in the sign network, positive links indicate agreement between sources, while negative links indicate conflict). In the last part of my PhD, I have introduced and investigated a more efficient rule. Although these works offer valuable insights, they are stylized theoretical models that overlook the effects of both human biases and distortions induced by digital media recommendation algorithms.

For these reasons, in this project I aim to extend the framework introduced in the above mentioned works and answer the following question: Which heuristic strategies can help individuals with bounded rationality identify unreliable sources in complex information environments? Specifically, I will investigate various inference heuristic rules for the identification of low-credible nodes on static and growing signed networks of information sources (both artificial and real) through network science methodologies. Unlike the previous models, my approach will include more explicitly the cognitive limitations of human decision-makers and the biases induced by digital media recommendation algorithms.
Finally, in a supplementary task, I will leverage recent insights into the emergent behavior of Large Language Models (LLMs) to replace laboratory experiments, which fall outside my area of expertise, with experiments conducted using LLMs to test the frameworks defined in the previous tasks.

The project contributes to cutting-edge research on opinion formation, introducing a novel methodology that combines network inference with human cognitive capabilities, with the ultimate goal to improve our ability to combat misinformation and foster more informed decision-making. Moreover, the framework can be used (in a future stage) to design empirical research, including behavioral experiments, on how people learn from signed network data. As a result, this research has potential beyond the network modeling community, attracting policymakers and academics from various domains.

Title: Reimagining Artificial Intelligence – Towards Establishing a Sociological Conception of AI
Abstract:
Background: The current mechanisms that define and drive the development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) have been widely criticized for being tech-oriented and market-led instead of starting from societal needs and challenges. Subsequently, numerous and notable initiatives have been proposed that argue for proactive engagement of various areas of social science in determining how AI should reach our societies. In these proposals, AI projects are still conceptualized within the tech sector while the attempt is to bring knowledge created in social sciences and humanities to the position of informing AI adoption policies.

Broad objective: In this project, we seek to examine a radically different placement for social sciences in the realm of AI. Our broad objective is to capture the constituents and structure of a distinctively sociological conception of AI that is not subordinate to or dependent on the technological trends (e.g. deep learning, pervasive sensing), but rather is grounded solely in the imaginaries of what humans need AI to be. 

Specific aims: To the interest of clarity and to be able to achieve a concrete outcome, we confine the scope of this proposal to a specific domain that is highly influenced by the discourses of “smart agenda”– the domain of urbanism.  Moreover, we focus our research on the context of European cities. Therefore, the questions that this project seeks to answer are as follows: In the vision of European cities as urban sociologists would describe (through interviews with us or in their published discourses) what are the promoted ideas that can be associated with a form of non-human intelligence? For example, the notion of “knowledge-intensive” has been proposed in the context of smart urbanity in contrast to the current “technology-intensive” model (Mcfarlane and Söderstrom 2017). Can a collection of such notions and their interrelations create a (domain-specific) alternative “conception of AI”? Also, compared to the existing conception of AI what are the main dissimilarities and similarities?

Methods to be used: Methodologically, our project is composed of a data collection phase followed by coding and theory generation attempts. First, we conduct semi-structured interviews with 15-20 urban sociologists complemented with the published material the interviewees may refer to. Then we will analyze and annotate the collected material, using qualitative and quantitative methods of discourse analysis, but also we consider other methods such as designing a thought experiment and disseminating it as an online survey. In the last part, we extract common patterns in the annotated data and explore the possibilities for structuring an alternative conception, in discussion with some of the interviewees.

Expected results and their impact: The outcome will provide a new ground for discussions of AI projects in cities. We do not expect the creation of a new conception of AI lead to the creation of new type of AI devices and tools. Rather, by developing such a radically shifted standpoint the main impact is to achieve a distant sight, pronouncing what AI should bring to societies and making visible the nature and nuances of tensions between what can be beneficial to our societies and how AI is directed currently.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Urban Sociology

Title: Fast but not furious: rapid Bayesian inference in balanced cortical circuits
Abstract: Sensory perception is fast in human, and nonetheless almost Bayes-optimal. I propose a theoretical approach to this puzzle in which circuit mechanisms for fast dynamics (which I have explored as part of my PhD thesis) are related to the speed of perception, for wich the computational aspects are cast in the framework of probabilistic Bayesian inference. The host laboratory has recently collected experimental evidence for a sampling-based representation of posterior uncertainty in the cortex. We are thus combining methods from machine learning and statistical physics to understand how inference via sampling can be performed through the collective dynamics of large ensembles of neurons. The project has expected outcomes both in the field of machine learning and in neuroscience.
Keywords: Bayesian inference, cortical dynamics, sensory perception, synaptic plasticity

Title: Tackling domain shifts in pediatric neuroimaging: bridging advanced computational MR techniques and clinical practice
Abstract:
The successful combination of tailored image processing methods and non-invasive magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has led to a paradigm shift in pediatric healthcare and neurosciences. Notwithstanding technical challenges, tailored acquisition and image analysis techniques allow to obtain high-quality images of the brain anatomy in fetus and newborn populations. Pediatric neuroimaging standards in current clinical care rely on 1.5 and 3 Tesla MRI systems. However, access to this powerful imaging tool at a global scale is very limited or nonexistent.

Today, machine learning methods applied to brain MRI enable the extraction of imaging biomarkers of the early brain maturation and their association to later cognitive-psychological conditions and behavioral changes. Assessing the impact of brain development in fetal, preterm and newborn populations later in life is however limited by the domain shift between pre- and postnatal imaging techniques. In fact, the important methodological differences in acquisition schemes and processing pipelines in these populations strongly bias the comparison of the extracted biomarkers. Furthermore, at the global level, existing neurodevelopmental studies are also skewed by excluding a wide part of the population due to limited access to MRI, thus narrowing our understanding of brain development in normal conditions as well as in situations of malnutrition, infection or stress, which are predominant in middle- and low-income countries.
The recent push for low-field MRI could be the game changer towards a global dissemination of paediatric neuroimaging. Low-field MR scanners enable a more cost-effective and widely accessible MRI technology, particularly in developing countries with large pediatric populations. However, there is an important distributional shift arising from low magnetic field strength due to the associated reduction in signal-to-noise ratio and image spatial resolution.

This research project tackles the two aforementioned important domain shifts in pediatric MRI linked to the gap be- tween magnetic field strengths and populations. Our first research line is dedicated to developing new super-resolution reconstruction and segmentation methods for T2-weighted imaging at low field (0.55 Tesla). To do so, we will leverage information from high-magnetic field strengths by the inclusion of deep image priors and learned regularisation into an inverse problem formulation. Furthermore, we will adapt existing brain tissue segmentation models via domain adaptation strategies which exploit synthetic MR images from numerical simulations. Our second research line aims at addressing the population gap by developing a unified motion-robust high-resolution technique for T1 and T2 mapping of the fetal and newborn brain. A major contribution will be the development of a new self-supervised super-resolution strategy that will enable the estimation of relaxation times at fine scale using clinically relevant sequences and acquisition times. This project will be complemented by three feasibility studies for the clinical integration of these novel methods at high and low field strengths. Finally, a highly timely and relevant outcome will be the implementation of a comprehen- sive numerical simulation framework for pediatric brain MR imaging, leading to the first-front benchmark dataset for the development and validation of image analysis methods, both for low–field and clinical MR systems. At the end of the project, we will provide a unified and mathematically sound image processing framework for the longitudinal assessment of early brain development, both at low and clinical magnetic field strengths.

Title: Digital Tools For Mental Health: Closing The Loop For Personalized Treatment
Abstract:
Currently, the diagnosis of mental health disorders relies on subjective clinical evaluations performed using structured clinical interviews. It is difficult to capture disease progression in a rigorous when relying on clinic visits or assessments that are infrequent, incomplete, out of the context of a patient’s home environment, and might be biased by patients’ symptom status. The absence of objective metrics represent a limitation also for the improvement of the diagnostic process and the choice of personalized treatments. Many efforts have been made to identify markers representative of treatment response, but treating mental illness still remains a trial and error approach. The proliferation of mobile devices and wearable sensors for behavioral and physiological monitoring could help address these challenges. Digital sensors can be used to continuously and unobtrusively identify relevant digital biomarkers and objectively assess disease severity and progression, providing a feedback for treatment personalization. The adoption of digital tools can improve the patients’ quality of life and have a significant impact on making mental health care processes and decisions more efficient and cost-effective. Further research is needed to determine the effectiveness of digital tools applied to mental health and support their actual implementation in clinical routine. 
Therefore, with this project I aim to address technical and knowledge gaps in mental illness treatment and fundamentally advance the field by: (Objective 1) identifying digital biomarkers for unobtrusive and continuous characterization of the course of mental health disorders; (Objective 2) developing methods for modelling mental health disease progression and response to therapy; (Objective 3) understanding to what extent outcomes can be improved by using a closed-loop personalized treatment. Specifically, I will address these aims by developing: A multimodal monitoring pipeline: a flexible framework for collecting and exploiting multimodal data, detect patterns that define the patient’s status, and model the progression of the disease. A closed-loop dose/treatment adjustment framework based on digital biomarkers that enable automatic refinement of the therapy. The framework will include a simulator (‘digital twin’) for developing and testing the treatment personalization before its actual implementation.
The proposed framework will be tested into translational and clinical research. Depression is the leading cause of disease burden worldwide, and the leading burden of health amongst young people. Within this project, we will identify and validate digital biomarkers of diagnostic status and changes in multiple variables (e.g., sleep, activity, heart rate variability) directly related to depression severity. Furthermore, we will close the loop for treatment personalization using the identified set of digital biomarkers as feedback. Specifically, together with our collaborator, we will investigate the feasibility of personalized slow-wave-sleep modulation therapy, a promising solution for treating and alleviating depression symptoms. This will enable us to validate the developed pipeline and gain a better understanding of the dose/treatment response model for depression and slow-wave modulation. 
The development of the proposed framework to detect changes at the within-individual level will enable objective, shorter and less expensive evaluations. It represents the cornerstone of evidence-based methods for personalized mental health treatments. The proposed project is the foundational piece of my vision to make mental health care more accessible and efficient, and improve the lives of people that everyday deal with these debilitating conditions.

Title: Combining Image and Graph-based Neural Networks for Handwriting Recognition
Abstract: This proposal aims to develop models, data synthesis and training methods for document analysis tasks such as classification or retrieval that allow the application of deep learning models without the need for manually created annotations. Especially, considering historic documents or low resource language the heavy demand for labeled data hinders the application of learning-based methodology. A key factor in the proposed project is the exploitation of the structural nature of handwriting. In addition to the visual appearance, the underlying structure can represented as a graph. Recent developments in geometric deep learning allow to integrate this structural element on the level of model design. Additionally, explicitly modeling the geometric component serves as a form of regularization, increasing adaptability and the generalization capabilities of the developed models. Training of a model combining visual and geometrical information is then performed with as little supervision as possible. Therefore, data synthesis approaches will be developed that also include structural representations. This project extends the state-of-the art in deep learning based document analysis by developing methods that explicitly model the geometric components of handwriting. The resulting reduction of training data demand opens up a diverse set of application areas and tasks.
Keywords: Computer Vision, Document Analysis, Handwriting Recognition, Pattern Recognition

Title: Creating to perceive: The role of mental imagery in visual object recognition and categorisation
Abstract:
Background and rationale. Visual object recognition and categorisation determine how we interact with, and reason about the world. Successful recognition and categorisation require robust representations. Humans acquire such representations from remarkably little external input. The question of how this is accomplished is far from being solved. Whereas perceptually induced experience supports the acquisition of robust representations, it is unexplored whether this is also true for the internal creation of visual experience.

Overall objective. The goal of this project is to provide insights into how humans acquire robust representations from sparse external data.

Specific aims. I aim to develop a novel approach that permits the precise tracking of experience-dependent representational shifts across the course of learning novel representations. This approach is applied to investigate whether internally created visual experience enhances the acquisition of robust representations, and thus might explain
the remarkable data efficiency of the visual system.

Methods. In a learning task, participants are shown images of
novel objects and are trained to classify them. Thereby, changes in perceived similarity among objects are tracked across learning. Using machine learning-based methods, it is inferred how internal representations change as a function of accumulated experience. These representational shifts and classification performance are compared among groups of
participants who either learn only from physically presented images, or additionally engage in a mental imagery task to internally create supplementary visual experiences.

Expected results. Subjects endowed with mental imagery are predicted to learn robust representations from less externally presented stimuli than subjects who are not. Learning-
dependent changes in perceived similarity and the associated representational shifts are expected to be connected to gains in classification performance and to be similar regardless whether experience is accumulated perceptually
or internally.

Impact. This research will provide insights into how internally created visual experience can explain how humans acquire robust representations from little external input. This may not only reshape how we think about the visual system and the functions of mental imagery but also lead to a better understanding of learning-dependent representational changes, thereby providing benefits across the fields of cognitive science, computer science, as well as in clinical cases where object recognition is impaired.
Keywords: imagination, internal generative processes, mental imagery, mental representations, multidimensional scaling, object recognition, ordinal embeddings, perceptual categorisation

Title: Vector Leptoquarks as Portals to Dark Matter and Bayesian Modeling for Jet Clustering
Abstract:
In pursue of a complete theory of nature, particle physicists have long utilized the powerful technique of model building. In the traditional sense, model building concerns the construction of quantum field theories (QFTs) in the Lagrangian formalism suitable to explain current experimental data and provide testable predictions in the near future. Since at present, the predominant framework of particle physics is the Standard Model (SM), these new QFTs, referred to as Beyond the Standard Model (BSM) theories, are designed explicitly to address phenomena that are left unexplained within its scope. For instance, pivotal themes of this project are two major mysteries of Modern Physics : the presence of Dark Matter (DM) and the flavour puzzle. In particular, deviations from the SM predictions in certain flavour-dependend processes involving B-mesons, the so-called B-Physics anomalies, have reinstigated interest in the latter.
BSM theories propose the existence of new particles and interaction mediators, many of which could be probed by direct production at particle colliders and subsequent reconstruction of their decay products at particle detectors. One of the most important detector-level object is a highly collimated spray of hadrons, known as jet. The identification of jets is the goal of the jet clustering algorithms, which nowadays rely on sequential recombination schemes with hard clustering, i.e. there is a unique assignment of each particle to a jet of fixed radius. However, certain limitations of these schemes have motivated the use of probability theory and unsupervised Machine Learning (ML) well known in the computer science community in the design of search strategies for anomaly detection. Consequently, a novel form of model building is emerging in jet physics, which instead of Lagrangians employs probability distributions. 
The objectives of my project are twofold. First, the connection between dark matter and new flavorful interactions will be explored within the context of ultraviolet (UV) complete frameworks such as the ‘4321’ models, which have recently attracted a great deal of attention in the theory community. These models feature vector leptoquarks (LQs) at the TeV-scale that can at the same time act as mediators of the new interactions (and potentially explain the B-Physics anomalies) and as DM portals. Secondly, I will use Bayesian probabilistic modeling and state-of-the-art ML techniques in order to implement a jet clustering algorithm that is characterized by unprecedented flexibility in modeling overlapping regions at the detector and jets of variable size. Additionally, this algorithm aspires not only to complement the existing hard clustering schemes but also to provide an underlying statistical interpretation of them, which would be of major theoretical value. Ultimately, my results will facilitate the hunt for New Physics (NP) at the Large Hadron Collier (LHC) at CERN, directly benefiting the experimental collaborations by motivating the parameter space of dedicated LQ and DM searches and providing a new versatile tool for jet clustering.
Keywords: B-Physics Anomalies, BSM Physics, Bayesian Statistics, Clustering Algorithms, Dark Matter, Flavor Physics, High Energy Physics, Jet Physics, LHC searches, Machine Learning, Model Building

Title: OrChemSTAR – Organic Chemistry Science Teaching and Learning with Augmented Reality
Abstract:
Chemical compounds can be described with different chemical formulae (e.g., molecular formulae, condensed formulae, skeletal formulae, like Kekulé and Lewis structures, and perspective drawings, like Newman, Sawhorse, Fischer and Haworth projections). The different representations each focus on different aspects of chemical bonds. Reading the different representations, selecting a mode of representation appropriate for a particular purpose, and writing the chemical formulas require appropriate subject-specific skills from learners. While experts can mentally translate between different modes of representation, novices first have to build up appropriate mental representations and learn the design rules of the different modes of representation. This project investigates how learners can be supported by an augmented reality application that displays chemical compounds in multiple representations directly in the learning material in three dimensions, provides adaptive feedback to chemical formulas written or drawn by learners themselves, and guides adaptively through individualized learning paths.
To carry out this research project, an AR app (OrChemSTAR) will be developed with several features to support learners: 
1. Chemical formulas in printed or handwritten texts will be recognized after being captured by the camera, and multiple representations of the chemical compounds will be overlaid on the text at appropriate locations to support formula reading. Learning aids are provided for selected chemical compounds and any known learning difficulties. 
2. The app should also recognize typical errors in hand-drawn chemical formulas. For this purpose, drawings from learners are collected for selected compounds. With these drawings, an artificial intelligence module will be trained to recognize hand-drawn structural formulas. 
3. The app will have a tutor mode to support learners in learning a representation method and writing/drawing formulas by adaptively designing individual learning paths.
The app developed for this research project will be used to investigate (in laboratory and field experiments) the effectiveness of the adaptive assistance provided for learning modes of representation of chemical compounds as well as selected related organic chemistry content (esp. stereochemistry). In a mixed-methods pre-post design, learners are divided into three groups (EG1 – adaptive learning: AR adapts to learners and offers individual learning paths; EG2 - technical adaptivity: AR adapts to context and content; CG - no adaptivity: AR only) are interviewed about learning with the app and knowledge acquisition is measured. As a control, mental rotation ability is assessed in the pre-test, cognitive load and intrinsic motivation in the post-test, and attitudes towards augmented reality applications in particular and digital technologies in general at both times. Personal experiences during learning with the app and feedback on the app will also be surveyed. Additionally, participants in the lab study will be interviewed in more depth. Eye-tracking studies will be conducted to gain deeper insights into cognitive information processing during learning with the app.
Keywords: Artifical intelligence, Augmented reality, Chemical formulae, Chemistry education, Deep machine learning, Empirical pilot study, Eye-tracking research, Neural networks
