Title: A new method for charm tagging to probe the coupling of the Higgs boson to charm quarks
Abstract:
Eight years ago, the discovery of a new fundamental particle, the Higgs boson, was announced by the ATLAS and CMS collaborations at CERN. Since then, a great effort has been dedicated to measuring the Higgs boson decays to vector bosons, heavy quarks and leptons. While the most frequent decay modes have now been successfully observed, interactions with the light quark sector remain widely unexplored. There is still no experimental evidence that the Higgs boson couples to the 1st and 2nd generation of fermions. The next most promising candidate in the quark sector is the decay to a pair of charm quark and antiquark. 

In the ATLAS experiment, the reconstruction of charm quark signatures remains a challenge. Two distinct and parallel methodologies have been explored so far: the inclusive and exclusive reconstructions. Inclusive reconstructions, also known as charm tagging, exploit low level information related to the lifetime of hadrons in order to extract the flavour of the quark. Exclusive reconstructions focus on the precise identification of one or multiple subprocesses where a charm quark hadronised into a meson or a baryon decaying in well-defined final state particles measured in the detector. 

This project aims at developing and improving charm-tagging by using exclusively reconstructed charged $D$-meson signatures initiated by charm quarks in the ATLAS detector. The specific processes investigated here are the $D^{+}\rightarrow K^-\pi^+\pi^+$ and $D^{*+}\rightarrow D^0\pi^+ \rightarrow (K^-\pi^+)\pi^+$ decays. Starting from the event selection developed in Run 1, I will implement a feed-forward neural network to exploit optimally the various correlations of the input variables and create an exclusive $D$-meson tagger. One interesting possibility offered by neural networks is to train the multivariate algorithm to simultaneously disentangle between $D^+$, $D^{*+}$ and other hadrons by building multiple output nodes. In order to improve the reconstruction efficiency, additional information is required as input to the neural network. One possibility is to exploit the low track multiplicity of typical $D$-meson events and add kinematic variables (transverse momentum $p_T$, pseudo-rapidity $\eta$, angular displacement $\phi$, ...) to the neural network. In addition, further improvements can be achieved by using more sophisticated classes of algorithms such as recurrent neural networks. Extending the tagger to identify more decays of the $D$-meson will be studied as well.

The main objective of this project is to improve the reconstruction of charm quarks signatures, crucial for the measurement of the $H\rightarrow c\bar{c}$ process. By applying exclusive and inclusive reconstructions strategies on the same data set, it becomes possible to study the overlap between the two methodologies as well as the possibilities to improve both techniques.
Keywords: ATLAS, CERN, Charm quarks, Charm tagging, D-meson, Flavour tagging, Higgs, Machine Learning, Neural Networks, Particle physics

Title: Information-theoretic content identification in large-scale databases
Abstract:
This project is the continuation and extension of SNF project No 200021--119770 "Secure unclonable identification/authentication codes based on natural randomness'' where we have addressed a number of theoretical and practical aspects of physical object security based on microstructure images. The main challenge of the precedent project was to develop a practical framework for the characterization of physical objects based on their unique unclonable features as well as to establish theoretical fundamentals of reliable and secure identification and authentication. Such a unique characterization was discovered for most materials including paper, cartoon, metal and plastic. The obtained microstructure images served as input to the robust identification and authentication procedures allowing either to deduce the unique identification index or to decide about the object's authenticity. Therefore, both practical results have been obtained and theoretical limits have been derived demonstrating the huge potential of this technology. The results of this project have been published in a journal paper and presented at many reputable international conferences with an acceptance rate below 30\%. This success makes it also possible to extend the achieved results to other types of multimedia, biometrics and bioinformatics applications where similar problems are under active investigation and even to foster new applications.

At the same time one has to admit that to achieve these theoretical limits practically and explore this huge potential one needs to address a number of issues related to large--scale applications. In these applications the number of objects, items or contents can be in the order of hundred millions or billions. Being confirmed theoretically under asymptotic assumptions (infinite length or size, unbounded complexity and memory, etc.), one faces a number of  practical constraints that should be considered accordingly within the theoretical analysis. This concerns the theoretical investigation of identification performance under complexity and memory storage constraints as well as the proper handling of emerging security and privacy issues.

It is remarkable that the main bottleneck of identification systems related to accurate and reliable extraction of a candidate set of indices to be scored can be efficiently solved using a framework of digital fingerprinting (a.k.a. robust perceptual hashing or short binary codes) that recently attracted more and more attention. This makes the identification mechanism universal, scalable and adaptive to any type and size of content and computational architectures including distributed ones. Unfortunately, most of the methods, which are based on the above framework, are lacking a thorough theoretical analysis with respect to the achievable upper limits and have been proposed independently in different domains using different performance measures and terminology, which complicates fair comparison and benchmarking. Thus, the task of identifying, introducing and applying these fundamental common principles is of great theoretical and practical importance. In this context, the goal of the present proposal is to extend and further develop a new unified information-theoretic framework for efficient content identification in large-scale databases. This goal will be achieved based on novel interpretation and practical development of the concept of bit reliability that we would like to propose and explore in this project.

As detailed in the proposal, the proposed theoretical framework relies on the study of information theory, projection transforms and embedding, coding theory, cryptography and machine learning. It should provide not only  a unified theoretical basis for problems that are currently treated independently but also open doors to many practical applications.

In the scope of this proposal, the following subjects will be investigated:
(A) Information-theoretic performance analysis of the identification problem;
(B) Information-theoretic analysis of identification based on asymmetric mapping;
(C) Practical complexity-constrained identification systems attaining theoretical performance limits.
Keywords: complexity, cryptography, identification, information theory, machine learning, memory storage, privacy, projection, reliable bit extraction, security

Title: Precision measurement of the quark-coupling strength Vub
Abstract:
The Standard Model of Particle Physics is the theory of the elementary particles and their interactions. It has proven extremely successful in explaining observations in a broad energy range, as well as predicting the existence of new particles and interaction properties that have later been experimentally verified. The Higgs boson, predicted in 1964 [1], and discovered at the Large Hadron Collider in 2012 [2, 3], is one of the most recent confirmations of the Standard Model. Despite its success, the Standard Model is widely recognized as being incomplete, as it fails to explain several phenomena including gravity, dark matter, and the matter-antimatter asymmetry in the universe. For this reason, a lot of effort in particle physics goes into testing the predictions of the Standard Model to search for hints of new physics phenomena.

Precise determinations of Standard Model parameters are needed to reach a sensitivity to new physics effects. This includes the precise determination of the unitary Cabibbo–Kobayashi–Maskawa (CKM) matrix [4, 5], which describes the flavor-changing weak interactions in the quark sector. The least known CKM matrix element is |Vub|, which governs the b to u quark transition. Its most precise determination [6] is based on the exclusive semileptonic B -> pi l nu decay measured at the Belle and BaBar experiments [7]. A significant uncertainty originates from the limited precision of the hadronic form-factor predictions [6]. Thus, selecting a decay channel with a smaller uncertainty on these predictions can lead to a more precise determination of |Vub|. A good candidate is the exclusive semileptonic decay Bs -> K- mu+ nu, where the uncertainty of the hadronic form-factor predictions are significantly smaller, as demonstrated in Ref. [8]. Thus, this decay channel has the potential of providing the most precise |Vub| determination. While it is not possible to use this channel at the B factories, the decay Bs -> K- mu+ nu has already been used by the LHCb experiment to obtain |Vub| [9], however due to limited signal statistics and not exploiting the information of the differential branching fraction, its full potential of providing the most precise determination of |Vub| has not yet been achieved.  

In this project, the full Run 2 data sample collected by the LHCb experiment has been exploited to pursue a high precision determination of |Vub| based on the Bs -> K- mu+ nu decay. With a signal yield that is five to six times higher than that of the previous LHCb measurement, the branching fraction of the signal can be measured in several bins of the dilepton invariant mass squared (q^2). By fitting the measured differential branching fraction over the full q^2 region, precise determinations of |Vub|, as well as the hadronic form factor parameters, can be obtained. During the course of the project, several key analysis tools were developed, including a framework for modelling particle misidentification backgrounds and dedicated tools for the unfolding of the reconstructed q^2 distribution. The analysis has reached an advanced stage and represents an important step towards achieving the most precise |Vub| determination using this decay channel.

In addition to the Bs -> K- mu+ nu analysis, this project also included the development of LHCb software tools required for processing and analysing data collected during Run 3. In particular, this work focused on the development and deployment of an Inclusive Multivariate Isolation tool designed to reduce the size of events stored for offline analysis while preserving the information relevant for semileptonic decays. The tool has been integrated into the Run 3 data processing framework and is now used in the semileptonic data selection of the LHCb experiment. By significantly reducing the number of unrelated tracks stored in each event, it enables efficient data taking under the increased luminosity conditions of Run 3 while maintaining the high quality data required for physics analyses.

Title: Sensing Knowledge Emotions in Multimedia Discovery
Abstract:
Understanding why multimedia users prefer one image or video over another is key to enhancing user experience. Multimedia researchers have focused on user interaction and their explicit feedback to build content delivery systems, e.g., YouTube, Netflix. Recently, researchers and major industrial players have discovered the importance of emotions in the way content is perceived by the audience. In the last decade, the technologies of emotion detection and emotional analyses have been extensively developed, to the point of commercialization, e.g., Affectiva Affdex and GFK Verein EmoScan. However, emotion recognition has mainly been focused on basic emotions which are not necessarily useful in practical applications, e.g., we rarely experience disgust while listening to music. In this project, we target detecting knowledge emotions that are often experienced while watching or browsing multimedia content, namely interest, boredom, surprise and confusion. Despite their importance, tools to recognize knowledge emotions in response to multimedia have not been reported in the literature.
Psychologists have identified a set of facial expressions, physiological changes and head movements which are associated with knowledge emotions. For example, speech prosody features may be used to recognize interest in both group conversations and single speaker settings. The proposed research aims at studying and detecting knowledge emotions in response to multimedia considering users' personality and appraisal process. The studies on appraisal mechanisms of interest have shown that different people show interest in different items depending on their personality and background.  
This project will address the following research questions: (i) What are the most important appraisals that result in knowledge emotions and what is the effect of the user's personality on them? (ii)  Which spontaneous responses and expressions are related to knowledge emotions? Which machine learning techniques should be extended for such problems? (iii) Can automatic machine recognition of knowledge emotions be achieved?  If so, how accurately? (iv) Can recognizing knowledge emotions and users' intentions contribute to users' satisfaction? 
The project is timely in view of the very significant research and commercial interest in multimedia information retrieval and affective computing, at Swiss and international levels. This project will benefit from the close collaboration with the Swiss National Center of Competence in Research (NCCR) on Affective Sciences in Geneva.
Keywords: affective computing, boredom, emotion recognition, facial expressions, interest, knowledge emotions, multimedia browsing, multimedia retrieval

Title: Isogeometric Analysis for Vision
Abstract:
Computer Vision makes possible the analysis 3-dimensional scenes from physical measurements. The spectrum, scale and quality of these measurements are constantly expanding, introducing new research problems that require new solutions. Inverse problems provide a mathematical framework to formalize many of these applications, like reconstructing a 3D surface from 2D images, segmenting a video into the objects of a scene or estimating their motion.

Inverse problems in vision are usually ill-posed and must be solved by turning away from strict solutions and looking for ones that are optimal with respect to an application-dependent cost. This leads to optimization problems where the minimization variable is a smooth function and the objective functional includes regularization. Common regularizers are designed for functions over the image plane and are meaningless when extracting information of the scene, as the natural domain of the solution is the scene itself. These techniques, however, are popular in vision because they leads to minimization problems easy to solve, while its alternative requires doing analysis over complex domains. 

This project proposes to solve such problems with isogeometric analysis, an analysis technique based on finite elements that has been recently developed in computational science. Isogeometric analysis offers 3 advantages to inverse problems in vision: adaptation of the solution space to complex domains; control of the smoothness of the solution at each point; and efficient multiscale analysis. Despite these benefits, isogeometric analysis is still unexplored in vision because its numerical techniques exclude common penalties used to reconstruct sharp corners, obtain sparse decompositions or be robust to outliers. Our isogeometric framework will overcome these limitations by combining the spline representations of isogeometric analysis with advanced optimization techniques developed in convex analsysis.
Keywords: Computer Vision, Imaging, Isogeometric Analysis

Title: SPARCLING: Large-scale Annotation and Alignment of Parallel Corpora for the Investigation of Linguistic Variation
Abstract:
Translated documents in multiple languages (here: parallel corpora) are valuable resources for various tasks in natural language processing and linguistic research. Parallel corpora are useful for tasks as diverse as word sense disambiguation, machine translation and contrastive corpus linguistics. The usefulness of these resources for contrastive linguistics, in particular, has increased tremendously with the possibility to automatically align the texts on the word and phrase level.
We work on the automatic annotation and alignment of large parallel corpora from Europarl (the transcriptions of the debates in the European Parliament), with a focus on English and German, but moving beyond these to include French, Finnish, Italian, Polish, and Spanish. Linguistic annotations include Part-of-Speech tags, lemmas and syntactic dependencies. The early languages of the EU (DE, EN, ES, FR, IT) each have around 50 million words in the corpus, Finnish and Polish somewhat less. In sum, this amounts to several 100 million entries in the database. To this, we have to add the cross-lingual alignment links which number in the same order of magnitude.
This amount of data poses challenges for storage and efficient retrieval. We work on a powerful query language that will allow a linguist to access and view the linguistic data in a user-friendly fashion. 
However, the massive parallelism of the texts also offers interesting options for improving the annotation and alignments. It is thus one of the main aims of our project to investigate the advantages of multi-parallel corpora for improving the quality of word alignments.
On the linguistic side we will use a data-driven approach to modelling variation in English article use. Previously, it has been difficult to retrieve noun phrases without an article (so-called `bare NPs') from electronic corpora. Since German makes use of articles to a greater extent than English, retrieving NPs with an article in German but no article or other determiner in the aligned English NPs allows us to systematically target bare NPs in English. A similar approach is possible for the language pairs Italian-English and Spanish-English, since the Romance languages, again, make greater use of articles than English. For languages without articles - such as Polish - using English as a starting point and retrieving English NPs with articles will allow modelling the strategies that these languages employ to mark syntactic categories such as `definiteness' and `indefiniteness'. Finally, since our parallel corpus contains both original texts and translations, we will make use of the materials to study the impact of typological differences (i.e. article vs. no-article language) in language contact. The focus for this will be on the language pair English-Finnish.
This is a proposal for a one-year extension of our SNF project ``Large-Scale Annotation and Alignment of PARallel Corpora for the Investigation of LINGuistic Variation" which started in the fall 2013 and will end in 2016. The PhD students in this project have made remarkable progress. Additional supervision and support from Computational Linguist Simon Clematide played an important role in this. We now ask for funding for a 4th year so that we can ensure the sustainability of the corpus query system and allow the PhD students to conclude their research and finish their theses.
Keywords: Articles, Corpus Linguistics, Linguistic Variation, Parallel Concordancing, Parallel Corpora

Title: Neural mechanisms of Adaptive speech planning in natural conversation
Abstract:
Background: Human communication relies on the brain’s remarkable ability to seamlessly coordinate speech planning and
execution during natural conversations. Recent studies have used idealized and controlled conversations, showing involvement
of distinct networks for speech planning, articulation and monitoring. However, despite significant progress in understanding
isolated aspects of speech planning, little is known about how these networks dynamically interact in real-world conversational
contexts. Natural conversations require continuous adaptation to various factors, such as individual habits and familiarity with
interlocutors, geo-linguistic and sociolinguistic specificity, or interaction context. These adaptations manifest as hesitations,
repetitions, pauses, and backchannels like “yeah” or “uh-huh”. Research into these adaptive mechanisms has been hindered
by two main challenges: (1) the scarcity of high-resolution neural recordings during uncontrolled natural conversations, and
(2) the limitations of traditional computational models trained on idealized conversation scenarios in capturing the complex,
relational, and temporal dynamics of brain activity during natural speech. Yet, natural conversations can reveal crucial insights
into the inner workings of the speech planing and production systems. To address these gaps, advanced neurophysiological
recording techniques combined with appropriate computational models are essential to fully understand speech planning and its
adaptability.
Objective and approach: This project aims to investigate how the speech planning network dynamically interacts with the
articulation and monitoring networks to facilitate adaptive planning in natural conversations. The underlying hypothesis is
that adaptive speech planning is mediated by distinct neural signatures and network interactions that differentiate adaptive from
normal speech sequences. I hypothesize that conversation segments with adaptive features (e.g., hesitations, pauses, repetitions,
speech rate modifications, and prosodic adjustments) exhibit unique temporal and network connectivity patterns compared to
normal speech segments. Specifically, I propose a novel feedback mechanism in which the monitoring network directly influences
the planning network through rapid, phase-locked oscillatory coupling in the theta band (4–8 Hz), with the strength and
latency of this coupling predicting the speaker’s capacity to implement timely corrective adjustments, thereby affecting turn-taking

Title: Integrating literature mining of taxonomy and traits with genomics to transform species richness and distribution modelling applied to biodiversity assessments
Abstract: This interdisciplinary research project aims to harness complementary expertise in biodiversity genomics and text mining to revolutionise how data are used for species and habitat protection and restoration by delivering an open-access knowledge graph and modelling portal that links text-mined traits, genomic indicators, and environmental layers for transparent, reusable analyses. Specifically, it seeks to enhance the informativeness and precision of (1) spatiotemporal species distribution mapping and (2) species taxonomic richness modelling by integrating organismal traits extracted from literature using text mining with genomic data analyses and systematically benchmarking these integrative models against occurrence-only baselines. Current species distribution modelling is increasingly adopting integrative approaches that incorporate species traits and genomic data. However, progress is hindered by challenges in accessing these data, a gap we address through AI-assisted literature digitisation, named-entity recognition/normalisation, relationship extraction, and semi-automated expert curation that standardise heterogeneous sources into machine-actionable formats. Additionally, uncertainties in taxonomic richness and the presence of undescribed “dark taxa” create further obstacles that we will explicitly propagate into model predictions through taxonomic concept reconciliation and uncertainty quantification. Despite the importance of characterising past, present, and future species distributions and richness, applying the state-of-the-art in biogeographical species modelling approaches remains constrained by the heterogeneity and paucity of available data. We will mobilise relevant “grey datasets” and public genomic repositories to harmonise traits and genetics for modelling at scale. Addressing these issues requires advancing state-of-the-art text mining techniques for biodiversity and taxonomic literature while integrating them with genomic analyses for species and population differentiation and transferring these workflows through targeted training for Swiss partners and agencies to ensure long-term capacity. The geographic and taxonomic scope of the project is designed to address the research questions, with a focus on birds, bats, and fish of Switzerland, and on butterflies, bumblebees, and amphipods of Europe. They represent groups of species with different levels of taxonomic resolution (well-defined, cryptic species, hidden dark taxa), a spectrum of variable levels of accumulated knowledge that can be mined from the literature, existing trait-collection efforts of variable comprehensiveness that provide baselines against which to evaluate literature-mining trait-extraction efforts, and for which genomic data are increasingly available for many species within these groups. These case studies will also enable forward-time simulations to evaluate demographic and adaptive dynamics under climate and land-use scenarios. Integrating morphological, genomic, and ecological data within a unified framework offers significant benefits for biodiversity science, applied conservation, and academic research, yielding decision-ready maps, reproducible pipelines, and stakeholder-co-designed tools to support conservation planning in Switzerland and across Europe.

Title: Bandits on Networks: Regret, Optimization and Equilibria
Abstract:
Bandit problems have been extensively studied in machine learning as simple yet flexible models that capture the problem of repeated decision making with limited information (see [BCB12] for a survey). In multi-armed bandit problems, an agent is asked to repeatedly select one of many actions (arms) for which the agent receives an unknown reward; solutions require a careful tradeoff between exploration (gaining new knowledge about the rewards) and exploitation (using current knowledge to maximize rewards). This simple model has found modern applications in a many domains including e-Commerce (e.g., online advertising [CKRU08, LPP10]), Networking (e.g., adaptive routing [AK04]), Operations Research (e.g., scheduling and inventory systems [MT08]), Social Science (e.g., clinical trials and experimental design [HS91, OHS01]), Ecology [SRL13] and Finance (e.g., portfolio selection [GS11a, SLM12]).

In the classical setting, at each time step the agent only observes the reward for the action which she selects. However, in realistic settings, individuals often have access to additional side information, e.g., via their social or economic network, which they can use to make enhanced decisions. This phenomenon has been observed in the Social and Natural Sciences, for example, in the acquisition of consumer products by individuals, the adoption of new technologies in agriculture, the prevalence and spread of corruption, and in the behavior of animals such as squirrels (see, e.g., [LBG48, KL55, ZAA07, Yoo12, San06, ASC12]). Hence, a natural question arises: How should an agent incorporate side observations in order to maximize their rewards, and how much improvement can such information bring? Indeed, such questions have inspired much recent and exciting work in Computer Science and Economics due to the realistic and relevant framework they address.

The central goal of this project is to integrate the model of selfish agents in a network with the concept of reward maximization; both form key components of important settings and we believe that only in conjunction can relevant solutions be found. Specifically, we plan to consider bandit models where selfish agents playing against a multi-armed bandit are connected by a network; each agent can observe the actions and rewards of their neighbors in addition to their own, and each strives to maximize their own rewards. In summary, this project aims to lay the foundations for understanding selfish behavior in bandit optimization for networked agents, bridging gaps in an increasingly important problem from both theoretical and practical perspectives. It requires a unique synthesis of concepts from algorithms, game theory and networks, and has the promise to push forward state of the art techniques for the ubiquitous problem of adaptive decision making for networked agents.
Keywords: Game Theory, Learning, Multi-Armed Bandits, Networks

Title: Predicting individual cognitive performance in healthy aging subjects from multimodal brain imaging connectivity data
Abstract:
Healthy aging is accompanied by changes in brain structure and function, as well as by changes in cognitive performance. As this cognitive decline represents a severe burden for the afflicted individuals, understanding the basic relationship between the aging brain and changes in cognition, as well as predicting declining cognition on a single-subject level, therefore, are of utmost importance.
Recent progress in neuroimaging made it possible to characterize the brain as a complex network. With this approach the functional coupling between brain regions (functional connectivity) or the fibers connecting regions (structural connectivity) can be investigated based on data acquired with magnetic resonance imaging. The aim of this project is to shed light on how cognitive performance in healthy aging might be predicted from brain connectivity data. This will be done in a multimodal imaging approach, in which structural and functional connectivity will be combined and entered into machine learning algorithms to predict an individual’s cognitive performance. While this project seeks to investigate basic brain-behavior relationships, the framework used here is most suitable to be utilized in more applied research settings in the future. For instance, brain-based diagnosis or treatment selection becomes feasible, because these machine learning algorithms allow for a single-subject prediction or classification of behavior based on neuroimaging data.
I plan to conduct this project at the Max Planck Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences in Leipzig at the research group “Neuroanatomy and Connectivity” led by Dr. Daniel Margulies.

Title: Intuitionistic epistemic logic
Abstract: The goal of this project, broadly conceived, is to combine two successful logical systems - intuitionistic logic and epistemic logic - to study knowledge from an intuitionistic perspective. The motivation for such enterprise lies on the one hand in philosophy, namely to give an intuitionistic account of knowledge faithful to the BHK interpretation, and on the other hand in applications to computer science and artificial intelligence, namely to design and study logical systems capable of reasoning about the knowledge of agents in situations where information is uncertain. The project thus consists of two parts. One part addresses the philosophical motivation and develops intuitionistic epistemic logics where knowledge is interpreted in a way faithful to the BHK interpretation. This part includes a philosophical discussion of knowledge from the point of view of intuitionism, the development of formal semantics based on Medvedev’s finite problem semantics and the unpacking of intuitionistic epistemic logic into an explicit form. The second part deals with developing and studying intuitionistic modal fixed point logics where the modalities are interpreted as knowledge operators and the study of their mathematical and computational properties as well as applications. To this end recent proof theoretic developments such as cyclic and non-well founded proofs as well as model, game and automata theoretic techniques are employed.

Title: Autonomous navigation of magnetically guided robotic devices
Abstract:
The future impact of medical robotics on healthcare is tightly linked to the ability of robotic devices to provide increased levels of autonomy and assistance to the physician. Expected benefits of autonomy range from increased situational awareness for the surgeon due to task supervision assistance, reduced mental load when repetitive or tedious tasks are performed automatically, and increased patient safety and recovery time due to better motion accuracy and repeatability of the robotic device.
 
Remote Magnetic Navigation is an ideal actuation modality to navigate many next-generation autonomous medical robots. Magnetic microrobots can be used to deliver drugs to targeted locations in the human body, but they first need to be locally released near the disease site by catheters, which can also be guided magnetically. These magnetic soft continuum robots are also relevant for a large variety of minimally invasive surgeries, as forces and torques are applied remotely on the distal ends of these soft structures, which has important safety benefits for tissue interaction. Despite these promising advantages, achieving autonomy with magnetic robotic devices for medical interventions is vastly unexplored. The complexity of the anatomy in which the robot navigates during medical interventions, and the difficulty in predicting the behavior of magnetic devices interacting with their environment, render such tasks particularly challenging. 

In this project, we will develop key components to sense, plan, and act with autonomous magnetic robots for magnetically guided medical interventions. Our tasks will be to develop a real-time simulation framework for the navigation of soft magnetic robots in complex anatomies to predict and plan their behavior. The framework will incorporate a multi-physics dynamic model of the robot and environment to implement model-based autonomous navigation policies, to create virtual environments to train controllers with reinforcement learning, and to optimize the design of magnetic soft robots. The simulator will be built upon an open-source software framework to which our project will contribute by incorporating constitutive laws and physical interactions specific to magnetically guided robots. We will integrate magnetic Hall sensors within soft magnetic continuum robots to provide localization and shape sensing abilities to our custom robotic devices. We will also integrate force sensing technologies for increased navigation safety and awareness, and to allow force measurements to be integrated within our simulators. We will implement multi-sensor fusion based on medical imaging and endoscopic cameras to autonomously navigate magnetic robotic devices and reconstruct 3d anatomical environments using visual mosaicking. The magnetic robotic devices to be considered include magnetic catheters and endoscopes as well as magnetic microrobotic devices such as micro capsules and micro catheters. 

This project will help move magnetic medical robots to the next level of autonomy through several fundamental and technological contributions. We expect the outcome to have a broad impact on the research fields of medical robotics and soft robotics, and to create opportunities in the delivery and steering of microrobots in clinical therapies.

Title: Eye Labeling for Medical Image Data
Abstract:
Computer vision and machine learning are now critical to large scale medical image analysis. To train state-of-the-art methods for automatic detection and segmentation of biomedical structures, manually annotated, or labeled, image data must be provided by expert-users who have significant knowledge in specific subject matters (eg tumors, mitochondria, lesions, etc).

Due to this critical reliance on experts, acquiring training data remains a major bottleneck for large scale machine learning in medically relevant applications. While crowd-sourcing has been very successful in traditional computer vision, its success hinges on access to large populations of annotators. This makes it at odds with many medically driven applications where the number of experts capable of providing accurate annotations is often very small.

In addition, the data annotation bottleneck is particularly problematic as it not only strongly limits the quantity of data that can be acquired to train classification algorithms, which in turn reduces performances, but also places an overwhelming annotation burden on a small number of experts.

To reduce these burdens, the aim of this project is to leverage low-cost gaze-tracking hardware with machine learning and computer vision techniques to allow experts to seamlessly and effortlessly annotate large quantities of medical image data by simply looking at the them.

Title: Exploring the Human Dimension in Large-Scale Reforestation through Qualitative Research and Agent-Based Models
Abstract:
Given current evidence from the natural sciences, the global climate crisis is clearly a result of human actions (IPCC 2021). Increasingly, earth scientists now acknowledge that they require a better understanding of how humans and their socio-cultural-economic decision-making affect the earth-system. This includes monitoring, analyzing, and modeling complex systems resulting from interactions of networked socio-economic structures with the environment. The background and rationale of the project is thus that the multiple (climate, biodiversity, economic, and social) crises that the world is facing today require a re-evaluation of how social structures interrelate with and impact ecological systems (Ingold 2019; Hickel 2020). From the analysis of current structures and existing literature, this project intends to contribute to a vision for a more holistic and integrated understanding of coupled human-natural systems.
The overall objective of this research project is to create shared perspectives between social and natural sciences research communities in the emerging field of sustainability sciences. This is to be achieved through the project’s specific aim of assessing human-natural systems through ethnographic research methods and by translating findings into quantitative modelling with a focus on agent-based modelling (ABM). Agent-based modelling is one of the most promising computational methods used by social and earth-scientists to date, with its ability to simulate complex systems, accounting for feedbacks and nonlinearities as well as incorporating different levels of uncertainty. As technology advances in the areas of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and computing power, the field of integrated assessment and earth science has the potential to consider the cognitive abilities of both individual and collective agents in its analysis. 
Increasingly, global institutions and leading scholars in the field of integrated assessment such as the host professor call for more reflexivity and the involvement of affected groups, in order to more adequately integrate the human dimension into existing biophysical models. Emerging sub-fields of anthropology, with their deep understanding of indigenous knowledge and practices, as well as their critical reflectivity of Western epistemologies, are uniquely positioned to address existing gaps in theory and method, thereby contributing to the transformation of science as an institution. 
In order to overcome existing boundaries between these fields in sustainability science, this project adopts a novel and integrated methodological approach. It combines conceptual analysis based on theoretical work, empirical-qualitative field work, and collaborative research methods to enable effective knowledge co-production across disciplinary boundaries with members at the host university. Field work will be carried out in in a reforestation project in Thuwal, near the host university, King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST). The expected results are exploratory agent-based models that account for the attitudes of social actors in an environmental restoration project. The results and the novel methodology will have a high impact in sustainability science research communities. The integrated approach will help to incorporate more fully socio-political perspectives in earth sciences and in consequence be of great interest to policy-makers, applied and design anthropology, as well as to sustainability scientists from various backgrounds.

Title: Revolutionize mathematical modeling in pharmacology to accelerate clinical application in neonatology and pediatrics
Abstract:
Mathematical modeling in pharmacology, also called pharmacometrics (PMX), is an interdisciplinary discipline that applies ordinary differential equations to support decision-making in drug development, pharmacology, and clinical practice. Briefly, PMX modeling can be applied to characterize and predict drug concentrations, disease progression, and treatment effects. 
However, PMX modeling is in some sense a trial-and-error process since many different models are tested and developed to characterize the data. The current PMX modeling approach is therefore time-consuming and consequently computationally costly.
In neonates and especially in pre-term neonates, strong maturation processes occur which must be characterized with sophisticated mathematical models. From a mathematical perspective, explicit time-dependencies describing maturation process must be included in the PMX model. Consequently, development of PMX models for neonatal populations is even more complex and time-consuming.
Recently, neural ordinary differential equations (NODE) were introduced to model pharmacokinetic data. In such a NODE the right-hand-side is substituted with a neural network. Therefore, the mechanism is no longer explicitly and iteratively modeled by hand but is learned. These NODEs might impact all kinds of modeling fields, not only PMX.
The main goal of this proposal is to move away from the iterative trial-and-error process, either by testing different models by hand or with currently available automation algorithms, to real automation, i.e., learning the mechanism with NODEs and consequently get a tailored model for a specific disease situation in neonatology. 
It will be investigated how such NODEs must be implemented in the non-linear mixed effect modeling framework, by solving questions such as 
1)Which neural network parameters should obtain inter-individual variability?
2)What is a reasonable number of neurons?
3)How should covariate effects be implemented in the neural network?
In addition, NODEs will probably for the first time be applied to pharmacodynamics data, e.g., describing disease progression and treatment effects. Finally, the developed NODE will be implemented in an optimal control framework to compute the optimal individual dose for a new neonatal patient. In case of success a R package will be made freely available. 
The proposed new methodology can be the spark of a revolution in mathematical modeling in pharmacology. The potential impact is to accelerate clinical application in neonatology and consequently to establish a faster beneficial impact for the individual neonate. Application to neonatology was chosen since there is clear medical need for such more tailored models, also in view that on average 60% of neonates are treated off-label. In addition, if the proposed new methodology works in this complex neonatal environment with ongoing maturation processes, probability is very high that it can be easily translated to other populations in pediatrics or adults.
Keywords: artificial intelligence, mathematical modeling, neonatology, neural networks, pediatrics, pharmacology, pharmacometrics

Title: Natural and Neural Dialog Generation
Abstract:
Recent development in neural language modeling and machine translation has generated significant excitement and hope in the research community for automatically generating natural language dialogs in the so called end-to-end systems. This is to overcome some of the outstanding limitations of the traditional methods (the so called pipeline systems) which involve using tremendous manual labor to device rules and templates for machines to have conversations with humans. In the new end-to-end systems, the dialog generation is data-driven thus requiring a minimal amount of human intervention. At the same time, because of the properties of the neural networks, the generated dialogs are more natural because they are based on human expressions. They are also amazingly generative. In other words, the neural nets are capable of producing dialogs which never existed in the dataset used to train them. 

However, this field is relatively young. There are many interesting challenges and open issues to tackle, such as the fact that the dialogs generated can be very short, dull, or both. This is largely due to optimization functions that do not take into account users' perception of what it means to be natural and engaging, but instead focusing on what developers believe to be optimal. More importantly, we lack methods to treat human emotions in dialogs, both in terms of recognizing them and detecting them, and producing them according to human behaviors. 

In this project, we aim at designing a neural architecture capable of taking into speakers' emotions and producing "appropriate" and emotionally engaging responses, and the evaluation of these methods; in the other direction, we will pursue both qualitative and quantitative user studies to develop detailed guidelines for what we exactly mean by human-like (thus natural) and emotionally engaging dialogs. In other words, while the first objective focuses on the technical aspect of the project, the latter is a user-centric approach to identify evaluation criteria.
Keywords: dialog evaluation techniques, dialog generation, emotion detection in language, human computer interaction, machine learning

Title: A single-cell multi-omics approach to study mouse pre-implantation development
Abstract: Pre-implantation development in mammals involves complex processes at the level of genomic organization, DNA methylation and transcriptional activity, leading to embryonic genome activation. How different epigenetic markers interact in single mouse blastomeres at early stages of development to influence the transcription of genes, and to what extent these processes vary from cell to cell and between embryos, is not fully understood. Although, in recent years a number of methods that enable single-cell omics measurement have been described, their integration to measure more than one entity in a single cell has remained challenging. Here, I propose a novel strategy for the integrated measurement of different epigenetic markers in combination with the measurement of nascent transcripts in single cells. The strategy relies on the use of a combination of specific restriction enzymes, for the measurement of 5-methylcytosine (MspJI), 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (AbaSI) and accessible chromatin (MseI and/or NlaIII), as well as 2’-fluoro GTP analogues in combination with specific RNases for the measurement of nascent transcripts. The application of these technologies to pre-implantation mouse embryos will shed light into the relationships of different epigenetic markers and their influence on transcription at the single cell level, and how these processes result in cell differentiation during early development. I further propose to use new deep-learning libraries, such as TensorFlow or Caffe, to quantitatively model and gain understanding of these dynamic processes in single blastomere cells.
Keywords: Epigenetics, Pre-implantation development, Single-cell, Trancription

Title: How is GenAI reshaping knowledge collaboration in online communities? Impact on knowledge creation, coordination and sharing
Abstract:
Online communities serve as essential spaces for knowledge collaboration, enabling individuals and organizations to contribute, refine, and exchange knowledge in a decentralized and collective manner. Unlike traditional organizational settings with hierarchical structures, these communities operate through peer-driven coordination and governance, making them highly dynamic and adaptable. For example, the development of open-source software on platforms like GitHub has enabled global collaboration, resulting in successful projects such as the Linux operating system, which has benefited both organizations and society by providing a robust and cost-effective alternative to proprietary software. Similarly, Wikipedia has become a pioneering example of crowdsourced knowledge, where millions of contributors worldwide have created the largest and most widely used encyclopedia, empowering individuals and communities with free access to information. However, the increasing integration of GenAI technologies is reshaping how knowledge is created, coordinated, and exchanged in these digital ecosystems. AI-generated content is now widespread on platforms like Wikipedia, GitHub, and Stack Exchange, raising fundamental questions about its impact on content quality, editorial governance, task allocation, incentive structures, and community engagement. This has severe implications also for the sustainability of the current AI ecosystem as decreased knowledge creation in OCs will limit the training quality of future AI models. While previous research has explored human-driven collaboration in online communities, little is known about how AI-generated contributions influence participation dynamics, governance mechanisms, and long-term knowledge sustainability.
This project systematically studies the impact of GenAI across three key stages of knowledge collaboration: creation, coordination, and exchange. Study 1 focuses on knowledge creation, examining how AI-generated content influences the accuracy, neutrality, and quality of knowledge production in Wikipedia. It evaluates whether AI improves efficiency and coverage or exacerbates issues such as bias and misinformation. Studies 2 and 3 address knowledge coordination, analyzing how AI-driven coding assistants reshape task allocation, governance structures, and contributor participation in Open-Source Software communities. These studies explore whether AI centralizes or decentralizes complex coding tasks, affects peer review engagement, and alters decision-making hierarchies in platforms like GitHub. Finally, Studies 4 and 5 examines knowledge sharing, assessing how AI impacts knowledge seeking behaviors, contributor incentives, and sustainability on platforms like Stack Overflow. These studies examine whether AI-generated answers disrupt traditional status hierarchies, discourage expert participation, or improve knowledge accessibility.
By integrating these three interrelated phases into a comprehensive research framework, this project provides a holistic understanding of AI’s role in transforming digital knowledge ecosystems. It employs quantitative, qualitative, and computational methods, leveraging large-scale data from Wikipedia, GitHub, and Stack Exchange to generate empirical insights. The findings will contribute to theoretical advancements in digital collaboration, AI-human interaction, and governance in peer-production systems, while also informing platform administrators, policymakers, and AI developers on how to effectively integrate AI tools without undermining human participation and knowledge sustainability.
Keywords: artificial intelligence, generative AI, human-ai collaboration, online collaboration, online communities, open innovation

Title: Personalized Visual Analytics: Human Preference Elicitation for Ranking-based Multi-Criteria Decision-Support
Abstract:
Choosing between thousands of items is a common and challenging task, often requiring individuals to balance multiple preferences simultaneously. Item ranking is a popular approach to structuring unorganized item collections by multiple criteria. However, existing solutions in multi-criteria decision-making through item ranking are limited in addressing the nuanced nature of human decision-making. In interactive solutions, people can express multiple preferences, which are used by algorithms to compute human-centered and personal rankings. In this project, we will demonstrate how cutting-edge Visual Analytics (VA) principles can be transferred to item ranking to demonstrate effective and efficient interactive ranking creation solutions and empower broad audiences.

We will tackle various challenges: severe preference elicitation restrictions, shortcomings of item filtering, the lack of preference-oriented quality metrics and ground truth in preference-based scenarios, lack of transparency and ranking explainability, process-oriented shortcomings in analytic provenance and guidance, almost no support for uncertainty-aware Preference Elicitation (PE) and decision-making and linguistic uncertainty in textual inputs, the missing awareness of different people needing different solutions, semantic gaps and a lack of contextualization, as well as hardly any data processing support, missing awareness for a huge design space that is however weakly populated, and the missing adoption into application areas.

Novel contributions of this VA project are along the lines of the proposal's objectives. We will: (1) design and develop novel interactive interfaces for effective and efficient ranking-based PE; (2) combine item-based, attribute-based, and direct with indirect elicitation needs; (3)  propose novel methods for the quality assessment of preference-based rankings and for ranking explainability and its quantitative evaluation; (4) systematically study and extend the process modeling of item ranking through analytic provenance and guidance; (4) extend item ranking with uncertainty-aware ranking creation and decision-making support; (5) be at the forefront of studying human alignment and semantic-level interactions for personalized analytics and PE for item ranking; and (6) develop a VA framework that unifies these novel forms of interactive PE and VA support for evaluation and the application of four envisioned case studies.

Our project comprises 2 PhDs and 2 PostDocs tracks. The PhDs cover different PE techniques, direct and indirect, connecting the semantic space with the ranking space and the data space through formalized feedback. The PostDocs investigate methods to enhance the ranking process, i.e., provenance, guidance, and uncertainty modeling. All tracks will collaborate on tasks and applications, contributing to a joint VA and evaluation framework.

By developing novel interactive interfaces and targeted adaptive recommendations, this VA project intends to improve users' proficiency in articulating preferences, both visually and verbally, to empower users to express their preferences effectively. 
Additionally, the integration of uncertainty-aware ranking creation and decision-making support will enhance users' ability to make informed decisions. By developing and rigorously evaluating novel techniques within a modular VA framework, the project seeks to broaden the accessibility and applicability of its findings. Furthermore, by integrating quality assessment, explainability, and analytic provenance into ranking-creation processes, the project aims to address the critical need for transparency and accountability in AI-assisted decision-making. 

Ultimately, the project aspires to make a significant impact on how individuals engage with ranking creation and data-driven decision-making, fostering personalized visual analytics solutions tailored to meet diverse needs across various applications.

Title: Monitoring and mapping fungal diversity for nature conservation
Abstract:
Fungi constitute one of the largest groups of organisms on earth with central importance for ecosystem functioning. Despite their obvious relevance for understanding nature and ecosystem change, they have traditionally been neglected in conservation and monitoring, implying a wide-ranging knowledge gap. This project application has an overarching goal of closing this gap, by bringing fungi firmly on the biodiversity map. It will use existing citizen science data to explore spatiotemporal changes in fungal communities and analyse how well the Habitats Directive captures fungal biodiversity. Further, it will develop and test new tools and methods for fungal biodiversity mapping and monitoring, combining citizen science and standardized sampling of DNA from environmental sampling (eDNA). Finally, an important objective is to consolidate open data resources underlying collaboration on fungal biodiversity, by substantially improving taxonomic identification and data linked to DNA-based fungal occurrences. Overall, the project will hence address all three themes of the open Biodiversa call.

The project is structured into clearly delegated, yet interlinked thematic work packages (WPs):

1. Improving identification of and unambiguous communication on fungal species
2. Applying and Improving AI tools for fungal monitoring
3. Involving citizen scientists in biodiversity discovery and monitoring
4. Sampling fungal communities by eDNA
5. Analysing fungal biodiversity patterns in time and space

The project involves computer scientists, bioinformaticians, ecologists, taxonomists and citizen scientists collaborating to solve questions of societal interest. It is novel and seeking maximal applied impact by combining well-established, but so far isolated, tools in innovative ways. The consortium behind the project has a strong track record of previous collaborations and bridges research traditions in Northern, Central and Southern Europe, securing transfer of knowledge across regions, and a wide geographical scope on the ground for those WPs where this is central, i.e., WPs 1, 3 and 4.

The project will not only provide a much-needed insight into the conservation status of fungi in Europe. Due to the critical roles fungi play in ecosystems, and their sensitivity to ecosystem change, improved insights into the fungal dimension of biodiversity will be of huge importance for understanding, more broadly, how global change affect ecosystems and associated ecosystem services mediated by fungi. Finally, we believe that the project will have impact on conservation and monitoring in other organism groups, by showcasing how molecular and AI methods in combination with unambiguous communication on species can be combined to increase credibility and impact of biodiversity data.

Title: Multitask Learning with Multilingual Resources for Better Natural Language Understanding
Abstract:
In recent years, multi-task learning and transfer across tasks and languages have become an increasingly dominant paradigm in natural language processing (NLP). While some of my earlier research such as shared subword segmentation across languages has contributed to this success, our research within the project during the SNSF Professorship has focused on a number of directions, including
(1) an analysis of transfer learning performance in different settings to gain better insights into its working mechanisms and limitations,
(2) the creation of datasets to test cross-task and cross-lingual generalization, and take steps towards allowing NLP for more low-resource languages, and
(3) the development of novel methods to improve transfer in more challenging settings, e.g. parameter sharing strategies in massively multilingual models, cross-lingual transfer across writing systems, and multimodal settings including speech translation and vision-and-language models.

This follow-up proposal will allow me to continue and complete the ongoing research in these directions. The overarching goal of this follow-up project remains to improve NLP for tasks and languages where few (costly) training resources are available, which is true for most task/language combinations. One focus of this follow-up project are low-resource languages and language varieties such as Romansh and Middle Eastern languages. In addition to text-based transfer, the project will also target multimodal models (text + speech, or text + vision) as an area where cross-lingual transfer still lags behind the successes in textual models.

Because of the high cost of training NLP models on large-scale data, the currently most popular approach to unlock cross-task and cross-lingual transfer is (expensive) self-supervised pretraining on large-scale data, followed by (cheap) fine-tuning on small amounts of supervised data from the target task. While this approach is generally very effective, representational biases resulting from pretraining will typically also affect the fine-tuned model. A large body of work has been devoted to identifying and reducing representational biases that align with social biases (e.g. racism or sexism), but our analysis has also uncovered representational biases resulting in the confusion of numbers and names in downstream applications, specifically the selection of a Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) consensus translation from a set of machine translation hypotheses. Our future research will study the effect of text representation and learning objectives on these representational biases, and introduce methods to reduce them. This will lead to neural models that can be used more safely in applications where it is central that two texts retain the same meaning, such as summarization, translation, or data-to-text-generation.

With its focus on knowledge transfer across tasks and languages, this project will develop further techniques and insights that will not only have an impact on the research field, but will also lead to improved natural language processing services deployed by industry, with the biggest improvements expected for lower-resource languages.
Keywords: multilinguality, multimodality, natural language processing, transfer learning

Title: Intelligent Privacy-Preserving Mechanisms for Data-Sharing Mobile Applications
Abstract: The widespread use of smart mobile devices has fostered the development of a variety of successful mobile applications with which users share their information with others. The data that users disclose to untrusted entities (for example, service providers, and friends of friends) exposes aspects of their private life, which is not apparent at first but can be inferred from the revealed data. People are notoriously bad estimators of risks, including privacy risks. Moreover, due to various cognitive biases, lack of enough information, and the complexity of the decision problem, it is difficult for users to make the optimal decision about whether to reveal or obfuscate their information and, if necessary, how to obfuscate it. In this research proposal, I address the problem of protecting users' privacy in data-sharing mobile applications. My goal is to develop strategic algorithms and intelligent tools to automatically assess the users' privacy level from their shared data, to help the users find the right balance between revealing and hiding their data and develop privacy-sensitive sharing habits, and to provide them with effective yet useful alternatives (e.g., obfuscated data). To achieve this goal, my methodology comprises a sequence of data analysis, algorithm design, and field experiments. I will study the inner correlation of users' data (e.g., their consecutive location samples), which an adversary takes advantage of to infer their private information, and the impact of this correlation on their (location) privacy. Additionally, I will study how users influence privacy of each other, and how the sharing habit and privacy setting of one user affect the privacy of others. With a clear understanding of user data/network, I will design intelligent privacy-preserving mechanisms that learn and consider the privacy and service-quality requirements of users, their influence on each other, and their data-sharing habits. Additionally, the protection mechanisms strategically anticipate the inference attacks that can be run by untrusted entities (e.g., service providers) to discover users' private information. I will implement the designed mechanisms and test them, e.g., on location-sharing applications, and evaluate their effectiveness and usefulness in practice. I propose the idea of intelligent nudges, in which the protection mechanism learns a user's sharing habits as well as her reactions to privacy-sensitive suggestions, and identifies the optimal nudges (i.e., pieces of information about present privacy risks and countermeasures) that can maximize the user's privacy in the long run. This proposed project fills the gap between the theoretical work on privacy-preserving data-sharing mechanisms, and the research on behavioral decision theory and economics of privacy. It contributes to the research field of usable privacy and will enhance privacy of users in the emerging data-sharing applications.
Keywords: Bayesian Inference, Behavioral Decision Theory, Economics of Privacy, Game Theory, Machine Learning, Mobile Application, Privacy Enhancing Technologies, Usable Privacy and Security

Title: Regression discontinuity designs in electronic health record data: A novel step towards personalised healthcare
Abstract:
Background: The current clinical decision system relies mainly on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies. Although RCTs have high internal validity, they are costly and time-consuming, their study population is often not generalizable to diverse populations, and they are usually underpowered for examining the treatment effects variations across granular patient subgroups. While observational studies of large-scale electronic health record (EHR) data provide an affordable alternative, such studies are generally thought to yield unreliable causal effect estimates. 

Aims: The project broadly aims to analyse large-scale EHR data to establish the causal effects of clinical interventions with a focus on treatment effects variations across patient subgroups. Specifically, it aims to determine the feasibility and validity of a novel quasi-experimental study design for clinical research - regression discontinuity (RD) in EHR data - for estimation of causal effects within granular patient subgroups under minimal assumptions. 

Methods: We will test the feasibility and validity of RD on several datasets, including the Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) dataset, Optum health care dataset, and other EHR datasets from Stanford Healthcare (STARR). Following rigorous analyses using statistical inference and machine learning techniques, we will compare the resulting causal effect estimates to those from RCT data by weighting the population characteristics to those of a given RCT’s study population. 

Results and impact: The novel design of RD in EHR data could successfully combine the advantages of observational studies (low cost, large sample size, and representativeness) with those of RCTs (high internal validity), enabling causal effects estimation in personalised medicine.
Keywords: Causal inference, Electronic health record (EHR) data, Personalised healthcare, Precision medicine, Regression discontinuity (RD)

Title: A new framework integrating motivation and perception in the human brain
Abstract:
One of the central questions in neuroscience is how our brain enables us to be motivated and take good decisions. Despite recent advances, a mechanistic understanding of how neural activity gives rise to behavior remains elusive, and we are still far from understanding which neural dysfunctions trigger neuropsychiatric disorders, or from being able to build human-like behaving machines. One possible explanation for this gap is that current models of decision making may be too simplistic and do not incorporate details about how neuronal populations process information. Although this knowledge has been integrated into realistic, biologically-inspired models of perception, it has not yet been used to characterize motivation and goal-directed decision making. Here, we propose to take an important step in this direction, by testing whether the brain guides motivation and goal-directed decision making by similar neural computations as evident for perception and sensory systems.

A central hypothesis in decision neuroscience is that the brain guides goal-directed behavior by value signals that represent the motivational relevance of the available stimuli or actions. Yet, how exactly these signals are constructed and represented in the brain remains unknown. We propose to adopt the new perspective - originally developed by theories of perception - that values are computed in the brain by means of a probabilistic population code. This framework radically differs from current approaches since it allows the brain to represent, within the same probabilistic signal, both the value of an object and the uncertainty about this value. We will test central predictions of this new framework in a functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) experiment, investigating whether a model of these proposed computations allows us to decode both the identity and precision of represented values from fMRI activity in the brain’s motivation system. The experiment will also allow us to understand mechanistically how the computed value signals can be directly derived from, and combined with, visual representations of the world around us. 

Our new proposal is methodologically challenging, in that it tries to decipher probabilistic population codes underlying fMRI signals in sensory cortices and motivational areas at the same time. Our proposal is also risky, since it is not yet fully established whether neural populations in motivational brain systems employ similar neural coding principles as those in sensory brain areas. However, if proven to be true, our hypothesis will provide an important paradigm shift for the field of behavioral neuroscience: It gives a novel, different perspective on the concepts on value, confidence, and behavioral variability, and it supports a unified framework for how neural computations can link representations in low-level sensory cortices and higher-level motivational areas. Importantly, our framework relates the computational principles of value construction with biological knowledge about single-neuron and population-level activity, thereby filling the gap between basic neurophysiology and economic and psychological theories of decision making. Moreover, it changes the way we analyze functional imaging data of human brain activity and provides important links to invasive recordings in non-human brains. Last but not least, it puts forward new avenues for understanding and assessing the dysfunctional brain mechanisms underlying neuropsychiatric behavioral disorders, and for building human-like autonomous agents in artificial intelligence research.

In sum, our proposal outlines a new interdisciplinary research line on the brain basis of motivation that would greatly benefit from SPARK funding to kick-start this unconventional but potentially high-impact project.
Keywords: Decision-Making, Motivation, Perception, orbitofrontal cortex, value, ventromedial prefrontal cortex

Title: Smarter Model Learning in Syntax-based Statistical Machine Translation
Abstract:
Today, automatic translations from and into German are relatively bad compared to other language pairs, if we compare Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) systems with the same learning algorithms and similar amounts of training data. One reason are syntactic phenomena in German such as non-contiguous verb complexes and long-range inter-dependencies such as subject-verb agreement, which are poorly modelled in traditional SMT models. Syntactic models have been proposed which have the potential to overcome these technical limitations.

However, syntactic models introduce new challenges, primarily the fact that syntactic constraints at learning time result in sparser data compared to models without syntactic constraints. Thus, the constraints are typically relaxed to avoid a huge penalty in performance because of sparsity.
In this balancing-act of specific, but sparse, and (over-)generalized, less sparse translation units, I propose novel methods to achieve the necessary level of generalization, while discriminatively learning to penalize overgeneralized rules. I also plan to utilize the rich information from syntactic parsers to learn to better model morphology in SMT.

The goal of this research project is to advance the state of the art of SMT into German, yielding better translations in terms of word order and morphosyntactic correctness.
Keywords: English, German, Grammaticality, Morphology, Statistical Machine Translation, Syntax

Title: Phase diagrams and Algorithms for Inference and Learning
Abstract:
The fields of high dimensional statistics, modern inference and machine learning have witnessed transformative changes in the last few years. In particular, recent algorithmic advances on deep networks have convincingly shown that it is possible to learn non-trivial features in data in an unsupervised way. However these exciting advances are almost all empirical.  Although the new approaches find their roots in neural network systems; there is very little theoretical basis or understanding for their recent successes at discovering and correctly identifying features or good representations of data. 

The aim of the present interdisciplinary project is to benefit from the recent
developments in fields as diverse as theoretical statistical physics coding, signal processing, probability and random combinatorial optimization to uncover principles hidden behind the success of the new approaches in modern inference problems.
Keywords: Boltzman machines, algorithms, autoencoders, compressed sensing, dictionary learning, generative models, inference, learning, neural networks

Title: A novel procedure to support meaning-making at work: combining work and life design research with AI-enhanced narrative methods
Abstract: Meaning is a central predictor of health and a key component of positive wellbeing. It has been postulated that humans have an innate drive to make meaning of everyday experiences and to form a coherent view of the world around them. In the field of work design, occupational health psychologists have addressed this topic with a focus on job crafting, person-job fit, and basic needs satisfaction. In the field of life design, vocational psychologists have researched this topic with a focus on idiosyncratic processes of self-construction and identity narratives within people's vocational development. To understand and support meaning-making in the working population, we will combine the concepts and methods from both fields of research, in order to achieve the necessary depth of insight into such an existential issue. Furthermore, to balance both the depth and breadth of this research, we convey our approach through a digital platform. This will allow us to scale up meaning-making procedures - that are often conducted in a face-to-face setting - through a self-explanatory and stepwise process. We also see a unique and creative chance to enhance this procedure with generative artificial intelligence to provide inspiration to the participants. Thus, our research objectives are (1) to combine work and life design approaches into a novel procedure to support meaning-making at work, delivered via a digital platform called "Meaning@Work", then (2) to apply and test generative AI techniques to creatively enhance this procedure, and (3) to evaluate the adherence to and engagement with this procedure and the outcomes in terms of the experience of meaning at work, using mixed methods. This combination of concepts and methods will have an impact on both fields of research, expanding their repertoire and ways of studying the concept of meaning and meaning-making at work.
Keywords: Career construction theory, Digital intervention research, Generative artifical intelligence, Identity narratives, Job crafting, Meaning-making
