Title: PreDiMIX – Predicting and Understanding Diversity Benefits from Variety Mixtures
Abstract:
Agriculture faces enormous challenges: yields have to increase while fertilizer and pesticide inputs need to be reduced, and this in a time of increasing climatic uncertainty. Crop diversification is one of the few options that allows to address all of these challenges simultaneously. Traditionally, diversification is achieved "temporally" in the form of crop rotations. In contrast, the "spatial" diversification in the field, e.g. in the form of mixed crops, is less frequently applied because it often conflicts with mechanized practices. 
Variety mixtures offer an interesting middle ground between pure and mixed-species cultures, because they allow to increase within-field genetic and trait diversity, yet are similar to pure crops with respect to processing. However, it currently is not well understood how mixtures need to be assembled to optimize yield and ecological functioning. Here, we propose to investigate positive effects of diversity in variety mixtures of wheat, and to develop simple yet effective predictive methods for optimal mixture assembly. We will combine the expertise, ideas, and technological resources of five research teams and from molecular breeding, ecology, computer science, genetics to phenomics. Jointly, we will study the mechanisms underlying variety mixture benefits - specifically yield and disease suppression - at different levels: (1) adopting niche-based approaches inspired by coexistence theory, (2) using deep phenotyping and related trait-based methods, (3) focusing on crop productivity by mixing components with different environmental optima, and (4) at the level of genes and gene-by-environment interactions. Hypothesis testing and model development will be supported by both large historic field data sets and new, systematically-designed field experiments. 
The project consists of several work packages (WP) that capitalize on a common platform of data and experiments, and advanced field phenotyping methodologies. WP1 will combine ecological theory and multivariate analytical methods to identify functional complementarity among varieties and develop predictive models of diversity effects. WP2 will use high-throughput phenotyping of pure and mixed stands to determine traits that improve complementarity and yield under environmental variation. WP3 will search complementary wheat varieties for optimal disease suppression, examining the role of diversity of host genes and resistance mechanisms. WP4 will develop novel quantitative community-genetic approaches to resolve positive diversity effects to specific genetic differences between varieties and study the genetic architecture of mixture benefits. And WP5 will utilized genomic prediction and artificial intelligence methods to model gene-by-environment interactions and allow site-specific mixture recommendations. 
The combination of resources, analytical methods, and synergistic expertise will allow us to master the scientific and logistic challenges of this project, and to address major unsolved ecological and agronomic questions. It is hoped that this ambitious project lies the cornerstone to promote high-performing variety mixtures as a key component of agro-ecological production.

Title: The Impact of Physician Gender on Medical Decisions and Healthcare Costs
Abstract:
The large and persistent variation observed in the resource use and health spending in many countries may partly reflect physician discretion in care options. Numerous decisions in health care reside within a large grey area of clinical discretion, which may represent differing physicians’ beliefs and preferences about appropriate treatment. When the variation is not due to population need, it is unwarranted and may suggest inefficient resource allocation. The gender of physicians can occupy a central role in this setting. Gender may affect medical decision-making through 1) physicians’ perceptions of their patients’ health and wellbeing, and 2) physicians’ decisions for treatment. Evidence suggests that gender disparities exist in healthcare provision. Yet, the question of whether and how the gender of a physician could affect the cost and value of healthcare is under-researched and lacks a causal interpretation.
In this project, we aim to identify the causal impact of physicians’ gender on medical decision-making explaining part of the regional variation in healthcare costs in Switzerland, through variation in treatment decisions between male and female physicians, holding constant all other physician and patient characteristics. Our methodological approach plans to elicit both stated and revealed preferences. First, we plan to make use of patient vignettes to analyse physicians’ prescribing behaviour and uncover potential differences in behavioural characteristics. Physicians are presented with several patient vignettes for which they have to decide on diagnosis and treatment. While a set of vignettes will provide cases associated with clear diagnosis and treatment, another set of vignettes will depict patient symptoms for which it is uncertain when/how to evaluate and treat (as per clinical guidelines), opening for physician bias to influence decision-making. Second, the results from the vignettes will be linked to routine data aggregated at the practice level on mandatory health insurance claims, broken down to types and costs of prescribed treatments. Additional information from patient-level health claim data will supplement the analysis. The unique combined dataset will allow us to identify physician prescribing behaviour through machine learning algorithms and single out the role of gender in treatment decisions through counterfactual analysis. Through an interdisciplinary approach (health economists, epidemiologists, and health services researchers) this research will improve our understanding of how physician gender interplays with learned behaviour, practice environment, and patient preferences, and ultimately affects the clinical decision-making process and healthcare costs disparities. Gender could play two distinct roles: 1) differences in prescribing behaviour, where gender has a causal impact, or 2) differences in the effect on healthcare costs, whereby gender plays a moderating role. As our main outcomes, we analyze differences in treatment decisions, relative performance (as deviations from guidelines), and their cost implications across gender. Our project will improve our understanding of the interplay between gender and medical practice variation. The project outcomes will contribute to a better understanding of the role of the gender of physicians on medical decisions and design incentives to reduce unwarranted regional disparities and guarantee that variation in practices derives from the needs and preferences of patients.

Title: Deep learning for high throughput cryo-electron tomography
Abstract:
Cryo electron tomography (cryoET) is profiling itself as the method of choice for the study of biological compounds in their cellular context.  Recent developments on the instrumentation side have made possible the collection of large amounts of high quality data, bringing up the necessity of  establishing  efficient frameworks for data analysis that can operate with none to minimal human supervision.  Ideal efficiency would be marked by the ability to perform an online analysis of the raw data produced by the microscope.
This proposal devises the development and posterior integration of distinct numerical tasks that jointly cover the full computational pipeline that links the raw data gained in a session of tomographic data collection (i.e., a tilt series  of micrographs of the sample imaged at different orientations at the electron microscope) to the final results in the form of averaged models of the macromolecules of interest, possibly classified in different functional states, or as automated annotations of the tomogram contents.  The final aim of establishing a high-throughput analysis sets the goal of achieving a full and unsupervised completion of this workflow in the order of magnitude of the minutes, matching the time needed by current instrumentation to collect a full tilt series.
Already at the level of selection of recording sites on the carbon grid that supports the sample during the imaging session, we intend to refine the current, in-house developed image processing system for  computerized selection of viable holes (recording sites) through a deep learning system that learns and  automatically applies the selection patterns preferred by experienced human users.  After selection of the holes, the next automation requirement is the mutual alignment of the micrographs representing different views.  The approach suggested in this approach combines the two main procedural families  (location of gold bead fiducials and  alignment of micrographs to global tomogram reprojections), joining them through the introduction of an initial model computed by a  genetic algorithm type on the central tilts, typically the ones with the highest signal content. This initial model  allows for a gradual integration of micrographs of higher tilts through a mutual validation of global reprojection and individual gold bead identifications.
The final automation stage concerns the interpretation of the tomogram content, both regarding the off-line discovery of hidden structures, and the on-line identification of copies of compounds of interest, which might appear -depending of  the case- in a wide range of supporting geometries defined by the general architecture of the tomogram contents.
Algorithmic development will be closely followed by integration in our well established, in-house package  Dynamo, ensuring both the availability of an extensive codebase for efficient development of scientific software, and an enormous visibility of the output of this project, due to the widespread used of our software suite.
Keywords: cryo electron tomography, deep learning, gpu computing, high throughput microscopy, segmentation

Title: Representation Learning for Arbitrarily Long Richly Formatted Multimedia Documents
Abstract:
In the recent years, the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP) has seen a paradigm shift with the adoption of large-scale self-supervised pre-trained representations [Dai and Le 2015,Peters et al. 2018, Devlin et al. 2018, inter alia]. These models are pre-trained on large corpora of text without labels as language models and can be fine-tuned on any downstream task. Pre-trained representations have led to significant improvements in many traditional NLP tasks and are now being adopted to model text data in a variety of domains such as biomedicine [Lee et al. 2020], scientific documents [Beltagy et al. 2019] and patents [Lee and Hsiang 2019].

While the impact of pre-training in NLP is undeniable, current pre-training approaches have key shortcomings that prevent us from unleashing their true potential in the real world. In particular:

1. With increased digitization, there has been a growth in the number of long text documents such as blogs, stories, books, etc. However, our existing pre-training approaches use a moving "context window" and thus cannot be directly fine-tuned for settings which require us to model arbitrarily long text. 

2. With the growing use of typesetting software, text today is often written and presented with due formatting using multiple modalities of data (text, images, tables, figures, etc.) to convey information much more easily. However, pre-trained representations ignore this rich multimodal document structure which could be helpful in many applications.

There are many challenges in pre-training representations of long multimedia documents. Pre-training Transformer [Vaswani et al. 2017] based models such as BERT again from scratch on a dataset of long documents is computationally very expensive as the computational complexity of these models increases quadratically with the length of the document. Moreover, there are no computational studies of text layout features in formatted text and how they can be leveraged for AI problems. These features are in addition to more well-studied discourse features such as syntactic arrangement or rhetorical forms and thus, it is not straight-forward to extend pre-training models for text data to formatted documents.
Multimedia documents typically contain multiple modalities of data such as images, tables, figures, plots, etc. in addition to text. However, there isn't much work on pre-training generic multimodal feature representations and it would be very expensive to pre-train fresh generic multimodal feature representations.

In this research, we plan to incorporate discourse level features for document layout and rich multimodal context to pre-train generic feature representations of multimedia documents. This work can be seen as an augmentation of existing pre-trained representations where we model multimedia documents as graph data structures from various typesetting software such as Latex, Word, HTML, etc. and then combine existing pre-trained representations of text [Devlin et al. 2018], images [Girshick 2015], etc. corresponding to the elements in the document. We rely on recent advances in graph neural networks [Wu et al. 2019] to exploit the relationship between different elements of multimedia documents and  learn representations of multimedia documents. We have already conducted some preliminary studies in this direction. For example, our ongoing work on modeling long text documents shows promising results and in our past work [Sachan et al. 2020] on harvesting structured subject knowledge of geometry from textbooks, we have shown that formatting features can be used to improve a strong information extraction system in that domain, and the discourse and text layout features provide information that is complementary to the lexical semantic information commonly used for information extraction. If successful, we plan to also explore the utility of our generic pre-trained multimedia document representation in challenging tasks such as multimedia information extraction and multimedia question answering.
Keywords: Multimedia, Multimodal AI, Natural Language Understanding

Title: Climate modelling by theory, data and simulation
Abstract:
Mitigating and adapting to global warming and the accompanying climate changes are among the greatest scientific challenges of this century. To mitigate catastrophic impacts such as flooding cities, droughts, and more frequent wildfires, societies need to understand how the climate will evolve both globally and locally. This understanding hinges on the availability of reliable climate models capable of accurately predicting future climate changes. Unfortunately, existing climate models cannot predict climate change reliably. A notable example is the wide variance in model predictions concerning the timing of global temperature increases surpassing the Paris Agreement's 2°C warming threshold relative to pre-industrial levels, primarily because climate models fail to predict the cloud response to climate change reliably.

While the fundamental physics behind cloud formation and evolution is understood, the vast difference in scales between microphysical processes within clouds and large-scale atmospheric flows means that current climate models cannot accurately resolve all relevant scales. This necessitates the parameterization of cloud microphysics. Unfortunately, the parametrizations that existing models employ inadequately represent the role of cloud microphysics within the climate system. To enhance model accuracy, improvements in cloud microphysics parametrizations are essential.

The Climate Modelling Alliance (CliMA), a large multidisciplinary project at our host institute, unites scientists and engineers from diverse fields to refine earth system models. This endeavor builds on a synergy of theory, data, and simulations to develop coarse-grained models, which are then calibrated using extensive observational data and high-resolution simulations. My research has contributed to the CliMA project by focusing on the development and calibration of advanced cloud microphysics parametrizations. A cornerstone of my work has been the contribution to the development of the super-droplet method code, PySDM, a pivotal tool for conducting detailed particle-based simulations of microphysics. Through PySDM, I have created a comprehensive library of rainshaft simulations, encompassing a wide range of updraft momentum magnitudes and aerosol number densities. This dataset serves as a valuable resource for model calibration and further investigation. Moreover, we have devised a framework for the calibration of warm-rain bulk microphysics parameterizations using high-fidelity super-droplet simulations. This framework employs gradient-free methods to calibrate microphysics models and offers insights into parameter uncertainties and correlations. Utilizing this framework and the rainshaft simulation library, I successfully calibrated a single-moment microphysics scheme, markedly reducing model-data mismatches. Additionally, we have assessed a classic microphysics parameterization, demonstrating its potential for improvement through calibration with the rainshaft simulation library. This ongoing work underscores the significant strides possible in enhancing the reliability of climate models through dedicated efforts on cloud microphysics simulation and calibration.
Keywords: Bulk microphysics schemes, Climate modeling, Cloud microphysics, Ensemble Kalman methods, Machine learning, Super-droplet methods, Uncertainty quantification

Title: Natural language interface for controlling microscopes
Abstract:
Modern live-cell microscopy techniques are becoming increasingly complex, requiring expertise in diverse areas like biological probe design, wet-lab protocols, optics, electronics, and software. Microscopy automation leads to increasingly large data volumes that require complex image analysis pipelines to extract biologically relevant information. We are entering an era of "smart microscopy," where microscopes autonomously react in real-time to data and adjust parameters for optimal imaging across different time and length scales. Such complex experiments often require programming skills. 
Microscopy workflows are typically explained and shared through natural language, whether in research papers, software documentation, or lab discussions. Having experienced colleagues familiar with the often customized hardware setups is extremely valuable. Many institutions with enough financial resources invest in knowledge retention and transfer across generations of scientists, for example by creating imaging facilities. In this project we propose to build a natural language interface for microscopes, making complex microscopy experiments accessible to a wider audience.

We will use large language models (LLMs) that have proven to offer convenient access to knowledge: Trained on massive domain-specific datasets, they can answer questions posed in natural language. This technology can potentially address the lack of dedicated microscopy support. However, unlike human experts, current LLMs lack direct interaction capabilities with microscopes.

We propose a software stack empowering LLMs to:
• read real-time information about the microscope’s configuration
• execute hardware commands like changing filters or initiating image acquisition

This enables the LLM to go beyond merely answering general microscopy questions, as would be the case with simply using chatGPT. Instead, the LLM can respond to queries specific to the microscope at hand. "Which of my filters can be used to image DAPI?". By letting the LLM execute hardware commands, users can change the hardware configuration with simple language prompts. "Change the filters to image DAPI!". This intuitive interaction empowers users with the virtual presence of a microscopy expert.
Beyond accessibility, this approach opens doors to increased levels of automated microscopy. LLMs have demonstrated success in robotics, effectively planning tasks and controlling hardware trough code APIs. By integrating an LLM control layer with existing hardware, we can achieve substantial automation without requiring new equipment.

We envision a spectrum of LLM-powered microscope automation, ranging from simple to complex:
• Level 1: Conversational Assistant. The microscope answers user questions. Users can chat with the microscope documentation and ask questions about current settings. "What is the current filterset used for?"
• Level 2: Linear Code Execution. The next level of automation is unlocked when the LLM can execute hardware commands. "Acquire a timelapse movie in the UV channel with 20 frames and 1-second delay."
• Level 3: Feedback Control. Complex "smart microscopy" experiments involve iterative analysis and adjustment based on microscope output. For instance, the LLM might analyze camera data to instruct the microscope. "Scan the plate and if you find a dividing cell, take a movie."
• Level 4: Automated Experiment Planning. The ultimate goal is automating entire experiment design and execution based on a research question. "Identify differences between these two cell populations."

In a period of one year the project goal is to achieve level 2 (linear code execution). We will not develop LLMs or novel task planning algorithms; instead, we will set up a software environment that will consolidate a microscope control software, LLMs and a user interface. As LLM technology is developing at an incredible pace, we will focus on creating an ’LLM-ready’ platform, that is agnostic to the specific type or architecture of LLM used. 

The software stack we will comprise:
• LLM to microscope control software interface that provides the LLM with machine-readable real-time hardware information, and all other necessary data to generate valid microscope control code.
• user interface to communicate with the LLM, to preview LLM-generated code, and approve or abort its execution.
• virtual clones of microscope devices to simulate LLM-written code before execution on real hardware.

To test this software stack, we will develop a reference implementation of an LLM agent, based on existing textcompletion models. We expect the following outcomes:
• Simplified microscope use: The natural language interfaces will make microscopes more accessible to new users and simplify complex acquisition script writing for researchers.
• Improved accessibility: The language interface provides an alternative for individuals lacking the visual or motor skills required for conventional GUI interaction.
• Foundation for autonomous systems: This project lays the groundwork for future LLM-powered autonomous microscopy systems. The Level 2 implementation will demonstrate the project’s feasibility and pave the way for securing funding to develop Level 3 and 4 systems.
• Broad applicability: By building upon the open-source microscope control software µManager, the system will be compatible with a wide range of microscopes.
Keywords: Accessibility, Automatization, Large language models, Microscopy, functional imaging

Title: (Ro)Bot-Human Interaction – A Digital Shift in the Administration of Criminal Justice? Substantive Law, Procedure, & Verdicts in Ambient Intelligent Environments
Abstract:
Criminal law was designed by humans to create order amongst ourselves. Accordingly, its fundamental concepts, such as the notion of free will or the concept of a free appraisal of evidence or the claim of dignity and autonomy of parties to the criminal proceeding, are uniquely human. However, this human-centric approach is at risk of losing its place as a primary guiding principle as (ro)bot-human interactions increase. Until now, such collaboration has not had special standing in criminal law despite the fact that robots in various forms, software bots as well as standalone machines, already gather and process information, draw conclusions on behalf of humans and cooperate with them, or even act autonomously as their agents. Ongoing digitalization, or the increase in ambient intelligent environments, may gradually require a change in the traditional method of establishing the elements of alleged criminal conduct and in the way in which such elements are proven in court when human-robot collaboration turns detrimental. This, in turn, may have repercussions upon the narratives in criminal verdicts. 
This project assesses the consequences of (ro)bot-human interactions in ambient intelligent environments. It primarily uses the example of technology surveying human drivers in modern cars in the course of driving automation. This includes software bots as well as physically independent smart devices that are made for enhancing safety in road traffic in the context of Swiss penal law. The goal is to understand legal changes and predict further impacts upon criminal law. The project will cover three working packages; packages one and two will be dissertation projects and the third will be a joint project among a group of scholars in comparative criminal law, engineering and law and legal narratives. The working packages will build upon each other, addressing the following questions:
(1) Substantive Criminal Law: What are the potential changes in the assessment of subjective (mens rea) elements of crimes in penal traffic law cases, particularly when robots issue warnings to humans based on their assessment of drivers’ behavior? 
(2) Criminal Procedure: What are the challenges for fact-finding and evidence evaluation in criminal proceedings after fatal traffic accidents involving evidence from monitoring technology? Specifically, must defense rights be modified as a consequence to the use of certain machine-generated evidence so as to provide sufficient protection to the human driver standing trial? 
(3) Digital shifts and its impact on narratives in criminal verdicts: How do criminal courts assess and prove mens rea in traffic incidents? Does the approach change with driving automation? Where do different criminal justice systems, with diverging legal traditions, technology adoption and traffic regulations, differ in explaining and establishing responsibility? Are there any commonalities?

Smart safety devices in modern cars provide poignant examples of everyday human-robot collaboration that foreshadows a number of specific effects upon penal law. Within the domain of substantive criminal law, the demarcation of a negligent act from an intentional crime could change entirely when the mens rea could be inferred from a person’s response to (ro)bot advice. For instance, if a drowsiness detection system alerts a driver to take a break but the driver continues, eventually causing an accident, courts may be inclined to infer negligence or even intent as a result of the driver disregarding the advice. Yet, criminal procedure might not grant an adequate defense to human drivers. In criminal proceedings the importance of human testimony, most notably a defendant’s admission, will lose standing, while machine-based evidence will gain traction. For example, if a drowsiness detection system assesses a driver as sleepy, how can the driver challenge this machine-evidence if it is presented against him in court? Finally, verdicts will have to explain responsibility sharing in (ro)bot-human interactions and how machine-generated data was evaluated against human statements to justify an acquittal or conviction. With the ongoing automation of driving, robots monitoring humans will take over a crucial safety functions, like in Take Over Requests (TOR) when a car wants to hand over after having performed the dynamic driving tasks itself and must ensure the human driver is in fact capable of taking the steering wheel. As robots will likely become more embedded in our lives, similar issues will arise in other aspects of human life.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, automated driving and criminal liability, comparative criminal law, criminal liability and negligence, digital evidence and defense rights, driving automation, human robot interface, legal narratives and criminal verdicts, mens rea, robot-human-cooperation, robotics and criminal law

Title: Ultra-Low Power Closed-Loop Feature Extraction and Stimulation Platform for Implantable High-Density Neural and Cardiac Prostheses
Abstract: My proposed research plan aims at introducing an appropriate compression algorithm followed by a feature extraction platform as an efficient method to limit the amount of data acquired by an implantable neural or cardiac prosthesis. Following a reliable feature extraction, electrical stimulation will be implemented using extremely compact and power-efficient electronics. The final goal is to implement two prototypes of ultra compact and low-power implantable devices with higher channel counts than existing devices: (1) a 256-channel fully implantable intracranial EEG recording array with compressed-domain seizure detector, closed-loop stimulator and external classification processor for epilepsy treatment, and (2) a 64-channel ECG recording and heartbeat detection array with on-chip compression and stimulation capability for efficient heartbeat regulation in patients suffering from arrhythmia. Thus, the main contribution of this research is exploring an optimal sensing, compressing, feature extracting and stimulating framework with more than an order of magnitude denser integration compared to state of-the-art implantable microelectronic circuits for intracranial EEG (iEEG) and ECG signal acquisition. As a significant advantage, the proposed design can be easily scaled up to larger overall array sizes, while retaining the spatial resolution and power efficiency of the implantable device.

Title: Establishing Ecological Validity and Reliability of a Neurocognitive Supertask for Predicting Real-World Transdiagnostic Rigidity
Abstract: Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and major depressive disorder (MDD) share common symptoms such as difficulties in adaptation, emotion dysregulation, and stress reactivity (referred to as transdiagnostic rigidity). Traditional neurocognitive tasks fall short of disentangling the underlying mechanisms of transdiagnostic rigidity, limiting the development of targeted, real-time digital stress and mood interventions. To address this gap, I have developed GearshiftFellowship (GF) during my study abroad. GF is a neurocomputational supertask that integrates various clinical and neurocognitive domains. These domains have largely been studied in isolation, which poses a challenge for understanding adaptive mechanisms across different contexts and over time. GF allows the study of transdiagnostic rigidity in an adaptable environment, including cognitive and social contexts, designed for dissecting mechanisms with cognitive computational models. It has the potential for evolving into a digital therapeutic tool for predicting and addressing transdiagnostic rigidity. After establishing construct validity of GF and using it for computational phenotyping of ADHD, OCD, and MDD, the goal of the return grant is to establish GF’s ecological validity and assess its potential to guide real-time adaptive digital interventions that improve behavioral adaptation, emotion regulation, and reactivity to stressors.

Title: The development of a sorghum genotype to phenotype modelling pipeline
Abstract:
Adapting plants to current and future climate changes is an urgent necessity that requires developing new methods to better understand and predict plant growth. In this ambitious project I want to combine advanced genetic resources, new modelling approach, and state-of-the-art phenotyping technology to describe plant growth from the genotype to the phenotype (G2P) level integrating key plant environmental adaptations. For that purpose, I will use an existing sorghum multi-parent population (MPP), an advanced genetic resource with wide genetic diversity for adaptation traits like photoperiodism. I will use high throughput phenotyping experiments to complement the available MPP phenotyping data measuring traits like transpiration efficiency.

The first phase will involve comparing statistical genetics models (SGMs) and machine learning (ML) algorithms for their ability to model plant adaptation traits in terms of genotype and genotype by environment (GxE) information.  Then, I will evaluate the capacities of crop growth models (CGMs) to reconstruct plant adaptation functions and their interactions with the environment using data from the MPP characterized in different environments. Finally, I will integrate the MPP genetic variability into the CGM by estimating key plant genotype CGM parameters through SGMs or ML. This integration of SGM/ML with CGM will constitute an advanced CGM/G2P pipeline to explore the genotype by environment by management space exposing the large MPP genetic diversity to a wide range of simulated environmental conditions. Ultimately, the pipeline will help in the adaptation of sorghum varieties in West Africa, where climate change has major repercussions.

Title: First-principles models of precipitation in metallic alloys
Abstract:
Precipitation hardening is a commonly used processing technique to enhance the mechanical properties of modern engineering alloys made of aluminium, titanium, magnesium and nickel. Alloy chemistries and processing conditions are carefully tuned to achieve optimal microstructures that enhance material properties. Despite the ubiquity of precipitation hardening in modern engineering alloys, the precise nucleation mechanisms and barriers for precipitate formation remain unknown. This project seeks to answer fundamental questions on the atomistic mechanisms of precipitation by utilising electronic structure calculations, machine learning and statistical mechanics.
During age hardening, alloys form several intermediate metastable precipitates. Early stages typically induce order-disorder phase transitions. The precipitates formed through order-disorder phase transitions are long-range orderings on the same crystal structure as the disordered phase. Longer ageing times tend to induce structural phase transitions. Phases with a crystal structure different from that of the matrix phase emerge at this stage. Due to the large nucleation barriers associated with structural phase transformations, these precipitates are thought to primarily nucleate at defects. Through this research program, we will unravel the precise atomistic mechanisms for phase transformations and the thermodynamic and kinetic barriers associated with precipitate formation.
Atomistic models and statistical mechanics techniques will be utilised to elucidate precipitation mechanisms along pathways relating a disordered phase to ordered precipitates. Quantum-accurate interatomic potentials parameterised with machine learning will enable a rigorous exploration of nucleation mechanisms in metallic alloys. The interatomic potentials will then be used with statistical mechanics techniques to estimate homogeneous and heterogeneous nucleation barriers at elevated temperatures for phase transformations that occur during precipitation. Specifically, the nucleation mechanisms in multicomponent alloys comprised of magnesium, titanium, and aluminum will be studied.
Insights into homogeneous and heterogeneous precipitation mechanisms gained through this research program will enhance our ability to design metallic alloys and processing conditions. Quantifying nucleation barriers for homogeneous and heterogeneous nucleation will allow alloy designers to identify features such as defects that may need to be controlled to achieve optimal microstructures. Further, we will answer long-standing questions on the atomistic mechanisms of precipitate formation in metallic alloys. The tools developed as part of this project will enable the study of more complex alloys, phenomena and processing conditions.

Title: Structure and dynamics of materials based on advanced electronic structure calculations
Abstract:
In atomistic simulations the positions of all the involved atoms are individually known. In this way the structure as well as the dynamics  of molecular systems can be studied and understood in depth. A prerequisite for such atomistic simulations is the availability of a high quality potential energy surface and methods to explore it efficiently. Potential energy surfaces calculated on the density functional level
are usually considered to be state of the art, even though their accuracy is not sufficient in numerous cases. In this project several key aspects of atomistic simulations will be addressed. Based on our recently developed methods to navigate in the configurational space, the efficiency of our structure prediction schemes will be further improved and its applicability enlarged. In addition we will deduce
from our exploration of the potential energy surface not only structural but also dynamic properties. Improved density functional methods will be implemented to give higher accuracy potential energy surfaces and consequently improved predictability for atomistic simulations. We will work both on the validation of methods within mainstream density functional schemes as well as on some non-standard approaches inspired by quantum chemistry methods. For some specific systems, machine learning based force fields will be constructed that are not only highly accurate but also orders of magnitude faster to evaluate than potential energy surfaces resulting from density functional calculations. All these developments will allow to find new materials with useful properties faster and to predict their properties with higher reliability. In particular we will apply these methods to study molecular crystals and cluster assembled materials.
Keywords: electronic structure calculations, structure prediction

Title: Smart Beds for Obstructive Sleep Apnea for Individualized Diagnosis, Treatment, and Follow Up
Abstract:
Background and rationale
Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) affects about 1 billion people worldwide. OSA is characterized by a repetitive collapse or narrowing of the upper airway during sleep resulting in cyclic oxygen desaturations, intrathoracic pressure swings and arousals from sleep. Symptomatic OSA is associated with impaired sleep quality, impaired quality of life, and daytime sleepiness, and an increased risk of motor vehicle accidents. Severe OSA is associated with hypertension and an increased risk of cardio- and cerebrovascular events. The effective gold standard treatment for symptomatic OSA is continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy. CPAP splints the upper airway by means of pressurized air and normalises  breathing during sleep. However, many patients with OSA do not accept or tolerate CPAP well and thus do not use it every night all night. Socio-demographic patient characteristics, disease severity, psychological factors, and side effects often lead to suboptimal treatment adherence. Thus, a relevant number of symptomatic OSA patients need a different treatment approach or remain untreated. The existence of phenotypes with specific OSA features, symptom burden, systemic consequences, and comorbidities has been demonstrated in cross-sectional studies. However, a link between treatment outcomes and patient characteristics is needed to enable the implementation of tailored treatment plans.  Furthermore, OSA severity based on conventional severity markers such as the number of obstructive hypopneas or apnoeas per hour of sleep or monitoring shows a high night-to-night variability. Comprehensive sleep laboratory examinations, which are necessary for the clear typing of OSA, are time-consuming and expensive. Therefore, novel ways to monitor patients in the home environment to diagnose and classify OSA and to evaluate treatment response are of interest. Furthermore, novel therapy approaches that only intervene when apnoeic events occur might increase therapy compliance.   

Overall objectives and specific aims
The objective of this project is to facilitate personalization of OSA therapy by introducing unobtrusive sensors (microphones, ballistocardiography, and bio-radar) in combination with machine learning into the whole OSA diagnosis and treatment pathway. During diagnosis the use of unobtrusive sensors in the home environment allows for multi-night recordings to reduce the impact of night-to-night variability of OSA severity and classifying markers. In addition, non-contact detection of obstructive respiratory events during sleep can be used not only for more accurate diagnosis of OSA, but also for rapid therapy application (event-driven intervention) and therapy efficiency monitoring. Personalization at the level of therapy dosage will be addressed by robotic beds for providing mechanical interventions based on online detection of obstructive respiratory events. The beds will induce a change in body position that reduces the risk of upper airway collapse. The interventions should be carried out without causing sleep fragmentation. We will follow up to verify the control of OSA under different therapy modalities (e.g. CPAP, mandibular advancement splint, positional therapy) using non-contact patient-friendly home sleep measurements. By providing unobtrusive home measurements at 3 and/or 6 months follow-up, we will establish an easy method to get insight into personal therapy success. The combination of the follow-up and the baseline data will enable us to identify predictive features for therapy success.

Expected results
We will deliver a unique database  containing >500 datasets of OSA patients with clinical parameters, full in-laboratory cardiorespiratory polygraphy recordings, data from unobtrusive sensors, and follow-up data. Using this database and machine learning-based algorithms, we will identify potential predictors of treatment success. Furthermore, we will demonstrate personalization of the dosage of interventions by developing novel robotic beds for providing positional therapy triggered by apneic events. This closed-loop intervention will be validated in a proof-of-concept study. 

Impact on the field and beyond
Therapy personalization and new treatment methods for OSA are a cutting-edge focus of research in sleep medicine. Robotic beds are a promising pathophysiology-oriented individually tailored treatment approach. Novel robotic beds with closed-loop treatment capabilities being developed as part of this project, will account for the variability in manifestation of OSA during the night and intervene only when apneas or hypopneas occur, rather than intervening all night. Therefore, these beds could offer an innovative treatment approach for many patients and a real business opportunity for bedding manufacturers.

Title: Implementation of an Interprofessional Medication Adherence Program for vulnerable patients to support the transition of care from hospital to community  – The “OzIMAP project”
Abstract:
Background

Community health workers (CHWs) help bridge the cultural gap between health services and the communities they serve. CHWs work with physicians, nurses and social workers, but little is known about their collaboration with pharmacists.
The overall objective of this postdoctoral research was to explore the interprofessional collaboration between CHWs and pharmacists (through a scoping review), the impact of their collaboration on supporting patient medication adherence (through a systematic review), and the strategies and challenges CHWs and pharmacists working in Australia and New Zealand encounter in their collaborative practices (through a qualitative study).

Methods

In the scoping and systematic review, the English language scientific literature published in databases such as Embase, MEDLINE, Web of Science or CINAHL, was searched. Inclusion criteria of the scoping review were that the research (i) involved pharmacists and CHWs working collaboratively and (ii) included an intervention, service or program. Inclusion criteria of the systematic review were that (i) the intervention was delivered by pharmacists and CHWs and (ii) reported on medication adherence outcomes. The software Covidence was used to screen and select eligible articles. Data were extracted using a customized template using Excel and synthesized narratively.

As part of the qualitative study, semi-structured interviews were conducted with pharmacists and CHWs in Australia and New Zealand, to explore i) CHW-pharmacist interprofessional collaboration experiences, ii) how pharmacists perceived CHWs’ roles and vice-versa, iii), challenges to collaborative practices and iv) strategies to foster their collaboration. Interviews lasted approximately 30 minutes and were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and inductively thematically analysed.

Results

First, the eighteen studies included in the scoping review showed that most interventions involving CHWs and pharmacists working collaboratively involved medication reviews, support for medication adherence, disease prevention or addressing the social determinants of health. Pharmacists had primarily clinical roles (i.e., medication reconciliation and patient education), while the CHWs’ roles consisted of collecting patient information, supporting patient self-management, bridging the cultural gap by translating information in the patient’s language and ensuring patient follow-up. The collaborative practice occurred via interprofessional referral, ranging from the CHW facilitating the link between the patient and the pharmacist, and information sharing between the CHW and the pharmacist, to an interprofessional collaborative practice where CHWs and pharmacists delivered the intervention together.

Secondly, the systematic review exploring the impact of CHW-pharmacist interprofessional interventions on patient medication adherence showed that a significant improvement in medication adherence was observed in three of the eight studies. 

Thirdly, the qualitative study —including twenty-nine participants (16 pharmacists and 13 CHWs)— showed that CHWs connected the patient and the pharmacist and helped bridge cultural gaps, shared patient-related information with the pharmacist, supported patient medication management and adherence, and referred patients to pharmacists. CHWs helped patients to take up pharmacy services and reinforced pharmacists’ recommendations. There was a lack of understanding of each other’s role, but pharmacists and CHWs acknowledged the benefit of each other’s roles. Key challenges to collaborative practices were poor communication between CHWs and pharmacists, and lack of guidelines on the collaborative practices. Strategies to promote collaboration included clarification of their roles, improving the working relationship and knowledge of the mutual benefits of collaboration.

As part of this study, we have developed recommendations on how to prevent fraudulent participants from taking part in online research. Strategies included promoting the study to a closed network on social media, encouraging participants to provide sources that verify their identity and discouraging the use of artificial intelligence to answer questions.

Conclusion

CHWs have an important role to play in bridging the cultural gap between the patient and the pharmacist, in improving patient referral so that more patients can benefit from pharmaceutical services, and in identifying patients’ social determinants of health. CHWs and pharmacists can work synergistically and collaboratively to tailor an intervention to the patient’s needs, which can improve and optimize pharmaceutical services, and may ultimately improve patient health outcomes.
Collaborative practices were identified between CHWs and pharmacists working in Australia and New Zealand. However, challenges remain, including a lack of understanding of CHWs’ roles by pharmacists. Future research should focus on improving knowledge of the mutual benefits of collaboration, and co-designing a CHW-pharmacist collaborative intervention with guidelines to standardize and foster collaboration.

Title: Bridging the gap between behavioural traits and population dynamics
Abstract:
Background and rationale: Before a population exhibits a demographic response to environmental changes, individual animals often respond behaviourally to the altered conditions. Behavioural adjustments—such as shifts in time allocated to foraging—serve as a first line of defence, particularly for long-lived species facing climate change-induced resource scarcity. These behavioural responses help individuals cope with new resource landscapes but come with trade-offs, such as increased exposure to predation or adverse weather conditions. Understanding the repeatability of these behavioural traits and their impact on fitness is essential because demographic responses can lag, and by the time population-level effects are detected, it may already be too late for effective conservation interventions. Formalising the integration of behavioural traits into population ecology models is therefore critical for predicting and mitigating the demographic consequences of climate change.
In this Ambizione research proposal, I address this overarching objective through a series of interconnected research aims. I will use a model organism that represents a guild of prey species facing the trade-off between resource scarcity and increased predation pressure as climate-change driven droughts become more prevalent: the vulturine guineafowl (Acryllium vulturinum). Work I am conducting for my postdoc is revealing that these arid-adapted birds, native to East Africa, increase their foraging activity as conditions deteriorate (quantified via Normalized Difference Vegetation Index: NDVI), and that this foraging activity is repeatable within individuals. Crucially, preliminary survival analyses suggest that individuals that increase their foraging activity more relative to the average had a higher risk of being predated during a prolonged drought, highlighting a major trade-off between the risk of starvation and predation. This work lays the foundation for important questions that I am motivated to pursue as an independent lab leader:
Aim 1. How do environmental conditions affect foraging behaviour and physiological profiles?
Using machine learning to classify behaviour from biologging data, I will quantify how foraging activity and intermittent vigilance are adjusted to resource scarcity, and how repeatable individuals are in the mean expression of their foraging behaviour from one day to the next. I will compliment this with non-invasive (faecal) glucocorticoid measures to quantify the physiological stress profile of birds displaying different foraging strategies.
Aim 2. What are the underpinnings of individual variation in behavioural and physiological traits?
Determining the source of individual variation in behaviour is challenging. Individual differences in foraging activity (and associated physiology) result from the interplay between external factors (e.g., resource availability; Aim 1), demographic differences (age, sex), early-life experiences and individual ‘behavioural types’ (e.g., risk-taking propensity). Using life-history data and direct field observations, I will establish how these traits emerge and are represented within a population.
Aim 3. How do behavioural and physiological traits affect survival and reproduction?
Integrating behaviour and physiology into population dynamics requires establishing how foraging activity and physiological stress influence survival and reproduction. By monitoring life-history events (breeding success, death), I will link these traits to fitness outcomes under different environmental conditions (i.e., high to low resource availability) using survival analyses.
Aim 4. How do behavioural and physiological traits maintained within a population affect population dynamics? 
Finally, I will build Integral Projection Models (IPMs), incorporating behavioural and physiological traits and environmental covariates to predict vital rates and project population growth (or decline). As this is a single-organism approach, I will compliment my analysis with simulations to make broader predictions on how behaviour contributes to population dynamics.
Impact: Behavioural ecologists have been accused of being ‘aloof’ to the role our discipline could play in understanding how climate change will affect wildlife populations, particularly as idiosyncrasies between how different populations of the same species respond to climate change (often ascribed to ‘random noise’) may be driven by differences in behavioural responses expressed within these populations. My research will be a timely demonstration of how behavioural ecology matters to population processes and will forecast which behavioural traits will come under strong selective pressure under future climate change scenarios.
Keywords: Behavioural ecology, Climate change, Early warning signals, Fitness, Population dynamics, Stress physiology

Title: NeuraMod: Architectural Modelling with Neural Potentials
Abstract: The proposed research aims at assessing a new architectural modelling approach involving both human and artificial intelligences to decode and encode meaningful architectonic articulations from generated visuo-semantic tokens and neural responses as a next generation of grammar-less modelling methods, and based on information-communication technology and cognitive sciences paradigms. By the use of multimodal, gaze-dependent brain-computer interfaces, it will progressively elaborate a technical infrastructure for human-Machine-interaction, to allow for producing and evaluating visuo-spatial and physical experiments, and to finally reflect upon a synthetic and theoretical framework for the application of such methods.

Title: Reverse-engineering and digital reconstruction of a limb control circuit
Abstract:
State-of-the-art robots cannot match the abilities of animals to sense, decide, and act. Work in bio-inspired robotics, an area that attempts to reverse-engineer biological solutions to solve outstanding engineering challenges, has yielded impressive results in biomechanics and actuation. However, bio-inspiration has yet to distill the principles of behavioral control. Artificial systems have difficulty behaving autonomously in part due to the challenges of controlling their limbs in the presence of unexpected perturbations, sensory signal delays, and noise. Animals overcome these challenges by efficiently and intelligently exploiting a massive array of tactile (touch) and proprioceptive (position) limb mechanosensors. Using these signals, animals can construct high-level behaviors from low-level sensorimotor control loops, rather than from explicit kinematic models like those used to control robots. 

How animals use mechanosensory feedback to control their limbs remains unknown. Uncovering these mechanisms has enormous potential for transforming how we design robots and neuroprosthetics, and for understanding and treating movement disorders. Unfortunately, even with modern tools, the mammalian limb-spinal system’s complexity and physical inaccessibility make it intractable for comprehensive investigation. Instead, studies using Drosophila melanogaster provide an unparalleled opportunity to more rapidly understand how mechanosensory feedback enables dexterous limb control. Drosophila limb circuits are organized similarly to their mammalian counterparts. Flies use their limbs to groom, walk, fight, court, and reach. Limb circuits reside in the ventral nerve cord (VNC), a region that is functionally equivalent to the mammalian spinal cord. Individual, or populations of genetically-identified VNC neurons can be targeted using GAL4 driver lines from libraries of transgenic Drosophila. The small number of neurons (~10^5) also makes Drosophila circuits more amenable to bio-realistic in silico modeling.

I have developed three technologies that only now make it possible to reverse-engineer and digitally reconstruct biological algorithms controlling complex limb movements in Drosophila: (i) software for 3D limb pose estimation, (ii) an approach for imaging the VNC of behaving animals, and (iii) a physics-based 3D Drosophila simulation that can be driven by a neural network controller. By leveraging these tools and with a focus on Drosophila grooming, my laboratory will investigate four features of biological limb controllers that make them superior to state-of-the-art robotic controllers – closed-loop control using sensory feedback, integration of sensorimotor signals, efficiency, and adaptive flexibility:

Aim 1: Reveal how limb control circuits use mechanosensory feedback during movement correction

Aim 2: Uncover how limb control circuits integrate and use copies of motor signals and sensory feedback

Aim 3: Investigate theoretical predictions for how limb control circuits achieve efficiency

Aim 4: Identify how limb control circuits adapt to modify limb grooming behaviors across species

These aims will be pursued through a series of complementary in vivo and in silico experiments that are designed to test, refine, and possibly overturn influential theories of motor coordination. These experiments will also establish a framework for further exploring how limb control can be modified through changes in gene expression to generate the variety of motor behaviors seen across individuals and species.
Keywords: 2-photon imaging, Drosophila melanogaster, evolution, grooming, limb control, limb tracking, neural networks, simulations

Title: Grounding uncertainty: standards and agency in digital labour platforms
Abstract:
The ability of digital platforms to transform the world we live in and unremittingly feed artificial intelligence (AI) have become a key debate among scholars and wider policy circles. Such potential disruption includes many dimensions of future worlds of work globally. This study looks at practices likely to turn such uncertainty into action. It aims at examining how digital labour platforms organise and control a disaggregated and remote workforce, and how does such a workforce cope with current power asymmetries in platform-mediated work.
While a burgeoning scholarship exists on location-based platforms relying on workers to provide services such as ride-hailing (Uber, Lyft), (food) delivery (Deliveroo, Just Eat), and care (Care.com, Helpling), fewer studies investigate online web-based platforms relying on remote workers, also called ‘gig workers’ or ‘freelancers’ on platforms such as Appen, Upwork, or 99Design.
In its analysis of work carried out online via web-based platforms, the project supplements existing scholarship that examines digital labour platforms in light of structural transformations of capitalism, informal and non-standard employment relations, obstacles and opportunities to labour agency, workers subjectivities and governing infrastructures. It aims at filling the gap in the literature in three ways. First, drawing upon international political economy and cognate fields, it conceptualises the interplay between the uncertainty facing the worldwide provision of services intermediated by platforms, their governing infrastructure, and on-the-ground-labour relations. Second, it sheds light on standards as distinct instruments of the infrastructure governing the provision of services mediated by platforms. Third, while the existing literature portrays work performed on online web-based platforms as thwarting most potentials of labour agency, the project aims at providing a tailored research design to spot emergent and disparate forms of collective action in an under-studied segment of the gig economy in which voice is still viewed as unlikely.
With a focus on uncertainty, standards and labour agency affecting online web-based platforms, the project is organised around research propositions regarding contradictions and complementarities. The first one posits that standards used by digital labour platforms are set against the opposing political economy objectives of productivity, quality and security requirements, on the one hand, and protecting sustainable and decent work, on the other. The second one posits that the capacity of web-based online workers to draw on core principles and rights at work to voice their concerns about carrying out standardised tasks rests on the complementarity of pre-existing solidarities, digital communication tools, grassroot and established trade unions, and awareness of labour standards used by platforms and their broader regulatory environment.
The project combines desk research, in-depth semi-structured interviews, and participant observation. It relies on a qualitative extended case method and draws on practice tracing and interpretative content analysis. It uses a purposeful critical case sampling to select the three following countries: Bangladesh, Serbia, and Germany. The cases provide a graduation on the labour supply chain. They reflect a variety of occupations from low to higher skilled tasks and prospects for collective action. Such research design is set to provide further insights on on-the-ground practices upon which standards and labour agency respond to the uncertainty facing the worldwide provision of services intermediated by platforms.
Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Bangladesh, Digital labour platforms, Germany, Labour agency, Online web-based workforce, Serbia, Standards, gig economy, platform, standards, working conditions

Title: Steps against the burden of Parkinson’s Disease StepuP
Abstract:
Parkinson’s disease (PD) affects over 10 million people worldwide and is one of the most prevalent neurodegenerative diseases. Despite good effects of medication, unstable gait and falls continue to affect 70% of patients with PD. This leads to loss of confidence, social isolation, fractures, and hospital admissions. Treadmill training has demonstrated substantial and well-proven benefits in improving gait and reducing falls, which can be enhanced by the concurrent use of mechanical or virtual-reality triggered gait adaptations. However, the underlying mechanisms responsible for the effects of treadmill training are poorly understood. It is imperative to disentangle how PD patients benefit from treadmill training to improve and personalize training. To do so, we will determine how the well-proven outcomes from non-pharmacological treadmill training relate to the biomechanical, physiological, and neural changes that underlie intervention success and how these effects transfer to daily life.
Four clinical centers will recruit a total of 168 PD patients. Participants will be randomized 1:1 to intervention or control groups. The intervention groups will receive treadmill training, enhanced at selected sites by mechanical or virtual- reality triggered gait adaptations. All participants will undergo assessments before and immediately after training, and again after 12 weeks to investigate retention. We expect gait speed, step length and step variability to improve by clinically relevant extents. We hypothesize that sensorimotor integration underpinning feedback control of balance during gait explains these effects. This will be probed by analysis of biomechanical data, where we expect enhanced quality of feedback control regulating foot placement in walking. Neurophysiological changes underpinning these behavioral changes will be assessed using a combination of electroencephalography (EEG) and electromyography (EMG). After training, we expect to see improved feedback control of gait stability that is accompanied by decreased EEG beta band power and increased EEG-EMG (brain-muscle) coherence.
Improved gait as assessed in the lab does not always translate to increased daily-life walking. We hypothesize that gait self-efficacy mediates and/or modifies transfer of training effects and will therefore investigate the associations of the above mechanistic probes, gait efficacy and patients’ characteristics with mobility outcomes. Digital mobility outcomes over one week will be assessed remotely using our advanced sensor tools.
We will use machine learning to assess individual improvement, focusing, for example, on understanding why some individuals improve on the lab-based tests and in their daily life, but others do not or only in the lab. This will help us to understand the mechanisms that underlie (individual) translation of treatment outcomes into real-world outcomes and may empower and inform the development of personalized interventions.
In conclusion, the proposed project will provide a mechanistic understanding into how widely used treadmill training changes neural activity in patients with PD, how this translates to improved control of gait, and how this in turn translates to outcomes that are meaningful to patients in their daily life.

Title: Novel State-of-the-Art Graph Matching Algorithms
Abstract:
Due to fast developments in both storage media and data acquisition, we observe rapidly increasing amounts of data available in diverse areas in both science and industry. Simultaneously, we observe that in many applications the underlying data is inherently complex, making graphs the most useful and adequate data structure available to date. These two developments evoke the need for ongoing research of robust and efficient methods that assist humans in understanding and handling their pools of big sets of graph data.

A large amount of graph based methods for pattern recognition and related fields have been proposed. One of these methods is graph edit distance - a powerful and flexible graph dissimilarity measure and actually one of the main subjects of this proposal. Regarding graph edit distance (or more generally graph matching) we observe two substantial gaps in research that we aim to research and bridge. Formally, within the present project we will research...

- encodings of matching information in a novel data structure to formalize the stable cores of specific classes by means of graphs. The rationale of this matching-graph representation is that it can be beneficial to focus on stable/important parts of graphs during algorithmic comparisons (rather than on complete graphs). 

-  hierarchical graph representations in conjunction with linear time graph embedding. This procedure is motivated by the fact that hierarchical representations (including fast and expressive graph embeddings) can be exploited in filter-and-verify strategies in order to substantially speed up and improve the matching processes.

By verifying both hypotheses we plan to make significant advances in the field of structural pattern recognition and establishing novel paradigms that go beyond the current understanding.  In particular, the overall objective is the development and research of novel, robust graph edit distance methods that outperform the current state-of-the-art in graph matching on existing and novel data sets stemming from different real world scenarios. Hence, the proposed project involves both research on fundamental algorithms and solving concrete problems in applications. Last but not least, we aim at thorough comparisons of structural methods with recent deep learning methods in order to gain insights on where graph based methods actually rank to date.
Keywords: Big Graph Data, Graph Based Pattern Recognition, Graph Matching, Learning with Graphs

Title: Reduced-Basis Nonlinear Models for Simulating Synergistic Geometric Instabilities in Metal Structures under Extreme Loading
Abstract:
Recent studies, quantifying natural hazards, and their effects on infrastructure assets worldwide, recognize that the required simulation technologies should encompass a broad range of physical phenomena, so as to promptly thwart the consequences of environmental threats, prevent downtime, and plan for the future by enabling “virtual testing”. In steel structures, which form the main focus of this proposal, the magnitude of demands typically associated with extreme events require refined analyses, with local and member inelastic and geometric nonlinearities. Their interaction is often synergistic, detrimentally amplifying one another. These effects may prematurely trigger global collapse and/or downtime with prominent adverse consequences to the public in terms of safety, environmental impact and economic losses. 
The opportunities afforded by abundant computational resources currently allow detailed simulations of intricate physical phenomena. However, reproducing these analyses across multiple instances of an infrastructure network, and evaluating their vulnerability to numerous loading scenarios, remains challenging. Intelligent use of computation will require the development of high-fidelity and reduced-basis models, while enabling a vast number of simulations of the built-environment. Current approaches to structural modeling, in a computationally efficient manner, employ either point plastic hinge models, whose predictive capabilities are known to be significantly limited and often unrealistic; or standard fiber-based approaches that both suffer from spurious mesh dependency in nonlinear softening problems and conveniently neglect coupling of local and member instabilities. While continuum finite element approaches can trace synergistic instabilities of critical regions within a metal structure, the associated computational cost of such methods is outrageously high in parameterized simulations of complex systems. In an effort to tackle the computational expense, hybrid methods involving the interfacing of elements of various fidelities are evolving. Yet, the current state-of-the-art does not seem to properly transfer the force and/or kinematics across the elements' interface, thereby compromising the accuracy of predictions. This research project proposes fundamental theoretical developments and methods to address the above challenges. It aims at developing a family of adaptable reduced-order nonlinear physics-based models, which could be used to capture the synergy of physical mechanisms, causing loss of load carrying capacity in metal structures under extreme loading at a viable computational cost. 
The proposed models will be informed by means of material-level tests that will deliver reliable material properties of representative steels. The main outcomes of the research project will be timely. Title: A high-altitude air vehicle as cost-effective access to  Earth observation and space
Abstract:
This proposal concerns an extremely cost-effective approach to high-altitude flight - i.e. up to and in excess of 70,000 feet (the reference altitude in meters is 20,000). 

A novel approach to extreme high-altitude atmospheric flight is put forward which focuses on the development of air vehicles with extremely high aerodynamic efficiency values, an indispensable quality for flight in rarefied air, yet cheap and robust enough to fly through the lower atmosphere without incurring in structural failures or aeroelastic instabilities. 
The key original concept consists in a ``formation'' of drones, aerodynamically designed to be able to fly autonomously and in close formation, allowing an overall high aerodynamic efficiency at high altitude yet the ability to withstand wind gusts at lower altitude. 
The wing aspect ratio is the key parameter: a high value is essential for high aerodynamic efficiency, a smaller value allows the design of a structure which is able to withstand gusts much better. The "system" hence introduces a completely new degree of freedom: the ability to fly as "one aircraft" or as a a number of "individual" aircraft by varying the clearance between the drones in flight or the type of formation. High efficiency at higher altitude would be achieved in close formation whereas a robust aeroelastic response to wind gusts at lower altitude is possible because of the much more "robust" structure of each individual drone.   

Beside telecommunications, this kind of flights are instrumental for "low altitude" Earth Observation missions in which air vehicles can replace the much more expensive satellites in low Earth orbit and are often referred to as High Altitude Pseudo Satellites or HAPS.  The best known of such vehicles is possibly Airbus Zephir. 
Furthermore, a high-altitude flight can be the first step of the launch of satellites, the best known  of such  air vehicles are possibly the numerous WhiteKnights developed by Scaled Composites. Also in this case, the greatest advantage would be the much lower costs (with respect to conventional launchers). 

Several factors let us believe that the potential -- in terms of  the scientific and commercial interest  --  of this idea is significant. First and foremost, the growing commercial interest for ``space'', smaller satellites, in particular and for Earth Observation missions, may be  carried out by a HAPS at much cheaper costs than satellites. As far as access to space is concerned, the cost reduction efforts carried out by SpaceX  makes cost-effective solutions look much more attractive   then in the past. 
The feasibility of the idea is supported by  some technologies with a fast growing TRL: (i) control software exploiting artificial intelligence, (ii) electrical propulsion and energy storage, (iii) as mentioned above, high-altitude air vehicles like Airbus Zephyr and   WhiteKnights, (iv) high-fidelity simulations are now reliable design tools.  

The expected TRL is clearly as low as 1 or 2. This study shall provide a first feasibility assessment by trying to provide some efficiency numbers on the basis  of numerical simulations.
However, the  project shall not only investigate the aerodynamic and aeroelastic responses but also assess the requirements on the control system, which is of course of critical importance.
Keywords: Earth observation, access to space, aerodynamics, aeroelasticity, drones, formation flight, optimisation, rarefied air

Title: High-level Audio-Visual Descriptors for Content-Based Video Categorization
Abstract:
The pervasiveness of amateur media recorders either as stand-alone devices or embedded in smart-phones are revolutionizing the way private and public events are captured and reported. The decreasing cost of the hardware coupled with the popularization of social networks has therefore favored in the past few years the exponential distribution through the internet of user-generated multimedia content, and in particular videos. Unlike text that is now effectively indexed and searched, this huge (and ever growing) amount of multimedia information is highly unstructured and, as such, difficult to index and to retrieve. Manual indexing alone of user-generated videos is not feasible in practice, as tags and annotations – when available – are often subjective and potentially unreliable or misleading. There is therefore an urgent need to develop content-based algorithms for the automatic categorization of user-generated videos that would enable applications such as citizen journalism, forensic search and entertainment. The objective of my research project is to develop a multi-modal content-based video categorization that jointly exploits the information that is available in audio and visual modalities. 

To this end I will investigate accurate high-level features that effectively describe the audio and video content. These descriptors should capture the semantic content in a scene that can be obtained from each modality independently. Next I will study how to combine these unimodal features in order to create high-level audio-visual descriptors with a global meaning. The aim of these audio-visual features will be to capture information that is not possible to extract using one modality only or when dealing with each modality separately. Moreover this multimodal approach will be used to influence the reliability of the features extracted in a single modality: for example, a bride pictured while a wedding song is playing would give a stronger idea about the concept wedding and frames with texture and color representing sand, coupled with the sound of waves would strengthen the concept of beach. Video categorization can therefore become more reliable when using multimodal descriptors with high semantic content, as opposed to audio-only or video-only features. 

Although the importance of audio-visual analysis has been highlighted for more than a decade and high-level descriptors can be efficiently used in other applications in the joint audio-visual domain, few approaches explore the possibilities of semantic analysis for audio-visual signals. 

During this postdoctoral research at Queen Mary, University of London (QMUL) I will have a unique opportunity to broaden my knowledge in both computer vision and audio analysis. The School of Electronic Engineering and Computer Science combines excellent research groups in these fields, and their completed projects in "Multi-modal object tracking in a network of audiovisual sensors" and "Audiovisual semantic discovery" demonstrate a strong interest in my research domain.
Keywords: content-based video categorization, high-level descriptors, joint audio-visual analysis
