Title: ReCOUNT - Reasons of the others: concession and counterargument in polylogues
Abstract:
ReCOUNT is a collaborative corpus based investigation of discursive patterns of concession and counterargument (CO(u)N patterns) in the context of argumentative polylogue, relying on a qualitative and quantitative exploration of an extensive case study of discussions on issues related to Generative AI carried out via social media platforms.

The discursive practice of counterargument plays a crucial role in argumentation theory, as a bridge between the analysis of argumentative discussions and their evaluation, especially in the perspective of dialectical theories, which tie the quality of an argument to its ability to withstand criticism in a discussion setting. We hypothesize that, in a defeasible reasoning setting, counterargument inherently presupposes an act of concession (resuming, re-presenting and – to some extent – recognizing the reasons of the other), consequently adopting the concession and counterargument pattern (CO(u)N pattern) as the main unit of analysis and drawing on the rich linguistic and rhetorical literature on concession, with a special attention to the linguistic polyphony tradition.

Relying on multiple layers of analysis of the corpus, which include Inference Anchoring Theory (IAT), its enrichment and combination with the Argumentum Model of Topics (AMT), as well as an ad-hoc multidimensional annotation of CO(u)N we seek to bridge the gap between pragma-linguistic and rhetorical studies of concession and micro-inferential analyses of  counterargument from the perspectives of defeasible reasoning, informal logic and dialectics.

By placing the investigation in a polylogical setting and adopting a polylogical perspective, we mobilize this multi-layer analytical framework to capture hitherto undescribed phenomena relating to the resumption, re-presentation and countering of others’ reasoning that emerge when the reconstruction of the discussions abandons the traditional dyadic setting.

The proper description of these emerging polylogical phenomena involves the microscopic  analysis of CO(u)N patterns, accounting for anaphoric phenomena, reconstructing enthymematic inferences, and projecting the pattern’s polyphonic configuration of perspectives onto the polylogue’s participants, but also requires the macroscopic analysis of recurring large scale CO(u)N configurations, individual and communitarian CO(u)N styles characterizing discussion participants, as well as trends and tendencies emerging within discussions over time and across discussions. To this effect, the multi-layer analytical framework is applied at different levels of granularity to the annotation of sub-corpora within the broad case study of discussions on Generative AI on social media platforms to produce qualitative analyses of collections of highly detailed reconstructed examples and to develop quantitative analytics for mapping large discussions and capture trends, tendencies and styles across the whole corpus.

Expected results include, ranging from the micro- to the macro- level, a pragmatically grounded understanding of the functioning of different types of defeaters in enthymematic arguments, new understanding of the complex argumentative patterns incorporating conceded arguments (known as conductive arguments) as well as on the strategies for managing multi-dimensional configurations of (dis-)agreement in polylogue, with insights on the context-specific dynamics of the discussions on Generative AI and on the role of social-media platforms as desirable by-product of the research.    

The USI-IALS team and the WUT-New Ethos team, on the one hand, will leverage on their respective strengths by focusing respectively on in-depth reconstructive qualitative analysis of enthymemes and on the quantitative corpus analytics. On the other hand, they will closely collaborate in theory building, corpus design and collection, corpus annotation.
Keywords: Argumentum Model of Topics, Generative AI, Generative Artificial Intelligence, IAMT, Inference Anchoring Theory, Large Language Models, argumentation theory, case study, concession, counterargument, discourse analysis, discursive polyphony, polylogue, social media discussions

Title: Adaptive Learning-based Model Predictive Control for Varying-topology Multi-agent Systems
Abstract:
Cyber-physical systems are becoming increasingly sophisticated and interconnected in pursuit of higher efficiency and performance. Examples include microgrids, vehicle platoons, energy hubs, and electric vehicle charging infrastructures. Owing to their complex interconnected nature, these networks can be modeled as multi-agent systems. To further enhance their flexibility, these systems are being designed to allow for network topology changes, enabling them to dynamically adjust to evolving conditions. Such complexity necessitates the development of advanced control schemes that are robust against failures, maintain privacy, and adapt well to varying network topologies. To meet these requirements effectively, there is a growing shift from centralized control to distributed control, which offers improved scalability and resilience. This transition yields advanced control schemes which are better suited to handle the dynamic and complex nature of these systems.

Due to its strong theoretical guarantees and successful industrial applications, significant efforts have focused on developing model predictive control (MPC) schemes (e.g. distributed MPC) for multi-agent systems including varying-topology networks. A key limitation of MPC in this context is, however, its reliance on accurate models, which are often difficult to obtain or complex to use. To this end, simplified models are typically employed within the MPC framework. To compensate for the discrepancy between the actual and simplified models (i.e. the model uncertainty), several MPC variants (e.g. robust and stochastic MPC) have been developed. These variants, however, do not improve the simplified model and do not learn more about the uncertainty using online data. The main objective of this project is to reduce the conservatism of such variants for multi-agent systems with varying topologies by learning the model uncertainties online. The growing availability of data and the rigorous development of data-driven methods support the possibility of using system identification and machine learning methods for this purpose.

We aim to achieve the main objective by developing a modular adaptive learning-based MPC architecture for multi-agent systems with varying topologies. This architecture is mainly composed of two layers: a learning layer and an adaptation layer. In the learning layer, a better description of the uncertainty is learnt using online data. In the adaptation phase, the MPC problem is continually adapted based on the learnt uncertainties. We will consider using various system identification techniques and machine learning methods to identify various classes of uncertainty online. While these methods have shown success in single-agent systems, using them with varying topology networks is still an open problem. Beyond establishing theoretical guarantees, we also aim to demonstrate the framework on representative applications, including microgrids and vehicle platoons. We expect the proposed architecture to outperform existing MPC schemes through continual online uncertainty learning and adaptive reformulation of the MPC problem. In the longer term, this architecture has the potential to provide a standardized approach for developing scalable and efficient MPC solutions for modern, dynamic, and complex cyber-physical systems.
Keywords: Control Architectures, Learning-enabled Control, Mathematical Optimization, Model Predictive Control, Multi-agent Systems

Title: Grassland conservation across European landscapes protecting biodiversity and ecosystem services with ecological networks. (GreeNet)
Abstract:
Permanent grasslands are an important land cover type in European protected area
networks, valued for their biodiversity and ecosystem services (ES). Aligning the
biodiversity and ES conservation agendas whilst sustaining agricultural land-use on a
landscape scale is an important societal priority. Integrating social-ecological
knowledge on grassland use in protected areas would provide an important basis for
developing and maintaining protected landscapes and for optimizing the use of scarce
public resources.
GreeNet’s major objective, therefore, is to develop transition pathways for sustainable
management of European grasslands under a combined land sparing and land sharing
paradigm prototyping novel ways to develop and maintain protected landscapes.
GreeNet will analyse grassland case studies in Austria, Estonia, Germany, Ireland,
Norway, and Switzerland considering a gradient of protection status from currently
unprotected but highly valuable landscapes, to Natura 2000 areas, biosphere reserves,
nature parks, and national parks.
GreeNet brings together scholars from multiple disciplines and stakeholders across
multiple scales. Its inter- and transdisciplinary methodology integrates assessments of
conservation management options at the farm level with field and landscape scale
assessments of innovative indicators of biodiversity and ES considering spatial effects
from landscape coordination. Methodologies are jointly developed at consortium level
and applied at case study level. They include i) the design of integrated conservation
management options at the landscape scale through the mapping of grasslands with
machine-learning techniques, ii) the evaluation of landscape multifunctionality with
ecological tools across landscape intensity gradients, iii) the empirical assessment and
modelling of attitudes, preferences, and constraints of farmers regarding individual
and collaborative conservation management options and landscape protection
statuses, taking into account global change scenarios, iv) the analysis of
cost-effectiveness of conservation incentive schemes in different governance systems
using a policy planning model at landscape scale and v) the analysis and development
of governance strategies towards long-term protection of grassland landscapes.
Participatory processes are organised at three levels (farms, regions, international),
during different project stages, with different levels of engagement, and in multiple
participatory processes.
The social-ecological perspective in GreeNet on the spatially explicit field and landscape
scale allows to identify the barriers and enabling factors that make landscape
protection effective and acceptable by farmers and the public. Hence, GreeNet will
address local landscape scale design challenges and Pan-European policy goals such
as the national biodiversity strategies, the Aichi-targets, and SDGs.
Keywords: Agricultural Policy, Biodiversity, Conservation, Ecosystem Services, Grassland, Landscape, Synergies, Trade-offs

Title: Deep Learning Algorithms for High-Dimensional Dynamic Programming Jump-Diffusion Models
Abstract:
The goal of this project is to develop a machine learning toolbox for the 
numerical solution of financial, insurance and macroeconomic models with dynamics 
driven by stochastic volatility processes with jumps. A special focus will be to establish
a framework that is able to accommodate high-dimensional stochastic volatility models, Levy processes, jump-diffusions as well as Hawkes-diffusion models, a powerful device allowing to model contagion and negative feedback effects among shocks and disasters. The methods and algorithms developed in the 
project will make it possible to solve more realistic models than is possible with 
classical methods and, therefore, will yield new insights into important aspects
of finance, insurance, taxation, fiscal policy, environmental science and health economics. 
On the theoretical side, the project aims to develop new approaches to the approximation of solutions of partial integro-differential equations with input-convex neural networks in high-dimensions.

Title: Towards the understanding of the universe’s formation: finding the hydrogen 21 cm signal
Abstract:
- SKAO and its goal
The Square Kilometer Array Observatory (SKAO) is an ambitious project which aims at creating an array of observatories in a one square kilometer in Australia and South Africa, which should be completed in the coming years. The SKA project is an unprecedented ambitious project and global effort in radio astronomy to delve deeper and faster into the mysteries of the universe and could provide valuable insights into key periods of the universe creation, such as the cosmic Dark Ages, the cosmic dawn, and the epoch of reionisation. 
Funded in 2019, the SKAO Consortium has been created to support the preparation and processing of SKAO data. From 2022, Switzerland will be an active member of the SKAO Consortium, with various schools participating in its realization.
- SKAO SDC series
In order to be able to process the expected large and complex amounts of data that the SKAO will produce, a series of challenges, called SKAO Science Data Challenges (SDC) were created. These challenges consider difficult part of the data processing which need state-of-the-art methods to be addressed properly. 
- SKA 3rd SDC and the Hydrogen 21cm signal
This project aims at addressing the third SDC challenge, which aims at extracting the hydrogen 21cm signal from mock datasets created by the SKAO Consortium to represent real data that the SKAO will produce.  
A first round of the challenge provided interesting results and insights, and the Swiss team achieved 10th place using a SERENET approach. While promising, those results did not yield full satisfaction regarding the full hydrogen 21 cm signal extraction, which remains mostly unsolved. 
- Novel approach needed
To achieve satisfying result and solve the hydrogen 21 cm signal extraction, more complex, creative and risky methods are needed. The results of the 3rd SDC unveiled promising leads and interesting concepts that were not addressed despite their potential, because of their high complexity and low probability of success in such a short span. This project aims at thoroughly exploring those creative approaches beyond the scope of the 3rd SDC, allowing for a more in-depth analysis and secure a methodology for the hydrogen 21 cm signal extraction.
Keywords: Astrophysics, Deep Learning, Denoising, Epoch of Reionisation, Hydrogen 21cm signal, Machine Learning, Power spectrum, SKAO, Square Kilometer Array Observatory

Title: Probabilistic Multi-Label Learning for Chronic Diseases
Abstract: This project aims at applying multi-label learning (MLL) techniques (machine learning) for the analysis of medical data, such as laboratory tests or physical examinations, in order to identify patients affected by chronic diseases, such as diabetes and their comorbidities. Indeed, when physicians are in front of patients affected by several comorbidities, the decision making for a treatment becomes complex. In addition, with the technical progress in the medical area, patients are monitored in a more continuous way, which generates larger quantities of heterogeneous data. Hence, the analysis of temporal physiological signals and laboratory tests with MLL methods, which can model overlapped medical conditions, will help physicians to take optimal decisions against the worsening of illnesses. Our contributions will be a novel probabilistic framework that has the potential to address specific challenges in the medical domains such as the ability to discard unreliable diagnostic decisions.
Keywords: chronic disease, comorbidity, decision support, machine learning, multi-label learning

Title: Perceptive Dynamic Locomotion on Rough Terrain
Abstract:
Legged robotics and in particular quadrupedal robotics has made considerable advances in the past decade. Several groups around the world have realized versatile systems that show great locomotion skills  and  the  first  legged  solutions  are  currently  installed  in  industrial  applications.   Despite all advances by our research community, these machines are still far away from their full potential in their mobility and autonomy to navigate through challenging environments.  The primary reason is that, in contrast to wheeled or flying vehicles, legged robots have to discontinuously make and break contact with the terrain in order to balance and move forward. 
The  objective  of  this  project  is  to  overcome  these  challenges  and  realize perceptive  dynamic locomotion in challenging environments with legged robots.  To this end, we propose a hybrid algorithm, i.e., a combination of online and offline planning methods composed of sampling-based path planning, reinforcement learning, and model-based optimization.  This research project builds upon our extensive and world-leading expertise in locomotion planning, control, and environment perception, and combines modern ideas from the different communities of machine learning and optimal control.  Specifically, we use simplified models for the system dynamics and the environment representation to plan a rough initial path.  To overcome the highly non-convex problem of finding footholds and gait timings on uneven grounds of variable properties, we train neural network policies in simulation and use it on local, robot-centric maps.  On the last layer, we finally account for the full system dynamics and terrain knowledge to plan and control motion and ground reaction forces to move forward.  On all layers, we make use of semantic knowledge about the environment gained from experience. The proposed multi-layer approach allows exploration of different combinations of model-free Reinforcement Learning (RL) and model-based optimization tools in order to make the toolchain as performant as possible. 
We are convinced that true progress in this area is only possible with real systems and real data, which will be strongly emphasized during execution of our research.  Hence, in our project we will continuously test and validate the proposed methods and algorithms in simulation and real-world experiments with the existing quadrupedal robot ANYmal.  With this research, we are convinced we will enable new applications of legged systems in hardly accessible terrain.
Keywords: legged robotics, locomotion control, navigation, optimal control, reinforcement learning, robotics

Title: The role of sexual behaviour dynamics and treatment-as-prevention in the spread of HIV, Hepatitis C and syphilis: Predicting the conditions for control and elimination
Abstract:
Control and elimination of HIV, hepatitis C Virus (HCV) and syphilis transmissions is a clinical and research priority worldwide. Available treatments options, including recent therapeutic breakthroughs4, dramatically improve the health of infected individuals and substantially lower the risk of onward transmission. Yet, even in countries with high diagnosis and treatment rates such as Switzerland, we and others have shown that the incidences of HIV, HCV and syphilis associated with sexual risk behaviour have not declined. In order to overcome barriers to transmission control and elimination, well-orchestrated prevention initiatives which expand the current fragmented approaches are needed. This can only be achieved by an improved understanding of the complex interplay between prevention and treatment strategies, patterns of sexual behaviour, and sexual contact networks. This project will comprehensively address these questions by combining established and novel methodologies, and by exploiting unique nationwide data sources. For decades, Swiss surveillance systems and the Swiss HIV Cohort Study (SHCS, www.shcs.ch) have collected information on sexual behaviour in both HIV-negative and positive people, long-term incidence and clinical data, as well as viral genomic data. To the best of our knowledge, this will be the first study to jointly investigate sexual behaviour dynamics among HIV-negative and positive individuals, transmission networks inferred from viral phylogenies, and clinical outcomes for these three interacting infections. The overarching aim of this project is to identify the necessary conditions regarding sexual behaviour, diagnosis and treatment rates to control sex-related transmission of HIV, HCV  and syphilis, and to characterize effective interventions to achieve transmission control. This project will determine whether and how WHO elimination targets (90% reduction in transmissions by 2030) are achievable. We intend to set-up coupled mathematical models of sexual behaviour, and HIV, HCV and syphilis transmission. The models will emulate the past and project the future of these epidemics. A routine update procedure will enable the models to continuously learn from newly upcoming data and to produce projections that reflect all known relevant information at time of projection. This project will provide a platform for the study of further STI such as gonorrhoea and chlamydia. The project will first focus on men who have sex with men (MSM) to subsequently extend the methodology to other transmission groups. The proposed methodology can be applied to other regions and to other transmissible diseases. In particular, we aim:

Aim 1: To disentangle and model sexual behaviour structures and their relationship with transmission networks inferred from viral phylogenies. We will do this by: i) using unsupervised machine learning to infer clusters of sexual behaviour  based on longitudinal individuals’ records; ii) characterizing the relationship between behavioural clusters and transmission networks inferred from phylogenetic analyses of HIV and HCV; iii) using behavioural clusters, transmission networks and their relationships to inform the sampling process of a qualitative nested study aimed at overcoming information gaps on sexual behaviour that have historically led to oversimplified assumptions; iv) developing a mathematical model that based on the outcomes of (i-iii) emulates the dynamics of sexual behaviour. The model of sexual behaviour will capture the effects of interactions between individuals and external information (e.g., scientific releases, media coverage of disease outbreaks) including public health interventions like campaigns aimed at influencing sexual behaviour.

Aim 2: To model transmission of HIV, HCV and syphilis. We will integrate the model of sexual behaviour into previously developed models of HIV and HCV transmission, and will develop a model for syphilis transmission. These transmission models will be coupled to reflect interactions between the three infections, and time-updated to capture emerging information. 

Aim 3: To identify and project the impact of novel strategies for transmission control by exploiting the knowledge gained from Aims 1 and 2. Our models will identify target groups in which behavioural and treatment interventions are most likely to lead to the largest possible reduction in the incidence of the studied infections, and project the impact of such interventions. Modelled interventions will  include treatment-as-prevention (TasP) and HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). Interventions will consider different scenarios of future sexual behaviour. Time-updating projections will provide a novel tool to this field for implementing and surveying interventions to contain STI transmission, and a mechanism for assessing and improving the accuracy of model projections.

Title: The Nuts and Bolts of Language Models
Abstract:
Language models are transforming not only the field of natural language processing but many areas of life ranging from journalism to education. With the availability of ever more training data and computing resources, their ability to perform tasks without task-specific training is truly astounding. Thus, many technologists believe that language models are general-purpose reasoners, and even predict that they will become the basis for general AI. While their capabilities are increasing at astonishing rates and much engineering is done to make these models ever more effective, little is actually known about their capabilities on a theoretical level. Many claims about their abilities are made without a formal basis or even a technical definition. However, in the context of computer science the notion of general purpose reasoning is concretely defined, through the formalism of Turing machines (TMs) introduced in Alan Turing’s (1937) seminal paper. This gives us reasonable tools for testing claims about the reasoning- or algorithmic capabilities of language models. This grant proposes an investigation of Language Models (LMs) with the tools of the theory of computation and formal language theory. 

Almost all research relating neural language models and formal language theory treats models as unweighted recognizers, i.e., researchers seek to determine the set of strings the models accept. However, language models are inherently probability distributions over strings. In this proposal, we contend that we should treat language models as probabilistic recognizers and analyse them using probabilistic formal language theory. To
the authors’ knowledge, no published work in the literature currently does this despite—since language models are by definition probabilistic—it being the most natural path.

Our research plan is divided into six work packages. In Work Package #1, we build on prior work by Minsky (1967) to analyze when and how we can view language models as probabilistic finite-state machines. In Work Package #2, we then extend this to show how LMs based on recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can compress certain probabilistic formal languages into their representation. Then, we turn to the question of whether language models can represent any computable probabilistic language. We do this by proposing three projects that extend the celebrated result by Siegelmann and Sontag (1992), who showed that RNNs can encode a Turing machine, to the probabilistic case. In Work Package #3, we start by giving a lower bound of the expressivity of LMs by showing that they can encode probabilistic real-time Turing machines. In Work Package #4, we then give an upper bound on the expressivity by showing that language models that are allowed to output certain additional symbols in between the output can simulate any probabilistic Turing machine, thus showing how to extend Siegelmann and Sontag’s (1992) result to probabilistic Turing machines. Then, in Work Package #5, we ask, again under more realistic assumptions, what is the exact formal computational model that corresponds to RNN LMs. Finally, in Work Package #6, we turn our attention to chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al. 2022), which we analyze through the lens of our previous formal results. Chain-of-thought prompting is a novel technique of interacting with an already trained LM by giving it examples to a Language model on how to think step-by-step, which has been empirically shown to drastically increase their performance on algorithmic tasks. There has not been any theoretical analysis explaining this phenomenon. All in all, we believe our proposal offers several new results that shed light on the nature of large language models.
Keywords: computer science, formal language theory, large language models, machine learning, natural language processing, theoretical computer science

Title: The role of the cytokine GM-CSF in mammalian myelopoiesis during development, steady state and dysregulation
Abstract: The granulocyte macrophage-colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF or CSF-2) is emerging as a major player in the modulation of phagocyte function in tissue inflammation. During inflammation invariably, some tissue-invading lymphocytes produce high levels of GM-CSF, which in turn acts to license myeloid cells to cause immunopathology across different diseases. This lymphocyte-to-myeloid cell communication conduit represents a major focus in our research endeavors. Concomitantly to its role in tissue inflammation, GM-CSF has also been described for its impact on medullary and extra-medullary myelopoiesis. Yet, apart from its ability to shape the macrophage population of the lung, we understand very little about its function during development and steady-state homeostasis. Clinically, GM-CSF is targeted for neutralization in chronic inflammatory disease, but contrariwise, GM-CSF is also given to treat patients with hematological dysfunction. The focus of this proposal is to understand the role GM-CSF plays during mammalian embryogenesis and tissue macrophage development, as well as its impact on myelopoiesis during inflammation. For this, we have generated a series of gene-targeted mice, which allow us to fate-map and report cells, which express(ed) GM-CSF in the steady state and permits the manipulation these cells genetically. In addition, we can manipulate GM-CSF and GM-CSF-Receptor expression in an inducible and conditional fashion across natural GM-CSF producing and sensing cells. The aims of this proposal are to i) determine the cellular sources of GM-CSF during mammalian embryonic and neonatal development and in adulthood across all tissues, ii) to determine the role of GM-CSF plays in shaping the tissue-resident phagocyte compartment and iii) to understand the impact of dysregulated GM-CSF on myelopoiesis.
Keywords: cytokine networks, embryogenesis, machine learning, myelopoiesis, pattern recognition, single cell analysis, transgenic mice

Title: Dissecting the regulatory landscape of the human genome
Abstract: A large number of genetic variants linked to phenotypic changes are located in the non-coding regions of the genome, suggesting that their effects are most likely the result of changes in gene expression regulation. Expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) analyses allow finding of regulatory genetic variants, which are linked to changes in gene expression. However, the regulatory elements perturbed by the genetic variants must be identified to fully understand these mechanisms. I propose to develop a computational framework to predict enhancers and their target genes based on genome-wide chromatin and gene expression data in an eQTL study setting. First, a set of high-confidence enhancers in human lympoblastoid cell lines (LCL) will be created from published literature and available databases. A machine-learning algorithm will then be trained based on posttranslational histone modifications, transcription factor binding and DNA sequence conservation at these enhancers. This model will then be used to predict genome-wide enhancers in additional 47 LCLs. Furthermore, data on detected eQTLs and dynamics in gene expression and chromatin variability will be used to associate the predicted enhancers to target genes, thus deciphering the cis-regulatory network around eQTL genes and pinpointing candidate regulatory elements that are perturbed by genetic variants.
Keywords: Chromatin, Computational Biology, Gene expression, Gene regulation, Genomics

Title: Exploiting LHC data with machine learning and preparations for HL-LHC
Abstract: The proposal is to improve flavour tagging and so-called boosted-object tagging by using novel algorithms and machine learning such as deep learning.  The pattern recognition techniques for tracking of charged particles currently in use will no longer be able to cope with the huge amount of computation required during HL-LHC.  New machine learning techniques for particle track reconstruction for HL-LHC are proposed.  Fast high-fidelity calorimeter simulation is a bottleneck in the physics program.  A novel fast calorimeter simulation using Variational Auto Encoders is proposed.  The ITk upgrade of the ATLAS pixel detector is key to the HL-LHC project.  Contributions to the in-house construction steps are proposed, in line with FLARE grant 20FL20_173601.  The proposed research is complemented with a progamme to search for unconventional signatures due to new phenomena associated with a dark or hidden sector, and unseen Higgs boson decays: H->cc in VH production (V=W/Z).

Title: A Multi-perspective Assessment of Channel-related Unfairness in Voice Assistants
Abstract: Artificial Intelligence-based voice assistants (VAs) provide many advantages to e-commerce providers (e.g., by automating customer service or sales processes), and their overall importance is strongly growing. The worldwide E-Commerce transaction volume via VA is expected to increase from 4.6 billion USD in 2021 to 19.4 billion USD in 2023 (Statista 2022). However, research has shown that VA use is not always fair for consumers (Cram et al. 2020; Liang et al. 2021). Among others, unfairness can result from voice channel-related characteristics that restrict the amount and form of information presentation. Serious consequences for consumers may include a lack of transparency during product selection, excluding choice options, as well as higher prices (Robert et al. 2020; Greene et al. 2019). Algorithmic fairness has mostly used a technological lens that sought to develop probabilistic decision support that prevents disparate harm to different groups (Barocas & Selbst 2016). However, this perspective falls short (Dolata et al. 2022), since a) establishing fair VAs may even be potentially economically undesirable for e-commerce providers, b) customer perceptions may differ from objective fairness considerations, and c) customers and algorithms form an ensemble that needs to be studied jointly. While first qualitative works indicate that by neglecting certain fairness principles during VA design, relationships between firms and consumers might be harmed (Weith & Matt 2022; Robert et al. 2020), we still lack a broader multi-perspective assessment that considers technical aspects, consumer perceptions and responses, as well as firms’ economic considerations. If we do not close this gap, consumers could become reluctant, jeopardizing the broad adoption of VAs in the field, but also firms might stretch the borders of using unfair AI for themselves to gain economic advantages. We distinguish the computational parts of VAs from the underlying channel (audio), and its ability to transmit transaction related information (Ochmann et al. 2021). The projects focus on channel-related restrictions that can (deliberately or not) affect fairness during the interaction and the presentation of the decision outcome. As part of our multi-perspective assessment, we first assess VA technology and interaction experts from practice and research to obtain an understanding of the possibilities and restrictions of VA interaction design regarding fairness. We next classify and empirically test consumers' perceptions of unfair VAs and measure the effects on firms (e.g., attitudes towards the firm and churn, Araujo et al. 2020). Based on these insights, we then interview business decision-makers to develop an overall decision-framework for the configuration and integration of fair VAs. The framework jointly considers technological, perceptional, behavioral and economic factors, to help firms to better integrate VAs subject to fairness considerations while considering the associated risks of improper configurations. In addition to obtaining a better theoretical understanding of individuals’ fairness perceptions and responses, this also serves as a profound basis for regulators to establish fairness guidelines for VAs and take actions if required.
Keywords: Algorithmic Fairness, Consumer Perceptions, Decision Framework, Effects of Unfairness, Voice Assistants

Title: Rapid Deployment of Compliant, Sensorized Anthropomorphic Robot Hands
Abstract:
Human hands offer incredible capabilities that enable them to perform a wide range of dexterous grasping and in-hand manipulation tasks. These capabilities stem from the physical complexity of hands, their passive properties and sensing capabilities. Despite significant advances in robotics and machine learning there remains a significant gap between human capabilities and those of anthropomorphic robotic manipulators. This is particularly the case for ‘contact-rich’ manipulation tasks, those whose successful completion requires intricate and complex interactions between the hand and environment. Programming and deploying these robots is also slow and limited such that their full capabilities are often not exploited.

There is a specific need for anthropomorphic robotic manipulators as they can be seamlessly integrated into human environments to perform tasks which are designed for human hand kinematics and capabilities. They are also best suited for replicating or learning control policies which are demonstrated by human hands. Developing such manipulators with human-like capabilities could be transformative in addressing current global challenges. They could help enable sustainable agriculture through precision harvesting or provide universally accessible health-care by providing human-like assistance. They could also have significant economic, social and environmental impact in a number of application areas. Such tasks include the harvesting of delicate fruits and the performance of medical procedures as well as many household tasks that humans take for granted.  The robot hands could also perform tasks that are too dangerous or harmful for human hands, such as operation in hazardous laboratories or environments.

The goal of this project is to develop anthropomorphic robotic manipulators that have the physical capabilities to perform contact-rich manipulation and can be rapidly programmed and deployed. There are two key challenges that must be addressed to achieve this goal. Firstly, current fabrication methods and technologies for hands result in significantly different kinematics and passive properties to human hands, and lack the required force control and sensing capabilities.  Secondly, current means of programming or learning control policies for these robots are slow and do not fully exploit the embodied properties of the robot. This prevents their use in real world scenarios where their true impact could be realised.

To address these challenges, I propose the development of robotic hands which leverages hybrid soft-rigid structure to create a compliant, tendon-actuated hand. Through the use of novel flexure joints and Bowden cables, compliance and distributed actuation will be introduced into the palm and thumb to close the gap between human and robot hand kinematics and capabilities. The ability to apply variable force will be achieved through torque control, and distributed sensing will be enabled through a novel sensing skin.  
To address the challenge of rapidly programming or deploying this hand, teleoperation will be used via a sensing glove, which will leverage the similarity in the robot and human hand kinematics and capabilities. By finding the appropriate parameterization of control space through motor synergies, teleoperation will then be extended to learning from demonstration, to generate more robust and closed loop control policies. This approach will be applied to tasks from three high impact scenarios.

This project will be highly disruptive due to the resulting advances in robotic hardware coupled with the ability to deploy them. The interdisciplinarity and novelty of this work makes it ambitious, however, I have the interdisciplinary knowledge, fabrication facilities and background required. This project will push the boundaries on robotic manipulation, and can serve as a springboard for other research programs to leverage the hardware and capabilities enabled by this project.
Keywords: control, manipulation, robotics, sensing, soft robotics, tactile sensing

Title: Dynamic Macromolecular Crystallography from Cryocooled Crystals
Abstract:
The function of biomolecules is intricately linked to their structures and dynamics. Traditional methods like Macromolecular crystallography (MX) and cryogenic electron microscopy performed at cryogenic temperatures only provide static structures. The next frontier in structural biology is to move beyond these static snapshots and explore dynamic structures across biologically relevant temperatures and time scales. Recent advances in room-temperature (RT) MX and time-resolved (TR) MX hold great promise, but practical challenges in sample logistics and the complexity of experimental procedures currently constrain their impact. Transporting delicate macromolecular crystals at RT to synchrotron facilities is particularly challenging and incompatible with beamline automation. In addition, such experiments often require specialized MX instrumentations, which are often not accessible or affordable. 
To address these challenges, we propose a novel approach called Cryo2RT, which aims to leverage the well-established cryogenic workflows and automation capabilities at synchrotron MX beamlines to streamline the sample logistics for RT/TR experiments. The Cryo2RT workflow is designed to integrate the best features of cryogenic and room-temperature methodologies, allowing researchers to take advantage of the automation and high-throughput capabilities of cryo-crystallography while enabling the study of dynamic structures at room temperature. We aim to simplify complicated RT/TR-MX experiments using conventional MX tools at standard MX beamlines. Specifically, we will develop (1) high-throughput RT-MX for structural-based drug design; (2) automated multiple-temperature (MT) serial MX to probe protein conformational ensembles; (3) droplet-mixing for dynamic structural enzymology; (4) microsecond TR-MX to study protein dynamics. As a proof of concept, we will combine these four areas of research with our Cryo2RT workflow and apply it to the SARS-CoV-2 3CL protease, a key target for small molecule COVID-19 therapies, and to ß-lactamase and lactonase– two enzymes that play vital roles in bacterial antibiotic resistance.
One of the key motivations behind the Cryo2RT project is to disseminate RT/MT/TR-MX techniques and workflows at other synchrotron facilities and engage the broader scientific community in exploring dynamic structures and functions. We look forward to an exciting new era in determining X-ray dynamics structures. Only through global community efforts can experimental dynamic structures expand exponentially, which is essential for advancing molecular dynamics simulation to accurately model dynamic processes and training the next generation of machine-learning methods to predict the function of biomolecules.

Title: An application-based perspective on graph representation learning and sequence modeling
Abstract:
Graph-structured data, in particular sequential data, is ubiquitous in nature and engineering systems.
In this context, machine learning models have emerged as a powerful tool for analysing relational data, e.g. pictures, speech, language corpora, time series, and networks, among others. While machine learning methods applied to sequential data is typically referred to as sequence modeling, processing data given as general graphs (i.e., not necessarily regular grids) is referred to as graph representation learning or graph-based learning. Popular choices of machine learning models for sequence modelling are Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) with famous examples including Long Short-Term Memories (LSTMs) and Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), as well as more recently Transformers with famous examples including BERT and GPT. Message-passing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as the default machine learning model for graph-structured data with Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) and Graph Attention Networks (GAT) being prominent examples in this context.

Despite their successes it is known that RNNs and Transformers as well as GNNs suffer from central issues that makes it difficult to apply them to real-world data, e.g. RNNs struggle to learn long-term dependencies (LTDs) on account of the so-called exploding and vanishing gradients problem, the performance of Transformers is impaired on sequential decision making tasks, and deep GNNs suffer from the over-smoothing issue. Most, if not all, of these issues arise in applications in robotics as well as in the context of scientific computing, where higher-order interactions need to be learned over very long time-scales. Therefore, we propose for this SNF fellowship to analyse and construct novel approaches in sequence modeling and graph-based learning through an application-driven perspective on problems in scientific computing and robot learning.

In this project, we first aim to formalize a central issue in graph representation learning, referred to as over-squashing, which is known to significantly impair the performance of deep GNNs.
Afterwards, we focus on leveraging graph representation learning to solve partial differential equations (PDEs). In particular, we aim to incorporate structure from multi-scale dynamical systems into graph-based machine learning models to obtain more accurate predictions for multi-scale PDE systems. Moreover, based on the insights gained from formalizing over-squashing, we aim to improve the wiring of the underlying computational graph such that it is more efficient (i.e., mitigates over-squashing) as well as incorporates non-local information of the solution field. In the second half of our project, we focus on applying state-of-the-art (SOTA) sequence models and graph-based learning to problems in robotics. More concretely, we model the communication of multi-robot systems as GNNs and address several issues in this context, namely the challenges of expressive and efficient communication. Finally, we leverage sequence models to address major challenges in offline reinforcement learning, i.e., learning LTDs as well as using self attention for sequential decision making.
Keywords: Graph Neural Networks, Graph Representation Learning, Recurrent Neural Networks, Robot Learning, Scientific Computing, Sequence Modeling, Transformers

Title: Unveiling Mediators of Heterogeneity in PDAC carrying TP53 and KRAS mutations
Abstract:
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the deadliest cancers, with a mere 10% five-year survival rate due to late detection and therapy resistance. With only 20% of patients eligible for curative surgery at diagnosis, there is an urgent need for innovative approaches to both detection and treatment. This proposal addresses fundamental gaps in PDAC biology by investigating the epigenetic and transcriptional heterogeneity underlying tumor evolution and therapeutic resistance, particularly in the context of TP53 and KRAS mutations.
Our multi-pronged approach combines cutting-edge single-cell multiomics (ATAC-seq and RNA-seq) with epigenetic Cytometry by Time of Flight (CyTOF) to create comprehensive profiles of individual PDAC cells. Novel computational tools will integrate these datasets to identify distinct cellular subpopulations and correlate epigenetic patterns with key mutations.
Using patient-derived organoids (PDOs), we will investigate how epigenetic drugs, chemotherapies, and KRAS inhibitors influence tumor heterogeneity and cell survival. Artificial intelligence models will be developed to simulate drug responses at the single-cell level, enabling prediction of optimal treatment strategies.
A key deliverable is EPINUC-PDAC, an advanced platform for detecting PDAC-specific epigenetic signatures and protein biomarkers from plasma nucleosomes at single-molecule resolution. This tool will be validated using samples from both healthy donors and PDAC patients, with machine learning algorithms developed to classify samples and monitor treatment efficacy.
This research will provide unprecedented insights into PDACs epigenetic and transcriptional landscape, revealing how TP53 and KRAS mutations drive tumor evolution and therapy resistance. The findings will identify novel therapeutic targets while delivering a non-invasive diagnostic tool for early detection. Beyond PDAC, this integrated approach to genetic and epigenetic analysis has broad implications for cancer diagnosis and treatment.

Title: Solvable Models of Learning with Artificial Neural Networks
Abstract:
Deep learning brought remarkable progress into many applied domains. Yet it is surrounded by many theoretical questions about its functioning, properties, and limitations. We still do not know how to predict the number of samples needed for a given neural network to learn a given task nor why a highly non-convex loss landscape can be efficiently explored by a gradient-based descent to find minima of good generalization properties.

Understanding neural networks require understanding the subtle interplay between the structure of the data, the architecture of the network, and the efficiency of the learning algorithm. While many classical approaches are omitting one or two of them, our approach is based on statistical physics methods to describe high-dimensional spaces and probability distributions together with the theoretical physics paradigm of building simplified models that never-the-less capture the behaviour and properties that we aim to explain. With this approach, we address a range of the key open theoretical question about learning with neural networks keeping into consideration the interplay between data, architecture and algorithm.

In this project we work our way towards a theory of learning with neural networks that will one day be able to predict the needed number of samples, explain why overparametrization is needed and under which condition, predict which versions of learning algorithms will have the best performance, give guarantees on the uncertainty of the learned functions, or design algorithms that require fewer data and smaller networks thus mitigating the hunger for computational resources that machine learning currently suffers from. The proposed work will also have an impact back on the physics of disordered systems as the key technical problems we are proposing to solve are also of interest there (e.g. systems
with non-i.i.d. disorder, or an explicit description of out-of-equilibrium dynamics).

The proposed work is divided into 4 work packages (WP). WP1 where we study how the structure of data influences learning largely inspired by recent striking results on universality with simple Gaussian models of data. In WP2 we build a theory of gradient-based algorithms that is able to predict and analyze their trajectory in non-convex landscapes. In WP3 we aim to solve the problem of extensive rank matrix factorization that is currently the main bottleneck in carrying forward the overall program of analyzing multi-layer neural networks in an explicit form. WP4 builds on the
results of WP3 (and WP1-2) to provide an analytic understanding of learning with multi-layer neural networks.
Keywords: Analysis of algorithms, Exactly solvable models, Learning theory, Machine learning, Replica Method, Statistical Physics, Theory of Neural Networks, Theory of disordered systems

Title: Daily Weather Reconstructions to Study Decadal Climate Swings
Abstract:
On top of anthropogenic changes, the climate system exhibits mulitannual-to-multidecadal variability that is relevant for society, but not well understood. Decades of warm, dry European summers, cold winters or storm or flood rich periods have been observed in the past and will recur in the future. Long records are required to study this variability. To better understand the underlying processes, we will analyse such periods on a daily time scale by generating daily weather reconstructions and ana-lysing them together with monthly reconstructions and model simulations. Atmospheric processes operate on short time scales and it is often weather rather than climate that matters for society. Recon-structing weather rather than climate is thus closer to the mechanisms and closer to impacts. 
Several long European measurement series are available, but more information is required for daily weather reconstruction. The first part of the project will provide additional daily measurement series as well as weather diaries for central Europe. Our work will focus on the period 1683-1737; we will rely on available sources for later periods. The second part of the project will provide daily weather reconstructions back to 1683 in two ways. (1) We will provide daily weather types for Central Europe back to the 17th century based on measurements and observations from weather diaries using a machine-learning classification algorithm. (2) We will provide daily fields of temperature, precipi-tation, and sea-level pressure for central-western Europe back to the 18th or 17th century using an analog approach. Analogs will be sampled from daily 0.1° resolved fields (E-Obs) and augmented using a data assimilation (Ensemble Kalman Filter) algorithm. The fields will be used for the analyses. We will also generate impact-relevant indices such as growing degree days, frost days, and dry spells.
The third part of the project provides subdaily high-resolution fields using data assimilation and dy-namical donwscaling. Title: Learning-based 3D Infant Face and Head Model for Medical Applications
Abstract:
Realistic 3D digital models of human heads and faces have the potential to transform current
medical practices for pre-treatment diagnostics, treatment planning, patient documentation and
quantitative assessment of treatments. In contrast to entertainment where 3D digital faces have
become stunningly detailed and realistic with the help of artificial intelligence (AI), medical settings entail several challenges due to the small sizes of real patient data and under-representation of different age groups in the existing datasets.

In this project, we aim at building high-quality models of the human infant face and head learned from real datasets that derive from the medical treatment of infants. Using these models as priors, we will develop methods to reconstruct individual optimal target morphologies, which can be used as a reference in the treatment planning of infants with craniofacial malformations. 3D morphable models (3DMMs), which are classical and powerful tools for face modeling, have not been explored in depth for infant face and head modeling and the use of models for adults gives suboptimal results on infants. Therefore, our starting point will be developing these models for infants. To increase the quality of modeling and to obtain photo-realistic reconstructions, we will design generative adversarial networks (GANs). Since the knowledge of underlying bone structure is an integral part of treatment planning for craniofacial malformations, we then develop deep learning-based methods to reconstruct the skull using 3D face and head surface scans, as an alternative to computed tomography (CT) scans with the goal of reducing the ionized radiation burden on infants.

We focus on three common craniofacial malformations observed in infants: positional cranial deformity, cleft lip and palate and craniosynostosis. For each type of these malformations, we will conduct clinical assessments of the computational methods that we will develop on patient data originating from the specific craniofacial treatments.

Our work proceeds according to the following work packages (WPs): We first develop high-quality 3DMMs (WP1) and deep learning methods (WP2) for craniofacial modeling and treatment planning for infant heads and faces. We then design deep learning-based methods for skull reconstruction (WP3). In parallel to this computer graphics research at ETH, we conduct data collection and clinical validations at the University of Basel for each of the infant craniofacial malformations that we address in this project (WP4-WP6). 

In this collaboration between two major Swiss engineering and medical institutions, we expect
to achieve a highly valuable impact in the intersection of computer science and medicine. The
developed AI-based solutions will not only forward the state-of-the-art in computer graphics and
face modeling, but will also have a high potential to facilitate malformation treatments, decrease
the burden on physicians and increase the satisfaction of patients. In the future, the developed
methods can be extended for adults and other anatomical malformations. The insights gained
in the project will also be valuable for potential applications such as surgery training, surgery
simulation and virtual reality-based surgery.
Keywords: 3D infant face models, Computer graphics, Deep learning, Infant craniofacial malformations

Title: Discovering the connectome spectral signatures of behavior
Abstract:
BACKGROUND and RATIONAL Many types of neuroimaging data are nowadays represented as networks, i.e. connectomes. This approach is very promising since it captures efficiently information that is represented in a biologically relevant fashion. It has helped, over the last 10 years, to improve our understanding of the organization of the brain, how brain functional activity is related to the underlying structure, characterized the networks alterations related to diseases or declining cognition. However, we are is still facing difficulties when it comes to fingerprinting specific phenotypes and disentangling population differences, i.e. developing useful biomarkers. This is related to the way traditionally phenotypes and brain networks are represented and analyzed. Indeed, behavioral phenotypes have historically been subject to a categorial classification (e.g. DSM), while phenotypes most likely span over a continuum of multiple behavioral dimensions from normal to pathologic. This latter view is currently promoted by the Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) scheme with the hope of tightening the link with the underlying biology. On the other side brain graph analytics is facing difficulties related to the fact that the explicit graph representation is a challenging combinatorial object to analyze. Hence solely “simple” or “hand crafted” nodal or edge measures are used, hence limiting the characterization of graphs. Graph spectral analysis enables to express fully graph related signals as a spectrum of orthogonal functions (i.e. harmonics) via the Graph Fourier Transform (GFT). This approach has already proven its utility in many contexts of physics and biology. More particularly, the decomposition of the brain into spatially distributed functional systems that relate to specific behavioral domains is well established and strongly overlaps with the resting state networks, which themselves have been expressed in sparse graph Fourier spectra. GFT is the linear form of more general methods that aim at embedding data on a relevant representation. Such network embeddings techniques, of which the most powerful are based on deep learning, come as a solution in non-linear systems, and learn directly from the data structure the optimal projection to express the data as a sparse spectrum. 
OBJECTIVES MR connectomics provides a large diversity of functional and structural brain graphs. Those multi-modal connectomes contain rich subject specific information that is potentially related to cognition/behavior, as well as psychopathology. We propose to express connectomics data as a graph spectrum and show that specific behavioral and psychopathologic dimensions relate to specific sparse spectral representations. Hence, we expect to discover specific connectome spectral signatures (brain imaging biomarkers) of behavioral and psychopathology domains. 
METHODS TO BE USED (1) We will work with 2 MRI neuro-imaging cohorts, the open Human Connectome Project cohort (for behavior and cognition) and the Lausanne Psychosis Cohort for psychopathology. (2) In terms of projection methods, we will first, express each subject’s connectome graph signal (e.g. cortical thickness) as a spectrum using graph Fourier transform and in a second step use supervised deep autoencoding to define data driven spectra of entire multimodal connetomes. (3) Behavior and psychopathology are expressed in terms of continuous domains using either the RDoc framework or data driven groupings using factor analysis. (4) Linking behavior to connectome spectra is done by using either multiple regression analysis for the linear case and gradient descent on the auto-encoded embedding space. 
EXPECTED RESULTS With this work we should be able to obtain A) for each subject an individual connectome spectral signature correlating to its behavioral profile (hence defining a new imaging biomarker); B) at the population level we will be able to characterize each behavioral domain with a unique connectome spectrum. 
IMPACT The advent of MR connectomics is an unprecedented chance to develop relevant imaging biomarkers of behavior and psychopathology. However appropriate tools are still lacking. Here we propose a principled method for such discovery, which will find its application in a broad range of scientific and clinical disciplines. Furthermore, the presented method can be applied to discover other biomarkers, e.g. of genomic and other biologic traits.
Keywords: behavior, brain MRI, cognition, connectome, deep learning, graph fourier transform, network science, neuroimaging biomarkers, psychosis, variational autoencoder

Title: QuanTOR – Quantitative Analysis of Textual Organisation across Registers
Abstract:
In linguistic research, registers are usually analysed at the level of 
entire texts, despite the fact that common definitions of register are 
linked to the situational context. Situations unfold dynamically over 
time and language users make different choices at different points in 
this process. As a consequence, texts are linguistically different at the 
beginning, in the middle and at the end, and this dynamic organisation
at the sub-textual level needs to be integrated in register studies. This
project aims at enriching linguistic register studies with an account of 
the dynamic nature of situations and hence registers as well as 
quantitative methods for studying this phenomenon. Our focus on the 
temporal dynamics of text organisation requires an approach that is 
capable of extracting patterns of linguistic features and the underlying 
(latent) dimensions of variation from short text segments. It also 
necessitates automatic identification and classification of relevant 
segments in order to scale to the analysis of very large corpora. In 
order to achieve these goals, the project adopts a three-pronged 
approach to corpus analysis, leveraging the respective expertise of its
three applicants. Our work programme combines linguistic 
interpretation, theory development and manual annotation with 
multivariate quantitative analysis as well as unsupervised and 
supervised machine learning. To this end, we develop a novel 
Bayesian version of Geometric Multivariate Analysis, a reliable and 
fine-grained approach to the investigation of linguistic variation, as 
well as machine-learning approaches for the segmentation and 
labelling of texts that apply state-of-the-art neural and statistical 
language models. In an iterative process, we develop a theory of the 
dynamics of language use in situational context, a gold standard of 
manually segmented and labelled texts, the BayesGMA approach for 
studying multivariate feature distributions in text time, as well as 
readily applicable language models for automatic text segmentation 
and labelling. All components and quantitative results are carefully 
evaluated and validated. The project uses components of the 
International Corpus of English (ICE), which not only facilitate the 
analysis of temporal dynamics across a range of different registers – 
in the spoken and written mode – but also allow us to submit 
theoretical claims to an empirical test, for instance, concerning the 
theoretical relationship between genre and register. The results of the 
computationally supported corpus analysis will provide a new 
perspective on a theory of register as a dynamic linguistic reflection of
human behaviour in situational context, based on quantitative 
empirical insight, which, in turn, will feed into our understanding of the
architecture of language.
Keywords: World Englishes, computational linguistics, corpus linguistics, genre, quantiative linguistics, regional variation, register studies, stylistics

Title: TomoPath: High-resolution analysis of protein packing flexibility by in situ structural biology showcased on dynamics of corynephage architecture.
Abstract: Flexibility of functional biomolecules is one of the major factors that prevent the characterization of protein structures at high-resolution in their physiological context, and thus, the use of cryo-electron microscopy for the completion of mechanical studies. In this project, we will show how a new multidisciplinary Ansatz allows to integrate techniques of biophysical modeling into the analysis of in situ cellular data acquired by cryo-electron tomography on active corynephages, leading to the characterization at atomic resolution of the multiple conformations adopted locally by capsid, tail and fiber proteins at different functional stages. The different scales of the phage architecture will thus be analyzed simultaneously, enabling a dynamic interpretation of the interaction between its different building pieces. Our main goal is to reformulate subtomogram averaging so that it is driven by molecular dynamics simulations harnessed by artificial intelligence. Such advance framework will be integrated in the open-source software package Dynamo for subtomogram averaging. Generalization of the developed algorithms will be explicitly considered, with a final aim at offering flexible, well documented computational tools to the community.
Keywords: cryo-electron tomography, deep learning, in situ structural biology, molecular dynamics, subtomogram averaging

Title: Artificial intelligence for patient information and self management support in childhood cancer survivorship
Abstract:
Background. Childhood cancer survivors (CCS) are at a high risk of experiencing late effects of treatment, which include chronic conditions and secondary malignancies that can affect their quality of life and lead to premature mortality. Therefore, CCS and their caregivers must be informed about these risks, empowered to self-manage their well-being, and attend lifelong long-term follow-up (LTFU) care to address any complications in time. Despite the abundant information available to CCS and their families, they still report multiple information needs after treatment, mainly because they struggle to select information relevant to their context.
Aims. The proposed project aims to: 1) identify ways in which artificial intelligence (AI) can support CCS and their families during cancer survivorship; 2) assess perceptions about beliefs, benefits, and barriers associated with the use of AI-based e-health tools for patient information, self-management, and health monitoring among CCS and their caregivers; and 3) develop a concept AI-based e-health tool to support CCS and their families during cancer survivorship.
Methods. The proposed project will be conducted at the University of Oslo (Norway) and consists of three studies, one to address each aim. The first study is a systematic literature review of state-of-the-art empirical research on existing tools that use AI-based technologies to provide patient information and support self-management and health monitoring in oncology survivorship. The data extracted from the included studies will be analyzed using narrative synthesis and, if feasible, meta-analysis. The second study is a cross-sectional questionnaire-based survey. CCS older than 14 years (n=350) and their caregivers will be surveyed about their use and perceptions about AI-based technologies for health-related purposes, including information, self-management, and health monitoring. Collected data will be analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics. The third study will use focus groups with stakeholders (n=30, including a subgroup of CCS and their caregivers from Study 2, as well as healthcare professionals from different areas). Focus groups will allow for gathering further in-depth insight into the needs and experiences, beliefs, and suggestions for additional features that can improve information, self-management, and health monitoring in childhood cancer survivorship. Recordings of the focus groups will be transcribed and analyzed following the principles of thematic analysis.
Results. The project will identify the possible uses of AI-based e-health tools for patient information, self-management, and health monitoring, specifically for the needs reported by the stakeholders involved in childhood cancer survivorship. Furthermore, it will provide information on the perceptions of such technologies among the possible end users, which will be essential to address before making AI-based e-health tools available to this population.
Impact. Tailored health information is a significant need reported in childhood cancer research. Using AI can reform the provision of health information to CCS and their caregivers, bridging gaps in health literacy and addressing common barriers to LTFU care attendance. The project will provide the foundation for successfully integrating AI-based tools into childhood cancer survivorship care by producing comprehensive and contextually relevant results to guide the development of medically trained and validated AI-based tools for childhood cancer survivorship.
Keywords: artificial intelligence, childhood cancer, health information, self-management, survivorship

Title: Urban Landscape Perception - Gamification of Urban Blue and Green Spaces
Abstract:
This project aims to investigate the complex interactions between urban blue and green spaces (UBGS) and urban populations through gamified crowdsourcing, focusing on how these spaces are perceived and interacted with. With an increasing global urban population, expected to rise from 55% to 68% by 2050, understanding the diverse roles of UBGS is crucial. These areas offer both ecological benefits, such as biodiversity and climate change mitigation, and social benefits, including tranquillity, recreation and aesthetic appreciation. However, the perceptions of and interactions with UBGS are not yet fully understood.

Building on previous research and the development of a gamified spatial crowdsourcing platform, this project has two main objectives: (1) to generate high-quality perceptual data through gamified participatory approaches, and (2) to analyse the interactions with and perceptions of UBGS by different socio-demographic groups. The research will address the following questions: How can we generate high-quality underlying data through inclusive and motivating participatory approaches? What are the stated and revealed perceptions and preferences of and interactions with UBGS? And, how can the generated perceptual data guide decision and policy-making processes? 

Citizen science tasks will be integrated into the spatial crowdsourcing platform to collect data in form of natural language landscape descriptions, tags, single and multiple choice questions, and in-situ images. This data will be analysed using natural language processing, computer vision, and human annotation to identify patterns and preferences. Extracted features will be translated to affordances to facilitate the comparison of different UBGS as well as to uncover correlations between subjective well-being and respective urban areas. The findings will be published in scientific journals, presented at conferences, and shared with the public.

The project is expected to produce an engaging spatial crowdsourcing platform with a growing number of participants, resulting in a rich collection of high-quality multimodal data on UBGS. Detailed cross-sectional analyses will offer new insights into how different socio-demographic groups perceive and interact with these spaces. Additionally, translating perceptions and interactions into urban affordance arrays will enable comprehensive comparisons of UBGS, informing policy and decision-making processes.

This research will significantly enhance our understanding of the socio-demographic variations in the perception and use of UBGS, contributing valuable knowledge to urban planning and policy-making. The innovative use of gamified crowdsourcing will set a precedent for inclusive and motivating data collection methods. Furthermore, by fostering an open dialogue between academics and the general public, the project will promote greater public engagement with urban sustainability issues, ultimately supporting more livable and resilient urban communities.

The project involves collaboration with the Game Technology Center (Swiss Federal Institute of Technology), the Gamification Group (Tampere University), and the Geocomputation Group (University of Zurich) to leverage interdisciplinary expertise in gamification and data analysis. The ultimate goal is to reconcile urban livability and resilience with increasing urbanisation, ensuring the well-being of urban populations in Switzerland and beyond.

Title: Using Deep Neural Networks to Bridge Clinical and Quantitative Analysis of Intracranial EEG in Epilepsy
Abstract:
The electroencephalogram (EEG) is a key diagnostic tool in epilepsy. Our project aims to bring the separated clinical and quantitative EEG (qEEG) analysis communities closer together. Using intracranial EEG recorded during the evaluation of epilepsy patients for the possibility of surgical therapy, neurologists will annotate specific wave forms (spikes, spike-and-wave discharges, focal slowing, …) that support the decision about target tissue for surgery. Results of quantitative EEG analysis will be analyzed for its relation to these specific wave forms. We will engineer generative adversarial networks (GANs, a special application of deep neural networks) to synthesize patient-specific EEG that is free of the wave forms under investigation. Comparing the results for the original and synthetic signals we will study the impact of epilepsy specific wave forms on qEEG markers. 

Scrutinizing which qEEG measures are sensitive to which clinical observations and wave forms, the project will contribute to a better clinical acceptance of quantitative methods. In the unlikely case that qEEG does not yield information complementary to visual expert analysis, engineering and computational effort can be focused towards reliable detection of the specific wave forms. Otherwise, visual analysis, which still serves as a clinical gold standard, can be enhanced by information about yet underused wave forms. In addition, channel selection for future development of computationally and energy efficient wearable and implantable devices can be supported.
Keywords: deep neural networks, electroencephalogram, epilepsy, time series analysis

Title: Mining Narratives from Large Text Corpora
Abstract:
When making sense of the world, human beings often rely on narratives: relatively simple stories or explanations that are easy to understand and relate to. For example: “Immigrants steal our jobs”, or “Taxes make people work less.” Though these narratives structure the public and political debate on many policy issues, little is known on the determinants of their formation, spread, and persistence over time (Shiller, 2017).

The major reason for this lack of evidence is that narratives are embedded in language. Researchers have not yet settled on a satisfactory automated approach to reading narratives from texts and producing reliable measurements. As social scientists have become more interested in empirically analyzing narratives, a greater need has been felt for new approaches to this challenge.

The task of this research is to leverage natural language processing tools from computer science to the challenge of measuring narratives. As outlined in this proposal, we are building a system for taking the plain text of documents and extracting latent narrative structures. We draw upon a number of recently developed techniques from deep learning, namely semantic role labeling (to extract entities and associated actions and attributes) and word embedding (to vectorize these semantic components and produce interpretable narrative clusters).

This system could be applied to a variety of future empirical applications in social science research. In the research plan, we illustrate the method with a pilot analysis of news articles about rape cases in the Times of India. The grant funding would be used to rapidly build out the narrative extraction system and apply it to an analysis of historical narratives surrounding taxation and sexual assault over the last 200 years.

This research will be useful to social scientists because a range of theoretically important questions concern phenomena that are embedded in text. The proposed methods will help researchers analyze the role of narratives in political and cultural change. Therefore the scientific benefits could be substantial, but this research would not have been feasible even five years ago since the language tools did not exist. Admittedly, even now there is significant risk in this project as the proposed system may not work satisfactorily. The applicant hopes that the revewers will agree that the potential benefits outweigh these potential risks.
Keywords: computational linguistics, narratives, political economy, quantitative history
