Title: Alternative Media, Alternative Norms? Understanding the Effects of Mainstream and Alternative News Media on Norms of Compliance and Opposition in Times of Crisis
Abstract:
Most measures of crisis management only fulfil their full potential if the majority in the population complies with them. Social norms indicate what others do (descriptive norms) and approve of (injunctive norms) and are thus a key mechanism for coordinating collective action. This has been demonstrated in the context of the Covid-19 pandemic and is currently being discussed regarding the climate crisis. However, not all people adhere to population-wide social norms and engage in collective efforts; instead, certain groups of people share norms of measure opposition. This not only influences the effectiveness of crisis measures but also increases the polarization of society. 
The present project aims to understand opposition to majority norms of risk mitigation in the context of the climate crisis. It therefore introduces the notion of alternative norms, which refers to norms of measure non-compliance, critique, and protest, and interrogates the role of alternative media in the formation of such norms. As a full understanding of “alternativeness” requires the consideration of the counterpart – the “mainstream” – the project will examine both alternative and mainstream processes of norm formation. This allows for gaining a comprehensive picture of the society’s resources for handling crises. The specific aims of the project are to (1) describe the prevalence of the use of mainstream and alternative media and mainstream and alternative norms regarding the climate crisis; (2) identify differences between mainstream and alternative media in their coverage of norms of the climate crisis; and (3) analyse the relationship between the use of (alternative) news media and the development of (alternative) norms regarding the climate crisis within the population. 
These aims will be addressed in three work packages, which will be undertaken in the German-speaking part of Switzerland. The first work package will assess (mainstream and alternative) media use and norms in the context of the climate crisis, based on a three-wave panel study in the German-speaking area of Switzerland (W1: N = 1,900, Sep 2024; W2: N = 1,330, Mar 2025; W3: N = 1,000, Sep 2025). The quota-based online survey will be administered in cooperation with the research institute Intervista. The second work package will compare the coverage of crisis norms of German-speaking mainstream and alternative news media with the widest reach. To this end, it will use two approaches that will complement and validate each other in several terms (e.g., variables, sample): a) a manual content analysis of the valence and salience of climate crisis measures, conducted with the Research Center for the Public Sphere and Society at UZH and b) an artificial intelligence-based content analysis to identify norm messages, in cooperation with the Linguistic Research Infrastructure at UZH. The third work package will link the survey and content analysis data to analyse the relationship between the use of mainstream and alternative media and the formation of mainstream and alternative norms regarding the climate crisis.
The project will make three main contributions. First, it will be the first study to provide an empirical description of the German-speaking Swiss society in terms of norms of measure compliance and opposition as well as (alternative) media use, which will help in assessing its resources to manage the climate crisis. Second, the project will provide insights on the meaning of alternative media in today’s society by revealing how they cover crisis topics and related norms in comparison to mainstream media. Third, the results will add a nuanced understanding of the process of norm formation in times of crisis by disentangling influences of mainstream and alternative media in different societal groups. These findings are more relevant than ever given that humanity is currently facing multiple severe crises that require a tremendous collective effort to mitigate a global polycrisis.
Keywords: Alternative Media, Climate Crisis, Crisis Communication, Medie Effects, News Media, Social Norms, climate change, collective action, content analysis, longitudinal design, media effects, quantitative research, risk mitigation, social norms, survey study

Title: Practical algorithms with rigorous guarantees for large-scale semidefinite programming
Abstract:
With the ever-growing data sizes along with the increasing complexity of the data models, modern applications in science and engineering impose heavy burdens on computational resources. As a result, there is a recent trend where heuristic approaches with unverifiable assumptions are overtaking more rigorous, conventional methods at the expense of reproducibility.  

Storage, rather than arithmetic computation, is the critical bottleneck that prevents us from solving many large scale optimization problems. 
For example, semidefinite programs (SDP) often have low-rank solutions that can be represented with O(n)-storage, yet SDP algorithms require us to store a matrix decision variable with size O(n^2). This observation leads to a question central to my research: Suppose that the solution to an optimization problem has a compact representation. Can we develop storage-optimal algorithms that provably approximate a solution to this problem?

With my collaborators, we have proposed a new convex optimization paradigm that achieves this goal for a model problem. This proposal describes my future research directions in three inter-related thrusts, which aims to turn our theoretical findings into a practical algorithm. 

(1) The first thrust aims to extend our paradigm for other templates including the general SDPs. This requires developing algorithms that can operate without direct knowledge of the decision variable, and that forms the decision variable as a stream of compact updates (e.g., sparse or low-rank). The most established approaches to design such algorithms are based on the conditional gradient frameworks, which are contingent to slow sublinear convergence rates. Since our target problems do not admit desirable global geometric properties (typically nonsmooth), we will explore convex optimization methods that can adapt to the local geometry for better empirical performance. 

(2) Many SDP formulations require the problem data to be readily available. However, in many modern applications, the data can be streaming, or simply too large to work with. This thrust aims to attack SDPs in stochastic settings. The main challenge is twofold: First, the literature on stochastic SDP formulations (in particular with stochastic constraints) is relatively young and immature. Second, the majority of the stochastic conditional gradient methods rely on an increasing mini-batch size, which eventually eliminates the storage benefits. 

(3) Optimization on manifolds is well suited for dealing with the low-rank constraints that arise in SDP templates. Geometric structures such as geodesic convexity play a crucial role in the analysis and design of effective optimization algorithms. Expanding Riemannian optimization for generic SDPs is an important and challenging task, both in deterministic and stochastic settings. This thrust explores the benefits and limitations of manifold optimization for low-rank matrix optimization problems. 

SDP formulations are key in signal processing, machine learning, and other engineering applications. By greatly enhancing the scalability of optimization methods for solving SDPs, my research has the potential to unlock new results in important scientific applications, including quadratic assignment, optimal power flow, and Fourier ptychographic microscopy imaging.  With my expertise in the field, the resources of my host institute, and the experience of the principal investigator Prof. Suvrit Sra, I am confident about achieving these goals.
Keywords: convex optimization, large-scale optimization, matrix sketching, non-convex optimization, projection-free methods, semidefinite programming, semidefinite relaxation, stochastic optimization

Title: Algorithmic sorting in education
Abstract:
The digital transformation of education raises pressing issues of social justice. This is specifically true for currently emergent technologies that employ artificial intelligence (AI) to sort and classify students for different purposes. The potential uses of such AI-based tools include automatic grading of exams, adapting learning content to individual needs and interests, providing tailored feedback, matching tasks to students’ motivational states, or supporting classroom management. Although mostly still in a development stage, these technologies have already yielded considerable debate regarding their social consequences. Numerous studies argue that AI-based sorting will enhance educational equity by radically personalizing teaching and learning. Recent critical scholarship has challenged these claims, maintaining that algorithmic black-boxes might actually reinforce rather than abolish educational disadvantages. These studies highlight that whether or not AI-based technologies will ever develop into equitable and practicable pedagogical tools will depend on many choices made during their development and implementation, such as the kind of algorithmic technique employed, the data used to train algorithms, the way social categories are represented and processed, or the concrete pedagogical settings they are eventually applied in. The problem that motivates the proposed project is that  we know little about how these various decisions are made, negotiated, and justified. 

Against this background, this study’s objective is to understand the interplay of normative assumptions, pedagogical and technological imaginaries, and professional practices that shape the formation and implementation of AI-based technologies “on the ground”. Its main research question is how actors from two key fields of practice – teaching and technology – envision and shape the role of algorithmic sorting in education. Although the relations, intersections, and tensions between these two fields are crucial for understanding how educational technologies function as pedagogical and social devices, they have so far hardly ever been studied in their interplay.

The project builds on French pragmatic sociology to grasp the complexity of normative considerations, socio-technical visions, institutional settings, technologies, and everyday work situations at play in these processes. On this basis, the study moves beyond existing research by putting the plurality of moral orders (including understandings of educational equity and justice) and the deep entanglement of normative and factual judgements (of what seems desirable and of what seems plausible and necessary in a given educational and social context) centre stage. Empirically, the study investigates (1) how actors in teaching and technology draw on different established understandings of “good and fair school education” when imagining and evaluating the role of algorithms in education, (2) how these understandings translate into concrete technological designs and educational practices, and (3) what tensions arise within and between both fields of practice that help understand the equitable or discriminatory potentials of AI-based tools in education. 

The project employs a qualitative research strategy that combines two components: (A) Focus groups are organized at different institutions in Germany and Switzerland to unravel normative, pedagogical, and technological visions and assumptions that guide how actors reason about algorithmic sorting in education. (B) In-depth case studies are conducted with participants from both fields to investigate how these visions and assumptions relate to everyday professional practices. A series of interdisciplinary synthesis workshops is organized to relate findings from focus groups and case studies across fields of practice and to systematically link analyses to ongoing research in the sociology of education and critical data studies. On this basis, the study will significantly further understanding of how AI-based tools might transform social sorting in education and will allow to identify key points to be considered for designing and using algorithmic sorting in an equitable and sustainable manner.
Keywords: algorithms, artificial intelligence, big data, critical data studies, qualitative research, school education, social sorting, sociology of critique

Title: Computational Capabilities of Brain-Like Models
Abstract:
How does the brain compute? How is the information encoded and processed in the brain? What makes the brain so much more appropriate than classical computers for several intelligent tasks? What are the computational potentialities of the brain? Do they transcend the limits of classical Turing machines?

The general understanding of the mind and its processes obviously represents a most challenging scientific issue. In this context, the encoding and processing of information in biological as well as in artificial neural networks is nowadays being studied from a wide range of multi-disciplinary perspectives, spanning from strictly experimental to purely theoretical methods. This global line of research has not only led to invaluable implications in cognitive science and neurophysiology in general, yet also to relevant achievements in the fields of artificial intelligence, machine learning, bio-inspired computing, robotics, etc.

In theoretical neural computation, the issue of the computational capabilities of brain-like models has mainly been approached from a so-called comparative perspective, which consists in comparing the computational powers of various neural models to those of diverse abstract machine models of computation. In this context, the computational potentialities of a multitude of neural network models have been shown to be able to range from the finite state automata up to the super-Turing level.

The proposed research project aims to pursue this theoretical approach to neural computation, by studying the computational capabilities of neural network models capturing relevant biological features and involved in biologically plausible paradigms of computation. Our goal consists in providing a precise characterization of the expressive power of various recurrent neural network models in terms of their attractor dynamics. The expected characterizations have to be provided at two distinct levels: first, in terms of computational equivalence between the neural network models under consideration and some specific abstract machine model; second, in terms of the topological complexity of the neural languages recognized by the neural models under consideration.

The methodology used in this research project lies at the crossroads of of Mathematics, Theoretical Computer Science, and Neuroscience. The biological specificities to be included in our models come from purely neuroscientific considerations. The modelling task of the neural networks involves a mathematical approach. The characterization of the computational capabilities of the neural models are studied from a theoretical computer scientist and a mathematical perspective.

From a general viewpoint, the proposed research direction aims at understanding those intrinsic features of neural computation which, if they exist, lie beyond the Turing barrier of computation -- in the set of super-Turing potentialities. Accordingly, such comparative studies between the computational capabilities of brain-like models and abstract machine models might ultimately bring further insight to the understanding of the intrinsic natures of both biological and artificial intelligences.

More globally, the proposed project presents some significance beyond the philosophical issue of the possibility of hypercomputational capabilities in neural systems or in nature in general. In fact, similarly to the theoretical work from Turing which played a seminal role in the practical realization of modern computers, further foundational studies of alternative models of computation might as well not only lead to relevant theoretical considerations, yet also to the emergence of novel computational technologies and algorithmic methods, and step by step, open the way to the next computational era. Our research project hopes to make a step in that direction.
Keywords: analog computation, attractors, automata theory, computability theory, computational power, evolving dynamical systems, hypercomputation, neural computation, recurrent neural networks, super-Turing, theoretical computer science

Title: Consumer Perceptions of AI-enabled Technologies
Abstract: Groundbreaking advances in artificial intelligence (AI) permit today’s virtual assistants (e.g., Amazon Alexa or Google Assistant) to develop from reactive to proactive agents, capable of initiating their own behavior and of making decisions autonomously on behalf of consumers. Proactive agents (PAs) are highly promising due to their potential to improve efficiency and reduce costs while increasing consumers’ convenience. However, drawing on research in consumer behavior, information systems, and innovation management, we argue that PAs challenge well-established human-machine interactions due to the delegation of decisions and experiences to technology. Furthermore, PAs may endanger the meaningfulness of consumers’ lives, as they deprive consumers of opportunities to generate meaning by completing everyday tasks. Based on a scenario-inspired qualitative study in emerging and developed markets, we identified trade-offs between functional and psychological consumption motives in connection with PAs. In addition, preliminary experimental evidence suggests that task delegation to PAs can affect consumers’ meaning in life. The primary objective of the proposed program of research is to shed light on how consumers perceive and use PAs. A series of studies aim to quantitatively validate the preliminary findings and to investigate the key success factors determining whether PAs tend to be either beneficial or harmful to consumers. The proposed research contributes to the literature on consumer behavior, information systems, and innovation management by advancing our understanding of the implications of AI-enabled technologies for consumers and society at large.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Autonomous Products, Consumer Behavior, Innovation Management, Meaning in Life, Smart Technologies

Title: ISAAC: Infinite Symmetry in Algebra, Applications, and Computability
Abstract:
In a time when the opportunities and curses of high-dimensional data are dawning upon us, and statisticians, computer scientists, and engineers develop increasingly complex mathematical models, an important task emerges for mathematicians: to develop the mathematical theory that underlies tomorrow's models.

Over the last decade, it has become clear that this endeavour touches all of mathematics, not just those areas traditionally thought of as applied maths. Two new facets are commutative algebra and algebraic geometry. On the one hand, existing algebraic and algebro-geometric techniques are being applied to problems in areas as diverse as machine learning, computer vision, and evolutionary biology.  On the other hand, these areas call for new mathematical theory---especially in algebra and geometry, where a key challenge is in dealing with very high-dimensional models.

Project ISAAC is situated on the latter side of this interaction. From challenges arising in the sciences, we distill new algebraic and geometric research questions, we will develop the theory required to answer these, and we will close the cycle by disseminating our work among researchers in the original areas of application.  In ISAAC, it is the systematic use of symmetry in all its manifestations that enables us to deal with high-dimensional models effectively.

More specifically, in ISAAC we will 
- develop the theory of infinite, discrete families of highly symmetric algebraic models and their infinite-dimensional limits;
- develop finite algorithms that can deal with these (a priori infinite) structures; and
- extend our understanding of the algebraic matroids arising from such families.

Throughout the project, graphical statistical models serve as an important source of examples, both as testing ground for our new mathematical methods and because of their central role in current applications.

ISAAC builds on recent developments and breakthroughs in commutative algebra and its applications to which my collaborators and I have already made significant contributions. Our recent work most relevant to this project includes general finiteness results forclosed subsets of polynomial functors; research on algebraic matroids that streamlines and generalises work from 1980's; work on algebraic techniques for minimising the distance from a data point to a real-algebraic variety; and algebraic-combinatorial research of several graphical models.
Keywords: Algebraic matroids, Applied algebraic geometry, Commutative algebra, Graphical models, Polynomial functors

Title: Inverse design of biolocomotion strategies
Abstract:
All natural creatures that swim, fly or slither share a common challenge: they are constantly confronted with the physics of the surrounding media of locomotion, water, air or ground. Whether physics can be turned to their advantage and up to which point natural creatures can push their performance within the physical limits dictated by the surrounding media, depends on their locomotion strategies.

During millions of years of evolution animals have refined their shapes, gaits and collective behaviors to master the complex interplay between their bodies, their senses and the environment. This constant effort has produced and extraordinary rich array of solutions which often largely outperforms current engineering designs, and that work in ways we still do not fully understand. Yet, they bear a great potential for technological innovation .

Here we wish to inquire into the fundamental physical mechanisms underlying swimming, flying and slithering phenomena via automatic inverse design methods based on numerical simulations, theoretical modeling and robot replicas. We set a goal, for example maximum energetic efficiency, and we numerically `evolve' solutions (shapes, gaits or collective behaviors) to optimally achieve the specified goal in a given environment. The virtual optimized solution is then theoretically analyzed and compared with both biological and robot replicas experimental data. This approach allows us to: 1) identify optimal solutions in relation to a purpose. 2) unveil by direct comparison the function of existing natural designs and inquire into their optimality. 3) analyze and experimentally test optimized designs to understand the mechanisms at play.

The rationalization of the fundamental principles underlying swimming, flying and slithering is certainly a challenging problem, but it carries the promise of being beneficial in a wide range of engineering applications, from collaborating underwater devices and swarms of unmanned air vehicles to efficient propulsive systems as well as energy harnessing applications.
Keywords: biolocomotion, collective beahvior, flying, inverse design, optimization, reinforcement learning, slithering, swimming

Title: Intention-Aware Gaze-Based Assistance on Maps
Abstract:
The concept of “one map fits all users” is surely obsolete. Adaptive and context-aware technologies have facilitated digital maps which offer personalized assistance by sensing, inferring, and utilizing the map user’s environmental, technological, and user context. Map adaptation is specifically helpful when the interaction possibilities with the map are restricted, or when time constraints apply. Despite maps becoming increasingly adaptive, the semantic gap between the contextual information used for adaptation and the user’s high-level cognitive processes that should finally be supported remains high. If a map-based assistance system could reliably infer a user’s intentions, it would be able to provide highly personalized assistance and support the user’s goals in an optimal way. Since vision is the primary sense for perceiving cartographic maps the user’s gaze behavior while interacting with a map is likely to provide valuable information on the user’s cognitive states in terms of intentions. With eye tracking technology it is possible to sense the user’s gaze on a cartographic map, relate it to the map contents, and use the acquired information for gaze-based adaptation. 
The proposed project envisions intention-aware gaze-based assistance on cartographic maps. A future intention-aware gaze-based assistive map could, for instance, recognize from the user’s gaze that he or she is planning a touristic round trip, and adapt to the user’s needs accordingly. The main objective of this project consists in the investigation of methods for the recognition of activities and intentions from gaze data, collected from cartographic map users. The project intends to investigate the following research questions:
1.How can visible map features (points, lines, polygons) be used to assign meaning to a user’s gaze on a cartographic map?
2.How can a map user’s activities be recognized from an incomplete gaze track (i.e., online), and how can a change in the performed activity be detected (segmentation problem)?
3.How can the recognized basic activities be combined and interpreted at a higher semantic level, i.e., with respect to the map user’s intentions?
Methods used in geographic data processing (e.g., map matching), mobile assistance systems (e.g., trajectory interpretation), activity recognition (e.g., machine learning from gaze tracks), and general plan recognition (e.g., Dynamic Bayes Models) will be extended and adapted to recognize a map user’s activities and intentions from gaze. 
The expected outcomes of the project include a) algorithmic approaches for online geometric matching of gaze with cartographic vector features, b) an evaluation of machine learning techniques for the recognition and segmentation of activities on cartographic maps, c) a methodology for the recognition of intentions from gaze on cartographic maps, d) an annotated eye tracking corpus, to be published online with the goal of stimulating further research in the eye tracking, artificial intelligence (A.I.), and geographic information science (GIScience) research communities. The eye tracking corpus will be created by collecting gaze data with studies in a controlled experimental setting (remote eye tracking) using various cartographic stimuli and tasks.
Keywords: Activity Recognition, Context, Eye Tracking, Gaze-Based Assistance, Gaze-Based Interaction, Intention Recognition, Map Adaptation

Title: Game design methodology and adapted tools for therapeutic games
Abstract:
Serious games (i.e. games having a serious purpose) are a current trend in research and industry. In our study, we are interested in Games for Health, that is, a serious games’ sub-genre where the serious purpose is to provide a therapy.
One of the biggest issues in therapy is the patient's observance or treatment adherence. As most therapies are focused on effectiveness, patients are asked to do repetitive and boring tasks. As a result, many experiments have been conducted where the patient motivation is fostered by mixing a game with the therapy, showing encouraging results. But therapeutic game design is a young and experimental field. We still have to create game design and development guidelines, as well as a set of transferable development tools, in order to improve the overall quality of therapeutic games. The same kind of work has already been tackled for Educational Games, using well established pedagogical scales and goals. Our research project intends to answer this issue, at least partially, by providing a transferable and specific game design methodology with adapted tools to design and develop therapeutic games. 
First of all, we study related works about definitions and taxonomies of serious games. We thus build a better understanding of therapeutic games and of their place in the broader scope of serious games. We also study existing therapeutic game experiments, and yet unpublished projects like Gabarello or SGCogR. These projects tackle very different therapies such as physical rehabilitation, behavior modification (e.g. treatment adherence), or cognitive rehabilitation, and provide insights on the design and development process used during the experiments.
In the same time, we study game design approaches such as player models, game component models, and models of what makes a game fun or compelling. Most of these works emphasize the player importance, as for example in Salen and Zimmerman game design definition: “Game design is the process by which a game designer creates a game, to be encountered by a player, from which meaningful play emerges”.
From the study of all these works, we are building a three-component therapeutic game model (i.e. the player, the therapy, and the game). By providing an analysis framework of existing and in-development therapeutic games, this model intends to deepen our understanding of the targeted players, games and therapies, and of their underlying relationships. Moreover, this model is also a key step for the development of our game design methodology, as it allows game designers to gather information, to formalize his work with health experts, and to get a clearer evaluation of the coherencies of their choices. For instance, a therapeutic game which intends to improve fine-motor control should reward accuracy over speed, and thus not use an as-fast-as-you-can scoring system.
The next step of our research is to analyze existing game design methods and studies on therapeutic games and other serious games. Then, we will design a modular architecture of tools for the game design and development of therapeutic games. We will study commercial game engines, as well as works on interactive storytelling tools, and artificial intelligence systems. Understanding these works will help us to design a suitable modular architecture. Then, among these tools, we will choose the most valuable one and develop it. At the end, we will integrate the tool to the under-development therapeutic game SGCogR (Serious Game for Cognitive Rehabilitation, also known as “Le village aux oiseaux”), which is a therapeutic game project in which our laboratory is involved. SGCogR aims to slow down the decline due to the Alzheimer’s disease by training attention network. The project is designed to be a full-featured game providing a game world, a story and different gameplay activities.

Title: Delineating Trees in Noisy 2D Images and 3D Image-Stacks
Abstract:
Tree-like structures appear at many different scales and in many different contexts. They can be micrometer scale dendrites in light microscopy image-stacks, centimeter-scale blood vessels in retinal scans, or meter-scale road networks in aerial images. Extracting them automatically and robustly is therefore of fundamental relevance to many scientific disciplines. However, even though the topic has received sustained attention ever since the inception of the field of Computer Vision, both robustness and automation remain elusive. Fully automated techniques exist but require very clean data; substantial amounts of manual intervention is required for any other kind.

In this project, we will therefore develop a fully automated approach to addressing these shortcomings. We will first develop an approach to finding optimal trees that accounts both for global image and geometric properties. We will then implement a practical algorithm to build near-optimal ones in an acceptably short time, even though the underlying problem is closely related to one known to be NP-Hard.
Keywords: Computer Vision, Delineation, Dendritic Trees

Title: Development of transferable machine learning potentials for simulation of metal-ligand interactions in complex environments
Abstract:
Metal complexes are ubiquitous chemical species with a broad range of applications in catalysis, functional materials, and electrochemistry. Furthermore, they are fundamental in vital biological processes, such as signaling, osmosis balance, protein assembly, and enzyme catalysis. Indeed, almost half of all enzymes require the presence of a metal atom to function, with Mg and Zn being the most prevalent species. The disruption of metal-ligand interactions in these systems leads to a large number of severe disorders, such as cancer, bacterial infections, Parkinson's, and Alzheimer's diseases. The detailed understanding of the role of the metals in the origin of the protein malfunctions and their possible treatments is, therefore, one of the biggest challenges nowadays.

Despite the profound importance of metal complexes in biochemical processes, the underlying mechanisms of action are often poorly understood as both experimental and theoretical methods to study them remain limited. Therefore, there is an urgent need for methods capable of efficiently and accurately describing metal-ligand interactions in their natural environment (e.g., in aqueous solutions and proteins). Machine learning (ML) approaches aimed at reproducing ab initio potentials offer a novel and powerful tool to model these interactions in complex chemical environments.

This fellowship aims to enhance the computational toolbox for modeling metal-ligand interactions in biological systems. I will achieve this goal by developing transferable machine learning potentials that efficiently describe metal-ligand interactions in complex environments without sacrificing the accuracy of the underlying ab initio method. I will target biochemically relevant metallo-complexes with ligands resembling peptides, drugs, and metabolic products. Small molecule-metal complexes in water, such as ATP and isocitrate in complexes with Mg2+ will serve as initial model systems, providing the foundations for modeling metallo-complexes within the enzyme's active sites.

This work will include (a) building a database of biologically relevant metal-ligand complexes; (b) assessment of the appropriate electronic structure methods for reference computations; (c) benchmark of the available descriptors and ML models; (d) training and testing of the potentials in the molecular dynamics; and (e) application of these models to study metalloproteins via the development of ML/MM interface. Overall, this project will introduce efficient computational tools that will help us advance our understanding of metallo-complexes in diverse biological environments and, consequently, the design of efficient inhibitors and drugs.

Title: PRISE Positive eneRgy dIstrict Step ahEad
Abstract:
Positive Energy Districts (PED) are a cornerstone of city-wide strategies for achieving urban sustainability and climate-neutrality, focusing on producing more energy than they consume through renewable energy integration, energy efficiency and flexibility, and systemic management. This project aims to develop an interdisciplinary, scalable framework for valorising potential PED areas within European cities, integrating energy planning with urban planning. At its core, PRISE bridges energy and urban planning, linking bottom-up community needs with top-down urban strategies through a spatially grounded, data-enhanced approach. 
Ostend (BE) serves as the primary case study and experimental ground for PRISE. In the Vuurtorenwijk district, a complex urban fabric of social and private housing, vulnerable populations, and fragmented ownership, PRISE will pilot scenario-based PED planning, including mobility and heating and cooling solutions. The presence of engaged local partners, such as Beauvent (energy cooperative), Woonsprong (social housing provider), and the city of Ostend, offers a rich ecosystem for co-creation, combining community engagement, technical innovation, and long-term regeneration strategies. An additional case study in Sion (CH) and the support of follower cities of Çankaya (TR) and Reggio Emilia (IT) further ensure geographic diversity and support the development of adaptable, Europe-wide methodologies. The case studies will serve to validate the methodology and assess its replicability and scalability across diverse urban contexts. 
After a preliminary step of mapping the existing best practices of PEDs across Europe, PRISE is structured in three key phases.  First, a Europe-wide assessment maps area-based PED readiness using a multi-scale, multi-domain framework combining geo-spatial, technical, morphological, and socio-economic data, including mobility and heating/cooling networks essential for energy flexibility and climate resilience. Machine learning techniques and participatory co-design ensure that urban typologies are matched with suitable PED pathways.
Second, PED concepts and scenarios are developed with stakeholders in the pilot sites. Here, a shared systems understanding is created using the New European Bauhaus Impact Model and the Integrated Modification Methodology. In this phase, data collection is done. This phase integrates active mobility, low-carbon heating and cooling strategies, and business model innovations (e.g., energy-as-a-service, aggregators). Title: Novel Image Processing Methods for Fetal MR Imaging: 3D Reconstruction and Segmentation with Soft Priors
Abstract:
The last decades witnessed an impressive development of image rocessing techniques devoted to the study of the human brain. Along with technical improvements and increasing sample size of the studied population, the study of the adult brain anatomy and function progressively shifted to the assessment of earliest stages of cerebral development (i.e. the postnatal brain growth). If most of neuroimaging research studies are conducted in children and adults, recent advances in clinical imaging of the fetus provide an unprecedented opportunity to image the process of the human brain growth in utero. Quantitative studies of structural fetal Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) would be of major importance in addressing the fundamental neuroscience question of early brain development. Moreover, in a clinical perspective, quantitative analysis of fetal MRI would help to better characterize the timing and the nature of prenatal pathologies, like ventriculomegaly, intra-uterine growth restriction or brain alterations in fetuses with congenital heart disease. New fast multi-slice MR techniques allow high contrast imaging of brain tissues but clinical acquisitions still have many critical limitations that restrain the use of computer-based methods for large scale studies. Consequently, the research project presented here, oriented to robust and accurate image processing methods for fetal MRI reconstruction and segmentation, will have an important impact for both neuroscience and clinics. 

Image processing methods for fetal MRI have to face major challenges like motion artifacts due to fetal movements inside the amniotic cavity, a poor spatial resolution due to fast sequences, the partial volume effect, intensity inhomogeneities, natural local intensity variations and the rapid changing anatomy of the developing fetal brain. The stateof-the-art of reconstruction and segmentation dedicated to fetal MRI is scarce. Reconstruction methods mostly rely on registration-interpolation strategies. However, these methods lack of mathematical proof of convergence and their results
present excessive blurring due to scattered data interpolation techniques. State-of-the-art segmentation methods are mostly applied to young fetus and they need anatomical priors and dynamic atlases to succeed. The use of such strong prior information faces a risk of circularity: each brain will be analyzed and deformed using the template of its biological age, potentially biasing the effective developmental delay. Thus, there is a need to develop solid mathematical framework for the fetal MRI reconstruction as well as for robust and accurate segmentation methods of fetuses at second and third trimester of pregnancy.

The primary aim of this project resides in developing advanced fetal MR imaging processing, providing significantly improved reconstruction and segmentation methods as compared to state-of-the-art techniques. The originality of our research project resides in the use of soft priors in both reconstruction and segmentation problems. By soft priors, we mean prior information coming from the image data itself, like sparsity constrains, local spatial priors or label priors. Our first contribution will be a general and flexible reconstruction framework for fetal MRI, thanks to the large versatility of the sparsity constraints and of the convex optimization methods. We aim at solving the inverse problem formulation with regularization constraints like Total Variation (TV) or Generalized TV regularization. We are supported by results in other computer vision domains, like denoising or Super Resolution (SR), where these sparsity priors proven sharp edges reconstructed images while being robust to noise and motion-corrupted frames. The problem we are facing in fetal MRI
is though more complex and thus further research will be done here, mainly dedicated to the development of iterative schemes and fast minimization algorithms to solve the 3D fetal MRI reconstruction. As regards segmentation, we aim at performing atlas-free segmentation of fetal brain tissue in MRI to avoid the risk of circularity in further quantitative
studies. We will present a flexible non-local variational framework based on a graph representation of the image with patches were any kind of regularization priors can be included, from new sparsity constraints like non-local TV to data driven priors. The use of patches (non-local information) is particularly appropriated in fetal MRI where we aim at preserving tiny structures and well-adapted to any gestational age. The proposed novel segmentation method will represent the second major methodological contribution of this project.
Keywords: Convex Minimization, Fetal imaging, Inverse problem, Magnetic Resonance Imaging, Sparsity priors, Super-resolution Reconstruction, Variational Segmentation

Title: State-dependent Sensorimotor Processing in Silicon Spiking Neural Networks
Abstract:
Spiking neural networks implemented using electronic VLSI circuits are promising information processing architectures for carrying out complex cognitive tasks in real-world applications, optimally suited for advanced and future VLSI processes.
Properly configuring these systems to solve sophisticated tasks, however, has been surprisingly difficult, mainly due to two facts: 1) the conceptual challenges in evoking sophisticated behavior with spiking neural networks, that is robust to the variability of real-world cues, and 2) the technical difficulties in mapping the spiking neuron parameters onto those of its hardware counterpart.
This project will address these problems by applying recent parameter translation techniques for mapping a desired theoretical neural network models onto the hardware, and developing state-of-the-art models of spike-based inference and decision-making. 
The objective is to synthesize a VLSI neuromorphic architecture able to control an agent in real-time to take task-relevant action in a stochastic, partially observable environment, according to a pre-determined policy.
I will demonstrate this approach using the experimental infrastructure developed at the host institute in UC San Diego, that include large-scale neuromorphic chips emulating thousands of neurons and synapses.
The achievements of this project will constrain and guide the development of new generations of brain-inspired processing systems and will contribute to bridging the gap between computational models implemented in neuromorphic neural networks and probabilistic inference algorithms.
Keywords: Computational Neuroscience, Decision Making, Learning and Plasticity, Machine Learning, Markov Decision Process, Neuromorphic Engineering, Reinforcement Learning, Robotics, Working Memory

Title: Modeling and Improving the Content and Usage of Multilingual Online Encyclopedias
Abstract:
With 27 billion words spread over 40 million articles in 293 languages, Wikipedia is the largest encyclopedia ever created. Millions of contributors have self-organized to create this vast resource in an unprecedented collaborative effort, producing a resource whose reliability is up to par with traditional encyclopedias. These impressive facts have led to a tremendous amount of research on Wikipedia and the processes by which it is created and edited.

Beside editors, however, there is another, in fact much larger, group of Wikipedia users: readers. They make Wikipedia the fifth most popular website in the world, serving hundreds of millions of pageviews to millions of users every day. It may hence at first seem counterintuitive that most research on Wikipedia’s users focuses on the smaller group of editors, while readers are much more poorly understood. It is explained, however, by the fact that the complete edit logs of all Wikimedia projects are publicly available, such that any researcher can contribute to our understanding of editor behavior, whereas usage logs need to stay private to the Wikimedia Foundation due to privacy considerations, such that only a very limited number of researchers (including the PI) can contribute to a data-driven understanding of reader behavior.

Understanding users is of paramount importance. Information systems cannot be effective without understanding users’ needs, and how they go about fulfilling them. Content and its usage are tightly coupled in this context: to study how a resource is used, we need to account for what is being used; and conversely, in order to optimize content, we need to keep in mind how it is consumed by people. Therefore, the goal of this project is to model and improve both the content and usage of Wikipedia. We structure the proposal along two principal thrusts:

Thrust I: Navigability and exploration:
An encyclopedia is a network of interconnected articles. Users find the information they require by navigating this network. The strategies by which they navigate are rather well understood in settings where they seek one precise piece of information. It is much more poorly understood in settings where they browse the network in an exploratory, rather than targeted, fashion. The PI’s group is in a unique situation to make significant progress with regard to these open questions, based on significant prior research on network navigation and by collaborating with the Wikimedia Foundation, which gives us access to Wikipedia’s access logs (including clicks on external links leading users off Wikipedia) and explicitly supports our proposed research. Based on Wikipedia’s access logs, we will conduct the first comprehensive analysis of Wikipedia reading behavior in the wild at the intended level of detail. We will turn our insights into mathematical models of navigation behavior that will form the basis for several downstream analyses and tools. For instance, we will conduct the first analysis of the evolution of Wikipedia’s hyperlink network from its inception in 2001 until today. We ask: As Wikipedia grew organically over time, did it become more or less navigable? Can we model the processes by which networks become and stay navigable? For practical impact, we will turn our insights and models into action by developing recommender systems for making suggestions to users on what content to read next.

Thrust II: Multilingual content:
Our second line of work is focused on multilingual encyclopedic content. As mentioned, content and its usage are tightly coupled. Hence, this thrust will draw on, and be useful for, the navigation models developed in the first line of work on navigability and exploration. We will research methods for supporting editors across languages via fine-grained action recommendations, suggesting what entities should be mentioned at what position in what article, by leveraging browsing logs. To facilitate the handling of multilingual content, we also propose algorithms for using Wikipedia’s multilingual content for learning to represent texts in language- independent ways, such that texts become comparable across languages, and we will put those representations to work in multiple applications.

Expected results and impact:
We expect our work to result in better models of multilingual encyclopedic content and its usage. With support from Wikimedia engineers, we will build tools for improving Wikipedia’s content and navigability across all its 200+ languages, thus improving the experience of millions of users. Moreover, navigation is everywhere on the Web, so we expect our models to be adaptable to other domains beyond encyclopedias. Similarly, the Web is just as multilingual as Wikipedia is, so we foresee a multitude of applications for our multi-lingual techniques. Finally, by understanding how users browse Wikipedia’s web of knowledge, we will also better understand how they think about the world, which will create research opportunities across field boundaries, e.g., with psychologists, cognitive scientists, and learning scientists.
Keywords: Applied machine learning, Computer science, Data mining, Data science, Multilingual content, Navigation, Network analysis, Online encyclopedias, User modeling, Web browsing, Wikipedia, World Wide Web

Title: Minimizing Door to Reperfusion Times in Drip and Ship Model for  Patients with Acute Ischemic Stroke (MDR in AIS)
Abstract:
Acute ischemic stroke (AIS) represents an important health and economic issue for Swiss National Healthcare System, as it is the second cause of mortality and the first cause of disability. AIS is a time-dependent pathology and therefore reperfusion therapies should be administered rapidly. Acute treatments include intravenous thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy (MT). For these reasons, time-dependent networks have been developed. Functional and technical outcomes of AIS patients are in close association with in-hospital stroke workflow timing. However, as avoidable delays are still an important issue, in-hospital stroke care pathways have to be improved, especially for patients primarily transferred to the closest primary stroke center (PSC) and secondarily to a comprehensive stroke center (CSC) for performing MT.
There are basically two organizational model for stroke management: the so-called “mothership” and the “drip-and-ship” (DS) approaches. 
In the first model, patients with suspected AIS are directly transferred to the CSC, which provides all diagnostic and therapeutic strategies to achieve reperfusion. This model, which is preferred in metropolitan areas, with short distances and high population density, minimizes time to MT delays.
On the contrary, in DS approach the patient is primarily transferred to the closest PSC to perform rapid diagnostic, imaging and administration of IVT followed by transport to the nearest CSC for MT, if it is indicated. This model is preferred in non-urban areas and with increasing distance between the CSC and PSC, as it is time-sparing for IVT administration, even if it cannot provide fast MT. 
Several technologic solutions, such as telemedicine assisted networks, mobile videoconferences and artificial intelligence algorithms, help to coordinate territory, PSCs and CSCs and to ensure proper selection of patients and setup of fast processes. 
Therefore, at CHUV we have developed in 2016 a streamlined in-hospital workflow for LVO AIS patients secondarily transferred to our CSC because eligible for MT, avoiding acceptance and assessment work-up at the emergency department (ED), leading to a significant gain of time. Our in-hospital workflow could be implemented with the introduction of a telemedicine application to accelerate the transfer of information and images from the PSC and our CSC.
Compared to the Siena standard in-hospital workflow, which still provides admittance at the ED, our door-to-groin (DTG) puncture is definitely lower (40 minutes vs 81 minutes). 
Vaudois Stroke Network Organization:
Our stroke network constitutes of three PSCs and one CSC at the Centre Hospitalier Universitaire Vaudois (CHUV). The catchment area covers a population of 1’500’000 inhabitants. It includes urban and non-urban areas of Sion, Nyon and Rennaz. Depending on the location of the patient presenting with AIS symptoms, the transfer can occur directly to CSC or to one of the PSC, with the decision of transportation destination performed by an emergency medical team. After a shared consultation by phone (conference call), patient deemed eligible for MT is secondarily transferred from PSC to CHUV. Blood test and neurological examen (NIHSS) performed in the PSC are sent to CHUV by e-mail with also every other medical information known before transfer. The patient is transported by helicopter or ambulance to CHUV and then directly to the angiography suite where he/she is assessed by the neurologist and the anesthesiologist. He/she undergoes CBCT scan before intervention if the clinical conditions change.  At this point, patients will undergo MT, if still eligible. 
Specific aims 1
To evaluate our performance in term of gain of time and patient clinical outcome comparing retrospectively our data before and after the introduction in 2016 at CHUV of the present in-hospital workflow, avoiding complicated and time-consuming evaluation at the ED. 
Specific aims 2
To compare our performance in term of DTG time and clinical outcome comparing retrospectively our data during the period from 1st January 2016 to 31st December 2022 with those of Siena data from 1st January 2018 to 31st December 2021.
Specific aims 3
To compare prospectively collected results of an optimized CHUV workflow with the introduction of telemedicine application to those recorded retrospectively during the period from 1st January 2016 to 31st December 2022.
Keywords: Acute Ischemic Stroke, Reperfusion Time, Thrombectomie

Title: Cognition 2.0: Physiological and Contextual Computing for Augmenting Human Cognition
Abstract: Evolution has always been the main driving force behind slow but steady change for the human brain. However, living in the Information era, our cognitive capacities cannot simply rely on natural evolution to keep up with the immense advancements in emerging technologies. Despite great strides in processing power, storage, and even usability, systems we use daily (e.g., smartphones, PCs, and soon IoT etc.) remain largely uninformed about our cognitive states. As a result, a so-called “cognitive gap” is forming between the human (user) and the machine (system), preventing us from fully harnessing the benefits of emerging technologies, by expending instead significant portions of our yet finite cognitive resources (e.g., working memory). The purpose of Cognition 2.0 is twofold: a) it will bridge the cognitive gap by building and deploying a “cognitive information layer” in-between human and machine, responsible for informing the machine side about user’s cognitive states and adapting ongoing human-machine interaction respectively. b) Cognition 2.0 will serve as an application framework, encompassing design and development guidelines for future cognition-aware applications. Through numerous user studies in the lab and in the wild, we will collect multimodal contextual and physiological data streams, that we will link to cognitive states and adequate interaction interventions for augmenting certain cognitive aspects (e.g., attention). Finally, we will utilize implications and knowledge stemming from user studies for eliciting the Cognition 2.0 framework for supporting cognition-aware applications.

Title: Clarifying the neurocognitive mechanisms of prospective memory through a working memory framework
Abstract:
Prospective memory (PM), i.e., our memory for future intentions, is integral for executing daily life plans. Consequences of PM failures range from inconvenient (forgetting to take the pizza out of the oven after 15 minutes) to dangerous (forgetting to take blood pressure medication after a meal). Yet, PM failures are one of the most common daily memory problems, and in old age, PM failures can seriously hamper independence and quality of life (Hering et al., 2018; Woods et al., 2012). In response, several theoretical models have been developed to characterize the cognitive mechanisms of PM. Surprisingly, these models give little focus to working memory (WM), i.e., the ability to briefly maintain limited information for achieving a goal, and thus, one of the key cognitive mechanisms of goal-directed behavior. Importantly, WM research has shown crucial differences in the maintenance of to-be-remembered information in different states of accessibility – from continuous activation in focal attention to passive retention and retrieval via long-term memory processes. These findings impact both the neurocognitive processes implicated in different situations, and the nature of age differences in WM. Such theoretical and methodological advancements in WM research have not yet been applied to PM. However, doing so could help PM models more accurately capture how the brain maintains future intentions.
The project addresses an important conceptual gap in PM research and will apply a WM framework onto the systematic study of PM, with the goal to further clarify the neurocognitive mechanisms of PM and their decline with healthy aging. This overall aim will be addressed over three work packages (WP) with specific aims. First, WP1 will conduct experiments within a Bayesian sampling and analysis framework, using manipulations established by the WM field, that can distinguish between different accessibility states. This fine-grained behavioral approach will constitute the first ever empirical detection of PM cues’ accessibility states. Next, WP2 will combine a time-resolved electroencephalography (EEG) measurement during a PM task with state-of-the-art machine learning analyses, to track potential accessibility state changes over the course of the task. This will situate our findings in contemporary theories of PM as a dynamic process and provide a more accurate neurocognitive appraisal of PM mechanisms. Finally, WP3 will apply WP1 and WP2 tasks in older adults, to investigate how aging affects PM cue accessibility state patterns. Such patterns will also be explored in high and low PM performers per age group. Thus, the project will investigate PM differences across old age, potentially uncovering factors contributing to age-associated and individual PM efficiency.
Leveraging the combined theoretical and methodological expertise of multiple WM and PM researchers, the proposed project will impact PM theory and practice in two key ways. First, it will shed new light on PM mechanisms by clarifying the precise accessibility states that younger and older adults dynamically store future intentions in throughout a PM scenario. Second, by testing whether low-PM older adults have trouble strategically shifting intentions into adaptive accessibility states, it can provide a first step toward developing targeted interventions to support such older adults’ PM performance. With this, the project presents an innovative and comprehensive mechanistic investigation of PM that can advance our understanding of PM and provide a scientific basis for addressing everyday PM problems.
Keywords: EEG, aging, cognitive aging, neurocognitive mechanisms, prospective memory, working memory

Title: Self-Organizing Machine Architecture - SOMA
Abstract: The tremendous increase of transistors integration during the last few years has reached the limits of classic Von Neuman architectures. This has enabled a wide adoption of parallel processors by the industry, enabling many-core processing architectures as a natural trend for the next generation of computing devices. Nonetheless, one major issue of such massively parallel processors is the design and the deployment of applications that cannot make an optimal use of the available hardware resources. This limit is even more acute when we consider application domains where the system evolves under unknown and uncertain conditions such as mobile robotics, IoT, autonomous vehicles or drones. In the end, it is impossible to foresee every possible context that the system will face during its lifetime, making thus impossible to identify the optimal hardware substrate to be used. Interestingly enough, the biological brain has ''solved'' this problem using a dedicated architecture and mechanisms that offer both adaptive and dynamic computations, namely, self-organization. However, even if such neuro-biological systems have often been a source of inspiration for computer science (as recently demonstrated by the renewed interest in deep-learning), the transcription of self-organization at the hardware level is not straightforward and requires a number of challenges to be taken-up.The first challenge is to extend the usual self-organization mechanisms to account for the dual levels of computation and communication in a hardware manycore architecture. From a biological point of view, this corresponds to a combination of the so-called synaptic and structural plasticity. We intend to define computational models able to simultaneously self-organize at both levels, and we want these models to be hardware-compliant, fault tolerant and scalable thanks to a neuro-cellular structure.The second challenge is to prove the feasibility of a self-organizing hardware structure. Considering that these properties emerge from large scale and fully connected neural maps, we will focus on the definition of a self-organizing hardware architecture based on digital spiking neurons. The third challenge consists in coupling this new computation paradigm with classical Von Neumann programming. This will require the definition of a programming model using the learning of input data to better and automatically divide and allocate functional elements.Hence, this project is a convergence point between past research approaches toward new computation paradigms: adaptive reconfigurable architecture, cellular computing, computational neuroscience, and neuromorphic hardware:  - SOMA is an adaptive reconfigurable architecture to the extent that it will dynamically re-organize both its computation and its communication by adapting itself to the data to process.  - SOMA is based on cellular computing since it targets a massively parallel (many-core), distributed and decentralized architecture.  - SOMA is based on computational neuroscience since its self-organization capabilities are inspired from neural mechanisms.  - SOMA is a neuromorphic hardware system since its organization emerges from the interactions between neural maps transposed into hardware from brain observation.This project represents a significant step toward the definition of a true fine-grained distributed, adaptive and decentralized neural computation framework. Using self-organized neural populations onto a cellular machine where local routing resources are not separated from computational resources, it will ensure natural scalability and adaptability as well as a better performance/power consumption tradeoff compared to other embedded solutions. This new computing framework may indeed represent a viable alternative to the classical Von Neumann architecture and could endow hardware systems with novel adaptive properties.
Keywords: architecture des ordinateurs, auto-organisation, calcul cellulaire, dispositifs numériques reconfigurables, machines neuromorphiques

Title: THE EFFECT OF KINETOCHORE SIZE IN CANCER
Abstract:
Human cells divide by equally separating their chromosomes into two daughter cells. A protein complex called kinetochore is responsible for chromosome segregation during cell division. Errors in chromosome segregation generate aneuploidy, a condition in which the number or structure of chromosome is altered. Aneuploidy is linked to several pathological conditions. About 70% of all solid tumors are aneuploid, and in cancer, aneuploidy correlates with aggressiveness and poor prognosis.
Here, I propose a combination of microscopy, machine-learning based image analysis and cell biology to investigate how kinetochore size affects chromosome segregation fidelity in cancer cells and organoids.
To determine the exact mechanisms triggering aneuploidy in malignances is of primary importance to understand cancer progression and drug resistance.
Keywords: Cancer, Chromosomal Instability, Image Analysis, Kinetochore, Mitosis, Organoids

Title: Detailed Real-World Shape Reconstruction of Reflective Surfaces and Objects
Abstract:
In the field of computer vision, graphics and surveying substantial progress has been made over the last years in developing techniques for capturing 3D models [Debevec et al. 1996; Levoy et al. 2000; Pollefeys et al. 2004; Newcombe et al. 2011] and measuring surface properties [Marschner et al. 2000; Dana et al. 1999; Chen et al. 2002] to generate faithful copies of the real-world. For instance, there has recently been a lot of interest in capturing visual models of cities [Frueh and Zakhor 2004; Pollefeys et al. 2008; Xiao et al. 2009; Nan et al. 2010] but it is clearly also desirable to reconstruct objects such as cars or scan industrial installations, glossy furniture at home, smart phones or windows. However, existing capturing techniques struggle with reflective scenes and objects as these do not reflect sufficient laser-light back to a range sensor or due to their reflective nature violating the Lambertian assumption underlying most image-based techniques. Consequently, resulting 3D models contain holes or erroneous data wherever reflection occurs and have to be post-processed after capturing. Typically, this would remove gross errors or close holes in bigger models but for the reflective parts themselves, no practical techniques exist to capture them in real-world settings.
The goal of this research effort is to improve the geometrical understanding of the behavior of reflective surfaces, in particular with respect to useful and practical approximations when observing. In particular we want to focus not only on the rough shape of the object (almost flat glass, cylindrical cooking pot, …) but on the details and subtle changes in surface normal (due to design, imperfections in manufacturing or tension) that dominate the reflection of the scenery. Based on these insights, we plan to develop techniques that allow to scan such reflective surfaces by means of standard cameras in real-world scenarios and then to infer their shape with very high detail. Earlier works for reconstructing reflective surfaces proposed scanning techniques in controlled lab environments based on well-known calibration targets. In contrast, the proposed line of research for this project is to extend the successful idea of structure-from-motion in unknown environments to reflective scenarios. This means that no artificial calibration targets will be placed into the scene but the existing scenery should be exploited in all steps to reconstruct the surface/object when a camera films the object or a survey car passes through a street with reflective facades.
The steps to achieve this can be categorized roughly as 1) estimation of camera ego-motion in reflective settings, 2) tracking of reflections on the surface (or specular flow), 3) estimation of what is being reflected and 4) estimation of surface normal maps/geometry. Finally, a reflective bundle adjustment (joint optimization of all camera and scene parameters) would improve a solution. All four problems will be addressed in this project and for all of them practical solutions are either limited to very restricted scenarios (lab conditions) or do not exist nowadays such that each step will mean substantial scientific progress towards automatic 3D scene understanding.
Practically, the developed methodology would allow to faithfully reconstruct reflective surfaces and objects for planning, visualization, and simulation, where nowadays models look artificial (e.g. houses with perfect mirrors as windows), require a huge amount of manual interaction (somebody adding the windows manually to the scan/model) or simply cannot be obtained in real-world situations. Second, the developed techniques have the potential for a much broader impact, e.g. they could enable automated quality control processes in manufacturing and civil engineering, to scan for defects or to detect stress or pressure visible through subtle defor-mations of the material‘s normals, and finally might even be deployed to autonomous cars or other robotic vehicles to be able to interact in or scan more complex environments.
Keywords: 3D modeling, Computer Vision, Shape from Reflection, Shape from Specularities

Title: From atomistic exploration of chemical compound space towards bio-molecular design:  Quantum mechanical rational compound design (QM-RCD)
Abstract: Atomistic details of matter determine physical and chemical properties. Much research has been carried out in order to understand and model this relationship using quantum mechanical (QM) first principles, statistical mechanics, and the ever increasing role of the computational sciences. Employed methods are based on a physico-chemical framework that nowadays permits to routinely compute relevant properties for any combinations of atomic configurations and composition, also called chemical compound space (CCS). The task of using QM for the discovery of novel compounds with improved properties is therefore equivalent to a combinatorial optimization problem in CCS. Tackling this task through QM based high-throughput screening, albeit straight-forward, is the least efficient way. The overall goal of this proposal is to make a comprehensive exploration of CCS possible by developing QM based rational compound design (QM-RCD) schemes that are drastically more efficient than screening. The proposed QM-RCD approach is based on two of the most fundamental and complementary strategies in numerical optimization theory, namely variational and correlational methods. For the former, differential, response-like, QM predictions of properties will be studied for compounds that are ``close'' in CCS. For the latter, intelligent data analysis methods (machine learning) will be applied to exploit complex correlations. Such models promise to dramatically accelerate the estimation of QM properties, enabling the modeling of massive numbers of compounds within discrete combinatorial optimization implementations, e.g. evolutionary or Monte Carlo based. While many QM properties are amenable to such efforts, the focus of this proposal lies on the archetypical problem of ligand design. The usefulness of this highly interdisciplinary endeavor, tightly linking theoretical physics with computational chemistry and biochemistry, and with computer sciences, will be exemplified for realistic and relevant ligand leads, such as DNA intercalating drugs (dominated by pi-pi-interactions) and ligand-protein (dominated by hydrogen bonding and polarization) interactions.
Keywords: chemical compound space, computational drug design, computational ligand design, density functional theory, gradient based optimization, machine learning, rational compound design, van der Waals interactions

Title: Optimal design of observational studies of area-based crime prevention using geospatial data mining
Abstract:
This project establishes a bridge between geospatial data mining and geographic criminology by proposing innovative methods to draw up optimal research designs for area-based criminological studies that allow causal inferences from non-experimental data. In geographic criminology, the optimal unit of analysis has received increasing attention of late over a growing awareness that an inappropriate aggregation level leads to undue amounts of heterogeneity within study areas that may obscure otherwise detectable neighborhood effects. Similarly, investigators using observational study designs have sought to divide the overall study population into meaningful subgroups or latent strata in order to reduce within-group heterogeneity and diminish design sensitivity to unmeasured covariates. 
The current project combines these two recent research strands by using both unsupervised and supervised data mining algorithms to identify the optimal spatial units of analysis for observational research designs that divide the study sample into meaningful strata, for which the effect of treatment may vary. More specifically, this project aims to develop a clustering procedure that will aggregate the grid cells of raster data on area ecological characteristics and georeferenced survey data to geographic areas of flexible shape and size in order to minimize between-cluster similarity for the theoretical constructs of interest. 
The current study hence has a double objective. First, the development of a clustering algorithm to aggregate raster cells flexibly in order to achieve maximum within-cluster homogeneity of the area ecological data and survey response patterns and, second, to select comparable treated and control areas to achieve optimal balance on the observed covariates and outcome measures. The study will use geostatistical tools in combination with advanced machine learning and data mining techniques to detect spatiotemporal patterns in the high-dimensional input space in order to identify the optimal units of analysis to separate the study area into homogenous sub-areas. Data mining tools also serve to meet the optimization criteria of balancing both observed covariates and pertinent outcome measures in order to identify the optimal research design for observational studies of area-based crime prevention. 
This project benefits from a unique constellation of available data to develop and test these methodologies at an exceptionally fine level of spatial granularity, namely the 2011 Swiss Crime Survey with more than 15,000 completed interviews, geocoded to the uniform Swiss map projection system, paired with the 2010 national population and housing census counts available in raster format with grid cells the size of one hectare. The main fundamental contributions of the present study are the following: 
1Development of new methodologies for the optimal design of observational studies of area-based crime prevention or other criminological phenomena that allow causal inferences 
2Development, exploration, and adaptation of new tools for the spatial analysis and geo-visualization of victimization survey data 

The research team combines the necessary expertise in data mining and geostatistical modeling and already disposes of most of the data and software tools for the analyses envisioned by this study. The main results will be presented at academic conferences and published in scientific journals.
Keywords: Crime prevention, Data mining, Geostatistics, Machine learning, Neighborhood profiling, Observational studies

Title: Reconstructing the long-term Human Occupation and Resilience Strategies in the Eastern Mediterranean: the case of Euboea (Central Greece)
Abstract:
What determines socio-environmental and economic resilience? What are the vulnerabilities, path dependencies, and tipping points involved in local responses to climate and social dynamics, and how can archaeology contribute to these fundamental questions today? The aim and ambition of this project is to obtain a comprehensive knowledge of the adaptation and resilience strategies developed by ancient populations in the Eastern Mediterranean, facing climate and environmental change over the long-term perspective (from the Neolithic to the Ottoman Period), performing analysis on the key study area of the island of Euboea, Central Greece. 
Euboea is a privileged area of study for multi-proxy and multi-disciplinary approaches, since the earliest traces of human presence date back to the Final Neolithic (4th millennium BC) and persist until modern age. Moreover, this region has witnessed the development of significant adaptation strategies to fluctuating water courses, evolving floodplains, and changing coastal dynamics during different periods of time at generational or multi-generational timescale, which may have influenced settlement location choices, as well as periods of population movement and urbanisation of the inland, by means of intensive agriculture and resource exploitation. Although some of the Euboean sites show signs of disruption or abandonment, the repeated occupation of some key locations, along with evidence of architectural and spatial adaptation, reflects the resilience of past societies. Despite the abundance of research and data generated for the Eastern Mediterranean, these data have been largely under deployed in making historical and diachronic conclusions. The resilience and vulnerabilities of past societies in this geographical frame have never been researched in parallel to climate and paleoclimate data in a deep time perspective, and are thus still poorly understood. 
This research will take a multi-dimensional approach by deploying and combining the most cutting-edge computational techniques. It will focus on i) formalising, modelling and testing existing and new hypotheses on Euboean landscape occupation, ii) evaluating the resilience of ancient populations to known and new modelled climate perturbations that affected the territory at different time-frames and iii) assessing how and to which degree Eastern Mediterranean landscapes were transformed by local climate variability and understanding the interaction between local communities and paleoenvironments (e.g. natural resource management; environmental impacts). These objectives will be achieved through three main research strategies: 1) collect and couple paleoclimate, paleoenvironmental and archaeological data in an innovative methodological and comparative framework based on sedimentological coring and Machine Learning techniques ; 2) generate a major georeferenced archaeological database for Euboea, using Remote Sensing and Deep Learning techniques; 3) simulate different scenarios and hypothesis for past population dynamics with Agents-based modelling. The results will be useful to archaeology and beyond by providing valuable insights into ancient human-environment interactions and impacts on cultural landscapes and long-term adaptations. In a contemporary perspective, they will contribute to help modern society respond to the challenges associated with climate and environmental changes and with the protection and conservation of the archaeological heritage exposed to human and natural disasters. Finally, they will be relevant to opening new interpretive and comparative terrains to understand similar dynamics realised in different study areas and temporal frameworks.
Keywords: Agents-based modelling, Climate change, Human-Environment interaction, Machine Learning, Paleoclimate, Paleoenvironment, Remote Sensing, Resilience & Adaptation strategies
