Title: Novel Architectures for Photonic Reservoir Computing
Abstract:
This proposal addresses the challenges of the Big Data era by developing high performance devices in the context of a recently established machine learning paradigm known as reservoir computing (RC). RC is well adapted to applications that require real-time online computing and is a serious candidate to outperform conventional Turing machines whose algorithms run on von Neumann architectures. Additionally, It is one of the few computing approaches that can be directly mapped to dedicated hardware. We articulate the proposed research around three main axes:

As dedicated hardware, we will design and fabricate compact photonic reservoirs. Integrated photonics has proved to be a promising approach to physically implement RC chips. In NAPRECO, we will follow two approaches to compact designs that bring hardware RC to a new level of performance. Scaled networks of coupled semiconductor optical amplifiers (SOAs) will be first studied experimentally, going beyond what has so far only been shown in simulations. A novel concept of compact photonic RC will be developed next, based on the dynamics in an optical interference pattern. Inspired by a RC demonstration using surface water waves our photonic equivalent would yield drastically smaller length scales and time constants.

In synergy with the development of the hardware concepts, the RC architecture will be optimized from a theoretical perspective. A strong mathematical guidance will be first provided to physically implement the two approaches highlighted. First, the RC concept based on interference requires an accurate mathematical modeling to optimize its architecture. Second, various theoretical results show the universality of RC as a computational paradigm both for digital and analog inputs but mapping RC to a dedicated hardware implies important restrictions that might limit the validity of those results. Finally, we will characterize the class of problems to which our concepts can be applied, quantify their performances, identify possible limitations, and suggest routes for improvement.

Specific machine learning applications will be explored in the financial and medical domains. We will focus on multivariate time series forecasting based on mixed frequency explanatory input signals, multivariate financial volatility forecasting, and classification of high-resolution electroencephalographic signals (Hi-Res EEG). Having in common a large volume of data and an unfavorable signal to noise ratio, such applications require a powerful signal processing tool, and will ideally demonstrate the potential of hardware RC solutions to impact relevant economic sectors.

NAPRECO is an intrinsically multidisciplinary collaboration that combines state-of-the-art knowledge in the mathematical and experimental realization of RC systems. It will advance the scientific understanding in a complex field, establish Swiss researchers in a world-leading role, and develop a vision towards critical applications. The expertise in integrated photonics and material science is covered by IBM Research-Zurich. The Sankt Gallen group will focus on the theoretical optimization of the reservoir architecture and on the development of the applications, having a well-grounded track record in both tasks. Both applicants have working experience, and are well embedded in international partnerships. Scientific results are therefore expected at a sustained rate and with a significant impact in strategic fields such as macroeconometrics, financial econometrics, and clinical neuroscience.
Keywords: Hi-Res EEG classification, brain-inspired computing, echo state networks, integrated optics, liquid state machines, neural computing, optical neural networks, reservoir computing, time series forecasting, volatility forecasting

Title: Open many-body quantum systems and machine learning
Abstract:
This proposal asks the question "How can machine learning enable new discoveries and breakthroughs in many-body physics?". I propose three projects that investigate how state-of-the-art learning techniques, such as reinforcement learning and restricted Boltzmann machines, may aid solve outstanding physics problems. 

In Project 1 I investigate how the algorithm "AlphaZero", initially developed by the Google DeepMind team to defeat the world-champion Go player, can be used to solve the problem of error decoding on topological quantum codes such as the toric code. This problem can be formulated as a game, and is hence amenable to such techniques. Preliminary results show that "ErrorZero" is able to reproduce a well-known solution (MWPM).

Project 2 centers around the objective of finite-size-scaling methods for numerical and experimental results. Measurement results in such systems are often obscured by effects that are solely present at small sizes, and one wishes to separate these contributions in order to infer the large (infinite) system size results. This is currently done using a scaling collapse with one or two parameter fitting. Here we investigate if a neural network can be used to do this collapse automatically, by showing it data of various system sizes simultaneously. In addition, we employ visual attention networks to extract finite size effects of 2D snapshots. 

In Project 3 we use the restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) Ansatz to construct phase diagrams of a 1D and, more importantly, a 2D Rydberg model that is currently being studied experimentally at Caltech by Prof. Dr. Manuel Endres. The phase diagram of this 2D model has not been studied for large system sizes, and the RBM approach is expected to outperform other methods. Moreover, it is very promising to study time-evolution with these RBMs, since the only other available method (PEPS) is notoriously difficult and hard to converge. Building a framework around this new approach will make a significant impact for all 2D models.

These projects allow me to expand my current research in the field of machine learning and physics, in which I have been at the forefront during the last 1.5years. My main contributions so far are in finding phase transitions using machine learning techniques, and have enabled me to get invited talks at international conferences. With this proposal I will be able to both continue research and strengthen my position in the field, so that in the coming year I hope to be able to find a more permanent position (ideally in Switzerland).
Keywords: Error correction, Finite Size Scaling, Machine learning, Phase transitions, Quantum computing, Rydberg Atoms

Title: Supporting personalized medicine for patients with multiple chronic conditions: Machine Learning to Augment Benefit Harm Analysis
Abstract:
Background: Most clinical guidelines and clinical decisions in multimorbidity are based on evidence from single disease studies. As a result, patients are treated for each condition in isolation, leading to a “treatment cocktail”, with unclear benefit-harm balance. An informed multidisciplinary approach and the use of high-dimensional routine care data could be potential solutions to address the challenges of multimorbidity.

Objectives: This study aims to (1) apply machine learning (ML) methods to estimate best possible treatment combinations for defined multimorbidity from observational data. (2) inform the benefit-harm balance assessment with the ML results to identify treatment combinations with the best possible outcome for defined multimorbidity.

Methods: To address objectives (1) Causal variational autoencoders (VAE) and conditional generative adversarial networks (GAN) will be used to understand, generate complete and representative data conditional on patient characteristics, the treatments and outcomes of interest. The generated data will then be used to create counterfactual ("what-if") scenarios to estimate effects under different treatment combinations. The effects will be anchored to state-of-the-art conventional methods available for estimating treatment effects from observational studies, as well as to field knowledge and prior evidence. Once we have confidence in the procedure for one or two treatments at a time and the results are consistent with conventional methods, we will use ML methods only for more complex conditions, as conventional methods cannot capture factorial complexity for more than two treatments. (2) We will perform the benefit-harm balance to weigh the benefit against the harms of the treatment combinations identified in step 1. The analyses will be performed for patient subgroups since the treatment effects, baseline risks, and patient preferences vary from patient to patient. Moreover, a personalized and interactive visualization dashboard will also be developed to assist treatment decision making for individual patient.

Significance: This will be used as a case study to demonstrate that reductionist single-disease studies cannot address multimorbidity and a paradigm shift toward an informed multidisciplinary approach that makes use of conventional methods, advanced calculations, observational or routine care data, and field knowledge to address the challenges of multimorbidity.
Keywords: Benefit-harm balance, HIV, Machine learning, Multiple chronic conditions, Personalized medicine

Title: AI-enabled Budget Slack Prediction and Explanation for Public Budgeting: How can AI help improve public budgeting?
Abstract:
Administrative divisions of the Swiss public sector have been found to project significant deficits but have substantial surpluses, undermining trust in the budgeting process and suggesting a lack of fiscal discipline. This budgetary slack can lead taxpayers to overpay for services not rendered or delay necessary investments, distorting public perceptions of government efficiency and eroding trust in the public sector. For the public sector, accurate budgeting is essential for fiscal responsibility and efficient resource allocation. Compared to the private sector, the public sector has received relatively little research on their budgeting practices and potential improvements. This is despite the public sector’s unique complexities of managerial reforms, promising emerging opportunities for processual improvements and large share of spending in most Western countries amounting to 40% to 50% of a country’s gross domestic product. 
This collaborative project aims at examining the possibilities in improving budgeting in the public sector by using AI. Together with public organizations, we explore collaborations between humans and artificial intelligence (AI) in budgeting aiming at reducing unfortunate outcomes of heightened budgetary slack. We formulate our guiding research question as follows: How can an AI help reduce public sector budgetary slack?
The project is structured in two phases. Phase 1 involves the development of a Budget Slack Prediction and Explanation System for public budgeting in close cooperation with public sector officials. The system has two key components: a Budget Slack Prediction Model and an AI Explainer, that is, a fine-tuned Large Language Model (LLM) explaining the budget prediction and potential budgetary slack (“PublicBudgetingGPT”) that we open source. The AI Explainer component provides information about slack predictions that aim at helping individuals increase understanding of a budgeting context and increase the efficacy of an AI slack prediction. Phase 2 involves experimental validation of the two key components of the system. In Phase 2, we intend to enhance our understanding of how AI can be embedded in budgeting by providing evidence on the role of perceived AI budgeting competence, added efficacy of an AI Explainer, and the role of risk aversion and process accountability when budgets are formed. 
The project contributes to the literature in accounting on budgeting and AI. While accounting academics are starting to show a strong interest in the way decision-makers use AI systems in accounting tasks, the accounting literature is in its early stages and has employed hypothetical cases to explore this question. Conceptually, we contribute to the participation literature in accounting and budgeting by examining how AI can be effectively embedded in budgeting processes considering decision-maker’s possible AI aversion/appreciation, risk, and accountability considerations. 
The project further contributes to explainable AI (XAI) research by proposing a novel approach enabling laymen to better understand budget predictions, that is, time series predictions for which we face a scarcity of explanation methods. We reach that goal via the development of a Budget Prediction and Explanation System that features a conversational interface with which users can pose their explanation needs in natural language instead of investigating static statistical explanations that reflect the status quo. Creating a novel instruction data set for budget explanation, we fine-tune a pre-trained LLM for explaining budget predictions. 
Ultimately, our work advances the understanding of human-AI collaboration in public administration, offering theoretically grounded research insights into explainable AI’s role in fostering trust and accountability in governmental decision-making.
Keywords: artificial intelligence, budgetary slack, budgeting, public budgeting, public sector, slack

Title: How proximate factors underlying decision making may affect the evolution and maintenance of cooperation
Abstract:
The evolution and maintenance of cooperation for direct fitness benefits is a topic of great interdisciplinary interest. Existing game theoretic models assume either that genes code directly for a strategy, or that gene-environment interactions lead to conditional strategies. However, in organisms with more complex central nervous systems, gene-environment interactions can affect brain development, allowing individuals to make decisions based on learning, memory and experience. Decision-making in the brain is also influenced by information sent by the body: for instance, through the production of hormones. Such processes may cause ubiquitously observed inter-species and inter-individual variation in levels of cooperation that is poorly explained by current models. In order to advance evolutionary questions about cooperation, we need to first understand how differences in personal experience, cognition, and physiology influence variation in cooperative interactions. 
I propose to address these questions using marine cleaning mutualisms as a model system. In these mutualisms, small fish called ‘cleaners’ remove ectoparasites from so-called ‘client’ fish species. Conflict arises when some cleaner fish species prefer to eat the protective mucus layer of their clients, which constitutes cheating. The major focus of this proposal is to study factors influencing decisions during cooperative interactions, and their link to variable behaviour in the cleaner fish L. dimidiatus, our main study system. Individual cleaners differ with respect to levels of cooperation and expression of cognitive abilities; in turn, client species differ with respect to the quality of the service they receive. Recent evidence suggests that the complexity of the cleaner’s interspecific social environment and/or cleaner-cleaner competition over access to clients may cause variation in cognition and cooperation due to ontogenetic effects. Therefore, one aim is to explicitly test for ontogenetic effects by translocating cleaners between sites that differ in social complexity and by experimentally reducing the cleaner-to-client ratio for 12 months in a large area in the field. We will investigate the consequences of cleaner reduction (i.e., increased cleaning demand) on service quality and client strategies via cleaning observations, individual follows of clients, transects and remote monitoring of home range use in various client species. Lab experiments testing the swimming performance and mucus quality of 18 client species belonging to 14 families will provide insights into the physiological costs that may limit partner control mechanisms like punishment and partner switching, which may explain variation among client species in received service quality. Furthermore, experiments on translocated cleaners and cleaners from the experimentally reduced density area will allow us to test whether these manipulations changed individual levels of cooperation and cognition. Finally, we will use a comparative approach to test in how far the physiology underlying a cleaner’s decisions in cooperative interactions varies with strategic options. Hormone and neurotransmitter levels offer the brain information about the individual’s current physiological state or life history stage, often causing pleiotrophic effects on behaviour. We have established that arginine-vasotocin, serotonin, and cortisol affect levels of cooperation in L. dimidiatus. This species prefers ectoparasites over client mucus. Our working hypothesis is that the same effects exist in other cleaner species with such food preference, while service quality will not be affected in species that prefer to eat ectoparasites and hence do not have to solve a conflict with clients over what to eat.
In parallel with empirical research, we aim to develop models that explicitly link parameters affecting social complexity with costs and benefits of more or less sophisticated decision rules, i.e. rules that use different amounts of information about the social environment. Our variables of interest will affect the efficiency of different updating rules that would lead to more or less knowledgeable / cognitively enabled individuals. The updating rules should take into account likely learning mechanisms used by animals, like reinforcement learning. We will explore the effects of social complexity and learning on both ecological and evolutionary time scales. The powerful combination of modelling and empirical data, especially the explicit links between mechanisms and function, should provide us with novel insights concerning the conditions promoting stable cooperation.
Keywords: behavioural ecology, cooperation, decision rules

Title: Rapid Beamforming for Massive MIMO using Machine Learning on RF-only and Multi-modal Sensor Data
Abstract:
Massive Multiple Input Multiple Output (mMIMO) antenna systems will be an important technology for future generation, e.g., 6G, mobile telecommunication networks to meet emerging throughput, reliability, and latency requirements. Directional transmission becomes increasingly important for exploiting spatial multiplexing in future mobile and wireless networks. In an mMIMO system, signals are transmitted in parallel between antenna arrays, and by selecting phases and amplitudes directional behaviour of the antenna system can be steered. The massive number of antennas in an mMIMO system makes it challenging to find optimized parameters in real-time. Machine Learning (ML) concepts such as Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Deep Learning (DL) can be used to not only estimate but also predict channel conditions and to determine parameters for rapid beamforming. Federated Learning (FL) allows performing ML in a distributed fashion. This approach is promising since many user devices can be involved in the learning process, but FL for channel estimation and beamforming is not well explored and understood. 

The project has two major scientific objectives, namely to advance the state-of-the-art in  Resilient and Personalized Channel Estimation using Distributed and Federated Learning (Objective 1) and Efficient Beamforming by utilizing Multi-Modal sensor data (Objective 2). The concepts, approaches, and algorithms developed for Objectives 1 and 2 will be validated in real-world experiments and simulations based on realistic collected data (Objective 3). Each Objective is divided into several tasks, most of which are jointly investigated by PhD students and faculty of the two collaborating universities in the USA and Switzerland (Northeastern University, NEU, and University of Bern, UniBE). While NEU has extensive experience in DL for MIMO systems and multi-modal beamforming, UniBE has experience in Federated and Split Learning as well as mobility prediction using advanced ML techniques. 
 
Objective 1 concerns fast and resilient channel estimation using Deep Learning to achieve better spectral efficiency. Several improvements addressing the pilot contamination effect will be targeted. Personalized FL for channel estimation exploiting shared knowledge among users will be investigated. Users with similar channel characteristics will be grouped, and group models will be personalized. In this context, partial FL will be applied, i.e. only subsets of model layers will be exchanged to come up with efficient communication. Moreover, RL will be leveraged to support federated model personalization. 

Objective 2 focuses on beamforming that goes beyond classical radio frequency-only approaches by utilizing multimodal sensor data. Again, various ML techniques will be applied for optimizing beams and predicting required beam directions. To minimize training costs and delays as well as to improve scalability, transfer learning will be used to transfer pre-trained models to other nodes. Mobility prediction is another technique for beamforming to predict user movements and adapt the beamforming parameters accordingly. Attention-based transformer neural networks will be investigated for faster and more scalable training. FL will also be investigated for beamforming to exploit the shared knowledge of user devices when diverse data from sources like LiDAR and cameras are available. However, such approaches must be scalable and avoid control channel overloads. Techniques that compress and reduce relaying of control data, such as model pruning and dynamic federated split learning, will be investigated and compared. 

Objective 3 will create a programmable infrastructure for simulation and emulation experiments to evaluate the concepts and approaches developed under Objectives 1 and 2. NEU manages the NSF Colosseum, a large Radio Frequency Channel Emulator, which collects data for the ML-based concepts and approaches of Objectives 1 and 2 as well as for testing those under realistic conditions. Moreover, additional experiments on a vehicular testbed and simulation studies will be performed using servers.
Keywords: 6G, Beamforming, distributed machine learning, federated learning, massive MIMO

Title: Unveiling Dark Matter in a Hidden Valley at particle colliders
Abstract: Research in the field of High Energy Physics (HEP) has achieved astonishing results in the last decades, rewarding us with deep insight into the Universe structure. The Standard Model (SM) of particle physics gives an outstanding description of observed particle phenomena with few exceptions: one of the most striking being the cosmic abundance of a non ordinary kind of matter, called Dark Matter (DM). The DM problem is central to the fields of particle and astroparticle physics, however, despite decades of searches and an immense experimental effort, DM has not been observed yet, suggesting that new theoretical and experimental strategies are essential. The research project proposed here will address the DM problem exploring a new class of theoretical models and experimental signatures, using proton-proton collision data recorded by the Compact Muon Solenoid experiment at the Large Hadron Collider at the energy frontiers. The discovery potential of the project will be maximised by devising novel algorithms for signal identification based on advanced machine learning techniques and developing sophisticated experimental methods of background mitigation. The outcome of this search will greatly advance our exploration of DM.
Keywords: CMS, Dark Matter, High Energy Physics, LHC, Machine Learning, Pixel Detector

Title: Tracking Opinion Change Over Time (OpiTrack)
Abstract: Recent years have seen the rapid growth of social media platforms that enable people to express their thoughts and opinions on the web and share them with other users. Many people write their opinion about products, movies, people or events on blogs, forums or review sites. In this project we will extend the latest models of opinion retrieval and sentiment analysis by incorporating time in the opinion analysis. We will develop models that track sentiment over time also covering different aspects of a topic. We will also develop models that will attempt to predict the sentiment change toward a topic at a certain time in future. The models developed will be evaluated with real data.
Keywords: information retrieval, language modelling, opinion retrieval and mining, santiment dynamics, temporal topic modelling

Title: Structural Intrinsic Dimensionality
Abstract:
Information is generally organized by similarity, itself often derived from a distance function. It is via neighborhoods that the data makes sense, as opposed to being a set of arbitrary unrelated items. Hence, studying neighborhoods in metric spaces is a fundamental operation, driving nearly any data processing or analysis, and that has applications in a large variety of domains.
 A common issue that data modeling and analysis techniques face is the degradation of their performance as the dimensionality of the data at hand increases. With the increase of dimension, the data shows adverse properties that degrade our ability to model neighborhoods and impede the effectiveness of any processing. This is often referred to under the generic label of ``curse of dimensionality'', which bears many facets and finds several definitions and origins in the literature. In this project, we wish to associate to every data point a value (named Structural Intrinsic Dimensionality) related to some true local dimensionality value at the location and to use this value to inform any further processing in order to circumvent this curse.

Neighboring relationships naturally relate to graphs constructed over the data. This project therefore proposes to install graph spanners as maps for driving the modeling and analysis of high-dimensional data. We wish to achieve this objective by defining the Structural Intrinsic Dimensionality as a inherent property that emerges from such structures over the data. We organize this investigation into two complementary and parallel objectives that directly shape the project. Objective 1 targets the definition of graph structures supporting the computation of Structural Intrinsic Dimensionality by operations such as diffusion and Objective 2 uses these structures, which encode local dimensionality, as basis for developing operational tools for data exploitation.

The overarching research question that we want to answer in this project therefore derives from the generic domain of high-dimensional data modeling and can be formulated as: ``How to construct and use graphs as maps for high-dimensional data spaces?'' The project also addresses the wider question of the power of graphs to retain geometric information, which is in direct relation with that of optimal graph embedding and manifold learning. Our research plan is organized into the work of two PhD researchers collaborating with one Post-Doctoral researcher. Each researcher has a well-defined objective and the collaboration of these lines of research form a coherent direction towards Structural Intrinsic Dimensionality.

To anchor our project in a real situation, we wish to develop a specific case study around Flow Cytometry data analysis. We believe that this use case offers a rich context for modeling, and that all operations we target such as density estimation, visualization, or classification are relevant there. More importantly, our existing collaboration with hematologists at Geneva University Hospital offers us a unique opportunity to address this challenge.

Title: Adaptive robot control inspired by the development of Drosophila melanogaster larvae (fruit flies)
Abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly improving and has moved beyond the capabilities of human masters in the games of chess and Go. While the methods used to develop board game-intelligence work well in that specific domain, they are of limited use to design adaptive robots even for seemingly simple tasks like picking up objects or locomotion. In part, the questionable performance of artificial intelligence in robot-environment interaction tasks is but a mere reflection of the Bernstein Problem – a fundamental problem in neuroscience named after the neurophysiologist Nikolai Bernstein. Bernstein’s problem addresses the fact that animals can learn to control their motion despite their complexity, which relates to a central scientific question: is the development of motor control as observed in natural organisms based on unsupervised learning rules? An answer to this question will not only have a significant impact on the fields of biology and complex systems, but it will provide the urgently needed paradigm shift in robotics. Although scientists have been studying this problem for over 100 years, recent findings in the field of neuroscience and the rapid advancement of machine learning now provide the potent tools to solve it. Therefore, I propose to computationally study the onset of coordinated motion as observed in the development of the fruit fly larva D. melanogaster and translate the findings to palpable methods for robot control using unsupervised learning. The outcome of this project will shed light into the unknown learning process for motor coordination in the fruit fly larva  and will help deepen our understanding of the onset of motor coordination in nature. Furthermore, the project will translate the biological findings into engineering principles which will provide control methodologies for the field of robotics.
Keywords: Applied mathematics, Neuromechanics, Robotics, Unsupervised learning

Title: Developing Smart Privacy Profiles for A Personal Data Marketplace using Fuzzy Logic: Case of Bitsabout.me
Abstract:
Every day people are confronted with privacy compromises and trade-offs while using online services. Due to the complexity of privacy controls it becomes problematic for people to precisely express their privacy preferences and estimate the potential risks of their disclosure behavior, thus leading to an uncertainty in privacy decision-making. The disclosure behaviour may differ from person to person, and can vary depending on the personal motives and the situational context, consequently every person has a personalised need for privacy. Thus, the research community increasingly focuses on user privacy profiling which involves the analysis of people’s individual privacy preferences and the development of an automated privacy settings configuration.

Bitsabout.me startup runs an online personal data marketplace (Me2B), where users are proposed to share their various data types to data processors or partners (e.g., companies, academic institutions or various types of government) for the specified amount of monetary reward (e.g., Coop offers 5 CHF to users for using their email for the distribution of Coop’s newsletter). The proposed project uses a real-world dataset provided by Bitsabout.me to investigate underlying characteristics of users’ actual privacy behaviour and to develop an intelligent engine that will generate smart privacy profiles. The project will be based on the design science in information system research methodology. This means that the project will go through the following actions: a) acquiring the dataset from Bitsabout.me; b) designing user privacy model using fuzzy inference system; c) implementing the prototype generating smart privacy profiles; d) testing the prototype with real users. This project will revolutionise the way in which people set their privacy settings. With valuable insights derived from a real-world dataset and fuzzy logic, this project will consider cognitive implications of the smart privacy profiles’ design. In the process, the project will contribute to the personal data marketplace development of Bitsbout.me, contributing guidelines and recommendations. Moreover, the developed prototype will have a generalisable nature, meaning that it can be applied to platforms other than personal data marketplaces.
Keywords: Data marketplace, Machine learning, Privacy profiles, Privacy settings, Recommender system

Title: Rapid lateral crystallization of Ge1-xSnx films, overcoming underlying substrate lattice mismatch and Sn solubility.
Abstract:
The crystalline quality of semiconductors relates directly to their functional properties such as charge carrier mobility and radiative recombination efficiency. Compared to bulk substrates, thin film technology provides the path of combining different materials for an increased functionality and a strong reduction in material utilization. 
Monocrystalline thin films may grow seamlessly on crystalline substrates, which provide the crystallographic orientation as well as mechanical support. Defects on the film appear when lattice constants between the two become too important. To circumvent this, a buffer layer may be employed to relax the strain and limit the defect formation close to the interface with the substrate. Alternatively, limiting growth at the nanoscale also results in single crystalline structures.  In a hybrid strategy, growth can start in nanoscale regions that then overgrow laterally forming a thin film in the so-called lateral epitaxy method. 
Alternatively, amorphous thin films can be crystallized in a heating pulse or cycle by applying a laser pulse or an ultra-fast broad-band flash lamp. This strategy is used for example to re-crystallize amorphized regions of devices after ion implantation. These processes can also be applied to amorphous layers on glass, for example in transistors addressing pixels in flat panel displays. Critical to the final quality layer is limiting the nucleation to a low density so that the crystallized grains can be as large as possible. This reduces the amount of grain boundaries, resulting in improved functional properties. 
The goal of this project is to obtain crystalline thin films of metastable Ge1-xSnx semiconductor alloys on a silicon substrate. Ge1-xSnx with x>0.06 exhibits a direct bandgap in the mid-infrared, rendering this material interesting for optoelectronic and photo-detection applications in LiDAR, imaging and biosensing. Our approach combines the selective initiation of crystallization at nanoscale regions and the use of ultra-rapid annealing cycles. The amorphous Ge1-xSnx layer is first deposited on a patterned oxidized Si substrate, with nanoscale openings to the crystalline Si. Prior to the Ge1-xSnx  deposition, the oxide is covered by a graphene layer. A few-ms flash annealing pulse is applied to trigger the crystallization. Crystallization should preferentially start in the nanoscale openings, adopting the crystalline orientation of the substrate. We will look for conditions in which crystallization then proceeds out of the nanoscale openings to laterally crystallize the whole film. The high speed of the thermal process (few ms) should suppress the diffusion of Sn out of the structure. The graphene should foster a higher selectivity of the crystallization process, compared to just using an oxide as a mask. The crystalline properties and functionality of the layers will be first scanned by Raman spectroscopy and X-Ray diffraction. The best samples will in addition be investigated in more detail by high-resolution transmission electron microscopy.  The conditions leading to the best crystalline quality will be found by a machine-learning design of experiment approach. The routine will optimize the linewidth of the (004) diffraction peak. 
Crystalline Ge1-xSnx layers constitute a real alternative to much more costly and less sustainable materials absorbing in the mid-infrared such as InGaAs and lead-based compounds. In addition, we believe this process will be of general nature and will open new avenues for the defect-free thin film formation of other materials systems.

Title: Multi-level modeling of molecular circuitry to facilitate precision medicine of complex disease
Abstract:
Within the past decade next generation sequencing technologies have enabled a systems perspective on gene expression and its regulation at various co- and post-transcriptional levels. Systems biology studies have provided fundamental insights into cell biology and drastically improved our understanding of the complexity of human disease, including cancer. Between-patient tumor heterogeneity indicates that therapeutic successes can be improved through molecular characterization, personalized forecasts of a patient course of disease and personally tailored therapeutic decisions.
Within the project proposed here we aim to implement a system, termed MoCi-PMS system (for Molecular Circuitry-based Precision Medicine Support system), which will elucidate molecular circuitries that are deregulated within patients. Making use of a multitude of sophisticated computational approaches developed over recent years MoCi-PMS will provide integral insights into complex disease and support precision medicine research as well as clinical decision making. In particular, for a given patient the MoCi-PMS system will (i) identify deregulated molecular circuitries at multiple regulatory levels, (ii) compare patient-specific molecular alterations to the ones found in other patients having similar disease patterns and (iii) estimate the probability of the patient to have the assumed disease and a specific pathological stage, respectively, making use of a computational approach that integrates predictive features inferred from multiple types of data, including cancer stage estimates, whole-genome sequencing and RNA sequencing.
MoCi-PMS feeds directly into current efforts to advance precision medicine by providing fine-grained, multi-level analyses of complex disease thereby facilitating clinical decision making, but also drug target discovery. By identifying features that are common and predictive for the pathological stage of patients having similar disease patterns, the system will provide novel insights into the molecular mechanisms that are characteristic to specific pathologies, thereby revealing actionable signatures that will feed into research of patient-tailored therapies.
Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Cancer, Clinical decision making, Complex disease, Deep learning, Drug target identification, Genomics, Machine learning, Personalized medicine, Precision medicine, Transcriptomics

Title: Sensory predictions in the human brain
Abstract:
The world around us is full of rich sensory experiences, which often follow repetitive rules. Through exposure to reoccurring sensory stimuli, we are able to learn patterns and form predictions that help us anticipate future events before these occur, or, infer the state of the world in cases where sensory information is incomplete. The brain continuously operates as a predictive machine not only supporting active predictions (i.e. when these are consciously generated and relevant to our immediate actions), but also when conscious access to incoming sensory stimuli can be excluded, such as during sleep, coma or anesthesia. Predictive traces manifest in multiple stages of sensory information processing, with the most prevalent theory being that ‘higher’ regions of the cortical hierarchy, i.e. frontal areas, propagate predictions to ‘lower’ regions, i.e. sensory areas. Although the electrophysiology of this basic predictive network has been well investigated, it remains unknown what are its computational contents and how these are modulated by conscious access to the environment. 
The present project will combine electrophysiological recordings in humans with computational modelling techniques to achieve two main goals: first, to investigate the neural mechanisms that underlie the formation of sensory predictions across cortical hierarchies, and second, to study how these are modulated by consciousness. 

This project will shed light on the computational and neural mechanisms that underlie the formation of sensory predictions in the human brain. A mechanistic understanding of how these are modulated by consciousness in healthy conditions promises to improve our understanding of pathological cases where sensory predictions are impaired, such as in patients with disorders of consciousness and a host of neuropsychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia.
Keywords: auditory, consciousness, electroencephalography, machine learning, sensory predictions

Title: Dark Matter and Cosmology with Gravitational Lenses
Abstract:
The current model of cosmology, LambdaCDM, is mainly based on three components: baryonic matter, Dark Matter (DM) and Dark Energy (DE). It explains an impressive amount of observations, ranging from the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) to the large scale structures of the Universe. In the recent years, however, new analyses revealed a number of limitations regarding DM and DE. DM does not explain all observations at the scales of individual galaxies, as formulated by the Cusp-Core, Missing Satellites, and Too-Big-to-Fail problems (Vogelsberger et al., 2020). Many alternative DM models have been proposed so far (e.g. warm, self-interacting, primordial black holes), but none has been successful at solving all three. DE is responsible for the accelerated expansion of the Universe, measured today as the Hubble constant (H0). There is a strong disagreement between Early Universe (e.g. the CMB) and Late Universe (e.g. the cosmic distance ladder) measurements of H0, known as the Hubble tension, which suggests either that unknown errors are affecting the measurements, or that LambdaCDM is not a complete description of the Universe (Di Valentino et al., 2021).
Strong gravitational lensing is one of the most powerful ways to study both DM and DE. First, it allows to probe the distribution of DM, because it is sensitive to the total mass of the lens galaxy. Second, the strong lensing of quasars is at the core of a competitive method to measure H0, known as time-delay cosmography, which does not share any data sets nor modeling assumptions with other methods.
In this project, I will use ~ 50 strong lenses to detect and quantify the impact of DM structures onto gravitational arcs. I will compute a collection of the most promising locations of DM structures, called sensitivity maps, in order to improve our knowledge of the DM mass function, a central property to discriminate between different DM models. This task is computationally expansive, hence I will rely on image processing (wavelets and sparsity) and machine learning (automatic differentiation) techniques I developed during my thesis to make it possible, by increasing the number of model parameters at a low computational cost (Galan et al., 2021, Galan et al. 2022 in prep.). Additionally, I will combine constraints from strong lensing with stellar kinematics to measure the shape of the baryonic and DM content of the lens galaxy, on the scales of a few kiloparsecs, helping to solve the Cusp-Core problem. To this aim, I will use new high signal-to-noise spectroscopic data of the lensed quasar RX J1131–1231, observed with the James Webb Space Telescope.
The improved understanding of the DM content of galaxies will provide better mass models in the context of time-delay cosmography. Based on the experience acquired during my thesis, I will incorporate these new constraints to the analysis of Hubble Space Telescope observations of two additional lensed quasars suitable for time-delay cosmography, in order to increase the constraints on H0. Additionally, I will provide a careful assessment of known systematic errors inherent to strong gravitational lensing, which is critical to shed the light on the Hubble tension.
This postdoc will be conducted at the Technical University of Munich (TUM), with Prof. Sherry Suyu as my sponsor. She is a recognized expert in gravitational lensing and cosmology, and will provide me with the data needed for this project. As members of the leading program on time-delay cosmography (TDCOSMO), we will have access to data sets suitable to measure H0. In addition, I will collaborate with DM and cosmology experts from the neighboring Max Planck Institute for Astrophysics (including Prof. V. Springel, Dr. S. Vegetti).
The proposed research and the new techniques I will use will be beneficial for the analysis of the ~ 300,000 new strong lenses that LSST and Euclid surveys will soon discover (Collett, 2015). It will help solving current limitations of DM and the possibility of new physics beyond our cosmological model.
Keywords: automatic differentiation, cosmology, dark matter, sparsity, strong lensing, time delay cosmography, wavelets

Title: Automatic Bone Segmentation in MRI using Statistical Shape and Appearance Models
Abstract:
The aim of the research proposed in this document is to find a general framework for detection
and segmentation of bones in MRI. This is considered a challenging task as the bones do not emit
sufficient electromagnetic signals leading to poor visibility in MRI.
Based on my prior work on detection of ribs in MRI, I propose the use of statistical shape models,
 machine learning-based appearance models and population-based stochastic optimization methods for this purpose. The modules
 in each step of the framework can be adapted to the specific properties of the target organ.
Keywords: Appearance Models, MRI, Segmentation, Statistical shape Models

Title: Projectable Epitope and Metabolic Index couple Multi-omics by sequencing (PrEMIuM-seq):  An innovative platform for delineating metabolism-guided immune regulations
Abstract: Emerging studies unveil the importance of metabolic programming and adaptations on guiding differentiation and functions of immune cells by instructing signaling cascades and epigenetic reprogramming[1, 2]. Interestingly, deregulated metabolism in cancer cells has also been shown to disturb metabolic fitness of immune cells that in turn leads to suppressive nature of the tumor microenvironment (TME). Thus, it is generally believed that we can understand immunometabolic regulations by learning from the metabolic crosstalk within the TME and develop superior cancer immunotherapy by rewiring metabolic programs of tumor-infiltrating T cells. Although the development and improvement of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) allow us to estimate metabolic preference of cells with defined transcriptomic information, the accuracy on predicting metabolic preference by utilizing mRNA levels of metabolic enzymes remain extremely low. Moreover, due to the low depth of mRNA reads, this type of analysis can not provide spatial information to simultaneously reflect metabolic preference and transcriptomics of cells in a single cell resolution. Here we proposed a single-cell approach called “Projectable epitope and metabolic index couple multi-omics by sequencing (PrEMIuM-seq)”, which is designed for “absolute projecting the protein information” through DNA barcode link with antibodies that recognize surface markers and metabolic enzymes and regulators. By combining with machine learning and network analysis, PrEMIuM-seq can empower us to understand how immune cells adapt metabolic challenges in tumors as well as other inflamed tissues in a single cell resolution. Most importantly, PrEMIuM-seq design allows us to integrate metabolomes, transcriptomics, and epigenomics in a single-cell resolution, which can provide an unexplored dimension to delineate the impacts of metabolic adaptations on orchestrating differentiation and activation states of immune cells (Figure 1). Ultimately, we anticipate to apply this approach for spatial analyses, which can improve our understanding in metabolic crosstalk in the TME as well as other inflamed tissues and lymph nodes during infection and vaccination.
Keywords: Hepatocellular carcinoma, anti-tumor immunity, exhaustion, immunometabolic regulation, immunosuppression, macrophage, tumor microenvironment

Title: One-Shot-NMR: Synergizing High-Field Spectroscopy with Deep Learning for Efficient and Cost-Effective Macromolecular Structural Studies
Abstract:
Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is one of the key techniques for protein structures and interactions studies. Its rapid growth in 80s and 90s resulted in standardized research protocol that involves: (a) expression of protein labelled with 13C and 15N isotopes, (b) measurement of multidimensional NMR spectra, and (c) manual analysis of signals recorded in the spectra. For decades, this protocol was the dominant approach in protein NMR spectroscopy, which contributed with over 14000 depositions in the protein databank (PDB), and numerous protein interaction and dynamics studies.

Unfortunately, annual NMR structure depositions in PDB peaked in 2008, and have since been on decline. In contrast, techniques like X-ray crystallography and cryo-EM have seen growing interest and increasing number of annual depositions. While NMR spectroscopy offers unique insights into protein structures, the protocol established in 80s and 90s is becoming too expensive, laborious and limiting for contemporary standards. Four key challenges associated with standard NMR protocol are: (1) the research requires expensive and scarce 13C and 15N isotopes, (2) isotope labelling involves protein expression in bacterial cells, typically E. Coli, limiting research scope to systems that can be expressed in bacterial cells, (3) recording the set of multidimensional NMR spectra takes typically about 2 weeks on expensive multi-million-dollar device, and (4) converting NMR spectra to protein structure model requires weeks or months of manual work. 

We believe that protein structure studies with NMR can be changed in radical manner, as the synergy between deep learning and high-field measurements (900 MHz - 1.2 GHz) can overcome all above-mentioned limitations. Our goal is to establish a deep learning approach that automatically delivers cross-peak positions, chemical shifts and protein structure from just three 2D homonuclear 1H-1H experiments. Specifically, we plan to use 2D COSY, TOCSY and NOESY experiments, which are stacked together to form single 3-channel spectrum (similarly to RGB channels in digital images). These channels encode information about pairs of hydrogens that are direct neighbours (COSY), belong to the same residue (TOCSY) or have through-space contact (NOESY). The 3-channel spectrum and protein sequence are inputs for deep architecture (e.g. Vision Transformer) that predicts distribution over shift assignments for each cross-peak observable in the spectrum. Then, the model output is used to reconstruct shift assignment and, if needed, protein structure.

The proposed approach directly tackles the previously outlined limitations of standard protocol: (1) 13C and 15N isotopes are no longer required, as the method relies only on 1H measurements, (2) no protein expression is necessary, enabling studies of native proteins or those previously challenging to express in E. Coli, (3) measurement time is reduced from 2 weeks to just about 1 day, optimizing utilization of costly instruments, and (4) the data analysis is automated, taking hours of computational time, rather than weeks or months of manual work. Importantly, our method’s output remains fully interpretable, allowing for manual verification of cross-peak positions, chemical shift assignment and protein structure. 

Our method isn’t exclusive to proteins or structure determination. It is applicable to other systems like RNA, DNA or protein-ligand complexes. However, in our pioneer work on this topic, we are choosing proteins as our primary focus to assess technique’s potential. The proposed research builds upon our previous work in developing ARTINA, a deep learning approach for protein structure determination with standard protocol. Its public implementation (nmrtist.org) got substantial attention in NMR community, being used to analyze over 9000 multidimensional spectra and complete over 3000 shift assignments.
Keywords: Deep Learning, NMR spectroscopy, Protein Structures and Interactions, Vision Transformer

Title: Fluency in Speech and Signing
Abstract:
Fluency in spoken communication – the ability to speak with smooth and natural timing properties and speed – serves as the foundation for successful spoken interaction, enabling efficient and effective communication. It is one of the most salient features of spoken language proficiency.  While fluency has been extensively studied in speech communication, the role of fluency in sign language—where language is conveyed exclusively through visual-spatial mode—remains largely obscure. The central aim of the present project is therefore to understand whether sign language relies on comparable utterance production and cognitive mechanisms as speech. We want to understand whether the mechanisms relevant for fluency in speech play a critical role in sign language fluency as well. 
The project will follow three major inter-related research directions: (1) Understanding fluency across modalities and proficiency levels: Following a linguistic approach, we aim at understanding fluency aspects within and across modalities (speech, signing) as well as within and across proficiency levels (first language, second language). Thus, we will analyze fluency in first-modality first-language (M1L1) and first-modality second-language (M1L2) signers as well as second-modality second-language (M2L2) signers and first-modality second-language (M1L2) speakers. (2) Automatic analysis of fluency in speech and signing: Focusing on the aspects of fluency identified as part of the first research direction, we will leverage machine learning methods—more specifically, deep learning methods—to investigate the automation of fluency analysis in speech and signing. Complementarily to this linguistic approach, we will apply methods to the raw signal—the acoustic and the visual signal—to find the best correlates for aspects of fluency in speech and signing. (3) Common cognitive processes in speech and signing: Our aim is to better understand common information processing mechanisms in speech and signing. Recent compelling evidence showed that signing reveals similar timing properties compared to speech by following a rate-of-event rule at a modulation rate of approximately <5 Hz, suggesting common neural oscillation mechanisms in the two modes. Here we will analyse the consequences of this phenomenon for information processing by testing intelligibility of speech and signing at different rates. 
The project will be based at the University of Zurich and the University of Teacher Education in Special Needs Zurich, in collaboration with Leiden University. This setup provides a unique combination of expertise in both speech and sign language. The partnership also ensures access to relevant test populations to carry out production, signal and cognitive processing experimental and exploratory paradigms. 
By investigating common fluency mechanisms in both signing and speaking, the project aims to provide a fundamental theoretical understanding of how human communication operates across different modalities and to identify shared cognitive and linguistic processes. The project will also inform the field of second language acquisition, as it is yet unclear whether the relation between L1 and L2 fluency is moderated by proficiency. Additionally, the project’s practical applications will contribute to advancements in sign and spoken language recognition and synthesis, paving the way for improved assistive technologies in the context of accessibility. The project will also lay the foundation for future testing of neural mechanisms underpinning possible common cognitive processes in multi-modal communication.
Keywords: Swiss German Sign Language (DSGS), computer vision, fluency, language assessment, natural language processing, second language acquisition, second language acquistion, sign language, speech

Title: Human-AI decision-making: Disrupting industries - disrupting passion?
Abstract:
Decision-making - the choice of the alternative that is expected to lead to a preferred result - depends on people's emotional states and their motivation to process information. (Langley, Mintzberg, Pitcher, Posada, & Saint-Macary, 1995; Seo & Barrett, 2007). The rise of artificial intelligence (AI) – machines performing cognitive functions such as learning or problem solving (Nilsson, 1971) – is fundamentally changing organizational decision-making (Shrestha, Ben-Menahem, & Von Krogh, 2019; von Krogh, 2018). While AI increases the efficiency to process large amounts of data (Brynjolfsson & Mcafee, 2017; Shrestha et al., 2019) some evidence suggests it may also be detrimental due to the loss of control and autonomy (Davenport & Ronanki, 2018; Kellogg, Valentine, & Christin, 2020; Raisch & Krakowski, 2020). Since control and autonomy over one’s work are central drivers of positive affect and motivation in the workplace (Deci & Ryan, 1987; Gagné, M., & Deci, 2005; Rich, Lepine, & Crawford, 2010), AI has the potential to disrupt employee passion, which refers to strong positive affect and sense of personal value triggering actions (Vallerand et al., 2003; Vallerand & Houlfort, 2003). However, empirical research on the effect of AI for organizational decision-making on the passion of workers is lacking. 

To bridge this gap, the proposed two-year research project seeks to explore how to design human-AI decision-making processes to mitigate potential downsides of AI on employee passion. Specifically, this research sets out to pinpoint why, how and for whom AI might disrupt passion and result in poor decision-making and to subsequently design interventions to overcome these challenges. Theoretically, I will draw upon prior research on AI-based decision-making (Kellogg et al., 2020; Shrestha, Krishna, & von Krogh, 2021), motivation and affect (f.ex. Gohm & Clore, 2002; Grant, 2008). Empirically, I will study employees using AI-based solution to make decisions. Given the lack of research on the link between passion and AI, I will first apply qualitative methods (interviews, observations, and surveys) to develop a process model of the conditions under and the mechanisms through which AI-driven decision-making aids foster or hinder employee passion. Second, I will design a study to quantitatively test the derived model. This research will contribute to theory and practice in three significant ways. First, I will advance a theory on the affective underpinnings impacting human-AI decision-making. I will shift away from a merely efficiency-driven view and develop a human-oriented lens to fully reap the potential benefits of AI. Second, I will employ both qualitative and quantitative methods to develop a holistic understanding of an under researched phenomenon. Third, I will theorize on the structural, cultural, relational and individual factors that allow individuals to sustain passion when applying AI for decision-making. Together with my industry partner, I will develop recommendations and host workshops to support decision-makers in designing future workplaces with highly passionate employees.

Title: Automatic Categorization of Potsherds
Abstract: The Tepalcatl project will focus on advancing the state-of-the-art in computational archaeology. More precisely, this project will investigate the potential of using clustering and classification methods, that provide stable quantitive results, to address the problem of automatic categorization of potsherds, which often requires qualitative analysis and expert knowledge. On the one hand, the Tepalcatl project has the technical objective of advancing the state-of-the-art in methods for efficient clustering and classification of image collections. On the other hand, it will provide tools to assist archaeologists in the automatic categorization of potsherds. The importance of this research project lays upon the fact that potsherds are the most studied material in any excavation site, as they provide with the relevant knowledge regarding the cultural and historical context for a given site, thus their categorization is an important challenge that requires efficient tools that can be used at excavation sites. Overall, this work represents a bi-disciplinary effort towards bringing the potential that computer science methods have in providing tools to satisfy archaeological needs.
Keywords: computer vision, cultural heritage, image categorization, machine learning, potsherds

Title: Improved methods for theoretical materials design
Abstract:
Materials design has become one of the most rapidly increasing fields of condensed matter science during the last years. Discovery of novel materials are called for with potential applications in various technologically relevant fields such as energy production and storage, novel electronic devices, data storage, medical application and catalysis. Instead of synthesizing and characterizing novel materials in
time-consuming, expensive experiments, theoretical material scientists have started to create databases obtained from all materials known to date and to systematically analyze them with high-throughput computation methods, trying to gain insight on how chemistry and structures are linked to material properties and to extract patterns from the underlying data. New, innovative computational methods are needed to efficiently characterize the continuously growing amount of materials data, and techniques need to be developed to extrapolate materials properties to design novel, undiscovered compounds with improved properties.

The presented project is aimed at solving two key limitations in materials design. First, most structure prediction methods do not access the knowledge stored in the large structural databases. By combining the Minima Hopping structure prediction scheme and machine-learning techniques a sophisticated method will be developed to explore new chemistries and to discover compounds with improved or new properties in energy applications. The new method will be applied to real-life challenges in materials design to find thermoelectric and hydrogen storage materials, or materials for use in photovoltaic applications. Second, Quantum Monte Carlo methods will be used to refine the energetic ordering of different phases in various compounds to significantly improve the predictive power by going beyond the accuracy of conventional density functional theory calculations used in current approaches. The outcome of this project will be of great value for many material scientists and will considerably accelerate the theoretical discovery of novel materials.
Keywords: Data Mining, Electronic Structure, Machine Learning, Materials Design, Simulation, Structure Prediction

Title: Astronomy Technology and Cutting-Edge Science with HIRAX: Precision Beam Calibration
Abstract:
Cosmology has undergone tremendous changes over the past decades, with an exponential growth of observational results that have allowed us to build a very precise model of what happened over the last 13.8 billion years, from the big bang until today. This development has gone hand-in-hand with technological progress that has enabled the observation of the Universe during different stages in its evolution, and the analysis of the resulting data. This revolution in observations is still ongoing, and one of the most data intensive fields in the coming decades will be radio astronomy where new, huge telescopes will deliver incredible amounts of data, that however require powerful analysis techniques in order to extract valid scientific results. These results are desperately needed to convert our precise models of the Universe into an improved understanding of the fundamental physical principles that govern the cosmological behaviour on the largest scales.

One of the upcoming radio telescopes is HIRAX, the Hydrogen Intensity and Real-time Analysis eXperiment, a South African led project with significant Swiss contributions that has led to an active and successful collaboration between the two countries. HIRAX will map baryon acoustic oscillations in the distribution of neutral hydrogen gas over a significant fraction of the sky between redshifts 0.8 and 2.5. HIRAX will be situated in one of the most radio-quiet locations on Earth, the SKA South Africa site in the Karoo desert. However, in order to fully exploit the HIRAX data, we need to also understand the instrumental response to exquisite precision. The diffuse synchrotron emission from our galaxy or from bright extragalactic sources is many orders of magnitude larger than the cosmological  signal. It will be critical for HIRAX to understand the spectral response of the instrument well enough to avoid contamination of the cosmological signal from spectrally smooth foreground sources. 
 
The goal of this proposal is to tackle precisely this challenge, leveraging the successful Swiss - South African collaboration to develop an integrated beam model for the HIRAX telescope, using a variety of scientific and engineering techniques. We will draw on the skills and expertise of South African and Swiss researchers at all levels, both students and staff, to combine a range of approaches, from beam measurements and associated analysis techniques, to beam simulations and beam model fitting. In addition to the scientific results that we expect from the project, this will also lead to more exchanges between the two communities, and to the training of young scientists in cutting-edge fields in science and technology. The detailed aims of the proposal are
   * Implementation and coordination of beam calibration techniques
   * Development of a simulation and modelling pipeline focused on beam calibration
   * Development of an integrated instrument beam model
   * Development of a beam calibration strategy
The results from this work will be instrumental for the success of the HIRAX telescope.

Title: The Evolutionary Epidemiology of HIV Elimination
Abstract:
Thanks to antiretroviral treatment and pre-exposure prophylaxis, prevention of HIV transmission has made substantial progress in the last years, bringing elimination of HIV transmission within reach in the next decade.  However, major obstacles and challenges threaten this goal both locally and globally. These include localized transmission, e.g. from difficult to reach populations, and, especially in resource-limited settings, the emergence and transmission of drug-resistant strains.  Both challenges underline the importance of viral evolution and genomics for understanding infectious disease epidemiology and prevention. In the first case, molecular epidemiology, which tracks the evolution of the virus, is the principal approach to reconstruct transmission chains and identify foci of transmission - in the second case, understanding the threat of antiretroviral resistance results from the interaction of epidemiological and evolutionary processes. This proposal aims to advance this field by analyzing rich data from observational cohorts and using mathematical models to integrate the different data sources. We will address these challenges in two work-packages:

WP-1 Viral genomics and real-time precision public health as tools for HIV micro-elimination:  We will monitor the growth of transmission clusters in real-time and determine the transmission context of newly diagnosed patients using viral nucleotide sequences from the Swiss HIV Cohort Study. We will use statistical learning approaches to predict the growth of transmission clusters and the probability that newly diagnosed individuals will be linked with future cases based on behavioral, epidemiological, and molecular data. We will then develop an individual-based transmission model and evaluate the potential of these tools to enhance and target prevention measures such as pre-exposure prophylaxis, test and treat, or partner notification to reduce HIV transmission and promote micro-elimination. 

WP-2 Investigating the drivers of antiretroviral resistance at the population level in resource-limited settings: We will develop a compartmental stochastic HIV-1 transmission model that can simulate the evolution of antiretroviral resistance to high-genetic barrier drugs such as dolutegravir (DTG). We will parameterize this model using the epidemiological data from the International epidemiology Databases to Evaluate AIDS (IeDEA) and data from a large multiregional study determining genotypic and phenotypic resistance from patients failing on DTG-based therapy (both funded by the NIH).  The integration of these unique data sources in the model will allow to assess the extent to which DTG can prevent the spread of resistance at the population level, identify the drivers of resistance and the populations at highest risk of resistance evolution, and assess the potential of public health interventions to curb the spread. In follow-up work, we will consider the feedback between the control of HIV transmission and antiretroviral resistance by combining approaches from WP-1 and WP-2.  

The challenges addressed in this proposal are relevant both for eliminating or at least sustainably reducing HIV transmission and, more generally, for advancing the molecular epidemiology of infectious diseases and predicting in real-time the relevance of ongoing evolutionary processes.
Keywords: Antiretroviral Resistance, Epidemiology, HIV-1, Mathematical Modelling, Molecular Epidemiology

Title: Kernel-based Dimensionality Reduction
Abstract: Real world systems generate high dimensional complex data. Some are also dealing with large scale datasets. In Dimensionality Reduction (DR) the goal is to search and project the data to a lower dimensional space while maintaining sufficient richness to represent the statistical properties of the data. This  is particularly difficult to achieve since no prior knowledge about data can be hypothesized, and there is need for a proper structure dependent measure. Another challenging task is to automatically define the sufficient lower dimension, which is instead commonly a subjective and user-defined parameter. Statistical kernel-based methods are state-of-the-art techniques that outperformed prior approaches in a broad range of applications, by mapping the data samples to a rich Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) and then linearly handle statistical dependency of the data in the destination space. They are particularly useful when the analytical functions over data are not available or not explicitly defined. They can be applied on high dimensional data with any arbitrary complex structure. Having low computational cost, they make for good candidates to work on large scale datasets. In this work I present a novel application of these methods to automatically capture the intrinsic structure of the data. I also investigate application of this approach to solve some complex problems in Computer Vision, Robotics, and Reinforcement Learning. Selection of a data dependent statistical kernel is also considered as a fundamental component.
Keywords: Dimensionality reduction, Intrinsic structure, Reinforcement learning, Statistical Kernel-based methods

Title: Multimodal patient-specific eye model for delineation and treatment planning of ocular tumors
Abstract:
In the past few years, retinoblastoma and uveal melanoma, the most common cancers of the eye, have witnessed an important advance in the field of medical imaging and its applications in ophthalmology. 
MRI, CT, Fundus Photography and Ultrasound are among the image modalities of reference for treatment planning and diagnosis confirmation of the disease. However, existing methods for modeling the eye are still imprecise and they do not benefit from state of the art techniques developed in other medical image processing applications. In addition, there is a disconnection between the different image modalities due to the lack of common anatomical landmarks and to the difficult method standardization in ophthalmic radiation oncology. This situation mainly affects the treatment planning (radiation dose optimization) step involved in External Beam Radiotherapy (EBRT), Cryotherapy and Brachytherapy, thus precluding optimal preservation of healthy tissue in patients. Furthermore, some patients need to undergo eye surgery prior to treatment planning, with the objective of offering a better tracking of the tumor location during therapy, therefore they require the implant of tantalum fiducial markers in the posterior part of the eye. Hence, techniques for preventing eye surgery while providing similar tracking results would offer an unprecedented opportunity for improving the patient’s quality of life during and after treatment. 
During the last two years we have developed a method to fully automatically segment the eye in the 3D MRI, and collaborated in the preliminary fusion of MRI with Fundus photography. These contributions follow the motivations of the presented project: i) create a method for the automatic delineation of pathological areas inside the eye in the MRI by combining multiple MRI sequences and machine learning techniques, ii) propose a framework for the fusion of MRI and Fundus photography for robust and accurate eye tumor delineation towards preventing eye surgery and iii) to set the basis for techniques to predict the tumor growth based on the shape and location of the tumor, and the technique applied for treatment. These ideas and the extended motivation can be read in detail in the research plan.
Keywords: machine learning, medical image analysis, ophthalmology, radiation oncology, registration, segmentation, statistical modeling, treatment planning

Title: Connectivity and dynamics of recurrent neuronal circuits
Abstract:
Background and general aim:
Cognitive brain functions arise from synaptic interactions between neurons in structured networks but it remains unclear how network connectivity determines the dynamics of neuronal population activity, and how modifications of connectivity update information processing during learning. We will combine 2-photon measurements of population activity, dense network reconstructions by volume electron microscopy, and computational modeling to analyze how connectivity defines computational functions of neuronal circuits in larval and adult zebrafish. The focus will be on memory-related computations by balanced-state networks in the olfactory bulb and telencephalic area Dp, the homolog of olfactory cortex.
Specific aims:
Aim 1: Structural and functional variability of OB networks. We will reconstruct wiring diagrams of complete olfactory bulbs from multiple zebrafish larvae after 2-photon imaging of odor-evoked population activity. Correlated variability in connectivity and neuronal dynamics will be analyzed within and across bulbs to examine structure-function relationships at the resolution of individual neurons and synapses. 
Aim 2: Reconstruction of an associative memory network. We will reconstruct the complete circuitry of Dp after measuring odor-evoked activity across >1000 neurons in adult zebrafish trained in an odor discrimination task. This will allow us to examine the structural underpinnings of memory-related changes in neuronal activity and to test key predictions of influential theories of memory.
Aim 3: Computational analysis of connectivity. To examine how connectivity determines the dynamics of population activity we will analyze spiking network models with natural and modified wiring diagrams. We will specifically explore whether balanced ensembles of tuned excitatory and inhibitory neurons define distinct manifolds in neural state space that represent maps of memories or valence.
Expected value: Our unique datasets will allow us to establish systematic links between the topological organization of recurrent neuronal circuits and their functional dynamics. Similar datasets cannot be obtained from larger vertebrates where exhaustive circuit reconstructions are prohibitively expensive. We will directly test key predictions of theoretical models that cannot be addressed without dense circuit reconstructions and corresponding activity measurements. The insights will be critical for a mechanistic understanding of neuronal computations underlying memory and cognition, which is a major challenge in neuroscience and important to understand circuit dysfunctions in disease. Moreover, our results are expected to be of high interest for the design of next-generation networks in artificial intelligence.
