Title: NSF-SNSF: Urban Harmony: Bridging City Forms and Human Well-Being Across Philadelphia and Lausanne
Abstract:
The question of how urban environments influence human well-being has been gaining attention as a critical area of study for modern cities. Answering this question requires data-driven approaches combined with experimental methods to compare current urban developments worldwide and their impact on residents. The following proposal puts forward a novel cross regional framework to investigate how urban form features such as land use, street network and connectivity affect various aspects of human well-being, across two distinct cities, Philadelphia and Lausanne. This framework starts by clustering urban regions based on urban form characteristics (e.g., land use diversity, street network design), helping to identify urban environments that can be directly compared both within and across Philadelphia and Lausanne. Through a series of experiments across experimentation mediums, we will assess how different urban forms influence human stress, physiology, cognition, and emotional states across detected clusters. The findings of our experiments will be then translated into actionable urban planning guidelines through direct collaboration with various stakeholders. By identifying cross-regional differences and similarities, this research will provide valuable insights for urban planners and policymakers both in the US and Europe, offering a framework for creating healthier urban environments.

The first objective is to build a robust framework leveraging machine learning methods to cluster neighborhoods in Philadelphia and Lausanne based on urban form features such as land use. This objective allows for finding candidate neighborhoods that are comparable across two vastly different cities in two different continents (OBJ-1). The second objective involves conducting controlled experiments within the detected clusters to understand the pathways in which the urban form affect indicators of well-being, such as higher stress levels in dense environments (OBJ-2). In contrast to prior work, we will perform the experiments across various mediums, i.e., online surveys, virtual reality experiments and field studies. Within each experimental platform, participants will observe (in an online survey), virtually walk (in virtual experiments), or walk on a controlled path (in field study), while we monitor biosignal metrics, including their physiological and cognitive responses, through an array of sensors (e.g., smart watches, brain activity monitoring, and eye tracking glasses) as well as various standardized questionnaires. The third objective aims to inform urban design guidelines that can promote well-being in diverse contexts (OBJ-3). In this objective, we will link our findings from field experiments with existing urban planning and design practices, identifying pathways by which our experimental findings can inform decision-making. The comparative nature of this research will shed light on whether certain urban design principles are universally beneficial or region-specific. 

The proposed project offers significant societal benefits by identifying urban form features that universally or regionally promote well-being, which will inform urban design and policy-making, helping cities worldwide to foster healthier and more resilient environments. The collaboration between the two universities will enhance the educational experience of students at both institutions, helping to further develop global perspectives. The project material will be used to develop a novel course titled human centered urban environments. Lastly, the project will involve interdisciplinary training in urban planning and design, mobility, physiological monitoring, and data analytics and will prepare the next generation of urban planners and researchers to address the complex challenges of human well-being in cities.
Keywords: physiological response, urban form, walkability, well-being

Title: A normative approach to uncertainty in habitual and goal-directed decision making
Abstract:
Decisions of humans and animals can be traced back to neuronal activity in multiple brain areas. The dominant computational paradigm for modeling psychological and neural aspects of decision-making tasks is reinforcement learning (RL). It is concerned with how to take decisions in an environment so as to maximize some notion of reward. Animals face a range of such optimization problems, which are critical to their longevity, and solve them effectively.
This goal can be achieved using habitual or goal-directed decision making. Past research has been dominated by the finding that the firing rate of dopamine neurons appears to mimic the prediction error signal in one "habitual" algorithm, which uses the difference between successive temporal predictions of future reward. In contrast, less research has been devoted to neural representations underlying goal-directed decision making and in particular how uncertainty might be incorporated into them. This question also has important clinical implications since pathologies of the representation of uncertainty have been linked to psychiatric disorders such as anxiety and schizophrenia. The principled way to take uncertainty into account is to deploy a Bayesian formulation. Within neuroscience this normative perspective has already played an important role in perception and motor control. 
In the present project, we propose to investigate it within the framework of reinforcement learning. Given the universality of principles the brain employs, the success of the normative account is prone to extend to decision making as well. For that, we will combine theory and simulation with validation through comparison with experimental literature. We will especially draw on probabilistic graphical models, Monte Carlo methods and neural network simulations, which will enable us to address several essential questions. We will first investigate how a normative account of uncertainty impacts habitual decision making. Then, we will study the implications of a Bayesian framework on goal-directed decision making. Finally, we will examine how habitual and goal-directed decision making are combined. Solving those questions will allow us to shed light on how the brain incorporates uncertainty into its neuronal computations. Moreover, it will be an essential step towards a better understanding of not only normal but also of pathological decision making in general. In particular, with regard to clinical relevance, impaired decision making has been linked to suicide attempts, addiction and Parkinson's disease, and the work proposed here will lay some important theoretical foundations for understanding these pathologies.
Keywords: Bayesian inference, decision making, neural computation, neuroscience, reinforcement learning

Title: Interpreting Exoplanets Using Machine Learning
Abstract:
The detailed characterisation of exoplanets, including those that may harbour life, is a core science goal of the next generation of major observatories, such as the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the European Extremely Large Telescope (E-ELT). These will lead to an explosion in the sensitivity and precision of exoplanet spectra, allowing us to study exoplanets as the three-dimensional, dynamic systems that they are. Current techniques comparing observations to models (known as atmospheric retrievals) rely on simplified 1-D models that will soon become insufficient. However, due to computational restrictions, traditional retrievals will be unable to cope with more complex physical models. During my PhD, I developed a brand-new machine learning retrieval method, which uses a Random Forest to drastically speed up the process. I have proven this method to be effective on both low-resolution, spaced-based data and high-resolution, ground-based data. With the SNSF Postdoc.Mobility fellowship, I will use this tool to deliver game-changing advancements in our interpretation of the detailed behaviour of exoplanet atmospheres. 

For my first project, I will use the Random Forest to simultaneously analyse exoplanet spectra from ground- and space-based telescopes. The two types of data provide different but equally valuable information about a planet’s atmosphere. I will start by focussing on gas giants, which already have excellent ground-based spectra available. These objects teach us about exoplanet diversity, and their composition can provide clues about their system’s formation history. The efficiency of the Random Forest allows for more complex and accurate physical models to be implemented. Furthermore, the forest enables an information content analysis, which can be used to advise the community on which datasets to use and support proposals for telescope time. This method can be used with both currently available data from the Hubble Space Telescope and existing high-resolution spectrographs, as well as upcoming data from JWST and the E-ELT. 

My second project will focus on three-dimensional analysis of exoplanets. With the improving quality of data, studies have shown that one-dimensional models can lead to biased results for the atmospheric composition of a planet. This could have detrimental effects when determining its potential habitability. The 3-D structure of an exoplanet can be simulated using General Circulation Models (GCMs). By taking advantage of the speed of our machine learning method, I will use these GCMs to consistently analyse many types of data, which has proven challenging due to their long computation time. This will give us an entirely new window into atmospheric circulation on exoplanets.

I will advance the field of exoplanet atmospheres by improving our analysis of these alien worlds. The conditions of these planets will teach us about the bigger picture of the universe, by answering questions about planet formation, potential habitability, and the uniqueness of our solar system.
Keywords: Atmospheric Retrieval, Exoplanet Atmospheres, Machine Learning

Title: Development, deployment and field testing of web-based augmented reality systems for interactive molecular modeling in educational settings using ordinary computers
Abstract:
Modern human-computer interaction technologies using augmented and virtual reality (AR/VR) have been attributed enormous potential in assisting thinking and learning processes, especially in chemistry and related disciplines that deal with abstract, intangible and/or idealized concepts such as molecules, electronic orbitals, forces, etc. Despite a number of studies, prototypes and a few computer programs putting forward AR and VR for education in areas of science involving chemistry (i.e. also molecular biology, biophysics, etc.) they all suffer from problems that strongly limit wide availability and usability: they rely on ad hoc hardware, which despite the dropping costs still preclude worldwide adoption, and cumbersome software setups.
  This Spark project seeks to develop an AR platform for immersive molecular visualization and modeling based entirely in web pages that run in common web browsers on ordinary webcam- and internet-enabled computers. With such web platform teachers and students will be able to explore (i.e. view, manipulate, interact with) molecules in 3D as if they were tangible but actually through an AR interface that brings in all the power of computer graphics and calculations at their hands, providing a mixed physical and computational pedagogical experience richer than that offered by either plain computer graphics or plastic-made molecular models. By using one AR marker on each hand, users will be able to manipulate virtual molecules in 3D to explore shapes, chirality, orbitals, surface properties, etc., and to force and test rotations and other deformations, probe bond formation and breaking, test non-covalent interactions, and more. All this at the cost of a standard computer, hence available not only at schools/universities but also accessible by students at their homes.
  Starting from preliminary feasibility tests about the use of web-based technologies for AR-based molecular display and calculations, the project will entail (i) development of a complete AR system for molecular visualization and handling based on standard computer vision techniques adapted to the web, and of a library of interesting examples (although users will also be able to load their own molecules); (ii) extension of existing rigid-body physics web engines to incorporate phenomena they do not account for, like electrostatics, bond breaking and formation, certain quantum effects; and (iii) extensive testing of the AR platform by teachers and students of institutions in Switzerland and abroad to evaluate the actual effect of such technologies on learning. 
  We will finally open the tool to the world and promote it through organizations dedicated to science education and outreach on a budget. Successful achievement of this project’s goals will not only (i) lead to a new tool that every student and teacher can use, but will also (ii) enable actual mass testing of the utility of these technologies in enhancing education, (iii) help integrate research groups working on human-computer interactions, pedagogy, artificial intelligence, molecular modeling, etc. at the host institution, and (iv) set the stage for more complex versions where web-based AR/VR are used for actual scientific research, beyond education.

Title: Decadal Variability of Daily Weather (DVDW)
Abstract:
Climate reconstructions serve science and society in many ways. Apart from documenting past climate states, they allow placing current climatic changes into context, quantifying decadal-to-centennial variability, and unravelling new climate mechanisms. This is also relevant in the con-text of decadal climate prediction, which has become a foremost research topic and which bene-fits from comprehensive reconstructions that go beyond temperature. In an ongoing ERC Ad-vanced Grant, we generated a global 3D reconstruction of monthly climate back to 1421, ModE-RA, based on data assimilation and making use of a large observational database. It allows a dynamical view of past climate. The proposed project builds on this new resource to analyse mechanisms behind multiannual-to-decadal variability. 
However, analysing monthly climate bears limitations. Therefore, we will address the daily scale, which is relevant for impacts and is closer to the scale of atmospheric processes. Also, many climate indices - phenological, late frost, growing season length, fire weather – as well as climate impact models – crop models, hydrological models, snowpack models - require daily input. Atmospheric data products such as reanalyses are extended backward but uncertainty gets large as we go back to the early 19th century. In an ongoing SNF project (WeaR) we have devel-oped and applied other methods of weather reconstructions that allow going further back in time, such as analog approaches. In the proposed project we combine the monthly ModE-RA with sub-monthly weather variability over Europe based on WeaR data. 
The goal of this project is to (1) provide daily weather fields for Europe back to ca. 1684, (2) to analyse decadal weather variability and their relation to large-scale climate mechanisms and (3) to calculate impact-relevant climate indices and analyse them together with historical sources.
First, we will improve the existing monthly reconstruction with a better implementation of the Kalman Filter and on a higher resolution. Then we will use historical instrumental data and weather diaries to add sub-monthly information using machine learning. On this time scale, bias-es in historical observations matter the least, and we preserve the monthly mean. Our approach makes use of the covariance matrix of the fields and of their time sequence. It will be trained on ERA5 reanalyses (soon extending back to 1940) and applied to past centuries. After 1806, an additional approach will be used, namely off-line assimilation of pressure and temperature ob-servations into the ensemble of the “Twentieth Century Reanalysis” 20CRv3. Fields from both approaches will be analysed with respect to interannual-to-decadal variability, which will be compared to corresponding results from a large ensemble of atmospheric model simulations for the period 1421-2008 (30,000 yrs in low resolution, 3000 yrs high resolution) performed within the current ERC project. We will focus on the relation of weather variability to Atlantic Ocean variability as well as the tropical and subtropical circulations such as monsoons or the subtropi-cal jet. From the daily fields, perhaps combined with scenarios (CORDEX), impact-relevant in-dices will be calculated and analysed. Results will be compared with historical sources on im-pacts.
Keywords: Historical data, meteorological measurements

Title: Attacking Deep Networks to Better Understand Them
Abstract:
Deep neural networks (DNNs) have led to tremendous strides in computer vision, addressing diverse tasks such as image classification, semantic segmentation, monocular depth and surface normal prediction, 6D object pose estimation, and 3D reconstruction. As such, they are now being deployed in many real-world applications, such as automated driving, surveillance and security, and image analysis in social media. While this has the potential to greatly benefit our society, it also raises important new concerns, in particular regarding the robustness of these DNNs.

Specifically, it has been shown that DNNs are vulnerable to different types of attacks. They include, among others, adversarial attacks, which aim to affect a DNN’s prediction by adding an imperceptible noise to the input image, and privacy inference attacks, which seek to extract private information from the features computed by a DNN from the input image. Much research has then focused on designing increasingly effective attacks, strategies to detect these attacks, or solutions to increase the DNNs’ robustness to them. In other words, the bulk of this research has been dedicated to the scenario where a malicious adversary aims to attack a DNN.

While we acknowledge the importance of this research, the goal of this proposal is to study DNN attacks for an entirely different purpose, specifically, that of improving our understanding of DNNs. In the recently-finished SNSF project 200021 175581, we started investigating the use of standard adversarial attacks to analyze the behavior of DNNs for semantic segmentation and human pose estimation. In this proposal, we aim to go well beyond this and will design new attack strategies whose main goal will not be to fool a DNN or steal information from it, but rather to query some specific properties to obtain an interpretable understanding of its behavior. We will achieve this by developing:
- Information Inference Attacks. We will develop strategies to study the perceptual information contained in a trained DNN’s features. Specifically, we will analyze whether one can extract semantically-meaningful properties, such as color, texture, edges, object categories, pose, and 3D shape, from the DNN’s features. The success or failure of the prediction of such quantities will tell us what information is exploited by a DNN trained for a target task.
- Semantic Adversarial Attacks. We will design attacks that modify a specific, interpretable property to fool a trained DNN. In particular, we will investigate attacks that alter sensor properties, color, texture, edges, viewpoint, depth, normals, and 3D shape. We will achieve this by either directly modifying the input image to alter these properties, or via rendering and NeRF based strategies to reason in 3D. As before, the success or failure of our attacks will provide an understanding of the sensitivity of a trained target DNN to different scene properties.

We will study such attacks for different tasks, including object recognition, semantic segmentation, monocular depth and normal prediction, and 6D object pose estimation. Our attacks will let us analyze not only the behavior of existing frameworks tackling these tasks, but also the influence of different deep learning factors on the DNNs’ behavior. To achieve this, we will develop strategies to study:
- The Impact of the Data. We will investigate how the training inputs (i.e., images), outputs (i.e., labels), and target tasks (single vs multiple) affect the information exploited by DNNs for their predictions. In turn, we will design meta-learning algorithms to search for data augmentation, sample selection, and task selection strategies to achieve robustness to specific phenomena.
- The Impact of Training and Architecture. We will study the influence of the training strategy (e.g., hyper-parameters, self-supervised learning), and of the architecture (e.g., normalization, CNNs vs transformers, compact networks) on the DNNs’ behavior. We will then develop AutoML techniques to discover the best training strategy and DNN architecture for a desired behavior.

In short, this project will investigate DNN attacks from a completely new perspective, with a view to provide a better understanding of DNNs. We will develop a general framework, publicly available to other deep learning practitioners for them to analyze their DNNs. As such, we are confident that our research will lead to significant advances in computer vision, and machine learning in general.
Keywords: Adversarial Attacks, Computer vision, Deep learning, Interpretability, Privacy

Title: An autonomous platform for the accelerated discovery of polyurethane degrading enzymes
Abstract:
Background: Polyurethane (PUR), a synthetic polymer, accounts for ~10% of global plastic waste, and is particularly recalcitrant due to its complex structural properties. Enzymes, also known as nature's catalysts, offer eco-friendly alternatives to incineration and landfilling, which are energy intensive and environmentally unsustainable. Nonetheless, wild-type PUR-degrading enzymes, e.g. urethanases and amidases, exhibit low activity, and their degradation mechanism remains elusive. Addressing these limitations demand innovative approaches beyond traditional enzyme design-test cycles.

Aim: To develop an interdisciplinary high-throughput enzyme screening platform, by combining machine learning (ML) concepts in directed evolution protocols for accelerated discovery of PUR degrading enzymes. Once potent enzymes are identified, structure-function relationships will be established to gain mechanistic insights into the mode of enzymatic PUR depolymerization. 

Methods: The project will synergize my expertise in building foundational to advanced ML models with expertise in enzyme engineering for plastic waste management from Prof. Dr. Uwe Bornscheuer’s group. The entire project involving cross-disciplinary methodologies will be carried out in three distinct phases:

Phase 1: Data analysis and ML model development 
• In-depth statistical analysis of existing enzymatic PUR degradation data in the Bornscheuer group. 
• Develop uncertainty-based and large language model (LLM)-based surrogate models to map enzyme 
  function based on their amino acid sequences.
Phase 2: Implementation of active learning-guided directed evolution 
• ML-guided directed evolution to recommend novel PUR degrading enzymes or variants.
• Screen several thousand enzymes using the integrated platform to identify potent candidates.

Title: Untangling Researcher Mobility, Productivity, and Knowledge Fit
Abstract:
When researchers move, they carry with them the skills and knowledge they have developed throughout their career. Mobility plays a critical role in the diffusion of knowledge, but also in the creation of knowledge. Regarding the latter, it is well established that there is a positive correlation between mobility and productivity, that is, mobile researchers exhibit greater productivity than non-mobile researchers. The direction of causation in that relationship is, however, unclear. Are mobile researchers more productive due to the additional skills developed and knowledge acquired in their new job? Or are researchers of greater talent simply more likely to be given the opportunity to move?

Promoting researcher mobility is given high priority in science policy. Indeed, many funding programs carry explicit mobility criteria -- including the program under which this proposal is being submitted. But the effects of mobility are not yet well understood: the scientific literature does not clearly answer a number of questions regarding the causal relationship between mobility and productivity and the factors influencing it.

This project will rely on data science and machine learning tools to develop a large-scale data set (in the hundreds of thousands) of researcher profiles from bibliographic databases. It will develop novel approaches for quantifying the topics a researcher is working on and for tracking the researcher's topic portfolio. With these it will answer three important questions regarding the mobility of researchers:

1) What are the general patterns of how mobility shapes a scientist's research topics?
2) What is the causal effect of researcher mobility on productivity?
3) What is the role of 'knowledge fit' in the mobility-productivity relationship?

The first question will provide insight into the effectiveness of mobility as a means for developing new skills and knowledge. The second will put to rest a long-running debate as to whether mobility directly boosts productivity or simply appears due to the overall higher talent level of the researchers offered the opportunity to move. The third question draws on 'person-organization fit' theory from management science and 'job matching' theory from economics. It will test whether productivity gains observed post mobility arise from a better fit between the researcher's topics and his or her new department.

In answering these questions this project will make a significant contribution to the academic literature concerning mobility, knowledge flows, and spillover. But, more importantly, it will provide key insights into the validity of assumptions promoting mobility in science policy. This project will push cutting-edge tools from big data and machine learning into mainstream economics of science research by making available the code and software developed for constructing the data set of researcher profiles. It will also expand the boundaries of causal estimation techniques through application to very large data sets -- a direction towards which empirical economics is moving.

Care has been taken to craft this proposal in such a manner that it optimally serves the career goals, and career advancement potential, of both the applicant and the PhD student for which funding is requested. A pair of collaborators, experts in the topic of mobility, have been carefully selected to enhance the quality, feasibility, and reach of the project.

This project will answer important academic questions, provide novel insight to science funding policy makers, produce powerful tools for the economics of science research community and position all participants to achieve their long-term career goals.
Keywords: Economics of Science, Empirical Economics, Mobility, Science Policy, Science of Science

Title: Formation and Evolution of planetary systems
Abstract:
The field of exoplanetary science is, since the pioneering discovery of the first extrasolar planet around a solar star by M. Mayor and D. Queloz, in exponential growth. New planetary exploration missions, new laboratory discoveries, new observatories in space or on the ground, are providing evidence of numerous other planetary systems: we know now that planetary systems are of common occurrence but also that their characteristics are much more diverse than originally thought possible. These discoveries triggered a renewed interest in the origin of these remote worlds, as well as on the sustainability of life in these environments.
The work proposed here is an extension of our previous efforts in providing a framework in which theoretical studies of the different processes at work in planet formation and evolution can be studied, and compared with observations. Such a comparison requires that these different processes are assembled in an end-to-end simulator which can be used to predict the expected population of extrasolar planets, and, ultimately, compared with real data. This comparison finally can be used not only to understand the origin of planetary systems (including ours), but can also guide future observations.
Planet population synthesis allows establishing the required theoretical framework. During the last funding periods, we have developed our models, known in our field as the ‘Bern Model’, based on actual physical/chemical descriptions of individual processes, trying to reduce as much as possible free parameters. These descriptions result from state-of-the-art numerical studies developed either in-house (as part of this proposal or with colleagues at the University of Bern), in collaboration, in particular inside the NCCR PlanetS, or taken from the literature. The different sub-projects in part B of this proposal aim at developing our models by considering different scenarios of planet formation and new important physics, and encapsulating them in a population synthesis approach.
One major goal of our models is the prediction of a variety of observable quantities that can be confronted with observations. Out of these latter, CHEOPS observation will occupy during the next funding period a special position. Indeed, we have been working in the past five years in the development of the satellite, as well as in the preparation of the GTO program of the mission. The next funding period will see our efforts bear fruits as we will obtain the first data to be confronted with results of models! Part A describes this effort, that will be developed in full collaboration with the CHEOPS science team. Using the Bayesian models we have developed during the last funding period, and extending them using novel deep learning techniques, we will aim at extracting the maximum of scientific information from CHEOPS light curve, and study the correlation between the composition of planets in the same system, and the origin of the density variability among small planets. Finally, these results will provide new constraints on important processes governing the characteristics of extrasolar planets, and will ultimately advance our knowledge of planet formation and evolution.
Keywords: CHEOPS, exoplanets, numerical simulations, planet formation, population synthesis

Title: Zero-Shot Classification with Large Language Models for Automatic Coding of Patient-Therapist Transcripts in Psychotherapy
Abstract:
The study of psychotherapy for treating mental health issue is of prime importance – the World Health Organization estimates that approximately 12 billion working days are lost each year to anxiety and depression. Observational coding techniques provide an essential means for understanding psychotherapeutic processes, facilitating research aiming to improve mental health treatments and therapist training. For example, one might use a team of human coders to code displays of empathy and validation, as recorded in transcripts of patient-therapist psychotherapy interactions. In turn, one can use these codes to understand the degree to which certain patient-therapist interactions tend to yield beneficial outcomes. Unfortunately, observational coding is extremely time consuming and expensive, requiring hours of coder training, and involves lengthy coding sessions whereby coders critically evaluate transcripts word by word.  
Recently, techniques from the domain of Machine Learning (ML) and artificial intelligence are beginning to be used to automate observational coding. Currently, the most common approach involves the use of algorithms which can be trained to identify patterns between certain features of the data and the codes assigned by trained human coders. The advantages of these algorithms are that they can be used to automatically code data, thereby dramatically reducing the cost and time associated with observational coding. However, the current ML techniques must be trained on example codes, and therefore do not eliminate the need to train coders who can produce high-quality examples. Furthermore, existing techniques are yet to integrate very recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), leaving room for dramatic improvements in performance. LLMs are a ML technique which have seen wide success in demonstrating close-to-human level generation of human language. 
We aim to develop an open-source solution which can automatically code transcripts with state-of-the-art LLMs, and which does not require any training data. Automatic coding systems provide a means to evaluate the effectiveness of therapy sessions by providing line-by-line summaries of patient-therapist interactions (e.g., displays of validation or emotion). These summaries can then be used to build a profile against which to measure the efficacy of therapy interactions for improved therapist training and patient recovery tracking. The innovation in our project, in contrast to the current approaches to automating observational coding using ML, lies in the use of zero-shot classification with state-of-the-art LLMs.  Zero-shot classification alleviates the need for training data and involves the use of pre-trained LLMs with software-based system for identifying the most likely codes for a set of input sentences. The system performance will be established by evaluating and validating it using a team of psychotherapists and pre-labelled datasets, and then applied to a couples’ therapy dataset to measure therapist adherence and session efficacy. 
The approach is risky because it deviates significantly from both the typical approach to observational coding in psychology as well as the newer approach with ML. However, this interdisciplinary approach, combining knowledge from the domains of machine learning and psychology, has the potential to create numerous opportunities for evaluating session quality, identify new therapeutic interventions to improve mental health treatments and training, and dramatically reduce the cost of observational coding.
Keywords: language models, machine learning, observational coding, psychotherapy

Title: Non-randomness in Morphological Diversity: A Computational Approach Based on Multilingual Corpora
Abstract: Linguistic diversity has inspired many linguistic theories since the development of the discipline in the nineteenth century till the present day. The factors involved in language diversification are complex, and often defy scientific explanation. As a consequence, linguistic research has shifted its focus towards – and away from – explaining linguistic diversity several times in its history. The recent development of large digital data sets and computational methods creates an opportunity for a new take on this fascinating topic: an interdisciplinary approach combining linguistic expert knowledge with general data science.In this context, an old view of language as an adaptive system has reemerged as an extension of linguistic typology. This framework specifically targets to explain non-randomness of linguistic diversity relying on statistical modelling to test dependence between elements of linguistic environment (e.g. demography, location) and elements of linguistic structure (e.g. sound inventory, morphological complexity). In these studies, information about relevant linguistic structures is commonly extracted from linguistic databases.The project proposed here intends to extend the study of language adaptation to linguistic data extractedfrom multilingual corpora. Statistical modelling of word frequency distributions in corpora across languagesis a systematic and reproducible means of inferring the nature and cross-linguistic variation of the underlying linguistic structures. Corpus measures, such as the Shannon entropy of word forms, for  nstance, have been employed in the study of linguistic diversity as general indicators of the size of the morphological inventory of a language. The rationale behind this method is the following causal chain: more morphological categories (e.g. gender marking, case, tense, aspect) ? more potential word types ? lower probability of individual word types ? higher Shannon entropy.Such approaches to corpus-based language comparison demonstrate the relevance of word frequency distributions to the study of linguistic diversity. However, there are two important obstacles to a full integration of the evidence from quantitative text analysis into linguistic accounts of language variation and change.First, corpus measures used so far can describe morphological diversity only at a fully aggregated level without discriminating between traditional morphological categories such as vocabulary diversity, inflection, and derivation. As a consequence, such comparisons are hard to relate directly to the traditional analysis incorporated in the existing linguistic descriptions. Second, corpus-based findings are dependent on the particular sample of texts contained in the corpora, which calls generalised claims into question.We propose to overcome the identified obstacles by applying the knowledge, methods, and tools that arerapidly developing in the domain of use-inspired natural language processing. In order to make a step to-wards a deeper text analysis, we will discriminate between the main lexical and morphological factors behind the observed word frequency distributions — vocabulary diversity, inflection, derivation. To this end, we will process language corpora automatically using state-of-the-art systems for lemmatisation, segmentation and morphological analysis. We will address the issue of corpus representativeness by breaking down corpus-based language representations into a set of features whose values are collected from texts of different size, genre and topic.Similarly, we will address language adaptation at a more fine-grained level by focusing on a set of geographical features extracted using geographical information systems and by testing the relation between these features and the structural linguistic features inferred from quantitative corpus analysis. As language adaptation and historical change are closely related topics, we aim to add a temporal dimension to our study by including in the analysis data from corpora of texts created in different historical periods.In addition to the theoretical findings, the project will provide a major methodological contribution facilitating future use of corpus-based computational methods in scientific approaches to linguistic diversity and change.
Keywords: Shannon entropy, Zip'f law, corpus-based typology, data science, derivation, inflection, language adaptation, linguistic diversity, morphological segmentation, morphology, multilingual corpora, natural language processing, vocabulary diversity, word frequency distribution

Title: Determinants of pattern learning: What role for attentional control?
Abstract:
The aim of the present proposal is to characterize the factors that enhance learning. We have recently hypothesized that attentional control plays a critical role in learning. This view holds that, by enhancing the ability to distinguish task-relevant information from sources of noise, attentional control benefits learning. Although grounded in sound computational models, the empirical evidence that directly supports this view is scarce, has focused on group averages and did not take into account other possible sources of variability. Here, we propose to evaluate the determinants of learning at the individual level. We will investigate further how individual attentional control abilities relate to learning capacities. In addition, we will measure higher cognitive constructs, such as working memory and fluid intelligence, as well as motivational characteristics such as mindset, intrinsic motivation and grit. We will thus be in a unique position to characterize how these factors jointly contribute to learning.

We will focus on two well-characterized forms of pattern learning: perceptual learning and statistical learning. We propose to investigate the determinants of these forms of learning by using complementary behavioral, modeling and neurocognitive approaches, both in a specific population known to have enhanced attentional control and in the general population. Indeed, we will first make use of the fact that action video game play enhances attentional control to test the hypothesis that improving attentional control results in enhanced learning. Second, we will use on-line testing protocols to collect data from a large number of participants (N=250). This will allow us to evaluate the link between attention, learning and other cognitive and motivational factors by comparing alternative quantitative models. Finally, we will concurrently collect behavioral and fMRI data on a novel learning paradigm we have developed. By applying the proper modeling procedures, we will track how the BOLD signal changes as learning proceeds. In this way, we will be able to characterize the neural systems that support perceptual and statistical learning as they unfold. A key question will be to determine the contribution of attentional control regions to the process of learning.

Overall this work will advance our theoretical understanding of the factors that may facilitate learning. Importantly, it will provide key practical knowledge about how to efficiently assess and improve individuals’ learning capacities. Such knowledge holds promises for fields as varied as rehabilitation of brain damaged patients, skill learning or education.

Title: Quantifying subjective visual experiences in the human brain
Abstract:
Intuitively, we often assume that everyone experiences the world in a similar way to us as we typically use common language to refer to how things look, sound, or feel. However, some stimuli such as “#TheDress” or special populations with unique perceptual experiences such as synesthetes, who experience additional, consistent sensations to ordinary stimuli (e.g., colours for sounds), highlight that there are vast differences in how people experience their surroundings. Despite these individual differences, the neuroscience literature is dominated by studies using central tendencies to understand perceptual processes. 

The core of my research program sees individual differences as an untapped opportunity to link perception to physical stimulus properties as well as individual genetic, anatomical, and experience-dependent variations. The overall objective is to gain comprehensive insights into how differences in perception arise by characterising subjective visual experiences in the human brain using dense sampling of neural and behavioural responses in large-scale stimulus spaces. 

In the current project, colour will be used as a model to map subjective experiences in the human brain. Colour space is the ideal testing ground for individual differences in perception, as it is a biophysically well-defined and constrained space (i.e., photopigments and receptors can react to a limited number of wavelengths of light), and it varies substantially across people. Variability in terms of the sensory apparatus can be characterized well with genetic screening (i.e., opsin arrays can capture the type and severity of colour vision deficiencies) and high-resolution retinal imaging (i.e., individual cone mosaics can be imaged in the eye). At a higher level, we also know that there is variability in colour perception that is experience-dependent and to some extent influenced by language. The current project aims to make precise predictions about subjective colour experiences based on variability in the sensory apparatus, genetic profile, and language, and relate these to densely sampled neural data from individuals. The specific aims of the project are to (1) characterise individual neural colour-space geometries, (2) link genetic profiles of colour vision to individual neural data, and (3) examine when language affects the neural representation of colour. Collectively, the proposed research will significantly advance our understanding of colour processing in the human brain by linking different sources of variability with perception. Beyond colour, the proposed work will provide novel avenues to gain comprehensive insight into how subjective experiences are generated.

Title: Global-scale prediction of cryosphere/hydrosphere variations using machine learning
Abstract:
Variations in the cryosphere and hydrosphere are of fundamental importance because these variations are affected by–and contribute to–climate change, which has far-reaching implications for people and society, including food security and production, and rise of sea-level in coastal areas. Tremendous efforts have been put into designing models that can project (i.e., predict) the cryosphere/hydrosphere (C/H) variations years and decades ahead, to take preventive measures to mitigate consequences such as excessive sea-level rise in coastal areas. However, due to modelling deficiencies and uncertainty in the observations, the mentioned projections exhibit large uncertainties and deviations from one projection to another, thus rendering them not much reliable. As more observational data become available, these projections are improved. Notwithstanding, deficiencies in the fundamental mathematical models are not resolved and still vastly contribute to the inaccuracies in the projections. To overcome this problem and present accurate projections, I introduce the idea of using machine learning (ML). ML algorithms are data-driven approaches that learn the underlying spatio-temporal structure in the observational data. Therefore, by exploiting the currently available datasets of C/H variations it is possible to predict their future evolution. Furthermore, ML algorithms can encode the physical laws governing the evolution of C/H using the concept of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs).
In this project, I will focus on the global evolution of C/H. The project is composed of two parts. In the first part, I will analyze the continental mass redistribution, which includes melting of mountain glaciers and polar ice sheets (Greenland and Antarctica), as well as variations in terrestrial hydrology (known as terrestrial water storage). This mass redistribution results in the so-called barystatic sea-level change, a major component of the hydrospheric variations. In the second part, I will investigate the so-called steric sea-level change, which involves thermosteric (thermal expansion) and halosteric (salinity variations) effects. The sum of barystatic and steric components is the total sea-level change that is of fundamental importance for sea-level research. For the analysis, I will follow two approaches. In the first approach I will deal with purely data-driven ML algorithms, while in the second approach, I will explore PINNs to account for the underlying physics of the C/H variations, primarily through laws of thermodynamics and fluid dynamics. In both parts, I train the algorithms on the historical maps of the steric sea-level change as well as mass redistribution across continent-ocean system (primarily since 1900). I do this by using algorithms for spatio-temporal modelling in computer vision, including the so-called convolutional long short-term memory and vision Transformers. I will also utilize additional climatic features such as greenhouse gas emission (e.g., CO_2 and methane) to enhance the prediction accuracy. While my primary focus will be to predict on decadal time scale, I will also investigate the capability of my method on longer horizons.
Based on my previous experience with ML and PINNs, I expect the projections to be accurate. Simple tests with currently available observational data can demonstrate the prediction capability of my algorithm. Furthermore, from comparison with state-of-the-art models I expect my predictions to be more accurate. The improved projections are of particular interest and importance to the climate research community and contribute to understanding of the climate system, thus might be useful for policymaking and enhancing peoples' quality of life.

Title: Accurate nonequilibrium lattice simulations
Abstract:
Correlated electron materials exhibit some of the most remarkable properties found in condensed matter systems. Their complexity arises from the interplay between multiple active degrees of freedom (spin, charge, orbital, lattice) and the competition between different low-energy states. The complex free-energy landscapes of these materials also provides a playground for interesting nonequilibrium phenomena, such as light-induced hidden phases.

Important insights into strongly correlated electron behavior have been gained over the past 30 years with the help of dynamical mean field theory (DMFT), which maps a lattice system onto a self-consistently determined quantum impurity model. The extension of DMFT to the nonequilibrium domain opened a path to simulations of laser-induced phenomena in strongly correlated systems and the exploration of nonthermal phases. However, most nonequilibrium studies up to now presented approximate solutions of the DMFT equations, with limited predictive power. DMFT also lacks nonlocal correlations and cannot be used to investigate the effects of long-ranged spin, charge and pair fluctuations on the nonequilibrium evolution. The latter effects are captured in moderately correlated lattice systems by diagrammatic formalisms like GW or the fluctuation exchange approximation (FLEX). However, since nonequilibrium implementations of these methods are very memory intensive, such simulations have been limited to short times and small lattices.   

To overcome these limitations, I propose two work packages, WP1 and WP2. In WP1, we will realize accurate nonequilibrium DMFT descriptions of strongly correlated systems by developing a new generation of impurity solvers based on the combination of the self-consistent strong-coupling expansion and tensor cross interpolation (TCI). TCI is a machine learning approach which enables a highly efficient evaluation of the multi-dimensional integrals appearing in the strong-coupling diagrammatic formalism. With the new solvers, we will be able to obtain accurate DMFT descriptions of nonequilibrium steady-states, even in the case of multi-orbital systems. In WP2, we will overcome the memory bottleneck in nonequilibrium Green's function calculations by employing the recently proposed quantics representation of correlation functions. This innovative computational approach, which imports techniques developed in the tensor network community into diagrammatic many-body theory, will enable simulations of large lattices. 

The improved nonequilibrium DMFT framework will be used to clarify the properties of nonthermal electronically ordered states in photo-doped Mott systems. The calculation of reliable observables for nonthermal magnetic, superconducting and excitonic insulator phases will help to interpret experimental results and stimulate the search for hidden phases in cold-atom systems and photo-excited materials. We will also study the role of dynamical screening in photo-induced insulator-metal transitions and the possibility of a screening-induced Mott gap collapse, which was proposed to occur in photo-excited materials such as VO2 and V2O3.

The lattice simulations based on quantics-compressed nonequilibrium Green's functions, on the other hand, will produce important information on the evolution of nonlocal spin, charge, excitonic and superconducting correlations in nonequilibrium lattice systems, and allow us to study nonthermal critical scaling. We will also study the thermalization of electrons which couple to optical and acoustic phonons to reveal the energy flow between electronic and lattice degrees of freedom after a photo-excitation. This will allow us to test the validity of phenomenological two-temperature models, which are often used to interpret experimental data.
Keywords: correlated electron systems, dynamical mean field theory, electron-phonon systems, impurity solvers, nonequilibrium Green's functions, nonequilibrium dynamics, nonthermal criticality, nonthermal phases, quantics compression, tensor cross interpolation

Title: Chemoselective, machine learning-guided investigation into the biodegradation potential of uncultivated members of environmental microbial communities
Abstract: Over 350’000 different chemicals and chemical mixtures are documented for human production and use. Many of these chemicals have negative effects on ecosystems and human health, driving a need for their environmental removal. Microbes are adept at degrading anthropogenic chemicals. However, most of the key taxa and enzymes involved in pollutant biotransformations in complex environmental microbiomes are unknown. We aim to address this knowledge gap by developing cultivation-independent techniques to characterize chemical biotransformations. We will conduct genome-resolved metagenomic analysis of wastewater-impacted stream biofilms. Based on these data, we will construct and screen pollutant-degrading enzyme libraries which will be integrated into machine learning models to predict enzyme-substrate specificity. Overall, this project seeks to mine the hidden natural diversity of enzymes that biotransform contaminants in stream biofilms. More broadly, this research advances methods for culture-independent analysis generalizable to other enzyme families and environmental microbiomes.
Keywords: Biofilms, Enzymes, Machine learning, Metagenomics, Microbial biodegradation, Microbiomes, Organic pollutants

Title: From atomistic simulations to giant planets
Abstract:
Simple elements when compressed at planetary pressures (Mbar) undergo physical transformations that defy expectations: hydrogen (H) metallizes and may become superconducting, noble gases develop remarkable chemistry, water may create new phases of matter, methane dissociates into diamond rain. Rationalizing the high-pressure physics of hydrogen-rich materials is not only of fundamental and technological interest but it is the current road-block to a robust understanding of Giant Planets structure, origin, and evolution.
High pressure conditions mean that even at temperatures well above 1000K the physics and chemistry of dense hydrogen-rich materials does not approach a trivial classical limit, but rather displays a staggering array of exotic behaviors driven by H physics, including
demixing of helium(carbon) into H leading to He(diamond) rain, and superionic water ices.

Interestingly, technological advances, leading to increasing accurate planetary measurements, e.g. the gravitational fields of Jupiter (in 2018) and Saturn (in 2019), concerning the planetary science side, as well as revolutionary high-pressure techniques in experimental high-pressure physics, outpaced the progress in the theoretical methods to understand the physics of dense H in both the low and high-temperature regime.
At low temperatures, new generations of numerical techniques are essential to assist experiments, which are challenging, and often lead to controversial results, in the search for metallic H, one of Ginzburg's top three most important questions in physics waiting to be solved in this century.
 As we recently highlighted severe drawbacks of previous state-of-the-art numerical investigations, we also showed a clear path forward to overcome their traditional accuracy, size, and time scale limitations.

In this project, I will develop and apply a machine-learning powered strategy to scale-up computationally prohibitive first-principle simulations and provide a new quantitative understanding of the thermodynamics of H-rich dense material. 

In concrete I will: 1 Develop and apply a suite of numerical methods understand H metallization and its complex polymorphism;
2 construct an accurate equation of state for dense H, a building block for planetary interiors models,
3 Probe the existence of "Helium rain" to assess how relevant is this process in Jupiter and Saturn;
4 Unravel the extremely rich high-P,T chemistry of hydrocarbons to explain the remarkably different measured properties of Uranus and Neptunes;
5 Quantitatively describe the phase diagram and transport properties of black hot icy water along the Giant Planets isentropes.

These accurate simulations, that would otherwise require several hundreds of CPU years if performed with standard methods, will inform and guide new generations of experiments as well as contribute to answering long-standing and fundamental questions concerning H metallization, polymorphism, Jupiter's evolution, the explanation of the anomalous luminosity of Saturn and Neptune, and the non-dipolar magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune.

Finally, in a cross-disciplinary sub-project, I will continue my work on developing electronic structure and machine learning methods for quantum computing architectures.
Keywords: atomistic simulations, dense hydrogen, electronic structure, high pressure physics, machine learning, molecular dynamics, planetary science, quantum Monte Carlo, quantum computing

Title: New physics searches with b-tagging, top-tagging and machine learning, and HL-LHC pixel upgrade using ATLAS at LHC
Abstract:
The search for new phenomena beyond the Standard Model of particle physics (SM) is the main goal of ATLAS and CMS, the two general purpose particle physics experiments at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC).  The increase in the center-of-mass energy from 8 to 13 TeV, and an increased integrated luminosity in the ongoing Run-2 (2015-2018) significantly extends LHC's sensitivity to discover physics beyond the SM (BSM), including naturalness-motivated new physics. Composite Higgs models are an alternative to Supersymmetry to address this hierarchy problem. The generic predictions of Composite Higgs models are the presence of heavy partners of the top quark, i.e. vector-like quarks, and new heavy resonances.  These new particles are expected to be in reach of the LHC and can have dominant decay modes to heavy flavor (top and bottom quarks).  A discovery would be nothing short of a revolution in particle physics.  Not finding any hints of new physics in LHC's Run-2 would severely constrain naturalness and decisively shape the future of particle physics both for theory and experiment.

The higher center-of-mass energy in Run-2 allows for searches for higher-mass objects, resulting in decay products with transverse momenta of unprecedented magnitude, which require dedicated identification techniques, in particular for the identification of b-jets (b-tagging) and high-pT hadronically decaying top quarks, which are reconstructed as so-called fat jets in the calorimeter from the top quark decay products (top-tagging).  Machine learning is a promising tool to fully exploit the detector performance for the proposed b- and top-tagging techniques.

The proposed research for the period of this funding request can be summarised as follows:
- Improve the understanding, calibration and the performance of the identification of high-pT b-jets and hadronically decaying top quarks.
- Machine learning is applied to b-tagging and top-tagging to assess the benefits and to learn where and how these novel algorithms are best applied in HEP. 
- Employ the advancements in the first two bullets in searches for physics beyond the SM.

In addition contributions to the HL-LHC pixel upgrade are proposed for the pixel module production.
Keywords: BSM physics, HL-LHC pixel upgrade, flavor-tagging, machine learning, top-tagging

Title: REducing SPEECH-related side-effects of deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease via automated speech analysis (RESPEECH-PD)
Abstract:
REducing SPEECH-related side-effects of deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease via automated speech analysis (RESPEECH-PD)

Background. Deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus (STN-DBS) is an effective treatment of L-dopa sensitive motor symptoms of Parkinson’s disease (PD), but its effects on speech are equivocal. Speech is the most complex learned motor program and it is of uppermost importance for social interaction. Although some aspects of speech might improve with STN-DBS, stimulation-induced dysarthria represents the most common side effect, with a prevalence of up to 90%. Worsening of speech can neutralize the motor benefits of STN-DBS in terms of overall benefit in quality of life. The pathophysiology behind STN-DBS-induced dysarthria includes current diffusion to myelinated fiber tracts surrounding the STN, mainly the pyramidal tract, located at the lateral border of the sensorimotor STN, leading to dysarthria. STN-DBS-induced dysarthria has to be distinguished from parkinsonian dysarthria. Unfortunately, the human ear has very limited capacities in the qualitative and quantitative evaluation of speech; thus improvement of STN-DBS induced dysarthria is still an unmet need. New methods of automated speech assesment based on acoustic analysis and machine-learning algorithms have quantified subtle speech alterations and distinguished different types of dysarthria. These new tools are outperforming the capacity of speech analysis of the most skilled clinicians. Modern directional DBS-systems allow for current steering, bearing the potential of reducing or completely avoiding stimulation-induced dysarthria. To leverage steering, detailed stimulation maps and improved dysarthria analysis are required that indicate regions of therapeutic effect and side effects. 

Aims and methods. The applicants unite several experts with complementary and proven high expertise in postoperative management of STN-DBS for PD, automated speech analysis in PD, imaging of precise electrode position and tractography, as well as modelling of current diffusion, which are fundamental prerequisites for achieving the following aims:
Aim 1.To identify the most sensitive and specific speech variables for STN-DBS-related improvement of parkinsonian dysarthria and STN-DBS-induced speech-related side-effects, by application of an automated speech analysis technique, comparing stimulation off and on states, as well as increasing stimulation amplitudes. 
Aim 2.Mapping of stimulation related speech changes: to investigate the anatomical and pathophysiological substrate of STN-DBS induced changes in speech production. Dysarthria severity, as measured by automated speech analysis, volume of tissue activated (VTA), and tractography of fiber tracts adjacent to the STN, will be set into context to determine a sweet spot for dysarthria reduction and to reveal speech parameters that correlate with current diffusion to the pyramidal tract. 
Aim 3.To investigate whether an automated speech analysis technique reliably detects improvements of STN-DBS-induced dysarthria in a longitudinal interventional cross-over study and to compare sensitivity for dysarthria reduction between automated, perceptive, and subjective speech analysis. 

Expected results. With successful completion of the presented protocol, we will be able to reliably detect the footprint of STN-DBS in speech and to identify the anatomical substrates for both improvement and deterioration of speech in PD, laying the foundation for better conventional and closed-loop postoperative management of STN-DBS in PD.

Expected value.  Systematic implementation of automated speech analysis would facilitate not only time-consuming postoperative management but also improve overall outcomes of STN-DBS in PD patients treated with STN-DBS. This would be the first use-inspired step towards fully automatized closed-loop DBS based on speech as a biomarker, allowing to standardize and improve outcomes of DBS across centers worldwide in the near future.

Title: Hydrogeomorphological Prediction of Source to Sink Sediment Pathways in the Alpine Rhine
Abstract:
The transfer of sediment from land to oceans is an important part of the global denudation and geochemical cycle, and it affects critical functions of river and coastal ecosystems. While most of this sediment is delivered to rivers from alpine basins, we only have a very rough understanding of where and how the sedimentary material is produced, and what are the source to sink pathways, leading to the questions: Is the entire basin involved in sediment production? How are local sources activated? What are the timescales involved in transport and storage? And how do we budget such pathways?
The proposed research focuses on answering these questions using the Alpine Rhine as a natural laboratory. We aim to do this by a new physics-based hydrogeomorphological approach to analyze sediment pathways, which combines distributed hydrological modeling and connectivity mapping with geological and geomorphological field observations. We start from the observation that rainfall-driven overland flow triggers erosion and sediment transport along sediment pathways from sources to sinks. Consequently, different local sediment sources distributed in space and time may be activated, and if these sources have distinct sediment properties, then tracing their source signals through a channel network is possible with the numerical model. We will use concentrations of cosmogenic nuclides for such tracing, together with other petrographic, geochemical, mineralogical and grain size properties, both for fine sediment transported in suspension and for bedload. This physics-based view is a major advancement over existing statistical mixing approaches to sediment source apportionment.
The research is organized around 3 subprojects that will be completed by 3 doctoral students. Doc1 will map the potential sediment sources and quantify their connectivity to the channel network. Such maps will first be prepared for small basins (Glogn, Plessur, Landquart), and the results (connectivity indexes, sediment yields) will be upscaled to the entire Alpine Rhine basin through deep learning methods with climatic inputs. Doc2 will use the source area information to model the sediment transfer (suspended load and bedload) through the landscape from the sediment production sites to the basin outlet using climatic forcing. She/he will first develop the necessary new components into an existing coupled hydrology-sediment model at the scale of the smaller basins, and calibrate it with observations. Then, he/she will upscale this model to simulate the routing of sediment and source identification in the entire mesoscale Alpine Rhine basin using field information of Doc3 as constraint. Doc3 will collect the field data for the characterization of source signals for bedload (grain size, bulk petrographic composition of clasts) and suspension loads (concentrations of cosmogenic nuclides, bulk geochemical and mineralogical composition). Cosmogenic nuclides will also be used to identify sites of sediment storage. The collected data will allow her/him to trace the source signals through the channel network. The maps of Doc1 will serve as basis for the selection of sample sites in the field.
The results will improve our understanding of the relative role of various sediment supply mechanisms on the bulk sediment budget of a basin. In a changing climate, understanding the origin of the sediment is key to predicting the direction and magnitude of changes in sediment transfer in the future. In a broader context, the three Docs will create a framework consisting of models and tracers, which are tested and validated for the scale of the Alpine Rhine. This framework will then be ready to be used by the community for the hydrogeomorphological analysis of other mountainous basins.

Title: CrowdAlytics: Large-Scale Human-Machine Systems for Data Science
Abstract:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly taking over work domains that used to be the realm of people (Brynjolfsson and McAfee, 2014). In recent history, the industrial revolutions fueled similar fears of unem- ployment, but eventually led to a new distribution of labor. Indeed, humans and machines present different, and, therefore, complementary characteristics that suggest that they are not perfect substitutes of each other (Chui et al., 2016). While some systems have occasionally proven to be capable of beating humans in specific well-defined tasks (High, 2012; Wang et al., 2016), humans’ innate ability/creativity/versatility to deal with incomplete or ill-specified tasks gives them an advantage in many work settings. Especially in groups, they are able to accomplish astonishing tasks that seem difficult to automate (Malone et al., 2010). Machines, in contrast to humans, are able to work systematically, homogeneously, and repeatedly without being bored or tired. Humans exhibit varying work quality, cognitive diversity (i.e., they have vastly varying skill sets), and need to be motivated (Bernstein et al., 2012). Assuming that well-structured tasks will eventually be automated and that humans have some innate capabilities difficult to completely replicate by machines the main question to be answered is: How can we combine groups of human and machine intelligences to effectively perform ill-structured tasks that are not achievable by either party alone?

One field that seems to crystalize itself as in dire need of combined, cooperative human-machine intelligence is data-driven knowledge discovery (Gil, 2017) or Data Science (Cao, 2017b,a). The explosion of available data on the Web and from sensors as well as the advances in machine learning have facilitated knowledge discovery in society, science, and the economy faster than ever before: Data-driven findings are shaping the way organizations take decisions (Business, 2012), new empirical scientific disciplines have emerged, citizens are constantly exposed to data journalism (Gray et al., 2012), and participants of civic coding events analyze/visualize data to better understand and improve their own environment. However, at the same time this rise in data and methods introduces several challenges for data scientists, who must specify what questions are worthy of pursuing and how to find, integrate, interpret, summarize, and analyze a vast number of sources of diverse nature at different stages of their multidisciplinary work. But Data Science professionals are very short in supply. To address this need, scientists have proposed statistical expert or intelligent discovery systems (Bernstein et al., 2005; Serban et al., 2013). In practice, though, the success of these systems is limited as well-trained data scientists are still an indispensable part of the process. Other AI-oriented efforts have developed methods to automatically search and digest scientific publications (Gil et al., 2014), and dynamically update analyses with the appearance of new related data (Gil et al., 2017). However, there is still a massive amount of manual work to identify gaps in the literature and design new Data Science problems to be investigated. Furthermore, mosts data analyses are still mostly pursued by individuals or small groups (ignoring AI-based support), as much of the tooling for collaborative Data Science is either inspired by software engineering tools and is not always suited for the explorative data analysis process or from collaborative writing lacking the capability to structure analyses and capture rationale.

To address this shortcoming, the goal of this proposal is to investigate how human-machine cooperatives (from now on HuMaCs) (Malone and Bernstein, 2015) can review, define and solve Data Science problems and results, in order to facilitate systematic progress in data-driven discoveries. Specifically, we will design, build, deploy, and evaluate HuMaCs that allow both novice and expert users as well as machines to collaborate on complex Data Science tasks. In pursuing this goal, the project will combine insight from statistics, Data Science, collective intelligence, computer supported collaborative work, and crowdcomputing to pioneer the exploration of human-machine collaboration for the data analysis task—a topic of utmost importance with the our life in the age of the smart machine.
Keywords: Business Process Management, CSCW (Computer Supported Cooperatie Work), Collective Intelligence, Crowdsourcing, Group Decision Processes, Human Computation, Human-Computer Interaction, Social Computing

Title: Next-Generation Multiscale Molecular Dynamics: Promoting Computational Chemistry with Artificial Intelligence
Abstract:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing our daily life from speech and facial recognition to self-driving cars, traffic cameras, intelligent robots, search engines, and video streaming to expert systems to predict consumer preferences and perform medical diagnosis. A similar quantum jump is currently starting to take place in computational sciences where an increasing number of applications are starting to emerge that apply machine learning (ML). AI also opens new possibilities for Computational Chemistry (CC) both in electronic structure calculations and molecular simulations. This is a natural evolution since the ever-increasing amount of data (generated by more powerful computers and more efficient algorithms) necessitates and enables the use of ML techniques. However, AI is not limited to ML but also includes other approaches such as analysis tools based on Bayesian inference or evolutionary algorithm (EA) based optimization.
In this proposal, we want to promote the fruitful interplay of AI algorithms with traditional CC approaches via close feedback loops (CC ? AI: CC data used for AI, AI predictions used in turn for advancing CC applications). This is a natural extension of our work in the framework of our two previous SNF grants where we introduced ML algorithms such as feature selection and causality inference to analyze high-dimensional simulation data and developed the EA toolbox EVOLVE for a broad range of inverse design applications (in molecular materials and protein design). Here we want to further extend these approaches and combine them with our long-standing efforts in the development and application of quantum based multiscale Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations in ground and excited states. 
In particular, we propose the development of a completely new highly flexible multiscale interface to the CPMD (www.cpmd.org) code called MIMIC. MIMIC is based on a multiple program-multiple data strategy and will allow for flexible combinations of different electronic structure and force fields while maintaining fast communication between the processes. MIMIC will thus allow multi-shell MM/QML/QMH schemes (with different parts of the system represented by different methods) as well as multiple- time step (MTS) based multi-rung QML-QMH approaches (in which a lower level QML method is used to drive and accelerate the actual dynamics with a higher level QMH method) that we have developed during the last two SNF grants. Furthermore, we want to enhance the capabilities of MIMIC through extensive combinations with AI approaches. In particular, we will use genetic algorithms (GA) to explore (and push) the accuracy limits of current exchange-correlation (XC) functionals in Density Functional Theory (DFT) via a GA-DFT approach. We will also develop a new GA based approach (GA-CI) to reduce the cost of high-level wavefunction based electronic structure methods (Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) and multireference active space methods CASCF and CASPT2) by several orders of magnitude. We also want to extend our ML based MD to a fully adaptive ML-MD approach with learning on-the-fly that can also be used as lower level method in MTS based combinations. This powerful new simulation methodologies can be applied to a large range of applications, here we will focus on three areas: the de-sign of biomimetic catalysts, the development of metal based two-centre anticancer drugs and the study of metal halide perovskites for photovoltaic applications.
Keywords: Biomimetic Design, Computational Biophysics, Computational Chemistry, Photovoltaics, Protein Engineering, QM/MM, artificial intelligence, machine learning, molecular dynamics, multiscale modelling
