Title: Modern Times Without Us! Determinants and Effects of Technology Skepticism, Grisons 1900-1940
Abstract:
From the implementation of mechanical looms and threshing machines during the Industrial Revolution to artificial intelligence (AI) and mRNA vaccines today, societies have always been skeptical about new and innovative technologies. On the one hand, technical innovations have led to enduring increases in living conditions and life expectancy over the last 200 years. On the other hand, innovations bring social change, uncertainty and a reshuffling of the wage structure. However, little is known about the determinants of technology skepticism and its effects on economic, health-related and political outcomes. This is surprising given its relevance to the public and political debate. One core problem in addressing the determinants and effects of innovation skepticism is the nature of technical change and its consequent aversion: Change occurs steadily over time, which makes it difficult to identify causal effects.

This project aims to address the determinants of technology skepticism and its effects on economic, health-related and political outcomes. In three different subprojects we explore quasi-natural experiments in the Swiss canton of Grisons from 1900 to 1940. First, we address how a major health-related shock cause mistrust of health-related policies and technologies. We link overmortality during the 1918 influenza pandemic to political support for compulsory vaccination and to vaccination behavior before and after the pandemic. We rely on the unique 1922 popular vote in Grisons on compulsory vaccination and on local smallpox vaccination campaigns from 1907 to 1933. The study will shed light on the determinants of technology skepticism and discuss parallels with the COVID-19 pandemic. Second, we aim to understand the initial opposition, gradual acceptance and adoption of one of the most influential technologies of the 20th century—automobiles. We use the repeated popular votes on Grisons' automobile ban from 1900 to 1925 to describe initial technology skepticism and test whether access to substitute technologies, role models or political leaders shape technology skepticism over time. Third, we use the unexpected abolition of the automobile ban in 1925 to estimate the causal effect of the end of a technology ban on economic development. We link the abrupt change in accessibility of rural places in 1925 to subsequent regional growth. We also test whether an overoptimistic perception of the benefits of this technology spurs over-investments and subsequent waves of bankruptcies in some sectors—mainly in the lodging industry. We also discuss parallels with the current debate on mobility cost and how it affects regional inequality.

Our project combines a battery of self-compiled archival data on, among others, vaccination behavior, local death registers, firm registers and voting patterns. We analyze these granular data in quasi-experimental settings that are used for empirical identification, predominantly relying on difference-in-differences models and event-study setups for causal analyses. We have already checked the availability of data and we are confident that our strategies work. Moreover, we show in a pilot study that higher 1918 influenza overmortality reduces both political support for compulsory vaccination and the use of vaccination technologies, while vaccination hesitancy—a measure for technology skepticism—surges.  

Our project will fill largely-unexplored gaps in the literature on the determinants and consequences of technology skepticism.  We are confident that our five planned papers and the respective data sets will attract a lot of attention, lead to publication in top journals in economics, and that the junior team members at CERGE-EI and Lucerne will be able to establish themselves as researchers with unique profiles.
Keywords: Economic History, Regional Economics, Technology Adoption, Technology Skepticism, Vaccination, Voting Behavior

Title: Pooled genetic perturbations with highly multiplexed image-based phenotyping in human neural organoids
Abstract:
Human neural organoids, generated from pluripotent stem cells in vitro, are useful tools to study human brain development, evolution, and disease. The three dimensional and multilineage environment enables emergent cell shapes, behaviors, interactions, and functions within a complex tissue microenvironment. We have previously established multiplexed, pooled CRISPR perturbation experiments with single-cell sequencing readouts to study the functions of developmental transcription factors and autism spectrum disorder risk genes in high throughput within human neural organoids. However, these methods disrupt the tissue context and therefore do not allow for detection of cell and tissue morphological phenotypes as well as non-cell autonomous perturbation effects. Further, effects of genetic perturbations on protein expression and localization cannot be revealed. Optical pooled screening (OPS) technologies are highly multiplexed, pooled CRISPR perturbations with imaging-based spatial omic readout that enable the evaluation of many genetic manipulations in a multicellular system while preserving spatial tissue features. In this project, we will establish OPS in human neural organoids and apply the technology to study neuronal migration disorders and the effect of microglia state on tissue microenvironments. The project will be realized through the following work packages:

Work package 1: Spatial phenotyping genetic loss of function associated with neuronal migration disorders in neural organoids. We will genetically disrupt proteins associated with neuronal migration disorders and assess perturbation effects on organoid cell states, morphologies and localization, as well as tissue architecture. Targets include transcription factors, signaling and cytoskeletal proteins, and extracellular matrix components. We will follow-up on the pooled experiments by establishing stable loss of function lines for selected genes and assess phenotypes using a combination of high-information content phenotyping methods.

Work package 2: Programming human iPSC-derived microglia integrated in neural organoids to explore the spectrum of microenvironmental phenotypes. We will activate and inhibit gene expression specifically in microglia that are mosaically incorporated into human neural organoids. Perturbation targets include genes associated with microglia-specific maturation, inflammation, and neurodegeneration (e.g. Alzheimer’s disease). We will test predictions about transcriptional regulators of microglia maturation and study how programmed microglia impact local brain organoid microenvironments.

Work package 3: Computational framework for assessing spatial perturbations in neural organoids. We will establish a machine learning based computational framework to process and analyze multimodal single-cell imaging and genomic data that can be used for morphological phenotyping and perturbation assessment. 

The combination of human model systems and single-cell genomic and imaging technologies continue to open up inroads into understanding human biology and disease. This project provides an exciting new direction for the field to link genotype to cellular and tissue phenotypes at scale in human context. Our vision is that these new techniques will help us to move toward a foundation model of causal cell and tissue biology. Importantly, the project will establish a multi-modal computational framework to assess spatial phenotypes across molecular, cellular, and tissue scales. These tools will be broadly applicable to diverse in vitro models of human development.

Title: What do Hedge Funds Think? Textual Analysis of Investor Letters
Abstract:
Hedge funds play a critical role in the asset management industry due to their use of complex strategies and the flexibility to operate with fewer restrictions than other institutional investors. They also move significant amounts of capital, influencing market liquidity and prices. Understanding the factors driving their performance and investment decisions is important for investors, researchers, and policymakers. However, the literature has faced hurdles in examining these due to the low disclosure requirements for hedge funds and the discretion fund managers have in revealing their strategies. The project addresses these gaps by utilizing a large corpus of hedge fund letters to investors spanning multiple decades. Some letters pre-date publicly available databases. 

Existing literature has only been able to infer hedge fund managers' views indirectly from market data. In this project, we overcome this limitation by extracting their perspectives directly from their own words. Our analysis draws on investor letters from a representative sample of long-short equity and global macro funds, both active and defunct, to avoid survivorship bias. We identify four topics that are crucial for understanding hedge fund performance with significant societal value: macroeconomic expectations, stock market expectations, approaches to sustainable investing, and communication strategies used to explain performance to investors.

Macroeconomic Expectations: Hedge fund managers are sophisticated investors, and their expectations of macroeconomic variables are crucial for asset pricing and the transmission of economic and monetary policies. The project will investigate whether hedge fund managers’ expectations are more accurate than those of professional forecasters, particularly after public announcements, and how their views reflect their interpretation of policy communications.

Stock Performance Expectations: Hedge fund managers often discuss individual stocks in their letters. This research will assess whether fund managers can predict future stock performance better than other professional forecasters, such as analysts, and will explore the events and analyses that cause managers to change their views on stocks.

Sustainable Investing: The project will examine hedge fund managers’ attitudes toward sustainable investing and whether they exploit opportunities created by green investors divesting from certain assets. It will explore whether hedge funds view climate change as a risk to be hedged or a speculative opportunity, contributing to either the reduction or the maintenance of climate-related risk premia.

Communication Strategies and Trading Styles: Hedge fund managers’ explanations of their past performance in investor letters can reveal their investment styles and risk-taking behavior. The project will explore how managers justify underperformance or overperformance and whether their communication strategies affect their clients’ decisions, such as preventing capital redemptions or causing panic-driven withdrawals.

To address these questions, we will employ state-of-the-art NLP techniques to analyze the content of the investor letters. Our analyses will encompass sentiment analysis, unsupervised topic modeling, and keyword discovery drawing on the BERT language architecture. For example, to extract macroeconomic expectations, we identify forward-looking portions of the text referring to macroeconomic policies and then measure the sentiment using FinBERT.

In conclusion, this research aims to bridge existing gaps in comprehending hedge fund strategies and behavior by providing direct insights from managers' own communications. The findings will deepen our understanding of hedge funds' influence on financial markets and the economy, shaping perceptions of their role in areas such as market stability, policy transmission, and sustainable investing.

fibrillation (af), the most common arrhythmia, affects more than 10 million individuals in europe, and is expected to increase, up to 17.9 million people by 2060. the associated healthcare costs promising for long term ambulatory screening of arrhythmias and more specifically for intermittent af and non sustained arrhythmias. the main goal of the present project is to develop a robust and reliable algorithm to detect and classify arrhythmias in everyday life with a ppg based sensor. important issues need to be addressed to efficiently diagnose arrhythmias in ambulatory settings. first, inspired project is a novel framework to reliably detect and classify arrhythmias in ambulatory settings based on ppg. this development paves the way to an effective low cost diagnostic tool for early Title: Large-scale Programmable Visible and Near-Infrared Photonics with Integrated Lasers for Cold Atom Manipulation
Abstract:
Cold atom arrays are among the leading hardware platforms for quantum information processing. For high-fidelity quantum operations, low-noise coherent visible near-infrared (VIS-NIR) laser beams are essential to precisely control multiple atomic transitions. However, the current reliance on bulky bench-top optical control systems in these experiments largely limits the scalability of atomic quantum processors.

Replacing room-size optical tables with wafer-scale programmable photonic integrated circuits (PICs) is a highly promising solution to this problem. This enables fast, tunable generation and manipulation of large coherent laser beam arrays for cold atom manipulation using compact, scalable photonic chips. Most recently, a programmable atom-control PIC based on silicon nitride (SiN) platform, an ultra-low loss material in VIS-NIR wavebands (WBs), has been reported as a proof of principle. However, this platform only has 16 channels and still relies on free-space light sources.

The overall objective of this project is to develop advanced simulation models to facilitate the design of large-scale programmable PICs with fully integrated tunable, ultra-narrow linewidth, VIS-NIR lasers for control of beyond thousands of cold atoms. The established theoretical design frameworks will be used to provide guidance for real device fabrication that will be done by other researchers in my host group. Specifically, I will seek to accomplish this goal via the following two subprojects:

(i) Integrated tunable, ultra-narrow linewidth VIS-NIR lasers on SiN PICs:
Electrically pumped external-cavity tunable lasers will be used to pump on-chip stimulated Brillouin scattering lasers to deliver gain with sub-100 Hz linewidth, which is crucial to manipulate cold atoms with high fidelity. A variety of III-V semiconductors will be employed as gain materials to cover the VIS-NIR WBs: InGaN (400-590 nm), AlInGaP (590-760 nm), and GaAs/AlGaAs (760-900 nm). I will develop multi-physics simulation models to simulate the proposed lasers and further evaluate their performance such as lasing threshold and linewidth.

(ii) Programmable high-speed, low-loss, large-scale SiN modulator array:
Novel designs for ultra-low loss (sub-10 dB/m), power efficient (above 50%), high-speed (> 10 GHz) Mach Zehnder modulators (MZMs) at VIS-NIR wavelengths will be investigated. Design architecture for large arrays consisting of over 1000 MZMs will be explored. Numerical simulations utilizing both forward design and deep-learning-based inverse design methods will be employed to optimize the performance of individual MZMs and large modulator arrays. The possibility of incorporating optical gain to compensate for the photon loss will also be investigated.
Keywords: integrated photonics, photonics for cold atom control, programmable modulator array, visible semiconductor lasers

Title: Guiding the Search for Drugs in Chemical Space with Automatically Generated Knowledge
Abstract:
In dire need to improve the yield and reduce the tremendous cost of 
bringing drugs to the market, computer-aided methods are routinely 
applied due to their low cost and low time expenditure. This project is 
focused on computational fragment-, structure-based de novo drug design. 
This form of design assembles potential drug molecules from smaller 
fragment-sized building blocks while taking the structure of the target 
protein into account. The molecules are built up inside a binding site of a 
disease-associated target protein. Notwithstanding its use in both academic 
research and pharmaceutical companies, computational de novo drug 
design is still afflicted with several shortcomings. Constructing a molecule 
inside a binding site and determining its feasibility as a potential drug 
molecule, the difficulty to synthesize the molecules with organic chemistry 
and the unachievable number of combinations of how fragments can be 
connected are the major limitations of de novo drug design. Sampling all 
potential drug molecules - chemical space - exhaustively is thus 
impractical or even impossible.
    Because of these difficulties modelers have to often rely on expert 
knowledge. This project aims at ameliorating this issue by employing 
algorithms from machine learning that automatically learn relationships 
from examples. The method of this proposal is inductive logic 
programming (ILP), which obtains rules (hypothesis) in the form of logic 
programs that are human-understandable. ILP will be used to infer general 
rules that describe known inhibitors. These rules will be obtained for two 
well studied protein families, protein tyrosine kinases and human 
immunodeficiency virus (HIV) protease. These systems were selected 
because of their association with severe diseases and as a consequence 
multiple structures co-crystallized with inhibitors are available. Proteins will 
be aligned to the target structure and the inhibitors will serve as input to 
the ILP algorithm. ILP rules describing the inhibitors will then be used to 
guide the design of the existing fragment-based de novo design method 
GANDI. The idea is to restrict the search in chemical space to areas that 
are occupied by known inhibitors (activity islands) using the ILP rules as 
design criteria. These activity islands are presumed to not just contain a 
single, but multiple active molecules against the protein target. Thus using 
a search strategy that biases the design process is a major advantage for 
de novo drug design. The performance of the approach will be assessed by 
measuring the similarity of the de novo molecules against the known 
inhibitors.
    In particular for novel proteins targets or proteins that are difficult to 
crystallize, structural information is sparse. Thus the shortage of structural 
data makes it difficult to obtain design rules. The second project simulates 
this situation by only using structural information from related protein 
structures of HIV protease to derive ILP rules, but not the actual protein 
family itself. In order to avoid the design of molecules that bind to the 
related proteins a negative design approach is employed that avoids the 
generation of the inhibitors of related proteins while only considering their 
general features with ILP. This approach thus mimics the design process 
against a novel target and would provide the experienced and novice 
modeler with a design strategy for specific inhibitors of novel targets.
    ILP has been used before to derive hypotheses of known inhibitors, but 
its application as design rules in a de novo design programs is novel. This 
strategy will improve de novo drug design and help that it can be applied 
more routinely. The advantages of using ILP are that rules are human-
understandable and can be instructive for modelers. In addition, the use of 
an automatic method allows the analysis of large data sets, which might be 
difficult to achieve manually. Furthermore, potential novel drug molecules 
against HIV protease and tyrosine kinases are expected.
Keywords: computational, design, drug, learning, logic, machine, programming

Title: The Perils and Prospects of Big Data in Finance
Abstract:
The goal of this research project is to highlight the dangers of excessive data mining in financial research. The scale of this problem has increased since the advent and widespread use of machine learning techniques in investment research. Equally importantly, incentives for research seem to be skewed in favor of finding false positives.

Harvey (2017) reports that the problem of p-hacking, by which the statistical significance can be enhanced, is widespread. Most of the studies in this area look at only published research. Our goal in the first project is to evaluate all information contained in the most commonly used finance datasets and construct a large set of over two million trading strategies, some of which have been studied and published, as well as some that have been studied but not published, and those that have yet to be studied. We will use advances in statistics, specifically techniques from multiple hypothesis testing, to attempt to put a bound on p-hacking and to gauge whether truly abnormal trading strategies exist.

The second project is motivated by the advent of machine learning techniques in finance. Nowadays, researchers routinely use web crawlers to extract news and their impact on stock returns. There have also been a spate of papers using elastic net regression techniques to learn more about the cross-sectional patterns in stock returns. Chinco, Clark-Joseph, and Ye (2017) find an impressive predictability in high-frequency returns using LASSO regression. Despite safeguards such as cross-validation, very few controlled experiments in finance document the efficacy of these techniques. Our goal is to construct such a simulation and be able to put an estimate on the statistical significance of results usually reported using real data.

The third project justifies the word “prospects” in the title of this research proposal. Here we turn from the challenges of big data to opportunities of big data. We will use big data to analyze the strength of connections in money management industry. In particular, we will study whether connections (more broadly defined than just social media connections) between money managers and pension plan sponsors influence the probability of hiring. We will also study whether these connections have a positive or negative impact on the outcome of greater interest, viz., returns generated by money managers. 

Research methods in this proposal come from a variety of fields including (i) multiple hypothesis testing from statistics and econometrics, (ii) machine learning techniques, and (iii) network analysis. One of sub-projects does not require much data, another sub-project uses data regularly used by finance researchers, while the third sub-project requires purchase of new data. All projects are heavy on computational requirements.
Keywords: Connections, Investment strategies, Machine learning, Multiple hypothesis testing, Pension funds

Title: Predictive Algorithms for Public Policy and Economic Research
Abstract: Algorithms in machine learning (ML) have been developed to enhance the accuracy of predictions of a label variable (Y) using other feature variables (X) for out-of-sample scenarios. This project highlights that the outcomes of these machine predictions (Y) can be beneficial for economic research and the execution of public policies. I will utilize tools from ML, causal inference, and field experiments to enhance the identification of public agents' misbehavior, which will lead to more effective public policies and fresh data for academic research.

Title: Learning to Create Realistic Human Avatars
Abstract:
Human digitalization is required in many applications, such as animation, games, AR/VR, and social networking. Commercial solutions have made tremendous progress in recent years, such as MetaHuman from Unreal Engine or Neon from Samsung. Yet, creating these human avatars still needs significant artist efforts. Furthermore, to animate the avatars realistically, marker-based optical motion capture systems (mocap) are often employed to record detailed facial expression and motion, which require expert knowledge and expensive setup. Recent advances in deep learning have enabled human pose, shape and motion estimation and animatable avatar generation from monocular sequences. However, avatars generated from images are often of low quality and suffer from severe geometric artifacts due to limited image-to-3D datasets and shape ambiguities in the RGB observations. Furthermore, recovered human motions often exhibit severe skating and jitters. The reconstruction quality is still far behind that obtained with commercial mocap systems.

In this project, we focus on advancing the frontier of realistic human digitalization from affordable commodity sensors, such as monocular RGB(D) cameras. While the ultimate goal is to build virtual humans, from RGB(D) cameras, that look, move and behave in the way that they are indistinguishable with real humans, here we aim to propose fundamental algorithms and efficient implementations for various aspects of human digitalization, ranging from clothed body reconstruction and animation, gen- erative models for human hand, realistic grasping synthesis, human motion estimation and generation. Concretely, the research agenda of this project focuses on two related strands:

1). Learning generative models for clothed human body and hand. The key challenge of per- ceiving and modeling humans from monocular sequences is the partial and noisy image observations. Our approach is to leverage powerful generative models. To generate animatable clothed human avatars, we will explore meta-learning to enable effective prior learning and produce animatable avatars with desirable physical properties such as pose-dependent cloth deformation using only limited monocular observations. Furthermore, humans interact with the physical world with their hands. We will also introduce novel hand representations that will be driven by keypoint-based skeleton articulation and provides a high fidelity, resolution independent neural implicit surface. This will be an important step toward synthesizing realistic human-object interaction for virtual humans.

2). Learning to capture and synthesize human motion and interaction. Humans move in and interact with the 3D world. Their existence and experience is defined by the interactions with the objects and 3D scenes. Recovering realistic human motions in everyday 3D environments is essential for human behaviour understanding and virtual avatar creation. The key challenge is to capture the complex and rich interactions in lightweight and unobtrusive settings. With this project, we aim to bring recent advances in learning techniques to address the problem of capturing and modeling complex interactions between humans and the 3D world, meanwhile, to build computational models to synthesize realistic motions for virtual humans doing realistic things in the virtual world.
Keywords: Generative Models, Human Motion Capture, Human Motion Synthesis, Virtual Humans

Title: Market Predictability and its Rationale: new insights in the Theoretical and Empirical Analysis of the Pricing Kernel
Abstract:
In recent years, rapid advancements in technology are reshaping financial markets. McKinsey (2016) and the Boston Consulting Group (2015), forecasted that by 2025, financial risk management, corporate finance and asset management will be dominated by the interaction between big data and machine learning. While all of the major market players (HSBC, J.P. Morgan, UBS) are hiring computer science experts to integrate new technologies in their business activities, academic research in financial economics is still largely ignoring these developments. The aim of this study is to update our understanding of one of the cornerstones of the theory of finance, the pricing kernel, by exploiting these new technologies.

This project studies expected returns at different frequencies using new techniques provided by machine learning and data science. The out of sample predictability of financial markets using these new powerful techniques will be investigated extensively, however the core objective of this project is to understand the rationale underpinning predictability and how this can affect the pricing kernel. Indeed, we propose a conceptual framework able to unify the rational and the behavioural approach toward asset pricing, solving some of the most puzzling anomalies in the field: momentum, post earnings announcement drift, and underreaction-overreaction.

In the first part of the research we will focus on yearly returns, studying the interactions among fundamentally and behaviourally based predictors. To conduct our analysis in an elegant and rigorous way, we will start from the framework proposed by Campbell and Shiller (1988). We will continue by showing how expected returns and dividend growth cannot be forecasted beyond a few years even if employing the most sophisticated machine learning techniques currently available. This implies that the current price is mostly the result of two perpetuities: one of expected dividend growth and one of expected returns. Then, we will study how the dynamics of these perpetuities are affected by the interaction between behaviourally and risk based components and how this can enhance our understanding of equity returns in terms of return predictability and pricing kernel formulation.

In the second part of the research we will study intra-daily returns which are the domain of algorithmic trading. Here, we propose a novel approach: rebuilding the main trading strategies commonly employed in professional trading desks and demonstrating how, while short term returns are unconditionally unpredictable on average, they are conditionally predictable on average when observing a strong trading signal. This will lead us to investigate the rationale underpinning the emergence of trading signals and how their existence can be reconciled with current economic theories. Then, we will study how the interdependencies among inter-market and inter-temporal signals are the basis of the phenomenon called contagion and of numerous patterns (“flows of predictability”) across securities and markets. Finally, we will investigate the links among trading signals and the empirical dynamics of the pricing kernel.
Keywords: Algorithmic Trading, Big Data, Data Science, Machine learning, Market predictability, Pricing Kernel

Title: Computer  Assisted  Precision  Medicine  for Breast Cancer
Abstract:
Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women and the second most common cancer overall. It occurs when some breast cells begin to grow abnormally. A number of different breast cancer sub-types can be identified based on the tumor location, grade, size and whether the cancer cells are sensitive to particular hormones or the immune system of the patient. The diagnosis and staging of breast cancer is heavily based on mammograms and sonography as well as histopathological images, while Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is usually an additional source of information. Typically, after the diagnosis of breast cancer, an operation is performed in order to remove the tumor while additional therapeutic procedures are also carried out such as chemotherapy, hormone therapy, radiation or immunotherapy. Different tumor sub-types are subject to different clinical outcomes and treatment decisions and therefore genetic information from the tumor is also taken into consideration. 

With the latest major advances on machine learning, a great number of algorithms became able to generate very informative models that are built on data. These models can provide powerful solutions, assisting physicians on their everyday practice. This project's aim is to propose a novel, modular, scalable and computationally efficient artificial visual perception paradigm towards personalized medicine for breast cancer. The proposed project is highly interdisciplinary, as it lies at the interface between (a) technical aspects, such as medical image analysis, machine learning, optimization and (b) clinical aspects, such as biological representation of breast tumors, diagnosis, treatment decisions and clinical outcomes. The final goal is that all the developed algorithms will have a tremendous impact not only on the medical image analysis community, but in the everyday practice of all the physicians and also patients that suffer from breast cancer.

This project will be among the first studies that aims to establish and evaluate strong relations between imaging and clinical data for breast cancer, integrating knowledge coming from engineers, medical doctors and biologists in each and every part of it. More specifically, machine learning algorithms with an emphasis on deep learning will be designed and utilized as tools to extract, combine and find correlations and relations of data that are not easily established with the human eye, by integrating multi-omics information, with well-established evidence driven knowledge from doctors and biologists. By modeling the problem towards that direction, a number of biomarkers and signatures that will assist clinicians in their everyday practice are expected to emerge and move the community a step closer to precision medicine.
Keywords: Artificial Inteligence, Breast Cancer, Genomics, Pathomics, Precision Medicine, Radiomics

Title: Mapping the flow of information between cellular, signaling, and chromatin states.
Abstract: The ability of individual cells to sense their environment and internal state, and to transmit this information in a context-dependent manner to downstream cellular processes is a fundamental property of life. Recently, we have shown that heterogeneous growth factor responses do not reflect a limited information processing capacity but adaptive information processing, in which the response of a signaling node is adapted to the physicochemical state of the cell. Since signaling nodes do this in different ways, they collectively, as a multimodal percept, capture a comprehensive picture of a cell’s multicellular context and internal state. This project aims to extend this concept to the level of chromatin, in which we hypothesise that heterogeneity in chromatin marks, associated transcription factors, and the subnuclear spatial organization of chromatin reflects another multimodal encoding of information about the cell's physiochemical state and environment, transmitted through cellular information processing. To address this, we will need methods that can holistically map these various internal representations within the same single cells. Here we will for the first time achieve that by: 1) establishing scalable multiplexed imaging of gene loci and their activities in single human cells; 2) combining this with 4i, our approach for highly multiplexed multiscale imaging of protein states in the same single cells; and 3) to map information flow between three internal cellular representations, namely cellular state, signaling state, and chromatin state, during the process of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition. This work will will significantly extend the capabilities of image-based systems biology and make it more comprehensive, both in the set of measurements we can obtain and the range of length scales we can cover in the same sample. The approach outlined here, and the datasets it will generate, has the potential to reveal generalisable rules by which cells encode information at multiple levels of biological organization and use it to make context-aware decisions, enabling higher levels of prediction of how individual cells respond to stimuli.

Title: One size fits all? Towards individual prediction of treatment success for posttraumatic stress disorder ini post-conflict settings (TRAUMA-FIT)
Abstract:
In war-affected countries, posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) represents a major mental health problem. Accumulating evidence indicates, that next to the individual trauma history, relevant contextual factors of the social and societal environment, as well as ongoing stressors and adversity play a major role in PTSD development and its treatment after war and conflict.
While trauma-focused psychotherapy is recommended as first-line treatment for PTSD, the individual treatment effects vary strongly, and a substantial number of individuals do not benefit from this type of treatment. This high treatment-effect heterogeneity for PTSD indicates that an individual allocation of treatments could lead to improved treatment outcomes. This is especially important in war-affected countries with limited resources for mental health care. 
Against this background, the present project aims to conduct a large precision mental health trial on effective treatment options for PTSD in the post-conflict region of Northern Uganda. A total number of N = 660 individuals will be randomized to the two arms of the trial: Narrative Exposure Therapy (NET), a trauma-focused short-term intervention, and Problem Management + (PM+), a present-centered intervention that aims to facilitate coping with current stress. Importantly, both treatments have been effectively implemented by local health workers in low-resource settings. 
Employing machine learning, the optimal treatment condition for each individual will be determined based on a set of individual predictors and relevant social and societal factors. In the next step, the performance of the algorithm will be evaluated by comparing mean treatment effects and rates of clinically significant changes between individuals who received their optimal versus sub-optimal treatment condition.
All in all, the project will provide knowledge on relevant predictors of treatment success in trauma-focused versus present-centered interventions for PTSD patients. Furthermore, knowledge regarding treatment personalization and optimal utilization of treatment resources in post-conflict settings will be generated.
Keywords: mental health, narrative exposure therapy, posttraumatic stress disorder, present-centered intervention, problem menagement plus, treatment predictors, war-affected

Title: Understanding and Improving the Society-level Effects of Navigation Techniques
Abstract: Hundreds of millions of people rely on navigation technologies like Google Maps and “SatNavs” to define how they move around the world. While navigation technologies provide obvious benefits to their users on a trip-by-trip basis, early evidence is emerging that these technologies may have societal severe side effects (i.e., negative externalities). For instance, there are reports of routing algorithms turning previously quiet neighbourhoods into traffic jams, helping wealthy people avoid areas that they perceive to be undesirable, and potentially increasing carbon emissions. Navigation technologies have even been linked to significant injuries and dozens of deaths due to algorithmic errors and user interface issues. In our project, “Understanding and Improving Society-level Effects of Navigation Technologies (SENT)”, we seek to (1) understand and (2) address the negative externalities of existing and upcoming navigation technology algorithms and interfaces. The first phase of the project will examine the algorithmic mechanisms behind and characteristics of these negative externalities. This phase will focus on the causes of catastrophic incidents associated with navigation technologies (i.e., deaths and significant accidents) and the societal effects of new routing algorithms (e.g., those that seek to provide “shortcuts”, increased safety, and other trip-by-trip benefits). Based on this research, we will develop a series of design implications to reduce the negative externalities associated with navigation technologies. The second phase of our work will focus on implementing and evaluating our proposed designs. For instance, we will develop sociotechnical routing algorithms that include input from local communities and routing algorithms that balance improvements to the trip-by-trip experience with the minimization of externalities (e.g., traffic, carbon emissions). We will also develop improvements to navigation technologies to reduce the number of catastrophic incidents associated with their use. We will additionally produce datasets and new technologies that will significantly facilitate the consideration of externalities by other navigation technology researchers. New technologies created through the course of this work will include navigation technologies that are less likely to play a role in catastrophic incidents (e.g., fatal accidents) and routing algorithms that avoid externalities like excessive traffic and bolstering the geographic filter bubble. The research in this proposal is situated at the intersection of Human-Computer Interaction and Geographic Information Science and uses mixed-methods approaches. Key outcomes are expected between the two main phases of the project: First, by systematically analyzing catastrophic incidents associated with navigation technologies and the behaviour of routing algorithms, we will seek to gain a much deeper understanding of the society-level effects (i.e., negative externalities) of existing navigation technologies. Secondly, building upon this knowledge, we will select several findings that emerge from the first phase, for which we will develop proof-of-concept solutions. This will include the development of datasets and technologies that will greatly facilitate the consideration of externalities by navigation technology researchers. The results will be a new generation of navigation technologies that minimize negative externalities while maintaining good trip-by-trip experiences.
Keywords: Algorithmic Bias, Artificial Intelligence, Computer science, GeoHCI, Geographic information science, Geographic information visualization, Human-computer interaction, Mobile HCI

Title: The Embodied Dreaming Project - Linking Body Stimulation and Virtual Reality Training to Lucid Dreaming
Abstract:
Every night the brain generates an almost perfect simulation of reality: during sleep, we perceive a complex dream world with all our senses, move seamlessly through it and interact in complex ways with the dreamed environment. However, whereas highly active sensory and motor regions of the brain support this intriguing reality simulation, a deactivated prefrontal cortex prevents our higher cognitive capacities to work in a similarly wake-like manner: even in the face of highly unusual dream events, we typically do not reflect on our current situation and do not realize that we are dreaming. The rare exception from this rule is the phenomenon of lucid dreaming: dreams during which the dreamer becomes aware of the ongoing state of mind without waking up. Lucid dreaming has a num-ber of applications in sleep research, clinical practice, professional sports, and everyday life. The main obstacle to both its scientific investigation and practical application is its rarity: only about half of the population knows the phenomenon from own experience and only few people have lucid dreams on a regular basis. Several strategies to increase lucid dreaming frequency exist, however none induces lucid dreams with high reliability in a given night. Most previous lucid dreaming induc-tion strategies either have targeted higher cognitive functions with metacognitive training, their under-lying prefrontal brain regions with electrical brain stimulation, or have used auditory or visual cues to make the dreaming subject aware of their current state of mind. Rarely have such attempts targeted bodily senses, despite the dreamed body in some cases is tightly bound to the real-life body. In the project proposed here, we aim for an embodied approach to lucid dream induction. We will in particu-lar focus on the vestibular system, considering that radical vestibular experiences are rare during wakefulness, however common in dreams of falling or flying. The technique of galvanic vestibular stimulation (GVS) during wakefulness allows on button press to induce very convincing experiences of falling. We will first induce dreams of falling and potentially flying by galvanic vestibular stimula-tion during REM sleep, investigating how - and how reliably - the vestibular experiences gets incorpo-rated into the dream plot. We will then train participants to associate such vestibular experience during wakefulness with the metacognitive thought “This is a dream!”, which we in turn aim to reactivate dur-ing sleep, thus eliciting full-blown lucid dreams. We will finally refine this strategy by combining gal-vanic vestibular stimulation with virtual reality (VR) scenarios of flying/falling experiences, thus devel-oping a highly immersive training environment for effective lucid dream induction. With a combined EEG-VR approach, we will further elucidate the neural correlates of metacognitive introspection, as well as vestibular experiences, during both wakefulness and sleep, levering machine learning strate-gies to compare between the two states. As both a control condition for other bodily senses, as well as a risk mitigation strategy in case of lower than expected efficacy of the vestibular stimulation strategy, we will in the early parts of the project also test electric muscle stimulation (EMS) and haptic stimulation (HS) as alternative lucid dreaming induction strategies. Thus delivering a comprehensive investigation of embodied dream experiences and their potential use in lucid dream induction. As a whole, the project will allow for novel insights into embodied dream experiences on both a cognitive and neural level, will develop a potentially highly effective new lucid dreaming induction strategy ‘on button press’, and will thus pave the way for applications in research, medical treatment, sports, and everyday life.

Title: Machine Learning-Enhanced Strategic Synthesis Planning
Abstract:
Organic synthesis is still perceived as an art that only human experts can do. As there are far too many possible moves to try them all, successful chemists make decisions based on the intuition that they have developed over decades of experience. Although computer-assisted retrosynthetic tools exist, designing syntheses is mostly trial and error. What is the recipe/route to a molecule that was never made before? Synthesis is the current bottleneck in the molecular design cycle, and unlocking 
machine learning-enhanced synthesis planning with strategy could accelerate the discovery of novel molecules and shorten syntheses at later development stages. 
Large databases of chemical reactions, continuously increasing computational power and open-source software to make deep learning approaches accessible have enabled new machine learning-driven synthesis planning tools. The advantage of such methods is that they can be trained on the available literature and extract the knowledge in it in a matter of days; a task that would take more than a lifetime for a human. After capturing patterns from millions of previously performed reactions, those machine learning approaches can then be queried with unseen inputs and predict what could happen in this new situation based on what they have seen during training. Ideally, chemists could do the creative process of designing a new molecule, input it into a synthesis planning tool and get ideas/suggestions on how the target molecule could be synthesised over multiple steps from less complex, possibly commercial building blocks. 
In current machine learning solutions, retrosynthetic models are trained on single reaction steps, and only in a second stage search algorithms are used to apply the trained single-step models and explore suggested synthesis trees. However, this leads to a discrepancy between the tasks the models are trained on and the actual goal. In comparison, a human expert would have a global strategy in mind and prefer, for example, to disconnect reactive functional groups first so that they only must be dealt with in the last steps of the synthesis. Moreover, the most accurate models on single-step evaluation benchmarks do not perform best in the multi-step prediction task. As the strategic component is missing, the artificial intelligence predicted routes often do not meet the high standards of synthetic chemists.

The purpose of this project is to advance the current ML approaches for strategic multi-step synthesis planning. As for any machine learning project, the data is crucial. Hence, we will start by defining a standardised synthesis format, convert two open-source reaction datasets into this format by stitching single-step reactions together and make an extended analysis of synthesis strategies. The created open-source synthesis datasets will enable us to train machine learning synthesis planning models that capture synthesis strategies. To advance the field, we will suggest a benchmark for synthesis planning tools, on which they can be evaluated and compared. With an easily accessible synthesis idea generator, we will strengthen the explainability of machine learning models, facilitate adoption by organic chemists, and collect valuable feedback to improve our approaches continuously.

During the project, we will train one doctoral student and one post-doc at the intersection of chemistry and artificial intelligence. In the age of chemical digitalisation, educating such young researchers to speak both languages (chemistry & machine learning) is crucial for Swiss academia and industry. Throughout the project, we will collaborate with expert synthetic chemists to ensure that the quality of the curated synthesis data, benchmark, and metrics is high and that the developed approaches are relevant.

The ultimate goal is to advance the field of machine learning for strategic synthesis planning, provide synthetic chemists with new ideas outside their area of expertise which can be experimentally validated, and accelerate the synthesis of novel molecules - going towards increasingly complex compounds and more sustainable routes.
Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Chemical reactions, Machine learning, Open science, Retrosynthesis, Synthesis planning, Synthesis strategy

Title: Learning for Safety in Data-driven Control
Keywords: control theory, data-driven, safety, uncertainty
grant_text: learning for safety in data driven control. background: in several complex systems, such as the transportation network, manufacturing or drug dose management, deriving an accurate physics based model of the system is challenging due to the scale of the system and the uncertainties in the parameters and processes involved. meanwhile, with the explosion of sensing and data processing capabilities, we can collect data from the systems at an unprecedented rate. this has resulted in a paradigm shift in control: from physics based to data driven. however, unless we prove safety of the data driven approaches, we cannot employ them in safety critical tasks such as autonomous driving, robot human interactions or personalized medicine. safe data driven control problem: with the advent of data driven control, the problem of safe data driven control has gained an increasing attention. this problem can be formulated as control of a dynamical system under state and input constraints, with the caveat that the dynamical model or the constraints are a priori uncertain. open challenges: past work on safe data driven control has mainly focused on the case of unknown dynamics but known constraints. the case in which the constraint sets themselves are being learned based on data is not sufficiently explored. this realistic case arises in several applications including autonomous driving, where the trajectories of nearby traffic are uncertain; autonomous robots operating in unexplored environments or along humans/other robots; or personalized medicine, where the effects of a drug on a given patient is a priori unknown. goal and specific aims: the goal of this project is to develop the theory and algorithms for safe data driven control, under uncertainties in the safe sets and their evolution. the specific aims are as follows: 1. developing fundamental understanding of safe data driven control by characterizing its sample complexity; 2. modeling probability distributions capturing the uncertainties in an estimation module used to learn safe sets; 3. synthesizing controllers that ensure satisfaction of suitably defined notions of risk and safety; 4. verification of the algorithms on realistic simulation test beds and on an in house experimental platform. expected outcome: i will contribute to both the scientific advancement of the problem and the training of researchers. i will publish the scientific results in strictly peer reviewed conference and journal venues, across automatic control and machine learning communities, and publicize them through international talks. i will work closely with my trainees to build their fundamental optimization, control and learning technical skills and to support them in scientific communication. additionally, i will organize workshops and online courses pertinent to the research objectives and outcomes, to exchange ideas and disseminate the research to a larger scientific community. impact: the future automated systems, e.g. in intelligent transportation and personalized medicine, need to ensure safety and efficiency despite uncertainties arising from coupled subsystems, human interactions and partial data. given the importance of this problem, the control and learning communities have been increasingly focusing on it, making breakthroughs on various formulations of this problem. my proposed research complements these efforts by bridging tools from stochastic control, online optimization and learning, all within my past contributions and expertise, to guarantee safety in a practically important but theoretically less explored problem class, namely, uncertain safe sets. it advances fundamental understanding for this problem class, designs robust control algorithms leveraging this understanding, and offers a holistic approach by verifying and benchmarking the theoretical results on realistic test beds.. control theory, data driven, safety, uncertainty

Title: Data imputation for SCADA data using Graph Neural Networks and Transfer Learning
Abstract:
In the era of digitalisation, data-driven approaches, particularly deep learning methods, can leverage the abundance of available data. 
However, the reliability of these models depends heavily on the quality of the historical data used for training.

In the context of wind energy, particularly wind turbine generators (WTGs), this data is provided by the Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) system, which includes variables such as wind speed, wind direction, power output and others. 
However, faulty and missing data can arise due to sensor errors, software issues, icing, dirt, or even human intervention.
This becomes especially problematic when long periods of data are missing or faulty.

Missing or faulty data can be addressed by deletion or imputation strategies, the latter trying to estimate missing values. 
Recent advances in data imputation strategies include the use of Graph Neural Networks
(GNNs).
GNNs, part of graph representation learning, encode structural information of graph structured data into features for machine learning tasks. 
Casting data of a wind farm into a graph structure allows for the use of GNNs, accounting for spatial relationships within the wind farm.

This project aims to employ, for the first time, GNNs for imputing faulty wind speed and power output data.
We will use open-source datasets from the Kelmarsh and Penmanshiel wind farms in the UK.
We will also explore transfer learning, using simulation data for the initial model training. The pre-trained models are then fine-tuned with the available SCADA data. 
This addresses the challenge concerning the requirement of large amounts of data for training neural networks.
Keywords: Data imputation, Graph Neural Network, Graph representation learning, SCADA data, Transfer learning, Turbine upgrade quantification, Wind energy

Title: PCS-OBEY: enabling People-Centric Sensing by Overcoming the privacy BarriEr
Abstract:
Imagine that you are in an intimate situation with your whole family in a cosy suburban restaurant (second birthday of your younger son) and your location is disclosed on Facebook to your work colleagues, who are catching up a deadline and desperately need you, but you do not answer their calls. Or imagine that a video when you are playing a silly clown in a bar with friends is posted automatically by your Google Glasses on a public server, such that anybody, including your boss, can see it. In both cases it was you who initially agreed that an application that you have recently downloaded and installed on your smartphone, automatically collects content from you. This application collects data from you and from many unknown to you individuals, following the people-centric sensing (PCS) approach, but you just simply did not oversee the negative personal consequences of using it. What counts for you is that, given the fact that you have agreed to share this data, the application provides you with better service quality. 
The PCS-OBEY targets users like you and it develops theoretical framework and mechanisms for modelling the individual user privacy for accessing sensor data/content from smartphones, while taking into account the user’s current context. The project focuses on smartphone, on a growing scale leveraged for PCS-based solutions.
The approach for researching PCS-OBEY involves real smartphones users in the multiple studies and it is as follows: 1) collection of sensor data/content from smartphones and understanding the user’s individual privacy preferences; the privacy preferences are related to the user’s intimacy state and willingness to share data in the given intimacy state 2) collection of context from smartphone (user’s location, activity, etc.) and relating it to the user privacy preferences, i.e., using machine learning techniques to learn intimacy state from the user’s context and building the user’s individual privacy model; 3) inferring/predicting (now/future) user’s intimacy, solely based on the context collected and analysed on the smartphone, while getting the user’s feedback on the prediction accuracy – to update the privacy model.
PCS-OBEY aims at truly individually tailored privacy management where control is at the user’s device – close to the sensors generating potentially disadvantageous content. PCS-OBEY is contrasted with the current population-based approaches – focusing on data anonymisation and storage, and not on the individual’s preferences.
The proposed project lies at the frontier of HCI and people-centric sensing, pervasive and ubiquitous computing, privacy management and machine learning. The project is timely - there is a significant for research and commercial interest for privacy-enabled PCS-based solutions, as smartphones became personal communication and computing devices affordable for masses, and applications (‘apps’) exploiting smartphone’s sensors/content are available for these devices on a growing scale. The challenge is that many of these applications collect smartphone-generated content either without the users being explicitly informed about it or, without informing the user about the purpose of collecting of this content, i.e., when installing an app, the user is asked to accept the app’s ‘permissions’, which may be unrelated to the way the app works, e.g., permission to share the location or calls for a simple stationary game.
To conduct the proposed research we have the necessary equipment including smartphones and sensors, as well as infrastructure for collecting smartphone-based data from mobile users called mQoL Living Lab. So far in our research we have focused on the PCS-based system (called QoSIS) for collecting of network performance data from mobile users and using machine learning over that data to provide them back with the best choice of connectivity. Mr Gustarini - the PhD student proposed for this project has already started the research towards the PCS-OBEY framework and mechanisms, defined the research questions enumerated in this proposal and acquired preliminary results, published at the prestigious conferences in the field.
Based on our previous experience and scientific expertise we aim to conduct the fundamental research beyond the state of the art in HCI and people-centric sensing, research on modelling of the individual user’s privacy preferences, and the PCS-based solutions enabled by privacy profiles and the context the user is in. We aim at the use of the context to determine real-time privacy settings in unconstrained environments, i.e., for privacy-based processing and distribution of sensor’s data. PCS-OBEY solution significantly enhances the current PCS-based approaches through the modelling of the user’s context. 
There are various potential uses of PCS-OBEY research, including PCS-based solutions for sociology research, 
for novel applications development, for common good of community caring for pollution or road traffic, or enabling e-government solutions. These solutions will leverage the data/content collected from masses while ensuring that the privacy of an individual is not violated. The PCS-OBEY will be firstly exploited via our on-going research projects and collaborations in the area of mobile computing and communications, applied in wellbeing and disease management, or in a sociology research.
Keywords: People-Centric Sensing, content sharing, context-awareness, mobile computing, opportunistic sensing, privacy

Title: Digital Transformation at the Local Tier of Government in Europe: Dynamics and Effects from a Cross-Countries and Over-Time Comparative Perspective (DIGILOG)
Abstract:
Digital transformation constitutes one of the most important innovations at the local level of government and is expected to reshape local service delivery, public administration, and governance in Europe fundamentally. Most recently, the COVID-19 pandemic has shown the fundamental importance of a well-prepared digital administration to replace analog processes, not only but most urgently needed in times of physical distancing (Kuhlmann et al., 2020a). In many countries, local government is the most significant tier of public service delivery, ensuring proximity to citizens and a key player of digital transformation (Steiner et al., 2018; Kuhlmann, 2009, p. 21; Bouckaert/Kuhlmann, 2016).
Against this background, it is a matter of concern and criticism that in current comparative research concerning the digital transformation of state and administration, local levels of government have been insufficiently investigated. Indeed, there is no systematic, cross-countries comparative knowledge available regarding the state of implementation and the effects of digital transformation at local government level in Europe. This collaborative research project is intended to remedy those deficits. Its first main research questions address the dynamics, scale, and pace of digital transformation in European local government, i.e., to what extent there has been radical/rapid revolutionary or gradual/slow evolutionary change and how and why these dynamics differ when considered from a cross-countries and inter-municipal perspective. The second main research question addresses the (intended and unintended) effects of digitalization on local self-government in Europe in terms of outputs (service delivery, organization, processes, and human resources), outcomes (performance and accountability), and impacts (citizens’ acceptance, governance, new cleavages). The independent variables include explanatory factors on the macro-level (institutional properties of the local government systems), meso-level (internal organizational arrangements and procedures), and micro-level (actor strategies, interests, motives).
The project will generate coherent data for a systematic comparison using methodological triangulation, i.e., quantitative and qualitative methods. It will take the form of a regular and automated quantitative survey of all local authorities in 47 European countries (members of the Council of Europe), based on web crawling and machine learning techniques - this is a novel approach in the context of the social sciences - and qualitative research, namely case studies in selected European countries. Renowned scholars from the University of Potsdam, ZHAW, and the Vienna University of Economics and Business, with extensive experience in local government and comparative research, form the consortium of this project.
Key deliverables of the project will be an openly accessible monitoring platform of digital transformation at the local tier of government, journal articles, an edited volume, and publications for practitioners. The real-time platform “Monitoring Digital Transformation in European Local Governments” is accessible to researchers and practitioners worldwide and contributes to a better understanding of long-term developments. The duration of the project being submitted to the SNSF/DFG is three years; however, by automating the process, the real-time platform will continue to exist and be updated regularly beyond this timeframe. The research project will yield policy-relevant knowledge concerning local digitalization measures from a European perspective, which can then be utilized to improve policymaking for future public sector modernization.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, European municipalities, comparative public administration, digital government, digital transformation, digitalization, dynamics of change, local government, machine learning

Title: INTACT - INTerstitial pneumonia pattern Analysis for  CompuTer-aided diagnosis
Abstract:
Interstitial Lung Diseases (ILDs) is a group of more than 200 chronic lung disorders characterized by scarring and/or inflammation of the lung tissue that leads to respiratory failure. In most cases, ILDs have unknown causes so they are described as Idiopathic Interstitial Pneumonia (IIP). Clinical examination, chest radiography and Computed Tomography (CT) constitute the first steps of the ILD diagnosis procedure, however most forms of ILD require additional invasive histological confirmation which introduces potential risks for the patient and increases common health care costs. Although there is currently no permanent cure, the precise diagnosis of ILDs is crucial for achieving the optimal treatment as well as investigating novel therapies. Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) constitutes the most prevalent IIP and carries a rather poor prognosis. Non-Specific Interstitial Pneumonia (NSIP) is a pathological subtype of IIP that mimics IPF in its clinical presentation, having though a more favorable prognosis. The high prevalence of IPF and NSIP among the ILDs combined with their similar clinical/radiological manifestations and their rather different prognosis and treatment make the corresponding differential diagnosis both crucial and challenging.
The aim of the proposed project is to develop a computational system that will assist clinicians with the diagnosis of ILDs while avoiding the dangerous, expensive and time-consuming invasive biopsies. The system will provide a computerized differential diagnosis, based on radiological data and clinical/biochemical markers and will focus on the discrimination between the IPF and the NSIP while keeping a generic architecture that could be expanded to most types of ILDs. The appropriate interpretation of the available radiological data combined with clinical/biochemical information can provide reliable diagnosis able to improve the diagnostic accuracy of the clinicians.
The proposed system will consist of two major modules: the image analysis module and the diagnosis support module. The former will segment the lung parenchyma from the CT images and perform detection/classification of the existing ILD patterns. Then, the extent and distribution of the lung abnormalities will be quantified. The second module will take as input the image analysis results together with the available clinical/biochemical data and based on the existing medical knowledge and machine learning techniques will provide as output a ranked list indicating the most likely disease. New methods for describing the 2D and 3D texture of CT patterns will be proposed and evaluated comparatively to the well-established literature. Moreover, the most appropriate artificial intelligence tools will be determined for classifying the CT patterns and producing the final diagnosis. For the purposes of the project two databases will be used: the publicly available Talisman database by the University Hospital of Geneva and the Inselspital database containing complementary 3D data from Multiple Detector CT (MDCT) scanners which will be created within the framework of the project.
The project will strengthen ILD lung CT-image analysis by introducing novel computer vision and machine learning techniques and evaluating comparatively the existing literature. The improvement of the clinicians’ diagnostic accuracy on ILDs will result in optimizing the corresponding treatment so the patient life will be prolonged and its quality will be improved. Furthermore, the research for novel treatments will be promoted. By achieving a reliable diagnosis based on CT, the patients will avoid the potential risks of bleeding and general anaesthesia as well as the high costs that come with a surgical biopsy.
Keywords: Classification, Computed Tomography, Decision Support System, Interstitial Lung Diseases, Pattern Recognition, Texture Analysis

Title: HYPER-EDGE: Harmonic Ptychography for Ultrafast Structural and Charge Dynamics at Interfaces
Abstract:
Interfaces are dynamic landscapes where charge transfer, molecular reorganisation and phase transitions dictate material functionality across fields ranging from energy storage and catalysis to quantum materials. However, existing ultrafast techniques lack the spatiotemporal resolution needed to directly resolve sub-femtosecond charge and structural dynamics at interfaces. Resolving these processes is critical for advancing technologies that rely on interfacial control. What makes HYPER-EDGE disruptive? Unlike conventional ultrafast spectroscopies, which require external probes and struggle to resolve spatial and temporal information simultaneously, HYPER-EDGE exploits HHG generated within the interface itself, encoding charge and structural dynamics into the emitted spectrum. Subsequent reconstruction using ptychographic phase retrieval provides background-free, high-resolution snapshots of the underlying interfacial dynamics. This ability to simultaneously extract attosecond temporal and nanometre spatial information has never been realised for complex liquid-based interfaces, making HYPER-EDGE a first-of-its-kind experimental framework.
Research roadmap and anticipated breakthroughs: The project will first establish proof-of-principle at solid–solid interfaces, investigating structural reconstruction, charge transfer, phase transitions and ion transport. Subsequent developments will extend the approach to reflection-mode harmonic ptychography, enabling surface-sensitive measurements at solid–solid, liquid–liquid and liquid–air interfaces. These steps will open access to plasmon-enhanced HHG, interfacial charge injection and nanoscale surface fluctuations, which are crucial for quantum materials, optoelectronics, energy conversion and nanofluidics. As a disruptive, untested approach, HYPER-EDGE faces challenges such as signal-to-noise limitations in solid-phase HHG, phase-retrieval complexities and interfacial mixing effects that may introduce variability. To mitigate these risks, the project will employ optimised HHG parameters for enhanced phase matching, systematic interface control using precision layer deposition and structured substrates, as well as reference-spectra calibration and machine-learning-based phase retrieval.
Despite these challenges, HYPER-EDGE has the potential to establish harmonic ptychography as a new standard methodology for ultrafast science across solid, liquid and heterogenous interfaces. The ability to monitor charge transport and molecular interactions in (quasi) real time will benefit optoelectronics, neuromorphic computing and biomedical sciences, with concrete applications in quantum technologies, energy storage and molecular self-assembly.

Title: Phenix - Alternative stochastic models for data integration and robust uncertainty quantification in hydrogeology
Abstract:
Aquifer heterogeneity is the result of a long history of geological processes leading to hydraulic conductivity variations that can span many orders of magnitudes. A major difficulty in groundwater modeling is to construct an adequate representation of the heterogeneity and to constrain it properly by indirect data. While it is straightforward to quantify the first statistical moments of this  variability using spatial statistics techniques, it is still considerably more difficult to integrate properly available conceptual geological information with geophysical and hydrogeological data.  

The aim of the PheniX project is to  develop a complete suite of tools allowing to integrate these different types of data in a Bayesian framework and provide robust uncertainty estimates. 

To reach that aim, the project includes three interrelated parts.
The first one focuses on the definition of new random function models and parameter inference techniques. These models are the key underlying components of the geological models and will be able to represent connectivity uncertainty. This is why we propose to work both on the extension of our current multiple point statistics technique and on substitution random functions because these models offer a parsimonious representation allowing to cover a wide range of connectivity patterns. 
The second part of the project focuses on the formalization of the relations between the random function models and the geological concepts. The aim is to allow constructing reliable 3D heterogeneity models for Quaternary formations in Switzerland in a semi automated manner. Finally, the third part of the project focuses on the data integration and inverse problem. Specific inverse methods are required to handle non multiGaussian random functions and especially discrete parameters. Here we propose to extend the Posterior Population Expansion (PoPEx) technique. We think that this approach will be sufficiently robust to handle the joint inversion of geophysical and hydrogeological data at the regional scale while accounting for a well defined geological prior. Machine learning will be employed to accelerate the inversion procedure. We plan to test the applicability of the method using synthetic highly realistic benchmarks and the upper {Aar aquifer located between Bern and Thun. Around 3'000 boreholes with lithological information are available at the site. We will complement that data set with a ground based time domain electro magnetic (TEM) geophysical campaign.

The expected results are a set of new models and efficient algorithms allowing to represent aquifer heterogeneity in 2D and 3D while integrating various types of data in a consistent manner. In addition, the benchmark data and the geophysical data set will be made public as well as the new algorithms that will be developed during the project.
Keywords: Alluvial aquifer, Data integration, Geophysics, Geostatistics, Hydrogeology, Inverse technique, Quaternary formations, Stochastic models

Title: ML2 - Multilevel and Domain Decomposition Methods for Machine Learning
Abstract:
Learning takes time. The dominant method for training deep neural networks, the stochastic gradient method, requires a substantial amount of steps until acceptable weights have been identified. As a consequence, a huge amount of computational resources, time, and energy has to be spent when a network is trained. 

Various approaches towards finding  more efficient training process have been developed, e.g. accelerated gradient methods or methods based on the approximation of second order information. Alternative approaches, such as using less accurate floating point representations for storing the weights can also help to reduce the computational impact of training. 

Still, the development of efficient training methods remains an open challenge.
Two major obstacles can be identified on the way to more efficient training methods. The first obstacle is the non-convexity of the loss functionals, which is related to a quite rich energy landscape with distinctive features. A good set of weights is usually thought to be characterised by a "stable" stationary point in the sense that a smaller variation of the weights will not influence the loss functional significantly. In other words, the properties of the training method directly influence the quality and stability of the resulting approximation provided by the network.

The second obstacle is the shear size of the problems - big data induces large scale Hessians, which prevents the straight forward application of many classical techniques from optimization. In fact, whenever classical Newton-like techniques are applied, linear systems have to be set up and possibly solved, which might simply be too large for the available (GPU) memory.

Within this project "ML2  - Multilevel and Domain Decomposition for Machine Learning" we will address both of the difficulties explained above by transferring ideas from multilevel methods, in particular multigrid (MG), and domain decomposition (DD) to  machine learning. 

Originally developed for the solution of symmetric positive definite linear systems arising from the discretization of elliptic PDEs, MG and DD  are nowadays used as massively parallel solution methods with (quasi-)optimal complexity for various types of linear and non-linear large-scale systems. 

During the last two decades, the idea of multi-level decompositions has also be applied to convex and non-convex minimization problems, leading to multi-level minimizations methods such as RMTR, Monotone Multigrid, or MG/OPT. These methods show significant to drastic improvements in terms of robustness and speed for large-scale minimization problems, when compared to a simple gradient method. Additionally, they allow for massive  parallelism.

Within ML2, we will develop parallel multi-level minimization methods for training neural networks, which will be designed to deal with the large scale non-convex minimization problems at hand  in an efficient way. 
ML2 will exploit the optimality of advanced parallel iterative solution methods for machine learning. 

The binding component between both worlds will be the multilevel decomposition, which can be found in both, neural networks and multigrid methods, as a hierarchy of problem dependent approximation spaces.
Keywords: Domain Decomposition, Machine Learning, Multigrid and Multilevel Methods, Multiscale Minimization, Neural Network, Nonlinear Preconditioning, Optimization, Training
