Title: Quantum Decision Theory: other classical paradoxes, losses, functional attraction factors, quantum artificial intelligence, large scale experimental tests and application to management
Abstract:
Over the last few years, our group has advanced a novel approach to decision theory, invoking mathematical techniques used in quantum measurement theory and quantum information theory, because of which this approach has been called Quantum Decision Theory (QDT) (Yukalov and Sornette, 2008). The mathematical basis of this approach has been developed in several publications (Yukalov and Sornette, 2009a,b,c; 2010a,b; 2011). In the last three years, the development of our theory has reached a level of maturation such that it is time to put more efforts on on-going experimental tests, novel experiments and practical applications, helped by a Ph.D. student who profits at the same time from this unique schooling environment. The goal of this project is precisely the use of our Quantum Decision Theory for practical applications. It seems that QDT is on its way to become the sole parsimonious predictive decision theory that allows not only for the quantitative resolution of all existing paradoxes of classical decision theory, but also for a variety of practical applications. But, to support this ambition, significant work needs to be carried out. Concretely, we shall concentrate on the following problems.
1-Using the criteria formulated in our published papers, we shall analyze the known classical paradoxes in decision making in order to classify them in two groups: the first group requires the full use of QDT; the second group necessitates only mild adaptation from classical utility theory extended into a probabilistic framework.
2-We shall extend the applicability of QDT, until now formulated for lotteries with gains to the case of lotteries with losses. On the basis of such an extension, we shall develop the associated method of risk management taking into account behavioral biases.
3-We shall extend our previous suggestions and develop the adequate framework, based on Quantum Decision Theory, for quantum information processing, quantum computing, and creation of quantum artificial intelligence.
4-We plan to formulate analytical specifications of attraction factors as a function of the parameters defining prospects and lotteries and dependent on context and framing. We recall that the attraction factor is the key novel ingredient of QDT. This will open the road towards an operational calibration of QDT to experiments performed both on ensemble of individuals and on single decision makers.
5-We will pursue a collaboration with the group of Prof. Hans-Rudolf Heinimann in the context of the Collegium Helveticum at ETH Zurich as well as within the Singapore-ETHZ (SEC) project on \future resilient systems", for explaining and interpreting, in the frame of QDT, the results of their experimental studies of decision making.
6-We will pursue a collaboration with the group of Prof. Ryan Murphy at ETH Zurich within the ETH Risk Center for developing a general methodology characterizing the empirical data obtained in a large number of experiments accomplished by this group.
7-We will develop a collaboration with the group of Prof. Y. Barral of the Institute of Biochemistry at the ETH Zurich for the purpose of formulating behavioral decision making at the level of biological cells.
The demonstration and operational application of a decision theory, such as the proposed QDT that is free of the numerous paradoxes plaguing the classical decision making, would be a major breakthrough. The development of the general theory to the level at which quantitative predictions become possible would provide essentially more relevant and robust decision making, cascading into the social sciences. Given our recent output, there is little uncertainty that our endeavor will be highly successful. Overall, we estimate that the present research proposal has a remarkable low-risk high-return potential impact.
Keywords: Complex Probabilities, Decision Theory, Entanglement, Fallacies, Hilbert Space, Interference, Quantum Mechanics

Title: High-throughput microfluidic platform interconnecting robotic image and single-cell RNA-seq (IRIS) processing
Abstract:
High-throughput sequencing methods for single-cell analyses are quickly becoming indispensable for biomedical research. This is because they uniquely allow the genome-wide exploration of genetic and transcriptional variation at the single cell level, thereby providing novel insights into the extent of cellular heterogeneity. The latest generation of single-cell analysis platforms, involving microdroplets for ultra-high throughout cell capture, provide in this regard an exciting research avenue for the whole field. Indeed, combined with additional single cell technologies such as microscopy and flow cytometry, which can rapidly assess protein expression intensities for several markers, these approaches have the potential to, for the first time, enable artificial intelligence (AI)-driven exploration of cellular diversity, whereby specific morphological phenotypes of individual cells could be linked to their respective molecular fingerprints.
However, to make this vision a reality, all of these approaches will need to be seamlessly integrated, whereas they currently function mostly as stand-alone techniques. To harvest the anticipated synergistic properties of these methods, we therefore propose to establish a robotic machine vision-controlled platform to precisely handle single cells on microfluidic chips. Having so far implemented a first proof-of-concept, we now intend to expand our platform to incorporate a real-time control framework, driven by image analysis and advanced data processing algorithms. Thus, the grand goal of this Spark proposal is to develop an automated, versatile and holistic single-cell processing approach onto which imaging and sorting of individual cells will be combined with single-cell tracking and RNA capture for downstream transcriptional profiling.
We anticipate that such a ground-breaking IRIS robot, interconnecting robotic image and single-cell RNA-seq, will open up entirely new research avenues to address outstanding fundamental research questions pertaining to the organization, function, dynamics, and heterogeneity of individuals cells. In addition, we envision that IRIS will be revolutionizing clinical practice as, in combination with machine-learning, it will enable highly precise and personalized diagnoses in the fields of cancer, metabolic, and immune diseases driven by the single-cell molecular profiling and classification of specific image-based cellular phenotypes in liquid biopsy samples.
Keywords: diagnostics, imaging, microfluidics, scRNA-seq

Title: Hyper-Representations: Learning from Populations of Neural Networks
Abstract:
In the last years, Neural Networks (NNs) have evolved from laboratory environments to the state-of-the-art technology tackling many real-world problems. With that, safety, robustness, and reliability requirements have become more important than ever. On the other side, the success of NNs is not guaranteed, considering the hard optimization problem to be solved during training of NNs. To be more specific, NN training is NP-complete, the loss surface and optimization problem are non-convex, and the parameter space to fit during training is high dimensional. Additionally, NN training is non-deterministic given its random initialization and sensitivity to hyper-parameter selection.

Our hypothesis is that neural network models (i.e., their weights and biases) evolve on unique trajectories in weight space during training. We think that curvature and geometry of the trajectories contain information on the state of training and can be used to reveal latent factors of individual models such as accuracy, convergence, or other properties of the neural network. Following, a population of neural network models trained on the same dataset, with the same architecture, and solving the same task (we refer to such a population as a “model zoo”) might populate lower-dimensional structures in weight space being rich on information about individual neural network models.

In our previous work, we have shown that we were able to learn lower dimensional representations of populations of NN models (we coined them hyper-representations). These representations can be exploited for several discriminative downstream tasks such as e.g., neural network accuracy prediction (by linear probing the model’s encoded hyper-representation embedding). In another work by us, we were able to show that hyper-representation can be used as generative models to sample unseen neural networks with desirable properties from its latent representation.

In this proposal we aim to extend our work on representation learning from populations of neural networks to learn task-agnostic representations from large-scale populations of neural networks across different model zoos. Firstly, we aim to scale hyper-representation learning towards large-scale neural network models such as ResNets and ViT-S models. We aim to accomplish this by fundamentally changing the current transformer backbone to process windowed snippets of token sequences representing model parameter instead of processing the entire flattened weight vector at once. Secondly, we aim to improve their transfer learning capabilities with the objective to exploit the learned hyper-representations for discriminative and generative downstream tasks across different model zoos. We have already trained 27 model zoos on 8 image datasets with over 3,844,360 collected model states. These model zoos will serve as foundation for hyper-representation learning. 

The research outlined in this proposal will be relevant and highly valuable for future machine learning research. It will impact areas such as “Trustworthy AI”, “Responsible AI” considering the discriminative downstream tasks and “Sustainable AI”, and “Transfer Learning” considering the generative downstream tasks, as outlined in this proposal.
Keywords: Deep Neural Networks, Model Zoos, Neural Networks, Representation Learning, Transformer, Trustworthy AI, Weight Space Learning

Title: Modeling Developmental Trajectories with Intensive Longitudinal Data from Large-Scale Formative Assessments
Abstract: By referring to intensive longitudinal data from the large-scale formative assessment system implemented in primary and secondary schools of four cantons in Switzerland (N = 100,000), we propose developing and implementing a novel methodology to analyze the developmental trajectories of students from a truly intraindividual perspective. Based on previous research showing that interindividual differences rarely correspond with intraindividual change (e.g., Molenaar & Campbell, 2009), this project aims to contribute to a paradigmatic shift in education science by reinstating the individual student as the primary focus of empirical research. In doing so, we suggest four hierarchically related approaches that address issues that are both fundamental in developmental science and highly relevant in the domain of education. These approaches are built around four increasingly complex statistical concepts (i.e., mean, variance, covariance, and multilevel). First, we suggest comparing different modelling approaches in order to determine a valid developmental score despite the challenge of imbalanced categorical data that has been collected at varying time intervals with different test items at each assessment. Second, we want to explore interindividual heterogeneity within intraindividual change by growth-mixture modelling, dynamic latent class analysis, generalized mixture modelling with dynamic structural equation models, and graph models based on higher-order time-series data. Third, we would inspect intraindividual covariation between the different concepts and content domains underlying the developmental score using dynamic systems, as well as machine learning approaches. Fourth and finally, using a summer vacation design, we would disentangle the institutional from the noninstitutional effects on students’ intraindividual learning progress in order to explore how much of the heterogeneity in learning progress can be explained by which factors. The methods developed and the lessons learned in the proposed project will enable future researchers in education science to conduct research based on data from digital learning platforms and show how such data repositories can provide an opportunity for future long-term longitudinal research on learning trajectories.

Title: Measuring Political Performance
Abstract:
Democratic principles are founded on the notion that elected representatives follow through on their campaign promises and stay true to their political beliefs postulated during the pre-election phase. Unfortunately, once elected, it becomes challenging for citizens to stay informed about their representatives' daily activities. The problem lies in the fact that legislative work is nuanced and spans many different aspects, such as agenda-setting (e.g., drafting legislation), fostering coalitions, gathering information and expertise, doing committee work, or preparing and delivering speeches on behalf of their own agenda or against an opponent's agenda. This makes it difficult for citizens to judge the performance of their elected representatives. 

The goal of this project is to study the political performance of Swiss members of parliament (MPs) and provide Swiss voters with clear and concise measures of their elected representatives' performance. Three aspects of performance are examined: political success, election promise fulfillment, and legacy.

We propose to follow established research and divide political success scores into three categories. We rely on existing operationalizations and develop computationally based methods for measuring career-, reputation-, and policy-based success.
While these three indicators inform voters about the success of their elected representatives, they do not inform them whether or not the MP adhered to their campaign promises. We, therefore, propose to develop a text-based method for eliciting campaign promises from political text data (e.g., personal websites, or transcribed campaign ads). Using text embeddings and supervised learning (helped via expert coding), we link promises to legislative actions, allowing us to quantify whether or not promises have been fulfilled.
Our last aspect for measuring the political performance of MPs is rooted in their legacy. Once MPs enter the political arena, the legislation they propose (or help shape) can be seen as their legacy. This legacy has two angles: (i) the longevity of the legislation and (ii) the substantiveness or potential impact of the legislation. We propose to measure the former not simply by examining the duration of legislation but also by taking into account the extent to which enacted proposals and legislative changes serve as a catalyst for future legislative changes. We further consider the potential impact legislative proposals can have on society. We propose text-based methods for estimating the substantiveness of a proposed legislation or amendment. This allows us, for instance, to compare the work of two MPs: one passing a bill on the adjustment of a law on animal husbandry of cows in the Alps and another pushing through a change in the wording of the long-standing labor law that affects Swiss employers.  Without accounting for substantive contributions to the legislative landscape, we run the risk of misinforming the public about the effectiveness of their representatives, potentially making both MPs appear to perform equally.

The aim of this project is to improve political accountability in Switzerland at the national level. By providing easy-to-understand and transparent indicators of how Swiss MPs perform their duties, this project can help prevent democratic erosion, improve representation, and promote equality. The methods we develop are universal and may be applied to other legislative bodies (e.g., text-based promise detection). The performance scores, however, are tailored to the Swiss Federal Assembly and designed to help Swiss voters assess the performance of their elected representatives. 
By providing Swiss citizens with theory-driven, scientific, and politically neutral performance scores of their elected representatives, we forgo the risk of citizens being misinformed (or losing interest due to lack of time) while trying to find the information themselves.
Keywords: interdisciplinary, legislative politics, machine learning, natural language processing, parliament, political methodology, political performance, political success, representation

Title: STEPS - Satellite-based Tracking of global CO2 and NOX Emissions of Point Sources
Abstract:
Point sources such as power plants and industrial facilities account for more than half of global emissions of carbon dioxide (CO2), making them critical targets for greenhouse gas emissions monitoring. Likewise, nitrogen oxides (NOx=NO2+NO) are a critical air pollutant co-emitted with CO2. The next generation of polar-orbiting CO2 satellites will provide images of CO2 and NO2 emission plumes from point sources with unprecedented accuracy, resolution and coverage. Images of NO2 will also be available from geostationary satellites, providing further critical information on the sub-daily variability of anthropogenic emissions that can be used for estimating CO2 emissions using CO2:NOx emission ratios. The combination of CO2 and NO2 measurements will thus enable the long-term monitoring of the emissions from large point sources across the globe, which will be critical for tracking progress in reducing air pollution and achieving net-zero emissions under the Paris Agreement.
To derive emissions from the CO2 and NO2 observations, the satellite measurements must be combined with detailed wind information, which is subject to large uncertainties due to uncertainties in the 3D wind fields, the vertical extent of the plumes, and the impact of atmospheric turbulence. To enable the use of NO2 satellite measurements to quantify NOx emissions, it is also necessary to acquire information on NOx:NO2 ratios and NOx lifetimes, which is governed by the complex chemistry inside the plumes that is currently not well characterized.
The vast number of images acquired by the next generation of satellites and the large number of observable sources requires lightweight emission quantification methods. Mass-balance (MB) methods and especially machine-learning (ML) models have been identified as the most promising candidates in this regard. However, applying these methods on the global scale requires realistic training and validation data. Such data are currently unavailable but can be generated with high-resolution model simulations closely mimicking real observations. Training with these synthetic images must account for inherent discrepancies between simulated and real satellite observations (the "domain gap"), ensuring that models generalize effectively to real-world data. Given the political significance of emission monitoring, the data and methods must meet stringent standards for quantifying uncertainty, interpretability, and adhering to open research data (ORD) guidelines.
STEPS will advance MB methods and ML models to quantify CO2 and NOX point source emissions from CO2 and NO2 imaging satellites. The project will generate and publicly release an unprecedented library of highly realistic, globally representative satellite images based on high-resolution chemical transport simulations. The library will be validated with in situ and remote sensing data and used for training and validating MB methods and ML models. The ML models will then be adapted to real satellite imagery to minimize the domain gap. Once developed and tested, the novel methods will be applied to the next generation of polar and geostationary satellites to monitor the CO2 and NOx emissions from power plants and industrial facilities.
STEPS will establish an advanced framework to develop, validate and apply ML models for emissions quantification. The framework will be proposed as a key component of future operational CO2 and NOX emission monitoring systems, including the Copernicus CO2 Monitoring and Verification Support (CO2MVS) capacity and WMO's Global Greenhouse Gas Watch (G3W) program.
The project will be conducted over four years by Empa, University of Zurich (UZH) and Wageningen University and Research (WUR). The team includes 2 PhD students (at Empa and UZH) and 1.5 full-time equivalent (FTE) scientists at Empa, UZH and WUR. STEPS builds upon the team's expertise in remote sensing, atmospheric modelling, machine learning and emission quantification from satellite images.

Title: Advanced Feature Extraction via Information Theory
Abstract: Feature extraction in high-dimensional data emerged as a promising solution when the computational resources are limited. While feature extraction is regularly applied on data to capture and perpetuate the relevant information and eliminate the redundant information, we focus on extraction of common features on multiple data. We seek for a novel feature extraction method using information theoretic tools namely common information component analysis. The proposed method hinges on a relaxed variant of Wyner’s common information that extracts from high-dimensional data sets, low-dimensional features that capture the common information between the data sets. The number of extracted features is controlled by a relaxing criterion. A promising algorithmic implementation known as machine learning tool is a tweaked variant of gradient descent.
Keywords: data science, feature extraction, information theory

Title: Rapid prediction of T-cell receptor specificities for cancer immunotherapy using structure-based fingerprinting approaches
Abstract: Cancer immunotherapy has produced great advances recently. For further improvements, promising approaches like adoptive cell therapy or vaccination would require the precise knowledge of which T-cell receptor (TCR) recognizes what cancer epitope (i.e. peptide-MHC, pMHC) in the tumor of a given patient. However, prediction of TCR specificities, the Holy Grail of immunoinformatics, is generally considered intractable due to the virtually unlimited number of pMHC and TCR sequences. Our project intends to tackle this question using unconventional structure-based machine-learning tools. Our pioneering idea is to modify existing shape-recognition approaches, successfully used in small-molecule design, for application in protein-protein binding prediction. Typically, these approaches encode the 3D-shape of molecules into 1D-vectors, making shape comparison as simple and rapid as calculating distances between vectors. By developing a method to recapitulate the shapes of pMHCs and of TCRs into such vectors, we plan to tackle two purposes. First, we hypothesize that such structure-based fingerprints will allow clustering TCRs based on their surface properties, and that these clusters will correlate with the ability of corresponding TCRs to bind identical or very similar pMHC. Second, we also hypothesize that, by carefully choosing the definition of the TCR and pMHC fingerprints, it will be possible to train machine learning approaches to rapidly predict, among a pool of TCR and pMHC found in a patient’s tumor, which TCR are recognizing which pMHC. Algorithm training will be based on available 3D structures of pMHC:TCR complexes, databases of interacting pMHCs and TCRs (e.g. VdJdb database), and on the large amount of experimental data available in-house. To our knowledge, this approach is entirely novel and is not explored in any other academic group or biotech company.We plan to meet these challenging objectives by addressing the following specific aims.In Aim 1, we will retrieve experimental data necessary for the project. Sufficient amount of experimentally determined 3D structures of TCR:pMHC complexes and pairs of interacting pMHCs and TCRs are available from the Protein Databank and VdJdb databases. These data will be curated and optimized by fine-tuning the selection criteria for data retrieval and by carefully curating them thanks to our molecular modelling and cancer biology expertise.In Aim 2, we will develop dedicated structural 1D fingerprints to encode the shape, electrostatics and lipophilic properties of the TCR surface. These fingerprints will be used to cluster TCR based on their surface similarity and validate our hypothesis that members of the same cluster will be more likely to bind similar or identical pMHC. The approach will be first developed and tested using available experimental 3D structures of TCR:pMHC complexes, and then further optimized and validated for its ability to perform satisfactorily using TCR homology models.In Aim 3, we will use TCR and pMHC fingerprints to train machine learning approaches able to predict TCR specificities.In Aim 4, we will ultimately experimentally validate the predictions made in Aim 3 to predict correct pMHC targets for given TCRs.The feasibility of the project is illustrated by positive preliminary results and endorsed by the long-term experience of the applicant in the fields of bioinformatics, biophysics and molecular interactions – notably protein-protein binding, machine learning and computer-aided drug-design. The project will benefit from the ongoing collaboration with Alexandre Harari’s group at the Lausanne University, who specializes in the experimental identification of tumor rejection antigens that are recognized by T cells and in the discovery of the T-cell features associated with better efficacy. His expertise will have a critical impact on the relevance of the data employed and on the quality of the experimental validation.The result of this project will open the road to widely applicable high-precision adoptive T-cell therapy and personalized vaccination in oncology, while laying the foundation for deeper fundamental mechanistic understanding in tumor immunology in particular and immunology in general.
